text: "Welding" Kumar was an Indian criminal from Chennai, born in Navalar Street near Korukkupettai, originally known as Jeyakumar, and believed to be around 47 to 48 years old at the time of his death. He began his career as a welder in Tondiarpet and was married to Shanthi, with a daughter named Divya and a son named Sushil Kumar. He was accused in 25 criminal cases, including four murders, and was described by the Deccan Chronicle as the henchman of some Tamil Nadu politicians. He was accused of killing Radhakrishnan in 1985 and Lambamani in 1992, and had attacked Chera inside court complexes and Veeramani from Ayodhya kuppam. He also attacked lawyer Vijayan on his way to court. Kumar received life imprisonment for attacks on Radhakrishnan and Shanmugasundaram. He continued to resort to violence even while in prison, attacking John Pandian in Cuddalore jail and V. Mullaivendhan in Salem jail. He gained notoriety in Tamil Nadu after the attack on DMK lawyer R. Shanmugasundaram on 30 May 1995, which left him severely injured. The attack, which occurred as Shanmugasundaram was preparing a case against then Chief Minister Jayalalitha in the TANSI land scam case, sparked widespread outrage in the legal community and led to statewide protests. The local court convicted him in that case and sentenced him to life imprisonment, a ruling later confirmed by the High Court. On 10 June 2009, he was killed by fellow inmates in Puzhal Prison, having been transferred from Coimbatore prison two months prior. Prison officials stated that his murder resulted from the hostility he generated by taking control of the prison racket, in which "well-to-do" remand prisoners deposited their mobile phones with convicts for a fee.

126 Velleda is a main-belt asteroid classified as an S-type, likely representative of a typical but sizable member of this group. It is named after Veleda, a priestess and prophet of the Germanic Bructeri tribe. The asteroid was discovered on 5 November 1872 in Paris, France, by Paul Henry, marking his first credited discovery. Together with his brother Prosper Henry, they discovered a total of 14 asteroids. 126 Velleda orbits the Sun with a period of 3.81 years and an orbital eccentricity of 0.11, and its orbital plane is inclined by 2.9° relative to the ecliptic plane. It has a cross-sectional diameter of approximately 45 km. The asteroid completes one rotation every 5.36 hours, and its brightness varies by 0.22 magnitudes during each rotation. This article on an S-type asteroid from the asteroid belt is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad and commonly referred to as Helsinki 1952, were an international multi-sport event held from 19 July to 3 August 1952 in Helsinki, Finland. Originally selected to host the 1940 Summer Olympics, which were canceled due to World War II after Japan withdrew due to the Second Sino-Japanese War, Helsinki was awarded the 1952 Games by the International Olympic Committee in 1947, following a successful bid that leveraged completed venues from earlier preparations. Helsinki is the northernmost city to have hosted a summer Olympic Games, and 1952 marks the most recent time when two consecutive summer Olympics were held entirely in Europe, following the 1952 Winter Olympics in Oslo, Norway. The 1952 Games set a record for the most world records broken until surpassed by the 2008 Summer Games in Beijing. The Bahamas, Guatemala, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Israel, Netherlands Antilles, Nigeria, the People's Republic of China, Saarland, the Soviet Union, Thailand, and Vietnam made their Olympic debuts at these Games. The United States won the most gold and overall medals. The Games were held amid a tense Cold War atmosphere, with the Korean War beginning in 1950, prompting the organizing committee to secure war insurance from Lloyd's of London. The Soviet Union, which had been accepted into the IOC in May 1951 and officially invited in December 1951, participated after its athletes were in medal condition, despite initial skepticism about the Games as a bourgeois event. The Soviet Union spent billions of rubles on athlete training and planned daily flights between Leningrad and Helsinki or stayed in the Porkkalanniemi garrison, but Finland required all competitors to reside in the Olympic village, leading to the establishment of a second village in Espoo, Otaniemi, for Eastern Bloc athletes. The Finnish team lived at the Santahamina Army School (later the Cadet School, now the National Defence University). The Games featured a record 5,469 participants from 67 countries during the inaugural march, with 4,925 athletes from 69 nations competing in 149 events. The opening ceremony on 19 July, held in the rain at the Olympic Stadium without a roof, drew 70,435 spectators. President J. K. Paasikivi delivered the shortest Olympic opening speech in history, mistakenly referring to the event as the "Fifteenth Olympic Games" and the "12th World Olympics" due to the cancellations of 1916, 1940, and 1944. The Olympic flame was lit by Paavo Nurmi and Hannes Kolehmainen, with athletes from the Soviet Union and Finland remaining in line as others dispersed to view Nurmi. German athlete Barbara Rotbraut-Pleyer, known as the "White Angel of the Games," jumped onto the track to deliver a peace message before being removed. Heikki Savolainen, a gymnast competing in his fifth consecutive Olympics, swore the Olympic oath. The torch relay began in Olympia, traveled to Athens, then via a miner's lamp on a SAS plane to Aalborg, Denmark, and continued by land, cycling, rowing, and paddling to Copenhagen, then by ferry to Malmö, Sweden, where it was carried by 700 messengers to Haparanda, crossed into Finland at Tornio, and was brought to the Tornio sports ground by Ville Pörhölä. The flame was then lit at Pallastunturi on 6 July using liquefied petroleum gas due to cloudy weather, and transported through Finland to Helsinki, covering a total of 7,870 kilometers over a period from 25 June to 19 July. The Olympic flame was officially lit for the Olympic Stadium. The event also saw the debut of OMEGA's OMEGA Time Recorder, a quartz clock that recorded times to 1/100 of a second and earned the Croix du Mérite Olympique award. Finland introduced cable television for the first time during the Games, with live broadcasts sent from the stadium to the Stockmann department store window. The city prepared extensively, building a new airport in Seutula (now Helsinki-Vantaan lentoasema), the 11-story Hotelli Palace, and the Olympic Pier in South Harbor, while also paving roads, painting buildings, and installing the city's first traffic lights at the intersection of Aleksanterinkatu and Mikonkatu in October 1951. A residential area, Kisakylä (Olympic Village), was constructed south of Käpylä's Koskelantie to house athletes, and female athletes had their own race village at the Nursing College in Meilahti. The organizing committee included the Finnish Olympic Committee, the Finnish State, the City of Helsinki, and 26 sports organizations, with Erik von Frenckell as chairman. The anthem was composed through a competition, with an unknown teacher, Jaakko Linjama, winning after using lyrics by Toivo Lyy, and the only Finnish composer to congratulate him being Jean Sibelius. The Olympic torch was designed by Aukusti Tuhka and the glass cover by Sakari Tohka.

The 1952 Helsinki Olympic Games were a complete success. The Olympic flame was lit by running heroes Paavo Nurmi, who ran to the stadium, and Hannes Kolehmainen, who ran to the stadium tower. When Nurmi arrived, athletes from participating countries broke formation to see him, with only the Soviet Union and Finland maintaining their lines. After the flame was lit, Archbishop Ilmari Salomies was scheduled to pray, but German Barbara Rotbraut-Pleyer, nicknamed "White Angel of the Games," jumped from the auditorium onto the track and ran to the speaker's seat; organizers quickly removed her, who managed to deliver a brief message of peace. Heikki Savolainen, a gymnast competing in his fifth consecutive Olympics, swore the Olympic oath on behalf of the athletes. There were 4,925 athletes from 69 countries, including the Soviet Union's Olympic debut and Germany's return since World War II. A total of 149 events were held across 17 sports. The most-medalling athletes were Viktor Chukarin of the Soviet Union, who won four gymnastics gold medals, and Emil Zátopek of Czechoslovakia, who won three track golds. The United States won the most gold and total medals (40 and 76), while Finland earned 6 gold, 3 silver, and 13 bronze. Shooting took place in seven events, six at the Malmi Shooting Range under moderate wind conditions, with top deer shooting results breaking world records and world records for knee position in rifle events; shotgun events were held at Huopalahti. Ten countries won medals in shooting, with Norway securing two golds (the only country to do so), and the Soviet Union winning the most medals; Boris Andreyev was the only Soviet shooter to win multiple medals. In a miniature rifle event, Finnish winner Vilho Ylönen was celebrated on the radio playing Björneborgarnas marsch, but Norwegian Erling Asbjørn Kongshaug was declared the winner after an hour-long countdown. The football tournament began before the official opening with qualifiers on 15–16 July in Kotka, Lahti, Tampere, Turku, and Helsinki; 27 countries registered, but Saarland and Mexico withdrew. Hungary's Golden Team won gold by defeating Yugoslavia 2–0 in the final, with Sweden winning bronze; the final drew 58,553 paid spectators, the largest crowd in Finland for a football match. The first Soviet-Yugoslavia football match remains famous; after a 5–1 Yugoslav lead, a Soviet comeback in the final 15 minutes led to a 5–5 draw, which was replayed with Yugoslavia winning 3–1. The defeat severely impacted Soviet football, leading to CSKA Moscow's withdrawal from the league and the stripping of Boris Arkadiev's Merited Master of Sports title. Twenty-three teams entered basketball, with ten advancing directly to the tournament and the remaining 13 qualifying before the official opening. The United States won gold by defeating the Soviet Union 36–25 in the final, which was slow-paced as the Soviets tried to match the Americans; the U.S. had previously beaten them 86–58. Uruguay won bronze after protesting the referee. Field hockey was included with a maximum of 12 teams allowed; 16 applied, and after four dropped out, 12 participated. The tournament began with two rounds before the Games opened, and the final was on July 24; India defeated the Netherlands 6–1 in the Velodrome final, winning its fifth consecutive gold under captain Kunwar Digvijay Singh. Canoeing took place at Taivallahti from 27–28 July with 159 participants from 21 countries in eight races. Canoeing was a highlight for Finland, as four of the nine sports were hosted there; the Finns won one silver and one bronze. Kurt Wires and Yrjö Hietanen won double gold in the kayak duo's 1,000 and 10,000 meters; Sylvi Saimo became the first Finnish female gold medalist in summer sports in the 500-meter kayak. Sweden won one gold and three silvers. Fencing events were held at the Espoo Westend Tennis Hall, with men competing in épée, sabre, and foil (individual and team), and women in foil (individual only). There were 250 men and 37 women from 32 countries. Italy, Hungary, and France won all the gold medals; six countries earned medals. The Mangiarot brothers Edoardo and Dario won double victories, and Hungarian swordsmen won a triple victory. The Modern Pentathlon was held at Ahvenisto in Hämeenlinna with 51 competitors from 19 countries, including the first-ever team competition. Sweden, Hungary, and Finland shared the medals; Lars Hall of Sweden won the individual event, and Hungary won the team event. Hall, a carpenter by profession, was the first non-officer to win the individual title. Boxing took place at Töölö Sports Hall from 28 July to 2 August in ten weight classes with 240 participants; 17 countries won medals. The United States won five golds, the Soviet Union won the most medals but no golds, and Finnish boxers earned five medals. Floyd Patterson knocked out Vasile Tiță in 42 seconds in the middle series; Norvel Lee won the heavyweight and was named the most technical boxer; Ed Sanders won gold in the heavyweight after Ingemar Johansson was rejected for passivity, with Johansson receiving his silver medal only in 1982. Wrestling was held in eight weight classes (Greco-Roman and freestyle) in Helsinki, with finals in Exhibition Hall I and freestyle events in Exhibition Hall II; free button events were on 20–23 July, Greco-Roman on 24–27 July. The Soviet Union was the most successful, winning six gold and ten total medals; Sweden dominated free wrestling and earned the second-highest medal count. Soviet Johannes Kotkas won the heavy Greco-Roman class by defeating all opponents in under five minutes. Weightlifting took place in seven weight classes (including a new light heavyweight class, increasing the limit from 82.5 to 90 kg) at the Exhibition Hall on 25–27 July with 141 competitors; all seven golds went to athletes from the U.S. and Soviet Union. The Soviets won seven medals, the Americans four golds, and five world records were set. John Davis won the heavyweight, continuing his undefeated streak since 1938. Sailing took place from 20 to 28 May in five categories; 93 crews from 29 countries participated. The U.S., Norway, and Sweden won medals; the U.S. won two golds, the only country to do so. Danish Paul Elvstrøm won the Finn class (from the Firefly class), securing his second gold and becoming the first athlete to win the same individual sport four times in a row. Cycling included six events (four track, two road), with 214 competitors from 36 countries; track events were on 29–31 July, road on 2 August. Italy, Australia, and Belgium won gold; Italy had five medals. Russell Mockridge of Australia won gold in the kilometer time trial and tandem race; André Noyelle of Belgium won gold in the 190 km road race and team event. Equestrian events included dressage, eventing, and show jumping in individual and team formats; eight countries won medals, with Sweden being the most successful, winning both dressage and eventing events. For the first time, non-military officers and women were allowed in dressage; Danish Lis Hartel, paralyzed from the knees down, became the first woman to win a riding medal after finishing second in show jumping. Rowing took place from 20 to 23 July at Meilahti (due to Taivallahti's sea breeze); 409 entrants from 33 countries participated. Fourteen countries won medals, with only American rowers winning two golds; the youngest Olympic winner was 14-year-old Bernard Malivoire of France in the coxswain duo. Diving included four men's and women's events; the U.S. won nine of the 12 medals, with France, Mexico, and Germany also winning medals. Patricia McCormick won gold in both the women's three-meter springboard and ten-meter platform. Swimming took place at the Helsinki Swimming Stadium from July 25 to 2 August; men competed in six events, women in five. The U.S. dominated men's events, Hungary women's events; both won four golds. Ford Konno won two golds and one silver; Katalin Szőke won two golds, Éva Novák two silvers and one gold. The Hungarian women's 4 × 100 meter freestyle team set a world record. The Helsinki Olympics were the last to include breaststroke and butterfly stroke; no male breaststroke swimmer reached finals, while Novák won silver. Water polo involved 21 countries; initial offshore matches were moved to the Swimming Stadium due to cold water, with some matches starting at 6 a.m. Hungary and Yugoslavia drew 2–2 in the final block; Hungary won gold on goal difference. Gymnastics was dominated by the Soviet Union, which won nine golds and 22 total medals in its debut; Finland, Germany, and Switzerland had modest success. Fifteen medals were awarded (eight men's, seven women's). Viktor Chukarin won four gold and two silver in men's events; Maria Gorokhovskaya won medals in every women's event, with a record seven medals (two gold, five silver) in one Olympics. Although the official report does not explicitly state that individual medals for women were awarded for the first time, it notes that individual women's gymnastics competitions were included for the first time. World Gymnastics confirmed that 1952 marked the first year an individual women's competition was held in addition to team events. Athletics included 33 events (24 men's, 9 women's); the U.S. won 31 medals (nine gold), the Soviet Union 17 (two gold), Germany eight (no gold), and Czechoslovakia four (five medals, all in women's events). Emil Zátopek won the 5,000 meters, 10,000 meters, and marathon—all in new Olympic record times. Marjorie Jackson of Australia won the 100 and 200 meters. World records were set in seven events; Adhemar Ferreira da Silva broke the triple jump world record four times; Bob Mathias won the decathlon with 7,887 points, over 900 points ahead of second place. Josy Barthel of Luxembourg won the 1500 meters. The Games allowed two demonstration sports: one from abroad and one from Finland. A handball match between Sweden and Denmark was held at the Olympic Stadium; Sweden won 19–11 despite poor weather. A pesäpallo match between the Finnish Baseball Federation and Finnish Workers' Sports Federation took place at the Olympic Stadium; the Baseball Federation won 8–4. During breaks, Finnish male and female gymnasts performed for the audience. With an annual average temperature of 5.9 °C (42.6 °F), Helsinki is one of the coldest cities to host the Summer Olympics. Most venues were located in the Helsinki Metropolitan Area, with the Modern Pentathlon and some field hockey events held in Hämeenlinna.

Barthel of Luxembourg won the 1500 m race. For the Helsinki Olympics, the organizing committee could select one foreign and one Finnish demonstration sport; a handball match between Sweden and Denmark and a pesäpallo (Finnish baseball) match were held at the Olympic Stadium. The handball match was affected by heavy rain, resulting in a modest level of play, with Sweden winning 19–11. The pesäpallo match saw the Finnish Baseball Federation defeat the Finnish Workers' Sports Federation 8–4. During breaks in both events, Finnish male and female gymnasts performed for the audience. Helsinki, with an annual average temperature of 5.9 °C (42.6 °F), was one of the coldest cities to host the Summer Olympics. Most competition venues were in the Helsinki Metropolitan Area, including Hämeenlinna for modern pentathlon and field hockey, and Tampere, Lahti, Kotka, and Turku for football. The main venue, the Olympic Stadium, hosted the opening and closing ceremonies, athletics, football semi-finals and finals, and the "Prix des Nations" show jumping event. Built for the 1940 Olympics and opened in 1938, the stadium was damaged during World War II and underwent expansion and refurbishment, including the addition of temporary wooden auditoriums on the south, north, and east sides, increasing its capacity to about 70,000. Swimming events took place at the Helsinki Swimming Stadium, located a few hundred meters east of the Olympic Stadium, which had three pools—racing, diving, and children's—and could accommodate about 9,500 spectators, with additional stands holding about 6,000. Indoor events were held in the Fair Hall (now Töölö Sports Hall) in two halls: the larger hall hosted men’s gymnastics, wrestling, and boxing, while the smaller hall hosted women’s gymnastics, freestyle wrestling, weightlifting, and basketball finals. Basketball first-round matches were held at the Tennis Palace, and fencing at the Westend tennis center in Espoo. Shooting events occurred at the Malmi shooting range, 11 kilometers from Helsinki, except for clay pigeon shooting, which took place at the Huopalahti track of the Finnish Hunters' Association. Dressage and field riding events were held in Ruskeasuo, Tali, and Laakso. The Töölö Rowing Stadium, located one kilometer from Taivallahti, was not used for rowing due to exposure to sea breeze; instead, rowing took place in Meilahti, three kilometers away, which was more sheltered. Harmaja, a lighthouse island off Helsinki’s coast, served as the start and finish for larger sailing classes, and Finn was the start and finish for the Liuskasaari race near the coast. The marathon route went north from the stadium to Käpylä, Pakinkylä, Tuomarinkylä, Vantaa, Tikkurila, and Korso, with a turning point at Mätäkivenmäki in Tuusula from which runners returned to the stadium; a 50-kilometer walk followed the same route, and a memorial stone was later placed at the turning point on Old Tuusulantie. A swimming stadium was built in Hämeenlinna for Ahvenisto to host the pentathlon, with the other four events held nearby. A total of 69 nations participated, up from 59 in 1948; thirteen made their first Olympic appearance: the Bahamas, the People's Republic of China, Gold Coast (now Ghana), Guatemala, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Israel, Netherlands Antilles, Nigeria, Soviet Union (USSR), Thailand, and Vietnam. Japan and Germany were reinstated after being banned in 1948 for their role in World War II; due to Germany’s division, athletes from Saar competed in a separate team, while only West Germany participated in the official German team, as East Germany refused a joint team. Romania returned to the Games. Nations absent in Helsinki 1952 but present in London 1948 were Afghanistan, Colombia, Malta, Peru, and Syria. Puerto Rico is a U.S. unincorporated commonwealth; the Bahamas, Bermuda, Gold Coast (modern-day Ghana), Hong Kong, Jamaica, Nigeria, Singapore, Trinidad and Tobago, and British Guyana were part of the British Empire; Netherlands Antilles was a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The Soviet Union sent the largest delegation. The top ten medal-winning nations at the 1952 Games are listed. The 50th anniversary of the Helsinki Olympics was commemorated in a 2002 Finnish euro silver coin (€10), featuring part of the Olympic Stadium and a section of the 1952 500 markka coin; the obverse includes "SUOMI FINLAND 10 EURO," a flame, and highlights Finland on Earth. A total of 2,394,099 admission tickets were printed for the Games, with about two million produced by the Bank of Finland’s banknote printing works. Tickets were printed on watermark banknote paper, beginning in July 1951 and lasting four months. In early 1952, the organizers opened ticket offices for domestic and international sales, with tickets sold in 52 countries; half of the over two million tickets were available abroad, though only about 250,000 were sold. A total of 1,376,512 tickets were sold for various events, with four price categories ranging from 300 to 2,100 FIM (approximately 9–65 euros today). Ticket revenue totaled about FIM 965 million, or EUR 29.7 million. Tickets were printed in ten colors based on venue and auditorium, with similar flag designs; texts in Finnish, Swedish, English, and French were included, and the sport was indicated by a symbol in the upper left corner. A spectator map was printed on the back; domestic tickets showed only price category, while foreign tickets also included the price in U.S. dollars. The City of Hämeenlinna printed simpler tickets for its modern pentathlon events. The Olympics had a significant impact on Finns, Helsinki, and perceptions of foreigners, symbolizing a key post-war achievement. Land reconstruction was practically complete by 1952, with the last war reparations paid in September 1952 and regulatory policy abolished at the same time. On the closing day, 3 August 1952, President J.K. Paasikivi noted in his diary that the Olympics were a great success, with foreign praise for the organization, which was beneficial for Finland’s image. Helsinki’s urban development had begun in the late 1930s with the construction of Parliament House, Lasipalatsi, and Pääposti; Olympic ambitions spurred many construction projects. Helsinki’s entertainment and nightlife were modest compared to previous hosts, with many temporary restaurants and venues established. The city had long planned a fair, but the Olympics provided the final push; Linnanmäki Amusement Park opened on 27 May 1950 on land leased in December 1949. The Olympics also advanced Helsinki’s infrastructure with a new airport, Olympic Pier, new asphalt, and the city’s first traffic lights. A rest stop for motorists was opened in Lahnajärvi in 1952 along the former Highway 1 (now road 110). The Olympics boosted Finnish self-confidence and provided new contact with non-Caucasian foreigners for the first time. The Games also united Finns during disputes, such as between the Finnish Workers' Sports Federation and the Finnish Sports Federation, which paused during the Olympics despite continuing afterward. Internationalization introduced new products, including Coca-Cola (introduced in the 1930s via Stockmann), chewing gum (imported for the first time), and Alko’s new drinks like the Gin Long Drink. Finland’s relations with the United Kingdom improved, especially after Prince Philip’s warm reception, signaling Finland’s integration into the Western world. In Finland, the Helsinki Olympics are sometimes called the "last real Olympics," emphasizing their status as a true, non-commercial sporting event; this phrase, invented in the 1970s–1980s in response to doping, the Munich massacre, and boycotts at the 1976, 1980, and 1984 Games, is not used internationally. The Helsinki Games were relatively small due to Finland’s size as the smallest country to host the Summer Olympics, though the 1956 Games had fewer athletes; marketing was present, with Kodak supporting the Games since 1896, and although the Polish press criticized the Helsinki Olympics as "competitions for disgusting traders," marketing was well established.

Local elections for Kathmandu's municipal council, known as the "Nepali: काठमाडौ नगरपालिका चुनाव सन् १९५३," were first held on September 9, 1953. Candidates nominated by the illegal Communist Party of Nepal received 50% of the total votes cast. Out of the 19 total seats, six were won by communists, four by the Nepali Congress, four by Praja Parishad, one by Gorkha Parishad, and four by independents. Among the elected communists was Janak Man Singh, who became the chairman of the council. However, his tenure was brief due to a jurisdictional dispute between the municipal council and the national government. A no-confidence vote ousted Singh from office, and the national government banned him from entering the municipal council office. When Singh attempted to enter the office, he was arrested and jailed.

Presidential elections were held in France on 5 December 1965, with a second round on 19 December. They were the first direct presidential elections in the Fifth Republic and the first since the Second Republic in 1848. This was the second presidential election since the beginning of the Fifth Republic. Under the first draft of the 1958 constitution, the president was to be elected by an electoral college to appease concerns about de Gaulle's allegedly authoritarian or Bonapartist tendencies, as there had been a historical reluctance in France to have a directly elected president due to Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte's 1851 coup d'état before the end of his term. However, a direct presidential election had always been essential to de Gaulle's political vision, and he had it adopted by the 1962 referendum. When the electoral campaign started, most political commentators believed de Gaulle would win re-election in a single round, leading opposition leaders to be reluctant to challenge him. Some potential candidates, such as former Prime Minister Pierre Mendès-France, declined to run due to their opposition to direct presidential elections. De Gaulle did not expect a significant challenger, announced his candidacy only one month before the first round, and did not lead an active campaign. The centre-left paper L'Express campaigned for a non-Communist opposition candidate; one potential challenger was Gaston Defferre, Mayor of Marseille and an internal opponent of SFIO leader Guy Mollet, who led a coalition of the SFIO, the Radical Party, and the centre-right MRP. Nevertheless, the leaders of these parties refused to support his candidacy. Defferre's failed candidacy led to other politicians entering the race. MRP leader Jean Lecanuet was nominated by his party and the CNIP to represent the centre, running a liberal and pro-European campaign influenced by John F. Kennedy, criticizing de Gaulle's "archaism" and "nationalism" to appeal to younger and more moderate conservatives. François Mitterrand, a former Fourth Republic minister not belonging to any party, offered to run as the sole candidate of the left. Mitterrand had been an opponent of de Gaulle since 1958, like the Communists but contrary to the SFIO leadership, and had written the book The Permanent Coup d'État, strongly criticizing de Gaulle's policies. He obtained support from several left-wing parties, including the French Communist Party (PCF), which wished to end its isolation. Despite a lacklustre campaign, de Gaulle won the first round by over three million votes but fell short of a majority, forcing a runoff two weeks later against Mitterrand. Tixier-Vignancour supported Mitterrand in the second round, and Lecanuet urged his voters not to vote for de Gaulle. De Gaulle defeated Mitterrand by a decisive margin in the runoff, though Mitterrand performed better than expected, signaling one of the first warnings that de Gaulle's popularity was waning. De Gaulle retained his Prime Minister Georges Pompidou but decided to carry out a cabinet reshuffle, dismissing his Economy Minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, which damaged relations within the majority coalition with Giscard's party, the Independent Republicans, the last allies of the Gaullists.

The 1972 Republican National Convention took place from August 21 to August 23, 1972, at the Miami Beach Convention Center in Miami Beach, Florida. It nominated then President Richard Nixon and then Vice President Spiro Agnew for reelection. The convention was chaired by House minority leader and future Nixon successor Gerald Ford of Michigan. This was the fifth time Nixon had been nominated on the Republican ticket for vice president (in the 1952 and 1956 United States presidential elections) or president (in the 1960 and 1968 United States presidential elections), with his five appearances matching the major-party standard set by Franklin D. Roosevelt, a Democrat who had been nominated for vice president once (in the 1920 United States presidential election) and president four times (in the 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944 United States presidential elections). Nixon was the first Republican to be nominated three times for president. The convention was the first Republican convention scheduled for only three days since 1944 and, along with the 2012 Democratic National Convention, remains the only three-day conventions in modern history. Originally, San Diego, California, was selected as the host city on July 23, 1971, with the event planned for the San Diego Sports Arena. Columnist Jack Anderson uncovered a memo from Dita Beard, a lobbyist for the International Telephone and Telegraph Corp., indicating that ITT could pledge $400,000 for the San Diego bid if the Department of Justice settled its antitrust case against ITT. Fearing scandal and citing labor and cost concerns, the GOP moved the convention—just months before it was to begin—to Miami Beach, Florida, which also hosted the Democratic National Convention. This marked the sixth and final time both national party conventions were held in the same city; Chicago had hosted double conventions in 1884, 1932, 1944, and 1952, and Philadelphia in 1948. The Republican convention did not return to San Diego until 1996. The convention set a new standard as it was scripted as a media event to an unprecedented degree. Anne Armstrong of Texas delivered the first national convention keynote address by a woman. First Lady Pat Nixon became the first Republican First Lady and the first First Lady in over 25 years to address a party's national convention; her speech established a precedent followed by Republican First Ladies Nancy Reagan, Barbara Bush, Laura Bush, and Melania Trump, as well as Democratic First Ladies Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, and Jill Biden. Nixon easily defeated primary challenges from Representative John M. Ashbrook of Ohio (on the right) and Representative Pete McCloskey of California (on the left); however, under New Mexico state law, McCloskey earned one delegate, which the convention refused to seat, fearing he might nominate himself and deliver an anti-war speech. Congressman Manuel Lujan of New Mexico, a strong Nixon supporter, honored state law by voting for McCloskey. The final vote was 1,347 for Nixon, one for McCloskey, and none for Ashbrook. Throughout the precisely scripted convention, delegates repeatedly chanted "Four more years! Four more years!" Spiro Agnew was renominated for vice president with 1,345 votes, one vote for NBC television journalist David Brinkley, and two abstentions. The convention was expected to face widespread protests, particularly against the Vietnam War, and the Nixon administration made efforts to suppress them. This tension was documented by Top Value Television in the independent film *Four More Years*, which juxtaposed protest footage outside the convention with internal political proceedings. The next day, *The New York Times* reported that 900 demonstrators had been arrested and that 52 people, including 12 police officers, had been injured. In 2005, files released under a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit revealed that the Federal Bureau of Investigation monitored former Beatle John Lennon after he was invited to perform at Yippie protests; the surveillance concluded he was not a dangerous revolutionary, as he was "constantly under the influence of narcotics." The Justice Department indicted Scott Camil, John Kniffen, Alton Foss, Donald Perdue, William Patterson, Stan Michelsen, Peter Mahoney, and John Briggs—collectively known as the Gainesville Eight—for conspiracy to disrupt the convention, but all were exonerated. Oliver Stone's film *Born on the Fourth of July*, based on Ron Kovic's autobiography, depicts Kovic and fellow Vietnam Veterans Against the War activists Bobby Muller, Bill Wieman, and Mark Clevinger being spat upon at the convention. This scene did not appear in Kovic's autobiography but was adapted directly from a 1972 documentary titled *Operation Last Patrol*, created by filmmaker and actor Frank Cavestani and photo journalist Catherine Leroy.

The 1980 Gillette Cup was an English limited overs county cricket tournament played between 2 July and 6 September 1980. It was the eighteenth and last edition of the Gillette Cup before it was renamed the NatWest Trophy in 1981. Middlesex won the tournament, defeating Surrey by 7 wickets in the final held at Lord's on 2 September 1980. The competition included the seventeen first-class counties along with five Minor Counties: Cornwall, Devon, Durham, Oxfordshire, and Suffolk. This tournament also marked the first time Ireland participated. Teams that won their first-round matches advanced to the second round; the second-round winners moved on to the quarter-finals; the quarter-final winners progressed to the semi-finals, and the semi-final winners eventually reached the final at Lord's on 2 September 1980.

Patrick Galbraith and Todd Witsken were the defending champions, but played with different partners this year. Witsken partnered with Ken Flach and was eliminated in the second round by Bryan Shelton and Kenny Thorne. Galbraith partnered with Danie Visser and won the title, defeating Andre Agassi and John McEnroe 6–4, 6–4 in the final. The first four seeds received a bye into the second round.

A referendum on joining the European Union was held in Norway on 27 and 28 November 1994. After prolonged debate, the "no" side won with 52.2 per cent of the vote, achieved on a turnout of 88.6 per cent. Norway had previously rejected EU membership in a 1972 referendum and had also been blocked from joining in 1962 by a French veto. As of 2025, this remains the most recent referendum in Norway. The "No" campaign was led by Anne Enger Lahnstein, leader of the Centre Party. Key arguments of the "No" side included concerns over loss of sovereignty and fundamental differences in economic structure, as Norway's economy relies heavily on natural resources such as oil and fish, unlike the EU's more industrial economy. Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland led the "Yes" campaign; her Labour Party was divided on the issue, and unlike Trygve Bratteli in 1972, she did not threaten to resign if the referendum resulted in a "no" vote, citing the risk of deeper party divisions. The "Yes" campaign argued that Norway, as a European country, should be part of the European Union and that membership would benefit Norway's economy. According to John Erik Fossum, a political science professor at ARENA, Centre for European Studies, University of Oslo, the fact that Norway had already signed the EEA agreement made it easier for people to vote "no" because they knew Norway had secured EU market access.

The 7th All-Africa Games (Zulu: imiDlalo yesi-7 yase-Afrika; Afrikaans: 7de Afrika-Spele), also known as Johannesburg 1999 (Zulu: eGoli 1999), was a sporting event held from 10 to 19 September 1999 in Greater Johannesburg, South Africa. Fifty-three countries participated in eighteen sports, with netball included as a demonstration sport. South Africa hosted approximately 25,000 visitors, including 6,000 athletes and 3,000 officials from across the continent. The opening ceremony featured dancing, African parables, and Zulu warriors, but due to the size of the props, it was held in an arena with fewer than 15,000 spectators. South Africa, which had lost its bid to Greece for the 2004 Olympic Games, aimed to impress FIFA in hopes of securing the 2006 World Cup, ultimately winning the 2010 edition. The games were a success, with South Africa outperforming Nigeria and Egypt in the medals race. Challenges included 600 children contracting food poisoning after eating boxed lunches during the practice session for the opening ceremony, laborers striking outside venues and displaying placards that read "No Wages, No All Africa Games," the demotion of women's field hockey to a non-medal event after Nigeria withdrew, a melee at the end of an Angola–Egypt basketball game that required police to escort the Egyptian team from the court, and Haile Gebrselassie, the world record holder in the 5,000 and 10,000 meters, opting out for health reasons, removing one of the event's major attractions. Despite these issues, IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch commended South Africa's organization, stating, "this shows that you can organize big events." Olympic stars Maria de Lurdes Mutola (athletics, 800 m), Penny Heyns (swimming), and Gete Wami (athletics, 10,000 m) excelled in women's events. South African pole vaulter Okkert Brits won his second African Games gold medal, and Assefa Mezgebu of Ethiopia claimed the men's 10,000 m title. Cameroon defeated Zambia 4–3 on penalties to win the football final, becoming the second team to win the tournament twice. Maria de Lurdes Mutola of Mozambique secured her third consecutive 800 meters title. Nigeria won all four relay races—men's and women's 4x100 meters and 4x400 meters. South African men won all four throwing events. New women's events introduced included pole vault, hammer throw, and the 10-kilometre road walk. The tournament's soccer champion was Cameroon, and the coach was Ben Bamfuchile.

2-XL is an educational toy robot marketed from 1978 to 1981 by the Mego Corporation and from 1992 to 1995 by Tiger Electronics. It was the first "smart-toy" to exhibit rudimentary intelligence, memory, gameplay, and responsiveness, and was given a personality that kept children engaged through verbal interactions, jokes, and funny sayings. The toy was invented and patented by Michael J. Freeman, Ph.D., who also voiced the robot using a synthesizer to create a high-pitched robot-like sound, shaping its personality. First introduced in 1978 by Mego, a US-based toy company in New York City, 2-XL became a commercial success and was sold in multiple countries with tapes translated into seven foreign languages. It used 8-track tapes that presented multiple-choice questions, with users selecting answers via buttons that changed the tape's path, enabling interactive gameplay. The robot could respond verbally based on user input, and its personality was highlighted by lines such as "Perhaps your brain went on strike! You are Wrong" or "Nice try but (whispering) you are wrong, but go ahead, I will be a nice little toy robot and give you a second chance now." If correct, it praised the user with phrases like "You must be a genius. Good work" or "Nice answer, football is correct." The original 2-XL had a brown plastic body with white facial features, two red light bulbs for eyes that flashed during operation, four red buttons for answering questions, and a volume/power knob. It played up to two hours of content covering sports, the Guinness Book of World Records, the metric system, general knowledge, and jokes. A 1980 revision featured brighter red eyes that responded to voice, a glossier plastic finish, and a rounder speaker. A school-specific version included earphone jacks, curriculum tapes, and a teacher's manual. In 1992, Tiger Electronics re-introduced 2-XL with cassette tapes that were twice as long as the original 8-track tapes and offered better sound quality, using all four tracks of a cassette to create interactive audio responses. Freeman again recorded the voice in a professional studio, and the new version included a light-up circular mouth and a headphone jack, allowing it to run on batteries. The cassette version used the same interactive logic as the original, leveraging the four-track structure to provide different audio outputs based on button presses. This concept was inspired by the Talk 'n Play system and earlier home cassette recorders. New tapes featured popular characters and media such as Spider-Man, X-Men, Star Trek: The Next Generation, Power Rangers, Jurassic Park, Superman, and Batman, allowing users to make choices that influenced story outcomes, similar to Choose Your Own Adventure books. The second version was available from 1992 to 1996, with about 45 tapes released, sold internationally including in Japan, Germany, Hungary, Italy, France, the UK, Ireland, Canada, and Brazil (distributed by Playtronic), and translated into many languages—though not recorded by Freeman. The original version included a program called "The World of 2-XL" with each unit, while other programs were sold separately. One final Mego tape, "Trilex," was a board game with a pyramid-shaped board and four colored slots aligned with the robot’s buttons, enabling users to drop checkers that would press the corresponding track buttons, aiming to form lines or triangles of three checkers of the same color, simulating a game-playing AI. Secondary products under the 2-XL name included laptop bags, earphones, and lunch boxes. Both versions won numerous awards, including FamilyFun’s 1992 best toy award, Right Start Magazine’s 1993 Europe’s best toy for ages 3–5, and Playthings magazine’s 75th anniversary cover naming 2-XL one of the top ten toys of all time. The Tiger 2-XL also won the 1992 Walt Disney Company Best Learning Toy award. The toy's success also inspired a game show, Pick Your Brain, and it served as a spokesrobot for basketball player Michael Jordan and his foundation in 1992 and 1993, appearing in several public service announcements with him. The name "2-XL" is a pun on "to excel."

The 2003 Badminton Asia Championships marked the 22nd edition of the Badminton Asia Championships and took place at the Tennis Indoor Gelora Bung Karno in Jakarta, Indonesia. Markis Kido is associated with the event.

The 2004 African Cup of Nations final was a football match played on 14 February 2004 between Tunisia and Morocco at the 7 November Stadium in Tunis, Tunisia. It determined the winner of the 24th edition of the biennial African tournament organized by the Confederation of African Football (CAF). Morocco qualified for the final for the first time in their history, while Tunisia reached the final for the third time. Tunisia won the match in regulation time with a score of 2–1, securing their first Africa Cup of Nations title, while Morocco finished in second place. Tunisia took the lead in the 5th minute with a goal from Francileudo Santos, but Morocco responded with a goal from Youssef Mokhtari in the 38th minute before Ziad Jaziri restored Tunisia's lead in the 52nd minute. The African Cup of Nations, organized by CAF, is the primary international association football competition for African national teams, with the 2004 tournament being its 24th edition since its inception. This was the first time the two teams faced each other in the final, having previously met twice in the group stage in 1978 and 2000. Tunisia had not won the title before 2004, having lost the final in 1965 on home soil to Ghana 2–3 after extra time and again in 1996 in South Africa 0–2. Morocco had won the title once, in 1976 in Ethiopia. The 7 November Stadium, located in Radès, about 10 kilometers south-east of Tunis city center, is a multi-purpose stadium with a capacity of 60,000 and was built in 2001 for the 2001 Mediterranean Games. It features a covered area of 13,000 m², including a central area, three adjoining grounds, two warm-up rooms, two paintings, and an official stand of 7,000 seats, with a press gallery equipped with 300 desks. Tunisia entered the tournament for the 11th time as hosts and was one of the favorites, having never won the title before, with two prior final appearances. In the opening Group A match at the stadium, Tunisia defeated Rwanda 2–1, with Ziad Jaziri scoring in the 27th minute, João Elias Manamana equalizing in the 31st minute, and Francileudo Santos scoring in the 57th minute. In the second match against DR Congo, Tunisia won 3–0 after Lomana LuaLua received a red card, with Santos scoring in the 55th minute, Najeh Braham in the 65th, and Santos again in the 87th. In the match against Guinea, Tunisia drew 1–1 after Selim Benachour scored in the 85th minute and Titi Camara equalized late. Tunisia topped Group A with seven points from two wins and a draw and advanced to the quarter-finals. In the quarter-final against Senegal, Tunisia won 1–0 with a header from Jawhar Mnari via a scissor pass from Jaziri in the 65th minute. In the semi-final against Nigeria, the match ended 1–1 after Jay-Jay Okocha scored a penalty in the 67th minute and Khaled Badra equalized with a penalty in the 87th minute, with Tunisia winning 5–3 in penalties, including Ali Boumnijel saving Peter Odemwingie’s spot-kick and Tunisians converting all five of their penalties. Morocco entered the tournament for the 12th time, previously winning in 1976 in Ethiopia after topping their group and drawing their final match against Guinea 1–1. In Group D, Morocco beat Nigeria 1–0 with Youssef Hadji scoring in the 77th minute, defeated Benin 4–0 with Marouane Chamakh scoring in the 17th minute, an own goal by Anicet Adjamossi in the 73rd minute, Abdeslam Ouaddou in the 75th, and Talal El Karkouri in the 80th, and drew 1–1 with South Africa after Patrick Mayo scored in the first half and Youssef Safri equalized with a penalty eight minutes later. Morocco topped Group D with seven points from two wins and a draw and advanced to the quarter-finals. In the quarter-final against Algeria, the match ended in a draw after Abdelmalek Cherrad scored in the 84th minute, Chamakh equalized in stoppage time, Hadji scored in the 113th minute, and Jawad Zairi added a goal in the 120+1 minute, resulting in a 3–1 victory for Morocco. In the semi-final against Mali, Youssef Mokhtari opened the scoring in the 15th minute and doubled it in the 58th, Hadji scored in the 80th, and Nabil Baha sealed the win in the 90+1 minute, sending Morocco to the final for the first time. The final was officiated by Senegalese referee Falla N'Doye, assisted by Ali Tomusange of Uganda and Brighton Mudzamiri of Zimbabwe, with Coffi Codjia of Benin as the fourth official. N'Doye, who became an international referee in 1995 and officiated one match at the 2002 FIFA World Cup, had previously refereed matches between Rwanda and DR Congo and Nigeria and Morocco during the tournament. This was the second time a Senegalese referee had overseen an Africa Cup of Nations final, following Badara Sène in 1992. Key figures attending the match included President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and his wife Leïla Ben Ali, FIFA President Sepp Blatter, CAF President Issa Hayatou, and AFC President Mohamed Bin Hammam. The final, held in front of 60,000 supporters, began with Tunisia taking a 1–0 lead in the fourth minute when Mehdi Nafti centered to Francileudo Santos, who scored his fourth goal of the tournament. At the end of the first half, Morocco equalized through Youssouf Hadji on a pass from Youssef Mokhtari. Seven minutes into the second half, Jaziri scored again to give Tunisia the lead. The match ended 2–1, giving Tunisia their first Africa Cup of Nations title. After the final whistle, jubilation erupted, with Tunisian players performing a circuit of the pitch and climbing onto the podium to receive gold medals, while Moroccan players received silver medals. President Ben Ali presented the trophy to Khaled Badra and Riadh Bouazizi, who raised it high. The Super Eagles of Carthage became the 13th national team in history to win the African championship, and Roger Lemerre became the first coach to win two different continental tournaments after previously winning Euro 2000 with France. On 24 February, President Ben Ali received the Tunisian team at the Carthage Palace, accompanied by technical and administrative staff, and awarded them the National Order of Merit. Tunisia also won the African National Team of the Year award from CAF. The two teams faced each other again in Group 5 during the second round of the 2006 FIFA World Cup qualification, with the first leg in Rabat ending 1–1 and the second leg in Tunis ending 2–2, with Tunisia securing its fourth World Cup qualification by finishing top of the group, while Morocco failed to qualify, finishing one point behind.

The 2007 Special Olympics World Summer Games (Chinese: 2007年世界夏季特殊奥林匹克运动会; pinyin: 2007 Nián shìjiè xiàjì tèshū àolínpǐkè yùndònghuì) took place in Shanghai, China. During the games, The Special Olympics officially launched Young Athletes, a sports program for children aged 2–7 with intellectual disabilities, following its pilot run in 2006. The program aimed to introduce these children to sports and foster interest before they become eligible to compete in the Special Olympics. It was tested in 11 other countries and involved over 10,000 children. The event generated a total of $101,663,833 in revenue, gains, and other financial support, representing a $16,898,416 increase from the previous year. Total expenses amounted to $101,010,125, an increase of $19,841,738 compared to 2006. Two weeks after the closing ceremony on October 23, Special Olympics founder Eunice Kennedy Shriver was awarded the Minerva Award for Lifetime Achievement. The award, named after the Roman goddess Minerva, recognizes women who have driven change in their communities, states, and nations, and was given in appreciation of Shriver’s contributions to the Special Olympics and her broader efforts to support people with disabilities. This Olympics-related article is a stub and can be improved by adding missing information.

doc_name: 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships – Men's junior race
text: The Men's junior race at the 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships took place on Saturday, 27 January 2007, in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium. Riders Mattias Nilsson from Sweden and Eduardo Recasens Gasso from Spain were disqualified for riding through the pits without changing their bikes.
The 2007 UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships took place from 27 to 28 January 2007 at the Domenico Savio Park in Hooglede-Gits, Belgium.

The 2007 World Series was the championship series of Major League Baseball's (MLB) 2007 season and the 103rd edition of the event. It was a best-of-seven playoff between the National League (NL) champion Colorado Rockies and the American League (AL) champion Boston Red Sox, with the Red Sox sweeping the Rockies in four games. This marked the Rockies' first and only World Series appearance as of 2025. Boston’s victory was their second World Series title in four seasons, their second consecutive sweep, and their seventh overall; it also represented the third sweep in four years by AL champions. The series began on Wednesday, October 24 and concluded on Sunday, October 28. Terry Francona became the second Red Sox manager to win two World Series titles, following Bill Carrigan, who won in 1915 and 1916. Including the last three games of the AL Championship Series, the Red Sox outscored their opponents 59–15 over their final seven games. Francona also became the first manager to win his first eight World Series games. The Rockies became the first NL team to be swept in a World Series after previously sweeping the League Championship Series, and only the second team ever to suffer such a fate, following the Oakland Athletics in 1990; this outcome would later be repeated by the 2012 Detroit Tigers, who were swept by the San Francisco Giants after sweeping the New York Yankees in the ALCS. As of the end of the 2024 season, 2007 remains the most recent season an American League team has swept a National League team in the World Series. This was the fourth time since interleague play began in 1997 that a World Series matchup was a rematch from the regular season, with the Rockies having defeated the Red Sox 2–1 in a three-game series at Fenway Park from June 12–14. Over 29 days in September through mid-October, the Rockies won 21 games and lost only once, including sweeps of the Philadelphia Phillies in the NLDS and the Arizona Diamondbacks in the NLCS, and a win over the San Diego Padres in the NL Wild Card tie-breaker. Their 2007 run was one of the most unlikely postseason runs in MLB history, having just 33/1 odds at the start of the season to win the National League. The Rockies' eight-day layoff was the longest in MLB postseason history, caused by their NLCS sweep, the ALCS going seven games, and scheduling by MLB. The Red Sox were more conventionally dominant, leading the American League East for most of the season. In the postseason, they swept the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim in the ALDS and defeated the Cleveland Indians in the ALCS after trailing 3–1, winning the final three games by a combined score of 30–5. Several players from the famed 2004 curse-breaking Red Sox team remained with the team. Neither team had participated in the previous year's postseason. Under the 2006 Collective Bargaining Agreement, the Red Sox had home-field advantage in the World Series following the AL's 5–4 win in the 2007 All-Star Game, with the first two games in Boston and games 3 and 4 in Denver. On October 17, 2007, a week before the first game, the Rockies announced that tickets would be available only through online sales, despite prior plans for local retail outlets. Five days later, California-based ticket vendor Paciolan, Inc., the sole authorized distributor, suspended sales after less than an hour due to an excessive number of purchase attempts. The Rockies organization claimed it was a denial-of-service attack, prompting the FBI to begin its own investigation. Ticket sales resumed the next day, with all three home games selling out within 2+1⁄2 hours. The Red Sox relied primarily on online sales for tickets, though some Fenway Park tickets were sold by phone and at the box office. They held a random drawing for the right to buy postseason tickets on October 15, with winners purchasing at a private online sale. Street prices in Boston were lower than in 2004: according to StubHub, the average price was about $1500 in 2007, down $300 from three years prior. Some fans found it cheaper to travel to Denver than to pay street prices for Boston tickets. Boston won the series 4–0. In Game 1, the Red Sox won by a blowout behind ALCS MVP Josh Beckett, who struck out nine batters, including the first four he faced, over seven innings for his fourth postseason win. Mike Timlin and Éric Gagné pitched perfect eighth and ninth innings, respectively. Boston Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski threw the ceremonial first pitch, as he had in Game 1 of 2004. Rookie Dustin Pedroia led off the first inning with a home run over the Green Monster in Fenway Park off Jeff Francis; it was only the second lead-off home run to start a World Series (the other being Don Buford’s in 1969). Kevin Youkilis then doubled to right, moved to third on David Ortiz’s groundout, and scored on Manny Ramirez’s single. After Mike Lowell flew out, Jason Varitek singled before J. D. Drew doubled to score Ramirez and make it 3–0 Red Sox. The Rockies scored in the second when Garrett Atkins doubled with one out off Beckett and scored on Troy Tulowitzki’s double, one out later, but the Red Sox got the run back when Youkilis walked with two outs and scored on Ortiz’s double. In the fourth, the Red Sox loaded the bases with two outs on a single, double, and intentional walk, and Varitek’s two-run double put them up 6–1. They extended the lead with seven runs in the fifth: Julio Lugo hit a leadoff single off Franklin Morales, Jacoby Ellsbury bunted into a forceout at second, Pedroia popped out, a balk moved Ellsbury to second, and he scored on Youkilis’s double. Ortiz’s double and Ramirez’s single scored a run each. The Red Sox loaded the bases on a double and walk before Drew’s single scored another run. Ryan Speier relieved Morales and walked all three batters he faced to force in three more Boston runs. Matt Herges relieved Speier and got Youkilis to fly out to right to end the inning. Though Herges and two relievers held Boston scoreless for the rest of the game, the Red Sox finished with 13 runs, the most ever in a World Series Game 1, and tied another record with nine extra-base hits. The last 11 of the Red Sox runs came with two outs. The ceremonial first pitch in Game 2 was thrown by 13-year-old heart transplant recipient Andrew Madden, accompanied by Hall of Famer Dwight Evans. After the Game 1 debacle, the Rockies appeared to return to form, scoring quickly on a groundout by Todd Helton with runners on second and third in the first. However, this was the only time the Rockies led in the series. Postseason veteran Curt Schilling (5+1⁄3 IP, one run, four hits) and Boston’s bullpen (Okajima, 2+1⁄3 IP; Papelbon, 1+1⁄3 IP) allowed no other runs. The Red Sox tied the game in the fourth off Ubaldo Jimenez on Jason Varitek’s sacrifice fly with runners on second and third, then took the lead in the next inning on Mike Lowell’s RBI double with runners on first and second. Matt Holliday had four of Colorado’s five hits in Game 2, including a base hit off Papelbon with two outs in the eighth. Before throwing another pitch, Papelbon caught Holliday leaning too far off first base and picked him off—Papelbon’s first career pickoff. This was the first World Series game ever played in Colorado, lasting 4 hours and 19 minutes, making it the longest nine-inning game in World Series history. Game 3 was also the 600th World Series game ever played. Daisuke Matsuzaka pitched five innings of scoreless ball and left in the sixth with no runs allowed. The Red Sox scored six runs in the third inning: Jacoby Ellsbury hit a leadoff double, moved to third on Dustin Pedroia’s single, and scored on David Ortiz’s double. After Manny Ramirez was intentionally walked, Mike Lowell’s single scored two more runs. J. D. Drew popped out before Ramirez was thrown out at home on Jason Varitek’s single with Lowell advancing to third. After Julio Lugo walked to load the bases, Matsuzaka hit a two-run single for his first base hit and RBI in the Major Leagues. Ellsbury capped the scoring with his second double of the inning to knock Colorado starter Josh Fogg out of the game. The Rockies’ offense responded in the sixth and seventh innings against a shaky Boston bullpen. After Matsuzaka walked two straight in the sixth with one out, reliever Javier López allowed back-to-back RBI singles to Brad Hawpe and Yorvit Torrealba. Mike Timlin allowed two straight leadoff singles in the seventh before NLCS MVP Matt Holliday brought the Rockies within one with a three-run home run off Hideki Okajima. Brian Fuentes gave back those runs in the eighth by walking Lugo with one out and allowing a subsequent single to Coco Crisp before Ellsbury and Dustin Pedroia, who had four and three hits respectively, hit back-to-back RBI doubles, raising Boston’s lead to 9–5. Jonathan Papelbon came on for a four-out save, getting Holliday to fly out on one pitch, leaving runners on first and second. Jason Varitek added Boston’s tenth run in the top of the ninth off LaTroy Hawkins with a sacrifice fly, scoring Mike Lowell, who had just stolen third base—the first time a Red Sox baserunner stole third base in the World Series since 1975—after hitting a leadoff single and moving to second on a sacrifice bunt. Papelbon came back out in the bottom of the ninth to complete the save, getting the first two outs before surrendering a two-out triple to Brad Hawpe, then finishing with a groundout from Yorvit Torrealba. The Red Sox won Game 3 10–5. During Game 3, the Red Sox set several World Series records: they struck early with Ellsbury’s leadoff double and Pedroia’s groundout, followed by Ortiz’s RBI single. Series MVP Mike Lowell hit a leadoff double in the fifth and scored on Varitek’s single, making the score 2–0 Boston. In the seventh, Lowell hit a home run to give Boston a 3–0 lead and knock starter Aaron Cook out of the game. The Rockies responded when Brad Hawpe hit a home run off a Manny Delcarmen fastball, bringing them within two. Relief pitcher Brian Fuentes gave back that run when Boston pinch-hitter Bobby Kielty hit a ball into the left field stands on the first pitch of the inning, extending the Red Sox lead to 4–1. In the bottom of the inning, Hideki Okajima allowed a one-out single to Todd Helton followed by a Garrett Atkins two-run home run, bringing the Rockies within one. Jonathan Papelbon relieved Okajima and earned his third save of the series. At 12:06 a.m. EDT on Monday, October 29, Papelbon struck out Colorado pinch hitter Seth Smith for the final out of the 2007 season. Boston had won its second World Series title in four years and seventh all-time. There was controversy in the top of the eighth when Fox’s broadcast announced that Alex Rodriguez would be opting out of his contract with the Yankees to become a free agent. Commissioner Bud Selig stated that an embargo had been placed on all Major League Baseball stories until the top event ended. Rodriguez and his agent Scott Boras later apologized for the incident. The Rockies became the third team in Series history (the 1937 Yankees and 1966 Orioles being the others) not to commit an error in a World Series of any length, and they were the first team to do so while losing the World Series. 2007 World Series (4–0): Boston Red Sox (A.L.) beat Colorado Rockies (N.L.). While the celebratory crowd at Kenmore Square was not as unruly as in 2004, cars were overturned and 37 arrests were made. The Red Sox victory parade, again in duck boats and called a "Rolling Rally" as in 2004, took place on October 30, 2007, with closer Jonathan Papelbon performing his infamous "Irish Jig" while local punk band the Dropkick Murphys played their hit "I'm Shipping Up to Boston." The Red Sox World Series win in 2007 continued the success of Boston-area teams in recent years: the Celtics won their 17th championship, their first since 1986, the last time the Red Sox lost in the World Series, 7+1⁄2 months later; they would win their 18th championship in 2024. The New England Patriots had victories in 2001, 2003, 2004, 2014, 2016, and 2018, the Boston Bruins in 2011, and the Red Sox in 2004, 2013, and 2018. The World Series was televised by Fox in the United States, with Joe Buck and Tim McCarver as booth announcers, starting at 8:00 pm EDT (6:00 pm MDT). The series broke with the tradition of starting on a Saturday, as MLB had become convinced that weekend games drew lower television ratings; prior to this season, every World Series since 1985 had opened on a Saturday, except for 1990. This was the first World Series to start on a Wednesday since 1968. Rogers Sportsnet (RSN) in Canada used the MLB International feed with Dave O'Brien and Rick Sutcliffe as booth announcers. NASN showed the games live to most of Europe, while in the UK, all games were shown terrestrially on Five. NHK aired the series in Japan. On radio, the series was broadcast nationally by ESPN Radio with Jon Miller and Joe Morgan announcing. Locally, Joe Castiglione and Glenn Geffner called the series for the Red Sox on WRKO in Boston, while Jack Corrigan and Jeff Kingery called it for the Rockies on KOA in Denver. Per contractual obligation, non-flagship stations on the teams' radio networks carried the ESPN Radio broadcasts. The Red Sox won two more World Series titles in 2013 and 2018; both were managed by members of the 2007 team. Pitching coach John Farrell served as skipper of the 2013 Red Sox, featuring 2007 holdovers Clay Buchholz (DNP), Jacoby Ellsbury, Jon Lester, David Ortiz, and Dustin Pedroia. The 2018 Red Sox were managed by Alex Cora, an infielder on the 2007 team. The Red Sox finished as a wild-card team in 2008, winning 95 games, and were defeated in the ALCS by the Tampa Bay Rays in seven games. They again qualified as a 95-win wild-card team in 2009 but lost 3–0 to the Los Angeles Angels in the ALDS. In both 2010 and 2011, the Red Sox missed the postseason despite winning 89 and 90 games, respectively. The 2011 season saw the Red Sox hold a nine-game lead in the wild card heading into September, only to lose 13 of their final 20 games and miss the playoffs, leading to the dismissal of skipper Terry Francona and the end of an era. By their next championship in 2013, they had both a new general manager and manager. The Rockies’ World Series run was nicknamed “Rocktober,” a portmanteau of the Rockies team name and October.

The 2018 Red Sox were managed by Alex Cora, who had previously been an infielder on the 2007 Red Sox team. In 2008, the Red Sox finished as a wild-card team with a 95-win record and were defeated in the ALCS by the Tampa Bay Rays in seven games. They again secured a 95-win wild-card spot in 2009 but lost 3–0 to the Los Angeles Angels in the ALDS. In both 2010 and 2011, the Red Sox missed the postseason despite winning 89 and 90 games, respectively. The 2011 season saw the Red Sox hold a nine-game lead in the wild card heading into September, only to lose 13 of their final 20 games, resulting in missing the playoffs and leading to the dismissal of manager Terry Francona, marking the end of an era for Red Sox baseball. By their next championship in 2013, the team had appointed a new general manager and manager. The Rockies' World Series run was nicknamed “Rocktober,” a portmanteau of the team name and October. After reaching the World Series in 2007, the Rockies appeared in the playoffs only three times in the following 15 seasons, with 2007 being their sole World Series berth. In 2009, the Rockies earned a wild-card berth after winning 92 games, but lost in four games to the Philadelphia Phillies in a rematch of the 2007 NLDS. During that season, the Rockies fired Clint Hurdle and replaced him with Jim Tracy. Between 2010 and 2017, the Rockies never finished higher than third place in the NL West, though in 2017 they returned to postseason play as a second wild-card team, losing in the Wild Card Game to the Arizona Diamondbacks. The following season, the Rockies made consecutive postseason appearances for the first time in team history, winning the Wild Card Game against the Chicago Cubs but losing in the NLDS to the Milwaukee Brewers 3–0. After managing the Rockies, Hurdle was hired by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2011 and in 2013 ended a 20-year major North American professional sports record without a winning season. Under Hurdle, the Pirates made the postseason three consecutive years, winning the 2013 National League Wild Card Game during that span. Three members of the 2007 Rockies went on to win a World Series ring with other teams: outfielder Matt Holliday won in 2011 with the St. Louis Cardinals, pitcher Jeremy Affeldt won in 2010, 2012, and 2014 with the San Francisco Giants, and pitcher Franklin Morales won in 2013 with the Red Sox and in 2015 with the Kansas City Royals.

The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th edition of the world championship for men's national football teams, held in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The bidding process was open only to African nations, with five countries submitting bids: Egypt, Morocco, South Africa, and a joint bid from Libya and Tunisia. Following a vote in May 2004, South Africa was selected over Egypt and Morocco to become the first African nation to host the finals; the decision was announced by FIFA president Sepp Blatter in Zürich, with South Africa receiving 14 votes, Morocco 10, and Egypt zero. The tournament took place in 10 stadiums across nine host cities, with the opening and final held at Soccer City in Johannesburg. Thirty-two teams qualified through a worldwide qualification tournament that began in August 2007, with the host nation South Africa qualifying automatically. The teams were divided into eight groups of four for the group stage, where the top two teams from each group advanced to the knockout stage, which consisted of four rounds—round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and final—followed by a play-off for third and fourth place. In the final, Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time to win their first World Cup title, becoming the eighth nation to win the tournament and the first European team to win a World Cup hosted outside Europe. Spain also became the first national team to win the tournament after losing their first match and the first team since 1978 to win a World Cup after losing a group stage match. As a result, Spain represented the world at the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup. South Africa, the host nation, was eliminated in the group stage, as were the 2006 finalists Italy and France, marking the first time hosts had been eliminated in the group stage and the first of three consecutive World Cups in which the defending champions were eliminated in the group stage. New Zealand, with three draws, were the only undefeated team but also eliminated in the group stage. The qualification draw was held in Durban on 25 November 2007, and the tournament featured 204 of the 208 FIFA national teams, sharing the record for most competing nations with the 2008 Summer Olympics. Teams that failed to qualify included Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Croatia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Poland, Sweden, Ukraine, Russia, and Turkey. The highest-ranked team not to qualify was Croatia (ranked 10th), while the lowest-ranked team that qualified was North Korea (ranked 105th). As of 2025, this was the last time North Korea, Slovakia, and Slovenia qualified for a FIFA World Cup finals, and the last time Belgium, Iran, and Croatia failed to qualify. Five new stadiums were built and five existing venues upgraded, with construction costs estimated at R8.4 billion (just over US$1 billion or €950 million). Public transport infrastructure, including Johannesburg's Gautrain and other metro systems, was improved. Special safety measures were implemented, including temporary flight restrictions around stadiums. On 8 July 2009, 70,000 construction workers walked off their jobs due to allegations of underpayment, but the strike was resolved within a week, and all stadiums were completed on time. The total prize money was US$420 million, a 60 percent increase from 2006, including US$40 million paid to domestic clubs—a first for the World Cup due to an agreement between FIFA and European clubs to settle claims from past injuries. The 2010 World Cup used 12 provisional venues, narrowed to ten officially announced by FIFA on 17 March 2006. Six of the ten venues were over 1,200 meters above sea level, with the two Johannesburg stadiums—FNB Stadium (Soccer City) and Ellis Park Stadium—at approximately 1,750 meters. FNB Stadium, Cape Town Stadium, and Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium each hosted eight matches, while Ellis Park and Moses Mabhida hosted seven each, and Loftus Versfeld, Free State, and Royal Bafokeng hosted six each. Peter Mokaba and Mbombela hosted four matches each but no knockout-stage matches. The group draw was held in Cape Town on 4 December 2009, presented by Charlize Theron and Jérôme Valcke, with balls drawn by David Beckham, Haile Gebrselassie, John Smit, Makhaya Ntini, Matthew Booth, and Simphiwe Dludlu. FIFA selected 29 referees, including four from AFC, three from CAF, six from CONMEBOL, four from CONCACAF, two from OFC, and ten from UEFA. English referee Howard Webb officiated the final, becoming the first person to referee both the UEFA Champions League final and the World Cup final in the same year. Each team fielded 23 players, with final squads confirmed by 1 June 2010 and late replacements allowed for serious injuries up to 24 hours before a match. Of the 736 players, over half played in European leagues, primarily in England (117), Germany (84), Italy (80), Spain (59), and France (46). The English, German, and Italian squads consisted entirely of home-based players, while only Nigeria had no players from clubs in their own league. FC Barcelona contributed the most players (13), with seven other clubs contributing 10 or more. Honduras's squad included three siblings—Jerry, Johnny, and Wilson Palacios—marking a first for the tournament, and Germany and Ghana had two brothers playing for opposing nations, Jérôme Boateng and Kevin-Prince Boateng. The 32 teams played 64 matches, progressing through the group stage and knockout rounds, with rest days allocated for player recovery. Preliminary events were held to celebrate the tournament. All match times were in South African Standard Time (UTC+2). The South American teams performed strongly, with all five advancing to the round of 16 (four as group winners) and four reaching the quarter-finals, though only Uruguay advanced to the semi-finals. Of the six African teams, only Ghana advanced to the round of 16, and South Africa became the first host nation to be eliminated in the group stage despite beating France and drawing with Mexico. Ghana and Ivory Coast were the only African teams to win a match, and the overall African performance was considered disappointing by observers like Roger Milla. Only six of the 13 UEFA teams advanced to the round of 16, a record low since 1986, but the final was contested by two European teams. Italy and France, the 2006 finalists, were both eliminated in the group stage, with Italy becoming the third defending champion to be eliminated in the first round after Brazil in 1966 and France in 2002. New Zealand, despite being one of the lowest-ranked teams, drew all three of their group matches and ended the tournament as the only undefeated team. In a controversial incident, FIFA President Sepp Blatter apologized to England and Mexico for refereeing errors.

New Zealand, one of the lowest-ranked teams, surprised many by drawing all three of their group matches and ending the tournament as the only undefeated team. The knockout stage featured 16 teams advancing from the group stage, consisting of four rounds—round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and the final—with each round eliminating half the teams. Any draw at 90 minutes was followed by 30 minutes of extra time, and if the scores remained level, a penalty shoot-out determined progression. In the round of 16, each group winner (A to H) was paired against the runner-up from another group. The round was marked by controversial refereeing decisions, prompting FIFA President Sepp Blatter to apologize to England and Mexico for the errors, stating that "you can win some and you lose some," and promising to re-open discussions on goal-line technology and video replays, with the first opportunity to discuss it occurring at the July business meeting. The three quarter-finals between European and South American teams all ended in European victories: Germany defeated Argentina 4–0, the Netherlands came from behind to beat Brazil 2–1 (marking Brazil’s first loss in a World Cup match outside Europe since 1950), and Spain won 1–0 over Paraguay to reach the final for the first time since 1950. Uruguay, the only South American team to reach the semi-finals, advanced after a 1–1 draw with Ghana, which missed a penalty in extra time following Luis Suárez’s handball on the line. The Netherlands qualified for the final for the third time with a 3–2 win over Uruguay, and Spain reached their first final with a 1–0 victory over Germany, making it the first World Cup final without Brazil, Italy, Germany, or Argentina, and ensuring a new champion as neither Spain nor the Netherlands had previously won the tournament. Germany defeated Uruguay 3–2 to secure third place, holding the record for most third-place finishes (4), while Uruguay holds the record for most fourth-place finishes (3). The final was held on 11 July 2010 at Soccer City, Johannesburg, where Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 in extra time, with Andrés Iniesta scoring the goal in the 116th minute—the latest winning goal in a FIFA World Cup final. This victory gave Spain their first World Cup title, making them the eighth team to win it, the first new winner without home advantage since Brazil in 1958, and the first team to win after losing their opening match. The final saw 14 yellow cards, more than doubling the previous record set in 1986, and John Heitinga was sent off for a second yellow card. The Netherlands had a key chance in the 60th minute when Arjen Robben was released by Wesley Sneijder to face Iker Casillas, who saved the shot. Iniesta broke the deadlock with a volleyed shot from a pass by Cesc Fàbregas. This result marked the first time two teams from the same continent won consecutive World Cups (after Italy in 2006), and Europe reached 10 titles, surpassing South America’s nine. Spain became the first European nation to win a World Cup not hosted on European soil and the first team since West Germany in 1974 to win as European champions. Spain also set a record for the fewest goals scored by a World Cup-winning team (eight), the fewest goalscorers (three: Villa with five, Iniesta with two, Puyol with one), and the fewest goals conceded (two, equaling Italy in 2006 and France in 1998), and became the first team to win the World Cup without conceding a goal in the knockout stage.
