The four top scorers in the tournament each scored five goals, all from teams finishing in the top four—Spain, the Netherlands, Germany, and Uruguay. The Golden Boot went to Thomas Müller of Germany (three assists), the Silver Boot to David Villa of Spain (635 minutes), and the Bronze Boot to Wesley Sneijder of the Netherlands (652 minutes); Diego Forlán of Uruguay scored five goals and one assist in 654 minutes, and three other players scored four goals. Only 145 goals were scored at the 2010 World Cup, the lowest in any FIFA World Cup since the 64-game format began, following 171 in 1998, 161 in 2002, and 147 in 2006. Twenty-eight players were suspended for two yellow cards (13), one red card (8), or a yellow followed by a red (7). FIFA released a final ranking based on progress, results, and quality of opposition, and an All-Star Team based on the Castrol performance index. The Dream Team, selected by public vote until 11 July 2010, included six players from Spain (including the coach), two from Germany, and one each from Brazil, the Netherlands, and Uruguay. The 2010 World Cup amplified public awareness of the vuvuzela, a long horn blown by fans, with complaints from players like Patrice Evra, Lionel Messi, and broadcasters about the noise disrupting communication and commentary. Some viewers reported that the ambient audio feed contained only vuvuzela sounds. ESPN and the BBC explored options for noise-free broadcasts. The official mascot was Zakumi, an African leopard with green hair, named from "ZA" and "kumi" (ten), reflecting South Africa’s colors of yellow and green. The match ball, Jabulani, manufactured by Adidas, meant "bringing joy to everyone," featured 11 colors representing each player and the 11 official languages of South Africa, and used eight thermally bonded, three-dimensional panels made from EVA and TPU with a GripnGroove textured surface developed in partnership with Loughborough University. The ball was made in China, with latex bladders from India, TPU from Taiwan, and other materials from China. Some players criticized the ball’s unpredictable movement, with Júlio César calling it a "supermarket" ball and Maradona stating long passes were unlikely, though some Adidas-sponsored players praised it. The official song, "Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)," performed by Shakira and Freshlyground, was based on the traditional African song "Zangalewa" and performed at the pre-tournament concert, opening, and closing ceremonies. The official mascot song was "Game On," and the anthem was "Sign of a Victory" by R. Kelly with the Soweto Spiritual Singers, performed at the opening ceremony. Danny Jordaan dismissed concerns that the attack on the Togo team in Angola in January 2010 affected security, though reports of thefts against tourists from China, Portugal, Spain, South Korea, Japan, and Colombia emerged. After the England vs. Algeria match on 19 June, a fan broke into the England dressing room shortly after Prince William and Prince Harry left, was released before police intervention, and the Football Association filed a formal complaint with FIFA demanding improved security. The tournament was linked to evictions, with the Abahlali baseMjondolo movement taking the KwaZulu-Natal government to court over the Elimination and Prevention of Re-Emergence of Slums Act, and the N2 Gateway project in Cape Town planning to remove over 20,000 residents from Joe Slovo Informal Settlement to build rental flats. NGOs and human rights groups criticized the conditions in Blikkiesdorp and accused the project of displacing poor families. Some argued that evictions were common in South Africa and that many were wrongly attributed to the World Cup. FIFA’s media control led to legal disputes with an international rugby match, a South African airline, and TV networks. Group ticket holders who did not use all their tickets led to early-round matches with up to 11,000 unoccupied seats. While the event boosted South Africa’s image, it was a major financial disappointment: construction costs totaled £3 billion (€3.6 billion), with expected tourism revenue of £570 million (€680 million), but only £323 million (€385 million) was generated from 309,000 foreign visitors, far below the expected 450,000. Local vendors were banned from selling food and merchandise within 1.5 kilometers of stadiums, requiring a R60,000 registration fee—unaffordable for most—limiting access to local South African food and culture. FIFA President Sepp Blatter declared the event a "huge financial success" for Africa, South Africa, and FIFA, citing revenue of £2.24 billion (€2 billion), and in a December 2010 Quality Progress, rated South Africa’s organization a nine out of ten, citing a lack of public transportation as the main issue. The 2010 FIFA World Cup was expected to be the most-watched television event in history, with hundreds of broadcasters from about 70 countries reaching a cumulative audience of over 26 billion people, averaging approximately 400 million viewers per match, and around 700 million expected to watch the final. New digital media allowed live coverage through alternative platforms.

FIFA President Sepp Blatter declared the 2010 FIFA World Cup "a huge financial success for everybody, for Africa, for South Africa and for FIFA," with revenue to FIFA amounting to £2.24 billion (€2 billion). In a December 2010 article in Quality Progress, Blatter rated South Africa's organisational efforts a nine out of 10, stating that South Africa could serve as a plan B for all future competitions, with the South African Quality Institute (SAQI) assisting in facility construction, event promotion, and organisation; the main issue identified was a lack of sufficient public transportation. The 2010 FIFA World Cup was expected to be the most-watched television event in history, with hundreds of broadcasters from about 70 countries transmitting the event to a cumulative TV audience that FIFA officials estimated would exceed 26 billion people, averaging approximately 400 million viewers per match, and around 700 million viewers expected to watch the final. New digital media allowed viewers to access coverage via cell phones and computers, with Jake Coyle of the Associated Press stating that the World Cup would receive more online coverage than any major sporting event. In the United States, ABC, ESPN, and ESPN2 averaged a 2.1 rating, reaching 2,288,000 households and 3,261,000 viewers for the 64 matches, a 31 percent increase in rating from 2006's 1.6, with households rising 32 percent from 1,735,000 and viewers increasing from 2,316,000; during the first 50 games, the rating increased by 48 percent, households by 54 percent, and viewers by 60 percent. Univision averaged 2,624,000 viewers, up 17 percent, and 1,625,000 households, an 11 percent increase. A Nielsen Company executive described the viewership for the U.S. versus Ghana match as "phenomenal." Live streaming on ESPN3.com attracted some of the largest audiences in history, with 7.4 million unique viewers tuning in, generating 942 million minutes of viewing—over two hours per unique viewer—and all 64 live matches averaging 114,000 viewers per minute; the semi-final between Spain and Germany reached 355,000 viewers per minute, the highest average on ESPN3.com. Sony technology was used to film the tournament, with 25 matches captured using 3D cameras via Sony's proprietary multi-image MPE-200 processors in specially designed 3D outside broadcast trucks, employing its flagship HDC-1500 cameras and new HDC-P1 unit, a compact point-of-view camera with 3, 2/3-inch CCD sensors; the 3D games were produced for FIFA by Host Broadcast Services. In PlayStation Home, Sony released a virtual space based on the 2010 FIFA World Cup in the Japanese version on 3 December 2009, called "FevaArena," a virtual stadium featuring event areas, a FIFA mini-game, and a shop with FIFA-related content. On 27 April 2010, EA Sports released the official 2010 World Cup video game. FIFA expanded the FIFA Fan Fest, hosting events in Sydney, Buenos Aires, Berlin, Paris, Rome, Rio de Janeiro, Mexico City, and several venues around South Africa, with the Durban Fan Fest being the most popular in South Africa, followed by the Cape Town Fan Fest.

The 2010 UEFA Champions League final was an association football match played at the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium, home of Real Madrid, on 22 May 2010, to determine the winners of the 2009–10 UEFA Champions League. It was the first Champions League final to be held on a weekend, rather than the traditional Wednesday. The match was won by Inter Milan, who defeated Bayern Munich 2–0, completing the treble—a feat never before achieved by any team from either Italy or Germany. This victory marked Inter's third European Cup title and their first since 1965; it was also their first final appearance since 1972 and the first time an Italian team had reached the final since A.C. Milan's win in 2007. Bayern, who had last won the competition in 2001, were the first German side to reach the final since Bayer Leverkusen in 2002. The 2010 final was the first not to feature an English side since Porto beat Monaco in 2004, due to Manchester United being eliminated by Bayern Munich in the quarter-finals on away goals. The Santiago Bernabéu Stadium had previously hosted three European Cup finals: in 1957, 1969, and 1980. The venue was selected by the UEFA Executive Committee in Vaduz, Liechtenstein, on 28 March 2008, based on criteria including stadium capacity, facilities, and security, and the decision to play the final on a Saturday was made at a meeting in Lucerne on 30 November 2007. The stadium, opened in 1947, had a capacity exceeding 75,000 initially, increased to 125,000 in 1954, reduced to 90,800 after renovations for the 1982 FIFA World Cup, and later reduced to just over 75,000 after conversion to an all-seater stadium in 1998, with a slight increase to just over 80,000 in 2006; only around 75,000 seats were available for the 2010 final. Each finalist was allocated 21,000 tickets, with 11,000 available to the general public, and applications ran from 8 to 19 March 2010 via a random lottery, including 2,000 children's tickets from each club and 1,000 from the public, plus 500 for children at the UEFA Champions Festival. A ticketing launch event was held in Madrid on 5 March 2010, attended by Emilio Butragueño, Esperanza Aguirre, and representatives from UEFA, the Royal Spanish Football Federation, and Real Madrid, with Aguirre receiving the first ticket from players Cristiano Ronaldo and Raúl. A trophy handover ceremony took place at the Palacio de Cibeles on 16 April 2010, where Johan Cruyff and Joan Laporta returned the trophy to UEFA president Michel Platini, who then handed it to Ángel María Villar Llona and Alberto Ruiz-Gallardón for display until the final. The official match ball, the Adidas Finale Madrid, was unveiled on 9 March 2010 and featured a "Starball" design with gold stars incorporating elements from the logos of the last 10 Champions League finals, each with a red border referencing the Spanish flag and a white base matching Real Madrid's kit. The referee was Howard Webb of England, supported by Darren Cann and Mike Mullarkey as assistant referees and Martin Atkinson as the fourth official, all from England. Inter started without any Italian players, while Bayern began with five German internationals, including Franck Ribéry, who was suspended for three matches after being sent off in the semi-final, and Thiago Motta, suspended for two matches. The match opened with the UEFA Champions Festival on 15 May 2010 at Parque del Retiro, culminating in a match between former Spanish players and European ex-professionals on the final day. The UEFA Champions League Anthem was performed by Peruvian tenor Juan Diego Flórez. Inter won 2–0 with both goals scored by Diego Milito in the 35th and 70th minutes; the first followed a long clearance flicked down by Milito to Wesley Sneijder, who returned the pass to Milito, and the second came after Milito collected a pass from Samuel Eto'o and beat Daniel Van Buyten. Milito was substituted before the end of the match and was applauded by Inter supporters, stating the win brought "incredible happiness" and that his team deserved the victory. Bayern captain Mark van Bommel acknowledged Inter as the "most effective team" due to their counter-attacking strategy. José Mourinho, who had previously managed Porto in 2004 and won the Champions League with Ajax in 1995, became only the third manager in European Cup history to win with two clubs, following Ernst Happel and Ottmar Hitzfeld. As winners, Inter played against Atlético Madrid, the 2009–10 UEFA Europa League winners, in the 2010 UEFA Super Cup, losing 2–0 with goals from José Antonio Reyes and Sergio Agüero, and also entered the 2010 FIFA Club World Cup, where they beat Seongnam Ilhwa Chunma 3–0 in the semi-finals and then defeated TP Mazembe 3–0 in the final to win the title. Inter secured the treble for the first time in Italian football history after winning the Coppa Italia and Serie A titles in 2010. As a result of the victory, Italy retained its fourth berth in the 2010–11 UEFA Champions League, while if Bayern had won or the match had gone to penalties, Germany would have overtaken Italy and gained an extra entry. José Mourinho resigned as Inter manager on 28 May to join Real Madrid for the 2010–11 season, citing a desire to become the first manager to win the Champions League with three clubs, though he was unable to achieve this, being eliminated in three successive semi-finals before returning to Chelsea in June 2013, with Carlo Ancelotti replacing him at Real Madrid, who won their tenth title in his first season. UEFA Man of the Match was Diego Milito (Inter Milan), and Fans' Man of the Match was Wesley Sneijder (Inter Milan).

The 2012 Delhi gang rape and murder, known as the Nirbhaya case, occurred on 16 December 2012 in Munirka, Delhi, when 22-year-old Jyoti Singh, a physiotherapy intern, was gang-raped and tortured in a private bus while travelling with her friend, Awindra Pratap Pandey. The bus, which had only six passengers including the driver, deviated from its route and its doors were shut, prompting suspicion from Pandey, who was then taunted by the group. A scuffle followed, during which Pandey was beaten, gagged, and knocked unconscious with an iron rod, and Jyoti was dragged to the rear of the bus, where she was raped and severely injured with a blunt object—later identified as a rusted, L-shaped wheel jack handle—causing extensive damage to her abdomen, intestines, and genitals. Jyoti attempted to fight back, biting three of the attackers. After the assault, both victims were thrown from the moving bus; one of the perpetrators cleaned the vehicle, which was later impounded. The partially clothed victims were found by a passerby around 11 pm and taken to Safdarjung Hospital, where Jyoti received emergency treatment and was placed on mechanical ventilation. She had numerous bite marks and injuries, and medical staff confirmed penetration by a metal rod. On 27 December, she was flown to Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore for further treatment, where she suffered a cardiac arrest during a six-hour flight and died at 4:45 am on 29 December (2:15 am IST). Her body was cremated on 30 December in Delhi under high police security. The incident sparked widespread national and international outrage, leading to public protests in New Delhi and major cities across India, demanding better women's safety and security. Six men were arrested: Ram Singh, the driver, and his brother Mukesh Singh, both from Ravidas camp; Vinay Sharma, a 26-year-old assistant gym instructor; Pawan Gupta, a 19-year-old fruit seller; Akshay Thakur, a 28-year-old man seeking employment; and the juvenile Mohammed Afroz, 17 years and six months old, from Badayun. The juvenile was convicted under the Juvenile Justice Act and sentenced to three years in a reform facility. The adult defendants—Pawan Gupta, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Mukesh Singh—were found guilty of rape and murder on 10 September 2013 and sentenced to death; the Delhi High Court upheld the verdict on 13 March 2014, and the Supreme Court rejected their final appeals on 18 December 2019. The four adult convicts were executed by hanging on 20 March 2020. Ram Singh died in police custody on 11 March 2013, with authorities stating it was unclear whether it was suicide or murder. The case led to the formation of a judicial committee that reviewed 80,000 public suggestions and concluded that government and police failures were the root cause of crimes against women. In 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act was passed by President Pranab Mukherjee, introducing new laws and creating six fast-track courts for rape cases. Despite these reforms, critics argue the legal system remains slow, though public discourse on women's safety has significantly increased. The victim's father initially opposed revealing her name, but later stated that he wanted the world to know her real name, Jyoti Singh, to honor her courage and inspire other survivors. In compliance with Indian law, her name was not publicly released initially, and media used pseudonyms such as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless," Damini, or Delhi braveheart. The Delhi police registered a case against the editor of Mail Today for disclosing her identity under section 228(A) of the Indian Penal Code. A Special Investigation Team, led by Pramod Kumar Kushwaha, was formed to probe the case. The attackers had previously robbed a carpenter, Ramadhir Singh, who reported the incident to three police constables from Hauz Khas, who refused to act, citing jurisdictional issues. The Delhi High Court reprimanded the police for being evasive in their probe status report, and two Assistant Commissioners were suspended for failing to prevent the incident. The government appointed a medical committee on 21 December to ensure Jyoti received optimal care, and on 26 December, a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh decided to transfer her to Singapore, a decision criticized by some doctors as politically motivated. The juvenile defendant, later renamed Raju in media, was arrested at Anand Vihar terminal and had only met the others that day. The case led to significant changes in public awareness and policy, though the victim's father later expressed regret that justice had not been fully achieved.

The Delhi High Court approved the establishment of five fast-track courts to handle rape and sexual assault cases. The first of these courts was inaugurated on 2 January 2013 by Altamas Kabir, Chief Justice of India, at the Saket court complex in South Delhi. On 21 December 2012, the Delhi High Court criticized the Delhi police for being "evasive" in a probe status report detailing officers on patrol duty in an area covered by a bus route, with a further hearing scheduled for 9 January 2013. The next day, the Delhi Police took action against three Hauz Khas police station personnel for inaction in responding to a robbery that occurred on the same bus. On 24 December, two Assistant Commissioners of Police were suspended for failing to prevent a gang rape incident. The juvenile defendant Mohammed Afroz, later referred to as Raju in the media due to his age, was declared 17 years and six months old on the day of the crime by the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB), based on his birth certificate and school documents, and the JJB rejected a police request for a bone ossification test to verify his age. On 28 January 2013, the JJB ruled that Afroz would not be tried as an adult, rejecting a petition by Janata Party president Subramanian Swamy to prosecute him as an adult due to the violent nature of the alleged crime. The minor was tried separately in a juvenile court. The verdict was initially scheduled for 25 July 2013, deferred to 5 August, and then to 19 August; on 31 August, he was convicted of rape and murder under the Juvenile Justice Act and sentenced to three years' imprisonment in a reform facility, including the eight months he spent in remand. Reportedly, Jyoti's younger brother attempted to attack the juvenile after the verdict but was restrained by the crowd. Afroz was released on 20 December 2015. To support his rehabilitation and mainstreaming as required by the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, management committees were established before his release, and a 'post-release plan' was submitted to the Delhi High Court in December 2015. The plan, prepared by a committee headed by an officer from the District Child Protection Unit, recommended that Afroz should lead a new life with a new identity if permissible to avoid backlash, and noted that he had learned cooking and tailoring during his stay in the reform house. The report recommended a one-time government grant of ₹10,000 (US$120) and a sewing machine from an NGO, which the Department of Women and Child Development (WCD) committed to providing. Afroz's family had ostracized him after the crime, but after his release, he was reported to be working as a cook. Five days after Jyoti's death on 29 December 2012, on 3 January 2013, the police filed charges against five adult men for rape, murder, kidnapping, destruction of evidence, and attempted murder of the woman's male companion. Senior lawyer Dayan Krishnan was appointed as the special public prosecutor. Mukesh Singh, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Pawan Gupta denied the charges; some had previously confessed, but their lawyers claimed the confessions were coerced through torture. On 10 January, one of their lawyers, Manohar Lal Sharma, stated in a media interview that the victims were responsible for the assault because they should not have used public transportation or been out at night as an unmarried couple, and that the male victim was "wholly responsible" for failing to protect the woman. The Delhi police filed a charge sheet against the defendants on 13 March 2013 in connection with the robbery of Ramadhir. The four surviving adult defendants were tried in a fast-track court, where the prosecution presented evidence including witness statements, the victim's statement, fingerprints, DNA testing, and dental modelling, completing its case on 8 July. On 10 September 2013, the four adult defendants were found guilty of rape, murder, unnatural offences, and destruction of evidence. They faced the death penalty, and demonstrators outside the courthouse called for their hanging; the victim's father also demanded they be hanged, stating, "We will get complete closure only if all the accused are wiped off from the face of the earth." Lawyers for three of the four stated they would appeal the verdict. On 13 September 2013, the four men were sentenced to death by hanging. Judge Yogesh Khanna rejected pleas for a lesser sentence, stating the case had "shocked the collective conscience of India" and that "courts cannot turn a blind eye to such crimes." The victim's family was present, and her mother expressed satisfaction, saying, "We were waiting with bated breath, now we are relieved. I thank the people of my country and the media." After the verdict, people outside the courtroom applauded. Upon hearing he would be executed, Vinay Sharma collapsed and pleaded with the judge, saying, "Please sir, please sir," and as they left, they shouted, "Brothers, save us!" While on death row, Mukesh Singh blamed Jyoti for being raped, claiming a decent girl would not roam at night and that she was more responsible than a boy, and that she should have remained silent during the assault to avoid being killed. On 13 March 2014, the Delhi High Court confirmed the guilt of each defendant and upheld the death sentences, noting the crime fell into the "rarest of the rare" category allowing capital punishment. The lawyers of the four men filed appeals to the Supreme Court. On 15 March 2014, the Supreme Court stayed the execution of Mukesh Singh and Pawan Gupta to allow appeals on 31 March, later extending the stay to the second week of July. On 2 June, Sharma and Thakur also requested a stay to appeal their convictions, and on 14 July, their execution was stayed. On 27 August 2015, Vinay, Akshay, Mukesh, and Pawan were convicted of robbing Ramadhir and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment. On 5 May 2017, the Supreme Court rejected the convicts' appeal, upholding the death sentence, stating they had committed a "barbaric crime" that had "shaken society's conscience," and the verdict was well received by the victim's family and civil society. Legal experts noted the convicts still had the right to file a review petition. On 9 July 2018, the Supreme Court rejected a review petition by three of the convicts. In November 2019, the Supreme Court dismissed a review petition from Akshay, retaining the death sentence, and his lawyer requested three weeks to appeal to the President. In January 2020, a five-judge bench rejected the curative petitions of Vinay Sharma and Mukesh. On 7 January 2020, a Delhi court issued a death warrant for the Nirbhaya rapists, setting the execution date for 22 January 2020 at 7:00 a.m. IST in Tihar Jail. Government authorities and the victim's mother alleged the convicts were intentionally delaying the legal process by filing appeals in stages to postpone execution. Under prison rules, if one convict petitions for mercy, the execution of all others in the case is postponed until a decision is made. Mukesh Singh filed a mercy plea in January 2020. The Delhi government recommended rejection and forwarded it to the Lieutenant Governor. On 17 January 2020, the President rejected the plea, with both the Delhi government and the home ministry recommending rejection. Hours after the rejection, Judge Dharmender Rana issued a second death warrant for execution on 1 February 2020 at 6:00 a.m., following a mandatory fourteen-day reprieve. During the hearing, the court also rejected Mukesh's plea to postpone execution. On 17 February 2020, a third death warrant was issued with an execution date of 3 March 2020 at 6:00 a.m. On 4 March 2020, a fourth death warrant was issued with an execution date of 20 March 2020 at 5:30 a.m. Numerous appeals and petitions were filed by the families and the convicts, including three seeking a stay at the International Court of Justice, but the execution date remained unchanged. On 20 March 2020 at 5:30 a.m. IST, Mukesh Singh, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Pawan Gupta were executed at Tihar Jail. The gallows were specially designed for four people. According to prison officials, the convicts refused a last meal and new clothes, were blindfolded, and did not resist as they were led to the gallows; Vinay Sharma suffered a breakdown and pleaded with the guards. The four were pronounced dead after hanging for 30 minutes. Mukesh Singh reportedly requested to donate his organs. Public protests took place in New Delhi on 21 December 2012 at India Gate and Raisina Hill, the latter being near the Parliament and Rashtrapati Bhavan, with thousands clashing with police and battling Rapid Action Force units. Demonstrators were baton-charged, shot with water cannons and tear gas, and arrested. Similar protests occurred nationwide, including over 600 women in Bangalore, thousands in Kolkata, and online via Facebook and WhatsApp, with users replacing profile images with a black dot. Tens of thousands signed an online petition. Yoga guru Baba Ramdev and former Army chief General Vijay Kumar Singh were among those who clashed with Delhi Police at Jantar Mantar. On 24 December, activist Rajesh Gangwar started a hunger strike, saying, "If my death shakes the system and gets them hanged, I am ready to die," and ended it after 14 days, stating he would continue his fight for stricter rape laws. The Middle Finger Protests, a Chandigarh-based NGO led by Prabhloch Singh, played a key role in the agitations. Seven metro rail stations in New Delhi were closed on 22 December to discourage gatherings at Raisina Hill. On 24 December, police blocked roads to India Gate and Raisina Hill, closed nine metro stations, and imposed a curfew near the presidential residence, citing CrPC section 144. The Hindustan Times accused police of excessive force, reporting 375 tear gas canisters used at India Gate. First Post criticized the government for failing to act positively and using force, lathi-charging, pushing media out, and shutting down metro stations. Police claimed peaceful protests were "hijacked" by hooligans and activists. During one protest, police constable Subhash Tomar collapsed and later died in hospital. Two witnesses claimed he collapsed without being hit, while a third disputed this. Hospital doctors and the post-mortem gave conflicting reports: he died of cardiac arrest, but it is unclear if the heart attack was caused by blunt-force injuries to his chest and neck. Some experts suggest the injuries may have been a side effect of CPR. The Delhi Police arrested eight young men and charged them with Tomar's murder and rioting at India Gate. In March 2013, the police admitted in the Delhi High Court they had no evidence and dropped the murder charges, with the youths calling the move "irresponsible." After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, protests were held in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth over their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar, with minor clashes and police removal of some protesters. One group observed a one-day hunger strike. All roads to India Gate were closed, and areas where protests had occurred were made inaccessible. Some protesters drew graffiti and slogans condemning the incident and demanding stricter laws and faster justice.

After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, widespread protests erupted across India, including in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth across their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, where minor clashes occurred between protesters and police, leading to the removal of some demonstrators. A one-day hunger strike was observed at Jantar Mantar, and all roads leading to India Gate were closed, with areas where protests had gathered previously made off-limits to the public. Protesters spread papers with graffiti and slogans condemning the incident and demanding stricter laws and faster justice. The BJP renewed its call for a special parliament session to discuss the case and adopt stricter laws on crimes against women. New Year's celebrations in Delhi were significantly scaled back, with the Indian armed forces and several clubs and hotels cancelling their parties. The protests also spread across South Asia, with marches and rallies in Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. In Nepal, hundreds of demonstrators in Kathmandu called for legal reforms and a change in attitudes toward women. In Bangladesh, the human rights group Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) said the Delhi protests had energized demonstrations against sexual violence, noting that men were now participating and that the protests included people from diverse social backgrounds. In Paris, people marched to the Indian embassy, handing over a petition calling for action to make India safer for women. An author for the South Asia Analysis Group described the protests as expressions of middle-class angst stemming from a breakdown of the social contract between the middle class and the liberal state. New Delhi has the highest number of sex crimes among India's major cities, with police data showing an average of one rape reported every 18 hours; reported rape cases increased by nearly 17 percent between 2007 and 2011. Only one of the 706 rape cases filed in Delhi in 2012 resulted in a successful conviction. Between 16 December and 4 January, the Delhi Police recorded 501 calls for harassment and 64 for rape, but only four were followed up with inquiries. The regional program director for U.N. Women South Asia stated that rape cases occur in nearly all cities and rural areas, with victims often dying immediately due to the brutality of the crime, calling the incident a wake-up call. Members of Indian parliament demanded severe punishment for the perpetrators. Sushma Swaraj, then Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, stated that the rapists should be hanged. Sonia Gandhi, Chairperson of the ruling United Progressive Alliance, visited Safdarjang Hospital to meet doctors and obtain updates on the victim’s health. Mayawati, chief of the Bahujan Samaj Party, said proper investigation was needed and that action should be so strict that no one would dare commit such acts again. Jaya Bachchan, an actress and member of the Rajya Sabha, said she was "terribly disturbed" and "ashamed" and felt "helpless" for not being able to act. Meira Kumar, then Speaker of the Lok Sabha, stated that a new law should be introduced and passed to ensure women's safety, emphasizing that existing laws were insufficient and that stricter laws were needed. Delhi’s then Chief Minister, Sheila Dixit, said she lacked the courage to meet the victim and described Delhi as a "rape capital," calling for senior police officials to be held accountable and for the immediate establishment of fast-track courts to handle rape cases swiftly. Three constables who refused to act on Ram Adhar’s robbery complaint were suspended for dereliction of duty. On 24 December 2012, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh issued his first official response, appealing for calm and stressing that violence would serve no purpose. He assured the public that all efforts would be made to ensure women’s safety and expressed empathy, saying as a father of three daughters he felt the incident deeply. He cancelled all official events to celebrate the new year as a tribute to Nirbhaya. Then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav, announced a ₹2 million (US$24,000) financial package and a government job for the victim’s family. President Pranab Mukherjee’s son, Abhijit Mukherjee, argued that the women protesters were not students, comparing the situation to the "Pink Revolution" in Egypt, and claimed he saw many "beautiful women" among them, though he expressed doubt about their student status. The remark was widely condemned as sexist; his sister Sharmistha and their father, the president, disapproved. Maharashtra Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan also expressed disapproval. Abhijit quickly withdrew and apologised. Spiritual guru Asaram Bapu provoked public criticism by claiming the victim was to blame for her assault, saying she could have stopped it by chanting God’s name and falling at the attackers’ feet. Several celebrities, including Preity Zinta, Shah Rukh Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Amitabh Bachchan, and Farhan Akhtar, expressed outrage on social media, demanding the rapists be castrated or hanged. The incident was featured in the first episode of the second season of Satyamev Jayate, hosted by Aamir Khan, which also addressed other rape cases and the suffering of survivors at the hands of police, medical staff, and the public. The American embassy released a statement on 29 December 2012, offering condolences to Nirbhaya’s family and reaffirming its commitment to ending gender-based violence globally. Nirbhaya was posthumously awarded one of the 2013 International Women of Courage Awards by the US State Department, with the citation stating that her personal ordeal, perseverance in fighting for justice, and her family’s bravery were helping to reduce the stigma and vulnerability that drive violence against women. Indian politician Mulayam Singh Yadav opposed making rape a capital offence, saying "Boys will be boys. Boys commit mistakes." Two years later, in response to his comments and another rape incident in Uttar Pradesh where his party was in power, UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said "We say no to the dismissive, destructive attitude of, 'Boys will be boys'" and stated that violence against women must never be accepted, excused, or tolerated, asserting that every girl and woman has the right to be respected, valued, and protected. UN Women called on the Government of India and the Government of Delhi to take radical reforms, ensure justice, and provide robust public services to make women’s lives safer. In response to Western media criticism of India, Jessica Valenti, writing in The Nation, argued that rape is also common in the United States, but US commentators deny or minimize its systemic nature while attacking India for a supposed rape culture. Activist Eve Ensler, who organized One Billion Rising, said the gang rape and murder was a turning point in India and globally, noting that she had never seen sexual violence break through public consciousness so dramatically, appearing on every newspaper’s front page, in college discussions, and in restaurants, and that India was leading the world in fast-tracking laws, sexual education, and examining patriarchal structures and masculinity. In the aftermath, female tourism to India fell by 35% compared to the previous year, according to an ASSOCHAM industry survey. The UK Foreign Office revised its travel advice and advised women against traveling alone. In 2014, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley stated that one incident of rape in Delhi was enough to cost the country billions in lost tourism. In response to the protests, central and state governments announced measures to improve women’s safety. The Government of Karnataka launched a 24/7 dedicated helpline (1091) operated by state police for sexual abuse complaints and considered setting up fast-track courts for pending cases. The Government of Tamil Nadu announced a 13-point action plan, treating sexual assault as a grave crime, assigning top police officials to probe such cases, and conducting daily hearings in fast-track courts with women prosecutors appointed as government counsels. The Jammu and Kashmir government announced plans to revise state laws on sexual offenses and gender crimes. The Government of Himachal Pradesh established state and district-level committees to review progress in cases of crimes against women. Despite these responses, Singh endured significant hardship during and after the protests, facing a demeaning medical examination, a harsh court cross-examination, salacious media coverage, and an insensitive societal response, including from people who knew her. On 22 December 2012, a judicial committee headed by J. S. Verma, a former Chief Justice of India, was appointed by the central government to submit a report within 30 days suggesting amendments to criminal law to address sexual assault. The committee urged the public, legal professionals, NGOs, and women’s groups to share views on possible legal amendments to ensure quicker investigations, prosecutions, trials, and enhanced punishments for extreme sexual assaults. The committee held its first meeting on 26 December 2012 and received over 6,000 emails with suggestions. The report was submitted after 29 days, having considered 80,000 suggestions, and identified government and police failures as the root cause of crimes against women. It recommended reviewing the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 in conflict zones and setting the maximum punishment for rape as the death penalty, rather than life imprisonment. The committee did not support lowering the age of adulthood from 18 to 16. On 26 December 2012, a Commission of Inquiry headed by former Delhi High Court judge Usha Mehra was established to identify lapses, determine responsibility, and suggest measures to make Delhi and the National Capital Region safer for women. On 1 January 2013, a task force headed by the Union Home Secretary was formed to examine women’s safety in Delhi and review the functioning of the city police. On 3 February 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013 was promulgated by then President Pranab Mukherjee, amending the Indian Penal Code, Indian Evidence Act, and Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on sexual offences. The ordinance introduced the death penalty for rape. According to Minister of Law and Justice Ashwani Kumar, 90 percent of the Verma Committee’s suggestions were incorporated into the ordinance. Critics argue that key recommendations, including the criminalization of marital rape and trying military personnel under criminal law, were ignored. In a December 2013 interview, Nirbhaya’s parents, Badri Nath Singh and Asha Devi, said they were seeking to change the juvenile law in cases like their daughter’s rape and murder. They petitioned the Supreme Court to try the juvenile in a criminal court instead of a Juvenile Justice court. The juvenile defendant, who was just short of 18 years old at the time of the crime, was sent to a borstal youth detention center for three years and then released. In a March 2015 interview with The Tribune, Women and Child Development Minister Maneka Gandhi said the government was moving forward with a law treating juveniles as adults in grave crimes. On 22 December 2015, the Rajya Sabha passed the revised Juvenile Justice Act, proposing that individuals above 16 years of age accused of heinous crimes be treated as adults in court. On 16 December 2013, the first anniversary of the attack, activists held memorials in New Delhi to honor the victim, widely known as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless." Women’s organizations lit candles and protested against women’s exploitation. University students and others organized a candlelight march at the bus stand in South Delhi where Nirbhaya and her friend Pandey boarded the bus. At a commemorative prayer meeting, political leaders committed to increasing efforts to improve women’s security. Former Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit, speaking with the victim’s mother, said Delhi’s society and authorities would work together to build a permanent legacy for her daughter, promising to fulfill whatever the family desired and to ensure such an incident would never happen again. The parents said they were proud of their daughter’s courage, which they believe inspired more women to speak out. In December 2014, on the second anniversary, the parents remarked that little had changed: "Nothing in India has changed since 16 December 2012. All promises and statements made by our leaders and ministers have turned out to be shallow. Our suffering gives them their moment in the limelight. My daughter asks me what I have done to get her justice. She asks what am I doing so that many more like her get justice and I wake up to realise how helpless and trivial I am..." On 16 December 2015, the third anniversary of the attack, "Nirbhaya Chetna Diwas" was observed with candlelight vigils, prayer meetings, and other events at Jantar Mantar. In a "brave homage to her daughter," Jyoti’s mother, Asha Devi, said, "My daughter's name was Jyoti Singh and I am not ashamed to name her. Those who commit heinous crimes like rape, their heads should hang in shame, not the victims' or their families'." She spoke out against the upcoming release of the juvenile convict and put forth four demands for justice: the juvenile should be sentenced to death, fast-track courts should be established in all courts to offer speedy justice to sexual assault victims, amendments to the Juvenile Justice Act should be passed, and the Nirbhaya Fund should be used to set up high-quality forensic labs.

On 16 December 2015, women's and citizens groups, candlelight vigils, prayer meetings, and other events were held at Jantar Mantar to honor Jyoti on the third anniversary of her death. Jyoti's mother, Asha Devi, described the event as "a brave homage to her daughter" and stated, "My daughter's name was Jyoti Singh and I am not ashamed to name her. Those who commit heinous crimes like rape, their heads should hang in shame, not the victims' or their families'." Devi opposed the upcoming release of the juvenile convict and made four demands for justice: on the third death anniversary of the victim, the release of the juvenile convict is seen as unjust; she does not know if the convict is 16 or 18, but knows he committed a brutal crime and there should be no age limit for punishment; the juvenile convict should be sentenced to death, fast-track courts should be set up in all courts to provide speedy justice to sexual assault victims, amendments to the Juveniles Justice Act should be passed, and the Nirbhaya Fund should be used to establish high-quality forensic labs in all states. The public outrage following the rape and murder sparked hopes for change in India. The government responded by passing new sexual assault laws, including a mandatory minimum sentence of 20 years for gang rape, and creating six new fast-track courts for rape prosecutions. The "Nirbhaya" case was the only conviction among 706 rape cases filed in New Delhi in 2012. Between 16 December 2012 and 4 January 2013, Delhi police recorded 501 harassment allegations and 64 rape cases, but only four inquiries were launched. However, the "Nirbhaya" case increased the willingness of rape or molestation victims to report crimes; police records show that during the final nine months of 2013, nearly twice as many rape victims filed reports and four times as many molestation allegations were made. A National Crime Records Bureau report indicates that 95 percent of cases brought to police were classified as crimes, yet there is a large backlog, with fewer than 15 percent of those charged tried in 2012, leaving 85 percent waiting to come to trial. On 16 December 2013, the first anniversary of the rape was commemorated in London with a public memorial honoring the victim; Meera Syal, whose parents are from New Delhi, spoke about the anger expressed at the time and urged the Indian government to enforce changes from the Criminal Law Amendment Act, which expanded the definition of rape and included new offences such as acid attack, sexual harassment, voyeurism, and stalking. She also emphasized the need for activists to act in solidarity to stop violence against women and girls globally. Following the incident, the government established the Nirbhaya Fund for the empowerment, safety, and security of women and girl children, administered by the Department of Economic Affairs of the finance ministry. However, an Oxfam India report published in 2021 found the fund remains underused and underutilized. Observers note that the victim's ordeal changed public conversations about women's issues, with men joining the discussions; a young woman who participated in the protests said that the taboo on discussing rape and sexual violence had been broken, and that media coverage of sexual violence increased, though she saw no change in rape culture or related brutality, noting that teasing, catcalling, and sexual harassment remain widespread in public and private spaces. She acknowledged that a year is too short to undo centuries of patriarchal norms embedded in homes, institutions, and laws, and that police responsiveness is driven by fear of censure rather than duty. Women in urban India still feel unsafe and often wear clothing that covers their bodies to feel safe. Public officials and commentators frequently claim that women who wear "skimpy" clothing or go out with men "invite" attacks, thus denying it is rape. In reality, most women avoid Western clothing due to fear of sexual assault. The idea that women's attire "provokes assault" is described as victim blaming by government officials, social commentators, men, and even other women. As society and the Indian government have failed to address the root causes, women adopt safety strategies such as ignoring sexual commentary, avoiding eye contact, dressing more modestly, and refraining from going out at night, which has led to women avoiding public spaces, including public transportation, reinforcing the expectation that women should stay at home. Critics argue these avoidance tactics are only temporary fixes to deeper issues of victim-blaming and lack of accountability for men. A 2017 poll by Thomson Reuters Foundation, the first of its kind globally, found Delhi was the fourth most dangerous city in the world for women and the worst in the world for sexual violence, rape, and harassment. In response to the incident, Safecity, a non-profit and free website developed by the Red Dot Foundation and launched in 2012, allows users to make anonymous reports of gender-based harassment, abuse, and violence, and creates publicly available maps of these incidents to raise awareness and advocate for improved public safety. In December 2013, the victim's family and social entrepreneur Sarvesh Kumar Tiwari established the Nirbhaya Trust, an institute to assist women who have experienced violence with shelter and legal aid. Named "Nirbhaya" meaning fearless in Hindi, after the media's name for the victim, due to India's law prohibiting the publication of a rape victim's name, the victim's father stated, "So many people supported us, so... we want [to] help those girls who have no one." Inspired by the protests and international attention, women's rights activists organized the first Women of India Leadership Summit, later renamed the Women of India Summit, in 2013, an annual gathering to develop strategies to empower women, especially in the National Capital Region, so that Delhi is no longer known as the "rape capital of the world." India's Daughter (2015), a documentary directed and produced by Leslee Udwin as part of the BBC's Storyville series, was scheduled for broadcast on International Women's Day, 8 March 2015, on NDTV 24x7 in India and BBC Four in the UK. On 1 March, it was revealed that the filmmakers had interviewed one of the rapists while he was in Tihar jail, which was picked up by Indian media. The Indian government blocked the broadcast in India via a court order on 4 March, and the BBC complied, not broadcasting in India. In the UK, the BBC moved the screening to 4 March and aired it on that date. The film was uploaded to YouTube and went viral on social media; on 5 March, the Indian government directed YouTube to block the video in India, and YouTube complied. The film generated significant controversy in India and worldwide. Because India does not permit the publication of a rape victim's name, the victim was called "Nirbhaya," meaning fearless, due to her efforts to fight off her attackers and her insistence on making a detailed statement to police before her death. However, after her death, the parents were quoted as saying they had no objections to using their daughter's name. In the film, the father stated he was "happy" to reveal her name, Jyoti Singh, and on 5 March said he believed everyone should watch the documentary as it revealed "the bitter truth" about attitudes toward women in India. Still, on 6 March, The Hindu published an article titled "Father objects to revealing gangrape victim's name in 'India's Daughter'" in which the father was quoted as planning legal action over the use of her name. Director and producer Leslee Udwin said the courage and passion of ordinary men and women who protested in unprecedented numbers during the December freeze inspired her to make the film, noting that India led the world in commitment to women's rights. Nirbhaya's father, Badrinath Singh, said the film "holds up a mirror to society" and that its screening signifies the continuation of the struggle his daughter was part of. He stated that since her death, every girl on the street is now like a daughter to him and his wife, and that people need to understand that sons must be taught to respect women. Speaking on 5 March, Singh said: "My wife and I brought up our children with the sole intention of making them good citizens. I can proudly say that we have achieved that. Our daughter has shown society its true face. She has changed the lives of many young girls. She remains an inspiration even after her death. She fought back those devils. We are proud of our daughter." Indian-Canadian filmmaker Deepa Mehta's 2016 film Anatomy of Violence was also based on the incident, exploring the social conditions and lack of mental and sexual education in Indian society that enabled the crime. "A Nation Awakens" is the 296th and 297th special two-part episode of the fourth season of Sony TV's Crime Patrol, originally aired on 21 and 22 September 2013, written by Subramanian S. Iyer and directed by R. Amit Kumar Jha, with principal photography in Mumbai beginning in January 2013, hosted by Anup Soni, and featuring Sanjeev Tyagi as the head police inspector. Richie Mehta, a Canadian filmmaker, created a seven-part web television series titled Delhi Crime in 2019, based on the aftermath and manhunt of the perpetrators, starring Shefali Shah, Rasika Duggal, and Adil Hussain, released on Netflix, and winning Best Drama Series at the 48th International Emmy Awards. The comic book Priya's Shakti was inspired by the Nirbhaya case, with the protagonist fighting against gender-based sexual violence in India and globally. A book on the Nirbhaya case, Courting Injustice: The Nirbhaya Case and its Aftermath, was authored by Rajesh Talwar and published by Hay House in 2013. On 5 September 2014, Bandaru Dattareya, a Member of Parliament and BJP National Vice President, inaugurated "Wo Desh Ki Beti" (Nation's Daughter), a social event in Hyderabad showcasing sixteen poems by Sunil Kumar Verma that depicted the pain of a nation at the gang rape of its daughters. Several artists have created works based on Nirbhaya's story; in January 2014, artists from across India held an art exhibition on Nirbhaya and sexual assault. Contemporary scroll painter Kalam Patua created a painting titled Nirbhaya exhibited at the 8th Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art. Feminist artist Pritika Chowdhry created artworks reimagining Nirbhaya as a superheroine, including a Nirbhaya superheroine, an Anonymous Nirbhaya mask, and other art projects to advocate against sexual assault. Polish-American artist Monica Weiss created an art memorial for Nirbhaya.

The 2013 El Reno tornado was an extremely large, powerful, and erratic tornado that occurred on the early evening of Friday, May 31, 2013, in a rural area of Central Oklahoma. It was a rain-wrapped, multiple-vortex tornado that peaked at a record width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km), making it the widest tornado ever recorded. The tornado formed at 6:03 p.m. CDT (23:03 UTC), about 8.3 miles (13.4 km) west-southwest of El Reno, and rapidly grew in size and intensity as it tracked through central Canadian County. It remained over mostly open terrain and did not impact many structures, but mobile weather radar measurements revealed extreme wind speeds exceeding 313 mph (504 km/h), among the highest ever observed on Earth, just slightly below the 321 mph (517 km/h) recorded during the 1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado. The tornado reached its maximum width of 2.6 miles as it crossed U.S. 81, surpassing the previous record set in 2004, and then turned northeastward, weakening before dissipating around 6:43 p.m. CDT (23:43 UTC) after tracking 16.2 miles (26.1 km). It avoided densely populated areas near the Oklahoma City metropolitan area. The tornado killed four storm chasers—three professional and one amateur—marking the first known deaths in storm chasing history. These chasers, including TWISTEX scientists and engineers Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young, were caught off-guard by the tornado’s immense size and erratic movement. Paul Samaras and Young were ejected from their Chevrolet Cobalt by a sub-vortex, while Tim remained buckled in the passenger seat. Local resident Richard Henderson, who took a photo of the tornado before being struck, also died. Other chasers, such as Mike Bettes of The Weather Channel and Reed Timmer, were injured or had their vehicles damaged. A Doppler on Wheels analysis revealed that all teams were hit by an intense internal sub-vortex with winds approaching 200 mph (320 km/h), moving in a complex pattern. The tornado was responsible for eight fatalities and 151 injuries. Due to its size, ferocity, irregular movement, and the storm chaser deaths, it became one of the most studied and infamous tornadoes, with the National Weather Service calling it "the most dangerous tornado in storm observing history." The tornado developed within a larger weather system involving a mid-to-upper level trough and a closed mid-level low pressure area moving east-northeastward, with a strong polar jet over the southern Great Plains. Dewpoints ranged from the upper 60s°F (20°C) to lower 70s°F (20–22°C), temperatures were in the low to mid-80s°F (27–30°C), and CAPE values ranged from 3500 to 5000 J/kg, with deep layer wind shear of 45–55 kn (52–63 mph), creating favorable conditions for severe storms. A Particularly Dangerous Situation Tornado Watch was issued at 3:30 p.m. CDT, and a tornado warning was issued at 5:33 p.m. CDT for Canadian County. The tornado initially formed as multiple sub-vortices, deviated from its path at 6:15 p.m. CDT, looped before resuming east-southeast motion, and killed two people at 6:23 p.m. CDT as it passed south of El Reno across U.S. 81. It then moved into more populated areas of Canadian County, prompting a tornado emergency, before turning northeast and passing over Interstate 40 at 6:42 p.m. CDT, killing two more people. The tornado was on the ground for 40 minutes along a 16.2-mile (26.1 km) path. A strong anticyclonic multi-vortex satellite tornado formed southeast of the primary tornado at 6:28 p.m. CDT and remained on the ground for 15 minutes before lifting at 6:43 p.m. CDT. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) initially rated the tornado EF3 based on damage, but later upgraded it to an EF5 rating based on mobile radar data, with wind speeds preliminarily estimated at over 296 mph (476 km/h), and a revised analysis in 2015 showing peak winds of 313 mph (504 km/h). A 2024 NOAA and University of Oklahoma analysis estimated wind speeds between 115–150 m/s (257–336 mph; 414–540 km/h). Despite the radar-measured wind speeds, NOAA revised the rating to EF3 in August 2013 because ground damage surveys did not support a higher rating, citing the rural nature of the area and the fact that the EF5 wind speeds occurred in sub-vortices that did not impact structures. The tornado’s unusual behavior included abrupt direction changes, rapid expansion to 2.6 miles in about 30 seconds, a swift increase in forward speed from 20 to 55 mph (32 to 89 km/h), multiple vortices, and a translucent outer circulation obscured by rain. This made it a worst-case scenario for storm chasers, with many located in the "bear's cage" area northeast of the tornado, where visibility was good but reaction time was minimal. The wrapping rain bands were part of the tornado’s outer circulation, not a narrow corridor of clear air. Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young were among the first known tornado-related deaths of professional storm chasers or researchers. Tim drove a reinforced truck, while Carl drove an unmodified Chevrolet Cobalt, which was underpowered and poorly suited for high winds and rain-slicked roads. Mike Bettes had his SUV thrown 200 yards, suffering a broken neck and fractured vertebrae, while Emily Sutton and Kevin Josefy had their vehicle damaged by debris. Billy Prater and his family sought refuge under an overpass, Brandon Sullivan and Brett Wright were struck by barn debris, and Reed Timmer’s vehicle lost its hood. Dan Robinson escaped just ahead of the TWISTEX crew and is believed to be the last person to see Samaras, Paul, and Young. A tour group led by Randy Walton and Mike Phelps escaped after turning around as the tornado approached. A Doppler on Wheels analysis showed that all vehicles entered the tornado through the less intense north/northwestern side and were then hit by the intense internal sub-vortex. In response to the deaths, Kansas Emergency Management Association president Brian Stone called for storm chasing regulations, though implementation remains uncertain. AccuWeather Senior Vice President Mike Smith urged against overreacting, noting that the chasers were the first to die in 40 years and that storm chasing provides vital real-time data. On June 2, dozens of storm chasers coordinated a tribute using GPS transponders to spell out the initials of Tim, Paul, and Carl in North Dakota, South Dakota, and Nebraska. The Discovery Channel aired a special tribute episode titled "Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster" on June 5, honoring the chasers and covering the May 20 Moore tornado. The November 2013 National Geographic cover story featured Tim Samaras and a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers launched a crowd-sourcing project to collect video, photos, and GPS logs to reconstruct the event, creating the largest visual data set ever gathered on a tornado. The data is combined with radar and lightning information and aims to develop a standardized open-access database. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage.

A documentary titled *Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster* was released on June 5, honoring three storm chasers and covering the events of the EF5-rated tornado that struck Moore and parts of southern Oklahoma City eleven days earlier, on May 20. The November 2013 issue of *National Geographic* featured a tribute to Tim Samaras, a National Geographic Explorer supported in part by the Society, and included a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers conducted a crowd-sourcing survey to collect storm chaser data, such as video, photographs, and GPS logs, creating the largest visual dataset ever assembled on a tornado. This information was combined with radar and lightning data, and the project aims to develop a standardized open-access database for future events. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage; Anton Seimon, one of its architects, noted that while it had been used only in relation to the El Reno tornado, it could be applied to future tornadoes with sufficient footage. The tornado moved over mostly open terrain, resulting in relatively light damage—though still significant in isolated areas—according to National Weather Service surveys, with structures sustaining at most EF3-level damage. The Oklahoma City West Livestock Market was described as a "war zone," with several large steel-frame warehouse buildings destroyed, multiple large brick buildings at the Canadian Valley Technology Center heavily damaged or destroyed, and a large metal wind turbine prop blade thrown 100 yards (91 m) into a daycare building, with damage at that site estimated at up to $40 million. One farmstead, including a large barn, cattle barn, three machine sheds, granaries, and the owner’s home, was completely destroyed. Several rural homes were destroyed, large amounts of gravel were blown off roads leaving only dirt exposed, and multiple large metal electrical transmission poles, trees, and vehicles were damaged or tossed. At least 29 buildings and 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed, with repairs in the El Reno area expected to take at least a year. On June 1, the American Red Cross established a shelter at Redlands Community College in El Reno for storm victims. The following day, Oklahoma Governor Mary Fallin visited damaged areas of El Reno. A state of emergency was already in effect due to the May 20 tornadoes, enabling residents to quickly access emergency aid. Homeless residents were provided temporary housing in shipping containers, each equipped with a kitchen, bedroom, living room, and bathroom. Eight people died in the tornado, all in vehicles. Local hospitals, including OU Medical Center, INTEGRIS Southwest Medical Center, and Mercy Hospital in El Reno, reported at least 115 injured, including five critical patients, with a total of 151 injuries attributed to the event. As the tornadoes approached the Oklahoma City metro, thousands of residents evacuated, possibly due to memories of the May 20 EF5 tornado’s devastation, causing Interstates 35, 40, 44, and 240 to become "parking lots" with chaotic traffic, including people traveling southbound in northbound lanes. It has been suggested that the evacuation was partially driven by a controversial on-air recommendation from KFOR-TV chief meteorologist Mike Morgan, who advised residents without underground shelters to evacuate south of the tornado’s path, contrary to the recommended safety plan of seeking an interior room, bathtub, or closet without windows. Dr. Jeff Masters of Weather Underground stated that if the tornado had tracked directly over one of the congested highways, the death toll could have easily exceeded 500. The tornado’s location was 35°28′45″N 97°54′00″W (35.4792°N 97.9°W).

The 2013–14 CEV Challenge Cup marked the 34th edition of the European Challenge Cup volleyball club tournament, previously known as the CEV Cup. Turkish team Fenerbahçe Grundig won the final by defeating Italian club Andreoli Latina, securing their first CEV Challenge Cup title. Serbian player Ivan Miljković was awarded Most Valuable Player during the final tournament.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony occurred on Thursday, 14 June 2018, at 3:30 BST (about half an hour before the opening match) at the Luzhniki Stadium in Moscow, Russia, where Russia defeated Saudi Arabia 5–0.[2][3] The official mascot of the tournament was Zabivaka (English: "The one who scores"), a wolf designed to represent fun, charm, and character, which was voted for by a 53% margin.[4] Former World Cup-winning Brazilian striker Ronaldo was also a mascot and was originally intended to deliver the ceremonial first kick, but instead, he passed the official match ball—an Adidas Telstar 18—to the child mascot Zabivaka, who then kicked it off to begin the tournament. The match ball was sent into space with the International Space Station crew in March and returned to Earth in early June.[5] Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered the opening speech, describing Russia as "open, hospitable and friendly" and emphasizing the unifying power of football, stating that it transcends language, ideology, or faith. He concluded by saying: “Our duty is to preserve this power of humanity for generations to come for the sake of developing sports and strengthening peace and mutual understanding between people. I wish all the teams’ success and an unforgettable experience for the fans. Welcome to Russia.” FIFA President Gianni Infantino followed with a speech stating: “Welcome to the FIFA World Cup here in Russia. As of today, for one month, football will conquer Russia and from Russia, football will conquer the world. Enjoy the biggest celebration on earth. Thank you President Putin, thank you Moscow, Spasibo [thank you] Russia.” After the speeches, the ceremony performances began before the Russia vs. Saudi Arabia match.[6][7][8] British pop singer Robbie Williams performed "Let Me Entertain You" and later sang "Feel" and a duet of "Angels" with Russian soprano Aida Garifullina, as performers emerged dressed in the flags of all 32 teams, each carrying a sign with their nation's name. Williams then performed "Rock DJ" in an encore as the pitch was cleared for the match.[9] During the encore, Williams gave the middle finger, prompting Fox in the US to issue an apology, while ITV in the UK had cut away before the incident.[10] While singing "Rock DJ," Williams altered the lyrics to "But I did this for free," replacing "Every night"—the reason for this change remains unexplained. Williams appeared on This Morning on 19 June, explaining that under pressure with only one minute left before kickoff, he performed a one-minute countdown using his middle finger, which he admitted he regrets and cannot trust himself to avoid. When asked if he regrets it, he said: "Yeah, of course, yeah. I cannot trust me. And the last thing I said to my manager before we sat down on the sofa here was, 'what could go wrong,' because I don't know what I'm going to do at any time. There's no, sort of, plan. The plan was, sing in key, don't fall over. That was the plan and 99% of the plan, I pulled off.” He added that nothing actually popped into his head, stating there was a block between him and sense, and only later realized he had done it. A total of 21 foreign heads of state attended the match, marking the largest gathering of leaders for a FIFA World Cup match.

Muharrem İnce, a member of parliament for Yalova, was announced as the presidential candidate of the Republican People's Party (CHP) on 3 May 2018. The following day, on 4 May, party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu formally declared the CHP's support for İnce. Shortly after, the CHP initiated campaign preparations, including the production of campaign materials and merchandise. In early May, it was revealed that İnce's campaign would use the slogan “Türkiye’ye güvence Muharrem İnce,” meaning "Muharrem İnce, an assurance to Turkey." The campaign launched with an election rally in Yalova on 5 May. In a 26 May interview on his campaign trail, İnce addressed the Turkish currency and debt crisis, stating that while the central bank could temporarily halt the lira’s slide by raising interest rates, depreciation does not fundamentally stem from interest rates being too high or too low; instead, political and legal reforms are essential to address economic uncertainty. He emphasized the need for independent and autonomous institutions to manage the economy and noted that his economic team had been working together for a long time. At campaign rallies, İnce pledged to allow education in the Kurdish language and to resolve the Kurdish issue through dialogue, not violence. On EU-Turkey relations, İnce supports Turkey’s bid to join the EU, which he traces back to the 1830s during the Ottoman Empire’s Tanzimat period, and highlights youth support for better employment opportunities as a key reason for deeper European integration. He also pledged to restore dignity to the Foreign Ministry’s professional diplomats, who are mocked by Islamist government trolls. Regarding Syria-Turkey relations, İnce proposed ending Turkey’s longstanding opposition to Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, arguing that cooperation would enable the return of the 3.5 million Syrian refugees living in Turkish camps. He stated during a rally that, “When I become president, we will have an ambassador to Syria.” Turkey severed diplomatic relations with Syria in 2012. As of 31 May, media reported that even die-hard CHP critics acknowledged İnce was performing far better than expected, due to his nationwide campaign focused on restoring democracy, the rule of law, better pay, and education. With respect to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, İnce expressed a mix of contempt and near pity. Over the last week of May, İnce saw a 74 percent increase in social media popularity, reaching just over 1 million mentions and tags, close to Erdoğan’s 1.3 million, while competitors Meral Akşener had 280,852, Selahattin Demirtaş 201,922, and Temel Karamollaoğlu 181,703.

doc_name: 2019 Australian Open – Main draw wildcard entries
text: The 2019 Australian Open wildcard playoffs and entries consist of a series of events and internal selections to determine eight men and eight women for singles wildcard entries, seven male and seven female doubles teams, and eight mixed-doubles teams. The USTA granted a wildcard to the top-performing man and woman based on ranking points earned across a set of ATP/Challenger hardcourt events in October and November 2018. For men, the events were ATP Paris, $75K Canberra, $75K Charlottesville, $75K+H Shenzhen, €106K+H Bratislava, €85K+H Mouilleron-le-Captif, $150K+H Bangalore, $150K+H Houston, $75K Champaign, and $50K+H Kobe; for women, the events were $80K Macon, $80K Tyler, $80K Las Vegas, and $150K+H Houston. For men, only the best two results from the three-week period were considered, while for women, the best three results from the four-week period were taken into account. The winners of the wildcard challenge were Jack Sock and Whitney Osuigwe. Tennis Australia awarded a singles wildcard and a doubles wildcard to the Australian women who earned the most ranking points from two ITF hardcourt events in October and November 2018: the 2018 Bendigo Women's International and the 2018 Canberra Tennis International. The winners were Priscilla Hon, Ellen Perez, and Arina Rodionova. The Asia-Pacific Australian Open Wildcard Play-off featured 16 players in both men's and women's singles draws and took place from 26 November to 2 December 2018 at the Hengqin International Tennis Centre in Zhuhai, China. The December Showdown, held annually for two weeks in December, includes age championships for 12/u, 14/u, 16/u, and 18/u categories and hosts the 2019 Australian Wildcard Playoff, which occurred from 10 to 16 December 2018 at Melbourne Park, providing a main draw singles wildcard for men and women and a main draw women's doubles wildcard.

The 2019 Rugby World Cup (Japanese: ラグビーワールドカップ2019) was the ninth edition of the quadrennial men's rugby union world championship, hosted in Japan from 20 September to 2 November across 12 venues nationwide. The opening match was held at Ajinomoto Stadium in Chōfu, Tokyo, and the final took place at International Stadium Yokohama in Yokohama. This marked the first time the tournament was held in Asia and outside the traditional Tier 1 rugby nations. The event saw the first match cancellations due to Typhoon Hagibis, which affected three matches because of safety concerns. South Africa defeated England 32–12 in the final to win their third title, matching New Zealand's record and becoming the first team to claim the title after losing a pool-stage match. The defending champions, New Zealand, finished third after defeating Wales in the bronze final. The International Rugby Board (IRB), later renamed World Rugby, invited nations to express interest in hosting the 2015 and 2019 tournaments by 15 August 2008, with 10 unions responding and nine showing interest in the 2019 event. Russia initially bid for both tournaments but withdrew in February 2009 to focus on the 2013 Rugby World Cup Sevens; Australia withdrew on 6 May 2009. The three potential hosts—Italy, Japan, and South Africa—were announced on 8 May 2009. On 28 July 2009, the IRB confirmed England as hosts for 2015 and Japan for 2019, approved by Rugby World Cup Ltd with a 16–10 vote. From late 2013, the IRB, RWC Ltd, JRFU, and Japan 2019 conducted a process of gathering expressions of interest and meeting with potential hosts. In May 2014, 22 municipal and prefectural organizations in Japan expressed interest, with formal bids due by 31 October 2014; 14 bids were received on 5 November. Hong Kong and Singapore expressed interest in hosting matches and were included in Japan's bid but were not among the 14 stadiums announced in 2014. Nissan Stadium in Yokohama and Denka Big Swan Stadium in Niigata declined to bid. The JRFU's original 2009 bid was revised, excluding Chichibunomiya Stadium in Tokyo and including the larger 50,000-seat Nagai Stadium in Osaka. East Osaka City, which took over Hanazono Rugby Stadium from Kintetsu in April 2015, submitted a joint bid with Osaka Municipality to refurbish the stadium. Kamaishi, Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Ōita, Nagasaki, and Kumamoto were not included in the bid. Hosting areas excluded were Hokushin'etsu (Hokuriku and Kōshin'etsu) and Chūgoku (including Hiroshima and Shikoku), with no Chūgoku city hosting in the 2002 FIFA World Cup, though Hiroshima hosted in the 2006 FIBA World Championship. The new National Stadium in Tokyo, built for the 2020 Summer Olympics, was initially planned as the primary venue but was scrapped and rebid in 2015 due to design criticism and rising costs, leading to its completion being delayed. As a result, the opening match was moved to Ajinomoto Stadium and the final to Nissan Stadium in Yokohama. The top three teams from the 2015 World Cup received automatic qualification, with the remaining eight spots filled through regional qualifiers, six of which came from regional groups and two via play-offs. Qualifying groups were Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. The United States qualified on 1 July 2017 by defeating Canada in a two-leg match as America 1. Fiji and Tonga qualified as Oceania 1 and 2 respectively. Samoa secured the third Oceania spot by defeating Germany in a two-leg tie the following year. Uruguay qualified in January 2018 with a 10-point win over Canada as Americas 2. Romania initially qualified as Europe 1, but after complaints from Spain over ineligible players, all three—Romania, Spain, and Belgium—were penalized, resulting in Russia qualifying and Germany entering a play-off against Samoa. Namibia qualified in August 2018 by defeating Kenya in the Rugby Africa Gold Cup final. The final spot was decided in a repechage tournament in Marseille in November 2018, won by Canada after winning all three of their matches. The pool draw took place on 10 May 2017 in Kyoto, moved from its traditional December slot after the previous World Cup to allow nations more time to improve their world rankings. The seeding system from previous tournaments was retained, with the 12 automatic qualifiers from 2015 allocated based on their World Rugby Rankings on 10 May 2017. The remaining two bands were formed from the eight qualifying teams based on their previous World Cup performance. The 20 teams were seeded according to their world rankings as of that date. The draw involved randomly selecting a ball from a pot, with the first ball assigned to Pool A, the second to Pool B, the third to Pool C, and the fourth to Pool D. Each team submitted a squad of 31 players, the same as in 2015, with the deadline being 8 September, the United States being the last to reveal their squad on 6 September. World Rugby named 12 referees, seven assistant referees, and four television match officials for the 48 matches. The opening ceremony occurred at Ajinomoto Stadium in Tokyo on 20 September 2019 at 18:30 (JST), featuring a showcase of traditional and modern Japanese culture and the evolution of rugby in Japan. Richie McCaw, former All Blacks captain and 2015 World Cup winner, performed a ceremonial handover of the Webb Ellis Cup. Six jet aircraft from Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Blue Impulse aerobatic team flew over the stadium. Kiyoe Yoshioka of Ikimono-gakari performed World in Union, the official song. The tournament was officially opened by Fumihito, Prince Akishino of Japan, with World Rugby chairman Sir Bill Beaumont delivering a speech stating: "Over the next six weeks we will experience the very best of rugby and the very best of Japan as excitement sweeps this great nation. I know Japan will be the most welcoming of hosts, you are the best. The waiting is over and the stage is set. It’s now over to the teams and the fans to make this the best World Cup ever."
