The 20 teams were divided into four pools of five teams, each playing a single round-robin format of 10 games, with each team playing every other team in the pool once. Teams earned four points for a win, two for a draw, and zero for a loss. A bonus point was awarded for scoring four tries or for losing by seven points or fewer, with both conditions applying if both occurred. The top two teams in each pool advanced to the quarter-finals, and the top three teams qualified for the 2023 Rugby World Cup. If teams were tied on match points, the following tiebreakers applied: if three teams were tied, the criteria were applied to determine first place, then again (starting from criterion 1) to determine second place. The opening match of the tournament was Japan versus Russia in Pool A, with Japan winning 30–10. Kotaro Matsushima scored the first hat-trick by a Japanese player at a World Cup. Kirill Golosnitsky scored the first try of the tournament in the opening match after four minutes, the fastest try ever in a World Cup opening match. Two days later, Ireland defeated Scotland 27–3. On 24 September, Samoa beat Russia 34–9 in Kumagaya. Four days later, Japan defeated Ireland 19–12 in Tokyo, scoring four out of six penalties. World Rugby later admitted three of the four offside penalties were incorrectly awarded. Kenki Fukuoka scored a try in the 58th minute to give Japan a two-point lead after Ireland's Garry Ringrose and Rob Kearney scored the opening tries. Yu Tamura's conversion and fourth successful penalty sealed the win. Scotland recorded their first World Cup victory with a 34–0 win over Samoa in Kobe, with Samoan captain Jack Lam describing the ball as "a bar of soap." Three days later, Ireland defeated Russia 35–0 in Kobe, with five different players scoring tries. Jordi Murphy was substituted in the 27th minute due to a possible rib injury, adding to Irish back row pain after losing Jack Conan. Japan won 38–19 in Toyota with a 85th-minute try from Kotaro Matsushima securing a bonus point. Russia was defeated 61–0 by Scotland, with George Horne scoring a hat-trick, making Scotland the first team in World Cup history to not concede a point in two consecutive matches. A red card to Bundee Aki in the 29th minute reduced Ireland to 14 men, but they won 47–5 over Samoa in Fukuoka, with Johnny Sexton scoring two tries. The Japan–Scotland match was under threat due to Typhoon Hagibis, with the Scottish Rugby Union demanding legal action if cancelled. After an inspection confirmed the match could proceed, Japan won 28–21 with Kenki Fukuoka scoring two tries, becoming the first Tier 2 team to qualify since 2007, topping the pool while Ireland finished second. Pool B began with New Zealand defeating South Africa 23–13. New Zealand scored two tries in four minutes from George Bridge and Scott Barrett, leading 17–3 at half-time. Pieter-Steph du Toit scored a converted try to bring the score to 17–10, but two penalties from Richie Mo'unga and Beauden Barrett sealed the win. In Higashiōsaka, Italy conceded an early try to Namibia but won 25–0 with a bonus point. Italy earned a second bonus-point victory in Fukuoka, scoring seven tries in a 48–7 win over Canada. In Toyota, South Africa defeated Namibia 54–0, scoring nine tries while Namibia managed only a Cliven Loubser penalty in the 23rd minute. New Zealand won 63–0 over Canada at Ōita Stadium, with Brad Weber scoring his first two tries and the Barrett brothers (Jordie, Beauden, and Scott) each scoring a try, becoming the first trio of brothers to start for New Zealand. New Zealand then defeated Namibia 62–0 in Chōfu, with Sevu Reece, Ben Smith, and Anton Lienert-Brown scoring two tries in the second half after Namibia allowed only 24 points in the first half. South Africa defeated Italy 49–3 in Fukuroi, with Cheslin Kolbe scoring two tries. South Africa then beat Canada 66–7, with Cobus Reinach scoring the fastest hat-trick in World Cup history in 11 minutes. The final two matches of the group—New Zealand vs. Italy and Namibia vs. Canada—were cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis. New Zealand finished top of the pool, South Africa second. Pool C began with Argentina recovering from a 17-point half-time deficit against France at Tokyo Stadium, only for France's Camille Lopez to score a drop goal in the 70th minute to win 23–21. In Sapporo, England won a bonus-point match over Tonga with two tries from Manu Tuilagi. England followed with a 38–0 victory over the United States, with Joe Cokanasiga scoring two tries; the match was marred by the first red card of the tournament, given to United States' John Quill for a shoulder charge to Owen Farrell's head. Argentina rebounded from their loss to France with a 28–12 win over Tonga in Higashiōsaka, scoring all their tries in the first 28 minutes, including a hat-trick from Julián Montoya, before Tonga scored two tries to reduce the margin to 16. After Typhoon Mitag nearly cancelled the match, France lost consistency and allowed the United States to stay in the game before three late tries in the second half secured a 33–9 win in Fukuoka. In Chōfu, England defeated Argentina 39–10, with Tomás Lavanini shown a red card for a high tackle on Owen Farrell's head, forcing Argentina to play with 14 men. France qualified with a two-point win over Tonga at Kumamoto Stadium, after conceding the first 17 points, with Sonatane Takulua and Mali Hingano scoring tries to close the gap to three points, before Romain Ntamack scored two penalties in eight minutes to secure the win. Argentina finished their campaign with a 47–17 victory over the United States in Kumagaya, with Joaquín Tuculet and Juan Cruz Mallia each scoring two tries, their first since 2003. After the England–France match was cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis, Tonga ended their campaign with a 31–19 win over the United States, converting a match-winning try by Telusa Veainu and securing a bonus point. England finished top of the pool, France second. Pool D opened with Australia defeating Fiji 18–0 in Sapporo after Fiji led by two points at half-time, with Australia scoring four tries in the second half for a bonus point. Wales beat Georgia 43–14 at City of Toyota Stadium, leading 29–0 at half-time and 22–0 after three tries in the first half.

In the 2019 Rugby World Cup, matches were affected by Typhoon Hagibis, leading to the cancellation of the Pool B game between New Zealand and Italy and the Pool C game between England and France, which were declared 0–0 draws due to safety concerns for public transport and evacuation orders in Tokyo and Kamaishi. The Namibia–Canada match in Kamaishi was also cancelled, following a level 5 evacuation order, and recorded as a 0–0 draw; Canada stayed in Kamaishi to assist with cleanup, while Namibia interacted with fans in Miyako City. In contrast, the Wales–Uruguay and United States–Tonga matches proceeded as scheduled. Tonga ended their campaign with a 31–19 victory over the United States, with Telusa Veainu converting the match-winning try and securing a bonus point. In Kumagaya, Georgia defeated Uruguay 33–7, with a dominant second-half performance earning a bonus point. Australia beat Fiji 18–0 in Sapporo, scoring four tries in the second half for a bonus point, while Wales defeated Georgia 43–14, leading 29–0 at half-time. In Kamaishi, Fiji initially led against Uruguay before a try from Juan Manuel Cat brought them to 12–0 at half-time, but Uruguay won 45–10 over Georgia in a bonus-point victory due to Semi Radradra scoring two tries and setting up three more. Australia also beat Uruguay 35–0 at Ōita Stadium, with Tevita Kuridrani and Dane Haylett-Petty each scoring two tries. In a later match at Ōita, Wales won 29–17 over Fiji, with Josh Adams scoring two tries and Wales qualifying for the quarter-finals. Australia defeated Georgia 27–8 in Fukuroi, and Wales beat Uruguay 35–13 in Kumamoto to finish undefeated and secure a quarter-final spot. The knockout stage featured three single-elimination rounds, with extra time and sudden death periods used if needed, and a kicking competition if tied. England defeated Australia 40–16 in Ōita, with Jonny May scoring two tries and 18 turnovers by Australia, prompting Michael Cheika’s resignation. New Zealand beat Ireland 46–14 in Tokyo, with Aaron Smith scoring two tries and a penalty try. France defeated Wales 20–19 in a match where Sébastien Vahaamahina was sent off, and Wales won with a 74th-minute try. South Africa beat Japan 26–3, with Makazole Mapimpi scoring two tries. In the semi-finals, England defeated New Zealand 32–12, with Mapimpi and Cheslin Kolbe scoring tries, while South Africa beat Wales 32–12, with Damian de Allende and Josh Adams scoring tries. England started as favorites in the final but faced early setbacks, including Kyle Sinckler’s injury and injuries to South Africa’s Bongi Mbonambi and Lood de Jager, and were behind 12–6 at halftime due to handling errors. South Africa led 25–12 after Makazole Mapimpi’s try and 32–12 after Cheslin Kolbe’s try. The bronze medal was won by New Zealand in a convincing win over Wales. The tournament’s broadcasting was handled by International Games Broadcast Services (IGBS), using resources from Australia, France, New Zealand, South Africa, and the UK, with NHK covering selected games in 8K resolution. World Rugby streamed matches for unsold markets, Sport24 held in-flight broadcast rights, and in South Africa, SuperSport had rights, with SABC broadcasting the final via agreement with MultiChoice. The cancellations impacted pool standings, with France unable to claim top position and Italy eliminated from the tournament, while South Africa’s pool position remained unaffected due to their prior qualification.

On 14 January 2019, a Boeing 707-3J9C, serial number 21128 and registered as EP-CPP, operated by Saha Airlines on a cargo flight crashed at Fath Air Base, near Karaj, Alborz province, Iran. This aircraft was the last civil Boeing 707 in operation. It was owned by the Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force (IRIAF) and had been leased to Saha Airlines. The aircraft was 42 years old at the time of the accident, having first flown on 19 November 1976 and been delivered to the Imperial Iranian Air Force as 5–8312. It was transferred to Saha Airlines on 27 February 2000, re-registered as EP-SHK, and subsequently returned to the IRIAF in December 2015 before being re-leased to Saha Airlines in May 2016 with the registration EP-CPP. The aircraft had suffered substantial damage from an uncontained engine failure on 3 August 2009 during a flight from Ahvaz International Airport to Mehrabad International Airport, Tehran, leading to an emergency landing at Ahvaz, after which it was repaired. The flight was intended to carry meat from Manas International Airport in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to Payam International Airport in Karaj, Iran, but the crew mistakenly landed at Fath Air Base, likely confusing its shorter runway with the longer Payam runway, as the two are only a few kilometres apart and aligned similarly. A Boeing 707 typically requires a runway longer than 2,500 meters (8,200 feet), but Fath Air Base's runway is only 1,300 meters (4,300 feet). Poor weather conditions were also reported. The aircraft overran the runway, crashed through a wall, and collided with a house in the Farrokhabad neighborhood of Fardis County, Alborz province. Security footage captured the crash and subsequent fire. The houses were unoccupied at the time, and no ground injuries occurred. Fifteen of the sixteen crew members on board died; one, flight engineer Farshad Mahdavinejad, survived but was seriously injured and taken to Shariati Hospital in critical condition. There were no passengers. Early reports indicated either 16 or 17 people on board, all but one of whom died. An investigation was launched, and the cockpit voice recorder, flight data recorder, and control display unit were recovered from the wreckage on 14 January.

The 2019–20 Primeira Liga, also known as Liga NOS due to sponsorship, marked the 86th season of Portugal's top professional football league. The season began on 9 August 2019 and concluded on 26 July 2020. Benfica were the defending champions, having won their 37th league title in the prior season. Paços de Ferreira and Famalicão were promoted from the 2018–19 LigaPro, while Gil Vicente were promoted directly from the 2018–19 Campeonato de Portugal by court decision. These three teams replaced Chaves, Nacional, and Feirense, who were relegated to the 2019–20 LigaPro. A total of eighteen teams competed: the top fifteen from the previous season, the two promoted from LigaPro, and one promoted from the third-tier Campeonato de Portugal. Paços de Ferreira returned to the top division one season after being relegated, while Famalicão secured their return after a 25-year absence; Gil Vicente, who had been relegated in the 2018–19 season, were reinstated by court decision five years after their last participation. On 12 March 2020, the Liga Portuguesa de Futebol Profissional (LPFP) suspended the Primeira Liga due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Portugal. Following government approval, the league resumed on 3 June with the remaining ten matchdays played behind closed doors. On 15 July 2020, Porto won their 29th league title with two matches remaining after defeating Sporting CP 2–0 at home. After the season ended, Desportivo das Aves and Portimonense were relegated to the 2020–21 LigaPro, but two days later, both Desportivo das Aves and Vitória de Setubal were relegated to the 2020–21 Campeonato de Portugal by LPFP decision after failing to meet registration requirements. On 10 March 2020, the LPFP announced that matchday 24 (6–8 March) fixtures would be played behind closed doors due to government restrictions on events with more than 5,000 people in open spaces or more than 1,000 participants in closed settings, effective until 3 April. Two days later, the LPFP suspended both the Primeira Liga and LigaPro due to the pandemic, following the Portuguese Football Federation's suspension of non-professional competitions and an emergency meeting involving the Sindicato dos Jogadores Profissionais de Futebol (SJPF), LPFP, and FPF, with the SJPF warning of aggravated financial losses in case of infection. LPFP president Pedro Proença met with club presidents to assess the impact and announced a COVID-19 economic support plan and the creation of an Economic Impact Monitoring Group to support clubs. The FPF also established a €1 million credit line for non-professional clubs. On 28 April, Prime Minister António Costa met with the presidents of the "Big Three" clubs (Benfica, Sporting CP, FC Porto), the FPF, and LPFP to discuss football's return, which caused controversy as clubs like Braga and Vitória de Guimarães felt excluded. On 11 May, several teams had players test positive for COVID-19, including a player from Benfica’s reserve team, and three players from Famalicão, Moreirense, and Vitória de Guimarães were sent home and isolated. On 20 May, LPFP president Pedro Proença proposed that matches be broadcast on free-to-air RTP instead of pay TV, supported by the Portuguese government, but the proposal sparked controversy with NOS and other sponsors, including Benfica and Porto, leading to rumors of Proença being forced out, which he later denied. Benfica subsequently left the LPFP board due to the controversy. On 14 May, following a meeting of clubs, five substitutions were permitted under IFAB’s temporary allowance, proposed by FIFA to reduce fixture congestion. On 22 May, the LPFP confirmed the league would resume on 3 June. On 27 May, an assistant referee for a Benfica vs. Marítimo match tested positive and was replaced. On 30 May, the LPFP approved a plan to resume the league, but Marítimo refused the five-substitution rule; the rule was eventually accepted on 8 June by the LPFP despite the refusal. The table of team positions reflects results after each week, with postponed matches not included in their original scheduled round but added to the subsequent full round. Annual awards were announced on 29 August 2020.

Three-time defending champion Rafael Nadal defeated Novak Djokovic in the final of the 2020 French Open, winning 6–0, 6–2, 7–5 to claim the men's singles title. This victory marked Nadal’s 13th French Open title and his 20th major title overall, tying Roger Federer’s all-time record for men's singles titles. For the fourth time in his career, Nadal did not lose a set during the tournament, following previous instances in 2008, 2010, and 2017. This was the first time in French Open history that neither the men's nor women's singles champions lost a set in their respective tournaments. Nadal also became the first player, male or female, to win 100 matches at the French Open and only the second man—after Federer at the Australian Open and Wimbledon—to win 100 matches at the same major. Djokovic, who was attempting to become the first man in the Open Era to achieve a double career Grand Slam, would accomplish this feat the following year; however, he suffered his worst-ever defeat in a major final, winning only seven games and losing his first and only bagel (0–6 set). In the third round, Taylor Fritz and Lorenzo Sonego played the longest tiebreak in French Open history, with Sonego winning the third set tiebreak 19–17. Jannik Sinner reached the quarterfinals on his tournament debut, becoming the first man to do so since Nadal won in 2005 and the youngest quarterfinalist since Djokovic in 2006; he was also the first man born in the 21st century to reach a major quarterfinal. Nadal and Sinner’s quarterfinal match was the first men's match at the French Open to start at night, beginning after 10:00 pm CEST and finishing at 1:26 am, making it the first French Open match to end after midnight. All seedings were based on ATP rankings.

The 2020 French Open was a major tennis tournament held on outdoor clay courts at Stade Roland Garros in Paris, France, and was the 119th edition of the event. Originally scheduled for 24 May to 7 June, it was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, first moved to 20 September to 4 October 2020, then later adjusted to 27 September to 11 October 2020. This marked the first time since 1947 that the tournament was not held in May–June and the first time since the Open Era that a major tournament was postponed rather than cancelled. The event was part of the 2020 ATP Tour and WTA Tour calendars under the Grand Slam category and was run by the International Tennis Federation. It included men's and women's singles and doubles, as well as junior and wheelchair tournaments. Qualifying matches for singles and doubles began on 21 September, with the main singles draws featuring 16 male and 12 female qualifiers out of 128 players each. The tournament was the only Grand Slam to retain the advantage set in the final set, unlike the Australian Open and Wimbledon, which had switched to tiebreaks. The men's singles title was won by Rafael Nadal, who secured his 13th French Open title and 20th Grand Slam title, defeating Novak Djokovic in straight sets; this victory made Nadal equal Roger Federer's all-time record of 20 Grand Slam titles and marked his fourth consecutive and 13th overall French Open title, with no set lost throughout the tournament. The women's singles title was won by Iga Świątek, who claimed her first WTA singles title by defeating Sofia Kenin in straight sets, becoming the first player from Poland, male or female, and the first player born in the 21st century, male or female, to win a Grand Slam singles title. Świątek also did not drop a set during the entire tournament. The 2020 French Open was also the 124th edition of the tournament and the last Grand Slam event of 2020. It was the first year with a retractable roof on Court Philippe-Chatrier (completed in late 2019), with plans for a roof on Court Suzanne-Lenglen by 2023, and the first year with evening tennis due to floodlights installed on the twelve courts. Because of the September–October sunset in Paris occurring before 8:00 pm CEST, evening matches were possible, with the first women's evening match occurring during Iga Świątek and Martina Trevisan's quarterfinal, and the first men's evening match between Rafael Nadal and Jannik Sinner, which started after 10:00 pm and finished at 1:26 am—marking the first French Open match to end after midnight. The mixed doubles event did not take place, continuing the trend after the US Open. The men's doubles began on 29 September with 16 seeded pairs, and the women's doubles began on 30 September with 16 seeded pairs. In men's doubles, Pavić and Soares won the title in straight sets after defeating Krawietz and Mies in the final, marking their second Grand Slam title. In women's doubles, Hsieh Su-wei and Barbora Strýcová, along with other seeded pairs, were eliminated, and the defending champions Tímea Babos and Kristina Mladenovic successfully defended their title in straight sets. In wheelchair men's singles, Hewett won the title in straight sets, defeating Gérard in the final, securing his fourth Grand Slam singles title. In wheelchair women's singles, Yui Kamiji won her fourth French Open title and 24th Grand Slam title by defeating Momoko Ohtani, 6–2, 6–1. In wheelchair quad singles, Dylan Alcott defeated Sam Schröder in the opening round, and Andy Lapthorne defeated David Wagner in three sets, with the semifinal results leading to the final. The tournament had a maximum spectator capacity of 11,500 across the three main courts, with 5,000 in each of Court Philippe Chatrier and Court Suzanne Lenglen and 1,500 in Court Simonne Mathieu, while qualifying matches were played without spectators. Spectator capacity was reduced to 5,000 in the main courts on 17 September and to 1,000 starting on the eve of the main tournament due to a surge in coronavirus cases. Players were required to undergo two virus tests upon arrival and stay in designated hotels. The Laver Cup, originally scheduled for 24–27 September, was postponed to 2021, conflicting with the initial French Open dates. The men's singles event began on 27 September with 32 seeded players, and the women's singles began on the same date. In the men's singles, 11 seeded players were defeated in the first round, including No. 4 Daniil Medvedev, No. 8 Gaël Monfils, and No. 11 David Goffin, and 10 seeded players lost in the second and third rounds. In the women's singles, 12 seeded players lost in the first round, including No. 9 Johanna Konta, No. 12 Madison Keys, and No. 15 Markéta Vondroušová, and seven more lost in the second round. Serena Williams withdrew before her second round match due to an Achilles injury. In the men's doubles, only one seeded pair lost in the first round, and six of the remaining twelve seeded pairs were eliminated in the third round. In the women's doubles, five seeded pairs and three unseeded pairs advanced to the quarterfinals, with the final between Babos and Mladenovic and Guarachi and Krawczyk, won by the former in straight sets. The tournament took place across 23 courts, including the three main showcourts: Court Philippe Chatrier, Court Suzanne Lenglen, and Court Simonne Mathieu.

In each match, the Japanese player prevailed; Ohtani defeated top-seeded de Groot and Kamiji beat Van Koot, both in straight sets. The final was played on 9 October between the lone Japanese players in the event. In the final, No. 2 Yui Kamiji defeated Momoko Ohtani, 6–2, 6–1, to win her fourth French Open singles title and her 24th Grand Slam title overall. The wheelchair quad singles tournament began on 8 October with the semifinal round. The field consisted of four players; defending champion Dylan Alcott and Andy Lapthorne received the top two seeds, with the other two players unseeded. In the opening round, Alcott faced wild card entry Sam Schröder in a rematch of the final of the US Open some weeks earlier. Alcott was victorious in two sets. The other semifinal saw Lapthorne defeat David Wagner in three sets, with Lapthorne winning the first and third. The third place match took place between Schröder and Wagner, and was won by Schröder in straight sets. The final was played between No. 1 Alcott and No. 2 Lapthorne, with Alcott winning both sets by a score of 6–2 to capture his eleventh Grand Slam singles title. The wheelchair men's doubles competition featured the same eight players as in the singles event. Houdet and Peifer formed the top-seeded pair, while Hewett and Reid were the second seeds. The other pairings were Fernandez with Kunieda, and Cattanéo with Gerard. Houdet and Peifer were beaten 12–10 on a tie-break in their semifinal by Fernandez and Kunieda, after both sides had won a set each, while Hewett and Reid advanced to the final with a straight-sets victory over Cattanéo and Gerard. In the final, Hewett and Reid won the first set on a tie-break before losing the second 6–1, but finished victorious after the deciding tie-break finished 10–3 in their favour. As with the men's competition, the wheelchair women's doubles event featured the same eight players as in the singles event. Two of the four pairs were seeded: Diede de Groot and Aniek van Koot received the top seed, and the second seed went to Yui Kamiji and Jordanne Whiley. In the semifinals, De Groot and van Koot defeated the pair of Kgothatso Montjane and Momoko Ohtani, and Kamiji and Whiley defeated the pair of Marjolein Buis and Charlotte Famin. The final was played between the pair of de Groot and van Koot, the defending champions, and the pair of Kamiji and Whiley. The Dutch pair took the first set 7–6 in a tiebreak, but the latter pair came back to win the second set 6–3 and force the match into a third. The third set, consisting solely of a tiebreak, was won 10–8 by de Groot and van Koot, completing their successful title defense. The wheelchair quad doubles event consisted of a single match, played on 9 October between the pair of Dylan Alcott and Andy Lapthorne and the pair of David Wagner and Sam Schröder. Alcott and Wagner had won this event as partners the previous year, but chose to partner with different players for this edition. The first set was won by Alcott and Lapthorne, 6–4, but Schröder and Wagner responded with a 7–5 win in the second set. The third set consisted only of a tiebreak, which was won by Schröder and Wagner, 10–8, to capture their second and nineteenth overall Grand Slam titles, respectively. Of the sixteen seeded players, only two made it through the first three rounds and into the quarterfinals: No. 7 Dominic Stricker and No. 8 Leandro Riedi. Stricker defeated Lukas Neumayer in his quarterfinal matchup, while Riedi battled from behind to defeat Alex Barrena. The other two matches saw Juan Bautista Torres defeat Lilian Marmousez and Guy den Ouden defeat Sean Cuenin. In the semifinals, Stricker beat Torres in three sets (with both of his wins coming by virtue of bagels), while Riedi booked a place in the final by defeating den Ouden in two sets. The all-Swiss championship match was won by Stricker, as he defeated Riedi 6–2, 6–4, to claim his first junior Grand Slam title. Of the sixteen seeded players, five made it past the first three rounds and qualified for the quarterfinals. Among them was No. 3 Elsa Jacquemot, who was awarded a wild card into the main competition, but lost to qualifier Renata Zarazúa in the first round; she then entered the Girls' Singles competition. Jacquemot defeated No. 10 Kristina Dmitruk in straight sets in her quarterfinal match; the other matches saw Alina Charaeva upset No. 9 Alexandra Vecic, No. 4 Polina Kudermetova defeat Océane Babel, and No. 2 Alexandra Eala defeat Linda Nosková. In the semifinals, Charaeva pulled another upset by defeating Kudermetova, while Jacquemot defeated Eala. The final was played between Jacquemot and Charaeva, and was won by the former, 4–6, 6–4, 6–2. Of the four pairs that qualified for the semifinals, two were seeded. Only three seeded pairs of the original eight made it past the second round, notably No. 1 Arthur Cazaux and Harold Mayot, who withdrew before their opening match. The only seeded pair to lose their quarterfinal match was No. 7 Mikołaj Lorens and Kārlis Ozoliņš, who retired before the second set began. The No. 8 pair of Bruno Oliveira and Natan Rodrigues qualified for the semifinals, defeating Martin Krumich and Dalibor Svrčina in two sets to book a place in the final. The No. 3 pair of Flavio Cobolli and Dominic Stricker defeated Lilian Marmousez and Giovanni Mpetshi Perricard in a third-set tiebreak to win their semifinal match and advance to the final. In the championship match, Cobolli and Stricker defeated Oliveira and Rodrigues, 6–2, 6–4, to win the title. Of the eight pairs that were seeded at the start of the tournament, two were among the four pairs that qualified for the semifinal round. Notably, the top-seeded pair of Weronika Baszak and Elsa Jacquemot were defeated in straight sets in the first round, while No. 3 Alexandra Eala and Elvina Kalieva were knocked out in the third-set tiebreak of their opening match. The semifinals saw the fifth-seeded pair of Maria Bondarenko and Diana Shnaider come from behind to defeat Jéssica Bouzas Maneiro and Guillermina Grant, and No. 2 Kamilla Bartone and Oksana Selekhmeteva lose in an upset to Eleonora Alvisi and Lisa Pigato. This set up a final between No. 5 Bondarenko/Shnaider and unseeded Alvisi/Pigato, which was won in an upset by the latter in straight sets, 7–6(7–3), 6–4. The 2021–22 season marked the 120th season in the history of Brighton & Hove Albion and their fifth consecutive year in the top flight of English football. The club competed in the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the EFL Cup, exiting both cup competitions in the fourth round. Brighton finished ninth in the league, their highest-ever top-flight finish, surpassing their previous best of 13th place from the 1981–82 season. The season began with three pre-season friendlies: a goalless draw against Rangers at Ibrox on 24 July, featuring former Albion player Connor Goldson; a 3–1 win over Luton Town a week later, with goals from Aaron Connolly, Enock Mwepu, and Percy Tau, managed by former Seagulls player and coach Nathan Jones; and a 2–0 home defeat to La Liga side Getafe on 7 August, following the return of key players like captain Lewis Dunk and Leandro Trossard. Brighton opened the league campaign with a 2–1 victory over Burnley, with goals from Neal Maupay and Alexis Mac Allister, and followed it with a 2–0 win against Watford on 21 August, marking their best start in a top-flight campaign and their first match in front of a full stadium since March 2020. In the EFL Cup second round, they defeated Cardiff City 2–0, with Jakub Moder and Andi Zeqiri scoring their first goals for the club. Their first league loss came on 28 August, a 2–0 home defeat to Everton, with Taylor Richards making his league and Premier League debut. In a first derby match against Crystal Palace on 27 September, Brighton were behind after Trossard conceded a penalty scored by Wilfried Zaha, but Joël Veltman's long ball led to Neal Maupay scoring a 90+5th-minute equalizer. A second league loss occurred on 23 October, a 4–1 home defeat to Manchester City, with the City side scoring their first three goals in 18 minutes. In the EFL Cup fourth round, they lost to Leicester City on penalties after a 2–2 draw, with Mwepu scoring his first goal for the club and Jürgen Locadia making his first start and only second appearance in over two years. On 24 October, Brighton drew 2–2 with Liverpool after coming from 2–0 down, with Mwepu scoring his first league goal. On 20 November, manager Alex Potter made his 100th appearance in charge with a 2–0 away loss to Aston Villa. On 6 December, Brighton were drawn away to West Bromwich Albion in the third round of the FA Cup, to be played on 8 January 2022. Their fixture against Tottenham Hotspur on 12 December was postponed due to high COVID-19 cases in the Spurs squad. Brighton played a 1–0 home loss against Wolves on 15 December, with several absences due to injury, suspension, and COVID-19, and their match against Manchester United on 18 December was also postponed two days before kickoff due to cases in both squads. After a 12-game winless run starting on 19 September, Brighton beat Brentford 2–0 on Boxing Day, moving into the top half of the table and securing a double over the Bees after a prior away win in September. In the FA Cup third round on 8 January, Brighton won 2–1 after extra time against West Brom, with Odel Offiah making his first start and Kjell Scherpen making his debut as goalkeeper. In the reverse fixture against Palace on 15 January, Pascal Groß's penalty was saved by Jack Butland, Maupay's goal was disallowed for a high boot, and Joachim Andersen scored an own goal in the 87th minute after a low-paced pass from Maupay. Brighton were knocked out of the FA Cup in the fourth round on 5 February, losing 3–1 to Tottenham after a Harry Kane double and a Solly March own goal, with Yves Bissouma providing a brief hope before Kane scored his second. Their record-breaking seven-match unbeaten run ended on 15 February in Potter's 100th league match, with a 2–0 away loss to Manchester United at Old Trafford, after Dunk was sent off for denying Anthony Elanga a run on goal—initially shown a yellow card, but VAR reviewed and deemed it a sending-off. After six consecutive defeats, Brighton drew 0–0 with Norwich City on 2 April, with Maupay's penalty narrowly missing the target. A week later, on 9 April, they defeated Arsenal 2–1, with Mwepu scoring and assisting on his first start since a long injury absence, and Moisés Caicedo making his Premier League debut and assisting Mwepu's goal. Seven days later, on 16 April, Trossard scored two goals in consecutive games, including a 90th-minute goal, helping Brighton go six games unbeaten in the capital. On 30 April, Brighton beat Wolves 3–0 at Molineux, reaching 44 points—breaking their previous record of 41—and winning 10 league matches, surpassing their previous record of nine. On 7 May, Brighton defeated Manchester United 4–0 at the AMEX, their biggest ever top-flight result and first home win of 2022, in front of a record crowd of 31,637. Moisés Caicedo and Marc Cucurella scored their first goals for the club, Pascal Groß scored his first of the season, and Trossard scored one and assisted two others, ending Brighton's hopes for UEFA Champions League qualification in the 2022–23 season. At the end-of-season awards, Marc Cucurella won both Players' Player and Player of the Season, Jeremy Sarmiento won Young Player of the Season, Enock Mwepu won The Seagulls Goal of the Season for his 20-yard strike against Liverpool in October. Brighton finished ninth after beating West Ham 3–1 in the final match, with Joël Veltman scoring his second goal for the club. The victory brought their points total to 51, 10 points above their previous record, and 42 goals—the most in a Premier League season. This was also the first time since joining the Premier League that Brighton finished ahead of rivals Crystal Palace, who finished 12th. Pre-season fixtures included matches against Rangers, Luton Town, and Getafe. Key player movements included Florin Andone joining Cádiz on a season-long loan on 23 August, Percy Tau joining Al Ahly on a permanent deal on 26 August, Michał Karbownik joining Olympiacos on a season-long loan on 27 August, Christian Walton signing with Ipswich Town on a season-long deal on 30 August (later joining them permanently on 19 January 2022), Andi Zeqiri moving to FC Augsburg on loan on 30 August, Moisés Caicedo joining Beerschot on a season-long loan on 31 August (recalled on 12 January 2022), Aaron Connolly joining Middlesbrough on loan on 2 January 2022, Jürgen Locadia joining VfL Bochum on a permanent deal on 5 January 2022, Taylor Richards joining Birmingham City on loan on 8 January 2022, Dan Burn signing with Newcastle United on a permanent deal on 31 January 2022, and Kjell Scherpen joining Oostende on loan on 31 January 2022.

The 2021–22 season marked Liverpool Football Club's 130th season in existence and their 60th consecutive season in the top flight of English football. The club was on track to achieve a unique quadruple, securing a record-breaking ninth EFL Cup and winning the FA Cup by defeating Chelsea on penalties in both finals after each match ended in a goalless draw. However, they lost the Premier League title by just one point to Manchester City and, in a repeat of the 2018 final, were defeated by Real Madrid in the Champions League final. This season was the first since 2015–16 without Georginio Wijnaldum, who moved to Paris Saint-Germain, and the first since 2017–18 without Xherdan Shaqiri, who transferred to Lyon. Liverpool excelled in both the FA Cup and EFL Cup, beating Chelsea on penalties in both finals after goalless draws. On the final day of the season, Liverpool played Wolverhampton Wanderers at Anfield while Manchester City faced Aston Villa at the Etihad Stadium. Liverpool were down 0–1 early, but City were also a goal down to Villa. Sadio Mané equalized for Liverpool, keeping their title hopes alive as City were now 0–2 down. However, City scored three goals in five minutes to take the lead, and despite Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson scoring two late goals to win 3–1 against Wolves, Liverpool were denied the title by a single point. In the UEFA Champions League, Liverpool made history by becoming the first English club to win all six group stage matches, advancing to the final against Real Madrid, a rematch of the 2018 final. The final took place on 28 May 2022 in Paris, where Liverpool, who had previously faced Real Madrid in 1981, lost 0–1 as Vinícius Júnior scored the only goal. The club's spending was £36,000,000 in the summer and £37,500,000 in the winter, totaling £73,500,000. Their income was £45,050,000 in the summer and £1,500,000 in the winter, totaling £46,550,000, resulting in a net expenditure of £9,050,000 in the summer and £36,000,000 in the winter, amounting to £26,950,000 overall. On 12 July 2021, Liverpool announced a pre-season training camp in Austria featuring four friendlies. On 19 July, they confirmed completing their pre-season with two home friendlies. On 29 July, they confirmed a two-match training camp against Bologna in France between previously scheduled fixtures. Liverpool began the FA Cup in the third round at home to Shrewsbury Town and entered the competition in the third round. They entered the Champions League in the group stage, with the group draw held on 26 August 2021 and fixtures announced the next day. The round of 16 draw took place on 13 December 2021 in Nyon, Switzerland, with Liverpool facing Inter Milan. The quarter-final draw occurred on 18 March 2022, pairing Liverpool with Benfica. The semi-final draw followed on the same day, with Liverpool being drawn against Villarreal, the reigning Europa League champions. The final was held on 28 May 2022 in Paris, marking Liverpool's tenth European Cup final—the most of any English club—and their third in five years, repeating the 2018 final outcome. Players with no appearances are not included in the list. The monthly fan-voted award was given to the player chosen by fans voting on Liverpoolfc.com.

The 2021–22 Premier League marked the 30th season of the league since its founding in 1992 and the 123rd season of top-flight English football. The season began on 25 March 2021 and ended on 30 May 2022, with fixtures released on 16 June 2021. Manchester City defended their title for the second consecutive year, winning their sixth Premier League title and eighth English league title overall, making it their fourth title in the last five seasons. They were the defending champions, having won the previous season's title. The season featured full attendance after the restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which had limited or halted matches in the final third of 2019–20 and the entire 2020–21 season. It also included a winter break with no matches scheduled between 23 January and 7 February 2022. The early title race was led by Liverpool, Manchester City, and Chelsea, who were within two points of each other by early December. Chelsea led briefly after a run of 14 unbeaten matches until a defeat to West Ham United gave City the advantage. City then won 12 consecutive games, including a victory over Chelsea, building a 13-point lead by January (though Liverpool had two games in hand due to COVID-19 postponements). Liverpool responded with a 10-game winning streak, including their games in hand, and a 2–3 home loss to Tottenham Hotspur in February reduced City's lead to one point before their match on 10 April. A 2–2 draw preserved City's narrow lead. On 7 October, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund acquired an 80% stake in Newcastle United for £300 million, ending Mike Ashley's 14-year ownership. An emergency meeting on 12 October involving the other 19 clubs expressed anger over the takeover, with Newcastle excluded from the meeting. On 18 November, clubs voted to tighten financial controls to limit Newcastle's spending. At the time of the takeover, Newcastle were in 19th place after failing to win any of their first seven games; Steve Bruce was dismissed and Eddie Howe appointed. Newcastle did not win until their 15th match, but after five January signings, they won 12 of their final 18 games to finish 11th. In December, multiple matches were postponed due to COVID-19 outbreaks, with clubs calling for a league shutdown; a meeting on 20 December led to fixtures being played over Christmas if safe, with clubs advised to play if they had 13 fit players plus a goalkeeper. On 2 March, Roman Abramovich announced plans to sell Chelsea, intending to donate all proceeds to Ukraine victims of the Russian invasion. Reports followed of interest from Hansjörg Wyss, Todd Boehly, Javed Afridi, and others. On 10 March, the UK government froze Abramovich's assets due to his ties with Vladimir Putin, halting Chelsea's ability to sell tickets, merchandise, or players, and negotiate contracts. A government licence allowed football operations, employee payments, and season-ticket access. For the first time in Premier League history, all title, Champions League, Europa League, Conference League qualifications, and relegation battles were decided on the final day. With a one-point lead over Liverpool, Manchester City needed to match or exceed Liverpool's result to secure back-to-back titles; Liverpool needed a win and hope City lost to Aston Villa, managed by Steven Gerrard. Liverpool fell behind Wolves early but equalised; Aston Villa took a 2–0 lead after 63 minutes via goals from Matty Cash and Philippe Coutinho. Manchester City scored three goals in under six minutes (Ilkay Gundogan and Rodri as substitutes) to take the lead. Liverpool responded with late goals from Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson to win 3–1, but the result was irrelevant as City won 3–2 against Villa to claim their fourth title in five seasons. The season is remembered for the high quality of play by Manchester City and Liverpool, resulting in a fierce title race similar to the 2018–19 season, but also for VAR issues in its third season in England, including a high intervention threshold that led to few decisions, such as the failure to award a penalty in the Everton–Manchester City match due to a handball by Rodri, which impacted the title race. Norwich City, promoted from the Championship, were relegated with four games to spare after a 10th loss in 12 matches, recording the worst goal difference since Derby County in 2007–08. Watford, also promoted, were the second team to be relegated after a defeat to Crystal Palace. The final relegation spot was contested by Everton, Burnley, and Leeds United, all of whom struggled in the final months. Everton won only three games between October and April, but victories over Manchester United, Chelsea, and Leicester City meant a 3–2 win over Crystal Palace in their final home game secured safety; Dominic Calvert-Lewin's 85th-minute goal led to fans storming the pitch. Fans again invaded the pitch at full time after avoiding relegation since 1951, extending their top-flight status to 69 years. Burnley and Leeds were level on 35 points, with Burnley having a better goal difference. Burnley fell behind 2–0 to Newcastle, while Raphinha scored a penalty to put Leeds ahead against Brentford in the 54th minute. A 78th-minute equaliser from Brentford and a Maxwel Cornet goal gave Burnley hope, but Jack Harrison's added-time goal confirmed Leeds' safety and relegated Burnley after six consecutive seasons in the Premier League. Chelsea secured a top-four finish for the fourth consecutive season, leaving only Tottenham and Arsenal in contention for the Champions League spot. Arsenal were in 4th with three games left, but losses to Tottenham in the North London derby and to Newcastle in their final away game, combined with Tottenham's win over Burnley, saw them fall behind. Spurs needed only a point against already relegated Norwich to qualify for the first time in three years and won 5–0, with Son Heung-min scoring two goals to share the Golden Boot with Mohamed Salah. Arsenal failed to qualify for the Champions League for the sixth season despite a 5–1 win over Everton. Manchester United had a difficult season, culminating in the sacking of Ole Gunnar Solskjær on 21 November 2021 after a 4–1 loss to Watford; Ralf Rangnick took over as interim manager. The club finished 6th with a zero goal difference and the worst points total in the Premier League era at 58, losing on the final day. They qualified for the Europa League, but not back-to-back spots, as West Ham's 3–1 defeat at Brighton meant they settled for the Europa Conference League. Brentford manager Thomas Frank had a strong first season, aided by the January signing of Christian Eriksen, winning seven of their last 11 games, including a 4–1 win over Chelsea. The team finished 13th, 11 points above the relegation zone and never spent a week in the bottom half. Brighton had their best top-flight season under Graham Potter, finishing ninth with 51 points despite a poor home record; their 4–0 win over Manchester United was their biggest top-flight victory. Twenty teams competed: the top 17 from the previous season and three promoted from the Championship—Norwich City, Watford, and Brentford. These replaced Fulham, West Bromwich Albion, and Sheffield United, all of whom were relegated after brief top-flight spells. Brentford's return marked their first season in the Premier League after a 74-year absence. Four players scored four goals: one for the home team, one for the away team.

Ons Jabeur won the women's singles title at the 2022 Madrid Open by defeating Jessica Pegula 7–5, 0–6, 6–2, marking her first WTA 1000 title and making her the first Arab and African woman to achieve this feat. Aryna Sabalenka, the defending champion, lost in the first round to Amanda Anisimova. Pegula reached the final after being a match point down against Camila Giorgi in the first round. This was the last professional appearance of 2016 Olympic gold medalist Monica Puig, who lost to Danielle Collins in the first round. The seeded players were determined based on the entry list as of 25 April 2022, with rankings and points prior to that date also reflecting that date. Players who did not qualify in 2021 had their points reduced by the points from their 16th best tournament. Some players who would have been seeded withdrew before the tournament began, and one such player is exempt from receiving zero points due to a long-term injury.

On 6 March 2022, a militant threw a grenade at a marketplace located on Hari Singh High Street in Srinagar, Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, near the Amira Kadal bridge, at approximately 4:20 P.M. The attack injured twenty-four people and killed two. The street was crowded with a large number of individuals at the time of the bombing. The terrorist targeted security forces, injuring dozens of people, including at least one policeman. Later that day, 60-year-old Muhammad Aslam Makdhoomi from Nowhatta died from his injuries. The 19-year-old Rafiya Jan passed away the following day. The attack drew widespread condemnation across India, including from Manoj Sinha, Farooq and Omar Abdullah, Mehbooba Mufti, the Jammu Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee, the Bharatiya Janata Party, and other prominent figures.

259 Aletheia is a large main-belt asteroid discovered by German–American astronomer Christian Peters on June 28, 1886, at Litchfield Observatory in Clinton, New York. Classified as an X-type (Tholen: CP-type) asteroid, it is dark and composed of heterogeneous materials containing primitive carbonaceous substances, which account for its low albedo of 0.04. The asteroid has a diameter of approximately 185 kilometers and is among the largest in the main asteroid belt. Its orbit has a semi-major axis of 3.1 AU, an inclination of 11 degrees, and a period of 5.55 years. In 2003, Richard P. Binzel and Schelte Bus contributed to the understanding of Aletheia through the Small Main-belt Asteroid Spectroscopic Survey, Phase II (SMASSII), a lightwave survey that collected visible-wavelength (0.435–0.925 micrometre) spectral data between August 1993 and March 1999. Lightcurve observations have also been conducted by astronomers at the Antelope Hill Observatory, which is officially recognized by the Minor Planet Center. The asteroid is named after Aletheia, the Greek goddess of truth, who is the daughter of Zeus and one of the nurses of Apollo.

3412 Kafka, with the provisional designation 1983 AU2, is an asteroid located in the inner regions of the asteroid belt and is approximately 6 kilometers in diameter. It was discovered on 10 January 1983 by American astronomers Randolph Kirk and Donald Rudy at Palomar Observatory in California, United States. The asteroid was first identified as 1942 YB at the Finnish Turku Observatory in 1942, extending its observation arc by 41 years before its official discovery. It orbits the Sun in the inner main belt at a distance of 2.0–2.5 AU, completing one orbit every 3 years and 4 months (1,212 days), with an orbital eccentricity of 0.10 and an inclination of 3° relative to the ecliptic. According to data from NASA's Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer and its NEOWISE mission, Kafka has a diameter of 6.1 kilometers and a surface albedo of 0.231. It is classified as a superslow rotator, with a rotation period of 2,766 hours (about 115 days), which is among the longest known for any asteroid. The asteroid was named after Franz Kafka (1883–1924), the Austrian–Czech writer known for novels and short stories in which protagonists encounter bizarre or surrealistic situations. The official naming citation was published by the Minor Planet Center on 13 February 1987 (M.P.C. 11641).

454 Mathesis is a main-belt asteroid discovered by German astronomer Friedrich Karl Arnold Schwassmann on March 28, 1900, with the provisional designation 1900 FC. Photometric observations conducted at the Altimira Observatory in 2004 revealed a light curve featuring a period of 8.37784 ± 0.00003 hours and a brightness variation of 0.32 in magnitude. This period contrasts with earlier reported values of 7.075 hours from 1994 and 7.745 hours from 1998. This article on an asteroid native to the asteroid belt is a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

The 5th Annual Streamy Awards, the fifth installment of the awards honoring streaming television series, took place on September 17, 2015, at the Hollywood Palladium in Hollywood, California. The event was hosted by YouTube stars Grace Helbig and Tyler Oakley and was broadcast live on VH1 while simultaneously livestreamed online, marking the first time the Streamy Awards were televised.[2][3][4] Several new award categories were introduced, including Social Video awards for content on Instagram, Snapchat, and Vine, subject categories such as Lifestyle and Documentary or Investigative, and Breakout Creator and Breakthrough Artist to recognize emerging creators.[5] Nominees were announced on August 12, 2015,[9][10] with finalists for the Audience Choice Award categories revealed on September 3.[11][12] On September 14, 35 of the award categories were unveiled during the Official Streamys Nominee Reception at the YouTube Space LA,[13] while the remaining nine "marquee categories" were announced during the main ceremony on September 17.[3][14] Winners were selected by the Streamys Blue Ribbon Panel, except for the Audience Choice awards, which were determined by public vote.[5] Rae Votta of The Daily Dot highlighted the unique and creative video segments introducing each award category, produced by online content creators, and noted that the strict runtime due to the televised format improved the show's flow compared to prior years.[3] The musical performances received positive reviews, with Future's performance of "March Madness" being particularly praised by writers from Spin, Vulture, MTV News, and Vice,[6][16][17][18] and Hailee Steinfeld's performance receiving acclaim from Teen Vogue.[19] Votta described the performances as "flashy and impressive" but felt they were disconnected from YouTube and online content creation.[3] Deepa Lakshmin of MTV News lauded Lilly Singh's acceptance speech, in which she credited Google and YouTube for featuring a brown girl on a billboard, calling it "badass" and especially meaningful for Indian fans of Singh's.[20] Social media reception was overwhelmingly positive, with analysis by social TV platform Canvs—using Nielsen Twitter TV ratings—showing that 41.5% of reaction tweets expressed "love" and 16.2% expressed "congrats."[1] The show was also recognized as the leading social non-sports program on television on the day it aired.[21]

61 Danaë is a stony (S-type) asteroid located in the outer asteroid belt's background population, with a diameter of approximately 84 kilometers. It was discovered by French astronomer Hermann Goldschmidt on 9 September 1860 from his balcony in Paris, France. Goldschmidt was ill at the time and asked his colleague Robert Luther to name the asteroid, who named it after Danaë, the mother of Perseus in Greek mythology. Danaë holds the distinction of being the first asteroid to feature a diacritical character in its official name. The asteroid orbits the Sun with a period of 5.15 years and rotates once every 11.45 hours. A 1985 study of lightcurve data indicated that Danaë might have a moon; if it does, the main body would be an ellipsoid measuring 85 km × 80 km × 75 km (53 mi × 50 mi × 47 mi), and the moon would orbit 101 kilometers (63 mi) away, measuring 55 km × 30 km × 30 km (34 mi × 19 mi × 19 mi). Both the main body and the moon have a density of 1.1 g/cm³.

66 Maja is a carbonaceous background asteroid located in the central regions of the asteroid belt, with a diameter of approximately 71 kilometers. It was discovered on 9 April 1861 by American astronomer Horace Tuttle at the Harvard College Observatory in Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States. The asteroid is named after Maia from Greek mythology, who is one of the Seven Sisters of the Pleiades and the mother of Hermes (Mercury), daughter of Atlas and Pleione. Maja belongs to the main belt's background population and orbits the Sun at a distance of 2.2–3.1 AU, completing one orbit every 4 years and 4 months (1,571 days) with a semi-major axis of 2.65 AU. Its orbit has an eccentricity of 0.17 and an inclination of 3° relative to the ecliptic. The observation arc for Maja begins at the Harvard Observatory, one night after its discovery. In the Tholen classification, Maja is a carbonaceous C-type asteroid, while in the SMASS classification, it is categorized as a "hydrated" carbonaceous subtype (Ch). Rotational lightcurves of Maja have been studied since 1988; analysis of a high-quality lightcurve by French amateur astronomers Maurice Audejean and Jérôme Caron from February 2011 yielded a rotation period of 9.73509 hours and a brightness amplitude of 0.25 magnitude (U=3). A modeled lightcurve from 2016, based on photometric data, confirmed a sidereal period of 9.73570 hours and identified two spin axes at (49.0°, −70.0°) and (225.0°, −68.0°) in ecliptic coordinates. Infrared surveys by IRAS, Akari, and NEOWISE indicate that Maja has a diameter between 62.87 and 82.28 kilometers and a surface albedo between 0.03 and 0.0759. The Collaborative Asteroid Lightcurve Link uses IRAS data, adopting an albedo of 0.0618 and a diameter of 71.82 kilometers based on an absolute magnitude of 9.36. The naming was proposed by Harvard's former president, J. Quincy, and officially cited in Paul Herget's *The Names of the Minor Planets* in 1955 (H 10). The asteroids 130 Elektra, 233 Asterope, and 1051 Merope were also named after the Seven Sisters, raising a minor concern in 1861 by George Phillips Bond, the observatory director, because these names were already used for some of the brightest stars in the Pleiades constellation in Taurus. As of now, no spacecraft has visited Maja. Although a flyby of Maja was initially planned for March 1997 during the Cassini–Huygens mission's departure from the inner solar system, delays in the launch—moved from April 1996 to October 1997—eliminated this possibility. Instead, Cassini-Huygens passed by asteroid 2685 Masursky on 23 January 2000.

Arthur Wallis Myers CBE (24 July 1878 – 17 June 1939) was an English tennis correspondent, editor, author, and player, recognized as one of the leading tennis journalists of the first half of the 20th century. He was the son of the Rev. John Brown Myers, secretary of the Baptist Missionary Society, and Agnes Traphena (née Nutter), and attended the Watford Endowed School and The Leys School in Cambridge. In 1900, he married Lilian Gentry, daughter of Captain George Gentry of Maldon, Essex; the couple had seven children, with the youngest, Prue, writing a tribute to her father titled A. Wallis Myers: A Testament to Tennis. Myers was an active amateur tennis player, primarily competing in doubles. In April 1906, he won the doubles title with New Zealander Anthony Wilding at the Championships of Barcelona. He also won the Monte Carlo doubles championship in 1910 and 1921. In mixed doubles, he competed at Monte Carlo in 1909 and reached the semi-finals at the 1914 World Hard Court Championships with Phyllis Satterthwaite. In 1923, he partnered with Molla Bjurstedt Mallory at the Monte Carlo tournament and also won the doubles title at the South of France Championships. He served as captain of British tennis teams on tour in Europe, South Africa, and India. Myers began editing the Ayers Lawn Tennis Almanack in 1908 and became the lawn tennis correspondent for The Daily Telegraph the following year, a position he held until his death in 1939. He also served as lawn tennis editor of The Field and authored several books on tennis, including a biography of four-time Wimbledon champion Anthony Wilding, who died in the First World War. During the war, Myers worked in the Ministry of Information. In 1924, he founded the International Lawn Tennis Club of Great Britain with Lord Balfour, former Prime Minister and later a Member of the Cabinet, as its first President. Myers was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 1920 New Year Honours, dated 30 March 1920, for his work at the Ministry of Information. He was appointed Chevalier (Knight) of the Legion of Honour by French President Paul Doumer on 29 April 1932 for his service to the game of tennis.

The American Chemical Society Award in Pure Chemistry is given each year by the American Chemical Society (ACS) to honor and promote fundamental research in pure chemistry conducted in North America by young men and women. "Young" is defined as individuals born within 35 years of the award ceremony, which occurs during the ACS Spring meeting. To qualify, a nominee must have demonstrated research of exceptional quality during the early stages of their career, with special emphasis on independence of thought and originality. The award was first presented in 1931, with Linus Pauling named as the first recipient. It is jointly sponsored by the Alpha Chi Sigma fraternity and the Alpha Chi Sigma Educational Foundation.

Aabria Iyengar (née Lipscomb; born May 11, 1985) is an American web series actress known primarily for tabletop role-playing game anthologies, streams, and podcasts. She is one of the creator-owners of the actual play podcast Worlds Beyond Number, which premiered in March 2023 and ranked in Patreon's top twenty accounts within a month. Iyengar served as the Dungeon Master (DM) for the first season of Exandria Unlimited and was the DM for two actual play anthology web series in 2021: Misfits and Magic (the tenth season of Dimension 20) and the first season of Exandria Unlimited, making her the first Critical Role DM after Matthew Mercer outside of one-shots. She has been both a player and a Game Master for multiple seasons of Dimension 20 and a guest DM on The Adventure Zone. Iyengar joined the main cast of Critical Role as a player in the fourth campaign, which premiered in October 2025, and also joined the third campaign as a guest star playing as gnome cleric Deanna in March 2023. In November 2023, she became the game master for the third chapter of Candela Obscura. She returned to Dimension 20 as the gamemaster for Burrow's End in 2023 and for the second season of Misfits and Magic in 2024, the first Side Quest campaign to receive a sequel season. In 2022, she appeared as gamemaster on Dimension 20: A Court of Fey & Flowers and joined the cast of the Vampire: The Masquerade web series NY by Night, playing as Margot "Fuego" Walker. In 2025, she reprised her player role in The Twenty-Sided Tavern and acted as the show's first guest Dungeon Master, also guest starring during the U.S. national tour in Chicago. Following a delay in filming the third season of NY by Night, Iyengar and other cast members formed Project Ghostlight to create independent, non-official World of Darkness actual plays; she stars in Private Nightmares, the group's first show, which premiered in March 2025. Iyengar contributed to the Critical Role sourcebook Tal'Dorei Campaign Setting Reborn (2022) and wrote a short story in the anthology Critical Role: Vox Machina–Stories Untold (2025). She is the writer, with artist Mari Costa, on the comic series The Fade, with the first issue published by Boom! Studios in November 2024. Born Aabria Lipscomb on May 11, 1985, she attended the University of Iowa, where she was a member of their Division I volleyball team, and the University of California, Los Angeles, where she competed for the UCLA Bruins track and field team. Iyengar first played Dungeons & Dragons in 2015 or 2016 when invited to her now husband's board game group and was given a cleric character sheet to play. Wired noted that she was often the only woman or person of color at the table and faced questioning and harassment, which she now addresses as a DM to ensure players do not face similar challenges. In April 2023, WizKids announced a new miniature boxed set of Exandria Unlimited characters including a figurine of Iyengar. She also appeared as both a player and as the Dungeon Master in multiple actual play podcasts between 2018 and 2020 on the Happy Jack's RPG Network. Iyengar was originally a guest player, acting as Laura Bennett, in the actual play web series Kollok: 1991 on the Hyper RPG Twitch channel before joining the main cast in the second season in 2019. In 2022, she reprised her role in the sequel set 30 years after the first show – Kollok was broadcast on AMC Networks' FearHQ Twitch channel. Iyengar has been part of the main cast, playing as Koseh, for Into the Mother Lands since 2020. She was the former chief marketing officer for the dice-maker Dice Envy. In Game Changer's seventh season, Vic Michaelis and Iyengar were elected as honorary presidents of Dropout. Chase Carter of Dicebreaker stated that both of her 2021 appearances were hits, leading many to clamor for more, and Christian Hoffer of ComicBook.com highlighted her fantastic storytelling and rapport with players. Carter also noted that Iyengar has become a household name in tabletop actual play, with her fame being a welcome change as a Black woman gaining respect and excitement in a historically white hobby. Iyengar gave the Storytime keynote at the 2021 PAX Unplugged. She also participated in Roll20 series using the Strixhaven: A Curriculum of Chaos module, appeared in vignette mini-episodes and spin-off one-shots, and contributed to a Patreon exclusive prequel podcast for The Wizard, the Witch, and the Wild One. All of these are Patreon exclusive.

Aaron Leo Brody (August 23, 1930 – July 26, 2021) was an American food scientist known for developing innovations in food processing and packaging. He created the first frozen fish sticks in the 1950s and, while working at Mars, Incorporated, introduced Starburst to the United States. Brody was born in Boston, Massachusetts, as the elder of two children to Nathan Brozozek and Lillian Gorman, Jewish immigrants from Poland; his father’s name was Americanized to Brody upon entry through Ellis Island. He attended Solomon-Lewenburgh Junior High School and then Boston English School in 1947. Brody entered the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1947, earning a B.S. in Food Technology in 1951. He worked as an illustrator for the MIT school newspaper, primarily using pen on paper to depict sports figures. He was drafted into the Korean War and served from 1952 to 1954 at Fort Pickett in Blackstone, Virginia, where he reported on wounded soldiers returning from the war as a newspaper correspondent. After his military service, he pursued a graduate degree in the Food Packaging Department at MIT, earning a Ph.D. in 1957 under Bernard E. Proctor, a prominent food scientist involved in early food irradiation research and the chair of the MIT Food Technology Department. His work, "Masticatory Properties of Foods by the Strain Gage Denture Tenderometer," was featured in Life magazine on October 29, 1956, with a full-page illustration of the machine chewing mozzarella cheese; the device is on display at the MIT Museum and enabled food manufacturers to control product qualities for process design. Brody later earned an M.B.A. from Northeastern University in 1970. While still in school, he began working at the Birdseye Fisheries Lab Division of General Foods in 1951, contributing to the development of the first frozen precooked foods, including fish sticks. As a graduate student, he worked part-time at Raytheon Manufacturing Company, where he helped develop the first microwave oven, enabling microwave cooking, heating, and browning of foods. After completing his graduate studies, he joined the Whirlpool Corporation in Benton Harbor, Michigan, where he led the development of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP), invented an odor control system for refrigerators, a thermoelectric refrigerator/freezer, the Total Environmental Control “Tectrol” controlled atmosphere process for food preservation, a progenitor of MAP for fresh-cut vegetables, and radiation pasteurization of foods. He also patented an apparatus and method for storing perishable animal and plant materials, as well as non-food materials. At Mars, Inc.’s M&M Candies Division, Brody developed commercial confectionery products including Starburst and Pop Rocks; his team adapted the British candy Opal Fruits into M&M Fruit Chewies, which were later renamed Starburst due to the connotation of M&M’s with chocolate. At Mead Packaging, he invented the Crosscheck Aseptic Packaging System for high-acid fluid foods like juices and sauces, receiving patents US4,152,464, US4,391,080, and US4,409,775. At Container Corporation of America, he led the development of the Versaform insert injection molding system and served as Marketing Development Manager, his final corporate role. By the mid-1980s, Brody transitioned into independent consulting and teaching, offering courses in food packaging and product development and marketing at The University of Georgia, MBA strategic marketing and product development at Saint Joseph's University, and packaging courses at Michigan State University. He authored numerous articles and ten textbooks on food packaging, food technology, marketing, and packaging, including The Encyclopedia of Packaging Technology, which covers packaging technologies across industries from food to automobiles, soft drinks to pharmaceuticals, and Modified Atmosphere Packaging for Fresh-Cut Fruits and Vegetables, which details modern MAP technologies for fresh-cut fruits. Brody married Carolyn Goldstein on April 11, 1953, and remained married until her death in April 2021; they had three children. He died on July 26, 2021, from congestive heart failure. In 1964, he received the Industrial Achievement Award from the Institute of Food Technologists and the Leadership Award from the Packaging Institute. He was named Packaging Man of the Year in 1985 by the National Association of Packaging, Handling, and Logistics Engineers. In 1988, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists awarded him the Riester-Davis Award for Lifetime Achievement in Food Packaging, the highest industry honor in the field. In 1994, he was the first recipient of the Institute of Food Technologists' Industrial Scientist Award for technical contributions to the food industry. In 1995, he was inducted into the Packaging Hall of Fame. In 2000, he received the Nicholas Appert Award from the Institute of Food Technologists for his lifetime contributions. The Michigan State School of Packaging established the Annual Aaron Brody Distinguished Lecture in Food Packaging as an endowment created by family and friends in recognition of his lifelong achievements. In 2015, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists renamed the Riester-Davis Award to the Riester-Davis-Brody Award in his honor. Brody was quoted in The New York Times and featured on National Public Radio and CNN. One of his NPR interviews, titled "The Weird, Underappreciated World Of Plastic Packaging," explained that plastic packaging has become an integral part of the food system, and on CNN, he described how new plastics could prevent soft drinks from falling flat.

The Abasto Shopping is one of the largest shopping mall centers in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Originally, it functioned as the central wholesale fruit and vegetable market, known as the "Mercado de Abasto," from 1893 to 1984. Since 1999, it has operated as a shopping mall. It is also renowned for being the area where tango singer Carlos Gardel, known as "El Morocho del Abasto" ("the dark-haired guy from Abasto"), lived for most of his life. Today, although located within the Balvanera neighbourhood, the surrounding area is often referred to as Abasto. The shopping center is accessible via the adjacent underground station Carlos Gardel on Line B of the metro (subte). By the end of the 19th century, Buenos Aires was expanding rapidly due to European migration, and following the demolition of the Mercado Modelo near Plaza Lorea, the Devoto brothers, who had acquired land in the Balvanera neighbourhood in 1875, proposed building a supply market. The land was situated near the Sarmiento railway and halfway between La Boca and Olivos, two key zones for fruit and vegetable production. The town hall approved the proposal on November 29, 1888, and the Deliberating Council sanctioned it on January 8, 1889, authorizing the construction of the Mercado Central de Abasto ("Central Supply Market") on a 25,000 m² plot bounded by Corrientes Avenue, Lavalle, Anchorena, and Laprida streets. The municipality permitted the market to sell fruit, vegetables, and other foodstuffs but prohibited meat sales. The former marketeers of Mercado Modelo formed the Sociedad Anónima Mercado de Abasto Proveedor ("Market Supply Provider Anonymous Society") in 1889, which purchased the land and the building rights from the Devoto brothers. Construction began after mayor Francisco Seeber approved the sale, with the first section opening on April 1, 1893, covering 1,300 m². Ten years later, a refrigerated storage facility and an ice factory were established to meet hygiene standards. As population and consumer demand grew, a parking area for horses and vehicles was needed, and in 1928, an annex for retail sales was built between Guardia Vieja, Lavalle, Gallo, and Bustamante streets. Continued demand led to overcrowding, prompting architects José Luis Delpini, Viktor Sulčič, and Raúl Bes to design a new market on the same site. Work began on December 28, 1931, with foundations and was completed in 1934. The new Mercado de Abasto covered 44,000 m² (473,612 sq ft), included railway access, and had underground parking. In 1939, the sale of meat and fish was permitted. On October 14, 1984, the central market was relocated to the present Mercado Central outside Buenos Aires, and the original Abasto market was closed and abandoned. A redevelopment project for a shopping mall was proposed in the mid-1990s. In 1996, the building was sold to "Inversiones y Representaciones Sociedad Anónima" (IRSA), which restored the facade and remodeled the interior. The Abasto Shopping Centre opened in 1999 and currently features many locally known brands such as Akiabara, Cuesta Blanca, and Sarkany, along with a limited number of foreign brands including Adidas, Lacoste, and Nike.

Abdul Bari (1892–1947) was an Indian freedom activist, academic, and social reformer who aimed to promote social reform in Indian society by educating people and awakening them to the need for change. He envisioned a free India free from slavery, social inequality, and communal disharmony and actively participated in the freedom movement, for which he was killed. He opposed the Two-nation theory. Born on 21 January 1884 to Md Qurban Ali as the eldest of four children, he was born in Kansua but resided in Koilwar and was a descendant of Malik Ibrahim Baya, a 14th-century sufi saint and warrior. He enrolled at the T. K. Ghosh Academy in Patna, completed his matriculation there, and later earned a Master of Arts degree from Patna University in 1918. In 1937, he signed his first historical agreement with the TISCO (now Tata Steel) management. He served as president of the Bihar Pradesh Congress Committee from 1946 until his death on 28 March 1947. He was killed by three men during an altercation at Bari Path in Khusrupur, Bihar Province, while returning from Dhanbad to Patna. Mahatma Gandhi described him as "living like a fakir in the service of his countrymen," while Congress President J. B. Kripalani called his death a loss of "India's bravest and most selfless soldier of freedom," emphasizing his complete absence of communal bias and his identity as an Indian dedicated to serving the working classes. On the first anniversary of his death, Rajendra Prasad remembered his contributions in a message dated 22 March 1948, published in Mazdur Avaz. Abdul Bari was married to Zulaikha Begum of Koilwar and had two sons—Salahuddin Bari and Shahabuddin Bari—and three daughters—Tahira, Hamida, and Saeeda. The Government of Bihar honored him by naming Bari Path and Abdul Bari Bridge. On March 20, 2021, and March 28, 2024, the Tata Workers Union, led by Sanjiv Kumar Chowdhary, president of the TWU, paid tribute to Abdul Bari on his death anniversary.

Abdul Hamid Hamidi (7 January 1927 – 11 July 2019) was a field hockey player from Pakistan, born in Bannu. He scored 48 international goals in 55 appearances for the Pakistan national team. He won a silver medal at the 1956 Summer Olympics and served as captain of the gold medal-winning team at the 1960 Summer Olympics. After retiring from professional play, he managed the national team during the 1966 and 1970 Asian Games and held the position of secretary general of the Pakistan Hockey Federation. As of 2017, he resided in Islamabad. He passed away on 11 July 2019 at the Combined Military Hospital in Rawalpindi at the age of 92. This article about a Pakistani Olympic medalist is a stub.
