The Art of Design is a Netflix original documentary series that showcases artists in the field of design. It premiered on Netflix on February 10, 2017. The series was created by Scott Dadich, who was formerly the editor-in-chief of Wired. The first season featured interviews with illustrator Christoph Niemann, Nike shoe designer Tinker Hatfield, stage designer Es Devlin, architect Bjarke Ingels, automotive designer Ralph Gilles, graphic designer Paula Scher, photographer Platon, and interior designer Ilse Crawford. In 2019, Netflix announced a renewal for a second season, which was released on September 25, 2019. This article pertains to an American television documentary and is currently a stub; additional information can be contributed to Wikipedia.

Abu Baker Asvat (/ɑsfat/) (23 February 1943 – 27 January 1989), also known as Abu Asvat or Abu, was a South African medical doctor who practised in Soweto during the 1970s and 1980s. Born in Fietas into a Gujarati Indian family, his father was a migrant shopkeeper, and he had two brothers. After attending local high school, Asvat studied medicine in Karachi, Pakistan, where he was involved in student politics, founded a student organisation affiliated with the Pan Africanist Congress of Azania (PAC), and hosted its cadres en route to China. He married Zorah in 1977 and had three children. Upon returning to South Africa, he worked at Johannesburg’s Coronation Hospital (now Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital), but was fired after confronting a white pharmaceutical representative who refused to engage with black doctors. He took over a small surgery in Soweto from his brother, establishing a thriving practice that treated over 100 patients daily, often on a pro bono basis. During the 1976 Soweto Uprising, he treated children shot by police, and his surgery was protected by residents of a nearby squatter camp. He opened a creche and soup kitchen for informal settlement residents and was known as "the people's doctor" in Soweto. Asvat promoted the educational methods of Brazilian radical educator Paolo Freire and was drawn to the Black Consciousness movement, particularly Steve Biko’s concept of blackness. He served as a key link between Lenasia and Soweto, breaking racial and social taboos, and was beaten and threatened by a Special Branch policeman in 1978. He received the first annual human rights award from The Indicator, a Lenasia-based newspaper, where he advocated for social mingling and immediate action against apartheid injustices. Asvat was a keen cricketer and initially supported Ali Bacher’s "Normal Cricket" initiative allowing black teams to play at white grounds, but became disillusioned when racial segregation persisted. He co-founded the Transvaal Cricket Board (TCB), which rejected "multi-racial" approaches and instead promoted a "non-racial" vision, organizing successful boycotts and growing the TCB league under his leadership. He voluntarily stepped down as TCB leader in 1981 but remained active as a cricketer, playing for The Crescents and organizing a junior league in the late 1980s. In 1982, Azapo launched the Community Health Awareness Project (Chap), which involved Asvat and others travelling across South Africa on weekends with medically equipped caravans, treating between 150 and 500 patients and delivering health lectures to groups of up to 6,000 people. In 1984, he compiled a 20-page manual on basic healthcare, distributed in English, Sotho, Northern Sotho, and Zulu, and worked with the Black Allied Mining and Construction Workers Union to expose hazardous asbestos mining conditions. He and associates visited the Vaal Triangle in 1984 during unrest to treat victims and document injuries from apartheid security forces. By the mid-1980s, Asvat was frequently quoted in major newspapers and became a prominent voice in the anti-apartheid movement on health issues, criticizing the government’s handling of the emerging AIDS epidemic in 1988 and maintaining a regular health column in The Sowetan. In 1984, he hired Albertina Sisulu, a co-president of the United Democratic Front and wife of imprisoned ANC leader Walter Sisulu, as his nurse. Despite banning orders, Sisulu was employed, paid during detention, and allowed to visit her husband at Robben Island. Despite political differences between the UDF and Azapo, which led to violence, Sisulu and Asvat continued working together, treating casualties from both sides. Asvat advocated for Soweto squatters, rushing to assist those whose shacks were threatened by the Soweto Town Council and West Rand Administration Board, often arranging emergency shelter in Lenasia or feeding displaced persons in his home. He was elected president of the People’s Education Committee (PEC) in Lenasia, despite his Black Consciousness views differing from the pro-ANC stance of the group, which aimed to enable black youth education after the 1976 riots and campaigned for African children to attend segregated Indian schools, achieving success by 1990 when 15% of Lenasia students came from African areas. During the 1986 State of Emergency, unknown forces attempted to fire-bomb his home, and eight months later, he survived an attempted stabbing at his surgery, slightly wounded in the face, with Albertina Sisulu raising the alarm. His wife was routinely harassed by Special Branch police. In 1988, a gunman pulled a weapon on Asvat but fled when a patient entered the room. The authorities planned to develop the squatter camp where his practice was located in Soweto’s "Chicken Farm" area, but Asvat refused to move unless alternative accommodations were provided. He and Sisulu continued working despite power cuts, eventually relocating to Rockville, where they remained harassed by the Security Police. On 27 January 1989, two men arrived at Asvat’s surgery, claiming to need treatment; once admitted by Sisulu, they drew a firearm and shot him twice, killing him. Sisulu sat beside him as he died, later telling his relatives that "My son died in my hands." In the days before his death, Asvat became unusually fearful, drove home on a flat tyre and told his wife he believed an unspecified 'they' were trying to set him up, and made two attempts to see his lawyers the next morning. Investigations identified Zakhele Mbatha and Thulani Dlamini as suspects, who were sentenced to death for robbery (the sentences were commuted after the abolition of the death penalty), though no money was taken, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found the police negligent in assigning a robbery motive and failing to thoroughly investigate the attack. Rumours quickly emerged linking Asvat’s murder to Winnie Mandela, as they had first met during one of his rural clinics in Brandfort, where she was banished. Asvat provided medical care for her, and she regularly dined with the family and attended parties. After Asvat’s murder, Winnie Mandela claimed he was killed because he could corroborate baseless allegations that Methodist minister Paul Verryn had molested Stompie Seipei. Media reports circulated that Asvat had examined the boy and insisted he be taken to hospital, making his death part of a cover-up. In 2018, Fred Bridgland’s biography of Winnie Mandela argued she was behind the murder. The allegations stemmed from Kenny Kgase, one of four boys taken from Verryn’s manse and brought to Winnie Mandela’s Diepkloof house by her Mandela United Football Club, who escaped and reported seeing Stompie and being assaulted. Thabiso Mono, another boy, stated Winnie Mandela accused him and others of allowing Verryn to sleep with them and accused Stompie of being a police informant, and claimed he was beaten by Winnie and the United Football Club guards. Winnie ordered Katiza Cebekhulu to file a police report accusing Verryn, requiring a medical certificate from a doctor. Cebekhulu stated that Winnie shouted, “If you don’t cooperate, I’ll deal with you,” and left without Asvat providing the certificate, which angered her. Years later, Cebekhulu was ordered to show two youths, Mbatha and Dlamini, the location of Asvat’s clinic. At the TRC, Cebekhulu testified to a "volcanic row" between Mandela and Asvat after Asvat refused to support her false allegations. The hearings were adjourned due to claims of intimidation by Winnie Mandela. Mbatha and Dlamini testified that Winnie Mandela paid them R20,000 (equivalent to $8,000) and provided them with a gun to kill Asvat, and both claimed they were intimidated before testifying. Mbatha claimed he immediately implicated Mandela but was tortured into changing his statement to robbery. Dlamini’s 1989 confession implicated Winnie Mandela, but it was not presented to the court, with police justifying suppression by saying it was "at odds" with their investigation. Mbatha’s lawyers accused a group of men in combat fatigues linked to Winnie Mandela of intimidating his family during a TRC hearing. Winnie Mandela’s lawyer exposed inconsistencies in the testimonies. When Albertina Sisulu testified, she failed to confirm an appointment card placing Winnie Mandela at the surgery on the morning of the killing, claiming to have forgotten the details, and when questioned about not wanting to be remembered as having implicated a comrade, she denied it. Thabiso Mono stated he saw Winnie Mandela assaulting the boys with fists and sjamboks. During her own testimony, Madikizela-Mandela denied the allegations. The TRC’s final report stated it could not verify Winnie Mandela’s involvement, criticized the police for quickly concluding the motive was robbery and for failing to investigate the connection between Cebekhulu and Dlamini’s accounts, and deemed Mbatha and Dlamini’s testimonies not credible. In January 2018, prior to Winnie Mandela’s death, ANC MP Mandla Mandela, Nelson Mandela’s grandson by Evelyn Mase, called for a probe into Winnie Mandela’s role in the Asvat and Seipei murders. Asvat was buried the day after his death in accordance with Muslim rites at Avalon Cemetery. Thousands of people, both African and Indian, attended the funeral, with marchers toyi-toyied and singing struggle songs. Apartheid police attempting to seize Azapo banners were driven off by Lenasia residents, and many women were present. The section of the R554 road linking Soweto to Lenasia was renamed Abu Baker Asvat Drive by the post-apartheid government. A junior cricket tournament was instituted in his memory in 2002. In 2021, he was awarded the Order of Luthuli in Silver by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

The Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves of 1807 (2 Stat. 426, enacted March 2, 1807) is a United States federal law that bans the importation of enslaved people into the United States, taking effect on January 1, 1808—the earliest date allowed by the U.S. Constitution. President Thomas Jefferson advocated for the law, calling for its enactment in his 1806 State of the Union Address, and had supported the idea since the 1770s. The law built upon earlier efforts, including the Slave Trade Act of 1794, which prohibited American ships from participating in the international slave trade, and the 1800 Act, which banned U.S. citizens from investing in or working on slave-trading ships. The 1807 law went further by criminalizing the importation of slaves from abroad, even on foreign vessels. It did not affect the domestic slave trade, which grew in importance after the end of imported slaves, and some smuggling continued. The law applied only to importation and exportation of enslaved people, not internal trade between states. Article 1, Section 9 of the Constitution had protected states' participation in the Atlantic slave trade for twenty years, and this provision could not be altered by constitutional amendment, meaning federal prohibition could only begin on January 1, 1808. While all Thirteen Colonies had banned the international slave trade during the American Revolution, some states later reopened it: North Carolina banned imports in 1794 and strengthened the ban in 1795; Georgia allowed the trade until 1798; and South Carolina reopened the trade in December 1803, importing 39,075 enslaved people between 1804 and 1808. By 1807, only South Carolina allowed the Atlantic slave trade. The Migration or Importation of such Persons as any of the States now existing shall think proper to admit, shall not be prohibited by the Congress prior to the Year one thousand eight hundred and eight, but a tax or duty may be imposed on such Importation, not exceeding ten dollars for each Person. Historians estimate that up to 50,000 enslaved people were illegally imported after 1808, mostly through Spanish Florida and Texas, and South Carolina Governor Henry Middleton estimated 13,000 smuggled African slaves arrived annually in 1819. The 1808 law spurred demand for fast vessels, with records indicating seven slavers were regularly fitted out in New York as late as 1859 and many more in major ports. In 1820, slave trading became a capital offense, with 74 cases prosecuted between 1837 and 1860, though few captains were convicted and only Nathaniel Gordon, hanged in 1862, was executed. After 1808, many Americans continued the slave trade by transporting Africans to Cuba, with nearly one-third of all slave ships between 1808 and 1860 owned by American merchants or built and outfitted in American ports, and it is possible U.S. citizens transported twice as many Africans to Cuba and Brazil as to U.S. ports. The U.S. Navy delayed anti-slaving patrols, only gaining authority in 1820, and enforcement was sporadic and ineffective; U.S. ships falsely flew the American flag to evade British patrols, and the first U.S. warship sent to intercept slavers was the USS Cyane, which arrested 11 American slavers in 1820–1821. No further patrols occurred until 1842, when they were limited by political pressure from slave-owning states. The Atlantic slave trade was not fully ended until the U.S. Civil War, when American-built and -managed ships were barred from operating. In the South, the Fire-Eaters—pro-slavery extremists—called for repealing the 1807 law and legalizing the international slave trade, viewing it as a way to assert the morality of slavery, drive down slave prices, balance Northern immigration, and maintain Southern congressional representation. They believed that if slavery was morally acceptable, then the slave trade must be too, a view that alarmed even pro-slavery figures like former President John Tyler, who condemned the proposal. As cotton prices rose in the 1850s, demand for enslaved labor increased, leading to calls to reopen the trade to meet demand or lower prices. While some Southerners opposed the idea, the general sentiment supported reopening the trade as a logical extension of pro-slavery ideology. Conventions of Southern planters repeatedly urged the re-opening, but such efforts failed in Congress, and state attempts to allow the importation of "apprentices" from Africa were unsuccessful. When repeal failed, some ignored the law, with notable cases including the smuggling of enslaved people aboard the Wanderer and the Clotilda.

Adolfo Alsina Maza (January 4, 1829 – December 29, 1877) was an Argentine lawyer and Unitarian politician, one of the founders of the Autonomist Party and the National Autonomist Party. Born in Buenos Aires, he was the son of Unitarian politician Valentín Alsina and Antonia Maza, daughter of Manuel Vicente Maza. When Juan Manuel de Rosas became Governor of Buenos Aires Province for the second time in 1835, Alsina moved to Montevideo, Uruguay, where he began his law studies. After the Battle of Caseros in 1852, his family returned to Argentina, and his father was appointed Minister by President Vicente López y Planes. Alsina completed law school and joined the Unitarian army during the civil war. In 1860, following the Battle of Pavón and the National Union Pact, he participated in the commission responsible for the 1860 constitution reform and was elected a deputy in 1862. When federalisation, supported by Bartolomé Mitre, was discussed in the Chamber of Deputies, Alsina caused a split in the Partido Unitario and founded the Partido Autonomista. In 1866, he was elected governor of the Buenos Aires Province; although he considered running for president, he withdrew after realizing he lacked support from most of the province. Domingo Sarmiento was elected president and named Alsina his vice-president. Upon Sarmiento’s presidency ending in 1874, Alsina joined Nicolás Avellaneda to establish the Partido Autonomista Nacional, through which Avellaneda became president and appointed Alsina Minister of War and Navy. In late 1875, Native Americans of Patagonia and the Pampas, particularly the Mapuche, launched organized resistance against the expansion of the nation’s southern border, marking the beginning of the "Conquest of the Desert." The first phase involved the construction of a two-meter deep, three-meter wide trench known as the zanja de Alsina to block the movement of horses and stolen cattle. Alsina also ordered the building of interconnected forts linked by telegraph. Seeking to understand the native peoples, he personally studied the situation but fell ill in the Pampas town of Carhué and died of renal failure at the age of 48.

Adrienne Camille Nelson (born 1967) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Oregon since 2023. She previously served as a justice of the Oregon Supreme Court from 2018 to 2023 and as a judge on the Multnomah County Circuit Court from 2006 to 2018. Nelson was born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1967, and grew up in southwestern Arkansas. She graduated from Gurdon High School in Gurdon, Arkansas, in 1985. Her mother successfully sued her school district to allow Nelson to be valedictorian after the school initially named a white student with a lower GPA to that position. Nelson graduated from the University of Arkansas in 1990 with a Bachelor of Arts, summa cum laude, in English literature and criminal justice. She then attended the University of Texas School of Law, graduating in 1993 with a Juris Doctor. Nelson moved to Portland, Oregon, in 1993 to be closer to her mother, who had previously relocated to the state. She worked as a contract analyst for an insurance company for two years, then served as an attorney in private practice in Portland as a public defender with Multnomah Defenders Inc, a non-profit public interest law firm, from 1996 to 1999, and for the law firm Bennett, Hartman, Morris & Kaplan LLP from 1999 to 2004. She was a senior attorney in Student Legal and Mediation Services for Portland State University from 2004 to 2006 and served as an adjunct professor at Lewis & Clark Law School from 2002 to 2005. Nelson has been a member of the American Bar Association House of Delegates and the ABA Commission on Disability Rights. She received the Oregon Women Lawyers (OWLs) Judge Mercedes Deiz Award in 2003 and the Oregon State Bar President's Public Service Award in 2007. She has also served as president of the Multnomah Bar Foundation and president of the Oregon State Bar Foundation Board. In 2021, a school in Happy Valley, Oregon was named after Nelson. Governor Ted Kulongoski appointed Nelson as a judge on the Multnomah County Circuit Court in February 2006, to replace Sidney Galton, and she was re-elected to a new six-year term in 2012. Governor Kate Brown appointed Nelson to the Oregon Supreme Court in January 2018, to replace justice Jack Landau, who retired on December 31, 2017. Nelson's term on the Supreme Court ended in January 2019, but she was elected to a full six-year term in November 2018. Nelson is the first African-American to serve on the Oregon Supreme Court or on any state appellate court in Oregon. On July 14, 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Nelson to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Oregon, to fill the seat vacated by Judge Michael W. Mosman, who assumed senior status on December 27, 2021. On October 12, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee. On December 1, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote. On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6 of the United States Senate; she was renominated later the same day. On February 2, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote. On February 14, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 53–44 vote. On February 15, 2023, she was confirmed by a 52–46 vote. She received her judicial commission on February 23, 2023. She is the first African-American woman to serve on the United States District Court for the District of Oregon. On December 10, 2024, Nelson issued an injunction blocking a merger between Kroger and Albertsons. The FTC sought to block the merger as a violation of antitrust law, arguing that a merger between the two companies would stifle competition.

After the Deluge, also known as The Forty-First Day, is a Symbolist oil painting by English artist George Frederic Watts, first exhibited in an incomplete form as The Sun at St Jude's Church in Whitechapel in 1886 and completed in 1891. The painting depicts a scene from the story of Noah's Flood, showing Noah opening the window of his Ark to see that after forty days of rain the floodwaters have not yet subsided but the rain has stopped. Watts, who was born in 1817 to a London musical instrument manufacturer, developed a lifelong obsession with death following the deaths of his two brothers in 1823 and his mother in 1826. He was apprenticed as a sculptor at age 10 and by his mid-teens earned a living as a portrait painter; he joined the Royal Academy of Arts at 18, though he disliked its methods and attended intermittently. From 1837, he became fully dedicated to painting, and after traveling to Italy in 1843 for four years, he returned to London suffering from melancholia and painted many gloomy works. His skills were widely recognized, and in 1856 he focused on portrait painting, which was highly regarded, leading to his election to the Royal Academy in 1867—the highest honor available to an artist at the time—though he soon became disillusioned with its culture. From 1870, he gained fame as a painter of allegorical and mythical subjects, becoming one of the world’s most respected artists. In 1881, he added a glass-roofed gallery to his home at Little Holland House, which opened to the public and boosted his visibility. Despite his father’s strict evangelical Christianity and his personal dislike of organized religion, Watts had a deep knowledge of the Bible and frequently painted Noah and the Flood, seeing modern society’s prioritization of wealth over moral values as a decline akin to the biblical cleansing of a degenerate world. He believed this societal shift, which he described as "the hypocritical veiling of the daily sacrifice made to this deity," was leading to societal collapse. The painting illustrates the moment when sunlight first becomes visible after 40 days of rain, with a bright sunburst breaking through clouds, a highly stylized seascape where light rays project beyond the canvas. This composition echoes J. M. W. Turner’s 1843 painting Light and Colour (Goethe's Theory) – The Morning after the Deluge – Moses Writing the Book of Genesis, which features a circle of light but includes recognizable human figures, unlike Watts’s abstract approach. Watts’s interest in the sun as a divine symbol stemmed from his acquaintance with Max Müller, who promoted solar theories of mythology. His widow, Mary Seton Watts, wrote that Watts deliberately avoided depicting the Creator directly, stating that he wanted viewers to imagine the Creator’s hand moving through light and heat to re-create, emphasizing the power of light rather than painting a portrait of the sun. Although he had previously painted an orange sun above a flat sea in The Genius of Greek Poetry (1878), which evoked pantheism, After the Deluge was explicitly intended as a monotheistic image, reflecting the magnificence and redemptive mercy of a single, all-powerful God. The completed painting was first exhibited at the New Gallery in 1891, and accompanied by an explanatory note stating: "A transcendent power of light and heat bursts forth to re-create; darkness is chased away; the waters, obedient to the higher law, already disperse into vapoury mists and pass from the face of the earth." Between 1902 and 1906, it was exhibited across the United Kingdom in Cork, Edinburgh, Manchester, Dublin, and at Little Holland House, and in 1904 it was transferred to the newly opened Watts Gallery in Compton, Surrey, shortly before Watts’s death that year. Although Watts did not include After the Deluge in his 1886 donation of his 23 most significant non-portrait works to the nation, it was greatly admired by fellow artists and has been cited as an influence on painters such as Maurice Chabas, Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo, and Edvard Munch. Despite its omission from the national collection, it remains in the Watts Gallery’s collection and is recognized as a landscape stripped of materialism, offering a poetic, sublimated vision of nature.

The Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) is a private hospital located in Karachi, Pakistan, established in 1985 with a US$300 million investment from Prince Karim Aga Khan. The government of Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq provided an 84-acre site for the hospital at no cost. AKUH serves as the primary teaching hospital for the Aga Khan University's Faculty of Health Sciences and offers secondary and tertiary care, including disease diagnosis and team-based patient management. The hospital has 560 beds, comprising 122 private and 117 semi-private air-conditioned rooms, 251 General Ward beds, and 52 special care beds in the ICU, CCU, and NICU. It features 17 main operating theatres, 4 in Surgical Day Care, and 2 in Obs/Gyn Day Care, where day care surgeries are performed. AKUH provides a range of specialized services, including pharmacy, radiology (including nuclear medicine), laboratory, cardiopulmonary, neurophysiology, and physiological measurement. Its laboratory operates 47 phlebotomy or specimen collection centers across Karachi and all major cities in Pakistan. A new private wing was added to the hospital, with construction completed in 2020. The Aga Khan Medical Complex, situated on a 65-acre site in Karachi, was planned and designed by Payette Associates, a Boston-based architectural firm, and incorporates a 721-bed hospital, a medical school for 500 students, a school of nursing, staff and student housing, and a mosque. The complex is designed to reflect the history, climate, environment, symbolism, and spiritual values of Muslim culture. AKUH is accredited by both the Joint Commission International (JCI) and the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Pakistan. In 2017, a joint board was formed between AKUH and the Karachi Municipal Corporation (KMC) to study all major hospitals in Karachi and assist in upgrading KMC-affiliated medical facilities. AKUH is recognized as a leader in introducing new healthcare technology in Pakistan; in 2016, The Express Tribune reported that it became the first medical center in the country to introduce the Neuro-Robotic Exoscope, an advanced brain surgery technology. The hospital's geographic coordinates are 24°53′36″N 67°04′28″E (24.8933°N 67.0744°E).

The Agusta A.106 was a single-seat light helicopter developed to serve as an anti-submarine warfare (ASW) platform for the Impavido-class destroyers of the Italian Navy. It was equipped with a sophisticated electronics suite supplied by Ferranti, enabling autostabilisation and contact identification. The helicopter could carry two torpedoes beneath its fuselage. Its tail and two-bladed main rotor were designed to fold for storage on ships, and the skid undercarriage included fittings for flotation bags. Two prototypes were constructed, with the first one achieving flight in November 1965. A planned pre-production batch of five aircraft was cancelled by the Italian Navy in 1973. Data for this information is sourced from Jane's All The World's Aircraft 1969-70 [1]. General characteristics, performance, armament, and comparisons with other aircraft of similar role, configuration, and era are also documented.

Ahmed Jamal, born on 3 September 1988, is a Pakistani first-class cricketer who plays for Sui Southern Gas Company. He stands at six feet four inches (193 cm) and is a right-arm pace bowler. In October 2017, he achieved his career-best bowling figures by taking nine wickets for 50 runs against Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited in the 2017–18 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy while representing Sui Southern Gas Corporation. Jamal gained recognition by winning Pakistan’s “King of Speed” competition in 2013, where he recorded a bowling speed of 143 km/h. Ahmed Samir Farag (Arabic: أحمد سمير فرج; born 20 May 1986) is an Egyptian footballer who plays for El-Daklyeh and the Egyptian national football team. He primarily plays as a left back but is also capable of playing as a left midfielder or left winger. In June 2008, Farag was selected for the Egypt national football team and featured in the line-up for five matches during the 2010 World Cup Qualifiers, making his debut against Congo DR on 1 June 2008. He was part of the Egypt national under-21 football team in two consecutive World Youth Cups: the 2005 tournament held in the Netherlands and the 2003 tournament in the UAE. Following his performance in 2003, Farag signed his first professional contract with FC Sochaux-Montbéliard at the age of 17, transferring from Al Ahly in Egypt. He was nominated for Young Player of the Year in Africa in 2005. In 2011, he won the best player award at the Nile Basin Tournament in Egypt. On 27 February 2014, he joined Zamalek SC for a period of 2 and a half years.[citation needed]

Ajoy Nath Ray, born on 31 October 1946 in Kolkata, is an Indian retired judge who served as the former Chief Justice of both the Allahabad and Sikkim High Courts. His father, Mr. A. N. Ray, was the 14th Chief Justice of India. Ray earned a degree in Science with Physics Honours from Calcutta University and completed his B.A. at the School of Jurisprudence, Oriel College, Oxford. He began practicing as an Advocate in civil matters at the Calcutta High Court on 4 August 1970 and was promoted to permanent Judge of the same court on 6 August 1990. On 6 June 2004, he assumed the role of Acting Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court. He was appointed Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court on 11 January 2005 and later transferred to become Chief Justice of the Sikkim High Court on 27 January 2007. Ray retired from the judiciary on 30 October 2008. This Indian law–related biographical article is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Ako Adjei (17 June 1916 – 14 January 2002) was a Ghanaian statesman, politician, lawyer, and journalist. He was a founding member of the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) and one of the six leaders detained during Ghana's struggle for independence from Britain, a group known as The Big Six. Adjei became a member of parliament as a Convention People's Party (CPP) candidate in 1954 and held ministerial offices until 1962, when he was wrongfully detained as Minister for Foreign Affairs following the Kulungugu bomb attack. Born in Adjeikrom, a small farming community in the Akyem Abuakwa area of the Eastern Region of Ghana (then the Gold Coast), Adjei’s father was Samuel Adjei, a farmer and trader, and his mother was Johanna Okaile Adjei, both from La near Accra. He had many siblings but was the youngest of his father’s children. His early education began at the Busoso Railway Primary School, where he walked 14 miles each day, followed by studies at the La Presbyterian Junior and Senior Schools. In March 1933, he won a scholarship to Christ Church Grammar School, but returned to the La Presbyterian Senior School after a month due to disliking the environment. He then entered the Accra Academy in April 1933, where he walked four miles to school and passed the Junior Cambridge examination in 1934. In December 1936, he passed the Cambridge Senior School Leaving Certificate Examination, one of only two students exempted from the London Matriculation Examination Board. While at the Accra Academy, he developed an interest in journalism and wrote for the African Morning Post, a newspaper owned by Nnamdi Azikiwe. Azikiwe arranged for him to study at Lincoln University, Pennsylvania, where he lived at Houston Hall and played football. He shared a room with K. A. B. Jones-Quartey and was adjacent to Kwame Nkrumah’s room, with whom he formed a close relationship. They frequently held discussions about African decolonization, including with Ozuomba Mbadiwe, Nwafor Orizu, and Ikechukwu Ikejiani. After one and a half years, he won a Phelps-Stokes Fund scholarship to attend Hampton Institute, then transferred to Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, earning a master’s degree in June 1943. He later became a lecturer at Fisk University through Dr. Edwin W. Smith, who invited him to assist in establishing the African Studies Department. To pursue a law career, Adjei moved to the United Kingdom, enrolling at the Inner Temple in May 1944. His father leased a family house in Accra to a Lebanese merchant for £10 per year for 50 years, with 30 years’ rent paid in advance, though the deal was completed after his father’s death and signed by Adjei and his brothers. In Britain, he became active in colonial politics and joined the West African Students Union (WASU), becoming its president. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in London in 1945, Adjei hosted him at his home until he found accommodation and introduced him to WASU members, including Kankam Boadu, Joe Appiah, and Kojo Botsio. Together, they organized the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester in 1945, which was attended by W. E. B. Du Bois, Hastings Banda, and Jomo Kenyatta and is regarded as a turning point in the independence struggle. Adjei enrolled at the London School of Economics and Political Science for an M.Sc. degree while studying law at the Inner Temple, though his dissertation on "The Dynamics of Social Change" was not completed due to time constraints. He passed all bar examinations and was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple in January 1947. Returning to the Gold Coast in May 1947, he enrolled at the Ghana bar and initially intended to launch a chain of newspapers to promote self-rule, but due to financial constraints, he joined Adumoa-Bossman and Co. chambers as a legal practitioner. He met J. B. Danquah, who was discussing the formation of a national political movement, and within four days joined a meeting of the UGCC Planning Committee. He became a member of the committee and, on 4 August 1947, one of the leading members when the UGCC was inaugurated at Saltpond. On 22 August 1947, the Accra branch was inaugurated, with Edward Akufo-Addo as president and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey and J. Quist-Therson as vice-presidents. As the movement grew, the leaders decided to convert it into a political party and needed a full-time secretary. J. B. Danquah recommended Ako Adjei, but he declined to focus on his newspaper and legal practice, instead suggesting Kwame Nkrumah, who was then running the West African National Secretariat (WANS) in London. Adjei recommended Nkrumah because he had observed his organizational skills and had been assured by Nkrumah that he would return to London after gaining experience in Ghana. Adjei wrote to Nkrumah and sent him £100, provided by George Alfred Grant, the UGCC’s founder and financier, for his trip to the Gold Coast. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in December 1947, Adjei introduced him to key UGCC members, including G. A. Grant, J. B. Danquah, and R. S. Blay. As general-secretary, Nkrumah began expanding the UGCC’s reach and focused on the plight of ex-servicemen, who had not received their emoluments after World War II. The UGCC lawyers helped draft a petition to the governor, which was presented on 24 February 1948, coinciding with the Nii Kwabena Bonnie III-led boycott campaign and resulting in the 1948 Accra Riots. As a result, Ako Adjei and other UGCC leaders, including J. B. Danquah, Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey, Edward Akufo-Addo, William Ofori Atta, and Kwame Nkrumah, were arrested and blamed by the British government for the unrest, with Adjei detained at Navrongo. The release of the Big Six led to a split between Nkrumah and the UGCC, with Nkrumah forming the Convention People's Party (CPP) in 1949. Ako Adjei remained with the UGCC and later criticized Nkrumah in his newspapers, the African National Times and the Star of Ghana. In the 1951 Gold Coast legislative election, he stood for the UGCC in the Accra Central Municipal Electoral District, polling 1,451 votes compared to Nkrumah’s 20,780 and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey’s 1,630. After the UGCC’s poor performance, he joined efforts to merge opposition parties and became Secretary of the Ghana Congress Party (GCP) in May 1952. He later refused to attend meetings due to criticism over introducing Nkrumah to dismantle the UGCC. In March 1953, under pressure from E. C. Quaye, Sonny Provençal, and Paul Tagoe, he joined the CPP and delivered his first speech at a major rally in Accra. In the 1954 Gold Coast legislative election, he ran for the CPP in Accra East, polling 11,660 votes against Nai Tete’s 768, Kwamla Armah-Kwarteng’s 471, and Nii Kwabena Bonnie III’s 317, and entered parliament on 15 June 1954. On 28 July 1954, he was appointed Minister of Trade and Labour by Prime Minister Kwame Nkrumah, a move intended to include middle-class professionals in the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford, and was re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent Accra East. Following Ghana’s independence on 6 March 1957, major cabinet appointments were made by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah. After his release in 1966, Ako Adjei lived in relative obscurity, focusing on his family and legal career. In 1992, he published a biography of George Grant. In 1997, he was awarded the Order of the Star of Ghana, the highest national honor in Ghana, for his contributions to the independence struggle. He died after a short illness in 2002.

Ako Adjei was appointed a member of the Gold Coast cabinet on 28 July 1954 by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, serving as Minister of Trade and Labour. This appointment was partly due to his status as a middle-class intellectual and professional, a move seen as a strategy to attract such individuals to the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford; he was also re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent the Accra East district. Following Ghana's independence on 6 March 1957, Ako Adjei remained in the Ministry of Interior and Justice, which was split in August 1957 into separate ministries, with Ako Adjei becoming Minister of Justice. It was rumored that Nkrumah made this change because Ako Adjei, though Ga, was considered "too gentlemanly" to manage the Ga-Adangbe Shifimo Kpee, a tribal organization active in Accra. Supporters believed he was better suited to handle judicial matters as a trained lawyer, and as Minister of Justice, he managed the Land Boundaries Settlement Commission, financial and ministerial affairs related to the Supreme Court, local courts, and customary law, and foreign processes. In 1958, he was moved to the Ministry of Labour and Cooperatives, where he helped establish labor structures that continue to exist and led Ghanaian delegations to the United Nations. In February 1959, he replaced Nathaniel Azarco Welbeck as Resident Minister of Guinea and was appointed Minister of External Affairs in April of the same year, holding both positions until September 1959 when he was relieved of his duties in Guinea and replaced by J. H. Allassani. On 8 April 1961, Nkrumah announced the removal of African Affairs from the Ministry of External Affairs and appointed Imoru Egala as Minister of State for African Affairs, a position without a successor. Ako Adjei returned to Ghana to argue for a more coordinated foreign policy, believing African unity would fail without integration of African relations under his ministry, but his efforts were unsuccessful. In May 1961, the portfolio was renamed Minister of Foreign Affairs, making Ako Adjei Ghana’s first Minister of Foreign Affairs in the first republic. He played a key role in shaping Ghana’s foreign policy during the Cold War, presenting a sober image of Ghana at international forums and advocating for a Union of African States, an Africa Customs Union, an Africa Free Trade Zone, and an Africa Development Fund—proposals later adopted by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and the Africa Union (AU). He announced a complete boycott of South African goods, ships, and airlines, allowing entry only to those who opposed apartheid. Ako Adjei remained Minister of Foreign Affairs until August 1962 when he was charged with treason in connection with the Kulungugu bomb attack on 1 August 1962, a failed assassination attempt on President Nkrumah. He, along with Tawia Adamafio and Hugh Horatio Cofie Crabbe, were accused of plotting the assassination. The Supreme Court acquitted them, citing circumstantial and fraudulent evidence, with the basis of the accusation centered on internal CPP dissensions. A member of Parliament, F. E. Techie Menson, described their actions during the incident as isolating themselves from the President and riding in separate vehicles. The three judges who acquitted them—Justice Sir Kobina Arku Korsah, Justice Edward Akufo-Addo, and Justice Kofi Adumua Bossman—were forced to resign, and two other judges, William Bedford Van Lare and Robert Samuel Blay, were dismissed for protesting. Nkrumah then appointed a 12-man jury headed by Justice Julius Sarkodee-Addo, which found the three guilty based on the testimony of a fetish priest. Ako Adjei and the others were sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment and then to 20 years by a presidential address on 26 March 1965. Ako Adjei stated he was innocent and that Adamafio and Cofie Crabbe were also innocent, recounting that he accompanied Nkrumah to a meeting with Upper Volta’s President Maurice Yameogo on 31 July 1962, and that during the return journey, a grenade was thrown at the President after he stopped to receive a bouquet from a boy at Kulungugu, killing the boy and injuring the President. He was arrested on 29 August 1962, during a reception for a visitor, and remained in detention for four years. Ako Adjei, along with his colleagues, was released by the National Liberation Council after the 24 February 1966 military coup that overthrew Nkrumah. He was released from Nsawam Medium Security Prison on 6 September 1966. After his release, he completely forswore politics, dedicating himself to his family and legal practice, reorganizing his chambers, Teianshi Chambers, and resuming private legal work. In 1978, he was appointed to a constitutional drafting commission by the Supreme Military Council for the Third Republic. The last time he was seen in a high-profile gathering was during a senior citizens event organized by former President Rawlings, though his relatives denied interviews due to his health. Ako Adjei was the last surviving member of the Big Six and died on 14 January 2002 at the age of 85 at Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital, survived by his wife and four children. His death drew tributes from leaders including President John Agyekum Kufour, who declared a state burial, stating that the nation owes him gratitude for advancing democratic rule and that the era of the Big Six had ended but their legacy remains. President Nana Akufo-Addo noted that the death marked the end of the founding fathers’ era and that their vision for free democratic rule now prevails. Jake Obetsebi-Lamptey emphasized that the chapter of the Big Six has not been erased and that their experiences are valuable for future generations. On the day of burial, all flags flew at half-mast; the state funeral was held at the state house, attended by politicians, ministers, diplomats, chiefs, relatives, and sympathizers. Wreaths were laid by President Kufour, Minister Hackman Owusu-Agyeman, President of the Ghana Bar Association Paul Adu-Gyamfi, and a family member. Joseph Henry Mensah read the government tribute, stating that Ako Adjei was a key figure in articulating African unity and bridging the CPP and UGCC, and lamenting that Ghana lost a gem whose wisdom could have been fully utilized. A private burial followed at the Holy Church of God, Okoman, Dome, in Accra. Ako Adjei was married to Theodosia Ako Adjei (née Kote-Amon), with whom he had four daughters. He was a Christian and a member of the Presbyterian Church of Ghana, believing that God controls all affairs and that individuals should serve Him as tools. The Ako Adjei Interchange in Accra (formerly Sankara Interchange) and Ako-Adjei Park in Osu, Accra, are named in his honor. He once said, "Ghana is our country. We have nowhere to go. This is where God has placed us and the earlier we realized this the better for all of us."

Al-Zabadani District (Arabic: منطقة الزبداني, romanized: manṭiqat al-Zabadani) is a district within the Rif Dimashq Governorate in southern Syria, with its administrative centre in the city of al-Zabadani. As recorded in the 2004 census, the district had a population of 63,780.[1] Prior to February 2009, the sub-districts of Ayn al-Fijah and al-Dimas were part of Al-Zabadani District; they were later incorporated to form the newly established Qudsaya District.[2] The town-resort of Bloudan, located within the al-Zabadani district, is a popular tourist destination for both locals and foreigners. The district is divided into three sub-districts or nawāḥī, with population data from 2004.[1] According to the Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS), the district comprises various villages, towns, and cities.[1] This article about a location in Rif Dimashq Governorate, Syria is a stub. Sir Alec John Jeffreys, CH FRS MAE (born 9 January 1950), is a British geneticist renowned for developing techniques for genetic fingerprinting and DNA profiling, which are now used worldwide in forensic science to assist police detective work and to resolve paternity and immigration disputes. He is professor of genetics at the University of Leicester and became an honorary freeman of the City of Leicester on 26 November 1992. In 1994, he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to genetics. Born into a middle-class family in Oxford, Jeffreys spent his first six years there before moving to Luton, Bedfordshire in 1956. He attributes his curiosity and inventiveness to his father and paternal grandfather, who held patents. At age eight, his father gave him a chemistry set, which he enhanced with extra chemicals, including a small bottle of sulphuric acid; an accidental splash caused a burn that left a permanent scar on his chin (now under his beard). His father also bought him a Victorian-era brass microscope, which he used to examine biological specimens. At about 12, he made a small dissecting kit, including a scalpel crafted from a flattened pin, to dissect a bumblebee, and later a deceased cat he found on the road while doing his paper round; dissecting the cat caused a foul smell when he ruptured its intestines. Jeffreys attended Luton Grammar School and Luton Sixth Form College, winning a scholarship to study at the University of Oxford’s Merton College, where he graduated in 1971 with first-class honours in biochemistry. He completed his Doctor of Philosophy degree on the mitochondria of cultured mammalian cells in the genetics laboratory. After his doctorate, he worked as a research fellow at the University of Amsterdam before joining the University of Leicester in 1977, where in 1984 he discovered a method of showing variations between individuals' DNA, inventing and developing genetic fingerprinting. He had a "eureka moment" in his lab on 10 September 1984 after observing an X-ray film of a DNA experiment that unexpectedly showed both similarities and differences between family members' DNA, realizing the potential of DNA fingerprinting to identify individuals. The method is now used in forensic science, paternity testing, and immigration disputes, and can also be applied to non-human species. Before commercialization in 1987, his laboratory was the only center in the world conducting DNA fingerprinting and received global inquiries. In 1985, his method was first used in a disputed immigration case to confirm the identity of a British boy from Ghana, whose DNA proved close relation to the family, bringing relief to the mother. DNA fingerprinting was first used in a police forensic case to identify the killer of Lynda Mann and Dawn Ashworth, murdered in 1983 and 1986 respectively in Narborough, Leicestershire; Colin Pitchfork was identified and convicted after DNA matches from his semen samples, and Richard Buckland, initially a suspect, was exonerated. The case is detailed in Joseph Wambaugh's 1989 book The Blooding and featured in Episode 4 of the 1996 American TV series Medical Detectives, with a further mini-series released in 2015 titled Code of a Killer. In 1992, Jeffreys' methods were used by German prosecutors to confirm the identity of Josef Mengele, who died in 1979, by comparing DNA from a femur bone of his exhumed skeleton with DNA from his mother and son, similar to paternity testing. DNA profiling, based on typing individual highly variable minisatellites in the human genome, was developed by Jeffreys and his team in 1985, with the term "DNA fingerprinting" retained for the initial test that types many minisatellites simultaneously. By focusing on a few highly variable minisatellites, DNA profiling became more sensitive, reproducible, and suitable for computer databases, becoming the standard forensic DNA system globally. The development of DNA amplification via the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enabled automation, increased sensitivity, and the use of alternative marker systems. The most commonly used markers are now variable microsatellites, or short tandem repeats (STRs), which Jeffreys first exploited in 1990 in the Mengele case. STR profiling was refined by Peter Gill’s team at the Forensic Science Service in the 1990s, leading to the launch of the UK National DNA Database (NDNAD) in 1995. With automated and sophisticated equipment, modern DNA profiling can process hundreds of samples daily. The current NDNAD system uses sixteen microsatellites plus a sex determination marker, providing a discrimination power of one in over a billion. Under British law, anyone arrested in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland has their DNA profile taken and stored in the database, regardless of conviction (different rules apply in Scotland). As of 2020, the national database contained DNA information from about 5.6 million people. Jeffreys has opposed the current use of DNA profiling with government access to the database and has proposed a database of all people's DNA, with access controlled by an independent third party. His former doctoral students include Turi King. Jeffreys met his future wife, Sue Miles, in a youth club in central Luton before becoming a university student and married her on 28 August 1971. He has one brother and one sister and two daughters, born in 1979 and 1983.

Aleister Crowley (/ˈælɪstər ˈkroʊli/; born Edward Alexander Crowley; 12 October 1875 – 1 December 1947) was an English occultist, ceremonial magician, poet, novelist, mountaineer, and painter. He founded the religion of Thelema, identifying himself as the prophet entrusted with guiding humanity into the Æon of Horus in the early 20th century. A prolific writer, he published widely over the course of his life. Born to a wealthy family in Royal Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, England, on 12 October 1875, Crowley was the son of Edward Crowley (1829–1887), an engineer who retired from a brewing business, and Emily Bertha Bishop (1848–1917), who came from a Devonshire-Somerset family and described her son as "the Beast," a name he embraced. The couple married in November 1874 at London's Kensington Registry Office and were evangelical Christians; Crowley's father converted to the Exclusive Brethren, a fundamentalist Christian group, and read a Bible passage to his wife and son daily after breakfast. After the death of their baby daughter in 1880, the family moved to Redhill, Surrey. At age 8, Crowley attended H. T. Habershon's evangelical Christian boarding school in Hastings and later Ebor preparatory school in Cambridge, run by Reverend Henry d'Arcy Champney, whom Crowley viewed as a sadist. In 1887, when Crowley was eleven, his father died of tongue cancer, an event he described as a turning point in his life and maintained an admiration for, calling him "my hero and my friend." Inheriting a third of his father's wealth, he began misbehaving at school and was punished harshly by Champney; his family removed him after he developed albuminuria. He then attended Malvern College and Tonbridge School, both of which he despised and left after a few terms. He became increasingly skeptical of Christianity, pointing out Biblical inconsistencies, and engaged in behaviors contrary to Christian morality, including smoking, masturbation, and having sex with prostitutes from whom he contracted gonorrhea. Sent to live with a Brethren tutor in Eastbourne, he took chemistry courses at Eastbourne College and developed interests in chess, poetry, and mountain climbing. In 1894, he climbed Beachy Head and visited the Alps, joining the Scottish Mountaineering Club. The following year, he climbed the Eiger, Trift, Jungfrau, Mönch, and Wetterhorn. He adopted the name Aleister over Edward, believing it fulfilled the ideal of a dactyl followed by a spondee, as in "Jeremy Taylor," and noted that Aleister is the Gaelic form of Alexander. In March 1896, while on holiday in Stockholm, Crowley had his first significant mystical experience, which several biographers, including Lawrence Sutin, Richard Kaczynski, and Tobias Churton, believe resulted from his first same-sex sexual experience, enabling him to recognize his bisexuality. At Cambridge, he maintained a vigorous sex life with women, mostly prostitutes, from one of whom he contracted syphilis, and eventually participated in same-sex activities despite their illegality. In October 1897, he met Herbert Charles Pollitt, president of the Cambridge University Footlights Dramatic Club, with whom he entered into a relationship; they broke apart because Pollitt did not share Crowley's growing interest in Western esotericism, a relationship Crowley regretted for years. In 1897, Crowley traveled to Saint Petersburg, Russia, intending to learn Russian for a future diplomatic career, but a brief illness in October 1897 triggered reflections on mortality and the futility of human endeavor, leading him to abandon diplomacy in favor of the occult. In March 1898, he obtained A. E. Waite's The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts and Karl von Eckartshausen's The Cloud upon the Sanctuary, furthering his occult interests. That same year, Leonard Smithers published 100 copies of Crowley's poem Aceldama: A Place to Bury Strangers In, which was not a success. He also published a string of other poems, including White Stains, a Decadent collection of erotic poetry printed abroad to avoid British prohibition. In July 1898, he left Cambridge without a degree, despite a "first class" showing in his 1897 exams and consistent "second class honours" results prior to that. In August 1898, he was in Zermatt, Switzerland, where he met chemist Julian L. Baker, with whom he discussed alchemy. Back in London, Baker introduced Crowley to George Cecil Jones, Baker's brother-in-law and a fellow member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888. On 18 November 1898, Crowley was initiated into the Outer Order of the Golden Dawn at the Isis-Urania Temple in London's Mark Masons Hall by Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers, taking the magical motto and name "Frater Perdurabo," which he interpreted as "Brother I shall endure to the end." He moved into a luxury flat at 67–69 Chancery Lane and invited Allan Bennett, a senior Golden Dawn member, to live with him as his personal magical tutor. Bennett taught Crowley ceremonial magic and the ritual use of drugs, and together they performed Goetia rituals until Bennett left for South Asia to study Buddhism. In November 1899, Crowley purchased Boleskine House in Foyers on the shore of Loch Ness in Scotland, describing himself as the "Laird of Boleskine" and wearing traditional highland dress even in London. He continued writing poetry, publishing Jezebel and Other Tragic Poems, Tales of Archais, Songs of the Spirit, Appeal to the American Republic, and Jephthah in 1898–99; most received mixed reviews, though Jephthah was a critical success. Crowley progressed through the lower grades of the Golden Dawn and was ready for the inner Second Order, but was unpopular due to his bisexuality and libertine lifestyle, developing feuds with members including W. B. Yeats. When the London lodge refused to initiate him into the Second Order, he visited Mathers in Paris, who personally admitted him into the Adeptus Minor Grade. A schism had developed between Mathers and the London members, who were dissatisfied with his autocratic rule. Acting under Mathers' orders, Crowley, with the help of his mistress and fellow initiate Elaine Simpson, attempted to seize the Vault of the Adepts at 36 Blythe Road in West Kensington from the London lodge members. In court, the judge ruled in favor of the London lodge, as they had paid for the space's rent, leaving both Crowley and Mathers isolated from the group. In 1900, Crowley traveled to Mexico via the United States, settling in Mexico City and beginning a relationship with a local woman. He developed a love for the country, continued experimenting with ceremonial magic using John Dee's Enochian invocations, and later claimed to have been initiated into Freemasonry. He wrote a play based on Richard Wagner's opera Tannhäuser and a series of poems published as Oracles (1905). Eckenstein joined him in 1900, and together they climbed several mountains, including Iztaccihuatl, Popocatepetl, and Colima, which they had to abandon due to a volcanic eruption. Leaving Mexico, he went to San Francisco before sailing for Hawaii aboard the Nippon Maru, where he had a brief affair with a married woman named Mary Alice Rogers, whom he later wrote about in a series of poems published as Alice: An Adultery (1903). Briefly stopping in Japan and Hong Kong, Crowley reached Ceylon, where he met Allan Bennett, who was studying Shaivism. The pair spent time in Kandy before Bennett decided to become a Buddhist monk in the Theravada tradition and traveled to Burma. Crowley then toured India, devoting himself to the Hindu practice of Rāja yoga, believing he achieved the spiritual state of dhyana, and studied at the Meenakshi Temple in Madura. He also wrote poetry published as The Sword of Song (1904) and contracted malaria, recuperating in Calcutta and Rangoon. In 1902, he was joined in India by Eckenstein and several other mountaineers: Guy Knowles, H. Pfannl, V. Wesseley, and Jules Jacot-Guillarmod. Together, the Eckenstein-Crowley expedition attempted K2, which was never climbed, reaching an altitude of 20,000 feet (6,100 m) before turning back due to illness, including influenza, malaria, and snow blindness. In November 1902, he socialized with painter Gerald Kelly in Paris and became a fixture of the Parisian arts scene. While there, he wrote poems on sculptor Auguste Rodin, later published as Rodin in Rime (1907). W. Somerset Maugham, after briefly meeting Crowley, used him as a model for the character of Oliver Haddo in his novel The Magician (1908). He returned to Boleskine in April 1903 and, in August, married Gerald Kelly's sister Rose Edith Kelly in a "marriage of convenience" to prevent her from entering an arranged marriage; the marriage appalled the Kelly family and damaged his friendship with Gerald. On a honeymoon to Paris, Cairo, and then Ceylon, Crowley fell in love with Rose and wrote a series of love poems, published as Rosa Mundi and other Love Songs (1906), as well as authoring the religious satire Why Jesus Wept (1904). In February 1904, Crowley and Rose arrived in Cairo, where they pretended to be a prince and princess and rented an apartment in which Crowley set up a temple room to invoke ancient Egyptian deities while studying Islamic mysticism and Arabic. Rose regularly became delirious and informed him "they are waiting for you." On 18 March, she explained that "they" were the god Horus, and on 20 March proclaimed that "the Equinox of the Gods has come." She led him to a nearby museum, where she showed him a seventh-century BCE mortuary stele known as the Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu; Crowley believed the exhibit's number, 666, was significant as the "Number of the Beast" in Christian belief and later called it the "Stele of Revealing." According to Crowley's later account, on 8 April he heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat. He wrote down everything the voice told him over the next three days and titled it Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book proclaimed that humanity was entering a new Aeon and that Crowley would serve as its prophet, stating that a supreme moral law was "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," and that people should live in tune with their True Will. This book and its philosophy became the cornerstone of Thelema. Crowley said he was unsure what to do with The Book of the Law and often resented it, ignoring its commands, including taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his own island, and translating the book into all the world's languages. According to his account, he instead sent typescripts of the work to several occult groups.

On 8 April, Crowley heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat, and recorded everything the voice told him over the next three days, titling the work Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book declared that humanity was entering a new Aeon, with Crowley as its prophet, and introduced the supreme moral law "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," urging people to live in tune with their Will. This text and its philosophy became the foundation of Thelema. Crowley initially doubted the book's significance and often resented it, ignoring its commands, such as taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his island, and translating the book into all languages. Instead, he sent typescripts to known occultists, stored the manuscript, and neglected it. Returning to Boleskine, Crowley believed Mathers was using magic against him, leading to a breakdown in their relationship. On 28 July 1905, Rose gave birth to their first daughter, Lilith, and Crowley wrote the pornographic Snowdrops from a Curate's Garden to entertain his recovering wife. He founded a publishing company, the Society for the Propagation of Religious Truth, parodying the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and published works like Crowley's Collected Works, edited by Ivor Back. His poetry received strong reviews but did not sell well; to gain publicity, he offered a £100 reward for the best essay on his work, won by J. F. C. Fuller, whose 1907 essay, The Star in the West, praised his poetry as among the greatest ever written. Crowley planned to climb Kanchenjunga in Nepal, the world's most treacherous mountain, but the expedition, involving Jacot-Guillarmod, Charles Adolphe Reymond, Alexis Pache, and Alcesti C. Rigo de Righi, was marred by conflict, with the others mutinying against his leadership as nightfall approached, resulting in the deaths of Pache and several porters, for which Crowley was widely blamed. In Moharbhanj, Crowley participated in big-game hunting and wrote The Scented Garden, a homoerotic work, before meeting Rose and Lilith in Calcutta and being forced to leave India after non-lethally shooting two men who attempted to mug him. He briefly visited Bennett in Burma, then toured southern China with his family, hiring porters and a nanny, smoking opium throughout the journey from Tengyueh to Yungchang, Tali, Yunnanfu, and Hanoi, and daily reciting the "Bornless Ritual" to invoke his Holy Guardian Angel. While Rose and Lilith returned to Europe, Crowley went to Shanghai to meet Elaine Simpson, who was fascinated by The Book of the Law; together they performed rituals to contact Aiwass. He then sailed to Japan and Canada before going to New York City, where he unsuccessfully sought support for a second Kanchenjunga expedition. Upon returning to Britain, he learned that his daughter Lilith had died of typhoid in Rangoon, which he later blamed on Rose's increasing alcoholism; under emotional distress, his health deteriorated, and he underwent several surgical operations. He began short-lived romances with actress Vera "Lola" Neville and author Ada Leverson; Lola Zaza was born in 1906, either in late summer, September, or the following winter, and contracted bronchitis and nearly died. With George Cecil Jones, Crowley continued performing the Abramelin rituals at the Ashdown Park Hotel in Coulsdon, Surrey, believing he attained samadhi or union with the Godhead, a turning point in his life. Using heavy amounts of hashish, he wrote "The Psychology of Hashish" (1909), championing the drug as a tool for mysticism. He claimed to have been contacted again by Aiwass in late October and November 1907, who dictated two additional texts, "Liber VII" and "Liber Cordis Cincti Serpente," later classified in Thelema's Holy Books. During the last two months of 1907, he wrote more Thelemic Holy Books, including "Liber LXVI," "Liber Arcanorum," "Liber Porta Lucis, Sub Figura X," "Liber Tau," "Liber Trigrammaton," and "Liber DCCCXIII vel Ararita," all received from a preternatural source. In June 1909, when the manuscript of The Book of the Law was rediscovered at Boleskine, he concluded that Thelema represented objective truth. His inheritance was dwindling; he was hired by George Montagu Bennett, the Earl of Tankerville, to protect him from witchcraft, recognizing Bennett's paranoia stemmed from cocaine addiction, and took him on holiday to France and Morocco. In 1907, he began taking paying students in occult and magical practice. Victor Neuburg, met in February 1907, became his sexual partner and closest disciple; in 1908, they toured northern Spain before going to Tangier, Morocco. The following year, Neuburg stayed at Boleskine, where they engaged in sadomasochism. Crowley continued writing prolifically, producing works such as Ambergris, Clouds Without Water, Konx Om Pax, and his first autobiography, The World's Tragedy, and wrote horror stories some of which were published, as well as articles in Vanity Fair, edited by Frank Harris. He also wrote Liber 777, a book of magical and Qabalistic correspondences borrowing from Mathers and Bennett. In November 1907, Crowley and Jones founded the A∴A∴, a successor to the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, aided by Fuller. The group's headquarters were at 124 Victoria Street in central London, with rites derived from the Golden Dawn but incorporating Thelemic elements. Early members included Richard Noel Warren, Austin Osman Spare, Horace Sheridan-Bickers, George Raffalovich, Francis Henry Everard Joseph Feilding, Herbert Edward Inman, Kenneth Ward, and Charles Stansfeld Jones. In March 1909, Crowley began publishing a biannual periodical, The Equinox, billed as "The Review of Scientific Illuminism," which became the "Official Organ" of the A∴A∴. Crowley grew increasingly frustrated with Rose's alcoholism and divorced her in November 1909 on grounds of his own adultery; Lola was placed in Rose's care, and the couple remained friends, with Rose continuing to live at Boleskine. Her alcoholism worsened, and she was institutionalized in September 1911. In November 1909, Crowley and Neuburg traveled to Algeria, touring from El Arba to Aumale, Bou Saâda, and Dā'leh Addin, with Crowley reciting the Quran to combat feelings of awe and dread. During the trip, he invoked the thirty aethyrs of Enochian magic, with Neuburg recording the results, later published in The Equinox as The Vision and the Voice. After a mountaintop sex magic ritual, he performed an evocation to the demon Choronzon involving blood sacrifice, which he considered a watershed in his magical career. Returning to London in January 1910, he found Mathers suing him for publishing Golden Dawn secrets in The Equinox; the court ruled in Crowley's favor, and the case gained widespread press coverage, increasing his fame. Crowley embraced the sensationalist image of being a Satanist and advocate of human sacrifice, despite neither being true. The publicity attracted new members to the A∴A∴, including Frank Bennett, James Bayley, Herbert Close, and James Windram. Leila Waddell soon became Crowley's lover. To expand his teachings, he developed the Rites of Artemis, a public performance of magic and symbolism featuring A∴A∴ members as deities, first performed at the A∴A∴ headquarters with attendees given fruit punch containing peyote; press reports were largely positive. In October and November 1910, he staged the Rites of Eleusis at Caxton Hall, Westminster, with mixed press reviews. West de Wend Fenton, editor of The Looking Glass, criticized Crowley as "one of the most blasphemous and cold-blooded villains of modern times," accusing him and Jones of homosexual activity; Crowley did not mind, but Jones sued for libel unsuccessfully, and Fuller broke off his friendship with Crowley. Crowley and Neuburg returned to Algeria for further magical workings. The Equinox continued publishing, and various books, including Ambergris, The Winged Beetle, The Scented Garden, Neuburg's The Triumph of Pan, and Ethel Archer's The Whirlpool, were published under its imprint. In 1911, Crowley and Waddell holidayed in Montigny-sur-Loing, where he wrote prolifically, producing poems, short stories, plays, and 19 works on magic and mysticism, including the two final Holy Books of Thelema. In Paris, he met Mary Desti, who became his next "Scarlet Woman," and they performed magical workings in St. Moritz; Crowley believed one of the Secret Chiefs, Ab-ul-Diz, spoke through her. Based on Desti's trance statements, he wrote the two-volume Book 4 (1912–13) and at the time developed the spelling "magick" to distinguish paranormal phenomena from stage magic. In early 1912, Crowley published The Book of Lies, described by biographer Lawrence Sutin as "his greatest success in merging his talents as poet, scholar, and magus." Theodor Reuss accused him of publishing O.T.O. secrets in The Book, but Crowley convinced Reuss the similarities were coincidental, and the two became friends. Reuss appointed Crowley head of O.T.O.'s British branch, the Mysteria Mystica Maxima (MMM), and at a Berlin ceremony, Crowley adopted the magical name Baphomet and was proclaimed "X° Supreme Rex and Sovereign Grand Master General of Ireland, Iona, and all the Britons." With Reuss's permission, Crowley advertised the MMM and rewrote many O.T.O. rituals, which were largely based on Freemasonry; the incorporation of Thelemite elements proved controversial. Fascinated by O.T.O.'s emphasis on sex magic, Crowley devised a magical working based on anal sex and included it in the syllabus for O.T.O. members initiated into the eleventh degree. In March 1913, Crowley acted as producer for The Ragged Ragtime Girls, a group of female violinists led by Waddell, performing at London's Old Tivoli theatre and later in Moscow for six weeks, where he had a sadomasochistic relationship with Hungarian Anny Ringler. In Moscow, he continued writing plays and poetry, including "Hymn to Pan" and the Gnostic Mass, a Thelemic ritual that became a key part of O.T.O. liturgy. Churton suggested Crowley had traveled to Moscow on orders of British intelligence to spy on revolutionary elements. In January 1914, Crowley and Neuburg settled in Paris, where Crowley was involved in the controversy over Jacob Epstein's monument to Oscar Wilde. Together, they performed the six-week "Paris Working," involving intense rituals and strong drug use, invoking Mercury and Jupiter, with acts of sex magic and journalist Walter Duranty present; inspired by the results, Crowley wrote Liber Agapé, a treatise on sex magic. After the Paris Working, Neuburg began distancing himself from Crowley, leading to an argument in which Crowley cursed him. By 1914, Crowley lived hand-to-mouth, relying on donations from A∴A∴ members and O.T.O. dues. In May, he transferred ownership of Boleskine House to the MMM for financial reasons, and in July he went mountaineering in the Swiss Alps, during which the First World War began. After recovering from phlebitis, he sailed for the United States aboard the RMS Lusitania in October 1914. Arriving in New York City, he moved into a hotel and began earning money writing for the American edition of Vanity Fair and doing freelance work for astrologer Evangeline Adams. In the city, he continued experimenting with sex magic using masturbation, female prostitutes, and male clients of a Turkish bathhouse, all documented in his diaries. Professing Irish ancestry and supporting Irish independence from Britain, Crowley began advocating for Germany in its war against Britain, becoming involved in New York's pro-German movement. In January 1915, pro-German propagandist George Sylvester Viereck employed him as a writer for The Fatherland, dedicated to keeping the U.S. neutral; in later years, detractors denounced him as a traitor to Britain. Crowley entered a relationship with Jeanne Robert Foster, touring the West Coast. In Vancouver, headquarters of the North American O.T.O., he met Charles Stansfeld Jones and Wilfred Talbot Smith to discuss Thelema's propagation on the continent. In Detroit, he experimented with peyote at Parke-Davis, then visited Seattle, San Francisco, Santa Cruz, Los Angeles, San Diego, Tijuana, and the Grand Canyon before returning to New York. There, he befriended Ananda Coomaraswamy and his wife Alice Richardson; they performed sex magic in April 1916, after which she became pregnant and then miscarried. Later that year, he took a "magical retirement" to a cabin by Lake Pasquaney owned by Evangeline Adams, where he used heavy drugs, performed a ritual, and proclaimed himself "Master Therion," writing short stories based on James George Frazer's The Golden Bough and a literary criticism work, The Gospel According to Bernard Shaw. In December, he moved to New Orleans, his favorite U.S. city, before spending February 1917 with evangelical Christian relatives in Titusville, Florida. Returning to New York City, he moved in with artist and A∴A∴ member Leon Engers Kennedy in May, learning of his mother's death. After The Fatherland collapsed, Crowley continued working with Viereck, who appointed him contributing editor of arts journal The International, which he used to promote Thelema before it ceased publication. He then moved to the studio apartment of Roddie Minor, who became his partner and Scarlet Woman; through their "Amalantrah Workings," he believed they were contacted by a preternatural entity named Lam. The relationship ended. In 1918, Crowley went on a magical retreat in the wilderness of Esopus Island on the Hudson River in upstate New York.
