He then moved to the studio apartment of Roddie Minor, who became his partner and Scarlet Woman; through their rituals, which Crowley called "The Amalantrah Workings," he believed they were contacted by a preternatural entity named Lam, a relationship that ended soon after. In 1918, Crowley went on a magical retreat on Esopus Island in upstate New York, where he began an adaptation of the Tao Te Ching, painted Thelemic slogans on riverside cliffs, and later claimed to experience past life memories of being Ge Xuan, Pope Alexander VI, Alessandro Cagliostro, and Éliphas Lévi. Back in New York City, he moved to Greenwich Village, where he took Leah Hirsig as his lover and next Scarlet Woman. He took up painting as a hobby, exhibiting at the Greenwich Village Liberal Club and attracting attention from The Evening World. With financial support from sympathetic Freemasons, Crowley revived The Equinox with the first issue of volume III, known as The Blue Equinox. He spent mid-1919 on a climbing holiday in Montauk, New York, before returning to London in December. Now destitute and back in London, Crowley faced attacks from the tabloid John Bull, which labeled him a traitorous "scum" for his work with the German war effort; though friends urged him to sue, he declined. When suffering from asthma, a doctor prescribed heroin, to which he soon became addicted. In January 1920, he moved to Paris, renting a house in Fontainebleau with Leah Hirsig; they were soon joined in a ménage à trois by Ninette Shumway and Leah's newborn daughter Anne "Poupée" Leah. Crowley had plans to form a Thelemite community called the Abbey of Thelema, inspired by the Abbaye de Thélème in François Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel. After consulting the I Ching, he chose Cefalù in Sicily as the location and began renting the old Villa Santa Barbara on 2 April. Moving to the commune with Hirsig, Shumway, and their children Hansi, Howard, and Poupée, Crowley described the situation as "perfectly happy ... my idea of heaven." They wore robes, performed rituals to the sun god Ra at set times, and occasionally conducted the Gnostic Mass; the rest of the day they followed their own interests. Crowley continued widespread correspondences, painted, wrote a commentary on The Book of the Law, and revised the third part of Book 4. He offered a libertine education for the children, allowing them to play all day and witness acts of sex magic. He occasionally traveled to Palermo to visit rent boys and buy supplies, including drugs; his heroin addiction dominated his life and cocaine eroded his nasal cavity. There was no cleaning rota, and wild dogs and cats wandered throughout the building, making it unsanitary. Poupée died in October 1920, and Ninette gave birth to a daughter, Astarte Lulu Panthea, shortly after. New followers continued to arrive at the Abbey, including film star Jane Wolfe, who arrived in July 1920, was initiated into the A∴A∴, and became Crowley's secretary; Cecil Frederick Russell, who disliked same-sex sexual magic and left after a year; and Frank Bennett, an Australian Thelemite who spent several months at the Abbey. In February 1922, Crowley returned to Paris for a retreat in an unsuccessful attempt to quit heroin. He then went to London to seek money, where he published articles in The English Review criticizing the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920 and wrote a novel, The Diary of a Drug Fiend, completed in July; the book received mixed reviews and was lambasted by the Sunday Express, which called for its burning and prevented further reprints. A young Thelemite, Raoul Loveday, moved to the Abbey with his wife Betty May; while Loveday was devoted to Crowley, May detested him and life at the commune, claiming Loveday was made to drink the blood of a sacrificed cat and required self-cutting with razors each time using the pronoun "I"; Loveday drank from a polluted stream, developed a liver infection, and died in February 1923. Returning to London, May told the press about her experience. John Bull proclaimed Crowley "the wickedest man in the world" and "a man we'd like to hang," and although Crowley considered many accusations slanderous, he could not afford legal fees to sue, so the attacks continued, spreading across Europe and North America. The Fascist government of Benito Mussolini learned of Crowley's activities and issued a deportation notice in April 1923, forcing him to leave Italy; without Crowley, the Abbey closed. Crowley and Hirsig went to Tunis, where, suffering from poor health, he unsuccessfully tried again to quit heroin and began writing his "autohagiography," The Confessions of Aleister Crowley. They were joined by Norman Mudd, who became Crowley's public relations consultant. Employing a local boy, Mohammad ben Brahim, as his servant, Crowley went with him on a retreat to Nefta, where they performed sex magic together. In January 1924, Crowley traveled to Nice, France, where he met Frank Harris, underwent a series of nasal operations, and visited the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man, developing a positive opinion of its founder George Gurdjieff. Destitute, he took on a wealthy student, Alexander Zu Zolar, and later another American follower, Dorothy Olsen. Crowley took Olsen to Tunisia for a magical retreat in Nefta, where he also wrote To Man (1924), a declaration of his status as a prophet entrusted with bringing Thelema to humanity. After spending the winter in Paris, in early 1925 Crowley and Olsen returned to Tunis, where he wrote The Heart of the Master (1938) as an account of a vision from a trance. In March, Olsen became pregnant, and Hirsig was called to care for her; she miscarried, after which Crowley took Olsen back to France. Hirsig later distanced herself from Crowley, who then denounced her. According to Crowley, Reuss named him head of O.T.O. upon his death, but this was challenged by Heinrich Tränker, who called the Hohenleuben Conference in Thuringia, Germany, which Crowley attended; prominent members like Karl Germer and Martha Küntzel supported Crowley's leadership, while Albin Grau, Oskar Hopfer, and Henri Birven backed Tränker, resulting in a split in O.T.O. Moving to Paris, where he broke with Olsen in 1926, Crowley had numerous lovers over the following years with whom he experimented in sex magic. Throughout, he was plagued by poor health due to heroin and cocaine addictions. In 1928, Crowley met Israel Regardie, a young Englishman who embraced Thelema and became his secretary for three years; that year, he also met Gerald Yorke, who began organizing Crowley's finances but never became a Thelemite; he also befriended journalist Tom Driberg, who did not accept Thelema. It was in this period that Crowley published Magick in Theory and Practice, which received little attention at the time. In December 1928, he met the Nicaraguan Maria Teresa Sanchez (Maria Teresa Ferrari de Miramar). Crowley was deported from France by authorities who disliked his reputation and feared he was a German agent. To allow her to join him in Britain, he married Sanchez in August 1929. Now based in London, Mandrake Press agreed to publish his autobiography in a limited six-volume set, also publishing his novel Moonchild and the short story collection The Stratagem. Mandrake went into liquidation in November 1930, before the full set of The Confessions could be published. Mandrake's owner, P. R. Stephensen, wrote The Legend of Aleister Crowley, an analysis of media coverage surrounding him. In April 1930, Crowley moved to Berlin, where he took Hanni Jaegar as his magical partner; the relationship was troubled. In September, he went to Lisbon, Portugal, to meet poet Fernando Pessoa, where he decided to fake his own death, doing so with Pessoa's help at the Boca do Inferno rock formation. He then returned to Berlin, where he reappeared three weeks later at the opening of his art exhibition at the Gallery Neumann-Nierendorf. Crowley's paintings aligned with the fashion for German Expressionism; few sold, but press reports were largely favorable. In August 1931, he took Bertha Busch as his new lover; their relationship was violent and involved frequent physical assaults. He continued to have affairs with both men and women in the city and met notable figures such as Aldous Huxley and Alfred Adler. In January 1932, he took the communist Gerald Hamilton as a lodger, through whom he was introduced to figures in the Berlin far left; it is possible he was operating as a spy for British intelligence, monitoring the communist movement. Crowley left Busch and returned to London, where he took Pearl Brooksmith as his new Scarlet Woman. Undergoing further nasal surgery, in 1932 he was invited as guest of honor at Foyles' Literary Luncheon and by Harry Price to speak at the National Laboratory of Psychical Research. In need of money, he launched court cases against those he believed had libelled him; some were successful. He gained publicity in a lawsuit against Constable and Co for publishing Nina Hamnett's Laughing Torso (1932), which he alleged libeled him by calling his occult practices black magic, but lost the case. The case worsened his financial situation, and in February 1935 he was declared bankrupt. During the hearing, it was revealed that Crowley was spending three times his income for several years. Crowley developed a friendship with Deidre Patricia Doherty, who offered to bear his child, born in May 1937; named Randall Gair, Crowley nicknamed him Aleister Atatürk. He died in a car accident in 2002 at age 65. Crowley continued to socialize with friends, holding curry parties where he cooked particularly spicy food. In 1936, he published his first book in six years, The Equinox of the Gods, which contained a facsimile of The Book of the Law and was considered volume III, number 3 of The Equinox periodical; the work sold well and received a second print run. In 1937, he gave a series of public lectures on yoga in Soho. Crowley was now living largely off contributions from O.T.O.'s Agape Lodge in California, led by rocket scientist Jack Parsons. He was intrigued by the rise of Nazism in Germany and, influenced by his friend Martha Küntzel, believed Adolf Hitler might convert to Thelema; when the Nazis abolished the German O.T.O. and imprisoned Germer, who fled to the U.S., Crowley then criticized Hitler as a black magician. When the Second World War broke out, Crowley wrote to the Naval Intelligence Division offering his services, but they declined. He associated with various figures in Britain's intelligence community, including Dennis Wheatley, Roald Dahl, Ian Fleming, and Maxwell Knight, and wrote that he originated the "V for Victory" sign first used by the BBC; this has never been proven. In 1940, his asthma worsened and, with German-produced medication unavailable, he returned to using heroin, becoming addicted again. As the Blitz hit London, Crowley relocated to Torquay, where he was briefly hospitalized with asthma and entertained himself with visits to the local chess club. Tiring of Torquay, he returned to London, where he was visited by American Thelemite Grady McMurtry, to whom Crowley awarded the title of "Hymenaeus Alpha." He stipulated that Germer would be his immediate successor, but McMurty should succeed Germer after Germer's death. With O.T.O. initiate Lady Frieda Harris, Crowley developed plans to produce a tarot card set, designed by him and painted by Harris, accompanied by a book, The Book of Thoth, published in a limited edition by Chiswick Press in 1944. To aid the war effort, he wrote a proclamation on the rights of humanity, "Liber OZ," and a poem for the liberation of France, La Gauloise. Crowley's final publication during his lifetime was a book of poetry, Olla: An Anthology of Sixty Years of Song. Another project, Aleister Explains Everything, was posthumously published as Magick Without Tears. In April 1944, Crowley briefly moved to Aston Clinton in Buckinghamshire, where he was visited by poet Nancy Cunard, before relocating to Hastings in Sussex, where he took up residence at the Netherwood boarding house. He took a young man named Kenneth Grant as his secretary, paying him in magical teaching rather than wages. He was also introduced to John Symonds, whom he appointed as his literary executor; Symonds held little regard for Crowley and later published unfavorable biographies. Corresponding with illusionist Arnold Crowther, it was through him that Crowley was introduced to Gerald Gardner, the future founder of Gardnerian Wicca; they became friends, and Crowley authorized Gardner to revive Britain's ailing O.T.O. Another visitor was Eliza Marian Butler, who interviewed Crowley for her book The Myth of the Magus. Other friends and family also visited him, including Doherty and Crowley's son Aleister Atatürk. On 1 December 1947, Crowley died at Netherwood of chronic bronchitis aggravated by pleurisy and myocardial degeneration, aged 72. His funeral was held at Woodvale Crematorium, Brighton on 5 December; about a dozen people attended, and Louis Wilkinson read excerpts from the Gnostic Mass, The Book of the Law, and "Hymn to Pan." The funeral generated press controversy and was labeled a Black Mass by tabloids. Crowley's body was cremated; his ashes were sent to Karl Germer in the U.S., who buried them in his garden in Hampton, New Jersey. Crowley's belief system, Thelema, has been described by scholars as a religion, more specifically as a new religious movement and as a "magico-religious doctrine." Although The Book of the Law, composed in 1904, is its central text, Thelema developed as a complete system in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley wrote that his purpose in life was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though what he meant by "paganism" was unclear.

Thelema, Crowley's belief system, has been described by scholars as a religion, a new religious movement, and a "magico-religious doctrine," with The Book of the Law (composed in 1904) serving as its central text, though the system fully developed in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley stated his purpose was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though the meaning of "paganism" remained unclear. He also wrote in the 4th Book of Magick about a great pagan Umbral fleet ruled by Ottovius that would be passed to the great Spartan, a detail whose esoteric nature was unclear. His thought was influenced by diverse sources, including eastern religious traditions like Hindu yoga and Buddhism, scientific naturalism, and Western esotericism such as ceremonial magic, alchemy, astrology, Rosicrucianism, Kabbalah, and the Tarot. He was deeply influenced by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, though he expanded upon their teachings with his own interpretations. Crowley incorporated concepts from South Asian traditions like yoga and Tantra into Thelema, believing in a fundamental resemblance between Western and Eastern spiritual systems. Historian Alex Owen noted that Crowley followed the "modus operandi" of the Decadent movement throughout his life. Crowley believed the twentieth century marked the beginning of the Aeon of Horus, a new era in which humans would take greater control of their destiny, following the Aeon of Osiris (dominated by paternalistic religions like Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism) and the Aeon of Isis (maternalistic and goddess-centered). He considered Thelema to be the proper religion of the Aeon of Horus and saw himself as its prophet. Thelema centers on the idea that each person has a True Will that should be discovered and pursued, in harmony with the Cosmic Will. This process, referred to as "the Great Work" or the attainment of the "knowledge and conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel," was achieved through the Abramelin operation, a ceremonial magic ritual from a 17th-century grimoire. The moral code "Do What Thou Wilt" is regarded by Thelemites as the religion's ethical law, though historian Marco Pasi noted it was not anarchistic or libertarian, as Crowley viewed individuals as part of a larger societal organism. Crowley believed in the objective existence of magic, which he spelled as "Magick," an archaic form of the word. In Magick in Theory and Practice, he defined Magick as "the Science and Art of causing change to occur in conformity with Will." He told his disciple Karl Germer that "Magick is getting into communication with individuals who exist on a higher plane than ours. Mysticism is the raising of oneself to their level." He saw Magick as a third way between religion and science, giving The Equinox the subtitle "The Method of Science; the Aim of Religion." He expressed positive views toward science and the scientific method, urging magicians to keep detailed records of their experiments, stating, "The more scientific the record is, the better." His understanding of magic was influenced by James Frazer, particularly the idea that magic preceded science in cultural evolution, though unlike Frazer, Crowley did not see magic as a relic to be eradicated, but rather as a force to be adapted to the new age of science. In his alternative framework, old systems of magic declined so that science and magic could synthesize into magick, which would accept both the supernatural and an experimental method. Crowley adopted a broad definition of magick that included almost all forms of technology, using an instrumentalist view of magic, science, and technology. To Crowley, the greatest aim of the magician was to merge with a higher power connected to the wellsprings of the universe, though he never consistently defined that power—sometimes as God, the One, a goddess, or one's own Holy Guardian Angel or higher self—and ultimately accepted that the nature of divinity remained a mystery. As a result, he wrote at times like an atheist, at times like a monotheist, and at other times like a polytheist. Sexuality played a central role in Crowley's ideas about magick and practice, and is described as central to Thelema. He outlined three forms of sex magick—autoerotic, homosexual, and heterosexual—and argued such acts could focus a magician's will on specific goals like financial gain or creative success. For Crowley, sex was a sacrament, with the consumption of sexual fluids interpreted as a Eucharist, often manifested through the Cakes of Light—a biscuit containing menstrual blood or a mixture of semen and vaginal fluids. The Gnostic Mass is the central religious ceremony in Thelema. Crowley's theological beliefs were inconsistent; historian Ronald Hutton noted that some writings suggest atheism, others polytheism, and others mystical monotheism. Based on The Book of the Law, Crowley described a pantheon of three deities from ancient Egypt: Nuit, Hadit, and Ra-Hoor-Khuit, and in 1928 stated all true deities derived from this trinity. Jason Josephson Storm argued that Crowley synthesized Christian theology and Neopaganism, drawing on 19th-century works like Frazer's Golden Bough, while remaining critical of institutional Christianity. Crowley did not consider himself a Satanist nor did he worship Satan, rejecting the Christian worldview in which Satan exists. He used Satanic imagery, such as describing himself as "the Beast 666" and referring to the Whore of Babylon, and sent "Antichristmas cards" to friends. In some writings, he identified Aiwass as Satan and called him "Our Lord God the Devil." Scholar Gordon Djurdjevic stated that Crowley was "emphatically not" a Satanist, "if for no other reason than simply because he did not identify himself as such." Crowley expressed strong anti-Christian sentiment, stating he hated Christianity "as Socialists hate soap," likely stemming from his experiences with the Plymouth Brethren. He was influenced by the King James Bible, especially the Book of Revelation, and was accused of advocating human sacrifice due to a passage in Book 4 stating that "a male child of perfect innocence and high intelligence is the most satisfactory victim" and that he had sacrificed about 150 annually—a tongue-in-cheek reference to ejaculation, not understood by critics. Crowley considered himself one of the outstanding figures of his time. Hutton described him as a self-indulgent, flamboyant young man who deliberately flouted social and religious norms, shielded from public outrage by his inherited wealth. Hutton also noted his "unappeasable desire" to control organizations and his "tendency to quarrel savagely" with challengers. Biographer Martin Booth described Crowley as "self-confident, brash, eccentric, egotistic, highly intelligent, arrogant, witty, wealthy, and, when it suited him, cruel." Richard B. Spence noted he was "capable of immense physical and emotional cruelty." Biographer Lawrence Sutin described him as showing "courage, skill, dauntless energy, and remarkable focus of will" alongside "blind arrogance, petty fits of bile, [and] contempt for the abilities of his fellow men." Thelemite Lon Milo DuQuette noted that Crowley "was by no means perfect" and "often alienated those who loved him dearest." Crowley enjoyed being outrageous and flouting conventional morality, with John Symonds noting he was "in revolt against the moral and religious values of his time." His political thought was studied by Marco Pasi, who found that socio-political concerns were subordinate to metaphysical and spiritual ones. He was neither on the left nor right but is best categorized as a "conservative revolutionary," despite not being affiliated with the German movement of the same name. Pasi noted Crowley's fascination with Nazism and Marxism–Leninism due to their anti-Christian stance and revolutionary potential, seeing in them the possibility of destroying old religious traditions and creating a void for Thelema to fill. He described democracy as an "imbecile and nauseating cult of weakness" and cited The Book of the Law stating "there is the master and there is the slave; the noble and the serf; the 'lone wolf' and the herd," influenced by Social Darwinism and Friedrich Nietzsche. Although he had contempt for most of the British aristocracy, he regarded himself as an aristocrat and styled himself as Laird Boleskine, once describing his ideology as "aristocratic communism." Crowley was bisexual but preferred women, with relationships with men being fewer and mostly early in life. He was particularly attracted to "exotic women," and stated he fell in love multiple times; Kaczynski noted that when he loved, he did so with his whole being, though the passion was typically short-lived. Even in later life, he attracted young bohemian women due to his charisma. He applied the term "Scarlet Woman" to female lovers he believed played an important role in his magical work. During homosexual acts, he usually played the passive role, which Booth believed appealed to his masochistic side. A recurring theme in his writings is that spiritual enlightenment arises through transgressing socio-sexual norms. Crowley advocated complete sexual freedom for both men and women, arguing that homosexual and bisexual people should not suppress their orientation, stating that a person "must not be ashamed or afraid of being homosexual if he happens to be so at heart; he must not attempt to violate his own true nature because of public opinion, or medieval morality, or religious prejudice which would wish he were otherwise." On other issues, he adopted a more conservative stance, opposing abortion on moral grounds, believing no woman following her True Will would desire one. Biographer Lawrence Sutin stated that "blatant bigotry is a persistent minor element in Crowley's writings." He described Crowley as a "spoiled scion of a wealthy Victorian family" who embodied many of the worst John Bull racial and social prejudices of his time, noting the contradiction between societal racism and fascination with people of color. Crowley insulted his close Jewish friend Victor Neuburg with antisemitic slurs and held mixed opinions about Jewish people as a group, praising their "sublime" poetry and qualities like imagination, romance, loyalty, probity, and humanity, while also claiming centuries of persecution led some to exhibit "avarice, servility, falseness, cunning and the rest." He praised the Chinese for exhibiting "spiritual superiority" over the English and Muslims for showing "manliness, straightforwardness, subtlety, and self-respect." Critics and adherents of Thelema have accused Crowley of sexism. Booth described him as exhibiting "general misogyny," which the biographer attributed to a bad relationship with his mother. Sutin noted that Crowley largely accepted the Victorian notion of women as secondary in intellect and sensibility. Scholar Manon Hedenborg White noted that some of Crowley's statements are "undoubtedly misogynist by contemporary standards," though characterized his attitude as complex and multi-faceted. His views on women varied dramatically in his writings. He described women as "moral inferiors" who needed to be treated with "firmness, kindness and justice," while also arguing that Thelema was essential to women's emancipation. Biographers Richard B. Spence and Tobias Churton have suggested that Crowley was a spy for British secret services, claiming he joined the Golden Dawn under their direction to monitor Mathers, who was a Carlist. Spence suggested the conflict between Mathers and the London lodge was part of an intelligence operation to undermine Mathers' authority. He proposed that Crowley's trip to Mexico was to explore Mexican oil prospects for British intelligence and that his trip to China was part of a British scheme to monitor the opium trade. Churton suggested that Crowley traveled to Moscow at the orders of British intelligence to spy on revolutionary elements. Spence and Sutin both wrote that Crowley's pro-German work in the United States during World War I was a cover for being a double agent for Britain, citing his hyperbolic articles in The Fatherland to make the German lobby appear ridiculous to Americans. Spence also wrote that Crowley encouraged the German Navy to destroy the Lusitania, informing them it would keep the US out of the war, while in reality hoping it would bring the US into the war on Britain's side. Today, Crowley is regarded as a source of inspiration by many seeking spiritual enlightenment or magical practice. While his books sold poorly and his disciples were few during his lifetime, his important works are now constantly in print, and the number of self-identified "thelemites" worldwide is several thousand. His influence on magically oriented new religious movements has been deep and pervasive; understanding aspects of Anglo-Saxon neo-paganism and contemporary satanism requires knowledge of Crowley's doctrines. In poetry, alpinism, and painting, he may have been a minor figure, but in the context of occultism, he has played and continues to play a major role. Crowley remains an influential figure among occultists and in popular culture, particularly in Britain and other parts of the world. In 2002, a BBC poll ranked him 73rd in a list of the 100 Greatest Britons. Richard Cavendish wrote that "In native talent, penetrating intelligence and determination, Aleister Crowley was the best-equipped magician to emerge since the seventeenth century." Scholar Egil Asprem described him as "one of the most well-known figures in modern occultism."
