Asbjørn Dyrendel, James R. Lewis, and Jesper Petersen noted that despite not being a Satanist, Crowley embodies the pre-Satanist esoteric discourse on Satan and Satanism through his lifestyle and philosophy, with his "image and ought" becoming an important influence on religious Satanism, notably affecting figures like Anton LaVey and Michael Aquino. Following his time in Cefalù, various "literary Crowleys" emerged in fiction: Shelley Arabin in John Buchan's 1926 novel The Dancing Floor, Damien Mocata in Dennis Wheatley's The Devil Rides Out, characters in Dion Fortune's The Secrets of Doctor Taverner (1926) and The Winged Bull (1935), and Dr. Trelawney in Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time. Crowley appeared on the cover art of The Beatles' 1967 album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and his motto "Do What Thou Wilt" was inscribed on the vinyl of Led Zeppelin's 1970 album Led Zeppelin III. Jimmy Page, co-founder of Led Zeppelin, bought Boleskine in 1971, part of the band's film The Song Remains the Same was filmed there, and he sold it in 1992. David Bowie referenced Crowley and his works in songs such as After All, "Quicksand" (1971), Station To Station, and it has been suggested that the lyrics of his 1983 hit "Let's Dance" substantially paraphrase Crowley's 1923 poem "Lyric of Love to Leah." Ozzy Osbourne and lyricist Bob Daisley wrote a song titled "Mr. Crowley" in 1980. A prophetic quote from Crowley's Magick in Theory and Practice (1911) was used as the opening introduction to the video game Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996). Crowley began to receive scholarly attention from academics in the late 1990s.

Alexander Henderson Manning (11 May 1819 – 20 October 1903) was a Canadian contractor, businessman, and the 20th Mayor of Toronto, serving a single term in 1873 and a second in 1885. Born in Dublin, Ireland, on 11 May 1819, he was educated there and immigrated to Toronto in 1834. Four years later, he lived in Ohio before returning to Toronto after two years. He worked as a builder and was a partner in a sawmill business. He worked on the construction of several projects, including the Welland Canal, the Library of Parliament, and the Toronto Normal and Model School. In the 1850s, he invested in real estate in Toronto. In the 1860s, he demanded overtime payments for road construction in Grey County, which was used to politically attack him for seeking excessive public funds. From 1870 to 1874, he worked on masonry and brickwork for the Canadian Library of Parliament. He was also an investor in the Toronto Street Railway and constructed railways in Vermont, Pennsylvania, New York, and other parts of Canada. Manning was unsuccessful in his first election as alderman for St. Lawrence Ward in 1855 but was elected in 1856 and reelected in 1857. He was not an alderman in the following council term but returned in 1867 and was reelected annually until 1873. He nominated himself for mayor in 1872 but was not selected by the city council; in 1873, he nominated himself again and was elected. During his first term, he advocated for a commissioner to oversee public projects and helped establish a system to assess and collect taxes. The city controversially purchased privately owned waterworks, which divided city council and the public. In 1874, he ran in the mayoral election that returned to popular vote but lost due to public allegations of misconduct in the waterworks tendering process. He won his first government contract to build the Welland Canal and Cornwall Canal. His 1879 contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was criticized for being awarded due to his influence in the Conservative Party. A royal commission found the price was not rigged but noted irregularities in the awarding process, which damaged his ability to secure further contracts and led to his company going bankrupt in 1883. Manning ran for mayor in 1879 and came in third; he declined the nomination in 1881, but in 1884, over 5,000 citizens signed a petition for him to run. As an independent candidate, he focused on his prior experience as mayor, promising financial restraint and clean water. His opponent, John Jacob Withrow, criticized tax assessments on Manning’s income and businesses, and Manning responded by reading his assessor reports and defending the reductions he received. He won the mayoral race with support from Conservative voters. As mayor, he maintained low tax rates and was an effective city administrator. He advocated for a better sanitation system, though his reputation was hampered by associations with dishonest individuals. He also supported the creation of the Home for Incurables and called for the formation of the Toronto Volunteers Reception Committee to prepare for the return of troops from the North-West Rebellion, and formed a committee to build a monument to those who fought for the government in the rebellion, which was erected in 1895. Initially believing he would be unchallenged in his reelection, he faced a growing civic reform movement that produced candidate William Holmes Howland, a temperance advocate who highlighted Manning’s presidency of the Toronto Brewing and Malting Company. Manning supported the Daily Mail in its dispute with the Toronto Typographical Union, leading the union to campaign against him. He lost his reelection bid in 1885. Manning was active in several Toronto social organizations, including the Irish Protestant Benevolent Society, the St. Patrick's Society, and the National Club. He was an investor in the Grand Opera House and purchased it when it went bankrupt in 1876. In 1884, he hired E. J. Lennox to design the Manning Arcade and funded the construction of Old City Hall. He was a member of the Toronto Board of Trade, a director of the Traders Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and president of the Toronto Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company and the North American Land Company Limited. He married Adeline Augusta Whittemore on 6 February 1850; she died in 1861, and he married Susan Celina Smith on 1 August 1861. They had two sons and two daughters. Manning died in Toronto on 20 October 1903 and was buried at St. James Cemetery in a tomb he built for his family. At the time of his death, he was the largest individual taxpayer in Toronto.

Alexei Alexeyevich Abrikosov (Russian: Алексе́й Алексе́евич Абрико́сов; June 25, 1928 – March 29, 2017[4][5]) was a Soviet, Russian, and American[6] theoretical physicist known primarily for his work in condensed matter physics. He shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics with Vitaly Ginzburg and Anthony James Leggett for theories explaining how matter behaves at extremely low temperatures.[6][7][8] Born in Moscow, Russian SFSR, Soviet Union, on June 25, 1928, to physicians Aleksey Abrikosov and Fani (née Wulf), Abrikosov was of Jewish descent.[9] After graduating from high school in 1943, he studied energy technology and earned a degree from Moscow State University in 1948. From 1948 to 1965, he worked at the Institute for Physical Problems of the USSR Academy of Sciences, where he received his Ph.D. in 1951 for his work on the theory of thermal diffusion in plasmas and his Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences degree in 1955 for research on quantum electrodynamics at high energies. He moved to the United States in 1991 and resided there until his death in Palo Alto, California, in 2017 at the age of 88.[19] During his time in the U.S., he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2000 and became a foreign member of the Royal Society in 2001.[3][10] From 1965 to 1988, he worked at the Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics (USSR Academy of Sciences) and remained a professor at Moscow State University since 1965. He also held tenure at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology from 1972 to 1976 and at the Moscow Institute of Steel and Alloys from 1976 to 1991. He served as a full member of the USSR Academy of Sciences from 1987 to 1991 and became a full member of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1991. In 1952 and 1957, Abrikosov published work explaining how magnetic flux can penetrate certain superconductors, leading to the classification of these materials as type-II superconductors, with the resulting pattern of magnetic flux lines known as the Abrikosov vortex lattice.[11] Together with Lev Gor'kov and Igor Dzyaloshinskii, he authored a foundational textbook on theoretical solid-state physics used for decades to train physicists. From 1991 until his retirement, he worked at Argonne National Laboratory in Illinois, where he was an Argonne Distinguished Scientist in the Condensed Matter Theory Group. At the time of receiving the Nobel Prize, his research focused on the origins of magnetoresistance—the property of some materials to change their electrical resistance under a magnetic field.[12][13][14][15][16] He received the Lenin Prize in 1966, the Fritz London Memorial Prize in 1972, the USSR State Prize in 1982, and the Landau Prize from the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1989. In 1991, he was awarded the Sony Corporation's John Bardeen Award and became a Foreign Honorary Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was also a member of the Royal Academy of London, a fellow of the American Physical Society, and a recipient of the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics. His father, Alexey Ivanovich Abrikosov (1875–1955), was a physician, and his mother, Fania Davidovna Woolf (1895–1965), was also a physician; through his father, he was the nephew of the Catholic nun Anna Abrikosova (1882–1936). His sister, Maria Alekseevna Abrikósova (1929–1998), was also a physician. He married Svetlana Yuriyevna Bunkova and had three children.[6][3]

Alfred Carlton Gilbert (February 15, 1884 – January 24, 1961) was an American inventor, athlete, magician, toy maker, and businessman. As the founder of the A. C. Gilbert Company, he is known for inventing the Erector Set and American Flyer Trains. Born in Salem, Oregon, Gilbert attended the Tualatin Academy and Pacific University in Forest Grove, Oregon, where he was a member of the Gamma Sigma Fraternity. He left Pacific after 1902 and transferred to Yale University, financing his education through work as a magician and earning a degree in medicine. His thesis was titled The Genito-Urinary Phenomena of Athletes. An accomplished athlete, he broke the world record for consecutive chin-ups (39) in 1900 and the distance record for the running long dive in 1902. He invented the pole vault box and set two world records in the pole vault, including a record of 12′ 3″ (3.66 meters) at the Spring meet of the Irish American Athletic Club at Celtic Park, New York, in 1906. At the 1908 Summer Olympics, he tied for gold with Edward Cook, setting an Olympic record. Choosing not to pursue medicine, Gilbert founded Mysto Manufacturing in 1907 with his friend John Petrie, which later became the A. C. Gilbert Company. He developed the Erector Set in 1913, inspired by steel construction girders used on the New York, New Haven & Hartford Railroad; the set was preceded by Frank Hornby’s Meccano, which Hornby patented as "Mechanics Made Easy" in 1901. In 1918, during World War I, when the Council of National Defense considered banning toy production, Gilbert successfully argued against it, earning the nickname "The man who saved Christmas." He had previously contributed to the war effort by becoming one of the Four Minute Men who gave lectures to encourage war bond purchases. By 1935, the company had sold more than 30 million Erector Sets. He expanded the product line to include chemistry sets, microscope sets, and other educational toys, amassing over 150 patents over 50 years. In 1938, he acquired the rights to the American Flyer toy train line from W. O. Coleman and moved production from Chicago to New Haven. He adopted a 3/16 scale for the trains while retaining the three-rail O-gauge track associated with Lionel. After World War II, O-gauge track was replaced with two-rail S-gauge track. Gilbert was praised for his commitment to scale realism, making American Flyer trains appear more authentic. He is credited with originating employee benefits such as free medical and legal advice and maternity leave. In 1915, he founded the Toy Manufacturers of America trade association and served as its first president. Frustrated that invention was not taught in schools, in 1941 he opened the Gilbert Hall of Science in New York City, which promoted science interest and sold his products. In 1950–1951, he marketed the Gilbert U-238 Atomic Energy Laboratory, which included radioactive ore samples of autunite, carnotite, torbernite, and uraninite. In 1908, he married Mary Thompson, whom he met at Pacific University; they had three children: two girls and a boy. In the 1930s, they lived at Maraldene in Hamden, Connecticut, which included kennels where Gilbert bred German Shepherds, one of which won the Max von Stephanitz award. He also owned a 600-acre estate called Paradise, used for hunting and housing big-game trophies, and served as a venue for entertaining clients and guests at the Yale Bowl. Upon retiring in 1954, he transferred the company to his son. That same year, he published his autobiography, The Man Who Lives in Paradise. After his death in 1961, the family sold the remaining shares of the A. C. Gilbert Company to Jack Wrather, which went out of business in 1967, though the Erector trademark continued to be used. A museum in Salem, Oregon, named A. C. Gilbert's Discovery Village, honors him and includes historic structures such as the house of his uncle Andrew T. Gilbert, opening in 1989. The television movie The Man Who Saved Christmas, released on December 15, 2002, dramatizes Christmas during 1917–1918 in the context of World War I and features Jason Alexander as Gilbert; the film takes several historical liberties. Pacific University in Forest Grove, Oregon, opened a residential hall named after Gilbert in 2009.

Alma S. Woolley (October 3, 1931, New York City – December 17, 2005, Baltimore) was an American nurse, nurse educator, nursing historian, and author. She led several schools of nursing and authored numerous books and articles on nursing education, the history of nursing education, and nurses. Woolley grew up during the Depression in the Bronx, New York City: her father died after being hit by a truck on his way to a public hospital; her maternal grandmother, who worked in a sweatshop, made all her clothes; her widowed mother worked as a stenographer for GM; and at age twelve, Woolley admired the smart gray uniforms with red trimming of the Cadet Nurse Corps during World War II, leading to her selection to attend the elite all-girls Hunter College High School, which she commuted to by public transport one hour each way. At Hunter, she won the all-city Latin Poetry Contest in 1949 and graduated second in her class, then attended Queens College and Cornell University's School of Nursing, earning a bachelor's degree in 1954. She joined the Visiting Nurse Service of New York, married, and worked at hospitals including Mary Immaculate Hospital in Jamaica, Queens, and later at Philadelphia General Hospital and Jefferson Medical College after moving to Philadelphia with her husband, Arthur E. Woolley. She became a nursing instructor at the University of Pennsylvania, enrolled in their graduate program, and earned an M.S. in medical-surgical nursing in 1965, an achievement that led to her early article in The American Journal of Nursing, "My Lamp Is Refueled," explaining how and why she maintained her professional engagement while raising four small children. In 1969, after moving to New Jersey with her husband and children, Woolley became an instructor at Atlantic Community College and was soon offered the task of creating a B.S. degree program in nursing for The Richard Stockton College of New Jersey, which opened in 1971. The original program she designed was for registered nurses, R.N.'s, without a university degree, to complete a Bachelor of Science in nursing. Woolley advocated for the transition of nursing education from non-university-trained R.N.'s to 4-year B.S.N. programs or their equivalents and published several pieces demonstrating the benefits of university-based nursing programs. In 1980, she earned a doctorate in nursing education from the University of Pennsylvania. In 1981, she was appointed Director of the School of Nursing at Illinois Wesleyan University and the Caroline F. Rupert Professor of Nursing; in 1986, she left Wesleyan to become Dean of Georgetown University School of Nursing and Health Studies. In 1989, she received the Distinguished Alumnus Award from the Cornell School of Nursing Alumni Association. She stepped down as dean of Georgetown's School of Nursing in 1992 and returned to teaching and writing, retiring as professor emeritus of nursing in 1996 and becoming a visiting professor at both the University of Maryland School of Nursing in Baltimore, Md, and the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences. She wrote or contributed to biographies of nurses including Maude Francis Essig, who served with American combat troops in World War I, and Virginia Matthews Dunbar, an early advocate of university curricula for nurses. Reflecting her belief that "the history of nursing education is an important lacuna in general histories of nursing" and that "as part of public history in the United States, nursing education can cite many accomplishments in the realm of health care policy," Woolley also published histories of nursing schools, including "Nuns and Guns" and Learning, Faith and Caring. Before her death in 2005, she was working on oral histories of women who, like her, had been recently admitted as members to the once all-male Cosmos Club of Washington, D.C.

Alnham is a hamlet and civil parish in Northumberland, England, located about 14 miles (23 km) west of Alnwick and approximately 6 miles (10 km) from the Scottish border, situated on the south side of a small tributary of the River Alnham. The village lies on uneven ground, sloping from south to north, at the foot of the southern outliers of the Cheviot Hills, with the River Alnham flowing eastward through it from its source in the Cheviot Hills to the coast. The village's layout is influenced by the river. The 2011 Census estimated the population at around 245. Evidence of human occupation in Alnham and its surroundings dates back to prehistoric times, with a cup-marked stone found at Alnham Northfield indicating Neolithic habitation. Bronze Age occupation is evident through a rare bronze spearhead found at High Bleakhope, possibly indicating elite presence, and the spearhead may have been placed as an offering to a deity due to the site's remote and elevated position. Numerous cairns and unenclosed settlements are found in the surrounding area, and two Iron Age palisaded enclosures have been discovered on High Knowes. Castle Hill, a Cheviot multivallate hillfort, is an Iron Age site located to the west of Alnham, standing at 289 metres (948 ft) above Ordnance Datum, with a sub-circular enclosure and ramparts made of earth and stone, and at least five hut circles within it. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks may date from the Bronze Age. The site shows at least four phases of development, beginning with a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by bivallate and then multivallate forms. There is also evidence of Romano-British settlement and agricultural activity, including prehistoric cord rig. The name "Alnham" comes from Old English hām (homestead) and the Celtic river-name Aln or Alaunos, meaning "homestead on the River Aln," with recorded variations including Alneham (1331), Elnam (1509), Ayneham (1557), and Ailnham (1663); it has also been historically known as "Yeldom" and in the Magna Britannia of 1724 as "Yarwell." Alnham was part of the Barony of Alnwick held by the Vesci family from the early 12th century until 1310, when it was sold to Henry de Percy, 1st Baron Percy, and has remained in the Percy family since. The Church of St Michael and All Angels, a Grade I listed building and part of the Diocese of Newcastle, was first recorded in an 1184 charter when William de Vesci granted it to Alnwick Abbey; it was later restored in the 13th century and again in 1664 and 1953. The church was damaged during Anglo-Scottish border conflicts and was in a ruinous state by the mid-1800s, with a detailed 1862 description noting damp, mildewed walls, rotting windows, and fungi. F. R. Wilson restored the church in 1870, and Gustav Adolph Renwick carried out further work in 1953. A medieval cross base, 2 feet (61 cm) high and Grade II listed, is located about 20 yards (18 m) south of the church. Tower House, also Grade II listed, was first recorded in 1541 as a "lytle toure" and served as the vicarage; it collapsed in 1651 and remained uninhabitable until 1844, when it was rebuilt with new battlements, turrets, and a residential wing. It is now a private residence. The medieval settlement at Alnham is a scheduled monument located south of St Michaels Church, consisting of earthworks, a toft, two houses, a small hill, and a group of three houses and an enclosure, likely originally larger and centered on the Church. Alnham Castle, a scheduled monument, includes the remains of a medieval tower house with a rectangular plan measuring 22 metres (72 ft) by 18 metres (59 ft) and up to 2 metres (6.6 ft) high, first mentioned in 1405 as one of Harry Hotspur's strongholds, and situated on a low ridge with a triangular annex to the east and south and a well-defined lynchet bank to the north, likely representing a garden and meadow. The former farmhouses of Alnham Castle, known as Castle Farm, are now the Pennywells—two Grade II listed cottages from the early 18th century—along with a Grade II listed garden wall and adjacent farm buildings (byres, stable, and shelter sheds built between 1830 and 1840), all of which have separate Grade II listings. Alnham has historically been affected by Anglo-Scottish border conflicts, with Scottish raids during Henry VIII's reign described in letters from the Earl of Northumberland in October and November 1532, and the tower reportedly in bad condition by 1541. A 1615 survey noted the village's vulnerability due to its location between the two realms. Alnham was a significant agricultural centre in the early 17th century, with Robert Norton's 1619 map showing four large common fields, 70 acres of arable land, and 168 acres of "Alnham oxe pasture." From the 18th century, the village declined due to land leasing policies that consolidated holdings, with the number of cottages dropping from five in Seymour's Survey of c. 1756 to two farms and three cottages by 1776. Alnham Common was first recorded in 1702 and divided in 1776. The 19th century saw Alnham consist of three farms, a church, a vicarage, a Church of England school (built in 1870), and six cottages, with farming remaining the primary economic activity. The population in 1801 was 233 and declined to 205 by 1891, with the 1831 census showing 45 male residents over 20 as labourers or servants, 8 as employers or professionals, and 15 as "middling sorts." In the 20th century, the only new building was the War Memorial Hall, erected in 1921, and the population gradually declined due to mechanisation and reduced farming incomes. Alnham is part of the North Core Strategy Delivery Area of Northumberland, one of the least populated areas in England with 26 residents per square km compared to the county average of 63. In 2001, the parish of Whittingham and Alnham had a total usual population of 505, and in 2011, Alnham Parish had an estimated population of 245. 20.4% of residents were aged 0–15 and 10.2% were aged 65+, with 100% identifying as white; 68.6% were Christian, and 81.3% of those aged 16–74 were economically active, primarily in agriculture, forestry, and fishing (25.7%). Alnham is part of the Berwick-upon-Tweed Parliament constituency, represented since May 2015 by Anne-Marie Trevelyan (Conservative), previously held by Alan Beith (Liberal Democrats), and is part of the Rothbury Ward, represented by Steven Christopher Bridgett (Independent). At the parish council level, Alnham is part of Whittingham Parish Council, which includes the former parishes of Alnham, Callaly, and Whittingham. There are seven listed structures in Alnham, including the Church, Tower House, the medieval settlement, and Alnham Castle.

The site contains a sub-circular enclosure within concentric ditches, with ramparts constructed from earth and stone excavated from the hillfort itself. It also includes remains of a Romano-British settlement and at least five hut circles within the hillfort’s interior. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks, defined by a curving out bank, represent the earliest remains and may date back to the Bronze Age. There were four possible phases of development for the earthwork defences during the Iron Age: the first phase involved a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by the construction of ramparts and ditches forming a bivallate hillfort (phase 2), while phases 3 and 4 led to Castle Hill becoming a multivallate hillfort. Several trackways near Castle Hill may date from the prehistoric or Romano-British periods, and there is evidence of agricultural activity from the Bronze Age, Iron Age, and Romano-British times. A prehistoric cord rig was found on the north-west of the hilltop, and prehistoric or Romano-British ploughing has created lynchets on the north-east side. Medieval cultivation extended from Alnham village and ceased at a boundary bank on the south-east face of the hill. The most significant 20th-century structure in Alnham is the War Memorial Hall, built in 1920 to reflect the impact of World War I on small rural communities; it is a stone-built village hall with a stone incision above the porch door, and no names are inscribed because there were no village deaths during the war. Alnham is an isolated rural community, with the nearest main road being the A697, approximately 7.5 miles (12 km) away. The village lies on a north-south local road from Prendwick to Scrainwood, and from a junction near the centre, another road heads northwest from Alnham, past Castle Hill, for about 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) to Ewartly Shank, where it ends. In the mid-to-late 19th century, plans existed for a Northumberland Central Railway line to pass through Alnham, positioned to the east of Pennylaws Cottage, but the project was never constructed.

Aloha Township is a civil township located in Cheboygan County, Michigan. As of the 2020 census, the population was 937. The township has a total area of 32.38 square miles (83.86 km²), of which 29.50 square miles (76.40 km²) is land and 2.88 square miles (7.46 km²), or 8.89%, is water. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, as of the 2000 census, there were 1,041 people, 423 households, and 321 families residing in the township. The population density was 35.4 inhabitants per square mile (13.7/km²), with 670 housing units at an average density of 22.8 per square mile (8.8/km²). The racial makeup was 95.29% White, 2.50% Native American, 0.38% Asian, 0.10% from other races, and 1.73% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race made up 0.38% of the population. Of the 423 households, 27.0% had children under 18, 70.0% were married couples living together, 3.5% had a female householder with no husband present, and 23.9% were non-families; 19.9% of households consisted of individuals, and 9.5% had someone living alone who was 65 years or older. The average household size was 2.45, and the average family size was 2.80. The age distribution showed 23.8% under 18, 3.8% from 18 to 24, 23.0% from 25 to 44, 30.7% from 45 to 64, and 18.6% aged 65 or older, with a median age of 45. For every 100 females, there were 105.3 males, and for every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 106.5 males. The median household income was $34,853, and the median family income was $41,406. Males had a median income of $32,955, while females earned $22,206. The per capita income was $18,656. Approximately 9.6% of families and 13.9% of the population were below the poverty line, including 17.1% of those under 18 and 8.9% of those 65 or older.

doc_name: American Classical Music Hall of Fame and Museum
text: The American Classical Music Hall of Fame and Museum is a non-profit organization dedicated to honoring individuals and institutions that have made significant contributions to classical music—specifically, "people who have contributed to American music and music in America," as stated by Samuel Adler, co-chairman of the organization's first artistic directorate. The organization was established in 1996 by Cincinnati businessman and civic leader David A. Klingshirm and began inducting honorees in 1998. Its offices and exhibits are located in the Hamilton County Memorial Building, adjacent to the Cincinnati Music Hall in the Over-the-Rhine neighborhood of Cincinnati, Ohio. While the exhibits are not open to the public, they are accessible during certain events at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati and through a virtual museum. In 2012, the "Classical Walk of Fame" was inaugurated in Washington Park, outside the steps of the Cincinnati Music Hall, featuring pavement stones inscribed with the names of American Classical Music Hall of Fame inductees. A mobile app enables park visitors to read biographies of the inductees, listen to samples of their music, view related images, and play classical music through a mobile jukebox that activates the park's "dancing fountain."

The American Dialect Society (ADS), established in 1889, is a learned society dedicated to the study of the English language in North America, and of other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it. The Society publishes the academic journal American Speech. Founded as part of an effort to create a comprehensive American dialect dictionary, the ADS was established in 1889 by a group of American philologists when Joseph Wright began editing the English Dialect Dictionary, with the goal of producing a similar work for the United States. Its original constitution from 1890 defined its objective as "the investigation of the spoken English of the United States and Canada," a mission that has remained essentially unchanged, only expanded in 1991 to include "the English language in North America, together with other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it." Members of the Society, which has never had more than a few hundred active members, include linguists, lexicographers, etymologists, grammarians, historians, researchers, writers, authors, editors, professors, university students, and independent scholars. The Society's activities include a mailing list that primarily focuses on American English but also covers other linguistic topics. Members began collecting material, much of which was published in the journal Dialect Notes, but significant progress toward compiling a nationwide dictionary was not made until Frederic G. Cassidy was appointed Chief Editor in 1963. The first volume of the Dictionary of American Regional English, covering the letters A-C, was published in 1985. The Society's other major project is the Linguistic Atlas of the United States and Canada. Since 1991, the ADS has designated one or more words or terms as the word of the year, with the New York Times noting that the Society "probably started" the "word-of-the-year ritual." The "Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache" (GfdS) has selected a word of the year since 1977. The Society also holds special votes each year to select words in various categories, such as "most original," "most unnecessary," "most outrageous," or "most likely to succeed." Several words chosen by the ADS appear on Merriam-Webster's Words of the Year lists.

Amrita Sher-Gil (30 January 1913 – 5 December 1941) was a Hungarian–Indian painter recognized as "one of the greatest avant-garde women artists of the early 20th century" and a pioneer in modern Indian art. She began painting from an early age, receiving formal art lessons at eight and painting servants in her household as a child, an experience that later influenced her return to India. Born Dalma-Amrita on 30 January 1913 at 4 Szilágyi Dezső square, Budapest, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, she was the daughter of Umrao Singh Sher-Gil Majithia, a Punjabi Indian Jat Sikh aristocrat and scholar in Sanskrit and Persian, and Marie Antoinette Gottesman, a Hungarian-Jewish opera singer from an affluent bourgeois family. Her parents first met in 1912 in Lahore, and her mother came to India as a companion to Princess Bamba Sutherland, granddaughter of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Sher-Gil was the elder of two daughters; her younger sister was Indira Sundaram (née Sher-Gil, born March 1914), mother of artist Vivan Sundaram. The family remained in Budapest until after the First World War. She was the niece of Indologist Ervin Baktay, who noticed her artistic talent during a 1926 visit to Shimla and advocated for her to pursue art, guiding her through critiques and academic training. In 1921, the family moved to Summer Hill, Shimla, India, where Sher-Gil began studying piano and violin and, by age nine, performed in concerts and plays at the Gaiety Theatre. She was expelled from her Catholic school, Convent of Jesus and Mary, for declaring herself an atheist. In 1924, after meeting an Italian sculptor in Shimla, her mother moved to Florence, where Sher-Gil enrolled at Santa Annunziata, exposing her to Italian masters, though she returned to India shortly after. At sixteen, she traveled to Europe with her mother to train in Paris, first at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière under Pierre Vaillent and Lucien Simon (where she met Boris Taslitzky) and later at the École des Beaux-Arts (1930–1934). She drew inspiration from Paul Cézanne, Paul Gauguin, and Amedeo Modigliani, and her work in Paris showed a maturity rarely seen in a 16-year-old. In 1931, she was briefly engaged to Yusuf Ali Khan, with rumors of an affair with her first cousin and later husband Viktor Egan; her letters reveal same-sex affairs. Her early works displayed Post-Impressionist influences, and her 1932 oil painting *Young Girls* marked a breakthrough, earning her a gold medal and election as an Associate of the Grand Salon in Paris in 1933—making her the youngest ever member and the only Asian to receive this honor. Her Paris period included self-portraits, nude studies, still lifes, and portraits of friends. One of her professors noted that her rich color palette suggested she was not at home in Europe, and that her true artistic atmosphere lay in the East. In 1933, she began feeling a strong longing to return to India, which she did at the end of 1934. In May 1935, she met English journalist Malcolm Muggeridge, with whom she had a brief intense affair and painted a portrait now held by the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. By September 1935, she saw him off for England. In 1936, at the behest of art collector and critic Karl Khandalavala, she traveled to India to explore her Indian roots, where she was deeply influenced by Mughal and Pahari schools of painting and the Ajanta cave paintings. In 1937, she toured South India and produced her South Indian trilogy—*Bride's Toilet*, *Brahmacharis*, and *South Indian Villagers Going to Market*—reflecting her passion for color and empathy for impoverished subjects. She declared, "I can only paint in India. Europe belongs to Picasso, Matisse, Braque.... India belongs only to me," marking a shift in her artistic mission to depict Indian life. Her work during this phase, including *Village Scene*, *In the Ladies' Enclosure*, and *Siesta*, showed influences from miniature and Pahari schools. Though acclaimed by critics like Karl Khandalavala and Charles Fabri as the greatest painter of the century, her paintings found few buyers; the Nawab Salar Jung of Hyderabad returned them, and the Maharaja of Mysore chose Raja Ravi Varma's works. A Congress sympathizer, Sher-Gil was drawn to the poor and distressed, and her depictions of Indian villagers and women reflect their conditions. She admired Gandhi’s philosophy and lifestyle, and Nehru was charmed by her beauty and talent; he visited her at Saraya in October 1940 and attended her 1937 exhibition in New Delhi. Though she exchanged letters with Nehru, her parents burned them when she was away marrying in Budapest. In September 1941, Sher-Gil and Viktor Egan moved to Lahore, where she lived and painted at 23 Ganga Ram Mansions, The Mall. She was known for her affairs with both men and women, and painted several of her female lovers; *Two Women* is believed to depict her and her lover Marie Louise. Her later works include *Tahitian* (1937), *Red Brick House* (1938), *Hill Scene* (1938), and *The Bride* (1940); her last work was left unfinished just before her death. In 1941, at age 28, she became seriously ill just days before her first major solo show in Lahore, slipping into a coma and dying around midnight on 5 December 1941. The cause of death remains unknown; a failed abortion and subsequent peritonitis have been suggested, and her mother accused her husband Egan of murdering her. The day after her death, Britain declared war on Hungary, and Egan was interned as an enemy alien. Sher-Gil was cremated on 7 December 1941 in Lahore. Her art has influenced generations of Indian artists, including Sayed Haider Raza and Arpita Singh, and her depictions of women have made her a beacon for women globally. The Government of India has declared her works National Art Treasures, with most housed in the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi and some at the Lahore Museum. A postage stamp featuring her painting *Hill Women* was released in 1978 by India Post, and Amrita Shergil Marg is a road in Lutyens' Delhi named after her. Her work proved to Western societies that Indians could create fine art, and when sold in India, the government mandates that the art remain in the country—fewer than ten of her works have been sold globally. In 2006, *Village Scene* sold for ₹6.9 crores at an auction in New Delhi, the highest price ever paid for an Indian painting at the time. The Indian cultural centre in Budapest is named the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre. Contemporary artists have recreated her works. The 1969 documentary *Amrita Sher-Gil*, directed by Bhagwan Das Garga and produced by India’s Films Division, won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film. In 1993, she inspired the Urdu play *Tumhari Amrita*. UNESCO designated 2013, the 100th anniversary of her birth, as the International Year of Amrita Sher-Gil. Her work is a key theme in the novel *Faking It* by Amrita Chowdhury. Aurora Zogoiby, a character in Salman Rushdie’s *The Moor’s Last Sigh* (1995), was inspired by Sher-Gil. Claire Kohda references Sher-Gil and her painting *The Three Girls* in her 2022 novel *Woman, Eating*, where the protagonist, Lydia, identifies with the subjects and speculates they were vampires. Sher-Gil was sometimes called India’s Frida Kahlo due to her revolutionary blending of Western and traditional art forms. On 30 January 2016, Google celebrated her 103rd birthday with a Doodle. In 2018, *The New York Times* published a belated obituary. That year, at a Sotheby’s auction in Mumbai, *The Little Girl in Blue* (a 1934 portrait of her cousin Babit, aged eight) sold for a record-breaking 18.69 crores. In 2021, *Portrait of Denyse* (1932, featuring Parisian art critic Denyse Proutaux) was auctioned by Christie’s with an estimated value of $1.8–2.8 million; Proutaux appeared in other Sher-Gil paintings, including *Young Girls* and *Denise Proutaux*, both exhibited in the "Amrita Shergil: The Passionate Quest" show at the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. On 18 September 2023, her 1937 painting *The Story Teller* fetched $7.4 million (Rs 61.8 crore) at a SaffronArt auction, setting a record for the highest price achieved by an Indian artist—just 10 days after Syed Haider Raza’s *Gestation* sold for ₹51.7 crore at Pundole.

Anant Gangaram Geete, born on 2 June 1951, is an Indian politician who served as the Union Cabinet Minister for Heavy Industries and Public Sector Enterprises from 2014 to 2019 in the Narendra Modi cabinet. He previously held the position of Union Cabinet Minister for Power from August 2002 to May 2004. He is a member of the Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) political party in Maharashtra, India. Geete has been elected to the Lok Sabha six times. In the 2009 general election, he won from the Raigad constituency by a margin of 145,000 votes, defeating the then sitting MP and former Cabinet Minister A.R. Antulay. In the 2014 general election, he retained his seat in Raigad by a margin of 2,110 votes over Sunil Tatkare, who was then the Minister for Water Resources in Maharashtra; however, Tatkare lost the seat in 2019 by a margin of 31,740 votes. Prior to representing Raigad, he served four terms in the Ratnagiri constituency from the 11th to the 14th Lok Sabha. He was born in Tisangi, a village in the Ratnagiri District of Maharashtra. Geete has held several key positions, including Chief Whip of the Shiv Sena Parliamentary party, Member of the Consultative Committee of the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Leader of the Shiv Sena Parliamentary Party, Member of the General Purposes Committee, Member of the Railway Convention Committee, Chairman of the Committee on Chemicals and Fertilizers, Member of the Committee on Petitions, Leader of the Shiv Sena Parliamentary Party in the Lok Sabha, and Member of the Committee on Food, Consumer Affairs & Public Distribution and the Business Advisory Committee.

Anant Maral Shastri (1912–1999) was an Indian freedom fighter, journalist, literary figure, poet, Sanskrit scholar, linguist, and administrator. He left Ambikapur, now in Chhattisgarh, at a young age to join Kashi Vidyapeeth in Varanasi, where he studied under Acharya Narendra Dev and Acharya JB Kriplani, both prominent freedom fighters. His grandfather, Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma, was the official tutor of Raja Bahadur Raghunath Saran Singh Deo, Maharaja of Sarguja (1879–1917), who was the great-grandfather of Madaneswar Saran Singh Deo, who later became Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh. Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma owned extensive landed property in Ambikapur, Sarguja, which his only son and heir, Anant Maral, abandoned when he joined Kashi Vidyapeeth and the freedom movement at a young age and never returned to claim it after Independence. During the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1932), when the British suppressed the press, Anant Maral went underground and published the Congress Bulletin and Congress Samachar from Allahabad. He wrote the articles by hand, cut stencils to print copies, and distributed them by foot across villages to spread the Congress message. He also served as Youth League secretary in Varanasi. After earning the Shastri degree, he moved to Lahore, where he briefly worked as a college professor before becoming editor of Hindi Milap, a leading newspaper, gaining significant popularity in literary circles. In 1945, he published a well-researched treatise on the Bhakti Movement titled "Ram Bhakti Shakha" in Lahore (now in Pakistan), which was adopted as a textbook for MA Hindi Literature by Punjab University during the pre-Independence era, with preface by renowned Hindi scholar and former All India Radio director Udayshankar Bhatt. In 1942, during the Quit India Movement, he was arrested and imprisoned at Patna Camp Jail, where Sitaram Kesri, later Congress President, was also a cellmate. Upon Independence, he relocated from Lahore to Delhi and joined the Publications Division of the Government of India as editor of Ajkal, the most circulated and popular Hindi magazine of the time, which became a launching pad for many future poets. At the Publications Division, he played a key role in compiling and editing Mahatma Gandhi's Prayer Speeches, which were recorded earlier by All India Radio, and these were published as "Bhaiyon aur Behnon" (Brothers and Sisters). In 1949, Anant Maral Shastri was appointed Director of Information and Publicity in Madhya Bharat, a position he retained after the state reorganisation in 1956, serving until 1971. During his tenure, the Tansen Samaroh in Gwalior—honoring Miyan Tansen, one of Akbar’s nine gems—and the Kalidas Samaroh in Ujjain, celebrating the great Sanskrit poet and dramatist Kalidas, reached their peak of glory. India’s first President, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, inaugurated the first Akhil Bharatiya Kalidas Samaroh (National Kalidas Festival) in 1958, with Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru as chief guest at the second, during which Nehru was presented with Kalidasa’s epic Raghuvansh, translated from Sanskrit to Hindi by Anant Maral Shastri. This initiative was taken by Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting BV Keskar (1952–1962), who transformed the Tansen Samaroh into a national music festival. For nearly two decades, Anant Maral also led the Madhya Pradesh Shasan Sahitya Parishad and Kala Parishad (State Councils for Literature and Arts). Major events such as the Tagore Centenary, Alauddin Khan Centenary, and the 1960s celebration at Khandwa honoring the legendary Hindi poet Makhanlal Chaturvedi marked significant highlights in the state’s cultural history and remain sources of pride for Madhya Pradesh.

Anantnag district is an administrative district in the Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, located in the disputed Kashmir region and one of ten districts comprising the Kashmir Valley. Its headquarters is the city of Anantnag. As of the 2011 census, it was the third most populous district in Jammu and Kashmir (out of 22), following Jammu and Srinagar. The district includes six tehsils—Anantnag, Bijbehara, Dooru, Kokernag, Pahalgam, and Shangus—and is divided into seven blocks: Breng, Shangus, Achabal, Dachnipora, Qazigund, Khoveripora, and Shahabad. It covers a total area of 3,574 square kilometres (1,380 sq mi) and is bordered by Kargil and Kishtwar to the east, Doda and Ramban to the south, Ganderbal to the north, and Kulgam, Srinagar, Pulwama, and Shopian to the west. Anantnag has a moderate climate (Köppen classification), characterized by cool springs and autumns, mild summers, and cold winters, influenced by the Karakoram to the east and the Pirpanjal range to the south. The hilly eastern areas are cooler than the flat northern regions. Summer is mild with high humidity and cool nights, and precipitation occurs throughout the year, with July being the hottest month (mean max 32°C, mean min 6°C) and December–January the coldest (mean max 0°C, mean min −15°C). The record high is 33°C and the record low is −18°C. On 5–6 January 2012, heavy snowfall and low temperatures led to a state of emergency, with school closures on 6 and 7 January. Over recent years, there has been an increase in relative humidity and annual precipitation, likely due to commercial afforestation projects that expanded parks and green cover, making suburban areas more lush than the central region. The district shares the typical climate of the Kashmir Valley, as described by Pandit Kulan or Kalhana, who noted the mild sunshine, saffron, iced water, and grapes, and compared it to places like Peshawar, Baghdad, Damascus, Fez, and South Carolina, though it does not match any single climate. Sir Walter Lawrence observed that every hundred feet of elevation brings a new climate and vegetation phase. Anantnag has seven assembly constituencies: Anantnag, Anantnag West, Dooru, Kokernag, Shangus-Anantnag East, Bijbehara, and Pahalgam, and one Lok Sabha constituency. The current Member of Parliament for Anantnag-Rajouri is Mian Altaf Ahmed Larvi of the JKNC, and the District Development Commissioner (DDC) is Yousuf Gorsi of the JKNC, part of the PAGD. According to the 2011 census, the district had a population of 1,078,692, roughly equivalent to the nation of Cyprus or the U.S. state of Rhode Island, ranking 425th in India (out of 640). The population density is 375 inhabitants per square kilometre (970/sq mi), with a 37.48% growth rate between 2001 and 2011. The sex ratio is 927 females per 1,000 males (varying by religion), and the literacy rate is 64.32%. About 26.23% of the population lives in urban areas, with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes constituting 0.17% and 10.75% of the population, respectively. Anantnag city, with a population of 108,505, is the largest city in the district, and the Anantnag Urban Agglomeration has a population of 158,785. Kashmiri is the predominant language, spoken by 85.10% of the population, followed by Gujari at 11.46% and Pahari at 1.21%. The nearest airport is Sheikh ul-Alam International Airport in Srinagar, 60 kilometres from Anantnag, and there is an Indian Air Force airbase in Awantipora. The district is well-connected by rail, with the Jammu–Baramulla line passing through it and numerous railway stations. It is also well-connected by roads, including NH 44, NH 244, and NH 501, which run through the district alongside other intra-district roads.

Andrea Carol Arpaci-Dusseau (also published as Andrea Dusseau) is an American computer scientist specializing in operating systems, file systems, data storage, distributed computing, and computer science education. She is a professor of computer sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Along with her husband, Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau, she co-authored the free 2018 textbook "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces" (OSTEP), which is downloaded millions of times annually and is used at hundreds of institutions worldwide. Arpaci-Dusseau earned her bachelor's degree in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University, graduating in 1991, and completed her Ph.D. in computer science at the University of California, Berkeley in 1998; her dissertation, "Implicit Coscheduling: Coordinated Scheduling with Implicit Information in Distributed Systems," was supervised by David Culler. After conducting postdoctoral research at Stanford University, she joined the University of Wisconsin–Madison faculty as an assistant professor in 2000 and became a full professor in 2009. She primarily teaches undergraduate and graduate-level operating systems courses. Arpaci-Dusseau is married to Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau, who is also a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and an expert in data storage; the two are frequent collaborators. In 2018, Arpaci-Dusseau and her husband received the SIGOPS Mark Weiser Award "for outstanding leadership, innovation, and impact in storage and computer systems research." She was named an ACM Fellow in 2020 "for contributions to storage and computer systems."

Emory Andrew Tate III, born on 1 December 1986 at the Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C., is an American and British social media personality, businessman, and former professional kickboxer who gained notoriety for promoting controversial positions within the manosphere. He has been described as the "king of toxic masculinity," has called himself a misogynist, and is politically categorized as both right-wing and far-right. As of June 2025, he has 10.7 million followers on Twitter and was the third-most googled person in 2023. He is multiracial, with an African American father, Emory Tate (1958–2015), a chess international master, and a White English mother, Eileen Tate, who worked as a catering assistant. He has a younger brother, Tristan, and a younger sister, Janine. Raised in Chicago, Illinois, and Goshen, Indiana, he moved to Luton in Bedfordshire, England, in 1997 after his parents divorced, living on Marsh Farm, which he described as the "worst area of the worst town." He was educated at Halyard High School and Luton Sixth Form College. Tate began practising boxing and martial arts in 2005 and worked in television advertising. From 2005, he began his kickboxing career in England, winning several titles, including the English ISKA Full Contact Cruiserweight Championship in 2009 and the International Kickboxing Federation Full Contact Cruiserweight British Title, and earned the nickname "King Cobra." In 2011, he won his first ISKA full contact world title in a rematch against Jean-Luc Benoît via knockout at 81.5 kg. He competed in the Enfusion 3: Trial of the Gladiators tournament in 2011 and 2012, winning a semi-final match but losing in the final. In 2013, he won his second ISKA world title in the Light Cruiserweight division. He held the Enfusion 90 kg world title in 2014 and became a four-time kickboxing world champion, retiring in 2014 due to eye injuries sustained during his career, which required surgical repair and led to a permanent retirement by age 30. In 2020, he returned to kickboxing, winning knockouts over Miralem Ahmeti, Iulian Strugariu, and Cosmin Lingurar in Romania, before retiring again with a 76–9–1 record. His brother Tristan, who also competed in kickboxing, retired early with a 43–9 record due to a shoulder injury. In 2016, Tate appeared on Big Brother's 17th series as a member of "The Others," but was removed after six days due to an ongoing police investigation into him for rape, which was later dropped. In December 2022, Tate and his brother were arrested in Romania with two women, and in June 2023, all four were charged with rape, human trafficking, and forming an organised crime group to sexually exploit women. Accusers reportedly went into hiding after a campaign of online harassment, and the Tate brothers filed a $5 million defamation lawsuit. In March 2024, British police obtained an arrest warrant for the brothers. In July 2024, a civil case in the UK was brought against the brothers and a third person for alleged tax evasion. In August 2024, Romanian police raided four properties owned by Tate and expanded the investigation to include trafficking minors, sex with a minor, money laundering, and attempting to influence witnesses. Tate and his brother have denied all charges. In May 2025, the UK Crown Prosecution Service brought multiple charges against Tate and his brother Tristan, including rape, actual bodily harm, and human trafficking. Tate and his brother launched a webcam business employing up to 75 models, selling "fake sob stories" to male callers, which they later admitted was a "total scam." They operated Hustler's University, a platform where members paid $49.99 monthly for courses on wealth accumulation and male–female interactions, including cryptocurrency, copywriting, and e-commerce, with an affiliate marketing program that was later shut down by Stripe and criticized as a pyramid scheme. The platform was rebranded as The Real World, which targets male teenagers and features a "cult-like atmosphere," with members referring to each other as "G" and Tate as "Top G," centered on his "41 Tenets for men." The Real World also offers cryptocurrency, e-commerce, and drop shipping. In 2023, Google and Apple removed The Real World's app, the Real World Portal, from their app stores. In January 2024, analysis found the Real World YouTube channel had 450 million views and a third-party channel had nearly 300 million views, with researchers estimating YouTube earned up to £2.4 million from ads, though YouTube disputed the figures. In May 2024, a misconfigured database leaked personal data of 968,447 users, including email addresses and passwords, and 22 million messages. In November 2024, a cyberattack exposed 794,000 usernames, 324,382 email addresses, and the contents of 221 public and 395 private chat servers. The War Room, advertised at $8,000, promotes self-discipline, confidence, and personal responsibility, claiming to teach men physical, mental, emotional, spiritual, and financial development. According to a BBC investigation, the group is an all-male, secretive society with a leader, Miles Sonkin (Iggy Semmelweiss), who met Tate in 2018 and established the group in 2019. Leaked chat logs revealed a "Pimpin' Hoes Degree" course (abbreviated to PhD) that taught techniques to "romantically seduce, emotionally manipulate, and socially isolate women" before luring them into webcam work, described by a human trafficking expert as using "Lover Boy" strategies. Victims reported that sex was used as a manipulation technique and that members engaged in "Pavlovian conditioning," including submission tests like receiving tattoos of members' initials. A whistleblower claimed to have been "brainwashed" by the group. As of August 2022, the group had 434 members and 45 potential victims. In 2024, Tate launched a meme coin called DADDY, which reached a market capitalisation of $217 million, a play on Iggy Azalea's $MOTHER coin, with Tate stating it was "for the patriarchy" and saying, "We're bringing the Gs back, make me a f***ing sandwich females." As of March 2025, Tate is facing six legal investigations—four criminal and two civil—in Romania, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Andrew Tate is an influencer in the manosphere and "alpha male" community, described as right-wing and far-right, and identified as a libertarian; he is dubbed the "king of toxic masculinity." He has been criticized for promoting views that women "belong in the home," "can't drive," and are "given to the man and belong to the man" as "a man's property," and for claiming men prefer dating 18- to 19-year-old women to "make an imprint" on them, labeling women who do not stay home as "hoes." In 2017, Tate expressed views on sexual harassment that suggested victims share responsibility for assaults and supported Russell Brand after allegations of sexual assault. He is associated with far-right ideologies and individuals, including Tommy Robinson, and has appeared on InfoWars and with figures like Mike Cernovich, Jack Posobiec, and Paul Joseph Watson; he attended CPAC in 2019. Hope not Hate has accused Tate of a "long history of racist statements, homophobia and links to the organised far-right," and Thierry Baudet called him an "outspoken political dissident." Tate has questioned whether the Nazis were the "bad guy" in WWII, performed Nazi salutes, and advocated bringing the Nazi salute back, responding to Elon Musk's salute in January 2025 by saying, "we're so back." In a 2023 BBC interview, Tate claimed he was "acting under the instruction of God" and preached hard work, discipline, anti-drugs, religion, no alcohol, and no knife crime. He has stated that depression "isn't real" and named conspiracy theorist Alex Jones a hero; in March 2024, he falsely claimed the Francis Scott Key bridge collapse was due to a cyber-attack. Tate was accused of inciting online hate after amplifying misinformation about the Southport stabbing, leading to far-right riots in the UK. Regarding the Gaza war, he accused Israel of "genociding" Palestinians and said the October 7 attacks were "an eye for an eye," and stated, "I can only pray for a death as heroic as Yahya Sinwar." He promoted an antisemitic conspiracy claiming the "Matrix" is the Jewish mafia and said, "stop crying over the Hitler crap" and questioned whether lies about WWII were also told about Gaza. Beginning in 2022, Tate's influence on teenage boys and young men has raised concerns among parents, teachers, and mental health experts globally, including in North America, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand. The New York Times described his views as "brainwashing a generation," and the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) considers his misogyny mainstream, stating he teaches that women are inferior and morally deficient and deserve physical, sexual, and emotional abuse, equating his philosophy to pickup artists. The White Ribbon Campaign called his commentary "extremely misogynistic" and its effects on young males "concerning," while Hope not Hate warned his content presents a "dangerous slip road into the far-right" and criticized his ties to far-right groups. Rape Crisis England and Wales said it is "unacceptable" that such misogyny is given a platform, and the Centre for Countering Digital Hate labeled his videos "extreme misogyny" for referencing leaving an imprint on young women. In response, Tate claimed his content includes "many videos praising women" and aims to teach audiences to avoid "toxic and low-value people," saying he plays a "comedic character" and that people believe "absolutely false narratives" about him. Tim Squirrell of the Institute for Strategic Dialogue said Tate poses a risk of radicalising young men into misogynist extremism, and Hope not Hate's director of policy called him a "legitimising force" for misogynistic views, while the End Violence Against Women Coalition said it is "hugely concerning" that he continues to influence younger men who agree with his views on women, masculinity, and how to be a man. Teachers in Australia reported a rise in sexism, misogyny, and sexual harassment in classrooms, with some quitting their jobs. In February 2023, teacher training courses on addressing Tate's views sold out. The UK's head of counter-terror policing expressed concern about the effect of such rhetoric on young boys, and the Department for Education discouraged discussion of Tate due to his influence on sexual harassment and misogyny. The Australian government allocated AUD$3.5 million (£1.8 million) to counter harmful gender stereotypes online, responding to young fans bringing misogynist views into schools. In February 2024, the UK shadow education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, proposed peer-to-peer mentoring programs to counter Tate's misogyny, a plan welcomed by the National Education Union. A 2023 survey by "The Man Cave" found 28% of 500 teenage Australian boys looked up to Tate and 36% found him relatable, with half of 24 schools reporting a significant negative impact. A Hope not Hate survey found 80% of British males aged 16–17 had viewed Tate's content, with 45% of those aged 16–24 having a positive view compared to 1% of British females aged 16–17. YouGov data in September 2023 found 26% of men aged 18–29 and 28% of men aged 30–39 agreed with Tate's views on women, with 6% of adults who had heard of him holding a positive view (12% men, 3% women) and half having a negative view. A 2023 Women's Aid and ORB International survey found 40% of 7–18 year-olds had heard of Tate, including 21% of 7–11 year-olds and 43–53% of 11–18 year-olds, with children exposed to his content being five times more likely to think hurting people is OK. A 2024 King's College London, Center for Women's Global Leadership, and Ipsos study found one in five men aged 16–29 who had heard of Tate held a favourable view (7% of women in the same age group), with only 6% overall holding a favourable view and over three-quarters holding an unfavourable view; one in seven agreed with his views on male identity and gender roles, while 61% disagreed. Tate's early YouTube channel, "the Hateful Tates," gained attention, and by July 2022, he was searched more than both Donald Trump and COVID-19. In August 2022, TikTok videos of Tate were viewed 11.6 billion times. By December 2023, he had over 8.5 million followers on X (Twitter), an increase of 5 million since December 2022, and as of August 2024, had 9.9 million followers. He was the third-most googled person in 2023, and his Wikipedia article was among the top 25 English Wikipedia articles in 2023. In December 2022, Tate tweeted to environmentalist Greta Thunberg, boasting about his 33 cars, including a Bugatti with a w16 8.0L quad turbo and two Ferrari 812 competizione models with 6.5L v12s, and requested her email to share details of his car collection and emissions. Thunberg responded with the satirical email "smalldickenergy@getalife.com," which went viral. Tate gained notoriety for promoting a "hyper-masculine, ultra-luxurious lifestyle" and "hyper-macho image," and is popular among British teenage boys who mimic his phrases and philosophies. Virtually every parent in Britain had heard of him, and parents and teachers expressed concern about his influence leading to misogynistic and aggressive behavior. In January 2023, the BBC reported that Tate and his brother used social media to contact young women to join their webcam business. The Center for Countering Digital Hate found YouTube earned up to £2.4 million from Tate's content, accusing YouTube of turning a blind eye; YouTube disputed the figure as "wildly inaccurate and overinflated." Three of Tate's Twitter accounts have been suspended, with one account created to evade a ban being verified by Twitter before being permanently banned. In August 2022, after an online campaign to deplatform him, Tate was permanently banned from Facebook and Instagram, losing 4.7 million followers, and Meta cited violations of policies on "dangerous organizations and individuals." TikTok removed his account for violating policies on content that attacks, threatens, incites violence against, or dehumanises individuals or groups. Shortly after, YouTube suspended his channel, which had 760,000 subscribers, citing hate speech and COVID-19 misinformation, and Tate later deleted his Twitch channel.

Three of Andrew and Tristan Tate’s Twitter accounts have been suspended at different times. In 2021, an account created by Tate to evade a prior ban was verified by Twitter, contrary to its policies, and was later permanently banned, with Twitter stating the verification occurred in error. In August 2022, after an online campaign to deplatform him, Tate was permanently banned from Facebook and Instagram, losing 4.7 million followers from the latter; Meta cited violations of its policy on "dangerous organizations and individuals." TikTok removed his account after determining it violated policies on content that attacks, threatens, incites violence against, or dehumanises an individual or group, with videos featuring Tate’s name as a hashtag receiving over 13 billion views. YouTube suspended his channel, which had 760,000 subscribers, citing multiple violations, including hate speech and COVID-19 misinformation, and Tate later deleted his Twitch channel, which had 50,000 subscribers. In November 2022, after Elon Musk acquired Twitter, Tate’s Twitter account was reinstated. Tate responded by stating that while most of his comments were taken out of context, he took responsibility for how they were received. Jake Paul denounced Tate’s sexism but called the bans censorship. Tate’s content continues to circulate on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok via fan accounts. After the bans, Tate moved to alt-tech platforms Gettr and Rumble, causing Rumble to briefly become the most downloaded app on the Apple App Store. In 2025, Tate stated he launched the BRUV (Britain Restoring Underlying Values) Party as part of his plan to become prime minister, with the party’s website declaring it a "war to reclaim Britain" to defend borders, crush crime, purge corruption, and restore national pride. The party launch was widely ridiculed, with one user calling its manifesto a "mix of North Korea and homoeroticism" and another calling it the "very worst idea in the history of British politics"; some speculated it was a PR stunt, but Tate dismissed it, stating he was "100% serious" and would run in the next election. The party’s Twitter handle was suspended but was restored after Tate made a complaint to Elon Musk. In 2017, Tate and his brother moved from the UK to Romania, where they run multiple businesses; Tate cited a preference for countries where corruption is accessible and claimed he would face fewer rape charges there, noting that Romanian police require "evidence" or "CCTV proof" for rape reports, unlike the Western world during the #MeToo movement. He reportedly has several children in Romania whom he visits occasionally. Tate was raised Christian but later became an atheist; by early 2022, he identified as Christian again, tithing £16,000 monthly to the Romanian Orthodox Church. After a viral video of him praying at a mosque in Dubai in October 2022, he announced on Gettr that he had converted to Islam; scholars such as Mufti Menk have commended the decision, calling him a "very sincere brother." In March 2023, during incarceration in Romania, Tate’s legal team reported a "dark spot on his lung, most likely a tumor" following a Dubai medical consultation, sparking online rumors about lung cancer; Tate denied having cancer on Twitter. In June 2025, it was revealed Tate received Vanuatu citizenship through the country’s citizenship by investment scheme in December 2022; a Vanuatu government spokesperson stated they were "definitely looking into" revoking his citizenship. Tate was first arrested in Britain in July 2015 after two women accused him of rape and assault, and was arrested again in December 2015; in 2019, the Crown Prosecution Service declined to file charges. Canadian alt-right activist Lauren Southern wrote in her 2025 memoir that she met Tate in Romania in 2018; she described being taken from a nightclub to her hotel room, kissing him briefly, and then being strangled unconscious after resisting his advances, stating she would prefer not to share the rest. In April 2022, the US embassy received a report that an American citizen was being held against her will in a property owned by the Tate brothers in Pipera, Romania; Romanian police raided the home and a nearby webcam studio, discovering four women, two of whom (the American and a Romanian woman) claimed they were held against their will, triggering an investigation by DIICOT into human trafficking and rape. In December, the Tates and two women were arrested; all four were suspected of human trafficking and forming an organised crime group, with one suspected of rape; Romanian authorities seized 29 assets, including cars, properties, watches, and money, totaling nearly US$4 million. In June 2023, DIICOT upgraded the charges to "human trafficking in continued form," a more serious charge, with seven victims identified; the four accused were indicted on charges of rape, human trafficking, and forming an organised crime group to sexually exploit women; they deny all charges and remain under investigation for money laundering and trafficking of minors. In the same month, the Tate brothers filed a defamation lawsuit against one accuser, their parents, and two others in Palm Beach County, Florida, seeking $5 million in damages, claiming the five conspired to falsely accuse them. In January 2024, the Romanian criminal case was heard in the preliminary chamber, and three months later, the Bucharest Tribunal ruled that the case met legal criteria. That month, US District Judge Robin L. Rosenberg dismissed another defamation lawsuit by the Tates against a former US Marine who reported them to the US Embassy and military officials. In March 2024, Westminster Magistrates' Court issued a European arrest warrant against Andrew and Tristan Tate, based on allegations of sexual aggression from 2012 to 2015; the brothers categorically reject all charges. In July, Devon and Cornwall Police began civil proceedings against Tate, Tristan, and a third person for tax evasion with their online businesses; two months later, three women involved in the British investigation and a fourth British woman filed a civil case against Tate. In August 2024, Romanian police expanded their investigation to include trafficking minors, sex with a minor, money laundering, and attempting to influence witnesses; prosecutors said the new investigation involves 35 alleged victims, including a woman who was a minor at the time; the Tate brothers, among six detained, denied all allegations. In December 2024, the Westminster Magistrates' Court ruled in favor of Devon and Cornwall Police, allowing them to seize £2.8 million in unpaid taxes from the Tate brothers’ online businesses. In February 2025, Alison Hernandez, Police and Crime Commissioner for Devon and Cornwall, announced the force received around £1.2 million, which she intended to support victims of violence against women and girls. In the US, following pressure from the Trump administration on Romanian authorities to lift travel restrictions, Tate left Romania by private jet and arrived in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, where he became the subject of a statewide criminal investigation. In March 2025, Florida’s Attorney General, James Uthmeier, initiated a criminal investigation into Tate upon his arrival. Tate’s ex-girlfriend, Brianna Stern, accused him of choking and beating her at The Beverly Hills Hotel on 10 March, claiming she was later diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome; she filed a lawsuit against him for physical and sexual abuse. Tate denies the accusations. In May 2025, the UK Crown Prosecution Service brought 21 charges against Tate and his brother Tristan, including rape, actual bodily harm, and human trafficking.

Andrew Chi-Chih Yao (Chinese: 姚期智; pinyin: Yáo Qīzhì; born December 24, 1946) is a Chinese computer scientist, theoretical physicist, and computational theorist. He is currently a professor and the dean of the Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences (IIIS) at Tsinghua University. Yao used the minimax theorem to prove what is now known as Yao's principle. Born in Shanghai (then part of the Republic of China) on December 24, 1946, Yao was raised in Hong Kong and then Taiwan after his parents moved there. He attended Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School, graduated from National Taiwan University with a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in physics in 1967, and pursued graduate studies in the United States at Harvard University, where he earned a Master of Arts (M.A.) in physics in 1969 and a Ph.D. in theoretical physics in 1972; his doctoral thesis, titled "Internal Symmetries and Positivity," was completed under Nobel Prize laureate Sheldon Glashow. In 1975, after only two years of study, Yao completed a second Ph.D. in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign as a National Science Foundation fellow, with his dissertation "A Study of Concrete Computational Complexity" supervised by Taiwanese computer scientist Chung Laung Liu. He served as an assistant professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (1975–1976), assistant professor at Stanford University (1976–1981), and professor at the University of California, Berkeley (1981–1982). From 1982 to 1986, he was a full professor at Stanford University. In 1986, he became the William and Edna Macaleer Professor of Engineering and Applied Science at Princeton University, a position he held from 1986 to 2004, during which he continued research on algorithms and complexity. In 2004, he became a professor at the Center for Advanced Study, Tsinghua University (CASTU) and the director of the Institute for Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS) at Tsinghua University in Beijing. Since 2010, he has served as the dean of IIIS at Tsinghua University and initiated the Conference on Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS). He is also the Distinguished Professor-at-Large in the Chinese University of Hong Kong. Yao was a naturalized U.S. citizen and worked in the U.S. for many years; in 2015, he renounced his U.S. citizenship and became an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences alongside Yang Chen-Ning. He received the Knuth Prize in 1996, the Turing Award in 2000—recognized for his fundamental contributions to the theory of computation, including complexity-based theory in pseudorandom number generation, cryptography, and communication complexity—and the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology in 2021. In 2022, he was listed on the Asian Scientist 100. In May 2024, Yao joined Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, and others in publishing an expert consensus paper warning about the extreme risks posed by AI, stating that AI safety research is lagging and calling for "proactive, adaptive governance mechanisms" for policymakers ahead of the AI Seoul Summit. Yao is a member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the Association for Computing Machinery, and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. His wife, Frances Yao, is also a theoretical computer scientist.

André Lallemand (French pronunciation: [ɑ̃dʁe lalmɑ̃]; September 29, 1904 – March 24, 1978)[1] was a French astronomer and director of the Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris. He made significant contributions to the development of photomultipliers for astronomical applications and invented the "electronic telescope" (or Lallemand camera). He received the Lalande Prize from the French Academy of Sciences in 1938[2] and the Eddington Medal from the Royal Astronomical Society in 1962 for his scientific achievements. Lallemand served as President of the Société astronomique de France (SAF), the French astronomical society, from 1960 to 1962.[3] The crater Lallemand on the Moon is named in his honor, and the French Academy of Sciences bestows a biennial award in astronomy known as the "Prix Lallemand". Angelos Postecoglou (/ˈændʒ ˌpɒstəˈkɒɡluː/ ANJ POS-tə-KOG-loo; born 27 August 1965) is a soccer manager and former player who was most recently the head coach of Premier League club Nottingham Forest. Born in Nea Filadelfeia, a suburb of Athens, Greece, Postecoglou was born to a family that migrated from the Alaşehir district of Manisa during the 1923 population exchange between Turkey and Greece. After his father, Dimitris ("Jim"), lost his business following the 1967 Greek military coup, the family moved to Australia in 1970 when Postecoglou was five years old. He grew up in Melbourne, Victoria, and at age 10, his parents changed his surname to "Postekos" due to a trend among Greeks to shorten names at the time, though he legally retains Postecoglou. Postecoglou began playing for South Melbourne Hellas at age nine and played 193 games in the National Soccer League from 1984 to 1993, contributing to their 1984 and 1990–91 titles, the latter as captain in a penalty shootout win over Melbourne Croatia. He was coached by Hungarian Ferenc Puskás, whose 4–3–3 formation with rigid full-backs and attacking wingers influenced Postecoglou’s own coaching style, though he later used attacking full-backs in an inverted position. A knee injury ended his NSL career at age 27. He was named starting left back in South Melbourne's team of the century in 2000 and played four senior international games for Australia between 1986 and 1988, including a debut on 3 August 1986 against Czechoslovakia and appearances in both legs of the 1988 Trans-Tasman Cup, which Australia won 4–1 on aggregate. He also represented Australia at youth level in 1985. After retiring, Postecoglou served as an assistant coach at South Melbourne under Jim Pyrgolios and Frank Arok, becoming head coach in 1996 after Arok’s firing. He led South Melbourne to consecutive National Soccer League titles in 1997–98 and 1998–99, and won the 1999 Oceania Club Championship, qualifying for the 2000 FIFA Club World Championship. He stepped down from South Melbourne in 2000 to become coach of Australia’s youth teams, where he helped identify and develop players, though he was replaced in February 2007 after Australia failed to qualify for the 2007 FIFA U-20 World Cup. He worked as a football pundit for Fox Sports and as an elite consultant to Football Federation Victoria.
