Postecoglou coached Panachaiki in the Greek third division and Whittlesea Zebras in Melbourne while running coaching clinics. On 16 October 2009, he was appointed head coach of Brisbane Roar, replacing Frank Farina. He released several players and acquired others, including Tommy Oar, Michael Zullo, and Adam Sarota, who moved to Utrecht, and striker Sergio van Dijk to Adelaide United. The 4–0 win against Adelaide United in round 13 was widely praised. Postecoglou led the Roar to the Premiership and Championship in the 2010–11 season, winning the Grand Final 4–2 on penalties against Central Coast Mariners in front of 52,168 people at Lang Park, going on a 36-game unbeaten run and losing only one game all season. He signed a two-year extension until the 2013–14 season on 18 March 2011. In the 2011–12 season, Brisbane Roar became the first team to win back-to-back A-League championships, and Postecoglou became the most successful Australian domestic football coach with four national titles. He announced his resignation as head coach of Brisbane Roar on 24 April 2012 after two-and-a-half years. On 26 April 2012, he signed a three-year contract with Melbourne Victory as head coach. His first game was a 2–1 loss to Melbourne Heart, and his first win came against Adelaide United in Round 4. The following year, Melbourne Victory reached the A-League Preliminary Final after beating Perth Glory 2–1 in an Elimination Final. Postecoglou was appointed head coach of the Australia national team on 23 October 2013, replacing Holger Osieck, tasked with regenerating a team seen as overly reliant on the 2006 Golden Generation. In his first match, a friendly against Costa Rica, Australia won 1–0 thanks to a goal from Tim Cahill. For the 2014 FIFA World Cup, Australia was drawn in Group B with Spain, the Netherlands, and Chile, losing to Chile 3–1 and the Netherlands 3–2, and finishing with a 3–0 loss to Spain, but their competitive performances led to belief in a new Golden Generation. In 2015, Australia won the AFC Asian Cup by defeating Kuwait 4–1 and Oman 4–0, beating China 2–0 in the quarter-final and the United Arab Emirates 2–0 in the semi-final, and winning the final 2–1 after extra time against South Korea. On 22 November 2017, two weeks after qualifying for the 2018 FIFA World Cup, Postecoglou announced his resignation as Socceroos coach. On 19 December 2017, he was appointed head coach of Yokohama F. Marinos, beginning after the 2017 Japanese Emperor's Cup. His first domestic game ended in a 1–1 draw against Cerezo Osaka. After a difficult start, he guided the club to the J-League Cup final and a 12th-place finish in the league. He extended his contract with Yokohama after receiving interest from the Greece national team. In 2019, he won the J1 League with Yokohama F. Marinos, securing their first title in 15 years. On 10 June 2021, Postecoglou became head coach of Scottish Premiership club Celtic, signing a 12-month rolling contract, making him the first Australian manager to coach a major European club. Celtic had just lost their league title to Rangers for the first time in a decade and had not hired English manager Eddie Howe. His first game was a 1–1 draw against FC Midtjylland in a UEFA Champions League qualifier, followed by a 2–1 loss in the second leg, leading to elimination. He lost his first league game 2–1 away to Heart of Midlothian on 31 July. On 19 December 2021, Celtic won the Scottish League Cup after defeating Hibernian 2–1 at Hampden Park. On 2 February 2022, a 3–0 win over Rangers put Celtic at the top of the league for the first time in the season, ending a 13-game unbeaten start for opposing manager Giovanni van Bronckhorst. The league title was sealed on 11 May with a 1–1 draw at Dundee United. Postecoglou won the Scottish League Cup a second time in February 2023 after beating Rangers 2–1 in the final. Celtic ended the 2022–23 season with a record eighth domestic treble after winning the Scottish Cup at Hampden Park against Inverness Caledonian Thistle on 3 June. He was named a candidate for The Best FIFA Football Coach after winning the domestic treble. On 6 June 2023, Postecoglou was appointed head coach of Tottenham Hotspur, starting 1 July on a four-year contract, becoming both the first Australian and first Greek to manage in the Premier League. After an unbeaten start to the 2023–24 season with two wins and a draw in his first three matches, he won the Premier League Manager of the Month award for August, becoming the first manager since David Wagner to win it in his first month. On 24 September, he became the first Tottenham manager to earn points from Arsenal away at the Emirates Stadium in four years, after a 2–2 draw. After continuing the unbeaten streak for a second month, he won the September Manager of the Month award, becoming the first ever manager to win it in each of his first two months. On 1 October, he guided Spurs to their first victory against Liverpool in five years, winning 2–1 at home. On 23 October, he achieved his seventh victory in his ninth league game with a 2–0 win over Fulham. He broke the record for most points earned by a Premier League manager in their first nine games, accumulating 23 points and surpassing Guus Hiddink’s 22 from Chelsea in the 2008–09 season. Postecoglou led Tottenham to three consecutive wins and the league's top spot in October, winning Manager of the Month for a third consecutive time, becoming the first manager to win the award for the first three months of a single season. On 6 November, he suffered his first defeat as Tottenham manager in a 4–1 home loss to Chelsea, during which his side was reduced to nine men after a straight red card to Cristian Romero and a second yellow card to Destiny Udogie. The loss began a five-game winless streak, during which the club drew one match and lost the rest, dropping from first to fifth. Leading Tottenham to an unbeaten run in their first ten games contributed to Postecoglou winning Manager of the Year honours at the London Football Awards on 29 February 2024. However, Tottenham was unable to recapture their strong season start.

Postecoglou, who grew up in Melbourne, Victoria, played Australian rules football from a young age and became a lifelong supporter of the Carlton Football Club in the Australian Football League (AFL), as well as of Liverpool and AEK Athens. He married his first wife, Georgia, in December 1988 and had a son from that marriage; he is currently married to a Georgia, who worked as a marketing manager at South Melbourne during his tenure there, and they have two sons together. His father, who died in 2018, worked hard every day to provide opportunities for Ange to have a better life, and Postecoglou stated that his motivation as a manager is to produce teams his father would enjoy watching. Postecoglou is fluent in Greek and is a Greek Orthodox Christian, and he is often referred to as "Big Ange" or mononymously as Ange or Angie in the media. In November 2022, he was inducted into the Football Australia Hall of Fame for his contributions to Australian football. In a 2018 interview, he cited Paul Keating as his favorite Australian Prime Minister and quoted him during the post-match press conference of the 2025 UEFA Europa League final, saying, "After an unlikely victory, this is one for the true believers." Postecoglou began his managerial career with South Melbourne, Brisbane Roar, Yokohama F. Marinos, Celtic, and Tottenham Hotspur, and also coached Australia U17 and Australia U20. From Chelsea in the 2008–09 season, Postecoglou guided Tottenham to three consecutive wins and the league's top spot in October, earning him Manager of the Month for a third consecutive time, making him the first manager to win the award for the first three months of a single season. On 6 November, he suffered his first defeat as Tottenham manager in a 4–1 home loss to Chelsea, following a straight red card to Cristian Romero and a second yellow card to Destiny Udogie, marking the start of a five-game winless streak where they drew one match and lost the rest, dropping from first to fifth. His leadership contributed to winning Manager of the Year at the London Football Awards on 29 February 2024, following an unbeaten run in their first ten games. However, a 4–2 loss to Liverpool on 5 May marked the club's first four-game league losing streak in 20 years, and despite the poor form, Tottenham finished fifth, qualifying for the 2024–25 UEFA Europa League after a year-long absence from European football. Prior to the 2024–25 season, Postecoglou stated in an interview that he usually wins things in his second year, though after a 1–0 loss to Arsenal on 15 September, he clarified, "I'll correct myself – I don't usually win things, I always win things in my second year. Nothing's changed. I've said it now. I don't say things unless I believe them," which many in the media interpreted as a promise of a trophy. The campaign was hampered by injuries, resulting in Tottenham's worst-ever Premier League finish at 17th, one spot above relegation, with the most defeats and lowest points tally in a single season. This poor performance raised speculation about his dismissal. Despite the league struggles, Postecoglou led Tottenham to their first trophy in 17 years by defeating Manchester United 1–0 in the 2025 UEFA Europa League final on 21 May 2025, their first title since the 2007–08 Football League Cup and their first European trophy since the 1983–84 UEFA Cup. The victory earned a league phase spot in the 2025–26 UEFA Champions League and the right to play against the 2024–25 UEFA Champions League winners for the 2025 UEFA Super Cup, making Postecoglou the first Australian and first Greek manager to win a European competition. During the Europa League victory parade on 23 May, he openly campaigned to return for the next season, stating "all the best TV series, season three is better than season two." However, on 6 June, exactly two years after his appointment, he was relieved of his duties as Tottenham's head coach. On 9 September 2025, he was announced as head coach of Nottingham Forest, signing a two-year contract as successor to Nuno Espírito Santo. He lost his first game as Forest manager 3–0 to Arsenal, followed by defeats to Swansea City in the League Cup and to Sunderland and Newcastle United in the Premier League, and a loss to FC Midtjylland in the Europa League, with draws against Burnley and Real Betis, resulting in a winless start in his first seven fixtures—the worst start by a Forest manager in over a century—and his job security being questioned after less than a month. After a 3–0 home defeat by Chelsea on 18 October 2025 that dropped the team into the relegation zone, Forest announced Postecoglou's departure just 18 minutes after the final whistle, making him the shortest-reigning manager in the club's history. Evangelos Marinakis had already left his seat when the team was 2–0 down. Postecoglou won none of his 8 games in charge, drawing 2 and losing 6, with a managerial reign of just 39 days—the second shortest in English Premier League history, only behind Sam Allardyce's 30-day tenure at Leeds United—and was replaced by Sean Dyche.

Anil Biswas (2 March 1944 – 26 March 2006), commonly known as Keru, was an Indian communist politician who served as the secretary of the West Bengal State Committee of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and as a member of the party's politburo from 1998 until his death in 2006. Born into a middle-class Mahishya family in Darermath village near Karimpur, Nadia district, to Ashutosh Biswas and Prafulla Kumari Debi, he lost his father at a young age. While in high school, he became interested in the Left movement and joined Krishnagar Government College in 1961, where he was influenced by Marxist leaders Harinarayan Adhikari and Dinesh Majumdar and became an active member of the Students' Federation of India, serving as a student leader in college elections. After completing an Honours degree in Political Science, he moved to Kolkata for further studies. He became a full-fledged member of the CPI(M) in 1965 and was arrested under the Defence of India Rules 1962, spending 11 months in prison, during which he completed his master's degree in political science. In 1969, he became a whole-time party member and began his party work as a journalist with Ganashakti, the party's daily newspaper. He was elected to the CPIM West Bengal state committee in 1978 and to the state secretariat in 1982. He edited Ganashakti between 1983 and 1998, during which the newspaper achieved its peak circulation. In 1985, he was elected to the party's Central Committee. In 1998, he joined the politburo, mentored by Pramod Dasgupta, and took over as secretary of the West Bengal State Committee after his predecessor Sailen Dasgupta resigned due to ill-health and old age. He was reelected as state secretary in 2002 and 2005. He also served as editor of Marxbadi Path (The Road of the Marxist), the theoretical quarterly in West Bengal. Known for his strategic acumen, he played a key role in the party's political decisions, including the decision to appoint Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee as Chief Minister of West Bengal in place of Jyoti Basu before the 2000 West Bengal Legislative Assembly Elections—a move that addressed public frustration with over two decades of the same chief minister and led to a major victory for the Left Front despite strong opposition from Mamata Banerjee's TMC. His effective management of media and ground workers during the 2006 West Bengal Assembly Election significantly reduced the opposition's seat count, as he had a deep understanding of public sentiment both in the media and on the ground. It is widely believed that the deaths of Anil Biswas and other key ground leaders like Subhas Chakraborty created opportunities for the opposition to come to power and replace the Left Front. He died on 26 March 2006 after being hospitalized due to a brain haemorrhage on 18 March. According to his last wishes, his body was donated to NRS Medical College and Hospital. He is survived by his wife Gita and daughter Ajanta.

Anna Krzeptowska-Żebracka (26 July 1938 – 1 December 2017)[1] was a Polish cross-country skier who competed in the women's 10 kilometres event at the 1960 Winter Olympics. She is the sister of Zofia Krzeptowska.[2] This biographical article about Polish cross-country skiing is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information on Wikipedia.

Anna Stepanovna Politkovskaya (née Mazepa; 30 August 1958 – 7 October 2006) was a Russian investigative journalist known for her reporting on political and social events in Russia, particularly the Second Chechen War (1999–2005). Born in New York City in 1958, she was the daughter of Ukrainian Soviet diplomats Stepan Fedorovich Mazepa (1927–2006) from Kostobobriv and Raisa Aleksandrovna (née Novikova; 1929–2021) from Kerch in Crimea. Her father, ethnically Ukrainian, attended a Ukrainian-language school in Chernihiv before the 1941 Nazi invasion and met her mother at a Russian-language night school in Kerch after the war. By 1952, her father was studying in Moscow, where he married her mother, and later became a founding member of the Special Committee against Apartheid in 1962, serving as its secretary until 1974. Her parents bought an apartment in central Moscow in 1962, where she mostly grew up, attending a music school and training in figure skating, and frequently visiting the Krupskaya Library. She graduated from Moscow State University's school of journalism in 1980 with a thesis on the poetry of Marina Tsvetaeva, under the supervision of Yasen Zasurskii, a close friend of the Mazepas. She married fellow student Alexander Politkovsky in 1978, and by 1981 they had two children, Ilya and Vera. Her initial journalistic work began with a brief internship in the mailroom at Izvestia in 1982, and she later worked as a reporter and editor for the Aeroflot emergencies and accidents section at Vozdushnyi transport, gaining access to travel across Russia. She also worked with the creative union Eskart and the St Petersburg publishing house Paritet. After her husband's declining influence following the 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, her career took off; from 1994 to 1999, she served as assistant chief editor of Obshchaya Gazeta, and from June 1999 to 2006, she wrote columns for the investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta. She published several award-winning books about Chechnya, life in Russia, and Russia under Vladimir Putin, including Putin's Russia (2004). Her reporting from Chechnya established her national and international reputation, and she frequently visited hospitals and refugee camps to interview victims of the conflict. She documented alleged abuses by Russian military forces, Chechen rebels, and the Russian-backed administration led by Akhmad and Ramzan Kadyrov, including the brutalization of civilians and the systematic torture, abduction, and murder of individuals. In 1999, she helped evacuate elderly residents from a bombed ethnically-mixed home in Grozny. In 2001, she was detained in Khattuni, Chechnya, where she was interrogated, beaten, and subjected to a mock execution using a BM-21 Grad rocket launcher, after which she was poisoned with tea. In September 2004, while attempting to fly to Beslan to mediate during the school hostage crisis, she fell violently ill and lost consciousness after drinking tea provided by an Aeroflot flight attendant, leading to her being taken off the flight and requiring medical treatment in Moscow. She was a U.S. citizen with a U.S. passport but never relinquished her Russian citizenship. She received numerous international awards for her work and used these platforms to urge Western governments to be more vigilant about Putin's policies after the September 11 attacks. In her book Putin's Russia, she accused the FSB of suppressing civil liberties to establish a Soviet-style dictatorship, admitting that society's apathy had enabled the rise of authoritarianism and warning that without information, Russia was hurtling back into a Soviet abyss. She concluded her essay "Am I Afraid?" with the statement that "If anybody thinks they can take comfort from the 'optimistic' forecast, let them do so. It is certainly the easier way, but it is the death sentence for our grandchildren." In May 2007, Random House posthumously published A Russian Diary, containing extracts from her notebook and writings from December 2003 to August 2005, covering the decline of Russian parliamentary democracy, the Beslan crisis, and the "winter and summer of discontent." The book was edited without her input due to her murder on 7 October 2006, the 54th birthday of Vladimir Putin. She was murdered in the elevator of her apartment block in Moscow on that day, an assassination that drew international attention. In 2014, five men were sentenced to prison for the murder, but it remains unclear who ordered or paid for the contract killing. Politkovskaya received death threats, including threats of rape and a mock execution, and claimed that Kremlin officials only spoke to her in secret, outside public view. She also stated that she was targeted for her work, and that people sometimes paid with their lives for speaking out. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving threats related to a police officer, Sergey Lapin, whom she had exposed for torture and disappearances; Lapin was later convicted in 2005. A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with the motive possibly being revenge for her role in Lapin's conviction. The European Court of Human Rights found the Russian Federation responsible for the forced disappearance of Khadzhi-Murat Yandiyev in 2006, and Colonel-General Alexander Baranov, mentioned by Politkovskaya as ordering the detention of militants in pits, was filmed giving orders to execute Yandiyev.

Anna Politkovskaya, an investigative journalist for Moscow's liberal newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was assassinated on 7 October 2006, Putin's birthday, in the lift of her apartment block in central Moscow. She had been shot twice in the chest, once in the shoulder, and once in the head at close range. The murder sparked widespread international reaction. Before her burial on 10 October 2006 at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, over one thousand mourners paid their respects; no high-ranking Russian officials attended. She was buried near her father, who had died shortly before her. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving email threats from a police officer, Corporal Sergey Lapin, whom she had accused of atrocities in Chechnya; Lapin was later convicted in 2005 for torture and disappearance of a Chechen civilian, a case she exposed in her article "Disappearing People." A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with revenge being a suspected motive. In 2004, Politkovskaya had a conversation with Ramzan Kadyrov, then Prime Minister of Chechnya, who reportedly said, "You're an enemy. To be shot," and one of his assistants suggested she should have been shot in Moscow. On the day of her murder, she had planned to publish a lengthy story on torture by Chechen security detachments known as Kadyrovites. She had described Kadyrov as the "Chechen Stalin of our days" in her final interview. In May 2007, a posthumous collection of her articles, With Good Reason, was published by Novaya Gazeta at the Gorbachev Foundation, shortly after Vera's daughter was named Anna in her honor. In 2008, ten men were detained on suspicion of involvement in her murder; four were brought before the Moscow District Military Court. Three were charged with aiding the killer, who was allegedly the brother of two suspects; there was insufficient evidence to charge an FSB colonel, though he was suspected of organizing the murder and stood trial for another offense. The case was held before a jury, a rare occurrence in Russia, and was open to the press and public. On 25 November 2008, Murad Musayev, a lawyer for the defendants, stated that case notes suggested a Russian politician (not named) had ordered her death. On 5 December 2008, Sergei Sokolov, a senior Novaya Gazeta editor, testified that Dzhabrail Makhmudov was an FSB agent and that his uncle, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, also worked for the FSB and was serving a 12-year sentence for an attempted murder. After the three men were acquitted in February 2009, Politkovskaya’s children, Vera and Ilya, along with their lawyers and Sokolov, criticized the trial. Andrew McIntosh, a Council of Europe official, condemned the lack of progress in the investigation, calling it a "blatant failure" and urging a relaunch of the probe, citing similar cases like the killings of Georgy Gongadze and Paul Klebnikov. On 19 January 2009, Stanislav Markelov, a lawyer who had investigated abuses documented by Politkovskaya, was assassinated in Moscow; journalist Anastasia Baburova died from injuries while trying to intervene. On 15 July 2009, Natalia Estemirova, a board member of Memorial and a key colleague of Politkovskaya in Chechnya, was abducted in Grozny and found dead in Ingushetia. In August 2009, the Supreme Court upheld the prosecution's objection to the acquittals and ordered a new trial. In August 2011, Russian prosecutors claimed to be close to solving the murder after detaining Dmitry Pavliuchenkov, a former policeman, alleged to be the principal organizer. In December 2012, Pavliuchenkov was found guilty and sentenced to 11 years in a high-security penal colony. In May 2014, five men were convicted of her murder, including three previously acquitted defendants; in June 2014, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev and Rustam Makhmudov received life sentences, though it remained unclear who ordered or paid for the killing. In September 2016, Vladimir Markin, an official of the Investigative Committee, included Politkovskaya’s killing in a list of the Most Dramatic Crimes in 21st century Russia and claimed it had been solved. Her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta protested that without identifying the instigator or sponsor, the case was not closed. On 7 October 2016, Novaya Gazeta released a video in which staff members repeatedly stated, "The sponsor of Anna's murder has not been found." Deputy chief editor Sergei Sokolov published a critical summary of the investigation, describing its false turns and shortcomings, and noted that after the 2014 convictions, the investigative team was reduced to one person who retired within a year, replaced by a lower-ranking investigator. He referenced the 2000 killing of Igor Domnikov, which was later solved, as evidence that perpetrators could be identified. The Intercept published a top-secret document from Edward Snowden showing that on 5 December 2005, the Russian Federal Intelligence Services (likely FSB) launched a cyberattack on Politkovskaya’s webmail account using malicious software not available in the public domain; it was unclear if this attack was linked to her death. Politkovskaya was described as brave, bold, and beautiful, and her fearless reporting on state abuses made her a lonely but powerful voice. A biographical film, initially titled Anna and later renamed Words of War, began production in 2022 with Maxine Peake, Jason Isaacs, and Ciaran Hinds, and had a limited release on 2 May 2025. The 2007–2008 academic year at the College of Europe was named in her honor. The international human rights organization RAW in WAR, founded in 2006 by Mariana Katzarova, established the annual Anna Politkovskaya Award to recognize a woman human rights defender in a conflict zone who stands up for victims at great personal risk. The award was first given on the first anniversary of her murder to Natalia Estemirova, who was abducted and killed in 2009. There is also a "Journalism-prize Anna Politkovskaja" awarded annually in Ferrara, Italy, by the magazine L'internationale and the comune of Ferrara.

Anne Legendre Armstrong (December 27, 1927 – July 30, 2008) was a United States diplomat and politician who made history as the first woman to serve as Counselor to the President and as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. She held these positions under the administrations of Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, and Jimmy Carter. Armstrong was born on December 27, 1927, in New Orleans, Louisiana, and graduated from Vassar College in 1949. She married Tobin Armstrong, a cattle rancher from Texas, in 1950. From 1966 to 1968, she served as vice chairman of the Texas Republican Party, and from 1971 to 1973, she was co-chairman of the Republican National Committee. She delivered the keynote address at the 1972 Republican National Convention, becoming the first woman from either major party to do so. On December 16, 1972, at a White House Christmas dinner, she praised both "Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace" and President Nixon, who had ordered the Christmas Bombing of North Vietnam, in the same breath. Nixon appointed her Counselor to the President on December 19, 1972, a role she held from January 19, 1973, to November 1974 under President Ford. During her time as Counselor, she founded the first Office of Women's Programs in the White House, which preceded the current White House Council on Women and Girls. Fluent in Spanish, she served as Nixon’s liaison to Hispanic Americans and was a member of a Cabinet committee on opportunities for Spanish-speaking people. From 1976 to 1977, she was the first woman to serve as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. At the 1976 Republican National Convention in Kansas City, Missouri, there was a draft effort to nominate her as vice presidential candidate with President Gerald Ford, but Senator Robert Dole was selected instead. In 1978, she supported George W. Bush in his successful primary challenge to Jim Reese in Texas's 19th congressional district. Armstrong was a strong advocate for the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), stating in 1971 that it had become a symbol of meaning for many and would resolve numerous legal questions. In 1987, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Ronald Reagan. In 1989, she was awarded the Golden Plate Award by the American Academy of Achievement. She also received an honorary Doctor of Laws from St. Mary's University in 1978. Armstrong died of cancer in 2008 and is buried at Oakwood Cemetery in Austin, Texas.

Anne Morgan, Baroness Hunsdon (c. 1529 – 19 January 1607), was an English official born around 1529 at Arkestone, Herefordshire, the daughter of Sir Thomas Morgan and Anne Elizabeth Whitney, daughter of Sir James Whitney and Blanche Milbourne. The Morgan family was of Welsh origin. On 21 May 1545, she married Henry Carey, son of Sir William Carey and Mary Boleyn, the elder sister of Queen consort Anne Boleyn; due to Carey's mother having been a mistress of King Henry VIII, some, including John Hales, vicar of Isleworth, speculated that Carey was the King's illegitimate son. Henry Carey was created Baron Hunsdon on 13 January 1559, after which Anne was styled Baroness Hunsdon. Following her elevation, she served Queen Elizabeth I as a Lady of the Privy Chamber, who was also her husband's first cousin and held the couple in high favour. Carey was appointed Captain of the Gentlemen-at-Arms, serving as the Queen's personal bodyguard. A painting by an unknown artist commemorates a visit by the Queen to Anne and Carey at Hunsdon House in Hertfordshire in September 1571; Anne is believed to be depicted among the Queen's Ladies in the royal procession as the foremost lady dressed in white. Anne's portrait, painted by a follower of George Gower, is displayed at Hatfield House. The couple had thirteen children, two of whom died in infancy. Henry Carey had several illegitimate children, including Valentine Carey; one of his mistresses was Emilia Bassano, believed by some, including A. L. Rowse, to have been the inspiration for William Shakespeare's sonnet The Dark Lady, due to her black hair and dark complexion; her son Henry, born in 1592, may have been fathered by her, although she was 63 at the time of the child's birth. Upon Henry Carey's death on 23 July 1596, he left his family in debt; Queen Elizabeth I paid for his funeral expenses, gave Anne a gift of £400, and provided her with an annual pension of £200 from the Exchequer. Anne used part of the funds to erect a monument to her husband in Westminster Abbey. On 14 December 1595, seven months before Carey's death, Queen Elizabeth appointed Anne as Keeper of Somerset House, a royal residence where the Queen had lived before her accession; Anne held this post for life, having previously held it in 1574 with her husband. Anne died on 19 January 1607 and was buried in Westminster Abbey; her will, dated 10 January 1607, was proved on 22 January.

Annie Jump Cannon (December 11, 1863 – April 13, 1941) was an American astronomer whose cataloging work was essential to the development of modern stellar classification. Alongside Edward C. Pickering, she developed the Harvard Classification Scheme, the first systematic effort to classify stars based on temperature and spectral type. Cannon became nearly deaf after 1893 due to scarlet fever, which affected her social life and led her to focus intensely on her research. Born in Dover, Delaware, she was the eldest of three daughters of Wilson Cannon, a shipbuilder and state senator, and Mary Jump; her mother introduced her to astronomy and encouraged her to study mathematics, chemistry, and biology at Wellesley College. Using an old astronomy textbook, Cannon and her mother identified stars from their attic, and her mother also taught her household economics, which she applied to organize her research. At Wilmington Conference Academy and later Wellesley College, Cannon excelled in mathematics and became valedictorian, graduating with a physics degree in 1884. She developed skills in photography during a 1892 trip through Europe, and her photos and writings from Spain were published in a pamphlet titled "In the Footsteps of Columbus" for the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. After her mother’s death in 1894, Cannon sought employment through her former instructor, Sarah Frances Whiting, who hired her as a junior physics teacher at Wellesley, allowing her to take graduate courses and learn spectroscopy. In 1894, she enrolled at Radcliffe College as a "special student" to access the Harvard College Observatory. In 1896, Pickering hired her as an assistant at the Observatory and she joined the Harvard Computers, a group of women tasked with completing the Henry Draper Catalogue, which aimed to map and classify every star to a photographic magnitude of about 9. Cannon used "Int" in her notes to denote brightness. By 1913, she could classify 200 stars per hour, classifying three stars per minute by spectral patterns and even identifying stars down to the ninth magnitude using a magnifying glass. Her work was highly accurate. Initially, disagreements arose over star classification, with Nettie Farrar leaving early, and conflicting approaches from Antonia Maury and Williamina Fleming; Cannon resolved this by applying a new system dividing stars into spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M based on Balmer absorption lines, which later aligned with stellar temperature. In 1901, she published her first catalog of stellar spectra. Despite initial criticism for being outside traditional gender roles, Cannon gained respect through her "tidiness" and patience, and she helped men in the observatory gain recognition by facilitating international partnerships. In 1911, she became Curator of Astronomical Photographs at Harvard; in 1914, she was admitted as an honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society; in 1921, she received an honorary doctorate in math and astronomy from Groningen University; in 1925, she became the first woman to receive an honorary doctorate of science from Oxford University. On May 9, 1922, the International Astronomical Union formally adopted her stellar classification system, which remains in use today with minor adjustments. In 1922, she spent six months in Arequipa, Peru, photographing southern hemisphere stars. In 1933, she represented professional women at the Chicago World's Fair (Century of Progress), and in 1935, she established the Annie J. Cannon Prize for distinguished contributions by women in astronomy. In 1938, she became the William C. Bond Astronomer at Harvard. Cecilia Payne collaborated with Cannon and used her data to demonstrate that stars are primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. Cannon’s career spanned over 40 years, ending with retirement in 1940, but she continued working actively in the observatory until shortly before her death. She classified approximately 350,000 stars in her lifetime, discovered 300 variable stars, five novas, and one spectroscopic binary, and compiled a bibliography of about 200,000 references. She died on April 13, 1941, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at age 77, after being ill for over a month. The American Astronomical Society awards the Annie Jump Cannon Award annually to female astronomers for distinguished work in astronomy.

Anselm Kiefer, born on 8 March 1945 in Donaueschingen, Germany, the son of a German art teacher, grew up in a city heavily bombed at the end of World War II, experiencing the war's devastation firsthand. His family moved to Ottersdorf in 1951, and he attended public school in Rastatt, graduating in 1965. He initially studied pre-law and Romance languages at the University of Freiburg before switching to art, studying at art academies in Freiburg and Karlsruhe, where he studied under Peter Dreher, a realist and figurative painter. He received an art degree in 1969. In 1971, Kiefer moved to Hornbach (Walldürn) and established a studio, remaining in the Neckar-Odenwald-Kreis until 1992, during which time his work is known as The German Years. In 1992, he relocated to France, first to Barjac, and from 2008 lived primarily in Paris in the Marais district with his second wife, the Austrian photographer Renate Graf, and their two children; they divorced in 2014. Kiefer has lived and worked in France since 1992, and since 2008 has resided primarily in Paris. In 2018, he was awarded Austrian citizenship. His works incorporate materials such as straw, ash, clay, lead, and shellac, and he values a "spiritual connection" with these materials, extracting the spirit already within them through processes like acid baths and physical blows with sticks and axes. He is particularly drawn to lead for its alchemical properties, noting its colorful appearance during heating and melting, especially the gold-like hues associated with alchemists. Straw represents energy due to its gold color and heat when burned, with the resulting ash symbolizing new creation and transformation. Kiefer emphasizes a balance between order and chaos, stating that too much order makes a piece dead and too much chaos prevents coherence, and he believes his works lose their power if placed in inappropriate spaces. His early career included performances documented in photographs titled Occupations and Heroische Sinnbilder, in which he dressed in his father's Wehrmacht uniform and mimicked the Nazi salute in France, Switzerland, and Italy to provoke German reflection on the Third Reich's xenophobia. In 1969, he presented his first solo exhibition, "Besetzungen (Occupations)," at Galerie am Kaiserplatz in Karlsruhe. His paintings have grown increasingly large, incorporating lead, broken glass, and dried plants, resulting in encrusted surfaces and thick impasto. By 1970, while studying informally under Joseph Beuys at Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, his style resembled Georg Baselitz’s, using glass, straw, wood, and plant parts, creating temporary, fragile works that emphasized natural forms. He returned to his birthplace in 1971 and later incorporated German mythology and studied Kabbalah, including the works of Robert Fludd. He made extended journeys throughout Europe, the US, and the Middle East, which influenced his work. In the 1970s and early 1980s, he created works based on Richard Wagner’s Der Ring des Nibelungen, and in the early 1980s produced over thirty paintings referencing Paul Celan’s poem "Todesfuge" ("Death Fugue"). Between 1980 and 1983, he painted looming stone edifices referencing National Socialist architecture, particularly buildings by Albert Speer and Wilhelm Kreis; the grand plaza in To the Unknown Painter (1983) specifically refers to the outdoor courtyard of Hitler’s Chancellery in Berlin. Between 1984 and 1985, he made works on paper with manipulated black-and-white photographs of desolate landscapes with utility poles and power lines, such as Heavy Cloud (1985), in response to West Germany’s controversy over NATO’s nuclear missile stationing. By the mid-1980s, his themes expanded to include art and culture’s fate, occult symbolism, theology, and mysticism, focusing on societal trauma and renewal. His 1980s paintings became more physical, featuring unusual textures and materials. He incorporated ancient Hebrew and Egyptian history, as in Osiris and Isis (1985–87), and in the 1990s shifted to universal myths of existence and meaning. From 1995 to 2001, he produced a cycle of large cosmic paintings. One of his most unusual works is 20 Years of Solitude (1971–1991), a ceiling-high stack of hundreds of white-painted ledgers and handmade books strewn with dirt and dried vegetation, with pages stained by his semen; the title references his frequent masturbation during its creation. He shocked the art world in May 1993 at a dinner party in New York, where he and Renate Graf decorated a candlelit loft with white muslin, skinned animals on hooks, white sand, and waiters dressed as mimes, serving arcane white organ meats, which guests found unappetizing; performers including Johanna Constantine, Lavinia Coop, Armen Ra, and Flotilla DeBarge were hired, and Anohni sang for the guests. Since 2002, he has worked with concrete, creating towers for Pirelli warehouses in Milan, paintings of the sea and boats with leaden objects (2004–05), rune motif paintings (2004–06), and other sculptures. In 2003, he held his first solo show at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac, Salzburg Villa Katz, titled Am Anfang, focusing on history and myths. In 2005, he held a second exhibition, Für Paul Celan, at the same gallery, focusing on books and Germanic mythology linked to Paul Celan’s poetry, featuring eleven canvas works, bound books, and five sculptures, including a monumental outdoor concrete and lead sculpture, lead books with bronze sunflowers, lead ships and wedges, and two lead books from The Secret Life of Plants. The exhibition toured to Paris and Galerie Yvon Lambert. In 2006, his exhibition Velimir Chlebnikov was shown in a studio near Barjac, then at White Cube in London, and finally at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Connecticut; it consists of 30 large (2 × 3 meters) paintings in two banks of 15, hung in a corrugated steel building mimicking the studio, referencing the Russian futurist Velimir Chlebnikov’s theories of a "language of the future" called "Zaum" and cataclysmic sea battles every 317 years, with toy-like, battered, rusted battleships hanging in paint and plaster waves, using black, white, gray, and rust colors. In 2007, he became the first artist since Georges Braque in 1970 to be commissioned to install a permanent work at the Louvre, Paris, and inaugurated the Monumenta exhibitions series at the Grand Palais, honoring Paul Celan and Ingeborg Bachmann. In 2009, he mounted two exhibitions at White Cube in London: Karfunkelfee, a series of forest diptychs and triptychs in glass vitrines filled with Moroccan thorns, referencing a term from German Romanticism by Ingeborg Bachmann, and The Fertile Crescent, a group of epic paintings inspired by a trip to India, linking Mesopotamian civilizations to post-WWII German ruins, with historian Simon Schama noting its meditation on the instability of built grandeur. In Morgenthau Plan (2012), a golden wheat field sculpture is enclosed in a five-meter-high steel cage. That year, he inaugurated a gallery space in Pantin, with the exhibition Die Ungeborenen, accompanied by a publication with a letter by Kiefer and essays by Alexander Kluge and Emmanuel Daydé. He continues to be represented by Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac and participates in group and solo exhibitions at their locations. In 1969, Kiefer began designing books; early examples are worked-over photographs, while recent ones consist of lead sheets layered with paint, minerals, or dried plant matter, such as the lead books on steel shelves symbolizing stored, discarded historical knowledge. The book Rhine (1981) comprises 25 woodcuts suggesting a journey along the Rhine River, with scenes of the unspoiled river interrupted by dark, swirling pages representing the sinking of the battleship Bismarck in 1941 during an Atlantic sortie codenamed Rhine Exercise. Kiefer’s first large studio was in the attic of his home in Hornbach, later moved to a factory in Buchen, and in 1988 he transformed a former brick factory in Höpfingen into an extensive artwork with installations and sculptures. In 1991, after twenty years in the Odenwald, he traveled to India, Mexico, Japan, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. In 1992, he established himself in Barjac, France, where he transformed his 35-hectare studio compound La Ribaute into a Gesamtkunstwerk—a derelict silk factory now housing an extensive system of glass buildings, archives, installations, storerooms, subterranean chambers, and corridors. Sophie Fiennes filmed the studio complex in Barjac for her documentary Over Your Cities Grass Will Grow (2010), which captured both the environment and the artist at work, with one critic noting that the project spans acres, featuring miles of corridors, large studio spaces, landscape paintings, sculptures, and serpentine excavated labyrinths resembling stalagmites or termite mounds, with no clear boundary between work and finished product.

Anselm Kiefer established himself in Barjac, France, in 1992, transforming a derelict silk factory into a 35-hectare studio compound called La Ribaute, which functions as a Gesamtkunstwerk and serves as a commentary on industrialization. The studio features an extensive system of glass buildings, archives, installations, storerooms, and subterranean chambers and corridors. Sophie Fiennes filmed the studio for her 2010 documentary Over Your Cities Grass Will Grow, which captured both the environment and Kiefer at work; one critic described it as a monumental, evolving concept-art organism with miles of corridors, large studio spaces, landscape paintings, sculptures, and earthy, labyrinthine structures resembling stalagmites or termite mounds, where the finished product remains indistinct and in constant transformation. In 2008, Kiefer left Barjac and moved to Paris, relocating his work to a 35,000 sq ft warehouse in Croissy-Beaubourg, formerly the depository for the La Samaritaine department store, transported by a fleet of 110 lorries. His abandoned Barjac studio is now maintained by a caretaker and left uninhabited, quietly awaiting nature’s takeover, as the film’s title suggests. Kiefer returned to Barjac in the summer of 2019 to live and work there. In 1969, he held his first solo exhibition at Galerie am Kaiserplatz in Karlsruhe, and in 1980, along with Georg Baselitz, represented Germany at the Venice Biennale. In 1997, he exhibited at the Museo Correr in Venice with a one-man show focusing on paintings and books. Comprehensive solo exhibitions have been held at the Kunsthalle Düsseldorf (1984), Art Institute of Chicago (1987), Sezon Museum of Art in Tokyo (1993), Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin (1991), Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York (1998), Fondation Beyeler in Basel (2001), Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth (2005), Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington D.C. (2006), and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (2007). In 2007, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao presented a major survey of his recent work, and in 2009, the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibited Broken Flowers and Grass: Nature and Landscape in the Drawings of Anselm Kiefer. In 2007, Kiefer created a permanent site-specific installation at the Louvre with the triptych Athanor and sculptures Danae and Hortus Conclusus, becoming the first living artist to do so since Georges Braque in 1953. In 2008, he installed Palmsonntag (Palm Sunday) (2006) at the First Baptist Church of Los Angeles, reconfiguring the space with sanded floors and a new wall for the reliquary paintings, and later exhibited it at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto with eight new panels. In 2010, he presented Next Year in Jerusalem at Gagosian Gallery, explaining that each work responded to a personal "shock" from recent news. In September 2013, The Hall Art Foundation, in partnership with MASS MoCA, opened a long-term installation in a 10,000 square-foot repurposed building, including Étroits sont les Vaisseaux (Narrow are the Vessels) (2002), The Women of the Revolution (Les Femmes de la Revolution) (1992), Velimir Chlebnikov (2004), and a new large-format lead photograph. In 2015, the Centre Pompidou, Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris, and Museum der bildenden Künste in Leipzig hosted a retrospective celebrating Kiefer’s 70th birthday. In 2016, the Albertina in Vienna held an exhibition of 35 woodcuts from 1977 to 2015. In 2017, the Met Breuer presented Provocations: Anselm Kiefer at The Met Breuer, spanning his career. In May 2018, Kiefer unveiled his first public art commission in the United States at Rockefeller Center, the Uraeus sculpture, inspired by Egyptian religious symbols and Thus Spoke Zarathustra, on view until 22 July. From October 18, 2025, to January 25, 2026, the Saint Louis Art Museum exhibited Anselm Kiefer: Becoming the Sea, a retrospective of his 60-year career, accompanied by a catalog. Kiefer received the Wolf Prize in 1990 and the Praemium Imperiale from the Japan Art Association in 1999, with the latter’s explanatory statement noting his complex engagement with history, his use of figures like Wagner and Goethe to address German cultural history, and his belief in art’s duty to confront the past and ethical questions, enabling the possibility of absolution through human effort. In 2008, he was awarded the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade, the first given to a visual artist, with art historian Werner Spies noting Kiefer’s passion for literature. In 2011, Kiefer was appointed chair of creativity in art at the Collège de France. Due to the spontaneous nature of his process, many of his works face stability concerns, which he acknowledges as part of the transformation process, a theme rooted in alchemy. He favors materials like lead for their alchemical properties—particularly its color shifts during heating, including gold, and its oxidation, which he accelerates with acid—and associates lead with the planet Saturn and magic numbers. Shellac is another favored material, valued for its color and energy, becoming warm when polished. Straw is used for its golden hue and energy, releasing heat and warmth when burned, symbolizing new creation and the cycle of life. The best-selling painting, The Fertile Crescent (2009), sold for $3,997,103 at China Guardian on June 3, 2019, surpassing the previous record of $3,554,500 for To the Unknown Painter (1983) sold at Christie's New York on May 11, 2011, and $3,549,350 for Let a Thousand Flowers Bloom (1999) sold at Christie's London on February 8, 2007. Kiefer’s works are held in public collections including the Hamburger Bahnhof, Berlin; Museum of Modern Art and Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; Detroit Institute of Arts; Tate Modern, London; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto; North Carolina Museum of Art, Raleigh; High Museum of Art, Atlanta; Albright-Knox Art Gallery, Buffalo; Philadelphia Museum of Art; National Gallery of Australia, Canberra; Tel Aviv Museum of Art; and the Albertina, Vienna. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York owns 20 of his rare watercolors. Notable private collectors include Eli Broad and Andrew J. Hall.

Antonio de Padua María Severino López de Santa Anna y Pérez de Lebrón (21 February 1794 – 21 June 1876) was a Mexican general, politician, and caudillo who served as the 8th president of Mexico on multiple occasions between 1833 and 1855 and held the office of vice president from 1837 to 1839. He is widely regarded as a controversial and pivotal figure in 19th-century Mexican politics, often referred to as an "uncrowned monarch" and associated with the "Age of Santa Anna." Born in Xalapa, Veracruz, into a respected Spanish family, he was named after his father, licenciado Antonio López de Santa Anna y Pérez, a lawyer, and his mother, Manuela Pérez de Lebrón y Cortés. His family prospered in Veracruz, where the merchant class dominated politics; his paternal uncle, Ángel López de Santa Anna, was a public clerk who became disgruntled when barred from moving to Mexico City due to the Spanish crown’s preference for peninsular-born Spaniards. Santa Anna’s mother supported his military career over his father’s preference for commerce, and her relationship with the intendant of Veracruz secured his early military appointment. The family had seven children, including four sisters and two brothers, with Santa Anna being close to his sister Francisca and brother Manuel, who also joined the army. His origins in Veracruz gave him immunity from yellow fever, a significant advantage in military campaigns, and contributed to his rise as a provincial leader. He began his military career in 1810 at age 16 with the Fijo de Veracruz regiment, fought against insurgents during the Mexican War of Independence, and was wounded in 1811. He later served in Texas and earned recognition for bravery at the Battle of Medina. When Agustín de Iturbide switched sides in 1821 to support independence, Santa Anna joined him, was granted command of Veracruz, and later rebelled against Iturbide in 1822, claiming the dissolution of the Constituent Congress as justification. He then participated in the Plan of Casa Mata, which led to the end of the First Mexican Empire and the establishment of a republic. In 1823, he was sent to Yucatán, where he planned an invasion of Cuba but abandoned it when Spanish reinforcements arrived. After the 1828 election, when conservative Manuel Gómez Pedraza won, Santa Anna rebelled, nullified the results, and expelled Spanish nationals, leading to Gómez Pedraza’s resignation and the rise of Guerrero. In 1829, Santa Anna defeated a Spanish invasion at Tampico, earning the title "Victor of Tampico" and "Savior of the Patria," and styled himself the "Napoleon of the West." When Vice President Anastasio Bustamante overthrew Guerrero in 1829, Santa Anna seized Veracruz’s customs revenues and declared rebellion, forcing Bustamante’s cabinet to resign and leading to new elections in 1833. Santa Anna was elected president on 1 April 1833, but he was not interested in governing and is described as an "absentee president," with Vice President Valentín Gómez Farías managing day-to-day affairs. Gómez Farías implemented liberal reforms, including abolishing tithing, seizing church property, closing the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, and secularizing Franciscan missions in Alta California. These actions provoked strong opposition from the church and army, leading to the Plan of Cuernavaca, which called for the repeal of the Ley del Caso, the removal of reform supporters, and the recognition of Santa Anna as the sole authority. As opposition grew, Santa Anna returned to the presidency, and Gómez Farías resigned, marking a shift from a federalist republic to a unitary central republic. Historians debate the number of his presidencies: Will Fowler cites six, the Texas State Historical Association claims five, Alexander Dawson and the University of Texas Libraries state eleven, though the latter notes he was only president for six years due to short terms. Santa Anna is viewed negatively in Mexican history, often ranked as "the principal inhabitant even today of Mexico's black pantheon of those who failed the nation," and considered one of the most unpopular and controversial Mexican presidents. After being overthrown and exiled in 1855 through the Plan of Ayutla, he faded from prominence during the Reform War, the Second French Intervention, and the establishment of the Second Mexican Empire. An elderly Santa Anna was allowed to return in 1874 by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada and died in relative obscurity in 1876. He is best known in the United States for his roles in the Texas Revolution and the Mexican–American War, where his leadership prolonged the conflict and contributed to the Mexican Cession and the Gadsden Purchase in 1853. His intermittent rule from 1832 to 1853 saw the loss of Texas, military failures, and territorial concessions. Historian Alexander Dawson notes that Santa Anna switched sides between the Liberal and Conservative Parties, playing a key role in both discarding and restoring the liberal Constitution of 1824. He is remembered as a populist caudillo who used military power to dissolve Congress and referred to himself as "His Most Serene Highness."

Santa Anna's influence was marked by secret political maneuvers involving Masonic lodges; he declared void the laws passed by Congress and local legislatures in favor of reforms, requested protection from Santa Anna to implement his plan and recognize him as the sole authority, removed deputies and officials enforcing reform laws and decrees, and provided military support to Gómez Farías to carry out the reforms. As public opinion turned against the reforms, Santa Anna returned to the presidency and Gómez Farías resigned, setting the stage for conservatives to transform Mexico from a federalist republic into a unitary central republic. Conservatives viewed Gómez Farías's liberal reforms as radical and a threat to elite power; Santa Anna's initial support for the reforms—followed by a more extensive one in 1855—may have been a test of liberalism, allowing him plausible deniability while monitoring reactions to attacks on army and church privileges and the confiscation of church wealth. In May 1834, Santa Anna ordered the disarmament of civic militias and urged Congress to abolish the controversial Ley del Caso; on 12 June, he dissolved Congress and announced the Plan of Cuernavaca, establishing a new Catholic, centralist, and conservative government. In exchange for preserving church and army privileges, the church agreed to provide a monthly donation of 30,000–40,000 pesos, which the santanistas succeeded in achieving, forcing the church to financially support the republic. On 4 January 1835, Santa Anna returned to his hacienda, appointing Miguel Barragán as acting president, and replaced the 1824 constitution with the "Siete Leyes" ("The Seven Laws"). He did not participate in the conservative efforts to replace the federalist constitution with a unitary system, remaining uneasy with their political direction, and was not present during any deliberations that led to the abolition of the federalist charter or the creation of the 1836 Constitution. Several states rebelled, including Alta California, Nuevo México, Tabasco, Sonora, Coahuila y Tejas, San Luis Potosí, Querétaro, Durango, Guanajuato, Michoacán, Yucatán, Jalisco, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, and Zacatecas, with some forming independent governments such as the Republic of the Rio Grande, the Republic of Yucatán, and the Republic of Texas; resistance was fueled by Santa Anna's reprisals against defeated enemies. The Zacatecas militia, led by Francisco García Salinas and armed with .753 caliber British 'Brown Bess' muskets and Baker .61 rifles, was defeated by Santa Anna's "Army of Operations" on 12 May 1835, resulting in nearly 3,000 prisoners and a 48-hour looting of Zacatecas City. After conquering Zacatecas, Santa Anna planned to move to Coahuila y Tejas to suppress the rebellion supported by U.S. settlers. In 1835, Santa Anna repealed the Mexican constitution, citing that American settlers in Texas were not paying taxes or tariffs because they did not receive government services, and thus new settlers were barred from Texas, a response to U.S. attempts to purchase the territory. Late in 1835, the Texas Department of Coahuila y Tejas rebelled and declared independence on 2 March 1836, with the northeastern region settled by American immigrants, including those from Moses Austin's party, who had been accepted by Spanish authorities for defense against foreign threats, though Mexico had declared independence from Spain before Austin's death. Santa Anna marched north to reassert control over Texas with brutal force, facing severe logistical challenges including cold weather, inadequate clothing, food shortages, poor medical supplies, and a lack of horses, mules, cattle, and wagons, with hostile Indigenous groups attacking stragglers and waterborne diseases spreading rapidly. The army's officers were largely incompetent, and the rigid hierarchy prevented Santa Anna from being informed of these problems. At the Battle of the Alamo on 6 March 1836, Santa Anna's forces killed 189 Texan defenders, and at the Goliad Massacre on 27 March 1836, over 342 Texan prisoners were executed; Santa Anna claimed that killing the Alamo defenders was necessary because Texan commander William B. Travis was disrespectful to him and that sparing them would have allowed Sam Houston to gain power threatening Santa Anna. The Mexican victory at the Alamo provided time for Houston and his forces to gain experience and weaponry. Despite Houston's poor command, Texas forces completely defeated Santa Anna's larger army at the Battle of San Jacinto on 21 April 1836. The day after, James Austin Sylvester captured Santa Anna near a marsh; he had hastily dressed in a dead Mexican dragoon's uniform but was quickly recognized. After three weeks in captivity, Texas President David G. Burnet and Santa Anna signed the Treaties of Velasco, in which Santa Anna acknowledged the full, entire, and perfect independence of the Republic of Texas, in exchange for guarantees of his safety and transport to Veracruz. In Mexico City, a new government declared the treaties null and void. Poinsett criticized Santa Anna, saying he had no sympathy for him now after having once been a passionate advocate of liberty, to which Santa Anna replied that he had once supported liberty with sincerity but soon realized its folly, stating that Mexico's people were unenlightened and under the influence of Catholic clergy, making despotism a proper and wise government. After time in exile and meeting U.S. President Andrew Jackson in 1837, Santa Anna was allowed to return to Mexico and retired to his hacienda in Veracruz, where he wrote a manifesto reflecting on his decisions. In 1838, Santa Anna found redemption after Mexico rejected demands for financial compensation for losses, prompting France to launch the Pastry War by landing forces in Veracruz. The Mexican government gave Santa Anna control of the army and ordered him to defend the nation; he engaged the French at Veracruz, retreated after a failed assault, and sustained injuries to his left leg and hand, requiring amputation of much of his leg, which he buried with full military honors. Despite Mexico's eventual capitulation, Santa Anna used his war service and sacrifice to re-enter politics. When Bustamante's presidency collapsed, supporters asked Santa Anna to take control of the provisional government, and he became president for the fifth time, ruling a nation with an empty treasury, facing rebellion led by Generals José de Urrea and José Antonio Mexía, which he crushed in Puebla. Santa Anna ruled more dictatorially, banning anti-Santanista newspapers and imprisoning dissidents. In 1842, he launched a military expedition into Texas, inflicting casualties without political gain, but it persuaded Texans of the potential benefits of annexation by the United States. After the 1842 elections, when a new Congress opposed his rule, Santa Anna attempted to restore the treasury by raising taxes, leading several states to withdraw from the central government, with Yucatán and Laredo declaring independence. With growing resentment, Santa Anna stepped down and fled Mexico City in December 1844; his buried leg was dug up by a mob and dragged through the streets until nothing remained. Fearing for his life, he tried to evade capture but was apprehended in January 1845 by Native Americans near Xico, turned over to authorities, and imprisoned; his life was spared, and he was exiled to Cuba. In 1846, following American victories at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma in the Mexican-American War, President Mariano Paredes was removed, and the new government sought to restore the 1824 constitution, with Santa Anna again assuming the presidency. Santa Anna, having been in exile for only a year, returned to Mexico on 6 August 1846, two days after Paredes' removal, stating he had no ambition for the presidency but would use his military experience in the conflict with the U.S. U.S. President James K. Polk sought to acquire northern territory by purchase or force, but Mexico refused. Polk sent agents to secretly meet with exiled Santa Anna, believing they had secured a promise for him to lift a blockade and broker a deal; however, upon returning to Mexico with an army, Santa Anna reneged and took up arms against the U.S. invasion. With no quick resolution, Polk authorized an invasion to take Mexico City, redirecting most of General Zachary Taylor's troops to General Winfield Scott's army. Santa Anna mobilized troops and artillery and rapidly marched north; his forces outnumbered Taylor's, but were exhausted, ill-clothed, hungry, and poorly equipped when they clashed at the Battle of Buena Vista on 22–23 February 1847. After two days of hard fighting, Santa Anna withdrew just as victory was imminent, taking war trophies such as cannons and battle flags. When Scott's army landed at Veracruz, Santa Anna quickly moved south to defend the capital. He set defenses at Cerro Gordo, but U.S. forces outflanked him and defeated his army. The path to Mexico City was clear; Santa Anna aimed to protect the capital and waged defensive warfare, placing strong defenses at El Peñon, which Scott avoided. Battles at Contreras, Churubusco, and Molino del Rey were lost; at Contreras, General Gabriel Valencia, a political and military rival of Santa Anna, disobeyed his orders and was routed. The Battle for Mexico City and the Battle of Chapultepec were hard-fought losses, and American forces captured the capital. Despite his tactical flaws and political ambition, Santa Anna was committed to fighting to the end, prolonging the war by at least a year and denying Polk's dream of a short war. One of Santa Anna's most personal and humiliating incidents was the capture during the Battle of Cerro Gordo of his prosthetic cork leg, which remains a war trophy in the Illinois State Military Museum and is no longer on display; a second leg, a peg, was captured by the 4th Illinois and used as a baseball bat, displayed at the home of Illinois Governor Richard J. Oglesby in Decatur; a replacement leg is displayed at the Museo Nacional de Historia in Mexico City. The prosthetic leg later influenced international politics; as U.S.-Mexico relations improved before World War II, Illinois considered returning the leg, and in 1942 a bill was introduced in the state legislature, with the Association of Limb Manufacturers wanting to participate in the repatriation. The state passed a non-binding resolution to return the leg, but the National Guard denied the transfer; as of 2025, the leg remains in the Illinois State Military Museum in Springfield. Following Mexico's defeat in 1848, Santa Anna went into exile in Kingston, Jamaica, then moved to Turbaco in New Granada (now Colombia). In April 1853, conservatives who had overthrown a weak liberal government under the Plan de Hospicio, drawn up by clerics in the cathedral chapter of Guadalajara, invited him to return to Mexico. Santa Anna was elected president on 17 March 1853; he honored his promises to the church by revoking a decree denying protection for monastic vows, a reform from 20 years earlier by Gómez Farías. The Jesuits, expelled from Spanish realms in 1767, were allowed to return to Mexico to educate poorer classes, and much of their property, confiscated and sold by the crown, was restored. Although he gave himself exalted titles, including "Most Serene Highness" and the full title "Hero [benemérito] of the nation, General of Division, Grand Master of the National and Distinguished Order of Guadalupe, Grand Cross of the Royal and Distinguished Spanish Order of Carlos III, and President of the Mexican Republic," his administration was no more successful than previous ones, relying on loans from moneylenders and support from conservative elites, the church, and the army. A major miscalculation was Santa Anna's sale of territory to the U.S. in the Gadsden Purchase, where the land in northwest Mexico (La Mesilla) was easier for building a transcontinental railway in the U.S. The purchase money was supposed to go to Mexico's treasury, but Santa Anna wanted immediate access to funds and bargained with American bankers for immediate cash, while they gained rights to future revenue. The deal netted Mexico only $250,000 against $650,000 in credit to the bankers, with James Gadsden believing the amount was likely higher. A group of liberals, including Alvarez, Benito Juárez, and Ignacio Comonfort, overthrew Santa Anna under the Plan of Ayutla in 1855, and he went into exile once again. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the United States paid.

Santa Anna made a major miscalculation by selling territory to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase, which involved land in northwest Mexico known as La Mesilla. This area was considered easier for building a transcontinental railway in the U.S., and the purchase money was intended to benefit Mexico’s empty treasury. However, Santa Anna sought immediate access to funds and negotiated with American bankers to receive cash upfront, with the bankers gaining rights to future revenue. The deal resulted in Mexico receiving only $250,000 against a credit of $650,000 going to the bankers, a sum James Gadsden believed was likely much higher. A group of liberal leaders, including Alvarez, Benito Juárez, and Ignacio Comonfort, overthrew Santa Anna under the Plan of Ayutla, leading to his exile in 1855. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the United States paid Mexico $15 million for the land, known as the Mexican Cession. Santa Anna married twice: first in 1825 to Inés García, daughter of wealthy Spanish parents in Veracruz, with whom he had four children—María de Guadalupe, María del Carmen, Manuel, and Antonio López de Santa Anna y García. His family background was of modest means, but his creole lineage and the dowry from Inés allowed him to purchase his first hacienda, Manga de Clavo, in Veracruz. The first Spanish ambassador to Mexico, Fanny Calderón de la Barca, visited Inés at Manga de Clavo and noted the hospitality, including a breakfast where Inés offered her a cigar and others followed suit. Two months after Inés’ death in 1844, Santa Anna married 16-year-old María de los Dolores de Tosta; they rarely lived together, with De Tosta residing in Mexico City and Santa Anna traveling for political and military duties. They had no children, and biographer Will Fowler speculated the marriage was either platonic or that De Tosta was infertile. Several women claimed to have borne Santa Anna natural children; in his will, he acknowledged and provided for four—Paula, María de la Merced, Petra, and José López de Santa Anna—and biographers have identified three more: Pedro López de Santa Anna, Ángel and Augustina Rosa López de Santa Anna. From 1855 to 1874, Santa Anna lived in exile in Cuba, the United States, Colombia, and Saint Thomas, leaving Mexico due to his unpopularity after his defeat in 1848. During exile, he engaged in gambling and business ventures, and was a passionate fan of cockfighting, maintaining many roosters for competitions. In the 1850s, he traveled to New York City with a shipment of chicle, intending to sell it for carriage wheels, but failed to convince U.S. manufacturers of its usefulness in tires. Although he introduced chewing gum to the U.S., he did not profit from it. Thomas Adams, assigned to assist Santa Anna, experimented with chicle and, though his attempts to use it as rubber failed, helped found the chewing gum industry with a product called "chiclets." In 1865, Santa Anna tried to return to Mexico to serve during the French invasion, but was refused by Juárez. That year, a schooner owned by Gilbert Thompson, son-in-law of Daniel Tompkins, brought him to Staten Island, where he attempted to raise funds for an army to retake Mexico City. In 1874, Santa Anna returned to Mexico under a general amnesty issued by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, having become crippled and nearly blind from cataracts. He died at his home in Mexico City on 21 June 1876 at age 82 and was buried with full military honors in a glass coffin at Panteón del Tepeyac Cemetery. Santa Anna was highly controversial, with Will Fowler describing him as a liberal, Republican, army man, hero, revolutionary, and regional strongman, but never a politician, who presented himself as a mediator against party politics and was more willing to lead armies than govern. Historian Gates Brown considers Santa Anna one of history’s worst military leaders due to his errors in two wars that cost Mexico significant territory. During the Texas Revolution, Santa Anna attacked the Alamo after knowing the defenders would not be reinforced, despite having time to build a logistical base at San Antonio. He lost more men than the defenders, sacrificing a third of his force, and his subsequent executions at the Alamo and Goliad fueled rebellion. He also mistakenly believed General Houston would not attack with a smaller, tired force, contributing to his defeat at San Jacinto. In the Mexican-American War, Santa Anna marched newly recruited and inexperienced troops across 385 kilometers (239 miles) of desert in winter without resupplying, leading to heavy Mexican casualties at Buena Vista. At Cerro Gordo, he dismissed advice from officer Manuel Robles Pezuela to reinforce Atalaya hill, believing the terrain made it unnecessary; the U.S. attack and flanking maneuver destroyed Mexico’s chance to stop General Winfield Scott’s advance on Mexico City. Santa Anna became prominent in Tejano folk memory due to his role in the Texas Revolution and the Alamo. Texas educators, writers, and officials portrayed him as the central antagonist in Texas’ independence narrative, contributing to an exaggerated view of his personal influence and a symbolic representation of Mexican autocracy, rather than a complex figure navigating internal Mexican instability. Stephen Oleszek argues that Santa Anna’s rise as a Texas folk legend is tied to myth-making around the Alamo, where he was depicted as a symbol of despotism while Alamo defenders like William B. Travis and James Bowie were portrayed as heroes, reinforcing a hero-villain dichotomy to unify Anglo-Americans and justify the Texas Revolution. This narrative has been embedded in textbooks, media, and the slogan "Remember the Alamo!" More recent works, such as Santa Anna in Texas: A Mexican American Viewpoint, show that Mexican perspectives on Santa Anna were divided and often did not align with the villainous Texan narrative. In the 21st century, historians emphasize the distinction between cultural memory and historical reality, noting that Santa Anna’s reputation evolved from a historical figure into a legend centered on the Battle of the Alamo.

Antonio Mucci was an Argentine politician who served as Minister of Labor under President Raúl Alfonsín. He advocated for reducing the influence of Peronism within Argentine unions and assisted the President in drafting a bill to be presented to Congress for that objective. However, he resigned from his position after the bill was rejected by Congress. This article about an Argentine politician is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Antonio Negri (/ˈnɛɡri/; Italian: [ˈneːɡri]; 1 August 1933 – 16 December 2023) was an Italian political philosopher renowned as one of the most prominent theorists of autonomism and co-author of the books *Empire* and *Multitude: War and Democracy in the Age of Empire* with Michael Hardt. Born in Padua, in the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, Negri’s father was a communist militant from Bologna in Emilia-Romagna, and although he died when Negri was two, his political engagement influenced Negri’s early exposure to Marxism; his mother was a teacher from Poggio Rusco in Lombardy. Negri began his activism in the 1950s with the Roman Catholic youth organization Gioventù Italiana di Azione Cattolica (GIAC), joined the Italian Socialist Party in 1956, and became a communist in 1955 while working at the Nahsonim kibbutz in central Israel, a Jewish communist community based on Zionist socialism. He earned a doctorate in philosophy in 1956 and was hired as a professor of dottrina dello Stato ("state doctrine"), a field akin to the philosophy of law, at the University of Padua, where he taught state and constitutional theory. In the early 1960s, he joined the editorial group of *Quaderni Rossi*, a journal that marked the intellectual revival of Marxism outside the Communist Party. In 1969, he co-founded the Potere Operaio (Worker Power) group with Oreste Scalzone and Franco Piperno, launching the operaismo (workerism) movement. On 16 March 1978, former Italian prime minister Aldo Moro was kidnapped in Rome by the Red Brigades (Brigate Rosse or BR), and nine days before his death, the BR called Moro’s family to inform them of his impending death—this call was later revealed to have been made by Valerio Morucci, not Negri. On 7 April 1979, Negri was arrested and charged with kidnapping, assassination, and insurrection, including leadership of the Red Brigades, masterminding the 1978 kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro, and plotting to overthrow the government. While a leader of the BR testified that Negri had nothing to do with the group, charges such as "armed insurrection against the state" were dropped, but he was sentenced in absentia to 30 years in prison in 1984 after fleeing to France, with an additional four years for moral responsibility for political violence in the 1960s and 1970s, specifically for instigating the murder of Carlo Saronio and for "morally concurred" involvement in the murder of Andrea Lombardini during a failed bank robbery. Michel Foucault remarked, "Isn't he in jail simply for being an intellectual?" and French philosophers Félix Guattari and Gilles Deleuze signed *L'Appel des intellectuels français contre la répression en Italie* in 1977 in protest against Negri’s imprisonment. Italian President Francesco Cossiga described Negri as "a psychopath" who "poisoned the minds of an entire generation of Italy's youth." In 1983, while still in prison, Negri was elected to the Italian legislature as a member of the Radical Party, used parliamentary immunity to be freed, and fled to France with the help of Félix Guattari and Amnesty International, though his immunity was later revoked by the Chamber of Deputies. Protected by the Mitterrand doctrine, he taught at Paris VIII (Vincennes) and the Collège international de philosophie, alongside Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, and Gilles Deleuze. In 1997, after a plea-bargain that reduced his sentence from 30 to 13 years, he returned to Italy to serve the remainder of his sentence, during which time he wrote many of his most influential works. He was released in 2003 and lived in Venice and Paris with his partner, the French philosopher Judith Revel. He was the father of film director Anna Negri. Negri was a central theorist of autonomist Marxism and a prominent figure in libertarian socialism, communism, and Marxism. In *Empire*, co-authored with Michael Hardt, they ask how labor, with its life-affirming potential, has become a tool of capitalist discipline, exploitation, and domination, and they critique liberal and socialist notions of labor and institutional reform from a radical democratic perspective, challenging the state-form itself. They argue that the rise of "Empire" marks the end of national conflict, where the enemy is no longer ideological or national but is instead a criminal threatening the law, and is both "banalized" and "absolutized." Empire is constituted by a monarchy (the United States and G8, and institutions like NATO, IMF, WTO), an oligarchy (multinational corporations and nation-states), and a democracy (NGOs and the UN). The book asserts that resistance to Empire is only possible through negation—“the will to be against”—and that although Empire is total, economic inequality persists and the identity of the poor endures. *Multitude* picks up where *Empire* leaves off, analyzing war and its contradictions, and focusing on the multitude and democracy.
