It is presented as a reiteration from a new point of view in a more accessible style, remaining a philosophical work aimed at shaping a conceptual ground for democratic political processes rather than offering a concrete program. In 2009, Negri completed *Commonwealth*, the final book in a trilogy beginning with *Empire* and continuing with *Multitude* in 2004. In *Commonwealth*, the authors introduce the concept of "the republic of property," stating that property remains the foundation of every modern political constitution. Part two explores altermodernity, which involves breaking with the fixed dialectic between modern sovereignty and antimodern resistance, transforming tradition, identity, and resistance into new forms. They argue that communism is defined by the common, capitalism by the private, and socialism (identified with statism) by the public. Alex Callinicos notes that the "common" includes not only natural resources but also languages, social practices, and modes of sociality, which are both means and results of biopolitical production. David Harvey observes that Hardt and Negri seek an altermodernity outside the binary of modernity and anti-modernity, proposing a new form of communism that operates beyond the choice between capitalism and socialism, and that revolutionary thought must engage identity politics as the primary vehicle for struggle against the "republic of property." In a discussion with Harvey, Hardt and Negri clarify that singularity refers to a multiplicity of others, internal division, and a process of becoming over time. After *Commonwealth*, Negri wrote articles on the Arab Spring and Occupy movements. In May 2012, he self-published (with Michael Hardt) an electronic pamphlet titled *Declaration*, arguing that the Occupy and encampment movements explore new forms of democracy; the introduction was published at Jacobin under the title "Take Up the Baton." In October 2011, he and Hardt published an article in *Foreign Affairs* titled "The Encampment in Lower Manhattan Speaks to a Failure of Representation." In 2013, Negri published *Spinoza: Politics and Postmodernity*, a collection of essays on Spinoza and his contemporary relevance, translated by William McCuaig. In 2017, Negri and Michael Hardt published *Assembly*, which reflects on contemporary capitalism and social movements, drawing on concepts from their Empire trilogy such as the common, the multitude, and globalization. It introduces the concept of "assembly," inspired by Deleuze and Guattari’s "assemblage," as a way of understanding mass movements and constituent power. The book analyzes events since *Commonwealth* was published in 2009, including the rise of right-wing populism, Occupy Wall Street, automation, and the digital economy. It proposes that leadership in movements should serve specific, tactical, and short-term ends, while the multitude (or collective) articulates long-term goals to which leadership must submit. The book received generally positive reviews, with Kyle Perry arguing that advocates for a democratic world must embrace leadership, strategizing, and institution-building, and that new institutions should be "nonsovereign" and foster continuity and organization. Terence Renaud notes that while much of Hardt and Negri’s project may appear exhausted given the changed political terrain, they effectively highlight the internal challenges facing a resurgent left, such as sectarianism, heavy-handed leadership, and complacency, and insist on a self-critical, internally democratic left. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays, translated and compiled into English. The first volume, *Marx and Foucault*, was published on 16 December 2016, in which he aims to show how the thinking of Marx and Foucault was synthesized into an original theoretical framework.

Terence Renaud, writing for the Los Angeles Review of Books, notes that given the significant changes in the political landscape since the publication of Empire in 2000, much of Hardt and Negri's project now appears to have concluded its contribution. Nevertheless, the authors effectively highlight the internal challenges a resurgent left faces, such as degenerating into sectarian conflict, authoritarian leadership, and complacency in its self-perception. Hardt and Negri advocate for a self-critical and internally democratic left that continuously questions its own assumptions, emphasizing that to transform society, the left must first transform itself. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays translated and compiled into English. The first volume, Marx and Foucault, was released on 16 December 2016, aiming to demonstrate how Marx and Foucault's thought were synthesized, particularly in the context of Italy from May '68 onward. The second volume, From the Factory to the Metropolis, published in February 2018, analyzes the shift from the traditional industrial proletarian 'mass worker' to the contemporary 'socialised worker' and examines the modern 'metropolis' as a space of antagonism between finance capital (operating through rents) and the 'cognitive proletariat,' with the central question being how the 'common' of the latter can be mobilized to destroy capitalism. The third volume, Spinoza: Then and Now, published in February 2020, explores how Spinoza's thought represents a radical departure from past ideas and serves as a vital tool for envisioning politics beyond capitalism. On 29 October 2021, Negri released the first volume of a new trilogy, Marx in Movement: Operaismo in Context, which provides an account of the history of Italian Autonomist (or 'Autonomist Marxist') thought, especially focusing on Negri's development of the concept of the 'social worker' as a way to update Marxism in response to changes since Marx's era of factory-based labor. Negri married Paola Meo in 1962; they had two children, Anna and Francesco, and later divorced. He has another daughter, Nina Negri, from a separate relationship. He met the philosopher Judith Revel in 1996 and married her in 2016. Negri died in Paris on 16 December 2023, at the age of 90. The works listed in order of their first publication in English are: Transcendence, Spirituality, Practices, Immanence: A Conversation with Antonio Negri by Judith Revel, published in Rethinking Marxism, 28(3–4), 470–478 (2016).

The Applied Catalysis Award, established in 2008 by the Royal Society of Chemistry, recognizes individuals for creativity and excellence in novel approaches or the application of catalysis in industry. The winner is selected by the Industry & Technology Division Awards Committee and is presented with £2000, a medal, and a certificate.

The Applied Inorganic Chemistry Award was established in 2008 and is awarded biennially by the Dalton division of the Royal Society of Chemistry for "outstanding contributions to the development of any branch of inorganic chemistry which has an application in industry." The recipient delivers a lecture tour across the UK, receives a medal, and is awarded £2000. The award was discontinued in 2020.

A total lunar eclipse occurred at the Moon’s descending node of orbit on Monday, April 24, 1967, with an umbral magnitude of 1.3356. This event took place when the Moon moved into Earth's shadow, causing it to be darkened, and specifically, the Moon's near side completely passed into Earth's umbral shadow, defining a total lunar eclipse. Unlike solar eclipses, which are visible only in a small region, a lunar eclipse can be observed from anywhere on the night side of Earth. A total lunar eclipse can last up to nearly two hours, whereas a total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes at any given location due to the smaller size of the Moon's shadow. Occurring just 16 hours after perigee on April 23, 1967, at 20:00 UTC, the Moon’s apparent diameter was larger. This eclipse was the first in a tetrad, a series of four total lunar eclipses occurring consecutively, with the others on October 18, 1967; April 13, 1968; and October 6, 1968. The Surveyor 3 probe was active on the Moon during this eclipse. It was completely visible over northeast Asia, Australia, and much of the Pacific Ocean, rising over most of Asia and setting over North America and western and central South America. This eclipse is part of an eclipse season, which occurs roughly every six months and lasts about 35 days, repeating every 173 days; two or three eclipses typically happen during each season, with each eclipse separated by a fortnight. It is also part of a semester series, repeating approximately every 177 days and 4 hours at alternating nodes of the Moon’s orbit. The penumbral lunar eclipse on August 27, 1969, occurs in the next lunar year eclipse set. The Metonic cycle, repeating nearly every 19 years, aligns the Earth's shadow with the same calendar date and background stars. This eclipse belongs to Saros series 121, which repeats every 18 years, 11 days, and contains 82 events, beginning with a penumbral lunar eclipse on October 6, 1047, and ending with a penumbral eclipse on March 18, 2508. The series includes partial eclipses from May 10, 1408 to July 3, 1498; total eclipses from July 13, 1516 to May 26, 2021; and a second set of partial eclipses from June 6, 2039 to August 11, 2147. The longest duration of totality occurred in member 43 on October 18, 1660, lasting 100 minutes and 29 seconds. All eclipses in this Saros series occur at the Moon’s descending node. Eclipses are tabulated in three columns, with every third eclipse in the same column being one exeligmos apart, meaning they cast shadows over similar parts of Earth. This eclipse is part of a tritos cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 135 synodic months (≈ 3986.63 days, or 11 years minus 1 month), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, though groupings of three tritos cycles (≈ 33 years minus 3 months) show similar eclipses. It is also part of the long period inex cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 358 synodic months (≈ 10,571.95 days, or 29 years minus 20 days), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, but groupings of three inex cycles (≈ 87 years minus 2 months) show similar eclipses. A lunar eclipse is typically preceded and followed by solar eclipses by 9 years and 5.5 days (a half saros), and this lunar eclipse is related to two annular solar eclipses of Solar Saros 128.

Arch Linux is an open source, rolling release Linux distribution that is kept up-to-date by regularly updating its individual software components. It provides monthly "snapshots" used as installation media and is intentionally minimal, requiring users to configure the system manually during installation to include only the software they need. The distribution uses Pacman, a package manager specifically developed for Arch Linux, to install, remove, and update software packages, with support for automatic dependency resolution. Pacman manages binary packages with a .pkg.tar.zst extension (zstd compression) or .pkg.tar.xz, and packages are compiled for the x86-64 architecture. All official packages are obtained from the Arch Linux package tree. The Arch User Repository (AUR) is a community-driven repository that hosts PKGBUILD scripts for software not included in the official repositories or alternative versions of existing packages; these scripts are built using the Arch build system (ABS) via the makepkg command and are not binary packages. AUR packages can be built manually or installed using AUR helper tools, though Arch developers emphasize that automatic downloading and execution of PKGBUILDs is not included in official repositories due to security risks, such as a malware incident on 19 July 2025 involving a modified Firefox build that was a remote access trojan (RAT). The AUR allows users to contribute PKGBUILDs, with those receiving 10 or more votes or over 1% usage from pkgstats eligible for promotion to the extra repository. The official repositories include core, extra, community, and testing, with community merged into extra in May 2023 and the unstable repository discontinued in July 2008; core-staging and extra-staging are used for rebuilds but are discouraged for use. The distribution does not schedule releases or provide traditional versions, instead relying on a rolling release model where packages are frequently updated, allowing systems to stay current. Manual interventions are occasionally required, as noted in the news section. Arch Linux's design emphasizes simplicity and transparency, avoiding complex abstractions and instead promoting direct user interaction through clean, well-documented configuration files, which has earned it a reputation as a distribution for advanced users who prefer the command line. The current logo was designed by Thayer Williams in 2007. Installation can be done manually via the Arch Wiki or automatically using the default 'archinstall' script introduced in April 2021, or through the 'pacstrap' utility. The distribution supports x86-64 processors and originally only targeted IA-32 CPUs, with the first x86-64 ISO released in April 2006. i686 support ended with the February 2017 ISO, making it unsupported in November 2017, and the community derivative Arch Linux 32 continues support for 32-bit hardware. The migration to systemd as the default init system began in August 2012 and became standard in October 2012, replacing the earlier SysV-style init. Until Pacman version 4.0.0, package signing was not supported, and packages were not verified for authenticity; however, package signing became mandatory for new builds in November 2011 and fully enabled by default in March 2012. The Arch build system enables source compilation and allows users to create custom PKGBUILD scripts to build packages compatible with Pacman. Arch Linux includes both libre and nonfree software, with the default kernel containing proprietary blobs, meaning it is not endorsed by the GNU project; the linux-libre kernel can be installed via the AUR or Parabola's repositories. The distribution is working toward making all official packages reproducible, allowing verification of package integrity across different environments. Arch Linux has a comprehensive community-run documentation site, the ArchWiki. The project was initiated in March 2002 by Judd Vinet, who chose the name for its meaning of "the principal," as in "arch-enemy," and stepped down in October 2007, transferring leadership to Aaron Griffin. Griffin stepped down in February 2020 after a voting period, transferring control to Levente Polyak, with a new two-year term added for the Project Leader position. In March 2021, developers considered porting packages to x86_64-v3 (Intel Haswell-era processors), and in February 2022, debug packages were introduced. In late 2021, Pacman 6.0 was released with support for parallel downloads. On 14 August 2025, the Arch User Repository, forums, and website were hit by a distributed denial-of-service attack, causing temporary unavailability and severely slowing or blocking AUR downloads. SteamOS 3.0, used in the Steam Deck, is based on Arch Linux. CachyOS is a gaming-focused distribution based on Arch Linux. Projects like PacBSD and Arch Hurd are adapting Arch Linux tools to other kernels, and the Arch Linux ARM project aims to port the distribution to ARM devices like the Raspberry Pi. Arch Linux has received reviews from OSNews, LWN.net, Tux Machines, and DistroWatch Weekly, with Greg Kroah-Hartman praising its performance and community feedback. In a 2023 DistroWatch poll, 17% of respondents used Arch and 30% used an Arch derivative, and as of 2025, Arch holds the third-highest average rating (9.18) on DistroWatch, behind only Artix Linux and BigLinux, both Arch derivatives.

Argentina competed at the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens, Greece, from 13 to 29 August 2004, marking its twenty-first appearance at the Olympic Games, with absences from the 1904 Summer Olympics in St. Louis, the 1912 Summer Olympics in Stockholm, and the 1980 Summer Olympics in Moscow due to support for the United States-led boycott. Carlos Espínola served as the nation's flag bearer at the opening ceremony. A total of 152 competitors—106 men and 46 women—participated in 86 events across 22 sports. Argentina's total medal count of six represented its best performance since the 1948 Summer Olympics, securing its first gold medals since 1952 and achieving its highest position in the medal table up to that point, placing 35th overall. Argentina qualified athletes in athletics events (up to three at the 'A' Standard and one at the 'B' Standard), qualifying a men's team, two competitors for the canoeing flatwater event, one fencer, nine judoka, and a team for the men's indoor tournament. The men's basketball roster, men's field hockey roster (headed by Jorge Ruiz), women's field hockey roster (headed by Sergio Vigil), men's football roster (headed by Marcelo Bielsa), and men's volleyball roster (headed by Alberto Armoa) were all officially listed. Argentina had one woman competing in artistic gymnastics as an individual. Swimmers earned qualifying standards in events with a maximum of two at the A-standard and one at the B-standard. Qualification results used the legend: Q = Qualify to final; q = Qualify to semifinal; FA = Final A (medal); FB = Final B (non-medal); FC = Final C (non-medal); FD = Final D (non-medal); FE = Final E (non-medal); FF = Final F (non-medal); SA/B = Semifinals A/B; SC/D = Semifinals C/D; SE/F = Semifinals E/F; R = Repechage. M = Medal race; OCS = On course side of the starting line; DSQ = Disqualified; DNF = Did not finish; DNS = Did not start; RDG = Redress given. One athlete was noted as over-aged.

Arshad Sauleh (Urdu: ارشر صالح) is an artist and radio broadcaster from a Muslim family, born in Srinagar, the summer capital of Kashmir. He has served as a host and judge in several prominent art exhibitions and is currently teaching art at the Government College of Education in Srinagar. Arshad Sauleh represented India at the 2002 International Exhibition of Quranic paintings in Iran and was honored by the Ministry of Heritage and Islamic Guidance, Government of Iran, for his participation in the tenth International Exhibition on Quranic Paintings. This recognition occurred during the period of the Kashmir conflict.

Arthur William Bacot (28 April 1866 – 12 April 1922) was an entomologist at the Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine. Born in North London, he was the third son and fourth child of Edmund Alexander Bacot and Harriet. Bacot was a poor attender at school, leaving at the age of sixteen in 1882, and subsequently worked as an office worker in the City of London. He had no formal scientific training beyond membership in the London Natural History Society. A dedicated butterfly collector, he authored over fifty papers on British lepidoptera between 1893 and 1909. In 1908, he began researching morphological and genetic topics, conducting breeding experiments with the geometrid moth Acidalia virginaria (binomial name Scopula modicaria), which he presented to the London Hospital Medical School. Professor Greenwood of the Advisory Committee for Plague Investigation sought someone to study the breeding habits of the rat flea and its transmission of the plague virus; Bacot was asked to undertake this research in his spare time with a small fee and all expenses covered. The project succeeded, leading to his appointment at the Lister Institute. In 1914, during the First World War, he traveled to Sierra Leone in British West Africa to study Yellow Fever. By autumn 1917, concerns arose about the reduced efficiency of the British Expeditionary Force in France due to trench fever; Bacot, alongside Joseph Arkwright, investigated the disease's cause and prevention, identifying the link between lice and both typhus and trench fever. Bacot contracted trench fever himself while in Warsaw. In 1922, he went to Cairo with Arkwright at the request of the Egyptian Government to study typhus; both contracted the disease from lice. Arkwright survived after a prolonged illness, while Bacot died at the age of 55.

The Asia–Europe Meeting (ASEM) is a political dialogue forum designed to strengthen relations and promote various forms of cooperation between its partners. It was officially established on 1 March 1996 at the 1st ASEM Summit (ASEM1) in Bangkok, Thailand, by the then 15 Member States of the European Union (EU) and the European Commission, the then 7 Member States of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and the individual countries of China, Japan, and South Korea. Over time, the forum expanded through a series of enlargements, including India, Mongolia, Pakistan, and the ASEAN Secretariat in 2008, Australia, New Zealand, and Russia in 2010, Bangladesh, Norway, and Switzerland in 2012, and Croatia and Kazakhstan in 2014. The ASEM Process is structured around three main pillars and is viewed by its partners as a means to deepen Asia–Europe relations at all levels to achieve a more balanced political and economic world order. This is supported by biennial meetings of Heads of State and Government, alternating between Asia and Europe, and biennial meetings of Foreign Ministers, along with other Ministerial Meetings and political, economic, and socio-cultural events at various levels. As of now, the ASEM Partnership comprises 53 Partners: 51 countries and 2 regional organizations. The countries include Australia, Austria, Bangladesh, Belgium, Brunei, Bulgaria, Cambodia, China, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Laos, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Malta, Mongolia, Myanmar, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Pakistan, the Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Thailand, the United Kingdom, and Vietnam. The regional organizations involved are the European Union and the ASEAN Secretariat. Biennial Summits are held alternately in Asia and Europe and are attended by the Heads of State and Government of the respective partner countries and organizations. In addition, regular Ministerial Meetings are held on foreign affairs, financial, cultural, economic, educational, labor and employment, transport, or environmental issues, attended by the relevant ministers.

Asim Ahmed Khan is an Indian politician from Delhi and a former cabinet minister in the Delhi government, serving in the ministries of Food and Civil Supply, Environment and Forest, Minority Affairs, and Elections. He was a member of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and represented the Matia Mahal Assembly constituency in the 6th Delhi Assembly. Born in Delhi, he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from Chaudhary Charan Singh University. He is a member of the AAP minority wing and contested the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) elections in 2012, receiving 6,300 votes. The AAP party website notes that he has worked in the Old Delhi area for 12 years and participated in various social activities. In the 2015 Delhi Legislative Assembly elections, Khan contested as an AAP candidate from Matia Mahal, raising issues of education and health. He won the seat with 47,584 votes, defeating five-time MLA Shoaib Iqbal, who ran on an Indian National Congress ticket, by a margin of 26,096 votes. Khan was described as a "less acknowledged 'giant killer'" despite having a "poor experience in politics," as Shoaib Iqbal had previously won five times, including in 2013 on a Janata Dal (United) ticket. The AAP secured 67 out of 70 seats in the Delhi assembly. Khan was one of four Muslim MLAs in the Sixth Legislative Assembly of Delhi and was considered "key" to AAP's success, which captured 80% of the Muslim vote. The AAP's minority wing played a crucial role in shifting Muslim votes—traditionally going to Congress—from Congress to AAP, contributing to AAP's decisive victory. Khan was sworn in as a cabinet minister on 14 February 2015 under Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal, being assigned responsibility for the Food and Civil Supply, Environment and Forest, Minority Affairs, and Elections ministries. On 9 October 2015, Kejriwal dismissed Khan from the cabinet on corruption charges, specifically for allegedly cutting a deal worth Rs. 6 lakh with a local builder. However, Khan was later cleared by the CBI due to lack of evidence.

doc_name: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira
text: On the evening of 6 April 1994, the aircraft carrying Rwandan president Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian president Cyprien Ntaryamira, both Hutu, was shot down with surface-to-air missiles as it prepared to land in Kigali, Rwanda; both were killed. The assassination triggered the Rwandan genocide, one of the bloodiest events of the late 20th century. Responsibility for the attack is disputed, with most theories pointing to either the Tutsi rebel Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) or government-aligned Hutu Power followers opposed to negotiations with the RPF. The Rwandan Civil War began in 1990 when the RPF, dominated by the Tutsi ethnic group, invaded northern Rwanda from Uganda. Most of the RPF fighters were refugees or sons of refugees who had fled ethnic purges by the Hutu government during the Rwandan revolution. The attempt to overthrow the government failed, though the RPF maintained control of a border region. As the war reached a stalemate, peace negotiations began in May 1992, resulting in the signing of the Arusha Accords in August 1993 to establish a power-sharing government. The war radicalized internal opposition, with the RPF's show of force strengthening support for the "Hutu Power" ideology, which portrayed the RPF as an alien force intent on reinstating the Tutsi monarchy and enslaving the Hutus. The Coalition for the Defense of the Republic (CDR) embraced these racist principles, known as the Hutu Ten Commandments, and led to the collapse of the first Habyarimana government in July 1993 when Prime Minister Dismas Nsengiyaremye criticized the president for delaying a peace agreement. Habyarimana dismissed Nsengiyaremye and appointed Agathe Uwilingiyimana, who was seen as less sympathetic to the RPF, in his place. The main opposition parties split into factions: one committed to Hutu Power and another, labeled "moderate," seeking a negotiated settlement. Uwilingiyimana was unable to form a coalition, making ratification of the Arusha Accords impossible. The CDR, which openly called for ethnic cleansing of the Tutsi, was entirely unrepresented in the Accords. The security situation worsened throughout 1993, with armed Hutu militias attacking Tutsis and high-ranking Hutu Power figures considering how to turn the security forces to genocide. In February 1994, Roméo Dallaire, head of the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR), warned his superiors that political discussions were running out of time due to the risk of catastrophic consequences. In early April 1994, the United Nations Security Council faced a dispute between the United States and non-permanent members over UNAMIR. Despite a classified February Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analysis predicting half a million deaths if the Arusha process failed, the U.S. sought to reduce its international commitments following the Somalia debacle and lobbied to end the mission. A compromise extending UNAMIR's mandate for three more months was reached on the evening of 5 April. Habyarimana was traveling regionally: on 4 April he flew to Zaire to meet with President Mobutu Sese Seko, and on 6 April to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, for a one-day summit convened by Tanzanian President Ali Hassan Mwinyi. For the return trip, Habyarimana offered to take Tanzania's Ambassador to Rwanda, Saleh Tambwe, with him, then extended the offer to President Ntaryamira, who accepted, preferring Habyarimana's faster Dassault Falcon 50 to his own transport. Several Burundian ministers joined the flight, and as a result, Tambwe was not brought on board. According to interim Prime Minister Jean Kambanda's testimony to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), Mobutu had warned Habyarimana not to go to Dar es Salaam on 6 April, claiming the warning came from a senior official at the Élysée Palace in Paris. Mobutu linked this warning to the suicide of François de Grossouvre, a senior official working for President François Mitterrand, who died by suicide on 7 April after learning about the downing of the Falcon. Shortly before 8:20 pm local time (18:20 UTC), the presidential jet circled Kigali International Airport once before final approach in clear skies. A weekly flight by a Belgian C-130 Hercules carrying UNAMIR troops returning from leave had been scheduled to land before the presidential jet but was waved off to give the president priority. A surface-to-air missile struck one of the wings of the Dassault Falcon, followed by a second missile hitting its tail. The plane erupted into flames mid-air and crashed into the garden of the presidential palace, exploding on impact. The plane carried three French crew members and nine passengers. The attack was witnessed by numerous people. One of two Belgian officers in Kanombe saw and heard the first missile climb into the sky, saw a red flash, and heard the aircraft engine stop, followed by another missile. He immediately called Major de Saint-Quentin, who advised him to protect his Belgian comrades. Another Belgian officer in an unused airport control tower saw the lights of an approaching aircraft, a light rising from the ground, and the aircraft lights going out, followed by a second light rising from the same place and the plane turning into a falling ball of fire. He immediately radioed his company commander, who confirmed with the operational control tower that the plane was the presidential aircraft. A Rwandan soldier in Camp Kanombe recalled that the president's engine sound was different from other planes; he saw a projectile, a ball of flame, and the plane go down. As the leader of the bloc, he told soldiers to get up and said, "Kinani has been shot down," though they initially denied it. He then put on his uniform and heard the bugle sound. A Rwandan officer cadet at the airport, listening to Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, heard the announcer state the presidential jet was coming in to land, then the broadcast abruptly switched to classical music. All twelve aboard the Falcon were killed. The French aircraft crew were: The crash caused chaos on the ground. Presidential Guards, who had been waiting to escort the president home, threatened people with their weapons. Twenty Belgian peacekeepers stationed along the airport perimeter were surrounded and some disarmed. The airport was closed, and the circling Belgian Hercules was diverted to Nairobi. In Camp Kanombe, the bugle call immediately after the crash was interpreted as a sign that the RPF had attacked the camp. Soldiers rushed to their armories, and the para-commando brigade Commandos de recherche et d'action en profondeur assembled on the parade ground at around 9:00 pm, while other units gathered elsewhere. At least one witness reported gunfire in Kanombe about an hour after the crash, and munitions explosions were initially reported. The senior officer for the Kigali operational zone called the Ministry of Defence; Defence Minister Augustin Bizimana was out of the country, and the officer who took the call failed to reach Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, who was at a reception with UNAMIR's Bangladeshi officers. The news of the crash, initially reported as an explosion of UNAMIR's ammunition dump, was relayed to UNAMIR Force Commander Dallaire, who ordered Kigali sector commander Luc Marchal to send a patrol to the crash site. Numerous people called UNAMIR for information, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana and Lando Ndasingwa. Uwilingiyimana informed Dallaire she was trying to gather her cabinet but many ministers were afraid to leave their families. She reported that all hardline ministers had disappeared. Dallaire asked her to confirm it was the president's plane, and called UNAMIR political head Jacques-Roger Booh-Booh. Uwilingiyimana confirmed it was the president's jet and that he was presumed on board. She also requested UNAMIR assistance in regaining control of the political situation, as she was legally next in line of succession, though some moderate ministers had already fled. At 9:18 pm, Presidential Guards, described as "nervous and dangerous," established a roadblock near the Hotel Méridien. Several other roadblocks had been set up in advance for Habyarimana's arrival. A patrol of UNAMIR Belgian soldiers sent to investigate the crash site was stopped at a Presidential Guards roadblock at 9:35 pm, disarmed, and sent to the airport. The para-commando brigade was ordered to collect bodies from the crash site, and UN peacekeepers were prevented from accessing it. Akingeneye was quickly recovered, but most corpses were damaged beyond immediate recognition. Habyarimana was identified lying in a flowerbed at about 21:30 on 6 April, while Ntaryamira was recognized at about 03:00 on 7 April. One Rwandan advisor was identified after his wife told the search party about his clothing. The last to be identified were the French aircrew, discovered at dawn outside the palace gardens. The bodies were taken into the Presidential Palace living room. Plans were initially made to take them to the hospital, but renewed conflict made this difficult, so the two presidents' bodies were stored in a freezer at a nearby army barracks. Two French soldiers arrived at the crash site and asked to be given the flight data recorder once it was recovered. The whereabouts of the flight data recorder were later unknown. The French military contacted Dallaire and offered to investigate the crash, which he refused immediately. A Rwandan colonel who called the army command about 40 minutes after the crash was told there was no confirmation that the president was dead. About half an hour later, at roughly 9:30, the situation remained confused, though it appeared clear the presidential aircraft had exploded and had likely been hit by a missile. News arrived that Major-General Déogratias Nsabimana, the army chief of staff, had been on the plane. Officers realized they needed to appoint a new chief of staff and began a meeting to decide who should take the role. Col. Bagosora joined them soon afterward. At about 10:00 pm, Ephrem Rwabalinda, the government liaison officer to UNAMIR, called Dallaire to inform him that a crisis committee was about to meet. After informing his superiors in New York, Dallaire went to attend the meeting, where he found Bagosora in charge. Observers feared that President Ntaryamira's death would lead to widespread violence in Burundi, as had occurred when his predecessor, Melchior Ndadaye, was assassinated in October 1993. However, unlike in Rwanda, the situation in Burundi remained peaceful. The Burundian government declared the plane crash an accident, and President of the National Assembly Sylvestre Ntibantunganya made a television broadcast, flanked by the minister of defence and the army chief of staff, appealing for calm. Several hundred Tutsis marched through the capital to celebrate the deaths of the presidents. Diplomats reported that most Burundians believed the assassination targeted Habyarimana, not Ntaryamira. On 16 April, a requiem mass was held for Ntaryamira at the Regina Mundi Cathedral in Bujumbura, attended by thousands, and he and his two ministers were buried in a state funeral. Ntibantunganya succeeded Ntaryamira as President of Burundi and believed Ntaryamira's death was "by the facts of circumstance" and that he was not targeted. In response to the assassination, President Mwinyi declared three days of national mourning in Tanzania and sent messages of condolence to the Rwandan and Burundian governments and the families of the deceased presidents. He wrote in his memoirs that the Tanzanian government was "shocked" by the downing of the plane. A group of about 70 Rwandans and Burundians at the New Mwanza Hotel celebrated the assassination, leading Prime Minister John Malecela to order their arrest. This action was countermanded by the attorney general, who stated their actions were not illegal. A mourning period was also established in Zaire. President of the UN Security Council Colin Keating appealed for peace in Rwanda and Burundi and sent condolences to the families of the late presidents. Following the 6 April assassination, Juvenal Habyarimana's remains were obtained by President Mobutu of Zaire and stored in a private mausoleum in Gbadolite, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Mobutu promised Habyarimana's family that his body would eventually be given a proper burial in Rwanda. On 12 May 1997, as Laurent-Désiré Kabila's ADFL rebels advanced on Gbadolite, Mobutu had the remains flown by cargo plane to Kinshasa, where they waited on the tarmac of N'djili Airport for three days. On 16 May, the day before Mobutu fled Zaire, Habyarimana's remains were cremated under the supervision of an Indian Hindu leader. The Hindu leader's presence reflected the need to cremate the body and Mobutu's insistence on a religious ceremony rather than Habyarimana's own religion. Two prominent investigations, internationally recognized, have identified the Kanombe barracks as the likely source of the missile. In 2010, the "Mutsinzi Report," carried out by Rwandan officials in collaboration with British ballistics experts from the Royal Military Academy, identified a small area including a portion of the airport, the Kanombe camp, and a small area near the presidential residence as the launch site. In January 2012, a French report was made public with similar findings. Despite these reports, some have continued to cast doubt on the conclusion. French Judge Jean-Louis Bruguière led a 2004 inquiry that accused the RPF of shooting down the plane from Masaka Hill, but it was found to be based on the testimonies of witnesses not regarded as credible. A 1994 Belgian inquiry concluded that the missile was fired from Masaka Hill, but stated it would have been virtually impossible for a rebel soldier to reach Masaka carrying missiles. The base was controlled by FAR forces, including the Presidential Guard and the para-commando battalion, and the Anti-Aircraft Battalion (LAA) were also based there. This report was widely reported to exonerate the RPF, although according to Filip Reyntjens, it did not actually do so. While initial suspicion fell on Hutu extremists who carried out the subsequent genocide, several reports since 2000 have stated that the attack was carried out by the RPF on the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became president of Rwanda. All such evidence is heavily disputed, and many academics and the United Nations have refrained from issuing a definitive finding. Mark Doyle, a BBC News correspondent who reported from Kigali during the 1994 genocide, noted in 2006 that the identities of the assassins "could turn out to be one of the great mysteries of the late 20th century." A now-declassified US Department of State intelligence report from 7 April 1994 reports an unidentified source telling the US ambassador in Rwanda that "rogue Hutu elements of the military—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible for shooting down the plane." This conclusion was supported by other U.S. agencies, including the Defense Intelligence Agency.

doc_name: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira
text: The assassination of Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira on 6 April 1994, which triggered the Rwandan genocide, remains widely debated. Although initial suspicion focused on Hutu extremists, including figures like Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, several reports since 2000 have alleged that the RPF carried out the attack at the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became Rwanda’s president. These claims are heavily disputed, with no definitive conclusion from the United Nations or major academic institutions. A declassified U.S. Department of State report from 7 April 1994 cited an unidentified source stating that rogue Hutu military elements—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible, a view supported by the Defense Intelligence Agency, which reported on 9 May that the crash was an assassination by Hutu military hardliners. Philip Gourevitch, in his 1998 book, highlighted the lack of positive identification of the assassins, with Bagosora being a key suspect due to his close ties to Habyarimana and his statements about preparing an "apocalypse." The Belgian Senate’s 1997 report found insufficient information to determine specifics, while the 1998 French National Assembly report proposed two theories: Hutu extremists acting due to fears of RPF advances, or the RPF acting due to stalled Arusha Accords negotiations; it offered no definitive conclusion. The Organisation of African Unity’s 2000 report avoided assigning responsibility. In January 2000, Louise Arbour, chief prosecutor of the ICTR, terminated an investigation into the shootdown after three Tutsi informants accused Kagame and the RPF of being part of an "elite strike team," with one whistleblower, Jean-Pierre Mugabe, making a declaration in April 2000. A three-page memorandum by investigator Michael Hourigan was sent to the ICTR, and Hourigan stated he was "astounded" when Arbour reversed her position, claiming the investigation was outside her mandate; this was supported by Jim Lyons, a former FBI agent, who believed Arbour acted under orders, though Luc Reydams’ investigation concluded the decision was based on practical and legal assessments, not orders. Arbour later stated it was her personal decision, noting that the plane crash did not clearly constitute a war crime or crime against humanity under the law, and that the focus should have been on RPF actions during the genocide period. In 1998, French magistrate Jean-Louis Bruguière opened an investigation on behalf of the French crew families, concluding the attack was ordered by Kagame and issuing arrest warrants against nine of his aides in 2006; Rwanda responded by severing diplomatic ties. Bruguière’s key witness, Abdul Ruzibiza, a former RPF lieutenant, claimed involvement in the downing using SA-16 missiles and published his testimony in 2004 and a book in 2005, asserting Kagame’s responsibility; however, in November 2008 he retracted his claims, stating they were due to personal security concerns, and later claimed he did not personally participate but knew someone who did. Critics, including Linda Melvern and Colette Braeckman, questioned the reliability of Bruguière’s evidence, with Braeckman suggesting French military involvement. Kagame responded in a 2007 BBC interview by offering cooperation with an impartial, neutral inquiry, though the BBC doubted such a judge would accept the task. Paul Rusesabagina, known for his role in Hotel Rwanda, supported the theory that Kagame and the RPF were responsible, arguing it defied logic that the UN Security Council did not investigate, as it had after Rafic Hariri’s 2005 assassination. In February 2008, Spanish judge Fernando Andreu issued an 182-page indictment and international arrest warrants against 40 high-ranking RPF officials, charging them with crimes from 1990 to 2002, including the plane shootdown, based partly on universal jurisdiction. Kagame also ordered a Rwandan commission to investigate French involvement in the genocide, which issued its report in November 2007 and stated it would await Kagame’s validation. In January 2010, Rwanda released the Mutsinzi Report, which implicates Hutu Power proponents in the attack; Philip Gourevitch noted that France and Rwanda reestablished diplomatic relations shortly after Rwanda’s admission to the Commonwealth, and that the report had been shared with France prior to that, implying France’s acceptance of its findings. Ntaryamira’s death is commemorated annually in Burundi on 6 April, though it has been overshadowed by Habyarimana’s death and the subsequent genocide.

The attorney general of Guatemala (fiscal general de la República de Guatemala) serves as the chief public prosecutor and head of the Ministerio Público (Department of Justice). Under article 251 of the Constitution of Guatemala, the attorney general is appointed by the president from a group of six candidates who must be lawyers and possess the same qualifications as the magistrates of the Supreme Court. These candidates are nominated by a commission composed of the chief justice of the Supreme Court, the deans of the law schools at the country's universities, and both the chairman of the bar association and the chairman of its honor tribunal. The attorney general serves a four-year term and enjoys the same immunity as the magistrates of the Supreme Court. The president may remove the attorney general only if there is a justified reason, as specified in article 14 of the Organic Law of the Ministerio Público, which states that removal is permitted only in cases of conviction of the attorney general for committing a crime while carrying out their duties.

doc_name: Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002
text: The Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002, informally known as the Iraq Resolution, was a joint resolution passed by the United States Congress in October 2002 as Public Law No. 107-243, authorizing the use of the United States Armed Forces against Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist Iraqi government in what would become Operation Iraqi Freedom. The resolution cited several justifications for military action, including support and encouragement of diplomatic efforts by President George W. Bush to strictly enforce through the U.N. Security Council all relevant Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq and to obtain prompt and decisive action to ensure Iraq abandoned its strategy of delay, evasion, and noncompliance and promptly complied with all such resolutions. It authorized President Bush to use U.S. Armed Forces "as he determines to be necessary and appropriate" to defend national security against the continuing threat from Iraq and to enforce all relevant U.N. Security Council Resolutions on Iraq. President Bush sought congressional authorization shortly after his September 12, 2002 statement before the U.N. General Assembly requesting swift Security Council action. Among the legislative proposals introduced in response, S.J.Res. 45 (Senators Daschle and Lott), H.J.Res. 114 (Rep. Hastert and Rep. Gephardt), and S.J.Res. 46 (Sen. Lieberman) were based on or modified from the White House proposal, while H.J.Res. 110 (Rep. Hastings) was a separate proposal never considered on the floor. Ultimately, the Hastert–Gephardt proposal became the focus of congressional action. Introduced on October 2, 2002, H.J.Res. 114 passed the House on October 10, 2002, by a vote of 296–133, and the Senate on October 11, 2002, by a vote of 77–23, and was signed into law as Pub. L. 107–243 on October 16, 2002. The resolution was supported by a list of senators including Baucus, Bayh, Biden, Breaux, Cantwell, Carnahan, Carper, Cleland, Clinton, Daschle, Dodd, Dorgan, Edwards, Feinstein, Harkin, Hollings, Johnson, Kerry, Kohl, Landrieu, Lieberman, Lincoln, Miller, Nelson (FL and NE), Reid, Rockefeller, Schumer, and Torricelli, as well as Akaka, Bingaman, Boxer, Byrd, Conrad, Corzine, Dayton, Durbin, Feingold, Graham, Inouye, Kennedy, Leahy, Levin, Mikulski, Murray, Reed, Sarbanes, Stabenow, Wellstone, and Wyden. In 2003, the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit refused to review the legality of the invasion, citing a lack of ripeness, and a three-judge panel dismissed the case, stating the judiciary cannot intervene absent a fully developed conflict between the President and Congress or if Congress granted the President "absolute discretion" to declare war. Similar judicial review efforts have been dismissed on various justiciability grounds. United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan stated in 2004 that the invasion was illegal and not in conformity with the UN Charter. Debate over the legality under international law centers on ambiguous language in U.N. Resolution 1441 (2002), which declared Iraq was in "material breach" of the cease-fire under U.N. Resolution 687 (1991), requiring cooperation with weapons inspectors. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties allows a party to invoke a "material breach" to suspend a multilateral treaty, and the U.S. and U.K. argue that this right enabled them to suspend the cease-fire under Resolution 687 and continue hostilities under the authority of U.N. Resolution 678 (1990), which originally authorized force after Iraq invaded Kuwait—this argument was previously used in Operation Desert Fox in 1998. They also assert that while Resolution 1441 required the Security Council to assess inspector reports, it did not require agreement on action, and if Iraq was found to have breached the resolution, no member state was constrained from acting to defend itself. The U.S. government further claimed the right to pre-emptive self-defense against terrorism fostered by Iraq. It remains unclear whether any party other than the Security Council can determine Iraq's breach of Resolution 1441, as U.N. members argue interpretation and enforcement of resolutions is not the responsibility of a single member. Other nations have maintained that a second resolution was required to initiate hostilities. On June 17, 2021, the House of Representatives voted to repeal the 2002 resolution by a vote of 268–161, with 219 Democrats and 49 Republicans supporting repeal and 160 Republicans and 1 Democrat opposing it. In July 2021, Senators Christopher Murphy, Mike Lee, and Bernie Sanders introduced S.2391, the National Security Powers Act of 2021, to repeal previous war authorizations and establish new procedures, but a Senator placed a quasi-anonymous hold on it in committee, preventing advancement; its House companion, H.R.5410, did not include repeal language and was similarly held in committee. On March 16, 2023, Senators Tim Kaine and Todd Young introduced S.316 to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, which passed the Senate 68–27, but its House companion, H.R.932, was quasi-anonymously held by a Representative in the House Committee on Foreign Affairs since February 9, 2023. On July 13, 2023, Kaine and Young introduced S.Amdt.427 to S.2226, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, but failed to propose it on the floor in time, so when the bill passed the Senate, the amendment was not acted upon and was excluded by law. Both AUMFs were ultimately repealed when President Donald Trump signed the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 on December 18, 2025.

Axitinib, marketed under the brand name Inlyta, is a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor developed by Pfizer. It has demonstrated significant inhibition of breast cancer growth in animal xenograft models and has shown partial responses in clinical trials for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and other tumor types. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved axitinib for the treatment of RCC after it demonstrated a modest increase in progression-free survival, although fatal adverse effects have been reported. Approval for RCC was granted by the FDA in January 2012, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in September 2012, the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in September 2012, and the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) in July 2012. A Phase II trial indicated good response when axitinib was combined with gemcitabine for advanced pancreatic cancer, but Pfizer halted a Phase III trial on 30 January 2009 due to lack of improved survival compared to gemcitabine alone. A 2010 Phase III trial for previously treated metastatic RCC showed significantly extended progression-free survival compared to sorafenib, leading the Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee (ODAC) to unanimously recommend FDA approval in December 2011 for axitinib as second-line treatment for advanced RCC. Axitinib has also been studied in combination with the ALK1 inhibitor dalantercept. A 2015 study showed that axitinib effectively inhibits the BCR-ABL1[T315I] mutated gene, common in drug-resistant chronic myeloid leukemia and adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia, representing one of the first instances of a new indication for an existing drug discovered through screening patient cells. Common side effects include diarrhea, hypertension, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dysphonia, hand-foot syndrome, weight loss, vomiting, asthenia, and constipation, occurring in more than 20% of patients. Coadministration with strong CYP3A4/CYP3A5 inhibitors or inducers should be avoided due to potential increases or decreases in axitinib plasma exposure. Its primary mechanism of action involves inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1–3, c-KIT, and PDGFR, thereby suppressing angiogenesis in tumors; it may also induce autophagy, similar to sorafenib. Axitinib has been shown to bind to the BCR-ABL fusion protein in a conformation distinct from VEGF binding, specifically inhibiting the drug-resistant T315I mutant isoform. In July 2024, the European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use adopted a positive opinion recommending marketing authorization for Axitinib Accord, developed by Accord Healthcare S.L.U., for the treatment of adults with RCC. Pfizer reported US$1.036 billion in revenue for Inlyta in 2023. In the European Union, axitinib is sold under the brand name Inlyta.

Bacthafucup (stylized as BacTHAfucUP, BacTHAfu*UP, or B.T.F.U) is the first studio album by Indian singer and songwriter Karan Aujla, with music produced by Tru Skool. The album was released on 15 September 2021 by Times Music and Speed Records, and the music video for "Chu Gon Do?" was released on 8 July 2021. It consists of 13 tracks and features Harjit Harman, 5 Rivers, Nave Suave, Gurlez Akhtar, and Amaal. The album was streamed more than 95 million times on Spotify. In November 2020, Karan Aujla announced he was working on his debut album and revealed Tru Skool as the producer. In May 2021, he titled the album as BacDAfucUP, and in June 2021, the album's intro was released by Speed Records under its final title, BacTHAfucUP. Aujla released the track listing on 2 July 2021. On 8 July 2021, he released "Chu Gon Do?"'s music video, directed by Rupan Bal. In an interview, Aujla disclosed that each track from the album is of a different kind and that there would be a surprise collaboration. In an interview with Red FM Canada, he stated the album would be out on 30 July 2021, but it was delayed. On 2 September, Aujla released the second intro, "Vibe Check," and stated the album would be about Punjabi folk music, also showing snippets of 3-4 songs. In the intro, he announced the official video for "Click that B Kickin It" would be released on 9 September and that the full album would be out on 15 September. On 9 September 2021, the official video for "Click That B Kickin It" was released, directed by Rupan Bal. The full album was released on all streaming platforms on 15 September 2021. The track "Chu Gon Do" debuted at number 6 on the UK Asian chart published by the Official Charts Company. The album charted at #19 on the Billboard Top Canadian Albums. On 27 September, Karan Aujla became No. 1 Digital Artist in India and No. 37 in the world. All tracks are written by Karan Aujla.

The Bader Award is an annual prize in organic chemistry presented by the Royal Society of Chemistry since 1989. The recipient receives £2,000 and a medal, and is also required to give a lecture tour throughout the UK.

Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad (20 July 1907 – 15 July 1972) was an Indian politician who served as the prime minister of Jammu and Kashmir from 1953 to 1964, holding the longest continuous tenure of any prime minister or chief minister in the state's post-independence history and is recognized as a period of stability. Born in 1907 in a lower middle-class family in the Safakadal area of Srinagar, within the then princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, he had a father, Abdul Ghaffar Bakshi, who was unemployed, and six siblings—four brothers and two sisters. He received education at C.M.S Tyndale Biscoe School up to the eighth grade, which was considered a reasonable qualification at the time. He began his career as a school teacher in Christian missionary schools in Skardu and Leh, and due to family pressure, returned to Srinagar to marry. In 1925, he joined the Kashmir branch of the All India Spinners’ Association and worked as a karyakarta at Gandhi Ashram in Srinagar, founded on Mahatma Gandhi’s principles for rural development, where he was exposed to the Indian National Congress and Gandhi’s ideas, earning the epithet "Kashmiri Gandhi" for advocating the boycott of British goods. In 1927, he joined Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah in the agitation for civic and political rights for Kashmir's Muslim population, leading to the formation of the Muslim Conference, where he demonstrated organizational talent by mobilizing students and workers and establishing unions; he was arrested multiple times, including for sixteen months in Reasi sub-jail, and earned the sobriquet "Khalid-e-Kashmir" within the party. By 1938, with demands for responsible government spreading across communities, the Muslim Conference was renamed the National Conference, and Bakshi worked underground to evade state police. In 1946, during the "Quit Kashmir" movement, he escaped to British India when arrested and traveled widely to build public support for the Kashmir agitation; after Mahatma Gandhi’s visit to Kashmir in August 1947, the warrant against him was withdrawn, and he returned home after seventeen months. On 30 October 1947, Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah was appointed Head of Emergency Administration as Kashmir faced attacks from Pakistani raiders, and Bakshi became his deputy head. In March 1948, the administration was upgraded to a popular interim government, and Bakshi was given the Home portfolio. After the 1951 constituency assembly elections, Abdullah was elected prime minister and Bakshi was appointed deputy prime minister. In August 1953, Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah was dismissed and arrested with the help of the head of state Karan Singh, and Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad became prime minister, winning a unanimous vote of confidence in October and also becoming president of the National Conference by majority vote of the State Cabinet. During his tenure, the famous Kashmir Conspiracy Case was initiated against Abdullah and others. Bakshi proved to be an effective administrator and is remembered as the "Architect of Modern Kashmir" for his role in advancing the ideal of "Naya Kashmir," establishing direct rapport with people at the grassroots, and gaining widespread popularity across regions. Politically, he faced a strong challenge from the Plebiscite Front, formed by Sheikh Abdullah’s loyalists in 1955. In May 1963, after losing three parliamentary by-elections, the Congress party, under the Kamaraj plan, recommended that some ministers resign to focus on party work; Jawaharlal Nehru made the final decision, and Nehru suggested Bakshi resign. Upon Bakshi’s recommendation, Khwaja Shamsuddin, a loyalist, was appointed to succeed him, but Shamsuddin led the state only briefly. In 1964, Bakshi headed the opposition to Chief Minister Ghulam Mohammed Sadiq; in the late summer of that year, the majority of legislators compelled him to move a vote of no-confidence against the government, but he was arrested and detained under the Defence of India Rules despite having majority support from MLAs, and the assembly was prorogued by the governor. He was released on health grounds in December. In June 1965, he announced his decision to retire from politics. In the 1967 Indian general election, he was elected to the Lok Sabha from the Srinagar constituency on a National Conference ticket, defeating the ruling Congress nominee, Ali Mohammed Tariq, by a large margin, and remained a member until 1971. Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad died on 9 July 1972. He steadfastly resisted any attempts to undermine Jammu and Kashmir's special status within the Union of India.

Baleka Mbete, born on 24 September 1949 in Clermont, a township in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, to a Hlubi family, is a South African politician who served as Deputy President of South Africa from September 2008 to May 2009. She was the Speaker of the National Assembly for two non-consecutive terms: from 2004 to 2008 and from 2014 to 2019, and served as Deputy Speaker between 1996 and 2004. A member of the African National Congress (ANC) since 1976, she was first elected to the National Assembly in the first post-apartheid elections in 1994 and held the seat until 2019, with a break from 2009 to 2014. She qualified as a teacher in 1973 and taught in KwaMashu before becoming involved in the Black Consciousness Movement, which led to her detention in 1976. She left South Africa for Swaziland on 10 April 1976 and later moved to Tanzania, where she worked with the ANC's Women's Section and headed the Medu Art Ensemble, also publishing poetry under her married name, Baleka Kgositsile. She returned to South Africa in June 1990 and participated in the negotiations to end apartheid, serving as secretary-general of the ANC Women's League from 1991 to 1993. In 1995, she was appointed chair of the ANC's parliamentary caucus and a member of the Presidential Panel on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. In May 1996, she became Deputy Speaker, succeeding Bhadra Ranchod, and was re-elected to that office in June 1999. In April 2004, she was elected Speaker of the National Assembly unopposed, with Gwen Mahlangu as deputy. During her term, she faced criticism over the Travelgate scandal and the use of parliamentary travel vouchers, and in January 2006, she chartered a jet costing R471,900 to attend the inauguration of Ellen Johnson Sirleaf in Liberia. In December 2007, she won election as ANC national chairperson with 61% of the vote, defeating Joel Netshitenzhe, and served in that role until December 2017. On 25 September 2008, she was appointed Deputy President following the resignation of Thabo Mbeki, though she did not become President, as Kgalema Motlanthe was appointed to that role. In May 2009, she was re-elected to the National Assembly but declined to be sworn in, leading to her stepping back from Parliament. She returned in May 2014 as Speaker, defeating Nosimo Balindlela in a vote of 260 to 88, and faced a no-confidence motion in September 2014 that was rejected 234 to 0 after opposition parties walked out. She has faced accusations of bias toward the ANC and being a puppet of President Zuma, and in March 2016, the Constitutional Court ruled that the National Assembly under her leadership breached the Constitution by failing to implement the Public Protector's Nkandla report. In April 2016, she identified herself as a presidential contender, but endorsed Cyril Ramaphosa at the ANC's 54th National Conference in December 2017, after being disappointed that Jacob Zuma did not support her campaign. She did not run for re-election as national chairperson and was not re-elected to the National Executive Committee at the 2017 conference, though she remained a member until 2022. In May 2019, she was re-elected to her parliamentary seat but was subsequently removed from the party list, and the ANC announced Thandi Modise would succeed her as Speaker. In March 2022, she stated she was "done with politics," but was appointed interim convener of the ANC Women's League in September 2022, serving until a new leadership was elected. At the ANC's 55th National Conference in December 2022, she was not re-elected to the National Executive Committee, marking her first loss since 1994. Mbete has been linked to business ventures, including shares in Dyambu Holdings, which is involved in the Gautrain project and has ties to Brett Kebble, and was implicated in a R25 million Gold Fields bribe in 2010. She married Keorapetse Kgositsile in 1978, divorced in 1992, and remarried Nape Khomo in 2016. She has three sons and two daughters.

Balendra Shah, commonly known as Balen, was born on 27 April 1990 in Naradevi, Kathmandu, to a Maithili Madhesi family; his parents are Late Ram Narayan Shah, an Ayurvedic practitioner, and Dhruvadevi Shah, who moved to Kathmandu from Mahottari District after his father’s posting at Naradevi Ayurvedic Hospital. Shah pursued his 10+2 education at V.S. Niketan Higher Secondary School and earned a bachelor’s degree (BE) in civil engineering from Himalayan Whitehouse International College, followed by a master’s degree (MTech) in structural engineering from Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) in Karnataka, India. He is currently pursuing a PhD in Civil Engineering at Kathmandu University, supported by a KU Researcher's Fellowship, with a research focus on "Conservation of Newa Heritage Structure to promote Tourism and Economy." From an early age, Shah showed interest in music and poetry, releasing his first single, Sadak Balak, in 2012 during his ninth grade, and gaining prominence in 2013 through his appearance on the YouTube battle rap series Raw Barz. In July 2022, he drew controversy for using a sacred crown in Nephopko Shreepech, a hip-hop reality show he judged. As mayor, Shah introduced live telecasts of municipal council meetings, initiated garbage disposal from 7 June 2022 through an agreement with the Ministry of Urban Development, and directed private companies to manage uncollected solid waste in August 2022. He also ordered the demolition of private properties above the Tukucha River to uncover it, leading to a writ petition and an interim court order halting the demolition. Shah requested the removal of unauthorized police sub-stations on sidewalks and clashed with the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal over the removal of unapproved construction materials at Tribhuvan International Airport, resulting in a legal dispute and a high court stay. His office issued a 7-day public notice to evict landless squatters on riverbanks, leading to clashes, injuries, and a subsequent complaint from the Home Ministry, which escalated tensions with the federal government, culminating in the suspension of garbage collection from Singha Durbar. Shah has faced criticism from Human Rights Watch and social activists for using disproportionate force against street vendors, with videos circulating of police chasing, beating, and confiscating vendor properties, which critics argue harms the urban poor. In September 2023, activist Iih stood for 199 hours outside Kathmandu City Hall, demanding vendor rights, supported by figures including Gagan Thapa, Kamal Thapa, and Surendra Pandey; Shah responded by citing existing laws and expressed concern over confiscated properties, leading to an agreement on temporary permits, return of goods, and an alternative plan. Shah is known for his confrontational style, including removing illegal buildings, uncovering the Tukucha River, and clearing street vendors. In 2023, he placed a map of Greater Nepal in his office—a symbolic act interpreted as a response to the “Akhanda Bharat” mural in India’s new Parliament building, which some in Nepal saw as depicting Nepali territory as part of undivided India. This action drew strong objections from India. He also temporarily banned the screening of Indian films after Adipurush included the line “Sita is the daughter of India,” a claim disputed in Nepal where Sita is traditionally believed to have been born in Janakpur; despite a court order to remove the ban, Shah initially refused, prompting a contempt of court petition before allowing screenings to resume. During the Gen-Z Protests, the Nepal Student Union filed a police complaint accusing Shah of inciting violence against heritage sites, though he denied the claims, stating city teams worked continuously to ensure safety. Shah is a supporter of the irredentist Greater Nepal theory, which claims territories beyond Nepal’s current borders, including areas now in Indian states, that were once under Nepalese control before the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli. He was elected mayor on 26 May 2022 with 38.6% of the votes, defeating Nepali Congress candidate Sirjana Shrestha and CPN (UML) candidate Keshav Sthapit by a margin of over 23,000 votes, becoming the first independent candidate to hold the office. He was sworn in on 30 May 2022 and served until his resignation on 18 January 2026. He is currently contesting in the upcoming general elections as a candidate for the Prime Minister of Nepal and joined the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) in late 2025. Shah is married to Sabina Kafle, a public health professional, and lives in Gairigaun, Tinkune. His campaign emphasized waste management, road traffic control, public service delivery, anti-corruption, and cultural heritage preservation. TIME Magazine included him in its 'The 100 emerging leaders who are shaping the future' list in 2023.

Band of Joy is the ninth solo studio album by English rock singer Robert Plant and the first released with his new backing group, the Band of Joy. It was released on 13 September 2010 in the UK and 14 September in the US. The album is notable for the song "Monkey," originally by the band Low, which is slowed down to a grinding, spooky gothic rock tempo and mood, differing significantly from Low's version. This track is arguably the least similar to other songs on the album (except for "Satan"), which mostly feature folk rock or progressive rock styles. Although not a regular part of Plant's live performances, it has been performed on occasion. The album debuted at #5 on the Billboard 200 chart and at #3 on the UK Albums Chart. The first single released from the album was "Angel Dance." Band of Joy received positive reviews, with Metacritic assigning it an aggregate score of 80 out of 100, indicating "generally favorable reviews." Rolling Stone gave it a three-and-a-half-star rating and ranked it #8 on its list of the 30 Best Albums of 2010. Q Magazine, in its January 2011 edition, ranked Band of Joy as the second best album of 2010, noting that Plant, free from the need to imitate his 20-year-old self from Zeppelin, sings to his strengths with Miller and Griffin as key contributors, showcasing a range of styles including gentlemanly country-blues ("Cindy, I'll Marry You Some Day"), spooky lo-fi ("Silver Rider"), and charming '60s pop ("You Can't Buy My Love"). The album was nominated for two Grammy Awards: Best Americana Album and Best Solo Rock Vocal Performance for the song "Silver Rider." Robert Plant was also nominated for Best British Male Solo Artist at the Brit Awards 2011. Sales figures are based on certification alone.

Bandipore, the headquarters of the Bandipore district in the Indian-administered union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, lies on the northern banks of Wular Lake, the second-largest freshwater lake in Asia and one of the largest in South Asia. The lake, formed due to tectonic activity and fed by the Jhelum River and streams Madhumati and Arin, varies in size seasonally from 30 to 189 square kilometres, though much of it has been drained due to willow plantations built in the 1950s. Wular is home to numerous migratory birds, but pollution from the Jhelum River—carrying waste from Srinagar and surrounding areas—has led to a pandemic growth of algae, threatening the lake’s ecosystem. Despite being the richest wetland in South Asia and the largest freshwater lake in Asia, no conservation measures have been implemented. Bandipore is situated on the banks of Wular and serves as a stepping stone to the higher reaches of Razdan, Gurez, and Tragbal. It is also adjacent to the Lolab Valley in Kupwara, just 30 kilometres away via Aloosa village, and upgrading this road would provide a lifeline to the Lolab valley. Historically, Bandipore was a key link between North India and Central Asia via the Silk Road, with a customs and immigration post at Pazalpora now functioning as a forest check-post, earning Bandipore the title of gateway to Central Asia. Strong cultural and trade links exist between Skardu, Gurez, and Bandipore. As per the 2011 Indian census, the district had a population of 37,081, with males constituting 54% and females 46%, and an average literacy rate of 66.53%—lower than the national average of 74%—with 75% of males and 55% of females literate, and 12% of the population under 6 years of age. The region is Muslim-majority, though prior to the early 1990s, Pandits lived in villages such as Ajar, Sonerwani, Kaloosa, Kharapora, Mantrigam, and Aragam, with some families in Ajar and Kaloosa not migrating. The Sharda Mandir at Kaloosa, featuring a rare, ancient tree known as Bran—believed to be several hundred years old—is a significant site. Villages like Chakreshipora, named after Chakerishwar, reflect the region’s Hindu heritage, and the famous Ziariat of Kausar Sahab Afghani is located near Chekreshipora. The Forest Training and Research Institute of Jammu and Kashmir, established in 1905 (originally founded in 1911), is located 3 km from the main town and is a premier body in forest conservation. The majority of the population speaks Kashmiri, with some speaking Gojri and Pahari; Tehsil Gurez and Tulail are Shina-speaking areas with a Shina majority, and there are a few Pashtun villages on the Line of Control. The Kishan Ganga Hydro Electric Power Project, located in Gurez Tehsil, is worth INR 15,000 crores and currently generates 330 MW of electricity for Jammu and Kashmir. A degree college, named after Hassan Khoyihami and established on a hilltop near Putushai village, approximately 6 km from the main market, began functioning in 2005 in the higher secondary school at Kaloosa. Nishat Park in Bandipore, constructed in 1954 under the supervision of then Prime Minister Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad, is modeled after the Nishat Garden in Srinagar and is located on the outskirts of the main market, offering a peaceful environment with beautiful flowers and trees. The town is well-connected by road via the Bandipora–Srinagar and Bandipora–Sopore roads but lacks railway connectivity; the nearest railway station is Sopore, 34 km away, and the nearest airport is Srinagar, 65 km away. Bandipore is known for trekking, mountaineering, and fishing, with Langmarg being a scenic meadow and Arin Nallah hosting exotic trout species. Mount Harmukh, located on the eastern side of the town, is a major attraction for mountaineers, with Sheera Sar (Lake of Spirits) serving as the base camp; commercial cabs operate up to Kudara, after which a 17-kilometre trek is required to reach the higher reaches. To the north lies Gurez, 86 kilometres away, accessible by commercial cabs in summer but closed in winter due to snowfall. The surrounding ranges—Sirandar, Kudara, Vewan, Mowa, and Tresangam—are inhabited by Gujjars and Bakarwals. A centuries-old shrine in Butho village, locally known as Ded Mouj and rumored to house the burial of Moses, is a myth and not historically verified. The Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, the largest Islamic institution in Jammu and Kashmir, is headed by Moulana Mohammad Rahmatullah Mir Qasmi. Notable individuals associated with Bandipore include Qazi Ghulam Nabi Jan (Chairman Land Development Bank & social activist), Qazi Ghulam Ali Jan (Assistant Conservator Forest), Hassan Khoehami (historian), Siyad Kashmiri Abdul Samad Lone (retired headmaster and poet), Naeem Akhtar (politician), Raheem Lone and Khalil Lone (noted hunters documented in Roosevelt’s book *East of the Sun and West of the Moon*), Nizam Uddin Bhat (politician), Faisal Ali Dar (social activist), Prof. Manzoor Fazili (academician and writer), Prof. Mohd Amin Malik (academician and columnist), Dr. Maroof Shah (writer), Masood Samoon (IAS and writer), and Asgar Samoon (IAS).

Barack Hussein Obama II (born August 4, 1961) is an American politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017. A member of the Democratic Party, he was the first African American president. Obama previously served as a U.S. senator representing Illinois from 2005 to 2008 and as an Illinois state senator from 1997 to 2004. Born in Honolulu, Hawaii, at Kapiolani Medical Center for Women and Children, Obama is the only president born outside the contiguous 48 states. He was born to an 18-year-old American mother, Ann Dunham (1942–1995), of English, Welsh, German, Swiss, and Irish descent, and a 27-year-old Kenyan father, Barack Obama Sr. (1934–1982), a married Luo Kenyan from Nyang'oma Kogelo. His last name, Obama, was derived from his Luo descent. His parents met in 1960 in a Russian language class at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where his father was a foreign student on a scholarship, and married in Wailuku, Hawaii, on February 2, 1961, six months before Obama was born. In late August 1961, shortly after his birth, Obama and his mother moved to the University of Washington in Seattle, where they lived for a year. During that time, Obama Sr. completed his undergraduate degree in economics in Hawaii, graduating in June 1962, and later earned a Master of Arts in economics from Harvard University. The couple divorced in March 1964. Obama Sr. returned to Kenya in 1964, where he married for a third time and worked as the senior economic analyst in the Ministry of Finance; he visited his son in Hawaii only once, at Christmas 1971, before being killed in an automobile accident in 1982 when Obama was 21 years old. In 1963, Dunham met Lolo Soetoro, an Indonesian East–West Center graduate student in geography, who married her on Molokai on March 15, 1965. After two one-year extensions of his J-1 visa, Lolo returned to Indonesia in 1966, and his wife and stepson followed in 1967. The family initially lived in the Menteng Dalam neighborhood in the Tebet district of South Jakarta and later moved to a wealthier neighborhood in the Menteng district of Central Jakarta. When Obama was six, he and his mother moved to Indonesia to join his stepfather. From age six to ten, he was registered in school as "Barry" and attended local Indonesian-language schools, supplemented by English-language Calvert School homeschooling by his mother, and became fluent in Indonesian. During his time in Indonesia, his stepfather taught him to be resilient and gave him a hardheaded assessment of how the world works. In 1971, Obama returned to Honolulu to live with his maternal grandparents, Madelyn and Stanley Dunham. He attended Punahou School, a private college preparatory school, with a scholarship from fifth grade until graduating in 1979. In high school, he continued to use the nickname "Barry" until making a visit to Kenya in 1980. From 1972 to 1975, he lived with his mother and half-sister, Maya Soetoro, in Hawaii while she was a graduate student in anthropology at the University of Hawaii. When she and Maya returned to Indonesia in 1975, Obama stayed in Hawaii so she could begin anthropology field work.
