His mother spent most of the next two decades in Indonesia, divorced Lolo Soetoro in 1980, earned a PhD in 1992, and died in 1995 in Hawaii from ovarian and uterine cancer. Obama wrote that the opportunity Hawaii offered to experience a variety of cultures in a climate of mutual respect became an integral part of his worldview. He also used alcohol, marijuana, and cocaine during his teenage years to "push questions of who I was out of my mind" and was a member of the "Choom Gang," a self-named group of friends who smoked marijuana. After graduating from high school in 1979, Obama moved to Los Angeles to attend Occidental College on a full scholarship. In February 1981, he made his first public speech calling for Occidental to disinvest from South Africa. In mid-1981, he traveled to Indonesia to visit his mother and half-sister and visited the families of college friends in Pakistan. Later in 1981, he transferred to Columbia University in New York City as a junior, where he majored in political science with a specialty in international relations and English literature, lived off-campus on West 109th Street, graduated in 1983 with a Bachelor of Arts degree and a 3.7 GPA, and worked briefly at the Business International Corporation as a financial researcher and writer and as a project coordinator for the New York Public Interest Research Group. Two years after graduating from Columbia, Obama moved to Chicago and was hired as director of the Developing Communities Project, a faith-based community organization in Roseland, West Pullman, and Riverdale. He worked as a community organizer from June 1985 to May 1988, helping set up a job training program, a college preparatory tutoring program, and a tenants' rights organization in Altgeld Gardens, and also worked as a consultant and instructor for the Gamaliel Foundation. In mid-1988, he traveled to Europe for three weeks and then to Kenya for five weeks, meeting many of his paternal relatives for the first time. Despite being offered a full scholarship to Northwestern University School of Law, he enrolled at Harvard Law School in the fall of 1988, living in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts. He was selected as an editor of the Harvard Law Review at the end of his first year, became president of the journal in his second year, and served as a research assistant to constitutional scholar Laurence Tribe. During summers, he worked at law firms Sidley Austin (1989) and Hopkins & Sutter (1990). His election as the first black president of the Harvard Law Review gained national media attention and led to a publishing contract and advance for a book about race relations, which evolved into a personal memoir, published in mid-1995 as Dreams from My Father. He graduated from Harvard Law in 1991 with a Juris Doctor magna cum laude. In 1991, he accepted a two-year position as Visiting Law and Government Fellow at the University of Chicago Law School to work on his first book and then taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago Law School for twelve years, first as a lecturer from 1992 to 1996 and then as a senior lecturer from 1996 to 2004. From April to October 1992, he directed Illinois's Project Vote, a voter registration campaign that registered 150,000 of 400,000 unregistered African Americans, leading Crain's Chicago Business to name him to its 1993 list of "40 under Forty" powers to be. In a 2006 interview, Obama highlighted the diversity of his extended family, describing it as "like a little mini-United Nations," noting he has a half-sister, Maya Soetoro-Ng, and seven other half-siblings from his Kenyan father's family, six of whom live. His mother was survived by her Kansas-born mother, Madelyn Dunham, who died on November 2, 2008, two days before Obama's election to the presidency. Obama has roots in Ireland; he met his Irish cousins in Moneygall in May 2011. In Dreams from My Father, he ties his mother's family history to possible Native American ancestors and distant relatives of Jefferson Davis and shares distant ancestors in common with George W. Bush and Dick Cheney. Obama lived with anthropologist Sheila Miyoshi Jager while a community organizer in Chicago in the 1980s; he proposed to her twice, both times being turned down, and the relationship was not made public until May 2017. In June 1989, Obama met Michelle Robinson when employed at Sidley Austin; she joined him at social functions and declined his initial requests to date. They began dating later that summer, became engaged in 1991, and were married on October 3, 1992. After suffering a miscarriage, Michelle underwent in vitro fertilization to conceive their children. Their first daughter, Malia Ann, was born in 1998, followed by a second daughter, Natasha ("Sasha"), in 2001. The daughters attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and, when they moved to Washington, D.C., in January 2009, began at the Sidwell Friends School. The Obamas had two Portuguese Water Dogs; the first, a male named Bo, was a gift from Senator Ted Kennedy, and in 2013 was joined by Sunny, a female. Bo died of cancer on May 8, 2021. Obama is a supporter of the Chicago White Sox and threw out the first pitch at the 2005 ALCS when a senator, and in 2009 at the All-Star Game while wearing a White Sox jacket. He is primarily a Chicago Bears football fan in the NFL, but as a child and adolescent was a fan of the Pittsburgh Steelers and rooted for them ahead of their victory in Super Bowl XLIII, 12 days after he took office as president. In 2011, Obama invited the 1985 Chicago Bears to the White House, the first visit since their 1986 Super Bowl win due to the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster. He plays basketball, a sport he participated in as a member of his high school's varsity team, and is left-handed. In 2005, the Obama family applied the proceeds of a book deal and moved from a Hyde Park, Chicago condominium to a $1.6 million house (equivalent to $2.6 million in 2024) in neighboring Kenwood, Chicago. The purchase of an adjacent lot and sale of part of it to Obama by the wife of developer, campaign donor, and friend Tony Rezko attracted media attention due to Rezko's subsequent indictment and conviction on political corruption charges unrelated to Obama. In December 2007, Money Magazine estimated Obama's net worth at $1.3 million (equivalent to $2 million in 2024), and their 2009 tax return showed a household income of $5.5 million—up from about $4.2 million in 2007 and $1.6 million in 2005—mostly from book sales.

Barack Obama, who played basketball as a member of his high school's varsity team and is left-handed, was involved in the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster.[93] In 2005, the Obama family used proceeds from a book deal to move from a Hyde Park, Chicago condominium to a $1.6 million house (equivalent to $2.6 million in 2024) in neighboring Kenwood, Chicago. The purchase of an adjacent lot and the sale of part of it to Obama by the wife of developer, campaign donor, and friend Tony Rezko drew media attention due to Rezko's later indictment and conviction on political corruption charges unrelated to Obama.[97] In December 2007, Money Magazine estimated Obama's net worth at $1.3 million (equivalent to $2 million in 2024).[98] His 2009 tax return showed a household income of $5.5 million—up from $4.2 million in 2007 and $1.6 million in 2005—mostly from book sales.[99][100] In 2010, with an income of $1.7 million, he donated 14 percent to non-profit organizations, including $131,000 to the Fisher House Foundation, which assists wounded veterans' families in residing near medical treatment sites.[101][102] According to his 2012 financial disclosure, Obama may be worth as much as $10 million.[103] Obama is a Protestant Christian whose religious views developed in adulthood; he wrote in The Audacity of Hope that he "was not raised in a religious household," describing his mother as spiritually awakened but detached from religion and his father as a "confirmed atheist" and his stepfather as viewing religion as "not particularly useful." He came to understand the power of African-American religious traditions through community organizing in his twenties.[105] In January 2008, Obama told Christianity Today that he is a Christian and a devout Christian, believing in the redemptive death and resurrection of Jesus Christ and that faith provides a path to being cleansed of sin and having eternal life.[106] On September 27, 2010, he stated: "I'm a Christian by choice. My family didn't go to church every week. My mother was one of the most spiritual people I knew, but she didn't raise me in the church. So I came to my Christian faith later in life, and it was because the precepts of Jesus Christ spoke to me in terms of the kind of life that I would want to lead—being my brothers' and sisters' keeper, treating others as they would treat me."[107][108] Obama met Trinity United Church of Christ pastor Jeremiah Wright in October 1987 and became a member in 1992.[109] During his 2008 presidential campaign, he resigned from Trinity after some of Wright's statements were criticized.[110] Since moving to Washington, D.C. in 2009, the Obama family has attended several Protestant churches, including Shiloh Baptist Church, St. John's Episcopal Church, and Evergreen Chapel at Camp David, though they do not attend regularly.[111][112][113] In 2016, Obama said he is inspired by a collection of items, including rosary beads from Pope Francis, a Hanuman figurine, a Coptic cross from Ethiopia, a small Buddha statue from a monk, and a metal poker chip once used as a lucky charm by a motorcyclist in Iowa, which remind him of the people he has met.[114][115] From 1994 to 2002, Obama served on the boards of the Woods Fund of Chicago and the Joyce Foundation, and from 1995 to 2002 on the Chicago Annenberg Challenge, serving as founding president and chairman of the board from 1995 to 1999.[52] His law license became inactive in 2007.[116][117] Obama was elected to the Illinois Senate in 1996, succeeding Alice Palmer in Illinois's 13th District, which included neighborhoods from Hyde Park–Kenwood south to South Shore and west to Chicago Lawn.[118] He gained bipartisan support for ethics and health care reforms, sponsored legislation increasing tax credits for low-income workers, negotiated welfare reform, and promoted childcare subsidies.[121] In 2001, as co-chairman of the bipartisan Joint Committee on Administrative Rules, he supported Republican governor George Ryan's payday loan and predatory mortgage lending regulations to prevent home foreclosures.[122][123] He was reelected in 1998 and 2002, defeating Republican Yesse Yehudah in 1998.[124][125] In 2000, he lost a Democratic primary for Illinois's 1st congressional district to Bobby Rush by a two-to-one margin.[126] In January 2003, Obama became chairman of the Illinois Senate's Health and Human Services Committee after Democrats regained a majority.[127] He sponsored and led bipartisan passage of legislation requiring police to record the race of detained drivers and made Illinois the first state to mandate videotaping of homicide interrogations.[121][128][129][130] During his 2004 Senate campaign, police credited him with advancing death penalty reforms.[131] He resigned from the Illinois Senate in November 2004 after being elected to the U.S. Senate.[132] In May 2002, Obama commissioned a poll to assess his chances in a 2004 Senate race, created a campaign committee, and by August 2002 had lined up political media consultant David Axelrod. He formally announced his candidacy in January 2003.[133] Obama was an early opponent of the George W. Bush administration's 2003 invasion of Iraq; on October 2, 2002, he addressed the first high-profile Chicago anti-Iraq War rally and spoke out against the war, and in March 2003 told the crowd "it's not too late" to stop it.[134][135][136][137][138] With Republican Peter Fitzgerald and Democratic Carol Moseley Braun not running, the 2004 Democratic and Republican primaries featured 15 candidates. In the March 2004 primary, Obama won in an unexpected landslide, becoming a rising star in the national Democratic Party and prompting the reissue of his memoir, Dreams from My Father.[140] In July 2004, he delivered the keynote address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention, seen by nine million viewers, which elevated his status within the party.[141][142] His expected opponent, Jack Ryan, withdrew in June 2004, and Alan Keyes accepted the Republican nomination to replace him.[143][144] In the November 2004 general election, Obama won with 70 percent of the vote, the largest margin of victory for a Senate candidate in Illinois history, taking 92 of the state's 102 counties, including areas where Democrats traditionally do not perform well.[145][146] Obama was sworn in as a senator on January 3, 2005, becoming the only Senate member of the Congressional Black Caucus.[147][148] He introduced two initiatives: Lugar–Obama, which expanded the Nunn–Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction concept to conventional weapons; and the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006, which authorized USAspending.gov, a web search engine for federal spending.[149][150] On June 3, 2008, Senator Obama, along with Senators Tom Carper, Tom Coburn, and John McCain, introduced the Strengthening Transparency and Accountability in Federal Spending Act of 2008.[151] He also cosponsored the Secure America and Orderly Immigration Act.[152] In December 2006, President Bush signed the Democratic Republic of the Congo Relief, Security, and Democracy Promotion Act, the first federal legislation enacted with Obama as its primary sponsor.[153][154] In January 2007, Obama and Senator Feingold introduced a corporate jet provision to the Honest Leadership and Open Government Act, which was signed into law in September 2007.[155][156] In 2007, Obama sponsored an amendment to the Defense Authorization Act adding safeguards for personality-disorder military discharges, which passed the full Senate in spring 2008.[157][158] He sponsored the Iran Sanctions Enabling Act supporting divestment of state pension funds from Iran's oil and gas industry, which was never enacted but later incorporated into the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act of 2010;[159] and co-sponsored legislation to reduce risks of nuclear terrorism.[160] He also sponsored a Senate amendment to the State Children's Health Insurance Program, providing one year of job protection for family members caring for soldiers with combat-related injuries.[161] Obama held assignments on the Senate Committees for Foreign Relations, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs through December 2006.[162] In January 2007, he left the Environment and Public Works committee and took additional assignments with Health, Education, Labor and Pensions and Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.[163] He also became Chairman of the Senate's subcommittee on European Affairs.[164] As a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Obama made official trips to Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, and Africa, meeting with Mahmoud Abbas before he became President of the Palestinian National Authority and giving a speech at the University of Nairobi condemning corruption in the Kenyan government.[165] He resigned his Senate seat on November 16, 2008, to focus on his presidential transition.[166] On February 10, 2007, Obama announced his candidacy for President of the United States in front of the Old State Capitol building in Springfield, Illinois, a site symbolic of Abraham Lincoln's 1858 "House Divided" speech.[167][168][169] He emphasized ending the Iraq War, increasing energy independence, and reforming the health care system.[170] Numerous candidates entered the Democratic primaries, narrowing to Obama and Senator Hillary Clinton, with Obama gaining a steady lead in pledged delegates due to better long-range planning, superior fundraising, dominant organizing in caucus states, and better exploitation of delegate allocation rules.[171] On June 2, 2008, Obama had enough votes to clinch his nomination. After initially hesitating, Clinton ended her campaign and endorsed Obama on June 7.[172] On August 23, 2008, Obama announced Joe Biden as his vice presidential running mate, selected from a field that included Evan Bayh and Tim Kaine.[173] At the Democratic National Convention in Denver, Colorado, Hillary Clinton called for her supporters to endorse Obama, and she and Bill Clinton gave speeches in his support.[174][175] Obama delivered his acceptance speech at Invesco Field at Mile High stadium to a crowd of about eighty-four thousand, viewed by over three million people worldwide.[176][177][178] During both the primary and general election, Obama's campaign set numerous fundraising records, especially in small donations.[179] On June 19, 2008, Obama became the first major-party presidential candidate to turn down public financing in the general election since the system was created in 1976.[180] John McCain was nominated as the Republican candidate and selected Sarah Palin as his running mate. Obama and McCain engaged in three presidential debates in September and October 2008.[181] On November 4, 2008, Obama won the presidency with 365 electoral votes to McCain's 173, winning 52.9 percent of the popular vote to McCain's 45.7 percent, becoming the first African-American elected president.[182][183][184] He delivered his victory speech before hundreds of thousands of supporters in Chicago's Grant Park.[185][186] He is one of three U.S. senators moved directly from the Senate to the White House, the others being Warren G. Harding and John F. Kennedy.[187] On April 4, 2011, Obama filed election papers with the Federal Election Commission and announced his 2012 reelection campaign in a video titled "It Begins with Us" posted on his website.[188][189][190] As the incumbent, he ran virtually unopposed in the Democratic primaries and secured the 2778 convention delegates needed to win the nomination on April 3, 2012.[191][192] At the Democratic National Convention in Charlotte, North Carolina, Obama and Joe Biden were formally nominated by former president Bill Clinton as the party's presidential and vice-presidential candidates. Their main opponents were Republicans Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan.[193] On November 6, 2012, Obama won 332 electoral votes, exceeding the 270 needed for reelection, with 51.1 percent of the popular vote, becoming the first Democratic president since Franklin D. Roosevelt to win the majority of the popular vote twice.[194][195][196][197][198][199] After his reelection, Obama addressed supporters and volunteers at Chicago's McCormick Place and said: "Tonight you voted for action, not politics as usual. You elected us to focus on your jobs, not ours. And in the coming weeks and months, I am looking forward to reaching out and working with leaders of both parties."[200][201] The inauguration of Barack Obama as the 44th president took place on January 20, 2009. In his first days in office, Obama issued executive orders and presidential memoranda directing the U.S. military to develop plans to withdraw troops from Iraq.[202] He ordered the closing of the Guantanamo Bay detention camp,[203] but Congress prevented the closure by refusing to appropriate required funds[204][205] and blocking the transfer of any detainees.[206] Obama reduced the secrecy of presidential records.[207] He also revoked President George W. Bush's restoration of the Mexico City policy, which prohibited federal aid to international family planning organizations that provide or counsel on abortion.[208] The first bill signed into law by Obama was the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, which relaxed the statute of limitations for equal-pay lawsuits.[209] Five days later, he signed the reauthorization of the State Children's Health Insurance Program to cover an additional four million uninsured children.[210] In March 2009, Obama reversed a Bush-era policy limiting embryonic stem cell research and pledged to develop "strict guidelines" on the research.[211] Obama appointed two women to the Supreme Court in the first two years of his presidency: Sonia Sotomayor, nominated on May 26, 2009, to replace David Souter, confirmed on August 6, 2009, becoming the first Supreme Court Justice of Hispanic descent; and Elena Kagan, nominated on May 10, 2010, to replace John Paul Stevens, confirmed on August 5, 2010, bringing the number of women on the Court to three for the first time in American history.[212][213][214] On March 11, 2009, Obama created the White House Council on Women and Girls, established by Executive Order 13506, to advise him on issues relating to the welfare of American women and girls, chaired by Senior Advisor to the President.

On September 9, 2009, Obama delivered a speech to a joint session of Congress addressing concerns over a 1,017-page health care reform plan introduced by House Democratic leaders, which he wanted Congress to approve by the end of 2009. On March 21, 2010, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA, colloquially "Obamacare") passed in the House by a vote of 219 to 212 and was passed by the Senate in December, after being passed in the House in November 2009 with a public option. On December 24, 2009, the Senate passed its own health care bill without a public option on a party-line vote of 60–39. On March 11, 2009, Obama created the White House Council on Women and Girls through Executive Order 13506, which advised him on issues relating to the welfare of American women and girls and was chaired by Senior Advisor Valerie Jarrett. On January 22, 2014, Obama established the White House Task Force to Protect Students from Sexual Assault with a broad mandate to advise on sexual assault on college and university campuses, co-chaired by Vice President Joe Biden and Jarrett, a development stemming from the White House Council on Women and Girls and the Office of the Vice President, and preceding the 1994 Violence Against Women Act drafted by Biden. On May 26, 2009, Obama nominated Sonia Sotomayor to replace retiring associate justice David Souter, who was confirmed on August 6, 2009, making her the first Supreme Court Justice of Hispanic descent. On May 10, 2010, Obama nominated Elena Kagan to replace retiring Associate Justice John Paul Stevens, who was confirmed on August 5, 2010, bringing the number of women on the Court to three for the first time in American history. On October 8, 2009, Obama signed the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, expanding the 1969 federal hate-crime law to include crimes motivated by a victim's actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability. On October 30, 2009, Obama lifted the ban on travel to the United States by those infected with HIV, an action celebrated by Immigration Equality. On December 22, 2010, Obama signed the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010, fulfilling a 2008 campaign promise to end the policy that had prevented gay and lesbian people from serving openly in the U.S. Armed Forces. In 2016, the Pentagon ended the policy that barred transgender people from serving openly in the military. On February 17, 2009, Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, a $787 billion (equivalent to $1153 billion in 2024) economic stimulus package aimed at recovering from the deepening worldwide recession, which included increased federal spending for health care, infrastructure, education, tax breaks, and direct assistance. In March 2009, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner introduced the Public–Private Investment Program for Legacy Assets, which included provisions for buying up to $2 trillion in depreciated real estate assets. In March 2009, Obama intervened in the automotive industry by renewing loans for General Motors and Chrysler to continue operations while reorganizing, setting terms for both firms' bankruptcies, including the sale of Chrysler to Italian automaker Fiat and a reorganization of GM giving the U.S. government a temporary 60 percent equity stake. In June 2009, dissatisfied with the pace of economic stimulus, Obama called on his cabinet to accelerate investment. He signed the Car Allowance Rebate System, known as "Cash for Clunkers," which temporarily boosted the economy. The Bush and Obama administrations authorized spending and loan guarantees totaling about $11.5 trillion from the Federal Reserve and the Department of the Treasury, though only $3 trillion had been spent by the end of November 2009. On August 2, 2011, after a lengthy congressional debate, Obama signed the bipartisan Budget Control Act of 2011, which enforced limits on discretionary spending until 2021, established a procedure to increase the debt limit, created a Congressional Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction with a goal of achieving at least $1.5 trillion in budgetary savings over 10 years, and established automatic spending reductions of up to $1.2 trillion if the committee failed to achieve savings. The legislation prevented a U.S. government default on its obligations. The unemployment rate peaked in October 2009 at 10.0 percent and averaged 10.0 percent in the fourth quarter, falling to 9.6 percent in the second quarter of 2010 and remaining there for the rest of the year, with employment rising by 0.8 percent between February and December 2010, less than the 1.9 percent average during prior recoveries. By November 2012, the unemployment rate fell to 7.7 percent, decreasing to 6.7 percent in the last month of 2013, and continuing to decline to 6.3 percent in the first quarter of 2014. GDP growth returned in the third quarter of 2009 at 1.6 percent, increasing to 5.0 percent in the fourth quarter, followed by a 3.7 percent increase in the first quarter of 2010, with lesser gains later, and overall growth of 2.9 percent in 2010. In July 2010, the Federal Reserve noted that economic activity continued to increase but had slowed, with chairman Ben Bernanke stating the outlook was "unusually uncertain." The Congressional Budget Office and many economists credit Obama's stimulus plan for economic growth, with the CBO reporting that the stimulus increased employment by 1–2.1 million, though it conceded that it is impossible to determine how many of those jobs would have existed without the stimulus. An April 2010 survey of members of the National Association for Business Economics showed an increase in job creation, but 73 percent of 68 respondents believed the stimulus had no impact on employment. The U.S. economy grew faster than other original NATO members by a wider margin under Obama than at any time since the end of World War II, with the OECD crediting the U.S. stimulus and European austerity measures for the faster growth. Within a month of the 2010 midterm elections, Obama announced a compromise deal with congressional Republican leadership that included a temporary two-year extension of the 2001 and 2003 income tax rates, a one-year payroll tax reduction, continuation of unemployment benefits, and a new rate and exemption amount for estate taxes. The resulting $858 billion (equivalent to $1.2 trillion in 2024) Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010 passed with bipartisan majorities and was signed by Obama on December 17, 2010. In December 2013, Obama declared growing income inequality a "defining challenge of our time" and called on Congress to strengthen the safety net and raise wages, following nationwide fast-food worker strikes and Pope Francis' criticism of inequality and trickle-down economics. He urged Congress to ratify a 12-nation free trade pact called the Trans-Pacific Partnership. On April 20, 2010, an explosion at the Macondo Prospect in the Gulf of Mexico caused a major sustained oil leak; Obama visited the Gulf, announced a federal investigation, formed a bipartisan commission to recommend new safety standards, and announced a six-month moratorium on new deepwater drilling permits pending regulatory review. Prior to the oil spill, on March 31, 2010, Obama ended a ban on oil and gas drilling along most of the East Coast and northern Alaska to gain support for an energy and climate bill and reduce foreign oil and gas imports. In July 2013, Obama expressed reservations and stated he would reject the Keystone XL pipeline if it increased carbon pollution or greenhouse emissions. On February 24, 2015, Obama vetoed a bill authorizing the pipeline, which was his third veto and first major veto. In December 2016, Obama permanently banned new offshore oil and gas drilling in most U.S.-owned waters in the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans using the 1953 Outer Continental Shelf Act. Obama emphasized conservation of federal lands, using the Antiquities Act to create 25 new national monuments and expand four others, protecting a total of 553,000,000 acres (224,000,000 ha) of federal lands and waters, more than any other U.S. president. Obama called for Congress to pass health care reform legislation, a key campaign promise, proposing expansion of health insurance coverage for the uninsured, capping premium increases, allowing people to retain coverage when changing jobs, spending $900 billion over ten years, including a government insurance plan (public option) to compete with corporate insurers, making it illegal for insurers to drop sick people or deny coverage for pre-existing conditions, requiring every American to carry health coverage, and including medical spending cuts and taxes on insurers offering expensive plans. On March 11, 2009, Obama lifted a ban on using federal funds for embryonic stem cell research, reversing a Bush-era policy that had limited such funding and pledging to develop "strict guidelines" on the research. In a major space policy speech in April 2010, Obama announced a shift in NASA's direction, ending plans for a return to the moon, development of the Ares I and Ares V rockets, and the Constellation program, in favor of funding earth science projects, a new rocket type, research and development for an eventual crewed mission to Mars, and ongoing missions to the International Space Station. On January 16, 2013, one month after the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, Obama signed 23 executive orders outlining sweeping gun control proposals, including urging Congress to reintroduce an expired ban on military-style assault weapons, impose limits on ammunition magazines to 10 rounds, introduce background checks on all gun sales, pass a ban on armor-piercing bullets, impose harsher penalties for gun-traffickers, especially unlicensed dealers who buy arms for criminals, and approve the appointment of the head of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives for the first time since 2006. On January 5, 2016, Obama announced new executive actions extending background check requirements to more gun sellers. In a 2016 editorial in The New York Times, Obama compared the struggle for "common-sense gun reform" to women's suffrage and other civil rights movements. In 2011, Obama signed a four-year renewal of the Patriot Act. Following the 2013 global surveillance disclosures by Edward Snowden, Obama condemned the leak as unpatriotic but called for increased restrictions on the National Security Agency (NSA) to address privacy violations, while continuing and expanding surveillance programs established by George W. Bush and supporting legislation to limit the NSA's bulk collection of phone records and increase transparency in the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC). In his speeches, Obama did not make more overt references to race relations than his predecessors, but according to one study, he implemented stronger policy action on behalf of African-Americans than any president since the Nixon era. Following Obama's election, many pondered the existence of a "post-racial America," but racial tensions quickly became apparent, and many African-Americans expressed outrage over what they saw as intense racial animosity directed at Obama. The acquittal of George Zimmerman following the killing of Trayvon Martin sparked national outrage, leading Obama to say in a speech that "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." The shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, sparked widespread protests, leading to the birth of the Black Lives Matter movement, which campaigns against violence and systemic racism toward black people. Though Obama entered office reluctant to discuss race, by 2014 he began openly discussing the disadvantages faced by many members of minority groups. Several incidents during Obama's presidency generated disapproval from the African-American community and law enforcement, and Obama sought to build trust between law enforcement and civil rights activists, with mixed results. Some in law enforcement criticized Obama's condemnation of racial bias after police actions that led to the deaths of African-American men, while some racial justice activists criticized his expressions of empathy for the police. In a March 2016 Gallup poll, nearly one third of Americans said they worried "a great deal" about race relations, a higher figure than in any previous Gallup poll since 2001.

On January 14, 2009, House Democratic leaders introduced a 1,017-page plan to overhaul the U.S. health care system, which President Obama wanted Congress to approve by the end of 2009. After public debate during the congressional summer recess of 2009, Obama delivered a speech to a joint session of Congress on September 9 to address concerns over the proposals. In March 2009, Obama lifted a ban on using federal funds for stem cell research. On November 7, 2009, a health care bill featuring the public option was passed in the House. On December 24, 2009, the Senate passed its own bill—without a public option—on a party-line vote of 60–39. On March 21, 2010, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA, colloquially "Obamacare") passed in the House by a vote of 219 to 212, having previously passed the Senate in December. Obama signed the bill into law on March 23, 2010. The ACA includes health-related provisions, most of which took effect in 2014, such as expanding Medicaid eligibility for people making up to 133 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL) starting in 2014, subsidizing insurance premiums for people making up to 400 percent of the FPL ($88,000 for a family of four in 2010) so their maximum "out-of-pocket" payment for annual premiums would be from 2 percent to 9.5 percent of income, providing incentives for businesses to provide health care benefits, prohibiting denial of coverage and denial of claims based on pre-existing conditions, establishing health insurance exchanges, prohibiting annual coverage caps, and supporting medical research. According to White House and CBO figures, the maximum share of income that enrollees would have to pay would vary depending on their income relative to the federal poverty level. The costs of these provisions are offset by taxes, fees, and cost-saving measures, such as new Medicare taxes for those in high-income brackets, taxes on indoor tanning, cuts to the Medicare Advantage program in favor of traditional Medicare, and fees on medical devices and pharmaceutical companies; there is also a tax penalty for those who do not obtain health insurance, unless they are exempt due to low income or other reasons. In March 2010, the CBO estimated that the net effect of both laws would be a reduction in the federal deficit by $143 billion over the first decade. The law faced several legal challenges, primarily based on the argument that an individual mandate requiring Americans to buy health insurance was unconstitutional. On June 28, 2012, the Supreme Court ruled by a 5–4 vote in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius that the mandate was constitutional under the U.S. Congress's taxing authority. In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, the Court ruled that "closely-held" for-profit corporations could be exempt on religious grounds under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from regulations adopted under the ACA that would have required them to pay for insurance covering certain contraceptives. In June 2015, the Court ruled 6–3 in King v. Burwell that subsidies to help individuals and families purchase health insurance were authorized for those doing so on both the federal exchange and state exchanges, not only those purchasing plans "established by the State," as the statute reads. In February and March 2009, Vice President Joe Biden and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton made separate overseas trips to announce a "new era" in U.S. foreign relations with Russia and Europe, using the terms "break" and "reset" to signal major changes from the policies of the preceding administration. Obama attempted to reach out to Arab leaders by granting his first interview to an Arab satellite TV network, Al Arabiya. On March 19, Obama released a New Year's video message to the people and government of Iran. On June 4, 2009, Obama delivered a speech at Cairo University in Egypt calling for "A New Beginning" in relations between the Islamic world and the United States and promoting Middle East peace. On June 26, 2009, Obama condemned the Iranian government's actions toward protesters following Iran's 2009 presidential election. In 2011, Obama ordered a drone strike in Yemen which targeted and killed Anwar al-Awlaki, an American imam suspected of being a leading Al-Qaeda organizer; al-Awlaki became the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and killed by a U.S. drone strike. The Department of Justice released a memo justifying al-Awlaki's death as a lawful act of war, while civil liberties advocates described it as a violation of al-Awlaki's constitutional right to due process. The killing led to significant controversy. His teenage son and young daughter, also Americans, were later killed in separate U.S. military actions, although they were not targeted specifically. In March 2015, Obama declared that he had authorized U.S. forces to provide logistical and intelligence support to the Saudis in their military intervention in Yemen, establishing a "Joint Planning Cell" with Saudi Arabia. In 2016, the Obama administration proposed a series of arms deals with Saudi Arabia worth $115 billion. Obama halted the sale of guided munition technology to Saudi Arabia after Saudi warplanes targeted a funeral in Yemen's capital Sanaa, killing more than 140 people. In September 2016, Obama was snubbed by Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party as he descended from Air Force One to the tarmac of Hangzhou International Airport for the 2016 G20 Hangzhou summit without the usual red carpet welcome. On February 27, 2009, Obama announced that combat operations in Iraq would end within 18 months. The Obama administration scheduled the withdrawal of combat troops to be completed by August 2010, decreasing troop levels from 142,000 while leaving a transitional force of about 50,000 in Iraq until the end of 2011. On August 19, 2010, the last U.S. combat brigade exited Iraq. Remaining troops transitioned from combat operations to counter-terrorism and the training, equipping, and advising of Iraqi security forces. On August 31, 2010, Obama announced that the United States combat mission in Iraq was over. On October 21, 2011, President Obama announced that all U.S. troops would leave Iraq in time to be "home for the holidays." In June 2014, following the capture of Mosul by ISIL, Obama sent 275 troops to provide support and security for U.S. personnel and the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad. ISIS continued to gain ground and commit widespread massacres and ethnic cleansing. In August 2014, during the Sinjar massacre, Obama ordered a campaign of U.S. airstrikes against ISIL. By the end of 2014, 3,100 American ground troops were committed to the conflict and 16,000 sorties were flown over the battlefield, primarily by U.S. Air Force and Navy pilots. In early 2015, with the addition of the "Panther Brigade" of the 82nd Airborne Division, the number of U.S. ground troops in Iraq increased to 4,400, and by July American-led coalition air forces counted 44,000 sorties over the battlefield. In his election campaign, Obama called the war in Iraq a "dangerous distraction" and that emphasis should instead be put on the war in Afghanistan, the region he cites as being most likely where an attack against the United States could be launched again. Early in his presidency, Obama moved to bolster U.S. troop strength in Afghanistan. He announced an increase in U.S. troop levels to 17,000 military personnel in February 2009 to "stabilize a deteriorating situation in Afghanistan," an area he said had not received the "strategic attention, direction and resources it urgently requires." He replaced the military commander in Afghanistan, General David D. McKiernan, with former Special Forces commander Lt. Gen. Stanley A. McChrystal in May 2009, indicating that McChrystal's Special Forces experience would facilitate the use of counterinsurgency tactics in the war. On December 1, 2009, Obama announced the deployment of an additional 30,000 military personnel to Afghanistan and proposed to begin troop withdrawals 18 months from that date; this took place in July 2011. David Petraeus replaced McChrystal in June 2010, after McChrystal's staff criticized White House personnel in a magazine article. In February 2013, Obama said the U.S. military would reduce the troop level in Afghanistan from 68,000 to 34,000 U.S. troops by February 2014. In October 2015, the White House announced a plan to keep U.S. Forces in Afghanistan indefinitely in light of the deteriorating security situation. Regarding neighboring Pakistan, Obama called its tribal border region the "greatest threat" to the security of Afghanistan and Americans, saying that he "cannot tolerate a terrorist sanctuary." In the same speech, Obama claimed that the U.S. "cannot succeed in Afghanistan or secure our homeland unless we change our Pakistan policy." Starting with information received from Central Intelligence Agency operatives in July 2010, the CIA developed intelligence over the next several months that determined what they believed to be the hideout of Osama bin Laden. He was living in seclusion in a large compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, a suburban area 35 miles (56 km) from Islamabad. CIA head Leon Panetta reported this intelligence to President Obama in March 2011. Meeting with his national security advisers over the course of the next six weeks, Obama rejected a plan to bomb the compound and authorized a "surgical raid" to be conducted by United States Navy SEALs. The operation took place on May 1, 2011, and resulted in the shooting death of bin Laden and the seizure of papers, computer drives and disks from the compound. DNA testing was one of five methods used to positively identify bin Laden's corpse, which was buried at sea several hours later. Within minutes of the President's announcement from Washington, DC, late in the evening on May 1, there were spontaneous celebrations around the country as crowds gathered outside the White House, and at New York City's Ground Zero and Times Square. Reaction to the announcement was positive across party lines, including from former presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. Since the spring of 2013, secret meetings were conducted between the United States and Cuba in the neutral locations of Canada and Vatican City. The Vatican first became involved in 2013 when Pope Francis advised the U.S. and Cuba to exchange prisoners as a gesture of goodwill. On December 10, 2013, Cuban President Raúl Castro, in a significant public moment, greeted and shook hands with Obama at the Nelson Mandela memorial service in Johannesburg. In December 2014, after the secret meetings, it was announced that Obama, with Pope Francis as an intermediary, had negotiated a restoration of relations with Cuba, after nearly sixty years of détente. Popularly dubbed the Cuban Thaw, The New Republic deemed the Cuban Thaw to be "Obama's finest foreign policy achievement." On July 1, 2015, President Obama announced that formal diplomatic relations between Cuba and the United States would resume, and embassies would be opened in Washington and Havana. The countries' respective "interests sections" in one another's capitals were upgraded to embassies on July 20 and August 13, 2015, respectively. Obama visited Havana, Cuba for two days in March 2016, becoming the first sitting U.S. president to arrive since Calvin Coolidge in 1928. During the initial years of the Obama administration, the U.S. increased military cooperation with Israel, including increased military aid, re-establishment of the U.S.–Israeli Joint Political Military Group and the Defense Policy Advisory Group, and an increase in visits among high-level military officials of both countries. The Obama administration asked Congress to allocate money toward funding the Iron Dome program in response to the waves of Palestinian rocket attacks on Israel. In March 2010, Obama took a public stance against plans by the government of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu to continue building Jewish housing projects in predominantly Arab neighborhoods of East Jerusalem. In 2011, the United States vetoed a Security Council resolution condemning Israeli settlements, with the United States being the only nation to do so. Obama supports the two-state solution to the Arab–Israeli conflict based on the 1967 borders with land swaps. In 2013, Jeffrey Goldberg reported that, in Obama's view, "with each new settlement announcement, Netanyahu is moving his country down a path toward near-total isolation." In 2014, Obama likened the Zionist movement to the civil rights movement in the United States. He said both movements seek to bring justice and equal rights to historically persecuted peoples, explaining: "To me, being pro-Israel and pro-Jewish is part and parcel with the values that I've been fighting for since I was politically conscious and started getting involved in politics." Obama expressed support for Israel's right to defend itself during the 2014 Israel–Gaza conflict. In 2015, Obama was harshly criticized by Israel for advocating and signing the Iran Nuclear Deal; Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had advocated the U.S. Congress to oppose it, said the deal was "dangerous" and "bad." On December 23, 2016, under the Obama administration, the United States abstained from United Nations Security Council Resolution 2334, which condemned Israeli settlement building in the occupied Palestinian territories as a violation of international law, effectively allowing it to pass. Netanyahu strongly criticized the Obama administration's actions, and the Israeli government withdrew its annual dues from the organization, which totaled $6 million, on January 6, 2017. On January 5, 2017, the United States House of Representatives voted 342–80 to condemn the UN Resolution. In February 2011, protests in Libya began against long-time dictator Muammar Gaddafi as part of the Arab Spring. They soon turned violent. In March, as forces loyal to Gaddafi advanced on rebels across Libya, calls for a no-fly zone came from around the world, including Europe, the Arab League, and a resolution passed unanimously by the U.S. Senate. In response to the passage of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1973 on March 17, the Foreign Minister of Libya Moussa Koussa announced a ceasefire. However, Gaddafi's forces continued to attack the rebels. On March 19, a multinational coalition led by France and the United Kingdom with Italian and U.S. support, approved by Obama, took part in air strikes to destroy the Libyan government's air defense capabilities to protect civilians and enforce a no-fly-zone, including the use of Tomahawk missiles, B-2 Spirits, and fighter jets. Six days later, on March 25, by unanimous vote of all its 28 members, NATO took over leadership of the effort, dubbed Operation Unified Protector. Some members of Congress questioned whether Obama had the constitutional authority to order military action in addition to questioning its cost, structure and aftermath. In 2016 Obama said "Our coalition could have and should have done more to fill a vacuum left behind" and that it was "a mess." He has stated that the lack of preparation surrounding the days following the government's overthrow was the "worst mistake" of his presidency. On August 18, 2011, several months after the start of the Syrian civil war, Obama issued a written statement that said: "The time has come for President Assad to step aside." This stance was reaffirmed in November 2015. In 2012, Obama authorized multiple programs run by the CIA and the Pentagon to train anti-Assad rebels. The Pentagon-run program was later found to have failed and was formally abandoned in October 2015. In the wake of a chemical weapons attack in Syria, formally blamed by the Obama administration on the Assad government, Obama chose not to enforce the "red line" he had pledged and, rather than authorize the promised military action against Assad, went along with the Russia-brokered deal that led to Assad giving up chemical weapons; however attacks with chlorine gas continued. A written statement stated: "The time has come for President Assad to step aside," a position reaffirmed in November 2015. In 2012, Obama authorized multiple programs run by the CIA and the Pentagon to train anti-Assad rebels; the Pentagon-run program was later found to have failed and was formally abandoned in October 2015. Following a chemical weapons attack in Syria, formally blamed by the Obama administration on the Assad government, Obama chose not to enforce the "red line" he had pledged and instead authorized the Russia-brokered deal that led to Assad giving up chemical weapons, though attacks with chlorine gas continued. In 2014, Obama authorized an air campaign primarily aimed at ISIL. On October 1, 2009, the Obama administration implemented a Bush administration program, increasing nuclear weapons production through the "Complex Modernization" initiative, which expanded two existing nuclear sites to produce new bomb parts. In November 2013, the Obama administration began negotiations with Iran to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, including an interim agreement, with negotiations lasting two years and a deal announced on July 14, 2015, titled the "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action," which saw sanctions removed in exchange for measures to prevent Iran from producing nuclear weapons. Obama hailed the agreement as a step toward a more hopeful world, though it drew strong criticism from Republicans, conservatives, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; the transfer of $1.7 billion in cash to Iran shortly after the deal was announced was also criticized by the Republican party, with the Obama administration stating the payment was due to the "effectiveness of U.S. and international sanctions." To advance the deal, the Obama administration shielded Hezbollah from the Drug Enforcement Administration's Project Cassandra investigation and from the Central Intelligence Agency. In December 2015, Obama started a $348 billion program to back the largest U.S. nuclear buildup since Ronald Reagan left office. In March 2010, an agreement was reached with Russian President Dmitry Medvedev to replace the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty with a new pact reducing long-range nuclear weapons by about a third; the New START treaty was signed in April 2010 and ratified by the U.S. Senate in December 2010. In December 2011, Obama instructed agencies to consider LGBT rights when issuing financial aid to foreign countries; in August 2013, he criticized Russia's law that discriminates against homosexual people, though he did not advocate a boycott of the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi. After Russia's invasion of Crimea in 2014, military intervention in Syria in 2015, and interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election, George Robertson stated that Obama had "allowed Putin to jump back on the world stage and test the resolve of the West," adding that the legacy of this would last. Obama's presidency ended on January 20, 2017, with Donald Trump's inauguration. The family moved to a rented house in Kalorama, Washington, D.C. On March 2, the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum awarded the Profile in Courage Award to Obama "for his enduring commitment to democratic ideals and elevating the standard of political courage." His first public appearance after leaving office was a seminar at the University of Chicago on April 24, where he appealed for a new generation to participate in politics. On September 7, Obama partnered with former presidents Jimmy Carter, George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush to assist victims of Hurricane Harvey and Hurricane Irma. From October 31 to November 1, Obama hosted the inaugural summit of the Obama Foundation, which he intended to be the central focus of his post-presidency and part of his ambition for more consequential activities after office. On May 22, 2018, Barack and Michelle Obama signed a deal to produce docu-series, documentaries, and features for Netflix under Higher Ground Productions. Higher Ground's first film, American Factory, won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature in 2020. On October 24, a pipe bomb addressed to Obama was intercepted by the Secret Service, one of several sent to Democratic lawmakers and officials. In 2019, Barack and Michelle Obama purchased a home on Martha's Vineyard from Wyc Grousbeck. On October 29, Obama criticized "wokeness" and call-out culture at the Obama Foundation's annual summit. In December 2019, Obama stated that women are "indisputably better" than men. Obama was reluctant to endorse in the 2020 Democratic primaries to unify the party, and on April 14, 2020, endorsed Joe Biden, stating he has "all the qualities we need in a president right now." In May 2020, Obama criticized President Trump for his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, calling it "an absolute chaotic disaster" and stating the consequences of the Trump presidency had unleashed "our worst impulses," diminished the U.S. reputation globally, and threatened democratic institutions. On November 17, Obama's memoir, A Promised Land, was released. Obama and his wife attended Joe Biden's inauguration in January 2021. In February 2021, Obama and musician Bruce Springsteen launched a podcast called Renegades: Born in the USA, discussing their backgrounds, music, and "enduring love of America." Later that year, Regina Hicks signed a deal with Netflix in a venture with Higher Ground to develop comedy projects. On March 4, 2022, Obama won an Audio Publishers Association (APA) Award for best narration by the author for his memoir A Promised Land. On April 5, Obama visited the White House for the first time since leaving office to celebrate the 12th anniversary of the Affordable Care Act. In June, the Obamas and Higher Ground signed a multi-year deal with Audible. In September, Obama visited the White House to unveil his and Michelle's official White House portraits. Around the same time, he won a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Narrator for his narration in the Netflix documentary series Our Great National Parks. In 2022, Obama opposed expanding the Supreme Court beyond nine justices. In March 2023, Obama traveled to Australia as part of his speaking tour, meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and visiting Melbourne for the first time; he was reportedly paid over $1 million for two speeches. In October 2023, during the Gaza war, Obama declared that Israel must dismantle Hamas following the October 7 attacks; weeks later, he warned Israel that its actions could "harden Palestinian attitudes for generations" and weaken international support, stating any military strategy ignoring human costs could "backfire." In July 2024, Obama expressed concerns about Biden's campaign viability after his poor debate performance against Trump; on July 21, Biden withdrew and endorsed Vice President Harris, who then ran as the Democratic nominee. Obama endorsed Harris alongside Michelle five days later and delivered a speech at the 2024 Democratic National Convention formally supporting her. He joined Harris on the campaign trail in October, visiting swing states and emphasizing her record as a prosecutor, senator, and vice president, advocating for increased voter turnout, and criticizing Donald Trump and the Republican Party, with these criticisms widely reported. After Trump was declared the winner on November 6, Obama and Michelle congratulated him and Vice President–elect JD Vance, praising the Harris campaign and urging liberal voters to support democracy and human rights. Obama attended Donald Trump's second inauguration in January 2025. Obama's family history, upbringing, and Ivy League education differ from those of African-American politicians who rose in the 1960s through civil rights activism. In an August 2007 meeting with the National Association of Black Journalists, Obama expressed puzzlement over being questioned about whether he is "black enough," stating, "we're still locked in this notion that if you appeal to white folks then there must be something wrong," and in an October 2007 campaign speech remarked, "I wouldn't be here if, time and again, the torch had not been passed to a new generation." Obama is frequently described as an exceptional orator. During his pre-inauguration transition and throughout his presidency, he delivered a series of weekly video addresses on YouTube. Obama avoided rigid political labels but described himself as a New Democrat, shifting the New Democrat faction from centrist, fiscally conservative Clintonism toward greater openness to social liberal policies. According to Gallup, Obama began his presidency with a 68 percent approval rating, the fifth highest for a president after inauguration. His ratings remained above the majority level until November 2009 and by August 2010 had dropped to the low 40s, a trend similar to Reagan and Clinton's first years. After Osama bin Laden's death on May 2, 2011, Obama saw a small poll bounce and maintained 50–53 percent approval for about a month before dropping back to the low 40s. His approval fell to 38 percent in late 2011 before recovering in mid-2012 to an average of 50 percent. After his second inauguration in 2013, approval remained stable around 52 percent before declining and bottoming out at 39 percent in December. Before the 2014 midterms, approval was at its lowest, with a disapproval rating reaching 57 percent. Approval lagged throughout most of 2015 but reached the high 40s by year-end. Gallup reported Obama's approval reached 50 percent in March 2016, the first time since May 2013. In polling from January 16–19, 2017, his final approval rating was 59 percent, placing him on par with George H. W. Bush and Dwight D. Eisenhower. Obama maintains relatively positive public perceptions post-presidency; Gallup's retrospective approval polls in 2018 and 2023 showed a 63 percent approval rating, ranking him fourth most popular since World War II. Polls showed strong support for Obama in other countries before and during his presidency. In a February 2009 poll by Harris Interactive for France 24 and the International Herald Tribune in Western Europe and the U.S., Obama was rated the most respected and most powerful world leader. In a May 2009 poll by Harris, he was rated the most popular world leader and the figure most people would rely on to pull the world out of the economic downturn. On October 9, 2009, the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded Obama the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize "for his extraordinary efforts to strengthen international diplomacy and cooperation between peoples," drawing mixed reactions; he became the fourth U.S. president to win the prize and the third to do so while in office. He called it a "call to action" and stated it was not a recognition of his own accomplishments but an affirmation of American leadership on behalf of global aspirations. Obama is described as one of the most effective campaigners in American history (particularly in 2008) and one of the most talented political orators of the 21st century. Historian Julian Zelizer credits Obama with a keen sense of how government institutions work and how his team could design policy proposals, noting policy successes such as the economic stimulus package that ended the Great Recession, the Dodd-Frank financial and consumer protection reforms, and the Affordable Care Act. Zelizer also notes the Democratic Party lost power and elected officials during Obama's term, calling this the "defining paradox of Obama's presidency." The Brookings Institution noted Obama passed only one major legislative achievement—the Affordable Care Act (ACA)—a fragile one—and that his legacy mainly rests on its symbolic importance and a patchwork of executive actions. David W. Wise noted Obama fell short in areas valued by Progressives, including continuing drone strikes, not targeting big banks during the Great Recession, and failing to strengthen his coalition before pushing for Obamacare, calling his legacy "a disappointingly conventional president." Obama's most significant accomplishment is generally considered to be the Affordable Care Act, provisions of which went into effect from 2010 to 2020. Many Senate Republican attempts to repeal the ACA, including a "skinny repeal," have failed. In 2017, the penalty for violating the individual mandate was repealed, effective 2019. Together with the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act amendment, it represents the most significant regulatory overhaul and expansion of coverage in U.S. healthcare since Medicare and Medicaid in 1965. Many commentators credit Obama with averting a threatened depression and pulling the economy back from the Great Recession. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Obama administration created 11.3 million jobs from the month after his first inauguration to the end of his second term. In 2010, Obama signed the Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, the most significant financial regulation changes since the Great Depression-era reforms under Franklin D. Roosevelt. In 2009, Obama signed the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, which included the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act—the first addition to federal hate crime law since Bill Clinton signed the Church Arson Prevention Act of 1996—expanding federal hate crime laws to include assault based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability. As president, Obama advanced LGBT rights by signing the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act in 2010, ending the policy banning open service by LGBT individuals in the armed forces, which took effect the following year, and in 2016 ending the ban on transgender people serving openly in the armed forces. A Gallup poll taken in the final days of Obama's term showed that 68 percent of Americans believed the U.S. government had acted appropriately in protecting LGBT rights.

In 2009, President Obama signed the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, which included the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act—the first expansion of federal hate crime laws since President Bill Clinton signed the Church Arson Prevention Act of 1996. This act made it a federal crime to assault someone based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability. During his presidency, Obama advanced LGBT rights by signing the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act in 2010, ending the policy that prohibited open service by LGBT individuals in the U.S. military, which took effect the following year. In 2016, his administration ended the ban on transgender people serving openly in the armed forces. A Gallup poll conducted in the final days of his term found that 68 percent of Americans believed the U.S. had made progress on LGBT rights during his eight years in office. Obama significantly increased the use of drone strikes against suspected militants and terrorists linked to al-Qaeda and the Taliban; in 2016, the U.S. dropped 26,171 bombs on seven countries. At the end of his presidency, he left approximately 8,400 troops in Afghanistan, 5,262 in Iraq, 503 in Syria, 133 in Pakistan, 106 in Somalia, seven in Yemen, and two in Libya. From December 31, 2009, to December 31, 2015, the number of inmates sentenced in U.S. federal custody declined by five percent—the largest such decline since Jimmy Carter—while the federal prison population rose under presidents Ronald Reagan, George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush. Human Rights Watch described Obama's human rights record as "mixed," noting that he often treated human rights as a secondary concern, supporting them only when the cost was low. Obama left office in January 2017 with a 60 percent approval rating; he gained 10 spots in a 2015 Brookings Institution survey, ranking as the 18th-greatest American president. In Gallup's 2018 job approval poll of the past 10 U.S. presidents, he received a 63 percent approval rating. The Barack Obama Presidential Center, his planned presidential library, will be hosted by the University of Chicago and located in Jackson Park on the South Side of Chicago. Obama received the Norwegian Nobel Committee's Nobel Peace Prize in 2009, the Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History and Education's Ambassador of Humanity Award in 2014, the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award in 2017, and the Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice and Human Rights Ripple of Hope Award in 2018. He was named TIME Magazine's Time Person of the Year in 2008 and 2012. He earned two Grammy Awards for Best Spoken Word Album for *Dreams from My Father* (2006) and *The Audacity of Hope* (2008), and three Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Narrator for *Our Great National Parks* (2022), *Working: What We Do All Day* (2023), and *Our Oceans* (2025), plus two Children's and Family Emmy Awards. In 2024, he became the first and only President from the Democratic Party to win the Sylvanus Thayer Award.

Baron Blitzkrieg is a supervillain appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics. The character, also known as Baron Reiter and simply the Baron, was created by Gerry Conway and Don Heck and first appeared in World's Finest Comics #246 (September 1977). Originally a vicious German army officer during World War II, Baron Reiter was blinded and disfigured when a concentration camp prisoner threw a bottle in his face. German scientists experimented on him as a Nazi, restoring his sight but not his appearance. As a result, he gains superhuman strength, invulnerability, optical energy beams, and the ability to fly. Initially, he could manifest these abilities one at a time, but underwent training to use them together. His early appearances were primarily antagonistic encounters with Wonder Woman and Superman. He later became a frequent opponent of the All-Star Squadron, brainwashed Commander Steel, confronted Hourman resulting in Red Bee's death, conspired with Zyklon to use the Liberty Bell to destroy Philadelphia before being defeated by the original Liberty Belle, Johnny Quick, and Jay Garrick / Flash, tried to stay hidden in Jamaica, and served as a benefactor of Axis Amerika. The Baron leads Shadowspire and collaborates with Vandal Savage's Symbolix organization in experimental research on Damage and an assassination attempt that is foiled by Deathstroke. During the "Infinite Crisis" storyline, he joins the Secret Society of Super Villains and is killed by Superboy-Prime during the Battle of Metropolis. In the "Blackest Night" storyline, his corpse is entombed below the Hall of Justice and later revived as a Black Lantern. In a flashback from JSA (vol. 2), during the 1940s, he led Gudra the Valkyrie, Horned Owl, Zyklon, and Nazi soldiers in an attempt to steal the Spear of Destiny, which was thwarted by the Justice Society of America and the Blackhawks. He possesses enhanced strength, agility, and endurance, wears body armor that provides some protection from physical attacks, has heat vision, and the ability to fly, and can travel between Earth-2 and Earth-X. In the alternate Flashpoint timeline, he makes a minor appearance and is killed by Frankenstein.

Basanti Dulal Nag Chaudhuri (6 September 1917 – 25 June 2006) was an Indian nuclear scientist and academic who served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, and played a pivotal role in India's nuclear program. He is recognized as one of the pioneers of nuclear physics in India. As Director General of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), he was instrumental in Pokhran-I (Smiling Buddha), India's first successful nuclear bomb test on 18 May 1974, which made India the sixth nation in the world to become a nuclear superpower, following the United States of America, Soviet Union (now Russia), England, France, and China. He also initiated the first feasibility studies on India's ballistic missile program. Born into a Bengali Hindu family in Narayanganj, Dhaka, Bengal Presidency, British India (present-day Bangladesh), his family relocated to West Bengal, India, following the partition of India in 1947 and the communal violence in East Bengal. His father became a professor of English at Banaras Hindu University (now IIT-BHU), Varanasi. Nagchaudhuri earned a Bachelor of Science degree from Banaras Hindu University and a Master's degree from Allahabad University. In Allahabad, he met lawyer Parmeshwar Narayan Haksar and renowned physicist Meghnad Saha, with whom he became close and joined his research group. In July 1938, when Saha moved to Rajabazar Science College, University of Calcutta, Nagchaudhuri followed. With Saha's support and funding from the Tatas, he moved to the University of California, Berkeley in 1938 to pursue a doctorate in Nuclear Physics, under Ernest Lawrence, completing it in 1941. After returning to India, he joined Saha's research group at Rajabazar Science College and, in 1949, became affiliated with the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP), later serving as its Director after Saha's retirement in 1952. His research focused on nuclear isomers, induced radioactivity, Cherenkov radiation, and nonthermal plasma. Before returning to India, he had arranged for the shipment of parts for a cyclotron magnet to Calcutta University, but the second consignment was sunk by the Japanese; the team, led by Saha and later Nagchaudhuri, built the remaining components, overcoming persistent issues with vacuum pumps and demountable oscillators. The cyclotron began functioning in 1954 after Emilio Segre's visit, and Nagchaudhuri is credited with building the first cyclotron in India. In 1953, he succeeded Meghnad Saha as Palit Professor of Physics at Calcutta University, holding the position until 1959. He was a visiting professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1961–62 and was nominated as a Lincoln Lecturer. Through his connections with B.C. Roy and P.N. Haksar, he was appointed Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on Science & Technology from 1969 to 1972 and served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence during this period. He became a Member of the Planning Commission in 1970 and served as Scientific Advisor to the DRDO from 1970 to 1974. In October 1972, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi approved the Smiling Buddha test, and Nagchaudhuri was a member of the steering committee for its preparations. The explosive lenses for the test were fabricated in the DRDO laboratories under his leadership. In 1970, he was tasked by Indira Gandhi to prepare a classified feasibility study for long-range ballistic missiles, leading to the initiation of Project Valiant in 1972 to develop a liquid-fuelled intermediate-range ballistic missile and Project Devil at DRDL for short-range surface-to-air missiles. Both projects were terminated in 1974 due to internal conflicts and lack of progress but laid the groundwork for the Integrated Guided Missile Development Program in the early 1980s. In 1970–71, he chaired a committee on India's maritime security, recommending coastal patrols, a registry of offshore fishing vessels, and a force to intercept illegal vessels—recommendations that formed the basis of the Rustamji Committee in 1974, leading to the establishment of the Indian Coast Guard. From 1 July 1974 to 1 January 1979, he served as Vice Chancellor of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). From 1975 to 1977, he chaired the National Committee on Environmental Planning and Coordination. He also served on the Board of Governors of the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. Nagchaudhuri was a member of numerous Indian and international scientific councils, including the Scientific Council of the International Centre for Theoretical Physics from 1976 to 1984 and the Research Advisory Council of the National Physical Laboratory from 1980 to 1982, and served as a member and vice-chair of the Board of Governors of the East-West Center. He also served on the boards of Bharat Dynamics Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. He maintained an active interest in Hindustani Classical Music and Bengali literature and culture. He was elected a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy in 1964, awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1975, and received honorary doctorates from Andhra University and Kanpur University. He died of a cerebral infarction on 25 June 2006 and was survived by his wife, Dipali Nag, his son, and his family.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Spanish: Basílica Menor de Nuestra Señora de la Merced) is a minor basilica located in Yarumal, Colombia, and belongs to the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos, serving as the seat of the parish of the same name. It is dedicated to the Virgin Mary, with the Virgin of Mercy as its patron saint, and functions as the titular church of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. Designed and constructed in the Renaissance Revival style as a larger replacement for Yarumal's original church, the project began in 1866 and faced numerous setbacks, including its high cost, the Colombian civil wars in the late nineteenth century, a partial collapse in 1890, and an earthquake in 1938, which delayed completion until 1944 when it was consecrated. During construction, the Chapel of Saint Aloysius—originally the cemetery chapel—was elevated to parish status. The basilica is rectangular and divided longitudinally into three parts, with a main façade composed of two domed towers joined by the central nave. It houses several artworks, including Nuestra Señora de la Merced, a 1798 painting of the Virgin of Mercy considered miraculous. In 1998, the Municipal Council of Yarumal declared both the basilica and the Chapel of Saint Aloysius a cultural and architectural landmark. On 12 August 1999, Pope John Paul II granted the church the title of minor basilica. Since 2000, the church has housed the remains of poet Epifanio Mejía, author of the Himno Antioqueño. Yarumal, originally named Saint Luis of Góngora, was founded in 1787 and initially had a straw chapel where priests from Santa Rosa de Osos held services. In 1790, the parish of Saint Luis of Góngora was established, later renamed to Our Lady of Mercy. By 1850, with a population of 3,000, it was clear that a larger church was needed. On 20 December 1860, Father Julián Palacio convened the townspeople to discuss the need for a new church and formed the first committee. On 15 January 1861, he proposed starting construction in April and authorized the first purchase of boards for rammed earth walls. On 5 February 1861, Gregorio Álvarez offered to work as bricklayer and project director for two reals and three pesos per day, and on the sixth, Palacio planted the first stone and began fundraising. A request for bishop’s authorization was approved on 2 March 1861, with the bishop urging organizational efficiency and the committee drafting seven regulatory chapters. The construction was financed through alms, collections, mandatory contributions, raffles, bazaars, and the sale of donated farms. On 4 July 1865, Santos Sánchez offered to direct architecture and masonry for five pesos per day but was not approved. On the same date, Policarpo Rivera donated land for free, including rights to build a shed and use mud, with the condition that it be returned after construction. Around this time, the committee hired laborers from Lime kilns in the Sepultura villages. On 25 August 1865, José María Zapata Muñoz was hired to direct architecture and masonry for four pesos per day, with the agreement to provide paintings and statues; he was later joined by Floro Hernández in 1868 and by Francisco Arroyave and Francisco Puerta on 18 July 1869. On 2 April 1866, Gregorio Álvarez began demolishing the old church, which stood on land belonging to the parish adjacent to municipal land north of Bolivar Square (now Epifanio Mejía park), with boundaries later clarified. On the same day, Palacio sent a letter to judicial vicar Valerio Antonio Jiménez requesting permission to build the Chapel of Our Lady of Carmen (now the Chapel of Saint Aloysius), which was granted on 17 April 1866. On 1 July 1866, Palacio requested to expand the chapel after the demolition of the old church, initially planning to sell the cemetery lot, but villagers instead proposed using funds to purchase land in front of the chapel to form a small square, which was approved by Monsignor Valerio Antonio Jiménez. On 14 February 1868, Pope Pius IX moved the seat of the Diocese of Antioquia to Medellín, renaming it Diocese of Medellín and Antioquia, though the Yarumal parish remained under its jurisdiction. With the chapel expanded and remodeled, Palacio requested and received approval from Bishop José Joaquín Isaza Ruíz to bless the chapel for Mass and sacraments while the main church was under construction. On 4 February 1873, the Diocese of Antioquia was restored, and Yarumal’s parish returned to its jurisdiction, with the seat in Medellín renamed simply as the Diocese of Medellín. In 1876, construction was halted due to the political–religious civil war from 1876 to 1877. On 1 September 1881, the board restarted work, contacting architect José María Zapata to begin on 1 December and hiring Manuel Antonio Misas to provide six thousand bricks for 38 pesos, though the agreement was canceled due to disagreements, with a 24-peso fine imposed. José María Zapata arrived in Yarumal in the first week of December 1881 to take charge, fulfilling his agreement with the board and with Father Aldemar Palacio (priest from 26 September 1875 to 5 August 1895). On 6 June 1884, priest Uladislao Ortiz and Marco A. Mejía requested approval to begin building the right tower, which was granted with a budget of 3,000 pesos. This marked the beginning of ongoing construction interruptions due to unrest, financial difficulties, and the urgent need to build a bridge over the Nechí River. On 18 June 1889, Bishop Jesús María Rodríguez authorized Mass and the Sacrament of Penance to be celebrated in the church during construction and ordered work to resume during his pastoral visit on 17 August.
