On 25 January 1890, work stopped when senior officer Ricardo Pérez and architect Zapata retired without notice, and José María Zapata Muñoz resigned on 6 February, when the portico and dome collapsed. At a meeting on 15 February, the board accepted Zapata’s resignation, attributing the collapse to either structural design flaws or construction interruptions. The community blamed those in charge, leading to a public meeting on 17 February 1890 where all members resigned, though the villagers urged them to stay, and they ultimately retained their positions. The board then met two days later to assess the situation, appoint an architect to examine the structure, determine what needed to be demolished, and take charge of the work. Zapata never returned to Yarumal. The frame of the church was designed by Victoriano Palacio and reviewed on 21 May 1894 by Tomás Vásquez, who found it satisfactory. However, due to the collapse, the board commissioned an engineer review. Heliodoro Medina was assigned to find the engineer, who hired Heliodoro Ochoa to evaluate the project. On 10 August 1894, a well-attended meeting was held, and Ochoa recommended not building the portico due to stability concerns. The board and townspeople agreed, and Ochoa was hired to design the front face of the building. Ochoa later proposed roofing the rear of the church with wood instead of the original stone dome, a proposal approved by majority vote. After this, Ochoa examined the previous work and found the carpentry and masonry to be stable. On 21 February 1895, work stopped again due to lack of funds and difficulties in collecting contributions. Only masons continued working at half speed, storing materials until work resumed. All board members were asked to resign on that date, and construction remained practically paralyzed from 4 August 1895. The board ordered the church condemned on 12 October 1895. Father Ildefonso Tirado began holding religious ceremonies in the new church on 11 May 1899 to encourage donations, coinciding with the start of the Thousand Days War. In February 1900, wooden grilles for stained glass windows were begun. On 27 December 1900, the board authorized Díaz to begin work on the bell tower. On 15 February 1901, construction began on the wooden side doors; the main door started on 20 July 1903. On 20 May 1901, the Daughters of María installed the altar of the Immaculate Conception, commissioned with board approval in 1898. Heliodoro Ochoa was brought back to Yarumal from Medellín to continue work on the bell tower and buildings, and along with Juan Nepomuceno Gómez, worked on the latches. On 22 July 1901, Victoriano Palacio was chosen to direct the tiling of the church. Work stalled until July 1903, when it resumed after the visit of Bishop Manuel Antonio López de Mesa. By then, Victoriano Palacio had been commissioned to install the altar, work on the chancel molding, create two holy water fonts, and build the bell tower. However, the bishop realized the work had only resumed due to his visit and blamed both the war and the board, leading him to remove all board members and appoint a new one. He also recognized that Yarumal needed two churches due to its population and importance, and ordered the new board to focus on both the new church and maintenance of the cemetery chapel. According to Ochoa’s calculations, the dome required 210 large planks, 700 small planks, 12 hundredweights of copper, and 2 of tin. On 22 November, the board approved José María Hoyos’s proposal to install a temporary altar with the image of Saint Joseph in a side nave. On 6 January 1906, it was agreed to begin tiling the building. In the same meeting, Carlos Mejía Vargas, supported by other doctors, recommended moving all religious ceremonies to the old cemetery chapel due to health concerns, and the priest agreed. In June 1908, structural problems in one of the towers became evident, prompting Ochoa to provide advice from Medellín to reinforce it with wood. Ochoa arrived in Yarumal on 24 December and visited the site with the full board. The board followed all recommendations except those to remove the bells, believing the tower modifications provided sufficient support. On 21 April 1914, priest Leónidas Lopera Roldán ordered construction of the atrium under the direction of José López and Jesús María Saldarriaga, with designs by Joaquín Pinillos. The following year, Roldán commissioned the altar, which served as the main altar for many years, from craftsmen in Carvajal. On 5 February 1917, Pope Benedict XV issued the papal bull Quod catholicae, creating the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos, splitting the former Diocese of Antioquia, and making Yarumal part of the new diocese. On the night of 4 February 1938, an earthquake caused serious damage, including wall damage, settlement of the main arch’s foundation, and cracks in the apse. Father Gerardo Martínez Madrigal requested technical advice from architects and engineers, who conducted photographic studies. Evaluations varied, with some recommending iron reinforcement, others suggesting demolition and a new concrete arch with columns. The pastor chose to rebuild damaged portions brick by brick using the recommendations of Jesús Mejía. After repairs, Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes consecrated the Church of Our Lady of Mercy on 11 February 1944. In 1947, Father Francisco Gallego Pérez purchased the first organ for the church, a Hammond organ for 7,000 pesos, delivered on 16 July and blessed on 14 September. Efraím Jiménez, priest from 9 March 1953 to 24 March 1968, hired Raúl Bohórquez to decorate the towers with nickel silver. Jiménez also obtained the current marble altar, consecrated on 7 June 1955 by Builes, and bought the current church organ from Walcker Orgelbau of Ludwigsburg, Germany for 102,000 pesos. The Hammond organ was later sold for 25,000 pesos to the Chapel of the Theological Seminary of Santa Rosa de Osos. Meanwhile, the cemetery chapel began to deteriorate, and in 1992, Father Luis Enrique Restrepo Muñoz established a board to restore it as a historical site. On 23 November 1998, the Municipal Council of Yarumal declared the Church of Our Lady of Mercy and the Chapel of Saint Luis architectural landmarks. On 12 August 1999, under the leadership of Father Gilberto Melguizo Yepes, the temple was granted the title of Lower Basilica. The consecration was performed in a ceremony chaired by Bishop Jairo Jaramillo Monsalve. Yepes ordered the replacement of a fallen church lamp, obtained stained glass windows, three new bells, a new baptismal font, and the picture of Blessed Mariano of Jesús Euse Hoyos. He restored marble tiles in the temple, which were in terrible condition. Additionally, in an initiative by Yepes and the Municipal Council of Culture, in August 2000, the remains of poet Epifanio Mejía were moved from the San Pedro Cemetery to the basilica.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The Church of Our Lady of Mercy in Yarumal, built in the Renaissance Revival style, is a historicist structure primarily developed in the 19th and 20th centuries, featuring a rectangular floor plan with three longitudinal naves—main and two lateral—crossed by a transept that projects slightly but does not form a cruciform. The intersection of the transept and central nave supports a dome. The building has a symmetrical main façade facing the Epifanio Mejía Park, composed of two domed towers joined by a section framing the central nave, with three entrances—one central and two on the sides—each aligned with a nave. The side view reveals the towers, then the naves (with lateral naves lower than the central one), followed by the transept wall at the same height as the central nave, topped by the dome. The roof is tiled in clay, with gabled roofs on the central nave and transept and single-slope roofs on the lateral naves. The interior includes areas beneath the towers and choir loft, separated by walls, each containing Stations of the Cross paintings. The central nave is wider and taller, flanked by arcades of seven pillars each with square bases, shafts, and capitals, supported by semicircular arches; above, there is a wide decorative entablature with two series of six windows on each side, and a dropped ceiling with three large glass lamps. The transept is square, with corner pillars supporting an eight-window raised dome; lateral naves are nearly the same length as the central nave, have two series of six windows with decorative cornices, and include four Stations of the Cross paintings and two wooden confessionals. The southern side wall has a door, and the left wall connects to the chapel of the Fallen Christ, which links to the corridor of ossuaries and stairs to the towers and high chorus. The transept opens east–west, has the same width and height as the central nave, and features a marble railing and three steps leading to the main area, with additional steps near the presbytery emphasizing the altar. Niches in the transept walls contain images and windows; the baptismal font is in the western transept, with a niche in the north wall housing a high relief of the baptism of Jesus and a Chi Rho above it. The presbytery, elevated by seven steps, has a vaulted apse and includes the altar in a half baldachin, the table of sacrifice, the priest’s seat, and the ambon—all in marble. The reserve altar is a rectangular room four steps above, located at the end of the right nave. The basilica is constructed primarily of solid brick, with some side walls in rammed earth, both plastered internally and externally, with simulated block sizes. Bricks are held with lime mortar (calcium oxide, sand, water), which dries into a hard substance but is less resistant and impermeable than cement; cement was used after the 1938 earthquake. The façades are load-bearing, averaging 80 cm in thickness, with square-based nave pillars measuring 100 cm per side, and a stone foundation supported by brick. The roof is a wooden structure covered in clay tiles; the main dome is brick with a wooden structure and copper plates, and the tower domes are similarly constructed with copper plates appearing silver externally. The walls are tiled with multicoloured marble, similar in design to the Church of Nuestra Señora del Rosario, featuring marble inlays and fleurs-de-lis, with white marble terraces; the nave flooring uses coloured cement (hydraulic tile), common between the early and mid-20th century. During Father Gilberto Melguizo Yepes’ tenure, the marble tiling was restored after settling and sinking, with affected areas injected with grout and the paving polished to restore its appearance. The veneration of the Virgin of Mercy in Yarumal dates back to the founding of San Luis de Góngora in 1787, when the colonists declared her patron saint and protector, as recorded in a document from Medellín issued on 21 December 1787 by Visitor Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde. A painting of the Virgin of Mercy was commissioned in 1789 by Nicolás Valencia, a trader from Rionegro, and donated to the parish. It was solemnly installed in 1790 by Priest Nicolás Francisco Agudelos and confirmed as patron saint by Bishop Ángel Velarde y Bustamante on 27 January 1792. In 1915, Father Leónidas Lopera installed the image in the upper niche of a wooden altar; in 1930, Father Julio Ortega purchased a new frame and added protective glass. Gerardo Martínez Madrigal, before the Second Marian Congress in 1942, secured a hammered silver frame, shield, filigree brooch, and gold crown from Santa Fe de Antioquia, costing 950 pesos in labor and 2,000 pesos total, with the three gold items weighing 108 grams, the crown containing 24 gemstones and three pearls. The silver frame, weighing 11.5 kilograms, was donated by Yarumal women, with the top showing the Virgin of Mercy’s shield and the bottom in gold bearing the inscription "The parish of Yarumal of its exalted patron saint in the Second Marian Congress." On 28 August 1942, Father Francisco Galician Pérez removed the painting from its original frame to transfer it to the silver frame, discovering on the reverse a caption confirming Nicolás Valencia as the commissioner: "True portrait of the miraculous image of Our Lady of Mercy, redeemer of captives. A gift of Nicolás Valencia. Year 1789, a Hail Mary by the painter." On 23 September 1942, Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes blessed the jewels, which were then affixed to the painting and placed in the niche of honour in the 1915 wooden altar, with 3 mm glass installed for protection at a cost of 70 pesos. In 1987, during Yarumal’s bicentennial, the painting was canonically crowned by the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos and received the title "Perpetual Mayor of Yarumal"; in 1998, Monsignor Melguizo Yepes added a belt and gold sceptre. False legends, such as one claiming a traveler from Medellín left the painting at the "Contento" inn, are contradicted by historical records and the painting’s documented presence in the early church of San Luis de Góngora. The first altar was donated by the Salesian Sisters of Don Bosco in 1898 and installed on 20 May 1901. In 1915, Father Leónidas Lopera commissioned a wooden altar from Carvajal cabinetmakers, which served as the primary altar; due to the small size of the patron saint’s chapel, the image was placed outside the niche for visibility. A marble altar was later commissioned for the 1954 Marian year. Franco Lucarini of Marmolería Italiana de U. Luisi Eredi in Medellín was selected after receiving bids from masons in Medellín, Italy, and Bogotá. The church signed the agreement on 19 February 1954 and extended the contract on 10 June to include tiling of the presbytery and side chapel for 25,300 pesos. The unveiling was planned for 15–20 September 1954 during the Marian Congress, but delays occurred due to strikes in Italy. Work was sent by sea: the first shipment left on 19 September 1954, taking 25 days and 10 days to clear customs and arrive in Yarumal; the final shipment left on 15 December. A total of 18 trips transported 184 boxes weighing 100,820 kilograms from Cartagena to Yarumal, at a transport cost of 9,997.01 pesos. Assembly and placement began on 1 February 1955, with Manuel Rave Ángel and his son Gilberto hired for 16,000 pesos, as they had previously placed the marble altar from Santa Rosa de Osos in 1936. Before installation, the stone of the 1944 consecrated altar was removed, along with the relics of saints Teódulo, Martial, Modestina, and Amanda, to be placed in the new altar stone upon consecration.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: It took 25 days to transport the altar components from Cartagena to Yarumal, with 10 days spent passing customs and arriving in Yarumal; the rest of the materials were sent by sea, with the final shipment departing on 15 December. A total of 184 boxes, weighing 100,820 kilograms, were transported in 18 trips from Cartagena to Yarumal, at a cost of 9,997.01 pesos. On 1 February 1955, work began to assemble and install the altar, with Manuel Rave Ángel and his son Gilberto hired for 16,000 pesos, considered ideal due to their prior work placing the marble altar from Santa Rosa de Osos in 1936. Before installation, the altar stone from the 1944 consecrated altar and the relics of saints Teódulo, Martial, Modestina, and Amanda were removed and stored in a metal box, sealed with the episcopal seal of Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes, who transferred them to the parish priest. Construction of the altar’s foundation began on 7 February 1955, made of metre-thick concrete; lifting of the eight three-tonne columns started on 19 February and was completed on 26 February. On 2 March, the capitals were installed on the columns, the 17th entablature (including architrave, frieze, and cornices) was placed, and five medallions representing the Four Evangelists and titular saint Aloysius Gonzaga were added; the cross was placed on 31 March. The altar rails were completed on 19 April, the altar of the Blessed Saint was ready on 21 April with a Venetian mosaic of Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper, the shrine was finished on 28 April, and the painting of the Virgin of Mercy was set in the niche on 30 April. The altar was consecrated on 8 June 1955 by Bishop Builes, accompanied by clergy, the Seminar of Missions, and priest Efraím Jiménez, during a two-hour ceremony when the relics were placed in the new altar stone. On 10 April 1955, Antonio Boroughs Rendón of Medellín was contracted for 1,600 pesos to build an indirect lighting system; the church also purchased a red rug for greater splendour. On 24 August 1955, the wooden altar in the reserve chapel was removed and replaced with the 1915 altar, carried out by Eugenio Salazar between 26 August and 3 September, though the altar table remained in place due to deterioration. After the liturgical reforms of the Second Vatican Council, which ended the practice of celebrating mass with the priest facing away from the congregation, priest Roberto Arroyave Vélez needed the "Altar of the Sacrifice," also made of marble and consecrated by Bishop Ordóñez, which occurred on 18 September 1970. The altar is 12 metres (39 ft) high, 7 metres (23 ft) wide at the base, weighs 70 tonnes (77 short tons), and cost $23,000; it features eight monolithic columns, each 6 metres (20 ft) and 55 centimetres (22 in) in diameter, arranged in two semicircular rows, with Corinthian style matching the church’s architecture. The semicircular entablature rests on the capitals and includes an east-facing semi-dome with high relief ornaments, a central shield bearing the "I.H.S." monogram of Jesus Christ, and a cross at the top; at the base of the semi-dome are five medallions representing Aloysius Gonzaga and the Four Evangelists on a Venetian mosaic background. The half-dome and columns form a canopy sheltering the altar, the church tabernacle, a green marble shrine for the Virgin of Mercy with a monogram and ducal crown, the throne of the saint, and a reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper in Venetian mosaic. Interest in acquiring a musical instrument for religious celebrations began in 1880 when Father Aldemar Palacio received a letter from Jesús María Rodríguez, Provisor of the Bishop of Antioquia, ordering all churches in the diocese to have an organ; due to construction-related economic difficulties, the purchase was postponed. On 11 October 1900, Presbyter Emigdio A. Palacio requested the purchase of a musical instrument, and the Board of Manufacture agreed to contribute 1,000 pesos, up to 1,500 pesos if the organ was purchased. In 1947, Presbyter Francisco Galician Pérez bought a Hammond organ for 7,000 pesos, unveiled on 16 July by teacher Cabral and blessed by the parish priest on 14 September. The current pipe organ was obtained by priest Efraím Jiménez from Oskar Binder & Cia. Ltda. of Bogotá, the exclusive Colombian representative for E.F. Walcker of Ludwigsburg, Germany, founded in 1785 and experienced in building organs for tropical climates. A delegate from the firm visited Yarumal to assess the church’s style and acoustics, recommending a pipe organ with 17 registrations (1,020 pipes) valued at 102,000 pesos to be paid over three years. Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes approved the contract, congratulating priest Jiménez. The agreement was signed on 19 February 1961 by Presbyter Jiménez, Benedicto Soto Mejía, and Oskar Binder. The organ, weighing four tonnes, was shipped from Bogotá via Sonsón on 6 March 1963, arriving in Yarumal three days later and installed through the "Door of the Pardon"; installation began on 11 March, overseen by Oskar Binder, and the organ debuted on 19 March, the Day of Saint Joseph. It was blessed from the pulpit by Bishop Builes before the Sunday liturgy on 24 March. The Hammond organ was sold to the Chapel of the Conciliar Seminary of Santa Rosa de Osos for 25,000 pesos. The E.F. Walcker organ has 17 stops across two manual keyboards (61 keys each) and a pedal keyboard for bass, all in a console facing the altar; it controls 1,020 pipes of varying length and calibre. It functions as an orchestra with trumpets, bombards, oboes, clarinets, flutes, and human voices, made of varnished and sealed mahogany, powered by an electrical fan and a 14-volt dynamo. Of the 32 organs in Antioquia, the basilica’s is the eighth largest in area and volume. Early representations of Jesus’ passion and death were 50 x 60 cm oil paintings obtained by Bárbara Palacio of Mejía, aunt of Father Benedicto Soto, donated to the parish and later given to the chapel of the Pontifical Seminar of Missions, canonically erected by J. Buenaventura Marín on 7 October 1903 with Emigdio Palacio and vicar witnessing. The current Stations of the Cross paintings, made in 1945 and 1946, were commissioned by Francisco Galician Pérez to Mariela Ochoa U. of Medellín, copied from illustrations brought by Father Gallego from Germany, each costing 100 pesos. The church initially had simple stained glass windows; Monsignor Melguizo Yepes commissioned artistic stained glass from an artist in Cali using cathedral glass. There are 11 windows in total, covering the lower series between the transept and towers; the rest remain simple. Five stained glass windows face the Rosenda Torres school from north to south: Jesus with apostles, Saint Francis Xavier, Pope John Paul II (who beatified Father Mariano and granted the church the title of lower basilica), Mariano de Jesús Euse Hoyos (blessed and born in Yarumal, coadjutor), and Saint Joseph. Six windows face the eastern nave from north to south: Baby Jesus and Holy Family, the Good Shepherd, the birth of Jesus, the Trinity, the gubernatorial decree declaring the Virgin of Mercy perpetual mayor of Yarumal, and a replica of the Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Mercy. The central nave has four large crystal chandeliers, 3.2 metres (10 ft) high and 2.3 metres (7.5 ft) wide, purchased and installed between 1959 and 1960 by Presbyter Efraím Jiménez after a demonstration by a lamp seller. Two chandeliers were initially ordered as a trial; the first was permanently installed on 23 October 1959. The plan, finalized that year, included two more chandeliers in the central nave and smaller ones for Easter 1960 in the presbytery, reserve altar, side naves, and under the basilica’s dome, totaling 13 chandeliers ordered from French firm Baccarat at 60,000 pesos; the final chandelier was installed on 11 February 1960. On 2 December 1882, during construction, José María Díaz donated the first clock, originally installed in the tower above the "Door of the Pardon," moved to the circular area between windows on the central door in 1920. It remained until 24 May 1966, when it was replaced by a new four-faced clock from Vitoria, Spain, solemnly blessed by Bishop Builes the day before installation, with plans to place the old clock in the cemetery of Carmen. The clock rings every fifteen minutes using its own bells, activated by ropes that pull hammers to strike the bell. The original bells were in poor condition due to cracks reducing volume; Monsignor Melguizo Yepes arranged their replacement, removing the damaged ones from the right tower and sending them to the Tristancho workshops, a Colombian bellmaking dynasty with 250 years of history, where they were melted to create new bells using the lost mould technique. The process involves mixing three types of clay with horse manure, building a bamboo frame, layering the clay, and repeating the process; the interior and exterior are machined into bell shape, sheep tallow is applied to release the mould, a countermould is heated to absorb the tallow, and both are burned, leaving a cavity filled with molten copper and tin. The foundry uses mud ovens with dry firewood, melting the metal at 1,200 degrees Celsius; each bell is made in one piece and takes only three seconds to fill a mould for a 300 kg bell, then cools for two days before hand-polishing. The three new bells are large, bronze, and cost 7,500,000 pesos; unveiled by Melguizo in 1997, they were baptized from highest to lowest as the Lady of Mercy (500 kg), Saint Aloysius Gonzaga (310 kg), and Benedicto (300 kg), used to announce religious events and operated manually via ropes from the tower’s lower part. The church has had four baptismal fonts: the first in what is now the chapel of the Fallen Christ, formerly the baptistry, decorated with the Holy Trinity; the second built by Gallego Pérez, placed equidistant between the chapel of the Fallen Christ and the chapel of Our Lady of Perpetual Help; the third located in the left nave, constructed in 1975 by Father Roberto Arroyave from bogotana sandstone under the signature "Enchapes Sacatín" for 80,000 pesos; the fourth and current font is in the same location, acquired by Gilberto Melguizo Yepes, built from marble with a staggered octagonal base, square pillar, and octagonal basin. Two holy water fonts were purchased in 1945 by Father Ernesto Acosta Arteaga from Marmolería Artistica of Hermenegildo Bibolotti, each 160 centimetres (63 in) high, with base, column, basin, and a central angel statue. In 1924, Presbyteries Rafael and José Manuel Yepes Carvajal donated 12 large French candelabras (1.5 metres high) used during eucharistic vigils from 6 June to 16 July, concluding with the Virgin of Carmen celebration; Presbytery Luis Enrique Restrepo Muñoz restored them during his first five years; they remain mostly at the foot of the main altar. The basilica originally had a pulpit made by the Carvajales Martínez, finished with imitation marble and allegorical depictions of the evangelists, which was demolished on 25 January 1971; the rosettes are preserved in the Traditional Museum of Monsignor Juan N. Rueda. Before the Second Vatican Council, the church had a wide variety of art; these were removed on 18 July 1967 due to council provisions. Among the removed works were paintings of the Holy Family, Sacred Heart, Immaculate Heart of Mary, Saint Joseph, Saint John Eudes, Saint Roch, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Saint Tarcisius, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, Infant Jesus of Prague, Infant Jesus of the Small Flock, the ancient Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Our Lady of Sorrows and Child Mary. Some remained temporarily, including the patron saint Our Lady of Mercy, titular saint Aloysius Gonzaga, Our Lady of Perpetual Help, the three pictures of the Ordeal, Our Lady of Fátima, Saint Augustine of Hippo, Saint Antonio, the embrace of Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, the Fallen Christ, and the divine countenance. Some images remained under review for retention: the Virgin of Carmen, one of the Immaculate Conception (by Bartolomé Esteban Murillo), Christ the King, and the Stations of Christ.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The paintings of the Holy Family, the Sacred Heart, the Immaculate Heart of Mary, Saint Joseph, Saint John Eudes, Saint Roch, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Saint Tarcisius, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the Infant Jesus of Prague, the Infant Jesus of the Small Flock, the ancient Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Our Lady of Sorrows and the Child Mary were removed from the church on 18 July 1967. Some of these images, including the patron saint Our Lady of Mercy, the titular Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, Our Lady of Perpetual Help, the three pictures of the Ordeal, the Our Lady of Fátima, Saint Augustine of Hippo, Saint Antonio, the embrace of Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, the Fallen Christ, and the divine countenance, remained for a time before being removed. Other images, such as the Virgin of Carmen, one of the Immaculate Conception (by Bartolomé Esteban Murillo), Christ the King, and the pictures of the Stations of Christ, were still under determination for retention or removal; the final placement of the Stations of Christ was decided on 14 August 1967 based on the considerations of the parish priest and Bishop Félix María Torres Parra. The current images in the church are located in the transept: the Immaculate Conception, the Virgin of Carmen, Saint Francis of Assisi embracing Christ on the cross, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, Saint Joseph, and the Blessed Mariano de Jesús Euse Hoyos. The painting of the Fallen Christ is in the chapel, and at the reserve altar are the paintings of Mary Help of Christians, Salvator Mundi, and six angels. The early church of Yarumal originally had the image of the Christ on the Column, noted in the 1845 inventory, but today its details and current location are unknown. Due to the absence of a Passion scene, in 1935 Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes ordered the rector to commission the Fallen Christ image. Presbyter Gerardo Martínez Madrigal began preparations for the chapel adjacent to the presbytery, and on 10 September 1938 made the final payment to Misael Osorio. The statue of the Fallen Christ was carved by Constantino Carvajal in 1935 for 400 pesos, and the corresponding urn was made by Francisco Gómez Estrada for 100 pesos. The image was inaugurated on days celebrating the Eucharistic Congress and the patron saints and is currently located in a chapel at the foot of the temple, previously the baptistry, next to the left nave. Fernando Ramírez and his wife Elena Rivera, from Sopetrán, acquired in the late 19th century a Barcelonan picture of the Dormition of the Mother of God. Upon the death of their daughter Carmen Ramírez Rivera of Botero on 22 March 1955, her brother Germán Ceballos Ramírez transferred the image to the parish. The Assumption of Mary, symbolizing the elevation of Mary’s body and soul to heaven, originated in the apostolic period and was formally established as dogma by Pope Pius XII on 1 November 1950. This image arrived in Yarumal on 6 January 1963, carved by Josué Giraldo Mejía, and depicts three invocations: the Infant Mary, the Immaculate Heart of Mary, and Our Lady of the Rosary. It features blue clothing without a mantle, a rosary in her hands, a garland of pink roses symbolizing the joyful mysteries, a crown of red roses around her heart representing the painful mysteries, and a third crown of yellow roses around her feet symbolizing the glorious mysteries. On the night of 8 to 9 January 1958, a fire in the altar stone destroyed the crucifix; a new one was donated by Antonio Hoyos Mejía. The cross was crafted in Yarumal by cabinetmaker Alfonso Areiza Medina for 20 pesos, and artist David Pérez of Medellín created the Christ sculpture for 300 pesos. The work was delivered on Holy Thursday, 3 April of that year, and unveiled on Good Friday for public veneration. Christ is depicted carrying the three powers of gold from the Divine Boy Jesus of Prague, donated by Mercedes Ramírez Rivera. The cross has a glow produced by a copper encasement ordered by rector Roberto Arroyave, designed to imitate the image of the Lord of the Miracles, a crucifix in the Basilica of San Pedro of the Miracles. In the basilica, three masses are celebrated Monday through Saturday, and eight on Sundays; schedules may vary due to celebrations of the patron saint, Holy Week, Christmas, or the Catholic calendar.

The Beilby Medal and Prize is awarded annually to a scientist or engineer for outstanding practical significance in chemical engineering, applied materials science, energy efficiency, or a related field. The prize is jointly administered by the Institute of Materials, Minerals and Mining, the Royal Society of Chemistry, and the Society of Chemical Industry, with the award being made in rotation among these organisations. It is open to members of these three institutes as well as scientists and engineers from around the world, with a specific aim of recognising early-career achievements; nominees must be no older than 39 years of age. The award is given in memory of Sir George Thomas Beilby FRS, a Scottish scientist born in 1850 who joined the Oakbank Oil Company in 1869 after studying at the University of Edinburgh. He served as President of all three organisations or their predecessor societies: the Society of Chemical Industry from 1898 to 1899, the Institute of Chemistry from 1902 to 1912, and the Institute of Metals from 1916 to 1918. Recipients receive a medal, a certificate, and a prize of £1,000, with the first award being presented in 1930. The list of recipients since 1930 is available.

The Bell UH-1 Iroquois, commonly known as the "Huey," is a utility military helicopter designed and manufactured by Bell Helicopter. It is the first model in the Huey family and the first turbine-powered helicopter to enter U.S. military service. Development began in the early 1950s, driven by a U.S. Army requirement for a medical evacuation and utility helicopter. The Bell 204, first flown on 20 October 1956, was praised for its single turboshaft engine, outperforming piston-engine helicopters. An initial production contract for 100 HU-1As was signed in March 1960. In response to power limitations, Bell developed improved models; the prototype used a Lycoming YT53-L-1 engine producing 700 shaft horsepower (520 kW), while by 1966, the Lycoming T53-L-13 engine, capable of 1,400 shaft horsepower (1,000 kW), was installed on some variants. A stretched version, first flown in August 1961, was developed to carry more troops, featuring a 41-inch (104 cm) extended fuselage with seating for 15, including crew, and the ability to carry six stretchers and a medic. Modifications included all-aluminium construction, a rotor brake, and alternative powerplants. The Iroquois first saw combat in the Vietnam War in March 1962, serving in roles such as general support, cargo transport, aeromedical evacuation, search and rescue, electronic warfare, and ground attack. Armed gunships were equipped with rockets, grenade launchers, and machine guns and were frequently modified in the field. The U.S. Air Force used Iroquois for reconnaissance, psychological warfare, and support missions in Vietnam, as did the Royal Australian Air Force. Approximately 7,000 Iroquois were deployed in Vietnam, with over 3,300 believed destroyed. The helicopter also saw combat in the Rhodesian Bush War, Falklands War, War in Afghanistan, and the 2007 Lebanon conflict. Originally designated HU-1, the nickname "Huey" became widely used and persisted even after the official redesignation to UH-1 in 1962. Derivatives include the Bell AH-1 Cobra attack helicopter, the Bell 204 and 205 for civilian use, the twin-engine UH-1N Twin Huey developed in the late 1960s, the four-blade Bell 412 introduced in Canada but not the U.S., and the UH-1Y Venom developed in the early 21st century for the U.S. Marine Corps. In U.S. Army service, the Iroquois was phased out in the early 21st century by the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk and Eurocopter UH-72 Lakota, though hundreds remained in service over 50 years after introduction. More than 16,000 Iroquois have been built since 1960. New orders from Japan and the Czech Republic have kept production active. Several countries, including Canada, Germany, Taiwan, Japan, and Italy, have produced the helicopter under license. Operators are found worldwide in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Pacific. In 1952, the U.S. Army sought a new helicopter for MEDEVAC, instrument training, and general utility, noting existing models were too large, underpowered, or complex. In November 1953, revised requirements were submitted. Twenty companies submitted designs, including Bell with the Model 204 and Kaman with a turbine-powered H-43. On 23 February 1955, the Army selected Bell to build three Model 204s for evaluation, designated XH-40. The XH-40, powered by the Lycoming YT53-L-1 engine producing 700 shp (520 kW), first flew on 20 October 1956 at Fort Worth, Texas, with Floyd Carlson at the controls. The Army ordered six YH-40 service test helicopters before the first flight, and two additional prototypes were completed in 1957. In 1959, Bell received a production contract for 182 aircraft, designated HU-1A and named Iroquois after Native American nations. The nickname "Huey" derived from the HU-1 designation became so popular that Bell began casting it on the anti-torque pedals. Even after the official designation changed to UH-1 in 1962 under a unified Department of Defense system, the nickname remained in common use. Army reports found the early YH-40 underpowered with the T53-L-1A engine producing 770 shp (570 kW), prompting the development of the UH-1B with a Lycoming T53-L-5 engine producing 960 shp (720 kW) and a longer cabin for seven passengers or four stretchers and a medic. Testing began in November 1960, with first deliveries in March 1961. In 1960, Bell developed the UH-1C to correct aerodynamic issues in the armed UH-1B, using a 1,100 shp (820 kW) T53-L-11 engine and a new rotor system to improve maneuverability and speed. A new tail boom with a wider vertical fin and larger synchronized elevators was designed. A dual hydraulic control system and improved inlet filter were added for Southeast Asian conditions. Fuel capacity increased to 242 US gallons (920 L), gross weight to 9,500 lb (4,309 kg), and useful load to 4,673 lb (2,120 kg). Production began in June 1966, with 766 units built, including five for the Royal Australian Navy and five for Norway. The Model 205 prototype flew on 16 August 1961, with seven pre-production aircraft delivered to Edwards AFB in March 1961. The 205 initially used a 44-foot (13 m) rotor and T53-L-9 engine with 1,100 shp, later lengthened to 48 feet (15 m) with a 21-inch (53 cm) chord and a longer tail boom, resulting in a gross weight of 9,500 lb (4,309 kg). The Army ordered production in 1963 with the T53-L-11 engine for multi-fuel capability; prototypes were designated YUH-1D and production models UH-1D. In 1966, the UH-1H was introduced with the 1,400 shp (1,000 kW) T53-L-13 engine, and the pitot tube was moved from the nose to the roof of the cockpit to prevent damage during landing. In 1962, the U.S. Marine Corps selected the UH-1B to replace the Cessna O-1 and Kaman OH-43D, resulting in the UH-1E, modified with all-aluminium construction, Marine-compatible radios, a rotor brake for shipboard use, and a roof-mounted rescue hoist. The UH-1E first flew on 7 October 1963, with deliveries starting on 21 February 1964; 192 units were built. Due to production constraints, two versions were produced under the UH-1E designation: the first 34 used the T53-L-11 engine, and later units benefited from UH-1C upgrades. The Marine Corps later upgraded UH-1E engines to the T53-L-13 producing 1,400 shp (1,000 kW). The U.S. Air Force selected a version with the General Electric T58 turboshaft engine for missile base support, requiring a separate offset gearbox due to the rear-mounted T58 output shaft. The UH-1N Twin Huey (Bell 212), developed for Canada in 1968 with a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6T twin-engine set, was also adopted by the U.S. Marine Corps and Navy, with first deliveries in 1971. In 1996, the U.S. Marine Corps launched the H-1 upgrade program, leading to the development of the UH-1Y and AH-1Z variants. The UH-1Y features a lengthened cabin, four-blade rotor, and two more powerful GE T700 engines and entered service in 2008. The Bell 412 is a four-blade version of the twin-engined Bell 212, not adopted by the U.S., but selected by Canada (CH-146 Griffon), licensed in Italy as the Augusta-Bell AB412, and planned for Japan by Subaru. It is a popular commercial and military helicopter and competed in the early 2000s Army Light Utility Helicopter program, losing to the UH-72 Lakota, which replaced aging UH-1 and OH-58A/C models in U.S. National Guard units. The UH-1 has a semi-monocoque metal fuselage with tubular landing skids and two rotor blades. Early models used a single Lycoming T53 turboshaft engine with power ratings from 700 to 1,400 shp (520 to 1,040 kW), while later models often featured twin engines and four-blade rotors. All UH-1 family members share similar construction. The UH-1H is the most-produced version and represents the family. The main structure includes two longitudinal main beams under the cabin, separated by transverse bulkheads, supporting the cabin, landing gear, fuel tanks, transmission, engine, and tail boom. The beams are joined at the lift beam, a short aluminum girder attached to the transmission via a lift link and cargo hook at the center of gravity. Steel lift beams were later introduced due to cracking on high-time airframes. The semi-monocoque tail boom attaches to the fuselage with four bolts. Dynamic components include the engine, transmission, rotor mast, main rotor blades, tail rotor driveshaft, and 42-degree and 90-degree gearboxes for the tail rotor. The main rotor transmission includes a 90-degree bevel gear with a 2.14:1 ratio, followed by a two-stage planetary gearset with a 9.53:1 ratio (3.087:1 each), and an engine output gearbox with a 3.19:1 ratio, resulting in 324 rpm at the main rotor. The two-bladed, semi-rigid rotor design, with pre-coned and underslung blades, is derived from early Bell models like the Bell 47, sharing features such as a damped stabilizer bar. The two-blade system reduces storage space but increases vibration, producing the characteristic "Huey thump" sound, especially during descent and turns. The tail rotor is driven from the main transmission via directional gearboxes, operating at approximately six times the main rotor speed. The UH-1H includes a synchronized elevator on the tail boom linked to the cyclic control, allowing a wider center of gravity range. The standard fuel system has five interconnected tanks, three behind the transmission and two under the cabin floor. The landing gear consists of two arched cross tubes joining skid tubes, with replaceable sacrificial skid shoes. Skis and inflatable floats can be fitted. While the five main fuel tanks are self-sealing, the UH-1H was not factory-armed, though armored pilot seats were available. Internal seating includes two pilot seats and up to 13 passengers or crew, with a maximum configuration of a four-man bench seat.

The UH-1H produces the characteristic 'Huey thump' sound during flight, especially during descent and turning, due to the tail rotor being driven from the main transmission via two directional gearboxes that provide a tail rotor speed approximately six times that of the main rotor to enhance its effectiveness. It features a synchronized elevator on the tail boom linked to the cyclic control, enabling a wider center of gravity range. The standard fuel system includes five interconnected fuel tanks—three mounted behind the transmission and two under the cabin floor—each of which is self-sealing, though the UH-1H was not factory-armed, with armored pilot seats available. Internal seating includes two pilot seats and up to 13 passengers or crew, arranged in a four-man bench seat behind the pilot seats, a five-man bench seat in front of the transmission, and two two-man bench seats on either side, all constructed with aluminum tube frames and canvas seats that are quickly removable and reconfigurable. The cabin can be fitted with up to six stretchers, an internal rescue hoist, auxiliary fuel tanks, spotlights, or other mission kits, and access is via two aft-sliding doors and two forward-hinged panels, which may be removed or pinned open; pilot access is through individual hinged doors. The UH-1H has dual conventional controls with a single hydraulic system boosting the cyclic stick, collective lever, and anti-torque pedals; the collective levers have integral throttles used only for engine start and shutdown, not rotor rpm control, which is automatically governed, while the cyclic and collective control main rotor pitch via push-pull tube linkages to the swashplate, and the anti-torque pedals adjust tail rotor pitch via a tensioned cable arrangement; some UH-1Hs were modified to replace tail rotor control cables with push-pull tubes like the UH-1N Twin Huey. The HU-1A (later UH-1A) first entered service with the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, the 82nd Airborne Division, and the 57th Medical Detachment, with Hueys from the 57th Medical Detachment arriving in South Vietnam in March 1962; the UH-1 has become one of the world's most recognized helicopters due to its role in U.S. involvement in Southeast Asia, particularly Vietnam, where primary missions included general support, air assault, cargo transport, aeromedical evacuation, search and rescue, electronic warfare, and later ground attack. A larger version based on the Model 205 was initially designated the UH-1D and flew operationally from 1963; the first batch of 77 UH-1Ds arrived in South Vietnam in April 1965. UH-1B/C gunships were replaced by the AH-1 Cobra from 1967 to late 1968 due to increasing North Vietnamese anti-aircraft defenses making continued use of UH-1 gunships impractical, after which the Cobra became the Army's primary attack helicopter. UH-1 gunships were often called "Frogs" or "Hogs" when equipped with rockets and "Cobras" or "Guns" when armed with machine guns; troop transport UH-1s were called "Slicks" due to the absence of weapons pods, though they had door gunners and were used in troop transport and medevac roles. UH-1s flew hunter-killer teams with observation helicopters such as the Bell OH-58A Kiowa and Hughes OH-6 Cayuse (Loach); during the 1972 Easter Offensive, two UH-1B helicopters with the XM26 Armament Subsystem were deployed to counter the invasion, with pilots receiving brief crash courses and successfully hitting 151 of 162 fired TOW missiles, including two tanks; these airborne TOW launchers were known as "Hawks Claws" and were based at Camp Holloway. During the Vietnam War, 7,013 UH-1s served in Vietnam, of which 3,305 were destroyed, and 1,151 pilots and 1,231 other crew members were killed. Post-Vietnam, the U.S. Army continued to operate large numbers of UH-1s, using them in combat during the invasions of Grenada (1983), Panama (1989), and the Gulf War (1991), where over 400 Iroquois performed missions, accumulating 31,000 flight hours over nine months with a 70% mission-capable rate, comprising over 20% of all coalition rotorcraft and recording 21% of total flying hours; more than 2,800 UH-1s remained in inventory, with 389 UH-1Vs making up 76% of Army medevac aircraft. Plans to phase out the UH-1 began as early as 1992, with the UH-1 being phased out starting in the 1980s via the introduction of the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk, though the Army UH-1 Residual Fleet retained around 700 units until 2015, primarily for training at Fort Rucker and in selected National Guard units; Army support ended in 2004, and the UH-1 was retired from active Army service in early 2005. Army National Guard retirements accelerated in 2009 with the introduction of the Eurocopter UH-72 Lakota; in 2009, the Guard marked 50 years of Huey service and 40 years with the National Guard with a ceremonial end to service; final flights occurred in Washington, D.C. in 2011 and Pennsylvania in 2010; the final U.S. Army UH-1 was retired in late 2016 and transferred to a state police department. The Huey remains in service with other Armed Forces, with the Air Force UH-1N still in service as of 2024 and scheduled for replacement; on 24 September 2018, the Boeing/Leonardo MH-139 won the competition to replace the UH-1N fleet, with the UH-1N fleet in service as of 2025. The U.S. Navy acquired surplus UH-1B helicopters from the Army, modifying them into gunships known as Seawolves for use with Navy Helicopter Attack (Light) (HA(L)-3), and also acquired UH-1C helicopters in the 1970s; Seawolves operated with Navy river patrol units. After HA(L)-3 was disestablished in 1972, the Navy established two new Naval Reserve Helicopter Attack (Light) Squadrons in 1976: HA(L)-5, the "Blue Hawks," at Naval Air Station Point Mugu in June 1977, and HA(L)-4, the "Red Wolves," at Naval Air Station Norfolk in July 1976. The last regular Navy Huey HH-1 search and rescue helicopters were retired in 2009 and replaced by H-60 Seahawks, and the last Marine Corps UH-1N was retired in 2014. The DEA used UH-1Hs, initially borrowed from the Army, for operations such as Operation Snowcap in Latin America and conducted counter-narcotics raids in Afghanistan, including a July 2009 raid that led to the arrest of an Afghan Border Police commander. Nine Argentine Army Aviation UH-1Hs and two Argentine Air Force Bell 212s were deployed during the Falklands War, performing general transport and SAR missions based at Port Stanley; two were destroyed and the remainder captured by British forces, with three surviving as museum pieces in England and the Falklands. The Royal Australian Air Force operated the UH-1H until 1989, with No. 9 Squadron deploying to South Vietnam in mid-1966 with M60 door guns; four helicopters were converted to gunships known as 'Bushrangers' with two fixed forward-firing M134 7.62 mm miniguns and 7-round rocket pods on each side, and aircrew armed with twin M60 flexible mounts; No. 35 and No. 5 Squadrons also operated the Iroquois through the 1970s and 1980s, contributing to the Multinational Force and Observers in Sinai from 1982 to 1986; in 1988, the RAAF began re-equipping with S-70A Blackhawks. In 1989 and 1990, the RAAF's UH-1Hs were transferred to the 171st Aviation Squadron in Darwin and the 5th Aviation Regiment in Townsville, following a decision to operate battlefield helicopters under the Australian Army; the last Bell UH-1 was retired on 21 September 2007 in Brisbane, replaced by MRH-90 and Tiger helicopters. The Royal Australian Navy's 723 Squadron operated seven UH-1Bs from 1964 to 1989, with three lost in accidents, and deployed during the Vietnam War as part of the Experimental Military Unit. The Salvadoran Air Force operated numerous UH-1s, becoming the largest and most experienced combat helicopter force in Central and South America during the 1980s, fighting for over a decade.

In 1989 and 1990, the Royal Australian Air Force's UH-1H Iroquois were transferred to the 171st Aviation Squadron in Darwin, Northern Territory, and the 5th Aviation Regiment in Townsville, Queensland, following the decision that all battlefield helicopters would be operated by the Australian Army. On 21 September 2007, the Australian Army retired its last Bell UH-1 helicopters, with the final flight occurring in Brisbane, and these were replaced by MRH-90 medium helicopters and Tiger armed reconnaissance helicopters. The Royal Australian Navy's 723 Squadron operated seven UH-1Bs from 1964 to 1989, with three lost in accidents during that period, and deployed Iroquois aircraft and personnel as part of the Experimental Military Unit during the Vietnam War. The Salvadoran Air Force operated numerous UH-1s, becoming the largest and most experienced combat helicopter force in Central and South America during the 1980s, fighting in the Salvadoran Civil War for over a decade and having been trained by the US Army in Vietnam-era tactics; by early 1985, El Salvador had 33 UH-1s in its inventory, some configured as gunships and others as transports, with further expansion supported by US government assistance. Several Salvadoran UH-1M and UH-1H helicopters were modified to carry bombs instead of rocket pods, enabling the military to avoid ground routes vulnerable to guerrilla ambushes, with gunships used to suppress hostile forces ahead of troop insertions. Dornier constructed 352 UH-1Ds under license between 1967 and 1981 for the West German Bundeswehr, which served with both the German Army and Air Force in utility and search and rescue (SAR) roles; after being replaced by twin-engine Eurocopter EC145s, the last UH-1Ds were withdrawn on 12 April 2021. Israel retired its UH-1s in 2002 after 33 years of service, replacing them with Sikorsky UH-60 Blackhawk helicopters, with an initial batch of 10 delivered in 1994; some were passed to pro-Israeli militias in Lebanon, while eleven UH-1Ds were reportedly sold to a Singapore-based logging company but were instead delivered in October 1978 to the Rhodesian Air Force to circumvent a United Nations embargo during the Rhodesian Bush War. In 1960, Subaru agreed to produce the HU-1B for Japan, renamed UH-1B in 1962, along with the HU-1H, renamed UH-1H, and Bell and Subaru developed the UH-1J. Starting in 1993, 130 UH-1Js were produced by Fuji for the Japanese Self-Defense Force. In 2005, two Japan Ground Self-Defense Force (JGSDF) UH-1s were deployed to Pakistan for earthquake relief, and in 2010, after floods, UH-1s were again deployed to assist in disaster relief; Japanese UH-1s have also been used periodically for water bombing against fires. Following the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, Japan's UH-1 fleet was extensively deployed for disaster relief and conducted reconnaissance flights over the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant carrying radiation detection equipment. By the early 2020s, Japan's Acquisition, Technology & Logistics Agency was planning to replace the remaining UH-1s in the JGSDF with a locally-built twin-engine multirole Bell 412, designated the H-2 in JSDF service; the first flight of the Subaru UH-2 occurred in 2022. During the early 1990s, the Lebanese Air Force inducted its first UH-1 helicopters; during the 2007 Lebanon conflict at the Battle of Nahr el-Bared, the Lebanese Army modified several UH-1Hs to carry 500 lb (227 kg) Mark 82 bombs, installing special mounting points on the sides for these high-explosive weapons to strike militant-held positions. After the 2020 Beirut explosion, UH-1s participated in disaster response and were used to extinguish fires. The fleet typically performs search and rescue, troop transport, aerial firefighting, and utility missions; in the late 2010s, specially modified UH-1Ds participated in the first LIDAR mapping exercise in Lebanon, and in February 2021, three additional Bell UH-1H-IIs were delivered to the LAF to augment its fleet. The Royal New Zealand Air Force operated 13 Iroquois with No. 3 Squadron, with the first five UH-1Ds delivered in 1966, nine UH-1Hs in 1970, and one more UH-1H in 1976; all UH-1D aircraft were upgraded to 1H specification during the 1970s, and two ex-US Army UH-1H airframes were purchased in 1996, with three lost in accidents. The RNZAF retired the Iroquois, replacing them with NHIndustries NH90 helicopters, with eight active NH90s and one spare procured; the process was initially expected by the end of 2013 but was delayed until 2016, with aircraft retired as they reached their next major group servicing intervals; the UH-1H was retired as the NH90 fleet stood up. On 21 May 2015, the remaining six UH-1H helicopters conducted a final tour before their planned retirement on 1 July, marking 49 years of service in areas including the UK, Southeast Asia, Timor, the Solomon Islands, various South Pacific nations, and the Antarctic. One UH-1 was preserved at the New Zealand National Museum after retirement in 2013, delivered in 2015, having entered service in 1966. During the 1973 Pakistan floods, the US sent six UH-1H helicopters, operating mainly in southern Pakistan, which were later left at Dhamial and then gifted to Pakistan by the US government following a proposal to Prime Minister Bhutto before his 1974 state visit. The Philippine Air Force (PAF) acquired Bell UH-1s, receiving the first in March 1969, with a unit reorganized into the 205th Tactical Helicopter Wing; the first four helicopters (tail numbers 290–293) were factory-new, with US Army production beginning just two years prior. In PAF service, the Hueys were used to combat insurgents and conduct disaster relief after earthquakes and typhoons; following this, the PAF armed them with M-60 machine guns, with aircrew undergoing gunnery training at Fort Magsaysay in February 1971, and the enhanced firepower was demonstrated in punitive operations at Barrio Talbac, San Ildefonso, Bulacan, on 7–8 April 1971, during which Huk Commander Beto and his aide Yoyong were killed. Francis Ford Coppola filmed Apocalypse Now in the Philippines, using Philippine Hueys for the iconic scene with Robert Duvall as Lt. Colonel Kilgore, due to President Ferdinand Marcos's agreement. In 2004, the PAF procured 20 refurbished UH-1H helicopters from Singapore Technologies Aerospace (ST Aero) for $12 million. In 2013, due to urgent operational needs, the PAF procured new Bell 412 units delivered in 2015; it also acquired 21 refurbished Bell UH-1D units with Night Vision Compatible Cockpit under a PHP1.26bn ($28 million) contract with Rice Aircraft Services and Eagle Copters joint venture, delivered in 2015. In October 2019, the Philippines made a deal with Japan to acquire spare parts to restore seven stored UH-1s to flightworthy condition. By January 2021, the PAF had 13 UH-1H and 10 UH-1D helicopters in operational service. In 2021, a plan to retire all remaining UH-1s was raised after a series of crashes; on 14 October 2021, the PAF officially decommissioned its UH-1D fleet, with retired aircraft stored at Clark Air Base, though airworthy airframes were returned to service due to lack of aircraft. The UH-1's role is now being fulfilled by recently delivered Poland-built PZL Mielec (Sikorsky S-70i) helicopters acquired under a Multi-Year Contractual Authority (MYCA); in January 2022. In 2022, the Philippines announced that some retired Hueys would be reactivated with Turkish company ASFAT's assistance, and Japan planned to donate UH-1s from its service to the Philippine Army; Japan is introducing new Hueys as replacements. As of December 2024, twenty-three units are in active service. Very late in the Rhodesian Bush War, the Rhodesian Air Force obtained 11 former Israeli Agusta-Bell 205As in violation of sanctions, allegedly using intermediaries to evade them; locally known as Cheetahs, these were restored to flightworthy condition and assigned to No. 8 Squadron, functioning as armed gunships and troop transports; one Cheetah was lost in combat in September 1979 after being hit by an RPG over Mozambique, and at least three other UH-1s were lost; the surviving helicopters were put up for sale in 1990. In July 2009, Yemen received four UH-1Hs, which remained grounded for most of their service, with at least one heavily damaged during Saudi-led airstrikes on Al Daylami and Al Anad Air Bases. In U.S. service, the G, J, Q, R, S, T, W, and Z model designations are used by the AH-1; the UH-1 and AH-1 are considered members of the same H-1 series, and the military does not use I (India) or O (Oscar) for aircraft designations to avoid confusion with "one" and "zero" respectively. Data from Jane's All the World's Aircraft 1987-88 is cited. The image of American troops disembarking from a Huey became an iconic image of the Vietnam War, appearing in films such as The Green Berets, The Deer Hunter, Platoon, Hamburger Hill, Apocalypse Now, Casualties of War, and Born on the Fourth of July, and prominently in We Were Soldiers, which depicts the Battle of Ia Drang. Author Robert Mason recounts his career as a UH-1 "Slick" pilot in his memoir, Chickenhawk. The 2002 journey of Huey 091, displayed in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, is detailed in the 2004 documentary In the Shadow of the Blade.

Beloit College is a private liberal arts college located in Beloit, Wisconsin, United States, founded in 1846 when Wisconsin was still a territory and is the state's oldest continuously operating college. It has an enrollment of approximately 1,000 undergraduate students. The college was established by the Friends for Education, a group formed by seven pioneers from New England who, upon arriving in the Wisconsin Territory, decided a college was needed. They raised funds and convinced the territorial legislature to grant a charter on February 2, 1846, with the first building, Middle College, constructed in 1847 and still in operation. Classes began in the fall of 1847, and the first degrees were awarded in 1851. Aaron Lucius Chapin served as the college's first president from 1849 to 1886. Beloit became coeducational in 1895, and in 1904, Grace Ousley became the first African-American woman to graduate. Although independent, the college has historically been unofficially associated with Congregationalism. It remained small for nearly its first century, with enrollment exceeding 1,000 only during the influx of World War II veterans in 1945–46. The "Beloit Plan," a year-round curriculum with three full terms and a field term, was introduced in 1964 and later replaced by a two-semester program in 1978. The campus is within the Near East Side Historic District and features 20 conical, linear, and animal effigy mounds built between 400 and 1200 by Late Woodland Native Americans, one of which, a turtle-shaped mound, inspired the college's symbol and unofficial mascot. These mounds are catalogued burial sites and may not be disturbed without a Wisconsin Historical Society permit; some have been partially excavated and restored, with artifacts like pottery and tool fragments held in the Logan Museum of Anthropology. In 2008, the college completed a 120,000 sq ft (11,000 m²) Center for the Sciences, renamed the Marjorie and James Sanger Center for the Sciences in 2017, which received LEED green building certification and won a Design Excellence Honor Award in Interior Architecture from the Chicago chapter of the AIA in 2009. In 2010, the Hendricks Center for the Arts, a 58,000-square-foot (5,400 m²) facility previously housing the Beloit Post Office and Public Library, opened and is named after Diane Hendricks and her late husband Ken Hendricks, a former college trustee; it is the largest single gift in the college's history. Two public museums, the Logan Museum of Anthropology and the Wright Museum of Art, founded in the late 19th century, are operated by college staff and students. The Logan Museum, accredited by the American Alliance of Museums, holds over 300,000 ethnographic and archaeological objects from 125 countries and over 600 cultural groups, while the Wright Museum has over 8,000 objects, including a large collection of original prints and Asian art, and features temporary exhibitions year-round. The campus includes two sculptures by Siah Armajani: Gazebo for One Anarchist: Emma Goldman (1991) and The Beloit College Poetry Garden. Beloit offers over 70 undergraduate majors, minors, and programs and partners with institutions such as Blackhawk Technical College, Johns Hopkins School of Nursing, Marquette University, Des Moines University, and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, as well as the Medical College of Wisconsin, to provide continuing education and accelerated degree pathways. The average class size is around 12 students, with one-third of courses having 10 or fewer students. Beloit is ranked in the top 100 of U.S. News & World Report's 2025 Best Colleges rankings and has high rankings in Most Innovative, Best Value, First-Year Experience, and Undergraduate Teaching. The college's most popular majors among 2024 graduates were Social Sciences, Biological/life sciences, and Physical sciences, a shift from 2021's top majors of Biology/Biological Sciences, Psychology, and Business/Managerial Economics. In 2012, it ranked among the top 20 American liberal arts colleges for Ph.D. graduates. Beginning in late 2023, Beloit launched five schools: the School of Business, which launched in late 2023, offers majors in business management, economics, and quantitative economics and operates in Pearson's Hall, part of a $20 million campus renovation, led by Diep Phan, a professor of economics and business since 2009; the School of Health Sciences, opened in late 2023/early 2024, offers healthcare-focused paths and partners with the Medical College of Wisconsin (November 2023) and Des Moines University (October 2025) for degree pathways, and with Edgewood University (2024) for a dual-degree RN to BSN program, led by Rachel A. Bergstrom, PhD; the School of Environment and Sustainability, launched in 2024, offers majors in biology, chemistry, education and youth studies, environmental biology, environmental chemistry, environmental communication and arts, environmental geology, environmental justice and citizenship, geology, and political science, directed by Jay Zambito, department chair of Geology; the School of Global and Public Service, launched in November 2024, offers majors in anthropology, critical identity studies, education and youth studies, French and Francophone studies, history, international relations, Japanese language and culture, political science, psychology, sociology, and Spanish language and culture, led by Beth Dougherty, Manger Professor of International Relations; and the School of Media and the Arts, which houses artistic and visual majors including creative writing, media studies, performing and applied arts, and studio art, led by Cullyn Murphy, Assistant Professor of Music and Media Studies, with the Hendricks Center for the Arts housing its studios and performance spaces. Student housing options include substance-free dorms and special interest houses such as Art, Spanish, Outdoor Environmental Club (OEC), and interfaith houses; the college has fraternities and sororities and over 45 student organizations and clubs, including the Aardvark Authors, founded in 2022. The student newspaper, The Round Table, was founded in 1853 as the Beloit Monthly, and the student radio station WBCR-FM operates at 88.3 MHz and streams online. Beloit has a frisbee golf course entirely on campus and in April 2006, students broke the world record for the longest Ultimate Frisbee game, lasting over 72 hours. In 2011, the college received the Senator Paul Simon Award for Comprehensive Campus Internationalization; 48 states are represented, and about 14% of the student body is international, with approximately half studying abroad in countries such as China, Russia, Brazil, Germany, India, and Spain, and sharing experiences on "Beloit and Beyond" Day each year. The "Mindset List," an annual list of freshman life experiences, originated at Beloit in 1998 and moved to Marist College in 2019. In 1969, Black students presented "The Black Demands," which led to protests including the occupation of Middle College as a Black Cultural Center and gatherings before a trustees meeting; while the demands were met, the college has not fully implemented all, such as increasing Black faculty and student representation to 10%. In 2018, Beloit updated its bias policy to include a section on hate acts, responding to incidents in 2006, 2015, and 2017. Beloit teams are known as the Buccaneers and compete at the NCAA Division III level in the Midwest Conference, fielding varsity teams in football, baseball, softball, volleyball, men's and women's swimming and diving, men's and women's basketball, men's and women's cross country, men's and women's track and field, men's and women's lacrosse, men's and women's hockey, men's and women's soccer, and esports. Notable achievements include baseball coach Dave DeGeorge reaching 558 career wins, three conference titles in twelve tournament appearances, and student-athletes earning All-American and Scholar All-American honors. Beloit plans to build on these successes by appointing Pat Miller as Athletic Director. In 2025, The Princeton Review named Beloit among the 391 Best Colleges, and U.S. News & World Report ranked it in the top 100 for Best Colleges, Most Innovative, Best Value, First-Year Experience, and Undergraduate Teaching. It consistently ranks among the nation's top 100 liberal arts colleges and is ranked 23rd nationally by Washington Monthly in its public good assessment. Niche ranks Beloit 737 of 1,613 in Best Colleges in America, 13 of 33 in Best Colleges in Wisconsin, 43 of 1,615 in Most Diverse Colleges, 68 of 932 in Most Liberal Colleges, and 101 of 181 in Best Liberal Arts Colleges.

Belvagene Davis (née Melton; October 13, 1932 – September 24, 2025) was an American television and radio journalist who became the first African-American woman to serve as a television reporter on the U.S. West Coast. Born in Monroe, Louisiana, on October 13, 1932, to John and Florence Melton, she was the oldest of four children; her mother was 14 years old at the time of her birth, and Belva spent her early years living with relatives. At age eight, she and her family moved to a two-bedroom apartment in West Oakland, California, where eleven people lived. Davis graduated from Berkeley High School in 1951, becoming the first in her family to do so. Though accepted into San Francisco State University, she could not afford college and worked as a typist at the Oakland Naval Supply Depot earning $2,000 annually. In 1957, she began writing freelance articles for Jet, a magazine focused on African-American issues, receiving $5 per piece with no byline, and later wrote for publications such as the Sun Reporter and Bay Area Independent, editing the latter from 1961 to 1968. In 1961, she became an on-air interviewer for KSAN, a San Francisco AM radio station targeting Black listeners, and made her television debut in 1963 for KTVU covering an African-American beauty pageant. She worked as a disc jockey for KDIA, a soul-gospel radio station in Oakland, when covering the 1964 Republican National Convention at the Cow Palace, where she and Louis Freeman were chased out by attendees throwing food and shouting racial slurs. In 1966, she joined KNEW as an announcer and became the first female African-American television journalist on the West Coast when hired by KPIX-TV, the CBS affiliate in San Francisco. She later worked for KRON-TV, the local NBC affiliate, becoming an anchorwoman in 1970. Over her career, she covered major events including the Berkeley riots of the Free Speech Movement, the Black Panthers, the Jonestown mass suicide-murder, the Moscone–Milk assassinations, the AIDS and crack epidemics, and the 1998 U.S. embassy bombing in Tanzania. From 1981 to 1999, she co-hosted KRON’s Sunday-morning show "California This Week" with Rollin Post. In the 1990s, she hosted "This Week in Northern California" on PBS member station KQED, retiring in November 2012. Her final broadcast featured a taped interview with Maya Angelou, a personal friend, to emphasize the theme of friendship. Davis was recognized for her coverage of politics, race, and gender, as well as her calm presence; Rita Williams, a KTVU reporter, described her as having "so much class, so much presence, so much intuition" and called her "the grande dame." Her autobiography, Never in My Wildest Dreams: A Black Woman's Life in Journalism, was published in 2010, with Bill Cosby writing in the foreword that she had symbolic value to the African-American television audience, noting that "we looked forward to seeing her prove the stereotypical ugliness of those days to be wrong." Davis married Frank Davis on January 1, 1952, and had two children and a granddaughter. She met her second husband, Bill Moore, in 1967 while working at KPIX-TV, and they lived in Presidio Heights and later in Petaluma, California. Davis maintained a separation between her personal and professional life, allowing African-American woman and American Women in Radio and Television member Kathleen H. Arnold (now anthropologist Kathleen Rand Reed) to produce Belva Davis – This is Your Life in 1975, and mentored Reed for decades. She served on the boards of the Museum of the African Diaspora, the Institute on Aging, and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, raising $5 million for the Museum of the African Diaspora in one year. Davis won eight Emmy Awards from the San Francisco/Northern California chapter and was an honorary member of Alpha Kappa Alpha. She received lifetime achievement awards from the American Women in Radio and Television and the National Association of Black Journalists. She died in Oakland, California, from a long illness on September 24, 2025, at the age of 92.

Benazir Ahmed, a retired police officer, served as the 28th inspector general of the Bangladesh Police, appointed in April 2020. Prior to this, he was the director general of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) from January 2015 to April 2020, succeeding Mukhlesur Rahman. Born in Gopalganj, he completed his SSC exams in 1978 from SM Model High School and HSC exams in 1980 from Jagannath College, both in second division. He earned his undergraduate degree in 1982 and a master’s in English literature from the University of Dhaka in 1982, followed by a Ph.D. in business administration from the same university, with enrollment qualifications relaxed by his supervisor, Shibli Rubayat Ul Islam. Ahmed joined the Bangladesh Police Service as assistant superintendent of police in 1988 and held various positions, including commissioner of Dhaka Metropolitan Police. In 2013, he criticized a Transparency International Bangladesh report on the police, calling it "cruelly" and "unjustly" critical. On 30 December 2014, he was appointed director general of RAB. In 2022, the Home Ministry announced a 9-day visit to Germany for the inspection of 100,000 bed sheets and pillows for the police, which sparked controversy and was later canceled after public outcry, with the Bangladesh Police claiming the reports were "untrue and misleading" due to "linguistic confusion." On 10 December 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury added Ahmed to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list under the Global Magnitsky Act, restricting financial dealings with him and blocking his assets. Ahmed denied all allegations, attributing the sanctions to "propaganda" and "anti-state forces," and accused human rights organizations—specifically one with a "Pakistani" South Asia director—of misleading U.S. politicians. An Interpol Red Notice was issued against him for crimes against humanity and economic corruption. In April 2024, Bangladesh Pratidin and Kaler Kantho published articles titled "Benazirer Ghore Aladiner Cherag" and "Boner Jomite Benazirer Resort," alleging Ahmed had amassed illegal wealth. The articles claimed he built the Savannah Eco Resort in Bairagitol village, Gopalganj, by illegally seizing land from Hindu families. On 23 May 2024, a court ordered the freezing of his properties and bank accounts over corruption charges. On 3 June 2024, he left the country. Transparency International Bangladesh raised alarms over the corruption allegations, and the Anti-Corruption Commission stated that evidence of corruption had been found and a case would be filed. On 12 June 2024, the court ordered the confiscation of additional properties of Ahmed and his family. Ahmed is married to Zeeshan Mirza and has three daughters: Farheen Rishta Binte Benazir, Tahseen Raisa Binte Benazir, and Zahra Zareen Binte Benazir.

Benjamin Abramowitz, also known as "Ben Hoffman" during the late 1930s and early 1940s, was an American painter, printmaker, and sculptor. First recognized at age 19 as senior artist with the Federal Art Project of the Works Progress Administration (WPA) in New York City, he is among the most respected Washington, D.C., artists of the past century. Born in Brooklyn, New York in 1917 to Russian immigrants, Abramowitz studied life drawing at the Brooklyn Museum School and held his first solo exhibition there at age 16. He attended the National Academy of Design and joined the Work Projects Administration (W.P.A.) in 1936 under the name Ben Hoffman, serving as a teacher, mural assistant, senior printmaker, and painter. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York holds eleven lithographs from the young artist. In 1941, Abramowitz moved to Washington, D.C., taking on U.S. government graphic assignments and chose Greenbelt as his base for home and studio for more than half a century. During the postwar years, he experienced critical personal and artistic evolution; by day a lithographer, each night he drew and painted with discipline. By his early 30s, he had become a celebrated figure in the growing Washington, D.C.-Baltimore regional art scene, with critics, curators, and collectors actively seeking his work. His art was acquired by major regional collections, including the Baltimore Museum of Art and the Phillips Collection, and the Corcoran Gallery of Art selected his work annually for its biennial exhibitions. By the mid-20th century, he was recognized not only as a painter but also as a teacher and "art coach" throughout the Washington metropolitan area, with among his students the D.C. painter and sculptor Lilian Thomas Burwell. The Ford Foundation sent him nationwide to lecture, conduct seminars, and deliver critiques as an artist-in-residence, while he maintained journals and corresponded regularly with critics, curators, and students. By the 1970s, he shifted from painting to creating wall works and freestanding sculptures and designed four books illustrating the basic principles of the creative experience. Until his mid-80s, when diminishing vision halted his work, he continued creating with the same discipline and vigor as before. His distinguished career has been cited in numerous prestigious biographical volumes, and the National Archives of American Art holds hundreds of papers, letters, and other materials. Walter Hopps, museum director and curator, stated at a memorial service for artist Gene Davis at the National Gallery of Art in 1985 that "the modern art movement in the Washington region started mid-century, and the first was the work of Ben Abramowitz." The prolific and complex achievements of master artist Benjamin Abramowitz in painting, sculpture, works on paper in drawing and watercolor span almost eight decades. Noted for his compelling aesthetic vision, Abramowitz has been hailed by critics, curators, and collectors as one of the most important artists of the 20th century. His vast body of work resists categorization, and despite working outside the geographical spotlight of the New York art world, his recognized mastery has been remarkably overlooked.

Bernard Sanders, born on September 8, 1941, in Brooklyn, New York, is an American politician and activist serving as the senior United States senator from Vermont, a seat he has held since 2007. He is the longest-serving independent in U.S. congressional history but maintains a close relationship with the Democratic Party, having caucused with House and Senate Democrats for most of his congressional career and sought the party's presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020. Ideologically a democratic socialist, Sanders is regarded as one of the main leaders of the modern American progressive movement. Born into a working-class Jewish family, Sanders attended Brooklyn College from 1959 to 1960 before transferring to the University of Chicago, where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in political science in 1964. While a student, he was a protest organizer for the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) during the civil rights movement. In 1962, he protested the University of Chicago's segregated housing policy by entering the administration building and camping outside the president's office, leading to the end of racial segregation in private university housing by 1963. He also attended the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the "I Have a Dream" speech, and was fined $25 (equivalent to $257 in 2024) for resisting arrest during a demonstration against segregation in Chicago's public schools. Sanders opposed the Vietnam War and applied for conscientious objector status, though his application was denied due to age.
