On May 16, 2024, a bronze statue of Graham was unveiled in the U.S. Capitol by House Speaker Mike Johnson. Graham's "My Answer" advice column appeared in newspapers for more than 60 years as of 2017. He authored several books, many of which became bestsellers; in the 1970s, *The Jesus Generation* sold 200,000 copies in the first two weeks after publication; *Angels: God's Secret Agents* achieved sales of one million copies within 90 days of release; and *How to Be Born Again* made publishing history with its first printing of 800,000 copies.

Bhupinder "Bindy" Singh Johal (January 14, 1971 – December 20, 1998) was an Indo-Canadian gangster from Vancouver, British Columbia, known as a self-confessed drug kingpin with a reputation for outspokenness, disregard for authority, and a long-standing rivalry with Robbie Kandola and the Dosanjh Brothers, who led a rival Punjabi Mafia faction. Johal operated alongside international drug lord Ranjit Cheema and controlled his own faction within the Punjabi Mafia, a loosely affiliated criminal organization originating in British Columbia that became increasingly ethnocentric over time and remained active and notorious in Vancouver since the early 1990s. He was born in 1971 (some sources note 1972 or 1973) in Shankar Nakodar, Punjab, India, to a Jatt Sikh family, and immigrated to Vancouver at age four, being raised by his mother after his parents separated. He was considered a "problem child" by teachers, displayed temperamental behavior, lacked respect for authority, and suffered severe depression after his parents cut his hair following an armed assault in Canada linked to the assassination of Indira Gandhi. He was expelled from Sir Charles Tupper Secondary School and sentenced to 60 days in jail in 1989 after assaulting his vice-principal, a defense he made that was dismissed by the judge as "cold-blooded cynicism" due to lack of evidence of racism. After moving to Richmond, he enrolled at McNair Secondary School, where he smashed a car window with a baseball bat and was convicted of possessing a dangerous weapon. He dropped out of college after his first semester to begin a criminal career, joining the Hispanic gang Los Diablos, which later became the Punjabi Mafia. He built a reputation as a hit-man for Jimmy and Ron Dosanjh, later betraying and killing both of them—Jimmy in February 1994 and Ron in April 1994—after the latter had taken out a contract to kill Johal for over C$230,000. The Dosanjh brothers were killed by men loyal to Johal, with Ron being shot in his red pickup truck while waiting for a traffic light and dying instantly from multiple bullets to the face. Johal was charged with two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the Dosanjh killings, along with Sarbjit Gill, Rajinder "Big Raj" Benji, Michael Kim Budai, Sun News Lai, Preet "Peter" Sarbjit Gill, and Kim "Phil" Ho-Sik, with the Crown alleging that Peter Gill was the actual gunman. The trial, one of the most expensive in Canadian history due to required security, resulted in acquittals for all defendants, including Gill, who was later convicted of obstruction of justice and sentenced to six years in prison; Gillian Guess, an active juror, was sentenced to 18 months for obstruction of justice. The Crown appealed the acquittals, but Johal was killed before a new trial began. Johal earned approximately $500,000 to $900,000 per week through illegal activities such as murder for hire, debt collection, and drug dealing, and was affiliated with the Buttar brothers, known for brutal gangland slayings. He formed a hit squad called "The Elite," consisting of five Indo-Canadian hit men, responsible for 25 murders over five years. Johal had a legendary bad temper, was convicted in 1997 of aggravated assault for attacking two men in a bar with a broken beer bottle, and had convictions for obstruction of justice, possession of dangerous weapons, and aggravated assault. In 1996, Chinese-Canadian drug dealer Randy Chan was kidnapped by Roman Mann, one of Johal’s associates, due to dissatisfaction with the quality of cocaine sold; Johal negotiated Chan’s release in exchange for 5 kilograms of cocaine and $500,000 from the Lotus triads. Johal openly admitted his gangster status and threatened rivals in interviews, becoming a folk hero among young Indo-Canadians who admired his success, wealth, and defiance of societal expectations, with many citing him as an inspiration to join organized crime. His gang was responsible for several murders, including the killing of Amarjit Singh Dheil in January 1997, Gorinder Singh Khun Khun on October 21, 1997 (after Johal believed Khun Khun was involved in the murder of neighbor Greg Olson), and Vinuse News MacKenzie on July 1, 1998, to eliminate a romantic rival. On September 19, 1998, Derek Chand Shankar insulted Johal, prompting Johal to order his murder after Buttar drove Shankar to the Queensborough Bridge, where he was shot. On November 29, 1998, Johal punched Roman "Danny" Mann after Mann expressed a desire to leave the gang, and Mann was later found dead in an industrial lot with a single bullet through his head; Johal blamed the Hells Angels. On December 20, 1998, at 4:30 a.m., Johal was fatally shot in the back of the head at the Palladium nightclub in Vancouver and died four hours later at Vancouver General Hospital. No witnesses described the assailant. Four months prior to his death, at least three of Johal’s associates had been killed, according to Bal Buttar’s confessions. In 2004, Buttar claimed he ordered Johal’s assassination out of fear that Johal would kill him. Buttar was never convicted of Johal’s murder due to his quadriplegic condition. Kash Heed, commanding officer of the 3rd Police District in Vancouver, stated it was disappointing that someone as intelligent and bright as Johal would turn to crime, noting that young people who emulate gangsters like Bindy see the benefits of criminal life without understanding the dangers.

Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev (Nepali: श्री ५ महाराजाधिराज वीरेन्द्र वीर विक्रम शाह देव; 29 December 1945 – 1 June 2001) was King of Nepal from 1972 until his assassination in 2001. He was the second son of King Mahendra and became crown prince because Mahendra's first son, Rabindra Shah, was born out of wedlock to a Gurung woman, making him an "illegitimate child." Birendra was born at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu and became crown prince upon his grandfather King Tribhuvan's death in 1955. He studied at St Joseph's School in Darjeeling and later at Eton College in the United Kingdom from 1959 to 1964, before returning to Nepal to travel to remote villages. He then studied at the University of Tokyo and political theory at Harvard University from 1967 to 1968. Birendra married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin, on 27 February 1970; the wedding cost $9.5 million and was one of the most lavish Hindu nuptial ceremonies in history. He ascended the throne on 31 January 1972 at age 26, with his coronation delayed until 24 February 1975, when he was 29, due to mourning and religious inauspiciousness traditions. As an absolute monarch, he inherited the panchayat system, which banned political parties; prominent leaders of the Nepali Congress were frequently arrested. In the 1980s, liberal student-led groups demanded constitutional change, and in May 1980, a referendum was held offering a multi-party or panchayati system, with the party-less system winning 55% to 45%. Following this, Birendra restructured the country into five development regions and visited each annually until 1990. In April 1990, after pro-democracy riots, he lifted the ban on political parties and agreed to become a constitutional monarch, appointing a Constitution Recommendation Commission that presented a draft constitution on 10 September 1990. The draft was approved by Prime Minister Krishna Prasad Bhattarai and his cabinet, and on 9 November 1990, Birendra promulgated the new constitution, transforming Nepal into a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. As a constitutional monarch, he gained popularity due to his democratic views and the inability of political parties to govern. However, he could not prevent the Nepalese Civil War, which lasted from 1996 to 2006. On 1 June 2001, Birendra and his family were massacred by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra, during a dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace; after shooting himself, Dipendra was declared king but failed to regain consciousness and died days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. During his reign, Birendra maintained Nepal's independence despite influences from India, China, and the Soviet Union. His first trips as king were to India in October 1973 and China two months later. He prevented the breakup of Mustang from Nepal and Tibet, disarmed Khampas rebels in the north by offering land, money, and citizenship to those who surrendered arms and confiscating weapons, and prohibited movement toward Tibet for those who did not surrender. He blocked the use of the army to suppress the Maoist revolution, which would have worsened the situation. Birendra was a lover of nature and a strong supporter of conservation. He established the Rhino Patrol force in 1970, introduced National Park law, and gazetted Chitwan National Park in December 1970 with borders delineated the following year and established in 1973. In 1976, he established Royal Karnali Wildlife Reserve (later Royal Bardiya), added Babai River Valley in 1984, and proclaimed it a national park in 1988. The fourth protected area, Langtang National Park, was established in 1976 with a 1,710 km² area in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Sindhulpalchok. He also established Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve and Royal Shuklaphanta Wildlife Reserve in 1976, which were later enlarged and converted to national parks in the late 1980s. Rara National Park was established in 1976 to fulfill his father's dream of a pristine reserve with a 106 km² area in Mugu and Jumla, including Rara Lake. Sagarmatha National Park was established in 1976 with a 1,148 km² area in Solukhumbu. In 1984, Khaptad National Park (225 km²) was established in Bajhang, Bajura, Achham, and Doti, and Parsa Wildlife Reserve was established and later extended to a national park. Shey Phoksundo National Park, a trans-Himalayan park of 3,555 km² in Dolpa and Mugu, was also established in 1984. To preserve royal hunting traditions and prevent wildlife depletion, he established Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve in 1987. The King Mahendra Trust for Nature Conservation was established in 1990 with Gyanendra as chairman, and he declared the Annapurna Conservation Area. Under his efforts, Sagarmatha National Park (1979) and Chitwan National Park (1984) were inscribed in UNESCO World Heritage Sites, along with the Durbar squares of Kathmandu, Lalitpur, and Bhaktapur, and religious sites such as Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath, and Changu Narayan in 1979. On 28 December 1975, a trolley bus system was established with Chinese aid. He followed his father by establishing industrial estates: Nepalgunj (1973), Pokhara (1974), Butwal (1976), Bhaktapur (1979), Dhankuta (1980), Birendranagar (1981), and Gajendranarayan (1986). Birendra is credited with devising the Melamchi water project to Kathmandu. Industries such as Gorakhali Tires, Udayapur Cement, Nepal Metal, and Nepal Pharmaceuticals were established during his reign. He was the patron of the Pashupati Area Development Trust. In April 1979, the Nepal Oriental Magnesite factory was established with joint investment from Nepal and Orissa Industries, India, at Lakuri Danda in Dolakha. In 1983, a Nepal-Pakistan Joint Economic Commission was established, bringing significant foreign investment. A 60 megawatt hydropower project at Kulekhani began operation in 1982 with aid from the World Bank, Kuwait, and Japan. TU Teaching Hospital was established in 1982 with support from Japan International Cooperation Agency. Nardevi Ayurvedic Hospital was established in 1974, and the Nepal Police Hospital was established on 27 Chaitra 2040 BS to provide free health services to police and their families. In 1976, he established Securities Exchange Center Ltd, which later evolved into the Nepal Stock Exchange. He also established Nepal Television in 1984, which launched its first channel in 1985 with French aid. By 1986, there were 2,054 industrial establishments employing about 125,000 workers. By 1990, television reach made video rental and satellite dishes common. In 1986, with Rastriya Panchayat approval, Mahendra Sanskrit University was established in Dang, becoming the second university in the country. Studies in 1972 showed that road connectivity in hilly and rural areas was more expensive than air connectivity, leading the government to prioritize airport development. Airports such as Baglung (1973), Dhorpatan, Mahendranagar, Rukum Chaurjahari, Sanphebagar (1975), Simikot (1977), Dolpa (1978), Ramechhap (1979), Doti (1973), Talcha (1975), Taplejung (1976), Rolpa (1980), Manang (1981), Bajura (1984), and Darchula (1986) were established. The Lamosangu-Jiri road to Solukhumbu was commissioned in 1985 with Swiss aid. The government focused on agriculture, with nearly 90% of the population involved by 1990. Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper was established in 1985 with Chinese support. Corn production increased from 500,000 tons in 1961 to over 1 million tons in 1991. Lumbini Sugar Mills at Sunwal, Nawalparasi was built in 1982 with Chinese technical assistance. Gorakhali Rubber Industries led to rubber cultivation in Jhapa, Illam, and other eastern areas. Agricultural-based industries such as Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper, Hetauda Textile, and numerous carpet and garment industries were established, contributing significantly to the economy. A referendum in 2037 BS (equivalent to 1980 in the Gregorian calendar) was held for democracy, offering a multi-party or panchayati system. During the panchayati system option, the referendum was held in May 1980.

In 1985, under the Companies Act 2021 (Bikram Sambat) with support from the People's Republic of China, agricultural lands and the agricultural workforce expanded, leading to increased food supplies and improved nutrition. Corn production rose from 500,000 tons in 1961 to over 1 million tons by 1991. The Lumbini Sugar Mills at Sunwal, Nawalparasi was established in 1982 with technical assistance from China. The Gorakhali Rubber Industries led to the first cultivation of rubber in Jhapa, Illam, and other eastern regions of Nepal. Agriculture-based industries such as Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper, Hetauda Textile, and numerous carpet and garment industries were established to process raw agricultural products, significantly contributing to the economy. During King Birendra’s reign, a referendum was held in 2037 BS to choose between a multi-party system or a Panchayati system. To promote balanced development, he divided the nation into five development regions and visited each annually until the 1990 democracy movement, after which the visits ceased. Despite being an autocratic ruler, King Birendra adhered strictly to constitutional limits, acting as a constitutional monarch and intervening during political crises. Mid-term elections in 2051 and the general election in 2056 are attributed to his good governance. He regularly sought the Supreme Court’s advice on constitutional matters and established a weekly meeting between the king and prime minister at his palace to discuss state affairs. Recognizing low literacy as a major barrier to progress, he prioritized education, with the five-year plan from 1971 focusing on building new institutions and improving the education system. On the occasion of his coronation, he declared primary education free for all Nepalese citizens. In 1978, with royal approval, all educational materials were distributed free of cost. He became the patron of the Royal Nepal Academy of Science and Technology and established Mahendra Sanskrit University in 1986 to preserve language and culture. The dowry system was criminalized in 1976 under the Social Practices Reform Act (2033 B.S.). Under the five-year plan, he introduced National Service, requiring post-graduate students to serve one year in rural development. He initiated the preservation of history by establishing the Natural History Museum in 1975 and enacted the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 2033 (1976) to prohibit drug trade, smuggling, and trafficking. Birendra promoted road development based on population and traffic, connecting rural areas with airports, and restructured governmental organizations to achieve developmental goals, emphasizing roadbuilding, sanitation, and technical training. A comprehensive study led to the restructuring of the National Planning Commission in 1972 and minor adjustments in 1987. Government policies focused on environment conservation, agriculture, and education. Though remembered as a development-friendly ruler, he is criticized for lacking the skills to drive rapid development, similar to his father King Mahendra, and his emphasis on sustainable development—such as nature conservation, culture, and history—was seen as hindering economic progress. The Panchayat regime under Birendra is considered a failure by historians, as he failed to attract significant foreign investment and implemented reforms that continued his father’s legacy. He restructured organizations established by his father and introduced development plans envisioned by him. However, his development efforts largely failed, with many newly built roads and airports being rarely used due to low vehicle ownership or access, thus not contributing to economic growth. Some historians and anti-egalitarians blame Birendra for the fall of the Panchayat regime, as the easing of restrictions in the 1980s allowed previously powerless political parties to emerge. From a young age, Birendra was described by his Eton teachers as a kind prince and was remembered by classmates as a "very, very nice bloke" who was embarrassed when his full title was read aloud. Nepalese media personality Neer Shah described him as a kind and development-loving king. Royalists and scholars view him as a simple king who listened to others’ views, though they criticize his weakness in refusing requests from others and his tendency to work like a clerk rather than delegate. In 2036 B.S. (1980), he allowed the Janmat Sangraha referendum, seen as a step toward democracy, though leaders and historians claim it was rigged. After the People's Movement I, he established a constitutional monarchy in Nepal. Some historians speculate that his democratic views and simple nature contributed to the success of the People's Movement I (1990). He is credited with introducing SAARC to strengthen Nepal’s foreign relations with South Asian countries. Birendra was diagnosed with coronary artery disease; in November 1999, he suffered a mild heart attack and was admitted to Cromwell Hospital in London, where he underwent angioplasty. Numerous structures, institutions, and honors were named after him. Monuments bearing his name were renamed after the restoration of parliament in 2006 and the end of the monarchy in 2008. Following the 2006 political changes, an effort was made to rename the highway built in his honor as Lok Marg.

The Black Widow pulsar (PSR B1957+20) is an eclipsing binary millisecond pulsar in the Milky Way, discovered in 1988 and located approximately 6,500 light-years (2,000 parsecs) from Earth. It rotates with a period of 1.6074 milliseconds and orbits a substellar companion, likely a brown dwarf or super-Jupiter, with a period of 9.2 hours and an eclipse duration of about 20 minutes. At the time of its discovery, it was the first known such pulsar. The prevailing theory suggests that the companion is being destroyed by the powerful outflows or winds of high-energy particles from the neutron star, leading to the name "black widow." Since then, similar systems have been identified, and as of February 2023, around 41 black widows are known. Observations have revealed a bow shock in H-alpha and a smaller shock in X-rays (detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory), indicating a forward velocity of about one million kilometers per hour. In 2010, the neutron star's mass was estimated to be at least 1.66 M⊙ and possibly as high as 2.4 M⊙, with the latter value potentially surpassing PSR J0740+6620 as the most massive neutron star detected and approaching the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit. However, by January 2023, the upper mass limit was revised down to 1.8 M⊙. The pulsar's companion is believed to be a brown dwarf. Artist impressions of the Black Widow pulsar are available.

Blenheim Palace, located in Woodstock, Oxfordshire, England, is the seat of the Dukes of Marlborough and one of the largest country houses in the country. Originally known as Blenheim Castle, it has been called Blenheim Palace since the 19th century. Built between 1705 and 1722, the palace was named after the 1704 Battle of Blenheim, a military victory achieved by the 1st Duke of Marlborough during the War of the Spanish Succession against the French and Bavarians. The land for the palace was granted by the Crown as a reward for these triumphs, with Parliament providing funds and the rent for the land set at one copy of the French royal flag annually, displayed in Windsor Castle. The palace was designed in the rare and short-lived English Baroque style by Sir John Vanbrugh, with assistance from Nicholas Hawksmoor, following the success of their earlier work on Castle Howard. The project faced significant financial difficulties, including the Crown cancelling support in 1712, leading to a three-year exile of the Marlboroughs on the Continent and a breakdown in relations with the Duchess, who criticized Vanbrugh for extravagance and impracticality. Despite initial funding, no exact sum was allocated by Parliament, and work halted after £220,000 had been spent and £45,000 owed. The Duke contributed £60,000 initially, and after his death in 1722, the Duchess, driven by ambition, completed the palace and its park, with Hawksmoor designing the Arch of Triumph and finishing key interior elements. The palace's design emphasizes grandeur over comfort, featuring massive stone structures, a severe Baroque style, and a strong visual axis that culminates in a procession celebrating the Duke’s military achievements. The palace includes a grand entrance with two approaches, a monumental East Gate that functions as a water tower, and a central axis leading to a painted saloon where the Duke was to be enthroned, with a 30-tonne marble bust of Louis XIV positioned above the south portico to symbolize his defeat. The palace is unique as a family home, mausoleum, and national monument and is the birthplace and ancestral home of Sir Winston Churchill. The estate, originally a royal deer park known as the Palace of Woodstock, had a long history, including being used to imprison Elizabeth I and later ruined during the Civil War. The 1st Duchess wanted the historic ruins demolished, while Vanbrugh advocated for preservation, and the ruins were ultimately removed. The palace was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. A parliamentary warrant from 1705 appointed Vanbrugh as architect but did not mention the Crown or Queen. The final completion date is unknown, but the Duchess was still negotiating costs as late as 1735 and noted in 1732 that the chapel was finished and more than half the tomb was ready. The palace's design, intended to be viewed from a distance, uses perspective and massed stone to create a pantheonesque effect, with statues of Britannia, chained French captives, and the English lion devouring the French cock, many by Grinling Gibbons, reinforcing its heroic and national character. The palace was completed after the Duke's death, and the entire structure, including its park, was finalized under the Duchess’s direction.

Blenheim Palace, designed with its principal and secondary rooms on the piano nobile, features an internal layout defined by court etiquette, with state apartments arranged along an axis of increasing importance and public use, culminating in the central saloon ("B"), which served as the communal state dining room. To either side of the saloon are suites of state apartments, decreasing in importance but increasing in privacy: the first room ("C") was intended as an audience chamber, the next ("L") as a private withdrawing room, and the next ("M") as the occupant's bedroom, the most private. A small room between the bedroom and the internal courtyard was designated as a dressing room, and this arrangement mirrors the layout on the east side of the saloon, where the Duke and Duchess had their own suites, with the bow room ("O") corresponding in importance to the saloon. The palace includes a 30-tonne marble bust of Louis XIV, positioned high above the south portico so that the defeated king is forced to look down on the parterre and spoils of his conqueror, a design intended to honor the Duke but never realized as he died before completion. The Duke was to have sat enthroned in the painted saloon, whose ceiling was originally to be painted by James Thornhill, depicting Marlborough kneeling to Britannia with a map of the Battle of Blenheim, but the Duchess objected to his overcharging, so the commission was given to Louis Laguerre. Laguerre's trompe l'œil painting features Peace as a woman holding back John Churchill, who holds a zigzag thunderbolt of war, with the walls showing nations at peace, and includes a self-portrait alongside Dean Jones, a chaplain disliked by the Duchess, and a depiction of French spies with large ears and eyes. The room also has four marble door-cases displaying the Duke's crest as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, only one of which was carved by Gibbons; the others were copied by the Duchess's cheaper craftsmen. The long library (H), designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor in 183 ft (56 m), was intended as a picture gallery with saucer domes to be painted by Thornhill, but this was not done due to the Duchess's displeasure. The library is furnished with the Duke's war spoils and art collection, including a large statue of Queen Anne, whose base records their friendship. From the northern end of the library, which houses the largest pipe organ in private ownership in Europe, built in 1891 by Henry Willis & Sons at a cost of £3,669 and replacing a 1888 organ by Isaac Abbott, access leads to the raised colonnade and chapel. The chapel, designed with the Duke's gargantuan tomb and sarcophagus as the dominant feature, was altered by the Earl of Godolphin to place the high altar against the west wall, and was commissioned by the Duchess in 1730, designed by William Kent, with statues of the Duke and Duchess as Caesar and Caesarina. The tomb was completed after the dowager Duchess's death in 1744, when the Duke's coffin was returned from Westminster Abbey and both were interred together. Successive Dukes and their wives are also buried in the chapel vault, and other family members are interred in St. Martin's parish churchyard at Bladon. The palace is Grade I listed on the National Heritage List for England since August 1957, and its park, woodlands, and formal gardens are Grades I listed on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens and are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. The park features the River Glyme, which Vanbrugh envisioned being crossed by the "finest bridge in Europe," containing some 30-odd rooms, though it was later modified by Capability Brown, who flooded and submerged the lower stories of the bridge, creating a more harmonious English landscape garden. The bridge, originally seen as incongruous by Alexander Pope and Horace Walpole, was narrowed at its base and the three small canal-like streams were absorbed into a single river-like stretch. The great parterre, nearly half a mile long (800 m) and as wide as the south front, was grassed over by Brown, and the Great Court was re-paved by Duchêne in the early 20th century. The Column of Victory, 134 ft (41 m) high, terminates a great avenue of elms planted in the positions of Marlborough's troops at the Battle of Blenheim, and Vanbrugh had originally intended an obelisk to mark the site of the former royal manor and Henry II's trysts, which the 1st Duchess rejected as "very odd things." Following the 1st Duke's death in 1722, his daughter Henrietta succeeded him, an unusual succession requiring a special Act of Parliament, and after her death, the title passed to Charles Spencer, Earl of Sunderland, whose mother was the Duke's second daughter Anne. The 1st Duke, a soldier, was not wealthy and used his fortune to complete the palace; the Marlboroughs were not particularly rich compared to other ducal families. The 5th Duke (1766–1840) was a spendthrift who depleted the family's fortune, selling the Boccaccio for £875 and his own library in over 4000 lots, and upon his death in 1840, the family faced financial difficulties. By the 1870s, the Marlboroughs were in severe financial trouble, and in 1875 the 7th Duke sold the Marriage of Cupid and Psyche and the famed Marlborough gems for £10,000, which was insufficient. In 1880, the 7th Duke petitioned Parliament to break the entail on the palace under the Blenheim Settled Estates Act 1880, allowing the dispersal of assets. The Sunderland Library was sold in 1882 for nearly £60,000, including rare books like Horace's Epistles (1480) and Josephus's works (1648); Raphael's Ansidei Madonna sold for £70,000; Van Dyck's Equestrian Portrait of Charles I for £17,500; and the Rubens painting, given by Brussels in 1704, was sold for a record sum and is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. These sales failed to cover debts, and the maintenance of the palace remained unaffordable, worsened by the British agricultural depression. When the 9th Duke inherited in 1892, the land was generating dwindling income. Charles, 9th Duke of Marlborough (1871–1934), saved the palace and family by marrying the American railroad heiress Consuelo Vanderbilt in 1895 for $2.5 million (equivalent to $94.5 million today), in 50,000 shares of the Beech Creek Railway with a 4% dividend guarantee, plus £100,000 annual income each. The marriage was negotiated with her parents, who paid for it, and the bride was locked in her room until agreeing. The wedding was signed in the vestry of St. Thomas Episcopal Church, and on the return carriage, the Duke told Consuelo he loved another woman and would never return to America, as he "despised anything that was not British." The honeymoon began with the replacement of the Marlborough gems, and the Duke commissioned European tapestries, paintings, and furniture to restore the palace. He then undertook an exhaustive restoration and redecoration, including gilt boiseries in the west staterooms to imitate Versailles, undermining Vanbrugh's rivalry with Louis XIV, and moving the state and principal bedrooms upstairs.

The teenage Consuelo was locked in her room by her mother until she agreed to the marriage, which was formally signed in the vestry of St. Thomas Episcopal Church, New York, immediately after the wedding vows. In the carriage leaving the church, Marlborough told Consuelo he loved another woman and would never return to America, stating he "despised anything that was not British." On their honeymoon, the replenishing of Blenheim began with the replacement of the Marlborough gems, and tapestries, paintings, and furniture were purchased in Europe to restore the depleted palace. Upon returning, the Duke initiated an exhaustive restoration and redecoration, with the staterooms west of the saloon being redecorated with gilt boiseries imitating Versailles, undermining Vanbrugh's original design as the interiors became mere pastiches of Louis XIV’s palace. While this redecoration had flaws and the Duke later regretted it, other improvements were well received. A key issue was that the state and principal bedrooms were moved upstairs, turning the staterooms into an enfilade of similar, unremarkable drawing rooms. On the west terrace, French landscape architect Achille Duchêne created a water garden, and on a lower terrace, two large fountains in the style of Bernini were placed—scaled models of those in the Piazza Navona presented to the 1st Duke. Blenheim once again became a place of wonder and prestige, yet Consuelo was deeply unhappy, documenting her struggles in her biography The Glitter and the Gold (1956). In 1906, she shocked society by leaving her husband, and they divorced in 1921. She married Frenchman Jacques Balsan in 1921 and died in 1964, living to see her son become Duke of Marlborough. She frequently returned to Blenheim, the house she had hated yet saved as an unwilling sacrifice. After the divorce, the Duke married Gladys Deacon, an American former friend of Consuelo with an artistic disposition; a painting of her eyes remains on the ceiling of the great north portico. Before her marriage, while staying with the Marlboroughs, she caused a diplomatic incident by encouraging Crown Prince Wilhelm of Germany to form an attachment with her, prompting the recovery of a ring he had given her through combined diplomatic efforts. After marriage, Gladys habitually dined with the Duke with a revolver by her plate; when he grew tired of her, he temporarily closed Blenheim and cut off utilities to drive her out. They separated but did not divorce. The Duke died in 1934, and his widow died in 1977. The 9th Duke was succeeded by his and Consuelo’s eldest son, John, 10th Duke of Marlborough (1897–1972), who married the Hon. Alexandra Mary Cadogan in 1920 and had two sons and three daughters. She died in 1961, and after eleven years as a widower, he remarried at age 74 to (Frances) Laura Charteris, formerly the wife of the 2nd Viscount Long and the 3rd Earl of Dudley, and granddaughter of the 11th Earl of Wemyss. The marriage was short-lived; the Duke died just six weeks later on 11 March 1972. The bereaved Duchess complained of "the gloom and inhospitality of Blenheim" after his death and soon moved out, referring to the palace as "The Dump" in her autobiography Laughter from a Cloud (1980), and died in London in 1990. The coming-out party for 17-year-old Lady Sarah Consuelo Spencer-Churchill at Blenheim Palace on 7 July 1939 was considered the highlight of the social season and has been styled as "the last season ever," with over 700 guests attending, including Winston Churchill, Anthony Eden, Ian Fleming, and a 22-year-old John F. Kennedy. The house and gardens were illuminated for miles, and the Ambrose band played in a pavilion as guests danced on the lawn into the early morning. Henry (Chips) Channon noted in his diary that he had never seen anything like the event. During the war, the 10th Duke welcomed evacuees from Malvern College and allowed the Security Service (MI5) to use the palace as a base until the end of the war. John Spencer-Churchill, 11th Duke of Marlborough (13 April 1926 – 16 October 2014), was the elder son of the 10th Duke and Alexandra Mary Hilda Cadogan, known as "Sunny" from his courtesy title of Earl of Sunderland. He ranked 224th in the Sunday Times Rich List 2004 with an estimated wealth of £185 million. In 1972, upon inheriting the dukedom, he assumed management of Blenheim Palace and the estate, opening it to visitors and as a film set, and establishing businesses such as a garden furniture company and a water bottling plant. He was active in organizations including the Thames and Chilterns Tourist Board and Oxford United Football Club, serving as vice-president of the Witney Conservative Association, the local party of David Cameron. He died in 2014 at age 88. The palace remains the home of the Dukes of Marlborough, with the present incumbent being Charles James (Jamie) Spencer-Churchill, 12th Duke of Marlborough, who succeeded his father on 16 October 2014. As of October 2016, the Marlboroughs still tender a copy of the French royal flag to the monarch on the anniversary of the Battle of Blenheim as rent for the land on which the palace stands. The palace, park, and gardens are open to the public for an entry fee (maximum £32 as of September 2022), with attractions including the Formal and Walled Gardens, Marlborough Maze, and Butterfly House. The palace is connected to the Walled Garden by the Blenheim Park Railway. The public has free access to about five miles (8 km) of public rights of way through the Great Park, accessible from Old Woodstock and the Oxfordshire Way, near the Column of Victory. Lord Edward Spencer-Churchill, the brother of the current Duke, founded the Blenheim Art Foundation (BAF), a non-profit, to present large-scale contemporary art exhibitions in the palace. BAF launched on 1 October 2014 with the UK’s largest ever exhibition by Ai Weiwei. In September 2019, during an exhibition of Maurizio Cattelan’s work, thieves entered the palace and stole "America," a gold toilet valued at £4.75 million installed in one of the bathrooms, which was not recovered. Blenheim Palace appears in 71 film and television productions, more than any other English country house, with a tour of filming locations available. In July 2024, the palace hosted the 4th summit of the European Political Community. The palace’s coordinates are 51°50′29″N 1°21′39″W.

Stiven Mesa Londoño, born on 27 January 2000 in Itagüí, a suburb of Medellín, is a Colombian rapper, singer, and songwriter known professionally as Blessd. His parents separated when he was young, and he moved with his mother to Bogotá, where he described his adolescence as difficult due to communication issues with his stepfather and being far from his family. He spent time in a detention center for minors after a fight, which led him to change his path and return to Medellín, where he lived with his maternal grandparents. Before leaving school to pursue music, he studied at the Institución Educativa Pedro Estrada. Inspired by his uncle, a rapper who played songs and helped him practice freestyling, Blessd began performing as a hobby at age 15 and competed in rap battles in Bogotá. He worked with his father and grandparents selling fruits and vegetables at the Central Mayorista de Antioquia starting at 2:00 am to earn money for recording songs. Initially a rapper, he shared his songs via WhatsApp in Medellín; his producer Lil Jay encouraged him to explore Reggaeton and create romantic songs, leading to the viral success of "Una," which gained over three million YouTube views after being filmed with the help of Megastore Tienda. After "Una" went viral, Blessd performed in over 500 schools across Antioquia and left school to focus on music. He was signed by manager Dr. Velasquez to JM World Music. In October 2020, he released "Viernes Social" with Puerto Rican artists Alexis, Yomo, Amaro, and Xantos, which became number one on Colombian radio and had over one million plays in 24 hours. In November 2020, he released "Lejania" with Ryan Castro, which gained popularity in Medellín, Colombia, and Costa Rica. In January 2021, he released "Imposible," which led to a remix with Maluma, produced by Prodigiez and released in May 2021 after they met at Maluma’s home for the video shoot. In summer 2021, "Hace Tiempo" gained over 10 million YouTube views in one month and earned him a spot in YouTube’s Foundry Class of 2021. In August 2021, he released a remix of "Dos Problemas" featuring Javiielo, Big Soto, and Neutro Shorty. In late 2021, he released his first studio album, Hecho en Medellín, which includes the songs "Hace Tiempo," "Quien TV," and "Medallo," and completed tours in the United States (New Jersey, Massachusetts, Florida) and Europe (Madrid, Barcelona, Paris, Málaga, Bilbao), serving as an opening act for Karol G’s Bichota tour in Medellín and performing in Mexico City, Caracas, Venezuela, and Guayaquil, Ecuador. In January 2022, he was nominated for a Lo Nuestro Award in the "Artista Revelación Masculino" category and was highlighted by Billboard as one of 22 Latin artists to watch in 2022. In the same month, he released "Niña de Mis Sueños" and a "Quien TV" Remix with Ryan Castro, after a year-long hiatus due to label disagreements over the "Lejania" remix. On 14 February, MonitorLatino reported that "Quien TV" Remix became the most popular song in Colombia and "Niña de Mis Sueños" charted at number 6 on Billboard. Blessd is a Catholic who learned about religion from his grandmother and named himself Blessd due to his faith; he has tattoos of Jesus, The Virgin Mary, a cross on his neck, and the word "bendito" (blessed) on his fingers, and is often seen praying on his knees before performances. He is inspired by Arcángel, Akapellah, Diomedes Diaz, and Joe Arroyo. He previously dated Colombian influencer Nicole Rivera, known as La Suprema, who appears in the "Confia en Mi" video, and confirmed the end of their relationship on 15 March 2022 via Twitter. He is a fan of football, supporting his hometown club Atlético Nacional, which featured his logo on its kits, and also supports F.C. Barcelona. In October 2024, he became part-owner of the Danish football club Vendsyssel FF, and on 15 December 2024, released "Himno de la grandeza," a song expressing his love and respect for Atlético Nacional.

Boavita is a town and municipality located in the Colombian Department of Boyacá, within the Northern Boyacá Province subregion. Its urban center lies in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes at an elevation of 2,114 metres (6,936 ft), approximately 184 kilometres (114 mi) from Tunja, the department's capital. The municipality shares borders with Capitanejo, Santander, and the Nevado River to the north, San Mateo and La Uvita to the east, Tipacoque and Soatá to the west, and Susacón to the south. The name Boavita originates from the Chibcha language and does not mean "good life"; instead, it signifies "Point on the hill worshipping the Sun" or "Gate of the Sun." Before the Spanish conquest, the area was inhabited by a tribe known as the Guavitas, part of the Laches and Muisca groups, and was governed by a cacique who remained loyal to the Tundama of Tundama. Modern Boavita was officially founded on February 9, 1613, by Sr. Hugarte. The primary economic activities in the municipality are agriculture, livestock farming, and mining, with key agricultural products including dates, sugarcane, yuca, coffee, cotton, potatoes, maize, chick peas, beans, peas, wheat, and arracacha. Mining in the region involves carbon extraction. Boavita experiences a subtropical highland climate (Köppen classification: Cfb), characterized by moderate temperatures year-round. Its geographic coordinates are 6°20′N 72°35′W (6.333°N 72.583°W).

Boliney, officially known as the Municipality of Boliney (Ilocano: Ili ti Boliney; Filipino: Bayan ng Boliney), is a municipality in the province of Abra, Philippines. According to the 2024 census, it has a population of 3,778 people. The municipality covers a land area of 216.92 square kilometres (83.75 sq mi), which constitutes 5.21% of Abra’s total area of 4,165.25 square kilometres (1,608.21 sq mi). It is bordered to the north by Sallapadan, Bucloc, and Daguioman, to the east by Tubo and the provinces of Kalinga and Mountain Province, and to the west by Luba and Manabo. Boliney is located 52.93 kilometres (32.89 mi) from the provincial capital Bangued and 422.00 kilometres (262.22 mi) from Manila. The municipality is politically subdivided into 8 barangays, each consisting of puroks and some having sitios. The population density is 17 inhabitants per square kilometre (44/sq mi). The residents are primarily of Cordillera sub-tribes, including the Masadiit of the Tingguian Tribes, Belwang of the Igorot, and Balatoc of the Kalinga tribe, with descendants of other Tinguian sub-tribes such as Binongan, Banao, Maeng, and Ammotan (now called Muyadan of Manabo) also present. The main livelihood of the people comes from rice terraces, though most rice lands were severely damaged or lost due to landslides, mud piles, and the killer quakes in 1990 and 1992; they now obtain most of their rice from Bangued and receive some from other mountain municipalities. Rehabilitation efforts for communal facilities such as roads, trails, irrigation systems, footbridges, and rice fields have been carried out by the Masadiit Farmers Cooperative Inc. (MFCI) with a fund of ₱2,903 million from the Presidential Management Staff, and by the Inter NGO Disaster Relief Services (INDRS) with C$292,516.00 and ₱7 million from Oxfam. Boliney is part of the lone congressional district of Abra and is governed by a mayor as its local chief executive and a municipal council as its legislative body, in accordance with the Local Government Code. The mayor, vice mayor, and councilors are elected directly by the people every three years. The municipality is situated 52.93 kilometres (32.89 mi) from Bangued and is accessible by road, which was completed in 1974; prior to that, access was only possible via a 24-kilometre (15 mi) mountain trail. After 1974, the road was extended by about 14 kilometres (8.7 mi) to reach Danac, the farthest barangay; the current road extends to the Poblacion, while the rest has been abandoned. The Boliney Schools District Office oversees all educational institutions within the municipality, managing and operating both public and private schools from primary to secondary levels.

The Bourke Award, presented by the Royal Society of Chemistry, is an annual prize available to academics from outside the UK. It was originally established by the Faraday Society under the name Bourke Lectures and is now known as the Bourke Award. The award provides £2000 to experts in physical chemistry or chemical physics to present their research in the UK and includes a commemorative medal. In 2020, the Bourke Award was merged with the Liversidge Award to form the Bourke-Liversidge Award.

Breng Valley, also known as The Golden Crown of Kashmir, is situated in the Anantnag district of the Indian union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. The valley is named after the rivulet Brengi, which is a right-bank tributary of the Jhelum River. It extends over 40 km on either side of the Brengi and Kokernag, which serves as the central point of the valley and is home to the renowned Kokernag Garden. The valley has been lauded by the Kashmiri Sufi saint Sheikh Noor-u-din Wali, who referred to it as Breng Gov Sonsun Preng, meaning the Breng Valley is a Golden Crown. Located along the banks of the Brengi River, the valley is encircled by mountains that are part of the Pir Panjal range. It provides access routes to the Wardwan Valley via Margan Top and to Kishtwar via Sinthon Top. This article related to a location in Jammu and Kashmir is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Briana Collette Scurry, born on September 7, 1971, is an American retired soccer goalkeeper. She was the starting goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team at the 1995 World Cup (3rd place), 1996 Summer Olympics (gold medal), 1999 World Cup (champions), 2003 World Cup (3rd place), and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games (gold medal). She played in the semi-final and playoff for third place in the 2007 Women's World Cup (3rd place). Scurry was a founding member of the WUSA, playing three seasons as starting goalkeeper for the Atlanta Beat from 2001 to 2003. Her career total of 173 international appearances is the second most among female soccer goalkeepers and the fifteenth most of any American female player, as well as the thirty-second most among all women. Scurry was elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on August 3, 2017, becoming the first woman goalkeeper and the first black woman to receive the honor. She is openly gay and married Chryssa Zizos, CEO of Live Wire Strategic Communications, LLC, on June 1, 2018. In 2022, she released her best-selling memoir, *My Greatest Save*, and was the subject of the CBS feature-length documentary *The Only*, released that year. Scurry was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to parents Ernest and Robbie Scurry and is the youngest of nine children, with three brothers and five sisters. She played goalie for the Anoka High School Tornadoes for four years and was instrumental in their Minnesota State Championship win in 1989, which ended in a shootout victory. In high school, she ran track and played floor hockey and softball, but basketball was her first and deepest love. She was named Anoka High School's Athena Award winner, High School All American, and Minnesota's top female athlete. In 2010, she was inducted into the Minnesota State High School Hall of Fame, and in September 2011, she was named to the inaugural class of the Anoka High School Hall of Fame. Scurry attended the University of Massachusetts Amherst, completing her four-year collegiate career with 37 shutouts in 65 starts and a career record of 48–13–4 with a 0.56 goals-against-average. She split time in the net in 1992, starting 13 games and earning seven shutouts, and played three games as a forward that year. In 1993, she helped lead the UMass Minutewomen to a 17–3–3 record, to the semifinals of the NCAA Women's Soccer Championship, and titles in the Atlantic 10 Conference regular season and tournament. In her senior season, she started all 23 games, recorded 15 shutouts, and had a 0.48 goals-against-average, the third best in the nation. She was named National Goalkeeper of the Year in 1993 by the Missouri Athletic Club Sports Foundation and was a 1993 second-team All-American, All-Northeast Region, and All-New England first-team selection. Scurry was a founding player for the Atlanta Beat in the Women's United Soccer Association (WUSA), the world's first women's professional league, where she served as starting goalkeeper for the three seasons (2001–2003). She helped the Beat reach two WUSA Championship Games and was named Goalkeeper of the Year in 2003. On March 13, 2009, she was named to the preseason roster of the Washington Freedom in the inaugural season of Women's Professional Soccer (WPS), but suffered a season-ending concussion early in the 2010 season and announced her retirement on September 8, 2010. Scurry was a goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team from 1994 to 2008, earning 173 caps, starting 159 games, and finishing her international career with a record of 133–12–14 and 71 shutouts. Her first appearance for the US team was on March 16, 1994, against Portugal, during which she recorded her first shutout. In her first year, she earned seven shutouts in 12 starts. She was a member of the gold-medal-winning US Women's National Team at the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta, starting and playing every minute of the team's five matches, conceding only three goals. In the 1999 Women's World Cup, she played every minute, allowing only three goals and recording four shutouts, and saved one penalty during the shootout in the final against China, leading to the United States' victory. Following the World Cup, she announced her intention to play in the WNBA. She started for the US in the 2003 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games, played two matches in the 2007 FIFA Women's World Cup, and was the alternate goalkeeper on the 2008 Olympic Team. On June 23, 2008, coach Pia Sundhage announced that Scurry would not be on the Olympic team; her last match for the United States was on November 5, 2008, against the Korea Republic. While playing in the Women's Professional Soccer league in 2010, she suffered a traumatic brain injury when a player from the opposing team collided with her knee into her right temple, leaving her temporarily totally disabled and dealing with severe depression. To address her symptoms, she underwent occipital nerve surgery in 2013. Scurry has since rebuilt her life and become an advocate for increased concussion awareness and research, testifying before Congress twice. In 2011, she was appointed general manager of the WPS franchise magicJack. In February 2021, The Washington Post reported that Chelsea Clinton, Jenna Bush Hager, Dominique Dawes, and Scurry were part of an investment group investing in the Washington Spirit. Scurry served as part of the rotation of studio commentators for ESPN's telecasts of the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup. Since 2021, she has served as a broadcast analyst for CBS soccer coverage, including serving as the lead desk analyst for the 2022 CONCACAF W Championship. On December 6, 2017, she was announced as the First Assistant Coach of the Washington Spirit and would serve as Technical Advisor for the Spirit Academy programs in Maryland and Virginia. Scurry appeared as a fictionalized version of herself in the 2000 film *Air Bud: World Pup* and was the subject of the 2022 Paramount Plus documentary *The Only*, directed by Anthony J. Cortese, which featured interviews with other USWNT players such as Mia Hamm, Brandi Chastain, Kristine Lilly, and Abby Wambach.
The Briggs & Stratton Raptor series consists of single-cylinder, four-cycle flathead engines. This series encompasses various models within the lineup.

The Bright Star Catalogue, also known as the Yale Catalogue of Bright Stars, Yale Bright Star Catalogue, or YBS, is a star catalogue that includes all stars of stellar magnitude 6.5 or brighter, which corresponds to roughly every star visible to the naked eye from Earth. The catalog lists 9,110 objects, of which 9,095 are stars, 11 are novae or supernovae that were "bright stars" only at their peak, and four are non-stellar objects: the globular clusters 47 Tucanae (HR 95) and NGC 2808 (HR 3671), and the open clusters NGC 2281 (HR 2496) and Messier 67 (HR 3515). The catalogue has a fixed number of entries, but its data is maintained and continuously updated, with a comments section about the objects being steadily enhanced. The abbreviation for the catalog is BS or YBS, but all citations of stars in it use HR before the catalog number, a tribute to its predecessor, the Harvard Revised Photometry Catalogue, published in 1908. The earliest predecessor, titled Harvard Photometry, was published in 1884 by the Harvard College Observatory under Edward Charles Pickering and contained about 4,000 stars. Pickering then promoted a similar survey for the southern celestial hemisphere, conducted by Solon I. Bailey between 1889 and 1891, resulting in the publication of the Revised Harvard Photometry in 1908, which included stars down to magnitude 6.5 in both hemispheres, a work continued by John A. Parkhurst through the 1920s. The Yale Bright Star Catalogue was first published in 1930 by Yale astronomer Frank Schlesinger; although the number of entries remains fixed at 9,110, the data for listed objects is corrected and extended, and a comments section is appended. The 1991 edition was the fifth in sequence and introduced a significant expansion of the comments section, which grew to just over the size of the catalogue itself. This edition, along with earlier ones, was compiled and edited by Ellen Dorrit Hoffleit of Yale University. The Harvard Revised Photometry, based on visual observations, has been replaced by photo-electric measurements using band pass filters, most notably the UBV photometric system, which can differ substantially—up to 1.8 magnitudes—from the older system. As a result, many stars brighter than V=6.50 are not included in the YBSC, and hundreds of stars in the YBSC are fainter than V=6.50. In 1983, Dorrit Hoffleit, Michael Saladyga, and Peter Wlasuk published a Supplement adding 2,603 stars with V magnitudes brighter than 7.10 measured at that time. The YBS has one predecessor and five editions.

doc_name: Bruno Kreisky Prize for Services to Human Rights
text: The Bruno Kreisky Prize for Human Rights is a biennial award established in October 1976 to mark the 65th birthday of Bruno Kreisky. It recognizes individuals and organizations for their significant contributions to human rights. In 1993, the prize was split into two components: a human rights prize, awarded between 7,000 and 30,000 Euros, and a prize for merit. The Bruno Kreisky Foundation for Human Rights has presented the award in 14 conferments, honoring more than 130 individuals, institutions, and human rights projects for exceptional service in advancing and protecting international human rights and for outstanding achievements in humanitarian aid. The selection of prize winners is carried out jointly by the board of trustees of the Bruno Kreisky Foundation and an international jury.

The Burlington Sock Puppets are a summer collegiate baseball team in the Appalachian League, based in Burlington, North Carolina, and playing their home games at Burlington Athletic Stadium, commonly known as "Sockville." Professional baseball was first played in Burlington from 1958 to 1964 by the Burlington Indians, who competed in the Carolina League (Class B until 1962, then Class A) as a Cleveland Indians farm club. Twenty-two years later, from 1986 to 2006, Cleveland affiliated the team with the Appalachian League as a Rookie-level team. During the period from 2007 to 2020, the team was known as the Burlington Royals due to their affiliation with the Kansas City Royals. As part of a Minor League Baseball contraction starting in 2021, the Appalachian League was restructured into a collegiate summer baseball league for rising college freshmen and sophomores, and the Burlington Royals were renamed the Burlington Sock Puppets. The nickname reflects Burlington's historical connection to the textile industry.

Busbie Castle was located in what is now Knockentiber (Scottish Gaelic: Cnoc an Tobair, hill of the well), a village in East Ayrshire, Parish of Kilmaurs, Scotland. Knockentiber lies 2 miles (3.2 km) WNW of Kilmarnock and 1/2 mile NE of Crosshouse. The castle overlooked the Carmel Glen and its Burn, which flows into the River Irvine, a mile or so to the south, after passing through the old Busbie Mill. Ainslie's map of 1822 labels the settlement as Bushby, while Armstrong's map of 1775 shows Busbie Castle in a ruinous state but still with its old woodland policies. The 1860s first edition of the Ordnance Survey (OS) indicates a pre-reformation chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary was situated near the castle site. A small hamlet of thatched cottages was clustered nearby; in 1860, the OS shows 'Old Busbie' on the opposite side of the road from the castle. Over time, Busbie and Knockentiber grew together. The castle was a simple keep, approximately 50 feet (15 m) high and about 40 feet (12 m) long by 25 feet (7.6 m) wide. Its entrance was on the ground floor, leading to a wheel-stair to the first-floor hall in the north-west angle and to two cellars or stores on the ground floor. The first-floor hall featured a large fireplace and two window seats. Historical records from the Registrum Magni Sigilli in 1465 list "Terras de le Moite," and in 1539, "9 marcat. de Busby, viz., lie Mote, Knokintibber, et Hallethornis," and in 1541, "Terras de Moite, Knokintebir," and in 1571, "Terras de Moit," and in 1583, "20 solidatas terrarum antiqui extentus de Moit-Mowat cum earum mansione," and in 1599, "9 marcat. terrarum de Busbeyis (viz., lie Mote, Knockiutibber et Halythornis)." In 1691, the Laird of Busbie's dwelling had six hearths and seven other dwellings were associated with the castle and its lands. The castle was a ruin since at least the 1770s and was demolished in 1949 or 1952 due to safety concerns and lack of funds to consolidate it. H. Ritchie built Busbie House as a replacement. Busbie Estates and Collective Securities Limited owned significant land in the 1950s. MacIntosh in 1894 describes the castle as a "prominent object in an otherwise monotonous landscape," noting gun ports, arrow slits, and a sculptured cable winding fantastically around the walls. He claims the castle likely had three floors, was roofless and in decay, and dates it to the 14th century, possibly built by the Mowat family from Flintshire in the 12th century. A Robert de Montealt is recorded in Scotland during the time of King David I; later, several soldiers with that name led armies into Scotland. William Craufurd of Wallston married a daughter of Mowat of Busbie around 1400. Charles Mowat of Busbie is mentioned in 1534 for involvement in the murder of William Cunyngham of Craganis and his servant; he was tutor to Hugh, Earl of Eglinton in 1546 and fined £47 in 1571–2 for celebrating mass at Eglinton Castle. In 1547, Charles Mowat was involved in the murder of Lord Boyd, with Sir Neil Montgomerie of Lainshaw as the victim; he was required to remain in France until Sir Neil Montgomerie’s son allowed him to return. A brother of the Earl of Eglinton appeared in court for provoking John Mowatt, Laird of Busby, and his servant Andrew Stevenston in Stewarton. The Mowat involved in the Montgomerie murder was later killed by William and Harrie (Sic) Stewart, sons of Lord Ochiltree, in 1577. Alexander, the eldest son, did not inherit; instead, James, his younger brother, succeeded to the Busbie lands. James’s son, also named James, is the last Mowat to appear in public records. The name de Monhaud or de Monte Alto is recorded as being pronounced 'Mowat' by Dalrymple. James Ritchie of Craigton obtained the lands in 1763, succeeded by his son Henry in 1799, who also acquired the Cloncaird estate. William Wallace of Cairnhill (now Carnell), the nephew of Henry, next inherited the estate. General Sir James Wallace died in 1867 and passed the property to William Wallace of Busbie and Cloncaird. In 1661, Hugh, Earl of Eglinton inherited the lands of Busbie, Knockentiber, and Robertown, a family holding these lands as far back as 1638. The barony, formerly part of the Barony of Kilmaurs, extended from Kilmaurs south to the River Irvine. It had no manor house and was later held by the Eglinton family. Hugh Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Eglinton, received a charter on 3 February 1499 from James V for the £40 lands of old extent of Roberton in Cunninghame. These lands were part of the Lands and Barony of Ardrossan, which included parts of Kilmaurs, Knockentiber, Craig, Gatehead, Woodhills, Greenhill, Altonhill, Plann, Hayside, Thorntoun, Rash-hill Park, Milton, Windyedge, Fardelhill, Muirfields, and Corsehouse. The present Busbie farm appears on older maps, such as the 1860 OS, as a mill with a clear millrace or lade and a sluice. The water was drawn from the Carmel near a dwelling marked as Busbie Holm, rejoining the burn just beyond the mill. The exact date when the mill ceased operation is unclear. It is likely the mill was associated with the castle and the Lairds of Busbie. A Robertown mill is known to have existed, named after the barony.

The Bust of Charles I was a sculptural work created by the Italian artist Gianlorenzo Bernini, which one historian described as "setting the visual conventions for centuries... [establishing itself as] the official portrait of secular absolutism." The sculpture depicted King Charles I of England, who wrote to Bernini praising the artist's name as "exalted above those of all men of talent who have exercised your profession." Bernini never traveled to London to complete the bust; instead, he used a painted triple portrait of Charles I, created by the Flemish artist Anthony van Dyck, specifically for this purpose. Although Bernini never met Charles I in person, the bust was regarded as a success at the time, and Charles rewarded Bernini with jewelry valued at over 4,000 Roman scudi—more than 60 times the average yearly salary of a worker in Rome. Pope Urban VIII sent the bust to Charles's queen, Henrietta Maria, in 1637, in an effort to promote reconciliation between the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of England. The bust was presented in 1637 and was admired for its craftsmanship and resemblance to the king. Charles also gave Bernini a valuable diamond ring. Henrietta Maria commissioned a companion bust of herself, but the English Civil War prevented its completion. After the English Civil War, the bust was sold but was later recovered and added to the Royal Collection during the Restoration, only to be destroyed by a fire at Whitehall Palace in January 1698. Numerous copies of the bust exist in various forms, including engravings and bronze sculptures. For a period in the 19th and early 20th centuries, there was a belief in England and elsewhere that Bernini had also produced a bust of Oliver Cromwell, the victor over Charles I in the English Civil War; however, this attribution was refuted in 1922. Media related to the Bust of King Charles I (Bernini) is available at Wikimedia Commons.

Henry Franklin "Buster" Smith (August 24, 1904 – August 10, 1991), also known as Professor Smith, was an American jazz alto saxophonist and mentor to Charlie Parker. He played a key role in developing the Texas Sax Sound while working with Count Basie and Lester Young in the 1930s. Smith performed with several prominent band leaders, including Duke Ellington, Earl Hines, and vocalist Ella Fitzgerald. He recorded his only album as leader in 1959, titled *The Legendary Buster Smith*, released by Atlantic Records, which featured songs such as "Kansas City Riffs," "Buster's Tune," "E Flat Boogie," and Kurt Weill's "September Song." For the sessions, he enlisted his brother Boston Smith to play piano and included musicians from throughout his career. Despite intending to record a follow-up, Smith was injured in an auto accident in the 1960s, which ended his ability to play the saxophone. He then began playing bass guitar in Dallas and continued to participate in the local music scene, leading a dance music band until 1980 and performing in the Legendary Revelations in the mid-1980s. Smith was born and raised in Alsdorf, Texas, a small township near Telico in the outskirts of Dallas, where he attended school as a child. He earned the nickname "Buster" from his parents due to being born as an overweight child; he was the third of five boys with no sisters, and both of his older brothers died in childhood from measles. His early musical influences were his mother and father, who played guitar; at age four, he played the organ with his brother, Boston Smith, who played the piano. His grandfather later gave away the family organ, believing it would lead Buster toward a life of sin. In 1919, Smith picked cotton for a week to earn $3.50 to buy a clarinet. By age eighteen, he had learned to play several instruments. In 1922, his family moved to Dallas, where he joined the Voodie White Trio, playing alto saxophone and clarinet. In 1923, he began his professional music career playing alto saxophone with medicine shows, where he had to play loudly to attract customers—an experience that shaped his loud musical style. In 1925, Oran "Hot Lips" Page invited him to join the Oklahoma City Blue Devils, where he wrote much of the group's music, learning from banjo player Johnny Clark and writing lyrics with co-workers from the bank. The Blue Devils' lineup included Walter Page, Oran Page, Lester Young, Count Basie, Jimmy Rushing, and Emir "Bucket" Coleman. They toured the Kansas City area and the Midwest, playing jazz for a year and bringing all members into prominence. Basie and Page left the group, but Smith stayed briefly before leaving as well. After leaving, he and Basie formed the Buster Smith-Count Basie Band of Rhythm, where they developed a louder style of jazz. Smith achieved a louder sound by using a tenor saxophone reed in his alto saxophone, and Lester Young complemented this by using a baritone saxophone reed on his tenor saxophone, a combination later known as the Texas Sax Sound. Smith gained significant influence in the Texan music community and mentored Charlie Parker during the 1930s, forming a "father-son relationship" through mentorship. In 1941, Smith returned to Dallas and stopped touring, remaining active in the local music scene. He wrote for jazz and blues bands, performed frequently, and taught young Texan musicians such as Aaron "T-Bone" Walker and Red Garland. He also performed session work with artists including Pete Johnson's Boogie-Woogie Boys, Eddie Durham, Leo "Snub" Mosley, Bon and His Buddies, and the Don Redman Orchestra. Smith died in Dallas on August 10, 1991, from a heart attack.

Cabell Calloway III (December 25, 1907 – November 18, 1994) was an American jazz singer, songwriter, and bandleader who became a prominent figure in the swing era through his regular performances at the Cotton Club in Harlem. He gained acclaim for blending jazz and vaudeville, a career that spanned over 65 years. A master of energetic scat singing, Calloway led one of the most popular dance bands in the United States from the early 1930s to the late 1940s, featuring trumpeters Dizzy Gillespie, Jonah Jones, and Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham, saxophonists Ben Webster and Leon "Chu" Berry, guitarist Danny Barker, bassist Milt Hinton, and drummer Cozy Cole. He achieved several hit records in the 1930s and 1940s, becoming the first African-American musician to sell one million copies of a record, with his most famous song, "Minnie the Moocher," originally recorded in 1931. This song earned him the nickname "The Hi-de-ho Man" and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999 and added to the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry in 2019. Calloway reached the Billboard charts in five consecutive decades (1930s–1970s). He made numerous stage, film, and television appearances, including roles in Stormy Weather (1943), Porgy and Bess (1953), The Cincinnati Kid (1965), and Hello Dolly! (1967), and experienced a career resurgence in the 1980s with his appearance in The Blues Brothers (1980). He was the first African-American to have a nationally syndicated radio program and received the National Medal of Arts from the U.S. Congress in 1993. He posthumously received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2008. Born in Rochester, New York, on December 25, 1907, Calloway's father, Cabell Calloway Jr., graduated from Lincoln University of Pennsylvania in 1898, and his mother, Martha Eulalia Reed, was a Morgan State College graduate, teacher, and church organist who also worked as a lawyer and in real estate. The family moved to Baltimore, Maryland, in 1919, where Calloway grew up in the West Baltimore neighborhood of Druid Hill. He skipped school to earn money by selling newspapers, shining shoes, and cooling down horses at the Pimlico racetrack, where he developed an interest in racing and gambling. After being caught playing dice on the church steps, he was sent to Downingtown Industrial and Agricultural School in 1921. Upon returning to Baltimore, he resumed hustling and worked as a caterer while improving his education. He began private vocal lessons in 1922 and studied music throughout his schooling. Despite his parents' and teachers' disapproval of jazz, he began performing in nightclubs in Baltimore, with mentors including drummer Chick Webb and pianist Johnny Jones. He joined his high school basketball team and played professionally with the Baltimore Athenians in the Negro Professional Basketball League during his senior year, graduating from Frederick Douglass High School in 1925. He briefly attended law school in Chicago before leaving to pursue a singing career. In 1927, he joined his older sister, Blanche Calloway, on tour for the revue Plantation Days, whom he credited as his inspiration for entering show business. After the tour ended, he enrolled at Crane College in Chicago but refused an opportunity to play basketball for the Harlem Globetrotters to pursue singing. He performed at "Black and tan" clubs such as Chicago's Dreamland Café, Sunset Cafe, and Club Berlin, where he was an understudy for Adelaide Hall and met Louis Armstrong, who taught him scat singing. He left school to join the Alabamians band. In 1929, the band opened at the Savoy Ballroom and, after the Alabamians disbanded, Armstrong recommended Calloway to join the musical revue Connie's Hot Chocolates, where he established himself as a vocalist singing "Ain't Misbehavin'" by Fats Waller. When the Missourians asked him to front their band in 1930, they became known as Cab Calloway and His Orchestra. In 1931, the band was hired at the Cotton Club in Harlem to substitute for Duke Ellington, leading to a permanent position. The band performed twice a week for NBC radio broadcasts, and Calloway appeared on programs with Walter Winchell and Bing Crosby, becoming the first African American to have a nationally syndicated radio show. During the Great Depression, he earned $50,000 a year at age 23. In 1931, he recorded "Minnie the Moocher," the first single by an African American to sell a million copies. He performed the song and others, "St. James Infirmary Blues" and "The Old Man of the Mountain," in the Betty Boop cartoons Minnie the Moocher (1932), Snow-White (1933), and The Old Man of the Mountain (1933), providing voice-over and using rotoscoping to base the characters' movements on his dance steps. The success of "Minnie the Moocher" made him known as "The Hi-de-ho Man." He appeared in a series of short films for Paramount, where his and Ellington's groups were featured more than any other jazz orchestras of the era. In these films, he performed a gliding backstep dance move, described by some as a precursor to Michael Jackson's moonwalk, which he called "The Buzz" in later years. The 1933 film International House featured his song "Reefer Man," about a man who smokes marijuana. Fredi Washington was cast as his love interest in Cab Calloway's Hi-De-Ho (1934), and Lena Horne made her film debut as a dancer in Cab Calloway's Jitterbug Party (1935). In 1936, he made his first Hollywood feature film appearance opposite Al Jolson in The Singing Kid, singing several duets with Jolson and featuring Calloway's band and 22 Cotton Club dancers. Film critic Arthur Knight noted that the film reflected a shift in American culture through Calloway's rhythmic and melodic singing style. In 1938, he released Cab Calloway's Cat-ologue: A "Hepster's" Dictionary, the first dictionary published by an African American, which became the official reference book of the New York Public Library. A revised version was released in 1939 with Professor Cab Calloway's Swingformation Bureau, and the final edition, The New Cab Calloway's Hepsters Dictionary: Language of Jive, was published in 1944. Poet Lemn Sissay stated in a 2014 BBC documentary that Calloway was taking ownership of language for a people whose languages had been taken away. His band included notable musicians such as Ben Webster, Illinois Jacquet, Milt Hinton, Danny Barker, Doc Cheatham, Ed Swayze, Eddie Barefield, and Dizzy Gillespie. Calloway recalled that he expected precision in his musicians, as he built songs around scat or dance steps. The band formed baseball and basketball teams, playing each other and local semi-pro teams, and participated in charity games. In 1941, he fired Dizzy Gillespie after a fracas when Calloway was hit with spitballs; he wrongly accused Gillespie, who stabbed Calloway in the leg with a small knife. From 1941 to 1942, he hosted a weekly radio quiz show called The Cab Calloway Quizzicale, a parody of Kay Kyser's The College of Musical Knowledge. During World War II, he entertained U.S. troops before they departed overseas. The band recorded songs with social commentary, including "Doing the Reactionary," "The Führer's Got the Jitters," "The Great Lie," "We'll Gather Lilacs," and "My Lament for V Day." In 1943, he appeared in Stormy Weather, one of the first mainstream Hollywood films with a black cast, featuring Bill "Bojangles" Robinson, Lena Horne, the Nicholas Brothers, and Fats Waller. He hosted Horne's character Selina Rogers as she performed the title song in a big all-star revue for soldiers. In 1946, he published a humorous pseudo-gossip column called "Coastin' with Cab" for Song Hits magazine. In the late 1940s, poor financial decisions and gambling led to the breakup of his band. In 1956, his daughter Lael and he recorded "Little Child," an adaptation of "Little Boy and the Old Man," which charted on the Billboard Hot 100. In 1958, Lee Sherman was the choreographer for The Cotton Club Revue of 1958, which starred Calloway and featured tap dancing prodigies Maurice Hines and Gregory Hines. That year, he released the album Cotton Club Revue of 1958 on Gone Records, produced by George Goldner and conducted and arranged by Eddie Barefield. In 1958, he appeared in St. Louis Blues, the life story of W.C. Handy, featuring Nat King Cole and Eartha Kitt. The Cotton Club Revue of 1959 toured South America, visiting Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, and also stopped in Uruguay and Argentina before returning to North America, including a Broadway run. He remained a household name through TV appearances and concerts in the U.S. and Europe, touring with the Harlem Globetrotters in 1961 and 1962 for halftime entertainment. In 1965, he appeared in The Cincinnati Kid with Steve McQueen, Ann-Margret, and Edward G. Robinson. He performed on The Ed Sullivan Show on March 19, 1967, with his daughter Chris Calloway. In 1967, he co-starred with Pearl Bailey as Horace Vandergelder in an all-black cast of Hello, Dolly! on Broadway, with Chris Calloway joining as Minnie Fay, reviving the show's business and leading to a rare RCA Victor cast recording. In 1973–74, he was featured in an unsuccessful Broadway revival of The Pajama Game with Hal Linden and Barbara McNair. His autobiography, Of Minnie the Moocher and Me, was published in 1976, including his complete Hepster's Dictionary as an appendix. In 1978, he released a disco version of "Minnie the Moocher" on RCA Victor that reached the Billboard R&B chart. He appeared in The Blues Brothers (1980), introducing him to a new generation. In 1985, he and his Orchestra performed at The Ritz London Hotel for a 60-minute BBC TV show, with Adelaide Hall, Doc Cheatham, Max Roach, and the Nicholas Brothers also appearing. A performance with the Cincinnati Pops Orchestra in August 1988, directed by Erich Kunzel, was recorded and featured a classic rendition of "Minnie the Moocher," 57 years after its original recording. In January 1990, he performed at the Meyerhoff Symphony Hall with the Baltimore Symphony. That year, he made a cameo in Janet Jackson's music video "Alright." He continued performing at jazz festivals, including the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival and Greenwood Jazz, and in 1992 embarked on a month-long tour of European jazz festivals. He was booked to headline "The Jazz Connection: The Jewish and African-American Relationship" at New York City's Avery Fisher Hall in 1993 but withdrew due to a fall at home. In January 1927, he had a daughter named Camay with Zelma Proctor. His daughter was one of the first African Americans to teach in a white school in Virginia. He married his first wife, Wenonah "Betty" Conacher, in July 1928; they adopted a daughter named Constance and divorced in 1949. He married Zulme "Nuffie" MacNeal on October 7, 1949. The family lived in Long Beach on the South Shore of Long Island, New York, bordering Lido Beach, and in the 1950s moved to Westchester County, New York, where he and Nuffie raised their daughters Chris Calloway (1945–2008), Cecilia "Lael" Eulalia Calloway, and Cabella Calloway (1952–2023). Calloway was an Episcopalian. In December 1945, he and friend Felix H. Payne Jr. were beaten by police officer William E.
