Todd in Kansas City, Missouri, after attempting to enter the whites-only Pla-Mor Ballroom to visit bandleader Lionel Hampton. They were hospitalized and charged with intoxication and resisting arrest, but the charges were dismissed. When Hampton learned of the incident, he refused to continue the concert. Todd claimed they refused to leave and struck him, but Calloway and Payne maintained they were sober; six civil rights organizations, including the NAACP, demanded Todd be fired, though he had already resigned after a pay cut. In 1952, Calloway was arrested in Leesburg, Virginia, on his way to a race track in Charles Town, West Virginia, charged with speeding and attempted bribery of a policeman. On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held.

Cab Calloway was arrested in Leesburg, Virginia in 1952 on his way to a race track in Charles Town, West Virginia, and charged with speeding and attempted bribery of a policeman. In 1946, six civil rights organizations, including the NAACP, demanded that Todd be fired, but he had already resigned after a pay cut. On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held at Cathedral of St. John the Divine. He was survived by his wife, who died in 2008, five daughters, and seven grandsons, and was buried at Ferncliff Cemetery in Hartsdale, New York. Music critics have noted his influence on later entertainers such as James Brown, Michael Jackson, Janet Jackson, and modern-day hip-hop performers. John Landis, who directed Calloway in The Blues Brothers, stated, "Cab Calloway is hip-hop." Timothy White wrote in Billboard (August 14, 1993): "No living pathfinder in American popular music or its jazz and rock 'n' roll capillaries is so frequently emulated yet so seldom acknowledged as Cabell 'Cab' Calloway. He arguably did more things first and better than any other band leader of his generation." In 1998, the Cab Calloway Orchestra, directed by Calloway's grandson Chris "CB" Calloway Brooks, was formed. In 2009, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy released an album titled How Big Can You Get?: The Music of Cab Calloway. In 2012, Calloway's legacy was celebrated in a PBS American Masters episode titled "Cab Calloway: Sketches." In 2019, plans were announced to demolish Calloway's boyhood home at 2216 Druid Hill Avenue in Baltimore, replacing it and the block with Cab Calloway Legends Park. Family members and the National Trust for Historic Preservation advocated for preservation due to its significance as an African-American cultural heritage site. Although the block is designated "historically significant" on the National Register of Historic Places, Baltimore City officials stated at a July 9, 2019 hearing that the Calloway house and adjacent properties have "extensive structural damage." The Commission on Historical and Architectural Preservation's executive director noted that properties in worse condition than the Calloway House have been restored with city tax credit support. Maryland Governor Larry Hogan urged the demolition be postponed to allow for preservation as a historic house museum, similar to the Louis Armstrong House in New York. Design options for Cab Calloway Square included an archway from the facade as part of the entrance, proposed by architects working with Baltimore City and the Druid Heights Community Development Corporation. Despite objections, the house was razed on September 5, 2020. In 1985, Town Supervisor Anthony F. Veteran declared a "Cab Calloway Day" in Greenburgh, New York. In 1990, Calloway received the Beacons in Jazz Award from The New School in New York City, and New York City Mayor David Dinkins proclaimed the day "Cab Calloway Day." In 1992, the Cab Calloway School of the Arts was founded in Wilmington, Delaware. In 1994, Calloway's daughter Camay Calloway Murphy founded the Cab Calloway Museum at Coppin State College in Baltimore, Maryland. The New York Racing Association (NYRA) annually honors Calloway, a native of Rochester, New York, with a stakes race for New York-bred three-year-olds as part of their New York Stallion Series. First run in 2003, The Calloway has undergone various distance and surface changes and is currently run at Saratoga Racecourse in Saratoga Springs, New York. The race celebrated its 13th renewal on July 24, 2019, and was won by Rinaldi. In 2020, Calloway was inducted into the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame. Calloway received accolades in positions and features, including short subjects.

Camilla Antoinette Clifford (29 June 1885 – 28 June 1971), known professionally as Camille Clifford, was a Belgian-born stage actress whose brief theatrical career was defined by her performance as "Miss New York" in the Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen, a role in which she portrayed a "Gibson Girl"-like woman. Although her towering coiffure and hourglass figure embodied the Gibson Girl style, she only performed the role on stage and never modeled for any of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations. Clifford was born on 29 June 1885 in Antwerp, Belgium, to Reynold Clifford and Matilda Ottersen, and was raised in Sweden, Norway, and Boston. On 31 August 1903, she made her stage debut as Mazie Manhattan, the New York Girl in "The Song of the Cities," in a Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen at the Tremont Theatre in Boston. The role required her to walk across the stage in the style of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations, leading to a misconception that she was a Gibson model—when in fact, she imitated his work, not the other way around. In early 1904, the Savage company signed a contract with George Musgrove and Frank McKee for a European tour, and to select an actress to join the new "London Company," a contest was held among those who had played Mazie Manhattan; Clifford won and the company departed in late April 1904. Clifford performed in the United States from 1902 and in England from 1904, returning to Boston on 3 July 1906. While typically playing walk-on, non-speaking roles, she gained fame for her beauty and, in the musical show The Catch of the Season, which opened at London's Vaudeville Theatre on 9 September 1904, she sang the song "Sylvia, the Gibson Girl." Her signature style included a long, elegant gown wrapped around a tightly corseted, eighteen-inch wasp waist. She retired from the stage after marrying Captain the Hon. Henry Lyndhurst Bruce (1881–1914), the eldest son and heir apparent of Henry Bruce, 2nd Baron Aberdare, in 1906; they had one child, Margaret, who died five days after birth. Her first husband was killed during the Great War in 1914, and his younger brother, Clarence, succeeded to the barony. In 1917, she married Captain John Meredyth Jones Evans; after the war, she left the stage permanently and later owned a stable of successful racehorses. Together, they were the parents of children, though the specific names are not provided. Her second husband died in 1957, and she died on 28 June 1971. Despite being known as "the quintessential Gibson Girl," she was not the only person to imitate the character on stage or screen. Photographs of her taken by Lizzie Caswall Smith in 1905 are frequently featured in historical fashion books and on websites to illustrate the Edwardian style.

The cancelled expressways in Toronto were a series of planned municipal expressways in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, that were only partially built or cancelled due to public opposition. Metropolitan Toronto's system of superhighways or freeways was intended to manage suburban growth and connect to the downtown core, in conjunction with the province's developing 400-Series Highways that would link to municipalities outside Metro. However, these expressways faced strong resistance from citizens in the downtown core, who opposed the demolition of homes and parklands, air pollution, noise, and the high cost of construction. The Spadina Expressway, planned since the 1940s, was cancelled in 1971 after only partial construction. Following its cancellation, other expressway plans, including a 'ring' around the central core, were abandoned. By the 1940s, urban development had extended beyond Toronto’s borders, and the city’s planning department recognized that population growth would require development of farmlands outside the city. In 1943, the City of Toronto Planning Board developed a plan for a nine-mile radius around Yonge Street and Queen Street, including a network of superhighways. With the creation of Metropolitan Toronto (Metro) in 1953, a new level of government was established with authority to build infrastructure such as highways, sewers, and public transit, while local governments handled land use planning. Metro planned to build an extensive network of highways that crisscrossed the city, with the province covering 50% of road project costs. Metro focused on roads serving the downtown core and connecting it to the suburbs, with key routes including the "Toronto-Barrie Highway" (Highway 400) on the north-west and the Queen Elizabeth Way on the southwest. The province was already planning Highway 400 in farmland areas, and Metro would extend these highways into the city. Construction began with the Lakeshore Expressway, which connected the QEW to the downtown core; the western section opened in 1958, continued eastward as an elevated highway to York Street in 1962, and reached the Don River by 1964. During construction, it was renamed the Gardiner Expressway after Fred Gardiner, the first chair of Metro and a major supporter. The Don Valley Parkway opened between Bloor Street and Eglinton Avenue in 1961 and expanded north and south to connect with Highway 401 in the north and the Gardiner in the south. These plans were part of a larger network first proposed in 1959 and fully developed by 1966 as the official plan. The inner ring included the Crosstown east-west along Davenport connecting to the Don Valley in the east and the Highway 400 extension to the west, the Highway 400 extension down Christie and Grace Streets from Davenport to the Gardiner near Fort York, and the Gardiner and Don Valley Expressways. The outer ring consisted of Highway 401 along the north, Highway 427 on the west, the Gardiner on the south, and the Scarborough Expressway to the east, connecting the Gardiner to Highway 401 in the far east. Other links included the Richview, a shorter at-grade expressway connecting the western end of the Crosstown at the Highway 400 extension to Highway 27 further west, eventually linking to the proposed Ontario Highway 403 and the Spadina Expressway, which ran north–south and connected the middle of Highway 401 to the downtown core, ending on Spadina Avenue near the University of Toronto. By 1962, the Spadina Expressway was approved and construction began in 1963 from Wilson Avenue to Lawrence Avenue. Initially, Metro approved only the Lawrence to Wilson section, but the province would not fund it unless the full route was approved, which it was. During construction, priority was given to access to the Yorkdale Shopping Centre, which opened in 1964, allowing drivers to travel from Lawrence Avenue north to Yorkdale via a paved section. The interchange with Highway 401 was completed later. In 1961, the Crosstown was cancelled by Metro Council, though carried forward by planning officials. Toronto and Metro proposed alternate routes for Highway 400, with Toronto favouring a route along railway lines. Metro developed its official transportation plan in 1964, evaluating three concepts: a road-oriented plan that included all expressways and omitted the Spadina subway, a transit-oriented plan that included Eglinton Avenue and Queen Street subways, extended the Spadina north to Vaughan, extended the Bloor-Danforth line east into Scarborough, and included express bus routes and commuter rail, and a mixed system that included all roads but omitted a Queen Street subway. The balanced plan, expected to be implemented by 1980, was estimated to cost $1 billion to construct, with the expressway component (Crosstown, Spadina, and Gardiner and Don Valley extensions) costing $210 million. The mixed system, though the most expensive, was approved by Metro Council in December 1966. The official plan included the Crosstown again, though it was not approved for construction. Toronto rejected the Crosstown, and the Ontario government revised the city’s official plan to allow for its possible construction. Construction of the Crosstown was not expected until the 1970s. After the Spadina south to Lawrence was completed, approval was given to proceed south to Eglinton, with the process of expropriating homes and parklands beginning, though without an interchange for the Crosstown. Construction plans became a point of growing protests in the late 1960s. The Gardiner and Don Valley Parkway had initially run through industrial areas, parkland, or unused areas, generating little public concern. As the Gardiner approached the downtown core, it began demolishing long-established neighbourhoods, and the planned expressways generally ran through well-settled areas. The Spadina Expressway passed through Forest Hill, The Annex, Harbord Village, Kensington Market, and Chinatown, while the Crosstown would have created a below-grade barrier on The Annex’s northern border and run beside Rosedale, displacing a forested ravine. Jane Jacobs, a new resident in The Annex who had previously blocked the Lower Manhattan Expressway in New York City, played a key role in opposing the Spadina Expressway. With David and Nadine Nowlan, she formed the "Stop Spadina And Save Our City" group, which became a major rallying point for anti-expressway sentiment. By the late 1960s, the Spadina Expressway had become a politically 'hot' topic. By 1969, construction had reached Eglinton Avenue (though paved only to Lawrence Avenue), less than half the planned route, and had already spent almost all of its $79 million budget. Metro Toronto had to return to the Ontario Municipal Board for additional loans, which were approved in a two-to-one decision. Stop Spadina appealed, and construction was halted pending the outcome. In 1971, Premier John Robarts retired and William Davis took office, who agreed to hear the appeal. On June 3, 1971, Davis stated in the Provincial Legislature: “If we are building a transportation system to serve the automobile, the Spadina Expressway would be a good place to start. But if we are building a transportation system to serve people, the Spadina Expressway is a good place to stop. It is our determination to opt for the latter.” Davis agreed to continue funding for the TTC subway line (now Line 1 Yonge–University) and later in 1972 agreed to complete the unfinished portion of the Spadina between Eglinton and Lawrence. The debate over continuing the Spadina further south from Eglinton continued throughout the 1970s. The cancellation of the Spadina Expressway marked the end of expressway construction in Toronto. Work on other expressways in the system was abandoned. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street, where the province left it, and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive, scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway instead of a six-lane freeway. The western terminus of the Richview forms the oversized interchange between Highways 401 and 427 and Eglinton Avenue near Pearson Airport. Highway 403 was built and now connects further west to Highway 401 at a major interchange that also connects to Highway 410. Both ends of the Scarborough Expressway were built: in the east as a large interchange that quickly turns into a smaller one with Kingston Road, and in the downtown core as a several-kilometre extension of the Gardiner past the Don Valley Parkway to Leslie Street. Lands acquired for the proposed Scarborough and Richview Expressways remained in municipal ownership for another twenty years and much of it remains in public ownership today, though future uses are undetermined. In 2001, the Gardiner East extension was demolished between the Don Valley Parkway and Leslie Street, and there were plans to remove the connection to the Don Valley Parkway, as of 2021 the connection is being realigned. In subsequent decades, the Peel and York Regions have expanded significantly in population and industrial development. An extensive highway network of Highways 403, 407, 410, 427, and 404 has developed in these suburbs and remains in the provincial inventory. Metro Toronto has not built any new expressways since the Spadina cancellation, with new expressways instead constructed by the province, some later transferred to municipal control. The province revised the Belfield Expressway route to terminate at Toronto International Airport instead of crossing Malton to Brampton, expropriated the right-of-way, and opened it as Highway 409. The segment of Highway 404 in Metro Toronto was originally intended as a northern extension of the Don Valley Parkway between Sheppard Avenue and Steeles Avenue, with the province continuing it into York Region, though the province ultimately assumed the entire project. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive (scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway) and transferred from the province to Metro Toronto upon completion in 1982. Highway 2A and a section of QEW (east of Highway 427, re-designated as part of the Gardiner) were transferred to municipal control in 1997, drawing criticism from local politicians as a financial burden. As an alternative to road construction, the city and province have expanded TTC services and GO Transit commuter rail. Although TTC ridership declined in the 1980s and 1990s, it has recently reversed the trend, setting a new record in 2008, indicating growing demand for alternatives to private vehicles. Since expressways reached capacity in the 1970s, commuting has been handled by increased transit, with only 10% of commuters using the Gardiner Expressway to get downtown, according to 2006 figures. Highway advocates, such as political candidate Abel Van Wyk, argue that expressways are necessary to meet demand from suburban growth and automobile traffic between suburbs and the downtown core, and believe new expressways are needed to reduce congestion. Opposing groups, including residents of the core, oppose expansion due to air pollution, noise, and health effects that degrade urban living standards and hinder urban growth. Transit advocates argue that transit lines have higher capacity than expressways and represent better use of government resources. Cycling advocates promote cycling routes as alternatives for commuting and recreation. Special interest groups, such as the Citizens' Transportation Alliance of Greater Toronto, advocate for expressway construction, proposing a new expressway to the northwest (likely an expansion of Black Creek Drive) and one to the east through Scarborough along a hydro corridor or an expansion of Kingston Road, and supporting the filling in of 'missing links' in the arterial road grid. The Canadian Automobile Association published a 2004 plan including a new Scarborough Expressway over Lake Ontario, new expressways and arterial roads, and the Richview Expressway, which was quickly dismissed by Toronto City Council. The City of Toronto and the Government of Ontario focus instead on transit alternatives, aiming to reduce highway dependence through improvements to the current transit network as described in the Transit City plan. In April 2009, the province announced accelerated construction of several Transit City initiatives, including an east–west Eglinton Light Rail line connecting to the airport. Line 1 was extended north to Vaughan, and the Eglinton Crosstown LRT is under construction. It is proposed that Line 1 be extended north to Richmond Hill, Line 2 east to Scarborough City Centre, Line 5 west to Toronto Pearson International Airport, and a new Ontario Line serve the core and neighbourhoods in former North York and East York. Other plans debated during municipal elections included new toll highways or expansions of existing expressways via tolling, though toll highways have been seen as political poison and no politician has included them in any election campaign. The Crosstown Expressway was a planned east–west expressway through central Toronto. Although consistently opposed by Toronto City Council, it remained in the Metro Toronto plan until it was cancelled after the Spadina cancellation. In 1944, it was first proposed and included in the City of Toronto Official Plan in 1949 as the 'north-west arm' of the Don Valley Roadway system. The highway would have connected to Highway 400 at Old Weston Road and St. Clair Avenue, proceeded south-easterly between Davenport Road and Dupont Street, entered the Rosedale Ravine to connect with the main Don Valley roadway south of the Bloor Street Viaduct at the intersection of today’s Rosedale Valley Road and Bayview Avenue, and was estimated to cost $15 million as part of a $179 million development plan. As part of the 1959 Metropolitan Toronto plan, the expressway would have connected the Highway 400 extension along an east–west route near Christie Street and Dupont Street, east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange. The expressway would continue east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through Rosedale to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961. Almost immediately, transportation officials lobbied Toronto and Metro to revive the project. In May 1962, Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford proposed the construction of the Crosstown, along with an extensive one-way street plan for downtown Toronto, arguing it would absorb Spadina traffic and eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential amenities, and encourage development. He stated that it would be folly to proceed otherwise.

An east–west route was proposed near Christie Street and Dupont Street, extending east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner Expressway. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange, running from north of Highway 401 through the Cedarvale and Nordheimer ravines and Spadina Road, with only a partial section built and now known as Allen Road. The expressway would have continued east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through the Rosedale neighbourhood east of Mount Pleasant Road to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section to be built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown expressway was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961 and later revived in May 1962 by Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford, who proposed it alongside a one-way street plan for downtown to absorb Spadina Expressway traffic, eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential areas, and encourage development; he also stated it would be folly to terminate the Spadina at anything other than a controlled-access expressway. Metro Planning Commissioner Murray Jones estimated 40,000 daily vehicles would move between Highway 400 and the Don Valley Parkway, and Metro Traffic Director Samuel Cass noted the plan would prevent heavy traffic from using residential streets in Rosedale and Moore Park. In 1964, Metro Planning Commissioner Eli Comay proposed extending Bay Street north of Davenport to connect with the Crosstown, criticizing the city for allowing an apartment development in the path of the extension; Toronto Controller William Dennison accused Comay of setting policy unilaterally, and the Toronto Board of Control rejected Comay and allowed the development to proceed. Metro Council twice instructed planners to cease work on the Crosstown, with Chairman William Allen joking that the only way to get it out of his mind was to leave the country. The Crosstown reappeared in the 1965 transportation plan and was approved by Metro Council, though the City of Toronto’s official plan had no such expressway and the Ontario Minister of Municipal Affairs rejected and rewrote that section to align with the Metro plan. The City of Toronto remained consistently opposed. Although land was acquired, the expressway was not built, though a short connecting road between the Don Valley Parkway and the Bayview Avenue Extension and Bloor Street would have likely been integrated. When the first section of the Don Valley Parkway opened from Bloor Street to Eglinton Avenue, it served as the southern terminus and remains an on/off ramp, with the unnamed roadway being a four-lane arterial with interchanges at either end, including the named 'Chester Hill' interchange. The East Metro Freeway was a proposed north–south expressway beginning at Highway 401 east of Morningside Avenue, following the Rouge River valley to Highway 407, with phase 2 extending beyond Highway 407 between the Ninth Line and York-Durham Line in Markham to Stouffville; it was a last priority for the province, with construction not planned until after the Scarborough Expressway was completed, and was not an extension of the Scarborough Expressway, as the latter’s western terminus would have been 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) west of the East Metro’s southern terminus. After the Spadina Expressway was cancelled, the Scarborough Expressway was put on hold and reviewed; with the Scarborough plan dropped, the East Metro route became less necessary and faced serious opposition from Rouge River naturalist groups, leading to its official removal from planning documents on June 1, 1994. Part of the Donald Cousens Parkway follows the East Metro Freeway route from 14th to 16th Avenue, though this arterial road now lies entirely within Markham, whereas the original Metro plan intended a terminus in Stouffville. Markham continues to seek a southern arterial connection to Highway 401, while Toronto has not rerouted Morningside Road to meet the Ninth Line at Steeles Avenue; instead, the current plan is to extend Morningside Avenue from McNicoll Avenue to Steeles Avenue just east of Tapscott Road using a private right of way and widen Steeles from just east of Markham Road to Ninth Line, with new traffic lights and a six-lane roadway to eliminate the bottleneck; a direct connection is not possible due to needing to cut across Cedar Brae Golf Club and build near the Rouge River. The Richview Expressway, named after the Richview Sideroad (now Eglinton Avenue through Etobicoke), was only partially completed due to low use and local opposition, resulting in a wide right-of-way from Black Creek Drive to Highway 427, which now includes high-speed flyover ramps at the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange originally intended for the Richview Expressway. The expressway was also known as the Hamilton Expressway because the original routing of Highway 403 (to Hamilton) was planned to terminate at the present site of the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange; had that routing been followed, the Richview would have been considered a municipal extension of Highway 403. However, the province realigned Highway 403 to turn north and meet Highway 401 at a new junction, also accommodating Highway 410 to Brampton, while widening Highway 401 between Highway 403 and Highway 427. A portion of the right-of-way between Highway 403 and the Richview Expressway was later used for Eastgate Parkway, which runs a short distance before curving north and terminating at Eglinton Avenue just west of Mississauga’s boundary with Etobicoke, while the rest of the corridor remained unbuilt. Lands allocated for the Richview Expressway were sold, with several apartment buildings now constructed on the old right-of-way. The corridor was revisited in the 2014 Toronto municipal election when John Tory’s SmartTrack plan proposed heavy rail, with challenger Olivia Chow highlighting the existing buildings; Tory was elected, but the heavy rail proposal was dropped in 2016 in favor of extending the Eglinton Crosstown LRT west to the city’s border with Mississauga. Although the expressway was never completed, plans included on/off ramps for the Scarborough Expressway (Gardiner Expressway Eastern Extension), which was intended to connect the Gardiner to Highway 401 at Toronto’s eastern boundary, with one segment built before public opposition halted the project. Traffic from the east would have gone directly downtown and served southeast Toronto; instead, such traffic now combines with northbound traffic on the Don Valley Parkway, where daily volumes exceed capacity, prompting ongoing proposals for new routes. The Scarborough Expressway was first conceived in the 1940s, with detailed planning beginning in 1967, and construction expected after the Spadina Expressway. Early plans had the route beside the CN route in southern Scarborough, later shifting to an eastern extension of the Gardiner along Lake Ontario’s base, following the Scarborough Bluffs, connecting to Highway 401 via Ontario Highway 2A, a short stub freeway part of the original 401 alignment. The 1967 proposal would have required demolishing 1,200 homes; after fierce opposition, the city redesigned the route in 1973, moving it entirely into the Lakeshore East CN/GO railway corridor from the Don Valley Parkway/Gardiner interchange, depressed in a deep ditch, reducing demolitions to 706 homes. This still did not satisfy east Toronto residents, who continued to oppose the plan, leading the city to shelve it in 1974. Property had been acquired by Metro Toronto, and some infrastructure, such as an overpass for roadway and railway tracks, was built, but opposition from residents, especially in eastern Toronto, caused the route to be severed from the Gardiner. The fiercest resistance came from eastern Toronto, leading to the deletion of the section beyond the Toronto/Scarborough boundary, which would have ended at Victoria Park Avenue and potentially flooded east-end neighbourhoods. Residents continued to oppose the plan and appeared before the Ontario Municipal Board each time Metro sought additional land. Metro and Scarborough continued to promote the expressway, renamed the "Scarborough Transportation Corridor," with parts of Eglinton Avenue East considered as a potential arterial to relieve Highway 401. Until the early 1990s, Metro and Scarborough maintained the plan, but by 1994 expressway development was no longer a priority. By 1996, Metro began planning to demolish the eastern end of the Gardiner Expressway, effectively ending the Scarborough Expressway/Scarborough Transportation Corridor. The intended connection between the Don River and Leslie Street was demolished in 2001, leaving only an offramp from the Gardiner to Carlaw Avenue, which was removed in 2021 to realign ramps between the Gardiner and the Don Valley Expressway. All that remains are concrete pillars from the elevated expressway to Leslie Street. Much of the land acquired across Scarborough remains vacant, with the City of Toronto conducting studies on its future use, including local streets, housing, and public parkland. Bridges along the CN/GO corridor were built with space for two lanes on either side of the railway, which are now empty and available for future rail upgrades. In the early 2000s, much of the land east of Manse Road in Scarborough was sold; the parcel between Kingston Road and Lawrence Avenue was developed into homes, as was a portion south of the railway and east of Poplar Road. A police station, Toronto Police 43 Division, was built on a parcel south of Lawrence Avenue.

The Canon EOS R50 is an entry-level APS-C mirrorless interchangeable-lens camera manufactured by Canon, announced on 27 February 2023 alongside the full-frame Canon EOS R8. It functions as an RF-mount replacement for Canon's discontinued EOS M50 Mark II and EOS 250D. Designed following the compact and lightweight principles of the EOS M50 Mark II and EOS 250D, the R50 incorporates the RF lens mount system and features from earlier EOS R series cameras, fitting the internal components of the EOS R10 into a more travel- and vlogging-friendly form factor. The camera features a 24.2-megapixel APS-C CMOS sensor, DIGIC X processor, Dual Pixel CMOS AF II focus system, and a 2.36-million-dot OLED electronic viewfinder, though physical controls have been simplified for beginner photographers. It lacks features such as a fully mechanical shutter, sensor self-cleaning, and in-body image stabilization, though in-lens stabilization is supported. The R50 includes a fully-articulating 1.62-million-dot LCD touchscreen, a built-in stereo microphone, a 3.5mm audio jack for external microphones, a UHS-I SD card slot, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity. It can shoot at 12 fps with a buffer of up to 42 JPEG images using the electronic first curtain shutter, or 15 fps with a buffer of up to 37 images using the electronic shutter, with shutter speeds ranging from 1/8000 seconds to 30 seconds. For video, it records up to 4K UHD resolution oversampled from the full sensor width at up to 29.97 fps and supports 1080p slow motion at up to 120 fps. The DIGIC X processor enables subject detection in multiple modes, up to 651 autofocus zones and 4503 autofocus points, and in-camera focus bracketing. Upon release, the EOS R50 received generally positive reviews; Engadget awarded it 87/100, calling it "a good balance between power and affordability," while Digital Photography Review gave it 84%, praising its photo and video quality and autofocus, though noting a lack of available RF-mount APS-C lenses. Some critics were more critical, with TechRadar and PCMag both giving it 3.5 stars and criticizing its ergonomics and limited physical controls, with PCMag noting the small size made it difficult to hold comfortably. On 26 March 2025, Canon introduced the EOS R50 V, a vlogging-focused variant that removes the built-in flash and electronic viewfinder but adds improved video recording capabilities, enhanced wired and wireless connectivity, and more video-oriented physical and digital controls, including the ability to shoot in Canon Log Clog3. Other Canon APS-C mirrorless cameras from the same period feature processors such as DIGIC 5/5+, DIGIC 6/6+, DIGIC 7, DIGIC 8, and DIGIC X; video capabilities including 1080p, 4K, 7K, and 8K; screen types such as flip (tilt), articulating, and touchscreen; body features like in-body image stabilization, multi-function hot shoe, and weather sealing; specialty models including astrophotography, Cinema EOS, and high-resolution cameras; and firmware add-ons like Magic Lantern Support.

The Cape Town Cycle Tour, formerly known as the Cape Argus Cycle Tour, is an annual cycle race held in Cape Town, South Africa, typically covering a distance of 109 km (68 mi). It is the first event outside Europe to be included in the Union Cycliste Internationale's Golden Bike Series. South Africa hosts three of the world's largest sporting events by number of entrants, with the Cape Town Cycle Tour, which can attract up to 35,000 cyclists, being the world's largest individually timed cycle race. The other two are the Comrades Marathon, the world's largest ultra-marathon running event, and the Midmar Mile, the world's largest open water swim. The Cycle Tour was the final leg of the Giro del Capo, a multi-stage race for professional and leading registered riders, which was last held in 2010. Traditionally staged on the second Sunday of March, the event has featured well-known competitors such as Miguel Indurain, Jan Ulrich, Matt Damon, Helen Zille, and Lance Armstrong. The race usually follows a scenic 109 km circular route starting at Grand Parade in Cape Town, traveling along Nelson Mandela Boulevard (N2), the M3 to Muizenberg, Main Road along the False Bay coast to Simon's Town and Smitswinkel Bay, then crossing the peninsula westward past the entrance to the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park (including Cape Point), heading north along the Atlantic coast through Scarborough, Kommetjie, Noordhoek, Chapman's Peak, Hout Bay over Suikerbossie Hill to Camps Bay, and ending near the Cape Town Stadium in Green Point. Between 2009 and 2010, and prior to 1999, the route varied in length between 104 km (65 mi) and 110 km (68 mi). The course records for conventional bicycles on the 110 km course over Chapman's Peak are documented. Penny Krohn holds the record for the most consecutive age group victories with 25. The fastest time ever recorded—also the highest average speed—was set in 1993 on the 105 km course by Wimpie van der Merwe in a fully faired recumbent, completing it in 02:16:40 at an average speed of 46.1 km/h. Japie Malan, at 92 years old during the 2012 Cycle Tour, is the oldest cyclist to complete the race within the seven-hour limit on a tandem, finishing in 05:49:00; he is also the oldest man (90 years old at the time) to complete the race on a single bicycle during the 2010 Cycle Tour, finishing in 06:48:52, and the oldest man to ride the Argus for the first time, which he did in 2004 at age 84. Mary Warner, at 80 years old during the 2006 tour, is the oldest woman to complete the race, finishing in 06:43:38. In 1978, Bill Mylrea and John Stegmann organized the Big Ride-In to advocate for cycle paths in South Africa, which drew hundreds of cyclists, including the Mayor of Cape Town at the time, and was first won by Lawrence Whittaker in September 1978. The original plan for the race was 140 km (87 mi), including a leg to Cape Point, but it was reduced to 104 km (65 mi) after being denied entry to the then Cape Point Nature Reserve; organizers convinced the initially reluctant Cape Argus, a local newspaper and sponsor, to allow the event to use its name. The event is now part of a week-long series of five cycling events that begin a week before the Cycle Tour and conclude with the main race. Between 2000 and 2003, the route was altered due to the closure of Chapman's Peak Drive, with a return via Ou Kaapse Weg and the Blue Route. The race has been halted three times due to extreme weather—twice when many competitors had already completed it, and once significantly shortened due to fire—and once cancelled. Key information about each event is provided in the document.

Johann Carl Friedrich Gauss (/ɡaʊs/ ⓘ; German: Gauß; [kaʁl ˈfʁiːdʁɪç ˈɡaʊs] ⓘ; Latin: Carolus Fridericus Gauss; 30 April 1777 – 23 February 1855) was a German mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist whose contributions spanned number theory, algebra, analysis, geometry, statistics, and probability. He served as director of the Göttingen Observatory and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855. From an early age, Gauss was recognized as a child prodigy in mathematics; while studying at the University of Göttingen, he developed several mathematical theorems. As an independent scholar, he authored the masterpieces Disquisitiones Arithmeticae and Theoria motus corporum coelestium. He produced the second and third complete proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra and introduced the triple bar symbol (≡) for congruence. In number theory, he made significant contributions including the composition law, the law of quadratic reciprocity, and proved the triangular case of the Fermat polygonal number theorem. He also advanced the theory of binary and ternary quadratic forms and hypergeometric series. At age 19, he proved the construction of the heptadecagon, the first such progress in regular polygon construction in over 2000 years. He introduced the concept of Gaussian curvature and proved its key properties, especially with his Theorema Egregium. Gauss was the first to prove Gauss's inequality and instrumental in developing the arithmetic–geometric mean. Over 100 mathematical and scientific concepts are named after him. Gauss played a key role in identifying Ceres as a dwarf planet; his work on the motion of planetoids led to the introduction of the Gaussian gravitational constant and the method of least squares, which he discovered before Adrien-Marie Legendre published it. He also introduced the recursive least squares algorithm. Gauss led the geodetic survey of the Kingdom of Hanover from 1820 to 1844 and was one of the founders of geophysics; he provided the first absolute measurement of Earth's magnetic field in 1832 and applied spherical harmonic analysis to show that most of Earth's magnetic field was internal. He was the first to discover and study non-Euclidean geometry, which he named. Gauss developed a fast Fourier transform some 160 years before John Tukey and James Cooley. His practical work led to the invention of the heliotrope in 1821, a magnetometer in 1833, and—along with Wilhelm Eduard Weber—the first electromagnetic telegraph in 1833. Gauss received the Lalande Prize in 1809 for his work on planetary theory and orbits and the Copley Medal in 1838 for his mathematical research in magnetism. He was known for not publishing incomplete work, and many of his discoveries were delayed due to posthumous editing. He believed that the act of learning, not the possession of knowledge, brought the greatest enjoyment. Though not an enthusiastic teacher, some of his students, such as Richard Dedekind and Bernhard Riemann, became influential mathematicians. Gauss married twice and had six children, several of whom later emigrated to the United States. He was born on 30 April 1777 in Brunswick, in the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (now in Lower Saxony), a family of relatively low social status. His father, Gebhard Dietrich Gauss (1744–1808), worked as a butcher, bricklayer, gardener, and treasurer; Gauss described him as honourable and respected but rough and dominating. His mother, Dorothea, was nearly illiterate. He had one elder brother from his father's first marriage. Gauss was a child prodigy; when teachers noticed his abilities, they brought him to the Duke of Brunswick, who sent him to the Collegium Carolinum from 1792 to 1795, with Eberhard August Wilhelm von Zimmermann as a teacher. The Duke then funded his studies in mathematics, sciences, and classical languages at the University of Göttingen until 1798. His mathematics professor was Abraham Gotthelf Kästner, whom Gauss called "the leading mathematician among poets, and the leading poet among mathematicians" due to his epigrams. Astronomy was taught by Karl Felix Seyffer, with whom Gauss maintained correspondence; Olbers and Gauss mocked each other in their letters. Gauss admired Georg Christoph Lichtenberg in physics and Christian Gottlob Heyne in classics. Fellow students included Johann Friedrich Benzenberg, Farkas Bolyai, and Heinrich Wilhelm Brandes. Gauss was likely self-taught in mathematics and independently rediscovered several theorems. In 1796, he solved a geometrical problem that had puzzled mathematicians since ancient times by determining which regular polygons can be constructed with compass and straightedge, leading him to choose mathematics over philology as a career. His mathematical diary, containing short remarks from 1796 to 1814, shows that many ideas for Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) originated during this time. An apocryphal story recounts that as a student, Gauss quickly calculated the sum from 1 to 100 as 5050 by recognizing it as 50 pairs of 101. Gauss graduated as a Doctor of Philosophy in 1799, not at Göttingen, but at the University of Helmstedt, the only state university in the duchy, under the Duke of Brunswick's request, with his thesis assessed by Johann Friedrich Pfaff and awarded in absentia without an oral examination. The Duke then provided him with financial support as a private scholar in Brunswick. Gauss declined calls from the Russian Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg and Landshut University. The Duke promised to fund an observatory in Brunswick in 1804, but plans were cancelled due to Napoleon's wars; the Duke died in the battle of Jena in 1806, the duchy was abolished the following year, and Gauss lost financial support. In the early 1800s, Gauss collaborated with astronomers in Bremen and Lilienthal—especially Wilhelm Olbers, Karl Ludwig Harding, and Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel—forming the informal group known as the Celestial police, whose goal was discovering new planets. They compiled data on asteroids and comets, which Gauss later published in Theoria motus corporum coelestium (1809). In November 1807, Gauss was hired by the University of Göttingen, then under Jérôme Bonaparte’s Kingdom of Westphalia, as full professor and director of the astronomical observatory, a position he held until his death. He was required to pay two thousand francs as a war contribution, which he could not afford; both Olbers and Laplace offered help, but Gauss refused. An anonymous person from Frankfurt, later identified as Prince-primate Dalberg, paid the sum. Gauss took over the 60-year-old observatory, founded in 1748 by Prince-elector George II and built on a converted fortification tower, which had outdated instruments. A new observatory had been approved by George III since 1802 and continued to be planned by the Westphalian government, but Gauss could not move until September 1816. He received new, up-to-date instruments, including two meridian circles from Repsold and Reichenbach and a heliometer from Fraunhofer. Gauss's scientific work can be divided into three periods: astronomy (first two decades of the 19th century), geodesy (third decade), and physics, mainly magnetism (fourth decade). Gauss disliked giving academic lectures and often complained about the burden, though he delivered lectures continuously from 1808 until 1854. Most of his lectures focused on astronomy, geodesy, and applied mathematics, with only three on pure mathematics. Several of his students became renowned in mathematics, physics, and astronomy, including Moritz Cantor, Dedekind, Dirksen, Encke, Gould, Heine, Klinkerfues, Kupffer, Listing, Möbius, Nicolai, Riemann, Ritter, Schering, Scherk, Schumacher, von Staudt, Stern, Ursin; and geoscientists Sartorius von Waltershausen and Wappäus. Gauss did not write textbooks and avoided popularizing science; his only attempts were on the date of Easter (1800/1802) and the essay Erdmagnetismus und Magnetometer (1836). He published exclusively in Latin or German, using classical Latin with contemporary modifications. Gauss gave his inaugural lecture at Göttingen in 1808, describing astronomy as based on reliable observations and accurate calculations. He was supported by lecturers such as Thibaut, Mayer, Weber (from 1831), and Harding, who led practical astronomy lectures. After Harding's death in 1834, the university appointed an assistant. Gauss and Harding had once been on friendly terms but became alienated, possibly because Gauss wanted Harding to be no more than an assistant. Gauss used the new meridian circles almost exclusively and limited joint observations with Harding. Brendel divided Gauss's astronomical activity into seven periods, with the years after 1820 considered a "period of lower astronomical activity." The new observatory did not perform as effectively as others; Gauss's research was a one-man effort without a long-term observation program, and the university only established an assistant after Harding's death. Gauss twice declined offers to join the Prussian Academy (1810 and 1825) and Leipzig University (1810) and Vienna University (1842), possibly due to family financial difficulties. His salary increased from 1000 Reichsthaler in 1810 to 2500 Reichsthaler in 1824, making him one of the best-paid professors later in life. In 1810, when Bessel was in trouble at Königsberg due to lacking an academic title, Gauss granted him a doctorate honoris causa from Göttingen's Philosophy Faculty in March 1811. He recommended an honorary degree for Sophie Germain but only shortly before her death, so she never received it. He also supported Gotthold Eisenstein in Berlin. Gauss remained loyal to the House of Hanover; after King William IV died in 1837, the new king Ernest Augustus annulled the 1833 constitution. Seven professors, known as the "Göttingen Seven," protested, including Gauss's friend Wilhelm Weber and his son-in-law Heinrich Ewald. All were dismissed, with three expelled; Ewald and Weber remained in Göttingen. Gauss was deeply affected but saw no way to assist them. Gauss participated in academic administration, serving three times as dean of the Faculty of Philosophy. He managed the university's widow's pension fund, dealing with actuarial science and writing a report on stabilizing benefits. He was appointed director of the Royal Academy of Sciences in Göttingen for nine years. Gauss remained mentally active into old age despite suffering from gout and general unhappiness. He died of a heart attack on 23 February 1855 in Göttingen and was buried in the Albani Cemetery. Heinrich Ewald and Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen delivered eulogies at his funeral. Gauss was a successful investor, accumulating wealth in stocks and securities valued at over 150,000 Thaler; after his death, about 18,000 Thaler were found hidden in his rooms. The day after his death, his brain was removed, preserved, and studied by Rudolf Wagner, who found its mass to be slightly above average at 1,492 grams (3.29 lb). Wagner's son Hermann estimated the cerebral area at 219,588 square millimetres (340.362 sq in) in his doctoral thesis. In 2013, a neurobiologist at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry in Göttingen discovered that Gauss's brain had been mislabeled soon after initial investigations, being mixed with that of physician Conrad Heinrich Fuchs, who died in Göttingen a few months after Gauss. Further investigation found no remarkable anomalies in either brain. Thus, all brain studies prior to 1998, except the first by Rudolf and Hermann Wagner, actually referred to Fuchs's brain. Gauss married Johanna Osthoff on 9 October 1805 in St. Catherine's church in Brunswick. They had two sons and one daughter: Joseph (1806–1873), Wilhelmina (1808–1840), and Louis (1809–1810). Johanna died on 11 October 1809, one month after Louis's birth, who died a few months later. Gauss named his children after Giuseppe Piazzi, Wilhelm Olbers, and Karl Ludwig Harding, the discoverers of the first asteroids. On 4 August 1810, Gauss married Wilhelmine (Minna) Waldeck, a friend of his first wife, with whom he had three children: Eugen (1811–1896), Wilhelm (1813–1879), and Therese (1816–1864). Minna died on 12 September 1831 after being seriously ill for over a decade. Therese then took over the household and cared for Gauss for the rest of his life; after his death, she married actor Constantin Staufenau.
