One month after the birth of Louis, who died a few months later, Gauss named his children after Giuseppe Piazzi, Wilhelm Olbers, and Karl Ludwig Harding, the discoverers of the first asteroids. On 4 August 1810, Gauss married Wilhelmine (Minna) Waldeck, a friend of his first wife, with whom he had three children: Eugen (later Eugene) (1811–1896), Wilhelm (later William) (1813–1879), and Therese (1816–1864). Minna Gauss died on 12 September 1831 after being seriously ill for more than a decade; Therese then took over the household and cared for Gauss for the rest of his life, and after his death, she married actor Constantin Staufenau. Her sister Wilhelmina married the orientalist Heinrich Ewald. Gauss's mother Dorothea lived in his house from 1817 until she died in 1839. The eldest son Joseph, while still a schoolboy, helped his father during the survey campaign in the summer of 1821. After university, in 1824, Joseph joined the Hanoverian army and assisted in surveying again in 1829; in the 1830s, he was responsible for expanding the survey network into the western parts of the kingdom. With his geodetical qualifications, he left the service and became director of the Royal Hanoverian State Railways, studying the U.S. railroad system for some months in 1836. Eugen left Göttingen in September 1830 and emigrated to the United States, where he spent five years with the army, then worked for the American Fur Company in the Midwest, later moving to Missouri and becoming a successful businessman. Wilhelm married a niece of the astronomer Bessel, moved to Missouri, started as a farmer, and became wealthy in the shoe business in St. Louis. Eugene and William have numerous descendants in America, but the Gauss descendants in Germany all derive from Joseph, as the daughters had no children. In the first two decades of the 19th century, Gauss was the only important German mathematician comparable to the leading French mathematicians; his Disquisitiones Arithmeticae was the first mathematical book from Germany to be translated into French. Gauss was "in front of the new development" with documented research since 1799, due to his wealth of new ideas and rigorous demonstration. Unlike earlier mathematicians like Leonhard Euler, who allowed readers to follow their reasoning including erroneous paths, Gauss introduced a direct and complete exposition that did not show the reader his thought process. Gauss was the first to restore the rigor of demonstration admired in the ancients, which had been pushed aside by earlier emphasis on new developments. In a letter to Farkas Bolyai, he stated: "It is not knowledge, but the act of learning, not possession but the act of getting there, which grants the greatest enjoyment. When I have clarified and exhausted a subject, then I turn away from it, in order to go into darkness again." His posthumous papers, scientific diary, and short glosses in his textbooks show he empirically worked extensively. He was a lifelong enthusiastic and fast calculator, checking results through estimation, though not always free from mistakes; he used skillful tools, including numerous mathematical tables, examined their exactness, and constructed new tables for personal use, such as developing Gaussian elimination. His calculations and tables were often more precise than necessary, likely providing additional material for theoretical work. Gauss only published work when he considered it complete and above criticism, consistent with his personal seal motto "Pauca sed Matura" ("Few, but Ripe"). Colleagues encouraged him to publish new ideas and criticized his delays, to which he responded that initial discovery was easy but elaboration was demanding due to lack of time or "serenity of mind." He published many short communications in journals but left a large literary estate. Gauss referred to mathematics as "the queen of sciences" and arithmetic as "the queen of mathematics," and reportedly believed that immediately understanding Euler's identity was a benchmark for becoming a first-class mathematician. Gauss claimed that the ideas of others had already been in his possession, so his concept of priority was "the first to discover, not the first to publish," differing from contemporaries. His citations were criticized as negligent, but he justified them by stating he only gave complete references to important previous authors, which required knowledge of the history of science and more time than he wished to spend. Soon after his death, Sartorius published the first biography (1856), describing Gauss as a serene and forward-striving man with childlike modesty and "iron character" and unshakeable mental strength, though others saw him as reserved and unapproachable "like an Olympian sitting enthroned on the summit of science." His contemporaries agreed he had a difficult character, often refusing compliments and displaying grumpy behavior, though his mood could change quickly to become a charming, open-minded host. Gauss disliked polemic natures and, with Hausmann, opposed the appointment of Justus Liebig to a university chair in Göttingen because he was always involved in polemics. Gauss's life was marked by severe family problems: his first wife Johanna died shortly after the birth of their third child, and he expressed his grief in a last letter to her in the style of an ancient threnody. His second wife and two daughters suffered from tuberculosis; in a letter to Bessel dated December 1831, Gauss described himself as "the victim of the worst domestic sufferings." Due to his wife's illness, both younger sons were educated in Celle, far from Göttingen. Joseph's military career ended after over two decades at the poorly paid rank of first lieutenant, though he had acquired considerable knowledge of geodesy and needed financial support from his father after marriage. Eugen shared his father's computational and linguistic talent but had a lively, sometimes rebellious character; he wanted to study philology, while Gauss wanted him to become a lawyer. After running up debts and causing a public scandal, Eugen left Göttingen dramatically in September 1830 and emigrated via Bremen to the United States, wasting his initial funds and after which his father refused further financial support. Wilhelm wanted to qualify for agricultural administration but faced educational difficulties and eventually emigrated as well. Only Gauss's youngest daughter Therese accompanied him in his final years. In later years, Gauss habitually collected various numerical data, such as the number of paths from his home to places in Göttingen or people's ages in days; he congratulated Humboldt in December 1851 for reaching the same age as Isaac Newton at death in days. Beyond Latin, Gauss was acquainted with modern languages and read classical and modern literature in English and French. At age 62, he began teaching himself Russian, likely to understand scientific writings from Russia, including those of Lobachevsky on non-Euclidean geometry. Gauss liked singing and attended concerts and was a busy newspaper reader, visiting an academic press salon at noon in his last years. He did not care much for philosophy and mocked the "splitting hairs of the so-called metaphysicians," meaning proponents of Naturphilosophie. Gauss had an "aristocratic and through and through conservative nature," with little respect for people's intelligence and morals, following the motto "mundus vult decipi." He disliked Napoleon and his system and was horrified by all forms of violence and revolution, condemning the methods of the Revolutions of 1848 though agreeing with some of their aims, such as a unified Germany. He had a low estimation of constitutional systems and criticized parliamentarians for their ignorance and logical errors. Some biographers have speculated on his religious beliefs; he sometimes said "God arithmetizes" and "I succeeded – not on account of my hard efforts, but by the grace of the Lord." Gauss was a member of the Lutheran church, like most of northern Germany's population, but it seems he did not believe all Lutheran dogma or fully understand the Bible literally. According to Sartorius, Gauss's religious tolerance, "insatiable thirst for truth," and sense of justice were motivated by his religious convictions. In his 1799 doctoral thesis, Gauss proved the fundamental theorem of algebra, stating that every non-constant single-variable polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. Mathematicians including Jean le Rond d'Alembert had produced false proofs before him, and Gauss's dissertation includes a critique of d'Alembert's work. He later produced three other proofs, the last in 1849 being generally rigorous, leading to considerable clarification of complex numbers. In the preface to the Disquisitiones, Gauss dates the beginning of his work on number theory to 1795, noting that previous mathematicians like Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Legendre had already found much of what he independently discovered. The Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, written in 1798 and published in 1801, consolidated number theory as a discipline and covered both elementary and algebraic number theory. It introduces the triple bar symbol (≡) for congruence and uses it for a clean presentation of modular arithmetic. It deals with the unique factorization theorem and primitive roots modulo n. In the main sections, Gauss presents the first two proofs of the law of quadratic reciprocity and develops the theories of binary and ternary quadratic forms. The Disquisitiones include the Gauss composition law for binary quadratic forms and the enumeration of the number of representations of an integer as the sum of three squares. As an almost immediate corollary of his theorem on three squares, he proves the triangular case of the Fermat polygonal number theorem for n = 3. From several analytic results on class numbers given without proof at the end of the fifth section, it appears Gauss already knew the class number formula in 1801. In the last section, Gauss proves the constructibility of a regular heptadecagon (17-sided polygon) with straightedge and compass by reducing the problem to an algebraic one—this was the first progress in regular polygon construction in over 2000 years. He shows that a regular polygon is constructible if the number of its sides is a power of 2 or the product of a power of 2 and any number of distinct Fermat primes. In the same section, he gives a result on the number of solutions of certain cubic polynomials with coefficients in finite fields, which amounts to counting integral points on an elliptic curve. An unfinished chapter, consisting of work done during 1797–1799, was found among his papers after his death. One of Gauss's first results was the empirically found conjecture of 1792—the later called prime number theorem—giving an estimation of the number of primes using the integral logarithm. In 1816, Olbers encouraged Gauss to compete for a prize from the French Academy for a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem; he refused, considering the topic uninteresting. However, after his death, a short undated paper was found with proofs of the theorem for the cases n = 3 and n = 5. The case n = 3 was proved earlier by Leonhard Euler, but Gauss developed a more streamlined proof using Eisenstein integers, which was simpler than the real integer case. In 1831, Gauss contributed to solving the Kepler conjecture by proving that the greatest packing density of spheres in three-dimensional space is achieved when their centers form a cubic face-centred arrangement, after reviewing a book by Ludwig August Seeber on the theory of reduction of positive ternary quadratic forms. Having noticed flaws in Seeber's proof, he simplified arguments, proved the central conjecture, and noted that this theorem is equivalent to the Kepler conjecture for regular arrangements. In two papers on biquadratic residues (1828, 1832), Gauss introduced the ring of Gaussian integers Z[i], showed it is a unique factorization domain, and generalized key arithmetic concepts such as Fermat's little theorem and Gauss's lemma. The main objective was to formulate the law of biquadratic reciprocity, as Gauss discovered that rings of complex integers are the natural setting for such higher reciprocity laws. In the second paper, he stated the general law of biquadratic reciprocity and proved several special cases. In an earlier 1818 publication containing his fifth and sixth proofs of quadratic reciprocity, he claimed the techniques (Gauss sums) could be applied to prove higher reciprocity laws. One of Gauss's first discoveries was the notion of the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM) of two positive real numbers. He discovered its relation to elliptic integrals in 1798–1799 through Landen's transformation, and a diary entry recorded the discovery of the connection of Gauss's constant to lemniscatic elliptic functions, a result he stated would "surely open an entirely new field of analysis." He also made early inroads into the foundations of complex analysis, and from a letter to Bessel in 1811, it is clear he knew the "fundamental theorem of complex analysis" — Cauchy's integral theorem — and understood the notion of complex residues when integrating around poles. Euler's pentagonal numbers theorem, together with research on the AGM and lemniscatic functions, led to results on Jacobi theta functions, culminating in the discovery in 1808 of the Jacobi triple product identity, which includes Euler's theorem as a special case. His works show he knew modular transformations of order 3, 5, 7 for elliptic functions since 1808. Several mathematical fragments in his Nachlass indicate he knew parts of the modern theory of modular forms. In his work on the multivalued AGM of two complex numbers, he discovered a deep connection between the infinitely many values of the AGM and its two "simplest values." In his unpublished writings, he recognized and made a sketch of the key concept of fundamental domain for the modular group. One of his sketches was a drawing of a tessellation of the unit disk by "equilateral" hyperbolic triangles with all angles equal to π/4. An example of Gauss's insight in analysis is his cryptic remark that the principles of circle division by compass and straightedge can also be applied to the division of the lemniscate curve, which inspired Abel's theorem on lemniscate division. Another example is his publication "Summatio quarundam serierum singularium" (1811) on the determination of the sign of quadratic Gauss sums, in which he solved the main problem by introducing q-analogs of binomial coefficients and manipulating them using several original identities that seem to stem from his work on elliptic function theory; however, Gauss cast his argument in a formal way that does not reveal its origin in elliptic function theory.

Gauss discovered a deep connection between the infinitely many values of the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM) and its two "simplest values," and in his unpublished writings recognized and sketched the concept of a fundamental domain for the modular group. One of his sketches depicted a tessellation of the unit disk by "equilateral" hyperbolic triangles with all angles equal to π/4. He made a cryptic remark that the principles of compass and straightedge circle division could also apply to lemniscate division, inspiring Abel's theorem on lemniscate division; in his 1811 publication "Summatio quarundam serierum singularium," he solved the sign problem of quadratic Gauss sums by introducing q-analogs of binomial coefficients and using original identities derived from his work on elliptic function theory, though he presented the argument formally without revealing its elliptic origin, later exposed by Jacobi and Hermite. In "Disquisitiones generales circa series infinitam..." (1813), he provided the first systematic treatment of the general hypergeometric function F(α,β,γ,x), showing that many known functions are special cases, and this work marks the first exact inquiry into the convergence of infinite series in mathematical history; it also introduced infinite continued fractions arising as ratios of hypergeometric functions, now known as Gauss continued fractions. In 1823, Gauss won the Danish Society prize with an essay on conformal mappings, stating that angle-preserving mappings in the complex plane must be complex analytic functions and using the Beltrami equation to prove the existence of isothermal coordinates on analytic surfaces, concluding with examples of conformal mappings into a sphere and an ellipsoid of revolution. Gauss often deduced theorems inductively from empirical numerical data, making significant contributions to numerical analysis, including the method of Gaussian quadrature published in 1816. In a 1823 private letter to Gerling, he described a solution to a 4x4 system of linear equations using the Gauss-Seidel method—an "indirect" iterative method—and recommended it over direct elimination for systems with more than two equations. Gauss invented an algorithm for computing what is now called the discrete Fourier transform when calculating the orbits of Pallas and Juno in 1805, 160 years before Cooley and Tukey developed their similar Cooley–Tukey algorithm; he developed it as a trigonometric interpolation method, but the paper Theoria Interpolationis Methodo Nova Tractata was published posthumously in 1876, after Fourier's 1807 introduction of the subject. The geodetic survey of Hanover sparked Gauss's interest in differential geometry and topology, leading to his 1828 publication that marks the birth of modern differential geometry of surfaces, departing from treating surfaces as graphs of functions and instead exploring them from the "inner" perspective of a two-dimensional being; this work established the Theorema Egregium, which states that the curvature of a surface can be determined solely by measuring angles and distances on the surface, independent of its embedding in three-dimensional or two-dimensional space. This leads to the abstraction of surfaces as doubly-extended manifolds, distinguishing intrinsic properties (the metric) from physical realization in ambient space, and implies that surfaces of different Gaussian curvature cannot be isometrically transformed, meaning a sphere or ellipsoid cannot be flattened to a plane without distortion, a fundamental issue in map projections. The work includes a proof of the local Gauss–Bonnet theorem on geodesic triangles and generalizes Legendre's theorem on spherical triangles to geodesic triangles on surfaces with continuous curvature, showing that the angles of a "sufficiently small" geodesic triangle deviate from those of a planar triangle of the same side lengths in a way depending only on the surface curvature at the vertices. Gauss's 1828 memoir lacks the concept of geodesic curvature, but in an unpublished manuscript from 1822–1825, he introduced the term "side curvature" (German: "Seitenkrümmung") and proved its invariance under isometric transformations, a result later obtained by Ferdinand Minding and published in 1830; this work contains the core of his lemma on total curvature and its generalization, found and proved by Pierre Ossian Bonnet in 1848 and known as the Gauss–Bonnet theorem. During his lifetime, the parallel postulate of Euclidean geometry was widely debated; Gauss considered the problem from the 1790s, realizing in the 1810s that a non-Euclidean geometry without the parallel postulate could resolve it. In a 1824 letter to Franz Taurinus, he outlined what he called a "non-Euclidean geometry," but forbade Taurinus from using it; Gauss is credited with being the first to discover and study non-Euclidean geometry and coining the term. The first publications on non-Euclidean geometry were by Nikolai Lobachevsky in 1829 and Janos Bolyai in 1832; Gauss wrote on the topic but did not publish, avoiding influence on contemporary discussions. He commended Bolyai's ideas in a letter to his father and friend Farkas Bolyai, claiming they were congruent with his own thoughts from decades earlier, though the extent of his prior work to Lobachevsky and Bolyai remains unclear due to vague and obscure writings. Sartorius first mentioned Gauss's work on non-Euclidean geometry in 1856, and only the publication of Gauss's Nachlass in Volume VIII of the Collected Works (1900) revealed his ideas, at a time when the subject was still controversial. Gauss was also an early pioneer of topology or Geometria Situs; his first proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra in 1799 contained an essentially topological argument, which he further developed in his fourth proof fifty years later. In 1804, during astronomical work, he determined the limits of the region on the celestial sphere where comets and asteroids might appear, calling it "Zodiacus," and discovered that if Earth's and comet's orbits are linked, then by topological reasoning the Zodiacus is the entire sphere; in 1848, in connection with the discovery of asteroid 7 Iris, he published a further qualitative discussion of the Zodiacus. In letters from 1820–1830, Gauss thought deeply about topics related to Geometria Situs and became aware of semantic difficulties; fragments from this period show he tried to classify "tract figures," closed plane curves with finite transverse self-intersections, which may be planar projections of knots, and devised a symbolic scheme—the Gauss code—that captured their essential features. In a 1833 fragment, Gauss defined the linking number of two space curves via a double integral, providing the first analytical formulation of a topological phenomenon; he lamented the little progress in Geometria Situs and remarked that one central problem would be "to count the intertwinings of two closed or infinite curves," and his notebooks indicate he also considered braids and tangles. Gauss influenced the emerging field of topology through occasional remarks and oral communications to Möbius and Listing. He applied complex numbers to solve known problems in a concise way, such as in a 1836 note on ternary forms and crystallography, where he stated the fundamental theorem of axonometry, describing how to represent a 3D cube on a 2D plane with complete accuracy using complex numbers; he described rotations of the sphere as linear fractional transformations on the extended complex plane and gave a proof that the altitudes of a triangle meet at a single orthocenter. Gauss studied John Napier's "Pentagramma mirificum" for several decades, gaining a full understanding of its geometric, algebraic, and analytic aspects, and in 1843 stated and proved several theorems connecting elliptic functions, Napier spherical pentagons, and Poncelet pentagons. He also contributed a solution to the problem of constructing the largest-area ellipse inside a given quadrilateral and discovered a surprising result about the area of pentagons. On 1 January 1801, Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered Ceres, which he believed was the planet between Mars and Jupiter according to the Titius–Bode law and named Ceres; he could track it only briefly before it disappeared behind the Sun. The mathematical tools of the time were insufficient to predict its reappearance from the limited data, and Gauss tackled the problem, predicting a position in December 1801, which was accurate within a half-degree when Franz Xaver von Zach and Heinrich Olbers independently identified the object near the predicted location. Gauss's method led to an eighth-degree equation, one solution of which is the Earth's orbit; the sought solution is separated from the remaining six based on physical conditions, using comprehensive approximation methods he developed. This work led to the publication in 1809 of Theoria motus corporum coelestium in sectionibus conicis solem ambientum, introducing the Gaussian gravitational constant. After the discovery of new asteroids, Gauss studied their orbital perturbations; initially using methods similar to Laplace's for Ceres, he focused on Pallas due to its high eccentricity and inclination, where Laplace's methods failed; he used his own tools: the arithmetic-geometric mean, the hypergeometric function, and his interpolation method. In 1812, he found an orbital resonance with Jupiter in the 18:7 ratio, giving this result as a cipher and revealing its meaning only in letters to Olbers and Bessel; after years of work, he completed the study in 1816 without a result he considered sufficient, marking the end of his theoretical astronomy activities. One outcome of his work on Pallas perturbations was the Determinatio Attractionis... (1818), introducing the "elliptic ring method," which replaced a planet in orbit with a fictitious ring of mass density proportional to the time spent on each orbital arc; Gauss presented a method to compute the gravitational attraction of such an elliptic ring, involving a direct application of the AGM algorithm to calculate an elliptic integral. Even after ending his theoretical astronomy work, Gauss remained active in observational astronomy throughout his career, beginning with work on determining longitude via lunar parallax in 1799, developing more convenient formulas than those in common use; after becoming director of the observatory, he emphasized fundamental astronomical constants in correspondence with Bessel, providing tables of nutation and aberration, solar coordinates, and refraction; he made many contributions to spherical geometry and solved practical navigation problems using stars, publishing numerous observations, with his last being the solar eclipse of 28 July 1851. Gauss's first publication after his doctoral thesis dealt with determining the date of Easter (1800), aiming to provide a convenient algorithm for people without knowledge of ecclesiastical or astronomical chronology, avoiding terms like golden number, epact, solar cycle, or religious connotations; this choice likely stemmed from historical confusion in the Holy Roman Empire due to the calendar transition from Julian to Gregorian, which was not fully resolved in Germany until 1700, and continued until 1776 when the difference in Easter dates between Protestant and Catholic territories was abolished; in Protestant regions like the Duchy of Brunswick, the first Easter calculated in the new manner was in 1777, five weeks before Gauss's birth. Gauss likely used the method of least squares to minimize measurement error when calculating Ceres's orbit; the method was first published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805, but Gauss claimed in Theoria motus (1809) that he had used it since 1794 or 1795, leading to the "priority dispute over the discovery of the method of least squares" in statistics; in his two-part 1823 paper Theoria combinationis observationum erroribus minimis obnoxiae, Gauss proved that the method has the lowest sampling variance among linear unbiased estimators under the assumption of normally distributed errors (Gauss–Markov theorem). In the first paper, he proved Gauss's inequality (a Chebyshev-type inequality) for unimodal distributions and stated without proof another inequality for fourth-order moments (a special case of the Gauss-Winckler inequality); he derived bounds for the variance of the sample variance. In the second paper, he described recursive least squares methods, which he discovered. His work on the theory of errors was extended by geodesist Friedrich Robert Helmert into the Gauss-Helmert model. Gauss also contributed to probability theory beyond error theory; in a diary note, he derived the asymptotic distribution of entries in the continued fraction expansion of a random number uniformly distributed in (0,1), now known as the Gauss-Kuzmin distribution, as a by-product of discovering the ergodicity of the Gauss map for continued fractions—this is the first result in the metrical theory of continued fractions. Since 1799, Gauss had been involved in geodetic problems, helping Karl Ludwig von Lecoq with calculations during a survey in Westphalia; beginning in 1804, he taught himself practical geodesy in Brunswick and Göttingen. Since 1816, his former student Heinrich Christian Schumacher, then professor in Copenhagen but living in Altona (Holstein) near Hamburg as head of an observatory, carried out a triangulation of the Jutland peninsula from Skagen in the north to Lauenburg in the south.

The Helmert model [212] is associated with Gauss's contributions to probability theory, where he derived the asymptotic distribution of entries in the continued fraction expansion of a random number uniformly distributed in (0,1), now known as the Gauss-Kuzmin distribution. This result emerged as a by-product of Gauss's discovery of the ergodicity of the Gauss map for continued fractions and represents the first-ever result in the metrical theory of continued fractions [213]. Since 1799, Gauss had been involved in geodetic problems, assisting Karl Ludwig von Lecoq with calculations during a survey in Westphalia [214]. Beginning in 1804, he taught himself practical geodesy in Brunswick and Göttingen [215][216]. Starting in 1816, Heinrich Christian Schumacher, then professor in Copenhagen and living in Altona near Hamburg as head of an observatory, conducted a triangulation of the Jutland peninsula from Skagen to Lauenburg, aiming to determine the geodetic arc between terminal sites and support map production. Schumacher requested Gauss to extend this work southward into the Kingdom of Hanover, which Gauss agreed to after a brief hesitation, and the project was officially authorized by King George IV in May 1820 [217]. For astronomical measurements, Gauss and Schumacher exploited the near-same longitude of their observatories in Göttingen and Altona, using a Ramsden zenith sector transported to both locations to measure latitude [218][219]. By October 1818, they had already determined angles between Lüneburg, Hamburg, and Lauenburg. From 1821 to 1825, Gauss personally directed triangulation work from Thuringia to the Elbe, including the largest triangle he ever measured—between Hoher Hagen, Großer Inselsberg, and Brocken, spanning 107 km (66.5 miles). In the sparsely populated Lüneburg Heath, he faced difficulties finding suitable points, often cutting lanes through vegetation [205][220]. To send pointing signals, Gauss invented a device with movable mirrors and a small telescope that reflected sunlight to triangulation points, which he named the heliotrope [221]; he also developed a sextant with an additional mirror, called the vice heliotrope [222]. Gauss was assisted by Hanoverian soldiers, including his eldest son Joseph. He participated in the baseline measurement (Braak Base Line) near Hamburg in 1820, using the result for evaluating the Hanoverian triangulation [223]. This work led to a better value for the flattening of the Earth's ellipsoid [224][x] and the development of the universal transverse Mercator projection (which he named conform projection) for representing geodetic data on plane charts [226]. After completing the arc measurement, Gauss expanded the triangulation westward to cover the entire Kingdom of Hanover under a royal decree dated 25 March 1828, with practical work directed by three army officers, including Lieutenant Joseph Gauss. The full data evaluation was conducted by Gauss, who applied his methods of least squares and elimination. The project concluded in 1844, and Gauss submitted a final report to the government; his projection method was not published until 1866 [228][229]. In 1828, Gauss first defined a physical approximation of the Earth's shape as the surface everywhere perpendicular to gravity, later named the geoid by his doctoral student Johann Benedict Listing [230][231]. Gauss had been interested in magnetism since 1803 [232]. After Alexander von Humboldt visited Göttingen in 1826, both began intensive research on geomagnetism, sometimes independently and sometimes collaboratively. In 1828, Gauss met physicist Wilhelm Weber at a conference in Berlin, where Humboldt was a guest. When Weber was appointed to the physics chair in Göttingen in 1831 by Gauss's recommendation, they began a productive collaboration, leading to a new understanding of magnetism and the definition of a unit of magnetism in terms of mass, charge, and time. They founded the Magnetic Association (Magnetischer Verein), an international group of observatories that conducted standardized measurements of Earth's magnetic field from 1836 to 1841. In 1836, Humboldt proposed a worldwide network of geomagnetic stations in the British dominions, suggesting standardized observations under fixed times and intervals, with Göttingen mean time as the standard. Sixty-one stations across five continents participated. Gauss and Weber established a publication series for the results, with six volumes edited between 1837 and 1843. Weber's departure to Leipzig in 1843, due to the Göttingen Seven affair, marked the end of the Magnetic Association's activities [236]. Gauss ordered the construction of a magnetic observatory in the garden of the Göttingen observatory, but disagreements arose over instruments—Gauss favored stationary ones for greater precision, while Humboldt preferred movable ones. Gauss studied temporal and spatial variations in magnetic declination, inclination, and intensity, distinguishing between "horizontal" and "vertical" intensity. With Weber, he developed methods to measure magnetic field components and constructed a magnetometer capable of measuring absolute values of Earth's magnetic field, achieving about ten times greater precision than previous instruments. This work made Gauss the first to derive a non-mechanical quantity from basic mechanical quantities [239]. He also developed spherical harmonic analysis to describe potential fields and used it to show that most of Earth's magnetic field originated from internal sources [241][242]. In his 1839 General Theory of Terrestrial Magnetism, Gauss presented observations using spherical harmonics rather than proposing a physical theory; the work predicted the existence of exactly two magnetic poles, rendering Hansteen's idea of four poles obsolete, and allowed precise determination of their locations [243][244]. Gauss influenced the beginning of geophysics in Russia when his former student Adolph Theodor Kupffer established a magnetic observatory in St. Petersburg, following the Göttingen model, and similarly, Ivan Simonov in Kazan [244]. The discoveries of Hans Christian Ørsted on electromagnetism and Michael Faraday on electromagnetic induction drew Gauss's attention. Gauss and Weber formulated rules for branched electric circuits, later independently discovered and named Kirchhoff's circuit laws [247], and constructed the first electromechanical telegraph in 1833, connecting the observatory to the physics institute in Göttingen via Weber, though they did not pursue commercial use [248][249]. Gauss's main theoretical interests in electromagnetism included formulating quantitative laws for electromagnetic induction. In notebooks from this period, he recorded several innovative formulations, including the discovery of the vector potential function (independently rediscovered by Franz Ernst Neumann in 1845) and in January 1835 wrote down an "induction law" equivalent to Faraday's law, stating that the electromotive force at a point equals the instantaneous rate of change of the vector potential function [250][251]. He attempted to find a unifying law for long-distance effects in electrostatics, electrodynamics, electromagnetism, and induction, analogous to Newton's law of gravitation, but this effort ended in a "tragic failure" [252][239]. Since Newton had shown that rotating bodies like Earth and stars assume non-spherical shapes, the problem of attraction of ellipsoids became significant in mathematical astronomy. In his 1813 publication "Theoria attractionis...", Gauss provided a closed-form expression for the gravitational attraction of a homogeneous triaxial ellipsoid at any point in space, using elliptic integrals instead of the methods of Maclaurin, Laplace, and Lagrange. In the process, he proved and applied special cases of what is now known as Gauss's theorem in vector analysis [253][254]. In his 1840 work on general theorems concerning attractive and repulsive forces acting in reciprocal proportions of quadratic distances, Gauss developed a basic theory of magnetic potential based on Lagrange, Laplace, and Poisson; it appears unlikely he was aware of George Green's prior work on the subject [246]. However, Gauss never developed a physical theory of magnetism or a model like Newton's for gravitation that could predict geomagnetic effects [239]. Gauss's calculations enabled instrument maker Johann Georg Repsold in Hamburg to construct a new achromatic lens system in 1810, addressing chromatic aberration in double lenses. In a 1817 article, Gauss computed necessary adjustments to lens shape and refractive index to minimize aberration; his work was noted by Carl August von Steinheil, who in 1860 introduced the achromatic Steinheil doublet, partly based on Gauss's calculations [255][256]. Many results in geometrical optics are scattered in Gauss's correspondence and hand notes [257]. In his Dioptrical Investigations (1840), Gauss provided the first systematic analysis of image formation under paraxial approximation (Gaussian optics), characterizing optical systems by their cardinal points and deriving the Gaussian lens formula, applicable without restrictions regarding lens thickness [258][259][260][261]. Gauss's first work in mechanics concerned Earth's rotation. When his friend Benzenberg conducted experiments on the deviation of falling masses from the vertical in 1802 (now known as the Coriolis force), Gauss developed a theoretical system for motion and found results that matched Benzenberg's data, which Benzenberg later included as an appendix in his book [262]. After Foucault demonstrated Earth's rotation with a pendulum in 1851, Gerling asked Gauss for further explanations, prompting Gauss to design a new apparatus using a shorter pendulum, observed with a telescope, vertical scale, and mirror attached to the pendulum. This is described in the Gauss–Gerling correspondence, and Weber conducted experiments with it in 1853, though no data were published [263][264]. Gauss's principle of least constraint from 1829 combined D'Alembert's principle with Lagrange's principle of virtual work and showed analogies to the method of least squares [265]. In 1828, Gauss was appointed head of the board for weights and measures of the Kingdom of Hanover, where he created standards for length and measure and personally oversaw the mechanical construction. In correspondence with Schumacher, he proposed new ideas for high-precision scales [266]. He submitted final reports on the Hanoverian foot and pound to the government in 1841. This work gained international significance due to an 1836 law linking Hanoverian measures to English ones [205]. Gauss first became a member of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1802 [267]. He received further memberships (corresponding, foreign, or full) from the Academy of Sciences in Göttingen (1802/1807), the French Academy of Sciences (1804/1820), the Royal Society of London (1804), the Royal Prussian Academy in Berlin (1810), the National Academy of Science in Verona (1810), the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1820), the Bavarian Academy of Sciences in Munich (1820), the Royal Danish Academy in Copenhagen (1821), the Royal Astronomical Society in London (1821), the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (1821), the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in Boston (1822), the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences in Prague (1833), the Royal Academy of Science, Letters and Fine Arts of Belgium (1841/1845), the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala (1843), the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin (1843), the Royal Institute of the Netherlands (1845/1851), the Spanish Royal Academy of Sciences in Madrid (1850), the Russian Geographical Society (1851), the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna (1848), the American Philosophical Society (1853), the Cambridge Philosophical Society, and the Royal Hollandish Society of Sciences in Haarlem [268][269][270][271][272][273][274][275][276][277][278][279][280][281][282][283][284][285]. Both the University of Kazan and the Philosophy Faculty of the University of Prague appointed him honorary member in 1848 [284]. Gauss received the Lalande Prize from the French Academy of Sciences in 1809 for his theory of planets and methods for determining orbits from three observations [286], the Danish Academy of Science prize in 1823 for his memoir on conformal projection [278], and the Copley Medal from the Royal Society in 1838 for "his inventions and mathematical researches in magnetism" [285][287][37]. He was appointed Knight of the French Legion of Honour in 1837 [288] and became one of the first members of the Prussian Order Pour le Merite (Civil class) when it was established in 1842 [289]. He received the Order of the Crown of Westphalia (1810), the Danish Order of the Dannebrog (1817), the Hanoverian Royal Guelphic Order (1815), the Swedish Order of the Polar Star (1844), the Order of Henry the Lion (1849), and the Bavarian Maximilian Order for Science and Art (1853) [285][282]. The Kings of Hanover granted him the honorary titles "Hofrath" (1816) and "Geheimer Hofrath" (1845) [55]. In 1949, on the occasion of his golden doctor degree jubilee, he received honorary citizenship of both Brunswick and Göttingen [282]. Soon after his death, a medal was issued by order of King George V of Hanover with the back inscription "to the Prince of Mathematicians" [291]. The "Gauss-Gesellschaft Göttingen" (Göttingen Gauss Society) was founded in 1964 to research Gauss's life and work and related figures, publishing the Mitteilungen der Gauss-Gesellschaft (Communications of the Gauss Society) [292]. The Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities maintains an online collection of all known letters from and to Carl Friedrich Gauss, and the literary estate is available.

The Order of Henry the Lion was awarded in 1849, and the Bavarian Maximilian Order for Science and Art was conferred in 1853. The Kings of Hanover granted him the honorary title "Hofrath" in 1816 and "Geheimer Hofrath" in 1845. In 1949, on the occasion of his golden doctor degree jubilee, he was honored with honorary citizenship by both Brunswick and Göttingen. Following his death, King George V of Hanover issued a medal with the reverse inscription dedicated "to the Prince of Mathematicians." The "Gauss-Gesellschaft Göttingen" was established in 1964 to conduct research on Carl Friedrich Gauss and related individuals, and it publishes the Mitteilungen der Gauss-Gesellschaft (Communications of the Gauss Society). The Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities maintains an online collection of all known letters from and to Carl Friedrich Gauss. The literary estate is preserved and made available by the Göttingen State and University Library. Additionally, written materials from Carl Friedrich Gauss and his family are held in the municipal archive of Brunswick.

Carl Olof Trygg (December 21, 1910 – 1993) was one of the recognized masters of 20th century woodcarving, renowned for the Scandinavian flat-plane style. Born in Stora Tuna, Kopparberg county, Dalarna, Sweden, he was one of three sons of Carl Johan Trygg and Maria Axelina Andersson. Carl Olof worked with his father carving wooden figures of common people in the Scandinavian flat-plane style. Together with his father Carl Johan and two brothers, Nils and Lars, they produced over 10,000 carvings. Many of these figures were sold to tourists for approximately US$10.00; adjusted for inflation, that amount would be equivalent to $108.05 in 2005. At age 17, Carl Olof immigrated to Canada with his mother Maria (43), brother Nils Johan (13), and an unknown relative, possibly his sister Kally Maria Trygg (8), arriving in Halifax, Nova Scotia on October 7, 1928. His father Carl Johan had arrived in Halifax on March 3, 1928. The family eventually settled in Montreal, Quebec, where they continued carving. Between Carl Johan Trygg and his sons, over 10,000 figures were carved. Trygg was a craftsman aligned with the tourist trade, typically creating solo figures from basswood or pine, mounted on a base, with clean cuts and a stylized execution from a single piece of wood. A notable feature of his work is the use of vibrant paint, often applied to clothing in plaid patterns. Carl Johan Trygg and Carl Olof Trygg later returned to Sweden, where they continued their careers; Carl Johan died there in 1954, and Carl Olof was producing figures as late as 1987. Trygg family woodcarvings remain highly sought after as collectibles, with over 10,000 figures produced by family members, priced between $50 and $500 based on age, size, and condition. The carvings can be identified by signatures and dates on the bases, with common signatures including the carver’s name and year, such as "C.O. Trygg 1961 Sweden," indicating the piece was carved by Carl Olof Trygg in 1961 while living in Sweden.

Carla Hall, born on May 12, 1964, is an American chef, television personality, and former model who was born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee. She graduated from Hillsboro High School and earned a degree in accounting from Howard University's Business School in 1986. After working as a Certified Public Accountant at Price Waterhouse in Tampa, Florida for two years, she left due to disliking the job. She then worked as a model on the runways of Paris, Milan, and London, during which time she decided to pursue a culinary career. Upon returning to the United States, she moved to Washington, D.C., where she started a lunch delivery service called the Lunch Bunch after her friend's coworkers expressed interest in her leftover sandwiches. After four years, she enrolled at L'Academie de Cuisine in Bethesda, Maryland, earning a Culinary Career Training certificate and later completing an externship at the Henley Park Hotel, where she was promoted to sous chef. By 1999, she became the executive chef at the Garden Cafe in the State Plaza Hotel and later served as executive chef at the Washington Club. In 2001, she founded Alchemy Caterers in Wheaton, Maryland, which she later renamed Alchemy by Carla Hall, and she remains in charge of the company. She authored the cookbook Cooking with Love: Comfort Food that Hugs You. Her big break came in 2008 when she competed on Top Chef: New York, where her crawfish gumbo earned her top-rated dish in the Thanksgiving challenge and Super Bowl XLIII tickets; she won two more challenges and was in the top for several others, impressing judges Jacques Pépin and Emeril Lagasse. She finished as runner-up to Hosea Rosenberg in the final challenge of the season. Hall gained popularity on the show for her personality and her call-and-response phrase "Hootie Hoo!", which she and her husband used to locate each other. She promoted the philosophy of "cooking with love," stating that cooking with care and calmness results in better food, and if one is not in a good mood, the only thing to make is a reservation. She participated in Top Chef: All-Stars, the eighth season, where she finished fifth overall and was awarded "Fan Favorite" by viewers, beating out Fabio Viviani. Since September 26, 2011, she has been one of the five co-hosts on The Chew, a one-hour ABC show centered on food from all angles that replaced All My Children, and remained a cohost until its cancellation in 2018. In 2014, she launched a Kickstarter campaign that raised $264,703 from 1,550 backers, exceeding her $250,000 goal, to open her restaurant Carla Hall's Southern Kitchen, which opened on June 17, 2016, in Brooklyn, New York, and closed in August 2017. She appeared on the May 3, 2009, cover of the Washington Post Magazine in a feature titled "Fit for Fame" about exercising while being famous. She portrayed a version of herself named "Spaghetti Scientist Carla Hall" in the BoJack Horseman episode "That Went Well," voiced Mpishi the harrier hawk in a season 2 episode of The Lion Guard titled "Ono and the Egg," and voiced the president in Season 1, Episode 5 of Butterbean's Café titled "A Grilled Cheese for the Big Cheese!" In 2016, she made a cameo in Fox's The Passion: New Orleans as a food truck operator. In 2018, she made a guest appearance on ABC's General Hospital as the Quartermaine family's cook. She has served as a judge on Food Network's Halloween Baking Championship and, in 2020, also hosted the season. She appeared as a judge on Season 7 of Food Network's Holiday Baking Championship as a replacement for Lorraine Pascal due to COVID-19 restrictions. In 2020, she judged the Channel 4 competition series Crazy Delicious, which took place on an edible set and was hosted by Jayde Adams alongside Heston Blumenthal and Niklas Ekstedt. As of 2020, she is featured in segments with Sesame Street characters Cookie Monster and Gonger in Snack Chat. In 2021, she appeared in Antiques Roadshow Celebrity Edition, episode 2, hosted Worst Cooks in America with Anne Burrell, and is a host and judge on Best Baker in America. In 2022, she was the headliner judge for the National Gingerbread House Competition. Hall lives in Washington, D.C. and married Matthew Lyons in 2006; she has a stepson named Noah.

Carlos Gardel is a station on Line B of the Buenos Aires Underground. It is located in the Balvanera barrio at the intersection of Avenida Corrientes and Calle Agüero and was opened on 17 October 1930 as part of the inaugural section of the line between Federico Lacroze and Callao. The station runs beneath the Abasto de Buenos Aires, one of the city's most prominent landmarks, and features an underground connection that allows access to the shopping centre without exiting to street level. Initially named Agüero after the road it crosses, the station was later renamed Carlos Gardel in honor of the famous tango singer, who was known as "El Morocho del Abasto" (The Brunette boy from Abasto). Media related to Carlos Gardel (Buenos Aires Underground) is available at Wikimedia Commons. This Buenos Aires Underground-related article is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Carlotta Gall is a British journalist and author who covered Afghanistan and Pakistan for The New York Times for twelve years and is currently covering the war in Ukraine. She is the daughter of veteran Scottish journalist Sandy Gall and began her newspaper career with The Moscow Times in Moscow in 1994, where she covered the first war in Chechnya extensively and reported on various events across the former Soviet Union. She also freelanced for British publications such as The Independent, The Times, and The Sunday Times, as well as American outlets including USA Today, Newsweek, and The New York Times. In 1996, she co-authored Chechnya: A Small Victorious War with Thomas de Waal; the following year, they published Chechnya: Calamity in the Caucasus, which won the James Cameron Prize for Distinguished Reporting in the UK. Gall received the Kurt Schork award for international freelance journalism in 2002, the Interaction award for international reporting in 2005, and the Edward Weintal Prize for diplomatic reporting from Georgetown University's Institute for the Study of Diplomacy in 2007. In 1998, she moved to the Financial Times and The Economist, reporting from Baku, Azerbaijan on the Caucasus and Central Asia. From 1999 to 2001, she worked in the Balkans for The New York Times, covering the wars in Kosovo, Serbia, and Macedonia, as well as developments in Bosnia and the rest of the former Yugoslavia. From 2001 to 2013, she served as a correspondent for The New York Times covering Pakistan and Afghanistan. From 2013 to 2017, she was the newspaper's North Africa correspondent based in Tunis and then became the Times' bureau chief in Istanbul, Turkey. Gall is featured in the Academy Award-winning documentary Taxi to the Dark Side (2007), where she was the first journalist to report on two Afghans who died in US custody at Bagram air base (Parwan Detention Facility); the documentary centers on the case of Afghan taxi driver Dilawar, who was beaten to death in 2002 while in US-military custody, with the military officially stating the cause of death was natural, but Gall uncovered what she considers incontrovertible evidence to the contrary. In 2014, in her book The Wrong Enemy: America in Afghanistan, 2001–2014, she accused Pakistan's clandestine intelligence service, the ISI, of hiding and protecting Osama bin Laden and his family after the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Cary High School is one of six public high schools in Cary, North Carolina, and is part of the Wake County Public School System. It became the first state-funded public high school in North Carolina in 1907, when the North Carolina legislature approved a statewide public education system, and the school’s board of directors sold it to the Wake County Board of Education for $2,750 on April 3, 1907—its estimated value at the time was over $8,000—half of which was paid by the state. This made Cary High School the first county high school in North Carolina, the first state-funded high school in the state, and the first high school in the state system. The school opened in 1896 as a private boarding school at the head of Academy Street, established to provide a higher course of instruction than local one-room schools, with its first class graduating in May 1897 and Edwin Lee Middleton serving as its first principal. In 1907, the State Legislature authorized a Cary School District and approved a school tax of up to 30¢ for every $100 of real estate, which was approved by voters in a referendum on May 7, 1907, with 100 in favor and two against. Students from outside the district paid $14 per term for freshmen and sophomores and $16 for juniors and seniors. Middleton remained principal during the transition, retiring in 1908, and was succeeded by superintendent Marcus Baxter Dry. The curriculum included one year of French, three years of science, and four years of English, history, Latin, and mathematics, with arithmetic, algebra, and geometry included in the latter; domestic science was added in 1910 for female students, and students could add art, elocution, music, or piano for an extra fee. In 1912, 119 students enrolled, including eighty boarding students from other counties, and the curriculum expanded to include agriculture, botany, and chemistry. That year, the Girls Athletic Club was formed. By 1913, the student body had outgrown the campus, prompting Dry to request a tax increase for a new building; voters approved $25,000 in bonds for a 33-room brick building, with an additional $5,000 from the state, which was considered the best high school building in the state. Dry noted that many school officials from across the state visited to study it. In 1914, the school changed its name to Cary Public High School and Farm Life School to reflect its expanded vocational curriculum, including agriculture and home economics. The next year, fifteen acres on what is now Walnut Street were donated by James M. Templeton Jr., and an additional $1,500 from others and the Town of Cary funded a barn, farmhouse, dairy cows, and other stock for the model farm (the farmhouse survives at 510 Walnut Street); students in the agricultural program milked the cows and consumed the milk with breakfast. In 1915, the Chsite yearbook premiered; in 1919, students formed a student council, a general athletic association, and The Echo campus newspaper; in 1921, a marching band was formed, school colors of olive green and white were selected, and the white rose became the school flower, with the motto "service." In 1920, Cary voters approved $45,000 in bonds for a new farm life department building, completed in 1922 as the Walter Hines Page Vocational Education Building. The following year, a State Normal Class for Teachers began at Cary High School, one of four sites in the state and operating for five years. By 1924, students could earn academic, agriculture, home economics, or teacher training diplomas. In 1925, a new gymnasium, the James M. Templeton Physical Education Building, costing $12,000, was added, seating 500 and featuring a wooden basketball court; by 1926, campus athletics included baseball, basketball, football, tennis, and track, and student clubs included the Boys Glee Club, Dramatic Club, Girls Glee Club, Home Economics Club, four literary societies, and the Science Cub. In 1926, the school acquired its first bus, traveling 24 miles a day for 22 students; in 1927, the Wake County Board of Education expanded the Cary School District from the Raleigh City limits to the Durham County line, enabling busing to consolidate schools in Morrisville, Reedy Creek, and Sorrell's Grove. The Board allocated $38,000 for a new building and $12,000 for heating upgrades, and the school had a library with 1,970 volumes. During the Great Depression, property values dropped, reducing school tax income; the Board closed Mount Herman and Ebenezer schools and sent their students to Cary; state funding increased and eventually ended the local school tax in 1933. Budget cuts included no new library books and the cessation of the Chsite yearbook; dormitories were closed, ending the boarding era. Grades 1 through 11 were taught at Cary High School under a consolidated program. WPA funding expanded athletic fields by five acres and enabled the construction of a football stadium with seating for 1,500. The success of the football field project led to a collaborative funding effort for a new central school building, with the Board providing $70,000 and the WPA covering the remaining $62,000 of the $132,000 cost. The dedication stone read: "Cary High School – First State Public High School – Established in North Carolina on April 3, 1907," and the building was completed in 1938, though mostly constructed in 1939. The three-story building included a cafeteria, fire doors, first aid room, intercom system, movie projector, sound-proof typing room, and an auditorium with 834 seats. At the dedication on March 4, 1940, Governor Clyde Hoey called Cary a "beacon of hope and inspiration," and the News and Observer noted Cary High School and its predecessor had led secondary education in Wake County and the state for 75 years. In 1941, Cary had the largest high school in Wake County with 460 students; Dry retired after 34 years as principal, then taught algebra in summer school; Thaddeus N. Frye became the new principal. In 1943, the school year was extended from eight to nine months after Wake County added the 12th grade. In 1956, Cary High School became the first in Wake County to be accredited by the Southern Association of Secondary Schools. In 1958, the Wake County Board of Commissioners purchased forty acres for $30,000 from Luther M. Maynard for a new campus; 150 residents debated the location, with some criticizing its distance from downtown and poor road access. Construction proceeded, and the last graduating class to attend the original campus was the Class of 1960, also the first with over 100 graduates. The original campus became Cary Junior High and Elementary School, then Cary Elementary School, and on August 13, 2011, opened as the Cary Arts Center. The new Cary Senior High School campus opened on September 7, 1960, with principal Samuel Arbes; it opened at full capacity with 573 students (sophomores, juniors, and seniors), including three classroom buildings, a gymnasium, library, auditorium, cafeteria, and shop building, designed by William A. Deitrick and built by J. M. Thompson Construction Company of Raleigh, at a cost of $771,251 plus $38,000 for design fees. By 1962, the school needed ten more classrooms, and expansion allowed freshmen to join in 1963, restoring the school’s name to Cary High School. In 1963, the Wake County Board approved the voluntary transfer of six African-American students from Berry O'Kelly School under the "freedom of choice" policy following the U.S. Supreme Court’s desegregation decision; Cary became the first school in Wake County outside of Raleigh to desegregate, selected because it was rapidly changing and more open to change. White parents sued, but the case was dismissed by the North Carolina Supreme Court. The students—seniors Lucille Evans and Frances Louise White, juniors Gwendolyn Matthews and Brenda Lee Hill, sophomore Ester Lee Mayo, and freshman Phyllis Rose—faced intense opposition upon arrival, with protests lasting ten days and dwindling to fewer than fifty students; Evans and White graduated in 1964; Gregory Crowe became the first African American male student in 1964. In 1967, the Board integrated Cary High School by making the former black high school a 9th-grade junior high for all races and transferring all black sophomores, juniors, and seniors to Cary Senior High School, which then had 764 whites and 112 blacks, or a 12.8% minority rate. By 1972, the school was overcrowded and used two mobile classrooms; in 1973, enrollment exceeded 1,500, requiring eight classroom trailers; a county-wide bond referendum provided $700,000 for expansion, with construction beginning in May 1974 on an eight-classroom building for foreign languages, library expansion, auto mechanics shop, stadium field house, and new lobby and offices. In 1989, a $4.5 million construction project added Building 10, including a new air-conditioned media center, allowing freshmen to return to campus after the mid-1960s. In 1995, the school had about 1,800 students in a space designed for 1,455; in 1996, a $3.44 million bond approved improvements including a new classroom, administrative space, Building A renovations for the performing arts, a career center, and computer labs, expanding capacity to 1,585 students, with work beginning on a new main entrance. In 2004, Clark Nexsen approved plans to renovate and expand campus, including a new auditorium, gymnasium, music classrooms, and a new classroom building; construction was completed by J. M. Thompson of Cary, and the new three-story classroom building opened in August 2008. As part of the project, the existing auditorium, band room, Building E, Building F, and part of Building B were demolished—78,063 square feet were removed, 135,839 added, and 26,831 renovated. In 2012, Clark Nexsen designed a master plan for Phase III, including a dining addition and a 100,000-square-foot classroom, to begin when funding is available. As of the 2021–22 academic year, Cary High School had 2,071 students, with 1,080 male and 991 female; the student population was 44.5% White, 27.5% Hispanic, 17.2% Black, 6% Asian, 4.4% two or more races, and 0.3% American Indian, with a total minority population of 55.5%; 28% of students are economically disadvantaged, with 23% receiving free lunch and 4% reduced lunch. The graduation rate is 87%, and 41.7% of students are ready for college, above the district average of 37.8%. The school has 120 teachers with a student-teacher ratio of 17:1; 97% of teachers have three or more years of experience and are certified. The student–counselor ratio is 299:1, better than the state average of 361:1, and the faculty includes a social worker. In 2019, Nolan Bryant received the Maggie Award for Best High School Principal in Western Wake County, and Jerry Dotson, track and cross country coach, received the Maggie Award for Best High School Coach in Western Wake County. Cary High School includes grades 9 through 12 and operates on a traditional calendar with a block schedule. The school offers Advanced Placement® courses, with 53% of students participating and 38% passing at least one AP® exam; 53% of students take the SAT, with an average score of 1146; 64% of graduates pursue college or vocational training. Students have received the Morehead-Cain Scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the John T. Caldwell Scholarship to North Carolina State University. The Career & Technical Education Department aims to prepare students for employment.

Cary High School serves students in grades 9 through 12 and operates on a traditional calendar with a block schedule. The school offers Advanced Placement® courses, with 53% of students participating and 38% passing at least one AP® Exam. Fifty-three percent of students take the SAT, achieving an average score of 1146, and 64% of graduates pursue college or vocational training. Students have received the Morehead-Cain Scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the John T. Caldwell Scholarship to North Carolina State University. The Career & Technical Education Department aims to prepare students for employment, incorporating internships into classroom learning, with educational areas including agriculture, business, finance and marketing, career development, computer science and information technology, family and consumer sciences, health sciences, and trade, technology, engineering and industrial education. Since the fall of 2022, the school has included The Academy of Technology and Advanced Manufacturing, a four-year immersive learning community focused on advanced manufacturing, design, engineering, and technology, which received over $100,000 in investment for electrical, electronic, instrumentation, pneumatic/flow control, and robotic equipment. As of 2024, U.S. News & World Report ranks Cary High School 18th in Wake County, 91st in North Carolina, and 3,446th nationally, while Niche gives it an "A" rating and ranks it #95 among the best public high schools in North Carolina. Juniors and seniors with a 3.6 GPA can apply to join the National Honor Society; the top twenty juniors by GPA serve as Junior Marshalls for senior events, and Honor Graduates receive a reception and Academic Awards Night, with students earning gold, silver, or red tassels and a patch for a GPA of 3.75 or higher. The media center employs two staff members and provides access to online databases and a physical book collection, including student-written book reviews on its website. In 1960, the student council held a design contest for a school seal, with the winning design featuring pine cones, dogwood blossoms, and the Latin phrase "Cognito Vincit" or "Knowledge Conquers." The Cary High School Alma Mater is sung to the tune of "Over the Summer Sea" or "La Donna e mobile" from Rigoletto by Giuseppe Verdi; the tune was discovered in 2021 during a performance by the Cary High Marching Band and Concert Chorus at a football game on October 22, 2021, and the revised lyrics are: "Cary! here’s love to thee / And we will ever be / Filled with true loyalty / And with devotion. / Long we will ever claim / The blessings of thy name, / And may thy spirit reign / From crest to ocean. / Fond hearts entwining, / Cease all repining, / Near us is shining / Cary’s bright smile." A tradition involves the rising senior class painting their year on the water tower across Maynard Road, a practice taken over by the Town of Cary for the Class of 1986, with locals contributing to the cost, and the town continuing the tradition. The Cary High School Band, established in 1921, is a corps-style marching band that has gained local, national, and international acclaim, with current director Christopher R. Foster and support from the Cary Band Boosters; it hosts Cary Band Day annually since 1958. In 1959, the band marched in Charlotte's Shrine Bowl Parade, Raleigh's Christmas Parade, and Wilmington's Azalea Festival Parade under James Johnson; in 1963, it represented North Carolina at a national festival in Sioux City, Iowa under Jack White; in 1965, it marched in Governor Dan K. Moore's inaugural parade under A. J. Moore. In 1972, the band won the Sun-Fun Festival in Myrtle Beach, beating Wilson High from Pennsylvania, and was listed in the top twenty nationally by Ruffles and Flourishes; in January 1973, under Jimmy Burns, it became the first North Carolina band to march in the Tournament of Roses parade, raising $30,000 for the trip, and also competed on the television show Sounds of '73, viewed by twenty to thirty million people; it also marched in parades for Governor James Holshouser and President Richard Nixon, and in the King Orange Bowl Festival parade in Miami on December 31, 1973. In August 1974, the band performed at the Fêtes de Genève in Geneva, Switzerland, a yearly honor limited to one U.S. band; the town celebrated Jimmy Burns Day. In 1975, the band played at the Kentucky Derby; on January 1, 1976, it became the first out-of-state band to march in the Cotton Bowl parade in Dallas; later that year, it won the Pennsylvania Festival of the Colonies parade competition and came in third overall. In 1977, the band returned to the Tournament of Roses; in 1978, it participated in the Festival of States in St. Petersburg, Florida, and under Don Stubblefield, it marched in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, seen by eighty million viewers; in March 1980, it toured Romania as Friendship Ambassadors; in 1982, it performed for President Ronald Reagan at a Raleigh Civic Center campaign event and in the Gimbel's Thanksgiving Day parade in Philadelphia; in 1984, it marched in the Tournament of Roses, becoming the first non-California band to do so three times; in 1987, it placed third at the Citrus Bowl Music Festival; in 1989, it marched in the inaugural parade for Governor James G. Martin and the San Diego Holiday Bowl Music Festival. In 1991, the band won the Citrus Bowl Music Festival parade event; in 1993, it marched in the inaugural parade for Governor James B. Hunt; in 1996 under Tony Robinson, it earned fourteen of fifteen first-place awards at the Gator Bowl in Jacksonville, including the Grand Champions trophy for best in both parade and field show. In 2016, the band marched in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade under Matt Minick. The Ambassadors Club represents Cary High to new transfer students and ninth graders during transition. The IDEA Club promotes student engagement and activism in government and politics, participated in fighting censorship of books related to gender, sexuality, and race in the school library in March 2022, and conducts voter registration drives. In 1996, alumnus Del Richards donated $40,000 to launch a Navy Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (NJROTC) program, which includes competitive teams in academics, athletics, drill, marksmanship, and physical fitness. Cary High School Performing Arts encompasses the choral group and drama club, typically producing a fall play and a spring choral concert; during the pandemic, live performances were replaced with videos edited by alumnus Michael Shorb and streamed to audiences; the group is supported by the Cary High School Performing Arts Booster Club. The school's yearbook, YRAC, began in 1948, reviving a prior publication discontinued during the Great Depression; in 1987, The Spirit student newspaper won first place at the American Scholastic Press Association Writing Contest under Janice Richardson; other student publications include The Page, founded in 2018 by Stephen Atkinson and Claire Perry. The Speech and Debate team is part of the Tarheel Forensics League and competes statewide; formed around 2010, it finished second in its first year, second at the state championship the next year, and qualified for the National Speech and Debate Tournament; it has competed at the national tournament seven of its first ten years and hosts local tournaments. The school's mascot is the Imp; Albert H. Werner, football and baseball coach starting in 1935, influenced the choice, having played at Duke where the junior varsity teams were called the Blue Imps; the name was initially the White Imp to balance college favorites, incorporating the White Phantoms of UNC Chapel Hill; initially used only by the football team, the name was later adopted for all sports; after the 1971–72 school year, "white" was dropped to avoid racial connotations during desegregation, and the Imp is now green. The current Imp illustration was designed by student Lee Mauney in the 1960s, who later became the school's art teacher and athletic director; in January 2010, Cary premiered a costumed Imp mascot at a basketball game against Apex High School, funded by donations and student efforts from the Ambassador Club, produced by Stagecraft in Cincinnati, Ohio. ESPN named the Cary Imp one of the best nicknames for a football team in 2009, and Sports Illustrated recognized it as the fourth most unique high school nickname in 2010; in 2023, the Cary Imp was voted the best high school mascot in the country in the Sports Illustrated High School Fan National annual competition. Historically, the school's colors were olive green and white; today, they are Kelly green and white. Cary's historic rival was Garner High School, noted as "as intense a rivalry as there was," and as the community grew and students were sent to Apex High School, that rivalry became the biggest. Cary is a member of the North Carolina High School Athletic Association (NCHSAA). Co-ed sports include cheerleading, junior varsity cheerleading, cross country, indoor track, track, and swim and dive; women's sports include varsity and junior varsity basketball, golf, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, volleyball; men's sports include varsity and junior varsity baseball, basketball, football, golf, lacrosse, soccer, tennis, and wrestling. The school's first football team was organized in 1917 under Tal Stafford, a former North Carolina A&M All American, who later disbanded the team due to World War I and the influenza epidemic; it was reorganized in 1923, and in 1935, Albert H. Werner became the football coach. In 1955 under John Ebby, the team went undefeated and won the Class A state championship, with players John Yarborough and Charles Maison, who later became an All-American at Elon College. On September 15, 1961, the new campus football field was dedicated as the Paul W. Cooper Athletic Field; in 1970, the Imps Booster Club pledged $100,000 to expand the field with locker rooms, restrooms, showers, and seating; in 1973, a press box was added, and A. E. Finley donated $15,000 to reduce debt, leading to the renaming of the stadium as Cooper Field at A. E. Finley Stadium; in 1982, the press box was replaced for $29,500. In 1976, under coach Dave Riggs, the football team won the conference title with a 6–1 record, winning the first round of the playoffs before losing to undefeated Richmond County High School, marking its best season until 1995; in the 1995–96 season under Bill Devine, the team was undefeated, won the conference title, allowed only 45 points, won their first playoff game, and set records for most points scored in a season and most interceptions, with the second-longest winning streak in school history. Under coach Jerry Winterton from 1981 to 2010, the wrestling team won 19 state championships (11 state tournament and 8 dual team titles), 21 regional championships, and 28 consecutive conference tournament championships; in 1987, it was ranked 25th nationally by Amateur Wrestling News and featured on ESPN's Scholastic Sports America; in 1988, it reached as high as 11th nationally; in 1990, its consecutive match win streak ended at 188 wins. Including playoffs, the Imps had a record of 621–16 under Winterton from 1981 to 2010; during this time, he coached 44 individual state champions and wrestlers who earned All-American and National Champion honors. Winterton was inducted into the Cary High School Hall of Fame in 1995, the North Carolina Chapter of the National Wrestling Hall of Fame in 2004, the NCHSAA Hall of Fame in 2014, and the National High School Hall of Fame (NFHS) in 2017. In 1994, the first class was inducted into the Cary High School Hall of Fame, which includes individuals who have played, coached, or served in the school's athletic program. The school's geographic coordinates are 35°46′18″N 78°45′57″W or 35.7717°N 78.7659°W. The faculty also includes a social worker.

Castlebridge (Irish: Droichead an Chaisleáin) is a small town in County Wexford, Ireland, located approximately 5 km north of Wexford town and just north of Wexford Harbour on the R741 road. It has become a rapidly expanding suburb of Wexford Town, with its population increasing from 783 in 1996 to 1,840 in 2016—a rise of nearly threefold over 20 years.[1][3] The original castle in the town was dismantled to construct buildings, including the Church of Ireland church, one of the oldest structures in Castlebridge. The river flowing through the town is actually a canal that replaced the original river; it was dug by hand to enable sailing cots loaded at Castlebridge’s docks to reach Wexford Town more efficiently.[citation needed] Fr James Dixon, the first Catholic priest allowed to minister in Australia, was born in Castlebridge in 1758.[4] Castlebridge is also the founding place of the Guinness Book of World Records. On 10 November 1951, Sir Hugh Beaver, then managing director of the Guinness Breweries, participated in a shooting party in the North Slob near the River Slaney in County Wexford, where he became involved in a debate over whether the golden plover or the red grouse was Europe’s fastest game bird (the golden plover being correct).[6] That evening at Castlebridge House, he realized that existing reference books did not provide answers to such questions, and he recognized that a book offering definitive answers to common pub debates could be popular.[7][8][9] In 2019, Diageo and the Pattison Group, who hold the rights to the Guinness Book of Records, expressed strong interest in Castlebridge House, which has remained derelict, with feasibility studies now underway by Wexford County Council to assess the damage and plan for its restoration, with the goal of developing it into a tourist attraction linked to the book’s origins.[10] This interest was highlighted by the launch of the first annual Castlebridge Record Makers Family Fun Festival in 2019, featuring exhibits on the book’s history and significance to the town.[11] Wexford Bus operates an hourly service, route 877 "The Bridge Loop," to and from Wexford on Mondays and Saturdays since February 2019.[12] Bus Éireann route 379 (Wexford–Gorey via Kilmuckridge and Courtown) serves Castlebridge on Mondays and Saturdays. The town’s center includes a 60x30 foot handball alley, where the handball club has produced several county and Irish champions and members have competed at World Championships in the United States.[citation needed] Nearby, opposite the Old School (now the Castlebridge Community Centre), is the local soccer club, Bridge Rovers FC.[citation needed] Patrick Breen, who lived in Castlebridge and was originally from Bannow in southern County Wexford, was the first Wexford person to serve as President of the Gaelic Athletic Association from 1924 to 1926—among only two Wexford individuals to hold the position.[13] He also founded the Irish Handball Council and the past pupils union of St. Peters College and is buried in the Castlebridge cemetery.[citation needed] Community groups in the area include the Castlebridge Gospel Choir, founded in 2003. Local businesses include the Porter House, which was named 'Pub of the Year' in 2017 before closing, along with several fast food restaurants, a local Londis supermarket, a furniture shop, an antiques store, and a post office.
