Catherine Sue Opie, born in 1961 in Sandusky, Ohio, is an American fine art photographer and educator who lives and works in Los Angeles. She earned a Bachelor of Arts from the San Francisco Art Institute in 1985 and a Master of Fine Arts from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) in 1988, where she was a strictly black-and-white photographer before transitioning to color work. Opie's early artistic development began when she received a Kodak Instamatic camera on her 9th birthday and created her first photograph—a self-portrait making muscles—followed by establishing her own darkroom at age 14. Her family moved to California in 1975, and in 1988, she moved to Los Angeles, where she worked as a lab technician at the University of California, Irvine, while also setting up working studios with her former partner, painter Julie Burleigh, in South Central Los Angeles. Her work explores the connections between mainstream and marginalized societies, focusing on portraiture, studio, and landscape photography to examine sexual identity, community, and the American dream. She is known for her portraits of the Los Angeles leather-dyke community, including the series *Being and Having* (1991) and *Portraits* (1993–1997), which depict queer identities such as drag kings, cross-dressers, and F-to-M transexuals, drawing visual references to 17th-century Old Master portraiture and using symbolic elements like blood in works such as *Self Portrait/Pervert* (1994) and *Self-portrait/Cutting* (1993). Opie's work also includes the *American Cities* (1997–present) series of panoramic black-and-white photographs of American cities and the *Domestic* (1995–1998) series documenting lesbian families on an RV road trip. She has curated exhibitions, including a selection of Tony Greene’s work at the 2014 Whitney Biennial with Richard Hawkins, and has served on the Artist Council and board of overseers at the Hammer Museum, as well as on the board of the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, and the Andy Warhol Foundation. In 2011, she photographed Elizabeth Taylor’s home in Bel Air, Los Angeles, taking 3,000 images with 129 forming the completed study, published as *700 Nimes Road*. Her first film, *The Modernist* (2017), composed of 800 still images, features Pig Pen (Stosh Fila) as a protagonist and is described as both an ode to Los Angeles and a critique of American modernism. Opie has used a range of printing technologies, including Chronochrome, Iris prints, Polaroids, and silver photogravure, and has referenced art history through bright color backgrounds (alluding to Hans Holbein) and frontal full-body portraits (inspired by August Sander), as seen in *Self Portrait/Nursing* (2004). She teaches photography at the University of California, Los Angeles, where she was named the inaugural endowed chair in 2019, funded by a $2-million gift from Lynda and Stewart Resnick. Opie has also taught at Anderson Ranch Arts Center and the Fine Arts Work Center. Her work balances personal and political themes, emphasizing community, identity, and the role of architecture, and she has explored controversial topics influenced by photographers like Robert Mapplethorpe and Nan Goldin. Her name appears in the lyrics of the Le Tigre song "Hot Topic." Her work is held in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and she has received awards including the United States Artists Fellowship (2006) and the President’s Award for Lifetime Achievement from the Women’s Caucus for Art (2009).

Cecil Edward Gibbon (Urdu: سیسل ایڈورڈ گبن) was a Pakistani politician who served as the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly of Pakistan from 1955 to 1958. He was born in 1906 in Allahabad, British India, to an Anglo-Indian family and received his education at St. Joseph's College, Nainital, and St. Edmund's College, Shillong. Gibbon began his career in 1938 when he became the President of the All-India Anglo-Indian Association in Hyderabad. He joined the Indian National Congress but had criticisms of its approach. In 1941, he worked in the Government of India's Food Department in Punjab and later became the president of the Anglo-Indian community's Punjab chapter. In 1946, he was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly and served as the Parliamentary Secretary to Chief Minister Khizar Hayat Tiwana. In 1947, Gibbon supported the creation of Pakistan, resulting in his expulsion from the Congress and the Anglo-Indian Association. He co-founded the Anglo-Pakistan Association and was one of the three Punjab Assembly legislators who voted for Pakistan's creation on 23 June 1947. The main reason for Gibbon's support for Pakistan was the promise of separate electorates (see Communal Award) for Christians, thereby freeing the Anglo-Indians from the dominance of the Hindu majority. Gibbon was a member of the first and second Punjab Assemblies and the National Assembly, participating in debates on various legislative matters. He was the lone non-Muslim representative from Punjab in the Second Constituent Assembly, and alongside Peter Paul Gomez of East Bengal, were the only Christian members in that body. He also served as the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly of Pakistan and advocated for separate electorates for minorities, especially displaced Christian families. However, Prime Minister Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy passed the Electoral Amendment Bill of 1957, formally abolishing separate electorates for non-Muslim minorities of the country. He remained as the Speaker of the National Assembly until 1958, when he retired from politics on being accused of corruption. Following the imposition of military rule under Ayub Khan, Gibbon emigrated out of the country.

The A Century of Progress International Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, was a world's fair held in Chicago, Illinois, United States, from 1933 to 1934, celebrating the city's centennial and registered under the Bureau International des Expositions (BIE). Designed primarily in Art Deco and Moderne styles, the fair promoted technological innovation as its theme, with the motto "Science Finds, Industry Applies, Man Conforms," emphasizing the connection between science and American life. Its architectural symbol was the Sky Ride, a transporter bridge perpendicular to Lake Michigan’s shore allowing passage between sides. The fair was organized as an Illinois nonprofit corporation in January 1928 and held on a 427-acre (1.73 km²) portion of Burnham Park, located on three and a half miles of newly reclaimed land between 12th and 39th streets on the Near South Side. Opened on May 27, 1933, by U.S. Postmaster General James Farley at a four-hour ceremony at Soldier Field, the fair’s opening night featured automatic lighting triggered by the star Arcturus, chosen because its light began its journey around the time of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The rays were detected by photoelectric cells in astronomical observatories and converted into electrical energy transmitted to Chicago. The fair buildings were multi-colored, creating a "Rainbow City" contrast to the "White City" of the 1893 fair, and were constructed using five-ply Douglas fir plywood, ribbed-metal siding, and prefabricated materials like Masonite, Sheetrock, and Maizewood, with windowless but brightly lit structures. The architectural commission, led by Paul Cret and Raymond Hood, included Edward Bennett, John Holabird, and Hubert Burnham, and excluded Frank Lloyd Wright due to his poor collaboration skills, though he developed three conceptual designs. The commission emphasized modern, forward-looking architecture rather than past styles, enabled by the fair’s location on state-owned, code-free land. Key pavilions included the Hall of Science (Cret), Federal Building (Bennett, Burnham, Holabird), General Motors Building (Albert Kahn), Sears Pavilion (Nimmons, Carr, Wright), the twelve-sided House of Tomorrow (George Frederick Keck), Italian Pavilion (Mario de Renzi and Adalberto Libera), Belgian Village (Burnham Brothers with Alfons De Rijdt), and Streets of Paris (Andrew Rebori and John W. Root), where Sally Rand performed. The fair also featured exhibits such as the "Lincoln Group" reconstructing Lincoln’s birth cabin, the Lincoln-Berry General Store, the Chicago Wigwam, and the Rutledge Tavern, and a replica of Jean Baptiste Point du Sable’s cabin, following a campaign by African American groups. The fair included the arrival of the German airship Graf Zeppelin on October 26, 1933, which landed at Curtiss-Wright Airport in Glenview for twenty-five minutes before departing. American automobile manufacturers showcased "dream cars," including a Rollston-bodied Duesenberg called the Twenty Grand, Cadillac’s V-16 limousine, Nash’s vertical parking garage, Lincoln’s rear-engined concept car precursor to the Lincoln-Zephyr, and Pierce-Arrow’s "Suddenly it's 1940!" Silver Arrow, with Packard winning best of show for its Packard Twelve. The 1933 Homes of Tomorrow Exhibition displayed modern home designs and materials. Marine artist Hilda Goldblatt Gorenstein painted twelve murals for the Navy exhibit depicting sea power from Jamestown in 1607 through World War I, and William Mark Young painted murals for the Ohio State Exhibit, later relocated to the Ohio Statehouse. The first Major League Baseball All-Star Game was held at Comiskey Park. In May 1934, the Union Pacific Railroad exhibited its streamlined M-10000 and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad’s Zephyr, which completed a record-breaking 13-hour 5-minute run from Denver to Chicago on May 26, known as the "Dawn-to-Dusk Dash," arriving at the fair’s "Wings of a Century" pageant. Both trains entered revenue service as the City of Salina and the Pioneer Zephyr, the latter now on display at the Museum of Science and Industry. Frank Buck’s Jungle Camp, visited by over two million people, was later moved to Amityville, New York. From June to November 1933, an amoebic dysentery outbreak affected over a thousand people, resulting in 98 deaths, eventually controlled by Joel Connolly through the discovery of defective plumbing contaminating drinking water. Originally scheduled to close on November 12, 1933, the fair reopened from May 26 to October 31, 1934, due to its success. It was financed through membership sales, raising over $800,000 (equal to $18,803,980 today), and a $10 million bond issued on October 28, 1929, before the stock market crash, with half retired by 1933 and the full debt paid by 1934—making it the first international fair in U.S. history to pay for itself. The fair attracted 48,769,227 visitors, with 22,565,859 admissions during the 170 days from May 27, 1933, and 16,486,377 during the 163 days from May 26, 1934, totaling 39,052,236. Much of the site is now part of Northerly Island Park and McCormick Place; the Balbo Monument, given by Benito Mussolini to honor General Italo Balbo’s 1933 trans-Atlantic flight, remains near Soldier Field, and Chicago added a third red star to its flag in 1933, now represented by the fourth of four stars. The Italian-American community donated a statue of Christopher Columbus to Grant Park. The Polish Museum of America holds Stanisław Kaczor-Batowski’s painting of Pulaski at Savannah, which won first place at the fair and was later unveiled by Eleanor Roosevelt at the Art Institute of Chicago in July 1934, before being purchased by the Polish Women's Alliance. The U.S. Post Office issued a fifty-cent Air Mail stamp (Scott C-18), informally known as the Baby Zep, depicting the fair’s Federal Building, the Graf Zeppelin in flight, and its hangar in Friedrichshafen, Germany, along with 1-cent and 3-cent commemorative stamps showing Fort Dearborn and the Federal Building, printed in souvenir sheets of 25 (Scott 728–31), later reprinted in 1935 (Scott 766–67). From October 2010 to September 2011, the National Building Museum in Washington, D.C. hosted an exhibition titled Designing Tomorrow: America's World's Fairs of the 1930s, prominently featuring the Century of Progress fair. The official records and papers of Lenox Lohr, general manager of the fair, are archived in Special Collections at the University of Illinois, Chicago, and materials including photographs, guidebooks, maps, architectural drawings, and souvenirs are held by the Ryerson & Burnham Libraries at the Art Institute of Chicago, with specific collections including the Chicago Architects Oral History Project, Daniel H. Burnham Jr. and Hubert Burnham Papers, Edward H. Bennett Collection, and Voorhees, Gmelin, and Walker photographs.

Chadwell O'Connor (October 9, 1914 – September 5, 2007) was an American inventor and steam engine enthusiast best known for inventing an improved fluid-damped tripod head with counterbalance and adjustable drag, for which he won Academy Awards in 1975 and 1992. He came from a distinguished family; his father, Johnson O'Connor, was a prominent psychometrician and pioneer in aptitude testing, and his mother died when he was young; his father later remarried Eleanor Manning, an MIT-trained architect and educator. The family lived in Boston, and O'Connor often visited his father at the General Electric factory in Lynn, Massachusetts, where he developed an interest in engineering. He earned a degree in mechanical engineering from the Stevens Institute of Technology and the California Institute of Technology. Shortly after graduating, World War II began, and O'Connor joined Douglas Aircraft, where he managed aircraft production and repair. After the war, he became chief engineer at Pasadena Power and Light, where his early interest in steam engines helped improve power production and incineration. In 1974, he developed the O'Connor Rotary Combustor to burn municipal garbage for steam power generation; a pilot plant was built in Japan, and in 1980, a production facility in Gallatin, Tennessee, burned 200 short tons (179 long tons; 181 t) of municipal waste daily. This technology was spun out of O'Connor Engineering to a separate company later acquired by Westinghouse. O'Connor was deeply fascinated by steam locomotives, recognizing them as a dying breed, and began photographing them. He later refurbished and reproduced classic steam locomotives, owning an 1891 0-4-0 locomotive from 1952 to 1967. With his company, O'Connor Engineering Laboratories, he recreated the Union Pacific No. 119 and Central Pacific Jupiter locomotives, which were used in the driving of the Golden Spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, and have operated at the Golden Spike National Historic Site since May 10, 1979. Disney animator Ward Kimball painted the artwork on the No. 119. In later years, O'Connor maintained a steamboat that he operated in Newport Beach, California. In the 1990s, the O'Connors donated one of their steam engines to the Minnesota Transportation Museum for the restoration of the streetcar steamboat Minnehaha, which returned to service as a working museum in 1996 and continues to offer historic steamboat cruises on Lake Minnetonka, Minnesota. His interest in photographing steam locomotives led to the invention of the improved tripod head, which he developed to solve the jerky motion in photos of moving trains by creating a silicone-filled platform between the tripod and camera for smooth panning and tilting. He shot over 100,000 feet of film during the waning days of steam locomotives. In 1952, while filming near Glendale, California, he met Walt Disney, a fellow steam enthusiast, who was impressed by the tripod head and asked O'Connor to produce more. O'Connor agreed, building them in his garage. At the time, Disney was filming The Living Desert, one of his first nature studies, and needed smooth shots of moving animals; the O'Connor head was so effective that Disney ordered 10 more, and the film won the first Academy Award for Documentary Feature in 1953. O'Connor founded a part-time business in 1952 to manufacture the heads, and by 1969, the business was so successful that he left the power company to work full-time on camera heads and steam engines at O'Connor Engineering. He and Disney maintained a lifelong friendship and business relationship, with O'Connor designing the power systems for the steam launches and paddlewheelers at Disney World in Florida. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences awarded O'Connor a Scientific and Engineering Award (Class II) in 1975 and an Award of Merit in 1992 for the concept and engineering of the fluid-damped camera head. Throughout his life, O'Connor received 29 U.S. patents. Chadwell O'Connor died on September 5, 2007.

doc_name: Chairman of the Senate of Pakistan
text: The chairman of the Senate of Pakistan, known as the president-chair of the Senate, is a presiding official elected by the Senate members and serves a three-year term, as stipulated in Article 60(1)–60(2) of Part III, Chapter 2 of the Constitution of Pakistan. The Senate must elect a chairman and deputy chairman at its first meeting and whenever the office becomes vacant, with the term beginning on the day the member assumes office. During the president's absence, the chairman of the Senate performs presidential duties; if the chairman is also unavailable, the speaker of the National Assembly assumes these duties. The chairman is the first in the line of succession to the presidency, preceding the speaker of the National Assembly. The first chairman of the Senate was Retired Senior Justice Habibullah Khan Marwat, who served until 1977, and Wasim Sajjad holds the record for the longest tenure. Senator Yusuf Raza Gilani, elected to the Senate in the April 2024 election, became the current chairman, assuming office on 9 April 2024. The Senate was established to provide equal representation to all federating units, balancing provincial disparities in the National Assembly and promoting national cohesion and harmony. It serves as a legislative body representing provinces and territories, fostering equality, peace, and mutual understanding essential for national growth. After Pakistan's creation on 14 August 1947, the first Constituent Assembly, elected in December 1945, passed the Objectives Resolution on 12 March 1949, which later became part of the constitution. It was dissolved in 1954, and the Second Constituent Assembly, convened by the governor-general in 1955, passed the first constitution on 29 February 1956, which was promulgated on 23 March 1956 and provided for a unicameral legislature. From 14 August 1947 to 1 March 1956, the Government of India Act, 1935, remained in effect. On 7 October 1958, martial law was declared and the constitution was abrogated. A Constitution Commission was appointed in February 1960 to draft the 1962 Constitution, which introduced a presidential system with a unicameral legislature and was abrogated on 25 March 1969. A civil government, following the 1970 elections in December 1971, introduced an interim constitution in 1972. The comprehensive 1973 Constitution, finalized on 12 April and promulgated on 14 August 1973, established a parliamentary system with a bicameral legislature consisting of the National Assembly and the Senate. The Senate initially had 45 members, increased to 63 in 1977, 87 in 1985, and reached 100 in 2002 through a legal framework enacted on 21 August 2002; currently, there are 104 members. The Parliament of Pakistan comprises the president and the two legislative houses: the National Assembly and the Senate. The president is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament and the four provincial assemblies and may be removed or impeached by a resolution passed by not less than two-thirds of the total membership of Parliament in a joint sitting. If the president's office becomes vacant or if the president is absent or unable to perform duties, the chairman of the Senate, or if unavailable, the speaker of the National Assembly, acts as president until a new president is elected. The Parliament includes political parties such as the Independent, Muslim League (N), Muslim League (Q), Pakistan Peoples Party, and Balochistan Awami Party.

Chanie Rosenberg (20 April 1922 – June 2021)[1][2] was a South African-born artist, former teacher, and socialist. She was the sister of Michael Kidron, the partner of Tony Cliff, and a founder member of the Socialist Workers Party in Britain.[3] Born into a Jewish Zionist family from Lithuania in South Africa, she had a relative named the poet Isaac Rosenberg; she studied Hebrew at Cape Town University.[1] In 1944, she moved to Palestine to live on a kibbutz, where she became an anti-Zionist and a revolutionary socialist and met Yigael Gluckstein, better known as Tony Cliff. After the war, she relocated to Britain, where she was a member of the Revolutionary Communist Party from 1944 to 1949, subsequently joining the group that later became the Socialist Workers Party.[1] She participated in numerous anti-racist and anti-fascist mobilisations. She worked as a teacher and was active in the National Union of Teachers in Hackney.[4] Additionally, she was an artist whose sculptures have been exhibited in the Royal Academy of Arts.[5]

Charles Allen Parker Bartlett was an American politician from Pennsylvania who served in the Pennsylvania State Senate, representing the 18th district from 1939 to 1942. The 18th district covered Northampton County, Pennsylvania. Born in Concord, Massachusetts, on November 17, 1880, to Charles H. Bartlett and Mary A. Née Hobson, Bartlett moved to Easton, Pennsylvania, where he completed a public high school education and did not attend college. From 1904 to 1933, he worked as a secretary, treasurer, and sales agent for local manufacturing firms. He joined the Pennsylvania National Guard in 1904 and during World War I, served as a Captain commanding Company A of the Rainbow Division's 149th Machine Gun Battalion within the American Expeditionary Forces from 1917 to 1919. After the war, he served as a Major in the Pennsylvania National Guard's coastal artillery until 1923. Following his military service, Bartlett was elected president of Wilson, Pennsylvania, for four years and served as the borough's Treasurer for nine years before being elected to the Pennsylvania State Senate from 1939 to 1942, during which he chaired the welfare committee. He then served as the Pennsylvania Senate Librarian from 1943 to 1948. Bartlett married Mildred E. Née Richards. He died on March 18, 1948, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, at the age of 67, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in his native Concord.

Charles Bentley (1805/6–4 September 1854) was an English watercolour painter known for his coastal and river scenery. Born in 1805 or 1806, he was the son of a master-carpenter and builder residing in Tottenham Court Road, London. He began working on colouring prints for Theodore Fielding and was eventually apprenticed to him to learn aquatinting. During this time, he was sent to Paris, likely to assist with the plates for *Excursion sur les Cotes et dans les Ports de Normandie* (Paris, 1823–5), most of which were based on watercolours by Richard Bonington. After completing his apprenticeship, Bentley earned some income through engraving or designing plates for periodicals but gradually shifted focus to painting watercolours. He exhibited four works at the first Exhibition of the New Society of Painters in Water-Colours (later the Royal Institute of Painters in Water-Colours) in 1832 and six the following year. He lived at 15, Bateman's Buildings, on the south side of Soho Square, where he resided for six years. In February 1834, he was elected an Associate-Exhibitor of the Old Water-Colour Society (later the Royal Society of Painters in Water-Colours). By 1838, he had moved to 11, Mornington Place, Hampstead Road, where he remained except for a three-year period when he lived with William Callow in Charlotte Street. His 1838 exhibitions included two imaginative compositions: *From the Red Rover*, depicting a naval battle, and *From Tom Cringle's Log*, showing a sinking slave-ship. He first exhibited at the British Institution in 1843 and became a full member of the Old Society the next year. In 1851, he exhibited at the Society of British Artists. Bentley painted scenes throughout Britain, in Jersey, the north of Ireland, and Normandy, which he visited multiple times with Callow between 1836 and 1841. He also exhibited views of Venice, Holland, and Düsseldorf, though it is uncertain whether he visited these places, as some works—such as those of Trebizond and Abydos, shown in 1841 and 1849—were based on drawings by Coke Smyth. He also prepared illustrations for *12 Views in the Interior of Guiana*, published by Rudolf Ackermann in 1841, using studies from an expedition to South America led by John Morison. Bentley was not financially successful; Samuel Redgrave described him as "uncertain in his transactions, and always poor." He died of cholera on 4 September 1854, leaving a widow, and was buried in the western side of Highgate Cemetery. The grave (no. 6056) no longer has a headstone or marker.

Charles Philip Snyder (July 10, 1879 – December 3, 1964) was a four-star admiral in the United States Navy and served as the U.S. Navy's first Naval Inspector General during World War II. Born in Charleston, West Virginia, in Kanawha County to future West Virginia Congressman Charles P. Snyder and Jane Goshorn, he attended Washington and Lee University for one year before entering the U.S. Naval Academy in 1896. Graduating fourth in his class in 1900, he served two years at sea as a passed cadet before being commissioned an ensign in 1902 and assigned to the battleship Alabama. Promoted to lieutenant, he reported to the Naval Academy on August 16, 1905 as an instructor in navigation and mechanics. In February 1906, he testified before a Congressional subcommittee regarding his role as disciplinary officer during a hazing incident in which an upper class man was acquitted at court-martial for injuring a fourth class man, as the court found that Snyder had tacitly encouraged the hazing. During World War I, he commanded the battleship Oregon, flagship of the Pacific Fleet; the cruiser Minneapolis; and the transport Mongolia. He graduated from the Naval War College in 1925. Promoted to captain, he served as commandant of midshipmen at the Naval Academy, on staff at the Naval War College, and as manager of the Portsmouth Navy Yard. Promoted to rear admiral with date of rank March 1, 1933 while serving as chief of staff to Admiral David F. Sellers, who was Commander Battleships, Battle Force, U.S. Fleet from 1932 to 1933 and Commander in Chief, U.S. Fleet from 1933 to 1934. Snyder served as commandant of the Portsmouth Navy Yard from 1934 to 1935, then commanded a heavy cruiser division of the Scouting Force, followed by a battleship division of the Battle Force, before serving as President of the Naval War College from January 2, 1937 to May 27, 1939. He returned to sea in 1939 as Commander Battleships, Battle Force, with the temporary rank of vice admiral. On January 6, 1940, he hoisted his four-star flag on board the battleship California as Commander Battle Force with the temporary rank of admiral. As commander of the Battle Force, he was second in command of the U.S. Fleet, under Admiral James O. Richardson. In January 1941, Richardson was relieved over a dispute about fleet basing and replaced by Husband E. Kimmel, a junior rear admiral. Simultaneously, the fleet was reorganized and the position of Commander Battle Force was downgraded to three stars, a change scheduled to take effect upon the completion of Snyder's tour that summer. For reasons of his own, Snyder had no desire to serve under Kimmel and asked to be relieved immediately. He was succeeded by Vice Admiral William S. Pye on January 31, 1941, one day before Kimmel ascended to command and eleven months before most of the Battle Force's battleships were sunk at anchor during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. Upon relinquishing command of the Battle Force, he reverted to his permanent rank of rear admiral and became a member of the General Board with additional duty as the president of the Board for Inspection of Military Readiness in Naval Districts. As a member of the General Board, Snyder participated in the debate over the role of African American sailors in the Navy. The Navy's policy was to confine black sailors to menial duties as stewards and messmen, excluding them from general service on the grounds that they were unable to maintain discipline among white subordinates and therefore had to be segregated, which was impractical at sea. When the General Board convened on January 23, 1942, Snyder suggested expanding black enlistment in rigidly segregated support roles outside the service branches: in the Aviation Branch, following the Army's lead; aboard auxiliaries and minor vessels, especially transports; or in the Musician's Branch, because "the colored race is very musical and they are versed in all forms of rhythm." From May 1942 until April 1946, he served as the first Naval Inspector General. The Naval Inspector General was used as a troubleshooter during World War II, inspecting shore facilities and investigating misconduct. As one of 24 inspection authorities concerned with Navy procurement and administration of activities ashore, he was instructed to keep the organization small and to rely on augmentation from the Fleet. He retired in August 1943 upon reaching the statutory age, and was advanced to admiral on the retired list as the highest rank in which he had served, but remained on active duty as inspector general until the end of the war. In early 1946, he investigated the sinking of the heavy cruiser Indianapolis in his official capacity as inspector general, but agreed to curtail his investigation so that Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King and Navy Secretary James V. Forrestal could immediately court-martial Indianapolis's commanding officer, Captain Charles B. McVay III. Snyder was decorated with the Navy Distinguished Service Medal for his service during World War II. He married the former Cornelia Lee Wolcott on July 10, 1902, and had three children: Elizabeth; Philip, who retired from the Navy as a rear admiral; and Jane. He died at the Naval Hospital in Bethesda, Maryland in 1964 and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. He married Edith Hanlon Christian in 1949. His decorations include the Navy Cross for eminent and conspicuous service in World War I, and a special letter of commendation from the War Department. He received an honorary Doctor of Laws degree (LL.D.) from Washington and Lee College on January 24, 1943, and the Sigma Chi fraternity distinguished medal for conspicuous public service in 1940. His great-granddaughter is actress Elizabeth McGovern.

Charlotte Lee, Lady Baltimore (born 13 March 1678, (13 March 1678 OS); died 1 February 1721, (22 January 1721 OS)), was an English noblewoman and granddaughter of King Charles II of England and his mistress Barbara Villiers, Countess of Castlemaine, Duchess of Cleveland. She was the eldest of at least fourteen children of Edward Henry Lee, 1st Earl of Lichfield (4 February 1663 – 14 July 1716), and Lady Charlotte Fitzroy (5 September 1664 – 17 February 1718), who was the illegitimate daughter of King Charles II by Barbara Villiers. Her mother was thirteen and her father was fifteen at the time of Charlotte's birth. Her paternal grandparents were Sir Francis Henry Lee of Ditchley, 4th Baronet of Quarendon, and Elizabeth Pope, daughter of Thomas Pope, 2nd Earl of Downe. On 2 January 1699, at the age of twenty, she married Benedict Leonard Calvert, son of Charles Calvert, 3rd Baron Baltimore, and Jane Lowe. In February 1715, she assumed the title of Lady Baltimore after her husband succeeded to the title of 4th Baron Baltimore upon the death of his father, the third Baron. The title of Proprietary Governor of the Province of Maryland had been lost during the Glorious Revolution and would be restored to Charles Calvert, the son of Charlotte and Benedict, upon his death on 16 April 1715. Charlotte and Lord Baltimore had six children, including Charles Calvert, 5th Baron Baltimore, and Benedict Leonard Calvert, who served as Governor of Maryland from 1727 to 1731. The couple separated in 1705; in 1706, Charlotte had an affair with Colonel Robert Fielding, then the bigamous husband of her grandmother the Duchess of Cleveland, and it was rumoured she bore a child by him, born on 23 April 1707. In 1711, Lord Baltimore introduced a Bill before the House of Lords to confirm their divorce, settle their finances, and declare any future children of Charlotte illegitimate. In 1719, before 10 December, she married Christopher Crowe (c.1681 – 9 November 1749), Consul at Leghorn, who was three years younger than her. This marriage produced five additional children. Charlotte Lee died of rheumatism on 22 January 1721 at Woodford Hall, Woodford, Essex, and was buried there on 29 January 1721. She died intestate, and her estate was administered on 4 March 1721 at Woodford Hall. Charlotte Lee is a minor character in Anya Seton's historical romance Devil Water.

Chattahoochee State Park was a public recreation area situated in the extreme southeast corner of Alabama, managed by the government of Houston County, Alabama. The park spanned 596 acres (241 ha) along Irwin's Mill Creek on the Florida-Alabama border. It closed after much of the park was destroyed by Hurricane Michael in 2018. Land adjacent to the park was the site of an 1818 skirmish during the First Seminole War. The state park was developed in the 1930s by members of the Civilian Conservation Corps, who constructed a natural stone dam to form the 23-acre (9.3 ha) CC Pond and built the park’s dirt roads; remnants such as chimneys from the CCC workers' camp were once visible. Most of the park’s facilities and trees were damaged by Hurricane Michael in October 2018, leading to its permanent closure due to the state’s inability to fund clearing, repair, and rebuilding efforts. In 2022, slow progress was being made toward reopening the park, with hopes of having it reopened by 2024.

Chiharu Shiota (塩田 千春, Shiota Chiharu), born in 1972 in Osaka, is a Japanese performance and installation artist who has lived and worked in Berlin, Germany since 1996. Her parents operated a business manufacturing fish boxes, producing a thousand wooden boxes daily, and although they did not directly support her artistic ambitions, they permitted her to formally study art. Shiota studied at Kyoto Seika University in Kyoto from 1992 to 1996, where she studied under contemporary sculptor Saburo Muraoka; she was an exchange student at Canberra School of Art, Australian National University, in 1993, and later attended Hochschule für Bildende Künste, Braunschweig (1997–1999), and Universität der Künste, Berlin (1999–2002), where she also served as Artist in Residence at Akademie Schloss Solitude, Stuttgart. In Berlin, she studied under Rebecca Horn and was influenced by Marina Abramović, who became a significant figure in shaping her artistic development. Her early works, including From DNA to DNA (1994) and Becoming Painting (1994), used materials like woolen threads and red enamel paint applied to her body, marking her first physical artworks and serving as acts of liberation. Shiota's artistic practice spans performance, sculpture, and installation, with her most recognized works being vast, room-spanning webs of threads or hoses that connect abstract networks to everyday objects such as keys, window frames, dresses, shoes, boats, and suitcases. Materials hold symbolic meaning in her work: menstruation blood is used as artistic material, and red threads represent human relationships; thin plastic tubing filled with blood-like liquid symbolizes the umbilical connection, suggesting nurturing and the beginning of life. She draws on psychogeography—the relationship between psyche and space—and has stated that she could not have created major installations like A Room of Memory (2009) and Memory of Skin (2005) without living in Berlin. Shiota has collaborated with choreographers and composers such as Toshio Hosokawa, Sasha Waltz, and Stefan Goldmann. Arriving in Berlin in 1999, she observed the city’s lingering Cold War relics and later focused on abandoned areas, collecting hundreds of old windows from former East Berlin, which she used in House of Windows (2005), exhibited at her solo show Raum at Haus am Lützowplatz and later at the 3rd Fukuoka Asian Art Triennale. She equates windows to skin, exploring physical and interpersonal boundaries in a rapidly changing urban environment, and views her own dislocation as a central theme in her work. Since the 2000s, Shiota has produced cobweb-like installations worldwide, adapting their scale to gallery spaces and incorporating found objects such as beds, dresses, shoes, keys, and chairs. These objects carry personal and lived experiences, and the red or black threads stretch, connect, enclose, and obscure them, reflecting the tangled, tense nature of human relationships. The creation process involves hours of labor by Shiota and her assistants, embedding performative elements into the works. In Dialogue with Absence (2010), an oversized white wedding dress hangs on a wall, with red liquid flowing from peristaltic pumps into it via plastic tubes, evoking themes of womanhood, societal burdens, and possibly her own battle with cancer. For Manifesta 14 in Pristina, she hung hundreds of red yarn threads from the Great Hammam’s ceiling, attracting over 150,000 visitors. She has also engaged in community-based projects, such as Further Memory (2010), a tunnel-like structure on Teshima Island, Japan, constructed from 600 used local windows, echoing House of Windows and reflecting on ecological beauty and the islanders’ connection to nature, offering a sense of hope amid depopulation.

The Chinese paddlefish (Psephurus gladius; simplified Chinese: 白鲟; traditional Chinese: 白鱘; pinyin: báixún; literal translation: "white sturgeon"), also known as the Chinese swordfish, is an extinct species of fish that was formerly native to the Yangtze and Yellow River basins in China. It was one of the largest freshwater fish, with records of specimens over 3.6 metres (12 ft) and possibly up to 7 m (23 ft) in length, though definitive evidence of lengths exceeding 3 metres (9.8 ft) is limited, and a reported 7-metre specimen attributed to C. Ping (1931) as cited by John Treadwell Nichols in 1943 is considered likely due to a translation error by Lance Grande and William Bemis in 1991. The last known specimen, a mature female caught in 2003, measured 3.63 metres (11.9 ft) and weighed approximately 200 kilograms (440 lb). A 1996 study estimated the largest females and males could reach 4.363 metres (14.31 ft) and 3.685 metres (12.09 ft), respectively, with FishBase and the World Wide Fund for Nature citing a conservative maximum weight of 300–500 kg (660–1,100 lb). The species was the only member of its genus Psephurus and one of two recent paddlefish (family Polyodontidae), the other being the still-living American paddlefish (Polyodon spathula). Unlike the American paddlefish, which feeds on plankton, the Chinese paddlefish was a piscivorous predator that primarily consumed small to medium-sized fish such as anchovies, cyprinids, gobies, bagrid catfish, and bothid flounders, as well as crustaceans like shrimp and crabs. It had a white underbelly and grey back and head, with dorsal and anal fins located far back on the body, a narrow and pointed paddle-like rostrum between a quarter and a third of total body length, small and round eyes, and a heterocercal tail fin with a well-developed lower lobe. Its skull was more elongate and narrower than that of the American paddlefish and lacked sculpturing, with fewer stellate bones on the rostrum; its teeth were small, sharp, canine-shaped, inward-curling, and fused into the bone in mature adults, with shorter, narrower jaws and a proportionately smaller gape, and the upper jaw not firmly attached to the braincase. The skeleton was largely cartilaginous, and the body lacked scales except for small ones in the caudal peduncle and caudal fin. Juveniles reached about 1 to 1.5 kilograms (2 to 3 lb) and 1 metre (3 ft) by their first winter, and about 3.3 kilograms (7 lb 4 oz) by age one; beyond that, weight gain increased dramatically, reaching about 12.5 kilograms (28 lb) at 1.5 metres (5 ft), with sexual maturity occurring at around 25 kilograms (55 lb). Females were suggested to grow larger than males after maturity, though growth rates were similar prior to that. The species had a lifespan estimated at 29–38 years, though the theoretical maximum was likely higher due to anthropogenic impacts. It was first classified under Polyodon by Eduard von Martens in 1862 and later placed in its own monotypic genus by Albert Günther in 1873; Spatularia angustifolium, named by Johann Jakob Kaup in 1862, is considered a junior synonym. Paddlefish are one of two living families of Acipenseriformes, alongside sturgeons, with the oldest Acipenseriformes records dating to the Early Jurassic (over 190 million years ago), and the oldest paddlefish fossil, Protopsephurus, from the Early Cretaceous in China (around 120 million years ago). The genus Polyodon, containing the American paddlefish, dates back to around 65 million years ago (beginning of the Paleocene), and molecular clock estimates for the divergence between the American and Chinese paddlefish range from 68 to 100 million years ago (middle to Upper Cretaceous). The Chinese paddlefish was native to the Yangtze River basin and its estuary at the East China Sea, historically also found in the Yellow River basin and its estuary at the Yellow Sea, and occasionally in coastal waters of the East and Yellow Seas, including the lower reaches of the Qiantang and Yong rivers in Zhejiang. It primarily inhabited the lower-middle reaches of the Yangtze, which were more prey-rich, and sometimes entered large lakes. Breeding adults migrated from the Yangtze to the lower Jinsha River (upper Yangtze) near Yibin, Sichuan, in fall and winter to spawn in spring (mid-March to early April), with males reaching maturity at 5 years and females at 6 years, and spawning males typically 5–10 years old and females 6–16 years old. Spawning sites were around 500 metres (1,600 ft) long, with a maximum depth of 10 metres (33 ft) and rapid flow, and the bottom was shingly in the lower reaches and muddy/sandy in the upper. Females likely spawned every other year or less frequently. The ovaries contained over 100,000 eggs, each about 2.7 mm (3⁄32 in) across with a sticky surface, which sank and attached to pebbles after fertilization. The species was amphidromous, with juveniles migrating 2,750 kilometres (1,710 mi) downriver after hatching in the upper Yangtze, reaching the Yangtze estuary near Shanghai by 4–5 months of age, then spending time in brackish and saline coastal waters, before migrating back upriver as subadults at 1.5–2 years old and progressing up to spawning grounds between Chongqing and Yibin. It was largely solitary and occupied the lower-mid water column, and was noted for being a strong swimmer. It used passive electroreception via ampullae in the head and rostrum to detect prey. The species was first named as Polyodon by von Martens in 1862, and later moved to Psephurus by Günther in 1873. The last records in the Yellow River basin and its estuary date to the 1960s, with declines noted between the 13th and 19th centuries, and annual harvests reaching 25 tonnes by the 1970s. A 2024 study estimated the spawning-age population in 1980 to be around 3,000. In 1983, the Chinese government banned fishing of the species due to its decline. Small numbers were still caught in the 1980s (e.g., 32 in 1985), and young individuals were seen as late as 1995. Attempts to establish a captive breeding program failed due to the rarity of the fish and difficulty in keeping adults alive. Since 2000, only two confirmed live sightings have occurred in the Yangtze basin: a 3.3-metre (10 ft 10 in), 117-kilogram (258 lb) female caught in Nanjing in 2002, which died despite rescue efforts, and a 3.52-metre (11 ft 7 in), 160-kilogram (350 lb) female accidentally caught in Yibin in January 2003 by fisherman Liu Longhua, which was radio-tagged and released but the tag failed after 12 hours. From 2006 to 2008, a research team from the Chinese Academy of Fisheries Science in Jingzhou failed to catch any paddlefish, though two possible specimens were detected via hydroacoustic signals. A 2019 study by scientists from the Yangtze River Fisheries Research Institute concluded the species was extinct based on its absence from extensive capture surveys between 2017 and 2018, estimating extinction between 2005 and 2010, with functional extinction occurring by 1993. The IUCN Species Survival Commission Sturgeon Specialist Group unanimously agreed to declare it extinct on 15 September 2019, and the official IUCN Red List status was formally updated to "extinct" in July 2022. The primary cause of extinction was the construction of the Gezhouba Dam in 1981, which blocked migration to upriver spawning grounds and fragmented the population, effectively preventing reproduction and leading to long-term population collapse. Overfishing also contributed significantly, as the species was heavily overfished at all life stages, from fry to adults, compounded by its long generation time. The fish was fished for caviar, though it made up less than 1% of total Yangtze fish catches by weight in the late 20th century. Historical references include a gold belt from the Jinsha site (c. 1000 BC) with paddlefish depictions, mentions in the Classic of Poetry (11th–7th century BC) as a sacrificial animal, the Huainanzi (2nd century BC) stating it was attracted to music, Guo Pu’s Jiang Fu (Eastern Jin), and a 9th-century Tang dynasty text suggesting killing the fish could cause rain. It appears in numerous historical Chinese paintings, and Sichuanese fishermen referred to its large size, with common names comparing its rostrum to an elephant’s trunk.
By weight, the 20th century holds the greatest amount.

Chivor is a town and municipality in the Eastern Boyacá Province, within the Colombian department of Boyacá. It is situated at 215 kilometres (134 mi) from the department capital, Tunja, and has a mean temperature of 18 °C (64 °F) in the Tenza Valley. The municipality is bordered to the north by Macanal, to the south by Ubalá, Cundinamarca, to the east by Santa María, and to the west by Almeida. The name Chivor originates from the Chibcha language and means "Our farmfields - our mother" or "Green and rich land," the latter referring to the abundant emerald deposits. The area was inhabited by the Muisca prior to the Spanish conquest, who were part of the Muisca Confederation, with the zaque of Hunza in the north and the zipa of Bacatá in the south. The Muisca already knew and mined the rich emerald deposits, using emeralds as religious offerings, decorations, and currency. Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada discovered the emerald deposits in 1537, but the mines were abandoned until 1886. Modern Chivor was officially founded on December 16, 1930, by Florencio Novoa. Its main economic activities are agriculture, including maize, yuca, bananas, sugarcane, beans, chayote, coffee, and fruits such as papayas, blackberries, lulo, and tree tomatoes, as well as emerald mining. In 2014, emeralds worth 30 million US dollars were extracted in Boyacá, and the rich deposits have led to numerous regional conflicts, including in Chivor. The Gran Esmeralda de Moctezuma, a 21-centimetre (8.3 in) high, 17-centimetre (6.7 in) long, and 16-centimetre (6.3 in) thick emerald, was found in Chivor and is currently in Vienna, Austria. Other notable emeralds from Chivor include Patricia, weighing 632 carats (126.4 grams or 4.46 oz), and La Magnífica, measuring 1225 carats (245 grams or 8.6 oz). The Embalse la Esmeralda, a hydroelectric reservoir governed from Chivor, Macanal, and Almeida, produces hydroelectric energy. Chivor has a subtropical highland climate (Cfb) characterized by heavy to very heavy rainfall throughout the year.

Clover "Chloe" Delight Esther Eudaly (1969/1970) is an American politician from Oregon who served as Portland's City Commissioner from 2017 to 2021. Eudaly won her position in November 2016 by promising to focus on the needs of renters, people with disabilities, and individuals with lower incomes, running as a tenants' rights advocate and pledging to encourage the construction of lower-cost housing. She was elected to Position 4 on the Portland City Commission and took office with the Office of Neighborhood Involvement, which she renamed the Office of Community & Civic Life (OCCL). Eudaly has a strong opposition to neighborhood associations, stating they "tend to be dominated by older, white homeowners and push their interests rather than the needs of a diverse, growing city." On September 18, 2019, Willamette Week reported that Eudaly sent an angry email to her City Council colleagues threatening political consequences if they did not support her stance on neighborhood associations. The Fair Access In Renting (FAIR) ordinance, which Eudaly introduced and successfully passed in June 2019 after working on it for two years, changed rental application screening in Portland. FAIR requires a first-come-first-serve approach, prioritizes accessible units for people with disabilities, limits landlords from requiring tenant incomes to be 2 to 2.5 times higher than rent, and restricts the use of credit and criminal histories in rental denials. FAIR passed on a 3–1 vote, with Mayor Ted Wheeler and Commissioner Nick Fish voting in favor along with Eudaly, while Commissioner Amanda Fritz voted against it and Commissioner Jo Ann Hardesty was absent. Eudaly voted to defund the Portland police department, but the proposal was defeated 2–3. The ordinance initially passed as a temporary measure set to expire with Portland’s housing emergency declaration in October 2017, but became permanent by unanimous vote in 2018. Rental fees are based on unit size: $2,900 for a studio or single room occupancy, $3,300 for a one-bedroom, $4,200 for a two-bedroom, and $4,500 for a three-bedroom or larger. In 2018, Eudaly became head of the Portland Bureau of Transportation (PBOT), where she spearheaded the Rose Lane Project, announced in June 2019 in response to the Enhanced Transit Corridors Plan adopted by City Council on June 20, 2018. The project includes dedicated bus-only lanes and adjusted traffic signals to give buses head starts at intersections. Trial runs on Southwest Madison Street, Northwest Everett Street, and the Burnside Bridge showed up to 76% reductions in bus delays, with buses crossing the Burnside Bridge nearly two minutes faster. On February 13, 2020, the Rose Lane Project was unanimously approved by Portland City Council. Eudaly grew up near Forest Grove, Oregon, moved to the Portland suburbs at age nine, attended Tigard High School, dropped out, and moved to Portland in 1988. She opened her bookstore, Reading Frenzy, in 1994 and is a founder of the Independent Publishing Resource Center, a maker's space for independent publishers. She resides in the Woodlawn neighborhood, has a son named Henry, and self-identifies as queer. Eudaly lost her November 2020 re-election bid to Mingus Mapps.

Chris Nwabueze Ngige (born 8 August 1952) is a Nigerian politician and medical doctor who served as Minister of Labour and Employment under President Muhammadu Buhari from 2015 to 2023. He was elected Senator for Anambra Central Constituency in April 2011. Ngige was governor of Anambra State from May 2003 to March 2006 under the People's Democratic Party (PDP). A medical doctor by profession, he graduated from the University of Nigeria-Nsukka in 1979 and served in the civil service, including at the National Assembly and state house clinics, retiring in 1998 as deputy director in the Federal Ministry of Health. He joined the PDP in 1999, serving as Assistant National Secretary and Zonal Secretary in the South East region. His 2003 gubernatorial election was controversial, and after an unsuccessful attempt on 10 July 2003 to have him removed via a fabricated resignation letter accepted by the state assembly, he broke ranks with his political godfather, Chris Uba, brother of Andy Uba. In August 2006, an Election Tribunal led by Justice Nabaruma nullified Ngige's 2003 victory, and the Nigerian Federal Court of Appeal confirmed the annulment on 15 March 2006, awarding the win to Peter Obi of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA). Ngige accepted the judgment in good faith and called on the people of Anambra to support Obi. Following Obi's impeachment, which was later overturned, Ngige attempted to run for governor in April 2007 but was disqualified by the Independent National Electoral Commission, despite a Federal High Court voiding the disqualification; Obi ultimately served out his term. Ngige faced criticism for appearing naked at the Okija voodoo shrine during his gubernatorial campaign. On 6 February 2010, he contested again for governor, facing 25 candidates including Andy Uba, Charles Soludo, Nicholas Ukachukwu, Mrs. Uche Ekwunife, Ralph Nwosu, and incumbent Peter Obi, who won the election. In April 2011, Ngige ran for senator on the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN) platform, winning with 69,765 votes to Professor Dora Akunyili's 69,292 after voting issues in some areas led to a re-vote on 25 April. His senatorial tenure ended when he lost the 2015 election to Hon. Mrs Uche Ekwunife, who was sworn in as senator for Anambra Central in the 8th National Assembly. On 11 November 2015, Ngige was appointed Minister of Labour and Employment by President Muhammadu Buhari. In 2019, he was nominated by President Buhari for screening by the National Assembly and was sworn in on 21 August 2019 as Minister of Labour and Employment. On 19 April 2022, Ngige declared interest in running for President of Nigeria under the All Progressive Congress (APC) banner, describing himself as "jack of all trade and masters of all". His 2003 gubernatorial election was annulled in March 2006 by the Court of Appeal, which declared Peter Obi the rightful winner, and a 2012 profile noted the annulment was based on "electoral malpractice". On 12 December 2025, Ngige was arraigned before the Federal Capital Territory High Court in Gwarinpa, Abuja, on an eight-count charge filed by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). The charges relate to his tenure as supervising minister of the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) between September 2015 and May 2023, alleging he conferred unfair advantages on companies linked to his associates through contract awards under Sections 19 and 17(a) of the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act, 2000. Ngige is also accused of corruptly accepting monetary gifts totaling ₦119.78 million from contractors, allegedly funneled through the "Dr Chris Nwabueze Ngige Campaign Organisation" and the "Senator (Dr) Chris Ngige Scholarship Scheme". Ngige pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Lieutenant-Colonel Christopher Codrington (c. 1668 – 7 April 1710) was an English Army officer, planter, and colonial administrator who served as governor of the Leeward Islands from 1699 to 1704. Born in Barbados around 1668, he was the eldest son of Christopher Codrington and Gertrude, and inherited one of the largest sugar plantations in Barbados, making the Codrington family extremely wealthy. He had a younger brother who suffered from a mental disability. Codrington never married but had a natural mixed-race son, William, from a relationship with a Black woman named Mauldline Morange; William received £500 in his father's will and became a plantation owner in Jamaica. Educated in England, he studied at Christ Church, Oxford, and was elected to All Souls College in 1690, where he was part of an intellectual circle that included Charles Boyle and Joseph Addison and became known as an avid book collector. In 1693, he returned to the West Indies to participate in an unsuccessful attack on the French possession of Martinique, then served in Flanders during the Nine Years' War, fighting notably at Huy and Namur in 1695. William III granted him a commission as captain in the English Army's 1st Regiment of Foot Guards, a largely honorary post where only 16 of the 24 companies were formed; under double-ranking, Codrington held the rank of lieutenant colonel. His father died shortly after the Peace of Ryswick in 1697, and Codrington was appointed governor of the Leeward Islands in 1699. He faced accusations of abuse of power and local disputes, which were investigated by Parliament, but he was exonerated just before the War of the Spanish Succession began in 1702. After successfully retaking Saint Kitts from the French, he resigned following a failed attack on Guadeloupe in 1703, which severely damaged his health. He attempted to re-enter politics unsuccessfully and spent his later years in retirement on his Barbadian estates. Upon his death on 7 April 1710, his body was brought to England and buried on 19 June 1710 in All Souls Chapel. His will bequeathed £10,000 and £6,000 worth of books to endow the Christopher Codrington Library at All Souls College, Oxford, which includes a statue by Sir Henry Cheere. In November 2020, his name was removed from the library due to his ownership of slaves, and a plaque was placed outside to commemorate the enslaved workers held on his plantations. His will also provided £1,500 for a monument to his father in Westminster Abbey, and the Codrington Plantations and part of Barbuda were left to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts to establish a college in Barbados. Delays from legal challenges meant Codrington College was not completed until 1745 and was initially restricted to white students; it remains an Anglican theological school and is now part of the University of the West Indies. The Codrington School, first established in 1917 and closed in the 1990s, was reopened in 2002 as an International Baccalaureate school. The Codrington baronets retained ownership of Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua until 1944.

Christopher Crowe (c. 1681 – 9 November 1749) was an English consul and landowner. In 1705, at the age of 24, he was appointed English Consul at Livorno, in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. He was awarded a "lucrative" contract to supply the British Mediterranean fleet with wine and olive oil during the War of the Spanish Succession, from 1703 to 1711. Crowe also served as a prize agent for captured enemy merchant ships, acquired artworks on behalf of the English nobility, and became wealthy. In 1707, he purchased Woodford Hall, a large house and estate in Woodford, Essex, adjacent to Epping Forest, from Sir Richard Child. In 1715, he married Charlotte Lee, Lady Baltimore, who had previously been married to Benedict Leonard Calvert, 4th Baron Baltimore, and they had five children. In 1727, he sold Woodford Hall to William Hunt, having secured a private act of Parliament, known as Crowe's Estate Act 1727 (1 Geo. 2. St. 2. c. 8 Pr.), to authorize the sale.

Christopher Mark Luxon, born on 19 July 1970 in Christchurch to a Roman Catholic family of Irish, Scottish, and English descent, is a New Zealand politician and businessman who has served as the 42nd prime minister since 2023. A member of the National Party, he has been the Member of Parliament for Botany since 2020 and previously led the Opposition from 2021 to 2023. Before entering politics, he was the chief executive officer (CEO) of Air New Zealand from 2013 to 2019. Luxon grew up in Howick, East Auckland, studied commerce at the University of Canterbury from 1989 to 1992, earning a Master of Commerce (Business Administration), and worked part-time at McDonald's and as a porter at the Parkroyal Hotel during his school and university years. He joined Unilever in 1993, working in Wellington, Sydney, London, and Chicago, becoming president of Unilever Canada in 2008. He joined Air New Zealand as group general manager in May 2011 and became CEO in June 2012, leading the company to record profits through a booming tourism market, the elimination of underperforming regional routes, and job cuts. Air New Zealand was named Australia's most trusted brand multiple times during his tenure. In 2014, he joined the Virgin Australia board as a representative of Air New Zealand, which sold its 25.9% stake in 2016, leading to his departure from the board. He resigned from Air New Zealand in 2019 and was encouraged by former Prime Minister John Key to enter politics. He won the National Party candidacy for Botany in November 2019 after Jami-Lee Ross resigned, and was elected in 2020 with 52% of the vote. He was appointed spokesperson for local government, research, science, manufacturing, and land information, and associate spokesperson for transport in the Shadow Cabinet of Judith Collins. After Collins stepped down on 25 November, Luxon was named party leader on 30 November 2021, following the withdrawal of Bridges from the leadership race. In the 2023 general election, the National Party won 38.1% of the party vote and 48 seats, a plurality but not enough to govern, leading to negotiations with ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First that lasted six weeks and concluded on 24 November. A formal three-party coalition was formed, with separate agreements between National and each junior party, and Luxon was sworn in as prime minister on 27 November 2023 by Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro. Under his premiership, the Sixth National Government has implemented significant cuts to the civil service, including the elimination of 9,500 public sector jobs by May 2025 and the scaling down or cancellation of over 240 government programmes, amounting to approximately $6 billion in savings. The government introduced $14.7 billion in tax cuts, replaced the Three Waters reform programme with the Local Water Done Well policy, and reduced co-governance initiatives while discouraging the use of the Māori language in the public service. It also reintroduced the three-strikes sentencing law and launched a pilot military-style boot camp for youth offenders. The government contributed to the construction of the City Rail Link metro system in Central Auckland and agreed to support the Treaty Principles Bill to its first reading, though it stated it would not support the bill beyond that stage. Luxon defended the boot camp and the prison population growth, calling higher prisoner numbers a "good thing" and stating the cost would be "what the cost will be." The government repealed New Zealand's world-leading smoke-free legislation, returning around $1 billion in annual tax revenue, despite warnings from researchers that thousands of New Zealanders would die needlessly. Luxon also introduced a "traffic light" regime for welfare, requiring jobseekers to reapply every six months and introducing a community work sanction. In August 2024, he and Education Minister Erica Stanford announced a new mathematics curriculum to be introduced in early 2025 and confirmed the eventual scrapping of the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) over five years. In November 2024, he delivered a national apology to survivors of abuse in state and faith-based care and introduced legislation to ban strip searches on children and strengthen security checks for those working with children. In early 2025, he announced openness to abolishing regional councils as part of reforming the Resource Management Act 1991. In August 2024, he criticized so-called "nice to have projects" and called for local councils to focus on rubbish collection and water infrastructure, while also confirming Cabinet's agreement to revise the Local Government Act and scrap its four wellbeing provisions. In April 2024, he stripped Melissa Lee of her Media and Communications portfolio and Penny Simmonds of her Disability Issues portfolio during a cabinet reshuffle due to criticism over their handling of media and disability funding. On 5 May 2024, he and Simeon Brown announced that Auckland would avoid a 25.8 percent rates increase under the Local Water Done Well plan. In early August 2024, he visited Hawke's Bay to discuss post-flood and Cyclone Gabrielle relief, confirming that work on the Napier-Wairoa railway line would be paused to focus on State Highway 2, and announced a NZ$63 million contribution to remove sediment and debris. As of March 2024, his net worth was estimated between NZ$21 million and NZ$30 million, making him the second-wealthiest National Party leader after John Key, owning seven properties including a home in Remuera valued at NZ$7.68 million. In late 2024, he stated, "Let's be clear, I'm wealthy," in response to questions about his property sales. After becoming prime minister, he initially claimed a NZ$52,000 accommodation allowance, but later repaid all amounts received, stating the issue had become a distraction. He sold three properties in 2024, with Stuff estimating a potential profit of up to $769,500. As Leader of the Opposition, he used public funds to pay for Māori language lessons, stating it was relevant to his role, but once prime minister, the government considered discontinuing incentive payments for public servants to learn te reo. The government's economic policies, centered on tax cuts and reducing public spending, led to a protracted recession with per capita GDP falling 4.6% since September 2022, inflation peaking at 7.3%, unemployment rising from 3.7% in June 2023 to 5.2% by late 2025, and persistent GP shortages, with over 250,000 unregistered patients and productivity losses exceeding $1 billion annually. Emergency department wait times and staffing shortages have worsened, and despite efforts to recognize overseas qualifications and establish a third medical school, little progress has been made. Luxon has consistently defended the scale of job losses and public service cuts, and in August 2024, he warned young unemployed people that their "free ride" under Labour would end under National, stating the government would make sweeping cuts to the Ministry of Social Development in favor of privatised employment agencies. His coalition dynamics with deputy prime ministers Winston Peters and David Seymour have been controversial, as they have openly challenged his authority. In foreign policy, his government increased military spending and Five Eyes cooperation, reflecting a general pro-United States shift.

The Government introduced legislation to combat abuse in care, including banning strip searches on children and strengthening security checks for individuals working with children. In August 2022, Luxon warned young unemployed people that their "free ride" under Labour would end if National won the 2023 election, stating that under National, such benefits would end and that the Ministry of Social Development would face sweeping cuts in favour of privatised employment agencies, with no funding for failure. In August 2024, Luxon and Louise Upston announced a "traffic light" regime for welfare, introducing escalating consequences for beneficiaries who fail to meet job-seeking obligations; from early 2025, jobseeker beneficiaries must reapply for benefits every six months instead of annually, and a new community work sanction requiring beneficiaries to "build skills and confidence" was introduced. When interviewed on TVNZ and RNZ's Morning Report, Luxon could not answer questions about how much beneficiaries actually receive. In October 2025, Luxon and Upston confirmed that welfare eligibility for 18 and 19-year-olds would be tightened, with those whose parents earn over NZ$65,000 becoming ineligible for Jobseeker and other emergency benefits from November 2026; 18 and 19-year-olds with dependent children or who are estranged from their parents would remain eligible. Luxon stated: "We're here to help and support as much as we can, but you also have to take responsibility for that and actually just consigning you to a life of welfare for 18 years is unacceptable." Since becoming prime minister, Luxon has made overseas trips to Australia, the Pacific, Southeast Asia, Japan, and the United States, where he met Chinese leaders. According to The Economist and Foreign Policy, New Zealand's foreign policy under the National-led coalition has shifted away from China toward closer ties with its traditional Five Eyes partners—United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. During an interview with The Economist, Luxon said he was looking to "diversify New Zealand's diplomatic and trade relationships away from its reliance on China," a shift described as the country's biggest pivot since the 1986 ANZUS dispute over nuclear policy. Foreign Policy columnist Derek Grossman noted that Luxon and Foreign Minister Winston Peters were continuing a thaw in New Zealand–United States relations initiated under John Key in 2010 and continued by Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins, with examples including the Royal New Zealand Navy sailing through the Taiwan Strait and the government's expressed interest in AUKUS and NATO. In late August 2024, Luxon supported Taiwan's participation in the Pacific Islands Forum in response to Chinese efforts to exclude Taiwan from the 2025 event. In April 2025, the Government announced a $12 billion allocation for defence over four years, raising spending to 2% of GDP from 1%; this amount matches the Treasury's estimate needed to halve child poverty by 2028. The Child Poverty Action Group highlighted the auditor-general's criticism of the government for lacking a coherent plan to address rising child poverty, raising public concerns about defence spending versus social welfare. On 20 December 2023, Luxon made his first state visit to Sydney, meeting Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, reaffirming New Zealand's nuclear-free policy while expressing openness to joining the non-nuclear pillar of AUKUS and stating a commitment to "heavy lifting" in the Australia–New Zealand defence relationship. Between 9 and 10 August 2025, Luxon hosted Albanese in Queenstown for annual bilateral talks, discussing trade, defence, the Gaza war, and Australia's 501 deportation policy; local and civil society leaders including Mayor Glyn Lewers, MP Joseph Mooney, Ngai Tahu Tipene O'Regan, Edward Ellison, and Cliff Curtis attended. The leaders laid wreaths at a memorial to fallen ANZAC soldiers in Arrowtown on 10 August. Luxon has consistently opposed Australia's 501 deportation policy, calling it "regrettable" and "not right," especially when it results in people with minimal ties to New Zealand being deported; he expressed disappointment that Australia reversed its more lenient approach, which considered length of residence and family connections. He stated, "It's just not right that people who have no connection to New Zealand are deported to New Zealand." Following discussions with Albanese, Luxon said: "We respect the fact that Australia has its own policies around deportation," but hoped common sense would prevail. Luxon's leadership has been challenged by his coalition partners, David Seymour (ACT) and Winston Peters (NZ First), with concerns over his perceived lack of control. A 2024 poll found that 51% of respondents believed Luxon was the decision-maker. David Seymour has openly challenged Luxon's authority, particularly on the Treaty Principles Bill, and has publicly contradicted the prime minister, reinforcing perceptions of weak leadership; Seymour asserts Luxon cannot unilaterally sack ACT ministers. Winston Peters is seen as unpredictable and influential, having, for example, in March 2024, undercut Finance Minister Nicola Willis by claiming a $5.6 billion fiscal hole from her tax cuts. Luxon's background as a corporate executive has led to criticism of his communication style, including the use of business jargon such as referring to voters as "customers," and appearing out of touch. Janet Wilson, former chief press secretary for the National Party, said he memorises talking points and sounds like a "talking robot." Luxon has also been criticised for avoiding direct answers, notably during the Andrew Bayly resignation saga, when he sidestepped questions about whether he would have sacked Bayly, eventually conceding he would have "demoted" him and that "you can call it sacked," a performance widely described as evasive. His handling of the Treaty Principles Bill—supporting its introduction but pledging to vote against it later—has been seen as lacking conviction and clarity, with Luxon claiming that allowing a first reading was "worth it to form government." In April 2024, a 1News-Verian poll showed the coalition government behind the left bloc, with 51% of respondents believing Luxon was the decision-maker. A Talbot Mills poll suggested a Labour-led government would have a bare majority of 62 seats, while Roy Morgan found 54% of respondents believed New Zealand was heading in the wrong direction, with only 35% believing it was in the right direction. In June, a poll showed Luxon fell behind opposition leader Chris Hipkins in net favourability for the first time. Opinion polls indicate that Luxon's unpopularity has deepened over his first 18 months in office, with his net favourability lower than that of previous first-term prime ministers such as Helen Clark, John Key, and Jacinda Ardern. Max Rashbrooke, a senior research associate at Victoria University of Wellington, noted that a common criticism is Luxon's "inability to articulate what he stands for" or what he aims to achieve. In October 2025, The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll found that 27% of voters viewed Luxon positively, while 51% had an unfavourable view. Luxon is an evangelical Christian and a social conservative. In his maiden parliamentary speech, he described himself as centre-right and moderate; the government is described as conservative and right-wing, one of the most so since the 1990s. Luxon supports low taxes, cuts to the Ministry of Social Development, military-style boot-camps for young offenders, stringent anti-gang legislation, and opposes welfare dependency and co-governance with Māori. In November 2019, he said he was against abortion, euthanasia, and legalising recreational cannabis, though he supported medicinal cannabis; he previously supported a "no jab, no pay" policy for unvaccinated children, but after becoming leader of the National Party, he stated he did not support cutting benefits for parents who do not vaccinate children against COVID-19. He has also firmly opposed efforts to reform New Zealand's water system. His anti-abortion views drew media attention after his election as National leader; he confirmed his personal opposition to abortion but stated that National would not contest the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. After previously declining to answer whether he believed abortion was tantamount to murder, he said in an interview with Newshub that he is "a pro-life person," and when asked again, responded "that's what a pro-life position is." In response to the Gaza war, Luxon stated he was shocked and saddened by Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel, condemned Hamas's actions, and stated Israel had a right to defend itself. He committed New Zealand to active military support, saying "I want us to be in lockstep with our partners who have common interests and actually be right there with them at that time." In January 2024, he authorised the deployment of 6 NZDF personnel to support military action against Houthi forces in the Red Sea, stating it was about standing up for beliefs and demonstrating real capability. On 30 January 2024, Luxon announced New Zealand would suspend its annual NZ$1 million aid to UNRWA following allegations that some UNRWA workers participated in the October 7 attacks, following a Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade review of aid to UNRWA. On 29 February 2024, he designated Hamas in its entirety as a terrorist entity. As the Gaza war continued, Luxon's position evolved; on 2 December 2024, he confirmed New Zealand would comply with an International Criminal Court arrest warrant if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited New Zealand, stating: "We believe in the international rules-based system, we support the ICC, and we would be obligated to do so." In June 2025, he described sanctions on Israeli ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir as "entirely appropriate." On 9 August 2025, Luxon and Albanese called for a ceasefire in Gaza and opposed Israeli plans to occupy Gaza City. On 13 August 2025, Luxon made remarks in Parliament criticising Israel's conduct, describing it as "utterly, utterly appalling" and stating that "I think Netanyahu has gone way too far. I think he has lost the plot." In late November 2021, Luxon said conversion therapy was "abhorrent"; in early February 2022, he supported the LGBT+ community and announced National MPs would have a conscience vote on the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill, which passed its third and final reading on 15 February 2022, with Luxon voting in favour. Although he frequently criticised Labour's pandemic management, on 8 January 2022, he stated National strongly supported COVID-19 vaccination, describing it as the best protection for people and families. In response to US President Donald Trump's 2025 APEC announcement to resume nuclear testing, Luxon expressed disapproval and reiterated his commitment to New Zealand's nuclear-free policy. On 20 September 2024, Luxon said the coalition was open to holding a referendum to extend the parliamentary term from three to four years at the 2026 election. On 27 February 2025, the government introduced the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Bill to conduct a referendum. On 3 May 2023, Luxon acknowledged the historical sensitivity of the 1970s dawn raids, which disproportionately targeted Pasifika New Zealanders, but stated Immigration New Zealand needed to "reserve the option" to use police raids against individuals involved in serious criminal offending or posing a security risk. He also stated there were 14,000 overstayers in New Zealand, in response to media coverage of recent dawn raid tactics criticised by Deputy Prime Minister Carmel Sepuloni for re-traumatising the Pasifika community. On 11 December 2023, Luxon said New Zealand's 118,000 annual net migration rate was unsustainable and that infrastructure needed better management to support growth, following Australia's announcement of a new migration strategy. In late January 2023, Luxon stated National opposed co-governance in health, education, and critical infrastructure, though he supported "self-driven" Māori initiatives such as Whānau Ora, kohanga reo, and charter schools. On 25 January, he said the existence of Māori seats "doesn't make a lot of sense." During Waitangi Day on 6 February 2023, Luxon described the Treaty of Waitangi as a "challenging, imperfect but ultimately inspiring document" through which New Zealand sought to understand the intentions of those who signed it, acknowledging the Crown had not upheld its promises and expressing hope that the Treaty settlement process would be completed by 2030.
