During a Question Time on 20 August 2024, Luxon said he believed Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown by signing the Treaty, and when questioned by Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, reiterated that the Treaty was New Zealand's founding document and protected both Māori and Crown interests. On 19 December 2024, Luxon confirmed he would not attend events at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds on 4 February 2025, stating he intended to celebrate Waitangi Day across New Zealand with different iwi. National Waitangi Trust chairperson Pita Tipene expressed disappointment, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that Luxon's decision was not in line with the spirit of the Treaty.

During Waitangi Day on 6 February 2023, Luxon described the Treaty of Waitangi as a "challenging, imperfect but ultimately inspiring document through which New Zealand had sought to understand what was intended by those who signed it." While acknowledging that the New Zealand Crown had not upheld the Treaty's promises and obligations, he expressed hope that the Treaty settlement process would be completed by 2030. During a Question Time in Parliament on 20 August 2024, Luxon stated that he believed Māori ceded sovereignty to the New Zealand Crown by signing the Treaty of Waitangi, and reiterated that the Treaty was New Zealand's founding document, protecting both Māori and Crown interests. On 19 December 2024, Luxon confirmed he would not attend events at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds on 4 February 2025, stating his intention to celebrate Waitangi Day around New Zealand with different iwi; National Waitangi Trust chairperson Pita Tipene expressed disappointment with the decision, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Luxon was "running away from problems of his own creation." Luxon describes himself as a "soft republican" and believes New Zealand will "ultimately" become a republic, but that the change would not happen "in my Government and in my time." On 1 March 2025, Luxon said the school lunch programme was experiencing "teething issues" due to quality and delivery problems, adding that Associate Education Minister Seymour "will work his way through those issues... and I expect he will [find a solution]." On 4 March, during a press conference, he told parents dissatisfied with the programme to "make a marmite sandwich and put an apple in a bag," a remark that drew criticism from Hora Hora School principal Pat Newman, Child Poverty Action Group executive officer Sarita Divis, and East Otago High School principal Helen Newcombe, who argued that school lunches are needed to improve student health and educational outcomes and combat child poverty. In response, Luxon defended his remarks and reiterated the Government's commitment to resolving programme issues. In February 2024, Luxon stated that sex education should be age appropriate and that parents should be able to withdraw their children from such classes if they choose. In March 2023, when asked if anti-transgender activist Posie Parker should be allowed into New Zealand, Luxon affirmed people's right to free speech but said he "absolutely" supported the rights of New Zealand's transgender community. In mid-August, he said there is no need for laws specifying which toilets transgender people can use, and during a TVNZ debate with Prime Minister Chris Hipkins in September, he stated that transgender participation in sports should be left to sporting bodies. Luxon met his wife Amanda at a church youth group and they married on 8 January 1994 when he was 23; they have a son and daughter, and the couple share the same faith, saying "it quietly guides what they care about." In late July 2022, Luxon confirmed he was on a family holiday in Hawaii during the parliamentary recess when a Facebook video post on 21 July implied he was visiting Te Puke; he attributed the confusion to a delay in his social media team updating his whereabouts, which he called a mistake. Luxon had a Catholic upbringing but describes himself as a non-denominational Christian; after returning to New Zealand in 2011, he attended the Upper Room church in Auckland, but now does not go to a regular church, stating he doesn't even go to church every Sunday. In his maiden speech in Parliament, he said “My faith is personal to me. It is not in itself a political agenda.” Luxon has never drunk alcohol in his life, making that decision at about seven or eight years old, citing his grandfather's drinking problems as the reason. He enjoys DIY, listening to country music, waterskiing, and fishing; he is a supporter of the Crusaders rugby union team and Auckland FC in association football, attending Auckland FC's first ever A-League Men match in 2024, where he was pranked by a fan who flicked his nose while posing for a photo. Luxon has a long-standing friendship with former Prime Minister John Key, with whom he used to ask questions about the pros and cons of being a prime minister; in an interview with podcaster Dom Harvey, he said the friendship includes their wives, who spend considerable time together and try to catch up every weekend. He described the relationship as "really special" and said it is especially meaningful as a Prime Minister to have a former Prime Minister as a friend, though he emphasizes that when they talk, they are "mates first, and politics is second." In 2017, while Luxon was chief executive at Air New Zealand, John Key was appointed as an Air New Zealand director; both resigned from Air New Zealand in 2019. In 2015, Luxon was named the Deloitte Top 200 CEO of the Year for his leadership at Air New Zealand, and in 2019, he won a BLAKE Award for his sustainability initiatives at Air New Zealand.

Sir Christopher Edward Nolan, born on 30 July 1970 in Westminster, London, is a British and American filmmaker recognized as a leading figure of the 21st century. His films have generated over $6 billion worldwide, making him the seventh-highest-grossing film director. He has won two Academy Awards, a Golden Globe Award, and two British Academy Film Awards. Nolan was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2019 and knighted in 2024 for his contributions to film. He developed an interest in filmmaking from a young age, beginning to make films at seven using his father's Super 8 camera and action figures, including a stop motion animation titled Space Wars. His uncle, who worked at NASA, sent him launch footage that he re-filmed and edited. From age 11, he aspired to be a professional filmmaker. He studied English literature at University College London, where he was president of the Film Society and co-screened feature films in 35mm with his future wife, Emma Thomas. After graduating in 1993, he worked as a script reader, camera operator, and director of corporate films. He directed, wrote, and edited the short film Larceny (1996), which premiered at the Cambridge Film Festival and is considered one of UCL's best shorts, and later made Doodlebug (1997). He and Thomas attempted to make a feature film titled Larry Mahoney, which they abandoned due to lack of industry support. His first feature film, Following (1998), which he wrote, directed, photographed, and edited, was made on a budget of around £3,000 with friends and used minimal equipment, and was well-received by critics who compared it to Hitchcock. It led to the creation of Memento (2000), a film developed from a short story by his brother Jonathan, which told the story in reverse and earned critical acclaim, including nominations for Best Screenplay and Best Director, and was listed as one of the best films of the 2000s. Memento earned Nolan two Independent Spirit Awards and led to the founding of Syncopy Inc. with Thomas in 2001. After Memento, he was recommended by Steven Soderbergh to Warner Bros. to direct Insomnia (2002), a remake of the 1997 Norwegian film, which received positive reviews and earned $113 million against a $46 million budget. Following Memento and Insomnia, Nolan established himself as an auteur. He was briefly attached to direct a Howard Hughes biopic and a Ruth Rendell novel adaptation before choosing to direct Batman Begins (2005), which revived the franchise and was praised for its psychological depth and realism. The film starred Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, Morgan Freeman, and Liam Neeson and was the biggest project he had undertaken to that point. He then directed The Prestige (2006), an adaptation of a Christopher Priest novel co-written with his brother Jonathan, which received critical acclaim and two Academy Award nominations. The Dark Knight (2008), the sequel to Batman Begins, expanded on the noir quality of the first film and became one of the best superhero films ever made, earning over $1 billion worldwide and winning two Academy Awards: Best Sound Editing and a posthumous Best Supporting Actor award for Heath Ledger. The film's failure to receive a Best Picture nomination prompted the Academy to increase the number of nominees from five to ten, known as "The Dark Knight Rule." Nolan then directed Inception (2010), a film he had conceived around nine years earlier, which became a critical and commercial success, named the best film of 2010 by Mark Kermode and praised for its philosophical themes. The film grossed over $836 million worldwide and was nominated for eight Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay, winning Best Cinematography. After the release of Tenet (2020), Nolan parted ways with Warner Bros. Pictures and signed with Universal Pictures for Oppenheimer (2023), which won him Academy Awards for Best Director and Best Picture. Nolan's films are known for their metaphysical themes, exploration of epistemology, existentialism, ethics, time, memory, and personal identity, use of mathematically inspired imagery, unconventional narrative structures, practical special effects, experimental soundscapes, large-format film photography, and materialistic perspectives. He is a strong advocate for traditional film stock over digital cameras. He has co-written several films with his brother Jonathan and runs the production company Syncopy Inc. with his wife, Emma Thomas. Nolan and Thomas have maintained strong ties with University College London, with both receiving honorary fellowships and Nolan receiving an honorary doctorate in 2017.

Christopher Nolan's success with The Dark Knight led Warner Bros. to sign him to write, direct, and co-produce Inception (2010), an idea he had developed around nine years earlier. Described as a contemporary sci-fi action film set within the architecture of the mind, Inception starred a large ensemble led by Leonardo DiCaprio and became a critical and commercial success, grossing over $836 million worldwide. Film critic Mark Kermode named it the best film of 2010, calling it proof that cinema can be both blockbuster and art. Philosophy professor David Kyle Johnson praised it as a classic almost immediately, highlighting its exploration of philosophical themes like leap of faith and the allegory of the cave. The film earned nominations for eight Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay, and won in Best Cinematography, Best Sound Mixing, Best Sound Editing, and Best Visual Effects. Nolan also received a BAFTA and a Golden Globe nomination for Best Director. Around the release of The Dark Knight Rises (2012), Joseph Bevan of the British Film Institute noted that Nolan had transitioned from promising British indie director to master of intelligent escapism. After initial hesitation, Nolan agreed to direct the film, working with his brother and David S. Goyer to develop a story that would conclude the trilogy on a high note. The film received positive reviews, with Kenneth Turan calling it "potent, persuasive and hypnotic" and Christy Lemire describing it as "typically spectacular, ambitious" though criticizing its "overloaded" story and grimness. It became the thirteenth film to gross $1 billion and was followed by a tragic shooting at a midnight showing in Aurora, Colorado, where 12 people were killed and 58 injured; Nolan issued a statement expressing condolences for the victims. The Dark Knight trilogy inspired a trend in superhero films to adopt its gritty, realistic tone, with Ben Child of The Guardian calling the trilogy "thrilling totems of the genre for decades to come." During story discussions for The Dark Knight Rises, Goyer proposed Man of Steel (2013), which Nolan produced after being impressed by Zack Snyder’s work in 300 (2006) and Watchmen (2009), and hired Snyder to direct. The film, starring Henry Cavill as Clark Kent, received mixed reviews and grossed over $660 million against a $220 million budget. Nolan then directed, wrote, and produced Interstellar (2014), originally scripted by Jonathan Nolan and initially intended for Steven Spielberg. Based on scientific theories by Kip Thorne, the film follows astronauts traveling through a wormhole in search of a new home for humanity. In a 2014 discussion, Nolan expressed admiration for scientific objectivity, wishing it were applied broadly. Interstellar, starring Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, and Jessica Chastain, received positive reviews and grossed $773 million worldwide. A. O. Scott of The New York Times called it a "sweeping, futuristic adventure driven by grief, dread and regret," while documentary filmmaker Toni Myers praised its exploration of multi-generational storytelling. The film was lauded for its scientific accuracy, leading to two academic papers and a call from the American Journal of Physics for its inclusion in school science curricula. At the 87th Academy Awards, it won Best Visual Effects and received four other nominations. In 2014, Nolan and Emma Thomas served as executive producers on Transcendence, the directorial debut of cinematographer Wally Pfister. In the mid-2010s, Nolan supported film preservation through Syncopy’s joint venture with Zeitgeist Films to release Blu-ray editions of Zeitgeist’s films. He directed the documentary short Quay (2015) for the Brothers Quay’s animation films and initiated a theatrical tour showcasing their works. As an advocate for analogue film, Nolan and visual artist Tacita Dean hosted an informal summit on Reframing the Future of Film at the Getty Museum in March 2015, with follow-up events in London, Mexico City, and Mumbai. In April 2015, he joined the board of directors of The Film Foundation and was appointed, alongside Martin Scorsese, to the National Film Preservation Board by the Library of Congress as a DGA representative. He also serves on the Motion Picture & Television Fund Board of Governors. After serving as an executive producer on Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016) and Justice League (2017), Nolan returned to directing with Dunkirk (2017), a film based on his original screenplay and co-produced with Thomas. Set during World War II in 1940, it follows the evacuation of Allied soldiers from Dunkirk, France, and is structured as a survival tale with minimal dialogue. Nolan waited to make it until he earned trust from a major studio to produce it as a British film with an American budget. Before filming, he sought advice from Spielberg, who advised him to prioritize research over imagination. The film, starring an ensemble cast, received widespread critical acclaim and grossed over $526 million worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing World War II film of all time. Mick LaSalle of the San Francisco Chronicle called it "one of the best war films ever made," and it earned Nolan his first Oscar nomination for Best Director. In 2018, Nolan supervised a new 70 mm print of Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), made from the original camera negative, and presented it at the 2018 Cannes Film Festival, where it was met with a standing ovation. In 2019, Nolan and Thomas received executive producer credits on The Doll's Breath, an animated short by the Quay brothers. His next film, Tenet (2020), described by Tom Shone as a "globe-spinning riff on all things Nolanesque," had been in development for over a decade and took more than five years to write. Delayed three times due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was the first major Hollywood tent-pole to open in theatres after the shutdown. The film follows an unnamed protagonist (played by John David Washington) who travels through time to stop a world-threatening attack. It grossed $363 million worldwide on a $200 million budget, becoming Nolan’s first box-office underperformer. Critics found it polarizing, praising its ambition and technical aspects while criticizing its confusing narrative. Peter Bradshaw awarded it five stars, calling it a "cerebral cadenza" with "supercharged energy and imagination," while Leslie Felperin described it as "a chilly, cerebral film" that is "easy to admire but almost impossible to love." At the 93rd Academy Awards, it won Best Visual Effects and was nominated for Best Production Design. Following its release, Nolan joined the Advisory Board of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers and served as an executive producer on Zack Snyder’s Justice League (2021), a director’s cut of the 2017 film. Nolan’s 12th film, Oppenheimer (2023), is a biopic based on J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in developing the atomic bomb, marking his first R-rated film since Insomnia (2002) and his first feature not made for Warner Bros. Financed and distributed by Universal Pictures, it was made with a $100 million production budget and equal marketing budget, offering Nolan total creative control, 20% of first-dollar gross, a 100-day theatrical window, and a blackout period. The film received critical acclaim, with Matthew Jackson of The A.V. Club calling it a "masterpiece" and the best of Nolan’s career, and BBC Culture’s Caryn James describing it as "boldly imaginative and his most mature work yet," combining the action of The Dark Knight trilogy with the cerebral depth of Memento, Inception, and Tenet. It grossed over $975 million worldwide, becoming the third-highest-grossing film of 2023. Nolan won the Academy Awards for Best Director and Best Picture. In 2025, he was elected president of the Directors Guild of America, representing over 19,500 members. His next directorial effort, The Odyssey, an adaptation of Homer’s epic poem, is scheduled for release in July 2026 and follows Odysseus (played by Matt Damon) on his journey home after the Trojan War, including encounters with Polyphemus, the Sirens, and Circe, and his reunion with Penelope. With an estimated $250 million budget, it will be the most expensive film of his career and the first mainstream blockbuster shot entirely on IMAX film. Nolan is married to Emma Thomas, whom he met at University College London when he was 19; she has worked as a producer on all his films since 1997. The couple has four children and resides in Los Angeles. They were included in the Sunday Times Rich List of 2025 with an estimated net worth of £360 million. Nolan prefers to maintain mystery about his work, refusing to discuss his personal life and stating he does not want audiences to think of him while watching his films. He does not own a smartphone or email address, instead hand-delivering scripts to actors and having his wife manage outreach. His films are centered on metaphysical themes such as time, memory, and personal identity, featuring mathematically inspired ideas, unconventional narratives, materialistic perspectives, and evocative sound. Guillermo del Toro called him an "emotional mathematician," and Will Gompertz described him as an "art house auteur making intellectually ambitious blockbuster movies that can leave your pulse racing and your head spinning." Joseph Bevan wrote that his films allow arthouse audiences to enjoy superhero films and multiplex crowds to engage with complex plots. Nolan views himself as "an indie filmmaker working inside the studio system." Critics have noted that Nolan defies Hollywood norms by creating original, complex genre films that challenge studio expectations, yet his films consistently draw large audiences. In The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan, professional philosophers and writers analyzed his work, identifying themes of self-destruction, truth, and the nature of heroes and villains. Robbie B. H. Goh described Nolan as a "philosophical filmmaker" who integrates existentialism, morality, epistemology, and the distinction between appearance and reality into action and suspense-driven films, maintaining engagement while offering deeper reflection. David Bordwell described Nolan’s work as experiments with cinematic time using subjective viewpoints and crosscutting. His use of practical effects, miniatures, models, and shooting on celluloid has been influential in early 21st century cinema. IndieWire noted that Nolan kept a viable alternative to computer-generated filmmaking alive. Stuart Joy described him as a "complete filmmaker" who oversees all aspects of production and manages external cultural and industrial factors. Nolan has made some of the most influential and popular films of his time, with many regarded as among the best of their decades. According to The Wall Street Journal, his ability to combine box-office success with artistic ambition has given him significant industry clout. His films have earned over $6 billion. Memento and The Dark Knight have been selected by the National Film Registry.

Christopher Nolan's use of practical, in-camera effects, miniatures, models, and shooting on celluloid film has been highly influential in early 21st century cinema. IndieWire noted in 2019 that Nolan "kept a viable alternate model of big-budget filmmaking alive," emphasizing that in an era where blockbuster filmmaking has become "a largely computer-generated art form," his approach remains significant. Due to his deep involvement in the technical and creative aspects of production, Stuart Joy described him as a "complete filmmaker" who "oversees all aspects of production while also managing cultural and industrial factors outside of the text." Nolan has produced some of the most influential and popular films of his time, with many regarded by critics as among the best of their respective decades. According to The Wall Street Journal, his ability to combine box-office success with artistic ambition has given him substantial industry clout. His films have earned more than $6 billion. Memento and The Dark Knight have been selected by the US Library of Congress for preservation in the National Film Registry for their cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance. These films, along with Inception, appeared in BBC's 100 Greatest Films of the 21st Century and The Hollywood Reporter's poll of best films ever made. In 2017, The Dark Knight, Inception, and Interstellar were included in Empire magazine's "The 100 Greatest Movies." In 2018, The Hollywood Reporter listed Nolan as one of the 100 most powerful people in entertainment, describing him as a "franchise unto himself." Parade ranked him number eight in its 2022 list of 75 Best Movie Directors of All Time. Five of his films were included in The New York Times 2025 list of The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century, and Memento, The Dark Knight, and Oppenheimer appeared in Rolling Stone's list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century." His work has been "intensely embraced, analysed and debated by ordinary film fans as by critics and film academics." Geoff Andrew of the British Film Institute called him a "persuasively inventive storyteller" and noted that his films are notable for their brilliant narrative ingenuity and adult engagement with complex philosophical questions rather than technical virtuosity. David Bordwell considers Nolan "one of the most accomplished living filmmakers," citing his ability to transform genre films into art and event films, along with his critical acclaim, box office success, and popularity. In 2008, Philip French named Nolan "the first major talent to emerge this century." Mark Kermode praised him for bringing the discipline and ethics of art-house filmmaking to Hollywood blockbusters, stating he proves profitability without appealing to the lowest common denominator. The Observer's Ryan Gilbey described Nolan as a "skillful, stylish storyteller" capable of merging Spielberg's spectacle with Roeg's or Resnais' intellectual depth. Mark Cousins applauded Nolan for embracing big ideas, noting that Hollywood filmmakers generally avoid such concepts—unlike Nolan. Scott Foundas of Variety called him "the premier big-canvas storyteller of his generation," while Justin Chang of the Los Angeles Times labeled him "the great proceduralist of 21st century blockbuster filmmaking, a lover of nuts-and-bolts minutiae." Nolan has been praised by contemporaries, with Kenneth Branagh calling his approach to large-scale filmmaking "unique in modern cinema" and stating he remains an artist and auteur, a heroic figure for audiences and behind-the-scenes professionals. Michael Mann credited Nolan with "inventing the post-heroic superhero" and highlighting his "singular vision." Nicolas Roeg noted that while "commercial art" is often self-negating, Nolan's work is deeply poetic despite being in the commercial arena. Martin Scorsese described Nolan as creating "beautifully made films on a big scale." Damien Chazelle praised Nolan for making seemingly impersonal projects like superhero epics and deep-space mind-benders feel deeply personal. Steven Spielberg referred to Nolan's Dark Knight series as an example of both art and blockbuster, and has described Memento and Inception as "masterworks." Denis Villeneuve expressed admiration for Nolan's ability to maintain his identity and create a distinct universe at scale, bringing intellectual concepts to the screen in a rare and impressive way. Nolan has been nominated for eight Academy Awards (winning two), eight British Academy Film Awards (winning two), and six Golden Globe Awards (winning one). From 2011 to 2014, he appeared on Forbes Celebrity 100 list based on income and popularity. In 2015, he was included in Time's 100 most influential people in the world. In 2006, he was named an Honorary Fellow of UCL; in 2017, he received an honorary doctorate in literature. In 2012, he became the youngest director to receive a hand-and-footprint ceremony at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles. In 2019, he was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire for services to film. In 2023, he received the Federation of American Scientists' Public Service Award for his depiction of scientists in Oppenheimer. In 2024, he was awarded the British Film Institute Fellowship for his "extraordinary achievements and enormous contribution to cinema" and the Honorary César award for "continually pushing the boundaries of storytelling." In March 2024, Nolan was made a knight bachelor for his contributions to film, and his wife Emma Thomas was honoured with a damehood.

ChromeOS, a proprietary operating system developed by Google, is derived from the open-source ChromiumOS, which itself originates from Gentoo Linux, and uses the Google Chrome web browser as its primary user interface. Google announced the project in July 2009, initially describing it as a cloud-based operating system where applications and user data reside in the cloud, primarily running web applications. The operating system first shipped with Chromebooks in 2011 and has since been offered as an installable Linux distribution called ChromeOS Flex since 2020. ChromeOS supports progressive web applications, Android apps from Google Play, and Linux applications. In 2025, Google confirmed that ChromeOS will transition from the Linux kernel to the Android kernel, resulting in a merged development path with Android, formally announced at the Snapdragon Summit in September 2025 under the internal codename "Aluminium OS." The new operating system will be desktop-optimized, running the same Android software on both desktop and mobile devices, adapted for different screen sizes, and will support both ARM and x86 processors, with the x86 version expected to be the first mainline maintained x86 architecture version of Android. Jeff Nelson, a Google employee, created the concept of ChromeOS in 2006 as "Google OS," initially a Linux distribution focused on speed, and early versions used Firefox before switching to Chrome in 2007. To determine marketing needs, developers analyzed usage patterns from 200 Google employee machines and their own usage. Google required hardware partners to use solid-state drives for performance and reliability, noting that ChromeOS requires only one-sixtieth the drive space of Windows 7; in 2019, ChromeOS recovery images were still between 1 and 3 GB in size. On November 19, 2009, Google released the source code as the ChromiumOS project, and at a news conference, Sundar Pichai demonstrated an early version that booted in seven seconds and featured a desktop resembling Chrome with application tabs. Chris Kenyon of Canonical announced a contract to contribute engineering resources, and Canonical was an early engineering partner; initially, ChromiumOS could only be built on Ubuntu, but in February 2010, the team switched to Gentoo Linux due to its flexible package management system, and the build environment is no longer restricted to any distribution, though installation guides use Debian (and thus Ubuntu) apt syntax. In 2010, Google released the unbranded Cr-48 Chromebook in a pilot program, with retail hardware delayed until 2011. On May 11, 2011, Google announced two Chromebooks from Acer and Samsung at Google I/O; the Samsung model launched on June 15, 2011, and the Acer model in mid-July. In August 2011, Netflix announced official support for ChromeOS, and later that month, Citrix released a client for remote access to Windows applications. Dublin City University became the first European educational institution to provide Chromebooks to students in September 2011. By 2012, demand for Chromebooks grew, and Google introduced new devices from Samsung, including the first Chromebox, the Samsung Series 3, and a lower-priced Chromebook in October 2012 priced at $250, using an ARM processor from Samsung's Exynos line, with reduced memory and screen resolution; Acer followed with the C7 Chromebook at $199, using an Intel Celeron processor and a laptop hard disk to reduce cost. In April 2012, Google introduced the Aura window manager and a conventional taskbar, marking a shift from a single-browser interface to a more traditional desktop experience. Google Drive integration was added in ChromeOS version 20, released in July 2012, and Adobe Flash support was fully sandboxed by the end of 2012. Before 2013, Google did not manufacture its own ChromeOS devices, which were designed and marketed by third-party partners; this changed in February 2013 with the release of the Chromebook Pixel, which featured an Intel Core i5 processor, a 2,560×1,700 touchscreen, and a price competitive with business laptops. By the end of 2013, analysts were divided on ChromeOS's future, despite predictions of its demise since 2009, as device sales continued to grow. In mid-2014, Time magazine published a piece highlighting conflicting views on Chromebooks' success. Intel's announcement of Intel-based Chromebooks, Chromeboxes, and LG's Chromebase further fueled uncertainty. Seizing the opportunity from the end of Windows XP support, Google offered significant discounts in early 2014 to promote Chromebooks in businesses. ChromeOS devices outsold Apple Macs worldwide in 2020. Since July 2021, ChromeOS's embedded controller has been based on a Google-maintained fork of Zephyr, a real-time operating system. In March 2014, Google hosted a hacking contest called Pwnium, where two exploits were demonstrated and a third at Pwn2Own; all were patched within a week. Google Native Client has been available since 2010, but few apps existed initially; in June 2014, Google announced ChromeOS would sync with Android phones and run Android apps from Google Play, expanding app availability. Google also adopted Material Design, with a new default wallpaper introduced in 2014 and fully integrated in Chrome 117. Chrome Enterprise, launched in 2017, includes ChromeOS, Chrome Browser, and device management features for businesses, offering standard features like bookmark and extension syncing, cloud printing, multi-layered security, remote desktop, and automatic updates, and advanced features such as Active Directory integration, unified endpoint management, advanced security, device policies, guest access, kiosk mode, and app whitelisting/blacklisting. The education sector was an early adopter, and Chromebooks are widely used in classrooms, with cloud-based computing advantages gaining traction in financial services, healthcare, and retail. ICT managers cite benefits such as advanced security, simplified management, reduced operational costs, and secure file access across devices. Google's Grab and Go program allows businesses to provide employees access to fully charged Chromebooks for checkout and return. In February 2014, Google released Chromebox for Meetings, a kit for conference rooms with a Chromebox, camera, noise-cancelling microphone, speakers, and remote control, supporting Google Hangouts, Vidyo, and UberConference. Partners released various models, and in 2016, Google introduced an all-in-one Chromebase for smaller meeting rooms. Google targeted the consumer market with the Chromebook in 2011 and the Chromebook Pixel in 2013, and expanded into enterprise with the Pixelbook in 2017, with a second-generation model released in 2019. In 2021, several vendors offered all-in-one Chromebase devices. Google has partnered with OEMs including Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Samsung; in August 2019, Dell launched the Latitude 5300 2-in-1 Chromebook Enterprise and Latitude 5400 Chromebook Enterprise, designed for security-conscious organizations and bundled with cloud-based support services. Other OEMs like Acer and HP also launched devices with Chrome Enterprise Upgrade. With a broader hardware range, ChromeOS became a viable option for enterprises avoiding migration to Windows 10 before Windows 7 support ended. Laptops running ChromeOS are known as Chromebooks; the first was the CR-48, released to testers in December 2010, with retail models following in May 2011. A desktop design, the Chromebox, was released by Samsung in May 2012, and a partnership with AOPEN led to the first commercial Chromebox in March 2015. In early 2014, LG introduced the first Chromebase, a monitor with built-in camera, microphone, and speakers. The Chromebit is an HDMI dongle that turns a TV or monitor into a personal computer; the first, an Asus model, shipped in November 2015 and reached end of life in November 2020. In March 2018, Acer launched the Chromebook Tab 10, a tablet with a screen size and resolution identical to the Apple iPad and a Wacom-branded stylus that does not require charging. ChromeOS supports multi-monitor setups via video-out ports, USB 3.0 Standard-A, or USB-C, with USB-C being preferred. On February 16, 2022, Google announced a development version of ChromeOS Flex, a distribution that can be installed on conventional PC hardware to replace Windows or macOS, similar to CloudReady, which Google acquired in 2020. ChromeOS automatic updates are available for 10 years for all Chromebooks manufactured in 2019 and onwards, covering the operating system, browser, and hardware; Google maintains a web page detailing the auto-update policy and end dates. Previously, the update period was 8 years, and shorter before that, though earlier models received updates for longer. Initially, ChromeOS was a thin client relying on servers for web applications and data; Google later encouraged developers to create packaged applications using HTML5, CSS, Adobe Shockwave, and JavaScript. In September 2014, Google launched App Runtime for Chrome (ARC), initially with four Android apps—Duolingo, Evernote, Sight Words, and Vine—and in 2016, ARC++ was introduced using Linux kernel features to run Android apps in isolated containers, enabling Google Play availability. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Nougat and Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS (Crostini), allowing desktop Linux applications, which was released to the stable channel in October 2018 as a beta feature.

OS. Runtime was launched with four Android applications: Duolingo, Evernote, Sight Words, and Vine. In 2016, the second version, ARC++, was introduced, using Linux kernel features cgroups and namespaces to create isolated containers that can run Android apps, eliminating the need to recompile apps and enabling access to Google Play for ChromeOS devices. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Android Nougat and Android Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for improved security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS, known as Crostini, allowing desktop Linux applications; this feature was released to the stable channel with Chrome 69 in October 2018 as a beta option and officially released with Chrome 91. All Chromebooks made since 2018, and some earlier models, can run Linux apps, which can be installed and launched alongside other apps. Google maintains a list of devices launched before 2019 that support Linux apps. Since 2013, Linux applications have been run in ChromeOS via Crouton, a third-party script set for distributions like Ubuntu. In 2018, Google officially introduced Crostini, named as a pun on Crouton, which runs a virtual machine via crosvm, using Linux's KVM tool, with the Termina VM containing a Gentoo-based ChromeOS kernel and LXD containers. Linux apps run in isolated containers, not on the VM itself, with a default Debian container and support for installing programs via APT or .deb files, or granting access to files and USB devices. As of ChromeOS 121, Debian 12 (Bookworm) is the default container base image. ChromeOS is built on the Linux kernel, originally based on Ubuntu, changed to Gentoo in February 2010. ChromeOS includes the Chromium Shell ("crosh") with minimal functionality like ping at startup; in developer mode, a full-featured bash shell is accessible via VT-2 or the crosh command shell, with a root password required for full privileges, defaulting to "chronos" or "facepunch" initially, later set to empty. ChromeOS is partially developed under the open-source ChromiumOS project, with ChromeOS receiving only Google and partner support and automatic updates to the latest version. Early in the project, Google shared design goals for ChromeOS, including minimal screen space through a single tab strip, reduced window management, floating "panels" for secondary tasks, and split screens for viewing content side by side, leveraging HTML5 offline modes, background processing, and notifications. On April 10, 2012, ChromeOS offered a choice between a full-screen interface and overlapping, resizable windows via the Ash window manager and Aura graphics engine, including translucent tabs, torn tabs, and a mouse-enabled shortcut list. In 2016, ChromeOS included "Native CUPS Support" as an experimental feature, becoming stable in 2020, enabling most printers even without Google Cloud Print support. Google Cloud Print, which allowed any device to print to supported printers via a proxy installed on ChromeOS, was discontinued after December 31, 2020, and ceased operations on January 1, 2021. ChromeOS stores user files on remote servers, and handling local files offline may cause confusion about which application opens them, a problem noted by Matthew Papakipos as similar to issues in Windows. ChromeOS uses a three-channel release system: Stable, Beta, and Developer (Dev), with a fourth canary channel confirmed by entering the ChromeOS shell in developer mode and using the command update_engine_client -channel canary-channel -update, which requires a powerwash to return to other channels. In 2022, two new channels, LTC (Long-term support candidate) and LTS (Long-term support), were added, available only to Enterprise admins, with LTC providing three months of support before switching to LTS. ChromeOS features a hardened design with auto-updating, sandboxing, and a verified boot process that checks for system compromises, shipped with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and a physical switch under the battery to enable developer mode, which reverses security functions but increases flexibility. Full disk encryption is enabled by default, with the decryption password stored in the TPM, which can be updated manually via settings, resetting the device to factory defaults. The user's Google Account password is the default sign-in method, with additional authentication like PINs, passwords, fingerprint, facial recognition, or smart unlock (via a paired phone) to prevent unauthorized access. If multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled on the Google Account, users may be prompted during setup, with the device designated as "trusted" for subsequent logins, and MFA can be required for each sign-in using hardware tokens like YubiKeys. At its debut, ChromeOS was seen as a competitor to Microsoft Windows and its cloud-based applications, though engineering director Matthew Papakipos argued that ChromeOS is designed for netbooks with limited computational power, unable to run resource-intensive programs like Adobe Photoshop. Some observers, including Tony Bradley of PC World, claimed that existing operating systems like Windows or Linux-based netbooks already provided a web-centric experience similar to ChromeOS, questioning the need for a new system. In 2016, Chromebooks were the most popular computer in the US K–12 education market. In 2020, Chromebooks became the second most-popular end-user operating system, growing from 6.4% in 2019 to 10.8% in 2020, with most growth occurring at the expense of Windows, which fell from 85.4% in 2019 to 80.5% in 2021. Google's offer of multiple open-source operating systems, including Android and ChromeOS, drew criticism, with Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer accusing Google of indecision and Steven Levy noting the dissonance between the two systems at Google I/O 2011.

In 2016, Chromebooks were the most popular computer in the US K–12 education market. In 2020, ChromeOS became the second most-popular end-user oriented operating system, growing from 6.4% in 2019 to 10.8% in 2020, with the majority of growth coming at the expense of Windows, which fell from 85.4% in 2019 to 80.5% in 2021. Google offers several open-source operating systems, including Android and ChromeOS, a setup that has drawn criticism, similar to Apple Inc.'s dual operating systems of macOS and iOS. At the time, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer accused Google of being indecisive. Steven Levy noted that "the dissonance between the two systems was apparent" at Google I/O 2011, where Android's Andy Rubin and Chrome's Sundar Pichai "unconvincingly tried to explain why the systems weren't competitive." Google co-founder Sergey Brin acknowledged that owning two promising operating systems was "a problem that most companies would love to face" and suggested that the two systems "will likely converge over time." This speculation intensified in March 2013 when Sundar Pichai replaced Andy Rubin as senior vice president in charge of Android, placing Pichai in charge of both operating systems. At Google I/O 2014, developers demonstrated native Android software running on ChromeOS via a Native Client-based runtime. In September 2014, Google introduced a beta version of the App Runtime for Chrome (ARC), enabling selected Android applications to run on ChromeOS through a Native Client-based environment without requiring modifications, though some adjustments could improve mouse and keyboard support. At its launch, ChromeOS support was limited to selected Android apps. In October 2015, The Wall Street Journal reported that ChromeOS would be folded into Android to create a single operating system by 2017, with the resulting OS being Android expanded to run on laptops. Google responded by stating that while the company has been working on integrating the best features of both systems, there is no plan to phase out ChromeOS. In 2016, Google enabled full access to Google Play for Android apps on supported ChromeOS devices, replacing the previous Native Client-based solution with a container based on Android Marshmallow that allows direct access to the ChromeOS platform and interaction with Android contracts like sharing. Engineering director Zelidrag Hornung explained that ARC was discontinued due to its limitations, including incompatibility with the Android Native Development Toolkit (NDK) and failure to pass Google's compatibility test suite. On November 18, 2024, Android Authority reported that Google is planning to completely merge ChromeOS into Android.

Cynthia Morris Sherman, born on January 19, 1954, in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, is an American artist known primarily for her photographic self-portraits, in which she portrays herself in diverse roles and imagined characters. She is the youngest of five children, born to Dorothy and Charles Sherman; her father worked as an engineer at Grumman Aircraft, and her mother taught reading to children with learning difficulties. Sherman has described her mother as good to a fault and her father as strict and cruel, and she was raised Episcopalian. In 1972, she enrolled at Buffalo State University, where she majored in painting but soon began exploring ideas that would define her work, dressing in various characters using thrift-store clothing. Frustrated by the limitations of painting, she switched to photography, recalling that "there was nothing more to say [through painting]" and that she could instead focus on an idea. She met Robert Longo at college, who encouraged her to document her "dolling up" process, which became the foundation of her Untitled Film Stills series. In 1974, she co-founded Hallwalls with Longo, Charles Clough, and Nancy Dwyer as an arts center for diverse artists. She was exposed to contemporary art at institutions such as the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, SUNY Buffalo campuses, Media Studies Buffalo, the Center for Exploratory and Perceptual Arts, and Artpark. Influenced by artists like Hannah Wilke, Eleanor Antin, and Adrian Piper, Sherman is considered part of the Pictures Generation. She graduated with a BA in 1976. Sherman works in series, photographing herself as a director, make-up artist, hairstylist, wardrobe mistress, and model, often in her studio. Her Bus Riders series (1976–2000) features meticulously observed characters, including the use of blackface, which some critics argue shows insensitivity to race, while others interpret it as exposing societal racism; American critic Margo Jefferson noted the work reflects a "stale visual myth." Other early works include cutout figures such as Murder Mystery and Play of Selves. Her landmark series, Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980), consists of 69 black-and-white photographs in which she portrays B-movie and film noir actresses in roles like librarians, hillbillies, and seductresses, set in streets, yards, pools, beaches, and interiors, evoking Italian neorealism or American film noir. The series avoids titles to preserve ambiguity, and her heroines are often alone, expressionless, and rebellious, challenging conventional ideas of marriage and family; the gaze in the images is typically from a male viewer, highlighting the male gaze. The photographs are 8 1/2 by 11 inches, displayed in identical black frames. Sherman used her own possessions or borrowed items as props, such as the doggy pillow in Untitled Film Still #11, and shot most in her apartment. The series is divided into distinct groups. In 1995, the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan purchased the series for an estimated $1 million, and Untitled Film Still #21 was listed among TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential photographs. Sherman has appropriated various visual forms, including the centerfold, fashion photograph, historical portrait, and soft-core sex image, with early works like the 1980s Fairy Tales and Disasters series first shown at Metro Pictures Gallery. In 1980, she created Rear Screen Projections, a series in which she poses in front of rear-projected landscapes, often as "hitchhiker" or "runaway" types, emphasizing artifice and theatricality, continuing themes from Untitled Film Stills. In 1981, she produced Centerfolds/Horizontals, 12 large (24 by 48 inches) photographs inspired by fashion and pornographic magazine center spreads, initially commissioned but not used by Artforum’s Ingrid Sischy; she poses recumbent, often supine, and aims for psychological depth, sometimes feeling tormented by the characters. In 1982, she began the Pink Robes series, including Untitled #97, #98, #99, and #100. In 1985, she created Fairy Tales, using prosthetics and mannequins to depict grotesque, disturbing characters inspired by classic fairy tales, subverting idealized representations with vivid color, theatrical staging, and a focus on decay and psychological distress. In 1989, provoked by the NEA funding controversy involving Robert Mapplethorpe and Andres Serrano and Jeff Koons’ "Made in Heaven" series, Sherman produced the Sex series, in which she removed herself from the images, using pieced-together medical dummies in sexualized positions; Hal Foster described it as an effort to "erode the subject and tear at the screen," and Jerry Saltz called it "anti-porn porn," noting the use of pubic hair, tampons, and sausages in excretion. Between 1989 and 1990, she made 35 large color photographs restaging European portrait paintings from the 15th to early 19th centuries under the title History Portraits. In 2008, she created Society Portraits, featuring wealthy, older women in elaborate costumes, styled hair, and heavy makeup, posed in luxurious but sterile settings, with digital manipulation enhancing wrinkles and sagging skin to convey loneliness and anxiety. Sherman stated she is trying to erase herself rather than reveal herself, clarifying that people often misinterpret her work as revealing secret fantasies. Between 2003 and 2004, she produced the Clowns cycle, using digital photography to create chromatically garish backdrops and montages of characters. In 2010–11, her exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art included a photographic mural, where she photoshopped her face into decorative backdrops to explore reality and fantasy. Based on a 32-page insert for POP using vintage Chanel clothes, a 2012 series of large-scale images depicts outsized, enigmatic female figures standing alone before ominous painterly landscapes from Iceland during the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruptions and on Capri. In 2017, she collaborated with W Magazine on a "selfie" project based on the "plandid" concept, using photo-correction apps to create Instagram portraits. From 2019, she exhibited self-portraits executed as tapestries by a Belgian workshop. Sherman has also created fashion series for Prada, Dolce & Gabbana, and Marc Jacobs; in 1983, she made advertisements for Dianne B. for Interview magazine, with Untitled #122 being especially iconic for de-emphasizing clothing; she also created photographs for a Harper's Bazaar editorial in 1993 and the Post Card Series for Comme des Garçons in 1994 with Rei Kawakubo. In 2006, she created fashion ads for Marc Jacobs, photographed by Juergen Teller and released as a monograph by Rizzoli; in 2008, she produced the six-image series Cindy Sherman: Untitled (Balenciaga), first shown in 2010. In 2010, she collaborated with Anna Hu on a jewelry design. She returned to working with Teller on Marc Jacobs’ Spring/Summer 2024 campaign. In the early 1990s, she worked with Minneapolis band Babes in Toyland, providing album cover photography for Fontanelle and Painkillers, creating a stage backdrop, and acting in the promotional video for "Bruise Violet." She also worked as a film director, moving to film with her 1997 movie Office Killer, starring Jeanne Tripplehorn, Molly Ringwald, and Carol Kane, in which Dorine, played by Carol Kane, serves as a stand-in for Sherman, and both share an interest in arranging bodies in diorama-like scenes.

Cindy Sherman is a conceptual photographer whose work explores the construction of identity, gender, and social roles through self-portraiture. She often assumes multiple characters using costumes, makeup, and props to transform herself, challenging traditional representations of women in media and popular culture. Her early work, such as the Untitled Film Stills series, features cinematic references and portrays archetypal female figures, highlighting the influence of visual culture on individual identity. In later series, Sherman experimented with digital manipulation and grotesque imagery to question notions of beauty, fame, and social perception. Her artistic style is widely recognized for its critical approach to representation, blending realism with theatricality and making the viewer aware of the artificiality inherent in images. Sherman created the six-image series Cindy Sherman: Untitled (Balenciaga) in 2008, which were first shown publicly in 2010. In the same year, she collaborated with Anna Hu on a jewelry design. She returned to working with Teller on Marc Jacobs' Spring/Summer 2024 campaign. In the early 1990s, she worked with the Minneapolis band Babes in Toyland, providing photographs for the albums Fontanelle and Painkillers, creating a stage backdrop for live concerts, and acting in the promotional video for "Bruise Violet"; she also worked as a film director. Sherman moved from photography to film with her 1997 movie Office Killer, starring Jeanne Tripplehorn, Molly Ringwald, and Carol Kane, in which Dorine, played by Carol Kane, serves as a stand-in for Sherman, reflecting their shared interest in arranging bodies in diorama-like scenes. According to author Dahlia Schweitzer, Office Killer is a comedy, horror, melodrama, noir, feminist statement, and art piece, featuring artistically executed murder scenes reminiscent of her Untitled Horror series. The film grossed $37,446 and received poor reviews, described as "crude" and "laugh-free," with art critic Roberta Smith noting it lacks the artist's usual finesse and calling it a "fascinating if lumpish bit of Shermaniana," while Stephen Holden called it "sadly inept." Sherman had a cameo in John Waters' film Pecker and appeared in The Feature in 2008, starring her ex-husband Michel Auder, which won a New Vision Award. In 2009, Paul Hasegawa-Overacker and Tom Donahue completed a documentary, Guest of Cindy Sherman, about their relationship with Sherman, which she initially supported but later opposed. In the catalog essay by Philipp Kaiser for Sherman's 2016 exhibition at Metro Pictures Gallery, he noted six short films she made in college that preceded Office Killer, and included a conversation between Sherman and Sofia Coppola in which Sherman admitted she may star in an upcoming film project. Sherman's first solo show in New York was at The Kitchen in 1980, and her photographs were the first show at the newly opened Metro Pictures Gallery that year. "Untitled Film Stills" were first shown at Artists Space, where Sherman was a receptionist. Her first solo exhibitions in France were presented by Galerie Chantal Crousel in Paris. Sherman has participated in many international events, including SITE Santa Fe (2004), the Venice Biennale (1982, 1995), and five Whitney Biennials. Her work has been featured in solo exhibitions at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam (1982), Whitney Museum of American Art in New York (1987), Kunsthalle Basel (1991), Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C. (1995), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1998), Serpentine Gallery in London and the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (2003), and Martin-Gropius-Bau in Berlin (2007). Major retrospectives have been organized by the Museum Boymans-van Beuningen in Rotterdam (1996), the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles and the Museum of Modern Art in New York (1997), sponsored by Madonna, and Kunsthaus Bregenz, Austria, Louisiana Museum for Moderne Kunst, Denmark, and Jeu de Paume in Paris (2006–2007). In 2009, she was included in "The Pictures Generation, 1974–1984" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. In 2012, the Museum of Modern Art mounted a show chronicling her work from the mid-1970s, including over 170 photographs, which traveled to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. In 2013, she was invited to organize a show at the Venice Biennale. In 2016, after a sabbatical spent "coming to terms with health issues and getting older," Sherman produced and staged her first photo gallery in five years, the series "The Imitation of Life," named after a 1959 Douglas Sirk melodrama, which presents her in highly stylized glamour portraits inspired by old Hollywood divas such as Gloria Swanson, Mary Pickford, and Ruby Keeler. The series was exhibited at Metro Pictures Gallery in New York City and the Broad Museum in Los Angeles in 2016, and later at Spruth Magers in Berlin and the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio in 2017. In 2019, the National Portrait Gallery in London organized a major retrospective of her work from the mid-1970s to the present. In 2024, at the Goulandris Museum of Cycladic Art in Athens, Sherman held her first exhibition in Greece, gathering over a hundred of her early works. In 2024, at Fotografiska Stockholm, she exhibited Tapestries, a series of tapestries based on her digitally altered Instagram selfies, marking her first major exploration of this medium. In her Imitation of Life series, Sherman poses in vintage costume and theatrical makeup as various ageing actress-like women. Scholar Douglas Crimp describes her work as a "hybrid of photography and performance art that reveals femininity to be an effect of representation." Sherman does not consider her work or herself to be feminist, stating "The work is what it is and hopefully it's seen as feminist work, or feminist-advised work, but I'm not going to go around espousing theoretical bullshit about feminist stuff." Many scholars emphasize the relationship between her work and the concept of the gaze, particularly Laura Mulvey's analysis of the male gaze in relation to her Untitled series, where she notes that "the accouterments of the feminine struggle to conform to a facade of desirability haunt Sherman's iconography," functioning as a parody of different voyeurisms. Others question whether this confrontation with the male gaze and the feminine struggle was intentional, and whether such intentionality is important in understanding the feminist standpoint of her photography. Sherman herself has expressed uncertainty about the Untitled series' relationship with the male gaze, stating in a 1991 interview with David Brittain that she did not analyze it at the time as a feminist issue, though now she has mixed feelings about the series being too reminiscent of original pin-up images. Her work is also analyzed through the lens of abjection, with scholars like Hal Foster and Laura Mulvey interpreting her use of the grotesque in projects like Vomit Pictures as de-fetishizing the female body. Scholar Michele Meager interprets Sherman as having been "crowned a resistant celebrity" to feminist theory. In 2010, Sherman's nearly six-foot-tall chromogenic color print Untitled#153 (1985), featuring her as a mud-caked corpse, was sold by Phillips de Pury & Company for $2.7 million, near the $3 million high estimate. In 2011, a print of Untitled#96 sold for $3.89 million at Christie's, making it the most expensive photograph at that time. Sherman was represented by Metro Pictures for 40 years and by Sprüth Magers before moving to Hauser & Wirth in 2021. In April 2023, Phillips NY auctioned Untitled #546 (2010), sized 159 cm x 359 cm, for $355,600, well above estimate. Sherman's work is credited as a major influence on contemporary portrait photographers, including Ryan Trecartin, and extends to artists in other mediums such as painter Lisa Yuskavage, visual artist Jillian Mayer, and performance artist Tracey Ullman. In April 2014, actor and artist James Franco exhibited a series of photographs at the Pace Gallery called New Film Stills, restaging twenty-nine images from Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, which received mainly negative reviews, calling the appropriations 'sophomoric,' 'sexist,' and 'embarrassingly clueless.' Sherman lived with artist Robert Longo from 1974 to 1980, who also included her in his 'Men in the Cities' series. She married director Michel Auder in 1984, making her stepmother to Auder's daughter Alexandra and her half-sister Gaby Hoffmann; they divorced in 1999. She was in a five-year relationship with Paul Hasegawa-Overacker, creator of the documentary Guest of Cindy Sherman, and from 2007 to 2011 had a relationship with artist David Byrne. Between 1991 and 2005, Sherman lived in a fifth-floor co-op loft at 84 Mercer Street in Manhattan's Soho neighborhood, which she later sold to actor Hank Azaria. She bought two floors in a 10-story condo building overlooking the Hudson River in West Soho and currently uses one as her apartment and the other as her studio and office. For many years, she spent her summers in the Catskill Mountains. In 2000, she purchased songwriter Marvin Hamlisch's 4,200-square-foot house on 0.4 acre in Sag Harbor for $1.5 million. She later acquired a 19th-century home on a ten-acre waterfront property on Accabonac Harbor in East Hampton, New York. Sherman has expressed contempt for social media platforms, calling them "so vulgar," yet maintains an active Instagram account featuring her selfies. She serves on the artistic advisory committee of the Stephen Petronio Company in New York City and on the Artists Committee of the Americans for the Arts. Along with David Byrne, she was a member of Portugal's Estoril Film Festival jury in 2009. In 2012, she joined Yoko Ono and nearly 150 other artists in founding Artists Against Fracking. In 2023, Sherman served on the jury that selected Sarah Lucas as the first winner of the New Museum's $400,000 Hostetler/Wrigley Sculpture Award. Ahead of the 2024 United States presidential election, she was one of 165 leading contemporary artists who contributed pieces to Artists for Kamala, an online sale with all proceeds going directly to Kamala Harris' campaign. Her works are held in various collections.

Clara Burel, born on 24 March 2001, is a French professional tennis player who peaked at No. 42 in the WTA singles rankings on 10 June 2024. In 2018, she reached the junior singles final at the Australian Open, the US Open, and the Youth Summer Olympics (YOG), and won a mixed-doubles bronze medal with compatriot Hugo Gaston at the YOG. She qualified for the ITF Junior Masters in October 2018, winning her first major title and becoming the junior world No. 1 the following week on 29 October 2018. Burel was selected as an alternate in the French Fed Cup team for the 2018 first-round match against Belgium. In September, she reached her first final on the ITF Circuit in Clermont-Ferrand, losing to Lesley Kerkhove. She was a wildcard entrant at the Australian Open, where she lost in the first round to Carla Suárez Navarro. In March, she received a wildcard into the Lyon Open but lost in the first round to Jil Teichmann. In September at Strasbourg, she defeated Kateryna Bondarenko before losing to Zhang Shuai in the second round. At the French Open, she entered as a wildcard, defeated Arantxa Rus in the first round and Kaja Juvan to reach the third round—becoming the youngest Frenchwoman since 18-year-old Alizé Cornet achieved the same in 2008—before losing to Zhang Shuai for the second consecutive tournament. She qualified for the Australian Open again, losing to Alison Van Uytvanck in the first round. Burel made her top 200 debut on 8 March 2021, rising 37 positions to world No. 181 after reaching the quarterfinals in Lyon. She qualified for Wimbledon, making her first main draw appearance at the grass-court Grand Slam, defeating Ellen Perez before losing in the second round to Kaja Juvan. Burel reached her first WTA Tour final at the Ladies Open Lausanne, losing to Tamara Zidanšek, and achieved her top 100 debut at world No. 98 on 19 July 2021. She made her WTA 1000 debut at the Canadian Open as a qualifier, losing to 13th seed Ons Jabeur in the first round. Burel reached a new career-high WTA singles ranking of No. 74 on 21 February 2022 and recorded her first WTA 1000 win at the Miami Open against qualifier Magdalena Fręch, though she lost to 28th seed Petra Kvitová in the second round. She qualified for the US Open, reaching the third round by defeating 25th seed Elena Rybakina and Alison Van Uytvanck, before losing to sixth seed Aryna Sabalenka. Burel qualified for the Australian Open again, defeating wildcard Talia Gibson in the first round, her first win at this major. In April, she qualified for the WTA 1000 Madrid Open, losing to Camila Osorio in the first round and then to 20th seed Barbora Krejčíková in the second round. She reached the final at the Ladies Open Lausanne, losing to Elisabetta Cocciaretto. Burel won her first WTA 125 title at the Open Angers Arena Loire in December, defeating compatriot Chloé Paquet in three sets. At the Australian Open, she reached the third round for the first time at this major, defeating Aleksandra Krunić and fifth seed Jessica Pegula, her first top-10 win, before losing to Océane Dodin, which led to a new career-high singles ranking of world No. 44, reaching the top 50 for the first time on 5 February 2024. At the Upper Austria Ladies Linz, she reached the quarterfinals, defeating Sinja Kraus and Kateřina Siniaková, before losing to third seed Donna Vekić. At the upgraded WTA 500 in Strasbourg, she reached the quarterfinals, defeating wildcard Karolina Plíšková and seventh seed and defending champion Elina Svitolina, her second career top-20 win, before losing to third seed Danielle Collins. Burel recorded a first-round win over Eva Lys at Wimbledon, losing her next match to qualifier Sonay Kartal. At the Cleveland Open, she reached the quarterfinals, defeating lucky loser Elvina Kalieva and eighth seed Sofia Kenin, before losing to top seed Beatriz Haddad Maia. Moving to the US Open, she defeated former champion Sloane Stephens but lost to 20th seed Victoria Azarenka in the second round. On her debut at the China Open, she won her first-round match over lucky loser Tamara Korpatsch before losing to fourth seed Coco Gauff in the second round. Only main-draw results in WTA Tour, Grand Slam tournaments, Billie Jean King Cup, United Cup, Hopman Cup, and Olympic Games are included in win–loss records. The information is current through the 2024 Jasmin Open and the 2024 US Open.

Claude Bourdet (28 October 1909 – 20 March 1996) was a writer, journalist, polemist, and militant French politician. He was the son of the dramatic author Édouard Bourdet and the poet Catherine Pozzi, and was born and died in Paris, France. In 1935, he married Ida Adamoff. He left the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich with an engineering diploma in technical physics in 1933. After completing his military service in the Artillerie de Montagne, he was assigned to a mission for the Economy Ministry during the government of the Front populaire. Bourdet was active in French Resistance movements and participated in the foundation of the resistance newspaper Combat alongside Henri Frenay. He served on the management committee of Combat until Frenay's departure to London and later Algeria in 1943, when Bourdet became its representative. From 1942, he contributed to the creation and development of the newspaper, focusing on dividing public administrations. In 1944, he was arrested by the Gestapo, imprisoned at Fresnes, and subsequently deported to various concentration camps, including Neuengamme, Sachsenhausen, and Buchenwald. After the war, he continued writing for Combat, but due to a conflict with Henri Smadja, the newspaper's owner, he left in 1950. In 1950, with the assistance of Gilles Martinet and Roger Stéphane, he founded L’Observateur, which was renamed L’Observateur Aujourd’hui in 1953 and then France-Observateur in 1954. Bourdet advocated for the union of the left and social justice and supported the anti-colonial struggle, condemning repression in Madagascar and torture in Algeria. In 1961, he investigated and denounced Maurice Papon, the prefect of the police, in relation to the shootings of Algerian FLN demonstrators on 17 October of that year, known as the Paris massacre of 1961. His political activism led to a major rift within the France-Observateur team in 1963, resulting in his departure from the publication. He continued to publish articles in Témoignage chrétien, Politique Hebdo, or Politis, and participated in special issues of the Nouvel Observateur. In 1985, Bourdet was a member of the "Jury of Honor" that evaluated whether the film Des terroristes à la retraite should be aired in France. The "Jury of Honor" reported that while it was desirable for a film to inform French audiences of all generations about the FTP-MOI saga, such a film had not yet been made. Bourdet described the film as "racist and anti-Semitic."

Claudio Bunster Weitzman (Latin American Spanish: [ˈklawðjo ˈβunsteɾ]; born April 15, 1947) is a Chilean theoretical physicist. Until 2005, his name was Claudio Teitelboim Weitzman. Until 2005, he believed he was the biological son of Volodia Teitelboim, but later learned that his biological father was lawyer Bruno Bunster. He believed this was a deliberate act by the leadership of the Communist Party and became estranged from his adoptive father, changed his name, and did not attend his funeral. Bunster attended Instituto Nacional General José Miguel Carrera, a prestigious public high school in Santiago. He was educated at the University of Chile and earned his doctorate in physics from Princeton University in 1973. He has conducted frontier research and taught at Princeton University and the University of Texas at Austin, and has served as a "Long Term Member" of the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton. Bunster has been Director of the Center for Scientific Studies (CECS) since its founding in 1984. Originally based in Santiago, CECS moved to Valdivia, South of Chile, in 2000, located at the 40S parallel, where its research expanded and deepened in the areas of life, the planet, and the cosmos. In addition to his research and leadership at CECS, Bunster has engaged in public service, serving as Scientific Adviser to President Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle from 1994 to 2000. During this time, the Presidential Chairs in Science and the Millennium Science Initiative were established. He was also a member of the Panel on Human Rights, a government-established body involving both civilian and military representatives to address human rights issues. Bunster has been particularly involved in integrating the armed forces into scientific initiatives as a means of strengthening democracy through science. This has led to joint scientific efforts between CECS and the Chilean Army, Navy, and Air Force, as well as with distinguished foreign institutions. Among the outcomes of these collaborations are several unprecedented expeditions to Antarctica in which Bunster was directly involved. He received Chile's National Prize for Exact Sciences in 1995, was elected to the Academy of Sciences of the United States in 2005, and was made Honorary Member of the Solvay Institutes in Brussels in 2007. In 2013, he was awarded the TWAS-Lenovo Prize by the World Academy of Sciences for the advancement of science in developing countries.

Clinton Conger Ballard Jr. (May 24, 1931 – December 23, 2008) was an American songwriter, singer, and pianist who wrote two Billboard Hot 100 number one hits. The first was "Game of Love" by Wayne Fontana and The Mindbenders in 1965, which reached number one in the US and peaked at number two in the UK. The second was "You're No Good," a 1975 hit by Linda Ronstadt, first sung by Dee Dee Warwick, covered by The Swinging Blue Jeans, Betty Everett, and later recorded by Van Halen; Betty Everett's version reached the Top Ten of the US Billboard R&B chart, while the Linda Ronstadt version reached number one on the Billboard chart. He also wrote two UK number one singles: "Good Timin'" by Jimmy Jones in 1960 and "I'm Alive" by The Hollies in 1965. When Ballard was three, he played the piano for KTSM, an El Paso radio station; at age 11, he attended a musical program for gifted students at the University of North Texas. After serving in the US Army, he moved to New York and became a songwriter and composer, including of the musical *Come Back Little Sheba*. His song "Hey, Little Baby" was recorded by Mitch Miller and became the theme for the 1958 World's Fair in Belgium. In 1957, he discovered the Kalin Twins and became their manager, writing their Decca debut single "Jumpin' Jack," which was followed by "When," a US Top Ten hit and number one on the UK Singles Chart. After leaving the Kalins in 1958, he wrote "Ev'ry Hour, Ev'ry Day of My Life" for Malcolm Vaughan and "Ginger Bread" for Frankie Avalon, the latter a Top Ten hit. His own recording career was less successful; in 1960, he adopted the pseudonym Buddy Clinton to record a two-sided single featuring "Take Me to Your Ladder (I'll See Your Leader Later)" and "Joanie's Forever," both co-written by Burt Bacharach and Bob Hilliard. In 1963, he wrote "You're No Good," first recorded by Dee Dee Warwick, with Betty Everett's version reaching the US Billboard R&B Top Ten; The Swinging Blue Jeans also recorded it in 1966. His songs were frequently recorded by British Invasion artists: The Swinging Blue Jeans recorded "It Isn't There," the Zombies recorded "Gotta Get a Hold of Myself" in 1966, and The Hollies recorded "I'm Alive," which reached number one in the UK in 1965. He also wrote "The Game of Love" for Wayne Fontana and The Mindbenders in 1965, as well as their subsequent chart singles "It's Just a Little Bit Too Late" and "She Needs Love." Ballard wrote songs for the Ricky Nelson film *Love and Kisses* and composed a series of commercial jingles, including a theme for Greyhound Lines. He died in Denton, Texas, in December 2008, two years after suffering a stroke. He is not to be confused with fellow songwriters Russ Ballard, Glen Ballard, or Hank Ballard.

Clive John Derby-Lewis (22 January 1936 – 3 November 2016) was a South African politician who initially joined the National Party and later served in the Conservative Party after its split from the National Party in 1982 due to a softening of apartheid policies. He served as a town councillor for Bedfordview (1972–1977), Deputy Mayor (1973–1974), and Mayor (1974–1975), and was made a Freeman of the Johannesburg Mini-Council. He represented Edenvale, Gauteng, on the Transvaal Provincial Council (1972–1981), where he was the National Party spokesman for Education and Hospital Services, and served on various boards including hospitals, primary and high schools, and a school for physically challenged children. He was a founder member of the Conservative Party, serving on its General Council, Parliamentary Caucus, and Transvaal Party Council, including its Information and Financial Committee. After losing his seat in the 1989 election, he was appointed to the State President's Council, where he served on the Economic Affairs and Amenities Committees. He visited London twice as part of a Conservative Party delegation, including in June 1989, and joined the Western Goals Institute as an honorary Vice-President, participating in the 22nd World Anti-Communist League Conference in Brussels in July 1990. Derby-Lewis was known for racially inflammatory remarks, such as claiming in Parliament in 1989 that "If AIDS stops Black population growth it will be like Father Christmas" and remarking "What a pity" about a black man on a runway, which he later apologised for. He was described as a "right-wing extremist" by The Daily Telegraph and as a "rabid racist" by journalist John Carlin. In October 1993, he was convicted of conspiracy to murder Chris Hani, the leader of the South African Communist Party, and sentenced to death, a sentence later reduced to life imprisonment when capital punishment was abolished in 1995. He confessed to his role in the assassination during his amnesty application to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, stating it was encouraged or sanctioned by senior Conservative Party leaders and that he acted "in defence of my people, who were threatened with a Communist take-over," citing his Christian faith in the Afrikaanse Protestant Church as central to his actions. His amnesty application was denied in April 1999, and in 2000, the Cape High Court dismissed an appeal to overturn the decision. Derby-Lewis applied for parole in June 2010, citing his age over 70 and having served more than 15 years, and was denied medical parole in 2011, 2013, and 2015. His medical parole was granted on 29 May 2015 by a judge, and he was released in June 2015 after serving 22 years due to terminal lung cancer. He died from the disease on 3 November 2016. Born in Cape Town, Derby-Lewis had German and Scots ancestry and grew up in Kimberley, being educated at the then-Christian Brothers' College. He worked as a chartered accountant, served as an extraordinary minister of Holy Communion at Blessed Sacrament Church in Johannesburg before leaving the Catholic Church in the early 1980s, and later joined the Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk, a staunch supporter of apartheid. He spent nineteen years as a volunteer in the South African Citizen Force and became the youngest ever commanding officer of the Witwatersrand Rifles Regiment, affiliated with the Cameronians, earning the John Chard Medal for meritorious service. He married Gaye Derby-Lewis, a former nun from Australia, in 1986, which was his second marriage, and had three children from his first marriage. He was the only member of the Conservative Party Parliamentary Caucus to have served in all four levels of government in South Africa. During his time in Parliament, he was opposed by the Progressive Federal Party, and in March 1988, opposition leader Harry Schwarz called him the "biggest racist in Parliament." He was also a member of the Standing Committees on Provincial Affairs of Natal and Trade and Commerce, and served as Chief Spokesman on Economic Affairs, Technology and Mineral Affairs when the Conservative Party became the Official Opposition. A list of senior ANC and South African Communist Party figures, allegedly developed by Arthur Kemp and including Nelson Mandela and Joe Slovo, was reportedly used in the planning of Hani's assassination. Derby-Lewis had abetted Janusz Waluś, a Polish immigrant, by delivering him the gun used in the assassination on 10 April 1993.
