His representative advocate, Roelof du Plessis, stated that the medical parole advisory board found his lung cancer to be stage 3b with probable or inconclusive spread to the left adrenal glands, inoperable, with marginal response to treatment and poor prognostic features.

Cléo Hamon, born on 25 November 2001 in Cormeilles-en-Parisis, France, is a French pair skater. With her former partner Denys Strekalin, she is a two-time French national champion (2020, 2021), a 2018 Volvo Open Cup champion, and has competed in the final segment at three World Junior Championships (2017–2019). Her brother, Axel, is a triathlete. Hamon began learning to skate in 2006 and competed in ladies' singles, winning silver in the advanced novice category at the Rooster Cup in April 2016 and placing 13th at the Golden Bear of Zagreb in October 2016. In the 2014–2015 season, she partnered with Xavier Vauclin and became the French national novice champions in March 2015. She also skated with Brice Panizzi. In August 2016, Hamon teamed up with Ukraine's Denys Strekalin to compete for France in pairs, coached by Mehdi Bouzzine in Courbevoie. They made their international debut in February 2017, placing seventh in junior pairs at the Bavarian Open, and finished fourteenth at the 2017 World Junior Championships in Taipei, Taiwan. In September 2017, they debuted on the ISU Junior Grand Prix (JGP) series, placing eighth in Riga, Latvia. In December, they won silver at the French Championships behind Lola Esbrat / Andrei Novoselov. At the 2018 World Junior Championships in Sofia, Bulgaria, they finished eleventh. Competing in the 2018 JGP series, they placed sixth in Linz, Austria, and fifth in Ostrava, Czech Republic. They won gold at the Volvo Open Cup in November 2018. At the 2019 World Junior Championships in Zagreb, Croatia, they finished ninth. After placing eighth at the 2019 JGP United States, they debuted on the senior Challenger series with a seventh-place finish at the 2019 CS Finlandia Trophy, placing tenth at the 2019 CS Warsaw Cup, and ninth at their first European Championships. Hamon/Strekalin won the French senior national title for the first time due to the absence of James/Cipres and finished the season at the 2020 World Junior Championships, placing fifth. They were scheduled to participate in the 2020 World Championships in Montreal, which would have been their senior World debut, but the event was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. With the pandemic ongoing, they began the new season at the 2020 CS Nebelhorn Trophy, where only pairs training in Europe competed; they were fourth after the short program and, after the top-ranked Hase/Seegert withdrew, placed third in the free and won the bronze medal. They were scheduled to make their Grand Prix debut at the 2020 Internationaux de France, but the event was canceled due to the pandemic. In February, they won their second straight National title. Later that month, they placed fifth at the International Challenge Cup. On March 1, they were named to the team for the 2021 World Championships, where they placed twentieth in their World Championship debut. They finished the season at the 2021 World Team Trophy, where they finished fifth in both segments and Team France finished in fifth place overall. They began the season at the 2021 Lombardia Trophy, where they finished in fourth place. They were originally scheduled to compete at the Nebelhorn Trophy, where the final Olympics spots would be decided, but were later replaced by Coline Keriven / Noël-Antoine Pierre. It was later announced that Hamon would be taking a break from figure skating due to health issues from burnout, which was the reason for their replacement at the Nebelhorn Trophy. The team later split, and Strekalin began looking for a new partner in October. (with Strekalin) GP: Grand Prix; CS: Challenger Series; JGP: Junior Grand Prix.

The Cochiquito Volcanic Group is a minor volcanic cluster located north of the town of Buta Ranquil in Argentina. Its primary volcano is Volcán Cochiquito, a stratovolcano believed to have formed during the Pleistocene–Holocene period. The volcanic field includes eight satellite cones, such as Volcán Sillanegra, which is a pyroclastic cone complex, and Volcán Ranquil del Sur, a small stratovolcano. This article concerning a location in Neuquén Province, Argentina, is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional details.

Youna Kang[4][5] (born 27 February 1990), known online as CodeMiko and alias The Technician, is a South Korean-American Twitch streamer and YouTuber. She is best known for her live streams on Twitch, where she interviews other streamers, content creators, and internet personalities as her virtual persona CodeMiko,[6] and for advancing interactivity in VTuber technology.[7] Kang created the CodeMiko persona using Unreal Engine, a motion capture suit from Xsens, motion capture gloves from Manus VR, and a facial tracking helmet from MOCAP Design.[a][b][7] The avatar consists of 36,000 polygons, modeled in Autodesk Maya and textured using Adobe Substance. Originally developed alone, the project is now managed by a team including an engineer, an artist / animator / rigger,[8] a publicist, a personal assistant, and a manager.[9] Kang now leads development efforts in broadcasting and idea generation, focusing on introducing new standards of interactivity with her audience.[8] CodeMiko's virtual environment is quasi-interactive, allowing viewers to influence the avatar and surroundings through live chat or donations.[7] Kang conceived the idea for CodeMiko while working at Nickelodeon.[8] After being laid off due to the COVID-19 pandemic,[9] she transitioned to full-time streaming.[8] Early earnings were around $300 per month, insufficient to cover rent,[8] and she incurred over $20,000 in debt to purchase the necessary equipment, including the Xsens Mo-cap suit,[10] which she has credited as pivotal to her success despite poor risk management.[10][9] Since the project's success, she can now afford a comfortable living.[9] Her streaming breakthrough occurred in 2021, following a viral tweet on Twitter[11] and going viral on r/LiveStreamFails on Reddit.[10] The CodeMiko avatar has an in-universe backstory as a video game character without a game, who always wanted to be in a mainstream video game but failed due to her 'Glitch'—a narrative arc similar to Vanellope von Schweetz from Wreck-It Ralph. She was forced into minor roles, like a bush in The Last of Us, mirroring the struggles of a Hollywood actress seeking any role in a film, and for her, any video game.[10] She eventually found her place in Kang’s Unreal Engine project, becoming a Twitch streamer and currently roaming various game worlds, including the world of dead memes and The Sims. The avatar is aware of the Technician and frequently breaks the fourth wall, both indirectly through cross-over interviews such as CodeMiko interviewing The Technician,[13] and directly via augmented reality.[14] The character's "glitchiness" is expressed through occasional transitions into her evil alter ego, "Glitch," who replaces her pink-haired avatar with a semi-transparent, Matrix-inspired digital rain avatar and speaks with a deeper, hoarser voice via a voice changer, often being profane and offensive. It was previously believed that CodeMiko was initially released under the name 'mikoglitch',[15] but in a VOD,[16] Youna clarified this was false and explained that 'mikoglitch' was created to circumvent a temporary shadow ban on her 'CodeMiko' channel. The interview format has been likened to the 1990s animated parody show Space Ghost Coast to Coast.[8] Kang described Glitch as "kind of stupid, unfiltered, and not afraid to say whatever is on her mind or what she sees."[8] In 2021, CodeMiko participated in PogChamps 3, placing last with four losses and zero wins, alongside streamer Myth,[17] and was coached by WGM Anna Rudolf[18] and Andrea Botez.[19] Kang developed "TOS PTSD" after unintentionally violating Twitch's terms of service, resulting in bans, leading to economic anxiety and seeking help from psychiatrist Alok Kanojia on stream.[8][20] She expressed concern about Twitch's proposed "Brand Safety Score" system, fearing her X-rated humor might make her content unsuitable for advertisers and threaten her income, though she later noted her concerns lessened due to brand sponsorships.[22][9] The project has received positive reception, with Kotaku calling CodeMiko "The Future Of Streaming"[8] and Designboom stating she is "Revolutionizing the digital space."[7] The Financial Times reported her content as signaling "The next frontier of digital entertainment",[12] and Quartz described her as "The talk show host of the future."[23] The Verge noted she is "reshaping the Twitch landscape in her image."[10] The project has also attracted interest from producers of sexually explicit content.[12]

The Codex Arundel (British Library Arundel MS 263) is a bound collection of pages of notes written by Leonardo da Vinci, primarily between 1480 and 1518, and spans a 40-year period from 1478 to 1518. It consists of 283 paper leaves of various sizes, most measuring around 22 cm × 16 cm, with only a few being blank; two folios, 100 and 101, were incorrectly numbered twice. The codex contains short treatises, notes, and drawings on diverse subjects such as mechanics and the flight of birds, reflecting Leonardo's practice of using a single folio sheet for each subject, arranged as a cohesive treatise across both sides of the pages. Later book binders cut these folios into individual pages and stacked them, disrupting the original structure and creating a seemingly random arrangement. The manuscript is similar in format to the Codex Leicester, which also compiles notes, diagrams, and sketches, and is recognized as second in importance to the Codex Atlanticus. Written in Italy during the late 15th and early 16th centuries, most of the pages date from 1480 to 1518. The manuscript was acquired in the early 17th century by Thomas Howard, 2nd Earl of Arundel (1585–1646), and later presented to the Royal Society in 1667 by his grandson, Henry Howard, 6th Duke of Norfolk (1628–1684). It was first catalogued in 1681 by William Perry as a scientific and mathematical notebook. In 1831, the British Museum purchased it along with 549 other Arundel manuscripts (half of Arundel's collection) from the Royal Society; it was catalogued by the British Museum in 1834 and remained in the British Library as MS Arundel 263 after the library separated from the British Museum in 1973. The most recent facsimile was published in 1998, and on 30 January 2007, it was digitized along with the Codex Leicester as part of the British Library's "Turning the Pages" project and made available in the 2.0 format, reuniting the two Leonardo notebooks online.

The Communist League (Danish: Kommunistisk Forbund; KF) was a political party in Denmark, founded on 21 January 1973 in Århus by the "Leninist Fraction," a group that had split from the Left Socialists (VS) in 1970 due to disillusionment over a lack of focus on labour struggles. The faction succeeded in adopting a new party programme and gained leadership of VS at its fourth congress in 1971, but internal conflicts intensified, peaking at the fifth congress in November 1972, after which the faction left VS despite securing a majority of delegates. They formed KF, with around 300 members following them, leaving VS with approximately 300 members. KF was primarily centered in Aarhus and Aalborg, the former being home to student activists in the 'Students Front,' while its Copenhagen branch remained weak. The party established new branches in Odense and Helsingør and became the leading force in the revolutionary left in those regions. KF launched the publications Vejen til Socialismen in 1976 and Arbejderpolitik in 1977. In 1975, factional conflicts arose within KF, with a group in Aarhus known as the "Coffee Club" (Kaffeklubben) proposing strategic changes; a document based on their inputs was approved ahead of the 1977 congress. In 1977, about 6% of delegates from Copenhagen formed the splinter group Kommunistisk Forbund - politik (KF-p), which adhered more closely to Leninism and argued that the 1917 October Revolution was the foundation of communist revolution in Denmark; after leaving KF, KF-p sought to join VS but were rejected due to political disagreements. The party was dissolved in 1980, with all members rejoining VS. During its existence, KF held seven congresses and organized various annual summer camps.
Conalia baudii is a species of beetle belonging to the genus Conalia and the family Mordellidae. It was first described in 1858 by Mulsant & Rey.

Conalia helva is a species of beetle belonging to the genus Conalia and the family Mordellidae. It was first described in 1862 by John Lawrence LeConte. This beetle has been observed in dead logs of Pinus taeda and in peach wood. [1][2][3] This Mordellidae-related article is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

The Constitution of Pakistan (Urdu: آئینِ پاکستان, romanised: Ā'īn-e-Pākistān), also known as the 1973 Constitution, is the supreme law of Pakistan, guiding the country’s legal framework, political culture, and institutional structure. Drafted by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto with input from opposition parties, it was unanimously approved by the 5th Parliament on 10 April 1973 and ratified on 14 August 1973. It establishes a federal parliamentary republic with Islam as the state religion and outlines the separation of powers among a bicameral legislature, an executive led by the Prime Minister, and an apex judiciary headed by the Supreme Court. The President serves as a ceremonial Head of State. The first six articles define the political system as a federal parliamentary republic and affirm Islam as the state religion. The Constitution mandates that all laws conform to Islamic injunctions from the Quran and Sunnah, and establishes institutions such as the Shariat Court and the Council of Islamic Ideology for interpreting and applying Islamic principles. It provides fundamental rights including freedom of speech, religion, press, movement, association, thought, life, liberty, property, and the right to bear arms, with due process rooted in British common law. The Constitution establishes a bicameral Parliament with the National Assembly as the lower house and the Senate as the upper house, ensuring equal provincial representation. It sets eligibility requirements for the President and Prime Minister—only Muslims of at least forty-five years of age—and prohibits laws that are repugnant to Islam. The Constitution introduces the Council of Common Interests to manage inter-provincial policy issues, including water distribution, and the National Finance Commission to regulate revenue sharing between the federation and provinces. It also promotes local government, women’s participation, minority protection, and social and economic well-being. The Constitution was adopted on 23 March 1956 as the first constitution, celebrated annually as Republic Day, and was later abrogated in 1958 and 1972. The 1962 Constitution introduced a presidential system and concentrated power in the President, but was suspended in 1969 and abrogated in 1972. The 1973 Constitution, framed by elected representatives, restored a parliamentary democracy with executive power in the Prime Minister. It has been amended 23 times, with three amendments failing to pass Parliament. The current promulgated Constitution is the 7th longest in the world, containing 56,240 words. The Objectives Resolution, passed in March 1949, was incorporated as a preamble into all subsequent constitutions and affirmed democracy and Islamic principles. Jinnah, in a 1948 radio talk, emphasized that the future constitution would be democratic and rooted in Islamic ideals. The 1973 Constitution was formally adopted on 2 February 1973, ratified unanimously on 19 April 1973, and came into full effect on 14 August 1973. On that day, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was elected Prime Minister after relinquishing the presidency to Fazal-i-Ilahi. The Constitution includes provisions for individual equality, prohibition of slavery, fair trial, and safeguards against discrimination in services and access to public places. It also preserves Urdu as the national language and English as the official language, while protecting all other languages, scripts, and cultures. The Constitution is divided into parts and includes schedules that categorize governmental activities and policies. Amendments to the Constitution require a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament, unlike earlier constitutions. The Constitution defines Pakistan as a Federation of Four Provinces and establishes a delicate balance between traditionalist and modernist elements, reflecting compromises on religious rights and humanism.

The Constitution of Pakistan establishes an Islamic way of life, promotes local government, ensures full participation of women in national life, protects minorities, advances social and economic well-being, and strengthens ties with the Muslim world to achieve international peace. Fundamental Rights include security of person, safeguards against arrest and detention, prohibition of slavery and forced labour, freedom of movement, association, speech, religion, and protection of religious institutions, non-discrimination in access to public places and services, and preservation of languages, scripts, and cultures. The judiciary holds full supremacy over other state organs. Urdu is declared the national language and English the official language, with all other languages preserved by the Constitution. Key Islamic principles from the 1956 Articles were incorporated into the Constitution. The Constitution is divided into parts containing individual articles, and schedules list governmental bureaucratic activities and policies. Unlike previous documents, the Constitution cannot be altered directly; instead, amendments are passed through Parliament requiring a two-thirds majority in both houses, and certain federal-related amendments must be ratified by a majority of provincial legislatures. As of 2019, 25 amendments have been made. The Eighth (1985) and Seventeenth (2004) Amendments shifted the government to a semi-presidential system, while the Eighteenth Amendment (2010) reversed this, restoring a parliamentary republic and defining attempts to subvert, abrogate, or suspend the Constitution as high treason. The second amendment (1974) declared Ahmadis to be non-Muslims and was passed unanimously by Parliament. The Twenty-Fifth Amendment incorporated the Federally Administered Tribal Areas into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In 2017, the Twenty-Seventh Amendment Bill, aimed at implementing recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms, failed to secure required majorities or presidential assent and was not adopted. In 2024, the Twenty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, enacted on 21 October, introduced landmark judicial reforms focusing on the Supreme Court and High Courts. In 2025, the Twenty-Seventh Amendment Bill proposed changes to Article 243, reflecting decades of shifts in civil-military authority: the 1985 Revival of the Constitutional Order gave the president control over military appointments, the 13th Amendment restored this to the prime minister, the 17th Amendment reversed it, and the 18th Amendment (2010) re-empowered the prime minister. The 27th Amendment proposed abolishing the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee and making the Chief of Army Staff, with life-long constitutional immunities, the Chief of Defence Forces, a move critics argue further consolidates military authority. It also proposed giving the prime minister the power to appoint or remove Supreme Court judges and establishing a Federal Constitutional Court, which analysts say would reduce the Supreme Court’s power. After the bill passed in November, two senior Supreme Court judges, Syed Mansoor Ali Shah and Athar Minallah, resigned in protest, citing 'crippled judicial independence.' The Constitution begins with the assertion that sovereignty over the universe belongs to Allah alone, and that the authority of the people of Pakistan is a sacred trust. It establishes a democratic order where the state functions through elected representatives, upholds Islamic principles of democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance, and social justice, enables Muslims to live according to Quranic and Sunnah teachings, ensures minorities can freely practice their religions and develop their cultures, and creates a federal structure with autonomous provinces. Fundamental rights include equality, opportunity, and before the law, social, economic, and political justice, and freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, and association, subject to law and public morality. The Constitution guarantees safeguards for minorities and backward classes, ensures judicial independence, and protects the integrity of Pakistan’s territories, including sovereign rights over land, sea, and air. The people of Pakistan, cognizant of their responsibilities before Allah and humanity, and inspired by Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah’s vision of a democratic state based on Islamic social justice, adopt, enact, and give this Constitution through their representatives in the National Assembly. All Members of the National Assembly (MNAs) from West Pakistan elected in the 1970 general election signed the Constitution except Mian Mahmud Ali Kasuri (PPP, Lahore-III), Abdul Hayee Baloch (NAP(W), Kalat-I), Abdul Khaliq Khan (PPP, Mardan), Haji Ali Ahmed Khan (PPP, Hyderabad-IV), and Nizamuddin Haider (CML, Bahawalpur-I). Sahibzada Muhammad Nazeer Sultan (MJUP, Jhang-III) was the last MNA elected in 1970 and one of the last signatories of the 1973 Constitution. Unlike the 1956 Constitution, which included 23 Hindus, 2 Christians, and 2 women in its creation, the 1973 Constitution had no representation from minorities or women.

doc_name: Contract Law of the People's Republic of China
text: The Contract Law of the People's Republic of China came into force on October 1, 1999, and was abolished on January 1, 2021, when the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China came into effect. It served as the primary source of contract law in the PRC. The most recent version consolidated various components of Chinese contract law that had previously been scattered across other substantive laws, contributing to greater legal uniformity. The law encompasses both general and specific provisions and includes legal rules concerning the formation, fulfillment, and breach of contracts. It recognizes a variety of contract types that can be entered into. The principles of freedom of contract, good faith, and the promotion of transactions have guided the law's development and are reflected in many of its key provisions. According to Article 1, the law was enacted to protect the legitimate rights and interests of contract parties, maintain socio-economic order, and advance socialist modernization. Article 2 defines a contract as an agreement establishing, altering, or terminating a civil right-obligation relationship between natural persons, legal persons, or other organizations with equal status; however, agreements concerning personal relationships such as marriage, adoption, and guardianship are governed by other laws. The Contract Law consists of 23 chapters and 428 articles. This article on a contract law topic is a stub and can be improved by adding missing information. This article on the law of the People's Republic of China is also a stub and can be enhanced with additional details.

The Coppa Italia Serie C (Italian: Serie C Italian Cup), previously known as Coppa Italia Lega Pro, is a straight knockout competition featuring teams from Serie C in Italian football, first held in 1972. The tournament consists of six rounds and starts in August with the first set, involving 56 of the 60 participating teams. The remaining four teams, which also compete in the Coppa Italia, join the competition during the second set. All matches are played as single legs, except for the semi-finals and the final. In the event of a tie—whether after a single leg or on aggregate—extra time is played, and if necessary, a penalty shootout determines the winner. In addition to receiving the trophy, the winning team qualifies for the next edition of the Coppa Italia and for the third round of Serie C promotion play-offs. If the winning team's spot is not available, it is awarded to the runners-up, or, as a secondary option, to the 4th-placed team in the same group as the winners.

Cornelia Ann Parker CBE RA (born 14 July 1956) is an English visual artist renowned for her sculpture and installation art. Born in Cheshire, England, her early life, marked by a mentally fragile mother and a violent father, significantly influenced her work. Her German mother served as a nurse in the Luftwaffe during the Second World War, and her British grandfather fought in the Battle of the Somme during the First World War. Parker studied at the Gloucestershire College of Art and Design (1974–1975) and Wolverhampton Polytechnic (1975–1978), earning her MFA from Reading University in 1982. She received honorary doctorates from the University of Wolverhampton (2000), the University of Birmingham (2005), the University of Gloucestershire (2008), and the University of Manchester (2017). In 1997, she was shortlisted for the Turner Prize alongside Christine Borland, Angela Bulloch, and Gillian Wearing, who won. She served as Honorary Professor at the University of Manchester from 2015 to 2018 and as Visiting Fellow at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford from 2016 to 2019, and was appointed Honorary Fellow at Trinity Hall, Cambridge in 2020. Her first solo museum exhibition was at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston in 2000; a survey exhibition followed at MCA Sydney in 2019, and a major retrospective opened at Tate Britain in May 2022. Parker has one daughter, Lily, with her former husband Jeff McMillan, and lives and works in London. She is best known for large-scale installations such as Cold Dark Matter: An Exploded View (1991), first shown at the Chisenhale Gallery in Bow, East London, where she had a garden shed blown up by the British Army and suspended its fragments, with a central light casting dramatic shadows on the walls; this inspired an orchestral composition by Joo Yeon Sir. In 1997, she exhibited Mass (Colder Darker Matter), suspending charred remains of a church struck by lightning in Texas; eight years later, she created Anti-Mass (2005) using charcoal from a black congregation church in Kentucky destroyed by arson. Hanging Fire (Suspected Arson) (1999) features charred remains of an actual suspected arson case. The Maybe (1995) at the Serpentine Gallery, London, was a performance piece conceived by Tilda Swinton, who lay apparently asleep in a vitrine; Parker collaborated to create an installation with glass cases containing relics such as Freud's couch pillow, Mrs. Simpson's ice skates, Charles Dickens' quill pen, and Queen Victoria's stocking; a version was later re-performed in Rome (1996) and MoMA, New York (2013). Avoided Object is an ongoing series developed in collaboration with institutions including the Royal Armouries, British Police Forces, Colt Firearms, and Madame Tussauds. Parker has intervened in historical artworks, such as exhibiting the backs of Turner paintings (Room for Margins, 1998) and wrapping Rodin's The Kiss with a mile of string (2003), titled The Distance (A Kiss With String Attached), as part of the 2003 Tate Triennial Days Like These; this piece was later re-staged at the Whitworth Art Gallery, Manchester (2015) and Tate Britain (2022). Subconscious of a Monument (2005) consists of dry soil fragments suspended from the ceiling, taken from beneath the Leaning Tower of Pisa to prevent collapse. These "avoided" objects have been transformed through burning, shooting, squashing, stretching, drawing, exploding, cutting, or being dropped from cliffs; Parker describes them as 'preempted' objects, like Embryo Firearms 1995, or non-objects such as cracks, creases, shadows, dust, or dirt, including The Negative of Whispers (1997), earplugs made from fluff gathered in the Whispering Gallery, St Paul's Cathedral. Another example is Pornographic Drawings (1997), made from ink derived from solvent dissolved from confiscated pornographic video tape by HM Customs and Excise. Parker states: "I resurrect things that have been killed off... My work is all about the potential of materials—even when it looks like they've lost all possibilities." In 2009, for Jupiter Artland, she created Nocturne: A Moon Landing, a firework display containing a lunar meteorite, making the moon "land on Jupiter"; the following year, she made Landscape with Gun and Tree, a nine-metre-tall cast iron and Corten steel shotgun leaning against a tree, inspired by Thomas Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews, using a facsimile of the gun owned by Robert Wilson, a founder of Jupiter Artland. For the 2011 Folkestone Triennial, she created The Folkestone Mermaid, a life-size, life-cast sculpture of Georgina Baker, a 38-year-old mother of two from Folkestone, celebrating womankind. To mark the 800th anniversary of Magna Carta, she created Magna Carta (An Embroidery) in 2015, a hand-embroidered version of the Wikipedia article on Magna Carta as it appeared on 15 June 2014, completed with embroiderers including members of the Embroiderers Guild, HM prisoners, Peers, MPs, judges, human rights lawyers, a US ambassador and his staff, and public figures such as Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, Jimmy Wales, Jarvis Cocker, and Doreen Lawrence. While the embroidery was on display at the British Library, Parker presented One More Time, a Terrace Wires commission for St Pancras International Station, London, co-presented by HS1 Ltd. and the Royal Academy of Arts. In 2016, she became the first female artist commissioned to create a new work for the Roof Garden of the Met in New York: Transitional Object (PsychoBarn), a scaled-down replica of the house from the 1960 Hitchcock film Psycho, constructed from a salvaged red barn. Parker curated the Found exhibition at The Foundling Museum in 2016, incorporating sixty-eight artists and contributing her own piece, A Little Drop of Gin, a limited-edition photogravure using a 1750s gin glass and droppings of gin, which earned her the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016. She appeared in the BBC Four series What Do Artists Do All Day? (2013), the Brilliant Ideas series (May 2015), "Danger! Cornelia Parker" on BBC One (summer 2016), and Gaga for Dada (autumn 2016), and contributed to the BBC Four production Bricks! (21 September 2016). On 1 May 2017, she was chosen as the official election artist for the UK general election, the first woman to hold that role; she observed the campaign leading to the vote on 8 June and produced two films and 14 photographic works, previewed on BBC Newsnight on 2 February 2018 and made available online via the UK Parliament website prior to an exhibition in Westminster Hall. In 2017, she created a series of blackboard drawings with 5- to 10-year-old children from Torriano Primary School, asked to copy news headlines from UK and US newspapers, noting that at that age children have a barely formed view of the world and will be profoundly affected by political turmoil. In November 2019, she opened her first major retrospective in Australia at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney for the Tenth Sydney International Art Series. In May 2022, she exhibited 100 artworks at Tate Britain in her largest solo exhibition to date, including films such as Chomskian Abstract 2007, Made in Bethlehem 2012, War Machine 2015, American Gothic 2016, Left, Right & Centre 2017, Election Abstract 2018, Thatcher’s Finger 2018, and Flag 2022. Tabish Khan of Culture Whisper praised her work as accessible and playful yet intellectually rigorous. In May 2023, her photograph "Snap" was used as the cover artwork for Peter Gabriel's song "Four Kinds of Horses". In November 2024, her glass rendition of the chandelier from Van Eyck's The Arnolfini Portrait was suspended in the Procuratie Vecchie in St Mark's Square, Venice, as part of Murano Illumina il Mondo, the first time in living memory that artworks were displayed in the colonnade. In 2011, she curated Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain at the Whitechapel Gallery using works from the Government Art Collection arranged as a colour spectrum. For the 2014 Royal Academy Summer Exhibition, she curated the Black and White Room, featuring well-known artists she believed should become Royal Academicians. In 2016, during her Hogarth Fellowship at the Foundling Museum, she curated a group exhibition titled FOUND, presenting works from over sixty artists responding to the theme of "found". In 2010, she was elected to the Royal Academy of Arts and appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2010 Birthday Honours. She received honorary doctorates in 2000, 2005, 2008, and 2017 from Wolverhampton, Birmingham, Gloucestershire, and Manchester respectively. She won the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016, with shortlisted artists including Carmen Herrera, David Hockney, Ragnar Kjartansson, Jannis Kounellis, and Helen Marten. In politics, prior to the 2015 general election, she endorsed Caroline Lucas of the Green Party, and in 2024 she participated in a plea to end the Gaza genocide. She was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2022 Birthday Honours for services to the arts.

Countdown is a British game show featuring word and mathematical tasks that began airing on 2 November 1982 and is broadcast on Channel 4. It was the first programme to be broadcast on Channel 4 and has aired 92 series since its debut, with over 8,000 episodes, making it one of Britain's longest-running game shows. The original French version, Des chiffres et des lettres (Numbers & Letters), ran on French television from 1965 until 2024. Each episode features two contestants competing in three game types: a ten-letter round where they attempt to form the longest word from nine randomly selected letters, a four numbers round in which they use arithmetic to reach a random target from six numbers, and a conundrum, a buzzer round to solve a nine-letter anagram. During series heats, the winning contestant returns the next day until they either lose or retire with eight wins as an undefeated "Octochamp"; the best eight contestants are invited to the series finals, decided in knockout format. Contestants of exceptional skill have received national media coverage, and the show is widely recognised and parodied in British culture. Produced by Yorkshire Television, Countdown was recorded at The Leeds Studios for 27 years before moving to Granada Studios in 2009 and then to Dock10 in Greater Manchester in 2013 following the development of MediaCityUK. Richard Whiteley presented the show for 23 years until his death on 26 June 2005; after his death, Des Lynam presented from October 2005 to December 2006, Des O'Connor from January 2007 to December 2008, Jeff Stelling from January 2009 to December 2011, and Nick Hewer from January 2012 until his retirement in June 2021, with Colin Murray standing in for him during part of the COVID-19 pandemic. Anne Robinson presented from June 2021 to July 2022, after which Murray returned on 14 July as a stand-in host. On 25 July 2022, Les Dennis guest hosted from 4 to 15 August, followed by Jenny Eclair from 16 to 19 August after Murray tested positive for COVID-19. Guest hosts including Floella Benjamin, Richard Coles, Trevor McDonald (for a second time), and Moira Stuart hosted one week each during the show's 40th anniversary celebrations in 2022. Murray was named the permanent host in January 2023. In the early years, the show had multiple assistant presenters: Carol Vorderman, hired for Series 1 as "vital statistician," alternated with Dr Linda Barrett until Barrett left after Series 2; letters were initially placed by Cathy Hytner, then by Karen Loughlin in Series 14 (1987) and Lucy Summers in Series 17 (early 1989); numbers were handled by Beverley Isherwood, later taken over by Hytner mid-Series 3. From Series 18 (July 1989) onwards, Vorderman permanently handled both letters and numbers. After 26 years, she left in December 2008 (alongside O'Connor) and was replaced by Rachel Riley, who has held the role since January 2009. Dr Anne-Marie Imafidon stood in for Riley from December 2021 to March 2022, and Dr Tom Crawford, an Oxford and Cambridge lecturer, stood in for Riley for three weeks in early 2025, making his first appearance on 24 February as the show's first-ever male arithmetician. Susie Dent first appeared in June 1992 as a rotating lexicographer and became a recurring member in 2003; since 2005 she has been the sole lexicographer and has been credited as a co-presenter since January 2015, appearing in "Dictionary Corner" with a weekly celebrity guest. Notable past lexicographers who appeared in more than 100 episodes include Catherine Clarke, Damian Eadie, Alison Heard, Mark Nyman, Richard Samson, Julia Swannell, Della Thompson, Freda Thornton, and Yvonne Warburton. The show originated from the French format Des chiffres et des lettres, created by Armand Jammot, which debuted in September 1965 under the name Le Mot Le Plus Long (The Longest Word) before adding numbers in January 1972. Belgian record executive Marcel Stellman brought the format to Britain, proposing it to several networks. Yorkshire Television purchased the concept in 1981 and produced two non-televised pilot episodes under the title Calendar Countdown, aired in Yorkshire between April and June 1982. Richard Whiteley, who hosted the spin-off, earned the nickname "Twice Nightly Whiteley" due to his daily appearances on both Calendar and the spin-off. He was assisted by Cathy Hytner and Denise McFarland-Cruickshanks for letters and numbers, Robina Sharp for selecting numbers and operating a fruit machine for the target, and Angela Garbut as the vital statistician; Ted Moult, who appeared in the pilot episodes and throughout the regional series, was the first Dictionary Corner guest and only appeared in the first seven episodes. After an additional, unbroadcast pilot episode with a refined format, the show was bought by Channel 4, which launched in November 1982. The show was renamed Countdown, expanded its hosting team, and was initially commissioned for four times a week for seven weeks, but due to its success, it has continued to be recommissioned as of 2024. A proposed spin-off, Junior Countdown, hosted by Gyles Brandreth and Ted Moult, was abandoned after a flawed pilot. Countdown was the first programme broadcast by Channel 4 on 2 November 1982, with Whiteley opening with the line: "As the countdown to a brand new channel ends, a brand new Countdown begins." Production staff recruited additional hostesses through national newspaper ads, with clear emphasis on mathematical skill for number experts; Beverley Isherwood and Linda Barrett were hired to handle number and letter tile selection, and a lexicographer was required for Dictionary Corner to verify words and provide entertainment. The lexicographer role was traditionally filled by an Oxford University Press member or production staff member, with past guests including Nigel Rees, Jo Brand, Martin Jarvis, Richard Digance, Geoffrey Durham, Ken Bruce, Magnus Magnusson, Pam Ayres, Paul Zenon, Jenny Eclair, Al Murray, John Sergeant, and Gyles Brandreth. Over time, the additional hostesses were dropped, retaining Vorderman primarily for tile selection and calculation verification. The role of lexicographer rotated among over thirty individuals until January 2005, when Susie Dent was permanently appointed after her 1992 debut. On 26 June 2005, Richard Whiteley died after a failed heart operation; the episode scheduled for that day was postponed as a mark of respect, with no episode aired, and the remaining episodes were broadcast after his death, preceded by a tribute from Carol Vorderman. The show went into hiatus from 1 July to determine its next steps, with no repeats aired. In October 2005, Des Lynam took over as main presenter, having previously participated in Celebrity Countdown in April 1998; his tenure ended in December 2006 due to a demanding schedule, with viewers reacting angrily to a proposed move from Leeds to Worthing. In January 2007, Des O'Connor took over; during his tenure, Susie Dent went on maternity leave in 2007–2008, with Alison Heard temporarily replacing her until 6 February 2008. By July 2008, both O'Connor and Vorderman announced they would leave at the end of that year after Series 59; O'Connor left to focus on other projects, and Vorderman left after rejecting a 33% salary decrease and being offered a 90% cut, with her agent stating the show could survive without her. Media reports suggested Rory Bremner or Alexander Armstrong as possible successors, but both declined. Several prominent women, including Anthea Turner, Ulrika Jonsson, and Myleene Klass, were considered, but Channel 4 selected an unknown male or female arithmetician with "charm and charisma." When Lynam became presenter, the show drew an average of 1.7 million viewers daily, around half a million more than in Whiteley's final years; the Series 54 final on 26 May 2006 attracted 2.5 million viewers. Daily viewership had previously ranged from 3 to 4 million in its 16:15 slot, and a drop in viewership after scheduling changes led Labour MP Jonathan Shaw to propose returning the show to a later time. The show has since moved to 14:10 as of 2025. In November 2008, Jeff Stelling was confirmed as host, and Rachel Riley was confirmed as Vorderman's replacement. Stelling left in December 2011 due to football commitments with Sky Sports, and Nick Hewer was announced as his replacement, taking over on 9 January 2012. During the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, Colin Murray filled in for Hewer during his isolation. Des O'Connor died on 14 November 2020 after a fall at home; the episode aired two days later was dedicated to his memory. On 7 December 2020, Hewer announced he would step down at the end of Series 83 in summer 2021, calling it a "privilege and a pleasure." On 15 February 2021, Anne Robinson, who first appeared in Dictionary Corner in 1987, was announced as Hewer's successor, beginning Series 84. Hewer's final episode aired on 25 June 2021. On 28 June 2021, Robinson became the show's first female host in its 39-year history. In May 2022, it was announced she would leave after one year, with Murray taking over for most of Series 86; she recorded 265 episodes, equivalent to two full series and the first three weeks of Series 86. The show quickly gained cult status in British television and maintains that image today, with its audience primarily consisting of students, homemakers, and pensioners due to its "teatime" broadcast slot and inclusive format. It has been one of Channel 4's most-watched programmes for over twenty years but has never won a major television award. Each episode awards the winner of the reigning champion (or the championship when two new contestants compete) a teapot styled to resemble the clock used in each round, introduced in December 1998 and custom-made, obtainable only by winning. Defeated contestants and retiring undefeated champions receive Countdown-themed merchandise. Initially, the series winner received a leather-bound copy of the twenty-volume Oxford English Dictionary, worth over £4,000; David Acton (Series 31 winner) opted for a CD-ROM version due to veganism and donated the price difference to charity. Between 2011 and 2021, the prize included ordinary hardback twenty-one-volume dictionaries, a laptop, and a lifetime subscription to Oxford Online (replaced by a MacBook Pro from Series 68); the physical dictionaries were discontinued after Series 83 as obsolete. Since Series 54 in 2006, the series champion also receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy. Runner-up prizes in finals increased from a £100 book voucher to £250, then £500, then £1,000, and from Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a 25th-anniversary celebration. On 2 November 2007, the show celebrated its 25th anniversary with a special 'birthday episode' featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills; VIP guests selected the letters and numbers. Guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on the success of Countdown.

The series champion of Countdown receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy in memory of the show's original presenter. Runner-up prizes in the finals have increased over the years from a £100 book voucher to £250, then to £500, and finally to £1,000, with beginning in Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode of Countdown was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a celebration of its 25th birthday. On 2 November 2007, Countdown aired a special 'birthday episode' to mark its 25th anniversary, featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills as players, with VIP guests selecting the letters and numbers; guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from the French TV network France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on Countdown's success. On 26 March 2010, Queen Elizabeth II congratulated Countdown for reaching 5,000 episodes, and on 5 September 2014, the programme received a Guinness World Record at the end of its 6,000th show for being the longest-running television programme of its kind during Series 71. Countdown has occupied a daytime broadcast slot since its inception in a 30-minute format, and since 2001, episodes last around 45 minutes including advertising breaks. During normal series, the winner of each game returns for the next day's show; a player who wins eight games is declared an "octochamp" and retires. At the end of each series, the eight best players—ranked first by number of wins and then by total score to break ties—are invited back for the series finals, where they compete in a knockout tournament seeded so that the first plays the eighth, the second plays the seventh, and so on. The winner of the knockout, culminating in the Grand Final, becomes the series champion. Each series lasts approximately six months with about 125 episodes. Approximately every four series, a Champion of Champions tournament occurs, inviting sixteen of the best players since the previous championship, selected by producer Damian Eadie, typically including series winners and other notable contestants. Series 33 was designated a "Supreme Championship," in which 56 of the best contestants from all prior series participated in a knockout tournament, with Series 10 champion Harvey Freeman declared Supreme Champion after defeating Allan Saldanha in the final. There are also occasional special episodes featuring past contestants in themed matches, such as David Acton and Kenneth Michie returning for a rematch of their Series 31 final, and brothers Sanjay and Sandeep Mazumder playing against each other on 20 December 2004. Since the shift to 45-minute episodes, the game is divided into three sections with advertising breaks. The first section includes two letters rounds and one numbers round; the second includes two letters rounds and one numbers round, followed by the Dictionary Corner anecdote, then two further letters rounds and one numbers round; the third section includes two letters rounds, Susie Dent's "Origins of Words" feature since September 2007, two further letters rounds, one numbers round, and a final "Conundrum" puzzle. Contestants swap control after every round, so each has five letters rounds and two numbers rounds. Since Series 46 in 2001, the host poses a "Teatime Teaser" at the end of the first two sections, giving a set of short words and a cryptic clue to a single word that can be anagrammed from them, with the solution revealed at the start of the next section; the anagram length has varied between seven and nine letters. The contestant in control chooses between two stacks of face-down letter tiles—one with vowels (A-E-I-O-U) and one with consonants—and the assistant reveals the top tile, repeating this nine times to form a nine-letter group with at least three vowels and four consonants. Contestants have 30 seconds to form the longest valid single word using the letters, with no letter used more than it appears; letter frequencies are weighted according to natural English usage, similar to Scrabble, and are periodically altered by producers. The two stacks are not replenished between rounds. Both contestants write down their words; after time runs out, the host asks for declared word lengths, starting with the contestant who chose the letters. If one has not written their word, they must state this; if both declare the same length, the one who chose the letters must give their word first to prevent cheating. If both state they have not written their words, the host allows a moment to do so, typically edited out. The contestant with the longer valid word scores one point per letter or 18 points if all nine are used. If the words are identical or of the same length, both score. If a contestant is visually impaired, Dictionary Corner verifies the word. Inaccurate declarations of word length result in zero points, even if the word is valid. Dictionary Corner reveals the longest and any unusual words formed from the letters at the end of each round. Most words in the Oxford Dictionary of English are valid, as are accepted forms not explicitly listed. Words not allowed include those that are not in the dictionary or not in accepted forms. The contestant in control selects six of 24 shuffled number tiles—two each of numbers 1 to 10 (small numbers) and four large numbers (25, 50, 75, 100)—and decides how many large numbers to use, after which the tiles are randomly drawn and placed on the board. A random three-digit target from 100 to 999 is generated by "CECIL" (Countdown's Electronic Calculator In Leeds). Contestants have 30 seconds to find a sequence of calculations using the numbers and basic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), not using any number more than it appears, and only exact division is allowed; fractions and negative numbers are not permitted. Both contestants must declare their results, and if both declare the same result and have not written their calculations down, the one who made the selection goes first. The contestant whose result is closer to the target scores points: ten for exact match, seven for within one to five, five for within six to ten; no points if more than ten away, or if calculations are flawed, too slow, or not written down. Both score if they reach the same result or are equally close. If neither reaches the target exactly, the assistant attempts a solution. Some games have multiple exact solutions; for example, 7 × (75 + 50 + 2 – 8 – 3) = 812. Not all games are solvable, especially when six small numbers are chosen and the target is large. Selecting one large and five small numbers is the most common choice, though two large numbers offer the best chance of an exact solution; selections with zero or four large numbers are generally considered hardest. The 24 tiles are laid out in four rows, with the top row containing only the large numbers; the contestant may specify how many tiles to draw from each row or simply state how many large and small numbers to use, with the assistant drawing them randomly. Numbers are usually placed from right to left, starting with small ones, though sometimes in scrambled order. On rare occasions, the contestant makes no choice, and the assistant selects the tiles. Unlike the letters round, the number tiles are fully replenished after each numbers round. A special edition on 15 March 2010 for previous champions Kirk Bevins and Chris Davies used instead of the four large numbers, the numbers 12, 37, and two unrevealed numbers. In a further special broadcast on 16 August 2010 between Series 59 finalists Charlie Reams and Junaid Mubeen, the other two numbers were revealed as 62 and 87. The final round is the Countdown Conundrum, where contestants are shown a combination of two or three words totaling nine letters and must form a single word using all letters in 30 seconds, buzzing in to respond (a bell for the champion, a buzzer for the challenger). Each contestant is allowed only one guess; the first to answer correctly scores 10 points. If a contestant buzzes in and either responds incorrectly or fails to respond, they are frozen out and the remaining time is given to the opponent. If neither solves it, the presenter asks the audience if anyone knows the answer and chooses someone to call it out (this practice was temporarily stopped in 2009 due to camera angle issues after a studio change). The Conundrum is intended to have one solution, though on occasion more than one valid word is found (e.g., MISSATTEE can become ESTIMATES or STEAMIEST), and any such result is accepted. On rare occasions, the Conundrum is presented as a nine-letter word to be anagrammed into another (e.g., SMARTENED becoming TRADESMEN). If the contestants' scores are within ten points going into the Conundrum, it is called a "Crucial Countdown Conundrum"; since ten points are at stake, solving it will either win the game or force a tiebreaker. If scores are tied after the Conundrum, additional Conundrums are played until the tie is broken. There have been several instances with two Conundrums to decide the winner, but only a handful of episodes required three, and there have been rare cases requiring even more, though not all such episodes are included in the broadcast. The rules of Countdown are derived from Des chiffres et des lettres, with the main difference being round length—DCedL's number rounds are 45 seconds, Countdown's are 30 seconds. DCedL also features "duels" with short tasks like mental arithmetic, forming themed words, or spelling correctly. Other differences include a different scoring system (9 points for exact solution, 6 for closest in DCedL) and a different proportion of letters to numbers rounds (10 to 4 in Countdown, 8 to 4 in DCedL). The pilot episode had different rules: only eight letters were selected per letters round; if two contestants offered a word of the same length or equally close solution in a numbers game, only the contestant who selected the round received points; five points were awarded for an exact numbers solution, three for within five, and one point for the closer solution regardless of distance. The style and colour scheme of the set have changed many times, and the show moved to Manchester after over 25 years in Leeds, but the clock has always been the centrepiece, and the clock music composed by Alan Hawkshaw remains a well-recognized feature. Executive producer John Meade commissioned Hawkshaw to revise the music for extra intensity at the start of Series 31 in January 1996, but after hundreds of viewer complaints, the original tune was reinstated after just 12 shows. The original set, known as the Pastel set, was used from 1982 until Series 17 in early 1989. A brown wooden set was introduced in Series 18 in July 1989 but remained in use for less than two years. Series 22 in July 1991 introduced the familiar "Wings" set in red, used until 1995. Series 31 in January 1996 changed the colour scheme to purple, then to tangerine at the end of 1999 with updated score and CECIL displays. In January 2003, the set was updated to a pink and purple striped theme with the letters and numbers boards on separate islands. In January 2009, a new numerical blue theme was introduced with the boards on opposite sides of a single display stand. New modern displays for scores and numbers came in January 2013, and a slight redesign occurred in July 2017 while retaining the blue background used up to the most recent series. The original clock was used until September 2013, when it was replaced. Until the end of Series 21, if contestants had equal scores after the first conundrum, the match was declared a draw and both returned for the next show. A significant format change occurred in September 2001, when the show expanded from nine rounds and 30 minutes to the current fifteen rounds and 45 minutes. The older format was split into two halves, each with three letters and one numbers game, plus a conundrum at the end of the second half. Under the old format, Grand Finals were extended to fourteen rounds, but now all shows use the fifteen-round format. The rules regarding valid words have changed over time; American spelling was allowed until 2002, and more unspecified inflections were assumed valid. In September 2007, Susie Dent began the "Origin of Words" feature, which follows the eighth letters round, partway through the third section of each episode; it was omitted during her maternity leave and reinstated upon her return. When the 15-round format was first introduced in September 2001, the round composition differed from today's: each of the first two sections had four letters rounds and one numbers round, and the third section had three letters rounds, one numbers round, and the conundrum. This created an imbalance, with one contestant making letters rounds six times and choosing numbers only once, while the other made letters five times and numbers twice. Dictionary Corner's guest spot was immediately before the first advertising break, and Susie Dent's Origin of Words spot preceded the second numbers game before the second break. The change to the current format was implemented on 25 March 2013, three weeks into the second section of Series 68, to comply with Channel 4's decision to increase advertising and alter its timing, reducing the actual show length from 36 to 35 minutes. Since its debut in 1982, Countdown has had more than 8,600 televised episodes and 92 complete series, and there have been sixteen Champion of Champions tournaments, the most recent in January 2023. Several of the programme's most successful contestants have received national media coverage; teenager Julian Fell set a record score of 146 in December 2002. In 2006, 14-year-old Conor Travers became the youngest series champion in the show's history, and 11-year-old Kai Laddiman became the youngest octochamp in 20 years. Conor Travers went on to win the 30th Anniversary edition.

The first advertising break and Susie Dent's Origin of Words spot occurred just before the second numbers game, shortly before the second break. The format change to the current structure was implemented on 25 March 2013, three weeks into the second section of Series 68, in response to Channel 4's decision to increase advertising and adjust its timing, which reduced Countdown's actual show length from 36 to 35 minutes. Since its debut in 1982, the programme has aired more than 8,600 televised episodes and completed 92 series, with sixteen Champion of Champions tournaments held, the most recent in January 2023. Several top contestants have received national media attention; in December 2002, teenager Julian Fell set a record score of 146. In 2006, 14-year-old Conor Travers became the youngest series champion in the show's history, and 11-year-old Kai Laddiman became the youngest octochamp in 20 years. Conor Travers later won the 30th Anniversary Champion of Champions series in March 2013 with a record-equalling 146. On 17 January 2019, Zarte Siempre, who won that tournament, set a new record of 150, which was surpassed in May 2019 by Elliott Mellor’s 152. On 29 September 2022, Tom Stevenson scored 154, a record later equalled by Cillian McMulkin on 31 January 2023. At eight years old, Tanmay Dixit was the youngest player ever to appear, winning twice in March 2005, and gained press attention for using words like 'fannies' and 'farted' in letters rounds. On Christmas Day 1987, Nic Brown achieved the highest score difference in a standard 14-round game, beating Joel Salkin 108–36, a margin of 72 points, and became one of only two contestants to achieve an undefeated 'grand slam'—becoming an Octochamp, winning a series, and winning a Championship of Champions. In April 2013, Giles Hutchings, a student at Royal Grammar School, Guildford, set the highest octochamp score at 965 points over eight games and won Series 68. This record was later beaten by Dylan Taylor, who scored 974 in August 2013 but lost the Grand Final. In 2019, Elliott Mellor broke the record by 87 points, becoming the first octochamp to surpass 1,000 points with a total of 1,061 over eight games, though he finished as runner-up. Three former contestants have returned to the show’s production team: Michael Wylie, Mark Nyman (as producer and occasional lexicographer in Dictionary Corner), and Damian Eadie (current series producer). In 1998, sixteen celebrities participated in Celebrity Countdown, a series of eight games broadcast weekly over eight weeks, including Des Lynam, who beat Siân Lloyd. In one game, Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall scored 47 against Jilly Goolden, who scored 9, making the highest and lowest scores in the same game. On Christmas Day 1997, Richard Whiteley and Carol Vorderman competed in a special episode, with William G. Stewart hosting in Whiteley’s chair and Susie Dent taking over Vorderman’s role, while Mark Nyman and Magnus Magnusson were in Dictionary Corner. The game was decided by the conundrum 'mistletoe', which Vorderman solved in two seconds after Whiteley accidentally buzzed after one second due to his habit of revealing the conundrum before solving it. Notable contestants include Pete Cashmore (Nuts magazine editor), Ayoola Erinle (rugby player), Neil MacKenzie, Clarke Carlisle, and Matt Le Tissier (footballers), Jon Marsh and Nick Saloman (musicians), Alex Horne (comedian), Peter Sheridan (Irish playwright), and Kirk Bevins (darts referee), who won Series 60 and reached the quarter-finals of the 30th Birthday Championship. Countdown is frequently referenced and parodied in British culture. In 1992, Saint Etienne used the host’s lead-in as the opening for "Stoned to Say the Least". In the 2002 film About a Boy, protagonist Will Freeman is a regular viewer. The Doctor Who episodes "Bad Wolf" (2005) and "Last of the Time Lords" (2007) reference a futuristic version of Countdown, with Professor Docherty commenting on the show’s change after Des Lynam took over. Fairport Convention guitarist Simon Nicol titled one of his albums Consonant Please Carol, echoing a show catchphrase. The show is mentioned in episode one of series 4 of Misfits (2012). A Countdown video game was released for the Nintendo DS and Wii in 2009, and mobile apps have also been developed. The programme has generated numerous widely viewed outtakes, including a round where the word 'gobshite' was offered, featured in TV's Finest Failures (aired 10 January 2000), and a 1991 episode where contestants Gino Corr and Lawrence Pearse both declared 'wankers', which was edited out but later appeared on outtakes. On 21 October 2008, Charlie Reams declared 'wankers', which was kept in but the word was bleeped. Other instances with mildly offensive words, such as 'wanker' or 'fart' (as the first four letters on the board in a 2001 episode, also featured in 100 Greatest TV Moments from Hell), and an anagram of 'fucked' appearing as 'A U O D F C K E G' (without either player using the word or Dictionary Corner finding two seven-letter words) have been aired. On 2 February 2017, the letters round board was 'M T H I A E D H S', and Dictionary Corner found 'shithead', which was bleeped in audio and censored on screen with a poo emoji. The show is referenced in episodes of Father Ted ("The Old Grey Whistle Theft"), Still Game ("Wireless"), Little Britain (2003), and BBC sketch show Dead Ringers, which parodies it multiple times. The Big Breakfast also parodied it in a feature called "Countdown Under". In a sketch "Countdown to Hell" from A Bit of Fry and Laurie, Stephen Fry mocked Richard Whiteley’s punning style and Hugh Laurie played a contestant, while Gyles Brandreth (played by Steve Steen) presented with the letters 'bollocsk' and produced the non-word 'sloblock' (meant to be equivalent to 'bollocks'). The show is briefly referenced in The Office when Chris 'Finchy' Finch mocks a temporary worker by saying he was 'professor in charge of watching Countdown every day', commenting on its student audience and the fact that viewers during its 'hometime' slot cannot be at work. The format has been parodied on Have I Got News for You: in 1999, during Whiteley’s guest appearance, the numbers game and clock music were copied, ending with the conundrum 'PHANIOILS' whose answer was Ian Hislop; in 2004, during Vorderman’s guest appearance, a news-based conundrum round was introduced; in 2006, when Vorderman hosted the show, a 'Spinning Conundrum Numbers Round' was introduced, combining a news picture with a number puzzle. In 1998, Richard Whiteley was the victim of a practical joke on Noel's House Party, where contestants and rounds were planted in a 'Gotcha!' prank. Both contestants and Dictionary Corner missed the word in 'OMETHINGS', and both declared 'I've got diarrhoea'. In the numbers round, the male contestant 'answered' by combining 6, 2, and 3 to make 623. Whiteley discovered the joke when Noel Edmonds appeared on set and revealed the short conundrum 'HOGCAT' meant 'gotcha'. In a 2003 episode of Top Gear, Whiteley participated in the 'Star in a Reasonably Priced Car' segment, with Jeremy Clarkson playing a Countdown game with him using words like 'imin' (Mini), 'sexul' (Lexus), 'nevor lard' (Land Rover), 'mushi bits' (Mitsubishi), and 'pianos shiazu' (Hispano-Suiza). The show was referenced twice on Harry Hill's TV Burp: once when 'Dev' (Coronation Street) made a sound like the Countdown end-of-round beep, and again when the competition 'Where Has The Knitted Character Been This Week?' had the answer 'on Rachel Riley's chair'. On 2 July 2010, the game appeared in The IT Crowd’s series 4 episode "The Final Countdown", where Moss declares that the nine-letter string TNETENNBA is a word, later becoming an octochamp and joining an underground club called '8+' to compete in a spoof of Boogie Town, featuring a cameo by Gyles Brandreth. British entertainer Stevie Riks has parodied the show in a YouTube video. In a 2011 episode, the Blackpool-based producer set the conundrum 'PNECRISIS' ('priciness') as a joke about Preston North End’s relegation. The game has also been featured as the first challenge in "What's Next" on Ant and Dec's Saturday Night Takeaway, with the pair versus an old head teacher. In 2010, it was used as a shopping task in the final Channel 4 series of Celebrity Big Brother, where housemates competed against champion Chris Davies via satellite and failed. In 2008, Charlie Reams, who was runner-up in Series 59, created a website called Apterous, allowing online play; all series champions since 2008 have been members. Since 2005, Ben Wilson, champion of Series 46, has organised a Countdown event in Lincoln, known as COLIN, held annually on a Saturday in January. COLIN features three rounds, with players drawn into tables of three (bots used if not divisible by three), each contestant hosting once and playing twice per round. In Round 1, tables are randomly assigned; in Rounds 2 and 3, tables are assigned based on performance. A final is held between the top two players, ranked by wins and points. Since 2014, a hangover event takes place the day after the main event, featuring two rounds with players split into White and Blue teams. In-person events have expanded to other locations, such as Bristol and Edinburgh. Since 2016, most events have been part of 'FOCAL' (Finals of the Co-events Annual League), where players earn points based on performance. The top eight are invited to a final, where they play against each other, and a final is held between the two best players, ranked by wins and points; the winner is declared FOCAL Champion.

Cyanothamnus ramosus is a species of plant in the citrus family Rutaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is an erect, mostly glabrous shrub that grows to a height of 30 cm (10 in), with pinnate leaves measuring 10–30 mm (0.4–1 in) long and having between three and seven leaflets on a petiole 1–11 mm (0.039–0.433 in) long; the leaflets are 5–15 mm (0.20–0.59 in) long. The plant produces up to three flowers in the leaf axils, on pedicels 2–15 mm (0.079–0.591 in) long, with four thick, glabrous, egg-shaped sepals 1.5–5 mm (0.059–0.20 in) long and white petals with blue or pale green backs, which are broadly elliptic, 3–5 mm (0.12–0.20 in) long and prominently glandular. Flowering occurs from May to October. The species was first formally described in 1839 by John Lindley, who named it Cyanothamnus ramosus in A Sketch of the Vegetation of the Swan River Colony. In 1863, George Bentham reclassified it as Boronia ramosa. In a 2013 paper in the journal Taxon, Marco Duretto and others restored Lindley's name Cyanothamnus ramosus based on cladistic analysis. The specific epithet "ramosus" is Latin for "full of branches." In 1971 and 1998, Paul Wilson described three subspecies in the journal Nuytsia, which have since been updated to reflect the genus change: subspecies anethifolius occurs between the Murchison River, the Stirling Range, and Cape Le Grand, subspecies lesueuranus is known only from near Mt Lesueur, and subspecies ramosus is mainly found in the Darling Range. The species is widespread on slopes and hillsides, sometimes in disused gravel pits, from near Shark Bay to near Esperance. Cyanothamnus ramosus is classified as "not threatened" by the Western Australian Government Department of Parks and Wildlife, but subspecies lesueuranus is listed as "Priority Two" by the Western Australian Government Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, indicating it is poorly known and restricted to one or a few locations.

Cylindrovertilla kingi, commonly known as King's amber pupasnail, is a small, air-breathing land snail belonging to the family Vertiginidae, a group of whorl snails. It is a terrestrial pulmonate gastropod mollusc, classified as a micromollusc. This species is native to Australia and is found exclusively in the states of New South Wales and Queensland. This Vertiginidae-related article is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information on Wikipedia.

Cómbita is a town and municipality located in the Colombian Department of Boyacá, within the Central Boyacá Province subregion. It lies on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense and shares borders with Arcabuco and the department of Santander to the north, Sotaquirá to the northeast, Tuta and Oicatá to the east, the department capital Tunja, which is 8.5 kilometres (5.3 mi) away, to the west and south, and both Arcabuco and Motavita to the west. Prior to the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors, the area was inhabited by the Muisca people, who were organized into the Muisca Confederation. The northern Muisca were ruled by the zaque of Hunza, corresponding to modern-day Tunja, and the cacique of Cómbita was a loyal subject of the zaque. In the Chibcha language spoken by the Muisca, the name Cómbita means either "Hand of the jaguar and wheel of life" or "Force of the summit." Modern Cómbita was officially founded in 1586. The primary economic activities in the town include agriculture, specifically the cultivation of potatoes, barley, wheat, maize, and peas, as well as livestock farming. Its geographic coordinates are 5°45′N 73°15′W (5.750°N 73.250°W).

Danavorexton (developmental code name TAK-925) is a selective orexin 2 receptor agonist that functions as a small-molecule compound and is administered intravenously. In a phase 1 clinical trial, it was shown to produce wakefulness in a dose-dependent manner comparable to modafinil. As of March 2021, danavorexton is being developed for the treatment of narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia, and sleep apnea. It is related to firazorexton (TAK-994), another orexin receptor agonist, whose development was discontinued in October 2021 due to safety concerns.

Darsheel Safary, born on 9 March 1997, is an Indian actor known for his work in Hindi and Gujarati films and television. He made his film debut in 2007 with the critically acclaimed drama Taare Zameen Par, directed by Aamir Khan, where he played the leading role of Ishaan Nandkishore Awasthi, a dyslexic student. Safary was discovered by script writer and creative director Amol Gupte in late 2006 while searching for a male lead; after reviewing hundreds of auditions, Gupte selected him from Shiamak Davar's dancing school, "Summer Funk," during a scene where boys were asked to describe how they would "bunk" school. Gupte recalled, "It was a tough call. But Darsheel has the mischief in his eyes to be Ishaan. Everyone just naturally gravitated towards him." His performance was widely praised by critics, with Taran Adarsh of indiaFM calling him a "Master" and stating his performance deserved a special award, while Rajeev Masand of CNN-IBN described Safary as a revelation, saying he "steals your heart" and "carries this film completely on his shoulders." Other reviewers hailed him as the "real star of the film" and noted his performance as "brilliant." In a 2007 interview, Safary mentioned that his career aspirations included singing, dancing, or becoming a businessman or jewellery designer. His second film, Bumm Bumm Bole, released in 2010, reportedly earned him ₹3 lakh, the highest amount paid to any child actor at the time. He also starred in Disney India's superhero film Zokkomon (2011) and Deepa Mehta's Midnight's Children (2012). In 2012, he participated in the dance reality show Jhalak Dikhhla Jaa with Avneet Kaur, finishing in seventh position. He took a break from acting to focus on his studies. In 2016, he appeared as Abhay in the anthology series Yeh Hai Aashiqui. In 2023, he featured in the Hindi sports drama film Hukus Bukus and the Gujarati film Kutch Express.

Darwin is the core Unix-like operating system underlying macOS, iOS, watchOS, tvOS, iPadOS, audioOS, visionOS, and bridgeOS. It was initially released as an independent open-source operating system by Apple in 2000 and is composed of code derived from NeXTSTEP, FreeBSD, and other BSD operating systems, Mach, and other free software projects, as well as code developed by Apple. Darwin's unofficial mascot is Hexley the Platypus. It is mostly POSIX-compatible but has never been certified as compliant with any version of POSIX; however, starting with Leopard, macOS has been certified as compatible with the Single UNIX Specification version 3 (SUSv3). The heritage of Darwin traces back to Unix derivatives enhanced by NeXTSTEP (later known as OPENSTEP, from version 4.0 onward), first released in 1989. After Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it announced it would base its next operating system on OPENSTEP, which evolved into Rhapsody in 1997, Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999, Mac OS X Public Beta in 2000, and Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. In 1999, Apple announced the release of the Mach 2.5 microkernel, BSD Unix 4.4 OS, and Apache Web server components of Mac OS X Server. At that time, interim CEO Steve Jobs referenced British naturalist Charles Darwin by saying "because it's about evolution." In 2000, the core operating system components of Mac OS X were released as open-source software under the Apple Public Source License (APSL) as Darwin, while higher-level components like Cocoa and Carbon frameworks remained closed-source. Up to Darwin 8.0.1, released in April 2005, Apple provided a binary installer (as an ISO image) after each major Mac OS X release to allow installation of Darwin as a standalone operating system on PowerPC and Intel x86 systems; minor updates were distributed as separate packages. Darwin is now only available as source code, and as of January 2023, Apple no longer mentions Darwin by name on its Open Source website, publishing only an incomplete collection of open-source projects related to macOS and iOS. The kernel of Darwin is XNU, a hybrid kernel using Open Software Foundation Mach Kernel (OSFMK) 7.3 from the OSF, elements of FreeBSD (including the process model, network stack, and virtual file system), and an object-oriented device driver API called IOKit, providing the flexibility of a microkernel and the performance of a monolithic kernel. The last bootable full release of Darwin supported 32-bit and 64-bit Apple PowerPC systems and 32-bit Intel PCs. Darwin currently supports the 64-bit x86-64 variant of Intel x86 processors in Intel-based Macs and 64-bit ARM processors in the iPhone 5S and later, the 6th generation iPod Touch, the 5th generation iPad and later, the iPad Air family, the iPad Mini 2 and later, the iPad Pro family, the fourth generation and later Apple TVs, the HomePod family, and Macs with Apple silicon such as the 2020 Apple M1 Macs, as well as the Raspberry Pi 3B. An open-source port of the XNU kernel exists for Intel and AMD x86 platforms not officially supported by Apple, though it has not been updated since 2009, and another exists for ARM platforms, though it has not been updated since 2016. Older versions supported some or all of 32-bit PowerPC, 64-bit PowerPC, 32-bit x86, and 32-bit ARM. Darwin supports the POSIX API through its BSD lineage (largely FreeBSD userland), enabling many programs written for other UNIX-like systems to be compiled without source code changes. Darwin does not include key macOS components such as the Carbon and Cocoa APIs or the Quartz Compositor and Aqua user interface, so it cannot run Mac applications, though it does support lesser-known macOS features like mDNSResponder (a core component of Bonjour) and launchd (an advanced service management framework). In July 2003, Apple released Darwin under version 2.0 of the APSL, which the Free Software Foundation (FSF) qualifies as a free software license. The APSL is similar to AGPL and is incompatible with the GNU General Public License. Earlier versions of the APSL did not meet the FSF's definition of free software, though they met the Open Source Definition. A table of major Darwin releases with their dates and corresponding derivative operating system releases is provided, noting that OS releases may have been issued on different dates. The version jump from Darwin 1.4.1 to 5.1 with the release of Mac OS X v10.1.1 was designed to align Darwin with the Mac OS X version and build numbering system, inherited from NeXTSTEP. In macOS build numbering, each version has a unique beginning build number identifying the whole version (e.g., Mac OS X v10.0 started with build numbers beginning at 4, v10.1 began at 5). Build dates for Darwin versions are not publicly available; the command `uname -r` shows the Darwin version number (e.g., "20.3.0"), and `uname -v` shows the XNU build version string including the Darwin version number.
