She has exhibited internationally in events such as Carnegie International (1995), XXIV São Paulo Biennial (1998), Documenta XI (2002), and the 8th Istanbul Biennial (2003), and has had solo exhibitions at The New Museum of Contemporary Art (1998), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1999 and 2005), Tate Britain (1999), Tate Modern (2007), and the Harvard Art Museums (2016–17). Her installation “Plegaria Muda” traveled to museums across Europe and South America from 2010 to 2013, including MUAC (Mexico), Moderna Museet (Malmö), CAM Gulbenkian (Lisbon), MAXXI (Rome), Pinacoteca São Paulo (2012), Museum of Contemporary Art (Chicago, 2015), and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (2015). In Atrabiliarios, she uses pairs and singles of women’s shoes, encased in translucent animal skin with medical sutures, to evoke the memory of those who have disappeared, highlighting the survivors’ uncertainty, longing, and mourning. Salcedo’s work consistently explores the intersection of personal and collective memory, the trauma of political violence, and the enduring presence of loss and resistance.

Downey is a city in southeastern Los Angeles County, California, United States, located 13 miles (21 kilometers) southeast of Downtown Los Angeles and considered part of the Gateway Cities. It is the birthplace of the Apollo space program and Taco Bell and is home to the world's oldest operating McDonald's restaurant, the Speedee McDonald's Store, which opened in 1953 at the southwest corner of Florence Avenue and Lakewood Boulevard. The store was damaged in the 1994 Northridge Earthquake and reopened in 1996 with a museum and gift shop. As of the 2020 census, the city had a total population of 114,355, with a population density of 9,215.5 inhabitants per square mile (3,558.1/km²). The city covers a total area of 12.6 square miles (33 km²), of which 12.4 square miles (32 km²) is land and 0.2 square miles (0.52 km²) is water. The racial makeup was 23.4% White, 3.7% African American, 2.1% Native American, 6.7% Asian, 0.3% Pacific Islander, 40.0% from other races, and 23.9% from two or more races, with 75.1% of the population identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race. The city is adjacent to South Gate and Bell Gardens to the west and northwest, Pico Rivera to the northeast, Santa Fe Springs and Norwalk to the east, and Paramount and Bellflower to the south. According to the Köppen Climate Classification system, Downey has a semi-arid climate (BSk). Mission San Gabriel Arcángel was initially founded on September 8, 1771, near Tongva settlements on a bluff overlooking the Rio Hondo, near the modern intersection of San Gabriel Blvd and Lincoln Avenue, and was later relocated to its present site in San Gabriel after five years due to flooding. In 1784, Governor Pedro Fages granted former soldier Manuel Nieto (1734–1804) a land concession of 300,000 acres (120,000 hectares) stretching from the Santa Ana River to the Old San Gabriel River (now the Rio Hondo and Los Angeles River) and from the mission highway (approximately Whittier Boulevard) to the ocean, though the acreage was later reduced due to encroachment on Mission San Gabriel lands. The land, known as Rancho Los Nietos, passed to Manuel Nieto’s four children after his death and was partitioned in 1833 by Mexican Governor José Figueroa; the northwestern portion, including the Downey-Norwalk area, was granted as Rancho Santa Gertrudes to Josefa Cota, widow of Antonio Nieto, covering approximately 21,000 acres (8,500 hectares) and containing the old Nietos homestead, a center of social life east of the pueblo of Los Angeles. Dairy was a major industry, with the Central Milk Agency marketing milk for "seven hundred dairymen whose dairy herds range from thirty to two thousand head" valued at over $1,000,000 per month. Some settlers came from Ireland, and the city was founded and named for John Gately Downey, the former and youngest governor of California, born in Ireland, who supported Republican Lincoln during the Civil War and pioneered modern subdivision development between the Rio Hondo and San Gabriel River around 1865. He believed oranges would flourish in Southern California and imported several varieties, leading to oranges becoming one of the state’s biggest cash crops. Two small settlements—College Settlement and Gallatin—were established along the Rio Hondo River, with Gallatin building a school known as the "Little Red Gallatin School House" in the late 1860s, later expanded to a two-story building in 1871 and moved to its present site in 1893. By 1883, College Settlement, Gallatin, and Downey joined, and with Governor Downey’s efforts, the Southern Pacific Railroad was convinced to route through and stop in Downey, making the depot area the new center of activity and forming a larger Downey. Farmers grew grain, corn, castor beans, and fruit, and by 1935 Downey was characterized as an "orange-grove town." Downey was incorporated in 1956 and adopted a charter form of government in 1964. After World War II, suburban homes and factories replaced farms. During World War II, Vultee Aircraft was Downey’s largest employer, producing 15% of all American military aircraft by 1941 and pioneering the use of women in manufacturing and the first powered assembly line for airplanes. After WWII, the plant was idle from 1945 to 1948 before being occupied by North American Aviation, which later became North American Rockwell, then Rockwell International, and eventually Boeing. In 1961, the facility was transferred to NASA and became the birthplace of the Apollo Space Program and the Space Shuttle, producing and testing many of the 20th century’s greatest aviation, missile, and space endeavors. The Rockwell plant closed in 1999, and the site was demolished and replaced by the Columbia Memorial Space Center, Downey Landing shopping center, Promenade at Downey shopping center (formerly Downey Studios), a Kaiser Permanente hospital, and a city recreation fields park. In the 1960s, Downey Records gained notoriety with recordings such as The Chantays' "Pipeline," and later, the local music scene led to the founding of The Blasters and Dark Angel. Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Center, the main public rehabilitation hospital for Los Angeles County, is located in Downey and is renowned worldwide for its innovations in spinal cord injury and post-polio syndrome care. Downey was featured in the 2008 film Pineapple Express, with many buildings along Florence Avenue appearing in a driving sequence. In 2010, the population was 111,772 with a density of 8,893.3 inhabitants per square mile (3,433.7/km²), and the median household income was $60,939, with 11.8% of the population below the poverty line. In 2023, the median household income was estimated at $87,400 and the per capita income at $37,122, with 7.0% of families and 9.1% of the population below the poverty line. In 2022, the Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count reported 218 homeless individuals in Downey, with approximately 30–40 homeless residents in the area. Crime reports from 2008 show a drop in robberies, aggravated assaults, and petty thefts, but auto thefts reached a 10-year high with 1,231 vehicles reported stolen, along with 252 robberies, 172 aggravated assaults, 24 rapes, 711 burglaries, and 2,038 larceny/thefts. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, gang activity increased, and although it persists in the southern area today, the city formed GOOD (Gangs Out Of Downey) to engage youth aged 10–20 in anti-gang programs, including sports, after-school care, scholarship programs, and counseling, maintaining a partnership with the Downey Police Department. In 2017, Downey was recognized as L.A. County's "Most Business-Friendly City" by the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation. The city is in California's 30th senatorial district, represented by Democrat Bob Archuleta, and the 64th Assembly district, represented by Democrat Blanca Pacheco, and in the 42nd congressional district, represented by Democrat Robert Garcia. Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his 1968 book "The Pump House Gang," including an article titled "The Hair Boys" about Harvey's Drive-in and the fashion of the hair boys, with a drawing of one appearing in "In Our Time." In 1955, a global news story emerged when truck driver George Di Peso at 7739 Alderdale Street tried to drown a gopher by placing a hose into its hole, only to find the hose being slowly pulled down, which was reported worldwide in a July 3, 1955, Los Angeles Times article titled "Tokyo Awaits Arrival of Downey Hose."

Downey is located in California's 42nd congressional district and is represented by Democrat Robert Garcia. Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his article "The Hair Boys," which described Harvey's Drive-in and the distinctive fashions worn by the hair boys, claiming Harvey's was one of the world's great unacknowledged centers of fashion. The essay appears in Wolfe's 1968 book "The Pump House Gang," and a drawing of a hair boy is included in his book "In Our Time." In 1955, Downey gained international attention when truck driver George Di Peso, living at 7739 Alderdale Street, attempted to eliminate a gopher by placing a hose into its hole and turning on the water, only to find the hose disappearing into the ground. Wire services reported the incident worldwide, and a July 3, 1955, front-page Los Angeles Times article ("Tokyo Awaits Arrival of Downey Hose") quoted a message from Tokyo stating, "Tell Di Peso in Downey the other end of his hose has not turned up here, but we're all still looking." The hose eventually vanished entirely, and the most likely explanation was an underground river pulling it down. In the early 1960s, a rumor circulated that Downey's City Library had banned Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan books because Tarzan was not married to Jane when they conceived Boy. This rumor was perpetuated in Los Angeles Times articles from the 1970s, such as "Downey Sends L.A. Back to the Bush League" (May 8, 1970). However, the rumor was false; according to "Zane Grey Also Safe: Tarzan’s Marital Status No Issue as Downey School Ban Is Denied" (December 28, 1961), a parent had placed two Zane Grey books "out of site in a desk drawer" in one elementary school, and no Tarzan books were removed. The books were later returned to the shelves. Most of Downey lies within the Downey Unified School District, with its two main public high schools named after Governor John G. Downey and Governor and Chief Justice Earl Warren. Downey has three public high schools: Downey, Warren, and Columbus High School. Other public schools are located in the Montebello Unified School District, Little Lake City Elementary School District, and Whittier Union High School District. Private schools are available, and Roman Catholic schools fall under the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles. The Downey City Library serves the city; the first library was established in 1901 by a women's social club founded in 1898. The County of Los Angeles Public Library opened a branch in Downey in September 1915, which moved several times, ending at the County Civic Center. In 1958, the Downey City Council voted to establish its own library and leave the county system. City library services initially operated from the back of a bookstore and opened on July 1, 1958, in the former cafeteria of the Downey Elementary School, which was then used as city hall and police station. A permanent building was constructed on December 7, 1959, with nearly 16,000 square feet (1,500 m²) and a cost of $186,200, or $11.97 per square foot, and was dedicated on December 17 and opened on December 18. In February 1984, an addition of nearly 12,000 square feet (1,100 m²) was completed and dedicated. In March 2019, the city announced it would use Measure S funds to begin remodeling the library, originally scheduled for 15 months but delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The remodeled library opened on May 3, 2021, with features including mobile app support for checkouts and a multi-use community space. The headquarters of the County of Los Angeles Public Library are located in Downey. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health operates the Whittier Health Center in Whittier, which serves Downey. The United States Postal Service operates three post offices in Downey: the Downey Post Office at 8111 Firestone Boulevard, the North Downey Post Office at 10409 Lakewood Boulevard, and the South Downey Post Office at 7911 Imperial Highway. Los Cerritos Community News serves the city. Four freeways provide access to Downey: I-105 and the Metro C Line pass through the southern part, I-5 through the northern region, I-605 along the eastern side, and I-710 just west of the city. The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro) provides bus services, with service available at the Lakewood Boulevard station on the C Line, and Downey also operates a local bus service called DowneyLINK. Downey's sister cities are listed in the document. The Downey Patriot is a weekly community newspaper, while the Los Angeles Times and the Press-Telegram provide daily local coverage in Los Angeles County and the Gateway Cities region.

Dragnet is an American crime drama television series starring Jack Webb and Harry Morgan that aired for four seasons, from January 12, 1967, to April 16, 1970. To distinguish it from the earlier 1950s Dragnet series, the ending year of each season was included in the on-screen title, beginning as Dragnet 1967 and concluding as Dragnet 1970. The series aired every Thursday from 9:30 to 10:00 pm (ET) and was directed by Jack Webb. All four seasons have been released on DVD; Season 1 ("Dragnet 1967") was released by Universal Studios Home Entertainment, while Seasons 2 ("1968"), 3 ("1969"), and 4 ("1970") were released by Shout! Factory. This was the second television series in the Dragnet media franchise, which includes film, television, books, and comics, and it holds the distinction of being one of the first examples of a discontinued American TV series being revived years later with some original cast members. Actors who played multiple roles during the series include Don Ross, Olan Soule, Marco Lopez, Herb Vigran, Clark Howat, Art Balinger, Alfred Shelly, Art Gilmore, Ralph Moody, Virginia Gregg, Ed Deemer, Howard Culver, Bert Holland, Don Stewart, Bobby Troup, Len Wayland, William Boyett, Stacy Harris, Stuart Nisbet, Kent McCord, Robert Brubaker, Harry Bartell, Jill Banner, Robert Patten, Sidney Clute, Anthony Eisley, Virginia Vincent, Don Dubbins, James McEachin, Peggy Webber, Jack Sheldon, and Vic Perrin. Each episode typically begins with stock footage of Los Angeles followed by Sgt. Joe Friday’s introduction, "This is the city," after which he specifies the day and time and describes the watch or shift he and Gannon are working. Friday, usually the lead investigator, and Gannon investigate each case, with Friday maintaining a polite but terse, clipped, and rigid manner of questioning witnesses or suspects, often responding to irrelevant details with, "Ma’am (Sir), we just want to get the facts." At the end of each episode, the legal fate of the arrested suspects is revealed. Friday and Gannon are rarely shown outside their professional relationship; Gannon occasionally mentions his wife, Eileen, and family, and sometimes encourages Friday, who is single, to have a social life. In a rare departure from the crime drama, the 1968 episode "Homicide: DR-06" shows Friday inviting the Gannons to his apartment for a steak dinner, only to have the evening repeatedly interrupted by other tenants seeking his assistance. In 1965, Jack Webb was approached by Universal Pictures to produce a Dragnet television movie for NBC; NBC programming director Mort Werner was impressed and decided to develop Dragnet into a weekly series. Webb was initially more interested in continuing the franchise with TV movies but ultimately agreed. The movie, which had a working title of Dragnet 1966, was released on January 27, 1969 (midway through the third season) on The NBC Monday Movie under the promotional title World Premiere: Dragnet, and is commonly referred to as Dragnet 1966 to distinguish it from other franchise works. It is included as an extra in the Dragnet 1968 DVD set. All episodes of the series were directed by Jack Webb. In one episode, Friday and Gannon investigate a bank robbery committed by a man and a woman; tracking their car leads them to a woman who matches the suspect’s description, initially lies to them, and is already on probation, leading the detectives to believe they have a suspect—until additional reports reveal other women being forced to rob banks in the same way. Though the first woman is cleared, the spree continues until one victim fights back. Sergeant Carl Maxwell, a fellow detective, goes AWOL after a case he worked on is dismissed; Friday and Gannon are given three days to find him before he is terminated from the LAPD. When they locate him drinking at a resort, he rants about the stresses of policing and claims he is a minority for being a cop, but a speech from Friday convinces him to return. Friday and Gannon also investigate an officer accused of police brutality following a drunk driving arrest; officers Pete Malloy (Martin Milner) and Jim Reed (Kent McCord), the main characters of Adam-12, appear as witnesses. In another episode, 17-year-old Hal Rustin (Michael Burns) is a car thief whose mother, Eunice Rustin (Peggy Webber), is unable to stop him. He is given a tour of jail to illustrate the consequences of crime, but it fails, and he later kills someone with a shotgun. Note: Harry Morgan had a bloody nose the night before filming.

Dua Lipa (/ˈduːə ˈliːpə/ ⓘ DOO-ə LEE-pə; born 22 August 1995) is an English singer and songwriter with seven Brit Awards and three Grammy Awards. Born in London, England, she is the eldest child of Kosovo Albanian parents Anesa (née Rexha) and Dukagjin Lipa from Pristina, FR Yugoslavia (present-day Kosovo), and has a sister, Rina, and a brother, Gjin. The name Dua, suggested by her grandmother, means "love" in Albanian, and her maternal grandmother is of Bosniak descent; both of her grandfathers were historians, with her father's ancestry traced to Peja, Kosovo. Musically influenced by her father, the lead singer and guitarist of the Kosovan rock band Oda, who played music at home including works by David Bowie, Bob Dylan, Radiohead, Sting, the Police, and Stereophonics, Lipa began singing at age five. She attended Fitzjohn's Primary School, where she took cello lessons and was initially told she could not sing in the choir; at nine, she began weekend singing lessons at the Sylvia Young Theatre School. After Kosovo declared independence in 2008, she moved to Pristina, where she attended Mileniumi i Tretë School and considered a music career. At 15, she returned to London alone and shared a flat with a family friend, attending Parliament Hill School to pass her A-Levels and later re-entering Sylvia Young Theatre School part-time. She uploaded songs to SoundCloud and YouTube, covering tracks like "If I Ain't Got You" and "Beautiful." In 2013, she modelled with Topshop, signed with Tap Management (directed by Ben Mawson and Ed Millett), and was introduced to Mawson by her lawyer, who discouraged her from signing another publishing deal. Mawson and Millett offered her a monthly salary to leave her job as a waitress in a cocktail bar to focus on music; during a session, she co-wrote "Hotter than Hell," which led to her signing a record deal with Warner Bros. Records in 2014. In August 2015, she released her first single, "New Love," produced by Emile Haynie and Andrew Wyatt; her second single, "Be the One," reached number one in Belgium, Poland, and Slovakia, charted in the top ten in over eleven European territories, and became an airplay success in Australia and New Zealand. In November 2015, she was named on the BBC Sound of... 2016 long list. Her first tour in the UK and Europe began in January 2016 and concluded in early December 2016. On 18 February 2016, she released "Last Dance," followed by "Hotter than Hell" on 6 May, which peaked at number 15 in the UK; on 26 August, "Blow Your Mind (Mwah)" was released, peaking at number 30 in the UK and becoming her first entry on the US Billboard Hot 100, debuting at number 72, while topping the Billboard Dance Club Songs chart and reaching number 23 on the Billboard Mainstream Top 40 chart. In November 2016, she was featured on Sean Paul's single "No Lie," which reached number ten in the UK and became a top-ten hit in ten countries six years after its release, becoming Sean Paul's most-streamed song as of December 2022, with the music video surpassing 1 billion views on YouTube by April 2022. A documentary about her, See in Blue, was commissioned by The Fader in January 2017. That month, she won the EBBA Public Choice Award and released "Scared to Be Lonely" with Martin Garrix, which reached number 14 in the UK. In May 2017, she performed at the anniversary of Indonesian television channel SCTV and won the award for Young and Promising International Artist at the SCTV Music Awards. Her debut album, Dua Lipa, was released on 2 June 2017; its sixth single, "New Rules," released the following month, became her first number one in the UK, the first by a female solo artist to reach the top since Adele's "Hello" in 2015, and charted in the top ten in Australia (number two), the US (number six), and Canada (number seven). As of 2024, the music video for "New Rules" has streamed over three billion views on YouTube. In June 2017, she performed at the Glastonbury Festival, in July at the We The Fest in Jakarta, and on BBC's Later... with Jools Holland in October. In December 2017, she was named the most streamed woman of 2017 in the UK by Spotify. In 2017, she had four singles reach the UK top 10: "Be the One," "New Rules," "No Lie," and "Bridge over Troubled Water," a charity single for the families of the victims of the Grenfell Tower fire. In January 2018, she received five nominations at the Brit Awards, more than any other artist that year, including British Album of the Year, British Single of the Year, British Video of the Year for "New Rules," British Female Solo Artist, and British Breakthrough Act, winning the latter two—making her the first female artist to receive five nominations. She performed at the awards ceremony on 21 February at the O2 Arena in London. In February 2018, she collaborated with American DJ Whethan on "High" for the Fifty Shades Freed soundtrack. In April 2018, she and Calvin Harris released "One Kiss," which topped the UK Singles Chart on 20 April, making it her second number one, and became the best-selling song of 2018 in the UK, staying at number one for eight consecutive weeks. She performed in the opening ceremony of the 2018 UEFA Champions League Final in Kyiv on 26 May. In September 2018, she performed at the F1 Singapore Grand Prix and endorsed Jaguar's new electric car, the I-PACE; the brand created a remix of her song "Want To" and launched a service allowing fans to create and share their own version of the song on Join the Pace, setting a world record for the "most remixed song ever." In October 2018, she released Dua Lipa: The Complete Edition, an expanded version of her debut album including three new songs, such as "Want To" and a collaboration with South Korean girl group Blackpink titled "Kiss and Make Up." In January 2019, she released "Swan Song" for the film Alita: Battle Angel. That month, she stated she had spent the previous year writing her second studio album, which she described as a "nostalgic" pop record that "feels like a dancercise class." In August 2019, she partnered with Yves Saint Laurent to endorse their fragrance Libre. In December 2019, her second album, Future Nostalgia, and its accompanying tour were announced. The album's lead single, "Don't Start Now," peaked at number two on both the UK Singles Chart and the US Billboard Hot 100, earning the longest top-ten stay for a British female artist on the UK Singles Chart and the longest top-ten stay without reaching number one in that chart's history; it also peaked at number one on the UK Big Top 40 and the US Billboard Mainstream Top 40 chart. Her second single leading up to the album's release was "Physical," released on 30 January 2020, with the music video released the next day; it debuted at number 60 on the US Billboard Hot 100. Future Nostalgia was released on 27 March to widespread critical acclaim, following the release of the record's third single, "Break My Heart," on 25 March. The album debuted at number two on the Official UK Albums Chart, 5550 copies behind 5 Seconds of Summer's Calm, and peaked at number one the following week in April 2020, while four of its singles entered the top ten of the Official Singles Chart. The album holds the record for the lowest one-week sales while at number one in the 21st century, with only 7,317 sales during the week beginning 15 May 2020. At the time of release, Lipa became the first British female artist since Vera Lynn to have three top-ten singles in a single calendar year, with Lynn having three in 1952; she later surpassed this with "Levitating," which also peaked within the top ten on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming her third top-ten in the US overall. The music video for "Physical" was nominated for Best Art Director at the Berlin Music Video Awards in 2020, with Anna Colomer Nogué as the art director. On 27 April 2020, DJ Ben Howell released a remix of "Hallucinate" with the BBC news theme, created during the coronavirus lockdown in Glasgow, Scotland, which garnered over a million views on YouTube by July 2023 and was well-received by Lipa and BBC Radio 1 DJ Greg James. On 11 August 2020, she was named global ambassador of the French mineral water brand Évian. On 13 August, she released a remix of "Levitating" featuring Madonna and Missy Elliott, which served as the lead single from Club Future Nostalgia, a remix collection of Future Nostalgia tracks by the Blessed Madonna and Mark Ronson, released on 28 August. On 2 October 2020, she released a second remix of "Levitating" featuring DaBaby, along with the music video for the remix. On 14 October 2020, she and Belgian singer Angèle were photographed on the set of a music video; later that month, they announced their collaboration, "Fever," released on 30 October 2020 and included on the French re-release of Future Nostalgia. In November 2020, she was featured on "Prisoner," a song from Miley Cyrus' Plastic Hearts album, released on 19 November with a music video. In November, it was announced she would be the musical guest on the 19 December episode of Saturday Night Live. On 27 November, she performed in a livestream concert titled Studio 2054, where she sang songs from Future Nostalgia, a new unreleased track with FKA Twigs, and previous singles such as "New Rules," "One Kiss," and "Electricity," featuring special guests including the Blessed Madonna, Angèle, Kylie Minogue, and Elton John. Lipa and Belgian singer Angèle were photographed on the set of a music video. Later in the month, the singers announced the release of their collaboration, "Fever," which was released on 30 October 2020 and is included on the French re-release of Future Nostalgia. Lipa was featured on "Prisoner," a song from Miley Cyrus' seventh studio album Plastic Hearts, released on 19 November 2020 alongside its music video. In November, it was announced that Lipa would be the musical guest on the 19 December episode of Saturday Night Live. On 27 November, Lipa performed in a livestream concert titled Studio 2054, where she sang various songs from Future Nostalgia, a new unreleased track with FKA Twigs, as well as previous singles such as "New Rules," "One Kiss," and "Electricity." The event featured special guests including the Blessed Madonna, Angèle, Kylie Minogue, and Elton John. Future Nostalgia was the most streamed album by a woman (and fifth most streamed album overall) on Spotify in 2020. On 11 February 2021, Lipa released a single titled "We're Good" along with Future Nostalgia: The Moonlight Edition. On 26 February 2021, Aleyna Tilki released her debut English-language single "Retrograde," co-written by Lipa. Lipa released the song "Can They Hear Us" from the soundtrack of the film Gully on 4 June 2021. On 13 August 2021, Lipa worked again with Elton John on the song "Cold Heart (Pnau remix)," released as the lead single from John's studio album The Lockdown Sessions, which reached number one on the UK Singles Chart on 15 October, becoming Lipa's third song to achieve this feat. In February 2022, Lipa launched a weekly lifestyle newsletter entitled Service95 and its accompanying podcast Dua Lipa: At Your Service. On 18 February 2022, a source close to the issue confirmed to Variety that Dua Lipa had parted ways with her longtime management business, Ben Mawson and Ed Millet's TaP Management, though the insider claimed she is not currently meeting with other management firms but will do so in the future. On 1 March 2022, reggae band Artikal Sound System filed a suit against Lipa and her label Warner Records alleging copyright infringement, asserting similarities between "Levitating" and their 2017 song "Live Your Life," which was dropped with prejudice in June 2023. A second suit by songwriters L. Russell Brown and Sandy Linzer claimed that "Levitating" infringed on their 1979 disco song "Wiggle and Giggle All Night." On 11 March 2022, Lipa and Megan Thee Stallion released "Sweetest Pie" accompanied by its music video, marking their first collaboration and serving as the lead single from Megan's second studio album Traumazine. On 27 May, Lipa collaborated with Calvin Harris and Young Thug to release "Potion," serving as the lead single from Harris's sixth studio album Funk Wav Bounces Vol. 2, marking the second collaboration between Harris and Lipa following their 2018 single "One Kiss." On 26 May 2023, Lipa released "Dance the Night" as the lead single of the Barbie film soundtrack, making her acting debut in the movie as Mermaid Barbie. In November 2023, Lipa acquired full ownership of all her songs, music, and publishing rights in a new deal completed with her former music publishers, TaP Music, which included all of her master recordings from her entire music catalogue, reaching 40 billion streams by February 2024. On 9 November 2023, Lipa released the lead single from her third studio album titled "Houdini," stating that Kevin Parker, who produced the song with Danny L Harle, was among her "core collaborators" on the album, with Spin referring to Harle as the co-producer. The follow-up singles "Training Season" and "Illusion" were released on 15 February 2024 and 11 April 2024, respectively, with the album Radical Optimism following on 3 May 2024. She continued her acting career with a starring role in the 2024 spy action comedy Argylle. In March 2024, Dua Lipa announced a short tour of European arenas in June of the same year, performing at the Arena of Nîmes, the Waldbühne in Berlin, and the Pula Arena, all of which are amphitheatres. In June, she headlined at Glastonbury Festival 2024, closing the festival's Pyramid Stage on 28 June. On 18 March 2024, Lipa announced the Radical Optimism Tour, a concert tour in support of the album. On 17 October, she performed at the Royal Albert Hall in London for an ITV television special titled An Evening with Dua Lipa, where she sang her biggest hits and songs from Radical Optimism, backed by the Heritage Orchestra. Dua Lipa co-wrote her songs with her co-writers and cites Kylie Minogue, Pink, Nelly Furtado, Jamiroquai, Prince, Kendrick Lamar, and Chance the Rapper as musical influences. In a 2018 GQ interview, she stated that her idea of pop includes P!nk, Christina Aguilera, Destiny's Child, and Nelly Furtado. Early in her career, her stage presence drew criticism, exemplified by a YouTube comment on her "New Rules" BRIT Awards performance that became an internet meme, which she credited as motivation to improve. A study by the Office for National Statistics found that the number of people born with the name "Dua" in England and Wales rose from 63 in 2017 to 126 in 2019, the year she earned her first UK number-one with "New Rules." In May 2018, she was named one of British Vogue’s 25 most influential British women of 2018 at age 22, with the review calling "New Rules" an "anthem of female empowerment" and describing her as a "culture definer." Lyndsey Havens of Billboard credited her with leading the revival of disco in 2020 through "Don't Start Now" (2019), and she was dubbed "the Future of Pop" due to the success of Future Nostalgia. She inspired French photographer Hugo Comte’s first photo-book and was included in Time’s 100 Next list by Kylie Minogue, who called her a "shining star." Mark Sutherland and Jem Aswad of Variety rated her one of the most impactful women in global entertainment. Wax figures of Dua Lipa are displayed at Madame Tussauds in major cities worldwide. She has won seven Brit Awards from nineteen nominations, three Grammy Awards from ten, two MTV Video Music Awards from twenty-three, two MTV Europe Music Awards from sixteen, two American Music Awards from seven, three iHeartRadio Music Awards from nineteen, nine Spotify 1 billion streams plaques, and one Bambi Award. She holds two Guinness World Records: in 2020 for most tickets sold for a livestreamed concert by a solo female artist, and in 2021 for most monthly listeners on Spotify for a female artist, though she did not surpass Ariana Grande’s prior peak. In 2024, she won the Top Dance/Electronic Song award at the Billboard Music Awards for "Houdini," which topped the Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart for 17 weeks. Time included her in its 2024 Time 100 list of the world’s most influential people, and Billboard ranked her number 25 on its 2025 "Top 100 Women Artists of the 21st Century" list. Lipa identifies as a feminist and has spoken out against sexism in the music industry and advocated for social equality in the LGBT community. On 12 February 2018, she raised a rainbow flag during a performance of "Be the One" at the Hollywood Palladium as part of The Self-Titled tour. At the 2018 Brit Awards red carpet, she wore a white rose dress in support of the Time's Up movement and stated in her acceptance speech her delight at women being present and winning awards, clarifying that her feminism is about equal opportunities, not misandry. In September 2018, some fans were removed from a Shanghai concert for waving rainbow flags, despite homosexuality being decriminalized in China in 1997; Lipa expressed pride and gratitude for their visibility. In November 2018, she criticized Brexit, stating that no refugee leaves without having to, based on her personal experience. In June 2019, she publicly supported Sudan’s democratic transition by sharing a "Stand with Sudan" image, rejecting the Khartoum massacre as an act of "brutal murder and rape" and a violation of freedom and human rights. In December 2019, she endorsed the Labour Party led by Jeremy Corbyn, calling the election "the most important in a generation" and describing Boris Johnson’s victory as a "total disaster." She participated in a Global Feminism short film directed by Annie Lennox’s The Circle, released ahead of International Women’s Day to raise awareness of misogyny, rape, and violence against women. In July 2020, she signed an open letter to the UK government, delivered to then Minister for Women and Equalities Liz Truss, requesting the banning of conversion therapy. She supports universal health care, noting that in the UK, the National Health Service is considered a right. In June 2020, she criticized the Israel Defense Forces’ treatment of Palestinians and referred to "fake Jews" and "fake Christians" in the Israeli government and U.S. midwest, claiming they created Hamas to justify occupation and oppression. An Im Tirtzu petition with over three thousand signatories demanded that Lipa’s songs be banned from Israeli Army Radio and Galgalatz due to what they called antisemitism and conspiracy theories; the radio responded that it does not boycott artists.
