Dulcie Evonne September (20 August 1935 – 29 March 1988) was a South African anti-apartheid political activist who was assassinated in Paris, France, in 1988. The second eldest daughter of Jakobus and Susan September, she grew up in Gleemore, a suburb of Cape Town. While in Cape Town, she developed a strong awareness of apartheid’s injustices and became deeply involved in political activism, advocating for national liberation, democracy, and social justice. She began her primary education at Klipfontein Methodist Mission and later attended Athlone High School, where she experienced firsthand the segregation enforced by Bantu education laws, which became central to her political beliefs. Several of her teachers at Athlone High School were active in civic and political organizations, which helped shape her political consciousness. Though her formal schooling ended halfway through Standard Eight (Grade 10), she continued her education through night classes and passed her Standard Eight exams in 1952. In 1954, she enrolled at the Wesley Training School in Salt River to become a teacher and completed her Teacher’s Diploma in 1955 at Battswood Training College. She began teaching at City Mission School in Maitland and later at Bridgetown East Primary School in Athlone in 1956. In 1957, she joined the Cape Peninsula Students' Union (CPSU), affiliated with the Unity Movement of South Africa, where she met political allies such as Dr. Kenneth Abrahams, Ottilie Abrahams, Neville Alexander, Marcus Solomon, and Fikile Bam. She was also a member of the Athlone branch of the Teacher's League of South Africa (TLSA). After growing frustrated with TLSA, she joined the African Peoples' Democratic Union of Southern Africa (APDUSA) in 1960 and was elected to its finance committee. The APDUSA soon split due to internal conflict, and under the leadership of Dr. Kenneth Abrahams and Neville Alexander—both suspended in 1962—September and others formed the unofficial Caucus to resolve divisions. After the Sharpeville massacre, she and other activists adopted a militant stance. Under Neville Alexander’s direction, she co-founded the Yu Chi Chan Club (YCCC) in July 1962, inspired by the Chinese Communist Revolution and named after Chinese guerilla warfare, which was disbanded by the end of that year and replaced by the National Liberation Front (NLF) in January 1963. On 12 July 1963, security police raided both her and Neville Alexander’s homes, and when NLF materials were found, September was detained on 7 October 1963 and imprisoned without trial at Roeland Street Prison. She was charged under the Criminal Procedure Act for "conspiracy to commit acts of sabotage and incite acts of politically motivated violence," and after months of court proceedings, judgment was delivered on 15 April 1964. She was sentenced to five years in prison, during which she endured severe physical and psychological abuse. Along with Elizabeth van der Heyden, Doris van der Hayden, and Dorothy Alexander, she was transferred to Kroonstad, a facility for political prisoners, after authorities discovered they were radicalizing illiterate female prisoners. In March 1965, the Bloemfontein Appeal Court dismissed their appeals. She was released in April 1969 under a strict five-year banning order imposed by the Pretoria regime. The restrictions, under the Suppression of Communism Act of 1950, prohibited her from social gatherings, political activities, and teaching in South Africa, imposed a curfew, restricted her movement to “Bantu areas,” banned communication with other banned individuals, and limited visitors to medical personnel and her father—later changed to her sister and brother-in-law. In 1973, as her banning order neared expiration, she applied for a permanent departure permit after securing a position at Madeley College of Education in Staffordshire. She left South Africa on 19 December 1973. In London, she joined the Anti-Apartheid Movement, participated in rallies at South Africa House in Trafalgar Square, and later joined the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa. In 1976, she joined the African National Congress (ANC) and worked in the ANC Women's League, where she gained recognition for her work on women’s issues and helped welcome newly exiled South Africans. In 1979, during the International Year of the Child (IYC), she was elected chairperson of the IYC Committee of the ANC Women's Section in London. As an ANC representative, she attended conferences in Finland, Canada, and France and worked with the United Nations (UN), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and the Women’s International Democratic Federation (WIDF) to promote children’s and women’s rights. In 1981, she was called to work full-time in the Regional Preparatory Committee (RPC) at ANC headquarters in Lusaka, where she was elected chairperson. By the end of 1983, she was appointed ANC Chief Representative in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg, and underwent short military training in the Soviet Union. In this role, she campaigned for economic sanctions against the South African government. Between October 1986 and September 1987, she was involved in the Albertini Affair, an anti-apartheid campaign that ended with embarrassment for both South African and French governments, during which she campaigned for the release of Pierre Andre Albertini, a French national imprisoned by South Africa, and petitioned French President Francois Mitterrand to deny South Africa’s new ambassador, Hennie Geldenhuys, until Albertini was freed. By 1987, she had become a significant threat to the South African government, leading strong anti-apartheid campaigns in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg and building strong alliances with anti-apartheid groups and left-wing politicians. On the morning of 29 March 1988, she was shot five times with a silenced .22 caliber rifle outside the ANC’s Paris office at 28, Rue des Petites-Écuries as she was opening the office after collecting mail. She was 52 years old. Her death sparked a strong public reaction in Paris, with more than 20,000 people gathering to mourn. The case remains unsolved, with speculation that South African hitmen were involved, possibly with French secret service collaboration. The French government concluded there was insufficient evidence to arrest suspects and closed the case after ten years. Before her assassination, she had been investigating illegal arms trafficking between France and South Africa. According to the Truth Commission Files, the motive may have been linked to her knowledge of illegal arms deals and possible nuclear collaboration between the French government and South African Armscor. Upon discovering this, she reportedly said she “feared for her life.” During her investigation, she reported her concerns to ANC superiors, who dismissed her. Some of her friends allege she reported being followed and threatened and requested protection from French authorities, which was denied. Charles Pasqua, the interior minister, denied these claims, stating she never made such a request. However, sources claim the French had intelligence that South Africa planned to kill her by December 1987, though this is officially denied. On the day after her murder, Alfred Nzo, secretary-general of the ANC, stated: "If ever there was a soft target, Dulcie September was one." Jean-Michel Jarre composed a song titled "September" for his 1988 Revolutions album, dedicated to her, which was performed at his Destination Docklands concert in October 1988 and included in the album recording Jarre Live (1989). Conceptual artist Hans Haacke created a 1989 installation titled "One Day, The Lions of Dulcie September Will Spout Water in Jubilation," modifying a defunct fountain in front of the Grande halle de la Villette in Paris as part of the Magiciens de la terre exhibition. Her short story "A Split Society – Fast Sounds on the Horizon" was included in the 1992 anthology Daughters of Africa, edited by Margaret Busby. The solo play Cold Case: Revisiting Dulcie September, written by Basil Appollis and Sylvia Vollenhoven, pays tribute to her and was performed at a French cultural festival in Paris, winning the inaugural Adelaide Tambo Award for Human Rights in the Arts. A book about her murder, Dulcie: Een Vrouw Die Haar Mond Moest Houden by Evelyn Groenink, was published in the Netherlands in 2001. A podcast titled They Killed Dulcie by Open Secrets and Sound Africa was released in March 2019. The 2021 documentary Murder in Paris, directed by Enver Samuel and edited by Nikki Comninos, explores her life and assassination. An online awareness campaign and petition for justice were launched using the hashtags “#justicefordulcie” and “#mercidulcie.” A 300-page graphic novel, Dulcie from Cape Town to Paris, published by Benoît Collombat and Grégory Mardon, revisits her murder investigation 30 years after her death. A square in the 10th arrondissement of Paris is named after her, officially inaugurated on 31 March 1998, with the inscription “Dulcie September Square: Representative of the African National Congress: Assassinated in Paris on 29 March 1988.” A street in Cléon, near Rouen, is named after her, as is a place in Nantes and a primary school in Évry-sur-Seine, as well as a middle school (collège) in Arcueil, near Paris. In August 2010, the first Dulcie September Memorial Lecture took place at the University of the Western Cape’s Centre for Humanities Research, and the Dulcie September Fellowship Awards in the Humanities and Social Sciences were launched, featuring speakers including Barbara Masekela and Margaret Busby. In October 2011, Staffordshire University Students' Union renamed their boardroom the "September Room" and erected a plaque in her memory. She was a former student of Madeley College of Education, one of the founding colleges of North Staffordshire Polytechnic. In 2013, the Athlone Civic Centre was renamed the Dulcie September Civic Centre. In Amsterdam, a road in the Transvaalbuurt is named Dulcie Septemberpad, and other buildings and streets in the neighborhood bear the names of prominent South Africans, including Steve Bikoplein, Nelson Mandela School, and Retiefstraat.

EGOT is an acronym for the Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Awards, designating individuals who have won all four of the major performing art awards in the United States. These awards recognize outstanding achievements in television, audio recording/music, film, and theatre, respectively, and achieving the EGOT has been referred to as the "grand slam" of American show business. Including those with honorary or special awards, 27 people have achieved this status, with only Robert Lopez having won all four awards twice. The term was coined by actor Philip Michael Thomas in late 1984 while starring in Miami Vice, when he expressed a desire to achieve the EGOT within five years. The acronym gained wider recognition after a 2009 episode of 30 Rock introduced EGOT status as a recurring plotline. There is debate over whether only the Primetime Emmy Award should count, as some—including Thomas—consider other Emmy categories subordinate to the Primetime honor. Starting in 2016, the Daytime Emmy Awards had a category for Outstanding Musical Performance in a Daytime Program, which was removed after the 2019 ceremony because three of the four winners were Broadway ensembles, including five individuals (Cynthia Erivo, Rachel Bay Jones, Katrina Lenk, Ben Platt, and Ari'el Stachel) who already had Tony and Grammy awards and only needed an Oscar to complete their EGOT. In 2023, TheaterMania writer Zachary Stewart criticized the practice of "selling" producer credits for shows favored to win a Tony as a "shortcut" to EGOT status, distinguishing between producers who do the actual work and those who merely finance it, often late in the award season. American composer Richard Rodgers (1902–1979) received his fourth distinct award in 1962, with 10 competitive awards between 1946 and 1979; he was the first person to win all four and primarily a composer. Helen Hayes (1900–1993) received her fourth distinct award in 1977, with six competitive awards between 1932 and 1980; she was the first woman and first performer to achieve the EGOT, and the first to win the Triple Crown of Acting, with a 45-year interval between her first and fourth award—the longest among EGOT winners. Rita Moreno (born 1931) received her fourth distinct award in 1977, with five awards between 1961 and 1978; she was the first Latina and the first to win a Grammy as her second award, and became a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2015 and a Peabody Award winner in 2019; she is the second EGOT recipient and the first Hispanic actress to win the Triple Crown of Acting. John Gielgud (1904–2000) received his fourth distinct award in 1991, with five competitive awards between 1948 and 1991; he was the first to win a Tony as his first award, won his Emmy at age 87, and became the oldest winner, the first male performer, the first LGBTQ winner, and the first non-American. Audrey Hepburn (1929–1993) received her fourth distinct award posthumously in 1994, with four competitive awards between 1954 and 1994; she was the fifth person to complete the feat and the first to do so posthumously, and the first to win two awards in consecutive shows (the 1994 Grammys followed her 1993 posthumous Emmy), and is the only EGOT winner to not win multiple awards in any of the four fields. Marvin Hamlisch (1944–2012) received his fourth distinct award in 1995, with 12 competitive awards between 1974 and 2001; he had the most Oscars of any EGOT winner (three, all in the same year), won "General Field" Grammys in 1974 (Song of the Year and Best New Artist), and was the first EGOT winner to have won both an Oscar and a Grammy for the same work ("The Way We Were"). Jonathan Tunick (born 1938) received his fourth distinct award in 1997, with five awards between 1977 and 2024; he was the first EGOT winner to win an Emmy as his second award and the first to win the Tony as his fourth award. Mel Brooks (born 1926) received his fourth distinct award in June 2001, with 11 awards between 1968 and 2002; he was the first to win the Emmy as his first award and the first to win his Oscar for screenwriting; he is the only person to have won the Triple Crown of Writing, with an Oscar, Emmy, and Tony in writing categories. Brooks is one of only two people to have two awards of each type, though one of his Oscars was honorary; when he appeared on the January 30, 2015 episode of Real Time with Bill Maher, he called himself an EGOTAK, noting he had also received awards from the American Film Institute and Kennedy Center. Mike Nichols (1931–2014) received his fourth distinct award in November 2001, with 15 awards between 1961 and 2012; he was the first to win the Grammy as his first award, the first to win multiple awards for directing (an Oscar, several Tonys, and two Emmys), and has the longest timespan of awards among EGOT winners at 51 years; he is one of only two people (the other being Bob Fosse) to achieve the Triple Crown of Directing. Whoopi Goldberg (born 1955) received her fourth distinct award in 2002, with five competitive awards between 1985 and 2009; she is the first African American winner, the first to win the Oscar as her second award, and the third person after Audrey Hepburn (1954) and Marvin Hamlisch (1974) to win two qualifying awards in the same year (her Tony and first competitive Emmy in 2002). Scott Rudin (born 1958) received his fourth distinct award in 2012, with 21 awards between 1984 and 2021, tying with Alan Menken for the most competitive EGOT awards; he is the only EGOT winner who is solely a producer and did not win any of his four awards for a creative endeavor (singing, writing, acting). Robert Lopez (born 1975) received his fourth distinct award in 2014, with 12 awards between 2004 and 2022; he is the first Filipino and Asian to achieve the EGOT, the youngest winner (39 years, 8 days) to receive all four awards in competitive categories, and at the time the fastest to complete his qualifying run (9 years, 8 months), with a subsequent shortest interval of 7 years, 8 months (June 27, 2010 to March 4, 2018) until 2024 when Benj Pasek and Justin Paul surpassed it. Lopez is the first person to win each EGOT award twice; as of 2025, he is one Oscar away from becoming the first triple EGOT winner; he is currently the only winner to have two of each EGOT award in competitive categories, as Mel Brooks' second Oscar in 2023 was honorary; his first two Emmys were Daytime Emmys, followed by a Primetime Emmy in 2021 for WandaVision; he is the only EGOT recipient to follow a Daytime Emmy win with a subsequent Primetime Emmy win. Lopez received his Grammy for The Book of Mormon in collaboration with Scott Rudin, making them the first pair of EGOT winners to co-win the same award; he is also the first person to have won the Oscar last, sharing it with his wife Kristen Anderson-Lopez in 2014 and again in 2018; as of 2024, Kristen Anderson-Lopez lacks only a Tony to achieve EGOT status in her own right. Andrew Lloyd Webber (born 1948) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 12 competitive awards between 1980 and 2025; on September 9, 2018, he, John Legend, and Tim Rice simultaneously became EGOTs after being awarded the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Variety Special (Live) for Jesus Christ Superstar Live in Concert. Tim Rice (born 1944) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 12 awards between 1980 and 2018, sharing all awards with Elton John, John Legend, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Alan Menken; on September 9, 2018, he, Lloyd Webber, and Legend became EGOTs via the same Emmy. John Legend (born 1978) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 21 awards between 2006 and 2025; he has the most Grammy Awards (12) of any competitive EGOT recipient, is the first African American man to achieve EGOT status, and the first person to receive the four awards in four consecutive years; he is the first EGOT recipient to have won both a competitive Primetime and Daytime Emmy, matched by Robert Lopez in 2021; on September 9, 2018, he, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Tim Rice became EGOTs via the same Emmy. Alan Menken (born 1949) received his fourth distinct award in 2020, with 21 competitive awards between 1990 and 2020, tying with Scott Rudin for the most competitive EGOT awards; if his special Emmy is counted, he becomes the fully competing EGOT with the most overall awards; if EGOT status is recognized without regard to non-competitive awards, Quincy Jones holds the record with 30 fully competitive awards, including 29 Grammys; Menken has the most Oscar wins (8) by an EGOT. Jennifer Hudson (born 1981) received her fourth distinct award in 2022, with five competitive awards between 2007 and 2022, making her the youngest competitive female EGOT to date. Viola Davis (born 1965) received her fourth distinct award in 2023, with five competitive awards between 2001 and 2023, becoming the eighteenth person to competitively win each of the four awards; she acknowledged her new EGOT status while accepting her 2023 Grammy; she is the third EGOT recipient and the first African American actress to win the Triple Crown of Acting. Elton John (born 1947) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with nine competitive awards between 1987 and 2024, becoming the nineteenth person to competitively win each of the four awards. Benj Pasek (born 1985) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with seven competitive awards between 2017 and 2025, becoming the twentieth person to competitively win each of the four awards; he and Justin Paul set a new record for achieving EGOT status in the fastest time (7 years, 7 months); Pasek shares all seven of his competitive award wins with his writing partner Justin Paul. Justin Paul (born 1985) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with seven competitive awards between 2017 and 2025, becoming the twenty-first person to competitively win each of the four awards; he and Benj Pasek set a new record for achieving EGOT status in the fastest time (7 years, 7 months); Paul shares all seven of his competitive award wins with his writing partner Benj Pasek. Six additional artists have received all four awards, though one was for an honorary or similar non-competitive distinction: Barbra Streisand lacks a competitive Tony; Liza Minnelli lacks a competitive Grammy; and Harry Belafonte, James Earl Jones, Quincy Jones, and Frank Marshall lack a competitive Oscar. Barbra Streisand (born 1942) received her fourth distinct award in 1970, with 18 awards between 1963 and 2001, three of which were non-competitive; at age 28, she obtained her fourth award with a special Tony, making her the youngest special EGOT winner; with only six years between her first award (1964 Grammy) and her 1970 Tony, she held the record for the fastest special EGOT until 2023 when Frank Marshall achieved it in four years. Streisand is the only EGOT to win an Oscar in both music and acting, and the only winner to have three competitive awards for debut performances (first studio album, first feature film, first television special); she also has the Peabody Award, AFI Life Achievement Award, Kennedy Center Honor, Cecil B. DeMille Award, National Medal of Arts, American Society of Cinematographers Board of Governors Award, and Presidential Medal of Freedom. Liza Minnelli (born 1946) received her fourth distinct award in 1990, with seven awards between 1965 and 2009, two of which were special. James Earl Jones (1931–2024) received his fourth distinct award in 2011, with eight awards between 1969 and 2017, two of which were special. Harry Belafonte (1927–2023) received his fourth distinct award in 2014, with six awards between 1954 and 2014, including a Grammy Hall of Fame Award and the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award (six special awards). Quincy Jones (1933–2024) received his fourth distinct award in 2016, with 33 awards between 1964 and 2024—the highest number of any EGOT winner; he won 28 Grammys, one Tony, and one Emmy, plus a special Grammy Legend Award and two special Oscars (Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award and Academy Honorary Award); his final qualifying award was a fully competitive 2016 Tony for The Color Purple. Frank Marshall (born 19) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with nine competitive awards between 1980 and 2024, becoming the twentieth person to competitively win each of the four awards.

Between 1954 and 2014, American singer, activist, and actor Harry Belafonte (1927–2023) received a total of six awards, including a Grammy Hall of Fame Award and the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award, with two of those being special awards. He received his fourth distinct award in 2014. American record producer, musician, songwriter, composer, arranger, and film and television producer Quincy Jones (1933–2024) received his fourth distinct award in 2016. Between 1964 and 2024, Jones received a total of 33 awards—the highest number among any EGOT winner—comprising 28 Grammys, one Tony, one Emmy, a special Grammy Legend Award, and two special Oscars (the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award and the Academy Honorary Award). His final qualifying award was a fully competitive 2016 Tony for The Color Purple. American film producer and director Frank Marshall (born 1946) received his fourth distinct award in 2023. Between 2019 and 2023, Marshall received a total of four awards and is the only EGOT winner to have won a Sports Emmy Award and to have received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. With just four years between his first award (a 2019 honorary Oscar), a long format TV sports documentary, and competitive Grammy and Tony music awards, Marshall completed his EGOT collection in the shortest time of any person to achieve this status. As of July 2025, 74 living people are one award away from achieving (competitive) EGOT status. Additionally, 12 living individuals are one award away from achieving EGOT status, including those who have won at least one non-competitive award. As of 2024, 16 out of the 21 EGOT winners were American nationals, while the remaining five—John Gielgud, Audrey Hepburn, Elton John, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Tim Rice—were British. There are conflicting definitions for the PEGOT: some define it as including the Peabody Award, others as the Pulitzer Prize. As of 2024, Mel Brooks, Rita Moreno, Mike Nichols, and Barbra Streisand have achieved PEGOT status via Peabody wins, while Marvin Hamlisch and Richard Rodgers have achieved it via Pulitzer wins. The REGOT includes a Razzie Award; Alan Menken has a REGOT due to his Razzie win (with Jack Feldman) for Worst Original Song for "High Times, Hard Times" from Newsies, and Liza Minnelli has a REGOT if her non-competitive Grammy Legend Award is counted. Lady Gaga reordered the acronym as EGORT after hosting Saturday Night Live and joking about her win for Worst Screen Combo (with Joaquin Phoenix) from Joker: Folie à Deux. Publications such as Vulture have listed the REGOT as including an induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame; Elton John is the only person with such a REGOT, though Harry Belafonte and Quincy Jones would be included if non-competitive awards are counted. In 2018, Leah Collins of CBC Arts proposed a Canadian equivalent of the EGOT—comprising the Canadian Screen Awards (and predecessors Gemini and Genie Awards), the Juno Awards, and the Dora Mavor Moore Awards—referred to by Toronto-based game show Trivia Club as the "Two-Can-Ju-Do," with no individual having won in all four categories. In 2019, Caitlin Welsh of Nova Entertainment proposed the "LAHA" as an Australian equivalent—Logie Awards, ARIA Music Awards, Helpmann Awards, and AACTA Awards—with no winners of all four awards identified, though Noni Hazlehurst has received nominations in all four.

Edward Maurice Charles Marsan OBE (born 9 June 1968) is an English actor who won the London Film Critics Circle Award and the National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance in the film Happy-Go-Lucky (2008). He was born in the Stepney district of London to a working-class family; his father was a lorry driver and his mother was a school dinner lady and teaching assistant. He was raised in Bethnal Green and attended Raine's Foundation School. He left school at 16 and initially worked as a printer before starting his career in theatre. Marsan trained at the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, graduating in 1991, and later studied under Sam Kogan at the Kogan Academy of Dramatic Arts, now known as The School of the Science of Acting, of which he is now a patron. His first year at drama school was funded by Mr Benny, a bookmaker who ran a menswear shop where Marsan worked; he received scholarships for the remainder of the course. It took many attempts for Marsan to secure a place at drama school. His first television appearance was in 1992 as a "yob" in the London Weekend Television series The Piglet Files. One of his more significant early television roles was in the mid-1990s BBC sitcom Game On, where he played an escaped convict who was an old flame of Mandy's. He went on to appear in Casualty, The Bill, Grass, Kavanagh QC, Grange Hill, Silent Witness, Ultimate Force, Southcliffe, and more. He also voiced the Manticore in the Merlin episode "Love in the Time of Dragons". In 2011, he starred alongside Olivia Colman and Peter Mullan in the British drama film Tyrannosaur. In 2013, he began portraying Terry Donovan, the brother to the lead character in seven series and 82 episodes of Showtime's drama series Ray Donovan, and also played Ludwig Guttmann in the television film The Best of Men. In May 2015, he appeared as the practical magician Gilbert Norrell in the BBC period drama Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell. His film roles include the main villain in the 2008 superhero film Hancock alongside Will Smith, as Inspector Lestrade in Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes, and other films such as Sixty Six, Gangs of New York, 21 Grams, The Illusionist, V for Vendetta, Gangster No. 1, Miami Vice, Mission: Impossible III, I Want Candy, Vera Drake, Happy-Go-Lucky, Filth, Tyrannosaur, and Heartless. In 2021, he played anti-Fascist activist Soly Malinovsky in the television adaptation of the novel Ridley Road. In 2022, he portrayed the real-life John Darwin in ITV's drama series The Thief, His Wife and the Canoe. In 2024, he appeared as Mitch Winehouse, father of Amy Winehouse, in the biopic Back to Black. Marsan married make-up artist Janine Schneider in 2002; they have four children. He is a humanist and was appointed a patron of Humanists UK in 2015. In 2015, he criticized the lack of representation of working-class people in the arts on BBC Radio 5 Live, stating that too much drama is written from "the white, privileged, middle class perspective". In 2024, he was interviewed on HARDtalk in an episode entitled "Do the arts neglect working-class people?". Marsan was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2025 New Year Honours for service to drama.

Eduardo Le Monnier (born Edouard Stanislas Louis Le Monnier; 30 September 1873 in Paris – 14 February 1931 in Buenos Aires) was a French architect known for his work in Brazil, Uruguay, and primarily in Argentina.[1][2][3] He studied at the National School of Decorative Arts in Paris and moved to Brazil in 1894, where he worked on projects such as the General Carneiro station in Belo Horizonte and served as a professor at the School of Fine Arts in Curitiba. He arrived in Buenos Aires on 1 November 1896, where he developed most of his projects and concrete works. One of his first works there was the bakery La Burdalesa (Paraná nº 861/9, year 1898, already demolished). In 1901, he revalidated his diploma at the University of Buenos Aires and joined the Central Society of Architects (SCA). In 1902, he completed the Artistic Ironworks Motteau, featuring a remarkable Art Nouveau style (Avenida Juan de Garay no. 1272, demolished), followed by the headquarters of the mutual savings society La Bola de Nieve in Buenos Aires and in Rosario, province of Santa Fe (Cordoba and Laprida streets, year 1906). He won the Municipal Prize for the Best Facade in 1903 for the residence he built for Bartolomé Ginocchio on Lima Street No. 1642. Two years later, in 1905, he received the third prize for the façade of Felix Egusquiza's residence on Libertad Street No. 1394, and in 1907 he presided over the SCA. Due to these recognitions, several aristocratic families hired him to build large residences in the Barrio Norte; the most notable is the Fernández Anchorena Palace, now housing the Apostolic Nunciature, located at Avenida Alvear 1637, constructed between 1907 and 1909. Another residence, smaller but equally opulent, was built on Avenida de los Incas 3260 and still stands today. In the second half of the 1920s, up to the crisis of 1929, there was a significant rise in financial institutions in Argentina, which established large parent companies in downtown Buenos Aires, becoming the financial city that persists today. Le Monnier designed the headquarters of the Uruguayan Argentine Bank (Avenida Roque Sáenz Peña nº 501, year 1928) and the adjacent buildings of the Bencich brothers, owners of a construction company (Edificio Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña 615 and Edificio Miguel Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña nº 614/6). He also taught at the National Academy of Visual Arts and Architecture. He died in Buenos Aires on 14 February 1931, at the age of 58.[citation needed]

Edward William McBride (ca 1791 – September 3, 1834) was a businessman and political figure in Upper Canada. Born in Newark (Niagara-on-the-Lake) around 1791, he was the son of a United Empire Loyalist. He served in the local militia during the War of 1812. He worked as assistant to King's Printer John Cameron and assumed the role when Cameron became ill in April 1815, continuing until February 1816, several months after Cameron's death. After that, he operated an inn at Niagara. In 1824, he was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Upper Canada for the town of Niagara as a Reformer. He supported government funding for the Welland Canal and defended those who supported Robert Gourlay. For a time, he co-published the Niagara Herald, a newspaper owned by John Crooks, alongside Bartemas Ferguson. As a freemason, he was accused of being associated with the kidnapping and presumed murder of Captain William Morgan, who is said to have revealed secrets of the order. Although McBride denied these accusations, this contributed to his defeat in the 1828 election. He died in Niagara in 1834.

Eger Vaughan Murphree (November 3, 1898 – October 29, 1962) was an American chemist best known for co-inventing the process of fluid catalytic cracking. Born in Bayonne, New Jersey, he moved to Kentucky as a child and graduated from Kentucky University with degrees in chemistry and mathematics in 1920, earning a master's degree in chemistry in 1921. He played college football as a tackle for Kentucky and served as captain of the 1920 Kentucky Wildcats football team. After teaching physics and math and coaching football for one year at Paris High School in Paris, Illinois, Murphree worked several years at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as a staff assistant and research associate in the Chemical Engineering Department. In 1930, he joined Standard Oil of New Jersey. During the Second World War, he was a member of the committee that organized the Manhattan Project and was recognized as a leader in synthetic toluene, butadiene and hydrocarbon synthesis, fluid catalytic cracking, fluid hydroforming, and fluid coking. He participated in the early Manhattan Project as a member of the S-1 Section, served as head of the centrifuge project (which was later abandoned), and was the overall engineer for the Manhattan Project in June 1942. He described Deputy District Engineer Kenneth Nichols as "more like the industrial engineers I was accustomed to dealing with—stable, conservative, thorough and precise." He was scheduled to be on the Lewis Committee reviewing the project in November 1942 but was ill; he (along with James Conant) opposed the committee’s recommendation to build only a small electromagnetic plant, and a full-size plant was constructed. In the 1950s, he served in the Defense Department on missile scheduling and coordinating the programs of the three military services, a role previously held by Nichols. From 1947 to 1962, he served as Vice President of research and engineering at Standard Oil of New Jersey, the company later known as Exxon. He received the Perkin Medal in 1950 and the Industrial Research Institute (IRI) Medal in 1953. The E. V. Murphree Award in Industrial and Engineering Chemistry, awarded annually by the American Chemical Society, is named in his honor. Murphree died on October 29, 1962, at Overlook Hospital in Summit, New Jersey, from coronary thrombosis. He was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1999.

Eintracht Frankfurt e.V., based in Frankfurt, Hesse, is a German professional sports club founded on 8 March 1899. Its football club, established as Frankfurter Fußball-Club Victoria von 1899 and Frankfurter Fußball-Club Kickers von 1899, merged in May 1911 to form Frankfurter Fußball Verein (Kickers-Victoria), which later joined the gymnastics club Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861 in 1920 to create TuS Eintracht Frankfurt von 1861. The name "Eintracht" means 'harmony' or 'concord' and is equivalent to 'United' in English. In 1927, due to pressure from nationalistic gymnastics authorities, the football and gymnastics sections separated. The club has spent a total of 56 seasons in the top division of German football, making it the seventh longest continuously participating club in the Bundesliga. Eintracht is currently in the Bundesliga, the top tier of the German football league system, and has won the German championship once, the DFB-Pokal five times, the UEFA Europa League twice, and finished as runners-up in the European Cup once. It was one of the founding members of the Bundesliga in 1963 and played in the top division for 33 consecutive seasons, finishing in the top half of the table in most of those years. The club has 155,000 members, making it the fourth largest football club in Germany. Since 1925, the club has played at the Waldstadion, currently known as Deutsche Bank Park due to sponsorship. Eintracht has won or drawn more than three-quarters of their games and finished in the top half of the table in most seasons, despite having the highest number of losses in the league (657). With an average attendance of 47,942 since 2013, the club ranks eighth among the 36 Bundesliga and 2. Bundesliga teams for attendance. Charly Körbel, who made 602 appearances in the Bundesliga, spent his entire senior career as a defender with the club. The primary rival is Kickers Offenbach, though the two have only played two league matches in the last 40 years. In 2024, Eintracht Frankfurt has nearly 14,000 active athletes across over 50 sports, making it the largest multi-sports club in the world with a professional football team. The club won its first German championship in 1959, defeating rivals Kickers Offenbach 5–3 after extra time in front of 75,000 fans at Berlin's Olympiastadion. This victory earned them a place in the 1959–60 European Cup, where they defeated BSC Young Boys and Wiener Sport-Club to reach the semi-finals, winning 6–1 at home and 12–4 on aggregate against Rangers, who gave them a guard of honour. They lost 7–3 to Real Madrid in the final at Hampden Park, a match remembered for a hat-trick by Alfredo Di Stéfano and four goals by Ferenc Puskás. After 1959, Eintracht finished as runners-up in 1961 and 1962 in the Oberliga, missing the final both times. From 1973 to 1981, the club achieved its most successful period in the Bundesliga era, winning three DFB-Pokals and the UEFA Cup. The first DFB-Pokal title came in 1973–74, defeating Hamburger SV 3–1, with the final delayed until August 1974 due to the 1974 FIFA World Cup. They won again in 1975, beating MSV Duisburg 1–0, and reached the semi-finals of the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1975–76. Under coach Gyula Lóránt, Eintracht went unbeaten in the second half of the 1976–77 season, finishing fourth, only two points behind champions Borussia Mönchengladbach. Lóránt left for Bayern Munich, and Dettmar Cramer took over before being replaced by Otto Knefler, who left due to health issues. In January 1979, Friedel Rausch became head coach, and Cha Bum-kun joined in July, becoming the first Korean to play in Europe, scoring 12 goals in his debut season. Eintracht reached the UEFA Cup semi-finals, defeating Aberdeen, Dinamo București, Feyenoord, and FC Zbrojovka Brno, before being drawn against Bayern Munich and winning 5–1 in extra time. In the final, they lost 3–2 in the first leg to Borussia Mönchengladbach, but won on away goals after teenager Fred Schaub scored the decisive goal in the return leg. After Lothar Buchmann succeeded Rausch, Eintracht won their third DFB-Pokal in 1981, marking the end of their golden era. In 1984, they avoided relegation by defeating MSV Duisburg 6–1 on aggregate after finishing 16th. In 1986 and 1987, they finished 15th. In 1987–88, they finished in the top half of the league for the first time since 1982 and won the DFB-Pokal 1–0 over VfL Bochum, with Hungarian Lajos Détári scoring the goal; he was sold to Olympiacos two days later. In 1988–89, Jörg Berger led them to safety in a 4–1 aggregate win over 1. FC Saarbrücken in the relegation playoff. In 1990, Berger took the club to third place and was recognized as the best coach in the league. He left in 1991 after a fourth-place finish, but the squad included top Bundesliga players such as Uwe Bein, Uli Stein, Jørn Andersen, Manfred Binz, Tony Yeboah, and Andreas Möller. Dragoslav Stepanović took over and led the team to third place in both seasons, with his tenure considered one of the best in Bundesliga history. In 1991–92, Eintracht came close to winning the Bundesliga, leading the table until the final match, when they lost 2–1 after a disputed penalty decision, allowing VfB Stuttgart to win the title. In 1993–94, they led the table at halftime but fell to fifth place and Klaus Toppmöller was sacked. In 1994, Jupp Heynckes was appointed coach, but fell out with key players Tony Yeboah, Maurizio Gaudino, and Jay-Jay Okocha, leading to suspensions and departures; Heynckes left after the club finished 13th. Relegation occurred in 1995–96, ending 33 consecutive Bundesliga seasons, alongside 1. FC Kaiserslautern. After a difficult debut in the 2. Bundesliga, Eintracht won the title in 1997–98 and returned to the Bundesliga. Promotion coach Horst Ehrmantraut left in December, and Jörg Berger returned, saving the club on the final day of the 1998–99 season with a 5–1 win over Kaiserslautern due to a late goal by Jan Åge Fjørtoft. In 1999, the club was docked two points for license violations and survived on the last day of the season by beating SSV Ulm, who were relegated. In 2000, the club was relegated under Friedel Rausch and failed to return in 2001–02. Eintracht secured a Bundesliga return on the final day of the 2002–03 season with a 6–3 win over Reutlingen, scoring three goals in the last 10 minutes. They were immediately relegated back to the 2. Bundesliga but were promoted the following season under Friedhelm Funkel, who also led them to the DFB-Pokal final in 2005–06, losing to Bayern Munich. This also earned them a spot in the UEFA Cup. After years of stability, Michael Skibbe replaced Funkel in 2009. In 2010–11, the club suffered its fourth Bundesliga relegation after setting a record for most points in the first half of the season, then going seven games without scoring a goal. Coach Skibbe was replaced by Christoph Daum, but the club was relegated again after winning only once in the second half. In 2011–12, Eintracht defeated Alemannia Aachen 3–0 on the 32nd matchday to secure promotion. In 2012–13, they finished sixth in the Bundesliga, qualifying for the Europa League. In 2014–15, they finished in the top half of the league, with Alexander Meier as the league's top scorer. In 2015–16, they struggled and Niko Kovač was appointed in March 2016. They survived through the relegation playoff, finishing 16th and beating 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate. In Kovač's first full season, they survived comfortably and reached the 2017 DFB-Pokal final, losing to Borussia Dortmund. In 2017–18, they reached their second DFB-Pokal final in a row, winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich, despite Kovač agreeing to join the club the following season. He was replaced by Adi Hütter. In 2018–19, the attacking trio of Luka Jović, Ante Rebić, and Sébastien Haller scored 41 league goals and 16 Europa League goals, receiving widespread praise.

During the 2014–15 season, Eintracht Frankfurt's Alexander Meier was the league's top scorer, but the team struggled in 2015–16, finishing 16th and surviving only through a relegation playoff, where they defeated 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate. Niko Kovač was appointed coach in March 2016, and in his first full season, the team survived comfortably and reached the 2017 DFB-Pokal final, losing to Borussia Dortmund. In 2017–18, Eintracht reached their second consecutive DFB-Pokal final, winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich—Kovač had already agreed to join Bayern from the next season—and he was replaced by Adi Hütter. In 2018–19, Luka Jović, Ante Rebić, and Sébastien Haller formed an attacking trio that scored 41 league goals and 16 Europa League goals, earning the nickname "the Buffalo Herd," and Eintracht won all six group games in the Europa League against Lazio, Apollon Limassol, Marseille, Shakhtar Donetsk, Inter Milan, and Benfica, drawing both legs 1–1 in the semi-finals against Chelsea before losing on penalties at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea won the tournament, and Eintracht missed Champions League qualification after dropping from 4th to 7th. After Jović, Rebić, and Haller left in summer 2019, the team regressed in 2019–20 and failed to qualify for Europe, but returned to the Europa League with a 5th-place finish in 2020–21, after which Adi Hütter left for Borussia Mönchengladbach. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht topped their group, stunned Barcelona in the quarter-finals with a 3–0 lead at Camp Nou and won 3–2, with approximately 30,000 Frankfurt fans in attendance, and beat West Ham home and away in the semi-finals to reach their first European final since 1980. In the final at Seville's Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium, Frankfurt beat Rangers 5–4 on penalties after a 1–1 draw in extra-time, with Rafael Santos Borré scoring Eintracht's goal and the winning penalty; goalkeeper Kevin Trapp was named man of the match after making a crucial late save from Ryan Kent and saving Aaron Ramsey's penalty. Eintracht won the competition unbeaten, qualifying for the 2022–23 UEFA Champions League, their first appearance since 1960; they finished second in their group and advanced to the knockout stages, but lost in the round of 16 to S.S.C. Napoli. In the 2022–23 DFB-Pokal, the team reached the final on 3 June 2023, losing 2–0 to RB Leipzig, and a 7th-place finish secured qualification for the UEFA Europa Conference League. Since November 2024, the executive board consists of Axel Hellmann (CEO), Markus Krösche (head of sports), Julien Zamberk (head of finances), and Philipp Reschke (head of fan relations, merchandising and HR). The club crest originates from the coat of arms of Frankfurt, referencing the 13th-century one-headed Imperial Eagle, and evolved with little change until 1980, when a stylized black and white eagle was adopted; in 1999, during its centenary, the club re-adopted a more traditional eagle crest. Since 2005, Eintracht has had a living mascot, a golden eagle named Attila from the Hanau Zoo, who has been present at over 200 games. The official club colours—red, black, and white—come from the founding clubs Frankfurter FC Viktoria (red and white) and Frankfurter FC Kickers (black and white); red and white are from the city coat of arms, and black and white from Prussia. After the merger, both sets of colours were adopted, and since Kickers Offenbach wear red and white, Eintracht avoids that kit, preferring black and red or black and white; in the 2023–2024 season, the home kit is black and red. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht played an unbeaten campaign with an all-white kit, earning the nickname "la bestia blanca" (the white beast), a play on "la bestia negra" (the black beast), after knocking out Barcelona. The club is nicknamed "Die Adler" (The Eagles), derived from the logo, and supporters also use "SGE," from the old name Sportgemeinde Eintracht (Frankfurt), meaning "Sports Community Harmony." The nickname "Launische Diva" (Moody Diva) was common in the early 1990s when Eintracht defeated top teams but lost to weaker ones. "Schlappekicker" (Slipper Kickers) dates back to the 1920s, when J. & C. A. Schneider, a local slipper manufacturer, was a major backer. Green denotes the highest level of German football; yellow the second. The club's initial games from 1899 to 1906 were played on the former Hundswiese field, near Hessischer Rundfunk; in 1906, they established Victoriaplatz by Eschersheimer Landstraße, purchasing stands for 350 marks in 1908; from 1912, they moved to Roseggerstraße in Dornbusch, then to the former Riederwaldstadion in 1920 after merging with Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861. The stadium was inaugurated as Waldstadion in 1925 with the German championship final between FSV Frankfurt and 1. FC Nürnberg; it was renovated for the 2006 FIFA World Cup and has a maximum capacity of 59,500 for Bundesliga fixtures as of 2025. Though officially called Deutsche Bank Park, fans typically refer to it as Waldstadion. Eintracht Frankfurt U21 is the reserve team, previously known as U23 to emphasize its role as a youth-pro to professional link; the club dissolved the team after the 2013–14 season in the Regionalliga Süd. On 14 February 2022, the club applied to re-admit the reserves to the Hessenliga for the 2022–23 season, and in their first season back, Frankfurt II won the Hessenliga and was promoted to the Regionalliga Südwest, where they now play. The main rival is Kickers Offenbach, across the Main River, with the two clubs having played in the 1959 German championship final, which Eintracht won. Eintracht also has regional rivalries with Darmstadt 98 (Hesse derby) and with 1. FSV Mainz 05 and 1. FC Kaiserslautern in Rhineland-Palatinate. The original rival was FSV Frankfurt, with a fierce early rivalry that faded after World War II due to Eintracht's dominance and lack of contact; today, fan relations are generally friendly. In the 2011–12 season, Eintracht played FSV in a league match for the first time in nearly 50 years—the last being on 27 January 1962 in the Oberliga Süd—first on 21 August 2011 at Eintracht's stadium (due to FSV's Bornheimer Hang holding fewer than 11,000), which ended 4–0, and again on 18 February 2012, which ended 6–1. A friendship between Eintracht fan clubs and Oldham Athletic supporters has lasted over 30 years, with small sections visiting each other's grounds at least once a season. Eintracht also has an international friendship with Atalanta supporters. The sports club Eintracht Frankfurt e.V. has nineteen sections, including athletics, where Betty Heidler (2007 hammer throw world champion) and Olympians Andrea Bunjes, Ariane Friedrich, Kamghe Gaba, and Kathrin Klaas were members; the rugby union section reached the German championship final twice, in 1940 and 1965. Within football, the club directly manages only the youth system and the reserve team; professional footballers are managed by Eintracht Frankfurt Fußball-AG, a subsidiary of the parent club.

El Anatsui, born on 4 February 1944 in Anyako, in the Volta Region of Ghana, is a Ghanaian sculptor who has spent much of his career in Nigeria. He gained international recognition for his "bottle-top installations," which consist of thousands of aluminum pieces collected from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire to form metallic, cloth-like wall sculptures. Though the materials appear stiff and sturdy, they are actually flexible, which aids in installation. Anatsui was included in the 2023 Time 100 list of the world's most influential people, with art historian Okeke-Agulu noting that his work transforms ordinary materials like printer’s plates or liquor-bottle caps into magnificent, globally displayed compositions. The youngest of his father’s 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle; his first artistic experience was drawing letters on a chalkboard, which his school headmaster encouraged, and he viewed the forms as images rather than letters. He earned a B.A. in 1968 and a postgraduate diploma in Art Education in 1969, both from the College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST) in Kumasi. Influenced by artists like Oku Ampofo, Vincent Akwete Kofi, and Kofi Antubam, who rejected foreign influences in favor of indigenous art, Anatsui taught at Winneba Specialist Training College (now University of Education) after graduating and later moved to the University of Nigeria, Nsukka in 1975, becoming a senior lecturer in 1982, head of the Fine and Applied Arts department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he held until 2011. He is affiliated with the Nsukka group and has built a global reputation while living and working in Nsukka. Anatsui noted that his education emphasized Western art, lacking focus on African culture, prompting him to visit the National Cultural Centre in Kumasi, where he encountered Adinkra, a system of signs and symbols, which introduced him to abstract art. In the 1970s, he worked in wood, carving trays and creating wall panels with Adinkra symbols and designs using hot rods, chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint. In the late 1970s, he began working in clay, exploring themes of fragility and transformation, particularly in broken pots that he saw as acquiring spiritual uses for ancestors and deities. He later explored food-related materials such as mortars and bottle tops. Much of his work uses found materials, emphasizing their history of use and the human hand’s imprint; he believes used objects carry energy from those who touched them, grounding his art in culture and environment. Bottle caps are especially favored because they resemble cloth, allowing both sculptural and painterly interpretations, and they reflect political and sociological contexts through brand names and colors. He sees the transformation of these materials—removed from their functional roles—as a way to generate reflection, thought, or wonder. Themes in his work include the destruction and reconstitution of materials as a metaphor for Africa’s colonial and post-colonial history, traditional West African textile motifs, and resistance to Western misinterpretations of African history. The concept of Sankofa ("go back and retrieve") is central to his practice, representing a return to African cultural roots as a path to self-discovery. His career began in Nsukka and expanded to Enugu, Lagos, and internationally. In 1990, he had his first major group show at the Studio Museum in Harlem and was featured in the exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions," which ran for five years. He has exhibited globally, including at the Brooklyn Museum (2013), Clark Art Institute (2011), Rice University Art Gallery (2010), Metropolitan Museum of Art (2008–09), National Museum of African Art (Smithsonian, 2008), Fowler Museum (UCLA, 2007), Venice Biennale (1990 and 2007), Hayward Gallery (2005), Liverpool Biennial (2002), and the Arab Museum of Modern Art (2019) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 1995, he held his first solo exhibition outside Africa in London, where he demonstrated African art in non-traditional, conceptually rich ways. In 2005, he appeared in the permanent collection at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and had his first display of metal sheets at Skoto Gallery in New York, which popularized his bottle-cap works. In 2006 and 2007, he was invited to the Venice Biennale, where he created two hanging metal tapestries displayed at Palazzo Fortuny, including Dusasa, which featured golds, reds, and blacks and created a gentle, unique aesthetic. Art curator Robert Storr described the series as exalting and distinct from postwar European art. Anatsui began referring to his metal works as "hangings" rather than "cloths" during this period. A 2010 retrospective, "When I Last Wrote to You About Africa," opened at the Royal Ontario Museum and toured the U.S. for three years. A major exhibition, "Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui," premiered at the Brooklyn Museum in 2013 and traveled to the Des Moines Art Center (2013–14) and the Bass Museum of Art (2014). A career-spanning survey, "Triumphant Scale," organized by Okwui Enwezor and Chika Okeke-Agulu, opened in March 2019 at Haus der Kunst in Munich and traveled to the Arab Museum of Modern Art (Doha) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 2023, Anatsui was selected for the Hyundai Commission at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, where his work "Behind the Red Moon," made from thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, addresses the transatlantic slave trade and will be on view through April 14, 2024. He was elected to the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992, a founding member and fellow of the Forum for African Arts in 2000, and a member of the International Selection Committee for the Dakar Biennale in 2000. He was a fellow at the Civitella Ranieri Foundation in 2001. Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First Ghana National Art Competition in 1968 and was named Best Student of the Year at KNUST in 1969. In 1983, he received a commission for two large terrazzo-surfaced cement sculptures on the Nsukka campus. In 1984, he was invited to the Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste residency in Cuxhaven, West Germany. In 1990, he received an honorable mention at the 44th Venice Biennale and was included in the documentary Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits. In 2015, he was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, and in 2017, he received the Praemium Imperiale, becoming the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.

El Peñol is a town and municipality in the Antioquia Department of Colombia, with a population of 16,223 as recorded in the 2018 census. It is situated in the Eastern Antioquia subregion and is nationally recognized for the nearby monolith, also known as El Peñol, which serves as a major tourist attraction. The town was originally established in 1714 along the Negro-Nare River by Fray Miguel de Castro y Rivadeneiro, while the area had previously been inhabited by the indigenous Tahamí people before Spanish colonization. In 1971, Empresas Públicas de Medellín decided to dam the Negro-Nare River at Guatape to supply additional water and power to the rapidly expanding city of Medellín, located about 50 miles (30 km) to the west, leading to the flooding of the river valley where El Peñol was situated. The original town was taken by eminent domain, and a new town was constructed several miles west, displacing several thousand residents who were forced to relocate without legal recourse. The dam was completed and the valley flooded in 1978, resulting in the creation of the El Peñol-Guatapé Reservoir, which now covers the former site of El Peñol. A cross marks the location above the former parish of El Viejo Peñol that once fronted the town plaza, and some rural areas of Guatape were also submerged and lost. El Peñol has a subtropical highland climate (Köppen classification: Cfb), characterized by consistently warm temperatures and abundant rainfall. El Santuario is a town and municipality located in the Antioquia Department of Colombia, within the Eastern Antioquia subregion. It was founded on 11 March 1765 by Captain Antonio Gómez de Castro. The town lies at an elevation of 2,150 meters above sea level and has an average temperature of 17 °C. It is situated 57 kilometers from Medellín, the capital of the Antioquia Department, and covers a total area of 83.45 km². El Santuario is notable for being the birthplace of comedian Guillermo Zuluaga, known as "Montecristo," and actor Crisanto Alonso Vargas, known as "Vargasvil." The primary economic activity in the town is agriculture, focusing on the cultivation of vegetables, beans, potatoes, and legumes.
