Dame Elisabeth Joy Murdoch, Lady Murdoch AC DBE (née Greene; 8 February 1909 – 5 December 2012), was an Australian philanthropist and matriarch of the Murdoch family. She married Sir Keith Murdoch in 1928, 23 years his junior, and inherited the bulk of his fortune upon his death in 1952. She was the mother of Rupert Murdoch, international media proprietor, and had other children: Janet Calvert-Jones AO (born 1939), Anne Kantor AO (1937–2022), and Helen Handbury AO (1929–2004). Born in Melbourne on 8 February 1909, she was the youngest of three daughters of Marie Grace de Lancey (née Forth) and Rupert Greene; her grandfather, William Henry Greene, was an Irish railway engineer who emigrated to Australia and married Fanny, the fourth of George Govett’s 10 daughters. Her mother’s ancestors were Scottish and English, with one maternal great-grandfather, Frederick Forth, serving as a lieutenant governor in the West Indies. She was educated at St Catherine's School in Toorak and Clyde School in Woodend. Before marriage, she volunteered with the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. She joined the management committee of the Royal Children's Hospital in 1933, serving as its president from 1954 to 1965, and was designated to succeed her predecessor Ella Latham; she oversaw the hospital’s relocation from Carlton to a new campus in Parkville. In 1961, she was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (CBE) for her work at the hospital, and in 1963, a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (DBE) for her role in building the new children's hospital. In 1989, she received a Companion of the Order of Australia, Civil Division (AC) for community services, and in 2001, the Centenary Medal for philanthropic contributions to the Australian arts. She was a Life Governor of the Royal Women's Hospital, patron of the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the Australian American Association (Victoria), a founding member of the EW Tipping Foundation and the Deafness Foundation of Victoria, and the first woman on the council of trustees of the National Gallery of Victoria. She was also a founding member of the Victorian Tapestry Workshop and a member of the Patrons Council of the Epilepsy Foundation of Victoria. Her garden, "Cruden Farm" at Langwarrin, designed by Edna Walling, is one of Australia’s finest landscape gardens and is open to the public. In 1983, she was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Laws by the University of Melbourne and became a fellow of Trinity College, Melbourne in 2000. A portrait of her by Christopher Pyett, adapted by Normana Wight and woven by Merrill Dumbrell, was commissioned for the National Portrait Gallery in 2000. In 2001, she was inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women and a rose, Treloars, was named after her. A Tasmanian Boronia species, Boronia elisabethiae, was named in her honour following donations to the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne. In 2002, she received recognition from the French government for funding an Auguste Rodin exhibition in Melbourne. In 2003, she joined Philanthropy Australia as a life member and was awarded the key to the City of Melbourne. In 2004, Langwarrin Secondary College was renamed Elisabeth Murdoch College. In 2005, at age 96, she received the Victorian of the Year award. In 2009, the main performance venue of the Melbourne Recital Centre was named in her honour, and she was elected an Honorary Fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities. In 2010, Geelong Grammar School named a new girls' boarding house after her. In January 2007, at age 97 years and 11 months, she surpassed Dame Alice Chisholm as Australia’s longest-lived dame. She was also a patron of the Australian Family Association. She died in her sleep at Cruden Farm, Langwarrin, Victoria, on 5 December 2012, at the age of 103. At the time of her death, she had 77 living descendants.

Elizabeth Michelle Belding is a computer scientist specializing in mobile computing and wireless networks. She is a professor of computer science at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Belding graduated from Florida State University in 1996 with a degree in computer science and a second degree in applied mathematics, both earned with Summa Cum Laude and Honors. She attended the University of California, Santa Barbara on a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship and completed her Ph.D. in electrical and computer engineering in 2000. Her dissertation, titled Routing in Ad hoc Mobile Networks: On-Demand and Hierarchical Strategies, was written under the name Elizabeth Michelle Royer and jointly supervised by P. Michael Melliar-Smith and Louise Moser. She has served as a member of the computer science faculty at the University of California, Santa Barbara since 2000. Belding was named a Fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in 2014 for "contributions to mobile and wireless networking and communication protocols" and was elected an ACM Fellow in 2018 for "contributions to communication in mobile networks and their deployment in developing regions." One of her publications on Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector Routing in mobile networks received the SIGMOBILE Test of Time Award in 2018.

Dame Elizabeth Anne Loosemore Esteve-Coll DBE FRSA (née Kingdon; 14 October 1938 – 16 September 2024) was a British academic, museum director, and librarian. She was born in Ripon, West Riding of Yorkshire, the daughter of Percy Kingdon, a bank clerk, and his wife Nora Rose. She attended Darlington High School and studied English and Spanish at Trinity College, Dublin, followed by Art History at Birkbeck College (now Birkbeck, University of London).[2][3] From 1977 to 1982, she served as head of learning resources at Kingston Polytechnic (now Kingston University London).[4] In 1982, she became the first female director of the University of Surrey Library.[4][5] In 1985, she was appointed Keeper of the National Art Library at the Victoria and Albert Museum, where she initiated changes to increase accessibility for a broader audience.[7] In 1987, she became the UK's first woman director of a national arts collection, succeeding Sir Roy Strong, and held the position until her resignation in 1994, midway through her second term, to become Vice-Chancellor of the University of East Anglia.[8][9] Alan Borg succeeded her as director, taking office on 1 October 1995.[8] She served as Vice-Chancellor of the University of East Anglia from 1995 to 1997 but stepped down after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, stating: "It is with real sadness and disappointment that I must acknowledge that I am not able to lead the university into the 21st century."[11][12] She served as Chancellor of the University of Lincoln for seven years and was a Trustee of the Sainsbury Institute for the Study of Japanese Arts and Cultures since its foundation in January 1999.[13][14] At the age of 21, she married José Esteve-Coll, a Spanish refugee sea captain who was 30 years her senior; he died in 1980.[15] She was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours list in 1995. In November 2005, she received the Order of the Rising Sun, Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon (3rd class) for her "outstanding contribution to the promotion of Japanese culture and studies to British people".[16] In November 2008, she was awarded an honorary doctorate of arts and named Chancellor Emerita by the University of Lincoln during a farewell ceremony at Lincoln Cathedral.[17][18] She died on 16 September 2024, at the age of 85.[15]

Nnoseng Ellen Kate Kuzwayo (29 June 1914 – 19 April 2006) was a South African women's rights activist and politician who taught from 1938 to 1952. She served as president of the African National Congress Youth League in the 1960s and was secretary of the ANC Youth League in the 1940s. In 1994, she was elected to the first post-apartheid South African Parliament at the age of 79 and served for five years until June 1999, becoming South Africa's longest-serving parliamentarian. Her autobiography, Call Me Woman (1985), won the CNA Literary Award, making her the first black writer to receive South Africa's leading literary prize. Born Nnoseng Ellen Serasengwe in Thaba 'Nchu, Orange Free State, she came from an educated, politically active family. Her maternal grandfather, Jeremaiah Makgothi, was taken to the Cape in circa 1875 to attend the Lovedale Institute, where he qualified as a teacher, worked as a court interpreter, and served as a Methodist lay preacher; he was the only layman to work with Robert Moffat on the translation of the Bible into Setswana. Both Makgothi and her father, Philip S. Mefare, were politically active—Makgothi was secretary of the Orange Free State branch of the South African Native National Congress, and Mefare was a member of its successor, the African National Congress. Kuzwayo began her schooling at a school built by Makgothi on his farm in Thabapatchoa, about 12 miles from Tweespruit, and attended Adams College, Amanzimtoti, before completing a teacher training course at Lovedale College in Fort Hare, graduating at age 22. She married Ernest Moloto in her late twenties, had two sons, and after enduring abuse, fled to Johannesburg. She had a part as a shebeen queen alongside Sidney Poitier in the 1951 film Cry, the Beloved Country. After her first marriage ended, she married Godfrey Kuzwayo in 1950. She taught in the Transvaal until 1952, when she gave up teaching due to the introduction of the Bantu Education Act, 1953, which limited black education opportunities. She then trained as a social worker from 1953 to 1955. After the 1976 Soweto uprising, she was the only woman on a committee of 10 tasked with organizing civic affairs in Soweto, and was detained for five months in 1977–78 under the Prevention of Terrorism Act; she later recounted her arrest in her 1996 testimony to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. She also served as president of the Black Consumer Union of South Africa and the Maggie Magaba Trust. In 1979, she was named Woman of the Year by The Star, and was nominated again in 1984. In 1987, she received an honorary doctorate of Laws from the University of the Witwatersrand, becoming the first black woman to receive such an honor from the university, and also received honorary doctorates from the University of Natal and the University of Port Elizabeth. She was awarded the Order of Meritorious Service by Nelson Mandela in 1999. With director Betty Wolpert, she co-produced the documentary films Awake from Mourning (1982) and Tsiamelo –– A Place of Goodness (1983), based on the story of her family's land dispossession. Kuzwayo died in Johannesburg at the age of 91 from complications of diabetes, survived by her sons Bobo and Justice Moloto, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. A South African marine research ship, the Ellen Khuzwayo, was named after her and launched in 2007.

Elsie Tu CBE GBM (née Hume; Chinese: 杜葉錫恩; 2 June 1913 – 8 December 2015), formerly known as Elsie Elliott, was a British-born Hong Kong social activist who served as an elected member of the Urban Council of Hong Kong from 1963 to 1995 and a member of the Legislative Council of Hong Kong from 1988 to 1995. Born on 2 June 1913 in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, into a working-class family of John and Florence Hume, she was the second of four children. After attending Benwell Secondary Girls' School and Heaton Secondary School, she studied at Armstrong College, graduating in 1937 with a Bachelor of Arts. From 1937 to 1947, she worked as a schoolteacher in Halifax, where she volunteered in Civil Defence during the Second World War. She converted to Christianity in 1932 during her university years. In 1946, she married William Elliott and moved to China in 1947 as a missionary with the Christian Missions in Many Lands, stationed in Yifeng. After the Chinese Communist Party took power in 1949 and expelled foreign missionaries from mainland China, she relocated to Hong Kong, living in an illegal apartment in the Wong Tai Sin squatter community known as Kai Tak New Village, where she observed corruption involving triad protection money. Disillusioned with her husband's rigid Protestant faith and the Plymouth Brethren's refusal to engage in social issues, she left the church in 1955 and divorced him in 1964. She lived briefly in a kitchen in a Kowloon Walled City tenement and founded Mu Kuang English School in 1954 in an old army tent near Kai Tak, starting with 30 pupils; she remained principal until 2000. The school now serves 1,300 children in low-income families on Kung Lok Road in Kwun Tong. She met Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei at the school, who became her husband 30 years later. Elliott was shocked by the injustices in Hong Kong, including child labour and poor working conditions, and wrote to The Guardian, prompting UK Parliament debate and eventually leading to labour reforms. She became politically active, winning her first Urban Council seat in 1963, and later served as vice-chairman from 1986 until her defeat in 1995, consistently receiving the highest votes. She was also the spokeswoman for the United Nations Association of Hong Kong, advocating for self-government. In 1966, she opposed a proposed 5-cent to 25-cent increase in Star Ferry fares, collecting over 20,000 signatories and flying to London to protest, which led to a hunger strike by So Sau-chung and eventually the Kowloon riots. She faced accusations of inciting the riots, dubbed the "Elliott riot," and was subjected to official inquiries. She campaigned against triad protection money and police corruption, reporting minibus rackets and corruption to various officials, including Governor Murray MacLehose and ICAC Director G. A. Harknett, and helped Mak Pui-yuen, who was victimised for reporting corruption. Her activism contributed to the establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in 1974. In 1979, she co-founded the Association for the Promotion of Public Justice (APPJ) with Andrew Tu, which later established a Filipino Overseas Workers Group. She advocated for gay rights, urging decriminalisation as in the UK in 1967, though the government cited local opposition; homosexuality was decriminalised in Hong Kong in 1991. In 1980, after John MacLennan, a police inspector, was shot in his home during an investigation into homosexuality, she suggested he was persecuted for knowing too much and corresponded with MacLehose and other officials, leading to a Commission of Inquiry. In 1980, she was found under surveillance by the Standing Committee on Pressure Groups (SCOPG), but she remained unbothered, stating she had done nothing wrong. She was appointed to the HKSAR Basic Law Consultative Committee in 1985 and, when the Urban Council became an electoral college in 1985, she was elected to the Legislative Council in 1988, serving until 1995, during which she chaired the House Committee from 1991 to 1995 and remained the most popular legislator. In the lead-up to the 1997 handover, she supported a gradual pace of democratisation preferred by the Chinese government, opposing Governor Chris Patten's electoral reforms and criticising him as a hypocrite. In the March 1995 Urban Council election, she lost to Szeto Wah by 2,397 votes, and in the September 1995 Legislative Council election, she lost again in Kowloon East to Szeto Wah, supported by the pro-Beijing Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB). She was appointed to the Beijing-controlled Provisional Legislative Council from December 1996 to June 1998, serving on the Selection Committee responsible for electing the first Chief Executive. After the Provisional Legislative Council was dissolved in 1998, her political career ended. She stepped away from active politics but continued to comment on social issues and write critical articles. In 2002, she supported the enactment of the anti-subversion law under Basic Law Article 23, and in 2003, she publicly endorsed Regina Ip, who promoted the law, during the 1 July Protest with over 500,000 demonstrators. In 2013, she criticised widening income inequality and expressed sympathy for dock workers striking against billionaire Li Ka-shing's Hutchison Whampoa, marking her 100th birthday in June 2013. The Mu Kuang alumni established the Elsie Tu Education Fund in her honour. She died on 8 December 2015 at the age of 102 from pneumonia-related complications at Kwun Tong United Christian Hospital. All three former Chief Executives—Tung Chee-hwa, Donald Tsang, and Leung Chun-ying—were pallbearers at her funeral on 20 December, and her ashes were buried with those of her husband, Andrew Tu, at the Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan. Her father, John Hume, a grocer's assistant who fought in the First World War and was gassed, profoundly influenced her conscience and world-view, instilling in her a hatred of war and compassion for people, as well as a left-leaning perspective on religion, Marxism, and workers' rights. She married William Elliott, eight years her junior, and described the period as the lowest point in her life, eventually divorcing him in 1964. She later married Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who came to Hong Kong from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s, and they worked together at Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching other Form 1 subjects. She believed Andrew's ideas reminded her of her father's values.

Elsie Tu's worldview was shaped by her father's influence, leading her in her youth to believe that "I could at least be good and useful in life"; her father died when she was in China. She married William Elliott, who was eight years her junior, and worked with the Plymouth Brethren missionary group in 1946. In 1947, she traveled to China with her husband, but grew increasingly disillusioned with his fundamentalism and their church, describing the period as "the lowest point in [her] life" and considering suicide. The couple separated during an abortive trip back to England, and she returned to Hong Kong alone, later divorcing him in 1964. In Hong Kong, she met her second husband, Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who had come from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s. They became working partners at the Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching all other Form 1 subjects; despite cultural and language differences, Elsie found Andrew's ideas brought her back to her father's values. In 1985, 30 years after meeting, they married when Elsie was 71 and Andrew was 63, remaining married until Andrew died in 2001. Andrew was also a social activist and leader of the Chinese Alliance for Commemoration of the Sino-Japanese War Victims, which demands justice, reparations, and apologies for victims of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Tu authored two volumes of autobiography and other works; Colonial Hong Kong in the Eyes of Elsie Tu was published in 2003, and Shouting at the Mountain: A Hong Kong Story of Love and Commitment, co-written with Andrew Tu, was completed after his death in 2001 and published in 2005. She also completed the publication of her husband's autobiography of his childhood in Inner Mongolia, Camel Bells in the Windy Desert. In the 1960s, Tu was recognized as a champion fighting for the underprivileged and against corruption; Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying praised her "passion and devotion to Hong Kong and her tremendous contributions to social reform and development" after her death, and Chief Secretary Carrie Lam recalled meeting her during her university days, describing her as an exemplary champion of social justice who commanded respect. Founding chairman of the Democratic Party Martin Lee praised her as a pioneer in fighting for democracy, and other democrats such as Lau Chin-shek, Lee Wing-tat, Fred Li Wah-ming, and Frederick Fung acknowledged that their involvement in social activism was inspired or assisted by Elsie Tu. Tu received numerous honours, including the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Government Service in 1975, a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 1977 for her anti-corruption work, and the Grand Bauhinia Medal (GBM) in 1997 as one of the first recipients of the highest honour in the SAR award system. She also received honorary degrees: an honorary doctoral degree in Social Science from the University of Hong Kong in 1988, honorary doctoral degrees in Laws from the Hong Kong Polytechnic University and in Social Science from the Open Learning Institute of Hong Kong in 1994, and honorary doctoral degrees in Civil Law from both Armstrong College (later Newcastle University) and Durham University in 1996.

The Embraer EMB 110 Bandeirante, meaning "pioneer," is a Brazilian twin-turboprop light transport aircraft designed by Embraer for both military and civil use. It was designed by French engineer Max Holste in accordance with specifications issued by the Brazilian Ministry of Aeronautics in 1965, aiming to create a general-purpose aircraft with low operational costs and high reliability for civilian and military operations. The aircraft was to have turboprop engines, a low-mounted wing, and sufficient capacity for eight personnel, based on a study of Brazilian commercial air traffic and existing airport infrastructure. This specification, known as IPD-6504, significantly influenced the aircraft's design. Early development predated the founding of Embraer, which was established in August 1969; construction of the prototype was supervised by Brazilian aeronautical engineer Ozires Silva, who also played a key role in founding the company. The first prototype, designated YC-95, made its maiden flight on 26 October 1968 from São José dos Campos Airport, piloted by José Mariotto Ferreira and accompanied by flight engineer Michel Cury, landing after approximately 50 minutes. Prior to this, 110,000 project hours were logged, producing 12,000 manufacturing drawings and 22,000 hours of structural and aerodynamic calculations, with an estimated 282,000 hours spent on manufacturing and tooling. The prototype was officially presented four days later, with a repeat of the maiden flight. The positive results led to the approval of production in mid-1969, with Embraer assuming responsibility on 2 January 1970. Two additional prototypes, designated EMB 100, flew on 19 October 1969 and 29 June 1970, respectively; however, due to shifting market conditions, the EMB 100 was quickly redesigned into the EMB 110 Bandeirante, which featured greater capacity and technological improvements. In May 1970, the Brazilian Air Force (FAB) placed an initial order for 80 production aircraft. The Bandeirante received its Brazilian airworthiness certificate in late 1972 and entered service with the Brazilian airline Transbrasil on 16 April 1973. A typical configuration seats between 15 and 21 passengers and is flown by two pilots; the EMB 110P1A/41 model has a length of 15.1 metres (50 ft), a height of 4.92 metres (16.1 ft), and a wingspan of 15.33 metres (50.3 ft). It has a maximum cruising speed of 411 km/h (222 kn), an economical cruising speed of 341 km/h (184 kn), achieving a range of 1,964 km (1,060 nmi) with 45 minutes of reserve fuel, and a service ceiling of 21,500 feet (6,600 m). During the 1970s, Embraer developed the EMB 120 Brasilia, an enlarged derivative with a pressurized cabin, greater speed, and capacity for up to 30 passengers, leading to the decision to halt further EMB 110 development and focus on the EMB 120. Between 1968 and 1990, Embraer produced a total of 494 aircraft in various configurations for diverse roles. The passenger model first flew on 9 August 1972 and entered commercial service on 16 April 1973 with Transbrasil. Ryanair operated a 15-seat EMB 110 starting on 8 July 1985, continuing until 1989. By October 2018, about 150 EMB 110s were still in service with airlines, air taxis, government entities, and air forces worldwide. Production ended in 1990, with the EMB 110 being superseded by the EMB 120 Brasilia. Deliveries to the Brazilian Air Force began in February 1973, with the first delivery on 9 February 1973. Two EMB 111A Patrulha maritime patrol aircraft were leased to the Argentine Navy during the Falklands War as a stop-gap between the retirement of the last Lockheed SP-2H Neptune and the introduction of modified Lockheed L-188 Electras. On 15 December 2010, the Brazilian Air Force flew its first upgraded EMB 110, designated C/P-95, equipped with modern avionics from Israeli firm Elbit Systems' Brazilian subsidiary, Aeroeletronica; at that time, the FAB had 96 active EMB 110s, which reduced to 48 by 2017. In 2020, 39 Bandeirantes were still in airline service with 15 operators: 31 in North/South America, 1 in Africa, and 7 in Asia Pacific & Middle East.

The emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis), a green buprestid beetle native to temperate northeastern Asia—including Russia, Mongolia, northern China, Japan, and Korea—is native to that region where it typically occurs at low densities and does not cause significant damage to ash trees (Fraxinus spp.). Females lay eggs in bark crevices, flakes, or cracks, and the eggs, measuring 0.6 to 1.0 mm in diameter and initially white, turn reddish-brown if fertile, hatch about two weeks later, and the larvae chew through the bark to feed on the phloem, cambium, and outer xylem, creating long serpentine galleries. The larvae go through four instars, with fully mature fourth-instar larvae being 26 to 32 mm long; they excavate J-shaped chambers in the sapwood or outer bark in the fall, where they develop into pupae and emerge as adults the following spring. Adults are bright metallic green, about 8.5 mm long and 1.6 mm wide, with darker green elytra that may have copper hues, and a small spine at the tip of the abdomen; they have serrate antennae beginning at the fourth segment. Adults emerge after 400–500 degree-days above 10 °C (50 °F), peaking at around 1,000 degree-days, feed on ash leaves for one week before mating, and males locate females by visual cues, dropping directly onto them to mate, with mating lasting up to 50 minutes and females mating with multiple males. A typical female lives about six weeks and lays 40–70 eggs, with longer-lived females laying up to 200. Larvae can overwinter in their galleries and may require an additional summer of feeding before overwintering again, with a two-year life cycle more common in cool climates like European Russia. The beetle is invasive in North America, where it was first identified in Canton, Michigan in 2002 (though possibly present since the late 1980s), likely introduced via shipping materials such as packing crates, and has a core population in Michigan and surrounding states and provinces, spreading to Ontario, northern Louisiana, Nebraska, New Brunswick, Colorado, and the Pacific Northwest (Oregon), with a population found in Moscow, Russia in 2003, spreading westward at up to 40 km (25 mi) per year and expected to reach central Europe between 2031 and 2036. It has spread to far eastern Ukraine from Russia and is not recorded in the European Union as of 2019. In North America, it primarily infests green ash (F. pennsylvanica), black ash (F. nigra), white ash (F. americana), and blue ash (F. quadrangulata), with blue ash showing higher resistance due to high tannin content in its leaves, a trait absent in most American ash species except blue ash. In Europe, F. excelsior is the main host, moderately resistant to infestation. The beetle can also infest non-ash species such as white fringe tree and Olea europaea (in lab settings), though it is unclear if these trees were healthy when infested. Ash trees in pure stands or in landscaping are more vulnerable due to environmental stresses like compacted soil, pollution, road salt, and urban heat, and because most landscaping ashes come from a few cultivars with low genetic diversity. Damage occurs as larval feeding disrupts nutrient and water transport, effectively girdling the tree and killing it; stressed trees may regenerate via stump sprouting or produce higher seed crops. Without natural suppressors like resistant trees, predators, or parasitoid wasps present in its native range, populations grow rapidly and all ash trees in an area are expected to die within 10 years. Every North American ash species is susceptible, though some Asian ash species like F. baroniana, F. chinensis, F. floribunda, F. mandshurica, and F. platypoda are resistant. In North America, the beetle has killed tens of millions of ash trees and threatens to kill most of the 8.7 billion ash trees, eliminating nearly all ash trees in the National Capital Region in nine years, reducing the density from 17–18 per hectare to 5–6 per hectare and transforming ash-dominated swamplands into shrublands, impacting wildlife. The loss of ash affects soil nutrients, increases invasive plants, and alters species that depend on ash. Control efforts include monitoring via visual surveys and traps using purple or green colors or volatile pheromones, girdling trees as trap trees, and quarantines restricting transport of ash firewood or live plants without inspection or treatment. Infested trees are often removed in urban areas, with replacements using non-ash species like maple, oak, or linden, and in rural areas, trees may be harvested for lumber or firewood under quarantine. Insecticides such as azadirachtin, imidacloprid, emamectin benzoate, and dinotefuran are used, with dinotefuran and imidacloprid being systemic and effective for one to three years; treatments are typically applied via direct injection or soil drench and are mainly used in urban areas with high-value trees, though not feasible for large forested areas. Insecticide use does not stop damage progression. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service ended all EAB quarantine activities on 14 December 2020 due to ineffectiveness, shifting focus to biological controls. Government agencies in the U.S. and Canada use the native parasitoid wasp Cerceris fumipennis for biological surveillance—volunteers catch the wasps as they return with beetles, indicating infestation—without significantly reducing beetle populations. The native range of the emerald ash borer in Asia was surveyed for parasitoid species that target the beetle without attacking other insects, in hopes they could suppress populations when introduced.

It is recommended to choose monotypic species such as the pawpaw, yellowwood, Franklin tree, Kentucky coffeetree, Osage orange, sourwood, and bald cypress. Insecticides containing active ingredients like azadirachtin, imidacloprid, emamectin benzoate, and dinotefuran are currently used; dinotefuran and imidacloprid are systemic and remain effective for one to three years depending on the product.[8][47][48] Insecticides are generally only considered viable in urban areas with high-value trees near an infestation.[47] Ash trees are primarily treated through direct injection into the tree or soil drench, and some insecticides require licensed applicators due to application restrictions. Damage from emerald ash borer can continue to increase over time even with insecticide use.[8] Insecticide treatments are not practical for large forested areas outside of urban settings.[8] The native range of emerald ash borer in Asia was surveyed for parasitoid species that target emerald ash borer without attacking other insects, with the goal of introducing them to suppress populations in North America.[49] Three species imported from China were approved for release: Spathius agrili, Tetrastichus planipennisi, and Oobius agrili by the USDA in 2007 and in Canada in 2013, and Spathius galinae was approved for release in 2015.[50][51] Excluding Spathius galinae, which was recently released, the other three species have been documented parasitizing emerald ash borer larvae one year after release, showing survival through winter, though establishment varied by species and location.[51] Tetrastichus planipennisi and Oobius agrili have established and shown increasing populations in Michigan since 2008; Spathius agrili has had lower establishment success in North America, possibly due to a lack of available emerald ash borer larvae at adult emergence in spring, limited cold tolerance, and better suitability to regions below the 40th parallel.[51] The USDA is also evaluating the use of Beauveria bassiana, an insect fungal pathogen, in combination with parasitoid wasps for controlling emerald ash borer.[52]

The Emil J. Oberhoffer House is a historic residence located in Lakeville, Minnesota, United States, situated overlooking Orchard Lake. Emil Oberhoffer, who founded and served as the first conductor of the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra, owned the home. The house was designed by Paul Haugen, an architect who worked for the firm Purcell and Elmslie, known for its Prairie School architectural style. Haugen began his career as an apprentice in Fargo, North Dakota, and after relocating to Minneapolis, he became influenced by Prairie School design principles. During a brief period of independence around 1913, Haugen designed this home as well as several other residences and a school in Burnsville. Later, the property was owned by the parents of golfer Patty Berg.

Emilio Marcos de Palma Morella (born 7 January 1978) is an Argentine man recognized as the first person born on the continent of Antarctica.[1][2] He was born at Fortín Sargento Cabral, located at Esperanza Base near the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, and had a birth weight of 3.4 kg (7 lb 8 oz). His father, Captain Jorge Emilio Palma, served as the head of the Argentine Army detachment at the base.[3] Silvia Morella de Palma, who was seven months pregnant at the time, was airlifted to Esperanza Base in late 1977 to complete her pregnancy.[4] Emilio was born on 7 January 1978 and baptized at the Chapel of St. Francis of Assisi on the base.[5] He is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the first person born on the continent.[6] This Argentine biographical article is a stub. An emoticon, a portmanteau of "emotion" and "icon," is a pictorial representation of a facial expression using characters such as punctuation marks, numbers, and letters to convey a person's feelings, mood, or reaction without detailed description. ASCII emoticons have roots dating back hundreds of years, with early examples including Robert Herrick’s 1648 poem "Tumble me down, and I will sit Upon my ruins, (smiling yet:)"—though experts question whether the colon was intentionally used to represent a smile. In the 17th century, punctuation like colons and semicolons were often placed within parentheses, as seen in Richard Baxter’s 1653 work with 14 instances of ":)". Typographical art using punctuation to express emotions appeared in newspapers as early as 1881, and in 1912, Ambrose Bierce proposed a bracket "‿" to represent a smiling face, while in 1936, Alan Gregg suggested using brackets and other punctuation to depict various moods. A 1953 New York Herald Tribune article used a dash and right bracket to represent a tongue in cheek, and MAD magazine in 1962 featured typewriter-generated artwork with emoticon-like elements. In the 1970s, a student at the University of Illinois developed pictograms resembling smiling faces on the PLATO IV system, likely in 1972, which Mary Kalantzis and Bill Cope consider the first emoticons. In 1982, computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the use of ASCII symbols, specifically the smiley :-) and frown :-(, on the Carnegie Mellon University bulletin board system to convey humor or sarcasm, and this protocol became widely adopted. The emoticon spread to ARPANET and Usenet, with other suggestions including * and &, and the smiley became integral to digital communication. In 1996, The Smiley Company, founded by Nicolas Loufrani and his father Franklin, launched The Smiley Dictionary, cataloging over 500 ASCII emoticons, which removed the hyphen to create :) instead of :-), influencing modern usage. Loufrani later created graphical representations of emoticons, registered in the U.S. Copyright Office in 1997 and released as GIFs in 1998, and developed a set of 640 icons published in 2001 and 2002. These portrait emoticons, which include hand gestures like white gloves, became the foundation for modern emojis. In 2007, Google began petitioning the Unicode Technical Committee (UTC) to standardize emojis, leading to a 2009 proposal with 625 new emoji characters, including many emoticon-style designs. The Smiley Company auctioned an NFT of 42 original graphical emoticons in 2022, with proceeds going to its non-profit arm. Emoticons and emojis are often confused, but most commonly used emojis are emoticons representing emotions. In 2024, the BBC reported that two of the top three emojis were portrait emoticons. Scott Fahlman auctioned his original 1982 emoticons as NFTs in 2021, selling for $237,500. In Western usage, emoticons typically have eyes on the left, followed by a nose and mouth, with the two-character version :) being very popular. Variants include :( for sadness, :(( for extreme sadness, :'( for weeping, :"> for a blush, ;) for a wink, :D for a grin, :P for a tongue-out expression, and :-> for a smug look. The combination <3 represents a heart, </3 a broken heart, :O shock, :/ melancholy, and :| neutrality. Crinkled eyes in XD or XDDDD suggest amusement. The equal sign = is used for eyes as in =), and the hyphen is often omitted. Younger users increasingly use :) without a hyphen, a shift linguists interpret as a form of covert prestige. In some countries, keyboard layouts influence emoticon use: Scandinavia uses =), and in Cyrillic-using regions, the right parenthesis ) is used as a smiley, with multiple parentheses indicating greater happiness. The shrug emoticon ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ uses the Japanese katakana character ツ. Kaomoji, popularized in Japan on ASCII NET in 1986, are distinct from the Scott Fahlman movement and evolved into forms like owo, uwu, and TwT, especially in anime and furry communities. Users of 2channel developed emoticons using scripts like Kannada, such as ಠ_ಠ for disapproval and ಥ for a tearing eye, which spread to 4chan and other Western sites. In South Korea, emoticons use Hangul letters, with consonants like ㅅ, ㅁ, or ㅂ for the mouth/nose and ㅇ, ㅎ, or ㅍ for eyes, and vowels like ㅜ and ㅠ for crying, as in ㅜㅜ. Semicolons and carets are common, with -;/ indicating sweating. The character 囧 (U+56E7), meaning "patterned window," was used as an emoticon as early as January 20, 2005, and can be combined with Orz, such as 囧rz. Other variants include 崮, 莔, 商, and 囧興.

Using quotation marks " and apostrophes ' are commonly used in Korean emoticons. Vowel jamos such as ㅜ and ㅠ can represent a crying face, with ㅜㅜ functioning similarly to the letter T in Western style. Sometimes ㅡ (a vowel jamo, not an em-dash), a comma (,), or an underscore (_) is added, and these character sets can be combined, as in ㅠ.ㅡ, ㅡ^ㅜ, and ㅜㅇㅡ. Semicolons and carets are also frequently used; semicolons can indicate sweating, as seen in -;/, --^, and -_-;;. The character 囧 (U+56E7), meaning 'patterned window', may be combined with the posture emoticon Orz, such as 囧rz. This character existed in Oracle bone script but was rarely used until its adoption as an emoticon, documented as early as January 20, 2005. Other variants include 崮 (king 囧), 莔 (queen 囧), 商 (囧 with a hat), 囧興 (turtle), and 卣 (Bomberman). The character 槑 (U+69D1), a variant of 梅 'plum', represents a double of 呆 'dull' or a greater degree of dullness. In Chinese, full characters are typically duplicated to express emphasis. Orz (other forms include Or2, on_, OTZ, OTL, STO, JTO, _no, _冂○, and 囧rz) is an emoticon depicting a kneeling or bowing person (the Japanese version is called dogeza), with "o" as the head, "r" as the arms and part of the body, and "z" as part of the body and legs. It can represent respect or kowtowing, but is commonly used to express frustration, despair, sarcasm, or grudging respect. It was first used in late 2002 on the Techside forum, a Japanese personal website, where a poster asked about a cable cover and typed "_|￣|○" to show a cable and its cover. Others noted it resembled a kneeling person, leading to its popularity. These comments were later deleted as they were considered off-topic. By 2005, Orz had spawned a subculture, with blogs dedicated to it and URL shortening services named after it. In Taiwan, Orz is associated with the concept of nice guys. o7 or O7 is an emoticon showing a person saluting, with "o" as the head and "7" as the arm. An emotisound is a brief sound transmitted and played back during message viewing, typically in IM or email, intended to convey emotional subtext. Some services, like MuzIcons, combine emoticons with music players in an Adobe Flash-based widget. In 2004, Trillian introduced "emotiblips," allowing users to stream files as the voice and video equivalent of an emoticon. In 2007, MTV and Paramount Home Entertainment promoted "emoticlip" as viral marketing for The Hills' second season, featuring twelve short dialogue snippets uploaded to YouTube. The concept is credited to Bradley & Montgomery, which hoped it would become "greeting cards that just happen to be selling something." In 2000, Despair, Inc. obtained a U.S. trademark for the frowny emoticon :-( on greeting cards, posters, and art prints. In 2001, they issued a satirical press release claiming to sue Internet users for typing the frowny, which drew protests when posted on Slashdot. Several patent applications have been filed for inventions aiding emoticon communication; some have been issued as U.S. patents. US 6987991, for example, describes a 2001 method to send emoticons over cell phones using a drop-down menu, designed to ease emoticon entry. The emoticon :-) was filed in 2006 and registered as a European Community Trademark in 2008. In Finland, the Supreme Administrative Court ruled in 2012 that the emoticon cannot be trademarked, reversing a 2006 administrative decision that had trademarked :-), =), =(, :) and :(, thus invalidating those trademarks. In 2005, a Russian court rejected a legal claim against Siemens by a man who claimed a trademark on the ;-) emoticon. In 2008, Russian entrepreneur Oleg Teterin claimed to have been granted a trademark on the ;-) emoticon, offering a license for tens of thousands of dollars to companies but free for individuals. In the Unicode Standard, a different use of "emoticon" refers to a subset of emoji that display facial expressions. The standard references existing systems that allow textual emoticons to be substituted with image or emoji versions. Some smiley faces were included in Unicode since version 1.1, including a white frowning face, a white smiling face, and a black smiling face ("black" refers to a filled glyph, "white" to an unfilled one). The Emoticons block was introduced in Unicode 6.0 (October 2010) and extended in 7.0, covering the range U+1F600 to U+1F64F. After that block was filled, Unicode 8.0 (2015), 9.0 (2016), and 10.0 (2017) added additional emoticons from U+1F910 to U+1F9FF. Currently, U+1F90C–U+1F90F, U+1F93F, U+1F94D–U+1F94F, U+1F96C–U+1F97F, U+1F998–U+1F9CF (excluding U+1F9C0 which contains the 🧀 emoji), and U+1F9E7–U+1F9FF do not contain emoticons since Unicode 10.0. For historical and compatibility reasons, other heads and figures, mostly representing genders, activities, and professions rather than emotions, are found in Miscellaneous Symbols and Pictographs (especially U+1F466–U+1F487) and Transport and Map Symbols. Body parts, primarily hands, are also encoded in the Dingbat and Miscellaneous Symbols blocks.

The English Ladies' Football Association (ELFA) was established in 1921 in response to the Football Association (FA)’s ban on women's football, with its founding meeting held in Liverpool on 10 December 1921, attended by representatives from about 30 women's teams. The ELFA was formed to support women footballers, popularise the game among women, and assist charity, and initially included a league of 57 amateur teams. Leonard Bridgett, manager and coach of Stoke Ladies, was elected as its first president. W. Henley was appointed as Secretary of the Association's pro team and helped organise a subsequent meeting in Blackburn on 17 December, where 57 clubs attended and many others expressed interest. The ELFA approved changes to rules to accommodate women players, including adjustments to pitch sizes and ball usage. On 7 January 1922, a meeting in Manchester approved the ball and pitch dimensions and saw the presentation of a cup for the Ladies' English Cup Competition. The ELFA also arranged a representative team for a match against Grimsby and District Ladies on 21 January. On 18 February 1922, a council meeting in Birmingham removed the Northern Union’s ground ban for ELFA-affiliated clubs and organised the draw for the first round of the ELFA Cup competition. The competition saw 23 clubs participate, with matches held on 18 March 1922 (first round), 22 April 1922 (second round), 20 May 1922 (third round), and a semi-final. The ELFA Cup was won by Stoke Ladies, who defeated Doncaster and Bentley Ladies 3–1 on 24 June 1922. The ELFA folded within a year, and women continued playing in local parks and dog-tracks without support from the FA, lacking money, infrastructure, coaches, or pitches—restrictions that persisted for fifty years until 1971. Women's football had existed before World War I but gained momentum during the war when women, especially in munitions factories, took on male roles and played football during breaks, leading to the formation of organised teams for war charity fundraising. The Munitionettes' Cup was established in August 1917, with Blyth Spartans as the first winners. After the war, factories closed and women were pressured to return to traditional roles, and football was deemed unladylike and dangerous by medical experts. On 5 December 1921, the FA formally cited concerns about football's unsuitability for women and requested clubs to refuse use of their grounds for women's matches. Despite its short lifespan, the ELFA laid the foundation for the revival of women's football. Preston Ladies competed in the British Ladies' Football World Championship at least twice in the 1930s, winning in 1937 by a 5–1 score and losing in 1939 to Edinburgh Ladies 5–2. A successor, the Women's Football Association (WFA), was formed in 1969, promoting a national England team and a premier league, though it remained voluntary with limited resources and often rescheduled or cancelled matches. In the 1970s, international recommendations and the Sex Discrimination Act of 1975 (with a clause exempting sports) helped advance the cause, but the FA only lifted its ban on women's football in 1992. In March 2018, the National Football Museum opened an extension to its permanent gallery dedicated to women's football, including the English Ladies Football Association Winner's Medal awarded to Lilian Bridgett of Stoke Ladies in 1922.

A solar equinox occurs when the Sun appears directly above the equator, rising due east and setting due west, happening twice annually around 20 March and 23 September. This event is also defined as the moment when Earth's equatorial plane passes through the center of the Sun's disk and when Earth's rotation axis is perpendicular to the Sun-Earth line, with no tilt toward or away from the Sun. Modern definitions use the Sun's ecliptic longitude, with equinoxes occurring when the apparent geocentric longitude is 0° and 180°. The term derives from Latin *aequinoctium*, meaning "equal night," as daytime and nighttime are approximately equal globally, though not exactly due to the Sun's angular size, atmospheric refraction, and rapid changes in day length near the equinoxes. A properly aligned sundial shows 12 hours of daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere, the March equinox is known as the vernal or spring equinox and marks the start of spring in many cultures, including the Assyrian, Hindu, and Persian calendars, while the September equinox is the autumnal or fall equinox marking the beginning of autumn; in the Southern Hemisphere, these names are reversed. The March equinox is called the northward equinox, as the Sun's declination crosses the celestial equator northward, and the September equinox is the southward equinox, with the declination crossing southward. Equinoxes alternate with solstices, and leap years cause slight variations in dates. Daylight increases most rapidly at the vernal equinox and decreases most rapidly at the autumnal equinox. The solar terminator is perpendicular to the equator, resulting in equal illumination of both hemispheres. For about four days, both the North and South Poles experience daylight; for example, in 2021, sunrise on the North Pole occurred on 18 March 07:09 UTC and sunset on the South Pole on 22 March 13:08 UTC, while sunrise on the South Pole was on 20 September 16:08 UTC and sunset on the North Pole on 24 September 22:30 UTC. The subsolar point is on the equator during equinoxes, crossing northward at March and southward at September. Julius Caesar set 25 March as the spring equinox in the Julian calendar in 45 BC, but due to a 11.3-minute annual drift, by 300 AD it had shifted to about 21 March and by the 1580s to 11 March. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar to correct this, reducing leap years from every 100 years to 97 every 400 years, maintaining the vernal equinox near 21 March. Despite this, a residual variation of ±27 hours remains. The dates of equinoxes shift over the 400-year Gregorian cycle; in the 21st century, the earliest March equinox was 19 March 2096 and the latest 21 March 2003, while the earliest September equinox was 21 September 2096 and the latest 23 September 2003 (Universal Time). On equinox, the Sun's center spends roughly equal time above and below the horizon, making day and night about equal, though sunrise and sunset are defined as when the Sun's upper limb is level with the horizon, resulting in days being about 14 minutes longer than nights at the equator and longer near the poles. The real equality of day and night occurs only at latitudes far from the equator, with seasonal differences of at least 7 minutes, and happens a few days before the spring equinox and after the fall equinox in mid-latitudes. The equilux—the date when day and night are exactly equal—is a neologism from the 1980s, gaining recognition in the 21st century, and is rare due to rapid day length changes, with mid-latitude equilux occurring a few days before spring and after fall equinoxes. The March to September interval is about 186 days, and September to March is about 179 days, making the polar day at the North Pole about 7 days longer than at the South Pole. Mirror-image conjugate auroras have been observed during equinoxes. Equinoxes are sometimes considered the start of spring and autumn, with traditional harvest festivals celebrated on these dates. In Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Central Asia, Nowruz, the Persian New Year, is celebrated on the northern hemisphere's spring equinox. Religious architecture, such as Angkor Wat in Cambodia, is often aligned with equinox events. Catholic churches have traditionally oriented their buildings to the equinox, following Charles Borromeo's recommendations. Around equinoxes, geostationary satellites experience temporary disruptions due to the Sun being directly behind them, causing solar noise that degrades or disrupts signals, lasting from minutes to an hour, with larger antennas experiencing shorter outages. Satellites also face power issues during equinoxes because they pass through Earth's shadow, relying on batteries for longer durations than at other times. Equinoxes occur on any planet with a tilted axis; Saturn's equinox, when its rings are edge-on to the Sun, happens every 14.7 years and was most recently on 6 May 2025, with minimal sunlight and more planetshine than solar light. Mars's most recent equinoxes were on 12 January 2024 (northern autumn) and 26 December 2022 (northern spring).

Erkki Oja, born on 22 March 1948, is a Finnish computer scientist and Aalto Distinguished Professor in the Department of Information and Computer Science at Aalto University School of Science. He is known for developing Oja's rule, a model that describes how neurons in the brain or in artificial neural networks learn over time. Oja was born in Helsinki and studied at Helsinki University of Technology, where he earned his diploma engineer in 1972, licentiate in technology in 1975, and Doctor of Technology in 1977. From 1976 to 1981, he served as a research fellow at the Academy of Finland, and from 1977 to 1978, he was a research associate at the Center for Cognitive Science at Brown University. Since 1981, he held a professorship in applied mathematics at Kuopio University (now University of Eastern Finland). From 1983 to 1984, he was a visiting research scholar at Tokyo Institute of Technology. From 1987 to 1993, he was a professor in computer science at the Lappeenranta University of Technology. He returned to the Helsinki University of Technology (now Aalto University) in 1993 as a professor in computer science and retired in 2015. Oja is a Fellow of the International Association for Pattern Recognition and the IEEE, and a member of the Finnish Academy of Sciences. He served as chairman of the European Neural Network Society from 2000 to 2005 and as chairman of the Academy of Finland’s Research Council for Natural Sciences and Engineering from 2007 to 2012. In 2019, he was awarded the Frank Rosenblatt Award for his contributions to artificial intelligence research. Oja was a member of the Board of Governors for the International Neural Network Society (INNIS) in 2003 and received honorary doctorates from Uppsala University and Lappeenranta University of Technology in 2008.

Erling Norvik (9 April 1928 – 31 December 1998) was a Norwegian politician affiliated with the Conservative Party. He was born in Vadsø and is the son of Erling Johannes Norvik, who served in the Norwegian parliament (Stortinget) from 1949 to 1961. The younger Norvik began his professional career as a journalist for the regional newspaper Finnmarken at the age of 12 and was elected to Stortinget in 1961 from Finnmark, succeeding his father. He served in the legislature for three consecutive terms from 1961 to 1973, after which he resigned to become the leader of the Conservative Party, a position he held from 1974 to 1980 and again from 1984 to 1986. In 1981, he declined a ministerial appointment and instead worked in the prime minister's office of his party colleague Kåre Willoch. In 1986, he was appointed Governor ("Fylkesmann") of Østfold county, a role he held for 12 years. This article about a Norwegian politician born in the 1920s is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

The Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania (ELCT; Swahili: Kanisa la Kiinjili la Kilutheri Tanzania) is the federation of Lutheran churches in Tanzania and one of the largest Lutheran denominations globally, with over 6 million members, representing 13% of the Tanzanian population. It is the second largest Lutheran church in the world and the largest in East Africa. The church is led by a presiding bishop and twenty-eight diocesan bishops, representing 28 dioceses, with its head office located in Mbeya since 1967. It is affiliated with the All Africa Conference of Churches (AACC), the Christian Council of Tanzania, the Global Confessional and Missional Lutheran Forum, and the Lutheran World Federation. The ELCT offers worship, Christian education, and a range of social services, including disaster response, healthcare, and AIDS education and relief. The first Lutheran missionaries arrived in German East Africa in 1887 when the Evangelical Missionary Society for East Africa (EMS), based in Berlin, Germany, established a station at Kigamboni, Dar es Salaam. A second group of German missionaries entered via South Africa and settled in the Southern Highlands. Missions from Germany continued throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries despite interruptions from the Hehe Wars (1891), the Maji Maji Uprising (1905–1907), World War I, and World War II. In 1938, seven Lutheran churches formed the Federation of Lutheran Churches in Tanganyika, which later merged into the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania. In 1964, Johannes Lilje, presiding bishop of the United Evangelical Lutheran Church of Germany, consecrated Stefano Moshi, elected as the first president of the new church body and a proponent of episcopacy, as the first presiding bishop of the ELCT. The church's seat is in Arusha and is primarily financed through collections, donations, and project grants from churches in the Global North. The ELCT is led by a presiding bishop, or "Mkuu," elected to four-year terms from among the bishops, and 24 bishops who oversee local dioceses; the current presiding bishop is Alex Malasusa. The church employs 1,360 ordained pastors (28 overseas), 3,000 lay evangelists, and 300 community officers (2014 figures). Women are not ordained in all dioceses, though the national church began ordaining women as of 1990; ordination remains a sensitive issue, with local dioceses making independent decisions. The ELCT is one of the fastest-growing churches globally, with an annual increase of approximately 8% in baptized members. Social services are central to its mission and include departments focused on disaster response, healthcare, and AIDS education and relief. The ELCT comprises regional dioceses in Kenya, South Sudan, Tanzania, Indonesia, Mongolia, Germany, Norway, Sweden, and Peru. Lutheranism is rooted in the theology of Martin Luther, with official confessional writings in the Book of Concord. The ELCT accepts the unaltered Augsburg Confession as a true witness to the Gospel and does not adhere to biblical inerrancy, instead supporting scholarly methods of biblical analysis, aligning with moderate Protestant traditions. Like other Lutheran bodies, the ELCT recognizes two sacraments: Communion (Eucharist) and Holy Baptism (including infant baptism); Confession and absolution is often included but is considered a return to the forgiveness of baptism, so strictly speaking, only two sacraments exist. The ELCT holds to the Lutheran doctrine of sacramental union, affirming that Christ's body and blood are truly present "in, with and under" the bread and wine, with all communicants receiving both bread and wine and the actual body and blood of Christ. This is sometimes referred to as consubstantiation, though Lutherans reject a philosophical explanation, viewing the presence as a mystery rather than a philosophical concept. This belief is more aligned with Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions than with most Protestant views, which often doubt or deny the actual presence of Christ's body and blood in communion. In August 2013, the ELCT established a relationship with the North American Lutheran Church through a "Memorandum of Understanding," paving the way for full communion between the two churches.

EverQuest II is a 3D fantasy massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) originally developed and published by Sony Online Entertainment for Microsoft Windows PCs and released in November 2004. It serves as a sequel to the original EverQuest, which was released five years earlier, and includes updated graphics, more streamlined gameplay, and an abundance of voice acting featuring actors such as Christopher Lee, Heather Graham, Minnie Driver, Wil Wheaton, Dwight Schultz, Richard Horvitz, Alan Dale, and Danica McKellar. According to SOE, the game featured 130 hours of spoken dialog recorded by 266 voice actors in October 2004, with additional dialog added through updates, including player voice emotes introduced in September 2005 via the Desert of Flames expansion. The music, composed by Emmy-award-winning Laura Karpman and recorded by the FILMharmonic Orchestra Prague, spans over ninety minutes and features unique themes for each location, aiming for a cinematic feel; the expansions Echoes of Faydwer and Rise of Kunark include themes from the original EverQuest arranged by Inon Zur, and Rise of Kunark introduced a new combat music system with 14 contextual themes based on enemy strength and battle tide. The game is set in an alternate future 500 years after the original EverQuest's events, functioning as a parallel universe that diverges at the conclusion of the Planes of Power expansion, allowing both games to develop independently without interfering with each other. Characters and locations from the original are altered by centuries of war and destruction, and players can access familiar places and characters through "heritage items" obtained via heritage quests. Each player creates a character in the 3D world of Norrath, choosing from races such as human, barbarian, dwarf, erudite, ogre, iksar, troll, gnome, half elf, high elf, halfling, Vah Shir, wood elf, dark elf, Kerra, Ratonga, Sarnak, Fae, and Arasai, with the Froglok race initially locked until a server-wide quest was completed. Players select one of four archetypes—Fighter, Scout, Priest, or Mage—and choose a class at level 10 and a subclass at level 20, though this system changed in 2006 so that the final class is selected at character creation. Characters gain experience through quests, exploration, and monster kills, with no experience loss or level loss upon death; instead, they respawn with full gear at revival locations, though a minor experience debt is repaid, and gear degrades after 10 consecutive deaths, requiring repair for a fee. The game emphasizes quests, with over 6,000 existing, and supports player interaction through grouping (up to six players), raids (up to 24), voice chat, mail, global chat, a marketplace, and tools like "looking-for-group" and "looking-for-work." Guilds are central to gameplay, with experience bars and levels up to 150 earned primarily through "writs" and killing epic monsters, unlocking rewards such as housing, mounts, house items, apparel, titles, guild halls, and a hosted website with forum and bank features. Guild recruitment tools are integrated, and players can maintain houses. A secure commission system allows players to sell crafting skills or use the common market to sell finished items. The game originally operated on a subscription model, but in July 2010, a free-to-play version called EverQuest II Extended was released on a separate server, funded by microtransactions or optional subscriptions. By November 2011, the subscription service was fully cancelled, transitioning all servers to free-to-play with microtransactions as the revenue stream. In February 2005, the game partnered with Pizza Hut, allowing players to order pizza via the "/pizza" chat command, a promotion that ended but generated significant press. In June 2005, Station Exchange—an official auction system on designated servers—was introduced, and in December 2008, Station Cash, a real-money trading (RMT) feature, was added. In January 2009, EverQuest II became available on Steam through a collaboration with Valve. In March 2006, SOE ended its Chinese and Korean operations for EverQuest II, which were managed by Gamania, with beta access ending on March 29 and all accounts moved to US servers by March 30. In October 2012, Krono was introduced as a real-money purchase option that grants 30 days of Gold subscription and can be traded or gifted, offering a safer alternative to purchasing SC cards. The game was nominated for "Best Massively Multiplayer Online Game" at GameSpot's 2004 awards and runner-up for "Best Persistent World Game" at IGN's 2004 awards, both losing to World of Warcraft. It was named the seventh-best computer game of 2004 by Computer Games Magazine and won "Most Improved Game" at GameSpy's 2006 awards for the addition of PvP servers and the Echoes of Faydwer expansion. After adopting free-to-play in 2011, it won "Best Bang for the Buck" at Massively's annual awards. EverQuest II reached 100,000 active accounts within 24 hours of release and grew to over 300,000 in January 2005, with a subscriber peak of 325,000 in 2005. As of September 2020, it had 21,000 subscribers and 29,000 monthly active players. EverQuest II: East, an alternate edition for East Asia, was developed by Sony Online Entertainment and launched in April 2005, featuring localized tutorials, a separate "SOGA Model" character design, and proprietary missions, but failed due to poor localization; Gamania terminated its operations on March 29, 2006, and all Chinese, Taiwanese, and Korean accounts were transferred to US servers. In February 2015, Sony Computer Entertainment sold Sony Online Entertainment to investment company Inception Acquisitions, which rebranded the studio as Daybreak Game Company, which continues to develop and publish EverQuest II. The game has been used in academic studies to analyze virtual economic behavior, with findings showing real-world patterns in production, consumption, and money supply, and that less than one percent (0.43%) of players are Platinum Farmers, with over 77% of them being Chinese. It received mostly positive reviews, earning an 83 out of 100 average on Metacritic, with critics noting it as more convenient and forgiving than the original, though less groundbreaking, with its extensive voice acting being a major advancement. While praised for its presentation and photorealistic graphics, performance issues were common on higher settings, requiring powerful systems for optimal play. The game's expansions, including Tears of Veeshan (which includes Chains of Eternity), introduce new zones, features, creatures, items, and player races, with access to levels above 92 requiring the purchase of Tears of Veeshan. Free-to-play accounts have access to the same areas as subscription accounts but face restrictions such as limited bag slots, coin limits, quest journal limits, race and class restrictions, and gear limitations, though many restrictions have been removed, including the inability to buy or sell items on the broker, spell tier limits, and the alternate advancement slider. The game's feature set has expanded since its 2004 release, including the introduction of Adventure Packs—smaller digital expansions with plot lines, zones, creatures, and items—though the development team now releases free zones and content instead. Expansions are available through retail or digital download and often include bonus features like in-game creatures. EverQuest II: East used similar settings to the original, with localized content and local language character naming, but most dialogue remained in English except for the novice tutorial, which was localized by Gamania.

Evi Nemeth (born June 7, 1940 – missing-at-sea June or July 2013) was an engineer, author, and teacher renowned for her expertise in computer system administration and networks. She was the lead author of the "bibles" of system administration: UNIX System Administration Handbook (1989, 1995, 2000), Linux Administration Handbook (2002, 2006), and UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook (2010, 2017). Known in technology circles as the matriarch of system administration, she earned her bachelor's degree in mathematics from Penn State in 1961 and her PhD in mathematics from the University of Waterloo, Ontario in 1971. She taught at Florida Atlantic University and the State University of New York at Utica (SUNY Tech) before joining the computer science department at the University of Colorado Boulder (CU-Boulder) in 1980, where she served as manager of the college's computing facility from 1982 to 1986. She also held visiting Associate Professor positions at Dartmouth College in 1990 and UC San Diego in 1998, while on sabbatical from CU-Boulder. At CU-Boulder, she was well known for her undergraduate systems administration program, which enabled students to gain in-depth knowledge and skills in Unix system administration. Together with Steve Wozniak, she established the Woz scholarship program at CU-Boulder to fund inquisitive undergraduates. Nemeth was also recognized for her ability to inspire and teach young people, mentoring numerous middle- and high-school students—known as "the munchkins"—and talented young undergraduates, who worked with her to support computing at the university and attended national meetings where they installed networks and broadcast sessions on the Internet via the multicast backbone. She coached the university's student programming teams in the ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest. From 1998 to 2006, she worked with the Cooperative Association for Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) at the University of California, San Diego, on Internet measurement and visualization projects. Outside the United States, she contributed to bringing Internet technology to the developing world through programs of the Internet Society and the United Nations Development Programme. A network guru T-shirt from the 1980s, featuring OSI Model layers with an added "financial" Layer 8 and a "political" Layer 9, was credited to her. During the Summer 1994 USENIX conference in Boston, she coordinated the production of a commemorative deck of playing cards celebrating the 25th anniversary of UNIX. After retiring, she sailed her 40-foot sailboat Wonderland around the world, including a circuit of the Atlantic, through the Panama Canal, and across the Pacific to New Zealand. In late May 2013, she traveled with six others aboard the vintage yacht Niña across the Tasman Sea en route to Australia from New Zealand. On June 4, the last message sent by Nemeth from Niña was received, as the Tasman Sea had 65 mile-per-hour winds and swell height reaching 26 feet; a natural disaster (e.g., a rogue wave) may have caused the boat’s disappearance. On July 5, New Zealand authorities officially ended the search for the Niña, though relatives of the crew continued to search.

Evolution Festival was an annual music festival held in Newcastle upon Tyne and Gateshead, England, from 2002 to 2013.[1][2] It drew tens of thousands of attendees each year and typically took place on the Quayside.[3] The festival was briefly known as Orange Evolution due to a sponsorship agreement with the mobile phone company Orange.[4] It has been described as "the biggest festival Tyneside has ever staged".[5] Headline acts included Dizzee Rascal, The Wombats, Paolo Nutini, and Maxïmo Park.[6][7][8] Florence + The Machine, Amy Winehouse, and Ellie Goulding performed at the festival before achieving widespread fame.[9][10][11] The event first took place on the Quayside in 2003, with performances by Moloko, Biffy Clyro, and Inspiral Carpets.[13] In 2004, due to funding issues, it reverted to a multi-venue format, including a Shindig event headlined by Eric Morillo and Deep Dish.[14] It returned to the Quayside in 2005, sponsored by Orange, with a three-stage lineup headlined by Dizzee Rascal and The Futureheads.[15] Maxïmo Park headlined the 2007 event.[8] In 2008, the festival ended its sponsorship with Orange and reverted to being called Evolution Festival, introducing a £3 entry charge for the first time.[16] In 2009, it expanded to a two-day format with performances by The Wombats, White Lies, and Florence + The Machine.[6] A folk stage was added in 2010.[7] In 2012, a one-off edition was held at Avenham Park, Preston, as part of the Preston Guild celebrations, titled GFest, featuring Maverick Sabre, Labrinth, and Stooshe and attracting thousands of attendees.[17][18] The 2013 main event in Newcastle featured The Vaccines, Ellie Goulding, Paloma Faith, and Jake Bugg.[19] In 2014, the festival did not take place, and although organisers Jim Mawdsley and Dave Stone stated it was only a "pause", the event has not been held since.[2] The Evolution brand continues through Evolution Emerging, a multiple venue event showcasing local new bands, which operated until 2019 when it rebranded into Tipping Point live.[12]

FC Baltika (Russian: Акционерное Общество «Футбольный клуб «Балтика») is a professional association football club based in Kaliningrad, Russia. The club was founded on 23 August 1954 as Pishchevik Kaliningrad and was renamed Baltika in 1958. It entered the Soviet League in 1957 and played in Class B (1957–1965), Class A, Group 2 (1966–1970), and the Second League (1971–1991). The best result was achieved in 1984, when Baltika won the regional group tournament. In 1992, Baltika entered the Russian Second Division and won the regional tournament to gain promotion to the First Division. After finishing fourth in 1993 and third in 1994, Baltika won the division in 1995. In 1996, Baltika achieved the best result in club history by finishing 7th in the Top Division, the Russian Premier League. The club was relegated in 1998, spending a total of three seasons in the top flight. In 1998, Baltika participated in the Intertoto Cup and reached the third round. Since then, Baltika played in the First Division, except for the 2002 and 2005 seasons when they were in the Second Division. In the 2018–19 Russian Football National League, they finished 16th (a relegation spot), but PFL zone East winners FC Sakhalin Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk did not apply for the FNL license, keeping Baltika in the league. On 19 May 2023, Baltika secured promotion to the Russian Premier League for the first time in 25 years. In the 2023–24 Russian Cup, Baltika advanced to the Superfinal. Baltika finished 15th in the league season and was relegated back to the second tier after one year in the Premier League. On 2 June 2024, Baltika lost the 2024 Russian Cup final to Zenit St. Petersburg with a score of 1–2; Baltika initially led 1–0 but conceded two goals in the 81st minute and in the 5th added minute. On 10 May 2025, Baltika secured a top-2 finish in the First League season and earned promotion back to the Russian Premier League for the 2025–26 season. As of 10 January 2026, according to the official Russian Premier League website. Baltika's reserve team played professionally in the Russian Third League in 1994 as FC Baltika-d Kaliningrad and in the Russian Second Division in 2006 and 2007 as FC Baltika-2 Kaliningrad. These players had international caps for their respective countries. Players whose name is listed in bold represented their countries while playing for Baltika. Flags indicate national team as defined under FIFA eligibility rules; some limited exceptions apply. Players may hold more than one non-FIFA nationality.

The Faraday Lectureship Prize, formerly known as the Faraday Lectureship, is awarded every two years (approximately) by the Royal Society of Chemistry for "exceptional contributions to physical or theoretical chemistry." Named in honor of Michael Faraday, the first Faraday Lecture was delivered in 1869, two years after Faraday's death, by Jean-Baptiste Dumas. As of 2009, the prize consisted of £5000, a medal, and a certificate, and the recipient is also required to give a public lecture outlining their research.

The Faraday Medal is presented by the Electrochemistry Group of the Royal Society of Chemistry. It has been awarded since 1977 to recognize outstanding mid-career electrochemists who are based outside the United Kingdom and Ireland for their contributions to research advancements.

Sri Chautaria Fateh Jang Shah, also known as Fatya Jang Shah or Fatte Jang Chautariya, served as the 6th prime minister of Nepal. Born in 1805, he was the eldest son of Sri Chautaria Prana Shah and Chautaryani Moha Kumari Devi, belonging to the 6th generation of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha. He was the nephew of Prime Minister Chautariya Pushkar Shah and had four brothers: Colonel Sri Chautaria Guru Prasad Shah, Rajguru Ram Krishna Bahadur Shah, Captain Sardar Bir Bahadur Shah, and Colonel Sri Chautaria Rana Sher Shah. His sister was Hiranya Garbha Devi, who became the third wife of Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana. Fateh Jung Shah received private education. He was appointed Mukhtiyar from 1840 to 1843 and lived in exile at Gaya, India from 1843 to 1845. In 1845, after his exile, he was promoted to Full General and Commander of Three Regiments. He then served as Mukhtiyar and Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1845 to 1846. He had three sons: Sri Chautaria Khadga Bikram Shah (Khadga Babusaheb), who was killed with him during the Kot Massacre on 14 September 1846, and Guru Prasad Shah and Guna Bahadur Shah. Fateh Jung Shah was killed in the Kot Massacre at the courtyard of Hanuman Dhoka Palace on 14 September 1846.

M. Fathima Beevi (30 April 1927 – 23 November 2023) was an Indian judge who served as a justice of the Supreme Court of India. Appointed to the apex court in 1989, she became the first female judge of the Supreme Court of India and the first Muslim woman to be appointed to any of the higher judiciaries in the country. She retired from the Supreme Court on 29 April 1992. After her retirement, she served as a member of the National Human Rights Commission and later as the Governor of Tamil Nadu from 25 January 1997 to 2001. In 2023, she was honoured with the Kerala Prabha Award, the second-highest honour given by the Government of Kerala, and posthumously awarded the Padma Bhushan in the 2024 honours list. Born on 30 April 1927 in Pathanamthitta, then part of the Kingdom of Travancore (now in Kerala), she was the daughter of Annaveettil Meer Sahib and Khadeeja Beevi, belonging to the Rowther family. She attended Town School and Catholicate High School in Pathanamthitta, earned a BSc in chemistry from Women's College, Thiruvananthapuram, and obtained her LL.B. from Government Law College, Thiruvananthapuram. Enrolled as an Advocate on 14 November 1950, she topped the Bar Council exam that year and began her career in the lower judiciary in Kerala, becoming Munsiff in May 1958, Sub-ordinate Judge in 1968, Chief Judicial Magistrate in 1972, and District & Sessions Judge in 1974. In January 1980, she was appointed Judicial Member of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, and elevated to the High Court as a Judge on 4 August 1983. She became a permanent Judge of the High Court on 14 May 1984 and retired from the High Court on 29 April 1989. As Governor of Tamil Nadu, she rejected mercy petitions filed by four condemned prisoners in the Rajiv Gandhi assassination case, invoking her power under Article 161 of the Constitution. She faced controversy for giving a clean chit to the law and order situation in Tamil Nadu, prompting the Central government to request her resignation. She resigned under controversial circumstances after accepting Jayalalithaa's assembly majority following the May 2001 elections and over the arrest of former Chief Minister M. Karunanidhi, who had previously advocated for her appointment. Jayalalithaa defended her decision, stating that as a former Supreme Court judge and legal expert, she did not require instruction on law or the Constitution, and her decision was not justiciable. Despite not being eligible to contest an election under constitutional provisions, Fathima Beevi administered the oath of office to J. Jayalalitha as Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu on 14 May 2001, based on the majority party's election of her as their leader.
