Several Public Interest Litigations were filed in the Supreme Court challenging the validity of her appointment, and she justified her action by citing the majority party's election of Jayalalithaa. The Supreme Court later overturned her appointment, ruling that a Governor cannot appoint a non-member of the legislature as Chief Minister, as such an action would be contrary to the Constitution and laws. During her tenure as Governor, she also served as Chancellor of Madras University, where her withholding of approval for the establishment of a new department for contemporary Tamil literature reportedly led to the Vice-Chancellor, P.T. Manoharan, resigning. She had previously served as Chairman of the Kerala Commission for Backward Classes (1993) and member of the National Human Rights Commission (1993), and received the Hon. D. Litt. and Mahila Shiromani Award in 1990, as well as the Bharat Jyoti Award. There were discussions among left parties about her potential nomination as President of India, during which the NDA Government proposed Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. Fathima Beevi passed away on 23 November 2023 at the age of 96.

Fazal Elahi Chaudhry (1 January 1904 – 2 June 1982) was a Pakistani barrister, politician, and statesman who served as the fifth president of Pakistan from 1973 until his resignation in September 1978, following the 1977 coup d'état that overthrew Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government and established martial law under Zia-ul-Haq. He was the first legislatively-elected president in Pakistan's history and served as a constitutional figurehead under the 1973 constitution, which shifted executive power to the prime minister. Born in Marala, Kharian Tehsil of Gujrat District, Punjab, into an influential Punjabi Muslim Gujjar family, Chaudhry received his early education in Kharian, then attended Aligarh Muslim University in 1920, earning his LLB in civil law in 1924. He later returned to Punjab, studied at the University of the Punjab, obtaining a master's degree in political science in 1925 and an advanced LLM in Law and Justice in 1927. After establishing a law firm in Lahore, he began practising civil law and returned to Gujrat. In 1930, he was elected unopposed to the Gujrat District Board. He joined the All-India Muslim League in 1942, became president of the Punjab Muslim League for Gujrat District in 1945, and participated in the 1946 Indian provincial elections on the Muslim League ticket. After Pakistan's independence in 1947, he was appointed parliamentary secretary and later served as education and health minister in Liaquat Ali Khan's cabinet. He represented Pakistan at the United Nations in 1952 and was elected to the West Punjab Assembly in 1951. In 1956, he was elected to the West Pakistan Assembly and served as its first Speaker from 20 May 1956 to 7 October 1958. He joined the Convention Muslim League and was elected deputy speaker of the National Assembly in 1965, serving until 1969 when Yahya Khan declared martial law. In 1970, he was elected to the National Assembly on the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) ticket and later became its speaker in 1972. Under the 1973 constitution, Chaudhry contested the presidential election against Khan Amirzadah Khan of the National Awami Party (Wali), winning with an absolute electoral college majority of 139 votes to Khan's 45, and was sworn in on 14 August 1973, becoming the first ethnic Punjabi president. He succeeded Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became prime minister. As a figurehead, the presidency had become ceremonial, with executive authority vested in the prime minister. After the 1977 coup d'état, Bhutto's government and all provincial governments were overthrown by Zia-ul-Haq, who assumed the role of chief martial law administrator; Chaudhry continued as president but had no influence over governmental, military, or national affairs. Due to contentious relations with the Zia-led military regime, he resigned on 16 September 1978, handing over the presidency to Zia-ul-Haq. Chaudhry remained a respected legislator and politician throughout his career and died of a heart ailment on 2 June 1982 in Lahore at the age of 78.

doc_name: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act
text: The Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) is a U.S. federal law that established the foundational system for pesticide regulation to protect applicators, consumers, and the environment. It is administered and regulated by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and appropriate state environmental agencies. FIFRA has been amended several times, with a major revision in 1972 through the Federal Environmental Pesticide Control Act (FEPCA), which expanded EPA's authority by shifting the burden of proof to chemical manufacturers, enforcing compliance against banned and unregistered products, and establishing a regulatory framework to address gaps in the original law. The Federal Insecticide Act of 1910 was the first pesticide law, ensuring quality by protecting farmers and consumers from fraudulent or adulterated products, though it did not address environmental or health risks. During World War II, increased wartime research led to a surge in pesticide use, with synthetic organic insecticide usage rising from 100 million pounds in 1945 to over 300 million pounds by 1950, contributing to post-war food surpluses due to reduced pest damage. The 1947 Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act addressed shortcomings of the 1910 law, assigning initial regulation to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which was later transferred to the EPA in 1972 with a shift in focus to human health and environmental protection. The 1972 FEPCA amendment required the EPA to evaluate potential risks to humans, the environment, and wildlife and take action when risks outweighed benefits. In 1988, Congress mandated the reregistration of many pesticides registered before 1984, and in 1996, the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) required older pesticides to pose no unreasonable risk to infants, children, or sensitive individuals with "reasonable certainty," and established a 15-year review cycle for all pesticides. In 2012, the Pesticide Registration Improvement Extension Act amended the registration process. As of May 2007, there are 28 listed restricted pesticides, and any area where they are used is considered a restricted area. Pesticides must undergo 120 safety and effectiveness tests; only 1 in 139,000 passes, and the law explicitly forbids certain substances and uses, unlike other pesticide laws that only impose costs. FIFRA establishes regulations requiring that pesticides not cause unreasonable adverse effects on human health or the environment, defined as risks that are unreasonable considering social, economic, and environmental costs, or dietary risks violating food standards under Section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). Applicants must provide scientific data from over 100 tests under EPA guidelines. The EPA sets tolerance levels for pesticide residues on or in food/feed, establishing a "reasonable certainty of no harm," and may exempt certain residues if they meet FDCA standards. Registered pesticides must conform to approved uses and labeling. Most older pesticides were required to be reregistered under 1972, 1988, and 1996 amendments to meet current safety, labeling, and risk standards. Reregistration fees for food/feed active ingredients are $50,000 (initial) and $100,000–$150,000 (final), with non-food use fees at $50,000–$100,000; annual maintenance fees are $425 per product up to fifty, with a maximum of $20,000 per company, and $100 per product over fifty, capped at $35,000. Fees may be reduced or waived for small businesses, public health, or minor use pesticides, and failure to pay results in cancellation. Adjuvants—chemicals added to enhance efficacy or alter physical properties—are regulated by the EPA, with over 200 registered pesticides recommending their use; the EPA sets tolerance levels for adjuvants but does not require registration. Devices used to trap or kill pests (excluding standalone application equipment) and pesticide intermediates used in manufacturing are regulated but not required to be registered under FIFRA, though intermediates may be regulated under the Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976. Under FIFRA, no individual may sell, use, or distribute a pesticide not registered with the EPA, except in limited cases, and all pesticides must have a label with detailed safe use instructions. Pesticides are classified as "general use" (available to the public) or "restricted use" (requiring certified applicator credentials). While the EPA primarily enforces FIFRA, state agencies have enforcement authority under Sections 23, 24, 26, and 27, though EPA authority supersedes state authority and can be rescinded if states fail to ensure safe enforcement. Section 9 authorizes inspections of pesticides in storage, Section 13 allows the EPA to issue Stop Sale, Use, or Removal Orders (SSURO) and seize violative pesticides, Section 15 provides indemnity for suspended or cancelled registrations, and Section 16 allows judicial review. Section 14 imposes civil penalties, with commercial applicators, wholesalers, dealers, and retailers facing fines of up to $5,000 per offense, private applicators receiving warnings for first offenses and fines up to $1,000 for subsequent violations. Violations are treated as misdemeanors with fines and/or imprisonment: private applicators face up to $1,000 and 30 days, commercial applicators up to $25,000 and one year, and manufacturers up to $50,000 and one year. The EPA must continuously monitor registered pesticides and require registrants to report new adverse effects and conduct ongoing studies. If new evidence of harm is found, the EPA may conduct a special review and amend or cancel the registration. The Endangered Species Act requires the EPA to consider impacts on endangered species and habitats when registering pesticides, ensuring they do not harm listed species or their habitats, with labels providing guidance through bulletins. The EPA implements usage limitations and monitoring to protect endangered species while minimizing disruption to pesticide users.

doc_name: Fencing at the 1896 Summer Olympics – Men's masters foil
text: The men's masters foil was one of three fencing events at the 1896 Summer Olympics programme and was the sole event featuring professional athletes, taking place immediately after the amateur event on 7 April. It consisted of a single match between Leonidas Pyrgos of Greece and Joanni Perronet of France, which Pyrgos won 3–1, becoming the first Greek champion in the modern Olympics. This was the first time the event was held and it occurred only once more in Olympic history. Fencing masters were an exception to the early Olympics' amateurs-only policy, with the men's foil masters event held in 1896 and all three weapons for men, plus a special épée match between top professionals and amateurs, in 1900. By 1904, only amateur events were conducted. With only two fencers, the competition involved a single bout to three touches, following standard foil rules: touches had to be made with the tip of the foil, the target area was the torso, and priority determined the winner in cases of double touches. The exact start time of the master's event is unknown, but fencing began at 10 a.m. on the second day of events with the amateur men's foil and followed with the master's foil. The Official Report states that fencing ended at noon. Pyrgos won the only bout, 3–1.

doc_name: Fencing at the 1908 Summer Olympics – Men's sabre
text: The men's sabre was one of four fencing events at the 1908 Summer Olympics programme and marked its fourth appearance, making it the only fencing event held at every Summer Olympics. The top two positions in the individual event were claimed by Hungarian fencers: Jenő Fuchs won gold and Béla Zulawszky took silver, while bronze was awarded to Bohemian Vilém Goppold von Lobsdorf. A total of 76 competitors from 11 nations participated, with each nation allowed to enter up to 12 fencers. This was the fourth time the event was held, and Georges de la Falaise of France, the 1900 gold medalist, returned after skipping the 1904 Games. Belgium, Bohemia, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and South Africa each made their debut in the men's sabre, while Austria made its third appearance, having missed only the 1904 Games. The competition consisted of four rounds, with each pool conducting a round-robin format to three touches. European sabre rules at the time used a full-body target area, unlike the above-the-waist target used in the 1904 Games, which later became standard post-World War I. Barrages were used to determine advancement when necessary. The first round featured pool sizes ranging from 4 to 8 fencers, with the three fencers who lost the fewest bouts advancing; a three-way tie for two spots led to the elimination of the British fencer. Renaud lost both playoff matches, allowing Grade and Jack to advance, while Lichtenfels suffered two losses in the playoff. The fifth pool had only four fencers, resulting in only one elimination—Langevin. Petri defeated van Tomme in the playoff for third place after losing to the Belgian in the main pool, and Badman defeated van Minden in the playoff for third place. The tenth pool, the largest at twice the size of the fifth, had eight fencers, with five eliminated; von Lobsdorf defeated all seven of his opponents to win first place, with no match between Sarzano and Stohr. Chapuis was eliminated in the three-way playoff for second and third. The final pool included seven fencers. Eight second-round pools were held, ranging from 4 to 5 fencers. Notley won two playoff matches to secure second place in his pool and advance. Doorman, who had lost to Petri in the main pool, defeated the German in the playoff for second place. Two semifinals, each with eight fencers, were held, with the top four from each advancing to the final. Four fencers tied at 5-2 records and all advanced to the final; Ceccherini withdrew after his first four bouts, resulting in walkover wins for Tóth, van der Voodt, and Doorman. Fuchs and von Lobsdorf did not finish within the time limit and were both recorded as losers. The gold medal playoff was won by Fuchs, who secured victory with a one-touch bout decided by a parry and riposte to his fellow Hungarian's head.

doc_name: Fencing at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Women's team foil
text: The women's team foil was one of eight fencing events featured in the fencing programme at the 1964 Summer Olympics and marked its second appearance as an event. The competition took place from October 16 to October 17, 1964. A total of 47 fencers from 10 nations participated. In the event, ties between teams were resolved first by individual victories (as noted in parentheses), and then by the number of touches received.

At the 1964 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, eight fencing events were held. Men participated in both individual and team competitions across the three weapon types: épée, foil, and sabre, while women competed exclusively in foil events. A total of 259 fencers—203 men and 56 women—from 30 nations took part in the Games.

The Fernández Anchorena Palace is an architecturally significant former residence located in the Recoleta section of Buenos Aires, Argentina, and currently functions as the Apostolic Nunciature in Argentina. It was commissioned by Juan Antonio Fernández and his wife, Rosa de Anchorena, to the French Argentine architect Eduardo Le Monnier (1873–1931), who designed it in 1907 in the Second Empire style, which was popular among Argentine high society at the time. The palace was completed in 1909, although the Fernández-Archorena couple never lived there. Over the years, the family used the mansion for social events and public ceremonies, and from 1922 to 1928, it served as the official residence of President Marcelo Torcuato de Alvear and his wife, the opera chanteuse Regina Pacini de Alvear. In 1940, the property was sold to Adelia María Harilaos de Olmos, the widow of prominent Córdoba Province landowner Ambrosio Harilaos de Olmos. She was the founder of the Catholic Ladies' League and a financier of a working women's assistance fund, as well as a contributor to several churches and a hospital pavilion. In 1947, she bequeathed the residence to the Holy See. Following her death in 1949, the palace became the Apostolic Nunciature in Argentina. At the time, Pope Pius XII had previously been a guest of hers (as Cardinal Pacelli) during his visit to Buenos Aires in 1934 for the Eucharistic Congress. The palace's geographic coordinates are 34°35′22″S 58°23′09″W (34.58944°S 58.38583°W).

doc_name: Figure skating at the 2010 Winter Olympics – Ice dance
text: The ice dance competition at the 2010 Winter Olympics took place at the Pacific Coliseum in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, on February 19 (compulsory dance), February 21 (original dance), and February 22 (free dance), 2010. The compulsory dance on February 19 featured the Tango Romantica. The original dance was performed on February 21, and the free dance occurred on February 22, 2010. Tessa Virtue and Scott Moir became the first ice dancers from Canada and North America to win an Olympic gold medal. They were the first former World Junior Ice dance champions to achieve Olympic gold, the first ice dance team to win Olympic gold on home ice, and the first ice dancers to win gold on their Olympic debut since the inaugural Olympic ice dance event in 1976. They were also the youngest ice dance Olympic champions at 20 and 22 years of age. Isabelle Delobel competed at the Olympics with partner Olivier Schoenfelder just four-and-a-half months after giving birth. The event included roles for a Referee, Technical Controller, Technical Specialist, Assistant Technical Specialist, Judges (CD), Judges (OD), and Judges (FD).

doc_name: Figure skating at the 2022 Winter Olympics – Ice dance
text: The ice dance competition in figure skating at the 2022 Winter Olympics took place on 12 February (rhythm dance) and 14 February (free dance) at the Capital Indoor Stadium in Haidian District, Beijing. Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron of France won the event, with Victoria Sinitsina and Nikita Katsalapov, representing the Russian Olympic Committee, securing silver, and Madison Hubbell and Zachary Donohue of the United States earning bronze. The 2018 champions Tessa Virtue and Scott Moir, along with bronze medalists Maia Shibutani and Alex Shibutani, retired from competition. Papadakis and Cizeron achieved the highest score of the 2021–22 season prior to the Olympics, while Sinitsina and Katsalapov recorded the second-highest score of the season and are the 2021 World champions, during which Papadakis/Cizeron did not compete. In ice dance, major errors are rare, and Olympic scores generally align with those from the season, making Papadakis/Cizeron and Sinitsina/Katsalapov the top contenders, with Papadakis/Cizeron as the favorites. During the rhythm dance, Papadakis and Cizeron broke their own world record to gain a two-point lead over Sinitsina and Katsalapov, which they then extended by winning the free dance by five points, narrowly missing their own world record. Their combined total score set a new world record, and they claimed gold by 6.5 points over Sinitsina/Katsalapov. Hubbell and Donohue finished third in both segments to win bronze by four points ahead of their American teammates Madison Chock and Evan Bates. Before the competition, the existing ISU best scores were recorded, and the following new best scores were established during the event. The rhythm dance was held on 12 February, the free dance on 14 February, and skaters were ranked based on their total combined (overall) score.

Filip Hašek, born on 20 March 1997, is a Czech professional footballer who plays as a midfielder for Jelgava, a club in the Latvian Higher League. He made his professional debut with Bohemians 1905 in a match against Slovácko on 22 July 2018. This biographical article concerning association football in the Czech Republic, focusing on a midfielder, is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information on Wikipedia.

Firebrand is a name used by several characters in American comic books published by DC Comics. Rod Reilly, the first Firebrand, appeared in Police Comics #1 through #13 from August 1941 to November 1942, published by Quality Comics; he was the bored and wealthy son of a steel tycoon who fought crime with his servant and friend, "Slugger" Dunn. Originally drawn by Reed Crandall, Rod wore a transparent shirt and red pants with a bandana mask covering the top half of his face, and he used a lariat and could climb buildings with vacuum cups. After DC acquired Quality Comics, Firebrand was largely inactive until the mid-1970s when he joined the Freedom Fighters. He was killed in a fight with the Silver Ghost in a photocopied issue of Cancelled Comic Cavalcade, which was never released and thus it is uncertain if this event is part of the current DC Universe. When DC collected characters into the All-Star Squadron, it was retconned that Rod had been injured in a surprise attack and replaced by his sister, Danette Reilly. In All-Star Squadron #5 (1981), Danette discovers Rod's identity while staying at his penthouse and muses on his relationship with Slugger Dunn, wondering why a bachelor playboy would need a bodyguard, and finds a hidden closet that makes her realize she didn't know her brother as well as she thought. Danette, a volcanologist, was first introduced in a special "All-Star Squadron" preview in Justice League of America #193 (August 1981), where she was studying volcanoes north of Hawaii when kidnapped by time-traveling villain Per Degaton and sorcerer Wotan. During her escape, Wotan hit her with a magical blast and hurled her into a pit of lava; the combination of magic and lava gave her the ability to control heat and project fire blasts. Her powers emerged after she put on Rod's costume, and since Rod was injured in the attack, she decided to become the new Firebrand. Because Degaton returned to the future after being defeated, the All-Star Squadron forgot the attack. Danette was initially racist toward the Japanese, but after visiting her brother in the hospital, he revealed he had been saved by a soldier whose parents were Japanese, who later died from his wounds, and she realized her prejudice and began showing more respect to people of Japanese descent. Danette appeared in Crisis on Infinite Earths, where she briefly reunited with her former lover, the reluctant supervillain Cyclotron, who, though deceased, phased into her time to assist her and assumed partial custody of his daughter Terri alongside the Atom. In Stars and S.T.R.I.P.E. (2000), Firebrand was revealed to have been killed by the Dragon King; she has remained dead since. During the Absolute Power event (2024), Firebrand's spirit was found in the Well of Souls in Themyscira and was used as a power source by the Amazo android Paradise Lost. Her name is a tribute to creator Roy Thomas' wife, Danette Thomas. The Quality Comics character Wildfire was originally intended to play a major role in All-Star Squadron, but DC objected due to her name being shared with a Legion of Super-Heroes member, so Danette Reilly was introduced instead. Firebrand was ranked 67th in Comics Buyer's Guide's "100 Sexiest Women in Comics" list. In February 1996, DC introduced a third Firebrand, former police detective Alejandro "Alex" Sanchez. After nearly dying in an explosion that destroyed his apartment, Sanchez underwent experimental surgery to restore mobility, paid for by philanthropist Noah Hightower, who later offered him advanced armor combined with implants to give him enhanced strength and speed for up to four hours. After his partner was attacked, Sanchez agreed to become Firebrand, and his armor emitted green flame, giving him a demonic appearance. Sanchez's storyline reflected concerns about racial injustice and violence against people of color. His tenure lasted only nine issues in his self-titled comic, and he reappears in JSA: Secret Files #2, where he is killed by a Checkmate knight in Roulette's arena. In April 2006, Andre Twist was introduced in The Battle for Blüdhaven after being exposed to Chemo, gaining control over fire; he also appears in Uncle Sam and the Freedom Fighters as a member of the new Freedom Fighters, carrying a bo staff and possessing athletic and martial arts skills. In the 2007 Freedom Fighters series, Firebrand develops a relationship with Red Bee and is devastated when she is taken over by an alien insectoid race; together, the Freedom Fighters save Red Bee and repel the invasion. In the 2010 Freedom Fighters series, Firebrand is killed by Charles Lane, the grandson of the Jester. The fifth Firebrand, Janet Fals, appeared in The Unexpected, released in June 2018. Janet was killed during the Dark Multiverse invasion, but her father used his CIA connections to bring her back to life, releasing her remains to Civil Solutions, a futurist arms developer, who resurrected her with a new heart called the "Conflict Engine," which requires her to start fights to stay alive, preventing her from returning to her old life or identity. She quenches her needs by fighting in underground matches as Firebrand. She had a flirtation with Joy, a female receptionist at V.A. Hospital in Mammoth City, and her creator Steve Orlando has confirmed she is a lesbian. Rod Reilly's Firebrand had no true super-powers but was personally trained by ex-heavyweight boxer "Slugger" Dunn to achieve physical perfection.

The First Ōkuma Cabinet was Japan's eighth cabinet and was headed by Prime Minister Ōkuma Shigenobu from June 30 to November 8, 1898. It marked Japan's first party-based government, with all ministers except the two service ministers coming from the Kenseitō. The cabinet was established just days after the Kenseitō was created through the merger of Ōkuma's Shimpotō and Itagaki Taisuke's Jiyūtō. Despite this formation, internal disagreements continued, resulting in a party split and the cabinet's dissolution by November 1898.

Fleabag is a British comedy-drama television series created and written by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, adapted from her 2013 Edinburgh Festival Fringe one-woman play of the same name, which won a Fringe First Award. The series was produced by Two Brothers Pictures for BBC Three and co-produced with Amazon Studios. Waller-Bridge stars as Fleabag, a free-spirited but angry and confused young woman living in London, while Sian Clifford co-stars as her sister Claire, and Andrew Scott joins in the second season; most main characters are unnamed, including Waller-Bridge and Scott. The protagonist frequently breaks the fourth wall, delivering exposition, internal monologues, and commentary to the audience. The show premiered on 21 July 2016 and concluded its second and final series on 8 April 2019. It received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, and the unique personality of the title character, with many critics and viewers calling it one of the greatest comedy and television series of all time. Waller-Bridge won the British Academy Television Award for Best Female Comedy Performance for the first series, and the second series earned her Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Comedy Series, Outstanding Lead Actress, and Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series; additional acting nominations were given to Clifford, Olivia Colman, Fiona Shaw, and Kristin Scott Thomas. The series also won the Golden Globe Awards for Best Television Series and Best Actress for Waller-Bridge, with a nomination for Scott. The initial concept for Fleabag came from a challenge by a friend to create a 10-minute sketch for a stand-up storytelling night. BBC Three originally broadcast the show, with a repeat run on BBC Two from 21 August to 25 September 2016; the second series aired simultaneously on BBC One and BBC Three, with BBC Three only offering it online. The show was picked up by Amazon Prime Video and premiered in the United States on 16 September 2016, with Series 2 released on 17 May 2019; it is also available on IFC in the US and Net5 in the Netherlands. A French remake titled Mouche (meaning 'fly') was produced by Jeanne Herry and aired on 3 June 2019 on Canal+, set in Paris with Camille Cottin in the lead role. Filming took place in and around London, primarily in North West and Central areas, with key locations including Dartmouth Park, Southampton Road, Laurier Road, Croftdown Road, Highgate Road, York Rise, Twickenham, Hampton Hill, Highgate, Tufnell Park, Belsize Park, Maida Vale, Kentish Town, Parliament Hill Fields, Southwark, Bloomsbury, Soho, Stanmore, Lincoln's Inn Fields, and Finsbury Square. Specific sets include Bold Café & Restaurant in Dartmouth Park as Fleabag's Guinea Pig Café, Cambridge Park Road in Twickenham for Dad and Godmother's house, the British Museum's Lecture Theatre in Russell Square for the feminist lecture, Kensal Green Cemetery for the daily jog, Hedsor House in Maidenhead for the silent retreat, Smith & Wollensky in Covent Garden for the family dinner party, St. Andrew's in Kingsbury for Hot Priest's church, the Tate Modern in Bankside for Godmother's sexhibition, Heron Tower in Bishopsgate for Claire's penthouse office, St Dunstan and All Saints Church in Stepney for the funeral, and 137 – Taylor and Taylor in Shoreditch for the hair salon. Filming for the first series began in late April 2016 and aired from 21 July to 25 August 2016; filming for the second series started in late August 2018 and aired from 4 March to 8 April 2019. Isobel Waller-Bridge, Phoebe's sister, composed the music for both series. Both series received 100% approval ratings on Rotten Tomatoes, with the first averaging 8.5/10 based on 42 reviews and the second 9.3/10 based on 99 reviews; Metacritic awarded the first series a score of 88 out of 100 and the second 96 out of 100, both indicating universal acclaim. Critics such as Emily Nussbaum of The New Yorker described the first series as a "precision black-humour mechanism, a warped and affecting fable about one single woman's existence," Maureen Ryan of Variety called it "scathingly funny" and noted it reveals itself as a tragedy, Hank Stuever of The Washington Post described it as a "funny, highly profane but surprisingly poignant dramedy," Mike Hale of The New York Times praised its "restless, almost feral energy and its slap-in-the-face attitude," and Mary McNamara of the Los Angeles Times commended its unpredictability and "clear eye for truth that often becomes, like all good comedy, quite devastating." The second series received unanimous acclaim and was considered a cultural phenomenon, with Serena Davies of The Daily Telegraph calling it "a near-perfect work of art," Mary Elizabeth Williams of Salon praising it as a "brilliant swan song," Alan Sepinwall of Rolling Stone calling it a "tragicomic masterpiece reaching new heights," James Poniewozik of The New York Times noting it feels "immediately confident, if inevitably less groundbreaking" but continues to push its form, and Hannah Jane Parkinson of The Guardian describing the conclusion as "the most electrifying, devastating TV in years," stating that many who did not watch or appreciate the first series were converted. Fleabag was ranked second-highest among shows of the 2010s by Metacritic's decade-end list and has since been recognized by multiple publications as one of the greatest television series of all time. Former U.S. President Barack Obama named the second season among his favorite films and television series of 2019, including it in his annual list on Twitter on 29 December 2019 with the addendum: "and a quick list of TV shows that I considered as powerful as movies: Fleabag: Season 2, Unbelievable, and Watchmen."

Florence Ann Farmer (24 January 1873 – 26 June 1958) was a pioneering woman in politics in Stoke on Trent, Staffordshire, England, becoming the first female councillor on the county borough council and later the first female Lord Mayor of the city in 1931–32. She was one of the children of George and Mary Farmer, born in Longton, Staffordshire, and her father, George, was an active Liberal local politician who served as secretary of the local party, a Justice of the Peace, and mayor of Longton from 1895 to 1896. After leaving school, Farmer trained as a teacher and served as headmistress of Uttoxeter Road Girls School in Longton from 1895 to 1906. She resigned from teaching to co-found the Phoenix Steam Laundry company with her brother George, and after his death in 1917, continued the business with his widow, Maude, until 1927 when Maude retired, leaving Florence in charge. Farmer was a founding member of the National Federation of Launderers and became the first woman to sit on its national executive committee. Women could only be elected to the local board of guardians since the Local Government Act 1894, and it was not until 1907 that women were allowed to serve on borough councils under the Qualification of Women (County and Borough Councils) Act 1907. Initially a Liberal, Farmer shifted to socialism and joined the Labour Party after the end of the First World War. In 1915, she was elected to the County Borough of Stoke on Trent board of guardians, and in November 1919, she became the first woman elected to the Stoke-on-Trent Council, winning unopposed for No. 23 ward (Longton). She served on various committees, including the watch committee, where she proposed the appointment of women constables; although initially defeated, the proposal was later accepted, leading to the first women constables in Stoke being appointed in 1921. Appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1920, she became the first woman to be made an Alderman of the City of Stoke-on-Trent in 1928. She chaired the local Labour Party branch from 1929 to 1931. When Lady Cynthia Mosley, the MP for Stoke-on-Trent, resigned from the Labour Party in 1931 to join her husband Oswald Mosley’s New Party, Farmer was nominated as the Labour candidate but was not selected; the nomination went to Ellis Smith. In October 1931, she was unanimously chosen to be Lord Mayor of Stoke-on-Trent for 1932–33, becoming the first woman to hold the office and only the fourth woman in England to serve as a Lord Mayor. At her investiture in November 1931, she wore the same mayoral chains that her father had worn as mayor of Longton in 1895. Farmer remained on the city council until 1945 and was granted the Freedom of the City in 1946. She never married and died in June 1958 at the age of 85.

Fort Oglethorpe is a city primarily located in Catoosa County with some areas extending into Walker County in the U.S. state of Georgia. As of the 2020 census, the city had a population of 10,423, with 3,994 households and 2,240 families. The city covers a total area of 13.9 square miles (36.0 km²), all of which is land, and is situated at 34°56′44″N 85°14′44″W (34.94556°N 85.24556°W). It lies 9 miles (14 km) south of Chattanooga, Tennessee, via U.S. Route 27, which continues 18 miles (29 km) south to LaFayette, Georgia. The Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park occupies the southern two-thirds of the city. The city is part of the Chattanooga, Tennessee–Georgia Metropolitan Statistical Area. Fort Oglethorpe was established on land originally owned by William Hamilton Hargrave and his wife Amelia Cecilia Strange-Hargrave, a Confederate soldier and landowner, near the Chickamauga National Battlefield. The U.S. Army established a cavalry post at the site in 1902, later naming it Fort Oglethorpe after James Oglethorpe, founder of the Colony of Georgia. During and after World War I (1917–1920), the fort served as a detention camp for civilian internees and prisoners of war. During World War II, it functioned as a war-time induction and processing center and again housed prisoners of war, and also served as a major training center for the Women's Army Corps. The post land was declared surplus in 1947 and returned to civilian use, leading to the incorporation of the town in 1949. As of the 2000 U.S. census, the population was 6,940, with 2,873 households and 1,881 families, and a population density of 532.6 inhabitants per square mile (205.6/km²). The racial makeup was 93.14% White, 2.38% African American, 0.19% Native American, 2.07% Asian, 0.03% Pacific Islander, 0.56% from other races, and 1.63% from two or more races, with 1.41% identifying as Hispanic or Latino. Household data showed 29.3% had children under 18, 47.0% were married couples, 15.0% had a female householder with no husband, and 34.5% were non-families; 30.6% were made up of individuals, and 13.3% had someone 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.29, and average family size was 2.86. The age distribution included 22.8% under 18, 9.5% aged 18–24, 26.3% aged 25–44, 21.8% aged 45–64, and 19.6% aged 65 or older, with a median age of 38. For every 100 females, there were 82.2 males, and for every 100 females aged 18 and over, there were 76.9 males. The median household income was $32,095, median family income was $40,643, male median income was $28,160, and female median income was $21,141. The per capita income was $16,288, with 11.5% of families and 17.4% of the population below the poverty line, including 30.8% of those under 18 and 11.3% of those 65 or older. As of circa 2024, 9,013 residents lived in Catoosa County and 250 lived in Walker County. The portion in Catoosa County is within the Catoosa County School District, which includes Lakeview–Fort Oglethorpe High School, while the Walker County portion is within the Walker County School District.

Fox Broadcasting Company, LLC, stylized in all caps as FOX, is an American commercial broadcast television network and the flagship property of Fox Corporation, operated through Fox Entertainment. Launched by News Corporation on October 9, 1986, it emerged as a competitor to the Big Three networks—American Broadcasting Company (ABC), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS), and National Broadcasting Company (NBC). Fox became the most successful attempt at a fourth television network, achieving the highest-rated free-to-air position in the 18–49 demographic from 2004 to 2012 and again from 2020 to 2021, and was the most-watched American television network in total viewership during the 2007–08 season. It is a member of the North American Broadcasters Association and the National Association of Broadcasters. Unlike other major networks, Fox does not operate its own news division and instead relies on Fox News, Fox Business Network, and Fox Weather for news programming. Fox and its affiliated companies operate entertainment channels internationally, though programming differs from the American network. In Canada, most viewers have access to at least one American-based Fox affiliate via over-the-air or pay television, but Fox's NFL broadcasts and most prime time programming are subject to simultaneous substitution rules imposed by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to protect domestic network rights. Fox is headquartered at 1211 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan, New York City, with additional offices at the Fox Network Center in Los Angeles and the Fox Media Center in Tempe, Arizona. 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios) began television production as early as 1948 under TCF Television Productions until 1958, producing syndicated programs. After the DuMont Television Network closed in August 1956 due to financial difficulties, the NTA Film Network was launched as a fourth network, with 20th Century Fox producing content for it, though the film network failed after a few years. 20th Century Fox continued producing content for the Big Three networks, including Perry Mason, Batman, and M*A*S*H. While running Paramount Pictures, Barry Diller attempted to create a fourth network with the Paramount Television Service in 1977, which was canceled before broadcasting. Diller later joined 20th Century Fox. In March 1985, News Corporation paid $255 million for a 50% interest in TCF Holdings, the parent of 20th Century Fox. In May 1985, News Corporation paid $2.55 billion to acquire six major U.S. independent stations—WNEW-TV in New York, WTTG in Washington, D.C., KTTV in Los Angeles, KRIV-TV in Houston, WFLD-TV in Chicago, and KRLD-TV in Dallas—from Metromedia. WCVB-TV in Boston was part of the original deal but was spun off to Hearst Broadcasting. Two years later, News Corporation acquired WXNE-TV in Boston and changed its call letters to WFXT. Radio personality Clarke Ingram suggested that Fox is a revival or linear descendant of DuMont, as Metromedia was formed from DuMont’s remaining stations, WNEW-TV and WTTG, and DuMont’s original operations in Manhattan became the Fox Television Center. In 1985, 20th Century Fox announced plans to form a fourth network using its studios and the Metromedia stations for production and distribution. Organizational plans were delayed until regulatory hurdles were cleared. In December 1985, Rupert Murdoch paid $325 million to acquire the remaining equity in TCF Holdings from Marvin Davis. The Metromedia station acquisition was approved by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in March 1986, with WNEW-TV and KRLD-TV changing call letters to WNYW and KDAF, respectively. These six stations, reaching 22% of U.S. households, formed the Fox Television Stations group. All original owned-and-operated stations (except KDAF, which was sold to Renaissance Broadcasting in 1995 and became a WB affiliate) remain part of Fox today. Fox initially affiliated with the top-rated independent station in each market, but in some cases, such as Denver, Phoenix, and St. Louis, it affiliated with a second-tier independent station when a more established one declined. Due to these factors, Fox was forced to affiliate with UHF stations in most markets, similar to DuMont’s experience. Barry Diller, then head of Fox Inc., is credited with creating the network, with the New York Times noting in October 1986 that his "current obsession" was creating a network to compete with NBC, CBS, and ABC. The network officially debuted with a soft launch at 11:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific Time on Thursday, October 9, 1986, featuring a late-night talk show, The Late Show, hosted by Joan Rivers. The show quickly declined in ratings and was discontinued by early 1987 after Rivers and her husband Edgar Rosenberg left due to creative disagreements. The program then used guest hosts, and some affiliates, such as WCGV-TV in Milwaukee and WDRB-TV in Louisville, signed on under the condition they would not carry The Late Show. Before its April 5, 1987 launch, Fox rebranded from FBC to "Fox" under original President Garth Ancier, with ad man Jay Chiat suggesting the use of the "Fox" heritage and "searchlight" iconography to link the network to 20th Century Fox. Several station groups, including Media Central and Pappas Telecasting, initially avoided Fox but later joined. On April 5, 1987, Fox held its "grand opening" by expanding into prime time, premiering Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show on Sunday nights. Both shows were rebroadcast at 7:00 and 7:30 p.m. Eastern/Pacific to allow viewers to sample programming without missing major network programs. Over the next several weeks, Fox added new shows, including 21 Jump Street, Mr. President, and Duet, completing its Sunday schedule. On July 11, 1987, the network launched its Saturday night lineup with the two-hour pilot of Werewolf, followed by The New Adventures of Beans Baxter, Karen's Song, and Down and Out in Beverly Hills, which were canceled by the start of the 1987–88 season and replaced by Second Chance and Women in Prison, both canceled by mid-1988. Fox had planned to cancel The Late Show and develop The Wilton North Report, but after a ratings resurgence under guest host Arsenio Hall, the network could not reach a deal with Hall to return as host and instead revived The Late Show in early 1988. The show then used guest hosts and eventually selected Ross Shafer as permanent host, only to be canceled by October 1988, while Hall signed a deal with Paramount Television to develop The Arsenio Hall Show. Fox aired the 39th Primetime Emmy Awards and the next five editions. Although Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show had modest success, several affiliates, including KMSP-TV in Minneapolis and KPTV in Portland, Oregon, disaffiliated in 1988 due to weak programming, citing that the network’s offerings harmed their syndicated programming. At the start of the 1989–90 season, Fox added a third night of programming on Mondays. The season marked a turnaround, with the debut of The Simpsons, an animated series that originated as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show. Ranked a three-way tie for 29th in the Nielsen ratings, it became a breakout hit and the first Fox series to break into the Top 30. As of 2025, The Simpsons is the longest-running American sitcom, the longest-running American animated program, and the longest-running American scripted primetime television series. In 1989, Fox introduced the documentary series Cops and the crime-focused magazine program America's Most Wanted, which debuted as a half-hour series on Sundays before expanding to an hour and moving to Fridays in the 1990–91 season. These series became staples on the network for over two decades and formed the nucleus of Fox’s Saturday night schedule starting in the 1994–95 season. Married... with Children, which centered on a dysfunctional lower-middle-class family, saw a significant increase in viewer interest after Michigan homemaker Terry Rakolta began a boycott in 1989 over risqué humor and sexual content. The show became Fox’s longest-running live-action sitcom, airing for 11 seasons. Fox survived where DuMont and other fourth-network attempts had failed because it operated just under the FCC’s legal threshold for a network, allowing it to generate revenue without adhering to the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules that applied to the Big Three. DuMont faced regulatory barriers, including a ban on acquiring additional stations and tighter FCC ownership limits, which restricted its growth. In contrast, Murdoch was willing to invest heavily in programming and talent. DuMont operated on a shoestring budget and could not retain programs or stars. Most later startup networks, such as UPN and The WB, followed Fox’s model. DuMont operated during a time when the FCC did not require television manufacturers to include UHF capability, so viewers had to buy expensive converters to access UHF stations, which had poor signal quality compared to VHF stations. By the time Fox launched, cable allowed UHF stations to compete equally with VHF stations. Fox was not initially considered a major competitor to the Big Three, as it targeted a younger demographic—adults aged 18 to 34—with edgier content, while the Big Three focused on older audiences. Until the early 1990s, most Fox stations were formatted as independent stations, airing first-run or acquired programming, and during prime time, either syndicated shows or movies. Few stations carried local newscasts, especially in early years, with only a few in larger markets retaining long-standing newscasts, and those were limited to one newscast per day. On September 6, 1990, Fox reached an agreement with TCI, the nation’s largest cable company, to establish a cable-only national feed, Foxnet, for markets without over-the-air affiliates. Foxnet launched on June 6, 1991, bringing Fox programming to smaller markets and reaching 1.3 million subscribers by 1992. As Fox expanded its prime time offerings to Thursday and Friday nights in the 1990–91 season, it scheduled The Simpsons against NBC’s The Cosby Show, and later introduced Beverly Hills, 90210, which became the network’s longest-running drama, airing for ten seasons. The show performed well in its Thursday slot, spending four seasons there and helping launch Martin, a Fox comedy that became a hit when it debuted in August 1992. The Simpsons returned to Sunday nights in the fall of 1994 and has remained there since. In Living Color, which debuted in April 1990, created memorable characters and launched the careers of Jim Carrey, Jamie Foxx, Damon Wayans, Marlon Wayans, Keenen Ivory Wayans, Chris Rock, Tim Meadows, Rosie Perez, and Jennifer Lopez. The show gained international prominence when Fox aired a live special during Super Bowl XXVI in January 1992, replacing CBS’s halftime show, marking the start of Fox’s rivalry with the Big Three and popularizing counterprogramming. The early and mid-1990s saw the debuts of several soap opera-style prime time dramas aimed at younger audiences, including Beverly Hills, 90210, Melrose Place (which initially had mediocre ratings but saw a significant viewership increase after Heather Locklear joined), the short-lived spin-off Models Inc., and the family drama Party of Five.

A television network that debuted in April 1990 created many memorable characters and launched the careers of future movie stars Jim Carrey, Jamie Foxx, Damon Wayans, Marlon Wayans, Keenen Ivory Wayans, guest stars Chris Rock and Tim Meadows, and both members of the show's dance troupe, the "Fly Girls," Rosie Perez and Jennifer Lopez. The series gained international prominence after Fox aired a special live episode in January 1992 as an alternative to the halftime show during Super Bowl XXVI, which was broadcast on CBS, marking the start of Fox's rivalry with the "Big Three" networks while popularizing the counterprogramming strategy against the Super Bowl telecast. During the early and mid-1990s, several soap opera-style prime time dramas aimed at younger audiences debuted and became quick hits, including Beverly Hills, 90210, its adult-focused spin-off Melrose Place (which initially had a mediocre ratings performance, before viewership rose significantly midway through its first season following Heather Locklear's addition to the cast), its short-lived spin-off Models Inc., and family drama Party of Five. The network also launched several series aimed at a black audience, including Martin, Living Single, and police procedural New York Undercover. Despite having a few successful shows like the science fiction drama The X-Files, Fox still lacked credibility among viewers, with many in the television industry viewing it as "the one that has that cartoon show" (The Simpsons), and more than 85% of affiliates in 1993 were UHF stations. Fox became a viable competitor to the older networks when it won broadcast television rights to the National Football League (NFL) away from CBS. In December 1993, Fox signed a contract with the NFL to televise games from the National Football Conference (NFC)—which had been airing its games on CBS since 1956—starting with the 1994 season. The initial four-year contract, which Fox bid $1.58 billion to obtain—while CBS offered $295 million per year to retain the rights—also included the exclusive U.S. television rights to Super Bowl XXXI in 1997. The network lured Pat Summerall, John Madden, Dick Stockton, Matt Millen, James Brown, Terry Bradshaw, and behind-the-scenes production personnel from CBS Sports to staff its NFL coverage. Shortly afterward, News Corporation began striking affiliation deals with, and later purchasing, more television station groups. On May 23, 1994, Fox agreed to purchase a 20% stake in New World Communications, a television and film production company controlled by investor Ronald Perelman that had recently entered broadcasting through its 1993 purchase of seven stations owned by SCI Television. As a result of Fox acquiring a 20% minority interest in the company, New World signed an agreement to switch the affiliations of twelve stations (eight CBS affiliates, three ABC affiliates [two of which were subsequently placed in a blind trust and then sold directly to Fox due to conflicts with FCC ownership rules], and one NBC affiliate) that it had either already owned outright or was in the process of acquiring from Citicasters and Argyle Communications to Fox starting in September 1994 and continuing as existing affiliation contracts with their existing major network partners expired. That summer, SF Broadcasting, a joint venture between Fox and Savoy Pictures founded in March 1994, purchased four stations from Burnham Broadcasting (three NBC affiliates and one ABC affiliate); through a separate agreement, those stations would also switch to Fox between September 1995 and January 1996 as existing affiliation agreements lapsed. These two deals were not the first instances in which a longtime "Big Three" station affiliated with Fox: in Miami, the affiliation moved from WCIX (channel 6) to NBC affiliate WSVN in January 1989 as the result of a complicated six-station affiliation swap in two South Florida markets spurred by NBC's purchase of CBS affiliate WTVJ (channel 4) and CBS's purchase of WCIX. WSVN immediately attracted industry notice for featuring a news-intensive tabloid format uncharacteristic of any Fox affiliate or independent station, with then-Fox network president Lucie Salhany calling WSVN "the future of television" in May 1994. WSVN remains the largest Fox affiliate in terms of market size to have entirely eschewed any prominent on-air branding with the network name. The NFC contract was the impetus for the affiliation deal with New World and SF Broadcasting's purchase of the Burnham stations, as Fox sought to improve local coverage of its new NFL package by aligning the network with stations that had more established histories and advertiser value than its charter affiliates. The deals spurred a series of affiliation realignments between all four U.S. television networks involving individual stations and various broadcasting groups such as those between CBS and Group W (whose corporate parent later bought the network in August 1995), and ABC and the E. W. Scripps Company (which owned three Fox affiliates that switched to either ABC or NBC as a result of the New World deal), affecting 30 television markets between September 1994 and September 1996. The two deals also had the side benefit of increasing local news programming on the new Fox affiliates, mirroring the programming format adopted by WSVN upon that station's switch to the network (as well as expanding the number of news-producing stations in Fox's portfolio beyond mainly charter stations in certain large and mid-sized markets). Fox Television Stations acquired New World outright on July 17, 1996, in a $2.48 billion stock purchase, making the latter's twelve Fox affiliates owned-and-operated stations of the network; the deal was completed on January 22, 1997. Later, in August 2000, Fox bought several stations owned by Chris-Craft Industries and its subsidiaries BHC Communications and United Television for $5.5 billion (most of these stations were UPN affiliates, although its Minneapolis station KMSP-TV would rejoin Fox in September 2002 as an owned-and-operated station). These purchases, for a time, made Fox Television Stations the largest owner of television stations in the U.S. (a title that has since been assumed by the Sinclair Broadcast Group, one of the network's largest affiliate groups). Fox completed its prime time expansion to all seven nights on January 19, 1993, with the launch of two additional nights of programming on Tuesdays and Wednesdays (the method of gradually adding nights to the programming schedule that began with the network's April 1987 prime time launch was replicated by The WB and UPN when those networks debuted in January 1995), making it the fifth broadcast network (behind the Dumont network) to air programming on a nightly basis. September 1993 saw the heavy promotion and debut of a short-lived western series that incorporated science-fiction elements, The Adventures of Brisco County, Jr. However, it was the supernatural investigative drama that debuted immediately following it on Friday nights, The X-Files, that would find long-lasting success, and would become Fox's first series to crack Nielsen's year-end Top 20 most-watched network programs. After several other failed attempts at late night programming following the cancellation of The Late Show (most notably, the quick failure of The Chevy Chase Show in 1993), Fox finally found success in that time period with the debut of MADtv on October 14, 1995; the sketch comedy series became a solid competitor to NBC's Saturday Night Live for over a decade and was Fox's most successful late night program as well as one of its most successful Saturday night shows, running for 14 seasons until 2009. An attempt to make a larger effort to program Saturday nights by moving Married... with Children from its longtime Sunday slot and adding a new but short-lived sitcom (Love and Marriage) to the night at the beginning of the 1996–97 season backfired with the public, as it resulted in a brief cancellation of America's Most Wanted that was criticized by law enforcement and public officials and was roundly rejected by viewers, which brought swift cancellation to the newer series. Married... quickly returned to Sundays (before moving again to Mondays two months later); both it and Martin would end their runs at the end of that season. The Saturday schedule was revised in November 1996, to feature one new and one encore episode of Cops, and the revived America's Most Wanted: America Fights Back. Cops and AMW remained the anchors of Fox's Saturday lineup, making it the most stable night in American broadcast television for over 14 years; both shows eventually were among the few first-run programs remaining on Saturday evenings across the four major networks after decreasing prime time viewership— as more people opted to engage in leisure activities away from home rather than watch television on that night of the week—led ABC, NBC and CBS to largely abandon first-run series on Saturdays (outside newsmagazines, sports and burned off prime time shows that failed on other nights) in favor of reruns and movies by the mid-2000s. America's Most Wanted ended its 22-year run on Fox in June 2011, and was subsequently picked up by Lifetime (before being cancelled for good in 2013); Cops, in turn, would move its first-run episodes to Spike in 2013 after 23 seasons (ending its original run on Fox as the network's longest-running prime time program), leaving sports and repeats of reality and drama series as the only programs airing on Fox on Saturday evenings. During the 1997–98 season, Fox had three shows in the Nielsen Top 20 (in terms of total viewers); The X-Files (which ranked 11th), King of the Hill (which ranked 15th) and The Simpsons (which ranked 18th), all of which aired on Sunday nights. Building around its flagship animated comedy The Simpsons, Fox would experience relative success with animated sitcoms in prime time, beginning with the debut of the Mike Judge-produced King of the Hill in 1997. Family Guy (the first of three adult-oriented animated series from Seth MacFarlane to air on the network) and Futurama (from Simpsons creator Matt Groening) would make their debuts in 1999; however, they were canceled in 2002 and 2003 respectively. Due to strong DVD sales and highly rated cable reruns on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim, Fox later decided to order new episodes of Family Guy, which began airing in 2005. Futurama would be revived with four direct-to-DVD films between 2007 and 2009 and would return as a first-run series on Comedy Central, where it ran from 2010 to 2013. Less successful efforts included The Critic, starring Saturday Night Live alumnus Jon Lovitz (which Fox picked up in 1994 after it was cancelled by ABC, only for the series to be cancelled again after its second season), and The PJs (which moved to The WB in 2000, after Fox cancelled that series after its second season). Other notable shows that debuted in the late 1990s included the quirky David E. Kelley-produced live-action dramedy Ally McBeal, the short-lived game show Greed, and the period comedy That '70s Show, the latter of which became Fox's second-longest-running live-action sitcom, airing for eight seasons. Throughout the 1990s and into the next decade, Fox launched a slate of cable channels beginning with the 1994 debuts of general entertainment network FX and movie channel FXM: Movies from Fox (now FX Movie Channel), followed by the debut of Fox News Channel in August 1996. Its sports operations expanded with the acquisition of controlling interests in several regional sports networks (including the Prime Network and SportsChannel) between 1996 and 2000 to form Fox Sports Net (which launched in November 1996), its 2000 purchase of Speedvision (later Speed Channel, which was replaced in the United States by Fox Sports 1 in August 2013; however, it continues to exist in other North American and Caribbean countries as Fox Sports Racing), and the launches of Fox Sports World (later Fox Soccer, which was replaced by FXX in September 2013) and Fox Sports en Español (now Fox Deportes) in the early 2000s. By 2000, many staple Fox shows of the 1990s had ended their runs. During the late 1990s and carrying over into the early 2000s, Fox put much of its efforts into producing reality shows many of which were considered to be sensationalistic and controversial in nature—such as Who Wants to Marry a Multi-Millionaire?, Temptation Island, Married by America, and Joe Millionaire (which became the first Fox program to crack the Nielsen Top 10), as well as video clip shows such as World's Wildest Police Videos and When Animals Attack!. After shedding most of these programs, Fox gradually filled its lineup with acclaimed dramas such as 24, The O.C., House, and Bones, and comedies such as The Bernie Mac Show, Malcolm in the Middle, and Arrested Development. As the decade wore on, Fox began surpassing ABC and NBC in the ratings, first in age demographics, then in overall viewership, and placed second behind a resurgent CBS in total viewership, beginning in 2002. Fox hit a major milestone in 2005 when it emerged as the most-watched U.S. broadcast network in the lucrative 18–49 demographic for the first time, largely boosted by the strength of the reality singing competition series American Idol. Regarded as the single most dominant program on 21st-century U.S. television, as well as the first Fox show to lead the Nielsen seasonal ratings, American Idol had peak audiences of up to 38 million viewers during the 2003 season finale and double-season average audiences of around 31 million viewers in 2006 and 2007. Subsequently, it leapfrogged over Fox's Big Three competition to become the highest-rated U.S. television program overall starting with the 2003–04 season, becoming the first reality singing competition series in the country to reach first place in the seasonal ratings. American Idol remains the most recent American television program to date to lead the national prime time ratings and attract at least 30 million viewers for multiple and consecutive television seasons. It is the most-watched program on American television by seasonal average viewership in the 2000s decade, as well as the most recent program scheduled to have successfully established a graveyard slot on American television since the end of NBC's Friends in 2004 and the subsequent decline of NBC's previously dominant "Must See TV" Thursday timeblock. By 2005, reality television succeeded sitcoms as the most popular form of entertainment in the United States as a result of Fox's rise with American Idol and NBC's network declines. House, which aired as American Idol's lead-out program on Tuesday nights, earned international prominence in the 21st century and became Fox's first prime time drama series (and the network's third program overall) to reach the Nielsen Top 10 beginning 2006. Beginning 2004, CBS and Fox, which ranked as the two most-watched broadcast networks in the U.S. during the 2000s, have tended to equal one another in demographic ratings among general viewership, with both networks winning certain demographics by narrow margins; however, while Fox has the youngest-skewing viewer base, CBS is consistently regarded to have the oldest audience demographics among the major broadcast networks. Fox hit a milestone in February 2005 by scoring its first sweeps victory in total viewership and demographic ratings, boosted largely by its broadcast of Super Bowl XXXIX and the strengths of American Idol, 24, House, and The O.C. In September 2006, as a result of the increasing number of over-the-air Fox affiliates and the increased availability of digital subchannels carrying Fox in certain markets, Foxnet was discontinued. Then, a sweeping milestone came by the conclusion of the 2007–08 season on May 21, 2008, shortly after the widely acclaimed seventh-season finale of American Idol, when Fox outranked longtime leader CBS as the most-watched television network overall in the United States, attributed to the strengths of Super Bowl XLII and its NFL game coverages, Idol and House during that season. To date, Fox is the only non-Big Three network to top the overall Nielsen ratings since its inception in the 1950–51 season. In the late 2000s, Fox launched a few series that proved to be powerful hits in different respects. In 2007, the network began production on the game shows Are You Smarter than a 5th Grader? and Don't Forget the Lyrics!; both shows ran for a total of three seasons each, making them the longest-running game shows in Fox's history. In 2008, the supernatural mystery series Fringe debuted to moderate ratings but earned critical acclaim during its first season on Tuesdays. Throughout its run, the series developed a large loyal fanbase that turned the show into a cult favorite. In 2009, Glee premiered to average ratings when its pilot aired as a lead-out program of the eighth-season finale of American Idol, but earned positive reviews from critics. The cast of the series has been acknowledged by Barack Obama and Oprah Winfrey, who have each asked the cast to perform live for various national events. At the beginning of the 2010s, new comedies Raising Hope and New Girl gave Fox its first live-action comedy successes in years. The second season of Glee delivered that series' highest ratings during the 2010–11 season, with viewership peaking during its Super Bowl lead-out episode in February 2011 (marking the most expensive post-Super Bowl episode ever produced on U.S. television). Fox has maintained several long-running game shows, making them the longest-running in the network’s history. The supernatural mystery series Fringe debuted in 2008 with moderate ratings but received critical acclaim during its first season on Tuesdays, eventually developing a large loyal fanbase that made it a cult favorite. Glee premiered in 2009 with average ratings when its pilot aired as a lead-out program for the eighth-season finale of American Idol, but earned positive reviews from critics. The show’s cast has been acknowledged by Barack Obama and Oprah Winfrey, who have each asked them to perform live at national events. In the early 2010s, Fox achieved its first live-action comedy successes in years with the new comedies Raising Hope and New Girl. The second season of Glee reached its highest ratings during the 2010–11 season, peaking during its Super Bowl XLV lead-out episode in February 2011, which was the most expensive post-Super Bowl episode ever produced on U.S. television. Glee consistently attracted worldwide media attention and built a large, loyal international fanbase. Fox’s live telecast of Super Bowl XLV in 2014 helped it become the first U.S. television network to earn an average single-night prime time audience of at least 100 million viewers. American Idol lost its position as the top-rated prime-time program during the 2011–12 finale, falling to second behind NBC Sunday Night Football, ending its eight-year streak as the top-rated prime-time broadcast network series in American television history, which included dominance in both the Adults 18–49 demographic and total viewership. Idol remained in the Nielsen Top 10 from 2003 to 2013 and was the highest-rated non-sports prime-time program and reality series in the U.S. from 2003 to 2012, marking the longest Nielsen ratings streaks for any Fox program in those categories. The 2012 season finale of American Idol marked the end of the 25th anniversary of the Fox network, during which it won the 18–49 demographic for the eighth consecutive season, the longest such streak according to Nielsen records (still standing as of 2026). However, Fox experienced a significant viewership decline during the 2012–13 season, with American Idol and Glee suffering steep ratings drops, and the network falling to third in total viewership (a 22% decrease) and second in the 18–49 demographic (a position it held as of 2014). This decline continued into the 2013–14 season, when Fox placed fourth among major networks in total viewership for the first time since 2001. On January 13, 2014, Fox announced it would abandon the traditional pilot season concept and instead directly pick up shows to series. The network achieved renewed ratings success with its February 2014 broadcast of Super Bowl XLVIII, which became the second most-watched television broadcast by average in U.S. history, and the lead-out programs New Girl and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. In May 2014, Kevin Reilly resigned as chairman of Fox Entertainment. On July 15, 2014, 21st Century Fox announced a merger of the network and 20th Century Fox Television into the newly created Fox Television Group, with Dana Walden and Gary Newman appointed as co-chairpersons. The 2014–15 season saw the series finale of Glee and the debut of new dramas Gotham and Empire. Empire’s ratings increased week-to-week throughout its first season, becoming the network’s first successful American Idol lead-out since House and the first American television program to consistently increase its episode-to-episode viewership during its first five weeks since ABC’s Roseanne in 1992. Empire ended its first season as the first American television show to increase its episodic viewership consistently throughout a single season and as Fox’s fourth program (and first since the 2013 finale of American Idol) to enter the Nielsen Top 10 by the end of the 2014–15 season. The 2015–16 season marked a notable turnaround for Fox, as it jumped ahead of ABC to third place in nationwide ratings (in both overall viewership and the 18–49 demographic) and achieved several firsts. This improvement was driven by the transfer of the Miss Universe and Miss USA pageants from NBC, as well as the return of The X-Files after its 2002 season end and the live musical special Grease: Live, which became the first live American television musical special of the 21st century to be broadcast in front of a live studio audience and the first live musical special aired by a non-Big Three network on primetime. By 2016, Empire and The X-Files ranked in the Nielsen Top 10 for the season, marking the first season since the 2007–2008 American Idol-House tandem that Fox had two programs in the Top 10 without American Idol or any other Fox reality show. The same year, American Idol concluded its original run on Fox after fifteen seasons, ending an era of one of the most successful shows in American television history. In February 2017, Fox broadcast Super Bowl LI, which attracted an average of 111.3 million viewers—ranking among the top five most-watched Super Bowl games and the second-highest audience in network history behind Super Bowl XLVIII. In March 2017, Rob Wade was named Fox’s new president of alternative entertainment and specials, having previously worked as a showrunner for Dancing with the Stars, head of entertainment for BBC Worldwide, and executive producer of America’s Got Talent and The X Factor. On July 27, 2018, 21st Century Fox shareholders agreed to sell most of its key assets—including 20th Century Fox and FX Networks—to The Walt Disney Company for $71.3 billion, following a spin-off of certain businesses. The sale did not include the Fox Broadcasting Company, television stations, or the Fox Sports, Fox News, and Fox Business cable channels, which were to be maintained under a new entity tentatively called "New Fox." Because Disney already owns ABC, the acquisition would have violated the FCC’s rules against merging any of the four major broadcast networks. As a result of the Disney/Fox deal and the December 4, 2019, merger of CBS and Viacom, Fox became the only major American broadcast network without a film studio. After the deal, Fox emphasized sports programming in its upfronts, including acquiring the NFL’s Thursday Night Football package and the rights to the FIFA World Cup. On June 27, 2018, WWE announced that SmackDown would move to Fox on Friday nights beginning October 4, 2019, under a five-year contract valued at $205 million per year. Fox also increased its non-scripted output, announcing The Masked Singer (based on the South Korean format King of Mask Singer), Mental Samurai, and Spin the Wheel for the 2018–19 season. In August 2018, Fox Television Group CEO Dana Walden stated the network planned to commission more series from independent studios not co-owned with the Big Three, citing limited opportunities due to vertical integration, and noted that top programs like The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us were distributed by third parties. Fox also planned to acquire new pitches directly from writers and offer them to outside producers, while gradually reducing scripted programming development from 20th Television, though The Simpsons would remain. Following the sale, Dana Walden became chairwoman of Disney Television Studios and ABC Entertainment. Charlie Collier succeeded Gary Newman as chairman and CEO of Fox on November 1, 2018, with Newman temporarily remaining in a transitional role. In early 2019, The Masked Singer premiered to Fox’s highest ratings for a non-scripted premiere without an NFL lead-in since 2011 and recorded the largest-ever Nielsen ratings gain for a non-scripted series after three days of delayed viewership. On January 30, 2019, Fox ordered a second season, with the first-season finale drawing an average audience of 11.5 million viewers. The next day, the "New Fox" entity, officially named Fox Corporation, began trading on March 19, 2019. At its 2019–20 upfronts, Fox announced 10 new scripted series, with three (Almost Family, Bless the Harts, and Prodigal Son) for the fall, and the second and third seasons of The Masked Singer scheduled for October 2019 and February 2020 (with the latter premiering after Super Bowl LIV). Fox also established Fox Alternative Entertainment, led by Rob Wade, for investments in non-scripted formats, with its first production being the second season of The Masked Singer. Thursday Night Football finished as the second highest-rated series of the 2018–19 season in the key demographic, behind only Sunday Night Football, while The Masked Singer tied for third with The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us. In the 2019–20 season, Thursday Night Football and The Masked Singer again finished as the second and third highest-rated programs in the key demographic, and Fox finished the season as the highest-rated network among viewers 18–49 (with CBS leading in overall viewers). Fox repeated this victory in the 2020–21 season but was narrowly beaten by NBC in the 2021–22 season by a tenth of a ratings share. In October 2022, Collier stepped down to join Roku, with Rob Wade promoted to president and CEO of Fox Entertainment. That season, Fox lost Thursday Night Football to Amazon Prime Video. In May 2023, Fox dropped its procedural drama 9-1-1 after six seasons, which had been the network’s scripted tentpole since 2018. As a 20th Television production, ABC picked up the series for a seventh season. Its spin-off, 9-1-1: Lone Star, remained on Fox and was renewed for a fifth season. In September 2024, it was announced that 9-1-1: Lone Star would conclude after its fifth season, becoming the last 20th Television-produced drama to air on the network. Fox also lost SmackDown to USA Network in September 2024, and began a strategy of regular sports programming on Friday nights, starting with a package of primetime college football games, leveraging its contract extension with the Big Ten Conference, which included options to carry Friday-night games after the addition of west coast teams. On April 2, 2025, Fox and 20th Television Animation announced a four-season, 15-episode renewal for The Simpsons, Bob’s Burgers, Family Guy, and American Dad!, marking the return of the latter to the network after an 11-year run on TBS from October 2014 to March 2025. As of 2015, Fox provides 17 hours of regularly scheduled network programming each week, including fifteen hours of prime time programming from Monday through Saturday (8:00 to 10:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific) and Sunday (7:00 to 10:00 p.m.), and one hour of late night programming on Saturdays (11:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.), which is currently a repeat of primetime series. The network also airs a Sunday morning political discussion show, Fox News Sunday with Shannon Bream (9:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. Eastern and Pacific), its only regular national news program. Sports programming is typically aired on weekends, mostly between 11:00 a.m. and 11:30 p.m. ET, with the Saturday and Friday prime time blocks (starting in 2024) mainly scheduled for sports, and encores airing when no sports are scheduled. Except for The Critic, The PJs, and Futurama, which were cancelled in 1995, 2000, and 2003, Fox typically airs a Sunday night lineup of original adult animation sitcoms, all produced or co-produced by 20th Television. This block, known as Animation Domination from May 1, 2005, to September 14, 2014, was rebranded as Sunday Funday in 2014 after the reintroduction of live-action comedy series, though animated series remain a key part of the schedule.
