Animation shows like Tiny Toon Adventures, Animaniacs, and Batman: The Animated Series (which were moved to Kids' WB in September 1995); Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, from Saban Entertainment, was the block's most successful series, debuting in 1993 and serving as its flagship until it moved to ABC and Toon Disney in 2002. In October 2001, Fox sold its children's division, including Saban Entertainment and Fox Family Worldwide, to The Walt Disney Company for $5.3 billion; in January 2002, the Fox Kids block was reduced to Saturdays, with weekday hours turned over to affiliates; on September 14, 2002, it was replaced by FoxBox, later renamed 4Kids TV in January 2005, which aired programs such as Yu-Gi-Oh!, Kirby: Right Back at Ya!, Sonic X, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (2003), Shaman King, and One Piece. Fox discontinued 4Kids TV on December 27, 2008, due to disputes over unpaid lease fees and failure to guarantee station carriage, citing stiff competition from cable channels as a reason for ending children's programming; the network turned two of the four Saturday morning hours over to affiliates for local newscasts or educational content, while retaining two hours for Weekend Marketplace, which debuted on January 3, 2009. On September 13, 2014, Xploration Station, a two-hour syndicated block produced by Steve Rotfeld Productions that complies with the Children's Television Act and focuses on STEM fields, began airing on Fox stations owned by affiliate groups including Fox Television Stations and Tribune Broadcasting; stations may choose to carry Xploration Station, continue with Weekend Marketplace (as Sinclair Broadcast Group did, though it added the block to most affiliates in September 2016), or not carry it at all (as Gray Television did in Birmingham due to existing E/I contracts). Unlike ABC, CBS, and NBC, Fox does not air national news programs—morning, evening, or overnight—focusing instead on prime time, sports, and ancillary programming; although Fox Corporation owns Fox News Channel, which launched in October 1996 and has near-universal distribution via pay TV, it operates as a separate entity under the Fox News Group. Fox does produce content for the broadcast network, including prime time news segments anchored by Bill Hemmer, especially during political events, and coverage of the State of the Union, presidential debates, national elections, and breaking news branded as a "Fox News Special Report," "Fox News Alert," or "Fox News Red Alert," with carriage varying by station and often limited to prime time; Fox also airs Fox News Sunday on Sunday mornings and rebroadcasts it later, and operates Fox NewsEdge, launched in 1996, which provides national and international news for local newscasts. Fox first attempted a national news program with The Reporters, a weekly newsmagazine from 1988 to 1990, which was cancelled due to low ratings; from 1987 to about 1996, it aired news capsules branded as Fox News Extra and later Fox News Updates; in 1993, it launched Front Page with hosts Ron Reagan and Josh Mankiewicz, which failed to capture a younger audience; in 1998, Fox Files, hosted by Catherine Crier and Jon Scott, lasted over a year before cancellation; its last newsmagazine attempt was The Pulse in 2002–03, hosted by Shepard Smith; on May 17, 2016, the network aired an interview special with Megyn Kelly, Megyn Kelly Presents. Fox attempted national morning programs, beginning with Fox After Breakfast (1996–1998), hosted by Tom Bergeron, Laurie Hibberd, and Vicki Lawrence, which aired at 9:00 a.m. to accommodate local newscasts; it originated as Breakfast Time on FX in 1994; in 2002, it launched Good Day Live, a syndicated, entertainment-focused version of Good Day L.A., which was cancelled in 2005; on January 22, 2007, Fox premiered The Morning Show with Mike and Juliet on owned-and-operated stations, hosted by Mike Jerrick and Juliet Huddy, with a lighter, entertainment-oriented format that shifted during major news events; it was syndicated in 2007 to stations affiliated with ABC, NBC, and CBS and cancelled in June 2009. Fox believed sports, particularly professional football, would drive growth, and in 1987, offered the NFL $13 million per game for Monday Night Football, but the NFL renewed with ABC; in 1993, Fox bid $1.58 billion for the National Football Conference, winning the rights and ending CBS's football coverage for the first time since 1955, which established Fox as a major network and led to affiliation deals with New World Communications; Fox also acquired rights to the NHL (1994–99), Major League Baseball (since 1996), and NASCAR (since 2001, initially with NBC and TNT); from 2007 to 2010, it aired the Bowl Championship Series and the BCS National Championship Game (excluding Rose Bowl events); after the deal ended, it acquired rights to the Big Ten and Pac-12 football championship games (alternating yearly with ESPN); in 2017, Fox secured tier 1 rights to the Big Ten Conference. In August 2011, Fox and the UFC reached a multi-year agreement to broadcast four live events annually in prime time or late night, with the first event, Velasquez vs. Dos Santos, airing on November 12, 2011; the deal ended in 2018, with UFC events moving to ESPN and ESPN+. Fox's 2023 telecast of Super Bowl LVII remains the highest-rated U.S. television program on average in history, while its 2017 telecast of Super Bowl LI holds the record for the largest overall audience in U.S. television history. On June 13, 2024, Fox announced a multi-year deal to be the sole broadcaster of the IndyCar Series and its subsidiary Indy NXT. Fox has 18 owned-and-operated stations and affiliation agreements with 226 additional stations across 50 states, the District of Columbia, and three U.S. possessions; through Fox Television Stations, it has the most owned-and-operated stations among major American commercial networks. The network reaches 95.77% of U.S. households (299,268,292 Americans with at least one TV set); New Hampshire, New Jersey, and Delaware are the only states without a locally licensed Fox affiliate (New Hampshire via WFXT, New Jersey split between WNYW and WTXF, Delaware via WTXF and WBOC-DT2). Fox largely discontinued analog broadcasts on June 12, 2009, as part of the digital transition; it maintains a few low-power affiliates, such as WYFX-LD in Youngstown, Ohio, and in some markets, these stations simulcast on subchannels of co-owned full-power stations; Fox also has numerous subchannel-only affiliations in markets outside the top 50 Nielsen-designated markets, with WSYX-DT3 in Columbus, Ohio (No. 34 by Nielsen) being the largest by market size. Nexstar Media Group is Fox's largest affiliate group by market and numerical reach, with 42 stations (including former O&Os spun off in 2008 to Local TV, later acquired by Tribune in 2013, and purchased by Nexstar in 2019); the Sinclair Broadcast Group is the second-largest operator of Fox stations, owning or providing services to 26 affiliated stations. Fox previously distributed programming to underserved markets via Foxnet, a cable channel launched in 1991 and shut down on September 12, 2006, which aired syndicated and brokered programming; the concept influenced The WB 100+ Station Group (launched September 1998) and The CW Plus (launched September 2006), which allow localized branding and local advertising sales. Fox's programming schedule differs from the "Big Three" networks by airing only two hours of prime time programming on Monday through Saturday evenings and three hours on Sundays, compared to three hours on weekdays and four hours on Sundays for ABC, CBS, and NBC; this is referred to as "common prime," with the 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific)/9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain) hour programmed only by the Big Three. Fox traditionally avoids programming the 10:00 p.m. hour, ceding it to local affiliates for newscasts, though exceptions exist for select special film presentations based on their running time.

Fox's prime time programming schedule differs from the "Big Three" networks (ABC, CBS, and NBC) by airing only two hours on Monday through Saturday evenings and three hours on Sundays, compared to the three hours from 8:00 to 11:00 p.m. on weekdays and four hours from 7:00 to 11:00 p.m. on Sundays (Eastern and Pacific Time) for the older networks. This schedule, known as "common prime," includes the 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain) hour, which is programmed exclusively by ABC, CBS, and NBC. Fox traditionally avoids programming the 10:00 p.m. hour, allowing local affiliates to air local newscasts during that time, though exceptions occur for special film presentations that exceed a two-hour timeslot, live sports overruns, or primetime entertainment following NFL playoff games. Fox did schedule programming in the 10:00 p.m. hour on Sundays from September 1989 to September 1993, but never added programming at that hour on other nights. The original reason for the reduced prime time hours was to avoid FCC requirements that would have classified Fox as a network and imposed associated regulations, though these rules have since been relaxed. Unlike the "Big Three," Fox does not air national morning or evening newscasts or any network daytime programming (such as soap operas, game shows, or talk shows), and instead relies on its owned-and-operated stations and affiliates to produce or distribute syndicated daytime content, including programs like Divorce Court and The Wendy Williams Show, distributed by corporate sister 20th Television. Fox also does not carry children's programming on Saturday mornings or late-night programming on Monday through Friday nights, with local affiliates producing their own content or airing syndicated programs. Due to irregular sports scheduling, many Fox stations fill weekend afternoons with syndicated programming, infomercials, and movies. Fox produces two versions of program promotions: one with standard airtimes based on time zones and another with "clean" end tags allowing stations to insert local airtime and station information via graphical and verbal continuity. This practice, different from ABC, NBC, and CBS, which only allow station logo insertions, was later adopted by The WB, UPN, The CW, and MyNetworkTV. A third promo version is used for cable network advertising, featuring "check local listings" in the end tag. Fox is the only broadcast network that currently airs adult animated comedies, beginning with The Simpsons in 1989, followed by King of the Hill (1997, until 2009, with a return to Hulu in 2025), Family Guy (cancelled twice, revived by Adult Swim in reruns, returned by Fox in 2005 due to home video sales), Futurama (1999, until 2003, picked up by Adult Swim, then Comedy Central from 2008–2013, returned to Hulu in 2023), American Dad! (2005, until 2014, picked up by TBS until March 2025, returned the next year), The Cleveland Show (2009, until 2013), Bob's Burgers (2011), The Great North (2021, until 2025), Krapopolis (2023), and Grimsburg and Universal Basic Guys (2024). Other adult animated shows like The Critic, The PJs, Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Son of Zorn (Fox's only live-action/animated hybrid sitcom), Bless the Harts, Duncanville, and Housebroken were short-lived and unsuccessful. While ABC, CBS, and NBC have attempted to replicate Fox's success with adult animated shows, none have succeeded. Within Fox's station group, locally produced news varies significantly compared to ABC, NBC, and CBS, which typically offer at least 4½ hours of local newscasts on weekdays and one hour on weekends. Most Fox stations run a late-evening newscast at 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain), lasting 30 minutes to one hour, due to the network not programming that hour. Several charter stations, such as WNYW in New York City, which launched its 10:00 p.m. newscast in March 1967, already aired prime time newscasts before Fox's launch. Most Fox stations also offer a weekday morning newscast from 7:00 a.m., one to three hours long, as a local alternative to national morning news. Fox has fewer stations with independent news operations than the "Big Three"; as of October 2015, 70 of its 236 stations (including all 18 owned-and-operated stations) had in-house news departments, compared to roughly 5/8–7/8 of stations on the other networks. KVVU (channel 5) in Las Vegas has the highest weekly news programming hours among Fox stations at 78½ hours. Many Fox stations use a newscast-intensive schedule similar to ABC, NBC, or CBS affiliates, including midday or early-evening newscasts, often extended by half-hour to compete with national evening newscasts. Some stations, especially those not owned by Fox Television Stations or formerly owned by Tribune Broadcasting, air early-evening newscasts only Monday through Friday due to weekend sports overruns. WSVN in Miami was the first Fox station to adopt this format, moving its late newscast from 11:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. and expanding it to one hour in 1989, and increasing its weekday morning newscast by two hours. This format was later adopted by former major network stations that switched to Fox between 1994 and 1996. Many upstart news departments begin with only a prime time newscast before adding more over time. In smaller to mid-sized markets outside the top 50 Nielsen-designated markets, local Fox newscasts are often outsourced to NBC, ABC, or CBS affiliates due to lack of funds, studio space, or legal duopolies or management agreements. For example, WEMT (channel 39) in Greeneville, Tennessee, produces its newscasts via a local marketing agreement with WCYB-TV (channel 5), an NBC affiliate, owned by Sinclair Broadcast Group. Fox affiliates that outsource news often carry less programming than standalone stations, as the contracting affiliate avoids competition in common time slots, unlike same-market ABC, CBS, or NBC affiliates that may simulcast. Exceptions include KFOX-TV (channel 14) in El Paso and WXIN, which began producing newscasts for their CBS-affiliated duopoly partners in September 2014 and January 2015, respectively, maintaining their prior news programming levels. KNPN-LD (channel 26) in St. Joseph, Missouri, is the smallest Fox affiliate by market size with an in-house news operation since its July 2012 sign-on; after KNPG-LD (channel 21) and KCJO-LD (channel 30) joined NBC and CBS in November 2016 and June 2017, News-Press & Gazette Company expanded KNPN's production, though the station maintained roughly the same amount of programming. WPGH-TV (channel 53) in Pittsburgh, the largest Fox station by Nielsen market ranking (#23), outsources its news programming; WPXI (channel 11), an NBC affiliate, has produced its 10:00 p.m. newscast since 2006 after WPGH shut down its news department. The largest Fox station without news programming is WSYT (channel 68) in Syracuse, New York, which discontinued its 10:00 p.m. newscast in 2006. In Dayton, Ohio, Sinclair Broadcast Group adopted Fox 45 News as its universal brand in August 2015, even though the news department belongs to WKEF (ABC affiliate), due to WKEF's weaker ratings; in 2019, WRGT and WKEF switched to a 24/7 web news service called "Dayton 24/7 Now," and in 2021, Fox affiliation moved to WKEF's second subchannel as part of Sinclair's consolidation to address regulatory concerns. Fox offers video on demand through Fox on Demand, available on cable, satellite, streaming, and telecom providers, and streams programming on Hulu and via the Full Episode portal on Fox.com. The most recent episodes are typically available the day after broadcast on Fox on Demand, with fast forwarding disabled and original advertisements included for a week before being replaced by direct response ads. Due to a January 2012 policy to encourage live or same-week DVR viewing, Hulu and Fox.com impose an eight-day delay for most viewers, restricting day-after-air access to subscribers of certain pay providers (such as Dish Network and Verizon FiOS) or Hulu's free service with Yahoo! Stream; however, Hulu offers newer episodes to paid subscribers with a user login. In March 2020, Fox began streaming the full schedule of its owned stations through Fox Now. In April 2020, Fox acquired the ad-supported streaming service Tubi, which initially offered third-party licensed content but later began adding episodes of Fox original series a week after television premiere. Fox discontinued the Fox Now app in July 2023, with streaming continuing on Hulu, Fox Local, or Tubi; the service was effectively relaunched as Fox One two years later. Fox began broadcasting in 720p high definition on September 12, 2004, during the first week of the 2004 NFL season. Until March 14, 2016, the network did not display an on-screen logo in the bottom-right corner of the screen, except for a ten-second "Fox HD" promotional logo (until the end of 2010, which included a DirecTV sponsor tag); instead, a station logo bug was triggered in the right-hand corner of the 16:9 screen, disappearing during commercial breaks, even during local pre-emptions for breaking news or severe weather, though some stations like WGGB-DT2 in Springfield, Massachusetts, displayed only a "FOX" logo. Network or affiliate bugs are not shown during Fox Sports programming. During high-profile or live programs like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance, Fox displays its network logo instead of the affiliate's for promotional reasons due to fair use of clips by other media. Until 2014, the bug was placed in the 4:3 safe area. Fox News Sunday displayed the "Fox HD" logo continuously due to both promotional and tape-delay reasons. On March 14, 2016, the standard Fox logo with hashtag was implemented across all programming, with the station bug flashing briefly at program start or after commercial breaks, as traditionally done by ABC, CBS, and NBC. The Fox HD bug was discontinued; it was still used on Fox News Sunday until late 2019–early 2020. On some Fox programs, a hashtag appears above the affiliate's logo (e.g., #newgirl or #bones) to provide viewers with program references.

During high-profile or live programs like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance, Fox displayed its network logo instead of the affiliate's logo, primarily for promotional reasons due to fair use of clips by media outlets such as news programs, talk shows, and review or satirical content; until 2014, this bug was placed in the 4:3 safe area. Fox News Sunday displayed the "Fox HD" logo continuously due to both promotional reasons and because many stations aired the program on tape delay later in the morning. Beginning March 14, 2016, the standard Fox logo with hashtag was adopted for all programming, with the station bug flashed briefly at the start of a program or after commercial breaks, as traditionally done by ABC, CBS, and NBC stations; the Fox HD bug was discontinued, though it remained on Fox News Sunday until around late 2019–early 2020. On some Fox programs, a hashtag appears above the affiliate's logo (e.g., #newgirl or #bones) to link viewers to the network’s official Twitter search tag for discussions during broadcasts. In April 2012, episode-specific tags related to plot points (e.g., #saturdaynightGLEEver for a Glee episode) were introduced to generate trending topics and spread conversations on Twitter. When the Fox bug appears instead of the station logo, the Twitter hashtag is directly above the Fox logo in the safe area. Fox's World Series coverage began in HD with Game 1 of the 2002 World Series. During the analog-to-digital transition, Fox was the only U.S. commercial network to air widescreen programs not available in HD, labeled "Fox High Resolution Widescreen" from 2001 to 2006. Prior to its HD feed launch, some sitcoms and dramas aired in widescreen standard-definition, while reality, talk, and game shows (American Idol being the first major exception, starting in 2008) aired only in widescreen enhanced definition. This Week in Baseball began airing in widescreen in 2009, and Fox News Sunday transitioned to HD when the Fox News Channel moved to new high-definition facilities in November 2008; prior to the unified widescreen presentation on both HD and standard-definition feeds in September 2010, it was the last Fox News program to use 4:3 safe area graphics and camera positions. MADtv aired only in 4:3 until September 2008, likely due to tape-delaying by stations and producers not adopting the 16:9 format. The final Fox show to convert to HD was Family Guy, beginning with its September 26, 2010, episode; all programming is now broadcast in widescreen and high definition as of 2013, with Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound. Fox is unique among American broadcasters in distributing its HD feed over satellite as an MPEG transport stream for bit-for-bit broadcast transmission; during network programming hours, local commercials are inserted using a transport stream splicer. Affiliates of other networks typically decode and re-encode compressed satellite feeds for over-the-air transmission. After Fox began broadcasting sports programming with 16:9-optimized graphics in late July 2010, it requested cable and satellite providers to use the No. 10 Active Format Description (AFD) flag, which displays 16:9 content in letterboxed format on 4:3 screens to ensure full display of graphical elements. Many Fox O&Os and affiliates began disseminating the AFD No. 10 flag for HD local news and syndicated programs, incorporating on-air graphics and logo bugs optimized for letterboxed presentation. In the early 1990s, Fox stations began using a branding structure combining "Fox" with the channel number and call letters (e.g., WNYW as "Fox 5"), later minimizing call letters to remain compliant with FCC rules, a trend followed by other networks. Branding varied by market: some stations used city or regional names (e.g., WFLD as "Fox Chicago" from 1997 to 2012, WTXF-TV as "Fox Philadelphia" from 1995 to 2003); others reduced "Fox" branding, using call letters or generic names (e.g., WSVN in Miami as "WSVN 7" and "(Channel) 7 News," KHON-TV in Honolulu changing from "Fox 2" to "KHON 2" in 2003, WDRB in Louisville dropping "Fox 41" to "WDRB" in 2011, KVRR in Fargo switching to "KVRR 15" in 2015). Stations that joined Fox through the 1994 New World deal retained Big Three-era branding (e.g., WJW in Cleveland dropped "TV8" and "Newscenter 8" for "Fox is ei8ht" and "ei8ht is News," KDFW in Dallas/Fort Worth rebranded to "Fox 4 Texas" and later to "Fox 4" with "Fox 4 News" since 1996). KTVU in Oakland-San Francisco retained "Channel 2" branding, rebranding to "KTVU Fox 2" in 1996 (adding the Fox logo beneath its "Circle Laser 2" logo), and adopting full-time "KTVU Fox 2" branding in February 2015, retaining the "Circle Laser 2" in both the standardized "boxkite" logo and an alternate version with a prominent Fox wordmark. KCPQ in Seattle retained "Q13 Fox" and "Q13 News" until September 2021, when it dropped "Q13" and rebranded to "Fox 13," aligning with other Fox O&Os. Starting in 2006, Fox O&Os adopted a standardized on-air look inspired by Fox News Channel, featuring a red, white, and blue boxkite logo with red pillars (rotating on-air, especially in logo bugs). After News Corporation acquired Myspace (sold in June 2011 to a group including Justin Timberlake), some O&Os launched websites with identical layouts and "MyFox" domains (e.g., MyFoxDC.com for WTTG). On-air use of the FNC-inspired logos declined in August 2012 with a new standardized graphics package using wordmark bugs; several O&Os discontinued "MyFox" domains by 2015. The use of Fox News Channel boxkite logos and connections to it was drastically reduced after Roger Ailes' July 2016 resignation, shifting to a simpler, more flexible "call-channel number" horizontal wordmark style suitable for traditional TV and mobile screens. In 2017, Stephen Arnold Music released a new news music package, "Beyond," which excluded all previous Fox News Channel sonic elements and was rolled out across all Fox O&O local news operations. As of 2017, Fox O&Os with sister MyNetworkTV stations began downplaying that network, with many adopting "Fox (channel number) Plus/Xtra/More" branding to suggest they are extensions of their sister Fox station, and many now carry extended newscasts or rebroadcasts of earlier newscasts during primetime, pushing MyNetworkTV’s schedule to late night. When Fox launched on October 9, 1986, as the Fox Broadcasting Company, it used a logo with three squares containing "FBC" similar to the UK’s BBC logo from 1997–present, with the network name in a rectangle below, mostly matching the color of ITV’s 1998–2004 logo, used primarily in the opening of The Late Show with Joan Rivers. On April 5, 1987, a more familiar logo based on 20th Century Fox’s design was introduced, featuring "FOX" with searchlights and a double-pane platform; Fox O&Os used a variant from 1987 to 1989 with an "O" and searchlight in negative space intersecting the "X" and panes; until the mid-1990s, some affiliates using CGI or local production houses emulated this design. In September 1993, the logo was modernized with a current proprietary logotype, angle changed (removing tilt), and the "O" gained a trademark pillar-like bowl, becoming a key element in advertising; the 1987 logo remained in print ads through 1993–94. Starting with this logo, Fox displayed an on-screen bug in the lower right corner (initially for one minute per segment, later throughout the program, then reverting after the 2009 digital transition). The "O" was later redesigned with the pillar, replacing the searchlight motif. A 1995–96 logo removed searchlights but kept two lower panes and added a third pane above the wordmark; a 1996 variant excluded the panes and restored searchlights behind the "F" and "X." The current logo, introduced in 1999, removed searchlights entirely and used only a wordmark. Despite this, searchlights remained part of 21st Century Fox branding, appearing in Fox News Channel’s logo and in the universal station logo introduced in 2006 by Fox O&Os (retained by seven former O&Os sold to Local TV in 2008 and spread to Tribune Broadcasting affiliates, modified in 2012 to feature one searchlight); the 1996–99 searchlight logo is still used by a few affiliates; searchlights were also in FX’s logo until 2008. The screen bug was used from 1999 to 2014; when the network upgraded to HD, the watermark remained in the 480i format. Until March 14, 2016, the network did not display the on-screen bug, only the hashtag without the Fox bug on some affiliates. For the 2019–20 season, Fox implemented branding by Trollbäck + Company, slightly thickening the logo and incorporating animations of its shapes into advertising and on-air elements, including an animation of abstract shapes morphing into the main Fox logo. Controversy arose in 2002 and 2003 over profanity by Cher and Nicole Richie during live broadcasts of the Billboard Music Awards on Fox affiliates in the Eastern and Central Time Zones, despite five-second audio delays; the indecent content was edited out in time zones west of the Mountain Time Zone. The Parents Television Council condemned both incidents as among the worst on television from 2001 to 2004 and filed tens of thousands of complaints with the FCC. Fox representatives’ apology was labeled a "sham" by PTC president L. Brent Bozell III, who argued the network could have easily used audio delays to remove the language. In 2004, Fox announced extending live delays to five minutes to allow easier editing of obscenities. In June 2007, the U.S. Second Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Federal Communications Commission v. Fox Television Stations that the FCC could not fine broadcasters for fleeting expletives, such as during the Billboard Awards; the FCC later appealed the decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari and oral arguments began on November 4, 2008. The Parents Television Council has also criticized many popular Fox shows for perceived indecent content, including Family Guy, The Simpsons, American Dad!, Futurama, Cops, Hell's Kitchen, 24, House, Married... with Children, Bones, Arrested Development, Prison Break, 'Til Death, Malcolm in the Middle, The O.C., and That '70s Show, and has filed complaints with the FCC regarding such content.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) does not have the authority to fine broadcasters for fleeting expletives, as demonstrated in the case of the Billboard Awards. The FCC later decided to appeal the Second Circuit Court's decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari in FCC v. Fox, et al., and oral arguments began on November 4, 2008. The Parents Television Council has criticized numerous popular Fox shows for perceived indecent content, including Family Guy, The Simpsons, American Dad!, Futurama, Cops, Hell's Kitchen, 24, House, Married... with Children, Bones, Arrested Development, Prison Break, 'Til Death, Malcolm in the Middle, The O.C., and That '70s Show. The Council has filed complaints with the FCC regarding indecent content in these programs, specifically for That '70s Show and Married by America. The FCC successfully fined the network nearly $1 million for airing Married by America. This fine was reduced to $91,000 in January 2009 after Fox appealed, following the FCC's admission that it originally claimed to have received 159 complaints about the show, but later acknowledged receiving only 90—coming from just 23 individuals. A study by blogger Jeff Jarvis found that all but two of the complaints were nearly identical, indicating the $1.2 million judgment was based on original complaints from only three people. On September 21, 2012, the United States Department of Justice dismissed the lawsuit.

François de Malherbe (1555–16 October 1628) was a French poet, critic, and translator. Born in Le Locheur (near Caen, Normandie), he came from a family of standing, though its noble lineage did not meet the heraldic standards for pre-16th century nobility. He was the eldest son of François de Malherbe, a conseiller du roi in Caen’s magistracy. Malherbe received an elaborate education in Caen, Paris, Heidelberg, and Basel. At twenty-one, he entered the household of Henri d'Angoulême, the illegitimate son of Henry II and governor of Provence, serving as secretary and marrying there in 1581. According to Tallemant des Réaux, his early verses were of poor quality. After Henri d'Angoulême died during Malherbe’s visit to Provence, he had no steady employment, though he earned a significant sum from Henry III through servile verses, which he later libelled. For many years, he lived between Provence and Normandy, with little known about this period. His work *Larmes de Saint Pierre*, imitated from Luigi Tansillo, was published in 1587. In 1600, he composed an ode of welcome for Maria de' Medici, marking the first of his notable poems. It took several years for his fortunes to improve; he was introduced to Henry IV by Cardinal Du Perron, though the king initially showed little interest, eventually summoning him to court and providing him with support, though the promised pension was not paid until after Henry IV’s reign. His father died in 1606, and Malherbe inherited his estate. From then on, he lived at court, maintaining a close correspondence with his wife, though seeing her only twice in twenty years. In old age, he suffered a major tragedy when his son, Marc Antoine, died in a duel against Paul de Fortia de Piles. Malherbe suspected foul play and used his influence to have de Fortia and Jean Baptiste de Covet brought to justice; he died before the case was resolved, reportedly from disease contracted during the siege of La Rochelle, where he had gone to petition the king. He died in Paris on 16 October 1628, at the age of seventy-three, just 15 months after his son’s death. The football team from Caen, France, Stade Malherbe de Caen, founded in 1913, is named after him. Malherbe had a significant and lasting impact on French literature, particularly in establishing the poetic rules of "Classicism" that would dominate for nearly two centuries until the Romantic era. His emphasis on technical perfection, simplicity, and vocabulary purity offered a corrective to the excesses of Pierre de Ronsard and La Pléiade, though Boileau-Despréaux’s praise in "Enfin Malherbe vint" is limited by his lack of knowledge of earlier French poetry. Malherbe’s personal character, marked by a bludgeon-like wit, was not amiable, as noted by his contemporary and rival Mathurin Régnier, who opposed him not only for his loyalty to Ronsard but also due to Malherbe’s discourtesy toward Régnier’s uncle, Philippe Desportes, whom Malherbe had initially plagiarized. While his poetic output is limited and often frigid, his best-known works include the *Consolation a Duperier* (featuring the line “Et, rose, elle a vécu ce que vivent les roses”), his odes to Marie de' Medici and Louis XIII. His prose is more extensive and highly refined, including translations of Livy and Seneca and numerous well-written letters, many addressed to Peiresc, as well as a detailed and critical commentary on Desportes. His most important disciples were François Maynard and Racan; Claude Favre de Vaugelas is credited with purifying French diction around the same time. Two of his poems were set to music by Maurice Jaubert. The primary biographical sources are Racan’s *Vie de Malherbe* and Tallemant des Réaux’s *Historiette*. The standard edition of his works is *Oeuvres poétiques*, edited by René Fromilhague and Raymond Lebègue (1968), while Antoine Adam’s popular collection *Poésies* is based on the Pléiade edition (1982). Key secondary sources include G. Brunot’s *La Doctrine de Malherbe* (1891), René Fromilhague’s *Malherbe: Technique et création poétique* (1954), David Lee Rubin’s *High Hidden Order* (1972) and its appendix in *The Knot of Artifice* (1981), and Claude K. Abraham’s *Enfin Malherbe* (1971), which focuses on Malherbe’s prosody.

Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón (Spanish pronunciation: [ˈfɾiða ˈkalo]; 6 July 1907 – 13 July 1954) was a Mexican painter renowned for her portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by nature and Mexican artifacts. Influenced by the country’s popular culture, she used a naïve folk art style to explore themes of identity, postcolonialism, gender, class, and race in Mexican society. Her paintings often had strong autobiographical elements and blended realism with fantasy. Associated with the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, Kahlo has also been described as a surrealist or magical realist and is known for depicting her chronic pain. Her 1940 self-portrait, The Dream (The Bed), holds the record as the most expensive work by a female artist ever auctioned, selling for $54.7 million. Born to a German father and a mestiza mother of Purépecha descent, Kahlo lived most of her life at La Casa Azul in Coyoacán, now the Frida Kahlo Museum. Though disabled by polio as a child, she was a promising medical student until a severe bus accident at 18 caused lifelong pain and medical issues. During recovery, she returned to art, initially considering a career as a medical illustrator. Her mother provided her with a specially-made easel and oil paints from her father, and a mirror was placed above the easel so she could see herself. Painting became a means to explore identity and existence, as she stated, "I paint myself because I am often alone and I am the subject I know best," and later, "to begin again, painting things just as [she] saw them with [her] own eyes and nothing more." Most of her early works were portraits of herself, her sisters, and schoolfriends, drawing inspiration from Renaissance artists like Botticelli and Bronzino and avant-garde movements such as Neue Sachlichkeit and Cubism. After moving to Cuernavaca in 1929 with Diego Rivera, she adopted a folk art style influenced by Adolfo Best Maugard’s treatise, incorporating elements from pre-Columbian and colonial Mexican art. In San Francisco in 1930, she met American artists like Edward Weston and Nickolas Muray, developed her folk art style, and created works such as Frieda and Diego Rivera (1931) and The Portrait of Luther Burbank (1931). Though she publicly presented herself as Rivera’s spouse, her work was included in the Sixth Annual Exhibition of the San Francisco Society of Women Artists. In Detroit, she faced health issues from a failed pregnancy and explored new techniques like etching and frescos, emphasizing themes of terror, suffering, wounds, and pain, and created retablo-style works such as Henry Ford Hospital (1932), My Birth (1932), and Self-Portrait on the Border of Mexico and the United States (1932). Despite no exhibitions in Detroit, she gave an interview to the Detroit News, titled "Wife of the Master Mural Painter Gleefully Dabbles in Works of Art." After returning to Mexico City in 1934, she made few paintings due to health issues, but in 1937 and 1938, following her divorce and reconciliation with Rivera, she produced more works than in all previous years, including My Nurse and I (1937), Memory, the Heart (1937), Four Inhabitants of Mexico (1938), and What the Water Gave Me (1938). The National Autonomous University of Mexico exhibited her work in early 1938, and she made her first significant sale in 1938 when Edward G. Robinson bought four paintings for $200 each. André Breton, impressed by her work, called it "a ribbon around a bomb," arranged her first solo exhibition at Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938, and later invited her to Paris in 1939. In New York, her colorful Mexican dress caused a sensation, and the exhibition, attended by Georgia O'Keeffe and Clare Boothe Luce, received positive press despite condescending reviews; she sold half of the 25 paintings. She received commissions from A. Conger Goodyear and Clare Boothe Luce. In Paris, despite Breton’s invitation, her paintings were not cleared by customs and the gallery refused to show most of them, considering them too shocking, and they were displayed alongside photographs, pre-Columbian sculptures, and Mexican market items. The exhibition opened in March 1939, received less attention due to the looming Second World War, and made a financial loss, leading her to cancel a planned London exhibition. However, the Louvre purchased The Frame, making her the first Mexican artist in their collection. She was warmly received by artists like Pablo Picasso and Joan Miró and by the fashion world, with Elsa Schiaparelli designing a dress inspired by her and Vogue Paris featuring her. Kahlo remained critical of the Surrealists, calling them "this bunch of coocoo lunatics and very stupid surrealists." In the United States, her work continued to gain attention, being featured at the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston in 1941 and in two high-profile exhibitions in New York in 1942: the Twentieth-Century Portraits exhibition at MoMA and the Surrealists' First Papers of Surrealism exhibition. In 1943, she was included in the Mexican Art Today exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Women Artists at Peggy Guggenheim's The Art of This Century gallery. In Mexico, she became a founding member of the Seminario de Cultura Mexicana in 1942, participated in exhibitions at the Benjamin Franklin Library in 1943 and 1944, and was invited to "Salon de la Flor." She also taught at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado ("La Esmeralda") starting in 1943, encouraging informal, non-hierarchical teaching and a focus on Mexican folk culture and street subjects. When her health prevented commuting, she held classes at La Casa Azul, and four students—Fanny Rabel, Arturo García Bustos, Guillermo Monroy, and Arturo Estrada—became devoted followers, known as "Los Fridos." She secured three mural commissions for herself and her students. Kahlo struggled to earn a living from her art until the mid to late 1940s, refusing to adapt her style, and received two government commissions in the early 1940s—one not completed and one rejected. However, she had regular private clients, such as engineer Eduardo Morillo Safa, who ordered over thirty family portraits. Her financial situation improved with a 5000-peso national prize for Moses (1945) in 1946 and the purchase of The Two Fridas by the Museo de Arte Moderno in 1947. By the mid-1940s, her paintings were featured in most group exhibitions in Mexico, and she could sell whatever she painted, sometimes incomplete works. As her health declined, she underwent a failed spinal surgery and painted works like Broken Column (1944), Moses (1945), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflecting her physical state. In her final years, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, painting still lifes of fruit and flowers with political symbols such as flags or doves. She expressed concern about expressing her political convictions, stating, "I have a great restlessness about my paintings... I must struggle with all my strength to ensure that the little positive my health allows me to do also benefits the Revolution, the only real reason to live." Her painting style became more intense, with brasher colors and faster brushstrokes. Photographer Lola Alvarez Bravo staged her first solo exhibition in Mexico at Galería Arte Contemporaneo in April 1953, despite her doctors’ bed rest orders; she arrived in an ambulance and was carried to the gallery, where she stayed for the event. The exhibition was a major cultural event and received global media attention. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, then resumed painting after a one-year break, creating political works such as Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954), Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), and the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates vary on the total number of paintings she produced, ranging from fewer than 150 to around 200.

In 1953, despite her doctors prescribing bed rest, Frida Kahlo ordered her four-poster bed to be moved to the gallery for the opening of a major exhibition, which was a significant cultural event in Mexico and received international media attention. She arrived in an ambulance, was carried on a stretcher to the bed, and remained there throughout the event. That same year, the Tate Gallery in London held an exhibition on Mexican art that included five of her paintings. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, after which she resumed painting following a one-year break. Her final works include the political paintings Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954) and Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), as well as the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates of her total output range from fewer than 150 to around 200 paintings. Her early works from the mid-1920s show influence from Renaissance masters and European avant-garde artists like Amedeo Modigliani, while by the end of the decade, she drew inspiration from Mexican folk art, particularly its themes of fantasy, naivety, and fascination with violence and death. Her style blended reality with surreal elements and frequently depicted pain and death. André Breton, a key early supporter, claimed her as a Surrealist, stating she developed her style without knowing the movement’s ideological foundations, and described her work as situated at the intersection of political and artistic lines. Bertram D. Wolfe called her a "sort of 'naïve' Surrealism," though Kahlo herself detested Surrealism, viewing it as bourgeois art. Some art historians, like Andrea Kettenmann, see her as a symbolist focused on inner experience, while Emma Dexter argues her work aligns more with magical realism or New Objectivity due to its roots in Aztec mythology and Mexican culture rather than Surrealism. Influenced by Mexicanidad, a romantic nationalism emerging after the revolution, Kahlo aimed to paint for the Mexican people and rejected the idea of formal art education, instead cultivating an image of being self-taught and naive. While muralists dominated the Mexican art scene in the 1920s, Kahlo focused on small-scale self-portraits, especially inspired by votive paintings or retablos—religious images made by amateurs to thank saints for surviving calamities—whose format emphasized figures over realistic backgrounds. She owned approximately 2,000 retablos, displayed in La Casa Azul, and used their narrative potential to explore allegory and iconography. Her self-portraits often mimicked colonial-era bust-length portraits but subverted them by portraying her as less attractive, reflecting shifting societal values in the 1930s as Mexicans moved away from socialism toward individualism. Her mask-like faces were linked to Indigenous and Catholic depictions of goddesses and saints. She was influenced by Mexican folk artists Hermenegildo Bustos and José Guadalupe Posada, as well as European artists Hieronymus Bosch and Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and poet Rosario Castellanos, whose works addressed female suffering and patriarchal structures. Root imagery in her paintings symbolizes personal growth, entrapment, and the influence of the past on the present; in My Grandparents and I, a young Kahlo holds a ribbon from an ancient tree bearing her ancestors’ portraits, with her left foot as a tree trunk, reflecting her view of humanity’s unity with the earth and Mexico. Trees represent hope, strength, and intergenerational continuity, while hair symbolizes growth and the feminine; in Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair, she wears a man’s suit and shorn hair, holding scissors menacingly near her genitals, interpreted as a threat to Rivera or a projection of her anger toward patriarchal values and machismo. Kahlo’s lifelong suffering from a youth bus accident led to frequent hospitalizations and surgeries, often performed by quacks, and her medical-themed paintings frequently depict bleeding and open wounds, especially in childbirth and miscarriage, reflecting guilt over living at the expense of others. Her paintings, though personal, are ambiguous and raise questions about Mexican society, particularly gender, race, and class. Historian Liza Bakewell notes Kahlo recognized the contradictions of being Mexican—modern yet pre-Columbian, young yet old, anti-Catholic yet Catholic, Western yet New World, independent yet colonized, mestizo yet not Spanish or Indian—and used pre-Columbian and Christian symbols, including monkeys, skeletons, skulls, blood, and hearts, often tied to Aztec myths like Coatlicue, Quetzalcoatl, and Xolotl. She also frequently depicted La Llorona and La Malinche, figures associated with suffering and misfortune, such as in Henry Ford Hospital (1932), where she painted herself weeping with an exposed heart, traditionally seen as a depiction of grief but now interpreted as a commentary on the taboo of remaining childless in Mexican society. Kahlo often portrayed her body in various states—wounded, as a child, or in different clothing like the Tehuana dress, a man’s suit, or a European gown—using it as a metaphor to explore societal roles. Her depictions of the female body, especially during miscarriages or childbirth and cross-dressing, position the viewer as a voyeur, making it difficult to avoid a conscious response. According to Nancy Cooey, Kahlo made herself into the central figure of her own mythology as a woman, a Mexican, and a suffering person, expressing spiritual resistance and sexuality. Nancy Deffebach notes she created a subject who was female, Mexican, modern, and powerful, diverging from traditional gender roles. Until the late 1980s, her work was often seen as less political and more naïve than that of male muralists. Art historian Joan Borsa criticizes that critical reception has frequently ignored or downplayed the politics in her exploration of personal history, including sexuality, marginality, cultural identity, female subjectivity, and power. Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, near Mexico City. While she claimed to have been born at La Casa Azul, the official registry lists the birth at her maternal grandmother’s home. Her parents were photographer Guillermo Kahlo (1871–1941) and Matilde Calderón y González (1876–1932), who were 36 and 30 when she was born. Guillermo, originally from Germany, moved to Mexico in 1891 after an accident ended his university studies. Kahlo claimed her father was Jewish, but genealogists in 2006 found he was Lutheran. Matilde was born in Oaxaca to an Indigenous father and a Spanish mother. The couple had daughters Matilde (c. 1898–1951), Adriana (c. 1902–1968), and Cristina (c. 1908–1964), and two half-sisters, María Luisa and Margarita, raised in a convent. Kahlo described her childhood as "very, very sad," with both parents often ill and their marriage lacking love. Her relationship with her mother was tense; she described her as kind, active, intelligent, but also calculating, cruel, and fanatically religious. Her father’s photography business declined during the Mexican Revolution due to the loss of government commissions and reduced private clients. At age six, Kahlo contracted polio, which caused her right leg to grow shorter and thinner, leading to isolation and bullying. This experience made her reclusive but also close to her father, who shared her experience of disability. He taught her literature, nature, philosophy, sports, and photography, and encouraged her to pursue strength despite societal norms. Due to polio, she began school later and attended kindergarten and primary school in Coyoacán, then was homeschooled for grades five and six. Her sister Cristina went to a convent school, while Kahlo was enrolled in a German school due to her father’s wishes; she was expelled for disobedience and sent to a vocational teachers’ school, where she was sexually abused by a female teacher. In 1922, she was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only 35 female students out of 2,000, and she excelled academically, becoming deeply committed to Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, emphasizing Indigenous heritage and rejecting European superiority. Nine of her classmates, with whom she formed the informal group known as the "Cachuchas," became prominent figures in the Mexican intellectual elite.

In 1922, Kahlo was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only recently begun admitting women, with just 35 girls out of 2,000 students. She performed well academically, was a voracious reader, and became deeply immersed in Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, a movement that emphasized Mexico's Indigenous heritage and rejected European colonial superiority. Nine of her schoolmates, with whom she formed an informal group called the "Cachuchas," became leading figures in the Mexican intellectual elite; they were rebellious, staged pranks and plays, and debated philosophy and Russian classics. To conceal her age and to declare herself a "daughter of the revolution," she claimed to have been born on 7 July 1910, the start of the Mexican Revolution, a date she maintained throughout her life. She fell in love with Alejandro Gomez Arias, the group's leader and her first love; her parents disapproved. Due to political instability and violence, they were often separated and exchanged passionate love letters. On 17 September 1925, Kahlo and Arias were on their way home from school when they got off a bus to retrieve an umbrella Kahlo had left behind, then boarded a second crowded bus. The driver attempted to pass an oncoming electric streetcar, which crashed into the wooden bus, dragging it a few feet. Several passengers were killed; Arias suffered minor injuries, but Frida was impaled by an iron handrail through her pelvis. She later described the injury as "the way a sword pierces a bull," and the handrail was removed by Arias and others, causing her immense pain. Kahlo suffered multiple injuries: a fractured pelvic bone, punctured abdomen and uterus, a broken spine in three places, eleven fractures in her right leg, a crushed and dislocated right foot, a broken collarbone, and a dislocated shoulder. She spent a month in hospital and two months recovering at home before returning to work. X-rays revealed that the accident had displaced three vertebrae, and she was required to wear a plaster corset for the better part of three months, confining her to bed rest. The accident ended her dreams of becoming a physician and caused her lifelong pain and illness; her friend Andrés Henestrosa stated that Kahlo "lived dying." By late 1927, her bed rest ended, and she began socializing with her former schoolfriends, who were now university students and involved in student politics. She joined the Mexican Communist Party (PCM) and met political activists and artists such as Julio Antonio Mella and photographer Tina Modotti. At one of Modotti's parties in June 1928, Kahlo was introduced to Diego Rivera. They had met briefly in 1922 when he was painting a mural at her school. Shortly after their 1928 introduction, Kahlo asked Rivera to judge whether her paintings showed enough talent for her to pursue a career as an artist. Rivera recalled being impressed by her work, stating it demonstrated "an unusual energy of expression, precise delineation of character, and true severity... They had a fundamental plastic honesty, and an artistic personality of their own... It was obvious to me that this girl was an authentic artist." Kahlo soon began a relationship with Rivera, who was 21 years her senior and had two common-law wives. They were married in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Coyoacán on 21 August 1929. Her mother opposed the marriage, referring to it as a "marriage between an elephant and a dove," a comment based on Rivera's size and Kahlo's fragility; her father approved, as Rivera was wealthy and could support Kahlo, who could not work and required expensive medical treatment. The wedding was reported by Mexican and international press, and the couple became the subject of constant media attention, referred to simply as "Diego and Frida." In late 1929, Kahlo and Rivera moved to Cuernavaca in Morelos, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Palace of Cortés. Around the same time, she resigned from the PCM in support of Rivera, who had been expelled shortly before the marriage for supporting the leftist opposition within the Third International. During the civil war in Morelos, life in Cuernavaca deepened Kahlo's sense of Mexican identity and history. Like many other Mexican women artists and intellectuals, she began wearing traditional Indigenous Mexican peasant clothing to emphasize her mestiza ancestry: long colorful skirts, huipils, rebozos, elaborate headdresses, and jewelry. She especially favored the dress of women from the matriarchal society of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which represented an authentic Indigenous Mexican cultural heritage in post-revolutionary Mexico. The Tehuana outfit allowed her to express her feminist and anti-colonialist ideals. After Rivera completed the commission in late 1930, he and Kahlo moved to San Francisco, where he painted murals for the Luncheon Club of the San Francisco Stock Exchange and the California School of Fine Arts. The couple was "feted, lionized, and spoiled" by influential collectors and clients. Her long love affair with Hungarian-American photographer Nickolas Muray likely began around this time. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico for the summer of 1931 and traveled to New York in the fall for the opening of Rivera's retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). In April 1932, they headed to Detroit, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Detroit Institute of Arts. By this time, Kahlo had become bolder in her interactions with the press, impressing journalists with her fluency in English and stating on her arrival that she was the greater artist of the two. "Of course he [Rivera] does well for a little boy, but it is I who am the big artist," she said in an interview with the Detroit News in February 1933. The year in Detroit was difficult for Kahlo. Although she enjoyed San Francisco and New York, she disliked aspects of American society, which she viewed as colonialist, and found most Americans "boring." She disliked socializing with capitalists such as Henry and Edsel Ford and was angered that many Detroit hotels refused to accept Jewish guests. In a letter to a friend, she wrote that although she was interested in U.S. industrial development, she felt "a bit of a rage against all the rich guys here, since I have seen thousands of people in the most terrible misery without anything to eat and with no place to sleep, that is what has most impressed me here, it is terrifying to see the rich having parties day and night while thousands and thousands of people are dying of hunger." Kahlo's time in Detroit was also complicated by a pregnancy. Her doctor agreed to perform an abortion, but the medication was ineffective. Kahlo had previously undergone an abortion in her marriage to Rivera and was deeply ambivalent about having a child. After the failed abortion, she reluctantly agreed to continue the pregnancy, but miscarried in July, which caused a serious hemorrhage requiring two weeks in the hospital. Less than three months later, her mother died from complications of surgery in Mexico. Kahlo and Rivera returned to New York in March 1933, as Rivera had been commissioned to paint a mural for the Rockefeller Center. During this time, she worked on only one painting, My Dress Hangs There (1933), and gave further interviews to the American press. In May, Rivera was fired from the Rockefeller Center project and hired to paint a mural for the New Workers School. Although Rivera wanted to stay in the U.S., Kahlo was homesick, and they returned to Mexico soon after the mural's unveiling in December 1933. Back in Mexico City, Kahlo and Rivera moved into a new house in the wealthy neighborhood of San Ángel, commissioned by Juan O'Gorman, a student of Le Corbusier. The house consisted of two sections joined by a bridge; Kahlo's was painted blue and Rivera's pink and white. The bohemian residence became a key meeting place for artists and political activists from Mexico and abroad. Kahlo experienced further health problems—undergoing an appendectomy, two abortions, and the amputation of gangrenous toes—and her marriage to Rivera became strained. He was unhappy to be back in Mexico and blamed Kahlo for their return. Although he had been unfaithful before, he now began an affair with her younger sister Cristina, which deeply hurt Kahlo. After discovering the affair in early 1935, she moved to an apartment in central Mexico City and considered divorcing him. She also had an affair with American artist Isamu Noguchi. Kahlo was reconciled with Rivera and Cristina later in 1935 and moved back to San Ángel. She became a loving aunt to Cristina's children, Isolda and Antonio. Despite the reconciliation, both Rivera and Kahlo continued their infidelities. In 1936, she resumed her political activities, joining the Fourth International and becoming a founding member of a solidarity committee to aid Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. She and Rivera successfully petitioned the Mexican government to grant asylum to Leon Trotsky and offered La Casa Azul as a residence for him and his wife Natalia Sedova. The couple lived there from January 1937 until April 1939, during which time Kahlo and Trotsky became good friends and had a brief affair. Kahlo painted Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky in 1937, including a written inscription to Trotsky in the painting on a letter that her figure holds. After opening an exhibition in Paris, Kahlo sailed back to New York. She was eager to reunite with Muray, but he ended their affair, as he had met another woman he planned to marry. Kahlo returned to Mexico City, where Rivera requested a divorce from her. The exact reasons are unknown, but Rivera stated publicly it was merely a "matter of legal convenience in the style of modern times... there are no sentimental, artistic, or economic reasons." According to their friends, the divorce was mainly due to their mutual infidelities. They were granted a divorce in November 1939, but remained friendly; she continued to manage his finances and correspondence. Following her separation from Rivera, Kahlo moved back to La Casa Azul and, determined to earn her own living, began another productive period as an artist, inspired by her experiences abroad. Encouraged by growing recognition, she moved from using small tin sheets since 1932 to large canvases, which were easier to exhibit. She adopted a more sophisticated technique, limited graphic details, and began producing more quarter-length portraits, which were easier to sell. She painted several of her most famous works during this period, including The Two Fridas (1939), Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair (1940), The Wounded Table (1940), and Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940). Three exhibitions featured her work in 1940: the fourth International Surrealist Exhibition in Mexico City, the Golden Gate International Exposition in San Francisco, and Twenty Centuries of Mexican Art at MoMA in New York. On 21 August 1940, Trotsky was assassinated in Coyoacán, where he had continued to live after leaving La Casa Azul. Kahlo was briefly suspected of involvement, as she knew the murderer, and was arrested and held for two days with her sister Cristina. The following month, Kahlo traveled to San Francisco for medical treatment for back pain and a fungal infection on her hand. Her continuously fragile health had declined since her divorce and worsened due to heavy alcohol consumption. Rivera was also in San Francisco after fleeing Mexico City following Trotsky's murder and accepted a commission. Although Kahlo had a relationship with art dealer Heinz Berggruen during her visit, she and Rivera were reconciled. They remarried in a simple civil ceremony on 8 December 1940. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico soon after. The union was less turbulent than before for its first five years. Both were more independent; while La Casa Azul was their primary residence, Rivera retained the San Ángel house as his studio and second apartment. Both continued having extramarital affairs; Kahlo had affairs with both men and women, with evidence suggesting her male lovers were more important to her than her female lovers. Despite medical treatment in San Francisco, Kahlo's health problems persisted throughout the 1940s. Due to spinal issues, she wore twenty-eight separate supportive corsets, ranging from steel and leather to plaster, between 1940 and 1954. She experienced leg pain, a chronic hand infection, and was treated for syphilis. The death of her father in April 1941 plunged her into depression. Her ill health increasingly confined her to La Casa Azul, which became the center of her world. She enjoyed caring for the house and garden and was accompanied by friends, servants, and pets, including spider monkeys, Xoloitzcuintlis, and parrots. While gaining recognition in her home country, her health continued to decline. By the mid-1940s, her back had worsened to the point that she could no longer sit or stand continuously. In June 1945, she traveled to New York for an operation that fused a bone graft and steel support to her spine to straighten it. The operation was a failure. According to biographer Hayden Herrera, Kahlo sabotaged her recovery by not resting as required and by once physically reopening her wounds in a fit of anger. Her paintings from this period, such as The Broken Column (1944), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflect her declining health. In 1950, Kahlo spent most of the year in Hospital ABC in Mexico City, where she underwent a new spine bone graft surgery. The surgery caused a difficult infection and required several follow-up procedures. After discharge, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches to move. During these final years, Kahlo dedicated her time to political causes as her health allowed. She had rejoined the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigned for peace, such as by collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. Kahlo's right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene in August 1953. She became severely depressed and anxious, and her dependence on painkillers escalated. When Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. She wrote in her diary in February 1954, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that."
