After discharge, she was largely confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches for mobility. During her final years, she remained active in political causes, rejoining the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigning for peace, including collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. In August 1953, her right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene, leading to severe depression and anxiety, with her reliance on painkillers increasing significantly. When Diego Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. In her diary from February 1954, she wrote, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that he would miss me... But never in my life have I suffered more. I will wait a while." In her last days, she was mostly bedridden with bronchopneumonia but made a public appearance on 2 July 1954, participating with Rivera in a demonstration against the CIA invasion of Guatemala. She anticipated her death, speaking about it to visitors and drawing skeletons and angels in her diary, with the last drawing being a black angel interpreted by biographer Hayden Herrera as the Angel of Death. Her final words were "Espero Alegre la Salida – y Espero no Volver jamás" ("I joyfully await the exit – and I hope never to return – Frida"). The demonstration worsened her illness, and on the night of 12 July 1954, she developed a high fever and extreme pain. At approximately 6 a.m. on 13 July 1954, her nurse found her dead in bed; she was 47 years old. The official cause of death was pulmonary embolism, though no autopsy was performed. Herrera has argued that Kahlo committed suicide, and the nurse reported that Kahlo had taken eleven painkillers that night, exceeding her prescribed maximum of seven. That evening, she had also given Rivera a wedding anniversary gift over a month in advance. On the evening of 13 July, Kahlo's body was taken to the Palacio de Bellas Artes, where it lay in state under a Communist flag. The following day, it was carried to the Panteón Civil de Dolores for an informal funeral attended by friends and family, with hundreds of admirers outside. In accordance with her wishes, she was cremated in a spectacular manner, with legend stating that mourners saw her hair catch fire, her corpse sit up, and her face form a final seductive grin. Rivera, who described her death as "the most tragic day of my life," died in 1957. Kahlo's ashes are displayed in a pre-Columbian urn at La Casa Azul, which opened as a museum in 1958. In the twenty-first century, Frida has become both a commercial icon and a symbol for various groups, including feminists, the LGBTQ community, and Chicanos, with the term "Fridamania" coined to describe her widespread appeal. The Tate Modern considers her "one of the most significant artists of the twentieth century," and art historian Elizabeth Bakewell calls her "one of Mexico's most important twentieth-century figures." Her reputation as an artist developed late in life and grew posthumously, as during her lifetime she was primarily known as Diego Rivera’s wife and an eccentric in the international cultural elite. Recognition increased in the late 1970s due to feminist scholars challenging the exclusion of female and non-Western artists from art history and the Chicano Movement elevating her as an icon. The first two books about Kahlo were published in Mexico in 1976 and 1977 by Teresa del Conde and Raquel Tibol, and in 1977, The Tree of Hope Stands Firm (1944) became the first Kahlo painting sold in an auction, netting $19,000 at Sotheby's. The first two retrospectives of her work were held in 1978, one at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City and another at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. A joint retrospective of her paintings and Tina Modotti’s photographs at the Whitechapel Gallery in London, curated by Peter Wollen and Laura Mulvey, opened in May 1982 and traveled to Sweden, Germany, the United States, and Mexico. The 1983 publication of Hayden Herrera’s biography Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo became an international bestseller. By 1984, Mexico declared her works part of national cultural heritage, prohibiting their export. As a result, her paintings rarely appear in international auctions, and comprehensive retrospectives are rare. Nevertheless, her works have broken records for Latin American art: in 1990, Diego and I was auctioned for $1,430,000, making her the first Latin American artist to exceed one million dollars; in 2006, Roots (1943) sold for $5.6 million; and in 2016, Two Nudes in a Forest (1939) sold for $8 million. Her popularity has led to the term "Fridamania," and she is considered "one of the most instantly recognizable artists," with her image used as frequently as those of Che Guevara or Bob Marley. Her life and art have inspired a wide range of merchandise and fashion. A biopic, Julie Taymor’s Frida, released in 2002, starred Salma Hayek (who co-produced it), grossed $56 million worldwide, and earned six Academy Award nominations, winning for Best Makeup and Best Original Score. The 2017 Disney-Pixar film Coco features a fictionalized Kahlo as a supporting character, voiced by Natalia Cordova-Buckley. Her appeal stems from a fascination with her painful and tragic life story, and she is seen as a symbol of non-conformity and a "cultural minority," simultaneously a victim and a survivor. Scholars note that her popularity is tied to the sharing of pain as a means of finding dignity and hope in modern society. Kirk Varnedoe stated that Kahlo resonates with contemporary sensibilities due to her self-obsession, creation of a personal world, and constant redefinition of identity—qualities shared by artists like Cindy Sherman and Kiki Smith and popular figures like Madonna. However, critics argue that her life has been mythologized, with dramatic elements overshadowing her art and reducing her works to literal depictions of her biography. Stephanie Mencimer notes that Kahlo has been embraced as a symbol for every politically correct cause and that, like a game of telephone, her story has been distorted, omitting uncomfortable details that reveal her complexity and flaws. This elevation of her life over her art diminishes understanding of her historical significance and obscures deeper truths in her work. Critics also warn that by sanitizing her biography, her image is set up for eventual decline, as is typical of women artists. Baddeley compares interest in Kahlo to that in Vincent van Gogh, noting that while Van Gogh is associated with his paintings, Kahlo is recognized through an image of herself—an observation on how male and female artists are perceived. Peter Wollen draws a parallel between Kahlo’s cult following and that of Sylvia Plath, whose complex art has been overshadowed by a simplified focus on her life. Kahlo’s legacy is commemorated through La Casa Azul, opened in 1958 and visited by about 25,000 people monthly, and Casa Roja (Museo Casa Kahlo), which focuses on her family. In 1985, Mexico City dedicated Parque Frida Kahlo in Coyoacán, featuring a bronze statue. In 2001, she became the first Hispanic woman honored with a U.S. postage stamp, and in 2012, she was inducted into the Legacy Walk in Chicago. In 2007 and 2010, commemorations were held on the centenary of her birth and the birthyear she attested to, including the Bank of Mexico releasing a $500-peso note featuring her painting Love's Embrace of the Universe, Earth, (Mexico), I, Diego, and Mr. Xólotl (1949) on the reverse and Diego Rivera on the front. A major retrospective at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 2007 attracted approximately 75,000 visitors. Her influence extends to various artistic fields: Paul Leduc released a biopic in 1984, and she is the protagonist of novels by Barbara Mujica (2001), Slavenka Drakulic (2008), and Barbara Kingsolver (2009). James Newton released an album titled Suite for Frida Kahlo in 1994, Michael Marra wrote a song titled "Frida Kahlo's Visit to the Taybridge Bar," and in 2017, Monica Brown and John Parra published a children's book, Frida Kahlo and her Animalitos. In 1996 and 2005, the Mexican Cultural Institute in Washington, DC hosted "Homage to Frida Kahlo" exhibitions showcasing global artists’ works inspired by her. Notable artists such as Marina Abramovic, Alana Archer, Gabriela Gonzalez Dellosso, Yasumasa Morimura, Cris Melo, and Rupert Garcia have used or appropriated her imagery. Kahlo has also been the subject of stage performances, including Annabelle Lopez Ochoa’s one-act ballet Broken Wings (2016), with Tamara Rojo as the lead, and a full-length version, Frida, premiered in 2020 by Dutch National Ballet with Maia Makhateli as Kahlo. Three operas have been composed about her: Robert Xavier Rodriguez’s Frida (1991), Kalevi Aho’s Frida y Diego (2014), and Gabriela Lena Frank’s El último sueño de Frida y Diego (2022). She is the main character in plays such as Dolores C. Sendler’s Goodbye, My Friduchita (1999), Robert Lepage and Sophie Faucher’s La Casa Azul (2002), Humberto Robles’ Frida Kahlo: Viva la vida! (2009), and Rita Ortez Provost’s Tree of Hope (2014). In 2018, Mattel released seventeen new Barbie dolls for International Women’s Day, including one of Kahlo, which drew criticism for its slim waist and missing unibrow. In 2014, she was honored in the Rainbow Honor Walk in San Francisco’s Castro neighborhood. In 2018, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors unanimously renamed Phelan Avenue to Frida Kahlo Way, which is located near City College of San Francisco and Archbishop Riordan High School. In 2019, Rafael Blanco painted a temporary mural titled “Frida Kahlo” that won third place at the Reno Mural Festival. Also in 2019, Frida’s “Fantasmones Siniestros” (“Sinister Ghosts”) was burned to ashes, publicizing an Ethereum NFT. Time created 89 covers to celebrate women of the year from 1920 onward, selecting Kahlo for 1938. In 2022, as part of a collaboration with Centre Pompidou, Swatch released a watch based on The Frame.
From 1920, a selection was made; Kahlo was chosen in 1938.[317] In 2022, as part of a collaboration with Centre Pompidou, Swatch released a watch inspired by The Frame.[318][319]

Friedrich Wilhelm Ernst Paulus (23 September 1890 – 1 February 1957) was a German Generalfeldmarschall during World War II, best known for the surrender of the German 6th Army during the Battle of Stalingrad (July 1942 to February 1943). The battle ended in disaster for the Wehrmacht, with Soviet forces encircling the Germans within Stalingrad, resulting in the death or capture of most of the 265,000-strong 6th Army, their Axis allies, and collaborators. Paulus had fought in World War I in France and the Balkans, rising to captain by the war's end. After the armistice, he served in the Reichswehr as a brigade adjutant and was selected among 4,000 officers allowed to serve in the limited defensive army. He joined the 13th Infantry Regiment at Stuttgart and held various staff positions from 1921 to 1933, including guest lectures in Moscow during the 1920s as part of military cooperation between the Weimar Republic and the Soviet Union. In 1934–35, he briefly commanded a motorized battalion; in October 1935, he became chief of staff at Panzer Troop Command, overseeing the training of the Panzerwaffe. In February 1938, he was appointed chief of staff to General Heinz Guderian’s XVI Army Corps, where Guderian praised his intelligence and diligence but expressed doubts about his decisiveness and command experience. Paulus remained in that role until May 1939, when he was promoted to major general and became chief of staff for the German Tenth Army, which later became the Sixth Army. He saw action in the invasions of Poland and the Low Countries and was promoted to lieutenant general in August 1940. In November 1941, after Field Marshal Walter von Reichenau, his patron, was reassigned, Paulus was promoted to General der Panzertruppe and appointed commander of the Sixth Army, taking command on 20 January 1942, six days after Reichenau’s death. Paulus led the drive on Stalingrad, where his troops engaged in over three months of brutal urban warfare. In November 1942, during Operation Uranus, the Soviet Red Army launched a massive counter-offensive that surrounded the 6th Army. Paulus refused to request evacuation and followed Hitler’s orders to hold Stalingrad at all costs. Operation Winter Storm, a relief effort by Army Group Don under Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, was launched in December, but Paulus was not given permission to break out, and Manstein’s forces failed to reach Stalingrad due to Soviet offensives elsewhere. Kurt Zeitzler eventually convinced Hitler to allow a breakout, provided Paulus continued to hold Stalingrad—an impossible task. For two months, Paulus and his forces fought on, but the lack of food, ammunition, and deteriorating conditions gradually weakened the defense. On 7 January 1943, General Konstantin Rokossovsky offered surrender terms, including normal rations, medical care, and retention of badges and uniforms. Paulus requested permission from Hitler to surrender, but the High Command rejected the request, stating that holding out helped the entire front. On 25 January, after the Soviets overran the last airstrip, Paulus again requested permission, emphasizing that his men were without food or ammunition, with 18,000 wounded, and that collapse was inevitable. Hitler rejected the request once more and ordered Paulus to hold Stalingrad to the death. On 30 January, Paulus informed Hitler that his forces were only hours from collapse. Hitler responded by promoting Paulus to field marshal, noting there was no precedent of a German field marshal being captured alive, implying Paulus must commit suicide. On 31 January 1943, Paulus and his staff surrendered. According to Colonel Wilhelm Adam’s diary, Paulus read the promotion order and said, “One can't help feeling it's an invitation to suicide. However I'm not going to do them such a favour,” before learning that Soviet forces were at the door. He recorded his new rank in official documents, stamped them with the seal, and threw the seal into a fire. The Soviet general informed Paulus that they would take him to the rear at 9:00, and he was transported in his personal car. The surrender marked the end of the 6th Army’s resistance. On 2 February 1943, the remainder of the army formally capitulated. Hitler was enraged by the surrender, vowing never to appoint another field marshal, though he later appointed seven more during the war’s final years. Hitler claimed that 18,000 to 20,000 Germans committed suicide annually in peacetime, and questioned how Paulus could surrender when 50,000 to 60,000 soldiers had died defending Stalingrad. Paulus, a Roman Catholic, opposed suicide and told General Max Pfeffer, “I have no intention of shooting myself for this Bohemian corporal,” and forbade his soldiers from standing on their trenches to be shot. Before surrendering, he sent his wedding ring back to his wife, who died in 1949 while he remained in captivity. Initially refusing to collaborate with the Soviets, Paulus became a vocal critic of the Nazi regime after the July 1944 assassination attempt, joining the Soviet-sponsored National Committee for a Free Germany. As a result, his wife and daughter Olga von Kutzschenbach were placed under Sippenhaft. He later served as a witness for the prosecution at the Nuremberg Trials. In 1953, he moved to East Germany, where he worked in military history research and lived in Dresden. At the Nuremberg Trials, when asked about the Stalingrad prisoners, he told a journalist to inform the wives and mothers that their husbands and sons were well. However, of the 100,000 German prisoners taken at Stalingrad, half died during the march to Siberian camps, nearly as many died in captivity, and only about 6,000 survived and returned home. In a 1954 talk in Berlin titled "On the vital issues of our nation," Paulus honored General Heinz Guderian, whom he had served with as chief of staff for the armored forces, and criticized the political leadership of the German Empire and Nazi Germany for causing military defeats in both world wars. He noted that Germany had great military experts like Clausewitz, Moltke the Elder, and Schlieffen, who assessed the political-military situation with sobriety, but that even the best army fails when ordered to perform impossible tasks. He also criticized U.S. foreign policy as aggressive and called for reconciliation between Germany and France, stating that German-French relations must be resolved to prevent the U.S. from using the conflict between the two nations as a tool of dominance.

American policy is described as "power politics," a concept that deeply affects Germans, who have experienced the consequences of pursuing aggressive, forceful strategies that prioritize national strength at the expense of others. Germans have learned from the 20th century that such policies inevitably fail unless they suppress the national will and independence of other peoples. The idea that the age of nations has ended because the United States relies on such dominance is a misconception and dangerous. Establishing positive neighborly relations with neighboring countries, especially France, is essential for Germany's national survival. The old enmity and disputes between Germany and France must be permanently resolved, as their relationship is a key link in the American strategy of dividing European nations and using them as tools for U.S. policy. Former Chancellor Heinrich Brüning advocated for improved relations between West Germany and the Eastern Bloc, criticizing West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's pro-American stance and opposing the EDC and Bonn conventions. Brüning supported negotiating with the East whenever possible, and another prominent German politician agreed that final implementation of the EDC agreement would be harmful to the German nation, arguing that no reasonable person can understand why Adenauer, under American influence, resists opportunities for economic and cultural engagement with Eastern peoples. As a former military officer and sector commander, based on his experiences, Paulus concluded that Germany must pursue any path leading to strengthened East-West relations. He emphasized that focusing on German unity, independence, and the affirmation of national rights best serves peace, international détente, and reconciliation. Good relations with other nations that respect Germany's rights are essential for European collective security and a prosperous future for Germany. A reunited Germany with balanced relations with the two major powers would ensure European peace and lay the foundation for general prosperity. From 1953 to 1956, Paulus lived in Dresden, East Germany, where he served as the civilian chief of the East German Military History Research Institute. In late 1956, he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and gradually became weaker. He died in Dresden on 1 February 1957, at the age of 66. According to his last will, his body was transported to Baden-Baden, West Germany, to be buried at the Hauptfriedhof next to his wife.

"Full Leather Jacket" is the 21st episode of the HBO original series The Sopranos and the eighth episode of the show's second season. It was written by Robin Green and Mitchell Burgess, directed by Allen Coulter, and originally aired on March 5, 2000. Meadow hopes to attend Berkeley, but her parents, Tony and Carmela, want to prevent it. Their neighbor, Jean Cusamano, has a sister, Joan O'Connell, who is a distinguished alumna of Georgetown University. Carmela persuades Jean to ask Joan to write a letter of recommendation for Meadow. Joan declines, but Carmela visits her, offers her a ricotta pie, and insists, "I want you to write that letter." Jean informs Carmela that the letter has been written, and Carmela requests a copy. Silvio and Paulie pressure Richie to build a wheelchair ramp for Beansie's house as partial reparation for crippling him. Richie refuses scornfully, but when he learns the request comes from Tony, he sends his nephew Vito Spatafore and his construction workers to fully adapt Beansie's house. Richie owns a leather jacket he obtained years ago from the feared mobster Rocco DiMeo. He gives it to Tony, who accepts it reluctantly but politely. Richie values the jacket and the act of giving it to Tony deeply. He is deeply offended when he sees it being worn by the husband of the Sopranos' maid. Adriana, embarrassed by Christopher in a restaurant, leaves him and returns to her mother's. Christopher goes to her, proposes marriage, and presents her with a ring. She says she loves him and the ring. In bed, he tells her, "I'm back on track, rededicating myself"—to her and to Tony. Matt and Sean continue working with Christopher, breaking into safes. After enduring various slights and snubs from members of the DiMeo family, they feel they are making no progress and decide to take drastic action. They ambush Christopher as he leaves a diner, believing this will earn them favor with Richie. Christopher is shot three times and left unconscious; Sean is killed. Matt flees and asks for Richie's protection; Richie, furious, chases him away. As Christopher lies comatose in the hospital, Tony asks, "How could this happen?" The episode's title is a play on the 1987 film Full Metal Jacket, whose title refers to full metal jacket bullets. Here, it alludes to the leather jacket that Richie gave to Tony. Additionally, after Christopher is shot, the camera pans the sidewalk showing the metal cartridge casings expelled from the weapons. Thematically, Matt and Sean ambushing Christopher to prove themselves to Richie reflects the killing of the Vietnamese sniper by Joker in the film Full Metal Jacket, which—on one level—can be seen as a reluctant act by Joker to prove himself to Animal Mother and the others. Richie is shown as being abusive of others around him in a manner similar to how Animal Mother abuses the other Lusthog Squad marines, who still rely on him for their safety. More generally, this episode is connected to the film referenced in its title through the theme of "loss of innocence." Gael García Bernal (Spanish: [ɡaˈel ɣaɾˈsi.a βeɾˈnal]; born 30 November 1978) is a Mexican actor and filmmaker known for his roles in films such as Amores perros (2000), Y tu mamá también (2001), Bad Education (2004), The Motorcycle Diaries (2004), Babel (2006), Coco (2017), Old (2021), Cassandro (2023), and Magellan (2025). On television, he played music conductor Rodrigo De Souza in the series Mozart in the Jungle (2014–2018) and starred as the titular character in the Disney+ special Werewolf by Night (2022). He was nominated for a BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role in 2005 for his portrayal of young Che Guevara in The Motorcycle Diaries and won his first Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Musical or Comedy in 2016 for Mozart in the Jungle. He co-founded the production company Canana Films with fellow actor Diego Luna in Mexico City. In 2016, Time magazine included him in its annual Time 100 list of the most influential people, and in 2020, The New York Times ranked him No. 25 in its list of the 25 Greatest Actors of the 21st Century. Born in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico, he is the son of Patricia Bernal, an actress and former model, and José Ángel García, an actor and director; his stepfather is Sergio Yazbek, whom his mother married when he was young. He began acting at age one and spent much of his teen years in telenovelas. García Bernal and Diego Luna were friends from childhood in Mexico City. At age fourteen, he taught indigenous people in Mexico to read, often working with the Huichol people; at fifteen, he participated in peaceful demonstrations supporting the Zapatista uprising of 1994. He studied philosophy at UNAM but took a sabbatical during a student strike to travel in Europe, later becoming the first Mexican accepted to study at the Central School of Speech and Drama in London and attending the European Graduate School for a master's in media and communication. After gaining success in telenovelas, Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu offered him a role in his debut feature, Amores perros (2000), which won critical acclaim and was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. His next role was in Alfonso Cuarón's Y tu mamá también (2001), which achieved crossover success in the U.S. and became the second-highest grossing Spanish-language film there. The following year, he portrayed Che Guevara in the 2002 TV miniseries Fidel and Father Amaro in the box-office record-breaking El crimen del Padre Amaro (2002). He reprised Che Guevara in The Motorcycle Diaries (2004), which broke the box office record set by Y tu mamá también three years earlier and earned him a BAFTA nomination in 2005. He also performed in theatre, including a 2005 production of Bodas de Sangre by Federico García Lorca at the Almeida Theatre in London. He has worked with acclaimed directors such as González Iñárritu, Pedro Almodóvar, Walter Salles, Alfonso Cuarón, Michel Gondry, and Iciar Bollaín, and has taken on English-language roles, including in Gondry's The Science of Sleep and The King, which received positive reviews. In 2007, he directed his first feature film, Déficit. He starred in the 2008 film Blindness, an adaptation of José Saramago's Nobel Prize-winning novel, where characters have no names or histories; director Fernando Meirelles noted that García Bernal focused on what his character wanted rather than their past. He again collaborated with Diego Luna in Rudo y Cursi, directed by Carlos Cuarón. The duo owns Canana Films, which recently partnered with Golden Phoenix Productions to produce television documentaries on the unsolved murders of over 300 women in Ciudad Juárez. In May 2010, he made a cameo as himself playing Cristiano Ronaldo in the Nike advertisement Write the Future. In 2010, he co-directed with Marc Siver four short films titled "Los Invisibles" for Amnesty International, focusing on Central American migrants in Mexico, their journey, risks, hopes, and contributions to Mexico, the U.S., and the world; he directed the films, conducted interviews, and narrated them. He starred in Even the Rain (2010), Spain's official entry for the 2011 Academy Awards. He narrated Human Planet for Hispanic audiences, which premiered on Discovery en Español on 25 April 2011 and aired on Discovery Channel in Latin America on 12 May. In 2014, he appeared in the American Spanish-language comedy film Casa de mi padre, opposite Will Ferrell, where he played a feared drug lord, marking his third collaboration with Diego Luna. He was also set to star in film adaptations of José Agustín's Ciudades Desiertas and Jon Stewart's directorial biopic Rosewater, in which he portrayed Maziar Bahari to critical acclaim, and was scheduled to appear in the 20th Century Fox reboot Zorro film Zorro Reborn, with a script by Glen Gers, Lee Shipman, and Brian McGeevy. In April 2014, he joined the main competition jury at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival. In June 2014, he began production on the dramatic comedy Zoom, directed by Pedro Morelli. In 2014, he was cast as Rodrigo de Souza in the Amazon Studios series Mozart in the Jungle, a role that earned him a Golden Globe in 2016. In 2016, he starred in two films submitted for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film: Desierto (Mexico) and Neruda (Chile). In 2017, he was named a member of the U.S. Dramatic Jury at the 2017 Sundance Film Festival and provided the voice of Héctor, a trickster protagonist, in the Pixar film Coco. He founded The Ambulante Documentary Film Festival, which brings documentary films to underserved areas, and helped create the Amnesty International series Los Invisibles; for this work, he received the Washington Office on Latin America's Human Rights Award in 2011. In October 2019, he and Diego Luna joined the Creative Advisory Board for EXILE Content alongside Adam Grant. In 2021, he starred in the M. Night Shyamalan thriller Old. In November 2021, he was cast in the Disney+ special Werewolf by Night by Marvel Studios. In 2024, he starred with Diego Luna in the Hulu original miniseries La Máquina. In 2025, he played Ferdinand Magellan in the historical drama Magellan, directed by Lav Diaz; the film is an international co-production between the Philippines, Spain, Portugal, Taiwan, and France and premiered at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival, being announced as the Philippines' official submission for Best International Feature Film at the 98th Academy Awards. García Bernal met Argentine actress Dolores Fonzi on the set of Private Lives in 2001; their son was born on 8 January 2009 in Madrid, Spain, and their daughter on 4 April 2011 in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He divides his time between Buenos Aires and Mexico City. He has been in a relationship with Mexican journalist Fernanda Aragonés since 2019 and had a child with her on 30 September 2021. He describes himself as "culturally Catholic but spiritually agnostic." He has received awards including the Ariel Award, BAFTA Awards, Cannes Film Festival recognition, Golden Globe Awards, and Goya Awards.

Gallium is a chemical element with the symbol Ga and atomic number 31. It was discovered by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in Paris, France, in 1875. Elemental gallium is a soft, silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure, and in its liquid state, it appears silvery white. When sufficient force is applied, solid gallium fractures conchoidally. Its melting point is 29.7646 °C (85.5763 °F; 302.9146 K), which is just above room temperature and approximately equal to average summer daytime temperatures in Earth's mid-latitudes. This melting point is used as a temperature reference point in the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90) established by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), and the triple point of gallium, 302.9166 K (29.7666 °C, 85.5799 °F), is preferred by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Gallium melts in a person's hands at normal human body temperature of 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) and has a strong tendency to supercool below its melting point; Ga nanoparticles can remain liquid below 90 K, and seeding with a crystal helps initiate freezing. Gallium is one of four non-radioactive metals (with caesium, rubidium, and mercury) that are liquid at or near room temperature; unlike mercury, it is neither highly reactive nor highly toxic and can be used in metal-in-glass high-temperature thermometers. It has one of the largest liquid ranges for a metal and a low vapor pressure at high temperatures. Its boiling point is 2676 K, nearly nine times higher than its melting point on the absolute scale, the greatest ratio between melting point and boiling point of any element. Liquid gallium wets glass and skin, as well as most other materials (except quartz, graphite, gallium(III) oxide, and PTFE), making it mechanically difficult to handle. Gallium's volume expands by 3.10% when it changes from liquid to solid, requiring care when storing it in containers that may rupture. It shares the higher-density liquid state with water, silicon, germanium, bismuth, and plutonium. Gallium does not occur as a free element in nature but is found in trace amounts as gallium(III) compounds in zinc ores like sphalerite and in bauxite. It is obtained by smelting and is a silvery blue metal that fractures conchoidally like glass. Gallium does not crystallize in simple crystal structures; its stable phase under normal conditions is orthorhombic with 8 atoms per conventional unit cell, where each atom has one nearest neighbor at 244 pm, and the remaining six neighbors are spaced at 27, 30, and 39 pm, grouped in pairs. The bonding between nearest neighbors is covalent, forming Ga₂ dimers, which explains its low melting point compared to aluminum and indium. This structure is similar to iodine and results from interactions between gallium's single 4p electrons, farther from the nucleus than the 4s electrons and the [Ar]3d¹⁰ core. In the liquid state, gallium exhibits a complex low-coordinated structure where each atom is surrounded by 10 others, rather than the 11–12 typical of most liquid metals. The physical properties of gallium are highly anisotropic, with significant differences between linear and volume thermal expansion coefficients, especially near the melting point, where the coefficient of thermal expansion increases by several hundred percent upon melting. Gallium has 30 known isotopes, ranging from mass number 60 to 89; only two are stable and occur naturally: gallium-69 (60.1% abundance) and gallium-71 (39.9% abundance). All other isotopes are radioactive; gallium-67 has the longest half-life at 3.2617 days. Isotopes lighter than gallium-69 decay via beta plus decay or electron capture to zinc isotopes, while those heavier than gallium-71 decay via beta minus decay to germanium isotopes; gallium-70 can decay to either zinc-70 or germanium-70. Gallium-67 and gallium-68 (half-life 67.84 minutes) are used in nuclear medicine imaging. Gallium primarily exists in the +3 oxidation state, with the +1 state found in some compounds, such as GaCl₂, which contains both gallium(I) and gallium(III) and can be formulated as GaIGaIIICl₄; the monochloride is unstable above 0 °C and disproportionates into elemental gallium and gallium(III) chloride. True gallium(II) compounds include GaS (formulated as Ga₂⁴⁺(S²⁻)₂) and Ga₂Cl₄(C₄H₈O₂)₂. Strong acids dissolve gallium, forming gallium(III) salts such as Ga(NO₃)₃, and aqueous solutions contain the hydrated ion [Ga(H₂O)₆]³⁺. Gallium(III) hydroxide, Ga(OH)₃, can be precipitated from gallium(III) solutions by adding ammonia and dehydrated at 100 °C to form gallium oxide hydroxide, GaO(OH). Alkaline hydroxide solutions dissolve gallium, forming gallate salts containing the Ga(OH)₄⁻ anion; gallium hydroxide, which is amphoteric, also dissolves in alkali to form gallate salts. Gallium reacts with chalcogens at high temperatures; at room temperature, it is unreactive with air and water due to a protective oxide layer, but at higher temperatures, it reacts with oxygen to form gallium(III) oxide, Ga₂O₃. Reducing Ga₂O₃ with elemental gallium at 500–700 °C yields dark brown gallium(I) oxide, Ga₂O, a strong reducing agent capable of reducing H₂SO₄ to H₂S, which disproportionates back to gallium and Ga₂O₃ at 800 °C. Gallium(III) sulfide, Ga₂S₃, has three crystal modifications and can be formed by reacting gallium with H₂S at 950 °C or Ga(OH)₃ at 747 °C. Reacting alkali metal carbonates and Ga₂O₃ with H₂S produces thiogallates containing the [Ga₂S₄]²⁻ anion, which decompose in strong acids to release H₂S; HgGa₂S₄ is used as a phosphor. Gallium also forms lower oxidation state sulfides, such as gallium(II) sulfide and green gallium(I) sulfide, produced by heating gallium(II) sulfide to 1000 °C under nitrogen. The binary chalcogenides Ga₂Se₃ and Ga₂Te₃ have the zincblende structure and are semiconductors but are easily hydrolyzed and have limited utility. Gallium reacts with ammonia at 1050 °C to form gallium nitride (GaN), and forms binary compounds with phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony: gallium phosphide (GaP), gallium arsenide (GaAs), and gallium antimonide (GaSb), all with the same structure as ZnS and important semiconducting properties. These compounds are synthesized by direct reaction of gallium with elemental phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony, or by reacting Ga₂O with phosphorus at low temperatures; GaP also exhibits higher electrical conductivity than GaN. Gallium forms ternary nitrides, such as examples with lithium and phosphorus or arsenic (e.g., Li₃GaP₂ and Li₃GaAs₂), which are easily hydrolyzed by dilute acids and water. Gallium(III) oxide reacts with fluorinating agents like HF or F₂ to form gallium(III) fluoride, GaF₃, an ionic compound insoluble in water but soluble in hydrofluoric acid, forming GaF₃·3H₂O; dehydration of this adduct forms GaF₂OH·nH₂O, and the adduct reacts with ammonia to form GaF₃·3NH₃, which can be heated to form anhydrous GaF₃. Gallium trichloride is formed by reacting gallium metal with chlorine gas and exists as dimeric molecules, Ga₂Cl₆, with a melting point of 78 °C; similar dimers exist with bromine and iodine. Like other group 13 trihalides, gallium(III) halides are Lewis acids, reacting with alkali metal halides to form salts with GaX⁻₄ anions and with alkyl halides to form carbocations and GaX⁻₄. When heated, gallium(III) halides react with elemental gallium to form gallium(I) halides; for example, GaCl₃ reacts with Ga to form GaCl. At lower temperatures, the equilibrium shifts back, and GaCl disproportionates into elemental gallium and GaCl₃. GaCl can also be produced by reacting gallium with HCl at 950 °C, yielding a red solid. Gallium(I) compounds are stabilized by forming adducts with Lewis acids; so-called "gallium(II) halides," GaX₂, are actually adducts with the structure Ga⁺[GaX₄]⁻. Gallium forms a hydride, GaH₃ (gallane), produced by reacting lithium gallium hydride (LiGaH₄) with gallium(III) chloride at −30 °C. In the presence of dimethyl ether, gallane polymerizes to (GaH₃)ₙ; without solvent, it forms dimer Ga₂H₆ (digallane), a gas with a structure similar to diborane, unlike α-AlH₃ where aluminum has a coordination number of 6. Gallane is unstable above −10 °C and decomposes into elemental gallium and hydrogen. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminum compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds; alkylgalliums are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, so organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers. They form stable peroxides and are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, being mobile and flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for organogallium compound synthesis, such as in carbogallation reactions, and reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaC.

Organoindium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds. Alkylgallium compounds are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, meaning organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers like organoaluminium compounds. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds and do form stable peroxides. These alkylgalliums are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, are mobile, and are flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for forming organogallium compounds, such as in carbogallation reactions; it reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaCp3. Gallium(I) forms complexes with arene ligands like hexamethylbenzene, which is bulky enough to give a half-sandwich structure [Ga(η6-C6Me6)]+, while less bulky ligands such as mesitylene allow two ligands to bind in a bent sandwich structure. Benzene, being even less bulky, allows dimer formation, as in [Ga(η6-C6H6)2][GaCl4]·3C6H6. In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev predicted the existence of gallium, naming it "eka-aluminium" and accurately forecasting its density, melting point, oxide character, and bonding in chloride. He predicted eka-aluminium would be discovered by spectroscope, would dissolve slowly in acids and alkalis, not react with air, that M2O3 would dissolve in acids to form MX3 salts, that eka-aluminium salts would form basic salts, that eka-aluminium sulfate would form alums, and that anhydrous MCl3 would be more volatile than ZnCl2—all of which were later confirmed. Gallium was discovered in 1875 by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran using spectroscopy from a sample of sphalerite, and he later obtained the free metal by electrolysis of its hydroxide in potassium hydroxide solution. He named the element "gallia" from Latin Gallia, meaning Gaul, his native region, and it was later speculated (though denied by Lecoq in 1877) that he named it after himself due to "le coq" (rooster) and "gallus" (rooster). De Boisbaudran initially measured gallium's density as 4.7 g/cm³, which did not match Mendeleev's prediction; Mendeleev suggested a remeasurement, which yielded the correct value of 5.9 g/cm³, exactly as predicted. From 1875 until the semiconductor era, gallium's primary uses were high-temperature thermometry and metal alloys with unusual stability or low melting points, some of which are liquid at room temperature. The development of gallium arsenide as a direct bandgap semiconductor in the 1960s marked the most significant stage in gallium's applications. In the late 1960s, the electronics industry began using gallium commercially for light-emitting diodes, photovoltaics, and semiconductors, while the metals industry used it to reduce alloy melting points. First blue gallium nitride LEDs were developed in 1971–1973 but were weak; only in the early 1990s did Shuji Nakamura combine GaN with indium gallium nitride to develop modern blue LEDs, now the basis of ubiquitous white LEDs, commercialized by Nichia in 1993. Nakamura and two other Japanese scientists received a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for this work. Global gallium production slowly increased from several tens of tons per year in the 1970s to about 100 t/yr by 2010 and rapidly accelerated, reaching approximately 450 t/yr by 2024. Gallium does not exist as a free element in Earth's crust; high-content minerals like gallite (CuGaS2) are too rare to serve as primary sources. Its crustal abundance is approximately 16.9 ppm, making it the 34th most abundant element, comparable to lead, cobalt, and niobium. Unlike these elements, gallium does not form its own ore deposits with concentrations above 0.1 wt.% and occurs at trace levels in zinc ores (~50 ppm) and slightly higher in aluminum ores, extracted as a by-product. This lack of enrichment is due to gallium's geochemical behavior. The USGS estimates over 1 million tons of gallium is contained in known bauxite and zinc ore reserves. Some coal flue dusts contain small amounts of gallium, typically less than 1% by weight, but these are not extractable without mining the host materials. Gallium is produced exclusively as a by-product during processing of bauxite and sulfidic zinc ores (mainly sphalerite), with minor amounts from coal. During the Bayer process, gallium accumulates in sodium hydroxide liquor and is extracted via methods such as ion-exchange resins; at a typical feed concentration of 50 ppm, about 15% of the gallium is extractable. The remainder goes to red mud and aluminum hydroxide streams. Gallium is removed from the resin in solution and then electrolyzed to produce gallium metal. For semiconductor use, it is further purified by zone melting or the Czochralski process, achieving purities of 99.9999% routinely and commercially. Gallium production is constrained by the annual extraction of bauxite, sulfidic zinc ores, and coal. Supply potential is defined as economically extractable amounts under current market conditions and includes at least 2,100 t/yr from bauxite, 85 t/yr from sulfidic zinc ores, and potentially 590 t/yr from coal—significantly exceeding current production of 375 t in 2016. The average price for low-grade gallium was $120 per kg in 2016 and $135–140 per kg in 2017. In 2017, world low-grade gallium production was about 315 tons, a 15% decrease from 2016. China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, and Ukraine were leading producers, while Germany ceased primary production in 2016. High-purity gallium production was about 180 tons in 2017, mostly from China, Japan, Slovakia, the UK, and the U.S. The 2017 annual production capacity was estimated at 730 tons for low-grade and 320 tons for refined gallium. China produced about 250 tons of low-grade gallium in 2016 and 300 tons in 2017, accounting for more than half of global LED production. As of July 2023, China produced between 80% and 95% of global gallium output. As of August 2023, China produced 80% of the world's gallium and 60% of germanium, and began restricting exports of both, key materials in the semiconductor industry, amid a "chip war" with the U.S. In 2024, China produced 98% of the world’s low-purity gallium (USGS). Semiconductor applications dominate commercial demand, accounting for 98% of total use, with 44% used in light fixtures and 36% in integrated circuits, and smaller shares in photovoltaics and magnets. Extremely high-purity gallium (>99.9999%) is commercially available for semiconductors. In 2007, gallium arsenide and gallium nitride in electronic components accounted for about 98% of U.S. gallium consumption, with 66% used in integrated circuits (mostly GaAs) for ultra-high-speed logic chips and MESFETs in cell phones, and 20% in optoelectronics. Worldwide, gallium arsenide makes up 95% of annual gallium consumption, valued at $7.5 billion in 2016, with 53% from cell phones, 27% from wireless communications, and the rest from automotive, consumer, fiber-optic, and military applications. The rise in GaAs consumption is linked to 3G and 4G smartphones, which use up to 10 times more GaAs than older models. Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride are used in optoelectronic devices with a market share of $15.3 billion in 2015 and $18.5 billion in 2016. Aluminium gallium arsenide is used in high-power infrared laser diodes, while gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride are used in blue and violet optoelectronic devices, such as laser diodes and LEDs. For example, gallium nitride 405 nm diode lasers are used as violet light sources in higher-density Blu-ray Disc drives. Other major applications of gallium nitride include cable television, wireless infrastructure, power electronics, and satellites. The GaN radio frequency device market was estimated at $370 million in 2016 and $420 million in 2016. Multijunction photovoltaic cells for satellite power use molecular-beam or metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy of gallium arsenide, indium gallium phosphide, or indium gallium arsenide; the Mars Exploration Rovers and several satellites use triple-junction gallium arsenide on germanium cells. Gallium is also a component in photovoltaic compounds like copper indium gallium selenium sulfide (Cu(In,Ga)(Se,S)2), used in solar panels as a cost-efficient alternative to crystalline silicon. Gallium readily alloys with most metals and is used in low-melting alloys. The nearly eutectic alloy of gallium, indium, and tin is a room-temperature liquid used in medical thermometers, known as Galinstan (with "-stan" referring to tin), having a melting point of −19 °C (−2.2 °F). This alloy is used to cool computer chips and as a thermal paste replacement in high-performance computing. Gallium alloys have been evaluated as substitutes for mercury dental amalgams but have not gained wide acceptance. Liquid gallium-indium alloys have been found to precipitate gaseous CO2 into solid carbon and are being researched for carbon capture and removal. Due to high surface tension and deformability, gallium-based liquid metals can be used to create actuators by controlling surface tension, with potential applications in artificial muscle for robotic actuation. Plutonium in nuclear weapon pits is stabilized in the δ phase and made machinable by alloying with gallium. Although gallium has no biological function, gallium ions behave like iron(III) in the body and are used in pharmaceuticals and radiopharmaceuticals. Interest in gallium's anticancer properties arose when 67Ga(III) citrate localized to tumor sites in animals. Clinical trials show gallium nitrate has antineoplastic activity against non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and urothelial cancers. New gallium-ligand complexes such as tris(8-quinolinolato)gallium(III) (KP46) and gallium maltolate are under development. Gallium nitrate (brand name Ganite) is used intravenously to treat hypercalcemia from bone tumor metastasis by interfering with osteoclast function. Gallium maltolate, an oral, highly absorbable gallium(III) ion, is anti-proliferative to cancer and some bacteria that take it instead of ferric iron (Fe3+), and is being tested for cancer, infectious, and inflammatory diseases. When gallium ions replace iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active while gallium is not. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound MR045 is selectively toxic to chloroquine-resistant malaria parasites by inhibiting hemozoin crystallization. Gallium-67 salts such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate are used as radiopharmaceuticals in gallium scans, where the radioactive isotope 67Ga is used and the gallium compound is unimportant. The body handles Ga3+ as if it were iron(III).

Ferric iron (Fe³⁺) is a key component in biological respiration, and researchers are investigating a compound containing gallium in clinical and preclinical trials for treating cancers, infectious diseases, and inflammatory conditions. When gallium ions substitute for iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active and facilitates electron transfer, whereas gallium is redox-inactive, leading to bacterial death. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound, MR045, is selectively toxic to malaria parasites resistant to chloroquine, as both compounds inhibit the crystallization of hemozoin, a byproduct of blood digestion in parasites. Gallium-67 salts, such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate, are used in nuclear medicine imaging (gallium scan) where the radioactive isotope ⁶⁷Ga is employed; the specific gallium compound is unimportant because Ga³⁺ behaves like Fe³⁺ in the body, concentrating in areas of inflammation or rapid cell division, enabling imaging of these sites. Gallium-68, a positron emitter with a half-life of 68 minutes, is used in PET-CT diagnostics when linked to pharmaceuticals like DOTATOC (for neuroendocrine tumors) and DOTA-TATE (for neuroendocrine metastasis and lung neuroendocrine cancers, including certain microcytomas); it is produced via chemical extraction from germanium-68 in gallium-68 generators. Gallium is used in neutrino detection, notably in the SAGE experiment at the Baksan Neutrino Observatory in Russia, which contains 55–57 tonnes of liquid gallium, and in the earlier GALLEX experiment in Italy, which used 12.2 tons of watered gallium-71; solar neutrinos caused a few ⁷¹Ga atoms to become radioactive ⁷¹Ge, detected in the experiment, revealing a 40% deficit in solar neutrino flux compared to theory—later explained by improved detectors and theories (e.g., SNO). Gallium serves as a liquid metal ion source in focused ion beams, such as in creating the world's smallest book, Teeny Ted from Turnip Town. It is also an additive in glide wax for skis and low-friction materials. Materials scientists consider gallium promising for flexible and wearable electronics. Gallium disrupts the protective oxide layer on aluminum, enabling water to react with aluminum in AlGa to produce hydrogen gas. A common chemist joke involves using gallium spoons to serve tea, as gallium resembles aluminum in appearance, and the spoons melt in hot tea. Advances in trace element analysis have detected dissolved gallium in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, with concentrations in the Beaufort Sea recently reported; typical dissolved gallium levels in the Pacific at depths <~150 m are 4–6 pmol/kg, while in the Atlantic at depths >~350 m, they are 25–28 pmol/kg. Gallium enters oceans primarily via aeolian input and is geochemically similar to aluminum, being less reactive; due to its similar dissolved profile and longer surface water residence time, gallium acts as a tracer for aluminum and for aeolian inputs of iron, particularly in the northwest Pacific, south and central Atlantic Oceans; for instance, low gallium surface waters in the subpolar northwest Pacific suggest low dust input, explaining high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll conditions. Metallic gallium is not toxic, but several gallium compounds are; gallium halide complexes are toxic, and the Ga³⁺ ion in soluble gallium salts forms an insoluble hydroxide when injected in large doses, causing nephrotoxicity in animals; at lower doses, soluble gallium is well-tolerated, does not accumulate, and is excreted mainly through urine in two phases: a first phase with a biological half-life of 1 hour and a second phase with a half-life of 25 hours. Inhaled Ga₂O₃ particles are likely toxic.

Gang Chen, born in China and known in Chinese as 陈刚 (pinyin: Chén Gāng), is a Chinese-born American mechanical engineer and nanotechnologist. At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), he holds the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering position and served as head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering from July 2013 to June 2018. He directs the Solid-State Solar-Thermal Energy Conversion Center, an energy frontier research center previously funded by the United States Department of Energy. Chen was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2010 and to the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering in 1984 and a Master of Engineering in 1987, both in power engineering, from the Huazhong University of Science and Technology, and a Doctor of Philosophy in mechanical engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1993. He worked as an assistant professor at Duke University from 1993 to 1997 and as a tenured associate professor at the University of California, Los Angeles from 1996 to 2001 before joining MIT in 2001. Chen has made significant contributions to thermoelectricity, nanotechnology, and thermal engineering. In 2022, he and colleagues discovered that cubic boron arsenide is a highly effective semiconductor with potential applications in electronics. He has received the K.C. Wong Education Foundation fellowship and the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation fellowship (2002–2003), the NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award (2008), and the ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award (2008). He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. In 2010, he was elected to the National Academy of Engineering for contributions to heat transfer at the nanoscale and thermoelectric energy conversion technology; in 2014, he was elected an academician of Academia Sinica in the Division of Engineering Science and received the Nukiyama Memorial Award of the Heat Transfer Society of Japan. He was elected a Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in April 2018 and of the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. On January 14, 2021, Chen was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and charged under the now-abolished China Initiative for allegedly failing to disclose connections to several Chinese educational programs in a U.S. Department of Energy grant application and for omissions in IRS filings, including allegations of wire fraud, failure to file a foreign bank account report (FBAR), and false statements on tax returns. The wire fraud charge stemmed from alleged omissions in an electronically submitted federal grant proposal form (Current and pending support). The FBI documents alleged that Chen received $19 million from China's Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech). In response, MIT President L. Rafael Reif stated the news was "surprising, deeply distressing and hard to understand," and on January 21, 2021, over 100 MIT faculty signed a letter protesting Chen's arrest, citing "deeply flawed and misleading statements" and ending with "we are all Gang Chen," which was shared on Twitter. On January 22, 2021, MIT's president clarified that the funds went to MIT, not Chen, to support a departmental research collaboration with SUSTech that Chen directed on MIT's behalf. The charges provoked widespread criticism, with many MIT faculty joining the protest, stating the defense of Chen was the defense of the scientific enterprise. Bloomberg noted that U.S. science has historically flourished by attracting international talent, and an MIT researcher stated the Department of Justice's China Initiative fundamentally misunderstands research and international collaboration. On January 14, 2022, the Wall Street Journal reported that federal prosecutors recommended dropping the charges, and the Washington Post reported that the DOE forms did not require Chen to disclose his connections to Chinese educational programs, undermining the basis of the charges. On January 20, 2022, federal prosecutors filed a motion to dismiss the charges "in the interests of justice," and the U.S. District Court dismissed the case. In a New York Times interview after his exoneration, Chen described the experience as "traumatic and deeply disillusioning" and stated, "I didn't do anything wrong." After the charges were filed, he was banned from the MIT campus and from contacting MIT employees, and his postdocs were moved to other labs. He lost his research group and funding and worked alone on other topics until the charges were dropped, after which he returned to his MIT office the day following the dismissal of the case.

PJSC Gazprom, a Russian majority state-owned multinational energy corporation headquartered in the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg, derives its name from the Russian phrase gazovaya promyshlennost (gas industry). In January 2022, Gazprom surpassed Sberbank to become the largest company in Russia by market capitalization. In 2023, the company reported a revenue of 8.5 trillion rubles, a significant drop from 11.7 trillion rubles in 2022. Gazprom is vertically integrated and operates in all segments of the gas industry, including exploration and production, refining, transport, distribution, marketing, and power generation. In 2018, it produced 497.6 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas and 15.9 million tonnes of gas condensate, accounting for 12% of global natural gas output. That year, Gazprom had proven reserves of 35.1 trillion cubic meters of gas and 1.6 billion tons of gas condensate. It exported gas via pipelines it builds and owns, such as Power of Siberia and TurkStream, producing 359 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas in 2018, a 13% decline from the prior year. Gazprom Neft, a subsidiary, produces about 41 million tons of oil with reserves of 2 billion tons. The company also holds stakes in finance, media, and aviation. Gazprom was established in 1989 when the Soviet Ministry of Gas Industry was converted into a corporation, becoming the first state-run corporate enterprise in the Soviet Union. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, Gazprom retained its Russian assets and secured a monopoly in the gas sector, while other national companies like Naftogaz and Turkmengaz took over assets abroad. In December 1992, following a presidential decree and government resolution, Gazprom became a joint-stock company and began distributing shares via vouchers, with 33% of shares acquired by the public by 1994 and 15% allocated to employees, while the state retained 40%, later reduced to 38%. Foreign ownership was limited to 9% until 1996, when 1% of equity was offered as Global Depository Receipts, and a $2.5 billion bond issue was launched in 1997. Under Viktor Chernomyrdin, who became Prime Minister in 1992, Gazprom evaded taxes, engaged in asset stripping, and shared assets with its executives and relatives, including the company Itera. Chernomyrdin was removed from office in 1998 and later became Gazprom's chairman. In 2000, Vladimir Putin, aiming to increase state control over key companies, replaced Chernomyrdin and Rem Viakhirev with Dmitry Medvedev and Alexei Miller, both of whom were Putin’s prior associates in Saint Petersburg. Miller and Medvedev were tasked with halting asset stripping and recovering losses, leading to Itera being denied access to Gazprom pipelines and nearly going bankrupt, with Itera eventually agreeing to return stolen assets in 2006. In April 2001, Gazprom acquired NTV, Russia’s only nationwide independent television station, from Vladimir Gusinsky’s Media-Most Holdings, after Gusinsky criticized the Kursk submarine disaster and the Second Chechen War and fled Russia. In June 2005, Gazprom subsidiaries sold a 10.7399% stake to Rosneftegaz for $7 billion, completing the sale by December 2005, which, combined with the state’s 38% share, gave the Russian government full control. The government then lifted the 20% foreign ownership cap, allowing foreign investment. In September 2005, Gazprom bought 72.633% of Sibneft for $13.01 billion, renaming it Gazprom Neft and using a $12 billion loan; the deal valued the company at £69.7 billion (US$123.2 billion) on the day of completion. In July 2006, the State Duma passed the On Gas Export law, granting Gazprom exclusive rights to export Russian natural gas. In December 2006, Gazprom signed an agreement with Royal Dutch Shell, Mitsui, and Mitsubishi to take a 50% plus one share stake in Sakhalin Energy. In June 2007, TNK-BP agreed to sell its stake in the Kovykta field to Gazprom after the Russian government questioned BP’s export rights. On 1 August 2007, Gazprom’s Sergey Kuprianov threatened Belarus with a 300% price increase on gas if debts were not paid, which was later resolved. On 23 June 2007, Russia and Italy signed a memorandum to build a 558-mile (900 km) South Stream pipeline to deliver 1.05 trillion cubic feet (30 km³) of gas annually to Europe, with a south fork to Italy and a north fork to Hungary. On 18 December 2007, Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Dmitry Medvedev signed an agreement with BASF to exploit a gas field, despite German academic warnings about overreliance on Russian gas. On 11 February 2008, Kuprianov threatened Ukraine with a gas flow halt, which was implemented in January 2009, beginning the 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas dispute. In December 2014, during a visit to Turkey, Putin announced the South Stream project would not proceed and instead committed to shipping 63 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/y) to Turkey, citing Bulgaria’s EU contract violations. In September 2012, the European Commission launched an anti-trust investigation into Gazprom, citing concerns about its dominant market position in upstream gas supply. In November 2013, Gazprom acquired Profmedia from Vladimir Potanin to expand its media interests. In May 2014, Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation signed a $400 billion contract for 38 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to China starting in 2018. Construction of the Power of Siberia pipeline began in August 2014 with pipe deliveries to Lensk, Yakutia, and gas supply to China began on 20 December 2019 as part of the energy pact; Beijing and Moscow are now negotiating a second Far Eastern gas pipeline. In June 2014, Gazprom negotiated a 24.9% stake in OMV with the Abu Dhabi-based IPIC. In July 2014, Gazprom acquired Central Partnership, one of Russia’s largest film distributors. In September 2015, Nord Stream 2 contracts were signed and the pipeline was commissioned by July 2021. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Gazprom’s export market shrank from 185 bcm in 2021 to 100 bcm in 2022 and further declined in 2023, leading to a revenue collapse and a 34% price increase in the domestic market over three years. Gazprom has also faced compensation claims for failing to supply gas under long-term contracts. In April 2025, Gazprom announced it would begin producing home appliances. In 2011, Gazprom produced 513.17 billion cubic meters of natural gas—17% of global output and 83% of Russian production—with Yamburg producing 41%, Urengoy 23.6%, Nadym 10.9%, Noyabrsk 9.3%, and others 15.2%. It also produced 32.28 million tons of oil and 12.07 million tons of gas condensate. The majority of Gazprom’s fields are in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region of Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug in Western Siberia, with the historically largest fields being Medvezhe, Urengoy, and Yamburg. After over two decades of production, these fields are in decline, with annual production dropping by 20 to 25 bcm. Production at Zaporliarnoe, Gazprom’s fourth-largest field, increased until 2004, offsetting the decline in others. Since 2004, Gazprom has maintained production by activating new smaller fields and purchasing assets from other companies. Gazprom Neft was acquired in 2005 for $13.1 billion, purchasing 75% of its shares. Gazprom’s domestic and reexport gas supply relies heavily on imports from Central Asia: 42.6 bcm from Turkmenistan, 8.5 bcm from Kazakhstan, and 9.6 bcm from Uzbekistan in 2007, with 75% of Turkmenistan’s gas exports purchased to supply Ukraine. In 2008, Gazprom paid $130/mcm to $180/mcm for Central Asian gas. In 2015, Gazprom’s proved and probable natural gas reserves were 23.705 trillion cubic meters (837.1 trillion cubic feet), a 3.8% increase from 2011, representing 18.4% of global reserves; crude oil reserves were 1.355 billion tons and gas condensate reserves were 933.3 billion tons. Of these, 59.8% of natural gas reserves (Categories A+B+C1) were in the Urals Federal District (decreasing), 20.5% in the Arctic shelf (increasing), and 8.3% in the Southern Federal District and North Caucasus Federal District. Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain supply. Nearly 37% of its reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and the Barents Sea. One of its major projects is the Blue Stream Pipeline, which delivers natural gas to Turkey via the Black Sea; the agreement was signed in 1997, the first joint was welded in 2000, and it transports 16 billion cubic meters annually. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found over 10 trillion cubic meters of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60% located in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated annual production capacity of 115 billion cubic meters (4.1 trillion cubic feet), with potential for increase.

Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain its supply. Nearly 37 percent of Gazprom's reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and in the Barents Sea. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found reserves of over 10 trillion cubic metres of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60 percent of these reserves in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated natural gas production capacity of 115 billion cubic metres per annum (4.1 trillion cubic feet per annum), with potential to increase to 140 billion cubic metres per annum (4.9 trillion cubic feet per annum). The Shtokman field, located 650 kilometres (400 mi) northeast of Murmansk and 1,000 kilometres (620 mi) west of the Yamal Peninsula in the central part of the Barents Sea, is estimated to contain up to 3.7 trillion cubic metres (130 trillion cubic feet) of gas, with potential production of 71 billion cubic metres per annum (2.5 trillion cubic feet per annum) in initial phases and up to 95 billion cubic metres per annum (3.4 trillion cubic feet per annum). Gazprom, TotalEnergies (France), and Statoil (Norway) formed Shtokman Development AG for the field's development. In 2013, in Amsterdam, Alexey Miller, chairman of Gazprom's management committee, and Jorma Ollila, chairman of Royal Dutch Shell's board, signed a memorandum outlining cooperation in Arctic shelf hydrocarbons exploration and development, in the presence of Putin and Mark Rutte. In 2008, Gazprom conducted 284.9 kilometres (177.0 mi) of explorative well drilling, 124,000 kilometres (77,000 mi) of 2D seismic, and 6,600 square kilometres (2,500 sq mi) of 3D seismic survey, resulting in a 583.4 billion cubic metre (20.60 trillion cubic feet) increase in gas reserves and a 61 million ton increase in crude oil and gas condensate reserves. Gazprom conducts prospecting in India, Pakistan, Algeria, Venezuela, Vietnam, Libya, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. Its Unified Gas Supply System (UGSS) includes 158,200 kilometres (98,300 mi) of gas trunklines and branches and 218 compressor stations with a 41.4 GW capacity, making it the world's largest gas transmission system; in 2008, it transported 714.3 billion cubic metres (25.23 trillion cubic feet) of gas, and Gazprom has claimed the UGSS has reached its capacity. Major transmission projects include Nord Stream pipelines and internal Russian pipelines. In 2021, Russia had two large LNG production plants, Yamal LNG and Sakhalin-2 LNG, both of which Gazprom has an interest in. In March 2021, the Russian Government authorized a long-term programme to develop and expand the LNG industry with nine additional LNG plants to meet the growing global LNG market. In August 2021, Russia's first LNG bunkering vessel, Dmitry Mendeleev, was completed for Gazprom. In October 2021, Gazprom and RusGazDobycha announced the construction of Baltic LNG at Ust-Luga, with access to the Baltic Sea for westward sea transportation, processing ethane-containing natural gas with a capacity of 13 million tons of LNG per year. In 2024, Gazprom faced a significant LNG tanker shortage, leading it to use the Marshal Vasilevskiy floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) for exporting LNG from its Portovaya facility, as its regular tankers like the Pskov were engaged in extended voyages to Asia, avoiding the Suez Canal and Red Sea due to Houthi attacks. In 2006, Gazprom sold 316 billion cubic metres (11.2 trillion cubic feet) to domestic customers, 162 billion cubic metres (5.7 trillion cubic feet) to Europe, and 101 billion cubic metres (3.6 trillion cubic feet) to CIS countries and the Baltic states; about 60 percent of its revenue came from European sales. In 2008, the average gas price for Russian industrial customers was $71/mcm, while households paid $54/mcm. Natural gas prices fluctuated since 2000; in late 2007, the NYMEX price was $7.53 per million Btu ($25.7/MWh), equivalent to $285 per 1,000 cubic metres, while German customers paid $250 per m3, Polish customers $290 per m3, Ukrainian customers $130 per m3, and Russian customers $49 per m3. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, due to falling export revenue, the domestic market is expected to see price increases of 34% by July 2025. Gazprom delivered gas to 25 European countries; its main export arm, Gazprom Export LLC (founded in 1973, previously known as Gazexport until November 1, 2006), holds a monopoly on gas exports to countries outside the former Soviet Union and sells most Russian gas in Europe under 25-year contracts. In late 2004, Gazprom was the sole gas supplier to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Estonia, Finland, Macedonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Slovakia, providing 97 percent of Bulgaria's gas, 89 percent of Hungary's, 86 percent of Poland's, nearly 75 percent of the Czech Republic's, 67 percent of Turkey's, 65 percent of Austria's, about 40 percent of Romania's, 36 percent of Germany's, 27 percent of Italy's, and 25 percent of France's gas. By December 2010, Italy's gas supply from Russia increased from 25 percent in 2004 to 70 percent with support from Alexander Medvedev and Antonio Fallico. In May 2006, the European Union received about 25 percent of its gas supply from Gazprom, and Gazprom entered several long-term gas contracts with European companies, with prices mainly linked to oil. In 2014, Europe accounted for 40% of Gazprom's revenue, and the proportion of gas bought in the spot market in Europe rose from 15 percent in 2008 to 44 percent in 2012. In September 2013, during the G20 summit, Gazprom signed an agreement with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to exclude the Henry Hub index from price settlements. In May 2014, Putin met with Xi Jinping and negotiated a $400 billion deal, under which Russia would supply 38 billion cubic metres annually over 30 years at $350 per thousand cubic metres starting in 2018. In 2013, the average price of Gazprom's gas in Europe was about $380 per thousand cubic metres. China offered a $50 billion loan to finance gas field development and pipeline construction to the Chinese border, with China building the remaining pipeline. In January 2023, due to sanctions following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom's gas exports fell 45% from 185 billion cubic metres (Bcm) to 101 Bcm, mainly due to the loss of the European market; in 2023, Europe purchased only 28 Bcm, the lowest level since the 1970s. In December 2025, Turkey finalized a one-year extension of its expiring gas import contracts with Russia totaling 22 Bcm; Turkish Energy Minister Bayraktar stated that supplies would continue but that the focus is on short-term contracts. On 1 January 2006, during a Russia-Ukraine gas dispute, Gazprom ceased gas supply to Ukraine and called for higher payments in line with global fuel prices; a temporary deal was reached on 3–4 January 2006. On 3 April 2006, Gazprom announced a threefold price increase for gas to Belarus after 31 December 2006; on 1 January 2007, it threatened to cut supply unless Belarus increased payments from $47 to $200 per 1,000 cubic metres or ceded control of its distribution network. Some analysts suggested the penalty was aimed at President Lukashenko for failing to pursue closer integration with Russia, while others noted Armenia paid similar prices. Gazprom requested $105, but Belarus refused; it responded that cutting supplies would deny Gazprom access to its pipelines, impairing gas transport to Europe. On 1 January 2007, a last-minute agreement was signed, with Belarus paying $100 per 1,000 cubic metres and allowing Gazprom to purchase 50 percent of Beltransgaz shares; immediately after, Belarus imposed a $42/ton transportation tax on Russian oil passing through its pipelines. On 13 March 2008, after halving gas supplies to Ukraine for three days, Gazprom agreed to supply it for the remainder of the year, removing intermediary companies. On 1 April 2014, Gazprom increased the gas price to Ukraine from $268.50 to $385.50 (£231.00) per 1,000 cubic metres; Ukraine's unpaid gas bills stood at $1.7 billion (£1.02 billion). On 30 October 2014, Russia agreed to resume gas supplies to Ukraine over winter through a deal brokered by the European Union. Gazprom is a vertically integrated company, owning its supply and distribution activities, including all main gas processing facilities in Russia, operating high-pressure pipelines, and since 2006 holding a legal export monopoly; other producers like Novatek are required to use Gazprom's facilities for processing and transport. At the end of 2008, Gazprom had 221,300 employees across subsidiaries in production, transportation, storage, and processing, with 9.5 percent in management, 22.9 percent as specialists, 63.4 percent as workers, and 4.2 percent as other employees. Gazprom's headquarters were in the Cheryomushki District, South-Western Administrative Okrug, Moscow until 2021, when they moved to the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg. Gazprom is a national champion, a concept promoted by Putin, where strategic companies serve national interests, such as selling gas domestically at prices below the global market; in 2008, Gazprom's activities accounted for 10 percent of Russia's GDP. Due to large-scale projects including Nord Stream 1 and Turkish Stream, Gazprom was a major revenue source for domestic suppliers and contractors. As of 2017, Gazprom's main shareholders were the Federal Agency for State Property Management (38.37%) and Rosneftegaz (10.97%), with Rosgazifikatsiya holding 0.89%, giving the Russian government majority control; the rest were held by investors, including 25.20% by ADR holders and 24.57% by other legal entities and individuals. Gazprom is listed on the Moscow and Karachi stock markets and is the top component of the MICEX and RTS indices; it was previously listed on London, Berlin, Frankfurt, and Singapore markets before 2022 sanctions. Gazprom has several hundred subsidiaries in Russia and abroad, directly or indirectly owned, including Gazprom International UK Ltd and Gazprom International Projects BV. Gazprom is the owner and sponsor of FC Zenit Saint Petersburg and its sports departments (basketball, volleyball), VC Zenit-Kazan, Gazprom-Ugra Surgut, and SKA St Petersburg of the KHL. On 1 January 2007, Gazprom became a sponsor of FC Schalke 04 at a cost of up to €25 million per year, extending the partnership for five years in November 2009; the sponsorship was suspended after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and was worth $150 million over five years. On 9 July 2010, Gazprom became a sponsor of Red Star Belgrade in the Serbian SuperLiga. In 2010, Gazprom was a Gold Partner of Team Katusha, alongside Itera and Rostekhnologii. On 17 July 2012, Gazprom became the official Global Energy partner of Chelsea FC for the UEFA Champions League 2012 winners, a sponsorship lasting until 2015. In September 2013, Gazprom became an official partner of FIFA tournaments from 2015 to 2018, including the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia. Gazprom was also a sponsor of the defunct Minardi F1 team in 2002–2003. In April 2021, Gazprom became a sponsor of the International Amateur Boxing Association (AIBA, now International Boxing Association) as a "general partner," a sponsorship that became controversial due to the IBA's increased Russian involvement.

On 9 July 2010, Gazprom became a sponsor of the Serbian SuperLiga football club Red Star Belgrade. In 2010, Gazprom was a Gold Partner of the Russian professional cycling team, Team Katusha, alongside Itera and Russian Technologies (Rostekhnologii). On 17 July 2012, Gazprom became the official Global Energy partner of the UEFA Champions League 2012 winners Chelsea, with the sponsorship continuing for three years until 2015. On 9 July 2012, Gazprom also became a sponsor of the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Super Cup, a partnership that lasted for three seasons until 2015 and was later extended until 2024; however, due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom's sponsorship for the Champions League and Euro 2024 was voided, ending their 10-year partnership with UEFA. In September 2013, Gazprom became an official partner of FIFA tournaments from 2015 to 2018, including the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia. Gazprom was also a sponsor for the defunct Minardi F1 team in 2002–2003. In April 2021, Gazprom became a sponsor of the International Amateur Boxing Association (AIBA, now the International Boxing Association) as a "general partner," a relationship that became controversial due to the IBA's increased Russian ties under president Umar Kremlev and ended in 2023. Gazprom is one of the world's largest greenhouse gas emitters, primarily due to methane leaks and its many gas-fired power plants. It has repeatedly been accused of using natural gas supply and pricing as a political and economic weapon against Europe and Ukraine.
