Donald Tusk, former prime minister of Poland, stated in April 2014 that excessive dependence on Russian energy makes Europe weak. Two boycott campaigns in Ukraine occurred in 2005 and 2013, and Russia denies weaponizing energy via Gazprom. In December 2019, Gazprom paid $2.9 billion to Ukrainian counterpart Naftogaz as ordered by a Stockholm court ruling on damage claims from alleged economic harassment. Following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom faced issues with EU countries and stated it would cut off supplies to French energy supplier Engie over failure to pay in full, a claim disputed by France's Energy Transition Minister Agnes Pannier-Runacher, who stated Russia was using gas as a weapon of war and that a complete supply interruption was a possible scenario. Yuganskneftegaz, a core production subsidiary of the Yukos Oil Company previously run by Mikhail Khodorkovsky, was targeted in 2003 when Russian tax authorities charged Yukos and Khodorkovsky with tax evasion, presenting a bill of over US$35 billion and demanding full payment on the same day. Requests for deferral, installment payments, or asset sales, including Sibneft, were rejected. Bailiffs froze Yukos' shares in Yuganskneftegaz, and on 19 November 2004, a notice was placed in Rossiyskaya Gazeta stating that Yuganskneftegaz would be sold at auction thirty days later on 19 December 2004. The auction required an advance deposit of US$1.7 billion and prior clearance by the Russian Federal Antimonopoly Service. In early December 2004, Gazprom applied through its wholly owned subsidiary Gazpromneft. On 15 December 2004, Yukos filed for bankruptcy protection in a Houston court and obtained a temporary injunction blocking Gazprom's participation. On 16 December 2004, Western banks withdrew support for Gazprom's application, and Baikalfinansgrup, a previously unknown company, submitted an application. On 19 December 2004, only Gazpromneft and Baikalfinansgrup appeared at the auction; Gazpromneft declined to offer, and Baikalfinansgrup acquired Yuganskneftegaz on its first bid. On 23 December 2004, Baikalfinansgrup was acquired by Rosneft, which later disclosed in its annual financial statement that it financed the acquisition. At the time, Sergey Bogdanchikov was the president of Rosneft and CEO of Gazpromneft. Shortly after the auction, the planned merger between Gazprom and Rosneft was abandoned, and Bogdanchikov resigned as CEO of Gazpromneft. On 7 February 2006, Vladimir Putin disclosed that Rosneft used Baikalfinansgrup as a vehicle to acquire Yuganskneftegaz to protect itself against litigation. On 22 April 2015, Gazprom was charged by the European Commission with using territorial restrictions to engage in anticompetitive behavior and imposing unfair prices, preventing gas imports at competitive prices and restricting access to high-demand areas while avoiding areas of excessive supply. Gazprom was also accused of compelling entities to consent to the now-defunct South Stream pipeline through mandatory consent clauses in long-term contracts. In 2018, Gazprom agreed to a settlement that dropped all contractual barriers to the free flow of gas in Central and Eastern European markets, granted customers explicit rights to trigger price reviews when prices diverged from competitive benchmarks, and allowed more frequent and efficient reviews. Gazprom agreed not to seek damages from its Bulgarian partners after the South Stream project ended. Had the case gone to court, it could have resulted in fines of up to $12 billion. In 2020, Gazprom agreed to reimburse Poland's PGNiG nearly $1.5 billion for years of compelling overpayment for gas supplies. In June 2021, a massive methane plume over Russia resulted from the partial shutdown of a Gazprom PJSC pipeline for emergency repair on 4 June, releasing 2.7 million cubic meters (1,830 metric tons) of methane, which has a short-term warming impact equivalent to 40,000 internal-combustion cars in the U.S. driving for a year, according to the Environmental Defense Fund. Methane's climate-warming effect is estimated to be 86 times more potent than carbon dioxide. Nord Stream is a system of offshore natural gas pipelines in Europe, running under the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany, owned and operated by Gazprom subsidiaries. The projects have been opposed by the United States, Ukraine, and other Central and Eastern European countries due to concerns over increased Russian influence and reduced transit fees. German Chancellor Olaf Scholz suspended certification of Nord Stream 2 on 22 February 2022 after Vladimir Putin recognized the Donetsk and Luhansk regions of Ukraine as independent republics. On 2 March 2022, Nord Stream 2 AG, a Gazprom subsidiary, ended business operations and laid off all 106 of its staff due to international sanctions, though earlier reports of bankruptcy were denied. On 26 September 2022, a severe drop in pressure in both NS1 and NS2 was linked to a sabotage-induced rupture in both pipes. Gazprom's Arctic oil drilling has drawn protests from environmental groups, particularly Greenpeace, which opposes drilling due to ecosystem damage and lack of safety plans. In August 2012, Greenpeace protested against the Prirazlomnaya oil platform, the world's first offshore Arctic drill site. On 18 September 2013, the Greenpeace vessel MV Arctic Sunrise staged a protest and attempted to board the Prirazlomnaya platform. After arresting two campaigners attempting to climb the rig, the Russian Coast Guard seized the ship by dropping from a helicopter and arrested thirty Greenpeace activists, towing the Arctic Sunrise to Murmansk. The Russian government intended to charge the activists with piracy and hooliganism, carrying a maximum penalty of fifteen years, but Greenpeace argued they were in international waters. The government's actions sparked global protests from governments and environmentalists. According to Phil Radford, Executive Director of Greenpeace in the U.S. at the time, the response was the "stiffest response that Greenpeace has encountered from a government since the bombing of the Rainbow Warrior in 1985." The piracy charges were dropped in October 2013, and in November 2013, 27 of the 30 activists were released on bail. In May 2014, the first shipment of Arctic oil arrived at a refinery in the Netherlands and was purchased by TotalEnergies. The episode is portrayed in the 3-hour television documentary On Thin Ice: Putin v Greenpeace. Following Russia's continued aggression toward Ukraine, the U.S. tightened debt financing restrictions on Gazprombank on 17 July 2014. On 12 September 2014, the U.S. barred U.S. persons from selling goods and services to Gazprom and Gazprom Neft related to deepwater, Arctic offshore, and shale projects. On 31 July 2014, the EU placed financial restrictions on Gazprombank, and on 8 September 2014, the EU placed financial restrictions on Gazprom Neft. In April 2018, the U.S. placed CEO Alexey Miller on the Specially Designated Nationals list, barring U.S. individuals and entities from dealing with him, with entities outside the U.S. also facing penalties if deemed to aid a sanctioned entity. Miller stated he was proud of the sanction, saying it confirmed that Gazprom was doing everything right. In December 2019, the U.S. sanctioned firms involved in the Nord Stream 2 project. On 24 February 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. expanded penalties on Nord Stream 2 AG, a Gazprom subsidiary, and sanctioned its CEO Matthias Warnig. It also expanded debt and equity prohibitions against Gazprombank, Gazprom, and Gazprom Neft. In March 2022, the European Union formally approved a ban on investments in the Russian energy sector, including Gazprom Neft. The UK banned Gazprom from its debt and equity markets on 2 March 2022, sanctioned Gazprombank on 24 March 2022, and Gazprom board members on 1 March 2023. Gazprom Energy, a UK firm, stated that it supplies 20.8% of non-domestic gas volume in Great Britain and sources gas through commodity exchanges like competitors, without depending on Russian gas supplies. In 2022, due to economic sanctions, Gazprom took the unprecedented step of suspending dividends for the first time since 1998. On 18 July 2022, during a Nord Stream 1 maintenance period, Gazprom sent a letter declaring force majeure, claiming it could not guarantee a gas supply due to extraordinary circumstances. On 26 September 2022, a rupture occurred in both Nord Stream 1 and 2 due to sabotage. In the first half of 2022, Gazprom reported high profits, roughly equal to 2021's profit, due to high prices. In the second half of 2022 and into 2023, Gazprom likely did not make a profit due to falling exports. Overall, Gazprom made a profit of 1.226 trillion roubles ($15.77 billion) in 2022, down 40% after an extra tax was levied in late 2022. On 19 December 2022, European Energy ministers agreed on a price cap of €180 per megawatt-hour for natural gas to prevent Russia from driving European prices upward. Gazprom's gas exports from Russia in 2021 were 185 billion cubic meters (Bcm), fell by 45% to 100 Bcm in 2022, and decreased again to 62 Bcm in 2023. In February 2023, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin signed an order granting Gazprom Neft the right to form its own private army. After the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the introduction of Western sanctions, Western gas companies continued to pay Gazprom Bank accounts in euros and dollars, which became blocked by sanctions. On 31 March, President Vladimir Putin signed Decree 172, requiring payments to be made by alternate means. Many Western companies refused to pay except under contract, leading Gazprom to cease supplying them. This resulted in the 2022–2023 Russia–European Union gas dispute. Arbitration cases have been initiated by several Western companies with long-term contracts for damages due to short supply or cessation of supply, including Germany's Uniper, which is claiming €11.6 billion from Gazprom, and Engie, which opened proceedings in February 2023 for short delivery. Gazprom went to arbitration for €300 million in unpaid gas from Gasum in Finland, which the arbitration ruled was payable but not in rubles. India's GAIL is also seeking compensation through a London arbitration court over Gazprom's short delivery of LNG to India, disrupted by sanctions against a Gazprom subsidiary in Germany.

Gender-affirming surgery (GAS) is a surgical procedure or series of procedures that alter a person's physical appearance and sexual characteristics to align with their gender identity. It is most commonly associated with transgender health care but is also pursued by cisgender individuals. The term is also known as sex reassignment surgery (SRS), gender confirmation surgery (GCS), and other names; however, "sex change" is generally considered offensive. Feminizing surgeries, such as vaginoplasty, vulvoplasty, and breast augmentation, result in female-looking anatomy, while masculinizing surgeries, including phalloplasty, mastectomy, and hysterectomy, result in male-looking anatomy. Patients often require lifelong hormone replacement therapy to support their endocrine system. Professional medical organizations, such as the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH), have established Standards of Care that require psychological evaluation and a period of real-life experience living in the desired gender before surgery is considered. Sweden became the first country to allow transgender people to change their legal gender after reassignment surgery and provide free hormone treatment in 1972, followed by Singapore in 1973 as the first in Asia. GAS is sometimes referred to as bottom surgery (in contrast to top surgery on the chest), and WPATH defines it broadly to include any surgical procedure for gender dysphoria. For trans women, genital reconstruction typically involves vaginoplasty using techniques like penile inversion, rectosigmoid vaginoplasty, or peritoneal pullthrough vaginoplasty; a less invasive option is vulvoplasty, which creates external female genitalia without a vaginal canal. For trans men, procedures may include phalloplasty or metoidioplasty to construct a penis, with metoidioplasty using the clitoris and resulting in a sensation-perceiving penis head, and scrotoplasty with possible testicular implants. Bigenital operations, such as androgynoplasty or vagina-preserving phalloplasty, allow individuals to retain original organs and are rarely performed. Gender nullification, which removes all external genitalia except the urethral opening, is pursued by some individuals assigned male at birth. GAS is also pursued by cisgender people for procedures like mammaplasty, penile implants, or testicular implants after orchiectomy. The term is often misrepresented by anti-trans activists as "genital-mutilation surgery." WPATH lists medically necessary procedures as including complete hysterectomy, bilateral mastectomy, chest reconstruction or augmentation, genital reconstruction, and certain facial plastic reconstructions, as well as facial hair electrolysis. Historical cases include Roman Emperor Elagabalus (2nd century), Alan L. Hart (1917), Dora Richter (1922–1931), and Lili Elbe (1930–1931), who underwent multiple surgeries including orchiectomy, penectomy, vaginoplasty, and an experimental uterine transplant that was rejected. In 1951, Harold Gillies developed a phalloplasty technique that became a standard. In 1971, Roberto Farina performed Brazil’s first male-to-female surgery, and in 1984, Jalma Jurado developed a technique used in over 500 surgeries. In 1999, Lebovic and Laub developed metoidioplasty. In 2003, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favor of Carola van Kück, affirming access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy. In 2011, Christiane Völling won a landmark case against a surgeon for non-consensual sex reassignment. As of 2017, some European countries require forced sterilization for legal gender recognition, and Japan requires sterilization as of 2020. The prevalence of transgender-related surgeries is difficult to measure, with a 2015 U.S. survey reporting that 25% of respondents had undergone such surgery. Medical conditions like diabetes, asthma, and HIV can complicate treatment, and patients typically require a multidisciplinary healthcare team, including endocrinologists and pharmacists, for medication management and education. Fertility is a key consideration, as orchiectomy or oophorectomy results in irreversible infertility. Surgery is generally not performed on children under 18, though rare exceptions exist with long-term mental health counseling and parental or court consent. Infants with intersex conditions may undergo early interventions, which are controversial due to human rights concerns. Negative outcomes, including PTSD and suicide, can occur when the surgically assigned gender does not match gender identity. Milton Diamond recommended delaying surgery until children can give informed consent and suggested introducing them to others with differences of sex development to reduce stigma. Access to GAS is limited by financial barriers, insurance coverage, and provider availability, with many surgeons trained under Standards of Care, particularly WPATH’s, which are widely recognized but criticized for being rigid and restrictive. Many surgeons require two letters of recommendation, one from a mental health professional with over a year of experience diagnosing gender dysphoria, confirming surgery is appropriate. While many medical professionals oppose requiring surgery for legal gender change, many jurisdictions still require a physician’s letter attesting to surgery for legal recognition. In the U.S., an increasing number of insurance plans cover GAS, including genital reconstruction, chest reconstruction, breast augmentation, and hysterectomy, with some requiring proof of psychological evaluation and real-life experience (RLE). In June 2008, the American Medical Association stated that denying treatment for gender dysphoria constitutes discrimination and supports insurance coverage as recommended by physicians. In 2017, the U.S. Defense Health Agency approved payment for sex reassignment surgery for an active-duty trans woman, performed at a private hospital due to lack of expertise in military facilities. Long-term quality-of-life research is limited by small sample sizes and baseline mental health disparities. A 2020 meta-analysis found low-quality evidence that chest reconstruction improves quality of life; a 2022 review found reduced suicide attempts, anxiety, depression, and gender dysphoria, along with higher life satisfaction; a 2024 review found genital surgeries improved depression and dissociation, with mixed results for other mental health outcomes and less conclusive evidence of improvement compared to hormonal therapy. A secondary analysis of the U.S. Transgender Survey found that gender-affirming surgery was significantly associated with lower rates of psychological distress, smoking, and suicidal ideation among those who underwent it compared to those who desired but did not undergo surgery.

A 2020 meta-analysis found "evidence of low quality" that gender-affirming surgery, especially chest reconstruction for trans men, improves quality of life.[71] A 2022 systematic review indicated that gender-affirming surgical procedures were linked to reduced rates of suicide attempts, anxiety, depression, and gender dysphoria, along with higher levels of life satisfaction, happiness, and quality of life after surgery.[72] A 2024 systematic review found that genital surgeries significantly improved depression and dissociation in trans and gender-diverse individuals, with "mixed results" for other mental health outcomes, concluding there was "less conclusive evidence" of mental health improvement after trans surgical procedures compared to hormonal therapy, though expressing tentative support for both.[70] A secondary analysis of the U.S. Transgender Survey found that gender-affirming surgery was significantly associated with lower rates of psychological distress, smoking, and suicidal ideation compared to those who desired surgery but had not undergone it; this was the largest controlled study on the subject to date (N=19,960), though limitations due to survey design and self-reported responses introduced possible response bias.[73] Gender-affirming surgery can be viewed as human enhancement.[74] Transgender people often face social obstacles such as discrimination, prejudice, harassment, and stigmatizing behaviors, with rejection being more severe than for lesbians, gays, and bisexuals,[72][75] which may limit quality of life improvements from surgery and prevent full alleviation of mental health disparities post-procedure.[77] Regret after gender-affirming surgery may stem from poor social and group support, late-onset gender transition, poor sexual functioning, and mental health problems; however, a 2021 systematic review found regret to be low, at around 1% among 7.928 transgender patients studied.[78] Regarding genital sensitivity, both trans men and trans women can maintain sensitivity after surgery, depending on surgical techniques used to preserve it; preserving the clitoral hood and clitoris under the reconstructed phallus is critical for maintaining sensitivity and achieving orgasm after phalloplasty.[79][80] Erogenous sensitivity is measured by the ability to reach orgasm during masturbation or intercourse; studies show both trans men and trans women report increased orgasms in sexual activities,[81][82] indicating the potential to maintain or enhance genital sensitivity. Most trans individuals report improved sex lives and greater sexual satisfaction after surgery,[82] with this enhancement positively linked to satisfaction with new primary sex characteristics.[82] Before surgery, trans patients had unwanted sex organs they wished to remove, leading to lack of enthusiasm for sexual activity; after surgery, they report greater body satisfaction and less stress during sexual activity.[82] Most report experiencing sexual excitement during sexual activity and masturbation,[82] with orgasm frequency and intensity differing between trans men and trans women—almost all female-to-male individuals report increased sexual excitement and can achieve orgasm through partnered sex or masturbation,[82][81] while only 85% of male-to-female individuals achieve orgasm after surgery.[83] Both groups report qualitative changes in orgasm experiences: female-to-male individuals report intensified and stronger excitement and orgasms, while male-to-female individuals report longer, gentler experiences.[82] Masturbation frequency increases after surgery for both trans women and trans men; a study found 78% of transsexuals can achieve orgasm through masturbation post-surgery,[81][82][84] with female-to-male individuals masturbating more frequently than male-to-female, possibly due to increased libido from testosterone therapy or reduced gender dysphoria.[81] Among life aspects, sexual satisfaction is the lowest among physical, emotional, and social domains; when compared to cisgender peers, trans women have similar sexual satisfaction to cis women, but trans men have lower satisfaction than cis men, and trans men also report lower sexual satisfaction than trans women.[81]

Cyprus is an island in the Eastern Basin of the Mediterranean Sea, ranking as the third-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily and Sardinia and the 80th-largest island globally by area. It lies south of the Anatolian Peninsula and is part of the Cyprus Arc. Geographically, it is classified in West Asia, though it is considered a European country in political geography. The island has experienced prolonged periods of Greek influence, along with intermittent Anatolian, Levantine, Byzantine, Ottoman, and Western European influence. It is dominated by two mountain ranges—the Troodos Mountains and the Kyrenia Mountains (also known as Pentadaktylos)—with the central plain, the Mesaoria, lying between them. The Troodos Mountains cover about half the island and stretch from Pomos Point in the northwest to Larnaca Bay in the east, featuring a complex, fragmented structure with steep valleys and stepped foothills in the southwest. The Kyrenia Range, a narrow limestone ridge along the northern coast, rises suddenly from the plains and extends into the Karpas Peninsula, which points toward Asia Minor, reflecting Cyprus’s geological connection to that region. The Kyrenia Range is known for its jagged, Gothic-like peaks and is less than half the height of Mount Olympus (1,952 m or 6,404 ft), the highest point in Cyprus, which is located in the Troodos Mountains. The Kyrenia Range is also referred to as the Pentadactylon Mountains due to its five-fingered summit shape. Ancient copper deposits were found on the Troodos slopes, originating from massive sulphide deposits within an ophiolite complex formed at a spreading centre under the Mediterranean Sea and uplifted during the Pleistocene. Access to year-round water is difficult across much of the island, traditionally attributed to deforestation and erosion, though Grove and Rackham challenge this view; instead, winter rivers originate in the Troodos and flow in various directions, including the Yialias and Pedhieos rivers flowing eastward into Famagusta Bay and the Serraghis River flowing northwest through the Morphou plain, all of which dry up in summer. An extensive network of dams and waterways has been built to supply farming areas. The Mesaoria plain is the island’s agricultural heartland, with crop productivity depending heavily on winter rainfall, and other crops grown under irrigation. Historically, the island was richly forested, especially in the Troodos and Kyrenia ranges and in the Mesaoria, though ancient conquerors removed much of the timber for shipbuilding, leaving little evidence today. About 12% of the island is classified as woodland, with shrub communities like golden oak, strawberry tree, terebinth, olive, kermes oak, and styrax found in non-forested areas, though maquis is uncommon. Most untended land is covered by garrigue, composed of low bushes such as Cistus, Genista sphacelata, Calicotome villosa, Lithospermum hispidulum, Phagnalon rupestre, and locally Pistacia lentiscus; excessive grazing leads to impoverished batha with stunted herbs. The island has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers (mid-May to mid-September) and mild, rainy winters (November to mid-March), with temperature and rainfall variations influenced by altitude and distance from the coast. The total area of Cyprus is 9,251 km², of which 5,896 km² are under the Republic of Cyprus and 3,355 km² under the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus; land area is 9,241 km² and water area is 10 km². The island has no land boundaries and a coastline of 648 km. Its maritime claims include a territorial sea of 12 nmi (22.2 km; 13.8 mi), a continental shelf extending to 200 m depth or to the depth of exploitation, and an exclusive economic zone of 98,707 km² (38,111 mi²). The elevation extremes are 0 m at sea level and 1,952 m at Mount Olympus. Natural resources include copper, pyrite, asbestos, gypsum, timber, salt, marble, and clay earth pigment. Land use in 2012 shows 9.90% arable land, 3.24% permanent crops, and 86.86% other land. Irrigated land was 457.9 km² in 2007, and total renewable water resources were 0.78 km³ in 2011. Freshwater withdrawal in 2009 was 0.18 km³ per year (10% domestic, 3% industrial, 86% agricultural), with a per capita rate of 164.7 m³/year. Natural hazards include moderate earthquake activity and droughts. Current environmental issues involve water resource problems due to the lack of natural reservoirs, seasonal rainfall disparities, seawater intrusion into the island’s largest aquifer, increased salinization in the north, water pollution from sewage and industrial waste, coastal degradation, and loss of wildlife habitats from urbanization. Cyprus is a party to international environmental agreements including Air Pollution, Air Pollution-Persistent Organic Pollutants, Biodiversity, Climate Change, Climate Change-Kyoto Protocol, Endangered Species, Environmental Modification, Hazardous Wastes, Law of the Sea, Marine Dumping, Nuclear Test Ban, Ozone Layer Protection, Ship Pollution, and Wetlands, with no signed but unratified agreements.

Georgi Ivanov Peev (Bulgarian: Георги Пеев; born 11 March 1979) is a Bulgarian former footballer who played as a midfielder. A youth product of Lokomotiv Sofia, he spent three seasons in the Bulgarian A Group with the first team before transferring to Dynamo Kyiv, where he won six major honours. He was discovered at the age of 21 by Dynamo Kyiv manager Valery Lobanovsky while playing for Lokomotiv and signed for €2.5 million. He also played for FC Dnipro Dnipropetrovsk. Peev made his official debut for Lokomotiv in a match against Litex Lovech on 8 August 1998, playing 13 minutes as a substitute, and scored his first professional goal on 5 December 1998 against Spartak Varna in the 10th minute. He was capped 45 times from his debut in 1999, appearing at the UEFA Euro 2004, and featured in 40 games for Bulgaria between 1999 and 2007. A right back or right winger known for his pace and attacking attitude, he was part of the Bulgarian squad at the 2004 European Football Championship, which exited in the first round, finishing bottom of Group C after topping Qualifying Group 8 in the pre-tournament phase. In January 2007, he moved to Amkar Perm in Russia for a reported fee of €500,000. In 2008, he was named fans' favorite player of the Russian Premier League and received a rare revolver from 1936 used by the Red Army. On 10 May 2010, following strong performances for his club, he was recalled to the national team for a friendly match against Belgium. On 27 March 2011, Georgi Peev announced his retirement from international football. His brother Daniel Peev is also a professional footballer.

Gerald M. Friedman (1921–2011) was a distinguished professor in Geology and one of the founders of modern rock sedimentation. He held professorships at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, the Graduate Center of the City University of New York, and Brooklyn College. Born in Berlin, Germany, on July 27, 1921, Friedman, being Jewish, fled the Nazis in 1938 and settled in England. He earned a bachelor's degree from the University of London in 1945, majoring in chemistry and minoring in geology. In 1945, he immigrated to the United States and worked as a Chemist for three years at Squibb. Friedman authored 573 papers and 19 books, including the highly cited work "Principles of Sedimentology." He received several awards, such as the William H. Twenhofel Medal in 1997, the Sidney Powers Memorial Award in 2000, and the Mary C. Rabbitt History And Philosophy of Geology Award in 2005. Friedman founded and directed the Northeastern Science Foundation, which organizes symposia and publishes journals such as Northeastern Geology, Environmental Science, Carbonates and Evaporites, and the Carbonates and Evaporites journal. The Sue Tyler Friedman Medal, named in honor of his wife, Sue (Tyler) Friedman, was established in recognition of her contribution.

The Gerard P. Kuiper Prize is given each year by the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society to recognize exceptional lifetime contributions in planetary science. The award is named in honor of Gerard P. Kuiper.

The Gerbrandy Tower (Dutch: Gerbrandytoren) is a radio tower located in IJsselstein, the Netherlands, and is also known as the Lopik tower due to its proximity to the town of Lopik. It was constructed in 1961 and is used for directional radio services, FM- and TV-broadcasting. The tower features a concrete structure 100 meters (328') high, upon which a guyed aerial mast is mounted. Its original total height was 382.5 metres (1,255 ft), but it was reduced to 375 metres (1,230 ft) in 1987. On August 2, 2007, its analog antenna was replaced with a digital one, reducing its height by another 9 metres (30 ft), bringing its current height to 366.8 metres (1,203 ft). This structure is a partially guyed tower, combining a lower free-standing concrete tower with an upper guyed mast. If counted as a tower, it is the tallest in Western Europe. A similar but smaller partially guyed tower exists in the Netherlands—the Zendstation Smilde radio tower—consisting of an 80-metre (260 ft) concrete tower with a 223.5-metre (733 ft) guyed mast. This tower collapsed after a fire on July 15, 2011, and was rebuilt starting in late 2011, completed in October 2012, with the replacement structure now standing at 303 metres (994 ft). The tower is named after Pieter Gerbrandy, who served as Prime Minister of the Netherlands during World War Two. Nearby, the KNMI-mast Cabauw is used for meteorological measurements, and the 196-metre (643 ft) high mediumwave transmitter Lopik was demolished on September 4, 2015. On July 15, 2011, a small fire occurred in the Gerbrandy Tower, prompting the immediate shutdown of all transmitters in the tower as a precaution, resulting in large parts of the Netherlands losing FM-radio and digital TV (DVB-T) reception, as the Smilde tower also caught fire and collapsed shortly after. Ownership of the tower is complex: the concrete main structure and the first three meters (10') of ground around the base are owned by Alticom, a company established in 2007 that acquired assets from KPN and was part of the European TDG Group; in June 2011, all Alticom shares were acquired by Infracapital, an infrastructure specialist of Prudential plc. The metal mast is owned by NOVEC, a subsidiary of TenneT. The ground surrounding the base, excluding the first three meters (10'), remains owned by KPN. Annually, from December 6 to January 6, the tower is decorated with 120 LED lamps attached to its 12 guy-wires, creating the appearance of a giant Christmas tree at night. In 1998, it was awarded by The Guinness Book of Records as the tallest Christmas tree in the world in a construction. The Mount Ingino Christmas Tree is also noted as the largest Christmas tree, though it is constructed on a hill slope.

Gerhard Heinrich Friedrich Otto Julius Herzberg, PC CC FRSC FRS, born on December 25, 1904, in Hamburg, Germany, to Albin H. Herzberg and Ella Biber, was a German-Canadian physicist and physical chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1971 "for his contributions to the knowledge of electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals." He is renowned for his work in atomic and molecular spectroscopy, using these techniques to determine the structures of diatomic and polyatomic molecules, including free radicals, and for the chemical analysis of astronomical objects. Herzberg served as Chancellor of Carleton University in Ottawa from 1973 to 1980. He had an older brother, Walter, born in January 1904, and his family was atheist, a fact they kept hidden. His father died in 1914 at age 43 due to dropsy and complications from a prior heart condition. Herzberg attended Vorschule (pre-school) late after contracting measles and graduated shortly after his father's death. He married Luise Herzberg (née Oettinger), a spectroscopist and fellow researcher, in 1929; Luise died in 1971. In 1933, the Nazi Party enacted a law banning men with Jewish wives from teaching at universities; as Luise was Jewish, Herzberg and his wife began planning to leave Germany. With help from John Spinks, a visiting physical chemist from the University of Saskatchewan, Herzberg secured a position at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. When they left Germany in 1935, the Nazis allowed them to take only the equivalent of $2.50 each and personal belongings. Initially considering a career in astronomy, Herzberg was rejected by the Hamburg Observatory due to lack of private financial support. After completing high school at the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums, he studied at Darmstadt University of Technology with a private scholarship and earned his Dr.-Ing. degree under Hans Rau in 1928. His most significant recognition was the 1971 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, during which he was described as "generally considered to be the world's foremost molecular spectroscopist." Herzberg received numerous honors, including being elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1951, winning the Frederic Ives Medal from the OSA in 1964, and being named an Honorary Member of the Society. The NSERC Gerhard Herzberg Canada Gold Medal for Science and Engineering, Canada's highest research award, was established in his honor in 2000. The Canadian Association of Physicists also has an annual award named after him, and the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics is named for him. An asteroid, 3316 Herzberg, bears his name. At Carleton University, Herzberg Laboratories, belonging to the Physics and Mathematics/Statistics Departments, is named after him. The main building of John Abbott College in Montreal and a public park in Saskatoon's College Park neighborhood are also named after him. Herzberg authored influential works, including Atomic Spectra and Atomic Structure and the four-volume encyclopedic series Molecular Spectra and Molecular Structure, often referred to as the spectroscopist's bible. The first three volumes were re-issued by Krieger in 1989 with extensive new footnotes by Herzberg, and Volume IV, "Constants of diatomic molecules," is a reference work compiling known spectroscopic constants of diatomic molecules up to 1978. Gerhard Herzberg fonds are held at Library and Archives Canada and the National Research Council Canada.

The German Air Force, known in German as Luftwaffe (literally "air weapon," pronounced [ˈlʊftvafə]), is the aerial warfare branch of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces. It was established in 1956 during the Cold War as part of the Bundeswehr, the armed forces of West Germany, following West Germany's accession to NATO in 1955. After German reunification in 1990, the Luftwaffe integrated elements of the former East German air force, the Luftstreitkräfte der NVA, which had been founded in 1956 as part of the National People's Army. There is no organizational continuity between the current Luftwaffe and the pre-1945 Wehrmacht Luftwaffe, which was disbanded in 1945/46 after World War II. The term Luftwaffe is used generically in German for any air force. The commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. As of 2015, the Luftwaffe operates from eleven air bases, two of which host no flying units, and maintains a presence at three civil airports. In 2012, it had an authorized strength of 28,475 active airmen and 4,914 reservists. After World War II, military aviation in Germany was banned by the Allied Control Commission, which disbanded the Nazi-era Luftwaffe in August 1946. The new Luftwaffe began operations in January 1956 with its first volunteers arriving at Nörvenich Air Base and receiving the US-made Republic F-84 Thunderstreak. Initially, it was divided into two operational commands: one in Northern Germany aligned with the British-led Second Allied Tactical Air Force and one in Southern Germany aligned with the American-led Fourth Allied Tactical Air Force. In 1957, the Luftwaffe took command of Army Air Defence Troops in Rendsburg and began expanding its air defense missile capabilities. The first operational unit was Air Transport Wing 61 at Erding Air Base, followed by the 31st Fighter-Bomber Squadron at Büchel Air Base. In 1958, the Luftwaffe received its first conscripts. In 1959, the 11th Missile Group in Kaufbeuren, armed with MGM-1 Matador surface-to-surface tactical nuclear cruise missiles, became operational. That same year, Fighter Wing 71 (Jagdgeschwader 71) equipped with Canadair CL-13 fighters became operational at Ahlhorner Heide Air Base. All aircraft, including current ones, feature the Iron Cross on the fuselage, a symbol from pre-March 1918, and the national flag of West Germany on the tail. In 1960, the Luftwaffe received its first Lockheed F-104 Starfighter jets, which remained in service until 1991. A total of 916 Starfighters were acquired, 292 of which crashed, resulting in 116 pilot deaths. This led to the Starfighter crisis in 1966, following 27 crashes and 17 casualties in 1965 alone. The West German public referred to the F-104 as the Witwenmacher (widow-maker), fliegender Sarg (flying coffin), Fallfighter (falling fighter), and Erdnagel (tent peg). On 25 August 1966, Defence Minister Kai-Uwe von Hassel relieved Chief Inspector Werner Panitzki and appointed Colonel Erich Hartmann, commander of the 71st Fighter Squadron, as Chief Inspector, due to public criticism of the Starfighter acquisition. On 2 September 1966, Johannes Steinhoff, with Günther Rall as deputy, became Chief Inspector. Steinhoff and Rall concluded that the non-German F-104s were safer and visited the US to study the aircraft, identifying deficiencies in training—such as lack of mountain and foggy-weather training and the aircraft's handling characteristics, including rapid, high-G turns—which contributed to accidents. They revised the training regimen, reducing accident rates to those comparable or better than other air forces and establishing a culture of high professionalism and tactical combat training outside Germany. Despite this, the F-104 retained its "widow-maker" reputation and was replaced earlier than in other nations by the McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II and the Panavia Tornado. On Steinhoff's initiative, the Luftwaffe established the German Air Force Command USA/Canada in Fort Bliss for missile and air defense training and pilot basic training, and a Tactical Training Command in Beja, Portugal, for Close Air Support training. Between 1967 and 1970, the Luftwaffe reorganized its forces, dissolving the two operational commands and dividing the four mixed Air Force divisions into two flying and two air defense divisions, with the remainder forming functional commands. Over the next decade, it received new equipment: in 1968, the first C-160 Transall transport planes; in 1974, the F-4 Phantom II fighter-bombers; in 1978, the first Alpha Jet Version A light attack jets; and in 1979, the first of 212 Panavia Tornado fighters. In 1986, the air defense forces began replacing Nike Hercules missiles with the MIM-104 Patriot and Roland short-range missile systems. Germany participates in NATO's nuclear sharing concept, allowing member nations without nuclear weapons to participate in nuclear weapon delivery. The Luftwaffe began training with the US Seventeenth Air Force in handling, arming, and delivering nuclear weapons. Initially, the F-104 was intended as a nuclear delivery platform with nuclear air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles and bombs. The Tornado became the second aircraft capable of delivering nuclear weapons, limited to B61 bombs. From 1965 to 1970, Missile Wings 1 and 2 operated 16 Pershing 1 missile systems with nuclear warheads under US Army custody, upgraded to Pershing 1a with 72 missiles in 1970. Although not directly affected by the 1988 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the Luftwaffe removed the Pershing 1a missiles from its inventory in 1991 and destroyed them. At the end of the Cold War, over 100,000 soldiers served in the Luftwaffe. The United States continues to lend nuclear weapons for hypothetical use under the nuclear sharing agreement. In 2007, 22 B61 nuclear bombs were stored at Büchel Air Base for use with Tornado IDS fighter-bombers of Tactical Air Force Wing 33. American nuclear weapons previously stored at Nörvenich, Ramstein, and Memmingen were withdrawn during the mid- to late-1990s. By international treaties with the "Big Four" powers—United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, and France—East Germany was a nuclear-free zone; the latter three no longer have nuclear weapons in Germany. After reunification in October 1990, the aircraft and personnel of the former East German air force were integrated into the Luftwaffe. The remnants were placed under the newly formed 5th Air Force Division (5. Luftwaffendivision) in Strausberg, renamed in 1993 to the 3rd Air Force Division (3. Luftwaffendivision), moved to Gatow in Berlin, and assigned to NATO in 1995. By 1990, East German aircraft markings were replaced by the Air Force Iron Cross, marking the first time Soviet-built aircraft served in a NATO air force. However, due to incompatibility with Western NATO equipment, most of the East German aircraft—such as the Sukhoi Su-17, MiG-21, MiG-23, and MiG-29—were retired and sold or transferred to NATO members in Eastern Europe, including Poland and the Baltic states. An exception was Fighter Wing 3 "Vladimir Komarov" (Jagdfliegergeschwader 3 "Vladimir Komarov") at Preschen Air Base, which flew new MiG-29 fighters. On 1 June 1993, it was renamed Fighter Wing 73 (Jagdgeschwader 73) and moved to Laage Air Base on 1 October 1994. The pilots were among the world's most experienced MiG-29 operators and served as aggressor pilots for dissimilar combat training. The United States sent fighter pilots to Germany during the Red October exercise to practice tactics against MiG-29s. The MiG-29s were fully integrated into the Luftwaffe's air defense structure and became the first Soviet Bloc aircraft to be operationally deployed within NATO. With the introduction of the Eurofighter Typhoon, the decision was made to withdraw the MiG-29s. All MiG-29s, except one, were sold to Poland for €1 each. On 9 August 2004, the last MiG-29s arrived in Poland and continue to serve in the 41st Tactical Squadron of the Polish Air Force. The Luftwaffe experienced its first combat action since World War II in September 1995 during Operation Deliberate Force, when six IDS Tornado fighter-bombers, equipped with forward-looking infrared devices, and escorted by eight ECR Tornados, supported NATO artillery missions against Bosnian Serb positions near Sarajevo. In March 1999, during the Kosovo War, the Luftwaffe participated directly in combat with Fighter Bomber Wing 32, equipped with ECR Tornados, which conducted missions to suppress enemy air defenses in Kosovo. These aircraft were equipped with an electronic countermeasures pod, one AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile, and an AGM-88 HARM air-to-ground missile. The wing flew 2,108 hours and 446 sorties, firing 236 HARM missiles at hostile targets, with no manned aircraft lost. In 2005 and 2008, Luftwaffe F-4F Phantom II fighters participated in the Baltic Air Policing operation, supplemented in 2009 by Typhoon units. In 2006, the Luftwaffe deployed several Panavia Tornado reconnaissance planes from the 51st Reconnaissance Wing "Immelmann" stationed in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, and German Army helicopters also operated from the Luftwaffe air base there. Additionally, C-160 Transall transport aircraft conducted missions in and around Afghanistan. Since the 1970s, the West German and post-reunification German Luftwaffe, along with other European air forces, has pursued the development of European-made warplanes, including the Panavia Tornado and the Eurofighter Typhoon, introduced in 2006. On 13 January 2004, Minister of Defence Peter Struck announced plans to reduce the number of fighter planes from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015. Assuming full implementation of the order for 180 Typhoons and the removal of all F-4 Phantoms, the number of Tornado fighter-bombers would be reduced to 85. Previously, the Bundesmarine's naval air wing (Marineflieger) operated 112 Tornado IDS aircraft; however, the last unit was disbanded in late 2004, and the entire maritime combat role was transferred to the Luftwaffe, with one unit equipped to carry Kormoran II and American HARM missiles. As of 2014, a significant portion of Germany's military aircraft was unserviceable, with approximately half of the Eurofighters and Tornados not airworthy, and the aging C-160 fleet operating in limited service while awaiting the introduction of the Airbus A400M, the first of which was delivered in December 2014. Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged that due to the poor state of Bundeswehr equipment, Germany could no longer fulfill its NATO commitments. The Luftwaffe was one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC) headquartered in Eindhoven, Netherlands, and most of its transport and tanker assets are managed under EATC. In 2018, the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTTs with Airbus A330 MRTTs was approved, with four units acquired by the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with Boeing CH-47 Chinook or Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter (STH) program was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe also participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, simulating extreme combat scenarios. The German Air Force contributed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock.

The German Air Force is one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC), headquartered in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, and most of its Transport & Tanker assets are now under EATC management. In 2018, the German Air Force approved the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTT aircraft with four Airbus A330 MRTT aircraft, a decision made in conjunction with the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with either the Boeing CH-47 Chinook or the Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter program (STH) was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, for the first time, with six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock. In 2018, the Air Force issued a request for information on four aircraft to replace the Panavia Tornado—Eurofighter Typhoon, F-15 Advanced Eagle, F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, and F-35 Lightning—before dropping the F-35 in January 2019, leaving the Eurofighter Typhoon and Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet as options. The German Air Force will acquire three C-130J Super Hercules transport and three KC-130J tanker aircraft, with deliveries planned for 2020–2021, jointly operated with the French Air Force’s two C-130J and two KC-130J aircraft (delivered 2018–19). In April 2020, the German government announced plans to purchase 30 F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, 15 EA-18G Growlers, and 55 Eurofighter Typhoons to replace the Tornado fleet, though approval was unlikely before 2022. The Super Hornet was selected for its compatibility with nuclear weapons and availability of an electronic attack variant, though as of March 2022, it had not been certified for the B61 Mod 12 nuclear bombs, with Boeing stating it believed it could meet German requirements with U.S. government support. In December 2021, Air Transport Wing 63 at Hohn Air Base, including the last remaining German C-160 Transalls, was disbanded, with the A400M and C-130J now serving as the primary tactical transport aircraft. In March 2022, Minister of Defence Christine Lambrecht announced Germany would buy 35 Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II fighter jets instead of Super Hornets, the only aircraft capable of carrying U.S. nuclear weapons, with an additional ten potentially added; Germany also planned to order 15 Eurofighter Typhoon electronic warfare aircraft to replace Growlers. In April 2022, Germany selected the CH-47F Chinook to replace its CH-53 Sea Stallion fleet as part of the STH program, with a contract worth approximately €5 billion (US$5.40 billion) for 60 aircraft. In August 2022, Germany deployed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets, three Airbus A330 MRTT tankers, and four Airbus A400M Atlas transports to Exercise Pitch Black in Australia, its largest peacetime deployment. From 12 to 23 June 2023, the German Air Force hosted Air Defender 23, the largest NATO air exercise since its creation, involving 25 nations and up to 10,000 troops. The current commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. The Inspector of the Air Force (Inspekteur der Luftwaffe) is the commander of Air Force Command (Kommando Luftwaffe), established in 2013 through the merger of the Air Force Office, German Air Staff, and Air Force Forces Command. This command, similar to the U.S. Air Force Air Staff, is a force-providing command, not an operational one, responsible for ensuring combat readiness of combat units, which during operations are commanded by NATO or the Joint Operations Command of the Bundeswehr. The Air Force Command directly controls three higher commands. The creation of the Air Force Command was part of a 2011 Bundeswehr reorganization announced by Thomas de Maizière, which reduced the Air Force to 23,000 personnel and led to the disbanding of the three air divisions, Air Force Training Command, and Air Force Weapon Systems Command. The three surface-to-air missile units merged into a single wing at Husum, fielding 14 MIM-104 Patriot and 4 MANTIS systems. The three air transport wings were merged into a single wing at Wunstorf Air Base, fielding 40 A400M Atlas transport planes. The Luftwaffe will field three Multirole Eurofighter Wings, each with two squadrons for a total of 143 Eurofighter Typhoons. A fighter-bomber wing with Panavia Tornado IDS remains at Büchel Air Base, and Reconnaissance Wing 51 at Schleswig Air Base will retain its Tornado ECR squadron and add one drone squadron. The Kommando Luftwaffe has two main elements: individual units fall under the Air Force Operational Forces Command or Support Forces Command, and only come under Air Operations Command during deployment or EU/NATO attachments. In 2021, the Space Component Command (Weltraumkommando der Bundeswehr) was established. The main subordinate elements of the Air Operations Command, Air Force Operational Forces Command, and direct subordinated institutions are detailed in the document. The Air Force operates 12 air bases in 2020, four of which host no flying units, and has a presence at three civilian airports, including Berlin Tegel, which closed in November 2020. In 2012, the Air Force had an authorized strength of 44,565 active airmen/women and 4,914 reservists; civil personnel are being reduced to 5,950, mostly in maintenance and the Air Force Fire Department. On 20 September 2011, Defense Minister Thomas de Maizière announced the Air Force would shrink to 23,000 airmen/women. The Luftwaffe has five training institutions: Offizierschule der Luftwaffe, Unteroffizierschule der Luftwaffe, Luftwaffenausbildungsbataillon, Fachschule der Luftwaffe, and Technische Ausbildungszentrum der Luftwaffe. Originally, German Air Force aircraft featured an Iron Cross on all four wing positions and on both sides of the fuselage rear, with a small tricolor flag on the vertical stabilizer and a serial number of two letters (service and combat wing) followed by three numbers (squadron and aircraft number), resembling U.S. Air Force buzz numbers. This system was replaced in 1968 with a four-digit registration code, separated by an Iron Cross: the first two digits identify the aircraft type, the last two are sequential per type. For example, Tornado IDS are numbered 4301–4622, Tornado ECR 4623–4657, and Eurofighters 3001–3399; the format is often written with a "+" as a placeholder, e.g., "10+01" for the A350 fleet. Air Force ranks match those of the German Army, with the same field dress and dark blue dress uniform featuring gold-yellow winged collar patches; dark blue side or peaked caps are worn, and members of the German Air Force Regiment wear a dark blue beret. The rank insignia for commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers/enlisted personnel are as described. Germany participates in the MRTT program for aerial refueling and contracts Noordzee Helikopters Vlaanderen for H145 rotorcraft training. As of August 2025, Germany plans to invest €350 billion in new equipment through 2041, in addition to a special fund of €100 billion, covering specific budget allocations. Numerous books, magazines, and articles have been written about the Luftwaffe.

Gertrude Katherine Lathrop (December 24, 1896–March 16, 1986) was an American sculptor renowned for her medallion work and sculptures of small animals. She was born in Albany, New York, to artist Ida Pulis Lathrop and Cyrus Clark Lathrop, and her sister Dorothy P. Lathrop was also an artist. Lathrop studied at the Art Students League in 1918 and at the School of American Sculpture, both under Gutzon Borglum. Her first exhibition was at the National Academy of Design in 1921. In 1924, she traveled to Gloucester, Massachusetts to study with Charles Grafly. She received an Honorable Mention from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1924, as well as the Helen Foster Barnett prize and the National Academy of Design award in 1928. In 1936, she designed the Albany Charter half dollar, and in 1938, she was commissioned by the Westchester County Coin Club of New Rochelle, New York, to design the New Rochelle 250th Anniversary half dollar. In 1964, she was awarded the Allied Artists of America's Medal of Honor; in 1967, she received the Pen and Brush Club's silver medal; and in 1970, she won the John Sanford Saltus Gold Medal from the British Numismatic Society. Lathrop was skilled in medal design and portrait modeling, but her primary passion was sculpting animals, a choice she explained by stating, "I chose to model animals because of their infinite variety of form and texture and their great beauty, for even the lowliest of them have beauty, yes even the ward bug, with his magnificent tusks." In 1954, she moved to Falls Village, Connecticut with her sister, a noted illustrator of children's books, where she resided for the rest of her life. Her works are held in the collections of the Seattle Art Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the Albany Institute of History & Art, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. She died in Falls Village, Connecticut in 1986.

Ghana, officially the Republic of Ghana, is a country in West Africa located along the Gulf of Guinea and the Atlantic Ocean, sharing borders with Côte d'Ivoire to the west, Burkina Faso to the north, and Togo to the east. It covers an area of 239,567 km² (92,497 sq mi) and has an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres (350 miles), situated between latitudes 4°45′N and 11°N and longitudes 1°15′E and 3°15′W. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra, making Ghana the country closest to the intersection of the Prime Meridian and the Equator (0°, 0°). The country spans diverse ecologies, including coastal savannas, tropical rainforests, and grasslands mixed with shrublands and forests, with forest extending northward 320 kilometres (200 miles) and eastward up to 270 kilometres (170 miles). Ghana is home to five terrestrial ecoregions: Eastern Guinean forests, Guinean forest–savanna mosaic, West Sudanian savanna, Central African mangroves, and Guinean mangroves. The climate is tropical, featuring a wet and dry season, and Ghana lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones—warm and dry in the east, hot and humid in the southwest, and hot and dry in the north. The White Volta River and its tributary, the Black Volta, flow south through Ghana to Lake Volta, the world’s third-largest reservoir by volume and largest by surface area, formed by the hydroelectric Akosombo Dam completed in 1965. The Volta exits Lake Volta into the Gulf of Guinea. The northernmost point is Pulmakong and the southernmost is Cape Three Points. With over 35 million inhabitants, Ghana is the thirteenth-most populous country in Africa and the second-most populous in West Africa. The capital and largest city is Accra. The earliest kingdoms to emerge in Ghana were Bonoman in the south and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north, with Bonoman existing in the area during the 11th century. From the 17th century, different Akan states emerged from the Bonoman area, primarily based on gold trading, including Bonoman (Brong-Ahafo), Adansi and Asante (Ashanti), Denkyira, Mankessim, Akyem, and Akwamu. By the 19th century, the southern part of Ghana was included in the Asante Kingdom, which developed from a loose network into a centralized kingdom with a specialized bureaucracy based in Kumasi. Prior to European contact, the Akan people developed an economy centered on gold and gold bars traded with other African states. European contact began with the Portuguese in the 15th century, who established the Portuguese Gold Coast (Costa do Ouro) and built a trading lodge at Anomansah, renamed São Jorge da Mina, with Elmina Castle commissioned in 1481 and completed in three years. By 1598, the Dutch joined the trade, establishing the Dutch Gold Coast and building forts at Fort Komenda and Kormantsi, capturing Elmina Castle in 1617 and Fort St Anthony in 1642. Other European powers, including the Swedes, Danes, and Germans, established their own Gold Coast territories, with the Germans building the Brandenburger Gold Coast or Groß Friedrichsburg. By 1874, Great Britain established control over parts of the country, assigning them the status of the British Gold Coast. Military conflicts between British colonial forces and Akan states, including the Anglo-Ashanti wars, culminated in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, after which the Ashanti lost control. In the late 19th century, cocoa cultivation expanded through the tropical forests, supported by the British administration. In 1947, the United Gold Coast Convention, led by "The Big Six," called for self-government within the shortest possible time following the 1946 legislative election. Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana from 1957 to 1966 as its first prime minister and president, formed the Convention People's Party in 1949 with the motto "self-government now" and initiated a "positive action" campaign involving non-violent protests, strikes, and non-cooperation with British authorities. Nkrumah was arrested and sentenced to one year in prison, released after being elected to Parliament in the 1951 general election, and became prime minister in 1952, implementing a policy of Africanization. On 6 March 1957, the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories, and British Togoland were unified as an independent dominion within the British Commonwealth under the Ghana Independence Act 1957, adopting the name Ghana. The current flag, consisting of red, gold, green, and a black star, dates from this unification. On 1 July 1960, following a constitutional referendum and presidential election, Nkrumah declared Ghana a republic and assumed the presidency. 6 March is celebrated as Independence Day and 1 July as Republic Day. Nkrumah led an authoritarian regime, repressing political opposition and conducting non-free and non-fair elections. In 1964, a constitutional amendment made Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life. He was the first African head of state to promote Pan-Africanism, merging teachings from Marcus Garvey, Martin Luther King Jr., and W. E. B. Du Bois, and played a key role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement and establishing the Kwame Nkrumah Ideological Institute to teach his ideologies of communism and socialism. His centenary was celebrated as a public holiday, known as Founders' Day. In 1966, a military coup codenamed "Operation Cold Chop" overthrew Nkrumah while he was in China, led by Colonel Emmanuel Kwasi Kotoka and Brigadier Akwasi Afrifa, forming the National Liberation Council chaired by Lieutenant General Joseph A. Ankrah. From 1966, Ghana was ruled by alternating military and civilian governments, often affected by economic instability, ending with Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings of the Provisional National Defence Council coming to power in 1981. In 1981, the constitution was suspended and political parties banned. Rawlings negotiated a structural adjustment plan, leading to economic recovery in the mid-1980s. A new constitution restoring multi-party politics was introduced in the 1992 presidential election, in which Rawlings was elected and again in the 1996 general election. In 1994, a tribal war in Northern Ghana between the Konkomba and other ethnic groups, including the Nanumba, Dagomba, and Gonja, resulted in between 1,000 and 2,000 deaths and 150,000 displacements. After the 2000 general election, John Kufuor of the New Patriotic Party became president on 7 January 2001 and was re-elected in 2004, marking the first peaceful transfer of power under the fourth republic. In the 2008 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo was defeated by John Atta Mills of the National Democratic Congress. Mills died of natural causes and was succeeded by Vice President John Mahama on 24 July 2012. Following the 2012 general election, Mahama became president in his own right, and Ghana was described as a "stable democracy." After the 2016 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo became president on 7 January 2017 and was re-elected in 2020. Akufo-Addo’s presidency ended in January 2025, and John Mahama succeeded him as president. To combat deforestation, on 11 June 2021, Ghana inaugurated Green Ghana Day with the goal of planting five million trees. On 6 August 2025, shortly after takeoff at Kotoka International Airport, a Harbin Z-9 crashed into a forested mountainside, killing eight people, including ministers Edward Omane Boamah and Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed. Ghana declared three days of mourning on 7 August and held a state funeral on 15 August at Black Star Square in Accra. Ghana is a multi-ethnic country with diverse linguistic and religious groups; the Akan are the largest ethnic group but constitute a plurality. Most Ghanaians are Christians (71.3%), nearly a fifth are Muslims, and a tenth practice traditional faiths or report no religion. Ghana is a unitary constitutional democracy led by a president who serves as both head of state and head of government. It ranked seventh in the 2022 Ibrahim Index of African Governance and fifth in the 2024 Fragile States Index. Since 1993, it has maintained one of the freest and most stable governments on the continent, performing well in healthcare, economic growth, and human development. Ghana has significant influence in West Africa and across Africa as a whole. It is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement and the African Union, and a member of the United Nations, South Atlantic Peace and Cooperation Zone, Economic Community of West African States, the Group of 24, and the Commonwealth of Nations. The name Ghana originates from Wagadu, a West African empire from the 3rd to 12th centuries, which Arab traders referred to as Ghana, derived from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning "ruler of gold." Rev. J. B. Anaman proposed a historical connection between the peoples of the Gold Coast and ancient Ghana in the early 20th century, drawing on D. W. Cooley’s interpretations of Arabic sources, and suggested an alternative derivation from the Wangara. Lady Flora Shaw compiled Arabic and European writings to present the kingdom as a major African power comparable to contemporary Western European states. Between 1907 and 1911, Rev. W. T. Balmer promoted the theory that the Akan peoples migrated from the medieval Empire of Ghana, a hypothesis later supported by Jack Goody, who noted it lacked linguistic and historical evidence but became influential among educated elites and nationalist intellectuals. The theory gained popularity in the 1920s in educational institutions, especially at Achimota, and was publicized by J. B. Danquah, who used Arabic and French translations to claim the Akan migrated from the Upper Niger region and associated the name Ghana with Akane or Akana, linking it to the ancient region of Akkad. Eva L. R. Meyerowitz expanded this narrative, claiming Akan origins and culture came from the Sahara and the Near East, suggesting Akan culture was Libya-Berber or connected to Mediterranean or Near Eastern cultures. By the time of independence, the name "Ghana" was widely accepted as a symbol of precolonial prestige, cultural unity, and national legitimacy. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Climate change is having significant impacts, with increasing temperatures, changing rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise expected to negatively affect infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods. Diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera are predicted to increase due to changes in water conditions.

The northernmost part of Ghana is Pulmakong, located near the Burkina Faso border, while the southernmost point is Cape Three Points. Ghana has a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons and lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones: the eastern coastal belt is warm and comparatively dry, the south-west corner is hot and humid, and the north is hot and dry. Climate change is significantly affecting Ghana, with rising temperatures, altered rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise negatively impacting infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods such as farming and fisheries. These changes threaten climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, energy, and forestry, and are expected to increase diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera due to shifting water conditions. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to a business-as-usual scenario, with a commitment to net zero by 2060. The country's geography includes low coastal plains, forested hills in the center, and savanna in the north, with Mount Afadja (885 m) in the Akwapim-Togo Range being the highest point. The Volta River system is dominant, with the White Volta and Black Volta converging in the north and flowing into Lake Volta, one of the world's largest artificial reservoirs created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965. The Volta exits into the Gulf of Guinea east of Accra, and other major rivers include the Pra, Ankobra, and Tano. Ghana is a unitary presidential constitutional democracy with a parliamentary multi-party system dominated by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) and the New Patriotic Party (NPP), having transitioned to the Fourth Republic in 1993 after civilian elections. Presidents are limited to two four-year terms; Nana Akufo-Addo won the 2016 and 2020 elections, defeating John Mahama, and his presidency ended in January 2025, after which Mahama became president. In 2012, Ghana ranked 67th least fragile globally and fifth least fragile in Africa, 64th least corrupt globally and fifth least corrupt in Africa, and seventh in Africa on the Ibrahim Index of African Governance. According to the 2023 V-Dem Democracy Index, Ghana is ranked 67th as an electoral democracy worldwide and 10th in Africa. Since independence, Ghana has adhered to nonalignment and is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement, actively participating in the United Nations and African Union. Ghana has strong ties with the United States, with three U.S. presidents—Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama—and Vice President Kamala Harris having visited officially. Notable Ghanaian figures such as Kofi Annan, Akua Kuenyehia, Jerry John Rawlings, and John Agyekum Kufuor have held international diplomatic roles. In 2010, President John Atta Mills visited China to mark the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations, and China reciprocated in 2011 with a visit by Zhou Tienong. China has become a top investor in Ghana, focusing on infrastructure, natural resources, and manufacturing, though concerns remain about sustainability, environmental impacts, and transparency. In 2013, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad met with Mahama to discuss the Non-Aligned Movement and co-chair a bilateral meeting at Flagstaff House. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are integrated into Ghana’s development agenda and budget through a decentralized planning approach involving UN agencies, traditional leaders, civil society, and academia. President Akufo-Addo noted that Ghana was the first Sub-Saharan African country to halve poverty as per Goal 1 of the Millennium Development Goals. In 1957, the Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) consisted of headquarters, support services, three infantry battalions, and a reconnaissance squadron; by 1964, it had expanded to six battalions, including a parachute unit. Today, Ghana is considered a regional power and hegemon, with Canadian Forces commander Roméo Dallaire highly praising its military personnel. Military operations are guided by the constitution, the Law on Armed Force Military Strategy, and agreements with the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre, executed under the Ministry of Defence. Despite being relatively peaceful, Ghana has experienced political violence, with an upward trend in politically motivated incidents in 2017. The Ghana Police Service and the Criminal Investigation Department are the primary law enforcement agencies, operating in 12 divisions, including specialized units such as a Militarized Rapid Deployment Force and Marine Police Unit, which handles offshore oil and gas issues. The Ghana Prisons Service and the Borstal Institute for Juveniles manage incarceration, and Ghana retains the death penalty for treason, corruption, robbery, piracy, drug trafficking, rape, and homicide. The UN's new SDGs emphasize promoting the rule of law, equal access to justice, reducing corruption, and building accountable, transparent institutions. Ghana is a key transshipment point for narcotics, primarily from South America and some African nations, with drug cartels exploiting weak border controls and porous borders. In 2013, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime stated that drug cartels from Colombia and Latin America use Africa as a route to Europe. Narcotics trafficking remains underground, and seizures declined in 2011; the Narcotics Control Board has impounded container ships at Sekondi Naval Base carrying thousands of kilograms of cocaine with a street value in billions of cedis. Drug cartels are using new methods to evade security agencies. President Mills initiated efforts to reduce the role of airports in drug trafficking. Homosexual acts are illegal in Ghana, and a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found that 96% of Ghanaians believe homosexuality should not be accepted. In rural areas, especially in northern Ghana, witchcraft accusations are common, with so-called "witch camps" housing around 1,000 people accused, and the government has announced plans to close them. Ghana possesses industrial minerals, hydrocarbons, and precious metals and is an emerging digital economy with a mixed economy. The "Ghana Vision 2020" economic plan aims for Ghana to become the first African country to become developed between 2020 and 2029 and a newly industrialized country between 2030 and 2039, excluding South Africa. Ghana has economic ties to the Chinese yuan renminbi, with the Bank of Ghana beginning to circulate renminbi as a second national trade currency in 2013. Between 2012 and 2013, 38% of rural dwellers lived in poverty compared to 11% of urban dwellers, with 94% of rural poor households engaged in agriculture. The Volta River Authority and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation are the two major electricity producers. The Akosombo Dam (1965), Bui Dam, Kpong Dam, and other hydroelectric dams provide hydropower, and the government plans to build a second nuclear power plant in Africa. The Ghana Stock Exchange is the fifth largest in continental Africa and third largest in Sub-Saharan Africa with a market capitalization of GH¢57.2 billion (CN¥180.4 billion) in 2012, and was the second best-performing exchange in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2013. Ghana produces high-quality cocoa and is the second largest global producer, supported by ICCO membership. It is classified as a middle-income country, with services accounting for 50% of GDP, manufacturing 24.1%, extractive industries 5%, and taxes 20.9%. The economy features a growing manufacturing sector and exports of digital technology products, including automobiles and ships, and benefits from diverse resource exports such as cocoa, industrial minerals, and agricultural products. The ICT sector is vital, with Rlg Communications, a state-affiliated company, producing tablets, smartphones, and consumer electronics. Urban electric cars have been manufactured in Ghana since 2014. In autumn 2021, Ghana became the first African country to issue social and green bonds, planning to borrow up to $5 billion to refinance debt for social and environmental projects and fund education and health initiatives, despite a low economic growth rate in 2020. Ghana exports hydrocarbons such as sweet crude oil and natural gas; the 100%-state-owned Ghana Oil Company is the leading filling station provider, and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation oversees exploration and production. Ghana aims to increase oil output to 2.2 million barrels (350,000 m³) per day and gas to 34 million cubic meters (1.2×10⁹ cu ft) per day. The Jubilee Oil Field, discovered in 2007, contains up to 3 billion barrels (480 million m³) of sweet crude oil. Ghana is believed to have 5 to 7 billion barrels (790 million to 1.1 billion m³) of petroleum reserves, the fifth-largest in Africa and 21st to 25th globally, and up to 1.7×10¹¹ cubic meters (6×10¹² cu ft) of natural gas reserves. The government plans to nationalize petroleum and natural gas reserves to boost revenue. In 2015, Ghana produced 88 metric tonnes of gold, and by 2019 it was the seventh largest gold producer globally, producing about 140 tonnes, surpassing South Africa to become the largest gold producer in Africa. Ghana exports silver, timber, diamonds, bauxite, and manganese, ranking 9th globally in diamond exports and reserves. The government also plans to nationalize the mining industry. In 2015 and 2016, electricity shortages—known as "dumsor"—led to persistent outages, increasing interest in renewables; by 2019, there was an electricity surplus. According to Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana was ranked 78th out of 180 countries with a score of 41, indicating perceived public sector corruption. Ghana launched a cellular mobile network.

Ghana exports gold, silver, timber, diamonds, bauxite, and manganese, and has other mineral deposits; it ranks 9th globally in diamond export and reserve size. The government has planned to nationalize the mining industry to increase government revenue. Electricity shortages in 2015 and 2016 led to "dumsor," defined as persistent, irregular and unpredictable power outages, increasing interest in renewable energy; as of 2019, there is a surplus of electricity. The judicial system addresses corruption, economic malpractice, and lack of economic transparency; according to Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana was ranked 78th out of 180 countries with a score of 41, where 0–9 indicates highly corrupt and 90–100 very clean. Ghana launched a cellular mobile network in 1992, later connecting it to the Internet and introducing ADSL broadband services. In 2025, Ghana was ranked 101st in the Global Innovation Index. The Ghana Space Science and Technology Centre (GSSTC) and Ghana Space Agency (GhsA) oversee space exploration and programs; they worked to launch a national security observational satellite into orbit in 2015. Ghana spends 1% of its GDP annually on space exploration to support science and technology research. In 2012, Ghana was elected to chair the Commission on Science and Technology for Sustainable Development in the South (Comsats) and has a joint space exploration effort with the South African National Space Agency. In 2011, tourist arrivals numbered 1,087,000, including South Americans, Asians, Europeans, and North Americans; tourist attractions include waterfalls such as Kintampo and Wli (the largest waterfall in West Africa), coastal palm-lined sandy beaches, caves, mountains, rivers, reservoirs, lakes like Lake Bosumtwi and Lake Volta (the largest human-made lake by surface area), forts and castles, World Heritage Sites, nature reserves, and national parks. Notable castles are Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle, which mark sites of bloodshed during the slave trade and preserve African heritage; UNESCO named the Castles and Forts of Ghana World Heritage Monuments, stating they shaped Ghana’s and the world’s history over four centuries as centers of the gold and slave trades and as symbols of European–African encounters and the African Diaspora. In 2010, Ghana ranked 108th out of 139 countries in the World Economic Forum’s list of favorite tourist destinations, moving two places from 2009; in 2011, Forbes ranked Ghana as the 11th most friendly country in the world, based on a 2010 traveler survey, with the highest rank among African countries included.
