In 1973, a meeting at the Pentagon led to the creation of the Defense Navigation Satellite System (DNSS), later named Navstar, with the full constellation designated Navstar-GPS. Ten Block I prototype satellites were launched between 1978 and 1985, with one launch failure. The Air Force Geophysical Research Lab developed the Klobuchar model for ionospheric corrections, with contributions from Elizabeth Essex-Cohen. After the 1980s, civilian use of GPS was limited by Selective Availability (SA), a deliberate error introduced into the signal to degrade civilian accuracy to about 100 meters, which military receivers could correct. Following the Korean Air Lines Flight 007 incident in 1988, President Ronald Reagan directed that GPS be made available for civilian use. During the Gulf War, the temporary disabling of SA occurred due to a shortage of military GPS units, as many U.S. soldiers used civilian receivers. Differential GPS systems from the U.S. Coast Guard, Federal Aviation Administration, and other countries began broadcasting local corrections in the 1990s, reducing both SA and atmospheric effects. The U.S. military also developed local GPS jamming, reducing the need for global degradation. On May 1, 2000, President Bill Clinton signed a directive to disable Selective Availability, providing civilians with the same accuracy as military users, a change proposed by Secretary of Defense William Perry in response to the growth of differential GPS services and military advancements in denial technologies. Selective Availability was removed from the GPS architecture beginning with GPS-III. After its discontinuation, GPS accuracy improved to about 5 meters (16 ft), with L5-band receivers achieving 30 centimeters (12 in) accuracy and high-end applications reaching within 2 cm (3/4 in), even sub-millimeter accuracy with long-term measurements. Consumer devices like smartphones can achieve 4.9 meters (16 ft) or better with assistive services such as Wi-Fi positioning. As of July 2023, 18 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals, considered pre-operational, with a full complement of 24 expected by 2027. The U.S. Department of Defense is required by law to maintain a continuous, worldwide Standard Positioning Service and to prevent hostile use of GPS without unduly disrupting civilian applications. The Interagency GPS Executive Board (IGEB) oversaw GPS policy from 1996 to 2004, after which the National Space-Based Positioning, Navigation and Timing Executive Committee was established in 2004 to advise federal agencies, chaired jointly by the Deputy Secretaries of Defense and Transportation, with members from State, Commerce, Homeland Security, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and NASA. The GPS satellites carry very stable atomic clocks synchronized with ground control stations, and any clock drift is corrected regularly. Each satellite broadcasts a signal containing its position and time, and a receiver calculates its four-dimensional position in spacetime using data from at least four satellites, solving for three spatial coordinates and its own clock deviation. The receiver measures the time of arrival (TOA) of signals from four satellites, computes pseudo-ranges based on the time of transmission (TOT), and determines its position and clock offset. The system's development was recognized with numerous awards, including the 1992 Robert J. Collier Trophy, the 2003 Charles Stark Draper Prize, the 2011 IAF Global Positioning System 60th Anniversary Award, and the 2018 induction of Gladys West into the Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame. In 2019, four founding members of the project received the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering. USA-203 from the Block IIR-M series is currently unhealthy. The GPS program cost, including satellite launches but not user equipment, was estimated at US$5 billion (equivalent to $11 billion in 2024) by 1994. Modernization efforts, including the next generation of GPS Block III satellites and the Next Generation Operational Control System (OCX), were authorized by the U.S. Congress in 2000. As of early 2015, high-quality Standard Positioning Service (SPS) receivers provided horizontal accuracy better than 3.5 meters (11 ft).

The signal transmitted by a GPS satellite and received by a ground station is proportional to the distance between them; using distance data from multiple ground stations, the precise location coordinates of a satellite at any given time can be determined. Each GPS satellite carries an accurate record of its own position and time and continuously broadcasts this data. A GPS receiver calculates its four-dimensional position in spacetime—three spatial coordinates and a clock deviation—by receiving signals from at least four satellites, as it must solve for four unknowns. The receiver measures the time of arrival (TOA) of signals according to its own clock, computes time of flight (TOF) values from the TOAs and time of transmission (TOT), and derives pseudo-ranges—ranges plus the time difference between the receiver and satellite clocks multiplied by the speed of light—using the speed of light. These pseudo-ranges are then used to compute the receiver’s three-dimensional position and clock offset, which are solved simultaneously using navigation equations. The resulting Earth-centered position is typically converted to latitude, longitude, and height relative to an ellipsoidal Earth model, and the height may be further adjusted to mean sea level (geoid). As of 2025, GPS modernization through GPS III and GPS IIIF satellites enhances performance with more accurate atomic clocks and stronger, secure, interoperable signals (L1C, L2C, L5), improving time-of-flight measurement precision and resistance to interference. Conceptually, time differences of arrival (TDOAs) define a hyperboloid geometry, with the receiver located at the intersection of three such hyperboloids; however, it is a misconception that three spheres define the user location—this only holds if the receiver’s clock is synchronized with satellite clocks, which would allow three satellites to determine position. In practice, a tracker algorithm improves position and time accuracy, rejects erroneous measurements, and estimates velocity, though velocity changes are delayed and inaccurate at short distances. GPS requires four or more satellites for accurate navigation, but fewer can suffice if one variable—such as altitude—is known (e.g., a ship at near-zero elevation or an aircraft with known height), and receivers may use dead reckoning, inertial navigation, or vehicle data to provide degraded position when fewer than four satellites are visible. The GPS system consists of three segments: space (24 to 32 satellites in medium Earth orbit, with six orbital planes at approximately 55° inclination and 60° separation, orbiting every 11 hours 58 minutes at about 20,200 km altitude), control (managed by the U.S. Space Force via monitoring stations in Hawaii, Kwajalein, Ascension, Diego Garcia, Colorado Springs, and Cape Canaveral, with data processed at Schriever Space Force Base by the 2nd Space Operations Squadron), and user segments (including military and civilian users). As of February 2019, there were 31 satellites in the constellation, with 27 in use and four as spares; a 32nd was launched in 2018 but remained in evaluation. The constellation now has nine satellites typically visible from any point on Earth with a clear horizon, improving redundancy. The control segment uses a Kalman filter to synchronize satellite atomic clocks and update ephemeris data, with the operation control segment (OCS) serving as the current control system until the Next Generation GPS Operation Control System (OCX) is fully operational. OCX, which began development in 2011 and faced delays, was expected to launch in 2021 but was pushed to 2024 and officially accepted by the U.S. Space Force on July 1, 2025, over 8 years and $4 billion behind schedule; OCX Block 3F is being developed to support GPS IIIF satellites, scheduled to launch in 2027. The user segment includes hundreds of thousands of military and tens of millions of civilian and commercial users, with receivers typically containing an antenna, processor, and stable clock. Many receivers support differential corrections via RTCM SC-104 (RS-232, 4,800 bps), though internal DGPS receivers often outperform external ones; as of 2006, low-cost units commonly include WAAS receivers. GPS data can be relayed via NMEA 0183 (used by open-source tools like gpsd) or proprietary protocols such as SiRF and MTK, through serial, USB, or Bluetooth connections. Originally a military system, GPS is now widely used in commerce, science, tracking, and surveillance, with its accurate time enabling applications in banking, mobile operations, and power grid control. The U.S. government restricts export of certain GPS receivers capable of operating above 60,000 ft or at speeds over 1,000 kn, classifying them as munitions requiring export licenses—even if used only for civilian purposes—though disabling high-altitude operation exempts them. These restrictions apply only to U.S.-origin units, with a growing trade in non-U.S. GPS components sold as ITAR-free. GPS was first used in combat during the 1991 Persian Gulf War, demonstrating both utility and vulnerability to jamming, which has since grown as adversaries like Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran have deployed jamming to disrupt operations, including the downing of Flight PS752. In the Russo-Ukrainian War, Russian electronic warfare reduced the effectiveness of GPS-guided munitions from 70% to 6%. Satellite atomic clocks operate on GPS time, which is not adjusted for leap seconds and is 18 seconds ahead of UTC as of January 2017 (due to a leap second added in December 2016), with receivers subtracting this offset to compute UTC. The GPS navigation message includes the GPS-UTC offset, which can accommodate up to 255 leap seconds.

While most clocks derive their time from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the atomic clocks on GPS satellites are set to GPS time, which is not adjusted for Earth's rotation and thus does not include leap seconds or other periodic corrections. GPS time was aligned with UTC in 1980 but has since diverged; as of January 2017, GPS time is 18 seconds ahead of UTC due to the leap second added on December 31, 2016. The difference between GPS time and UTC is included in the GPS navigation message, and receivers subtract this offset to compute UTC and specific time zone values. New GPS units may not display correct UTC until they receive the UTC offset message, and the GPS-UTC offset field can accommodate up to 255 leap seconds (eight bits). GPS time is theoretically accurate to about 14 nanoseconds due to clock drift relative to International Atomic Time (TAI), with TAI – GPS equaling 19 seconds, though most receivers are only accurate to about 100 nanoseconds due to signal interpretation errors. GPS applies two major relativistic corrections: one for the relative velocity between satellite and receiver (special relativity) and one for the difference in gravitational potential (general relativity); satellite acceleration is typically not separately corrected. GPS date is expressed as a week number and seconds into the week, with the week number transmitted as a ten-bit field in the C/A and P(Y) navigation messages, resetting every 1,024 weeks (19.6 years). GPS week zero began at 00:00:00 UTC (00:00:19 TAI) on January 6, 1980, and the week number returned to zero on August 21, 1999 and again on April 6, 2019. To determine the current Gregorian date, a receiver must have an approximate date within 3,584 days. The modernized GPS civil navigation (CNAV) message will use a 13-bit field that repeats every 8,192 weeks (157 years), lasting until 2137. GPS satellites broadcast navigation messages on L1 (1.57542 GHz) and L2 (1.2276 GHz) frequencies at 50 bits per second, with each complete message taking 750 seconds (12.5 minutes) and consisting of a 1500-bit frame divided into five 300-bit subframes, each 6 seconds long. Subframes 4 and 5 are subcommutated 25 times, resulting in a total message length of 37,500 bits. The first subframe contains the week number, time within the week, and satellite health; subframes 2 and 3 contain ephemeris data (precise orbital parameters), while subframes 4 and 5 contain almanac data (coarse orbit and status for up to 32 satellites and error correction). Receivers must demodulate signals from each satellite for 18 to 30 seconds to obtain ephemeris data and up to 732 to 750 seconds (12.5 minutes) to collect all almanacs. All satellites use code-division multiple access (CDMA) with unique pseudo-random (PRN) codes: the coarse/acquisition (C/A) code, accessible to the public, transmits at 1.023 million chips per second, and the precise (P/Y) code, encrypted for military use, transmits at 10.23 million chips per second. The satellites' internal clocks operate at 10.22999999543 MHz to compensate for relativistic effects. The L1 carrier is modulated by both C/A and P/Y codes, while L2 is modulated only by the P/Y code. The P/Y code can be encrypted for military access. The L3 signal (1.38105 GHz) is used by the U.S. Nuclear Detonation Detection System (USNDS) to detect and report nuclear detonations, and the L4 band (1.379913 GHz) is being studied for ionospheric correction. The L5 frequency (1.17645 GHz), added during GPS modernization, was first provided by a Block IIF satellite launched in May 2010 and completed with the 12th and final Block IIF satellite launched on February 5, 2016; it consists of two phase-quadrature carriers, each bi-phase shift key (BPSK) modulated, and supports safety-of-life aviation applications. In 2011, LightSquared sought a conditional waiver to operate a terrestrial broadband service near the L1 band, raising concerns about interference with GPS signals, especially in the upper 10 MHz of its spectrum, with testing in early 2011 showing minimal effects in the lower 10 MHz (less than 1% of GPS devices affected) and some concern in the upper range, with Aviation Week reporting "significant jamming" in June 2011. Signals are separated by unique Gold codes assigned to each satellite, and receivers identify satellites by their distinct C/A code patterns. If almanac data is already stored, the receiver selects satellites by their PRNs (1 to 32); otherwise, it enters a search mode until a lock is obtained, requiring an unobstructed line of sight. A delay of up to 30 seconds may occur before the first position estimate due to ephemeris data reading. The receiver uses satellite messages to determine satellite positions and transmission times. The satellite position and time are designated as [xi, yi, zi, si], and the true reception time is ti = t~i − b, where b is the receiver's clock bias relative to the more accurate satellite clocks. The message transit time is t~i − b − si, and the distance traveled is (t~i − b − si)c. With n satellites, the equations are solved for the receiver position [x, y, z] and clock bias b, requiring at least four satellites. The pseudoranges pi = (t~i − si)c are biased versions of true ranges, and the system has four unknowns, requiring at least four signals. When more than four satellites are available, the system is overdetermined and a fitting method is used. Position errors vary with satellite sky configuration, and receivers calculate error estimates using geometric dilution of position (GDOP) factors. The receiver position is typically expressed in WGS 84 coordinates or a country-specific system. The solution can be interpreted as the center of an inscribed sphere of radius bc, touching spheres centered at satellites with radii equal to pseudoranges. The measured pseudoranges contain clock errors, and in idealized cases, the true ranges represent the radii of spheres centered on satellites, with the receiver at their intersection via trilateration. However, in practice, random errors and precision loss from subtracting close numbers reduce accuracy, and three satellites alone are insufficient. More satellites improve accuracy by reducing random errors and increasing sphere separation, though multiple intersections occur, and a best-fit solution is computed via least squares. Subtracting pseudoranges from different satellites cancels the clock bias, resulting in a difference of distances di − dj, which defines a hyperbola in 2D or a hyperboloid in 3D, allowing the receiver to be located at the intersection of three hyperboloids from four satellites. With more satellites, multiple intersections exist, and a best-fitting solution is used. The receiver position and clock bias are solved simultaneously in a four-dimensional spacetime, with each signal describing a hypercone centered on a satellite. When more than four satellites are available, the system uses the best signals or all visible ones, depending on receiver channels, processing power, and GDOP.

The clock in a GPS receiver is typically less accurate than that of the satellites and is not precisely synchronized with them, leading to pseudoranges that differ significantly from true distances. To address this, the time difference between the receiver and satellite clocks is modeled as an unknown bias, denoted as b, and the system of equations is solved simultaneously for the receiver’s position [x, y, z] and the clock bias b. This solution space is viewed as a four-dimensional spacetime, requiring signals from at least four satellites, each of which defines a hypercone (or spherical cone) with its vertex at the satellite and a spherical base; the receiver’s position lies at the intersection of four or more such hypercones. When more than four satellites are available, the system becomes over-determined and solved using least-squares or weighted least-squares methods, as no unique solution exists. These equations are non-linear and typically require iterative methods like the Gauss–Newton algorithm for resolution. Initially, GPS was designed with a numerical least-squares approach before closed-form solutions were developed. One such closed-form solution, by S. Bancroft, is well-documented and claimed to perform better in low-geometric dilution of precision (GDOP) scenarios compared to iterative methods. Bancroft’s method is algebraic and applicable to four or more satellites; with four satellites, it involves inverting a 4x4 matrix and solving a single-variable quadratic equation, yielding one or two solutions, of which only one is typically a near-Earth, physically meaningful solution. For more than four satellites, Bancroft uses the generalized inverse (pseudoinverse). While some argue that iterative methods generally provide more accurate results, Leick et al. (2015) state that Bancroft’s (1985) solution is one of the earliest, if not the first, closed-form solution, with later closed-form solutions published but unclear adoption in practice. GPS error analysis identifies residual errors from sources such as signal arrival time, atmospheric delays (ionospheric and tropospheric), ephemeris and clock data, multipath, and interference, with error magnitude influenced by GDOP. Artificial errors, including jamming and selective availability—which previously limited accuracy to approximately 6–12 meters (20–40 feet) and was discontinued on May 1, 2000—remain a concern. GNSS enhancement techniques improve positioning accuracy by integrating external data, such as error corrections or direct measurements of signal deviations, into the calculation. In the U.S., GPS receivers are regulated under FCC Part 15 rules, which require them to accept interference and to reasonably discriminate against signals outside their allocated spectrum. GPS operates in the 1559 to 1610 MHz band, while LightSquared’s Mobile Satellite Service (MSS) band is 1525 to 1559 MHz. Since 1996, the FCC has authorized use of the adjacent spectrum for LightSquared. In 2001, LightSquared’s predecessor applied for an integrated satellite-terrestrial service; in 2002, the U.S. GPS Industry Council agreed to an out-of-band-emissions (OOBE) agreement to prevent ground-based transmissions from interfering with the GPS band. In 2004, the FCC adopted this agreement, authorizing LightSquared’s Ancillary Tower Components (ATCs) as ancillary to the satellite service, not as a standalone offering. This authorization was reviewed by the U.S. Interdepartment Radio Advisory Committee. In January 2011, the FCC conditionally authorized LightSquared’s wholesale customers—such as Best Buy, Sharp, and C Spire—to resell integrated services using only the 1525 to 1559 MHz band, contingent on interference studies led by LightSquared with GPS industry and federal agency participation. On February 14, 2012, the FCC vacated the conditional order after the NTIA concluded there was no practical way to mitigate GPS interference. GPS receivers are designed to operate beyond the GPS band, up to 400 MHz in either direction of 1575.42 MHz, due to mobile satellite services broadcasting at similar power levels. As per FCC Part 15, GPS receivers are not protected from out-of-band signals, explaining the coexistence of both bands. In 2003, the FCC allowed MSS licensees to build small ancillary ground towers to promote efficient terrestrial spectrum use, noting that the services are imperfect substitutes and operate in different market segments. In 2004, the FCC reiterated that the ground towers remain ancillary. In 2010, the FCC stated LightSquared would offer mobile broadband services to enhance competition, but GPS manufacturers argue this contradicts the 2003 and 2004 rulings that the ATC is ancillary. To support public interest, Trimble Navigation Ltd. formed the "Coalition To Save Our GPS." Both the FCC and LightSquared committed to resolving GPS interference before operation. Aviation experts warn that interference could cause aircraft to go off course undetected, affecting air traffic control, defense guidance, and emergency services like 911. On February 14, 2012, the FCC barred LightSquared’s national broadband network due to the NTIA’s finding that interference could not be mitigated, a decision LightSquared is challenging. Following the U.S. deployment of GPS, other nations have developed their own satellite navigation systems. In the event of space weather or anti-satellite attacks, the U.S. lacks a terrestrial backup; the LORAN-C system was shut down in North America in 2010 and Europe in 2015. eLoran is proposed as a U.S. terrestrial backup but has not received approval or funding as of 2024. China continues to operate LORAN-C transmitters, and Russia has a similar system called CHAYKA ("Seagull").

"Gluten Free Ebola" is the second episode of the eighteenth season of the American animated television series South Park, marking the 249th overall episode. It was written and directed by series co-creator Trey Parker and premiered on Comedy Central in the United States on October 1, 2014. The episode satirizes the gluten-free diet trend and the frequent changes to the Western pattern diet and the then-current food guide. After the events of "Go Fund Yourself," Stan, Cartman, Kyle, and Kenny return to school and are ostracized for having insulted their friends before their startup. At a staff meeting, Mr. Mackey boasts about adopting a gluten-free diet, which irritates others. To regain popularity, Cartman organizes a party for Scott Malkinson's diabetes, announcing it over local radio station WSPIC. Principal Victoria, who has been converted to gluten-free by Mr. Mackey, asks if the party has gluten-free food, to which the boys provide no answer. At the community center, a USDA scientist attempts to debunk gluten-related fears by extracting gluten from wheat dough; Mr. Mackey pressures him to drink the sample, leading to his violent death and a town-wide food panic. Cartman, panicked, calls Kyle and claims the entire town has taken all gluten-containing food, making the party impossible. The USDA works to resolve the crisis. At the Marsh home, two USDA agents find a can of beer in the garbage, which Randy dismisses as harmless—unaware that beer contains wheat—leading to his quarantine at a Papa John's restaurant with Mr. Garrison and an unnamed civilian. Stan, tasked with getting pop star Lorde to perform, tries to identify Randy’s co-worker who knows Lorde before being pushed back into Papa John's. Cartman dreams of Aunt Jemima (a parody of Mother Abigail), who tells him the food pyramids are upside-down, though Cartman misunderstands. As gluten-free toppings at Papa John's run out, the unnamed resident eats pizza dough containing gluten, believing it's a setup, and dies shortly after. At the radio station, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny cancel the party to focus on educating the public about gluten dangers. Cartman, claiming to know the solution, calls the USDA and asserts the food pyramid is upside-down. Surprisingly, the new dietary model works. The boys then host a successful party, with Stan reconciling with Wendy, who asks him to dance as the credits append "GF" (gluten-free) to a handful of cast and crew. Randy Marsh performs as Lorde at the party, foreshadowing the next episode. The episode's concept originated from Trey Parker and Matt Stone observing how people, including themselves, adopted gluten-free diets, leading them to create a satire of the trend. The A.V. Club's Josh Mordell gave the episode a C, finding the gluten-free panic "reasonably funny" but criticizing the lack of a B-story. IGN's Max Nicholson rated it 7 out of 10, praising the gluten panic but criticizing the party storyline, calling the radio segments "among the least funny South Park moments in recent memory." Spin magazine's Brennan Carley criticized the Lorde parody, questioning whether she had done anything worthy of the cartoon creators' ire; South Park responded in the following week's episode "The Cissy" with a subplot involving a Spin reporter named "Brandon Carlile" investigating the concert and stating: "It would be a shame if someone was…having fun at her expense." In January 2026, the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., introduced a new food pyramid model that inverted the traditional structure, placing meats, dairy, fats, fruit, and vegetables at the top. This sparked social media claims that "Gluten Free Ebola" had predicted the pyramid inversion and that the "Make America Healthy Again" movement was merely recycling South Park jokes. In response, Kennedy's Twitter account @SecKennedy posted an edited clip from the episode showing the traditional pyramid reorganized into the 2026 model.

Golda Meir (originally Meyerson; née Mabovitch; born 3 May 1898 – died 8 December 1978) was the prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974 and the country's first and only female head of government. Born into a Jewish family in downtown Kiev (now Kyiv), present-day Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire, she was the daughter of Blume Neiditch and Moshe Yitzhak Mabovitch, a carpenter. Meir had two sisters, Sheyna (born 1889) and Tzipke (later Clara; born 1902), and five siblings who died in infancy. Her earliest memories included her father boarding up the front door in response to rumors of a pogrom. She was named after her grandmother Golde. In 1903, Moshe left Russia for New York City, and after his absence, the family moved to Pinsk, present-day Belarus. In 1905, he moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where he found work in the railroad yard workshops and saved enough money to bring his family to the United States. Meir, along with her parents and sister, arrived in Quebec and traveled to Milwaukee by train. Blume ran a grocery store on Milwaukee’s north side, and by age eight, Meir often managed the store. She attended the Fourth Street Grade School (now the Golda Meir School) from 1906 to 1912 and, as a leader, organized the American Young Sisters Society in 1908 to fund her classmates’ textbooks. She graduated as valedictorian despite frequent tardiness due to work. In 1912, she began studying at North Division High School and worked part-time at Schuster’s department store and the Milwaukee Public Library. Her parents wanted her to marry and leave school, but she declined. In 1914, after a disagreement with her sister, she left North High School, moved out, and found work. After reconciling with her parents, she returned to Milwaukee and resumed studies, graduating in 1915. She became an active member of Young Poale Zion, which later became Habonim, embracing Socialist Zionism. In 1916, she attended the Milwaukee State Normal School (now University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee), and in 1917, she took a position at a Yiddish-speaking Folks Schule, further embracing Labor Zionism. On 9 July 1917, she became a naturalized U.S. citizen by descent, as her father had naturalized. On 24 December 1917, she married Morris Meyerson, with the condition that they settle in Palestine. Her plans to immigrate immediately were disrupted when transatlantic passenger services were canceled due to the U.S. entering World War I, so she focused on Poale Zion activities. After the war ended in 1921, the couple moved to Mandatory Palestine with Meir’s sister Sheyna, Sheyna’s daughter, and her childhood friend Regina, arriving via the SS Pocahontas from New York to Naples and then by train to Tel Aviv. Meir’s parents followed in 1926. The family was accepted into kibbutz Merhavia in the Jezreel Valley after an initial rejection; her duties included picking almonds, planting trees, working in chicken coops, and running the kitchen. Recognizing her leadership, the kibbutz elected her as its representative to the Histadrut. In 1924, the couple left Merhavia and lived briefly in Tel Aviv before settling in Jerusalem, where they had two children: Menachem (1924) and Sarah (1926). Meir returned to Merhavia in 1925. In 1928, she was elected secretary of Moetzet HaPoalot (Working Women's Council), and from 1932 to 1934, she served in the United States as an emissary to obtain medical treatment for her daughter’s kidney illness. In 1934, upon returning from the U.S., she joined the Executive Committee of the Histadrut and became head of its Political Department, a key training role for her future leadership. In July 1938, she served as the Jewish observer at the Évian Conference, where delegates from 32 countries expressed sorrow over Jewish refugees but refused to admit them; the only exception was the Dominican Republic, which pledged 100,000 refugees. Meir expressed disappointment and stated, "There is only one thing I hope to see before I die and that is that my people should not need expressions of sympathy anymore." During World War II, she held several key roles in the Jewish Agency, the Zionist Organization’s arm in British Palestine. In June 1946, after the British arrested Moshe Sharett and other Yishuv leaders in Operation Agatha, Meir became acting head of the Political Department, becoming the principal negotiator between the Jewish community and the British. After Sharett left for the U.S. to attend UN Partition Plan talks, Meir led the department until Israel’s establishment in 1948. In 1947, she traveled to Cyprus to meet Jewish detainees in internment camps and successfully persuaded them to prioritize families with children for entry into Palestine. On 17 November 1947, she met King Abdullah I of Jordan, who was seen as the only Arab leader willing to ally with a future Israeli state; the meeting confirmed his unwillingness to invade and his willingness to cooperate. Throughout the war, Meir played a minor role, feeling pushed aside, but she was critical in fundraising. In January 1948, the Jewish Agency needed funds for the war and the new state; the treasurer believed they could raise only $7 to $8 million from the American Jewish community, but Meir raised over $30 million, largely due to an emotional speech delivered in Chicago on 22 January. She toured dozens of U.S. cities and returned to Israel on 18 March. The funds were vital to the war effort, as the Arab Higher Committee’s annual budget was around $2.25 million, similar to Haganah’s pre-war budget. Ben-Gurion later called her the "Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible." However, upon returning, she was excluded from the 13-member cabinet of the provisional government and included in the 37-member People's Council, a decision Ben-Gurion protested as "inconceivable" and "a moral and political necessity." On 13 April, she was hospitalized in Tel Aviv due to a suspected heart attack; Ben-Gurion and political leaders urged her to recover and take on the role of "mother of this city," believing her words would inspire 100,000 residents. Instead, on 6 May, she visited Haifa after its occupation by Haganah and described the mass expulsion and flight of Arabs as "dreadful," likening it to the fate of Jews in Nazi-occupied Europe. She returned to Tel Aviv and eventually to Jerusalem two weeks before the end of the mandate. On 11 May, she met Abdullah I again, after being denied a meeting at Naharayim due to safety concerns and being forced to travel to Amman in secret as an Arab woman. At the meeting, Abdullah claimed he had made a promise when alone but now was "one of five" and could not fulfill it alone. He proposed integrating Jordan into Palestine with Jewish representation in the Jordanian parliament, but Meir refused. The meeting ended without agreement, and Abdullah stated he would be forced to invade due to Arab League pressure. Meir expressed openness to meeting again after Israel won the war. On 14 May 1948, Meir became one of 24 signatories (including two women) of the Israeli Declaration of Independence, recalling that she cried upon signing, saying she could not imagine real people doing such a thing. A day after independence, the second phase of the war began, and Meir lost her administrative role as the Political Department became the provisional Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with Dov Yosef taking over in Jerusalem. On 18 May, she launched a second fundraising tour, raising around $50 million, bringing her total fundraising to about $90 million—roughly one-third of the war’s $275 million cost. During preparations, she was issued the first Israeli passport. Over ten weeks, Israel faced significant war changes. On 25 June, while still in the U.S., she was appointed by Sharett as minister plenipotentiary to the Soviet Union, which had recently recognized Israel. Meir was displeased, as she spoke no Russian and feared loneliness in Moscow, stating, "At last we have a state. I want to be there. I don't want to go thousands of miles away. Why do I always have to go away?" Her return was delayed by a car crash that injured her leg and fractured a bone; Soviet officials refused to believe she was in the hospital and insisted on her return, so she ignored medical advice and returned on 29 July. She served as minister plenipotentiary from 2 September 1948 to 10 March 1949. She was impatient with diplomatic niceties and interpreters, did not drink or ballroom dance, and had little interest in gossip or fashion. When asked by a Russian ambassador how she traveled to Moscow, she replied, "tell His Excellency the Ambassador that we arrived riding on donkeys." This role was significant and difficult, as good Soviet relations affected Israel’s access to arms from Eastern Europe. Stalin and Molotov viewed the relationship as a tool for advancing Soviet influence in the Middle East. Soviet policies against religious and nationalist movements, including closing Jewish religious institutions and banning Hebrew language study and emigration to Israel, complicated relations. Just 20 days after her appointment, antisemitic crackdowns began in response to an article by Ilya Ehrenburg. Meir and her team responded by visiting Russian Jewish businesses, synagogues, and cultural events. On 3 October, during Rosh Hashanah at the Moscow Choral Synagogue, she was mobbed by thousands of Russian Jews chanting "Nasha Golda" ("Our Golda"), an experience she described as overwhelming and heart-stopping. This event was commemorated on the Israeli 10,000-shekel banknote issued in November 1984, which featured her portrait and the image of the crowd. To her close friends, she admitted.

Soviet–Israeli relations were complicated by Soviet policies targeting religious institutions and nationalist movements, including the shutdown of Jewish religious institutions, the ban on Hebrew language study, and the prohibition of promoting emigration to Israel. Just 20 days after her term began, antisemitic crackdowns started in response to an article by Soviet Jewish writer Ilya Ehrenburg. Meir and other Israeli representatives responded by visiting Russian Jewish businesses, synagogues, and cultural events. On 3 October, during Rosh Hashanah at the Moscow Choral Synagogue, she was mobbed by thousands of Russian Jews chanting "Nasha Golda," meaning "Our Golda," an event she described as overwhelming and emotionally powerful, with her heart slowing from the intensity of the love. This moment was commemorated by the Israeli 10,000-shekel banknote issued in November 1984, which featured her portrait on one side and the image of the Moscow crowd on the other. To her close friends, she admitted she had little to do in Moscow and felt isolated from Israeli politics. Despite being a socialist born in Ukraine, her Jewish identity caused friction with the Soviets, making progress difficult, and by the end of her term, she felt she had accomplished little and expressed guilt for not doing more for Russian Jews, as she would have been in their position if her father had not moved to the United States. She planned to run for the first Knesset elections on 25 January 1949, returned to Israel the month before, campaigned for Mapai, which won 35% of the votes and formed a coalition, and Ben-Gurion invited her into the cabinet. She was sworn in on 8 March and served in the Knesset until 1974. Ben-Gurion initially offered her the position of deputy prime minister, which she rejected due to its vague responsibilities and the need to coordinate with many departments. Instead, she took the role of Labor Minister from 10 March 1949 to 19 June 1956, which she called her "seven beautiful years," enjoying the ability to act quickly and independently and being one of the most powerful Israeli politicians at the time. A major source of friction was funding, especially for the millions of immigrants arriving in the new state. In October 1950, Meir announced a three-year development plan with a $15 billion price tag over 15 years, securing 40% of the budget through U.S. government and American Jewish loans, while Israel Bonds contributed only a small amount, though later became a major economic contributor. Meir assisted in building over a hundred ma'abarot—temporary immigrant camps with tin-roofed huts and tents—drawing criticism from new immigrants and politicians, but defended her actions by citing limited budgets and the time needed to build permanent housing. By 1953, she helped eliminate ma'abarot, with two-thirds eliminated by 1956 and 120,000 families moved to permanent housing. Meir considered herself highly productive, implementing welfare state policies, integrating immigrants into the workforce, and launching major housing and road construction projects. From 1949 to 1956, 200,000 apartments and 30,000 houses were built, large industrial and agricultural developments began, and new hospitals, schools, and roads were constructed. Despite Finance Ministry complaints, she established social security, maternity benefits, work-related accident insurance, benefits for widows and orphans, and burial costs. In 1954, she supported Ben-Gurion against Pinhas Lavon in the Lavon Affair. In the summer of 1955, she reluctantly ran for mayor of Tel Aviv at the request of her party, lost by two votes due to the religious bloc withholding support on grounds of her gender, and was happy to rejoin the cabinet. On 3 August 1955, she was hospitalized and diagnosed with arrhythmia. In October 1955, Ben-Gurion appointed her foreign minister, replacing Sharett, due to escalating disagreements between Ben-Gurion and Sharett, and although Meir was less experienced in foreign affairs than Sharett, she had a loyal and friendly relationship with Ben-Gurion, though she disliked the lingering pro-Sharett colleagues in her department. She served as foreign minister from 18 June 1956 to 12 January 1966. Her first months as foreign minister coincided with the 1956 Suez Crisis, in which Israel, Britain, and France invaded Egypt to regain Western control of the Suez Canal, remove President Gamal Abdel Nasser, and secure freedom of navigation through the Straits of Tiran. Meir planned and coordinated with the French government and military prior to the invasion and took charge of the Israeli delegation during United Nations debates. After the fighting began, the United States, the Soviet Union, and the United Nations forced the invaders to withdraw. As foreign minister, she promoted ties with newly established African states to gain international allies, believing Israel’s experience in nation-building could serve as a model for African nations, stating that both had overcome foreign rule and faced similar challenges in reclaiming land, increasing crop yields, irrigating, raising poultry, living together, and defending themselves. She also worked to convince the United States to sell Israel weapons, achieving success in 1962 when the White House quietly agreed to sell Hawk missiles. Israel’s relationship with the Soviet Union remained frosty during her tenure. On 29 October 1957, Meir’s foot was slightly injured when a Mills bomb was thrown into the Knesset debating chamber; David Ben-Gurion and Moshe Carmel were more seriously injured. The attack was carried out by 25-year-old Moshe Dwek, born in Aleppo, whose motives were attributed to a dispute with the Jewish Agency, and he was described as mentally unbalanced. In 1958, shortly after the death of Pope Pius XII, Meir praised him for assisting the Jewish people, a legacy that remains controversial. That same year, during the wave of Jewish migration from Poland to Israel, Meir sought to prevent disabled and sick Polish Jews from immigrating, writing in a letter to Israel’s ambassador in Warsaw, Katriel Katz: "A proposal was raised in the coordination committee to inform the Polish government that we want to institute selection in aliyah, because we cannot continue accepting sick and handicapped people. Please give your opinion as to whether this can be explained to the Poles without hurting immigration." In late 1965, 67-year-old Meir was diagnosed with lymphoma. In January 1966, she retired from her role as foreign minister, citing exhaustion and ill health, though she continued to serve in the Knesset and as secretary-general of Mapai. During the 1960s, Meir lived in a flat on the upper level of a house once known as Villa Harun al-Rashid, built in 1926 by Hanna Bisharat and later rented to British officers, then given to Zionist militias due to its prominent view. According to Hanna Bisharat’s grandson George Bisharat, Meir had the front tiles sandblasted to obliterate the name "Villa Harun al-Rashid" and conceal that she was living in an Arab home. Prime Minister Levi Eshkol died suddenly on 26 February 1969, leading to the appointment of Yigal Allon as interim prime minister and an election to replace him. Before the vote, most suspected Meir would be elected. On 7 March 1969, the party’s central committee voted Meir as the new party leader. At age 71, she had mixed feelings about her health but eventually agreed, saying she would honor the party’s decision as she had all past decisions. Meir served as prime minister from 17 March 1969 to 3 June 1974, maintaining the national unity government formed after the Six-Day War, in which Mapai merged with Rafi and Ahdut HaAvoda to form the Israeli Labor Party. Six months after taking office, she led the reconfigured Alignment, comprising Labor and Mapam, into the 1969 general election, which achieved the best showing for a single party or faction in Israeli history, winning 56 seats—the only time a party approached an outright majority—and retained the national unity government. In 1969 and the early 1970s, Meir met with world leaders to promote her peace settlement ideas, including Richard Nixon (1969), Nicolae Ceaușescu (1972), and Pope Paul VI (1973), and hosted West German Chancellor Willy Brandt in Israel. In August 1970, she accepted a U.S. peace initiative calling for an end to the War of Attrition and an Israeli pledge to withdraw to "secure and recognized boundaries" in a comprehensive peace settlement. The Gahal party quit the coalition in protest, but Meir continued to lead. On 28 February 1973, during a visit to Washington, D.C., Meir agreed with Henry Kissinger’s peace proposal based on "security versus sovereignty": Israel would accept Egyptian sovereignty over all Sinai, while Egypt would accept Israeli presence in some strategic positions in Sinai. In June 1969, on the second anniversary of the Six-Day War, Meir stated in an interview with The Sunday Times on June 15, 1969, that "there was no such thing as Palestinians," a comment later described by Al Jazeera as "one of her defining – and most damning – legacies" and considered a key example of Israeli denial of Palestinian identity. In the wake of the 1972 Munich massacre, Meir appealed to the world to "save our citizens and condemn the unspeakable criminal acts committed" and ordered the Mossad to hunt down and assassinate suspected leaders and operatives of Black September and the PFLP. During the 1970s, about 200,000 Soviet Jewish emigrants were allowed to leave the Soviet Union for Israel via Austria. When seven were taken hostage at the Austria–Czechoslovakia border in September 1973 by Palestinian militants, Austrian Chancellor Bruno Kreisky closed the Jewish Agency’s transit facility in Schönau. A few days later in Vienna, Meir tried to convince Kreisky to reopen it by appealing to his Jewish heritage, calling his position "succumbing to terrorist blackmail," but Kreisky refused, so Meir returned to Israel, infuriated. A few months later, Austria opened a new transition camp. A common criticism is that she could have avoided the Yom Kippur War in 1973. For months before the attack, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat made repeated peace overtures in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai, which were rebuffed by Meir, who had previously offered to discuss ceding "most of the Sinai" but refused to restore pre-1967 borders, and Egypt had no interest in peace talks under her conditions. In the days leading up to the war, Israeli intelligence could not confirm an imminent attack. On 5 October 1973, Meir received information that Syrian forces were massing on the Golan Heights and was alarmed, believing the situation resembled that before the Six-Day War. However, her advisers advised her not to worry, saying they would have adequate warning before war broke out, a view common after the Six-Day War. Despite the Knesset passing a resolution granting her power to demand a full-scale military call-up, Meir did not mobilize early. Soon, the threat became clear. Six hours before hostilities began, Meir met with Defense Minister Moshe Dayan and General David Elazar. While Dayan argued that war was unlikely and favored calling up only the air force and two divisions, Elazar advocated full-scale mobilization and a preemptive strike. On 6 October, Meir approved full-scale mobilization but rejected a preemptive strike, citing concerns that Israel might be seen as initiating hostilities, which would damage access to crucial foreign aid and military support, especially from the United States. She prioritized informing Washington of her decision. U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger later confirmed that if Israel had launched a preemptive strike, it would not have received U.S. backing. After the Yom Kippur War, Meir’s government faced infighting and questions over Israel’s lack of preparation. The Agranat Commission cleared her of "direct responsibility," stating that she wisely and quickly approved full mobilization of the reserves as recommended by the chief-of-staff, despite political considerations, performing a vital service for national defense. Her party won the December 1973 elections, but the coalition lost seats and could not form a majority. Meir resigned as prime minister on 11 April 1974 and gave up her Knesset seat on 7 June 1974, believing it was the "will of the people" and that she had served enough, stating that "five years are sufficient... It is beyond my strength to continue carrying this burden." Yitzhak Rabin succeeded her on 3 June 1974. In 1975, Meir published her autobiography, My Life, which became a New York Times Best Seller. On 21 November 1977, she spoke at the Knesset on behalf of the Labor Party to Egyptian President Anwar Sadat during his historic visit as the first Arab leader to visit Israeli-controlled territory, praising his courage and vision and expressing hope that mutual understanding could resolve differences for future generations. In May 1978, Meir was interviewed live by video link by Barbra Streisand at the finale of the American television special The Stars Salute Israel at 30, broadcast to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the state of Israel. On 8 December 1978, Meir died of lymphoma (lymphatic cancer) in Jerusalem at the age of 80 and was buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem. Her husband Morris Meyerson (also "Myerson") was born on 17 December 1893 in Chicago, Illinois. They married on 24 December 1917 and remained married until his death in Jerusalem on 25 May 1951. She never remarried. Despite never divorcing, the couple grew apart over time. When Meir took her children to the United States in the 1930s, Morris stayed behind in Jerusalem. Meir had two children.

Many differences remained to be resolved, that vision would be achieved in a spirit of mutual understanding.[76][77] In May 1978, Meir was interviewed live by video link by Barbra Streisand at the finale of the American television special The Stars Salute Israel at 30, broadcast to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the state of Israel.[78] On 8 December 1978, Meir died of lymphatic cancer (lymphoma) in Jerusalem at the age of 80. She was buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.[79][80] Meir's husband Morris Meyerson (also "Myerson") was born on 17 December 1893 in Chicago, Illinois. They married on December 24, 1917, and remained married until his death in Jerusalem on 25 May 1951. She never remarried. Despite never divorcing, the couple grew apart over the course of the marriage. When Meir took her children with her to the United States in the 1930s, Morris stayed behind in Jerusalem.[citation needed] Meir had two children. Her son, Menachem, was born in Jerusalem in 1924 and died on 14 December 2014 in Tel Aviv. He was a professional cellist who studied at the Israel Conservatory and Manhattan School of Music.[81] Her daughter Sarah was born on 17 May 1926 and died on 30 January 2010 in Revivim.[82] She had two sisters, Sheyna (1889–1972) and Tzipke (1902–1981), as well as five other siblings who died in childhood.[citation needed] Morris, Sheyna Korngold and her husband Shamai were buried on Nahalat Yitzhak Cemetery in Givatayim.[citation needed] In 1956, after becoming Foreign Minister, she changed her surname from "Meyerson" to "Meir", meaning "illuminate", as her predecessor Moshe Sharett had all members of the foreign service take a Hebrew surname.[citation needed] She was a heavy smoker and coffee drinker, and did not exercise often, which may have contributed to her recurring heart problems.[25] Of her Jewish identity, Meir said in the 1975 edition of her autobiography My Life that: "It is not only a matter, I believe, of religious observance and practice. To me, being Jewish means and has always meant being proud to be part of a people that has maintained its distinct identity for more than 2,000 years, with all the pain and torment that has been inflicted upon it."[83] She strongly identified with Judaism culturally, but was an atheist in religious belief.[84][85][86] She is famously reported to have stated: "I believe in the Jewish people, and the Jewish people believe in God."[87] In her later years she widened her religious attitude, especially concerning the State of Israel: "This country exists as the fulfillment of a promise made by God himself. It would be ridiculous to ask it to account for its legitimacy."[88] In 1974 Meir was awarded the James Madison Award for Distinguished Public Service by Princeton University's American Whig–Cliosophic Society.[89] Also in 1974, Meir was awarded the honor of World Mother by American Mothers.[90] In 1975, Meir was awarded the Israel Prize for her special contribution to society and the State of Israel.[72][91] In 1985, Meir was inducted into the Colorado Women's Hall of Fame.[92] In 2019, Time created 89 new covers to celebrate women of the year starting from 1920; it chose her for 1956.[93] Biographer Meron Medzini argues that a perspective of forty years makes possible an appreciation of her deep nationalism and Zionism. Historians find her main legacy includes effective leadership of the Labor Movement, and building good relationships with Third World nations. Medzini states, "Apart from laying the foundations for Israel’s presence in Africa, she was never taken with the routine and often dull diplomatic work in the Foreign Ministry and abhorred its outer manifestations of ceremonies and rites."[94] Most historians agree she was a success as Secretary of Labor and Housing, but a failure as prime minister.[7] A controversial figure in Israel, she has been lionized as a founder of the state and described as the "Iron Lady" of Israeli politics, but also widely blamed for the country being caught by surprise during the 1973 Yom Kippur War. She was also criticized for her dismissive statements towards the Palestinians.[68] Meir's story has been the subject of many fictionalized portrayals. In 1977, Anne Bancroft played Meir in William Gibson's Broadway play Golda. The Australian actress Judy Davis played a young Meir in the television film A Woman Called Golda (1982), opposite Leonard Nimoy. Ingrid Bergman played the older Meir in the same film. Actress Colleen Dewhurst portrayed Meir in the 1986 TV movie Sword of Gideon.[95] In 2003, American Jewish actress Tovah Feldshuh portrayed her on Broadway in Golda's Balcony, Gibson's second play about Meir's life. The play was controversial for implying that Meir considered using nuclear weapons during the Yom Kippur War.[citation needed] Valerie Harper portrayed Meir in the touring company production and in the film version of Golda's Balcony.[96] In 2005, actress Lynn Cohen portrayed Meir in Steven Spielberg's film Munich.[citation needed] Tovah Feldshuh assumed the role of Meir again in the 2006 English-language French movie O Jerusalem. She was played by the Polish actress Beata Fudalej in the 2009 dramatic film The Hope directed by Márta Mészáros.[97] English actor Helen Mirren portrayed Meir in the 2023 biopic film Golda, directed by Guy Nattiv and produced by Michael Kuhn. The film centres on the Yom Kippur War.[98] As of April 2021, a TV miniseries Lioness starring Shira Haas is also currently being produced and will be directed by Barbra Streisand.[99] In Israel, the term "Golda's shoes" (na'alei Golda) has become a reference to the sturdy orthopedic shoes that Golda favored. These shoes were also supplied to women soldiers in the Israel Defense Forces from its foundation to 1987.[108]

The Golden Temple, also known as Harimandir Sahib or Durbār Sahib, is a gurdwara located in Amritsar, Punjab, India, and is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism, alongside the Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur and the Gurdwara Janam Asthan in Nankana Sahib, both in Punjab, Pakistan. The sarovar (holy pool) on the site was completed by the fourth Sikh Guru, Guru Ram Das, in 1577. In 1604, Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the Golden Temple and played a key role in its development. The gurdwara was repeatedly rebuilt by the Sikhs after facing persecution and was destroyed several times by the Mughal and invading Afghan armies. Maharaja Ranjit Singh, after founding the Sikh Empire, rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809 and overlaid the sanctum with gold leaf in 1830, leading to its name "Golden Temple." The Golden Temple is spiritually the most significant shrine in Sikhism and became a center of the Singh Sabha Movement (1883–1920s) and the Punjabi Suba Movement (1947–1966). In the early 1980s, it became a center of conflict between the Indian government and a radical movement led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale. In 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ordered Operation Blue Star, a military action from 1 to 8 June 1984, to remove Bhindranwale and his followers from the complex, resulting in thousands of deaths among soldiers, militants, and civilians, significant damage to the gurdwara, and the destruction of the nearby Akal Takht—the prime seat of Sikh authority. The gurdwara complex was subsequently rebuilt. The Golden Temple is an open house of worship for all people, with a square plan, four entrances, and a circumambulation path around the pool; the four entrances symbolize Sikh beliefs in equality and inclusivity. The complex includes the Akal Takht, a clock tower, offices of the Gurdwara Committee, a museum, and a langar—a free vegetarian kitchen serving all visitors without discrimination. Over 150,000 people visit daily. The site has been nominated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with its application pending on the tentative list. The land for the site was chosen by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and named Guru Da Chakk; Guru Ram Das founded the town Ramdaspur, which later became Amritsar, after acquiring the land—either through donations of 700 rupees from the village of Tung or a donation from Emperor Akbar to Ram Das’s wife. Construction began in 1581, with the pool kept dry for eight years; Guru Arjan designed the gurdwara at a lower level to emphasize humility and ensured the compound was open on all sides to promote inclusivity. The sanctum had only one bridge, symbolizing the unity of the end goal. In 1589, the brick gurdwara was completed; some sources claim Guru Arjan invited the Sufi saint Mian Mir to lay the foundation stone, though this is unsubstantiated; traditional sources state he laid it himself. After the inauguration, the pool was filled with water, and on 16 August 1604, Guru Arjan completed the Adi Granth and appointed Baba Buddha as the first Granthi. The Ath Sath Tirath, a raised canopy on the circumambulation path, reflects the belief that visiting the temple is equivalent to 68 Hindu pilgrimage sites. The completion of the first version of the Golden Temple was a major milestone, providing a central pilgrimage site. Guru Arjan’s growing influence drew Mughal attention; he was arrested by Emperor Jahangir, tortured, and executed in 1606. His son, Guru Hargobind, fought a battle at Amritsar and left in 1635 for Kiratpur. The temple was occupied by the Minas for about a century. In the 18th century, Guru Gobind Singh sent Bhai Mani Singh to reclaim it. The temple remained a target of persecution by Mughal rulers and Afghan Sultans. After destruction, it was reconstructed in 1764 (confirmed by H.H. Cole) or 1776 (per Giani Gian Singh’s Tawarikh Sri Amritsar), with most decorations added in the early 19th century. Ranjit Singh, at age 22 in 1802, took Amritsar from the Bhangi Misl, paid homage at the temple, and announced plans to rebuild it in marble and gold. He donated gilded copper panels worth 500,000 rupees, with Mistri Yar Muhammad Khan overseeing the work under Bhai Sand Singh; the first panel was placed in 1803. Various individuals, including Tara Singh Gheba, Partap Singh, Jodh Singh, and Ganda Singh Peshawari (who donated in 1823), contributed to the ceiling decoration. Raja Sangat Singh of Jind State helped with the Darshani Deori. Due to the temple’s central importance, every Sikh sardar contributed to its renovations. The temple was renovated in marble and copper in 1809 and gold-leafed in 1830; an inscription at the entrance commemorates the work by Ranjit Singh and Giani Sant Singh of the Giani Samparda. A Gurmukhi inscription states that Maharaja Ranjit Singh was regarded as the chief servitor of the Great Guru. The 7th Nizam of Hyderabad, Mir Osman Ali Khan, began annual grants after learning of the temple through Ranjit Singh. Ranjit Singh took over management of the Durbar Sahib complex, appointing Sardar Desa Singh Majithia and making land grants to fund operations. Hari Singh Nalwa decorated the Akal Takht with gold and added the golden dome. Ranjit Singh made the position of temple officials hereditary; the Giani family were the only ones allowed to perform Katha from 1788 until 1921, when the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee took over, and they built the Bungas around the temple, including the gold and marble overlay. One of the main Bungas destroyed in 1988 was the Burj Gianian; the Kapurs were made heads of the Granthis, including ancestors of Bhai Jawahir Singh Kapur, who attempted but was denied the position. The temple complex was destroyed during Operation Blue Star, a military operation from 1 to 8 June 1984, ordered by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi after Harchand Singh Longowal invited Bhindranwale to reside in the complex to evade arrest. The government claimed Bhindranwale turned the temple into an armory and headquarters. After failed negotiations, the army attacked on 3 June 1984, with fighting lasting three days and ending on 8 June. The army used tanks and heavy artillery, facing resistance from militants with rocket-propelled grenade launchers and fortified positions at the Akal Takht. Casualty figures include 83 dead and 249 injured among soldiers, 1,592 militants apprehended, and 493 militant and civilian casualties; the government attributed high civilian deaths to militants using pilgrims as human shields. Foreign reporter Brahma Chellaney, the only one to remain in Amritsar, reported a death toll about twice the official figure—780 militants and civilians and 400 troops—stating that eight to ten men suspected of being militants were shot with hands tied and that a doctor was forced to perform postmortems. The Indian government charged Chellaney with violating press censorship, fanning sectarian hatred, and sedition. The operation was widely criticized by Sikhs worldwide as an assault on their religion, leading to many Sikh soldiers deserting and civil servants resigning. Five months later, on 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh. The public outcry led to over 3,000 Sikh killings in Delhi during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. Following the operation, hundreds of houses were demolished, and a security corridor called Galliara (Galiara or Galyara) was created around the compound and later opened as a public park in June 1988.

The military action in the temple complex was criticized by Sikhs worldwide, who viewed it as an assault on the Sikh religion. Many Sikh soldiers deserted their units, and several Sikhs resigned from civil administrative offices, returning awards received from the Indian government. Five months after the operation, on 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her two Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, in an act of revenge. Public outrage over her death led to the killing of more than 3,000 Sikhs in Delhi during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. Following the operation, the central government demolished hundreds of houses and created a security corridor called "Galliara" (also spelled Galiara or Galyara) around the compound. This corridor was later transformed into a public park and opened in June 1988. In December 2021, a young man was allegedly beaten to death after disrupting the Rehras Sahib (evening prayer) at the sanctum by jumping over a railing, picking up the sword before the Guru Granth Sahib, and attempting to touch it; he was overpowered by pilgrims and suffered fatal head injuries. The 2023 Golden Temple blasts occurred on 7 May and 9 May 2023. The Golden Temple's architecture reflects various architectural practices from the Indian subcontinent, with the first Harmandir Sahib built by Guru Arjan combining dharamsaals and holy water tanks (sarovar), constructed lower than the surroundings so devotees would have to walk down to reach it. The four entrances symbolize openness to all four traditional Indian caste classifications (varnas). No surviving record of the pre-1764 Harmandir Sahib built by the Sikh gurus exists, though Kanwarjit Singh Kang believes the original structure was similar to the 1764 version. James Fergusson considered the temple a specimen of 19th-century Hindu temple architecture. The colonial Punjab government in 1875 claimed the design, as built by Ranjit Singh, was based on the shrine of Sufi saint Mian Mir. Louis Rousselet described it as a "handsome style of Jat architecture," while Major Henry Hardy Cole noted it drew primarily from Islamic sources with Hindu influences. Percy Brown classified it as a synthesis of Islamic and Hindu styles with unique characteristics. Hermann Goetz viewed it as a "Kangra transformation of Oudh architecture," praising it but criticizing its "gaudy" elements, such as rococo-style art. Scholars like Ian Kerr describe it as a mixture of Indo-Islamic Mughal and Hindu Rajput architecture. The sanctum is 12.25 x 12.25 metres with two storeys and a gold leaf dome, sitting on a 19.7 x 19.7 metre marble platform within a 154.5 x 148.5 m² pool called Amritsar or Amritsarovar, which is 5.1 metres deep and surrounded by a 3.7-metre-wide circumambulatory marble passage. The sanctum is connected to the platform by a causeway, with the gateway called the Darshani Deorhi. Pilgrims can take a dip in the pool, believed to purify karma, and some carry water home for sick relatives. The pool is maintained by volunteers through periodic kar seva, including draining and desilting. The Har-Ki-Pauri section, located on the back of the temple, provides water for sipping and daily cleaning, with the cleaning solution mixed with milk. The Guru Granth Sahib is seated on the lower floor for about 20 hours daily and moved to its bedroom in the Akal Takht for four hours each day for sukhasana and Prakash. The upper floor is a gallery connected by stairs. The ground floor and surrounding path are lined with white marble, the exterior has gilded copper plates, doors are gold leaf-covered copper with nature motifs, the upper ceiling is gilded, embossed, and decorated with jewels, and the dome is semi-spherical with a pinnacle. The sides have arched copings and small domes, with corners adorned by cupolas, all covered in gold leaf. A pavilion called the Shish Mahal (mirror room) is on the second floor. Floral designs on the walls are Arabesque, arches contain verses from the Guru Granth Sahib in gold letters, and frescoes include animal, bird, and nature motifs. Stair walls feature murals of Sikh Gurus, such as a falcon carrying Guru Gobind Singh on horseback. The Darshani Deorhi houses temple management offices and treasury. The Prasada facility serves Karah prasad, a flour-based sweet offering. Pilgrims enter and circumambulate clockwise around the pool before entering the sanctum. There are four entrances to the gurdwara complex, symbolizing openness, but only one entrance to the sanctum via a causeway. In front of the sanctum is the Akal Takht, the chief Takht meaning "throne of the Timeless (God)," established by Guru Hargobind after his father's martyrdom as a center for spiritual and secular affairs, issuing binding writs. The Akal Takht is also known as Takht Sri Akal Bunga and is the primary seat among the five Sikh Takhts, located in Anandpur, Patna, Nanded, Talwandi Sabo, and Amritsar. It is the headquarters of the Shiromani Akali Dal (Supreme Akali Party). The Teja Singh Samundri Hall is the office of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, overseeing major Sikh temples. The Ramgarhia Bunga, two red sandstone minaret-style towers visible from the parikrama, was built in the 18th century by Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, a Sikh warrior and Ramgarhia misl chief, as watchtowers to defend against military raids. Over 70 such Bungas were built during the 18th century to house soldiers, provide accommodation, and serve as centers of learning; most were demolished during British rule, but the Ramgarhia Bunga remains a symbol of the community's identity and historical defense. The Clock Tower did not exist originally; in its place was a building called the "lost palace," which the British wanted to demolish after the Second Anglo-Sikh War. The Sikhs opposed it, but the demolition proceeded. The clock tower, designed by John Gordon in a Gothic style with red bricks, was built from 1862 to 1874 and later demolished by the Sikh community about 70 years later. A new entrance on the north side was constructed in its place, featuring a clock, a museum on the upper floor, and continuing to be called ghanta ghar deori. The original complex was open with many trees; now it is a walled, two-storey courtyard with four entrances, preserving three Ber trees. One, to the right of the main ghanta ghar deori, is called Ber Baba Buddha, believed to be where Baba Buddha sat during the pool and temple construction. A second, Laachi Ber, is where Guru Arjan rested during construction. The third, Dukh Bhanjani Ber, is on the other side of the sanctum, where a Sikh was cured of leprosy after bathing, earning it the name "suffering remover"; a small gurdwara is beneath it. The Ath Sath Tirath, or equivalent of 68 pilgrimages, is under this tree, and bathing nearby is believed to offer the same spiritual benefits as visiting 68 pilgrimage sites. The main north entrance has a Sikh history museum on the first floor, displaying paintings of gurus and martyrs, and historical items like swords, kartar, comb, and chakkars. A new underground museum near the clock tower also shows Sikh history. According to Louis E. Fenech, the display emphasizes persecution, martyrdom, and bravery, though it is partly ahistorical, such as a headless body continuing to fight. The main entrance has memorial plaques commemorating Sikh historical events, saints, martyrs, Ranjit Singh's contributions, and all Sikh soldiers who died in the two World Wars and Indo-Pakistan wars. The Amrit Sarovar is the main temple tank, measuring approximately 150 meters by 150 meters, with the shrine in the center, surrounded by a marble walkway. Construction began in November 1573 under Guru Amar Das, with major work by Guru Ram Das and expansion by Guru Arjan. The Udasis of Brahm Buta Akhara dug a hansli in 1783 to feed the sarovar, later made redundant by the construction of the Amritsar-Lahore and Kasur-Sabraon branches. Since 1866, the sarovar has been fed from the Jethuwal distributory of the Upper Bari Doab between the Beas and Ravi, via a connection between Kaulsar Sarovar and Amrit Sarovar; the canal was originally kachcha but later lined and covered. Since the 1900s, the sarovar has been regularly cleaned through kar seva, with the first modern cleaning held on 17 June 1923. Other prominent sarovars in Amritsar include Santokhsar, Ramsar, Kaulsar, and Bibeksar. Daily rites treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a living person, including ceremonies for its seating and movement. The complex includes a langar, a community-run free kitchen and dining hall attached to the east side near the Dukh Bhanjani Ber, outside the entrance. Vegetarian food is served to all visitors regardless of faith, gender, or economic status, with everyone sitting on the floor in rows called sangat. Over 100,000 meals are served daily. The art of the Golden Temple has rarely been seriously studied. The Shish Mahal features mirror-work with small mirror pieces inlaid into walls and ceilings, highlighted by floral designs. Ceilings, walls, and arches are embellished with intricate murals. Pietra dura artwork, featuring avian and animal designs using semi-precious stones, is inspired by Mughal tradition. The premises are also decorated with embossed copper, gach, tukri, jaratkari, and ivory inlay. External upper walls have beaten copper plates with raised floral and abstract designs, including human figures. Two embossed copper panels on the front depict Guru Nanak with companions Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, and an equestrian portrayal of Guru Gobind Singh. Gach is a type of stone or gypsum, transformed into paste and applied to walls like lime-plaster, then decorated with steel cutters and tools; colored glass pieces placed on it are known as tukri, with many examples in the Shish Mahal. Jaratkari involves placing inlaid and cut stones of various colors and types into marble, with surviving examples found in the temple.

Plates at the Golden Temple often feature raised designs, typically floral or abstract, though some include human figures. Two embossed copper panels on the front of the temple prior depict Guru Nanak with his companions, Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, on either side, and another shows an equestrian portrayal of Guru Gobind Singh. Gach, a type of stone or gypsum, was transformed into a paste similar to lime-plaster and applied to walls, where it was shaped using steel cutters and other tools; sometimes coloured glass pieces, known as tukri, were embedded, as seen extensively in the Shish Mahal. Jaratkari, an art form involving inlaid and cut stones of various colours and types into marble, is found on the lower exterior walls of the temple, using semi-precious stones like lapis lazuli and onyx, classified as pietra dura. Unlike Mughal jaratkari, which does not include human or animal figuratives, Sikh jaratkari art features such depictions. Inlaid ivory work is visible on the doors of the Darshani Deori, constructed from shisham wood, with the front overlaid in silverwork and the back adorned with floral, geometric, and animal designs including deer, tigers, lions, and birds; portions of the ivory were coloured red or green, praised by H.H. Cole for their harmony. The oldest surviving murals date to the 1830s, with most destroyed during renovations under the guise of kar seva, such as by covering walls with marble slabs. A prominent mural artist was Gian Singh Naqqash, whose works include floral designs with scattered animal themes and over 300 distinct patterns across the walls. Naqqashi artists developed a specialized language for their designs, with the most prominent category being dehin, defined as an imaginative expression of idealised forms, rooted in gharwanjh—a decorative motif of knotted animals like cobras, lions, and elephants holding or carrying floral vases with fruit and fairies—while the border of dehin is called patta, often featuring creepers or aquatic creatures. The only mural of human figures inside the temple is on the wall behind the northern staircase, depicting Guru Gobind Singh on horseback with his retinue leaving Anandpur, adapted from a Kangra miniature painting. H.H. Cole noted that murals of Indic mythological scenes once existed but have since been lost. W. Wakefield reported erotic murals in 1875, but Kanwarjit Singh Kang considers this account spurious due to lack of corroboration. Most artists and craftsmen involved in the temple’s artwork remain unidentified, though Hari Singh compiled a list including Kishan Singh, Bishan Singh, Kapur Singh, Kehar Singh, Mahant Ishar Singh, Sardul Singh, Jawahar Singh, Mehtab Singh, Mistri Jaimal Singh, Harnam Singh, Ishar Singh (distinct from Mahant Ishar Singh), Gian Singh, Lal Singh Tarn Taran, Mangal Singh, Mistri Narain Singh, Mistri Jit Singh, Atma Singh, Darja Mal, and Vir Singh. Most lost artwork, especially murals, disappeared over time, beginning in the late 19th century when devotees started donating inlaid marble panels that covered previously painted walls, hiding or destroying the murals. The traditional bungas surrounding the temple, which housed many murals, were demolished over time under the guise of modernisation and expansion of the parikrama, leading to the loss of their artwork. When the Darshani Deori was covered with marble panels, murals by Mahant Ishar Singh were also lost. The Singh Sabha movement, beginning in the 1870s, aimed to reform Sikhism in response to conversions to Christianity and Hinduism, with the Tat Khalsa group becoming dominant by the early 1880s. Before 1905, the Golden Temple had Brahmin priests and idols for over a century, but by the 1890s, reformist Sikhs opposed these practices, and in 1905, under the Tat Khalsa campaign, idols and images were removed. The movement led to the reassertion of the Khalsa in gurdwara administration, displacing the mahant class. In 1919, during the Baisakhi festival, Sikhs gathered at the Golden Temple and proceeded to Jallianwala Bagh, where Colonel Dyer opened fire on a crowd, killing 379 and wounding thousands. This massacre intensified opposition to British rule and led to non-violent protests that pressured the British to transfer control of the Golden Temple’s management and finances to the elected Shiromani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee (SGPC), which continues to manage it. The Punjabi Suba movement, initiated by the Shiromani Akali Dal in April 1948, demanded a Punjabi-speaking state in East Punjab after the States Reorganisation Commission failed to address linguistic boundaries. The Golden Temple complex served as its main centre, hosting key events such as the 1955 government raid and the Amritsar Convention, where Sikh sentiments were conveyed to the central government. The complex was also a site for speeches, demonstrations, mass arrests, and hunger strikes, with movement leaders residing in huts during such periods. The movement culminated in 1966 with the establishment of the modern state of Punjab and the official recognition of Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script. In the early 1980s, militant groups such as the Dharam Yudh Morcha led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, Babbar Khalsa, AISSF, and the National Council of Khalistan occupied the Golden Temple and Akal Takht. In December 1983, Harchand Singh Longowal invited Bhindranwale to reside there, and under General Shabeg Singh’s military leadership, bunkers and observation posts were built, and armed militants were organised at Harmandir Sahib in June 1984. The temple became a site for weapons training, and Shabeg Singh’s defences made a commando operation on foot impossible. Supporters circulated maps proposing historical and future boundaries of Khalsa Sikh territories in northwest India, north Pakistan, and eastern Afghanistan. In June 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ordered Operation Blue Star, resulting in severe damage, destruction of the Akal Takht, and official death tolls of 492 civilians and 83 Indian soldiers. Within days, around 2,000 Sikh soldiers mutinied and attempted to reach Amritsar to liberate the temple. On 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards. In 1986, her son Rajiv Gandhi ordered repairs to the Akal Takht, which were later removed and rebuilt by Sikhs in 1999.
