Google Chrome is a cross-platform web browser developed by Google, launched in 2008 for Microsoft Windows, built using free software components from Apple WebKit and Mozilla Firefox. Versions were later released for Linux, macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and Android, where it is currently the default browser. The browser is also the main component of ChromeOS, serving as the platform for web applications. Most of Chrome's source code comes from Google's open-source project Chromium, but Chrome is licensed as proprietary freeware. Initially using the WebKit rendering engine, Google forked it in 2013 to create the Blink engine, which all Chrome variants except iOS used as of 2017. As of December 2025, StatCounter estimates Chrome has a 75.23% worldwide browser market share on personal computers, is the most-used browser on tablets and smartphones, and holds a 71.22% market share across all platforms combined, making it the most-used web browser globally. Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page spearheaded a software demonstration using Mozilla Firefox developers, which convinced CEO Eric Schmidt—initially opposed to entering the browser market due to concerns about "bruising browser wars" and Google's size—to prioritize Chrome as a core business, leading to its commercial success. Schmidt stated that the demonstration was so good it "essentially forced me to change my mind." Rumors of Google developing a browser first appeared in September 2004, following the rise of Mozilla Firefox 1.0 and Internet Explorer's security issues. Chrome development began in 2006 and was spearheaded by Sundar Pichai. The browser was first publicly released as a beta version on September 2, 2008, for Windows XP and newer with support for 43 languages, and later released as a stable version on December 11, 2008. A passage in the initial beta's Terms of Service granting Google a license to all content transferred via Chrome was criticized and removed after being inherited from general Google terms. Chrome quickly gained about 1% usage share, dropped to 0.69% in October 2008, then rose back above 1% by December 2008. Google planned to release versions for macOS and Linux in early 2009, with developer previews announced on June 4, 2009, and beta versions released in December 2009. Chrome 5.0, announced on May 25, 2010, was the first stable release supporting all three platforms. Chrome was one of twelve browsers offered on BrowserChoice.eu for European Economic Area Windows users in 2010. Chrome was assembled from 25 code libraries, including Mozilla's Netscape Portable Runtime, Network Security Services (dropped in version 45), Skia Graphics Engine, SQLite, and others, with the V8 JavaScript engine, developed by a team in Denmark led by Lars Bak, being a key component due to its performance benefits for web applications like Gmail. Chrome initially used WebKit, then forked it to create Blink in 2013, using only WebKit's WebCore components while replacing other parts like its multi-process architecture. Chrome is internally tested with unit testing, automated user action testing, fuzz testing, and WebKit layout tests (99% passed), as well as against commonly accessed websites within 20–30 minutes. Google created Gears for Chrome to add web application features like offline support, which were later replaced by HTML5 standards. In March 2011, Google introduced a simplified logo to reflect Chrome's focus on a clutter-free, easy-to-use web experience. On January 11, 2011, Chrome removed H.264 video codec support for its HTML5 player to align with open codecs in the Chromium project, though hardware-accelerated H.264 decoding was added in November 2012. In October 2013, Cisco open-sourced its H.264 codecs. On February 7, 2012, Google launched Chrome Beta for Android 4.0 devices, and on many new Android 4.1+ devices, Chrome became the default browser. In May 2017, Google announced a version of Chrome for augmented and virtual reality devices. Chrome features a minimalistic interface, including the merging of the address and search bars into the omnibox. The first release passed Acid1 and Acid2 tests, and from version 4.0 passed all aspects of Acid3, though as of April 2017 it no longer passes Acid3 due to evolving web standards. In May 2011, Chrome scored 10 failed/11,578 passed in the ECMAScript Test 262 (ES5.1), outperforming Firefox 19 (193 failed) and Internet Explorer 9 (600+ failed), with IE10 scoring 7 failed. On the W3C CSS 2.1 test suite, Chrome's rendering engine passed 89.75% of tests. On the HTML5 test, Chrome 41 scored 518 out of 555, ahead of the five most popular desktop browsers, with Chrome 41 on Android scoring 510 out of 555, and Chrome 44 scoring 526, just 29 points below the maximum. The default interface includes back, forward, refresh/cancel, and menu buttons, with a home button available via Settings. Tabs are positioned at the top of the window, and can be transferred between containers by dragging. Each tab includes an omnibox with URL and search functions. When a user types in the omnibox, Chrome provides suggestions based on visited sites, popular websites, and searches, with instant suggestions based on visited sites not being turnable off. If keywords are typed and Enter is pressed, a search is conducted using the default search engine. The New Tab Page displays thumbnails of the most visited sites, frequent searches, bookmarks, and recently closed tabs, with features like rearranging, pinning, and removing thumbnails, and a "Recently closed" bar and "tips" section. Starting with version 3.0, users can install themes to customize the browser, with many free themes available in an online gallery. Chrome includes a bookmarks submenu with access to the Bookmark Manager and a toggle for the bookmarks bar. On January 2, 2019, Google introduced Native Dark Theme for Chrome on Windows 10. In 2023, Chrome was completely revamped using Google's Material You design language, including more rounded corners, dynamic color systems similar to Android 12, a revamped address bar, new icons and tabs, and a simplified 3-dot menu. Starting with version 4.1, Chrome included a built-in translation bar using Google Translate, available for 52 languages, which prompts users to translate when a foreign language is detected. Chrome allows users to synchronize bookmarks, history, and settings across devices via a chosen Google Account, updating all signed-in instances. For web developers, Chrome includes an element inspector to examine a webpage's DOM structure. Chrome has special URLs that load application-specific pages and a built-in feature to enable experimental functions, originally called about:labs and later renamed to about:flags. The desktop edition can save pages as HTML with assets in a "_files" subfolder or as unprocessed HTML-only documents, or in MHTML format. Users can create local desktop shortcuts to open web applications without the regular interface, allowing web apps to run alongside local software. This feature was enhanced with the Chrome Web Store, launched on December 7, 2010, allowing users to install web applications as extensions. In September 2013, Google introduced Chrome apps "For your desktop," enabling offline access, desktop shortcuts, and less dependence on Chrome, with apps launching in separate windows resembling native applications. The Chrome Web Store, opened on February 11, 2011, with Chrome 9.0, allows users to install extensions and apps, with themes and extensions integrated into a searchable catalog. Browser extensions can modify Chrome, are supported on desktop but not mobile, and are written using HTML, JavaScript, and CSS, distributed through the Chrome Web Store. Extensions include accessibility features like Google Tone, which uses speakers to share URLs with nearby devices. Extensions were enabled by default on the developer channel in September 2009, with a beta gallery launching in December with about 300 extensions, expanding to approximately 1,500 by January 2010. In 2014, Google began restricting Windows users from installing extensions not hosted on the Chrome Web Store, expanding this to all Windows and Mac users in 2015 after reporting a 75% drop in customer support requests for uninstalling unwanted extensions. In October 2018, Google introduced Manifest V3, a major update to the extension API that modernizes the architecture, improves security and performance, uses declarative APIs to reduce broad access, replaces background pages with limited "Service Workers," and prohibits remotely-hosted code. This change drew criticism for limiting ad blockers' ability to check rules and update filter lists independently. The V8 JavaScript engine used by Chrome features dynamic code generation, hidden class transitions, and precise garbage collection. In 2008, several websites conducted benchmark tests using the SunSpider JavaScript Benchmark and Google's own computationally intense benchmarks, including ray tracing and constraint solving, which unanimously reported Chrome's performance.

Google announced a major update to Chrome's extension API known as "Manifest V3," which modernizes the extension architecture to improve security and performance by adopting declarative APIs to reduce broad access and enable more efficient browser implementations, replacing background pages with feature-limited "Service Workers" to lower resource usage, and prohibiting remotely-hosted code. This change drew criticism because it restricts the number of rules and types of expressions that ad blockers can check and prevents independent updates to ad-blocking filter lists. Chrome uses the V8 JavaScript engine, which includes features such as dynamic code generation, hidden class transitions, and precise garbage collection. In 2008, benchmark tests using SunSpider and Google's own computationally intensive benchmarks—such as ray tracing and constraint solving—showed Chrome outperformed competitors including Safari (Windows), Firefox 3.0, Internet Explorer 7, Opera, and Internet Explorer 8; however, by October 11, 2010, independent tests revealed Chrome was scoring behind Opera's Presto engine after version 10.5. Mozilla claimed its TraceMonkey JavaScript engine (in beta) was faster than Chrome's V8 in some tests, with John Resig noting Chrome's strong performance on recursion-intensive benchmarks but questioning whether Google's suite reflected real-world applications, citing Firefox 3.0's poor performance due to missing recursion-tracing. Two weeks after Chrome's 2008 launch, the WebKit team introduced SquirrelFish Extreme, which reported a 36% speed improvement over V8. Chrome uses DNS prefetching to speed up website lookups, a feature shared with Firefox, Safari, Internet Explorer (via DNS Pre-resolution), and Opera (as a UserScript). Chrome previously used the SPDY protocol instead of HTTP for servers supporting it, such as Google services, Facebook, and Twitter, but SPDY support was removed in Chrome version 51 due to its replacement by HTTP/2. In November 2019, Google began developing "speed badging" systems to inform users why pages load slowly, with no release date provided. Chrome once had a Data Saver feature called Lite Mode, which automatically lazy-loaded images and iframes to speed up page loads, announced by engineers Addy Osmani and Scott Little; however, Lite Mode was disabled in Chrome 100 due to a decrease in mobile data costs in many countries. Chrome periodically retrieves updates from two blacklists—one for phishing and one for malware—and warns users when visiting flagged sites; this service is also available via the free public "Google Safe Browsing API." Chrome uses a process-allocation model to sandbox tabs, applying the principle of least privilege so that each tab process cannot access critical memory functions or interact with other tab processes, similar to Microsoft's "Protected Mode" in Internet Explorer 9 and later; on Linux, this uses seccomp mode. In January 2015, TorrentFreak reported that using Chrome with a VPN could pose serious security risks due to WebRTC support. On September 9, 2016, Chrome 56 introduced warnings for visiting insecure HTTP websites to encourage migration to HTTPS. On December 4, 2018, Google released Chrome 71 with new security features, including a built-in ad-blocking system and a plan to combat websites that enable involuntary mobile subscription sign-ups. On September 2, 2020, Chrome 85 extended support for Secure DNS on Android, enabling automatic switching to DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) when the DNS provider supports it. Since 2008, Chrome has been criticized for lacking a master password to protect user passwords; developers argue it does not provide meaningful security against determined attackers and have refused to implement one, with related bugs marked "WontFix"; as of February 2014, Chrome requires the user to enter their Windows account password before showing saved passwords. On Linux, Chrome/Chromium stores passwords in three ways: GNOME Keyring, KWallet, or plain text, with automatic selection based on the desktop environment; passwords in GNOME Keyring or KWallet are encrypted and protected by dedicated daemons, while plain text passwords are not; previously stored unencrypted passwords are automatically moved to encrypted stores when these services are used; support for GNOME Keyring and KWallet was added in version 6 and became the default in version 12. As of version 45, Chrome's password manager is no longer integrated with Keychain due to lost interoperability. No Chrome security vulnerabilities were exploited in the 2009–2011 Pwn2Own events; at Pwn2Own 2012, a French team exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in the Flash version bundled with Chrome to gain full control of a fully patched 64-bit Windows 7 machine via a booby-trapped website that bypassed Chrome's sandboxing. Chrome was also compromised twice at the 2012 CanSecWest Pwnium; Google's response, delivered by Jason Kersey, praised the researchers and noted the exploits were "works of art," with fixes deployed within 10 hours of submission. A significant number of Chrome vulnerabilities stemmed from Adobe Flash Player; for example, the 2016 Pwn2Own attack on Chrome relied on four vulnerabilities—two in Flash, one in Chrome, and one in the Windows kernel. In 2016, Google announced plans to phase out Flash Player in Chrome, beginning with version 53, initially disabling it for ads and background analytics, with the ultimate goal of full disablement by the end of the year, except on sites deemed broken without it; Flash was later re-enabled on a site-by-site basis excluding ads and analytics. Leaked documents from 2013 to 2016, codenamed Vault 7, detail the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency's capabilities, including the ability to compromise web browsers like Chrome. Google introduced download scanning protection in Chrome 17; in February 2018, it added an ad-blocking feature based on Interactive Advertising Bureau recommendations, giving sites employing invasive ads a 30-day warning before blocking their ads; Consumer Reports advised users to install dedicated ad-blocking tools for better protection against malware and tracking. Incognito mode prevents Chrome from storing local history, cookies, site data, or form inputs, though downloaded files and bookmarks are saved; user activity remains visible to websites and Internet service providers. Incognito mode is similar to private browsing in other browsers and does not prevent saving across all windows—users can switch between incognito and regular windows, with only the incognito window operating in private mode. The iOS version of Chrome supports locking incognito tabs with Face ID, Touch ID, or device passcode; in 2022, Google began implementing this feature on Android versions, now available on Android 12 and above if hardware supports it. In 2024, Google agreed to destroy billions of records to settle a lawsuit alleging it secretly tracked internet use of users who believed they were browsing privately in incognito mode. In February 2012, Google introduced the Do Not Track (DNT) standard to inform websites of a user's preference not to be tracked, implemented in version 23; the protocol is turned off by default in Chrome, in line with the W3C draft standard. Chrome uses a multi-process architecture where each site instance and plugin runs in a separate process, known as process isolation, enhancing security and stability by preventing interference between tasks; an attacker gaining access to one tab cannot access others, and a crash in one instance results in a "Sad Tab" screen instead of a full browser crash; this architecture reduces memory fragmentation over time and was later adopted by Safari and Firefox. Chrome includes a Task Manager that allows users to monitor memory usage, download volume, and CPU consumption by sites and plugins and to terminate them; Chrome version 23 improved battery life on systems with GPU-accelerated video decoding. The first production release occurred on December 11, 2008, ending the initial beta period and beginning production; on January 8, 2009, Google introduced a three-channel release system: Stable, Beta, and Developer (Dev), replacing the previous two channels; all Developer users were moved to Beta, with Dev builds becoming less stable. Each channel has a distinct release cycle and stability level: Stable updates roughly quarterly with features and fixes that passed thorough Beta testing, Beta updates monthly with stable features migrated from Dev, and Dev updates once or twice weekly, exposing new features that may be unstable. In July 2010, Google shortened the Stable release cycle from quarterly to six weeks; Beta releases followed at a similar rate, one month earlier, and Dev releases occurred weekly or biweekly, allowing time for basic testing. A fourth channel, Canary, was introduced, updated daily from a build at 09:00 UTC from the most stable of the last 40 revisions, named after the canary-in-a-coal-mine practice to detect crashes; if a Canary build fails, it is blocked from migrating to Dev until fixed. Canary is the most bleeding-edge official version of Chrome, running side by side with other channels and allowing different profiles, themes, and preferences; it does not natively become the default browser, though it can be set via System Preferences on Windows and macOS. Canary was initially Windows-only, with a macOS version released on May 3, 2011. The Chrome beta channel for Android launched on January 10, 2013, running side by side with the stable channel; Chrome Dev for Android launched on April 29, 2015. Chrome channels are automatically distributed according to their release cycles; on Windows, updates are managed via Google Update, controllable via Group Policy; users can also download standalone installers that do not auto-update. On macOS, updates are managed via Google Update Service, controllable via macOS "defaults"; on Linux, updates are handled by the system's package manager. This auto-updating behavior contrasts with Chromium, the open-source core of Chrome, which provides continuous source code builds and requires users to manage their own updates. In March 2021, Google announced that starting with Chrome 94 in the third quarter of 2021, Stable releases would occur every four weeks instead of six weeks since 2010, and a new release channel for system administrators and browser embedders with eight-week releases was introduced. Releases are identified by a four-part version number, e.g., 42.0.2311.90 (Windows Stable release April 14, 2015); the components are major.minor.build.patch. Chromium and Chrome release schedules are linked through annual Branch Point dates, which precede the final Developer build release by four days and the Stable initial release by about 53 days. For example, the version 42 Branch Point was on February 20, 2015; Developer builds stopped at build 2311 with release 42.0.2311.4 on February 24 (four days later); the first Stable release, 42.0.2311.90, was on April 14, 2015 (53 days after the Branch Point). Chrome supports color management using system-provided ICC v2 and v4 support on macOS and ICC v2 profiles by default on other platforms starting from version 22. When not connected to the internet, Chrome displays an "8-bit" Tyrannosaurus rex on the "No internet" error screen; pressing the space bar, clicking, or tapping the T-Rex causes it to jump and dash across a cactus-ridden desert, revealing it as an Easter egg in the form of an infinite runner game with no time limit and periodic black tinting; school or enterprise managers can disable the game. As of April 2016, stable 32-bit and 64-bit builds are available for Windows, with only 64-bit stable builds available for Linux and macOS; 64-bit Windows builds became available in the developer channel and as Canary builds on June 3, 2014, in the beta channel on July 30.

When Chrome is not connected to the Internet and displays a "No internet" message, an "8-bit" Tyrannosaurus rex appears at the top of the screen; pressing the space bar, clicking it with a mouse, or tapping it on touch devices causes the T-Rex to jump and dash across a cactus-filled desert, revealing it as an Easter egg in the form of a platform game. The game is an infinite runner with no time limit, progressing faster over time and periodically tinting to a black background. A school or enterprise manager can disable this game. As of April 2016, stable 32-bit and 64-bit builds of Chrome are available for Windows, with only 64-bit stable builds available for Linux and macOS. 64-bit Windows builds became available in the developer channel on June 3, 2014, in the beta channel on July 30, 2014, and in the stable channel on August 26, 2014. 64-bit macOS builds became available as canary builds on November 7, 2013, in the beta channel on October 9, 2014, and in the stable channel on November 18, 2014. Starting with version 89, Chrome will only be supported on Intel/Intel x86 and AMD processors with the SSE3 instruction set. A beta version for Android 4.0 devices was launched on February 7, 2012, available in a limited number of countries via Google Play. Notable features include synchronization with desktop Chrome for shared bookmarks and tabs, page pre-rendering, and hardware acceleration. Chrome supports many HTML5 features such as GPU-accelerated canvas, CSS 3D Transforms, CSS animations, SVG, WebSocket (including binary messages), Dedicated Workers, overflow scroll, strong HTML5 video support, IndexedDB, WebWorkers, Application Cache, File APIs, date- and time-pickers, and parts of the Media Capture API. Mobile customizations include swipe gesture tab switching, link preview with zooming to ensure the correct link is clicked, and font size boosting for readability. Features missing in the mobile version include sandboxed tabs, Safe Browsing, apps or extensions, Adobe Flash (now and in the future), Native Client, and the ability to export user data like open tabs or browsing history into portable files. Development changes include remote debugging and part of the browser layer being implemented in Java, communicating with Chromium and WebKit via Java Native Bindings; Chrome for Android is a fork of the Chromium project, with a priority to upstream new and modified code to Chromium and WebKit. The April 17, 2012, update added support for 31 additional languages and availability in all countries where Google Play is available, allowing users to request a desktop version of a website instead of a mobile one, and enabling Android users to add bookmarks to their home screens and choose which apps handle links. On June 27, 2012, Chrome for Android exited beta and became stable. Chrome 18.0.1026311, released on September 26, 2012, was the first version to support mobile devices based on Intel x86. Starting from version 25, the Chrome version for Android aligns with the desktop version, with new stable releases available simultaneously. A separate Chrome for Android beta channel was launched on January 10, 2013, with version 25, and as of 2013, a separate beta version is available in the Google Play Store and can run alongside the stable release. Chrome is available on Apple's iOS and iPadOS, released on June 26, 2012, supporting iPad, iPhone, and formerly iPod touch; the current version requires iOS 17.0 or greater or iPadOS 17.0 or greater. Due to Apple's App Store requirements, this version uses iOS WebKit, Apple's rendering engine, and thus cannot use Google's V8 JavaScript engine. Chrome is the default browser for the iOS and iPadOS Gmail app. In a Chitika review from July 18, 2012, Chrome had 1.5% of the iOS browser market; by October 2013, it had 3% of the market. On Linux, 32-bit Intel processor support ended in March 2016, though Chromium remains supported; as of Chrome version 26, Linux installations require GCC v4.6 and GTK v2.24 or later, making systems like Debian 6 (2.20) and RHEL 6 (2.18) deprecated. Support for Chrome on Windows XP and Vista ended in April 2016; the last version compatible with these systems was Chrome 49.0.2623.112, released on April 7, 2016, and re-released on April 11, 2016. Support for Windows 7 was initially set to end on July 15, 2021, but was moved back to January 15, 2022, then again to January 15, 2023, due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and enterprise migration delays; support for Windows 7, 8, and 8.1 ended on this date, with Chrome 109 being the last version supporting these operating systems. "Windows 8 mode" was introduced in 2012 for the developer channel, enabling a full-screen, tablet-optimized interface with snapping, sharing, and search features; it was changed in October 2013 to use a desktop-like ChromeOS interface with a dedicated windowing system and taskbar, and was removed in version 49, with users upgrading to Windows 10 losing this feature. Google dropped support for Mac OS X 10.5 with Chrome 22; 32-bit Chrome support ended in November 2014 with Chrome 39; support for Mac OS X 10.6, 10.7, and 10.8 ended in April 2016 with Chrome 50; support for OS X 10.9 ended in April 2018 with Chrome 66; OS X 10.10 ended in January 2021 with Chrome 88; OS X 10.11 and macOS 10.12 ended in August 2022 with Chrome 104; macOS 10.13 and 10.14 ended in September 2023 with Chrome 117; macOS 10.15 ended in September 2024 with Chrome 129; macOS 11 ended in August 2025 with Chrome 139. Google Chrome is the foundation of ChromeOS, which ships on hardware from Google's manufacturing partners, featuring a minimalist interface resembling the Chrome browser and being designed for users who spend most of their time online; the only applications are a browser with media player and file manager. Google announced ChromeOS on July 7, 2009. Upon release, Chrome received acclaim; Matthew Moore of The Daily Telegraph noted it was "attractive, fast and has some impressive new features." Initially, Microsoft downplayed the threat from Chrome, predicting most users would stick with Internet Explorer 8, while Opera said Chrome would strengthen the web. By February 25, 2010, BusinessWeek reported that Google's Chrome had forced Microsoft to re-engage with browser development after years of inactivity. Mozilla stated Chrome's entry was not surprising and that it would not affect Google's revenue relationship with Mozilla. Chrome's design bridges desktop and cloud computing by allowing desktop, Start menu, or QuickLaunch shortcuts to any web page or application, blurring the line between online and desktop experiences. Google has been accused of using Chrome and Blink to promote in-house web standards implemented first in its services, leading to performance issues and compatibility problems, with some developers refusing to test on other browsers. Tom Warren of The Verge compared Chrome to Internet Explorer 6 due to its ubiquity. In 2021, computer scientist and lawyer Jonathan Mayer stated Chrome has become an agent for Google LLC rather than a user agent, lacking meaningful privacy protections, pushing users toward Google Account linking, and implementing invasive advertising. A class-action lawsuit seeking $5 billion in damages was filed in 2020 over misleading claims about incognito mode tracking; in December 2023, a settlement was agreed upon and filed in federal court on April 1, 2024, requiring Google to delete billions of browsing records, revise disclosures about data collection in incognito mode, and allow users to block third-party cookies for five years, without monetary damages and pending court approval. In June 2015, the Debian developer community discovered that Chromium 43 and Chrome 43 were programmed to download the Hotword Shared Module, which could enable the OK Google voice recognition extension, though it was off by default, raising privacy concerns; the module was removed in Chrome 45, released on September 1, 2015, and was only present in Chrome 43 and 44. Chrome sends user activity details to Google through both optional and non-optional tracking mechanisms. Some tracking features can be enabled or disabled during installation or through browser settings; unofficial builds like SRWare Iron aim to remove these features. The RLZ library, used to measure marketing success, is not included in the Chromium browser. In March 2010, Chrome began using a unique ID token for installation statistics only on the first connection made by Google Update. The optional suggestion service, which sends typed text in the Omnibox to search providers before return, has been criticized for providing search engines with IP-addressed web use data. Chrome previously suggested similar pages when a page was not found, contacting Google servers for this, a feature that has since been removed. A 2019 Washington Post review by Geoffrey A. Fowler found that Chrome stores thousands more cookies than Mozilla Firefox in a typical week, noting Google's financial interest in collecting user data and recommending a switch to Firefox, Safari, or Chromium-based Brave. On installation, tracking can be disabled in ChromeOS; for other operating systems, it can be disabled through the installation interface or browser options. In 2023, Google proposed a technology to "hide the IP and traffic of its users" by routing Chrome traffic to Google servers, drawing criticism as all traffic remains accessible to Google. Chrome is tied to Google's advertising business, which introduced FLoC and later Topics to replace third-party cookies and Manifest V3 API changes for extensions. In January 2021, Google announced progress on privacy-friendly alternatives to replace third-party cookies, promising to phase them out by 2022 with FLoC; this triggered antitrust investigations by the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission, and drew criticism from DuckDuckGo, Brave, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation for underestimating user tracking capabilities. On January 25, 2022, Google announced the end of FLoC development and the introduction of the Topics API as a replacement, which uses weekly web activity to determine five interests, refreshing every three weeks and not retaining data. Manifest V3 has faced criticism for changes to the WebRequest API used by ad blockers and privacy extensions, with the declarative version processing rules in the browser instead of sending all traffic through extensions, improving performance but limiting rule count and expression types. The prohibition of remotely-hosted code restricts filter list updates, and due to the Chrome Web Store's fixed review process, updates may not be timely. Google has been accused of using Manifest V3 to hinder ad-blocking software due to its interest in the advertising market. In June 2019, Google increased the rule cap from 30,000 to 150,000 entries to address concerns about filtering limitations.

The WebRequest API enables ad blocking and privacy extensions to block and modify network connections, with its declarative version, DeclarativeWebRequest, processing rules directly within the browser instead of routing all traffic through the extension—a change Google claimed would improve performance. However, DeclarativeWebRequest is limited in the number of rules that can be set and the types of expressions allowed, and the prohibition of remotely-hosted code restricts independent updates to filter lists, which may not be updated promptly due to the fixed length of Chrome Web Store reviews. Google has faced criticism for using Manifest V3 to hinder ad-blocking software, citing performance issues and malicious extension use; in June 2019, it increased the rule cap from 30,000 to 150,000 entries to address concerns. In 2021, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) stated Manifest V3 was "outright harmful to privacy efforts" due to its impact on ad-blocking functionality. In December 2022, Google paused the transition to Manifest V3 to address developer feedback and migration issues, resuming it in November 2023, with support for Manifest V2 extensions removed from non-stable Chrome builds starting June 2024 and full removal from the Chrome Web Store in June 2025. These changes affected other Chromium-based browsers like Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi; Microsoft chose to support MV2 adblockers, while Brave maintained MV2 support as long as possible, though its reliance on the Chrome Web Store limited this, eventually creating a separate section for downloading MV2 extensions such as AdGuard, uBlock Origin, uMatrix, and NoScript. Mozilla stated it is adding Manifest V3 support to Firefox’s Chrome extension API for compatibility but emphasized that its implementation would not impose limitations on privacy or content-blocking extensions and that MV2 support would not be deprecated. Some developers released MV3 versions of their extensions, such as uBlock Origin Lite (uBOL), which features a static filter list, slower threat response, exclusion of filters for smaller or regional sites, absence of default cosmetic filters, and fewer overall filters; similar restrictions were introduced in Ghostry, Adblock Plus MV3, AdGuard MV3, and Stands MV3. Researchers from Goethe University Frankfurt found that MV3 extension providers largely bypassed Google’s restrictions, with tested MV3 versions blocking as many or more requests to trackers and ads than their MV2 counterparts, though cosmetic filters were over 20% less effective. In August 2024, a U.S. federal judge ruled Google maintained an illegal monopoly over search services, and in November 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice demanded Google sell Chrome to end its search monopoly. On August 12, 2025, Perplexity AI made a $34.5 billion bid to acquire Chrome from Google, claiming the sale could resolve ongoing antitrust litigation. Chrome overtook Firefox in November 2011 in global usage, and as of January 2026, according to StatCounter, it held a 71% global usage share (Cloudflare reported 68%), making it the most widely used web browser. On Sunday, March 18, 2012, Chrome first became the most used browser globally, securing 32.7% of web browsing, just ahead of Internet Explorer at 32.5%. From May 14 to 21, 2012, Chrome generated more internet traffic than Internet Explorer for the first time, with 31.88% and 31.47% of traffic respectively, marking the first week-long lead. At the 2012 Google I/O conference, Google reported 310 million active Chrome users, nearly double the 160 million in 2011. In June 2013, Chrome overtook Internet Explorer for the first time in the U.S. In August 2013, 43% of global internet users used Chrome, with Statista noting 36% in North America—the lowest globally. In December 2010, Google introduced an official Chrome MSI package for business use, which allows system-level installation and administrator control over updates, unlike the standard user-level installer that places Chrome in the local app data directory and enables invisible background updates; the MSI package, initially limited, was enhanced with group policy objects to fine-tune Chrome behavior, with over 500 policies now available. Google launched Chrome Browser Enterprise Support in 2016, a paid service for IT administrators to access expert support, and Chrome Browser Cloud Management in 2019, a dashboard enabling IT managers to control content, app usage, and installed extensions. In September 2008, Google released a significant portion of Chrome’s source code as the open-source project Chromium, enabling third-party developers to study and port the browser to macOS and Linux; the Google-authored portion is under the permissive BSD license, while other parts are under various open-source licenses. Chromium is similar to Chrome but lacks built-in automatic updates, a built-in Flash player, Google branding, and has a blue logo instead of the multicolored Google logo; it does not implement user RLZ tracking. Initially, the Chrome PDF viewer, PDFium, was excluded from Chromium but was made open-source in May 2014 and can be used to fill PDF forms. Applications, extensions, and themes for Chrome are developed and packaged in .crx files containing a manifest.json file specifying version, name, description, privileges, and other UI elements like icons and popups, with Google providing an official developer guide for creation and publishing. Chrome has its own web store for uploading and downloading these tools. As with Internet Explorer, Chrome’s popularity has led to malware abuse, such as the adware "eFast" that appeared in late 2015, which mimicked Chrome’s appearance, hijacked file associations, and injected ads into web pages.

A Google Doodle is a temporary, special alteration of the Google homepage logo used to commemorate holidays, events, achievements, and historical figures. The first Doodle, created in 1998 to mark the Burning Man event in Black Rock City, Nevada, was designed by co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin to inform users of their absence in case the servers crashed. Early Doodles were managed by marketing employee Susan Wojcicki, who led initiatives such as an alien landing and holiday-themed logos. From 1998 to 2000, Doodles were designed by cartoonist Ian David Marsden, after which Page and Brin asked public relations officer Dennis Hwang to design a Bastille Day logo, marking the beginning of an internal team known as the Doodlers, who now organize and publish Doodles. Initially static and non-hyperlinked, Doodles evolved by the 2010s: on October 31, 2000, the first animated Doodle celebrated Halloween, and on May 21, 2010, the first interactive Doodle, a playable Pac-Man created in association with Namco, debuted, featuring the Google letters in a maze and mimicking the original arcade game’s sounds. The "Insert Coin" button allowed one or two players to play, with a third press triggering an "I'm Feeling Lucky" search. The Doodle was removed on May 23, 2010, but a permanent site to play it was later released due to high user demand, with an estimated 1 billion players worldwide. By 2014, Google had published over 2,000 regional and international Doodles, often featuring guest artists, musicians, and personalities, and by 2024, the Doodlers had created over 5,000 Doodles globally. Doodles honor artists, scientists, and historical events, such as the 50th anniversary of the Lego brick, and are used to mark Google’s own milestones. Some Doodles are country-specific, while others appear worldwide. Since the first Thanksgiving Doodle in 1998, many annual Doodles for holidays and events have been recurring. The Doodlers team includes illustrators, engineers, and artists such as Ekua Holmes, Sophia Foster-Dimino, Lynnette Haozous, and Eric Carle. Google also runs Doodle 4 Google, a student competition that began in the UK, expanded to the US and other countries, and included events in Ireland (2008), India (2009), and Singapore (2010 and 2015), with winning designs displayed on national homepages. In 2007, Google faced criticism for posting a Roald Dahl Doodle on the day of Rosh Hashanah, leading to its immediate removal with no record in the official archive. In the same year, Google featured a Veterans Day Doodle despite criticism for omitting other patriotic holidays. In 2014, Google faced backlash for not honoring the 70th anniversary of D-Day, instead featuring Japanese Go player Honinbo Shusaku, prompting the company to remove the logo and add links to D-Day images. In 2016, a Doodle honoring Yuri Kochiyama, an activist with controversial views, drew criticism from conservative commentators and Senator Pat Toomey, who called for an apology, though Google did not respond or alter the Doodle. A 2014 SPARK Movement report highlighted a gender and racial imbalance in Doodles, with most honoring white males, prompting Google to commit to increasing representation of women and racial minorities. Google officially states in its guidelines that it does not create Doodles for religious holidays, avoiding religious themes or iconography, though it recognizes non-religious celebrations derived from religious holidays such as Valentine’s Day, Holi, and Tu B'Av. Critics argue that Google inconsistently applies this policy, noting the absence of Doodles for major Christian holidays like Easter and Christmas, despite celebrating Holi and Tu B'Av. While Christmas is not explicitly named, a seasonal Doodle has appeared on December 25 since 1999, and since the mid-2010s, a similar Doodle has been shown on January 7 (Eastern Orthodox Christmas) without using the term "Christmas" or "Eastern Orthodox Church." Google first created an Easter Doodle in 2000 and only returned to it in 2019 with a desktop-only, atypical Doodle where the Google logo remained unchanged and clicking the "I'm Feeling Lucky" button triggered an Easter-themed animation with linked items; this entry was later removed from the official archive. The 2019 Doodle was not visible on mobile devices unless "Desktop mode" was enabled, and Google’s technologist Danny Sullivan explained it was difficult to make the interactivity work reliably on mobile. In 2020, Google celebrated Easter again with a non-Doodle Easter egg below the search buttons, with hovertext "Happy Easter" and a link to a search results page, similar to how it has recognized Memorial Day and Remembrance Day in the US.

The Gordon E. Moore Medal is an annual award presented by the Society of Chemical Industry (SCI America) to individuals who have achieved early career success through innovative contributions in the chemical industry. Recognition is based on the award's evaluation of both the market impact and the positive effects on quality of life resulting from the recipient's work.

The Gordon Heights Fire Department is a volunteer fire department located in and serving the hamlets of Gordon Heights, Medford, Middle Island, and Yaphank in the Town of Brookhaven, Suffolk County, on Long Island, New York, United States. It is the sole department within the Gordon Heights Fire District. Prior to its establishment in 1947, there were no fire services in the community, which was founded in 1927; neighboring departments did not have a responsibility to provide protection. After a fire destroyed a local church, the Civic Association initiated efforts to form a community fire department, which was officially incorporated shortly thereafter. By 1948, the department had acquired its first fire truck. When the fire house became too small, residents advocated for the creation of a fire district to generate taxes and fund expansion, leading to petitions submitted to the Town Board. The first commissioners were appointed in 1952–53, followed by an election one year later. The Gordon Heights Fire District has faced criticism in recent years, with some residents claiming it has the highest tax rates on Long Island, a situation partly due to the district's lack of a commercial tax base. Opponents also point out its small size, serving about 900 homes compared to surrounding districts that serve between 4,400 and 8,700 households and have lower tax burdens. Supporters of the 60-member district highlight its status as the first Black fire department in New York State and its ability to offer services not available to larger departments, such as assisting elderly residents with snow plowing during winter. In 2006, an attempt to dissolve the district was rejected by the Town of Brookhaven because the petition was improperly formatted. A second dissolution petition was filed on December 31, 2008, but both attempts failed, and the department remains active as of 2021.

Government House is the official residence of the lieutenant governor of Jersey and is located in the parish of St Saviour. It serves as a venue for ceremonial functions, receptions, and meetings with visiting foreign dignitaries and heads of state, and also functions as the official residence of the Duke of Normandy (currently King Charles III) when he is in Jersey. The current building is at least the fifth official residence of governors and lieutenant governors of Jersey. Early governors or their lieutenants lived at Mont Orgueil and later at Elizabeth Castle, though the latter’s status as a tidal island led to a preference for accommodation in Saint Helier. In 1727, Colonel Magnus Kempenfelt resided in a house belonging to Le Geyt. During the Battle of Jersey in 1781, Major Moise Corbet lived at Le Manoir de la Motte, where he was captured by French invaders. Around 1800, under General Andrew Gordon, a house adjacent to the Royal Square was acquired and described in 1809 as a "large, substantial and commodious stone mansion with appropriate offices, pleasure and kitchen gardens". Under General Sir George Don, offices for public business were added, but Major-General Sir Colin Halkett petitioned the British Government in 1821 to exchange this town-centre property due to expensive repair needs, susceptibility to flooding from Le Grand Douet, and inadequate suitability for public entertainment. In 1803, the rector of St Saviour's Church, Rev. Philip Le Breton, purchased the land where Government House now stands and built a family home. This was bought by shipowner François Janvrin in 1814, who demolished the house and constructed a small two-storey villa named Belmont, using mahogany imported from South America, including for the main staircase, which remains a notable feature. In 1822, Major-General Sir Colin Halkett, then lieutenant governor, exchanged the old Government House in Saint Helier and Le Pré au Roi in Saint Clement for the Belmont property and additional land, after which it has been the official residence of all subsequent lieutenant governors. Halkett had noted that the lieutenant governor would have the opportunity at Belmont to host inhabitants and strangers without apparent bias, but his ADC, John Le Couteur, criticized the property, stating the masonry was "shamefully done". A guardhouse was built at the time for £215, though the house was considered unprepossessing. Projects to add a third storey were considered but not implemented until the second half of the 19th century, with further improvements including the addition of a porte-cochère. The drive was formerly part of La Ruette du Sacrement, leading to St Saviour's Church, and was purchased in 1810, later replaced by the new military road (St Saviour's Hill or Lé Mont du Gouvèrneux). The 12-acre grounds, situated in a valley setting from the formal lawns, include an ornamental lake and fountain created in 2009 visible from the road, along with commemorative trees and monuments. The lieutenant-governor's flag is flown from a flagpole in the grounds when he is present in the island. During the German occupation of the Channel Islands in the Second World War, the house was used as the residence of Generalleutnant Rudolf Graf von Schmettow, the German commandant. The 1989 issue of a £50 Jersey banknote featured an image of Government House on the reverse. Its coordinates are 49°11′41″N 2°05′40″W or 49.19486°N 2.09442°W.

Grace Medes (November 9, 1886 – December 31, 1967) was an American biochemist who discovered tyrosinosis, a metabolic disorder now known as tyrosinemia, and studied fatty acid metabolism. She was awarded the Garvan-Olin Medal in 1955 for her contributions to chemistry. Grace May Medes was born in Keokuk, Iowa, as the daughter of William Johnson Medes and Kate Francisco Hagny Medes. She earned her bachelor's and master's degrees in zoology from the University of Kansas and a PhD in 1916 from Bryn Mawr College. After completing her PhD, she taught at Vassar College starting in 1916 as an instructor in zoology until 1919, then as an assistant professor of physiology until 1922, becoming the first female faculty member with a PhD in the physiology department there. She moved to Wellesley College in 1922, serving as associate professor of physiology until 1924, and then joined the University of Minnesota Medical School in 1924 as a fellow for her first year and later as an assistant professor until 1932. During her time at Minnesota, she discovered the human metabolic disorder she named "tyrosinosis" in 1932; although her patient was atypical and the mechanism she identified has since been questioned, her testing methods remain a useful model for current research on tyrosinemia. In 1932, she became head of the department of metabolic chemistry at the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where she specialized in sulfur and fatty acid metabolism, establishing foundational work that contributed to the later discovery of Coenzyme A. She remained a research faculty member at the institute, later merged with the Institute for Cancer Research, until 1952, serving as a senior member from 1954 to 1960. In 1955, she received the Garvan Medal (now the Garvan-Olin Medal) from the American Chemical Society as an outstanding woman in chemistry and was also named one of the year's five distinguished alumni by the University of Kansas. In retirement, she resumed her work on tyrosinosis at the Fels Research Institute at Temple University and co-authored the book Normal Growth and Cancer in 1963 with Stanley P. Reimann. A symposium on tyrosinosis was held in Oslo, Norway, in her honor in 1965. Medes died on December 31, 1967, at the age of 81.

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, also known as the Pacific trash vortex or North Pacific Garbage Patch, is a gyre of marine debris located in the central North Pacific Ocean, roughly between 135°W and 155°W, and 35°N to 42°N. It receives plastic and floating trash from the Pacific Rim, including countries in Asia, North America, and South America. Despite popular belief, the patch does not appear as a visible island of garbage; instead, it consists of a widely dispersed area with a low density of 4 particles per cubic metre (3.1/yd³), making it undetectable by satellite imagery or casual boaters and divers. The debris is primarily composed of suspended microplastics—particles as small as fingernail-sized or smaller—that float in the upper water column. Researchers from the Ocean Cleanup project estimated the patch covers 1.6 million square kilometres (620,000 square miles), equivalent to about twice the size of Texas, and contains 45,000 to 129,000 metric tons (50,000 to 142,000 short tons) of plastic as of 2018. By the end of 2024, Ocean Cleanup had removed over one million pounds of trash, representing 0.5% of the total accumulated waste. While microplastics dominate by count, 92% of the mass comes from larger objects, including plastic lighters, toothbrushes, water bottles, pens, baby bottles, cell phones, plastic bags, and nurdles, some of which are over 50 years old. The patch is rapidly accumulating, increasing by 10-fold each decade since 1945, and contains approximately six pounds of plastic for every pound of plankton. A similar patch exists in the Atlantic Ocean, known as the North Atlantic garbage patch. The patch was first predicted in a 1988 NOAA paper based on research by Alaska-based scientists who observed high concentrations of marine debris in the North Pacific, particularly in regions influenced by ocean currents, leading to the hypothesis of a stable accumulation zone in the North Pacific Gyre. Charles J. Moore, after returning from the Transpacific Yacht Race in 1997, reported encountering a vast stretch of floating debris and alerted oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer, who named the area the "Eastern Garbage Patch" (EGP). The JUNK Raft Project, a 2008 trans-Pacific voyage organized by the Algalita Marine Research Foundation, aimed to highlight the plastic pollution in the patch. In 2009, Project Kaisei/Ocean Voyages Institute vessels, the New Horizon and the Kaisei, conducted a research voyage to assess the feasibility of large-scale collection and recycling, supported in part by the Scripps Institute of Oceanography's 2009 SEAPLEX expedition, which also studied the impact of plastic on mesopelagic fish like lanternfish. In 2010, Ocean Voyages Institute conducted a 30-day expedition in the gyre to continue scientific research and test prototype cleanup devices. In July/August 2012, the institute sailed from San Francisco to the eastern limits of the North Pacific Gyre, ending in Richmond, British Columbia, and returned, focusing on tsunami debris from the 2011 Japanese earthquake. A 2015 study found that debris from Asia primarily originates from six countries: China, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, and Thailand, with China responsible for about 30% of plastic ocean pollution as of 2010. In 2017, the Ocean Conservancy reported that China, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam collectively dump more plastic in the sea than all other countries combined. Efforts to reduce land-based debris have been led by organizations such as the Coastal Conservancy, Earth Day, Ocean Cleanup, and World Cleanup Day. A 2019 study estimated that 80% of ocean plastic comes from land-based sources, with 20% from boats and marine activities; a 2018 study found that synthetic fishing nets accounted for nearly half the mass of the patch due to ocean currents and increased fishing activity. A 2022 study indicated that 75% to 86% of plastic pollution stems from fishing and agriculture, with emissions primarily from Japan, China, South Korea, the U.S., and Taiwan. A 2020 study identified the U.S. as the third-largest contributor of plastic pollution in coastal environments. After China banned plastic imports in 2018, countries with poor waste management, such as Indonesia, became dumping grounds for U.S.-origin plastic. A 2019 study of 6,093 debris items over 5 cm found that 99% of rigid items by count and 90% of the total debris mass (514 kg) were plastics, traced to five industrialized fishing nations. The hard plastic waste includes unidentifiable fragments, fishing and aquaculture gear (nets, fish boxes, oyster spacers, eel traps), and household items. Of 201 analyzed objects, the most common languages were Chinese, Japanese, English, and Korean. The Ocean Cleanup estimated that up to 86% of the plastics in the patch come from fishing activity. The patch formed gradually through ocean currents capturing waste from coastal waters off North America and Japan, which are drawn toward the center by the gyre's rotational pattern. A 2014 study found that discarded fishing gear, such as buoys, lines, and nets, accounted for over 60% of the mass of marine plastic debris. According to a 2011 EPA report, the primary source of marine debris is improper waste disposal, including littering and illegal dumping, occurring at land-based sites like marinas, ports, rivers, harbors, and storm drains, as well as at sea from fishing vessels and cargo ships. Debris ranges from miles-long abandoned nets to micro-pellets used in cosmetics and cleaners. A computer model predicts that debris from the U.S. west coast would travel to Asia and return to the U.S. in six years, while debris from the east coast of Asia would reach the U.S. in one year or less. Although microplastics make up 94% of the estimated 1.8 trillion plastic pieces, they account for only 8% of the 79,000 metric tons (87,000 short tons) of plastic, with the majority from fishing. A 2017 study concluded that of the 9.1 billion metric tons of plastic produced since 1950, nearly 7 billion metric tons are no longer in use, with 9% recycled, 12% incinerated, and 5.5 billion metric tons (6.1 billion short tons) in oceans and land. A 2021 study found more than 40 animal species on 90% of the debris studied, and a 2022 study suggested that the patch supports a thriving ecosystem of life, including coastal species like jellyfish and sponges, which survive and reproduce in the open ocean. Scientists are concerned that this mix may create unnatural "neopelagic communities" where coastal species compete with or consume open-ocean species. The patch's size is indefinite and its debris distribution is not precisely defined due to the rarity of large items; most debris consists of small particles that evade detection. The estimated size of 1.6 million square kilometres (about twice the size of Texas or three times the size of France) is based on sampling, though such estimates are conjectural due to sampling complexities and the lack of a standard to define "elevated" pollution levels. Net-based surveys, using neuston or manta trawl nets with 0.33 mm mesh, are less subjective than direct observations but are limited by net size and ship time, requiring many tows to capture average abundance. Long-term data show a dramatic increase in plastic abundance in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre: in 1999, plastic abundance was 335,000 items per square kilometre (870,000/sq mi) and 5.1 kilograms per square kilometre (29 lb/sq mi), roughly ten times higher than in the 1980s, with similar increases off Japan. However, extreme spatial heterogeneity and the need to compare equivalent water masses mean such findings must be interpreted with caution. In August 2009, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography/Project Kaisei SEAPLEX survey found plastic in 100 consecutive samples across 1,700 miles, showing that the patch contains larger items but is mostly composed of smaller, "confetti-like" pieces that increase in concentration toward the center, suggesting the affected area may be smaller than estimated. Data from Pacific albatross populations also indicated two distinct debris zones. In March 2018, the Ocean Cleanup published findings from the Mega- (2015) and Aerial Expedition (2016), which used 30 vessels and 652 survey nets to collect 1.2 million pieces, and a C-130 aircraft with LiDAR sensors. The study found the patch covers 1.6 million square kilometres with a concentration of 10–100 kilograms per square kilometre (57–571 lb/sq mi), containing an estimated 80,000 metric tons (88,000 short tons) of plastic, with 1.8 trillion pieces and 92% of the mass in objects larger than 0.5 centimetres (3/16 in). NOAA clarified that the term "Great Pacific Garbage Patch" misrepresents the situation, as the area is not a large, visible mass of debris and cannot be seen from space. A 2001 study found plastic concentrations at 334,721 pieces per square kilometre (866,920/sq mi) with a mean mass of 5.1 kilograms per square kilometre (29 lb/sq mi), seven times greater than zooplankton in many areas, and much lower concentrations in deeper water. In 2012, researchers Goldstein, Rosenberg, and Cheng found microplastic concentrations had increased by two orders of magnitude over the previous four decades. On 11 April 2013, artist Maria Cristina Finucci founded The Garbage Patch State at UNESCO in Paris. In March 2018, New Scientist predicted the patch's size as approximately 1.6 million square kilometres. In 2010, an IEEE conference argued that the patch poses a threat to human living conditions but is controllable, while a 2011 conference noted it disrupts marine ecosystems and creates new biological conditions, leading to a new ecosystem. In 2009, Ocean Voyages Institute removed over 5 short tons (4.5 t) of plastic during the initial Project Kaisei cleanup. In 2019, during a 25-day expedition, they removed over 40 metric tons (44 short tons). In 2020, over two expeditions, they removed 170 short tons (150 t; 340,000 lb), with the first removing 103 short tons (93 t; 206,000 lb) and the second 67 short tons (61 t). In 2022, over two summer expeditions, they removed 148 short tons (134 t; 296,000 lb) of ghostnets, consumer items, and mixed plastic debris. On 9 September 2018, the first collection system, Ocean Cleanup System 001, was deployed from San Francisco to a trial site 240 nautical miles (440 km; 280 mi) away.

The Ocean Voyages Institute set a record for the largest cleanup by removing 170 short tons (150 t; 340,000 lb) of plastic from the ocean. The first 45-day expedition removed 103 short tons (93 t; 206,000 lb) of plastic, and the second expedition removed 67 short tons (61 t) of plastic from the garbage patch. In 2022, over the course of two summer expeditions, the institute removed 148 short tons (134 t; 296,000 lb) of plastic ghostnets, consumer items, and mixed plastic debris from the garbage patch. On 9 September 2018, the first collection system was deployed to the gyre to begin the collection task. This initial trial run of the Ocean Cleanup Project started towing its "Ocean Cleanup System 001" from San Francisco to a trial site approximately 240 nautical miles (440 km; 280 mi) away. The initial trial of the "Ocean Cleanup System 001" lasted four months and provided the research team with valuable information relevant to the design of the "System 001/B". In 2021, the Ocean Cleanup collected 63,182 pounds (28,659 kg; 31.591 short tons; 28.659 t) of plastic using their "System 002", with the mission running from July 2021 to 14 October 2021. In July 2022, the Ocean Cleanup announced they had removed the first 100,000 kilograms (220,000 lb; 100 t; 110 short tons) of plastic from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch using "System 002" and announced its transition to "System 03", which is claimed to be 10 times as effective as its predecessor. In April 2024, they celebrated a milestone of 10 million kg of trash extracted, and just seven months later in November 2024, they reached 20 million kg of trash removed. The 2012 Algalita/5 Gyres Asia Pacific Expedition began in the Marshall Islands on 1 May, investigated the patch, and collected samples for the 5 Gyres Institute, Algalita Marine Research Foundation, and several other institutions, including NOAA, Scripps, IPRC, and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute. In 2012, the Sea Education Association conducted research expeditions in the gyre, conducting 118 tows and counting nearly 70,000 pieces of plastic. The coordinates 38°N 145°W (38; -145) are associated with the location.

The Green Chemistry Award was first given in 2001 and was presented biennially by the Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC) to recognize significant advancements in environmentally focused chemistry.[1] In addition to receiving a £2000 prize, each winner was required to undertake a lecture tour based in the UK.[1] The award was discontinued in 2020.[2]

The Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII through the papal bull Inter gravissimas issued on 24 February 1582, replaced the Julian calendar and is now used in most parts of the world. The primary change was a revised leap year rule: every year divisible by four is a leap year, except for years divisible by 100, unless they are also divisible by 400. For example, 1800 and 1900 were not leap years, but 1600 and 2000 were. This adjustment reduced the average calendar year from 365.25 to 365.2425 days, more closely matching the actual tropical year of 365.2422 days, thus correcting a drift of about 10 days that had accumulated since the First Council of Nicaea in 325. This drift caused the March equinox to fall before 21 March, disrupting the calculation of Easter, which is based on the vernal equinox. To correct this, the calendar was advanced by 10 days: Thursday, 4 October 1582, was followed by Friday, 15 October 1582. The reform also adjusted the lunar cycle used to calculate Easter, as astronomical new moons were occurring four days earlier than the calculated dates. Initially adopted by Catholic countries and their territories, including Spain, Portugal, the Papal States, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and France (which adopted it on 9 December, followed by 20 December), the calendar was gradually adopted by Protestant and Eastern Orthodox nations over the following three centuries. Greece adopted it for civil use in 1923, though many Orthodox churches continue to use the Julian calendar for religious observances. To avoid confusion during the transition, dates were labeled as "Old Style" (Julian) or "New Style" (Gregorian). The Gregorian calendar, like the Julian, is a solar calendar with 12 months of 28 to 31 days, totaling 365 days with a leap day added to February in leap years. The leap day is placed on 29 February, though historically it was inserted by doubling 24 February. Before 1969, the Catholic Church delayed certain February feasts after the 23rd in leap years, a practice still reflected in some masses. Gregorian years are identified by consecutive numbers, and a full date is specified by year, month, and day. The calendar cycle repeats every 400 years (146,097 days), consisting of 303 regular years and 97 leap years, resulting in a mean year of 365.2425 days (365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, 12 seconds), equivalent to exactly 20,871 weeks. The reform was authorized by the Council of Trent in 1545, with Pope Paul III tasked to restore the vernal equinox to its 325 AD position and prevent future drift. Lilius proposed reducing leap years in centuries from 100 to 97, and Clavius expanded and defended the reform, advocating for a single, immediate correction of the 10-day drift. The 19-year lunar cycle was also revised to align with observed moon phases. The bull had no legal authority beyond the Catholic Church and the Papal States, requiring civil adoption for legal effect. The Spanish monarchy decreed the change on 29 September 1582, and the British Empire adopted it in 1752, followed by Sweden in 1753. Prior to 1917, Turkey used the Julian calendar for fiscal purposes, with the fiscal year starting on 1 March; from 1 March 1917, the fiscal year switched to Gregorian, and by 1 January 1926, the Gregorian calendar was adopted for general use. The secular difference between the Gregorian and Julian calendars is calculated by the formula D = ⌊Y/100⌋ − ⌊Y/400⌋ − 2, where Y is the year in astronomical year numbering (using 1 − (year BC) for BC years), and D is the number of days the Gregorian calendar is ahead. In leap years that are Julian leap years but not Gregorian, the conversion requires adjusting the date by one day less or more than the calculated value, with February given its appropriate number of days in the target calendar. The Gregorian calendar is proleptic before 1582, and the difference between the two calendars increases by three days every four centuries.

The Julian calendar is ahead of the Gregorian calendar. The secular difference D is calculated using the formula D = ⌊Y/100⌋ − ⌊Y/400⌋ − 2, where Y is the year in astronomical year numbering (using 1 − (year BC) for BC years), and ⌊x⌋ denotes rounding down to the nearest integer. For years that are leap years in the Julian calendar but not in the Gregorian, the rule is to add one day less or subtract one day more than the calculated value when converting to the Gregorian calendar, with February given its appropriate number of days. When subtracting days to find the Gregorian equivalent of 29 February (Julian), 29 February is excluded; thus, if the calculated value is −4, the Gregorian equivalent is 24 February. During the Roman Republic and Roman Empire, the consular year began on the day consuls first entered office—probably 1 May before 222 BC, 15 March from 222 BC, and 1 January from 153 BC—though the civil year consistently followed the order of months from January to December. In the Middle Ages, many Western European countries shifted the start of the year to Christian festivals such as 25 December, 25 March, or Easter, while the Byzantine Empire began its year on 1 September and Russia on 1 March until 1492, when it moved to 1 September. In common usage, 1 January was considered New Year's Day, but from the 12th century until 1751, the legal year in England began on 25 March (Lady Day), so events like the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1648 were recorded in 1648 because the year did not end until 24 March, though later histories adjusted it to 1649. Most Western European countries changed the start of the year to 1 January before adopting the Gregorian calendar; Scotland did so in 1600 (making 1599 a short year), and England, Ireland, and British colonies in 1752 (making 1751 a short year with only 282 days). In September 1752, the Gregorian calendar was introduced throughout Britain and its colonies via the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750. In countries where a legal decree sets the start of the year as 1 January, a specific date when this became standard can be identified; in others, the start of the year varied based on customs and influences. Neither the papal bull nor its canons explicitly fix the start of the year, though the canons state that the "Golden number" of 1752 ends in December and a new year (and new Golden number) begins in January 1753. Between 1582 and 1923, when the last European country adopted the Gregorian calendar, dual dating such as "10/21 February 1750/51" was common to account for differing year starts. "Old Style" (O.S.) and "New Style" (N.S.) denote dating systems before and after calendar changes, typically from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar between 1582 and the early 20th century. In England, Wales, Ireland, and British colonies, two changes occurred in 1752: the start of the year shifted from 25 March to 1 January, and the Julian calendar was replaced by the Gregorian calendar, removing 11 days from the September 1752 calendar. Writers used dual dating to reflect both calendar systems. In countries like Russia, where no year start adjustment occurred, O.S. and N.S. simply indicate the Julian and Gregorian systems; many Eastern Orthodox countries still use the Julian calendar for religious purposes. Extending the Gregorian calendar backward to dates before its official adoption produces a proleptic calendar, which should be used cautiously. For events before 15 October 1582, dates are generally shown as they appeared in the Julian calendar with the year starting on 1 January, without conversion to a Gregorian equivalent. For example, the Battle of Agincourt is universally considered to have occurred on 25 October 1415. Between 15 October 1582 and 14 September 1752, confusion arises in English-language texts when the same event has different dates (and possibly different year numbers) due to the use of Gregorian dates in continental Europe and Julian dates in English sources; events on the Continent are usually reported in English histories using the local calendar, such as the Battle of Blenheim on 13 August 1704. However, confusion can occur when an event affects both regions, such as William III of England sailing from the Netherlands on 11 November 1688 (Gregorian) and arriving in England on 5 November 1688 (Julian). The Gregorian calendar retains the Julian months with Latinate names and irregular day counts. Europeans often use mnemonics like "Thirty days hath September" to remember the number of days in each month, with variations in English, Italian, French, and Portuguese, and a version from c. 1425 in English marginalia: "Thirti dayes hath novembir / April june and Septembir. / Of xxviij is but oon / And alle the remenaunt xxx and j." A common alternative is the knuckle mnemonic, using the knuckles of the hands to represent months with 31 days and the spaces between them for months with fewer days. A similar method involves moving up a piano keyboard from an F key, with white keys representing longer months and black keys shorter ones. The Gregorian calendar uses a system of weeks, with physical or electronic calendars showing the weekday for a given date. Calculating the day of the week is complex due to the irregularities in the Gregorian system. When countries adopted the Gregorian calendar, the weekly cycle continued uninterrupted; for example, on 15 October 1582 (Gregorian), the preceding date was 4 October 1582 (Julian). Opinions vary on the numbering of days of the week; ISO 8601, widely used, starts with Monday = 1, with Mondays in the first column and Sundays in the last; in North America, the week typically begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday. The Gregorian calendar improves on the Julian calendar by skipping three leap days every 400 years, resulting in an average year of 365.2425 mean solar days, with an error of about one day every 3,030 years relative to the mean tropical year. Due to precession of the equinoxes and movement of the perihelion, the error relative to the astronomical vernal equinox is variable, with an average interval of 365.24237 days implying an error of about one day every 7,700 years. The Gregorian calendar is substantially more accurate than the Julian calendar’s average error of one day every 128 years. In the 19th century, Sir John Herschel proposed a modification with 969 leap days every 4,000 years (instead of 970), reducing the average year to 365.24225 days and making the year 4000 and its multiples common instead of leap; though proposed repeatedly, it has never been adopted. Over thousands of years, the Gregorian calendar falls behind astronomical seasons because the Earth's rotation is gradually slowing (due to tidal acceleration and leap seconds), while the year maintains a more uniform duration. An image showing the difference between the Gregorian calendar and astronomical seasons displays the June solstice date over Gregorian years, with each point indicating the solstice date; the error shifts by about a quarter of a day per year. Centurial years are ordinary years unless divisible by 400, making 1700, 1800, 1900, 2100, 2200, and 2300 leap years. These corrections cause 23 December 1903 to be the latest December solstice and 20 December 2096 to be the earliest, with a variation of about 2.35 days compared to the astronomical event. Proposed reforms of the Gregorian calendar include precursors to the original reform.

The Gregorian telescope is a reflecting telescope design developed by Scottish mathematician and astronomer James Gregory in the 17th century, first constructed in 1673 by Robert Hooke. Gregory's design was published in 1663 in his work *Optica Promota* (The Advance of Optics) and predates Sir Isaac Newton's first practical reflecting telescope, the Newtonian telescope, built in 1668. However, Gregory's design remained theoretical, as he never built a working model and lacked the practical skills or access to an optician capable of constructing it. His early attempts failed, and it was not until ten years after his publication, with the involvement of experimental scientist Robert Hooke, that a functional Gregorian telescope was built—five years after Newton's first reflecting telescope. The design features two concave mirrors: a primary mirror, shaped as a concave paraboloid, which collects light and forms a real image, and a secondary mirror, a concave ellipsoid, which reflects the image back through a hole in the primary mirror and out the bottom end, where it is viewed via an eyepiece. This configuration allows the observer to stand behind the primary mirror and produces an erect image, making it suitable for terrestrial observations. The design also functions as a telephoto lens, with a tube length much shorter than its actual focal length. Although largely superseded by the Cassegrain telescope, the Gregorian design is still used in some spotting scopes due to its ability to produce an erect image without prisms. The Steward Observatory Mirror Lab has manufactured mirrors for large Gregorian telescopes since at least 1985. In the design, the primary mirror forms a real image before the secondary mirror, enabling the placement of a field stop (known as a Gregorian stop) that blocks stray light from outside the field of view—this is especially beneficial in solar telescopes, such as the Solar Optical Telescope on the Hinode satellite, where it reduces heat reaching secondary mirrors and optical components. For amateur telescope makers, the Gregorian design is often easier to fabricate than the Cassegrain because the concave secondary mirror can be tested using the Foucault method, unlike the convex secondary in a Cassegrain telescope.

The Grisons (/ɡriːˈzɒ̃/;[4] French: [ɡʁizɔ̃]) or Graubünden (Swiss Standard German: [ɡraʊˈbʏndn̩] ⓘ),[note 1] more formally the Canton Grisons,[5] is one of the twenty-six cantons of Switzerland. It has eleven districts and its capital is Chur. The German name, Graubünden, means "Grey Leagues," referring to the canton's origin in three local alliances—the Three Leagues. The other native names also reference the Grey League: Grischùn in Sutsilvan, Grischun in the other forms of Romansh, and Grigioni in Italian. Rhaetia is the Latin name for the area. The Alpine ibex is the canton's heraldic symbol. As the largest and easternmost canton of Switzerland, it is one of the three large southern Alpine cantons, along with Valais and Ticino. It is the most diverse canton in terms of natural and cultural geography, encompassing both sides of the Alps and several natural and cultural regions, and is often compared to Switzerland as a whole, earning it the name "Little Switzerland."[6][7] The Grisons is bordered by four Swiss cantons as well as Austria, Italy, and Liechtenstein. It is the only trilingual canton of Switzerland and the only one where Romansh, Switzerland's fourth national language, has official status. Romansh language and culture are an important part of local identity.[9] In 2020, the canton had a population of 200,096.[2] It is the least densely populated canton of Switzerland. The only sizable city is Chur, as the majority of the population lives in mountainous areas, including some of the most remote valleys. One of the birthplaces of winter sports, the canton is a major tourist destination year-round, including numerous Alpine resort towns, notably Davos and St. Moritz. It is also renowned for its extensive narrow-gauge railway network, operated by the Rhaetian Railway, linking the capital with most valleys of the Grisons. Formerly occupied by the Rhaeti, most of the lands of the canton became part of the Roman province Raetia, established in 15 BC, with Curia, a settlement dating back to the Pfyn culture, as its capital. The area later became part of the diocese of Chur. In the late Middle Ages, the League of God's House, the Grey League, and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions were founded. In 1471, an alliance formed the Three Leagues, and by the end of the 15th century, they became allies of the Old Swiss Confederacy. In 1803, the Three Leagues became one of the cantons of the Confederation. The Grisons is Switzerland's largest and easternmost canton. Its geography, marked by the Alps, is complex and includes a wide range of climates and ecosystems. It is one of the three large southern Alpine cantons, along with Ticino and Valais, which include regions on the south side of the Alps.
