However, unlike those and all other cantons, it fully extends on both sides of the great Alpine barrier, from the northern plains at Maienfeld to the southern plains at Roveredo. A large portion of the canton is neither clearly north nor south of the Alps; it is the Engadin (the "garden of the Inn"), a large inner Alpine valley oriented toward eastern Europe. Therefore, parts of the canton lie in four of the five drainage basins of the country. The north is drained by the Rhine (ending in the North Sea), the south by the Po and Adige through several affluents (Mediterranean Sea), and the Engadin by the Danube through the Inn (Black Sea).[10] The Grisons lies fully within the Alps, with elevations ranging from 260 to 4,049 metres (853 to 13,284 ft). It is both one of the highest and lowest cantons of Switzerland and the second-highest when considering mean elevation. Its topography is extremely rugged, with many of the highest settlements in the country (and Europe) located in the Upper Engadin. There are well over 1,000 summits in the canton.[11] The highest peak is Piz Bernina, closely followed by numerous peaks in the homonymous range. Other prominent mountains include Piz Russein, Piz Kesch, Calanda, Aroser Rothorn, and Rheinwaldhorn (see list of mountains of Graubünden for a more exhaustive list). The canton includes numerous subranges of the Alps other than the Bernina, such as the Albula, Bregaglia, Glarus, Gotthard, Lepontine, Livigno, Plessur, Oberhalbstein, Ortler, Rätikon, Samnaun, Sesvenna, and Silvretta. The northern regions are drained by the Rhine and form an intricate network of valleys. The Rhine is one of the longest rivers in the canton and the only one flowing directly into a sea. Its sources are in the west, forming the Anterior Rhine and the Posterior Rhine, which converge at Reichenau to form the Rhine in the strict sense. After convergence, the valley opens and its floor constitutes the flattest plains of the canton, from Domat/Ems to Fläsch at the St. Gallen border. Around Chur, at the foot of the Calanda, the Rhine changes direction from eastward to northward. The Anterior Rhine and Posterior Rhine have numerous tributaries. The former forms the long and straight Surselva valley, shut off from the lower plains by the Rhine Gorge. Its major tributaries are the Glogn, Valser Rhine, and Rabiusa, forming the Val Lumnezia, Vals Valley, and Safiental. The Posterior Rhine notably collects the waters of the Avers Rhine and the Albula, which in turn collects the waters of the Gelgia and Landwasser. Similarly, the upper portion of the Posterior Rhine is shut off by the Viamala Gorge. After merging with the Albula, the Posterior Rhine forms the wide Domleschg valley until it meets its anterior counterpart. After that, the Rhine collects the waters of the Plessur at Chur, forming the Schanfigg valley, and the Landquart at the homonymous town, forming the Prätigau.[10] The Engadin is entirely drained by the Inn and is the only valley in Switzerland in the Danube basin. The Inn is one of the longest rivers in the canton and forms an almost straight valley from the Maloja Pass to Martina, with a change of direction near Zernez. Despite its length and numerous tributaries, only a few long rivers converge with the Inn: the Flaz (forming the Val Bernina), the Spöl (forming the Val da Spöl), and the Clemgia (forming the Val S-charl). In the lower part of the Engadin is also the side valley of Samnaun. The main passes connecting the Engadin with the northern Grisons are (from west to east): the Julier Pass, the Albula Pass, and the Flüela Pass.[10] The southern valleys are not contiguous and form four distinct regions: the Mesolcina (drained by the Moesa), the Val Bregaglia (drained by the Mera), the Val Poschiavo (drained by the Poschiavino), and the Val Müstair (drained by the Rom). The first three are in the Po basin and the last in the Adige basin. The Mesolcina and Bregaglia are contiguous to the northern regions through the San Bernardino Pass and the Septimer Pass, respectively. The Bregaglia, Poschiavo, and Müstair are contiguous to the Engadin through the Maloja Pass, the Bernina Pass, and the Ofen Pass.[10] Although there are no large bodies of water in the canton, numerous mountain lakes (above 800 m elevation) dot the landscape, some used as reservoirs for hydroelectricity. The largest natural lakes are Lake Sils, Lake Silvaplana, Lago di Poschiavo, and Lake St. Moritz (all in Upper Engadin except Lago di Poschiavo). Artificial lakes are more numerous, with the largest (over 100 ha) being Lago di Livigno, Lago di Lei, Lai da Sontga Maria, Zervreilasee, Lago Bianco, Lai da Marmorera, and Lägh da l'Albigna. The total number of lakes is estimated at 600.[12][note 2] Unlike other large cantons, the Grisons includes very few cities. The largest and capital city is Chur. It is followed by Davos, Landquart, Domat/Ems, and St. Moritz, which are, however, far less populated. The canton is particularly renowned for its numerous Alpine resort towns, notably Davos and St. Moritz, but also Klosters, Arosa, Lenzerheide, Disentis, Flims, Pontresina, and Scuol.[13] The climate diversity is high and comparable to that of Switzerland. In the southernmost and lowest regions, vineyards and olives are grown,[14] while on the highest summits, snow is found year-round. The inner valleys, especially the Engadin, are significantly drier than the north and south sides of the Alps, being sheltered by the high mountains. On the south side, Grono is one of the warmest places in the country with an average of 12.4 °C (54.3 °F), where the nationwide record temperature of 41.5 °C (106.7 °F) was recorded. The southern valleys are also significantly wetter than the rest of the canton (1,476 mm in Grono, 849 mm in Chur, and 705 mm in Scuol). The coldest places are at high elevations, such as on Piz Corvatsch. The Upper Engadin is among the coldest inhabited regions, notably Samedan with an average temperature of 2.0 °C (35.6 °F). The cantonwide record-low temperature of −37.9 °C (−36.2 °F) was recorded there.[15] The low-elevation region of Chur, including the Bündner Herrschaft, experiences less harsh temperatures with an average of 10.0 °C (50.0 °F). The area of the Grisons is 7,105.2 square kilometres (2,743.3 sq mi), 19.2% larger than the canton of Bern, the second largest canton.[16] Only about a third of this area is considered productive land, with forests covering about a fifth of the total area.[16] The canton is almost entirely mountainous and is the most sparsely populated region of the country. In its southeastern part lies the only official Swiss National Park. In its northern part, the mountains were formed as part of the thrust fault declared a geologic UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 under the name Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona. Another Biosphere Reserve is the Biosfera Val Müstair adjacent to the Swiss National Park, while Ela Nature Park is one of the regionally supported parks. The Grisons is sometimes included in the larger region of Eastern Switzerland, together with six other cantons. It shares borders with numerous European regions, reflecting its cultural diversity, and is the only canton adjacent to three different countries. On the national level, it shares borders with Uri, Glarus, St. Gallen (essentially across the Glarus Alps), and Ticino (essentially across the Gotthard Massif and the Lepontine Alps, but also at the level of the plain at Roveredo). On the international level, it shares borders with Liechtenstein to the north, the Austrian regions of Vorarlberg and Tyrol to the northeast, and the Italian regions of Trentino-South Tyrol and Lombardy to the east and south.[17] The deep Alpine valleys of the present-day Grisons were originally settled by the Raetians (Rhaeti). In Chur, archaeological evidence of settlement goes back to the Pfyn culture (3900–3500 BC), making the capital one of the oldest settlements in Switzerland. Most of the lands of the canton were once part of the Roman province Raetia, established in 15 BC. The current capital, Chur, was known as Curia in Roman times. The area later became part of the lands of the diocese of Chur. In 1367, the League of God's House (Cadi, Gottes Haus, Ca' di Dio) was founded to resist the rising power of the Bishop of Chur. This was followed by the establishment of the Grey League (Grauer Bund), sometimes called Oberbund, in 1395 in the Upper Rhine valley. The name Grey League is derived from the homespun grey clothes worn by the people and was used exclusively after 16 March 1424.[20] The name of this league later gave its name to the canton of the Grisons. A third league was established in 1436 by the people of ten bailiwicks in the former Toggenburg countship, as the Toggenburg dynasty had become extinct. This league was called the League of the Ten Jurisdictions (Zehngerichtebund). The first step toward the canton of the Grisons was when the League of the Ten Jurisdictions allied with the League of God's House in 1450. In 1471, the two leagues allied with the Grey League. In 1497 and 1498, the Leagues allied with the Old Swiss Confederacy after the Habsburgs acquired the possessions of the extinct Toggenburg dynasty in 1496,[22] siding with the Confederacy in the Swabian War three years later. The Habsburgs were defeated at Calven Gorge and Dornach, helping the Swiss Confederation and the allied leagues of the canton of the Grisons to be recognized. However, the Three Leagues remained a loose association until the Bundesbrief of 23 September 1524.[23] The last traces of the Bishop of Chur's jurisdiction were abolished in 1526. The Musso war of 1520 drove the Three Leagues closer to the Swiss Confederacy. Between 1618 and 1639, it became a battleground during the Bündner Wirren. The Protestant party was supported by France and Venice, while the Catholic party was supported by the Habsburgs in Spain and Austria. Each side sought control of the Grisons to gain control over the important alpine passes. In 1618, the young radical Jörg Jenatsch became a member of the court of 'clerical overseers' and a leader of the anti-Habsburg faction. He supervised the torture to death of the arch-priest Nicolò Rusca of Sondrio. In response, Giacomo Robustelli of the pro-Catholic Planta family raised an army of rebels in the Valtellina. On the evening of 18/19 July 1620, a force of Valtellina rebels supported by Austrian and Italian troops marched into Tirano and began killing Protestants. When they finished in Tirano, they marched to Teglio, Sondrio, and further down the valley, killing every Protestant they found. Between 500[24] and 600[25] people were killed that night and in the following four days. The attack drove nearly all the Protestants out of the valley, prevented further Protestant incursions, and took the Valtellina out of the Three Leagues. In response, in February 1621, Jenatsch led a force of anti-Habsburg troops to attack Rietberg Castle, the home of a leader of the pro-Catholic faction, Pompeius Planta.[26] They surprised Planta and, according to legend, he was killed by Jörg Jenatsch with an axe.[27] The murder of Planta encouraged the Protestant faction, who assembled a poorly led and disorganized army to retake the Valtellina and other subject lands. However, the army fell apart before attacking a single Catholic town.[26] This Protestant invasion provided the Spanish and Austrians with an excuse to invade the Leagues. By the end of October, Spain and Austria had occupied all of the Grisons. The resulting peace treaty of January 1622 forced the Grisons to cede the Müstair, the Lower Engadine, and Prättigau valleys. The treaty also forbade the Protestant religion in these valleys. In response, in 1622, the Prättigau valley rebelled against the Austrians and drove them out of the valley. The Austrians invaded the valley twice more, attempting to reimpose the Catholic faith, in 1623–1624 and 1629–1631.[28] In 1623, the Leagues entered into an alliance with France, Savoy, and Venice. Jürg Jenatsch and Ulysses von Salis used French money to hire an 8,000-man mercenary force.

Of Planta supported the Protestant faction, who assembled a poorly led and disorganized army to retake the Valtellina and other subject lands, but the army collapsed before engaging any Catholic town. This Protestant invasion gave Spain and Austria a pretext to invade the Leagues. By the end of October, Spain and Austria had taken control of all of the Grisons. The peace treaty of January 1622 compelled Grisons to surrender the Müstair, Lower Engadine, and Prättigau valleys, and banned the Protestant religion in these areas. In response, the Prättigau rebelled in 1622 and expelled the Austrians. The Austrians invaded the valley twice more, in 1623–1624 and 1629–1631, attempting to reestablish Catholicism. In 1623, the Leagues allied with France, Savoy, and Venice. Jürg Jenatsch and Ulysses von Salis used French funds to hire an 8,000-man mercenary force to expel the Austrians. The peace treaty of Monzon (5 March 1626) between France and Spain confirmed the political and religious independence of the Valtellina. In 1627, France withdrew from the Valtellina, which was then occupied by Papal troops. Starting in 1631, the League, under the French Duke Henri de Rohan, began expelling Spaniards. However, Richelieu refused to hand the valley over to its residents. When it became clear the French intended to remain permanently in the Leagues without forcing the Valtellina to convert to Protestantism, Jürg Jenatsch (now a mercenary leader) converted to Catholicism in 1635. In 1637, he rebelled and allied with Austria and Spain; his rebellion, along with that of 31 other League officers, forced the French to withdraw without combat. On 24 January 1639, Jürg Jenatsch was killed during Carnival by an unknown attacker dressed as a bear, who may have been a son of Pompeius Planta or an assassin hired by the local aristocracy; according to legend, he was killed by the same axe he used on Pompeius Planta. On 3 September 1639, the Leagues agreed with Spain to bring the Valtellina back under League sovereignty, with the promise to allow free exercise of the Catholic faith. Treaties with Austria in 1649 and 1652 restored the Müstair and Lower Engadine valleys to the authority of the Three Leagues. In 1798, the Grisons' lands became part of the Helvetic Republic as the canton of Raetia, except Valtellina, which was separated in 1797 for joining the Cisalpine Republic. It later became part of the Empire of Austria in 1814 and joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1859. With the Act of Mediation, the "perpetual ally" of Switzerland became a canton in 1803. The canton's constitution dates from 1892 and has undergone about 30 changes in the following century. The arms of the three original leagues were combined into the modern cantonal coat of arms in 1933. The Grand Council (German: Grosser Rat; Italian: Gran Consiglio; Romansh: Cussegl Grond), the legislature, meets in Chur, the cantonal capital. Its 120 members, elected in 39 districts using a majority system, serve four-year terms; the last district elections were in 2014. The cantonal government, exercising executive authority, consists of five members elected by the people for four-year terms, limited to three terms under a majority system. The constitution of the Grisons, last revised on 14 September 2003, states in its preamble that the canton's purpose is to "safeguard freedom, peace, and human dignity, ensure democracy and the Rechtsstaat, promote prosperity and social justice and preserving a sane environment for the future generations, with the intention of promoting trilingualism and cultural variety and conserving them as part of our historical heritage." The constitution allows municipal-level enfranchisement of foreign residents at the discretion of local governments. In 2009, the municipality of Bregaglia became the first to grant voting rights to foreigners. As of January 2017, there are 100 municipalities in the canton (as of January 2025). The inhabitants are called Bündner or (rarely) Grisonians. The population (as of 31 December 2020) is 200,096; as of 2007, it included 28,008 foreigners, or about 14.84% of the total. The main religions are Catholicism and Protestantism, with Roman Catholics forming a slight plurality (47% to 41% Protestant). The Grisons is the only Swiss canton with three official languages: German (74.7%), Romansh (13.9%), and Italian (13.9%), with the remaining 13% speaking another language natively. More Romansh speakers live in the Grisons than in any other canton, though it has become a minority language. Romansh consists of five dialect groups—Sursilvan, Vallader, Puter, Surmiran, and Sutsilvan—with a common written language called Rumantsch Grischun. Romansh has been recognized as one of four "national languages" by the Swiss Federal Constitution since 1938 and was declared an "official language" of the Confederation in 1996, allowing Romansh speakers to use Romansh for federal correspondence and receive responses in Rumantsch Grischun. Romansh has official status at the canton level, with municipalities free to specify their own official languages. Agriculture remains essential for maintaining remote valleys and is supported by national and regional subsidies; eight percent of the population work in agriculture and forestry, where 50 percent of production is certified organic. Agriculture includes forests and mountain pasturage in summer, particularly for cows, sheep, and goats. Since wolves and bears have returned, Maremma Sheepdogs are commonly used. Mountain pastures dominate, but wine production occurs in the Rhine Valley, especially in Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins, and Malans, known as the Bündner Herrschaft. In the southern valleys of Mesolcina and Val Poschiavo, corn and chestnut farming are practiced due to the milder climate, and olive trees are grown in Mesolcina. Twenty-four percent of the workforce are employed in industry, while 68 percent work in the service sector. The most industrialized region is Chur, home to Ems-Chemie, a major employer. Tourism is a major economic force, accounting for 14 percent of GDP, concentrated in towns like Davos, Klosters, Lenzerheide, Arosa, Flims, St. Moritz, and Pontresina, which have large ski areas. Numerous other tourist resorts exist, categorized by the official tourist board into "Top – Large – Small and beautiful." St. Moritz is one of the oldest winter sport resorts, popular since 1864; Davos saw its first winter tourists the following year. St. Moritz hosted the 1928 and 1948 Winter Olympics. Summer tourism also contributes significantly, with trekking, mountaineering, and mountain biking as key activities. Business tourism, notably in Davos where the World Economic Forum is traditionally held, is another revenue source. The canton spans both sides of the great Alpine barrier, with many important mountain passes, especially along the north-south axis. Transport has historically been a challenge; Roman-era cart tracks were found on Julier Pass, and Septimer Pass was rebuilt in 1387 for cart use, though it later lost importance and remains in its 1800 form for hikers. Corniche paths were essential over long stretches, and gorges like Viamala posed construction difficulties. The first real roads, 3.7 meters wide, were built across the Alps from around 1816, one of which remains in excellent historical condition. This route lost significance after rail tunnels opened. The last valley connected to the road system was Avers, with its remote hamlet of Juf reached only in 1897. After the Swiss Post expanded its Postal Bus services, motorized traffic became more common; by 1925, there were 250 vehicles in service. The inhabitants eventually accepted individual motor traffic in 1926. In 1967, the San Bernardino road tunnel opened to handle tourism traffic and is now used by heavy goods vehicles, though it is not well suited due to steep gradients. Most other passes are no longer important for goods transport. Unlike Valais and Ticino, the Grisons lacks major railway axes such as the Lötschberg and Gotthard. The only standard gauge railway is in the Rhine Valley, ending at Chur station. Chur has become a major transport hub due to the Rhaetian Railway, which links most regions of the canton. Public transport ensures access to nearly every settlement through an integrated timetable. Even Juf, with only about 30 residents and a European record, is reached five times daily by public transport. The two main transport companies are PostBus and the Rhaetian Railway, which is largely owned by the cantonal government. The Rhaetian Railway operates the largest narrow-gauge network in Switzerland and serves most regions, with branches to Central Switzerland and Italy. It is notably traveled by two of Switzerland’s longest-distance trains: the Glacier Express and the Bernina Express. Swiss Federal Railways extend only a few kilometers into the canton, from Maienfeld, serving Landquart and Chur, where passengers transfer to the Rhaetian Railway and numerous PostBus routes. The Albula Line and the Bernina Railway, the highest and only railway crossing the Alps without a tunnel, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. In winter, some road passes are closed, while high mountain passes like Julier, Bernina, and Lukmanier remain open (subject to restrictions). As the highest-elevated canton in Switzerland, it hosts vast alpine areas inaccessible by any transport and requiring walking. A large number of cable transport facilities provide access to mountains, with the highest being on Piz Corvatsch. The Engadin valley has its own airport, Samedan Airport, the highest in Switzerland, though there are no scheduled flights. Residents typically use Zurich, Milan’s Malpensa, Linte, or Bergamo airports. The Grisons is culturally the most diverse region of Switzerland, united by a strong mountain culture marked by life in isolated rural communities, notably depicted in Johanna Spyri’s Heidi. Traditional customs include Alpine transhumance in spring and autumn and the Chalandamarz at the end of winter. The canton has a large number of medieval castles and ruins; the most notable in the Engadin is Tarasp, guarding the Inn valley. Many ruins are found in the Domleschg area, and the church of Zillis features a famous 1130/40 romanesque illustrated ceiling now recognized as national heritage. Three World Heritage Sites are located in the canton: the Benedictine Convent of Saint John, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona, and the Rhaetian Railway in the Albula and Bernina Landscapes. The gastronomy of the Grisons is known for Bündnerfleisch (dried beef), often called Grisons Meat, as well as dried sausages (especially Salsiz), speck, and ham. Cheeses are numerous; notable dishes include Capuns (hearty dumplings with meat wrapped in chard leaves, then gratinated with cheese and cream), made primarily in the western part; Maluns (boiled potatoes mixed with flour, fried in butter), typically served with apple compote and local products; and Pizzoccheri (buckwheat noodles with potatoes, vegetables, and cheese), eaten in the Poschiavo valley. The emblematic dessert is the Bündner Nusstorte, a shortcrust pastry filled with caramelized walnuts and honey; a similar pastry with chestnuts, Torta di Castagne, is made in the southern valleys, especially Val Bregaglia. Wines are mainly produced in the Bündner Herrschaft, with 42 types of vines, Pinot Noir being the most popular. Smaller quantities are produced in the southern valleys; the Mesolcina is contiguous with the Ticino wine region, and Poschiavo with the Valtellina wine region. Numerous breweries exist, with the largest located in Chur, Calanda Bräu. Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha is the Romansh-speaking division of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation and focuses on the Grisons. Die Südostschweiz (in German) and La Quotidiana (Romansh) are key written media. The Grisons successfully reintroduced the ibex in the early 20th century after it had nearly disappeared from the Alps, except in the Aosta Valley, Italy, Parco Nazionale Gran Paradiso. The bearded vulture and lynx were reintroduced in the 21st century, though the lynx remains rare.

Guido Fanti (27 May 1925 – 11 February 2012) was an Italian politician who belonged to the Italian Communist Party. Born in 1925, he attended university but was forced to leave during the Second World War. In 1943, he was called to arms but soon joined the partisan resistance. After the liberation of Bologna in 1945, he joined the Italian Communist Party. Fifteen years later, he became provincial secretary of the PCI. In 1960, he entered the central committee of the party, where he was reconfirmed in the subsequent two congresses, and in 1965, at the XI congress, he became a member of the national directorate. Fanti was elected city councilor of Bologna in 1957; on 2 April 1966, he was elected mayor of the city following Giuseppe Dozza's resignation due to health reasons, after Dozza had led the city's reconstruction and initiated economic and social recovery. During his tenure, the PEEP public housing plan and the construction of the "Fiera District" (based on a project by architect Kenzō Tange) were approved. On 29 July 1970, Fanti resigned as mayor to become the first president of the Emilia-Romagna Region. He later renounced his regional position because he was a member of the Chamber of Deputies from 1976 to 1983. In 1983, he was elected senator of the IX legislature and served until 1987. From 1979 to 1989, he served as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP), and in 1984, he became vice president of the European Parliament. Guido Fanti died in the night between 10 and 11 February 2012.

Gunfire, a DC Comics superhero and freelance anti-terrorist operative created by Len Wein and Steve Erwin, first appeared in Deathstroke Annual #2 (October 1993) and is one of the "New Bloods," a group of superpowered individuals introduced during the 1993 DC Comics Bloodlines crossover event. Andrew Van Horn is the son of an unnamed business executive who inherits the family business after his father's death. During the Bloodlines crossover, he is attacked by the alien parasite Venev and gains the ability to manipulate kinetic energy. In Infinite Crisis, he fights the Secret Society of Super Villains during their assault on Metropolis, where Prometheus amputates his hands. In Final Crisis, Superman rescues Gunfire along with others from Limbo, a dimension containing forgotten characters. In Heroes in Crisis, Gunfire is one of the patients at the Sanctuary therapy center who is killed in an unexpected attack. Gunfire can charge any object by touching it, causing it to emit energy and function like a gun before disintegrating.

The multi-billion rupee Gurgaon kidney scandal was exposed in January 2008 when police conducted raids on a residential building and a guest house owned by Amit Kumar in Gurgaon, an industrial township near New Delhi, India. The victims, mostly poor individuals from western Uttar Pradesh, including Moradabad, were lured with promises of job opportunities and offered about Rs. 30,000 for kidney 'donation'. Those who refused were drugged and operated on against their will. The racket, which had been ongoing for six to seven years, involved the transplantation of kidneys from these donors into clients from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Saudi Arabia, and Greece. The Haryana police issued arrest warrants against Upendra Aggarwal, a general physician and associate of Amit Kumar, and the raid rescued five people, who were shifted to a Gurgaon hospital. On 25 January 2008, U.S.-based non-resident Indian couple and three Greek nationals, two of whom were transplant patients, were detained. Police revealed that Dr. Amit Kumar and his accomplices had performed 600 kidney transplants over the past decade, with at least two hospitals involved in post-transplant care. Fingerprinting evidence showed Kumar used multiple aliases and had been previously arrested at least four times for illegal organ trade, with prior arrests in Delhi, Andhra Pradesh, and Maharashtra involving Kumar, his brother Jeevan Kumar, Upendra Aggarwal, and Saraj Kumar, all of whom were released on bail. On 7 January 2008, Kumar was arrested by Delhi Police but released after a bribe of Rs. 20 lakhs; Jeevan Kumar was arrested on 17 February 2008 in Delhi. The Indian Medical Association requested a probe by its three-member committee and a further investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). Haryana police also uncovered two hospitals and ten laboratories in Greater Noida and Meerut allegedly involved in the scandal. As suspicions grew that Kumar had fled, the Haryana police requested CBI to alert Interpol, leading to red corner notices for Kumar and his brother. On 7 February 2008, Amit Kumar was arrested in Nepal, hiding in a wildlife resort about 35 miles from the Indo-Nepal border, where he had Rs. 9,36,000 in bank draft and €145,000 and $18,900 in cash. He attempted to bribe Nepali police to escape but failed. The CBI filed charges against him under sections 326, 342, 420, and 120B. In March 2013, a CBI special court convicted five accused, including Dr. Upender Dublesh and Dr. Amit Kumar, who received seven-year rigorous imprisonment and fines of over Rs. 60 lakh each, with the latter being termed a 'quack' by the court.

Gustave "Gus" Fitzhugh Touchard Jr., also known as Gustav, was an American tennis player active in the early 20th century and reached a highest ranking of No. 4 in the United States. Born on January 11, 1888, in New York to Gustave and Margaret McPherson Touchard, he played his first tournament in 1907 at the New York Tennis Club Open, reaching the semi-finals. In 1908, he reached his first final at the New York Metropolitan Championships, where he lost to Ross Burchard. In 1909, he won four singles titles: the Amackassin Club Invitation against Frederick Clark Inman, the Harlem Tennis Club Invitation against Wylie Grant, the Bronx County Championships against Theodore Pell, and the New York Tennis Club Open against Theodore Pell; he also reached the final of the New England Championships that year. At the US Nationals, he partnered with Raymond D. Little to win the 1911 doubles title and reached the 1912 doubles final. At the Tri-State Championships in Cincinnati, he won the 1912 singles title over Richard H. Palmer and reached the singles final again in 1913, losing to William S. McEllroy. He won the U.S. National Indoor Tennis Championships three consecutive years—1913, 1914, and 1915—and claimed the singles title at the New Jersey State Championships in 1915. In 1912, he reached the final of the US Clay Court Championship, losing to Richard Norris Williams. On October 11, 1911, he married Emeline Williams Holmes, and the marriage produced at least one child, Emlen Holmes, born on May 24, 1914. In July 1915, he admitted to stealing 24 dozen golf balls from the sporting goods store where he was employed. After being rejected by the United States aviation corps, he joined the Royal Flying Corps Canada at Camp Borden and died in 1918 at Toronto General Hospital following a throat operation.

Gvulot (Hebrew: גְּבוּלוֹת, lit. 'Borders') is a kibbutz in southern Israel, situated in the north-western Negev desert and under the jurisdiction of the Eshkol Regional Council. As of 2023, it had a population of 438 and is located approximately 120 meters above sea level. The village was established on land owned by the Jewish National Fund (JNF) on 12 May 1943 by immigrants from Romania and Turkey, who were members of the "Kibbutz Eretz Israel Gimel" group of Hashomer Hatzair, with financial support from Keren Hayesod. It was initially named Mitzpe Gvulot (Hebrew: מִצְפֶּה גְּבוּלוֹת, lit. 'Borders lookout') and was the first of three lookouts, the others being Beit Eshel and Revivim. Gvulot was the second modern Jewish settlement in the Negev and the first in the Gaza area, with the primary purpose of guarding JNF land and conducting research on the region's soil and climate to assess agricultural suitability. It was officially recognized as a kibbutz in 1946. Prior to the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, the settlement was divided into two parts—a small group of families in its post-war location and the rest in a nearby military base. During the war, the base served the 8th Brigade. After the war, in 1949, all residents relocated to Gvulot's current site, about 1.5 kilometers south of the base. Simon Le Bon, the lead singer of Duran Duran, worked at Kibbutz Gvulot, where he wrote early lyrics for "Careless Memories", "The Chauffeur", "Sound of Thunder", and "Tel Aviv". An anaerobic waste plant is currently being constructed between Gvulot and Tzeelim.

A gyro monorail, also known as a gyroscopic or gyro-stabilized monorail, is a single-rail land vehicle that uses the gyroscopic action of spinning wheels to maintain balance on a single rail, overcoming its inherent instability. This technology was developed by Louis Brennan, August Scherl, and Pyotr Shilovsky, each building full-scale working prototypes in the early 20th century. A later version was developed in the US in 1962 by Ernest F. Swinney, Harry Ferreira, and Louis E. Swinney. Despite its advantages, the gyro monorail was never developed beyond the prototype stage. One key benefit cited by Shilovsky is the suppression of hunting oscillation, a speed limitation in conventional railways, and the ability to make sharper turns than modern high-speed trains like the TGV, as the vehicle automatically banks on curves like an aircraft, eliminating lateral centrifugal acceleration. A major drawback is that most vehicles—passenger or freight—would require powered gyroscopes to remain upright. Unlike lateral shifting or reaction wheels, the gyroscopic system is statically stable, meaning the control system functions primarily as a roll damper. Louis Brennan developed a 22-tonne (22-long-ton; 24-short-ton) unladen prototype and filed his first monorail patent in 1903. His first demonstration model was a 30.0-by-11.8-inch (762 by 300 mm) box containing the balancing system, which prompted the Army Council to recommend £10,000 for development, though this was vetoed by the Financial Department. The Army later provided £2,000 from various sources. Within this budget, Brennan built a larger model, 6.0 by 1.5 feet (1.83 by 0.46 m), balanced by two 5.0-inch (127 mm) diameter gyroscope rotors, which is still on display at the London Science Museum. The track was laid in the grounds of Brennan’s house in Gillingham, Kent, using ordinary gas piping on wooden sleepers with a 50-foot (15 m) wire rope bridge, sharp corners, and slopes up to one in five. Brennan demonstrated this model in a 1907 lecture to the Royal Society, showing it running back and forth "on a taught and slender wire" under his control. The reduced-scale railway validated the War Department’s initial interest, though funding ceased after the 1906 Liberal government election. In 1907, the India Office approved £6,000 (equivalent to £801,733 in 2023) for development in the North West Frontier, and in 1908, the Durbar of Kashmir provided £5,000 (equivalent to £659,406 in 2023), with nearly all funds spent by January 1909, followed by an additional £2,000 (equivalent to £263,333 in 2023). On 15 October 1909, the railcar ran under its own power for the first time, carrying 32 people at 22 miles per hour (35 km/h), powered by a 20-horsepower (15 kW) petrol engine with electric transmission, driving a generator that supplied power to the gyro motors and air compressor. The balancing system used a pneumatic servo, not friction wheels, and the gyros were located in the cab, though Brennan planned to reposition them under the floor before a public display, which was delayed due to Scherl’s demonstration. In December 1909, Brennan demonstrated the railcar to the Royal Society, carrying 40 people at 40 km/h (25 mph) on a 200-meter (660 ft) circular track, with dimensions 12.2 m × 4.0 m × 3.0 m (40 ft × 13 ft × 10 ft). The public debut at the Japan-British Exhibition in London in 1910 carried 50 passengers at 20 miles per hour (32 km/h), with Winston Churchill among the attendees. Interest led to the production of children’s clockwork monorail toys in England and Germany. Despite being a viable transport option, the monorail failed to attract further investment; of the two vehicles built, one was sold as scrap and the other used as a park shelter until 1930. Just as Brennan completed testing, August Scherl announced a public demonstration of his gyro monorail in Berlin on 10 November 1909 at the Berlin Zoological Gardens. Scherl’s full-size vehicle was smaller, measuring 5.5 by 1.2 m (18 by 4 ft), with only four passenger seats. It used vertical-axis gyros, weighing 57 kg (125 lb), rotating at 8,000 revolutions per minute, with a hydraulic servomechanism and electric propulsion. Two safety features were included: the gyros continued rotating for several hours without power, allowing safe stopping before balance loss, and small corner wheels could be lowered to stabilize the vehicle. Scherl provided financial backing, while Paul Fröhlich invented the righting mechanism and Emil Falcke designed the car. A Scientific American editorial questioned practicality due to potential rail and bridge modifications. Though well-received during demonstrations, Scherl failed to secure financial support and wrote off his investment. After Brennan and Scherl’s efforts failed, Pyotr Shilovsky continued development in London, using a different balancing principle that allowed a smaller, slower-spinning gyroscope. In 1922, the Soviet government began construction of a Shilovsky monorail between Leningrad and Tsarskoe Selo, but funds ran out shortly after. In 1929, at age 74, Brennan developed a gyrocar, which was rejected by a consortium of Austin/Morris/Rover. In October 2022, Technische Hochschule OWL, Bielefeld University of Applied Sciences, Fraunhofer-Institut für Optronik, Systemtechnik und Bildauswertung, and Landeseisenbahn Lippe e. V. presented a gyro-stabilized monorail based on Brennan’s system on a section of the Extertal railway in Germany, called Monocab. Monocab enables bi-directional service on a single track with autonomous, narrow cabins. It was funded in September 2020 by the European Regional Development Fund and the state of North Rhine-Westphalia with 3.6 million euros. The vehicle runs on a single conventional rail and would topple without the balancing system. A spinning wheel is mounted in a gimbal frame with its spin axis perpendicular to the precession axis, aligned such that at equilibrium, the spin, precession, and vehicle roll axes are mutually perpendicular. Forcing the gimbal to rotate causes precession, generating gyroscopic torques about the roll axis, which can right the vehicle when tilted. The wheel tends to align its spin axis with the gimbal axis, rotating the vehicle about its roll axis. Ideally, the control mechanism would be passive, but due to the system’s equilibrium requiring restoration of potential energy, an active servo is necessary. If constant side forces were resisted by gyroscopic action alone, the gimbal would rotate to stops, causing the vehicle to topple; instead, the mechanism causes the vehicle to lean into disturbances, resisting them with a component of weight. Inertial side forces from cornering cause the vehicle to lean into the corner, but a single gyro introduces asymmetry, leading to net side forces. To ensure correct banking, the gyroscopic torque from vehicle turn rate must be removed. A free gyro maintains orientation relative to inertial space, and rotating it about an axis perpendicular to its spin axis generates gyroscopic moments. However, when the control system deflects the gyro relative to the chassis—not inertial space—vehicle pitch and yaw introduce additional unwanted torques, causing instability in one direction and increased stability in the opposite. Shilovsky encountered this with his road vehicle, which could not make sharp left turns. Brennan and Scherl solved this with pairs of counter-rotating gyros, precessing in opposite directions, so that vehicle motion relative to inertial space produces equal and opposite torques, canceling out the effects. Shilovsky claimed difficulty with double-gyro systems, though the reason is unclear; his solution was to vary control loop parameters with turn rate to maintain balanced response in both directions. Offset loads and side winds cause the vehicle to lean until the center of gravity is above the support point, resulting in contact side forces that may cause more discomfort than cornering forces. These forces create a gimbal deflection bias, which can be used as input to a slower loop to shift the center of gravity laterally, keeping the vehicle upright. This combination of gyro and lateral center of gravity shift is described in a 1962 patent and was implemented in a vehicle built in the US in 1962 by Ernest F. Swinney, Harry Ferreira, and Louis E. Swinney, known as the Gyro-Dynamics monorail. Shilovsky claimed benefits such as reduced right-of-way issues due to steeper gradients and sharper corners, and a form of on-track braking that could offer much shorter stopping distances than conventional rail braking, reducing safe train separation and increasing track occupancy and capacity. He also claimed his designs were lighter than equivalent duo-rail vehicles, with the gyro mass accounting for 3–5% of the vehicle weight, comparable to the bogie weight saved by single-track design. For a vehicle negotiating a horizontal curve, if the gyro axis is vertical, a component of turn rate (Ω) acts about the gimbal pivot, introducing an additional gyroscopic moment into the roll equation, displacing the roll from the correct bank angle and altering the constant term in the characteristic equation. If the turn rate exceeds a critical value, the balancing loop becomes unstable. However, an identical gyro spinning in the opposite direction cancels the destabilizing roll torque and, when forced to precess in the opposite direction, produces a corrective control torque. In 1972, Canada’s Division of Mechanical Engineering rejected a monorail proposal based on this instability issue, though their analysis was limited to single vertical-axis gyro systems and not universally applicable. Gas turbine engines operate with peripheral speeds up to 400 meters per second (1,300 ft/s), and have done so reliably for decades. An estimate for a 10-tonne (9.8 long tons; 11 short tons) vehicle with a center-of-gravity height of 2 meters (6 ft 7 in), assuming half the peripheral speed of jet engines, results in a gyro mass of only 140 kilograms (310 lb), making Brennan’s recommendation of 3–5% of vehicle mass highly conservative.

Güicán de la Sierra, also known as Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria de Güicán, is a town and municipality located in the Colombian Department of Boyacá. It is situated near the national natural park El Cocuy National Park. As of 2020, the municipality has a total population of 6,426. The municipality is named after the Güicán tribe, an indigenous group that once inhabited the region and is related to the U'wa people; the name Güicán translates to "in the fence of the wife" in the indigenous language. The Spanish conquistador Hernán Pérez de Quesada arrived in the area in search of gold, and the indigenous people retreated behind the Sierra Nevada to avoid him. The municipality was officially founded by Jesuit friar Miguel Blasco on February 26, 1756. It shares borders with Chiscas and Cubará to the north, Fortul and Saravena to the east, Tame and El Cocuy to the south, and Panqueba and El Espino to the west. The average elevation of Güicán is 3,492 meters above sea level. The region has a Tundra Climate (ET), with the highest average rainfall occurring in April at 244 mm and the lowest in January at 83 mm.

Habba Khatoon (Kashmiri: [habɨ xoːt̪uːn]; born Zoon Rather or Zuni, Kashmiri: زوٗن, lit. 'Moon'), also known as The Nightingale of Kashmir, was a 16th-century Kashmiri Muslim poet and ascetic. She was the consort of King Yousuf Shah Chak, though scholarly debate exists over whether she was a lower-status mistress or a member of his harem. Born in the village of Chandur (Kashmiri: Tsandhor) in Pampore, Pulwama district, her birth name was Zoon, given to her due to her beauty. Her father, Abdi Rathar of Chandhur, was a well-to-do and courageous farmer who arranged for her education with a village maulvi, teaching her the Quran and Persian classics, which were popular at the time. She learned works like Gulistan and Bostan and gained recognition beyond her village. Her parents intended to marry her to a peasant boy, Aziz Lone, who was uninterested in her charm and love, leading her to endure hardship—fetching water, gathering firewood, spinning, and enduring criticism from her mother-in-law and society. In her song "Tche Kyoho Vaatiyo Myaeni Marnai" (What do you stand to gain by my death?), she reflects on her suffering and questions the value of her death, concluding with introspection. Seeking solace, she consulted Khwaja Masud, who gave her consolation and reportedly coined the name Habba Khatoon, which she adopted. One of her famous songs, "Wolo Myaeni Poshey Madano" (Come, my flowery Cupid), expresses her longing and bitterness. According to legend, Yousuf Shah Chak, the last independent emperor of Kashmir, heard her singing under a chinar tree and fell in love, leading to her entry into the palace around 1570. She became a central figure in his life, and the couple visited natural sites like Gulmarg, Aharabal, Achabal, and Sonamarg, with a hillock in Gurez named after her. During this time, Kashmir faced political instability, with the Chak dynasty weakened and the Mughal emperor Akbar eyeing the region. Yousuf Shah Chak lost the throne in 1580 and was later supported by Akbar, who helped him regain it in 1581 through Raja Man Singh’s intervention. After Yousuf’s departure, Habba Khatoon remained in Kashmir for nearly twenty years, moving without attachments. She composed songs like "Harmukh Bartal," expressing her sorrow and longing for her husband. Though Persian words like 'shamaa,' 'ishq,' and 'burqa' were already in Kashmiri, she used them sparingly, preserving the authenticity and musicality of her native language. She developed a new musical form, Raasti-Kashmiri, modeled on Raasti-Farsi, and mastered the Persian raga Muqaami-Iran. Her poems, including Harmukh Bartal, Char kar myon maalinyo, and Vaervain saeth vaar chas no, are known as Yadhaaq in Kashmiri. The taqleqkar of loal poetry was praised by Kalhana in Rajtarangini. The hillock in Gurez Valley and an underpass in Mughalpura, Lahore, are named after her, and the Indian Coast Guard named a ship CGS Habba Khatoon in her honor.

Habba Khatoon was skilled in both poetic and musical styles, and naturally made her own contribution through a new composition called Raasti-Kashmiri, which is based on Raasti-Farsi and is sung during the last quarter of the night. She gained recognition for her expertise in the Persian raga Muqaami-Iran. Her poems, including Harmukh Bartal, Char kar myon maalinyo, Vaervain saeth vaar chas no, and others, are known as Yadhaaq in the Kashmiri language. The pioneer of loal poetry, referred to as the taqleqkar, was lauded by Kalhana in his work Rajtarangini, who described the poet’s insight as surpassing the stream of ambrosia, resulting in a lasting embodiment of glory for both the poet and others. A hillock in the Gurez Valley, Kashmir, is named after her, and an underpass in Mughalpura, Lahore, bears her name. Additionally, the Indian Coast Guard named a ship, CGS Habba Khatoon, in her honor.

Hamilton: An American Musical is a sung-and-rapped-through biographical musical with music, lyrics, and a book by Lin-Manuel Miranda, based on the 2004 biography Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow. The musical chronicles the life of American Founding Father Alexander Hamilton, detailing his role in the American Revolution and early U.S. political history. Composed from 2008 to 2015, its music draws heavily from hip hop, as well as R&B, pop, soul, and traditional-style show tunes. It casts non-white actors as the Founding Fathers and other historical figures. Miranda described the musical as about "America then, as told by America now." The show received near-universal acclaim upon its opening off-Broadway on February 17, 2015, at the Public Theater in Lower Manhattan, where Miranda played Alexander Hamilton and the engagement was sold out. It won eight Drama Desk Awards, including Outstanding Musical, and transferred to the Richard Rodgers Theatre on Broadway, opening on August 6, 2015, receiving positive reviews and strong box office performance. At the 70th Tony Awards, it received 16 nominations and won 11 awards, including Best Musical, and was awarded the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A filmed version of the Broadway production was released on Disney+ in 2020, followed by a theatrical release in 2025 by Walt Disney Pictures. The Chicago production began preview performances at the CIBC Theatre in September 2016 and opened the following month. The West End production opened at the Victoria Palace Theatre in London on December 21, 2017, after previews from December 6, and won seven Olivier Awards in 2018, including Best New Musical. The first U.S. national tour began in March 2017, a second U.S. tour opened in February 2018, and the third U.S. tour began on January 11, 2019, with a three-week engagement in Puerto Rico where Miranda returned to play Hamilton. The first non-English production opened in Hamburg in October 2022, translated into German. As of 2025, no amateur or professional licenses have been granted for Hamilton. The musical is structured in two acts and covers Hamilton's early life as an orphan on the island of St. Croix, his immigration to New York City, his meeting with Aaron Burr, John Laurens, the Marquis de Lafayette, and Hercules Mulligan at King's College in 1776, and his involvement in the Revolutionary War as George Washington's aide-de-camp. It details his marriage to Eliza Schuyler, his career as a lawyer and Secretary of the Treasury, and his complex relationship with Aaron Burr, culminating in their duel that ends Hamilton's life. At a ball hosted by Philip Schuyler, Eliza falls in love with Hamilton, who reciprocates, leading to their marriage ("Helpless"), while Angelica suppresses her own feelings ("Satisfied"). After the wedding, Burr and Hamilton celebrate their successes ("The Story of Tonight (Reprise)"), with Burr reflecting on Hamilton's rapid rise and his own affair with Theodosia. During the Battle of Monmouth, Hamilton aids Laurens in a duel against Major General Charles Lee ("Ten Duel Commandments"), resulting in Washington suspending him ("Meet Me Inside"). Eliza reveals she is pregnant with their first child, Philip, and urges Hamilton to slow down ("That Would Be Enough"). Lafayette convinces Washington to recall Hamilton for field command at the Battle of Yorktown ("Guns and Ships"), and Washington tells him that his actions will be remembered forever ("History Has Its Eyes on You"). At Yorktown, Hamilton works with Lafayette to defeat the British and uncovers Mulligan's espionage ("Yorktown (The World Turned Upside Down)"). After Yorktown, King George III questions the new nation's ability to survive ("What Comes Next?"). Hamilton's son Philip is born, and Burr has a daughter, Theodosia, with the two fathers promising to protect their children ("Dear Theodosia"). After Laurens is killed in a post-war battle, Hamilton grieves and redoubles his work ("Tomorrow There'll Be More of Us (The Laurens Interlude)"). Over the next decade, both Hamilton and Burr work as lawyers, with Hamilton gaining influence, participating in the Constitutional Convention, co-authoring The Federalist Papers, and becoming Secretary of the Treasury under President Washington, while Eliza urges him to slow down and Angelica moves to London. In 1789, Thomas Jefferson returns from France as Secretary of State ("What'd I Miss"), and Jefferson and James Madison debate Hamilton's financial plans at a Cabinet meeting ("Cabinet Battle #1"). Washington orders Hamilton to find a compromise, which he achieves through a private dinner, resulting in Hamilton's financial plan being passed in exchange for the permanent capital being placed on the Potomac River. Burr is envious of Hamilton's power and defeats Hamilton's father-in-law Philip Schuyler in a Senate race ("Schuyler Defeated"). In a second Cabinet meeting, Hamilton argues for U.S. neutrality during France's conflict with Britain, which Washington supports ("Cabinet Battle #2"). Jefferson, Madison, and Burr then unite to discredit Hamilton ("Washington on Your Side"). After Washington retires, Hamilton helps write his farewell address ("One Last Time"). King George learns of Washington's departure and is replaced by John Adams ("I Know Him"), who fires Hamilton, prompting Hamilton to publish a critical critique of Adams ("The Adams Administration"). Jefferson, Madison, and Burr confront Hamilton about James Reynolds's blackmail, accusing him of embezzlement ("We Know"). To defend himself, Hamilton recalls his life and the role writing has played in saving him ("Hurricane"), then publicly releases the Reynolds Pamphlet, damaging his reputation ("The Reynolds Pamphlet") and destroying his relationship with Eliza, who burns all his letters to erase herself from history ("Burn"). At 19, Hamilton's son Philip duels George Eacker ("Blow Us All Away") and is fatally shot ("Stay Alive (Reprise)"), leading to reconciliation between Alexander and Eliza ("It's Quiet Uptown"). Hamilton's endorsement of Jefferson over Burr in the 1800 presidential election ("The Election of 1800") deepens the rivalry, prompting Burr to challenge Hamilton to a duel via letter exchange ("Your Obedient Servant"). Hamilton writes his final letter while Eliza tells him to go to bed ("Best of Wives and Best of Women"). Burr reflects on the events leading to the duel, while Hamilton reflects on his legacy before throwing away his shot. Burr fatally shoots Hamilton, lamenting that though he survives, he is remembered as the villain who killed Hamilton ("The World Was Wide Enough"). The musical closes with a reflection on historical memory, as Jefferson and Madison reflect on Hamilton's legacy, and Eliza recounts how she reinserted herself into history by recording veterans' memories, raising funds for the Washington Monument, speaking out against slavery, and establishing the first private orphanage in New York City ("Who Lives, Who Dies, Who Tells Your Story"). Eliza then turns to the audience and lets out a tearful gasp. The original Broadway cast recording was made available by NPR on September 21, 2015, released digitally by Atlantic Records on September 25, 2015, and physically on October 16, 2015, with a vinyl release following. The album debuted at number 12 on the Billboard 200, the highest entrance for a cast recording since 1963, reached number 2 on the Billboard 200, and number 1 on the Billboard Rap albums chart. It won a Grammy Award for Best Musical Theater Album. The Hamilton Mixtape, a collection of remixes, covers, and samples, was released on December 2, 2016, and debuted at number 1 on the Billboard 200. The Hamilton Instrumentals, an instrumental version of the original cast recording, was released on June 30, 2017. Producers announced free sing-along programs and authorized the use of the Hamiltunes name and logo for fan events, which had already occurred in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington D.C., and elsewhere. Miranda launched a series of 13 Hamilton-related recordings called Hamildrops, released monthly from December 2017 to December 2018. The first, "Ben Franklin's Song" by The Decemberists, released on December 15, 2017, contains lyrics Miranda wrote for an unused song, imagined as Benjamin Franklin singing in a "Decemberist-y way." The second, "Wrote My Way Out (Remix)," released on January 25, 2018, is a remixed version of a song from The Hamilton Mixtape featuring Royce Da 5'9", Joyner Lucas, Black Thought, and Aloe Blacc. The third, "The Hamilton Polka" by "Weird Al" Yankovic, released on March 2, 2018, is a polka medley of musical songs, with Yankovic jokingly calling March 2 "February 30th" due to his scheduling. After the show premiered on Disney+ in July 2020, Yankovic released a video version of the song synced to clips from the show. The fourth, "Found/Tonight," released on March 19, 2018, is a mash-up of "You Will Be Found" from Dear Evan Hansen and "The Story of Tonight," with proceeds benefiting the March for Our Lives initiative. The fifth, "First Burn," released on April 30, 2018, features five actresses who played Eliza: Arianna Afsar, Julia Harriman, Shoba Narayan, Rachelle Ann Go, and Lexi Lawson, and is the first draft of "Burn," with Miranda noting the original version was angrier and more reactive, while the final version gives Eliza agency. The sixth, a cover of "Helpless" by The Regrettes, released on May 31, 2018, was suggested by producer Mike Elizondo. The seventh, "Boom Goes the Cannon..." by Mobb Deep, released on June 18, 2018, samples "Right Hand Man" and was one of the last recordings by Havoc and Prodigy before Prodigy's death in June 2017; Havoc dedicated it to Queensbridge. The eighth, "Rise Up, Wise Up, Eyes Up" by Ibeyi, was released on August 31, 2018. The ninth, "A Forgotten Spot (Olvidado)," released on September 20, 2018, features Puerto Rican artists Zion & Lennox, De La Ghetto, Ivy Queen, PJ Sin Suela, and Lucecita Benítez, and was created to mark the one-year anniversary of Hurricane Maria. The tenth, a rendition of "Theodosia Reprise" by Sara Bareilles, released on Halloween 2018, features Alex Lacamoire on piano and Questlove of The Roots on drums and was originally intended for Act 2 but cut from the final production. The eleventh, "Cheering For Me Now," released on November 20, 2018, is an original song based on the 1788 Federal Procession in New York City, with Miranda performing as Hamilton and arranged by Alex Lacamoire. The final release, "One Last Time (44 Remix)," released on December 20, 2018, features Christopher Jackson (George Washington), BeBe Winans, and Barack Obama (reciting lines from Washington's farewell address), with the "44" referencing Obama as the 44th U.S. president. The Broadway show's orchestration includes the conductor playing the first keyboard part. While on vacation from In the Heights, Lin-Manuel Miranda read the 2004 biography Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow and began envisioning a musical, finding only a 1917 Broadway play starring George Arliss as Hamilton. Miranda began a project titled The Hamilton Mixtape, and on May 12, 2009, performed the first song from it at a White House event.

The musical *Hamilton* is based on lines from George Washington's farewell address and features a gospel-style arrangement of the song "One Last Time," with the number "44" in the title signifying that Barack Obama was the 44th president of the United States. Lin-Manuel Miranda, while on vacation from performing in his Broadway show *In the Heights*, read Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography *Alexander Hamilton* and began envisioning a stage musical about Hamilton’s life, discovering that a play on Hamilton had previously been performed on Broadway in 1917 starring George Arliss. Miranda developed a project called *The Hamilton Mixtape*, and on May 12, 2009, he performed an early version of "Alexander Hamilton" at the White House Evening of Poetry, Music and the Spoken Word. He later worked on "My Shot" over the next year. The musical’s story and lyrics are heavily researched, with many songs drawing directly from primary sources such as personal letters, The Federalist Papers, and the Reynolds Pamphlet, and Miranda has cited *The West Wing* as an influence. A workshop production titled *The Hamilton Mixtape* was held at Vassar College and the New York Stage and Film Powerhouse Theater on July 27, 2013, directed by Thomas Kail and musically directed by Alex Lacamoire, featuring Miranda as Hamilton, Utkarsh Ambudkar as Burr, Christopher Jackson as Washington, Daveed Diggs as Lafayette/Jefferson, Ana Nogueira as Eliza, Anika Noni Rose as Angelica, Javier Muñoz as Laurens, Presilah Nunez as Peggy/Maria, and Joshua Henry as Mulligan/Madison/King George. Only Miranda, Diggs, and Jackson from that cast joined the off-Broadway production; Ambudkar was replaced due to alcoholism, and Brian d'Arcy James was replaced by Jonathan Groff as King George III. A 2014 workshop at the 52nd Street Project included Miranda as Hamilton, Leslie Odom Jr. as Burr, Diggs as Lafayette/Jefferson, Phillipa Soo as Eliza, Renée Elise Goldsberry as Angelica, Anthony Ramos as Laurens/Philip, Okieriete Onaodowan as Mulligan/Madison, Ciara Renée as Peggy/Maria, James as King George III, and Isaiah Johnson as Washington, with an audio recording available on YouTube. Directed by Thomas Kail and choreographed by Andy Blankenbuehler, the musical premiered Off-Broadway at The Public Theater on January 20, 2015, with previews and an official opening on February 17, extended to April 5 and then to May 3, with Ron Chernow serving as historical consultant. It opened to universal acclaim and won 11 Tony Awards. Producer Jeffrey Seller wanted to move the show to Broadway before the end of the 2014–2015 season to qualify for the Tony Awards, but Miranda and Kail overruled him, wanting more time. Changes between off-Broadway and Broadway included cutting several numbers, rewriting Hamilton’s final moments, and shortening "One Last Ride" to "One Last Time" to focus on Washington’s decision not to seek a third term. The show premiered on Broadway at the Richard Rodgers Theatre on July 13, 2015, in previews and opened on August 6, 2015, produced by Seller, Jill Furman, and Sandy Jacobs, with sets by David Korins, costumes by Paul Tazewell, lighting by Howell Binkley, and sound by Nevin Steinberg. In April 2016, the cast reached a profit-sharing agreement with producers, an uncommon arrangement. The show suspended production on March 12, 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, resuming on September 14, 2021. It began previews at the CIBC Theatre in Chicago on September 27, 2016, with Miguel Cervantes as Hamilton, Joshua Henry as Burr, Karen Olivo as Angelica, Arianna Afsar as Eliza, Alexander Gemignani as King George III, Jonathan Kirkland as Washington, and Samantha Marie Ware as Peggy/Maria, receiving positive reviews on opening in October and closing on January 5, 2020, after 1,341 shows and grossing $400 million, with over 2.6 million attendees including 31,000 public school students through the Hamilton Education Program. Plans for a national tour emerged in January 2016, initially with over 20 stops from 2017 through 2020; tickets for the San Francisco debut sold out within 24 hours, with over 110,000 people entering the waiting room. The first tour began previews at the SHN Orpheum Theatre on March 10, 2017, officially opening on March 23, running in San Francisco until August 5, then transferring to Los Angeles’s Hollywood Pantages Theatre from August 11 to December 30, 2017. A second U.S. tour, the "Philip Tour," began previews at the Paramount Theatre in Seattle on February 6, 2018, officially opening on February 15, 2018. The "Angelica Tour" required 14 truckloads and over 60 traveling cast, crew, and musicians, with two portable sets built for each tour to allow for advance assembly. The Philip Tour premiered in Canada at the Ed Mirvish Theatre in Toronto on February 11, 2020, scheduled to run until May 17, but was canceled from March 14 due to the pandemic. The Angelica Tour concluded on June 25, 2023, at the Centro de Bellas Artes Luis A. Ferré in Puerto Rico, and re-opened on September 4, 2024, at the Hollywood Pantages Theatre alongside the Philip Tour. A third touring company, the "And Peggy Tour," was announced on November 8, 2017, to debut in January 2019 at the University of Puerto Rico’s Teatro UPR in San Juan, with Miranda reprising the title role, later moving to San Francisco. Due to union concerns over budget cuts, the engagement was moved to the Luis A. Ferré Performing Arts Center and shortened to January 11–27, 2019, with police standing outside on opening night. Miranda’s performance at the venue marked his return nine years after playing Usnavi in *In the Heights*. The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon taped segments in Puerto Rico, with Miranda and Fallon performing a version of "The Story of Tonight" ending with a salsa rendition of the show’s opening. In a review, Chris Jones noted Miranda’s deeper emotions, improved vocal and dance technique, and praised Donald Webber Jr.’s performance as Burr; the three-week run raised about $15 million for Miranda’s Flamboyán Arts Fund, including funding for Teatro UPR’s restoration. A filmed version of "Alexander Hamilton" from the Puerto Rico production was shown as the final part of *Hamilton: The Exhibition* in 2019. Julius Thomas III took over the role of Hamilton when the And Peggy Tour moved to San Francisco, opening on February 21, 2019, and was fixed in San Francisco with no traveling dates, closing on March 11, 2020, due to the pandemic, reopening on August 10, 2021, and closing on September 5, 2021, with its final performance in Toronto on August 20, 2023. A planned Los Angeles production from March 12 to November 22, 2020, was suspended due to the pandemic and later opened on August 27, 2021, running until March 20, 2022, named the Eliza Tour. Cameron Mackintosh produced a London production that reopened the Victoria Palace Theatre on December 21, 2017, after previews from December 6, receiving positive reviews; Prince Harry attended a charity performance in 2018, singing a few bars of "You'll Be Back" as King George III. The London production closed on March 16, 2020, due to the pandemic, announced to reopen in 2021, and reopened on August 19, 2021. The Australian premiere began at Sydney Lyric on March 17, 2021, with Jason Arrow as Hamilton, Chloé Zuel as Eliza, Lyndon Watts as Burr, Akina Edmonds as Angelica, Matu Ngaropo as Washington, Victory Ndukwe as Lafayette/Jefferson, Shaka Cook as Mulligan/Madison, Marty Alix as Laurens/Philip, Elandrah Eramiha as Peggy/Maria, and Brent Hill as King George III, suspended on June 25, 2021, and resuming on October 19. The production opened in Melbourne at Her Majesty’s Theatre on March 15, 2022, with a Ham4Ham show on March 22, and received positive reviews, with Jason Arrow praised and Standby Tigist Strode receiving acclaim; Sami Afuni took over Mulligan/Madison and Rowan Witt joined as King George, ending the season on January 15, 2023. The Australian tour continued in Brisbane at the Lyric Theatre, QPAC from January 2023, concluding on April 23. Stage Entertainment announced a German production in 2019 to open at the Operettenhaus in Hamburg, originally scheduled for November 2021, postponed due to the pandemic, with previews starting September 24, 2022, and opening on October 6, 2022, becoming the first non-English production, with lyrics translated by Kevin Schroeder and Sera Finale. The German production ended in October 2023 after one year due to poor ticket sales. The Australian producers announced an international tour to begin in Auckland, New Zealand at Spark Arena in May 2023, featuring the Australian cast and being the first staged in an arena. On March 28, 2023, Miranda announced the musical’s Asian premiere in Manila, Philippines, in September at the Solaire Resort & Casino, with previews starting September 21, 2023, and opening on November 11, 2023, featuring Australian cast members including Jason Arrow as Hamilton and Filipino actress Rachelle Ann Go as Eliza; the production ran until November 26, 2023, then moved to Abu Dhabi in 2024, running from January 17 to February 11 at the Etihad Arena.

The Australian producers, Michael Cassel Group, announced an international tour beginning in Auckland, New Zealand at Spark Arena in May 2023, featuring the Australian cast and marking the first arena staging of the production. On March 28, 2023, through GMG Productions' social media, Miranda announced the musical's Asian premiere in Manila, Philippines, at the Solaire Resort & Casino's theatre in September 2023, with previews starting on September 21 and opening night on November 11, 2023. Several Australian cast members, including Jason Arrow as Alexander Hamilton, returned for the first Asian production, which ran until November 26, 2023. Filipino actress Rachelle Ann Go reprised her role as Eliza from the original West End production. After Manila, the show moved to Abu Dhabi in 2024, running from January 17 to February 11 at the Etihad Arena, before transferring to Singapore on April 19 at the Sands Theatre, Marina Bay Sands. A UK and Ireland tour began at the Palace Theatre, Manchester on November 11, 2023, and toured to Edinburgh, Bristol, Birmingham, Dublin, Cardiff, Bradford, Southampton, Liverpool, Sunderland, Plymouth, and Norwich, with the full cast announced on September 21, including Shaq Taylor in the titular role. Hamilton's off-Broadway engagement at The Public Theater was sold out, and when it opened on Broadway, it had a multimillion-dollar advance, reportedly earning $30 million before opening. By September 2015, the show was sold out for most of its Broadway run and was the second-highest-grossing show on Broadway during the Labor Day week ending September 6, 2015, behind only The Lion King. In late November 2016, Hamilton set a Broadway box office record by grossing $3.3 million in a single eight-performance week, becoming the first show to exceed $3 million in eight performances. The musical offers a ticket lottery before each show, initially with 21 front-row seats and occasional standing room tickets; Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda began hosting outdoor mini-performances, called "Ham4Ham," before each daily drawing, allowing lottery participants to experience parts of the show and giving winners the chance to purchase two tickets for the price of one ($10 bill). HowlRound characterized Ham4Ham as part of a tradition of Latina/o theatremaking, emphasizing accessibility and social media engagement, noting it aligns with the philosophy of "taking the theatre to the people." The Ham4Ham shows drew unusually large crowds, causing congestion on West 46th Street, leading to an online ticket lottery beginning in early January 2016, which on its first day saw over 50,000 entries that crashed the website. After Miranda left the show on July 9, 2016, Rory O'Malley, who played King George III, took over as host of Ham4Ham, which officially ended on August 31, 2016. The online lottery continued, with a mobile app released in August 2017 that expanded the lottery to include touring productions and the Broadway show. Marilyn Stasio of Variety praised the off-Broadway production, noting the music was exhilarating and the lyrics were a surprise, with each character's singing style tailored to their persona, and that Miranda's narrative became a collective story of a nation built by immigrants. Jesse Green of New York highlighted the show's method of exploring the conflict between independence and interdependence, noting the references to Rodgers and Hammerstein, Gilbert and Sullivan, Sondheim, West Side Story, and 1776, as well as the excellence of the duels, which were handled superbly by director Thomas Kail and choreographer Andy Blankenbuehler. Elisabeth Vincentelli of the New York Post, which was founded by Hamilton's creator, criticized the show's portrayal of Hamilton and Burr's relationship, stating it fails to drive the narrative and that many numbers are exposition-heavy, especially those involving George Washington. Ben Brantley of The New York Times described the Broadway production as worth seeing, noting the characters' costumes and the set's period-appropriate tavern atmosphere. David Cote of Time Out New York called Hamilton a sublime blend of hip-hop, R&B, Britpop, and traditional showstoppers, praising its human drama and novelistic density, and named it a Critics' Pick with five stars. Andrew Schocket of the Journal of the Early Republic noted that while Hamilton strays from the "American Revolution Rebooted" genre, it remains rooted in it, and Marvin McAllister observed that the hip-hop influence works well because Miranda elevates the form through musical theater storytelling, ennobling both the culture and its creators. The Economist described the show's critical reception as "near-universal acclaim," and Barack Obama joked in 2016 that admiration for the musical is the only thing he and Dick Cheney agree on. In 2019, The Guardian ranked Hamilton the second-greatest theatrical work since 2000. Some feminist scholars have criticized the show for its depiction of women, with theatre professor Stacy Wolf noting that female characters are assigned limited and stereotypical roles, and musicologist Cheryl L. Keyes arguing that Eliza, Angelica, and Maria Reynolds conform to the "good wife," "gold digger," and "whore" tropes found in hip-hop. Andy Blankenbuehler received a Special Drama Desk Award for his choreography, which is described as "inspired and heart-stopping" and "indispensable" to the storytelling. The musical holds the record for most Tony Award nominations with 16 (though due to multiple actor nominations, it could have won only 13 unless a tie occurred), eventually winning 11 awards, the second-most ever for a single production, behind The Producers (2001), which won twelve. The New Yorker described the show as an achievement of historical and cultural reimagining, noting the costumes and set reflect the period with velvet frock coats and knee britches, a wooden scaffold against exposed brick, and warm lighting suggesting candlelight. The musical is mostly sung and rapped throughout, with little dialogue outside the score. Miranda stated that the portrayal of Hamilton, Jefferson, Washington, and other white historical figures by Black, Latino, and Asian actors does not require suspension of disbelief, saying the cast reflects how America looks now, allowing audiences to leave cultural baggage about the founding fathers at the door and making the story more immediate and accessible. The show emphasizes Hamilton's immigrant status, highlighting his work ethic and intelligence, and promotes a pro-immigration message by portraying him as an immigrant who "gets the job done," thus fostering a positive image of immigrants and illustrating America's complex racial history and identity. Renee Elise Goldsberry, who played Angelica Schuyler, said the show is a story about America told by a diverse cast with diverse musical styles, offering the opportunity to reclaim a history some feel is not theirs. Miranda has stated he is "totally open" to women playing the Founding Fathers, and the British production featured predominantly Black British artists. Although based on historical events, Miranda used dramatic license in retelling the story. Critics have pointed out a simplistic portrayal of Hamilton and a vilification of Jefferson; Joanne B. Freeman of Yale noted that real Hamilton was a contradictory figure who distrusted immigrants and valued law and order. Australian historian Shane White found the framing of the story "troubling," stating it centers on the Founding Fathers rather than including ordinary people, African-Americans, Native Americans, and women in a more inclusive narrative. Rutgers University professor Lyra Monteiro criticized the multi-ethnic casting for obscuring the absence of identifiable enslaved or free persons of color, and noted other commentators, such as Ishmael Reed, argued the show makes Hamilton and others appear more progressive on racial justice than they were. Policy analyst Matt Stoller criticized the musical's portrayal of Hamilton as an idealist, contrasting it with the historical record of Hamilton's reactionary, anti-democratic politics, citing his role in the Newburgh conspiracy, development of a financial system that empowered the wealthy, and use of military force, indefinite detention, and mass arrests during the Whiskey Rebellion. In 2018, Historians on Hamilton: How a Blockbuster Musical Is Restaging America's Past was published, with fifteen historians analyzing how the musical engages with and misinterprets history. Theatre scholars Meredith Conti and Meron Langsner have published analyses of firearms and dueling in the musical. Ishmael Reed wrote and produced the 2019 play The Haunting of Lin-Manuel Miranda, which critiques Hamilton's historical inaccuracies, initially running at Nuyorican Poets Cafe in May 2019 and again in October 2019. Philosopher Michael Sandel critiques Hamilton for oversimplistic multiculturalism, avoiding discussions on Hamilton's financial doctrines, and embracing liberal meritocracy in his 2022 edition of Democracy's Discontent. KQED News reported that a growing number of U.S. history teachers are using the Hamilton phenomenon to inspire students, with Cabinet rap battles engaging students on traditionally uninteresting topics. An elective course on Hamilton was offered at Ethical Culture Fieldston School in New York, and KQED noted that the show is especially galvanizing for students who find 18th-century America distant and irrelevant, as it presents the Founding Fathers as real humans with feelings and flaws, not as "bloodless, two-dimensional cutouts." A Bronx teacher noted his students were singing the songs like they would sing the latest releases from Drake or Adele, and one teacher emphasized Hamilton's ability to write his way out of trouble as a sign of scholarship and upward mobility. Hamilton's producers pledged to provide 20,000 New York City public high school students from low-income families with subsidized tickets at $70, with the Rockefeller Foundation contributing $1.5 million to reduce prices to $10 per student. The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History created a study guide to accompany the student-ticket program. Through a private grant, nearly 20,000 Chicago Public Schools students saw a special performance in 2017, with some performing original songs on stage. EducationWorld praised the musical for revitalizing interest in civic education, and Northwestern University announced plans in 2017 to offer coursework in history, Latino studies, and interdisciplinary studies inspired by Hamilton. In 2016, Moraine Valley Community College launched the "Straight Outta Hamilton" movement, hosting panels and events connecting the musical to current events. In 2015, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced a redesign of the $10 bill, with plans to replace Hamilton with a then-undecided woman from American history.

The Hamilton Education Program, founded in 2016 with funding from the Rockefeller Foundation, is a collaboration between the producers of Hamilton, the Miranda Family, and the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History. It established the Ham4Progress Award for Educational Advancement to support college-bound high school juniors from communities affected by social injustice or discrimination. The Gilder Lehrman Institute also created a study guide to accompany the student-ticket program, which aimed to lower ticket prices to $10 per student.
