Harnaam Kaur, born on 29 November 1990, is a British social media personality, postpartum coach, life coach, and motivational speaker. She was born in Slough, Berkshire, in a traditional Punjabi family. At the age of 12, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a condition characterized by elevated androgens in females, which causes hirsutism—the growth of excessive facial and body hair. As a result, Kaur grows a full beard. Initially, she tried to remove her facial hair due to constant bullying, but she has since embraced her appearance and become a spokesperson for the body positivity movement. In an interview with Rock N Roll Bride, she stated, "I decided to keep my beard and step forward against society's expectations of what a woman should look like. Today I am not suicidal and I do not self-harm. Today I am happy living as a young beautiful bearded woman. I have realised that this body is mine, I own it, I do not have any other body to live in so I may as well love it unconditionally." Before gaining media attention, Kaur worked as a primary school teaching assistant at Khalsa Primary School. She began receiving public attention in 2014 and later became a full-time public figure, freelance model, and motivational speaker. In March 2015, photographer Mr. Elbank included her in an exhibit at Somerset House in London featuring over 80 individuals with beards. In June 2015, she modeled for Rock N Roll Bride and was photographed by Louisa Coulthurst of Urban Bridesmaid Photography. In November 2015, she joined the "Eff Your Beauty Standards" campaign founded by Tess Holliday as a spokesperson. In March 2016, she became the first woman with a beard to walk at London Fashion Week, opening the show for designer Marianna Harutunian. She is signed to Wanted Models in Paris and appears in fashion spreads in both online and print magazines. In May 2016, conceptual artist Annelies Hofmeyr featured her in the project Trophy Wife Barbie, altering a Barbie doll to her likeness. In July 2016, musician Aisha Mizra included her in the music video for her song "Fuck Me or Destroy Me." In September 2016, Kaur was included in the Guinness World Records as the youngest woman in the world to have a full beard, with the citation stating: "Now with a beard measuring as long as six inches [15 cm] in places, she overcame years of bullying to take ownership of her appearance and achieve this record title at the age of 24 years 282 days." In March 2017, she was featured in a Teen Vogue article titled "Instagrammers Challenge Body and Facial Hair Stigma." In August 2017, she collaborated with grooming company Captain Fawcett to create and design a beard oil elixir, modeling in the advertisement campaign. In interviews and on social media, Kaur discusses the abuse and harassment she endured as a teenager, which led to self-harm and attempted suicide. In 2017, she participated in panel discussions in the House of Parliament on mental health, body image, cyberbullying, LGBTQIA+, and how social media, businesses, schools, and the government can support positive body images. Kaur uses Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, and YouTube to promote body-positive campaigns, raising awareness about body shaming, cyberbullying, and mental illness, and challenging gender stereotypes in media. She has said, "I don't think I believe in gender. I want to know who said a vagina is for a woman and a penis is for a man, or pink is for a girl and blue is for a boy. I am sitting here with a vagina and boobs – and a big beautiful beard." While she converted to Sikhism at age 16 as a reason for stopping hair removal, she now identifies as spiritual rather than religious. Traditionally, Sikhism forbids cutting hair, so she continues to wear a turban or other head coverings, a practice from the Khalsa tradition. Kaur is originally from Slough, England, and her younger brother, Gurdeep Singh Cheema, created the film Happy Ending? The Dangers of Online Grooming to raise awareness about online child grooming. To promote self-love and acceptance, Kaur named her beard Sundri, meaning beauty or beautiful, and refers to her beard as "she."

Harry Keen CBE (3 September 1925 – 5 April 2013) was an English diabetologist and professor of human metabolism at Guy's Hospital. He was the first to identify microalbuminuria as a predictor of kidney disease in diabetics and was an international authority on diabetes. Born in 1925 in London to a Jewish family, his parents were Sydney Keen, a tailor, and Esther (née Zenober), a teacher who had migrated to the United Kingdom from Poland. He attended St Ann's School in Hanwell and Ealing County Grammar School for Boys. He studied medicine at St Mary's Hospital Medical School, graduating on 5 July 1948, the day the National Health Service (NHS) was established. Keen began his medical career as a house officer at London's West Middlesex Hospital from 1948 to 1949, then enlisted in the Royal Army Medical Corps, serving for two years in Suez, Egypt. He returned to London in 1951, taking up a post at St Mary's Hospital under George Pickering, where he assisted on a large project studying hypertension in patients with diabetes and their first-degree relatives. In 1953, he began collaborating with Robert Daniel Lawrence, who headed the diabetes clinic at King's College Hospital, and spent seven years there studying diabetes and its long-term complications. In 1960, he travelled to Bethesda, Maryland, for a year-long research fellowship at the National Institutes of Health, where he experimented with insulin assays and early attempts to isolate pancreatic islets. Upon returning to London in 1961, he was hired as a lecturer by Guy's Hospital and its associated medical school, where he spent the rest of his career. In 1962, he conducted the Bedford Survey, in which every adult in Bedford provided a urine sample; around 70% of the population participated, and 250 participants were found to have undiagnosed diabetes. The study led to the first definition of prediabetes, which Keen called "borderline diabetes," and demonstrated the relationship between glucose intolerance and cardiovascular disease at a population level. In 1964, he and his colleagues became the first to show that trace amounts of the protein albumin in urine could predict kidney disease in diabetes, which is now the basis for routine kidney screening in diabetic patients. With the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, he conducted the Whitehall Survey in 1969, which led to the creation of different glucose thresholds for microvascular and macrovascular disease. He also pioneered the concept of the insulin pump, which delivers insulin continuously to type 1 diabetics who are reliant on insulin. In 1971, he was appointed professor of human metabolism at Guy's. He established one of the UK's first diabetes centres at Guy's Hospital. Keen chaired the 1980 and 1985 World Health Organization expert committees on diabetes. He was involved in the St. Vincent Declaration of 1989, which set international goals and benchmarks for diabetes care. He retired from medicine in 1990, becoming professor emeritus at King's College London. Keen chaired the British Diabetic Association between 1990 and 1996 and was appointed honorary president of the International Diabetes Federation in 1991. He was awarded a CBE and the first United Nations/UNESCO Hellmut Mehnert Award for the Prevention of Diabetes and its Complications in 1998. He received the American Diabetes Association's Kelly M. West Award for Outstanding Achievement in Epidemiology and Harold Rifkin Award for Distinguished International Service in the Cause of Diabetes in 1989 and 1992, respectively. Keen married Anna "Nan" Miliband, the sister of sociologist Ralph Miliband, in 1953; they had a son and a daughter. He was an uncle by marriage to Labour politicians Ed Miliband and David Miliband. He died on 5 April 2013.

Hassan Nasrallah (31 August 1960 – 27 September 2024) was a Lebanese Shia cleric and politician who served as the third secretary-general of Hezbollah, a Shia Islamist political party and militia, from 1992 until his assassination in 2024. Born the ninth of ten children into a Shia family in Bourj Hammoud, Matn District (an eastern suburb of Beirut), on 31 August 1960, Nasrallah’s father, Abdul Karim Nasrallah, was born in Al-Bazouriyah, a village in Jabal Amel (Southern Lebanon) near Tyre, and worked as a fruit and vegetables seller. Although his family was not particularly religious, Hassan was interested in theological studies and attended the al-Najah school and later a public school in Sin el Fil, a predominantly Christian neighborhood. In 1975, the outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War forced the family to move to their ancestral home in Bazourieh, where Nasrallah completed his secondary education at a public school in Tyre. There, he briefly joined the Amal Movement, a Lebanese Shia political group. He then studied at the Shia seminary in Baalbek, following the teachings of Iraqi Shi'ite scholar Mohammad Baqir al-Sadr, who founded the Dawa movement in Najaf during the early 1960s. In 1976, at age 16, Nasrallah traveled to Iraq and was admitted into al-Sadr’s seminary in Najaf, where al-Sadr reportedly recognized his leadership qualities, saying, "I scent in you the aroma of leadership; you are one of the Ansar [followers] of the Mahdi...". Nasrallah was expelled from Iraq in 1978, along with dozens of other Lebanese students, as Saddam Hussein expelled many Shias, including future Iranian supreme leader Ruhollah Khomeini and Abbas al-Musawi. He returned to Lebanon in 1979, having completed the first part of his studies. Back in Lebanon, he studied and taught at Amal’s leader Abbas al-Musawi’s school, later becoming Amal’s political delegate in Beqaa and a member of its central political office. In 1982, Nasrallah helped organize Hezbollah, which was formed to resist the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon, declaring that its confrontation with Israel "should only end when it has been removed from existence". In 1989, he traveled to Qom, Iran, to further his religious studies. In 1991, he returned to Lebanon and in 1992 replaced Musawi as Hezbollah’s leader after Musawi was killed by an Israeli airstrike. Under Nasrallah’s leadership, Hezbollah acquired rockets with a longer range, enabling them to strike northern Israel despite the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon. In 1993, Israel conducted Operation Accountability, which destroyed much of Lebanon’s infrastructure, and claimed success. An agreement followed, whereby Israel ended its attacks and Hezbollah agreed to stop rocket attacks on northern Israel. After a short pause, hostilities resumed. In 1996, Israel launched Operation Grapes of Wrath, blocking key Lebanese ports and bombing a Syrian military base. After 16 days of attacks, the Israeli–Lebanese Ceasefire Understanding was reached, with Hezbollah agreeing to cease rocket attacks in exchange for Israel halting its attacks—similar to the 1993 agreement. The peace did not last. In September 1997, Nasrallah’s public image changed dramatically after a speech about the killing of his eldest son by Israeli forces and his visits to other mourning families, which united Lebanese citizens and positioned him as a selfless, deeply rooted leader. In Israel, debates grew over whether the presence of Israeli forces in southern Lebanon was effective, as the security zone could not prevent Hezbollah rockets from reaching Israel. After heavy Israeli casualties, some Israeli politicians argued that the conflict would only end with Israel’s withdrawal. In 2000, Ehud Barak withdrew Israeli forces from Lebanon. The South Lebanon Army (SLA), supported by Israel, was quickly overrun by Hezbollah, with many members captured and some escaping to Israel. This success greatly increased Hezbollah’s popularity in Lebanon and the Islamic world. Nasrallah was credited with ending the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, significantly boosting the party’s political standing. In 2004, he negotiated a prisoner exchange deal with Israel, resulting in hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese prisoners being freed and many human remains, including that of his son, being returned to Lebanon. The agreement was hailed across the Arab world as a victory for Hezbollah. In December 2007, a London-based article in Asharq Al-Awsat reported that command of Hezbollah’s military wing was transferred to deputy Na'im Qasim, though Hezbollah denied this, calling it an attempt to "weaken the popularity" of the movement. In October 2008, Hashem Safieddine, his cousin, was assigned to succeed Nasrallah as secretary general. Widespread protests in Lebanon in October 2019 due to a deepening financial and economic crisis pressured government leaders, including Nasrallah, to resign. Hezbollah has been designated a terrorist organization by the United States, the European Union, and other nations, while the Arab League designated it as such in 2016 but no longer views it as one as of 2024. Russia rejects the terrorist designation, considering Hezbollah a legitimate sociopolitical organization, and as of 2012, China remains neutral and maintains contacts with Hezbollah. Nasrallah negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding with the Free Patriotic Movement led by Michel Aoun, agreeing to disarm upon the return of prisoners and the Shebaa Farms, and to pardon and return fugitive SLA members. In return, Aoun committed to reforming Lebanon’s confessional electoral system toward one man, one vote. Following an ambush by Hezbollah in Israeli territory that killed three soldiers and abducted two, the 2006 Lebanon War began. During the conflict, Israeli bombardments damaged parts of Beirut, especially the poorer, Shiite-controlled South Beirut. On 3 August 2006, Nasrallah vowed to strike Tel Aviv in retaliation, saying, "If you hit Beirut, the Islamic resistance will hit Tel Aviv and is able to do that with God's help," and claimed Hezbollah forces inflicted heavy casualties on Israeli troops. Nasrallah faced intense criticism from Arab countries, including Jordan, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia, with King Abdullah II and President Hosni Mubarak warning of regional "adventurism," and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud Al-Faisal calling the attacks "unexpected, inappropriate and irresponsible," stating they would pull the region back to earlier years. Lebanese leader Walid Jumblatt of the Progressive Socialist Party criticized Nasrallah, saying he was willing to let Beirut burn while haggling over surrender terms. After the war, Nasrallah’s speech solidified his image as a "charismatic leader in the media age" and a "symbol of pan-Arab national heroism," declaring that the victory was for Lebanon and all free people, not just Hezbollah, and highlighting the resistance’s steadfastness as a model for Arab and Islamic armies. The "Green Flood" (Al-sayl al-akhdhar) followed, referring to the distribution of $12,000 to citizens affected by the war, funded by Iran and delivered through militant networks. In a 2006 TV interview, Nasrallah stated he would not have ordered the capture of two Israeli soldiers if he had known it would lead to such a war, claiming the operation was a pretext for a pre-planned conflict. On 15 October 2008, Iraqi news source Almalaf reported that Nasrallah had been poisoned, citing sources in Lebanon who said a poisonous chemical was used and that Iranian doctors saved him. Hezbollah denied the poisoning, with Hezbollah member Al-Hajj Hassan stating it was a "lie and a fabrication," and confirming Nasrallah was okay. Iranian doctors arrived on a special military flight and reportedly considered flying Nasrallah to Iran for treatment. On 25 October 2008, in an interview with Al-Manar, Nasrallah denied the poisoning, accusing Israel and the United States of fabricating the story as part of a psychological war to imply internal disputes. He claimed that internet sources spreading the story were run from a single "dark room" and served American-Israeli interests, and stated that the organization had initially considered denying the claims in writing but chose a televised interview to refute them. On 25 May 2013, Nasrallah announced Hezbollah’s involvement in the Syrian civil war on the side of the Assad government against "Islamist extremists," pledging not to allow Syrian militants to control areas bordering Lebanon and confirming Hezbollah’s fighting in the strategic town of Qusair. In July 2014, his nephew was killed fighting in Syria. On 27 September 2024, it was reported that his daughter Zainab was killed by an Israeli airstrike, but this was later confirmed as false. Nasrallah consistently called for the end of the State of Israel and opposed reconciliation as the only path to justice, and highlighted Israel’s nuclear weapons as a security threat. Despite declaring "death to Israel" and "death to America," in a 2003 interview with The New Yorker, he stated that no one could go to war on behalf of the Palestinians, even if they disagreed with Palestinian agreements, and in 2004 said he would not sabotage a two-state settlement but would continue to encourage Palestinian resistance. Lebanese writer Amal Saad-Ghorayeb quotes Nasrallah as saying, "If we searched the entire world for a person more cowardly, despicable, weak and feeble in psyche, mind, ideology and religion, we would not find anyone like the Jew. Notice, I do not say the Israeli," though Charles Glass questions the attribution, noting the quote was originally attributed to a Hezbollah member of the Lebanese Parliament, Muhammad Fneish. In a 1998 speech marking the Day of Ashura, published on Nasrallah’s official website, he referred to Israel as "the state of the grandsons of apes and pigs – the Zionist Jews" and condemned them as "the murderers of the prophets."

Hassan Nasrallah, a prominent Lebanese leader and head of Hezbollah, has been a central figure in Middle Eastern politics, often referring to Israel as "the state of the grandsons of apes and pigs – the Zionist Jews" and condemning it as "the murderers of the prophets," statements interpreted by CAMERA, MEMRI, and Shaul Shai as broadly antisemitic. In a 1998 speech marking Ashura, he also claimed that Jews are "Allah's most cowardly and avaricious creatures," and that if they gathered in Israel, it would save the world from having to pursue them globally. After the Hebron Agreement in 1998, Nasrallah called for the assassination of Yasser Arafat, stating that Palestinian police should act like Khaled al-Islambuli and that Arafat’s presence is a "disgrace." In a 2002 speech cited by journalist Badih Chayban, Nasrallah said, "If they [the Jews] all gather in Israel, it will save us the trouble of going after them worldwide," though Charles Glass questioned the authenticity of this quote, noting it was attributed to a Hezbollah member, Muhammad Fneish, not Nasrallah himself, and that a Hezbollah spokeswoman, Wafa Hoteit, denied the statement. In 2009, Nasrallah disavowed opposition to Jews, stating that the issue with Israel is not its Jewish identity but its status as occupiers who are raping Palestinian land and holy sites. On Al Quds Day in 2013, he declared Israel "a cancer that must be eradicated." He condemned the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center, stating that Hezbollah neither favored nor opposed the act, and that while they do not endorse Osama bin Laden’s methods or operations, they condemn such actions. Nasrallah called the Hamas attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 a heroic operation and stated that Hezbollah’s missile and drone attacks on northern Israel were carried out in solidarity with Palestinians. In a 1988 speech, Nasrallah stated that Lebanon should become part of a Greater Islamic Republic governed by the Mahdi and Imam Khomeini. During the 2006 Jyllands-Posten Muhammad cartoons controversy, he claimed that if a Muslim had carried out Imam Khomeini’s fatwa against Salman Rushdie, the Danish, Norwegian, and French attackers would not have dared to offend the Prophet Muhammad. In February 2012, Nasrallah criticized the Quran burning in Afghanistan, calling the behavior of those who affront prophets and holy books "Israeli and let us say it is Jewish," and stated that such actions reflect a mentality that could lead to a global religious war. According to CAMERA, Nasrallah stated that Lebanese society refuses to grant Palestinian residents Lebanese citizenship and rejects their resettlement, a position supported by broad Lebanese consensus due to fears of reigniting civil war, while Palestinian refugees in Lebanon consistently favor the right of return. On 27 September 2024, the Israeli Air Force launched an airstrike on Hezbollah’s headquarters in Dahieh, reportedly targeting Nasrallah, killing at least six and injuring over 90, with several missing. The Israel Defense Forces claimed Nasrallah had died in the strike; Hezbollah and Lebanese authorities confirmed his death, and his body was found under rubble, reportedly from toxic fumes rather than physical wounds, though some sources suggest blunt force trauma. Hashem Safieddine was assumed to be his successor but was killed in a separate Israeli airstrike; Naim Qassem was elected secretary-general on 29 October 2024. Nasrallah’s body was temporarily buried in secret to avoid Israeli attacks during his funeral, which took place on 23 February 2025, attended by an estimated 450,000 to 1,400,000 people, including many flying Hezbollah flags and holding portraits of Nasrallah and Safieddine. Senior Hezbollah official Ali Daamoush claimed about 800 personalities from 65 countries attended. Representatives from Iran, Iraq, and Yemen attended, with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling them "two heroes of the resistance." Hours before the funeral, Israeli air strikes targeted Hezbollah rocket launchers in southern Lebanon, and Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz stated that Israeli planes flew over the stadium to send a message that anyone threatening Israel would face destruction. Nasrallah’s body was buried in Beirut and Safieddine’s in Deir Qanoun an-Naher. Nasrallah became a "national hero" in Lebanon, with the New York Times calling him the "most powerful man in the Middle East" and the "only Arab leader who actually does what he says he's going to do," and Al Jazeera comparing him to Yasser Arafat, Gamal Abdel Nasser, Che Guevara, and Fidel Castro, while Annia Ciezadlo described him as an "emblem of Islam and Arab pride." Amal Saad-Ghorayeb described him as "passionate" but "plainspoken and practical," and American activist Osama Siblani praised him as a "great leader" at a 2024 Gaza war protest rally. Nasrallah was often referred to as "al-Sayyid Hassan," indicating descent from Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Husayn ibn Ali. However, many Lebanese, especially Sunni Muslims and Christians, viewed him as an agent of Iranian interests, with Hezbollah seen as a state within a state serving Iranian objectives. Under his leadership, Hezbollah was implicated in assassinations of critics and March 14 Alliance politicians, and was often despised by anti-Assad Syrians, particularly in Idlib, who saw him as complicit in Assad’s atrocities; jubilant celebrations erupted in parts of Syria after his assassination. Two songs were composed about him during the 2006 war: "The Hawk of Lebanon" in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and "Yalla Ya Nasrallah" in Israel. In 2007, Lebanese singer Alaa Zalzali composed "Ya Nasrallah," and Julia Boutros released "Ahebba'i," inspired by a message Nasrallah sent to Hezbollah fighters in 2006. Nasrallah married Fatima Mustafa Yassine in 1978 and had four sons and one daughter: Mohammad Hadi, Mohammad Jawad, Zeinab, Mohammad Ali, and Mohammad Mahdi. On 12 September 1997, four Hezbollah fighters were killed in an Israeli ambush near Mlikh, including Muhammad Hadi, Nasrallah’s eldest son. Five Lebanese soldiers and a woman were killed in a simultaneous airstrike. Nasrallah said upon learning of his son’s death, "I am proud to be the father of one of the martyrs." When the IDF released photos of his son’s body and offered to exchange it for body parts of those killed in the earlier ambush, Nasrallah responded, "Keep it. We have many more men like Hadi ready to offer themselves to the struggle," and a seven-day mourning period followed, attended daily by an estimated two hundred thousand people. His son’s remains were returned to Lebanon in 2004 as part of a prisoner exchange deal involving Nasrallah. Syrian opposition media reported that Nasrallah was a brother-in-law of Hezbollah commander Wissam al-Tawil, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike in January 2024. On 25 May 2024, Hezbollah announced that Nasrallah’s mother, Hajja Umm Hassan, had died. On 2 October 2024, five days after Nasrallah’s assassination, his son-in-law Hassan Jaafar al-Qasir was killed by an Israeli strike.

Heinrich Vogl (15 January 1845 – 21 April 1900) was a German operatic heldentenor. He played the role of Loge in Richard Wagner's Das Rheingold at the Munich Court Opera on 22 September 1869, with his wife, Therese Vogl, performing as Wellgunde. He also sang the role of Siegmund in Wagner's Die Walküre at Munich on 26 June 1870, with Therese Vogl portraying Sieglinde, Siegmund's sister and lover. His debut at the Munich Court Opera was as Max in Weber's Der Freischütz. He performed at Bayreuth, Berlin, London, and the Metropolitan Opera in New York City. At Bayreuth, he played Loge in the first complete Ring cycle on 13 August 1876. His performance in the role earned fellow singer Lilli Lehmann's praise, who stated he was born for the part and that his Loge had never been equalled. His debut at the Metropolitan Opera was on 1 January 1890 in the title role of Lohengrin; he also performed Loge, Siegmund, the title role of Tannhäuser, Tristan in Tristan und Isolde, and Siegfried in both Siegfried and Götterdämmerung. Heinrich Vogl was the first to perform the roles of Loge and Siegfried in London, doing so in the first Ring cycle at Her Majesty's Theatre with Anton Seidl conducting and his wife playing Brünnhilde. His Wagner repertoire included all the leading tenor roles except Walther in Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg, for which Wagner rejected him for the 1868 premiere, stating at the age of 23 that Vogl was "totally incompetent." He and his wife Therese were among the first to sing the lead roles in Tristan und Isolde and were highly regarded in those roles. His non-Wagner roles included the title role in Verdi's Otello, Canio in Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, Aeneas in Berlioz's Les Troyens, and the title role of Berlioz's Benvenuto Cellini. He was known for his vocal power and stamina, enabling him to perform Loge, Siegmund, and both Siegfrieds from Wagner's Ring cycle on consecutive evenings multiple times. Heinrich Vogl is buried beside his wife in Tutzing, Bavaria.

Helen Hartness Flanders (May 19, 1890 – May 23, 1972), a native of Springfield, Vermont, was an internationally recognized ballad collector and authority on folk music in New England and the British Isles. At the initiative of the Vermont Commission on Country Life, she began a three-decade career collecting traditional songs from New England, many of which originated in the British Isles, during a time when people were shifting away from traditional music in favor of radio. Recognizing that these songs were at risk of being lost as the people who sang them passed away, Flanders dedicated herself to recording them. She was born in Springfield, where her father, James Hartness, was an inventor, industrialist, and one-term Governor of Vermont, and she graduated from the Dana Hall School in 1909, singing in the glee club and joining the French club. In 1911, she married Ralph Flanders, a mechanical engineer, industrialist, and U.S. Senator from Vermont (1946–1959), with whom she maintained homes in Springfield and Washington, D.C., entertaining notable figures such as Dorothy Canfield Fisher and Robert Frost. They had three children: Elizabeth (born 1912), Anna (also known as Nancy, born 1918), and James (born 1923); Elizabeth assisted her mother in collecting and transcribing songs. Flanders published two volumes of poetry and one children's play, and traveled with her husband to the British Isles, Europe, and Australia. In 1930, Vermont Governor John E. Weeks invited her to join the Committee on Traditions and Ideals of the Vermont Commission on Country Life, which tasked her with collecting Vermont folk songs passed down orally. Initially recording on wax cylinders, she later used aluminum and acetate discs from 1939 to 1949 and reel-to-reel tapes, often using her car’s cigarette lighter when electricity was unavailable. She worked with George Brown in 1930, Phillips Barry from 1931 to 1937, and Alan Lomax in 1939; from 1940 to 1958, Marguerite Olney made major contributions to both collection management and fieldwork. Between 1930 and 1939, she focused on Child ballads, resulting in a large number of cylinder recordings; of the 150 disc recordings with Lomax, many included songs, stories, and fiddle tunes. Over time, her recordings expanded to include religious songs, children's songs, 19th-century American popular songs, dance tunes, and folktales. George Brown, Alice Brown, Phillips Barry, Marguerite Olney, and Elizabeth Flanders Ballard all created musical transcriptions for her publications. An index of all recordings (collected between 1930 and 1958) was published in 1983. In 1941, due to insufficient space in her home, she donated the collection to Middlebury College, Vermont, where it is now housed in Special Collections and includes nearly 4,500 field recordings, her papers, and related materials. Copies are also available at the American Folklife Center of the Library of Congress and Harvard University, which holds files of her correspondence. Flanders observed that songs migrating from the British Isles or Europe often changed as singers incorporated details from life in the New World, such as the "Yorkshire Bite" becoming the "New Hampshire Bite," and many ballads reflect aspects of New England and Colonial history. In 1942, Middlebury College awarded her an honorary Master of Arts; she was a member of the National Committee of the National Folk Festival Association and vice president of the Folksong Society of the Northeast, and in 1966, the Vermont House of Representatives added her name to the state’s Roll of Distinction in the Arts. She authored eight books on ballads and folk music, wrote pamphlets, newspaper and magazine articles, and two books of poetry, and contributed a regular column on ballads to the Springfield Sunday Union and Republican (Massachusetts) during the 1930s. Folksingers such as Margaret MacArthur (1928–2006), who moved to Vermont in the late 1940s, promoted the collection through concerts and recordings, with Flanders encouraging her and providing copies of the recordings; MacArthur became known for her repertoire of songs from the Flanders Collection. In recent years, Vermonter Deborah Flanders has performed and recorded songs collected by her great-aunt Helen. The Flanders Ballad Collection at Middlebury College is organized as follows.

Helmut Lang, born on 10 March 1956, is an Austrian artist and former fashion designer and mentor who lives and works in New York and on Long Island. In 1986, he presented his first Helmut Lang runway collection in Paris at Centre Georges Pompidou; his first Helmut men's collection debuted in 1987, and a decade later he relocated his label from Vienna to New York. Lang utilized unconventional materials such as rubber, feathers, and metallic fabrics, redefining the silhouette of the 1990s and early 2000s. He broke from the opulent runway show traditions of the 1980s by becoming the first designer to stream his collection online in 1998. His brand was recognized for its utilitarian, minimalist aesthetic and its prestigious denim line. In 1999, Lang sold a 51% stake in his company to the Prada Group, which managed distribution and manufacturing, while Lang retained control of design and advertising. Prada subsequently launched Helmut Lang accessories like shoes, belts, and bags and opened Helmut Lang stores in Hong Kong and Singapore. Sales under the Prada Group declined from $100 million in 1999 to $37 million in 2003, with the cancellation of licensing for external companies to manufacture and market the profitable Helmut Lang Jeans cited as a key reason for the drop in revenue. In 2005, Lang left the label and retired from fashion, after which he has resided in New York City and on Long Island as a practicing artist. In 2006, Prada sold the Helmut Lang brand to Link Theory Holdings. Lang has collaborated with artists Jenny Holzer and Louise Bourgeois, and his recent artistic works explore abstract sculptural forms and physical arrangements beyond the human body. He held his first solo art exhibition, ALLES GLEICH SCHWER, at the Kestnergesellschaft in Hannover in 2008 and has since presented solo exhibitions internationally. Excerpts from his art projects, Long Island Diaries and The Selective Memory Series, have been published in various publications including Purple, BUTT Magazine, Fanzine 137, Visionaire, and most recently The Travel Almanac. The original Helmut Lang stores, all designed by Lang in collaboration with Gluckman Mayner Architects of New York, have been closed; the last to close was the Paris location in late 2005. Four scents created by Lang in cooperation with Procter & Gamble were discontinued with the 2005 closure of the brand. This timeline covers Helmut Lang's work in fashion and art up to 2021.

Henri de Valois, duc d'Angoulême (1551 – 2 June 1586, in Aix-en-Provence), also known as "Henri, bâtard de Valois" or "Henri de France," was a Légitimé de France, cleric, and military commander during the Wars of Religion. He was born the bastard son of Henri II of France and his mistress Janet Stewart, Lady Fleming, an illegitimate daughter of James IV of Scotland. As the most favored natural son of the king, he was legitimized and granted the title of Duke of Angoulême. Henri served as Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, Grand Prior of France of the Sovereign Order of Malta, and Admiral of the Levantine Sea, and ruled as Governor of Provence from 1579 until his death in 1586. In 1570, supporters of Mary, Queen of Scots, selected Henri as a potential leader of a French military force to assist them in their civil war against James VI of Scotland, believing his Scottish and French royal ancestry would earn him respect in Scotland and England; however, the plan was proposed to John Lesley, Queen Mary's ambassador in France, and ultimately, French soldiers and Henri were not sent to Scotland. Henri played a major role in the two prolonged military campaigns against Huguenot strongholds during the peak of the French Wars of Religion, participating in the Siege of La Rochelle (1572–1573), organized by the Duke of Anjou, future King Henry III of France, and leading the five-year Siege of Ménerbes (1573–1578), which took place at a citadel in the Luberon foothills favored by Pope Pius V. While serving as Governor of Provence, his secretary was the poet François de Malherbe, and Henri composed many sonnets, one of which was set to music by Fabrice Caietain. In 1586, Henri was killed in a duel at Aix-en-Provence with Philip Altoviti, who was also mortally wounded in the encounter.

The Henry Draper Catalogue (HD) is an astronomical star catalogue published between 1918 and 1924, providing spectroscopic classifications for 225,300 stars; it was later expanded by the Henry Draper Extension (HDE), published between 1925 and 1936, which added classifications for 46,850 more stars, and by the Henry Draper Extension Charts (HDEC), published from 1937 to 1949 in the form of charts, which provided classifications for 86,933 additional stars. In total, 359,083 stars were classified as of August 2017. The HD catalogue is named after Henry Draper, an amateur astronomer, and covers the entire sky almost completely down to an apparent photographic magnitude of about 9; the extensions added fainter stars in certain areas of the sky. The construction of the Henry Draper Catalogue was part of a pioneering effort to classify stellar spectra, and its catalogue numbers are commonly used to identify stars. The origin of the catalogue dates back to Henry Draper's first photograph of a star's spectrum, Vega, in 1872, followed by over a hundred more stellar spectrum photographs before his death in 1882. In 1885, Edward Pickering began supervising photographic spectroscopy at the Harvard College Observatory using the objective prism method; in 1886, Draper's widow, Mary Anna Palmer Draper, funded the work under the name Henry Draper Memorial. Pickering and his team began an objective-prism survey of the sky and classified the resulting spectra. A first result was the Draper Catalogue of Stellar Spectra, published in 1890, which included spectroscopic classifications for 10,351 stars, mostly north of declination −25°, with most classifications done by Williamina Fleming. The classification scheme subdivided the Secchi classes (I to IV) into letters A to N, with O for stars with bright lines, P for planetary nebulae, and Q for spectra not fitting into classes A through P; no star of type N appeared, and the only star of type O was HR 2583. Antonia Maury and Pickering published a more detailed study of bright northern hemisphere stars in 1897, using classifications from I to XXII, with groups I to XX corresponding to subdivisions of Draper types B, A, F, G, K, and M, and XXI and XXII corresponding to types N and O; she was the first to place B stars before A stars. In 1890, the Harvard College Observatory built the Boyden Observatory in Arequipa, Peru to study the southern sky, and in 1901, Annie Jump Cannon and Pickering published a study of bright southern hemisphere stars. Cannon used the Draper Catalogue's lettered types but dropped all letters except O, B, A, F, G, K, and M in that order, plus P for planetary nebulae and Q for peculiar spectra, and introduced types such as B5A for stars halfway between B and A, F2G for stars one-fifth of the way from F to G, and so on. Between 1910 and 1915, increased interest in stellar classification led to the start of work on the Henry Draper Catalogue in 1911, with Cannon and her coworkers classifying spectra at a rate of approximately 5,000 per month from 1912 to 1915. The catalogue was published in nine volumes of the Annals of Harvard College Observatory between 1918 and 1924, containing rough positions, magnitudes, spectral classifications, and cross-references to the Durchmusterung catalogs for 225,300 stars. The classification scheme was similar to Cannon's 1901 work, but types such as B, A, B5A, F2G were changed to B0, A0, B5, F2, and so on, with classes O through M, P for nebulae, and R and N for carbon stars. Pickering died on February 3, 1919, leaving six volumes to be overseen by Cannon. She classified 46,850 fainter stars in selected regions of the sky in the Henry Draper Extension, published in six parts between 1925 and 1936. She continued classifying stars until her death in 1941; most of these classifications were published in 1949 in the Henry Draper Extension Charts (the first portion of which was published in 1937), with Margaret Walton Mayall supervising the work after Cannon's death. The catalogue and its extensions were the first large-scale attempt to catalogue stellar spectral types and led to the Harvard classification scheme, still used today. Stars in the main catalogue are of medium magnitude, down to about 9th magnitude (about 1/15 as bright as the faintest stars visible to the naked eye), while the extensions include stars as faint as the 11th magnitude in selected sky regions. Stars in the original catalogue are numbered from 1 to 225,300 (prefix HD), in order of increasing right ascension for the epoch 1900.0; the first extension stars are numbered from 225,301 to 272,150 (prefix HDE); extension chart stars are numbered from 272,151 to 359,083 (prefix HDEC). However, the numbering is continuous, so the prefix HD may be used without ambiguity. Many stars are commonly identified by their HD numbers. The Henry Draper Catalogue and Extension were available from the NASA Astronomical Data Center as part of their third CD-ROM of astronomical catalogues and are currently available from the VizieR service of the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg as catalogue number III/135A. Due to their format, converting the Henry Draper Extension Charts into a machine-readable format was difficult, but it was completed by 1995 by Nesterov, Röser and their coworkers, and the charts are now available at VizieR as catalogue number III/182. The Henry Draper Catalogue and its extensions are available online free of charge at the VizieR service of the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg.

Sir Henry Ernest Gascoyne Bulwer, GCMG (11 December 1836 – 30 September 1914[1]), was a British colonial administrator and diplomat. He was the nephew of Sir Henry Lytton Bulwer and brother to Edward Earle Gascoyne Bulwer.[2][3] Bulwer was educated at Charterhouse School and Trinity College, Cambridge.[4] He held various administrative and diplomatic posts throughout his career.[3] In recognition of his service, he was appointed to the Order of St Michael and St George as Companion in 1864, Knight Commander in 1874, and Knight Grand Cross in 1883.[8] The town of Bulwer in Natal, South Africa, was named after him.[9] While serving as Governor of Labuan, he presented the type specimen of Bulwer's pheasant (Lophura bulweri) to the British Museum, a bird subsequently named in his honor.[10][3] The author H. Rider Haggard, who had worked on Bulwer's staff in Natal and was his friend, dedicated the novel Marie to Sir Henry Bulwer.[11] This British diplomat-related article is a stub. The Hessenlied is the official anthem of the German state of Hesse. The lyrics were authored by Carl Preser (1828–1910), and the melody was composed by Albrecht Brede (1834–1920). The song begins with the lines "I know a land so affluent and so beautiful, the fields full of golden grain," describing a landscape where forests "flourish from the valley to sunny heights" and "many dark, fragrant forests" are present. It recalls the speaker's childhood memories of sitting "in blossoms and flowers" under the care of their mother's hand. The anthem then expresses a greeting to the homeland as "thou magnificent land," calling Hesse "the heart of Germany, my thriving land Hesse." The geographical scope is defined as stretching "from the Main to the Weser, Werra and Lahn," with the text noting that the cities in this region "shine" and are "gorgeous to see in the light." The repeated lines emphasize both personal nostalgia and regional pride. This article about the music of Germany is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information. The Hickinbottom Award, also known as the Hickinbottom Fellowship, is given annually by the Royal Society of Chemistry to an early career scientist for outstanding contributions in organic chemistry. The recipient receives a monetary prize and is required to complete a lecture tour across the UK. The award is selected by the awards committee of the Royal Society of Chemistry's organic division. It was established in 1979 through a bequest from Wilfred Hickinbottom, who was recognized for his support of high standards in experimental chemistry. A portion of the monetary award is the Briggs scholarship, which was funded by a bequest from Lady Alice Lilian Thorpe, the daughter of William Briggs. The award was first presented in 1981 to Steven Ley and Jeremy Sanders. Subsequent recipients are listed in the records.

Himachal Pradesh, known in Hindi as Himācal Pradeś and literally meaning "snow-laden mountain province," is a mountainous state in northern India, situated in the Western Himalayas between 30°22′N and 33°12′N latitude and 75°47′E and 79°04′E longitude, covering an area of 55,673 square kilometres. It is the northernmost state of India and shares borders with Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to the north, Punjab to the west, Haryana to the southwest, Uttarakhand to the southeast, and a narrow border with Uttar Pradesh to the south, while also having an international border with the Tibet Autonomous Region in China. The state is characterized by extreme landscapes, including several peaks and extensive river systems, with the Zanskar range in the northeast, the great Himalayan range in the east and north, the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal ranges in the lesser Himalayas, and the Shiwalik range in the south and west. Reo Purgyil, at 6,816 metres, is the highest peak in the state. The drainage system includes perennial rivers such as the Chandra Bhaga (Chenab), Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Yamuna, which are fed by snow and rainfall and flow through valleys like the Satluj, Spiti, Baspa, Kullu, Kangra, Parvati, Lahaul and Pangi, and Chamba. These rivers contribute to both the Indus and Ganges basins. Due to elevation variations, the climate ranges from hot and humid in the south to cold, alpine, and glacial in the north and east; Dharamsala receives heavy rainfall, while Lahaul and Spiti are cold and nearly rainless. The state experiences three seasons: summer (mid-April to end of June), winter (late November to mid-March), and the rainy season. Himachal Pradesh is recognized as India's second open-defecation-free state in 2016 and was ranked as India's least corrupt state in a 2017 CMS-India Corruption Study. The state is divided into 12 districts, grouped into three divisions—Shimla, Kangra, and Mandi—and further subdivided into 73 subdivisions, 78 blocks, and 172 tehsils. It is one of the states in the Indian Himalayan Region (IHR), a global hotspot of biodiversity, with 463 bird, 77 mammalian, 44 reptile, and 80 fish species; the state bird is the Western tragopan (jujurana), and the state animal is the snow leopard. The state has five national parks—Great Himalayan National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), Pin Valley, Inderkilla, Khirganga, and Simbalbara—and 30 wildlife sanctuaries and 3 conservation reserves. Himachal Pradesh is also known as Dev Bhoomi ("Land of Gods") and Veer Bhoomi ("Land of the Brave"). The region has been inhabited since prehistoric times by tribes such as the Koli, Hali, Dagi, Dhaugri, Dasa, Khasa, Kanaura, and Kirata, with the Kols and Mundas believed to be the original inhabitants, followed by the Bhotas and Kiratas. The foothills were inhabited by people from the Indus Valley Civilisation (2250–1750 BCE). During the Vedic period, small republics (Janapada) existed, later conquered by the Gupta Empire, and later fragmented into local powers including Rajput principalities, which were invaded by the Delhi Sultanate, Mahmud Ghaznavi, Timur, and Sikander Lodi. Several hill states acknowledged Mughal suzerainty. The Kingdom of Gorkha conquered territories in Nepal in 1768, expanded its territory, and annexed Sirmour and Shimla, defeating Kangra's ruler Sansar Chand Katoch in 1806, though they failed to capture Kangra Fort, which came under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1809. After the First Anglo-Sikh War, Raja Ram Singh captured the Siba fort in 1846. The British came into direct conflict with the Nepali forces in the tarai belt, expelled them from the Satluj provinces, and emerged as the paramount power. During the 1857 revolt, hill states were largely inactive, except for some rulers like those of Chamba, Bilaspur, Bhagal, and Dhami, who supported the British. After Queen Victoria's proclamation in 1858, the British Crown took control. During World War I, rulers of Kangra, Jaswan, Datarpur, Guler, Rajgarh, Nurpur, Chamba, Suket, Mandi, and Bilaspur remained loyal and contributed to the war effort. On 15 April 1948, the Chief Commissioner's Province of Himachal Pradesh was established by integrating 30 princely states, including the Simla Hills States and four southern hill states of Punjab, under the Himachal Pradesh (Administration) Order, 1948. Bilaspur was merged into Himachal Pradesh on 1 July 1954 via the Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954. Himachal became a Part 'C' state on 26 January 1950 and had its first Legislative Assembly election in 1952. On 1 November 1956, it became a union territory. On 1 November 1966, areas from Punjab—Simla, Kangra, Kullu, Lahul and Spiti, Lohara, Amb, Una Kanungo, Santokhgarh Kanungo, parts of Dhar Kalan Kanungo, and some parts of PEPSU and Pathankot—were merged into Himachal Pradesh under the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966. On 18 December 1970, the Himachal Pradesh Act was passed, and the state came into being on 25 January 1971 as the 18th state of India, with Dr. Yashwant Singh Parmar as its first chief minister. The state operates under a parliamentary system with a unicameral Legislative Assembly of 68 Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLA), with terms lasting five years. The executive authority lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister, who is appointed by the Governor, the titular head of state appointed by the President of India. The Speaker and Deputy Speaker are elected by the members and preside over assembly meetings. The judiciary includes the Himachal Pradesh High Court and lower courts. Planning began in 1951, with the First Five-Year Plan allocating ₹52.7 million, of which over 50% went to transport and communication and 4.6% to power (rising to 7% by the Third Plan). Expenditure on agriculture increased from 14.4% in the First Plan to 32% in the Third Plan, declining to less than 10% by the Tenth Plan, while energy expenditure reached 24.2% in the Tenth Plan. The total GDP for 2005–06 was ₹254 billion, up from ₹230 billion in 2004–05, showing a 10.5% increase. In the November 2022 assembly elections, the Indian National Congress won 40 seats, the BJP won 25, and Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu was sworn in as the 15th Chief Minister on 11 December 2022, with Mukesh Agnihotri as deputy. The state government promotes sustainable development through its "Green Himachal vision," as highlighted by Town and Country Planning Minister Rajesh Dharmani in a statement on 29 March 2025. In 2002, a workshop on endangered medicinal plant species was held, attended by 40 experts, due to large-scale irrational extraction threatening biodiversity. According to the 2003 Forest Survey of India report, 66.52% of the state's area is legally defined forest. The state is known as the "fruit bowl of the country" with widespread orchards and cultivated flowers like white gladiolas, carnations, marigolds, roses, chrysanthemums, tulips, and lilies. The Himachal Pradesh Horticultural Produce Marketing and Processing Corporation Ltd. (HPMC) markets fresh and processed fruits. The state is also the first smoke-free state in India, with cooking free of traditional chulhas.

Planning in Himachal Pradesh began in 1951 alongside the rest of India with the implementation of the first five-year plan, which allocated ₹52.7 million to the state. More than 50% of this expenditure was directed toward transport and communication, while the power sector received only 4.6%, increasing to 7% by the Third Plan. Expenditure on agriculture and allied activities rose from 14.4% in the First Plan to 32% in the Third Plan, declining progressively to less than 10% by the Tenth Plan. Energy sector expenditure reached 24.2% in the Tenth Plan. The total GDP for 2005–06 was ₹254 billion, up from ₹230 billion in 2004–05, reflecting a 10.5% increase. In fiscal 2015–16, GDP was estimated at ₹1.110 trillion, rising to ₹1.247 trillion in 2016–17, a 6.8% growth, with per capita income increasing from ₹130,067 to ₹147,277. Fiscal 2017–18 advance estimates showed GDP at ₹1.359 trillion and per capita income at ₹158,462. As of 2018, Himachal Pradesh is the 22nd-largest state economy in India with a GDP of ₹1.52 lakh crore (US$18 billion) and the 13th-highest per capita income (₹160,000 or US$1,900). It ranks second in the country on human development indicators after Kerala. Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), Himachal Pradesh recorded a 46% share of workdays for women in 2009–2010, a sharp rise from 13% in 2006–2007. Agriculture contributes 9.4% to the net state domestic product and is the main source of income and employment, directly supporting 90% of the population and providing direct employment to 62% of total workers. Major crops include wheat, maize, rice, and barley, with cropping systems such as maize-wheat, rice-wheat, and maize-potato-wheat; pulses, fruits, vegetables, and oilseeds are also grown. The traditional Kuhl irrigation system is prevalent in the Kangra valley, though it faces threats from hydroprojects on small streams. Initiatives like the Mid-Himalayan Watershed Development Project and the Himachal Pradesh Reforestation Project (HPRP), the world’s largest clean development mechanism (CDM) undertaking, have improved agricultural yields and rural incomes. Apple is the principal cash crop, grown in Shimla, Kinnaur, Kullu, Mandi, Chamba, Sirmaur, and Lahaul-Spiti, with an average annual production of five lakh tonnes and per hectare output of 8 to 10 tonnes. Apple cultivation covers 49% of the area under fruit crops and 85% of total fruit production, generating an estimated economy of ₹3500 crore. Apple production increased from 90,347 hectares in 2000–01 to 104,000 hectares in 2011–12, and in fiscal 2015–16, it reached 753,000 tonnes, making Himachal the second-largest apple-producing state after Jammu and Kashmir. The state is also a leading producer of apricots, cherries, peaches, pears, plums, and strawberries. Kangra tea, introduced in 1849 and popular globally, peaked in the late 19th century, declined after the 1905 Kangra earthquake, and received geographical indication status in 2005. Himachal is known as Asia’s pharmaceutical hub, housing 652 pharmaceutical units and a thriving ₹40,000 crore drug manufacturing industry. Hydropower is a major source of income, with abundant perennial rivers supporting high-capacity plants that produce surplus electricity sold to states like Delhi, Punjab, and West Bengal. This electricity export revenue is used as a subsidy for state consumers. The state is nearly universally electrified, with 94.8% of houses receiving electricity as of 2001 (above the national average of 55.9%), though its hydroelectric potential of 27,436 MW across five river basins remains underutilized, with a capacity of 10,351 MW in 2016. Tourism is a major economic contributor, with hill stations like Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala, Dalhousie, Chamba, Khajjiar, Kullu, and Kasauli attracting domestic and foreign tourists. The state has five Shakti Peeths—Chintpurni, Jwalamukhi, Bajreshwari Mata, Shri Chamunda Devi, and Naina Devi—and prominent pilgrimage sites such as Baijnath, Bhimakali, Bijli Mahadev, and Jakhoo. Manimahesh Lake in Chamba hosts an annual August pilgrimage attracting lakhs of devotees. The state is referred to as "Dev Bhoomi" due to its presence in ancient Hindu texts and numerous historical temples. Adventure tourism includes ice skating in Shimla, paragliding in Bir and Solang Valley, rafting in Kullu, skiing in Manali, boating in Bilaspur, fishing in Tirthan Valley, trekking, and horse riding. Shimla hosts Asia’s only natural ice-skating rink. The state has some of the highest mountain passes in the world—Rohtang Pass, Baralacha La, Kunzum La, Borasu Pass, and Hamta Pass—and Spiti Valley, at over 3000 meters, is a popular destination with ancient Buddhist monasteries. Himachal hosted the first Paragliding World Cup in India from 24 to 31 October 2015 in Bir Billing, located 70 km from Mcleod Ganj in Kangra district, which is known as the launching site and considered the best for paragliding, with the landing site being Bir. The village also hosts cultural events like the Bir Music Festival. Over 2000 villages celebrate festivals such as Kullu Dussehra, Chamba’s Minjar, Renuka ji Fair, Lohri, Halda, Phagli, Losar, and Mandi Shivratri. There are approximately 6000 temples, including Bijli Mahadev, a 20-meter stone structure believed to attract lightning as a sign of divine blessings. The Great Himalayan National Park in Kullu, covering 620 km² from 1500 to 4500 meters, was established in 1984 and includes forest types like Deodar, Himalayan Fir, Spruce, Oak, and Alpine pastures, housing animals such as snow leopard, yak, Himalayan black bear, Western tragopan, monal, and musk deer. Sanctuaries like Naina Devi and Gobind Sagar (220 km²) in Una and Bilaspur host animals such as Indian porcupine and giant flying squirrel, with fish species including Mrigal, Silver carp, Katla, Mahaseer, and Rohu in Gobind Sagar Lake. Narkanda, located at around 8850 feet between the Giri and Sutlej river valleys, is known for its apple orchards. The state has three domestic airports in Kangra, Kullu, and Shimla districts, connecting it to New Delhi and Chandigarh. The only broad-gauge railway line runs from Amb Andaura–Una to Nangal Dam in Punjab and extends to Daulatpur, electrified since 1999, with a small section crossing into Himachal from the Pathankot–Jalandhar line. Himachal is known for narrow-gauge railways: the Kalka-Shimla Railway (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the Kangra Valley Railway, totaling 259 km; the operational railway network spans 296.26 km. Roads are the primary mode of transport due to the hilly terrain, with a total network of 28,208 km, including eight National Highways (1,234 km) and 19 State Highways (1,625 km). Hamirpur has the highest road density in the country. Some roads close during winter and monsoon due to snow and landslides. The state-owned Himachal Road Transport Corporation operates over 3,100 buses, and around 5,000 private buses serve the state. The 2011 Census recorded a total population of 6,864,602 (3,481,873 males, 3,382,729 females), representing 0.57% of India’s population with a 12.81% growth rate. The child sex ratio improved from 896 in 2001 to 909 in 2011. The total fertility rate (TFR) in 2015 was 1.7, one of the lowest in India. The state ranks 21st in population, followed by Tripura at 22nd, with Kangra District having the highest population at 1,507,223. Life expectancy increased from 52.6 years (1970–1975) to 72.0 years (2011–15), above the national average. The infant mortality rate was 40 in 2010, the crude birth rate declined from 37.3 in 1971 to 16.9 in 2010 (below the national average of 26.5 in 1998), and the crude death rate was 6.9 in 2010. The literacy rate nearly doubled between 1981 and 2011, reaching 83.78% in 2011. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes account for 25.19% and 5.71% of the population, respectively. The sex ratio is 972 females per 1,000 males, up from 968 in 2001. Main caste groups include Brahmins, Rajputs, Kanets, Gurjars, Kulindas, Ghirths, Kolis, Hollis, Chamars, Rehars, Lohars, Baris, Julahas, Turis, Batwals, and Dalits. Caste-based discrimination persists, especially affecting Dalit communities in rural areas, with recent incidents such as a 12-year-old Scheduled Caste boy’s suicide in Limbra village (17 September 2025) after being locked in a cowshed and harassed for allegedly entering an upper-caste woman’s house, leading to arrests under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Research shows upper castes hold fertile land, while depressed castes have less fertile land, and both major political parties rely on upper-caste votes. Hindi is the de jure official language, spoken as a lingua franca, with Sanskrit as the additional official language, encouraged for wider study and use. Most residents natively speak Western Pahari languages (locally called Himachali or Pahari), including Pahari (Mahasu Pahari, Pahari Kinnauri), Kangri, Mandeali, Bilaspuri, Chambeali, and Kullu.

The Prevention of Atrocities Act is referenced in the context of social dynamics in Himachal Pradesh, where fieldwork indicates that upper castes, particularly the Thakurs, hold predominantly fertile land, while depressed castes have limited access to land, which is often unfertile. Both major political parties in the state allocate election tickets and mobilize voters based on caste, with a clear dependence on Thakur or upper-caste support. Hindi is the de jure official language and serves as the majority lingua franca, with Sanskrit recognized as an additional official language, though it is primarily used in academic and symbolic settings. The majority of the population speaks Western Pahari languages—such as Kangri, Mandeali, Kullui, Bilaspuri, Chambeali, Gaddi, Sirmauri, Churahi, Hinduri, Pangwali, and Bhattiyali—locally known as Himachali or Pahari. Other spoken languages include Hindi (15.68%), Punjabi (4.42%), Nepali (1.30%), and Kinnauri (1.20%). Smaller communities speak Haryanavi (0.32%), Gujari (0.21%), Lahuli–Spiti (0.16%), Pattani (0.12%), Tibetan (0.3%), and various Kinnauri and Himalayan dialects such as Bhoti Kinnauri, Chitkuli Kinnauri, Bunan (or Gahri), Jangshung, Kanashi, Shumcho, Spiti Bhoti, Sunam, Tinani, Tukpa, Chinali, and Lahul Lohar. Hinduism is the dominant religion, with over 95% of the population adhering to it, primarily through Shaivism and Shaktism, which are evenly distributed across the state—Himachal Pradesh has the highest proportion of Hindus among all Indian states and union territories. Muslims are concentrated in Sirmaur, Chamba, Una, and Solan districts, making up 2.5–6.3% of the population, while Sikhs constitute 1.16% and are mainly urban; Buddhists account for 1.15%, forming a majority (62%) in Lahaul and Spiti and 21.5% in Kinnaur. The state remained largely untouched by external customs due to its difficult terrain, and has undergone rapid economic and social transformation. Culturally, Himachal is divided into three regions: Upper Himachal (Mahasu), Lower Himachal (Kangra, Hamirpur, Bilaspur, Una, and parts of Chamba), and the Lahaul and Spiti and upper Kinnaur districts. It is a multilingual state with Western Pahari languages widely spoken, including Kangri, Mandeali, Kullui, Chambeali, Bharmauri, and Kinnauri. Himachal is renowned for its handicrafts such as carpets, leather works, Kullu shawls, Kangra paintings, Chamba Rumals, stoles, embroidered grass footwear (Pullan chappal), silver jewellery, metal ware, knitted woolen socks, Pattoo, basketry (cane and bamboo), and woodwork, with growing domestic and international demand. Himachali caps, known for their color bands, symbolize political identity—Congress leaders like Virbhadra Singh wore green-banded caps, while BJP leader Prem Kumar Dhumal wore maroon-banded caps; Virbhadra Singh served six terms as Chief Minister, and Dhumal served two. Local music and dance are integral to cultural expression, especially during festivals and religious occasions. National and regional fairs, including temple fairs, occur in nearly every region, with Kullu Dussehra, Minjar mela, and Mahashivratri Mandi being nationally recognized. The local cuisine resembles northern Indian food with Punjabi and Tibetan influences, centered on lentils (Dāl), rice (chāwal or bhāț), vegetables (sabzī), and chapati, with non-vegetarian food more accepted due to limited fresh vegetables in hilly areas. Specialties include Siddu, Babru, Khatta, Mhanee, Channa Madra, Patrode, Mah ki dal, Chamba-style fried fish, Kullu trout, Chha Gosht, Pahadi Chicken, Sepu Badi, Auriya Kaddu, Aloo palda, Pateer, Makki di roti, Sarson ka saag, Chamba Chukh (Chouck), Bhagjery, and Chutney of Til. At independence, the literacy rate was only 8%, one of the lowest in India, but by 2011 it had risen to 82.8%, making Himachal one of the most literate states. There are over 10,000 primary schools, 1,000 secondary schools, and more than 1,300 high schools. Himachal became the first Indian state to make elementary education compulsory and accessible to every child, and it stands out for overcoming gender bias in education, with a female literacy rate of around 76% and near-universal primary school enrollment for girls. While gender disparities exist at higher levels, the state significantly outperforms others in closing the gap, with Hamirpur District showing particularly high literacy. The state government has invested heavily in education, shifting from quantitative expansion during the first six five-year plans to qualitative improvement and modernization after the seventh plan. In 2001, over 1,000 teacher aids were appointed through the Vidya Upasak Yojna. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan promotes universal elementary education and community school management, while the Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (launched in 2009) focuses on quality secondary education. The state’s education standards are high compared to other Indian states, with notable institutions including Baddi University of Emerging Sciences and Technologies, Indian Institute of Technology Mandi, Indian Institute of Management Sirmaur, Himachal Pradesh University in Shimla, Central University of Himachal Pradesh in Dharamsala, National Institute of Technology Hamirpur, Indian Institute of Information Technology Una, Alakh Prakash Goyal University, Maharaja Agrasen University, and Himachal Pradesh National Law University. Prominent medical institutes include Indira Gandhi Medical College and Hospital in Shimla, Dr. Rajendra Prasad Government Medical College in Kangra, Rajiv Gandhi Government Post Graduate Ayurvedic College in Paprola, and Homoeopathic Medical College & Hospital in Kumarhatti, with a Government Dental College in Shimla being the state’s first recognized dental institute. The state government plans to establish three major nursing colleges to strengthen healthcare. CSK Himachal Pradesh Krishi Vishwavidyalya Palampur is a globally recognized hill agriculture institute, and Dr. Yashwant Singh Parmar University of Horticulture and Forestry is unique in India for its teaching, research, and extension in horticulture, forestry, and allied fields. Jawaharlal Nehru Government Engineering College was inaugurated in 2006 at Sundernagar. The National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) also operates a campus in Kangra.

Hiram Rhodes Revels (September 27, 1827 – January 16, 1901) was an American Republican politician, minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and college administrator. Born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, in 1827 to free people of color, Revels had ancestors who were free before the American Revolution; his parents were of African American, European, and Native American ancestry, with his mother specifically of Scots descent and his father a Baptist preacher. He received his early education from a local free Black woman despite restrictions on free Black children’s education and lived with his older brother Elias B. Revels in Lincolnton, North Carolina, where he was apprenticed as a barber in his brother’s shop—a trade considered respectable and socially beneficial for Black Americans at the time. After Elias Revels died in 1841, his widow transferred the shop to Hiram Revels. He attended the Beech Grove Quaker Seminary in Indiana and the Union Literary Institute (Darke County Seminary) in Randolph County, Indiana. In 1845, Revels was ordained as a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and served as a preacher and religious teacher in Indiana, Illinois, Ohio, Tennessee, Missouri, and Kansas; he was imprisoned in Missouri in 1854 for preaching to Black people but was never physically harmed. In the 1850s, he married Phoebe Bass, a free Black woman, and studied religion at Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois, before becoming a minister in Baltimore, Maryland, where he also served as principal of a Black high school. During the American Civil War, Revels served as a chaplain in the United States Army and helped organize two regiments of the United States Colored Troops in Maryland and Missouri, participating in the Battle of Vicksburg. In 1865, he left the AME Church to join the Methodist Episcopal Church and was assigned to churches in Leavenworth, Kansas, and New Orleans, Louisiana; in 1866, he became a permanent pastor in Natchez, Mississippi, where he settled with his wife and five daughters and became an elder in the Mississippi District of the Methodist Church. He founded schools for Black children during this time. In 1868, he was elected alderman in Natchez, and in 1869, he was elected to represent Adams County in the Mississippi State Senate. Congressman John R. Lynch noted that Revels was a new figure in the community, having never voted or attended political meetings, but was seen as intelligent and capable, and believed to be a man of ability. On January 1870, Revels delivered an impressive opening prayer in the Mississippi state legislature, which made a profound impression and led to his election to the U.S. Senate. In 1870, he was elected by a vote of 81 to 15 in the Mississippi legislature to fill the vacant U.S. Senate seat previously held by Albert G. Brown, who withdrew in 1861 when Mississippi seceded. When he arrived in Washington, D.C., Southern Democrats opposed his seating, citing the 1857 Dred Scott Decision, which held that Black people were not citizens, and arguing that Revels had not met the nine-year citizenship requirement before the 14th Amendment in 1868. Supporters countered that Revels had been a citizen since voting in Ohio and that the Civil War and Reconstruction amendments had overturned Dred Scott, making it unconstitutional to bar him based on pre-war constitutional rules. Senator Charles Sumner declared that "the time has passed for argument" and stated that colored persons must be senators, asserting that the Declaration of Independence’s principle of equality was now a reality. On February 25, 1870, Revels was seated in the U.S. Senate by a party-line vote of 48 to 8, with Republicans voting in favor and Democrats voting against, and everyone in the galleries stood to see him sworn in. Senator Henry Wilson defended Revels, citing signatures from Mississippi legislative clerks and Adelbert Ames, the military governor of Mississippi, and argued that skin color was not a barrier to Senate service, invoking the Golden Rule. Revels advocated compromise and moderation, supporting racial equality and urging fellow senators to recognize the capabilities of African Americans. In his maiden speech on March 16, 1870, he called for the reinstatement of Black legislators from Georgia who had been illegally removed. He served on the Committee of Education and Labor and the Committee on the District of Columbia, focusing on Reconstruction issues, and supported amnesty and full citizenship for former Confederates who swore loyalty to the United States. He opposed a proposal by Senator Allen G. Thurman to keep Washington, D.C. schools segregated and advocated for integration, nominated a young Black man to the U.S. Military Academy (who was denied admission), and successfully supported efforts to allow Black workers access to the Washington Navy Yard. The Northern press praised his oratory, and Congressman James G. Blaine noted that Black senators were studious, earnest, and honorable. Revels supported legislation to develop infrastructure in Mississippi, including grants for the New Orleans and Northeastern Railroad (41st Congress 2nd Session S. 712) and levees on the Mississippi River (41st Congress 3rd Session S. 1136). After his Senate term ended on March 3, 1871, Revels was appointed as the first president of Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College (now Alcorn State University) in Claiborne County, Mississippi, where he taught philosophy. In 1873, he took a leave of absence to serve as Mississippi’s secretary of state ad interim. He was dismissed from Alcorn in 1874 after campaigning against the reelection of Governor Adelbert Ames and was reappointed in 1876 by the new Democratic administration, serving until his retirement in 1882. On November 6, 1875, Revels wrote a letter to President Ulysses S. Grant denouncing Adelbert Ames and carpetbaggers for manipulating the Black vote and perpetuating racial hatred. He remained active as a Methodist Episcopal minister in Holly Springs, Mississippi, becoming an elder in the Upper Mississippi District and serving briefly as editor of the Southwestern Christian Advocate. He also taught theology at Shaw College (now Rust College). Hiram Revels died on January 16, 1901, while attending a church conference in Aberdeen, Mississippi, and was buried at Hillcrest Cemetery in Holly Springs. His daughter, Susie Revels Cayton, edited The Seattle Republican in Seattle, Washington, and among his grandsons were Horace R. Cayton Jr., co-author of Black Metropolis, and Revels Cayton, a labor leader. In 2002, scholar Molefi Kete Asante listed Hiram Rhodes Revels as one of the 100 Greatest African Americans.

The history of Kashmir is deeply connected to the broader history of the Indian subcontinent and has been influenced by Central and East Asia. Historically, Kashmir referred only to the Kashmir Valley in the western Himalayas; today, it encompasses the Indian-administered union territories of Jammu and Kashmir (including Jammu and the Kashmir Valley) and Ladakh, the Pakistan-administered territories of Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and the Chinese-administered regions of Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract. In the first half of the 1st millennium, the region was a center of Hinduism and later Buddhism under the Mauryas and Kushanas. During the ninth century, the Karkota Dynasty fostered a native Shaiva tradition that flourished for seven centuries under the Utpala and Lohara dynasties, ending in the mid-14th century. Islam began spreading in the 13th century, accelerated during the 14th and 15th centuries, and led to the decline of Kashmiri Shaivism. In 1339, Shah Mir became the first Muslim ruler, founding the Shah Mir dynasty. Muslim monarchs ruled Kashmir for five centuries, including the Mughal Empire from 1586 to 1751 and the Afghan Durrani Empire from 1747 to 1819. In 1819, the Sikhs, under Ranjit Singh, annexed Kashmir after defeating the Afghans. Following the Sikh defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1846, the Treaty of Lahore and the Treaty of Amritsar transferred control to the Raja of Jammu, Gulab Singh, who became the new ruler. His descendants ruled under British paramountcy until 1947, when the former princely state became a disputed territory administered by India, Pakistan, and China. The name "Kashmir" is etymologically derived from Sanskrit "ka" (water) and "shimīra" (desiccate), meaning "desiccated land," based on the legend that sage Kashyapa drained a lake in the valley at Baramulla, creating the settlement known as Kashyapa-pura, linked to ancient geographical references like Kaspapyros and Kaspatyros. The Nilamata Purana (c. 500–600 CE) records early history, though it is considered inconsistent; Kalhana's Rajatarangini, completed by 1150 CE, chronicles Kashmir's dynasties and is credited as India's first historian, relying on traditional sources and personal observations. During Muslim rule, three supplements to Rajatarangini were written by Jonaraja, Srivara, and Prajyabhatta and Suka, ending with Akbar's conquest in 1586. These were translated into Persian by scholars like Nizam Uddin, Farishta, and Abul Fazl. Key Persian texts include Baharistan-i-Shahi and Haidar Mailk's Tarikh-i-Kashmir (completed in 1621), both based on Rajatarangini and Persian histories. Archaeological findings at the Lower-Middle Palaeolithic Galander site near Pampore show remains of Palaeoloxodon turkmenicus and stone tools dating to 400–300,000 years ago, suggesting early human activity. Neolithic sites in the Kashmir Valley date to around 3000 BCE, with Burzahom showing two phases: the first (c. 2920 BCE) with mud-plastered pit dwellings and coarse pottery, and the second (until c. 1700 BCE) with ground-level houses and animal burials, including evidence of wheat, barley, and lentils. The megalithic phase featured massive circles and black burnished pottery. During the Vedic period, the Uttara–Kurus settled in Kashmir. In 326 BCE, Porus sought help from Abhisares, the king of Kashmir, against Alexander the Great, who later submitted after losing the Battle of Hydaspes. Under Ashoka (304–232 BCE), Kashmir became part of the Maurya Empire and Buddhism was introduced, with stupas, Shiva shrines, and Srinagari (Srinagar) built. Kanishka (127–151 CE) conquered Kashmir and founded Kanishkapur; Buddhist tradition holds he held the Fourth Buddhist Council there, with scholars like Ashvagosha, Nagarjuna, and Vasumitra participating. By the fourth century, Kashmir became a center of learning for both Buddhism and Hinduism, with missionaries spreading Buddhism to Tibet and China, and pilgrims visiting from these regions. Kumārajīva (343–413 CE) traveled to China, influencing Emperor Yao Xing and translating Sanskrit works. The Alchon Huns, under Toramana, conquered Kashmir, and Mihirakula (c. 502–530 CE) led campaigns across North India, defeating Yasodharman and destroying Buddhist shrines before retreating to Kashmir. After his defeat, he ruled there and committed atrocities. The Huns' influence faded after his death. In 659, Kashmir submitted to the Tang Dynasty's protectorate under Emperor Gaozong. Hindu dynasties ruled from the 7th to 14th centuries, with significant developments in Kashmiri Hinduism, including the rise of Kashmir Shaivism through scholars like Vasugupta (c. 875–925 CE) and Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025 CE). The Karkota Empire (8th century) expanded under Chandrapida and Lalitaditya Muktapida, who defeated Tibetans, Yashovarman of Kanyakubja, and kingdoms in Magadha, Kamarupa, Gauda, and Kalinga, extending influence to Malwa and Gujarat and defeating Arabs at Sindh; the dynasty ended around 855–856 CE. The Utpala dynasty, founded by Avantivarman, was followed by Shankaravarman (885–902 CE), who fought the Gurjaras. Political instability in the 10th century led to the rise of the Tantrins, causing chaos until defeated by Chakravarman. Queen Didda, of Hindu Shahi descent, ruled in the second half of the 10th century. After her death in 1003 CE, the Lohara dynasty took over. Suhadeva, the last Lohara king, fled after a raid by Zulju (Dulacha), a Turkic–Mongol chief, around 1320; his wife, Queen Kota Rani, ruled until 1339 and is credited with building the "Kutte Kol" canal to divert Jhelum waters. Mahmud of Ghazni attempted to conquer Kashmir in the 11th century but failed due to the fortress at Lohkot. Historian Mohibbul Hasan argues that oppressive taxation, corruption, and the rise of feudal lords during the Lohara dynasty (1003–1320 CE) enabled foreign invasions. Rinchana, a Tibetan Buddhist refugee, ruled after Zulju; folklore suggests he converted to Islam due to political pressure from his minister Shah Mir, who then led a coup to establish Muslim rule. In the 14th century, Islam became dominant in Kashmir. Islamic preacher Sheikh Nooruddin Noorani (Nund Rishi) combined Kashmir Shaivism with Sufism. Sultans from 1354 to 1470 were generally tolerant, except Sultan Sikandar (1389–1413), who imposed taxes, forced conversions, and earned the title But–Shikan for destroying idols. Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (c. 1420–1470) invited artists from Central Asia and Persia, leading to prosperity in wood carving, papier-mâché, shawls, and carpets.
