In the 1470s, states of Jammu, Poonch, and Rajauri revolted against Sultan Hajji Khan but were subdued by his son Hasan Khan in 1472. By the mid-16th century, Hindu influence declined as Muslim missionaries from Central Asia and Persia arrived, and Persian replaced Sanskrit as the official language. The Chak nobility eventually unseated the Shah Mir dynasty. Mughal general Haidar Dughlat invaded Kashmir in c. 1540 on behalf of Humayun, but was overthrown due to persecution of Shias, Shafi'is, and Sufis and revolts. Kashmir came under direct Mughal rule in 1586 under Akbar, who added it to the Kabul Subah; Shah Jahan later carved it into a separate subah with its seat in Srinagar. Gardens, mosques, and palaces were built under successive Mughal rulers, but religious intolerance and discriminatory taxes returned under Aurangzeb in 1658. After his death, Mughal influence declined. In 1700, a Kashmiri merchant's servant brought Mo-i Muqqadas (the Prophet's hair) to the valley, which was housed in the Hazratbal Shrine. Nadir Shah's invasion in 1738 weakened Mughal control. The Afghan Durrani Empire took control in 1752; the governor Sukh Jiwan Mal rebelled in the mid-1750s but was defeated in 1762. The Durrani rulers oppressed the Hindu population through forced conversions, killings, and forced labor, with a heavy tax burden; historian Victoria Schofield notes the cruelty was mainly directed at Hindus, and many Kashmiris were sold into slavery. The Durrani Empire controlled Kashmir until 1819, after which it was annexed by the Sikh Empire. After the Battle of Shopian in 1819, the Sikhs took control. Initially welcomed due to suffering under the Afghans, Sikh rule proved oppressive, with anti-Muslim laws such as death sentences for cow slaughter, closure of the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, and banning the azaan, though these were later repealed by governor Muhyuddin. European visitors noted the poverty of the Muslim peasantry and exorbitant taxes under Sikh rule.

The empire controlled Kashmir until 1819, after which the region was annexed by the Sikh Empire. After four centuries of Muslim rule, Kashmir fell to the Sikhs under Ranjit Singh of Punjab following the Battle of Shopian in 1819. The Kashmiris, having suffered under the Afghans, initially welcomed the Sikh rulers, but Sikh governors proved to be hard taskmasters, and Sikh rule was generally considered oppressive, possibly due to the region's remoteness from the Sikh capital in Lahore. The Sikhs enacted anti-Muslim laws, including death sentences for cow slaughter, closing the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, and banning the azaan, though these laws were later repealed by governor Muhyuddin in the final decade of Sikh rule. European visitors noted the abject poverty of the Muslim peasantry and exorbitant taxes under the Sikhs, with high taxes reportedly depopulating large areas and leaving only one-sixteenth of cultivable land under cultivation. After the 1832 famine, the Sikhs reduced land tax to half the produce and began offering interest-free loans, making Kashmir the second highest revenue earner for the Sikh Empire. During this period, Kashmiri shawls gained global recognition, especially in the West. In 1780, after Ranjit Deo's death, the Sikh Empire captured the kingdom of Jammu and made it a tributary. Ranjit Deo's grandnephew, Gulab Singh, served at Ranjit Singh’s court, distinguished himself in military campaigns, and was appointed Raja of Jammu in 1820. With officer Zorawar Singh, Gulab Singh captured Ladakh and Baltistan for the Sikhs. Notable Sikh governors of Kashmir included Moti Ram, Hari Singh, Kirpa Ram, Mihan Singh, and Muhyuddin. In 1845, the First Anglo-Sikh War began, and Gulab Singh remained neutral until the Battle of Sobraon in 1846, when he acted as a mediator and trusted advisor to Sir Henry Lawrence. Two treaties were signed: the first saw the British receive the hill countries between Beas and Indus in exchange for ten million rupees; the second transferred to Gulab Singh, for seven point five million rupees, all mountainous territory east of the Indus and west of the Ravi (i.e., the Vale of Kashmir). The Treaty of Amritsar freed Gulab Singh from Sikh obligations and made him Maharajah of Jammu and Kashmir. The Dogras' loyalty proved valuable during the 1857 revolt, as they refused to shelter mutineers, allowed English women and children to seek asylum in Kashmir, and sent troops to fight for the British, leading the British to secure Dogra succession. After Gulab Singh's death in 1857, his son Ranbir Singh added the emirates of Hunza, Gilgit, and Nagar to the kingdom. The Princely State of Kashmir and Jammu (1820–1858) was artificial in composition and lacked a coherent identity due to its disparate origins and autocratic rule. It combined diverse regions, religions, and ethnicities: eastern Ladakh was ethnically and culturally Tibetan with Buddhist inhabitants; southern Jammu had a mixed Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh population; the central Kashmir Valley was predominantly Sunni Muslim with a small but influential Hindu minority (Kashmiri pandits); northeast Baltistan had a population ethnically related to Ladakh but practicing Shi'a Islam; northern Gilgit Agency had diverse, mostly Shi'a groups; and western Punch was Muslim but of a different ethnicity. Despite being a majority, Muslims faced severe oppression under Hindu rule through high taxes, forced labor, and discriminatory laws. Many Kashmiri Muslims migrated from the Valley to Punjab due to famine and Dogra policies. The Muslim peasantry was vast, impoverished, lacked education and political awareness, and was chronically in debt to landlords and moneylenders, organizing politically only in the 1930s. Ranbir Singh's grandson Hari Singh, who became ruler in 1925, was the monarch in 1947 at the time of British withdrawal and the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. An internal revolt began in Poonch against oppressive taxation, and in August, Maharaja’s forces fired upon pro-Pakistan demonstrations, burned villages, and massacred civilians. The Poonch rebels declared an independent "Azad" Kashmir on 24 October. Rulers were encouraged to accede to either India or Pakistan, considering geographical contiguity and people's wishes. In 1947, Jammu and Kashmir’s population was 77% Muslim and 20% Hindu. To delay a decision, the Maharaja signed a standstill agreement with Pakistan, pending with India. In October 1947, Pashtun tribesmen from Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province, recruited by Poonch rebels and incensed by atrocities, invaded Kashmir, engaging in looting and killing. The rebels’ goal was to intimidate Hari Singh into submission. Instead, the Maharaja appealed to the British, who agreed on the condition that he accede to India. After signing the Instrument of Accession, Indian troops entered Kashmir and expelled the Pakistani-sponsored irregulars from most of the state. India accepted the accession as provisional until the will of the people could be determined. Sheikh Abdullah endorsed the accession as temporary and was appointed head of the emergency administration. Pakistan immediately contested the accession, claiming it was fraudulent, that the Maharaja acted under duress, and that he had not terminated the standstill agreement with Pakistan. In early 1948, India sought a UN resolution on the Kashmir conflict. The United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan (UNCIP) was established, and the UN Security Council passed Resolution 47 on 21 April 1948, insisting that the people of J&K determine their accession through a free and impartial plebiscite. The Indian Prime Minister urged the UN to conduct a referendum on the results. However, India insisted no referendum could occur until all irregulars were cleared. On 5 January 1949, UNCIP stated that the accession of J&K to India or Pakistan would be decided by a plebiscite. Both countries accepted the principle that Pakistan withdraw its intruders and Indian forces, followed by a truce and plebiscite, but failed to reach a truce due to disagreements on demilitarization—specifically whether the Azad Kashmiri army should be disbanded during the truce or plebiscite phase. A ceasefire was agreed in late 1948 under UN auspices, but the plebiscite was never held, leading to deteriorating India-Pakistan relations and three subsequent wars in 1965, 1971, and 1999. India controls about half of the former princely state, Pakistan controls a third, governing it as Gilgit–Baltistan and Azad Kashmir. According to Encyclopædia Britannica, despite a clear Muslim majority in Kashmir before 1947 and its geographic and cultural ties to Muslim-majority Punjab, the region was divided. Pakistan ended up with thinly populated, inaccessible, and underdeveloped territory, while the largest Muslim group in the Valley—over half the region’s population—remained in Indian-administered territory, with its access to the Jhelum valley route blocked. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 39 in January 1948 to establish a special commission to investigate the conflict. Following the commission’s recommendations, Resolution 47 (21 April 1948) required the withdrawal of Pakistani forces from J&K and a plebiscite to determine accession, supervised by the UN. Subsequent resolutions noted India’s failure to hold the plebiscite, but no punitive action could be taken because the resolution was non-binding. Pakistan never withdrew its forces and retained occupation. The eastern region of the former princely state has faced a boundary dispute. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, boundary agreements between Britain, Afghanistan, and Russia over northern Kashmir were signed, but China never accepted them, and its position remained unchanged after the 1949 communist revolution. By the mid-1950s, the Chinese army entered northeastern Ladakh, completed a military road through Aksai Chin by 1956–57 to connect Xinjiang and western Tibet, and India’s discovery of this road led to border clashes culminating in the Sino-Indian War of October 1962. China has occupied Aksai Chin since 1962 and also acquired the Trans-Karakoram Tract from Pakistan in 1965. In 1949, the Indian government compelled Hari Singh to step down and transfer power to Sheikh Abdullah, leader of the National Conference Party. Since then, India and Pakistan have remained in bitter enmity, with three wars over Kashmir, and the growing dispute and democratic failure have fueled Kashmiri nationalism and militancy. In 1986, the Anantnag riots erupted after CM Gul Shah ordered the construction of a mosque at a Hindu temple in Jammu and made an incendiary speech. Hindu-Muslim riots, triggered by the opening of Babri Masjid to Hindu worshippers, spread to seven other states. Following the 1987 Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly election, widely seen as rigged, disgruntled youth such as the 'HAJY group'—Abdul Hamid Shaikh, Ashfaq Majid Wani, Javed Ahmed Mir, and Mohammed Yasin Malik—joined the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) as an alternative to the ineffective democratic system. This intensified the insurgency in the Valley. In 1989, conflict intensified as Mujahideen from Afghanistan infiltrated the region after the Soviet–Afghan War ended. Pakistan provided arms and training to both indigenous and foreign militants, worsening discontent. In August 2019, the Indian government repealed the special status granted to Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 of the Indian Constitution and passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, dissolving the state and reorganizing it into two union territories: Jammu and Kashmir (west) and Ladakh (east), effective from 31 October 2019. In the 1901 British Indian Empire Census, the princely state of Kashmir had a population of 2,905,578: 2,154,695 Muslims, 689,073 Hindus, 25,828 Sikhs, and 35,047 Buddhists. Hindus were mainly in Jammu, where they made up just under 50% of the population. In the Kashmir Valley, Hindus numbered only 524 per 10,000 (5.24%), and in Ladhakh and Gilgit only 94 per 10,000 (0.94%). The total Valley population was 1,157,394, of which 1,083,766 (93.6%) were Muslims. These percentages have remained stable for over a century. In the 1941 British India Census, Muslims accounted for 93.6% of the Valley population and Hindus for 4%. In 2003, Muslims in the Valley were 95% and Hindus 4%; in Jammu, Hindus were 67% and Muslims 27%. Among Kashmiri Muslims, four divisions were recorded: Shaikhs, Saiyids, Mughals, and Pathans. The Shaikhs, the most numerous, are descendants of Hindus who abandoned caste rules and have clan names such as Tantre, Shaikh, Bat, Mantu, Ganai, Dar, Damar, Lon. Saiyids are divided into religious practitioners and those in agriculture; their kram name is 'Mir,' used as a prefix for religious ones and as an affix for agricultural ones. Mughals, though few, have kram names like Mir, Beg, Bandi, Bach, Ashaye. Pathans, more numerous than Mughals, are mainly in the southwest, with notable colonies like Kuki-Khel Afridis at Dranghaihama, retaining old customs and speaking Pashtu. Major Muslim tribes include Butts, Dar, Lone, Jat, Gujjar, Rajput, Sudhan, and Khatri. Some Butts, Dars, and Lones use the title Khawaja; Khatri use Shaikh; Gujjars use Chaudhary. All these tribes are indigenous to the region and converted from Hinduism to Islam. Among Jammu’s Hindus, who numbered 626,177, the details of their distribution are not fully provided in the text.

The Mughals, who were not numerous, used kram names such as "Mir" (a corruption of "Mirza"), "Beg", "Bandi", "Bach", and "Ashaye". The Pathans, who are more numerous than the Mughals, are primarily found in the south-west of the valley, where Pathan colonies have been established over time; the most notable is the Kuki-Khel Afridis at Dranghaihama, who maintain traditional customs and speak Pashtu. The main Muslim tribes in the princely state include the Butts, Dar, Lone, Jat, Gujjar, Rajput, Sudhan, and Khatri. A small number of Butts, Dar, and Lone use the title Khawaja, while the Khatri use the title Shaikh and the Gujjar use the title Chaudhary. All these tribes are indigenous to the princely state and converted to Islam from Hinduism upon their arrival in the region. Among the Hindus of Jammu province, who numbered 626,177 (or 90.87% of the Hindu population of the princely state), the major castes recorded in the census were Brahmins (186,000), Rajputs (167,000), Khatris (48,000), and Thakkars (93,000).

Jack Dorsey began developing the early idea for Twitter in 2006 while working at the podcasting company Odeo. The concept originated during a "daylong brainstorming session" where Dorsey, then an undergraduate student, proposed using an SMS service to communicate with a small group. The original project code name was twttr, inspired by Flickr and the five-character length of American SMS short codes, with Evan Williams later attributing the name to Noah Glass. The domain twitter.com was already in use, so the team purchased it six months after launching twttr and renamed the service Twitter. The developers initially considered "10958" as the SMS short code but changed it to "40404" for ease of use and memorability. Work on the project began in February 2006, and Dorsey published the first Twitter post, "just setting up my twttr," in March 2006. The first prototype, developed by Dorsey and contractor Florian Weber, was used internally at Odeo, with the full version launched publicly on July 15, 2006. In October 2006, Biz Stone, Evan Williams, Dorsey, and others formed Obvious Corporation and acquired Odeo, including its assets. Williams fired Noah Glass, who remained silent about his role until 2011. Twitter spun off into its own company in April 2007. The service was initially ambiguous in definition, described as a social network or microblogging platform, but evolved into being primarily an information network. The term "tweet" emerged from a search by Craig Hockenberry for a shorter way to refer to posting a Twitter update, later adopted by Blaine Cook. The hashtag was introduced in 2007 by Chris Messina, inspired by Internet Relay Chat and Jaiku, and was eventually adopted by Twitter despite mixed initial reactions. Twitter's popularity surged at the 2007 South by Southwest Interactive (SXSWi) conference, where usage increased from 20,000 to 60,000 tweets per day, and the service won the festival's Web Award with the remark "we'd like to thank you in 140 characters or less. And we just did!" Elon Musk joined as a user in 2009. Twitter won the "Breakout of the Year" Webby Award in 2009 and was named Word of the Year by the Global Language Monitor that same year. By February 2010, users were sending 50 million tweets per day, and by March 2010, over 70,000 applications were registered. In June 2010, about 65 million tweets were posted daily, equating to roughly 750 tweets per second, increasing to about 140 million daily by March 2011. Twitter moved to third place among social networking sites by January 2009. The platform saw usage spikes during major events, such as the 2010 FIFA World Cup, where 2,940 tweets per second were posted after Japan scored against Cameroon, followed by 3,085 after the Lakers' NBA Finals victory and 3,283 after Japan's win over Denmark. A record of 7,196 tweets per second was set during the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup Final. When Michael Jackson died on June 25, 2009, Twitter servers crashed due to 100,000 tweets per hour containing "Michael Jackson." The highest recorded rate, 143,199 tweets per second, occurred in Japan during a screening of the movie Castle in the Sky on August 3, 2013. In June 2009, Tony La Russa sued Twitter for trade infringement after an impersonation of him, leading to a settlement and the introduction of Verified Accounts. Ashton Kutcher's account became the first with a million followers in 2009. Twitter played a major role in the 2009 Iranian presidential election protests. On January 22, 2010, NASA astronaut T. J. Creamer posted the first unassisted off-Earth Twitter message from the International Space Station. By late November 2010, an average of a dozen updates per day were posted on the astronauts' communal account, @NASA_Astronauts. Twitter acquired Atebits on April 11, 2010, which developed the Apple Design Award-winning Twitter client Tweetie, becoming the official client for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. The Library of Congress began archiving all tweets from 2006 onward, initially archiving all new tweets, though it switched to selective archiving in 2018. From September to October 2010, Twitter rolled out "New Twitter," allowing users to view pictures and videos directly within the platform and introducing a redesigned interface with '@mentions' and 'Retweets' above the stream and 'Messages' and 'Log Out' in a top black bar. The "New Twitter" experience was fully rolled out by November 1, 2010. In April 2011, Twitter tested a new homepage and phased out the "Old Twitter," though a glitch delayed the transition, with the retro homepage remaining until April 20. On December 8, 2011, Twitter introduced the "Fly" design, adding Connect and Discover tabs, a redesigned profile, and timeline, with a layout similar to Facebook. In February 2012, Twitter announced a partnership with Yandex, a Russian search engine, to leverage real-time news feeds. On March 21, 2012, Twitter celebrated its sixth birthday with 140 million users and 340 million tweets per day. In April 2012, Twitter opened an office in Detroit and expanded its Dublin office. In March 2011, a cobra escaped from the Bronx Zoo, leading to the creation of a parody account @BronxZoosCobra, which gained widespread attention. On June 5, 2012, Twitter unveiled a modified logo removing text to feature a redesigned bird. By December 18, 2012, monthly active users had increased by 42% and surpassed 200 million. Pope Benedict XVI joined Twitter on December 18, 2012, using the handle @pontifex, which answers questions via the hashtag #askpontifex. In 2012, "tweet" was added to the Oxford English Dictionary. Vine, a short video service, was launched in 2013. On January 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Crashlytics to expand its mobile developer products. On April 18, 2013, Twitter launched a music app called Twitter Music for iPhone. On August 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Trendrr, followed by MoPub on September 9, 2013. As of September 2013, 200 million users sent over 400 million tweets daily, with nearly 60% from mobile devices. In April 2013, the Syrian Electronic Army hacked the Associated Press account, causing a significant short-term market impact, and later hacked Barack Obama's account. During Super Bowl XLVII on February 3, 2013, Kraft Foods VP Lisa Mann tweeted "You can still dunk in the dark" after a power outage, a moment that became a milestone in daily cultural commentary. Twitter went public in 2013 through an IPO that raised $1.8 billion. 2014 was a difficult year for the company, with market pessimism. In April 2014, Twitter redesigned its site to resemble Facebook, featuring profile pictures and biographies on the left and a full-width header with parallax scrolling, which remained the main desktop layout until July 2019. Growth slowed in 2015. In September 2016, Twitter shares rose 20% after reports of takeover interest, with potential buyers including Alphabet, Microsoft, Salesforce, Verizon, and The Walt Disney Company. The board was open to a deal by the end of 2016, but no acquisition occurred due to concerns over abuse and harassment. In 2017, Elon Musk first expressed interest in acquiring Twitter. In June 2017, Twitter revamped its dashboard to improve the user experience. Vine was shut down in 2017. On April 29, 2018, Solstar sent the first commercial tweet from space using commercial infrastructure during a New Shepard flight. In May 2018, Twitter introduced an algorithm to hide replies deemed detractive, requiring users to click "Show more replies" to view them. From 2015 to 2018, Twitter suspended over a million accounts related to terrorism. In 2018, the tweet length limit was increased from 140 to 280 characters, after a trial in 2017. In 2019, Twitter released another user interface redesign. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Twitter experienced significant growth but also faced challenges with misinformation. The platform began marking tweets with misleading information and adding fact-check links, though it sometimes incorrectly flagged factual content as misleading. In May 2020, two tweets from U.S. President Donald Trump were marked as "potentially misleading" and linked to fact-checks. Trump responded by signing an executive order to weaken Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. After the January 6 United States Capitol attack, Twitter banned Trump, citing violation of its "glorification of violence" policy, drawing criticism from American conservatives and European leaders. In 2020, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian pushed pandemic conspiracy theories on Twitter, which is blocked in mainland China but used as a public diplomacy tool by Chinese officials. China's ambassador to South Africa also made these claims on Twitter. In May 2020, Twitter placed fact-check labels on two of these tweets.

In May 2020, Twitter moderators marked two tweets from U.S. President Donald Trump as "potentially misleading" and linked to a fact-check. Trump responded by signing an executive order to weaken Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which limits social media sites' liability for content moderation decisions. After the January 6 United States Capitol attack, Twitter banned Trump, claiming he violated "the glorification of violence policy." The ban drew criticism from American conservatives and European leaders, who viewed it as an interference with freedom of speech. In 2020, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian promoted conspiracy theories about the pandemic on Twitter, a platform blocked in mainland China but used by Chinese officials for public diplomacy. China's ambassador to South Africa also made these claims on Twitter. In May 2020, Twitter placed fact-check labels on two Chinese government tweets that falsely suggested the virus originated in the U.S. and was brought to China by Americans. In January 2021, Hua Chunying renewed the conspiracy theory that the SARS-CoV-2 virus originated in the United States from the U.S. military biology laboratory Fort Detrick, continuing to reference it on Twitter and urging the U.S. government to open Fort Detrick for investigation. In April 2021, Twitter announced the establishment of its African headquarters in Ghana. On June 5, 2021, the Nigerian government issued an indefinite ban on Twitter, citing "misinformation and fake news spread through it have had real world violent consequences," following the platform's removal of tweets by Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari. The ban was criticized by Amnesty International. In 2021, Twitter began the research phase of Bluesky, an open-source decentralized social media protocol allowing users to choose their preferred algorithmic curation. The same year, Twitter launched Twitter Spaces, a social audio feature; "super follows," a subscription model for exclusive content; and a beta of "ticketed Spaces," which makes access to certain audio rooms paid. Twitter unveiled a redesign in August 2021, featuring adjusted colors and a new Chirp font that improves left-alignment for most Western languages. In June 2022, Twitter announced a partnership with e-commerce giant Shopify to launch a sales channel app for U.S. Shopify merchants. On August 23, 2022, the contents of a whistleblower complaint by former information security head Peiter Zatko to the U.S. Congress were published. Zatko had been fired by Twitter in January 2022; the complaint alleges Twitter failed to disclose data breaches, had negligent security, violated U.S. securities regulations, and breached a prior settlement with the Federal Trade Commission over user data protection, and claims the Indian government forced Twitter to hire an agent to gain direct access to user data. Elon Musk initiated an acquisition of Twitter, Inc. on April 14, 2022, and concluded it on October 27, 2022. Musk began buying shares in January 2022, becoming the company's largest shareholder by April with a 9.1 percent ownership stake. Twitter invited Musk to join its board, an offer he initially accepted before declining. On April 14, Musk made an unsolicited offer to purchase the company, to which Twitter's board responded with a "poison pill" strategy before unanimously accepting Musk's $44 billion buyout offer on April 25. Musk stated he planned to introduce new features, make algorithms open-source, combat spambot accounts, and promote free speech, framing the acquisition as the cornerstone of X, an "everything app." In July, Musk announced he would terminate the agreement, claiming Twitter breached the agreement by refusing to crack down on spambot accounts. The company filed a lawsuit in the Delaware Court of Chancery, with a trial scheduled for the week of October 17. Weeks before the trial began, Musk reversed course and announced he would proceed with the acquisition. The deal closed on October 28, with Musk becoming the new owner and CEO of Twitter. The company was taken private and merged into a new parent company named X Corp. Musk fired several top executives, including former CEO Parag Agrawal. Musk proposed reforms and laid off half of the company's workforce. Hundreds of employees resigned after Musk issued an ultimatum demanding they commit to "extremely hardcore" work. Linda Yaccarino was appointed CEO of X Corp. In July 2023, the Twitter service was rebranded as X. Reactions to the buyout were mixed, with praise for Musk's planned reforms and vision, especially his emphasis on free speech, but criticism over fears of increased misinformation, disinformation, harassment, and hate speech. In the United States, conservatives largely supported the acquisition, while many liberals and former employees expressed concerns about Musk's intentions. Since becoming owner, Musk faced backlash for handling the company and account suspensions, including the December 2022 suspensions of ten journalists. Elon Musk completed his acquisition of Twitter in October 2022; Musk served as CEO until June 2023 when he was succeeded by Linda Yaccarino. The Twitter service was rebranded to X on July 23, 2023, and its domain name changed from twitter.com to x.com on May 17, 2024. Yaccarino resigned on July 9, 2025. Now operating as X, the platform closely resembles its predecessor but includes additional features such as long-form texts, account monetization options, audio-video calls, integration with xAI's Grok chatbot, job search, and a repurposing of the verification system as a subscription premium. Several legacy features were removed after Musk's acquisition, including Circles, NFT profile pictures, and the experimental pronouns in profiles feature. Musk's goals included transforming X into a "digital town square" and an "everything app" similar to WeChat. X has faced significant controversy post-rebranding, including the release of the Twitter Files, suspensions of ten journalists' accounts, labeling media outlets as "state-affiliated," and restricting their visibility. Criticism has also arisen over viral misinformation, hate speech (especially antisemitism), and child pornography. In response to allegations it deemed unfair, X Corp. has pursued legal action against nonprofit organizations Media Matters and the Center for Countering Digital Hate.

Hit Parader is an American music magazine that originally operated from 1942 to 2008 and was relaunched in 2025. Launched in 1942 by Charlton Publications in Derby, Connecticut, it published its first issue on September 16, 1942, with a mission statement targeting schoolchildren, college students, military personnel, radio listeners, moviegoers, jukebox users, record buyers, and people who whistle. The magazine's title referenced the "hit parade," a list of popular singles based on sales or airplay. Initially, it featured lyrics to current hit songs, a practice that ended in 1975 due to licensing costs, after which it included interviews, color photos, and feature articles on rock musicians. In the 1960s, Jim Delehant worked as a staff writer and editor, noting that the music scene was unexciting before the rise of acts like the Beatles and the Beach Boys, and that Hit Parader used traveling journalists to write authentic feature stories. Contributors included Ellen Sander, Keith Altham, Derek Taylor, Nick Logan, Barbara Charone, Lenny Kaye, Jonh Ingham, and Alan Betrock. During the 1970s, it covered major rock acts such as Led Zeppelin, the Rolling Stones, Elton John, David Bowie, Blue Öyster Cult, the Kinks, Three Dog Night, the Who, Cheap Trick, Kiss, and Van Halen, and later expanded to include punk and new wave artists. The magazine typically included song lyrics, artist photos, feature articles, album reviews, interviews, reader mail, trivia, and reader polls. Andy Secher joined as an assistant editor in 1979, hired after a New York Daily News interview with AC/DC, and later became editor in 1980 after replacing Lisa Robinson, who had been promoting new wave music. Secher led the magazine’s shift to exclusively focus on hard rock and heavy metal, a move that began in 1984 and resulted in a 450% increase in sales, reaching a monthly circulation of half a million copies. Secher described this shift as being timely due to the rise of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal and the West Coast Metal Explosion, and he identified its target audience as young suburban males, such as a 17-year-old in Iowa. The June 1984 issue, dedicated to Mötley Crüe, sparked controversy when Secher reported a scene involving the band’s lead vocalist Vince Neil and a woman, which was sanitized before publication, leading retailers like 7-Eleven to threaten to remove the magazine. Over the decade, Hit Parader became a leading heavy metal publication, covering acts like Mötley Crüe, Quiet Riot, Def Leppard, Ratt, and Ozzy Osbourne, and producing special issues such as Hit Parader's Heavy Metal Hot Shots and Hit Parader's Heavy Metal Heroes. Secher also produced a television spinoff, Hit Parader's Heavy Metal Heroes, on USA Network. The magazine declined in the 1990s due to financial struggles, with Charlton selling it in 1991, and a backlash from Guns N' Roses over a 1991 cover story that misrepresented an interview between Axl Rose and Sebastian Bach as exclusive when it was actually a transcript of a Howard Stern broadcast. The rise of Nirvana and grunge in 1991 marked a turning point in heavy metal's decline, leading to a steady drop in readership. Secher maintained that Hit Parader’s audience preferred short, pithy features and large color photos and defended the magazine’s support of heavy metal, stating it was a proud fanzine, not a critical publication like the New York Times. The magazine ceased publication after its December 2008 issue. It had also published "Top 100" lists, including "Top 100 Metal Bands," "Top 100 Guitarists," "Top 100 Vocalists," and "Top 100 Bassists & Drummers." In 2020, Matt Pinfield, Ash Avildsen, and Josh Bernstein acquired the rights and reestablished Hit Parader as a branded production company headquartered in Universal City with a mission to create original content and immersive experiences. They announced a television series, Paradise City, described as a blend of Euphoria, Entourage, and Sabrina, featuring Drea de Matteo and Bella Thorne, which premiered as an eight-episode season on Amazon Prime in 2021. The brand remained inactive except for sponsoring events like the 2024 relaunch of the Mayhem Festival. On October 2, 2025, Yungblud announced he would be the inaugural cover of the relaunched magazine, stating he grew up with it and the legends featured on its covers, and that the first edition was released in October with monthly releases following. He also played a surprise event at the private Hit Parader Club in Nashville, Tennessee, on September 25, 2025, during the final stop of his IDOLS Tour in the U.S. Subsequent covers have featured Orville Peck and Zedd.

Hlengiwe Buhle Mkhize (6 September 1952 – 16 September 2021) was a South African politician who served as Minister of Higher Education and Training and Minister of Home Affairs under President Jacob Zuma. A member of the National Assembly and national executive since May 2009, she was Deputy Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities when she died in September 2021. Born on 6 September 1952, she completed a Bachelor of Arts in psychology, social work, and sociology at the University of Zululand in 1976, where she was involved in student activism. She earned an Honours in psychology in 1978 and a Master's in clinical psychology in 1981, both from the University of Natal. Mkhize spent over a decade in academia as a senior lecturer at the University of Zululand from 1984 to 1990 and at the University of the Witwatersrand from 1990 to 1995, and also served as a visiting professor at the University of Illinois and University of Mississippi. In 1995, she was appointed to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, where she chaired the Reparations and Rehabilitation Committee, and held various civil society roles, including establishing the National Children and Violence Trust, serving as a reparations officer in the President's Fund, chairing the South African branch of Transparency International, and leading the University of Zululand’s council. She also had business interests, being a director in 15 private companies, including Aerosud, by the time she joined government in 2009. A long-serving member of the African National Congress (ANC), she served in her local branch executive from 1991 to 2004 and was national treasurer of the ANC Women's League from July 2008 to August 2015, during which she raised over R40-million in funds. She was elected to the National Assembly in the April 2009 general election, representing the ANC, and was re-elected in 2014 and 2019, serving until her death in 2021. In 2005, President Thabo Mbeki appointed her as South African Ambassador to the Netherlands, a post she held until 2008, during which she chaired the executive council of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and was vice-president of the International Criminal Court from 2006 to 2008. Between 2009 and 2017, she served as deputy minister in four portfolios: Deputy Minister of Correctional Services (2009–2010), Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Training (2010–2012), Deputy Minister of Economic Development (2012–2014), and Deputy Minister of Telecommunications and Postal Services (2014–2017). In February 2018, she was sacked by President Cyril Ramaphosa, who succeeded Jacob Zuma, and retreated to the Portfolio Committee on Communications, where she was elected chair in November 2018 and served until after the May 2019 general election. After the 2019 election, she was appointed Deputy Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities, deputising Minister Maite Nkoana-Mashabane, and served until her death. She was first elected to the National Executive Committee of the ANC in 2017, ranking 73rd out of 80 ordinary members. Mkhize was diagnosed with lung cancer in March 2017 and was hospitalised on 31 August 2021. She died in hospital in Johannesburg on 16 December 2021, aged 69. President Ramaphosa granted her an official funeral. She was married to Pat Mkhize and had four children – three daughters and a son – and a grandson. She was also chairperson of the June and Andrew Mlangeni Foundation.

The Honda Battle of the Bands (often abbreviated as The Honda or HBOB) is an annual marching band exhibition in the United States that showcases performances by bands from historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs). Sponsored by the American Honda Motor Company, the Invitational Showcase was held in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia from late January 2003 to 2020. In February 2023, Alabama State University in Montgomery, Alabama was selected as the first HBCU campus to host the in-person event, marking a significant shift in location. Since 2023, the event has moved to new venues, with the 2025 showcase taking place at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, making it the first time the event was held on the West Coast. The Honda Battle of the Bands Celebration Tour occurs between September and November at regular season football games, though the term "Honda Battle of the Bands" typically refers only to the invitational showcase, which began in 2003. Despite the name, Honda's "battle" is not a competition with a declared winner; instead, bands compete for audience and community favor. The event is one of the most popular collegiate marching band events in the nation, drawing over 50,000 fans annually. The program includes two components: a Voting Process from September to October and the Invitational Showcase. The first band is selected by popular vote, while the next three are chosen from three instrument categories—128 instruments or fewer, 129 to 160, and 161 or more—using a weighted vote from institution presidents, band directors, and an online opinion poll, with presidents and directors not allowed to vote for their own institutions. The final four bands are selected by American Honda and the Urban Sports & Entertainment Group based on, but not limited to, the voting results. A total of eight bands are invited to perform halftime routines in front of 50,000+ fans. The event was created in 2003 to celebrate, support, and recognize the excellence of Black college marching bands and the unique academic experience at HBCUs. Honda annually awards more than $205,000 in grants to participating bands and hosts a HBCU recruitment fair before the showcase. In 2018, the event was on a one-year hiatus in 2019 due to Super Bowl LIII being held in Atlanta; it resumed in 2020. In 2020, Honda announced a one-year pause in 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with the in-person event cancelled again in 2021, though a virtual event was likely held in 2022. In 2022, Honda announced the return of the in-person event in 2023 and released a four-part docuseries celebrating HBCU culture and bands on February 26, 2022. In November 2023, Honda announced a one-year hiatus in 2024 due to the Toad Bowl Game being held there and not being relocatable. In April 2024, Honda confirmed the return of the event in February 2025 at SoFi Stadium in Southern California. The event's coordinates are 33°57′11″N 118°20′20″W / 33.953°N 118.339°W / 33.953; -118.339.

The Honda Juno is a scooter that came in two versions: the K-series produced in 1954 (K, KA, KB) and the M-series introduced in 1962 (M80, M85). The Juno K, Honda's first scooter, was launched in 1954 as a deliberately sophisticated model, designed to compete with established scooters like the Fuji Rabbit and Mitsubishi Silver Pigeon. It featured the first electric start, a full windscreen with a tilt-back sun-shade, and built-in signal lamps, and introduced Fibre-Reinforced Plastic (FRP) body construction to Japan. Only 5,980 units were produced over a period of one and a half years. Kihachiro Kawashima, who retired as executive vice-president in 1979, recalled the Juno K as a "splendid failure" due to its high cost, engine overheating, heavier-than-expected FRP body that made it underpowered and clumsy, problematic cantilevered suspension, and customer dissatisfaction with the motorcycle-style clutch operation. The final Juno KB model is identifiable by enlarged rear vents and new vents on the windscreen. Technologies from the Juno K, including the electric start, were later used in the 1957 C71 Dream, and the Plastics department led by Shozo Tsuchida developed polyethylene components that became key in the Super Cub. The Juno M80/M85, introduced in November 1961, took a different design approach: it lacked an upper windscreen, used an exposed horizontal-twin engine instead of an enclosed fan-cooled unit, and featured conventional monocoque steel body construction rather than FRP panels over tube. It also introduced a clutchless Badalini-type hydraulic-mechanical transmission, which later influenced the development of Hondamatic motorcycle transmissions. The M80 and M85 are essentially identical, with the M85 designation denoting a mid-year engine enlargement. The Juno line was discontinued by year-end, with only 5,880 units produced in total.

Hong Joon-pyo (Korean: 홍준표; born 20 November 1953) is a South Korean retired politician and prosecutor who served as the mayor of Daegu from 2022 to 2025. He previously served as the governor of South Gyeongsang Province, a member of the National Assembly for five terms, and the party leader of the conservative Grand National Party in 2011 and its successor incarnations, the Saenuri Party and the Liberty Korea Party, from 2017 to 2018. He was the presidential nominee of the Liberty Korea Party in the 2017 South Korean presidential election and came in second place during the general election, losing to Moon Jae-in. Hong ran as a candidate in the 2022 South Korean presidential election for the nomination of the conservative People Power Party and came in second place during the primaries, narrowly losing to Yoon Suk Yeol. He was elected Mayor of Daegu in 2022, but resigned to launch his third campaign for the presidency in the 2025 South Korean presidential election. Although he advanced from the first round, Hong ultimately failed to win the party primary and subsequently announced his retirement from politics. Born in Changnyeong, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea, Hong graduated from Yeungnam High School and received a Bachelor of Laws degree from Korea University. Due to being underweight, he was discharged from the army after only fourteen months of service. In January 1996, Hong joined the New Korea Party and was elected for the Songpa A constituency during the 1996 election, entering the National Assembly for the first time. He was formerly the chairperson of the Grand National Party, which changed its name to the Saenuri Party in 2012 and again to the Liberty Korea Party in 2017; he stepped down as chairperson on 9 December 2011 and was replaced by future President Park Geun-hye. On 20 October 2011, Hong criticized Seoul Mayor Park Won-soon's The Beautiful Foundation for sending money to left-wing citizen groups and generated criticism against Park Won-soon regarding allegations of extorting tax money for overseas visits. He considered renaming the Grand National Party after Park Won-soon won the October 2011 election. Hong was first elected as Governor of South Gyeongsang Province in 2012 and re-elected in 2014. He secured the nomination of the Liberty Korea Party, with his campaign appealing to older, conservative voters by describing Hong as a "strongman," a reference to former president Park Chung Hee, a dictator popular with older conservatives whose daughter, Park Geun-hye, was impeached for corruption. Hong finished second among the five major candidates with 24% of the vote behind Moon Jae-in. After losing the presidential election, Hong was elected as the leader of the Liberty Korea Party. Following a massive loss in the 2018 local elections on 13 June 2018, Hong resigned as party leader on 14 June 2018. On 17 February 2020, the Liberty Korea Party dissolved and merged with several other parties to become the United Future Party. Hong left the United Future Party in March 2020 after party leaders decided not to give him a candidacy in any of the upcoming 2020 legislative elections. Running as an independent candidate, Hong won the National Assembly election of Suseong B in Daegu on 15 April 2020. On 24 June 2021, Hong rejoined the People Power Party (which had previously been called the United Future Party until 2 September 2020) and signaled a presidential bid in the upcoming 2022 South Korean presidential election. On 29 June 2021, Hong Joon-pyo officially entered the 2022 presidential election. He placed second in the final round of the primaries behind the winner Yoon Seok-yeol, winning 41.5 percent of the votes. On 26 April 2022, Hong resigned from the National Assembly after being chosen as the People Power Party's nominee for the mayor of Daegu. He went on to win the election for mayor of Daegu and began his term on 1 July 2022. Following the 2024 South Korean martial law crisis in December, Hong did not explicitly state his support for any side but said he understood the "loyalty" of President Yoon Suk Yeol while describing his actions as reckless and "making a scene." Later that month, Hong said he would run for president in the event of an early presidential election. In February 2025, Hong said he would step down as mayor if the impeachment of Yoon Suk Yeol was upheld. Hong claimed that in August 2022, Shincheonji leader Lee Man-hee told him that over 100,000 followers were directed to join the People Power Party as "responsible members" to support then-candidate Yoon Suk Yeol during the 2021 primary, with critics alleging this support was exchanged for Yoon, then Prosecutor General, obstructing a police raid on Shincheonji. A day after the removal of Yoon Suk Yeol from office by the Constitutional Court of Korea, Hong expressed interest in a presidential bid, stating on Facebook: "I have been thoroughly preparing for this election, considering it the final mission of my 30-year political career. Starting next week, I will proceed step by step with the necessary procedures." Shortly before officially announcing his campaign for the 2025 South Korean presidential election, Hong stepped down as Daegu mayor. He officially declared his candidacy on 14 April. Although he advanced from the first round, he ultimately failed to make it to the runoff in the primaries held by the People Power Party. After his loss, Hong announced that he would retire from politics and leave the People Power Party. Hong stated: "I am very thankful that I can graduate from my political life today honorably and cleanly thanks to the care shown to me by party members and the public over the last 30 years." Hong is known for his right-wing populism, advocating for social conservatism and hawkish approaches to diplomatic issues. He holds economically conservative views, supporting Korean conglomerates (chaebols) and wanting to reduce the power of trade unions. When asked how he would respond to growing concerns around corrupt practices among chaebols, such as those that brought down former President Park Geun-hye's administration, he stated he would reduce corruption by putting it through a "washing machine." Hong supports a vigilant approach to national security, including the deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) from the United States and "armed peace," and has stated support for South Korea's nuclear armament. Hong has publicly indicated that he believes AIDS and HIV are a result of homosexuality to attract conservative voters. In a televised presidential debate, Hong criticized Moon Jae-in on homosexuality and remarked that gay soldiers were a source of weakness in the Korean military. In 2023, Hong directed civil servants to obstruct the Daegu Queer Culture Festival after court attempts to halt the festival failed, though police intervened to allow the festival to proceed. Hong supports the death penalty; in 2017, he said he would revive capital punishment if elected.

Horacio Coppola (31 July 1906 – 18 June 2012) was an Argentine photographer and filmmaker, and the husband of the German photographer Grete Stern. Born in Buenos Aires, he was the youngest of 10 children; his Italian immigrant parents were well off, and he studied art, music, law, and languages. He began taking photographs around the age of 20. In the 1920s and ’30s, he traveled to Europe, where photography was emerging as an art form, characterized by unusual angles and cropping. He met Grete Stern in Germany and later worked in London, taking portraits of famous artists and contributing to a book about Mesopotamian artifacts in the Louvre and the British Museum. In 1936, he and Stern returned to Argentina, where he was commissioned to photograph Buenos Aires for its 400th anniversary, producing streetscapes that depicted the city’s romance, vitality, and squalor. The couple had a daughter, Silvia, and a son, Andres, and later divorced. In 1959, Coppola married Raquel Palomeque, a pianist. He authored the photographs featured in the first edition of "Evaristo Carriego" (biography) (1930) by Jorge Luis Borges and was one of the pioneering Argentine photographers and a key figure in Modernism. He studied at the Bauhaus during the 1930s. Coppola was awarded the title of "Illustrious Citizen of Buenos Aires" and, at the age of 100, had a retrospective exhibit at the Malba Museum in Buenos Aires.

Hugh Finlayson (December 12, 1810 – June 3, 1889) was an Ontario businessman and political figure who represented Brant North in the Legislative Assembly of Ontario as a Liberal member from 1867 to 1879. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland in 1810, he arrived in North America in 1832, initially settling in New York City before moving to Brantford in Upper Canada in 1835. He eventually settled in Paris, Ontario, where he worked as a saddle and harness maker and operated a tannery. Finlayson served as mayor of Paris in 1858 and represented East Brant in the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Canada from 1858 to 1861. He was elected to the Ontario Legislative Assembly in 1867 and remained a member until 1879. He died in Paris in 1889. This article about an Ontario Liberal Party MPP is a stub. Hum Kahan Ke Sachay Thay is a Pakistani drama television series based on a novel of the same name by Umera Ahmad, directed by Farooq Rind and co-produced by Soul Fry Films and MD Productions. The series stars Mahira Khan, Usman Mukhtar, and Kubra Khan in lead roles and premiered on 1 August 2021 on Hum TV. The show was first announced by Zainab Qayyum in late March 2021, who confirmed her participation along with Kubra Khan and the direction by Farooq Rind. Omair Rana, who plays Mehreen's father, revealed in an interview that he is starring in the serial and that Mahira Khan will return to television after five years with this show. The series received mixed to negative reviews, with praise for its premise and the performances of the lead actors, while facing criticism for glorifying toxic relationships and unrealistic elements, such as Aswad's character and the portrayal of suicide. Critics also pointed out the romanticization of cousin marriages, the slow pacing, and the depiction of mental health issues, including the use of therapy. Haneena Moosa of The Daily Times highlighted the powerful opening dialogue and praised the series' premise, while Maheen Zia and another reviewer from The News International criticized the glorification of toxic dynamics. A DAWN Images reviewer commended the acting and inclusion of mental therapy but noted the toxicity of Mukhtar's character and the suicide scene as negative aspects. Jasir Shahbaz of The Friday Times argued that the portrayal of cousin relationships perpetuates harmful traditions and limits women's agency. Despite the criticism, the series follows the story of three cousins—Aswad Ayub (Usman Mukhtar), Mehreen Mansoor (Mahira Khan), and Mashal Tahir (Kubra Khan)—who were best friends in childhood. Aswad is humble and friendly, while Mashal is beautiful and rich, and Mehreen is poor and average-looking. Mehreen's maternal grandmother hates her because her father, Mansoor (Omair Rana), is a drug addict. After Mansoor is caught stealing jewelry to buy drugs and is abandoned by his wife Rabia (Laila Wasti), he commits suicide by heroin overdose. Mashal overhears her parents saying Mansoor is a drug addict and tells Mehreen, causing a rift between them. Rabia remarries and neglects Mehreen, who then moves in with Mashal's parents and her paternal grandmother. She lives a lonely life but remains academically and artistically gifted, admired by her friends, which makes Mashal envious. Her only support comes from her aunt Saleha Ayub (Huma Nawab), Aswad's mother, who loves her like a daughter and knows her true reality. Mashal, who is not academically or artistically inclined, is constantly told by her mother Shagufta (Zainab Qayyum) to be like Mehreen, leading to an inferiority complex and obsession with her. She sneaks into Mehreen's room to read her diaries, discovering Mehreen's hatred for her. Mashal is in contact with Aswad, who lives in America, and becomes jealous of his affection for Mehreen, feeding him false information about her, claiming she smokes and has many boyfriends. Aswad is brainwashed and begins to dislike Mehreen. Saffwan (Haroon Shahid), Mehreen's friend's cousin, becomes romantically interested in her, but Mashal reveals Mehreen's past to him, creating a misunderstanding. Saffwan later realizes it was Mashal's doing and proposes to Mehreen, whom he rejects, saying he would hate her once he learns her full history. Saleha decides Mehreen should marry Aswad, a wish she has long held, and Mehreen, who has secretly loved him, does not object. Mashal then tells Aswad she loves him and wants to marry him, but Aswad, who also likes her, agrees to marry her, only for Saleha to reject her and insist Mehreen is the only one he can marry. Aswad tells Mashal he cannot marry her, breaking her heart, though she forgives him and secretly tries to dissuade Mehreen from marrying Aswad by tearing her wedding veil. That night, Mashal is found dead in her room, and everyone blames Mehreen, who is arrested. Shabbo, their maid, knows the truth but remains silent. Due to the trauma, Mehreen begins hallucinating about her father in jail. She is soon bailed out by Saleha, who arranges a lawyer. Tahir and Shagufta are unhappy about her release, still believing she poisoned Mashal. Aswad believes Mehreen killed Mashal and treats her rudely, leading to emotional abuse and worsening mental health. Mehreen starts hallucinating that Mashal tells her to kill herself, and Aswad forces her to sign an affidavit stating she killed Mashal. The stress causes a nervous breakdown, and she is hospitalized. The psychiatrist tells Aswad that great stress caused Mehreen's condition, and Aswad begins to feel guilty. Shagufta calls Aswad to inform him she plans to dispose of Mehreen's belongings, which he collects and sees are Mehreen's awards and paintings—something Mashal had previously shown off. Shabbo finally reveals the truth: Mashal tried to kill Mehreen by having sleeping pills placed in her cup, but mistakenly put them in Mashal's cup instead. Aswad learns from Mehreen's diary that Mashal and Mehreen had a conversation that night, both realizing they were manipulated by their parents and reconciling. Mashal, realizing she had ordered the pills for Mehreen, threw her cup to the ground, breaking it, and unknowingly drank the pills. They both apologized and promised to talk again the next day. Aswad is shocked and asks Mehreen for forgiveness, promising to love her as he did in childhood. Mehreen forgives him, and they reconcile. Later, Mehreen continues her incomplete degree with Aswad's full support and begins a new life together.

Hunter Schafer, born December 31, 1998, in Trenton, New Jersey, and raised in Raleigh, North Carolina, is an American actress, model, and activist. Her father was a pastor, and the family moved between churches in New Jersey, Arizona, and eventually Raleigh, where Schafer grew up. She has three younger siblings: two sisters and a brother. Schafer began expressing femininity as a toddler; in seventh grade, she came out to her parents as a gay boy, but developed gender dysphoria in eighth grade and came out as a transgender girl in ninth grade, beginning her transition after being diagnosed with dysphoria. She also questioned whether she had a non-binary identity and found support through YouTube and social media. In 2016, she became the youngest plaintiff in the ACLU and Lambda Legal lawsuit Carcaño v. McCrory against North Carolina's Public Facilities Privacy & Security Act, a "bathroom bill" that prohibited transgender people from using bathrooms matching their gender identity. The lawsuit led to the bill's repeal, and Schafer made a film protesting it released by Rookie and wrote an essay for Teen Vogue in July 2016. For her activism, she was named to Teen Vogue's "21 Under 21" list in 2017 and granted an interview with Hillary Clinton. Schafer studied watercolor painting and clothing design; she designed clothes in high school, inspired by Tim Burton and Skottie Young, and posted her artwork on Instagram, which gained popularity. Her designs, often featuring political messaging, were featured by Huffington Post in 2017. She attended Needham B. Broughton High School and transferred to the North Carolina School of the Arts, graduating from its visual arts program. In 2017, she was a semifinalist in the U.S. Presidential Scholars Program. After high school, she planned to attend Central Saint Martins in London to study clothing design for nonbinary people and intended to open a studio and gallery for trans artists using grant money from Teen Vogue. She signed with Elite Model Management in 2017 after meeting an agent on Instagram and moved to Brooklyn to model in New York City, working with brands such as Dior, Marc Jacobs, Converse, Gucci, Helmut Lang, Versus, and Versace. She walked for nine fashion houses in early 2018, made her debut at New York Fashion Week, and traveled to Europe. Marie Claire praised her for her ethereal yet edgy look and versatility. In 2019, she was cast in the HBO series Euphoria as transgender high school student Jules Vaughn, after finding a casting call on Instagram requiring no prior acting experience. She completed her final audition in Los Angeles, filmed the pilot there, and moved to Los Angeles to film the first season. At the time, trans television characters and trans actors in such roles were rare. She worked with creator Sam Levinson and costume designer Heidi Bivens to ensure Jules's experiences were accurate and was praised by Vulture for not being a passive victim of violence. Her performance was widely acclaimed, earning her a Shorty Award, an MTV Movie & TV Award, and a Dorian Award. The Advocate noted she should have been nominated at the 2020 Primetime Emmy Awards, and Queerty named her one of 50 queer people leading toward equality in 2020. In 2021, she co-wrote the Euphoria episode "Fuck Anyone Who's Not a Sea Blob," which featured Jules in therapy and was critically acclaimed. In 2020, she became the global brand ambassador for Shiseido Makeup; in 2021, Prada named her their new house ambassador, and Time included her on its Next list of emerging leaders, with a tribute by Euphoria co-star Zendaya. In 2022, she starred in the English dub of the Japanese film Belle and made her directorial debut with the music video for Girl in Red's song "hornylovesickmess," sharing storyboard sketches with the final shots. She directed the music video for Anohni and the Johnsons' "Why Am I Alive Now?" in 2023 and became the new face of Mugler's Angel perfume. She starred in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023) as Tigris Snow, a role praised as "excellent" and "underused," with director Francis Lawrence citing her disarming authenticity and warm audition. She continued modeling for Alexander McQueen, Prada, and Schiaparelli. At the 2023 Vanity Fair after-party for the 95th Academy Awards, she wore a white maxi skirt and a top with a horizontal feather covering her nipples, designed by Ludovic de Saint Sernin for Ann Demeulemeester, an outfit that became infamous and sparked widespread discussion, later referenced by Spanish pop singer Rosalía in a 2025 photoshoot. Since the Songbirds & Snakes press tour, she has been stylized by Dara Allen, whom she considers a close friend, and some attribute her fashion success to their collaboration. In 2024, she starred in Tilman Singer's horror film Cuckoo, her first lead role in a feature film, which she described as "the training wheels" turning off and which received praise for its "intense and emotional central performance"; she also appeared in a scene in Yorgos Lanthimos's anthology film Kinds of Kindness. In 2025, she starred in the horror short film The Hunt, directed by Nadia Lee Cohen, to promote Gentle Monster's autumn 2025 campaign. In 2025, a leaker reported she was initially considered for the role of Princess Zelda in the live-action The Legend of Zelda film, which was later given to Bo Bragason; the rumor sparked both supportive and transphobic reactions, with some outlets speculating Nintendo chose a cisgender woman to avoid backlash, though this has not been confirmed. Schafer has upcoming roles in David Lowery's Mother Mary, Tom Ford's Cry to Heaven, Zach Strauss' Palette, Hideo Kojima's horror video game OD, the Amazon series Blade Runner 2099, and a horror film by Arkasha Stevenson. In 2019, she identified as closer to a lesbian, and in 2021, described herself as bi or pan or something. She had a brief relationship with Rosalía from 2019 to 2020, which she confirmed in 2024, and considers her "family no matter what"; she dated Euphoria co-star Dominic Fike from February 2022 to around July 2023, ending the relationship after discovering he cheated. In 2019, she used she/her pronouns and the title "Mx. Schafer," stating in 2016 that she was not a cis girl. In 2024, she said she wanted to talk less about her trans identity as she had moved past the most difficult parts of her transition and no longer wanted to be seen solely as a "trans starlet," declining many trans roles. In an interview with Rolling Stone, she said, "No. I'm just a tranny who's famous, you know?" and in a 2024 Vogue interview, she discussed balancing visibility and responsibility in representation, saying she constantly "does the math of when to reel it in and when to lean into it." In 2022, she liked and commented "!!!!!" on an Instagram post criticizing certain non-binary activists who opposed trans identities being considered a medical condition requiring dysphoria, linking such activism to anti-trans legislation; this drew backlash from some fans, who accused her of endorsing transmedicalism, which she denied, stating she believed there was an imbalance in visibility between non-binary people and binary trans women, especially those of color or who rely on sex work, and that this deserved attention. On February 27, 2024, Schafer and fifty others were arrested in New York City during a Jewish Voice for Peace protest outside 30 Rockefeller Center, aimed at disrupting President Joe Biden's interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers. In February 2025, through an eight-minute TikTok video, she criticized the Trump administration and the U.S. Department of State for changing her passport gender marker from female to male without her consent, stating it was important to track national developments and that it was a "good, necessary point" to share. Marcy Rheintgen, the first person arrested under Florida's anti-trans bathroom law, described Schafer as a personal hero who inspired her to challenge the law after receiving a male passport.

I Am... Sasha Fierce is the third studio album by American singer and songwriter Beyoncé, released on November 12, 2008, by Columbia Records and Music World Entertainment. The album was recorded from November 2007 to August 2008 over a nine-month period, with production handled by Darkchild, Toby Gad, Jim Jonsin, Rico Love, Stargate, Tricky Stewart, Ryan Tedder of OneRepublic, and The-Dream, alongside others. Although there are no featured artists on the main track listing, Lady Gaga and Kanye West appear on the deluxe editions. The album is formatted as a double album, reflecting Beyoncé's dual artistic personas: the first disc, I Am..., features slow and midtempo pop and R&B ballads, while the second, Sasha Fierce—named after her on-stage alter ego—focuses on uptempo electropop and Europop tracks. Beyoncé co-wrote or co-produced all material on the album and worked with producers and songwriters including Babyface, Stargate, Tricky Stewart, The-Dream, Darkchild, Sean Garrett, Solange Knowles, Jim Jonsin, Rico Love, Ryan Tedder, Bangladesh, Ian Dench, Dave McCracken, Wayne Wilkins, and Blac Elvis. She also collaborated with Toby Gad and BC Jean on "If I Were a Boy" and worked again with Amanda Ghost on "Disappear." Beyoncé credited her husband Jay-Z and jazz singer Etta James for inspiring her songwriting. Musically, the I Am... disc draws from folk and alternative rock, incorporating acoustic guitar, while Sasha Fierce features electronic influences, with songs like "Radio" and "Sweet Dreams" showcasing those elements. The ballads were crafted to blend pop and soul, expanding both genres, and Beyoncé experimented with stronger lyrics to break from expectations. "Ave Maria" samples Franz Schubert's "Ave Maria" after being co-written with Ghost, who noted they were inspired by their recent marriages. "Smash Into You," originally intended for Jon McLaughlin's album, was given to Beyoncé after being leaked. During the recording process, Beyoncé recorded over seventy songs and eliminated those that were meaningless to her, resulting in twelve tracks on the standard edition and five additional tracks on the deluxe edition. Songs from producers like The Neptunes and Danja were not included. The album received mixed to positive reviews and was a commercial success, debuting at number one on the US Billboard 200 with first-week sales of 482,000 units, earning Beyoncé her third consecutive US number-one solo album. It has earned one diamond and over thirty platinum certifications worldwide, achieving seven-times platinum status by the RIAA after shipping over seven million units in the United States and selling 10 million copies globally, making it one of the best-selling albums of the 21st century. The album received seven Grammy nominations at the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards (2010), including Album of the Year, winning five, with a sixth win during the ceremony, making Beyoncé the female artist with the most awards won in one night. Singles such as "If I Were a Boy" and "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)" charted highly internationally, with the former topping charts in over ten countries and reaching number three on the Billboard Hot 100, and the latter becoming her fifth number-one single on the Hot 100. "Diva" and "Ego" were released exclusively in the United States, while "Halo" and "Sweet Dreams" were promoted internationally as the third and fourth singles, respectively. "Broken-Hearted Girl" was released internationally as the fifth single, and "Video Phone" was released in September 2009 as the eighth single, with "Why Don't You Love Me" released in July 2010 as the ninth and final single. The album was marketed with televised appearances and award show performances across Europe and America, and Beyoncé embarked on the worldwide I Am... Tour (2009–10). The recording took place at studios in Atlanta, New York, Ibiza, Los Angeles, Miami Beach, and Burbank. The I Am... cover, described as "underneath all the makeup," shows Beyoncé without clothing or makeup, while the Sasha Fierce cover features heavy makeup, a leotard, tall heels, and a "cyborg"-esque metallic glove, both shot by Peter Lindbergh. Beyoncé revealed in a 2021 Harper's Bazaar interview that she based the project on black and white photography after being upset by a fan survey suggesting her fans disliked black and white images, highlighting her frustration with corporate formulas and noting the album's commercial success. The album was released in the United States on November 18, 2008, previously in Japan on November 12, Australia and Germany on November 14, and France and the United Kingdom on November 17; the deluxe edition was released simultaneously. Beyoncé promoted the album through performances on shows including Music Station, the MTV Europe Music Awards, the World Music Awards, The Oprah Winfrey Show, Saturday Night Live, and various others, with her first live performance of "Halo" at the 40th NAACP Image Awards in February 2009 and a performance of "Sweet Dreams" at the 2009 MTV Europe Music Awards in November 2009. She performed "If I Were a Boy" at the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards in January 2010, along with a cover of Alanis Morissette's "You Oughta Know." The bonus track "Why Don't You Love Me" reached number one on the US Dance Club Songs chart in February 2010. A music video for the full-length track was released online on May 4, 2010. On June 16, 2009, Above and Beyoncé: Video Collection & Dance Mixes was released, including a remix of "Ego" with Kanye West and behind-the-scenes footage. Beyoncé was scheduled to perform "Sweet Dreams" at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards but only performed the bridge before switching to "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)." The platinum edition was released in Australia on September 4, 2009, and in the United States on October 20, 2009, including a cover of Billy Joel's "Honesty" and a DVD of music videos. The deluxe edition was reissued in the United States on November 23, 2009, with new tracks "Poison" and the remix of "Video Phone" with Lady Gaga, and an EP titled I Am... Sasha Fierce – The Bonus Tracks was released the same day for digital download, featuring those songs and "Why Don't You Love Me." The album formally introduces Sasha Fierce, who Beyoncé revealed was born during the making of "Crazy in Love" (2003), and described as her sensual, aggressive stage alter ego. In an interview with Emmet Sullivan, Beyoncé affirmed that Sasha Fierce is strictly for the stage. The I Am... disc was described by Beyoncé as having mainstream songs and traditional R&B for her long-time fans, with influences from Barbra Streisand, Karen Carpenter, and The Beatles from the 1970s. Music writer Andy Kellman noted the first disc as a set of adult contemporary ballads with roots in 1970s soft rock, while the second disc features consistent electronic elements. "Diva" was noted as a variation on Lil Wayne's "A Milli," and "Sweet Dreams" was praised for its electronic bassline, compared to Michael Jackson's "Beat It," and derived from contemporary R&B with 1980s funk influences. "Broken-Hearted Girl" is a midtempo piano ballad with strings and a drum machine beat. "Hello" includes the line "You had me at hello" and features sweet guitar-picking and delicate harmonies. "Video Phone" contains lyrics referencing Skype sex and a solo performance for a new acquaintance, with a remixed version featuring Beyoncé and Lady Gaga trading verses and gasps and groans. "Disappear" features sweet guitar-picking and delicate harmonies. "That's Why You're Beautiful" is a slow-tempo soft rock and rock power ballad with a grungy guitar riff and stuttering drums, compared to Alice in Chains and Jill Scott. The platinum edition includes a cover of Billy Joel's "Honesty" (1979). The album was titled I Am... Sasha Fierce to highlight the contrast between Beyoncé and her alter ego.

The platinum edition of I Am... Sasha Fierce was released in Australia on Beyoncé's twenty-eighth birthday, September 4, 2009, and in the United States on October 20, 2009; it included a cover version of Billy Joel's "Honesty" (1979) and a DVD with music videos from the album's singles. The deluxe edition was reissued in the United States on November 23, 2009, containing all previously released songs plus new tracks "Poison" and the remix of "Video Phone" with Lady Gaga. On the same day, an EP titled I Am... Sasha Fierce – The Bonus Tracks was released digitally in the United States, featuring "Poison," the "Video Phone" remix, and "Why Don't You Love Me." To promote the album, Beyoncé launched the I Am... Tour, beginning in Edmonton, Canada on March 26, 2009, with the European leg starting April 26 in Zagreb, Croatia, and ending June 9 in London, England. The third leg began June 21 in the United States and concluded in August with the I Am... Yours four-day residency at Encore Las Vegas on the Las Vegas Strip. The fourth leg started September 15 in Melbourne, Australia and ended September 24 in Perth, Australia, followed by performances in Asia, the Middle East, Europe, Africa, and the United Kingdom, finishing on November 24 in Belfast, Northern Ireland. The final leg in February 2010 began in Florianópolis, Brazil and ended in Trinidad on February 18. According to Pollstar, the 2010 shows earned $17.2 million, adding to the $86 million from the first 86 concerts in 2009, bringing the tour total to $103.2 million for 97 shows. The I Am... Yours residency at Encore Theater was recorded on August 2, 2009, and released as a DVD, audio CD, and television special titled I Am... Yours: An Intimate Performance at Wynn Las Vegas in late November 2009. Various tour performances were filmed worldwide for the live DVD I Am... World Tour, released on November 30, 2010. On October 8, 2008, Beyoncé premiered two lead singles, "If I Were a Boy," which peaked at number three on the US Billboard Hot 100, topped eight charts worldwide, and reached the top ten on many others, and "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)," which peaked at number one on the US Billboard Hot 100, becoming Beyoncé's fifth number-one single and reaching the top ten globally. Both singles were certified double platinum and quadruple platinum, respectively, by the RIAA. "Diva," released exclusively in the United States, peaked at number nineteen on the US Billboard Hot 100, becoming Beyoncé's twelfth top-twenty single and number three on the US Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs, and was certified gold by the RIAA. "Halo," released internationally, peaked at number five on the US Billboard Hot 100 and reached the top ten worldwide, certified double platinum by the RIAA on January 5, 2010. Two additional singles, "Broken-Hearted Girl" and "Sweet Dreams," were initially announced but became the sixth and seventh singles, respectively. "Sweet Dreams" reached the top ten in most countries, including the United States, topped the New Zealand Singles Chart, and was certified platinum by the RIAA on January 5, 2010. "Broken-Hearted Girl," the seventh single, reached the top forty globally without certification or release in the United States. "Video Phone," released as the eighth single on September 22, 2009, with a music video and digital download, featured a remix with Lady Gaga, reached the top forty worldwide, peaked at number sixty-five on the US Billboard Hot 100, and became Beyoncé's fourteenth number-one on the US Hot Dance Club Songs. "Why Don't You Love Me" was released as the ninth and final single on July 2, 2010, and peaked atop the US Hot Dance Club Songs before its official release. As of July 2010, digital tracks from the album had sold 12.3 million units in the United States, and according to Columbia Records, the album had sold fifteen million digital singles worldwide. I Am... Sasha Fierce received mixed reviews; at Metacritic, it received an average score of 62 based on 24 reviews, indicating generally favorable reviews. Sal Cinquemani of Slant Magazine praised the individual songs as a testament to Beyoncé's reliability as a singles artist but criticized the album's inability to reconcile the adult-contemporary style of "I Am" with the edgier sounds of "Sasha Fierce." Adam Mattera of The Observer found both discs lacking depth, criticizing the first for chasing radio formats and the second for its "independent woman anthems" that appeal to drag queens but confuse others. AllMusic's Andy Kellman called the double-disc "gimmick" flimsy, favoring the second disc's upbeat pop, noting that Beyoncé's vocal performance on the "I Am" disc almost rescues its staidness. Robert Christgau of MSN Music named it the "dud of the month," calling it a bad record with few details worth considering and criticizing its "split-personality" as "deeply vapid," noting only three good songs. Jonah Weiner of Blender described Beyoncé as a "beauty-shop feminist" with poise in describing love. Stacey Anderson of Spin noted the first disc meanders over down-tempo cuts and called "Sasha" an intriguing but diluted direction. Nana Ekua Brew-Hammond of The Village Voice found the "I Am" disc lacking cohesion but praised "Sasha Fierce" as "brassy, big-headed, confrontational, and witty," stating each track challenges the listener to leave inhibitions at the door. Christian Hoard of Rolling Stone noted the slow songs are full of bland self-affirmation but praised the "Sasha" disc as Beyoncé's most adventurous music yet. Colin McGuire of PopMatters called the album a little rough around the edges and viewed the "Sasha" disc as a more compelling dance-oriented experience. Leah Greenblatt of Entertainment Weekly stated the album offers two compelling sides of Beyoncé and suggested it might have been better as a single disc, noting that the lyrics offer little new emotional insight. Sasha Frere-Jones of The New Yorker found the album a "mess" due to the alter ego tripping on the idea of redefinition. Greenblatt ranked I Am...
