Sasha Fierce at number two on her list "10 Best CDs of 2008," highlighting "If I Were a Boy" and "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)" as highlights and noting the rest of the album is consistently satisfying on repeated listening. Mark Edward Nero of About.com ranked it ninth on his list of the Best R&B Albums of 2008. Christian Gerard of NBC Washington included it in his "Honorable Mentions" list for "Best Albums of 2008." Agence France-Presse, as reported by ABS-CBN News and Current Affairs, recognized it as the twelfth best-selling album of 2008. On The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop year-end lists, it was ranked 333rd in 2008 and 580th in 2009. It was ranked number twelve on Rolling Stone's Reader's Poll for the best albums of the 2000s decade and number eight on Entertainment Weekly's list of the "10 Best Albums of the Decade." The album won a Soul Train Music Award for Best Album of the Year at the 2009 Soul Train Music Awards. Beyoncé won the American Music Award for Favorite Soul/R&B Female Artist at the 2009 American Music Awards, with I Am... Sasha Fierce receiving a nomination for Favorite Soul/R&B Album. Beyoncé also won a BET Award for Best R&B Artist at the 2009 BET Awards, though she lost the same award to Alicia Keys at the following ceremony. She was nominated for the Brit Award for International Female Solo Artist at the 2009 Brit Awards, the Meteor Music Award for Best International Female at the 2009 Meteor Awards, and the International Dance Music Awards for Best Artist (Solo) and Best R&B/Urban Dance Track for "Sweet Dreams" at the 25th Annual International Dance Music Awards in 2010. At the MOBO Awards 2009, Beyoncé won the MOBO Award for Best International Act and I Am... Sasha Fierce was nominated for Best Album. Beyoncé won an MTV Europe Music Award for Best Female, "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)" won Best Video, and "Halo" won Best Song at the 2009 MTV Europe Music Awards. The album was nominated for the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Album at the 40th NAACP Image Awards in 2009 and for an NRJ Music Award for International Album of the Year at the NRJ Music Awards 2010. Beyoncé was nominated for a People's Choice Award for Favorite Female Artist and Favorite R&B Artist at the 36th People's Choice Awards in 2010, won a Teen Choice Award for Choice Music: R&B Artist at the 2010 Teen Choice Awards, and was nominated for World's Best R&B Artist at the 2010 World Music Awards. I Am... Sasha Fierce and its singles earned Beyoncé seven Grammy Award nominations at the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards in 2010, including Album of the Year; she won five, and also won a record-breaking sixth for her rendition of "At Last" from the Cadillac Records soundtrack, making her the most decorated female artist in one night in Grammy history. The album debuted at number one on the US Billboard 200, selling 482,000 copies in its first week and giving Beyoncé her third consecutive number-one album in the United States, her fourth overall, including Destiny's Child's Survivor (2001). This made her the third female artist of the 2000s to have her first three solo albums debut at number one. By the end of 2008, the album had sold 1,459,000 copies in six weeks and became the tenth best-selling album of the year according to Billboard. This achievement placed Beyoncé in a tie with Garth Brooks, Mariah Carey, and Shania Twain for having an album in Nielsen SoundScan's year-end top ten for the fifth time. The album became the second best-selling album of 2009 in the United States and was certified six-times platinum by the RIAA. As of July 2022, it has sold 8.12 million album-equivalent units in the United States. In the United Kingdom, it debuted at number ten on November 29, 2008, becoming Beyoncé's lowest-debuting album despite higher first-week sales than B'Day (2006), rose to number nine after a performance with Alexandra Burke on The X Factor fifth season finale on December 27, 2008, and reached its highest peak of number two in its thirty-ninth week on August 16, 2009, due to the success of singles like "Sweet Dreams," making it her best-selling album in the UK with over 1.5 million units sold and certified six times platinum by the British Phonographic Industry. In Australia, it debuted at number nine on November 24, 2008, climbed to number eight on January 5, 2009, and reached number three on two separate occasions in October 2009 following the success of "Sweet Dreams" and "Broken-Hearted Girl," later certified quintuple platinum by the ARIA in 2023. In New Zealand, it debuted at number sixteen on November 24, 2008, peaked at number six on March 2, 2009, and reached number three on September 21, 2009, after the success of "Sweet Dreams," certified platinum by RIANZ after twenty-three weeks on the chart with over 15,000 copies shipped. In Spain, it debuted and peaked at number seven on November 26, 2008, and was certified double platinum by PROMUSICAE for over 160,000 copies. The album was the best-selling international album of 2009 in Turkey. It topped Brazil's year-end chart and was certified double diamond for sales over 500,000 copies by Pro-Música Brasil. The album has sold over ten million copies worldwide and generated over 1 billion streams as of February 2017.
The figures provided are based solely on certification, not including sales and streaming data. Sales and streaming figures are also based only on certification.

"I See You" is the eighth episode of the third season of Breaking Bad and the 28th episode overall. Written by Gennifer Hutchison and directed by Colin Bucksey, it originally aired on AMC in the United States and Canada on May 9, 2010. The episode's title is a play on "ICU," referencing the intensive care unit of a hospital. As Jesse Pinkman leaves the hospital after Hank Schrader's attack, he sees Hank being admitted in critical condition with four gunshot wounds and smiles to himself, satisfied by the karmic justice, as Skinny Pete picks him up. Walter White tells confused and upset Gale Boetticher that they are not working well together and that he is being replaced; Jesse then arrives, upsetting Walt, and displays his uncouth and unprofessional behavior as he admires the lab, further confusing Gale, who realizes Jesse is his replacement. As Walt leaves, Victor reminds him not to fall behind on their weekly quota. Jesse informs Walt about Hank's condition, prompting Walt to go to the hospital, where Steve Gomez and George Merkert explain that two Cartel hitmen, Leonel and Marco Salamanca, attempted to kill Hank. Gomez is astonished that Hank defeated both without his gun, leading Marie Schrader to question why Hank didn't have his gun, as he had turned it in after being suspended for assaulting Jesse. Marie blames both Gomez and Merkert for not supporting Hank and also blames Walt, believing Hank would never have met Jesse if Walt hadn't "bought marijuana" from him. Leonel, now with amputated legs, is being treated in the same hospital as Hank. When Gomez and Walt visit him from the other side of his door, Leonel recognizes Walt and angrily crawls toward him before being hoisted back to his bed, startling Walt and making him realize he might have been the intended target. Gus Fring receives a call from Juan Bolsa, who suspects Gus orchestrated the hit on a DEA agent, as Marco and Leonel would not have attacked without approval. Bolsa tells Gus he intends to get the truth from Leonel about who authorized the attack. Walt spends the next few days at the hospital while Jesse stays at the lab, waiting for him to return so they can resume cooking to meet their quota. Walt eventually receives a call from Gus to check in; to avoid revealing that his brother-in-law is a DEA agent, Walt lies, claiming Gale has set them back and promises to produce 400 pounds (180 kg) of meth next week, which Gus agrees to. Walt is horrified when Gus suddenly appears at the hospital, bringing free food from Los Pollos Hermanos as a show of support for the DEA. Gus meets Walt's family and shares a memory from when he first met Hank, revealing to Walt that Gus already knew Hank was a DEA agent. In private, Walt assures Gus that Hank is not a problem for their business, and Gus subtly indicates that Leonel will no longer be a threat. As he leaves, Leonel suddenly goes into cardiac arrest and dies. Mike Ehrmantraut is then shown disposing of a syringe and leaving unnoticed, with Gus's appearance serving as a distraction for Mike's actions, and Gomez celebrates. Later that night, Gus receives another call from Bolsa, whose house is now surrounded by Mexican federales. With Leonel dead, Bolsa believes Gus is responsible and vows retaliation, but is interrupted by the federales. His bodyguards are shot and killed, and as Bolsa attempts to escape, he is shot to death. The episode was written by Gennifer Hutchison and directed by Colin Bucksey, and aired on AMC in the United States and Canada on May 9, 2010. Donna Bowman of The A.V. Club noted that the episode focuses on the organization employing Walter, highlighting its long reach and ruthless ambition, but criticized the hospital scene as "spouting clichés." Seth Amitin of IGN gave the episode a 9.4/10 rating, calling it "a great episode about the emotional debris left in the wake of last week's amazing melee." In 2019, The Ringer ranked "I See You" 47th out of the 62 total Breaking Bad episodes, and Vulture ranked it 61st overall. The episode's original broadcast was viewed by 1.78 million people, an increase from the 1.52 million who watched the previous episode, "One Minute."

The DST-ICTP-IMU Ramanujan Prize for Young Mathematicians from Developing Countries is an annual mathematics award given by the International Centre for Theoretical Physics in Italy. The prize is named in honor of the Indian mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan. It was established in 2004 and first presented in 2005. The award is conferred upon a mathematician from a developing country who is under 45 years of age and has carried out exceptional research within a developing country. The prize is jointly supported by the Ministry of Science and Technology (India) and the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters via the Abel Fund, with collaboration from the International Mathematical Union.

Immature, later known as IMx, is an American R&B boy band managed by record producer Chris Stokes, formed in Los Angeles, California in 1991 by Marques "Batman" Houston (born August 4, 1981), Jerome "Romeo" Jones (born October 25, 1981), and Don "Half Pint" Santos. Kelton "LDB" Kessee (born January 2, 1981), the group's drummer at the time, joined full-time in 1994 after Santos was removed due to his parents pulling him from the group following the filming of House Party 3. The group released four albums under the Immature name: On Our Worst Behavior (1992), which included original member Santos and featured singles "Da Munchies", "I Wanna Know U That Way", "Be My Girl", and "Tear It Up (On Our Worst Behavior)", the latter of which appeared on the Bebe's Kids soundtrack and reached number 29 on Billboard's Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs despite the album not charting on Billboard's charts; Playtyme Is Over (1994), released after signing with MCA Records and featuring singles "Never Lie" (their biggest hit), "Constantly", and "I Don't Mind", which peaked at number 88 on the Billboard 200 and number 26 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums; We Got It (1995), featuring singles "We Got It", "Lover's Groove", and "Please Don't Go", which peaked at number 76 on the Billboard 200 and number 14 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums; and The Journey (1997), their final album under the Immature name, featuring singles "I'm Not a Fool", "Give Up The Ghost" (featuring Bizzy Bone), and "Extra, Extra" (written by and featuring Keith Sweat), which peaked at number 92 on the Billboard 200 and number 20 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. In 1999, the group changed their name to IMx, feeling "Immature" no longer reflected them, and released Introducing IMx, their fifth album, featuring singles "Stay the Night", "Keep It On the Low", and "In & Out of Love", which peaked at number 101 on the Billboard 200 and number 31 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. On August 21, 2001, IMx released their sixth album, IMx, after signing with TUG Entertainment and New Line Records (now WaterTower Music), featuring singles "First Time", "Beautiful (You Are)", "Clap Your Hands Pt. 1", and "Ain't No Need" (which appeared on the soundtrack for The Adventures of Pluto Nash), peaking at number 126 on the Billboard 200 and number 26 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. The group also released a Greatest Hits album on February 27, 2001, featuring popular singles from the past nine years, including remixes and guest appearances such as Monteco's "Is It Me?". The song "Keep It On the Low" was used as the theme song for House Party 4: Down to the Last Minute, in which the group also starred. Immature branched out into film and television, appearing in House Party 3 and House Party 4: Down to the Last Minute, and on shows such as A Different World, Sister, Sister, Family Matters, Soul Train, and All That, where they collaborated with Kel Mitchell on the hit song "Watch Me Do My Thing" from the All That soundtrack. In 2002, the group disbanded. Houston and Jones (under the name Young Rome) pursued solo careers, with Houston releasing his debut solo album MH in 2003, followed by Food for Thought in 2004, and later releasing Naked (2005), Veteran (2007), Mr. Houston (2009), Mattress Music (2010), and Famous (2013). Jones also released his debut solo album, Food for Thought, in 2004. Houston and Jones both starred in the dance film You Got Served (2004), with Houston also co-starring in Fat Albert (2004) and landing a lead role in the UPN comedy sitcom Cuts, and appearing as Roger on Sister, Sister (1994–1998). In 2007, Houston starred in the horror film Somebody Help Me. The track "Tamika" appeared on the Sister, Sister episode "A Friend in Deed", which aired on October 29, 1997, where the group performed as themselves at a school fundraiser. In early 2015, the band reunited to release a comeback EP titled Remember, changing their name back to Immature, featuring mature-sounding remakes of "Never Lie" and "Please Don't Go" along with new songs "Let Me Find Out", "Oh My", and "Best Sex". On November 6, 2013, Immature performed their first show since reuniting at Club Nokia in Los Angeles with Next and Dru Hill. In September 2019, Immature announced their #TBTour with special guests Ray J, B5, and J. Holiday.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is the national space agency of India, headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka, and functions as the principal research and development arm of the Department of Space (DoS), which is overseen by the Prime Minister of India. The Chairman of ISRO also serves as the chief executive of the DoS. ISRO is primarily responsible for space-based operations, space exploration, international space cooperation, and the development of related technologies. It operates a constellation of imaging, communication, and remote sensing satellites and manages the GAGAN and IRNSS satellite navigation systems. The agency has conducted three lunar missions and one Mars mission. Formerly known as the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR), established in 1962 by then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on the recommendation of scientist Vikram Sarabhai, it was renamed ISRO in 1969 and initially subsumed into the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). In 1972, the Government of India established a space commission and the DoS, bringing ISRO under its purview, institutionalising space research in India. ISRO launched India's first satellite, Aryabhata, in 1975 via the Soviet Interkosmos launch vehicle. In 1980, it successfully launched the RS-1 satellite on board the indigenously built SLV-3 launch vehicle, making India the seventh country to achieve orbital launches. ISRO has since developed various small-lift and medium-lift launch vehicles, enabling it to launch satellites and conduct deep space missions. It is one of six global government space agencies with full launch capabilities, including the ability to deploy cryogenic engines, launch extraterrestrial missions, and deploy artificial satellites, and is the only one of four governmental agencies to have demonstrated unmanned soft landing capabilities. ISRO's programmes have significantly contributed to socio-economic development in civilian and military domains, including disaster management, telemedicine, navigation, and reconnaissance, and its spin-off technologies have advanced engineering and allied fields. ISRO adopted an official logo in 2002, featuring an orange arrow shooting upwards with two blue satellite panels and the name ISRO in orange Devanagari on the left and blue English in Prakrit typeface on the right. Modern Indian space research began in the 1920s with S. K. Mitra’s ionospheric experiments in Kolkata, followed by contributions from C. V. Raman and Meghnad Saha. After 1945, key developments were driven by Vikram Sarabhai and Homi Bhabha, who founded the Physical Research Laboratory and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, respectively. Early research included cosmic radiation, high-altitude testing, deep underground experiments at the Kolar mines, and upper atmosphere studies. In 1950, the DAE was established with Bhabha as secretary, providing funding for space research. The Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences (ARIES) was founded in 1954, and the Rangpur Observatory was established in 1957. The launch of Sputnik 1 by the Soviet Union in 1957 opened opportunities for global space exploration. INCOSPAR operated initially within the DAE, with IOFS officers, including H. G. S. Murthy and Waman Dattatreya Patwardhan, playing key roles in developing sounding rockets and propellants. The Rohini series of sounding rockets began launches in 1967. Under Indira Gandhi’s government, INCOSPAR was replaced by ISRO, and in 1972, the DoS was established to specifically oversee space technology development. India joined the Soviet Interkosmos programme and launched its first satellite, Aryabhata, via a Soviet rocket. Efforts to develop an orbital launch vehicle began after mastering sounding rockets, with the goal of launching a 35 kg mass into low Earth orbit. After seven years, the SLV-3 successfully launched a 40 kg payload into a 400-kilometre orbit in 1980, making India the seventh country to reach orbit. The SLV-3 had two more launches before being discontinued in 1983. In 1985, ISRO established the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) and began work on the Vikas engine based on the French Viking, with testing facilities established two years later. The Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), based on SLV-3, was developed to launch satellites into geostationary orbit but had limited success and was discontinued. Concurrently, the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) and Indian Remote Sensing Programme (IRS) were developed, leading to a large constellation of multi-band communication, radar, optical, and meteorological satellites. The PSLV, introduced in the 1990s, had over 50 successful flights (except for its first flight in 1994 and two partial failures), enabling India to launch all its low Earth orbit satellites, small payloads to geostationary orbit, and hundreds of foreign satellites. Development of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) began, but India was blocked by the US from obtaining cryogenic engines from Russia’s Glavkosmos, leading to the import of KVD-1 engines with limited success and the launch of an indigenous cryogenic technology project in 1994, which took two decades to complete. A new agreement with Russia provided seven KVD-1 cryogenic stages and a ground mock-up stage without technology transfer, used for initial GSLV Mk.1 flights. ISRO faced US sanctions from 6 May 1992 to 6 May 1994, and after the US refused to share GPS technology during the Kargil War, ISRO developed its own navigation system, IRNSS (now NaVIC). In 2003, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee urged the development of lunar and crewed space missions. ISRO launched Chandrayaan-1 in 2008, the first probe to confirm water on the Moon. In 2013, the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), launched on PSLV, became the first Asian spacecraft to enter Martian orbit and the first country to succeed on its first attempt. The cryogenic upper stage for GSLV became operational, making India the sixth country with full launch capabilities. In 2014, the heavier-lift LVM3 rocket was introduced for heavier satellites and future human missions. In September 2019, Project NETRA was announced to address space debris and near-Earth objects. On 23 August 2023, ISRO achieved its first soft landing on an extraterrestrial body, becoming the first nation to land near the lunar south pole and the fourth to land on the Moon with Chandrayaan-3, the third lunar mission. The Vikram lander successfully touched down at 6.04 pm IST (12:34 pm GMT) near the southern lunar pole, a world-first. On 2 September 2023, ISRO launched its first solar probe, Aditya-L1, on PSLV. On 30 December 2024, ISRO launched the SpaDeX mission, pioneering spacecraft rendezvous, docking, and undocking using two small satellites. On 16 January 2025, the Mission Operations Complex verified a successful docking, making India the fourth country (after the US, Russia, and China) to achieve successful space docking. ISRO also successfully controlled two satellites as a single entity after docking. In May 2025, ISRO completed the final abort test for the Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission, scheduled for launch in early 2027. In August 2025, ISRO completed the first integrated air drop test for Gaganyaan, hailed by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh as a step toward self-reliance. On 2 November 2025, ISRO launched its heaviest communication satellite, CMS-03, aboard the LVM3-M5 rocket from Sriharikota, marking a milestone as all eight LVM3 missions achieved 100% success. On 24 December 2025, ISRO launched AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird Block-2 aboard the LVM3-M6 rocket, the heaviest foreign satellite ever launched from Indian soil, weighing 6,100 kg (13,400 lb). ISRO pursues space-based applications such as research, reconnaissance, and communications, designs and develops rockets and satellites, and conducts upper atmosphere and deep space exploration. It has also incubated technologies in India’s private space sector, boosting its growth. Vikram Sarabhai, as INCOSPAR chairman in 1969, stated that India’s purpose was not to compete with economically advanced nations in lunar or planetary exploration or manned spaceflight, but to apply advanced technologies to real societal problems. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam noted that critics questioned the relevance of space activities in a newly independent nation struggling with food security, but Nehru and Sarabhai had a clear vision: to apply advanced technologies to real-life problems to play a meaningful role in the global community. India’s economic progress has made its space programme more visible and active, aiming for greater self-reliance. In 2008, India launched 11 satellites, including nine from other countries, becoming the first nation to launch 10 satellites on a single rocket. ISRO operates two major satellite systems: INSAT for communication and IRS for natural resource management. The DoS, under the Space Commission, manages ISRO and other agencies and institutes. Antrix, set up as ISRO’s marketing arm, promotes its products, services, and technologies. A separate entity focuses on marketing spin-off technologies, technology transfer, and industry interface. ISRO has established Space Technology Incubation Centres (S-TIC) at the National Institute of Technology, Agartala (east), Jalandhar (north), and Tiruchirappalli (south) to incubate startups aligned with space missions, bringing together industry, academia, and ISRO for R&D. In 2021, ISRO and the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) established a joint framework where ISRO approves space research projects of mutual interest, and IIST’s Advanced Space Research Group (ASRG) gains full access to ISRO facilities, aiming to transform IIST into a leading space research and engineering institute. To reduce dependence on NORAD for space situational awareness, ISRO is setting up telescopes and radars in Leh, Mount Abu, Ponmudi, and a future site in Northeast India to cover all directions. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota already supports the Multi-Object Tracking Radar (MOTR). All telescopes and radars will fall under the Directorate of Space Situational Awareness and Management (DSSAM) in Bengaluru, which will collect data on inactive satellites and conduct research on active debris removal, space debris modelling, and mitigation. For early warning, ISRO launched a ₹400 crore (US$53 million) project called Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis (NETRA), which will track atmospheric entry, intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), anti-satellite weapons, and other space-based threats. All radars and telescopes will be connected through NETRA, supporting remote and scheduled operations. NETRA will follow the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IASDCC) and United Nations guidelines.

ISRO is establishing telescopes and radars in four locations—Leh, Mount Abu, and Ponmudi—to cover the North, West, and South directions of Indian territory, with a fourth location in Northeast India to cover the entire eastern region. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota already operates the Multi-Object Tracking Radar (MOTR). All telescopes and radars will be managed by the Directorate of Space Situational Awareness and Management (DSSAM) in Bengaluru, which will collect tracking data on inactive satellites and conduct research on active debris removal, space debris modelling, and mitigation. ISRO launched a ₹400 crore (4 billion; US$53 million) project called Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis (NETRA) for early warning, enabling tracking of atmospheric entry, intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), anti-satellite weapons, and other space-based attacks. NETRA will connect all radars and telescopes, support remote and scheduled operations, and follow guidelines from the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IASDCC) and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOSA), aiming to track objects up to 36,000 kilometres (22,000 mi) in geostationary transfer orbit (GTO). India signed a memorandum of understanding on the Space Situational Awareness Data Sharing Pact with the US in April 2022, enabling collaboration between the Department of Space (DoS) and the Combined Space Operation Center (CSpOC) to protect space-based assets from natural and man-made threats. On 11 July 2022, the ISRO System for Safe and Sustainable Space Operations Management (IS4OM) was inaugurated at the Space Situational Awareness Control Centre in Peenya by Jitendra Singh; it provides information on on-orbit collision, fragmentation, atmospheric re-entry risk, space-based strategic information, hazardous asteroids, and space weather forecasts, safeguarding operational space assets and monitoring spacecraft with close approaches over the Indian subcontinent or those conducting suspicious manoeuvres or seeking re-entry in South Asia. On 7 March 2023, IS4OM successfully executed a controlled re-entry of the decommissioned Megha-Tropiques satellite by firing four on-board 11 Newton thrusters for 20 minutes each, involving 20 manoeuvres since August 2022 and consuming 120 kg of fuel, with final telemetry confirming disintegration over the Pacific Ocean, as part of compliance with international space debris mitigation guidelines. At the 42nd annual meeting of the IADC in Bengaluru, S. Somanath stated that the long-term goal is for all Indian space actors—governmental and non-governmental—to achieve debris-free space missions by 2030. Since the launch of Aryabhata in 1975, India has deployed numerous satellite series and constellations via Indian and foreign launchers; ISRO currently operates one of the largest constellations of active communication and earth imaging satellites for military and civilian use. The Indian Remote Sensing Programme (IRSP) comprises India’s largest collection of remote sensing satellites for civilian applications, placed in polar Sun-synchronous orbit (except GISATs), providing data in various spatial, spectral, and temporal resolutions for national development programs. Initial versions used the 1 (A, B, C, D) nomenclature, later divided into sub-classes such as Oceansat, Cartosat, HySIS, EMISAT, and ResourceSat, with all names unified under the "EOS" prefix in 2020. These satellites support optical, radar, and electronic reconnaissance, city planning, oceanography, and environmental studies. The Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) is India’s telecommunication system, consisting of multipurpose geostationary satellites developed and launched by ISRO to meet telecommunications, broadcasting, meteorology, and search-and-rescue needs. Since the first INSAT launch in 1983, it has become the largest domestic communication system in the Asia-Pacific region, jointly managed by DOS, the Department of Telecommunications, India Meteorological Department, All India Radio, and Doordarshan. The series was renamed from INSAT to GSAT, then to CMS from 2020 onwards. These satellites are also used by the Indian Armed Forces. GSAT-9, known as the SAARC Satellite, provides communication services to India’s smaller neighbors. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has implemented an indigenous Satellite-Based Regional GPS Augmentation System (SBAS), known as GAGAN—GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation—as part of a plan for civil aviation, with a Technology Demonstration System (TDS) completed in 2007 by installing eight Indian Reference Stations at airports linked to a Master Control Centre near Bengaluru. IRNSS, known operationally as NavIC, is India’s independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate positioning services within India and up to 1,500 km (930 mi) from its borders, with a position accuracy better than 20 m (66 ft) in the primary area, offering Standard Positioning Service (SPS) and Restricted Service (RS). Kalpana-1 (MetSat-1) was ISRO’s first dedicated meteorological satellite. The Indo-French SARAL satellite, launched on 25 February 2013, is a cooperative altimetry mission that monitors ocean surface and sea levels, with AltiKa measuring surface topography with 8 mm (0.31 in) accuracy and 2 km spatial resolution, surpassing the average 2.5 cm (0.98 in) of standard altimeters. During the 1960s and 1970s, India developed its own launch vehicles due to geopolitical and economic factors, creating a sounding rocket and by the 1980s achieving the Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3) and the Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), with supporting infrastructure. The SLV-3 was India’s first space rocket, with a failed launch in 1979 followed by a successful one in 1980, making India the sixth country with orbital launch capability. The ASLV, developed in the 1980s to enable geostationary orbit launches, faced repeated failures and was abandoned in favor of a new project due to insufficient funding. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), India’s first medium-lift launch vehicle, enabled the launch of all remote-sensing satellites into Sun-synchronous orbit; it failed in its first launch in 1993 and had two other partial failures, but has since become ISRO’s primary launch vehicle with over 50 successful launches placing hundreds of Indian and foreign satellites into orbit. The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), conceived in the 1990s to transfer significant payloads to geostationary orbit, faced delays due to the development of the CE-7.5 engine, with the US blocking India from acquiring cryogenic technology from Russia, leading to India’s independent cryogenic engine development. The Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3), previously known as GSLV Mk III, is ISRO’s heaviest operational rocket, equipped with a more powerful cryogenic engine and boosters than the GSLV, offering higher payload capacity and enabling India to launch all its communication satellites. LVM3 is expected to carry India’s first crewed mission to space and will serve as a testbed for the SE-2000 engine for future heavy-lift rockets. The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is a small-lift launch vehicle developed by ISRO to deliver 500 kg (1,100 lb) to low Earth orbit (500 km) or 300 kg (660 lb) to Sun-synchronous orbit (500 km), supporting multiple orbital drop-offs for small satellites. Rohini is a series of sounding rockets developed by ISRO for meteorological and atmospheric studies, capable of carrying 2 to 200 kg (4.4 to 440.9 lb) between 100 and 500 km altitudes, with current models including RH-200, RH-300 Mk-II, RH-560 Mk-II, and RH-560 Mk-III, launched from Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) and SDSC Sriharikota. The Advanced Technology Vehicle (ATV) is a modified Rohini-560 sounding rocket developed to test a native dual-mode air-breathing scramjet engine; as of 2016, two test missions were flown. ISRO first proposed human spaceflight in 2006, leading to infrastructure and spacecraft development. A 600 kg (1,300 lb) Space Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE) launched in 2007 using the PSLV safely returned to Earth after 12 days. In 2009, ISRO proposed a ₹124 billion (equivalent to ₹310 billion or US$3.7 billion in 2023) budget for its human spaceflight program, with an unmanned flight expected after seven years and a crewed mission after seven years of funding; however, crewed missions were not a priority for years. A 2014 space capsule recovery and a 2018 pad abort test preceded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 2018 Independence Day announcement that India would send astronauts into space by 2022 using the Gaganyaan spacecraft. ISRO has developed key technologies such as the crew module, crew escape system, space food, and life support systems. The Gaganyaan project, costing less than ₹100 billion (US$1.3 billion), aims to send two or three Indians to space at an altitude of 300–400 km (190–250 mi) for at least seven days using a GSLV Mk-III launch vehicle. The newly established Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) will coordinate the Indian Human Spaceflight (IHSF) campaign, with an astronaut training center being set up in Bengaluru to train personnel in rescue and recovery, microgravity survival, and radiation environment studies. ISRO built centrifuges for launch acceleration preparation and will upgrade existing launch facilities at SDSC. HSFC and Glavkosmos signed an agreement on 1 July 2019 for astronaut selection, medical examination, and space training. An ISRO Technical Liaison Unit (ITLU) was to be established in Moscow to support key technologies and facilities for space life. Four Indian Air Force personnel completed training at Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in March 2021. Axiom Mission 4 (Ax-4), launched in June 2025 by SpaceX from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, included Shubhanshu Shukla as mission pilot, marking the first time an Indian astronaut traveled to the International Space Station (ISS). Shukla flew alongside Axiom commander Peggy Whitson and mission specialists Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski (European Space Agency) and Tibor Kapu (Hungary), with Prasanth Nair serving as backup and participating in training at NASA’s Johnson Space Center. Shukla spent approximately two weeks aboard the ISS conducting around 60 experiments, at least seven of which were developed by ISRO or Indian academic institutions, covering cognitive effects of screen exposure, microbial adaptation, muscle atrophy, and crop resilience in microgravity. According to ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan, Shukla’s activities will advance India’s Gaganyaan program. Media reports estimate the Government of India spent approximately ₹548 crore (US$65 million) on the mission seat, drawing scrutiny amid India’s efforts to develop indigenous human spaceflight capability; ISRO and Axiom Space defended the cost, citing value in astronaut training, operational readiness, and scientific return. ISRO is developing an orbital crewed spacecraft, Gaganyaan, for the Indian Human Spaceflight Programme (IHSP), designed to carry up to three people, with a planned upgraded version featuring rendezvous and docking. The first crewed mission will have a mass of approximately 3 tonnes (6,600 lb), placed in low Earth orbit at around 400 km (250 mi) altitude, supporting a crew of two for up to seven days. India plans to develop a modular space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, with a mass of approximately 20 tonnes (44,000 lb), placed at 400 km (250 mi) altitude, initially supporting up to three astronauts for 15 to 20-day missions. The station is intended to be launched five to seven years after Gaganyaan’s completion and will be expanded in phases, serving as a platform for international collaboration in interplanetary exploration, microgravity science, space biology, and space medicine. ISRO and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research have operated a balloon launch base in Hyderabad since 1967, located near the geomagnetic equator where cosmic ray fluxes are low, making it ideal for studying diffuse cosmic X-ray background. ISRO contributed to the discovery of three bacterial species in the upper stratosphere (20–40 km), highly resistant to UV radiation and not found elsewhere on Earth, leading to speculation about extraterrestrial origin. These extremophiles are named Bacillus isronensis (in recognition of ISRO’s role), Bacillus aryabhata (after the ancient Indian astronomer Aryabhata), and Janibacter hoylei (after astrophysicist Fred Hoyle). Launched in 2015, Astrosat is a space observatory.

A platform for international collaboration in research related to interplanetary exploration, microgravity science, space biology, and space medicine exists. ISRO and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research have operated a balloon launch base in Hyderabad since 1967, benefiting from its proximity to the geo-magnetic equator, where primary and secondary cosmic ray fluxes are low, making it ideal for studying the diffuse cosmic X-ray background. ISRO contributed to the discovery of three bacterial species in the upper stratosphere between 20–40 km (12–25 mi), highly resistant to ultraviolet radiation and not found elsewhere on Earth, leading to speculation about extraterrestrial origins. These extremophiles are named Bacillus isronensis, Bacillus aryabhata, and Janibacter hoylei in recognition of ISRO’s role, India’s ancient astronomer Aryabhata, and astrophysicist Fred Hoyle. Launched in 2015, Astrosat is India’s first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, observing active galactic nuclei, hot white dwarfs, pulsars, binary star systems, and supermassive black holes at galactic centers. The X-ray Polarimeter Satellite (XPoSat), launched on 1 January 2024 via a PSLV-DL rocket, carries the Polarimeter Instrument in X-rays (POLIX) to study the degree and angle of polarization of X-ray sources in the 5–30 keV range, with an expected operational lifespan of at least five years. Chandryaan missions are India’s lunar exploration series, with the first, Chandrayaan-1, launched on 22 October 2008 using a modified PSLV from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, entering lunar orbit on 8 November 2008 and operating for 312 days, carrying 11 instruments—five Indian and six from foreign agencies including NASA, ESA, the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Brown University, and others—to map the Moon’s chemical composition and topography, especially its polar regions, and earning awards from the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, the International Lunar Exploration Working Group, and the National Space Society. Chandrayaan-2, launched on 22 July 2019 on a GSLV Mk III, included an orbiter, Vikram lander, and Pragyan rover, aiming to explore the lunar south pole; however, the Vikram lander crashed during descent on 7 September 2019 due to a software glitch after deviating from its trajectory at 2.1 km altitude, with telemetry lost seconds before touchdown; the orbiter successfully extended its service life to seven years. Chandrayaan-3, India’s second attempt to soft-land on the Moon, launched in 2023 and included only a lander-rover set, and on 23 August 2023, ISRO became the first space agency to successfully land near the lunar south pole, making it the fourth to land on the Moon; Prime Minister Narendra Modi declared August 23 National Space Day in India. The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), informally Mangalyaan, was launched on 5 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, becoming the first country to achieve Mars orbit on its first attempt at a record low cost of $74 million, with a launch mass of 1,337 kg and 15 kg of scientific instruments; the team received the 2015 Space Pioneer Award. Researchers from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences and Indian Institute of Science identified Ladakh as the best site for India’s first Mars and Moon analogue research station to support mission planning and training, with studies led by Binita Phartiyal, Aloke Kumar, and astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla, focusing on geological and astrobiological research, human studies, crew training, technology readiness, and life support testing. A 21-day Mars and Moon analog mission led by Aaka Space Studio and ISRO will simulate extraterrestrial conditions, testing human health, biometrics, circadian lighting, and life support technologies, following prior simulations in the Rann of Kutch in 2023. On 2 September 2023, ISRO launched the 400 kg Aditya-L1 mission to study the solar corona, the first Indian solar coronagraph to observe in visible and near-infrared bands, with the primary goal of studying coronal mass ejections and their magnetic fields to understand space weather; it successfully entered its final orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024, approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. Long-term plans include crewed landings on the Moon and other planets. Chandrayaan-4, a planned lunar sample return mission, is in its conceptual and design phases, expected to launch around 2028, returning up to 3 kg of regolith from near Shiv Shakti point, the landing site of Chandrayaan-3. The Lunar Polar Exploration mission (LUPEX), a joint ISRO-JAXA robotic mission, is planned for no earlier than 2028 to explore the lunar south pole, with JAXA providing the H3 launch vehicle and rover and ISRO responsible for the lander. ISRO aims to send an Indian astronaut to the lunar surface by 2040. The next Mars mission, Mangalyaan 2, is proposed for launch in 2030 and will include a rover, helicopter, sky crane, and supersonic parachute. ISRO is considering a Venus Orbiter Mission, approved by the Union Cabinet on 18 September 2024 under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s direction, with a budget of ₹1,236 crore (US$150 million), ₹824 crore (US$97 million) for the spacecraft, to study Venus’s atmosphere, surface, and subsurface processes, especially given its past habitability, and to understand planetary evolution; a payload called VIRAL, co-developed with LATMOS and Roscosmos, is planned. Conceptual studies are ongoing for missions to asteroids and Jupiter, with a launch window every 33 months and a Venus flyby required; development of RTEG power is being pursued to enable deeper space missions. AstroSat-2 is the successor to the AstroSat mission. Exoworlds, a joint proposal by ISRO, IIST, and the University of Cambridge, is a space telescope for exoplanet atmospheric studies planned for 2025, to be placed at the Earth-Sun L2 point, focusing on spectroscopy in the NUV-VISIBLE-IR ranges. The Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) will produce high-resolution deep UV-optical images and low to medium-resolution spectroscopy, recommended in March 2019 with seed funding and proposed collaboration with the Canadian Space Agency. DAKSHA is a proposed all-sky, high-energy transient mission to study gravitational waves and gamma-ray bursts from 1 keV to 1 MeV using twin LEO satellites with three identical instruments each, with seed funding issued and instrument development underway by teams from TIFR, IIT Bombay, Raman Research Institute, IUCAA, and PRL; ISRO has confirmed technical feasibility but has not approved funding. ISRO is studying a mission to the stable L5 Lagrange point, conceptually similar to ESA’s Vigil mission. A complement to Aditya-L1 is being proposed for a Low-Earth Orbit placement. A family of 50 artificial intelligence-based satellites will be launched between 2024 and 2028 to collect geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) using thermal, optical, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) technologies, with AI-enabled satellites capable of communication and collaboration to monitor military movements and border areas for national security. ISRO is developing the Satellite-Protection Project to safeguard India’s space assets from threats, initiated after a near-collision in mid-2024. ISRO is developing more powerful and less polluting rocket engines, including the semi-cryogenic SE-2000 engine based on RD-120, which will be less polluting and more powerful than the Vikas engine, and when clustered with LVM3, will increase payload capacity; on 28 March 2025, ISRO announced progress in designing a semi-cryogenic engine with 2,000 kN thrust for the LVM3 booster stage. Reusable methane and LOX-based engines are under development, with methane being less polluting and requiring minimal refurbishment, with cold flow tests beginning in 2020. ISRO’s current launch vehicles lack the capacity to launch satellites beyond 4-ton class to geostationary orbit, a gap planned to be addressed by the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), a family of five modular medium to heavy-lift rockets, initially called Unified Modular Launch Vehicle, powered by LOX-methane engines, capable of lifting from 4.9 t to 16 t to geostationary transfer orbit—nearly four times the capacity of the existing LVM3. ISRO is studying heavy (HLV) and super heavy-lift launch vehicles (SHLV), with modular designs featuring interchangeable parts to reduce production time, and has mentioned an HLV with 10-tonne capacity and an SHLV capable of delivering 50–100 tonnes into orbit. A rocket family of five medium to heavy-lift class modular rockets, the NGLV, is being planned to replace existing PSLV and GSLV rockets. Two reusable launcher projects are ongoing: ADMIRE, a VTVL test vehicle, and RLV-TD, a program to develop an autonomous spacecraft launched vertically and landing like a plane. To realize a fully reusable two-stage-to-orbit (TSTO) launch vehicle, a series of technology demonstration missions are being conceived.

ISRO is developing a family of five medium to heavy-lift modular rockets, known as the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), initially referred to as the Unified Modular Launch Vehicle or Unified Launch Vehicle, which will share components and replace the existing PSLV and GSLV rockets entirely. These rockets will be powered by LOX-methane engines and have a payload capacity ranging from 4.9 tonnes (5.4 short tons; 4.8 long tons) to 16 tonnes (18 short tons; 16 long tons) to geostationary transfer orbit, nearly four times the capacity of the current LVM3. Two reusable launcher projects are underway: the ADMIRE test vehicle, a vertical takeoff and vertical landing (VTVL) system, and the RLV-TD programme, designed to develop an autonomous spacecraft that launches vertically and lands like an aircraft. To advance a fully reusable two-stage-to-orbit vehicle, a series of technology demonstration missions have been planned, with the RLV-TD serving as a flying testbed for technologies such as hypersonic flight, autonomous landing, powered cruise flight, and hypersonic flight using air-breathing propulsion. The first mission, the Hypersonic Flight Experiment (HEX), was completed five months after the RLV-TD's test flight in February 2016, which reached a height of 70 km and weighed around 1.5 tonnes (1.7 short tons; 1.5 long tons). HEX is intended to serve as a fly-back booster for the winged TSTO concept, followed by a landing experiment (LEX) and a return flight experiment (REX). India is transitioning from conventional chemical propulsion to Hall-effect and plasma thrusters to reduce spacecraft weight; GSAT-4 was the first Indian spacecraft to carry electric thrusters but failed to reach orbit, while GSAT-9, launched in 2017, used a xenon-based electric propulsion system for in-orbit functions, and GSAT-20 is expected to be India’s first fully electric satellite. On 28 March 2025, ISRO reported that its 300 mN xenon-based Stationary Plasma Thruster (SPT) successfully completed a 1,000-hour life test under 5.4 kW full power in a vacuum chamber. The electric propulsion system (EPS), incorporating SPT, is designed to replace chemical propulsion in future satellites for orbit raising and station-keeping, offering at least six times greater specific impulse, enabling satellite buses to carry more transponders, and will be validated in the next Technology Demonstration Satellite (TDS-01) mission. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), also called alpha source thermoelectric technology by ISRO, use nuclear decay heat to power spacecraft; in January 2021, the U. R. Rao Satellite Centre issued an Expression of Interest (EoI) for a 100-watt RTG, which would extend spacecraft life and reduce mass compared to solar panels, enabling long-duration deep space missions to outer planets. Two radioisotope heater units developed by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) were included in the propulsion module of Chandrayaan-3 and functioned flawlessly. ISRO plans to collaborate with the Department of Atomic Energy to use nuclear propulsion technology in future missions. On 27 January 2022, the Space Applications Center and Physical Research Laboratory jointly demonstrated quantum entanglement-based real-time quantum key distribution over a 300-meter atmospheric channel, including quantum-secure text and image transmission and quantum-assisted two-way video chatting. At the Indian Mobile Congress 2023, ISRO presented satellite-based quantum communication using quantum key distribution technology, aiming to counter quantum computers that could break current encryption. A significant milestone was achieved in September 2023 when ISRO demonstrated free-space quantum communication over 300 meters, including live video conferencing using quantum-key encrypted signals. The SSLV Launch Complex, under construction in Kulasekarapattinam, Tamil Nadu, will serve as ISRO’s second launch facility, primarily for launching the SSLV and private launch vehicles, with an estimated 20 to 25 launches annually, and is expected to be commissioned by December 2026. India’s satellite communication network, one of the largest globally, supports applications such as land and water resource management, disaster forecasting, weather forecasting, meteorological imaging, and computer communication, benefiting sectors like business, administrative services, and the National Informatics Centre (NIC). The Integrated Space Cell, under the Ministry of Defence’s Integrated Defence Staff, has been established to effectively utilize space-based assets for military purposes and assess threats to them, promoting cooperation among the three armed services and civilian agencies. India operates 14 satellites, including GSAT-7A for exclusive military use and the rest as dual-use satellites, placing it fourth in the number of active satellites in orbit, with GSAT-7A enhancing the Indian Air Force’s network-centric warfare capabilities by linking ground radar stations, airbases, and airborne early warning systems like the Beriev A-50 Phalcon and DRDO AEW&CS, and also supporting the Army’s Aviation Corps for helicopters and UAVs. GSAT-7, launched in 2013, was built for the Navy to monitor the Indian Ocean Region with a 2,000-nautical-mile footprint and real-time input to warships, submarines, and maritime aircraft, while GSAT-7A, launched in December 2018, supports the IAF’s network-centric operations. The RISAT series of radar-imaging satellites are used for military purposes, and EMISAT, launched on 1 April 2019, is a 436-kilogram electronic intelligence (ELINT) satellite that improves situational awareness by detecting hostile radars. India’s space programme has contributed to military spin-offs, such as the Agni missile, which was derived from the SLV-3 technology; A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, who led the SLV-3 project at ISRO, later headed the Agni missile programme, using the SLV-3’s solid fuel first stage and a liquid-fuel second stage derived from the Prithvi missile. The IRS and INSAT satellites were primarily for civilian-economic applications but provided military benefits; in 1996, the Ministry of Defence temporarily restricted IRS-1C use for border missile monitoring, and in 1997, the Air Force adopted space assets for surveillance and battle management. Institutions like the Indira Gandhi National Open University and Indian Institutes of Technology use satellites for education; between 1975 and 1976, India conducted the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE), using NASA’s ATS-6 technology to broadcast educational content to 2,400 villages, significantly improving rural education. ISRO provides telemedicine services, connecting rural patients to urban doctors via satellite for real-time diagnosis, treatment advice, and follow-up at super-specialty hospitals, with mobile telemedicine vans deployed in remote areas. ISRO helped implement the Biodiversity Information System, completed in October 2002, which uses satellite remote sensing and geospatial modeling to create vegetation cover maps at a 1:250,000 scale, linking gene-level plant data with spatial information in a web-enabled BIOSPEC database for ecological hotspots such as northeastern India, Western Ghats, Western Himalayas, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, through collaboration between the Department of Biotechnology and ISRO. The IRS-P5 (CARTOSAT-1) satellite was equipped with high-resolution panchromatic equipment for cartography, followed by IRS-P6 for agricultural applications, and the CARTOSAT-2 project, with a single panchromatic camera, succeeded CARTOSAT-1 by providing scene-specific on-spot images. ISRO has diversified its research into spin-offs, including bionic limbs, silica aerogel for cold-weather soldier protection, distress alert transmitters, Doppler weather radar, and sensors for engineering inspections. ISRO has signed formal cooperative agreements with countries including Afghanistan, Algeria, Argentina, Armenia, Australia, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Brunei, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, China, Denmark, Egypt, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Israel, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Maldives, Mauritius, Mexico, Mongolia, Morocco, Myanmar, the Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Peru, Portugal, Russia, São Tomé and Príncipe, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, South Korea, Sweden, Switzerland, Syria, Tajikistan, Thailand, Tunisia, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States, Uzbekistan, Venezuela, and Vietnam, and with international bodies such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), European Commission, EUMETSAT, European Space Agency (ESA), and SAARC. ISRO has two collaborative missions with France’s CNES: the retired Megha-Tropiques, which studied the tropical water cycle, and the active SARAL for altimetry, with a third mission, TRISHNA (a thermal infrared imaging satellite for high-resolution natural resource assessment), currently being planned. The Lunar Polar Exploration Mission (LUPEX) is a joint Indo-Japanese mission to study the Moon’s polar surface, with India responsible for providing soft landing technologies. NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) is a joint Indo-US radar satellite using dual frequencies (L and S bands), making it the world’s first radar imaging satellite to employ both frequencies. In India, the electromagnetic spectrum is auctioned to telecom companies; in 2010, 20 MHz of 3G spectrum was auctioned for ₹677 billion (US$8.0 billion). In January 2005, Antrix Corporation signed a deal with Devas Multimedia for 70 MHz of S-band transponder capacity on GSAT-6 and GSAT-6A for ₹14 billion (US$170 million) over 12 years, using spectrum allocated for satellite-based communication. If this spectrum were auctioned at the 2010 price, its value would have exceeded ₹2,000 billion (US$24 billion), a hypothetical scenario considered by the Comptroller and Auditor-General as a government loss. There were procedural lapses: the satellite capacity was allocated exclusively to Devas, violating rules requiring non-exclusivity; the Cabinet was misinformed about other service providers, and the Space Commission was not informed when approving the second satellite, whose cost was reduced to avoid Cabinet approval. ISRO committed ₹7.66 billion (US$91 million) to build, launch, and operate the two satellites. In late 2009, ISRO insiders exposed the deal, leading to investigations and its annulment; G. Madhavan Nair, then ISRO Chairperson, was barred from holding any post in the Department of Space, and several former scientists were found guilty of "acts of commission" or "acts of omission." Devas and Deutsche Telekom demanded US$2 billion and US$1 billion in damages, respectively. The Department of Revenue and Ministry of Corporate Affairs initiated an inquiry into Devas’ shareholding. In March 2015, the Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case against the then executive director of Antrix, two officials of a USA-based company, a Bengaluru-based private multimedia company, and other unknown officials under Section 120-B, Section 420 of IPC, and Section 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the PC Act, 1988. Devas initiated arbitration proceedings in June 2011, and in September 2015, the International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce ruled in favor of Devas, ordering Antrix to pay US$672 million (Rs 44.35 billion) in damages. Antrix opposed the tribunal award in the Delhi High Court.

Devas Multimedia, a private multimedia company based in Bengaluru, along with other unknown officials of the Antrix Corporation or the Department of Space, was involved in a dispute. Devas initiated arbitration proceedings against Antrix in June 2011. In September 2015, the International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce ruled in favor of Devas and ordered Antrix to pay US$672 million (Rs 44.35 billion) in damages. Antrix contested Devas' request for the tribunal award in the Delhi High Court. The document also lists the chairpersons of ISRO since 1963.

Ida Fiyo Mntwana (1903 – March 1960) was a South African anti-apartheid and women's rights activist. She worked as a dressmaker and became politically active in the 1950s. After Madie Hall Xuma resigned as national president of the African National Congress Women's League (ANCWL) in 1949, Mntwana succeeded her and was more radical, organizing women in demonstrations, strikes, and other acts of civil disobedience. She was elected to the African National Congress (ANC) executive committee. In 1954, Mntwana became the first president of the Federation of South African Women (FEDSAW) and helped organize the Congress of the People. On the second day of the congress, police invaded the event and created a conflict between the people and the police; it was Mntwana who calmed the crowd by singing a freedom song from the platform, ensuring the congress continued. On 26 August 1952, she led a march in Germiston consisting of 29 women: 11 Indian, one Coloured (Susan Naude), and 17 African women. She and the group were detained and sentenced to fourteen days in Boksburg prison. She also led the FEDSAW march to the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 27 October 1955, with around 2,000 women participating to protest pass laws for women. Mntwana was one of the defendants in the 1956 Treason Trial and died in March 1960 during this trial. She is represented in one of 100 bronze statues as part of the National Heritage Monument's project, The Long March to Freedom, with her statue created by Sarah Lovejoy. In August 2000, Mntwana was cited as "torchbearer" during Thabo Mbeki's speech at the unveiling of South Africa's Women's Monument. She was awarded a posthumous Order for Meritorious Service in silver in 2003.

Ida F. Pulis Lathrop (1859–1937) was an American painter known primarily for her portraits, still lifes, and landscapes. She lived and worked in Albany, New York. Born on October 27, 1859, in Troy, New York, she was the daughter of Catherine (née Sheffér) and Abraham William Pulis. In 1885, she married Cyprus Clark Lathrop, with whom she had two daughters who also became artists: Gertrude K. Lathrop and Dorothy P. Lathrop. Lathrop was a self-taught artist. She passed away on September 7, 1937, in her home in Albany and is buried in the Albany Rural Cemetery. Her artworks are held in the collections of the Albany Institute of History and Art and the Smithsonian American Art Museum, among other institutions.

Iftikhar Hussain Ansari (26 April 1942 – 30 September 2014), widely known as Moulvi Sahib, was a Kashmiri Shia cleric, politician, businessman, and a proponent of the Grand Ashura Procession in Kashmir. He served as a Wakil (Representative) of Ayatollah Sistani and also represented Ruhollah Khomeini. One of the leading Shia clerics in Kashmir, he maintained close relationships with scholars such as Sayyid Jawad Shahristani, Mohammad Alavi Gorgani, and Lotfollah Safi Golpaygani. He studied at Sultanul Madaris Lucknow and Hawza Najaf. He succeeded his father, Muhammad Jawad Ansari, as president of the All Jammu and Kashmir Shia Association in 1962, a position he held for life. He was a four-time Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) from the Pattan Assembly segment for the Jammu and Kashmir People's Democratic Party (PDP), and had previously been a member of the National Conference and the Indian National Congress. In 1978, he co-founded the Jammu and Kashmir People's Conference with Abdul Ghani Lone, and his son and brother are now part of the party. Ansari was also a Member of the Legislative Council (MLC) for two non-consecutive terms. He gained a strong following among the Shia community due to his clerical background and served as a Minister of the State Government on multiple occasions, notably in the portfolio of Housing and Urban Development, which he revolutionized. He also focused on environmental issues and initiated a large-scale project to clean Dal Lake. His political career began in the 1960s. In 1973, he was elected as an MLC on the Indian National Congress ticket; in 1977, he switched to the Janata Party. He returned to the Indian National Congress in the 1980s and was appointed leader of the Legislature party in the Jammu and Kashmir State Assembly from 1983 to 1987. In 1996, he won the state legislative assembly elections on a Congress ticket and became a minister in the National Conference government led by Farooq Abdullah. In 2002, he joined the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference and won from Pattan; in 2006, he switched to the PDP but lost in the by-election. In 2008, he won a significant victory on a PDP ticket, reinforcing his political standing. As of 2014, he was nominated as the party's candidate for the upcoming assembly elections, reflecting his continued influence. After his death, his son, Molvi Imran Reza Ansari, who had previously been the candidate from Zadibal, was nominated for Pattan and won with a landslide victory in the 2014 J&K elections, achieving the highest margin of victory in the state's electoral history. Ansari was thrice the target of unsuccessful assassination attempts: in June 2000, he narrowly escaped a landmine explosion while addressing a religious gathering at Gund Khwaja Qasim, which killed twelve of his followers; on 1 September 2000, he was injured by an IED explosion that killed two policemen and a driver. The police suspected Hizbul Momineen, a terrorist group led by Mohammad Abbas Ansari and Ghulam Rasool Noori. Ansari died at his residence in Dar ul Jawad, Qamarwari, Srinagar, on 30 September 2014, after a prolonged battle with liver illness, having been undergoing specialized treatment in the United States. Political, religious, and social leaders expressed condolences. Hundreds of thousands of people attended his funeral, shops were closed, and all activities were suspended in Shia-dominated areas. People from all faiths and backgrounds participated in the event, and international condolences were also offered. His funeral procession was taken from his residence in Qamarwari to Imambargah Zadibal, where Namaz e Jenazah was offered. He was buried in his ancestral graveyard, Baba Mazar, Alamgari Bazar, Zadibal, Srinagar.

The Indie RPG Awards were annual, creator-driven honors recognizing independent role-playing games and supplements. Founded in 2002 by Andy Kitkowski, the awards concluded their final round in 2017. For the purpose of the awards, a specific definition of an Indie role-playing game was established. Throughout their history, certain categories were consistently used for nominations. In their early years, additional categories were also introduced and awarded.

Indonesian painting has a long tradition and history in Indonesian art, with some of the world’s oldest paintings found in Indonesia due to the preservation of early works in cave environments. The earliest Indonesian paintings are prehistoric rock art, such as petroglyphs in the Maros caves in Sulawesi, which are approximately 40,000 years old and among the oldest known paintings globally. In November 2018, scientists discovered a figurative painting of an unknown animal in Lubang Jeriji Saléh on Borneo (Kalimantan), dated to over 40,000 years, possibly as old as 52,000 years. In December 2019, figurative cave paintings depicting pig hunting in the Maros-Pangkep karst in Sulawesi were estimated to be at least 43,900 years old, recognized as “the oldest pictorial record of storytelling and the earliest figurative artwork in the world.” In 2021, a pig-related cave painting in Indonesia was dated to over 45,500 years. These prehistoric paintings were created on cave walls and rocks, using techniques such as the aerograph—where hands were placed on walls and sprayed with chewing leaves or colored mineral stones—and clay with natural dyes from minerals and animal fats. The themes were often magical, and examples can be seen in Leang Pattakere Cave in South Sulawesi, depicting hunting scenes, and on the south coast of West Papua, showing ancestors. Hand silhouettes are common across many sites, including Seram Island, Berau Gulf, Arguni, and Kai Island, alongside motifs like human figures, boats, sun, moon, birds, fish, turtles, lizards, legs, and hog deer. After the prehistoric period, Indonesian culture developed expertise in stone construction, metal casting, agriculture, tools, sculpture, and batik, influenced by Hinduism from around the 5th century AD, leading to the emergence of writing. Art themes during this era included religion, mythology, legends, and historical stories, such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata in Balinese paintings. The Majapahit era used a wayang style with stylized, horizontal compositions, reflecting similarities between wayang kulit and Balinese paintings. Paintings used natural pigments from bark, leaves, soil, and soot, were made on elongated fabric without frames, resembling scroll paintings, and served as educational tools in temples and lontar manuscripts. In Bali, Hindu culture faced Islamic influence, leading to unique hybrid paintings recognized internationally. This development is divided into three phases: Kamasan, Pita Maha, and Young Artists painting. Islamic art in Indonesia centers in the Kraton, where artists combine knowledge of science, philosophy, and other arts. Depictions of living beings are avoided; instead, stylized animal and human motifs combined with Arabic script are used in mosque decorations and crafts. Paintings often depict stories from wayang or candra sangkala and prophet history, with some originating as glass paintings from Cirebon. Modern Indonesian painting began with Dutch colonialism, influenced by European romanticism, and was shaped by figures like Raden Saleh Syarif Bustaman (1807–1880), who studied under A.A.J. Payen and later in Europe with Cornellius Krusemen and Andreas Schefhout, becoming the first Indonesian to study fine arts abroad and a respected court painter. Raden Saleh is considered a pioneer, though Indonesian painting did not follow the European Renaissance stages. After the revolution, painters shifted from romantic themes to "populist" themes, rejecting natural beauty as a symbol of capitalist enemies in the communist ideology. Limited access to paints and canvases led to simpler, abstract forms. The Cultural Manifesto Movement in the 1950s encouraged artists to free their work from political propaganda, leading to expressionism. Modernism later introduced alternative art forms like installation and performance art, which emerged widely in art colleges between 1993 and 1996, followed by "collaboration" as a trend in 1996–1997. Conventional painting became more of an investment than community appreciation. Modern Indonesian art is deeply connected to European traditions, influenced by post-impressionism (early 18th century), which emphasized individualism and experimentation in materials, techniques, and expression. This contact began through European painters visiting Indonesia, inspiring new artistic directions. In the mid-19th century, Indonesian artists primarily used traditional regional styles with decorative potential, such as in Bali, Java, Toraja, and Kalimantan. S. Sudjojono (1913–1986) led a group of painters who never studied in Europe, including Agus Djaya Suminta, L. Sutioso, Rameli, Abdul Salam, Otto Jaya, S. Sudiarjo, Emiria Sunassa, Saptarita Latif, Herbert Hutagalung, S. Tutur, Hendro Jasmara, and Sutioso. In 1938, they formed the Association of Indonesian Drawing Experts (PERSAGI) in Jakarta to promote an authentic Indonesian style through sketches of local life. After returning from Europe, Abdullah S.R. (1878–1941) developed the Indonesia Jelita (Mooi Indie) style in Bandung, emphasizing the beauty and peaceful nature of Indonesia, often portraying romantic and serene natural scenes for foreign tourists. Before this, Dutch colonial authorities employed foreign painters such as W. G. Hofker (Netherlands), R. Locatelli (Italy), Le Mayeur (Netherlands), Roland Strasser (Switzerland), E. Dezentje (Netherlands), and Rudolf Bonnet (Netherlands). During the Japanese occupation in 1942, PERSAGI was disbanded, but grassroots artists emerged. In 1945, Japan established Japan Keimin Bunka Shidoso (Cultural Center) with former PERSAGI members like Agus Djaya Suminta and S. Sudjojono as teachers, supporting artistic activities. Despite economic hardship, artistic life flourished, with exhibitions held by painters such as Basuki Abdullah, Affandi, Kartono Yudhokusumo, Nyoman Ngedon, Hendra Gunawan, Henk Nantung, and Otto Jaya to promote national identity. Post-independence, painting became a medium of national struggle, evident in struggle posters and battle sketches, notably by Djajengasmoro and his Front Painter group. In 1946, after the government moved to Yogyakarta, painters relocated there, forming the Community Arts Association in 1946, later joining the Young Indonesian Artists (SIM) group in 1947, founded in Madiun by Sudjojono. In 1949, R. J. Katamsi and other SIM members, along with People's Painters, POETRA, and Budayan Taman Siswa, established the Indonesian Fine Arts Academy (ASRI), now known as ISI, to train aspiring artists. Key figures included S. Soedjojono, Hendra Gunawan, Djajengasmoro, Kusnadi, and Sindusiswono. In Bandung, the Center for the Higher Education for Teachers of Pictures, led by Syafe'i Soemardja and assisted by Mochtar Apin, Ahmad Sadali, Sudjoko, and Edi Karta Subarna, became the Fine Arts Department at ITB in 1959. In 1964, the Department of Fine Arts Education at IKIP Bandung (now Indonesian Education University) was founded by Barli, Karmas, Popo Iskandar, Radiosuto, and Wiyoso Yudoseputo, with alumni including Oho Garha, Nana Banna, Hidayat, Dadang MA, and Hardiman. Fine arts departments later spread to other IKIPs across Indonesia. Around 1974, young artists emerged in various regions, including Jim Supangkat, Syahrinur Prinka, Satyagraha, F.X. Harsono, Dede Eri Supria, and Munni Ardi. Their first exhibition was at Taman Ismail Marzuki in Jakarta. These young artists challenged traditional definitions of art, rejected academic elitism, questioned established boundaries, avoided framing, used diverse media and concepts, and created works inspired by sacred elements.

The International Prize in Statistics is awarded every two years to an individual or team for major achievements using statistics to advance science, technology, and human welfare. Alongside the COPSS Presidents' Award, it is considered the two highest honours in the field of statistics. Modeled after the Nobel Prizes, Abel Prize, Fields Medal, and Turing Award, the prize includes a monetary award of $80,000 and is presented during the World Statistics Congress. It recognizes a single work or body of work that embodies a powerful and original idea with significant impact across other disciplines or practical benefits to the world. The recipient must be alive at the time of the award. The prize is administered by the International Prize in Statistics Foundation, which includes representatives from major learned societies. In addition to honoring statisticians, the Foundation seeks to educate the public about statistical innovations and increase the field's visibility. The recipient is selected by an international committee of experts in statistics. As of 2016, the committee members were Xiao-Li Meng (Harvard University), Sally Morton (Virginia Tech), Stephen Senn (Luxembourg Institute of Health), Bernard Silverman (University of Oxford), Stephen Stigler (University of Chicago), Susan Wilson (Australian National University), and Bin Yu (University of California, Berkeley). As of May 2022, the selection committee members are Yoav Benjamini, Francisco Cribari-Neto, Vijay Nair, Sonia Petrone, Nancy Reid, Sylvia Richardson, and Jane-Ling Wang.

The International Space Station (ISS) is a large space station assembled and maintained in low Earth orbit by five space agencies—NASA (United States), Roscosmos (Russia), ESA (Europe), JAXA (Japan), and CSA (Canada)—through a collaboration involving their contractors. As the largest space station ever built, it primarily serves as a platform for conducting scientific experiments in microgravity and studying the space environment. The station is divided into two main segments: the Russian Orbital Segment (ROS), developed by Roscosmos, and the US Orbital Segment (USOS), built by NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. A key structural component is the Integrated Truss Structure, which connects the station’s solar panels and radiators to its pressurized modules, which support functions such as scientific research, crew habitation, storage, spacecraft control, and airlock operations. The ISS has eight docking and berthing ports for visiting spacecraft and orbits Earth at an average altitude of 400 kilometres (250 miles), completing one orbit every 93 minutes and 15.5 orbits per day. The station originated from the combination of the United States' Space Station Freedom and the Soviet Union's Mir-2, with the first module launched in 1998 and long-term occupancy beginning on 2 November 2000 with the arrival of the Expedition 1 crew. Since then, the ISS has remained continuously inhabited for 25 years and 78 days, the longest continuous human presence in space. As of August 2025, 290 individuals from 26 countries have visited the station. Future plans include adding at least one module, Axiom Space's Payload Power Thermal Module, and the station is expected to remain operational until the end of 2030, after which it will be de-orbited using the US Deorbit Vehicle. The concept of international space collaboration began in the early 1970s, culminating in the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, the first docking of spacecraft from two different spacefaring nations. Concepts such as International Skylab, Skylab-Salyut, and Shuttle-Salyut were proposed but abandoned due to falling budgets and rising Cold War tensions. In the early 1980s, NASA planned Space Station Freedom, with ESA approving the Columbus laboratory by 1987 and Japan announcing the Japanese Experiment Module (JEM or Kibō) in 1985. In 1985, ESA science ministers approved the Columbus program, which aimed to evolve into a full-fledged European orbital outpost. Rising costs in the early 1990s led Congress to demand increased international participation to avoid cancellation of Freedom. Meanwhile, the USSR began constructing modules for Mir-2 in the mid-1980s, but the collapse of the Soviet Union led to its significant downsizing and potential cancellation. American and Russian officials then proposed combining the two projects. In September 1993, U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin announced plans for a new space station, which became the International Space Station, and agreed on the Shuttle–Mir program for American Shuttle docking with Mir. Originally intended as a laboratory, observatory, and factory with roles in transportation, maintenance, and as a staging base for future missions to the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, not all initial uses have been realized. The 2010 United States National Space Policy expanded the ISS’s roles to include commercial, diplomatic, and educational purposes. The ISS supports scientific research with power, data, cooling, and crew available for experiments, including small uncrewed spacecraft for zero gravity and space exposure studies, with long-term studies possible due to human researcher access. Experiments are conducted in fields such as astrobiology, astronomy, physical sciences, materials science, space weather, meteorology, and human research, including space medicine and life sciences. Scientists on Earth can access data and suggest modifications, and resupply missions allow routine hardware launches. Crews conduct expeditions of several months, providing about 160 man-hours per week with a six-member crew, though much of this time is spent on station maintenance. A notable experiment is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS), which detects dark matter and other cosmic phenomena; NASA considers it as important as the Hubble Space Telescope. On 3 April 2013, scientists reported hints of dark matter detected by AMS, noting an unexplained excess of high-energy positrons in cosmic rays. The space environment is hostile, featuring intense radiation, high vacuum, extreme temperatures, and microgravity; extremophiles and tardigrades can survive in dry conditions.
