Garland also succeeded in having San Francisco rename an alley on the same block from Adelaide Place to Isadora Duncan Lane.[84][85] In medicine, the Isadora Duncan Syndrome refers to injury or death.

Murals of the nine muses by Maurice Denis are located in the auditorium. In 1987, she was inducted into the National Museum of Dance and Hall of Fame. Duncan has drawn literary and artistic attention from the 1920s to the present, appearing in novels, film, ballet, theatre, music, and poetry. In literature, Duncan is portrayed in various works. Among the films and television shows featuring Duncan are several productions. Ballets based on Duncan include specific works. On the theatre stage, Duncan is portrayed in various performances. Duncan is featured in music across different compositions. Archival collections, organizations, and other related materials document her legacy.

Isham Warren Garrott (c. 1816 – June 17, 1863) was a colonel in the Confederate States Army during the American Civil War and was killed by a Union sharpshooter on June 17, 1863, shortly before his promotion to brigadier general was confirmed by the Confederate Senate or delivered and became effective. Born in either Anson County or Wake County, North Carolina, around 1816, Garrott graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and studied law. In 1840, he moved to Marion, Alabama, where he practiced law. He was a member of the Whig Party and a Mason, and served as an incorporator of the Marion and Alabama River Transportation Company and President of the Board of Trustees of Howard College. Garrott was elected to the Alabama House of Representatives in 1845 and 1847 and served as an elector for John C. Breckinridge's failed 1860 Presidential Election campaign. Alabama Governor Andrew B. Moore sent Garrott to North Carolina as a commissioner to enlist his home state's aid in joining the secession movement. When the Civil War began, Garrott formed the 20th Alabama Infantry Regiment, serving briefly as its lieutenant colonel from September 16, 1861, to October 7, 1861, and thereafter as its colonel. The brigade was stationed in Mobile, Alabama during 1861 and 1862, and was later sent to Mississippi as part of General Edward D. Tracy's brigade. Garrott participated in the Battle of Port Gibson and the Battle of Champion's Hill. His commission to the rank of brigadier general, dated May 28, 1863, was received at headquarters after his death, and because of his death, the posthumous appointment was not confirmed by the Confederate Senate. According to Warner's footnote, Garrott was buried under the window of a friend's (Finney) house in Vicksburg, and his remains were never moved, as noted in a letter from his wife. A Confederate undertaker's list of CS burials in Vicksburg was lost—though partially recovered years later—and reported a "Colonel Garnet" of the 20th Alabama with an unknown gravesite. It appears Garrott was reburied in Vicksburg's Cedar Hill/Confederate Cemetery, but due to a misspelling of his surname and an incorrect rank, his general commission was received after his death, leading to the reporting that his remains were not moved from the initial burial site. Consequently, the National Park Service listing for Garrott now has his correct rank and surname but no grave number. A stone cenotaph marker for him stands in Soldiers Rest Confederate Cemetery, ironically located in the Cedar Hill (Old Vicksburg City) Cemetery. Fort Garrott near Vicksburg was named in his honor. The fort did not fall to the Union Army in battle because the planned final assault on Confederate positions scheduled for July 6, 1863, was avoided due to Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton's surrender of his army to Major General Ulysses S. Grant on July 4, 1863. The Sons of Confederate Veterans Camp 764 in Marion, Alabama, is named in his honor.

doc_name: Islamia College of Science and Commerce, Srinagar
text: The Islamia College of Science and Commerce, Srinagar (commonly known as Islamia College or ICSC) is a University Grants Commission Autonomous College and has been accredited with an A grade by the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC). Located on a 12.17-acre (0.0493 km²) campus in Hawal, Srinagar, the college is situated in the state of Jammu and Kashmir and is affiliated with the University of Kashmir. It holds the distinction of being the first college in Jammu and Kashmir to implement the CBCS (Choice Based Credit System) starting from 2015. Established in 1961 during the Prime Ministership of Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad, the institute was founded as an Autonomous Educational Institute by the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. The NAAC accredited the college at the A level on 12 September 2017, with an institutional score of 3.27 CGPA, making it the highest-rated college in Jammu and Kashmir. It was also recognized as a College for Potential Excellence by the University Grants Commission (India) in April 2010. The college operates a Mountaineering & Trekking Club affiliated with the Jammu & Kashmir Mountaineering and Trekking Association, where students actively participate in club activities. The adventure club is led by Dr. Altaf Ur Rehman, with past leadership roles held by Aga Syed Ashtar, Jasim Ali, and Syed Kumail Madni. In 2018, the college announced the introduction of three post-graduation programs.

Ivan Karlović (c. 1485 – 9 August 1531), also known as Johannes Torquatus in Latin, was the Count of Krbava and the last male descendant of the Kurjaković family from the noble Gusić tribe. Born in Udbina as the son of Karlo Kurjaković and Dorothea Frankopan, he inherited vast estates including the županijas of Krbava, Odorje, Hotuča, Lapac, part of Lika, and several fortified cities after his father's death in 1493. He held the position of Ban of Croatia twice: from 1521 to 1524 and again from 1527 to 1531, and participated in the 1527 Election in Cetin as one of the leading Croatian magnates. During the Hundred Years' Croatian–Ottoman War, he actively resisted Ottoman expansion, engaging in military actions such as defeating an Ottoman army near Gradac in 1500 and fighting against them in Bosnia. He supported Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, during the Hungarian succession crisis in 1506 and held townships like Mutnik and Belaj (today Bilaj) between 1505 and 1509. In 1508, he temporarily fought against Maximilian I’s army in the Venetian hinterland and defended Mutnik from Croatian noblemen, possibly with Ottoman assistance. From 1509 to 1524, he entered into multiple Condottieri contracts with the Republic of Venice to defend its Dalmatian estates, though he refused to participate in a 1510 campaign to free Dalmatia from Venetian control due to financial constraints. In 1513, as Vice-Ban and Captain of Croatia and Dalmatia (1512–1513), he fought in the Battle of Dubica alongside Petar Berislavić and other nobles. In 1514, Ottoman raids targeted his estates in Krbava and Lika, and in 1519, his envoy Stjepan Posedarski delivered an anti-Ottoman speech to Pope Leo X, pleading for help in defense of faith, freedom, and survival. After Petar Berislavić’s death in 1520, Karlović found his severed head and body at Plješivica and had them transported to Bihać and then Veszprem. In 1521, he attempted to negotiate with the Ottomans unsuccessfully and was named Ban of Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia, but failed to prevent the fall of Knin, Skradin, and Ostrovica Fortress. Despite receiving military and financial aid from Archduke Ferdinand I, he resigned as Ban in 1524 due to financial strain and lack of noble support. In December 1526, he participated in the Croatian Election in Cetin, where Croatian nobility elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg as king to counter Ottoman threats, a move that occurred amid a civil war involving John Zápolya. In 1527, he was reappointed Ban and remained in office until his death in 1531, during which he lost key forts such as Obrovac, Udbina, Komić, and Mrsinj-grad, and received substitute estates in Turopolje—Medvedgrad, Lukavec, and Rakovec—from Ferdinand I. In 1528, he led a Croatian army reinforced by Carniolan forces to defeat thousands of Ottoman troops near Belaj, and in 1529, he helped during the Siege of Vienna. He died on 9 August 1531 in Medvedgrad and was buried in the Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Remete, Zagreb, under the great altar. According to the inheritance contract with Nikola III Zrinski, who married his sister Jelena Kurjaković, his estates passed to the Zrinski family due to having no descendants married to the niece of cardinal Tamás Bakócz. He owned 22 forts and cities across three županijas and two župas, including Udbina, Krbava, Kurjak-grad, Turan, Počitelj, Podlapčec, Mrsinj-grad, Lovinac, Gradac, Novigrad, Zvonigrad, Zelengrad, Kličevac, Bag, Obrovac, and Stari Obrovac. His sister Jelena was the mother of Nikola IV Zrinski, future Ban of Croatia and hero of Szigetvár. His nephews, Nikola and Ivan Zrinski, inscribed on his tombstone in 1541: "Sepultus genere Spectabilis militiaque praeditus magnificus dominus Torquatus, comes Corbaviae regnorumque Croatiae et Sclavoniae banus mole sub hac tegitur," which, along with the coat of arms, was later lost. A 16th-century Glagolithic document described the coat of arms as a goose on a shield with the letters I. C. (Joannes Caroli), and Samuel Timon (1736) and Károly Wagner (1802) described it, though their accounts were influenced by 17th-century armorials like Opus Insignium Armorumque (1687–1688) by Johann Weikhard von Valvasor. In folk tradition, ruined towns like Komić, Kozja Draga, and Mazin are still called Karlovića dvori ("Karlović's palaces"). Karlović is the central figure in Fran Binički’s novel Ivan Hrvaćanin (1926) and is remembered in folk poetry, including bugarštica such as "Kad se Ivan Karlović vjerio za kćer kralja Budimskoga," among Molise Croats in Southern Italy, Burgenland Croats in Austria, and Bosniaks, likely descendants of his former subjects. He is referred to in various forms such as Ivan or Jivan Karlović, Ive Karlovićev, Ivan Dovice, did Karlović, Karlo Vića, and Ivan Hrvaćanin. In Molise, fragmented versions of songs in Shtokavian-Chakavian with Ikavian accent and longer Chakavian versions with Ekavian-Ikavian accent are preserved. He is generally portrayed as a noble and tireless warrior against the Ottomans, though in Molise he is negatively depicted as feared by girls picking flowers in meadows, reflecting a folk theme where hero identity is less important and linked to fear and danger during Ottoman conquests, indicating the community’s migration and ethnic identity. Due to the loss of most personal holdings and the biblical reference to Job on his tombstone, he is sometimes called "Job of Croatia."

Ivan Rebroff (born Hans Rolf Rippert; 31 July 1931 – 27 February 2008) was a German vocalist allegedly of Russian ancestry, known for his distinctive and extensive vocal range of four octaves, spanning from a low F to a high F, one and a quarter octaves above C. An imposing figure on stage, he was typically bearded and dressed in Cossack clothing, with his height exceeding 2 metres. Born on 31 July 1931 in Berlin, he claimed to have been born prematurely at seven months on a train platform, a statement he made in his own account. His parents were Paul Rippert, an engineer born in 1897 in Liebenwerda, and Luise Fenske, born in Bromberg (now Bydgoszcz, Poland). While his Russian descent is often disputed, it has never been entirely refuted; in a 1989 interview with Izvestia, he stated "according to documents I am Ivan Pavlovich Rebroff" (Russian: Иван Павлович Ребров). He studied singing at the Hochschule für Musik und Theater Hamburg. Despite imperfect knowledge and pronunciation of Russian, he gained fame for performing Russian folk songs, as well as opera, light classics, and folk songs from various other countries. Known for his stage enthusiasm, he performed over 6,000 concerts, including a two-year, seven-day-a-week engagement at the Théâtre Marigny in Paris, where he portrayed Tevye in Fiddler on the Roof. In his seventies, he still performed 13 concerts in 21 days during an Australian tour. Rebroff described himself as the "connection between East and West." He was named an honorary citizen of the Greek Sporades island of Skopelos, his domicile. Rebroff was privately homosexual. In addition to singing, he was at least a reasonable violinist and keyboardist, as evidenced by photographs of him playing a church organ, though he may have also played the piano. He sang and could converse to varying degrees in Russian, French, Italian, English, and Greek, in addition to his native German. He died at the age of 76 in Frankfurt on 27 February 2008, following a long illness. Four days after his death, his brother Horst Rippert [de], who is nine years his senior and, according to his own unsubstantiated claims, shot down Antoine de Saint-Exupéry during World War II, claimed part of Rebroff's vast fortune.

Joseph Melville Broughton Jr. (November 17, 1888 – March 6, 1949) was an American politician who served as the 60th governor of North Carolina from 1941 to 1945 and later briefly as a United States senator from January 3, 1949, until his death in office approximately two months later. Born in Raleigh, North Carolina, he graduated from Wake Forest College in 1910, where he played football, attended Harvard Law School, and worked as a school principal and journalist before entering the legal profession. He served in the North Carolina Senate from 1927 to 1929 and later served one term as governor. Identified with progressive politics, including support for Roosevelt Administration social justice legislation, he implemented several reforms, most notably extending the public school term from six to nine months. The North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources describes him as a typical white moderate of his time, advocating for African American improvements such as equalizing teacher salaries and improving housing. In August 1941, he deployed the North Carolina National Guard to protect Cy Winstead, a Black man accused of raping a white woman, after he was nearly lynched in Roxboro. Following the incident, Broughton had police investigate the mob and charged ten white men; on April 24, 1942, a jury found five—Coy Harris, A.P. Spriggs, P.I. Holt, Johnny Holt, and Willie Aiken—guilty of unlawful assembly for an unlawful purpose, a misdemeanor punishable by up to two years in prison, while acquitting them of inciting to riot. Harris and Spriggs were each sentenced to 18 months in county jail, and the other three to 12 months. The jury recommended mercy for the Colt brothers, and Aiken did not deny his guilt. The verdict shocked the public, which had been sympathetic to the mob; in June 1942, 2,000 people submitted a petition demanding parole or pardon. Harris, Spriggs, P.L. Holt, and Aiken were paroled on July 23, 1942; Johnny Holt was denied parole due to his involvement in a California robbery and was paroled between then and 1943; all six were discharged from parole in September 1943. Winstead later pleaded guilty to assault with intent to commit rape and was sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison; in February 1943, the Person County NAACP petitioned for his parole, expressing doubt about his guilt, but he refused to apply due to strict conditions. Broughton resisted threats to segregation; in 1942, he urged African Americans not to make demands during World War II, stating, "Negroes are ill-advised if they take the position they are for victory in this war if something is to be done for them. Negroes should put their full energy into the war effort, for failure means slavery of the worst sort for white and Negro alike. The man or woman who uses this emergency as a means of stirring up strife between the races is not a friend to either race and is not a good American." In 1943, he wrote, "We believe in a policy of purity and high standard as to both races and we recognize the principle that race distinction does not imply race discrimination," and rejected NAACP criticism, claiming racism had no impact on North Carolina's judicial system. He was one of twelve nominated at the 1944 Democratic National Convention to serve as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate. In 1948, Broughton was elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating William B. Umstead in the Democratic primary; he won both a special election to complete the Senate term and a full-term election in November and took office on December 31, 1948, though his service was brief. Appearing healthy, he suddenly collapsed from a heart attack and died in Washington, D.C., on March 6, 1949. Governor W. Kerr Scott appointed Frank Porter Graham to fill his vacant Senate seat until the next election. Broughton was the son of Joseph Melville Broughton and Sallie Harris; he married Alice Willson in 1916 and had four children. He was the nephew of Needham B. Broughton and a first cousin of Carrie Lougee Broughton and medical doctor and Baptist minister Len G. Broughton. He and his wife lived in the Jolly-Broughton House in Raleigh's Hayes Barton Historic District before and after residing in the North Carolina Executive Mansion. He was interred at Montlawn Memorial Park in Raleigh. In 1959, the State Hospital at Morganton for psychiatric patients was renamed Broughton Hospital in his memory, and Broughton Hall at North Carolina State University was named in his honor. He was a member of Civitan International.

Jacen Solo is a fictional character in the Star Wars Legends continuity, the son of Han Solo and Leia Organa Solo, nephew of Luke Skywalker, and brother of Jaina Solo and Anakin Solo, as well as cousin of Ben Skywalker. He is a central figure in several novels, especially the New Jedi Order series, and becomes the antagonist of the Legacy of the Force series under the name Darth Caedus. Created for Timothy Zahn's Thrawn trilogy, set five years after Return of the Jedi, Jacen is introduced in the 1991 novel Heir to the Empire as one of a pair of twins Leia is pregnant with, born five minutes after his sister Jaina on Coruscant in the 1993 novel The Last Command. The twins, along with their younger brother Anakin, are sent to safe havens under the protection of Leia's handmaiden, Winter. In Jedi Search, they return to Coruscant at age three and have adventures, including becoming lost in the underworld of Imperial City with C-3PO before being rescued. In The Crystal Star, all three children are abducted by Hethrir, who attempts to brainwash them into becoming Dark Jedi, but they defeat him. In the Young Jedi Knights series, Jacen travels to Yavin 4 for Jedi training, discovers a strong connection to the Living Force, communicates with jungle creatures, keeps a menagerie of animals in his room at the Great Massassi Temple, and befriends the Wookiee Lowbacca and the warrior princess Tenel Ka. In Heirs of the Force and Shadow Academy, they discover a crashed TIE fighter from the Battle of Yavin, fix it with Jaina, and are captured by its pilot Qorl, who lives in the jungle for two decades; they escape, but Qorl also escapes and later discovers the Shadow Academy, a Dark Jedi training ground led by Brakiss and containing the remains of the Dathomiri Nightsisters. The twins and their friends are kidnapped by the Second Imperium, resist the dark side, and are rescued by Luke Skywalker and Tenel Ka. After returning to Coruscant, they reunite with Zekk, fight him several times, and eventually build their first lightsabers, with Jacen using a corusca gem for his focusing crystal. In Lightsabers, Tenel Ka's lightsaber shorts out during a sparring match with Jacen when his blade passes through thin air, severing her arm, causing Jacen to suffer guilt. In Darkest Knight, they visit Kashyyyk with Lowbacca to witness his sister's rites; in Jedi Under Siege, they defeat the Shadow Academy and the Second Imperium on Yavin 4. Throughout the series, Jacen and Jaina continue training, meet new friends like Raynar Thul, and cannot convince Zekk to stay at the Academy. They discover the Diversity Alliance, an alien anti-human group led by Twi'lek Nolaa Tarkona, sister of Oola, who was murdered by Jabba the Hutt in Return of the Jedi. In Jedi Bounty, they are briefly held captive on Ryloth to rescue Lowbacca, who joined the Diversity Alliance; in The Emperor's Plague, they uncover a plot involving General Evir Derricote's deadly diseases hidden in an Imperial storehouse, defeat Tarkona, who dies from one of the plagues, and Bornan Thul dies from the plague before his son's eyes. In Return to Ord Mantell, they visit the planet to watch a race, encounter Czethros, a bounty hunter who once hunted Han, and are ambushed by Black Sun agents, helped by Anja Gallandro, a lightsaber-wielding non-Jedi who blames Han for her father's death, though Solo reveals her father died in a trap. In Trouble on Cloud City, Czethros is revealed as a minor Black Sun leader trying to gain power, and Jacen, Tenel Ka, and Lowbacca are ambushed, with Jacen nearly killed. In Crisis at Crystal Reef, Jaina attempts to capture Czethros while Jacen helps Anja overcome her spice addiction and fight Black Sun; Anja recovers and accepts her father's death, and Jacen realizes she lacks Jedi potential, ending his infatuation when she joins Lando. In the New Jedi Order series, Luke takes Jacen as his apprentice, though they disagree on philosophical issues; Jacen believes the Force is a guide to destiny and tells Anakin that the Force is part of something greater. During the Yuuzhan Vong attack in Dark Tide: Onslaught, Jacen believes many Jedi are too aggressive and temporarily abandons his powers, but returns to battle due to his love for his mother, eventually making peace with his father. In Star by Star, Jacen joins a mission to Myrkr to infiltrate a Yuuzhan Vong cloning facility where the invaders create Voxyn; the mission fails with Anakin's death, and Jacen, forced into leadership, uses the Force Meld to unite the team. After destroying the voxyn queen, Jacen is captured by the Yuuzhan Vong under Vergere and Nom Anor, disappearing from the Force. In Traitor, he awakens in the Embrace of Pain, where he learns to use pain to sustain himself under Vergere's tutelage, who was once a Jedi of the Old Republic and met his grandfather, Anakin Skywalker. He works on Yuuzhan Vong ships, heals slaves, and uses a slave seed beneath his flesh to communicate with their technology, escaping by commanding amphistaffs to surround him. Jacen and Vergere flee to Coruscant, where the planet is transformed into a Yuuzhan Vong paradise. Vergere removes the slave seed, but Jacen still senses the Yuuzhan Vong; he is surrounded by warriors, channels Force lightning, runs away, and is later given full Force use by Vergere. He surrenders and becomes the "khattazz al'Yun," or Avatar of God, with Nom Anor intending to use him to sacrifice Jaina, fulfilling a prophecy. Jacen's true allegiance remains his own; when ordered to sacrifice Jedi Ganner Rhysode, he refuses and instead helps Ganner hold off the Yuuzhan Vong, confronting the World Brain and suggesting it work against the invaders. Ganner dies, but Jacen escapes with Vergere. He returns to the New Republic as a hardened man, joins Admiral Kre'fey's fleet, and participates in a successful deception at Ebaq 9, where Vergere dies. Her spectral form appears to him afterward. As the Galactic Alliance forms, Jacen accompanies Luke into the Unknown Regions to seek a solution to the Yuuzhan Vong threat, playing a key role in finding Zonama Sekot and convincing the planet to join the fight. He kills Supreme Overlord Onimi, using the Force as a conduit, after nearly being killed by Shimrra, and begins to believe he is beyond good and evil, marking the start of his fall. After the war ends, Jacen tells Luke he plans to travel the galaxy to learn more about the Force. On a five-year journey, he enters a realm of the Force known as beyond shadows, trained by a sect called the Mind Walkers, and gazes into the Pool of Knowledge, which holds the Throne of Balance, where all future events are shown. He sees a dark man ruling the galaxy and becomes determined to prevent this future. Following this, Jacen begins his descent into the dark side. In Dark Nest, he feels a Force urge, follows his sister to the Unknown Regions to help the Killik against a Chiss invasion, returns to Galactic Alliance space, and travels to the Hapes Cluster to ask Tenel Ka to assist with the conflict, sending a fleet of Hapan Battle Dragons to protect the Killiks. In The Unseen Queen, Tenel Ka gives birth to his daughter, Allana, who is attacked by the Gorog; Jacen repels the attack, uses the Force to send Tenel Ka's grandmother into a coma, and sees a vision of a never-ending war with the Killiks at its center. Determined to prevent it, he provokes the Chiss into destroying the Killiks, though he later reveals he does not know who started the war in the vision. In The Swarm War, Luke follows Jacen's advice, including when Jacen tells him he is not ready to face Lomi Plo, the Dark Queen of the Gorog. Jacen, with R2-D2, helps Luke confront his fears about Mara's involvement in his mother's death and accompanies him to face Plo. During the fight, Luke falters when Mara is injured, Plo holds him, and Jacen is critically wounded while saving Mara's life; Mara injures Plo and tends to Jacen's wounds. While recovering, Jacen urges Luke to embrace his darker emotions, but Luke refuses and defeats Plo and Raynar Thul without using the dark side. In the novel, Jacen watches holovideos of his grandparents, Anakin Skywalker and Padmé Amidala, seeing Anakin fall to the dark side and Padmé die in childbirth due to Anakin's actions; Jacen sympathizes with Anakin's desire to protect his wife and reminds Luke that Anakin was a fallible human. In Betrayal, Jacen begins training his cousin Ben in the Force. After a mission to Adumar ends in a life-threatening attack, they return to a dinner party at their parents' home, where Han expresses concern over Corellia's independence. Luke orders Jacen and Ben to disable the Centerpoint Station, which Thrackan Sal-Solo, Han's cousin, is using; Ben disables it while Jacen distracts Thrackan, ensuring a partial victory. While traveling to a subterranean base, Ben and Nelani are forced out of a mining car; their guide, Brisha Syo, creates a dark side phantom of Luke that nearly kills Jacen. Brisha stops the projections and takes Jacen to an office where Darth Vectivus, the supposed Sith Lord, lives. After fighting Force projections with Ben, Nelani catches up with them. Brisha is revealed to be Lumiya, the Dark Lady of the Sith, who reveals that Vergere is a Sith apprentice and that Jacen has already received Sith training. Lumiya claims Jacen will become the next Sith Lord. Unsure of his next move, Jacen creates visions of the future; in each vision where Lumiya is arrested, the galaxy falls into endless war and Jacen ends up fighting Luke. Horrified, Jacen spares Lumiya. Nelani attempts to arrest her, but Jacen intervenes, realizing she might fulfill the dark vision, and fights and kills her, asking for forgiveness before striking her down. He agrees to consider Lumiya's claims and leaves the asteroid with an unconscious Ben, erasing Ben's memories of Lumiya and Nelani, telling him both were killed by dark side phantoms. They return to Coruscant, but after Jacen departs, Lumiya says she has won. In Bloodlines, fully pledged to Lumiya, Jacen becomes head of the Galactic Alliance Guard, begins rounding up Corellians for internment, and during an interrogation of a suspected assassin (Ailyn Vel, Boba Fett's daughter), accidentally kills her using the Force. In Tempest, Jacen takes command of Rogue Squadron during the blockade of Corellia, shoots down a civilian freighter that had fired on him, relieves his sister from duty for refusing to participate, and uses the Anakin Solo to fire upon the Millennium Falcon, while both his sister and he are involved.

Jacen Solo, after agreeing to consider Lumiya's words and leaving the asteroid with an unconscious Ben, erases Ben's memories of Lumiya and tells him both she and Nelani were killed by dark side phantoms. They return to Coruscant, where after Jacen departs, Lumiya claims she has won. In Bloodlines, fully pledged to Lumiya, Jacen becomes head of the GFFA's secret police, the Galactic Alliance Guard, and, with Ben at his side, begins rounding up Corellians for internment and deportation. During an interrogation of a suspected assassin—Ailyn Vel, Boba Fett's daughter—Jacen attempts to use the Force to extract information and accidentally kills her. In Tempest, Jacen takes command of Rogue Squadron during the blockade of Corellia, shoots down a civilian freighter that had fired on him, relieves his sister from duty for refusing to participate, and uses the Anakin Solo to fire upon the Millennium Falcon while both his sister and parents are on board. He believes his parents were involved in a failed assassination of Tenel Ka, when in fact they were set up by Dur Gejjen, Prime Minister of Corellia. In Sacrifice, Lumiya says she is pleased with his progress and instructs him to undergo the Trial of Sacrifice—to kill what he loves most—believing this would allow him to use Sith powers without becoming evil and "immortalize his love" through sacrifice. Jacen decides the only way is to kill Tenel Ka and their daughter Allana. After Ben overhears Jacen communicating with Lumiya, Mara Jade tracks him down in the Hapes Consortium, where they fight in a long and heated battle, and Jacen kills Mara. The sacrifice required to become a Sith Lord is not Jacen's love, but Ben's. Ben suspects Jacen immediately upon meeting him at his mother's body. Eventually, Jacen chooses the Sith name Darth Caedus. By Fury, Darth Caedus becomes the principal antagonist, declared enemy of nearly every major character, including his parents, sister, Luke, and Ben. He kidnaps Allana to prevent Tenel Ka and the Hapans from leaving government, but Han, Leia, Luke, Jaina, Ben, and allies save her. After saving Allana, Leia tells Caedus to become a Jedi again, but he refuses. Han and Leia later discover Allana is Caedus and Tenel Ka's child. In Revelation, Caedus takes Tahiri Veila as his new apprentice to replace Ben and turns to ending the war, enticing the Imperial Remnant to attack Fondor. Though Admiral Niathal offers Fondor a chance to surrender, Caedus insists on making an example of it by crippling its shipyards and government. After sharing military secrets that cause hundreds of deaths and compromise the battle plan, Niathal arranges a cease-fire without consulting Caedus. Enraged by the treason, Caedus orders the fleet to ignore Niathal's orders and bombard major cities. Niathal orders ships loyal to her to attack the Anakin Solo. Two-thirds of the fleet sides with Caedus, while the rest ally with Niathal. When the Imperial Remnant refuses to assist Caedus, his apprentice assassinates Imperial Head of State Gilad Pellaeon and transfers control to the Moffs, who then support Jacen. A mysterious fleet led by Admiral Daala, loyal to Pellaeon, appears with one hundred Mandalorian mercenaries and, due to Daala's experimental weapons, forces the Galactic Alliance Fleet into retreat. Caedus then takes control of Coruscant and claims sole control of the Galactic Alliance. In Invincible, Jaina takes it upon herself to defeat her brother. Caedus's meditations are disrupted by Luke Skywalker, who attempts to hide Jaina's attack. Jaina, with several Mandalorian commandos, confronts Caedus, who quickly dispatches the Mandalorians while Jaina acts as a sniper. When she runs out of ammunition, she seizes a Mandalorian saber and severs Caedus's arm. Jaina withdraws due to her own injuries. After escaping an attack by Luke on the Anakin Solo's bridge, Caedus sees a vision of his daughter Allana on a white throne in a time of peace, which convinces him he has won—bringing peace to the galaxy and preventing future war and suffering. At the climax, Caedus and Jaina face off in a final lightsaber duel aboard the Anakin Solo. During the duel, Caedus returns to the light and tries to persuade Jaina of his intentions to protect Tenel Ka and Allana, but she refuses to listen and attacks after he deactivates and holsters his lightsaber. She later slams the door shut when he tries to leave. After a grueling battle in which both are seriously injured, Jacen is defeated when Jaina severs his Achilles tendon and stabs him in the heart. As he dies, Jacen reaches out to both his former lover and his child through the Force, warning them to flee from a bio-warfare attack designed by the Imperial Remnant. In this act of selflessness, Jaina sees the remnants of the good man her brother had once been. Following Caedus's death and the war's end, the Galactic Alliance defeats the Confederation and peace is restored to the galaxy, as Jacen had foreseen in a Force vision. Though Jacen makes few true appearances in Fate of the Jedi, which follows the Legacy of the Force series, his legacy is felt throughout, as Luke Skywalker is arrested for negligence of duty and sentenced to a ten-year exile, during which he and Ben investigate how and why Jacen turned to the dark side. Jacen's spirit makes its first appearance in Abyss, where it warns Luke and Ben about Abeloth, the main antagonist. In the final novel, Apocalypse, Jacen's spirit (along with Mara's) aids Luke as he partners with Darth Krayt in the final battle against Abeloth. After Abeloth is destroyed, Jacen reveals that Krayt was the dark figure he saw in his vision of the future and the source of his downfall; he saw Allana standing next to Krayt. In response, Krayt insists that Caedus's actions merely delayed the Sith, who will eventually succeed in their planned takeover of the galaxy. In aiding the Jedi against Abeloth, Jacen posthumously redeems himself, though he still refers to his fate as damnation. While Luke does not forgive his nephew for his role in Mara's death, he gains understanding of what led Jacen to that point. The second volume of the Legacy comic series, set about 140 years after Return of the Jedi, features Jacen's descendant Ania Solo as the protagonist. In this era, the descendants of Jacen, Jaina, and Ben are main characters, set during and after Darth Krayt takes over the galaxy. Though they do not appear as spirits, older characters like Luke and Mara do. IGN listed Jacen as #17 on their list of the top 100 Star Wars heroes, noting he had a more "profound effect" than any other Solo child on the Star Wars setting. Jesse Schedeen, writing for IGN, also listed Darth Caedus as #5 in a reader-inspired list of top Star Wars villains, calling his "defining moment of villainy" his murder of Mara Jade. UGO.com listed Jacen as their top Star Wars expanded universe character, calling him "one of the most fearsome - and most tragic - villains in the Star Wars universe." With the release of Star Wars: The Force Awakens in production in April 2014, most licensed Star Wars novels and comics produced since 1977 were declared non-canon. The epilogue of "Family Reunion – and Farewell," the series finale of Star Wars Rebels, introduces a character named Jacen Syndulla by series creator Dave Filoni in honor of Jacen Solo.

John Gilbert Layton PC MSC (July 18, 1950 – August 22, 2011) was a Canadian politician and academic who served as leader of the New Democratic Party (NDP) from 2003 to 2011 and as leader of the Official Opposition in 2011. He previously served on Toronto City Council, occasionally holding the title of acting mayor or deputy mayor. Layton was the member of Parliament (MP) for Toronto—Danforth from 2004 until his death. Born on July 18, 1950 in Montreal, Quebec, to parents Doris Elizabeth (née Steeves) and Progressive Conservative MP Robert Layton, he was the maternal great-grandnephew of William Steeves, a Father of Confederation, and his grandfather, Gilbert Layton, had served as a minister without portfolio in Quebec's Union Nationale under Premier Maurice Duplessis. Raised in Hudson, a largely Anglophone suburb of Montreal, Layton was student council president at Hudson High School and later credited longtime friend Billy Bryans for his student council victory. In 1969, he was appointed Quebec Youth Parliament prime minister until 1970. He graduated from McGill University in 1970 with a Bachelor of Arts (BA) in political science and economics, having switched from science to arts due to the influence of professor Charles Taylor, and studied at York University under C. B. Macpherson. He earned a Master of Arts (MA) in political science in 1972 and a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in political science in 1983 under David Bell. He taught political science at Ryerson Polytechnical Institute (now Toronto Metropolitan University) from 1974 and as an adjunct professor at the University of Toronto from 1978 to 1994. Layton joined the NDP in 1970, citing Tommy Douglas's opposition to the War Measures Act during the 1970 October Crisis as influential. He was a pacifist and participated in anti-Vietnam War demonstrations. In a foreword to Canadian Idealism and the Philosophy of Freedom, he described the idealist tradition as advocating for a society where equality includes positive liberty—enabling people to work together toward shared goals. In 1982, Layton was elected to Toronto City Council in a surprise upset against incumbent Gordon Chong. He became a leading left-wing figure, opposing the SkyDome project and advocating for AIDS patients' rights. In 1984, he was fined for distributing leaflets at the Toronto Eaton Centre during a strike, but the charge was dismissed on free speech grounds. He was also a vocal opponent of Toronto's bid to host the 1996 Summer Olympics. In 1985, he moved to the Metropolitan Toronto Council, and in 1988, he swapped roles with ally Dale Martin. He won a comfortable victory over Lois MacMillan-Walker in the 1988 municipal election, marking the first time a reformist coalition of New Democrats and independents controlled city council. On July 9, 1988, he married Olivia Chow, a Hong Kong-born Toronto District School Board trustee. Chow later joined the Toronto City Council and was elected to federal politics five times, winning her seat in 2006, re-elected in 2008 and 2011, and becoming the 66th mayor of Toronto in 2023 after resigning from federal politics in 2014 to run for mayor, placing third in the 2014 race. In 1990, a Toronto Star article by Tom Kerr accused Layton and Chow of unfairly living in a federal-subsidized housing cooperative despite their high income. They had lived in the Hazelburn co-op since 1985, paying $800 per month for a three-bedroom apartment and voluntarily contributing an additional $325 per month to offset the subsidy. By 1990, their combined annual income was $120,000, and the co-op's board argued that mixed-income tenants were essential to its success. The city solicitor cleared them of wrongdoing, and in June 1990, they left the co-op and bought a house in Toronto's Chinatown with Chow's mother. Layton ran for mayor in 1991 as the first official NDP candidate, facing incumbent Art Eggleton, who chose not to run again. He was opposed by Susan Fish, June Rowlands, and Betty Disero, with Rowlands gaining right-wing support. Layton lost the November 12, 1991 election by a considerable margin, though Olivia Chow won a city council seat. In November 1991, Layton co-founded the White Ribbon Campaign to end male violence against women. He returned to academia and founded Green Catalyst Group Inc. In 1993, he ran for the House of Commons in Rosedale for the NDP but finished fourth. In 1994, he returned to Metropolitan Toronto Council, succeeding Roger Hollander in the Don River ward, and after the 1998 "megacity" merger, he was re-elected to Toronto City Council in a two-member ward. He remained on council until pursuing federal leadership. He became chair of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and gained national attention. In 1997, he ran in Toronto—Danforth but lost to incumbent Dennis Mills. In June 1999, as chair of Toronto's environmental task force, the Toronto Atmospheric Fund, he helped launch the WindShare wind power cooperative. Layton was elected leader of the NDP on January 25, 2003, winning on the first ballot with 53.5% of the vote, defeating Bill Blaikie, Lorne Nystrom, Joe Comartin, and Pierre Ducasse. His campaign focused on revitalizing the party and was endorsed by former NDP leader Ed Broadbent. He did not seek a by-election and instead contested Toronto—Danforth in the 2004 federal election, appointing Bill Blaikie as parliamentary leader. He criticized Prime Minister Paul Martin's policies as conservative and argued the Liberal Party had shifted right. He emphasized strengthening the NDP's presence in Quebec, appointing Pierre Ducasse as his Quebec lieutenant and spokesperson. The party's support increased significantly, polling higher than both the Canadian Alliance and the Progressive Conservatives by the end of 2003. In the 2004 federal election, controversy arose over Layton's claim that Martin was responsible for homeless deaths due to lack of affordable housing funding. While homelessness and deaths increased during the Liberal government's tenure, affordable housing is a provincial matter, and the link to Martin's decisions was indirect. The charge was defended by some, including the Ottawa Citizen, but widely criticized as inaccurate and negative campaigning. Layton also proposed removing the Clarity Act, considered vital to Quebec's place in Canada by some and undemocratic by others, and promised to recognize any Quebec independence declaration after a referendum. This position was not part of the official NDP policy and drew criticism from prominent members like Bill Blaikie and Alexa McDonough. His stance on the Clarity Act was reversed in the 2006 election to support. The NDP ran French-language ads in Quebec, with Layton appearing in them due to his fluency in colloquial Québécois French. He advocated for electoral reform, calling for a referendum to replace first-past-the-post with proportional representation. He threatened to use the NDP's influence in a minority government, though the proposal was dismissed by Liberal and Bloc Québécois leaders, who benefit from the first-past-the-post system. The NDP achieved a 15% popular vote, its highest in 16 years, but won only 19 seats, two fewer than in 1997, and far below his prediction of 40. Some potential voters may have supported the Liberals to prevent a Conservative win. Olivia Chow and several other Toronto NDP candidates lost tight races, and Layton won his own seat against Dennis Mills by a narrower margin than early polls indicated. With the Liberal government reduced to a minority, the sponsorship scandal damaged its popularity, prompting the Conservatives and Bloc Québécois to push for a snap election. Prime Minister Martin approached the NDP for support. Layton demanded the cancellation of proposed corporate tax cuts and increased social spending. The resulting compromise, which passed on June 23, was opposed by other opposition parties, who used it to force non-confidence votes, which were defeated on May 19. Layton's civil conduct in a raucous parliament earned him increased credibility as a leader, becoming the major second-choice leader in many polls, including second in Quebec after Gilles Duceppe. In mid-November 2005, when Liberal support declined after the Gomery Commission's first report, Layton offered conditions for continued support, particularly on health care privatization, demanding strict controls on public spending on private delivery. He expressed disappointment at the lack of progress on the issue, with Martin offering only a "good meeting" comment.

On May 19, two motions of non-confidence were defeated, and Layton's amendments were passed on their final reading vote on June 23. As a result of this political coup and his apparent civil behaviour in a spitefully raucous parliament, many political analysts noted that Layton gained increased credibility as an effective leader of an important party, becoming the major second choice leader in many political polls—such as polling second in Quebec after Gilles Duceppe, despite the low polls for his party as a whole in the province. In mid-November 2005, when Liberal support dropped after the Gomery Commission delivered its first report, Layton offered the prime minister several conditions in return for the NDP's continued support, most notably on the issue of privatization of health care in Canada, where Layton wanted strict provisions for controlling public spending on private health care delivery, saying that without "significant action" on the issue, "Mr. Martin can't count on our support." Martin for his part offered no comment on a meeting held to discuss the issue, only saying that it was a "good meeting," while Layton publicly expressed his disappointment at the outcome. Layton announced he would introduce a motion requesting a February election. However, the Martin government refused to allow the election date to be decided by the opposition. A motion of non-confidence followed, moved by Stephen Harper and seconded by Layton, triggering the 2006 federal election. Layton was working with the Liberal government, but determined he would have a better chance of electoral success by voting against the government and having an election. On March 26, 2011, in response to Harper's allegations that a coalition is not a legitimate or principled way to form government, Duceppe stated that Harper had once tried to form a coalition government with the Bloc Québécois and NDP. In 2004 Stephen Harper privately met with Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe and Layton in a Montreal hotel. The meeting that took place between the three party leaders happened two months before the federal election. On September 9, 2004, the three signed a letter addressed to then-Governor General Adrienne Clarkson, stating, "We respectfully point out that the opposition parties, who together constitute a majority in the House, have been in close consultation. We believe that, should a request for dissolution arise, this should give you cause, as constitutional practice has determined, to consult the opposition leaders and consider all of your options before exercising your constitutional authority." On the same day the letter was written, the three party leaders held a joint press conference at which they expressed their intent to co-operate on changing parliamentary rules, and to request that the governor general consult with them before deciding to call an election. At the news conference, Harper said "It is the Parliament that's supposed to run the country, not just the largest party and the single leader of that party. That's a criticism I've had and that we've had and that most Canadians have had for a long, long time now so this is an opportunity to start to change that." However, at the time, Harper and the two other opposition leaders denied trying to form a coalition government. Harper said, "This is not a coalition, but this is a co-operative effort." One month later, on October 4, Mike Duffy, now a Conservative senator (appointed by Harper), said "It is possible that you could change prime minister without having an election," and that some Conservatives wanted Harper as prime minister. The next day Layton walked out on talks with Harper and Duceppe, accusing them of trying to replace Paul Martin with Harper as prime minister. Both Bloc and Conservative officials denied Layton's accusations. With a vote scheduled for January 23, 2006, many New Democrats expected Layton to deliver substantially more seats than he did in 2004. They hoped the NDP would hold the balance of power in a new minority Parliament, so that they could carry additional leverage in negotiating with the governing party. Mike Klander, the executive vice-president of the federal Liberals' Ontario wing, resigned after making posts on his blog comparing Chow to a Chow Chow dog and calling Layton an "asshole." Through the course of the campaign, Layton attempted to cast himself as the sole remaining champion of universal health care. Some opinion polls showed that Canadians found Layton the most appealing and charismatic of the leaders. Layton repeatedly insisted that "Canadians have a third choice," and urged Liberals to "lend us your vote." Some commentators and pundits mocked Layton for over-using these catchphrases instead of explaining the NDP platform. The NDP strategy had changed in that they were focusing their attacks on the Liberals rather than in 2004, where they criticized both the Liberals and Conservatives in equal measure, prompting some criticism from Paul Martin. Andrew Coyne suggested that the NDP not only wanted to disassociate themselves from the scandal-ridden Liberals, but also because the Liberals were likely to receive credit for legislation achieved under the Liberal-NDP partnership. The NDP had also lost close races in the 2004 election due to the Liberals' strategic voting. Early in the campaign, NDP MP Judy Wasylycia-Leis had asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) to launch a criminal investigation into the leaking of the income trust announcement. The criminal probe seriously damaged the Liberal campaign and preventing them from making their key policy announcements, as well as bringing alleged Liberal corruption back into the spotlight. Layton's campaign direction also caused a break between him and Canadian Auto Workers union head Buzz Hargrove over the issue of strategic voting. Hargrove preferred a Liberal minority government supported by the NDP and he had earlier criticized Layton for participating in the motion of non-confidence that brought down the Liberal government. Hargrove allied with the Liberals and publicly stated that he "did not like the campaign that Jack Layton was running," criticizing Layton for "spending too much time attacking the Liberals." During the final week of the campaign, knowing that last-minute strategic voting had cost the NDP seats in several close ridings during the 2004 election, Hargrove and Martin urged all progressive voters to unite behind the Liberal banner to stop a Conservative government. Layton intensified his attacks on the Liberal scandals, pledging to use his minority clout to keep the Conservatives in check. Shortly after the election, the Ontario provincial branch of the NDP revoked Hargrove's party membership because he had violated the party's constitution by campaigning for other parties during an election campaign, though Layton disagreed with this. Hargrove retaliated by severing ties with the NDP at the annual CAW convention. The election increased the NDP's total seats to 29 seats, up from 18 before dissolution. Among the new NDP candidates elected was Olivia Chow, making the two only the second husband-and-wife team in Canadian Parliament history (Gurmant Grewal and Nina Grewal were the first husband-and-wife team in Canadian Parliament after the 2004 federal election). In the end, the NDP succeeded in increasing their parliamentary representation to 29 MPs, though they had significantly fewer seats than the Bloc Québécois (51) or the Opposition Liberals (103). At the NDP's 22nd Convention, held on September 10, 2006, in Quebec City, Layton received a 92% approval rating in a leadership vote, tying former Reform Party leader Preston Manning's record for this kind of voting. This record was later broken in 2016 by Elizabeth May of the Green Party of Canada. At the same convention, the NDP passed a motion calling for the return of Canadian Forces from Afghanistan. On September 24, 2006, he met with Afghan President Hamid Karzai to discuss the NDP position. After the meeting Layton stated that Canada's role should be focused on traditional peacekeeping and reconstruction rather than in a front line combat role currently taking place. Layton and his caucus voted to support the new proposed rules for income trusts introduced by the Conservatives October 31, 2006. The short-term result of the tax policy announcement was a loss to Canadian investors of $20 billion, the largest ever loss attributed to a change in government policy. Layton threatened to move a motion of non-confidence against the government over the "Clean Air Act" unless action was taken to improve the bill and its approach to environmental policy. Prime Minister Harper agreed to put an end to the Parliamentary logjam by sending the bill to a special legislative committee before second reading. He released his proposed changes to the "Clean Air Act" on November 19, 2006. On June 3, 2008, Layton voted to implement a program which would "allow conscientious objectors ... to a war not sanctioned by the United Nations ... to ... remain in Canada ...". Layton led the NDP to be instrumental in taking action on the peace issue of Canada and Iraq War resisters. On June 11, 2008, Prime Minister Stephen Harper made it known that he had received private counsel from Layton on the matter of Indian residential schools and the apology to former students of the schools. Before delivering the apology, Harper thanked Layton. Layton started off the 2008 federal election campaign with a speech similar to that of US presidential nominee Barack Obama. Layton denied he was trying to draw comparisons with Obama, saying "I mean, I am a lot shorter than he is. He is a brilliant orator. I'm never going to claim to be that. But what I have noticed is that the key issues faced by the American middle class, the working people of the U.S. and their concerns about their families' futures, are awfully similar to the issues that I hear in Canada." Layton said that he has also written to Obama and Hillary Clinton saying that the North American Free Trade Agreement had hurt working people in both countries "and those stories have to be told." Layton, along with Prime Minister Harper and Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe, initially opposed the inclusion of Green Party leader Elizabeth May in the leaders' televised debates. Layton initially said that he was following the rules of the broadcast consortium, while NDP spokesman Brad Lavigne confirmed that Layton had refused to attend if May was present, noting that May had endorsed Liberal leader Stéphane Dion for prime minister, and arguing that her inclusion would in effect give the Liberals two representatives at the debate. Rod Love, former chief of staff to Ralph Klein, suggested that the Greens could potentially cut into the NDP's support. Layton's stance drew criticism from the YWCA, Judy Rebick, and members of his own party. Layton dropped his opposition to May's inclusion on September 10, 2008. "This whole issue of debating about the debate has become a distraction to the real debate that needs to happen," Layton said. "I have only one condition for this debate and that is that the prime minister is there." In October 2008, Layton posted an online video message speaking out in favour of net neutrality, torrent sites, video-sharing sites, and social-networking sites. In a separate interview he said that increasing corporate control "is very, very dangerous and we have put the whole issue of net neutrality right into the heart of our campaign platform," and that the Internet is "a public tool for exchanging ideas and I particularly want to say that if we don't fight to preserve it, we could lose it." In the end, the NDP gained 8 new seats, taking its tally to 37. This result still left the NDP as Canada's fourth party, behind the Bloc Québécois with 50. The NDP managed to retain Outremont, held by Tom Mulcair, its only seat in the province. The 40th session of Parliament began on November 27, 2008, with a fiscal update by the Conservatives that outlined their agenda for the upcoming term. This included a temporary suspension of federal employees' right to strike and a removal of monetary subsidies for political parties. All three opposition parties including the NDP stated that they could not support this position. Layton along with Liberal leader Stéphane Dion and Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe began negotiations to form a coalition that would replace the Conservatives as the government. The three opposition parties planned to table a motion of non-confidence in the House of Commons, and counted on the likelihood that the Governor General Michaëlle Jean, would invite the coalition to govern instead of dissolving parliament and calling an election so soon after the last election. On December 1, 2008, the three opposition leaders signed an accord that laid down the basis for an agreement on a coalition government. The proposed structure would be a coalition between the Liberals and the NDP, with the New Democrats getting six Cabinet positions. Both parties agreed to continue the coalition until June 30, 2011. The Bloc Québécois would not be formally part of the government but would provide support on confidence motions for 18 months. Opposition to the proposed coalition developed in all provinces except Quebec. On December 4, 2008, the governor general granted Prime Minister Harper's request to prorogue Parliament until January 26, 2009, at which time Harper had planned to introduce the budget. Dion had since been ousted from the leadership of the Liberals and his successor, Michael Ignatieff, had distanced himself from the coalition. Layton remained committed to ousting the Harper government, pledging that the NDP would vote against the Conservative budget regardless of what it contained. Layton urged Ignatieff's Liberal Party to topple the Conservatives before the shelf life of the coalition expired; constitutional experts said that four months after the last election, if the government fell, the governor general would likely grant the prime minister's request to dissolve Parliament instead of inviting the coalition. On January 28, 2009, the Liberals agreed to support the Conservative budget with an amendment, ending the possibility of the coalition, so Layton said "Today we have learned that you can't trust Mr. Ignatieff to oppose Mr. Harper. If you oppose Mr. Harper and you want a new government, I urge you to support the NDP." In March 2009, the NDP, under Layton's leadership, re-introduced a motion (first passed June 3, 2008) which, if implemented, would allow conscientious objectors to the Iraq War to remain in Canada. The motion again passed March 30, 2009, by 129–125, but it was non-binding. In a leadership review vote held at the NDP's August 2009 federal policy convention, 89.25% of delegates voted against holding a leadership convention to replace Layton. In October 2009, Layton paired up with the Stephen Lewis Foundation to raise money for HIV/AIDS affected families in Africa. As part of the foundation's A Dare to Remember campaign, Layton busked on a busy street corner. Layton's son, Mike was elected to Toronto City Council in the 2010 city council election. In early 2011, Layton was featured in an episode of CBC Television's Make the Politician Work. The Conservative government was defeated in a no-confidence vote on March 25, 2011, with the motion gaining full support of all opposition parties including the New Democrats, after the government was found in contempt of Parliament. It was the first time in Commonwealth history that a government lost the confidence of the House of Commons on the grounds of contempt of Parliament. The no-confidence motion was carried with a vote of 156 in favour of the motion, and 145 against, thus resulting in the prime minister advising a dissolution of Parliament and a federal election. The day after the successful passing of the motion, Layton started the NDP election campaign, first with a speech in Ottawa followed later in the day by an event in Edmonton, Alberta. Questions about Layton's health due to a recent hip surgery were often directed to him during the campaign, with Layton insisting that he was healthy enough to lead. On March 29, 2011, the New Democrats presented their first real campaign promise, a proposal to cap credit card rates to reduce credit card debt. Unlike the previous election, Layton stated he was in favour of Green Party leader Elizabeth May speaking at the leaders debates, despite the fact that she was once again being discouraged by the Canadian media networks. The NDP also embarked upon the largest advertising campaign in its history, focusing on the Harper government's health care record. He also dedicated the federal election campaign to former Saskatchewan premier Allan Blakeney, who died about halfway through the campaign. Despite entering the campaign with relatively low poll numbers, the NDP recovered and increased their support significantly after Layton's performance in the leaders debates. In the English-language debate, Layton criticized Michael Ignatieff's poor attendance record in the House of Commons, saying "You know, most Canadians, if they don't show up for work, they don't get a promotion!", to which Ignatieff was unable to respond effectively. The Globe and Mail described Layton's attack as a "knock-out punch" while the Toronto Star stated it was the "pivot in the debate [that] was a turning point in the federal campaign." Layton's New Democrats successfully capitalized on Ignatieff's attendance record in the Toronto area. On February 4, 2011, Layton attended a rally against usage-based billing in Toronto with MPs Dan McTeague, Olivia Chow, Peggy Nash and others. His attendance at this rally was accompanied by several press releases by the NDP denouncing metered internet usage in Canada. The NDP surge began in Quebec, with the NDP surprising many observers by surpassing the previously front-running Bloc in Quebec. In Canada overall, the NDP surged past the Liberals to take the second place behind the Conservatives; in Quebec, the NDP took first place. The NDP surge became.

Layton's attack on Ignatieff, which questioned his attendance at work and claimed he didn't get a promotion, left Ignatieff unable to respond effectively; the Globe and Mail described it as a "knock-out punch" while the Toronto Star called it the "pivot in the debate [that] was a turning point in the federal campaign." The New Democrats successfully used Ignatieff's attendance record in the Toronto area to their advantage. On February 4, 2011, Layton attended a rally in Toronto against usage-based billing with MPs Dan McTeague, Olivia Chow, Peggy Nash, and others, accompanied by several press releases from the NDP denouncing metered internet usage in Canada. The NDP surge began in Quebec, where the party surprised observers by surpassing the previously leading Bloc; in Canada overall, the NDP surged past the Liberals to take second place behind the Conservatives, and in Quebec, it took first place. This surge became the dominant narrative of the final week of the campaign, as other parties turned their attacks on the NDP and Layton. On April 29, 2011, a retired police officer told the Sun News Network and the Toronto Sun that in 1996, Layton had been found in a massage parlour during a raid targeting underage Asian sex workers, with police warning him about the potentially questionable use of the business and recommending he avoid it; no charges were filed. The Sun later published a follow-up in which Toronto city councillor Giorgio Mammoliti criticized Layton. Layton maintained there was no wrongdoing, stating he had simply "gone for a massage at a community clinic" and did not return after being advised not to, and he referred to the release of the police report as a smear campaign. Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe dismissed the claim, and a National Post columnist suggested a Liberal insider leaked the story, though a Liberal Party spokesman denied involvement. A Toronto Star column noted that most online contributors agreed there was a smear campaign against Layton. That same day, the Nanos Leadership Index saw Layton's score rise from 80 to 97, surpassing Harper's 88 and Ignatieff's 39, with the polling company attributing the improvement to public sympathy for a candidate unfairly maligned. The Toronto Police Service launched an investigation into how official police notes were leaked to Sun Media, noting that police notebooks are closely guarded and may contain unfounded allegations. On May 5, 2011, no charges were laid regarding the leaked information. Layton appeared on the Radio-Canada talk show Tout le monde en parle on April 3, credited with improving the NDP's standing among Francophone voters due to his informal Québécois French, as the show is the most popular program in Quebec; he also performed well in the televised French-language party leaders' debate on April 13. In the May 2, 2011, election, Layton led the NDP to 103 seats—more than double its previous high—enough to make the NDP the Official Opposition for the first time. The gains were largely due to a major surge in Quebec, where the NDP won 59 of the province's 75 seats, dominating Montreal and sweeping Quebec City and the Outaouais, although the NDP also won more seats than any other opposition party outside Quebec. The NDP had entered the election with only one seat in Quebec—Thomas Mulcair's—and had won only one seat in the province historically (Phil Edmonston in a 1990 by-election). Many of these gains came at the expense of the Bloc, which was reduced to a four-seat rump without official party status in Parliament. Layton came from a political family: his maternal great-granduncle, William Steeves, was a Father of Confederation; his great-grandfather, Philip E. Layton, was a blind piano salesman and activist who founded the Montreal Association for the Blind in 1908 and campaigned for disability pensions in the 1930s; he was the senior partner in Layton Bros. Pianos, a business established in 1837 in London, England, which Philip emigrated to Montreal at 19 and which continues to operate as Layton Audio; his 1898 composition, Dominion March, was played at Layton's lying in state. Layton's grandfather, Gilbert, served in Quebec's Union Nationale government under Maurice Duplessis as a cabinet minister, later resigning due to the government's lack of support for Canadian participation in World War II. Layton's father, Robert, was initially a Liberal Party activist in the 1960s and 1970s, later switching to the Progressive Conservatives and serving as a federal Cabinet minister under Prime Minister Brian Mulroney in the 1980s, as well as a member of Parliament. Layton was raised in the United Church of Canada and was a member of Bloor Street United Church in Toronto, though he also attended services at the Metropolitan Community Church of Toronto, whose pastor, Brent Hawkes, was a longtime NDP activist and personal friend. In 1969, at age 19, Layton married his high school sweetheart Sally Halford, with whom he had two children: Mike, who served as a Toronto city councillor from 2010 to 2022, and Sarah, who works for the Stephen Lewis Foundation; the marriage ended in divorce in 1983 after 14 years. Layton first met Olivia Chow in 1985 during an auction at Village by the Grange, where Jack was the auctioneer and Olivia was the interpreter; they had previously known each other and realized they were both candidates, so they had lunch to discuss the campaign. Three weeks later, they went on their first date; Olivia's mother initially did not approve of Layton due to his race and lack of being a lawyer or doctor. Layton was invited to dinner at Olivia's mother's home, where they played mahjong; after dinner, Layton attempted to thank her in Cantonese, incorrectly saying "Thank you for the good sex," which broke the ice and led to a long friendship. Layton was known for playing music and singing at gatherings; Alberta NDP leader Brian Mason recalled during a three-day board meeting when Layton was running for president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities that he would gather people in his hotel room, play guitar, and get them singing old folk songs from the 1960s, using his personality to engage people rather than politics. Layton was a keen Trekkie and had a custom Starfleet uniform made by a tailor, famously photographed wearing it at a Star Trek convention in 1991. At the 2005 Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner, Layton mocked himself and his party by playing guitar and singing three songs: "Party for Sale or Rent" (to the tune of "King of the Road"), a reworked version of "Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out" with humorous lyrics, and "If I Had Another $4.6 Billion." He once wrote: "My friends, love is better than anger. Hope is better than fear. Optimism is better than despair. So let us be loving, hopeful and optimistic. And we'll change the world. All my very best, Jack Layton." On February 5, 2010, Layton announced he had been diagnosed with prostate cancer, noting his father Robert had the same type 17 years earlier and had recovered; his wife, Olivia Chow, had thyroid cancer a few years before. He vowed to beat the cancer and said it would not interrupt his duties as MP or NDP leader. Following the 2011 federal election, Layton led the party into the first month of the new parliamentary session and attended the NDP Federal Convention in Vancouver. After Parliament adjourned for summer, Layton announced on July 25, 2011, that he would take a temporary leave from his post to fight an unspecified, newly diagnosed cancer, hoping to return as leader upon the resumption of the House of Commons on September 19, 2011, and recommended that NDP caucus chair Nycole Turmel serve as interim leader. Layton died at 4:45 a.m. ET on August 22, 2011, at his home in Toronto, aged 61. Upon hearing the news, there was a nationwide outpouring of grief, and Governor General David Johnston, Prime Minister Stephen Harper, NDP deputy leader Libby Davies, and US ambassador to Canada David Jacobson issued statements praising Layton and mourning his loss. Layton's family released an open letter written by Layton two days before his death, expressing his wishes for the NDP's leadership and addressing various segments of Canadian society. Layton was accorded a state funeral between August 25 and 27, 2011, with the final memorial service at Roy Thomson Hall in Toronto; he was the second leader of the Official Opposition to die in office, the first being Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a former prime minister who received a state funeral under prime ministerial protocol; Layton was the first Official Opposition leader to die for whom a state funeral would not otherwise have been granted, but Prime Minister Harper offered it to Layton's widow, who accepted. Layton's body was cremated after the funeral; a portion of his ashes was scattered under a jack pine planted on Toronto Island in his honour, a second portion at the Layton family's plot at Cote St. Charles United Church in Hudson, Quebec, and a third portion under a memorial sculpted by Chow at the Toronto Necropolis Cemetery on the first anniversary of his death. Layton's life is portrayed in a 2013 television movie entitled Jack, with Rick Roberts portraying Layton and Sook-Yin Lee as Olivia Chow, featuring Wendy Crewson and Erin Karpluk, released on March 10, 2013, and aired on CBC Television.

Jackie is the sixth studio album by American singer Ciara, released on May 1, 2015, through Epic Records. After leaving her previous record label and releasing her self-titled fifth studio album in July 2013, Ciara took a hiatus to focus on her relationship with American rapper Future, which inspired her sixth album. In May 2014, Ciara gave birth to her first child and later called off her engagement to Future following public claims of infidelity. After the breakup, Ciara postponed the album's release and focused on motherhood while quietly recording new music. During the recording process, Ciara worked with long-time collaborators Harmony "H-Money" Samuels and Polow da Don, as well as less frequent producers Dr. Luke and Cirkut, and songwriter Diane Warren. The album is a predominantly pop and R&B record influenced by hip hop, dance-pop, house, electropop, trap, drum and bass, and 1990s R&B, with themes centered on love, betrayal, and motherhood. Named after her mother, the album features guest appearances by Pitbull and Missy Elliott. The lead single, "I Bet," was released on January 26, 2015, and debuted at number 96 on the US Billboard Hot 100, peaking at number 43. The second single, "Dance like We're Making Love," was released on April 28, 2015, and the album was promoted with a third single, "Give Me Love," which received a US urban contemporary impact date on June 9, 2015. The album peaked at number 17 on the US Billboard 200 with 25,000 album-equivalent units (19,900 in sales), the lowest first-week sales among her first six albums, and placed at number 13 on the Top Album Sales chart. Ciara embarked on the Jackie Tour in 2015, which included 19 US dates and later expanded to include Canada, though the tour was ultimately cancelled. The album received mixed reviews from critics, with Metacritic assigning it a score of 60 based on 8 reviews, indicating "mixed or average" reception. Some critics praised its production and variety, while others noted a lack of depth or personal insight. The album opens with "Jackie (B.M.F.)," a trap and drum and bass track about motherhood, followed by "That's How I'm Feelin'," a synth-driven song featuring Pitbull and Missy Elliott, and "Lullaby," a dance-friendly track with a metaphor about a new mom putting her partner to bed. Other tracks include "Dance like We're Making Love," a sultry midtempo pop song, "Stuck on You," a brash pop song, "Fly" with an '80s electro sample and Squarepusher chords, "I Bet" with lyrics on betrayal, "Give Me Love" as an EDM/house track, "Kiss & Tell" as a retro-soul bounce, "All Good" as a disco-lite pop song, "Only One" as a pop ballad, and "One Woman Army" as a dance-pop track with a robo-military march, all of which are lyrically about self-reliance. The album closes with "I Got You," a lullaby for Ciara's one-year-old son, Future Jr. Ciara stated that "Jackie" is her best body of work, reflecting her growth as an artist and mother, and that the album captures her emotional journey through vulnerability, ambition, and personal transformation.

The album achieved 900 in sales and had the lowest first-week sales among her first six albums; its sales ranked it at number 13 on the Top Album Sales chart. Credits are adapted from liner notes and iTunes.

James Lusk Alcorn (November 4, 1816 – December 19, 1894) was a governor and U.S. senator during Mississippi’s Reconstruction era. A Moderate Republican and Whiggish "scalawag," he faced a bitter rivalry with Radical Republican Adelbert Ames, who defeated him in the 1873 gubernatorial race. Alcorn was the first elected Republican governor of Mississippi. Born near Golconda, Illinois Territory, to James Alcorn and Hanna Lusk, a Scots-Irish family, he studied at Cumberland College in Princeton, Kentucky, and practiced law in Salem, Kentucky, where he was admitted to the bar in 1838. He served in the Kentucky House of Representatives in 1843 and moved to Mississippi the following year. He established a law office in Coahoma County, where his property holdings and law practice grew, making him wealthy. In 1850, he built a three-story house at Mound Place Plantation in Coahoma County. By 1860, he enslaved nearly one hundred people and held lands valued at a quarter of a million dollars. He served in the Mississippi House of Representatives and Senate during the 1840s and 1850s as a leading Whig. He founded the levee system and was chosen president of the levee board; a levee district was established in 1858 through his efforts. He ran for Congress in 1856 but lost, and in 1857 was nominated for governor by the Whigs but declined. Alcorn attended the 1851 Mississippi convention called by Democratic governor John A. Quitman, who advocated secession, and joined the Mississippi Unionists to oppose secession, warning of a Northern-dominated South. However, in January 1861, he joined the secessionists and was elected to the Committee of Fifteen to prepare the Ordinance of Secession. Though born in the free, pro-U.S. state of Illinois, he joined the Confederate States of America and was appointed brigadier-general of the Mississippi Militia. Jefferson Davis refused to commission him due to political differences, and Alcorn served in the Confederate Army for about eighteen months in inconspicuous field duties, mainly raising troops and garrison duty. After several major generals resigned, including Davis, Earl Van Dorn, and Charles Clark, Alcorn became eligible for promotion but was passed over because John J. Pettus was governor. At the start of the Civil War, Alcorn was ordered to central Kentucky and later stationed at Fort Donelson, Tennessee. In October 1861, he raised three regiments of militia, designated the Army of 10,000, and led them to Camp Beauregard, Kentucky, under General Leonidas Polk. His field service ended in January 1862 when his brigade was disbanded. He was captured in Arkansas in 1862, paroled later that year, and returned to Mound Place Plantation. In 1863, he was elected to the Mississippi state legislature, where he joined critics of Confederate President Jefferson Davis. During the war, he spent a fortune raising and supplying troops; in 1863, his plantation was raided during the Yazoo Pass Expedition. He preserved part of his wealth by trading cotton with the North. In November 1863, he wrote to his wife that he had sold 111 bales of cotton, holding ten thousand dollars in Green backs and one thousand in gold. After the war, he was among the fifty wealthiest men in the South. He lost two sons to the war: Milton Stewart Alcorn, who committed suicide in 1879 after returning home partially deaf and a drunkard, and Henry "Hal" Alcorn, who ran away to join the military, became ill, was captured, and died of typhoid fever en route to Mississippi. Alcorn was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1865 but was barred from seating due to his participation in the Confederacy. He supported suffrage for freedmen and endorsed the Fourteenth Amendment. He led the scalawags, who made up about a fourth of Republican officials in Mississippi, in coalition with carpetbaggers and freedmen. Most Republican votes came from African Americans, despite most state officeholders being white. In the 1869 election, Alcorn defeated Lewis Dent to become governor, serving until 1871. As a modernizer, he appointed former Whigs, some previously Democrats, supported public schools for all, and established a new black college, now known as Alcorn State University, which he helped shape with Hiram Revels as its president. Many Republicans opposed him due to his patronage and resistance to civil rights legislation, as well as his unwillingness to appoint local Black officers when white alternatives existed. He opposed a state civil rights bill and believed in preserving the old Southern civilization. Alcorn resigned to become a U.S. senator from 1871 to 1877, succeeding Hiram Revels, the first African American senator.
