As a senator, he advocated for removing political disabilities of white Southerners, rejected federal efforts to end segregation in hotels, restaurants, and railroads, denounced the federal cotton tax as robbery, and defended separate schools for races. Though a former enslaver, he described slavery as "a cancer upon the body of the nation" and expressed satisfaction over its end. His estrangement from Adelbert Ames deepened in 1871, and by 1873, their rivalry turned into intense animosity. Ames won the 1873 gubernatorial race by 69,870 to 50,490 votes, defeating Alcorn, who won support from scalawags. Alcorn withdrew from state politics and accused Ames of being incapable and an enemy of the people. When Blanche Bruce was elected as the second African American senator in 1874, Alcorn refused to introduce him to the Senate, and Bruce was welcomed by Roscoe Conkling. In 1875, during a period of rising violence against Black Republicans, Alcorn led a white force against Black Republicans at Friar's Point, resulting in at least five Black deaths. Alcorn supported modernizing the South while believing in white supremacy and advocating civil and political rights for African Americans. In a letter to his wife, he stated that white Southerners must make African Americans their friends or the future would be "red with blood and damp with tears." He founded the Mississippi levee system and played a key role in rebuilding levees after the Civil War. After retiring from politics, he remained active in levee affairs, served as a delegate to the 1890 Mississippian constitutional convention, where he supported the black disenfranchisement clause introduced by Democrats. He was twice married: first in 1839 to Mary C. Stewart, who died in 1849, and in 1850 to Amelia Walton Glover of Alabama. In later life, he practiced law in Friars Point, Mississippi, and lived quietly at Eagle's Nest in Coahoma County. He died in 1894 and was buried at Eagle's Nest in the Alcorn Cemetery in Friars Point. He commissioned a statue of himself, which was placed on his grave. Alcorn County, Mississippi, and Alcorn State University, the first historically black land-grant university, are named in his honor.

James Luke Prendergast (April 7, 1800 – May 13, 1895) was a merchant and political figure in Newfoundland. He served in the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly, representing Conception Bay from 1842 to 1852, Harbour Grace from 1855 to 1859, and again from 1860 to 1861 as a Liberal. Born in Harbour Grace, he was the son of James Prendergast and married Margaret Bransfield in 1825. In an 1840 by-election, he ran as an independent Liberal against Edmund Hanrahan, but due to widespread violence during the campaign, Governor Henry Prescott invalidated the election results. Prendergast was first elected as a Liberal in 1842. He was defeated when he ran again as an independent Liberal in 1852. In 1855, after being elected as a Liberal, he served as acting superintendent of fisheries. His 1859 election was overturned, but he was elected in the subsequent 1860 by-election. The general election in Harbour Grace in 1861 did not open the polls due to the threat of violence, and Prendergast was defeated in a later by-election that year. He ran unsuccessfully for a seat in 1869 as an anti-Confederate. Later in life, he served as sheriff of Harbour Grace and as a justice of the peace. He died in Harbour Grace at the age of 95. James Randi, born Randall James Hamilton Zwinge on August 7, 1928, in Toronto, Canada, was a Canadian-American stage magician, author, and scientific skeptic who extensively challenged paranormal and pseudoscientific claims. He was the co-founder of the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry (CSI) and the founder of the James Randi Educational Foundation (JREF). Randi began his career as a magician under the stage name The Amazing Randi and later devoted most of his time to investigating paranormal, occult, and supernatural claims. He retired from practicing magic at age 60 and from his foundation at age 87. Although often called a "debunker," Randi disliked the term and preferred to describe himself as an "investigator." He wrote about paranormal phenomena, skepticism, and the history of magic and was a frequent guest on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson, where he famously exposed fraudulent faith healer Peter Popoff. He was also featured on Penn & Teller: Bullshit!. Before his retirement, JREF sponsored the One Million Dollar Paranormal Challenge, offering $1 million to applicants who could demonstrate evidence of any paranormal, supernatural, or occult power or event under agreed test conditions. Randi was the son of Marie Alice (née Paradis) and George Randall Zwinge, an executive at Bell Telephone Company, and had French, Danish, and Austrian descent. He took up magic after seeing Harry Blackstone Sr. and reading conjuring books during a 13-month period in a body cast following a bicycle accident, during which he confounded doctors who expected he would never walk again. He skipped classes and dropped out of high school at 17 to perform as a conjurer in a carnival roadshow, practiced as a mentalist in local nightclubs and at Toronto's Canadian National Exhibition, and wrote for Montreal's tabloid press. At a church, he exposed a pastor claiming to read minds by revealing the trick, leading to a four-hour jail sentence that inspired his career as a scientific skeptic. In his 20s, he posed as an astrologer under the name "Zo-ran" by randomly assembling items from existing astrology columns. In his 30s, he worked in the UK, Europe, Philippine nightclubs, and Japan, witnessing many tricks presented as supernatural, including an evangelist using the "one-ahead" technique. Randi began a professional stage magic and escapology career in 1946 under the name The Amazing Randi, performing escape acts globally. On February 7, 1956, he appeared live on NBC's Today show, remaining in a sealed metal coffin submerged in a hotel swimming pool for 104 minutes, breaking what was claimed to be Harry Houdini's record of 93 minutes, though Randi noted he was much younger than Houdini when he set the record. He was a regular on the Long John Nebel program on WOR, hosted The Amazing Randi Show until January 1966, and was fired from WOR due to complaints from the archbishop of New York over a comment that "Jesus Christ was a religious nut," a claim Randi disputed. Randi hosted numerous television specials and world tours, appearing regularly on Wonderama from 1959 to 1967 and auditioning for a revival of The Magic Clown in 1970, which was never picked up. In a 1974 issue of Abracadabra, he stated that the magician community relies heavily on mutual trust and faith. In a 2003 issue of The Linking Ring, it was noted that Randi's ethics made him "Amazing" and that he "talks the talk and walks the walk." During Alice Cooper's 1973–1974 Billion Dollar Babies tour, Randi performed as a mad dentist and executioner, building stage props including the guillotine, and in 1976 escaped from a straitjacket while suspended upside-down over Niagara Falls. Randi was accused of using psychic powers in spoon bending; when challenged by a professor at the University at Buffalo and Senator Claiborne Pell, he denied having any paranormal abilities, stating he was a trickster who used deception. Randi was a member of the Society of American Magicians (SAM), the International Brotherhood of Magicians (IBM), and The Magic Circle in the UK, holding the rank of "Member of the Inner Magic Circle with Gold Star." He authored ten books, including Conjuring (1992), subtitled "Being a Definitive History of the Venerable Arts of Sorcery, Prestidigitation, Wizardry, Deception, & Chicanery and of the Mountebanks & Scoundrels Who have Perpetrated these Subterfuges on a Bewildered Public, in short, MAGIC!" and co-authored with Bert Sugar in 1976, focusing on Houdini's life and art. His book The Magic World of the Amazing Randi (1989) was a children's introduction to magic, and he wrote educational works on paranormal claims, including biographies of Uri Geller and Nostradamus, and an encyclopedia on occult and supernatural hoaxes (1995). In 2011, he was working on A Magician in the Laboratory, which detailed his application of skepticism to science. He was a member of the all-male literary banqueting club the Trap Door Spiders, which inspired Isaac Asimov's fictional group, the Black Widowers. Other books include Flim-Flam! (1982), The Faith Healers (1987), James Randi, Psychic Investigator (1991), Test Your ESP Potential (1982), and An Encyclopedia of Claims, Frauds, and Hoaxes of the Occult and Supernatural (1995). Randi was a regular contributor to Skeptic magazine, penning the "'Twas Brillig ..." column and serving on its editorial board, and a frequent contributor to Skeptical Inquirer, published by CSI, of which he was also a fellow. In 1972, he publicly challenged Uri Geller, accusing him of using magic tricks and presenting his claims in The Truth About Uri Geller (1982). To educate columnists and TV personalities, Randi and CSICOP worked to influence the media, and he found Johnny Carson to be a strong supporter, noting that Carson, a former magician, was skeptical and would ask what he wanted emphasized in interviews. In 1973, Geller appeared on The Tonight Show, which is documented in the Nova special "Secrets of the Psychics." Randi revealed that Carson had prepared props without informing Geller and kept Geller and his staff away from them. Geller appeared surprised and said he was "scared" and "surprised" because he had been told about 40 questions, and he failed to demonstrate any paranormal abilities, saying he "didn't feel strong" and felt pressured. According to Adam Higginbotham, Geller was humiliated for 22 minutes and later returned to Tel Aviv, believing he was destroyed. However, the appearance backfired, as Geller was immediately booked on The Merv Griffin Show and became a paranormal superstar, with his failure making his abilities seem more real to a trusting public. This outcome led Randi to realize more needed to be done, so in 1976 he approached psychologist Ray Hyman, who had criticized Geller's Stanford tests, and together with Martin Gardner, formed the Committee for Scientific Investigation of Claims of the Paranormal (CSICOP). Using donations and sales of Skeptical Inquirer, they and philosopher Paul Kurtz took seats on the executive board, with Isaac Asimov and Carl Sagan as founding members. Randi became the public face of CSICOP and, according to Hyman, the face of the skeptical movement. András G. Pintér called Randi the grandfather of European skepticism for his role in launching several European organizations. Geller sued Randi and CSICOP for $15 million in 1991 and lost; the suit against CSICOP was dismissed in 1995, and Geller was ordered to pay $120,000 for filing a frivolous lawsuit. The legal costs Randi incurred used almost all of a $272,000 MacArthur Foundation grant awarded in 1986. Randi dismissed Geller's claims about psychic photography in the Ted Serios case, arguing it was trick photography using a hand-held optical device. During the legal dispute, CSICOP leadership asked Randi to refrain from commenting on Geller, which he refused, leading to his resignation, though he maintained a respectful relationship with the group, which changed its name to the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry (CSI) in 2006. In 2010, Randi was one of 16 new CSI fellows elected by its board. Randi wrote many articles criticizing paranormal beliefs and demonstrated flaws in studies suggesting paranormal phenomena, including his Project Alpha hoax, in which he planted two fake psychics in a privately funded psychic research experiment. He appeared on numerous TV shows to debunk claims, such as on That's My Line in 1981, where he exposed claimed psychic James Hydrick by arranging foam packaging peanuts to prevent the demonstration of moving a telephone book page, leading Hydrick to confess everything. Randi was awarded a MacArthur Foundation Fellowship in 1986, with a $272,000 five-year grant that supported his investigations of faith healers, including W. V. Grant, Ernest Angley, and Peter Popoff, whom he first exposed on The Tonight Show in April 1986. Carson invited Randi on the show without seeing the evidence, and after Randi showed a video from Popoff's broadcast in which he called out a woman, revealed personal information, and performed a laying-on-of-hands healing, Randi replayed the video with sound dubbed in from a radio scanner that detected Popoff's wife Elizabeth using a radio frequency to transmit information to a receiver in Popoff's ear. The information was gathered by assistants who distributed "prayer cards" to the audience. The exposé led to many TV stations dropping Popoff's show, eventually forcing him into bankruptcy in September 1987. However, Popoff returned with faith-healing infomercials that reportedly attracted over $23 million in 2005. The Canadian Centre for Inquiry's Think Again! TV documented one of Popoff's performances in Toronto on May 26, 2011. In February 1988, Randi tested media gullibility by perpetrating a hoax with Australia's 60 Minutes and releasing a fake press package.

Directions and information to a miniature radio receiver hidden in Popoff's left ear were gathered by Popoff's assistants, who had distributed "prayer cards" to the audience before the show, instructing them to write down all the information Popoff would need to pray for them. The news coverage from Randi's exposé on The Tonight Show led to many TV stations dropping Popoff's show, eventually forcing him into bankruptcy in September 1987. However, the televangelist returned soon after with faith-healing infomercials that reportedly attracted more than $23 million in 2005 from viewers sending in money for promised healing and prosperity. The Canadian Centre for Inquiry's Think Again! TV documented one of Popoff's more recent performances before a large audience who gathered in Toronto on May 26, 2011, hoping to be saved from illness and poverty. In February 1988, Randi tested the gullibility of the media by perpetrating a hoax with Australia's 60 Minutes program and a fake press package, building publicity for a "spirit channeler" named Carlos, who was actually artist José Alvarez, Randi's partner. While performing as Carlos, Alvarez was prompted by Randi using sophisticated radio equipment. According to the 60 Minutes program on the Carlos hoax, "it was claimed that Alvarez would not have had the audience he did at the Opera House (and the resulting potential sales therefrom) had the media coverage been more aggressive (and factual)", though an analysis by The Skeptic's Tim Mendham concluded that, while the media coverage of Alvarez's appearances was not credulous, the hoax "at least showed that they could benefit by being a touch more sceptical". The hoax was exposed on 60 Minutes Australia; "Carlos" and Randi explained how they had pulled it off. In his book The Faith Healers, Randi wrote that his anger and relentlessness arose from compassion for the victims of fraud. Randi was also critical of João de Deus, a.k.a. "John of God", a self-proclaimed psychic surgeon who had received international attention. Randi observed, referring to psychic surgery, "To any experienced conjurer, the methods by which these seeming miracles are produced are very obvious". In 1982, Randi verified the abilities of Arthur Lintgen, a Philadelphia doctor, who was able to identify the classical music recorded on a vinyl LP solely by examining the grooves on the record. However, Lintgen did not claim to have any paranormal ability, merely knowledge of the way that the groove forms patterns on particular recordings. In 1988, John Maddox, editor of the prominent science journal Nature, asked Randi to join the supervision and observation of the homeopathy experiments conducted by Jacques Benveniste's team. Once Randi's stricter protocol for the experiment was in place, the positive results could not be reproduced. Randi stated that Daniel Dunglas Home, who could allegedly play an accordion that was locked in a cage without touching it, was caught cheating on a few occasions, but the incidents were never made public. He also stated that the actual instrument in use was a one-octave mouth organ concealed under Home's large mustache and that other one-octave mouth organs were found in Home's belongings after his death. According to Randi, author William Lindsay Gresham told Randi "around 1960" that he had seen these mouth organs in the Home collection at the Society for Psychical Research (SPR). Eric J. Dingwall, who catalogued Home's collection on its arrival at the SPR, does not record the presence of the mouth organs. According to Peter Lamont, the author of an extensive Home biography, "It is unlikely Dingwall would have missed these or did not make them public". The fraudulent medium Henry Slade also played an accordion while held with one hand under a table. Slade and Home played the same pieces. They had at one time lived near each other in the U.S. The magician Chung Ling Soo exposed how Slade had performed the trick. Randi distinguished between pseudoscience and "crackpot science". He regarded most of parapsychology as pseudoscience because of the way in which it is approached and conducted, but nonetheless saw it as a legitimate subject that "should be pursued", and from which real scientific discoveries may develop. Randi regarded crackpot science as "equally wrong" as pseudoscience, but with no scientific pretensions. Despite multiple debunkings, Randi did not like to be called a "debunker", preferring to call himself a "skeptic" or an "investigator": if you go into a situation calling yourself a debunker then it is as if you have prejudged the topic. It's not neutral or scientific, and it can turn people against you. Skeptics and magicians Penn & Teller credit Randi and his career as a skeptic for their own careers. During an interview at TAM! 2012, Penn stated that Flim-Flam! was an early influence on him, and said "If not for Randi there would not be Penn & Teller as we are today". He went on to say "Outside of my family ... no one is more important in my life. Randi is everything to me". At the NECSS skeptic conference in 2017, Randi was asked by George Hrab what a "'skeptic coming of age ceremony' would look like" and Randi talked about what it was like as a child to learn about the speed of light and how that felt like he was looking into the past. Randi stated "More kids need to be stunned". At The Amaz!ng Meeting in 2011 (TAM 9) the Independent Investigations Group (IIG) organized a tribute to Randi. The group gathered together with other attendees, put on fake white beards, and posed for a large group photo with Randi. At the CSICon in 2017, in absence of Randi, the IIG organized another group photo with leftover beards from the 2011 photo. After Randi was sent the photo, he replied, "I'm always very touched by any such expression. This is certainly no exception. You have my sincere gratitude. I suspect, however that a couple of those beards were fake. But I'm in a forgiving mood at the moment. I'm frankly very touched. I'll see you at the next CSICon. Thank you all". In a 2019 Skeptical Inquirer magazine article, Harriet Hall, a friend of Randi, compares him to the fictional Albus Dumbledore. Hall describes their long white beards, flamboyant clothing, associated with a bird (Dumbledore with a phoenix and Randi with Pegasus). They both are caring and have "immense brainpower" and both "can perform impressive feats of magic". She states that Randi is one of "major inspirations for the skeptical work I do ... He's way better than Dumbledore!". Exploring Psychic Powers ... Live was a two-hour television special aired live on June 7, 1989, wherein Randi examined several people claiming psychic powers. Hosted by actor Bill Bixby, the program offered $100,000 (Randi's $10,000 prize plus $90,000 put up by the show's syndicator, LBS Communications, Inc.) to anyone who could demonstrate genuine psychic powers. In 1996, Randi established the James Randi Educational Foundation. Randi and his colleagues publish in JREF's blog, Swift. Topics have included the interesting mathematics of the one-seventh area triangle, a classic geometric puzzle. In his weekly commentary, Randi often gave examples of what he considered the nonsense that he dealt with every day. Beginning in 2003, the JREF annually hosted The Amaz!ng Meeting, a gathering of scientists, skeptics, and atheists. The last meeting was in 2015, coinciding with Randi's retirement from the JREF. Randi began a series of conferences known as "The Amazing Meeting" (TAM) which quickly became the largest gathering of skeptics in the world, drawing audiences from Asia, Europe, South America, and the UK. It also attracted a large percentage of younger attendees. Randi was regularly featured on many podcasts, including The Skeptics Society's official podcast Skepticality and the Center for Inquiry's official podcast Point of Inquiry. From September 2006 onwards, he occasionally contributed to The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe podcast with a column called "Randi Speaks". In addition, The Amazing Show was a podcast in which Randi shared various anecdotes in an interview format. In 2014, Part2Filmworks released An Honest Liar, a feature film documentary, written by Tyler Measom and Greg O'Toole, and directed and produced by Measom and Justin Weinstein. The film, which was funded through Kickstarter, focuses on Randi's life, his investigations, and his relationship with longtime partner José Alvarez (born Deyvi Orangel Peña Arteaga), to whom he was married in 2013. The film was screened at the Tribeca Film Festival, at Toronto's Hot Docs film festival, and at the June 2014 AFI Docs Festival in Silver Spring, Maryland, and Washington, D.C., where it won the Audience Award for Best Feature. It also received positive reviews from critics. The film was featured on the PBS Independent Lens series, shown in the U.S. and Canada, on March 28, 2016. In December 2014, Randi flew to Australia to take part in "An Evening with James Randi" tour, organized by Think Inc. This tour included a screening of An Honest Liar followed by a "fireside chat" with Randi on stage. Cities visited were Adelaide, Perth, Brisbane, Melbourne, and Sydney. MC in Adelaide was Dr. Paul Willis with Richard Saunders interviewing Randi. MC in Perth was Jake Farr-Wharton with Richard Saunders interviewing Randi. MC for Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney was Richard Saunders with Lawrence Leung interviewing Randi. In 2017, Randi appeared in animated form on the website Holy Koolaid, in which he discussed the challenge of finding the balance between connecting sincerely with his audience and at the same time tricking/fooling them with an artful ruse, and indicated that this is a balance with which many magicians struggle. The James Randi Educational Foundation (JREF) offered a prize of US$1,000,000 to anyone able to demonstrate a supernatural ability under scientific testing criteria agreed to by both sides. Based on the paranormal challenges of John Nevil Maskelyne and Houdini, the foundation began in 1996, when Randi put up $1,000 of his own money payable to anyone who could provide objective proof of the paranormal. The prize money grew to $1,000,000, and had formal published rules. No one progressed past the preliminary test, which was set up with parameters agreed to by both Randi and the applicant. He refused to accept any challengers who might suffer serious injury or death as a result of the testing. On April 1, 2007, it was ruled that only persons with an established, nationally recognized media profile and the backing of a reputable academic were allowed to apply for the challenge, in order to avoid wasting JREF resources on frivolous claimants. On Larry King Live, March 6, 2001, Larry King asked claimed medium Sylvia Browne if she would take the challenge and she agreed. Randi appeared with Browne on Larry King Live six months later, and she again appeared to accept his challenge; however, according to Randi, she ultimately refused to be tested, and the Randi Foundation kept a clock on its website recording the number of weeks since Browne allegedly accepted the challenge without following through, until Browne's death in November 2013. During a subsequent appearance on Larry King Live on June 5, 2001, Randi challenged Rosemary Altea, another claimed medium, to undergo testing for the million dollars, but Altea refused to address the question. Instead, Altea replied only, "I agree with what he says, that there are many, many people who claim to be spiritual mediums, they claim to talk to the dead. There are many people, we all know this. There are cheats and charlatans everywhere". On January 26, 2007, Altea and Randi again appeared on the show, and Altea again refused to answer whether or not she would take the One Million Dollar Paranormal Challenge. In October 2007, claimed psychic John Edward appeared on Headline Prime, hosted by Glenn Beck. When asked if he would take "the Amazing Randi's" challenge, Edward responded, "It's funny. I was on Larry King Live once, and they asked me the same question. And I made a joke [then], and I'll say the same thing here: why would I allow myself to be tested by somebody who's got an adjective as a first name?" Beck simply allowed Edward to continue, ignoring the challenge. Randi asked British businessman Jim McCormick, the inventor of the bogus ADE 651 bomb detector, to take the challenge in October 2008. Randi called the ADE 651 "a useless quack device which cannot perform any other function than separating naive persons from their money. It's a fake, a scam, a swindle, and a blatant fraud. Prove me wrong and take the million dollars". There was no response from McCormick. According to Iraqi investigators, the ADE 651, which was corruptly sold to the Baghdad bomb squad, was responsible for the deaths of hundreds of civilians who died as a result of terrorist bombs which were not detected at checkpoints. On April 23, 2013, McCormick was convicted of three counts of fraud at the Old Bailey in London; he was subsequently sentenced to ten years' imprisonment for his part in the ADE 651 scandal, which Randi was the first to expose. A public log of past participants in the Million Dollar Challenge exists. In 2015, after Randi's retirement, his foundation said the Million Dollar Challenge would no longer consider applicants unless they meet a set of minimum protocols, to reduce the amount of frivolous claims. Randi was involved in a variety of legal disputes, but said that he had "never paid even one dollar or even one cent to anyone who ever sued me". However, he said, he had paid out large sums to defend himself in these suits. Randi met magician Uri Geller in the early 1970s, and found Geller to be "Very charming. Likable, beautiful, affectionate, genuine, forward-going, handsome—everything!". But Randi viewed Geller as a con-man, and began a long effort to expose him as a fraud. According to Randi, Geller tried to sue him several times, accusing him of libel. Geller never won, save for a ruling in a Japanese court that ordered Randi to pay Geller one-third of one per cent of what Geller had requested. This ruling was cancelled, and the matter dropped, when Geller decided to concentrate on another legal matter. In May 1991, Geller sued Randi and CSICOP for $15 million on a charge of slander, after Randi told the International Herald Tribune that Geller had "tricked even reputable scientists" with stunts that "are the kind that used to be on the back of cereal boxes", referring to the old spoon-bending trick. The court dismissed the case and Geller had to settle at a cost to him of $120,000, after Randi produced a cereal box which bore instructions on how to do the spoon-bending trick. Geller's lawyer Don Katz was disbarred mid-way into this action and Geller ended up suing him. After failing to pay by the deadline imposed by the court, Geller was sanctioned an additional $20,000. Geller sued both Randi and CSICOP in the 1980s. CSICOP argued that the organization was not responsible for Randi's statements. The court agreed that including CSICOP was frivolous and dropped them from the action, leaving Randi to face the action alone, along with the legal costs. Geller was ordered to pay substantial damages, but only to CSICOP. In 1993, a jury in the U.S. District Court in Baltimore found Randi liable for defaming Eldon Byrd for calling him a child molester in a magazine story and a "shopping market molester" in a 1988 speech; however, the jury found that Byrd was not entitled to any monetary damages after hearing testimony that he had sexually molested and later married his sister-in-law. The jury also cleared the other defendant in the case, CSICOP. Late in 1996, Randi launched a libel suit against a Toronto-area psychic named Earl Gordon Curley. Curley had made multiple objectionable comments about Randi on Usenet. Despite suggesting to Randi on Usenet that Randi should sue—Curley's comments implying that if Randi did not sue, then his allegations must be true—Curley seemed entirely surprised when Randi actually retained Toronto's largest law firm and initiated legal proceedings. The suit was eventually dropped in 1998 when Earl Curley died at the age of 51 of "alcohol toxicity". Allison DuBois, on whose life the television series Medium was based.

A jury in the U.S. District Court in Baltimore found James Randi liable for defaming Eldon Byrd for calling him a child molester in a magazine story and a "shopping market molester" in a 1988 speech; however, the jury concluded that Byrd was not entitled to any monetary damages after hearing testimony that he had sexually molested and later married his sister-in-law. The jury also cleared CSICOP as a defendant. In late 1996, Randi filed a libel suit against Toronto-area psychic Earl Gordon Curley, who had made multiple objectionable comments about Randi on Usenet, including suggesting that if Randi did not sue, then his allegations must be true. Curley was surprised when Randi retained Toronto's largest law firm and initiated legal proceedings, and the suit was dropped in 1998 when Curley died at age 51 from "alcohol toxicity." Allison DuBois, whose life inspired the television series Medium, threatened Randi with legal action for using a photo of her from her website in a December 17, 2004, commentary without permission; Randi removed the photo and began using a caricature of DuBois starting with his December 23, 2005, commentary. In 2007, Sniffex, the producer of a dowsing bomb detection device, sued Randi and the JREF over comments regarding a government test in which the Sniffex device failed, and lost; Sniffex was later investigated and charged with fraud. Randi was a registered Democrat and, in April 2009, released a statement endorsing the legalization of most illegal drugs. He had been reported as a believer in Social Darwinist theories, though he denounced such ideologies and movements in 2013. Randi's parents were members of the Anglican Church but rarely attended services; he attended Sunday school at St. Cuthbert's Church in Toronto a few times as a child but stopped after receiving no response to his request for proof of the Church's teachings. In his essay "Why I Deny Religion, How Silly and Fantastic It Is, and Why I'm a Dedicated and Vociferous Bright," Randi, who identified as an atheist, argued that religious texts contain unbelievable accounts, such as the virgin birth, miracles of Jesus, and the parting of the Red Sea, describing the Virgin Mary as being "impregnated by a ghost" and questioning how Adam and Eve's family populated the Earth without incest, claiming that "The Wizard of Oz is more believable. And much more fun." Clarifying his view of atheism, Randi stated there are two types: one claiming no deity exists and the other claiming there is no evidence for a deity; he belonged to the latter because he could not prove the nonexistence of a deity, and religious people have an easier position by simply stating belief based on preference and reading. In An Encyclopedia of Claims, Frauds, and Hoaxes of the Occult and Supernatural (1995), he criticized Guru Maharaj Ji's meditation techniques, calling them convincing only to the "very naive." In 2003, he signed the Humanist Manifesto. Regarding his 2006 coronary artery bypass surgery, when asked if he was tempted by religious ideas about an afterlife, Randi said he allowed Daniel Dennett to speak for him, referencing Dennett's essay "Thank Goodness," in which Dennett expressed gratitude to medical staff and designers rather than a mythical being, stating, "Thank the goodness of the anaesthesiologist... Thank the goodness of the nurses who empty my bedpan... Thank the designers and makers of Dacron," and emphasized that "don't thank a mythical being." In a 2016 CSICon discussion with Kendrick Frazier, Randi stated that belief in a deity is an "unprovable claim" and "a rather ridiculous claim," an easy way to explain unanswerable phenomena, and concluded that belief in a god is "one of the most damaging things that infests humanity at this particular moment in history," though he saw signs of improvement. In the 1960s, while hosting his own radio show, Randi lived in a small house in Rumson, New Jersey, with a sign reading "Randi—Charlatan." In the 1970s and 1980s, he supported seven foster children. In 1987, Randi became a naturalized U.S. citizen, citing an incident during a tour with Alice Cooper when the Royal Canadian Mounted Police searched the band's lockers, ransacking the room but finding nothing illegal. In February 2006, Randi underwent coronary artery bypass surgery; during his hospitalization, weekly commentary updates were made by guests. He recovered and participated in organizing and attending The Amaz!ng Meeting in 2007 in Las Vegas, Nevada. In June 2009, Randi was diagnosed with colorectal cancer; small tumors were removed via laparoscopic surgery, and he announced the diagnosis at The Amaz!ng Meeting 7, stating he would begin chemotherapy soon and saying, "One day, I'm gonna die. That's all there is to it... I'm using a lot of oxygen and such—I think it's good use of oxygen myself, but of course, I'm a little prejudiced on the matter." He completed his final chemotherapy session in December 2009, describing it as less unpleasant than expected. In a video posted in April 2010, he stated he had been given a clean bill of health. In a 2010 blog entry, Randi came out as gay, inspired by the 2008 film Milk. On July 2, 2013, Randi married Venezuelan artist José Alvarez (born Deyvi Orangel Peña Arteaga) in Washington, D.C.; he first met Alvarez in 1986 at a Fort Lauderdale public library after moving to Florida. Alvarez, then known as Peña, had fled his native country due to threats for being homosexual. The alias "José Alvarez" was already in use in the U.S., causing legal and financial issues for the real Alvarez, who was arrested for identity theft and faced deportation. They resided in Plantation, Florida. In the 1993 documentary Secrets of the Psychics, Randi stated he never used narcotics, did not smoke or drink, because such substances could "fuzz the edges of my rationality" and he wanted to remain fully aware of reality, willing to give up comforting fantasies to live in a real world. In a video released in October 2017, Randi revealed he had suffered a minor stroke and was advised not to travel during recovery, so he would not attend CSICon 2017 in Las Vegas. Randi died at his home on October 20, 2020, at age 92; the James Randi Educational Foundation attributed his death to "age-related causes," and the Center for Inquiry described him as "the public face of skeptical inquiry, bringing a sense of fun and mischievousness to a serious mission," with Kendrick Frazier noting that despite his fierce challenges to nonsense, he was "a kind and gentle man." James Vernon the Younger (15 June 1677 – 17 April 1756) was a British government official, courtier, diplomat, and Whig politician who served in the House of Commons from 1708 to 1710. He served as British envoy to Denmark from 1702 to 1707 and was groom of bedchamber to the Prince of Denmark from 1702 to 1708. He was the eldest son of James Vernon and Mary Buck, daughter of Sir John Buck, 1st Baronet, of Hamby Grange, Lincolnshire; his father was Secretary of State under William III. Vernon was educated at Utrecht in 1690, at Rotterdam from 1690 to 1692, and again at Utrecht from 1696 to 1697. In 1691, he was appointed serjeant of the chandlery and in 1697 became an extra clerk of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council. His first parliamentary attempt was in a by-election in 1698 at Penryn, where he failed. From 1698 to 1700, he was groom of bedchamber to the Duke of Gloucester, from whose illness he contracted the disease that caused the Duke's death, and he recovered over several months. At the 1701 general election, he and his father contested St Mawes but were unsuccessful. From 1701 to 1702, he served as a Commissioner of the privy seal. In May 1702, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. In 1708, he was returned as Whig Member of Parliament for Cricklade. In early 1709, he supported the naturalization of the Palatines, and in 1710 voted for the impeachment of Dr Sacheverell, later expressing disappointment that Whig leaders had made a big deal about ‘a factious preacher much below their notice’. He became a Commissioner for excise in 1710, in compensation for his father's dismissal as teller of the Exchequer; the post, worth £800 a year, made him ineligible to stand in the 1710 general election. Vernon disengaged from politics and served the Tory administration as an official. In 1713, he married Arethusa Boyle, daughter of Charles Boyle, Lord Clifford of Lanesborough, and with whom he had issue, including Francis Vernon, who died in 1783 and was created 1st Earl of Shipbrook (I). When King George I ascended the throne in 1714 and the Whigs were in power, Vernon's Whig background benefited him; he retained his position and was appointed a Clerk of the Privy Council in 1715, a post he held for life. In 1716, he again served as Commissioner of the Privy Seal. He lost his excise post in 1726 due to a disagreement with Walpole, but it was restored in 1728. In 1727, he succeeded his father. Vernon devoted himself to religious and charitable works, including sponsoring the foundation of the colony of Georgia and serving as a trustee for Bray's charity. Though his government duties kept him in London, by 1733 he purchased an estate at Great Thurlow, Suffolk, for £15,000, and later built workhouses for several Suffolk parishes. He died on 15 or 17 April 1756 and was buried at Great Thurlow.

The Jammu division is a revenue and administrative division of the Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in the disputed Kashmir region, bordered by the Kashmir division to the north, Ladakh to the east, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to the south, and the Line of Control to the west, separating it from Pakistani-administered Kashmir. It consists of the districts of Jammu, Doda, Kathua, Ramban, Reasi, Kishtwar, Poonch, Rajouri, Udhampur, and Samba, with most of the land being hilly or mountainous, including the Pir Panjal Range that separates it from the Kashmir Valley and parts of the Great Himalayas in Doda and Kishtwar. The principal river is the Chenab. Jammu city is the largest city in the division and serves as the winter capital of Jammu and Kashmir, known as the "City of Temples" due to its numerous temples and shrines with prominent shikhars. It is a major pilgrimage center for Hindus, with a majority of the population practicing Hinduism, while Islam and Sikhism have strong cultural presence. Historically, the hilly regions south and southwest of the Kashmir Valley formed the Jammu Province of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, comprising 22 hill states during the declining Mughal Empire, known as the Dugar group of states, with "Durgara" being a medieval term linked to the region; the term appears in an 11th-century copper plate inscription from Chamba and is associated with Vallapura or Babbapura, though not mentioned in the Rajatarangini. Jammu is mentioned in Timur’s chronicles from 1398, and Raja Bhim Dev is noted as a supporter of Mubarah Shah against Jasrat, who conquered Jammu in 1423 after killing Bhim Dev and later appointed Manik Dev as a vassal. In the early 16th century, Jammu was described as a powerful state in the Punjab hills, and under Emperor Akbar, the hill kingdoms were brought under Mughal suzerainty with considerable autonomy. After the decline of Mughal power, the Jammu state under Raja Dhruv Dev of the Jamuwal family asserted dominance, reaching its peak under Raja Ranjit Dev (r. 1728–1780), who was widely respected. By the 1770s, the Sikh misls, including the Bhangi, Kanhaiya, and Sukerchakia, gained ascendancy, with the Bhangi misl attacking Jammu and forcing Ranjit Dev into tributary status, and Brij Lal Dev being defeated by Mahan Singh, who sacked and plundered the region. In 1808, Jammu was annexed to the Sikh Empire by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the son of Mahan Singh. Gulab Singh, a descendant of Dhruv Dev, joined the Sikh forces, earned a jagir near Jammu, and was made a hereditary Raja of Jammu in 1822 by Ranjit Singh, with his brother Dhyan Singh receiving Poonch and Chibhal and Suchet Singh receiving Ramnagar. By 1827, Gulab Singh had brought all principalities between Kashmir and Jammu under his control, placing the entire Jammu province under the three Jamwal brothers within the Sikh Empire. After Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s death in 1839, internal conflicts weakened the Sikh court, and Gulab Singh’s brothers and nephew were murdered. During the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–1846), Gulab Singh remained neutral but was later invited to Lahore and installed as prime minister, actions which contributed to a Sikh defeat. The British, seeking to weaken the Sikhs, demanded a war indemnity including all hilly territory between the Ravi and Indus rivers, which was transferred to Gulab Singh for 7.5 million Nanakshahee Rupees, establishing the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under the Dogra dynasty. During Dogra rule, Jammu and Srinagar alternated as capitals, six months to a year each, with Poonch and Chibhal granted as jagirs to Dhyan Singh’s sons, Jawahir Singh and Moti Singh; Jawahir Singh was exiled for conspiracies, Chibhal reverted to Gulab Singh, and Poonch remained under Moti Singh and his descendants under Jammu and Kashmir’s suzerainty. During the partition of India, Maharaja Hari Singh, facing a rebellion in the west and a Pashtun tribal invasion from Pakistan, acceded to India on 26–27 October 1947, after initially refusing to accede to either India or Pakistan due to the region’s mixed religious composition. India airlifted troops to repel the invasion, though major portions of Muzaffarabad, Poonch, and Mirpur remained under Pakistani control, with the rest incorporated into India under Article 370, granting autonomy. The division has eight geographical subregions: Ravi-Tawi Kandi plains, Shiwaliks, Pir Panjal belt, Chenab Valley, Bhaderwah Valley, Gandoh Valley, Paddar Valley, and Warwan-Marwah Valley. The climate varies with altitude: Jammu city has hot summers, rainy monsoons, and mild cold, foggy winters without snowfall, while higher hills are snow-capped; Patnitop is a popular winter resort, and the Vaishno Devi shrine is snow-covered in winter. The Banihal Pass often closes due to heavy snowfall. According to the 2011 census, the total population of Jammu Division is 5,350,811, with Scheduled Castes (Dalits) at 19.44% and Scheduled Tribes at 15–20%. Five districts—Rajouri, Poonch, Doda, Kishtwar, and Ramban—have Muslim majorities, while the southwest plains are predominantly Hindu. The Dogra ethnic group comprises approximately 47% of the population and is closely related to Punjabis. The Jammu district has 84% Hindus, 7% Muslims, and most of the remainder are Sikhs; Hindus are predominant in Jammu, Kathua, Samba, and Udhampur, and roughly half in Reasi. Hindus include native Dogras, Kashmiri Pandits, Punjabi Hindu migrants, and refugees from Kotli and Mirpur. Sikhs are mainly migrants from Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Dogri is spoken by a majority in Jammu, Udhampur, Kathua, Samba, and Reasi, with other languages including Gojri, Pahari, Kashmiri, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu. Hindu castes include 30% Brahmins, 27% Rajputs, 15% Thakkar (combined with Rajputs), 2% Jat, 10% Khatri, and 8% Megh and Chamar; Backward Classes make up 32%. Muslim-majority districts include Poonch and Rajouri, where Gujjar, Bakerwal, and Pahari groups are ethno-linguistically distinct from Kashmiri Muslims, and Kashmiri Muslims are present in Kishtwar, Ramban, Doda, and Reasi. The Jammu division has 10 districts as of April 2021, including Bhimber, Kotli, Mirpur, Poonch (western parts), Haveli, Bagh, and Sudhnati, which are now part of Pakistan-administered Jammu and Kashmir. Major political parties include Congress, BJP, National Conference, Jammu and Kashmir People's Democratic Party, and Jammu and Kashmir National Panthers Party. Various groups, including the BJP, have advocated for the separation of Jammu from Kashmir and its inclusion as a distinct entity in the Indian Union, citing neglect by Kashmir-centric administrations. In November 2020, IkkJutt Jammu was launched as a party demanding Jammu division’s separation and statehood and campaigned against the Roshni Act, declared unconstitutional by the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in 2020. The current legislative assembly structure (46 seats in Kashmir, 37 in Jammu) has been criticized for depriving Jammu of equal decision-making power, leading to repeated demands for a Delimitation Commission; after the state’s reclassification as a Union territory, a commission was established with retired Supreme Court judge Ranjana Prakash Desai as chairman. The Jammu Chamber of Commerce & Industry is the apex body for traders and industrialists in the region. Jammu is known for its landscape, ancient temples, Hindu shrines, Mubarak Mandi Palace, Amar Mahal Palace (now a museum), gardens, and forts. The Vaishno Devi shrine, located 48 km from Jammu in Katra on the Trikuta Hills at 1,700 meters, is a sacred cave shrine 30 meters long and 1.5 meters high, with shrines dedicated to Mahakali, Mahalakshmi, and Mahasarasvati; pilgrims trek 13 km to enter through a narrow opening and walk through icy waters. The shrine is associated with a legend of the goddess hiding from a demon. Purmandal, 35 km from Jammu, is an ancient holy place with Shiva temples and celebrates Shivratri with festive activities. Mansar Lake, 62 km from Jammu, is a 34 km² lake fringed by forest-covered hills, a holy site with legends similar to Lake Manasarovar, and features a shrine to Shesha, a six-headed serpent, with iron chains placed on a boulder; newlyweds perform three circumambulations for blessings. Nearby temples of Umapati Mahadev, Narasimha, and Durga are visited by devotees, and people take holy dips on festivals; certain communities perform the Mundan ceremony here. Boating facilities are provided by the Tourism Department.

Mansar Lake, located at 5.14694°E / 32.69611, is both an excursion destination and a holy site in Jammu, sharing the legend and sanctity of Lake Manasarovar. On the eastern bank of the lake stands a shrine dedicated to Shesha, a mythological snake with six heads, featuring a large boulder with iron chains possibly representing small serpents guarding the deity. Newlyweds perform three circumambulations (Parikarma) around the lake to seek Shesha’s blessings. Nearby are ancient temples of Umapati Mahadev and Narasimha, as well as a temple of Durga, visited by large numbers of devotees who take a holy dip in the lake during festivals. Certain Hindu communities perform the Mundan ceremony (first haircut) of their male children here. The lake offers boating facilities managed by the Tourism Department. With its religious significance and natural heritage, Mansar Lake is popular among tourists due to its flora and fauna. The lake is encircled by an illuminated path with viewing decks for observing seasonal birds, tortoises, and fish species. A nearby wildlife sanctuary houses spotted deer, neelgai, and water birds such as cranes and ducks. Visitors can also witness the traditional lifestyle of Gujjar and Backarwals, who live in open Kullhas in the hills around the lake and wear ethnic costumes. The Mansar Lake road connects to a major route linking Pathankot to Udhampur, a strategically important town on National Highway No. 1A. This by-pass road avoids Jammu city, and Surinsar Lake, linked to Mansar, is 24 km (15 mi) from Jammu via this route. Bahu Fort, situated about 5 km from Jammu city on the left bank of the Tawi river, is one of the oldest forts in the city, originally constructed by Raja Bahulochan over 3000 years ago and later improved by Dogra rulers. Inside the fort is a temple dedicated to Goddess Kali, known as Bave Wali Mata, the presiding deity of Jammu. Pilgrims gather here every Tuesday and Sunday for "Tawi flowing worship," and the fort is now surrounded by a terraced garden that is a favorite picnic spot. Bagh-e-Bahu, a Mughal-age garden on the Tawi riverbank, offers views of the old city and river, with a small canteen on one side. On the by-pass road behind Bahu Fort, the city forest surrounds the ancient Mahamaya Temple overlooking the Tawi river, with a small garden surrounded by woods providing a commanding view of the city. Opposite Bahu Fort, a temple dedicated to Mahamaya, a Dogra-descended goddess who died 14 centuries ago fighting invaders, stands. The present temple, built shortly after Maharaja Gulab Singh’s coronation in 1822 and known as Bawey Wali Mata or Mahakali, is considered second only to Mata Vaishno Devi in mystical power. The Raghunath Temple, located at the city center and built in 1857, was initiated by Maharaja Gulab Singh in 1835 CE and completed by his son Maharaja Ranbir Singh in 1860 CE. The temple’s inner walls are covered with gold on three sides, and it features many galleries with hundreds of thousands of shaligrams. It has seven shrines, each with its own tower, making it the largest temple complex in northern India. Though 130 years old, it boasts one of the richest collections of ancient Sanskrit scriptures and manuscripts in its library. The temple’s architecture blends Mughal influences with gold-plated interiors, and its main sanctuary is dedicated to Lord Rama, the eighth incarnation of Vishnu and the patron deity of the Dogras. The temple also houses a Sanskrit library with rare manuscripts. Along the Tawi river, the Peer Kho Cave temple, believed to be where Ramayana character Jamvant (the bear god) meditated, and the Panchbakhtar and Ranbireshwar temples dedicated to Lord Shiva exist. The Ranbireshwar Temple, located on Shalimar Road near the New Secretariat and built by Maharaja Ranbir Singh in 1883 CE, features a central Shiva lingam measuring 2.3 meters (7 ft 7 in) and twelve crystal lingams ranging from 150 to 380 mm (5.9 to 15.0 in), along with galleries containing thousands of Shiva lingams on stone slabs. The Shivkhori cave shrine, located in Reasi District, depicts a natural shivlingum and is one of the most venerated cave shrines of Lord Shiva in the region. The cave is approximately 150 meters (490 ft) long and contains a 4 ft (1.2 m) high Svayambhu Lingum that constantly bathes in milky lime fluid dripping from the ceiling. The first entrance is wide enough to accommodate 300 devotees at once, and the inner chamber is smaller. The cave contains natural images of various Hindu deities and is known as "the Home of Gods." An annual 3-day Shiv Khori mela is held on Maha Shivratri, usually in February or the first week of March, attracting thousands of pilgrims from across the state and beyond. To manage the growing influx, the Shiv Khori Shrine Board has developed facilities including a Shrine Guest House at Ransoo (cost: Rs. 19 lakh), a reception center and pony shed (cost: ₹7.959 million or US$94,000), tile work on a 3-kilometer-long track, plantation of ornamental and medicinal plants, and park development. Other planned improvements include electrification of the cave with modern systems, oxygen and electric generators, exhaust fans, shelter sheds with toilet facilities near the site, 15 shelter sheds along the route from Ransoo to the cave, a railing from the base camp to the cave, a 15,000/EfnrKing water reservoir, proper sanitation, a 25 kV electric transformer, a clock room, permanent bus services from Katra, Udhampur, and Jammu, a police post, a dispensary, and an STD PCO. Recently, the management of Shiv Khori has been transferred to the Sri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board. The Chandi Maa temple in Machel village, District Kishtwar, is about 290 km (180 mi) from Jammu. During the annual 'Chhadi Yatra' in August, thousands visit the shrine, which was first visited in 1981 by Thakur Kulveer Singh of Bhaderwah. Since 1987, he has organized the Chhadi Yatra annually. Travel agents and private cabs from Jammu, Udhampur, Ramnagar, and Bhaderwah arrange transport; the journey takes about 10 hours by road from Jammu to Gulabgarh, the base camp, with a 32 km foot journey that usually takes two days. People often stay overnight in villages along the way, and roadside 'langers' (free food points) are set up. The government provides basic amenities. A helicopter service from Jammu and Gulabgarh is available, with a helipad just 100 meters (330 ft) from the shrine. Jammu’s major attractions include the revolving restaurant Falak on the top floor of KC Residency hotel, Ragunath Bazar as the main tourist and shopping district, and Gandhi Nagar’s Gole Market on Apsara Road. Green Belt Park along Green Belt Road and Rajinder Park on Canal Road—situated between two canals and featuring a large fountain lit at night with a children’s area—are popular spots. The city has the "Big Bazaar" at Jewel Chowk and shopping malls such as 'Wave - The Wave Mall' and Palm Island near Canal Road. Bahu-Plaza in Trikuta Nagar is a commercial hub and youth hangout, housing most of the corporate sector and mobile phone companies including Airtel, BSNL, Vodafone, Aircel, and Tata Indicom. It also hosts cinema halls such as KC Cineplex, Wave Cinema, Palm Cinema, and a PVR near KC Cineplex. Jammu is known for its food specialties including chocolate barfi, sund panjeeri, patisa, and local dishes like rajma with rice and kalaadi, a processed cheese made with calf rennet in buffalo milk. Fiddlehead fern (kasrod), a GI-tagged item, is highly valued for taste and medicinal properties and is consumed as a vegetable or pickle. Kohlrabi, known as kaddam in Jammu, is another specialty, often eaten with rice. Kalari cheese, made in the Ramnagar region, is famous throughout the state. Dogri food specialties include ambal, khatta meat, kulthein di dal, dal patt, maa da madra, rajma, and auriya. Pickles typical of Jammu include those made from kasrod, girgle, mango with saunf, zimikand, tyaoo, seyoo, and potatoes. Auriya is a potato-based dish, and during weddings, kayoor and sund are prepared. Lohri, celebrated a day before Makar Sankranti, marks the end of Poh (Pausha) month and the beginning of Magha month in the Hindu solar calendar, known as Maghi Sangrand. It is celebrated with traditions such as Chajja making, Hiran Dance, Dandaraas, and preparing Lohri garlands. Children make a peacock replica called Chajja, carry it to houses, and perform a special dance with it, striking sticks in rhythm with drums (Dandaraas). In the hills, a special Hiran Dance is performed where dancers disguise as deer and visit homes with auspicious ceremonies and food. On Lohri, children wear garlands of groundnuts, dry fruits, and candies, and eat Tilcholi—a mixture of sesame, rice, and groundnuts. A pageant of Sassi-Punnu, two lovers from Sindhi folk tradition, is also performed on camels. The next day, Makar Sankranti is celebrated as Uttarain (from Sanskrit: Uttarayana), also called Attrain or Attrani. It is observed on the fourth day of Krishna Paksha of Magha month and is also known as Maghi Sangrand. Dogras observe a tradition of Mansana (charity) of Khichdi of Maah Dal, which is prepared on this day and thus the day is referred to as 'Khichdi wala Parva.' It is also a day for sending food to married daughters. Fairs are held on holy places and pilgrimage sites. People take holy baths in the Devika river and visit pilgrimages like Uttar Behni and Purmandal. This day is also celebrated as the birth anniversary of Baba Ambo ji, a local deity. At the Vasuki temple in Bhaderwah, the idols of Vasuki Nag are covered on Magh Sankranti and uncovered after three months on Vaisakha Sankranti. Sankashti Chaturthi, celebrated on the fourth day of Shukla Paksha of Magha month, is dedicated to Lord Ganesha and is observed by Dogra women who perform Arghya to Chandrama at night, donating and eating Bhugga (Til Jaggery mixture) and radish during the fast. Basant Panchami, dedicated to Goddess Saraswati, is celebrated with yellow, saffron, or orange clothing, saffron-colored food offerings, and folk songs like Aayi Basant and Paala Udant. This day is significant for Dogras as it marks the founding of the Dogri Sanstha in 1944. Gauri Tritiya, observed on the fourth day of Shukla Paksha of Magha month in hill districts like Bhaderwah, Doda, Kishtwar, and Ramban, is similar to Karwa Chauth but involves a fast completed after Gauri Puja. Married women worship Goddess Gauri for the health and longevity of their husbands, and the festivity lasts three days. During this time, women visit neighbors to offer 'Thel' (respect) and receive blessings of 'Suhagan Bho' (live long your husband). Holi is celebrated traditionally in Jammu with Holika Dahan on the eve and color play the next day. Earlier, people used to wear headgears called Patangi made of colored paper and silver ribbons. A Dogra sweet dish, Khaste (similar to Gujjiya), is prepared. A three-day fair is held at Narsingh Dev temple in Kathua. Rama Navami, the birth of Lord Rama, is celebrated with religious fervor and gaiety across Jammu, coinciding with the end of the nine-day Navaratra festival. A special function is held at the Raghunath Temple, where large numbers of devotees offer obeisance to Lord Rama. Even during Dogra rule, the rulers would personally visit the Raghunath Mandir to offer worship to Shri Rama.

Women in Jammu are encouraged to offer ‘Thel’ (respect) to other women and receive in return their blessing ‘Suhagan Bho’ (Live long your husband). Holi is celebrated traditionally in Jammu, with Holika Dahan performed on the eve of the festival, followed by color-playing the next day. Historically, people used to decorate themselves with special headgears called Patangi, made of colored paper and silver ribbons. A Dogra sweet dish named Khaste, similar to Gujjiya, is prepared on this day. A three-day fair is held at the Narsingh Dev temple in Kathua. Rama Navami, marking the birth of Shri Rama, is celebrated with religious enthusiasm and gaiety throughout Jammu and coincides with the culmination of the nine-day Navaratra festival. A special function is held at the historical Raghunath Temple in Jammu city, where many devotees offer obeisance to Lord Rama; even during the Dogra rule, rulers would personally visit the Raghunath Mandir to worship Shri Rama, their patron deity. In addition to worship, discourses on Bhagwan Ram’s life and the Ramayana are conducted. On this occasion, a Shobha Yatra is organized, featuring images of Shri Rama, Mata Sita, and Lakshman, along with tableaux depicting scenes from the Ramayana, which are taken in a grand procession. Devotees shower flower petals on the Yatra, and market unions and Hindu organizations organize Bhandaras. Baisakhi originates from the first month of the Hindu Vikram calendar and is celebrated on the first day of the Vaisakh month, marking Mesha Sankranti; it is also known as 'Basoa' in Dogri. Devotees take a ritual dip in rivers, canals, and ponds early in the morning, and in Dogra households, a Puja is performed afterward, with a portion of the food crop offered to deities. The new fruit of the year is enjoyed on this day. A ritual bath at the Tawi river during Baisakhi is common in Jammu. In Udhampur, Baisakhi is celebrated on the banks of the Devika river, where devotees enjoy folk songs for three days. At Sudhmahadev, the festival is celebrated with great pomp, including a folk song competition and vendors setting up stalls for eatables. Many people visit the Nagbani temple to witness the grand New Year celebration. Baisakhi is considered a harvest festival and is seen as auspicious, especially for marriages. Celebrations include Dogri Bhangra, which is closely related to the Punjabi variant in actions, costumes, and songs. The festival is marked by numerous fairs, with Airwan in Kathua hosting a Baisakhi fair attended by 10,000 people as per the 1961 Census. Around 15,000 pilgrims visit the 700-year-old Subar Nag Devta temple in Bhaderwah every year on Baisakhi. Other Baisakhi fairs are held in Doda Bridge and Ramban. A major festival is held twice a year at the Kali Temple in Bahu Fort. Chaitre Chaudash is celebrated at Uttar Behni and Purmandal, located about 25 km (16 mi) and 28 km (17 mi) from Jammu respectively; Uttar Behni derives its name from the Devak River (locally known as Gupt Ganga) flowing in a northerly direction. Purmandal, 39 km (24 mi) from Jammu city, celebrates Shivratri for three days, marking the marriage of Lord Shiva to Goddess Parvati, with people from Jammu visiting the Peer Khoh Cave Temple, Ranbireshwar Temple, and Panjbhaktar Temple. If one visits Jammu during Shivratri, celebrations are observed almost everywhere. Both Chaitre Chaudash and Shivratri are celebrated similarly. Dhamdeh, also known as Dharma Dhihada or Dharma Divas, is celebrated on the Sankranti of the Aashadha month. People take a ritual bath and perform Mansana (charity) of hand fans, water pitchers, and seasonal fruits like melons, offered in the name of Pitras (ancestors). A major celebration involves offering sweet water drinks and food to the poor and needy. Similar rituals are observed on Nirjala Ekadashi (celebrated on Jyestha Shukla Ekadashi), where a strict Vrata is observed in honor of Lord Vishnu. Rutt Raahde is a festival celebrated by Dogra women of all ages from Aashada Sankranti to Shravana Sankranti, with the last day, Shravana Sankranti, referred to as Sakolade or Minjraan. Young girls and women collect broken earthen pitcher necks, insert seeds of Kharif crops into them, and create Raahde, which are decorated with rangoli patterns using natural colors. Every Sunday, women gather at the site to sing folk songs and enjoy eatables like Rutt, Gheur, and Pudas. On the final day of the festival, Badda Rutt, women assemble again, sing folk songs, enjoy eatables, and immerse the Raahde in water bodies. Shravana Sankranti, also known as Sakolade (named after the ear ornaments worn on this day), is also referred to as Minjraan in parts of Himachal. Janmashtami in Dogri is known as Thongren Da Vrat, meaning a Vrata for Thakur (Lord Krishna). Adults observe a fast in honor of Sri Krishna, while children and youth enjoy kite flying. Girls and women decorate their palms with Teera, a dye from an indigenous plant. Some families keep cereal grains in the name of Kul Devtas, Pitras (ancestors), and family members, known as Deyaa Parna. These grains are offered to the wood of a holy tree called Jhand, known as Jhand Puja. The wood is covered with sacred cloth called shoaath, and clay sculptures of a couple and their children are placed on it and worshipped. They are offered Kheer (without sugar) and Makkhan. Dropads (a type of chapati) are then offered to cows, a practice known as ‘dropad mansnaa’. Some people also enjoy swinging on trees known as peengan. At night, children are dressed up like deities, and towns and cities witness processions. At midnight, Sund Panjeeri is offered as Naivedya to Sri Krishna. Vatsa Dwadashi is celebrated on the twelfth day of Krishna Paksha of Bhadrapada month as Bacch Dua, and Durvashtami on the eighth day of Shukla Paksha of Bhadrapada month as Drubadi. In both festivals, women prepare small-sized idols or sculptures of calves using wheat dough, which are worshipped on water bodies. Soaked black chickpeas and Durva grass are used for Puja, and Dogra dishes like Rutt and Dropad are offered as Naivedya. The festival is celebrated on the first day of the solar month of the Hindu calendar, i.e., Bhadrapada, and holds special significance in the Ramban district of Jammu division. People visit the Chandrabhaga river and offer floral offerings. It is popularly known as Singh Sankrant and is locally traced to the Pandavas. Tulsi Puja is performed in Dogra families from Kartika Shukla Ekadashi to Kartika Purnima, a five-day period known as Panj Bhikham (Bhishma Panchak). During Tulsi Puja, families decorate the Tulsi plant pot and write 'Ram Ram' on it, known as Tulsi Da Chauntra in Dogri. The plant is covered with a Red Dupatta or Chunni. A fast is observed on Kartika Shukla Ekadashi in honor of Lord Vishnu and Tulsi Mata. Women light Diyas from Ekadashi to Purnima on the Tulsi plant, a ceremony known as Deeve in Dogri. Some families may also organize a Tulsi Vivah with Shaligram, as it is believed that Tulsi has affinity with Shaligram. An annual fair is held in honor of Baba Jitto, a simple and honest farmer who committed suicide rather than submit to unjust demands of a local landlord to part with his crop, having died in the village of Jhiri, 14 km from Jammu. A legend has grown around Baba Jitto, and his followers gather at Jhiri on the appointed day from across North India, revere him for his compassion, courage, and honesty. Though the pilgrimage to Mata Vaishno Devi is a year-round event, a visit during the Navratras is considered the most auspicious. To highlight regional culture, heritage, and traditions, the State Tourism Department has instituted the Navratri Festival as an annual event during September or October for the nine auspicious days of the Navratras. A large number of tourists visit the shrine during this period, showcasing religious traditions and popular culture. An eight-day fair is held at the Narsingh and Annapurna temples in Ghagwal of Samba district, involving a procession of the deity on a chariot, known as Rath Kharda Mela. Thousands of devotees from neighboring states like Punjab and Himachal Pradesh and other parts of Jammu attend. People from hilly areas such as Basohli, Doda, Kishtwar, Bani, and Dudu Basantgarh set up stalls to sell handicrafts and woolen items like Pattus, blankets, and shawls. During the fair, the temple is decorated with flowers and lights. Devotees visit to pay obeisance to Bhagwan Narsimha, and a Bhandara is organized. Local farmers sow their fields in the name of Bhagwan Narsimha and offer a portion of the harvest to the temple during the fair. Besides Ghagwal, the Rath Kharda Mela is also held in Ramgarh tehsil of Udhampur district, Parnala village in Billawar tehsil, and Hatli village in Kathua. Shivaratri, meaning 'Shiva's night,' is a significant festival for Hindus, especially those of Kashmiri origin in Jammu. On this day, Lord Shiva and his spouse Parvati are worshipped with great devotion. Esoterically, it symbolizes the mystic union of Jiva (individual soul) with Paramatma (the Supreme Godhead), representing spiritual realization where the world of relativity fades and perfect peace prevails. Alongside worship, social and cultural gatherings are observed, with people rejoicing and exchanging greetings. The Jamnalal Bajaj Award is an Indian honor recognizing contributions to Gandhian values, community service, and social development. Established in 1978 by the Jamnalal Bajaj Foundation of the Bajaj Group, the award is presented annually in four categories and is typically conferred by the President, Vice President, Prime Minister of India, or a prominent national figure. The foundation, currently led by Rahul Bajaj, was founded in 1977 in memory of Jamnalal Bajaj, the group's founder, a philanthropist, and a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi. The award ceremony is held on 4 November, which is Jamnalal Bajaj's birth anniversary. Each recipient receives a citation, a trophy, and a cheque worth Rs Ten lakh.
