Janet Louise Hubert (born January 13, 1956) is an American film and television actress and dancer best known for playing the original Vivian Banks on the sitcom The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air from its first season in 1990 until the end of its third season in 1993. She was nominated for an NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Actress in a Comedy Series in 1991 for her performance. Her role as Mignon on the digital series King Ester earned her a Daytime Emmy Award nomination in 2020. Hubert was born in Chicago, Illinois, and spent her early years growing up on Chicago's South Side; at age nine, she moved with her family to rural Chicago. She won a scholarship to the Juilliard School in New York City but did not complete her studies. After performing in the national tour of Dancin', she made her Broadway debut in 1981 in the ensemble of The First, a musical about Jackie Robinson. She created the role of Tantomile in the original Broadway production of Cats and also understudied Grizabella and Demeter. She left Cats in April 1983 to join the national tour of Sophisticated Ladies, opposite Dee Dee Bridgewater and Gregg Burge. After being allegedly fired by the show's creators, Hubert's character, Aunt Viv, was recast and played by Daphne Maxwell Reid for the remainder of the series. Will Smith, the show's star, claimed that Hubert "brought her problems to work," and rumors suggested he fired her due to this, though Hubert has denied this, stating she left after being told she had two months and a half left on set and could not work on another project. Her role as Aunt Viv was subsequently played by Daphne Maxwell Reid. Hubert appeared in a 2002 episode of Friends as Chandler's boss. In 2005, she began playing the recurring role of Lisa Williamson, mother of attorney Evangeline Williamson, on One Life to Live, with occasional appearances since then. She appeared as Michel Gerard's mother in an episode of Gilmore Girls and has made appearances on episodes of All My Children, NYPD Blue, The Bernie Mac Show, and Tyler Perry's House of Payne. In November 2018, it was announced she had been cast on General Hospital, where she made her debut as Yvonne on December 7, 2018. Hubert appeared in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air Reunion on HBO Max in November 2020, where she and Smith spoke for the first time since her departure. Hubert discussed personal issues, including domestic violence, and clarified she had not been fired. Smith admitted he was neither "sensitive" nor "perceptive" at the time, attributing his behavior to being "very young" and "immature," and stated that being a parent had taught him to understand her situation, apologizing for his actions. Hubert then joined the rest of the guests at the reunion. She appeared on FX's Pose in season 3 as a family member of Billy Porter's character, Pray Tell, alongside Jackée Harry and Anna Maria Horsford. In 2022, she appeared on The Ms. Pat Show as the title character's mother-in-law, Jewell. In 1990, Hubert married James Whitten, who was verbally and physically abusive toward her until their separation in 1994; from this marriage, she gave birth to a son, Elijah Isaac Whitten. She has been married to Larry Kraft since 2005. Hubert suffers from osteoporosis and serves as ambassador for the National Osteoporosis Foundation.

Janice Burgess (March 1, 1952 – March 2, 2024) was an American television executive, screenwriter, and producer for Nickelodeon. She created the Nick Jr. series The Backyardigans and served as a writer and story editor for Nickelodeon's revival of Winx Club, both of which were produced at the Nickelodeon Animation Studio. Burgess joined Nickelodeon in 1995 as executive-in-charge of production. Born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, she grew up in the Squirrel Hill neighborhood and attended the Ellis School. She frequently played in her backyard, which later inspired The Backyardigans, describing it as a "wonderful, happy, safe place" where "you could have these great adventures just romping around. From there, you could go anywhere or do anything." She loved musicals, and her mother frequently played a wide array of music. Planning to become an art historian, she graduated from Brandeis University in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in art history. According to an interview with Investor's Business Daily, Burgess did not enjoy traveling "in art circles with collectors and high society," so she sought a different career after college and volunteered at public television station WQED, where she managed craft services. In the early 1990s, she held positions at the Children's Television Workshop, including as an assistant travel coordinator for 3-2-1 Contact and project manager for Ghostwriter, where she coordinated tie-in magazine and teacher materials with the show's content. She was notified of a job opening at Nickelodeon and joked she interviewed "about 11,000 times." She was hired as executive in charge of production for Nick Jr., overseeing the development of Blue's Clues and Little Bill, and later became vice president of Nickelodeon's Nick Jr. division. While working as an executive, she attended scripting and concept development meetings and helped creative teams with characters and storylines. She was given a creative opportunity by senior vice president Brown Johnson, who asked her to develop a new Nick Jr. show. Burgess produced a pilot episode called "Me and My Friends" at Nickelodeon Studios Florida in 1998, a live-action, full-body puppet show featuring music and dance, which was not picked up for a full series. Several months later, Brown Johnson asked her to retool the concept, as he liked the characters and music and believed the show would work better in animation. Using the characters from "Me and My Friends," she wrote a second pilot produced at Nickelodeon's New York studio in 2002, which was renamed The Backyardigans and greenlit for a 20-episode season. Reflecting on the shift, Burgess said, "Sometimes your first attempt is just not all that great. In this case, my second attempt was much better." The Backyardigans premiered on Nickelodeon on October 11, 2004. Burgess served as executive producer for the show throughout its four-season run. In 2006, she described her work positively: "making The Backyardigans has become sort of like an adventure that I go on with my friends. Of course, we get paid, but we do get to be carefree in our work, enjoy each other, hang around a lot, travel a little bit, and make up stuff." She drew inspiration from action films, such as Die Hard and Terminator 2, when writing episodes, aiming to adapt high-stakes stories for young children in a safe, non-scary, and non-imitatable way. The series received eight Daytime Emmy Award nominations, and Burgess won the 2008 Emmy for Outstanding Special Class Animated Program. After The Backyardigans concluded in 2010 with its fourth and final season, much of the staff, including Burgess, regrouped to work on Nickelodeon's Winx Club, where she served as a writer, story editor, and creative consultant. Burgess died in hospice care in Manhattan on March 2, 2024, the day after her 72nd birthday. She was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018, six years before her death.

Jay-Z & Ciara Live (also known as Jay-Z Live with Special Guest Ciara) was a 2009 summer concert tour headlined by American rapper Jay-Z and American R&B singer Ciara, in support of their respective albums The Blueprint 3 and Fantasy Ride. The six-city United States tour took place from July 2 to July 12, 2009, originally scheduled to have ten dates but later reduced to six. The opening act was rapper Fabolous. Ciara did not perform at the first show for an unknown reason but appeared at the second concert at The Palms. The July 12 date in Atlanta, Georgia, was cancelled due to heavy rain. All tour dates were announced and confirmed on Ciara's official website. The tour received positive to favorable reviews from critics. The Los Angeles Times gave the entire tour a very positive review, noting that Ciara worked hard during her brief set, performing impressive acrobatics with her four dancers. Her street-tough image was highlighted through her wearing ripped jeans and leather vests, resembling a sleeked-up girl gang, though her delivery was unfocused and she often appeared unenjoying, lip-syncing to half the songs. The paper also observed that she didn't seem to be enjoying herself. Meanwhile, Jay-Z received a positive review for his energetic and engaging set, which kept the audience highly excited. The review emphasized that Jay-Z's performances are fun because he is exceptionally skilled at crafting sharp, funny, and resonant thoughts using his nimble verbal delivery, and he interacts well with the audience.

The Jaynes Covered Bridge is a historic covered bridge located in northern Waterville, Vermont, carrying Codding Hollow Road across the North Branch Lamoille River. Constructed around 1877, it is one of three 19th-century covered bridges in Waterville and one of five that span the North Branch Lamoille River within a five-mile stretch. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974. Situated a short distance east of Vermont Route 109 on Codding Hill Road, the bridge is a single-span queen post truss structure measuring 56.5 feet (17.2 m) in length and 15 feet (4.6 m) in width, with a 12-foot (3.7 m) roadway width accommodating one lane. It features a gabled metal roof and vertical board siding that ends before the eaves. The bridge deck has been replaced with steel I-beams covered by wooden planking, meaning the trusses now support only the superstructure, and the joints between the truss posts and diagonals have been reinforced with steel plating. The bridge is one of three period bridges in the town that span the same river, and together with two others in the neighboring town of Belvidere, it represents one of Vermont's highest concentrations of bridges on a single waterway. The builder of the bridge is unknown. Media related to the Jaynes Covered Bridge is available at Wikimedia Commons.

Jean Galloway Bissell (June 9, 1936 – February 4, 1990) was a South Carolina attorney who advanced to a high-ranking position in banking and later served as a United States circuit judge on the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Born in Due West, South Carolina, she obtained a Bachelor of Science degree from the University of South Carolina in 1956 and a Bachelor of Laws from the University of South Carolina School of Law in 1958. From 1958 to 1971, she practiced law in Greenville, South Carolina, and then continued in Columbia, South Carolina, until 1976. From 1976 to 1984, she served as an executive at South Carolina National Bank in Columbia, where she became the highest-ranking female executive among the 100 largest bank holding companies in the United States. During the 1970s and early 1980s, she also lectured at the University of South Carolina. On May 24, 1984, President Ronald Reagan nominated Bissell to a newly created seat on the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, established by 96 Stat. 25. This nomination followed Reagan’s earlier attempt in 1982 to appoint Sherman Unger, a United States Department of Commerce official, to the same seat, which failed due to significant opposition and Unger’s death from terminal cancer in late 1983. Bissell was confirmed by the United States Senate on June 8, 1984, and received her commission on June 11, 1984, becoming the first female South Carolina lawyer to serve as a federal judge. She served on the court until her death. Bissell died of cancer on February 4, 1990, at Sibley Memorial Hospital in Washington, D.C., at the age of 53.

Jeffrey Edward Epstein (January 20, 1953 – August 10, 2019) was an American financier, human trafficker, child sex offender, and serial rapist. Born in Brooklyn, New York, to Pauline "Paula" Stolofsky and Seymour George Epstein, both of whom were Jewish and married in 1952, he grew up in the Sea Gate neighborhood of Coney Island with his brother Mark. Epstein was nicknamed "Bear" and Mark was called "Puggie." He attended public schools, including Public School 188 and Mark Twain Junior High School, where he earned money tutoring classmates and was described as "sweet and generous," "quiet and nerdy," and "very smart in math." In 1967, he attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen, where he showed musical talent. He graduated from Lafayette High School at age 16 after skipping two grades and studied mathematical physiology at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University from 1971 to 1974, leaving without a degree. In 1974, at age 21, he began teaching physics and mathematics at the Dalton School on Manhattan’s Upper East Side despite lacking a teaching credential. During his time there, he allegedly showed inappropriate behavior toward underage female students, including flirting and attending parties where young people were drinking. He became acquainted with Alan Greenberg, CEO of Bear Stearns, whose daughter, Lynne Koeppel, testified that Epstein influenced a parent to advocate for him to Greenberg. After being dismissed from Dalton in June 1976 for "poor performance," Greenberg offered him a job at Bear Stearns. Epstein joined Bear Stearns in 1976 as a junior assistant, quickly advancing to become an options trader and advisor to wealthy clients such as Edgar Bronfman. In 1980, he became a limited partner and in 1981 was asked to leave for a "Reg D violation" according to his sworn testimony. He remained close to Greenberg and James Cayne, the bank’s later CEO, and was a client until Bear Stearns collapsed in 2008. In August 1981, Epstein founded Intercontinental Assets Group Inc. (IAG), which he described as a high-level bounty hunter helping clients recover stolen funds, including Spanish heiress Ana Obregón in 1982 after the collapse of Drysdale Government Securities. In the 1980s, Epstein traveled extensively between the U.S., Europe, and the Middle East, meeting Steven Hoffenberg through Douglas Leese and John Mitchell. He possessed an Austrian passport with a false name and residence listed as Saudi Arabia. Hoffenberg hired Epstein in 1987 as a consultant for Towers Financial Corporation, a collection agency, paying him $25,000 per month (equivalent to $69,000 in 2024). Together, they operated as corporate raiders, attempting to take over Pan American World Airways in 1987 and Emery Air Freight Corp. in 1988. In 1993, Towers Financial imploded as one of the largest Ponzi schemes in U.S. history, losing over $450 million (equivalent to $1 billion in 2024), with Hoffenberg claiming Epstein was intimately involved; Epstein left by 1989 and was never charged. In 1988, Epstein founded J. Epstein & Company to manage assets of clients with over $1 billion in net worth. His only publicly known billionaire client was Leslie Wexner, chairman and CEO of L Brands (Victoria's Secret), whom he met in 1986 through mutual acquaintances. Wexner granted Epstein full power of attorney in 1991, allowing him to manage finances, sign checks, and handle property transactions. Epstein managed Wexner’s wealth, including the construction of his yacht, the Limitless, and helped models like Stacey Williams. He also served as a global talent scout for Victoria's Secret, using his position to sexually manipulate young women. By 1995, Epstein was a director of the Wexner Foundation and Wexner Heritage Foundation and president of Wexner’s Property, which developed New Albany, Ohio. He earned millions in fees from managing Wexner’s affairs and frequently corresponded with L Brands executives. In 1996, Epstein renamed his firm to Financial Trust Company and relocated it to St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, to reduce federal income taxes by 90 percent, leveraging connections with JP Morgan banker Jes Staley. In 2002, his financial-administrative staff numbered 150 employees across three locations. In 2012, JP Morgan general counsel Stephen Cutler criticized Epstein as "not an honorable person" and claimed Epstein lied during a meeting with Staley and Cutler, citing Bill Gates as a character reference; the bank did not terminate Epstein until 2013, coinciding with Staley’s departure, after increased federal regulatory pressure. Epstein then moved his business to Deutsche Bank. According to Forbes in 2025, the majority of Epstein’s wealth between 1999 and 2018 came from $490 million in fees—$200 million from Leslie Wexner and $170 million from Leon Black—with the remaining $310 million from investment returns, totaling $600 million at death. He donated $50,000 to Democrat Bill Richardson's 2002 and 2006 gubernatorial campaigns, $15,000 to Democrat Gary King's 2004 Attorney General campaign, $35,000 to King's 2014 gubernatorial campaign, $10,000 to Jim Baca's land commission bid, and $2,000 to Santa Fe County Sheriff Jim Solano's 2010 reelection bid. In 1991, Epstein was one of four donors pledging $2 million for Rosovsky Hall at Harvard University. In the 1990s, he donated $10,000 to the White House Historical Association. In 2000, Epstein established the Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation to fund science research and education; prior to 2003, it funded Martin Nowak's research at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton; in 2003, he pledged $30 million to create a mathematical biology and evolutionary dynamics program at Harvard, which was run by Martin Nowak, though the actual amount received was $6.5 million. Epstein was friends with and funded Gerald Edelman, Stephen Kosslyn, Danny Hillis, and Lawrence Krauss. In 2019, Forbes deleted a 2013 article calling Epstein "one of the largest backers of cutting edge science" after The New York Times revealed the author, Drew Hendricks, had been paid $600 to submit it falsely as his own. According to attorney Gerald B. Lefcourt, Epstein was "part of the original group that conceived of the Clinton Global Initiative" and donated $25,000 to the Clinton Foundation in 2006. Epstein co-organized a science event with illusionist and skeptic Al Seckel called the Mindshift Conference in 2010 on his private island Little Saint James, with attendees including scientists Murray Gell-Mann, Leonard Mlodinow, and Gerald Jay Sussman. The true extent of Epstein's donations is unknown; the Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation fails to disclose information routinely disclosed by other charities. In 2015, the New York Attorney General attempted to obtain information but was refused because the charities were based outside the state and did not solicit in New York. Scientists Murray Gell-Mann, Leonard Mlodinow, and Gerald Jay Sussman attended events related to Jeffrey Epstein. The true extent of Epstein's donations remains unknown, and the Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation does not disclose information that other charities routinely provide. In 2015, the New York Attorney General sought information about the foundation but was denied because the charities were based outside New York and did not solicit there. A New York Times investigation found that an Epstein-owned charity donated $2.3 million to former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak between 2004 and 2006 and invested $1 million in a partnership with Barak in 2015; Barak met with Epstein "dozens of times" starting in 2013. Epstein also made charitable donations through three private charities—Epstein Interest, the COUQ Foundation, and Gratitude America Ltd.—and, according to federal tax filings, donated $30 million between 1998 and 2018 through these entities. After his death, institutions such as Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) faced criticism for accepting funds from Epstein, with some offering to return the money. Beginning in the early 2000s, Epstein expressed interest in improving the human race via genetic engineering and artificial intelligence, including using his own sperm, and communicated his fascination with eugenics. In 2019, it was reported that Epstein planned to "seed the human race with his DNA" by impregnating up to 20 women at his New Mexico compound, which he called a "baby ranch," where mothers would give birth to his offspring. He supported cryonics and a personal version of transhumanism, stating he intended to have his penis and head frozen. Kathleen Hall Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center, stated that while scientists could accept funding from billionaires for legitimate work, it would have been wrong to do so if they knew Epstein was planning a eugenics experiment. Professor George Church apologized for meeting Epstein after his 2009 sentence, saying there should have been more discussion about whether they should have helped him, noting "a lot of nerd tunnel vision." Epstein had recurring sleep issues, and Deepak Chopra consulted him from 2016 to 2019; while in jail, he also experienced sleep issues and was given a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine. Epstein was believed to have been partially under the care of longevity doctor Peter Attia. On July 23, 2019, Epstein was found injured and semiconscious on the floor of his cell at 1:30 a.m. with marks around his neck. His cellmate, former New York City police officer Nicholas Tartaglione, denied knowing what happened. Correctional staff suspected suicide but did not rule out staging or assault. NBC News reported that some sources said Epstein may have tried to hang himself, others said the injuries were not serious and could have been staged, and a fourth said an assault by his cellmate was not ruled out. After the incident, Epstein was placed on suicide watch. Six days later, on July 29, 2019, he was taken off suicide watch and placed in a special housing unit with another inmate, and his close associates said he was in "good spirits." The jail informed the Justice Department that he would have a cellmate and that a guard would check on him every 30 minutes, but these procedures were not followed on the night of his death. On August 9, 2019, Epstein's cellmate was transferred out, and no replacement was assigned. Later that evening, contrary to normal procedures, Epstein was not checked every 30 minutes. The two assigned guards fell asleep and did not check on him for about three hours; they falsified records. The two cameras in front of Epstein's cell were also claimed to have malfunctioned that night. Epstein was found dead in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center (MCC) in New York City at 6:30 a.m. EDT on August 10, 2019. The Bureau of Prisons stated lifesaving measures were initiated immediately and that he was taken to a hospital. On August 10, 2019, the Bureau of Prisons and U.S. Attorney General William Barr declared the death an apparent suicide, though no final determination was made. The Department of Justice Inspector General's report, released on June 27, 2023, criticized jail officials for repeated "negligence, misconduct, and outright job performance failures" and denied any suggestion other than suicide. In May 2025, the FBI announced plans to release surveillance footage from the night of Epstein's death, stating the video clearly shows Epstein alone in his cell with no evidence of outside involvement, reaffirming the suicide ruling. On August 11, 2019, an autopsy was performed. It appeared likely that Epstein had thrown himself violently off the top bunk, which would explain the damage beyond strangulation. The preliminary autopsy found multiple breaks in his neck bones, including the hyoid bone. Hyoid bone breaks are more common in homicide by strangulation than in hangings; a 2010 study found them in 25% of hangings, while a 2010–2016 study found them in only 6% of cases. Hyoid breaks become more common with age due to bone brittleness. Forensic pathologist Cyril Wecht noted that hanging by leaning forward would not result in broken cervical bones. On August 16, 2019, Barbara Sampson, the New York City medical examiner, ruled the death a suicide by hanging. She only reviewed nine minutes of footage from one security camera. Epstein's defense lawyers were dissatisfied with the conclusion and conducted their own investigation, including legal action to view the pivotal camera footage, claiming the evidence was "far more consistent" with murder than suicide. Independent pathologist Michael Baden, hired by the Epstein estate, observed the autopsy and stated that the injuries, including a broken neck bone, are extremely unusual in suicidal hangings and more typical of homicidal strangulation, concluding the evidence points to homicide. On August 18, 2019, it was reported that Epstein had signed his last will and testament on August 8, 2019, two weeks after being found injured and two days before his death. Until then, he had been depositing money into other inmates' commissary accounts to avoid being attacked. Following the autopsy, Epstein's body was claimed by his brother Mark. On September 5, 2019, his body was interred in an unmarked crypt next to his parents at the I.J. Morris Star of David Cemetery in Palm Beach, Florida, and his parents' names were removed to prevent vandalism. Attorney General Barr ordered a Department of Justice inspector general investigation and said he was "appalled" by Epstein's death in federal custody. Two days later, he said there were "serious irregularities" in the prison's handling of Epstein and promised accountability. On August 14, 2019, federal judge Richard M. Berman wrote to the MCC asking whether the suicide investigation would include a probe into Epstein's prior July 23 injuries, noting that the incident's conclusion had never been explained. The president of the Council of Prison Locals C-33, E. Young, stated prisons "can't ever stop anyone who is persistent on killing themselves," noting that 124 inmates died by suicide between 2010 and 2016, or about 20 per year, out of a total inmate population of 180,000, with the previous suicide in that facility occurring in 1998. Young said it was unclear if there was video of Epstein's hanging or direct observations by jail officials, noting that while cameras are widespread, the interior of cells may not be within their range. He said union officials had raised concerns about staffing, citing the Trump administration's hiring freeze and budget cuts to the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP), calling it "all caused by the administration." President Serene Gregg of the American Federation of Government Employees Local 3148 said MCC was operating with only 70% of needed correctional officers, forcing many to work 60- to 70-hour weeks. In prior congressional testimony, Attorney General Barr admitted the BOP was "short" by about 4,000 employees and had lifted the freeze, beginning recruitment. Epstein's attorneys asked Berman to investigate, alleging the incident was "far more consistent with assault" than suicide. One week after signing his final will, it was reported that at least one camera in the hallway outside Epstein's cell had unusable footage, though other usable footage existed in the area. Two cameras in front of Epstein's cell were sent to an FBI lab for examination. Federal prosecutors subpoenaed 20 correctional officers regarding the cause of Epstein's death. On November 19, 2019, federal prosecutors charged MCC guards Michael Thomas and Tova Noel with creating false records and conspiracy after video revealed Epstein had been in his cell unchecked for eight hours before being found dead. On May 22, 2021, the guards admitted to falsifying records but were spared jail time under a deal. As part of a deferred prosecution agreement, they pleaded guilty to falsifying records and conspiracy to defraud the U.S., were sentenced to six months of supervisory release and 100 hours of community service. On December 19, 2023, Judge Loretta Preska ordered a list of 170 Epstein associates to be unsealed on January 1, 2024. Anyone on the list had until January 1 to appeal to have their name removed. In February 2025, the second Trump administration's attorney general Pam Bondi stated that Epstein's client list was "sitting on my desk" for review, and in June, Elon Musk alleged Trump was in the files. In July, Bondi and FBI head Kash Patel announced there was no list, no evidence Epstein had blackmailed anyone, that Epstein had killed himself, and released footage showing a partial view of a common area and an obscured view of the stairs leading to Epstein's cell block—though the footage was not independently verified. A minute was found missing, where the clock jumped from 11:58:58 to 12:00:00. An investigation found the video had been modified despite the FBI's claim it was raw, and three minutes were cut out. CBS News cited an unnamed official saying the video had been edited to remove a minute, and an unedited version is in the FBI's possession. On July 15, 2025, Representative Thomas Massie submitted House Resolution 119–581, co-sponsored by Ro Khanna, to force the Department of Justice to release the Epstein files. They announced on August 12 they would bring victims to the Capitol on September 3. Massie told ABC's Jonathan Karl that the motion would force a full release of the files, has the force of law, and is emblematic of President Trump's promise to hold rich and powerful individuals accountable. On August 25, 2025, the House Oversight Committee issued a subpoena to Acosta for testimony on the Epstein files. He was not included in the subpoenas sent in August, which included Bill Clinton, Hillary Clinton, and former attorneys general Loretta Lynch, Eric Holder, William Barr, Merrick Garland, Jeff Sessions, and Alberto Gonzales. Acosta testified in October about his plea deal with Epstein, defending his decision to pursue a state-level case due to perceived weaknesses in federal evidence, denying knowledge of Epstein's financial crimes—claims disputed by Democrats and highlighting contradictions with later evidence of investigations into financial aspects, and calling his testimony non-credible. On September 4, James O'Keefe published an exposé on Deputy Chief Joseph Schnitt of DOJ Special Operations, who said there were "thousands and thousands of pages of files" relating to Epstein and that the DOJ would "redact every Republican or conservative person in those files" while "[leaving] all the liberal, Democratic people in those files." Epstein's brother Mark Epstein alleged the same, stating he had heard from a "good source" that a team in Virginia was "sanitizing" and "scrubbing the files to take Republican names out." On November 12, Adelita Grijalva gave the final 218th signature to Massie's discharge position, forcing the creation of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which requires the attorney general to "make publicly available" all files related to the prosecution of Epstein within 30 days and to provide the Judiciary Committees with an unredacted "list of all government officials and politically exposed persons" named in the files. Epstein's death became the subject of widespread controversy and debate, with the belief that his death was a homicide, including Epstein himself, becoming a popular internet meme.

Jennifer Widom, born in 1960 or 1961, is an American computer scientist renowned for her foundational work in database systems and data management, particularly in semi-structured data management and data stream management systems. Since 2017, she has served as the dean of the School of Engineering and holds the position of professor of computer science at Stanford University. She is the Fletcher Jones Professor of Computer Science and has received multiple lifetime achievement awards from the Association for Computing Machinery. Widom earned a bachelor's degree in trumpet performance from the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music in 1982 and a PhD in computer science under David Gries from Cornell University in 1987. She began her career as a researcher at the IBM Almaden Research Center and joined Stanford University as a professor in 1993. She chaired the Stanford computer science department from 2009 to 2014 and served as senior associate dean for faculty and academic affairs in the School of Engineering from 2014 to 2016. In February 2017, she was named Dean of the School of Engineering. Widom is a fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery since 2005 and received the ACM-W Athena Lecturer Award in 2015 for her contributions to active database systems. She is also a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Widom has co-authored four academic textbooks on database systems that cover database design, use, and implementation of applications and management systems, and these materials are used at junior, senior, and graduate levels in the computer science department. In late 2011, she launched one of the first Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), titled "Introduction to Databases," which had over 100,000 enrolled students and launched simultaneously with two other MOOCs by Stanford University School of Engineering faculty. In 2018, she was awarded the Erna Hamburger prize by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne - Women in Science and Humanities Foundation for her work with MOOCs. Widom is the daughter of Lois Widom and Harold Widom, an American mathematician, and her uncle Benjamin Widom is a faculty member in chemistry at Cornell University. She is married to Alex Aiken, who previously served as chair of Stanford's computer science department, and they have a son and a daughter.

The Jensen Interceptor was introduced in 1950 as the second car produced by Jensen Motors after World War II, based on Austin components with a body crafted by Jensen and styled by Eric Neale. It featured a 3,993 cc (4.0 L; 243.7 cu in) straight-six engine and transmission from the Austin Sheerline, along with a chassis derived from the Austin A70 and modified independent coil sprung suspension. Production ran through 1957, and the name was later reused for a second-generation Jensen Interceptor launched in 1966, with subsequent revivals. The car initially debuted as a convertible with a mix of aluminium and steel on a wood frame, featuring a hinged front section for engine access and a rigid plastic (Perspex) wrap-around rear window that dropped into a well when the top was lowered. In 1952, a hardtop with a fabric-covered roof and a few sedan versions were introduced. Total production included 32 convertibles, 52 saloons, and 4 sedancas. The braking system initially used a mixed Girling hydraulic/mechanical setup, later upgraded to a full hydraulic system, while the four-speed manual transmission gained an optional overdrive in 1952, which required a 3.77:1 rear axle ratio. A 1952 convertible tested by The Motor achieved a top speed of 95 mph (153 km/h), accelerating from 0-60 mph (97 km/h) in 17.8 seconds with a fuel consumption of 20.3 miles per gallon (imperial). In 1952, the car was priced at £2645 (including tax) on the home market, with the overdrive adding an extra £116. In 1953, American race car legend Briggs Cunningham owned a left-hand drive Interceptor fitted with a 331 cu in (5.4 L), 180 bhp (134.2 kW) Chrysler "Firepower" hemi engine, achieving a top speed approaching 145 mph and ranking as the second fastest production car of 1955, behind the Mercedes-Benz 300SL. Jensen also produced the Austin A40 Sports, a smaller vehicle that resembled a scaled-down version of the Interceptor.

Jitendra Kumar Maheshwari (born 29 June 1961) is a judge of the Supreme Court of India. He was previously chief justice of the Sikkim and Andhra Pradesh high courts and served as a judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. Born in Joura, a small town in the Morena District of Madhya Pradesh, he graduated in arts in 1982 and obtained his LL.B. in 1985, followed by an LL.M. in 1991. He enrolled as an advocate with the Bar Council of Madhya Pradesh on 22 November 1985 and practiced in civil, criminal, constitutional, service, and tax matters. He was also an elected member of the M.P. State Bar Council. Appointed as an additional judge of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh on 25 November 2005, he was confirmed as a permanent judge on 25 November 2008. He served on various committees focused on improving the administration of the Madhya Pradesh High Court until 6 October 2019. He was elevated as Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court and assumed office on 7 October 2019, becoming the first Chief Justice of the newly established Andhra Pradesh High Court. In January 2021, the Supreme Court collegium swapped the chief justices of Andhra Pradesh and Sikkim high courts, after which Justice Maheshwari was transferred as Chief Justice of the High Court of Sikkim on 6 January 2021. In August 2021, the Supreme Court collegium, led by CJI N. V. Ramana, recommended his name along with eight other high court judges for appointment to the Supreme Court of India. He took oath as a Judge of the Supreme Court of India on 31 August 2021. As of 14 May 2025, he has become a member of the five-member Supreme Court collegium following the retirement of CJI Sanjiv Khanna.

Barry "Jock" Zonfrillo (4 August 1976 – 1 May 2023) was a Scottish chef, television presenter, and restaurateur who founded the Orana Foundation and served as a judge on MasterChef Australia. Born in Glasgow, Scotland, and raised in Ayr, his father Ivan was a barber from Scauri, Italy, and his mother Sarah was a hairdresser from Dalmellington, Ayrshire; he had an older sister, Carla. Zonfrillo attended Belmont Academy in Ayr. At age 12, he began working as a dishwasher at a restaurant where his sister was a waitress and started learning to cook three weeks later after a chef had a motorbike accident. He left school at 15 to begin an apprenticeship at The Turnberry Hotel, during which he began using drugs, including heroin. In 1993, at 16, he was named Young Scottish Chef of the Year. After completing his apprenticeship, he worked at the one-Michelin-starred Arkle Restaurant in Chester, where he claimed to have sold drugs to fund his addiction and was later fired after a foul-mouthed outburst. He then moved to London, working for Marco Pierre White at The Restaurant Marco Pierre White, Quaglino's, and Chapter One with David Cavalier, before going to Australia in 1994 for 12 months. Initially rejected by many restaurants, he was hired by Dietmar Sawyere at Restaurant 41 in Sydney, where he started as a line cook and became sous-chef after two months. After his visa expired, he worked for three months at Gordon Ramsay's Aubergine, then returned to White at the Oak Room and Les Saveurs, before joining Pharmacy. At age 22, he was appointed head chef at The Tresanton Hotel in Cornwall. In 2000, he immigrated to Australia, where he quit heroin cold turkey and remained clean. He became head chef at Restaurant 41 and began using Australian native ingredients. In 2002, he set fire to an apprentice chef's pants for working too slowly; the chef, Martin Krammer, sued him, was awarded damages exceeding $75,000 in 2007, and Zonfrillo was declared bankrupt in May 2007 after a creditor's petition. He was fired from Restaurant 41, then worked in kitchen equipment importation and consultancy, briefly at the Austral in Adelaide. In 2011, he became head chef at Penfolds Magill Estate Restaurant in South Australia but left after 18 months. In November 2013, he opened Orana and Street ADL in Adelaide, replacing Street ADL with Bistro Blackwood in September 2017. In August 2017, Orana was named Australia's 2018 Restaurant of the Year by Gourmet Traveller; in the same year, Zonfrillo was named Australia's 2018 Hottest Chef in The Australian. In October 2018, Orana was named Australia's 2019 Restaurant of the Year by The Good Food Guide and received three hatted recognition in the 2019 and 2020 Chef Hat Awards. From 2016 to 2017, he ran a food truck called Nonna Mallozzi serving Italian food; in December 2018, he opened a bar, Mallozzi, which closed in July 2019 after losses exceeding $140,000. Bistro Blackwood closed in late 2019, and Orana closed in March 2020. On 5 October 2020, the restaurant companies entered voluntary administration with unpaid debts of approximately $3.2 million; investigations were launched into trading while insolvent, unfair preferences, director duties, and related party loans. Zonfrillo sold his family home in the Adelaide Hills after Orana's closure. In 2016, he founded The Orana Foundation to preserve Indigenous Australian cooking techniques and ingredients, which was awarded The Good Food Guide Food for Good Award in October 2017. The foundation created a database of 1,443 Aboriginal food plants in partnership with the University of Adelaide, launched in September 2020, detailing nutritional profile, taste, flavour, and preparation methods. The Australian raised questions in August 2020 about Zonfrillo's foundation management; he launched defamation proceedings against the newspaper, which was settled by Nationwide News, with an apology published in The Australian on 17 December 2020. In 2014, he hosted Nomad Chef on the Discovery Channel, traveling to 10 countries to learn about Indigenous food practices; in 2015, he hosted Restaurant Revolution; in 2016, he co-hosted Chef Exchange with Qu Jianmin from Qingdao for two seasons. In October 2019, he was named a judge on MasterChef Australia alongside Melissa Leong and Andy Allen, having previously appeared as a guest chef in three seasons. In July 2020, he was announced as a judge for Junior MasterChef Australia. From 2016 to 2019, he served as programming director of the Tasting Australia food festival. In July 2021, he began selling "worry beads" bracelets with skulls for up to $500 under the brand Caim. On 28 July 2021, Simon & Schuster published his memoir, Last Shot; a feature in The Sydney Morning Herald questioned his claims, including visits to "hundreds of Indigenous communities" and drug use, with Marco Pierre White stating that "almost everything he has written about me is untrue," though Simon & Schuster defended the book as a "historical account written from the personal knowledge of the subject." Zonfrillo met his first wife, Kelly, in Sydney in 1996 and separated in 2002. On 1 January 2017, he married his third wife, Lauren Fried, whom he met on Twitter in October 2014; in February 2018, they had a son born two months premature weighing 1.2 kg; they had a daughter in October 2020. Zonfrillo had two other daughters from previous marriages. After the closure of his restaurants, the family moved to Melbourne around March 2020, residing in Carlton before relocating to Rome, Italy in 2023. Daily Mail Australia reported he had been battling bowel cancer since 2021 and was receiving treatment while not filming MasterChef. Zonfrillo died in Melbourne on 1 May 2023 at age 46; his body was found after a welfare check at Zagame's House hotel; there was no immediate cause of death, but police did not treat the death as suspicious and were preparing a report for the coroner. The 15th season of MasterChef Australia, which he had already filmed, was scheduled to premiere on 1 May 2023 but was postponed to 7 May; it was preceded by a special episode of The Sunday Project reflecting on his life. His funeral was held at the Macquarie Park Cemetery and Crematorium on 13 May 2023 and attended by around 200 people.

A jockey is a professional who rides horses in horse racing or steeplechase racing, and the term also applies to camel riders in camel racing. The word originated in England and was used to describe someone who rode horses in racing; it is a diminutive of "jock," a Northern English or Scots term for "John" or "boy," first recorded in 1529. In Shakespeare’s *Richard III*, the phrase "Jockey of Norfolk" appears. Originally, jockeys were all male, but female jockeys have since been allowed to compete, leading to many successful and well-known women in the sport. The term "jockey" was initially used in the 16th and 17th centuries for horse-dealers, postilions, itinerant minstrels, and vagabonds, often implying a trickster, and the verb "to jockey" meaning to outwit or deprive someone of something first appeared in that context. The current meaning of a race rider was first documented in 1670. Jockeys must be light, typically weighing between 100–120 lb (45–55 kg), and physically fit, with no official height limit, though they are usually short due to weight restrictions. Flat jockeys typically stand 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) to 5 ft 7 in (170 cm), while jump jockeys are often taller, with examples over 5 ft 10 in (178 cm); Lester Piggott, at 5 ft 8 in (173 cm), was nicknamed "Longfellow," and Jack Andrews, at 6 ft 4 in (193 cm), rides at 142 lb (64 kg); Bruce Hobbs, at 6 ft 1.5 in (186.7 cm), was the tallest jockey ever to win the Grand National. Jockeys are generally self-employed, nominated by trainers to ride their horses, and are paid a fee regardless of prize money and a percentage of the race winnings. In Australia, apprentice jockeys are employed under indenture to a master (trainer), and upon completing a four-year apprenticeship, they become senior jockeys and are considered freelance. Apprentices must successfully complete about 20 barrier trials before riding in races and are known as "bug boys" due to the asterisk symbol in race programs resembling a bug. All jockeys must be licensed and are not permitted to bet on races. Apprentices receive a weight allowance, allowing them to carry less weight than experienced jockeys in handicapped races, which incentivizes trainers to hire them. After their apprenticeship, senior jockeys may be paid a retainer by owners, giving the owner the right to require the jockey to ride their horses. Racing modeled on the English Jockey Club spread globally through colonial expansion. Jockeys wear the registered "colours" of their trainer or owner, a tradition rooted in medieval jousting and influenced by Italian city racing events, with traditional colours including purple, gold, or yellow/nude. The term "silks" refers to the white breeches and bib, stock, or cravat, and wearing silks is a rite of passage for new jockeys. Silks, which originated in the UK and were first mentioned in 1515, were formally established in the 1700s and are used to identify horses and owners; colours must be distinct and are registered by each Australian state’s Principal Racing Authority. Famous silks can be auctioned for high prices, reflecting their historical and cultural value. Jockeys must wear helmets, goggles, silks, vests, breeches, gloves, boots, saddles, girths, and stirrups during races, with safety vests worn beneath silks. The skivvy, a lightweight mesh or microfibre bodysuit, is worn under silks on race days and a heavier version during track work. Various annual awards are given to jockeys worldwide. The sport carries significant risks, including permanent, debilitating, and life-threatening injuries such as concussion, bone fractures, arthritis, trampling, and paralysis; jockey insurance premiums are among the highest in professional sports. Between 1993 and 1996, 6,545 injuries occurred, resulting in a rate of 606 per 1,000 jockey years. In Australia, race riding is considered the second most deadly job after offshore fishing, with five deaths and 861 serious injuries recorded from 2002 to 2006. Eating disorders, such as anorexia, are common due to the extreme pressure to maintain very low weights, often within a five-pound (2.3 kg) margin. The biography *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* documented these disorders, and cases like Kieren Fallon and Robert Winston highlight the physical toll of dehydration caused by weight restrictions. Sports Dietitians Australia warn that dehydration and energy depletion can impair concentration and coordination; research by the Irish Turf Club found that rapid weight loss leads to significant dehydration, though cognitive function is maintained, suggesting jockeys adapt to perform under dehydrated conditions. In January 2016, the International Concussion and Head Injury Research Foundation (ICHIRF) launched a study titled "Concussion in Sport," the first to examine concussion effects in athletes, including around 200 retired jockeys. In the U.S., women make up only 14% of working jockeys and ride only 10% of all race starts. In the 1850s, women-only events were held in Victoria, Australia, but women were not allowed to ride professionally or on men’s tracks. Wilhemena Smith rode as Bill Smith in north Queensland, using a male name and disguise, and was only officially recognized as a woman after her death in 1975. Elizabeth Williams Berry rode internationally as Jack Williams, disguising herself with cigars and a bowler hat. In Australia, female jockeys were restricted to "ladies only" events until the 1970s; the Victoria Racing Club allowed women to register for professional "ladies only" events in 1974, and New Zealand amended its rules in 1978. Pioneers like Pam O'Neill in Australia and Linda Jones in New Zealand pushed for equal competition, with O'Neill setting a world record on her first day. Bev Buckingham, Australia’s top female jockey, became the first in the Southern Hemisphere to win 1,000 races; she broke her neck in a 1998 fall at Elwick Racecourse but regained mobility. Clare Lindop won the Adelaide jockeys' premiership in 2004–05, becoming the first woman to win a metropolitan premiership in mainland Australia; Andrea Leek won the Grand National Hurdle in 2005. In 2009, women accounted for 17% of jockeys in Victoria but received only 10% of rides, especially in cities; about half of apprentice jockey intakes in some regions are women. In January 2015, all eight races at Mount Gambier were won by women jockeys. Michelle Payne became the first female jockey to win the Melbourne Cup on 3 November 2015. In Britain, women were banned from racing under Jockey Club rules, though records show women rode as men as early as 1804; Elizabeth Williams Berry rode in England as Jack Williams. In 1972, Meriel Patricia Tufnell won the first female race, the Goya Stakes; in 1976, Valerie Greaves became the first amateur woman to beat professionals under rules; in 1978, Karen Wiltshire became the first professional woman to win a British flat race. In 1996, Alex Greaves became the first woman to ride in the Epsom Dash. In the 21st century, women’s profiles rose in British flat racing: Hayley Turner became Champion Apprentice in 2005 and the first woman to ride 100 winners in a season in 2008; Kirsty Milczarek became the first woman to ride three winners at a single meeting in 2008, riding 71 winners that year. Amy Ryan and Josephine Gordon won apprentice championships in 2012 and 2016, respectively. In National Hunt racing, success has been limited, though amateur riders Nina Carberry and Katie Walsh (sister of Ruby Walsh) have won at the Cheltenham Festival. In 2010, both the winner and runner-up of a National Hunt Chase were ridden by women: Katie Walsh on Poker de Sivola and Nina Carberry on Becauseicouldntsee. On Boxing Day 2015, Lizzie Kelly won a Grade 1 race in Britain; she won another Grade 1 in 2017 at the Grand National Festival. In 2016, Rachael Blackmore became the first woman to win the Irish Conditional Jockeys title; in 2018, Lizzie Kelly became the first female professional to win at the Cheltenham Festival; in 2019, Bryony Frost became the first woman to ride a Grade 1 winner at Cheltenham; in 2021, Rachael Blackmore won the Grand National. The British Horseracing Authority encourages women, who make up three-quarters of graduates from the UK’s two main racing schools, to remain in the profession. In New Zealand, women constitute over 40% of jockeys; the first win by a woman was by Canadian jockey Joan Phipps in 1977. Linda Jones is believed to be the first New Zealand woman to apply for an apprentice licence, though she was denied, despite years of riding in lady rider events in New Zealand and abroad.

At the Cheltenham Festival, Bryony Frost became the first female jockey to ride a Grade 1 winner in 2019, riding Frodon in the Ryanair Chase. In 2021, Rachael Blackmore made history by becoming the first female jockey to win the Grand National, the most valuable jump race in Europe. The British Horseracing Authority (BHA) has been working to encourage the three-quarters of graduates from the two principal UK racing schools who are women to remain in the profession as jockeys. In New Zealand, women make up over 40% of jockeys in Thoroughbred racing. The first win by a woman in New Zealand was achieved by visiting Canadian jockey Joan Phipps at Te Awamutu in November 1977. Linda Jones is believed to be the first New Zealand woman to apply for an apprentice's licence, though she was rejected; she had previously ridden in lady riders events in New Zealand and overseas, including in Brazil, highlighting that New Zealand and Australia were outliers in not allowing women to compete with male jockeys in professional races. She eventually succeeded, and the New Zealand Racing Conference accepted female jockeys on 15 July 1978, with Joanne Hale (Giles) becoming the first New Zealand woman to ride in a totalisator race at Waimate that day. Sue Day (Christchurch), Joanne Lamond (Oamaru), and Vivienne Kaye (Awapuni) also rode in races on that day. Sue Day became the first New Zealand female jockey to win a totalisator race against males on 22 July 1978, winning with Jaws in the Waybrook Handicap at Timaru. Cherie Saxon (Hastings) was another female jockey active at the time. Linda Jones' first win was on Big Bickies at Te Rapa, followed by a win with Royal Petite, the first Open Handicap winner for a female jockey. Her other notable wins included Lovaro in the Queen Elizabeth Handicap and Holy Toledo in the Wellington Derby on 22 January 1979 (possibly the first female jockey worldwide to win a Derby). Jones was also the first female jockey to win a professional race against males at a registered meeting in Australia, winning aboard Pay The Purple in the Labour Day Cup at Doomben Racecourse, Brisbane on 7 May 1979. In 1982, Maree Lyndon became the first female jockey to win a Group I race in New Zealand, winning the New Zealand Cup on Sirtain. In 1986, Trudy Thornton became the first woman to ride in New Zealand's longest thoroughbred race, the Great Northern Steeplechase, and in 1995, Tina Egan became the first woman to win that race. In 1997, Catherine Hutchinson (née Tremayne) became the first female jockey to ride six winners in a day, achieving this at Ruakaka. Lisa Cropp won the New Zealand jockeys' premiership in 2005 and 2006. In recent years, the premiership has been won by Lisa Allpress (2012, 2016, 2019, and 2020), Samantha Collett (2018), and Danielle Johnson (2021). In April 2017 at Timaru, eight of the nine races were won by women jockeys: Alysha Collett, Kylie Williams, Tina Comignaghi, Amanda Morgan, and Samantha Wynne. On 10 October 2019 at Tauherenikau Racecourse, all eight races were won by women: Rosie Myers (4 races), Lisa Allpress (2), Charlotte O'Beirne (A), and Leah Mischewski. Eliza Carpenter (1851–1924) was an early African-American race horse owner in Ponca City, Oklahoma, where she trained horses and became one of the few African-American stable owners in the West; she sometimes rode her own horses as a jockey, winning some races, with recorded horses including "Irish Maid", "Blue Bird", "Jimmy Rain", "Sam Carpenter", and "Little Brown Jug", which she reportedly raced at Tijuana, Baja California. Anna Lee Aldred (1921–2006) received a license at age 18 in 1939 at Agua Caliente Racetrack in Tijuana, Mexico, when officials could not find a rule barring women jockeys, and she finished second by a nose in her first professional race. Hollywood stuntwoman Alice Van-Springsteen (1918–2008) also rode as a jockey and was one of the first women to receive a trainer's license for Thoroughbred horses. Wanta Davis (1918–2012) won over 1,000 races in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s, including a notable 1949 six-furlong match-race against Johnny Longden at Agua Caliente; she rode at some state-sanctioned pari-mutuel tracks without a license, with most events being dusty county fair or half-mile western circuit races, and although in demand as a training jockey, her license applications were repeatedly denied. Twelve years after Davis retired, the "modern era of female jockeys" began when Olympic equestrian and show jumping competitor Kathy Kusner, who had also ridden as a jockey, successfully sued the Maryland Racing Commission in 1967 under the Civil Rights Act, winning her case in 1968 and becoming one of the earliest women licensed in the United States, though an injury prevented her from racing. In late 1968, Penny Ann Early was the first woman to earn a mount as a licensed Thoroughbred jockey in the U.S., entering three races at Churchill Downs in November, but male jockeys boycotted those races, so she could not ride. On 7 February 1969, Diane Crump became the first licensed woman to ride in a parimutuel Thoroughbred race in the United States at Hialeah Park Race Track in Florida, requiring a police escort to reach the paddock. Two weeks later, on 22 February at Charles Town in West Virginia, Barbara Jo Rubin became the first woman to win a race, going on to win 11 of her first 22. Other women soon followed, and over time American women jockeys have proven their ability; Julie Krone has 3,704 victories, the most by an American woman, and as of June 2012, at least nineteen others have each ridden over 1,000 winners. Canada has generally followed the U.S. in opportunities for women jockeys, with only two female jockeys having over 1,000 wins, though in both actual and relative numbers and overall success rate, Canada has surpassed the U.S. in opportunities at the highest level, particularly in their respective Triple Crown series. Starting with Joan Phipps in the 1973 Breeders' Stakes, 10 different women have competed in 30 Canadian Triple Crown races, with a combined record of two wins, three places, and four shows. While no U.S. Triple Crown race has ever featured more than one female rider, that has occurred 10 times in Canada, with three women—Francine Villeneuve, Chantal Sutherland, and Emma-Jayne Wilson—racing in all three Canadian races, Sutherland doing it twice and Wilson three times. Since Diane Crump rode in the 1970 Kentucky Derby, six different women have competed in U.S. Triple Crown events, some multiple times: 10 times in the Derby, four times in the Preakness, and nine times in the Belmont, with a combined record of one win, one place, and one show. Julie Krone is the only woman to have won a U.S. Triple Crown race, on Colonial Affair in the 1993 Belmont. Rosie Napravnik became the first woman to ride in all three U.S. Triple Crown races with appearances in the 2011 Kentucky Derby, the 2012 Belmont Stakes, and the 2013 Preakness Stakes, and in 2013 she became the first woman to ride in all three U.S. Triple Crown races in the same year; she is also the only woman to have won the Kentucky Oaks, which she has won twice. To replace child jockeys whose use was deplored by human rights organizations, a camel race in Doha, Qatar, on 13 July 2005 featured robotic jockeys at the reins; seven camels were equipped with robots that operators controlled remotely, signaling them to pull reins and prod the camels with whips. In North America during the 1800s, most aspects of horse racing were primarily performed by enslaved African Americans; plantation owners brought enslaved workers and their horses to other plantations to organize and bet on races. Enslaved and free Black people were involved in horse racing, often in grooming, feeding, backing, exercising, and other auxiliary roles, eventually working up to becoming trainers and full-time racers. By the end of the 1800s, horse racing was almost exclusively run by African American jockeys, with Isaac Murphy, Willie Simms, and Jimmy Winkfield being the three most successful, Murphy winning the Kentucky Derby in 1884, 1887, and 1890. This dominance ended abruptly in 1896 after the Plessy v. Ferguson decision, which legalized segregation, leading to the end of African American jockeys' supremacy in the sport.

Joe Nzingo Gqabi OLS (6 April 1929 – 31 July 1981) was a South African African National Congress (ANC) activist who served as the ANC's chief representative in Zimbabwe at the time of his assassination by the South African Defence Force in Harare (then Salisbury), Zimbabwe, in 1981. Born on 6 April 1929 in Aliwal North, which is now part of the Joe Gqabi District Municipality, Gqabi's first language was Xhosa. In the 1950s, he worked as a journalist for New Age and maintained frequent contact with ANC leader Walter Sisulu. As a member of the South African Communist Party and UMkhonto we Sizwe, he was sent for guerrilla training in China in the early 1960s. He was captured along with 28 other members undergoing military training in Rhodesia and deported to South Africa, where he was sentenced to two years' imprisonment for illegally leaving the country and ten years under the Sabotage Act, leading to his incarceration at Robben Island. After his release in 1975, he rejoined the ANC. In 1976, he became co-chairman, alongside Martin Ramokgadi, of the clandestine ANC organisation in Johannesburg known as the Main Machinery. During this period, the South African security services attempted to assassinate him by placing a bomb in his car, which was discovered before detonation. He was arrested following the Soweto uprising, where Oliver Tambo later stated he acted as an intermediary between the ANC and the South African Students' Movement, but the police, lacking sufficient evidence, could not build a case against him. He was released in 1977, fled to Botswana, and then moved to Zimbabwe after its independence in 1980. On 31 July 1981, he was assassinated by the South African Defence Force in Ashdown Park, Salisbury (now Harare), Zimbabwe. His body was repatriated to South Africa in 2004 and he was reburied in Aliwal North on 16 December 2004. Posthumously, he was awarded the Order of Luthuli in silver by the South African government, and the Joe Gqabi District Municipality was named in his honour.

Sir John Bramston, GCMG, CB (14 November 1832 – 13 September 1921), was a politician in Queensland (now part of Australia) and a British colonial government administrator in Queensland and Hong Kong. He served as Assistant Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies in London for more than 20 years, retiring in 1898 and being created Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George (KCMG) upon retirement. Born on 14 November 1832 in Roxwell, Essex, Bramston was the second son of Thomas William Bramston (later MP for South Essex) of Skreens, Essex, and his wife Eliza, daughter of Admiral Sir Eliab Harvey. He was educated at Winchester College and Balliol College, Oxford, where he graduated with a B.A. in 1854, became Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford the following year, and earned a D.C.L. in 1863. He entered the Middle Temple in November 1854 and was called to the bar in June 1857. He went to Queensland in 1859 as private secretary to Sir George Bowen, the first Governor of Queensland, holding that post for two years before resigning. On 3 July 1863, he was appointed a Member of the Queensland Legislative Council and served in the first Ministry formed by his friend Sir Robert Herbert, the first Premier of Queensland, from July 1863 to February 1866, acting briefly as Attorney-General from 31 August 1865 to 11 September 1865. Although his membership of the Legislative Council was lifetime, he resigned on 17 November 1869. Robert Herbert established a farm in the Brisbane area and lived there with Bramston, who named their house Herston, a combination of their surnames, which later became the name of the suburb of Herston. Bramston returned to England, where he remained for two years, acting as Assistant Boundary Commissioner for Devon and Cornwall under the Reform Act of 1867. He returned to Queensland in 1868 and was elected in the by-election on 3 April 1871 following Charles Haley's resignation as Member of the Queensland Legislative Assembly for Burnett, holding the seat until 8 December 1873, when the electorate was abolished in a redistribution. During this time, he served as Queensland's Attorney-General in the Palmer Ministry from 3 May 1870 to 2 January 1874. On 12 December 1872 at St John's Cathedral in Brisbane, Bramston married Eliza Isabella Russell, daughter of Rev. Harry Vane Russell and niece of the Governor of Queensland, George Phipps, 2nd Marquess of Normanby (who had married Laura Russell, sister to Harry Russell), with the service conducted by Bishop Edward Tufnell. The Governor hosted a wedding reception at Government House, and the couple honeymooned in Sydney and Tasmania. In 1874, Bramston was appointed Attorney General of Hong Kong, replacing Julian Pauncefote, and at times acted as a judge in Hong Kong. In June 1876, he was appointed Assistant Under-Secretary of State in the Colonial Office, serving on a mission to Berlin in connection with the Angra Pequena negotiations in July 1886, in which year he was created Companion of the Order of the Bath. In October 1887, Bramston's death was announced in the Queensland newspapers, leading to the publication of many obituaries, but it was later revealed to be an error due to a misinterpretation of a telegram. In 1892, he was appointed Registrar of the Order of St. Michael and St. George. In 1899, he was sent as Royal Commissioner alongside Admiral Sir James Erskine to inquire into French treaty rights in Newfoundland, a dispute settled by the Entente Cordiale of 1904; he was also a member of the Royal Commission for the Paris Exhibition of 1900. In the 1900 New Year Honours list, he was promoted to Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George (GCMG), and received the order from Queen Victoria during an investiture at Windsor Castle on 1 March 1900. His wife, Lady Bramston, died in 1920. Bramston died at Wimbledon on Tuesday 13 September 1921 and was buried at the Wimbledon Cemetery.

The John Brophy Award is given to the ECHL coach deemed to have made the greatest contribution to his team's success, as selected by the coaches of all ECHL teams. The award has been presented since 1989 and was initially called Coach Of The Year before being renamed in honor of John Brophy in 2003. John Brophy coached in the ECHL for 13 seasons and holds the league record with 575 regular and postseason wins. Bob Ferguson is the only coach to have won the award more than once, receiving it in 1999 and 2000.

John Graham Lough (8 January 1798 – 8 April 1876) was an English sculptor renowned for his funerary monuments and portrait sculptures, as well as ideal classical male and female figures. Born at Black Hedley Port, Greenhead near Consett, County Durham, he was one of eleven children, the son of William Lough of Aycliff, County Durham, and Barbara Clementson of Dalton, Northumberland. His father was a farmer near Hexham, and Lough may have worked as a farmer in his youth. He later apprenticed to a stonemason at Shotley Field near Newcastle upon Tyne and worked in Newcastle as an ornamental sculptor, carving decorations for the building of the city's Literary and Philosophical Society. In 1825, he traveled to London by sea to study the Elgin Marbles at the British Museum, taking lodgings in Burleigh Street, above a greengrocer's shop, where he began moulding his colossal statue of Milo of Croton, inspired by the Elgin Marbles and Michelangelo’s work. In 1826, with support from John Thomas Smith, he joined the Royal Society Schools and became the protégé of painter Benjamin Haydon, exhibiting the completed statue the following year. This work so impressed London society that it brought him numerous patrons and established his career; a later 1863 bronze version of the statue survives at Blagdon, Northumberland. From 1826, he began exhibiting ideal figures and heads at the Royal Academy. Between 1834 and 1838, he spent time in Rome, where his portrait style was influenced by Neo-classicism. He received a provisional commission to carve four granite lions for the base of Nelson's Column, but in 1846, after consulting with the column’s designer William Railton, he withdrew due to unwillingness to work under the architect’s constraints; the commission was later given to Edwin Landseer, with assistance from Carlo Marochetti, who completed it in 1867. He was a close friend of surgeon Campbell De Morgan, who sat with Lough as he lay dying of pneumonia; a bust of De Morgan by Lough is held by the Middlesex Hospital medical school and on display there. Lough is buried in Kensal Green Cemetery, London. One of his younger brothers, Thomas, was a talented musician, artist, and poet, best known for "The Ramshaw Flood" (1848), but fell into vagrancy and poverty, dying at Lanchester Workhouse just one year after John Graham Lough’s death. His public works include a statue of Lord Collingwood in Tynemouth, a memorial to Thomas Noon Talfourd in the Shire Hall, Stafford, and a bronze George Stephenson memorial of 1862 opposite the North of England Institute of Mining and Mechanical Engineers in Newcastle upon Tyne. In London, he produced monuments to Henry Montgomery Lawrence and Bishop Middleton in St Paul's Cathedral, and created the Queen Victoria and Prince Albert for the Royal Exchange. In Canterbury Cathedral, he was responsible for the monuments to Bishop Broughton and Lt Col Frederick Mackeson. He produced many ideal works on classical, historical, and literary themes, including a series of marble statues of Shakespearean subjects for his chief patron, Matthew, 4th Baronet Ridley. Despite his prolific output, Lough was controversial, as his work divided opinion; the Literary Gazette hailed his first exhibition as a demonstration of "extraordinary genius" and later praised a sculptural group as one that "nineteen out of twenty people would prefer ... to any other work in the exhibition," while the Art Journal was fiercely critical, describing his statue of Queen Victoria for the Royal Exchange as "an odiously coarse production, in which not one feature of the Queen is recognisable" and of such "gross vulgarity" that it exceeded "the worst production that has ever been publicly exhibited." Media related to John Graham Lough is available at Wikimedia Commons.

John Joseph Hall (18 February 1884 – 30 June 1949) was an Australian politician and journalist. He was born in Eaglehawk to Joseph Hall, a miner and tea merchant, and Isabella, née Gray. He attended state school and later worked as a booking clerk with Victorian Railways and as a journalist for the Bendigo Advertiser, serving as mining correspondent for The Argus. He married Clarissa Jessamine Snell on 26 December 1907, and they had six children. Active in the Kyabram Reform Movement, Hall founded the Victorian Farmers' Union (VFU) in 1916 and served as its general secretary from 1916 to 1918. In 1917, he was elected to the Victorian Legislative Assembly as the member for Kara Kara, but was defeated on a recount in February 1918. He then ran as the VFU's candidate in the 1918 federal Flinders by-election, but withdrew after securing a promise from the Nationalist Party to introduce preferential voting. Despite multiple attempts, Hall never regained a seat in parliament. He continued his career in journalism, editing the Farmer's Advocate (1917–1924), the Morning Post (1924–1927), and the Leader (1946–1949). Hall died in Richmond in 1949.
