John II (French: Jean II; 26 April 1319 – 8 April 1364), known as John the Good, ruled as King of France from 1350 until his death in 1364. Upon ascending the throne, France faced severe crises: the Black Death, which killed between a third and a half of its population; widespread popular revolts known as Jacqueries; the activities of free companies (Grandes Compagnies) of routiers who plundered the country; and sustained English aggression, culminating in the catastrophic Battle of Poitiers in 1356, where John was captured. While imprisoned in London, his son Charles served as regent and suppressed several rebellions before concluding the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, which resulted in France losing significant territories and paying a massive ransom. As part of an exchange of hostages, including his son Louis I, Duke of Anjou, John was released to raise funds for the ransom. Upon returning to France, he introduced the franc to stabilize the currency and attempted to eliminate the free companies by sending them on a crusade, though Pope Innocent VI died before the meeting in Avignon. When informed that Louis had escaped captivity, John voluntarily returned to England, where he died in 1364 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Charles V. John was nine years old when his father, Philip VI, became king; Philip’s succession was unexpected because all three sons of Philip IV had died without male heirs and their daughters were passed over, as was King Edward III of England, Philip IV’s granddaughter through Isabella. To secure his throne, Philip married off his son John at age thirteen to King John the Blind of Bohemia, who sought French support for controlling Lombardy. A treaty was signed, stipulating that Bohemia would provide four hundred infantrymen in war and that the Lombard crown would not be contested if Bohemia obtained it. Bonne of Bohemia, selected as John’s wife due to her child-bearing age (16 years), brought a dowry of 120,000 florins. John reached the age of majority on 27 April 1332 and was granted the Duchy of Normandy, along with the counties of Anjou and Maine. The wedding took place on 28 July at Notre-Dame in Melun, attended by six thousand guests, and was followed by a two-month celebration culminating in his knighting at Notre-Dame in Paris. As duke, he was formally granted knightly arms before a gathering of European monarchs and dukes. Upon becoming duke, John faced the reality that most Norman nobility were aligned with England, as Normandy relied heavily on maritime trade across the English Channel. To maintain stability, Norman nobles were organized into interdependent clans with charters ensuring autonomy, primarily divided between the counts of Tancarville and Harcourt. In 1341, tensions flared when Geoffroy d'Harcourt raised troops against King Philip, demanding he be made duke to secure autonomy; royal forces captured Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte and exiled Geoffroy, with three of his companions decapitated in Paris on 3 April 1344. In 1342, John was in Avignon for the coronation of Pope Clement VI, and in 1343, he participated in peace negotiations with Edward III’s chancery clerk. By 1345, increasing numbers of Norman rebels defected to Edward III, threatening royal legitimacy. The French defeat at Crécy on 26 August 1346 and the fall of Calais on 3 August 1347 further damaged royal prestige. In response, Philip VI sought a truce, and John negotiated with Geoffroy d'Harcourt, agreeing to return confiscated goods and appointing him sovereign captain in Normandy. He then allied with the Tancarville family by marrying John, Viscount of Melun, to Jeanne, heiress of Tancarville, ensuring loyalty to John while allowing Geoffroy to continue defending Norman autonomy. On 11 September 1349, John’s wife, Bonne of Bohemia, died at Maubuisson Abbey from the Black Death. To escape the pandemic, John left Paris. On 9 February 1350, five months after her death, he married Joan I, Countess of Auvergne, at the Château de Sainte-Gemme near Saint-Germain-en-Laye. In 1343, negotiations began between Philip VI and dauphin Humbert II of Viennois over the inheritance of the Dauphiné, initially assigning it to John’s younger brother Philip, Duke of Orléans, but later changed to John as heir. By 1349, Humbert relinquished the Dauphiné to the House of Valois, designating John’s eldest son Charles as successor, with the condition that Dauphiné remain a distinct polity. Thus, in 1349, Charles became the first Valois Dauphin de Viennois, and in 1350, upon John’s coronation as king, Charles became heir presumptive, holding both the title of Dauphin de Viennois and the right to the French throne. Philip VI died on 22 August 1350, and John was crowned king of France on 26 September 1350 in Reims, with his second wife, Joanna, crowned queen at the same time. In November 1350, John had Raoul II of Brienne, Count of Eu, seized and executed, though the reasons remain unclear, with rumors suggesting he had pledged the County of Guînes for his release. John inherited a militarily disorganized and fragmented kingdom, and seven months after his coronation, he issued the ordinances of 1351 to address military issues, including poor organization, discipline, and payment, in response to defeats like Crécy. These ordinances are considered the first comprehensive military reforms in French history, surpassing earlier decrees by focusing systematically on army-wide structure. The reforms aimed to counter the English armies’ use of longbowmen and centralized command. However, resistance from the nobility—such as Charles of Navarre—undermined implementation, as they viewed the reforms as a threat to their feudal autonomy and traditional rights to command personal forces. Rivalries among noble factions, including Charles of Navarre and the Duke of Orléans, caused political instability and weakened royal authority. Nobles resisted discipline and resented serving under royal oversight or alongside common soldiers, leading to inconsistent enforcement and reliance on feudal levies with irregular payments. The failure to integrate these reforms contributed to the French defeat at Poitiers. The battle exposed military weaknesses and highlighted noble resistance, leading to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), which ceded territories to England (later recovered by Charles V) and caused thousands of French casualties, including nobles, further weakening the feudal structure. Although the ordinances were limited in effectiveness due to enforcement challenges and financial constraints, they laid the foundation for modernizing the French military, influencing later reforms by Charles V and Charles VII, including the creation of a standing army and permanent taxation. These changes transformed the feudal system from decentralized to one with royal oversight, integrating nobles into a royal framework and strengthening crown authority. On 16 November 1351, John established the Order of the Star, a chivalric order designed to unify the French nobility under royal leadership and counter Edward III’s Order of the Garter. Unlike religious military orders such as the Templars or Hospitallers, the Order of the Star was a royal, state-sponsored initiative with a clear military purpose tied to national defense, making it the first organized, state-backed knightly group in France. It aimed to foster loyalty among knights and prevent defections to foreign powers, especially among nobles with lands across multiple kingdoms. In 1354, John’s son-in-law and cousin, Charles II of Navarre, who held lands in Normandy and the Kingdom of Navarre, was implicated in the assassination of the Constable of France, Charles de la Cerda, John’s favorite. To secure a strategic ally against the English in Gascony, John signed the Treaty of Mantes on 22 February 1354. The peace was short-lived, and Charles eventually allied with Henry of Grosmont, the first Duke of Lancaster. In September 1355, John and Charles signed the Treaty of Valognes, but it lasted only briefly. On 5 April 1356, during a banquet at the Royal Castle in Rouen attended by John’s son Charles, John burst through the door in full armor, swords drawn, with over a hundred fully armed knights, shouting, “Let no one move if he does not want to be dead with this sword.” When Charles of Navarre and other nobles refused to comply, John grabbed him by the throat, yelling, “Traitor, you are not worthy to sit at my son's table!” He then ordered the arrest of all guests, and later that night, summarily executed John, Count of Harcourt, and several other Norman lords and notables while standing nearby—an act driven by revenge for the assassination of Charles de la Cerda. This action alienated remaining Norman support from the crown, pushing many lords to align with Edward III and the English, setting the stage for the English invasion and the Battle of Poitiers. In 1355, the Hundred Years' War flared again, and in July 1356, Edward, the Black Prince, launched a chevauchée through France. John pursued him with his own army, meeting him a few miles southeast of Poitiers in September. John believed his army was twice the size of the English force and did not immediately attack. While waiting, papal legates attempted to negotiate a truce; the Black Prince offered his wagon train, promised not to fight for seven years, and even offered to return Calais to France. John demanded 100 of the Prince’s best knights as hostages, including the Prince himself. No agreement was reached, and combat began. On the day of battle, John and 17 knights from his personal guard dressed identically to confuse the enemy. Despite this, the French knights were routed by English longbow volleys, and John was captured as the English force advanced. Though he fought valiantly with a large battle-axe and his helmet was knocked off, he surrendered when Denis de Morbecque, a French exile fighting for England, approached him and offered to lead him to the Prince of Wales. John surrendered by handing him his glove. That night, he dined in the Black Prince’s red silk tent, who attended to him personally. He was then taken to Bordeaux and then to England. The Battle of Poitiers was one of the most significant military disasters in medieval history for France. While negotiating peace, John was held first in the Savoy Palace, then in Windsor, Hertford, Somerton Castle in Lincolnshire, Berkhamsted Castle in Hertfordshire, and briefly at King John’s Lodge in East Sussex, before being transferred to the Tower of London. In France, the public reaction was not to the defeat at Poitiers but to the captivity of King John. When people learned of the French lords’ flight from battle, they believed it was due to treason. They questioned the meaning of honor and nobility, and some returning nobles were attacked by furious villeins, even those who had been on parole to collect ransoms. As a prisoner of the English, John was granted royal privileges that permitted him to maintain certain rights.

King John II of France was a central figure in one of the major military disasters of the Middle Ages, particularly due to his capture at the Battle of Poitiers in 1356. After being taken prisoner by the English, he was held in various locations including the Savoy Palace, Windsor, Hertford, Somerton Castle in Lincolnshire, Berkhamsted Castle in Hertfordshire, and briefly at King John's Lodge in East Sussex, before being transferred to the Tower of London. In France, the public reaction to his captivity overshadowed the defeat at Poitiers, as people believed the French lords’ flight was due to treason and cowardice, leading to widespread hatred of knights perceived as treacherous. Despite being a prisoner, John was granted royal privileges allowing him to travel and maintain a regal lifestyle, during which his account books show he purchased horses, pets, clothes, and maintained an astrologer and court band. The Treaty of Brétigny, drafted in May 1360, set his ransom at 3 million crowns—roughly two to three years of France’s national revenue, the largest budget in Europe at the time. On 30 June 1360, John left the Tower of London and went to Eltham Palace, where Queen Philippa hosted a farewell entertainment; he spent the night in Dartford, stopped at the Maison Dieu of St Mary at Ospringe, paid homage at St Thomas Becket’s shrine in Canterbury on 4 July, dined with the Black Prince at Dover Castle, and reached Calais on 8 July. Leaving his son Louis of Anjou in Calais as a hostage to ensure payment, John was allowed to return to France to raise the ransom, and the treaty was ratified in October 1360. On 1 July 1363, John learned that Louis had escaped from Calais, prompting him to voluntarily return to England in January 1364 to negotiate with Edward III in person, despite opposition from his advisors. He famously stated that “if good faith were banned from the Earth, she ought to find asylum in the hearts of kings.” Immediately after, he appointed his son Charles as Duke of Normandy and regent of France. John landed in England in January 1364, was met by Sir Alan Buxhull, Sir Richard Pembridge, and Lord Burghersh at Dover, and was taken to Eltham and the Savoy Palace, where he was warmly received and a frequent guest of Edward at Westminster. A few months later, he fell ill with an unknown malady and died at the Savoy Palace in April 1364. His body was returned to France and interred in the royal chambers at Saint Denis Basilica. John’s death at age 44 was not unusually young for the period, especially considering the impact of the Black Death and the stresses of captivity. Primary sources, including Jean Froissart and the Grandes Chroniques de France, do not specify the nature of his illness, only noting he “fell ill and died,” and neither describe him as frail or chronically unwell. Froissart’s account of John’s lavish lifestyle in captivity and his participation in festivities suggests physical capability, while his preference for hunting over jousting and reliance on advisors like Charles de la Cerda may reflect personal temperament or political strategy rather than illness. The claim of poor health is largely a modern historiographical construct based on inferences, not direct evidence. John II married Bonne of Bohemia and had 11 children in eleven years. His close relationship with Charles de la Cerda, who was appointed connetable and accompanied him on journeys, drew criticism from partisans of Charles II of Navarre, who accused him of having “no other God than him”; La Cerda was later stabbed to death in 1354, an event that deeply grieved John. John acquired the titles of Count of Anjou, Count of Maine, and Duke of Normandy in 1332, which were later absorbed into the royal domain upon his coronation in 1350. During his reign, he created seven duchies and counties—the most of any French monarch—expanding French territory and influence by acquiring the Duchy of Burgundy, creating the Duchy of Auvergne, and placing his sons in strategic positions. He elevated the Barony of Tancarville to a county and created Jean, Viscount of Melun, as Count of Tancarville, who served as Chamberlain, Hereditary Constable of Normandy, Sovereign Master of the Waters and Forests of France, and held key military roles, including a lieutenancy general in 1361 to pacify regions threatened by the Free Companies. He also elevated Castres to a county in 1356 and granted it to John VI of Vendôme, a loyal vassal who fought at Poitiers and was captured by the English, as a reward and to secure loyalty in a region vulnerable to English influence. In 1360, the Duchy of Anjou was created and granted to Louis I of Anjou, John’s second son, as part of the Treaty of Brétigny, to secure a loyal presence in a region near English-held Aquitaine and Brittany, with Louis serving as a hostage in England. Philip II the Bold initially received Touraine as an apanage in 1360, but after Burgundy became available in 1363, Philip was given Burgundy instead, and Touraine was temporarily reassigned or returned to the crown, reflecting John’s strategic flexibility. The Duchy of Auvergne was created from the Terre royale d’Auvergne and granted to John’s third son, John, alongside the Duchy of Berry, to strengthen royal control in a region with a history of autonomy and pro-English sympathies. John served as king’s lieutenant in Auvergne since 1358, making him a logical recipient of the apanage. John II was succeeded by his eldest son, Charles, who became Charles V, known as The Wise.

King John created the Duchy of Berry for his third son, John, encompassing the County of Berry and parts of Poitou, as part of his 1360 reorganization of apanages following the Treaty of Brétigny. Centered in central France, Berry was a relatively stable region strategically important for connecting northern and southern royal domains and serving as a buffer against internal dissent, such as the Jacquerie revolt (1358). John of Berry, appointed king’s lieutenant in 1358 for regions including Auvergne and Languedoc, was a key figure in John’s government, and the apanage provided him with the resources to govern effectively and support royal policies. Unlike Anjou or Burgundy, Berry was less exposed to immediate external threats, making it a stable base for administrative and artistic patronage. John of Berry became a renowned patron of the arts, commissioning works like the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry. His governance strengthened royal influence in central France, with Berry remaining closely tied to the crown. The Duchy of Auvergne was created from the Terre royale d’Auvergne (royal lands of Auvergne), while the County of Auvergne continued to exist in parallel. John granted it to his third son John alongside the Duchy of Berry. Auvergne, in south-central France, had been part of the royal domain since its confiscation by Philip II Augustus in 1209 and partial restoration to local counts. The elevation of Auvergne to a duchy was a strategic move to strengthen royal control in a region with a history of autonomy and pro-English sympathies among some local lords (e.g., the Counts of Auvergne). By granting it to John, King John aimed to secure Auvergne’s loyalty during the Hundred Years’ War. John’s role as king’s lieutenant in Auvergne (since 1358) made him a logical choice for the apanage. The grant formalized his authority, countering local resistance and English influence in the region. The creation of the duchy alongside Berry reflects John’s intent to consolidate central and southern France under a trusted son, especially after the territorial losses of the Treaty of Brétigny. John of Berry held Auvergne until his death in 1416, when it reverted to the crown. His daughter Marie inherited the title of Duchess of Auvergne, and it later passed to her husband, John I, Duke of Bourbon, in 1426, integrating Auvergne into the Bourbon domains. The apanage reinforced royal authority in Auvergne, though John’s heavy taxation to fund war efforts sparked revolts, such as the Tuchin Revolt, highlighting the challenges of governing the region. Touraine later became an apanage for other royal relatives under John’s successors, reinforcing its role as a “floating” apanage for royal cadets. On 28 July 1332, at the age of 13, John was married to Bonne of Luxembourg (d. 1349), daughter of John, King of Bohemia. On 19 February 1350, at the royal Château de Sainte-Gemme, John married Joanna I of Auvergne (d. 1361), Countess of Auvergne and Boulogne. Joanna was the widow of Philip of Burgundy, the deceased heir of that duchy, and the mother of the young Philip I, Duke of Burgundy (1344–61), who became John's stepson and ward. John and Joanna had three children, all of whom died shortly after birth. King John II faced extraordinary challenges: the Black Death, which killed a third to half of France’s population, the Hundred Years’ War with England, internal revolts like the Jacquerie, and plundering by free companies. His capture at the Battle of Poitiers (1356) and the subsequent Treaty of Brétigny (1360), which ceded significant territories and demanded a massive ransom, have often been focal points for criticism. However, applying modern standards of leadership to a medieval monarch risks oversimplifying the political, economic, and social constraints of the era. The trend of criticizing John II began with Jean Froissart’s influential but biased chronicle, which provided a narrative of bravery undercut by recklessness. Jules Michelet’s 19th-century reinterpretation transformed this into a nationalist critique, portraying John as a weak ruler who failed France. Subsequent historians—François Guizot, Charles Petit-Dutaillis, Edouard Perroy, Jean Deviosse, and Maurice Keen—built on Michelet’s framework, citing each other and Froissart to reinforce a narrative of incompetence. This historiographical chain reflects a tendency to judge John II by modern standards of statecraft, often ignoring the medieval emphasis on chivalric honor and the external pressures of war, plague, and noble factionalism. The reliance on citations created an echo chamber, where each historian reinforced the previous one’s conclusions without fully reevaluating primary sources like Jean de Venette or considering the broader context. Modern scholars like Françoise Autrand have begun to break this cycle by highlighting John II’s adherence to chivalric ideals and the impossible circumstances he faced, suggesting that the trend of criticism may be waning as historians adopt a more contextual approach. The earliest significant criticism of John II likely stems from contemporary or near-contemporary chroniclers, particularly Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1405), a Hainaut-born chronicler whose Chronicles are a primary source for the Hundred Years’ War. Froissart’s account, while vivid and detailed, often reflects a chivalric bias and the perspective of his patrons, who included figures aligned with the English or Burgundian factions. His portrayal of John II at Poitiers emphasizes the king’s bravery but also his tactical errors, such as ignoring advice against engaging the English due to their superior longbow tactics. Froissart writes of John’s decision to fight on foot with a poleaxe, portraying it as courageous but implying it was reckless given the French defeat. This narrative sets a tone of personal valor undermined by poor judgment, a theme later historians amplified. Froissart’s account was influential because it was widely circulated in medieval Europe and became a foundational source for later historians. His depiction of John II’s capture and lavish lifestyle in English captivity—engaging in feasts, hunting, and pilgrimages—contributed to perceptions of a king more concerned with personal honor than governance. While Froissart does not explicitly condemn John, his focus on the king’s extravagance and military failure provided raw material for subsequent criticism. Another contemporary source, Jean de Venette (c. 1307–c. 1370), a Carmelite friar, offers a more sympathetic view, emphasizing the external pressures John faced, such as the Black Death and economic collapse. However, Venette’s chronicle was less widely read than Froissart’s, so it had less impact on shaping the critical narrative. The critical trend solidified in the early modern period, particularly with Jules Michelet (1798–1874), a 19th-century French historian whose Histoire de France (1833–1867) is a landmark in French historiography. Michelet, a romantic nationalist, viewed the Valois monarchy, including John II’s reign, through the lens of France’s struggle for national unity. He criticized John II for his "weakness" and "extravagance," particularly highlighting the Poitiers defeat and the Treaty of Brétigny as catastrophic for French sovereignty. Michelet’s portrayal of John as a well-meaning but ineffectual ruler, overly reliant on favorites like Charles de la Cerda, set a precedent for later historians. His vivid prose and emphasis on national decline made his work highly influential, and he is a likely candidate for initiating the modern trend of criticizing John II. Michelet’s interpretation influenced a chain of historians who cited his work, either directly or indirectly, as they built the critical narrative around John II. Key figures include: 1. François Guizot (1787–1874): A prominent historian and statesman, Guizot’s History of France (1829–1830) drew on Michelet’s framework and Froissart’s chronicles. Guizot emphasized John II’s military failures and the economic devastation caused by the ransom payments, portraying the king as a symbol of feudal incompetence. 2. Charles Petit-Dutaillis (1868–1947): In his The Feudal Monarchy in France and England (1933), Petit-Dutaillis cited Michelet and Guizot, focusing on John II’s inability to centralize royal authority amidst noble defections and English aggression. He described John’s reign as a low point in Valois legitimacy. 3. Edouard Perroy (1901–1974): Perroy’s The Hundred Years War (1945) built on Petit-Dutaillis and Michelet, explicitly citing their works. He criticized John II for his strategic blunders at Poitiers and his failure to manage noble factions, particularly Charles II of Navarre. 4. Jean Deviosse (1920–1992): In Jean le Bon (1985), Deviosse offered a more nuanced view, acknowledging John’s courage and chivalric ideals but still framing his reign as a failure due to the Poitiers debacle and financial mismanagement. Deviosse cited Froissart, Michelet, and Perroy. 5. Maurice Keen (1933–2012): In The Pelican History of Medieval Europe (1969), Keen cited Perroy and Michelet, describing John II as a king overwhelmed by circumstances, with his capture at Poitiers symbolizing the collapse of French royal authority. Recent historians have begun to challenge the critical trend, arguing that John II’s reign must be understood within its medieval context. Françoise Autrand in Charles V: Le Sage (1994) contrasts John’s failures with his son Charles V’s successes but acknowledges John’s efforts to maintain Valois legitimacy amidst unprecedented crises. Autrand cites Deviosse and Froissart but emphasizes the structural challenges—such as the decentralized feudal system and the economic impact of the Black Death—over personal failings. D'Arcy Boulton highlights John II’s establishment of the Order of the Star in 1351 as a bold attempt to strengthen royal authority and unify the French nobility, though he notes its limited success due to political fragmentation and military defeats. Similarly, Georges Bordonove argues that John’s personal bravery, notably in battles such as Poitiers in 1356, and his commitment to chivalric ideals reflect his dedication to royal prestige and the reputation of the Valois. Bordonove further notes that, during his captivity in England, John upheld the dignity of the French crown through his steadfast adherence to honorable conduct despite political and personal adversity.

John William Robert Kerr, 7th Marquess of Lothian PC (1 February 1794 – 14 November 1841), was a Tory politician who styled himself Lord Newbottle from birth until 1815 and held the courtesy title Earl of Ancram from 1815 to 1824. He served briefly as Captain of the Yeomen of the Guard under Sir Robert Peel between September and November 1841. Kerr was the eldest son of William Kerr, 6th Marquess of Lothian, and Lady Harriet, daughter of John Hobart, 2nd Earl of Buckinghamshire. He entered the House of Commons in 1820 as one of two representatives for Huntingdon, a seat he held until he succeeded his father as Marquess of Lothian in 1824. He also succeeded his father as Colonel of the Edinburgh Militia, a position he held until his death. In September 1841, he was sworn of the Privy Council and appointed Captain of the Yeomen of the Guard in Sir Robert Peel’s Tory administration, a role he held until his death in November 1841. He served as Lord-Lieutenant of Roxburghshire from 1824 to 1841. In 1831, he married Lady Cecil Chetwynd-Talbot, daughter of Charles Chetwynd-Talbot, 2nd Earl Talbot; they had five sons and two daughters. Their two elder sons, William and Schomberg, both succeeded to the title. Their third son, Lord Ralph Kerr, became a major-general in the army and was the father of Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian; their fourth son, Lord Walter Kerr, became an admiral in the Royal Navy and was the grandfather of Peter Kerr, 12th Marquess of Lothian, and great-grandfather of Michael Kerr, 13th Marquess of Lothian. Lord Lothian died in November 1841 at the age of 47. After his death, the Marchioness converted to Catholicism with her two younger sons, Lord Ralph Kerr and Lord Walter Kerr, and her daughters. The Marchioness of Lothian died in May 1877, aged 69.

John Robert Lewis (February 21, 1940 – July 17, 2020) was an American civil rights activist and statesman who served in the United States House of Representatives for Georgia's 5th congressional district from 1987 until his death in 2020. He participated in the 1960 Nashville sit-ins and the Freedom Rides, served as chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) from 1963 to 1966, and was one of the "Big Six" leaders who organized the 1963 March on Washington. In 1965, Lewis led the first of three Selma to Montgomery marches across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, where, in an incident known as Bloody Sunday, state troopers and police attacked him and other marchers. A member of the Democratic Party, Lewis was first elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1986 and served 17 terms, representing a district that included most of Atlanta. Due to his length of service, he became the dean of the Georgia congressional delegation. He held key leadership roles in the Democratic Party in the House, serving from 1991 as a chief deputy whip and from 2003 as a senior chief deputy whip. He received numerous honorary degrees and awards, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011. Born near Troy, Alabama, on February 21, 1940, the third of ten children of Willie Mae (née Carter) and Eddie Lewis, his parents were sharecroppers in rural Pike County, Alabama. His great-grandfather, Frank Carter, had been born enslaved in the same county in 1862 and lived until Lewis was seven years old. As a boy, Lewis aspired to be a preacher and, at age five, preached to his family's chickens. He had little interaction with white people as a child, having seen only two white people by age six. He recalled growing up in rural Alabama, very poor, with few books at home and attending a Rosenwald School, the only school in the area. At age 16, he attempted to get a library card and was told the library was for whites only. He later learned about integrated schools, buses, and businesses from relatives in northern cities, including an experience in Buffalo, New York, at age 11. In 1955, Lewis first heard Martin Luther King Jr. on the radio and followed the Montgomery bus boycott. At age 15, he preached his first public sermon; at 17, he met Rosa Parks and at 18, met King. He also credited evangelist Billy Graham as someone who helped change him and inspired his desire to become a minister. After writing to King about being denied admission to Troy University, Lewis was invited to meet with him, who advised against suing due to risks to his family, and instead, Lewis enrolled at a small historically black college in Tennessee. He graduated from the American Baptist Theological Seminary in Nashville and was ordained as a Baptist minister, then earned a bachelor's degree in religion and philosophy from Fisk University, a member of the Phi Beta Sigma fraternity. As a student, Lewis became an activist, organizing sit-ins at segregated lunch counters in Nashville and participating in civil rights activities, including bus boycotts and nonviolent protests for voting rights and racial equality. He believed in "good trouble, necessary trouble" as a means to achieve change. While a student, he attended nonviolence workshops led by Rev. James Lawson and Rev. Kelly Miller Smith, adopting the philosophy of nonviolence for life. In 1961, Lewis became one of the 13 original Freedom Riders, riding interstate buses from Washington, D.C. to New Orleans to challenge segregated seating, which violated federal law. The Freedom Rides, initiated by the Fellowship of Reconciliation and revived by James Farmer and the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), aimed to enforce the Supreme Court decision in Boynton v. Virginia (1960). The rides revealed government inaction in the face of violence. After extreme violence in South Carolina and Alabama, the Kennedy Administration called for a moratorium. At age 21, Lewis was the first Freedom Rider to be assaulted in Rock Hill, South Carolina, when two white men attacked him, injuring his face and kicking him in the ribs. Two weeks later, he joined a Freedom Ride to Jackson, Mississippi. Near the end of his life, he said, "We were determined not to let any act of violence keep us from our goal. We knew our lives could be threatened, but we had made up our minds not to turn back." He was imprisoned for 40 days at the Mississippi State Penitentiary. In an interview with CNN during the 40th anniversary of the Freedom Rides, Lewis recounted violence in Birmingham, where Riders were beaten by a mob including KKK members with baseball bats, chains, lead pipes, and stones, and at the Greyhound station in Montgomery, where he was hit in the head with a wooden crate and left unconscious. When CORE abandoned the Freedom Ride, Lewis and Diane Nash arranged for Nashville students from Fisk and other colleges to continue the campaign. In February 2009, 48 years after the Montgomery attack, Lewis received a nationally televised apology from Elwin Wilson, a white southerner and former Klansman. In 2015, Lewis stated he had known Michael Schwerner, Andrew Goodman, and James Chaney, who were abducted and murdered in June 1964 in Neshoba County, Mississippi, by members of the Ku Klux Klan, including law enforcement. In 1963, when Charles McDew stepped down as SNCC chairman, Lewis, a founding member, was elected to lead the organization. He had been arrested 24 times in the nonviolent movement and was the youngest of the "Big Six" leaders organizing the March on Washington. He was the fourth of 12 speakers, preceding Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech. Lewis had written a response to Kennedy's 1963 Civil Rights Bill, criticizing it for failing to protect African Americans from police brutality or provide voting rights, calling it "too little and too late." Advance copies were distributed on August 27, but other leaders demanded revisions. James Forman rewrote the speech, replacing Lewis's original statement "we cannot support, wholeheartedly the [Kennedy] civil rights bill" with "We support it with great reservations." The speech, though censored, was the most prominent sustained criticism of police violence in the civil rights movement at that time. Lewis declared, "We are tired of being beat by policemen," adding that the bill did "nothing to protect the young children and old women who must face police dogs and fire hoses in the South," drawing enthusiastic cheers, the first of more than twelve times that applause forced him to pause. After Lewis, Dr. King delivered his famous "I Have a Dream" speech. Historian Howard Zinn noted that Lewis was prepared to ask, "Which side is the federal government on?" a question that was removed from his speech to avoid offending the Kennedy Administration. In 1964, SNCC launched Freedom Schools and the Mississippi Freedom Summer to register black voters and engage college student activists. Lewis coordinated SNCC's efforts for Freedom Summer. In 1965, he organized voter registration efforts during the Selma voting rights campaign and became nationally known during the Selma to Montgomery marches. On March 7, 1965—known as "Bloody Sunday"—Lewis and Hosea Williams led over 600 marchers across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama. At the city-county boundary, Alabama State Troopers ordered them to disperse. When the marchers stopped to pray, police discharged tear gas and charged with nightsticks, beating them. Lewis's skull was fractured, and he escaped to Brown Chapel, a church in Selma that served as the movement's headquarters. He bore scars on his head for the rest of his life. Lewis served as SNCC chairman until 1966, when he was replaced by Stokely Carmichael. In 1966, he moved to New York City to become associate director of the Field Foundation of New York, where he completed his degree from Fisk University. He returned to Atlanta to direct the Southern Regional Council's Community Organization Project. In 1970, he became director of the Voter Education Project (VEP), a position he held until 1977. Though initially a project of the Southern Regional Council, the VEP became independent in 1971. Despite challenges from the 1973–1975 recession, the VEP added nearly four million minority voters to the rolls and expanded its mission, including running Voter Mobilization Tours. In January 1977, incumbent Democratic Congressman Andrew Young resigned to become U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. under President Jimmy Carter. In the March 1977 open primary, Atlanta City Councilman Wyche Fowler ranked first with 40% of the vote, failing to reach 50%, while Lewis ranked second with 29%. In the April election, Fowler defeated Lewis 62%–38%. After the loss, Lewis accepted a position with the Carter administration as associate director of ACTION, responsible for the VISTA program, the Retired Senior Volunteer Program, and the Foster Grandparent Program, holding the role for two and a half years before resigning as the 1980 election approached. In 1981, Lewis ran for an at-large seat on the Atlanta City Council, winning with 69% of the vote and serving until 1986. After nine years in Congress, Wyche Fowler gave up the seat to run for the U.S. Senate. Lewis decided to run for the 5th district again. In the August Democratic primary, State Senator Julian Bond ranked first with 47%, just three points shy of winning, while Lewis finished second with 35%. In the run-off, Lewis defeated Bond 52% to 48%, a victory that strained relations in Atlanta's Black community, as many Black leaders had supported Bond. Lewis was endorsed by the Atlanta newspapers and favored by the white liberal establishment. His win was due to strong results among white voters, a minority in the district. During the campaign, he ran advertisements accusing Bond of corruption, implying Bond used cocaine, and suggesting Bond had lied about his civil rights activism. In the November general election, Lewis defeated Republican Portia Scott 75% to 25%. He was reelected 18 times, dropping below 70 percent of the vote in the general election only once in 1994, when he defeated Republican Dale Dixon by a 38-point margin, 69%–31%. He ran unopposed in 1996, 2004, 2006, and 2008, and again in 2014 and 2018. He was challenged in the Democratic primary only twice: in 1992 and 2008. In 1992, he defeated State Representative Mable Thomas 76–24%. In 2008, Thomas challenged Lewis again; Markel Hutchins also contested the race. Lewis defeated both, 69–16–15%. Lewis represented Georgia's 5th congressional district, one of the most consistently Democratic districts in the nation, which has been represented by a Democrat since its formalization in 1845. He was one of the most liberal congressmen to represent a district in the Deep South, categorized as a "Hard-Core Liberal" by On the Issues. The Washington Post described him in 1998 as "a fiercely partisan Democrat but ... also fiercely independent." Lewis characterized himself as a strong and adamant liberal. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution called him the "only former major civil rights leader who extended his fight for human rights and racial reconciliation to the halls of Congress" and referred to him as the "conscience of Congress" among U.S. senators and congressional aides. He cited Florida Senator and later Representative Claude Pepper, a staunch liberal, as the colleague he most admired.

He represented Georgia's 5th congressional district, one of the most consistently Democratic districts in the nation, which has been represented by a Democrat for most of its history since its formalization in 1845. Lewis was one of the most liberal congressmen to represent a district in the Deep South and was categorized as a "Hard-Core Liberal" by On the Issues. He admired Florida Senator and later Representative Claude Pepper, a staunch liberal, as his most admired colleague. Lewis supported gay rights and national health insurance. He opposed the 1991 Gulf War, the 2000 U.S. trade agreement with China that passed the House, the Clinton administration's NAFTA and welfare reform. After welfare reform passed, he was described as outraged, saying, "Where is the sense of decency? What does it profit a great nation to conquer the world, only to lose its soul?" In 1994, when Clinton considered invading Haiti, Lewis opposed armed intervention, but after a non-violent transition of power was negotiated, he supported U.S. troop presence in Haiti under Operation Uphold Democracy, calling it a "mission of peace." In 1998, when Clinton was considering a military strike against Iraq, Lewis said he would back the president if American forces were ordered into action. In 2001, three days after the September 11 attacks, Lewis voted to give President George W. Bush authority to use force against the perpetrators of 9/11 in a vote that was 420–1, calling it probably one of his toughest votes. In 2002, he sponsored the Peace Tax Fund bill, a conscientious objection to military taxation initiative reintroduced yearly since 1972. He was a "fierce partisan critic of President Bush" and an early opponent of the Iraq War; the Associated Press reported he was "the first major House figure to suggest impeaching George W. Bush," arguing the president "deliberately, systematically violated the law" in authorizing the National Security Agency to conduct wiretaps without a warrant, and said, "He is not king, he is president." Lewis drew on his Civil Rights Movement history in his politics, making an annual pilgrimage to Alabama to retrace the 1965 Selma to Montgomery march route, which he worked to include in the Historic National Trails program. The trip became a sought-after event among lawmakers, both Republican and Democrat, with Lewis stating, "We don't deliberately set out to win votes, but it's very helpful." However, Faith and Politics Institute faced criticism for selling seats on the trip to lobbyists for at least $25,000 each, and according to the Center for Public Integrity, even Lewis said he would feel "much better" if the institute's funding came from churches and foundations instead of corporations. On June 3, 2011, the House passed a resolution 268–145 calling for withdrawal of U.S. military from air and naval operations in and around Libya; Lewis voted against it. In a 2002 op-ed, Lewis quoted Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s response to an anti-Zionist student at a 1967 Harvard meeting, stating, "When people criticize Zionists they mean Jews, you are talking anti-Semitism," and included another statement from March 25, 1968: "Peace for Israel means security, and we must stand with all our might to protect its right to exist, its territorial integrity. I see Israel as one of the great outposts of democracy in the world, and a marvelous example of what can be done, how desert land can be transformed into an oasis of brotherhood and democracy. Peace for Israel means security and that security must be a reality." Lewis "strongly disagreed" with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel and co-sponsored a resolution condemning the pro-Palestinian group, but supported Representatives Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib's House resolution opposing U.S. anti-boycott legislation banning the boycott of Israel, explaining his support as "a simple demonstration of my ongoing commitment to the ability of every American to exercise the fundamental First Amendment right to protest through nonviolent actions." In January 2001, Lewis boycotted George W. Bush's inauguration by staying in his Atlanta district, not attending because he did not believe Bush was the true elected president. Later, he joined 30 other House Democrats who voted to not count the 20 electoral votes from Ohio in the 2004 presidential election. In March 2003, Lewis spoke to a crowd of 30,000 in Oregon during an anti-war protest before the Iraq War. In 2006 and 2009, he was arrested for protesting against the genocide in Darfur outside the Sudanese embassy. He was one of eight U.S. Representatives from six states arrested while holding a sit-in near the west side of the U.S. Capitol to advocate for immigration reform. In October 2007, Lewis endorsed Hillary Clinton for president. On February 14, 2008, he announced he was considering withdrawing his support and might instead cast his superdelegate vote for Barack Obama, saying, "Something is happening in America and people are prepared and ready to make that great leap." Ben Smith of Politico said that "it would be a seminal moment in the race if John Lewis were to switch sides." On February 27, 2008, Lewis formally endorsed Obama. After Obama clinched the Democratic nomination, Lewis said, "If someone had told me this would be happening now, I would have told them they were crazy, out of their mind, they didn't know what they were talking about ... I just wish the others were around to see this day. ... To the people who were beaten, put in jail, were asked questions they could never answer to register to vote, it's amazing." Despite switching his support to Obama, Lewis drew criticism from constituents for his support of Clinton for several months. One of his challengers in the House primary election set up campaign headquarters inside the building that served as Obama's Georgia office. In October 2008, Lewis criticized John McCain and Sarah Palin, accusing them of "sowing the seeds of hatred and division" in a way that brought to mind the late Gov. George Wallace and "another destructive period" in American political history. McCain said he was "saddened" by the criticism from "a man I've always admired" and called on Obama to repudiate the statement. Obama responded, saying he "does not believe that John McCain or his policy criticism is in any way comparable to George Wallace or his segregationist policies." Lewis later clarified that he had not compared McCain and Palin to Wallace himself, but rather that his earlier statement was a "reminder to all Americans that toxic language can lead to destructive behavior." On an African American being elected president, he said: "If you ask me whether the election ... is the fulfillment of Dr. King's dream, I say, 'No, it's just a down payment.' There's still too many people 50 years later, there's still too many people that are being left out and left behind." After Obama's swearing-in, Lewis asked him to sign a commemorative photograph, which Obama signed, "Because of you, John. Barack Obama." On June 22, 2016, House Democrats, led by Lewis and Massachusetts Representative Katherine Clark, began a sit-in demanding House Speaker Paul Ryan allow a vote on gun-safety legislation after the Orlando nightclub shooting. Speaker pro tempore Daniel Webster ordered the House into recess, but Democrats refused to leave the chamber for nearly 26 hours. In 1988, the year after being sworn into Congress, Lewis introduced a bill to create a national African American museum in Washington. The bill failed and was blocked in the Senate, most often by conservative Southern Senator Jesse Helms, for 15 years. In 2003, Helms retired. The bill won bipartisan support and President George W. Bush signed it, with the Smithsonian's Board of Regents to establish the location. The National Museum of African American History and Culture, located adjacent to the Washington Monument, held its opening ceremony on September 25, 2016. Lewis supported Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic presidential primaries against Bernie Sanders. Regarding Sanders' role in the civil rights movement, Lewis remarked, "To be very frank, I never saw him, I never met him. I chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee for three years, from 1963 to 1966. I was involved in sit-ins, in the Freedom Rides, the March on Washington, the March from Selma to Montgomery ... but I met Hillary Clinton." Former Congressman and Hawaii Governor Neil Abercrombie wrote a letter to Lewis expressing his disappointment with Lewis's comments about Sanders. Lewis later clarified, saying, "During the late 1950s and 1960s when I was more engaged, [Sanders] was not there. I did not see him around. I have never seen him in the South. But if he was there, if he was involved someplace, I was not aware of it ... The fact that I did not meet him in the movement does not mean I doubted that Senator Sanders participated in the civil rights movement, neither was I attempting to disparage his activism." In a January 2016 interview, Lewis compared Donald Trump, then the Republican front-runner, to former Alabama Governor George Wallace, saying, "I've been around a while and Trump reminds me so much of a lot of the things that George Wallace said and did. I think demagogues are pretty dangerous, really ... We shouldn't divide people, we shouldn't separate people." On January 13, 2017, during an interview with NBC's Chuck Todd for Meet the Press, Lewis stated: "I don't see the president-elect as a legitimate president." He added, "I think the Russians participated in having this man get elected, and they helped destroy the candidacy of Hillary Clinton. I don't plan to attend the inauguration. I think there was a conspiracy on the part of the Russians, and others, that helped him get elected. That's not right. That's not fair. That's not the open, democratic process." Trump replied on Twitter the following day, suggesting that Lewis should "spend more time on fixing and helping his district, which is in horrible shape and falling apart (not to [...] mention crime infested) rather than falsely complaining about the election results," and accusing Lewis of being "All talk, talk, talk – no action or results. Sad!" Trump's statement about Lewis's district was rated as "Mostly False" by PolitiFact, and he was criticized for attacking a civil rights leader such as Lewis, especially one who was brutally beaten for the cause, and especially on Martin Luther King weekend. Senator John McCain acknowledged Lewis as "an American hero" but criticized him, saying: "this is not the first time that Congressman Lewis has taken a very extreme stand and condemned without any shred of evidence for doing so an incoming president of the United States. This is a stain on Congressman Lewis's reputation – no one else's." A few days later, Lewis said he would not attend Trump's inauguration because he did not believe Trump was the true elected president. "It will be the first (inauguration) that I miss since I've been in Congress. You cannot be at home with something that you feel that is wrong, is not right," he said. Lewis had failed to attend George W. Bush's inauguration in 2001 because he believed he too was not a legitimately elected president. His statement was rated as "Pants on Fire" by PolitiFact. Lewis endorsed Joe Biden for president on April 7, 2020, a day before Biden effectively secured the Democratic nomination, recommending Biden pick a woman of color as his running mate. Lewis served on the following Congressional committees at the time of his death and was a member of over 40 caucuses, including. In 1991, Lewis became the senior chief deputy whip in the Democratic caucus. His 1998 autobiography Walking with the Wind: A Memoir of the Movement, co-written with Mike D'Orso, won the Robert F. Kennedy Book Award, the Anisfield-Wolf Book Award, the Christopher Award, and the Lillian Smith Book Award. It appeared on numerous bestseller lists, was selected as a New York Times Notable Book of the Year, was named by the American Library Association as its Nonfiction Book of the Year, and was included among Newsweek magazine's 2009 list of "50 Books For Our Times." It was critically acclaimed, with The Washington Post calling it "the definitive account of the civil rights movement" and the Los Angeles Times proclaiming it "destined to become a classic in civil rights literature." His life is also the subject of a 2002 book for young people, John Lewis: From Freedom Rider to Congressman. In 2012, Lewis released Across That Bridge, written with Brenda Jones, to mixed reviews. Publishers Weekly's review said, "At its best, the book provides a testament to the power of nonviolence in social movements ... At its worst, it resembles an extended campaign speech." In 2013, Lewis became the first member of Congress to write a graphic novel, launching a trilogy titled March. The March trilogy is a black and white comics trilogy about the Civil Rights Movement, told through the perspective of civil rights leader and U.S. Congressman John Lewis. The first volume, March: Book One, written by Lewis and Andrew Aydin, illustrated and lettered by Nate Powell, was published in August 2013; the second volume, March: Book Two, was published in January 2015; the final volume, March: Book Three, was published in August 2016. In an August 2014 interview, Lewis cited the influence of a 1958 comic book, Martin Luther King and the Montgomery Story, on his decision to adapt his experience to the graphic novel format. March: Book One became a number one New York Times bestseller for graphic novels and spent more than a year on the lists. It received an "Author Honor" from the American Library Association's 2014 Coretta Scott King Book Awards and became the first graphic novel to win a Robert F. Kennedy Book Award, receiving a "Special Recognition" bust in 2014. March: Book One was selected by first-year reading programs in 2014 at Michigan State University, Georgia State University, and Marquette University. March: Book Two was released in 2015 and immediately became both a New York Times and Washington Post bestseller for graphic novels. The release of March: Book Three in August 2016 brought all three volumes into the top 3 slots of the New York Times bestseller list for graphic novels for 6 consecutive weeks. The third volume was announced as the recipient of the 2017 Printz Award for excellence in young-adult literature, the Coretta Scott King Award, the YALSA Award for Excellence in Nonfiction, the 2016 National Book Award in Young People's Literature, and the Sibert Medal at the American Library Association's annual Midwinter Meeting in January 2017. The March trilogy received the Carter G. Woodson Book Award in the Secondary (grades 7–12) category in 2017. In 2018, Lewis and Andrew Aydin co-wrote another graphic novel as a sequel to the March series entitled Run, which documents Lewis's life after the passage of the Civil Rights Act. The authors teamed with illustrator Afua Richardson for the book, originally scheduled for release in August 2018 but later rescheduled. It was released on August 3, 2021, a year after his death, as it was one of his last endeavours before he died. Nate Powell, who illustrated March, also contributed to the art.

John Lewis received the 2017 Printz Award for excellence in young-adult literature, the Coretta Scott King Award, the YALSA Award for Excellence in Nonfiction, the 2016 National Book Award in Young People's Literature, and the Sibert Medal at the American Library Association's annual Midwinter Meeting in January 2017. The March trilogy won the Carter G. Woodson Book Award in the Secondary (grades 7–12) category in 2017. In 2018, Lewis and Andrew Aydin co-wrote Run, a graphic novel sequel to the March series that documents Lewis's life after the passage of the Civil Rights Act; the book was illustrated by Afua Richardson and Nate Powell, originally scheduled for release in August 2018 but released on August 3, 2021, a year after his death, as it was one of his last projects. Lewis met his future wife Lillian Miles at a New Year's Eve party hosted by Xernona Clayton; she worked at the library of Atlanta University at the time, and they married in 1968. They had a son who works in politics, and Lillian died on December 31, 2012, their 45th wedding anniversary. Lewis has a grandson who lives in Paris. On December 29, 2019, he was diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer and remained in the Washington D.C. area for treatment, stating, "I have been in some kind of fight – for freedom, equality, basic human rights – for nearly my entire life. I have never faced a fight quite like the one I have now." On June 7, 2020, the day after completing chemotherapy, he made his last public appearance at a large Black Lives Matter mural on Sixteenth Street in Washington, D.C., following protests that had been tear-gassed by U.S. Park Police and Secret Service under President Donald Trump's orders. Lewis died on July 17, 2020, at age 80 in Atlanta, the same day and city as his friend and fellow civil rights activist C.T. Vivian, making him the final surviving "Big Six" civil rights icon. President Donald Trump ordered all flags to be flown at half-staff in response to his death, and international leaders including Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Löfven, French President Emmanuel Macron, and Irish President Michael D. Higgins expressed condolences. Public ceremonies began in Troy, Alabama, at Troy University, which had denied him admission in 1957 due to racial segregation; his casket was then taken to a memorial at the historic Brown Chapel AME Church in Selma, Alabama. Calls to rename the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma in his honor grew after his death. On July 26, 2020, his casket, carried in a horse-drawn caisson, traveled the same route over the bridge that he walked during the Bloody Sunday march from Selma to Montgomery, before lying in state at the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery. U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell announced that Lewis would lie in state in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda on July 27 and 28, with a public viewing and procession through Washington, D.C.; he is the first African-American lawmaker to receive this honor, though in October 2019, Representative Elijah Cummings had previously lain in state in the Capitol Statuary Hall. Due to health concerns related to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, his casket was displayed outdoors on the East Front steps during public viewing hours instead of in the Rotunda. On July 29, 2020, his casket left the U.S. Capitol and was transported back to Atlanta, Georgia, where he lay in state at the Georgia State Capitol. At his final funeral service at Atlanta's Ebenezer Baptist Church, former U.S. Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama delivered speeches, with former President Jimmy Carter sending a statement due to his age and inability to travel; President Donald Trump did not attend. Lewis was buried at Atlanta's historic South-View Cemetery. He penned an op-ed for The New York Times on the day of his funeral, calling on the younger generation to continue the work for justice and an end to hate. In 1997, the sculpture by Thornton Dial, The Bridge, was dedicated to him at Ponce de Leon Avenue and Freedom Park, Atlanta; in 1999, he received the Wallenberg Medal from the University of Michigan and the Four Freedoms Award for Freedom of Speech. In 2001, he was awarded the Profile in Courage Award "for his extraordinary courage, leadership and commitment to civil rights," a special Lifetime Achievement award given only twice, the other being William Winter in 2008; the following year, he received the Spingarn Medal from the NAACP. In 2004, he received the Golden Plate Award of the American Academy of Achievement from James Earl Jones. In 2006, he received the U.S. Senator John Heinz Award for Greatest Public Service by an Elected or Appointed Official from the Jefferson Awards for Public Service. In September 2007, he was awarded the Dole Leadership Prize from the Robert J. Dole Institute of Politics at the University of Kansas. He was the only living speaker from the March on Washington present at Barack Obama's inauguration, and Obama signed a commemorative photograph for him with the words, "Because of you, John. Barack Obama." In 2010, he received the first LBJ Liberty and Justice for All Award from the Lyndon Baines Johnson Foundation, and in 2011, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama. In 2016, a future U.S. Navy underway replenishment oiler was named USNS John Lewis; that same year, Lewis and fellow Selma marcher Frederick Reese accepted Congressional Gold Medals for the "foot soldiers" of the Selma marchers, and he received the Liberty Medal at the National Constitution Center, coinciding with the 150th anniversary of the 14th Amendment. In 2020, he was awarded the Walter P. Reuther Humanitarian Award by Wayne State University, the UAW, and the Reuther family. Lewis gave commencement addresses at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in 2014, Bates College (Lewiston, Maine) and Washington University in St. Louis in 2016, Bard College and Bank Street College of Education in 2017, and Harvard University in 2018. He was recognized for his involvement with comics with the 2017 Inkpot Award. On July 30, 2018, the Atlanta City Council voted to rename Atlanta's Freedom Parkway John Lewis Freedom Parkway. On November 5, 2020, the Metropolitan Council of Nashville and Davidson County voted to rename part of Nashville, Tennessee's 5th Avenue John Lewis Way. On June 23, 2020, the Fairfax County Public School Board voted to rename Robert E. Lee High School in Springfield, Virginia to John R. Lewis High School, and a program called John Lewis Now was created in his vision to provide students with leadership and government curriculum using the nearby Washington, D.C. area. Following his death, support for renaming the historically significant Pettus Bridge in Lewis's honor grew, and the Board of Fairfax County Public Schools announced the renaming of Robert E. Lee High School to John R. Lewis High School. Troy University announced that its main building on the flagship campus would be named after John Lewis, previously named after Bibb Graves, a former Alabama governor and Ku Klux Klan officer. On August 1, 2020, a statue of Lewis by sculptor Gregory Johnson was revealed and installed at Cook Park in Atlanta, Georgia, in April 2021. On February 21, 2021, President Joe Biden marked Lewis's late birthday on Twitter, urging Americans to "carry on his mission in the fight for justice and equality for all," stating, "While my dear friend may no longer be with us, his life and legacy provide an eternal moral compass on which direction to march. May we carry on his mission in the fight for justice and equality for all." On October 2, 2021, Seattle opened the John Lewis Memorial Bridge. On October 27, 2021, the University of California, Santa Cruz named one of its residential colleges, formerly known as College Ten, John R. Lewis College. On August 16, 2024, a statue of Lewis by Basil Watson was installed in Decatur, Georgia, in the place where an obelisk monument to the Confederacy was previously erected by the United Daughters of the Confederacy in 1908 and removed in 2020. Lewis was awarded more than 50 honorary degrees. He was portrayed by Stephan James in the 2014 film Selma, made a cameo in the music video for Young Jeezy's song "My President" released during Obama's inauguration, voiced himself in the 2017 Arthur episode "Arthur Takes a Stand," and his life was chronicled in the 2017 PBS documentary John Lewis: Get in the Way and the 2020 CNN Films documentary John Lewis: Good Trouble. He appeared in the 2019 documentary Bobby Kennedy for President, where he commended Robert F. Kennedy for his civil rights support, and recounted his sorrow following the 1968 assassinations of Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. Lewis also presented Green Book as a nominee for Best Picture at the 91st Academy Awards on February 24, 2019, alongside Amandla Stenberg. He attended comics conventions to promote his graphic novel, notably San Diego Comic-Con in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017. During the 2015 convention, he led an impromptu simulated Selma civil rights march with children, wearing the same clothes as on Bloody Sunday, which drew thousands of participants and was repeated in 2016 and 2017.

Johnson Evan Gicheru (died 25 December 2020)[1][2] was a Kenyan lawyer and the 12th Chief Justice of the Republic of Kenya.[3] He was appointed by President Mwai Kibaki following his election in 2003 and served as Chief Justice from 21 February 2003 until his retirement on 27 February 2011, making him the longest-serving African Chief Justice in Kenya's history. He held various early career positions, including Senior State Counsel in the Office of the Attorney General and administrative officer in the Office of the President. He was appointed a Judge of the High Court in 1982 and became a member of the Court of Appeal on 8 June 1988. During his tenure, he served as chairperson of a judicial inquiry into the death of Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Ouko, though the commission was disbanded before releasing its findings.[4] He was married to Mrs. Margaret Gicheru and they had seven children.[5] Johnson Evan Gicheru passed away on 25 December 2020. Johnson O'Connor (January 22, 1891 – July 1, 1973) was an American psychometrician, researcher, and educator best known as a pioneer in aptitude testing and a strong advocate for the importance of vocabulary. Born into a prosperous Chicago family, he was the son of John O’Connor and Nelie Johnson O’Connor; his mother descended from early Puritan settlers of Massachusetts, and his father was an attorney who once shared an office with Clarence Darrow. O’Connor received a progressive education at the University of Chicago Laboratory School under John Dewey and graduated from Harvard University in 1913 with a degree in Philosophy. He later conducted research in astronomical mathematics under Percival Lowell and worked in electrical engineering at American Steel and Wire and General Electric. In 1922, F.P. Cox of General Electric commissioned O’Connor to develop the "human" engineering project, which aimed to match employees to positions aligned with their natural abilities and retrain them in those areas. This led O’Connor to study inborn aptitudes and create aptitude tests known as "work samples," developing classifications such as "Graphoria," "Ideaphoria," and "Structural Visualization." He became one of the first researchers to provide evidence that aptitudes are innate, showing that individuals with higher mathematical aptitude learn mathematics more efficiently than those with lower aptitude, and that despite equal training, those with higher aptitude consistently outperform others. In 1930, O’Connor founded the Human Engineering Laboratory at Stevens Institute of Technology, which later became the Johnson O'Connor Research Foundation, a non-profit with aptitude testing centers in major U.S. cities. While studying aptitudes related to specific vocations, he discovered that vocabulary level was the strongest single predictor of occupational success across all fields, and that vocabulary is not innate but can be acquired by anyone. This finding became central to his later work, where he focused on cataloging essential English words and ordering them by difficulty. He developed a method to assess students’ vocabulary levels through a multiple-choice diagnostic test, recommending that students enter a vocabulary program at a level matching their skill, with optimal learning occurring just beyond that level. He authored several books on vocabulary, including "The Johnson O'Connor English Vocabulary Builder," "The Johnson O'Connor Science Vocabulary Builder," and the "Ginn Vocabulary Building Program" (co-authored). His extensive vocabulary was notably showcased during a guest appearance on Groucho Marx’s "You Bet Your Life," where Groucho humorously remarked on his dual last names. In his final years, O’Connor continued researching, lecturing, and writing on human aptitudes and mental potential, publishing books such as "Structural Visualization," "The Unique Individual," and "Psychometrics." He also focused on vocabulary acquisition processes. O’Connor died in Mexico City, D.F., on July 1, 1973, and is buried beside his wife, architect Eleanor Manning O’Connor, in Newport Beach, California. He was survived by his son, Chadwell O’Connor, an engineer and Academy Award winner who designed the O'Connor Fluid-Head camera tripod.

Joseph Matthäus Aigner (18 January 1818, Vienna – 19 February 1886, Vienna) was an Austrian portrait painter who studied under Friedrich von Amerling and Carl Rahl. He painted portraits of Franz Joseph I of Austria and his wife Elizabeth, Franz Grillparzer, Friedrich Halm, Nikolaus Lenau, and Maximilian I of Mexico. In 1847, he married actress Fanny Matras (1828–1878). During the 1848 revolutions in Vienna, Aigner served as commander of the Academic Legion and was court-martialed for high treason, receiving a death sentence. However, Alfred I, Prince of Windisch-Grätz, pardoned him. According to Ripley's Believe It or Not!, a Capuchin friar, whose name Aigner never knew, saved his life three times—when he attempted to hang himself at ages 18 and 22 and when he was sentenced to death. Aigner died by suicide with a pistol in Vienna in 1886, and the same friar presided over his funeral. This article about an Austrian painter is a stub.
