Joshna Chinappa, born on 15 September 1986 in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, is an Indian squash player who became the youngest Indian national champion at 14, winning both junior and senior national titles. She is a two-time World Champion and four-time Asian Champion. Recognizing her contributions, she was awarded the Arjuna Award in 2013 and the Padma Shri in 2024. Her father, Anjan Chinappa, runs a coffee plantation in Coorg and was also her first coach and a member of the Tamil Nadu squash team. Her great granduncle K.M. Cariappa, the first commander-in-chief of the Indian Army in independent India, and her grandfather, father, and grandfather were all squash players. Joshna began playing squash at age seven and joined the Madras Cricket Club at eight, after deciding against badminton and tennis. She was the first beneficiary of the Mittal Champions Trust established by Mahesh Bhupati with funding from Lakshmi Mittal. In 2000, she won her first junior and senior national championships, becoming the youngest to hold both titles. In 2003, she won the British Junior Open U17 title at 16 and reached the U19 final the following year, losing to Omneya Abdel Kawy of Egypt. In 2005, she won the U17 title again by defeating Tenille Swartz of South Africa. In July 2005, she reached the finals of the World Junior Squash Championships in Belgium, losing to Raneem El Weleily of Egypt, having previously reached the last eight in 2003. In 2007, she switched coaches from Mohammad Medhaat to Malcolm Willstrop. In 2008, she won her first WISPA tour title at the NSC Super Satellite No 3 in Malaysia, defeating Low Wee Wern, and won a second tour title the following week by beating Wern again, reaching a career-best PSA World rank of 39. In 2010, she won the German Ladies Open, defeating Gaby Schmohl 11–6, 11–7, 11–6, marking her fourth tour title and first in Europe. In 2011, she won the Windy City Open by beating Dipika Pallikal 3–2 in the final. In August 2012, she faced an injury layoff during the Hamptons Open and returned in May after a seven-month break, winning the WISPA title at the 2012 Chennai Open by defeating Sarah Jane Perry 9–11, 11–4, 11–8, 12–10. In February, she won the Winter Club Women's Open; in April, she won the Richmond Open, defeating Australia's former world champion Rachael Grinham 11–9, 11–5, 11–8, her first win against her in six meetings. In March, she reached her new career-high PSA world ranking of 19. In August 2014, she and Dipika entered the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow as fifth-seeds in women's doubles, advancing through the group stage and reaching the quarterfinals, where they defeated Joelle King and Amanda Land-Murphy in straight games. They beat the second-seeded Australian pair of Rachael Grinham and Kasey Brown in the semifinals to reach the final, defeating the English pair of Jenny Duncalf and Laura Massaro in an upset win in less than 28 minutes with scores of 11–6, 11–8. This marked India's first-ever squash medal at the Commonwealth Games and made them the first Indian women to win a gold medal in squash. In May 2015, she reached the semifinals at the HKFC International but lost to Annie Au. In August, she won the Victorian Open in Australia for her tenth tour title, defeating Line Hansen 11–5, 11–4, 11–9. In September, she won the NSCI Open by beating Egypt's Habiba Mohamed 11–8, 11–9, 11–6, though she was injured during the second game after Mohamed struck her on the face with the racket. In October, she defeated Salma Hany of Egypt 11–9, 8–11, 5–11, 11–8, 11–9 to reach the semifinals of the 2015 Carol Weymuller Open, losing to Joelle King. In the first round of the Qatar Classic, she defeated Raneem El Welily, the World No. 1 at the time. In December 2015, she achieved her career-high world rank of 13, becoming the highest-ranked Indian woman player, overtaking Dipika. In February 2016, she lost in the quarterfinals of the Cleveland Classic to Camille Serme. At the 2016 South Asian Games in Guwahati as the top-seed, she won gold by defeating Maria Toorpaki Wazir 10–12, 11–7, 11–9, 11–7. In May 2016, she reached the semifinals of the HKFC International, defeating Annie Au 3–2 after losing the title the previous year, but lost in the final to Joelle King. In July, she rose to a career-high ranking of 10, becoming the second Indian to enter the world's top 10 after Dipika. In August, at the 2016 SRAM Invitational in Malaysia, she reached the finals after beating Joelle King in the semifinal but lost to Nicol David in the final. In October, she reached the finals of the 2016 Otters International in Mumbai after defeating Tesni Evans 3–1, 11–6, 15–13, 9–11, 11–8, losing to Annie Au in the final 9–11, 11–13, 7–11. In November, she participated in the 2016 World Team Squash Championships in Paris with Dipika, Akanksha Salunkhe, and Sunayna Kuruvilla, but the Indian team did not qualify for the knockout stage. In March 2017, she lost in the second round of the British Open to Raneem El Welily. In April, she participated in the 2017 Asian Individual Squash Championships in Chennai, reaching the final and defeating Palikkal 13–15, 12–10, 11–13, 11–4, 11–4, becoming the first Indian to win the Asian Squash Championship, which she described as her biggest achievement. In August, she and Dipika reached the quarterfinals of the World Doubles Squash Championship as second-seeds, defeating Samantha Cornett and Nikole Todd 10–11, 11–6, 11–8, and settled for a bronze medal after losing to Jenny Duncalf and Alison Waters. In September, she won her 15th national championship title at the 74th National Squash Championships in Greater Noida, one title short of the record. Later that month, she reached the final of the 2017 HKFC International as the third-seed but lost to Nour El Tayebl. In April 2018, she reached the quarterfinals of the women's singles event at the Commonwealth Games after defeating Tamika Saxby of Australia, but lost to Joelle King 11–5, 11–6, 11–9. Alongside Dipika Pallikal, she won the doubles silver medal at the 2018 Commonwealth Games. In April, she won her second-round match at the El Gouna International against eight-time world champion Nicol David in straight games, a notable upset. She lost in the quarterfinals. In August, she reached the semifinals of the 2018 Asian Games, defeating Nicol David 12–10, 11–9, 6–11, 10–12, 11–9, and lost to Sivasangari Subramaniam in the final, securing a silver medal. In October, she reached the quarterfinals of the Carol Weymuller Open. In March, she lost in the quarterfinals of the Black Ball Open to Joelle King. In April, she lost in the semifinals of the Macau Open. In May 2019, she won the Asian Individual Squash Championships by defeating Annie Au in the final. In June, she won her 17th national squash championship title, breaking the record previously held by Bhuvneshwari Kumari, who had won the title 16 times. In October, at the World Squash Championship, she lost to Nour El Sherbini of Egypt in the pre-quarterfinal. In February, she won her 18th national title at the 77th Senior National Championship. On 2 February 2014, she won the Winnipeg Winter Open, her maiden WSA world title, defeating Egypt's Heba El Torky 11–13, 11–8, 11–5, 3–11, 12–10. Joshna and Dipika are regarded as India's top-performing women squash players, both having reached the world's top 10. Joshna states that the rivalry between them is exaggerated by the media; they are competitive but get along well, often sharing rooms during events and competing together in events like the Commonwealth Games. Together, they won the Women’s Doubles Gold Medal at the 2022 Squash World Doubles Championships in Glasgow, Scotland.

Jovian (/ˈdʒoʊviən/; Latin: Jovianus; Ancient Greek: Ἰοβιανός, romanized: Iobianós; 331 – 17 February 364) was Roman emperor from June 363 to February 364. Born in 331 at Singidunum, Moesia Superior (modern Belgrade, Serbia), he was the son of Varronianus, commander of Constantius II's imperial bodyguards (comes domesticorum). Jovian joined the imperial bodyguard and, in 361, escorted Constantius' remains to the Church of the Holy Apostles. He married Charito and had two sons, Varronianus and another whose name is unknown. In 363, he accompanied Emperor Julian on the Mesopotamian campaign against Shapur II, the Sassanid king. At the Battle of Samarra, Julian was mortally wounded; Ammianus Marcellinus notes that Julian declined to name a successor, fearing he might overlook a worthy candidate or endanger a preferred one. Julian died on 26 June 363. The next day, the army offered the throne to Saturninius Secundus Salutius, praetorian prefect of the Orient, who refused it. Instead, despite Julian's reinstitution of paganism, the army chose the Christian Jovian, a senior officer of the Scholae, as emperor. On the morning of his accession, Jovian resumed the retreat begun by Julian. Though harassed by the Sasanids, the army reached Dura on the banks of the Tigris. Unable to cross the river, Jovian was forced to negotiate a peace treaty on humiliating terms: a thirty-year truce, withdrawal from the five Roman provinces—Arzamena, Moxoeona, Azbdicena, Rehimena, and Corduena—and cession of the fortresses of Nisibis, Castra Maurorum, and Singara to the Sasanids, along with the surrender of Roman interests in Armenia, leaving King Arsaces II without Roman support. The treaty was widely regarded as a disgrace. After crossing the Tigris, Jovian sent an embassy to the West to announce his elevation. With the treaty signed, he and his army marched to Nisibis, where the populace was given three days to leave before the city was handed over to the Sasanids. In September 363, upon arriving at Edessa, Jovian issued two edicts: one limiting the distance a soldier could be sent for straw to signal the end of hostilities, and another restoring estates of the res privata to the Imperial finances after Julian had transferred them to pagan temples. At Antioch in October 363, Jovian faced an enraged populace, with offensive graffiti and insulting authorless bills (famosi) throughout the city, prompting him to order the burning of the Library of Antioch. He left Antioch in November 363, heading for Constantinople, and by December 363 was at Ancyra, where he proclaimed his infant son Varronianus consul. His journey ended on 17 February 364, when he died in his tent at Dadastana, halfway between Ancyra and Nicaea, aged 33. His death, which went uninvestigated, may have resulted from suffocating on poisonous fumes from a brazier in a newly painted bedchamber. Jovian was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople in a porphyry sarcophagus. He was succeeded by Valentinian I and Valens, who divided the empire between them. To eliminate threats, they blinded Varronianus; according to John Chrysostom, Charito was spared but lived in fear. At Edessa, Jovian was met by bishops, including Athanasius, who had recently returned from exile. The Semi-Arian bishops received a poor reception, while Athanasius delivered a letter insisting on the Nicene Creed and rejecting Arianism. Athanasius was restored to his episcopal duties and allowed to accompany Jovian to Antioch. Upon arrival, Jovian received a letter from the Synod of Antioch requesting the restoration of Meletius as bishop. By September 363, Jovian restored the labarum ("Chi-Rho") as the army's standard, revoked Julian's edicts against Christians, but did not close any pagan temples. He issued an edict of toleration granting full liberty of conscience to his subjects, while banning magic and divination. Despite supporting the Nicene doctrines, he passed no edicts against Arians. Philostorgius, an Arian church historian, stated that Jovian restored churches to their original uses and freed them from the persecutions inflicted by the Apostate Julian. Jovian was consequently the last emperor to rule the entire Roman Empire for the whole of his reign, from his successors Valentinian I and Valens to the fall of the Western Roman Empire, all subsequent administrations involved co-emperors governing a split Eastern and Western jurisdiction.

Juan Manuel Barrientos Valencia is a Colombian chef and businessman, known by the nickname "Juanma." He was born in Medellín, Colombia, and completed his education at Colegiatura Colombiana in Medellín and Mariano Moreno in Buenos Aires. In 2006, he founded the El Cielo restaurant chain. In 2015, he opened the original El Cielo Miami, which was awarded a Michelin star in Florida's first-ever Michelin Guide in 2022. He has been recognized as one of the 50 best chefs of Latin America and received the Revelation Chef Award from Madrid Fusion. He is also a recipient of a Michelin Award. One of his projects is titled "In El Cielo, estamos cocinando la paz de Colombia," which translates to "In El Cielo, we are cooking up peace in Colombia."

Jules François Camille Ferry (French: [ʒyl fɛʁi]; 5 April 1832 – 17 March 1893) was a French statesman and republican philosopher who led the Moderate Republicans and served as Prime Minister of France from 1880 to 1881 and 1883 to 1885. He was a strong advocate of laicism and colonial expansion. Under the Third Republic, Ferry implemented laws that made primary education in France free, non-clerical (laïque), and compulsory. He reorganized the committee of public education through a law of 27 February 1880 and proposed regulations for university degrees, which sparked controversy due to Article 7 removing teaching rights from unauthorized religious orders. He successfully passed his eponymous laws of 16 June 1881 and 28 March 1882, establishing free, laical, and mandatory primary education. In higher education, the number of professors known as the "Republic's black hussars" doubled under his ministry. After France’s defeat by Prussia in 1870, Ferry promoted colonial expansion primarily for economic gain. In 1882, as Minister of Public Instruction, he launched a scientific exploration mission to Tunisia, led by botanist Ernest Cosson and including Napoléon Doumet-Adanson, with a geological section under Georges Rolland added in 1884, assisted by Philippe Thomas from 1885 and Georges Le Mesle in 1887. In a speech before the Chamber of Deputies on 28 March 1884, he stated that "it is a right for the superior races, because they have a duty. They have the duty to civilize the inferior races." He directed negotiations leading to a French protectorate in Tunis (1881), prepared the treaty of 17 December 1885 for the occupation of Madagascar, organized the conquest of Annam and Tonkin (Indochina), and initiated exploration in the Congo and Niger regions. The war with the Qing dynasty over these territories, triggered by the French retreat from Lạng Sơn, led to the Tonkin Affair, resulting in violent criticism from Clemenceau and other radicals, and Ferry’s resignation on 30 March 1885. Although the peace treaty of 9 June 1885, in which the Qing ceded suzerainty over Annam and Tonkin to France, was negotiated under his ministry, he never again served as premier. Ferry opposed monarchy, having witnessed Henri, Count of Chambord’s early bid, and conducted a widespread purge of monarchists from key state positions. In the 1890s, he visited Algeria and warned that a conflict between Indigènes and Europeans was inevitable. Ferry held the longest tenure as Prime Minister under the Third Republic until Georges Clemenceau became premier twice in the 20th century. He believed France should avoid confrontation with Wilhelmine Germany, favoring cooperation with Otto von Bismarck over threats of future war, a pragmatic but unpopular stance. Bismarck, though initially wary, accepted Ferry’s approach, supported French colonial expansion, and proposed Franco-German cooperation against the British Empire, leading to a colonial rivalry in Africa that nearly escalated into war at Fashoda in 1898—though both leaders died before the conflict materialized. The rivalry eventually led to the Entente Cordiale in 1904. Ferry remained a key figure in the moderate republican party and opposed General Boulanger. After Jules Grévy’s resignation on 2 December 1887, Ferry ran for president but was rejected by radicals and withdrew in favor of Sadi Carnot. On 10 December 1887, a man named Aubertin attempted to assassinate Ferry, who died on 17 March 1893 from complications of the wound. The Chamber of Deputies granted him a state funeral.

Heo Seung, born on May 7, 1991, is a South Korean rapper better known by his stage name Justhis. He released his debut album, titled 2 Many Homes 4 1 Kid, on June 14, 2016. Justhis is a member of the Korean hip hop crew IMJMWDP and is currently signed to the label GROOVL1N.

Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir, born on 4 October 1942 in Reykjavík, is an Icelandic politician who served as prime minister from 2009 to 2013. She was a member of the Althing (Iceland's parliament) for the Reykjavík constituencies from 1978 to 2013, winning re-election eight times. She studied at the Commercial College of Iceland and graduated in 1960 with a commercial diploma. From 1962 to 1971, she worked as a flight attendant with Icelandic Airlines, and from 1971 to 1978 as an office manager. She was active in trade unions, presiding over the Icelandic Cabin Crew Association and the Association of Former Stewardesses, and serving on the Board of the Commercial Workers' Union from 1976 to 1983. Elected to the Althing in 1978 on the Social Democratic Party list, she served as deputy speaker in 1979 and from 1983 to 1984, and was elected vice-chairperson of the Social Democratic Party in 1984, holding the position until 1993. She served as Minister of Social Affairs and Social Security from 1987 to 1994 and again from 2007 to 2009. In 1994, after losing the leadership bid for the Social Democratic Party, she declared "Minn tími mun koma!" ("My time will come!"), a phrase that became widely known in Iceland. She then left the party and founded the National Awakening (Þjóðvaki), which received 7.1% of the vote and four seats in the 1995 election, before all MPs joined the Social Democratic Party in 1996. In the 1999 election, National Awakening ran with the Social Democratic Alliance, and the parties officially merged in 2000. From 1994 to 2003, she was an opposition member in the Althing, serving on various committees. After the 2003 elections, she was re-elected deputy speaker from the Reykjavík South constituency. In the 2007 elections, from the Reykjavík North constituency, she returned to government as Minister of Social Affairs and Social Security with the Social Democratic Alliance and the Independence Party. On 26 January 2009, Prime Minister Geir Haarde resigned following the 2008 financial crisis, and President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson asked the Social Democratic Alliance and the Left-Green Movement to form a new government. Jóhanna was proposed as prime minister due to her public popularity and strong relations with the Left-Green Movement; a Capacent Gallup poll in December 2008 found 73% approval of her actions, the highest among cabinet members, with her approval ratings improving over 2008. The new government required support from the Progressive Party, and after negotiations ending on 31 January, the cabinet was appointed on 1 February 2009. A parliamentary election on 25 April 2009 followed the Kitchenware Revolution protests, resulting in the Social Democratic Alliance and the Left-Green Movement gaining overall majority seats, with the Progressive Party and the new Citizens' Movement also gaining seats, while the Independence Party lost support and seats. On 10 May 2009, Jóhanna remained prime minister in the new government. During her tenure, several referendums were held on Icesave bank debts; the first on 6 March 2010, followed by a second on 9 April 2011, both resulting in "no" votes. After the second referendum failed, the British and Dutch governments stated they would take the case to European courts. On 28 September 2010, the Althing voted 33–30 to indict former prime minister Geir Haarde on charges of negligence, but not other ministers, in a case heard by the Landsdómur, a special court established in 1905. The left coalition government, comprising the Social Democratic Alliance, the Left-Green Movement, the Progressive Party, and the Liberal Party, agreed to convene a constitutional assembly inspired by citizen protests. On 4 November 2009, a bill was introduced to involve citizens in drafting a new constitution. A National Forum, Þjóðfundur 2009, was held on 14 November 2009 at Laugardalshöll in Reykjavík, with 1,200 randomly selected participants from the national registry. On 16 June 2010, the Constitutional Act was passed by parliament, establishing a new Forum 2010 with a seven-member Constitutional Committee overseeing the process and the Anthill group organizing it. On 26 October 2010, 25 non-partisan citizens were elected to a Constitutional Council, though the Supreme Court invalidated the election results on 25 January 2011 due to procedural faults; the parliament upheld the process and accepted the candidates as part of the council. On 29 July 2011, the draft constitution was presented to parliament, which voted on 24 May 2012 to organize an advisory referendum on the proposal by 20 October 2012, with 35 in favor and 15 against, the only opposition coming from the former governing Independence Party. A proposed referendum to end Iceland's accession talks with the European Union was rejected, with 34 votes against and 25 in favor. In 2010, her government banned strip clubs, payments for nudity in restaurants, and other forms of employer profit from employee nudity—making it the first such ban in a Western democratic country. Jóhanna stated that the Nordic countries were leading in women's equality, recognizing women as equal citizens. Julie Bindel of The Guardian called Iceland the most feminist country in the world. In 2012, when asked about the most important gender-based issue, she said it was "to fight the pay gap between men and women." She married Þorvaldur Steinar Jóhannesson in 1970 and had two sons, Sigurður Egill Þorvaldsson (born 1972) and Davíð Steinar Þorvaldsson (born 1977). After divorcing in 1987, she entered a civil union with Jónína Leósdóttir (born 1954) in 2002. When same-sex marriage was legalized in Iceland in 2010, Jóhanna and Jónína converted their civil union into a marriage, becoming one of the first same-sex married couples in the country. In 2017, she published a biography titled Minn tími ("My Time"), covering the period from the 2008 financial crisis through the protests, emergency elections, and the recovery under the left-wing government.

The K-class blimp was a non-rigid airship built by the Goodyear Aircraft Company of Akron, Ohio, for the United States Navy. These blimps were powered by two Pratt & Whitney Wasp nine-cylinder radial air-cooled engines, each mounted on twin-strut outriggers, one per side of the control car that hung under the envelope. Before and during World War II, 134 K-class blimps were built and configured for patrol and anti-submarine warfare operations, and were extensively used in the Navy’s anti-submarine efforts in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean areas. In 1937, K-2 was ordered from Goodyear as part of a contract that also included the L-1, Goodyear’s standard advertising and passenger blimp. K-2 was the production prototype for future K-class airship purchases. K-2 flew for the first time at Akron, Ohio on December 6, 1938, and was delivered to the Navy at NAS Lakehurst, New Jersey on December 16. The envelope capacity of the K-2—404,000 ft³ (11,440 m³)—was the largest for any USN blimp up to that time. K-2 was flown extensively as a prototype, and continued to operate testing new equipment, techniques, and performing whatever tasks were needed, including combat patrols in World War II. On October 24, 1940, the Navy awarded a contract to Goodyear for six airships (K-3 through K-8) that were assigned the designation Goodyear ZNP-K. These blimps were designed for patrol and escort duties and were delivered to the Navy in late 1941 and early 1942. K-3 through K-8 had only minor modifications to K-2's design, the only major change being the engines, which were changed from Pratt & Whitney R-1340-16s to Wright R-975-28s. The Wright engine/propeller combination proved excessively noisy and was replaced in later K-ships with slightly modified Pratt & Whitney engines. The K-3 cost $325,000. A series of orders for more K-class blimps followed. Twenty-one additional blimps (K-9 through K-30) were ordered on October 14, 1942. On January 9, 1943, 21 more blimps (K-31 through K-50) were ordered. The envelope size of K-9 through K-13 was increased to 416,000 ft³ (11,780 m³) and those delivered thereafter used an envelope of 425,000 ft³ (12,035 m³). The final contract for the K-class blimp was awarded in mid-1943 for 89 airships. Four blimps from this order were later canceled. The remaining deliveries were assigned numbers K-51 through K-136. However, the number K-136 was not assigned to a specific airship as the control car assigned for K-136 was used to replace the car for K-113. The original car for K-113 was destroyed in a fire. The US Navy's experiences with K-ships in tropical regions showed a need for a blimp with greater volume than the K-class to offset the loss of lift due to high ambient temperatures. Goodyear addressed these concerns with a follow-on design, the M-class blimp, which was 50% larger. After World War II, a number of K-class blimps were modified with more advanced electronics, radar, sonar systems, and larger envelopes. These modified blimps were designated. The K-ships were used for anti-submarine warfare (ASW) duties in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans as well as the Mediterranean Sea. All equipment was carried in a forty-foot-long control car. The installed communications and instrumentation equipment allowed night flying. The blimps were equipped with the ASG radar, which had a detection range of 90 mi (140 km), sonobuoys, and magnetic anomaly detection (MAD) equipment. The K-ships carried four 350 lb (160 kg) depth bombs, two in a bomb bay and two externally, and were equipped with a machine gun in the forward part of the control car. An aircrew of 10 normally operated the K-ships, consisting of a command pilot, two co-pilots, a navigator/pilot, airship rigger, an ordnanceman, two mechanics, and two radiomen. On June 1, 1944, two K-class blimps of United States Navy (USN) Airship Patrol Squadron 14 (ZP-14) completed the first transatlantic crossing by non-rigid airships. K-123 and K-130 left South Weymouth, MA on May 28, 1944, and flew approximately 16 hours to Naval Station Argentia, Newfoundland. From Argentia, the blimps flew approximately 22 hours to Lajes Field on Terceira Island in the Azores. The final leg of the first transatlantic crossing was about a 20-hour flight from the Azores to Craw Field in Port Lyautey (Kenitra), French Morocco. The first pair of K-ships were followed by K-109 & K-134 and K-112 & K-101, which left South Weymouth on June 11 and June 27, 1944, respectively. These six blimps initially conducted nighttime anti-submarine warfare operations to complement the daytime missions flown by FAW-15 aircraft (PBYs and B-24s) using magnetic anomaly detection to locate U-boats in the relatively shallow waters around the Straits of Gibraltar. Later, ZP-14 K-ships conducted minespotting and minesweeping operations in key Mediterranean ports and various escort missions, including that of the convoy carrying Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill to the Yalta Conference in early 1945. In late April 1945, K-89 and K-114 left Weeksville NAS in North Carolina and flew a southern transatlantic route to NAS Bermuda, the Azores, and Port Lyautey where they arrived on May 1, 1945, as replacements for Blimp Squadron ZP-14. The ability of the K-ships to hover and operate at low altitudes and slow speeds resulted in detection of numerous enemy submarines as well as assisting in search and rescue missions. The K-ships had an endurance capability of over 24 hours, which was an important factor in the employment of ASW tactics. The mooring system for the K-ship was a 42 ft (12.8 m) high triangular mooring mast that was capable of being towed by a tractor. For advance bases where moving the mooring mast was not needed, a conventional stick mast was used. A large ground crew was needed to land the blimps and moor them to the mast. During the war, only one K ship was lost to enemy action. On July 18, 1943, K-74 was shot down by U-134 in the Straits of Florida. The crew was rescued eight hours later, except for one man who was attacked by a shark and drowned only minutes before the rescue. Five weeks later, U-134 was sunk by a British frigate in the Bay of Biscay on its return voyage to Germany. In 1947, Goodyear acquired the former Navy K-28 and operated it as part of its commercial advertising blimp fleet. The K ship was named Puritan and was the largest ever Goodyear blimp. The airship was purchased from the Navy primarily to experiment with Trans-Lux illuminated running copy advertising signs attached to the envelope. Costly to operate and maintain, Puritan was retired from the Goodyear fleet in April 1948 after only one year of operation. The blimp was deflated and placed in storage at Goodyear's base at Wingfoot Lake in Suffield, Ohio and was later sold back to the Navy. K-43, the last operational Navy "K Ship", was retired from service in March 1959. Several K-class blimps were used for nuclear weapon effects tests at the Nevada Test Site (NTS) during the Operation Plumbbob series of tests in 1957. K-40, K-46, K-77, and K-92 were destroyed in Project 5.2, events Franklin (Fissile) and Stokes (19 kt, XW-30 device). The tests were to "determine the response characteristics of the model ZSG-3 airship when subject to a nuclear detonation in order to establish criteria for safe escape distances after airship delivery of antisubmarine warfare special weapons." According to the Navy, the "airship operations were conducted with extreme difficulty." The Navy was trying to determine whether the airship could be among the aircraft to deliver its planned Lulu (W-34) nuclear depth charge. During the life of the K-class airship, the U.S. Navy used three different designation systems. From 1922 through World War II, the Navy used a four-character designator. The K-class blimps were designated ZNP-K where the "Z" signified lighter-than-air; "N" denoted non-rigid; "P" denoted a patrol mission; and "K" denoted the type or class of airship. In April 1947, the General Board of the U.S. Navy modified the designation system for airships. The second character of the designator was dropped as the Board dropped the code for rigid airships so that the "N" for non-rigid was no longer needed. The designation for the K-class blimps then became ZPK. In April 1954, the designation system for lighter-than-air airships was further modified so that it conformed to the designation system for heavier-than-air aircraft. By this time the ZPK blimps had been retired from service and only the later version K-Class blimps were in service. Under the 1954 system the ZP2K blimp became the ZSG-2, the ZP3K became the ZSG-3, the ZP4K became the ZSG-4, and the ZP5K became the ZS2G-1. In the new designation system, the "Z" signified lighter-than-air; the "S" was the type denoting an anti-submarine warfare mission; the numeral (i.e., "2") was the model; and the "G" was for Goodyear, the manufacturer's letter in the Navy's designation system. The final numeral denoted the series of the vehicle within the type/model. The US Navy ordered a new type of airship in 1951 for the Korean War. The new airship was designated ZP4K (later called ZSG-4), which had a different design than WW2 K-type. The first ZP4K was delivered in June 1954. A total of 15 were built. In 1955 an update version called the ZP5K (later called ZS2G-1) was delivered, a total of 15 were built. The ZP5K has an inverted “Y” tail.

Karl August Folkers (September 1, 1906 – December 7, 1997) was an American biochemist known for his major contributions to the isolation and identification of bioactive natural products. He graduated from the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences at the University of Illinois in 1928 and was awarded the Alumni Achievement Award by the institution in 1986. Throughout his career, Folkers primarily worked at Merck, where he played a key role in the isolation of vitamin B12 in 1947, a vitamin recognized as one of the most structurally complex. As part of the Merck Pharmaceuticals research team, Folkers, Fern P. Rathe, and Edward Anthony Kaczka were the first to isolate the antibiotic cathomycin in 1955, and his team also isolated the antibiotic cycloserine. In 1958, his team determined the structure of coenzyme Q10. Later, he served as director of the Institute of Biomedical Research at the University of Texas at Austin, holding the position of Ashbel Smith Professor of Chemistry. For his scientific achievements, he received the Perkin Medal in 1960, the William H. Nichols Medal in 1967, the Priestley Medal in 1986, and the National Medal of Science in 1990.
