Karl Ludwig, Count of Ficquelmont (German: [ˈfɪkɛlˌmɔnt]; French: Charles-Louis comte de Ficquelmont; 23 March 1777 – 7 April 1857), was an Austrian aristocrat, statesman, and General of the cavalry of the Austrian Imperial army of French noble origin. Born Gabriel-Charles-Louis-Bonnaventure, Count de Ficquelmont, at the Castle of Dieuze in the present-day French département of Moselle, he belonged to a noble family from Lorraine dating back to the 14th century (House of Ficquelmont) and was introduced to King Louis XVI at Versailles in 1789. Shortly after, the French Revolution began, and as aristocrats, his family was targeted; several relatives were beheaded and many estates were confiscated during the Terreur era. Ficquelmont joined the "Army of the Princes" to fight against revolutionary France. He entered the military service of the Habsburg monarchy in 1793 and participated in all Austrian campaigns during the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, earning a reputation as a brilliant military officer. In 1809, he rose to the rank of Oberst and was appointed chief of staff to Archduke Ferdinand Karl Joseph of Austria-Este. In 1811 and 1812, he led troops in Spain, where his victories drew the attention of Emperor Napoleon I, who unsuccessfully attempted to recruit him. He was elevated to the rank of Generalmajor in 1814 and received the capitulation of Lyon a few months later. Over the following decades, Ficquelmont advanced in the Austrian military, achieving various promotions. In 1815, due to his status as a skilled and loyal military officer, he was approached to represent Austria as a diplomat. After the War of the Sixth Coalition ended, he was sent to Stockholm as Austrian Ambassador Extraordinary to Sweden to smooth relations with the newly elected Swedish heir, Bernadotte, ensuring his inclusion in the coalition leading to the Congress of Vienna—mission successfully completed and marking the start of his diplomatic career. Following Napoleon’s fall, Italy became a key sphere of influence for the Austrian Empire, and in 1820, Ficquelmont was appointed Ambassador to Tuscany and Lucca to strengthen Austrian influence over Grand Duke Ferdinand III of Tuscany. During this time, he met his future wife, Russian countess Dorothea von Tiesenhaussen. In 1821, he was appointed ambassador plenipotentiary to Naples amid the political crisis following the 1820 Carbonari Revolution. A military revolt in Naples in July 1820 forced the king to adopt a constitution modeled on the Spanish Constitution of 1812. The Holy Alliance feared the unrest might spread, prompting Austria to send an army into Naples, which defeated the Neapolitans at Rieti on 7 March 1821 and entered the kingdom. Ficquelmont was sent to manage the subsequent occupation, gaining significant influence over King Ferdinand I and Neapolitan elites and effectively administering domestic and foreign policies. He was recognized as Austria’s key diplomatic asset for his political acumen and social skills, described as possessing Germanic seriousness, Italian subtlety, and the wit of 18th-century French nobility. In 1829, he was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary to Russia. His wife, countess Dorothea von Tiesenhausen, was the granddaughter of Prince Kutuzov and a member of the prominent Tiesenhausen family, becoming influential in the politics of Emperor Nicholas I. The Saltykov Mansion, the Austrian Embassy, was described as a "place of wisdom and intelligence" and as "(...) the setting of the two most illustrious salons of the period (1830s), reigned over by Ficquelmont's wife." Ficquelmont and Dorothea's influence in Russia was long-lasting, and as a sign of appreciation, Emperor Nicholas I awarded him the Orders of St. Andrew, St. Alexander Nevsky, St. Vladimir, and St. Anna. In 1839, Ficquelmont was recalled to Vienna to serve in the Foreign Office during Prince Metternich’s absence. In 1840, he was appointed Minister of the State and Conferences and chief of staff of the Imperial Army, becoming not only Metternich’s right-hand man but officially the second most senior statesman in the Empire, with the observation that "Count de Ficquelmont stands just behind or next to Prince Metternich (..) Every conference starts with Count de Ficquelmont and ends with Prince Metternich." In Vienna, the Ficquelmonts were among the most prominent social figures, with Ficquelmont’s salon being described as the most sophisticated, erudite, mindful, and beloved in the city. In 1841, his daughter, countess Elizabeth Alexandrine, married Prince Edmund von Clary-und-Aldringen, heir to one of the Empire’s most prominent princely families. In 1847, Ficquelmont was sent to Milan as acting Chancellor of Lombardy–Venetia and senior advisor to Archduke Rainer Joseph of Austria to restore Austrian rule amid growing resentment. After only a few months, he was recalled to Vienna to lead the Council of War as the Revolutions of 1848 began. From early 1848 to 13 March, he led the Austrian Council of War. On 13 March, Prince Metternich resigned and fled; Ficquelmont then assumed duties until 17 March, when Count Franz Anton von Kolowrat was appointed Minister-President. From 17 March until the fall of the Kolowrat cabinet on 3 April, Ficquelmont managed the Department of Foreign Affairs and the War Ministry. On 4 April, he became Minister-President of the Empire, but due to his close ties with the Metternich System and the Russian tsar, popular opposition forced him to resign on 4 May. The period was violent: his wife, Countess Dolly, was arrested twice by the Venetian guarda civil and eventually fled Venice on an English ship with her daughter, son-in-law, and grandchildren. Additionally, his kinsman in the War Ministry, Count Theodor Franz Baillet von Latour, was lynched during the Vienna Uprising of October 1848. After the revolutions ended, Ficquelmont refused to return to politics and dedicated himself to writing and publishing political essays that gained wide recognition across Europe. In 1852, Emperor Franz Joseph I of Austria made him a Knight of the Golden Fleece, the most prestigious order of the Empire. In his later years, he retired first to his palace in Vienna and later to his Venetian palace, where he died in 1857 at the age of 81. As a result of the French Revolution, the Ficquelmont family dispersed across Europe, with members settling in Italy, Hungary, England, and the Netherlands. One of Charles-Louis’s uncles, Count Antoine-Charles de Ficquelmont (1753–1833), recreated the title Count de Ficquelmont in the Dutch nobility on 16 July 1822. Charles-Louis had five siblings, of whom only one had children—a girl and a boy. His niece, Clotilde de Vaux (Paris 1815–Paris 1846), inspired philosopher Auguste Comte’s Religion of Humanity, organized around public veneration of Humanity through a Goddess modeled after her. In 1821, at age 44, Ficquelmont married countess Dorothea von Tiesenhausen (St. Petersburg 1804 – Venice 1863), 17, granddaughter of Prince Kutuzov. Countess Dorothea was renowned for her beauty; a famous Neapolitan proverb praised her as « Vedi Napoli, la Ficquelmont e poi muori » (« To see Naples, the countess Ficquelmont, and die »). She was also known for her letter-writing and diary, which were published in Italian and Russian in 1950, documenting her life as a high society aristocrat in 19th-century Europe. The couple had one daughter, Elisabeth-Alexandrine-Marie-Thérèse de Ficquelmont (Naples 1825 – Venice 1878), Countess de Ficquelmont by birth and Princess Clary und Aldringen by marriage to Edmund, 4th Prince of Clary-Aldringen. Through Elisabeth, he was a grandfather of Prince Siegfried von Clary-Aldringen (Teplitz 1848 – Teplitz 1929) and Count Manfred von Clary-Aldringen (Vienna 1852 – Salzburg 1928).

Kashmir Martyrs' Day (Urdu: یومِ شہداءِ کشمیر, Kashmiri: کٲشِرؠ شَہیٖدَن ہُینٛد دۄہ) or Kashmir Day was an official state holiday observed in Kashmir to commemorate 21 Muslims killed on 13 July 1931 by Dogra forces of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir in British India. On that day, Kashmiri Muslims were offering prayers outside the Srinagar Central Jail, where Abdul Qadeer, who had urged Kashmiris to resist the rule of Hari Singh, was present. As the crowd grew restless and the Islamic call to prayer began, the Dogra army opened fire, killing the first muezzin who was giving the Azan. Another muezzin attempted to continue the prayer and was also shot dead, and in total 23 people were killed in attempts to complete the Azan. The bodies were buried in the graveyard attached to the Shrine of Khwaja Bahawuddin Naqshbandi (Ziyarat Naqshband Sahab) in Srinagar, which is now known as Mazar-e-Shuhada or the Martyrs' Graveyard. The day was removed as an official holiday of Jammu and Kashmir by the Government of India in December 2019, although the Government of Pakistan continues to mark it. GM Lone, in Kashmir Life, identifies four incidents that led to the tragedy: a Hindu businessman in Udhampur converted to Islam, had his property taken and was denied inheritance under a 1882 Dogra decree; on 29 April 1931, Muslims were stopped from delivering Khutbah after police intervention, leading to a protest at the main masjid and increased unrest; on 4 June 1931, police constable Fazal Dad Khan’s copy of Panjsurah was thrown away by a sub-inspector, prompting him to go to the mosque; and on 20 June 1931, Quran leaves were found in a public lavatory. Prem Nath Bazaz, in "Inside Kashmir" (1941), stated that the mass agitation leading to 13 July was driven by Muslim discontent and that those who died at the jail gate fought against an unsympathetic government. Abdul Qadeer Khan, an employee of Major Butt of the Yorkshire Regiment, had been attending protest meetings and at Khanqah-i-Maula on 21 June 1931 delivered an impromptu speech, which was recorded by authorities and led to his arrest on 25 June for sedition and inciting riot under the Ranbir Penal Code. His trial began on 4 July in Srinagar, with large Muslim crowds gathering to witness it. On 13 July, the trial continued at Srinagar Jail, where about 160 police officers, including at least 31 armed with guns, were present. Around 4,000 to 5,000 people gathered, were denied entry, but about 200 entered peacefully. Khan’s lawyers addressed the crowd, who agreed to leave after the noon prayer. At noon, Muslims lined up for prayers; when officials including the District Magistrate and Superintendent of Police arrived, slogans such as "Allah-o-Akbar," "Islam Zindabad," and "Abdul Qadeer Zindabad" were shouted. As the call to prayer began, Governor Raizada Trilok Chand ordered police to open fire, killing the first muezzin instantly and shooting dead the second muezzin attempting to finish the Azan, after which police fired indiscriminately. A gun was snatched by a crowd member and he was shot dead by a policeman. According to the Dalal Inquiry Commission, 180 rounds were fired, resulting in 17 Muslims killed on the spot and 40 seriously injured, five of whom died later; The Hindu, Daily Tribune (28 July 1931), reported 21 Muslim deaths. GS Raghavan, in The Warning From Kashmir, described the event as a mob storming the jail, forcing open gates, and stoning officials and police, with the District Magistrate ordering fire, which led to further unrest and looting. The crowd later resumed stoning and was dispersed with a lathi charge and cavalry pursuit. The bodies were buried at the Shrine of Khwaja Bahawuddin Naqshbandi, now known as Mazar-e-Shuhada. Jyoti Bhusan Das Gupta wrote that modern Kashmir's 'freedom movement' began on 13 July 1931, while Prem Nath Bazaz called 13 July 1931 the most important day in contemporary Kashmir's history, marking the start of an open struggle for independence and freedom. Sheikh Abdullah compared the day to the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, and Chitralekha Zutshi emphasized the incident's multi-casualty nature and its roots in socio-economic and socio-political crises. In protest, the Reading Room Party announced a statewide shutdown, and at a public meeting at the Martyrs' Graveyard, Sheikh Abdullah declared 13 July as Martyr's Day. This unrest led to arrests of Sheikh Abdullah and Chaudhry Ghulam Abbas. The aftermath prompted Maharaja Hari Singh to appoint a commission chaired by B J Glancy to examine Muslim grievances and to democratize the monarchy, resulting in the proposal of a legislative assembly, which was established in 1934.

Kashmiri cuisine refers to the traditional culinary practices of the Kashmiri people, with rice serving as a staple food since ancient times. The equivalent of "bread and butter" in Kashmiri is haakh-batte, meaning greens and rice. The cuisine is generally meat-heavy, with the region having the highest per capita consumption of mutton in the subcontinent. In most Kashmiri meals, bread is not included; it is only consumed with tea in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Cooking methods for vegetables, mutton, homemade cheese (paneer), and legumes are similar among Muslims and Pandits, except that Muslims use onions, garlic, and shallots instead of asafoetida. Lamb or sheep is preferred, though beef is also popular. Cockscomb flower, known as "mawal" in Kashmiri, is boiled to create a red food coloring used in certain dishes, especially in Wazwan. Pandit cuisine uses Kashmiri red chili powder and ratanjot for color in dishes like rogan josh, while Kashmiri Muslim cuisine uses chilies in moderate amounts and avoids hot dishes at large meals. Vegetable curries are common, and meat is traditionally considered an expensive indulgence. Wazwan dishes, beyond weddings, are prepared on special occasions like Eids, alongside rice, vegetables, and salad. Global appreciation of Kashmiri cuisine has grown, with iconic dishes such as Rogan Josh, Gushtaba, Yakhni, and Kahwa featured in gourmet menus worldwide, and the cuisine gaining visibility in food festivals in London and Dubai, as well as fine-dining experiences in New York and Toronto. In India, upscale Kashmiri restaurants have opened in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad, run by members of the Kashmiri community or curated by chefs specializing in Wazwan, helping preserve and promote the region’s gastronomic heritage. This growth is supported by food influencers, YouTube chefs, and curated pop-up events. The cultural and culinary roots of Kashmiri cuisine are linked to South Asia, Persian, and Central Asian cuisines, blended with local ingredients. The term kabab is Arabic, korma has Turkish roots, and rogan josh, yakhaen, ab gosht, riste, and goshtabh originate from Persian sources. A legend states that the Kashmir valley was once a vast mountain lake, and soil layers contain remains of freshwater fish, fossil oysters, and water chestnut shells at 457 meters above the valley. Snake and fire worship from Iran influenced early Kashmiri culture, with serpents worshipped and buried with insects, and grains splashed at shrines and graves. The Bommai Sopore archaeological site, discovered in 2005, features a prehistoric rock engraving depicting chase and game scenes, the first of its kind in Kashmir. Recent excavations in Overa valley, Pahalgam, have revealed Paleolithic stone tools, including single-edged blades used for hunting. Even before the Megalithic period, there is evidence of wheat, barley, and lentil cultivation. Clear agricultural evidence, including large grain storages and rachises of wheat and barley, was found at Qasim Bagh after 2500 BC. The Kashmir Valley contains multiple Northern Neolithic sites, possibly dating as early as 3000 BC, with evidence of broom-corn millet movement across Inner Asian mountains. Lentil samples at Pethpuran Teng date back to around 2700 BC, one of the earliest pulse crops in the region. The valley’s lower latitude allowed crop cultivation without the need for traits found in higher latitudes. At Burzahom, stone hearths, ceramic structures with hollow stands and globular pots, rectangular harvesters with curved edges, and harpoons indicate hunting, fishing, and cultivation. Artistic depictions include a hunting scene with a dog and sun path diagram. Mortar and pestles made of volcanic rock are similar to those used today. The presence of lentils indicates contact with Central Asia, and harvesters with two holes suggest contact with China. At Gufkral, settlers engaged in wild game and domesticated animals such as wild sheep, goat, cattle, red deer, wolf, Himalayan ibex, and bear. Roasting was done outside, with no hearths inside dwellings. Piercers were used for flesh incisions, and scrapers for fat removal. In Phase IB, cattle and common peas were introduced, and pigs and fish appeared in the late Neolithic. Bones of hare, hedgehog, rodents, and beaver were also found. Emmer wheat at Kanispur suggests Harappan contact with Neolithic Kashmir. With the Aryan migration around the 8th century BC, fire worship became embedded in Kashmiri culture, including a phallic emblem of cooked rice. The local ceremony of vayuk resembles the Iranian Farvadin, where on a special day, Kashmiri Muslims visit graves and distribute rice. Earthen thalis and handis have been found from the Indo-Greek period to the Kushan era, with Kushan coins showing motifs of kings sacrificing at altars. The Kushan period features a double-cropping pattern, indicating agricultural change after a post-Neolithic decline. Horticultural and foraging items like grapevine, Indian gooseberry, wild jujube, walnut, and almond were part of the diet. At Kanispur, barley dominates, while at Semthan, wheat is more common. Kashmir had trade links with Rome via Gilgit and Yasin valley, exporting saffron and dolomiaea costus (kutha), which was used in Rome for food scenting and wine seasoning. Military contacts existed between the Karkota kingdom and the Tang Dynasty, with Kashmir supplying agricultural goods to Chinese troops in Gilgit in 722 AD. Islam arrived in Kashmir through mixed Iranian and Central Asian influences, and Kashmiri Hindus practiced vegetarianism, avoided garlic and onions, and had unique customs such as drinking water brought by Muslims and allowing Muslim foster-mothers to feed children. The rishi cult adhered to vegetarianism, non-injury to animals, and avoided garlic and onions. Nund Rishi is said to have eaten dried dandelion leaves, and Lal Ded practiced strict vegetarianism. When Yusuf Shah Chak signed a treaty with Akbar in 1586, one condition was that the mint, saffron, and game would remain under imperial control. In Srinagar, poor people’s meals included ghee, milk, beef, onions, wine, pickles, and vinegar. During the Mughal era, rice, fish, and vegetables were staples, and butter and fats were avoided due to the cold climate. River water was not drunk in South Kashmir; instead, people consumed warm Dal Lake water. In 1635–36, a conflict arose between Shias and Sunnis over mulberry eating at Maisuma, and in 1641, unprecedented floods and famine devastated villages. Shahjahan sent 30,000 rupees to Tarbiyat Khan to aid the poor and established five food centers. Cow slaughter was punishable by death, with many accused individuals publicly hanged. Rulers’ shortsighted policies led to an agrarian crisis, with Sikh rulers taking half of paddy production as government share, reducing the population from 800,000 in 1822–1823 to 120,000 in 1835. Coarse rice and haakh were the main foods, with wheat and maize used where paddy cultivation was limited due to terrain and irrigation. Aquatic products like singhara (water nuts) were consumed in certain areas. Kashmiri apples were transported over 12 days by coolies to Rawalpindi. The 1878–79 famine was deadly, and during Maharaja Ranbir Singh’s reign, catching and eating fish was made illegal. Those who killed cows were boiled in oil and hung publicly. People had no right to waste land, only to plant trees, which they owned. Officials often took milk and butter from gujjars without payment. Ancient Kashmiri scriptures and travelers' accounts mention foods including chicken, fish, game, and other items. Apart from chicken, fish, and game, Kashmiris use only mutton or goat meat. Over 75% of sheep are cross-breeds known as Kashmir Merino, providing both meat and wool. Bakkarwal goats belong to the rare Kaghani breed, prized for meat. Beef is consumed in towns and villages, especially for affordability. In some villages, beef-eaters are separated from mutton-eaters during wazwan feasts. A class divide exists between those who eat kat maaz (mutton), considered elite, and those who eat bad maaz (beef), considered lower-class. The largest rabbit breeding farm in North India is located in Wussan village, Baramulla, and rabbit meat is increasingly consumed as a substitute for sheep and goat meat, especially by people with cardiac issues due to its lean, white, nutritious profile. The Kashmir Aenz is the only recognized domestic goose breed in India, with rearing dating back to ancient times, as noted by Sir Walter R. Lawrence. In Srinagar, geese are sold in Batmaloo and Lal Chowk, with vendors purchasing from village rearers and selling live or slaughtered. Affluent families make geese pickles for winter use. The Duke of Bedford sent 10,000 trout eggs from the UK in 1899, which perished, but a second consignment from Scotland the next year succeeded. Rainbow and brown trout adapted well, while indigenous snow trout (known as alegaad) continues to thrive in both standing and flowing water. There were 137 private fish farms in Anantnag, declared the 'Trout District of India'. Poultry farms follow European standards, with free-range eggs produced using permaculture and no-dig gardening. Chick varieties like Kalinga brown, Vanraja, Kashmir Commercial Layer are collected to ensure a steady supply of organic brown eggs. The Kashmir Duck (batook) is reared across all districts, with the highest population in Bandipora, followed by Kupwara, Baramulla, Srinagar, and others. Kashmir duck eggs are either white or green-shelled and weigh 66.20 grams on average. Kalij pheasant (wan kokur) lays between 6 and 10 eggs per clutch and is traditionally served soft-boiled in olive-green shells with a sprinkle of celery salt and buttered soldiers. Kashmiris consume various rice varieties, including the nutty and fragrant Mushk Budji, grown in the higher reaches of the valley, which received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in February 2022. Kashmiri red rice, known as Zaag Batt, is grown in Tangdhar, near the Pakistan border, valued for its superior texture and taste. In 2009, farmers in the region harvested Basmati rice for the first time. The most commonly used Kashmiri vegetables include haakh (collard greens or kale), monj haak (kohlrabi), tsochael (mallow), bamchoont (quince), kral mound (shepherds purse), saze posh (holly hock), and nadur (lotus stem).

People in Kashmir consume a variety of rice, including the nutty and fragrant Mushk Budji, grown in the higher reaches of the Kashmir Valley, which received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in February 2022. This rice is known for its harmonious blend of taste, aroma, and rich organoleptic properties. Kashmiri red rice, locally called Zaag Batt, is cultivated in the village of Tangdhar on the border with Pakistan and is valued for its superior texture and taste. In 2009, farmers in the region first harvested Basmati rice. The most commonly used Kashmiri vegetables include haakh (collard greens or kale), monj Haak (kohlrabi), tsochael (mallow), bamchoont (quince), kral mound (shepherds purse), saze posh (holly hock), nadur (lotus stem), praan (shallots), aubuj (sorrel), mawal (cockscomb), wushkofur (camphor), tila gogul (mustard), and gor (water-chestnut). The floating vegetable garden on Dal Lake is the second largest wholesale market in the world, where men of all ages trade vegetables like tomatoes, carrots, cucumbers, turnips, water chestnuts, leafy greens, and the famous nadur on wooden boats, often sharing cigarettes or hookahs. The sweetness of Kashmir’s water influences the taste of its vegetables. Nadur, a porous and fibrous lake vegetable, has become an irreplaceable ingredient in traditional Kashmiri cooking and is said to have been discovered in the 15th century by Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin during a shikara ride on Gil Sar lake. A popular legend claims that the yarn threads thrown into Dal Lake by Lalla Ded (1320–1392), a Kashmiri mystic saint, transformed into nadur’s fibers. Sun-dried vegetables, known as hokh syun, are consumed when fresh produce is scarce; they are prepared by peeling, chopping, salting, and sun-drying during summer and include dried tomatoes (ruwangun haech), fenugreek leaves (meeth), lotus stem (nadir haech), Iberian knapweed (kretch), shallot leaves (praan), mint (pudna), bottle gourd (al haech), turnip slices (gogji haech), quince (bamchount haech), collard greens (hoech haak), and spinach (hoech palak). In the Charar Sharief area, dried pears (tang haech) are considered a delicacy. Shallots, known as praan, are a key flavoring ingredient in many Kashmiri dishes, including soups, stews, curries, and kebabs, and were featured in many of Mughal Emperor Akbar’s feasts in the 16th century. Buthoo village is renowned for producing prized organic shallots. Snow Mountain garlic, or Kashmiri garlic, is a rare single-clove variety of Allium sativum with a bright white to creamy-white clove and a strong, pungent flavor without acidity. The Kashmir Valley is the only place in India where asparagus grows, historically cultivated in Pulwama, Budgam, Rajbagh, Tangmarg, and Gulmarg, with current cultivation restricted to Tangmarg and Gulmarg. Sugarcane does not grow in Kashmir; sugar was imported from erstwhile united Punjab up to 1947 and was among the costliest imports. The Dogra government proposed cultivating sugar maple and beetroot sugar, but the plan did not materialize. In the absence of imported sugar, honey was used, with acacia flower honey produced in Tral, Verinag, and other areas, and Sidr honey, obtained from Sidr (jujube) trees, considered one of the world’s finest types of honey. Kashmiri apples are known for their juiciness and flavor, with over 1.9 million metric tonnes produced in 2019—more than any other Indian state—and Kashmir accounts for 90% of India’s walnut production. Kashmiri walnuts are nutrient-rich and in demand globally, with giant walnut trees reaching up to 75 feet in Srinagar. Walnut oil was traditionally used for cooking and imparted a sweeter, nuttier flavor. Muhammad Quli Afshar introduced cherries from Kabul during Akbar’s time; the Mishri variety is famous and sweeter than others, rich in minerals, vitamins, and plant compounds. Other exotic berries include sweet and sour mulberry (tuell and shah-tuell), raspberry (chhanchh), barberry (kaawducchh), and red berry (haapat maewaa). Strawberries (istaber) are harvested in the Gassu area near Srinagar. Orange cultivation began in Urossa village in Uri, where the warmer climate and soil are suitable for the crop. The region’s microclimate supports Mediterranean crops like lemons and olives; Kashmiri lemons are juicier than those from Punjab. A sub-species of wild olives that grows in harsh conditions is used for grafting, producing about 1,000 liters of extra virgin olive oil annually. Kashmiri grapes are cultivated on 500 to 600 hectares, with annual production ranging from 1,100 to 1,500 metric tonnes. Holstein Friesian and Jersey cows were introduced decades ago, producing 4 million liters of milk daily. Organic Kashmiri butter wrapped in Chinar leaves was traditionally common but is now sold only by a few. A traditionally ripened Himalayan cheese called milk chapati or maish krej is consumed in Kashmir. Kashmiri saffron is renowned for its aroma, color, and medicinal value; Pampore saffron has 8.72% crocin content, higher than Iran’s 6.82%, and received a GI tag in May 2020. Shahi zeera (imperial cumin) belongs to the Apiaceae family and was initially found in the jungles of Gurez Valley; its darker seeds are considered superior due to smell, rarity, and shape. Rock salt consumption is traditional in Kashmir, imported from Khewrah in Pakistani Punjab, where it was first discovered by Alexander the Great’s troops in 326 B.C. Pre-independence, it was imported via the Mughal Road (formerly Namak Route); after partition, supply was blocked. It is now consumed by nearly one-fourth of the population. Spring is a season of rejuvenation in Kashmir, with picnics centered around food. The countryside is filled with almond (badaam), peach (tsunun), cherry (gilaas), and pear (tang) blossoms, and mustard fields bloom in yellow. Apricot (Tser) blossoms are white with pink or reddish tints and grow from late spring to early summer. Beans are a spring vegetable, cherries are a late spring to summer fruit, coriander (danival) is a cool herb dominant in spring and summer, garlic (rohan) grows from spring through fall, and melons (kharbooz) are grown in spring and summer. Tender spring haakh is called kaanul. Harvesting of lotus stem (nadur) begins in September. A samovar bubbles in a corner, releasing the fragrance of saffron and cardamom. Cookie-shaped kandi kulchas made of flour, butter, sugar, and poppy seeds are passed around to be dipped in tea. Men fish under the shade of chinar trees in Dalgate. Dandelion leaves (haand) are foraged on foot. Paddy is cut with sickles and stacked to dry. Chestnuts are roasted in dying embers. Bulbous garlic and red potatoes grow together. Saffron fields in full bloom are seen in Pampore, Pulwama district. In hilly areas, maize and walnut trees are seen with fruit ready for harvest. In apple-producing areas like Sopore (North Kashmir) and Shopian (South Kashmir), cartons of apples are transported. During long winters, with short days and limited sunlight and electricity, food becomes a major source of comfort and interest. On window sills and terraces, aubergines, cherry tomatoes, gourds, and turnips are sun-dried. The daan (Kashmiri traditional stove) with twin stoves (Chaer) is always ready for long cooking sessions despite shortages. When roads are blocked by snow, families gather in the kitchen where the flavor of overnight shab deg fills the space. Kohlrabi (monje) is cold-tolerant and continues to grow in winter, with a little frost even helping it. Notable Kashmiri dishes include kababs, which originated from Turkish soldiers grilling meat on open fires and are now cooked with local spices and served with dips. For most Kashmiris, breakfast consists of fresh bread from a local bakery and a cup of noon chai (salt tea), with bread available year-round but its accompaniments varying. Some affordable luxuries include certain baked goods. Unlike most Indian subcontinent dishes where flavors are added during cooking, wazwan flavors are added before cooking by soaking meat in flavored water (osmosis). Wazas are trained for years to master meat cutting and grinding, traditionally mashed with walnut wood. Kashmir produces large quantities of vegetables and forest produce. Native to the Himalayan foothills, Guchhi or kanaguchhi mushrooms (Morchella species) are highly prized internationally, especially in European gastronomy, but large-scale cultivation has failed; wild harvesting is relied upon, and a kilogram can cost up to 30,000 INR (approximately €330/kg or US$350/kg) as of 2023. Paneer is known as tschaman in Kashmiri and is spiced with a sweet-savory blend including cinnamon, mace, clove, cumin, and ground coriander, with ground ginger being a staple due to the scarcity of fresh ginger. The shadowy underbelly of the wazwan, spicy spreads are served free when Kashmiris eat out or pack food. The traditional practice of shadow fishing, known as Tchaayi Gaad in Anchar Lake near Srinagar, involves fishermen breaking ice in the morning, hiding under blankets or straw umbrellas to create a shadow that attracts fish, which are then harpooned. Willows once lined the lake banks, providing shade for fish during summer. Common fish dishes are consumed. Kashmiris eat more rice than people in the Jammu region. In certain rural areas, individuals place an egg in a kanger (fire pot), and the scent of the cooking egg signals readiness. Estimates suggest 50 to 60 birds are killed daily in Kashmir’s wetlands; hunted game (shikaar) is not cooked immediately but hung for days (faisander) to make the meat softer and less fibrous. In British India, markhor (screw horn goat), the world’s largest wild goat, was considered a challenging game species and is locally regarded as the tastiest wild meat. Indian wild boar was introduced by Maharaja Gulab Singh, a Dogra military general, and was a delicacy for Dogras and Sikhs, though its population declined after 1947 in the Muslim-majority region. Game dishes include markhor and wild boar. Kashmiri Pandits, who were vegetarian and avoided onions and tomatoes, were known as Dal Battas (Dal Pandits). Various Kashmiri pickles are consumed. Nomadic Gujjars and Bakerwals move their herds and settlements seasonally. Kashmiris enjoy sugar, with common sweetmeats including traditional baked goods. Before 1918, Abdul Ahad Bhat of Ahdoos studied baking with English bakers at Nedou’s hotel in Srinagar, owned by Austro-Swiss Michael Nedou, and later opened the first Kashmiri bakery. Ahdoos specialized in English pastries and added Kashmiri items as India moved toward independence. Mughal Darbar was established in 1984 on Residency Road, and Jee Enn, founded by Ghulam Nabi Sofi in 1972, is located nearby. Many owners and staff of these bakeries trained at Ahdoos. The Kashmir Valley is noted for its bakery tradition, particularly in the production of qand.

Gujjars and Bakerwals migrate their herds of dairy cattle and their settlements up and down the mountains according to seasonal changes. Kashmiris have a strong affinity for sugar, and common sweetmeats are consumed in the region. Before 1918, Abdul Ahad Bhat from Ahdoos studied baking under English bakers at Nedou's, a hotel in Srinagar owned by Austro-Swiss Michael Nedou, and quickly mastered the craft, eventually founding the first bakery in Kashmir by a local Kashmiri. Ahdoos specialized in English pastries and, as India moved toward independence from British rule, introduced Kashmiri items to its menu. Mughal Darbar was established on Residency Road in 1984, and Jee Enn, founded by Ghulam Nabi Sofi in 1972, is located on a parallel road. Many owners and staff of these bakeries trained at Ahdoos. The Kashmir Valley is renowned for its bakery tradition, particularly the qandarwan, a variety of leavened breads unique to the region and indicative of Central Asian influence. Bakery shops on Dal Lake or in downtown Srinagar are elaborately arranged, selling breads with golden brown crusts topped with sesame and poppy seeds. Traditional Kashmiri breads include various types of leavened loaves. Wazwan, a multi-course meat-based meal originating in Kashmir, is popular throughout the region and is served internationally at food festivals and reunions. All dishes are prepared according to halal standards; vegetarians enjoy delicacies such as Dum Alve, Nadur (lotus stem), Haakh (collard greens), and Kashmiri vegetarian pulao, which is made with aromatic spices, vegetables, and dried fruits. Kashmiris are heavy tea drinkers and do not use the term "Kashmiri Chai"; instead, they refer to their signature pinkish, salted tea as "noon chai," which is made with black tea, milk, salt, and bicarbonate of soda, with the color resulting from the preparation method and soda. Kashmiri Hindus call it "Sheer Chai," while Muslims call it "Noon Chai" or "Namkeen Chai," both meaning salty tea. Noon Chai is a common breakfast drink taken with breads like baqerkhani, brought fresh from Qandur (Kashmiri: کاندر), or from bakers. It is a fundamental part of Kashmiri household life, traditionally served in large samavars, though now kettles are used instead. Nuts like almonds and pistachios, edible rose petals, and sometimes malai or fresh cream are added before serving to enhance flavor and texture. A 2022 University of Kashmir study found that 87% of springs in the valley have excellent to good water quality, and many rural and backward communities rely on spring water, which they consider the purest due to spiritual ties with shrines. The Kokernag Spring, one of the oldest and purest, produces Bringi Spring Water with high alkalinity and balanced minerals. Babribyol sharbat is a sweetened milk drink made with rose water or Rooh Afza syrup and soaked sweet basil seeds grown locally. Kashmiri lassi (lyaess) is a salty yogurt drink made by churning buttermilk with a wooden choomph or churner, requiring precise technique so that buttery fats float to the top in a froth and spices and dried mint are properly balanced. This fermented rice water drink is believed to benefit a sluggish liver. A berry juice drink is prepared at home during Ramadan and appears in the 1977 film Arnimaal, where guests sip it during wedding celebrations. The traditional wazwan, featuring slow-cooked meat dishes, pairs well with whisky, and Loire Valley’s Sancerre complements Kashmiri goshtabeh, while a ripe fruity red works well with roghan josh; Montepulciano is recommended. During Ramadan, Muslims avoid food during the day but enjoy special meals at dusk, including khajur ka laddoo, babribyol, kulfi, phirin, seemni, fruit chaat, fruit custard, kateer, and noon chai. The scent of slow-cooked mutton is prominent in Srinagar, and despite the city’s unpredictability, spirits are high during Eid Mubarak. Eid-ul-Fitr concludes 30 days of Ramadan and is marked by families returning home after prayers to serve Kehwa (saffron tea) and chai with bakery items like cakes, cookies, ghee tchot (a tandoor-baked flatbread), pastries, and savory snacks such as chicken and mutton patties. Well-to-do families often prepare select wazwan dishes like kebabs, rista, shami kebabs, chicken pieces, kanti (stir-fried meat), and mutton or chicken tikki with sauces and green chutney (dhaniya chutney), especially when entertaining guests like sons-in-law. Lunch is typically rice-based with a variety of meat dishes, including yakhni, a dish made with fresh curd and mild spices. The day begins with the Fajr prayer and a breakfast of bakery goods with dodh kehwa (milky green tea). As the festival ends, well-to-do families begin placing orders with wazas for the feast, which is prepared at their homes and then sold to customers. Sacrificial animals include Delhi Walla, Merino Cross, Bakerwal, and Kashmiri sheep varieties. Only vegetarian food is provided to devotees; in Batmaloo and surrounding areas, most people turn vegetarian and consume dried turnips (gogji aare), believed to have helped Kashmir survive a famine during Dawood’s time. In Pampore, people cook dried vegetables, eggs, cheese, and other food without meat and invite relatives and friends to maintain a saint’s tradition. In Khanyar and Sarai Bala, devotees gather outside shrines where local and non-local businesses sell traditional Kashmiri food, and pious men sing hymns over offerings of dates and sweets. In Anantnag, people in the southern region stop eating meat as a sign of respect for a 16th-century mystic, with few butcher shops open during these seven days; for three-and-a-half days before and after the saint’s Urs, people eat radish braised in tamarind. For Kashmiri Pandits, the prasad at Shivratri puja includes a charger with rice, cooked lamb, fish, and a raw fish on top. On the 9th day of ashad, Pandits offer yellow rice cooked with turmeric, a little oil, and salt along with tsarvan (goat’s liver). Navreh, the Kashmiri New Year, is incomplete without nadur and is often mistaken for Nowruz; it celebrates the arrival of spring and occurs around the March equinox. Tibetan exiles in Kashmir, including members of Tibet’s small Muslim population, live in Srinagar near the 18th-century Hari Parbat fort, and their children run popular momo (beef dumpling) shops and Tibetan restaurants, offering Cantonese chicken, kumloo wonton, and fried pasta stuffed with minced mushrooms. Kashmiri Sikh cuisine has influences from Punjab, such as onions and tomatoes, but uses Kashmiri elements like badyaan (saunf). Many Indian tourists rely on Vaishno Dhabas, which serve all-vegetarian North Indian food. Some Kashmiri cooking techniques include blanching dandelion stalks (haand) four times to remove bitterness, cooking food on both top and bottom with slow heat using charcoal, braising haakh leaves in water with a wooden spatula to keep them submerged, using mustard oil for flavor, relying on a fragrant meat stock made from onions and shallots, poaching meatballs (rista and goshtabeh) in this stock with cinnamon and black cardamom, frying whole spices like cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, and bay leaves in oil—neither too little nor too much—and adding hot ghee or mustard oil with fried praan (shallots) paste and saffron extract. Sliced onions are fried until golden brown and pureed with minimal water. Yogurt must be fatty and thick, with a pinch of dried mint added at the end. Dishes are enhanced with saffron extract (in rogan josh and rista) or mawal (dried cockscomb flower), and Kashmiri chilli is sometimes added in excess for color; tomatoes are incorrectly used as a substitute when mawal and rattanjot are unavailable and are not authentic in Kashmiri cooking. Flavors and textures come from slow-cooking spices with ingredients until they release juices and fats and meld together. Smoking mustard oil is a process called durust, which prepares it for use after cooling. In the shab deg, the cooking vessel is sealed with dough and cooked over a simmering fire through the long winter night. Dum cooking was popularized by Mughal courts in the 16th century. Goshtabeh and rista, two meatball dishes, are rarely found outside the valley due to their unique texture, which is difficult to replicate. The sheep must be freshly slaughtered and the meat pounded before rigor mortis sets; air is incorporated by folding and beating the meat. The quality of pots is important, as emphasized by wosta (ustad) Nazir Ahmed Aram, who notes the need for the right copper content and recommends walnut or apple wood; cooking on gas is not equivalent. Kashmiri cuisine is a blend of influences from Central Asia, Persia, China, and the Indian subcontinent. Food recipes have been passed down across cultures. Kashmiris are gregarious and value sharing, with language and food being central to regional identity. The saying "one who eats properly shall rule the country" reflects this. A wedding tradition involves newlyweds making roti together, with the bride flattening the dough and the groom flipping it. Kashmiris are very particular about taste, and food connoisseurs can identify the waza (chef) who prepared a dish or distinguish a Kashmiri aubergine from others by smell. When filmmaker Vivek Agnihotri suggested a vegetarian wazwan, social media protested, and Gordon Ramsay faced criticism for his Rogan Josh, with Kashmiris noting incorrect meat cut and gravy. In Kashmir, food must taste and look good, with an appealing aroma, and meals are seen as celebrations of life, from small gatherings to weddings or circumcisions. Dastarkhaans (white sheets) are spread on the floor to serve meals, and events often invite 100 to 500 people. Since the insurgency and violence, food has become a symbol of life and resilience. Wazas, descendants of Samarkandi cooks, are a significant political group in Srinagar. All dishes are eaten by hand, reflecting an intimate relationship with food; even elderly people eat marrow bones and ear cartilage after meals, with no shame. It is considered disrespectful to refuse food or an extra serving, and people go to great lengths to persuade others to accept it. Kashmiri language contains many food-related proverbs and idioms. Historically, Kashmiri women would pack extra mutton dishes in old newspapers or plastic bags, a practice that later spread to men who carried leftover meat in their traem (wazwan copper dish), evolving into a social movement with even elites providing special carry bags. Leftover rice at weddings is not wasted but served to animals like dogs and cattle. In the past, green Chinar leaves were used to package delicate items like mulberry, butter, mutton, and cheese to prevent contamination.

The practice of using carry bags to transport food evolved into a broader movement that gained social acceptance, with even elite groups participating by providing specially designed carry bags for leftover food. Leftover rice is no longer discarded; it is utilized in marriage ceremonies and served to animals such as dogs and cattle. In Kashmir, a previously abandoned tradition involved using green Chinar leaves to package sensitive items like mulberry, butter, mutton, and cheese, a method that helped keep these easily contaminated foods free from toxicity until consumption.

Katherine Stoneman (April 1841 – May 19, 1925) was an early 20th-century suffragist and the first woman admitted to the Bar Association in the State of New York. Born on her family's farm in Busti, Chautauqua County, New York, she was the fifth of eight children; her family operated in the lumber business, and her father served as a justice of the peace for several years. One of her brothers, George Stoneman, became the Governor of California, and her brother Edward served as a Judge on the Supreme Court of Illinois. In 1864, she began attending the Albany Normal School to become a teacher, where she also worked as a copyist for the New York Court of Appeals. She graduated from Albany Law School of Union University, founded in 1851, in 1866 and began teaching at the Glens Falls Seminary, later teaching at her alma mater, the Albany Normal School. She served as the first female president of their alumni association and as Vice-Principal. In 1885, Stoneman became the first woman to pass the New York Bar Exam, but her application to the bar was rejected in the spring of 1886 due to her gender. With support from local suffragettes, she advocated for a bill allowing admission of all qualified applicants regardless of race or gender. The bill was introduced, passed, and signed by Governor David Hill on May 20, 1886, just nine days after her rejection. Twelve years after her bar admission, she returned to study law formally at Albany Law School, where she became the first woman to graduate in 1898. She maintained a law office in Albany from 1889 to 1922. She died on May 19, 1925, and is buried in Albany Rural Cemetery. Stoneman was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame in October 2009. The eponymous Kate Stoneman Project celebrates and advances women in the legal profession.

Kathleen Gemberling Adkison (née Parks; July 5, 1917 – August 3, 2010) was an American abstract painter. She was born in Beatrice, Nebraska, to parents Rupert Parks and Henrietta Williamson. She attended Hawthorn High School in Kearney, Nebraska for three years and graduated from Garfield High School in Seattle, Washington. She studied art and painting under Leon Derbyshire at the Cornish Institute between 1938 and 1942. Adkison was the last surviving artist trained under Mark Tobey, who was Jackson Pollock's inspiration. Her work has been exhibited in museums as early as 1960, when the Frye Art Museum held a solo show of her work. She also had a solo exhibition at the Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture, formerly the Cheney Cowles Memorial Museum, in Spokane, Washington, from December 13, 1973 to January 13, 1974. Adkison was a critically acclaimed artist and highly recognized for her work. She was among only eight women included in Northwest Art Today at the 1962 Seattle World's Fair. She was the featured artist in a solo retrospective at the Cheney Cowles Museum in Spokane, Washington, from March 27, 1999, to June 27, 1999, which was the first such retrospective at that museum since 1974. Adkison married Thomas Adkison, an architect, in 1968; they had two children. She enjoyed hiking and climbed to the base camp at Mt. Everest twice. Thomas Adkison died in 1986. She died on August 3, 2010, in Spokane, Washington, aged 93.

Katharine Ellen Sykes OBE FInstP CPhys (born 20 December 1966) is a British physicist, broadcaster, and Professor of Sciences and Society at the University of Bristol. She previously held the position of Collier Professor of Public Engagement in Science and Engineering from 2002 to 2006. She has presented numerous BBC2 and Open University TV series, including Rough Science, Ever Wondered about Food, Alternative Therapies, and Alternative Medicine, and appeared in the documentary television miniseries Brave New World with Stephen Hawking in 2011. Sykes was educated at Fitzharrys School, a co-educational comprehensive school in Abingdon, and earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics from the University of Bristol in 1989, followed by a PhD in 1996, which focused on the crystallization and degradation of polyhydroxybutyrate, a biodegradable plastic. She helped create and co-directs the Cheltenham Science Festival and Famelab, a national UK competition that identifies and trains emerging talent in science communication. She served as Head of Science for Explore-At-Bristol, leading the team responsible for the content of the award-winning Hands-on Science Centre. Sykes is a member of the Council for Science and Technology (CST), the UK government's top-level advisory body on science and technology policy, and has served on advisory panels for public engagement in science with the Royal Society, the Wellcome Trust, and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). She is a trustee of NESTA and a board member of Explore-At-Bristol. In 2006, she received the Kohn Award for excellence in public engagement with science. She was awarded an honorary Doctor of Science degree and honorary fellowship from the University of Gloucestershire and won the Suffrage Science award in 2013. Sykes was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2009 Birthday Honours.

Ken Noda, born October 5, 1962, is an American concert pianist, accompanist, vocal coach, and composer. He began composing music and performing as a concert pianist before the age of 11. He has performed with symphony orchestras worldwide and has composed numerous art songs and five operas. He worked as a vocal coach at the Metropolitan Opera from 1991 until retiring from his full-time position in July 2019. Born to Japanese parents in Dobbs Ferry, New York, Noda grew up in Scarborough and was educated at the Hackley School, graduating in 1980. He began studying the piano at age five and was admitted to the Juilliard School on a full scholarship at age seven. He studied piano privately with Daniel Barenboim, Adele Marcus, and Sylvia Rabinof and studied singing with Beverley Peck Johnson, serving as her studio accompanist at Juilliard for many years. In 1986, he received an Avery Fisher Career Grant worth $10,000 (equivalent to $28,685 in 2024). Noda composed his first opera, *The Canary and the Baseball*, at age 10, which premiered at the Brevard Music Festival on August 18, 1973, and was later staged by the educational wing of the New York City Opera. At age 13, he received a National Endowment for the Arts grant to compose a three-act opera, *The Rivalry* (1976), his third opera. He composed two additional operas: *The Highwayman* (1979) and *The Magic Turtle* (1980). By age 16, he had composed 65 art songs. Noda began performing early, and by age 14, he had appeared as a soloist with the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra, the Minnesota Orchestra, the St. Louis Symphony, and the New York Philharmonic. He has also performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, the Boston Symphony Orchestra, the Chicago Symphony, the Cleveland Orchestra, the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Montreal Symphony Orchestra, the National Symphony Orchestra, the Orchestre de Paris, the Philharmonia Orchestra, and the Vienna Philharmonic. In 1980, he performed at Royal Albert Hall for the BBC Proms. In 1982, at age 20, he was invited by President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan to perform with violinist Itzhak Perlman in the East Room of the White House, the performance being recorded for the PBS television program *In Performance at the White House*. In 1983, he closed the Mostly Mozart Festival at Lincoln Center with Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 1 conducted by Leonard Slatkin. In 1989, he performed in concert with the Emerson String Quartet for the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center. In 1991, Noda ceased his performance career after becoming disillusioned with the classical musical world and the role he played in it. In a later interview with The New York Times, he stated that young people are drawn to romance, war, and good-and-evil stories because their emotional lives are largely fantasy, and that this imaginative capacity, while essential to talent, diminishes over time, leading many prodigies to experience midlife crises in their late teens or early twenties if their imagination is not replenished by experience. After halting his performance career, Noda joined the Metropolitan Opera as a vocal coach and administrator in 1991 and has since performed only rarely as a soloist. He continues to perform regularly as an accompanist to singers in recitals in New York City, having accompanied performers such as those listed. Since 1999, he has taught on the faculty at the Marlboro Music School and Festival. He has also spent four summers teaching at the Renata Scotto Opera Academy and gives master classes in opera at the Yale School of Music and the Juilliard School. He currently serves on the staff of the Metropolitan Opera as an instructor to singers in the Lindemann Young Artist Development Program and has served as a judge for the final round of the Metropolitan Opera National Council Auditions. He began working at the Met as a vocal coach in 1991.

Ken Skupski Jr., born on 9 April 1983 in Liverpool, is a British former professional tennis player who specialised in doubles. He achieved a career-high ATP doubles ranking of world No. 44 in July 2010 and won seven ATP Tour titles, most notably the 2021 Mexican Open with his younger brother Neal Skupski, with whom he regularly competed from 2013. Skupski is a three-time Grand Slam quarterfinalist, having reached the quarterfinals at the 2017 Wimbledon Championships in both men's and mixed doubles, and at the 2020 Australian Open in men's doubles. At the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi, he won a silver medal in men's doubles with Ross Hutchins and a bronze in mixed doubles with Sarah Borwell. He also represented Great Britain in the Davis Cup on two occasions in 2010. His father, Ken Sr., is a retired police officer of Polish descent, and his mother, Mary, is a golfer. Skupski is a devoted fan of Liverpool Football Club and a keen golfer with a handicap of six. As youngsters, the brothers lost a doubles match against a pairing with special educational and emotional needs, an experience they say motivated them to train harder and contributed to their future success. Skupski graduated from Louisiana State University in May 2007, where he was a NCAA Doubles finalist in 2005, a two-time Southeastern Conference Coaches Indoor Champion (the only player in the conference history to win back-to-back titles), fourth in the school's history for total wins with 107, and a six-time All-American (two in singles, one in doubles, three in academic categories). In June 2009, he and Colin Fleming defeated the world no. 1 doubles pair, Mike Bryan and Bob Bryan, at the Queen's Club tournament. However, he was eliminated in the first round at Wimbledon for the second consecutive year, again partnering Fleming, and lost in the mixed doubles second round. In September 2009, he was part of the Great Britain Davis Cup squad for the Europe/Africa Zone Group 1 relegation play-off against Poland, acting as cover and helping prepare for Poland's top-10 doubles team, but did not play; Great Britain lost 3–2 and were relegated to Group II. In September 2009, he won the Open de Moselle in France with Fleming, defeating Arnaud Clément and Michaël Llodra 2–6, 6–4, 10–5, and two months later won the St Petersburg Open, defeating Jérémy Chardy and Richard Gasquet 2–6, 7–5, 10–4. At the 2010 Australian Open, he and Fleming reached the second round before losing to Michael Kohlmann and Jarkko Nieminen 6–3, 4–6, 3–6; at the French Open, they lost in the second round to Wesley Moodie and Dick Norman 6–7(5–7), 6–4, 6–7(4–7). In June 2010, he reached the Eastbourne Open final, losing to Mariusz Fyrstenberg and Marcin Matkowski in three sets with Fleming; he finally won a match at Wimbledon in the first round, but lost in the second to the Bryan brothers in straight sets with Fleming. He competed at all four Grand Slams in the same year for the first time, but lost in the first round at the US Open in straight sets with Fleming. In July 2010, he and Fleming played in the Davis Cup tie against Turkey at Eastbourne, securing a 6–3, 6–4, 6–4 win that gave Great Britain a 3–0 lead, ending a five-match losing streak and marking their first Davis Cup win in three years. In October 2010, at the Commonwealth Games in Delhi, Skupski and Hutchins won the men's doubles silver medal, losing to Paul Hanley and Peter Luczak in the final, and later won the mixed doubles bronze medal by defeating Ross Hutchins and Anna Smith with Sarah Borwell, who had never played together before and were brought together by their shared coach, Louis Cayer. After a poor run of results, Skupski and Fleming ended their partnership in early 2011, with their final tournament being St. Petersburg, where they lost in the first round. In January 2011, he lost in the first round at the Australian Open with Travis Parrott in straight sets; in February, he partnered Robin Haase at the Marseille Open, reaching the final and winning the title by defeating Julien Benneteau and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga 6–3, 6–7(4–7), [13–11], marking his first title in over a year and a half. At the French Open, he lost in the first round to Fleming 4–6, 4–6 with Igor Zelenay; at Wimbledon, he lost in the first round with Robin Haase; in mixed doubles, he partnered Elena Baltacha and reached the second round before losing to Andy Ram and Meghann Shaughnessy 4–6, 4–6. At the Australian Open in January, he lost in the first round with Xavier Malisse in straight sets, marking his fifth consecutive first-round exit without winning a set. In mid-June, he reached the final of the Aegon International with Jamie Delgado, losing to Colin Fleming and Ross Hutchins 4–6, 3–6, his first final in over a year. At Wimbledon, he broke his Grand Slam curse by reaching the second round after winning a grueling five-set first-round match with Delgado, but lost in straight sets 6–7(2–7), 0–6, 2–6 to the Bryan brothers. In mixed doubles with Melanie South, they reached the third round before losing to Nenad Zimonjić and Katarina Srebotnik 4–6, 7–6(7–5), 7–9. A month later, he and Delgado reached their second final of the season at the Farmers Classic, losing to Ruben Bemelmans and Xavier Malisse 6–7(5–7), 6–4, [10–7]. At the US Open, he and Delgado reached the third round before losing to Marcel Granollers and Marc López in straight sets 2–6, 4–6, having defeated Jürgen Melzer and Philipp Petzschner in the second round in straight sets. Initially partnering with Delgado, Skupski increasingly played with his brother Neal from 2013 due to Neal's lower ranking, winning six Challenger titles and reaching the final at the Kremlin Cup. As their partnership did not qualify them for the French Open, they split; Ken partnered New Zealander Michael Venus, a fellow LSU alumnus, and Neal teamed with American Bradley Klahn, both losing in the first round. In July 2013, Neal was playing in World Team Tennis in the US, so Skupski partnered Divij Sharan, winning the doubles title at the Euro 42,500 men's Challenger in Recanati, Italy, defeating Ilija Bozoljac and Flavio Cipolla 4–6, 7–6(3), 10–6. In September, the Skupskis won the St. Remy Challenger in France, playing only two matches due to byes and a semi-final walkover, defeating Andrej Martin and Igor Zelenay 6–4, 6–1 as top seeds. At the 2017 Wimbledon Championships, Skupski reached the quarterfinals as a wildcard with his brother Neal, losing to the 4th seeded pair Łukasz Kubot and Marcelo Melo, and also reached the mixed doubles quarterfinals with Jocelyn Rae. The Skupski brothers won their first ATP title together at the Open Sud de France. At the 2020 Australian Open, Skupski reached the quarterfinals partnering Santiago González for the first time at a Major and second overall. In March 2021, he won his sixth ATP title and first at the ATP 500 level with Neal at the Mexican Open. In June 2021, he won the Nottingham Open on grass partnering Matt Reid. At the end of the year, he won his second ATP title of the season, the 2021 Sofia Open, partnering Jonny O'Mara. In June, partnering Jonny O'Mara, he defended his Nottingham Open title by defeating Julian Cash and Henry Patten in the final after saving three championship points. Skupski announced that Wimbledon 2022 would be his last professional tournament; partnering Jonny O'Mara again, he won the first round against Julio Peralta and Alejandro Tabilo, and the second round against Marcelo Melo and Raven Klaasen, but lost in the round of 16 to 11th seeds Andreas Mies and Kevin Krawietz, which was his final match. He was scheduled to play in the mixed doubles event with Heather Watson, but she withdrew before their first-round match due to a knee injury. Skupski played two seasons in World Team Tennis, debuting in 2017 with the Orange County Breakers and being named WTT's Male Rookie of the Year, and joining the expansion Orlando Storm in 2019 for their inaugural season. He rejoined the Orlando Storm in 2020, beginning on 12 July, marking his second time with the team. During the season, he partnered Tennys Sandgren in men's doubles and Jessica Pegula in mixed doubles, earning a season-high 56% of games won in men's doubles, helping the Storm secure a No. 3 seed in the WTT Playoffs, though they ultimately lost to the Chicago Smash in the semifinals.

Kenneth Jinghwa Hsu (simplified Chinese: 许靖华; traditional Chinese: 許靖華; pinyin: Xǔ Jìnghuá), Ph.D., M.A., born on 28 June 1929, is a Chinese scientist, geologist, paleoclimatologist, oceanographer, government advisor, author, inventor, and entrepreneur born in Nanjing, China. He earned a B.Sc. from the Chinese National Central University (later renamed Nanjing University in mainland China and reinstated in Taiwan) in 1948, followed by a M.A. from Ohio State University in 1950 and a Ph.D. from the University of California, Los Angeles in 1953. Hsu worked as a petroleum geologist for the Shell Development Corporation (now Shell Oil Company) in Houston, Texas, from 1954 to 1963, then served as an associate professor at two U.S. universities from 1963 to 1967. He became a professor of geology at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zürich) from 1967 to 1994, where he promoted experimental geology and established five leading international laboratories in rock mechanics (geophysics), mass-spectrometry (isotope geochemistry), Quaternary research (paleoclimatology), sedimentology, and tectonics. After retiring in 1994, he transitioned into environmental engineering. During his tenure at ETH Zürich, he was invited as lecturer, guest, or honorary professor in geology, climatology, or oceanography to numerous global institutions, including Beijing, San Diego, Cambridge, Columbia, Florence, Harvard, London, Milan, M.I.T., Moscow, Nanjing, Naples, Ohio, Oxford, Paris, Princeton, Taipei, Tokyo, Toronto, Washington, Woods Hole, and Yale. Post-retirement, he held guest professorships at National Taiwan University (1994–95), senior fellowships at the Berlin Institute of Advanced Studies (1995–96), Keck Professorship at Colorado School of Mines, guest professorship at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and university professorships at Nanjing University and Beijing University of Geosciences. Hsu contributed to the Earth Science Revolution of the 1960s by consolidating Plate Tectonics Theory and championed 'Process Oriented Geology,' aligning with the evolutionary biology of Lynn Margulis, the Gaia hypothesis of James Lovelock, and others, emphasizing physical, chemical, and biological processes in geological problems and advocating educational reform in geology. His research included sedimentation in isostatically driven tectonic basins, active margins of continental plates, physical chemistry of evaporites and pelagic diagenesis, granulite formation, catastrophic effects of meteorite impacts, extinction of life forms, and limnology of Lake Zurich. He participated in and led five deep-sea drilling cruises to the South Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Black Sea, and led international expeditions to Tibet, Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, South China, California Coast Ranges, and the Swiss Alps, traveling to 80 countries for Earth Science. Hsu received numerous medals and awards. He was elected a Member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in 1986, becoming a Foreign Associate due to circumstances, and was also an Associate of the Third-World Academy of Sciences, a Member of Academia Sinica (1988), the Mediterranean Academy of Sciences, and several other academies. He co-founded the European Geophysical Society and the science of paleoceanography, convened the First International Conference of Paleoceanography, founded the journal Paleoceanography, and assisted in founding the Asian Association of Marine Geology. He served 11 years as President of the International Association of Sedimentologists and convened the Third Workshop on Marine Geology of IUGS, the First Earth Science Colloquium of the European Science Foundation, several Dahlem Conferences, and numerous symposia and workshops for IGP, ILP, IGCP, SCOR, and JOIDE. Hsu edited numerous scientific journals and held advisory roles for governments of developing countries. He co-organized a consortium of 15 European member states to join the International Ocean Drilling Program. He successfully lobbied for the Chinese Geological Union to replace the Chinese Geological Society in Taipei as a member of the International Union of Geological Sciences and was part of the first IUGS delegation to China. He provided training programs for Sedimentology (1979), Field Geology of Tibet (1980), and Plate Tectonics (1992) for the Chinese Ministry of Geology and Mining, and from 1983 to 1995, assisted the Institute of Geology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences with a plate tectonics project and the publication of a new Geological Atlas of China. On his 60th and 70th birthdays, colleagues published two Festschrift symposia books: Controversies in Geology and Paradoxes in Geology. In September 2009, his contributions to China and science were recognized in a Beijing conference attended by government, industry, and academic dignitaries. After retirement, Hsu founded companies including Tarim Resource Recycling Limited (UK, 2003), Kenneth Hsu IHC Technology & Development Limited (China, 2005), and Lazarus Energy International Limited (UK, 2007), and held 16 patents in mining, petroleum, water, carbon, energy, and environmental management, including the Hydro-Transistor and Integrated Hydrologic Circuit (IHC). His technologies applied in China included enhanced oil recovery techniques. In 2000, Hsu combined hydro-fracturing, horizontal drilling, and water flooding to invent a new residual oil recovery (ROR) process called 3-dimensional fluid injection, which could increase world recoverable petroleum reserves by 50% or more, using water (or carbon dioxide). With support from Chinese Prime Minister Wen Jiabao, an expert panel convened by former Petroleum Minister Dr. Wang Tao unanimously approved the ROR invention for testing and application in China. In April 2006, PetroChina reported a successful test at the Changqing Oil Field (discovered in 1907), where annual production rose from about 10,000 tons prior to the test to 10 million tons in 2006 and 20 million tons in 2007. Hsu is active in institutions and organizations to apply new technologies in China and internationally, serving as president of the IHC Technology & Development Corporation (China), senior advisor and chief engineer at the Kenneth Hsu Institute for IHC Development (National Institute of Earth Sciences, Beijing), and director of the Center for Environmental & Health Engineering (Henan University, Kaifeng). His work on nitrite in drinking water and cancer was documented in The Ecologist journal. Hsu authored or edited over 20 books in multiple languages and was elected International Writer of the Year by the International Book Club (Cambridge, UK) in 2003. His books include The Mediterranean Was A Desert (1982), which detailed the Messinian Salinity Crisis and the 1970 D/V Glomar Challenger Leg 13 expedition, leading to the hypothesis that the Mediterranean was a desert 5.5 million years ago; the book was selected by Philip Morrison of Scientific American as one of the 100 most significant and influential science books of the 20th century and was adapted into a PBS film. Challenger At Sea (1983) served as an overview of marine geology and a textbook for non-majors. The Great Dying (1986) described the cometary impact theory behind the dinosaur extinction, sold over 170,000 copies worldwide, and reached 28,000 in the U.S. and 100,000 in mainland China in 1989, with 40,000 in Taiwan; it was featured in Taipei’s United Post best-seller list for over a year and named a top non-fiction book of the year in August 1992. The book challenged Charles Darwin’s theory of natural selection, arguing that most extinctions are caused by catastrophes and that evolution is governed by chance rather than gradual improvement, endorsing catastrophism and non-Darwinian evolution. Klima Macht Geschichte (2000) proposed a theory linking climate and history, predicting global cooling and a little ice age before 2500, supported by scientists including Khabibullo Abdusamatov, Yuk Yung, John Cassey, Nigel Calder, Henrik Svensmark, Alexander Chizhevsky, and John D. Hamaker; it was based on Hsu’s earlier paper 'Is Gaia Endothermic?' and referenced in a 1992 Geographical Magazine article. Amadeus & Magdalena (2002), published in Chinese, English, and German with a Chinese title "莫扎特的愛與死," presented Hsu’s musicological theory on the death of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Hsu has authored or co-authored more than 400 scientific articles across diverse fields including Archaeology, Cancer, Chronon Physics, Climatology, Cosmology, Cytology, Epistemology, Evolution, Fractal Geometry, Gaia, Geology, Heliobiology, History, Hydro-Physics, Languages, Marine Biology, Mathematics, Music, Oceanography, Palaeontology, Paleoclimatology, Philosophy, Politics, Religion, and Symbiogenesis.

Kim Fields Morgan (née Fields; born May 12, 1969) is an American actress and director. She first gained fame as a child actress on the television series Good Times (1978–1979), and rose to greater prominence for her role as Dorothy "Tootie" Ramsey on the NBC sitcom Diff'rent Strokes (1979–1981), as well as its spin-off The Facts of Life (1979–1988). Before appearing on The Facts of Life, she co-starred in a short-lived sitcom called Baby, I'm Back with Demond Wilson and Denise Nicholas and appeared in a television commercial for Mrs. Butterworth's syrup. She later appeared on two episodes of Good Times as a friend of Penny Gordon Woods, played by Janet Jackson (sister of Michael), in the episodes "The Snow Storm" and "The Physical." Fields played the role of Dorothy "Tootie" Ramsey on The Facts of Life from 1979 to 1988; even years later, many still recognize her catchphrase, "We're in troouu-ble!." When the show began production, Fields was so short that the producers put her on roller skates during the first season to avoid difficult camera angles. However, she later lost a role as Arnold Jackson's girlfriend on Diff'rent Strokes because she was taller than Gary Coleman, who played Arnold. In 1984, during the run of The Facts of Life, Fields released two singles on the Critique Records label: the disco/Hi-NRG "He Loves Me He Loves Me Not," which became a minor club hit, and "Dear Michael," which became a minor R&B hit, reaching No. 50. After taking time away from acting to attend Pepperdine University to earn her bachelor's degree in telecommunications, Fields appeared in a 1993 episode of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, in which Will Smith pretended to marry her in an attempt to seduce her. She had a starring role in the hit Fox sitcom Living Single as Regina "Reginé" Hunter from 1993 to 1998, acting alongside her real-life mother Chip Fields, who played her character's mother on the show. Following the end of Living Single, Fields began performing R&B and rap music with a group called Impromp 2. With her degree from Pepperdine University, she also began directing, directing a number of episodes of the All That! spin-off Kenan & Kel, in which she also appeared in two episodes, and has worked as a director on the sitcoms Tyler Perry's Meet the Browns, Tyler Perry's House of Payne, and BET's Let's Stay Together. Fields guest-starred on television shows such as UPN's One on One, The Golden Palace, and Martin, and appeared as herself on HBO's The Comeback. On February 1, 2007, Fields was reunited with her co-star Lisa Whelchel on WFAA-TV's Good Morning Texas, marking the first time in six years (since The Facts of Life Reunion movie) that Fields and Whelchel had seen each other. Fields has worked with her husband Christopher Morgan on projects. In 2010, she and Morgan produced and directed a Christmas television special called Holiday Love, which they shot in three days; the special aired on TV One, and a second episode aired for Christmas in 2011. Fields described the special as "restorative and transformative" of her Christian faith, and revived it on the Internet in 2013. On August 18, 2015, it was announced that she would be joining the cast of the Bravo reality television show The Real Housewives of Atlanta for its eighth season; on March 21, 2016, she announced that she would not return to the show for another season. On March 8, 2016, Fields was announced as one of the celebrities who would compete on season 22 of Dancing with the Stars, partnered with professional dancer Sasha Farber; during a double elimination on May 2, 2016, Fields and Farber were eliminated and finished the competition in 8th place. In 2017, Fields played the role of Theresa Newman in the Christian film A Question of Faith, which featured her first co-starring appearance in a feature film and premiered in theaters on September 29, 2017. Since May 2021, Fields has starred on Netflix's The Upshaws (2021–2026). Fields was married to film producer Johnathon Franklin Freeman from 1995 to 2001. She gave birth to her first child, Sebastian Alexander Morgan, by then-boyfriend Broadway actor Christopher Morgan, on May 4, 2007; the couple introduced their son the following week in People magazine. On July 23, 2007, they were married in a private ceremony officiated by Pastor Donnie McClurkin. In July 2013, Fields announced on the talk show The Real that she and her husband were expecting another son; on December 3, 2013, they welcomed Quincy Xavier Morgan in Atlanta, Georgia.

On November 9, 2008, he scored the K-League's historic 10,000th goal, which was against his own team.
