Kimberley (Khoekhoe: ǃ’Ās; Tswana: Kimbali) is the capital and largest city of the Northern Cape province of South Africa, located approximately 110 km east of the confluence of the Vaal and Orange Rivers. It holds significant historical importance due to its diamond mining heritage and the siege during the Second Boer War. British businessmen Cecil Rhodes and Barney Barnato built their fortunes in Kimberley, with Rhodes founding the De Beers diamond company in the early days of the mining town. On 2 September 1882, Kimberley became the first city in the Southern Hemisphere and the second in the world after Philadelphia, United States, to install electric street lighting. The first stock exchange in Africa, the Kimberley Royal Stock Exchange, opened on 2 February 1881. In 1866, Erasmus Jacobs found a 21.25-carat (4.3 g) diamond on the Orange River near Hopetown, which became known as the Eureka; it was purchased by Schalk van Niekerk and later sold. In 1869, an 83.5-carat (16.7 g) diamond, known as the Star of South Africa, was found nearby (29°3′S 23°58′E﻿ / ﻿29.050°S 23.967°E﻿ / -29.050; 23.967), sold by van Niekerk for £11,200 and later resold in London for £25,000. In 1871, Esau Damoense, the cook for prospector Fleetwood Rawstorne's "Red Cap Party", found diamonds on Colesberg Kopje, prompting Rawstorne to inform the De Beer brothers, sparking the "New Rush" with 900 claims and two to three thousand miners working the area, which eventually became the world-renowned Kimberley Mine. The Cape Colony, Transvaal, Orange Free State, and Griqua leader Nicolaas Waterboer all claimed the diamond fields, with the Free State Boers wanting the area due to its location within the Orange and Vaal River borders. After mediation by the Governor of Natal, the Keate Award favored Waterboer, who placed himself under British protection, leading to the proclamation of Griqualand West on 27 October 1871. Colonial Commissioners arrived in New Rush on 17 November 1871, and Governor Barkly visited in September 1872, proposing to make Griqualand West a Crown Colony. Richard Southey arrived as Lieutenant-Governor in January 1873, but delays in London, where Secretary of State for the Colonies John Wodehouse, 1st Earl of Kimberley, insisted on "decent and intelligible names" and rejected "New Rush" and "Vooruitzigt", led to a renaming. Colonial Secretary J.B. Currey renamed the area "Kimberley" by proclamation dated 5 July 1873, a move that was criticized in an editorial in the Diamond Field newspaper, which stated, "we went to sleep in New Rush and waked up in Kimberley, and so our dream was gone". After British government compensation to the Orange Free State, Griqualand West was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1877. Cape Prime Minister John Molteno initially opposed annexation due to financial concerns but passed the Griqualand West Annexation Act on 27 July 1877 after securing assurances of local consultation. From mid-July 1871 to 1914, 50,000 miners dug the Big Hole (or Kimberley se Gat in Afrikaans), which has a surface of 17 hectares (42 acres), is 463 metres wide, was excavated to 240 metres in depth, partially infilled to about 215 metres, and now has 40 metres of water, leaving 175 metres visible; beneath it, the Kimberley Mine was mined to 1097 metres. The Big Hole is the principal feature of a 2004 submission placing "Kimberley Mines and associated early industries" on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative Lists. By 1873, Kimberley was the second-largest town in South Africa with a population of approximately 40,000. Smaller mining companies were amalgamated by Cecil Rhodes and Charles Rudd into De Beers and by Barney Barnato into The Kimberley, and in 1888, the two merged to form De Beers Consolidated Mines, which held a monopoly over the world's diamond market. The city grew rapidly due to a large African migration seeking cheap labour from the De Beers company, and also attracted prostitutes from various ethnicities, earning a reputation as a city of limitless opportunity. Five big holes were dug into kimberlite pipes, named after the town; the largest, the Kimberley Mine or "Big Hole", covering 170,000 square metres (42 acres), reached a depth of 240 metres (790 ft) and yielded three tons of diamonds, closing in 1914, while Dutoitspan, Wesselton, and Bultfontein closed in 2005. On 14 October 1899, Kimberley was besieged at the start of the Second Boer War, with British relief forces suffering heavy losses; the siege ended on 15 February 1900, though the war continued until May 1902, during which British forces established a concentration camp for Boer women and children. The Boroughs of Kimberley and Beaconsfield amalgamated into the City of Kimberley in 1912. Urban segregation existed before apartheid, and the Group Areas Act enforced racial separation into European (White), Native (Black), Coloured, and Indian categories, with families split by measures like the 'pencil test' and communities relocated (e.g., Malay Camp) or selectively cleared (e.g., Greenpoint). New townships were created at the city's northern and north-eastern edges, and institutions like churches (e.g., Bean Street Methodist Church) and schools (e.g., William Pescod and Perseverance School) were affected, with some closing or relocating. The Reservation of Separate Amenities Act restricted African movement and designated public places as 'Europeans Only', and the Native Laws Amendment Act sought to divide church communities racially, a policy rejected by Archbishop Clayton in 1957. Resistance began in mid-1952 with the Defiance Campaign, when Dr Arthur Letele organized volunteers to occupy 'Europeans Only' benches at Kimberley Railway Station, leading to arrests; the Mayibuye Uprising on 8 November 1952, sparked by poor beer quality, resulted in shootings and a mass funeral on 12 November 1952, with detained leaders including Dr Letele, Sam Phakedi, Pepys Madibane, Olehile Sehume, Alexander Nkoane, Daniel Chabalala, and David Mpiwa. Archdeacon Wade of St Matthew's Church blamed apartheid policies, including poor housing, lighting, and transport, and unfulfilled promises, for the riots. Later anti-apartheid activists in Kimberley included Phakamile Mabija, Bishop Graham Chadwick, and provincial premiers Manne Dipico and Dipuo Peters. Prominent figures with Kimberley connections include Robert Sobukwe, founder of the Pan Africanist Congress, who was banished to the city after release from Robben Island in 1969 and died there in 1978; Benny Alexander (1955–2010), who later changed his name to Khoisan X and served as General Secretary of the Pan Africanist Congress and Pan-Africanist Movement from 1989, was born and raised in Kimberley. The Northern Cape Province became a political reality in 1994 with Kimberley as its capital; infrastructure existed since the 1940s, but post-1994 development included administrative departments, a Northern Cape Legislature, and an enlarged Kimberley City Council, now the Sol Plaatje Local Municipality, named after the prominent writer and activist who lived in the area. The former Diamantveld District Council became the Frances Baard District Municipality, named after the trade unionist born in Greenpoint, Kimberley. The Kimberley borough council adopted a coat of arms in 1878, registered with the Cape Provincial Administration in December 1964 and the Bureau of Heraldry in February 1968; the design combined the Union Jack with elements of the Cape Colony's coat of arms and a lozenge symbolizing the diamond industry: Azure, a cross and saltire superimposed Gules, both fimbriated Argent, in chief three bezants Or, each charged with a fleur de lis Azure, and in base three annulets Or; on a lozenge Or, superimposed over the fess point, a lion rampant Gules. The motto was Spero meliora. The divisional council for rural areas registered its own arms in August 1970: Per saltire, in chief, barry wavy of six Argent and Azure; in base, Argent, a pale Sable charged with three fusils Argent; dexter, Gules, a shovel and pick in saltire, handles downward, Or; sinister, a staff of Aesculapius, Or. In layman's terms, the shield was divided diagonally with (1) six silver and blue wavy stripes, (2) a crossed pick and shovel on a red background, (3) a golden staff of Aesculapius, and (4) three silver diamond-shaped fusils on a black vertical stripe on a silver background. The crest featured two crossed rifles in front of an upright sword; the supporters were two kudus; the motto was "Nitanir semper ad optima". Kimberley was the initial hub of industrialization in late 19th-century South Africa, transforming the agrarian economy into one based on mineral wealth, with migrant labour becoming a key feature, especially in the mines. The city hosted South Africa's first school of mines, opened in 1896 and later relocated to Johannesburg, becoming the foundation of the University of the Witwatersrand, with a Pretoria campus later becoming the University of Pretoria. The first two years of the school were attended at colleges in Cape Town, Grahamstown, or Stellenbosch, with the third year in Kimberley.

Africa's first stock exchange, the Kimberley Royal Stock Exchange, opened on 2 February 1881. On 2 September 1882, Kimberley became the first town in the Southern Hemisphere to install electric street lighting, a feat previously achieved only by Philadelphia, in the United States. In 1892, the first South African and international exhibition was held in Kimberley, opened by Sir Henry Loch, Governor of the Cape of Good Hope, on 8 September, featuring art, paintings from Queen Victoria’s royal collection, mining machinery, and other exhibits, sparking international interest and leading to a competition for display space. South Africa's first school of mines opened in Kimberley in 1896 and later moved to Johannesburg, becoming the foundation of the University of the Witwatersrand; a Pretoria campus later evolved into the University of Pretoria. The first two years of study were completed in Cape Town, Grahamstown, or Stellenbosch, the third year in Kimberley, and the fourth in Johannesburg, with buildings constructed at a total cost of 9,000 pounds, funded on a pound-for-pound basis by De Beers. In 1913, Kimberley established South Africa's first school of aviation to train pilots for the proposed South African Aviation Corps (SAAC), known as Paterson's Aviation Syndicate School of Flying, now commemorated in the Pioneers of Aviation Museum with a replica of the first Compton Patterson Biplane. In the 1930s, Kimberley had the best night-landing facilities on the African continent, hosted a major air rally in 1934, and during wartime, Kimberley Airport was taken over by the Union Defence Force and operated by the 21 Flying School for fighter pilot training. Today, Kimberley Airport (IATA: KIM, ICAO: FAKM) serves the area with regular flights from Cape Town and Johannesburg. Rail connections to the Cape Colony’s coastline began in 1872 under the Cape Government Railways, with the Cape Town to Kimberley line completed in 1885, accelerating passenger and goods transport and linking Kimberley to cheaper grain and coal supplies, thereby undercutting local African trade in fresh produce and firewood; the railway also played a role in the rapid spread of the Spanish Influenza in 1918. The rail network eventually connected Kimberley to Port Elizabeth, Johannesburg, Durban, and Bloemfontein, with De Aar serving as a major junction linking to Upington (later Namibia) and Calvinia; rail use declined from the 1990s. Today, passenger services to and from Kimberley are operated by Spoornet’s Shosholoza Meyl, connecting south to Cape Town and Port Elizabeth and north to Johannesburg, with luxury services offered by the Blue Train and Rovos Rail; the central station is Kimberley railway station. Wagon and coach routes developed rapidly as diamond mining expanded, with major routes from the Cape and Port Elizabeth; accounts from the 1870s describe poor road conditions and a lack of bridges. From the mid-1880s, the route through Kimberley and Mafeking (now Mahikeng) became the main axis of British colonial expansion, from which the Pioneer Column set out in 1890 to settle Rhodesia. Today, the main north-south route, the N1, goes via Bloemfontein, not Kimberley. Kimberley lies at the intersection of the N12 and N8 national roads. It is the seat of the Northern Cape Provincial Legislature and Provincial Administration, serving the region’s mining and agricultural sectors. The city presents itself as a significant tourist destination, known as the 'City that Sparkles,' with diverse museums and attractions, and acts as a gateway to Northern Cape destinations such as Mokala National Park, nature reserves, game farms, hunting lodges, and historic sites. Kimberley has hosted major meetings, including the founding of the Kimberley Process in 2000 and a follow-up in 2013, and the International Indigenous Peoples Summit on Sustainable Development in 2002, with the Mittah Seperepere Convention Centre and other facilities supporting these events. Under the Köppen system, Kimberley has a semi-arid climate (BSh) with long, wet summers and short, mild, dry winters with chilly nights. Water is drawn from the Vaal River at Riverton, about 15 km north of the city. According to the 2011 census, the population of Kimberley "proper" was 96,977, with Galeshewe and Roodepan having populations of 107,920 and 20,263 respectively, giving an urban total of 225,160; 63.1% identified as Black African, 26.8% as Coloured, 8.0% as White, and 1.2% as Indian or Asian; 43.2% spoke Afrikaans, 35.8% Setswana, 8.7% English, 6.0% isiXhosa, and 2.7% Sesotho. The city lies on a flat landscape with no prominent topographic features, except for debris dumps from over a century of diamond mining, which have been recycled and filled back into De Beers Mine by 2010, with some near the Big Hole designated as heritage features. The surrounding rural area consists of flat plains with hills of andesite to the north and northwest, and Karoo-age dolerite to the south and east, forming shallow pans. A notable feature is Kamfers Dam, a large pan north of the city, an important wetland supporting a breeding colony of lesser flamingos; conservation efforts aim to engage city residents with local wildlife, though in 2012 rising water levels flooded an artificial island built to enhance flamingo breeding, and in December 2013 an outbreak of avian botulism killed hundreds of birds, after which the island re-emerged. The administration of the Crown Colony of Griqualand West (from 1873) was based in Kimberley’s Government Buildings until its annexation to the Cape in 1880. Separate Borough Councils in Kimberley and Beaconsfield operated until their amalgamation into the City of Kimberley in 1912, after which a single City Council governed the city and a Divisional Council managed the rural district; in the 1980s, a separate political entity called Galeshewe (with Mankurwane) was created with its own council. Post-1994, the Kimberley City Council became the Sol Plaatje Local Municipality, and the successor to the Diamandveld Regional Services Council became the Frances Baard District Municipality. The idea of the Northern Cape as a distinct geographic entity began in the 1940s but became official in 1994, with Kimberley designated as the province’s legislative capital; the provincial legislature initially used the old Cape Provincial Administration building before moving to a purpose-built facility between a township and former white suburbs. Kimberley is also the seat of the Northern Cape Division of the High Court of South Africa. Education is a key sector in Kimberley’s social and economic life. Sol Plaatje University opened in Kimberley in 2014 with an initial intake of 135 students; former President Jacob Zuma highlighted its focus on heritage studies, including museum management, archaeology, indigenous languages, and restoration architecture. Former tertiary institutions in Kimberley have been absorbed into these structures. The city has historically attracted diverse faith communities, including various Christian denominations, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, and traditional African beliefs, notably in the Zionist Christian Church (ZCC); it is the seat of the Anglican Diocese of Kimberley and Kuruman and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kimberley (formerly the Apostolic Vicariate of Kimberley in Orange), with churches also belonging to the Methodist Church, Presbyterian Church, Congregational Church, Dutch Reformed Church, Baptist Church, Afrikaans Baptist Church, Apostolics, Pentecostals, and the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Notable artists include William Timlin, Walter Westbrook, and Philip Bawcombe. Writers from Kimberley or with strong ties include Diane Awerbuck, Benjamin Bennett, Lawrence Green, Dorian Haarhoff, Dan Jacobson, E P Lekhela, Z.K. Matthews, Sarah Gertrude Millin, Sol Plaatje, Frank Templeton Prince, Olive Schreiner, A.H.M. Scholtz, and Sabata-Mpho Mokae. Dr Victor is a notable reggae and rhythm and blues musician from the city. Memorials include the Diamond Field, the first newspaper published on 15 October 1870 at Pniel; other early papers were the Diamond News and the Independent; the current daily is the Diamond Fields Advertiser, first published on 23 March 1878. The Volksblad, with a free local supplement called Noordkaap, is read by Afrikaans-speaking residents. Two community radio stations were established in the 1990s. Kimberley has contributed significantly to cricket history, producing international players such as Frank (Nipper) Nicholson, Xenophon Balaskas (born to Greek parents), Ken Viljoen, Ronnie Draper, Pat Symcox, and coach Mickey Arthur; it hosted a match during the 2003 ICC Cricket World Cup, and Elsie McDonald was a Springbok bowler. Frank Dobbin, known as Uncle Dobbin, was part of Paul Roos’ original Springboks on the 1906/1907 tour to the British Isles; his memory is preserved in his colonial-style home in Roper Street with a brass plaque. Later Springboks to wear green and gold included Ian Kirkpatrick, Tommy Bedford, and Gawie Visagie, brother of Piet Visagie of Ammosal. Kimberley is home to the Griquas rugby team, which won the Currie Cup in 1899, 1911, 1970, and 2025; Ronnie Bauser, an ex-mayor of Kimberley, was involved with the team from 1950 to 1971. Richard Henyekane, a South African footballer, is from Kimberley, as is his younger brother Joseph, who played for Golden Arrows; Jimmy Tau is also from the city. Karen Muir, born in Kimberley, became in 1965 the youngest person to break a world record in any sport at age 12, setting the record in the 110-metre backstroke at the junior world championships in Blackpool, England; the record still stands. She was denied a spot at the 1968 Olympics due to South Africa’s apartheid policies. A world record was also broken in the municipal pool named after her, beaten by Johannesburg’s Anne Fairlie and Frances Kikki Caron. Charl Bouwer, the Paralympic swimmer who won gold in the 50m freestyle at the 2012 London Paralympics, was born in Kimberley. Bevil Rudd is an Olympic medallist. The first Maloof Money Cup World Skateboarding Championships were held in Kimberley in September 2011 and again in 2012; after the Maloof sponsorship ended in 2013, the event became known as the Kimberley Diamond Cup. H.F. Oppenheimer, in a 1976 foreword, stated that the discovery of diamonds in Kimberley was the first step in transforming South Africa from an agricultural to an industrial nation, noting that when gold and other minerals were later found to the north, Kimberley already had men of vision and enterprise with the capital and technology to develop them. Anthony Trollope visited Kimberley in 1877 and was deeply unimpressed by the heat, dust, and flies, remarking that the people were proud of their flies and dust and describing the town as having only one building with a storey above ground, no pavement, and an ugly market place surrounded by corrugated iron shops. A.H.J. Bourne, former headmaster of Kimberley Boys' High School, observed in 1937 that Kimberley’s rapid growth from a bare veld suggested a supermind behind its development. In the early 1990s, writer Dan Jacobson returned to Kimberley, where he had grown up in the 1930s, noting that the people and their language had vanished, and that Afrikaans had replaced English as the common language among whites, blacks, and Coloureds. Virtualtourist reviewer Catherine Reichardt asked if Kimberley was dull, and responded that the answer is a resounding 'No' for those passionate about history, as the city offers rich historical depth and is best appreciated with an overnight stay, providing a microcosm of South African history.

The Kingston Symphony (KS) is a Canadian orchestra based in Kingston, Ontario, with Evan Mitchell serving as its principal conductor since 2014. The ensemble primarily performs its concerts at The Grand Theatre. The orchestra was established in 1953 as the New Symphony Association of Kingston, with Graham George as its first principal conductor. George led the debut concert of Joseph Haydn's The Creation on 12 April 1954 at The Grand Theatre, featuring the Kingston Choral Society and baritone James Milligan. In its first three years, the orchestra held only two concerts annually, but the number of performances increased starting in 1957. Subsequent principal conductors included William Hill (1957–1959) and Edouard Bartlett (1960–1965). In 1963, the ensemble was renamed the Kingston Symphony, coinciding with the formation of the Kingston Symphony Association. Some concerts were held at the Kingston Gospel Temple. Alexander Brott became conductor in 1965 and oversaw the hiring of several professional string and wind players. The newly renovated Grand Theatre became the orchestra's primary concert venue. Brian Jackson served as conductor from 1982 to 1991, during which time the Symphony performed approximately twelve concerts per year. In 1992, Glen Fast assumed the conductorship. Under his leadership, the orchestra shifted toward performing new works by Canadian composers, including world premieres of Chan Ka Nin's Violin Concerto (1998), Marjan Mozetich's Piano Concerto (2000), Srul Irving Glick's last work, Isaiah (2002), John Burge's Clarinet Concerto (2004), István Anhalt's The Tents of Abraham (2005), and Peter Paul Koprowski's Tapestries of Love: Symphony for Soprano and Orchestra (2007). Fast remained conductor until 2014, when Evan Mitchell succeeded him.

Kissing Students (Estonian: Suudlevad tudengid) is a sculpture and fountain situated in Raekoja plats, Tartu, Estonia, located in front of Tartu Town Hall. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of the city, reflecting Tartu's status as Estonia's "intellectual capital" and "student capital," a reputation rooted in the city's home to the nation's oldest and most prestigious university, the University of Tartu.[1][2][3] The fountain was constructed in 1948 and was especially favored by newlyweds, who believed standing there would bring good fortune for their future.[1] The sculpture was designed in 1998 by Mati Karmin.[1] Its geographical coordinates are 58°22′49″N 26°43′23″E﻿ / ﻿58.38021°N 26.72296°E﻿ / 58.38021; 26.72296. Kliment Yefremovich Voroshilov (Ukrainian: Климент Охримович Ворошилов; Russian: Климент Ефремович Ворошилов), commonly known as Klim Voroshilov, was a prominent Soviet military officer and politician during the Stalin era (1924–1953). He was one of the original five Marshals of the Soviet Union, the second-highest military rank, junior only to the position of Generalissimo held by Joseph Stalin, and served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, the nominal head of state, from 1953 to 1960. Born on 4 February 1881 in Verkhnyeye, Bakhmut uyezd, Yekaterinoslav Governorate, Russian Empire (now part of Lysychansk city in Luhansk Oblast, Ukraine), Voroshilov came from a working-class family; his father was a former soldier who worked as a railway worker or miner and experienced periods of unemployment. Voroshilov described a childhood marked by extreme hardship, beginning work at age six or seven, receiving frequent beatings from wealthy peasants, and growing up illiterate until enrolling at age 12 in a nearby village school, where he received two years of education. He became close friends with Semyon Ryzhkov during his school years. In 1896, he began working in a factory near his village, led a strike in 1899, and joined the Bolsheviks in 1903 at a German-owned factory in Luhansk (renamed Voroshilov during the Stalin era), where he led strikes during the 1905 revolution. In April 1906, he traveled to Stockholm for the Fourth Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) under the pseudonym 'Volodya Antimekov' and shared a room with Josif Dzhugashvili, later known as Stalin. In spring 1907, he went to London for the Fifth RSDLP Congress, was arrested and deported to Arkhangelsk, escaped in December, and moved to Baku where Stalin was active. He was arrested again in 1908, released in 1912, and worked in an ordnance factory in Tsaritsyn (Stalingrad/Volgagrad). During the February Revolution, he was in Petrograd but returned to Luhansk, where he chaired the town soviet and was elected to the Constituent Assembly. His military career began in early 1918 when he commanded the Fifth Ukrainian Army, which was driven out of Ukraine by German forces; after a long retreat, his forces reached Tsaritsyn, where Stalin was posted as a party representative and Voroshilov was given command of the Tenth Army. Stalin and Voroshilov led the Red Army's defense of Tsaritsyn and sponsored the creation of the first Red Cavalry unit under Semyon Budyonny, composed mainly of southern Russian peasants. Voroshilov clashed with Leon Trotsky, who considered him undisciplined and threatened him with court martial in October 1918. He was later transferred to Ukraine as commander of the Kharkiv military district and then People's Commissar for War in the Ukraine soviet republic, where he supported the 'Military Opposition' opposing centralized army formation and the recruitment of former Tsarist officers. During the Polish–Soviet War, he served as political commissar with Budyonny’s First Cavalry. Voroshilov was elected to the Central Committee in 1921 and became commander of the North Caucasus military district in April 1921, then commander of the Moscow military district in March 1924. In 1925, after Mikhail Frunze's death, he was appointed People's Commissar for Military and Navy Affairs and Chairman of the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR, a position he held until 1934. Despite holding high offices, he was not part of the inner leadership; in November 1930, Sergey Syrtsov alleged a "tiny group" excluding Voroshilov made decisions behind the Politburo. His key achievement during this period was relocating key Soviet war industries east of the Urals to allow strategic retreat while preserving manufacturing capacity. Frunze, aligned with the Troika (Zinoviev, Kamenev, Stalin), died in 1925 from a massive chloroform overdose during surgery, which Stalin's doctors urged despite previous advice to avoid it. Voroshilov became a full member of the Politburo in 1926 and remained until 1960. In 1934, he was appointed People's Commissar for Defence and in 1935 became a Marshal of the Soviet Union. During the first Moscow trials in August 1936, he signed the order denying clemency and ordering executions. He was a main speaker at the March 1937 Central Committee plenum, where he denounced Nikolai Bukharin and Alexei Rykov as "renegades." Initially, he believed the purges would not affect the armed forces and was unprepared for the arrests of Marshal Tukhachevsky and others in April and May. He openly stated that saboteurs in the Red Army were few and tried to save officers like Lukin and Sokolov-Strakhov, sometimes succeeding. On 30 May 1937, he ordered commander Iona Yakir to travel to Moscow for a Military Revolutionary Council meeting, knowing he would be arrested. At the June 1937 meeting, Voroshilov vacated the chair and apologized, saying he could not believe so many high-ranking officers were corrupt. Afterward, he played a central role in Stalin's Great Purge, denouncing military colleagues and subordinates when ordered by Stalin. He wrote personal letters to exiled officers like Mikhail Ostrovsky, urging them to return and falsely assuring them of no retribution. Voroshilov personally signed 185 documented execution lists, fourth among Soviet leaders after Molotov, Stalin, and Kaganovich. He denounced officers he disliked, such as Tukhachevsky. Despite purging "mechanisers" who supported tanks over cavalry, he believed cavalry use should decrease and modern arms should be prioritized. Budyonny tried to recruit him to protect cavalry, but Voroshilov openly opposed it. He praised the Red Army's combined arms capabilities and initiative during the 1936 summer maneuvers but also identified issues in the army, including poor communication, ineffective staffs, lack of inter-arm cooperation, and rudimentary command structures in tank units. After the purge, reforms were introduced to align doctrine with the army's actual state; Voroshilov and Kulik were among the instigators. However, they failed to implement these reforms effectively. One reform, the reorganization of field units, was conceived by Kulik and implemented by Voroshilov, which inadvertently moved the Red Army to a less advanced state than in 1936. Voroshilov noted that territorial units were disbanded due to their inability to train conscripts in modern technology. He had openly criticized the system as inadequate in an era of imperialist military expansion, and territorial units were unpopular with him and the Red Army leadership. These units were ineffective; conscript Alexey Grigorovich Maslov noted he never fired a shot during training, and real training occurred only once a year when veterans returned. Voroshilov commanded Soviet troops during the Winter War from November 1939 to January 1940, but due to poor planning and his incompetence as a general, the Red Army suffered about 320,000 casualties compared to 70,000 Finnish casualties. At Stalin’s dacha in Kuntsevo, Stalin shouted at Voroshilov for the losses; Voroshilov responded by blaming Stalin for eliminating the army’s best generals and smashed a food platter on the table—Nikita Khrushchev said this was the only time he witnessed such an outburst. Voroshilov was made the scapegoat for the Finnish campaign and replaced as Defense Commissar by Semyon Timoshenko, later being appointed Deputy Premier for cultural matters. Initially, he argued for the release of thousands of Polish officers captured in September 1939, but later signed the order for their execution in the Katyn massacre of 1940. Between 1941 and 1944, he was a member of the State Defense Committee. After the German invasion in June 1941, he commanded the short-lived Northwestern Direction (July to August 1941) and then the Leningrad Front from September 1941. Working with Andrei Zhdanov as German forces threatened to cut off Leningrad, he displayed personal bravery, including rallying retreating troops and personally leading a counter-attack against German tanks with only a pistol at Ivanovskoye. However, his counterattack style was outdated and drew contempt from military colleagues; he failed to prevent the German encirclement of Leningrad and was dismissed on 8 September 1941, replaced by Georgy Zhukov. Despite this, Stalin needed popular wartime figures, and Voroshilov remained an important figurehead. Between 1945 and 1947, he supervised the establishment of a socialist regime in postwar Hungary and attributed the poor performance of the Hungarian Communist Party in the October 1945 Budapest municipal elections to the presence of non-Hungarian leaders, claiming it was "detrimental to the party." In 1952, he was appointed a member of the Presidium of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Following Stalin’s death on 5 March 1953, Voroshilov was approved as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet on 15 March 1953, with Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary and Georgy Malenkov as Premier. Voroshilov, Malenkov, and Khrushchev jointly arrested Lavrenty Beria after Stalin’s death. As Chairman, Voroshilov oversaw death row appeals, presiding over meetings and having the most influential voice, though split votes were common and he was sometimes outvoted. He generally advocated leniency, especially for those showing repentance or convicted of crimes of passion or under the influence of alcohol, while judging political crimes and financial offenses more harshly. Many death sentences were commuted to prison terms during his tenure, and his successor, Brezhnev, adopted a harder line. The contrast between his relatively lenient appeals in the 1950s and his active role in the 1930s purges was noted by Khrushchev, who asked him, "So when were you acting according to your conscience, then or now?" After Khrushchev removed most Stalinists like Molotov and Malenkov from the party, Voroshilov’s influence declined. On 7 May 1960, the Supreme Soviet granted Voroshilov’s request for retirement and elected Leonid Brezhnev as chairman. Voroshilov died on 2 December 1969 at the age of 88.

Kliment Voroshilov influenced the committee to show leniency, particularly for those who expressed repentance in their appeal documents or were convicted of crimes of passion or under the influence of alcohol, while he imposed harsher sentences on those convicted of political crimes or acts with financial motives. During his tenure, many death sentences were commuted to prison terms of varying lengths. His successor, Brezhnev, took a noticeably harder line in appeals cases. The contrast between Voroshilov's magnanimous approach to pardons in the 1950s and his involvement in the deadly purges of the 1930s was noted even at the time by Khrushchev, who asked him, "So when were you acting according to your conscience, then or now?" After Khrushchev removed most Stalinists like Molotov and Malenkov from the party, Voroshilov's career declined. On 7 May 1960, the Supreme Soviet granted Voroshilov's request for retirement and elected Leonid Brezhnev chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Council. The Central Committee also relieved him of duties as a member of the Party Presidium on 16 July 1960. In October 1961, he was excluded from election to the Central Committee at the 22nd party congress. Following Khrushchev's fall, Brezhnev brought Voroshilov out of retirement and re-elected him to the Central Committee in 1966. Voroshilov was awarded a second medal of Hero of the Soviet Union in 1968. In a winter night in 1969, Voroshilov felt unwell and refused to call an ambulance; in the morning, he put on his military uniform, called a car, and went to the hospital himself, fully decorated. He died on 2 December at the age of 88 and was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, in one of the twelve individual tombs between the Lenin Mausoleum and the Kremlin wall. Voroshilov was married to Ekaterina Voroshilova, born Golda Gorbman, a Ukrainian Jew from Mardarovka; she changed her name upon converting to Orthodox Christianity to marry him. They met while both were exiled in Arkhangelsk, where Ekaterina was sent in 1906. While serving on the Tsaritsyn Front in 1918, where Ekaterina was helping orphans, they adopted a four-year-old orphan boy named Petya. They also adopted the children of Mikhail Frunze after his death in 1925. During Stalin's rule, they lived in the Kremlin at the Horse Guards. Molotov described Voroshilov in 1974 as "nice, but only in certain times," noting he always supported the party's political line because he was from the working class, a common man, a good orator, and clean, and personally devoted to Stalin, though his devotion was not strong. He actively advocated for Stalin, supported him in everything though not always certain, which affected their relationship. This complexity explains why Stalin treated him critically and did not invite him to private conversations, though he did come by himself, and Stalin frowned. Under Khrushchev, Voroshilov behaved badly. The Kliment Voroshilov (KV) series of tanks used in World War II was named after him. Two towns were named after him: Voroshilovsk in Donbas (now Alchevsk), Voroshilovgrad in Ukraine (now changed back to Luhansk), Voroshilov in the Soviet Far East (now renamed Ussuriysk after the Ussuri river), and the General Staff Academy in Moscow. Stavropol was called Voroshilovsk from 1935 to 1943.

Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosomal condition in which a male has an extra X chromosome, resulting in a total of 47 or more chromosomes instead of the usual 46. It is named after American endocrinologist Harry Klinefelter, who first described the condition in 1942 with colleagues Fuller Albright and E. C. Reifenstein at Massachusetts General Hospital, and it was later confirmed in 1956 to result from an extra chromosome. The syndrome is diagnosed through karyotyping, which analyzes chromosomes in blood cells, and may also involve testing of oral mucosa cells to detect mosaicism. The birth prevalence of KS in Victoria, Australia is estimated at 223 per 100,000 males, and the overall prevalence in the general male population is approximately four per 10,000 (0.04%). KS occurs randomly due to nondisjunction during gametogenesis—either in paternal meiosis I, maternal meiosis I, or maternal meiosis II—where sex chromosomes fail to separate, leading to an XXY karyotype. The extra X chromosome is inherited from the mother in about 50% of cases, and maternal age is the only known risk factor, with women aged 40 having a four-times higher risk than those aged 24. In XXY males, most genes on the extra X chromosome are inactivated, except for those in pseudoautosomal regions that can be expressed. Symptoms often appear at puberty and include infertility, small testicles (typically less than 2 cm in length and 1 cm in width, with a volume of 4 ml or less), reduced muscle mass, less body and facial hair, broader hips, poor motor coordination, gynecomastia (breast growth), and low libido. Gynecomastia occurs in up to 80% of cases, with about 10% seeking surgical removal. Approximately 50% of males with KS can produce sperm, and advanced reproductive techniques like intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) with testicular sperm extraction (TESE) have enabled biological offspring in over 100 reported cases by 2010. Mosaic forms, such as 47,XXY/46,XY, occur in about 15–20% of cases and are associated with milder symptoms, including normal male secondary sex characteristics. Variants like 48,XXYY or 48,XXXY occur in one in 18,000–50,000 male births, and 49,XXXXY in one in 85,000 to 100,000 male births. Individuals with KS are at increased risk for autoimmune disorders, breast cancer, venous thromboembolic disease, osteoporosis, and cardiovascular disease due to metabolic issues like dyslipidemia and type 2 diabetes, though hypertension is not linked to the condition. The syndrome is associated with language delays, reading difficulties, executive function deficits, and a 10% autism prevalence, with 25% to 85% experiencing some language problem. Behavioral issues such as anxiety, depression, mood dysregulation, and poor social skills are common, and children may be quiet, shy, and less active. Despite these challenges, adults with KS often lead normal lives with friends and families, though some face social and emotional difficulties. The lifespan is reduced by about 2.1 years compared to the general male population. Hypogonadism in KS refers to decreased hormone production, not just small testicles, and is characterized by low testosterone, high follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels, leading to impaired spermatogenesis. Testicular dysfunction results from destruction of seminiferous tubules and reduced function of Sertoli and Leydig cells. Diagnosis is often prompted by symptoms such as small testes, infertility, gynecomastia, tall stature, long limbs, developmental delay, or learning issues. KS has been identified in ancient burials, including a 1000 AD man in Portugal and a person buried with the Suontaka sword, whose gender identity may have been non-binary. Historically, symptoms like infertility and gynecomastia led to social stigma due to perceived lack of masculinity, but awareness and advocacy have reduced stigma. The classification of KS as an intersex variation is debated; some intersex groups and academics include it, while traditional medical views have excluded it, often prioritizing physical appearance. A 2024 study found that 19% of KS respondents identified as intersex or non-binary, 12% as female, and 53% as male, with 56% noting a discrepancy between gender identity and physical appearance. Only about 25% of individuals with KS are diagnosed in their lifetime, and the syndrome is the main cause of male hypogonadism. The rate among infertile males is 3.1%, and it is more common in transgender women than in the general population.

Knud Nellemose (12 March 1908, Copenhagen – 14 January 1997, Copenhagen) was a Danish sculptor known for his figures of sportsmen and statues of famous Danes. Between 1927 and 1933, with some interruptions, he studied under Einer Utzon-Frank at the Danish Academy. After starting his career as a sports journalist and newspaper illustrator, he transitioned to sculpture, focusing on boxers, footballers, and athletes, often in motion. Initially influenced by Kai Nielsen, he developed a distinct style characterized by rhythmic movements of arms and legs. He traveled to Greece and Italy, where he was particularly impressed by Donatello, but the dynamic representations he created through accentuated muscle shaping and asymmetrical body positions are entirely his own. One notable pre-war work is Avismanden Leitriz (1935), depicting a newspaperman in the clothes he wore when selling papers in Copenhagen’s streets. Highly productive in both stone and bronze, Nellemose created the Marble Church statues of Søren Kierkegaard (1972) and Bernhard Severin Ingemann (1988), as well as numerous groups of footballers. Among his portraits, some focused on the face and others on half figures, include those of archaeologist Peter Vilhelm Glob (1979) and architect Steen Eiler Rasmussen (1988). During the German occupation of the Second World War, Nellemose was a member of the Frit Danmark resistance group, which led to numerous commissions for war memorials, such as those for Silkeborg (1946) and the 4th of May Dormitory in Aarhus (1953). His Erindring (Remembrance) from 1987 is a powerful depiction of a prisoner from a concentration camp. From 1939, he exhibited as a member of the Decembrist artists, and from 1946 at Den Frie Udstilling. His work was also included in the sculpture event of the art competition at the 1948 Summer Olympics. Knud Nellemose's sister, Karin (1905–1993), was a well-known actress who appeared in many stage productions and films.

Koichi Mizushima (水島公一, Mizushima Kōichi; born January 30, 1941) is a Japanese researcher recognized for discovering lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2) and related materials used in lithium-ion batteries (Li-ion battery). He was trained as a physicist at the University of Tokyo and earned a PhD in Physics from the same institution. He spent 13 years working in the Physics Department at the University of Tokyo. In 1977, he was invited by Professor John Goodenough from the Inorganic Chemistry Department at Oxford University to join as a research scientist. During his tenure at Oxford from 1977 to 1979, Dr. Mizushima, in collaboration with John B. Goodenough, discovered LiCoO2 and related compounds now utilized in the cathode of the Li-ion battery.[1][2][3] After his time at Oxford, he joined Toshiba.[4]

Kokernag (Urdu pronunciation: [koːkərnɑːɡ]; Kashmiri pronunciation: [kɔkarnaːɡ]) is a sub-district, town, and notified area committee located in the Breng Valley, also known as the Golden Crown of Kashmir, within the Anantnag district of the Indian union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. It is renowned for its botanical gardens, pristine freshwater springs, and rainbow trout farm and lies 25.3 km from Anantnag District via NH244. It is one of the most popular weekend getaways from the state capital, Srinagar. The etymology of the name 'Kokernag' (Kashmiri: کۄکرناگ) is disputed, with no conclusive historical proof; one theory suggests it comes from 'koker' (Kashmiri for chicken) and 'nag' (Sanskrit for springs), as the springs emerge from a hillside resembling a hen’s claw-foot. Another theory interprets 'koker' as 'fowl' and 'nag' as 'serpent'. A third theory proposes that 'Kokernag' derives from 'Koh' (mountain), 'kan' (from or under), and 'nag' (spring). The place is also known as Breng Kokernag, a name given by poet and scholar Shiekh ul Alam, who stated "kokernag breng chu sunsund preng," meaning "Kokernag is crown of gold." Kokernag is mentioned in Ain Akbari, which notes that its water satisfies hunger and thirst and acts as a remedy for indigestion. Situated at an altitude of approximately 2,000 meters above sea level, Kokernag is surrounded by towns including Wangam, Devalgam, Hangalgund, Nagam, Sagam, Zalengam, Magam, and Soaf Shali. The Kokernag trout farm covers a total area of about 400 kanals, of which 129 kanals are allocated for gardens and other purposes. The area is famous for its trout streams and is home to the largest freshwater spring in Kashmir. The Trout Fish Farming Project Kokernag, established in 1984 with assistance from the European Economic Community, functions as the mother unit for producing quality Rainbow Trout and Brown Trout. Under its extension program, 59 trout rearing units/hatcheries have been set up across nearly all districts of the state, including Leh and Kargil, with more units being developed. Trout is readily available to the public at all rearing units, including a special sale outlet at Gagribal. A rural mart has been established in Kokernag by NABARD to promote and market handicrafts made by local women self-help groups. According to the 2011 India census, Kokernag had a population of 6,553, with males making up 68% and females 32% of the population. The average literacy rate is 63%, higher than the national average of 59.5%, with male literacy at 77% and female literacy at 33%. Nine percent of the population is under six years of age. Kokernag is located about 25 km from Anantnag on the right side of NH244, and the easiest way to reach it is by hiring a Sumo in Anantnag or taking a local bus, which takes approximately one hour. The nearest railway station is Anantnag railway station on the 119 km-long Kashmir Railway line from Baramulla to Banihal, located 30 km away. The nearest airport is Srinagar International Airport, situated 85 kilometers from Kokernag.

The Krimchi temples are a group of seven ancient Hindu temples situated in the Udhampur District of the Jammu Division in Jammu and Kashmir, India. Located on the bank of the Birunala stream in the village of Krimchi, the complex is 12 km from Udhampur and is locally known as the Pandava Temples. According to the Archaeological Survey of India, the temples were constructed between the 8th and 9th centuries AD, with construction occurring in stages; temples No. 6 and 7 are believed to have been damaged several centuries ago. Local tradition suggests the temples date back to the protagonists of the Mahabharata War or a late Pandava dynasty that ruled in Jammu and Kashmir, a theory proposed by Alexander Cunningham. Legend claims that Raja Kichak founded the town of Krimchi and the surrounding kingdom, and that the Pandavas during their exile stayed in the area for an extended period. Given their 8th-century construction, the temple complex reflects elements of Indo-Greek architecture. The complex includes four large and three small temples, with the main temple standing 50 feet tall and dedicated to Hindu deities such as Shiva, Ganesha, Vishnu, and Parvati. The architectural style is similar to classical Kashmiri temples in India. This article is a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

Kristen Nygaard (27 August 1926 – 10 August 2002) was a Norwegian computer scientist, programming language pioneer, and politician. He is internationally recognized as the co-inventor of object-oriented programming and the programming language Simula, developed with Ole-Johan Dahl in the 1960s. Nygaard and Dahl were awarded the 2001 A. M. Turing Award for their contributions to computer science. Born in Oslo, he earned his master's degree in mathematics from the University of Oslo in 1956, with a thesis titled "Theoretical Aspects of Monte Carlo methods." From 1948 to 1960, he worked full-time at the Norwegian Defense Research Establishment, initially in computing and programming (1948–1954) and later in operational research (1952–1960). From 1957 to 1960, he led the first operations research groups in the Norwegian defense establishment and co-founded the Norwegian Operational Research Society (1959–1964). In 1960, he joined the Norwegian Computing Center (NCC), where he helped establish it as a research institute, becoming Director of Research in 1962. Together with Dahl, he developed the foundational concepts of object-oriented programming—such as objects, classes, inheritance, virtual quantities, and multi-threaded (quasi-parallel) execution—through the Simula I (1961–1965) and Simula 67 (1965–1968) languages, which were extensions of ALGOL 60. In 2004, the Association Internationale pour les Technologies Objets (AITO) established the Dahl–Nygaard Prize, awarded annually at the ECOOP conference to two individuals—senior and junior—making significant technical contributions to object-orientation in the spirit of Dahl and Nygaard’s pioneering work. Nygaard conducted research on planning, control, and data processing for Norwegian trade unions (1971–1973) with Olav Terje Bergo, and explored the social impact of computer technology and the general system description language DELTA (1973–1975) with Erik Holbaek-Hanssen and Petter Haandlykken. He served as professor at Aarhus University, Denmark (1975–1976), and became professor emeritus at the University of Oslo (part-time from 1977, full-time 1984–1996), contributing to the development of the Scandinavian School in System Development and participatory design. Starting in 1976, he co-developed and implemented the general object-oriented programming language BETA with Bent Bruun Kristensen, Ole Lehrmann Madsen, and Birger Møller-Pedersen, which is now available on many computer platforms. From 1976 to the 1980s, he chaired the steering committee of the Scandinavian research program System Development and Profession Oriented Languages (SYDPOL) and led the Cost-13 (European Common Market Commission)-financed project on extending profession-oriented languages for professional work involving artificial intelligence and information technology. From 1995 to 1999, his research focused on distributed systems, particularly as leader of the General Object-Oriented Distributed Systems (GOODS) project (1997–1999), funded by the Norwegian Research Council, which aimed to enhance object-oriented languages and system development methods by introducing concepts to describe relationships between layered or distributed programs and hardware and human users. The GOODS team included Haakon Bryhni, Dag Sjøberg, and Ole Smørdal. His final research interests were in introductory programming education and creating a process-oriented conceptual platform for informatics, leading to the development of the Comprehensive Object-Oriented Learning (COOL) project with international test sites. He delivered lectures and courses on these topics in Norway and abroad. In November 1999, he became chair of an advisory committee on Broadband Communication for the Norwegian Department for Municipal and Regional Affairs. From 2001, he held a part-time position at the Simula Research Laboratory. In June 1990, he received an honorary doctorate from Lund University, Sweden, and in June 1991, became the first individual to receive an honorary doctorate from Aalborg University, Denmark. He was elected a member of the Norwegian Academy of Sciences. In October 1990, he was awarded the Norbert Wiener Award for Social and Professional Responsibility by Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility. In 1999, he and Dahl received the Rosing Prize from the Norwegian Data Association for exceptional professional achievements. In June 2000, he was awarded an Honorary Fellowship by the Object Management Group for "his originating of object technology concepts." In November 2001, the IEEE awarded Nygaard and Dahl the IEEE John von Neumann Medal "For the introduction of the concepts underlying object-oriented programming through the design and implementation of Simula 67." In February 2002, they received the 2001 A. M. Turing Award from the Association for Computing Machinery, cited for "ideas fundamental to the emergence of object-oriented programming, through their design of the programming languages Simula I and Simula 67." In August 2000, he was made Commander of the Royal Norwegian Order of St. Olav by King Harald V. From 1971 to 2001, he was a member of the Labour Party and participated in its research policy committees. In 1984 and 1985, he chaired the Informatics Committee of the University of Oslo and contributed to the university’s plan for research, education, and computing and communication facilities. He was the first chairman of the Environment Protection Committee of the Norwegian Association for the Protection of Nature. He served as Norwegian representative in OECD activities on information technology for ten years in the 1970s and was a member of the Research Committee of the Norwegian Federation of Trade Unions, collaborating with unions globally. For several years, he managed an experimental social institution aimed at creating humane living conditions for socially outcast alcoholics. Nygaard was active in Norwegian politics, serving on the National Executive Committee of the Norwegian Liberal Party in the mid- and late-1960s and as chair of its Strategy Committee. He was a minor ballot candidate in the 1949 parliamentary election. During the 1972 referendum on Norway’s membership in the European Common Market (later the European Union), he coordinated youth organizations opposing membership. From 1971 to 2001, he was a Labour Party member and involved in research policy committees. In November 1988, he became chair of the Information Committee on Norway and the EEC, which was reorganized in August 1990 as Nei til EF, an organization focused on informing the public about Norway’s relationship with the Common Market and advocating against membership. In 1993, following the EEC’s ratification of the Maastricht Treaty and the formation of the European Union, the organization changed its name to reflect this. Nei til EF became the largest political organization in Norway (145,000 members in 1994, from a population of 4 million). Nygaard worked with Anne Enger Lahnstein, leader of the anti-EU Centre Party, in this campaign. In the 28 November 1994 referendum, "Nei til EU" won with 52.2% of the vote and the highest voter participation in Norwegian history: 88.8%. Nygaard’s strategy emphasized advocating for something in addition to opposition, specifically the Scandinavian welfare state, which he viewed as threatened by the Maastricht Agreement. He resigned as chair in 1995 and later served on the organization’s strategy committee and council. In 1996 and 1997, he coordinated efforts to establish the European Anti-Maastricht Movement (TEAM), a cooperative network of national organizations opposing the Economic and Monetary Union and the Maastricht Treaty, which was successfully launched on 3 March 1997. Nygaard married Johanna Nygaard in 1951; she worked at the Norwegian Agency for Aid to Developing Countries, specializing in recruiting and administrative support for specialists in East Africa. They had three children and seven grandchildren. Nygaard died of a heart attack in 2002.

Kristin Otto, born on 7 February 1966 in Leipzig, Bezirk Leipzig (present-day Sachsen), East Germany, is a former East German swimmer who became an Olympic, World, and European champion multiple times. She is most renowned for being the first woman to win six gold medals at a single Olympic Games, achieved at the 1988 Seoul Olympic Games. In long course swimming, she held world records in the 100 meter and 200 meter freestyle events. She was also the first woman to swim the short course 100 meter backstroke in under a minute, accomplishing this at an international short course meet at Indiana University in 1983. Otto began swimming at age 11 in an East German sports academy and competed in her first world championships in 1982, winning a gold medal in the 100 meter backstroke and two additional golds in the 4×100 m relays. After 1982, she changed coaches and focused on speed strokes; at the 1983 European Championships, she finished second in the 100 meter freestyle behind Birgit Meineke. In 1984, she set a world record in the 200 meter freestyle but was unable to compete at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics due to the boycott by 14 Eastern Bloc countries, including East Germany. In 1985, she fractured a vertebra, which prevented her from competing for most of the year or attending the European Championships. She returned in 1986 at the World Championships in Madrid, winning four gold medals (100 m freestyle, 200 m individual medley, 4×100 m medley relay, and 4×100 m freestyle relay) and two silver medals (50 m freestyle, 100 m butterfly), and continued her success at the 1987 European Championships, where she won five gold medals. At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, she won six gold medals and set Olympic records in the 50 m freestyle and 100 m butterfly. Otto retired from swimming in 1989 and currently works as a sports reporter for German television. She was named Female World Swimmer of the Year by Swimming World in 1984, 1986, and 1988, and received a Star of People's Friendship in gold (second class) in October 1986 for her sporting achievements. Her career was affected by the exposure of widespread doping in East German athletics, with former teammate Petra Schneider admitting to using banned substances; however, Otto stated she was unaware of doping and passed all doping tests, asserting: "The medals are the only reminder of how hard I worked. It was not all drugs."

Kungsängen Golf Club is located in Kungsängen, Sweden. It was established in 1989, when the first 18 holes were built. The club now operates two 18-hole golf courses: the 'Kings Course' and the 'Queens Course'. The club house was completed in 1993. The Queens Course is the oldest, opening in 1991, and runs through forests, featuring smaller greens and a shorter layout. The Kings Course opened in 1993 with 18 holes and was later renovated three years later to meet international championship standards. The renovation included widening the course to accommodate the public, and it now includes natural water hazards with fairways surrounded by pines. The club hosted the Scandinavian Masters, a European Tour event, in 1998, 2000, 2002, and 2005. The first Scandinavian Masters victory on the course was achieved by local professional Jesper Parnevik. Kungsängen is 25 minutes from Stockholm and is part of the PGA European Tour Courses. In 2001, the club hosted the STC Scandinavian International, a 54-hole event on the European Senior Tour.

The Kunming Metro, also known as Kunming Rail Transit, is a rapid transit system serving Kunming, the capital of China's Yunnan Province. The system currently comprises 6 operational lines, with 2 extensions to existing lines under construction and 3 additional lines planned, totaling 164.3 kilometers of track. Due to long-standing traffic congestion in Kunming's streets, discussions about a subway system have existed since the late 1990s. At the time of construction, the city had a population of just over 3 million, with the built-up urban area reaching over 5 million by 2020, making it one of the largest Chinese cities without a metro system prior to development. A 2006 proposal suggested starting construction in 2008 with a north-south and east-west line, while the current system was first announced in 2009, with construction beginning later that year. The metro was designed not only to relieve traffic in the city center but also to promote development in the southeast, particularly in the Chenggong District, which experienced a construction boom despite lacking adequate transit links. Construction on Lines 1 and 2 began officially in May 2010, after delays, with an elevated test section having been built since 2009. Lines 1 (34 km) and 2 (22 km) were initially scheduled for opening in 2012 but were delayed and opened in early 2013. Line 3 began construction in August 2010 and opened on 29 August 2017. The construction of Line 1 was estimated to cost up to 32 billion yuan (US$4.5 billion), with elevated sections costing around 250 million yuan per kilometer and underground sections ranging from 400 to 800 million yuan per kilometer; China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) is the primary contractor. Line 6 trains were manufactured by China South Locomotive & Rolling Stock Corporation Ltd (CSR, now CRRC) in Zhuzhou and operate as 6-car sets at 120 km/h; CSR discussed safety concerns related to these speeds in October 2011. Rolling stock has been updated over time: Line 1, 2, and 6 feature LED physical route maps, with some Line 1 and 2 trains upgraded to digital UIs; Line 3 uses a digital route map with a basic UI; Line 4 has darker flooring, a new info board UI, and a remade route map UI; Line 5 reverted to white flooring, updated its info board and route map UIs, and features projectors on the exterior that display advertisements on tunnel walls. Line 1 is 33.3 km long with 22 stations, running from South Ring Road to University Town (South) and Kunming South Railway Station, and currently has through service with Line 2, which will end when Line 1 Northwest Extension and Line 2 Phase 2 open, turning South Ring Road into an interchange. The first phase of Line 1 opened on 20 May 2013, the second phase on 30 April 2014, and a 5.3 km branch to Kunming South Railway Station opened on 26 December 2016. Line 1 includes an elevated section connecting Kunming to Chenggong and an underground section beneath Caiyun Road in Chenggong, with the northwest extension planned to be dug underground along the west side of the city center, serving as Kunming’s main rail link to Chenggong. Line 1’s color is red. Line 2 is 12.4 km long with 14 stations, running from North Coach Station to South Ring Road, and shares through service with Line 1, which will end when Line 2 Phase 2 opens, extending its route to Haidong Park. The first phase opened on 30 April 2014; the route includes a short elevated section to Longtou Street and an underground section beneath Beijing Road to South Ring Road. Phase 2 will be dug beneath Guannan Avenue and Fubao Road toward Haidong Park, making it Kunming’s main north-south line. Line 2’s color is blue. Line 3, which opened on 29 August 2017, is 19.16 km long with 20 stations, running from Western Hills Park to East Coach Station, and serves as Kunming’s main east-west line; its color is magenta. Line 4, which began operations on 23 September 2020, is 43.4 km long with 29 stations, running from Jinchuan Road to Kunming South Railway Station, connecting Northwest and Eastern Kunming to the metro and serving as a second link to Chenggong; it features cartoon mascots known as the "K4 Cats" to promote ridership; its color is orange. Line 5, which started on 29 June 2022, is 26.5 km long with 22 stations, running from World Horti-Expo Garden to Baofeng, and functions as a tourism line linking destinations such as World Horti-Expo Garden, Haigeng Great Dam, and Haigeng Park; its color is green. Line 6, 25.3 km long with 8 stations, runs from Kunming Airport to Tangzixiang; Phase 1 opened on 28 June 2012, and Phase 2 opened on 23 September 2020, extending it to Tangzixiang just south of the city center. It is an airport express line connecting the city center with Kunming Changshui International Airport; its original terminus at East Coach Station was not connected to other lines until Line 3 opened in 2017, and the two intermediate stations between East Coach Station and Kunming Airport were built as infill stations. Line 6 temporarily ceased operations on 5 March 2016 to complete the infill stations and resumed on 29 August 2017 with four stations; its color is teal. Extensions of Lines 1 and 2 are under construction but have faced delays, originally projected for 2022 and now expected to open in December 2026. Line 9 (Songming Line) and the Anning Line are planned, with all phase 1 station names confirmed. However, construction of the planned new lines is currently on hold due to a lack of funding and unstable leadership.

Kwadwo Baah-Wiredu (1952 – 24 September 2008) was a Ghanaian politician and a chartered accountant. He served as Member of Parliament for Asante Akim North Constituency from January 1997 until his death on 24 September 2008. He held ministerial positions under the Kufuor government from 2001, serving as Minister of Local Government and Rural Development (2001–2003) and Minister of Education, Youth and Sports (2003–2005), before becoming Minister for Finance and Economic Planning in 2005. In 2005, he became the first Finance Minister in Ghana's history to present the country's Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament before the start of the fiscal year 2006, a practice that has since become standard for all Finance Ministers. Baah-Wiredu was born in Asante Akim Agogo. He began secondary education at Kumasi High School in 1967, obtained the GCE Ordinary Level Certificate in 1972, and completed his sixth form at Prempeh College, both in Kumasi. He enrolled at the University of Ghana in 1974, earning a B.Sc. in Administration (Accounting option), and later completed a four-year course with the Institute of Chartered Accountants, qualifying as a chartered accountant in 1985. He worked at Ghana Airways and the Volta River Authority, served as a senior consultant on computer systems and finance manager at Ananse Systems, and was a partner in Asante Wiredu and Associates, an accounting firm. He began his political career in 1997 as Member of Parliament for Asante Akim North following his victory in the 1996 Ghanaian General Election. He joined the New Patriotic Party in 1992 and was elected to the Second Parliament of the Fourth Republic in 1996, retaining his seat thereafter. In 2000, he won the general election for Asante Akim North, securing 32,341 votes out of 45,227 valid votes cast (72.3%), defeating Kofi Opoku Manu (11,852 votes, 26.5%), Kwabena Anafi (168 votes, 0.4%), James K. Baah (151 votes, 0.3%), Emmanuel K. Adade (130 votes, 0.3%), and Joseph B. Frimpong (75 votes, 0.2%). In 2004, he won again on the New Patriotic Party ticket, receiving 40,497 votes out of 53,098 valid votes cast (76.3%), defeating Atobrah Isaac (0.8%), Thomas Osei Bonsu Nkansah (21.6%), and Kwabena Anarfi (1.3%). His constituency was part of the 31 seats won by the New Patriotic Party in the Ashanti Region in 2000 and 36 seats in 2004, with the party winning a total of 99 seats (200 total) in 2000 and 128 seats (230 total) in 2004. Baah-Wiredu was married with six children. He died on 24 September 2008 in South Africa, where he had been receiving medical treatment for a short illness.

Lal Narayan Sinha was a lawyer who served as the Attorney General of India from 9 August 1979 to 8 August 1983 and as the Solicitor General of India from 17 July 1972 to 5 April 1977. He was educated at Patna Law College, Patna University. He was the first Attorney General to represent a private party during their term in office. Before assuming the role of Solicitor General of India, he served as the Advocate General of Bihar for several years. His son, Lalit Mohan Sharma, became the Chief Justice of India, and his grandson, Justice Partha Sarthy, currently serves as a Judge in the Patna High Court. La Capilla is a town and municipality located in the Eastern Boyacá Province within the Colombian department of Boyacá. Its urban centre lies at an altitude of 1,600 metres (5,200 ft) in the Tenza Valley. The area was originally named La Capilla de Tenza due to the appearance of Our Lady of Candle in the outskirts of the village, which led to the construction of a chapel and the adoption of the name Capilla. The first inhabitants were the Muisca, part of the loose Muisca Confederation, and they were aligned with the caciques of Garagoa, Sutatenza, and Somondoco in the Tenza Valley. Conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada and his forces passed through the valley in 1537 en route to the territories of the zaque of Hunza. Modern La Capilla was officially established on November 13, 1793, by Juan de la Cruz Aguirre. The primary economic activity in La Capilla is agriculture, specifically the cultivation of cucumbers, tomatoes, and beans.

Lambda Istanbul is a Turkish LGBT organization that was established in 1993 as a cultural space for the LGBT community and became an officially registered organization in 2006. Clandestine Pride events began in Turkey in 1993, and with Lambda Istanbul's involvement, they transitioned into public marches. In May 2008, the organization was ordered dissolved by a court decision, with prosecutors asserting that its objectives were "against the law and morality." This decision drew criticism from Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. On November 25, 2008, the Supreme Court of Appeals overturned the dissolution order, and on April 30, 2009, a lower court granted Lambda Istanbul permission to continue operating. The national anthem of the secessionist African state of Biafra, formerly known as the Eastern Region of Nigeria, was titled "Land of the Rising Sun." The lyrics were authored by Nnamdi Azikiwe, and the melody was adapted from Jean Sibelius' "Finlandia," a choice influenced by Biafran president Emeka Ojukwu's appreciation for Sibelius's musical works. The anthem begins with the lines: "Land of the rising sun, we love and cherish, Beloved homeland of our brave heroes; We must defend our lives or we shall perish, We shall protect our hearts from all our foes; But if the price is death for all we hold dear, Then let us die without a shred of fear." It continues with: "Hail to Biafra, consecrated nation, O fatherland, this be our solemn pledge: Defending thee shall be a dedication, Spilling our blood we’ll count a privilege; The waving standard which emboldens the free Shall always be our flag of liberty." The final stanzas state: "We shall emerge triumphant from this ordeal, And through the crucible unscathed we’ll pass; When we are poised the wounds of battle to heal, We shall remember those who died in mass; Then shall our trumpets peal the glorious song Of victory we scored o’er might and wrong." The closing verses pray: "Oh God, protect us from the hidden pitfall, Guide all our movements lest we go astray; Give us the strength to heed the humanist call: To give and not to count the cost’ each day; Bless those who rule to serve with resoluteness, To make this clime a land of righteousness."
