According to the "National Report on caste/ethnicity, language & religion" from the National Population and Housing Census 2021, Nepal has 124 mother tongues. Of these, Nepali is the mother tongue for 44.86% of the population and serves as a second language for 46.2% of the total population. The languages of Nepal, referred to as Nepali languages in the country's constitution, are defined as those spoken by Nepalis with an ancient history or origin within Nepal's sovereign territory. These languages belong primarily to the Indo-Aryan and Sino-Tibetan language families, with only a few belonging to Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian families. The Indo-European family, specifically the Indo-Aryan (Indic) sub-family (excluding English), comprises 48 languages and accounts for nearly 82.1% of the population, including Nepali, Bhojpuri, Maithili, Awadhi, the Tharu languages, and Hindustani (Hindi-Urdu). The Sino-Tibetan family, part of the Tibeto-Burman group, includes about 63 languages and is spoken by 17.3% of the population, such as Tamang, Nepal Bhasa (Newar), Magar, and Limbu. The Dravidian family is represented by Kurux, and the Austro-Asiatic family by Santali and Mundari. Indigenous languages that predated the arrival of Indic, Tibeto-Burman, and other language families are nearly extinct, with only the Kusunda language surviving, though it is in a critical state. Nepal also has several indigenous village sign languages—Jhankot Sign Language, Jumla Sign Language, and Ghandruk Sign Language—as well as Nepali Sign Language for national use. The Constitution of Nepal 2015 (2072 B.S.) recognizes that all mother tongues spoken in Nepal are national languages. The Language Commission of Nepal in 2021 recommended 14 official languages for different provinces, with Nepali serving as the official working language at the federal level, while provinces are allowed to choose one or more additional official languages. Specific recommendations include Maithili and Limbu for Province No. 1; Maithili, Bhojpuri, and Bajjika for Province No. 2; Tamang and Nepal Bhasa for Bagmati Province; Magar and Gurung for Gandaki Province; Tharu and Awadhi for Lumbini Province; Nepali (Khas Bhasa) Karnali dialect and Magar for Karnali Province; Dotyali and Tharu for Sudurpashchim Province. Out of the 124 mother tongues, 111 were reported in the 2011 census, with 13 newly identified in 2021, including Bhote, Lowa, Chum/Nubri, Baragunwa, Nar-Phu, Ranatharu, Karmarong, Mugali, Tichhurong Poike, Sadri, Done, Munda/Mudiyari, and Kewarat. Some foreign languages from the 2011 census were included in the "Other Language" category due to very few speakers. In the 2021 census, 25 languages were used as a second language by more than 10,000 people each, compared to only 18 in the 2011 census. Most of Nepal's languages are found exclusively in oral form, and the Language Commission has identified fifteen scripts currently in use in the country.

The Lapworth Medal is the most prestigious award presented by the Palaeontological Association, bestowed upon individuals who have made a significant contribution to the field of palaeontology through a substantial body of research.

Laura Phillips "Laurie" Anderson, born on June 5, 1947, in Chicago and raised in Glen Ellyn, Illinois, one of eight children of Mary Louise (née Rowland) and Arthur T. Anderson, is an American avant-garde artist, musician, and filmmaker whose work spans performance art, pop music, and multimedia projects. Initially trained in violin and sculpting, she pursued performance art in New York City during the 1970s, focusing on language, technology, and visual imagery. Her first performance-art piece, a symphony played on automobile horns, was performed in 1969. In 1970, she drew the underground comix Baloney Moccasins, published by George DiCaprio. She worked as an art instructor and art critic for Artforum and illustrated children's books, including The Package (1971), a picture-only mystery. In the early 1970s, she performed in New York, with one of her most-cited works, Duets on Ice, involving her playing the violin while wearing ice skates with blades frozen into ice, ending only when the ice melted. Two early pieces, "New York Social Life" and "Time to Go," were included in the 1977 compilation New Music for Electronic and Recorded Media, along with works by Pauline Oliveros, and two others appeared on Airwaves. She recorded a lecture for Vision, a set of artist's lectures released by Crown Point Press as six LPs. Many of her earliest recordings remain unreleased or were issued in limited quantities, such as "It's Not the Bullet that Kills You (It's the Hole)," originally recorded for a jukebox art installation at the Holly Solomon Gallery in New York City, featuring musicians Peter Gordon, Scott Johnson, Ken Deifik, and Joe Kos. In the late 1970s, she released recordings through the Giorno Poetry Systems label, and in 1977, she was granted an artist-in-residence stay at the Cité internationale des Arts in Paris. In 1978, she performed at the Nova Convention, which included notable figures like William S. Burroughs, Philip Glass, Frank Zappa, Timothy Leary, Malcolm Goldstein, John Cage, and Allen Ginsberg. She also worked with comedian Andy Kaufman in the late 1970s. In 1980, she received an honorary doctorate from the San Francisco Art Institute; in 1982, she was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship for Creative Arts—Film; and in 1987, she received an honorary doctorate in the fine arts from the University of the Arts in Philadelphia. She gained widespread recognition in 1981 with the single "O Superman," originally released by B. George's One Ten Records in limited quantity, which reached number two on the UK singles chart, prompting a surge in orders that led to a seven-album contract with Warner Bros. Records, which re-released the single. "O Superman" was part of the stage work United States Live (1984) and appeared on her debut studio album Big Science (1982). Prior to Big Science, she recorded the collaboration album You're the Guy I Want to Share My Money With (1981) with William S. Burroughs and John Giorno, with each artist recording one side of a double-LP and a separate groove on the fourth side. This was followed by the back-to-back releases of Mister Heartbreak and United States Live (both 1984), the latter a five-LP (and later four-CD) recording of her two-evening stage show at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. She also appeared in a television special produced by Nam June Paik, "Good Morning, Mr. Orwell," broadcast on New Year's Day 1984. She starred in and directed the 1986 concert film Home of the Brave and composed soundtracks for the Spalding Gray films Swimming to Cambodia (1987) and Monster in a Box (1992). She contributed music to Robert Wilson's Alcestis at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and hosted the PBS series Alive from Off Center in 1987 after producing the short film What You Mean We? the year before. In that film, she introduced "The Clone," a digitally altered masculine counterpart to her, who later co-hosted with her on Alive from Off Center. Elements of the Clone were later used in the puppet of her later work, Puppet Motel. In 1991, she was a member of the jury at the 41st Berlin International Film Festival. That year, she appeared in The Human Face, a BBC documentary on the history of the face in art and science, where her face was transformed using latex masks and digital effects. In 1994, she created a CD-ROM titled Puppet Motel, followed by Bright Red, co-produced by Brian Eno, and a spoken-word album, The Ugly One with the Jewels (1995). In 1997, she appeared on the charity single "Perfect Day." In 1996, she performed with Diego Frenkel (La Portuária) and Aterciopelados for the AIDS benefit album Silencio=Muerte: Red Hot + Latin produced by the Red Hot Organization. After a more than half-decade gap, she released her next album in 1999 with Songs and Stories from Moby Dick. During this time, she wrote a supplemental article on the cultural character of New York City for the Encyclopædia Britannica and created multimedia presentations, including one inspired by Moby-Dick. A central theme in her work is the exploration of technology's effects on human relationships and communication. Starting in the 1990s, she collaborated with Lou Reed, whom she met in 1992, on recordings: Reed contributed to "In Our Sleep" (Bright Red, 1994), "One Beautiful Evening" (Life on a String, 2001), "My Right Eye" and "Only an Expert" (Homeland, 2010), which he also co-produced; Anderson contributed to "Call on Me" (The Raven, 2003), "Rouge" and "Rock Minuet" (Ecstasy, 2000), and "Hang On to Your Emotions" (Set the Twilight Reeling, 1996). In late 1998, Artist Space in New York presented an exhibit of her work from the 1970s to 1980s, including her 1990s work Whirlwind. Life on a String was released in 2001, after she signed a new recording contract with Nonesuch Records, a Warner Music Group label. The album combined new works, including one recalling the death of her father, with material from the Moby-Dick presentation. In 2001, she recorded the audiobook version of Don DeLillo's novella The Body Artist and toured performing her best-known musical pieces, including a performance of "O Superman" in New York City a week after the September 11 attacks, released in early 2002 as the double CD Live in New York. In 2003, she produced albums with French musicians La Jarry and Hector Zazou and performed with them; Zazou's album Strong Currents (2003) featured her alongside Jane Birkin, Lori Carson, and Irene Grandi. In 2003, she became NASA's first artist-in-residence, which inspired her performance piece The End of the Moon. In May 2004, she received an honorary doctorate from Columbia University. She was part of the team that created the opening ceremony for the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens and collaborated with choreographer Trisha Brown and filmmaker Agnieszka Wojtowicz-Vosloo on the multimedia project O Zlozony/O Composite, which premiered at the Palais Garnier in Paris in December 2004. She mounted themed shows and composed a piece for Expo 2005 in Japan. In 2005, she visited Russia's space program, including the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre and mission control, with Arts Catalyst and participated in the Arts Catalyst's Space Soon event at the Roundhouse. Her exhibition The Waters Reglitterized opened at the Sean Kelly Gallery in New York City in 2005, described as a diary of dreams and their literal recreation as art, including drawings, prints, and high-definition video, running until October 22, 2005. In 2006, she was awarded a residency at the American Academy in Rome and narrated Ric Burns' Andy Warhol: A Documentary Film, first televised in September 2006 as part of the PBS American Masters series. She contributed a song to Plague Songs, a collection of songs related to the 10 Biblical plagues, and performed at Came So Far for Beauty, a Leonard Cohen tribute event in Dublin, Ireland, on October 4–5, 2006. In November 2006, she published a book of drawings based on her dreams, titled Night Life. Material from Homeland was performed in small work-in-progress shows in New York throughout May 2007, supported by a four-piece band with live lighting and video by Willie Williams and Mark Coniglio. A European tour included performances in Dublin (September 28–29, 2007), Melbourne (October 17–19, 2007), and Russia (April 26, 2008) at the Moscow Dom Muzyky. The work was performed in Toronto, Canada, on June 14, 2008, with her husband Lou Reed, making "The Lost Art of Conversation" a duet. The Homeland Tour included performances at the Ferst Center for the Arts in Atlanta, Georgia; The Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts in New York City; and the Harris Theater for Music and Dance in Chicago, Illinois, co-presented by the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. In February 2010, she premiered a new theatrical work, Delusion, at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, Canada, commissioned by the Vancouver 2010 Cultural Olympiad and the Barbican Centre, London. She received the Women's Project Theater Woman of Achievement Award in March 2010. In May–June 2010, she curated the Vivid Live festival in Sydney with Lou Reed. Her new studio album Homeland was released on June 22. She performed "Only an Expert" on July 15, 2010, on the Late Show with David Letterman, and her song "Gravity's Angel" was featured on the Fox reality television dance competition show So You Think You Can Dance the same day. She appears as a guest musician on several tracks from experimental jazz musician Colin Stetson's studio album New History Warfare Vol. 2: Judges (2011). In 2012, she developed a theatrical work titled "Another Day in America," with first public showings in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, in January 2012 as part of Theatre Junction Grand's 2011–12 season and One Yellow Rabbit's annual arts festival, the High Performance Rodeo. In May 2012, she was named the Inaugural Distinguished Artist-In-Residence at the Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center (EMPAC) at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York. In March 2013, an exhibition titled Laurie Anderson: Language of the Future, selected works 1971–2013, was held at the Samstag Museum as part of the Adelaide Festival of the Arts in Adelaide, South Australia, with a performance of Duets on Ice on opening night. In 2013, she received the Honorary Doctor of Arts from the Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture. In June/July 2013, she performed "The Language of the Future" and guest curated at the River to River Festival in New York City. In November 2013, she was the featured Guest of Honor at the B3 Biennale of the Moving Image in Frankfurt, Germany. In 2018, she contributed vocals to a re-recording of David Bowie's "Shining Star (Makin' My Love)," originally from Bowie's 1987 album Never Let Me Down, produced by Mario J. McNulty, who knew Anderson and Bowie were friends. On February 10, 2019, at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in Los Angeles, Anderson and the Kronos Quartet's Landfall won the Grammy Award for Best Chamber Music/Small Ensemble Performance, marking her first Grammy and her first collaboration with the Kronos Quartet; the award was inspired by her experience of Hurricane Sandy, with Nonesuch Records noting the work juxtaposed lush electronics and traditional strings with Anderson's powerful descriptions of loss, from water-logged pianos to disappearing animal species to Dutch karaoke bars. Chalkroom is a virtual reality work by Anderson and Taiwanese artist Hsin-Chien Huang in which the reader flies through a structure made of words, drawings, and stories. To the Moon, a collaboration with Hsin-Chien Huang, premiered at the Manchester International Festival on July 12, 2019, as a 15-minute virtual reality artwork allowing audience members to explore a moon with donkey rides and Earth's rubbish in a non-narrative structure, accompanied by a film showing the development of the work. In 2021, Anderson was appointed the Charles Eliot Norton Professor of Poetry at Harvard University and presented a series of six lectures titled Spending the War Without You: Virtual Backgrounds over two semesters. In 2021, she created a show on the second floor of the Hirsh.

Laurie Anderson received her first Grammy Award in 2019 for her album *Landfall*, which was the second Grammy for Kronos and was inspired by her experience of Hurricane Sandy. The album, described by Nonesuch Records as juxtaposing lush electronics and traditional strings by Kronos with Anderson's powerful descriptions of loss—such as water-logged pianos, disappearing animal species, and Dutch karaoke bars—won the Grammy for Best Chamber Music/Small Ensemble Performance. In October 2012, Hurricane Sandy destroyed archives of her creative work, including photographs, performance props, audiovisual equipment, musical instruments, and other materials, which led to her writing the book *All the Things I Lost in the Flood* (2018) reflecting on her career and the ephemeral nature of art. Anderson moved to New York in 1966 and now lives in Tribeca; she met musician Lou Reed in 1992 and was married to him from April 2008 until his death in 2013. She is a foreign member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Music and a long-time student of Buddhism and meditation, having first learned meditation in 1977 with the Insight Meditation Society and later studying with Tibetan Nepali teacher Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche. Anderson invented several experimental instruments, including a tape-bow violin created in 1977 that uses recorded magnetic tape in the bow and a magnetic tape head in the bridge, which she has updated over the years and used in her film *Home of the Brave* with MIDI-based audio samples; and a six-foot-long baton-like MIDI controller called the "talking stick," developed in the late 1990s with Interval Research and Bob Bielecki, which uses granular synthesis to break sound into tiny segments called grains and reassemble them into new textures. A recurring motif in her work is the use of an electric pitch-shifting voice filter that deepens her voice into a masculine register, which she calls "audio drag." This voice, initially known as the "Voice of Authority" and later dubbed Fenway Bergamot at Lou Reed's suggestion, has been used as a "voice of authority" or conscience, and later as a tool for historical or sociopolitical commentary, as seen in "Another Day in America" from her 2010 album *Homeland*. In 2021, she was appointed the Charles Eliot Norton Professor of Poetry at Harvard University and delivered a series of six lectures titled *Spending the War Without You: Virtual Backgrounds* over two semesters. In 2021, she created a show titled *The Weather* at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C., described by *The New York Times* as "a sort of nonretrospective retrospective of one of America's major, and majorly confounding, modern artists." In mid-2023, her exhibit *Looking into a Mirror Sideways*, highlighting various styles of her art techniques, opened at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm, Sweden, and became her biggest solo show in Europe. In 2024, she withdrew from a guest professorship at the Folkwang University of the Arts in Essen, Germany, after university officials objected to her support of a "Letter Against Apartheid" organized by Palestinian artists, calling for "an immediate and unconditional cessation of Israeli violence against Palestinians." In November 2024, she staged *United States V*, a multimedia performance envisioned as a sequel to *United States*, commissioned by Factory International and staged at Aviva Studios in Manchester, England, featuring video appearances from Ai Weiwei as God and Anohni as an angel. She also collaborated with Taiwanese artist Hsin-Chien Huang on *Chalkroom*, a virtual reality work where the reader flies through a structure made of words, drawings, and stories, and *To the Moon*, a 15-minute virtual reality artwork that premiered at the Manchester International Festival on July 12, 2019, allowing audience members to explore a moon with donkey rides and Earth's rubbish in a non-narrative structure, accompanied by a film showing its development. The single "Sharkey's Day" was for many years the theme song of the cable channel Lifetime, and she has contributed to recordings by Peter Gabriel, Lou Reed, Jean-Michel Jarre, Philip Glass, and a tribute album for John Cage. Formal music videos have been produced for her work, and in lieu of a music video for her *Strange Angels* album, she created a series of one- to two-minute "Personal Service Announcements" in the early 1990s, which were frequently shown between music videos on VH1 and used music from her *Swimming to Cambodia* soundtrack. In 2013, Dale Eisinger of Complex ranked *United States* as the third greatest work of performance art ever, noting Anderson's ability to capture the climate of life in the United States without causing a standoff, with her *United States I – IV* performances being highlighted as a peak of her range.

Le Rêve (The Dream) is a 1932 oil on canvas painting (130 × 97 cm) by Pablo Picasso, then 50 years old, depicting his 22-year-old mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter. It was said to have been painted in one afternoon on 24 January 1932 and belongs to Picasso's period of distorted depictions, characterized by oversimplified outlines and contrasted colors reminiscent of early cubism. Critics have noted the painting's erotic content, specifically an erect penis in the upturned face of the model, which is believed to symbolize Picasso's own. Purchased for $7,000 in 1941 by Victor and Sally Ganz of New York City, the painting became part of their 50-year collection of works by only five artists: Picasso, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Frank Stella, and Eva Hesse. After the Ganzes died—Victor in 1987 and Sally in 1997—their collection, including Le Rêve, was sold at Christie's on 11 November 1997 to settle inheritance tax, with Le Rêve fetching an unexpectedly high $48.4 million, at the time the fourth most expensive painting sold (tenth when adjusted for inflation). The entire collection brought $206.5 million, while the Ganzes had spent approximately $2 million over their lifetime collecting these works. The 1997 buyer of Le Rêve was Wolfgang Flöttl, an Austrian-born investment fund manager who also briefly owned Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr. Gachet in the late 1990s. In 2001, under financial pressure, Flöttl sold Le Rêve to casino magnate Steve Wynn for an undisclosed sum, estimated at about $60 million. In 2006, Le Rêve was the centerpiece of Wynn's collection, and he had considered naming his Wynn Las Vegas resort after it, but abandoned the idea due to anti-French sentiment in the U.S. in response to France's opposition to the U.S. invasion of Iraq. On 26 October 2006, Wynn told a group of friends—including screenwriter Nora Ephron and her husband Nick Pileggi, broadcaster Barbara Walters, art dealer Serge Sorokko and his wife Tatiana Sorokko, and lawyer David Boies and his wife Mary—that he had agreed to sell Le Rêve to Steve Cohen for $139 million, a price that would have made it the most expensive artwork ever sold at that time. While showing the painting to his friends, Wynn reportedly put his right elbow through the canvas, creating a six-inch tear in the left forearm of the figure. Ephron suggested this was due to Wynn's habit of using wild gestures and his retinitis pigmentosa, which affects peripheral vision. Wynn later stated that the incident convinced him not to sell the painting. After a $90,000 repair, the painting was re-valued at $85 million. Wynn filed a claim with his Lloyd's of London insurers for $54 million, which he claimed represented the perceived loss from the damage, an amount covering most of the original purchase price. When the insurers refused, Wynn sued them in January 2007, and the case was settled out of court in March 2007. Cohen purchased Le Rêve from Wynn in 2013 for $155 million (approximately $134 million in 2006 dollars), a price that, ignoring inflation, was the highest ever paid by a U.S. collector until Kenneth C. Griffin's ~$300 million purchase of Willem de Kooning's Interchange in September 2015.

The Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (Russian: Физи́ческий институ́т имени П. Н. Ле́бедева Российской академии наук) is a Russian research institute located in Moscow, specializing in physics. It was established in its current form in 1934 by academician Sergey Vavilov and moved to Moscow that same year, being named after the Russian physicist Pyotr Lebedev. It is also known as the P. N. Lebedev Institute of Physics or simply the Lebedev Institute. In Russian, it is commonly referred to by the acronym FIAN (ФИАН), standing for "Physical Institute of the Academy of Sciences". The institute's research activities cover a wide range of fields, including laser technology, dark matter structure, nanostructures, superconductivity, cosmic rays, and gamma-astronomy. It developed a technique for crystallizing cubic zirconia, known in Russia as Fianit, named after FIAN. The institute operates a particle accelerator, a 1.2 GeV electron synchrotron called "Pakhra", located in Troitsk near Moscow at the LPI's HEP department. However, the institute is not entirely or primarily focused on accelerator or particle physics, as its research scope encompasses most areas of modern physics. The Andreyev Acoustics Institute is a part of the Lebedev Physical Institute and is named after Nikolay Andreyev. In 2021, a documentary titled "Mishik Kazaryan: The Path of an Explorer" (original title «Мишик Казарян: путь Искателя») was released, directed by Leonid Ioffe, and narrates the life and work of Professor Mishik Kazaryan, an experimental physicist and laureate of the USSR State Prize who worked at the Lebedev Physical Institute. The film provides insight into the daily life of the institute from the mid-1960s. The institute's geographical coordinates are 55°41′52″N 37°33′55″E (55.69778°N 37.56528°E).

The Leelavati Award recognizes outstanding contributions to public outreach in mathematics. It is named after the 12th-century mathematical treatise "Lilavati," authored by the Indian mathematician Bhāskara II, also known as Bhaskara Achārya. This treatise, focused on arithmetic, algebra, and the decimal system, presents a series of arithmetic problems in verse form addressed to a person named Leelavati (possibly his daughter), followed by hints for solutions. The work served as the primary source of learning arithmetic and algebra in medieval India and was later translated into Persian, influencing mathematical education in West Asia. The Leelavati Prize was first awarded at the closing ceremony of the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) 2010 in Hyderabad, India. It was established by the Executive Organising Committee (EOC) of the ICM with the approval of the IMU Executive Committee (EC) as a one-time international award for exceptional public outreach in mathematics. Due to its positive reception at the conference and in the mathematical press, the IMU decided to make the prize a recurring award given every four years, with the ceremony becoming a regular part of each ICM closing event. The prize is not intended to recognize mathematical research but rather outreach efforts in the broadest sense. It includes a cash prize of 1,000,000 Indian Rupees (equivalent to 14,000 US dollars) along with a citation, and has been sponsored by Infosys since 2014.

Lemonade is the sixth studio album by American singer and songwriter Beyoncé, surprise-released on April 23, 2016, by Parkwood Entertainment and Columbia Records, as a visual album paired with a film of the same name. It is conceived as a concept album that explores the historical Black female experience in the United States, allegorized as a personal journey through marital betrayal and healing, and structured as a song cycle based on the Kübler-Ross model. Categorized by critics as an eclectic, genre-blending album with avant-garde and art pop elements, Lemonade incorporates a wide range of genres including R&B, rock, country, soul, blues, hip-hop, jazz, reggae, pop, gospel, and funk. The album features guest vocals from Jack White, the Weeknd, James Blake, and Kendrick Lamar. Upon release, it topped the charts and received platinum certifications in several countries across Europe, the Americas, and Asia–Pacific, becoming the world's best-selling album of the year. It was supported by five singles and promoted through a series of televized performances and the Formation World Tour—the first all-stadium tour by a female artist. Lemonade was hailed as an instant classic and has since been named one of the greatest albums of all time, receiving praise for its experimental post-genre production, nuanced vocal performance, and political subject matter reflecting Beyoncé's personal life. It was music critics' top album of 2016 according to the BBC, named the greatest album of the 2010s by the Associated Press, and topped Rolling Stone's Greatest Albums of the 21st Century list. One of the most Grammy-nominated albums in history, Lemonade won Best Urban Contemporary Album and Best Music Video at the 59th Grammy Awards and also won a Peabody Award in Entertainment at the 76th Annual Peabody Awards, receiving four nominations at the 68th Primetime Emmy Awards. The album is considered a cultural phenomenon, sparking widespread discourse on its personal revelations and socio-political commentary, influencing the entertainment industry, inspiring other musicians and visual artists, and igniting trends across music, fashion, and pop culture. It has also been the subject of extensive analysis in academic journals, college courses, books, and museum exhibitions. Beyoncé's career transformed with the release of her fifth studio album, Beyoncé (2013), which received widespread commercial and critical success and influenced how music is released in the digital age, elevating her from a leading pop star to an auteur who defied industry conventions. The following year, her personal life became a subject of public scrutiny after rumors of Jay-Z's infidelity spread, fueled by leaked elevator footage at the 2014 Met Gala showing Beyoncé's sister Solange physically attacking Jay-Z. The family released a joint statement to assuage concerns, and although divorce rumors continued during their joint On The Run Tour (2014), the couple presented a unified front. On February 6, 2016, Beyoncé released "Formation" as a free download via Tidal, accompanied by an unlisted music video on YouTube. The track, blending trap and bounce, celebrated her culture, identity, and success as a Black woman from the Southern United States. The song and video were met with widespread acclaim, with critics praising it as a personal and political ode to Black Southern heritage. Beyoncé performed the song a day after its release during the Super Bowl 50 halftime show, and a commercial aired afterward announcing the Formation World Tour, with pre-sales opening two days later. The performance received rave reviews from fans and critics but was met with backlash, boycotts, and protests from some conservative figures and law enforcement organizations over perceived anti-police, anti-American, and anti-white racist messages. In an interview with Elle published on April 4, 2016, Beyoncé stated her desire to create art that promotes healing and transformation, saying: "I hope I can create art that helps people heal. Art that makes people feel proud of their struggle. Everyone experiences pain, but sometimes you need to be uncomfortable to transform. Pain is not pretty, but I wasn't able to hold my daughter in my arms until I experienced the pain of childbirth!" Lemonade was recorded between June 2014 and July 2015 across 11 studios in the United States. Beyoncé conceived the idea of writing each song to correspond to a specific emotion forming the chapters of the album and film, and posted mood boards around the studio to guide her collaborators. She and her team played music in the studio to inspire each other. The album was written in stages, with Beyoncé retreating to her home to work with recording and mixing engineer Stuart White and to care for her daughter. The process began at the Record Plant in Los Angeles for a month, followed by a break and a 45-day stay in Paris, where the team stayed in a hotel and set up two studios in separate rooms—one for Beyoncé and one for Jay-Z. Jay-Z described recording as "using our art almost like a therapy session" after his infidelity, and the music Beyoncé recorded separately became Lemonade and was released first. The album was produced through Beyoncé's synthesis of many collaborators, including both popular and lesser-known artists. Beyoncé oversaw all aspects of the writing and production process; co-writers MNEK and Jonny Coffer noted she had a clear vision for how the songs should sound, consistently offering direction and suggestions. The songs were developed piecemeal, with Beyoncé combining material she wrote herself with elements from other writers. Collaborator MeLo-X described her production style as highly distinctive, saying: "She has a way of creating that I've never seen before as an artist. She produces, alters and arranges tracks in ways I wouldn't think of." As a multimedia audiovisual artwork, Lemonade relates the emotional journey of Beyoncé after Jay-Z's infidelity in a generational and racial context through its music, lyrics, visuals, and poetry. The album is a song cycle referencing the classical compositional genre defined by Robert Schumann, Franz Schubert, and Johannes Brahms, with the tracks (excluding "Formation") corresponding to the eleven chapters of the Lemonade film: "Intuition", "Denial", "Anger", "Apathy", "Emptiness", "Accountability", "Reformation", "Forgiveness", "Resurrection", "Hope", and "Redemption." Melina Matsoukas, director of the "Formation" music video, stated that Beyoncé explained the concept behind Lemonade, saying she wanted to show the historical impact of slavery on Black love and how Black families, men, and women are socially conditioned not to be together. In a 2018 Vogue article, Beyoncé wrote about "generational curses" in her family, including a slave owner who married a slave, and explained that only after seeing this clearly was she able to resolve conflicts in her own relationship. She wrote: "Connecting to the past and knowing our history makes us both bruised and beautiful." This theme is repeated throughout Lemonade, with Beyoncé's grief, trauma, and struggle connected to that of her ancestors. The sixth track, "Daddy Lessons," acts as a turning point, linking Jay-Z cheating on her with her father Mathew Knowles cheating on her mother Tina. Towards the end of Lemonade, Beyoncé reveals the meaning behind the title, showing Jay-Z's grandmother Hattie White saying: "I had my ups and downs, but I always find the inner strength to pull myself up. I was served lemons, but I made lemonade," and describing her own grandmother, Agnez Deréon, as an "alchemist" who "spun gold out of this hard life" with instructions passed down through generations like a lemonade recipe. Miriam Bale for Billboard called Lemonade "a revolutionary work of Black feminism" as "a movie made by a black woman, starring Black women, and for Black women," in which Beyoncé is seen gathering, uniting, and leading Black women throughout the film. The album also chronicles the relationship between Black women and American society, including how the United States betrayed and continually mistreats Black women, with society needing to solve its problems to enable reformation and rehabilitation. Lemonade centralizes the experiences of Black women in a way rarely seen in media, celebrating their achievements despite adversity. "Don't Hurt Yourself" contains a quote from Malcolm X: "The most disrespected person in America is the Black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the Black woman. The most neglected person in America is the Black woman." The film features Black female public figures with successful careers despite facing misogynoir and racism, and includes clips of everyday Black women from working-class communities, bringing visibility to those often ignored. The film envisions a space where there was never oppression of Black women, with Beyoncé and other Black women forming a self-sufficient community to heal together. Lemonade defies and dismantles stereotypical representations of Black women as monolithic and angry, instead attributing them complexity, agency, strength, and vulnerability. To create Lemonade, Beyoncé drew from the work of many Black women often overlooked or forgotten. The music draws inspiration from Black female blues musicians such as Shug Avery, Bessie Smith, and Sister Rosetta Tharpe, who used personal trauma to empower Black women, as well as samples songs originally recorded by Black women like Memphis Minnie and Dionne Warwick, whose most famous recordings were by male or white artists. These musical references situate Lemonade within the broader tradition of blues women who used their art to voice Black women's emotional experiences and social realities. The visuals draw inspiration from Black feminists such as Julie Dash's Daughters Of The Dust, Alice Walker's In Search Of Our Mothers' Gardens, and Toni Morrison's The Bluest Eye. Other influences include literary works by Black women focusing on African-American folklore (such as Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God) and Afrofuturism (such as Octavia Butler's Kindred). Beyoncé specifically moves away from her typical music roots to develop a more communal spotlight on artistic hoodoo with other Black female creatives. Beyoncé also uses Lemonade as a form of recognition, commemoration, and celebration of the culture and history of Black people in the Deep South and the United States as a whole. The film contains allusions to slavery, such as the House of Slaves' Door of No Return in Senegal and the dungeons of Elmina Castle in Ghana, where slaves were taken before being shipped to the Americas. In "Love Drought," Beyoncé walks with her dancers into the sea, alluding to the Igbo Landing of 1803, where Igbo slaves took control of their slave ship and marched into the sea while singing in Igbo, drowning themselves. Beyoncé appears wearing a tignon, referencing Louisiana's tignon laws implemented in 1786 that limited African-American women's dress to maintain racist social hierarchies. The film includes references to African religion and spirituality, such as Yoruba ori body paint in "Sorry," allusions to the loa Erzulie Red-Eyes in "Don't Hurt Yourself," and Beyoncé's initiation into the Santería religion and embodiment of the Yoruba orisha Oshun in "Hold Up." Allusions to New Orleans culture include "Queen of Creole cuisine" Leah Chase, the Edna Karr Marching Band, jazz funerals, Mardi Gras Indians, and the Superdome. In Lemonade, Beyoncé is seen with other Black women on plantations. In the "Formation" video, the walls of plantation houses are covered with French Renaissance-style portraits of Black subjects; director Melina Matsoukas stated that "films about slavery traditionally feature white people in these roles of power and position. I wanted to turn those images on their head." Towards the end of Lemonade, Beyoncé and several Black women are on a plantation, with Chris Kelly for Fact writing that "Instead of an antebellum memory, these scenes portray a dream: the fantasy of an all-Black, matriarchal utopia when women dress up, prepare meals, take photographs, and perform shows, not for a master but for themselves." Throughout the film, Beyoncé can be seen in Fort Macomb, a Confederate States Army stronghold taken over by the 1st Louisiana Native Guard, eventually destroyed by Hurricane Katrina. On "Daddy Lessons," Beyoncé is seen standing in a hideaway in the fort, alluding to the Underground Railroad. However, on the closer "All Night," Beyoncé is seen above ground, walking on top of the ruins of the fort in an antebellum-style dress made in West African material, possibly inspired by artist Yinka Shonibare, known for reappropriating "European import — the cloth — to remake symbols of European cultural dominance in the spirit of Africa." On "Don't Hurt Yourself," Beyoncé samples Led Zeppelin's "When the Levee Breaks," originally written by Black Delta blues artists Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie, referring to the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 that displaced hundreds of thousands of African Americans. With this sample, Beyoncé reappropriates a song written by Black people about Black history. In general, she reappropriates genres influenced by African Americans that are now seen as predominantly white, such as rock in "Don't Hurt Yourself" and country in "Daddy Lessons." Lemonade is an eclectic, genre-blending album that explores many musical styles. Vox's Alissa Wilkinson described it as an R&B-rock-country-soul album, with other genres including blues, hip-hop, jazz, reggae, pop, gospel, and funk. The Nation's Erin Vanderhoof characterized it as avant-garde, while Pitchfork's Marc Hogan called it an art pop album. Kariann Goldschmitt, music lecturer at the University of Cambridge, described the album's experimentation with musical styles as a "recuperative historiography" of African-American contributions to diverse genres of music. The album features musicians Jack White, Kendrick Lamar, and bassist Marcus Miller, and samples folk music collected by John Lomax, Sr. and his son Alan Lomax on "Freedom." Beyoncé and her team reference the musical memories of all those periods, including a brass band, stomping blues rock, ultraslow avant-R&B, preaching, a prison song (both collected by John and Alan Lomax), and the sound of 1960s fuzz-tone guitar psychedelia (sampling the Puerto Rican band Kaleidoscope). The Washington Post called the album a "surprisingly furious song cycle about infidelity and revenge." The Chicago Tribune described it as not just a mere grab for popular music dominance, but a retrospective allowing the listener to explore Beyoncé's personal circumstances, with musical tones from the southern United States, harking back to her formative years in Texas. AllMusic wrote that Beyoncé "delights in her Blackness, femininity, and Southern origin with supreme wordplay." On the album, Isaac Hayes and Andy Williams are among the sampled artists. PopMatters noticed the album's nuanced theme of anger and betrayal with vast swathes of political context, though it remains a pop album at its essence with darker and praiseworthy tones. There are two suggested inspirations for the title. The song "Freedom" ends with an audio recording of Hattie White, grandmother of Beyoncé's husband Jay-Z, telling a crowd at her ninetieth birthday party in December 2015: "I had my ups and downs, but I always find the inner strength to pull myself up. I was served lemons, but I made lemonade."

Lemonade is a surprisingly furious song cycle about infidelity and revenge, described by the Chicago Tribune as more than a mere attempt to dominate popular music, instead serving as a retrospective that allows listeners to explore Beyoncé's personal circumstances, with musical tones reflecting her formative years in Texas. AllMusic praised Beyoncé for "delighting in her Blackness, femininity, and Southern origin with supreme wordplay," and noted that the album samples artists such as Isaac Hayes and Andy Williams. PopMatters highlighted the album's nuanced exploration of anger and betrayal, embedded with political context, while acknowledging its fundamental pop essence and darker, praiseworthy tones. The title is linked to two inspirations: the song "Freedom" ends with an audio clip of Hattie White, grandmother of Jay-Z, at her 90th birthday party in December 2015, reciting, "I was served lemons, but I made lemonade," a reference to the proverb encouraging turning difficulty into something positive; Beyoncé also draws on her own grandmother Agnez Deréon’s lemonade recipe as a metaphor for intergenerational healing. The album’s cover, taken from the "Don't Hurt Yourself" music video, features Beyoncé in cornrows and a fur coat, leaning against a Chevrolet Suburban and covering her face with her arm, noted for its stark, minimalist style that reflects the album’s raw emotional themes. In 2023, Joe Lynch of Billboard ranked it the 99th best album cover of all time. Lemonade was first released for online streaming via Tidal on April 23, 2016, through Parkwood Entertainment and Columbia Records, with a digital download the following day, and was released on CD and DVD on May 6, 2016. A limited edition box set titled How to Make Lemonade was available for pre-order on August 18, 2017, including a six-hundred-page coffee table book with behind-the-scenes content and a double vinyl LP; standalone vinyl followed on September 15, 2017. Initially exclusive to Tidal, the album was added to other streaming platforms on April 23, 2019, exactly three years after release, with the version including the original audio and the original demo of "Sorry" as a bonus. Beyoncé aimed to perform the entire Lemonade album live; she performed "Formation" at the Super Bowl 50 halftime show, which critics lauded and which sparked discussions on political symbolism. At the 2016 BET Awards on June 27, she performed "Freedom" with Kendrick Lamar, beginning with a clip of Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech, and the performance was critically acclaimed. At the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards on August 28, she performed a sixteen-minute medley of "Pray You Catch Me," "Hold Up," "Sorry," "Don't Hurt Yourself," and "Formation," including interludes from the Lemonade film, with critics noting political symbolism such as dancers falling as though shot, alluding to police brutality, and a black man in a black hoodie lifting her, referencing Trayvon Martin. On October 19, she performed "6 Inch" and "All Night" at a TIDAL X benefit concert in Brooklyn; on November 2, she performed "Daddy Lessons" with the Dixie Chicks at the 50th Annual CMA Awards, a performance praised by critics but criticized by conservative country fans, sparking debates about country music and Black presence in it, leading to a remix of "Daddy Lessons" featuring the Dixie Chicks. At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards on February 12, 2017, she performed "Love Drought" and "Sandcastles," a performance themed around motherhood that evoked female deities and Renaissance European Christian art, as well as non-European elements like Fulani facepainting, Ethiopian icons, Byzantine jewelry, and Latin American Baroque painting. To promote Lemonade, Beyoncé launched the Formation World Tour from April to October 2016, featuring Es Devlin’s 'Monolith' stage, a revolving seven-storey box with video walls, fire, and fireworks, which critics hailed as a "visual feast" and "emotional tour de force," winning Tour of the Year at the 2016 American Music Awards, being included in Rolling Stone’s 50 Greatest Concerts of the Last 50 Years, and named the best tour of the decade by Consequence of Sound in 2019. The tour ranked number one and number two on Pollstar’s 2016 mid-year Top 100 Tours chart in North America and worldwide, with a mid-year gross of $137.3 million from 25 shows, and a total gross of $256 million from 49 sold-out shows, ranking number two on the 2016 Year-End Tours chart. The album was accompanied by a sixty-five-minute film of the same title, produced by Good Company and Jonathan Lia, which premiered on HBO on April 23, 2016, logging 787,000 viewers and divided into eleven chapters: "Intuition," "Denial," "Anger," "Apathy," "Emptiness," "Accountability," "Reformation," "Forgiveness," "Resurrection," "Hope," and "Redemption." The film features poetry and prose by Warsan Shire, including "The Unbearable Weight of Staying," "Dear Moon," "How to Wear Your Mother's Lipstick," "Nail Technician as Palm Reader," and "For Women Who Are Difficult to Love." The cast includes Ibeyi, Laolu Senbanjo, Amandla Stenberg, Quvenzhané Wallis, Chloe x Halle, Zendaya, and Serena Williams; in "Forward," the mothers of Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, and Eric Garner are shown holding pictures of their sons. Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s daughter Blue Ivy, as well as Jay-Z’s grandmother Hattie White and Beyoncé’s mother Tina Knowles with her husband Richard Lawson on their wedding day in 2015, appear. The film samples Malcolm X’s speech "Who Taught You to Hate Yourself," featured on "Don't Hurt Yourself." The film appeared on several critics’ lists: Pitchfork ranked it number one on their best music videos of 2016; Sight & Sound placed it at number twenty-six on their best films of 2016; David Ehrlich placed it at number twenty-three on his Best Films of 2016 list; Jen Yamato ranked it number nine on her Top 10 Best Films of 2016 list. In June 2016, Matthew Fulks sued Beyoncé, Sony Music, Columbia Records, and Parkwood Entertainment for allegedly copying visual elements from his film Palinoia for the Lemonade trailer, but the lawsuit was dismissed by New York federal judge Jed S. Rakoff. Lemonade included five singles, three of which became major hits; all twelve songs charted on the US Billboard Hot 100. "Formation" was released as the first single exclusively on Tidal on February 6, 2016, with its music video, and was performed at the Super Bowl 50 halftime show; it peaked at number ten on the Hot 100, with its video uploaded to Vevo in December 2016. "Sorry" was released as the second single on May 3, 2016, to rhythmic adult contemporary radio, peaking at number eleven; its video was uploaded on June 22, 2016. "Hold Up" was released to German and UK contemporary hit radio on May 12, 2016, and to US radio on August 16, 2016, peaking at number thirteen; its video was uploaded on September 4, 2016. "Freedom" and "All Night" were released as the fourth and fifth singles, peaking at number thirty-five and thirty-eight respectively. The album received widespread acclaim, with many calling it an instant classic, masterpiece, and Beyoncé's magnum opus; at Metacritic, it received a weighted average score of 92 based on 33 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim." Greg Tate of Spin called it a "triumph of marketing and musicality, spectacle and song, vision and collaboration," praising its deep engagement with Southern Black feminist culture and its emotional and sonic power. Alexis Petridis of The Guardian said the album "feels like a success" and that Beyoncé sounded "genuinely imperious," noting the music’s progression from "Pray You Catch Me" to a "righteous frenzy" on "Don't Hurt Yourself." Jonathan Bernstein of The Daily Telegraph called it her strongest work to date and noted the thin line between love and hate. Nekesa Moody and Mohamad Soliman of The Washington Post described it as "deeply personal, yet a bold social and political statement." Jon Pareles of The New York Times praised Beyoncé’s vocals and her courage in addressing widespread issues, noting the album’s independence from radio formats. Greg Kot of the Chicago Tribune felt the artistic advances were "slight" in contrast to its personal, raw, and relatable aspects, calling it a "clearly conceived" piece with a unifying vision. Everett True of The Independent called it "fiery, insurgent, fiercely proud, sprawling and sharply focused," with Beyoncé picking up the mantles of Prince and Nina Simone. Kitty Empire of The Observer praised the celebration of female endurance and pragmatism with warmth, anger, and wit, calling it a rare unification of high art and low. Jillian Mapes of Pitchfork stated that the signature cadence, patois, and attitude on Lemonade reflect Beyoncé's status as a hip-hop pop star, yet she also demonstrates a new kind of post-genre pop star. Annie Zaleski of The A.V. Club called it a "seismic step forward" for Beyoncé as a musician, pushing pop music into "smarter, deeper places." Shahzaib Hussain of Clash described Lemonade as Beyoncé at her most benevolent and unadulterated, celebrating Blackness as a "celebratory beacon" and calling it a "long overdue, cathartic retribution." Sal Cinquemani of Slant Magazine called it her "most lyrically and thematically coherent effort to date." Maura Johnston of Time noted the tracks were "fresh yet instantly familiar" with an "over-the-top but intimate" sound. Jamie Milton of DIY said there is "so much more than an enthralling story" in the album, praising Beyoncé as a "risk-taker breaking new ground, up there with the bravest." Exclaim!'s Erin Lowers wrote, "If you've ever been handed lemons, you need Lemonade," calling it "an album in which millions will find their own struggles reflected back to them, as therapeutic as it is utterly dazzling." Britt Julious of Consequence of Sound described how Lemonade, the visual album, weaves emotional grief into art about the Black woman, drawing on Voudou and Southern Black gothic storytelling, and praised its song cycle structure as representing the grief process with "two dichotomous halves," noting it dismantles cycles of abuse and finds healing, purpose, and greatness. Evan Sawdey of PopMatters felt few albums could be considered "as bold, complex, or resolute as Lemonade," and the BBC's Mark Savage described it as having a "complex narrative arc" that "demands to be heard in one sitting," noting Beyoncé had become an albums artist beyond radio play. At the end of 2016, Lemonade was named the critics' top album of the year by the BBC and ranked number one by the most publications (37) on Metacritic, including Rolling Stone, Billboard, Entertainment Weekly, The Guardian, Digital Spy, The Independent, The Associated Press, The New York Times (Jon Pareles list), Los Angeles Times (Mikael Wood list), Pop Matters, Pretty Much Amazing, Idolator, Stereogum, Complex, Consequence of Sound, Wired, and US Weekly. It was named the best album of the 2010s by Consequence of Sound, The Associated Press, and Spex, and the best music video of the decade by The Daily Beast, as well as one of the best movies of the 2010s by Vox. It was included in the top-five albums of the decade by Rolling Stone, The Independent, New York Post, Billboard, Paste, The A.V. Club, WXPN The Key, Refinery29, Tampa Bay Times, Insider, The Young Folks, Genius, Variety, Uproxx, Noisey, The Independent, and The Wild Honey Pie. In January 2025, Rolling Stone named Lemonade the greatest album of the 21st century. Consequence of Sound named it the second best album of the last 15 years (2007–2022). BBC Radio 4 named it the eighth greatest risk in 21st century art, stating Beyoncé "resisted commercial pressure not to be political" and "let audiences into her personal life as never before." The Guardian listed it at number 25 on their 100 best albums of the 21st century. In 2020, Parade named Lemonade the best music video of all time. In 2017, it was ranked number 6 on NPR's list of the 150 Greatest Albums Made By Women. The Daily Telegraph named it the eighth greatest album of all time in 2025, describing it as a "bold, shapeshifting masterpiece channelling personal turmoil into visionary genre-hopping pop." The Quietus placed it at number 9 on their top 100 albums list. Apple Music ranked it number 10 on their list of the 100 Best Albums ever created. Consequence of Sound named it the 18th greatest album of all time in 2022. It is the 29th best album of all time by Metacritic score. On Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time list, it was placed at number 32, citing its exploration of "the betrayals of American blackness" and "all of the country's music traditions." Paste listed it at number 55 on their list of the 300 Greatest Albums of All Time. Lemonade was nominated for four Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Variety Special and Outstanding Directing for a Variety Special. It received eleven nominations at the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards, including Breakthrough Long Form Video for Lemonade, Video of the Year, Best Pop Video, Best Direction, Best Editing, and Best Cinematography for "Formation," Best Female Video and Best Art Direction for "Hold Up," and Best Choreography for "Sorry" and "Formation," winning eight, including Video of the Year and Breakthrough Long Form Video. At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards, it received three nominations: Album of the Year, Best Urban Contemporary Album, and Best Music Film; "Formation" received three: Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Music Video; "Hold Up" was nominated for Best Pop Solo Performance; "Don't Hurt Yourself" for Best Rock Performance; and "Freedom" for Best Rap/Sung Performance. Beyoncé won two awards: Best Urban Contemporary Album and Best Music Video for "Formation." Lemonade won a Peabody Award in Entertainment, with the board of jurors stating it "adroitly brings together stories about betrayal, renewal, and hope," drawing from Black cultural producers to create a "rich tapestry of poetic innovation," immersing viewers in the "sublime worlds of black women, family, and community," and challenging cultural ideas about women of color. In the United States, Lemonade debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with 653,000 album-equivalent units, 485,000 of which were pure album sales, making it the highest opening-week sales for a female act that year and the first artist in chart history to have their first six studio albums debut at number one. In the same week, Beyoncé became the first female artist to chart twelve or more songs on the US Billboard Hot 100 simultaneously. The album slipped to number two in its second week, selling 321,000 album-equivalent units (196,000 pure sales), and remained at number two in its third week with 201,000 album-equivalent units (153,000 pure sales). It was certified platinum by the RIAA in June 2016 and sold 1,554,000 copies and 2,187,000 album-equivalent units in the United States according to Nielsen's 2016 year-end report. After its April 23, 2019, release on streaming, it returned to the top ten on the Billboard 200 at number nine, with the original demo of "Sorry" debuting at number nineteen on the US R&B Songs. On May 20, 2019, it was certified double platinum (2 million copies) and triple platinum (3 million copies) on June 13, 2019. In Canada, it debuted at number one with 33,000 copies and had sold 138,000 album-equivalent units by the end of 2016, 101,000 of which were pure album sales. In the UK, it debuted at number one with 73,000 copies, with 10,000 equivalent sales (14% of total) from streaming—marking the largest ever for a number-one album since streaming was included—and was certified platinum by the BPI for 300,000 copies on September 9, 2016. All of its tracks debuted in the top hundred of the UK Singles Chart. In Australia, it sold 20,490 digital copies in its first week, debuted at number one, and received a double platinum certification from ARIA in 2023 for 140,000 equivalent units. It peaked at number one in Ireland, Belgium, Croatia, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Scotland, and Sweden, and debuted at number one in Brazil, receiving a platinum certification from Pro-Música Brasil. Lemonade is credited with reviving the album concept in an era dominated by singles and streaming and popularizing the release of albums with accompanying films. Jamieson Cox of The Verge called it "the endpoint of a slow shift toward cohesive, self-centered pop albums," stating it "sets a new standard for pop storytelling at the highest possible scale." Megan Carpentier of The Guardian wrote it "almost revived the album format" as an "immersive, densely textured large-scale work" that must be listened to in full. Myf Warhurst on Double J's "Lunch With Myf" explained that Beyoncé "changed [the album] to a narrative with an arc and a story and you have to listen to the entire thing to get the concept." Katherine Schulten of The New York Times asked, "How do you talk about the ongoing evolution of the music video and the autobiographical album without holding up Lemonade as an exemplar of both forms?" Joe Coscarelli noted that some brand-name acts, including Frank Ocean's Endless and Drake's Please Forgive Me, followed Beyoncé's blueprint with high-concept mini-movies. Other projects inspired by Lemonade include Lonely Island's The Unauthorized Bash Brothers Experience, Thom Yorke's Anima, Sturgill Simpson's Sound & Fury, and Kid Cudi's Entergalactic. Beyoncé's use of various genres on Lemonade is credited with setting the precedent for music to transcend genre, with NPR writing that the album "leads us to this moment where post-genre becomes a thing." The use of genres has also been credited with kickstarting the reclamation of certain genres by Black people. "Daddy Lessons" started a trend of "pop stars toying with American West and Southern aesthetics" and set the precedent for "The Yeehaw Agenda," the trend of reclaiming Black cowboy culture. "Don't Hurt Yourself" is credited with the reclaiming of rock by Black women, with Brittany Spanos of Rolling Stone writing that Beyoncé and her peers are giving rock a "second life – and may be what can save it." Several musicians were inspired by Lemonade: Snoop Dogg named his 2016 album Coolaid after it; Sabrina Carpenter said it inspired her to not limit herself, noting it "really transcended every genre"; Cardi B said her 2025 album Am I the Drama? is "going to have my Lemonade moments"; Fergie was inspired to create a visual counterpart for her 2017 album Double Dutchess; Little Mix cited it as inspiration for their 2016 album Glory Days; Ellie Rowsell of Wolf Alice named it one of her favorite albums and said it helped her "put in more thought to what makes a good album flow"; The-Dream wrote a response titled "Lemon Lean" in his 2018 EP Love You to Death; Victoria Monét cited it as inspiration; Lahna Turner released a visual album entitled Limeade; Matt Palmer created his visual EP Get Lost; Todrick Hall made his 2018 album Straight Outta Oz as a visual album due to Lemonade; and Arrow Benjamin said his 2016 EP W.A.R. (We All Rise) was inspired by Lemonade, as every piece was created from a visual perspective. Ann Powers of NPR said Fiona Apple was influenced by Lemonade when implementing Black musical traditions on her 2020 album Fetch the Bolt Cutters; Jenna Wortham of The New York Times drew a parallel between the two albums as "blueprints for how to take in all that emotion and kind of how to push it back out in a way that's cathartic and constructive"; Dan Weiss of Billboard wrote that Shania Twain's Now "couldn't have existed without" Lemonade, calling it an album that "completely changed the course of breakup album history"; Kadeen Griffiths from Bustle stated Lemonade "paved the way" for Alicia Keys' Here and Solange's A Seat at the Table; and Danielle Koku for The Guardian stated that Lemonade aided the return of African mysticism to music.

Lemonade has had a profound and wide-reaching impact across music, fashion, media, academia, and pop culture. Critics have noted that Fiona Apple was influenced by Lemonade when incorporating black musical traditions into her 2020 album Fetch the Bolt Cutters, while Jenna Wortham described both albums as "blueprints for how to take in all that emotion and kind of how to push it back out in a way that's cathartic and constructive." Dan Weiss of Billboard stated that Shania Twain's Now "couldn't have existed without" Lemonade, calling it an album that "completely changed the course of breakup album history" and highlighted as an example of an artist at their full creative peak. Kadeen Griffiths from Bustle noted that Lemonade "paved the way" for Alicia Keys' Here and Solange's A Seat at the Table, while Danielle Koku for The Guardian said Lemonade aided the return of African mysticism to pop music by "stripping it of its ancient pagan labels." Jay-Z's 2017 album 4:44 is seen as a response to Lemonade, with Jay-Z referencing the line "You better call Becky with the good hair" from Beyoncé's "Sorry" and retorting "Let me alone, Becky" in "Family Feud." At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards in 2017, Adele dedicated her Album of the Year award to Beyoncé, calling her "the artist of my life" and stating that Lemonade was "so monumental," and later claimed in a 2021 Vogue interview that Beyoncé should have won the award instead, saying she went into Beyoncé's dressing room to explain that the Grammys' leadership "don't know what a visual album is" and that the award she received was broken, with her wedging a lemon into it—emphasizing that for women of color, Lemonade was a major acknowledgment of their undermined grief. Stevie Wonder called Lemonade "a great work, a great art piece," and Bono included "Freedom" in his "60 Songs That Saved My Life" project, calling it "a platter I had rarely seen." The album inspired artists in film, television, literature, art, and theatre: Misha Green, creator of Lovecraft Country, said Lemonade influenced the show's score by using poetry as a "score"; Bill Condon, director of Beauty and the Beast, cited the visuals as inspiration for the film. The Royal National Theatre's 2018 production of Antony and Cleopatra featured a costume inspired by Lemonade, with designer Evie Gurney drawing a parallel between Cleopatra and Beyoncé as a woman who reclaimed her narrative. The character of Catherine of Aragon in the musical Six was inspired by "Lemonade-era Beyoncé," and Ellie Kendrick's 2018 play Hole at the Royal Court was described as a "stage version of Beyoncé's Lemonade album" focusing on feminism and historical oppression. Fashion stylist Salvador Camarena designed a room dedicated to Lemonade during Modernism Week, citing its "visually stunning" nature and iconic looks. The young adult anthology A Phoenix First Must Burn, edited by Patrice Caldwell, aims to "evocate Beyoncé's Lemonade for a teen audience," and a 2017 video game titled "Lemonade Rage" was created in homage to Lemonade and the "Hold Up" music video. The cover of Marvel's 2017 America comic book paid homage to the "Formation" music video, with the illustrator stating it was a "parallel" to Beyoncé's work on representation, feminism, and fighting for what's right. Marie Claire named the lemonade drop as one of the most influential pop culture moments of the 2010s. Sales for Warsan Shire's chapbook "Teaching My Mother How to Give Birth" increased by 700 to 800% after being included in the Lemonade film. Beyoncé's mention of Red Lobster in "Formation" increased sales by 33%, leading employees to rename menu items and call it the "Beyoncé Bounce." Designers of costumes from Lemonade, such as Natalia Fedner, who designed Beyoncé's dress for "Hold Up," reported career boosts, including being named a "designer to watch" on Entertainment Tonight. The inclusion of imagery from the 1991 film Daughters of the Dust in Lemonade helped bring the film back to theatres, with director Julie Dash stating it "re-confirmed a lot of things that I know to be true about visual style and visual metaphors" and redefined Creole culture. The popular "Lemonade braids" hairstyle is named after a hairstyle Beyoncé wore in Lemonade. Georgia Murray for Refinery29 credited Beyoncé's yellow dress in "Hold Up" with "kickstarting an obsession with yellow" still seen today. The use of the lemon and bee emojis gained meaning after Lemonade's release, with a Twitter spokesperson stating the lemon emoji "took on a meaning of its own." The MTV Video Music Award for Breakthrough Long Form Video, which Beyoncé won at the 2016 MTV VMAs, was reintroduced after 25 years due to Lemonade. Lemonade was parodied and paid homage to in various media: in an episode of Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt titled "Kimmy's Roommate Lemonades!", character Titus Andromedon parodied "Hold Up," "Sorry," and "All Night," coining the term "Lemonading," which was nominated for two Emmys. The "Hold Up" music video was also parodied in The Simpsons, Making a Scene with James Franco, The Ellen DeGeneres Show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, and The Daily Show. SNL produced two sketches: "The Day Beyoncé Turned Black" after the release of "Formation," and "Melanianade," parodying the "Sorry" video with impersonations of Donald Trump's female aides. In a Late Night with Seth Meyers sketch, female staffers paid homage to the visuals, costumes, songs, and poetry. The Late Late Show with James Corden produced a parody titled "Lemonjames: A Visual Monologue," recreating parts of the Lemonade film. Goldie Hawn and Amy Schumer produced a parody of "Formation." The Season 2 premiere of Crazy Ex-Girlfriend featured a musical number that paid homage to Lemonade, including parodies of "Formation" and "Pray You Catch Me." For Beyoncé's 36th birthday, public figures like Michelle Obama and Serena Williams recreated the costume from the "Formation" video. The first episode of James Acaster's 2020 podcast Perfect Sounds focused on "the genius of Lemonade." Scholars and authors outside the music industry have also engaged with Lemonade: a talk at Seminole State College discussed how Beyoncé embodies the conjure woman as a contemporary revision of Zora Neale Hurston's work. The Museum of Design Atlanta launched "The Lemonade Project," a twelve-month series exploring race, gender, and class. Kinitra Brooks and Kameelah Martin produced "The Lemonade Reader," an educational tool analyzing the album's Afrodiasporic influences, visual aesthetics, narrative of grief and healing, and ethnomusicological reach. University of Texas at Austin professor Omise'eke Tinsley wrote Beyoncé in Formation: Remixing Black Feminism (2018), analyzing the album in relation to Black women's sexuality and gender. University of Albany professor Janell Hobson created a lesson plan based on Lemonade, stating it stimulates discussions on Blackness, womanhood, and feminism. Dissect Podcast dedicated its sixth season to Lemonade, with hosts Cole Cuchna and Titi Shodiya offering interpretative analysis combining music theory, lyricism, and social analysis. In a 2020 New York Times article, actress Kerry Washington called Lemonade a "game changer" visually, musically, and sociopolitically. The release of "Formation" and Beyoncé's Super Bowl 50 halftime performance sparked conversation and controversy due to its "unapologetic Blackness," with articles from the BBC and TheWrap analyzing its significance. Many think pieces, particularly by Black women, have analyzed Lemonade's messages, such as Miriam Bale for Billboard who named it "a revolutionary work of black feminism." Megan Carpentier of The Guardian called it a "pop culture phenomenon," stating no other living musical artist could ignite such broad conversations with a new album. Syreeta McFadden noted that "Formation" depicts archetypal southern Black women in ways rarely seen in popular culture. Melissa Harris-Perry of Time said Beyoncé "publicly embraced explicitly feminist Blackness at a politically risky moment," and Candace McDuffie of Glamour said Lemonade made Beyoncé the cultural zeitgeist, reinforcing that her actions cause global pandemonium. Since its release, Lemonade has spawned a large body of academic literature and studies. The University of Texas at San Antonio offered a course in Fall 2016 titled "Black Women, Beyoncé and Popular Culture," which explored the album as a meditation on contemporary Black womanhood and delved into theoretical, historical, and literary frameworks of Black feminism. The University of Tennessee at Chattanooga hosted a "Lemonade Week" in April 2017 featuring discussions on feminism, theatrical performances, African-American women writers and poets, and choreography tutorials. Harvard University hosted "The Lemon Drop," a discussion exploring the nuances of Lemonade. The University of Arkansas offered a course analyzing Black feminism's influence on Beyoncé and Lemonade. The University of Pennsylvania ran two courses exploring politics, race, and gender through Lemonade. Michigan State University hosted a discussion on Lemonade as part of a series on underrepresented and marginalized communities. Chatham University based a writing class on Lemonade, where students examine their place in power systems. Valdosta State University offered a course unpacking themes in Lemonade, including Black identity, feminism, marital infidelity, sisterhood, and faith. The College of Charleston hosted a discussion by Black feminist scholars on Beyoncé's use of southern landscape, Black women, music, and African-based spirituality. The University of North Georgia offered a class titled "Okay, Ladies, Now Let's Get in Formation: Intersectional Feminism in Beyoncé's Lemonade," exploring the music, lyrics, and visuals. Credits from the album's liner notes, Beyoncé's official website, and Spotify are also referenced. Sales figures are based on certification alone, as are shipments and sales+streaming figures.

Leo Strauss (September 20, 1899 – October 18, 1973) was a German-American political philosopher and historian of philosophy whose work profoundly influenced twentieth-century political theory in the United States and the study of classical political thought. He is best known for his interpretations of ancient and medieval philosophy, his account of classical natural right, and his claim that philosophers often wrote esoterically, presenting different teachings to general and specialist audiences. Strauss argued that the modern turn in philosophy, beginning with Niccolò Machiavelli and culminating in historicism and relativism, marked a decisive break with classical understandings of politics and the good life. His work aimed to recover the questions and methods of ancient political philosophy as a corrective to the perceived crisis of modern thought. His scholarship encompassed studies of Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon, Thomas Hobbes, Baruch Spinoza, Friedrich Nietzsche, and the medieval Islamic and Jewish philosophical traditions, particularly Al-Farabi and Maimonides. Central to his writings were the tensions between reason and revelation, the nature of political prudence, and the relationship between philosophy and political authority. His methodological emphasis on close textual reading, the pedagogical value of classical texts, and the critique of modernity formed the basis of what became known as "Straussian" approaches to political theory. Born in Kirchhain, Hesse-Nassau (a province of the Kingdom of Prussia in the German Empire), to Jennie Strauss (née David) and Hugo Strauss, Strauss was raised as an Orthodox Jew, though his family did not fully embrace Orthodox practice. His father and uncle ran a farm supply and livestock business inherited from Meyer (1835–1919), a leading member of the local Jewish community. After attending the Kirchhain Volksschule and the Protestant Rektoratsschule, he studied at the Gymnasium Philippinum in Marburg, graduating in 1917. He served in the German army during World War I from July 5, 1917, to December 1918. He earned his doctorate in 1921 from the University of Hamburg with a thesis on F. H. Jacobi, supervised by Ernst Cassirer, and attended courses at the Universities of Freiburg and Marburg, including those taught by Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger. He joined a Jewish fraternity and worked for the German Zionist movement, meeting intellectuals such as Norbert Elias, Leo Löwenthal, Hannah Arendt, and Walter Benjamin, who remained an admirer of his work throughout his life. His closest friend was Jacob Klein, and he engaged intellectually with Gerhard Krüger, Karl Löwith, Julius Guttmann, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Franz Rosenzweig (to whom he dedicated his first book), Gershom Scholem, Alexander Altmann, and Paul Kraus, who married Strauss's sister Bettina; Strauss and his wife later adopted Paul and Bettina Kraus's child after both parents died in the Middle East. He maintained vigorous epistolary exchanges with several of these friends, many of which are published in the Gesammelte Schriften (Collected Writings), some in translation. He also had a discourse with Carl Schmitt, which he discontinued after Schmitt failed to respond to his letters. In 1932, after receiving a Rockefeller Fellowship, Strauss left his position at the Higher Institute for Jewish Studies in Berlin for Paris, where he married Marie (Miriam) Bernsohn, a widow with a young child, whom he had known in Germany. He adopted her son, Thomas, and later his sister's child, Jenny Strauss Clay (who later became a professor of classics at the University of Virginia); he and Miriam had no biological children. At his death, he was survived by Thomas, Jenny Strauss Clay, and three grandchildren. He became a lifelong friend of Alexandre Kojève and was on friendly terms with Raymond Aron and Étienne Gilson. Due to the Nazis' rise to power, he chose not to return to Germany. He found shelter in England, where in 1935 he secured temporary employment at the University of Cambridge with the help of his in-law David Daube. While in England, he became close to R. H. Tawney and had less favorable relations with Isaiah Berlin. Unable to secure permanent employment, he moved to the United States in 1937 under the patronage of Harold Laski, who helped him obtain a brief lectureship. After a short stint as a research fellow at Columbia University, he joined The New School, where he worked in the political science faculty from 1938 to 1948 and took on adjunct roles. In 1939, he served as a visiting professor at Hamilton College. He became a U.S. citizen in 1944 and in 1949 was appointed professor of political science at the University of Chicago, holding the Robert Maynard Hutchins Distinguished Service Professorship until 1969. In 1953, he coined the phrase reductio ad Hitlerum, a play on reductio ad absurdum, suggesting that comparing an argument to one of Hitler's is a fallacy of irrelevance. In 1954, he met Karl Löwith and Hans-Georg Gadamer in Heidelberg and delivered a public speech on Socrates. In 1965, he was offered a temporary lectureship in Hamburg, which he declined due to health reasons, and received an honorary doctorate from the University of Hamburg and the German Order of Merit through the German representative in Chicago. In 1969, he moved to Claremont McKenna College in California for a year and then to St. John's College, Annapolis in 1970, where he was the Scott Buchanan Distinguished Scholar in Residence until his death from pneumonia in 1973. He was buried in the Annapolis Hebrew Cemetery with his wife Miriam Bernsohn Strauss, who died in 1985, and Psalm 114 was read at the funeral service at the request of family and friends. Strauss's thought is characterized by two main themes: the critique of modernity and the recovery of classical political philosophy. He argued that modernity, emerging in 15th-century Italian city states especially through Machiavelli, represented a radical break from Western tradition, leading to nihilism, relativism, historicism, and scientism. He claimed that modern political and social sciences, based on empirical observation and rational analysis, failed to address fundamental questions of human nature, morality, and justice, reducing humans to objects of manipulation. He criticized modern liberalism for lacking moral and spiritual foundations and for undermining religion, tradition, and natural law. To counter modernity's crisis, Strauss advocated a return to classical political philosophy, arguing that ancient and medieval thinkers had a deeper understanding of human nature and society. He promoted careful, respectful reading of classical texts, asserting that their authors wrote esoterically—using layered meanings, irony, paradox, or self-contradiction—to protect themselves and the regime from persecution, to attract the right readers, and to engage in a dialogue across time, which he called "the great conversation." This esoteric writing, he argued, was not about hiding a secret message for a select few versus a public one, but about conveying a deeper, irreducible message at the tacit heart of the text. Influenced by his Jewish background and engagement with Islamic and Jewish medieval philosophy, especially Al-Farabi and Maimonides, Strauss saw these thinkers as models for reconciling reason and revelation, philosophy and theology, Athens and Jerusalem.
