For Strauss, politics and philosophy were necessarily intertwined; he viewed Socrates' trial as the moment political philosophy began, emphasizing that Socrates argued philosophers must consider human nature—defined by Aristotle as that of a "political animal"—before studying nature. However, he also held that the ends of politics and philosophy were irreconcilable and irreducible. Strauss distinguished "scholars" from "great thinkers," identifying himself as a scholar, noting that most self-described philosophers are actually cautious scholars who reason about the differences between great thinkers, while great thinkers boldly confront major problems. In Natural Right and History (1953), he critiqued Max Weber's epistemology, engaged with the relativism of Martin Heidegger (unnamed), analyzed the evolution of natural rights through Hobbes and Locke, and critiqued Rousseau and Burke, with excerpts from Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero at the heart of the work. Much of his philosophy was a reaction to Heidegger, whom he believed must be understood and confronted before modern political theory could be fully formulated, requiring engagement with ontology and the history of metaphysics. Strauss wrote that Nietzsche was the first philosopher to properly understand historicism, rooted in Hegelian philosophy of history; Heidegger, in Strauss's view, sanitized and politicized Nietzsche, while Nietzsche believed that all principles—including belief in progress—would eventually be shown to be false, and that the only way forward was to "voluntarily choose life-giving delusion instead of deadly truth, that one fabricate a myth." Heidegger believed Nietzsche's nihilism was a "myth" stemming from a defective Western conception of Being traced to Plato. In correspondence with Kojève, Strauss stated that Hegel was correct in asserting that an end of history implies an end to classical political philosophy. In the late 1930s, Strauss first called for a reconsideration of the distinction between exoteric (public) and esoteric (secret) teaching. In 1952, he published Persecution and the Art of Writing, arguing that serious writers use esoteric methods to protect themselves and the regime, attract the right readers, and repel the wrong ones, with the act of uncovering the interior message itself being a form of philosophical reasoning. Drawing on Maimonides and Al-Farabi and referencing Plato's Phaedrus, Strauss proposed that the classical and medieval art of esoteric writing is the proper medium for philosophic learning, as it guides readers to think independently rather than imparting knowledge. He presented Maimonides as a "closet nonbeliever" who obfuscated his message for political reasons. His hermeneutical argument, reiterated in works like The City and Man (1964), is that before the 19th century, Western scholars understood that philosophical writing does not belong in any polity, as it questions conventional wisdom at its roots and must guard against readers who believe themselves authoritative or defenders of the status quo. Philosophers of the past used esoteric communication to avoid persecution, especially from those few whom the many regarded as the most righteous guardians of morality. Strauss explicitly followed Gotthold Ephraim Lessing in arguing that medieval political philosophers, like their ancient counterparts, adapted their language to prevailing moral views to avoid being condemned as heretical or unjust—not by the "many" who did not read, but by the "few" who were seen as moral authorities. Modern social science is flawed, according to Strauss, because it assumes the fact–value distinction, a concept he found dubious, tracing its roots in Enlightenment philosophy to Max Weber, whom he described as a "serious and noble mind" but who, in Strauss's view, was deeply influenced by Nietzsche's relativism. For Strauss, politics could not be studied from afar; a political scientist using a value-free scientific eye was self-deluded. Positivism, as the heir to Auguste Comte and Weber, failed to justify its own existence, which requires a value judgment. While modern liberalism emphasized individual liberty, Strauss advocated greater attention to human excellence and political virtue, constantly raising the question of how freedom and excellence can coexist without providing a straightforward answer to the Socratic question: What is the good for the city and man? Two significant political-philosophical dialogues Strauss had with living thinkers were with Carl Schmitt and Alexandre Kojève. Schmitt, who later became chief jurist of Nazi Germany, was one of the first important German academics to positively review Strauss's early work, particularly on Hobbes, and his approval was instrumental in securing Strauss the scholarship that allowed him to leave Germany. According to Heinrich Meier's interpretation, Strauss's critique of Schmitt's The Concept of the Political led Schmitt to make significant emendations in its second edition. In a 1932 letter to Schmitt, Strauss summarized Schmitt's political theology as stating that because man is by nature evil, he needs dominion, which can be established only through unity against other men; every association of men is necessarily a separation from others, and thus the political, as understood, is not the constitutive principle of the state.

Freedom and excellence can coexist, according to Leo Strauss, who refused to offer a direct answer to the Socratic question of what is good for the city and man. Strauss engaged in two significant political-philosophical dialogues with living thinkers: Carl Schmitt and Alexandre Kojève. Schmitt, who later served as chief jurist of Nazi Germany, was one of the first prominent German academics to positively review Strauss’s early work, particularly his interpretation of Hobbes, and this endorsement helped secure Strauss the scholarship that enabled him to leave Germany. According to Heinrich Meier, Strauss’s critique of Schmitt’s *The Concept of the Political* prompted Schmitt to make substantial revisions in its second edition. In a 1932 letter, Strauss summarized Schmitt’s political theology as asserting that because man is by nature evil, dominion is necessary, and unity can only be achieved through a unity against others; every association is a separation from others, so the political is not the foundation of the state but a condition of it. Robert Howse, however, claims there is no clear evidence for this influence, suggesting the relationship was merely professional. Strauss directly opposed Schmitt, viewing Schmitt’s return to Hobbes as clarifying the nature of political existence and modern self-understanding, but arguing that Schmitt’s transformation of political thought into a political theology was inadequate. Strauss instead advocated a return to a broader classical understanding of human nature and a revival of ancient political philosophy. With Kojève, Strauss maintained a close and lifelong philosophical friendship, first meeting as students in Berlin; Kojève later stated that without befriending Strauss, he never would have known what philosophy is. Their central dispute centered on the role of philosophy in politics: Kojève, a senior civil servant instrumental in founding the European Economic Community, believed philosophers should actively shape political events, while Strauss maintained that philosophers should only participate in politics to the extent that philosophy remains free from political interference. Strauss argued that modern liberalism, oriented toward universal freedom rather than ancient liberalism focused on human excellence, contains an inherent tendency toward extreme relativism, leading to two forms of nihilism. Believing that 20th-century relativism, scientism, historicism, and nihilism contributed to the decline of modern society and philosophy, Strauss sought to trace these philosophical pathways and advocated a return to classical political philosophy as a basis for evaluating political action. He argued that Plato’s *Republic* is not a blueprint for regime reform (a reference to Karl Popper’s critique), but rather reveals the nature of political things—the nature of the city. Strauss claimed the city-in-speech is unnatural because it arises from the abstraction from eros. Though skeptical of progress, he was equally skeptical of political agendas of "return," fearing that attempting to resolve debates between rationalism and traditionalism would be dangerous. He expressed concern about efforts to establish a world state, fearing such a structure would inevitably become a tyranny, and thus remained distant from both fascism and communism. Strauss rejected Karl Popper’s views as illogical; in response to Eric Voegelin’s letter criticizing Popper’s understanding of Plato, Voegelin stated that Popper was philosophically uncultured and incapable of correctly understanding even a single page of Plato, calling the study a waste of time and an annoyance. Strauss shared this letter with Kurt Riezler, who used his influence to oppose Popper’s appointment at the University of Chicago. Strauss consistently emphasized two key dichotomies in political philosophy: Athens and Jerusalem (reason and revelation) and Ancient versus Modern. The "Ancients" include the Socratic philosophers and their heirs; the "Moderns" begin with Niccolò Machiavelli. The contrast reflects the unresolved tension between reason and revelation. The Socratics, reacting to early Greek philosophers, brought philosophy back to earth and to the political sphere. The Moderns, reacting to the dominance of revelation in medieval society, promoted reason, rejecting Aquinas’s fusion of natural right and natural theology, which they saw as vulnerable to theological disputes. Thomas Hobbes, influenced by Francis Bacon, shifted political thought toward human physical fears and hopes, setting a precedent for John Locke, David Hume, and Adam Smith. As a youth, Strauss was part of the German Zionist youth group with Gershom Scholem and Walter Benjamin, both of whom remained admirers throughout their lives. At age 17, Strauss was "converted" to political Zionism under Ze'ev Jabotinsky, writing essays on its controversies before abandoning the activities by his early twenties. While maintaining a sympathetic interest in Zionism, he later regarded it as "problematic" and became disillusioned with some of its goals. Strauss taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem during the 1954–55 academic year. In a letter to a *National Review* editor, he questioned why Israel had been labeled a racist state, arguing the author lacked sufficient proof, and concluded that political Zionism is problematic for obvious reasons, yet it served as a vital moral force in an era of dissolution by resisting the leveling of ancestral differences and fulfilling a conservative function. Strauss accepted the utility of religious belief but was openly disdainful of atheism and disapproved of contemporary "dogmatic disbelief," which he considered irrational. Like Thomas Aquinas, he believed revelation must be subject to rational examination. In *The City and Man*, he invites readers to consider "what is God?" (p. 241), and Edward Feser notes that Strauss was neither an orthodox believer nor a convinced atheist, maintaining that orthodoxy remains a defensible option alongside unbelief. In *Natural Right and History*, Strauss distinguishes a Socratic (Platonic, Ciceronian, Aristotelian) from a conventionalist (materialistic, Epicurean) reading of divinity, arguing that the question of religion is inseparable from the nature of civil society and authority. He defends the Socratic reading and rejects the conventionalist one, which includes atheism. This view contradicts interpretations by Shadia Drury and others who claim Strauss viewed religion instrumentally. Strauss’s works were admired by thinkers such as Gershom Scholem, Walter Benjamin, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Alexandre Kojève, and Jacques Lacan. Benjamin, who met Strauss as a student in Berlin, expressed lifelong admiration. Gadamer stated he largely agreed with Strauss’s interpretations. "Straussianism" refers to the research methods, concepts, presuppositions, central questions, and pedagogical style characteristic of many conservatives influenced by Strauss. It is especially influential among university professors of historical political theory and also serves as a common intellectual framework among conservative activists, think tank professionals, and public intellectuals. Harvey Mansfield, Steven B. Smith, and Steven Berg, though not students of Strauss, are considered Straussians. Mansfield argues there is no such thing as "Straussianism" but rather Straussians and a school of Straussians, describing the school as open to all of philosophy without requiring specific beliefs. Within political theory, the Straussian method involves a "close reading" of the "Great Books," aiming to understand a thinker as he understood himself, without concern for historical context or influence, and with an openness to finding timeless truths. Great books are seen as authored by thinkers of sovereign critical self-knowledge and intellectual power, beyond the reach of their historical context, while lesser works are considered epiphenomenal. This approach counters mid-20th-century historicism, which views political thought as progressing linearly, and suggests that past thinkers may hold truths that contemporary thinkers have missed. Almost all of Strauss’s writings have been translated into Chinese, with a notable school of Chinese Straussians, including Liu Xiaofeng and Gan Yang. "Chinese Straussians," often also interested in Carl Schmitt, exemplify the adaptation of Western political theory in non-Western contexts. As editors of a recent volume note, the reception of Schmitt and Strauss in the Chinese-speaking world reveals insights into Western modernity’s contradictions and non-liberal societies’ dilemmas. Critics have accused Strauss of being elitist, illiberal, and anti-democratic. Seymour Hersh has claimed Strauss endorsed "noble lies," myths used by leaders to maintain social cohesion. In *The City and Man*, Strauss discusses Plato’s Republic myths, including the belief that state land belongs to the state even if acquired illegitimately and that citizenship is based on more than birth. Shadia Drury, in *Leo Strauss and the American Right*, claims Strauss instilled an elitist strain in American political leaders linked to imperialist militarism, neoconservatism, and Christian fundamentalism, arguing that Strauss taught that perpetual deception of citizens by rulers is necessary because they need strong leaders to guide them. Some conservatives, like Claes G. Ryn, criticize Strauss for creating an artificial contrast between moral universality and the conventional, ancestral, and historical. Ryn argues Strauss wrongly assumes that respect for tradition undermines reason and universality, and that genuine universality is known in concretized, particular forms. He contends that Strauss’s abstract, ahistorical conception of natural right distorts true universality and that his views have led American conservatives—especially Catholic intellectuals—to reject tradition in favor of ahistorical theorizing, contrary to the Christian notion of the Incarnation, which unites the universal and historical. Ryn sees Strauss’s anti-historicism as connected to the French Jacobins, who also viewed tradition as incompatible with virtue and rationality. Paul Gottfried describes the "new Jacobinism" of neoconservatism as echoing the rhetoric of Louis Antoine de Saint-Just and Leon Trotsky, adopted by the philosophically unprepared American Right. In *Straussophobia*, Peter Minowitz offers a detailed critique of Drury, Xenos, and others, accusing them of bigotry and buffoonery. Steven B. Smith, in *Reading Leo Strauss*, rejects the link between Strauss and neoconservatism, asserting that Strauss was never politically active, never supported imperialism, and questioned the usefulness of political philosophy in shaping policy. He argues that Plato’s myth of the philosopher king should be read as a reductio ad absurdum, and that philosophers should engage politics only to preserve philosophy’s autonomy. Robert Alter, in reviewing Smith’s work, finds Smith’s argument persuasive in correcting misconceptions about Strauss’s political views. Strauss’s daughter, Jenny Strauss Clay, defended him against accusations of being the mastermind behind neoconservative foreign policy, stating he was a conservative in opposing the idea that change is always progress. Since contemporary academia leaned left with its faith in progress and science and discomfort with moral judgment, Strauss stood outside the academic consensus. If academia had leaned right, he would have questioned it too—on certain occasions he did. Mark Lilla argues that attributing neoconservative views to Strauss contradicts a careful reading of his texts, especially *On Tyranny*, summarizing Strauss as emphasizing the need for philosophy to recognize tyranny’s dangers and to defend its autonomy without believing it can shape politics. Responding to claims that Strauss’s teachings led to George W. Bush-era foreign policy, such as spreading liberal democracy through military force, Nathan Tarcov, director of the Leo Strauss Center at the University of Chicago, asserts that Strauss was essentially non-political. After analyzing the limited practical political views in Strauss’s writings, Tarcov concludes that Strauss reminds us of enduring political problems, but we are solely responsible for our flawed solutions. Books and articles on Maimonides and Jewish philosophy are also part of Strauss’s body of work.
Today, there are writings about Maimonides and Jewish philosophy, including books and articles.

Leon R. Rohde, born on 10 May 1995, is a German cyclist who competes in both road and track events. As of the most recent information, he rides for the UCI Continental team Santic–Wibatech. This biographical entry about a German cyclist born in the 1990s is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional details on Wikipedia.

doc_name: Leslie Fox Prize for Numerical Analysis
text: The Leslie Fox Prize for Numerical Analysis, established in 1985 by the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications (IMA), is a biennial award created in honour of the mathematician Leslie Fox (1918–1992). It recognizes "young numerical analysts worldwide" who are under 31 years of age. Candidates submit papers for evaluation by a committee, which then selects shortlisted individuals to present lectures at the Leslie Fox Prize meeting. The prize is awarded in two categories—First Prize and Second Prize—based on a combination of mathematical and algorithmic brilliance as well as presentational skills.

Annette Leslie Jones (born September 7, 1967) is an American stand-up comedian and actress. She was a cast member and writer for the NBC sketch comedy series Saturday Night Live from 2014 to 2019, and hosted the ABC game show Supermarket Sweep. She has also performed as a featured act at the Just for Laughs festival in Montreal and the Aspen Comedy Festival. In 2010, her one-hour comedy special, Problem Child, aired on Showtime. Jones starred in Ghostbusters (2016) as Patty Tolan. In 2017 and 2018, she was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her work on Saturday Night Live. Born in Memphis, Tennessee, Jones has a younger brother, Rodney Keith Jones (1971–2009). Her father, Willie Jones Jr., served in the U.S. Army, and the family moved frequently. They relocated to Los Angeles when her father took a job at Stevie Wonder's radio station, KJLH, as an electronics engineer. Jones attended high school in Lynwood, California, where she played basketball, a sport her father encouraged due to her height. She earned a basketball scholarship to Chapman University, where she worked as a disc jockey at KNAB and considered playing professional basketball overseas. When her coach, Brian Berger, left Chapman in 1986 for Colorado State University, Jones followed. At Colorado State, she considered a pre-law degree but switched majors to accounting and computer science before settling on communications. Jones began stand-up comedy in college in 1987 after winning a "Funniest Person on Campus" contest. After winning, she left school to move to Los Angeles, where she performed at comedy clubs while working at Roscoe's House of Chicken and Waffles and UPS. Comedians Mother Love and Dave Chappelle encouraged her to move to New York City, where she lived for over two years and appeared on BET's ComicView before returning to Los Angeles. She performed at The Comedy Store in West Hollywood, but her shows received negative reviews. She then went on tour, opening for Jamie Foxx, where she was booed; Foxx advised her to "live life for a little while," and she stopped performing for three years. She performed in smaller clubs until 2010, when she began requesting spots at The Comedy Store and secured prime-time slots. In 2012, Chris Rock saw her perform and introduced her to several top comedy managers, all of whom did not recognize her potential. The following year, Rock helped her secure an audition for Saturday Night Live, which she landed. In 2008, Jones participated in Katt Williams's It's Pimpin' Pimpin' tour. Netflix signed her for a stand-up special scheduled for 2020. In December 2013, SNL held a casting call to add at least one African American woman, and Jones auditioned. Before the audition, she criticized the show and Kenan Thompson, calling it "not funny." Sasheer Zamata was added as a featured player, while Jones and LaKendra Tookes were hired as writers. Jones appeared in the Weekend Update segment of the May 3, 2014 episode hosted by Andrew Garfield, where her jokes about dating and being a breeding slave caused controversy. She appeared in the first and third episodes of the 40th season, hosted by Chris Pratt and Bill Hader, respectively. On October 20, 2014, Jones was promoted to cast as a featured player and made her official debut on the October 25, 2014 episode hosted by Jim Carrey. At age 47, she became the oldest person to join SNL as a cast member, surpassing Michael McKean and George Coe, who joined at 46 in 1994 and 1975. Her addition marked the first time in SNL history that the cast included more than one African American woman; the 40th season also became the first to have five concurrent African American cast members, breaking the previous record of three. Jones returned for Seasons 41, 42 (where she was promoted to Repertory Status), 43, and 44. The 44th season was her final season on SNL. In 2006, Jones appeared in Master P's film Repos. In 2014, she appeared in Chris Rock's directorial film, Top Five; Rock later said a follow-up was in development, stating, "Some people really shine in Top Five. You might want to see a little more Leslie Jones." In 2015, she appeared in the Judd Apatow and Amy Schumer project, Trainwreck; Apatow and Schumer wrote a role specifically for her after seeing her in Top Five. In 2016, she starred in the Ghostbusters reboot as Patty Tolan, alongside Melissa McCarthy, Kristen Wiig, and Kate McKinnon. She also appeared in Coming 2 America with Tracy Morgan, Rick Ross, and KiKi Layne. Since 2017, she has been a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in the Actors Branch. During the 2016 Summer Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Jones regularly live-tweeted events and posted reaction videos. Her commentary gained popularity, with articles such as The Huffington Post's "Watching Leslie Jones Watch The Olympics Is Better Than the Actual Olympics" highlighting her enthusiasm. Television producer Mike Shoemaker, a follower, suggested to NBC executive producer Jim Bell that Jones join the Olympics coverage team; Bell responded by asking her to join, and she accepted, covering swimming, track and field, gymnastics, and beach volleyball. Jones reprised her role at the 2018 Winter Olympics in South Korea and live-tweeted for the postponed 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, Japan. She live-tweeted for the final time at the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing, China, and released a statement on Twitter saying this would be her last Olympics live-tweet, claiming NBC was pressuring her to stop. Jones and comedian Adam DeVine appeared in a 2016 Allstate Insurance ad campaign created by Leo Burnett Worldwide. In 2017, she hosted the BET Awards, marking her hosting debut. In 2018, she appeared in two advertisements for Amazon's Echo Spot. In 2020, she hosted a Supermarket Sweep reboot and returned for season 2 in 2021. She also hosted the 2021 MTV Movie & TV Awards. Jones has cited Eddie Murphy, Richard Pryor, Carol Burnett, Lucille Ball, John Ritter, and Whoopi Goldberg as her comedic influences. She is a fan of the Seattle Sounders FC and RuPaul's Drag Race. After the release of Ghostbusters in July 2016, Jones faced racist and misogynistic attacks on Twitter. The platform took action, permanently banning user and Breitbart editor Milo Yiannopoulos, who called her "barely literate." Jones temporarily left Twitter on July 18, 2016. She appeared on Late Night with Seth Meyers to discuss the incident and her meeting with Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey, where she stated that "hate speech and freedom of speech are two different things." A month later, her personal website was hacked, with its content replaced by photos of her passport and driver's license—an instance of doxxing—and alleged nude images, along with a video tribute to Harambe, the Cincinnati Zoo gorilla killed in May 2016, a reference to the racist remarks made about her. Her team took the site down immediately. Both incidents sparked widespread support from fans and celebrities using the hashtag #LoveForLeslieJ, which trended on Twitter and Instagram. Supporters included Paul Feig, Gabourey Sidibe, Ellen DeGeneres, Sara Benincasa, Ava DuVernay, Hillary Clinton, Corey Taylor, Katy Perry, Octavia Spencer, Anna Kendrick, Lena Dunham, and Loni Love. Jones addressed the hacks on the October 22, 2016 episode of Saturday Night Live. When she appeared on Late Night with Seth Meyers on May 12, 2015, a montage of fans showed their support for her.

Limpho Hani (née Sekamane; born 31 January 1948) is a Mosotho–South African activist and the widow of anti-apartheid activist Chris Hani. Born in Sea Point, Maseru, the capital of Lesotho, she married Chris Hani in 1974 at a magistrate's court in Lusaka, Zambia, with a celebratory wedding lunch at Wimpy. After returning to Southern Africa in late 1975, the couple moved into a house in Lithabaneng, Maseru, known as "Moscow House" by ANC members. They had three daughters: Neo (born 1973), Nomakhwezi (born 1978, died 2001), and Lindiwe (born 1981). Hani worked for the Lesotho Tourism Board but became increasingly involved in Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK) operations, including smuggling new MK recruits across the South African border through Swaziland after the 1976 Soweto Uprising. She was detained by South African authorities from 1977 to 1978 and, according to her husband's biographer Hugh Macmillan, gave evidence against Mountain Qumbela, a former ANC leader in the Cape. In 1982, after her husband faced an assassination attempt, she left her job to move with him to Lusaka. She returned to Maseru in 1984, working first with the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency and then at the Swedish Embassy from 1985. The couple moved to South Africa in 1990 after the ANC was unbanned. On 10 April 1993, Chris Hani was assassinated outside their home in Dawn Park, Boksburg, with his teenage daughter Nomakhwezi present. In the April 1994 post-apartheid elections, Hani was elected as an ANC Member of the National Assembly and re-elected in June 1999, resigning from her seat on 17 August 1999, when it was filled by Kay Moonsamy. She also served on the ANC's National Executive Committee, first elected at the 49th National Conference in Bloemfontein in December 1994 and re-elected in December 1997, before resigning during her second term due to other commitments. Following her husband's murder, Hani refused to forgive the killers, a stance described by Sisonke Msimang as "almost heretical" in contrast to Nelson Mandela's conciliatory approach. During the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Janusz Waluś and Clive Derby-Lewis expressed regret and applied for amnesty, but Hani and her family, represented by George Bizos, opposed amnesty. In 2014, when a court approved medical parole for Derby-Lewis, Hani expressed outrage, calling it "a very sad day in South Africa." In 2022, Waluś was granted parole after a sustained campaign by Hani and the SACP to block it. In a media statement, Hani said that Waluś murdered her husband and daughter, and that he had not apologized to her, stating she would never forgive him and only sought justice. The Constitutional Court ruled in November 2022 that the Minister of Justice and Correctional Services had been irrational in denying parole to Waluś, who had been eligible for release for over 15 years. Hani stormed out of the court, calling the verdict "diabolical" and accusing the court and Chief Justice Raymond Zondo of failing South Africa, saying, "This country is finished. In this country, a foreign white [Polish Waluś] can come into South Africa and kill my husband." She expressed sympathy with Minister Lindiwe Sisulu, whom she said was "the only one in this country who saw through these guys." A subsequent application by Hani and the SACP to rescind the court's order was unanimously dismissed.

The Line 6 of the Kunming Metro (Chinese: 昆明轨道交通6号线; pinyin: Kūnmíng Guǐdào Jiāotōng Liù Hào Xiàn), also known as the Airport line (Chinese: 机场线; pinyin: Jīchǎng Xiàn), is a rapid transit line that connects Kunming Changshui International Airport with Kunming's urban center. The line is 25.3 kilometres (15.7 mi) long and has 8 stations. It entered operation on 28 June 2012, initially serving two stations: East Coach Station and Kunming Airport, coinciding with the opening of the new airport to transport passengers to downtown Kunming. The line ceased operation temporarily starting in May 2016 to facilitate preparations for the opening of Line 3, which was scheduled for early 2017. It reopened in August 2017 alongside Line 3. On subway maps, Line 6 is represented in teal. The one-way fare is CN¥5. Service operates daily from 6:00 AM to 22:00 PM, with an average headway of 15 minutes. Trains on Line 6 travel at speeds of up to 100 kilometres per hour (62 mph), and during its initial operation, a one-way trip took approximately 20 minutes. The line runs through Panlong District and Guandu District. Construction began on 1 August 2010, with track-laying completed around December 2011.

The Line of Control (LoC) is a de facto military boundary between Indian- and Pakistani-controlled regions of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, established as part of the Simla Agreement following the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971. Though not a legally recognized international boundary, it replaced the original 1949 ceasefire line with a renamed "Line of Control" that both nations agreed to respect without prejudice to their positions. The Indian-controlled areas are divided into the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, while the Pakistani-controlled areas are Azad Kashmir and Gilgit–Baltistan. The northernmost point of the LoC is NJ9842, beyond which lies the Siachen Glacier, a site of armed clashes beginning in 1984. To the south, the border between Pakistani Punjab and the Jammu province is ambiguous: India considers it an "international boundary," while Pakistan refers to it as a "working border." A separate ceasefire line, known as the Line of Actual Control (LAC), separates Indian-controlled Jammu and Kashmir from Chinese-controlled Aksai Chin. After the 1947 First Kashmir War and the 1965 conflict, only minor changes were made to the original ceasefire line, with the 1972 Simla Agreement formalizing the LoC as a de facto border and stipulating that neither side would unilaterally alter it, regardless of differences in legal interpretation. The United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) was tasked with investigating ceasefire violations (CFVs), though its role diminished after 1971. In 2000, U.S. President Bill Clinton identified the Kashmir Line of Control as one of the world’s most dangerous regions. The LoC from Kargil to Gurez includes mountain passes and valleys with streams and rivers; areas up to 14,000 feet (4,300 m) are wooded, while higher peaks are exposed, with snowy winters and mild summers. From Gurez to Akhnoor, the terrain is mountainous and hilly, generally forested, with tracks and minor roads connecting settlements. Visibility and line of sight are significantly affected by the mix of flora and elevation. In 2018, two corps and multiple battalions of the Border Security Force manned the Indian side, while the Rawalpindi Corps guarded the Pakistani side. CFVs occur symmetrically on both sides, and responses to one incident can trigger firing at distant locations. Weapons used include small arms, rocket-propelled grenades, recoilless rifles, mortars, automatic grenade launchers, rocket launchers, and other direct and indirect arms. Soldiers face sniper attacks in moving vehicles, through bunker peepholes, and during meals. Civilian populations living near or ahead of forward posts have complicated the situation, with shelling and firing resulting in civilian deaths. Bunkers have been built for civilian protection during CFVs. India and Pakistan typically report only their own side’s casualties, blaming the other for firing and claiming adequate retaliation. According to Happymon Jacob, CFVs stem from operational reasons (such as defense construction, the "rule of the gun," lack of bilateral border mechanisms, and soldier or commander traits), politico-strategic motives, proportional responses (like land grabs, revenge firing, or "I am better than you"), accidental incidents (civilian-related or unclear line demarcation), and other factors (testing new recruits, honor, prestige, humiliation, fun, gamesmanship), with operational reasons being the primary cause. Mines were laid across the India–Pakistan border and the LoC in 1947, 1965, 1971, and 2001; the small stretch between fencing rows is mined with thousands of landmines. During the 2001–2002 standoff, thousands of acres along the LoC were mined, leading to civilian and military deaths and injuries. Between January 2000 and April 2002, 138 Indian military personnel were killed. Reinforced sandbagged and concrete posts and bunkers serve as the first line of defense, equipped with supplies for at least a week, allowing soldiers to sleep, cook, and monitor enemy positions continuously. Some posts are in remote locations, with animals used for transport or reared on-site. Living quarters and forward bunkers are often separated, and some post locations follow old 1947–1972 war-era positions with minor adjustments. India constructed a 550-kilometre (340 mi) Anti-Infiltration Obstacle System (AIOS) barrier along a 740–776 km stretch of the LoC by 2004, consisting of double rows of fencing, concertina wire 8–12 feet (2.4–3.7 m) high, electrified, and linked to motion sensors, thermal imaging, lighting, and alarms. Construction began in the 1990s, slowed in the early 2000s due to increased hostilities, resumed after a November 2003 ceasefire, and was completed in late 2004. The fence reduced militant infiltration by 80%, according to Indian military sources, and a proposal for an upgraded smart fence was accepted in 2017. Pakistan has not built a border fence, though several villages lie between the Indian fence and the zero line—13 in Tithwal, with an estimated total of 60 villages and at least one million people living in districts adjacent to the LoC from Rajouri to Bandipora. The Indian Ministry of Home Affairs reported 1,504 "terrorist" infiltration attempts in 2002, with only 105 successful ones in 2016. Infiltration was a key issue during the 2001–2002 standoff, and the reduction in such attempts reflects declining support within Pakistan. During the 2019 Balakot airstrike, Indian aircraft crossed the LoC for the first time in 48 years. Following the 2005 Kashmir earthquake, five official crossing points were designated: Nauseri-Tithwal, Chakoti-Uri, Hajipur-Uri, Rawalakot-Poonch, and Tattapani-Mendhar. The 2016 Azad Jammu and Kashmir Cross LoC Travel and Trade Authority Act lists trade points including Chakothi–Salamabad and Rawalakot (Titrinote)–Poonch (Chakkan-da-Bagh), with the 2011 ordinance establishing these. Between 2005 and 2017, approximately 14,000 people crossed from Muzaffarabad to Indian Kashmir, while about 22,000 crossed to Pakistan. Legal crossings require extensive documentation, including proof of family ties, and even temporary crossings invite government scrutiny. Security forces hold flag meetings and exchange sweets during festivals at these points. On 21 October 2008, cross-LoC trade was conducted for the first time in 61 years. Trade is barter-based, with nearly PKR 11,446 crore (₹5,000 crore or US$790 million in 2023) passing through Chakothi–Salamabad in ten years. The Teetwal crossing, across the Neelum River between Muzaffarabad and Kupwara, is open only in summer and for people, not trade. The Tithwal bridge, first built in 1931, has been rebuilt twice. The Salamabad crossing (Kamran Post) is a major trade and travel route in the Baramulla district, with banking and trade facilitation centers planned on the Indian side. The bridge, named "bridge of peace" in English, was rebuilt after the 2005 earthquake when a mountain collapsed on the Pakistani side and reopened for trade in 2008. The Srinagar–Muzaffarabad bus crosses this bridge. A road connects Kotli and Tatrinote on the Pakistani side to the Indian Poonch district via Chakan Da Bagh, a major trade and travel route with planned banking and trade centers. Most flag meetings occur here. The Tattapani–Mendhar crossing was opened on 14 November 2005. The LoC division severed the Jhelum valley route, the only access from Pakistani Punjab to the Kashmir Valley, cutting off villages and separating families. Some families could see each other across the LoC, such as along the Neelum River, but could not meet. Women on the Pakistani side have sometimes approached military camps to demand an end to infiltration, reducing Indian cross-LoC firing. Documentaries covering the LoC include *A journey through River Vitasta*, *Raja Shabir Khan's Line of Control*, and *HistoryTV18's Kargil: Valour & Victory*. Bollywood films depicting the LoC include *LOC: Kargil* (2003), *Lakshya* (2004), *Gunjan Saxena: The Kargil Girl* (2020), *Uri: The Surgical Strike* (2019), and *Bajrangi Bhaijaan* (2015), as well as the TV show *Avrodh* (2020). The coordinates of the LoC are 34°56′N 76°46′E / 34.933°N 76.767°E / 34.933; 76.767.

The Linus Pauling Award is an annual recognition of outstanding achievement in chemistry, presented by the Puget Sound, Oregon, and Portland sections of the American Chemical Society. The award is named after the renowned U.S. chemist Linus Pauling, who lived from 1901 to 1994, and was first bestowed in 1966. Additionally, another Linus Pauling Award is given each year by the Chemistry Department at Buffalo State College.

Doraemon, the co-protagonist of the anime and manga series, is a cat-like robot from the future with yellow skin who originally had ears, but they were eaten by a robotic mouse, causing him to become blue-skinned and heartbroken. People often mistake him for a raccoon dog, which frustrates him. He is sent back in time by Sewashi Nobi, Nobita's great-great-grandson, to assist Nobita. Doraemon possesses a 4-dimensional pocket from which he retrieves futuristic tools, gadgets, and playthings from a future department store. He tends to panic during emergencies, frantically pulling out a needed item only to produce a large number of unrelated household items. Despite his frequent mishaps, Doraemon is friendly and intelligent but suffers greatly due to Nobita's behavior. Since his arrival, he has lived as the unofficial fourth member of Nobita's family, acting like a second son to Nobita's parents, as he needs to eat and sleep. He is deeply afraid of mice, a fear stemming from the robot mouse that ate his ears, and often reacts with devastating gadgets when confronted with them; Nobita usually saves him in such situations. Although he lacks fingers in most media (though sometimes has bumps resembling fingers in his hands), he can hold objects due to suction cups in his hands. His favorite food is Dorayaki or Doracake. He has been shown to date a normal female cat named Mi Chan. He is the elder brother of Dorami, another robot from the future, who is at least as smart as Doraemon. Nobita Nobi, the other co-protagonist, wears glasses, a red or yellow polo shirt with a white collar, and blue or black shorts with white socks and light blue shoes. He is not good at sports but is skilled at shooting and string figures. He is the son of Tamako and Nobisuke Nobi, the future father of Nobisuke (his son), and the future husband or boyfriend of Shizuka and great-great-grandfather of Sewashi. Shizuka Minamoto, nicknamed Shizuka-chan, is a smart, kind, and pretty girl often associated with the color pink, wearing a pink shirt and skirt. The name "Shizuka" means "Quiet." She is Nobita's best friend and love-interest and does not avoid him due to his poor grades or laziness; instead, she encourages him, though she usually fails. She bathes several times a day, but is frequently interrupted by Nobita, Gian, or Suneo, often due to misuse of Doraemon's gadgets like the Anywhere Door. Her skirt is often flipped by Nobita's gadget misuse or the wind. Scenes showing her bathing or underwear have been removed from dubbed versions in India, Europe, the U.S., and the U.K. Her true passions are sweet potatoes and the violin, both of which she plays poorly, and she reluctantly takes piano lessons due to her mother's wishes. She is an animal lover and keeps two pets: a dog saved from illness by Nobita and Doraemon, and a canary that runs away repeatedly, leading Nobita and Shizuka to chase it. She sometimes likes handsome TV idols and is close to her classmate Dekisugi, though they remain friends. Takeshi Goda, known as Gian, is a strong, quick-tempered bully who frequently steals others' belongings, especially Nobita's and Suneo's, under the excuse of "borrowing" them unless the item is damaged. He has a terrible singing voice, which causes nausea in listeners; even when Nobita and Doraemon try to mute it in a silent world, the lyrics written on a board have the same effect. Despite his poor singing, a girl once liked it, and in some films, his singing is enhanced into a weapon. When he hears a recording of himself, he denies it is his voice and threatens to beat the person who sang it poorly. Gian is confident in cooking, but his homemade food is often terrible. Though he is seen as intimidating, he is sensitive and cries easily when touched, values his friends deeply, and has a soft spot for his younger sister Jaiko, often trying to prevent her from getting into trouble. He is fearful of his mother, who frequently punishes him. His catchphrase is "What's mine is mine. What's yours is also mine," known as Gianism in Japan. Suneo Honekawa, known as Sneech in the English dub, is a fox-faced, rich, and spoiled child who loves to show off his wealth, especially to Nobita, often provoking envy. He frequently teases Nobita and pushes him aside when inviting Gian and Shizuka to his parties. Despite his boastful nature, he is one of Nobita's closest friends and often asks for help from Nobita and Doraemon. In films, he is reluctant to join adventures and avoids trouble, showing cowardice. He has extensive scientific knowledge, is a talented artist and designer, and is extremely cunning. He is self-conscious about his height, being the shortest in class, and often brags about himself, sometimes staring in the mirror. He likes steak and melon and tries to win Shizuka's favor. Dorami is Doraemon's younger sister, yellow-skinned with a large red bow replacing her ears and a flower tail replacing her kitsune tails. She shares half the oil from a can with Doraemon during her creation, making them siblings. She lives in 22nd-century Tokyo with Sewashi and visits Nobita using the time machine when Doraemon is off-duty or during his health checkup. She likes melonpan and is afraid of cockroaches like Nobita's mother. She is a more advanced robot than Doraemon, capable of producing 10,000 horsepower compared to Doraemon's 129.3, and is the smartest student in her school, with better gadget skills. In one story, Nobita tries to replace Doraemon with her due to her superior abilities, but quickly realizes she does not understand him and does not tolerate his antics. She has her own spin-off manga, and in The Doraemons series, she is the love interest of Dora-the-Kid, Doraemon's friendly rival. Nobita's paternal grandmother, also known as Grandma, died when Nobita was in kindergarten before the main storyline. She is kind and eccentric, unlike her husband, and never scolded Nobisuke for not engaging in masculine activities. Nobita remembers her fondly, with many of his positive childhood memories involving her; many of his toys, including his old kendama, were given to him by her. When Nobita travels to the past, she recognizes him as her grandson. She appears in a few episodes and takes care of Nobita in his early years; in one Doraemons manga, she is proud to see him grow into a teenager. Shizuka's cousin appears in a few episodes. A character who lives with Sunetsugu in New York and raised him as his own son, is single, and sometimes appears in Doraemon episodes. He blamed himself for Doraemon being outdated but, after seeing the friendship and brotherhood between Doraemon and Nobita, he abandoned his reset in one episode. A character often seen with Gian and Suneo playing in a vacant lot or baseball field, wearing a baseball cap and often appearing with Haruo. Another character often seen with Gian and Suneo in the same settings, moderately fat, and often appears with Yasuo.

Girlfriends is an American situation comedy that aired for eight seasons, totaling 172 episodes, with its first six seasons on UPN and the final two on The CW. The series premiered on September 11, 2000, and concluded on February 11, 2008. Joan Clayton (played by Tracee Ellis Ross) is nearly 30, close to becoming a junior partner at her law firm, and has a strong friend circle. She hires Maya Wilkes (Golden Brooks) as her assistant and has been friends with colleague William (Reggie Hayes) for over three months. Joan is frustrated that she hasn't had a romantic partner in a year and believes she should be married by now. Her friends, the egotistical Toni Childs (Leslie Silva) and the lazy 27-year-old college student Lynn (Christina Cox), help cheer her up and get her a man, with Toni referring to Maya as "ghetto." Joan and William compete for a senior partner position, only to be shocked when the firm hires Sharon Upton Farley (Anne-Marie Johnson) as an outsider. They plan to protest by walking out, but only one of them actually does. Meanwhile, Lynn and Maya assist Toni in dealing with her fears after Todd asks her to take an HIV test. Joan and William confront Toni over her jealousy and negative attitude about her wedding, especially when Toni announces that Reesie Jackson, her college roommate, will be a bridesmaid. Reesie reveals that Brian, her husband and Joan’s ex-boyfriend, gave her AIDS. Lynn convinces Toni to visit Virginia to seek Sandy’s help before a grant presentation for her AIDS documentary; during the trip, Lynn meets her grandmother and learns a shocking secret about Sandy’s health. After discovering William’s new earnings, Maya tries to become his assistant to improve her salary and return to school, but William only agrees if Joan approves. Toni’s twin brother Antoine visits for a weekend with Maya, but becomes unsettling when he declares his love and says he won’t return to Boston; when she rejects him, he locks himself in the bathroom and refuses to leave. William orders Lynn to leave his house and continually sabotages her attempts to find a roommate. Toni agrees to help Joan clean out her house, but insists that Joan’s love life is what needs to be eliminated. Joan’s cousin Melanie Barnett (Tia Mowry), an aspiring med student, decides to abandon her medical career to pursue a professional athletic career. Maya moves into her new home, Toni and Todd attempt to reach a settlement, William pursues Monica, Joan attends an A-list party where she makes a dramatic mistake, and Lynn writes a song reflecting on the group’s growing distance. Concerned about William’s emotional state after his breakup with Monica, Maya, Joan, and Lynn travel to Chicago to convince Monica to reunite with William. Upon arrival, they learn Monica has been cut off from her family fortune, so Joan offers her a job at the J-Spot. William is initially thrilled when Monica returns, but she later demands half of what he earned during their relationship. Joan unexpectedly proposes to Aaron, but when he mishears his response, she concludes the relationship is over and walks away. Meanwhile, Maya and Darnell find their dream house, but when Darnell gets the chance to buy the garage, he must decide which purchase to make.

doc_name: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
text: The Ig Nobel Prizes are a parody of the Nobel Prizes, awarded each year in mid-September—around the same time as the genuine Nobel Prizes are announced—for ten achievements that "first make people laugh, and then make them think." These prizes are intended to celebrate the unusual, honor imaginative work, and spur public interest in science, medicine, and technology. All awards recognize real achievements, except for three in 1991 and one in 1994, which were due to an erroneous press release. The awards ceremony has taken place on various dates, including 6 October 1995, 3 October 1996, 9 October 1997, 8 October 1998, 30 September 1999, 5 October 2000, 4 October 2001, 3 October 2002, 2 October 2003, 30 September 2004, 6 October 2005, 5 October 2006, 4 October 2007, 2 October 2008, 1 October 2009, 30 September 2010, 29 September 2011, 20 September 2012, 12 September 2013, 18 September 2014, 17 September 2015 at Harvard's Sanders Theatre (the 25th First Annual ceremony), 22 September 2016, 14 September 2017, 13 September 2018, 12 September 2019, 17 September 2020 (webcast), 9 September 2021 (31st First Annual, webcast), 15 September 2022 (32nd First Annual, webcast), 14 September 2023 (33rd First Annual, webcast), 12 September 2024 (34th First Annual, held at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology), and 18 September 2025 (35th First Annual, held at Boston University). Each winner receives a medal shaped like a frying pan that makes noise when shaken and Cambridge parking passes valid from 3 a.m. to 4 a.m. the day after Christmas. The first nomination also included three fictional recipients for fictional achievements.

This list outlines the official symbols of India's states and union territories, which typically include a state emblem, an animal, a bird, a flower, a tree, and sometimes a second animal such as a fish, butterfly, reptile, aquatic animal, or heritage animal, along with fruits, plants, state songs, and state mottos. The state song "Truth alone triumphs" was composed by Sankarambadi Sundaraachari and sung by Suryakumari for the Telugu film Deena Bandhu (1942), starring V. Nagayya, and was released as a private label by the artist. The blackbuck has white fur on the chin and around the eyes, contrasting sharply with black facial stripes; males exhibit two-tone coats with dark brown to black upper parts and legs, and white underparts and inner legs, with darkness increasing with age; females and juveniles are yellowish fawn to tan. Albino blackbucks are commonly found in zoos such as the Indira Gandhi Zoological Park in Andhra. The striped snakehead is a fast-growing fish species in the genus, known for its air-breathing ability, and is suitable for intensive culture; it is sold live and commands high market prices due to its flavorful flesh and absence of fine bones. Andhra is the second-largest mango-producing state in India, covering approximately 4.31 lakh hectares and producing 43.5 lakh metric tons annually. In Andhra, the sport known as 'chedugudu' is popular. The state motto "Truth alone triumphs" is shared with "Satyameva Jayate," and "Victory to Haryana" is another state motto. The species listed include (Labeo calbasu), (Nelumbo nucifera), (Mangifera indica), and (Ficus religiosa). The emblem of Kerala features the Lion Capital of Ashoka without the bell and lotus foundation, flanked by the Indian flag, and behind it is a Gopuram based on the Srivalliputhur Temple; the seal includes Tamil script inscriptions: "Tamil Nadu Arasu" at the top and "Vaymaiye Vellum" at the bottom, meaning "Truth Alone Triumphs" or "Satyameva Jayate." This is the only state emblem that incorporates both the Indian flag and a Hindu temple tower. The state song for Telangana is "Jaya Jaya He Telangana" ("Victory to Mother Telangana!"), with Kerala Day celebrated on November 1 and the state language being Malayalam. The official symbols also include the Indian Elephant (Elephas maximus indicus), the Great hornbill (Buceros bicornis), the Malabar banded peacock (Papilio buddha), the Malabar gliding frog (Rhacophorus malabaricus), the Green chromide (Etroplus suratensis), the Golden Shower Tree (Cassia fistula), the Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), and the Coconut tree (Cocos nucifera). Other symbols include "Truth alone triumphs" (Gladiolus grandiflorus), (Citrus reticulata), (Dalbergia sissoo), (Antilope cervicapra), (Accipiter gentilis), and fish. Some autonomous administrative divisions established under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution have also adopted official symbols.

doc_name: List of Regional Transport Office districts in India
text: This document outlines the Indian Regional Transport Offices (RTOs) and their assigned vehicle registration codes, organized by state or union territory and district. These RTOs, managed by respective state and union territory Transport Departments and headed by Regional Transport Officers (RTOs), are responsible for enforcing the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and its associated rules. The Andhra Pradesh state government introduced a uniform registration system, assigning all new vehicles the AP-39 code since February 2019, making Andhra Pradesh the first state to adopt the "one state-one code" policy. In 2023, a new series, AP-40, was launched. The list includes numerous locations across various cities and regions, such as Civil Lines, Pratap Bagh, Kotwali, and others in Delhi, as well as areas in Bengaluru and surrounding districts, each covered by specific RTO jurisdictions. In Tamil Nadu, certain vehicle series are reserved for specific vehicle types. No RTO uses a number that sums to '8', meaning there are no codes like 08, 17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, or 80. In West Bengal, the "One RTO One Code" initiative introduced WB-05B for both commercial and private vehicles, replaced the earlier WB-13B series, discontinued the WB-18 series after WB-18AM and transitioned to WB-17B, and discontinued the WB-18TA series after WB-18TF, replacing it with WB-17N; the WB-22U series, used for private vehicles in Alipore RTO, remains active. The two-letter state code for Telangana was initially AP, changed to TS after state bifurcation, and then to TG in May 2024; however, both AP and TS codes remain valid. Due to the official respelling of the state name from "Orissa" to "Odisha," the Transport Department replaced "OR" with "OD" on vehicle plates on 1 September 2012. In Telangana, the state code is now TG. Specific RTO codes are listed, including RNK, RNU, RJL, RSL, RRL, RSM, RRM, RSG, RRG, RSB, RRB, RNB, RND, RNE, RNH, RNI, RNL, RNV, RNX, RNG, RNP, RPE, RPH, RPI, TPG, RPP, RNM, RNN, RNQ, RNS, RPK, RPL, RNR, RPF, RPM, RPN, RPJ, RPO. Note that some areas, like parts of GHMC Hyderabad, are covered by this RTO but are not within Hyderabad District. The "KA-57 F" series is exclusively for KSRTC and BMTC buses, and autorickshaw permits are available here, though registration must be done at other Bengaluru RTOs.

doc_name: List of The Cosby Show characters
text: The Cosby Show is an American television sitcom starring Bill Cosby that aired for eight seasons on NBC from 1984 to 1992, focusing on the Huxtable family, an upper middle-class African-American family living in Brooklyn, New York. Dr. Heathcliff "Cliff" Huxtable, who lives in Brooklyn Heights, New York, is known for his comical antics, playful admonishments, and relentless teasing humor. He had a brother, James Theodore Huxtable, who died of rheumatic fever at age 7. In his high school and college years, he was an athlete who competed in wrestling, American football, and track and field. He later served in the Navy before attending medical school and became an obstetrics and gynecology doctor who runs a practice from an office annexed to his home. Most characters outside the family and friends refer to him as "Dr. Huxtable," and he is well-respected in the community. Cliff is married to Clair Huxtable, both of whom attended the fictional Hillman College. Together, they have five children: Sondra, Denise, Theodore (Theo), Vanessa, and Rudith (Rudy). Cliff enjoys live jazz, has an extensive collection of albums, and tries to eat junk food whenever he can get away with it. He is eccentric and silly to most people, especially his family, but is kind-hearted and a dedicated father with a strong sense of humor. A running gag is his repeated attempts to get the grown children to leave the house. Cliff is very playful and enjoys competition, often making bets with Clair over things like the release date of a jazz song or a "Smooth Contest" judged by the children, and he plays a monthly game of pinochle against his father and friends, which sometimes becomes very passionate. He often loses these bets and games, such as never beating his father-in-law at chess, but eventually broke his losing streak at pinochle with the help of Dr. Foster, an expert player and their literary professor at Hillman College. In the pilot episode, Cosby's character is named Clifford, as shown on a house sign, but his full name was later changed to Heathcliff, even though Clair once called him "Heathclifford," and he is commonly known as "Cliff." Originally, Cliff was to be a chauffeur, with humor derived from customer interactions, but the show was changed to feature him as a doctor, with humor coming from his family interactions. Cliff appears in three episodes of A Different World: the pilot (with Rudy), "Rudy and the Snow Queen" (also with Rudy), and "If Chosen, I May Not Run." He is the only character to appear in every episode. Clair Olivia Huxtable (née Hanks) is the elegant, tough, eloquent, and engaging wife of Cliff, known for her relaxed confidence and sharp emphasis. She is intelligent, classy, and successful as a businessperson and a lawyer, rarely losing an argument, and skilled in recalling facts and dates, as shown when she quotes a book passage and page number during a television roundtable. She speaks Spanish and once speaks Portuguese to Theo's teacher. Despite her strictness, she is a loving mother and wife, with her catchphrase "Let the record show." Her character is loosely based on Bill Cosby's wife, Camille Cosby, and her maiden name is the same as Camille's. Her age is directly stated only once, and two episodes provide conflicting information: in season three, Cliff celebrates his 50th birthday, and in season five, Clair celebrates her 46th, indicating she is six years younger, but in the season four episode "The Locker Room," it is stated she is four years younger. Originally, she was supposed to be a housewife, but when the show aired, she became a lawyer and eventually became a partner in her law firm, helping her family with legal issues and successfully representing her daughter Sondra in a case over dishonest car repairs. She was the chief disciplinarian of the children, as shown when she delivers a scathing speech to Vanessa after she sneaks off to Baltimore to see a rock concert. Clair appears in four episodes of A Different World: "Clair's Last Stand," "Risky Business" (with Theo and Vanessa), "Forever Hold Your Peace" (with Martin and Olivia), and "Success, Lies and Videotapes." She has been ranked highly in several lists of the top television mothers, including being voted "Favorite TV Mom" in 2004 by the Opinion Research Company, included in Film.com's Top 5 Classic TV Moms in 2009, selected in iVillage's "Mommy Dearest: The TV Moms You Love" in May 2012, and named the ninth Most Memorable Female TV Character by AOL in 2012. Sondra Tibideaux (née Huxtable), the eldest daughter, did not appear in the pilot episode, as Clair says, "Why do we have four children?" and Cliff replies, "Because we did not want five." In her first appearance, she is a sophomore in college and 20 years old. She earned a degree from Princeton University and intended to become a lawyer like her mother. She married Elvin Tibideaux in season four and later gave birth to twins named after Nelson and Winnie Mandela. She is serious, responsible, and intelligent, fitting the characteristics of a first-born, though she occasionally has bizarre thoughts (e.g., dropping out of law school to open a wilderness store with Elvin), which she usually recovers from quickly. She is proud of her parents but held to a higher standard than her siblings. Sondra was created when Bill Cosby wanted to show the success of raising a child, and Whitney Houston was considered for the role. Sabrina LeBeauf almost missed out because she is only 10 years younger than Phylicia Rashad. The character is loosely based on Cosby's eldest daughter, Erika. Denise Kendall (née Huxtable) is the second daughter. At the start of the series, she is 16 years old, loves fashion and music, and does not want to attend school to pursue these interests. She is independent, learns lessons on her own, and after a two-year stint at Hillman College, goes to Africa as a photographer's assistant, where she meets and marries Navy Lt. Martin Kendall and becomes stepmother to his three-year-old daughter Olivia. She eventually decides to become a special education teacher and plans to attend Medgar Evers College, but leaves New York when Martin is posted to Singapore. In the series finale, she is revealed to be pregnant. In the first two seasons, she is a popular high schooler with many friends and a changing love life, often mocked by Cliff for her hairstyles and clothing. In later seasons, she becomes more flighty and expresses ideas that confuse Cliff and Clair. In season three, she leaves home to attend Hillman College, a fictional historically Black college where her mother, father, and grandfather were alumni. A spin-off series, A Different World, initially focused on Denise at college, but she was written out after the first season when Lisa Bonet became pregnant. In season five, she travels to Africa, falls in love with and marries Martin, and returns home in the season six premiere, shocking her parents with the news. Cliff and Clair accept the couple when they meet Olivia, who wins their hearts and is welcomed into the family. She appears regularly in the first three seasons, in four episodes each of seasons four and five (a picture of her appears in the opening credits of season four), regularly in season six, and in only a few episodes in season seven. The character is loosely based on Cosby's daughter Erinn, who was about the same age as Denise, and Denise attended Hillman College, modeled after Spelman College. Theodore Aloysius "Theo" Huxtable is the middle child and only son, athletic and obsessed with impressing girls and obtaining a sports car or motorcycle. He is 14 years old at the start of the series. In the pilot, he is lectured by his father for not applying himself at school. In early seasons, he is a troublemaker, such as letting his best friend's younger sister pierce his ear, leading to an infected earlobe, though his behavior improves by the time he leaves high school. A recurring theme in early seasons is his academic struggles, especially in sophomore-year geometry taught by Mrs. Westlake. As the series progresses, he evolves into a successful high school and college student, and in interviews, Cosby noted a similar change in his real-life son, Ennis. While at NYU, it is revealed he has dyslexia, a learning disability that motivates him to work harder and overcome it. By the final season, he becomes a volunteer student teacher helping children with dyslexia at a community center. He is offered a job in San Francisco but turns it down to attend graduate school and continue his volunteer work. In the final episode, he graduates from NYU with a degree in psychology. In the pilot and once in season one ("Bad Dreams"), Vanessa refers to him as "Teddy" instead of "Theo." He has a long-running, on-and-off relationship with Justine, mentioned many times but appearing in only nine episodes. During high school, his best friend is Walter Bradley (Carl Anthony Payne II), known as "Cockroach," who is a scholastic underachiever, though he presents convincing facts in a mock trial that closes the case. The two occasionally compose rap songs for school assignments. When Theo gets tickets to "Dance Mania," only one can enter, and he lets Cockroach have the spot, which makes him uncomfortable when he sees Cockroach on TV and at school the next day. This episode marks Cockroach's final appearance, and he is rarely mentioned afterward. Theo appears in two episodes of A Different World: "My Dinner With Theo" (with Rudy) and "Risky Business" (with Clair and Vanessa). Vanessa Huxtable is the fourth child and third daughter, 11 years old at the start of season one. As she grows, she faces typical teenage issues, such as wearing makeup before her 15th birthday and spending time on the phone with friends. Unlike her brother, she is an excellent student and enjoys school; by the start of season seven, she goes to college one year early. In the final season, she becomes engaged to Dabnis Brickey, a man in his late twenties, who is the head of maintenance at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, where she enrolls. However, she realizes she is not ready to marry and breaks off the engagement, maintaining they are "just friends" by the end. In early seasons, she is nosy, often sneaking to find out what goes on in the house, especially involving Theo. In a later episode, the tables are turned when Theo catches her friends smoking in her room, though she herself did not participate. She often fights with her younger sister, Rudy, over childish issues, and at one point, their fighting causes damage to their bedrooms and the kitchen ceiling, leading Cliff to declare their rooms off-limits and exile them to the basement until repairs are done. On one occasion, she gets into a physical fight with Denise over a sweater she stole from Denise's closet. During seasons five and six, she has a rebellious phase, engaging in shady activities such as creating a suggestive dance for a music video, sneaking out with a boyfriend after breaking curfew, playing a drinking game with friends, attempting to sneak to a college party, and most famously, sneaking out to a concert in Baltimore with her friends, where everything goes wrong, greatly upsetting Clair. One of her best friends is Kara (Elizabeth Narvaez), who rambles at high speed; when Cliff refers to her as "Turbo Tongue," he usually replies with a bewildered "Thank you." Vanessa appears sporadically in the final two seasons due to being away at college. The character is loosely based on Cosby's daughter Ensa, who was about the same age as Vanessa. Vanessa also appears in the A Different World episode "Risky Business" (with Clair and Theo). Rudith Lillian "Rudy" Huxtable is the youngest child, only five years old at the start of the series. Several of her friends appear throughout the series, including the quiet Peter Chiara, who repeatedly runs out the front door when frightened, and the chauvinist, blues-loving Kenny, whom she nicknames "Bud," who always gets advice from his unseen older brother, leading to misunderstandings and trouble, though he seems to grow out of it. Keshia Knight Pulliam was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award in season two, becoming the youngest nominee ever; one of her fellow nominees was Lisa Bonet, neither of whom won, as they lost to Rhea Perlman from Cheers. The Huxtable family was originally going to have two boys and two girls, but the youngest child, Rudy, was initially supposed to be a boy, and the character was rewritten for a girl (Keshia Knight Pulliam) due to a lack of boys auditioning. Jaleel White, later known for his role as Steve Urkel on Family Matters, revealed in a 2011 interview with Vanity Fair that he auditioned for the role of Rudy. The character is loosely based on Cosby's youngest daughter, Evin, who was about the same age as Rudy. Rudy also appears in three episodes of A Different World: the pilot (with Cliff), "Rudy and the Snow Queen" (also with Cliff), and "My Dinner with Theo" (with Theo). Elvin Tibideaux is Sondra's boyfriend and later husband. They met at Princeton University, where they both earned degrees. They constantly bicker in early episodes, until their interactions with the Huxtables, especially Clair, challenge him to confront his "male-chauvinist" attitudes. After their honeymoon, they shock Cliff and Clair by announcing their intention to forego medical school and law school and start a wilderness supply store in Brooklyn.

doc_name: List of The Cosby Show characters
text: The show features three boys and two girls. The youngest child, Rudy, was originally intended to be a boy, but the character was rewritten as a girl, Keshia Knight Pulliam, due to a lack of boys auditioning. Jaleel White, known for his role as Steve Urkel on Family Matters, revealed in a 2011 interview with Vanity Fair that he had auditioned for the role of Rudy. The character is loosely based on Bill Cosby's youngest daughter, Evin, who was approximately the same age as Rudy. Rudy appears in three episodes of A Different World: the pilot (with Cliff), "Rudy and the Snow Queen" (also with Cliff), and "My Dinner with Theo" (with Theo). Elvin Tibideaux is Sondra's boyfriend and later husband; they met at Princeton University, where they both earned degrees. The two frequently bicker during early episodes until Elvin's interactions with the Huxtables, especially Clair, challenge him to confront his "male-chauvinist" attitudes. After returning from their honeymoon, they shock Cliff and Clair by announcing they will forgo medical school and law school to start a wilderness supply store in Brooklyn. When their children are born, Elvin re-applies to medical school, a decision that convinces Sondra to resume her law school studies. Elvin was a high school wrestler and competed for one year at Princeton University before quitting due to a hip injury. During season three, he helps Theo with strategy and moves. Lt. Martin Kendall is a United States Navy officer, husband of Denise Huxtable, and father of Olivia. He is introduced to the Huxtables after Denise unexpectedly marries him in Africa, unbeknownst to the family. When the newlyweds return, they learn Denise's family does not know about their marriage or him at all, causing initial discomfort for Clair and Cliff, who eventually become accustomed to the blended family. Kendall had an ex-wife, Paula (played by Victoria Rowell), and in the finale, it is revealed that he and Denise are expecting a baby together. Joseph C. Phillips played Sondra's date in a season two episode, a different character than Martin. Martin appears frequently in the sixth season but is only seen in a few episodes of the seventh season, Phillips's final season as a regular, and makes his final appearance in the season eight episode "Olivia Comes Out of the Closet." Martin also appears in the Different World episode "Forever Hold Your Peace" (with Clair and Olivia). Olivia Kendall is Denise Huxtable's precocious stepdaughter, who is three years old when she first appears. Olivia is the only child of Martin and Paula Kendall. After a few years of marriage, her parents divorced, and Paula gave Martin full custody, as she felt overwhelmed by marriage and motherhood. Olivia was raised by her grandparents and father. When Olivia is almost four, Martin marries Denise Huxtable, whom he met in Africa. The new family moves in with Denise's parents, Clair and Cliff Huxtable, who become Olivia's step-grandparents. As a Naval officer, Martin travels frequently, so Olivia spends time with Denise during his absences. Olivia continues to live with her step-grandparents while her parents are in Singapore during the final season. The character Olivia was named after Bill Cosby's wife, Camille Olivia Hanks-Cosby. Raven originally auditioned for the Bill Cosby movie Ghost Dad but did not get the part because she was too young; however, Cosby liked her so much that he created the role of Olivia, his step-granddaughter, for her in the final three seasons. Olivia also appears in the Different World episode "Forever Hold Your Peace" (with Clair and Martin). Pam Tucker is the daughter of Clair Huxtable's first cousin, making her and Clair first cousins once removed. The daughter of a single mother, Pam moves in with the Huxtables after her mother relocates to California to care for Pam's grandmother. Upon moving in, Pam is a high school junior—younger than Vanessa but older than Rudy. At first, she is not used to the Huxtables' upper-middle-class lifestyle or close-knit family dynamics, but eventually fits in and becomes part of the Huxtable family. Pam makes her first appearance in the fourth episode, "A Period of Adjustment," in season seven. Frequently, Pam is shown interacting with her best friend, Charmaine Brown (Karen Malina White), and Charmaine's boyfriend, Lance Rodman (Allen Payne). The character had a mixed reception.

doc_name: List of The Dukes of Hazzard episodes
text: This is a list of episodes for the 1979–1985 CBS action-adventure/comedy series The Dukes of Hazzard. The show aired for seven seasons and consisted of 147 episodes. Many episodes followed a consistent structure: "out-of-town crooks pull a robbery, Duke boys blamed, spend the rest of the hour clearing their names, the General Lee flies and the squad cars crash." Additionally, almost every episode began with the Duke boys driving in the General Lee, either running an errand or on a leisurely drive, and inadvertently stumbling upon one of the sheriff's speed traps. The Duke family resides in Hazzard County, Georgia. Their patriarch is Jesse Duke, a farmer and former moonshiner who is very wise and likely the most trusted person in six counties; his nephews, Bo and Luke, and his niece, Daisy, live on the Duke farm with him. Jesse raised Bo, Luke, and Daisy after their parents died in an auto accident. The family has made moonshine for generations. A few years prior, Bo and Luke were stopped on a moonshine run, and Jesse swallowed his pride to sign a treaty with the U.S. government to stop making moonshine if they could be released on probation. Since then, Jesse has honored his word and no longer runs moonshine. Despite being on probation, Bo and Luke continue to have fun, helping Jesse manage the farm and operating a souped-up orange Dodge Charger called the General Lee. Daisy works as a waitress at the Boar's Nest, the most popular bar/restaurant in the county, which is owned by the corrupt Hazzard County commissioner, Boss Jefferson Davis "J.D." Hogg. Boss Hogg owns nearly everything in Hazzard County, including bumbling Sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane. Boss would do anything to make a dishonest dollar but does not condone violence. He plans to have Rosco receive a delivery of illegal slot machines, and Rosco is loyal enough to follow his orders. After about 20 years as one of the best lawmen in the state, most of Rosco's pension was lost in the last bond election in Hazzard County, making him bitter and corrupt. He is now running for re-election against an even more corrupt opponent. After hijacking the shipment of illegal slot machines, Bo and Luke plan to distribute them to civic clubs and organizations in the area and use the proceeds to help renovate the local orphanage before the health department shuts it down. Guest stars include Tisch Raye as Jill Rae Dodson; Ernie Brown as Dobro Doolan; Dan Fitzgerald as driver; Champ Laidler as Brodie; Gillaaron Houck as Leroy; Lou Walker as Workman; Dennis Haskins as Moss; Sandra Dorsey as Deputy Hazel; Ralph Pace as Harvey; Jason Lively as Rudy. Notes indicate that younger Dukes fans may recognize Dennis Haskins, who played Moss in this pilot episode, as he later became Mr. Belding on Saved by the Bell and had other recurring guest roles on The Dukes. Main characters Cooter Davenport (Ben Jones) and Deputy Enos Strate (Sonny Shroyer) do not appear in the opening credits and are only recognized in the end credits. In one episode, an Atlanta music-publishing outfit steals $50.00 from Daisy (a corruption of Boss Hogg's), and the FBI is monitoring the scam. Bo and Luke go to town to resolve the issue and end up interfering with a police raid. They devise a plan to catch the record pirates by having Daisy pretend to be a potential client to trick the music outfit's leader, Lester Starr, into believing she can fake recordings of real-life artists. Meanwhile, after being in the wrong place at the wrong time, Bo and Luke are targeted by the FBI and local law. Boss sees an opportunity to tie in with the syndicate, with a new singer Starr must audition for them and Boss, who just happens to be Daisy. This is a big mistake. Guest stars include Ronnie Schell as Lester Starr; Ginny Parker as Mabel; Clayton Landey as Max; Terry Browning as Ruby; Candy Bleick as Dodie; Wallace Merck as Jojo; Bill Gribble as Carson; J. Roy Tatum as FBI Agent #3; Wallace Wilkinson as FBI Agent #1; Bob Cleveland as FBI Agent #2. Notes state that while Bo and Luke discuss their plan in Atlanta, the sign of the first Mellow Mushroom pizza chain can be seen behind Bo. Loretta Lynn's name (as well as Coulter's) are dubbed over at several points in the episode. Bill Gribble, who appears as "Carson," also appeared in Moonrunners as Cooter Pettigrew. This episode marks the first time Cooter delivers his standard CB intro: "Breaker 1, breaker 1. I maybe crazy but I ain't dumb. Crrrrazy Cooter comin' at ya!" While fleeing from Enos in Cooter's car, Bo and Luke face a problem: the vehicle is loaded with moonshine that Cooter was supposed to deliver for Boss Hogg. Bo and Luke pick up a hitchhiker they recognize as their friend Mary Kaye Porter (Jeanne Wilson), who is now nine months pregnant and fleeing from Atlanta crime boss Quirt McQuade (Cliff Pellow), who believes Mary Kaye has $118,254.37 stolen from him.
