Bo and Luke help Terry Lee by getting him a basset hound from the pound. It turns out to be Maxine, the valuable purebred showdog that was kidnapped from wealthy John J. Hooper (Joe Dorsey) at a dog show, and the kidnappers, a man named B. B. (Billy Ray Sharkey) and his wife Mandy Jo (Jennifer Holmes), have demanded a $25,000 ransom. B. B. had worked for John for eight years before being fired. Maxine escaped and ended up in the pound when B. B. and Mandy Jo came to Hazzard. John and his wife (Toni Sawyer) have posted a $10,000 reward for Maxine's return. Boss Hogg, who wants the reward, learns Maxine is at the orphanage and, unaware of Terry Lee's feelings, takes her and holds her until John arrives. B. B. and Mandy Jo mistake Rosco's dog Flash for Maxine and, as a result, kidnap Flash. While everyone is looking for Flash, Boss Hogg remains hopeful about collecting the reward for Maxine. After everything is resolved, B. B. and Mandy Jo are found, Flash is rescued, and the Hoopers decide to adopt Terry Lee. Daisy and Lulu return from a shopping trip to New Orleans. At the airport, Lulu accidentally picks up a suitcase identical to her own, which contains a stolen $250,000 diamond necklace. When the thieves and their boss, Mr. Lipton (Robert Phalen), learn that Lulu and Daisy have the suitcase, they begin pursuing them, bent on retrieving the necklace by any means necessary. Boss Hogg wants the necklace to sell it to his crooked cousin, Big Dan Hogg (Marty Zagon), for $25,000—without realizing how valuable the necklace truly is. Bo, Luke, and Enos—later joined by Boss and Rosco—devise a plan to trap Lipton and his men and return the necklace to its owner, knowing that Lipton and his men have threatened to kill Daisy and Lulu if they fail to hand over the necklace or if any entrapment is detected. After returning from a Marine Corps reunion, Luke chases a woman who robbed a jewelry store in Capitol City, while at the same time, her identical twin sister is with Bo on the side of the road in a different part of the county, providing an alibi for the twins, Cindy (Randi Brough) and Sandy Ballou (Candi Brough). This causes a feud between Luke and Bo. Luke knows the woman he chased committed the robbery, and Bo refuses to believe Luke, thinking the woman in Capitol City is the same as the one on the road with Bo. The situation is resolved when Bo and Luke realize they are dealing with twins. In an effort to save money, Rosco and Enos have their patrol cars taken away by Boss Hogg, who gives them a pair of three-wheel ATVs to drive. While Enos was on the LAPD, he arrested and testified against hit man Frank Scanlon (Don Gordon). Now, Scanlon, who wears a different disguise for each job, has escaped from prison and arrived in Hazzard, determined to make Enos pay for putting him away. The Dukes help Enos capture Scanlon. Rosco's inattention allows Scanlon to escape from Hazzard jail, and Boss Hogg fires Enos for it. After Scanlon blows up Enos' empty car with a bomb, the Dukes and some friends set a trap to stop Scanlon before he can hurt Enos, but Scanlon turns the tables and kidnaps Daisy, believing the easiest way to get Enos is through Daisy. Scanlon demands that Enos give himself up alone or he will kill Daisy. The Dukes and everyone else in Hazzard set out to rescue Enos and Daisy and help Enos get his job back. Daisy, who has her pilot license, fills in for Hazzard County's crop duster, her boyfriend Joe Ward (Michael Crabtree), when Joe is injured. Boss Hogg has two crooks, Percy (Steven Williams) and Hector (Nick Benedict), secretly mix poisonous lye in the crop duster's pesticide mixer. As Boss had planned, Daisy kills Boss Hogg's crops so Boss can sue the Dukes for damages, hoping to win the Duke farm. However, Boss Hogg's scheme backfires when Percy and Hector form their own plan: they tell the county's farmers to pay a ransom or get lye dumped on their crops. The Dukes set out to stop Percy and Hector before Hazzard becomes a wasteland. 18-year-old Nancy Lou Nelson (Kim Richards) comes to Hazzard to see Cooter, and Nancy Lou turns out to be Cooter's long-lost biological daughter. Years ago, Cooter and local girl Beverly Hibbs ran away and got married. Back then, Cooter was still a wild man. Beverly's father had the marriage annulled, but not before Beverly became pregnant. Because of Cooter's wild side, Beverly and Cooter agreed it would be better if she raised Nancy Lou alone. Now, Cooter tries to be respectable, but seems unable to avoid brushes with strangers named Collins (David Gale) and Buck Morgan (Jack Yates), who lead a group planning to dump toxic waste in Hazzard County. Nancy Lou begins to believe Beverly was right about Cooter and plans to leave town. Bo, Luke, and Cooter set out to stop Collins and Morgan, and the Dukes try to help Cooter redeem his image in Nancy Lou's eyes. When Boss Hogg learns what Collins and Morgan are up to, he makes it clear he does not want toxic waste in Hazzard County. Private investigator Harry Bobo (Frank Birney) comes to Hazzard with a photo of heiress Vivian Stewart, the long-lost granddaughter of wealthy industrialist Carter Stewart (Lyle Talbot)—who is offering a $200,000 reward to anyone who finds Vivian. It turns out Vivian looks exactly like Daisy, so Boss Hogg, who wants the reward money, has Professor Crandall (Walker Edmiston) hypnotize Daisy into thinking she is Vivian. Boss Hogg tricks Harry into thinking Daisy is Vivian, and they visit Carter. But Vivian's cousins Alan Fairchild (Greg Michaels) and Vonnie Fairchild (Nancy Hinman), who would inherit Vivian's estate if she is killed, are out to kill Daisy because they also believe Daisy is Vivian. Bo and Luke chase armored truck robbers Phil (Charles Cyphers) and Lenny (Charles H. Hyman) through Chickasaw County, and Sheriff Ed Little mistakes the Dukes for the robbers. The only eyewitness who can clear Bo and Luke is their old friend, local artist Artie Bender (James Cavan)—but Boss Hogg has just hidden Artie away and declared him legally dead so Boss can sell Artie's paintings to an art dealer at inflated prices. Chickasaw County Sheriff "Big Ed" Little continues to pursue Bo and Luke after they escape from jail, as they try to unravel the mystery of whether Artie is really dead. Country music star Candy Dix (Roberta Leighton), a woman Luke courted before he enlisted in the Marines, comes to Hazzard to do a concert at the Boar's Nest and see Luke for the first time in seven years. As they try to rekindle their romance, Luke finds that Candy has a lot on her mind. Her current boyfriend and manager, Eddie Lee Memphis (Jeff Osterhage), is with her.

doc_name: List of The Dukes of Hazzard episodes
text: Through Chickasaw County, Sheriff Ed Little mistakes the Dukes for the robbers. The only eyewitness who can clear Bo and Luke is their old friend, local artist Artie Bender (James Cavan), but Boss Hogg has hidden Artie away and declared him legally dead so Boss can sell Artie's paintings to an art dealer at inflated prices. Chickasaw County Sheriff "Big Ed" Little continues to pursue Bo and Luke after they escape from jail, as they try to unravel the mystery of whether Artie is really dead. Country music star Candy Dix (Roberta Leighton), a woman Luke courted before he enlisted in the Marines, comes to Hazzard to do a concert at the Boar's Nest and see Luke for the first time in seven years. As they try to rekindle their romance, Luke finds Candy has a lot on her mind; her current boyfriend and manager, Eddie Lee Memphis (Jeff Osterhage), has been ill-tempered and abusive toward her, because Memphis owes a gambling debt to bookie Mr. Starkey (Ritch Brinkley), who threatens to kill him if the debt is not paid. Memphis is terrified, and the Dukes must protect Candy from Memphis and his accomplice Hoby Willis (Ned Bellamy), who are out to kill her so Memphis can use her $75,000 life insurance policy to pay off the debt. While protecting Candy, Memphis tries to prevent interference by visiting Boss Hogg and asking that Luke be arrested for kidnapping. Bo and Luke are offered a chance to return to the NASCAR circuit, racing for Mary Beth Carver (Lydia Cornell), the daughter of crime boss J. J. Carver (Ramon Bieri). Mary Beth is not involved in Carver's operations. Bo and Luke decline, vowing to uphold a promise they made to Jesse that they would never again leave the farm to race. A Federal Agent named Walden (Herbert Jefferson, Jr.) later approaches Bo and Luke, offering a healthy cash sum for them to work undercover as race car drivers for Mary Beth, since J. J. Carver is involved in a gambling racket involving murder, robbery, and illegal gambling. The offer is too good to pass up, and Bo and Luke agree to work for Walden, who tells them they cannot tell Jesse and Daisy what they are doing, leaving clueless Daisy angry. Daisy berates Bo and Luke for leaving her and Jesse to return to racing after their promise, even slapping Bo. Bo and Luke begin to infiltrate J. J. Carver's organization, compiling evidence to bring him to justice. The Tri-Counties 150 is underway at a track in Capitol City, and Bo is driving Carver's race car, but their cover is blown—thanks to Boss Hogg and Rosco, who think Bo and Luke are making gambling deals. After tying up Luke, Boss, and Rosco, Carver (Ramon Bieri) sends his henchman Jo Jo (Mike Moroff) to the track to kill Bo as soon as he crosses the finish line. When Jesse and Daisy show up at the track, Bo, unaware he is putting Daisy's life in danger, has Daisy secretly take his place in the race so he can go to Carver's home and help Luke, Boss, and Rosco recover the evidence. Once Carver is brought down and Bo and Luke are allowed to tell Daisy and Jesse what they were doing, Daisy realizes she made a mistake in getting angry and apologizes to them. Boss Hogg's nephew Dewey Hogg (Robert Morse), who is Hughie Hogg's older brother, returns to Hazzard for the first time in seven years and says he is dying from a rare and lethal sleeping disorder. Dewey convinces Boss that he wants to build the Dewey Hogg Memorial Clinic as his legacy, if Boss will put up $50,000 and get the town to contribute another $50,000. The plan works, and Dewey and Boss get Jesse to guard the money, which then goes missing, and Dewey frames Jesse for the scam. Luke and Daisy discover Dewey is faking his illness, and the Dukes devise a plan to get him to lead them to the money. Luke pretends to order a very expensive stomach pump to save his life, and Dewey, in distress, rushes to the bank to find the money to pay for it. It is revealed that Dewey had transferred the money into a different safety deposit box. However, Luke's plan goes sour when Boss and Rosco expose their scheme. Dewey escapes, and the Dukes must follow him in a long car chase. Dewey and his nurse assistant are stopped and made to march out of Hazzard in disgrace without the money. Daisy will play a nurse in a play at the church and carries her notes in a black book. Nervous Norman Willis (Mike Genovese), a neurotic crime boss, comes to Hazzard County to collect a debt from Boss Hogg. While Norman's limo is in front of the General Lee, the car backfires, and Norman, living up to his nickname, mistakes it for a gunshot. A scared Norman, thinking he is having a heart attack, has his driver Jake (Kaz Garas) rush him into town. In town, Norman and Jake see Daisy wearing a nurse uniform and do not realize she is practicing for the play. Jake gets Daisy's attention, and Daisy comes to help Norman. Norman puts his little black book next to him on the back seat. Daisy puts down her black book, which is identical to Norman's. Jake and Norman decide to go to the local hospital, but first, Daisy grabs her rehearsal notes—or so she thinks. She actually grabs Norman's black book, which contains information on all of his crooked operations. When Norman discovers he has the wrong book, he is terrified Daisy has the information that could put him in prison. He and Jake go out hunting for Daisy, intending to get the book and kill her to prevent her from revealing their activities. Bo, Luke, and Jesse decide to hide Daisy in Enos's house while they look for Norman and Jake. Norman tells Boss Hogg that his debt will be cleared if he helps Norman find Daisy. Enos unwittingly lets Daisy's location slip to Rosco, and Rosco and Boss tell Willis and Jake where to find her, promising she will be unharmed. Boss Hogg, who does not condone violence, is unaware Norman plans to have Jake kill Daisy. Norman and Jake kidnap Daisy from Enos's house, and it is up to the Dukes, Cooter, and Enos to rescue her. Recently, the cash flow from Boss Hogg's scams has slowed to a trickle. In Boss's opinion, things would be better if he could get Enos out of the way and hire a deputy who would look the other way and keep the Dukes out of the way. To achieve this, Boss promotes Enos to Hazzard Commissioner of Records and hires Billy Joe Coogan (Michael Alldredge), from Cedar City, as the tough new deputy, who proves to be an unexpected challenge for the Dukes. What Boss does not know is that Coogan is hatching a crooked plan with Eddie Hollis (Joseph Whipp). Coogan and Hollis have helped Boss Hogg with scams before, but now there is more than $150,000 that Boss skimmed from the county over the past years, and he placed it in a hidden account. Coogan learns about it when he sees Boss's secret ledger, and Coogan and Hollis demand that Boss give up the money or the spillway at the Hazzard dam will be opened as far as it will go. If the spillway is set wide open for long enough, all of Hazzard will be flooded under about 10 feet of water, and every farm in Hazzard County will be washed out. The Dukes are in a race against time to stop Coogan and Hollis and help Enos get his deputy job back. Boss Hogg is in a stew after discovering that Lulu is going to cash in the $100,000 in bonds that Boss already cashed in on and replaced with fake bonds. Boss must get rid of the fake bonds. The problem is, Lulu has changed the combination of the safe that she and Boss Hogg keep at home. Boss hires Madame Delilah (Leslie Easterbrook) and Three Pack (Tommy Madden), a pair of fortune-teller con artists, to get the safe combination from Lulu and get rid of the fake bonds. But complications arise because Madame Delilah and Three Pack have robbed the Boar's Nest. Rosco and Boss Hogg, unaware that Madame Delilah and Three Pack are the robbers, accuse Daisy of the robbery. Luke and Jesse must hide Daisy from Rosco. Daisy and Luke discover the truth about Madame Delilah and Three Pack. They have been robbing Hazzard blind with their scams. Boss Hogg is angry at their victimization of Lulu and demands that Madame Delilah and Three Pack be put in jail. Luke and Daisy try to find Madame Delilah and Three Pack and prove Daisy's innocence. Recurring guest: Peggy Rea as Lulu Coltrane Hogg. Jonas Jones (Hal Williams) rescued Cooter from a fire in Oklahoma 10 years ago, and they have been friends ever since. An auto parts supply distribution firm, scheduled to deliver a shipment of parts for Boss Hogg, is a front for a hijacking and theft ring led by John Harris (George McDaniel). When Jonas is framed for a hijacking by Harris's crew, Cooter takes the rap for Jonas to stop Harris from framing him. This is much to Boss and Rosco's delight, since Cooter unwittingly implicates Bo and Luke as accessories. With Jonas in hiding, Bo and Luke help Cooter escape from jail. While Jesse and Daisy try to infiltrate Harris's distribution firm, Luke goes undercover as a driver for their operation to set a trap for the hijackers, but when Rosco and Boss show up to arrest Bo and Cooter, they are forced to take drastic action. The Dukes are celebrating the anniversary of the day they got the General Lee eight years ago in 1976, and we see the story of how they got it. Eight years ago, Luke was just out of the Marines, and Bo was just out of high school. Two jewel thieves named Ginny (Janie Fricke) and Rick (Sam Melville) hid $50,000 worth of gold dust under the dashboard of a black Dodge Charger. The car was wrecked and taken to a junkyard. Bo and Luke were searching for a race car to compete in a local race with a $10,000 prize. Their search led them to the black Dodge Charger. The Dukes bought the car and took it to Cooter's garage to soup it up and paint it its current color, orange—the only color Cooter had at his garage at the time. It was Jesse's idea to name it the General Lee. The number 01, as Bo explained, means "From here on out, it's number one all the way." Ginny and Rick go after the Dukes to get the gold dust, but the Dukes manage to stop them, win the race, and keep the General Lee. After six seasons of complaining in song that they "keep showing my hands and not my face on TV," Waylon Jennings finally appears on The Dukes of Hazzard, on camera. An old friend of the Duke family, Waylon brings his tour bus and traveling museum to Hazzard County. Years ago, before his first professional gig, someone stole Waylon Jennings's guitar. With no money to replace it, he would have missed his opportunity, but then a stranger loaned him the money to replace it. That stranger was Jesse Duke. They have been friends ever since. Waylon enters Hazzard, traveling in a very valuable mobile country music history museum to use as a charity exhibit. This museum, considering its value, is a desirable item for a thief. Boss Hogg is always willing to do almost anything for money. Boss hires two crooks named Buddy (Stephen Lee) and Jeb (Terrence Evans) to steal the museum and hold it for ransom. Bo, Luke, and Daisy are on their way to an old-fashioned hay ride. Meanwhile, a truck carrying an experimental genetic drug accidentally drops a vial of it into the Hazzard pond. Shortly after, the Dukes must stop at the pond to get water for the General Lee's radiator, since it has overheated. While filling a jug of water from the lake, Luke also takes a small drink. He does not realize he is drinking water contaminated by the genetic drug. Luke begins to experience a severe personality change. He becomes obnoxious and turns on Bo. When they get to the hay ride, Luke insults Enos and says he now sees that Hazzard is just a joke of a town. When all the Dukes are back at the farm, Luke continues to insult his family. He forgoes the ceremony of saying grace and insults Uncle Jesse's cooking. For Bo, this is the last straw, and he wants to have it out with Luke. Jesse asks Bo to hold back. Luke takes off in the General. Out of respect for Jesse's wishes, Bo agrees to go look for the dramatically changed Luke. Luke, now under the full influence of the drug, goes on a rampage, even running Bo off the road. Luke is observed by Hurley (Alan Autry) and Ben (Greg Finley), two men planning to rob the Hazzard Bank, and they are looking for a good getaway driver. Luke, in his current frame of mind, agrees to help them for a cut of the money. Soon, Boss Hogg becomes aware of Hurley and Ben's plans to rob his bank and begins to devise his own plan to catch Hurley, Ben, and especially Luke in the act. Meanwhile, the remaining Dukes discover the empty genetic drug vial at the lake and go to the research company in Atlanta to find out more information, hoping to save Luke from its effects. Dr. Debbie Davis (Lori Hallier) tells them the drug will not wear off until 11:00 AM the following morning. The Dukes hurry back to Hazzard to try to prevent Luke from getting himself into trouble. However, they arrive too late. Luke has already done the robbery with Hurley and Ben, and he has been videotaped by Boss's surveillance cameras. It is up to Uncle Jesse and Daisy to catch up to Rosco and get the tape from him before he delivers it to the authorities. Rosco is unwilling to listen to their story, but Rosco's dog Flash chews the tape up. Bo and Enos find Hurley and Ben. Bo has it out with Luke. During the fight, the drug wears off, and Luke is his old self again. Luke apologizes to everyone he insulted while under the influence of the drug, and everyone is forgiving. A computer technician named Rance (Ray Colbert) is fired from his job shortly after completing work on a contract. He and a co-worker named Marv (William Allen Young) get revenge against their former employer by stealing a cache of electronics to sell on the black market, then stealing them back for ransom. One of those items is an advanced robot named Bobby Joe (Robert Shields). Bo and Luke, who had an earlier skirmish with Rance and Marv, become suspicious and investigate their van. Rosco catches the Duke boys inside the van but bungles the arrest. The robot, however, is easily able to apprehend the Dukes. Boss Hogg is impressed, buys the robot, and promptly promotes Bobby Joe to Hazzard County Sheriff. Boss Hogg is unaware that Marv and Rance have.

doc_name: List of The Dukes of Hazzard episodes
text: During the fight, the drug wears off, and Luke is his old self again. Luke apologizes to everyone he had insulted while under the influence, and everyone forgives him. A computer technician named Rance (Ray Colbert) is fired shortly after completing work on a contract. He and his co-worker Marv (William Allen Young) get revenge by stealing a cache of electronics to sell on the black market and later stealing them back for ransom. One of the stolen items is an advanced robot named Bobby Joe (Robert Shields). Bo and Luke, who previously had a conflict with Rance and Marv, become suspicious and investigate their van. Rosco catches the Duke boys inside the van but bungles the arrest. The robot easily apprehends the Dukes. Boss Hogg is impressed, buys the robot, and promotes Bobby Joe to Hazzard County Sheriff. Hogg is unaware that Marv and Rance plan to use Bobby Joe to rob the Hazzard Bank. The Dukes become suspicious and begin investigating, eventually finding the crooks' hideout and their ransom note to the electronics company, proving Bobby Joe was stolen. When Marv and Rance discover the Dukes have been snooping, they capture them and tie them up before heading to rob the bank. After loading all the loot into their truck, they have Bobby Joe hold Rosco at the scene to make it appear as if Rosco robbed the bank. When Boss Hogg arrives, he is angry at Rosco until the Dukes explain everything about Marv and Rance. The Dukes flee in the General, followed by Rosco and Enos, to find Marv and Rance. Bo and Luke stop Marv and Rance's truck and grab them. Rosco and Enos arrive just in time to capture Marv and Rance and recover the stolen money. Rosco is now a proud sheriff once again. A senator is visiting Hazzard to inspect law enforcement, and Boss Hogg frames the Dukes by convincing them that Daisy won prizes, including a fur coat and a diamond necklace, at the Capitol City Department Store as the 1,000,000th customer—though the prizes were stolen from Boss Hogg's own robbery. Just as Hogg plans to send the Dukes to prison, he takes a blow to the head and wakes up with amnesia. He suddenly becomes a nice guy and double-crosses his partners Stoney (John Matuszak) and Zack (Jan Eddy), who want to silence him. While a Hollywood production company is filming in Hazzard, star Brock Curtis (Barry Van Dyke) loses brake control in his car and is saved by the Dukes. The producers offer the Dukes a part in the movie. The Dukes, with Boss and Rosco, travel to Hollywood. In Hollywood, Boss and Rosco try to get into a movie, but Flash catches the attention of a talent agent. The Dukes discover that Brock's near-accident was no accident—producer Jason Dillard (Brett Halsey), who is facing severe financial problems, has taken out a $5,000,000 life insurance policy on Brock and has arranged for Blake (Frank Annese) to kill him to collect the money. The Dukes must stop Dillard and Blake. Boss Hogg's arch-enemy, Colonel Cassius B. Claybourne (Morgan Woodward), commissioner of Osage County, plans to take over Hazzard County. He arrests Bo and Luke while they pass through Osage County and puts them on the chain gang, where they are harassed by guards led by Captain Slater (Brion James). With public pressure mounting, Boss and Rosco give in to Claybourne's demand to surrender Boss's moonshine contracts in exchange for Bo and Luke's freedom. When they go to Osage County to retrieve Bo and Luke, Claybourne arrests them and places them on the road gang along with Bo and Luke. Claybourne exploits Boss's love for high-calorie food to extort him, eventually forcing him to give up most of Hazzard County. Bo, Luke, and Daisy, along with Jesse and General Lee, must break everyone out and reclaim Hazzard from Claybourne and his sheriff, R. P. "Droopy" Cathcarte (Claude Earl Jones). After inheriting his grandfather's estate, Boss Hogg finds a letter from Jesse's great-great-grandfather Jeremiah Duke stating that Jeremiah signed the Duke farm over to Boss Hogg's great-great-grandfather Thaddeus B. Hogg in 1872, when Hazzard was known as Sleepy City. Boss evicts the Dukes from the farm, but before leaving, they examine Jeremiah's diary, which reveals that Thaddeus Hogg pressured Jeremiah to sell the farm. Bo, Luke, and Daisy's great-grandparents—Joe Duke, Hank Duke, and Dixie Duke—came to help Jeremiah and faced Hogg's hired men: Frank James (Nick Benedict) and Jesse James (Paul Koslo). When they could not scare off the Dukes, Hogg framed Hank for horse rustling and traded Hank's freedom for the farm. Thinking he had won, Hogg headed to town just as the James boys robbed his safe, capturing him and Rufus Z. Coltrane, Rosco's great-great-grandfather, and fleeing to the hills. The Dukes of old may have saved the day then, and this history may help the present-day Dukes keep the farm from Boss Hogg. Cale Yarborough visits Hazzard to see Robbie (Chad Sheets), an orphan about to undergo surgery at Tri-County Hospital. Eddie Scoggins (Al White) and Elmo Smith (Dennis Haskins), who robbed the Capitol City Bank and bought a hideout from Boss Hogg, frame Bo, Luke, and Cale for the robbery. A train is coming through Hazzard County with a box car containing over $3,000,000 in valuables. Boss Hogg hires three men—Burke (Wayne Grace), Carney (Steve James), and Perry (Ted Markland)—and masterminds a plan to knock the boxcar off the train using a remotely controlled car. When that car is wrecked, Burke, Carney, and Perry steal the General Lee instead. Using the General Lee would implicate Bo and Luke, so when Bo and Luke search for it, they are captured, gagged, and planned to be killed—something Boss would never approve of. Jesse and Daisy must find Bo and Luke and help them. Boss is appalled by the plan to kill Bo and Luke, so he, Rosco, and Enos join in to stop it. Escaped convict and former Marine Lee Benson (Judson Scott) and his accomplice Brad Hixx (Robert Gray) go to Hazzard to settle a score with Luke. While in the Marines, Luke was a sergeant and Benson had robbed his best friend's foot locker, which Luke discovered and had Benson imprisoned for several years. Now, Benson wants Luke to pay for that. As part of his plan, Benson orders Bo and Luke to drive them out of state in the General Lee at gunpoint, without revealing anything is wrong when approached by authorities. Chickasaw County Sheriff Big Ed Little (Don Pedro Colley), tracking Benson and Hixx, assumes the Dukes are helping them. To avoid detection, Benson and Hixx force Bo and Luke to drive through a forest fire. When Sheriff Little locks everyone except Enos in a holding cell, Bo and Luke rely on Enos' help and their own wits to stop Benson and Hixx. A group of armored car robbers—Kate (Karen Lamm), Taylor (Bob Hastings), Budge (Chip Heller), and Cleary (Michael Prokopuk)—steal an armored car by lifting it with a helicopter, carrying Boss' uninsured bank money. The Dukes are blamed for the theft. When Bo and Luke are arrested, the robbers strike again. Knowing the Dukes are innocent, Boss and Rosco allow them to escape so they can pursue the hijackers. The robbers then kidnap Daisy. Bo, Luke, Jesse, Enos, Boss, and Rosco team up to rescue Daisy. Bo and Luke take to the air to locate the gang's hideout. Boss Hogg's great-uncle Silas Hogg has died and left $100,000 to charity at the discretion of the executor, Jesse. Boss, wanting the money, tries every trick to become executor. At Silas' farm, the Dukes, with the help of a ventriloquist and special effects wizard named Mr. Winkle (Bill McLean), set up gadgets to make it appear that Silas is haunting Boss, causing him to give up his plan. Boss's attorney, Larson (Jason Evers), tries to obtain the money. Hughie Hogg (Jeff Altman) returns to Hazzard with a plan to cheat Boss out of everything. With the help of Trixie (Katherine "Kitty" Moffat), Hughie makes Boss believe there is a genie in a magic lamp that grants untold wealth and a way to get rid of Bo and Luke. The Dukes must stop Hughie before Bo and Luke end up in prison, leaving Boss and Rosco with only a worthless lamp. There have been recent UFO sightings in Hazzard County, and Bo and Luke initially think people are crazy until an alien (Felix Silla) hides in the General Lee and returns to the Duke farm. Boss wants to use the visitor as a tourist attraction. At the same time, thieves Mickey Larsen (Dennis Burkley) and Buck Simmons (Britt Leach) are casing Hazzard for a planned bank robbery. Two crooks, Slade (Anthony De Longis) and Jerry (Scott Lincoln), force an unwilling Enos to hand over a bank transfer shipment. Daisy sees Enos with the money but does not see Slade and Jerry, who threaten to shoot her if Enos does not comply. Slade and Jerry escape. Because Daisy only sees Enos getting the money, the state's Deputy Attorney General (Michael Fairman) jails Enos for robbery. Daisy cannot refuse to testify against Enos or face contempt. Knowing Enos would never rob a bank, Daisy proposes marriage to him, as a wife cannot be legally forced to testify against her husband. Slade and Jerry try to stop the marriage because it would expose their frame-up. To clear Enos' name, Bo and Luke search for Slade and Jerry. Lulu Hogg stages her annual charity talent contest at the Boar's Nest. Rosco performs a magic act and names Boss Hogg as his assistant. Boss is annoyed because it conflicts with a scheduled business appointment. Knowing Lulu would walk out on him if he refuses, Boss agrees to participate. He schemes to use the "disappearance" to drive into town for his appointment. However, the disappearance works too well. Paroled convict Floyd Malone (Kevin Peter Hall) and his brother Bubba (Ji-Tu Cumbuka) want to make Boss pay for testifying against Floyd in a hijacking case three years ago. They kidnap Boss outside the Boar's Nest—unknown to Rosco, the Dukes, or others inside. After convincing Lulu that Boss's disappearance may have been foul play, Bo and Luke search for the Malones, who demand $1,000,000 or Boss will be killed. The Dukes struggle to convince grief-stricken Rosco that his magic was not responsible. Bo and Luke hatch a plan to rescue Boss. Once Boss is freed and the Malones are arrested, Bo and Luke convince Boss to complete the second half of Rosco's magic trick. Boss still refuses until he sees an emotional Rosco recalling their shared memories and how Boss was the only one who stood by him. Boss "reappears" on cue when Rosco performs the trick one last time. An overjoyed Rosco is happy to see Boss again. Guest starring includes Alan Autry as Hurley; Lori Hallier as Dr. Debbie Davis; Greg Finley as Ben; Ben Slack as Mr. Adams; James Bradford as Toby; Rick Johnson as Zeb (uncredited); Robert Shields as Bobby Joe the Robot; William Allen Young as Marv; Audrey Landers as Billie Jean; John Matuszak as Stoney; Jan Eddy as Zack; Barry Van Dyke as Brock Curtis; Joel Brooks as the Director; Brett Halsey as Jason Dillard; Frank Annese as Blake; Jason Bernard as the Chief Guard; Floyd Levine as G.S. Baldwin; Karen Witter as Jackie; Brion James as Captain Slater; Claude Earl Jones as Sheriff R. P. "Droopy" Cathcarte; James Avery as Charlie; Morgan Woodward as Col. Cassius B. Claiborne; Tom Willett as Deputy (uncredited); Paul Koslo as Jesse James; Nick Benedict as Frank James; Cale Yarborough as himself; Al White as Eddie Scoggins; Dennis Haskins as Elmo Smith; Chad Sheets as Robby; Wayne Grace as Burke; Steve James as Carney; Judson Scott as Lee Benson; Robert Gray as Brad Hixx; Karen Lamm as Kate; Bob Hastings as Taylor; Chip Heller as Budge; Michael Prokopuk as Cleary; Brenda Bowie as the aerobics instructor; Robert Resnick as the Driver; Jason Evers as Attorney Larson; Chris Mulkey as Sharp; Katherine Moffat as Trixie; Pat Studstill as Barclay; Roger Torrey as Norris; Dennis Burkley as Mickey Larsen; Britt Leach as Buck Simmons; Ritchie Montgomery as Elton Loggins; Felix Silla as "Little Cousin"; Anthony De Longis as Slade; Scott Lincoln as Jerry; Michael Fairman as Deputy Attorney General; Royce Applegate as Insurance Adjuster; Kevin Peter Hall as Floyd Malone; Ji-Tu Cumbuka as Bubba Malone. Recurring guests include Parley Baer as Doc Appleby, Peggy Rea as Lulu Coltrane Hogg, and Don Pedro Colley as Sheriff Ed Little. Recurring guest is Jeff Altman as Hughie Hogg.

doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: The Tom and Jerry animated series features a list of characters introduced in chronological order. Thomas "Tom" (originally named "Jasper") is a bluish grey and white domestic shorthair cat, typically living a comfortable, pampered life, while Gerald "Jerry" (originally called "Jinx"), a brown house mouse, lives nearby. Despite being larger and more energetic, Tom is no match for Jerry’s intelligence and strength, often able to lift heavy objects like anvils and withstand significant impacts. Though cats usually chase mice to eat them, Tom rarely attempts to eat Jerry; instead, he often taunts him or seeks rewards from humans for catching him. Jerry usually wins by the end of each cartoon, though Tom triumphs occasionally—such as in The Million Dollar Cat, where Jerry’s actions provoke Tom’s retaliation, or in Timid Tabby, where Tom’s cousin pushes Jerry too far. Rarely, both characters lose, like in Filet Meow, where Jerry’s trap backfires, or when Jerry overlooks something. They occasionally form temporary truces, such as in Posse Cat, where they agree to share a reward, but these break down when one reneges. In Snowbody Loves Me, they end on a friendly note. Both characters exhibit sadistic tendencies, enjoying tormenting each other, but show conscience when one is in danger from an unplanned event or a third party. They sometimes bond over shared negative experiences and act as allies against third-party tormentors, though these alliances dissolve when unexpected events occur or when one feels the other is no longer needed. Characters introduced in the theatrical shorts directed by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera include Spike, a stern, occasionally dim-witted grey bulldog who disapproves of cats but is gentle toward mice, with a possessiveness over his bone and ticklishness; Spike’s first speaking role was in The Bodyguard (1944), voiced initially by Billy Bletcher until 1949, and later by others including Patrick McGeehan, Jerry Mann, Bob Shamrock, John Brown, Fred Karbo, Stan Freberg, and Daws Butler; Spike is protective of his son Tyke, who does not speak in Tom and Jerry or the 2014 TV series (except for laughing in one short), but speaks in Tom and Jerry Kids, voiced by Patric Zimmerman. Nibbles (also known as Tuffy) is a small blue/gray, diaper-wearing orphan mouse who appears frequently with Jerry, especially in comics; his debut was in The Milky Waif (1946), and he was featured in the Academy Award-winning short The Little Orphan (1949); he is sometimes called Jerry’s nephew but is more accurately described as an orphan; he is often shown eating excessively and was left on Jerry’s doorstep in his first appearance; Tom chases him as much as Jerry. Though created as Tuffy in comics in 1942, early animated appearances used the name Nibbles; from the 1950s onward, he was called Tuffy on-screen; in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring (2002), he is named Nibbles again and is portrayed as a pet-store mouse unknown to Jerry. In Mouseketeer shorts, Nibbles speaks in French and English, and is not Jerry’s nephew but the son of François Mouse, whose name appears in Touché, Pussy Cat! (1954); he is often mistaken for a girl due to his high-pitched voice, voiced by Francoise Brun-Cottan, Lucille Bliss, Lou Scheimer, Frank Welker, Charlie Adler, Tara Strong, Reece Thompson, Chantal Strand, Kath Soucie (from 2010), and Alan Marriott (in video games). Butch, a black alley cat, first appeared in Baby Puss (1943) alongside Topsy and Meathead, though unnamed in The Alley Cat (1941), where he was referred to as "Tom" in a model sheet; in Baby Puss, he torments Tom after Tom is dressed up as a baby; he is the leader of alley cat bullies who help Tom catch Jerry and competes with Tom over Toodles Galore, creating a love triangle in Springtime for Thomas (1946) and Casanova Cat (1951); in A Mouse in the House (1947), he battles Tom to catch Jerry; in Blue Cat Blues (1956), he is portrayed as a millionaire; he appears in Scat Cats (1957) as a house cat owned by George and Joan. Butch is voiced by Harry E. Lang in The Alley Cat, Jack Mather in Baby Puss, Frank Graham in Springtime for Thomas and Trap Happy (1946), Raul Martinez in Springtime for Thomas (singing voice), Jerry Mann in Casanova Cat, Fred Karbo in Life with Tom, Daws Butler in Baby Butch (1954), Smarty Cat (1955), and Scat Cats (1957), Alan Marriott in Fists of Furry (2000), Marc Silk in War of the Whiskers (2002), Maurice LaMarche in The Magic Ring (2002), Tony Cervone in The Karate Guard (2005), Colin Murdock in Tom and Jerry Tales (2006–08), Joey D'Auria in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021) and Tom and Jerry in New York (2021), and Nicky Jam in Tom & Jerry (2021). Toodles Galore is an attractive white female cat with a large blue bow, considered Tom’s love interest though Tom is a playboy with other interests; she is the only love interest to appear more than twice; Tom lost her to Butch and Spike, and in Casanova Cat (1951), she fell in love with Jerry. Toodles is one of the more anthropomorphic animals, with human-like features such as sitting in human poses, walking on two feet, having human-shaped hands with painted nails, and human-like eyes and lips; she wears a bathing suit in Salt Water Tabby (1947) and has cat ears and nose; she never speaks and rarely moves. She appears in four episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales (2006–2008): "Joy Riding Jokers," "Spaced Out Cat," "Piranha Be Loved By You," "Abracadumb," and "Flamenco Fiasco," credited as "Senorita Cat" in the latter, voiced by Chantal Strand; in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021), she makes cameo appearances in "Belly Achin'", "Cat Napped," "Don't Cut the Cheese," and "A Star Forlorn," and has a full appearance in Season 4’s "Tap Cat"; she appears in Tom and Jerry in New York, voiced by Rachael MacFarlane; a similar white cat appears in the 2021 film. Mammy Two Shoes (voiced by Lillian Randolph) is an African-American woman whose role as a maid or homeowner is never clarified; her face is never seen except briefly in Saturday Evening Puss (1950), and she usually beats Tom (addressed as "Thomas") with a broom when he misbehaves or tries to get rid of Jerry; she appears in 19 cartoons from Puss Gets the Boot (1940) to Push-Button Kitty (1952); Anita Brown voices her in The Mouse Comes to Dinner; the character became controversial due to the Mammy archetype and was retired in 1953; Gene Deitch avoided her due to its outdated nature; MGM Animation/Visual Arts, under Chuck Jones, replaced her with a rotoscoped white woman (mostly stocky or thin), with Randolph’s voice replaced by June Foray’s Irish-accented or generic young adult voice; three years after Turner acquired the series, Lillian Randolph’s voice was replaced by Thea Vidale, who re-recorded dialogue to remove stereotypes. Little Quacker is a duck and recurring character appearing in Little Quacker (1950), Just Ducky (1953), Downhearted Duckling (1954), Southbound Duckling (1955), That's My Mommy (1955), Happy Go Ducky (1958), and The Vanishing Duck (1958); he speaks frequently, with a "duck voice" similar to Disney’s Donald Duck; he is trusting, even allowing Tom to eat him; he is a friend of Jerry but has no hard feelings toward Tom; in three cartoons, he is separated from his mother at birth and reunites with her in two; in That's My Mommy, he is adopted by Tom; in Little Quacker, his father Henry appears; due to differing birth depictions, he may have siblings; he has a girlfriend named Fifi in Downhearted Duckling; he appears in "The Lost Duckling" (1975) in The Tom and Jerry Show; he inspired Yakky Doodle in Hanna-Barbera shows and Hard Luck Duck in What a Cartoon! (1995), voiced by Russi Taylor. Quacker is voiced by Red Coffey in classic shorts, Don Messick in The Tom and Jerry Show (1975), Alan Marriott in Fists of Furry and War of the Whiskers (named "Duckling" in those games), and Sam Kwasman in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014) and Tom and Jerry in New York. Cuckoo, a canary first appearing in Kitty Foiled (1948), also appears in The Flying Cat (1952), Life with Tom (1953), Hic-cup Pup (1954), Two Little Indians (red version), and Matinee Mouse (reusing clips); he is Jerry’s best friend and can carry heavy objects, such as a bowling ball or a 2000 lb. weight. Lightning, a ginger orange cat, first appears in Old Rockin' Chair Tom (1948) as Tom’s rival, named for his speed; in later appearances, he is one of Tom’s alley cat rivals with the same design as Butch but in orange; in Mucho Mouse, he speaks Spanish and is a house cat; he appears in Switchin' Kitten (Gene Deitch) and Catty-Cornered (Chuck Jones), where he has a more orange-yellow color, black tail and ears; he also appears in the live-action film, voiced by Joey Wells. Topsy is a grey/brown Scottish Fold kitten, one of Tom’s alley cat friends/foes, though in Professor Tom he befriends Jerry; he first appears in Baby Puss and last in Scat Cats; in Tom and Jerry Tales, he has a more yellowish color; in Professor Tom, he is explicitly a house cat; more often, he is an alley cat or of unknown origin; in the live-action film, he is voiced by Harry Ratchford. Meathead is a brown, mangy alley cat with a red toupee, first appearing in Sufferin' Cats! (1943) as Tom’s rival; he appears in Baby Puss and other shorts as a rival or ally; he is known as Frankie in Heavenly Puss; in Scat Cats, his final appearance, he is portrayed with all-gray fur. Meathead appears in several episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales with an orange color similar to Lightning, and has a red nose; in two episodes, he has a bush.

doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: Jerry first appears in Baby Puss and makes his final appearance in the original theatrical shorts in Scat Cats. In Tom and Jerry Tales, he is depicted with a more yellowish color, similar to Life with Tom. Topsy, another character, is explicitly a house cat in Professor Tom; more often, he is shown as an alley cat or of unknown origin, as seen in Saturday Evening Puss and other shorts. In the live action film, Topsy is voiced by Harry Ratchford. Meathead is a brown, mangy alley cat who wears a red toupee, occasionally matching the color of his fur; he is generally portrayed as dull-witted and first appears in Sufferin' Cats! (1943) as Tom's rival. He also appears in Baby Puss and other shorts as one of Tom's alley cat buddies or foes, known as Frankie in Heavenly Puss. In Scat Cats, his final appearance, he is portrayed with an all-gray color. Meathead appears in several episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales with an orange color similar to Lightning, has a red nose, and in two episodes, a bushy tail. He reappears in the episode "Cruisin' for a Bruisin'" as a lead antagonist, while a drag version named "Meathelda" appears in "Hop to It!". He makes multiple appearances in later seasons, usually alongside Butch and other alley cats, and appears in the live action film, voiced by Na'im Lynn. George and Joan, voiced by Daws Butler (1954–1957; George), Richard Anderson (1958; George), June Foray (1954–1956; Joan), Julie Bennett (1956–1958; Joan), Pilar Arcos (1957; Joan), and Perry Sheehan (1958; Joan), are an average middle-class white couple who debut in Pet Peeve (1954), replacing Mammy Two Shoes. They own Tom, Jerry, and Spike, though Tom likes to keep Joan company and Spike likes to keep George company. Joan is often seen cooking or sitting on her armchair knitting or sewing a dress with Tom nearby. George hates monthly bills and complains they are too expensive, but when not complaining, he reads the newspaper in his smart purple or grey suit, with Spike keeping him company. Both are kind and polite to each other and to Tom and Spike. In Pet Peeve, they decide to keep Jerry as a pet because he is easy to care for and eats little, telling Tom and Spike to leave. However, in later shorts, Tom and Spike still live with them, and Jerry is not a pet. George and Joan appear in three other shorts: Tom's Photo Finish, Busy Buddies, and The Vanishing Duck (Quacker's last short), and one Spike and Tyke short, Scat Cats. In some shorts, Joan appears without George, such as in Mouse for Sale, The Flying Sorceress, Mucho Mouse, and Tot Watchers, suggesting George is working at his office. Jeannie, the babysitter of George and Joan's baby, is an average teenager who spends much of her time on the phone and is often called upon to look after the baby. She leaps straight onto the phone when George and Joan shut the front door, indicating negligence. Despite this, she is kind, friendly, cheerful, and rarely loses her smile—except when scolding Tom for "bothering the baby," which she believes Tom and Jerry do on purpose. Jeannie and the baby appear in only two cartoons: Busy Buddies (1956) and Tot Watchers (1958). Jeannie is voiced by Janet Waldo in the original shorts; in Tom & Jerry Kids, the babysitter is slightly younger and a redhead instead of a blonde. In Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring, the baby's name is changed to Freddie and he is hostile toward Jerry (though it could be a different mouse identical to Muscles). Due to modern sensibilities, this negligent climax is no longer used in newer entries because child neglect is now a serious issue. A handful of teenage babysitters in The Flintstones have a similar climax. The Ants are an army of red ants who steal food and appear in Cat Napping, Pup on a Picnic, Barbecue Brawl, and Carmen Get It!, and also in Tom & Jerry Kids. They are unusually heavy for their size, and their combined weight often breaks items like Tom's hammock or causes tables and diving boards to shake. It is unclear how or why they are so heavy. Each guardian devil for Tom and Jerry appears in three cartoons: Sufferin' Cats! (1943), Springtime for Thomas (1946), and Smitten Kitten (1952). In the first, one serves as an evil conscience for Tom and in the other for Jerry. A tiny goldfish lives in the same house as Tom and Jerry and first appears in The Little Goldfish (1939) by Rudolf Ising. Major roles come in Jerry and the Goldfish (1951) and Filet Meow (1966), where Tom's attempts to eat her lead to Jerry winning her affections. She appears in cameo roles in Puss Gets the Boot (1940), Puss n' Toots (1942), Baby Puss (1943), The Million Dollar Cat (1944), Casanova Cat (1951), The Missing Mouse (1953), Haunted Mouse (1965), and The Brothers Carry-Mouse-Off (1965). Muscles is Jerry's cousin and a mouse with incredible strength. In Jerry's Cousin (1951), Muscles appears to hate cats, including Tom. In Haunted Mouse, another mouse named Merlin, also a cousin of Jerry's, appears as a wizard with magical abilities. Muscles appears again in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring, where his name is changed to Freddie and he is hostile toward Jerry (though it could be a different mouse identical to Muscles). He is voiced by Paul Frees in Jerry's Cousin and by Billy West in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring. He also appears in The Tom and Jerry Show. George is the cat counterpart of Muscles, identical to Tom (though shorter) and a cousin. Unlike Muscles, George is a coward and afraid of mice. He first appears in Jerry's Cousin, where he is thrashed by Muscles (possibly explaining his fear), and has a bigger role in Timid Tabby (1957), where he overcomes his fear. He appears in Tom & Jerry Kids, where his fear seems to reappear even though he pretends it hasn't (his name is changed to Tim in that short). He is voiced by Bill Thompson. Fluff, Muff, and Puff are a trio of brown, black, and orange kittens who first appear in Heavenly Puss (1949) in a cameo during Tom's dream as charming kittens who drown. They also appear as cute but mischievous kittens in Triplet Trouble (1952) and on The Tom and Jerry Show. Chérie is a brown/grey female mouse who serves as Jerry's love interest. She first appears at the end of Springtime for Thomas (1946), then in Smitten Kitten (1952), Touché, Pussy Cat! (1954, where she has an identical twin), Tom and Chérie (1955, the first cartoon where she is named, seen only in silhouette), and The Mouse from H.U.N.G.E.R. (1967, as a ticking time bomb set by Tom). Toots refers to three different characters. The first is a fluffy beige cat in Puss n' Toots (1942) and The Mouse Comes to Dinner (1945), the latter being her only speaking role; she also has a cameo in The Bodyguard (1944) and Smitten Kitten (1952). This version appears in some 1940s Tom and Jerry comics and in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021), mistakenly credited as "Toodles" and voiced by Alicyn Packard. Toots is also a different cat in The Zoot Cat (1944) and in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Kitty Cat Blues." She is occasionally and erroneously called "Sheikie," but this is actually Tom's nickname, as seen on a gift card. Finally, Toots is a mouse who serves as Jerry's love interest in Blue Cat Blues (1956). Toots also appears as an antagonist in Love Me, Love My Mouse (1966). In some mouseketeer series, Tom serves as the king of France, a clear reference to Louis XIV, who is shown as extremely short-tempered and cruel. In The Two Mouseketeers (1952), the king executes Tom; in Royal Cat Nap (1958), he orders Tom's execution. Mechano cat first appears in Push Button Kitty (1952) as Tom's rival. Later, Mechano and Robot-Mouse appear as a cat-like-robot and mouse-like-robot who serve Tom and Jerry, except in Advance and Be Mechanized (1967), when they get revenge and switch roles, controlling their minds and making them do the work. Mechano's attempts to catch or trap Jerry or Robot-Mouse always backfire for Tom, except in Advance and Be Mechanized, where he initially succeeds in catching Robot-Mouse. In Guided Mouse-ille, he can stand upright and use hands to operate a gun from a mobile tank, which backfires, leaving him with a black face and crying in frustration. He sneaks back and shoots Tom, who attempts to shoot him back, but the shot comes out on the wrong end, causing Tom to faint, leaving Mechano laughing. He also appears in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Tin Cat of Tomorrow" (2006), where he is named Verminator 7000. Mechano (called "Robot Cat") appears as a fighter in the video game War of the Whiskers (2002) and is voiced by Marc Silk. The St. Bernard is a dog who first appears in Puttin' on the Dog (1944) and again in The A-Tom-Inable Snowman (1966). Unlike other dogs, he is not hostile to cats and once becomes Tom's medical aid. He also appears in War Dogs and Little Cesario. Eagle is an eagle that tries to steal Jerry for food from Tom. He first appears in Flirty Birdy, then in The Tom and Jerry Show episode "The Egg and Tom and Jerry" (1975, where he is female), and again in Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Bend it like Thomas" (2007). Eagle also appears as a playable character in War of the Whiskers (2002), voiced by Marc Silk. Lion debuted in Slap Happy Lion (1947) by Tex Avery. He transitions from a tame cat in Jerry and the Lion (1950) to a nervous one in "The Hypochondriac Lion" (1975) to a monster in "You're Lion" (2007). He is a playable character in Tom and Jerry in War of the Whiskers, voiced by Alan Marriott. A baby woodpecker first appears in Hatch Up Your Troubles (1949) and its remake The Egg and Jerry (1956), where he can peck into anything, including Tom's stomach or golf club in Tee for Two (1945). Baby Woodpecker and his Mama make cameo appearances in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014). Uncle Pecos is Jerry's cowboyish uncle who appears in Pecos Pest (1955). He is voiced by Shug Fisher and is known to play guitar, wear a black cowboy hat covering his eyes, and pluck each of Tom's whiskers to replace broken strings. Being from Texas, he is shown as super strong and has a stammer, especially while singing. He returns in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Cry Uncle" (2006), voiced by Scott McNeil, where he arrives at Tom and Jerry's house, annoys them with music, and leaves with Auntie Spinner at the end. He makes a second return in The Tom and Jerry Show, voiced by Stephen Stanton, in episodes "I Quit," "Uncle Pecos Rides Again," and "Cat-A-Tonic Mouse" (all 2018). A trio of cats—black, brown, and orange—offer extermination services and first appear in Jerry's Cousin and again in Karate Guard, failing to live up to their promise in each. Butch is the leader in Karate Guard, though he holds that role alone in Trap Happy. A radio with a male human voice broadcasts music, cookery shows, and warnings about escaped animals or bomb threats. In Jerry's Diary (1949), the radio is anthropomorphic (with announcer "Uncle Dudley"), though not in other cartoons. The radio's announcements often cause trouble for Tom, such as in Jerry and the Lion (1950), Little Runaway (1952), The Missing Mouse (1953), Down Beat Bear (1956), fear in Fraidy Cat (1942), embarrassment in Jerry's Diary (1949) and Life with Tom (1953), or as a cause of evil intentions in Jerry and the Goldfish (1951). The radio is voiced by Martha Wentworth in Fraidy Cat, Jerry Mann in The Zoot Cat and Life with Tom, Harry E. Lang in Jerry's Diary, Frank Graham in Jerry and the Lion, Daws Butler in Jerry and the Goldfish and Down Beat Bear, and Paul Frees in The Missing Mouse and Down Beat Bear. Unlike other characters, this is not a character per se but a substitution for another, such as Spike the Bulldog, used for a brief visual gag. A character turns into a jackass when fooled, such as Spike in Solid Serenade (1946), The Framed Cat (1950), and Pet Peeve (1954), or Tom in Polka-Dot Puss (1949). In Pup on a Picnic (1955), 'Jackass' is replaced with 'Sucker'. Characters introduced in the theatrical shorts directed by Gene Deitch in the early 1960s include an overweight, short-tempered, average height, middle-aged, bald white man who becomes Tom's owner in only three of the thirteen cartoons: Down and Outing (1961), High Steaks (1962), and Sorry Safari (1962). Unlike other owners, he has severe anger issues and is repeatedly violent toward Tom. He is voiced by Allen Swift. The Grumpy Owner bears a strong resemblance to Clint Clobber (also voiced by Swift), the property manager of a rundown apartment building created for Terrytoons in the mid to late 1950s. There is debate over whether they are the same character, but Deitch claimed they are different. He is a mad scientist reminiscent of Frankenstein, first appearing in Switchin' Kitten (1961). He is the owner of Jerry (who is also his assistant) and has numerous cats trapped in a prison. When Jerry picks an orange cat named Lightning, the other cats flee in terror as the scientist pulls him out for an experiment. He switches Lightning's mind with that of a bulldog and presents the bulldog as a gift to Jerry. An unnamed thin white lady is Tom's owner in Buddies Thicker Than Water (1962). Chuck Jones uses her in The Unshrinkable Jerry Mouse (1964) and in the revised version of Saturday Evening Puss. She also appears in the movie Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry (2005). Like many early owners, her face is never shown. Characters introduced in theatrical shorts produced by Chuck Jones in the mid to late 1960s include a nameless mouse-sized bulldog designed similarly to Spike the Bulldog, who is Jerry's pet dog companion.

doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: The mad scientist, first appearing in a theatrical short, is the owner of Jerry, who also serves as his assistant, and holds numerous cats in a prison; when Jerry selects an orange cat named Lightning, the other cats flee in fear as the scientist pulls him out for an experiment, switching Lightning’s mind with that of a bulldog and presenting the bulldog as a gift to Jerry. An unnamed thin white lady serves as Tom’s owner in Buddies Thicker Than Water (1962), and also appears in The Unshrinkable Jerry Mouse (1964), the revised version of Saturday Evening Puss, and Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry (2005); her face is never shown. In mid to late-1960s theatrical shorts produced by Chuck Jones, a nameless mouse-sized bulldog, designed similarly to Spike, appears in only two shorts—The Cat's Me-Ouch (1965) and Purr-Chance to Dream (1967)—as Jerry’s pet dog companion, defending him against Tom; he is presumed to be the oldest son of Spike before Tyke, with a big bite like the Tasmanian Devil, and shares Spike’s appearance and personality. A shark that attempts to eat Tom and Jerry appears in Puss 'n' Boats and Filet Meow (1966) and Surf-Bored Cat and Cannery Rodent (1967); it is a blue shark in Cannery Rodent and Surf-Bored Cat, and a great white shark in the other two. In the first half of the 1975 season of The Tom and Jerry Show television series, a gopher who eats vegetables appears in Gopher Broke and The Son of Gopher Broke; a parody of Robin Hood and His Merry Men, including the character based on the Robin Hood tales, appears in Robin Ho Ho and Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse (2012); the primary antagonist in both is based on the Robin Hood character; a love interest for both Tom and Jerry appears in The Ski Bunny and The Tennis Menace; a police officer appears in See Dr. Jackal and Hide and in The Police Kitten, where he is the superior officer to both Tom and Jerry. In The Tom and Jerry Comedy Show, a Basset Hound with a miserable expression, originally from Tex Avery’s 1940s shorts, first appears in a poster cameo in Matinee Mouse (1966) during the Chuck Jones era, and appears in Droopy and Dripple segments, Tom and Jerry Kids, and Tom and Jerry Tales, sometimes opposing Spike; an anthropomorphic, sluggish, sleepy bear from Harman-Ising’s 1930s shorts also appears in direct-to-video films. McWolf, initially named "Slick Wolf," is the villain in the Droopy and Dripple segments, a cruel wolf whose mission is to ruin Droopy’s (and Dripple’s) life and sometimes stay with Miss Vavoom in Tom & Jerry Kids; he is based on the wolf in Red Hot Riding Hood and is voiced by Frank Welker. In Tom & Jerry Kids, Dripple is the son of Droopy, an older version of the infant pup from Homesteader Droopy (1954), always with his father and sometimes thinking better than him; his mother is never mentioned, though Droopy’s frequent relationship with Miss Vavoom suggests she may be dead or divorced with no visitation rights; he is voiced by Charlie Adler. The recurring woman of the show is seductive, changes hairdos, is conquered by Droopy, and is often targeted by McWolf; she is based on Red from Red Hot Riding Hood (1943) and voiced by Teresa Ganzel; she is sometimes called Bubbles Vavoom, Ultra Vavoom, or Sugar Vavoom. A gold cat host of a demonstration and participation show, with a rancher accent and sometimes acting as an enemy to Tom, is purportedly inspired by Southern California car dealer Cal Worthington and voiced by Phil Hartman. Urfo, a six-legged alien dog, frequently arrives on Earth to help Jerry fight Tom; his owners often send people to retrieve him. Clyde, a fat cat who causes problems for Tom despite trying to be friendly and helpful, is voiced by Brian Cummings and appears uncredited in the live-action film Butch's gang. A mangy orange cat, first appearing as an antagonist of Spike or Tyke, is voiced by Pat Fraley. A medically challenged yellow swallow, friends with Jerry in Hard to Swallow, changes to blue in "Swallow the Swallow" and "Grab that Bird" due to being chased by Clyde and Kyle, is voiced by David L. Lander. A grayish-green, shaggy fanged mouse who occasionally replaces Jerry and outwits his foes, voiced by Frank Welker, first appears in "Wildmouse" and is last seen in "King Windmouse." A cougar who torments Spike and Tyke, wanting to eat Tyke’s lunch and prevented by Spike, is voiced by Frank Welker. The elderly sheriff of Hokey Finokey Swamp is arrogant, rude, and self-centered, threatening to send Swampy back to the circus, which he knows promotes animal cruelty, and envies the map Swampy made to find hidden treasure; he appears in "Cajun Gumbo" as the main antagonist and also serves as an antagonist with the Gator Brothers in another episode featuring Wild Mouse. The Gator Brothers are Sheriff Potgut’s henchmen and appear in "Cajun Gumbo" and another episode with Wild Mouse. Stinky Jr. is the son of McWolf and shares his father’s personality. Screwball Squirrel, based on the original Screwy Squirrel from 1944, now takes place in a public city park, where he messes with hot-headed park attendant Dweeble and his dumb guard dog Rumpley; he is voiced by Charlie Adler and appears in one direct-to-video film, Tom and Jerry's Giant Adventure, voiced by Paul Reubens, and makes a cameo in the Season 3 episode "Kid Stuff" of The Tom and Jerry Show. A squirrel superhero, flamboyant and campy, who throws lightning bolts and speaks with a slight Minnesotan accent, appears in the spin-off series Droopy, Master Detective and is voiced by Charlie Adler. In Tom and Jerry Tales, Mauricio, a very amorous octopus gentleman first appearing in the 1953 live-action musical film Dangerous When Wet during a Tom and Jerry sequence with Esther Williams, is voiced by Fernando Lamas and later by David Kaye in "Octo Sauve," where he mistakes Tom for a mermaid and wants to date him, leading them to get lost at sea. The princess appears in Medieval Menace, where she kisses Tom, who has turned into a frog, thinking he is a prince transformed by a spell; she is voiced by Nicole Bouma. Mrs. Two Shoes, a white woman with a personality and name similar to Mammy Two Shoes, appears in "Ho, Ho Horrors," where photos on a mantel suggest she has a family (a man and a boy, shown only as legs and partial torsos); she is voiced by Nicole Oliver. In the 2014 television series Tom and Jerry Show, Rick (voiced by Jason Alexander and later Stephen Stanton) and Ginger (voiced by Grey DeLisle) are a middle-class couple; Rick is more sympathetic toward Spike while Ginger favors Tom; their faces are never seen, but their voices are featured. The Hamster is a small, anti-social, overachieving hamster with light brown fur who wears glasses and is the smartest hamster in the lab. Bot is a robot that cleans the lab with a vacuum and control arm, has a red screen that spots trash, and often mistakes Tom for trash. Beatie and Hildie are witch sisters who serve as Tom and Jerry’s medieval owners. The detective, owner of Tom (and presumably Jerry), appears in first-season episodes such as "Feline Fatale," "One of a Kind," "Haunted Mouse," "Sleuth or Consequences," "Poof!," "Bone Dry," "Cat Napped," and "Curse Case Scenario," where Tom and Jerry work as sleuths using his name and fame in his absence. Dr. Bigby is an eccentric scientist whose experiments often go wrong, and is the owner of Jerry, Napoleon, the Hamster, and Bot. Skid, an orange cat who is always the leader and elected Top Cat, competes with both Tom and Butch for the Golden Fez in the Top Mouse Catchers. George and Junior are based on the original George and Junior from Tex Avery’s 1940s shorts and appear in the Season 4 episode "Shadow of a Doubt" of The Tom and Jerry Show. In various Tom and Jerry movies, Robyn Starling is a young girl whose father Tom and Jerry helped her find in Tom and Jerry: The Movie; she is voiced by Anndi McAfee. Biff Buzzard and Buzz Blister appear in Tom and Jerry: Blast Off to Mars and Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry; in the latter, they are news reporters, and in the former, they are astronauts; Biff is voiced by Billy West and Buzz by Jess Harnell. Blue Parrot Betty is a pet parrot owned by Blue Pirate Bob in Tom and Jerry: Shiver Me Whiskers; she is voiced by Kathy Najimy. Tin, Pan, and Alley are a trio of male Siamese cats created for direct-to-video films, serving as secondary antagonists in Tom and Jerry Meet Sherlock Holmes, Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse, Tom and Jerry's Giant Adventure, Tom and Jerry: The Lost Dragon, and Tom and Jerry: Spy Quest, acting as henchmen for main antagonists; in Tom and Jerry Meet Sherlock Holmes, they are local gravediggers for Professor Moriarty; in Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse, they work as spies for Prince John; in Tom and Jerry: The Lost Dragon, they are the Hench-cats of Drizelda; in Tom and Jerry: Spy Quest, they work for Doctor Zin; they also appear in Tom and Jerry: Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory; named after the 1943 Warner Bros. short Tin Pan Alley Cats; Tin is voiced by Greg Ellis, Pan by Jess Harnell, and Alley by Richard McGonagle. Butch, originally known as Spike until renamed to avoid confusion with Spike from the Tom and Jerry cartoons, is a bulldog from Tex Avery’s 1940s and 1950s shorts, a main antagonist in Droopy shorts (replaced by Hanna-Barbera’s Spike in the 1980s), and has a series of his own; he appears in movies such as Tom and Jerry and the Wizard of Oz and Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring.

doc_name: List of aftershocks of the April 2015 Nepal earthquake
text: After the main earthquake in Nepal on 25 April 2015, there was some seismic activity in the Jumla district prior to the main shock, but these events are not considered foreshocks. As of 7 June 2015, over 304 aftershocks had occurred, a number that seismologists describe as normal. Seismologist Roger Musson notes that the typical pattern for aftershocks is that the largest one occurs one day after the main shock and is one magnitude less. Thus, the 6.7 magnitude aftershock on 26 April 2015, following the 7.8 magnitude main shock, aligns with this pattern. It is highly unlikely that the earthquake was a foreshock to a larger future event, and therefore, an earthquake exceeding 7.8 magnitude is not expected in the near future after 25 April 2015. The list provided below is incomplete and may contain inaccuracies, and it includes only significant earthquakes.

doc_name: List of current members of the King's Privy Council for Canada
text: Members of the King's Privy Council for Canada are entitled to the title The Honourable, while Prime Ministers, Governors General, and Chief Justices are automatically granted the title The Right Honourable. Although Governors General receive the title The Right Honourable upon being sworn in, they are not inducted into the Privy Council until the end of their term, unless they were already members by virtue of another office. Other distinguished individuals, such as prominent former Cabinet ministers, may also be granted the title The Right Honourable. Leaders of opposition parties and provincial premiers are not automatically inducted into the Privy Council; opposition leaders may be added occasionally to mark significant events like the Canadian Centennial in 1967, the patriation of the Constitution, or to enable them to advise on national security issues under the Security of Information Act. Paul Martin introduced the practice of inducting parliamentary secretaries into the Privy Council, though this practice has not been continued by subsequent leaders. The Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act established the Security Intelligence Review Committee (SIRC), requiring its members to be drawn from Privy Council members who were not sitting in the Senate or House of Commons at the time of appointment; thus, individuals not already in the Privy Council were sworn in before being named to the committee. In 2019, the SIRC was replaced by the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency. Traditionally, the Order of Canada has been used to recognize prominent Canadians, but Brian Mulroney appointed 18 Canadians to the Privy Council on Canada Day in 1992 to commemorate Canada's 125th anniversary, and two additional individuals—W.O. Mitchell and Maurice Richard—were appointed later that year. Conrad Black, one of the 18 appointed, was expelled from the Privy Council in 2014 on the recommendation of Prime Minister Stephen Harper. This list details the longest-serving current members of the King's Privy Council for Canada.

Disneyland, a theme park located in Anaheim, California, was conceived by Walt Disney. This list includes attractions such as rides, shows, shops, and parades that have permanently closed at the park, excluding character meets and atmosphere entertainment like roving musicians. It also does not include permanently closed attractions from Disney California Adventure. The Main Street Opera House has hosted various shows over the years. Bear Country opened in 1972, was renamed Critter Country in 1988, and was subsequently renamed Bayou Country in 2024.

doc_name: List of presidents of the Philippines
text: Under the Constitution of the Philippines, the president is both the head of state and government and serves as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The president is directly elected by qualified voters to a six-year term and must be a natural-born citizen of the Philippines, a registered voter, able to read and write, at least forty years of age on the day of the election, and a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately preceding the election. No elected president can seek re-election; however, a successor who has not served more than four years can still run for a full term. Upon resignation or removal, the vice president assumes the presidency. The incumbent president is Bongbong Marcos, who assumed office on June 30, 2022. Emilio Aguinaldo became the first president of the Philippines under the Malolos Republic, known as the First Philippine Republic, which he led until 1901 when he was captured by U.S. forces during the Philippine–American War (1899–1902). The American colonization of the Philippines abolished the First Republic, leading to the U.S. governor-general exercising executive power. In 1935, the United States, fulfilling its promise of full Philippine sovereignty, established the Commonwealth of the Philippines following the ratification of the 1935 Constitution, which restored the presidency. The first national presidential election was held, and Manuel L. Quezon (1935–1944) was elected to a six-year term with no re-election provision as the second Philippine president and first Commonwealth president. In 1940, the Constitution was amended to allow re-election but shortened the term to four years. Three years later, the Second Philippine Republic was established under the 1943 Constitution imposed by Japan after the occupation of the Philippines in 1942 during World War II. José P. Laurel served as puppet president of the Japanese-sponsored government; his de facto presidency, not legally recognized until the 1960s, overlapped with the Commonwealth president, who went into exile. The Second Republic ended after Japan's surrender in 1945, and the Commonwealth was restored that year with Sergio Osmeña (1944–1946) elected as president. Manuel Roxas (1946–1948) succeeded Osmeña after winning the first post-war election in 1946 and became the first president of the independent Philippines when the Commonwealth ended on July 4 of that year, marking the beginning of the Third Republic, which included the administrations of the next five presidents, the last being Ferdinand Marcos (1965–1986), who imposed martial law in 1972 and established the New Society (Bagong Lipunan), leading to the Fourth Republic. Marcos's dictatorship ended in 1986 with his deposition during the People Power Revolution, and the current constitution came into effect in 1987, beginning the Fifth Republic. Among those elected as president, three died in office: Manuel L. Quezon and Manuel Roxas by natural causes, and Ramon Magsaysay in a plane crash (1953–1957). Ferdinand Marcos is the longest-serving president, with 20 years and 57 days in office, making him the only president to serve more than two terms; Sergio Osmeña is the shortest-serving, having served 1 year and 300 days. Two women have held the presidency: Corazon Aquino (1986–1992), who became president following the successful People Power Revolution of 1986, and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo (2001–2010), who ascended to the presidency as vice president upon Estrada's resignation and was later elected to a full six-year term in 2004. Some historians consider Andrés Bonifacio the first president of the Philippines; he was the third Supreme President of the Katipunan, which he transformed into a revolutionary government known as the Tagalog Republic upon the Cry of Balintawak in August 1896. While the term "Tagalog" referred to a specific ethnicity, Bonifacio used it to represent all indigenous Filipinos, replacing the colonial term "Filipino." Some historians argue that including Bonifacio as a president should also include Macario Sakay and Miguel Malvar, who continued Aguinaldo's leadership after his capture and revived the Tagalog Republic in 1902, respectively. These individuals are considered "unofficial presidents" by some scholars and are not recognized as presidents by the Philippine government. Emilio Aguinaldo is officially recognized as the first president of the Philippines, based on his term during the Malolos Republic, though he had previously led several revolutionary governments that are not counted in the official succession of Philippine republics. Manuel L. Quezon delegated his presidential duties to José Abad Santos, then-Chief Justice, when he fled the Philippines during Japanese occupation to establish a government-in-exile; Abad Santos is believed to have functioned as acting president, though no legal document confirms the transfer of the presidency. Three former vice presidents—S. Laurel, Binay, and Robredo—have made unsuccessful runs for the presidency. The list provided includes only cabinet secretaries who served full-time; vice presidents who served concurrently as cabinet secretaries are not included.

doc_name: List of prime ministers of Nepal
text: The position of the Prime Minister of Nepal (Nepali: नेपालको प्रधानमन्त्री, romanized: Nepālko Pradhānmantrī) has evolved through various names and structures throughout Nepalese history. In the early period of the Shah dynasty, the Mulkajis (Chief Kajis) or Chautariyas served as prime ministers within a council consisting of 4 Chautariyas, 4 Kajis, and other officers known as Bharadars, who were typically drawn from high-caste and politically influential families such as the Pande, Basnyat, and Thapa families. The nobility of Gorkha, primarily composed of Chhetri families, played a significant role in civil administration. In 1804, Rana Bahadur Shah established a single authoritative position called Mukhtiyar, which held executive powers of the nation. This position remained the head of the executive until November 1843, when Mathabar Singh Thapa was appointed as Mukhtiyar and Prime Minister and also became the Chief of the Nepalese Army. During the Rana dynasty, the prime ministerial office became hereditary, and officeholders were granted additional titles, including Maharaja of Lamjang and Kaski, Supreme Commander-in-Chief of Nepal, and Grand Master of the Royal Orders of Nepal. After the 1951 revolution, non-aristocratic individuals such as Matrika Prasad Koirala held the office under the authority of the King. The first general election was held in 1959, resulting in Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala becoming the first elected prime minister. However, he was removed and imprisoned in the 1960 coup d'état led by King Mahendra, who established the Panchayat system, a regime without democratic governance, until 1990. The Jana Andolan movement in 1990 led to the transformation of the Kingdom into a constitutional monarchy. This was later disrupted by the 2005 coup d'état by King Gyanendra. Following the Loktantra Andolan movement in 2006, the monarchy was abolished on 28 May 2008 by the 1st Constituent Assembly, and Nepal was declared a federal parliamentary republic. The current constitution was adopted on 20 September 2015, with KP Sharma Oli becoming the first prime minister under this constitution. All prime ministers of Nepal from 1768 to 1950 were Chhetris, except for Ranga Nath Poudyal, who was a Khas Brahmin. Among the 23 men elected since Nepal gained democracy after the Rana dynasty in 1951, 15 were Khas Brahmins, 3 were Thakuri, 2 were Newar Shresthas, 2 were Chhetri, and 1 was a Sanyasi/Dasnami. Executive power was historically shared between the Kajis and Chautariyas.

Roller coasters are amusement rides designed for amusement parks and modern theme parks. Early versions in the 16th and 17th centuries, popular in Russia, involved wooden sleds sliding down large ice slides. The first roller coasters with trains attached to wooden tracks emerged in France in the early 1800s. While wooden roller coasters are still manufactured, steel roller coasters, introduced in the mid-20th century, have become more widespread and are found on every continent except Antarctica. Amusement parks often compete to build the tallest, fastest, and longest rides to attract thrill seekers and increase attendance. Ranked by height, speed, length, and number of inversions, roller coasters have frequently served as key attractions in this competition. Computer-simulated models have driven innovations that enhance thrill levels while improving quality and durability. The debut of Magnum XL-200 in 1989 at Cedar Point marked the first complete-circuit roller coaster to exceed 200 feet (61 m), representing a turning point in the industry. This period, known as the Coaster Wars, saw intense competition as parks raced to set world records, with some records lasting only a year or less. The Smiler features fourteen inversions, the highest number of any roller coaster. Former record holder Kingda Ka, which stood as the world's tallest coaster at 456 feet (139 m) since 2005, held its record until its closure in 2024. Formula Rossa, previously the world's fastest roller coaster, reaches a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h). Steel Dragon 2000, once the world's longest at 8,133 feet (2,479 m), held its record from opening until the launch of Falcons Flight in 2025, which now holds the titles for tallest, fastest, and longest roller coaster. This listing includes all types of roller coaster inversions.

doc_name: List of solar eclipses in the 19th century
text: During the 19th century, there were 242 solar eclipses, consisting of 87 partial, 77 annular, 63 total, and 15 hybrid eclipses (which are a combination of total and annular). The highest number of eclipses in a single year was five, occurring in 1805, while the years 1801, 1812, 1819, 1823, 1830, 1841, 1848, 1859, 1870, and 1880 each had four eclipses.
