Two months, January 1805 and December 1880, each contained two solar eclipses: on January 1 and January 30, 1805, and on December 2 and December 31, 1880. These predictions were provided by Fred Espenak of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. The longest duration of totality, when the Moon fully covered the Sun, occurred on August 7, 1850, with a maximum duration of 6 minutes and 50 seconds; the longest possible duration for a total solar eclipse is 7 minutes and 32 seconds. The longest annular solar eclipse of the century happened on October 30, 1883, lasting 10 minutes and 17 seconds, with a maximum possible duration of 12 minutes and 29 seconds. Four instances of back-to-back hybrid solar eclipses within less than six months occurred in the 19th century: the first on June 6 and November 29, 1807; the second on June 16 and December 9, 1825; the third on October 20, 1827, and April 14, 1828; and the fourth on October 30, 1845, and April 25, 1846. The table lists the date and time of the greatest eclipse in dynamical time (equivalent to Ephemeris Time), the saros series number, the eclipse type (total, annular, partial, or hybrid), the gamma value (indicating how centrally the Moon's shadow hits Earth), and the magnitude (the fraction of the Sun's diameter obscured by the Moon). For total and annular eclipses, the duration, location of the greatest eclipse, and path width are included, along with the geographical areas where the eclipse is visible and a chart showing each eclipse's path.

doc_name: List of speakers of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly
text: The Speaker is the presiding officer of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, the primary law-making body for the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, and is elected by the members of the assembly from among them. The Madras Legislative Council, the first representative legislature for the Madras Presidency, was established in December 1920, with P. Rajagopalachari nominated as its first president, who took office on 17 December 1920. The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy in 1937, transforming the Madras Legislative Council into the upper chamber of a bicameral legislature, with its presiding officer thereafter known as the chairman of the council. This structure continued until the council was abolished in 1986, following Indian Independence. In 1937, the Madras Legislative Assembly was also established as part of this bicameral system, with its presiding officer designated as the speaker. Madras State, which served as the precursor to the current state of Tamil Nadu, was formed after India became a republic on 26 January 1950 and included present-day Tamil Nadu along with parts of present-day Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Kerala. The first legislature of Madras State elected on the basis of universal suffrage was constituted on 1 March 1952, following general elections held in January 1952. Madras State was officially renamed Tamil Nadu in January 1969.

doc_name: List of vice-chancellors of the University of Delhi
text: The vice-chancellor serves as the executive head of the University of Delhi. The list of vice-chancellors of the University of Delhi is available, with references cited as [1][2][3][4].

This list highlights women's firsts, documenting the initial instances when a woman or women achieved a significant historical milestone. The phrase "breaking the gender barrier" or "breaking the glass ceiling" is commonly used to describe such achievements.[1][2] Variants of this concept exist for specific fields, such as "breaking the brass ceiling" for women in the military and "breaking the stained glass ceiling" for women in religious leadership roles.[3][4] Inclusion on the list is limited to accomplishments by women that have had a major historical impact. The list also includes historic firsts involving women serving as heads of state or government. (History Portal is a "main page" linking to broader history topics.)

Elizabeth J. Magie Phillips (née Magie; May 9, 1866 – March 2, 1948) was an American game designer, writer, feminist, and Georgist who invented The Landlord's Game, the precursor to Monopoly, to illustrate the economic teachings of progressive era economist Henry George. Born in Macomb, Illinois, in 1866 to Mary Jane (née Ritchie) and James K. Magie, a newspaper publisher and abolitionist who accompanied Abraham Lincoln in the late 1850s, Magie moved to the D.C. and Maryland area in the early 1880s, where she worked as a stenographer and typist at the Dead Letter Office. She was also a short story writer, poet, comedian, stage actress, feminist, and engineer. At age 26, she received a patent for an invention that improved the typewriting process by allowing paper to pass through rollers more easily; at that time, women held less than one percent of all patents. She briefly worked as a news reporter in the early 1900s and married Albert Wallace Phillips in 1910 at age 44; they had no children. Magie was an outspoken advocate for feminism and Georgism, an economic theory advocating a universal land tax based on land's usefulness, size, and location (the "single tax"), with surplus funds distributed to the public, which aimed to eliminate landowner power, promote land cultivation, and redistribute wealth to low-income individuals. This belief formed the foundation of The Landlord's Game. She believed women were as capable as men in invention and business, a view considered novel and radical in the 1800s; as a stenographer, she earned about $10 a week, insufficient to support herself without a husband. To highlight women's and Black people's subjugated status, she published an advertisement auctioning herself as a "young woman American slave" seeking a husband, which sparked national attention and established her as a bold feminist. In 1903, she applied for a patent on The Landlord's Game, which was granted U.S. Patent 748,626 on January 5, 1904—before women gained national voting rights. The game was designed to demonstrate the negative effects of land monopolism and the benefits of a land value tax, featuring two settings: a monopolist version (Monopoly) where players aim to own industries and drive others out, and an anti-monopolist version (Prosperity) where players create products and interact with opponents. In 1906, she moved to Chicago and co-founded the Economic Game Co. with fellow Georgists to self-publish the game. In 1910, Parker Brothers published her humorous card game Mock Trial. The Newbie Game Co. in Scotland patented a version called "Bre'r Fox and Bre'r Rabbit," though no evidence confirms British patent protection. In 1924, after her original patent expired in 1921, she and her husband patented a revised edition of the game to regain control as it was being copied at colleges. In 1932, the Adgame Company of Washington, D.C. published her second edition, which included both Monopoly and Prosperity. She also developed Bargain Day (1937), a department store-themed game, and King's Men (1937), an abstract strategy game, as well as a third version of The Landlord's Game in 1939. Magie died at age 81 in 1948 and was buried with her husband Albert Wallace Phillips, who died in 1937, in Columbia Gardens Cemetery, Arlington, Virginia. She had no children and was not credited during her lifetime for her impact on board games or American culture. The game gained popularity among college students at Harvard, Columbia, and the University of Pennsylvania, as well as left-leaning middle-class families and Quakers in the Northeast. Thirty years after its invention in 1904, Parker Brothers released a modified version known as Monopoly, which Charles Darrow claimed to have invented in his basement. Magie publicly criticized Darrow and reported earning only $500 from her invention and receiving no credit. In a 1936 Washington, D.C. newspaper interview, she expressed her frustration over the similarities between Monopoly and The Landlord's Game and the lack of recognition and financial return. After Ralph Anspach, creator of the Anti-Monopoly game, discovered Magie's patents during a legal dispute with Parker Brothers, her contributions gained renewed attention. Despite Darrow and Parker Brothers claiming ownership, Magie has posthumously received credit for one of the most popular board games. Her game introduced the circular board format, a novel departure from linear games of the time, and provided entertainment that taught about Georgist principles, wealth distribution, and the dangers of monopolies—elements absent from Darrow’s version of Monopoly. Magie also contributed to the women's movement and Black people's rights by publishing political material in newspapers and inventing games during a period when women held less than one percent of U.S. patents.

Louis Daniel Armstrong (August 4, 1901 – July 6, 1971), nicknamed "Satchmo", "Satch", and "Pops", was an American jazz and blues trumpeter and vocalist, considered one of the most influential figures in jazz. His career spanned five decades and several eras in jazz history. He received numerous accolades, including the Grammy Award for Best Male Vocal Performance for "Hello, Dolly!" in 1965, and a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972. His influence extended across musical genres, with inductions into the DownBeat Jazz Hall of Fame, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame. Born in New Orleans, Armstrong rose to prominence in the 1920s as an inventive trumpet and cornet player, shifting jazz from collective improvisation to solo performance. In 1922, he moved to Chicago with mentor Joe "King" Oliver to join Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, where he gained fame through cutting contests and attracted the attention of Fletcher Henderson. He later moved to New York City, becoming a featured soloist and recording artist, and by the 1950s was an international musical icon, regularly appearing on radio, television, and film. Known for his rich, gravelly voice and skillful improvisation, Armstrong was also a pioneer in scat singing, first recording it on the Hot Five track "Heebie Jeebies" in 1926. His best-known songs include "What a Wonderful World", "La Vie en Rose", "Hello, Dolly!", "On the Sunny Side of the Street", "Dream a Little Dream of Me", "When You're Smiling", and "When the Saints Go Marching In". He collaborated with Ella Fitzgerald on three records: Ella and Louis (1956), Ella and Louis Again (1957), and Porgy and Bess (1959), and appeared in films such as A Rhapsody in Black and Blue (1932), Cabin in the Sky (1943), High Society (1956), Paris Blues (1961), A Man Called Adam (1966), and Hello, Dolly! (1969). Armstrong was one of the first popular African-American entertainers to cross over to wide popularity with white and international audiences. Though he rarely discussed racial issues publicly, he took a well-publicized stand for desegregation during the Little Rock Crisis and could access upper echelons of American society at a time when this was difficult for Black men. Armstrong was born on August 4, 1901, though he often claimed July 4, 1900, and his parents were Mary Estelle "Mayann" Albert and William Armstrong; Mary was from Boutte, Louisiana, and gave birth to her daughter Beatrice "Mama Lucy" Armstrong (1903–1987) when she was about 16. William abandoned the family shortly after. Armstrong was raised by his grandmother until age five, when he returned to his mother. He lived in poverty in The Battlefield neighborhood on Rampart Street and attended the Fisk School for Boys, a segregated school. At age six, he worked for the Karnoffskys, a Jewish family, collecting rags and bones and delivering coal. He sang "Russian Lullaby" with them when their son David was put to bed and credits them with teaching him to sing from the heart. The lyrics he quoted match Irving Berlin's 1927 song, about 20 years after he remembered singing it. In his 1969 memoir, Louis Armstrong + the Jewish Family in New Orleans, LA., the Year of 1907, he described being seven years old when he witnessed discrimination against the Karnoffskys and learned about real life and determination. He may have performed his first musical act at the side of the Karnoffskys' junk wagon, playing a tin horn to attract customers, and Morris Karnoffsky gave him an advance to buy a cornet. At age 11, he dropped out of school. His mother moved into a one-room house on Perdido Street with Armstrong, Lucy, and her common-law husband Tom Lee. Armstrong joined a quartet of boys who sang in the streets; Bunk Johnson taught him to play by ear at Dago Tony's honky tonk. He was arrested on December 31, 1912, for firing a blank from his stepfather's gun and was sent to the Colored Waif's Home, where life was spartan and corporal punishment was used. There, Peter Davis became his first teacher and chose him as bandleader. At age 13, he attracted the attention of Kid Ory. On June 14, 1914, he was released to his father and stepmother, Gertrude, and lived with two stepbrothers for several months before being rejected by his father and returning to his mother. He shared a bed with her and Lucy in a small home in The Battlefield and sought musical work. He found a job at a dance hall owned by Henry Ponce, met the drummer Black Benny, who became his guide and bodyguard, and at age 15 pimped for a prostitute named Nootsy, who stabbed him in the shoulder and was nearly choked to death by his mother. He briefly studied shipping management at a local community college but quit due to financial difficulties. While selling coal in Storyville, he heard spasm bands playing music from household objects and listened to early jazz from bands like Pete Lala's, where King Oliver performed. In the late 1910s, he played in brass bands and riverboats in New Orleans, touring with Fate Marable's band on the steamboat Sidney with the Streckfus Steamers. Marable praised Armstrong's musical knowledge and insisted he learn sight reading, which Armstrong described as "going to the university." In 1918, when King Oliver left Kid Ory's band, Armstrong replaced him and also became second trumpet in the Tuxedo Brass Band. By age 20, he could read music and began performing extended trumpet solos, injecting his own style and starting to sing. In 1922, he moved to Chicago at Oliver's invitation, though he returned to New Orleans periodically. Playing second cornet in Oliver's Creole Jazz Band at the black-only Lincoln Gardens in Chicago, he earned enough to quit day jobs. Chicago offered better job opportunities for Black people, including in factories and entertainment. Oliver's band was influential in the early 1920s. Armstrong lived luxuriously in Chicago with his first private bath and began writing letters to friends in New Orleans. He could blow 200 high Cs in a row and gained a reputation through cutting contests. His first studio recordings with Oliver for Gennett Records occurred on April 5–6, 1923, during a long train journey to Richmond, Indiana, with poor equipment, acoustics, and a cramped studio. The recordings were acoustic, with the band playing directly into a funnel connected to the needle. Because Armstrong played so loudly, Oliver could not be heard, so Armstrong stood 15 feet away. Lil Hardin, whom he married in 1924, urged him to seek more prominent billing and develop his own style. She encouraged him to play classical music in church concerts and dress more stylishly. Her influence strained his relationship with Oliver, especially over salary and withheld earnings. Armstrong's mother visited Chicago in 1923 after being told he was out of work, hungry, and sick; Hardin arranged and decorated an apartment for her. Armstrong and Oliver parted amicably in 1924. He was invited to join Fletcher Henderson's Orchestra, the top African-American band of the time, where he switched to trumpet to blend in. His influence on Coleman Hawkins, Henderson's tenor sax soloist, is evident in their recordings. Armstrong adapted to Henderson's tight style, playing trumpet and experimenting with trombone, and his emotional style affected the entire band. His performances included singing and stories about New Orleans preachers. The Henderson Orchestra played for white patrons only at venues like the Roseland Ballroom, with arrangements by Don Redman, and Duke Ellington's orchestra came to watch Armstrong. During this time, he recorded with Clarence Williams, the Williams Blue Five, Sidney Bechet, and blues singers Alberta Hunter, Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith. In 1925, he returned to Chicago at Lil's insistence, where she billed him as "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player." He joined her band and later formed Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five, recording hits such as "Potato Head Blues" and "Muggles" (a slang term for marijuana). The Hot Five included Kid Ory (trombone), Johnny Dodds (clarinet), Johnny St. Cyr (banjo), Lil Armstrong on piano, and no drummer. Over a 12-month period starting in November 1925, they produced 24 records. Armstrong's leadership style was easygoing, with St. Cyr noting the group felt relaxed and broad-minded. Recordings like "Cornet Chop Suey", "Struttin' With Some Barbecue", "Hotter Than That", and "Potato Head Blues" featured highly creative solos by Armstrong. According to Thomas Brothers, "Struttin' with Some Barbeque" was so well-planned with bluesyness and showiness that it was likely showcased at the Sunset Café. His recordings with pianist Earl "Fatha" Hines, including the 1928 "Weather Bird" duet and his trumpet introduction and solo in "West End Blues", remain among the most influential improvisations in jazz history. Young musicians across the country memorized his solos. Armstrong also played with Erskine Tate's Little Symphony at the Vendome Theatre, providing music for silent films and live shows, including jazz versions of classical pieces like "Madame Butterfly," giving him experience with longer musical forms and large audiences. He began scat singing and was among the first to record it on "Heebie Jeebies" in 1926. The recording's popularity made the Hot Five the most famous jazz band in the U.S., despite rarely performing live. After separating from Lil, Armstrong played at the Sunset Café for Joe Glaser, Al Capone's associate, in the Carroll Dickerson Orchestra, later renamed Louis Armstrong and his Stompers. Hines was the music director and Glaser managed the orchestra. Hines and Armstrong became close collaborators. At the Sunset Café, Armstrong accompanied singer Adelaide Hall, who developed her scat singing with his guidance. In the first half of 1927, Armstrong formed his Hot Seven group, adding drummer Al "Baby" Dodds and tuba player Pete Briggs while keeping most of the original Hot Five lineup, with John Thomas replacing Kid Ory on trombone. Later that year, he recorded nine more records with a new Hot Five lineup. In the second half of 1928, he recorded with Zutty Singleton (drums), Earl Hines (piano), Jimmy Strong (clarinet), Fred Robinson (trombone), and Mancy Carr (banjo). Armstrong made a significant impact during the 1920s Harlem Renaissance, influencing writer Langston Hughes, who admired him and acknowledged him as one of the era's most recognized musicians. Hughes wrote books celebrating jazz and recognized Armstrong as a leader of the Harlem Renaissance's embrace of African-American culture. The sound of jazz, including Armstrong's music, helped shape Hughes as a writer, with his work reflecting the jazz style. As "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player," Armstrong solidified his legacy and continued focusing on his vocal career, bringing together Black and white audiences. In 1929, he returned to New York to play in the pit orchestra for the musical Hot Chocolates, an all-black revue written by Andy Razaf and pianist Fats Waller.

Zutty Singleton played drums, Earl Hines played piano, Jimmy Strong played clarinet, Fred Robinson played trombone, and Mancy Carr played banjo. During the 1920s Harlem Renaissance, Louis Armstrong made a significant impact, influencing well-known writer Langston Hughes, who admired Armstrong and recognized him as one of the most prominent musicians of the era. Hughes wrote books that celebrated jazz and acknowledged Armstrong as a leader in the Harlem Renaissance's embrace of African-American culture, and the sound of jazz, including Armstrong's music, helped shape Hughes's writing style, which mirrored the rhythms and improvisation of jazz. Armstrong, known as "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player" during this time, transformed jazz and maintained a strong focus on his vocal career, drawing both Black and white audiences. In 1929, Armstrong returned to New York to play in the pit orchestra for the all-Black revue *Hot Chocolates*, written by Andy Razaf and Fats Waller, where he made a cameo as a vocalist and regularly stole the show with his rendition of "Ain't Misbehavin'"; his version became his biggest-selling record. He later worked at Connie's Inn in Harlem, a venue rivaling the Cotton Club, which was fronted by gangster Dutch Schultz, and achieved success with vocal recordings, including songs by Hoagy Carmichael. His 1930s recordings used the RCA ribbon microphone, introduced in 1931, which added warmth to vocals and became central to the "crooning" sound of artists like Bing Crosby. Armstrong's interpretation of "Stardust" became one of the most successful versions ever recorded, highlighting his unique vocal style. His radical reworking of "Lazy River," recorded in 1931, began with a trumpet solo, introduced a melody with sobbing horns, and featured Armstrong's growling interjections like "Yeah!... Uh-huh... Sure... Way down, way down," and in the first verse, he sang with a single note and strongly syncopated phrasing, while in the second stanza, he improvised a melody that evolved into a classic scat singing passage. His vocal innovations, rooted in his trumpet experience, influenced jazz vocal interpretation, with his gravelly voice becoming an archetype and his scat singing influencing white singers like Bing Crosby. The Great Depression severely affected the jazz scene; the Cotton Club closed in 1936, many musicians stopped playing, Bix Beiderbecke died, Fletcher Henderson's band disbanded, Sidney Bechet became a tailor and moved to Paris, and Kid Ory returned to New Orleans to raise chickens. In 1930, Armstrong moved to Los Angeles to seek new opportunities, playing at the New Cotton Club with Lionel Hampton on drums, drawing Hollywood crowds and radio audiences, and appearing in his first movie, *Ex-Flame*, while also being convicted of marijuana possession and receiving a suspended sentence. He returned to Chicago in late 1931, playing in bands similar to Guy Lombardo's and recording more standards; when the mob pressured him to leave, he visited New Orleans, received a hero's welcome, saw old friends, sponsored a baseball team called Armstrong's Secret Nine, and had a cigar named after him. After a national tour shadowed by the mob, he fled to Europe. Upon returning to the U.S., Armstrong undertook exhausting tours, but financial issues from his agent Johnny Collins's erratic behavior and his own spending, along with breach of contract violations, left him short of cash. He hired Joe Glaser as his manager, who helped resolve legal issues, mob problems, and debts. Armstrong also faced health issues with his fingers and lips, worsened by his playing style, leading him to develop his vocal style and make his first theatrical appearances, including in *Pennies from Heaven* (1936) and substituting for Rudy Vallee on CBS radio in 1937, becoming the first African American to host a sponsored national broadcast. After years on the road, Armstrong settled permanently in Queens, New York, in 1943 with his fourth wife, Lucille. Despite challenges from Tin Pan Alley, gangster influence, and anti-Black prejudice, he continued developing his music. Big band bookings declined in the 1940s due to shifting public tastes, with ballrooms closing and pop vocals gaining popularity, making it impossible to sustain a 16-piece touring band. A revival of interest in 1940s traditional jazz allowed Armstrong to return to small-group styles. He performed as a guest with Lionel Hampton's band at the second Cavalcade of Jazz in Los Angeles on October 12, 1946, and led a successful small-group concert at New York Town Hall on May 17, 1947, featuring Jack Teagarden, with the two performing a duet on "Rockin' Chair" that was recorded for Okeh Records. On August 13, 1947, Joe Glaser restructured Armstrong's big band into a six-piece traditional jazz group, the Louis Armstrong and His All-Stars, featuring initially Earl "Fatha" Hines, Barney Bigard, Edmond Hall, Jack Teagarden, Trummy Young, Arvell Shaw, Billy Kyle, Marty Napoleon, Big Sid "Buddy" Catlett, Cozy Cole, Tyree Glenn, Barrett Deems, Mort Herbert, Joe Darensbourg, Eddie Shu, Joe Muranyi, and percussionist Danny Barcelona. On February 28, 1948, Suzy Delair performed "C'est si bon" at the first Nice Jazz Festival, and Armstrong loved the song; on June 26, 1950, he recorded the American version with English lyrics by Jerry Seelen, which became a worldwide success and was performed by top international singers. Armstrong was the first jazz musician to appear on the cover of *Time* magazine on February 21, 1949. He and his All-Stars performed at the ninth Cavalcade of Jazz at Wrigley Field on June 7, 1953, alongside Shorty Rogers, Roy Brown, Don Tosti, Earl Bostic, and Nat "King" Cole. Over 30 years, Armstrong performed more than 300 times a year, made many recordings, and appeared in over 30 films. By the 1950s, Armstrong was a widely beloved American icon and cultural ambassador with a global fanbase, but a generation gap emerged with younger jazz musicians like Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, and Sonny Rollins, who viewed Armstrong's vaudevillian style as outdated and "Uncle Tomish," calling it a link to minstrelsy that they were ashamed of; Armstrong referred to bebop as "Chinese music," and when asked in 1954 if he could play bebop, he replied, "'Bebop?' he husked. 'I just play music. Guys who invent terms like that are walking the streets with their instruments under their arms.'" After finishing his contract with Decca Records, Armstrong went freelance and recorded for other labels. He maintained an intense international touring schedule but suffered a heart attack in 1959 in Italy and had to rest. In 1964, after over two years without studio work, Armstrong recorded "Hello, Dolly!" by Jerry Herman, originally sung by Carol Channing; his version stayed on the Hot 100 for 22 weeks, longer than any other record that year, reached No. 1, and made him the oldest person to achieve that feat at 62 years, nine months, and five days, displacing The Beatles from the top spot. Armstrong toured into his 60s, visiting parts of the Communist Bloc in 1965 and touring Africa, Europe, and Asia under U.S. State Department sponsorship, earning the nickname "Ambassador Satch" and inspiring Dave Brubeck to compose *The Real Ambassadors*, with performances in Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria. By 1968, Armstrong was approaching 70 and his health was failing due to heart and kidney ailments, forcing him to stop touring, though he continued recording, including "What a Wonderful World," which topped the British charts for a month. He did not perform publicly in 1969 and spent most of the year recovering; his longtime manager Joe Glaser died. By summer 1970, doctors deemed him fit to resume performances, and he began another world tour, though a heart attack forced a two-month break. Armstrong made his last recorded trumpet performances on his 1968 album *Disney Songs the Satchmo Way*. The Louis Armstrong House Museum notes that Louis pronounced his name as "Lewis"; on his 1964 record "Hello, Dolly!", he sings, "This is Lewis, Dolly," and in 1933, he recorded "Laughin' Louie." Many announcers, fans, and acquaintances called him "Louie," and Lucille Armstrong called him "Louie" in a 1983 videotaped interview; musicians and close friends usually called him "Pops." In a 1943–1944 memoir, Armstrong stated, "All white folks call me Louie," suggesting he did not use the nickname himself or that whites never addressed him by it. He was registered as "Lewie" on the 1920 U.S. census; "Lewie" is the French pronunciation of "Louis" and is common in Louisiana. In 1919, while performing at the Brick House in Gretna, Louisiana, Armstrong met Daisy Parker, a local prostitute, and began an affair. He visited her home several times and learned she had a common-law husband. On March 19, 1919, they married at City Hall. They adopted a three-year-old boy, Clarence, whose mother, Armstrong's cousin Flora, died shortly after giving birth; Clarence had a head injury and was mentally disabled, and Armstrong cared for him his entire life. Their marriage ended in 1923. On February 4, 1924, Armstrong married Lil Hardin Armstrong, King Oliver's pianist; she had divorced her first husband. She helped develop his career, but they separated in 1931 and divorced in 1938. Armstrong then married Alpha Smith, beginning the relationship during the 1920s at the Vendome and continuing afterward; their marriage lasted four years and ended in 1942. He married Lucille Wilson, a singer at the Cotton Club in New York, in October 1942, and remained married until his death in 1971. Armstrong had no biological children. In December 2012, Sharon Preston-Folta claimed to be his daughter from a 1950s affair with Lucille "Sweets" Preston, a Cotton Club dancer; in a 1955 letter to his manager Joe Glaser, Armstrong affirmed the baby was his daughter and ordered Glaser to pay $400 per month ($5,869 in 2024 dollars) to the mother and child. Armstrong was known for his colorful and charismatic personality, and his autobiography caused some biographers and historians concern due to his tendency to embellish stories, especially about his early childhood. He was a leading public figure, beloved by an American public that rarely engaged deeply with Black performers, and lived a private life of access and privilege rarely afforded to other Black Americans. Armstrong generally remained politically neutral, which sometimes alienated him from other Black Americans who expected him to be more vocal during the civil rights movement, though he criticized President Eisenhower for not acting forcefully on civil rights. The trumpet is hard on the lips, and Armstrong suffered lip damage due to his aggressive playing style and preference for narrow mouthpieces that dug into his inner lip. During his 1930s European tour, he suffered a severe ulceration that required him to stop playing for a year. He used salves and creams, cut scar tissue with a razor blade, and by the 1950s became an official spokesman for Ansatz-Creme Lip Salve. In a 1959 backstage meeting with Marshall Brown, Armstrong was advised to see a doctor for proper lip treatment, but he did not until his final years, when his health was failing and doctors considered surgery too risky. In 1959, Armstrong was hospitalized for pneumonia in Italy, with doctors concerned about his lungs and heart, but he recovered by the end of June. The nicknames "Satchmo" and "Satch" are short for "Satchelmouth"; the origin is uncertain. One common story is that as a young boy in New Orleans, he scooped coins from the street and stuck them in his mouth to prevent theft, earning the nickname "satchel mouth"; another is that his large mouth led to the nickname. Early on, he was known as "Dipper," short for "Dippermouth," referencing the song *Dippermouth Blues*. The nickname "Pops" came from Armstrong's habit of forgetting names and calling people "Pops," which was later used as a title for a 2010 biography by Terry Teachout. After a Savoy competition, he was crowned "King Menelik," after the Emperor of Ethiopia, for slaying "ofay jazz demons." Armstrong celebrated his identity as a Black man from a poor New Orleans neighborhood and avoided "putting on airs," though many younger Black musicians criticized him for performing in segregated audiences and not taking a stronger stand.

Louis Armstrong was known by several nicknames, including "satchel mouth," which originated from his large mouth, a trait that led to the nickname being shortened to "Satchmo," and "Dipper," short for "Dippermouth," referencing the song "Dippermouth Blues" and his unique embouchure. He was also called "Pops" because he often forgot people's names and referred to them as such, a nickname later used as the title of a 2010 biography by Terry Teachout. After a competition at the Savoy, he was dubbed "King Menelik" after the Emperor of Ethiopia for defeating "ofay jazz demons." Armstrong celebrated his identity as a Black man from a poor New Orleans neighborhood and avoided appearing elitist; however, younger Black musicians criticized him for performing in segregated audiences and not actively supporting the civil rights movement. In 1957, during a candid interview in Grand Forks, North Dakota, shortly after the Little Rock desegregation crisis, Armstrong denounced Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus and President Dwight D. Eisenhower, calling the President "two-faced" and "having no guts," and stated he would cancel a planned Soviet Union tour, saying, "The way they're treating my people in the South, the government can go to hell." The FBI maintained a file on him due to his outspoken views on integration. His comments drew both praise and backlash, with figures like Jackie Robinson and Lena Horne supporting him, while a Mississippi radio station banned his records; his longtime manager, Pierre Tallerie, attempted to retract the remarks, prompting Armstrong to sharply rebuke him and insist on speaking for himself. When asked about his religion, Armstrong said he was raised Baptist, wore a Star of David in honor of the Karnoffsky family who supported him as a child and lent him money to buy his first cornet, was baptized Catholic at the Sacred Heart of Jesus Church in New Orleans, and met Pope Pius XII and Pope Paul VI. Armstrong was concerned about his health and used laxatives to manage his weight, a practice he promoted in his diet plan "Lose Weight the Satchmo Way"; he initially used Pluto Water but became a strong advocate for Swiss Kriss, even distributing packets to people including members of the British royal family. He also created humorous risqué cards featuring himself sitting on a toilet viewed through a keyhole with the slogan "Satch says, 'Leave it all behind ya!'"—a claim sometimes mistakenly described as advertising Swiss Kriss. In a live recording of "Baby, It's Cold Outside" with Velma Middleton, he altered the lyric to "Take some Swiss Kriss while I pour." His laxative use began in childhood when his mother collected dandelions and peppergrass for her children's health. Armstrong was a heavy marijuana smoker throughout much of his life and was arrested in 1930 for drug possession, spending nine days in jail; he described marijuana as "a thousand times better than whiskey." His love of food is reflected in songs like "Cheesecake," "Cornet Chop Suey," and "Struttin' with Some Barbecue," though the latter was about a companion, not food, and he often signed his letters "Red beans and ricely yours." A fan of Major League Baseball, he founded a team in New Orleans called the Raggedy Nine and later transformed it into his "Secret Nine Baseball." Armstrong was gregarious and wrote constantly on the road, recording music, sex, food, childhood memories, his marijuana use, and even his bowel movements. He was not a Freemason; although sometimes cited as a member of Montgomery Lodge No. 18 (Prince Hall) in New York, no such lodge existed, and in his autobiography he stated he was a member of the Knights of Pythias of North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia, an African American fraternal organization. In 1949, he presided as King of the Zulu Social Aid & Pleasure Club during Mardi Gras, earning a cover feature in Time magazine. Early in his career, Armstrong was renowned for his cornet and trumpet virtuosity, known for "clarinet-like figurations and high notes" and his "intense rhythmic 'swing'" involving accented upbeats, slurring, and complementary rhythmic patterns. His most celebrated recordings include the Hot Five and Hot Seven sessions and those with the Red Onion Jazz Babies; his improvisations, though unconventional, were subtle and melodic, with the solo in "Potato Head Blues" widely regarded as his best. Prior to Armstrong, jazz ensembles typically varied melodies; he was virtually the first to base significant variations on chord harmonies rather than melodies, transforming jazz into a soloist's art form. He often re-composed pop tunes with more compelling variations and composed over 50 original songs, including jazz standards like "Gully Low Blues," "Potato Head Blues," and "Swing That Music." He performed with major artists such as Bing Crosby, Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Earl Hines, Jimmie Rodgers, Bessie Smith, and Ella Fitzgerald; Crosby notably emulated Armstrong's vocal techniques, including easing breath, using head voice, and singing on consonants, which influenced later popular singers. Armstrong recorded two albums with Ella Fitzgerald—Ella and Louis and Ella and Louis Again—with backing by the Oscar Peterson Trio and drummer Buddy Rich on the first and Louie Bellson on the second; Norman Granz later envisioned a Porgy and Bess recording. His Columbia Records albums, Louis Armstrong Plays W.C. Handy (1954) and Satch Plays Fats (all Fats Waller tunes) (1955), were both masterpieces and moderately successful. In 1961, the All-Stars recorded The Great Summit and The Great Reunion (combined) with Duke Ellington, featuring many of Ellington's famous compositions and two exclusive tracks, with Ellington playing piano. His performance in Dave Brubeck's The Real Ambassadors (1963) was critically acclaimed and included "Summer Song," one of his most popular vocals. In the week beginning May 9, 1964, his recording of "Hello, Dolly!" reached number one, and the album of the same name also hit number one, displacing The Beatles and selling well, eventually going "Gold" (500,000); it won best male pop vocal performance at the 1964 Grammy Awards. Armstrong had 19 "Top Ten" records, including "Stardust," "What a Wonderful World," "When The Saints Go Marching In," "Dream a Little Dream of Me," "Ain't Misbehavin'," "You Rascal You," and "Stompin' at the Savoy"; "We Have All the Time in the World" gained renewed popularity in the UK in 1994 via a Guinness ad, reaching number 3. In 1964, Armstrong became the oldest artist to have a number one song with "Hello, Dolly!" and his song "Bout Time" was later featured in the film Bewitched. In February 1968, he performed "Grassa e Bella" in Italian on the Italian RAI television channel with Lara Saint Paul for the C.D.I. label. In 1968, "What a Wonderful World" topped the British charts for a month. He appeared on Johnny Cash's show on October 28, 1970, singing "Ramblin' Rose" and re-creating Jimmie Rodgers' "Blue Yodel No. 9" with Cash. Armstrong enjoyed diverse music, from blues to Guy Lombardo's arrangements, Latin American folk songs, and classical symphonies and opera, often incorporating these influences, which sometimes surprised fans. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as an early influence, with solos like the hard-rocking version of "St. Louis Blues" from the WC Handy album showing mutual influence. He appeared in over a dozen Hollywood films, most notably as a bandleader and narrator in the 1956 musical High Society, starring Bing Crosby, Grace Kelly, Frank Sinatra, and Celeste Holm, where he sang the title song and performed "Now You Has Jazz" with Crosby. In 1947, he played himself in New Orleans, opposite Billie Holiday, chronicling the decline of Storyville and the exodus of musicians from New Orleans to Chicago; in The Five Pennies (1959), he played himself, sang, and performed classic numbers, including a duet with Danny Kaye, during which Kaye impersonated Armstrong. He also appeared in The Glenn Miller Story alongside James Stewart. In 1937, Armstrong became the first African American to host a nationally broadcast radio show. In 1969, he had a cameo in Gene Kelly's Hello, Dolly! as the bandleader Louis, singing the title song with Barbra Streisand. He appeared on radio programs such as The Story of Swing (1937) and This Is Jazz (1947), and made television appearances, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, including on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. In 1949, his life was dramatized by Richard Durham in the Chicago WMAQ radio series Destination Freedom. Argentine writer Julio Cortázar, a self-described admirer, claimed that a 1952 concert at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris inspired his creation of the fictional creatures Cronopios, calling Armstrong "Grandísimo Cronopio." A pivotal scene in Stardust Memories (1980) features Woody Allen being overwhelmed by a recording of Armstrong's "Stardust" and experiencing a nostalgic epiphany. In 2022, a documentary film titled Louis Armstrong's Black & Blues was released about him. Against his doctor's advice, Armstrong played a two-week engagement at the Waldorf-Astoria's Empire Room in March 1971, after which he suffered a heart attack and was hospitalized; he was released in May and resumed trumpet practice. Still hoping to return to performing, he died of a heart attack in his sleep on July 6, 1971, in Corona, Queens, New York City. He was buried in Flushing Cemetery, Flushing, Queens, New York City. His honorary pallbearers included Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Pearl Bailey, Count Basie, Harry James, Frank Sinatra, Ed Sullivan, Earl Wilson, Benny Goodman, Alan King, Johnny Carson, and David Frost. Peggy Lee sang "The Lord's Prayer," Al Hibbler sang "Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen," and Fred Robbins, a longtime friend, delivered the eulogy. Armstrong was posthumously awarded the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972 by the Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, recognizing outstanding artistic contributions to the recording field. Recordings of Armstrong were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, established in 1973, to honor recordings at least 25 years old with qualitative or historical significance.

Louis Armstrong died, and was interred in Flushing Cemetery, Flushing, in Queens, New York City. His honorary pallbearers included Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Pearl Bailey, Count Basie, Harry James, Frank Sinatra, Ed Sullivan, Earl Wilson, Benny Goodman, Alan King, Johnny Carson, and David Frost. Peggy Lee performed "The Lord's Prayer" at the services, Al Hibbler sang "Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen," and Fred Robbins, a long-time friend, delivered the eulogy. Armstrong was posthumously awarded the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972 by the Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, a Special Merit Award given by vote of the Recording Academy's National Trustees to performers who have made outstanding artistic contributions to the recording field. Recordings of Armstrong were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, established in 1973, to honor recordings that are at least 25 years old and have qualitative or historical significance. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame included Armstrong's "West End Blues" on its list of 500 songs that shaped rock and roll. In 1995, the U.S. Post Office issued a Louis Armstrong 32-cent commemorative postage stamp. In 1999, Armstrong was nominated for inclusion in the American Film Institute's 100 Years ... 100 Stars. In 1950, Bing Crosby, the most successful vocalist of the first half of the 20th century, stated, "He is the beginning and the end of music in America." Duke Ellington, in a 1971 DownBeat magazine article, said, "If anybody was a master, it was Louis Armstrong. He was and will continue to be the embodiment of jazz." Though Armstrong is widely recognized as a pioneer of scat singing, Ethel Waters and others had recorded scat singing in the 1920s prior to him, according to Gary Giddins and others. Literary critic Harold Bloom stated, "The two great American contributions to the world's art, in the end, are Walt Whitman and, after him, Armstrong and jazz ... If I had to choose between the two, ultimately, I wouldn't. I would say that the genius of this nation at its best is indeed Walt Whitman and Louis Armstrong." In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Armstrong at No. 39 on their list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time. In 1991, an asteroid was named 9179 Satchmo in his honor. In the summer of 2001, to commemorate the centennial of his birth, New Orleans's main airport was renamed Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport; the entrance to the airport's former terminal building features a statue depicting Armstrong playing his cornet. In 2002, Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–1928) were preserved in the United States National Recording Registry, selected annually by the National Recording Preservation Board for inclusion in the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry. The US Open tennis tournament's former main stadium was named Louis Armstrong Stadium in his honor, as Armstrong had lived a few blocks from the site. Congo Square, a historic gathering place for Black people in New Orleans for dancing and music, was later renamed Louis Armstrong Park. Dedicated in April 1980, the park includes a 12-foot (3.7 m) statue of Armstrong holding a trumpet. A Wonderful World, a musical based on his life, had its world premiere run at Miami New Drama from December 4, 2021, to January 16, 2021, after mounting previews beginning March 5, 2020, and canceling opening night (March 14) due to COVID concerns. Mirroring Armstrong's musical journey, the show stars James Monroe Iglehart and makes "pre-Broadway" stops in New Orleans on October 1–8, 2023, and Chicago on October 11–29, 2023. The musical, conceived by Drama Desk Award winner and Tony Award nominee Christopher Renshaw and novelist Andrew Delaplaine, and directed by Renshaw, features an original book by Aurin Squire and charts the rise of Armstrong from the perspective of his four wives. The show will debut on Broadway in 2024. The house where Armstrong lived for nearly 28 years was declared a National Historic Landmark and opened to the public for guided tours in 2003. The Louis Armstrong House Museum, located at 34–56 107th Street between 34th and 37th avenues in Corona, Queens, presents concerts and educational programs, operates as a historic house museum, and makes its archives of writings, books, recordings, and memorabilia available for public research. The museum is administered by Queens College, City University of New York, following the terms of Lucille Armstrong's will, and is operated by the nonprofit Louis Armstrong House Museum. It opened to the public on October 15, 2003. A new visitors center opened across the street from the Armstrong home in the summer of 2023. The museum's website includes the digitized Armstrong Archives, searchable 24 hours a day.

Louis Moreau Gottschalk (May 8, 1829 – December 18, 1869) was an American composer, pianist, and virtuoso performer of his own romantic piano works. Born in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Edward Gottschalk and Aimée Marie Bruslé, he had six siblings, five of whom were half-siblings by his father's biracial mistress. The family lived in a cottage at Royal and Esplanade in the Vieux Carré and later moved to 518 Conti Street, where his maternal grandmother Bruslé and nurse Sally, both Saint Dominican Creoles, influenced his exposure to diverse musical traditions. He began playing the piano early and made his informal public debut in 1840 at the St. Charles Hotel. At age 13, he left the United States for Europe to pursue classical training, but the Paris Conservatoire rejected his application without hearing him, with head of the piano faculty Pierre Zimmerman stating, "America is a country of steam engines." Despite this, he gained recognition through family connections. Compositions such as Bamboula (Danse Des Nègres) and La Savane established him as an authentic American composer, incorporating African musical traditions and serving as precursors to jazz; they are considered the first examples of Louisiana Creole music in classical culture. After a concert at the Salle Pleyel, Chopin praised him, saying, "Give me your hand, my child; I predict that you will become the king of pianists," and both Franz Liszt and Charles-Valentin Alkan acknowledged his exceptional talent. Returning to the United States in 1853, he traveled widely, including a sojourn in Cuba in 1854, which led to a series of trips to Central and South America. He visited Puerto Rico after his Havana debut and composed Souvenir de Porto Rico; Marche des gibaros, Op. 31 (RO250), probably in 1857, a march based on a Puerto Rican folk song form, with "gibaros" referring to the jíbaros or Puerto Rican peasantry. After his tour, he rested in New Jersey before returning to New York City, where he took on the young Venezuelan student Teresa Carreño, an exception to his skepticism about prodigies. Though he gave her only a few lessons, she remembered him fondly and performed his music throughout her life; she later performed for Abraham Lincoln and became a renowned pianist known as the "Valkyrie of the Piano." In late 1855 and early 1856, he connected with notable figures in the New York art world, including sculptor Erastus Dow Palmer, composer George William Warren, and landscape painter Frederic Edwin Church, who had also traveled in Latin America and produced large-scale paintings of South American subjects. Gottschalk dedicated a Mazurka poétique to Church, who gave him a small, now-unidentified landscape painting; he also possibly collaborated with Warren on The Andes, Marche di Bravoura, inspired by Church’s painting The Heart of the Andes. By the 1860s, he was the best-known pianist in the New World, though he only returned to New Orleans occasionally, always introducing himself as a native. He composed the tarantella, Grande Tarantelle, Op. 67, subtitled Célèbre Tarentelle, between 1858 and 1864. In May 1865, a San Francisco newspaper reported that he had traveled 95,000 miles by rail and given 1,000 concerts. Later that year, he was forced to leave the United States due to an alleged affair with a student at the Oakland Female Seminary in Oakland, California; he denied wrongdoing, claiming the incident was a smear campaign by a rival of the piano manufacturer Chickering & Sons, the brand he used for his tours. He never returned to the United States and instead traveled to South America, where he continued performing. On November 24, 1869, at the Teatro Lyrico Fluminense in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, he collapsed from yellow fever after finishing the piece Morte! (Death) and just as he began playing Tremolo. He never recovered. He died on December 18, 1869, at age 40, at his hotel in Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, likely from an overdose of quinine, with an essay by Jeremy Nicholas noting that he died of empyema due to a ruptured abdominal abscess. In 1870, his remains were returned to the United States and buried at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, New York City. His original burial site was marked by a marble monument with an "Angel of Music" statue, which was damaged by vandals in 1959. In October 2012, after nearly 15 years of fundraising, a new "Angel of Music" statue, created by Giancarlo Biagi and Jill Burkee, was unveiled. Gottschalk's music was popular during his lifetime, with early works like Bamboula, La Savane, Le Bananier, and Le Mancenillier based on his childhood memories in Louisiana and regarded as the earliest pieces of creole music in classical culture. His 13-minute opera Escenas campestres retains value, and the Bamboula theme appears in his Symphony No. 1: A Night in the Tropics. A melody from Souvenirs d'Andalousie forms the basis of Ernesto Lecuona’s popular 20th-century piece "Malagueña." Many of his compositions were lost or destroyed after his death. Richard Jackson edited a 1973 collection of his piano music and organized an exhibition at the New York Public Library. Vanguard Records released the first important recordings of his orchestral works, including A Night in the Tropics, by Maurice Abravanel and the Utah Symphony Orchestra. Vox Records issued a multi-disc collection, later reissued on CD, including world premiere recordings of the original orchestrations conducted by Igor Buketoff and Samuel Adler. In 1984, Nimbus Records released The Lady Fainted, a selection of piano fantasies, caprices, meditations, and paraphrases performed by Alan Marks. Lambert Orkis recorded a selection of his music on an 1865 Chickering concert grand in 1988 as part of The Smithsonian Collection of Recordings. Gottschalk’s music was used in the soundtrack for the Michel Deville film Aux Petits Bonheurs, played by Noël Lee on a Steinway piano and released by Erato Records in 1994. Beginning in the 1990s, Philip Martin recorded most of Gottschalk’s extant piano music for Hyperion Records. Howard Breslin wrote a historical novel about him, Concert Grand, in 1963. A version of Bamboula with added lyrics was recorded in April 1934 by Abel Beauregard’s dance band, the Orchestre Créole Matou from Guadeloupe, marking the first recording of the composition; the first classical piano recordings of his works were not made until 1956 by Eugene List. Other recordings of the bamboula rhythm heard in New Orleans’ Congo Square, such as the 1950 Haitian voodoo recording Baboule Dance (three drums), the 1962 Cuban folk tune Rezos Congos (Bamboula, Conga Music), and Dr. John’s 1970s recording of Litanie des Saints from Goin' Back to New Orleans, are linked to Gottschalk’s work. Comments by musicologist Bruno Blum are included in each of these releases.

The third season of Love Is Blind premiered on Netflix on October 19, 2022, and ended on November 9, 2022, with a reunion episode released on that same date. A three-part companion special titled After the Altar was released on February 10, 2023. This season featured singles from Dallas, Texas, all of whom lived in Dallas during filming. In 2023, Bartise Bowden appeared on the first season of Perfect Match, finishing as a finalist. According to Netflix and production company Kinetic Content, there were no unaired engagements in Season 3; all couples who got engaged in the pods were included in the show.

Lucas Valeriu Ntuba Radebe OIS (born 12 April 1969) is a South African former professional footballer who played as a centre back. Born to Emily and Johannes Radebe in the Diepkloof section of Soweto, near Johannesburg, he is one of 11 children and attended Bopasenatla Secondary School until age 15. His parents sent him to Bophuthatswana for Grade 10 to protect him from the violence in Diepkloof Zone Four, where he attended Ngotwane High School near Zeerust. He began playing in the now-defunct Bophuthatswana Soccer League (BOPSOL) with Stocks Birds in Lehurutshe, closer to Zeerust, before being scouted by Kaizer Chiefs in South Africa. Initially a goalkeeper, he switched to central midfield and then to central defence. In 1989, Patrick Ntsoelengoe recruited him to Kaizer Chiefs, where he became captain during his time at the club. In 1994, Radebe and Philemon "Chippa" Masinga moved to Leeds United for a transfer fee of £250,000; Radebe was included in the deal to please Masinga, though he became the more valuable player. Initially, the move was unsuccessful due to disagreements with then-Leeds manager Howard Wilkinson and injuries that prevented him from securing a regular first-team spot. In March 1996, he returned to goalkeeping after John Lukic's injury and again played in goal when Mark Beeney was sent off against Manchester United, earning 'cult-hero' status despite Leeds losing 1–0. When Wilkinson was replaced by George Graham, Radebe's career flourished, and he was made captain for the 1998–99 season. During that season, Leeds finished fourth in the FA Premier League and qualified for the UEFA Cup; in 1999–2000, they finished third and qualified for the Champions League, reaching the semi-finals. Radebe turned down offers to join Manchester United, AC Milan, and Roma. In 2000, he was awarded the FIFA Fair Play Award and also received the Contribution to the Community Award in the Premier League 10 Seasons Awards. That same year, he sustained serious knee and ankle injuries, missing nearly two years and struggling to regain form. He made his international debut for South Africa on 7 July 1992 against Cameroon and was part of the 1996 African Cup of Nations-winning squad. He captained South Africa at the 1998 and 2002 FIFA World Cups, though the team failed to reach the knockout stages in both; he scored a goal in 2002. He earned 70 caps and scored two goals, with his last match being against England on 22 May 2003. After retiring in May 2005, Leeds held a testimonial match at Elland Road on 2 May 2005, attended by over 37,886 fans, and he also played in a retirement match in Durban, with proceeds donated to charity. In August 2006, Radebe returned to Leeds after failing to secure a role in South Africa's 2010 World Cup preparations, stating he was "tired of waiting for unreliable people" who had promised him a position in the national team setup. In 2008, a Leeds brewery named a beer "Radebeer," reflecting fan admiration. On 8 October 2009, he was named an ambassador by the English Football Association to support the 2018 World Cup bid. A biography, *Lucas: From the Streets of Soweto to Soccer Superstar* by Richard Coomber, was published in 2010. In May 2010, he won the PFA Merit Award for his contributions to football. During the 2010 FIFA World Cup, he served as a pundit for ITV and a columnist for The Daily Telegraph. In September 2010, he expressed interest in managing Leeds United and the South African national team, stating those were the only coaching roles he would consider. In July 2012, he accepted a position as team manager with the South African national side. In October 2013, he was set to return to Elland Road, where he was presented to the crowd on 30 October 2013. On 23 January 2013, it was confirmed that boxer Josh Warrington would fight IBF world champion Lee Selby on 19 May at Elland Road, with Radebe joining Warrington for the ringwalk; Warrington won by split decision, and the band Kaiser Chiefs performed songs at the event. In 1991, while driving with his brother Lazarus to buy drinks for his mother, Radebe was shot; the bullet entered his back and exited halfway down his thigh, but he was not critically injured. The incident, which he attributes to someone being hired to prevent him from switching clubs, influenced his decision to join Leeds United in 1994. He was voted 54th in the Top 100 Great South Africans in 2004. His wife Feziwe died of cancer in October 2008; in December 2008, he was treated for a heart complaint after collapsing at the gym. He married his second wife at the end of 2015. The British indie/britpop band Kaiser Chiefs chose their name because Radebe is a former player of Kaizer Chiefs. Radebe has been an ambassador for FIFA's SOS Children's Villages and received the FIFA Fair Play Award in December 2000 for his efforts in eliminating racism in football and his work with children in South Africa.

Ludwig Prandtl (German pronunciation: [ˈluːtvɪç ˈpʁantl̩]; 4 February 1875 – 15 August 1953) was a German fluid dynamicist, physicist, and aerospace scientist who pioneered rigorous mathematical analyses in aerodynamics, forming the foundation of aeronautical engineering. In the 1920s, he developed the mathematical basis for subsonic aerodynamics, extending to transonic velocities, and established key theories including the boundary layer, thin-airfoil theory, and lifting-line theory. The Prandtl number is named after him. Born in Freising near Munich on 4 February 1875, Prandtl spent more time with his father, an engineering professor, who encouraged him to observe nature and reflect on his observations. He entered the Technische Hochschule Munich in 1894 and earned a Ph.D. under Professor August Foeppl in six years, with his thesis titled "On Tilting Phenomena, an Example of Unstable Elastic Equilibrium" (1900). After university, he worked at Maschinenfabrik Augsburg-Nürnberg, where he discovered that suction tubes failed due to flow separation, a phenomenon previously noted by Daniel Bernoulli, which led to his boundary-layer approach to fluid resistance. In 1901, he became a professor of fluid mechanics at the Technical School in Hannover, later the Technical University Hannover and University of Hannover, where he developed many of his most important theories. On August 8, 1904, he delivered a groundbreaking paper, "Über Flüssigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung" (On the Motion of Fluids in Very Little Friction), at the Third International Mathematics Congress in Heidelberg, introducing the boundary layer and explaining flow separation and stall for the first time. The paper's impact was so significant that he succeeded Hans Lorenz as director of the Institute for Technical Physics at the University of Göttingen later that year. In 1907, during his time at Göttingen, he established the Motorluftschiffmodell-Versuchsanstalt (MVA), later renamed Aerodynamische Versuchsanstalt (AVA) in 1919, focused on wind tunnel measurements for airship models with minimal air resistance. During World War I, the facility conducted research on lift and drag on airfoils, bomb aerodynamics, and cavitation on submarine propeller blades. In 1925, the university spun off his research arm to form the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Flow Research, now the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization. Due to the complexity of his 1904 boundary layer concept, its adoption was initially slow; only in 1908 did two of his students, Blasius and Boltze, publish dissertations on the boundary layer—Blasius on a flat plate in parallel flow and Boltze on spherical shapes—leading Prandtl to expand the theory to include a thermal boundary layer for heat transfer. By 1914, three more boundary layer papers were published by Göttingen researchers, but their dissemination remained limited until Theodore von Kármán published a 1921 paper on the momentum integral equation across the boundary layer. Following earlier work by Frederick Lanchester, Prandtl collaborated with Albert Betz and Max Munk on a mathematical tool for analyzing lift from real-world wings, resulting in the Lanchester–Prandtl wing theory, published in 1918–1919. He also developed a simplified thin-airfoil theory for cambered airfoils used in World War I aircraft and demonstrated that wing-tip effects are crucial, introducing the concept of induced drag and wingtip vortices, showing that an elliptical spanwise lift distribution minimizes induced drag. He later proposed a bell-like lift distribution that reduces tip loads by washing out wing tips to achieve minimum induced drag for a given structural weight, though this was initially ignored in aircraft design and has since been rediscovered and gained importance (see also the Prandtl-D experimental aircraft). In 1908, Prandtl and his student Theodor Meyer developed the first theories of supersonic shock waves and flow, including the Prandtl–Meyer expansion fans, enabling supersonic wind tunnel construction. In 1929, working with Adolf Busemann, he created a method for designing a supersonic nozzle, now used in all supersonic wind tunnels and rocket nozzles. His work on circulation was vital for ship propeller hydrodynamics, with most experimental work conducted at Göttingen from 1910 to 1918 with Albert Betz and Max Munk, and these discoveries remained secret from the West until after World War I. Prior to World War I, the Society of German Natural Scientists and Physicians (GDNÄ) was the only forum for applied mathematicians, physicists, and engineers in German-speaking countries. In 1920, they met in Bad Nauheim and concluded that a new umbrella organization for applied sciences was needed, leading to the formation of the German Physical Society (DGTP) that same year. In September 1921, the two societies met with the German Mathematical Society (DMV) in Jena, and in its first volume, ZAMM (Journal of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics) stated that this marked "for the first time, applied mathematics and mechanics coming to its own to a larger extent," highlighting the shared goals of Prandtl, von Kármán, Richard von Mises, and Hans Reissner. Prandtl and his peers co-founded GAMM (International Association of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics), which established a new international community of mathematicians, "scientific engineers," and physicists. Prandtl also contributed to the study of compressibility at high subsonic speeds through the Prandtl–Glauert correction, which became valuable during World War II as aircraft approached supersonic speeds. He worked on meteorology, plasticity, structural mechanics, and tribology. From 1921 to 1929, he investigated fluid instabilities, then shifted to developed turbulence, engaging in a competitive race with von Kármán to formulate a universal law of turbulence. Around 1930, both concluded that skin friction was inversely proportional to the square of the Reynolds number and logarithmically related to the product of Reynolds number and skin friction, resulting in a draw. Prandtl and von Kármán's boundary layer work was widely adopted by aerodynamic and hydrodynamic experts after World War I. In May 1932, the International Conference on Hydromechanical Problems of Ship Propulsion in Hamburg featured experiments by Günther Kempf that confirmed von Kármán and Prandtl's theoretical findings. After Hitler's rise and the establishment of the Third Reich, Prandtl continued as director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society. The Nazi air ministry, led by Hermann Göring, used his international reputation to promote Germany's scientific agenda. Prandtl openly supported the regime, writing in 1937 to a NACA representative that Fascism in Italy and National Socialism in Germany represented "very good beginnings of new thinking and economics," and in letters to G. I. Taylor and his wife in 1938 and 1939, he stated that Germany's struggle against Jews was "necessary for its self-preservation" and that "if there will be war, the guilt to have caused it by political measures is this time unequivocally on the side of England." As a member of the German Physical Society (DPG), he helped Carl Ramsauer draft the DPG Petition in 1941, published in 1942, which argued that German physics was falling behind the United States due to the rejection of "Jewish Physics" (relativity and quantum theory), leading to a decline in the belief in "German Physics" superiority and allowing German students to study these fields in schools. Prandtl remained at Göttingen until his death on 15 August 1953. His work in fluid dynamics remains foundational in aerodynamics and chemical engineering, and he is often referred to as the father of modern aerodynamics. A crater named Prandtl is located on the far side of the Moon, and the Ludwig-Prandtl-Ring is awarded by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Luft- und Raumfahrt in his honor for outstanding contributions in aerospace engineering. In 1992, Prandtl was inducted into the International Air & Space Hall of Fame at the San Diego Air & Space Museum.

Lygia Pape (7 April 1927 – 3 May 2004) was a Brazilian visual artist, sculptor, engraver, and filmmaker who played a key role in the Concrete movement and later co-founded the Neo-Concrete Movement in Brazil during the 1950s and 1960s. Born in Nova Friburgo, Brazil, she studied philosophy at the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFTJ) and received informal training in fine arts, studying with Fayga Ostrower at the Museum of Modern Art, Rio de Janeiro. At age 20, she joined the Concrete art movement, a term coined by Dutch artist Theo van Doesburg in 1930. In the 1950s, she created the Tecelares Series, woodblock prints characterized by precise geometric forms, minimalism, and the use of black ink on rice paper, with thin lines that reveal the white paper beneath. These works employed a weaving metaphor to connect with Brazil’s traditional and indigenous cultures, where geometry expressed collective identity rather than industrialization. The 1959 Tecelares print, Sem Título [Untitled], features parallel lines disrupted by non-orthogonal lines, creating the illusion of separate planes and space. Despite its Concrete origins, the work shows handmade qualities—slight line variations and ink feathering—indicating a human touch and marking a transition into Neo-Concrete art. The 1960 version is even more organic, with visible wood grain and subtle diagonal lines that create movement, opposing the mechanistic ideals of Concrete art. In 1952, at age 25, Pape met Hélio Oiticica, Ivan Serpa, and Aluísio Carvão, forming the Grupo Frente, which rejected traditional Brazilian painting and explored abstract and geometric forms. The group held exhibitions in 1954 at Ibeu Gallery and in 1955 at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio, emphasizing non-traditional use of line, form, and color. A debate between Grupo Ruptura and Grupo Frente over the rigidity of geometric abstraction inspired Pape and others to launch the Neo-Concrete Movement in 1959. Pape signed the Neo-Concrete Manifesto alongside Lygia Clark and Hélio Oiticica, emphasizing invention and a desire to discover new ways of knowing the world through art. During this period, she explored the idea of “living the body,” creating multi-sensorial experiences. Her work Livro da Criação [Book of Creation] consists of sixteen unbound cardboard pages, each depicting moments in the creation of the world, designed for phenomenological engagement where each reader interprets it differently. In the 1960s and 1970s, she produced videos and installations critical of the Brazilian dictatorship, with more subtle metaphors from the 1980s onward. Her 1975 film Eat Me features slow-motion sensual movements of mouths, interpreted as implicating gender and sexuality, and is seen as objectifying women despite Pape’s insistence it is not a thesis. In 1967, the installation O Ovo involved participants crawling into a wooden cube covered in plastic film and pushing through it to simulate birth. From 1972 to 1985, Pape taught semiotics at the School of Architecture at the Universidade Santa Úrsula in Rio de Janeiro, becoming a professor at the School of Fine Arts of the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro in 1983. She earned a master’s degree in philosophy from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in 1980 and introduced her students to the informal architecture of Rio’s favelas, especially Maré. In 1981, she received a Guggenheim Fellowship. Her first retrospective was in 2000, focusing on her print practice, which she viewed as a generative source of her artistic career. Ttéias (1979) is emblematic of her process; conceived in 1979 and fully realized in the 1990s, it began with experiments in arranging metallic strings at Parque Lage Gardens in Rio. The word "Ttéias" is a pun on "teia" (web) and "teteia" (a person or thing of grace), consisting of semi-transparent prisms made from gold thread, allowing immersive, interpretive experiences. Pape’s work is held in the Museum of Modern Art, the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, and the Tate. It was included in the 2021 exhibition Women in Abstraction at the Centre Pompidou. In 2025/2026, she received her first solo exhibition in France, Weaving Space, at the Pinault Collection, Bourse de Commerce. Pape did not work with a commercial gallery until later in life. Projeto Lygia Pape, established by her before her death in 2004 and managed by her daughter Paula Pape, was involved in a 2017 U.S. lawsuit against LG Electronics, several mobile phone vendors, and Getty Images Korea for copyright infringement of her 2003 sculpture TtEia 1, C, used in packaging and advertising for the K20 V mobile phone. Pape died on 3 May 2004 in Rio de Janeiro at the age of 77.

Lyndon Baines Johnson (/ˈlɪndən ˈbeɪnz/; August 27, 1908 – January 22, 1973), also known as LBJ, was the 36th president of the United States, serving from 1963 to 1969. He became president after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, under whom he had served as the 37th vice president from 1961 to 1963. A Southern Democrat, Johnson previously represented Texas in Congress for over 23 years, first as a U.S. representative from 1937 to 1949, and then as a U.S. senator from 1949 to 1961. Born in Stonewall, Texas, Johnson worked as a teacher and a congressional aide before winning election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1937. In 1948, he was controversially declared the winner in the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate election in Texas before winning the general election. He became Senate majority whip in 1951, Senate Democratic leader in 1953, and majority leader in 1954. Senator Kennedy bested Johnson and his other rivals for the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination before surprising many by offering to make Johnson his vice presidential running mate. The Kennedy–Johnson ticket won the general election. Vice President Johnson assumed the presidency in 1963, after President Kennedy was assassinated. The following year, Johnson won reelection to the presidency in a landslide, winning the largest share of the popular vote for the Democratic Party in history, and the highest for any candidate since the advent of widespread popular elections in the 1820s. Johnson's domestic policy agenda known as the Great Society was aimed at expanding civil rights, public broadcasting, access to health care, aid to education and the arts, urban and rural development, consumer protection, environmentalism, and public services. He sought to create better living conditions for low-income Americans by spearheading the war on poverty. As part of these efforts, Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965, which resulted in the creation of Medicare and Medicaid. Johnson made the Apollo program a national priority; enacted the Higher Education Act of 1965 which established federally insured student loans; and signed the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 which laid the groundwork for U.S. immigration policy today. Johnson's civil rights legacy was shaped by the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Due to his domestic agenda, Johnson's presidency marked the peak of modern American liberalism in the 20th century. Johnson's foreign policy prioritized containment of communism, including in the ongoing Vietnam War. Johnson began his presidency with near-universal support, but his approval declined throughout his presidency as the public became frustrated with both the Vietnam War and domestic unrest, including race riots, increasing public skepticism with his reports and policies (coined the credibility gap), and increasing crime. Johnson initially sought to run for re-election in 1968; however, following disappointing results in the New Hampshire primary, he withdrew his candidacy. Johnson retired to his Texas ranch and kept a low public profile until he died in 1973. Public opinion and academic assessments of Johnson's legacy have fluctuated greatly. Historians and scholars rank Johnson in the upper tier for his accomplishments regarding domestic policy. His administration passed many major laws that made substantial changes in civil rights, health care, welfare, and education. Conversely, Johnson is heavily criticized for his foreign policy, namely escalating American involvement in the Vietnam War. Lyndon Baines Johnson was born on August 27, 1908, near Stonewall, Texas, in a small farmhouse on the Pedernales River. He was the eldest of five children born to Samuel Ealy Johnson Jr. and Rebekah Baines. Johnson was not given a name until he was three months old, as his parents could not agree on a name that both liked. Finally, he was named after "criminal lawyer—a county lawyer" W. C. Linden, who his father liked; his mother agreed on the condition of spelling it as Lyndon. Johnson had one brother, Sam Houston Johnson, and three sisters, Rebekah, Josefa, and Lucia. Through his mother, he was a great-grandson of Baptist clergyman George Washington Baines. Johnson's paternal grandfather, Samuel Ealy Johnson Sr., was raised Baptist and for a time was a member of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ). In his later years, Samuel Sr. became a Christadelphian; Samuel Jr. also joined the Christadelphian Church toward the end of his life. Johnson was influenced in his positive attitude toward Jews by the religious beliefs that his family, especially his grandfather, had shared with him. Johnson grew up poor, with his father losing a great deal of money. Biographer Robert Caro described him as being raised "in a land without electricity, where the soil was so rocky that it was hard to earn a living from it." In school, Johnson was a talkative youth who was elected president of his 11th-grade class. He graduated in 1924 from Johnson City High School, where he participated in public speaking, debate, and baseball. At 15, Johnson was the youngest in his class. Pressured by his parents to attend college, he enrolled at a "sub college" of Southwest Texas State Teachers College (SWTSTC) in the summer of 1924, where students from unaccredited high schools could take the 12th-grade courses needed for admission to college. He left the school just weeks after his arrival and decided to move to California. He worked at his cousin's legal practice and in odd jobs before returning to Texas, where he worked as a day laborer. In 1926, Johnson enrolled at SWTSTC. He worked his way through school, participated in debate and campus politics, and edited the school newspaper, The College Star. The college years refined his skills of persuasion and political organization. For nine months, from 1928 to 1929, Johnson paused his studies to teach Mexican–American children at the segregated Welhausen School in Cotulla, Texas, 90 miles (140 km) south of San Antonio. The job helped him to save money to complete his education, and he graduated in 1930 with a Bachelor of Science in history and his certificate of qualification as a high school teacher. He briefly taught at Pearsall High School in Pearsall, Texas before taking a position teaching public speaking at Sam Houston High School in Houston. When he returned to San Marcos in 1965, after signing the Higher Education Act of 1965, Johnson reminisced: "I shall never forget the faces of the boys and the girls in that little Welhausen Mexican School, and I remember even yet the pain of realizing and knowing then that college was closed to practically every one of those children because they were too poor. And I think it was then that I made up my mind that this nation could never rest while the door to knowledge remained closed to any American." After Richard M. Kleberg won a 1931 special election to represent Texas in the United States House of Representatives, he appointed Johnson as his legislative secretary. This marked Johnson's formal introduction to politics. Johnson secured the position on the recommendation of his father and that of state senator Welly Hopkins, for whom Johnson had campaigned in 1930.
