In an interview with Revolver magazine, Stephenson described the project as "fucked-up electronic punk" and rejected the "industrial" label for being "very goth, and very black and white," emphasizing its "a lot more colorful" nature. Kerrang! recognized Machine Girl as one of the "bands expanding the definition of hardcore," characterizing them as "a particularly punky and ferocious breed of the electronic sub-genre breakcore that could easily pass for hardcore when they rip it live." Pitchfork defined their sound as "relentlessly smashing together bits of punk, grindcore, rave, industrial, and more," describing it as "unpredictable and dangerous, full of animalistic rage and uncontrollable energy." The project's name originates from the 2008 Japanese film The Machine Girl, which they occasionally sampled on their 2014 album WLFGRL. Stephenson is also a member of the electronic duo Prolaps with Bonnie Baxter from Kill Alters, beginning their collaboration on the track "Vomit" from ...Because I'm Young Arrogant and Hate Everything You Stand For, which they started releasing in 2020. In 2013, Machine Girl began posting self-directed videos on their YouTube channel, starting with the unfinished song "~*•°•.[g0o∂]_[∫3º¥].•°•*~," released on December 20, 2013. Their next upload was on February 7, 2014, for the song "Ginger Claps," nine days before the release of their debut album WLFGRL. On November 4, 2014, they posted a video titled "___________DJPH11252014," promoting a DJ performance at "DJ PHANTASY CLUB" featuring ABSRDST, Doss, DV-i, Ducky, Machine Girl, Ligaments, Legion, and The Magick Report, including a snippet of an early mix of "Loop Version" that later appeared on their 2018 album The Ugly Art. On July 31, 2015, Machine Girl released two videos titled "HEAVEN MIX" and "HELL MIX," featuring visuals by Videopunks and containing snippets from each side of their sophomore album Gemini. The next official music video was for "Bitten Twice," released on May 16, 2017, followed by "Sad Claps" on June 12, 2017. Subsequent visualizers were uploaded for ...Because I'm Young Arrogant and Hate Everything You Stand For (September 24, 2017), MRK90 MIX VOL 1 (December 17, 2017), and The Ugly Art (October 14, 2018). The next music video to be published was for "Fully In It" on August 28, 2020, featuring stop motion animation by Ellie Thatcher. On November 15, 2020, Machine Girl released a video titled "GLOBAL FANDEMIC [MACHINE GIRL SET @ A2B2 NIGHT OF FIRE]" as part of a 24-hour virtual music festival hosted by Andy Morin of a2b2, featuring Matt performing over fan-submitted visualizers and including almost entirely unreleased songs and a shortened version of "Athoth A Go!! Go!!" with a different bassline, as well as an early demo of "Just Because You Can," which later appeared on their 2024 album MG Ultra. A visualizer for Prolaps' album Guilted Hexitation was posted on January 3, 2021, titled "PROLAPS 2021 GUILTED HEXITATION," shot by Nicos Kennedy and edited by Lana Evoli. A visualizer for Ultra Cycle Pt. 1: Vernal Birth premiered on March 21, 2021, with visuals by Lucid Interval, followed by a video for Ultra Cycle Pt. 2: Estival Growth on June 22, 2021, featuring visuals by N3T4. On August 28, 2024, Machine Girl released an official music video for "Until I Die," from the album MG Ultra, directed by Bryan M. Ferguson. A week later, on September 4, 2024, they released a music video for "Motherfather" from the same album. Despite resembling AI-generated art, the video was confirmed to contain no AI-generated assets, as stated by director John Lee. On October 4, 2024, they released a music video for "Psychic Attack," the final track of MG Ultra. Two months later, on December 13, 2024, they released a music video for "Ass2Mars," another MG Ultra song, directed by Sandy Loaf. A video for "Grindhouse," another track from MG Ultra, premiered on January 1, 2025, directed, filmed, and edited by Sydney Villacortabuer, and features scenes of a fight at a supernatural party.

Madhur Canteen (Bengali: মধুর রেস্তোরা, romanized: Modhur restora, lit. 'Madhu's canteen') is a well-known landmark in the history of Dhaka University and in Bangladesh's national politics due to its association with various political movements that originated from the university. The canteen's current location holds significant architectural and heritage value. Madhusudan Dey (Modhu), the canteen's founder, is a key figure in the region's socio-political history; he was killed on 25 March 1971 during Operation Searchlight when the Pakistan Army attacked Dhaka University, taking him to Jagannath Hall where he was executed along with many university students. Madhusudan Dey was injured, arrested, and killed in the early morning hours of 26 March 1971 after the military stormed his house, during which his wife, son, and daughter-in-law were also killed. After the Liberation War, Arun Kumar Dey took over the management of the canteen. The canteen was established in 1921 when Madhusudan Dey, aged 15, came to Dhaka with his father, Aditya Chandra, who, with university authorities' permission, began selling food on the campus, which at the time was located in the present Dhaka Medical College building. The canteen was later relocated when the Arts Faculty moved to a new building at Nilkhet. Madhur Canteen played a central role in the Bangladesh Liberation Movement and was a focal point for political activism, including the Language Movements of 1948 and 1952, the 1949 movement by fourth-class Dhaka University employees, student protests against the university's black laws (kala kanoon), and the 1969 mass uprising in East Pakistan. During these events, it served as a social epicentre for student leaders and activists. The Pakistani army targeted the canteen on 25 March 1971, marking the beginning of Operation Searchlight. The canteen suffered severe damage during the liberation war and was subsequently reconstructed. It was relocated to an old structure that previously served as the Durbar Hall of the Dhaka Nawabs, a building constructed starting in 1873 and continued over several years. In 1906, a conference held in this building, sponsored by Nawab Bahadur Sir Khwaja Salimullah, the Nawab of Dhaka, led to the formation of the All-India Muslim League. The canteen continues to be a significant community gathering place. In 1995, a statue of Madhusudan Dey, created by Toufiq Hosen Khan, a student of fine arts, was installed in front of the canteen.

Mahlagha Mallah (Persian: مه‌لقا ملاح‎; 21 September 1917 – 8 November 2021) was an Iranian environmental activist and librarian, recognized as the "Mother of Iran's Environment." She was born on 21 September 1917 in a caravanserai near Now Kandeh, while her parents were en route to Mashhad on a pilgrimage. Her mother, Khadijeh Afzal Vaziri, and her grandmother, Bibi Khanoom Astarabadi, were both women's rights activists in Iran. Her father, Aghabzorg Mallah, worked for the government and resided in various cities. At 17, she married Hossein Abolhasani. After studying philosophy, social sciences, and sociology at the University of Tehran, she earned a master's degree in social sciences in 1958. In 1966, she moved to Paris to pursue a PhD at the University of the Sorbonne, which she completed in 1968, and also studied librarianship at the National Library of France. Upon returning to Iran, she worked as a librarian at the Psychology Research Institute Library at the University of Tehran. It was only after her retirement from librarianship in 1977 that she and her husband began environmental campaigning. Her interest in environmental issues was influenced by her mother's activism and deepened when, in 1973, she read a book on pollution to learn how to catalogue it. After retiring, she began researching pollution in Tehran, initially visiting homes and speaking with residents about environmental concerns. In 1993, she founded the Women's Society Against Environmental Pollution, the first non-governmental environmental organization in Iran, which was officially registered with the Ministry of the Interior in 1995. By 2012, it had become the largest environmental group in Iran, with branches in 14 Iranian cities and had enabled over 25,000 families to recycle. In 2011, it was considered the most popular environmental group in the country. In 2009, the society published a report titled "Water Rights," highlighting the urgent need to conserve wetland habitats in Iran, including in the Zayandeh Rud region. Mallah is described as an ecofeminist, emphasizing that women must be central to environmentalism. Her life story was featured in the 2015 documentary All My Trees, directed by Rakhshān Banietemad. She passed away on 8 November 2021, at the age of 104.

A mammal, derived from the Latin *mamma* meaning "breast," is a vertebrate belonging to the class Mammalia, characterised by milk-producing mammary glands, a broad neocortex, fur or hair, and three middle ear bones. These traits distinguish mammals from reptiles and birds, whose ancestors diverged from them during the Carboniferous Period over 300 million years ago. Approximately 6,640 extant species of mammals have been described and are divided into 27 orders. The largest orders by species count are Rodentia (including mice, rats, porcupines, beavers, capybaras), Chiroptera (bats), and Eulipotyphla (including hedgehogs, moles, and shrews). The next three are Primates (including humans, monkeys, and lemurs), Cetartiodactyla (including pigs, bovids, and whales), and Carnivora (including cats, dogs, and seals). Mammals are the only living members of Synapsida, a clade that, along with Sauropsida (reptiles and birds), forms the larger Amniota group. Early synapsids, known as pelycosaurs, evolved during the Pennsylvanian subperiod (~323 to ~300 million years ago), splitting from the reptile lineage. Therapsids, which emerged in the Middle Permian (~265 million years ago), became dominant land vertebrates and gave rise to mammals through a series of evolutionary stages culminating in cynodonts. Mammals originated from cynodonts during the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, with the first known mammals (in Kemp's definition) appearing around 225 million years ago. Crown group mammals evolved from earlier mammaliaforms during the Early Jurassic. The modern diversity of mammals developed in the Paleogene and Neogene periods of the Cenozoic era after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs, making mammals the dominant terrestrial group since 66 million years ago. Most mammals are quadrupedal, though some have adapted for life in water, air, trees, or underground; bipeds use only the lower limbs, while cetaceans and sea cows have reduced rear limbs. Mammals range in size from the 30–40 millimetres (1.2–1.6 inches) bumblebee bat to the 30-metre (98-foot) blue whale, the largest animal ever known. Lifespan varies from two years in shrews to 211 years in the bowhead whale. All modern mammals give birth to live young, except the five monotreme species, which lay eggs. The most species-rich group is viviparous placental mammals, which use a placenta to nourish offspring during gestation. Most mammals are intelligent, with some exhibiting large brains, self-awareness, and tool use; they communicate through vocalisations, ultrasound, scent marking, alarm signals, singing, echolocation, and in humans, complex language. Mammals form fission–fusion societies, harems, or hierarchies, though some are solitary and territorial, and most are polygynous, though some are monogamous or polyandrous. Domestication of mammals during the Neolithic Revolution shifted human societies from nomadic to sedentary, enabling farming and leading to the development of early civilisations. Domesticated mammals provide transport, agriculture, food (meat and dairy), fur, and leather, and are also used for sport, as pets, working animals, and in scientific research. Mammals have been depicted in art since the Paleolithic and appear in literature, film, mythology, and religion. Declines in numbers and extinctions are primarily due to human poaching and habitat destruction, especially deforestation. Mammal classification has evolved since Carl Linnaeus first defined the class in 1758, and no system is universally accepted; McKenna & Bell (1997) and Wilson & Reeder (2005) offer useful compendiums, while Simpson (1945) was widely taught until the end of the 20th century. However, since 1945, new paleontological data and cladistic methods have challenged Simpson’s classification, which remains the closest to an official system despite its flaws. Most mammals, including the six most species-rich orders, belong to the placental group. According to Mammal Species of the World, 5,416 species were identified in 2006, grouped into 1,229 genera, 153 families, and 29 orders; by 2008, the IUCN counted 5,488 species in its Global Mammal Assessment. Research published in the Journal of Mammalogy in 2018 identified 6,495 mammal species, including 96 recently extinct. The term "mammal" is modern, coined by Linnaeus in 1758 from *mamma*. Timothy Rowe (1988) defined Mammalia as the crown group—the most recent common ancestor of living monotremes (echidnas and platypuses) and therians (marsupials and placentals), and all descendants—dating its origin to the Jurassic Period, around 167 million years ago, based on fossils like Ambondro, Amphilestes, and Amphitherium. T. S. Kemp defines mammals as synapsids with a dentary–squamosal jaw articulation and transverse molar occlusion, with the earliest known example, Tikitherium, dating to 225 million years ago. Molecular studies based on DNA and retrotransposon data suggest three major placental lineages—Afrotheria, Xenarthra, and Boreoeutheria—diverging in the Cretaceous, with divergence times ranging from 105 to 120 million years ago depending on DNA type and paleogeographic interpretations. The relationships among these groups remain contentious, with hypotheses including Atlantogenata, Epitheria, and Exafroplacentalia. Boreoeutheria includes Euarchontoglires and Laurasiatheria. Phylogeny according to Álvarez-Carretero et al. (2022) includes Monotremata, Paucituberculata, Didelphimorphia, Microbiotheria, Notoryctemorphia, Peramelemorphia, Dasyuromorphia, Diprotodontia, Cingulata, Pilosa, Hyracoidea, Sirenia, Proboscidea, Tubulidentata, Macroscelidea, Afrosoricida, Eulipotyphla, Chiroptera, Pholidota, Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Scandentia, Lagomorpha, Rodentia, Dermoptera, and Primates. The first fully terrestrial vertebrates were amniotes, which evolved from amphibious tetrapods in the Pennsylvanian and had internal membranes allowing egg development on land. Two major amniote lineages emerged: Synapsida (including mammals) and Sauropsida (including reptiles, birds, and dinosaurs). Synapsids have a single temporal fenestra; early forms like Dimetrodon were large and predatory. Nonmammalian synapsids were incorrectly called "mammal-like reptiles" but are neither reptiles nor part of the reptile lineage. Therapsids evolved in the Middle Permian and became dominant. The Permian–Triassic extinction event (~252 million years ago) ended carnivorous therapsid dominance, with archosaurs (crocodiles, pterosaurs, dinosaurs) taking over large carnivore niches. Large cynodonts like Trucidocynodon and traversodontids still occupied herbivorous and carnivorous roles. By the Jurassic, dinosaurs dominated large herbivore niches. Mammals expanded from a nocturnal insectivore niche from the mid-Jurassic onward; Castorocauda, a Jurassic relative, had adaptations for swimming and digging. Most mammals remained nocturnal, contributing to their traits. Mesozoic mammal species were mostly multituberculates, eutriconodonts, and spalacotheriids. The earliest known metatherian, Sinodelphys, dates to 125 million years ago in China and includes fur and soft tissue imprints. The earliest known eutherian, Juramaia sinensis, is from 160 million years ago in the late Jurassic. Eomaia, from 125 million years ago, shares features with marsupials but not placentals, including epipubic bones extending from the pelvis—present in marsupials, monotremes, and early eutherians like Asioryctitheria but absent in modern placentals. These bones stiffen muscles and reduce pelvic space, suggesting a short gestation and small newborns, indicating the placenta evolved later. Epipubic bones are ancestral and lost in placental mammals. One of the earliest monotremes, Teinolophos, lived about 120 million years ago in Australia. Monotremes retain a cloaca (shared orifice for urination, defecation, and reproduction) and lay leathery, uncalcified eggs. Hadrocodium, from 195 million years ago in the early Jurassic, shows the first clear jaw joint formed solely by the dentary and squamosal bones, with no articular bone. The earliest clear evidence of hair or fur comes from Castorocauda and Megaconus, from 164 million years ago. In the 1950s, foramina in cynodont jaws were thought to indicate whiskers and fur, but modern lizards like Tupinambis have similar foramina without whiskers, so this evidence is not definitive. Studies of Permian coprolites suggest non-mammalian synapsids had fur, possibly as early as dicynodonts. Endothermy likely first evolved in non-mammalian therapsids. Monotremes have lower body temperatures and variable metabolic rates than marsupials and placentals, though some ancestors may have had therian-like body temperatures. Some modern therians, like afrotheres and xenarthrans, have secondarily evolved lower body temperatures. Erect limbs evolved incompletely—monotremes have sprawling limbs—while parasagittal limb posture appeared in the late Jurassic or early Cretaceous in eutherian Eomaia and metatherian Sinodelphys, both dated to 125 million years ago. Epipubic bones are a feature present in early mammals and lost in placentals.

Studies on Permian coprolites indicate that non-mammalian synapsids of that epoch already possessed fur, suggesting the evolution of hairs may have originated as early as in dicynodonts. The origin of endothermy in mammals is uncertain, though it is generally believed to have first evolved in non-mammalian therapsids. Modern monotremes have lower body temperatures and more variable metabolic rates than marsupials and placentals, but evidence suggests some of their ancestors, possibly including those of therians, may have had body temperatures similar to modern therians. Some modern therians, such as afrotheres and xenarthrans, have secondarily evolved lower body temperatures. The evolution of erect limbs in mammals is incomplete—both living and fossil monotremes have sprawling limbs. The parasagittal (nonsprawling) limb posture emerged during the late Jurassic or early Cretaceous and is found in eutherian Eomaia and metatherian Sinodelphys, both dated to 125 million years ago. Epipubic bones, a trait influential in mammal reproduction, first appear in Tritylodontidae and are considered a synapomorphy between them and Mammaliaformes; they are widespread in non-placental Mammaliaformes, though Megazostrodon and Erythrotherium appear to lack them. It is proposed that the original function of lactation was to keep eggs moist, primarily based on observations of monotremes. In human females, mammary glands develop fully during puberty regardless of pregnancy. Therians occupied medium- to large-sized ecological niches in the Cenozoic after the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event about 66 million years ago, which eliminated ecological space previously held by non-avian dinosaurs and other reptiles, leading to an exponential increase in body size (megafauna). This diversification was not solely due to expansion into large-bodied niches; mammals diversified rapidly, showing an exponential rise in diversity. For instance, the earliest-known bat dates to about 50 million years ago, only 16 million years after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. Molecular phylogenetic studies initially suggested most placental orders diverged between 100 and 85 million years ago, with modern families emerging from the late Eocene through the Miocene, though no placental fossils have been found before the end of the Cretaceous. The earliest undisputed placental fossils come from the early Paleocene, after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs; Protungulatum donnae was once considered one of the first placental mammals but has since been reclassified as a non-placental eutherian. Recalibrations of genetic and morphological diversity rates suggest a Late Cretaceous origin for placentals and a Paleocene origin for most modern clades. The earliest-known ancestor of primates is Archicebus achilles, dating to around 55 million years ago, weighing 20–30 grams and fitting within a human palm. Living mammals are identified by the presence of sweat glands, including those specialized for milk production, though in fossil classification, other features are used due to the absence of soft tissue. Many traits shared by all living mammals appeared in the earliest members of the group, which were not present in Triassic mammal ancestors. Nearly all mammaliaforms possess an epipubic bone, with modern placentals being the exception. On average, male mammals are larger than females, with males being at least 10% larger in over 45% of species; most orders show male-biased sexual dimorphism, though some, like Lagomorpha, show no bias or are female-biased. Sexual size dimorphism increases with body size (Rensch's rule), with male-biased dimorphism linked to male–male competition and sexual selection, which correlates with mating systems and both male and female size. Female mass is also under parallel selection, with higher weaning age in polygynous species and lower fecundity in larger females, indicating selection for smaller females. These patterns hold across mammals, though there is variation among orders. Most mammals have seven cervical vertebrae; exceptions include the manatee and two-toed sloth (six) and the three-toed sloth (nine). All mammals have a neocortex, a brain region unique to mammals. Placental brains have a corpus callosum, unlike monotremes and marsupials. The mammalian heart has four chambers—two atria and two ventricles—with four valves ensuring unidirectional blood flow. Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left atrium via pulmonary veins and flows into the left ventricle, with most blood entering passively during relaxation, and the left atrium contracting near the end of ventricular relaxation to pump blood. The heart is supplied with nutrients and oxygen via coronary arteries. Mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus to accommodate more hemoglobin, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. Mammalian lungs are spongy and honeycombed, with breathing primarily driven by the diaphragm, which contracts to increase thoracic volume and relaxes to decrease it, expelling air. During exercise, abdominal muscles contract to increase pressure on the diaphragm, forcing air out more forcefully. The rib cage expands and contracts via respiratory muscles, allowing air to move down its pressure gradient. This system is known as a bellows lung. The integumentary system consists of three layers: epidermis (10–30 cells thick, providing waterproofing), dermis (15–40 times thicker, containing blood vessels and bones), and hypodermis (adipose tissue for insulation and cushioning; thickness varies, with right whales having the thickest at 20 inches or 51 cm). No other animals have hair, which is a definitive mammalian trait, though some have very little. Herbivores have evolved diverse dental structures for plant consumption: frugivores and soft-leaf feeders have low-crowned teeth for grinding; grazers with silica-rich grasses have high-crowned teeth that wear less. Carnivores have carnassial teeth, long canines, and similar tooth replacement patterns. Even-toed ungulates (Artiodactyla) have a four-chambered stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum), where plant material is mixed with saliva, separated, and regurgitated as cud; cellulolytic microbes break down cellulose. Perissodactyls store digested food in an enlarged cecum for fermentation. Carnivores have a simple stomach adapted for meat digestion, with a short or absent cecum and a non-sacculated large intestine. Mammals are ureotelic, converting ammonia to urea via the liver's urea cycle; bilirubin, a byproduct of blood cells, is excreted through bile and urine, giving feces a brown color. Mammalian kidneys have a renal pelvis, pyramids, cortex, and medulla due to elongated loops of Henle; they are typically bean-shaped, though pinnipeds, cetaceans, and bears have multilobed kidneys. Most adult placentals lack a cloaca; in embryos, the cloaca divides into a posterior region becoming the anus and an anterior region that develops into the urogenital sinus in females or the penile urethra in males. Afrosoricids and some shrews retain a cloaca as adults; marsupials have a separate genital tract with a trace of the cloaca externally; monotremes have a true cloaca, with urine flowing into it rather than a bladder in placentals. Mammals have a larynx that opens and closes quickly to produce sounds, with a supralaryngeal vocal tract filtering sound. The lungs and surrounding muscles provide air and pressure for phonation. More primitive mammals like echidnas produce only hisses through exhalation; other mammals use vocal folds to generate sounds such as purring and screaming. Mammals can shift the larynx to breathe through the nose while swallowing through the mouth and produce oral or nasal sounds; nasal sounds are soft, oral sounds are loud. Some mammals, like the hammer-headed bat (Hypsignathus monstrosus), have a large larynx that occupies the thoracic cavity, lowering pitch; large vocal pads, such as in big cats, also lower pitch. Infrasound is produced by elephants and baleen whales; small mammals with small larynxes produce ultrasound, detectable via middle ear and cochlear modifications, used in mother-to-pup communication and echolocation in bats and toothed whales, which use a melon instead of a vocal membrane. Primates have air sacs attached to the larynx that may lower resonances or increase sound volume. Vocal production is controlled by cranial nerve nuclei in the brain, supplied by the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves (branches of the vagus), and the hypoglossal and facial nerves; electrical stimulation of the periaqueductal grey (PEG) region elicits vocalizations. The ability to learn new vocalizations is found only in humans, seals, cetaceans, elephants, and possibly bats, with humans having a direct connection between the motor cortex and spinal motor neurons. The primary function of fur is thermoregulation, with additional roles in protection, sensory functions, waterproofing, and camouflage. Hair length does not affect thermoregulation; for example, tropical mammals like sloths have similar fur length to arctic mammals but less insulation, while some tropical mammals with short hair have the same insulating value as arctic mammals. Fur denseness increases insulation, with arctic mammals like the musk ox having dense underfur and guard hairs up to 30 cm long, forming an airtight coat to survive −40°C. Desert mammals like camels use dense fur to block solar heat, with fur reaching 70°C while skin stays at 40°C. Aquatic mammals trap air in fur to conserve heat by keeping skin dry. Mammalian coat coloration is influenced by camouflage, sexual selection, communication, and thermoregulation, primarily due to melanin types: eumelanin for brown and black, pheomelanin for yellow to reddish hues. Some mammals, such as mandrills, vervet monkeys, and certain opossums, have blue skin due to light diffraction in collagen. Many sloths appear green because their fur hosts green algae, possibly a symbiotic relationship aiding camouflage. Camouflage is significant in many mammals, such as arctic foxes, collared lemmings, stoats, and snowshoe hares, which change color seasonally from brown in summer to white in winter. Arboreal mammals like primates and marsupials have violet, green, or blue skin, indicating adaptive advantages in arboreal habitats. Aposematism is mentioned.

Some mammals exhibit vibrant colors due to light diffraction in collagen fibers, such as mandrills, vervet monkeys, Mexican mouse opossums, and Derby's woolly opossums, which have blue skin. Many sloths appear green because their fur hosts green algae, possibly indicating a symbiotic relationship that provides camouflage. Camouflage is a significant factor in many mammals, helping them avoid predators or prey; for instance, arctic and subarctic mammals like the arctic fox (Alopex lagopus), collared lemming (Dicrostonyx groenlandicus), stoat (Mustela erminea), and snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus) change color seasonally—being brown in summer and white in winter—to match their environment. Arboreal mammals, including primates and marsupials, often have violet, green, or blue skin, suggesting an evolutionary advantage in tree-dwelling habitats through convergent evolution. Aposematism, or warning coloration, explains the black-and-white pelage of self-defense species like skunks and honey badgers. Coat color can be sexually dimorphic in many primates, with differences potentially reflecting nutrition and hormone levels relevant to mate selection. Darker coats absorb more solar radiation and help retain heat, with some small mammals like voles having darker fur in winter; in contrast, arctic mammals such as the polar bear have white, pigmentless fur that reflects solar radiation. The black-and-white striping of zebras may deter biting flies. Mammals reproduce through internal fertilization and are solely gonochoric, meaning individuals are born with either male or female genitalia. Males ejaculate semen through a penis, which may be enclosed in a prepuce, and some placentals urinate through the penis; some also possess a penis bone (baculum). Marsupials typically have forked penises, while echidna penises have four heads with only two functional. Erection can result from blood flow into spongy tissue or muscular action. Most mammals have testicles that descend into the scrotum, usually located posterior to the penis, though in marsupials it is often anterior. Females generally have a vulva (clitoris and labia) externally, with internal structures including paired oviducts, one or two uteri, one or two cervices, and a vagina; marsupials have two lateral vaginas and a medial vagina, while monotreme "vagina" is better described as a urogenital sinus. Placental uterine systems vary: duplex (two uteri and cervices), bipartite (two uterine horns with one cervix), bicornuate (Y-shaped), or simplex (single uterus). The ancestral mammalian reproductive condition involves giving birth to relatively undeveloped young, either via direct vivipary or short-lived soft-shelled eggs, likely due to epipubic bones restricting torso expansion. Kayentatherium, an early mammal, produced undeveloped perinates in litters of 38. Most modern mammals are viviparous, but the five monotreme species—platypus and four echidna species—lay eggs. Monotremes have a sex-determination system distinct from most mammals, with platypus sex chromosomes resembling those of chickens. Marsupials have a short gestation period, giving birth to underdeveloped young that continue developing in a pouch (marsupium), a plesiomorphic trait among viviparous mammals due to epipubic bones preventing torso expansion; even non-placental eutherians likely reproduced this way. Placentals give birth to more developed young after long gestation periods, thanks to the placenta, which connects the fetus to the uterine wall for nutrient exchange. In placentals, epipubic bones are either lost or transformed into the baculum, enabling torso expansion. Most mammals give birth multiple times in their lifespan, though a few are semelparous. Mammalian mammary glands produce milk, the primary nutrition for newborns; monotremes lack teats but have mammary glands, with young licking milk from patches on the mother’s belly. Marsupial milk changes in production and composition due to underdeveloped young, and mammary glands have autonomy to supply different milks at various developmental stages. Placental milk is dominated by lactose, while monotreme and marsupial milk is dominated by oligosaccharides. Weaning occurs when a mammal reduces dependence on maternal milk and transitions to solid food. Nearly all mammals are endothermic ("warm-blooded"), with hair aiding in thermoregulation, allowing them to forage in cold climates where ectothermic animals cannot survive. Endothermy requires high food intake, so mammals consume more per unit of body weight than reptiles; small insectivorous mammals eat large amounts, while the naked mole-rat produces little metabolic heat and is considered an operational poikilotherm. Birds are also endothermic, so endothermy is not unique to mammals. Mammalian lifespan varies widely—from one year in the yellow-sided opossum to 211 years in the oldest bowhead whale. DNA repair capacity is strongly linked to lifespan; a 1974 study by Hart and Setlow found that DNA excision repair increases with species lifespan, and species with longer lifespans show better recognition of DNA double-strand breaks and higher levels of the Ku80 protein. In a study of 16 mammalian species, DNA repair genes were up-regulated in longer-lived species, and the cellular level of poly ADP ribose polymerase correlated with lifespan in 13 species. Additional studies across various mammalian species also found a correlation between lifespan and DNA repair capability. Most vertebrates walk plantigrade, but many mammals like cats and dogs are digitigrade, walking on their toes for greater speed. Horses are unguligrade, walking on the tips of their toes for increased stride length and speed. Great apes, giant anteaters, and platypuses are knuckle-walkers. Some mammals, such as humans and great apes, are bipedal, using two limbs for locomotion, which provides a wider field of vision, energy conservation, and hand manipulation for foraging; some bipeds hop, such as kangaroos and kangaroo rats. Animals use different gaits depending on speed, terrain, and situation; horses have four natural gaits: walk, trot, canter, and gallop, with occasional unusual gaits like crawling. Quadrupeds use gaits categorized by support sequence: walking (some feet on ground), running (all feet off ground at some point), and leaping. Arboreal mammals often have elongated limbs to cross gaps, reach food, or brachiate; many, such as tree porcupines, silky anteaters, spider monkeys, and possums, have prehensile tails for grasping branches. Spider monkeys have adhesive pads or bare patches at the tail tip for increased friction. Claws help with climbing rough surfaces and reorienting forces, enabling squirrels to climb large, flat tree trunks, though they can interfere with grasping small branches. Primates use hairless fingertips to grip branches via friction, with grip strength depending on branch diameter. Squirrels have mobile ankle joints that allow them to rotate their feet into a reversed posture, enabling claws to hook into bark and counteract gravity. Small size offers advantages to arboreal species, including larger relative branch size, lower center of mass, increased stability, lower mass, and better movement in cluttered habitats. Size affects gliding animals like sugar gliders. Some primates, bats, and sloths achieve passive stability by hanging beneath branches, making pitching and tipping irrelevant. Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, using wing movements to generate lift and thrust. Their wings are thinner and contain more bones than birds, allowing greater maneuverability and lift with less drag. By folding wings during upstrokes, bats use 35% less energy than birds. Bat wing membranes are delicate but can regenerate small tears. Touch-sensitive receptors called Merkel cells, with tiny hairs in the center, are present on bat wings, enhancing sensitivity to airflow and enabling efficient flight through wing shape adjustments. Fossorial mammals, adapted to digging, include badgers, naked mole-rats, and many rodents; they live primarily underground, with subterranean species living exclusively underground and sub-fossorial species having limited adaptations. Fossorial mammals have fusiform bodies, thick at the shoulders and tapering at the tail and nose, with degenerated eyes (e.g., fully fossorial marsupial moles have useless eyes, while pocket gophers have small functional eyes); external ears are small or absent. They have short, stout legs for strength over speed, broad front paws with strong claws for digging, and webbed back paws with claws to throw dirt backward; most have large incisors to prevent dirt from entering their mouths. Shrews, hedgehogs, and moles were once classified under the obsolete order Insectivora. Fully aquatic mammals, such as cetaceans and sirenians, have lost their legs and use tail fins for propulsion; whales move their tail fins up and down for forward motion, with flippers used for steering; most have dorsal fins to prevent flipping. Sirenians move using flukes raised and lowered in long strokes, which can be twisted for turning, with paddle-like forelimbs aiding in turning and slowing. Semi-aquatic mammals, such as pinnipeds, have two pairs of flippers (fore and hind), with elbows and ankles enclosed; they reduce drag through streamlined bodies, smooth muscle bundles, and lack of arrector pili allowing fur to be streamlined. Fore-flippers are used for locomotion in a wing-like manner, with movement not continuous and gliding between strokes; reduced fore-limb length provides mechanical advantage at the shoulder and elbow joints, while hind-flippers serve as stabilizers. Other semi-aquatic mammals include beavers, hippos, otters, and platypuses. Hippos are large semi-aquatic mammals with barrel-shaped bodies and graviportal skeletal structures adapted to support their weight; their specific gravity allows them to sink and move along river bottoms. Many mammals communicate through vocalizations for mating, warning, food signaling, and social interaction. Males often call during mating to attract females and deter rivals, such as lions and red deer roaring. Humpback whale songs may signal to females and vary by region, forming distinct dialects. Social vocalizations include territorial calls.

The animal glides between each stroke, and compared to terrestrial carnivorans, its fore-limbs are reduced in length, providing greater mechanical advantage to the locomotor muscles at the shoulder and elbow joints; the hind-flippers function as stabilizers. Other semi-aquatic mammals include beavers, hippopotamuses, otters, and platypuses. Hippos are large semi-aquatic mammals with barrel-shaped bodies that have graviportal skeletal structures adapted to support their massive weight, and their specific gravity allows them to sink and move along the riverbed. Mammals communicate through vocalizations for purposes such as mating rituals, warning calls, indicating food sources, and social interaction. Males often call during mating to deter rivals and attract females, as seen in lions and red deer; humpback whale songs may signal to females and vary by ocean region; gibbons use territorial calls, and greater spear-nosed bats use frequency to distinguish groups; vervet monkeys emit distinct alarm calls for at least four predators, triggering different responses—such as climbing trees for a python or seeking ground cover for an eagle—and prairie dogs produce complex calls indicating predator type, size, and speed. Elephants use a range of sounds including snorting, screaming, trumpeting, roaring, and rumbling, some of which are infrasonic and can travel up to 6 miles (9.7 km) during still times near sunrise or sunset. Many mammals use visual anti-predator signals, such as deer and gazelle stotting to show fitness or white-tailed deer flagging their tails when alarmed to alert predators. Scent-marking is used by many mammals, likely for territorial defense and various social functions. Microbats and toothed whales, including oceanic dolphins, use vocalizations for both social interaction and echolocation. Maintaining a high body temperature is energetically costly, so mammals require a nutritious and abundant diet. Early mammals were likely predators, but species have since adapted; carnivores eat animals, herbivores consume plants containing complex carbohydrates like cellulose, and herbivores rely on gut bacteria in a multichambered stomach or large cecum to digest these substances. Some mammals are coprophagous, consuming feces to absorb undigested nutrients. Omnivores eat both plants and animals; carnivores have simple digestive tracts due to the ease of digesting meat, though baleen whales have multi-chambered stomachs like herbivores. Small mammals, weighing less than about 18 ounces (510 g; 1.1 lb), are mostly insectivorous because they cannot sustain a slow herbivorous digestive process; larger mammals can tolerate slower feeding or digestion. Some omnivores show varying degrees of carnivory and herbivory, categorized as mesocarnivory (50–70% meat), hypercarnivory (70% or more meat), or hypocarnivory (50% or less meat), with differences in dentition—hypocarnivores have dull, triangular teeth for grinding, while hypercarnivores have conical, sharp teeth and strong jaws for bone-crushing, as in hyenas, some of which had sabre-shaped canines. Some physiological carnivores consume plant matter and some physiological herbivores consume meat, which from a behavioral standpoint makes them omnivores, but from a physiological perspective, they may still be classified as carnivores or herbivores if they obtain nutrients from non-complementary sources; for example, giraffes, camels, and cattle gnaw bones for minerals, and cats eat grass to expel hairballs, aid hemoglobin production, or act as a laxative. Many mammals hibernate when food is scarce, with larger species like bears becoming polyphagic to build fat stores and smaller ones storing food; during hibernation, metabolism slows, heart and respiratory rates decrease, and internal temperatures drop—Arctic ground squirrels can reach −2.9 °C (26.8 °F), though their heads and necks remain above 0 °C (32 °F). Some mammals in hot environments aestivate during drought or extreme heat, such as the fat-tailed dwarf lemur (Cheirogaleus medius). Terrestrial animals in captivity learn to drink water, but most free-roaming mammals stay hydrated through moisture in food and learn to seek high-fluid foods; drinking methods vary: cats and canines lap with spoon-like tongues, with cats using only the tip of their smooth tongue to pull water into their mouths, while canines use a ladle-like tongue to scoop; ruminants and most herbivores partially submerge their mouths and use a plunging tongue action to draw water; cats drink more slowly than ruminants due to greater predation risks. Desert animals often avoid drinking and rely on succulent plants; in cold environments, hares, tree squirrels, and bighorn sheep consume snow and icicles; giraffes' drinking method, which appears to defy gravity, may involve a plunger-like function of their long necks; elephants draw water into their trunks and squirt it into their mouths. In intelligent mammals like primates, the cerebrum is relatively larger, and intelligence is indicated by learning and behavioral flexibility; rats are considered intelligent due to their ability to learn new tasks, and deer have smaller brains than cats, which must think to outwit prey. Tool use indicates learning and cognition; sea otters use rocks regularly to break open shells, with some populations spending 21% of their time making tools; chimpanzees use twigs to fish for termites, possibly learned through observation and representing true animal teaching; animals may experience a "Eureka moment" when solving puzzles; dogs can also have such moments. Brain size, relative to body mass, is a key indicator of intelligence, with allometric analysis showing brain size scales at approximately the 2⁄3 or 3⁄4 exponent of body mass; the encephalisation quotient compares an animal’s actual brain size to the expected size based on body mass. Sperm whales have the largest brain mass of any animal, averaging 8,000 cubic centimeters (490 cu in) and 7.8 kilograms (17 lb) in mature males. Self-awareness, measured by the mirror test, indicates abstract thinking and is shown in Asian elephants (some pass), chimpanzees, bonobos, orangutans, humans (from 18 months), common bottlenose dolphins, orcas, and false killer whales. Eusociality, the highest level of social organization, involves overlapping generations, division of reproductive labor, and cooperative care of young, typically seen in insects, but also in naked mole-rats and Damaraland mole-rats. Presociality involves communal living, cooperative care, or primitive reproductive division without all three traits of eusociality; humans and some Callitrichidae (marmosets and tamarins) show high levels of cooperative care; Harry Harlow’s 1958 rhesus monkey experiment showed that social interaction is essential for mental and sexual development. Fission–fusion societies change in size and composition, with a parent group splitting into smaller subgroups (fission) or reuniting (fusion) based on environmental or social needs; examples include primates (orangutans, spider monkeys), elephants, spotted hyenas, lions, and dolphins. Solitary animals defend territories and avoid social interactions except during breeding season to prevent resource competition and food depletion; they may also be less conspicuous to predators or prey. In hierarchies, individuals are either dominant or submissive; despotic hierarchies have one dominant individual (e.g., wolves, lemurs), while pecking orders are linear with a top and bottom, sometimes ranked by sex (e.g., hyenas); dominant individuals, or alphas, have high reproductive success, especially in harems where one or a few males have exclusive breeding rights, though non-resident males may be accepted in some cases, such as in common vampire bats. Some mammals are perfectly monogamous, mating for life and not taking other partners, including wolves, Eurasian beavers, and otters. Polygamy occurs in three forms: polygyny (one or multiple dominant males), polyandry (multiple males mating with one female), or polygynandry (multiple males with multiple females); polygyny is the most common, occurring in up to 90% of mammals, excluding leks; lek mating involves males gathering around females and displaying to attract them, as in harbour seals. All higher mammals (excluding monotremes) share live birth and lactation as key adaptations for young care, often building nests or burrows or feeding and guarding offspring for long periods; many are K-selected, investing more time and energy in their young than r-selected animals. When mating, both parents share interest in offspring success, though to varying degrees; mammalian females may exhibit maternal aggression toward other females or their young, though some mammals, like tenrecs, may "aunt" infants; male involvement in child rearing varies by species, such as southern pig-tailed macaques (no care) versus Japanese macaques (care). Non-human mammals play diverse roles in human culture, being the most popular pets with tens of millions of dogs, cats, rabbits, and mice kept globally; mammoths, horses, and deer are among the earliest subjects of art, found in Upper Paleolithic cave paintings like Lascaux; artists such as Albrecht Dürer, George Stubbs, and Edwin Landseer are known for mammal portraits; many species are hunted for sport and food, especially deer and wild boar; horses and dogs are widely raced with betting; there is a tension between animals as companions and as individuals with rights; mammals also play significant roles in literature, film, mythology, and religion.

Dogs, cats, rabbits, and mice are the most popular pets globally, with tens of millions of these animals kept by families worldwide. Mammals like mammoths, horses, and deer have been among the earliest subjects in art, appearing in Upper Paleolithic cave paintings such as at Lascaux. Major artists including Albrecht Dürer, George Stubbs, and Edwin Landseer are renowned for their mammal portraits. Deer and wild boar are especially popular as game animals, and mammals like horses and dogs are widely raced for sport, often involving betting. There is ongoing tension between animals as companions and their status as individuals with rights. Mammals play significant roles in literature, film, mythology, and religion. The domestication of mammals was crucial in the Neolithic transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture and civilization, leading to worldwide societal changes, biodiversity shifts, and environmental transformations. Domestic mammals form a major part of global livestock for meat, including approximately 1.4 billion cattle, 1 billion sheep, 1 billion domestic pigs (as of 2009), and over 700 million rabbits (as of 1985). Cattle and horses have long been used for work and transport, providing about 80% of power for small farms in the developing world and 20% of global transport, primarily in rural areas, with pack animals still used in mountainous regions. Mammal skins produce leather for shoes, clothing, and upholstery, and wool from sheep, goats, and alpacas has been used for centuries in clothing. Mammals are vital in scientific research, especially in genetics and medicine, with millions of mice and rats used annually; knockout mice, genetically modified with inactivated genes, help study gene functions, and non-human primates are used due to their similarity to humans. Despite their benefits, humans have severely impacted wild mammals, with wild mammal biomass now at just 4% of all mammals—96% being humans and their livestock—terrestrial wild mammals making up only 2%. Hybrids result from breeding genetically distinct individuals and include intra-specific (e.g., Bengal and Siberian tigers), interspecific (e.g., lions and tigers), and intergeneric (e.g., sheep and goats) crosses, occurring naturally in hybrid zones; some, like the red wolf, are recognized as species though controversially. Breeding-back efforts attempt to recreate extinct animals, such as Heck cattle resembling the aurochs, but lose the original wildtype gene pool. Purebred wild species face extinction due to genetic pollution—uncontrolled hybridization leading to gene swamping and outcompetition by hybrids—such as the endangered wild water buffalo threatened by domestic water buffalo. Defaunation, driven primarily by human activity, has led to empty forests and loss of large vertebrates, with the Quaternary extinction event suggesting human hunting of megafauna like the woolly mammoth. The IPBES 2019 Global Assessment Report states that wild mammal biomass has declined by 82% since the beginning of human civilization, with wild animals accounting for only 4% of mammalian biomass. Species like rhinoceroses, giraffes, primates, and pangolins are predicted to go extinct soon. The WWF’s 2020 Living Planet Report shows vertebrate wildlife populations have declined by 68% since 1970 due to human activities such as overconsumption, population growth, and intensive farming, indicating a sixth mass extinction. Hunting and poaching threaten hundreds of mammal species, especially near villages, such as peccaries, and the ivory trade severely impacts African elephants. Marine mammals face entanglement in fishing gear, with cetaceans suffering between 65,000 and 86,000 discard mortalities annually. Global conservation efforts include the Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio Accord), with 189 signatory countries, and the IUCN, which has over 1,200 member organizations. Recent extinctions, defined as those after 1500, include around 80 mammal species since that time and 2015. Some species, like the Père David’s deer, are extinct in the wild and survive only in captivity; others, like the Florida panther, are ecologically extinct due to critically low numbers; some are locally extinct (extirpated), such as Atlantic grey whales.

Mammoth Cave National Park is a U.S. national park located in south-central Kentucky, encompassing 52,007 acres (21,046 ha) primarily in Edmonson County, with small portions extending into Hart and Barren counties. The park includes the longest known cave system in the world, the Mammoth–Flint Ridge Cave System, which was formally named in 1972 after a connection was discovered between Mammoth Cave and the longer Flint Ridge system. As of 2025, more than 426 miles (686 km) of passageways have been surveyed, exceeding the length of Mexico's Sac Actun cave system by over 1.5 times. The park was established on July 1, 1941, following contentious eminent domain proceedings that continue to impact the region. It was designated a World Heritage Site on October 27, 1981, an International Biosphere Reserve on September 26, 1990, and an International Dark Sky Park on October 28, 2021. The park’s mission, as stated in its foundation document, is to preserve, protect, interpret, and study the internationally recognized biological and geologic features, including the cave system, the forested karst landscape, the Green and Nolin rivers, and evidence of human history, while providing public enjoyment, recreation, and understanding. The cave developed in Mississippian-aged limestone capped by the Big Clifty Sandstone, which has made the system stable; thin limestone layers within the sandstone create an epikarstic zone where tiny conduits dissolve due to acidic groundwater, leading to surface springs that later sink underground at the sandstone-limestone contact. The underlying limestone layers, in order from top to bottom, are the Girkin Formation, Ste. Genevieve Limestone, and St. Louis Limestone; the Main Cave passage is located at the base of the Girkin and top of the Ste. Genevieve. The cave’s stratigraphy is studied through correlation with explorer surveys to produce approximate three-dimensional maps without drilling. The sandstone caprock resists water penetration except through vertical cracks, making many upper passages dry and lacking stalactites or stalagmites, though erosion has created exceptions like the Frozen Niagara room. The contact between sandstone and limestone is visible when hiking from valley bottoms to ridgetops, where rock composition shifts from limestone to sandstone at a defined elevation. A massive sinkhole known as Cedar Sink exists in the southern part of the park, where a small river enters and disappears underground. The National Park Service offers several cave tours, including lighted tours of one to six hours featuring features like Grand Avenue, Frozen Niagara, and Fat Man's Misery, as well as two tours using only paraffin lamps. "Wild" tours explore remote, muddy, or dusty areas. The Echo River Tour, which involved boat rides along an underground river, was discontinued in the early 1990s due to logistical and environmental concerns. The park’s headquarters and visitor center are located on Mammoth Cave Parkway, accessible directly from I-65 at Exit 48, which connects with Kentucky Route 70 from the north and Kentucky Route 255 from the south. Human activity in the cave dates back five thousand years, with Native American remains, including mummies, recovered in the 19th and 20th centuries, reflecting intentional burial practices. In 1935, the remains of an adult male, named "Lost John," were found under a boulder after a pre-Columbian miner disturbed the rubble; the remains were publicly exhibited until the 1970s when they were interred in a secret location for preservation and political sensitivity. Research beginning in the late 1950s by Patty Jo Watson of Washington University in St. Louis used carbon dating and dietary analysis of preserved specimens to determine that the region’s Archaic and early Woodland peoples transitioned from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture. Experimental archaeology, where modern explorers used ancient tools, helped researchers understand the challenges faced by early cave users. Artifacts such as cane torches, drawings, gourd fragments, and woven grass moccasin slippers are found in Salts Cave in the Flint Ridge system. The 31,000-acre "Pollard Survey" was sold by indenture on September 10, 1791, in Philadelphia by William Pollard; 19,897 acres between Bacon Creek and the Green River were purchased by Thomas Lang Jr. on June 3, 1796, for £4,116.65, and were later lost to a county tax claim during the War of 1812. Legend attributes the first European visit to Mammoth Cave to either John or Francis Houchin in 1797, though John Decatur "Johnny Dick" Houchin, who was only 10 years old, is unlikely to have been involved; Francis "Frank" Houchin is more probable due to his proximity to the cave entrance, though Charles Houchin, a hunter, may have shot the bear that led to the discovery. Brucker and Watson’s work suggests the cave was known before 1797. Valentine Simon first surveyed and registered the land in 1798 and began exploiting the cave for saltpeter. During the War of 1812, increased demand due to the Jefferson Embargo Act of 1807 led to a surge in saltpeter production, making cave mining profitable. In July 1812, Charles Wilkins and Hyman Gratz purchased the cave and began industrial-scale mining of calcium nitrate using 70 enslaved laborers to build and operate leaching apparatus and haul soil. A half-interest in the cave was sold for $10,000 (equivalent to over $150,000 in 2020). After the war, mining ceased and the cave became a minor tourist attraction centered on a nearby Native American mummy. Wilkins’ estate sold his interest to Gratz, and in 1838, the Gratz brothers sold the cave to Franklin Gorin, who intended to operate it as a tourist attraction. Gorin was a slave owner who used enslaved people as guides; Stephen Bishop, one of them, became a celebrated guide, making extensive maps and naming many cave features. Gorin wrote that Bishop was the first to cross the Bottomless Pit and the only person known to have reached the bottom of Gorin’s Dome. After Bishop’s discovery, interest shifted from the "Old Cave" to new areas, which Bishop described as "grand, gloomy and peculiar." In 1839, John Croghan of Louisville purchased the estate, including Bishop and other slaves. Croghan briefly operated a tuberculosis hospital in the cave in 1842–43, believing the cave’s vapors would cure patients, but the disease ultimately killed him in 1849. In 1866, Charles Waldack, a photographer from Cincinnati, took the first photos inside the cave using magnesium flash photography. Throughout the 19th century, Mammoth Cave gained international fame, attracting writers such as Robert Montgomery Bird, Robert Davidson, Horace Martin, Alexander Clark Bullitt, Nathaniel Parker Willis, Bayard Taylor, William Stump Forwood, and John Muir. Famous visitors included actor Edwin Booth (brother of John Wilkes Booth, who assassinated Lincoln in 1865), singer Jenny Lind (who visited on April 5, 1851), and violinist Ole Bull, who gave a concert in the cave; two chambers are now known as "Booth's Amphitheatre" and "Ole Bull's Concert Hall." The difficult farming conditions in the region led to commercial exploitation of nearby caves, resulting in the "Kentucky Cave Wars," a period of intense competition where private cave owners used deception—such as misleading signs or "cappers" who falsely claimed Mammoth Cave was closed—to lure tourists. In 1906, Mammoth Cave became accessible by steamboat with the construction of a lock and dam at Brownsville, Kentucky. In 1908, Max Kämper, a German mining engineer, arrived from New York and spent several months exploring the cave with the help of Ed Bishop. He produced an accurate instrumental survey of many kilometers of the cave and a corresponding surface topographic map, which was suppressed by the Croghan family and is no longer known, though the cave map remains a significant achievement in cave cartography. Kämper speculated that Mammoth Cave was connected to Salts and Colossal Caves, a connection not proven until 60 years later. In the early 1920s, George Morrison created new entrances to Mammoth Cave via blasting on land not owned by the Croghans. Without access to the Croghan family’s unpublished surveys, it was proven that they had been exhibiting cave sections not on their land, leading to lawsuits and competition among entrances. Floyd Collins spent ten years exploring the Flint Ridge Cave System, discovering Floyd Collins' Crystal Cave and exploring Salts Cave, before dying in 1925 at Sand Cave after dislodging a rock on his leg and being unable to be rescued due to starvation. The rescue attempts generated widespread media attention and contributed to a movement that led to the establishment of Mammoth Cave National Park in 1941. As the last Croghan heirs passed away, advocacy grew among wealthy Kentuckians, who formed the Mammoth Cave National Park Association in 1924. The park was authorized on May 25, 192.

The geographic extent of Mammoth Cave revealed that the Croghans had long been exhibiting sections of the cave not owned by them, leading to lawsuits and the operation of different cave entrances in direct competition. In the early 20th century, Floyd Collins spent ten years exploring the Flint Ridge Cave System, during which he discovered Floyd Collins' Crystal Cave and explored Salts Cave, before dying in 1925 at Sand Cave, Kentucky, after dislodging a rock onto his leg during a tight crawlway and being unable to be rescued due to starvation. Rescue attempts generated widespread media attention, prompting prominent Kentuckians to form a movement that led to the establishment of Mammoth Cave National Park in 1941. As the last Croghan heirs passed away, advocacy grew among wealthy Kentucky citizens, who formed the Mammoth Cave National Park Association in 1924, and the park was authorized on May 25, 1926. Donated funds were used to purchase farmsteads, while other land within the proposed park boundary was acquired via eminent domain, displacing thousands of people and resulting in bitter disputes with inadequate compensation, a situation that received little outside attention. The federal government was legally barred from restoring or developing cleared farmsteads while the private Association held the land, a restriction evaded by operating a maximum of four CCC camps from May 22, 1933 to July 1942. According to the National Park Service, by May 22, 1936, 27,402 acres (11,089 ha) had been acquired and accepted, and the area was officially declared a national park on July 1, 1941, when a minimum of 45,310 acres (18,340 ha), comprising over 600 parcels, had been assembled. Superintendent Hoskins noted that a summer tanager named Pete arrived at the guide house around April 20 each year starting in 1938, eating from guides' hands and feeding his mate, delighting visitors. Mammoth Cave National Park was dedicated on July 1, 1941, and the same year saw the incorporation of the National Speleological Society. R. Taylor Hoskins, the second Acting Superintendent under the old Association, became the first official Superintendent and served until 1951. The New Entrance, closed since 1941, was reopened on December 26, 1951, becoming the starting point for the Frozen Niagara tour. By 1954, the park's land holdings included all lands within its outer boundary except for two privately held tracts; one, the old Lee Collins farm, was sold to Harry Thomas of Horse Cave, Kentucky, whose grandson William "Bill" Austin operated Collins Crystal Cave as a show cave in direct competition with the park, which maintained roads to the property. In February 1954, a two-week expedition under the National Speleological Society, known as C-3 or the Collins Crystal Cave Expedition, was organized at Austin's invitation. The expedition drew public interest through a photo essay by Robert Halmi in the July 1954 issue of True Magazine and a double first-person account by Joe Lawrence Jr. and Roger Brucker, confirming that passages in Crystal Cave extended toward Mammoth Cave proper, exceeding its boundaries, though the explorers kept this information secret due to fears of park restrictions. In 1955, Crystal Cave was connected by survey to Unknown Cave, the first connection in the Flint Ridge system. Some C-3 participants wished to continue exploring and formed the Flint Ridge Reconnaissance under Austin, Jim Dyer, John J. Lehrberger, and E. Robert Pohl, which was incorporated in 1957 as the Cave Research Foundation to support academic and scientific research; notable researchers included Patty Jo Watson. In March 1961, the Crystal Cave property was sold to the National Park Service for $285,000, and the Great Onyx Cave property, the only other private inholding, was purchased for $365,000; the Cave Research Foundation was allowed to continue exploration through a Memorandum of Understanding with the National Park Service. In 1960, Colossal Cave was connected to Salts Cave, and in 1961, Colossal-Salts was connected to Crystal-Unknown, forming a single cave system under much of Flint Ridge. By 1972, the Flint Ridge Cave System had been surveyed to 86.5 miles (139.2 km), making it the longest cave in the world. During the 1960s, CRF teams found passages in the Flint Ridge system that penetrated under Houchins Valley and came within 800 feet (240 m) of known Mammoth Cave passages. In 1972, CRF Chief Cartographer John Wilcox led expeditions from the Flint Ridge side and explored leads in Mammoth Cave to connect the systems. On a July 1972 trip, Patricia Crowther, weighing 115 pounds (52 kg), crawled through a narrow canyon called the "Tight Spot," a filter for larger cavers. On August 30, 1972, Wilcox, Crowther, Richard Zopf, and Tom Brucker passed through the Tight Spot and discovered the name "Pete H" inscribed on a river passage wall with an arrow pointing toward Mammoth Cave, believed to have been carved by Warner P. "Pete" Hanson, who died in World War II; the passage was named Hanson's Lost River. On September 9, 1972, a six-person CRF team—Wilcox, Crowther, Zopf, Gary Eller, Stephen Wells, and Cleveland Pinnix (a National Park Service ranger)—followed Hanson's Lost River downstream to its connection with Echo River in Cascade Hall of Mammoth Cave, completing the connection between the Flint Ridge and Mammoth Cave systems, an achievement known as the "Everest of speleology," resulting in a surveyed system of 144.4 miles (232.4 km) with fourteen entrances. Further connections followed, including to Proctor/Morrison Cave beneath Joppa Ridge in 1979; Proctor Cave was discovered by Jonathan Doyle during the Civil War and later owned by the Mammoth Cave Railroad, and Morrison Cave by George Morrison in the 1920s. This connection extended the frontier of Mammoth Cave exploration southeastward. Simultaneously, an independent group, the Central Kentucky Karst Coalition (CKKC), made discoveries outside the park, surveying tens of miles in Roppel Cave east of the park, discovered in 1976, which briefly ranked as one of the nation's longest caves before being connected to the Proctor/Morrison section on September 10, 1983, by a joint CRF and CKKC expedition entering through separate entrances and meeting in the middle. The resulting surveyed length reached nearly 300 miles (480 km). On March 19, 2005, a connection into the Roppel Cave portion was surveyed from a small cave under Eudora Ridge, adding about three miles; the entrance, now called the "Hoover Entrance," was discovered in September 2003 by Alan Canon and James Wells. Incremental discoveries since then have increased the total length to over 400 miles (640 km). It is certain that many more miles of cave passages remain undiscovered, with new natural entrances being rare and discovery primarily occurring through routine exploration of side passages from known entrances. At least two other major cave systems lie near Mammoth Cave: the Fisher Ridge Cave System, discovered in January 1981 by Michigan cavers associated with the Detroit Urban Grotto, mapped to 131 miles (211 km), and the Whigpistle Cave System, discovered in 1976 by Rick Schwartz, which connected to three nearby caves—Whigpistle, Martin Ridge, and Jackpot—now mapped to 42 miles (68 km) as of 2025, with ongoing exploration. Located 7 miles (11 km) from the visitor center is Diamond Caverns, where a stagecoach used to ferry visitors from the Bells Tavern train stop in Park City, Kentucky, to both Diamond Caverns and Mammoth Cave is on display. The park has a Humid subtropical climate (Cfa) according to the Köppen classification, and the Plant Hardiness zone at the visitor center, at 722 ft (220 m) elevation, is 6b with an average annual extreme minimum temperature of -3.2°F (-19.6°C). Bats inhabiting the caverns include the Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis), gray bat (Myotis grisescens), little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus), big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus), and tricolored bat (Perimyotis subflavus); rare species like the eastern small-footed bat have estimated populations of 9–12 million in the Historic Section, though numbers are now only a few thousand, and ecological restoration to support bat populations is ongoing. The red bat (Lasiurus borealis) is a forest-dweller and rarely found underground. Other cave animals include three species of cave crickets (Hadenoecus subterraneus, Ceuthophilus stygius, Ceuthophilus latens), a cave beetle (Pseudanophthalmus inexpectatus), fishing spiders (Dolomedes spp.), a cave salamander (Eurycea lucifuga), two eyeless cavefish (Typhlichthys subterraneus and Amblyopsis spelaea), a cave crayfish (Orconectes pellucidus), and the Kentucky cave shrimp (Palaemonias ganteri); some surface animals may use cave entrances but do not enter deep passages. The Green River flowing through the park is legally designated as "Kentucky Wild River" by the Kentucky General Assembly through the Office of Kentucky Nature Preserves' Wild Rivers Program. The park's potential natural vegetation type is Oak/Hickory (100) with an Eastern Hardwood Temperate broadleaf and mixed forest (25) form. Common fossils include crinoids, blastoids, and gastropods; Mississippian limestone has yielded fossils of over a dozen shark species, including part of a Saivodus striatus, comparable in size to a modern great white shark, and the species Glikmanius careforum and Troglocladodus trimblei, known only from within the cave. The cave's name refers to the large width and length of passages near the Rotunda entrance and was used long before the full system was explored, with no woolly mammoth fossils ever found, meaning the name has no connection to the extinct mammal. The list of information is incomplete. Roger W. Brucker has co-authored four nonfiction books and authored one historical novel on the Mammoth Cave System, presented here in the order of the events in their narratives, not publication order. Kenneth C. Carstens authored two academic works: "Archaeological Investigations in the Central Kentucky Karst" (1980, 2 vols.) and "Archaeological Reconnaissance in Mammoth Cave National Park" (1973), both from the Department of Anthropology at Washington University in St. Louis.

Manasbal Lake is the deepest freshwater lake in the Safapora area of Ganderbal district, Jammu and Kashmir, India, named after the sacred Manasarovar. It is surrounded by four villages: Jarokbal, Kondabal, Nesbal (on the north-eastern side), and Gratbal. The lake is known for its lotus blooms (Nelumbo nucifera) that appear along its periphery during July and August, enhancing the beauty of its clear waters. A Mughal garden, Jaroka Bagh (meaning bay window), built by Nur Jahan, overlooks the lake. It is a significant site for birdwatching as it serves as one of the largest natural spawning grounds for aquatic birds in Kashmir and is referred to as the "supreme gem of all Kashmir Lakes." The rootstocks of the lotus plant, which grow extensively in the lake, are harvested and consumed by local communities. The lake is accessible from Srinagar via a 30-kilometre (19 mi) road passing through Shadipora, Nasim, and Ganderbal, and also from Sonmarg via Ganderbal. It lies on the route to Wular Lake, the largest lake in Kashmir. Locals believe the lake is ancient, though exact dating remains undetermined. Near the northern shore are ruins of a 17th-century Mughal fort, Jharokha Bagh, historically used by caravans traveling from Punjab to Kashmir. The lake is bordered by the Baladar mountains to the east, a lacustrine, fluviatile, and loessic elevated plateau known as 'Karewa' to the north, and the Ahtung hills to the south, which are used for limestone extraction. Along the Jhelum River, Manasbal Lake belongs to the third series of high-altitude lakes of the Himalayas, situated at 1,585–1,600 m (5,200–5,249 ft), classified as valley lakes (including Dal, Anchar, and Manasbal), distinct from high-altitude wetlands (in the Pir Panjal ranges) and glaciated lakes (in the inner Himalayas at 3,000–4,000 m). A fissure runs east to west through the center of the lake. The catchment area, covering 10 km² (3.9 sq mi), has no major inlet channels and is primarily fed by precipitation and over 1,200 springs; water flows out to the Jhelum River via a regulated channel. The lake supports fishing, food and fodder plant harvesting, navigation, transportation, tourism, and recreation. Water quality parameters include recorded flora and fauna: zooplankton, benthos, and fish, with economically important species such as Cyprinus (an exotic species introduced in 1956) noted, though indigenous fish populations have declined due to environmental changes. Eutrophication has been confirmed, with Ceratophyllum demersum spreading, dense mono-specific weed stands forming, reduced species diversity, prolonged anoxic conditions, and accumulation of H₂S in deeper waters, along with pollution from the absence of wastewater treatment plants. The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), which surveyed the lake in 1997, identified the causes of its degradation, particularly the transformation of its banks into a stinking marsh. WWF recommended restoration measures, which were only implemented in 2007 with the establishment of the Wular-Manasbal Development Authority (WMDA) under the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. The WMDA initiated restoration efforts, with the chief executive officer stating that community participation was achieved after long discussions with locals, emphasizing that conservation is vital not only for tourism but also for livelihoods. A Shikara operator reported significant improvements in the lake’s condition. During restoration work, an ancient Hindu temple was discovered on the eastern shore, dating to 800–900 AD during the Avantivarman or Sankaravarman rule, constructed in local grey stone with a unique pyramid-shaped roof and floral motifs, serving as a new pilgrimage site for visitors to Amarnath and Kheer Bhawani temples. Other attractions include the Manasbal Temple, ruins of a terraced Mughal garden, and sculptured stones of Sufi shrines. The National Cadet Corps (NCC) began in Kashmir in 1965, but its training facility at Manasbal was abandoned in 1989 due to security issues. In September 2022, the Indian Navy revived NCC naval training at Manasbal, with 100 cadets—including girls from various colleges—participating in activities such as boat pulling, sailing, signaling, and ship modeling. The Manasbal Development Authority provided a suitable camping site and infrastructure. Previously, such training occurred in Nagrota and Mansar Lake. The lake offers pleasant weather in May and August, when water skiing is popular, supported by the Jammu & Kashmir Tourism Department (JKTD), which provides equipment and trained instructors. The lake’s surface sheen and size attract skiers, but concerns remain about the environmental impact of water skiing, as noise and turbulence could disrupt the lake’s tranquility and risk turning it into a second Dal Lake. There is ongoing debate about whether a more environmentally sensitive, sustainable tourism model would be better suited for preserving the lake’s peace and ecological integrity.

Manasseh Damukana Sogavare, born on 17 January 1955 in Popondetta, Northern Province, in the Territory of Papua (then part of the Australian-ruled Territory of Papua and New Guinea), is a Solomon Islander politician who served as prime minister of the Solomon Islands for a total of nine years, from 2000–2001, 2006–2007, 2014–2017, and 2019–2024. He has represented East Choiseul in the National Parliament since 1997 and served as minister of finance from 1997–1998, 2017–2019, and 2024–2025. Sogavare graduated with a bachelor’s degree in accounting and economics from the University of the South Pacific and a master’s degree in management studies from the University of Waikato in New Zealand. He previously held key positions including Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Finance (1994–1996), Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Director of the Central Bank of the Solomon Islands, and Chairman of the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund. He was first elected to Parliament in the 6 August 1997 election and became Minister of Finance and Treasury in 1997 under Prime Minister Bartholomew Ulufa'alu, though he was dismissed in mid-July 1998 without explanation, claiming the decision was made to maintain government stability. He withdrew support for Ulufa'alu, accusing him of authoritarianism, and later became deputy leader of the opposition in September 1998, then leader after Solomon Mamaloni's death in January 2000. Sogavare was elected prime minister on 30 June 2000 with 23 votes in favor and 21 against, following Ulufa'alu's resignation due to capture by rebels. He served until 17 December 2001. His party won only three seats in the 2001 election, but he remained in Parliament. In 2002 and again from 2005 to April 2006, he was a member of the Bills and Legislation Committee. After the 2006 general election, he led the Solomon Islands Social Credit Party into a coalition to oust Snyder Rini, receiving 11 of 50 votes to become prime minister on 18 April 2006, before switching support to Rini, who became prime minister and appointed Sogavare as Minister for Commerce, Industries and Employment. When Rini resigned on 26 April 2006, Sogavare won a parliamentary vote on 4 May 2006 with 28 votes against Fred Fono’s 22, and was sworn in. His tenure included managing recovery from riots during Rini’s premiership. On 11 October 2006, he survived a no-confidence vote with 28 votes against 17, prompted by deteriorating relations with Australia, including the expulsion of Australian High Commissioner Patrick Cole in September and the defense of suspended attorney general Julian Moti, who faces child sex charges in the Solomon Islands. On 13 October, Sogavare threatened to expel Australia from an assistance mission, and a week later, Australian peacekeepers raided his office. On 13 December 2007, he was defeated in a no-confidence vote with 25 votes in favor and 22 against, remaining in caretaker status until opposition candidate Derek Sikua was elected on 20 December 2007, when Sogavare became Leader of the Opposition.
