In 2010, he co-founded the Ownership, Unity and Responsibility Party, which won three seats in the 2010 general election. Following the 19 November 2014 general election, Sogavare became prime minister for the third time. On 22 September 2017, he spoke at the United Nations General Assembly, condemning North Korea’s ballistic missile tests and Indonesia’s violence in West Papua. On 7 November 2017, seventeen members of his Democratic Coalition for Change voted against him in a no-confidence motion, with Derek Sikua claiming Sogavare had lost touch with reality and fixated on conspiracy theories, while Sogavare blamed the defections on an anti-graft bill, saying some MPs feared imprisonment. Sogavare remained Acting Prime Minister until Rick Houenipwela was elected on 15 November 2017, after which he became finance minister and deputy prime minister. Shortly after the 2019 general election, Sogavare relaunched the OUR Party. On 24 April 2019, he was re-elected prime minister with more than half the vote, despite a court injunction to postpone the vote, as the Governor General, Frank Kabui, proceeded under constitutional immunity. The election triggered riots in Honiara, damaging the Pacific Casino Hotel, which Sogavare used as a campaign headquarters. On 16 September 2019, his government recognized the People's Republic of China (PRC), ending 36 years of recognition of the Republic of China, citing a bipartisan taskforce and Ministry of Foreign Affairs findings. Sogavare described the decision as a collective agreement by all Democratic Coalition Government for Advancement (DCGA) MPs. The move caused significant debate, leading to the sacking of ministers Rick Hou and Tautai Kaitu'u, with Hou claiming the decision was pre-determined. Deputy Prime Minister John Maneniaru and Education Minister Dean Kuku were also terminated, and Police Minister Lanelle Tanagada resigned. Malaita Province continued to support Taiwan and received $25 million in U.S. aid in 2020; its premier, Daniel Suidani, held an independence referendum dismissed by the national government as illegitimate. In November 2021, anti-government protesters, mostly from Malaita, burned buildings near the Parliament and looted Honiara’s Chinatown, with Sogavare resisting resignation, warning rioters would face consequences and accusing them of being politically motivated. Australia responded by deploying Federal Police and Defence Force personnel under the Australia–Solomon Islands Bilateral Security Treaty, with Papua New Guinea and Fiji also sending peacekeepers. On 6 December 2021, Sogavare survived a no-confidence motion. In 2022, he signed a wide-ranging security pact with China. The 2024 general elections were delayed from 2023 to 2024 by parliament, with Sogavare citing the country’s hosting of the Pacific Games as a reason, a move condemned by the opposition as a power grab. Sogavare led the OUR Party to win 15 seats and over 24% of the vote. On 29 April 2024, he announced he would step down as OUR Party leader and not seek re-election in the 2 May parliamentary vote, calling it a "collective decision." The Coalition of National Unity and Transformation, including Kadere and People First parties, nominated Foreign Minister Jeremiah Manele, who succeeded Sogavare as party leader and became prime minister on 2 May after defeating Matthew Wale. Sogavare was subsequently appointed finance minister. On 28 April 2025, he resigned as finance minister and joined an opposition coalition to unseat Manele, which also included Wale, Peter Kenilorea Jr., and Gordon Darcy Lilo. Manele secured enough support to avoid a no-confidence motion, and Sogavare became a backbencher for the first time since 1997. Sogavare is married to Emmy Sogavare, who owns Shadel Café, and has three children: Brandt, Shannon, and Maydrel. As prime minister, he earned a salary of 428,560 Solomon Islands dollars (approximately US$50,000). He holds a black belt in karate and is a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, having dedicated the Sogavare Memorial Seventh-day Adventist Church in memory of his father Sagavare Loko. Sogavare has been widely accused of promoting democratic backsliding, with critics describing the Solomon Islands under his leadership as increasingly autocratic or even authoritarian. Despite his modest formal salary, he has accumulated a vast real estate portfolio, raising questions about his sources of income.

Manny Díaz Jr., born on March 2, 1973, is an American politician currently serving as the president of the University of West Florida. He served as the 28th education commissioner of Florida from 2022 to 2025. A Republican, Díaz represented the 36th district in the Florida Senate from 2018 to 2022, which includes the Hialeah area in northwest Miami-Dade County. He previously served three terms in the Florida House of Representatives from 2012 to 2018, representing parts of Hialeah and Northwest Miami-Dade County. Díaz was born in Hialeah, graduated from Miami Springs High School, and earned a degree in human resources from St. Thomas University in 1994. He later obtained a master's degree in educational leadership from Nova Southeastern University in 1998. In 2006, he completed the Harvard University Graduate School of Education Principal's Summer Institute as part of the Superintendent's Urban Principal Initiative. He began his career as a teacher and baseball coach at Miami Springs High School, teaching social studies at Hialeah-Miami Lakes High School from 1995 to 1999, where he served as assistant principal for eight years. From 2013 to 2019, he was assistant principal at George T. Baker Aviation School, a public vocational school near Miami International Airport. Díaz denied allegations of discussing drug use or making inappropriate comments to a female student during his 1990s teaching career, attributing them to political attacks by a Democratic marketing consultant. In 2012, he filed for bankruptcy, citing $1.3 million in debts. From 2013 to 2022, he worked for Doral College, a private college affiliated with the for-profit Academica charter school operator founded by Fernando Zulueta, serving as its chief operating officer for most of that time; the institution failed to receive accreditation from the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools and eventually received accreditation from a minor accreditor. On July 14, 2025, Díaz was named interim president of the University of West Florida following the resignation of Martha Dunagin Saunders; during his interim tenure, he fired the university's general counsel after she objected to his hiring of Lawson Huck Gonzalez, a Ron DeSantis-linked law firm, as outside counsel for the presidential search. On January 8, 2026, Díaz was officially appointed president of the University of West Florida with a starting salary of $950,000; the selection process faced allegations of procedural irregularities, and contract requirements were changed to accommodate his lack of a doctoral degree. His advocacy for charter school expansion was also a point of concern. In 2010, Díaz ran for the Miami-Dade County School Board but lost in the primary to Perla Tabares Hantman, receiving 39% of the vote compared to her 61%. In 2012, after Florida House districts were reconfigured, he ran in the newly created 103rd district in the Republican primary against Renier Díaz de la Portilla and Alfredo Naredo-Acosta, winning 55% of the vote to their 39% and 6%, respectively, and faced only write-in opposition in the general election, winning by a wide margin. He was re-elected in 2014 and 2016. During his time in the legislature, he chaired the Choice and Innovation and K-12 Appropriations committee and was a key member of Representative José R. Oliva's team, who later became the second Cuban-American speaker of the Florida House. In 2018, Díaz was elected to the Florida Senate District 36, defeating Democrat David Perez 54.1% to 45.9%, with his re-election receiving substantial funding from health care and education companies. He chaired the Senate Education committee from 2018 to 2020 and the Senate Health Policy committee from 2020 to 2022. During the 2022 legislative session, he was the only Republican to vote against the congressional redistricting plan, indicating his alignment with Governor Ron DeSantis. On June 1, 2022, he assumed office as Education Commissioner after Richard Corcoran stepped down. In 2024, the Florida Board of Governors eliminated sociology as a core course at its public universities, a move Díaz defended by stating that sociology had been "hijacked by left-wing activists" and no longer served its intended purpose as a general knowledge course. While in the legislature, he sponsored legislation allowing more private online education providers, some from outside Florida, to offer classes to public school students, permitting students to take classes in public virtual schools in other counties, and requiring the Florida Department of Education to create a catalogue of online offerings. In 2017, he rejected allegations of conflict of interest when he co-sponsored, with Richard Corcoran and Michael Bileca, legislation directing $140 million in public funds to charter schools, noting that all three men and their wives were involved in the charter school industry. He sponsored the 2019 Family Empowerment Scholarship legislation and a 2020 bill that significantly expanded publicly-funded vouchers for private schools, widely regarded as the largest expansion of school choice in the nation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Díaz opposed vaccine requirements for students and in 2021 expressed interest in reviewing additional vaccine mandates, such as for mumps and measles; as of September 2021, he had not been vaccinated against COVID-19. In 2022, he sponsored SB148/HB7, an "anti-woke" bill supported by Governor Ron DeSantis; after being signed into law in April 2022, Chief U.S. District Judge Mark E. Walker blocked key provisions in November 2022, calling the law "positively dystopian." Díaz was a four-year letterman in college baseball at St. Thomas University, playing under head coach Al Avila. His second wife, Jennifer, worked in Miami-Dade Public Schools and Miami-Dade charter schools; they married on December 11, 2010. She previously served as vice-chair of the governing board of the Tallahassee Classical School, affiliated with Hillsdale College. They have three children; Díaz's son Dominic, from his first marriage to Linet Gonzalez, played baseball at Longwood University.

Sir Manuel Amadeo Esquivel KCMG, PC (2 May 1940 – 10 February 2022) was a Belizean politician who served as the second prime minister of Belize from 1984 to 1989 and again from 1993 to 1998. As leader of the United Democratic Party (UDP), his party's victory in the 1984 general election marked the first time an opposition party had won since universal suffrage was introduced in 1954. Born in Belize City, then the capital of the British Crown Colony of British Honduras, Esquivel attended St John's College and earned a Bachelor of Science degree in physics from Loyola University New Orleans. He later obtained a postgraduate certificate in physics education from Bristol University, England. After the 1969 British Honduras election, he became head of the pro-business Liberal Party, which merged with two other parties in 1973 to form the UDP. He served two terms on the Belize City Council and was UDP chairman from 1976 to 1982. In the 1979 election, he ran for the Freetown constituency but was defeated by George Cadle Price of the People's United Party (PUP). He was then appointed a minority member of the Belize Senate, where he defeated Philip Goldson in January 1983 to become the first and only politician elected leader of a major Belizean political party while serving as a senator. Acting opposition leader Curl Thompson remained UDP's House leader until the next election. Esquivel was elected to the House of Representatives in December 1984 from the newly formed Caribbean Shores constituency, becoming prime minister shortly after. He held the seat until the 1998 election, when he was defeated by Jose Coye of the PUP. During his first term, the Price government faced a financial crisis and entered a standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) after raising tax rates twice. Upon becoming prime minister, Esquivel implemented economic reforms advised by domestic experts such as Edney Cain, shifting Belize's economy away from a mixed model toward increased foreign direct investment and tourism growth. In his second term, he introduced unpopular austerity measures, including suspending public sector pay raises from 1995 to 1997, while transferring 450,000 shares of Belize Telecommunications to a trust for affected workers. The opposition PUP labeled him "VATMAN" for introducing a 15% value-added tax (VAT) in 1995; the VAT was repealed by his successor Said Musa in 1999, who later introduced a 10% goods and services tax (GST) in 2005. After the UDP won the February 2008 election, Esquivel was appointed senior advisor to government with the rank of minister by Prime Minister Dean Barrow on 12 February 2008. He was also appointed Chairman of the Central Bank of Belize on 18 January 2011, stepping down in September 2013 and resigning from the Cabinet in March 2014. Post-retirement, Esquivel continued to offer public commentary, advocating for a standardized definition of the national flag and coat of arms, supporting decriminalization of small amounts of cannabis in 2017, and publishing an editorial in the Amandala newspaper in support of the 2019 Belizean territorial dispute referendum. He and his wife were among the first citizens to receive the COVID-19 vaccine for those over 60 when the government began administering it. Esquivel met his future wife, Kathleen Levy, while studying in Bristol; they married in 1971 and had three children: David, Laura, and Ruth. Laura served as a Belize City councilor (2006–2012), Director of the Belize Tourism Board (2012–2014), and Deputy Chief of Mission at the Embassy of Belize in Washington, D.C. He was involved in two vehicle rollovers on the Western Highway in 1996 and 2009 due to wet road conditions; the first caused only minor injuries, while the second required facial surgery. Kathleen, Lady Esquivel, authored a biography titled *Still Waters*, published in 2021. Esquivel died on 10 February 2022 at the age of 81. He was appointed to the Privy Council of the United Kingdom by Queen Elizabeth II in 1986, earning the title "Right Honourable," and received an Honorary Doctorate of Humane Letters from Loyola University. He was appointed Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George (KCMG) in the 2010 New Year Honours. In 2021, the Belize City Council renamed an overpass and the coastal road connecting Belize District and Stann Creek District after him.

Manuleleua Paletasala Tovale is a Samoan politician and former member of the Legislative Assembly of Samoa, affiliated with the FAST Party. He was first elected to the Legislative Assembly in the 2021 Samoan general election. An election petition against him was dismissed in June 2021. On 28 July 2021, he was appointed Associate Minister for the Prime Minister and Cabinet. On 17 January 2025, he was removed from his position as associate minister by Prime Minister Fiamē Naomi Mataʻafa following his support for her expulsion from the FAST Party. He lost his seat in the 2025 Samoan general election. This article about a Samoan politician is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Marcel-André Baschet (5 August 1862 – 28 December 1941) was a French portrait painter renowned for his many portraits of the Presidents of the French Third Republic. Born in Gagny (Seine-et-Oise), he was the second son of Ludovic Baschet, who was the art editor of Panorama and the Revue illustrée. His brother René served as art critic for Salonsavant and edited L'Illustration from 1904 until the first half of the 20th century. At age 17, Baschet enrolled at the Académie Julian in the studio of Jules Lefebvre. He studied at the École des beaux-arts de Paris under Gustave Boulanger, and in 1883 won the Grand Prix de Rome for his painting Oedipus curses his son Polynices, becoming a pensionist at the Villa Médicis in Rome from 1883 to 1887. On 3 January 1888, he married Jeanne Guillemeteau, with whom he had one son and one daughter. He began teaching at the Académie Julian in 1889 and from 1900 taught Princess Mathilde. From 1907 to 1941, he operated a shop at 21 Quai Voltaire in Paris, where a commemorative plaque was installed after his death. In 1908, he received the médaille d'honneur for his portrait of Henri Rochefort, and his portrait of Claude Debussy was exhibited globally. He was awarded the Knight of the Légion d'honneur in 1898 and was elected a member of the Académie des beaux-arts in 1913. His artworks are held in private collections and museums, including the Musée d'Orsay and Château de Versailles. His younger brother Jacques (1872–1952) was a historian, art critic, artistic director, and editor of L'Illustration, as well as director of a national company.

Marcelo Miranda Viana da Silva, born on 4 March 1962 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a Brazilian mathematician specializing in chaotic dynamical systems and strange attractors. His parents were Portuguese, and he grew up in Portugal, where he completed his undergraduate studies at the University of Porto. He earned his Ph.D. from the Instituto Nacional de Matemática Pura e Aplicada (IMPA) in Rio de Janeiro under the supervision of Jacob Palis. Viana is currently the director of IMPA, a position he was elected to for the period 2016–2019. He proved the Zorich–Kontsevich conjecture in collaboration with Artur Avila. In 1993, he was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. He received the TWAS Prize in 1998 and the inaugural ICTP Ramanujan Prize in 2005 for his research achievements. Viana served as vice-president of the International Mathematical Union from 2011 to 2014 and as president of the Brazilian Mathematical Society from 2013 to 2015. In 1998, he delivered a plenary lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Berlin. He chaired the executive committee for the 2018 International Congress of Mathematicians held in Rio de Janeiro and is a columnist for Folha de S.Paulo.

Mari Lloyd-Williams is a Welsh medical consultant who specialises in palliative care. She taught at the University of Liverpool for more than two decades before moving to Liverpool John Moores University in 2022, where she was appointed Professor of Palliative and Supportive Care. Born to Margaret Winter Davies and county councillor Lloyd Williams, she was educated at Leicester Medical School. In 2000, she became a Consultant and Honorary Senior Lecturer for the University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust and LOROS Hospice following her palliative medicine training with them. In 2002, she joined the University of Liverpool as a Senior Lecturer and was granted a personal chair at the School of Population, Community and Behavioural Sciences in 2003. She also holds an honorary consultant position in palliative medicine with the Marie Curie Hospice, Liverpool and the Liverpool clinical commissioning group. As an academic, her specialism is palliative care, including leadership of a project involving more than a hundred elderly people in a rural village. With support from The Prince's Countryside Fund, she received a Churchill Fellowship in 2019 to travel to the Faroe Islands and Ireland to "[develop] volunteer-led palliative care facilities in rural communities", specifically planning a visit to Giljagarður, an elderly community in the Faroese town of Leirvík. She was elected Fellow of the Learned Society of Wales in 2011 and is also a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians and a Fellow of the Royal College of General Practitioners.

Mariam Nabatanzi Babirye, born around 1980 and known as Maama Uganda or Mother Uganda, is a Ugandan woman recognized for giving birth to 44 children, 38 of whom are still alive. As of March 2025, her eldest children are 33 years old and the youngest are eight years old. She first gave birth at age 13 after being forced into marriage the year prior, and by age 36, she had delivered 44 children, including three sets of quadruplets, four sets of triplets, and six sets of twins—totaling 15 births—due to a rare genetic condition causing hyperovulation from enlarged ovaries. In 2019, at age 40, she underwent tubal ligation to prevent further pregnancies after giving birth to her last set of twins via cesarean section, one of whom died in childbirth, marking her most recent child to pass away. Her mother abandoned her and her five brothers shortly after her birth, and at age seven, her stepmother mixed cut glass into the food of her older siblings while she was away, resulting in their deaths. In 1993, at age 12, she was married to a 40-year-old man who was polygamous and physically abusive; her father-in-law provided the family with land to support themselves. At age 13, she gave birth to twins, followed by triplets two years later and quadruplets one and a half years after that. She stated that her father had given birth to 45 children with different women, all in multiple births. After her sixth delivery, she consulted a doctor who advised her to continue having children, stating that stopping would lead to early death, and at age 23, she had given birth to 25 children with a high ovary count. In 2015, her husband abandoned the family, unable to support 42 children, and left her pregnant with twins; he later sold their homestead. She and her children were hosted by her grandmother, and after her grandmother’s death, relatives allowed her to remain in the homestead, though as of April 2023, she still owes a balance on the property before full ownership. Babirye and her household, consisting of sixty-odd individuals including children, grandchildren, and daughters-in-law, live in Kasawo, Mukono district, Central Uganda. They rely heavily on donations for food, beds, and other necessities, and Babirye works part-time as a tailor, herbalist, and hairdresser. Their home complex includes five cement-block houses with corrugated iron roofs and 17 rooms—15 bedrooms and two empty living/dining rooms—nine of which have no beds, six with a total of eight bunk beds (four of which are unusable), and the other four beds accommodate 24 children on mattresses. According to The Uganda Times, Babirye aims to receive UGX 5 million (about US$1,400) to pay off the homestead balance to her grandmother’s relatives to gain full ownership. She also plans to acquire new iron sheets to fix the leaking roofs, 25 new bunk beds, and 66 new mattresses so each person has their own bed, acquire land for farming and animal rearing, and establish a restaurant, bridal salon, and events management service to employ her children and achieve financial security for her dependents.

Marina Abramović, born November 30, 1946, in Belgrade, PR Serbia, FPR Yugoslavia, is a Serbian conceptual and performance artist. Her work investigates body art, endurance art, the relationship between performer and audience, the limits of the body, and the possibilities of the mind. Active for over four decades, she refers to herself as the "grandmother of performance art" and pioneered a new notion of artistic identity by involving observers, focusing on confronting pain, blood, and the physical limits of the body. In 2007, she founded the Marina Abramović Institute (MAI), a non-profit foundation for performance art. Abramović was raised by her grandparents until she was six years old; her grandmother was deeply religious, and she spent her childhood in church following her grandmother's rituals. When she was six, her brother was born, and she began living with her parents, taking piano, French, and English lessons, though she did not take art lessons and only enjoyed painting as a child. Life under her mother's strict supervision was difficult; her mother beat her for "supposedly showing off," and she described being under military-style control until age 29, which limited her performances to before 10 p.m. In a 1998 interview, she recalled her parents' terrible marriage, citing an incident when her father smashed 12 champagne glasses and left the house as the most horrible moment of her childhood. She studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Belgrade from 1965 to 1970 and completed post-graduate studies in the art class of Krsto Hegedušić at the Academy of Fine Arts in Zagreb in 1972. From 1973 to 1975, she taught at the Academy of Fine Arts in Novi Sad while launching her first solo performances. In 1976, after marrying Neša Paripović (between 1970 and 1976), she moved to Amsterdam permanently to perform there. From 1990 to 1995, she was a visiting professor at the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Paris and the Berlin University of the Arts; from 1992 to 1996, she taught at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg, and from 1997 to 2004, she was a professor for performance art at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Braunschweig. In her 1973 Edinburgh performance, she used ten knives and two tape recorders to explore ritual and gesture, cutting herself ten times and replaying the recordings to replicate the movements, thus examining the physical and mental limits of the body. In another performance, she lit a large petroleum-drenched star on fire, cutting her nails, toenails, and hair, throwing the clippings into the flames, and leaping into the center of the pentagram after losing consciousness due to lack of oxygen, which the audience initially failed to notice. She later commented that losing consciousness meant she could no longer be present and perform. Prompted by this, she created Rhythm 2 in 1974, which involved ingesting medications to induce muscle contractions and loss of bodily control while remaining aware, followed by a calming medication, lasting five hours. In Rhythm 4, performed at Galleria Diagramma in Milan, she knelt naked in a room with a high-power industrial fan, attempting to breathe in as much air as possible, and soon lost consciousness. To prevent audience interference, she had the cameraman focus only on her face, but after several minutes of unconsciousness, the cameraman stopped and called for help. In a 1976 performance in Naples, she placed 72 objects on a table for the audience to use as they wished, including a rose, feather, honey, whip, olive oil, scissors, scalpel, gun, and a single bullet. For six hours, the audience manipulated her body, leading to her being stripped, attacked, and devalued into an image she described as the "Madonna, mother, and whore," with one person aiming a gun at her head and others cutting her clothes. She later stated that if the audience is left to act, they can kill her and that she felt deeply violated. Abramović defines her identity in contrast to that of spectators, blurring roles to reveal collective human experiences and truths, and her work also explores the objectification of the female body, testing the limits of danger and exhaustion. In 1976, she met Uwe Laysiepen, known as Ulay, with whom she began a collaborative relationship exploring ego and artistic identity, creating "relation works" characterized by movement, change, and "art vital," forming a collective identity called "The Other" and speaking of themselves as parts of a "two-headed body." They dressed and behaved like twins, creating a relationship of complete trust, reducing individual identities. Critics have interpreted their work as a hermaphroditic state, but Abramović rejects this, emphasizing her focus on the body as a unit of individuality, rooted in her parents' military pasts, and their exploration of extreme states of consciousness and architectural space. Between 1981 and 1987, they performed Nightsea Crossing in twenty-two performances, sitting silently across from each other for seven hours a day. In 1988, after years of tension, they embarked on a spiritual journey to end their relationship, walking the Great Wall of China from opposite ends—Ulay from the Gobi Desert and Abramović from the Yellow Sea—each walking 2500 km to meet in the middle and say goodbye. She conceived the walk in a dream and described it as a dramatic, human, and film-like ending, emphasizing solitude. The journey took eight years to gain Chinese government permission, and by then, their relationship had dissolved. At her 2010 MoMA retrospective, she performed The Artist Is Present, sharing a period of silence with each visitor who sat in front of her; when Ulay arrived, she reached out to him across the table, an emotional moment that went viral. In November 2015, Ulay sued Abramović, claiming she had paid him insufficient royalties under a 1999 contract covering sales of their joint works, and in September 2016, a Dutch court ordered her to pay €250,000 in royalties, plus over €23,000 in legal costs, finding that Ulay was entitled to 20% net royalties as specified in the contract, and requiring her to credit all works from 1976 to 1980 as "Ulay/Abramović" and from 1981 to 1988 as "Abramović/Ulay." Cleaning the Mirror consisted of five monitors showing Abramović scrubbing a grimy human skeleton in her lap, with each monitor dedicated to a different body part—head, pelvis, ribs, hands, feet—each with its own sound, creating overlaps. As the skeleton became cleaner, Abramović became covered in the grayish dirt. The three-hour performance, including Cleaning the Mirror #1 at MoMA, #2 at Oxford University (90 minutes), and #3 at the Pitt Rivers Museum (five hours), is filled with metaphors of Tibetan death rites. In 1996, she worked with Jacob Samuel to produce a cookbook of "aphrodisiac recipes" called Spirit Cooking, with evocative instructions such as "13,000 grams of jealousy" and "mix fresh breast milk with fresh sperm milk," inspired by the belief that ghosts feed on emotions, sound, and light. In 1997, she created a multimedia Spirit Cooking installation at Zerynthia Associazione per l'Arte Contemporanea in Rome, featuring white gallery walls with "enigmatically violent recipe instructions" painted in pig's blood, described by Alexxa Gotthardt as a comment on humanity's reliance on ritual to organize and legitimize life. Spirit Cooking later evolved into a dinner party entertainment for collectors, donors, and friends. In a performance involving the scrubbing of thousands of bloody cow bones over four days, Abramović earned the Golden Lion award at the Venice Biennale. She created Balkan Baroque as a response to the Yugoslav Wars, recalling that other artists reacted immediately, but she could not create work soon due to the emotional impact. She returned to Belgrade, interviewed her mother, father, and a rat-catcher, and incorporated these interviews into the piece, including clips of her father holding a pistol and her mother's empty and crossed hands. While seated among a large pile of bones, she tried to wash them. The performance took place in Venice in 1997; she remembered the intense heat and that worms emerged from the bones.

Marina Abramović created the performance piece Balkan Baroque in response to the Yugoslav Wars, which took place in the 1990s. The four-day performance earned her the Golden Lion award at the Venice Biennale in 1997. She could not immediately create work about the war due to its personal impact, so she returned to Belgrade, where she interviewed her mother, her father, and a rat-catcher. These interviews were incorporated into the piece, along with clips of her father’s hands holding a pistol and her mother’s empty and later crossed hands. Abramović dressed as a doctor recounting the rat-catcher’s story while sitting among a large pile of bones, attempting to wash them. The performance occurred in Venice in 1997, and she remembered the extreme heat and the emergence of worms from the bones. She explained that scrubbing bones clean is impossible, symbolizing that blood and shame from war cannot be washed away—just as the war cannot be cleansed of its shame. The work was intended to speak not only about the war in Bosnia but about any war anywhere in the world. Beginning on November 9, 2005, Abramović presented Seven Easy Pieces at the Guggenheim Museum in New York City, performing for seven consecutive nights over seven hours, recreating works by five artists from the 1960s and 1970s, including Gina Pane’s The Conditioning and Vito Acconci’s 1972 performance involving masturbation under floorboards, and introducing a new piece on the final night. All performances were dedicated to her late friend Susan Sontag. From March 14 to May 31, 2010, the Museum of Modern Art held a major retrospective of Abramović’s work, curated by Klaus Biesenbach, which was the largest performance art exhibition in MoMA’s history. The exhibition featured the performance The Artist Is Present, which lasted 736 hours and 30 minutes, with Abramović sitting immobile in the atrium while visitors took turns sitting opposite her. Ulay made a surprise appearance at the opening night. She sat in a marked rectangle with a chair opposite her, and visitors were invited to sit and maintain eye contact; most sat for five minutes or less, while a few stayed for a full day. The line grew so large that museum security only noticed it on the last day, when a visitor vomited and another began to disrobe. Tensions arose due to the limited time for earlier visitors. Art enthusiasts speculated about whether Abramović wore an adult diaper, and noted her crying when a sitter cried or during her physical contact with Ulay. She sat across from 1,545 people, including Klaus Biesenbach, James Franco, Lou Reed, Alan Rickman, Jemima Kirke, Jennifer Carpenter, and Björk. A support group, "Sitting with Marina," and a blog, "Marina Abramović made me cry," were established. Marco Anelli took portraits of every sitter, which were published on Flickr, compiled into a book, and exhibited at the Danziger Gallery. Abramović said the show changed her life completely. After Lady Gaga saw and publicized the show, a new audience—particularly young people aged 12 to 18—began attending. In September 2011, a video game version of The Artist Is Present was released by Pippin Barr. In 2013, Dale Eisinger ranked The Artist Is Present ninth in his list of the greatest performance art works. The performance inspired Australian novelist Heather Rose to write The Museum of Modern Love, which was launched at MoMA in 2018. Balkan Erotic Epic is a four-hour durational performance by Abramović, presented at Factory International's Aviva Studios in Manchester from October 9 to 19, 2025, building on her 2005 multi-channel video installation of the same name. The work explores Balkan folklore, collective mythology, ancient myths, ritual, eroticism, spirituality, and tradition, featuring over seventy performers, including dancers, musicians, and singers, and allowing audiences to move freely through thirteen immersive scenes. It includes elements such as Fertility Rite, Massaging the Breast, and Scaring the Gods, re-examining the connection between sexuality, spirituality, and the body in ritual traditions. The performance is noted for its ritualistic use of nudity, multi-space choreography, and focus on reclaiming the body as a site of power and transformation. Frieze described it as a "reclamation, reinvention and perversion of personal and collective history, mythology and identity." The performance is touring in Barcelona (January 24–30, 2026), Berlin (October 14–17, 2026), and New York (December 8–20, 2026). In 2009, Abramović was featured in Chiara Clemente’s documentary Our City Dreams and a book of the same name, which highlighted five artists, including Swoon, Ghada Amer, Kiki Smith, and Nancy Spero, each of whom has a devotion to New York. Abramović is also the subject of the documentary Marina Abramović: The Artist Is Present, based on her 2010 retrospective, which aired on HBO in the United States and won a Peabody Award in 2012. In January 2011, she was on the cover of Serbian ELLE, photographed by Dušan Reljin. Kim Stanley Robinson’s science fiction novel 2312 mentions a performance art style known as "abramovics." In June 2013, a world premiere installation by Abramović was featured at Toronto’s Trinity Bellwoods Park as part of the Luminato Festival, and she co-created the theatrical production The Life and Death of Marina Abramović with Robert Wilson, which premiered at the festival and at the Park Avenue Armory in December. In 2007, Abramović founded the Marina Abramović Institute (MAI), a nonprofit foundation for performance art, in a 33,000-square-foot space in Hudson, New York, and also established a performance institute in San Francisco. She is a patron of the London-based Live Art Development Agency. In June 2014, she presented 512 Hours at London’s Serpentine Gallery, and in December 2014, at the Sean Kelly Gallery in Generator, participants were blindfolded and wore noise-canceling headphones in an exploration of nothingness. On November 30, 2016, to celebrate her 70th birthday, she held a birthday party at the Guggenheim titled "Marina 70," which included a 70-minute "Silence" segment ending with a gong crash, followed by "Entertainment" where she spoke and watched ANOHNI perform "My Way" while wearing a large black hood. In March 2015, she gave a TED talk titled "An art made of trust, vulnerability and connection." In 2019, IFC’s mockumentary show Documentary Now! parodied Abramović’s work and the documentary Marina Abramović: The Artist Is Present, with an episode titled "Waiting for the Artist" starring Cate Blanchett as Isabella Barta (Abramović) and Fred Armisen as Dimo (Ulay). Originally scheduled for September 26, 2020, her first major UK exhibition at the Royal Academy of Arts was postponed to autumn 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The exhibition, which brought together works spanning her 50-year career and new pieces reflecting on bodily changes and life-death transitions, was described by Tabish Khan of Culture Whisper as "intense, discomfiting, memorable, and performance art at its finest." In 2021, she dedicated a monument titled Crystal Wall of Crying at the site of a Holocaust massacre in Ukraine, at Babi Yar. In 2022, she condemned the Russian invasion of Ukraine. In September 2023, she became the first woman to have a solo exhibition in the Royal Academy’s main galleries, which she helped stage while recovering from a near-fatal pulmonary embolism, exploring how her works might be reinterpreted or reperformed by others using archival footage, installations, and live performances by artists trained in the Marina Abramović Method. In 2026, she is scheduled to have a solo exhibition titled Transforming Energy at Venice’s Gallerie dell'Accademia art biennale, which will be the first exhibition for a living female artist at the museum in its 275-year history. Abramović proposed a performance titled "Come to Wash with Me" in 1969 at Galerija Doma Omladine in Belgrade, where a gallery would be transformed into a laundry with sinks around the walls, and the public would remove their clothes and have them washed, dried, and ironed by Abramović before returning them. The proposal was refused. In 1970, she proposed a similar untitled performance at the same gallery, where she would stand in front of the public dressed in regular clothing, take clothing from a rack (including oversized items like a bra or slip), change into them, and then place a gun to her temple, pulling the trigger—resulting in a possible outcome of her death. Abramović directed a segment titled Balkan Erotic Epic in Destricted, a 2006 compilation of erotic films, and a segment titled Dangerous Games in 2008’s Stories on Human Rights. She also acted in the five-minute short film Antony and the Johnsons: Cut the World. The Marina Abramović Institute (MAI) is a performance art organization focused on performance, long-duration works, and the use of the "Abramović Method." In its early phase, it was a proposed multi-functional museum space in Hudson, New York, designed by Rem Koolhaas and Shohei Shigematsu of OMA, with an early design phase funded by a Kickstarter campaign that raised over 4,000 contributions, including Lady Gaga and Jay-Z. The building project was canceled in October 2017 due to excessive costs. MAI continues as a traveling organization, partnering with institutions and artists internationally in Brazil, Greece, and Turkey. In her youth, she was a performer in one of Hermann Nitsch’s Viennese actionist performances. She maintains a friendship with James Franco, who interviewed her for The Wall Street Journal in 2009, visited her during The Artist Is Present in 2010, and attended the 2012 Met Gala with her. In July 2013, Abramović collaborated with Lady Gaga on the Artpop album, with their work displayed at an event titled "ArtRave" on November 10. They also collaborated on projects supporting MAI, including a video using the Abramović Method and a nonstop reading of Stanisław Lem’s Solaris. In the same month, Jay-Z performed an Abramović-inspired piece at Pace Gallery in New York, performing his track "Picasso Baby" for six straight hours. During the performance, Abramović and several art world figures were invited to dance with him face to face. The footage was used in the music video. She allowed Jay-Z to adapt "The Artist Is Present" under the condition that he would donate to her institute, but stated he did not fulfill this obligation, calling it a "one-way transaction." Two years later, in 2015, she publicly apologized, stating she was never informed of his sizable donation. Abramović claims she feels "neither like a Serb, nor a Montenegrin," but an ex-Yugoslav, saying when asked where she is from, she always says she comes from a country that no longer exists. In February 2025, she endorsed the 2024–2025 Serbian anti-corruption protests. She has had three abortions and has stated that having children would have been a "disaster" for her work. Sculptor Nikola Pešić says she has a lifelong interest in esotericism and spiritualism. Among the Podesta emails was a message from Abramović to Podesta’s brother discussing an invitation to a spirit cooking, which was interpreted by conspiracy theorists.

Abramović describes her identity as neither Serb nor Montenegrin, but as ex-Yugoslav, stating that when asked where she is from, she always says she comes from a country that no longer exists. She claims to have had three abortions in her life and has stated that having children would have been a "disaster" for her work. Sculptor Nikola Pešić notes that Abramović has a lifelong interest in esotericism and spiritualism. In the Podesta emails, a message from Abramović to Podesta's brother about an invitation to a spirit cooking was interpreted by conspiracy theorists like Alex Jones as an invitation to a satanic ritual, and was used as evidence by Jones and others of Hillary Clinton's links to the occult. In a 2013 Reddit Q&A, she clarified that the context determines whether occult practices constitute art: if done in a gallery or artistic context, it is art; otherwise, it is not. On April 10, 2020, Microsoft released a promotional video for HoloLens 2 featuring Abramović, but withdrew it due to accusations from right-wing conspiracy theorists of her having ties to Satanism. Abramović responded by urging people to stop harassing her, emphasizing that her performances are simply the art she has created over the past 50 years. Two years after the initial deal, in 2015, Abramović publicly apologized, stating she was never informed of Jay-Z's sizable donation. In February 2025, she endorsed the 2024–2025 Serbian anti-corruption protests.

Marina Evseevna Ratner (Russian: Мари́на Евсе́евна Ра́тнер; October 30, 1938 – July 7, 2017[1]) was a professor of mathematics at the University of California, Berkeley who worked in ergodic theory.[2] Around 1990, she proved a group of major theorems concerning unipotent flows on homogeneous spaces, known as Ratner's theorems.[3] Ratner was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1992,[4] awarded the Ostrowski Prize in 1993 and elected to the National Academy of Sciences the same year. In 1994, she was awarded the John J. Carty Award from the National Academy of Sciences.[5] Ratner was born October 30, 1938 in Moscow, Russian SFSR. Her father was a plant physiologist and professor, and her mother was a chemist. Her family suffered from discrimination and antisemitism because they were Jewish. Ratner's mother was fired from work in the 1940s for writing to her mother in Israel, then considered an enemy of the Soviet state.[6] Ratner gained an interest in mathematics in her fifth grade.[6] She was able to go to Moscow State University because the university had limited discrimination against Jewish applicants as the Khrushchev era began.[7] From 1956 to 1961, Ratner studied mathematics and physics at Moscow State University. Here, she became interested in probability theory, inspired by A.N. Kolmogorov and his group.[6] After graduation, Ratner spent four years working in Kolmogorov's applied statistics group. Following this, she returned to Moscow State University for graduate studies under Yakov G. Sinai, also a student of Kolmogorov. She completed her PhD thesis, titled "Geodesic Flows on Unit Tangent Bundles of Compact Surfaces of Negative Curvature", in 1969.[8] During this time, Ratner studied the aforementioned geodesic flows as well as a special class of flows called Anosov flows. After earning her doctorate, she worked at the High Technical Engineering School in Moscow until she lost her job in 1970 due to applying for an emigration visa to Israel.[7] In 1971 Ratner emigrated from the Soviet Union to Israel and she taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem from 1971 until 1975. She continued to study geodesic flows, extending her results to higher dimensions. Ratner also proved that the trajectory of Anosov flows exhibited the Bernoulli property of randomness. She began to work with Rufus Bowen at Berkeley, who was studying similar Axiom A flows, and eventually was invited to join him as a professor in 1975.[7] Ratner then emigrated to the United States and became a professor of mathematics at Berkeley, with "some controversy" following within the department.[9] Ratner studied horocycle flows, proving that they are "loosely Bernoulli", and their Cartesian squares are not. In the early 1980s she described how rigidity applied to horocycle flows, and this led to her work on the Raghunathan conjecture.[7] During the 1980s Ratner published proofs of conjectures dealing with unipotent flows on quotients of Lie groups made by S. G. Dani and M. S. Raghunathan.[10] During this time she proved a property now named after her, showing that two unipotent flow trajectories that remain together for a period of time will remain close for a much longer time.[7] Much of Ratner's work focused on dynamical systems, especially over homogeneous spaces. Her results were abstract and had extensive consequences for different fields within math. In particular, a wide array of research in number theory has proceeded from her results.[11] Before earning her doctorate, Ratner had a daughter, Anna, from a brief marriage.[7] Ratner moved to Israel with her parents in the early 1970s. Her sister Judith remained in the Soviet Union, and lost her job as a research metallurgist in 1973 due to her family's emigration. When Ratner later moved to the U.S., her parents stayed in Israel. Judith applied to leave the Soviet Union in 1977 along with her husband, but they were denied permission and faced persecution because they were Jewish. Judith's family eventually received permission to leave in 1987.[9] Marina Ratner died July 7, 2017, at the age of 78.[11] In 1992, Ratner was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and in 1993, the National Academy of Sciences.[6] Ratner also won the Ostrowski prize in 1993.[7] For her theorems on unipotent flows and other work, she won the John J. Carty Award for the Advancement of Science in 1994.[12] Also that year, she became the third woman plenary speaker at International Congress of Mathematicians, and Ingrid Daubechies followed her at the same conference. Emmy Noether and Karen Uhlenbeck had been the only other women to speak there for decades. Ratner's talk was titled Interactions between ergodic theory, Lie groups and number theory.[6] In 2004, Ratner won the Donald Sterling Noyce Prize for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching.[11] In 2013, Ratner received an honorary doctorate from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and they hosted a conference about her work.[7] Some mathematicians claim that Ratner would have won the Fields Medal, the most prestigious prize in mathematics, if her work had been completed by the age of 40, as required by the prize. Elon Lindenstrauss and Maryam Mirzakhani won the Fields Medal for work that grew out of Ratner's results.[11] Her discoveries influenced many fields of mathematics, including geometry, dynamics, diophantine approximation, ergodic theory, and Lie group theory.[7]

Mark A. Nook is the 11th president of the University of Northern Iowa. Before assuming this role, he served as the chancellor of Montana State University Billings from 2014 to January 2017. Nook was born in Estherville, Iowa, and graduated from Holstein Community School in Holstein, Iowa. He earned a bachelor's degree in physics and mathematics from Southwest Minnesota State University in 1980, a master's degree in astrophysics from Iowa State University in 1983, and a Ph.D. in astronomy from the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 1990. He began teaching physics and astronomy at Concordia College in 1983, serving as an instructor until 1986. From 1986 to 1990, he worked on the Wisconsin Ultraviolet Photo-Polarimeter Experiment. In 1990, he joined St. Cloud State University as an assistant professor of physics and astronomy and director of the university's observatory and planetarium, becoming a full professor in 1998. He served in this position until 2007, during which time he chaired the department of physics, astronomy, and engineering science from 1999 to 2004 and served as dean of undergraduate studies from 2004 to 2007. From 2007 to 2009, and again from 2010 to 2011, he was provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point, serving as interim chancellor from 2009 to 2010. From 2011 to 2014, he held the position of senior vice president for academic and student affairs for the University of Wisconsin System. In 2017, he was inducted into Omicron Delta Kappa at the University of Northern Iowa as a faculty/staff initiate. In 2022, he was appointed to the board of directors for the American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education, and in 2023, he was appointed to the board of directors for the American Association of State Colleges and Universities.

The Marlow Medal and Prize is an early-career award in physical chemistry presented by the Royal Society of Chemistry. Each year, one or two recipients, who are junior researchers under the age of 35 or within 10 years of completing their doctorate, are selected to receive £2000 and deliver lectures at universities across the UK. The award was founded in 1957 and honors the chemist George Stanley Withers Marlow (1889–1948). Additionally, award winners are entitled to £3000 in travel expenses to participate in a lecture tour in Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, or Malaysia. This lecture series, established in 1981, is named in memory of Robert Anthony Robinson (1903–1979).

Martha "Matty" Louisa Cocke (October 9, 1855 – August 15, 1938) was an American educator recognized as the first woman to serve as president of Hollins College in Virginia. She was born in 1855 to Charles Lewis Cocke and Susanna Virginia Pleasants Cocke, one of nine children, and grew up on the grounds of the Hollins Institute, which her father founded and supervised as superintendent. She graduated from the collegiate department in 1874. Early in her career, she worked as a secretarial assistant to her father before becoming an instructor of English, French, German, and mathematics two years after graduation. In 1884, she was appointed registrar and librarian. Her father owned the deed to the school due to money owed by the trustees; after his death in 1901 and the predecease of his eldest brother, the heir apparent, the remaining heirs selected Matty Cocke as president. Although she avoided public events, she was well-liked on campus, and students established a short-lived literary society in her honor; beginning in 1930, they sang to her annually on her birthday. Under her leadership, the Institute experienced significant growth: faculty and staff expanded from about forty to more than sixty by 1933, over a dozen new buildings were constructed, and prominent intellectuals visited campus regularly. The school began awarding an A.B. degree in 1903 and officially changed its name to Hollins College in February 1911. By the time she retired in 1933, the institution had adopted a four-year college curriculum and achieved full accreditation. Upon retirement, she transferred ownership of the college from the family to a public board of overseers. In 1926, she received an honorary Doctor of Laws from Roanoke College. She died at home at Hollins College on August 15, 1938, and is buried in the family cemetery on campus. Her personal papers are held by Hollins University, and she is listed on the Wall of Honor of the Virginia Women's Monument.

Martin Creed, born on 21 October 1968 in Wakefield, England, is a British artist, composer, and performer who lives and works in London. He moved to Glasgow at age 3 when his father, a silversmith, took a teaching position there. Raised in a Quaker household, Creed attended Lenzie Academy and studied art at the Slade School of Art, University College London, from 1986 to 1990. He lived in London except for a period from 2000 to 2004 when he resided in Alicudi, an island off Sicily. Creed won the Turner Prize in 2001 for two exhibitions, Martin Creed Works and Art Now: Martin Creed, held across England during the preceding year. His submission for the Turner Prize show at the Tate Gallery was Work No. 227: The lights going on and off, an empty room where the lights switched on and off every five seconds. The jury praised the work for its audacity, strength, rigour, wit, and sensitivity to the site, despite controversy from visitors who protested by throwing eggs, claiming Creed’s work was not real art and that painting was at risk of extinction. Since 1987, Creed has numbered each of his works, with titles often descriptive, such as Work No. 79: some Blu-tack kneaded, rolled into a ball and depressed against a wall (1993) and Work No. 88: a sheet of A4 paper crumpled into a ball (1995). Work No. 200: Half the air in a given space (1998) is a room filled with half its cubic space in balloons. Work No. 19: An Intrusion And A Protrusion From A Wall, first exhibited at the Slade in 1989, was later replaced in 1990 by Work No. 21 with slightly different content, challenging ideas of reproducibility and authenticity in art. In 2009, he created Work No. 1020: Ballet, a live performance combining music, ballet, words, and film, originally produced by Sadler's Wells and performed in the Lilian Baylis Studio, later staged in Edinburgh in 2010, New York in 2013, and London in 2014. In 2015, he designed a work for Victoria Beckham’s store in London. His public works, such as The Scotsman Steps in Edinburgh, DON'T WORRY at St Peter's Church in Cologne, singing lifts at The Royal Festival Hall, London, and the spinning "MOTHERS" sign in Fort Worth, Texas, are freely accessible. Creed's works are held in museum collections worldwide, including at the Colleccion Jumex in Mexico City and The Lights Going On and Off at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Work No. 1000 consists of 1,000 hand prints made with broccoli, reflecting his comical, child-like approach. Work No. 975, Everything is Going to be Alright, was installed on the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art in November 2009; the phrase has appeared in other works, including a red neon text in New York’s Times Square (Work No. 225, 1999), a 30-metre-long version in Detroit (Work No. 790, 2007), and a 23-metre white neon version at the Rennie Museum in Vancouver (Work No. 851, 2008); a 46-metre multicoloured version was commissioned for Christchurch Art Gallery in 2017. In 2011, Creed was commissioned by Fruitmarket Gallery to create Work No. 1059, which clads 104 steps and landings in different marbles, described by Guardian critic Jonathan Jones as a "generous, modest masterpiece of contemporary public art." In 2012, he participated in Sketch, London’s long-term artist-conceived restaurant programme, creating Work No. 1343 where every piece of cutlery, glass, chair, and table was unique, and Work No. 1347, featuring 96 different types of marble in a herringbone pattern. In 2019, Work No. 2950: WHATEVER was installed on a building in Auckland, New Zealand, as a large multicoloured neon sign. Creed formed his first band, Owada, in 1994 with Adam McEwen and Keiko Owada, releasing their first CD, Nothing, in 1997 on David Cunningham's Piano label. Since 1999, he has not used the name Owada. In 2000, he released a solo recording titled I Can't Move under his own name with Art Metropole. A 2004 solo concert received a zero-star review in The Guardian. In 2010, he provided cover art for a Futuristic Retro Champions single and performed with his band, featuring Keiko Owada on bass, Genevieve Murphy on keyboards, Ben Kane on drums, and Anouchka Grose on steel guitar. Creed founded Telephone Records and released "Thinking/ Not Thinking" in early 2011, followed by "Where You Go" in 2012. In 2012, the Double AA Side single "Fuck Off" and "Die" was released on Moshi Moshi Records in May, ahead of the album Love To You, released in July, produced by David Cunningham, Martin Creed, and The Nice NIce Boys (Andrew Knowles of Johnny Marr & The Healers and Nick McCarthy of Franz Ferdinand). The Vinyl Factory produced a limited edition with hand-painted covers by Creed. "You're The One For Me" was released simultaneously with the album. In 2014, Mind Trap was released, featuring songs and instrumental pieces for orchestra, with Creed singing and playing instruments, supported by gospel singers Dee Alexander and Yvonne Gage and Andy Knowles on drums. Keiko Owada played bass on Gift Attack / Don't Won't. Co-produced by Martin and Andy Knowles, the album was recorded in London, Chicago, and the Czech Republic, with Nick McCarthy and Mark Ralph providing additional production. The Chicago tracks were recorded analog at Soma Studios. The Brno Philharmonic Orchestra, conducted by Mikel Toms, recorded three commissioned orchestral works: Work No. 955 for the Birmingham Symphony Orchestra, Work No. 994 for the Hiroshima Symphony Orchestra, and Work No. 1375 for the London Sinfonietta. All lyrics and music on the album are by Martin Creed, except "New Shutters," which is his arrangement of a traditional Neapolitan folk song. The album sleeve features Work No. 1674: Anouchka and was designed by Andy Knowles. Creed is well-regarded by Franz Ferdinand, who regularly attend his gigs and co-produced his Mind Trap album. In 2015, a new body of audiovisual work was released in response to the Syrian refugee crisis: the double A-side single “Let Them In / Border Control” was made available as free downloads on SoundCloud, accompanied by videos created by Creed. In July 2016, Creed released Thoughts Lined Up, including the singles "Understanding" and "Princess Taxi Girl," with accompanying videos. In a 2002 interview, Creed explained that he stopped making paintings because he didn’t like deciding what to paint, instead focusing on communicating with people, expressing himself, and wanting to be loved. He believes art is primarily emotional, driven by a desire to make something and connect with others. In 1996, Richard Long and Roger Ackling selected Creed for exhibition at EASTinternational. Since winning the Turner Prize, he has exhibited globally, including large survey shows at Trussardi Foundation, Milan ('I Like Things'), Bard College, New York ('Feelings'), and a touring exhibition from Ikon Gallery Birmingham to Hiroshima and Seoul. His first major survey, 'What's the point of it?', was held at the Hayward Gallery, London, in January 2014, featuring works such as Work No. 227, Work No. 293, and Work No. 1092 MOTHERS. In 2014, the Southbank Centre commissioned a new organ piece, Work No. 1815, performed alongside J.S. Bach’s works. His largest survey to date, The Back Door, took place at Park Avenue Armory, New York from June to August 2016, curated by Tom Eccles and Hans-Ulrich Obrist, featuring works from his over 20-year career. In 2017, he exhibited at Museum Voorlinden in the Netherlands titled Say Cheese, which included a wall of 1,000 broccoli prints in various colors, a room filled with blue balloons for walking through, and a room with metronomes ticking at different speeds. In 2019, the Centro Botín held an exhibition called Amigos from 6 April to 9 June, featuring new installations including one among trees surrounding the building. The Museum of Recent Art held an exhibition titled Thinking / Not Thinking from 12 February to 2 May 2019, showcasing several installations.

Mary Ann Willson (active 1810 to 1825) was an American folk artist based in Greene County, New York, whose work remained undiscovered for over a century until it appeared in an exhibition of American Primitive paintings in 1944. Little is known about her life, with available information derived from two anonymous letters—one accompanying a portfolio acquired by the Harry Stone Gallery in 1943 and a short biography in Richard Lionel De Lisser's *Picturesque Catskills, Greene County*, first published in 1894. These letters, which reference Thomas Cole, Asher Brown Durand, and Daniel Huntington as "modern" painters, are dated to the mid-nineteenth century. According to the documents, Willson and her "friend," Miss Brundage (also spelled Brundidge), left Connecticut around 1810 to settle in Greenville, Greene County, New York, where they purchased a few acres and built a log cabin. Brundage farmed the land while Willson painted, selling her works—described as rare and unique—to farmers and others from Canada to Mobile, Alabama. Her paintings, created with bright colors made from berry juice, vegetable dye, or brick dust, were stylistically untrained and based on popular prints of the day. Her surviving oeuvre consists of twenty-two watercolors, as listed in a 1976 checklist by N. F. Karlins. At Brundage's death, Willson reportedly became inconsolable and disappeared shortly after, with her last known work completed in 1825; her fate remains unknown. In 1944, the Harry Stone Gallery exhibited sixty-seven "American Primitive" paintings, including twenty of Willson's watercolors, which covered landscapes, still lifes, narrative scenes, portraits, mythological themes, and genre subjects. Curator Jean Lipman noted Willson's "teeming imagination, bold taste for primary color and geometric design, and total lack of inhibition," describing her style as close to modern abstract art. Although there was initial speculation at the time that the works were forgeries and the documentation fabricated to exploit the folk art market, Karlins concluded they were authentic, citing De Lisser's 1894 publication and records in the collection of Theodore Cole, the son of Thomas Cole and owner of two of Willson's watercolors. Karlins affirmed that despite unanswered questions about her origins and influences, the paintings are genuine and represent one of the most original early nineteenth-century folk watercolorists ever discovered. Willson's life and relationship with Brundage inspired Isabel Miller's 1969 novel *A Place for Us*, republished in 1971 as *Patience and Sarah*, and a 1998 opera by Paula M. Kimper.

Mary Fairchild MacMonnies Low (1858–1946) was an American painter known for her work in landscapes, genre paintings, and portraits. Born in 1858 in New Haven, Connecticut, she studied at the St. Louis School of Fine Arts, where she received a three-year scholarship, and later in Paris at the Académie Julian and under Carolus Duran. She maintained her own studio at 11 Impasse du Maine, which is now part of the Musée Bourdelle. She married Frederick MacMonnies in 1888 and divorced him in 1909, after which she married Will H. Low that same year. In April 1892, Low (then MacMonnies) was approached by Sarah Tyson Hallowell, agent for Bertha Palmer, the key figure behind the Woman's Building at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, to paint one of two mural tympana for the building's interior; the other was Modern Woman by Mary Cassatt. The subject of Low's mural was Primitive Women, which was considered more successful than Cassatt's at the time, and these were the only murals created by either artist. MacMonnies Low also exhibited her work at the Palace of Fine Arts during the 1893 Exposition. She is represented in the Museum of Rouen, France, where she won a gold medal in 1903 and again in 1911, as well as a gold medal in Dresden in 1902 and in Marseille in 1905, and the Julia Shaw prize from the Society of American Artists in 1902. She became an associate of the National Academy of Design.

Mary Renetta Hawton (née Bevis; 4 September 1924 – 18 January 1981) was an Australian tennis player whose career spanned the 1940s and 1950s. She won the women's doubles title at the Australian Championships five times and, in 1958, also secured the mixed doubles title with her compatriot Robert Howe. In 1948, she married Keith Ernest Hawton. Hawton served as captain of the Australian Fed Cup team in 1979 and 1980 and held the position of director at the NSW Tennis Association. In 1979, she published a book titled How to Play Winning Tennis. She passed away on 18 January 1981 in Sydney, Australia. The Mary Hawton Trophy, awarded to the winner of the Australian girls' team championships, and Hawton Place in the Canberra suburb of Chisholm, are both named in her honor. Hawton achieved significant success in Australia at the Australian Championships, reaching the semifinals in singles six times in 1948, 1952, 1953, 1954, 1956, and 1959, and reaching 12 finals, eight of which were consecutive. She also reached the doubles finals at Wimbledon and the French Championships in 1957 and 1958, partnering with Australian player Thelma Coyne Long. Hawton concluded her career with six Grand Slam titles: five in women's doubles and one in mixed doubles.

Mary Letitia Caldwell (December 18, 1890 – July 1, 1972) was an American chemist who taught chemistry at Western College, where she earned her bachelor's degree in 1913 and taught until 1918. Born in Bogotá, Colombia, to U.S. missionaries, she was part of a family of five siblings who all valued higher education. She earned her M.A. and Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1919 and 1921, respectively, and was hired as an instructor at Columbia in 1922. She became the first woman instructor in the chemistry department at Columbia University and later the first woman to attain the rank of assistant professor there in 1948, eventually becoming a full professor in 1948. She was the only female member of the senior faculty in the chemistry department at Columbia University. Caldwell had a progressive muscular disorder that made her reliant on a wheelchair for life, beginning to use it by 1960, and her 9th floor office at Chandler Hall remained unchanged despite this. She spent sixty years researching amylase, a starch enzyme, and developed a method for purifying crystalline porcine pancreatic amylase, which is now used by laboratories in America and Europe. In 1960, she received the Garvan Medal from the American Chemical Society, an annual honor awarded to a U.S. female chemist for significant contributions to chemistry. Her work focused on purifying enzymes, as she was dissatisfied with commercial enzyme materials, and she successfully developed a method for isolating crystalline pancreatic enzymes.

Maryon Lane (15 February 1931 – 13 June 2008) was a South African ballet dancer who gained prominence in Britain as a ballerina with the Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet and as a soloist with the Royal Ballet. Born Patricia Mills in Zululand, a district of Natal province (now KwaZulu-Natal) on the Indian Ocean coast of South Africa, she moved to Johannesburg, in the northern province of Transvaal (now Gauteng), at around 13 years old in 1944. There, she studied ballet with leading teachers, including Marjorie Sturman, a specialist in the Cecchetti method, and Reina Berman, who had trained in the Cecchetti method before transitioning to the Royal Academy of Dancing (RAD) syllabus. In 1946, shortly after the end of World War II, Mills emigrated to the UK, winning an RAD scholarship to attend the Sadler's Wells Ballet School in London. After one year of study, she joined the corps of the Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet, at which point she adopted her professional name, Maryon Lane, to distinguish herself from another South African dancer named Patricia Miller. The Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet was a small, young company founded by Ninette de Valois to develop dancers and choreographers following the relocation of the parent company to the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden. Due to the need to replace depleted leading dancers, Lane advanced quickly through the ranks; by 1948, at age 17, she became a principal dancer and performed in major works by de Valois and Frederick Ashton. Petite, with dark hair, a pretty oval face, and ideal proportions, she was noted for her vivid personality, strong technique, and natural musicality. De Valois regarded her as the ideal repertory dancer—capable of demi-caractère and dramatic roles as well as classical work. Throughout her career, she was celebrated for her musicality, attack, and commanding stage presence. She excelled in lighthearted roles such as Swanilda in Coppélia, Lise in Ashton's La Fille Mal Gardée, and the title roles in John Cranko's Pineapple Poll and Léonide Massine's Mam'zelle Angot, as well as in dramatic roles like the vapid Ballerina in Petrushka, the Betrayed Girl in The Rake's Progress, and the adulterous, runaway Bride in Blood Wedding. She was particularly praised for her performance in the demanding fairy variations in the prologue to The Sleeping Beauty and as Princess Aurora. Her most significant contribution was her involvement in creating new ballets, especially those by the young Kenneth MacMillan. In 1955, MacMillan cast her in a principal role in Danses Concertantes, set to Stravinsky’s score with designs by Nicholas Georgiadis, a work that led de Valois to transfer both the ballet and Lane to the main company at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden. She concluded her performing career there as a soloist in 1968. Among the roles she created were several new productions. She was married to Royal Ballet colleague David Blair, with whom she had twin daughters in 1960. In 1961, Blair was promoted to Margot Fonteyn’s regular partner but was soon overshadowed by Rudolf Nureyev’s arrival in 1962. Both Lane and Blair, along with other leading dancers, fell into relative obscurity amid the growing fame of Fonteyn and Nureyev. After leaving the Royal Ballet in 1968, she made occasional guest appearances with London Festival Ballet, Ballet Rambert, and her former company. She then dedicated herself to teaching, becoming an inspired and influential instructor at the London Ballet Centre, and later taught at the Royal Ballet and Ballet Rambert schools and with other companies and seminars. In middle age, after her husband died in 1976, she moved to Cyprus, a former British stronghold in the eastern Mediterranean, settling in the Greek Cypriot town of Kyrenia, a cultural hub and tourist destination on the northern coast. There, she founded the Maryon Lane Ballet Academy. After teaching local students for several years, she passed away in 2008 at the age of 77.

María Fernanda Cabal Molina (born August 8, 1966) is a Colombian political scientist, businesswoman, politician, and Senator of Colombia. A member of the Democratic Center Party, she has held her seat since 2018 and is the party's most voted-for member of Congress. Born in Cali, Cauca Valley, she lived there until her high school years before moving to Bogotá, D.C., where she graduated from the University of the Andes and joined the Political Science Department as coordinator of the Democracy Program, funded by the National Endowment for Democracy. She began her political career as a Member of the Chamber of Representatives in 2014 and was first elected to the Senate in 2018, being re-elected in 2022. Cabal is a female member of the Democratic Center and holds the highest-ranking position in the Senate. She is known for her far-right views and was one of the members of her party who voted against the plebiscite for the peace process. She is of Spanish ancestry from Asturias and Madrid. During the 1990s, she participated in the student movement that later promoted the Seventh Ballot, calling for constitutional reform through the convening of the National Constituent Assembly. Although baptized under the Catholic rite by her parents in 1964, she identifies as a Lapsed Catholic and has expressed admiration for the Evangelical Protestant rite, attending services on multiple occasions. Cabal is known for her conservative positions and has maintained close relations with the Donald Trump administration in the United States and Jair Bolsonaro of Brazil, while consistently criticizing leftist movements in Colombia and Latin America. She supports controversial policies, including the right of civilians to bear arms for self-defense and the rejection of the peace agreement between the FARC guerrillas and the Colombian government. She also signed the Madrid Charter of the Madrid Forum, joining the right-wing group organized by the Spanish political party Vox.

María Teresa Castillo (October 15, 1908 – June 22, 2012) was a Venezuelan journalist, politician, political activist, human rights activist, and cultural entrepreneur. She founded the Caracas Athenaeum, a prominent cultural institution that promotes the arts of Caracas, and served as its president from 1958 until her death in 2012. A strong advocate for human rights, she played a key role in establishing Amnesty International's Venezuelan chapter in 1978. Born on October 15, 1908, in the hacienda "Bagre" in Cúa, Miranda State, Venezuela, she graduated from the School of Social Communications at the Central University of Venezuela. In 1934, she emigrated to New York, United States, where she worked as a seamstress in a factory; however, her efforts to remain in the country were unsuccessful because she was labeled as a revolutionary. In 1989, she was elected to the Venezuelan Chamber of Deputies, the former lower house of the national legislature, and served as the first President of the Chamber's Permanent Commission on Culture. She was also a member of the Chamber's Committee on Regional Development during her time in office. Castillo married Venezuelan journalist Miguel Otero Silva in 1946; they had two children, Miguel Henrique Otero, who is currently the editor of El Nacional newspaper, and Mariana. She passed away in Caracas on June 22, 2012, at the age of 103. In Salou, a municipality in the Catalan province of Tarragona, there is a street named after María Castillo, called Carrer de Maria Castillo.

Masaki Tsuji (辻 真先, Tsuji Masaki; born March 23, 1932 in Nagoya) is a Japanese anime screenwriter, mystery writer, manga author, travel critic, essayist, professor, and mystery fiction novel writer.[1] He was most active in the industry from the 1960s through the 1980s and served as a scriptwriter for numerous popular anime television series produced by Mushi Production, Toei Animation, and Tokyo Movie Shinsha. Tsuji is particularly recognized for his collaborations on animated adaptations of the works of Osamu Tezuka and Go Nagai. In April 2007, he led Japan's first international anime research lab as part of Digital Hollywood University.[2] On December 4, 2007, he received a lifetime achievement award at the 11th Japan Media Arts Festival.[3] On September 24, 2008, he was awarded a Special Award at the 13th Animation Kobe for his contributions to animation writing.[1][4]

Matthew Dubourg (1703 – 3 July 1767) was an English violinist, conductor, and composer who spent most of his life in Ireland. He led the orchestra at the premiere of Georg Friedrich Handel's oratorio Messiah. Born in London as the illegitimate son of a court dancing master, with his mother's identity unknown, Dubourg performed a Corelli sonata at age nine in 1712 at the home of Thomas Britton, standing on a stool. At age eleven in 1714, he studied under the renowned Italian violinist, composer, and music theorist Francesco Geminiani and performed at the Queen's Theatre in March 1714, a benefit concert in May at Hickford's Room, and numerous other events during the London season. On 17 June 1727, he married Frances, daughter of musician Bernard Gates, at Stanmore, Middlesex; they had one daughter, Elizabeth, who married oboist Redmond Simpson on 22 September 1753, who had one child. Dubourg served as concert-master from 1728 to 1764 in Dublin, holding the official title "Chief Composer and Master of the Music attending His Majesty's State in Ireland" at Dublin Castle, and was a major force in Dublin's musical life alongside Geminiani, his long-time friend and teacher. In April 1730, Dubourg, styled "Mathew Dubourgh, Gentleman," entered into a property deal with Francis Barry, Senior, wife of Richard Barry of Dublin, whereby he received the dwelling house of tailor George Quay on Capel Street in Dublin for £110; the deed was witnessed by Elen Du Bourg (sic), possibly a relative. Four years later, a Deed of Mortgage or Conveyance was recorded between Frances Barry (widow of Richard Barry) and Dubourg, stating that Dubourg paid £460 for separate plots of land in Capel Street and Arbour Hill, Dublin; this deed was witnessed by Peter Gunan of Dublin, an instrument maker known for tuning and maintaining the organ at Trinity College Chapel. Dubourg was close friends with Handel and followed his career in London and the music scene across the Irish Sea. Around 15 May 1736, Benjamin Victor, theatre manager in London, wrote to Dubourg about the upcoming marriage of Frederick, Prince of Wales to Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha, noting that operas would not succeed due to the Prince's absence from public entertainments, and that music flourished in subscription concerts and private parties. Dubourg conducted the orchestra during the first performances of Handel's Messiah at Mr Neale's Music Hall in Dublin on 13 April 1742. Permission to use choir members from Dublin's cathedrals was initially granted by Dean Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), author of Gulliver's Travels, but Swift later withdrew it and reinstated it as the performance dates approached.
