Swift also criticized Dubourg's orchestra, calling them "a club of fiddlers in Fishamble Street," though Handel praised their performance, writing to Charles Jennens that the instruments were "really excellent" and the music "delightfully" sounded in the room. According to Redmond Simpson, Dubourg's son-in-law, Handel suffered a "violent and universal" paralytic stroke while dining with Dubourg in Dublin, but was quickly recovered by Doctors Barry and Quin and Mr Nichols, Surgeon General, through violent bleeding and evacuations, and never had a recurrence. During a 1742 concert conducted by Handel, Dubourg played a cadenza that wandered far from the theme, creating complex modulations, and when he returned to the original theme, Handel said, "Welcome home, Monsieur Dubourg." After the Messiah premiere, Dubourg traveled to London with Handel and performed several works at Covent Garden, including Samson, L'Allegro ed il Penseroso, and the London premiere of Messiah in 1743, before returning to Dublin in October. Dubourg composed several works still frequently performed, especially in Britain, including Variations of Druid Tunes, where he adapted famous Irish tunes in the late Baroque style, and variations on the sonatas (op. 5) of Arcangelo Corelli. In 1752, Dubourg became Master of the Royal Chapel in London, a position he held until his death in 1767. Upon Handel's death in 1759, money was left to Dubourg in his will. On 3 July 1767, Dubourg made a brief will leaving most of his estate to his wife Frances, and he died shortly thereafter; although there is some uncertainty about the exact date, his registered date of death is 5 July 1767. The inscription on his tombstone reads: "Here lyeth the body of Matthew Dubourg, chief composer and master of music in the kingdom of Ireland, servant to four generations of the illustrious House of Hanover, George I. and II., his Royal Highness the late Prince of Wales, and His present Majesty; as also instructor in Music to their Royal Highnesses the Duke of Cumberland and the late Prince Frederick. He died July 5, 1767, aged 64." Tho' sweet Orpheus thou couds't Bring Soft pleadings from the trembling string Unmov'd the King of Terror stands, Nor owns the magic of thy hands.

Matvey Isaakovich Blanter (10 February [O.S. 28 January] 1903 – 27 September 1990) was a Soviet composer and one of the most prominent creators of popular songs and film music in the Soviet Union. He composed over two thousand songs and remained active as a composer until 1975. Born in Pochep, then in the Chernigov Governorate of the Russian Empire, to a Jewish craftsman, Blanter studied piano and violin at the Kursk Higher Music School and continued his education in Moscow from 1917 to 1919, studying violin and composition. His early works in the 1920s included light dance and jazz music, such as "John Gray" (1923), a foxtrot that became a major hit. In the 1930s, under increasing ideological pressure, Blanter shifted to composing Soviet propaganda songs and became a key figure in the development of the Soviet "mass song." Among his notable works from this period are "The Song of Shchors" (1935), which tells the story of Ukrainian Red Army commander Nikolai Shchors, and "Partisan Zheleznyak" (1936), which blends military marching rhythms with a mournful ballad describing Commander Zheleznyak's heroic death, opening and closing with a stanza about his lonely burial mound in the steppes. Other significant songs include "Youth" (1937), a cheerful marching song asserting that "right now, everyone is young in our young, beautiful country"; "Stalin Is Our Battle-Glory" (1937), a widely performed hymn to Joseph Stalin; and "The Football March" (1938), whose music is still performed at the start of every football match in Russia. In 1938, Blanter began a long collaboration with poet Mikhail Isakovsky, producing the world-renowned "Katyusha," which combines elements of a heroic battle song and a peasant lament. In the song, a young woman named Katyusha sings of her beloved, compared to "a gray eagle of the steppes," who is far away serving on the Soviet border; the theme emphasizes that the soldier will protect the Motherland while the girl preserves their love. Though joyful and full of imagery of a fertile, blooming land, the song also conveys the sense that the motherland is under threat, and it gained fame during World War II as an inspiration to defend one's land. In 1937, Pravda called for thousands of Soviet girls to work in the Far East to help build military defenses, and Blanter was commissioned to write the operetta *On the Bank of the Amur River* to celebrate the initiative; it premiered at the Moscow Operetta Theatre in 1939 and was broadcast by Moscow Radio and performed nationwide. In early 1945, Blanter accompanied the Red Army to Berlin and was commissioned by Stalin to compose a symphony about the capture of Berlin. However, when Vasily Chuikov met with a German delegation led by Hans Krebs to negotiate surrender, Chuikov had war correspondents pretend to be members of his staff to appear more intimidating. Blanter, wearing civilian clothes, could not pass as an officer and was shoved into a closet just before the delegation arrived. He remained there for most of the meeting and eventually collapsed from lack of air, falling out of the closet into the room just as the delegates were leaving, embarrassing Chuikov and shocking the Germans. Blanter also composed several popular wartime songs, including "The Enemy Burned Down His Home" (1945), which depicts a soldier returning to find his entire family dead; the song was deemed too pessimistic by authorities and banned until it was performed for the first time in 1961. Postwar works include "The Migratory Birds Are Flying" (1949), a patriotic song in which the narrator watches migratory birds fly away and declares that he can think of no better place than the Motherland, and "Dark-Eyed Cossack Girl" (Russian: Черноглазая казачка), written specifically for bass-baritone Leonid Kharitonov. In 1983, Blanter joined the Anti-Zionist Committee of the Soviet Public, an organization established as an anti-Zionist propaganda tool. He died in Moscow in 1990 and was buried at Novodevichy Cemetery. Ayn Rand's 1936 novel *We the Living*, set in Petrograd between 1923 and 1925, includes a passage highlighting the immense popularity of "John Gray." In the 1966 novel *The Last Battle*, Cornelius Ryan notes that Blanter accompanied the Red Army into Berlin during the final days of the war and the collapse of Nazi power. In the 2004 film *Downfall*, Blanter has a minor role and is portrayed by Boris Schwarzmann, depicted as being stuffed into the closet of Vasily Chuikov's office, who is in a rush to meet Nazi general Hans Krebs.

Abul Kalam Ghulam Muhiyuddin (11 November 1888 – 22 February 1958), widely known as Maulana Azad and sometimes referred to as Abul Kalam Azad, was an Indian writer, activist in the Indian independence movement, and statesman. A senior leader of the Indian National Congress, he became the first Minister of Education in the independent Indian government, and his contributions to establishing India’s education foundation are commemorated by celebrating his birthday as National Education Day. Born in Mecca, then part of the Ottoman Empire (now Saudi Arabia), Azad’s family had origins in Herat. His father, Muhammad Khairuddin bin Ahmed Al Hussaini, was a Muslim scholar with thousands of disciples and claimed noble ancestry; his mother, Sheikha Alia bint Mohammad, was the daughter of Sheikh Mohammad bin Zaher AlWatri, a respected scholar from Medina. Azad settled in Calcutta with his family in 1890 and was home-schooled by family-appointed teachers. Fluent in Arabic, he mastered Bengali, Hindustani, Persian, and English, and was trained in the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali fiqh, Shariat, mathematics, philosophy, world history, and science. By age thirteen, he was married to Zulaikha Begum; by twelve, he wanted to write on Al-Ghazali; at fourteen, he contributed articles to Makhzan; at fifteen, he taught students older than him; and by sixteen, he completed the traditional curriculum nine years ahead of peers and launched a magazine. He began publishing a poetical journal, Nairang-e-Aalam, at age eleven and edited Al-Misbah by age twelve. In 1903, he launched Lissan-us-Sidq, which ran from December 1903 to May 1905 before closing due to funding issues. He joined Al-Nadwa in 1906 and edited Vakil from April 1906 to November 1906, later resuming the role until July 1908. In 1908, he traveled to Egypt, Syria, Turkey, and France, where he encountered revolutionaries like those of the Young Turk Movement and Iranian revolutionaries, which influenced his radical political views and led him to become a full-fledged Indian nationalist. He opposed British racial discrimination and Muslim communalism, rejecting the All-India Muslim League’s separatist stance. In 1905, he opposed the partition of Bengal and became active in revolutionary activities introduced by Aurobindo Ghosh and Shyam Sundar Chakravarty, organizing secret meetings in Bengal, Bihar, and Bombay. In 1912, he founded the Urdu weekly Al-Hilal in Calcutta, which openly criticized British policies and promoted Indian nationalism and Hindu-Muslim unity. Al-Hilal was banned in 1914 under the Press Act. In 1913, he became a founding member of the Anjuman-i-Ulama-i-Bangala, which later became the Jamiat Ulema-e-Bangala. He supported the Khilafat Movement to protect the Ottoman Sultan’s position as Caliph, which caused distress among Muslim conservatives. In 1916, he launched Al-Balagh, which was banned under the Defence of India Regulations Act, and was arrested; he was imprisoned in Ranchi until 1 January 1920. After release, he returned to a politically charged environment following the passage of the Rowlatt Acts in 1919 and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919. Gandhi, who had led successful non-violent revolts in Champaran and Kheda, organized the people and promoted Satyagraha. Azad and the Ali brothers welcomed Congress support for the Khilafat Movement and organized a non-cooperation campaign, including boycotts of British institutions and foreign goods. Azad joined the Congress and was elected president of the All India Khilafat Committee. He grew close to Gandhi and shared a deep passion for religion and non-violence (ahimsa), and developed friendships with Jawaharlal Nehru, Chittaranjan Das, and Subhas Chandra Bose. In 1921, he launched Paigham, which was banned by December 1921, and he and its editor, Abdul Razzak Mahilabadi, were arrested and sentenced to one year in prison. In 1922, the Khilafat and non-cooperation movements declined after violence at Chauri Chaura; Gandhi suspended the movement and fasted to repent. Despite this, Azad remained committed to Gandhi’s ideals. In 1923, at age 35, he became the youngest person to serve as President of the Indian National Congress. He led the Flag Satyagraha in Nagpur and presided over the 1924 Unity Conference in Delhi, which aimed to reunite Swarajists and Khilafat leaders under the Congress. He served on the Congress Working Committee and held positions as general secretary and president. In 1928, the Congress opposed the Simon Commission, which had no Indian members, and appointed the Motilal Nehru Commission to propose reforms. Azad endorsed the Nehru Report, which called for ending separate electorates and establishing a secular, independent India, and supported Gandhi’s call for dominion status within a year, or full independence otherwise. He aligned with Congress socialists like Nehru, Subhas Bose, and Jayaprakash Narayan and supported Nehru’s re-election in 1937. He advocated dialogue with Jinnah and the Muslim League between 1935 and 1937, rejecting the idea that the League represented only Muslims. In 1938, he mediated between Subhash Bose and Gandhi, standing by Gandhi and reluctantly supporting the Congress’s exit from provincial assemblies in 1939 after India’s entry into World War II without consultation. He criticized Jinnah for calling Congress rule “Hindu Raj” and the resignation of Congress ministries a “Day of Deliverance,” and opposed the Muslim League’s separatist agenda. At the 1940 Lahore session, when the League adopted a resolution for a separate Muslim state (Pakistan), Azad was elected Congress president in Ramgarh. In his presidential address, he strongly rejected the Two-Nation Theory, stating that Islam had a thousand-year claim on India and that all Hindus, Muslims, and Christians were Indians with equal pride in their religious identities.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, who served as Congress president from 1939 until 1946, strongly opposed the Muslim League's Two-Nation Theory and advocated for Hindu-Muslim unity, asserting that all Hindus and Muslims were Indians with shared bonds of brotherhood and nationhood. In his 1940 presidential address, he stated that Islam had a legitimate claim on Indian soil equal to Hinduism and that Indian Christians also had a rightful pride in being Indians. As the British faced growing unpopularity, Azad, along with Nehru and Gandhi, remained cautious about launching a full rebellion, fearing it would divide India and worsen the war situation. However, after intense debates in the Congress Working Committee in May and June 1942, Azad concluded that decisive action was necessary. He supported the "Quit India" call, traveled across India to rally support, and on 7 August 1942 inaugurated the struggle at Gowalia Tank in Mumbai. Two days later, he and the entire Congress leadership were arrested and imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort, where they remained under strict isolation and censorship for nearly four years. During imprisonment, Azad engaged in bridge, refereed tennis, taught Persian, Urdu, Indian and world history, and on 26 January each year commemorated the independence movement. He proposed negotiations with the British in 1943, arguing the rebellion had been mistimed, but the proposal was rejected. When Gandhi held talks with Jinnah in 1944, Azad criticized the move as counter-productive. After the war, the British agreed to transfer power, and all political prisoners were released in 1946. Azad led Congress in the elections for the Constituent Assembly and headed the delegation to negotiate with the British Cabinet Mission. He strongly supported the mission's 16 May proposal, which advocated a federal system with autonomy for provinces and grouping of provinces on religious lines—Group B for Muslim-majority West, Group C for Bengal and Assam, and Group A for the rest—arguing it would assuage Muslim concerns and bury Jinnah's demand for Pakistan. Despite opposition from Gandhi and others, the Working Committee approved the resolution with Azad and Patel's backing, and Azad secured Jinnah's agreement to the proposal. Azad resigned as Congress president in 1946, nominating Nehru, who led the interim government, and was appointed Minister of Education. He focused on rural education, girls' education, universal primary education, adult literacy, and vocational training, establishing the Central Institute of Education, the first Indian Institute of Technology in 1951, the University Grants Commission in 1953, and promoting the Indian Institute of Science and Delhi University's Faculty of Technology. He was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1952 from Rampur and won both Rampur and Gurgaon in 1957. Azad supported Nehru's socialist policies and social rights for women and underprivileged groups. He presided over the UNESCO General Conference in 1956 and wrote major works including India Wins Freedom, Ghubar-e-Khatir, and Tazkirah Tarjumanul Quran. Ghubar-e-Khatir, written between 1942 and 1946 during his imprisonment, consists of 24 letters to his friend Maulana Habibur Rahman Khan Sherwani, never sent due to restrictions, later published in 1946 by Ajmal Khan. The book covers complex topics like the existence of God, the origin of religions, and music in religion, with over 500 Persian and Arabic couplets. The book is seen as dealing with Azad’s social and spiritual life, while India Wins Freedom focuses on his political life. In 1989, the Ministry of Minority Affairs established the Maulana Azad Education Foundation and the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad National Fellowship to support minority students. In 1992, India posthumously awarded him the Bharat Ratna. Numerous institutions across India bear his name, including Maulana Azad Medical College, Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology, Maulana Azad National Urdu University, and the Maulana Azad Library at Aligarh Muslim University. His tomb, located next to Jama Masjid in Delhi, is a major national monument and receives many visitors; the Delhi High Court ordered its renovation in 2005. National Education Day is celebrated annually on 11 November, his birthday. Jawaharlal Nehru called him Mir-i-Karawan, and Gandhi described him as having the calibre of Plato, Aristotle, and Pythagoras. Azad was portrayed in the 1982 film Gandhi by Virendra Razdan, in a 1990s television series by Mangal Dhillon, in the docudrama Seher Hone Tak with Aamir Bashir, and in the 2019 film Woh Jo Tha Ek Massiah Maulana Azad with Linesh Fanse. Commemorative stamps were released by India Post.

The biographical film *Aashiq-e-Vatan* is about Maulana Azad, with the film *Woh Jo Tha Ek Massiah* released in 2019, directed by Rajendra Gupta Sanjay and Sanjay Singh Negi, and featuring Linesh Fanse in the lead role. Maulana Azad's birthday, 11 November, is observed as National Education Day in India. Commemorative stamps have been released by India Post, organized by year.

Mavis Constance Tate (born Maybird Hogg; 17 August 1893 – 5 June 1947) was a British Conservative politician and campaigner for British women's rights. She was the daughter of Guy Weir Hogg (1861–1943), a diplomat who served as British consul for Portugal, Sweden, and Norway, a justice of the peace, and had business interests as managing director of SA Advertising Contractors in Cape Town, South Africa, and general manager of the Uganda Company; his wife, Constance, was daughter of Henry Joseph Marsden. Guy Hogg was grandson of Sir James Hogg, 1st Baronet, a politician and chairman of the East India Company. Mavis Tate’s brother, Kenneth, succeeded as the 6th baronet. As a Conservative, she was elected Member of Parliament (MP) for Willesden West in 1931, a seat typically held by Labour, and in 1935 moved to Frome, which she held with a majority of 994; Frome had been a Labour seat during the 1920s and was defeated by Labour in 1945. She was an early member of Archibald Ramsay's Right Club, founded in May 1939, but publicly protested Germany's mistreatment of Jews after Kristallnacht in 1938. After a nervous breakdown in 1940, she distanced herself from the far-right. In 1932, as MP for Willesden West, she opposed a clause in the National Health Insurance and Contributory Pension Bill that would penalise married women as 'malingerers and cheats' despite their full contributions. On the 1933 Employment Bill, she advocated for more training of the unemployed, stating it was better to train a smaller number thoroughly than to flood the market with undertrained workers. In 1934, during discussion of the Employment Assistance Act, she argued that destitute men and women should receive the same benefit amounts. She supported improvements in midwifery training due to 'terrible figures of maternal mortality' in 1935 and raised concerns about research into mental disorder and deficiency, particularly when sterilisation was proposed, questioning whether padded cells were a cure. She was a passionate advocate for equal pay, arguing that work should be paid according to its worth and that women had historically performed most of the country’s productive work before being excluded from working for gain; she criticized the government for systematically paying women less than men in the civil service and teaching profession, noting that this led to more women being employed and fewer men. She supported women's equal rights in nationality, stating married women should be in the same position as men, and presented a petition from 100 Commonwealth women's groups. By 1936, she was MP for Frome and supported the Marriage Bill for removing abuses in divorce law, highlighting the negative effects of illegitimacy on children whose parents were legally bound to partners in prison or asylums. She challenged the employment of 14-year-olds in factories, expressing concern over health deterioration and long hours, and reiterated her support for equal pay. She argued for better pensions for women, noting that women had typically earned less than men and thus saved less. She objected to clauses in the Marriage Bill implying that prolonged desertion did not end a marriage, quoting a clergyman that such a situation amounted to no Christian marriage. During World War II, she advocated for arming women to resist a feared German invasion in 1940 and cited the antisemitic writer Douglas Reed to support her call for the mass internment of refugees in 1940, stating that Jews were capable of acting as spies for Nazism. She chaired the Women's Power Committee in 1941 and the Equal Pay Campaign Committee in 1942, and was vocal on equal pay during the war. In two instances, she went against scientific and professional advice: in 1936, she challenged the government’s use of a living virus in smallpox vaccination; in 1939, she claimed the lymph vaccination method for soldiers, derived partly from rabbits, was likely to spread encephalitis and was extremely dangerous. In 1937, she objected to milk pasteurisation, citing constituents who disliked it, claiming the milk had negligible nutritive value and a nauseating taste; in 1939, she asserted that pasteurisation killed vitamins and hormones, calling it a 'pernicious practice'. A Royal Commission she requested on pasteurisation was not approved, and despite general support among MPs, she continued to argue that many people loathed pasteurised milk, despite evidence that 40% of pulmonary tuberculosis cases were linked to milk from unpasteurised sources. In April 1945, shortly before the end of WWII, Tate travelled with nine other MPs to visit the Buchenwald concentration camp in Germany to report on the atrocities; she narrated the newsreel for British Pathé News, stating "do believe me when I tell you that the reality was indescribably worse than these pictures." On 25 April, Earl Stanhope submitted the report to Prime Minister Winston Churchill, who presented it to Parliament on 27 April 1945. She married Captain Gerald Ewart Gott in 1915, divorced in 1925; in 1925 she married Henry Burton Tate, divorced in 1944. She adopted the first name "Mavis" in 1930 by deed poll. She suffered a nervous breakdown in 1940. Tate committed suicide by gassing herself and died at 6 Bloomfield Terrace, Westminster, on 5 June 1947, leaving an estate valued at £35,482,978. At her 1947 inquest, the Coroner for Westminster concluded she had committed suicide due to mental disturbance from ill-health. In a note to her brother, she wrote: "As I have no one dependent on me, it seems to be the wiser thing to end my life. An invalid is only a national liability. Today I cannot endure the extensive, constant pain in my head and I have had practically no sleep at all for week after week." Medical evidence indicated the effects of intense overwork, including severe kidney pain. Her brother, Col. Kenneth Hogg, said she was always trying to do too much. Her illness began after her visit to the Buchenwald concentration camp in 1945.

Max Vuyisile Sisulu, born on 23 August 1945 in Soweto, is a South African politician and businessman who served as Speaker of the National Assembly from May 2009 to May 2014. A member of the African National Congress (ANC), he was part of the party's National Executive Committee (NEC) from December 1994 to December 2017. The son of anti-apartheid activists Albertina and Walter Sisulu, he is the eldest of five children, with siblings Mlungisi, Zwelakhe, Lindiwe, and Nonkululeko. In 1963, at age 19, he and his mother were arrested after his father went into hiding; his father was later sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial. After his release, Sisulu left South Africa for exile via Gaborone, Botswana, and moved to Tanzania, where he joined Umkhonto we Sizwe. Over the next decade, he lived in various regions of Africa and Europe, completing a master's degree in political economy from the Plekhanov Russian University of Economics in Moscow in 1969, a senior military training course in Skhodnya, Soviet Union in 1972, a one-year research fellowship at the University of Amsterdam in 1985, and serving as the ANC's representative in Budapest. From 1986 to 1990, he was head of the ANC's Department of Economic Planning at its headquarters in Lusaka, Zambia. In 1990, he returned to South Africa during the end of apartheid negotiations and became the founding director of the National Institute of Economic Policies in Johannesburg. In 1993, he earned a Master of Public Administration from the Harvard Kennedy School of Government. In April 1994, during South Africa's first democratic elections, Sisulu was elected to the National Assembly, the lower house of the new Parliament, and appointed as the inaugural chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on the Reconstruction and Development Programme (RDP), a policy he had helped draft. He was elected to the ANC NEC in 1994 and to the National Working Committee (NWC) in 1997. In February 1997, he became Chief Whip of the Majority Party, succeeding Arnold Stofile, and announced plans to restore the RDP committee's status and introduced academic training for MPs and staff. He resigned from Parliament in November 1998 to enter business, first joining Denel as deputy chief executive officer from 1998 to 2001, then becoming group general manager at Sasol from 2003 to 2006, and later holding various directorships, including at African Rainbow Minerals. He remained active in the ANC, being re-elected to the NEC and re-appointed to the NWC in December 2002 and December 2007, and served as chairperson of the NEC's Subcommittee on Economic Transformation until after the 53rd National Conference in December 2012, when Enoch Godongwana succeeded him. In the April 2009 general election, he returned to the National Assembly, ranked 39th on the ANC list, and was elected unopposed as Speaker on 6 May, replacing Gwen Mahlangu-Nkabinde, with Nomaindia Mfeketo as deputy. He was nominated by Andrew Mlangeni and was the first man to serve as Speaker since 1994 and the first black man ever to hold the position. He served throughout the Fourth Parliament, widely respected for his fairness and levity, and oversaw the establishment of the parliamentary budget office. During his tenure, he established an ad hoc parliamentary committee to examine the Public Protector's report on the Nkandla homestead upgrades, which found President Jacob Zuma had benefited unduly and should repay the state. Opposition parties welcomed his action, and he was later criticized by some within the ANC for initiating the committee, though the ANC denied such rebukes. The committee did not complete its work before the end of the parliamentary term. In the May 2014 general election, he was ranked 14th on the ANC list, but the party announced Baleka Mbete would replace him as Speaker, with observers suggesting this reflected a desire for stricter partisan control. Sisulu was sworn in as an ordinary MP on 21 May but resigned eight days later after failing to be appointed to President Zuma's cabinet, a move that surprised observers, though the ANC denied claims he was punished for the Nkandla investigation. After leaving Parliament, he remained active in the ANC, criticizing President Zuma in April 2016 following the Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker judgment, calling for his resignation, and condemning Zuma's failure to support Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan as "bloody foolish," attending a civil society march in Pretoria in support of Gordhan. He served the remainder of his NEC term but was not re-elected at the December 2017 national conference. On 31 January 2018, he was appointed as an independent non-executive director of Harmony Gold. In 1966, he married Mercy Vutela, the daughter of activist Greta Ncapayi, whom he had known since high school; they reunited in exile in Moscow. Their son, Mlungisi, became a diplomat in South African embassies to Khartoum and Prague and died of cerebral malaria in London in January 2008 at age 40. His first marriage was short-lived. In 1979, he married Elinor Sisulu, a writer he met in Amsterdam in 1985, who later published a biography of her parents-in-law.

Maxi Gnauck (born 10 October 1964) is a German former artistic gymnast who represented East Germany. She earned a total of 27 medals at the Olympic Games, World Championships, World Cups, and European Championships, making her one of the most successful female gymnasts Germany has ever produced. In 1980, she was awarded East German Sportspersonality of the Year. Her parents had planned to name their child Max, but when the baby was a girl, they added an 'i', resulting in the uncommon name Maxi for Germany. When Maxi was five, her mother enrolled her in a gymnastics center in their area. By age eight, she won her first medals at the Kreisspartakiade. At nine, she transferred to SC Dynamo Berlin, where she was coached by Jürgen Heritz. She is regarded as one of the best uneven bars competitors of all time and was also an outstanding tumbler; she was one of the first female gymnasts to perform a triple twist on floor. In April 1986, Maxi officially announced her retirement and began a four-year course in sports coaching at the University of Leipzig. In 1988, she suffered a severe injury while sliding down a waterslide during her work as an aide at a children's summer camp by the Baltic Sea, breaking her C5 vertebra and nearly becoming paralysed; three vertebrae were later reinforced with a metal plate. After the reunification of East Germany and West Germany, facing strong competition, she took temporary coaching positions in South Africa and Great Britain, both for a few months in 1990. From 1993 until 2004, she worked as a full-time coach at the Harksheide Gymnastics Center in Norderstedt near Hamburg. Since 2005, she has worked at the Artistic and Apparatus Gymnastics Center (Kunst- und Gerätturnzentrum) in Liestal, Switzerland. In 2000, she was inducted into the International Gymnastics Hall of Fame, becoming the first German gymnast to receive this honour.

The Mayor of Kathmandu is the head of the municipal executive of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, elected for a five-year term with a limit of two consecutive terms. The position was first established in 1932 during the Rana regime. Kathmandu was initially declared a municipality in 1932 through the Kathmandu Municipality Sabal Act, founded as a waste management department, and Singh Shamsher Jung Bahadur Rana was appointed as the first 'Mayor Man' by the government of Chandra Shumsher. In 1947, the first municipal elections were held, with Gehendra Shumsher Thapa appointed as chairman by the Rana regime and Shankar Dev Pant elected as his deputy. Following the fall of the Rana regime in 1953, Janak Man Shrestha became the first elected mayor through an indirect election by the council. After King Mahendra's coup in 1960, the mayor position was abolished, and the Pradhan Panch (Council Head) became the elected head. In 1995, mayor Prem Lal Singh declared Kathmandu a metropolitan city, and Keshav Sthapit was elected as its first mayor in 1997. The position has been held by fifteen individuals in a permanent capacity since its creation. The city is overseen by the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Municipal Assembly, and the mayor is supported by the Municipal Executive, composed of ward chairs from all 32 wards. Local government authority in Nepal is defined under Schedule 8 of the Constitution of Nepal, and the mayor's powers are derived from the Local Government Operation Act, 2017. The mayor's main functions include serving as a member of the Kathmandu District Assembly, an ex-officio member of the Pashupati Area Development Trust, the Boudhanath Area Development Committee, the senate of the National Academy of Medical Sciences, and as chairman of the Valley Municipal Forum. The current mayor is Sunita Dangol, who has been serving since January 18, 2025, and was elected as deputy mayor in the 2022 election, taking office on May 30, 2022.

The mayor of the City and County of San Francisco is the head of the executive branch of the city and county government, responsible for enforcing city laws, approving or vetoing bills passed by the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and administering city departments, setting policy agendas, preparing the city budget, and appointing personnel, including filling vacancies in elected offices and serving as acting mayor in emergencies. The mayor serves a four-year term and is limited to two successive terms. Since 1856, San Francisco has operated as a consolidated city-county, with a combined government structure. Since 1850, 45 individuals have served as mayor, with 46 mayoralties due to Charles James Brenham’s two non-consecutive terms, counted chronologically as both the second and fourth mayor. Prior to 1850, Californios held the office during the Spanish and Mexican eras starting in 1779. The current mayor is Democrat Daniel Lurie. Mayoral elections occur every four years, with the cycle aligned with U.S. presidential elections since 2022, following the passage of Proposition H, which was enacted due to low turnout in off-year elections—such as 42% in 2019 and 86% in 2020. Until 2019, elections were held one year before presidential elections on November election day. Candidates must live and be registered to vote in San Francisco. The mayor is typically sworn in on January 8 following the election. Under California’s non-partisan election rules, party affiliations are not listed on the ballot. Mayoral elections originally used a two-round system, but were reformed in 2002 to adopt instant-runoff voting, which allows voters to rank three candidates; if no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-voted candidate is eliminated and votes are redistributed until a majority is achieved. This system was first used in the 2004 Board of Supervisors election and implemented in the 2007 mayoral election. As of 2024, the mayor earns an annual salary of $364,582, the highest in the United States, with nine city public employees earning more, including the chief investment officer and managing director of the San Francisco Employees' Retirement System. Current mayor Daniel Lurie returned all but $1 of his salary to the city. San Francisco’s mayor does not have an official residence; Mayor Willie Brown unsuccessfully sought to acquire the Yerba Buena Island mansion for this purpose. When a mayor dies, resigns, or is incapacitated without designating an acting mayor, the president of the Board of Supervisors becomes acting mayor until the full Board selects a successor. This has occurred seven times: James Otis died and was succeeded by George Hewston; Eugene Schmitz was removed and succeeded by Charles Boxton; Charles Boxton resigned and was succeeded by Edward Robeson Taylor; James Rolph resigned and was succeeded by Angelo Rossi; George Moscone was assassinated and succeeded by Dianne Feinstein; Gavin Newsom resigned and was succeeded by Ed Lee; and Lee died in office and was succeeded by London Breed before the Board selected Mark Farrell as interim mayor. The longest mayoral term was James Rolph’s, lasting over 18 years, during which San Francisco expanded its transit system, built the Civic Center, and hosted the World’s Fair. The shortest term was Charles Boxton’s, which lasted only eight days. Three mayors have died in office: Otis from illness, Moscone in 1978 by assassination, and Lee from cardiac arrest. Dianne Feinstein and London Breed are the only women to have served as mayor, both by succession and election; Willie Brown and London Breed are the only African Americans to have served; Ed Lee is the only Asian American mayor. Four mayors have Jewish ancestry: Washington Bartlett (Sephardi), Adolph Sutro (Ashkenazi), Dianne Feinstein (Ashkenazi), and Daniel Lurie. Fourteen mayors are native San Franciscans: Levi Richard Ellert, James D. Phelan, Eugene Schmitz, James Rolph, Elmer Robinson, John F. Shelley, Joseph Alioto, George Moscone, Dianne Feinstein, Frank Jordan, Gavin Newsom, Mark Farrell, London Breed, and Daniel Lurie. Four mayors are foreign-born: Frank McCoppin and P.H. McCarthy (born in what is now the Republic of Ireland, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland), Adolph Sutro (born in Prussia, part of Germany since 1871), and George Christopher (born in Greece). Willie Brown is the first Black mayor of San Francisco; London Breed is the first Black female mayor. Breed, a District 5 supervisor and president of the Board of Supervisors, won a special election following the death of Mayor Ed Lee on December 12, 2017, and served out the remainder of Lee’s uncompleted term until January 8, 2020. After that, she was eligible to run for two full terms and won the 2019 mayoral election but lost the 2024 mayoral election. This list excludes acting mayors appointed when the mayor is out of the city.

"Me at the zoo" is the first video uploaded to YouTube on April 23, 2005, at 8:27 p.m. (UTC−7), and is recognized as the platform's inaugural upload. The 19-second video was recorded by Jawed Karim’s high school friend, Yakov Lapitsky, and features Karim standing in front of two elephants at the San Diego Zoo in California, where he comments on the length of their trunks, saying: "Alright, so here we are in front of the, uh, elephants, and the cool thing about these guys is that, is that they have really, really, really long, um, trunks, and that's, that's cool. And that's pretty much all there is to say." YouTube was founded in 2005 by Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim, with Hurley studying design at the Indiana University of Pennsylvania and Chen studying computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Karim was inspired to create the platform after being unable to find video clips of the Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show controversy and the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami online. Multiple journalists and publications have recognized the video as a milestone in YouTube's history, with Business Insider, The New York Observer, and BuzzFeed News ranking it as one of the most important YouTube videos, and it has been described as the first YouTube vlog. Reviewers have noted that its ordinary, amateur nature set the tone for user-generated content and established an era of short videos, with Aaron Duplantier and the Los Angeles Times highlighting its significance in media consumption. Greg Jarboe described the video as "extraordinary" for its time, emphasizing that it reflected Karim’s vision of empowering users to become "broadcasters of tomorrow," which helped YouTube grow into the world's most popular online video-sharing community. The official San Diego Zoo YouTube account left a now-pinned comment in 2020 stating, “We're so honored that the first ever YouTube video was filmed here!”, which became the most-liked comment on the platform by April 1, 2025, with 4.2 million likes. Karim has repeatedly updated the video’s description to express criticism of YouTube’s business decisions, including in November 2013 when he stated, "I can't comment here anymore, since I don't want a Google+ account," and in November 2021 when he wrote, "When every YouTuber agrees that removing dislikes is a stupid idea, it probably is. Try again, YouTube," followed by a longer condemnation. On December 16, 2023, the video’s thumbnail was changed to a MrBeast-style image of Karim with fiery eyes and pointing at stampeding elephants, but it was reverted two weeks later. In February 2025, Karim updated the description to include a statement about the danger of microplastics to the brain. The description also includes timestamps for chapters: "Intro", "The cool thing", and "End". As of January 2026, the video has received more than 379 million views.

Meaning of Life is the eighth studio album by American pop singer Kelly Clarkson, released on October 27, 2017, by Atlantic Records. Executive produced by Clarkson and Craig Kallman, it marks her debut release with the label after completing her recording contract with RCA Records, which she signed following her win on the first season of American Idol in 2002. Weary of the restrictive pop-focused structure of her prior deal, Clarkson sought to explore soul and R&B music—a genre she had long desired but had not pursued due to lack of opportunity—until being offered a long-term worldwide deal with Atlantic by Warner Music Nashville executive John Esposito, which included greater creative freedom. The album is her second foray into soul and R&B, following the lead single from her debut album "Miss Independent," and draws inspiration from the 1990s music of Aretha Franklin, Mariah Carey, Whitney Houston, En Vogue, and Bonnie Raitt, aiming to evoke a "soulful" spirit reminiscent of those artists' early works. Clarkson and Kallman commissioned a range of collaborators, including Jesse Shatkin, Greg Kurstin, Mozella, Jason Halbert, The Monarch, Mick Schultz, Harlœ, and James Morrison, with the album's tracks centered on interpersonal connections, specifically love and living in the moment. The album received generally positive critical reception, praised for Clarkson's confidence and cohesion, and debuted in the top three of the Billboard 200, marking her eighth consecutive studio album to achieve this. Three singles—"Love So Soft," "I Don't Think About You," and "Heat"—were released to promote the album, with the first and last topping the Billboard Dance Club Songs chart. "Love So Soft" earned two Grammy Award nominations: Best Pop Vocal Album and Best Pop Solo Performance at the 60th and 61st ceremonies. The album's supporting tour, Meaning of Life Tour, visited U.S. arenas between January and March 2019. After completing her seventh studio album, Piece by Piece (2015) and its companion remix album in 2016, Clarkson ended her contract with RCA Records and 19 Recordings, which held phonographic rights to her master recordings. RCA executives Peter Edge and Tom Corson offered her a three-album deal with a $1 million advance per album, contrasting with the previous six-album, $500,000-per-record agreement. Despite a successful relationship with Edge and Corson, Clarkson declined the renewal, calling it an "arranged marriage," and instead signed with Atlantic on June 24, 2016. The move reunited her with Pete Ganbarg, who had previously worked on her album All I Ever Wanted (2009), and led to her debut appearance on an Atlantic record with the Hamilton-inspired mixtape track "It's Quiet Uptown." Three of her previous producers—Greg Kurstin, Jason Halbert, and Jesse Shatkin—returned for Meaning of Life, while new collaborators included The Monarch, Nick Ruth, and Mick Schultz. Recording sessions began after her 2016 pregnancy and continued into 2017. To avoid a sound similar to Stronger (2011), Clarkson met with songwriters and showcased soulful tracks to define the album's direction. She contributed to a few songs, drawing lyrical inspiration from the novel Big Little Lies, though family life limited her writing efforts. Songwriters such as Ali Tamposi, Mozella, Harlœ, Sebastian Kole, Diztortion, and Warren "Oak" Felder submitted material in Nashville. Clarkson and Kallman jointly executive produced the album, with Kallman handling A&R, marking the first time in ten years Clarkson received executive producer credit. She described Kallman as "instrumental" in guiding the project and emphasized his role in preserving the soulful integrity of the music. Kallman personally invited the soul band Earth, Wind & Fire to perform at recording sessions for two tracks, and Clarkson requested her touring backup singers—Jessi Collins, Nicole Hurst, and Bridget Sarai—to be featured prominently, deviating from her past practice of recording her own background vocals. The album's theme is connection, with Clarkson stating that "life is about loving yourself enough so that you can love others" and that "we need to connect, we need to have conversations." She illustrated the album's logo as a circle to emphasize life's interconnectedness and that no one is in the middle of it. Clarkson emphasized that the album is not "great because of Kelly Clarkson," but because of the musicians, singers, engineers, and producers involved. Musically, the album is described as a mixture of soulful R&B pop, "soulful pop"/"pop-soul," or a soul and R&B record, with critics noting its blend of soulful anthems and empowerment pop. Atlantic promoted the album as a "sensual" pop record and her first documented soul and R&B album, while Clarkson described it as a "grown-ass woman's record" made after living life, reflecting mature themes such as emotional intimacy and self-acceptance. The album opens with "A Minute (Intro)," written and produced by The Monarch with input from Jim McCormick and Katie Pearlman, a self-care anthem for Clarkson. "Love So Soft," co-written and co-produced by Shatkin, Mozella, and Priscilla Renea, is a tribute to classic R&B. "Heat," produced by The Monarch and Mick Schultz with Harlœ and Michael Pollack, discusses full commitment in a relationship. The titular track "Meaning of Life" was written by James Morrison with Ilsey Juber and Shatkin, originally pitched for Piece by Piece but later used as a foundation for the new album. "Move You," written by Nick Ruth, Amy Kuney, and Molly Kate Kestner, bridges religious and secular music. "Whole Lotta Woman," co-written by Jussifer, Novawav duo Denisia Andrews & Brittany Coney, Fade Majah, and Shatkin, is an empowerment anthem rooted in Southern U.S. culture. Earth, Wind & Fire prominently features on this track. "Medicine," co-written and produced by Schultz and Harlœ, is inspired by Carey's "Emotions" (1991). "Cruel," written by The Monarch, Harlœ, and Pat Linehan and produced by Jason Halbert, speaks to commanding respect in a relationship. "Didn't I," written by the Davidsons, Audra Mae, and Pearlman, is a song where Clarkson bellows at a man for abandoning her. "Would You Call that Love," co-written with Greg Kurstin and produced by him, reflects on failed relationships. "I Don't Think About You," written by Harlœ, Michael Pollack, and The Monarch and produced by them, is a ballad based on a past relationship. "Slow Dance," written by Ruth, Kuney, and Kestner, is a sultry song about a woman demanding a man to take things slowly. The final two tracks, "Don't You Pretend" and "Go High," were co-written by Clarkson, Shatkin, and Mozella; the latter is inspired by Michelle Obama's 2016 Democratic National Convention speech. Originally scheduled for June 2017, the release was delayed to October 27, 2017. Atlantic's senior marketing manager Chris Ruff stated the rollout would prioritize physical sales before streaming promotion. The lead single "Love So Soft" was released digitally with "Move You" on September 7, 2017, peaked in the top fifty of the Billboard Hot 100, and topped the Billboard Dance Club Songs chart. The titular track "Meaning of Life" was released as a promotional single on October 19, 2017, followed by "I Don't Think About You" on February 9, 2018, and "Heat" on July 27, 2018. Clarkson announced the Meaning of Life Tour following her role as a coach on the fourteenth season of The Voice, with the tour visiting U.S. cities from January to March 2019. To promote the album, Clarkson performed at events including a Rainbow Room concert in New York City with Kallman, Greenwald, and Max Lousada on September 6, 2017, a "Nashville Sessions" series at the War Memorial Auditorium, an iHeartRadio Secret Session in Toronto broadcast in the following month, and an album release party in Los Angeles on the release date, aired live on iHeartRadio stations. In November 2017, she performed at two events in New York City—one hosted by Neil DeGrasse Tyson at YouTube Space and the other at the Gramercy Theatre with Sirius XM. Cracker Barrel sponsored a "Rocking and Stockings" series during the 2017 holiday season. Clarkson performed the album's songs on The Today Show, America's Got Talent, The Ellen DeGeneres Show, The Graham Norton Show, The Late Late Show with James Corden, The Voice of Germany, the 2017 We Day, the 2017 Invictus Games, the 2017 American Music Awards, Strictly Come Dancing, and other televised events.

Clarkson performed multiple selections from her album *Meaning of Life* across various televised events. She premiered "Love So Soft" on The Today Show the day after its release and performed it on programs including America's Got Talent, The Ellen DeGeneres Show, The Graham Norton Show, The Late Late Show with James Corden, The Voice of Germany, the 2017 We Day, the 2017 Invictus Games, and the 2017 American Music Awards. She performed the titular track on Strictly Come Dancing; "I Don't Think About You" on The Ellen DeGeneres Show; "Move You", "I Don't Think About You", and "Didn't I" on The Today Show; "Heat" on The Today Show and the Opening Ceremony of the 2018 US Open; "Whole Lotta Woman" on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, The Late Late Show with James Corden (during Carpool Karaoke), and the 2018 Billboard Music Awards; "I Don't Think About You" and "Didn't I" on Late Night with Seth Meyers; and "Medicine" and "I Don't Think About You" on The Voice. The album received generally positive reviews from music critics, with Gold Derby's consensus stating that the "intimate, R&B-drenched album is full of confidence," describing its soul emphasis as "euphorically liberated." On Metacritic, it received an average score of 73 based on eight reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews." AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine gave it a four-star rating, calling it one of her most satisfying albums and commending Clarkson for sounding "assured here in a way that differs from her earliest records." Leah Greenblatt of Entertainment Weekly gave it a "B+" rating, noting its cohesion and self-assurance, and stating it "swings low and sweet — a refreshingly real dispatch from an artist expressing exactly what she feels in this moment." Bruner of Time wrote that the album "finds her as fans prefer: a confident artist with a sense of humor and sass to spare." Shaun Kitchener of the Daily Express rated it five stars, saying Clarkson was "in her absolute element" and the album was a "peppier, more playful alternative to Adele's 25." Glenn Gamboa of Newsday gave it a four-star rating, calling it her best album and stating it was her most cohesive work, offering a "chance to declare her ambitions and deliver on them." Isaac Feldberg of The Boston Globe noted that Clarkson "has perhaps never sounded as confident or comfortable as she does" and that she "channels her delight at [her] newfound freedom into songs that, while signaling a new stage in her career, appear to flow directly from both her heart and soul." Mike Nied of Idolator said that "returning to her roots had truly opened a wealth of opportunities" for Clarkson. Craig Jenkins of Vulture described the album as "a simmering pot of warm grooves and powerful vocals, a career pivot to the music that Clarkson ought to have been allowed to make right out of the gate." Michael Cragg of The Observer rated it four stars, comparing its sound to Meghan Trainor and Mariah Carey and crediting its "big, syrupy" ballads for "accentuating Clarkson's undeniably powerful voice, creating a comfort zone that feels genuine." Some critics were ambivalent: Hannah Davis of The Guardian gave it a three-star rating, writing that it had "lots of filler" and evoked Christina Aguilera and Trainor, but noted its "strong, '90s diva-ish mood suits Clarkson's belting vocal style" as she enters a more soulful phase. Katherine St. Asaph of Spin said much of the album felt "dated, studiously attempting to recreate an era Clarkson's long since transcended," and was puzzled by an album that sounded like "contractual winner's filler" nearly 15 years after winning the competition. *Meaning of Life* was nominated for Best Pop Vocal Album at the 61st Grammy Awards and Best Pop Solo Performance for "Love So Soft" at the 60th Grammy Awards. Both nominations made Clarkson the most-nominated artist in both categories' history, sharing the Best Pop Vocal Album record with Justin Timberlake. During promotion, she received honors including the Powerhouse Award at the 2017 Billboard Women in Music event, the Icon Award at the 2018 Radio Disney Music Awards, and a Hall of Fame induction at the 2017 Nickelodeon HALO Awards. The album was included on several publications' year-end lists. It debuted on the Billboard 200 in the United States at number two with 79,000 album-equivalent units, of which 68,000 were traditional album sales, marking Clarkson's eighth consecutive top three studio album and her third to debut at number two. It also debuted at number one on the Billboard Digital Albums chart and became her first entry on the Billboard Vinyl Albums chart. Overseas, it entered the top ten of the Billboard Canadian Albums chart and the Australian ARIA Albums Chart, attained a top twenty debut on the Official UK Albums Chart, the Irish IRMA Artist Albums Chart, and the Swiss Hitparade, and a top forty entry on the national charts of Austria, Germany, and the Netherlands. The album received a RIAA Gold certification in 2021, selling 500,000 equivalent units in the US.

Mehbooba Bur Mufti Sayed (born 22 May 1959) is an Indian politician and leader of the Jammu and Kashmir People's Democratic Party (PDP), who served as the 9th chief minister of the erstwhile state Jammu and Kashmir from 4 April 2016 to 19 June 2018. She is the first female chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir. After the revocation of Article 370 of the constitution in August 2019, Mufti was detained without any charges at first and later under the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. She was the first woman to hold the office of chief minister in Jammu and Kashmir. She formed a coalition government in Jammu and Kashmir jointly with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). She resigned in June 2018 after the BJP withdrew from the coalition. Mufti was the president of the PDP and a member of the Indian parliament, representing Anantnag in the 16th Lok Sabha before being sworn in as chief minister. She also represented Anantnag in the 14th Lok Sabha (2004–09) and has been a Leader of Opposition in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly. She is the daughter of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed and Gulshan Ara, born in 1959 in Akhran Nowpora, J&K, India. She graduated in English literature from Government College for Women in Jammu and has a law degree from the University of Kashmir. Post 1989, she shifted to N. Delhi and joined the Bombay Mercantile Bank, after which she worked with East West Airlines, before moving back to J&K. She married Javed Iqbal Shah in 1984, but they later divorced. Her ex-husband is the first cousin of her father, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, meaning that before their marriage, Mehbooba Mufti was Javed Iqbal Shah's niece. She has two daughters, Iltija and Irtiqa. Her ex-husband is a political analyst, an animal-rights activist, and was briefly with the National Conference party. When elections for the state assembly were held in 1996, Mehbooba became one of the most popular members elected from Bijbehara on an Indian National Congress ticket. Her father had returned to the Congress, which he had left in 1987, angry at the alliance that party had formed with its traditional rival in the state, the National Conference. She later served as the leader of the opposition in the assembly, taking on the government of chief minister Farooq Abdullah with asperity. She resigned her assembly seat and went on to contest the parliamentary elections in 1999 from Srinagar, where she lost to incumbent member Omar Abdullah. She won the Pahalgam seat in the state assembly from South Kashmir, defeating Rafi Ahmed Mir, when assembly elections were held again in 2002. She was elected to the Lok Sabha from Anantnag seat in 2004 and 2014. She defeated Mirza Mehboob Beg, who was the incumbent MP, in the 2014 Lok Sabha Elections. After her father's death in January 2016, when he was heading the coalition government in Jammu and Kashmir, she took forward the same alliance with the BJP, the second time the BJP and the PDP formed a government in Jammu and Kashmir. On 4 April 2016, she took the oath and became the first woman Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir. On 25 June 2016, she won an Assembly seat in a by-election in Anantnag with the highest margin in any recent elections there and thereafter focused on settling of Rohingyas. On 19 June 2018, she resigned as chief minister of Kashmir. Her government had been an alliance between the Peoples' Democratic Party (PDP) and the BJP, but there was a rift in the alliance in February 2018, when two BJP ministers expressed public support for a man who was alleged to have raped and killed an eight-year-old girl in Kathua District. The BJP's National General Secretary, Ram Madhav, announced the end of the alliance between the BJP and the PDP, saying it was because of the deteriorating security situation. Mehbooba and the state government had tried suspending security operations for Ramadan, but the militants had not reciprocated, and 30 people were killed during the ceasefire. So the BJP withdrew from the alliance with the PDP so that the Indian government could get tough with the militants. When the alliance between the PDP and the BJP ended, Mehbooba resigned as chief minister. Mehbooba said "the muscular policy will not work in Kashmir". She contested the 2019 Lok Sabha elections from Anantnag seat but lost it to Hasnain Masoodi of the National Conference, and later also lost the 2024 Lok Sabha elections from Anantnag - Rajouri seat to Mian Altaf Ahmed Larvi of the National Conference with 2.3 lakh votes. On 5 August 2019, she was detained by the Central government. Her daughter Iltija Mufti took over her mother's Twitter account on the 46th day of detention. In November, Iltija Mufti wrote a letter to the Srinagar Deputy Commissioner to shift her mother to a place better equipped for the valley's winter. In February 2020 she was further detained under the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. She was released on 13 October 2020. On 25 November 2020, former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister and People's Democratic Party chief Mehbooba Mufti was detained by Jammu and Kashmir Police and was not allowed to visit South Kashmir's Pulwama to meet the family of senior PDP leader Waheed Para, who was arrested by the National Investigating Agency earlier that week. Mufti said that her daughter Iltija Mufti has also been placed under house arrest.

Meiosis is a specialized form of cell division in sexually reproducing eukaryotic organisms, including animals, plants, and fungi, that produces gametes—sperm or egg cells—through two successive divisions, resulting in four haploid daughter cells, each containing one copy of each chromosome. Before meiosis begins, during the S phase of the cell cycle, DNA is replicated so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids, held together by sister chromatid cohesion. This phase is referred to as the "premeiotic S-phase" or "meiotic S-phase." Following replication, cells enter meiotic prophase, a prolonged stage that lasts 13 out of 14 days in mice, during which homologous chromosomes pair, synapse, and undergo genetic recombination through programmed double-strand breaks initiated by the enzyme SPO11, leading to the exchange of genetic information via crossovers. These crossovers form physical links called chiasmata, which help ensure accurate segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I. The paired chromosomes, known as bivalents or tetrads, are further divided into substages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, and diakinesis. In pachytene, homologous recombination is completed, with most double-strand breaks repaired without crossovers and a subset forming crossovers between non-sister chromatids. In diplotene, the synaptonemal complex disassembles, and homologous chromosomes remain connected at chiasmata. In human fetal oogenesis, oocytes arrest in prophase I in a state known as dictyotene, which persists until puberty or later. During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes are segregated into two daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes (haploid), but each chromosome still consists of two sister chromatids. This division is called a reductional division. In meiosis II, which follows without DNA replication, sister chromatids separate, similar to mitosis, resulting in four haploid cells. In female animals, three of the four products are typically eliminated as polar bodies, and only one develops into an ovum. The process of meiosis ensures that gametes contain one set of 23 chromosomes in humans, with half maternal and half paternal origin. When a sperm and an egg fuse during fertilization, they form a diploid zygote with 46 chromosomes—23 from each parent—maintaining the species' chromosome number across generations. Errors in meiosis that lead to aneuploidy, an abnormal number of chromosomes, are the leading known cause of miscarriage and the most common genetic cause of developmental disabilities. Meiosis was first described in sea urchin eggs in 1876 by Oscar Hertwig, further detailed in Ascaris eggs in 1883 by Edouard Van Beneden, and its significance for inheritance was recognized by August Weismann in 1890. Thomas Hunt Morgan detected crossovers in Drosophila melanogaster in 1911, confirming that traits are carried on chromosomes. The term "meiosis," derived from the Greek μείωσις meaning "lessening," was introduced by J.B. Farmer and J.E.S. Moore in 1905 as "maiosis," later changed to "meiosis" by Koernicke and Pantel and De Sinety to follow Greek transliteration conventions. Meiosis is divided into meiosis I and II, each consisting of prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, with meiosis I involving reductional division and meiosis II involving equational division. During meiosis, specific genes are highly transcribed, and both transcriptional and translational controls regulate gene expression. In human and mouse oocytes, centrosomes are absent, and microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) form a spindle. Homologous chromosomes align at the metaphase plate in meiosis I due to bipolar attachments, with independent assortment occurring due to random orientation. Cohesin holds sister chromatids together until anaphase I, with arm cohesin degraded and centromeric cohesin protected by Shugoshin. After meiosis I, cytokinesis results in two daughter cells with cytoplasmic bridges, and cells may enter interkinesis without DNA replication. In meiosis II, prophase II involves reformation of the spindle, metaphase II features alignment of chromosomes at a new equatorial plate, anaphase II involves separation of sister chromatids, and telophase II concludes with the formation of four haploid cells. Meiosis does not occur in archaea or bacteria, which reproduce asexually via binary fission, though horizontal gene transfer in these organisms involves DNA transfer and recombination. In some eukaryotes like bdelloid rotifers, meiosis is absent, and reproduction occurs via parthenogenesis. Meiosis is essential for oogenesis and spermatogenesis and contributes to genetic diversity through recombination, resulting in offspring that are genetically distinct from either parent.

Meiosis II is the second meiotic division, typically involving equational segregation, where sister chromatids separate, and it mechanically resembles mitosis but produces genetically distinct outcomes. It results in four haploid cells (n chromosomes; 23 in humans) from two haploid cells (each with n chromosomes and two sister chromatids) formed in meiosis I. The four main phases are prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, and telophase II. In prophase II, nucleoli and the nuclear envelope disappear, chromatids shorten and thicken, and centrosomes move to the poles to form spindle fibers. In metaphase II, centromeres have two kinetochores that attach to spindle fibers from opposite poles, and the equatorial plate is rotated 90 degrees compared to meiosis I. During anaphase II, remaining centromeric cohesin, no longer protected by Shugoshin, is cleaved, allowing sister chromatids—now referred to as sister chromosomes—to move to opposite poles. Telophase II involves decondensation of chromosomes, spindle disassembly, reformation of nuclear envelopes, and cell division, resulting in four daughter cells, each with a haploid chromosome set. Meiosis is a fundamental feature of eukaryotes and likely existed early in eukaryotic evolution; organisms once thought to lack meiosis, such as Giardia intestinalis and Leishmania, have been found to possess meiotic genes and evidence of meiotic recombination. Amoebas were also previously considered asexual, but evidence suggests most lineages are ancestrally sexual, with asexual forms arising recently. Dacks and Rogers proposed facultative sex was present in the common eukaryotic ancestor. Meiosis generates genetic diversity through independent assortment—random orientation of homologous pairs and sister chromatids during metaphase I and II—and crossing over, where homologous regions exchange genetic material during prophase I. However, in silkworm oocytes (Bombyx mori), meiosis is completely achiasmate, lacking crossovers despite the presence of synaptonemal complexes. Female mammals and birds are born with all oocytes arrested at prophase I (dictyate stage), which may last decades and includes four copies of the genome; this arrest is thought to provide DNA repair redundancy, particularly through homologous recombination, which is crucial for germline integrity and fertility. Genetic recombination is viewed as a DNA repair mechanism, and experimental evidence shows that oxidative DNA damage, such as from hydrogen peroxide, increases mating and meiotic spore formation in yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe) and heat shock-induced meiotic sex in Volvox carteri, suggesting oxidative stress triggers meiotic activity. Meiosis occurs in eukaryotic life cycles involving sexual reproduction, alternating between haploid and diploid states through mitotic growth, gamete production via meiosis, and fertilization. In diplontic cycles (e.g., humans), the diploid organism develops from a zygote via mitosis, and germ-line cells undergo meiosis to produce gametes. In haplontic cycles (e.g., many fungi and protozoa), the haploid organism develops from a gamete, and the zygote undergoes immediate meiosis to form haploid spores. In haplodiplontic cycles (alternation of generations), the diploid organism produces spores via meiosis, which grow into a haploid organism that produces gametes; this cycle combines elements of both others. Meiosis occurs in all animals and plants, producing gametes with half the parent cell’s chromosome number, though the process differs: in animals, gametes are produced directly; in land plants and some algae, meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores that develop into gametophytes. Gametes fuse to form a zygote with the original chromosome number. In females, meiosis occurs in oocytes, which divide twice unequally: the first division yields a daughter cell and a small polar body, and the second division produces a second polar body and a single haploid ovum. Oocytes are arrested in prophase I and remain dormant in follicles, with the germinal vesicle present until resumption of meiosis stimulated by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). At the start of each menstrual cycle, FSH promotes folliculogenesis, leading to resumption of meiosis and arrest at metaphase II before ovulation. If fertilized, meiosis completes. In males, meiosis occurs during spermatogenesis in seminiferous tubules, initiated post-puberty when Sertoli cells produce retinoic acid, which stimulates spermatogonia differentiation and meiosis, with sensitivity modulated by nanos and DAZL proteins. In females, meiosis begins embryonically, possibly stimulated by retinoic acid from the mesonephros, though genetic studies show retinoic acid is not required for initiation. A rare one-divisional meiosis occurs in some flagellates from the gut of Cryptocercus. In humans, recombination among the 23 chromosome pairs redistributes chromosomal segments, with about 1.6 times more recombination in females than males, higher at centromeres in females and telomeres in males; 1 million base pairs correspond to 1 cMorgan. Approximately 200 double-strand breaks form per meiotic cell, but only 5–30% become crossovers, resulting in 1–2 crossovers per human chromosome. Recombination rates differ between maternal and paternal DNA. Errors such as nondisjunction—failure of proper chromosome separation—can lead to gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers, causing chromosomal disorders like trisomy or monosomy. Disjunction is normal separation in meiosis I or II, while nondisjunction results in gametes with too many or too few chromosomes and can occur in meiosis I, II, or mitosis. Most monosomic and trisomic embryos are nonviable, though some aneuploidies, such as trisomy 21, are tolerated. Nondisjunction in human oocytes increases with maternal age, likely due to cohesin loss. Comparing meiosis to mitosis highlights key differences. In oocytes, maturation promoting factor (MPF), regulated by CDK1 and cyclin B, induces germinal vesicle breakdown (GVB) and is active before and after GVB, with activity resuming in meiosis II and persisting until fertilization. In mammals, meiotic arrest is maintained by natriuretic peptide type C (NPPC) and natriuretic peptide receptor 2 (NPR2), which increase cGMP in cumulus cells, inhibiting phosphodiesterase 3A and cAMP hydrolysis. GPR3/12 activates adenylyl cyclase to generate cAMP, which activates PKA to phosphorylate WEE2 and CDC25B, keeping CDK1 activity suppressed. PKC may also inhibit meiotic progression. Meiosis resumes when luteinizing hormone (LH) increases, reducing cGMP via epidermal growth factor-like factors that disrupt gap junctions and lower NPPC/NPR2 activity, while also stimulating production of FF-MAS, which supports progression from metaphase I to II and stabilizes metaphase II arrest. Phosphodiesterases may be temporarily activated by PKA, and long-term regulation may involve protein expression changes. Hypoxanthine, a purine from the follicle, also inhibits oocyte meiosis.

LH-induced epidermal growth factor-like factors, such as amphiregulin and epiregulin, synthesized in mural granulosa cells, reduce cGMP levels in oocytes by restricting cGMP transport through cumulus cell-oocyte gap junctions and lowering NPPC levels and NPR2 activity; these factors may also cause destabilization and breakdown of gap junctions. They may trigger the production of additional oocyte maturation factors, including steroids and follicular fluid-derived meiosis-activating sterol (FF-MAS), in cumulus cells, with FF-MAS promoting progression from metaphase I to metaphase II and possibly stabilizing metaphase II arrest. Meiosis resumption is reinforced by the exit of WEE2 from the nucleus due to CDK1 activation. Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) metabolize cAMP and may be temporarily activated by PKA-mediated phosphorylation; longer-term regulation of PDEs may require modulation of protein expression, for example, hypoxanthine, a PDE inhibitor, may interfere with cAMP metabolism. Kinases such as protein kinase B, Aurora kinase A, and polo-like kinase 1 contribute to meiotic resumption. There are similarities between meiotic prophase I arrest and resumption and the mitotic G2 DNA damage checkpoint: CDC14B-based activation of APC-CDH1 in arrest and CDC25B-based resumption. Meiotic arrest requires inhibitory phosphorylation of CDK1 at Thr-14 and Tyr-15 by MYT1 and WEE1, as well as regulation of cyclin B levels via the anaphase-promoting complex (APC); CDK1 is regulated by cyclin B, whose synthesis peaks at the end of meiosis I; at anaphase I, cyclin B is degraded by an ubiquitin-dependent pathway; cyclin B synthesis and CDK1 activation drive entry into metaphase, while entry into anaphase follows ubiquitin-mediated cyclin B degradation, reducing CDK1 activity. Proteolysis of adhesion proteins between homologous chromosomes occurs in anaphase I, while proteolysis between sister chromatids occurs in anaphase II. Meiosis II arrest is mediated by cytostatic factor (CSF), which includes the MOS protein, mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MAPKK/MEK1), and MAPK; the protein kinase p90 (RSK) is a key target of MAPK and may block entry into S-phase between meiosis I and II by reactivating CDK1; there is evidence that RSK aids entry into meiosis I by inhibiting MYT1, which activates CDK1; CSF arrest may occur through regulation of the APC as part of the spindle assembly checkpoint. In budding yeast S. cerevisiae, Clb1 is the main meiotic regulatory cyclin, with Clb3 and Clb4 also expressed and activating a p34cdc28-associated kinase before the first meiotic division; the IME1 transcription factor drives entry into meiotic S-phase and is regulated by inputs such as nutrition; a1/α2 represses a repressor of IME1, initiating meiosis; IME1 enables sporulation of non-a/α diploids; IME2/SME1 enables sporulation when nitrogen is present, supports recombination in a/α cells expressing RME1 (an inhibitor of meiosis), and encodes a protein kinase homolog; MCK1 supports recombination in a/α cells expressing RME1 and encodes a protein kinase homolog; SME2 enables sporulation when ammonia or glucose are present; UME1-5 enable expression of certain early meiotic genes in vegetative, non-a/α cells. In fission yeast S. pombe, the Cdc2 kinase and Cig2 cyclin initiate premeiotic S phase, while cyclin Cdc13 and CDK activator Cdc25 are necessary for both meiotic divisions; the Pat1-Mei2 system is central to S. pombe meiotic regulation; Mei2 is the major meiotic regulator, moving between nucleus and cytoplasm and working with meiRNA to promote meiosis I; Mei2 is involved in exit from mitosis and induction of premeiotic S phase; Mei2 may inactivate the DSR-Mmi1 system by sequestering Mmi1 to stabilize meiosis-specific transcript expression; Mei2 may stall growth and induce G1 arrest; Pat1, a Ser/Thr protein kinase, phosphorylates Mei2 on Ser438 and Thr527, which may decrease Mei2 half-life by promoting its degradation via a proteasome complex involving E2 Ubc2 and E3 Ubr1; the Mei4 transcription factor is required to activate cdc25 transcription in meiosis, and mei4 mutants experience cell cycle arrest; Mes1 inhibits the APC/C activator Slp1, allowing Cdc2-Cdc13 MPF activity to drive the second meiotic division. It has been suggested that the yeast CEP1 gene product, which binds to centromeric region CDE1, may play a role in chromosome pairing during meiosis I. Meiotic recombination is mediated by double-stranded breaks catalyzed by Spo11, with Mre11, Sae2, and Exo1 involved in breakage and recombination; after breakage, recombination typically occurs homologously and may proceed via either a double Holliday junction (dHJ) pathway or synthesis-dependent strand annealing (SDSA), the latter producing noncrossover products. Checkpoints for meiotic cell division exist in S. pombe, where Rad proteins, S. pombe Mek1 (with FHA kinase domain), Cdc25, Cdc2, and an unknown factor are thought to form a checkpoint. In vertebrate oogenesis, cytostatic factor (CSF) plays a role in switching into meiosis II.

The Melvin Mooney Distinguished Technology Award is a professional honor given by the ACS Rubber Division. It was established in 1983 and is named in recognition of Melvin Mooney, who developed the Mooney viscometer and the Mooney-Rivlin hyperelastic law. The award includes an engraved plaque and prize money. It is presented to individuals who have demonstrated exceptional technical competence through significant and repeated contributions to rubber science and technology.

Merata Mita CNZM (19 June 1942 – 31 May 2010) was a New Zealand filmmaker, producer, and writer who played a pivotal role in the development of the Māori screen industry. She was the first indigenous woman and the first woman in New Zealand to solely write and direct a dramatic feature film, Mauri (1988). Born on 19 June 1942 in Maketu, Bay of Plenty, she was the third of nine children and grew up in a traditional rural Māori environment belonging to the iwi Ngāti Pikiao and Ngāi Te Rangi. She taught at Kawerau College for eight years, where she used film and video to engage high school students, many of whom were Māori and Pacific Islander, through oral storytelling and artistic expression, sparking her interest in filmmaking. Initially working as a liaison for film crews and later as a sound assistant and sound recordist, she gained recognition within the film industry and began a long career in film and television. In 1990, she moved to Hawaii and taught documentary filmmaking at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. Her debut feature film, Mauri (1988), challenged mainstream narratives by asserting Māori cultural sovereignty and honoring the Treaty of Waitangi, with its title meaning cycles of life and spiritual connection to the land. The film's hill is described as having filmic agency, representing the "mauri" or life force, and is central to the concept of "Fourth Cinema"—a term coined by Barry Barclay for indigenous cinema created by indigenous filmmakers for indigenous audiences. Prior to the 1970s, Māori were largely portrayed by male Pakeha filmmakers in ways that reduced their culture to colonial myths. A 37% increase in Māori urban residency from 1945 to 1966 contributed to cultural disconnection and loss of traditions, leading to the Māori Renaissance, a movement to preserve identity. Mita’s films were politically engaged, reflecting her belief that all aspects of life are political, and she actively participated in struggles such as Maori land occupations, anti-apartheid, and anti-racist movements. She co-directed To Love A Māori (1972) with Ramai Te Miha Hayward and directed landmark documentaries including Bastion Point: Day 507 (1980), which was the only media access permitted by Ngāti Whātua during their land protest, and Patu! (1983), about the 1981 South African Springboks rugby tours, as well as Hotere (2001) on artist Ralph Hotere and the music video Waka for Che Fu. In 1998, a documentary on her life, Rangatira: Merata Mita – Making Waves, was directed by Hinewehi Mohi. In 2014, NZ on Air funded a biographical film, Te Taki A Merata Mita – How Mum Decolonised The Screen, to be directed by her son Heperi Mita, which was accepted into the Sundance Film Festival in 2019.
