Mita mentored indigenous filmmakers internationally through organizations such as the Sundance Film Festival's Native Film Initiative, the National Geographic All Roads Indigenous Film Festival, and the Pacific Islanders in Communications consortium, and in 2016, the Sundance Institute established the Merata Mita Fellowship for indigenous filmmakers globally. She received numerous awards, including the Amiens International Film Festival's MRAP Award for Patu! (1983), the Rimini Film Festival's Best Film for Mauri (1989), the Flaherty Seminar's Leo Dratfield Award (1996), the Taos Film Festival's Mountain Award (1999), the Te Waka Toi "Making a difference" Award (2009), and was appointed a Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the 2010 New Year Honours. She was also nominated for the Asia Pacific Screen Awards' Best Children's Feature Film (2010) and the Aotearoa Film and Television Awards' Best Director – Television Documentary (2011). The National Geographic All Roads Festival established the Merata Mita Award in 2010 to honor a legacy of outstanding storytelling. Mita had seven children: Rafer, Richard, Rhys, Lars, Awatea, Eruera, and Hepi; her fourth son, Lars, died at 11 months. Her son Hepi Mita produced the documentary Merata: How Mum Decolonised the Screen, released in 2018. Mita died suddenly on 31 May 2010 after collapsing outside the studios of Māori Television. She directed or collaborated on numerous films and television shows.

Michael Anderson Pereira da Silva, born on February 16, 1983, is a Brazilian former professional footballer who played as a left midfielder. He began his professional career at Santo André before joining Cruzeiro, where he spent one season before transferring to São Paulo, playing for Palmeiras. After two seasons with Palmeiras, he signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian club Dynamo Kyiv in July 2007. Michael made his debut for Dynamo on 22 July against Arsenal Kyiv, scoring a double in the match. In UPL Round 2, he made his UEFA Champions League debut in a group stage game against the Italian team Roma. Throughout the autumn and winter of 2007, Michael was injured and received treatment in Brazil, but he recovered and returned to play. On 13 May 2009, he moved on loan from Dynamo Kyiv to Botafogo, with the loan lasting until 31 December 2009. He then transferred from Kyiv to Portuguesa on 23 May 2011. This information is confirmed by combined sources from the Flamengo official website and Flaestatística.

Michael John Creutz, born on November 24, 1944, in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is an American theoretical physicist at Brookhaven National Laboratory, specializing in lattice gauge theory and computational physics. His father, Edward Creutz, was also a physicist and was involved in the Manhattan Project at the time of Michael's birth. Creutz earned his bachelor's degree in physics with honor from Caltech in 1966 and completed his graduate studies at Stanford University under a NSF Graduate Fellowship, graduating in 1970. His thesis was conducted at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, with Sidney Drell as his adviser. Following graduation, he served as a research associate at SLAC before joining the Center for Theoretical Physics at the University of Maryland, College Park, as a fellow from 1970 to 1972. In 1972, he joined the High Energy Theory Group at Brookhaven National Laboratory, becoming a senior physicist in 1985 and serving as group leader from 1984 to 1987. In 2003, he became an adjunct professor at the C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics at Stony Brook University. His research covers various areas in particle physics and mathematical physics, but he is best known for his work on lattice QCD. His 1983 textbook, *Quarks, Gluons, and Lattices*, was the first full-length textbook on lattice QCD and is regarded as a classic in the field. Creutz is a fellow of the American Physical Society and received the Aneesur Rahman Prize for Computational Physics in 2000 "for first demonstrating that properties of QCD could be computed numerically on the lattice through Monte Carlo methods, and for numerous contributions to the field thereafter." In 2009, he was awarded the Humboldt Research Award.

Michael Stanley Dukakis (/dʊˈkɑːkɪs/ duu-KAH-kiss; born November 3, 1933) is an American politician and lawyer who served as governor of Massachusetts from 1975 to 1979 and from 1983 to 1991, making him the longest-serving governor in Massachusetts history and the second Greek-American governor in U.S. history, after Spiro Agnew. Born in Brookline, Massachusetts, to Greek immigrants, Dukakis attended Swarthmore College, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in political science in 1955, before enlisting in the United States Army from 1955 to 1957. After completing his military service, he received a J.D. from Harvard Law School in 1960. He began his political career as a town meeting member in Brookline and served in the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1963 to 1971. He won the 1974 gubernatorial election, defeating incumbent Francis Sargent, and pledged a "lead pipe guarantee" of no new taxes and a dismantling of the powerful Metropolitan District Commission (MDC), though he failed to achieve these goals. After losing his 1978 bid for re-nomination to Edward J. King, he defeated King in the 1982 Democratic primary and served as governor from 1983 to 1991, presiding over a period of economic growth known as the "Massachusetts Miracle." Building on his popularity, Dukakis sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1988, prevailing in the primaries and being formally nominated at the 1988 Democratic National Convention. He chose Senator Lloyd Bentsen of Texas as his running mate, while the Republicans nominated George H. W. Bush and Senator Dan Quayle. Dukakis made history as the first Greek-American and Aromanian presidential candidate, the first Greek Orthodox major-party nominee, and the first major-party nominee with ancestry outside Europe. Although he lost the election, carrying only ten states and Washington, D.C., he improved on the Democratic performances in the previous two elections. After the election, Dukakis announced he would not seek another term as governor and left office in 1991. Since the death of Jimmy Carter in 2024, Dukakis is the oldest living presidential nominee. Since leaving office, he has served on the board of directors for Amtrak and taught political science at Northeastern University and UCLA. He was considered a potential Senate appointee in 2009 following Ted Kennedy's death, though Governor Deval Patrick selected Paul G. Kirk. In 2012, Dukakis supported Elizabeth Warren in her Senate campaign and in the 2020 Democratic presidential primaries. Dukakis's father, Panos, was a Greek immigrant from Edremit in Turkey who settled in Lowell, Massachusetts, and graduated from Harvard Medical School in 1924, working as an obstetrician. His mother, Euterpe (née Boukis), was born in Larissa to Aromanian parents from Vrysochori and emigrated to Haverhill, Massachusetts, in 1913. Dukakis attended Brookline High School, where he was an honor student and a member of basketball, baseball, tennis, and cross-country teams, and ran the Boston Marathon as a 17-year-old senior. He married Katherine "Kitty" Dickson in 1963, and they remained together until her death in March 2025. Dukakis has a brother, Stelian, who was three years his elder; Stelian suffered a mental breakdown and attempted suicide when Michael was seventeen, was institutionalized for years, and later became a teacher, professor, and assistant city manager. He unsuccessfully attempted to sabotage Michael's 1964 campaign by distributing anti-Michael pamphlets and ran for the Brookline Board of Selectmen twice and once in 1972 for the Massachusetts House of Representatives as a Republican before dying in 1973 after being struck by a car while cycling. Dukakis served four terms in the Massachusetts House of Representatives between 1962 and 1970, ran unsuccessfully for Attorney General in 1966, and was the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor in 1970 on a ticket with Boston mayor Kevin White, but the ticket lost the gubernatorial election. After losing the lieutenant governor race, he returned to the private sector, practicing law at Hill and Barlow. During his first term as governor, he commuted the sentences of 21 first-degree murderers and 23 second-degree murderers and hosted President Gerald Ford and Queen Elizabeth II during their 1976 visits to Boston. He gained recognition for working during the Blizzard of 1978 and for exonerating Sacco and Vanzetti in 1977. His first term was undermined by backlash over high sales and property taxes, leading to his defeat in the 1978 primary by Edward J. King, a decision that his wife Kitty called "a public death." After that, he taught at Harvard University's John F. Kennedy School of Government and published the book State and Cities: The Massachusetts Experience in 1980. In 1982, after making peace with the Democratic Party, the MDC, state police, and public employee unions, he defeated King in the Democratic primary and went on to defeat Republican John Winthrop Sears in the November election, with John Kerry elected lieutenant governor on the same ballot. As governor, he presided over a high-tech boom and prosperity, earning a reputation as a 'technocrat,' and was voted the most effective governor by the National Governors Association in 1986. Residents of Boston and its surrounding areas remember him for improvements to the city's mass transit system, especially train and bus renovations, and he was known for riding the subway to work every day. In 1988, Dukakis and Rosabeth Moss Kanter co-authored Creating the Future: the Massachusetts Comeback and Its Promise for America, an examination of the "Massachusetts Miracle." He won the Democratic nomination in 1988, receiving 2,877 out of 4,105 delegates, and was pro-choice on abortion. He made history as the first non-Western European American major-party nominee and the only major presidential nominee with ancestry from outside Northwestern Europe until Barack Obama's nomination in 2008. He enjoyed strong support among Greek Americans, with the Associated Press reporting an "outpouring of pride" in April 1988, especially among older generations. Dukakis emphasized his working-class background as the son of impoverished immigrants and his fluency in Greek and other languages, using Neil Diamond's "America" as the campaign theme song. His reserved and stoic nature led to criticism, with him being referred to as "Zorba the Clerk," though he performed well in the first presidential debate, with The New York Times noting that analysts generally agreed he outperformed George H. W. Bush. In the second debate, his performance was poor and reinforced his image as cold. During the campaign, concerns about his mental health arose when he refused to release his full medical history, with persistent suggestions of past psychiatric treatment; President Reagan referred to him as an "invalid" at a White House press conference, and journalist Robert Novak revealed in the 2008 film Boogie Man: The Lee Atwater Story that Lee Atwater personally tried to spread these rumors. Editors at The Washington Times contributed to the rumors with a story headlined "Dukakis Kin Hints at Sessions," which was later corrected to show the full quote was "It's possible, but I doubt it." Dukakis faced criticism over capital punishment, the pledge of allegiance in schools, and a photograph of him in a tank during a 1988 photo op at the General Dynamics Land Systems plant in Sterling Heights, Michigan. The image, intended to portray him as a strong commander-in-chief, backfired when he was photographed without a helmet as the tank exited the garage, though most photographers captured him wearing a helmet during a high-speed pass. The image was ridiculed by Bush and the media, with a poll showing 25 percent of respondents were less likely to support him, and footage was used in a Bush campaign ad during the World Series. The Dukakis campaign responded with a 60-second ad featuring a television set playing the Bush ad being flicked off by a finger revealed to be Dukakis, who proclaimed he was fed up with "George Bush's negative TV ads," a tactic later labeled "pin-the-tail-on-the-donkey advertising." The phrase "Dukakis in the tank" remains a shorthand for backfired public relations efforts. In 2008, when asked about the photograph, Dukakis said "Should I have been in the tank? Probably not, in retrospect. But these days when people ask me, 'Did you get here in a tank?' I always respond by saying, 'No, and I've never thrown up all over the Japanese prime minister.'" The Dukakis/Bentsen ticket lost the 1988 election by a decisive margin in the Electoral College to George H. W. Bush and Dan Quayle, carrying only ten states and Washington, D.C.

Footage of Michael Dukakis in a tank was used in a television ad by the Bush campaign that aired during the World Series. In response, the Dukakis campaign produced a 60-second ad showing a television set playing Bush's ad, which is flicked off the screen by a finger later revealed to be Dukakis as he declares he is fed up with "George Bush's negative TV ads"; this "pin-the-tail-on-the-donkey" style advertising only drew further attention to the tank ride. The phrase "Dukakis in the tank" has since become shorthand for backfired public relations moments. In 2008, when asked about the image, Dukakis said he probably should not have been in the tank, but he now responds to questions about it by saying, "No, and I've never thrown up all over the Japanese prime minister." The Dukakis/Bentsen ticket lost the election by a decisive margin in the Electoral College to George H. W. Bush and Dan Quayle, winning only 10 states and the District of Columbia. Many believed the loss stemmed from Dukakis's failure to campaign nationally and his delayed response to Bush's attack campaign, which caused his 17-point lead in opinion polls to vanish as Bush defined the campaign's issues. Dukakis has stated that not responding to the Bush attack campaign was a "pretty dumb decision." Despite the loss, his performance improved over previous Democratic candidates, with Bush winning a majority of the popular vote but Dukakis's margin of loss (7.8%) being narrower than Jimmy Carter's in 1980 (9.7%) or Walter Mondale's in 1984 (18.2%), and earning 41.8 million votes nationally. Dukakis achieved strong results in states that had previously voted Republican, including New York (the second-largest state by electoral votes at the time), Rhode Island, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Oregon, and Washington, and won Iowa by 10 points—a state that had voted Republican in the previous five presidential elections. His popular vote share in South Dakota (46.51%), Kansas (42.56%), Oklahoma (41.28%), Wyoming (38.01%), and Idaho (36.01%) would not be matched by any subsequent Democratic presidential candidate. Although Dukakis reduced Republican dominance in the Midwest, he failed to challenge the growing GOP strength in the South, losing most Southern states by wide margins—Bush's popular vote margins exceeded 15% in most—though Dukakis carried most of the southern-central parishes of Louisiana, which was his best Southern popular vote margin. His second-lowest Southern margin was in Texas, where four overwhelmingly Mexican-American counties in South Texas delivered more than 81% of the vote to Dukakis, and these counties ranked among his top five nationally. In 2008, Dukakis stated during an interview with Katie Couric that he "owe[d] the American people an apology" because "if I had beaten the old man [i.e. George H. W. Bush], we never would have heard of the kid [i.e. George W. Bush], and we wouldn't be in this mess." His final two years as governor were marked by increased criticism of his policies and significant tax increases to address the economic effects of the U.S. economy's "soft landing" at the end of the 1980s and the 1990 recession, leading him to announce in early 1989 that he would not seek reelection to a fourth term. After leaving office, Dukakis served on the board of directors for Amtrak and became a professor of political science at Northeastern University, a visiting professor at Loyola Marymount University, and a visiting professor in the Department of Public Policy at the Luskin School of Public Affairs at UCLA. He retired from teaching by 2021. Along with other notable Greek-Americans, he is a founding member of The Next Generation Initiative, a leadership program for student involvement in public affairs. In November 2008, Northeastern named its Center for Urban and Regional Policy after Michael and Kitty Dukakis. Dukakis is a member of the ReFormers Caucus of Issue One. He retired from Northeastern at age 90 in 2024, and the documentary film *Dukakis: Recipe for Democracy*, about his time as a professor at Northeastern, premiered on October 22, 2024. In August 2009, at age 75, Dukakis was mentioned as one of two leading candidates to serve as an interim U.S. Senator after Ted Kennedy's death; instead, Governor Patrick appointed Paul G. Kirk, the other candidate and favorite of the Kennedy family, to fill the seat. Dukakis has advocated for effective public transportation and high-speed rail to address automobile congestion and airport space limitations, as well as for an extended learning time initiative in public schools. On January 31, 2014, he stated he was not in favor of renaming South Station as the "Gov. Michael S. Dukakis Transportation Center," though it was later renamed to that name; he did not object to naming the as-yet unbuilt North-South Rail Link after him. In 2012, Dukakis supported Elizabeth Warren's successful U.S. Senate candidacy. During the 2016 Democratic presidential primaries, he endorsed Hillary Clinton. He endorsed Setti Warren's unsuccessful 2018 Massachusetts Democratic gubernatorial nomination and Elizabeth Warren's 2020 Democratic presidential campaign. He later endorsed Joe Biden in the general election and, with his wife, endorsed Ed Markey for reelection to his Massachusetts U.S. Senate seat in 2020 during both the primary and general elections. Dukakis was married to Kitty Dukakis (née Dickson) for 61 years, from June 20, 1963, until her death on March 21, 2025. Their first child, a daughter, died from anencephaly shortly after birth. They later had two daughters, Andrea and Kara. A son, John Dukakis (né Chaffetz), was born in 1958 to Kitty and her first husband, Phoenix businessman John Chaffetz (who later fathered former Congressman Jason Chaffetz); Michael Dukakis adopted John Jr. Dukakis is the cousin of Academy Award–winning actress Olympia Dukakis. In 1988, Michael and Kitty Dukakis said they attended both Greek Orthodox and Jewish worship services out of respect for both spouses' faiths. The Dukakises primarily lived in a home they bought in the early 1970s in Brookline, Massachusetts, and also maintained a home in Los Angeles during his teaching career at UCLA.

Miguel Gerardo Velázquez Olivares[a] (born 2 July 1990) is a former Mexican professional footballer who last played as a right-back for Atlante. His career in association football in Mexico is primarily associated with the position of defender, and he was born in the 1990s. This biographical article on a Mexican football defender from the 1990s is currently marked as a stub and can be expanded with additional details on Wikipedia.

Michael Vincent Lawler, born on September 9, 1986, is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for New York's 17th congressional district since 2023. From 2021 to 2022, he was a Republican member of the New York State Assembly representing the 97th district in Rockland County. Lawler was born to Marie (née Fortino) and Kevin Lawler and was raised in South Salem, New York, and Suffern, New York; he is Catholic and of Irish and Italian descent. He graduated from Suffern High School and earned a Bachelor of Science degree in accounting and finance from Manhattan College in 2009, graduating as valedictorian. In October 2024, The New York Times reported resurfaced photos of Lawler wearing a Michael Jackson costume with blackface at a Manhattan College Halloween party in 2006; in response, Lawler stated the costume was a sincere homage to his musical hero, emphasizing that blackface was not part of his intent. It was also reported that in 2005, J. Randy Taraborrelli, a Michael Jackson biographer, helped get Lawler, then a high school senior, into the courtroom for Jackson's trial. He served as Rob Astorino's campaign manager in his 2014 gubernatorial run and later as an assistant to Astorino as County Executive. In 2016, Lawler served as a Republican convention delegate for Donald Trump. In 2018, he co-founded the political communications firm Checkmate Strategies. In 2020, Lawler was elected to the New York State Assembly for a two-year term, defeating Democratic incumbent Ellen Jaffee. In 2022, Lawler was the Republican nominee in New York's 17th congressional district, winning the August primary and narrowly defeating Democratic incumbent and DCCC chair Sean Patrick Maloney in the November general election. On November 5, 2024, Lawler was re-elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in the 17th congressional district, defeating Democratic nominee Mondaire Jones by 23,946 votes. The New York Times reported in September 2024 that Lawler was seen as a potential candidate for governor of New York in 2026, but in July 2025, he announced he would seek reelection to the House in 2026 instead. On January 4, 2023, Lawler criticized then-newly sworn Representative George Santos's conduct as "embarrassing and unbecoming" and "certainly a distraction," and called for Santos to resign. Lawler voted for Kevin McCarthy in the 2023 Speaker election, stating, "It's time for everybody to unify. It's time for everybody to move forward because the reality is the American people didn't elect us to fight over rules." On January 9, 2023, he voted in favor of the House rules package and delivered his first House speech supporting a bill to defund the IRS of funds allocated in the Inflation Reduction Act. He was one of five Republicans to vote against the Parents' Bill of Rights in March 2023, the only Republican not from the Freedom Caucus to do so, citing an unspecified amendment as going too far, though he co-sponsored the bill. On June 21, 2023, Lawler voted with 20 other Republicans to block the censure of Rep. Adam Schiff. On July 6, 2023, he introduced H.R.4493, the District of Columbia One Vote One Choice Act, to prohibit Washington, D.C., from adopting ranked-choice voting, with Representatives Claudia Tenney (R-NY-24) and Chuck Edwards (R-NC-11) as the only cosponsors. For much of 2023, Lawler banned television news cameras from his town hall meetings, rescinding the ban in early 2024. On October 5, 2023, he signed a letter with 15 House Republicans opposing the inclusion of the Ending Agricultural Trade Suppression (EATS) Act in the 2023 farm bill, which would have overturned state and local animal welfare laws restricting sales from animals raised in battery cages, gestation crates, and veal crates, arguing it would undermine states' rights and cede control to Chinese-owned pork producer WH Group and its subsidiary Smithfield Foods. In March 2024, Lawler was one of 10 House Republicans who signed a letter opposing the inclusion of the EATS Act in the 2024 farm bill. Lawler is a major supporter of raising the cap on the state and local tax deduction (SALT), a position that drew criticism from Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-GA) in May 2025; President Trump encouraged Republicans to pass a spending bill increasing the SALT cap to $30,000 from $10,000, and Lawler and other blue-state Republicans argued the increase was insufficient. Trump singled out Lawler in a May 2025 meeting, saying, "End it, Mike, just end it." On July 3, 2025, Lawler voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Lawler is described as a moderate Republican. In 2024, he was rated as the fourth most bipartisan member of the U.S. House during the 118th Congress by the Bipartisan Index. He is a co-sponsor of the American Families United Act, which addresses needs of mixed-status families in the U.S. immigration system. Lawler opposes abortion except in cases of rape or when the mother's life is at risk, but opposes a federal ban on abortion. In 2025, Lawler voted in favor of HR 1 of the 119th Congress. In August 2023, he signed a letter to the House Agriculture Committee opposing the EATS Act, which would have overturned state and local animal welfare laws, including California's Proposition 12. He also cosponsored the Puppy Protection Act to increase welfare standards for commercial dog breeders. In September 2024, Lawler was one of 11 House Republicans who signed a letter to Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines requesting an analysis of Chinese biotechnology and slaughter-free cultivated meat developments and recommendations to promote U.S. alternative proteins innovation. In May 2023, Lawler and Democrat Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced legislation expanding anti-boycott laws to include international governmental organizations, aiming to stop the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement in the U.S., but the bill faced heavy criticism from House Republicans and conservatives for violating First Amendment rights, leading House Republican leadership to scrap a vote in May 2025. In 2023, Lawler opposed the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's plan to implement congestion pricing in Manhattan, calling it an "outrageous cash grab," and in 2024, he asked President-elect Donald Trump to cancel the plan. Lawler voted for Trump in the 2024 Republican primary in New York and was one of six Republicans to sign a bipartisan letter pledging to respect the results of the 2024 presidential election. Lawler lives in Pearl River with his wife, Doina, born in Moldova, and their two daughters.

Michael Kent Young, born on May 1, 1963, is an American college basketball coach and currently serves as the head men's basketball coach at Virginia Tech. He was hired on April 7, 2019, after a 17-year tenure at Wofford College where he compiled a record of 299–244 (.545) as head coach. Born in Radford, Virginia, Young played collegiately at Emory & Henry College, where he served as team captain during his junior and senior seasons. After his playing career, he began coaching as an assistant at Emory & Henry. In 1988, he left to serve one year as an assistant under Oliver Purnell at Radford University. In 1989, Young started his assistant coaching role at Wofford, where he spent the next 30 years, guiding the Terriers through their transition from Division II to Division I independent status and eventually to the Southern Conference, where they compete today. In December 2001, Wofford promoted head coach Richard Johnson to athletic director, prompting Young to take over the team for the 2002–03 season. His first six years were uneventful, with highlights including a .500 conference record in his first season and overall .500 records in the 2004–05 and 2007–08 seasons. The 2008–09 season marked a turning point, as it set new school Division I records and marked the Terriers' first winning season as a Division I school and their first winning Southern Conference record in history. In 2009–10, Young led the Terriers to both the Southern Conference regular season and tournament championships, earning Wofford its first NCAA tournament bid. For these achievements, Young was named the 2010 Southern Conference Coach of the Year and the Hugh Durham National Coach of the Year. On December 21, 2017, Young led Wofford to a 79–75 victory over #5 North Carolina, the program's first win over a top 25 team. The following season, Wofford defeated Seton Hall 84–68 in the 2019 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament, marking Young's first NCAA Tournament win as a head coach. On November 5, 2019, Young recorded his 300th win, which was also his first as Virginia Tech's head coach, defeating Clemson 67–60. On November 20, 2019, Virginia Tech defeated Delaware State 100–64, setting a new school record and achieving an ACC record with 21 three-pointers made. On November 25, 2019, Young led Virginia Tech to a 71–66 victory over No. 3 Michigan State in the Maui Invitational, his first win over a ranked team as head coach of the Hokies. At the end of the 2020–21 regular season, Young was named ACC Coach of the Year. On March 12, 2022, Young led the Hokies to their first ACC Tournament title in school history. The final was against Mike Krzyzewski's Duke Blue Devils, in Coach K's final ACC tournament game; Virginia Tech, the seven seed, won 82–67 after defeating Clemson, Notre Dame, and North Carolina in consecutive nights, becoming the first seven seed to win the tournament in the program's history.

Ruth Mildred Barker (February 3, 1897 – January 25, 1990) was a musician, scholar, manager, and spiritual leader from the Alfred and Sabbathday Lake Shaker villages. Born in Providence, Rhode Island on February 3, 1897, she joined the Shakers on July 7, 1903, when her newly widowed mother placed her under the care of the Alfred village. She was assigned to the Second Family, where sister Harriet Coolbroth served as a mother figure, and she assisted the elderly sister Paulina Springer, with whom she befriended and learned the song "Mother Has Come with Her Beautiful Song." Springer died in 1905 and, on her deathbed, asked Barker to always remain Shaker, a promise Barker kept. Barker's interest in music grew through lessons from Coolbroth and Lucinda Taylor, and she later stated that the "vim and vigor" of Shaker song drew her to the faith. She was a member of the "Beacon Light Circle." Her mother returned in 1911 to take her home, but Barker insisted on staying at Alfred, and seven years later, in 1920, she signed the covenant as a member of the Alfred community. The Second Family closed that same year, and Barker moved to the Church Family at Alfred. In 1931, the Alfred community closed, and she relocated to Sabbathday Lake in New Gloucester, Maine, where she was placed in charge of the Girls' Order and formed the "Girls' Improvement Club" for poetry, recitations, and Bible study. She also managed preserves and candy making—specializing in hand-dipped chocolates—at the village store, where she sewed and knitted, overseeing these operations until 1968. In 1950, she was appointed trustee of Sabbathday Lake, responsible for the village’s businesses and finances. Since the 1940s, she served as de facto spiritual leader of the Sabbathday Lake community. Gertrude Soule, who had left and rejoined the community multiple times, was appointed Eldress in 1950 and felt uncomfortable with Barker’s influence. In 1957, Soule moved to the Parent Ministry at Hancock Shaker Village in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. In 1971, after Soule decided not to return to Sabbathday Lake, Barker was appointed Eldress in her place. In 1960, Theodore Johnson joined the Shakers, and the following year, he and Barker co-founded The Shaker Quarterly, a magazine and journal that published scholarly articles on theology and the Shakers, shared village news, and occasionally advertised community products. Barker served as business manager from its founding until 1974 and regularly contributed articles and the newsletter column Home Notes. Through her leadership, Sabbathday Lake reopened its religious meetings to public attendance. She traveled as a speaker on Shaker-related topics. From the 1940s onward, she worked with historian and musicologist Daniel W. Patterson to preserve Shaker music. She noted that she initially did not realize how vital the music was, but felt a deep connection to the tradition, believing it was essential and would endure through centuries. She appeared on four recordings, including Early Shaker Spirituals. In recognition of her contributions to traditional Shaker song, she received the National Heritage Fellowship in 1983 from the National Endowment for the Arts. She also received numerous other awards. Barker died on January 25, 1990, after battling cancer for several months.

The Minister of War (French: Ministre de la guerre) was the highest-ranking official in the French Ministry of War and served as a key position within the Government of France from 1791 to 1947. This role replaced the Secretary of State for War and, later, was merged with the offices of Minister of the Navy and Minister of Air to create the Minister of the Armed Forces. In 1791, during the French Revolution, the Secretary of State for War was renamed Minister of War. For the majority of its history until the early 20th century, the office was held exclusively by Marshals or Generals; however, the Third Republic gradually transitioned to civilian politicians occupying the position, though this shift was often disrupted by the governmental instability of the era, resulting in many ministers serving only for a few days. On 27 April 1791, the National Constituent Assembly passed a decree establishing the six ministries—Justice, Interior, Finances, War, Navy, and Foreign Affairs. This decree was formally enacted into law on 25 May 1791 by King Louis XVI. The law assigned the Minister of War full authority over the French Army and sole responsibility for the provost duties of the National Gendarmerie, as well as oversight of the administration and finances of the ministry.

The Royal Norwegian Ministry of Culture and Equality (Norwegian: Det kongelige kultur- og likestillingsdepartement; short name Kultur- og likestillingsdepartementet) is responsible for cultural policy, regulations, and matters related to the media and sports, as well as equality and non-discrimination. It was established in 1982 as the Ministry of Cultural and Science, replacing the previous Ministry of Church and Education Affairs, which had held overarching responsibility for cultural affairs until then. The ministry is currently led by Minister of Culture and Equality Lubna Jaffery (Labour), who has held the position since June 2023. The Secretary-General is Kristin Berge, and Aleksander Hagen serves as state secretary, while Mari Hansen Ingleson is the political adviser. The ministry reports to the Storting. The Ministry of Churches and Education, originally founded in 1818, was responsible for culture before the 1982 establishment of the independent Ministry of Culture and Science (Kultur- og vitenskapsdepartementet). In 1990, responsibilities were split into a Ministry of Churches and Culture (Kirke- og kulturdepartementet) and a Ministry of Education and Research (Utdannings- og forskningsdepartementet). In 1991, church responsibilities were transferred back from the Ministry of Culture to the newly renamed Ministry for Churches, Education and Research (Kirke-, utdannings- og forskningsdepartementet). In 2002, the Ministry of Culture regained responsibility for the churches and was renamed Kultur- og kirkedepartementet. From 2010 until the end of 2021, the ministry operated under the name Kulturdepartementet. In 2019, responsibility for equality was transferred from the Ministry of Children and Family to the Ministry of Culture. On 1 January 2022, the ministry was officially renamed Kultur- og likestillingsdepartementet (Ministry of Culture and Equality). The ministry is organized into six departments and an information unit.

doc_name: Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation
text: The Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation (MoCTCA) is the governmental body responsible for promoting tourism, culture, and private sector involvement in Nepal, and it also functions as the nation's aviation regulatory authority. The ministry is headquartered in Singha Durbar, Kathmandu. Originally established in 1978 as the Ministry of Tourism by the Government of Nepal, it incorporated the portfolios of Civil Aviation in 1982 and Culture in 2000. In 2008, the ministry was dissolved and divided into the Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation and the Ministry of Culture and State Restructuring. In 2012, the ministry was renamed and adopted its current structure as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation. The ministry comprises several departments and subdivisions.

Miriam Amanda "Ma" Ferguson (née Wallace; June 13, 1875 – June 25, 1961) was an American politician who served two non-consecutive terms as governor of Texas: from 1925 to 1927 and from 1933 to 1935. She was the first female governor of Texas and the second woman elected to the governorship of any U.S. state to assume office, after Nellie Tayloe Ross of Wyoming. Born in Bell County, Texas, she studied at Salado College and Baylor Female College. At age 24, she married James Edward Ferguson, a lawyer, at her father's farm near Belton in Bell County. Her nickname "Ma" came from her initials "M. A." and the fact that her husband was known as "Pa" Ferguson; they had two daughters, Ouida Wallace Ferguson and Dorrace Watt Ferguson. James Ferguson served as governor from 1915 to 1917, and during his second term, he was investigated by State Attorney General Dan Moody for actions against the University of Texas. The Texas State Senate impeached him, convicted him on ten charges, and barred him from holding state office again. After his impeachment, Ma Ferguson ran in the Democratic primary for governor and won, with open support from her husband, whom she said she would consult for advice. She ran in the 1924 general election, promoting the slogan "two governors for the price of one," and her speeches involved introducing her husband and letting him take the platform. A common campaign slogan was "Me for Ma, and I Ain't Got a Durned Thing Against Pa." Patricia Bernstein of the Houston Chronicle noted that it was never in doubt who was really running things during her tenure. After winning the primary, she defeated George C. Butte, a prominent lawyer and University of Texas dean, who was the strongest Republican nominee since Reconstruction. Due to her husband's corruption and impeachment, thousands of voters crossed party lines, and Butte won nearly 300,000 votes—many from women and suffragists—though Ferguson still won 422,563 votes (58.9%) to Butte's 294,920 (41.1%). Butte had been supported by former governor William P. Hobby, who succeeded James Ferguson in 1917 and won a full term in 1918. In 1924, Ma Ferguson became the first elected female chief executive of Texas, the second elected female state governor in the U.S. to assume office, and the first to be elected in a general election. Nellie Tayloe Ross had been sworn in to finish her late husband’s unexpired term two weeks before Ferguson’s inauguration, though both won their elections on the same day. Ferguson’s campaign manager was Homer T. Brannon of Fort Worth. In 1926, state attorney general Dan Moody, who had investigated her husband and recovered $1 million for Texas citizens, defeated her in a run-off election, becoming the next and youngest governor of Texas. Suffragist activism played a major role in her defeat, as these women rallied behind Moody. Ferguson ran again in 1932, narrowly winning the Democratic nomination over incumbent Ross S. Sterling, and then soundly defeating Republican Orville Bullington in the general election, 521,395 (61.6%) to 322,589 (38.1%). It was a year of Democratic successes as Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president. Bullington, a cousin of the first wife of John G. Tower, performed better than most Texas Republican candidates but did not match Butte’s 1924 showing. Her second term was less controversial than her first; rumors circulated that state highway contracts went only to companies that advertised in the Fergusons' newspaper, the Ferguson Forum, but a House committee investigated and no charges were filed. The Great Depression led to cuts in state and federal funding, reducing the number of commissioned officers in the Texas Rangers to 45 and limiting their transportation to free railroad passes or personal horses. In 1932, the Rangers supported Governor Ross Sterling in his re-election bid over "Ma" Ferguson, prompting her to immediately discharge all serving Rangers upon taking office in January 1933. The force’s salaries and funding were slashed, and its size was reduced to 32 men. This disorganization allowed Texas to become a haven for Depression-era gangsters such as Bonnie and Clyde, George "Machine Gun" Kelly, Pretty Boy Floyd, and Raymond Hamilton. The hasty appointment of unqualified Rangers proved ineffective. The legislature, convinced by the disorganization, hired a Chicago-based consulting firm, which concluded that Texas had extremely high criminality and underfunded, undermanned, loose, and obsolete law enforcement. The consultants recommended merging the Rangers with the Texas Highway Patrol to form the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS). After deliberation, the legislature approved the plan, and the resolution creating the DPS was passed in 1935 under Governor James V. Allred, with an initial budget of $450,000, making the DPS operational on August 10. In October 1933, Ferguson signed Texas House Bill 194, which helped establish the University of Houston as a four-year institution. "Fergusonism," the Fergusons' brand of populism, remains controversial in Texas. As governor, she addressed key issues, aligning with "wets" in the prohibition debate despite being a teetotaler like her husband, and opposing the Ku Klux Klan, which declined after 1925 due to a national scandal involving its president, D. C. Stephenson. She is described as a fiscal conservative but also supported a state sales tax and corporate income tax. She is often credited with a quote allegedly about bilingualism in Texas schools: "If English was good enough for Jesus Christ, it ought to be good enough for the children of Texas," though variations of this statement date back to 1881 and were used to ridicule certain Christians; Ferguson did not originate it. During her two non-consecutive terms, she issued almost 4,000 pardons, many to those convicted of violating prohibition laws. In 1930, Secretary of State Jane Y. McCallum published a pamphlet criticizing her pardons. Though never proven, rumors persisted that pardons were available in exchange for cash payments to her husband. In 1936, voters passed a constitutional amendment removing the governor’s power to issue pardons and transferring it to a politically independent Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles. Several labor laws were passed during her two terms. In a 1932 speech, her husband James E. Ferguson defended "Fergusonism," citing reforms such as child labor laws, workmen's compensation, aid for rural education, a free textbook law, and regulations on women’s working hours. Miriam Ferguson herself defended "Fergusonism," citing liberal measures like a semi-monthly pay day law, an eight-hour workday, the establishment of an Industrial Accident Board, and the creation of the Lower Colorado and Brazos River Authorities. Except for an unsuccessful bid to replace Governor W. Lee "Pappy" O'Daniel in 1940, the Fergusons remained retired after 1935. In that 1940 campaign, Ma Ferguson trailed O'Daniel’s main rival, Ernest O. Thompson of Amarillo, who was Texas Railroad Commissioner. Her husband James died of a stroke in 1944, and Miriam Ferguson died of congestive heart failure in 1961 at age 86. She was buried in the Texas State Cemetery in Austin.

Miss USA 1976 was the 25th edition of the Miss USA pageant, broadcast live by CBS from Niagara Falls, New York, on May 15, 1976. Barbara Peterson from Minnesota won the title, succeeding Summer Bartholomew of California, who had held the previous year's title. Peterson was the first and, as of now, the only woman from Minnesota to win the Miss USA crown. She went on to compete in Miss Universe 1976, becoming the first Miss USA titleholder to not advance to the semi-final round of that competition.

Miss World 1958 was the eighth edition of the Miss World pageant, held at the Lyceum Ballroom in London, United Kingdom, on 13 October 1958. Charles Eade and Bob Russell crowned Penelope Coelen of South Africa as Miss World 1958, marking South Africa's first victory and Africa's second win in the pageant's history. Twenty contestants participated in the event, with one contestant appointed to represent her country after contracting an illness from the previous edition. The pageant was hosted by Bob Russell. Miss Belgium 1958, Michele Gouthals, was scheduled to compete but did not participate because her organization appointed Miss Belgium 1957, Jeanne Chandelle, to represent Belgium again, as she had contracted the Asian Flu during the Miss World 1957 pageant and only attended the coronation day. This edition featured the debut of Brazil, and the returns of Turkey, which last competed in 1953, and Norway, which last competed in 1954. Hanni Ehrenstrasser of Austria withdrew after winning Miss Europe 1958, making her ineligible for Miss World; Elisabeth Schubel-Auer was set to replace her but did not proceed for undisclosed reasons. Leila Saas of Egypt, Pirkko Mannola of Finland, Hjördís Sigurvinsdóttir of Iceland, Lydie Schmit of Luxembourg, and Denise Orlando of Tunisia also withdrew for undisclosed reasons. Australia withdrew after failing to hold a national competition or appoint a candidate. Janet Ohene-Agyei Boateng of Ghana withdrew due to financial constraints, and Krystyna Żyła of Poland was barred by her government from competing; she was eventually found dead in December 1958. The number of placements was reduced from seven to six in this edition, with the six finalists selected through a preliminary competition on the day of the final, consisting of a swimsuit and an evening gown segment. Twenty contestants competed for the title.

Miss World is the oldest existing international beauty pageant, founded in 1951 in the United Kingdom by Eric Morley. Morley organized a bikini contest as part of the Festival of Britain celebrations, which was later dubbed "Miss World" by the press. The swimsuit competition was intended to promote the newly introduced bikini, which was still considered immodest, and when Kerstin "Kiki" Hakansson of Sweden was crowned in a bikini in 1951, it sparked controversy, leading to religious objections and a papal condemnation. As a result, the bikini was replaced in future pageants with more modest swimwear, and from 1976, evening gowns were used for crowning. Håkansson remains the only Miss World crowned in a bikini. Morley registered "Miss World" as a trademark and decided to make the pageant annual, though it was initially planned as a one-time Festival of Britain event. He announced winners in the order No. 3, No. 2, and No. 1 to maintain tension. The BBC began broadcasting the pageant in 1959, and it became one of the most watched programs in the UK during the 1960s and 1970s. In 1970, the London contest was disrupted by women's liberation protesters, and South Africa was banned due to sending two contestants, one black and one white. The pageant reached a peak viewership of over 18 million in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In the 1980s, it repositioned with the slogan "Beauty With a Purpose," adding intelligence and personality tests. In 1984, BBC1 controller Michael Grade announced it would cease broadcasting beauty pageants, calling them an anachronism. Thames Television aired the pageant from 1980 to 1988, after which ITV dropped it. Mainstream television broadcasts declined in the 1990s, and the pageant returned on Sky One in 1997 before moving to Channel 5 from 1998 to 2000. After Eric Morley's death in 2000, his widow Julia Morley became chair of the Miss World organization. The first black African Miss World winner, Agbani Darego of Nigeria, was crowned in 2001. That year, the organization launched a "Vote For Me" special, featuring delegates and allowing viewer voting, and also sold broadcasting rights for Talent, Beach Beauty, and Sports events. ITV broadcast the 2001 pageant from South Africa on digital channel ITV2, with the special airing a week earlier on main ITV. In 2002, the pageant was scheduled in Abuja, Nigeria, amid controversy over Amina Lawal, a woman awaiting stoning under Sharia law. The event faced boycotts from several nations including Denmark, Spain, Switzerland, Panama, Belgium, and Kenya, and protests led to inter-religious riots in Kaduna with over 200 deaths and destruction of religious sites. A fatwa calling for beheading of Isioma Daniel, who wrote a critical editorial, was issued but nullified by Saudi authorities. The pageant was moved to London due to safety concerns and the withdrawal of Canada and Korea, though many boycotting contestants later attended, including Kathrine Sørland of Norway. The eventual winner was Azra Akın of Turkey. In 2013, Islamic group protests led to the pageant being held in Hindu-majority Bali. Anastasia Lin of Canada missed the 2015 pageant due to a visa denial in China and was declared persona non grata for criticizing China's human rights; she later competed in 2016. The 2020 pageant was scheduled for Phuket, Thailand, but was canceled due to the global spread of COVID-19. The event was postponed indefinitely and later rescheduled to 16 December 2021, but due to positive cases among delegates—including Miss World Indonesia Carla Yules, Miss World India Manasa Varanasi, and Miss World Malaysia Lavanya Sivaji—the finale was postponed. On 15 December, 17 positive cases were confirmed in Puerto Rico, including contestants and staff, and on 16 December, Lavanya Sivaji tested positive and was isolated. The finale was ultimately held on 16 March 2022 at Puerto Rico's Coca-Cola Music Hall. Fast-track events, including Beauty With a Purpose (established in 1972), Talent (introduced in 1978), Sports (individual competition from 2006), Top Model (first held in 2004, resumed in 2007), and Multimedia (added in 2012), determine semi-finalist placements. Prior to 2016, fast-track winners earned points but did not guarantee a spot; since 2016, winners automatically qualify for quarter- or semi-finals. The Beach Beauty event, which ran from 2003 to 2015, was discontinued due to backlash from conservative countries and replaced the swimsuit competition, with a sarong introduced in 2013. The Miss World Organization manages the annual Miss World Finals, which has grown into one of the world's largest pageants, and since 1951 has raised over £1 billion for children's charities supporting disabled and underprivileged children. The pageant is franchised in more than 100 countries and has faced numerous controversies throughout its history.

The Mississippi Mass Choir is an American gospel choir based in Jackson, Mississippi. After considering the idea of forming a mass choir, Frank Williams, a member of the Jackson Southernaires and an executive in the gospel music division of Malaco Records, decided to establish the choir. He first secured the record company's support and then recruited Mississippi talents, including David R. Curry Jr., who became the choir's minister of music. Open auditions brought together over 100 voices from across the state, forming the Mississippi Mass Choir. After months of rehearsals, the choir recorded their eponymous debut album and video live at Thalia Mara Hall (formerly Jackson Municipal Auditorium) on October 29, 1988. In the spring of 1989, five weeks after its release, Billboard certified the album as the Number 1 Spiritual album in the country, and it remained on the Billboard charts for 45 consecutive weeks, setting a record for gospel recordings. At the 9th annual James Cleveland GMWA Awards, the choir won Choir of the Year-Contemporary and Best New Artist of the Year-Traditional. They also won four Stellar Awards in 1989 and were nominated in several categories for the 1989 Soul Train Music Awards and Dove Awards. The choir's second album, God Gets The Glory, was recorded live at the Mississippi Coliseum on December 8, 1990, and debuted at Number 16 on the Billboard chart, reaching Number 1 two weeks later. The choir recorded two live albums: one in 1991 with Frank Williams and James Moore as leads, and another in 1995 with Moore again. Their third and most popular album, It Remains to Be Seen..., was recorded live at Thalia Mara Hall in January 1993 and remained at the top of the charts for an entire year. This album was the last recorded with founder Frank Williams, who died of a heart attack in Savannah, Georgia, on March 22, 1993. Eight more albums have been released since his death. Executive director Jerry Mannery states, "We are all about our Father's business. We are not entertainers; we are ministers for Christ. Our mission remains constant; to serve the Lord and spread the Gospel of Jesus Christ." The choir has ministered in song in over 40 states within the United States, including Alaska, and has traveled to Japan, Italy, Spain, the Bahamas, and Greece, becoming the first gospel group to perform at the Acropolis. While attending the Umbria Jazz Gospel and Soul Easter Festival in Terni, Italy, the choir was invited to sing for Pope John Paul II at his summer residence. On June 19, 2009, the choir commemorated their 20th anniversary by recording their ninth album, ...Then Sings My Soul, live at the First Baptist Church in Jackson, which was officially released on February 1, 2011. In 2009, they also released a compilation CD/DVD titled The First Twenty Years, featuring popular songs and interviews with choir members. From December 8 to 26, 2010, the choir made a fourteen-city tour of Spain and the Canary Islands. According to concert promoter Luis Manjarres, "Since their first Spanish tour, Mississippi Mass Choir has become a classic of the European and the Spanish Christmas. They will showcase their talent in the main venues of Barcelona, Madrid, San Sebastian, Bilbao, Pamplona, Gijon, and Vigo. This tour of fourteen concerts will culminate on Christmas night, in the wonderful city of Santa Cruz de Tenerife at the Canary Islands, in a very special event with the 92-piece Tenerife Symphonic Orchestra, under the direction of Maestro Lu Jia. Mississippi Mass Choir will be the first African American choir to perform with a European Symphonic Orchestra before an audience of 20,000. It is the time for Mississippi Mass Choir ... It is the time for Classic Gospel." In October 2013, the choir celebrated their 25th anniversary by recording their 10th live album titled Declaration of Dependence. The album's hit single, "God's on Your Side" (featuring gospel artist/Sunday Best winner Le'Andria Johnson and Stan Jones), was released on April 11, 2014, and the album itself was released in June 2014. The choir began a 10-city tour and a 13-city Spain tour. On January 11, 2017, the choir was featured on an episode of ABC's Black-ish. On October 7, 2018, the choir appeared on an episode of Discovery Channel's Expedition Unknown, titled "Search For The Afterlife – Heaven and Hell", exploring different religions and cultures from around the world. On October 28, 2022, the choir recorded their eleventh live album at the Word of Life Church in Flowood, Mississippi. Special guests included Mary Mary's Tina Campbell, Crystal Aikin, Myron Butler, Brian Courtney Wilson, and Georgia Mass Choir's founder/leader Rev. Milton Biggham. On July 7, 2025, veteran choir member Mosie "Mama" Burks died at the age of 92. Burks joined the choir in the mid-1990s as a lead soloist and toured internationally with the choir for decades until her retirement in 2020.

The Mississippi River is the primary river of the largest drainage basin in the United States, the second-longest river in the country after the Missouri, and the world's tenth-largest by discharge flow and the largest in North America. It flows from its traditional source at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, 1,475 feet (450 m) above sea level, to the Gulf of Mexico over a distance of 2,340 miles (3,770 km), with a stream gradient of 0.01% and a total drop of 450 meters over 3,766 km. The river's watershed covers 1,151,000 square miles (2,980,000 km²), including all or parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces, and accounts for nearly 40% of the continental U.S. landmass. The highest point in the watershed is Mount Elbert at 14,440 feet (4,400 m), in the Rocky Mountains. The river's average annual discharge ranges between 200,000 and 700,000 cubic feet per second (6,000 to 20,000 m³/s), with a long-term mean discharge at Cairo, Illinois, of 281,500 cu ft/s (7,970 m³/s) from the Ohio River and 208,200 cu ft/s (5,900 m³/s) from the Mississippi. The river's flow is 8% that of the Amazon, which averages nearly 7 million cubic feet per second during wet seasons. Before 1900, the Mississippi transported an estimated 440 million short tons (400 million metric tons) of sediment annually; this has decreased to 160 million short tons (145 million metric tons) per year due to engineering modifications such as dams, meander cutoffs, and bank revetments. The river is divided into three sections: the Upper Mississippi, from Lake Itasca to the Missouri River confluence at St. Louis, Missouri; the Middle Mississippi, from St. Louis to the Ohio River confluence at Cairo, Illinois, covering 190 miles (310 km) and dropping 220 feet (67 m) over 180 miles (290 km); and the Lower Mississippi, from the Ohio River to the Gulf of Mexico, about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) long. The Upper Mississippi is regulated by 43 dams, including 14 above Minneapolis and 29 downstream, with locks and dams designed to improve navigation and manage flow. The head of navigation is currently at Minneapolis after the Coon Rapids Dam, though the St. Anthony Falls Lock and Dam, completed in 1963, previously held that position until 2015 when it was closed to prevent the spread of invasive Asian carp. The river's elevation drops from 799 feet (244 m) above sea level above the St. Anthony Falls Dam to 750 feet (230 m) below, a 49-foot (15 m) drop—the largest of any lock and dam on the Mississippi. The Upper Mississippi includes major tributaries such as the Minnesota, St. Croix, Cannon, Zumbro, Black, La Crosse, Root, Wisconsin, Rock, Iowa, Skunk, and Des Moines rivers. The river is a multi-thread stream with natural and artificial lakes, including Lake Winnibigoshish (over 11 miles wide), Lake Onalaska (over 4 miles wide), and Lake Pepin (over 2 miles wide). The Middle Mississippi is relatively free-flowing, with no major tributaries except the Missouri and Meramec rivers. The Lower Mississippi receives major tributaries including the White, Arkansas, Big Black, and Yazoo rivers. The river's flow is diverted at the Old River Control Structure in Louisiana, where 30% of the combined flow of the Mississippi and Red Rivers goes to the Gulf via the Atchafalaya River instead of continuing down the main channel to New Orleans. The river's mouth is located about 100 miles (160 km) downstream from New Orleans, and the average speed is about 26 miles (42 km) per day or 1 mile (1.6 km) per hour. The river's retention time from Lake Itasca to the Gulf is about 90 days. The lower Mississippi has undergone repeated avulsion events every thousand years due to sediment buildup, shifting its course and forming abandoned distributaries known as bayous, which have advanced the Louisiana coastline by 15 to 50 miles (24 to 80 km) over the past 5,000 years. The current active delta is known as the Birdfoot or Balize Delta. The river's basin was shaped by the Laurentide Ice Sheet during the most recent Ice Age and by geological processes including the formation of the Reelfoot Rift around 80 million years ago due to crustal subsidence after uplift from a volcanic hotspot. The river's water flows into the Gulf of Mexico, forming a distinct plume visible in NASA MODIS images that remains separate from salt water for a long distance before mixing, and in drought years, saltwater can travel up to 64 miles (103 km) upstream, contaminating drinking water, prompting the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to construct saltwater sills in 1988, 1999, 2012, and 2022 to contain it. The name "Mississippi" comes from the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe or Algonquin) term Misi-ziibi (Great River), rendered in French as Misi zipi. The river served as a border in the 18th century under the Treaty of Paris and later became a key boundary in the Louisiana Purchase and westward expansion, symbolized by the Gateway Arch in St. Louis and the Trans-Mississippi Exposition. The river is also used as a dividing line for broadcast call signs, with W to the east and K to the west, and regional landmarks are often classified relative to it, such as "the highest peak east of the Mississippi" or "the oldest city west of the Mississippi." The river is commonly nicknamed "The Mighty Mississippi River" or simply "The Mighty Mississippi."

The Mississippi River originates at Lake Itasca and is approximately 2,340 miles (3,766 km) long when measured from its traditional source, making it the fourth longest river in the world after the Nile, Amazon, and Yangtze. When measured from its longest stream source, Brower's Spring in Montana (the headwaters of the Missouri River), the river is 3,710 miles (5,971 km) long. When measured from the largest stream source by water volume—the Ohio River and its tributary, the Allegheny River—the Mississippi begins in Pennsylvania. At its source, the river is about 3 feet (0.91 m) deep; between Saint Paul and Saint Louis, the average depth is 9 to 12 feet (2.7–3.7 m), with Lake Pepin averaging 20–32 feet (6–10 m) and reaching a maximum depth of 60 feet (18 m). Between Saint Louis and Cairo, Illinois, the depth averages 30 feet (9 m), and below Cairo, where the Ohio River joins, it averages 50–100 feet (15–30 m), with the deepest point in New Orleans reaching 200 feet (61 m). The river flows through or along 10 states, from Minnesota to Louisiana, and defines portions of their borders, with Wisconsin, Illinois, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi on the east side and Iowa, Missouri, and Arkansas on the west. State borders are based on the middle of the riverbed at the time they were established, and despite shifts in the river’s course, the borders remain unchanged, leaving small isolated areas of one state across the new channel. The river’s course has changed dramatically over time due to natural processes such as avulsion, which occurs roughly every thousand years when sediment buildup raises the river’s level, prompting it to find a steeper, more direct route to the Gulf of Mexico. This process has advanced the coastline of south Louisiana by 15 to 50 miles (24 to 80 km) over the past 5,000 years. The current active delta lobe is known as the Birdfoot Delta or the Balize Delta, named after La Balize, Louisiana, the first French settlement at the river’s mouth. The river’s basin was shaped by the Laurentide Ice Sheet during the most recent Ice Age, with the southernmost extent of the ice sheet extending into present-day U.S. and the Mississippi basin. As the ice sheet retreated, hundreds of feet of rich sediment were deposited, forming the flat, fertile landscape of the Mississippi Valley. During the melt, glacial rivers established drainage paths into the Mississippi watershed, creating valleys such as the Minnesota, James, and Milk Rivers. After the ice sheet fully retreated, many of these rivers found paths to Hudson Bay or the Arctic Ocean, leaving the basin with features larger than what the existing rivers could have carved in the same time period. During the Illinoian Stage (300,000 to 132,000 years before present), the ice sheet blocked the Mississippi near Rock Island, Illinois, diverting it to its present western channel, which now forms the border of Illinois. The Hennepin Canal follows the ancient Mississippi channel from Rock Island to Hennepin, Illinois, and the current Illinois River follows the old Mississippi path from Hennepin to Alton, Illinois. In March 1876, the river suddenly changed course near Reverie, Tennessee, leaving a small part of Tipton County, Tennessee, attached to Arkansas and separated from the rest of Tennessee, but the state line still follows the old channel. The town of Kaskaskia, Illinois, once stood on a peninsula at the confluence of the Mississippi and Kaskaskia (Okaw) Rivers, serving as a French colonial community, the capital of the Illinois Territory, and the first state capital of Illinois until 1819. Starting in 1844, repeated flooding caused the river to slowly encroach eastward, and a major flood in 1881 overtook the lower 10 miles (16 km) of the Kaskaskia River, forming a new channel and cutting off the town. Later floods destroyed most of the town, including the original State House. Today, a remaining 2,300 acres (930 ha) island with 14 residents is known as an enclave of Illinois and is accessible only from Missouri. The New Madrid Seismic Zone, along the Mississippi near New Madrid, Missouri, is linked to an aulacogen (failed rift) that formed with the Gulf of Mexico and remains seismically active. Four major earthquakes in 1811 and 1812, estimated at 8 on the Richter scale, caused significant local damage and were felt widely across the Midwest and eastern U.S., creating Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee. The earliest bridge across the Mississippi was built in 1855 in Minneapolis, where the current Hennepin Avenue Bridge stands. The first railroad bridge was constructed in 1856 between the Rock Island Arsenal and Davenport, Iowa; it was attacked by the steamboat Effie Afton, which set it on fire, leading to a Supreme Court ruling in favor of the railroad. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, established in 1802, is responsible for maintaining a navigation channel, beginning with early surveys in 1829 of the Des Moines Rapids and Rock Island Rapids, both of which were considered impassable. The Corps recommended a 5-foot-deep channel at the Des Moines Rapids, which began in 1837, and later excavated the Rock Island Rapids. By 1866, excavation was deemed impractical, leading to the construction of a canal around the Des Moines Rapids, which opened in 1877, while the Rock Island Rapids remained an obstacle. In 1878, Congress authorized a 4.5-foot-deep channel via wing dams, and the Moline Lock, bypassing the Rock Island Rapids, opened in 1907. In 1907, Congress authorized a 6-foot-deep channel project, which was abandoned in the late 1920s in favor of a 9-foot-deep (2.7 m) channel. Lock and Dam No. 19 at Keokuk, Iowa, completed in 1913, was built by the Union Electric Company to generate electricity and eliminated the Des Moines Rapids. Lock and Dam No. 1 in Minneapolis was completed in 1917, and Lock and Dam No. 2 near Hastings in 1930. Before the 1927 flood, the Corps aimed to close side channels to increase main river flow, believing this would deepen the river and reduce flooding; the 1927 flood disproved this, leading communities to create their own levee breaks. The Rivers and Harbors Act of 1930 authorized the 9-foot-deep, 400-foot-wide navigation channel, achieved through 23 new locks and dams built in the 1930s. Until the 1950s, there was no dam below Lock and Dam 26 at Alton, Illinois; Chain of Rocks Lock (No. 27), added in 1953, bypasses rock ledges at St. Louis and protects city water intakes. In the 1950s, scientists determined the Mississippi was shifting to the Atchafalaya River due to its steeper path to the Gulf, prompting Congress to authorize the Old River Control Structure to prevent the river from switching to the Atchafalaya and leaving New Orleans on a side channel. An auxiliary flow control station was built in 1986 for the $300 million project. Dam 26 at Alton was replaced by the Mel Price Lock and Dam in 1990, and the original dam was demolished. The Corps now maintains spillways and floodways, including the Birds Point-New Madrid Floodway in Missouri, the Old River Control Structure and Morganza Spillway in Louisiana (directing water to the west and east sides of the Atchafalaya), and the Bonnet Carré Spillway (directing water to Lake Pontchartrain), to divert floodwaters and reduce pressure on New Orleans and Baton Rouge. Some pre-1927 strategies, such as cutting the necks of horseshoe bends, are still used to reduce flood heights. Approximately 50,000 years ago, the Central United States was covered by an inland sea, drained by the Mississippi and its tributaries into the Gulf of Mexico, creating large floodplains and extending the continent southward, resulting in rich soils in areas like Louisiana. The Mississippi basin was first inhabited by Native American peoples who practiced hunting and gathering and are considered one of the few independent centers of plant domestication in human history. Evidence of early cultivation of sunflower, goosefoot, marsh elder, and indigenous squash dates to the 4th millennium BC. After about 1000 BC, during the Woodland period, lifestyles became more settled with shelter construction, pottery, and weaving. From 200 to 500 AD, the Hopewell interaction sphere facilitated trade and cultural exchange across the region. After 800 AD, agriculture introduced from Mesoamerica, based on the Three Sisters (maize, beans, and squash), became dominant, leading to the rise of the Mississippian culture, characterized by complex chiefdoms and large population centers. The most prominent site, Cahokia, was occupied between 600 and 1400 AD, with a peak population of 8,000 to 40,000—larger than London at the time—and was later dispersed, with archaeological evidence indicating increased social stress at first contact with Europeans. Modern American Indian nations in the Mississippi basin include Cheyenne, Sioux, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Ho-Chunk, and Meskwaki.

The Hopewell interaction sphere was active between 200 and 500 AD, spreading common cultural practices across waterways from the Gulf of Mexico to the Great Lakes. After this period, communities became more isolated, and agriculture based on the Three Sisters—maize, beans, and squash—introduced from Mesoamerica gradually became dominant. Around 800 AD, an advanced agricultural society known as the Mississippian culture emerged, characterized by highly stratified chiefdoms and large population centers. The most prominent site, Cahokia, was occupied between 600 and 1400 AD and had a population between 8,000 and 40,000 at its peak, larger than London at the time. At first contact with Europeans, Cahokia and other Mississippian cities had dispersed, and archaeological evidence indicates increased social stress. Modern American Indian nations in the Mississippi basin include Cheyenne, Sioux, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Ho-Chunk, Meskwaki, Kickapoo, Tamaroa, Moingwena, Quapaw, and Chickasaw. The name "Mississippi" comes from Messipi, the French version of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe or Algonquin) name Misi-ziibi (Great River). The Ojibwe refer to Lake Itasca as Omashkoozo-zaaga'igan (Elk Lake) and the river from it as Omashkoozo-ziibi (Elk River); after flowing into Lake Bemidji, it is called Bemijigamaag-ziibi (River from the Traversing Lake); into Cass Lake, Gaa-miskwaawaakokaag-ziibi (Red Cedar River); out of Lake Winnibigoshish, Wiinibiigoonzhish-ziibi (Miserable Wretched Dirty Water River); after merging with the Leech Lake River, Gichi-ziibi (Big River); and finally Misi-ziibi (Great River) after the Crow Wing River confluence. After Giacomo Beltrami and Henry Schoolcraft's expeditions, the longest stream above the Crow Wing and Gichi-ziibi confluence was named the "Mississippi River." The Mississippi River Band of Chippewa Indians, known as the Gichi-ziibiwininiwag, are named after the Gichi-ziibi stretch. The Cheyenne called it Máʼxe-éʼometaaʼe (Big Greasy River), the Arapaho named it Beesniicíe, and the Pawnee called it Kickaátit. During French Louisiana, the river was spelled Mississipi or Missisipi and also known as the Rivière Saint-Louis. In 1519, Alonso Álvarez de Pineda was the first recorded European to reach the river; Hernando de Soto reached it on May 8, 1541, calling it Río del Espíritu Santo in present-day Mississippi, and in Spanish it is called Río Mississippi. Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette explored the river in the 17th century; Marquette traveled with a Sioux guide who named it Ne Tongo ("Big river") in 1673, and Marquette proposed calling it the River of the Immaculate Conception. When Jolliet explored the valley, natives guided him to the Chicago Portage, which he noted required only a canal of "half a league" (less than 2 miles or 3 kilometers) to connect the Mississippi and Great Lakes. In 1848, the Illinois and Michigan canal breached the continental divide between the Great Lakes and Mississippi Valley, accelerating development and permanently altering the region's ecology. In 1682, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, and Henri de Tonti claimed the entire Mississippi River valley for France, naming it the Colbert River and the region La Louisiane for King Louis XIV. On March 2, 1699, Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville rediscovered the river's mouth after La Salle's death and built the small fort of La Balise to control passage. In 1718, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, established New Orleans about 100 miles upriver, modeled after Mobile. In 1727, Étienne Perier began constructing the first levees on the river using enslaved African laborers. After Britain's victory in the Seven Years War, the Mississippi became the border between British and Spanish territories; the Treaty of Paris (1763) granted Britain all land east of the river and Spain all land west of it, with Spain ceding Florida to Britain to regain Cuba. Britain then divided the territory into East and West Florida. Article 8 of the Treaty of Paris (1783) stated that navigation of the Mississippi from its source to the ocean would remain free and open to British subjects and U.S. citizens. Britain ceded West Florida back to Spain to regain the Bahamas, and initial disputes were resolved when Spain signed Pinckney's Treaty in 1795. In 1800, under pressure from Napoleon, Spain secretly ceded an undefined portion of West Florida to France in the Treaty of San Ildefonso. The United States secured effective control of the river through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. A dispute arose over which parts of West Florida Spain had ceded to France, affecting which areas the U.S. acquired in the purchase. Due to U.S. colonization and military actions, Spain ceded both West and East Florida to the United States in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819. The last serious European challenge to U.S. control came at the end of the War of 1812, when British forces attacked New Orleans just 15 days after the Treaty of Ghent was signed, but were repelled by General Andrew Jackson. In the 1818 Treaty between the U.S. and Great Britain, the border from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains was set along the 49th parallel, effectively transferring the northwestern extremity of the Mississippi basin to Britain in exchange for the southern portion of the Red River basin. Zadok Cramer wrote a guidebook, The Navigator, detailing the river's features, dangers, and navigable waterways, which was updated and expanded into 12 editions over 25 years. The colonization of the area was not significantly slowed by three earthquakes in 1811 and 1812, estimated at 8 on the Richter scale, centered near New Madrid, Missouri. Mark Twain's book, Life on the Mississippi, covered steamboat commerce from 1830 to 1870, first published as a seven-part serial in Harper's Weekly in 1875 and fully published by James R. Osgood & Company in 1885, including a passage from the unfinished Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. The first steamboat to travel the full length of the Lower Mississippi from the Ohio River to New Orleans was the New Orleans, which made its maiden voyage during the 1811–12 New Madrid earthquakes. The Upper Mississippi was treacherous and poorly mapped, with only two steamboat trips per year to the Twin Cities landings until the 1840s, indicating limited profitability. In 1851, Secretary of War Charles M. Conrad authorized a scientific study of the river to prevent flooding, first published in 1861 as "Report upon the Physics and Hydraulics of the Mississippi River," the most extensive river study of its time. Steamboat transport remained viable for passengers and freight until the end of the first decade of the 20th century. The Anchor Line operated a luxurious fleet between St. Louis and New Orleans from 1859 to 1898. Giacomo Beltrami wrote about his journey on the Virginia, the first steamboat to reach Fort St. Anthony in Minnesota, describing it as a promenade once a journey. The steamboat era transformed the economic and political life of the Mississippi and introduced a flourishing tourist trade. Control of the river was a strategic objective in the American Civil War, part of the U.S. Anaconda Plan. In 1862, Union forces cleared Confederate defenses at Island Number 10 and Memphis, Tennessee, and naval forces captured New Orleans, Louisiana. The last major Confederate stronghold was at Vicksburg, Mississippi; the Union's Vicksburg Campaign (December 1862–July 1863) and the fall of Port Hudson completed control of the lower Mississippi River. The Union victory ended the Siege of Vicksburg on July 4, 1863, and was pivotal to the Union's final victory. The "Big Freeze" of 1918–19 blocked river traffic north of Memphis, Tennessee, preventing coal transport from southern Illinois, leading to widespread shortages, high prices, and rationing in January and February. In spring 1927, the river broke out in 145 places during the Great Mississippi Flood, inundating 27,000 mi² (70,000 km²) to a depth of up to 30 feet (9.1 m). In 1930, Fred Newton became the first person to swim the river from Minneapolis to New Orleans, completing the 1,836-mile journey in 176 days. In 1962 and 1963, industrial accidents spilled 3.5 million U.S. gallons (13,000 m³) of soybean oil into the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers, covering the Mississippi from St. Paul to Lake Pepin and causing an ecological disaster and a demand for pollution control. On October 20, 1976, the MV George Prince ferry was struck by a ship while crossing from Destrehan to Luling, Louisiana, resulting in 78 deaths and 18 survivors. In 1988, the water level at the Memphis gauge dropped to 10 feet (3.0 m) below zero, exposing wooden-hulled craft from the late 19th to early 20th centuries over 4.5 acres (1.8 ha) in West Memphis, Arkansas. The State of Arkansas, the Arkansas Archeological Survey, and the Arkansas Archeological Society conducted a two-month data recovery effort, receiving national media attention during a drought. The Great Flood of 1993 primarily affected the Mississippi above its confluence with the Ohio River at Cairo, Illinois. Two portions of the Mississippi were designated American Heritage Rivers in 1997: the lower portion around Louisiana and Tennessee, and the upper portion around Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, Missouri, and Wisconsin. The Nature Conservancy's "America's Rivershed Initiative" released a report card in October 2015, giving the basin a grade of D+, noting aging infrastructure and multiple environmental problems. In 2002, Slovenian swimmer Martin Strel swam the entire river from Minnesota to Louisiana in 68 days.
