In 2005, the Source to Sea Expedition paddled the Mississippi and Atchafalaya Rivers to support the Audubon Society's Upper Mississippi River Campaign. Geologists believe the lower Mississippi could take a new course to the Gulf via either the Atchafalaya Basin or Lake Pontchartrain if flood-control structures are overtopped or damaged. A failure of the Old River Control Structure between the Mississippi and Atchafalaya Basin could divert 30% of the river's flow to the Atchafalaya River, with a steep drop into the basin. If the structure fails during a major flood, there is concern the river could erode and capture its main channel. The structure was nearly lost during the 1973 flood but was repaired and improved, with additional facilities increasing flow capacity and reducing future failure risks. The Morganza Spillway, located slightly higher and well back from the river, is normally dry; even if it fails at the crest during a severe flood, floodwaters would need to erode to normal levels before a permanent channel shift could occur. During the 2011 floods, the Corps of Engineers opened the Morganza Spillway to 1/4 of its capacity, releasing 150,000 cubic feet per second (4,200 m³/s) to flood the Morganza and Atchafalaya areas, reducing stress on the control system. Army Corps geologist Fred Smith stated that the river "wants to go west" and that a major flood—when structures can't release all water and the levee gives way—would cause the river to jump its banks. Another possible diversion is through Lake Pontchartrain near New Orleans, controlled by the Bonnet Carré Spillway and an imperfect natural levee 12–20 ft (3.7–6.1 m) high. A diversion through Lake Pontchartrain would have consequences similar to an Atchafalaya diversion but to a lesser extent, as the current channel would remain in use past Baton Rouge and into New Orleans. Water skiing was invented on the river in a wide region between Minnesota and Wisconsin.

The Old River Control Structure is a key feature in managing the Mississippi River's course, as Army Corps of Engineers geologist Fred Smith noted, "The Mississippi wants to go west." In 1973, a forty-year flood occurred, and a larger flood event—when the structures can't release all the floodwaters and the levee must give way—is expected to happen in the future, leading to the river jumping its banks and breaking through. Another potential course change involves a diversion into Lake Pontchartrain near New Orleans, which is currently prevented by the Bonnet Carré Spillway and an imperfect natural levee approximately 12–20 ft (3.7–6.1 m) high. If the Mississippi were to divert through Lake Pontchartrain, the consequences would resemble those of an Atchafalaya diversion but to a lesser extent, as the main river channel would continue to be used past Baton Rouge and into the New Orleans area. Water skiing was invented in a wide region between Minnesota and Wisconsin known as Lake Pepin, with Ralph Samuelson of Lake City, Minnesota, creating and refining his technique in late June and early July 1922. He performed the first water ski jump in 1925 and was pulled at 80 mph (130 km/h) by a Curtiss flying boat that same year. There are seven National Park Service sites along the Mississippi River, with the Mississippi National River and Recreation Area dedicated to protecting and interpreting the river itself. The other six sites are listed from north to south. The Mississippi basin supports a highly diverse aquatic fauna and is referred to as the "mother fauna" of North American freshwater. Approximately 375 fish species are known in the basin, surpassing other North Hemisphere river basins in temperate/subtropical regions except the Yangtze. Streams originating in the Appalachian and Ozark highlands contain especially high numbers of species, including numerous endemics and relicts such as paddlefish, sturgeon, gar, and bowfin. The Upper Mississippi River alone hosts about 120 fish species, including walleye, sauger, largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, white bass, northern pike, bluegill, crappie, channel catfish, flathead catfish, common shiner, freshwater drum, and shovelnose sturgeon. The basin is also home to many reptiles, including American alligators, various turtle species, aquatic amphibians, and cambaridae crayfish. About 40% of U.S. migratory birds use the Mississippi River corridor during spring and fall migrations, and 60% of all migratory birds in North America (326 species) use the river basin as a flyway. Numerous introduced species are present, including Asian carp such as silver carp, which have outcompeted native fish and are known for their dangerous jumping behavior and have spread widely throughout the basin, approaching but not yet invading the Great Lakes. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources has designated much of the Mississippi River in the state as infested with zebra mussels and Eurasian watermilfoil.

Miya Masaoka (born 1958, Washington, D.C.) is an American composer, musician, and sound artist active in contemporary classical and experimental music. Her work includes contemporary classical composition, improvisation, electroacoustic music, inter-disciplinary sound art, sound installation, traditional Japanese instruments, and performance art. She is based in New York City and has performed on a 21-string Japanese koto, extended through software processing, string preparations, and bowing. She has created performance works and installations that incorporate plants, live insects, and sensor technology. Her full-length ballet was performed at the Venice Biennale in 2004. She has received the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Fellowship (2021), the Doris Duke Award (2013), the Herb Alpert Award (2004), and a Fulbright Fellowship for advanced research in Noh, gagaku, and the ichi gen kin. She is an associate professor in the MFA Visual Arts Department at Columbia University and the director of the MFA Sound Art Program. Masaoka began studying classical music at age eight. In her early 20s, she moved to Paris, France, and after returning to the U.S., enrolled at San Francisco State University, where she earned a BA in Music, magna cum laude, studying with Wayne Peterson and Eric Moe. She holds an MA from Mills College, where she received the Faculty Award in Music Composition, with teachers including Alvin Curran, Maryanne Amacher, and David Tudor. Her work spans voice, orchestra, installations, electronics, and film shorts, and includes handmade responsive garments (LED KIMONO) and pieces mapping insect movement, plant responses, and brain activity to sound (Pieces For Plants, The Sound of Naked Men, Thinking Sounds). Her works have been commissioned and premiered by Bang on a Can, So Percussion, Either/Or, Kathleen Supove, Joan Jeanrenaud, SF Sound, Volti, Rova Saxophone Quartet, Alonzo King’s Ballet, The Del Sol String Quartet, and others. Her orchestral work “Other Mountain” was selected for a reading by JCOI Earshot for the La Jolla Symphony in 2013. She founded and directed the San Francisco Gagaku Society (1989–1996) under Master Suenobu Togi, a former Japanese Imperial Court musician whose gagaku lineage traces back over 1000 years to the Tang Dynasty. Her interest in nature and resonant outdoor spaces led her to record migrating birds in the canyons near the San Diego Airport, resulting in “For Birds, Planes and Cello,” written for Joan Jeanrenaud. “While I Was Walking, I Heard a Sound” is scored for 120 singers, spatialized in balconies of a concert hall, with one movement featuring three choirs and nine opera singers making bird calls and environmental sounds. As a kotoist, she has performed and recorded with Pharoah Sanders, Pauline Oliveros, Gerry Hemingway, Jon Rose, Fred Frith, Larry Ochs, Maybe Monday, Steve Coleman, Anthony Braxton, Reggie Workman, Dr. L. Subramaniam, Andrew Cyrille, George E. Lewis, Jin Hi Kim, Susie Ibarra, Vijay Iyer, Myra Melford, Zeena Parkins, Toshiko Akiyoshi, William Parker, Robert Dick, Lukas Ligeti, Earl Howard, Henry Brant, and others. Masaoka describes herself as deeply moved by the sounds and kinetic energy of the natural world, emphasizing the complexity and fundamental nature of human heartbeat, lunar rhythms, oceanic cycles, and cultural soundscapes. She initiated and founded the San Francisco Electronic Music Festival in 1999. In 2004, she received the Alpert Award in the Arts, and previously received a National Endowment for the Arts award and a Wallace Alexander Gerbode Award. The New York Times describes her solo performances as exploring the extremes of her instrument, and The Wire describes her compositions as magnificent, virtuosic, and essential. She has been a faculty member at the Milton Avery Graduate Program at Bard College in Music/Sound since 2002 and has taught music composition at NYU. She received the Doris Duke Performing Artist Award in 2013 and a Fulbright Scholarship for Japan in 2016. Her recorded works include: Myths, Modes and Means (BMG/RCA, 1996), What We Live (Black Saint, 1996), Suite for Koto and Jazz Orchestra (BMG, 1997), Twelve Minor (Avant, 1998), Global Fusion (Erato, 1999), Trancepatterns (Dendroica Music, 2000), Burdocks (Tzadik, 2001), Legends and Legacies (Asian Improv Records, 2005), Cloud Plate (Cryptogramophone, 2005), Sequel (for Lester Bowie) (Intakt, 2006), Sound Body (samadhisound, 2007), and With Fred Frith and Maybe Monday.

Mohamed Abdelaziz Dja'it (1886–1970) (Arabic: محمد عبد العزيز جعيط) was an Islamic scholar who served as Mufti of the Republic of Tunisia from 1957 to 1960. He was born in 1886 during the French protectorate of Tunisia and was the son of Youssef Djaït, who served as Prime Minister under the Beylik of Tunis. In the early years of Tunisian independence, President Habib Bourguiba referenced Dja'it's 1949 majalla publication when justifying the new Code of Personal Status, which included laws on family life and women's status, from a religious perspective. Dja'it issued a fatwa opposing the code in September 1956 but later withdrew his opposition and was appointed Mufti of the Republic. He was eventually dismissed for criticizing Bourguiba's position on fasting.

Mohammed Racim (Arabic: محمد راسم, 24 June 1896 – 30 March 1975) was an Algerian artist who co-founded the Algerian School for Miniature Painting with his brother, Omar, and the institution continues to exist today.[1] Born in the Casbah of Algiers in 1896 into a distinguished family of artists,[1][2] Racim came from a lineage whose pre-colonial prosperity was diminished by the French regime's confiscation of property.[1][3] In 1880, his father had re-established a wood-carving and copper-working workshop in the Casbah, where Omar Racim engraved decorative tombstones. The family secured commissions to decorate public buildings and pavilions at French colonial exhibitions.[4] Racim's talent for drawing was recognized during his primary education when he was assigned to copy Islamic decorative motifs for state workshops established by Governor Charles Jonnart. Around 1914, he became familiar with Persian, Mughal, and Andalusian miniatures created for the private use of Muslim nobility and developed a personal style blending traditional materials and classical arabesque and calligraphic elements with figurative inserts that included modern features. As a teenager, he befriended Nasreddine Dinet, who advised him on painting the human figure and helped him secure commissions to decorate books with calligraphic plates. His primary patrons were businessmen and government officials who appreciated his depictions of old Algeria's cultural milieu.[1] By the late 1930s, Racim had become a prominent figure in Algerian culture.[3] His work "Women at the Cascade" presents an imagined pre-colonial past, depicting a time before French arrival when indigenous people were masters of the Maghreb, portrayed as prosperous, engaged in fine textiles, elaborate costumes, and the arts of music, architecture, and gardening.[5] Roger Benjamin has argued that Racim's work effectively erases the presence of French settlers in Algeria, celebrating a pristine Turkish city rather than the industrialized port shaped by a century of French modernization. Nevertheless, he was not an ideologue and acknowledged that his artistic success was made possible by French scholarly influence.[6] Mohammed Racim and his wife were killed in their home on 30 March 1975 and were buried together in the Thaalibia Cemetery of the Casbah of Algiers.[citation needed] On 24 June 2021, Google honored his 125th birthday with a Google Doodle.[7]

Mohinder Amarnath Bhardwaj, born on 24 September 1950 in Patiala, is a former Indian cricketer and cricket analyst, son of Lala Amarnath, the first post-independence captain of India. He served as vice-captain of the Indian team that won the 1983 Cricket World Cup, where he was named Player of the Final and also played a key role in the semi-final, earning Man of the Match honors in both matches. He was part of the Indian squad that won the 1985 World Championship of Cricket. Known widely by players and pundits as the best Indian batsman against express pace, Mohinder received the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award in 2009. He was the second eldest son of Lala Amarnath and Kailash Kumari; his elder brother Surinder was a former international cricketer, younger brother Rajinder a former first-class cricketer, and he has two sisters, Kamala and Dolly. He completed his schooling at MB High School, Mandir Marg, Delhi, and graduated from SGTB Khalsa College, Delhi University. Making his Test debut against Australia in December 1969 as a quick-bowling all-rounder, he was a top-order batsman, primarily playing at No. 3, known for being both attacking and defensive, and for reinventing his game over time. He was also skilled with the ball, bowling swingers and cutters with great control and had a unique run-up where he slowed down as he approached the crease. He played 69 Tests, scoring 4,378 runs at an average of 42.50, including 11 hundreds and 24 fifties, and took 32 wickets at 55.68; in 85 One Day Internationals, he scored 1,924 runs at an average of 30.53, with a highest score of 102 not out, and took 46 wickets at 42.84. Imran Khan of Pakistan and Malcolm Marshall of the West Indies praised his batsmanship, courage, and ability to endure pain. In the 1982–83 series against Pakistan and the West Indies, he scored over 1000 runs in the two series, and despite India losing the first three Tests 3–0, he was the sole saving grace for the batting line-up. Sunil Gavaskar, in his book "Idols," described Mohinder as the finest batsman in the world, and Imran Khan stated in his book "All Round View" that Mohinder was the best batsman in the world during the 1982–83 season and should have played continuously from his debut in 1969 until retirement. The series saw Imran Khan take 40 wickets and jointly win "Man of the Series" with Mohinder, who was instrumental in stabilizing India's batting. Sunil Gavaskar scored 434 runs in one innings during the series. Mohinder made his first Test century at Perth against Jeff Thomson at the WACA, the fastest and bounciest wicket in the world, and followed it with 10 more centuries against top-class fast bowling. In the 1983 World Cup semi-final against England, his accurate seam bowling led to the dismissal of David Gower and Mike Gatting, with only 27 runs given in 12 overs (2.25 per over), the lowest among Indian bowlers, and he scored 46 runs to provide a solid foundation, earning Man of the Match. In the final against the West Indies, India was dismissed for 183 in 54.4 overs, far below the 60-over target, but Amarnath's calm batting provided stability, occupying the crease for 80 balls and scoring 26 runs. Krishnamachari Srikkanth top-scored with 38, followed by Sandeep Patil with 27. India's chances were slim, but the Indian bowling, exploiting weather and pitch conditions, bowled out the West Indies for 140, winning by 43 runs. Amarnath and Madan Lal were joint highest wicket-takers with 3 wickets each, and he was again named Man of the Match for his economical bowling, conceding only 12 runs in 7 overs (1.71 per over), and also took the match-winning wicket. As vice-captain, he held the World Cup aloft in a famous photograph with captain Kapil Dev. Except for 1982–83, Mohinder never held a steady place in the Indian Test side and was frequently dropped, earning the nickname "Comeback Man" of Indian cricket. He was known for his batting technique, temperament, and skill, having experimented with a side-on batting stance. He was admired for his personality, courage, and determination; Vivian Richards called him "one of the nicest men to have ever played the game," and David Boon said "Concede didn't seem to be in his vocabulary." Gideon Haigh noted that despite being hit by Richard Hadlee, Imran Khan, Malcolm Marshall, and Jeff Thomson—suffering a skull fracture, being knocked unconscious, teeth knocked out, and a painful jaw injury—he never stopped hooking and continued playing, with Michael Holding stating that what separated him from others was his ability to withstand pain. During the Bridgetown Test in 1982–83, he retired for stitches after being hit on the head and returned to face Michael Holding, hooking a bouncer to the boundary. However, during the 1983/84 tour of India, the West Indies attack restricted him to just 1 run in six innings, with Holding dismissing him three times for ducks, leading to his drop shortly after his 1983 World Cup success. He played a key role in a famous chase at Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain, in 1976, scoring 85 in the second innings to take India to the brink of a historic win. He had notable conflicts with the Indian cricket selectors, famously calling them a "bunch of jokers," which often led to his exclusion. Mohinder is the only Indian to be dismissed on handling the ball, first in an ODI on 9 February 1986, and the only Indian to be dismissed for obstructing the field in ODIs; he is also the only international cricketer to have been given out for both handling the ball and obstructing the field. He carried a red handkerchief visibly in his trouser pocket while batting as a superstition. He presented a popular weekly cricket coaching TV program in the late 80s and early 90s titled "Cricket with Mohinder Amarnath," which featured technique presentations and guest speakers, mostly from the Indian national team, and gained a strong following among youth, especially after the 1987 Reliance Cup, broadcast on Doordarshan. The program's title song, "Khel hi hain hamara jeevan...", was very catchy; young Sachin Tendulkar, at 15, was interviewed by Amarnath and later joined the Indian team for the Pakistan tour after a year. Mohinder is married to Inderjit Amarnath and has one daughter. The 2021 Hindi film 83, based on India's 1983 World Cup victory, features Saqib Saleem as Amarnath and Amarnath himself as his father, Lala, and he also played the role of a cricket coach to Saleem's character, Viraj Sharma, in the 2016 film Dishoom.

doc_name: Molar ionization energies of the elements
text: These tables provide values for molar ionization energies expressed in kJ⋅mol−1, representing the energy required per mole to remove an electron from gaseous atoms or atomic ions. The first molar ionization energy corresponds to the removal of an electron from neutral atoms, while subsequent energies—such as the second, third, and so on—relate to the removal of electrons from singly, doubly, or higher charged ions. For ionization energies given in electron volts (eV), refer to the Ionization energies of the elements (data page). It should be noted that all data for elements starting with rutherfordium and beyond is predicted.

Morris Villarroel (born 1978 or 1979) is a Spanish professor of animal psychology at the Technical University of Madrid. Since February 2010, he has been lifelogging by writing in paper notebooks at 15 to 30 minute intervals, recording what he is doing, his location, the times he wakes up, the food he eats, and his ideas. He also tracks his movements using a fitness tracker. An example log entry reads: "I woke up at 05:45 in a hotel in Sweden. My hind leg muscles were hurting a bit." When notebooks are full, he indexes them in a spreadsheet with categories and keywords. In 2019, he estimated spending about an hour a day writing in his notebooks. Originally planning to continue for 10 years as an experiment, he decided to keep going after that period. He began lifelogging to improve his memory and time management and to maintain a clear record of his life experiences, which he says makes him feel like he has lived a longer life and enhances his emotional regulation. As of December 2019, he had filled up 307 notebooks. In April 2014, he started wearing a chest-mounted camera that took photos every 30 seconds, accumulating about 1,200 per day, which he used for most of the day except in private settings like the bedroom. He captured significant memories such as his father's death and his son's birth, and noted that while some people were uncomfortable, most were supportive. He discontinued using the camera after a few years due to difficulty managing the volume of photos. Both of his parents are psychologists, and he is married with five children.

Mount Everest, known locally as Sagarmāthā in Nepal and Qomolangma in Tibet, is Earth's highest mountain above sea level and lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas, marking part of the China–Nepal border at its summit. Its height was most recently measured in 2020 by Chinese and Nepali authorities as 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8+1⁄2 in). The mountain attracts many climbers, including experienced mountaineers, with two main routes: one from the southeast in Nepal (the standard route) and one from the north in Tibet. Despite not presenting substantial technical challenges on the standard route, Everest poses dangers such as altitude sickness, weather, wind, avalanches, and the Khumbu Icefall. As of May 2024, 340 people have died on Everest, and over 200 bodies remain on the mountain due to dangerous conditions. Climbers typically ascend from base camps above 5,000 m (16,404 ft), with the elevation gain varying; on the Tibetan side, climbers drive directly to the North Base Camp, while on the Nepalese side, they fly into Kathmandu, then Lukla, and trek to the South Base Camp, resulting in a climb from Lukla to the summit of about 6,000 m (20,000 ft). The first recorded attempts to reach the summit were made by British mountaineers, as Nepal restricted foreign entry. In 1921, the British reached 7,000 m (22,966 ft) on the North Col, and in 1922, they achieved the first ascent above 8,000 m (26,247 ft), pushing the North Ridge route to 8,321 m (27,300 ft). George Mallory and Andrew Irvine made a final summit attempt on 8 June 1924 but did not return, leading to debate over whether they were the first to reach the top. Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary made the first documented ascent in 1953 via the Southeast Ridge route, with Norgay having reached 8,595 m (28,199 ft) in 1952 as part of a Swiss expedition. The Chinese team of Wang Fuzhou, Gonpo, and Qu Yinhua made the first reported ascent from the North Ridge on 25 May 1960. The Nepali name Sagarmāthā (IAST: Sagarmāthā, Sanskrit: Sagar-Matha, lit. "goddess of the sky") derives from सगर (sagar, "sky") and माथा (māthā, "head"). The Tibetan name Qomolangma (ཇོ་མོ་གླང་མ, lit. "holy mother") was first recorded in the 1721 Kangxi Atlas and appeared in the West in 1733 as Tchoumour Lancma on a map by D'Anville. The official Chinese transcription is Zhūmùlǎngmǎ Fēng, a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan name, adopted in May 1952 after earlier names like Shèngmǔ Fēng were phased out. The British Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, beginning in 1802, used giant theodolites weighing 500 kg (1,100 lb) and required 12 men to carry, but was hindered by Nepal's refusal to allow entry. Observations were made from Terai, where conditions were difficult due to rain and malaria, resulting in three deaths and two retirements. In 1847, Andrew Scott Waugh observed a peak beyond Kangchenjunga, designated Peak XV, and in 1849, James Nicolson made observations from 190 km (120 mi) away, with data indicating Peak XV was higher than Kangchenjunga. Radhanath Sikdar identified Peak XV as the world's highest peak in 1852 using trigonometric calculations. Waugh officially announced in 1856 that Peak XV (later named Mount Everest) was 8,840 m (29,002 ft) high, with the height rounded to 29,002 ft to avoid implying an exact value. From 1952 to 1954, the Survey of India determined the height as 8,847.73 m (29,028 ft), reaffirmed in 1975 by China at 8,848.13 m (29,029.30 ft), both measuring the snow cap, not the rock head. The 8,848 m (29,029 ft) height was officially recognized by Nepal and China. In 1999, an American expedition led by Bradford Washburn measured a rock head elevation of 8,850 m (29,035 ft) and a snow/ice elevation 1 m (3 ft) higher, though it was not officially recognized by Nepal. Geoid uncertainty questions the accuracy of both the 1999 and 2005 surveys. In 2005, the Chinese Academy of Sciences and State Bureau of Surveying and Mapping announced a height of 8,844.43 m (29,017.16 ft) with ±0.21 m (8.3 in) accuracy, based on rock height, with a snow-ice depth of 3.5 m (11 ft), and a disagreement arose over whether the official height should be rock (8,844 m) or snow (8,848 m). In 2010, both countries agreed on 8,848 m, with Nepal recognizing China's claim of a rock height of 8,844 m. On 8 December 2020, Nepal and China jointly announced the new official height as 8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft). Plate tectonics at the Main Himalayan Thrust, where the Indian and Eurasian plates converge, are increasing Everest's height and moving the summit northeastward at rates of 4 mm (0.16 in) per year vertically and 3 to 6 mm (0.12 to 0.24 in) per year horizontally, though some accounts suggest lateral movement of 27 mm (1.1 in) or even shrinkage. The summit is the point where Earth's surface reaches the greatest distance above sea level. Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller when measured from its base, rising over 10,200 m (33,464.6 ft) from the ocean floor, though only 4,205 m (13,796 ft) above sea level. Denali in Alaska is taller when measured from base, with a height above base of 5,600 m (18,400 ft), despite its sea-level height of 6,190 m (20,308 ft). Everest's base elevations range from 4,200 m (13,800 ft) on the south to 5,200 m (17,100 ft) on the Tibetan Plateau, giving it a height above base of 3,650 to 4,650 m (11,980 to 15,260 ft). Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther from Earth's center (6,384.4 km or 3,967.1 mi) than Everest (6,382.3 km or 3,965.8 mi) due to Earth's equatorial bulge, despite having a lower peak elevation of 6,268 m (20,564.3 ft) versus Everest's 8,848 m (29,028.9 ft). Other nearby high mountains include Lhotse (8,516 m), Nuptse (7,855 m), Changtse (7,580 m), and Khumbutse (6,636 m). The Khumbu Icefall and glacier are major obstacles on the southwest side, affecting base camps and climbs. Geologists have divided the rocks of Mount Everest into three formations.

Mount Everest, at 8,848 meters (29,028.9 feet) above sea level, is not the farthest point from Earth's center due to the planet's equatorial bulge; Chimborazo, at 6,268 meters (20,564.3 feet) above sea level, is farther from Earth's center because the Earth bulges at the equator, with a distance of 6,382.3 kilometers (3,965.8 miles) compared to Everest's 6,371.2 kilometers (3,959.0 miles). Many of the world’s highest mountains are near Everest, including Lhotse at 8,516 meters (27,940 feet), Nuptse at 7,855 meters (25,771 feet), Changtse at 7,580 meters (24,870 feet), and Khumbutse at 6,636 meters (21,772 feet). On the southwest side, the Khumbu icefall and glacier serve as a major obstacle for climbers and base camps. Geologists have divided Mount Everest’s rock layers into three formations: the Qomolangma Formation, the North Col Formation, and the Rongbuk Formation, separated by low-angle faults called detachments. The Qomolangma Formation, also known as the Jolmo Lungama Formation, extends from the summit to about 8,600 meters (28,200 feet), composed of greyish to dark grey or white, parallel laminated Ordovician limestone interlayered with recrystallized dolomite and siltstone, containing microscopic fragments of crinoids, trilobites, and ostracods; a 60-meter (200-foot) thick thrombolite bed at the foot of the "Third Step" consists of sediments bound by cyanobacteria biofilms. This formation is broken by high-angle faults ending at the Qomolangma Detachment, which separates it from the Yellow Band. The North Col Formation, from 7,000 to 8,600 meters (23,000 to 28,200 feet), includes the Yellow Band (8,200 to 8,600 meters) made of Middle Cambrian diopside-epidote marble and phyllite, with up to five percent recrystallized crinoid ossicles; the upper five meters are deformed, separated from the Qomolangma Formation by a 5–40 cm (2.0–15.7 inch) fault breccia. Below 8,200 meters, the North Col Formation consists of deformed schist and phyllite, metamorphosed from Middle to Early Cambrian deep-sea flysch. Its base is the Lhotse detachment, a regional low-angle normal fault. Below 7,000 meters, the Rongbuk Formation underlies the North Col Formation and consists of sillimanite-K-feldspar schist and gneiss intruded by leucogranite sills and dikes (1 cm to 1,500 meters thick), part of a Late Oligocene–Miocene intrusive belt formed 20 to 24 million years ago from partial melting of Paleoproterozoic to Ordovician metasedimentary rocks during Indian Plate subduction. The mountain's sedimentary and metamorphic rocks were thrust southward over the Indian Plate's Archean granulites during the Cenozoic India-Asia collision, with the Qomolangma and North Col formations originating as marine sediments from India’s continental shelf. The Rongbuk Formation formed from high-grade metamorphic and granitic rocks that were pushed down, heated, and partially melted at depths over 15 to 20 kilometers (9.3 to 12.4 miles) before being forced upward. Mount Everest is rising at about 2 mm per year. The Ordovician limestone of Everest was recognized by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) in 2022 as a geological heritage site due to its fossiliferous marine origin and international scientific relevance. Very little native flora or fauna exist on Everest; a moss grows at 6,480 meters (21,260 feet), possibly the highest altitude plant species, and Arenaria grows below 5,500 meters (18,000 feet); satellite data from 1993 to 2018 shows vegetation expansion into previously bare areas. A black jumping spider, Euophrys, has been found at up to 6,700 meters (22,000 feet), possibly the highest confirmed non-microscopic permanent resident, with E. everestensis at 5,030 meters (16,500 feet), feeding on wind-blown insects; microscopic life is likely at higher altitudes. Bar-headed geese migrate over the Himalayas and have been seen flying over Everest’s summit, with George Lowe reporting this in 1953; choughs have been spotted as high as 7,906 meters (25,938 feet) and yellow-billed choughs at 7,900 meters (25,919 feet). Yaks are used to haul gear, carrying up to 100 kilograms (220 pounds), with thick fur and large lungs; other animals include the Himalayan tahr (prey of snow leopards), Himalayan black bear (up to 4,300 meters), and red panda. A pika and ten new ant species were found in a region expedition. From Nepal, Everest is protected in Sagarmatha National Park; from China, in Qomolangma National Nature Reserve. The mountain has an ice cap climate (Köppen EF) with all months below freezing. The base camp on the Nepalese side is located on the Khumbu Glacier, which is rapidly thinning due to climate change, prompting plans by Taranath Adhikari to relocate it to a lower altitude to improve safety, though resistance from climbers and Sherpas has delayed the move due to lack of viable alternative locations. In 2008, a weather station at 8,000 meters (26,000 feet) went online, operated by SHARE, which also installed the Mount Everest webcam in 2011. The Balcony Station, at 8,430 meters (27,660 feet), is the highest weather station on Earth, set up by Tom Matthews and Baker Perry in 2019 and ceased transmitting data as of January 20, 2020. Everest extends into the upper troposphere and stratosphere, with summit air pressure about one-third of sea level; winds commonly reach 160 km/h (100 mph), with a recorded speed of 280 km/h (175 mph) in February 2004; these winds can blow climbers into chasms or reduce oxygen by up to 14 percent via Bernoulli’s principle, prompting climbers to aim for spring or fall windows when the monsoon season ends or begins. The summit was first reached by humans in 1953; only about 200 people had summited by 1987, and as of December 2024, the Himalayan Database records just under 13,000 summits by around 7,200 individuals. Early attempts include Clinton Thomas Dent suggesting climbing Everest in 1885; George Mallory and Guy Bullock discovered the northern approach in 1921, reaching 7,005 meters (22,982 feet) at the North Col, where Mallory identified a route to the summit. In 1922, Mallory, Col. Felix Norton, and Howard Somervell reached 8,225 meters (26,985 feet) without oxygen, and George Finch and Geoffrey Bruce reached 8,321 meters (27,300 feet) using oxygen. In 1924, Mallory and Geoffrey Bruce’s attempt was aborted due to weather, and Norton and Somervell reached 8,572.8 meters (28,126 feet), ascending only 30 meters in the final hour; Mallory used oxygen with Andrew Irvine, who disappeared on June 8, 1924. Mallory’s body was found in 1999 on the North Face, and Irvine’s detached foot was found in 2024, sparking debate over whether they reached the summit. In 1933, Lady Houston funded the Houston Everest Flight, where two aircraft led by the Marquess of Clydesdale flew over the summit. Early expeditions from Tibet via the North Face were unsuccessful due to access closure in 1950 after China took control of Tibet; Bill Tilman and a small party in 1950 pioneered the standard southern route through Nepal. The 1952 Swiss Mount Everest expedition was granted permission to attempt a climb.

Years before the first confirmed ascent and safe descent in 1953, Irvine's detached foot, still in a boot and sock, was found in 2024. In 1933, Lady Houston, a British millionaire, funded the Houston Everest Flight of 1933, which saw a formation of two aeroplanes led by the Marquess of Clydesdale fly over the Everest summit. Early expeditions—such as Charles Bruce's in the 1920s and Hugh Ruttledge's two unsuccessful attempts in 1933 and 1936—tried to ascend the mountain from Tibet, via the North Face. Access was closed from the north to Western expeditions in 1950 after China took control of Tibet. In 1950, Bill Tilman and a small party which included Charles Houston, Oscar Houston, and Betsy Cowles undertook an exploratory expedition to Everest through Nepal along the route which has become the standard approach to Everest from the south. The 1952 Swiss Mount Everest expedition was granted permission to attempt a climb from Nepal. It established a route through the Khumbu icefall and ascended to the South Col at an elevation of 7,986 m (26,201 ft). Raymond Lambert and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay were able to reach an elevation of about 8,595 m (28,199 ft) on the Southeast Ridge, setting a new climbing altitude record. Tenzing's experience was useful when he was hired to be part of the British expedition in 1953. The Swiss made another post-monsoon attempt in the autumn; they made it to the South Col but were driven back by winter winds and severe cold. In 1953, a ninth British expedition, led by John Hunt, returned to Nepal. Hunt selected two climbing pairs to attempt the summit. The first, Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans, came within 100 m (330 ft) of the summit on 26 May 1953, but turned back after running into oxygen problems. As planned, their work in routefinding, breaking trail and oxygen caches were of great aid to the following pair. Two days later, the expedition made its second assault with the second pair: New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepali Sherpa climber. They reached the summit at 11:30 am local time on 29 May 1953 via the South Col route. At the time, both acknowledged it as a team effort by the whole expedition, but Tenzing revealed a few years later that Hillary had put his foot on the summit first. They took photos and buried sweets and a small cross in the snow before descending. On 23 May 1956, Ernst Schmied and Juerg Marmet ascended. Wang Fuzhou, Gonpo and Qu Yinhua of China made the first reported ascent of the peak from the North Ridge in May 1960. The first American to climb Everest, Jim Whittaker, joined by Nawang Gombu, reached the summit on 1 May 1963 on the American Mount Everest expedition and on 22 May on the same expedition Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld were the first to traverse the mountain by climbing via the North Face and descending via the South Col. In 1970, Japanese mountaineers conducted a major expedition. The centrepiece was a large "siege"-style expedition, working on finding a new route up the Southwest Face. Another element was an attempt to ski Everest. Despite a staff of over one hundred and a decade of planning, the expedition suffered eight deaths and failed to summit. However, Japanese expeditions enjoyed some successes. Yuichiro Miura became the first man to ski down Everest from the South Col—he descended nearly 1,300 vertical metres (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with extreme injuries. Another success was an expedition that put four on the summit via the South Col route. Miura's exploits became the subject of film, and he went on to become the oldest person to summit Everest in 2003 aged 70 and in 2013 aged 80. In 1975, Junko Tabei became the first woman to summit Everest. The 1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition led and organised by Chris Bonington made the first ascent of the Southwest Face from the Western Cwm. In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen. The Polish climber Andrzej Zawada headed the first winter ascent of Everest, the first winter ascent of an eight-thousander. On 15 January, the team managed to set up Camp III at 7,150 metres (23,460 ft) above sea level, but further action was stopped by hurricane-force winds. The weather improved after 11 February, when Leszek Cichy, Walenty Fiut and Krzysztof Wielicki set up camp IV on South Col at 7,906 metres (25,938 ft). Cichy and Wielicki started the final ascent at 6:50 am on 17 February. At 2:40 pm Andrzej Zawada at base camp heard the climbers' voices over the radio – "We are on the summit! The strong wind blows all the time. It is unimaginably cold." The successful winter ascent started a new decade of Winter Himalaism, which became a Polish specialisation. After 1980 Poles did ten first winter ascents on 8000 metre peaks. In 1989, Polish climbers under the leadership of Eugeniusz Chrobak organised an international expedition to Everest on a difficult western ridge. Ten Poles and nine foreigners participated, but only the Poles remained in the attempt for the summit. On 24 May, Chrobak and Andrzej Marciniak, starting from camp V at 8,200 metres (26,900 ft), overcame the ridge and reached the summit. But on 27 May, during an avalanche from the side of Khumbutse near the Lho La pass, four climbers were killed: Mirosław Dąsal, Mirosław Gardzielewski, Zygmunt Andrzej Heinrich and Wacław Otręba. The following day, due to his injuries, Chrobak died. Marciniak, who was injured, was saved by a rescue expedition in which Artur Hajzer and New Zealanders Gary Ball and Rob Hall took part. The organisation of the rescue included Reinhold Messner, Elizabeth Hawley, Carlos Carsolio and the US consul. On 10 and 11 May 1996, eight climbers died after guided expeditions were caught in a blizzard during a summit attempt on 10 May. During the 1996 season, 15 people died. These were the highest death tolls for a single weather event, and season, until the 16 deaths in the 2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche. The guiding disaster gained publicity and raised questions about the commercialisation of climbing and the safety of guiding clients on Everest. Journalist Jon Krakauer, on assignment from Outside magazine, was in one of the affected guided parties, and published the bestseller Into Thin Air, which related his experience. Krakauer was critical of guide Anatoli Boukreev. A year later, Boukreev co-authored The Climb, in part as a rebuttal of Krakauer's portrayal. The dispute sparked debate within the climbing community. Boukreev was awarded The American Alpine Club's David Sowles Award for his rescue efforts on the expedition. In 2004 researchers from the University of Toronto told the New Scientist that analysis of conditions on 11 May suggested that weather caused oxygen levels to plunge about 14 per cent. One survivor was Beck Weathers, left for dead about 275 metres (900 feet) from Camp 4 at 7,950 metres (26,085 feet). After spending a night on the mountain, Weathers made it back to Camp 4 with massive frostbite and vision impaired due to snow blindness. Fellow climbers considered his condition terminal and left him in a tent to die overnight. Weathers was lowered to Camp 2 and a helicopter rescue was organised by the Nepali Army. The storm's impact on climbers on the North Ridge, where several climbers also died, was detailed in a first-hand account by Matt Dickinson in his book The Other Side of Everest. Sixteen-year-old Mark Pfetzer was on the climb and wrote about it in Within Reach: My Everest Story. The 2015 feature film Everest is based on the events of this guiding disaster. In 2006, 12 people died. David Sharp's death triggered debate and years of discussion about climbing ethics. The question was whether climbers had left a man to die and whether he could have been saved. He attempted to summit alone with two bottles of oxygen, compared to the standard five used by most climbers. He arranged his permit through Asian Trekking, a Kathmandu-based company that provided basic services to base camp, but not beyond that point. Sharp climbed without a radio or guide. Multiple climbing parties encountered Sharp in distress. Double-amputee climber Mark Inglis said that on 15 May his climbing party, and many others, had passed Sharp, sheltering under a rock overhang 450 metres (1,480 ft) below the summit, without attempting a rescue. Inglis said 40 people had passed by Sharp, but he might have been overlooked as climbers assumed Sharp was the corpse nicknamed "Green Boots", but Inglis was not aware that climbers had tried to help Sharp despite being in the process of helping an injured woman, Burçak Özoğlu Poçan, down. There has been discussion about Himex in the commentary on Inglis and Sharp. In regard to Inglis's initial comments, he later revised details because he had been interviewed while he was "physically and mentally exhausted, and in much pain. He had suffered frostbite – he later had five fingertips amputated." It was estimated that Sharp summited on 14 May and began his descent, but on 15 May he was in trouble and being passed by climbers on their way up and down. It is believed he was suffering from hypoxia and was about 300 m (1,000 ft) from the summit on the North Side route. The Tribune, India, quoted someone who described what happened to Sharp as "the most shameful act in the history of mountaineering". Much of this controversy was captured by the Discovery Channel while filming Everest: Beyond the Limit. A crucial decision affecting Sharp is shown where a returning climber, adventurer Maxim Chaya, is descending and radios his base camp manager (Russell Brice) that he has found a frostbitten and unconscious climber in distress. Chaya is unable to identify Sharp, who had chosen to climb solo and did not identify himself to other climbers. The manager assumes Sharp is part of a group that has already calculated they must abandon him, and informs his lone climber there is no chance of him being able to help Sharp by himself. As Sharp's condition deteriorates and other descending climbers pass him, his opportunities for rescue diminish: his legs and feet curl from frostbite, preventing him walking; later descending climbers are lower on oxygen and lack the strength to offer aid; time runs out for Sherpas to return and rescue him. Sharp's body remained just below the summit on the Chinese side next to "Green Boots"; they shared a space in a rock cave that was an ad hoc tomb. Sharp's body was removed from the cave in 2007, and since 2014, Green Boots has been missing, presumably removed or buried. As the Sharp debate started, on 26 May Australian climber Lincoln Hall was found alive after being left. He was found by a party of four climbers who, giving up their own attempt, stayed with Hall and descended with him and 11 Sherpas sent up to carry him down. Hall fully recovered. His team had assumed he had died from cerebral edema, and were instructed to cover him with rocks. There were no rocks to do this and he was abandoned. The erroneous information of his death was passed to his family. On 21 May 2007, Canadian climber Meagan McGrath initiated the successful high-altitude rescue of Nepali Usha Bista. McGrath was selected as a 2011 recipient of the Sir Edmund Hillary Foundation of Canada Humanitarian Award, which recognises a Canadian who has contributed a significant service in the Himalayan Region of Nepal. By the end of 2010, there had been 5,104 summits by about 3,142 individuals, with 77 per cent accomplished since 2000. The summit was achieved in 7 of the 22 years from 1953 to 1974 and not missed between 1975 and 2014. An illustration of the explosion of popularity is provided by the number of daily ascents. Analysis of the 1996 Mount Everest disaster shows part of the blame was on the bottleneck caused by a large number of climbers (33 to 36) attempting to summit on the same day; this was unusually high at the time. By comparison, on 23 May 2010, the summit was reached by 169 climbers – more summits in a single day than in the 31 years from the first successful summit in 1953 to 1983. Nearly all attempts at the summit are done using one of two main routes. In 2005–07, more than half elected to use the more challenging, but cheaper northeast route. Sudarshan Gautam, a Canadian double-amputee, summited the mountain in 2013.[252] In the same year, Eli Reimer, a teenager with Down syndrome, hiked to the South Base Camp as part of a fundraising effort for his father's foundation.[253] Mount Everest has two main climbing routes, the Southeast Ridge from Nepal and the North Ridge from Tibet, as well as many other less frequently climbed routes.[254] Of the two main routes, the Southeast Ridge is technically easier and more frequently used. It was the route used by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953 and the first recognised of 15 routes to the top by 1996.[254] This was, however, a route decision dictated more by politics than by design, as the Chinese border was closed to the western world in the 1950s, after Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China.[255] Most attempts are made during May, before the summer monsoon season. As the monsoon season approaches, the jet stream shifts northward, thereby reducing the average wind speeds high on the mountain.[256][257] While attempts are sometimes made in September and October, after the monsoons, when the jet stream is again temporarily pushed northward, the additional snow deposited by the monsoons and the less stable weather patterns at the monsoons' tail end makes climbing extremely difficult. The ascent via the Southeast Ridge begins with a trek to Base Camp at 5,380 m (17,700 ft) on the south side of Everest, in Nepal. Expeditions usually fly into Lukla (2,860 m) from Kathmandu and pass through Namche Bazaar. Climbers then hike to Base Camp, which usually takes six to eight days, allowing for proper altitude acclimatisation in order to prevent altitude sickness.[258] Climbing equipment and supplies are carried by yaks, dzopkyos (yak-cow hybrids), and human porters to Base Camp on the Khumbu Glacier. When Hillary and Tenzing climbed Everest in 1953, the British expedition they were part of (comprising over 400 climbers, porters, and Sherpas at that point) started from the Kathmandu Valley, as there were no roads further east at that time. Climbers spend a couple of weeks in Base Camp, acclimatising to the altitude. During that time, Sherpas and some expedition climbers set up ropes and ladders in the treacherous Khumbu Icefall. Seracs, crevasses, and shifting blocks of ice make the icefall one of the most dangerous sections of the route. Many climbers and Sherpas have been killed in this section. To reduce the hazard, climbers usually begin their ascent well before dawn, when the freezing temperatures glue ice blocks in place. Above the icefall is Camp I at 6,065 metres (19,900 ft). From Camp I, climbers make their way up the Western Cwm to the base of the Lhotse Face, where Camp II or Advanced Base Camp (ABC) is established at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). The Western Cwm is a flat, gently rising glacial valley, marked by huge lateral crevasses in the centre, which prevent direct access to the upper reaches of the Cwm. Climbers are forced to cross on the far right, near the base of Nuptse, to a small passageway known as the "Nuptse corner". The Western Cwm is also called the "Valley of Silence" as the topography of the area generally cuts off wind from the climbing route. The high altitude and a clear, windless day can make the Western Cwm unbearably hot for climbers.[259] From Camp II, climbers ascend the Lhotse Face on fixed ropes.

Sherpas have been killed in this section of Mount Everest, prompting climbers to begin their ascent well before dawn to reduce hazards, as freezing temperatures glue ice blocks in place. Above the icefall is Camp I at 6,065 metres (19,900 ft). From Camp I, climbers proceed up the Western Cwm to the base of the Lhotse Face, where Camp II or Advanced Base Camp (ABC) is established at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). The Western Cwm is a flat, gently rising glacial valley with large lateral crevasses in the center, preventing direct access; climbers cross near the base of Nuptse to a passage called the "Nuptse corner." This area is known as the "Valley of Silence" due to its windless conditions, though high altitude and clear, still air can make it unbearably hot. From Camp II, climbers ascend the Lhotse Face on fixed ropes to Camp III at 7,470 m (24,500 ft), then another 500 metres to Camp IV on the South Col at 7,920 m (26,000 ft). Between Camp III and Camp IV, climbers face the Geneva Spur—an anvil-shaped black rock named by the 1952 Swiss expedition—and the Yellow Band, a section of interlayered marble, phyllite, and semischist requiring about 100 metres of rope. On the South Col, climbers enter the death zone, where they typically endure no more than two or three days; if weather is poor with high winds, they must descend, often back to Base Camp. From Camp IV, climbers begin their summit push around midnight, aiming to reach the summit (another 1,000 metres above) within 10 to 12 hours. They first reach "The Balcony" at 8,400 m (27,600 ft), a small platform for rest and viewing, then climb over a series of imposing rock steps that force them into waist-deep snow, a serious avalanche hazard. At 8,750 m (28,700 ft), a small table-sized dome of ice and snow marks the South Summit. From there, climbers follow the knife-edge Southeast Ridge, known as the "Cornice traverse," where snow clings to rock; a misstep to the left would send one 2,400 m (7,900 ft) down the Southwest Face, while to the right is the 3,050 m (10,010 ft) Kangshung Face. At 8,790 m (28,840 ft), the 12 m (39 ft) rock wall known as the Hillary Step is encountered. Hillary and Tenzing were the first to ascend it using primitive ice climbing equipment; today, climbers use fixed ropes set up by Sherpas. Above the step, the climb to the summit is moderately angled snow slopes, though exposure is extreme, especially on large snow cornices. With increasing numbers climbing, the Step has become a bottleneck, causing long waits. After the Step, climbers traverse a loose, rocky section with fixed ropes that can be problematic in bad weather; they typically spend less than half an hour at the summit to descend to Camp IV before darkness or due to running out of oxygen. The North Ridge route begins in Tibet, with expeditions trekking to the Rongbuk Glacier and setting up base camp at 5,180 m (16,990 ft). To reach Camp II, climbers ascend the medial moraine of the east Rongbuk Glacier to the base of Changtse at around 6,100 m (20,000 ft). Camp III (ABC) is located below the North Col at 6,500 m (21,300 ft). Climbers ascend to the North Col at 7,010 m (23,000 ft) via fixed ropes, then climb the rocky North Ridge to Camp V at around 7,775 m (25,500 ft), crossing the North Face diagonally to Camp VI at 8,230 m (27,000 ft) before making the final summit push. Climbers face a treacherous traverse from the base of the First Step (8,501 to 8,534 m / 27,890 to 28,000 ft) to the Second Step (8,577 to 8,626 m / 28,140 to 28,300 ft), which includes the "Chinese ladder," a semi-permanent metal ladder placed in 1975 by Chinese climbers and used by virtually all climbers. After the Second Step, the Third Step (8,690 to 8,800 m / 28,510 to 28,870 ft) is climbed, followed by a 50-degree snow slope to the summit ridge. The summit is described as "the size of a dining room table," capped with snow over ice over rock, with snow layer variation from year to year; the rock summit is made of Ordovician limestone, a low-grade metamorphic rock. Below the summit is "rainbow valley," filled with dead bodies in brightly coloured gear, and down to about 8,000 m (26,000 ft) lies the "death zone" due to low oxygen and high danger. At these high altitudes, temperatures can drop to very low levels, causing frostbite, and snow is well-frozen, leading to slipping and falling. High winds are also a threat. Atmospheric pressure at the summit is about 0.333 standard atmospheres (337 mbar), providing only about a third as much oxygen. A sea-level dweller exposed to altitudes above 8,500 m (27,900 ft) without acclimatisation would lose consciousness in two to three minutes. Blood oxygen saturation drops from 98–99% at sea level to 85–87% at base camp and very low levels at the summit, resulting in breathing rates of 80–90 breaths per minute, leading to exhaustion. Lack of oxygen, exhaustion, extreme cold, and climbing hazards contribute to the death toll; injured climbers are often left behind, and as of 2015, over 200 bodies remain on the mountain. Debilitating symptoms of high-altitude cerebral oedema commonly appear during descent, with profound fatigue and late summit times linked to death. A 2008 study found most deaths occur in the death zone, especially during descent. A 2014 article noted that while falling is a major danger for all 8000ers, avalanches are more common at lower altitudes. Despite this, Everest is safer than peaks like Kangchenjunga, K2, Annapurna, Nanga Parbat, and Eiger (especially the nordwand) in some measures, depending on the period. Factors affecting lethality include mountain popularity, climber skill, and climb difficulty. Retinal haemorrhages, affecting up to a quarter of climbers, can damage eyesight and cause blindness; in 2010, a climber went blind and died in the death zone. A team tried to rescue a climber who became incapacitated but failed due to difficult terrain. Rescuing someone who is incapacitated is extremely difficult, and in 2011, two Nepali men paraglided off the summit after running out of oxygen and supplies, descending to Namche Bazaar in 42 minutes. Most expeditions use oxygen masks and tanks above 8,000 m (26,247 ft); while Everest can be climbed without oxygen, only the most accomplished climbers do so, and the death rate is double for those who attempt it without supplemental oxygen. Travelling above 8,000 m causes cerebral hypoxia; one study found that Mount Everest may be the highest an acclimatised human can reach, but climbers may suffer permanent neurological damage despite returning to lower altitudes. The use of bottled oxygen was first used in 1922 by George Finch and Geoffrey Bruce, who climbed to 8,100 m (26,600 ft) at 270 m/h (900 ft/h) with oxygen, though the Alpine world initially rejected it as unsportsmanlike. George Mallory later concluded that he could not summit without it and used oxygen in his 1924 attempt. When Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953, they used open-circuit oxygen, and Griffith Pugh called the debate a "futile controversy," noting oxygen enhances the climber's appreciation of surroundings. For 25 years, bottled oxygen was standard for summit success. Reinhold Messner became the first to climb Everest without oxygen in 1978 with Peter Habeler, and in 1980 he summited solo without oxygen or support on the northwest route. After the climbing community accepted oxygen-free ascents, many purists insisted it should be the norm. The 1996 disaster intensified the debate; Jon Krakauer criticized oxygen use, arguing it allowed unqualified climbers to attempt the summit, leading to dangerous situations and more deaths. The disaster was partly caused by 34 climbers attempting the ascent, causing bottlenecks at the Hillary Step and delays beyond the usual 14:00 turnaround. Krakauer proposed banning oxygen except in emergencies to reduce pollution and keep only qualified climbers on the mountain. The guide Anatoli Boukreev's decision not to use oxygen was criticized by Krakauer, who argued that without oxygen, Boukreev could not assist clients in descending; supporters claim oxygen gives a false sense of security. Low oxygen causes cognitive impairment, described as "bradypsychia," and in severe cases, hallucinations; some studies show altered brain structure in high-altitude climbers. Everest is also climbed in autumn (post-monsoon season), such as in 2010 when Eric Larsen and five Nepali guides summited after a ten-year gap; autumn is considered more dangerous due to unstable new snow, though it attracts winter sports like skiing and snowboarding. Two Japanese climbers summited in October 1973, and Chris Chandler and Bob Cormack did so in October 1976 as part of the American Bicentennial Expedition, the first American autumn ascent. By the 21st century, summer and autumn have become more popular for skiing and snowboarding. In the 1980s, autumn climbing was more popular than spring. U.S. astronaut Karl Gordon Henize died in October 1993 on an autumn expedition conducting a radiation experiment. Winter climbing is not popular due to cold, high winds, and short days; by January, summit winds reach 270 km/h (170 mph) and temperatures average −33°F (−36°C).
