Chris Chandler and Bob Cormack reached the summit of Mount Everest in October 1976 as part of the American Bicentennial Everest Expedition, becoming the first Americans to make an autumn ascent of the mountain, as reported by the Los Angeles Times. By the 21st century, summer and autumn have become more popular for skiing and snowboarding attempts on Everest. During the 1980s, autumn climbing was more popular than spring climbing. U.S. astronaut Karl Gordon Henize died in October 1993 during an autumn expedition, conducting a radiation experiment, as background radiation increases with higher altitudes. Mount Everest has also been climbed in winter, but this is not popular due to extreme cold, high winds, and short days; by January, the peak is typically exposed to 270 km/h (170 mph) winds and has an average summit temperature of −33 °F (−36 °C). Some climbers have reported life-threatening thefts from supply caches; in May 2006, Vitor Negrete, the first Brazilian to climb Everest without oxygen and a member of David Sharp's party, died during descent, and theft of gear and food from his high-altitude camp may have contributed. Michael Kodas, in his 2008 book *High Crimes: The Fate of Everest in an Age of Greed*, described unethical guides and Sherpas, prostitution and gambling at the Tibet Base Camp, fraud in oxygen bottle sales, and climbers collecting donations falsely claiming to remove trash. In 2007, the Chinese side of Everest was described as "out of control" after a Canadian had all his gear stolen and was abandoned by his Sherpa, though another Sherpa helped him escape safely and provided spare gear; other climbers have also reported missing oxygen bottles, which can be worth hundreds of dollars each, and hundreds of climbers pass by tents, making theft difficult to prevent; reports of oxygen bottle theft became more common in the late 2010s. By the end of the 2010 climbing season, there had been 5,104 ascents by about 3,142 individuals. Notable firsts include Lucy, Lady Houston, who funded the Houston Everest Flight of 1933, where a formation of airplanes led by the Marquess of Clydesdale flew over the summit to photograph the terrain. On 26 September 1988, Jean-Marc Boivin made the first paraglider descent of Everest via the Southeast Ridge, setting records for the fastest descent and the highest paraglider flight; he noted he was tired due to trail damage and difficulty running at that altitude. In 1991, four men in two balloons achieved the first hot-air balloon flight over Everest; one balloon carried Andy Elson and Eric Jones, the other Chris Dewhirst and Leo Dickinson, who later wrote a book titled *Ballooning Over Everest*; the balloons were modified to operate up to 12,000 m (40,000 ft); Reinhold Messner called one of Dickinson’s Kodachrome photos the "best snap on Earth"; Dewhirst offered to take passengers on a repeat for $2.6 million per person. In May 2005, French pilot Didier Delsalle landed a Eurocopter AS350 B3 on the summit to set FAI records for the highest landing and take-off, staying for about four minutes, twice; he had also landed on the South Col two days earlier, and the landing was confirmed by the FAI; during the flight, he rescued two Japanese climbers at 4,880 m (16,000 ft), with one noting the record improved rescue chances. On 21 May 2011, Nepali climbers Lakpa Tsheri Sherpa and Sano Babu Sunuwar paraglided from the summit to Namche Bazaar in 42 minutes, then hiked, biked, and kayaked to the Indian Ocean, reaching the Bay of Bengal by 27 June 2011, becoming the first people to complete a continuous summit-to-sea descent; Babu had never climbed before, and Lakpa had never kayaked or swam; the duo won National Geographic Adventurers of the Year in 2012; footage of the flight was shown on Nightline in 2013. In 2014, mountaineer Wang Jing led a team that used a helicopter to fly from South Base Camp to Camp II to avoid the Khumbu Icefall and then climbed to the summit, sparking controversy over the legitimacy and propriety of the climb; Nepal investigated her, and she initially denied flying to Camp II, admitting only that support crew were flown there, but later stated in August 2014 that she had flown to Camp II because the icefall was impassable, saying, "If you don't fly to Camp II, you just go home," and insisting she had not hidden the fact; her team used the south side because the Chinese denied them a permit, and this refusal may have benefited Nepal by allowing it to showcase improved hospitals and promote a hybrid aviation/mountaineering style, sparking discussions about helicopter use; National Geographic noted a village honored Wang with awards after she donated $30,000 to the town’s hospital; she won the International Mountaineer of the Year Award from Nepal in June 2014. In 2016, increased helicopter use was noted for greater efficiency and for hauling supplies over the deadly Khumbu Icefall, saving icefall porters 80 trips but still increasing commercial activity; after many deaths in the icefall in 2014, the Nepali government wanted helicopters to transport climbers to Camp 1, but this was blocked by the 2015 earthquake, so it was implemented in 2016 (helicopters were instrumental in rescues in 2015); in that summer, Bell tested the 412EPI, which hovered at 5,500 m (18,000 ft) and flew as high as 6,100 m (20,000 ft) near Everest. Mount Everest has hosted winter sports and adventures such as skiing, snowboarding, paragliding, and BASE jumping. Yuichiro Miura became the first man to ski down Everest in the 1970s, descending nearly 1,300 vertical meters (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with severe injuries; Stefan Gatt and Marco Siffredi snowboarded Everest in 2001; other skiers include Davo Karničar of Slovenia, who descended from the top to South Base Camp in 2000, Hans Kammerlander of Italy in 1996 on the north side, and Kit DesLauriers of the United States in 2006; Marco Siffredi died in 2002 during a second snowboarding expedition; in 2025, Andrzej Bargiel completed the first ski descent of Everest without supplemental oxygen. Gliding descents have become more popular, noted for rapid descents; in 1986, Steve McKinney led an Everest expedition; in 1988, Jean-Marc Boivin made the first paraglider descent from the Southeast Ridge to a lower camp; in 2011, Sano Babu Sunuwar and Lakpa Tsheri Sherpa made a gliding descent from the summit down 5,000 meters (16,400 ft) in 45 minutes. The southern part of Mount Everest is considered one of several "hidden valleys" of refuge designated by Padmasambhava, a ninth-century Buddhist saint. Near the north side of Everest lies Rongbuk Monastery, described as the "sacred threshold to Mount Everest" with dramatic views; it is a key pilgrimage site for Sherpas in the Khumbu region, accessible via Nangpa La. Miyolangsangma, a Tibetan Buddhist "Goddess of Inexhaustible Giving," is believed to reside at the top of Everest; Sherpa Buddhist monks believe Everest is her palace and playground, and climbers are only partially welcome guests who arrive without invitation. Sherpas believe the mountain and its slopes are blessed with spiritual energy, and one should show reverence when passing through, as karmic effects are magnified and impure thoughts are discouraged. In 2015, the president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association warned that pollution, especially human waste, had reached critical levels; up to 12,000 kg (26,500 lb) of human excrement is left behind each season; waste is scattered along the route, making sleeping areas minefields; climbers above Base Camp typically bury waste in snow, sling it into crevasses, or defecate where convenient, often within meters of their tents; the only safe place to defecate without contaminating the mountain is Base Camp, located at approximately 5,500 m (18,000 ft), which sees the most activity; in the late 1990s, expeditions began using toilets made from blue plastic 190-liter (50-US-gallon) barrels with seats and enclosures. The waste problem is worsened by non-human waste such as used oxygen tanks, abandoned tents, and empty cans and bottles; the Nepali government now requires each climber to pack out eight kilograms of waste when descending. In February 2019, China closed the base camp on its side of Everest to visitors without climbing permits, allowing tourists to go only as far as Rongbuk Monastery. In April 2019, the Khumbu Pasanglhamu Rural Municipality launched a campaign to collect nearly 10,000 kg (20,000 lb) of garbage from Everest; in 2024, waste removal continues to receive attention.

Mr. Mackey Jr. is a fictional character in the adult animated television series South Park, voiced by series co-creator Trey Parker and debuting in the season one episode "Mr. Hankey, the Christmas Poo." He serves as the school counselor at South Park Elementary and occasionally teaches classes there. Known for ending or beginning most of his sentences with "m'kay," he is based on Parker's junior high school counselor Stan Lackey. Mackey has a disproportionately large head due to the tightness of his tie, wears a green long-sleeved shirt, a blue tie, dark blue pants, blue leather shoes, and black-rimmed glasses, and speaks with a Southern accent. He has black yet thinning hair. According to "Insheeption," Mackey was most likely born in 1965, placing him in Generation X, a conclusion supported by references to the 1980s in episodes like "Back to the Cold War" (e.g., his childhood bedroom, the WarGames parody, and dancing to Wang Chung's "Dance Hall Days" during a duck and cover drill) and "Taming Strange" (where 1980s songs like Lionel Richie's "All Night Long (All Night)" and Glenn Frey's "The Heat Is On" play from his computer). Mackey taught sex education with Ms. Choksondik, with whom he had a sexual relationship until her death, after which he took over the fourth-grade class until Mr. Garrison returned. In "Ike's Wee Wee," he taught Mr. Garrison's class about drugs, smoking, and alcohol, but was fired after marijuana he distributed to students was stolen by Mr. Garrison, leading to his eviction by his landlord and subsequent depression and drug use. He holds generally left-wing political views, as seen in his protest against the Iraq War in the season seven episode "I'm a Little Bit Country," but in season twelve's "About Last Night," he is shown supporting John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign and expressing disappointment upon his loss, and he signs up for I.C.E. in "Got a Nut." It was presumed in "Proper Condom Use" that his last sexual encounter was 21 years prior, when he was 19. In "Something You Can Do with Your Finger" and "Cat Orgy," it is hinted that bondage sex scenes occurred between Mackey and Liane Cartman, with the former featuring Eric Cartman watching a tape of Mackey and Liane, where the latter drinks from a cup of her own urine, and the latter showing Mackey flirting with Liane. In "Insheeption," it is revealed that Mackey is a hoarder due to a troubled childhood as a fourth-grader in 1974, when he was bullied and a fan of Woodsy Owl, and after the owl molested him during a field trip, he threatened to rape Stan Marsh in the mouth if Stan threw any clutter from his office. In "Trapped in the Closet," Mackey is shown as a member of the Church of Scientology, though this is not mentioned again later. He is fluent in Spanish, as demonstrated in "Rainforest Shmainforest." Unlike many major adult characters, his first name remains unknown.

Muhammad Ayub Sheikh is a Pakistani politician who served as a member of the National Assembly of Pakistan from 2008 to 2013. He was elected in the 2008 Pakistani general election as a candidate of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) from Constituency NA-254 (Karachi-XVI). During the election, he received 132,648 votes and defeated Syed Suhail Abrar, who ran as a candidate for the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP).

Mukul Chandra Dey (23 July 1895 – 1 March 1989) was one of five children of Purnashashi Devi and Kula Chandra Dey. He studied at Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan and is recognized as a pioneer of drypoint-etching in India. The entire Dey family exhibited artistic talent, with his brother Manishi Dey becoming a well-known painter and his sisters, Annapura and Rani Chanda, excelling in arts and crafts. Mukul Dey married Bina Roy from Khanakul, Bengal; they had one daughter, Manjari, affectionately named Bukuma, who later married Shantanu Ukil, a leading painter of the Bengal School of Art. He was the first Indian artist to travel abroad specifically to study printmaking. In 1916, while in Japan, he studied under Yokoyama Taikan and Kanzan Shimomura in Tokyo and Yokohama, and during his stay at Tomitaro Hara’s Sankeien, he lived with Rabindranath Tagore and studied classical Chinese and Nihonga style Japanese paintings, particularly the works of Sesshu Toyo. After returning to India, Dey trained in etching in Chicago under James Blanding Sloan and Bertha Jaques, introduced by American artists Roi Partridge and Imogen Cunningham, and remained a life-member of the Chicago Society of Etchers. In 1920, he traveled again to study etching and engraving under Frank Short and Muirhead Bone at the Slade School of Fine Art and the Royal College of Art in London, where he studied under Professor Henry Tonks. An exhibition of his drawings and paintings, including ten copies of Ajanta and one of Bagh Caves paintings, was held at 59 Onslow Square, London, on 4 February 1924, with the assistance of Lady Grant; his work had previously been displayed at the Royal Academy and the New English Art Club. According to Polish sculptor Stanislaw Szukalski, when Mukul was in America, he showed him his drawings, which impressed Szukalski, who then advised him against going to Paris to "finish his study," warning that such a move would lead to blind admiration for movements like Kandinski and Picasso, and urged Mukul to develop self-confidence to view European art with contempt and select only worthy examples. This advice convinced Mukul to return to Santiniketan, to Tagore’s delight. Dey used a Western medium—drypoint etching—to portray Indian life, unlike Haren Das, whose woodcut technique was more indigenous. His subjects included river scenes in Bengal, traditional baul singers, Calcutta markets, and the lives of Santhal villagers in Birbhum near Santiniketan. He was an active member of the Vichitra Club at Jorasanko, where young artists like Nandalal Bose, Asit Kumar Haldar, and Narayan Kashinath Deval were encouraged to experiment with new art forms. In 1925, Dey published a book on the Ajanta and Bagh cave paintings, which inspired him deeply, and later illustrated and published several other books. In 1928, he was appointed the first Indian Principal of the Government School of Art, Calcutta, where he removed teachers closely associated with Company School painting and established a women's section, previously open only to men. Gracefully drawn images of Bengali villagers in dry-point have become his most recognized works, with some pieces hand-coloured using watercolors, coloured pencils, or thin ink washes. He is also remembered for portraits of prominent Indian figures, including members of the Tagore and Tata families, Albert Einstein, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, and Josephine MacLeod, the promoter of Swami Vivekananda’s Ramakrishna order at Belur Math—MacLeod having first brought Okakura Kakuzo to India in 1901–1902. Manishi Dey, Mukul’s younger brother, was a member of the Progressive Artists' Group and a prominent painter of the Bengal School of Art, traveling extensively throughout India in contrast to his more steady brother. Dey’s works are held in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, the Indian Museum, Kolkata, the National Gallery of Modern Art in Mumbai, and the National Gallery of Art in New Delhi. The Mukul Dey Archives are preserved at Chitralekha, his former home in Santiniketan. He also served as an illustrator for several book projects, including the scholarly work *Shantiniketan Bolpur School of Rabindranath Tagore*, which he illustrated for the later Nobel Prize winner in 1916.

On 23 November 2022, dairy worker Janak Patel was murdered during a robbery at the Rose Cottage Superette in Sandringham, Auckland, New Zealand. The incident occurred at 8pm when Patel, a recent Indian migrant who had moved to Auckland from Hamilton just days before, and his wife were in a backroom living area of the store when masked offender Frederick Gilbert Hobson, an Ōtāhuhu resident repatriated from Australia, entered armed with a knife. Hobson had been stalking the area for 45 minutes, hiding in a telephone booth, and after confronting Patel, used a knife to attack him, stabbing him six times, including in the chest and back. Patel managed to fight back with a hockey stick, wrestled with Hobson, and was forced to the ground before being stabbed in the neck. Hobson fled with the stolen cash register, which was later found in a rubbish bin, and the suspect was confronted by Patel, who provided a description to police. On 24 November, police released images of the suspect, described as wearing a black cap, black and white bandanna, dark top, and black trousers emblazoned with "Raiders," and launched a homicide investigation, confirming they were hunting for a lone man. By 25 November, police had identified two suspects from CCTV footage showing two men and a black car, later confirmed as a dark-coloured Honda Inspire, and arrested them; a 34-year-old man was charged with murder and aggravated robbery, and a 42-year-old man with robbery. On 27 November, a 36-year-old man was charged with robbery. The three defendants appeared in the Auckland High Court on 14 December 2022, where the 34-year-old man (interim name suppression) and 42-year-old Shane Tane pleaded not guilty to robbery and murder charges, while Henry Ford, the third defendant, was granted a stay of proceedings due to terminal illness. On 8 March 2023, Fred and Tane had their charges upgraded from aggravated robbery to murder, and Hobson's name suppression lapsed. On 13 March 2024, Frederick Hobson pleaded guilty to murder and aggravated robbery. On 26 June 2024, Hobson was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum non-parole period of 15 years, and Shane Tane was sentenced to four years and six months for aggravated robbery. Henry Ford remained in stay of proceedings. Hobson's lawyer stated he was ashamed and remorseful, citing homelessness, unemployment, and drug addiction as contributing factors. Victim impact statements were heard during sentencing. In response to the incident, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern faced criticism from ACT Party leader David Seymour for not visiting Sandringham or postponing her trip to the Chatham Islands, which she defended by stating she had consulted community leaders and did not want to interfere with the investigation. On 26 November, Ardern met with Patel’s family and community leaders, acknowledged police efforts, and confirmed the government was investigating ways to support small businesses with security measures. On 28 November, the government announced a new retail crime package including a fog cannon subsidy scheme, a NZ$4 million fund for local councils in Auckland, Hamilton, and the Bay of Plenty, and expanded eligibility of the existing NZ$6 million Retail Crime Prevention Fund to include aggravated robberies. Dairy and Business Owners Association chairperson Sunny Kaushal announced a nationwide protest following Patel’s funeral, with thousands of dairies and small businesses ceasing operations for at least two hours, and called for self-defence laws to allow owners to use "acceptable force." Sandringham Business Association chair Jithin Chittibomma criticized the government for ignoring retail concerns. On 26 November, the Migrant Workers Association held a candlelit vigil outside the store, and on 28 November, the Dairy and Business Owners Group staged a nationwide protest, including a vigil outside Ardern’s electorate office in Mt Albert and others across the country. By 3 December, a Givealittle page had raised NZ$91,000 for Patel’s family, and by 23 December, over NZ$100,000 had been raised. In March 2022, Stuff reported a surge in retail crime including "ram raids," shoplifting, and repeat offending, prompting businesses to deploy countermeasures such as stab-proof vests, radios, body cameras, automatic number plate recognition, and facial recognition systems. In response, the New Zealand Police created a national retail investigation unit, which by October 2022 had dealt with over 70 offenders and laid nearly 600 charges. A University of Otago study estimated retail theft cost retailers NZ$1 billion annually and that retailers spent NZ$500 million a year on security, with retail crime costing the average household NZ$800 per year. Retail NZ chief executive Greg Harford estimated retail crime cost the average household NZ$800 annually. According to Kaushal, dairy and convenience store theft increased by 30 percent (1,402 offences) in the first 11 months of 2021 compared to 2020, while arrests for such crimes declined by 23 percent. The New Zealand Herald reported that retail crime incidents, including shoplifting and "ram raids," had doubled from 4,000 to under 8,000 between 2017 and the first six months of 2022, citing Police data. A 2019 Retail NZ survey estimated that 70% of retail crime was unreported. Police attributed the increase to improved reporting, while the National Party blamed it on Labour’s "soft on crime" policies. By late August 2022, police secured NZ$6 million in government funding for the Small Retailer Crime Prevention Fund to help small businesses install countermeasures such as shatterproof glass, bollards, fog cannons, and roller doors. Companies also hired door staff to deter offenders. In December 2014, Australia amended its Migration Act 1958 to make it easier to deport non-citizens imprisoned for at least one year. By March 2022, 2,544 New Zealanders had been deported from Australia over seven years, contributing to a surge in crime including over 2,000 dishonesty convictions, 1,387 violent crime convictions, 861 drug and anti-social behavior offenses, and 57 sexual crime offenses. Several Australian-based bikie gangs, including the Comanchero and Mongols, expanded into New Zealand. Police Commissioner Andrew Coster and National Party leader Christopher Luxon attributed the rising crime and gang membership to the repatriation of New Zealand deportees from Australia.

On 16 September 2021, Lauren Anne Dickason, a South African immigrant, murdered her three daughters—6-year-old Liané and 2-year-old twins Maya and Karla—at her home in Timaru, New Zealand. After admitting to the killings, she denied murder and instead pleaded insanity or infanticide. She was found guilty of murdering her three children on 16 August 2023 and sentenced on 26 June 2024 to 18 years in prison, with no minimum term and will remain in a mental health hospital until deemed mentally fit for prison. Dickason is the daughter of Malcolm and Wendy Fawkes. She attended a boarding school in Pretoria, South Africa, and from age 15 experienced depression and anxiety, along with post-natal depression. She studied medicine at the University of Cape Town, graduating in 2004, and completed rural health practice in Pretoria, where she met her husband Graham Dickason, an orthopaedic surgeon, in 2005. They married in 2006. Dickason faced multiple fertility issues, undergoing 17 rounds of IVF and using donor eggs; she had her first child, Sarah, in 2013, who died shortly after birth, prompting her to stop working and become a part-time surgeon assistant to Graham. She later had three more children: Liané, born in September 2014, and twins Maya and Karla, born in November 2018. Following the twins' birth, the family hired a nanny, Maria Mendy Sibanyoni, who worked from November 2018 to May 2020. Dickason was diagnosed in 2015 with "major depression with underlying anxiety," linked to postpartum depression following Sarah’s death, and experienced flashbacks, sleep difficulties, crying, suicidal thoughts, panic attacks, restlessness, detachment, and intrusive thoughts. Anxiety and depression also affected her during and after the birth of the twins, due to Karla’s cleft palate. In May 2019, after struggling to put her twins to bed, she saw a psychiatrist and reported homicidal thoughts, citing Karla’s frequent outbursts, including slapping and biting, and stating her children were "never enough." The family planned to emigrate to New Zealand in August 2020 but faced delays due to the global COVID-19 pandemic and immigration issues. Though she experienced depression and suicidal thoughts during the pandemic, her mood improved between late 2020 and June 2021, with the Crown claiming a remission lasting at least two months. Dickason stopped taking her antidepressants in March 2021 without consulting her doctor but resumed them in August 2021. Her mental health worsened in July 2021 during South African unrest following Jacob Zuma’s imprisonment, leading her to fear for her children’s safety and have thoughts of harming them; she confided in Graham, who convinced her to restart medication. She continued to have homicidal thoughts after a foot surgery but did not disclose them due to concerns about immigration plans. In July 2021, a friend sent her a TikTok video titled "Mom needs a minute," which she responded to by saying "Awesome xxx, that's exactly how I feel." Over the following months, she searched online for methods to overdose her children. In August 2021, after seeing her husband and daughters play with cable ties in the garage, she had thoughts of using them to asphyxiate her children, two weeks before the family moved to New Zealand. She became withdrawn, cried frequently, and her mother Wendy noted significant weight loss. The family arrived in Timaru on 11 September 2021, five days before the killings, and Dickason was unhappy with the town, describing it as "small, disgusting and creepy," fearing cyberbullying for her children and comparing New Zealand’s treatment of Māori to apartheid in South Africa. Defence experts stated these concerns became delusions reinforced by her depression. The children were murdered on the night of 16 September 2021. On that day, Karla and Maya attended their first day at preschool and Liané attended her second day at Timaru Christian School. After picking up her daughters, Karla threw a tantrum in the car. The family visited the local botanical gardens, where Dickason believed a group of girls warned her that a boy was photographing her children, leading her to believe New Zealand was as dangerous as South Africa. That day, she had thoughts of "brutally killing" the children by sedating them and cutting their femoral arteries. Graham went out with colleagues, leaving Lauren alone with the children. During a police interview, she told detectives the children were "being wild again, jumping on the couches, not listening to what I'm trying to tell them" and that "something just triggered me." She later told investigators that the trigger was an Immigration NZ request for medical information about Karla’s cleft palate and her own mental health, and her feeling she couldn’t make the children’s school lunches. After gathering the children in a bedroom, she told them they were making necklaces with cable ties and tricked them into wearing the ties around their necks, telling them "Mummy's very sick and is going to die. I can't leave you behind because I don't know who’s going to look after you." She then asphyxiated the children, starting with Karla, then Liané and Maya. She told police that Karla had been "really horrible" and that Liané had fought back, recalling that the oldest child was angry and asked why she was doing this, saying she loved her and was the best mum. Since the children were still breathing, she smothered them with a towel and their blankets. Afterwards, she attempted suicide with a knife and pills. The bodies were discovered in their beds by Graham upon returning home. He confronted a distraught Dickason, who told him it was "too late" before falling into a catatonic state. At 10 pm on 16 September 2021, police responded to a call from neighbours Karen and Brad Cowper, who found Graham distraught. At the house, police found the three dead children and Lauren Dickason, who was hospitalised in stable condition. Graham’s colleague Mark Cvitanich and his wife Cathy also responded to Graham’s phone call and called police and emergency services. Dickason was taken to Timaru Hospital. On 17 September, police interviewed Dickason, who admitted to killing her three children. Detective Inspector Scott Anderson confirmed the arrest of a 40-year-old woman in connection with the deaths and stated the incident was isolated and no one else was being sought. On 18 September, Dickason appeared in the Timaru District Court and was remanded to a forensic psychiatric ward at Christchurch’s Hillmorton Hospital, later placed in a hospital psychiatric unit. At Hillmorton, she was interviewed by five forensic psychiatrists and psychologists for 53 hours. Three—Susan Hatters-Friedman, Justin Barry-Walsh, and Ghazi Metoui—believed she was severely mentally unwell and could claim a defence of insanity or infanticide. The other two, Erik Monasterio and Simone McLeavey, believed she killed her children out of anger and control, including not wanting another woman to parent them if she died or Graham remarried. On 5 October 2021, her lawyer Kerryn Beaton QC sought an extended remand, delaying her court appearance due to a mental health assessment. On 15 October, Beaton told the Christchurch court that Dickason would plead not guilty to three charges of murder. She was unable to attend due to illness and sought further remand, which was not opposed by Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. A trial date for March 2023 was set. The trial began on 17 July 2023 at the Christchurch High Court, presided over by Judge Cameron Mander and with Andrew McRae as Crown prosecutor. McRae detailed the circumstances of the deaths and Dickason’s attempted suicide, while defence lawyer Anne Toohey outlined the defence’s arguments. The Crown argued Dickason murdered her children due to resentment over their impact on her marriage, while Dickason denied murder due to insanity or infanticide. Testimony included Graham, emergency responders, and the children’s teachers, along with digital forensic evidence and Dickason’s police interview. On 26 July, the Crown rested its case. Defence counsel Toohey argued that Dickason’s decision to kill her children was "spontaneous" because she believed her and the children’s lives were not worth living and that they were "all better off dead." The defence relied on expert witnesses: Dr Susan Hatters-Friedman, Dr Justin Barry-Walsh, and Dr Ghazi Metoui. The prosecution called Dr Erik Monasterio and Dr Simone McLeavey. On 11 August, McRae delivered his closing address, stating Dickason knew her actions were morally wrong and that the key drivers were "anger and control." He emphasized that the trial was by jury, not experts, and that defence experts had not assessed her at the time of the killing, while the Crown had. The Crown argued defence experts ignored crucial information and that Dickason’s accounts were inconsistent. It claimed postpartum depression had remitted and was at best a minimal contributor. The Crown said the defence experts’ evidence should be treated with caution, noting Dickason reported killing Karla first due to her misbehaviour, such as biting and scratching. The defence countered that Karla was killed first because she was closest to Dickason. When asked if postpartum depression caused the killings, Dickason said "no," and that the idea "just popped up," though the Crown later stated the thoughts did not just appear. The defence’s closing address, starting at 2:30 pm, mentioned her 16 rounds of IVF, the family’s move to New Zealand to provide a better life for the children, the world being dangerous for them, postpartum depression after the twins’ birth, her severe mental illness, her husband’s lack of understanding, her reliability and consistency with experts, that she was not asked by police why she killed them, and that she did not tell anyone she killed them out of anger. The defence also noted her brother, sister, or close family could have provided context. On the fifth week, Justice Mander summed up the case, discussing the police interview the day after the deaths and instructing the jury not to let emotion—such as sympathy or media-driven prejudice—alter their judgment. He noted there was no dispute that Dickason caused the deaths, and the issue was whether it was murder, infanticide, or insanity due to an undisputed mental imbalance. He summarised the expert evidence. On 16 August 2023, Dickason was found guilty of three counts of murder after 15 hours of deliberation, with a 11-1 majority verdict rejecting infanticide and insanity defences and accepting the Crown’s argument that she acted "methodically, purposefully and even clinically out of anger and control." Dickason stood motionless as the verdict was delivered and wept as she was led out. Both her lawyers and several jurors wept. Justice Mander remanded her to Hillmorton Hospital under a compulsory treatment order, stating prison was inappropriate and requested expert reports on her mental state and an appropriate sentence. Her parents, Malcolm and Wendy Fawkes, issued a statement blaming postpartum depression for the deaths of their grandchildren and urged greater awareness of its effects. The judge sought to determine the sentence length and type following a mental health assessment. The Sentencing Act presumes life imprisonment for murder unless it would be "manifestly unjust." The decision on whether Dickason would serve time in prison or remain in a psychiatric unit has not yet been made. She will not be extradited to South Africa. In early September 2023, her sentencing date was set for 19 December 2023, later postponed to 2024, then to 20 March, and finally rescheduled to 26 June due to delays in determining her placement. Until then, she remained at Hillmorton Hospital. On 26 June 2024, she was sentenced to 18 years in prison as three concurrent determinate sentences, with no minimum term and will remain in a mental health hospital until deemed mentally fit. During sentencing, victim impact statements from family members, including Graham and both paternal and maternal relatives, were read. Dickason has been served with a deportation order that will take effect upon her release. In early August 2024, her legal team lodged an appeal against the conviction in the New Zealand Court of Appeal on 23 July; the grounds have not been disclosed. If successful, a second trial could occur. The New Zealand government granted $709,000 for Dickason’s defence, including $153,970 for three psychiatric or psychological reports and $71,062.50 for other expenses.

On 26 June 2024, Lauren Dickason was sentenced to 18 years in prison, consisting of three concurrent determinate sentences of 18 years, with no minimum term of imprisonment. She will remain in Hillmorton Hospital until deemed mentally fit for prison. During the sentencing, she remained silent and showed no reaction, and victim impact statements from her family members, including Graham and both paternal and maternal relatives, were read. A deportation order has been served against her, which will take effect upon her release from prison. On 23 July 2024, her legal team lodged an appeal in the New Zealand Court of Appeal, though the grounds have not been disclosed; if successful, a second trial could occur. The New Zealand government provided $709,000 for her defence, including $153,970 for three psychiatric or psychological reports, $71,062.50 for a forensic psychologist, $58,700.81 for expert witnesses, $39,945.78 for other witness disbursements, $6,367.50 for a private investigator, $9,480 for computer forensics, and $3,000 for expert legal opinion. Her legal team spent 1714.25 hours on the defence, with Crown Solicitor Andrew McRae spending 732.5 hours. On 18 September 2021, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) assisted the Dickason family's relatives in traveling to New Zealand and securing managed isolation under COVID-19 quarantine rules. The former nanny Mari Sibanyoni expressed shock and grief upon learning of the children's deaths. On 23 September 2021, a candelight vigil was held in Timaru’s Queen Street in honour of Lianne, Maya, and Karla Dickason, during which Graham read a letter expressing forgiveness for his wife and thanking friends and family, and a similar service was held in Pretoria; Graham returned to South Africa in December 2021. Neighbours Rob and Jade Whaley built a memorial garden in Timaru, including an "Angel Dickason tree" with three white stones in memory of the girls. The Independent Online’s Jehran Naidoo compared Dickason to American mother Andrea Yates, noting both suffered from mental illness and post-partum depression, had experienced previous miscarriages, had professionally-accomplished husbands, and killed their children while their husbands were away. In mid-August 2023, Timaru Mayor Nigel Bowen welcomed the jury’s guilty verdict, stating it ended a dark period for the town and urged community members to check on one another, emphasizing that mental health was still stigmatized. Judge Mander, Detective Inspector Scott Anderson, chaplain Alan Cummings, and South Canterbury Chief Medical Officer Dr Ben Pearson all extended sympathies to the victims’ families and welcomed the verdict as closure. Current affairs bloggers David Farrar and Martyn "Bomber" Bradbury described the verdict as justice for the deceased children. Following her conviction, supporters established a Facebook group called "Support for Lauren Dickason" in July 2022, which grew to over 1,900 members from multiple countries, mostly women, with the spokesperson stating the verdict had silenced women’s voices. The group planned a march and picnic in Christchurch in November 2023, walking from the justice precinct to the Botanic Gardens with "support not silence" T-shirts and sunflowers, and holding a picnic in support of maternal mental health. Supporter Tanya Parker organized a petition urging Judge Mander to consider postpartum depression in sentencing and for the legal profession to recognize it as a public health crisis. The group also produced a 370-page book of supportive letters titled 'Lauren: Our love and support,' which was sent to Dickason on the second anniversary of the children’s deaths. In early October, The Press reported that Dickason wrote a letter to her supporters thanking them for their love during a difficult time, revealing she had made three teddy bears from her daughters’ clothing and stated she could never forgive herself for what happened. In response to media attention, Hillmorton Hospital restricted her communications, banning letters during the sentencing period, though these restrictions were later lifted, allowing her to receive letters again.

doc_name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Buenos Aires)
text: The National Museum of Fine Arts (Spanish: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes) is an Argentine art museum located in Buenos Aires, in the Recoleta section. It opened on 25 December 1895 in a building on Florida Street, which is now home to the Galerías Pacífico shopping mall. Eduardo Schiaffino, an Argentine painter and art critic, was its first director. In 1909, the museum moved to a building in Plaza San Martín, originally constructed in Paris as the Argentine Pavilion for the 1889 Paris exhibition, which was later dismantled and relocated to Buenos Aires. The museum participated in the International Centenary Exhibition in Buenos Aires in 1910. After the pavilion was demolished in 1932 as part of Plaza San Martín's remodeling, the museum relocated to its current site in 1943, a building initially built in 1870 as a drainage pumping station and adapted for its use by architect Alejandro Bustillo. During the 1955–64 period under director Jorge Romero Brest, the museum underwent physical and collection modernization. A temporary exhibits pavilion opened in 1961, and the museum acquired a significant amount of modern art through collaboration with the Torcuato di Tella Institute and other sources; a contemporary Argentine art pavilion opened in 1980. This 1,536 square metres (16,533 sq ft) hall is the largest of 34 currently in use, with the museum’s total exhibit space amounting to 4,610 square metres (49,622 sq ft). Its permanent collection includes 688 major works and over 12,000 sketches, fragments, potteries, and other minor works. The institution also maintains a specialized library with 150,000 volumes and a public auditorium. The museum commissioned architect Mario Roberto Álvarez to design a branch in Neuquén, inaugurated in 2004, which features four exhibit halls totaling 2,500 square metres (26,910 sq ft), a permanent collection of 215 works, temporary exhibits, and a public auditorium. The ground floor contains 24 exhibit halls with a fine international collection of paintings from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, along with the museum’s art history library. The first floor has eight exhibit halls showcasing works by prominent 20th-century Argentine painters, including Antonio Berni, Ernesto de la Cárcova, Benito Quinquela Martín, Eduardo Sívori, Sarah Grilo, Alfredo Guttero, Raquel Forner, Xul Solar, Marcelo Pombo, and Lino Enea Spilimbergo. The second floor, with two halls completed in 1984, features a photography exhibition, two sculpture terraces, and houses most of the institution’s administrative and technical departments.

The Museum of Recent Art (Romanian: Muzeul de Artă Recentă, or MARe) is a contemporary art museum situated in Bucharest, Romania, within the Primăverii district. Its collection includes over 1,000 artworks by more than 250 Romanian and international artists, spanning more than 150 pieces displayed across a five-level, 1,200 square meter facility. The term "recent" primarily denotes the temporal scope of the collection, covering Romanian art from the post-Stalinist period to the present, with international art featured through temporary exhibitions. The museum is designed to be more open and accessible than traditional Romanian museums, offering a library and other cultural spaces for the community. The building was constructed on the site of an interwar villa that previously stood in the area, which had architectural influences from Western (Moorish) design. This villa was demolished, and the museum's guided tours incorporate its historical narrative, including the fact that Ana Pauker, a prominent Communist Party leader during the proletkultist era, once lived there. There are also references to underground tunnels beneath the villa, contributing to its historical significance. The architectural design, by Youssef Tohme Architects & Associates, features a unified monolithic structure made of dark-colored brick resting on a fully glazed space, creating a large, open atrium facing the street. Notable artists represented in the collection include Ion Țuculescu, Andrei Cădere, Horia Bernea, Ion Grigorescu, Dan Perjovschi, Hermann Nitsch, Lucio Fontana, and Michelangelo Pistoletto.

The music for the Kingdom Hearts video game series was composed by Yoko Shimomura, with orchestral arrangements handled by Kaoru Wada. The original soundtracks have been released on three albums and a fourth compilation album. The series features musical pieces from both Square Enix and Disney, including "Mickey Mouse Club March" by Jimmie Dodd, "This Is Halloween" by Danny Elfman, and "One-Winged Angel" by Nobuo Uematsu, as well as well-known Disney film tracks such as "Winnie the Pooh" by Robert B. Sherman and Richard M. Sherman, "He's a Pirate" by Geoff Zanelli, Klaus Badelt, and Hans Zimmer, "Beauty and the Beast" by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, "Night on Bald Mountain" (rendered as "A Night on the Bare Mountain") by Modest Mussorgsky, and a remixed version of "One-Winged Angel" by Nobuo Uematsu. Several vocal songs are included, most notably the four main theme songs: "Hikari", "Passion", "Chikai", and "Face My Fears", with the two main themes written and performed by Japanese American pop star Hikaru Utada. The Japanese versions of "Hikari" and "Passion" are the theme songs for the Japanese releases of Kingdom Hearts and Kingdom Hearts II, respectively, while their English counterparts, "Simple and Clean" and "Sanctuary", are used for international releases and the Japanese re-release of the first game, Kingdom Hearts Final Mix. The songs share a similar melody but differ in lyrical meaning, with "Simple and Clean" not being a literal translation of "Hikari". "Hikari" was released in Japan on March 20, 2002, and sold over 270,000 copies in one week; "Simple and Clean" was included in Utada's single "Colors", which debuted at number one on Japan's Oricon charts and stayed for 19 weeks, and later appeared as a bonus track on Utada's 2009 English-language album This Is the One. Both songs have "PLANITb remix" versions and "Hikari" has a "Godson Mix", used at different points in the game. "Passion" was released on December 14, 2005, and "Sanctuary" was first previewed on MTV.com in early 2006; both the "Opening" and "After the Battle" versions of "Sanctuary" were released in May 2009 as bonus tracks on Utada's second American album, This Is the One. The "After the Battle" versions of "Passion" and "Sanctuary" serve as the ending theme songs for Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance. The music ranges from dark to cheerful to sorrowful and includes original tracks such as the title screen track "Dearly Beloved", and the theme songs "Simple and Clean" and "Sanctuary". The main themes are pop songs, distinct from the rest of the music, which features a mix of piano and orchestral pieces. Kingdom Hearts II includes vocal songs like "Part of Your World" and "Under the Sea" from The Little Mermaid, composed by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman. Yoko Shimomura began composing video game music in 1988, joined Square in 1993, and left in 2002 to work freelance. She draws inspiration from travel and emotional experiences and respects solo and orchestral works such as Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 7, Chopin's Ballade No. 1, and Ravel's La Valse. She was initially hesitant to compose for Kingdom Hearts due to the mix of Square's narrative and Disney characters, but enjoyed arranging Disney themes and worked to preserve their original mood while adapting to the PlayStation 2's technical limitations, such as using a trial-and-error method for "This Is Halloween". She created original music to accompany gameplay and felt emotions like happiness and sadness in fight music, discussing ideas with director Tetsuya Nomura and game planners. For Kingdom Hearts coded, 358/2 Days, and Birth by Sleep, she composed the main themes while others handled the rest. She has stated that the series successfully combined scenes and music and feels honored that her music has resonated with fans. Hikaru Utada was chosen by Nomura as the only singer for the first theme song due to her ability to cross language and cultural barriers, and her involvement was announced in January 2002. Her participation in the sequel was announced in July 2005, and Nomura chose not to use a different singer for the second theme because fans associated Utada with the series. Utada drew inspiration from the game's worlds and characters and received story explanations from Nomura, who noted that the second theme tied more closely to the game's narrative than the first. The music has been released in various formats, with the first soundtrack released in Japan, the United States, and Europe on March 27, 2002 (Japan), November 25, 2002 (Europe), and March 23, 2003 (United States), and subsequent albums released only in Japan. The first soundtrack is a 2-CD set containing most of the original game's music, with bonus tracks, composed by Shimomura, vocals by Utada for "Simple and Clean" and "Hikari", and orchestral arrangements by Wada performed by the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra. The soundtrack was released after Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, so it does not include additional tracks from that version. The soundtrack received positive reviews, with IGN ranking "Dearly Beloved" as number four on their top ten RPG title tracks, being nominated for the "Best Sound in a PlayStation 2 Game Editor's Choice Award" and runner-up for the "Best Sound in Game 2002 Reader's Choice Award", and rated 3 out of 5 by Allmusic. GameSpy described it as "pleasant, melodious, and fitting for the various situations" and praised the English version of "Simple and Clean". The Kingdom Hearts Final Mix Additional Tracks CD, released in Japan on December 26, 2002, features new tracks from the re-release. The Kingdom Hearts II Original Soundtrack, released in Japan on January 25, 2006, contains music composed and produced by Shimomura, with orchestral arrangements by Wada performed by the Tokyo Philharmonic Orchestra and vocals by Utada for "Passion". It received positive critical reception, with G4TV awarding it "Best Soundtrack" at the 2006 G-Phoria awards, GameSpy noting it was not as strong as the first soundtrack, Game Informer calling it "unforgettable", and GameSpot praising it as a "superb soundtrack" and rating it 9 out of 10. The Kingdom Hearts Original Soundtrack Complete is a nine-disc compilation released in Japan on March 28, 2007, containing music from Kingdom Hearts, Chain of Memories, and Kingdom Hearts II, with unreleased tracks, new and rearranged versions from Final Mix releases and Re:Chain of Memories. It includes printed images on each disc and a deluxe booklet with illustrations by Tetsuya Nomura and comments from Shimomura, and a special CD case featuring Sora and Roxas artwork. Discs one and two contain unaltered tracks from the original soundtrack, discs three to six contain longer, looped tracks from Kingdom Hearts II, discs seven and eight contain tracks from Re:Chain of Memories, and disc nine contains bonus tracks from Final Mix versions. On May 27, 2009, Square Enix released a piano arrangement album of popular pieces selected by members of their music website, with a preview concert in Tokyo attended by lottery winners; Shimomura described it as consisting of easy listening piano solo arrangements, with tracks 5 through 8 forming a sonata on the series' themes. "The Other Promise" and "Roxas" are used in a cutscene of Kingdom Hearts Re:coded in Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 ReMIX, and the Piano Collections arrangement of "Dearly Beloved" appears in the title screen of Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 ReMIX, HD 2.5 ReMIX, HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, and HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX. Piano Collections Kingdom Hearts Field & Battle, released in Japan on January 13, 2010, features battle and world themes arranged by Sachiko Miyano and Natsumi Kameoka. Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep & 358/2 Days Original Soundtrack, released on February 2, 2011, features music from Birth by Sleep, 358/2 Days, and Re:coded, composed by Shimomura, Takeharu Ishimoto, and Tsuyoshi Sekito, with discs one and two containing music from Birth by Sleep and disc three containing music from 358/2 Days (tracks 1–13), Re:coded (tracks 14–20), and Birth by Sleep: Final Mix (tracks 21–27); the 358/2 Days and Re:coded tracks are in pure orchestrated form. Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance Original Soundtrack, released on April 18, 2012, includes tracks from The World Ends with You, remixed by Ishimoto, with orchestral arrangements by Wada. Kingdom Hearts 10th Anniversary Fan Selection: Melodies & Memories, released in Japan on September 19, 2012, features tracks chosen by fans from the official website. The music has been well received overall, with Greg Kasavin of GameSpot noting that the background music fits each setting but criticizing the loops as too short and repetitive, and IGN reviewer David Smith praising the production values, including the use of the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra and arrangements of "Night on Bald Mountain" and "Under the Sea", and highlighting Shimomura's ability to maintain atmosphere while creating a consistent musical thread.

Kingdom Hearts 10th Anniversary Fan Selection: Melodies & Memories is a 2-CD album released in Japan on September 19, 2012, to commemorate the series' 10th anniversary. The tracks were selected by fans through the series' official website. The music of Kingdom Hearts was generally well received; Greg Kasavin of GameSpot praised the background music for being appropriate to each setting but criticized the loops as too short and repetitive. IGN reviewer David Smith commended the production values, including the use of the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra and arrangements of pieces like "Night on Bald Mountain" and "Under the Sea," and praised composer Yoko Shimomura for maintaining a consistent atmosphere with a unifying character thread throughout the soundtrack. Daniel Kalabakov of SoundtrackCentral.com described Shimomura's orchestral composition as "sophisticated" and noted the score's unique qualities, though he considered it one of her weaker albums overall. Adam Corn of SoundtrackCentral.com highlighted the Kingdom Hearts tracks as a standout on the compilation album Drammatica. Jim Cordeira of Gaming Age called the music one of the best aspects of the first game, noting the orchestrated soundtrack surpassed the "midi-sounding" tunes of earlier Final Fantasy titles. Benjamin Turner of GameSpy praised the main theme but found some world background music weak, while Gerald Villoria of GameSpy complimented both PlayStation 2 game soundtracks, stating that Kingdom Hearts II's soundtrack was not as strong as the first game's. Several tracks received special attention: "Hikari" debuted at number one on the Oricon Weekly Singles chart in Japan, remained at number one for three weeks, and stayed on the chart for thirteen weeks. It sold over 270,000 copies in its first week and surpassed 860,000 copies by August 2002, earning recognition from Guinness World Records in 2008 as the best-selling video game theme song in Japan. Kalabakov praised Utada's singing and instrumentation in "Hikari" but expressed a lack of preference for pop songs. Turner appreciated the English translation of "Hikari" and considered Utada's vocals a strong addition to the game's opening and ending segments. "Passion" debuted at number four on the Oricon Weekly Singles chart and remained on the chart for nine weeks. G4TV's Miguel Concepcion particularly liked "Dearly Beloved," the title screen track, which IGN also praised as number four on their top ten list of RPG title tracks, noting it lifted doubts about the game's potential. Kalabakov described "Dearly Beloved" as a fitting "fairy tale-style" piece with a simple yet emotionally rich composition.

The Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is a self-report questionnaire that makes pseudoscientific claims to categorize individuals into 16 distinct "personality types." The test assigns a binary letter value to each of four dichotomous categories: introversion or extraversion, sensing or intuition, thinking or feeling, and judging or perceiving, resulting in a four-letter result such as "INTJ" or "ESFP," representing one of 16 possible types.[7][8] Developed during World War II by Americans Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, the MBTI was inspired by Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung's 1921 book Psychological Types.[9] Isabel Myers was particularly fascinated by the concept of "introversion" and typed herself as an "INFP," though she felt Jung's book was too complex for the general public and sought to simplify his cognitive functions for broader accessibility.[10] Briggs began her research into personality in 1917, observing differences between her son-in-law's personality and that of other family members, and developed a typology with four temperaments: meditative (thoughtful), spontaneous, executive, and social.[20][21] After the 1923 English translation of Jung's book, Briggs recognized that Jung's theory resembled but extended beyond her own, and her four types were later identified as corresponding to the IXXXs (Introverts: "meditative"), EXXPs (Extraverts & Prospectors: "spontaneous"), EXTJs (Extraverts, Thinkers & Judgers: "executive"), and EXFJs (Extraverts, Feelers & Judgers: "social").[i][20][21] Her first publications were two articles in The New Republic: "Meet Yourself Using the Personality Paint Box" (1926) and "Up From Barbarism" (1928).[23][24] Neither Myers nor Briggs had formal training in psychology and were self-taught in psychometric testing; Myers apprenticed under Edward N. Hay, learning test construction, scoring, validation, and statistical methods.[26][27] Briggs and Myers began creating their indicator during World War II, believing that understanding personality preferences would help women entering the industrial workforce identify war-time jobs that would be "most comfortable and effective" for them.[26] The Briggs Myers Type Indicator Handbook was published in 1944 and re-published as the "Myers–Briggs Type Indicator" in 1956.[28] Myers' work attracted Henry Chauncey of the Educational Testing Service, who supported the first MBTI manual in 1962. The MBTI received further support from Donald W. MacKinnon, W. Harold Grant, and Mary H. McCaulley. The publication was transferred to Consulting Psychologists Press in 1975, and the Center for Applications of Psychological Type (CAPT) was founded.[29] After Myers' death in May 1980, Mary McCaulley updated the manual, and the second edition was published in 1985, with the third edition appearing in 1998.[30] In 1987, an advanced scoring system called the Type Differentiation Indicator (TDI) was developed for the longer MBTI, Form J, which includes 290 items from Myers' earlier work and yields 20 subscales (five under each of the four dichotomies) plus seven additional subscales for a "comfort-discomfort" factor, which parallels the NEO-PI factor of neuroticism. This factor indicates a sense of overall comfort and confidence versus discomfort and anxiety and loads onto one of the four type dimensions. A composite called "strain" and scales for type-scale and comfort-scale consistency are also included; 23 of the 27 TDI subscales have reliability greater than 0.50, considered acceptable given the brevity of the subscales.[31] In 1989, a scoring system for the 20 subscales of the original four dichotomies was developed, initially known as "Form K" or "the Expanded Analysis Report," now called MBTI Step II.[36] Form J or the TDI includes the items necessary to score Step III, which was developed in a joint project involving the Myers–Briggs Company, CAPT, and the MBTI Trust headed by Katharine and Peter Myers. CAPT advertised Step III as addressing type development and the use of "perception and judgment" by respondents.[39] The MBTI is based on Jung's 1921 theory of psychological types, which was partially based on the four elements of classical cosmology, proposing four cognitive functions—sensation, intuition, feeling, and thinking—with one dominant in an individual, and each function expressed in either an introverted or extraverted form, resulting in eight combinations, four of which are largely conscious and four unconscious.[40][44] The MBTI adds a judgment-perception preference, with J or P indicating a person's most preferred extraverted function, which is the dominant function for extraverts and the auxiliary function for introverts.[48] The MBTI sorts psychological differences into four dichotomies, producing 16 types, none of which are considered better or worse; Briggs and Myers theorized that people innately "prefer" one overall combination of type differences.[49] The 16 types are abbreviated by the first letters of each of their four preferences (with "N" used to distinguish intuition from introversion), such as "INTJ" or "ESFP." The interaction of two, three, or four preferences is known as "type dynamics," which has received little or no empirical support and is criticized for logical problems, reliance on anecdotal evidence, and failure to fit empirical facts; only one out of 540 test results showed the presumed order of functions 1 to 4.[50] Myers and Briggs asserted that each type has one dominant function, evident early in life, a secondary (auxiliary) function becoming more evident during adolescence, a tertiary function developed in mid-life, and a fourth, inferior function—seen as unconscious and most evident under stress—referred to as the "shadow."[51] The terms in the MBTI differ from everyday usage; for example, preferring judgment over perception does not mean being more "judgmental" or less "perceptive," nor does the test measure aptitude, only preference.[52] Myers emphasized the direction of preference (e.g., E vs. I) over its degree, leading to a bimodal distribution in scoring, though most studies show scores are centrally peaked, similar to a normal distribution, indicating most people are neither clearly introverted nor extraverted. To score the MBTI, a cut-off line is used at the midpoint of each scale, classifying those below as low and those above as the opposite type, which contradicts psychometric research showing most people lie near the middle of a continuous curve.[13][69] Despite its widespread use—estimated at 50 million people having taken it, with 10,000 businesses, 2,500 colleges and universities, and 200 U.S. government agencies using it—the MBTI is widely regarded as pseudoscience by the scientific community.[1][3][2] It has been criticized for poor validity, poor reliability, measuring non-independent dichotomous categories, and lack of comprehensiveness.[12][13][14][15] Most research supporting its validity has been conducted by the Center for Applications of Psychological Type, an organization run by the Myers–Briggs Foundation, and published in the Journal of Psychological Type (JPT), raising concerns about independence, bias, and conflict of interest.[5] University of Pennsylvania professor Adam Grant states there is no evidence behind the MBTI, as the traits measured have almost no predictive power for happiness, job performance, or marital satisfaction.[18] Psychologists such as Robert Hogan have called it "little more than an elaborate Chinese fortune cookie," and Nicholas Campion has described it as "a fascinating example of 'disguised astrology,' masquerading as science."[63][64] Media reports have labeled the test "pretty much meaningless" and "one of the worst personality tests in existence."[61][62] The test is not recommended in counseling and relies on the Barnum effect, flattery, and confirmation bias, leading participants to identify with vague, desirable, and widely applicable descriptions.[11][67] Hans Eysenck (1995) argued that the 16 MBTI types are incomplete, as Jung's original model included 32 types, 16 of which could not be measured by questionnaire, and it was unfair to claim the MBTI accurately measured Jungian concepts.[45] Both Jung's original model and the simplified MBTI remain hypothetical, with no controlled scientific studies supporting either.[46] Jung did not view type preferences as dualistic but as tendencies with the potential to balance.[47] According to Jung, each person uses all four cognitive functions, with one dominant and proficient, supported by the secondary (auxiliary) function, and to a lesser degree the tertiary function, while the fourth function is always the opposite of the dominant and is considered the inferior or "shadow" function.[57][58] Myers and Briggs added the judgment-perception preference, claiming people have a preference for using either the judging function (thinking or feeling) or their perceiving function (sensing or intuition) when relating to the outside world, with judging types preferring to "have matters settled" and perceptive types preferring to "keep decisions open."[59] A major task in interpretation is helping respondents with less clear preferences arrive at a comfortable and accurate assessment of their type through exploration of how type preferences appear in behaviors.[68]

The Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is considered somewhat desirable, vague, and widely applicable, but it is not recommended for use in counseling. Isabel Myers believed that the direction of preference—such as extraversion (E) versus introversion (I)—was more important than the degree of preference, implying a bimodal distribution where most people fall clearly into one category or the other. However, empirical studies show that scores on MBTI scales are typically centrally peaked, resembling a normal distribution, indicating that most individuals score near the middle and are neither clearly introverted nor extraverted. To assign types, a midpoint cut-off is used, classifying those below it as low and those above as the opposite type, which undermines the concept of categorical "types" and suggests most people lie near the middle of a continuous spectrum. Research fails to support the existence of distinct personality types, removing a key argument previously used by type advocates. Some supporters argue that applying type dynamics—such as assuming dominant or auxiliary functions like Se or Ni—is a logical error with little empirical backing, and instead claim the MBTI is most valid when viewed as independent dichotomies. The content of the MBTI scales is problematic: a 1991 National Academy of Sciences review found only the I-E scale has strong validity, while S-N and T-F scales show weak validity, and concluded there was insufficient well-designed research to justify its use in career counseling. The committee noted a discrepancy between the MBTI’s popularity and its lack of scientific support, calling the situation "troublesome." There is insufficient evidence to support claims about the utility of the four-letter type derived from MBTI responses. Accuracy depends on honest self-reporting, as the MBTI lacks validity scales to detect socially desirable or exaggerated answers, allowing individuals to fake responses; one study found a weak but significant correlation between the judging scale and the Eysenck lie scale, suggesting conformist individuals are more likely to be classified as judging. The MBTI ethical guidelines prohibit using results to screen job applicants, and the instrument's intent is to provide a framework for understanding individual differences and a dynamic model of development. The terminology is criticized as vague and general, potentially leading to the Barnum effect, though some argue the type descriptions are distinctive and precise. David Keirsey developed the Keirsey Temperament Sorter, mapping MBTI types to four temperaments and providing detailed descriptions of language, values, interests, and behaviors. Research shows the JP and SN scales correlate with each other, and a factor-analytic study of 1,291 college students found six factors instead of four, raising doubts about construct validity. According to Hans Eysenck, the E-I scale is mostly a sociability measure, correlating well with the MMPI and Eysenck Extraversion scale, but also loading on neuroticism, which correlates with introversion and various psychological traits like self-confidence and empathy, indicating a failure to separate introversion from neuroticism. The MBTI has low test-retest reliability: between 39% and 76% of people receive different type classifications after five weeks, with about 50% remaining the same type within nine months and only 36% after more than nine months. For Form M, reliability is reported as higher. One study found that only half of people chose the same type when comparing their self-assessed and MBTI-assigned profiles. A 2002 meta-analysis by Robert and Mary Capraro found that while MBTI scales showed strong internal consistency and some test-retest reliability, many studies did not report reliability data. Critics argue that MBTI criticisms stem from questions about its origins, not its usefulness, and some maintain it can be a reliable measure, though scores depend on sample and testing conditions. A 1973 study found that INFP was the most common type among fine arts and art education students (36% and 26%, respectively), and Intuitive-Perceptive types (ENFP, INFP, ENTP, INTP) were over-represented among teachers of English, social studies, and art, while science and math fields had more Sensing and Judging types. A survey of 27,787 high school students found INFPs showed a significant preference for art, English, and music. Isabel Myers claimed type proportions vary by career or study, but research shows type distributions in professions are similar to those in the general population, and concerns remain about type relevance to job satisfaction and misuse. The Myers–Briggs Company, formerly Consulting Psychologists Press (CPP), became the exclusive publisher in 1975 and calls the MBTI "the world's most widely used personality assessment," with up to two million assessments administered annually, claiming it meets or exceeds the reliability of other psychological instruments. The MBTI has poor predictive validity for job performance and is explicitly discouraged from being used as a predictor of job success in its manual. Its popularity persists due to ease of understanding, availability of supporting materials, and widespread administration. McCrae and Costa found that MBTI scales correlate with the Big Five personality traits—extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism—though the MBTI lacks a measure for emotional stability (neuroticism), and concluded that the MBTI measures four relatively independent dimensions rather than true dichotomous preferences or distinct types. During the COVID-19 pandemic, MBTI testing became popular in South Korea, especially among young people seeking dating partners, originating from the website 16Personalities.com, which offers a free version of the official test. Experts and the MBTI publisher have warned against using the test for dating, as it was not designed for this purpose. South Korea previously saw a similar trend with blood type personality theory. By December 2021, nearly half the population had taken the test, and it became a topic in the 2022 presidential election. In March 2022, Korea JoongAng Daily reported that many Korean companies began asking job candidates to disclose their MBTI results, prompting opposition from job seekers, with 60% of those in their twenties opposing such use. The trend spread to China, where some employers asked applicants about their MBTI or 16Personalities results, leading to MBTI-related products, services, and social media content. In 2021, Tim Travers Hawkins’s film *Persona: The Dark Truth Behind Personality Tests* premiered on HBO, and the MBTI publisher explicitly condemns its misuse, stating the test is not intended to be predictive and should never be used for hiring, screening, or making life decisions.

NGC 2298 is a globular cluster located in the southern constellation Puppis. It was discovered by James Dunlop on May 30, 1826, and is likely a former member of the disputed Canis Major Dwarf galaxy. The cluster is currently being disrupted by the galactic tide, which has caused it to trail a long tidal tail. The NHK Hall is a concert hall situated at the NHK Broadcasting Center, which serves as the main headquarters of Japan's public broadcaster, NHK. It functions as the primary venue for the NHK Symphony Orchestra and has also hosted events such as the 1979 Japan Music Awards and NHK's annual New Year's Eve special, Kōhaku Uta Gassen. The original NHK Hall opened in 1955 in Tokyo's Uchisaiwai-cho district and was used for live broadcasts including Song Plaza, Kōhaku Uta Gassen, and Personal Secrets. In 1973, a new NHK Hall was constructed in Shibuya, Tokyo, at the location of NHK's new headquarters, the NHK Broadcasting Center. The hall's acoustics were designed by Minoru Nagata, who later founded Nagata Acoustics, and TOA Corporation supplied the sound equipment. On April 9, 2019, it was announced that the hall would close from March 2021 to June 2022 for seismic retrofitting, construction, and renovation. The 72nd Kōhaku Uta Gassen, broadcast on December 31, 2021, was held at the Tokyo International Forum, marking the first time since the hall's opening in 1955 and the first time in 49 years—since the 23rd edition in 1972—that the event took place outside the NHK Hall. Nancy Marie Amato is an American computer scientist recognized for her research in the algorithmic foundations of motion planning, computational biology, computational geometry, and parallel computing. She holds the position of Abel Bliss Professor of Engineering and serves as Head of the Department of Computer Science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Amato is known for her leadership in broadening participation in computing and is currently a member of the steering committee of CRA-WP (formerly CRA-W), having been on the board since 2000. She earned a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and a Bachelor of Science in Mathematical Sciences from Stanford University in 1986. She obtained a Master of Science in Computer Science from the University of California, Berkeley in 1988, with advisor Manuel Blum. In 1995, she received a PhD in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign under advisor Franco P. Preparata for her thesis "Parallel Algorithms for Convex Hulls and Proximity Problems." She joined the Department of Computer Science at Texas A&M University as an assistant professor in 1995, was promoted to associate professor in 2000, to professor in 2004, and to Unocal professor in 2011. In July 2018, she was named the next head of the Department of Computer Science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, beginning in January 2019. Her notable contributions include a foundational paper on probabilistic roadmap methods (PRMs) that introduced the first PRM variant not using uniform sampling in the robot's configuration space. She co-authored a seminal paper with a student demonstrating how PRM can be applied to protein motions, particularly protein folding, thereby establishing a new research area in computational biology. Another paper with her students shows how global energy landscape statistics, such as relative folding rates and population kinetics, can be derived from approximate landscapes generated by her PRM-based method. She also developed a novel technique, approximate convex decomposition (ACD), for partitioning a polyhedron into approximately convex pieces. Amato co-leads the STAPL project with her husband Lawrence Rauchwerger, a computer scientist also on the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign; STAPL is a parallel C++ library. The third and final season of Narcos, an American crime thriller drama created and produced by Chris Brancato, Carlo Bernard, and Doug Miro, centers on the Cali Cartel. Pedro Pascal returns to the series in his role from the prior two seasons. All 10 episodes premiered on Netflix on September 1, 2017, and received highly positive critical reception. The show was originally renewed for a fourth season, which instead transitioned into Narcos: Mexico, a prequel/sequel companion series. On Rotten Tomatoes, the third season has a 97% approval rating from 23 reviews, with an average score of 7.46/10, and the critical consensus states, "Narcos continues to evolve in its third season, drawing on historical details to take viewers on a thoroughly gripping -- and unsettlingly timely -- journey into darkness." On Metacritic, the season is rated 78 out of 100 based on 9 critics, reflecting "generally favorable" reviews.

Narendra Krishna Karmarkar, born in 1956, is an Indian mathematician who developed Karmarkar's algorithm. He is listed as an ISI highly cited researcher. He invented one of the first provably polynomial time algorithms for linear programming, known as an interior point method, which is a cornerstone in the field. He published this result in 1984 while working at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey. Karmarkar earned his B.Tech. in electrical engineering from IIT Bombay in 1978, an M.S. from the California Institute of Technology in 1979, and a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of California, Berkeley in 1983 under Richard M. Karp. He served as a post-doctoral research fellow at IBM Research (1983), Member of Technical Staff and fellow at the Mathematical Sciences Research Center, AT&T Bell Laboratories (1983–1998), professor of mathematics at M.I.T. (1991), at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton (1996), and Homi Bhabha Chair Professor at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai from 1998 to 2005. He was the scientific advisor to the chairman of the TATA group from 2006 to 2007, during which time he was funded by Ratan Tata to scale up the supercomputer he designed and prototyped at TIFR. The scaled-up model outperformed a supercomputer in Japan at the time and achieved India's best-ever ranking in supercomputing. He was the founding director of the Computational Research Labs in Pune, where this scaling-up work took place. He continues to work on a new architecture for supercomputing based on concepts from finite geometry, particularly projective geometry over finite fields. Karmarkar's algorithm solves linear programming problems in polynomial time, represented by a set of linear constraints and variables. The traditional approach involved treating the problem as a high-dimensional solid with vertices and moving from vertex to vertex, whereas Karmarkar's method traverses through the solid, significantly reducing solution time. For instance, in a communications network optimization problem, solution time dropped from weeks to days, enabling faster business and policy decisions. His algorithm has inspired the development of several interior-point methods, some of which are used in current linear-programming solvers.

The National Fascist Party (Italian: Partito Nazionale Fascista, PNF) was established by Benito Mussolini as the political expression of Italian fascism and as a reorganisation of the previous Italian Fasces of Combat. It ruled the Kingdom of Italy from 1922, following the March on Rome, until the fall of the Fascist regime in 1943, when Mussolini was deposed by the Grand Council of Fascism. The PNF was succeeded by the Republican Fascist Party in the territories under the Italian Social Republic and was ultimately dissolved at the end of World War II. Rooted in Italian nationalism and the desire to restore and expand Italian territories, the party believed such expansion was necessary for national superiority and to avoid decay. Italian Fascists claimed modern Italy was the heir to ancient Rome and supported the creation of an Italian Empire to provide spazio vitale ("living space") for Italian settlers and to control the Mediterranean Sea. The party promoted a corporatist economic system in which employer and employee syndicates formed associations to represent economic producers and collaborate with the state in setting national economic policy, aiming to resolve class conflict through cooperation. It also strongly advocated autarky.
