Italian Fascism opposed liberalism and Marxist socialism due to their opposition to nationalism, and rejected reactionary conservatism as espoused by Joseph de Maistre, instead advocating respect for tradition and a shared Italian past alongside modernisation and a vision of Italy as the hegemonic power in Europe. The PNF and its successor, the Republican Fascist Party, are the only parties banned from re-formation by the Italian Constitution, which states that re-organisation of the dissolved Fascist party is forbidden under any form. After World War I, Italian nationalism claimed Italy was cheated in the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (1919), particularly over the loss of Fiume (Rijeka) to Yugoslavia and exclusion from the wartime Treaty of London (1915), which had promised territorial gains for Italy. In September 1919, war hero Gabriele D'Annunzio established the Italian Regency of Carnaro, promulgating the Carta del Carnaro, a syncretic blend of right-wing and left-wing ideas that influenced early Italian fascism. The Regency was deposed in December 1920 after the Treaty of Rapallo. The PNF was founded in Rome during the Third Fascist Congress on 7–10 November 1921, marking the transformation of the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento into a political party. The party played a key role in promoting Mussolini's ideology, with Blackshirts (squadristi) gaining support from landowners by violently attacking socialists and their institutions in the rural Po Valley. On 28 October 1922, Mussolini attempted a coup known as the March on Rome, involving nearly 30,000 fascists, led by quadrumvirs General Emilio De Bono, Italo Balbo, Michele Bianchi, and Cesare Maria de Vecchi, with Mussolini remaining behind and allowing himself to be photographed marching. Generals Gustavo Fara and Sante Ceccherini assisted in preparations, and other organisers included Marquis Dino Perrone Compagni and Ulisse Igliori. On 24 October 1922, Mussolini declared before 60,000 people in Naples: "Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy." Blackshirts had already taken control of the Po plain and key strategic points. On 26 October, former prime minister Antonio Salandra warned current prime minister Luigi Facta of Mussolini's demands, but Facta did not believe the threat and thought Mussolini would govern quietly. Facta ordered a state of siege for Rome, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the military order. On 30 October, the King handed power to Mussolini, who was supported by the military, business class, and right-wing population. The march involved fewer than 30,000 men, and the King feared civil war due to the fascists' control of the country. Mussolini was asked to form his cabinet on 31 October 1922, with around 25,000 Blackshirts parading in Rome, and thus legally attained power under the Statuto Albertino. The March on Rome was not a conquest but a constitutional transfer of power enabled by the surrender of public authorities to fascist intimidation. Many business leaders believed they could manipulate Mussolini, who initially emphasized free market and laissez-faire economics, but this proved optimistic as his corporatist model granted the state total control over businesses through industry bodies ("corporations"), with businesses retaining property rights but few freedoms. After the coup, a parallel agreement was reached between Mussolini and King Victor Emmanuel III, leading to Mussolini becoming head of government. On 15 December, the Grand Council of Fascism was founded as the supreme organ of the PNF. After modifying electoral legislation with the Acerbo Law, the Fascist Party won the controversial April 1924 elections. In early 1925, Mussolini abandoned democracy and established a total dictatorship, making the PNF the only legally permitted party in Italy, a status formalised by a 1928 law and maintained until 1943. This shift was strongly criticised by Giacomo Matteotti, whose speech in Parliament led to his kidnapping and murder by fascist blackshirts. The regime imposed Fascist ideology and symbols nationwide, requiring party membership for employment or government assistance, displaying fasces in public buildings, and promoting a personality cult around Mussolini as "Il Duce." The Italian parliament was replaced by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations, filled exclusively with PNF members. The party promoted Italian imperialism in Africa and racial segregation and white supremacy in colonies. In 1930, the Youth Fasces of Combat were established. In the 1930s, secretary Achille Starace, a loyalist from Southern Italy, launched a campaign of ceremonies, rallies, and youth organisations to shape national and personal identity. Starace brought the Opera Nazionale Balilla (ONB) under PNF control and dissolved the Youth Fasces, merging them into the Gioventù Italiana del Littorio (GIL). On 27 May 1933, party membership became required for public office; on 9 March 1937, it became mandatory for all public office holders; and from 3 June 1938, non-members were barred from working. In 1939, Ettore Muti replaced Starace, reflecting the increasing influence of Galeazzo Ciano, Mussolini’s son-in-law and Minister of Foreign Affairs. On 10 June 1940, from the balcony of Palazzo Venezia, Mussolini announced Italy's entry into World War II on the side of Nazi Germany. On 25 July 1943, following Dino Grandi's request due to war failures, the Grand Council of Fascism overthrew Mussolini, asking King Victor Emmanuel III to restore full authority and remove Mussolini as prime minister, which he did. Mussolini was imprisoned, the Fascist organisations collapsed, and the party was officially banned by Pietro Badoglio's government on 27 July. After the Nazi-engineered Gran Sasso raid liberated Mussolini in September, the PNF was revived as the Republican Fascist Party (Partito Fascista Repubblicano – PFR) on 13 September, as the sole party of the Northern Italian Social Republic (the Salò Republic), with Alessandro Pavolini as secretary. The PFR did not outlast Mussolini's execution and the collapse of the Salò state in April 1945, during the final Allied offensive in Italy. Italian Fascism was based on Italian nationalism and Georges Sorel's revolutionary syndicalism, evolving into national syndicalism, with many revolutionary syndicalist leaders becoming founders of the movement and holding key positions in Mussolini’s administration. The movement sought to restore and expand Italian territories to assert national strength and avoid decay, claiming modern Italy inherited Roman and Renaissance legacies and promoted the cultural identity of Romanitas ("Roman-ness"). It viewed ancient Rome as the "First Rome" and Renaissance Italy as the "Second Rome," with Mussolini emulating Julius Cæsar and Augustus. The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), ghostwritten by Giovanni Gentile, declared the Fascist state as a will to power and empire, with empire being both territorial and spiritual, guiding other nations without conquest. The regime promoted the restoration of the Mazzinian Risorgimento, claiming it had been abandoned in Giolittian-era Italy, and sought to incorporate "unredeemed" territories. To the east, the Fascists claimed Dalmatia as Italian due to its historical Italian cultural roots, including Venetian influence, and supported the return of Italians of Dalmatian heritage, especially after the 1919 revocation of the Treaty of London's promise to include Dalmatia. The regime supported the annexation of Slovenia into Italy, resulting in a quarter of Slovene ethnic territory and approximately 327,000 out of 1.3 million Slovenes being subjected to forced Italianization. It claimed Albania as Italian due to historical links with Illyrian and Roman populations, Roman and Venetian influence, and the presence of hundreds of thousands of Albanians in southern Italy, and endorsed assimilation and colonization of Albania with Italian settlers. The regime also claimed the Ionian Islands as Italian, citing their Venetian ownership from the mid-14th to the 18th century. To the west of Italy, the regime pursued similar imperial ambitions.

Albania was claimed by the Fascist regime as ethnically linked to Italy through prehistoric Italiotes, Illyrian, and Roman populations, with Roman and Venetian imperial influence justifying Italy's right to possess it. The regime also argued that hundreds of thousands of Albanians had been absorbed into Southern Italy, making the incorporation of Albania a reasonable step to unite people of Albanian descent. It endorsed Albanian irredentism, particularly targeting Kosovo and Epirus, especially the Chameria region with a significant Albanian population. After annexing Albania in 1939, the regime promoted assimilating Albanians into Italian culture and colonizing the country with Italian settlers from the Italian Peninsula to transform it into Italian territory. The Fascists claimed the Ionian Islands as Italian due to their historical possession by the Venetian Republic from the mid-14th to the 18th century. To the west, they asserted that Corsica, Nice, and Savoy belonged to Italy, citing historical, ethnic, and linguistic grounds. This claim stemmed from the 1860–1861 Italian unification, when Piedmont-Sardinia, under Count Cavour, was pressured by French Emperor Napoleon III to cede Nice and Savoy in exchange for French support of unification. The Fascist regime produced literature on Corsica and Nice, citing Petrarch’s statement that "the border of Italy is the Var; consequently Nice is a part of Italy" and Giuseppe Garibaldi’s assertion that "Corsica and Nice must not belong to France," claiming they would one day be reclaimed. Mussolini initially pursued Corsican annexation through encouraging autonomist movements and independence before annexation. To the north, the regime in the 1930s sought to annex Ticino and Graubünden in Switzerland, arguing that Romansch was an Italian dialect and that Graubünden should be incorporated into Italy. In November 1938, Mussolini declared to the Grand Fascist Council that Italy would extend its border to the Gotthard Pass. The regime accused Switzerland of oppressing the Romansch people and claimed Ticino due to its historical belonging to the Duchy of Milan until 1515, and areas in Graubünden, such as the Mesolcina and Hinterrhein, were held by the Milanese Trivulzio family. In 1940, Galeazzo Ciano proposed to Hitler and Ribbentrop the division of Switzerland along the central Western Alps, including Valais. To the south, the regime claimed Malta, which had been under British control since 1800, arguing that Maltese was an Italian dialect and that Malta was the cradle of Latin civilization; Italian had been an official language until 1937, when it was abolished by the British after Italy invaded Ethiopia. Italian irredentists claimed North African coastal territories as Italy’s Fourth Shore, citing Roman rule as justification. In January 1939, Italy annexed Libya’s coastal provinces—Tripoli, Misurata, Benghazi, and Derna—into metropolitan Italy, granting indigenous Libyans the right to apply for "Special Italian Citizenship" requiring literacy in Italian and valid only in Libya. Tunisia, a French protectorate since 1881, was seen as a loss to Italian ambitions, and upon entering WWII, Italy declared its intent to seize Tunisia and Algeria’s Constantine province. Italy also sought to annex Portugal’s colonies in the 1920s, viewing Portugal as weak and poorly managing its colonies, though relations were influenced by Salazar’s authoritarian, nationalist regime aligned with Britain. In 1925, the PNF declared the Fascist state to be totalitarian, initially a term used pejoratively by liberals, which the Fascists redefined positively as a state that unifies all values and creates politically active citizens. The Doctrine of Fascism (1932) stated that for the fascist, everything is in the state, and no human or spiritual value exists outside it, defining fascism as totalitarian. H. R. Knickerbocker noted in 1941 that Mussolini’s regime was the least terroristic among totalitarian states, citing mild treatment of a dissenting journalist, in contrast to Soviet or Nazi torture and execution. However, historians note extreme violence in Italian colonies: one-tenth of Libya’s population died during the Fascist era from gassings, concentration camps, starvation, and disease, and a quarter of a million Ethiopians died during and after the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. Italian Fascism promoted a corporatist economy with employer and employee syndicates working with the state to set national economic policy, criminalizing strikes and lockouts as harmful to national unity. The political anthem was "Giovinezza" ("The Youth"), emphasizing youth as a critical period for moral development. The regime promoted "moral hygiene" of youth, condemning homosexuality as deviant, criminalizing birth control and abortion, taxing bachelors, and viewing pre-pubertal male sexual excitement as a cause of criminality. It launched aggressive campaigns to reduce young women’s prostitution. Mussolini viewed women’s primary role as childbearers, stating "war is to man what maternity is to the woman," and introduced financial incentives for large families, policies to reduce female employment, and ceremonies honoring women as "reproducers of the nation." In 1934, he declared that women’s work was incompatible with childbearing and that unemployment for men could be solved by women’s exit from the workforce. Fascism emphasized a shared past and modernized Italy, with Mussolini calling for art that was "traditionalist and at the same time modern, looking to the past and the future." Traditional Roman symbols, such as the fasces (symbolizing unity, authority, and power) and the she-wolf of Rome, were used to represent shared heritage. In 1926, the fasces was adopted as a state symbol, though a redesign of the national flag incorporating it was blocked by monarchists; instead, the tricolour was raised with a black Fascist flag. Later, after Mussolini’s 1943 rescue by German forces, the Italian Social Republic used a fasces-variant flag. Initially republican and anti-monarchical, Italian Fascism shifted in 1922 to recognize the monarchy as a necessary compromise to gain support, especially given King Victor Emmanuel III’s popularity after WWI and army loyalty. The regime publicly linked Victor Emmanuel II and other historical figures like Cavour, Garibaldi, and Julius Caesar to a tradition of dictatorship. Despite this, the relationship with the monarchy remained strained, with Mussolini reducing the King’s power by creating the position of First Marshal of the Empire in 1938, giving him equal military authority. Mussolini privately resented the monarchy, envying Hitler’s dual role as head of state and government, and planned to dismantle the monarchy and establish a republic upon Italian military success. After being deposed in 1943 and Italy switching to the Allies, Fascism returned to republicanism and condemned the monarchy. In his 1943 speech, Mussolini praised Hitler and condemned Victor Emmanuel III for betraying the regime, stating that "it is not the regime that has betrayed the monarchy, it is the monarchy that has betrayed the regime," and that a new national and social Fascist state would be established. The regime did not denounce the House of Savoy entirely, praising Victor Emmanuel II for rejecting dishonorable pacts and blaming Victor Emmanuel III for betraying him by joining the Allies. The relationship with the Catholic Church was initially anti-clerical but shifted in the 1920s as Mussolini sought cooperation. In 1929, the Lateran Treaty created Vatican City, ending decades of conflict after the 1870 annexation of the Papal States. Fascism justified its 1938 antisemitic laws by claiming they fulfilled the Catholic Church’s mandate from the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, which required Jews to wear distinctive clothing. Italian Fascism influenced global movements, with admiration from Winston Churchill, Sigmund Freud, George Bernard Shaw, and Thomas Edison for its law and order, and its anti-Mafia stance. It influenced Adolf Hitler’s Nazi Party, the Russian Fascist Organization, Brit HaBirionim, the British Union of Fascists, the Romanian National Fascist Movement, and the Sammarinese Fascist Party, which established a government in San Marino. In Yugoslavia, Milan Stojadinović founded the Yugoslav Radical Union, with members wearing green shirts, Šajkača caps, and using the Roman salute, and calling himself Vodja. In Switzerland, pro-Nazi Colonel Arthur Fonjallaz, after visiting Italy in 1932, became a strong Mussolini admirer and advocated for Italian annexation of Switzerland, receiving Fascist foreign aid. Switzerland hosted two Italian politico-cultural activities: the International Centre for Fascism.

George Bernard Shaw and Thomas Edison are mentioned in the context of a statement about the Fascist Government combating organised crime and the Mafia with violence and vendetta (honour), though this connection appears to be an error or misattribution, as no factual link between these individuals and the Fascist Government is supported by the document. Italian Fascism influenced Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party, the Russian Fascist Organization, Brit HaBirionim, the British Union of Fascists, the Romanian National Fascist Movement (including the National Romanian Fascia and the National Italo-Romanian Cultural and Economic Movement), and the Sammarinese Fascist Party, which established a government in San Marino based on essentially Italian Fascism. In the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, Milan Stojadinović founded the Yugoslav Radical Union, a Fascist party, with members wearing green shirts, Šajkača caps, and using the Roman salute; Stojadinović also referred to himself as Vodja. In Switzerland, pro-Nazi Colonel Arthur Fonjallaz of the National Front became a strong admirer of Mussolini after visiting Italy in 1932 and advocated for Italian annexation of Switzerland while receiving Fascist foreign aid. Switzerland hosted two Italian politico-cultural activities: the International Centre for Fascist Studies (CINEF — Centre International d'Études Fascistes) and the 1934 congress of the Action Committee for the Universality of Rome (CAUR — Comitato d'Azione della Università de Roma). In Spain, writer Ernesto Giménez Caballero, in his 1932 work Genio de España (The Genius of Spain), called for Italian annexation of Spain under Mussolini leading an international Latin Catholic empire, but later became closely associated with Falangism, resulting in the abandonment of the annexation idea. In India, Italian Fascism, particularly the Opera Nazionale Balilla, influenced B.S. Moonje and the Hindu Mahasabha. In Brazil, Italian Fascism inspired and financed Plínio Salgado's Brazilian Integralist Action. Although the National Fascist Party was outlawed by Italy's postwar Constitution, several neo-fascist parties emerged to continue its legacy. Historically, the largest neo-fascist party was the Italian Social Movement (Movimento Sociale Italiano), which achieved its best electoral result with 8.7% of the vote in the 1972 general election. The MSI was disbanded in 1995 and replaced by National Alliance, a conservative party that distanced itself from Fascism, as its founder, former foreign minister Gianfranco Fini, stated during an official visit to the State of Israel that Fascism was "an absolute evil." National Alliance and other neo-fascist parties were merged in 2009 to form the short-lived People of Freedom party led by then Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, which eventually dissolved after the defeat in the 2013 general election. Many former members of the MSI and National Alliance later joined Brothers of Italy, including Giorgia Meloni, Ignazio La Russa, Adolfo Urso, Francesco Lollobrigida, Daniela Santanchè, Luca Ciriani, Tommaso Foti, Nello Musumeci, Gianni Alemanno, Giovanni Donzelli, Nicola Procaccini, Andrea Delmastro Delle Vedove, Marcello Gemmato, Paola Frassinetti, Galeazzo Bignami, Claudio Barbaro, Isabella Rauti, Wanda Ferro, Edmondo Cirielli, Giovanbattista Fazzolari, Alessio Butti, Francesco Acquaroli, Marco Marsilio, Federico Mollicone, Romano Maria La Russa, Marcello Taglialatela, and Michele Rallo.

doc_name: Nebula Award for Best Game Writing
text: The Nebula Award for Best Game Writing is one of the Nebula Awards, presented annually by the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association (SFWA) for science fiction or fantasy game writing. The Nebula Awards are regarded as one of "the most important of the American science fiction awards" and are described as the "science-fiction and fantasy equivalent" of the Emmy Awards. The Game Writing category is the newest addition to the Nebulas, which began in 1966 with awards for printed fiction only. The Nebula Award for Best Game Writing has been awarded annually since 2019. The push to establish this category was championed by then SFWA president Cat Rambo following the eligibility of game writers for SFWA membership in 2016. According to an SFWA statement from 2018, the category was introduced to reflect how technological advancements have expanded the media used in science fiction and fantasy storytelling. To be eligible, a work must be published in English in the United States, or in English elsewhere in the world if released on a website or in an electronic edition. A game is defined as "an interactive or playable story-driven work which conveys narrative, character, or story background," with no set word count required, but at least one credited writer is necessary. Nominees and winners are selected by SFWA members, though game writers do not need to be members. Works are nominated between December 15 and January 31 each year, with the six receiving the most nominations forming the final ballot—additional nominees may be included in case of ties. Members then vote on the ballot over a one-month period, and the results are announced at the Nebula Awards ceremony in May. Writers are not allowed to nominate their own works, and if a tie occurs in the final vote, it is broken by the number of nominations the work received. Over seven nomination years, 41 games by 121 writers have been nominated, primarily video games, but also including eight books for role-playing game systems and one interactive film. The first award was won by Charlie Brooker for the interactive film Black Mirror: Bandersnatch; the second by a team of nine writers led by Leonard Boyarsky for The Outer Worlds; the third by Greg Kasavin for Hades; the fourth by a team of six writers for Thirsty Sword Lesbians; the fifth by Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R. R. Martin for Elden Ring; the sixth by a team of 16 writers led by Adam Smith for Baldur's Gate 3; and the seventh by a team of writers led by Stewart C. Baker for the interactive fiction game A Death In Hyperspace. Eleven writers have been nominated more than once, with Kate Heartfield and Natalia Theodoridou each having three nominations. Interactive fiction developer Choice of Games has had the most games nominated, with nine over six years. SFWA identifies the awards by the year of publication, which is the year prior to the award year. Entries with a yellow background and an asterisk (*) next to the writer's name are winners or joint winners; all other entries are nominees on the shortlist.

Eddard "Ned" Stark is a fictional character in the 1996 high fantasy novel A Game of Thrones by George R. R. Martin and in HBO's adaptation of the A Song of Ice and Fire series. He is the lord of Winterfell and warden of the North, the second son of Rickard Stark, and a lifelong friend of King Robert Baratheon, who invites Ned to become Hand of the King after the sudden death of their mentor, Jon Arryn. Ned is married to Lady Catelyn Tully and is the father of five trueborn children—Robb, Sansa, Arya, Bran, and Rickon—and has a bastard son, Jon Snow, as well as a ward, Theon Greyjoy. In the novel, Ned is portrayed as a virtuous, honorable patriarch with a strong moral compass, content to avoid courtly intrigue and committed to loyalty and honor. His family name, Stark, reflects both the resilience of his house and his resistance to moral compromise. Despite his principles, he is drawn into political corruption in King's Landing and ultimately faces a crisis between protecting his family and upholding his honor. He discovers that Robert's children with Cersei Lannister are the result of incest with her twin brother Jaime, and suspects Jon Arryn was poisoned to cover this truth. After being injured by Jaime Lannister and betrayed by Petyr "Littlefinger," Ned is imprisoned for treason. A secret deal with Varys leads him to publicly confess to treason in exchange for sparing his family, but King Joffrey orders his execution for amusement, forcing his daughter Sansa to view his severed head mounted on a spike. His execution shocks readers and viewers alike, as it subverts expectations of a heroic protagonist. In the follow-up novel A Clash of Kings, Ned's death ignites a civil war between House Stark and House Lannister, leading to the War of the Five Kings. His remains are returned to Catelyn, who sends them north to be laid in House Stark's ancestral crypt, though it is not confirmed whether they ever reach Winterfell due to the road being cut off by Ironborn invaders. Lady Barbrey Dustin claims she will never allow Ned's bones to be laid to rest in Winterfell. Ned is mentioned in flashbacks and referenced throughout later novels, including A Storm of Swords and A Dance with Dragons, where surviving Stark children, Stannis Baratheon, Jorah Mormont, and Northern mountain clans remember him with respect and affection. The mountain clans join Stannis' campaign to retake Winterfell in honor of Ned's legacy. In A Feast for Crows, Queen Cersei is haunted by visions of Ned silently mocking her. In the HBO adaptation, Sean Bean portrays Ned in the first season, with Sebastian Croft playing him as a child in season six and Robert Aramayo as a young adult in seasons six and seven. Bean was nominated for a Saturn Award and a Scream Award for the role and the cast was nominated for a Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series in 2011. In the show, Ned is beheaded in the ninth episode, "Baelor," a move that shocked audiences and established a dramatic precedent that no one is safe. The producers, David Benioff and D. B. Weiss, stated that Ned's death was a key selling point for HBO, emphasizing the show's unpredictability and the idea that characters are not immune to danger. The image of Bean as Ned sitting in the Iron Throne appears on the covers of the 2011 Season 1 DVD and Blu-ray sets. Ned returns in season six through flashback visions seen by Bran and the Three-Eyed Raven. In the first season, Robert Baratheon visits Winterfell and asks Ned to become Hand of the King. Ned accepts to protect Robert and investigate Arryn's death, traveling to King's Landing with his daughters Arya and Sansa. Catelyn captures Tyrion Lannister, believing he orchestrated the assassination of Bran and the murder of Arryn. Ned and Robert disagree over Daenerys Targaryen, leading Ned to resign as Hand. After being attacked by Jaime Lannister, Ned is injured and his guards are killed. Robert reappoints him as Hand and orders Catelyn to release Tyrion. While Robert is hunting, Ned learns Tywin Lannister is besieging the Riverlands. He demands Tywin appear in King's Landing and sends forces to bring his bannermen to justice. Robert is killed during a boar hunt, and Ned is left to manage the kingdom. Before he can act against Cersei and place Stannis on the throne, he is betrayed by Littlefinger and imprisoned. Ned's eldest son, Robb, calls for action in response.

Catelyn has Tyrion Lannister captured, believing he was responsible for sending an assassin to kill Bran and that the Lannisters also killed Jon Arryn. Ned and Robert soon find themselves at odds regarding Daenerys Targaryen, and Ned steps down as Hand in defiance against Robert's wishes to have her killed. Soon after, Ned and his guards are attacked by Tyrion's brother Jaime Lannister; Ned is injured and his men are murdered. Robert reappoints Ned as Hand and commands him to have Catelyn release Tyrion and make peace with the Lannisters. While Robert departs for a boar hunt, Ned discovers that Tywin Lannister and his forces are laying siege to the Riverlands, the homeland of his wife's house, the Tullys. He demands Tywin present himself in King's Landing and sends a force to bring his bannermen to justice. Robert is killed just as Ned discovers that his three children by Cersei were actually fathered by the queen's twin, Jaime. Before Ned is able to neutralize Cersei and place Robert's brother Stannis on the throne, he is betrayed by Littlefinger, and the queen has him imprisoned for treason. Ned's eldest son Robb calls in his father's banners and marches an army south in an attempt to rescue his father. Ned makes a public confession to save his daughters from Cersei's wrath, but Joffrey has Ned beheaded anyway. In the season 6 episode "Home", Bran sees a vision of Ned (Sebastian Croft) as a child with his sister and brother, Lyanna and Benjen. In the following episode, "Oathbreaker", Bran witnesses the battle between a young Ned (Robert Aramayo) and the knight Ser Arthur Dayne at the Tower of Joy. In the episode "The Door", Bran watches Ned bid Benjen and his father, Rickard, farewell as he departs for his fosterage at the Vale. In the following episode, "Blood of My Blood", Bran briefly glimpses Ned's hand amongst someone's blood, revealed in the season finale, "The Winds of Winter", as belonging to Lyanna (Aisling Franciosi), dying of childbirth in the tower. She makes him swear to protect her son - Jon Snow. Bran revisits this moment in the season 7 finale, "The Dragon and the Wolf", where Lyanna whispers Jon's true name to Ned - Aegon Targaryen. Bean was nominated for a Saturn Award for Best Actor on Television, a Scream Award for Best Fantasy Actor, and an EWwy Award for Best Actor, Drama for the role. IGN named Ned its Best TV Hero of 2011, and Bean won the Portal Award for Best Actor.

The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) is the official national tourism organization of Nepal, dedicated to establishing the country as a premier holiday destination globally. It creates a platform for vision-driven leadership by combining government commitment with the innovation of the private sector. The NTB promotes Nepal in both domestic and international markets, works to reposition the nation’s image, and regulates product development in the tourism sector. The Board is chaired by the Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation and comprises 11 members: five from the government, five from the private sector, and the Chief Executive Officer. The current CEO of the Nepal Tourism Board is Deepak Raj Joshi. Established in 1998 through an act of Parliament, the NTB was formed as a partnership between the Government of Nepal and the private sector tourism industry, making it a pioneer in using the PPP (Public-Private Partnership) model. The official slogan of the NTB is "Nepal: Lifetime Experiences," which aims to redefine international tourism in Nepal as a destination offering unique and unmatched experiences for visitors.

Neptune and Triton is an early marble sculpture created by the Italian artist Gian Lorenzo Bernini, executed around 1622–1623 and standing 182.2 cm (71.7 in) tall. It was originally commissioned by Cardinal Alessandro Damascenti-Peretti Montalto in 1620 and completed from March 1622 to February 1623 as a fountain to decorate the pond in the garden of his Villa Peretti Montalto on the Viminal Hill in Rome. The sculpture was placed in the pre-existing oval pool, the Peschiera or Peschierone, designed by Domenico Fontana between 1579 and 1581. The work was initially referred to as "Neptune and Glaucus" in Filippo Baldinucci's biography of Bernini, but appears as "Nettvno, e Tritone" in Domenico de' Rossi's engraving from 1704 and was later corrected to "Neptune and Triton" based on Joshua Reynolds' notes. In 1786, the Englishman Thomas Jenkins purchased it, and later that same year, Joshua Reynolds acquired it. After Reynolds' death in 1792, it was sold to Charles Anderson-Pelham, 1st Baron Yarborough, who kept it in the garden of his home, Walpole House, in Chelsea, London. His descendants moved it in 1906 to Brocklesby Hall in Lincolnshire. The Victoria and Albert Museum in London bought the sculpture in 1950, although it had previously been exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1938. The scene draws loose allusions to Neptune and Triton aiding Trojan ships as described in Virgil's Aeneid and Ovid's Metamorphoses. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Neptune commands Triton to blow his shell to calm the waves, while in Virgil's Aeneid, Neptune calms the waves and later, with the nereid Cymothoe and Triton, dislodges Aeneas's ships using his trident. However, neither passage precisely matches the sculpture, and Bernini appears to have combined elements from various sources. The composition features Neptune standing astride over Triton, who is in a crouching position, both mounted on a large half-shell serving as socle. Neptune aims his trident seawards, while Triton blows his conch, designed to spurt water, making the sculpture functional as a fountain. Neptune's posture and the filling of the reverse-V-shaped negative space by Triton represent radical departures in Bernini's work, marking his first piece where the silhouette is broken and demonstrating "full Baroque freedom" according to Rudolf Wittkower, though Wittkower noted Bernini had not yet achieved the dynamism seen in later works like David and Pluto. Neptune is depicted as a mature, bearded, muscular figure of male authority, twisting his torso as if about to thrust his trident downward, wearing a cloak and being otherwise naked; his touseled hair and beard suggest storminess. Wittkower interpreted Neptune's angry expression as calming the waves with his trident, while John Pope-Hennessy noted the absence of the nereid in the Virgilian scene and suggested Ovid as a basis, though the Ovid passage fails to mention the trident. Collier pointed out the inconsistency of Neptune wearing a wrathful expression while calming the sea and proposed an Ovid passage where Neptune is in wrath, but this also lacks mention of the trident. Collier also suggested that if Virgil was the source, Neptune might be using the trident to dislodge ships from rocks, but the absence of any ships in the sculpture makes this implausible. Notably, the ends of Neptune's drapery resemble dolphin heads, possibly paying homage to Ovid's references to Neptune and dolphins in the Metamorphoses and the theme of transformation, or reflecting a light-hearted Hellenistic Rococo touch as perceived by Barrow. Triton, Neptune's son, is positioned below Neptune's legs, thrusting forward to blow the conch, appearing as a teenage boy with defined musculature; he grasps Neptune's leg and ducks his left shoulder between Neptune's thighs. Bernini's Triton is double-tailed, a feature also seen in his later Triton Fountain in Rome. The naturalism of the figures aims to evoke an immediate emotional response: Neptune's furrowed brow conveys fierce strength and divine power, while Triton appears submissive and anxious, reflecting human emotion and obedience. Bernini's work allows viewers to "see" the gods in motion, marking his first sculpture where the silhouette is broken, the climax of a transitory action is presented, and the action extends beyond physical limits. The sculpture's dramatic body positions and subtle naturalism are intended to make myths feel real and demand viewer belief in their truth.

New Balance Athletics, Inc. (NB), operating as New Balance, is an American multinational footwear and apparel company headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, founded in 1906 as the New Balance Arch Support Company by William J. Riley, an Irish immigrant. Riley named the company after observing chickens in his yard, noting their three-pronged feet provided balance, a concept he demonstrated by placing a chicken foot on his office desk. His first product, a flexible arch support with three support points, aimed to improve shoe fit. In 1927, Riley hired Arthur Hall as a salesman, and in 1934, Hall became a business partner; the company later operated as the New Balance Athletic Shoe Company. It gained recognition among baseball and track and field athletes during the 1930s. In 1956, Hall sold the business to his daughter Eleanor and her husband Paul Kidd, who continued selling arch supports until 1960, when they introduced the "Trackster," the first running shoe available in varying widths, which became popular through YMCA programs and was adopted by college track teams including MIT, Tufts, and Boston University. Sales declined until 1972, when 28-year-old Jim Davis acquired the company, believing in the potential of leisure-time products; at the time, the company employed six people and produced 30 pairs of shoes daily via mail-order and a few U.S. retailers. The Boston area became a hub for the running boom in the 1970s, leading to rapid growth. In 1982, New Balance opened a UK factory in Workington, relocating it to Flimby in 1991. In 2001, the company purchased PF Flyers and re-launched the brand in 2003; in February 2004, it acquired Warrior Lacrosse (now Warrior Sports) from Warren, Michigan. In 2011, New Balance placed Aravon, Cobb Hill, and Dunham under its Drydock Footwear affiliate. In 2015, New Balance’s parent company, along with Berkshire Partners, bought Rockport from Adidas and combined it with Drydock Footwear under the name The Rockport Group, which included the Aravon, Cobb Hill, Dunham, and Rockport brands. In 2018, The Rockport Group filed for bankruptcy and was sold. In February 2015, New Balance entered the global soccer market through its subsidiary Warrior Sports, which had a $40-million-a-year sponsorship deal with Liverpool F.C., and later rebranded to leverage the parent brand’s global reach. The UK High Court rejected New Balance’s legal challenge to Liverpool’s UK£70 million+ kit deal with Nike, which began in January 2020, and the Manchester United deal with Adidas for £75 million annually. In 2016, New Balance opposed the Trans Pacific Partnership, criticizing it for harming domestic manufacturing, while supporting the stance of Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and Donald Trump against the agreement; Matt Lebretton, the company’s vice president of public affairs, stated that all three candidates agreed the TPP was not the right policy. After Donald Trump won the 2016 election, Lebretton expressed optimism about improved trade relations, and some media interpreted his remarks as supportive of Trump, leading to an ad hoc boycott campaign. Owner and chairman Jim Davis donated nearly $400,000 to the Trump Victory Committee in September 2016. In December 2018, Joe Preston became president, succeeding Rob DeMartini. In March 2020, the company converted some of its New England manufacturing facilities to produce face masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. In April 2021, Teddy Santis, founder of Aimé Leon Dore, was named creative director of New Balance’s premium sneaker line. New Balance manufactures shoes and apparel with a U.S. and UK manufacturing presence, producing popular models like the 990 series in Europe, unlike many competitors who manufacture exclusively outside the U.S. and Europe, resulting in higher pricing. The company differentiates its products through technical features such as blended gel inserts, heel counters, and a broader range of sizes, especially for very narrow or very wide widths. Between 1992 and 2019, the company earned approximately $69 billion in profit. In 2017, New Balance’s Flimby, England facility produced 28,000 pairs of shoes weekly, accounting for 5% of European sales. New Balance sponsors a variety of sports, including the New York Road Runners (organizer of the New York City Marathon), the NBA, major league baseball teams the New York Mets and Boston Red Sox, Team Ireland at the Rio 2016 Olympics, and global football, athletics, and individual sports teams in basketball, baseball, cricket, cycling, tennis, rugby, lacrosse, motorsports, and skateboarding. The company has launched products in collaboration with Aimé Leon Dore, NBA star Kawhi Leonard, and British designer Paul Smith. In 2025, New Balance released a limited-edition line of Japan-made cotton T-shirts in collaboration with Shohei Ohtani, celebrating craftsmanship and cultural roots. On 1 December 2025, New Balance was named on-and-off field apparel supplier for the Perth Bears, an incoming National Rugby League (Australia) club entering the league in 2027—making the Bears the first NRL club to partner with the brand. The New Balance Foundation, established in 1981, supports national and Boston-based charities focused on health, nutrition, education, and physical activity. In 2015, New Balance committed to the Science Based Targets initiative to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius and aims to achieve 100% renewable electricity in operations by 2025. In February 2024, the company launched its resale program 'Reconsidered,' allowing pre-worn shoes to be sold on its online store. In 2011, a class-action lawsuit was filed against New Balance alleging false advertising regarding toning footwear, citing a University of Wisconsin–La Crosse study funded by the American Council on Exercise. Researchers found no statistically significant improvements in exercise response or muscle activation from wearing toning shoes, concluding there is no evidence that such shoes increase calorie burn, improve muscle tone, or enhance physical activity, though they may encourage people to walk more. In August 2012, New Balance settled the false advertising claims by paying $2.3 million.

There have been two New Brighton Piers in the Christchurch, New Zealand, suburb of New Brighton. The first pier, constructed from timber, opened on 18 January 1894 and was demolished on 12 October 1965. Construction began in 1891, and the opening ceremony was officially conducted by the Governor of New Zealand, the Lord Glasgow, with attendees including the Mayor of Christchurch (Walter Cooper), the Mayor of Linwood (J. R. Brunt), and two members of the House of Representatives (George John Smith and William Whitehouse Collins). The event ended as it started to rain, causing the planned fireworks to be postponed. The pier was built to a length of 700 feet (210 m), with plans for an octagonal end and a large building that were never realized. Over time, the structure deteriorated, and the city council ordered its demolition, which occurred during four and a half hours in the early morning of 12 October 1965 on a receding tide. For 30 years, the New Brighton community campaigned for a new pier, with the Pier and Foreshore Society leading efforts to save the original and later advocating for a replacement. When NZ$2 million was raised, Christchurch City Council matched the funding, and a new pier was designed using reinforced concrete. This current pier was built in the exact same location and officially opened on 1 November 1997. It spans 300 metres (980 ft), making it the longest ocean pier in Australasia. The New Brighton Pier is regarded as the icon of New Brighton and later the icon of Christchurch following the 22 February 2011 earthquake that severely damaged Christchurch's Cathedral. It is one of Christchurch's major tourist attractions and currently hosts various events, including regular skate-on-the-pier activities and the annual Guy Fawkes fireworks display on 5 November. The pier sustained damage from several earthquakes, with the 2016 Christchurch earthquake worsening the damage. Repairs began in February 2017, lasted 16 months, and cost NZ$8.5 million, after which the pier reopened in May 2018. Its coordinates are 43°30′23″S 172°43′59″E or 43.5065°S 172.7330°E.

Nicholas Kipyator Kiprono arap Biwott (22 February 1940 – 11 July 2017) was a Kenyan businessman, politician, and philanthropist who served in the governments of Jomo Kenyatta and Daniel arap Moi, holding eight senior civil servant and ministerial positions, including Minister of State (1979–82), Minister of Energy (1984–1985, 1990), Minister of East African and Regional Co-operation (1998–99), and Minister of Regional Development, Science, and Technology (1982). He was widely regarded as one of the most powerful and competent ministers under President Moi and a key figure in advancing regional cooperation. Former president Uhuru Kenyatta praised Biwott as a "patriot and diligent leader, who spent decades building schools and hospitals and spearheading every other kind of development including marketing Kenya abroad." Born on 22 February 1940 in Tot, Chebior village, Elgeyo-Marakwet District, Rift Valley Province of British Kenya, to Maria Soti and Joseph Cheserem Soti, a market trader and cattle herder in Eldoret, Biwott attended Tambach Intermediate School (1951–1954) and later Kapsabet High School. After finishing secondary school in 1959, he began working at the Department of Information in Eldoret and published the Kalenjin monthly newsletter with Kendagor Bett. He studied at the University of Melbourne, Australia, from 1962 to 1964, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and Political Science and a Diploma in Public Administration. He served as District Officer in Nkubu, South Imenti Division, Meru District (1964–1965), returned to Melbourne in 1966 for a master's degree in Economics under a Commonwealth scholarship, and completed it in 1968. Biwott entered government service in 1965 as District Officer in South Imenti and Tharaka, Meru District (January 1965–June 1966), where he implemented 'harambee' community fundraising for irrigation projects, roads, health centres, schools, employment at Igoji quarries, and coffee and tea planting. He also played a central role in the 'Land Transfer' programme under the 'Million Acres' scheme and helped rehabilitate the Mau Mau, persuading them to discontinue violence and resettling many on their own land. After his master's degree, he worked in the Ministry of Agriculture, GOK, as Personal Assistant to Minister Bruce MacKenzie (1968–1970), coordinating cereal production, marketing, fertiliser policy, and research into wheat and maize strains, and guiding Kenya’s regional policy with the East African Council of Ministers. In 1971, he moved to the Treasury as Senior Secretary under Minister of Finance and Economic Planning Mwai Kibaki, creating and heading the External Aid Division and technical assistance program, facilitating the establishment of the French School in Nairobi (now Lycee Denis Diderot), the French Cultural Centre with Alliance de Francais, and the German Friedrich Ebert Stiftung Foundation with Goethe Institut. In late 1978, he transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs on President Kenyatta’s personal recommendation to work with Vice-President Daniel arap Moi. In 1974, he ran unsuccessfully for Keiyo South Constituency; in 1979, he won the seat on the KANU ticket and retained it in 1983, 1988, 1992, 1997, and 2002, losing it in the 2007 election to Jackson Kiptanui Arap Kamai of the Orange Democratic Party (ODM), which won all but one of KANU’s Rift Valley seats. Following the 2002 election, he served on the Devolution Committee of the Constitution of Kenya Review Commission and abstained from the 2005 Constitutional Referendum, stating the draft constitution would divide the country along ethnic lines; it was rejected. In 2005, he contested the leadership of KANU but lost to Uhuru Kenyatta after a Kenyan High Court decision. Biwott served as Under Secretary (1974–1978) in the Ministry of Home Affairs under Moi, then as Deputy Permanent Secretary in the Office of the President (1978–1979) after Kenyatta’s death. After being elected MP in 1979, he returned to the Office of the President as Minister of State (1979–1982) responsible for science and technology, cabinet affairs, land settlement, and immigration, during which the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) was established. In September 1982, he became Minister of Regional Development, Science, and Technology, creating the Lake Basin Development Authority and the Kerio Valley Development Authority based on regional models from Australia and Tennessee. In September 1983, he was appointed Minister of Energy and Regional Development, and in March 1988, after ministry reorganisation, became Minister of Energy, holding the post until January 1991. During this period, he established the National Oil Corporation, built national oil storage facilities near Nairobi connected to the Mombasa refinery, extended the pipeline from Nairobi to Kisumu and Eldoret, and advanced rural electrification, the Sondu Miriu Dam, the Masinga Multi-Purpose Dam, the Kiambere Hydro Electric Dam, and the Turkwell Hydro Electric Multi-Purpose Dam. From 1991 until 1997, he held no government position, then returned as Minister of State in the Office of the President of East Africa in 1997, becoming Minister of East African and Regional Co-operation (1998–1999). He played a central role in COMESA, coordinating legislation for an East African Road Network and an East African Legislative Assembly, and serving as Chairman of both COMESA and the East Africa Council of Ministers. In September 1999, his portfolio expanded to include Trade and Industry, Tourism, and East African Cooperation (1999–2001), during which he established a Tourist Trust Fund with the European Union, set up the Tourist Police, and re-introduced the East Africa Safari Rallies. He was praised as "the hardest working minister of tourism Kenya has ever had" and "the best minister of tourism in 25 years." In May 2001, he continued as Minister of Trade and Industry and East African Tourism (2001–2002), establishing the Small Medium Trade Trust Fund with the European Union, introducing an Intellectual Property bill passed as an Act, achieving a free trade area with COMESA, establishing the Africa Trade Insurance Agency to cover foreign investments against political risk, and serving as Chairman of the African Caribbean Pacific Group (ACP) at the World Trade Organization. Biwott was a successful entrepreneur, having worked with his father in a fruit and vegetable business in Eldoret as a teenager, borrowing money to start a meat and egg sideline, and later forming ABC Foods in the late 1960s. In 1969, at age 29, he purchased the Eldoret Town International Harvester (IH) dealership (now FMD trading as Lima Ltd), a dairy farm, started an importer-exporter business in 1972, bought two wheat farms in 1974, established the sole agency for IH agricultural tractors and implements in 1975, and acquired a local air operator in 1977 (now Air Kenya). His business strategy of acquiring small or failing businesses and reinvesting in them proved successful, making him one of Kenya’s wealthiest businessmen. His businesses employ thousands and one of his major shareholder companies has been among Kenya’s top 10 corporate taxpayers. He supported education, health, and small business development, establishing the Mbegu Trust in 2008 to develop education and opportunity in Kenya. He actively promoted girls’ education by building schools such as the Maria Soti Educational Centre and Biwott Secondary School, and founded and patronized the Keiyo South Education Foundation, providing bursaries to needy students. He led health projects including at least two sub-district hospitals, three health centres, and eight dispensaries, and served as a member and later chairman of the National Fund for the Disabled of Kenya from 1980. Political detractors have raised controversies, particularly from 1989–1992, with allegations tied to the 1990 murder of Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Ouko. Scotland Yard detective John Troon named Biwott as a person of interest in his final report based on statements by Marianne Brinner-Mattern and Dominico Airgahi, directors of BAK Group, which had been awarded a contract to revamp a molasses plant in Kisumu but was terminated due to failure to raise funding and conduct a feasibility study, later awarded to US company F.C. Schaffer under USAID and the then Minister of Industry Dalmas Otieno. Before Ouko’s death, BAK Group claimed $150,000 in damages; after Ouko’s death, the claim rose to $5.975 million. Airgahi was on bail in Milan in 1987 for fraud and extortion, and Brinner-Mattern was a key witness in that case, with the Milanese judge calling her testimony "unreliable" and recommending a "compassionate veil." Ten government officials, including Biwott, were detained in November 1991, but a Kenyan police investigation found no evidence linking Biwott to Ouko’s disappearance or death. In December 2003, Biwott filed a formal complaint against New Scotland Yard, claiming Troon’s investigation was flawed and erroneous, requesting an investigation into Troon and an apology, which was rejected in December 2004 by the Metropolitan Police, citing lack of involvement of UK citizens or suspects and limited resources, and noting the Kenyan Parliamentary Select Committee (PSC) was investigating Ouko’s death. The PSC proceedings were abruptly terminated when Biwott began giving testimony; the committee, led by Gor Sunguh, refused to allow cross-examination of witnesses by Biwott’s lawyers, with six members resigning and four others leaving. New members were appointed, leaving ten members, four of whom did not sign Sunguh’s report. In 2005, Parliament refused to consider Sunguh’s report, which was re-tabled on 8 December 2010 and rejected as “shoddy” and used to “settle political scores.” In 2000, High Court Judge Alnashir Visram awarded Biwott Sh30 million in damages—the largest in a defamation case in Kenya—for linking him to the Ouko murder in a book titled 'Dr Iain West's Casebook' by Chester Stern and others. The court ordered author and pathologist Iain West and journalist Chester Stern to pay KES 15 million in compensatory and KES 15 million in exemplary damages, and bookshops Bookpoint and Bookstop to pay KES 10 million. Several local dailies were also sued; in March 2002, Kalamaka Ltd., publisher of the People Daily, was found guilty of “unmitigated and defenceless character assassination.”

Mr. Nicholas Biwott was awarded a record Sh30 million in damages, the largest settlement in a defamation case in Kenya, after suing British journalist Chester Stern and others for linking him to the Ouko murder in the book 'Dr Iain West's Casebook'. Chester Stern and the book's publishers, Little Brown, stated they would "vigorously defend" the action but ultimately did not defend it, resulting in an uncontested case. Judge Visram ruled that author and pathologist Iain West and journalist Chester Stern, the book’s co-authors, pay KES 15 million in compensatory damages and another KES 15 million in exemplary damages. Bookpoint and Bookstop, popular Nairobi bookshops, also paid Biwott KES 10 million in damages for stocking copies of 'Dr Ian West's Casebook'. Biwott also sued several local dailies for defamatory coverage; in March 2002, Kalamaka Ltd., the publisher of the People Daily, was found guilty of "unmitigated and defenceless character assassination" and awarded Kshs 20 million in damages. Biwott's case is said to have contributed to the development of defamation law in Kenya and was referenced in 2005 in a defamation and libel case filed by former Chief Justice Evans Gicheru, who sued Andrew Morton, author of the biography 'Moi - The Making of an African Statesman', and publisher Michael O Mara Books. On the morning of 11 July 2017, Biwott died of complications from kidney failure at a Nairobi hospital. A memorial service was held at Milimani AIC on 18 July 2017, and a second service was held at the Maria Soti Girls Educational Centre Kaptarakwa in Keiyo, Elgeyo/Marakwet County, with over 20,000 people attending. In his final speech at the funeral, President Uhuru Kenyatta eulogized Biwott as a "true patriot", stating that when the history of Kenya is written, it will include many men and women who quietly but firmly and confidently contributed to Kenya being a sound, stable country with a growing economy, and that Nicholas Biwott is one of those people. Biwott was buried in a wooden casket, contrary to misleading claims circulating on Kenyan social media prior to his burial that he would be buried in a gold coffin.

Nicholas Joseph LaLota (/ləˈloʊtə/ lə-LOH-tə; born June 23, 1978) is an American politician and veteran who has served since January 7, 2023, as the U.S. representative for New York's 1st congressional district. He is a member of the Republican Party and was born in Bay Shore, New York. LaLota graduated from St. Anthony's High School and earned a degree from the United States Naval Academy in 2000. He served in the U.S. Navy for eight years, including three overseas deployments. He obtained a Master of Business Administration and a Juris Doctor from Hofstra University. LaLota served as chief of staff to Suffolk County presiding officer Kevin McCaffrey, on the Suffolk Board of Elections, and as a trustee for the village of Amityville, New York. He ran for the U.S. House of Representatives in New York's 1st congressional district to succeed Lee Zeldin, who sought the governorship, and won the general election on November 8, 2022, by defeating Democratic nominee Bridget Fleming. On December 27, 2022, LaLota became one of the first Republicans to call for a full House Ethics Committee investigation into false claims made by fellow Long Island Republican George Santos. On March 7, 2024, during President Joe Biden's State of the Union address, Santos announced on social media that he planned to run against LaLota in the 2024 Republican primary. LaLota sought reelection in 2024 and defeated Democratic nominee John Avlon. He is one of six Republicans who signed a bipartisan letter led by centrist House Representatives, pledging to respect the results of the 2024 presidential election. LaLota married his high school sweetheart, Kaylie, who teaches at Northport High School; they have three daughters. He resides in Amityville, New York, and is Catholic.

The Nike Cortez is the first running shoe released by Nike in 1972 and is considered a significant factor in the company's success. It was designed by Nike co-founders Bill Bowerman and Phil Knight, who first met in 1957 when Knight competed on Bowerman's track team at the University of Oregon. Knight acquired the distribution rights for Onitsuka Tiger athletic shoes in the U.S., and the two founded Blue Ribbon Sports, which later changed its name to Nike in 1972. Bowerman believed athletes needed a better track shoe than what was available and finalized the design of the Cortez in 1968. The shoe's initial name was "Mexico," referencing the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City; after that, it was renamed "Aztec," but Adidas threatened legal action due to similarity with its Azteca Gold shoe. They then chose "Cortez," honoring Hernan Cortés, the Spanish Conquistador who led the expedition that ended the Aztec Empire. The shoe was introduced to the public at the peak of the 1972 Summer Olympics and gained widespread attention after U.S. Olympic athletes began wearing it. Sales reached $800,000 in the first year, a 100% increase over the 8,000 sales inquiries from the first year of selling Onitsuka Tiger shoes. The Cortez was initially made with leather, but Bowerman later switched to nylon and suede to reduce weight and improve comfort. The shoe features a simple design with the Nike swoosh on the sides and a streak on the lower sole, and its foam is generously placed to absorb road shock, reduce leg fatigue, and provide comfort, with one marathoner calling it "the most comfortable shoe ever." In 2009, the Cortez Fly Motion was released, incorporating flywire—lightweight Vectran threads—that further reduced the shoe's weight. The shoe has been redesigned multiple times and set an early standard for running shoes. It is also famously worn by George Costanza on Seinfeld and by Forrest Gump in the 1994 film Forrest Gump. The Nike Cortez is commonly worn by gangs in Los Angeles, notably MS-13; in January 2013, four Hispanic teenagers were shot in a Brentwood, California neighborhood after being asked why they were wearing Nike Cortez shoes, and all were injured. Nike eventually grew into a multi-billion dollar corporation operating in over 160 countries and employing more than 35,000 people. In 1974, Nike won a court battle to continue using the name "Cortez" after the shoe was previously known as the Onitsuka Tiger Cortez, and it was later renamed to the Onitsuka Tiger Corsair.

In mathematics, a Nikodym set is a subset of the unit square in ℝ² with a complement of Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., area 1), such that for any point in the set, there exists a straight line that intersects the set only at that point. The existence of such a set was first established by Otto Nikodym in 1927. Later, constructions were developed showing that each point in a Nikodym set has continuum many exceptional lines, and Kenneth Falconer identified analogues of these sets in higher dimensions. Nikodym sets are closely related to Kakeya sets, also known as Besicovitch sets. The existence of Nikodym sets is sometimes compared to the Banach–Tarski paradox, although a key difference exists: the Banach–Tarski paradox depends on non-measurable sets. Researchers have also studied Nikodym sets over finite fields, as opposed to ℝ.

Nikolai Vladimirovich Talyzin (Russian: Никола́й Влади́мирович Талы́зин; 28 January 1929 – 23 January 1991) was a Soviet bureaucrat and economist who served as head of the Gosplan, or the State Planning Committee. Born in Moscow to a working-class family, he graduated from the Moscow Communications Institute and worked at the Scientific Research Institute of Radio of the Soviet Ministry of Communications, where he held positions including engineer, leading designer, senior research fellow, and deputy director. Under his leadership, the world's first satellite television broadcasting system "Orbita" was developed and put into operation in 1967, enabling nearly 90 million citizens in Siberia and the Russian Far East to watch Soviet Central Television programs. He also oversaw the introduction of the satellite systems "Moscow" and "Moscow-Global." In October 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev appointed Talyzin to help initiate perestroika, following five years as the Soviet representative at Comecon, the Eastern European trade bloc. He was appointed head of the State Planning Commission when most sectors of the Soviet economy remained under state control and became one of the three First Deputy Premiers, as well as a non-voting member of the Communist Party Politburo. As Gorbachev advanced economic reforms, the planning commission's role shifted from setting production targets to formulating economic strategy. Talyzin faced significant criticism and was moved to head the Bureau for Social Development in 1988, a position he held due to being blamed for slowing reforms. In September 1989, when perestroika failed to achieve its intended outcomes, he was dismissed, along with many other conservatives in Nikolai Ryzhkov's government, whom he accused of hindering reform progress.

Annamaria Beatrice "Nina" Amenta is an American computer scientist serving as the Tim Bucher Family Professor of Computer Science and chair of the Computer Science Department at the University of California, Davis.[1][2] Her expertise lies in computational geometry and computer graphics, with a notable focus on reconstructing surfaces from scattered data points.[2][3] She was raised in Pittsburgh and earned a bachelor's degree in classical civilization from Yale University, graduating in 1979.[2][4] After working as a computer programmer for over ten years, she returned to graduate school and obtained her Ph.D. in 1994 from the University of California, Berkeley, with a thesis on the relations between Helly's theorem and generalized linear programming, under the supervision of Raimund Seidel.[5] Following postdoctoral research at The Geometry Center and Xerox PARC, she joined the faculty at the University of Texas at Austin and relocated to the University of California, Davis in 2002. She was appointed Bucher Professor and department chair in 2013.[2] Amenta co-chaired the Symposium on Computational Geometry in 2006 alongside Otfried Cheong.[6]

Noel Fielding (/ˈnəʊəl/; born 21 May 1973) is an English comedian, artist, and actor. In 1998, he co-created the comedy troupe The Mighty Boosh with Julian Barratt, playing the character Vince Noir and several others. Other notable roles include Richmond in the IT Crowd, the lead role of Dick Turpin in The Completely Made-Up Adventures of Dick Turpin (2024), and he has been a co-presenter of The Great British Bake Off since 2017. Fielding began performing stand-up comedy after graduating from art school in 1995 and first met Barratt in 1997 when they both performed at a pub in north London. In 1998, they performed their first comedy show together at Oranje Boom Boom, which was "very raw, but... hilarious," followed by a gig at Hen and Chickens Theatre in Islington, London. They took The Mighty Boosh to the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in 1998, then returned in 1999 with Arctic Boosh and in 2000 with Autoboosh. In 2001, The Mighty Boosh became a six-part radio show on BBC London Live, later transferring to BBC Radio 4. In 2004, it became an 8-part television show on BBC Three, airing for three series until 2007—20 episodes in total—with the first series set in a zoo operated by Bob Fossil, the second in a flat, and the third in a secondhand shop in Dalston called Nabootique. The show generated a cult following and won awards, with its style described as surreal, escapist, and new wave comedy. Fielding said he did all the animations for the first three weeks of the TV show, but due to lack of sleep, Ivana Zorn, Nigel Coan's partner, took over most of the painting, with Fielding designing the main characters. Fielding and Barratt formed Secret Peter Productions with Nigel Coan, who also directed and co-wrote Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy and helped animate series 1 and 2 of The Mighty Boosh. Dave Brown contributed graphics, and Julian Barratt composed all the music. The Mighty Boosh won the Shockwaves NME Best TV Award three times in 2007, 2008, and 2010. In 2006, they toured with The Mighty Boosh Live, and in 2008–2009, they toured again with The Mighty Boosh Live: Future Sailors Tour. Fielding and Barratt wrote two film scripts that did not reach production—one a "Rocky Horror Picture Show type thing" with Barratt as a man believing himself to be the last human, and another an Arctic adventure—due to their interest in the Arctic. Fielding appeared as a team captain on Never Mind the Buzzcocks from 2009 to 2015 and again since 2021, achieving the record for the highest team score, and appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year thirteen times between 2006 and 2017, including three with Russell Brand, nine with Richard Ayoade, and once with Eddie Izzard. He also appeared in Catherine Tate's TV movie Laughing at the Noughties (2011), performed Kate Bush's "Wuthering Heights" dance routine for Let's Dance for Comic Relief (2011), and took part in Channel 4's Comedy Gala in 2010 and 2014. In 2011, he produced his first solo series for E4, titled Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy, which aired in January 2012 and had a second series in 2014 titled Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy 2: Tales From Painted Hawaii. He also appeared in music videos for Mint Royale ("Blue Song"), Razorlight ("In the Morning"), Robots in Disguise ("Girl", "The Tears", "Turn It Up"), and Kasabian ("Vlad the Impaler", "Re-Wired", "La Fée Verte"), with the "Vlad" role reprised at the 2014 Glastonbury Festival. Fielding was scheduled to appear in the 2007 film Stardust but dropped out due to ill health. In November 2007, he starred in five episodes of Vic Reeves' House Arrest as a local vagrant. He was born in the Westminster area of London in 1973, the son of Royal Mail manager Ray Fielding and Yvonne Fagan, and grew up in Mitcham, Southwest London. He is of French descent through his father, who Fielding described as "..basically French," and when he was three, his father remarried, and Fielding was mostly raised by his paternal grandmother. His father and stepmother, Diane, became more involved in parenting during his mother's illness in the 1980s, and his mother died in 1990 at age 37 from complications of liver damage. Fielding has commented that "My parents had lots of parties... They were hopelessly bohemian." Michael Fielding, his younger paternal half-brother, played various characters in The Mighty Boosh and Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy, and his father and stepmother appeared in The Mighty Boosh, with his father making cameos as Chris de Burgh. When Fielding was around 6 or 7, he attended a Kiss concert, wearing a Kiss costume and was taken to the backstage dressing room so Gene Simmons could see it. At age 13, he began writing comedy sketches, and at 15, he became a goth and started using makeup, saying he loved being dressed up by his girlfriends. While studying at Croydon Art College, he met Dave Brown. From 1992 to 1995, he studied a BA in graphic design and advertising at Buckinghamshire College of Higher Education in High Wycombe, graduating in 1995. While at the college, Dave Brown and Nigel Coan were also on the same course, and all three shared a student house. Nigel Coan later collaborated with Fielding on The Mighty Boosh. After university, Fielding began performing comedy and started stand-up after graduating in 1995. In 1997, he first met Barratt at a pub in north London, where they both performed. Barratt had more experience in performing than Fielding, but they "had quite a good chemistry straight away." On the day they met, they went back to Barratt's place, where Barratt played music on his Akai sampler and Fielding used a ping-pong ball to make an eye patch. Both shared an interest in music—Fielding into rock and pop, Barratt into jazz and electro—and both had played in bands before meeting. They also shared a love of comedy, including Vic Reeves and Bob Mortimer. In 2010, Fielding was scheduled to perform a solo tour but cancelled it via Twitter, stating he was too busy to write the Mighty Boosh film and create a new album. In 2012, he toured Sydney and Melbourne with a solo stand-up show and hosted a stand-up comedy gala at the Just For Laughs festival in Sydney. From 2014 to 2015, he toured the UK and Australia with An Evening With Noel Fielding, which included stand-up, sketch comedy, and performances by his brother Michael Fielding and long-term collaborator Tom Meeten, with Nigel Coan creating the animation. In 2005 and 2010, Fielding performed at Montreal's Just For Laughs comedy festival, and in 2020, the festival moved online due to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Fielding and Jimmy Carr live-streamed a conversation from their homes. Barratt and Fielding first performed together in Stewart Lee's show Moby Dick and King Dong (Edinburgh Fringe Festival, 1997), in which Barratt played King Dong's penis. The name "Mighty Boosh" originated from a phrase used by a friend of Michael Fielding's to describe Michael's childhood hair. Fielding and Barratt said they used to place potted plants around Hen and Chickens to try and make it into a play, though they "didn't know anything about theatre or what you did." Fielding has said that his show is "magical and fantastical," telling intricate, weird stories, with Vince Noir being a modern, indie kid and Howard Moon being eccentric, relying heavily on Barratt's music and his own animation. Fielding formed Secret Peter Productions with Nigel Coan, and Coan also directed and co-wrote Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy. In 2017, it was revealed that Fielding would co-host The Great British Bake Off with Sandi Toksvig. In 2017, he appeared as a contestant on Taskmaster (Series 4), hosted by Greg Davies and Alex Horne, and won the series. In January 2018, he was a panellist on QI alongside Russell Brand and Aisling Bea. In 2024, he played Dick Turpin in The Completely Made-Up Adventures of Dick Turpin on Apple TV+. Fielding has exhibited his artwork in London and collaborated with Fendi for their autumn/winter 2021 menswear collection.

Noel Fielding made a brief appearance in the opening sequence of the film Baby Driver (2017) and appeared in the music video for Razorlight's "In the Morning". He featured in music videos for Robots in Disguise songs "Girl" (alongside Chris Corner, who was at the time boyfriend to Sue Denim), "The Tears", and "Turn It Up". In 2009, he was involved in the Kasabian video "Vlad the Impaler", in which he plays the titular character, and reprised the role at the 2014 Glastonbury Festival. The music video was directed by Richard Ayoade; Fielding is referenced in Kasabian's "La Fée Verte", a track on their Velociraptor! album, with Sergio Pizzorno noting "The line, 'I met Dalí in the street.' Dalí is Noel Fielding. And he is the modern-day Dalí". He also appears as Vlad in the "Re-Wired" video, riding a five-seater bicycle with the band, and as a patient in a psychiatric hospital in "You're In Love With a Psycho", re-enacting the broken mirror routine from the Marx Brothers film Duck Soup with Pizzorno and Tom Meighan. He appeared in Kate Bush's music video "Deeper Understanding" as a thank-you for the Let's Dance For Comic Relief performance. Fielding formed a band called Loose Tapestries with Sergio Pizzorno to provide music for Noel Fielding's Luxury Comedy; the band released two albums and a Christmas single. Fielding has exhibited his paintings in London; his first exhibition, entitled Psychedelic Dreams of the Jelly Fox, took place in December 2007 in a gallery above the patisserie Maison Bertaux in Greek Street, Soho. There, he listed inspirations including Henri Rousseau, René Magritte, Willem de Kooning, Roy Lichtenstein, Dexter Dalwood, a former tutor from the Croydon School of Art, and Salvador Dalí. A second exhibition, Bryan Ferry vs the Jelly Fox, ran from 5 July 2010 to 5 January 2011 at Maison Bertaux. In October 2011, he released an art book titled Scribblings of a Madcap Shambleton, co-produced with The Mighty Boosh cast member Dave Brown, featuring many of his old and new paintings, drawings, and photography. His video installation of The Jelly Fox was shown at the Saatchi Gallery, and in 2012 he created a unique piece inspired by The Beatles for Liverpool Love at the Museum of Liverpool. In March 2015, his exhibition He Wore Dreams Around Unkind Faces was shown at the Royal Albert Hall. In January 2021, luxury fashion house Fendi unveiled a collection featuring abstract takes on the brand's logo, created by Fielding. On 18 November 2025, British rock band Pink Floyd released a newly mixed version of Shine On You Crazy Diamond (Parts I–IX) along with an official YouTube video featuring a time-lapse painting by Fielding inspired by founding member Syd Barrett. On 6 September 2011, Fielding received an honorary master's degree from his alma mater, now called Buckinghamshire New University, for his ongoing interest in the graphics area and support for many art organisations. In 2015, Fielding was named one of GQ magazine's 50 best-dressed British men. He was formerly in a relationship with Robots in Disguise lead vocalist Dee Plume, who made minor appearances in The Mighty Boosh and its live adaptations. He began dating radio DJ Lliana Bird around 2010, and they have two children. During his time at art college, Fielding developed what was suspected to be the virus hepatitis A, though it was later confirmed to be glandular fever; Nigel Coan, who studied the same course at art college and shared a flat with him, helped Fielding during this period. Fielding was ill and exhausted for a year. His paternal half-brother is Michael Fielding.

The Nokia 2 is a budget Android smartphone manufactured by HMD Global under the Nokia brand, announced on 31 October 2017. It features a 5.0-inch LTPS IPS LCD display, a quad-core 1.3 GHz Cortex-A7 Qualcomm Snapdragon 212 processor, 1 GB of RAM, and 8 GB of internal storage that can be expanded via microSD cards up to 128 GB. The device is equipped with a 4100 mAh battery, offering a claimed two-day battery life. It includes an 8 MP rear camera with LED flash and a 5 MP front-facing camera, available in pewter and black, pewter and white, and copper and black colour options. The phone launched with Android 7.1.1 Nougat and can be upgraded to Android 8.1 Oreo; however, in June 2019, HMD Global announced it would not receive an update to Android 9 Pie due to the System-on-Chip's insufficient performance. Reviews of the Nokia 2 were mixed, with Andrew Williams of TechRadar commending its battery life and pricing, while criticizing its slow performance, poor cameras, and limited storage.

The Nokia 8110 is a mobile phone released in 1996 and announced on 9 September 1996 as the first device in Nokia's high-end 8000 series. It introduced the first 'slider' form factor, where a sliding cover protected the keypad when carried in a pocket and extended downward during use, bringing the microphone closer to the mouth; opening the cover also answered an incoming call. Its curved design, especially when open, led to it being nicknamed the "banana phone." It was the first Nokia phone to feature a monochrome graphic LCD. Designed for the business market, it was one of the smallest and lightest phones available at 152 grams, with better battery life than its predecessor, the Nokia 2110. It was also the first GSM cellphone to use an ARM processor. The improved 8110i model, launched in March 1997, was the first phone to include the SSMS (Smart SMS) engine. Handsets could be updated OTA (Over The Air) with an intelligent menu structure, enabling simple information input sent via structured text messages to an MT receiver, which could then interpret the data and send a structured response back. Ring tone receiving via SMS was also part of the smart messaging protocol, making the 8110i the first mobile phone to support it. Nokia eventually discontinued Smart messaging in favor of the WAP standard but has not removed smart messaging support from later models. The 8110 and 8110i models were succeeded by the Nokia 8810 in 1998, while the 8146 and 8148 models were succeeded by the Nokia 7110 in 1999. An altered version of the phone was famously featured in the science fiction action film The Matrix (1999), where it was modified with a spring-loaded mechanism—though this feature actually appeared on the Nokia 7110.

Nokia Corporation, a Finnish multinational telecommunications, information technology, and consumer electronics corporation, was originally established in 1865 as a pulp mill by mining engineer Fredrik Idestam near Tampere, Finland, with a second mill opened in Nokia in 1868. The company was formally named Nokia Ab in 1871 after the second site. Over time, it expanded into rubber and cables, and in 1922 partnered with Finnish Rubber Works and Kaapelitehdas.
