In 1967, the three entities merged to form Nokia Corporation, which was restructured into forestry, cable, rubber, and electronics, later entering networking and radio industries. In 1977, Kari Kairamo became CEO and led major acquisitions, including Salora, Luxor AB, and Oceanic, making Nokia the third-largest television manufacturer in Europe. In 1979, Nokia established Mobira, a mobile radio telephone manufacturer, which launched the world's first international cellular network, NMT, in 1981 and the first mobile phone, the Mobira Senator, in 1982. In 1984, Nokia acquired Mobira and later acquired Schaub-Lorenz in 1987, which was sold under the "ITT Nokia" brand. In 1988, Nokia bought Ericsson's Information Systems division, forming Nokia Data. After Kairamo's death in 1988, Simo Vuorilehto led a restructuring, divesting unstrategic units, including Nokian Tyres in 1988 and Finnish Rubber Works in 1990, and selling the computer division, Nokia Data, to ICL in 1991. Jorma Ollila succeeded Vuorilehto in 1992 and transformed the company into a telecom-oriented enterprise, leading to a significant rise in operating profit from negative in 1991 to $1 billion in 1995 and nearly $4 billion by 1999. Nokia assisted in developing the GSM standard and launched the world's first GSM call in 1991 using its equipment. The Nokia 1011 was the first commercially available GSM mobile phone, launched in November 1992. In 1996, Nokia sold its television business to Semi-Tech Corporation, closing its German plant in September 1996 and retaining brand rights until 1999. In 1997, Nokia launched the first digital satellite receivers in the UK and introduced the first with Common Interface (CI) support. In 1998, Nokia became the world's best-selling mobile phone brand, surpassing Motorola, and manufactured its 100 millionth mobile phone. The success was driven by fashion-oriented products like the Nokia 5110 and 3210, featuring colorful, replaceable back covers. In 1998, Nokia co-founded Symbian Ltd. with Psion to develop a new operating system for PDAs and smartphones, launching the Nokia 9210 Communicator in 2001 and the Symbian Series 60 platform, later introducing the Nokia 7650 as the first camera phone. Nokia became the largest shareholder of Symbian in February 2004 and fully acquired the company in June 2008, forming the Symbian Foundation as its successor. In 1999, Nokia introduced its first wireless LAN products and in 2000 employed over 55,000 people, with a 30% market share in mobile phones, nearly double that of Motorola. By 2000, Nokia had operations in 140 countries and was recognized as the "most trusted brand in Europe" in a Reader's Digest survey. Nokia pioneered camera phones, launching the first in North America with the Nokia 3600/3650 in 2003, and introduced the Nseries in April 2005. The Nokia N95, launched in 2006, won "best mobile imaging device" in Europe in 2007, while the N82 (2008) and N93 (2006) were also recognized for imaging. The N8 (2010) featured a 12-megapixel sensor, the 808 PureView (2012) had a 41-megapixel sensor, and the Lumia 920 (2012) implemented advanced PureView technologies. Nokia was a pioneer in mobile gaming, with Snake preloaded on many devices, and attempted to enter the handheld gaming market with the N-Gage in 2002, which failed despite efforts to revive it as a smartphone platform in 2008. In Q1 2004, Nokia's mobile phone market share dropped to 28.9%, but it recovered, reaching a peak of 40.4% in Q4 2007 with a 51% smartphone market share, being the largest vendor globally in all regions except North America. In 2005, Nokia launched mobile TV trials in Finland with Yle and in the UK with Arqiva and O2 using the DVB-H standard. In 2005, Nokia developed Maemo, a Linux-based operating system, which shipped on the Nokia 770 Internet Tablet. On 1 June 2006, Jorma Ollila became chairman and retired as CEO, replaced by Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo. In August 2007, Nokia introduced Ovi, an umbrella for its Internet services, including the N-Gage platform and Nokia Music Store, which faced competition from Apple's App Store in 2008. In October 2008, Nokia announced the Nokia 5800 Xpress. In 2020, Nokia employed approximately 92,000 people across over 100 countries, did business in more than 130 countries, and reported annual revenues of around €23 billion. It is a public limited company listed on Nasdaq Helsinki and the New York Stock Exchange, was the world's 415th-largest company by 2016 revenues according to the Fortune Global 500, having peaked at 85th place in 2009, and is a component of the Euro Stoxx 50 stock market index. The company's roots are in the Tampere region of Pirkanmaa, with its main headquarters in Espoo, Finland, in the Helsinki metropolitan area. At its peak in 2000, Nokia accounted for 4% of Finland's GDP, 21% of total exports, and 70% of the Nasdaq Helsinki market capital. Nokia is the world's third-largest network equipment manufacturer as of 2018. After a partnership with Microsoft and subsequent market struggles, Microsoft bought Nokia's mobile phone business in 2014, incorporating it as Microsoft Mobile. Following the sale, Nokia focused on telecommunications infrastructure and Internet of things technologies, divesting its Here mapping division and acquiring Alcatel-Lucent, including its Bell Labs research organization. The company also experimented with virtual reality and digital health through the purchase of Withings. The Nokia brand returned to the mobile and smartphone market in 2016 via a licensing arrangement with HMD. Nokia remains a major patent licensor for most large mobile phone vendors. Its history dates from 1865, with the first pulp mill established near Tampere, and a second near Nokia, and the company was named after the latter site. The coordinates of the original site are 60°13′30″N 24°45′22″E (60.225°N 24.756°E).

Nokia launched mobile TV trials in 2005 in Finland with content from public broadcaster Yle, using the DVB-H standard, and the service could be viewed on the widescreen Nokia 7710 smartphone with a special accessory for receiving DVB-H signals. The company also partnered with Arqiva and O2 to conduct trials in the UK in September 2005. In 2005, Nokia developed a Linux-based operating system called Maemo, which was released that year on the Nokia 770 Internet Tablet. On 1 June 2006, Jorma Ollila became chairman and retired as CEO, replaced by Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo. In August 2007, Nokia introduced Ovi, an umbrella name for its new Internet services, including the N-Gage platform and the Nokia Music Store; the Ovi Store faced strong competition from Apple's App Store when it launched in 2008. In October 2008, Nokia announced the Nokia 5800 XpressMusic, the first device to ship with the touch-centric S60 5th Edition, also known as Symbian^1, the first iteration of the platform since the Symbian Foundation's creation. In November 2008, Nokia announced it would end mobile phone sales in Japan due to low market share. Nokia's global mobile phone market share peaked in 2008 at 38.6 percent. That same year, Nokia acquired Trolltech and its Qt software development, which became a central part of its strategy until 2011 and was eventually sold in 2012. Nokia briefly returned to the computer market with the Booklet 3G netbook in August 2009. In late 2009 and 2010, the music-focused Xseries and consumer-focused Cseries were introduced respectively. In April 2010, Nokia introduced the Nokia N8, the first device to run on Symbian^3, though it was delayed for many months, tarnishing the company's image, especially after the failure of the N97 and increased competition from Apple and Google. On 10 September 2010, Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo was fired as CEO, and Stephen Elop from Microsoft was appointed as CEO, becoming the first non-Finnish director in Nokia's history; investors pressured the board to recruit an outsider to shake up management and break from the traditional "Nokia way." Ollila announced he would step down as chairman by 2012. On 11 March 2011, Nokia paid Elop a $6 million signing bonus as "compensation for lost income from his prior employer," in addition to his $1.4 million annual salary. The old Symbian OS became completely open-source in February 2010, but in November 2010, it was announced that the Symbian Foundation was closing and that Nokia would take back control of the Symbian operating system under closed licensing. By then, Nokia was the only remaining company using the platform, along with carrier NTT Docomo in Japan, after Samsung and Sony Ericsson moved to Android. In 2010, for its Linux ambitions, Nokia collaborated with Intel to form the MeeGo project, resulting from the merger of Nokia's Maemo and Intel's Moblin. Nokia's Symbian platform, which had been the leading smartphone platform in Europe and Asia for many years, became outdated and difficult for developers after the rise of iOS and Android. To counter this, Nokia planned to make its MeeGo Linux operating system, under development, the company's flagship on smartphones. Shortly after Elop's CEO tenure began, the Nokia board approved his ability to change the company's mobile phone strategy, including switching operating systems. Veteran Anssi Vanjoki, head of the smartphones division, left the company around this time, with his final appearance at Nokia World 2010 when the Nokia E7-00 and other Symbian^3 devices were introduced. On 11 February 2011, Nokia announced a "strategic partnership" with Microsoft, adopting Windows Phone 7 as its primary smartphone operating system and integrating its services, including Bing as search engine and Nokia Maps data into Bing Maps. Elop stated that Nokia chose not to use Android due to an apparent inability to "differentiate" its offerings, with critics noting his past ties to Microsoft may have influenced the decision. Although the MeeGo "Harmattan"-based N9 received a highly positive reception in 2011, Nokia had already decided to end MeeGo development and focus solely on its Microsoft partnership, though the CEO said the N9's "innovations" would live on in future products, eventually appearing on the Asha platform in 2013. After the Microsoft partnership announcement, Nokia's market share declined due to falling demand for Symbian as consumers realized the company's focus would shift. The company posted a large loss for the second quarter of 2011—only its second quarterly loss in 19 years. Nokia's first Windows Phone flagship was the Lumia 800, released in November 2011. Falling sales in 2011, not significantly improved by the Lumia line in 2012, led to consecutive quarters of huge losses. By mid-2012, the company's stock price fell below $2. CEO Elop announced cost-cutting measures in June, including shedding 10,000 employees by year-end and closing the Salo manufacturing plant. The Finnish prime minister announced that the government would not subsidize the company from an emergency state fund. Around this time, Nokia launched a new project codenamed "Meltemi," a platform for low-end smartphones. Under the Microsoft alliance and Elop's management, Nokia renewed its focus on the North American market, where Nokia phones had been almost irrelevant for many years. This strategy began in January 2012 with the introduction of the Nokia Lumia 900 smartphone in partnership with U.S. carrier AT&T. In March 2011, Nokia introduced a new corporate typeface called "Pure." On 1 August 2011, Nokia announced a new three-digit naming system for mobile phones, ending the use of letters and effectively ending the Nseries, Eseries, and Cseries; the Nokia 500 was introduced with the new system. Nokia last used three-digit names on analogue phones in the 1990s. When the Lumia 920 was announced in September 2012, it was seen as the first high-end Windows Phone with a feature set capable of challenging rivals, and Elop said the positive reaction created a sense of hope and optimism. The company also made gains in developing countries with its Asha series, which were selling strongly. Although Nokia's smartphone sales and market share increased throughout 2013, including in North America, it was still not enough to avoid financial losses. Ollila stepped down as chairman on 4 May 2012 and was replaced by Risto Siilasmaa. In September 2013, Nokia announced the sale of its mobile and devices division to Microsoft, which helped avoid further financial losses and benefited Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer, who wanted to expand Microsoft's hardware and become a devices and services company. Nokia chairperson Risto Siilasmaa described the deal as rationally correct but emotionally difficult—experts agree that Nokia would have faced a cash crisis without selling the division. Analysts believe Ballmer pushed for the buyout due to fears that Nokia was close to adopting Android and abandoning its Microsoft alliance. Indeed, in January 2014, the Nokia X was introduced, running on a customized version of Android, a surprising launch just weeks before the finalization of the Microsoft buyout. Others, including Ballmer's successor Satya Nadella, believed Microsoft thought merging its software teams with Nokia's hardware engineering and design would "accelerate" growth of Windows Phone. The sale was completed in April 2014, with Microsoft Mobile becoming the successor to Nokia's mobile devices division. Nokia also moved its headquarters to a new building complex at Karaportti. At the time, Ballmer was retiring as Microsoft CEO and was replaced by Satya Nadella, who opposed the Nokia mobile phones purchase, along with chairman Bill Gates. The purchased assets from Nokia were eventually written off by Microsoft in 2015. By 2014, Nokia's global brand value according to Interbrand fell to 98th place, a sharp decline from the 5th place it held in 2009. Nokia's downfall in the mobile phone market has been explained differently by analysts, with many divided over the CEO's decision to abandon its in-house operating system and adopt Windows Phone in 2011. Many researchers concluded that Nokia suffered from deep internal rivalries within management. Former employees claimed that management became complacent after early success. Some from the Symbian development team claimed that upper management rejected hundreds of proposed innovations during the 2000s, including a complete rewrite of Symbian's code. One former employee claimed the company was run as a "Soviet-style bureaucracy." In July 2013, Nokia bought Siemens' stake in the Nokia Siemens Networks joint venture for $2.2 billion, turning it into a wholly owned subsidiary called Nokia Solutions and Networks, later rebranded as Nokia Networks. During its financial struggles, its profitable networking division with Siemens provided much of its income; thus, the purchase was positive, especially after the sale of its mobile devices unit. After selling its mobile devices division, Nokia focused on network equipment through Nokia Networks. In October 2014, Nokia and China Mobile signed a US$970 million framework deal for delivery between 2014 and 2015. On 17 November 2014, Nokia Technologies head Ramzi Haidamus disclosed that the company planned to re-enter the consumer electronics business as an original design manufacturer, licensing in-house hardware designs and technologies to third-party manufacturers. Haidamus stated that the Nokia brand was "valuable" but "is diminishing in value, and that's why it is important that we reverse that trend very quickly, imminently." The next day, Nokia unveiled the N1, an Android tablet manufactured by Foxconn, as its first product following the Microsoft sale. Haidamus emphasized that devices under these licensing agreements would meet high production quality standards and "look and feel just like Nokia built it." Nokia CEO Rajeev Suri stated that the company planned to re-enter the mobile phone business in this manner in 2016, following the expiration of its non-compete clause with Microsoft. According to Robert Morlino, the spokesman for Nokia Technologies, the company planned to follow a brand-licensing model rather than direct marketing of mobile devices due to the sale of its mobile devices division to Microsoft. The company took aggressive steps to revitalize itself, evident through hiring software experts, testing new products, and seeking sales partners. On 14 July 2015, CEO Rajeev Suri confirmed that the company would return to the mobile phones market in 2016. On 28 July 2015, Nokia announced OZO, a 360-degree virtual reality camera with eight 2K optical image sensors, claiming it would be the most advanced VR film-making platform. The division behind the product stated that OZO would be "the first in a planned portfolio of digital media solutions," with more technological products expected. OZO was fully unveiled on 30 November in Los Angeles. The OZO, designed for professional use, was initially intended for retail at US$60,000; however, its price was reduced by $15,000 prior to release and is now listed as $40,000. On 14 April 2015, Nokia confirmed talks with French telecommunications equipment company Alcatel-Lucent regarding a potential merger. The next day, Nokia announced an agreement to purchase Alcatel-Lucent for €15.6 billion in an all-stock deal. CEO Rajeev Suri believed the purchase would give Nokia a strategic advantage in 5G wireless technology development. The acquisition created a stronger competitor to Ericsson and Huawei, whom Nokia and Alcatel-Lucent had surpassed in total combined revenue in 2014. Nokia shareholders hold 66.5% of the new combined company, while Alcatel-Lucent shareholders hold 33.5%. The Bell Labs division was to be maintained, but the Alcatel-Lucent brand would be replaced by Nokia. In October 2015, following approval by China's Ministry of Commerce, the merger awaited approval by French regulators. Despite the initial intent to sell the submarine cable division separately, Alcatel-Lucent later declared it would not. The merger closed on 14 January 2016, but was not complete until 3 November 2016. From the acquisition, Nokia is now also the owner of the Alcatel Mobile phone brand, which continues to be licensed to TCL. On 3 August 2015, Nokia announced a deal to sell its Here digital maps division to a consortium of BMW, Daimler AG, and Volkswagen Group for €2.8 billion. The deal closed on 3 December 2015. On 26 April 2016, Nokia announced its intent to acquire French connected health device maker Withings for US$191 million, integrating it into a new Digital Health unit of Nokia Technologies. Nokia later wrote off the cost of the acquisition and in May 2018 the health unit was sold back to Éric Carreel, a Withings co-founder and former CEO. On 18 May 2016, Microsoft Mobile sold its Nokia-branded feature phone business to HMD Global, a new company founded by former Nokia executive Jean-Francois Baril, and an associated factory in Vietnam to Foxconn's FIH Mobile subsidiary. Nokia entered into a long-term licensing deal with HMD to make it the exclusive manufacturer of Nokia-branded phones and tablets outside Japan, operating in conjunction with Foxconn. The deal also granted HMD the right to essential patents and featurephone software. HMD subsequently announced the Android-based Nokia 6 smartphone in January 2017. At Mobile World Congress, HMD unveiled the Nokia 3 and Nokia 5 smartphones, as well as a re-imagining of Nokia's classic 3310 feature phone. Nokia has direct investments in the company and has some input in the new devices. On 28 June 2016, Nokia demonstrated a 5G-ready network for the first time. In February 2017, Nokia carried out a 5G connection in Oulu, Finland using the 5GTF standard, backed by Verizon, on Intel architecture-based equipment. In July 2017, Nokia and Xiaomi signed a business collaboration agreement and a multi-year patent agreement, including a cross-license to each company's cellular standard-essential patents. In that year, Nokia's brand value was ranked 188th by Brand Finance, a jump of 147 places from 2016, attributed to its health portfolio and new mobile phones developed by HMD Global. In January 2018, Nokia signed a deal with NTT Docomo, Japan's largest mobile operator, to provide 5G wireless radio base stations in the country by 2020. Later that month, Nokia announced the ReefShark line of 5G chipsets, claiming it triples bandwidth to 84 Gbit/s. In March, Solidium, the investment arm of the Finnish Government, purchased a 3.3% stake in Nokia valued at €844 million. In 2017, Nokia and Xiaomi signed a business collaboration agreement and a multi-year patent agreement, including a cross-license to each company's cellular standard-essential patents. That year, Nokia's brand value was ranked 188th by Brand Finance, an increase of 147 places from 2016, attributed to its health portfolio and new mobile phones developed by HMD Global. In January 2018, Nokia signed a deal with NTT Docomo, Japan's largest mobile operator, to provide 5G wireless radio base stations in Japan by 2020. Later that month, Nokia announced the ReefShark line of 5G chipsets, claiming it triples bandwidth to 84 Gbit/s. In March 2018, Solidium, the investment arm of the Finnish Government, purchased a 3.3% stake in Nokia valued at €844 million. In May 2018, Nokia acquired a California-based IoT startup, SpaceTime Insight. In January 2019, the Canadian government announced $40 million in support for Nokia's 5G research. A 2019 study by Counterpoint Research found that 96 percent of Nokia phones were either shipped with or updated to the latest Android version since Pie was released in 2018, significantly outperforming competitors like Samsung, LG, Xiaomi, and Huawei, which averaged around 80 percent. On 2 March 2020, Nokia announced Pekka Lundmark as its new CEO. Later that month, Nokia completed the acquisition of Elenion Technologies, a U.S.-based company specializing in silicon photonics technology to improve the economics of advanced optical connectivity products. On 27 May 2020, Sari Baldauf succeeded Risto Siilasmaa as chairwoman of the board of directors, and Kari Stadigh was appointed vice chair. In June 2020, Nokia won a $450 million 5G contract from Taiwan Mobile to build out its next-generation network as the sole supplier. In October 2020, Nokia announced a $14.1 million contract with NASA to build a 4G mobile network for astronaut use on the moon, through its subsidiary Bell Labs, expected to begin in 2022. In 2020, Flipkart collaborated with Nokia to market Nokia-branded consumer products in India, including televisions, a laptop, and a range of air conditioners. In April 2022, Nokia announced it would exit the Russian market following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, stating the decision would not affect its financial outlook as Russia accounted for less than 2% of Nokia's net sales in 2021. In February 2023, Nokia introduced a new logo for the first time in nearly 60 years to modernize its brand identity, as the previous logo was still associated with mobile phones; the new logo was designed by Lippincott. In December 2023, Nokia acquired Fenix Group to strengthen its wireless offering in the defense segment for an undisclosed amount. In the same month, Nokia announced a €185 million deal with Lumine Group to carve out its device management and service management businesses (inherited from Alcatel-Lucent's purchase of Motive, Inc. and formerly Mformation), with the deal completed in April 2024 and involving the transfer of around 500 employees. In February 2024, Nokia accelerated its carbon neutrality target by 10 years to 2040, having previously committed to cutting its carbon footprint across emissions scopes in half by 2030 from a 2019 baseline. In June 2024, Nokia acquired Infinera for $2.3 billion. On 10 February 2025, Nokia announced that Pekka Lundmark would step down as president and CEO on 31 March and be succeeded by Justin Hotard. In September 2025, Nokia announced an artificial intelligence-based partnership with Supermicro, focusing on integrated data center network products. Nokia is a julkinen osakeyhtiö (public joint-stock company) listed on the Nasdaq Nordic/Helsinki and New York stock exchanges. It plays a major role in Finland's economy, contributing 1.6% to Finland's GDP and accounting for about 16% of the country's exports in 2006, and is a significant employer working with local partners and subcontractors. Nokia comprises two main business groups along with subsidiaries and affiliated firms. Nokia Networks is the largest division, a multinational data networking and telecommunications equipment company headquartered in Espoo, Finland, and the world's third-largest telecoms equipment manufacturer by 2017 revenues (after Huawei and Cisco). It operates in around 150 countries and provides wireless and fixed network infrastructure, communications and network service platforms and professional services to operators and service providers, focusing on GSM, EDGE, 3G/W-CDMA, LTE and WiMAX radio access networks, supporting core networks with increasing IP and multiaccess capabilities and services. The Nokia Siemens Networks (NSN) brand was launched in February 2007 as a 50.1% Nokia and 49.9% Siemens joint venture, now wholly owned by Nokia; in July 2013, Nokia bought back all shares for US$2.21 billion and renamed it first to Nokia Solutions and Networks, then to simply Nokia Networks. Nokia Technologies is a division that develops consumer products and licenses technology including the Nokia brand, focusing on imaging, sensing, wireless connectivity, power management, and materials, and includes three labs: Radio Systems Lab, Media Technologies Lab, and Sensor and Material Technologies Lab; it also runs the Invent with Nokia program. It was created in 2014 following a restructuring. In November 2014, Nokia Technologies launched the Nokia N1 tablet. In July 2015, it introduced the OZO VR camera for professional content creators in Tampere, Finland, featuring 8 synchronized shutter sensors and 8 microphones to capture stereoscopic 3D video and spatial audio; production ended in 2017, but immersive audio software under the OZO brand continues. On 31 August 2016, Ramzi Haidamus stepped down as president of Nokia Technologies, with Brad Rodrigues serving as interim president; on 30 June 2017, Gregory Lee, former CEO of Samsung Electronics in North America, was appointed CEO and president. Nokia Bell Labs, formerly the R&D arm of the American Bell System, became a subsidiary after the 2016 acquisition of Alcatel-Lucent. In December 2023, Nokia announced plans for a new research facility in New Brunswick, New Jersey, relocating from the 80-year-old Bell Labs facility in Murray Hill, New Jersey, expected to occur before 2028. NGP Capital (formerly Nokia Growth Partners) is a global venture capital firm focusing on growth-stage IoT and mobile technology companies, with investments in the U.S., Europe, China, and India; it manages $1 billion in assets after a $350 million funding round in 2016. Nokia had previously promoted innovation through Nokia Venture Partners, renamed BlueRun Ventures and spun off in 2005; the China arm became independent in 2010 as Lanchi Ventures; Nokia Growth Partners was founded in 2005 and renamed to NGP Capital in 2017. NGP's largest exits include GanJi, UCWeb, Whistle, Rocket Fuel, Swype, Summit Microelectronics, and Netmagic. Nuage Networks, formed by Alcatel-Lucent in 2013 to develop software-defined networking solutions, became part of Nokia after the 2016 acquisition; it secured deals with Vodafone and Telefónica in 2017 for its SD-WAN architecture, BT since 2016, and China Mobile in January 2017 for 2,000 public cloud servers, and with China Pacific Insurance Company in October 2017. The company is based in Mountain View, California, with Sunil Khandekar as CEO. Alcatel Mobile, a mobile phone brand owned by Nokia since 2016, was licensed to TCL since 2005 under Alcatel (later Alcatel-Lucent) until 2024. HMD Global, a mobile phone company based in Espoo, Finland, was founded by former Nokia employees and introduced Nokia-branded Android-based devices in 2017; initially, Nokia had no investment but retained some input in device development. Nokia has 10.10% ownership in HMD Global after investing alongside Qualcomm and Google in 2020; in the 2020 financial report, FIH Mobile disclosed a 14.38% ownership, with Finnish Nokia holding 10.10% and other investors including Google, Qualcomm, and others with undisclosed shares. Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), a provider of turnkey undersea network solutions, was acquired by Nokia in 2016; it develops technology and offers installation services for optical submarine cable networks globally. Nokia and ASN added the CS Ile d'Ouessant to their fleet in 2019 (originally built as CS Toisa Warrior in 2011) and requested two additional cable ships, CS Ile d'Yeu and CS Ile de Molène, in 2021. The cable-laying fleet includes six from Alcatel, six and seven from Alcatel-Lucent, and eight from Nokia. Key trends for Nokia are as of the financial year ending 31 December. Control and management are divided among shareholders at a general meeting and the Nokia Group Leadership Team, under the direction of the board of directors; the chairman and leadership team members are appointed by the board, with only the chairman belonging to both the board and leadership team. The board has Audit, Personnel, and Corporate Governance and Nomination Committees. Operations are managed under the Finnish Companies Act, Nokia's Articles of Association, and Corporate Governance Guidelines, supplemented by board charters; in November 2019, Nokia discontinued the role of Chief Operating Officer (COO), with Joerg Erlemeier stepping down on 1 January 2020. Nokia is a public limited liability company and the oldest company listed under the same name on the Helsinki Stock Exchange, beginning in 1915; it has had a secondary listing on the New York Stock Exchange since 1994 and shares were delisted from the London, Paris, Stockholm, and Frankfurt stock exchanges in 2003, 2004, 2007, and 2012, respectively; after acquiring Alcatel-Lucent in 2015, it listed again on the Paris Stock Exchange and was included in the CAC 40 index on 6 January 2016 but removed on 18 September 2017. In 2007, Nokia's market capitalization was €110 billion; by 17 July 2012 it fell to €6.28 billion, then rose to €26.0 billion by 23 February 2015; in 2020, it was 21.76 billion. Nokia's corporate culture manifesto since the 1990s is called The Nokia Way, emphasizing speed and flexibility in decision-making within a flat, networked organization. The official business language is English, used in all documentation and official internal communication. In 1992, Nokia adopted values defined by respect, achievement, renewal, and challenge; in May 2007, it redefined them to Engaging You, Achieving Together, Passion for Innovation, and Very Human based on global employee input; in August 2014, after the sale of its Devices business, it reverted to the original 1992 values. Nokia is headquartered at Karaportti in Espoo, Finland, since 2014, after moving from the Nokia House following the sale of the mobile phone business to Microsoft; the Karaportti building was previously the headquarters of NSN (now Nokia Networks). In 2018, Nokia received the Leading Lights award for most innovative cable/video product and was named to Ethisphere's 2018 list of the world's most ethical companies. In 2008, Nokia Siemens Networks reportedly provided Iran's telecom monopoly with technology enabling deep packet inspection to intercept Internet communications, allowing monitoring and alteration of emails, social media, and phone calls; during post-election protests in June 2009, Iran's Internet access slowed to less than 10% of normal speeds, suspected due to deep packet inspection. In July 2009, Nokia began experiencing a boycott of its products and services in Iran led by consumers supporting the protest movement, resulting in reduced demand for handsets and declining SMS usage. Nokia Siemens Networks stated in a press release that it provided only a "lawful intercept capability solely for monitoring of local voice calls" and denied providing deep packet inspection, web censorship, or Internet filtering. In October 2009, Nokia filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court of Delaware against Apple Inc., claiming infringement of 10 wireless communication patents, including data transfer; Apple responded with a countersuit in December 2009, accusing Nokia of 11 patent infringements.

During the post-election protests in Iran in June 2009, Iran's Internet access slowed to less than a tenth of its normal speeds, which experts suspected was due to the use of deep packet inspection.[279] In July 2009, Nokia began to face a boycott of its products and services in Iran, led by consumers sympathetic to the post-election protest movement and targeting companies perceived as collaborating with the regime; demand for handsets declined and users started avoiding SMS messaging.[280] Nokia Siemens Networks stated in a press release that it provided Iran only with a "lawful intercept capability solely for monitoring of local voice calls" and that it "has not provided any deep packet inspection, web censorship, or Internet filtering capability to Iran".[281] In October 2009, Nokia filed a lawsuit against Apple Inc. in the U.S. District Court of Delaware, claiming that Apple infringed on 10 of its patents related to wireless communication, including data transfer.[282] Apple responded by filing a countersuit in December 2009, accusing Nokia of 11 patent infringements; Apple's general counsel, Bruce Sewell, stated, "Other companies must compete with us by inventing their own technologies, not just by stealing ours." This led to a legal dispute between the two telecom companies, with Nokia later filing another suit with the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), alleging Apple had infringed its patents in "virtually all of its mobile phones, portable music players and computers," and requesting a ban on all U.S. imports of Apple products, including the iPhone, Macintosh, and iPod.[283] Apple countered by filing a complaint with the ITC in January 2010.[282] In June 2011, Apple settled with Nokia, agreeing to an estimated one-time payment of $600 million and royalties to Nokia, and also reached a cross-licensing agreement on some of their patented technologies.[284][285][286] In January 2013, Nokia's Indian subsidiary was charged with non-payment of Indian Tax Deducted at Source and violating transfer pricing norms in India; the unpaid TDS of ₹30 billion, accumulated over six years, stemmed from royalty payments made by the Indian subsidiary to its parent company.[287][288] In March 2019, it was reported that the Nokia 7 Plus phones were allegedly sending personal user data to China over several months; investigators found that the devices transmitted unencrypted data packages—including geographical location, SIM card number, and phone serial number—to an unidentified Chinese server each time the phone was turned on, the screen activated, or unlocked, enabling real-time tracking of the user's movements and actions.[289] Nokia brand owner HMD Global denied any such data transfers, claiming it was due to an error in the software packing process.[290] The Finnish Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman launched an investigation into the matter, assuming "that personal data has been transferred."[291] In 2020, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute accused at least 82 major brands, including Nokia, of being linked to forced Uyghur labor in Xinjiang.[292]

Norberto Santiago Raffo (27 April 1939 – 16 December 2008) was an Argentine footballer who played as a striker. He was the Copa Libertadores de América Topscorer in the 1967 season with 14 goals for Racing Club, the eventual champions, achieving the third highest goal total in a single Copa Libertadores season. Born in Avellaneda, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, he played for both Avellaneda giants Independiente and Racing Club, winning major titles with both teams. He is best remembered by Banfield fans for scoring 68 goals in 180 games between 1960 and 1966, making him the third top scorer in the club's history. Raffo also played for Atlanta, Lanús, Altos Hornos Zapla in Argentina, Huachipato in Chile, and América de Cali in Colombia. He managed several Argentine clubs, most notably Lanús on multiple occasions and Banfield, as well as Argentino de Quilmes, El Porvenir, Gimnasia y Esgrima de Jujuy, Altos Hornos Zapla, and Talleres (RE). He had a long tenure in charge of the Lanús youth team from 1987 to 1996. His son, Néstor Santiago, is a former footballer for Racing Club.

Norman Percevel Rockwell (February 3, 1894 – November 8, 1978) was an American painter and illustrator known for his depictions of everyday American life, which gained broad popular appeal. He is most famous for creating cover illustrations for The Saturday Evening Post over nearly five decades, producing 323 original covers during a 47-year relationship with the magazine. Among his best-known works are the Willie Gillis series, Rosie the Riveter, the Four Freedoms series, Saying Grace, and The Problem We All Live With. Rockwell maintained a 64-year professional relationship with the Boy Scouts of America (BSA), during which he produced covers for Boys' Life (now Scout Life), calendars, and other materials, including images such as The Scoutmaster, A Scout Is Reverent, and A Guiding Hand. He created more than 4,000 original works in his lifetime, with most surviving in public collections. He illustrated over 40 books, including Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, and painted portraits of U.S. Presidents Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon, as well as foreign leaders like Gamal Abdel Nasser and Jawaharlal Nehru, and Judy Garland. One of his last portraits was of Colonel Sanders in 1973. His annual calendar contributions for the BSA between 1925 and 1976 were only slightly less prominent than his "Four Seasons" illustrations for Brown & Bigelow, which were published for 17 years beginning in 1947 and reproduced in various styles and sizes since 1964. He also created artwork for advertisements for Coca-Cola, Jell-O, General Motors, Scott Tissue, and other companies, and illustrated booklets, catalogs, posters (especially movie promotions), sheet music, stamps, playing cards, and murals, including "Yankee Doodle Dandy" and "God Bless the Hills," completed in 1936 for the Nassau Inn in Princeton, New Jersey. Rockwell's work was dismissed by serious art critics during his lifetime, with many modern critics finding it overly sweet, especially his Post covers, which are seen as idealistic or sentimentalized, leading to the deprecatory term "Rockwellesque." Some contemporary artists regard his work as bourgeois and kitsch, and Vladimir Nabokov criticized his technique as being used "banally," stating in Pnin that Dalí was Norman Rockwell's twin brother kidnapped by gypsies in infancy. Critics often refer to him as an "illustrator" rather than an artist, a designation he accepted as his self-identification. In his later years, Rockwell gained more recognition as a painter through serious subjects, such as his civil rights-themed series for Look magazine, including The Problem We All Live With, which depicts Ruby Bridges walking to school past a wall with racist graffiti and was displayed in the White House when she met President Barack Obama in 2011. Rockwell was born in New York City on February 3, 1894, to Jarvis Waring Rockwell and Anne Mary "Nancy" Rockwell; his father was Presbyterian and mother was Episcopalian, and he converted to the Episcopal faith two years after their engagement. His earliest American ancestor was John Rockwell (1588–1662), who immigrated to colonial North America in 1635 aboard the ship Hopewell and settled in Windsor, Connecticut. He had one brother, Jarvis Jr., older by a year and a half. Rockwell attended the Chase Art School at age 14, then the National Academy of Design and the Art Students League of New York, where he studied under Thomas Fogarty, George Bridgman, and Frank Vincent DuMond. His early works appeared in St. Nicholas Magazine and Boys' Life. At 18, he illustrated Carl H. Claudy's book Tell Me Why: Stories about Mother Nature, and at 19 became art editor for Boys' Life, where he painted several covers, beginning with Scout at Ship's Wheel in the September 1913 edition. His family moved to New Rochelle, New York, when he was 21, and with help from cartoonist Clyde Forsythe, he submitted his first successful Post cover, Mother's Day Off, in 1916. He published eight Post covers in the first year and eventually created 323 covers over 47 years, including Sharp Harmony in September 1936. His success led to cover work for Literary Digest, Country Gentleman, Leslie's Weekly, Judge, Peoples Popular Monthly, and Life. During World War I, he was refused enlistment due to being underweight but gained enough weight to enlist and served as a military artist without seeing combat. In 1943, during World War II, he painted the Four Freedoms series—Freedom from Want, Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, and Freedom from Fear—inspired by a speech by Franklin D. Roosevelt, completing it in seven months and losing fifteen pounds. He used the Pennell family from Brunswick, Maine, as models for two paintings and combined photographs with his vision. The series was published in 1943 by The Saturday Evening Post, and the U.S. Department of the Treasury exhibited the originals in sixteen cities to promote war bonds. Rockwell considered Freedom of Speech the best of the four. A fire in his studio in 1943 destroyed numerous original paintings, costumes, and props, leading to a shift in his career toward modern subjects. He was approached by Elliott Caplin to create a daily comic strip with Al Capp and Rockwell, but the project was abandoned due to Rockwell's perfectionism and inability to meet daily deadlines. In the late 1940s, he spent winters at Otis College of Art and Design, occasionally using students as models. In 1949, he donated an original Post cover, April Fool, to a library fundraiser. After his wife Mary died in 1959 from a heart attack, he took time off and with his son Thomas produced his autobiography, My Adventures as an Illustrator, published in 1960, with excerpts appearing in eight consecutive Post issues, including the famous Triple Self-Portrait. His last Post cover was published in 1963, ending 47 years of coverage. He then worked for Look magazine for ten years, focusing on civil rights, poverty, and space exploration. In 1966, he was invited to Hollywood to paint portraits of the stars of Stagecoach and appeared as an extra playing a "mangy old gambler." In 1968, he created an album cover portrait for Mike Bloomfield and Al Kooper. For the 75th anniversary of his birth, he posed in Beyond the Easel for the 1969 Boy Scout calendar. In 1969, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation commissioned him to paint the Glen Canyon Dam. His final BSA calendar illustration, The Spirit of 1976, was completed when he was 82, concluding a 64-year partnership that produced 471 images for periodicals, guidebooks, calendars, and promotional materials. His legacy and style for the BSA was carried on by Joseph Csatari. In 1977, Rockwell was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the United States, by President Gerald Ford, with his son Jarvis accepting the award. Rockwell, a heavy smoker, died on November 8, 1978, of emphysema at age 84 in his Stockbridge, Massachusetts, home. First Lady Rosalynn Carter attended his funeral. He married Irene O'Connor on July 1, 1916, who modeled for Mother Tucking Children into Bed, published in January 1921, and they divorced on January 13, 1930. After a period of depression, he moved briefly to Alhambra, California, where he painted notable works like The Doctor and the Doll, and married schoolteacher Mary Barstow on April 17, 1930. The couple returned to New York and had three sons: Jarvis, Thomas, and Peter. They lived at 24 Lord Kitchener Road in New Rochelle. The family was not regular church attendees but were members of St. John's Wilmot Church, where their sons were baptized. Rockwell moved to Arlington, Vermont, in 1939, where his work began to reflect small-town life, later joined by friend John Carlton Atherton. In 1953, the family moved to Stockbridge, Massachusetts, so Mary could be treated at the Austen Riggs Center, near where Rockwell set up his studio. He also received treatment from analyst Erik Erikson, who noted that Rockwell painted his happiness but did not live it. Mary died unexpectedly on August 25, 1959. Rockwell married his third wife, Mary Leete "Mollie" Punderson, on October 25, 1961. His Stockbridge studio was on the second floor of a row of buildings, with the Back Room Rest (known as "Alice's Restaurant") directly below from 1966. Chief of police William Obanhein was a frequent model. From 1961 until his death, he was a member of the Monday Evening Club in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, with five members serving as pallbearers at his funeral alongside Jarvis Rockwell. A custodianship of his original works was established near his home in Stockbridge, and the Norman Rockwell Museum remains open year-round, housing over 700 original paintings, drawings, and studies. The Rockwell Center for American Visual Studies at the museum is a national research institute for American illustration. His work was exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 2001, and Breaking Home Ties sold for $15.4 million at a 2006 Sotheby's auction. A 12-city U.S. tour of his works occurred in 2008, and in 2008 he was named the official state artist of Massachusetts. In 2013, Saying Grace sold for $46 million (including buyer's premium), setting a new record. His works were also exhibited at the Reading Public Museum and the Church History Museum from 2013 to 2014. Films have referenced his art: in Annie Hall (1977), Alvy teases Annie with "What did you do, grow up in a Norman Rockwell painting?" In Empire of the Sun, a scene inspired by a Rockwell painting—Freedom from Fear (1943)—is shown as a young boy is put to bed and later keeps a reproduction during captivity. Forrest Gump includes a shot re-creating Rockwell's "Girl with Black Eye" with young Forrest in place of the girl, and the film draws heavy visual inspiration from his art. George Lucas owns the original of "The Peach Crop," and Steven Spielberg owns a sketch of Rockwell's Triple Self-Portrait, both of which hang in their workspaces. Rockwell is a major character in an episode of The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, "Passion for Life," portrayed by Lukas Haas. Some albums and tracks have drawn inspiration from his work: Prism's 1981 album Small Change used Girl at Mirror as its cover, "Dreamland" by Our Lady Peace (2009) was inspired by his paintings, Oingo Boingo's Only a Lad cover parodies a Rockwell-illustrated BSA handbook cover, and Lana Del Rey named her 2019 album Norman Fucking Rockwell! after him. Rockwell is among the figures depicted in Our Nation's 200th Birthday, The Telephone's 100th Birthday (1976) by Stanley Meltzoff.

Norman Rockwell's artwork has influenced various media and public spaces. The original of "The Peach Crop" and Steven Spielberg's sketch of Rockwell's Triple Self-Portrait each hang in the respective filmmaker's workspace. Rockwell is a major character in an episode of George Lucas' The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, "Passion for Life," portrayed by Lukas Haas. In 1981, Rockwell's painting Girl at Mirror was used as the cover for Prism's fifth studio album, Small Change. The track "Dreamland" from Our Lady Peace's 2009 album Burn Burn was inspired by Rockwell's paintings. The cover of Oingo Boingo's album Only a Lad is a parody of the Boy Scouts of America 1960 official handbook cover illustrated by Rockwell. Lana Del Rey named her sixth studio album, Norman Fucking Rockwell! (2019), after Rockwell. Rockwell is among the figures depicted in Our Nation's 200th Birthday, The Telephone's 100th Birthday (1976) by Stanley Meltzoff, which was based on Rockwell's 1948 painting The Gossips. Japanese carmaker Suzuki used excerpts from Rockwell's art in its 1986 brochure for the "Mighty Boy" small pickup truck, including an image from the April 29, 1922, issue of the Saturday Evening Post. Museum director Thomas S. Buechner stated that Rockwell's art remains timeless, saying that "When the last half century is explored by the future, a few paintings will continue to communicate with the same immediacy and veracity they have today." In 2005, May Corporation, which had previously purchased Marshall Field's from Target Corp., was acquired by Federated Department Stores. After the acquisition, Federated discovered that Rockwell's The Clock Mender, displayed in the store, was a reproduction. Rockwell had donated the original painting—depicting a repairman setting the time on a clock at the Marshall Field and Company Building and featured on the November 3, 1945, Saturday Evening Post cover—to the store in 1948. Target later donated the original to the Chicago History Museum. On February 3, 2010, on the anniversary of Rockwell's birth, Google featured his iconic image "Boy and Girl Gazing at the Moon" (also known as "Puppy Love") on its home page, causing such a surge in traffic that the Norman Rockwell Museum's servers were overwhelmed. In 2017, the original 1948 oil study for Tough Call (also known as Game Called Because of Rain), one of Rockwell’s best-known baseball-themed works, sold for US $1.68 million at Heritage Auctions. The painting had hung in a Texas family’s home for years before being identified as a Rockwell piece and became one of the highest prices ever achieved for a Rockwell study. On November 2, 2025, the Norman Rockwell family published an essay in the opinion section of USA Today denouncing the Donald Trump administration's Department of Homeland Security for unauthorized use of several Rockwell paintings in social media posts alongside nationalist slogans promoting anti-immigration policies. The essay stated, "If Norman Rockwell were alive today, he would be devastated to see [...] his own work has been marshalled for the cause of persecution toward immigrant communities and people of color." Rockwell provided illustrations for several film posters. He designed the album cover for The Live Adventures of Mike Bloomfield and Al Kooper (1969) and was commissioned by English musician David Bowie to design the cover for his 1975 album Young Americans, though the offer was withdrawn after Rockwell informed Bowie he would need at least half a year to complete the painting.

North Red Deer was a former village in central Alberta, Canada, located within the City of Red Deer. It was situated on the north shore of the Red Deer River along the Calgary and Edmonton (C&E) Railway, which was later acquired by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The former village is now part of Red Deer's Riverside Meadows neighbourhood, with some areas also falling within Highland Green and Oriole Park. Established as a hamlet in 1894 following the completion of the C&E rail line and the construction of the bridge over the Red Deer River, North Red Deer incorporated as the Village of North Red Deer on February 17, 1911, with the ministerial order signed on June 18, 1911. Walter Webb served as the village's first mayor, beginning on March 13, 1911. After an earlier unratified effort in 1946, the village officially amalgamated with the City of Red Deer on January 1, 1948, with the last village council meeting held on December 24, 1947. In 1999, the City of Red Deer renamed the area to Riverside Meadows. In 2000, the city adopted the Riverside Meadows Area Redevelopment Plan (ARP), which was later replaced by a new ARP in 2009. The city marked the centennial of the Village of North Red Deer on August 27, 2011. During its existence, the population grew from 304 in 1911 to 698 in 1946.

Novo Theatre, Dhaka (formerly known as Bhasani Novo Theatre and Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Novo Theatre), is a planetarium located on Bijoy Sarani Avenue in the Tejgaon area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. It opened to the public on 25 September 2004 and was initially named Bhasani Novo Theatre. The theatre was made autonomous through the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Novo Theatre Bill 2010. The space center was commissioned by the Ministry of Science and Communication Technology of the Government of Bangladesh. On 20 March 2025, the interim government of Bangladesh, via an ordinance, changed the name of the planetarium from Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Novo Theater to Novo Theatre. Built on 5.46 acres of land, the planetarium features spaces ranging from a 21-meter dome seating 275 people to three-meter inflatable and portable domes where visitors sit on the floor. Designed by architect Ali Imam, the planetarium's dome simulates Earth with a cool blue sky and uses a 120-degree projection system to display moving images of planets and stars on a large-screen dome. Visitors do not need to look up; instead, they experience space as if they are living within it, thanks to 150 projectors. The facility offers three main exhibits: "Journey to Infinity," which presents stars, planets, and other celestial bodies in virtual reality; "ai amader Bangladesh," which features Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's lecture delivered on 7 March; and "The Grand Canyon," which describes the settlement clan Garikhad in North America's Grand Canyon that existed four thousand years ago. In addition, the planetarium introduced a new capsule simulator, a smart-step floor, and 3D video. In 2013, it also established a Nuclear Industrial Information Centre.

Numbertime is a BBC educational numeracy television series for primary schools that aired on BBC Two from 20 September 1993 to 3 December 2001. For its first four series, it was presented by Lolita Chakrabarti. El Nombre, an animated character used throughout the series, eventually became the concept for his own educational BBC children's television program; his name means "The Name" in Spanish, not "The Number", which would be "El Número". The third line of his opening song and his farewell catchphrase were changed several times during the series' run to reflect the focus of each series, though the original ones—("Writing numbers in the desert sand", used in the seventh series, and "Adios amigos, and keep counting", used in the fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth series)—remain the most famous. In the second series, his tagline and farewell catchphrase were changed to "Drawing shapes in the desert sand" and "Adios amigos, and keep shaping up", respectively; in the third series, they were changed to "Righting wrongs in the desert sand" and "Adios amigos, over and out"; in the fourth series, his tagline was changed to "Counting numbers in the desert sand" (also used in the ninth series), and in the third episode of that series, his farewell catchphrase was changed to "Adios amigos, and fetch some water". In the fifth series, both tagline and farewell catchphrase were changed to "Telling time in the desert sand" and "Adios amigos, 'till the next time"; in the sixth series, his tagline was changed to "Using numbers in the desert sand"; in the eighth series, it was changed to "Counting money in the desert sand". The first series, aimed at four- to five-year-olds, had ten episodes focusing on numbers 1–10 in order. Each episode began with Lolita introducing herself, pulling the number from a string hanging from the ceiling, pushing it into its correct hole in a wall, and singing the main theme, "One to Ten", as each hole lit up. Between segments, there were comedy sketches based on nursery rhymes and fairy tales, animations featuring El Nombre, the Mexican gerbil who parodied Zorro, showing little Juan how to draw numbers while his four-piece mariachi band played "The Mexican Hat Dance" (with "Again!" after each performance), and a sequence encouraging viewers to spot things of the number of the episode—using the same video with a different number of items each time, accompanied by the recurring song "Numbers All Around", sung by a group of children. Each episode ended with Lolita singing a song or introducing an animation, followed by a challenge to find things related to the episode's number before she said she would "see them next Numbertime". The first series originally aired on Mondays as part of the Daytime on Two strand at 9:45 am, repeated at 2:00 pm on the same day; in Scotland, the 2:00 pm repeats were replaced with broadcasts of BBC Scotland's schools series Over the Moon with Mr. Boom. Episodes included the Narrator presenting Nursery Rhyme Theatre No. 1 – Little Miss Muffet with interruptions, and Little Jack Horner having one minute to find one plum on Sammy Sallow's game show, where success allows choosing a prize—either a mountain bike, a computer, or a picture of Sallow—ending with "One Finger, One Thumb, Keep Moving" sung by the children. The Narrator introduced Nursery Rhyme Theatre No. 2 with Marvo the Magician and his Two Amazing Dickie Birds, and Sammy Sport reported on Jack and Jill attempting to break the world record for running up a hill, filling a pail, and returning down in under two minutes; this episode ended with Lolita singing "The Animals Went in Two by Two". Sammy Sport joined Baa-Baa Black Sheep for the "Win a Bag of Wool" competition results, and Goldilocks invited viewers to Guess Whose House on Sammy Sallow's game show; the Numbertime Top Ten featured "Three-Sided Triangles" at No. 3, singing an original song titled "We're Triangles (Oh Yes We Are)". Farmer Giles introduced the finals of One Girl and Her Sheep, with Little Bo Peep and her dog Shep competing, and the Knave of Hearts conversing with the Queen of Hearts about her royal tarts; Lolita told viewers to "grab their partners and take the floor" as she introduced a quartet of dancing squares singing "Do the Square Dance". Australian chef Wally Bee and his assistant Bruce demonstrated how to cook five fat sausages on a barbecue for Barbecue Time, and Harry Headline visited the Five Pigs Family for Five Minutes' Fame; in the El Nombre sketch, Little Juan celebrated his fifth birthday, and the episode ended with Lolita singing "Fly, Little Dickey Birds, Round and Round". A gardener named Fred enlisted his family to pull up his enormous turnip for Garden Time, and Mr. and Mrs. Jones had to balance six eggs on a seesaw for Sammy Sallow's game show, with three attempts; the episode ended with Lolita singing "This Old Man" in voiceover. Sammy Sport traveled to Scotland to witness a fishing contest among the Seven Fat Fishermen to catch the largest fish on a bridge by the Clyde, and ordering seven portions of fish and chips caused trouble for the shopkeeper and his customer (who had seven children); the episode ended with Lolita singing "In My Little Garden, Now Promise You Won't Laugh" (also known as "One Potato, Two Potato"). Sammy Sport visited Shoeburyness to interview the Old Woman who Lives in a Shoe (who has eight children), and the Policeman asked viewers to help find Wee Willie Winkie for Crime Spot; it was evening in Little Juan's town in the El Nombre sketch, and the episode ended with Lolita imagining a world where everything was eight-shaped, visiting the Planet of the Eights to sing an original song—this was the only episode in which she did not wear her usual purple outfit but a silver spacesuit. Lucky the Cat recalled her nine lives on This Is My Life, and Harry Headline visited Miss Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary's garden for Garden Time, where he ruined her chances in the "Best Flowers Competition" and she ended up coming ninth; this was the only episode not to end with a song, instead featuring Lolita showing a homemade necklace with nine beads (three red, three blue, and three yellow), referencing the episode's third animated sketch. Farmer Giles and his dog Scruff demonstrated a new, quick method for mowing a meadow for Farming News, and Sammy Sport visited Ten Pin Alley to watch Ten Pin Pete attempt to become the new Ten Pin Champ; Lolita showed ten Russian dolls, and the episode ended with "Ten in the Bed", sung by the group of children who sang "Numbers All Around" earlier. Because this was the final episode, Lolita did not tell viewers she would "see them next Numbertime". In 1994, BBC Enterprises (now BBC Worldwide) released a video titled "Number Time" (BBCV 5359, spelled with two words), containing sixty minutes of edited highlights from the series (it was the only such release at the time); it was later rereleased in 1997 as the second half of a "two-on-one" video with "Alphabet Fun Time" (BBCV 5357), originally released around the same time and containing fifty-eight minutes of highlights from that show's 1992 series; the combined video was titled "Alphabet Fun Time and Number Time" (BBCV 5987) and rereleased in 1999. The series was later re-released in full as a "Video Plus Pack" in 1996, slightly altered to remove the episodes' opening titles. From 22 September to 1 December 1998, the BBC broadcast a "revised" version of the series as a lead-in to the sixth series; in place of Lolita, Bill (introduced in the fourth series) and Bernie (who joined in the fifth) introduced episodes with a number line, though Lolita's voice was still heard narrating reused animated sketches. All episodes except Numbers 1, 4, and 9 had the original live-action sketches replaced with the Dolls' House sketch (as in Series 5), though in episodes retaining original sketches, the prize scene in the "Find One Plum" sketch was cut and the "One Girl and Her Sheep" sketch was omitted. The El Nombre sketches were slightly lengthened, and sequences of children discussing the ten numbers (similar to those discussing time in Series 5) were introduced; although the Planet of the Eights sketch was reused, its vocal track was redubbed and Lolita was edited out. The "Numbers All Around" song by children was retained, but the "One Finger, One Thumb, Keep Moving" song had the children forming the number one and shouting its number cut at the end, and the "Ten in the Bed" song had a new video of the ten children in bed while retaining the original song. A lively maths series designed as a follow-on to the first series, featuring four colourful "clown-like" characters—Mo, Sappy, Grimble, and Jick—who live together. A robot named Trundle narrates each episode and helps them with maths. There are also animations and songs. The gang decide to have a barbecue, adding up sixteen guests and themselves to make twenty people; they learn to count in twos and fives, and Trundle shows a farmer using his sheepdog to count sheep. Trundle naughtily knocks over food boxes, which fall on Grimble and Jick, who rescue him but forget to send out invitations. It starts to rain, so they decide to restart the barbecue the next day. On a lovely day for a picnic, the gang learn about division by sharing food fairly—such as a quarter of a pizza, half a can of drink, or one banana each—though Grimble is upset, he is outshone by tapirs, tamarins, and wild horses shown at Marwell Zoo Park. Mo takes glass bottles to the bottle bank, leaving Grimble in charge of cleaning up and sorting by colour and shape; Trundle plays an odd one out game with the viewer at a Sainsbury's supermarket. When Mo returns, she sees the confusion and the group puts everything back in place. The gang learn about handling data when opening a pet shop; they try to ask people what their favorite animal is, but Sappy asks the right question without writing answers and Jick writes answers but asks the wrong question. Grimble goes out to find the correct data and discovers tigers are the world's favorite animal, so they close the pet shop. The gang learn about the number one hundred as they host a concert for one hundred people; they also learn to count in tens. Trundle shows that a hundred-year-old person receives a birthday card from the Queen, a century in cricket is one hundred years, and a centurion led one hundred Roman soldiers. He also shows how people count people in a football match, on a runaway train, and in a school orchestra. Sappy decides to conduct one hundred children. The gang learn that things are made to measure as Mo needs a shelf for her books, so Grimble and Jick build one but keep getting it wrong. Trundle shows two boys of different heights trying to set up goals, how goal widths vary in sports, and how the ancient Egyptians built pyramids using a cubit. The gang learn about weighing after Trundle receives a letter from a circus seeking a very light clown; the ringmaster assigns jobs to the gang to clear animal droppings, prepare hay, peanuts, and greens for Big Ears (thought to be an elephant), weighing them first on a seesaw and mixing custard pies without using scales. They discover Big Ears is actually a rabbit and are asked who among them is the lightest. The gang learn about measuring time as they prepare for Grimble's birthday; Mo and Sappy buy a green clock-shaped cake and a green alarm clock, and Jick makes a green jelly. Trundle shows Big Ben and explains how monks used sand clocks to ring the monastery bell and how ancient Romans used candles to measure time. The gang want to buy flowers and must first count their money and determine what they can afford; they are introduced to different coin denominations, combinations, and the concept that more coins do not mean a larger sum. Trundle shows a blind boy named Darren who identifies coins by touch. The gang are trapped in a board game called "Shape Master" and learn about 2D and 3D shapes; each finds a shape to escape—Mo finds a cube, Sappy finds a cylinder, Grimble finds a pyramid, and Jick finds a hexagon. Trundle explains how cubes and cuboids appear in buildings, how sticks of rock are made, and how shapes like hexagons, squares, rectangles, and diamonds tessellate. The second series, also aimed at four- to five-year-olds, had five episodes focusing on the four basic two-dimensional shapes. Each episode began with Lolita standing by a mobile with the shapes hanging from it, singing the main theme "Squares and Triangles, Circles and Rectangles" as the mobile turned. Once stopped, she walked to the nearest shape, asked viewers if they knew it, and it lit up when she named it—starting from this series, El Nombre had two sketches per episode: one showing Juan encountering that week's shape around town (with Juan being clumsy and facing villagers after El Nombre leaves), and the second showing him drawing it in the desert sand. The series featured four cut-out animated characters made from the shapes of the episode—circular man with magical powers, square robot with transformation powers, triangular knight with a magical lance, and rectangular man. In the final episode, they built a house together after the rectangular man built one from rectangles, and the square robot, triangular knight, and circular man transformed them into their own shapes. Each episode ended with Lolita singing an "extended" version of a song heard earlier during a montage of the shape in the real world (with the final one continuing over the credits), and viewers were challenged to find how many of that week's shape they could spot before the next episode. The first two episodes aired on Mondays at 9:45 am as part of the Daytime on Two strand, but due to May Day on 8 May 1995, the third episode aired the next day; the last two episodes aired on Mondays. In one episode, El Nombre shows Juan what a circle is (using a cart's wheel, a hoopla ring, a hoop with its stick), while Terry introduces the "Ring a Ring o' Roses Formation Dance Team" and their manager Cynthia, and a prehistoric couple attempt to invent the round wheel after square and triangular ones in Great Moments in History; in the second cut-out sketch, circular pawprints transform into a circular ladybird, circular bird, circular caterpillar (becoming a circular butterfly), circular fish blowing circular bubbles, circular car emitting circular smoke, circular man's head, and circular bear; in the CGI sketch, a circle gains two additional planes and transforms into a beach ball, a football, an orange, and the planet Earth. In another episode, El Nombre shows Juan what a square is (using Pedro and Juanita's frame, Señor Manuel and Señor Chipito's draughts board, The Maggot and Cactus saloon's sign, and a blackboard), while Bobby Cube asks the Shape Spotters on Let's Shape Up to name the square by pointing out its distinguishing features, and a square robot builds a square dog that turns on him after.

Terry introduces the world-famous "Ring a Ring o' Roses Formation Dance Team" (along with their manager, Cynthia) on Come Prancing, and a prehistoric couple attempts to invent the round wheel (after square and triangular ones) for their car in Great Moments in History; in the episode's second cut-out animated sketch, circular pawprints transform into a circular ladybird, a circular bird, a circular caterpillar (which becomes a circular butterfly), a circular fish that blows circular bubbles, a circular car emitting circular smoke from its circular exhaust, a circular man's head, and a circular bear; in its CGI animated sketch, a circle gains two additional planes and transforms into a beach ball, a football, an orange, and the planet Earth. El Nombre teaches Juan what a square is, using the then-unnamed Pedro and Juanita's frame, Señor Manuel and Señor Chipito's draughts board, The Maggot, Cactus saloon's sign, and a blackboard, while Bobby Cube asks the Shape Spotters on Let's Shape Up to name the square by highlighting its features; a square robot builds a square dog that turns on him after detecting his scent, but he scares it away by transforming into a larger square dog with a big square and running to and climbing up it; Jill Scoop reports on Old King Cole who wants his square bowl (after round, triangular, and rectangular ones) for Newsdesk; in the episode's CGI animated sketch, a yellow square in the bottom-right of a gameboard rises to become a cube with numbers 1–6 on its sides, which then transform into six groups of dots corresponding to those numbers as the cube becomes dice for Snakes and Ladders. El Nombre teaches Juan what a triangle is, using a musical triangle, a roadworks sign, and a stepladder, while Aladdin finds a lamp with a triangle on it (after those with a circle and square) for his Uncle Abanazer, but wastes three wishes (one for each side and corner) by turning Abanazer into a cat, himself into a mouse, and making the lamp disappear (causing Abanazer to turn on him, though both question why there was no Genie); a triangular knight attempts to slay a triangular dragon (burned the first time, rained on the second time when the dragon's fire is extinguished), and Bobby Cube again asks the Shape Spotters to identify the triangle by pointing out its features; in the CGI sketch, a triangle has a dotted line drawn inside it, folds up into a triangular-based pyramid, rotates to show numbers 1–4 on its sides lighting up, then unfolds back into a triangle. El Nombre teaches Juan what a rectangle is, using a plank of wood, the cart's side, and Pedro and Juanita's cardboard piece; Sammy Shape visits Old Mother Hubbard's cottage to find out "what makes a rectangle a rectangle" for Shapewatch (a spoof of Crimewatch), meeting her dog (who wants a bone but finds a rectangular biscuit instead); a rectangular man swims at a pool (after walking up a staircase, taking an elevator, and walking up another staircase), Humpty Dumpty identifies the shape of a brick in the wall he is sitting on (just before falling), and a woman named Jane writes a rectangular letter, posts it into a postbox with a rectangular slot and door, and receives it at her house. El Nombre helps Juan remember the shapes (using a square frame, a circular hoop with a stick, a rectangular book, and a triangular roadworks sign), while the rectangular man, square robot, triangular knight, and circular man (now with a circular body and a wheel for a foot) build a house together (after the rectangular man built one entirely from rectangles, and the others transformed them into their own shapes), showing that "all different shapes work well together"; Bobby Cube asks the Shape Spotters to identify the "Shy Shapes" in a cola can and a Battenberg cake; a rectangle folds into a hollow cylinder as two circles cover its ends and a second rectangle wraps around it to form a can of baked beans; in the episode's second El Nombre sketch, Juan draws "El Nombre" (a square, rectangle, circle, and triangle stacked) before drawing "the rope that hits him on the head and knocks him over"; El Nombre says it has never happened to him, so Juan swings a rope at him and tells him "It has now!"; the sombrero-less El Nombre chases Juan through the town to an extended version of his theme song (with the new tagline "Drawing shapes in the desert sand" at the end), but never catches him; this is the only old-style episode with just one live-action sketch. In 1996, both this series and the next were released on VHS as "Video Plus Packs" by BBC Educational Publishing (now BBC Active); the following year, they were rereleased together as a double "Video Plus Pack" named "Numbertime Shapes/Side by Side". After the 1997 corporate change, the BBC Education website (http://www.bbc.co.uk/education/) was superimposed onto the four shapes (a red circle, green triangle, yellow square, blue rectangle) at the end of this series' episodes and the next two series, but not the first series' episodes. The third series (aimed at four- to five-year-olds) has five episodes focusing on prepositions; each episode opens with Lolita singing "Under, Over, Everywhere" (with the previous series' mobile visible in the background, now with an apple, three stickmen, a rainbow, a cloud with a hot-air balloon, a sun, a snake, a spider, and a snail); Juan gains three new friends—Pedro Gonzales, Juanita Conchita, Maria Consuela Tequila Chiquita (Pedro and Juanita had previously appeared in the second series)—and a pet tarantula named Tanto; each episode ends with Lolita reciting a rhyme or singing a song (with the second episode's song being an extended version of one heard earlier in an animated sketch about a fox); a sketch in the second episode parodies EastEnders as "GreenGrocers"; this is the first series to credit the El Nombre voice actors at the end of its final episode (Sophie Aldred, Kate Robbins, and Steve Steen); although made in Autumn 1995, it was not broadcast until 28 February 1996. This series and the next aired on Wednesdays in the Daytime on Two at 10:25 am; this series premiered after a rerun of the second series, and the next series premiered after Daytime on Two returned following a two-week Easter break. Juan has no school concert activity, so El Nombre tells him to recite Incy Wincy Spider with Tanto; a bear flies a kite (which comes down in a tree, so he climbs it to retrieve it); a window cleaner is annoyed by her colleague's incompetence; Juan recites Incy Wincy Spider at the concert (but Tanto won't come down the drainpipe, so El Nombre coaxes him); three clowns named Boris, Doris, and Ethel compete to see who can raise the biggest laugh in Give Us a Giggle. Juan wants to take a photo of himself and Mama (but can't because he is behind the Polaroid); an engine driver pulls wagons (but the coupling snaps when going uphill, so when they roll back down, they are in front of him, and he must signal a second engine to help); Jack and Jill take Farmer Giles's horse and cart to market in Happy Ever After; a fox hides in his secret lair to escape a hunt (accompanied by a rhyme from Lolita in voiceover); Juan still cannot take a photo of himself and Mama (so El Nombre takes it and blows himself up in the process); the GreenGrocers proprietor tries to get his four customers to stand behind his stall and form a proper queue (until he is upstaged by a toy salesman). Juan cannot score past Pedro, so El Nombre (not in his usual outfit, but in what later becomes Santo Flamingo United's strip) tells him to kick the ball over him; Princess Perfect wants a bed that cannot have a pea under it; a tortoise named Toby goes to a party but cannot get over the hedge (unlike the bird, frog, squirrel, and rabbit, who all go over, but the last one tells him to go under); Pedro is on a stool so Juan cannot score past him (until El Nombre tells him to kick the ball under him, and when Pedro objects, they reduce the goal size, but El Nombre whispers to Juan to kick the ball to one side before Pedro leaves); the Cow (from Hey Diddle Diddle) is scared of jumping over the Moon (so the Little Dog volunteers the Dish instead, but suggests running under it). Mama wants to go to Hurrell's store but there is a hole in front (so El Nombre and Juan tell her to walk around it); a doll pushes three building blocks (numbered 1–3) together (but a clown driving a breakdown truck crashes into them, scattering them, so he must help rearrange them); Darren and Sharon Jam cannot decide where to place their new table on Lucky Lottery Winners; Mama comes out of Hurrell's store (but still thinks there's another way around the hole, so El Nombre tells her to jump across it if she is brave, but when he falls in, she chooses to go around it again); Lord and Lady Posh give instructions to their gardener, Jarvis, on where to plant their roses and daisies. Juan loses Tanto, so El Nombre helps him and Mama find him; the bear from the first episode tries to boil water in a saucepan but its bottom is missing; a magician turns a volunteer's watch and keys into an alarm clock and one big key; two burglars named Bob and Bert break into a sweet shop, eat all the sweets, grow too fat to escape through the window, and are caught by PC Nabb; from this point on, El Nombre returns to one sketch per episode (except in Episodes 21 and 26).
