The fourth series (aimed at five- to six-year-olds) has eight episodes focusing on "more than" (addition) and "less than" (subtraction); each episode opens with Lolita singing "More or Less" in a studio with pillars; this series introduces Bill (voiced by Paul Cawley), a green bird who can swallow and regurgitate almost any object whole; from the fifth series onwards, he is joined by a purple cat named Bernie (voiced by Laura Brattan), who appears at the beginning of each "revised" first-, sixth-, and seventh-series episode; the series also features a toad named Test who hops along the heads of fifteen multicolored people (wearing red jumpers with numbers 1–15) forming a numberline based on the episode's focus (their jumpers turn green when Test is on their heads); each episode ends with Lolita singing a song (the last one continues over the credits, and it is her final appearance, though she still says she will "see them next Numbertime"); two sketches in the first and seventh episodes parody Percy Thrower and Sir David Attenborough as "Percy Grower" and "David Attencoat"; a third sketch in the third episode parodies Surprise, Surprise as "What a Surprise" (with Cinderella receiving a surprise visit from her Fairy Godmother); the Bill sketches in the second and sixth episodes feature an enormous (unnamed) beetle who chases Bill after putting his feet into the eight wellingtons he regurgitates (in the second episode) and falls on top of him after pulling his last two wellingtoned legs off a wall (in the sixth episode); the fourth episode features a "female" version of Bill who falls on top of him after he shakes twenty mangoes off a tree; in the El Nombre sketches of the seventh and final episodes, Juan has his fifth birthday for the second time (this time, Pedro, Juanita, and Maria bring him an extra candle because he is one year older, so he ends up with eight), and El Nombre's town gains a female mayor, Señora Fedora, who is also a balloon seller. A little old woman, a little old man, and their little old cat enlist the help of the Little Old Mouse to pull up their enormous turnip for Growing Bigger; Little Juan needs to play two cymbals (not one); Test hops from 3 to 7; contestant Sharon plays Find One More to win two prizes; Bill adds four flowers together; Juan needs to hit the cymbals one more time (to make four hits); in the episode's second animated sketch, a slow butterfly tries to keep up with faster friends, but when he joins them on a tree, the branch breaks under their weight and they all fly away. Freda Fantastic from Fantastic Fairytales presents The Elves and the Shoemaker; Little Juan and El Nombre juggle seven of Mama's tomatoes (which they shouldn't play with); Test hops from 7 to 13; Fred Fantastic presents The Frog Prince; Bill adds eight wellingtons (belonging to an enormous beetle) which, when the beetle puts his feet into them, causes him to chase after Bill; in the episode's second animated sketch, Noah refuses to let a mammoth onto the Ark because there is only one of him, so he disguises himself as two bears with puppets and a tarpaulin, but is quickly discovered by Noah again. A ladybird's nine babies and three extra are saved from a fire (which is actually smoke from her husband Arnold's barbecue); Little Juan and his friends are about to have Mama's very hot chili with tacos but there are only three chairs; Test hops from 2 to 8; Fairy Godmother presents What a Surprise with surprising results for Cinderella; Bill puts twelve books on a shelf which collapses under their weight; in the episode's second animated sketch, a kiwi notices his (three-toed) footprints in the sand and tries to count them, but finds it too hard to count in threes and eventually runs away from the camera. Snow White goes to the Wild Wood Takeaway and gets seven Good Fairy Cakes (declining Grimbleshanks' first offer of Toad Burgers) for the dwarves' tea as it is Dopey's birthday; Little Juan accidentally blows Juanita's balloon up five more times, causing it to burst; Test hops from 1 to 11; Jack's mother will not let him climb the beanstalk as it only has ten leaves (it needs fifteen to change her mind); Bill shakes twenty mangoes off a tree, ending with a "female" version of himself falling on top of him; in the episode's second stop-motion sketch, a Tyrannosaurus Rex plans to eat a small Triceratops but is scared away when five larger Triceratopses, followed by five more, suddenly appear behind them to protect him. A magician makes six red balls disappear one at a time; Little Juan and his friends play musical chairs but all have a chair to sit on; Test hops from 12 to 8; Carlotta Bottle tries to sing Ten Green Bottles but the bottles "don't-a fall-a" because property master Reg is not present to knock them down; Bill eats three apples off a tree, causing the branch to break under his weight and the zero he was displaying to hit him on the head; in the episode's second animated sketch, three dogs wait to be picked by prospective owners at a pet shop (when only one remains, he does a dance with a hat and cane to pass the time). Rebecca Testament reports for Numbertime News and interviews Mr. Noah and one of his sons, Ham, who used to have only six animals on the ark (two elephants, two lions, two doves); Little Juan and Tanto go to get two melons for Mama's pie ("Melon Surprise") as a surprise, but Señor Manuel the greengrocer has to save two of his melons for a special customer; Test hops from 10 to 4; a woman wins two coconuts and then another two from a total of eight on a shy, Bill subtracts six of the enormous beetle's wellingtons (causing the beetle to fall on top of him); Little Juan discovers that Señor Manuel's special customer is Mama, who already has two melons; in the episode's second animated sketch, two monkeys.

Three apples fall from a tree, ending with the branch breaking under the weight and the zero displayed hitting the person on the head; in the second animated sketch, three dogs wait to be picked up by prospective owners at a pet shop, and when only one remains, he dances with a hat and cane. Rebecca Testament reports for Numbertime News, interviewing Mr. Noah and his son Ham, who previously had only six animals on the ark (two elephants, two lions, and two doves); Little Juan and Tanto go to get two melons for Mama's pie ("Melon Surprise"), but Señor Manuel the greengrocer must save two melons for a special customer, and later Little Juan discovers that the special customer is Mama, who already has two melons; Test hops from 10 to 4, a woman wins two coconuts and then another two from a total of eight, Bill subtracts six of the enormous beetle's wellingtons (causing the beetle to fall on top of him), and in the second animated sketch, two monkeys argue over two bananas and fall off their tree. The Early Bird loses all nine of his worms, and it is David Attencoat's fault for saying it isn't raining; Little Juan celebrates his fifth birthday for the second time, with more than five candles on his cake; Test hops from 11 to 5, Humpty Dumpty is afraid of heights so the crew removes the nine bricks of the wall three at a time, and Bill watches nine leaves blow off a tree before winter, ending with him being covered in snow; in the second animated sketch, three pegs blow off a washing line, three petals fall from three eight-petalled flowers (leaving five), a tricycle hits a stone and all three wheels fall off, three sides of a picture frame fall down (leaving one), and three mice steal three biscuits from a plate of eight (leaving five), one of whom returns with a note saying "Oh yes!" The magician from the fifth episode makes fifteen beads disappear under three beakers, five at a time; Little Juan nearly floats away with six of Señora Fedora's balloons, Test hops from 13 to 3, Simple Simon must find a penny for five of the Pieman's fifteen pies, which have all been sold to Old Mother Hubbard, Little Jack Horner, and the Queen of Hearts, and Bill recycles fifteen glass bottles (five green, five clear, five brown); in the second animated sketch, an enormous snail eats twenty trees from four gardens, scares away a smaller snail, a goat, a cow, and a flock of birds as it descends on each. In 1997, the series was released on VHS as a "Video Plus Pack" by BBC Educational Publishing, and on 16 May 2013 it was rereleased on DVD as a "DVD Plus Pack" by BBC Active with an accompanying teachers' book, though it is now out of print. The fifth series, aimed at four- to six-year-olds, had ten episodes focusing on time-related concepts, with Lolita no longer presenting; each episode began with an animated man with a pocket watch for a head, who also appeared in a musical sketch at the end of the sixth episode. El Nombre's town was named Santo Flamingo (first mentioned in the sixth episode in reference to their local football team, though the school sign read "San Flamingo School"), and Juan gained a new teacher, Constanza Bonanza; all but two episodes featured a rarely speaking man named Tim (played by Toby Jones) learning about time-related concepts, with his only spoken line being "Cook for half an hour" in the seventh episode when reading the instruction on a pie box. This series introduced the recurring sketch of the Dolls' House, featuring a cowgirl named Annie (Victoria Gay), a scarecrow named Scrap (Paul Cawley), a robot named Glimmer (Ashley Artus with a Geordie accent), a clock named Ticker (Mike Hayley), and from the sixth series onward, a butler named Branston (Brian Miller); they were frequently visited by a pirate named Captain Kevin (Roger Griffiths), on three occasions by a mechanic named Megamax (Fidel Nanton), Glimmer's girlfriend Princess Penelope (who visited Scrap when ill and ate all his chocolates), and a Russian ballet dancer named Nadia Nokoblokov (who performed Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin's Minute Waltz); in the seventh series, a detective named Shelley Holmes (Issy Van Randwyck) also visited frequently, though the sketch ended after that series. Although made after the BBC's corporate change in Winter 1997 (evidenced by the new logo at the end of episodes), it was not broadcast until 13 January 1998. This series and the next were originally aired on Tuesdays at 9:45 am as part of the Schools Programmes strand. In the first new-style episode, Tim wakes up in the middle of the night, brushes his teeth, and pours cornflakes but waits until morning for milk; Little Juan wakes up the village because he thinks a fiesta is in the morning instead of the evening; the residents of the Dolls' House take turns preparing meals, Bill takes a Polaroid of himself and new co-star Bernie (who comes in covered in mud, so she gives him a bath and takes another Polaroid); Bill gets covered in mud while trying to bathe her. Tim goes to referee a football match but the forecast is "windy," so he changes into his best suit; Little Juan has football practice but cannot remember the day; Bill decides to go on holiday to escape the rain, leaving Bernie with seven cans of cat food (one for each day of the week) and a can opener; Scrap and Glimmer argue over a teddy bear, and Captain Kevin resolves it. The newspaper in this episode's Tim sketch is dated before the BBC's corporate change (10 April 1997), but it incorrectly states that day was a Monday when it was actually a Thursday. Tim tries to put on his suit (jacket, trousers, hat, shoes, socks, tie) in the wrong order; El Nombre helps Mama make Delietta Smith's omelette with red and green peppers; Bill wakes Bernie for dinner but forgets the food; Scrap and Glimmer attempt to make a chocolate splodge cake for Annie. This is the first episode to refer to the Dolls' House by name. Tim grows two flowers and photographs them but cannot wait for the third; Pedro bets Juan he can find a spider faster than Tanto; Bernie wants an apple but cannot reach it, so Bill offers to fly up, but when he learns he can't, he challenges her to a tower-building contest; Megamax comes for tea, so Annie, Scrap, and Glimmer paint the house, but Glimmer runs down, and Megamax deduces he needs a new battery, giving him the "Max Pack Turbo Booster." El Nombre helps Little Juan learn about the clock face for homework; Scrap and Glimmer clean Ticker's spring; Bill trips over sleeping Bernie and flies into his clock, causing all numbers and hands to fall off; when he reassembles them with Bernie's help, the clock's cuckoo calls at 3:00 and causes him to faint. Little Juan and friends prepare for a school outing to see Santo Flamingo United play in the cup final at 3:00; Bernie naps at 2:00, but Bill plays a prank by moving the clock an hour ahead and replacing the cuckoo to wake her; Scrap waits for the postwoman to deliver his new "Scrap Jacket" (which he had been talking about all night, keeping Glimmer from sleeping). Tim (with his only line, "Cook for half an hour") cooks a big pie he bought, gets bored, and eats all his other groceries; Scrap is ill, so Annie asks Glimmer to take his temperature every hour and give him medicine every half-hour (but Princess Penelope visits); Bernie enjoys a "cattuccino" at the foot of a Big Ben-like clock tower until Bill bungee-jumps from its minute hand, steals it when he returns, drinks it, and returns the empty cup; Pedro, Juanita, and Maria agree to meet Juan for football at 2:30 (but Juan wonders how to know when it is 2:30). Tim has hiccups and tries to cure them by drinking water and holding his breath for ten seconds, but is interrupted by a crank phone call and a crank door-caller; San Flamingo School holds a three-legged race during its sports day; Bill and Bernie prepare to launch each other into outer space using only a seesaw; Nadia Nokoblokov visits the Dolls' House to help with her new dance (Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin's Minute Waltz). Tim receives a three-layered parcel at night (a birthday cake) with a musical birthday card playing a high-speed version of "Happy Birthday to You"; El Nombre helps Juan and Juanita order the four seasons correctly for homework (but they still need to draw a picture for each); Bernie puts a smile on a snowman (which turns out to be Bill) in winter, the snow melts and blossoms grow in spring, Bill waters flowers to help them grow and Bernie mows the lawn in summer, leaves blow off in autumn, Bernie throws a snowball at Bill and skates on the ice in winter, and puts another smile on a snowman (again, Bill); the residents of the Dolls' House also organize their clothes for each season (but Glimmer thinks they are being thrown away). In his last appearance, Tim is woken by a train, eats cornflakes, drinks coffee, and builds a house of cards, which falls when the last train passes; Ticker is broken because Annie, Scrap, and Glimmer failed to oil him, so Captain Kevin gives him a spare ship's bell; Bill and Bernie test each other's knowledge of time with their clock (Bill gets two wrong); Miss Constanza Bonanza, Pedro, Juanita, and Mama remind Juan that it is choir practice at 4:30, football practice at 5:00, tea at 5:30, and home at 6:00. The four shapes at the end of episodes were redesigned and differently colored (circle green, triangle yellow, square red, rectangle blue); in 1999, the series was released on VHS as a "Video Plus Pack" by BBC Educational Publishing. The sixth series, aimed at five- to six-year-olds, had ten episodes focusing on numbers 11 through 20; each episode opened with Bill and Bernie finding the episode's number on their number line (carried over from the 1998 revised version of the first series); Santo Flamingo gained an ice-cream seller named Señor Gelato, a carpenter named Señor Chipito (who previously appeared in the second series as owner of "The Maggot and Cactus" saloon), and a bandit named Don Fandango (who stole twenty gold coins from the bank managed by Señor Calculo in the final episode); former Blue Peter host Janet Ellis joined the El Nombre cast; although made in Winter 1998, it was not broadcast until 12 January 1999. Eleven soldiers (ten in two rows of five, the eleventh on the bottom) march around, ten form the number eleven; Little Juan and friends prepare for a second school outing to play football (but only have ten shirts, and El Nombre writes the episode number in desert sand); Scrap receives a "Soccerbox" football game from his great-aunt Laura Litterbin (which disappoints him as he dislikes football, and one of the eleven white players goes missing). In song, a pair of green slugs eat twelve plants (in three rows of four) and make the number twelve; Juan bets Juanita he can do more skips than her (mistakenly pronouncing her surname as "Chiquita"), and Pedro bets both that he can do more than either (counting as fast as possible); Captain Kevin does not want Branston to mention twelve because it reminds him of the final voyage of the good ship Rusty Bucket (when its crew found twelve biscuits). Thirteen balls (in three rows of four and one underneath) roll around; Mama told Juan and Pedro that Señor Gelato is having a lucky day and they must help him with thirteen lucky charms (but Juan initially thinks he wanted to help); Annie dances in the Dolls' House lounge (but Scrap does poorly if he had done thirteen steps). Fifteen cars (in three rows of five) go nowhere and no one cares; Señor Gelato accidentally drives his ice-cream tricycle into a three-legged table that Mama told Juan and Pedro to take to Señor Chipito for repair (they need a replacement wheel with fifteen spokes, but Juan initially thinks it has more as he cannot tell where he started counting); Scrap and Glimmer play marbles (Glimmer is losing badly, and his ten red marbles go missing). Seventeen windows (in four rows of four and one on the door) open on a building and lights switch on at night; El Nombre helps Juan, Pedro, and Señor Gelato collect all seventeen of Señor Manuel's tomatoes and put them in a bag; Scrap eats three lots of cake mix meant for three of twenty cakes for Captain Kevin's birthday party. A spaceship beams up twenty stars (in four rows of five) and beams them down again in the constellation of twenty; Don Fandango steals twenty gold coins from the bank (Tanto bites a hole in his bag, causing all to fall out); Nadia Nokoblokov visits the Dolls' House again to perform "The Dance of Twenty Turns"; Ticker realizes if he stays in the bedroom he does not have to watch, and Scrap eats a cake with twenty candles, so Annie and Nadia punish him by putting him on the revolving podium and telling Glimmer to make him do twenty "fast" turns; clips from the first and fourth series were reused in a musical sketch at the end of this episode. In 2000, both this series and the next were released on VHS as "Video Plus Packs" by BBC Educational Publishing; on 4 May 2012, this series was re-released on DVD as a "DVD Plus Pack" by BBC Active with an accompanying teachers' book and an audio CD (initially released as a cassette) — this one is still in print. The seventh series, aimed at five- to six-year-olds, had five episodes focusing on adding and identifying two-figure numbers up to 100; each episode opened with Bill and Bernie using a number square instead of a number line, joined by a caterpillar named Limo (voiced by Peter Temple) who crawls around to count the required numbers; in Santo Flamingo, Maria's sister Pepita Consuela Tequila Chiquita also started at San Flamingo School. This series, the last for the Dolls' House, was originally aired on Thursdays at 10:50 am as part of the Schools Programmes strand. Bernie stacks.

In 2000, both this series and the following one were released on VHS as "Video Plus Packs" by BBC Educational Publishing; on 4 May 2012, this series was re-released on DVD as a "DVD Plus Pack" by BBC Active, including an accompanying teachers' book and an audio CD featuring songs from the series (initially released as an audio cassette), which remains in print. The seventh series, aimed at five- to six-year-olds, consisted of five episodes focusing on adding and identifying two-figure numbers up to 100; each episode began with Bill and Bernie, whose number line was replaced by a number square, joined by a caterpillar named Limo (voiced by Peter Temple), who crawled around the square to count the required numbers. In Santo Flamingo, Maria's sister Pepita Consuela Tequila Chiquita also started at San Flamingo School. This series, which was the Dolls' House's final episode, originally aired on Thursdays as part of the Schools Programmes strand at 10:50 am. Bernie stacks twenty-nine plates (thrown to her by Bill) and does not know what comes after 29, so asks Limo for help; each time she adds ten more, she must ask again, but when she reaches 100, the plates fall over due to their weight. Scrap has lost all but one of his fifty buttons, so Shelley Holmes helps him find them, while Señor Gelato has only one cornet left and Juan volunteers to go to Hurrell's store to get twenty-four more, though he is later asked to bring three extra ones. While dusting the number square, Bernie sneezes out four numbers (18, 46, 69, and 83), and after Limo replaces them, she dusts Bill's beak, causing him to sneeze the entire number square over. Maria's sister Pepita also begins at San Flamingo School, which is seen for the first time in this episode, while Glimmer cooks apple pie and custard (using his Aunt Dimity's recipe), but Scrap has mixed up his cookbook and Limo must place four additional numbers (24, 38, 77, and 96) back into the square. Bernie takes a forty-wink nap, and Limo counts them by crawling along each row of the number square; Scrap is tired of licking envelopes (containing birthday party invitations), while Juan saves up money in his donkey bank and takes it to Santo Flamingo Bank, and Bill and Bernie ask Limo to find numbers 30 and 90 and add ten. Bill makes twelve sandwiches and ten iced buns for a party (and Bernie makes ten more of each, plus ten rock cakes each), while Scrap and Glimmer prepare party bags; Señora Fedora opens the 15th Annual Santo Flamingo Egg Festival and chooses Mama to make a giant omelette (requiring sixty-one eggs but only having twenty-one), and Bill and Bernie eat thirty of the party "goodies," but Bill drops ten buns and Bernie slides their remains into him, causing him to drop ten sandwiches; when they dance, he throws the remaining twelve into the air. Bill bought twenty packs of five fish fingers (but forgot the chips, as Bernie discovers when she puts them in the freezer), Glimmer paints a five-dot pattern, and San Flamingo School holds a jumble sale—this was also the final episode to feature the Dolls' House, even though it credits Victoria Gay at the end, she did not appear as Annie in this series. The eighth series, aimed at five- to seven-year-olds, had ten episodes focusing on coin recognition, money problems, coin equivalents, and change (previously covered in BBC's Numbers Plus and Megamaths); each episode opened with eight "money-spiders" (one for each coin: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, and £2) descending from a tree. This series introduced pounds and pence to Santo Flamingo, added a railway station named El Loco and a pizza delivery boy named Leonardo de Sombrero, and reworked the recurring song "Numbers All Around" to focus on coins. It also introduced the recurring sketch Screensaver, featuring a screen named Screen (voiced by Sue Elliott-Nicholls), customers (all played by Michael Fenton-Stevens), and a robot named T1L (pronounced "Til," voiced by Paul Vates). This series aired on each day of the working week for a fortnight as part of the Schools Programmes strand at 11:05 am. Juan, Mama, and Pedro go to the fair (but don't know if they have enough money for the coconut shy, roundabout, or candy floss), Bill runs a cake stall but Bernie can't decide whether to buy one, so flips four coins (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p) into the air—though they don't come down again—and a cricket player wants to buy glue from Screensaver to fix his broken bat. San Flamingo School holds another jumble sale (to raise money for a new school bell), Bill now runs a drink stall but closes after selling his last drink to Bernie for 8p, and Bernie disguises herself as a vending machine to trick Bill into giving her money back; a policeman wants to buy a timepiece from Screensaver (who try to sell him Big Ben for 10p). Little Juan and his friends visit Santo Flamingo National Park to see the Giant Cactus, while Bill runs an "everything" stall (but when Bernie collects 10p from a 5p, two 2p, and a 1p coin, she misinterprets "everything 10p" and wheels it away), and a sailor wants to buy a cake from Screensaver (who offer a wedding cake). Little Juan and his friends arrive at the park and see the Giant Cactus, while Bill and Bernie buy a snack (5p), juice (2p), and chocolate (3p) from three talking vending machines; an old man wants to buy a new wheel for his wheel-basket from Screensaver (they try to sell him a bicycle wheel). Juan and Maria notice Señor Manuel has set up a giant jellybean machine outside Hurrell's store, Bernie plays "Coin Sports" and loses Bill's 1p, 2p, 5p, and 10p coins after they roll into a river (totaling 18p), and a Russian secret agent wants to change his appearance at Screensaver (they sell him a Hawaiian shirt for 4p, a blond wig for 8p, and a striped bow tie for another 8p). Mama takes Juan back-to-school shopping at Hurrell's store (and has him try on a hat that is too big), Bernie pays 20p for an elephant ride and gets 5p change (finding it slow, she pays another 20p for a rocket ride and gets another 5p change, then masquerades as a cat ride to trick Bill into giving her a third 5p; after he gives it to her, he wants to do it again, but she is too tired to), and a chef wants to buy butter and eggs from Screensaver. Señor Gelato promises Juan and Juanita ice cream if they go to Santo Flamingo Bank and exchange 50p for coins, while Bill and Bernie try to exit a car park (when Bill collects 50p, the barrier catapults him into the air), and a businessman wants to buy a pet from Screensaver (they sell him a "Starpet" from their home planet for 50p). Miss Bonanza is getting married (and Juan organizes the school's 50p collection for her gift), Bill pays 50p for a photo and gets 20p change (but the booth takes it before he can enter, so Bernie pays another 50p and Bill counts her change; when she looks out, the booth takes a photo of her tail, so they combine their changes to have a joint photo), and a rock star wants new shoes from Screensaver (they sell him blue suede platforms for 15p each). Pedro, Juanita, and Maria sleep over at Juan's house (planning to watch a scary film), while Bill and Bernie do laundry (paying 10p for washing powder and £1 for the machine); when Bernie inserts a £1 coin into the washing powder machine, she gets ten cups, which she pours into the washing machine, causing it to spew foam over the floor. A cowboy named Tom ("Big T") wants to buy a shirt with a big T from Screensaver. Little Juan performs a concert to raise money for the school bell (with Don Fandango masquerading as Mama and trying to steal all his £1.60 earnings), while Bill and Bernie want to go on a boat trip for £2 (though Bernie has a £2 coin, they both have to go back so Bill can gather the coins; when they return, Bernie gets on the boat before it leaves, but Bill is not lucky—he carries all his coins in a giant sack). A non-speaking clown tries to get Screen and T1L (in their last appearance) to guess he wants a top hat (50p) and a rabbit (for £1.50) at Screensaver. In the ninth (and final) series, aimed at six- to seven-year-olds, ten episodes focused on adding and subtracting, similar to the fourth series (without Lolita, live-action sketches based on nursery rhymes, or Test the Toad); Numbertime News, which had appeared in five episodes of the first series with Sammy Sport (played by Andy McEwan, who had played Matt Dillon in Death Without Dishonour, episode 26 of Taggart), and one episode of the fourth series with Rebecca Testament (played by Issy Van Randwyck), became a recurring sketch, with anchorwoman Tara Boomdeay (played by Elisabeth Sladen, who had played Sarah Jane on Doctor Who and several characters in episodes of the third and fourth series) and roving reporter Brad Quiff (played by Ian Connaughton). This series saw Michael Fenton-Stevens return to join the El Nombre cast and introduced Addem (voiced by Richard Pearce), a green snake who discovered the series' concept with a yellow ant named Ann (voiced by Moir Leslie) and a whole civilization of multi-coloured ants (mostly voiced by Brian Bowles and Richard Pearce, with the Queen Ant voiced by Moir Leslie). The series originally aired on Mondays at 11:05 am, but 1 October 2001 was the first day of the Labour Party Conference, so its fourth episode was not shown until the following week. Brad Quiff investigates addition (with the "High Peaks Climbing Team"), Bernie challenges Bill by giving him numbers to add to make twenty, Addem discovers a civilization of ants (headed by Ann), and Little Juan enters a competition on Radio Flamingo. Juan and Pedro go shopping at Señor Calculo's barbecue, Bernie plants seeds in window boxes and Bill helps her add them, Brad Quiff investigates how many chocolate bars the Malarkey Gang have stolen and Ann must get twenty-nine ants into three houses. Addem helps Ann sort beds for the "adolescants," Little Juan faces Don Fandango in the final of the Santo Flamingo Darts Championships, Brad Quiff reports on the popularity of the "Princess Patsy" doll, and Bill and Bernie wash their socks at the launderette from the eighth series. Brad Quiff visits a country fair to meet bun makers, El Nombre reads Little Juan a bedtime story (about Don Fandango robbing the Santo Flamingo Bank), Ann needs to prepare twenty-five meals for the "Accounts Department," and Bill and Bernie try to make carrot juice. Ann learns about adding acorns in hundreds, Brad Quiff reports on the opening of the "Whizzo Lolly Factory," Bill helps Bernie count her pennies as she plans to "shop 'till she drops," and Juan and Pedro earn pocket money by picking lemons for Señor Manuel. Brad Quiff reports on an American football team passing the ball down a numberline, Bernie challenges Bill again by giving him numbers to subtract to leave ten, a pair of cowboy ants must take twenty-seven aphids to the milking shed, and Juan goes on holiday to Costa Fortuna with Mama, Pedro, Juanita, and Maria after winning the first episode's competition. The Queen Ant decides to hold a regatta, Juan and his party board the plane to Costa Fortuna, Bill washes more socks at the launderette but Bernie tells him to separate whites from coloureds, and Brad Quiff reports on crowds gathering for Punch and Judy performances all day; in this episode's adaptation of the story (also frequently adapted by Mr. Partridge on Hi-de-Hi!), Mr. Punch steals Judy's marbles while she is asleep. Brad Quiff reports on an annual tug-of-war contest between the Diddletown Dodgers and the Softville Saints, Ann needs eighty-two candles for the Queen Ant's birthday cake, Juan and his party arrive at the Sea View Hotel in Costa Fortuna (where they meet guide Pablo), and Bill and Bernie insert two 20p coins into two of the three talking vending machines from the eighth series to buy a snack (16p) and juice (14p), receiving 4p and 6p change respectively; they combine their changes to buy a bar of chocolate (10p) from the third machine. This is one of only two episodes with an El Nombre sketch not set in Santo Flamingo. Juan and Pedro go to the fair in Costa Fortuna (where their guide Pablo fronts a ring-toss game), Ann must fill forty-five places in the "Accountants'" new building, Bill runs an apple stall (but when Bernie wants to buy three, he has none, so they both pick some from an apple tree), and Brad Quiff reports on "Doreen's Sweet Shop" being robbed of a large pile of chocolate eggs. In the show's final episode, a squad of 100 marching ants keeps breaking up and reforming, Juan and his party return to Santo Flamingo (and are told at customs they can only bring a certain amount), Brad Quiff reports on the "Numbertime News Live Formation Climbing Team" (who show a trick to remember sums), and Bill and Bernie have tea (Bill puts ten sugar cubes in his, and when Bernie asks what he is doing, she makes him forget how many he added); even though this was the last episode, El Nombre received a second series in 2003. In 2001, by which time VHS was becoming obsolete, this series was released on VHS as a "Video Plus Pack" by BBC Educational Publishing. In 2002, by which time VHS was even more obsolete, this series was again released on VHS as a "Video Plus Pack" by BBC Educational Publishing. The first series was accompanied by a ten-part radio series on BBC School Radio entitled Radio Numbertime, focusing on numbers 1–10 in order, which aired from 21 September to 30 November 1993. Another radio series, simply titled Numbertime, aired on BBC School Radio from 29 September 2000 to 26 March 2003, and a third radio series, again titled Numbertime, aired from 1 May to 26 June 2014.
From 29 September 2000 to 26 March 2003, a third radio series titled Numbertime, matching the name of the previous defunct television series, was aired on BBC School Radio from 1 May to 26 June 2014.

The Nyholm Prize for Education honors the life and contributions of Sir Ronald Nyholm, an Australian-born chemist renowned for his work in coordination chemistry and his strong advocacy for enhancing science education. He served as president of the Royal Society of Chemistry from 1968 to 1970. Established in 1973, the prize is awarded biennially by the Royal Society of Chemistry to recognize exceptional achievements in chemical science education, particularly significant contributions to national or international research or innovation. Prior to 2008, it was known as the Sir Ronald Nyholm Lectureship (Education Division). Each recipient is awarded £5,000, a medal, and a certificate. The list of recipients is documented in the records.

The Odd Fellows Hall in Old Town Eureka, California, also known as the French Empire Mansard Building, is a building constructed in 1883 that features Second Empire architecture.[2] Historically, it has functioned as a department store, a professional building, a clubhouse, and a meeting hall for Odd Fellows.[1][3] The property was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.[3] This article about a California property on the National Register of Historic Places is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

Oicatá is a town and municipality located in the Central Boyacá Province, Department of Boyacá, Colombia. Its urban centre lies on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense at an altitude of 2,815 metres (9,236 ft), approximately 153 kilometres (95 mi) from Bogotá and 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) from Tunja, the department capital. It shares borders with Cómbita and Tuta to the north, Chivatá and Tunja to the south, Chivatá to the east, and Cómbita and Tunja to the west. The name Oicatá derives from the Chibcha language and means "Domain of the priests" or "Hailstoned farmlands." The municipality was established on May 9, 1539, by Pedro Ruiz Corredor. Prior to the Spanish conquest, the area belonged to the Muisca, the most advanced society in Colombia in terms of social, cultural, and productive development. After the conquest, governance was carried out by the Governor General, appointed directly by the King of Spain. The people achieved independence from Spain following the Battle of Boyacá on August 7, 1819, where Simón Bolívar's forces defeated Spanish troops. In 1821, the Constitution of Cúcuta introduced a hierarchical administrative structure, dividing the country into departments, provinces, counties, and parishes, and established Boyacá Department as comprising the provinces of Tunja, Pamplona, Socorro, and Casanare. The Act of June 15, 1857, declared Boyacá a sovereign state including the provinces of Tunja, Tundama, Casanare, and the counties of Chiquinquirá and Velez. The Act of October 31 of that year created four departments: Tunja with 42 districts, Tundama with 46, Casanare with 21, and Oriente (East) with 6. Under the Constitution of Rionegro in 1863, administrative divisions were modified, and Law 10 of that year reorganized Boyacá into six departments: Casanare, Tundama, North, West, East, and Centre. The centrist Constitution of 1886 established a structure of departments, provinces, and municipalities. In 1911, Executive Decree No. 306 abolished provinces and led to the creation of the commissariat of Arauca from several municipalities. Subsequently, municipalities in the Orinoco region formed the intendency of Casanare as part of Boyacá until 1973, when it separated again. The primary economic activity in Oicatá is agriculture, producing potatoes, maize, barley, wheat, peas, and beans. The climate of Oicatá is influenced by its location and altitude, with an elevation of nearly 3,000 metres, making it one of Colombia’s higher cities. It has a subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cfb) characterized by minimal temperature variation year-round and a distinct dry season from December to February.

Baroness Olga Vadimovna von Root (2 December 1901 – 28 June 1967) was a Russian stage actress and singer born in Sevastopol, Crimea. She was the daughter of Baron Vadim Nikolayevich von Root, a Czarist military officer and nobleman, and Lubov Karlovna Kostsyushko-Valyuzhinich, a member of a Polish landed gentry family. Her paternal ancestors were Volga German nobility who came to the Russian Empire during the reign of Peter the Great to serve in the Imperial Russian Army. Her maternal grandfather, Karl Kazimirovich Kostsyushko-Valyuzhinich, was Catholic and the founder of the Archeological Museum in Chersonesus, and her maternal grandmother, Maria Pavlovna Reveliotis, was a Russian Orthodox woman of Greek descent and the granddaughter of General Theodosios Reveliotis, a leader of the Greek War of Independence. Through her mother, Root was also a descendant of the Polish national hero Tadeusz Kościuszko. Root was educated at the Smolny Institute of Noble Maidens in Saint Petersburg, where she trained as a singer. At the age of fifteen, she ran away and performed with a troop of Romani performers, learning their music and dances from Nikolai Kroutchine, after which she was found and returned to her family. During the October Revolution, her family moved from Moscow to Kyiv; her father, loyal to Nicholas II, commanded troops in the White Army. To support her family, Root began singing in cabarets and nightclubs. She was arrested by Bolsheviks during a raid, imprisoned, and ordered to be executed, but her life was spared after a Bolshevik colonel recognized her from the stage and released her. The colonel later spared her mother and siblings from arrest and informed Root that her father would be granted amnesty if he defected to the Red Army. She wrote to her father and persuaded him to switch sides, after which he became an instructor at the Soviety Military Academy. During the rise of Communism, Root became a star of the stage as a singer and actress, performing under the name Olga Vadina and becoming one of the top stars of post-Revolutionary Russia's concert theatre, eventually marrying her manager. She performed a program of Romani ballads at a theatre in Paris and later performed in other European capitals. While living in New York City with her second husband, Armand Hammer, she worked with a musician to transcribe Russian and Romani music. In 1925, while performing in Yalta, she was introduced to Armand Hammer, a Jewish-American millionaire industrialist, and the two fell in love. She obtained a divorce from her first husband in Moscow and married Hammer in a civil ceremony in 1927. They had one son, Julian Armand Hammer, born in Moscow in 1928. The family left Moscow in 1930 and settled on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. They divorced in 1943. Root is the grandmother of American businessman Michael Armand Hammer and the great-grandmother of American actor Armie Hammer.

Oliver Heaviside (/ˈhɛvisaɪd/ HEV-ee-syde; 18 May 1850 – 3 February 1925) was a British mathematician and electrical engineer who invented a new technique for solving differential equations, equivalent to the Laplace transform, independently developed vector calculus, and rewrote Maxwell's equations in the form commonly used today. He significantly shaped the understanding and application of Maxwell's equations in the decades following Maxwell's death. In 1893, he extended them to gravitoelectromagnetism, which was confirmed by Gravity Probe B in 2005. His formulation of the telegrapher's equations became commercially important during his lifetime, after their significance was initially overlooked, as few others were familiar with his novel methodology. Born on 18 May 1850 at 55 Kings Street (now Plender Street) in Camden Town, England, the youngest of three children of Thomas Heaviside, a draughtsman and wood engraver, and Rachel Elizabeth West, Heaviside was a short and red-headed child who suffered from scarlet fever, resulting in a hearing impairment that hindered his communication and social interactions as a child. He described his time in Kings Street as miserable, which led him to hate craftspeople and influenced his lifelong abstention from alcohol. A small legacy allowed the family to move to a better part of Camden when he was thirteen, and he was sent to Camden House Grammar School, where he placed fifth out of five hundred pupils in 1865. His parents could not keep him at school after he turned 16, so he studied independently for a year with no further formal education. His uncle by marriage, Sir Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875), an expert in telegraphy and electromagnetism, took a strong interest in his education, and in 1867 sent him to work with his older brother Arthur Wheatstone in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. Two years later, he took a job as a telegraph operator with the Danish Great Northern Telegraph Company laying a cable from Newcastle to Denmark using British contractors, where he soon became an electrician. He continued studying while working, and by age 22 published an article in the Philosophical Magazine on 'The Best Arrangement of Wheatstone's Bridge for measuring a Given Resistance with a Given Galvanometer and Battery,' which received positive feedback from physicists including Sir William Thomson and James Clerk Maxwell. When he published an article on the duplex method of using a telegraph cable, he mocked R. S. Culley, the engineer in chief of the Post Office telegraph system, who had dismissed duplex as impractical. In 1873, his application to join the Society of Telegraph Engineers was rejected with the comment "they didn't want telegraph clerks," which angered Heaviside, prompting him to ask Thomson to sponsor him, and with the support of the society's president, he was admitted "despite the P.O. snobs." In 1873, Heaviside encountered Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, which he later recalled as "great, greater and greatest," and despite his initial ignorance of mathematical analysis, he spent several years mastering it before moving to his own interpretation of Maxwell's work. From home, he developed transmission line theory (the "telegrapher's equations"), showing mathematically that uniformly distributed inductance in a telegraph line would reduce both attenuation and distortion, and that with sufficient inductance and low insulation resistance, the circuit would be distortionless, allowing all frequencies to propagate at equal speeds. From 1882 to 1902, except for three years, Heaviside contributed regular articles to the trade paper The Electrician, which paid him £40 per year—insufficient for living but aligned with his desire to write. Between 1883 and 1887, he averaged 2–3 articles per month, which later formed the bulk of his Electromagnetic Theory and Electrical Papers. In 1880, he researched the skin effect and patented in England the coaxial cable. In 1884, he recast Maxwell's mathematical analysis from its original form (using quaternions) into modern vector terminology, reducing twelve of the original twenty equations in twenty unknowns to four differential equations in two unknowns—now known as Maxwell's equations—describing electric charges (static and moving), magnetic fields, and their relationship. Between 1880 and 1887, he developed the operational calculus using the differential operator p (previously denoted by D by Boole), providing a method of solving differential equations by treating them as algebraic equations. This caused controversy due to its lack of rigor; Heaviside famously stated, "Mathematics is an experimental science, and definitions do not come first, but later on. They make themselves, when the nature of the subject has developed itself," and once asked, "Shall I refuse my dinner because I do not fully understand the process of digestion?" In 1887, Heaviside worked with his brother Arthur on a paper titled "The Bridge System of Telephony," proposing the addition of loading coils (inductors) to telephone and telegraph lines to correct distortion. The paper was blocked by William Henry Preece of the Post Office, who viewed self-inductance as detrimental to transmission and had recently dismissed the editor of The Electrician, which ended Heaviside's long-running series of articles until 1891. Heaviside believed Preece was behind the sacking and considered him mathematically incompetent, a view supported by biographer Paul J. Nahin, who described Preece as "a powerful government official, enormously ambitious, and in some remarkable ways, an utter blockhead." Preece suppressed Heaviside's work to protect his own reputation and avoid admitting error. The importance of Heaviside's work remained unrecognized for some time. In 1897, AT&T employed George A. Campbell and Michael I. Pupin to extend Heaviside's work, filing patents for their research and the construction of coils previously invented by Heaviside. AT&T later offered Heaviside money in exchange for his rights, possibly influenced by their respect for his work, but Heaviside refused unless the company granted him full recognition. He was chronically poor, making his refusal especially notable. In 1959, Norbert Wiener published The Tempter and accused AT&T and Michael I. Pupin of usurping Heaviside's inventions. This setback redirected Heaviside's attention to electromagnetic radiation; in 1888 and 1889, he calculated field deformations around a moving charge, predicting what is now known as Cherenkov radiation and inspiring George FitzGerald to propose the Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction. In 1889, he first published a correct derivation of the magnetic force on a moving charged particle, the magnetic component of the Lorentz force. In the late 1880s and early 1890s, Heaviside worked on electromagnetic mass, treating it as material mass capable of producing similar effects; Wilhelm Wien later verified his expression for low velocities. In 1891, the British Royal Society named him a Fellow, and the following year devoted over fifty pages of the Philosophical Transactions to his vector methods and electromagnetic theory. He was elected to honorary membership of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1894. In 1905, he received an honorary doctorate from the University of Göttingen. In 1896, FitzGerald and John Perry granted Heaviside a civil list pension of £120 per year, which he accepted after rejecting other charitable offers from the Royal Society. In 1902, Heaviside proposed the existence of the Kennelly–Heaviside layer of the ionosphere, suggesting a mechanism for radio signals to travel around the Earth's curvature. The layer's existence was confirmed in 1923. His predictions, combined with Planck's radiation theory, likely discouraged further attempts to detect solar radio waves until Jansky's development of radio astronomy in 1932. Heaviside opposed Albert Einstein's theory of relativity; Howard Eves noted he was the only first-rate physicist at the time to criticize Einstein, with his invectives often bordering on absurdity. In later years, Heaviside became eccentric; according to B.A. Behrend, he became a recluse who delivered manuscripts to a grocery store where editors picked them up. Though he had been an active cyclist in his youth, his health declined in his sixth decade. During this time, he signed letters with the initials "W.O.R.M." and reportedly painted his fingernails pink, moving granite blocks into his house as furniture. In 1922, he became the first recipient of the Faraday Medal, established that year. He was a Unitarian but not religious, and reportedly mocked people who placed faith in a supreme being. He died on 3 February 1925 in Torquay at age 74 after falling from a ladder. He is buried just behind and to the right of the building near the southeast corner of Paignton cemetery, with his father Thomas and mother Rachel. The gravestone was cleaned by an anonymous donor in 2005. He was highly regarded by electrical engineers, especially after his correction to Kelvin's transmission line analysis was vindicated, though most recognition came posthumously. In July 2014, academics at Newcastle University and the Newcastle Electromagnetics Interest Group founded the Heaviside Memorial Project to restore the monument through public subscription. The restored memorial was unveiled on 30 August 2014 by Alan Heather, a distant relative of Heaviside, and attended by the Mayor of Torbay, the MP for Torbay, an ex-curator of the Science Museum (representing the Institution of Engineering and Technology), the Chairman of the Torbay Civic Society, and delegates from Newcastle University. A collection of Heaviside's papers is held at the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) Archive Centre, including notebooks with mathematical equations, annotated pamphlets on telegraphy, manuscript notes, drafts of papers, correspondence, and drafts of articles for 'Electromagnetic Theory.' An audio tribute from 1950 by Oliver E. Buckley, President of Bell Telephone Labs, has been digitized and is accessible on the IET Archives. In 1908, Heaviside was made an Honorary Member of the Institution of Electrical Engineers (IEE), with his entry reading "1908 Oliver Heaviside FRS" in the IEE Roll of Honorary Members and Faraday Medallists 1871–1921. In 1922, he received the Faraday Medal. In 1950, the IEE Council established the Heaviside Premium Award, recommending a £10 annual prize for the best mathematical paper accepted. Heaviside advanced vector methods and vector calculus; Maxwell's original formulation consisted of 20 equations in 20 variables, which Heaviside reduced to four equations in four variables (B, E, J, and ρ) using curl and divergence operators. Less well known is that Heaviside's equations and Maxwell's are not identical, and it is easier to modify Heaviside's version to align with quantum physics. He also discussed the possibility of gravitational waves using the analogy between the inverse-square law in gravitation and electricity. With quaternion multiplication, the square of a vector is negative, which displeased Heaviside; he is credited by C. J. Joly with developing hyperbolic quaternions, though this was largely the work of Alexander Macfarlane. He invented the Heaviside step function to calculate current when a circuit is switched on and was the first to use the unit impulse function now known as the Dirac delta function. He developed his operational calculus method for solving linear differential equations, which resembles the current Laplace transform method based on the "Bromwich integral," named after Bromwich who provided a rigorous justification for Heaviside's operator method using contour integration. Heaviside was familiar with the Laplace transform but considered his method more direct. He developed transmission line theory (the "telegrapher's equations"), which increased transmission rates over transatlantic cables by a factor of ten—reducing transmission time from ten minutes per character to one minute per character—and discovered that telephone transmission could be improved by adding electrical inductance in series with the cable. He also independently discovered the Poynting vector. He advanced the idea that the Earth's upper atmosphere contained an ionized layer, predicting the Kennelly–Heaviside layer. In 1947, Edward Appleton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for proving the layer's existence. He coined several terms in electromagnetic theory; however, he is sometimes incorrectly credited with coining susceptance (the imaginary part of admittance), which was coined by Charles Proteus Steinmetz in 1894, and reactance (the imaginary part of impedance), which was coined by Édouard Hospitalier in 1893.

Placing electrical inductance in series with the cable could significantly improve performance, and Heaviside independently discovered the Poynting vector. He proposed that the Earth's uppermost atmosphere contains an ionised layer, later known as the ionosphere, which he predicted was the Kennelly–Heaviside layer; this layer was later confirmed by Edward Appleton, who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1947 for proving its existence. Heaviside introduced several key terms in electromagnetic theory. However, he is sometimes mistakenly credited with coining susceptance (the imaginary part of admittance) and reactance (the imaginary part of impedance); in fact, susceptance was introduced by Charles Proteus Steinmetz in 1894, and reactance was introduced by Édouard Hospitalier in 1893.

Oliviero Diliberto, born on 13 October 1956 in Cagliari, is an Italian politician who has served as leader of the Party of Italian Communists. He was born into a family of public servants: his father, Marco, worked as an attorney in the Administration of the Region of Sardinia, and his mother, Lella, was a teacher. The death of his father in 1971 deeply affected him, after which he took on a fatherly role for his younger siblings, his sister Ludovica (then eight years old) and his brother Alessio, who was born two months before. At age 13 in 1969, during a period of turmoil in Italian schools, Diliberto became involved in the student movement and rose through the ranks of the student activism. In 1978, the same year he graduated, he became Secretary of the FGCI (Federation of Young Italian Communists, the youth organization of the PCI) for the province of Cagliari. After graduating from high school, he traveled to Paris, where he briefly worked at the city morgue to support himself, preparing corpses for autopsies, a period influenced by his fascination with Michel Foucault's philosophical thought. From 1978 to 1986, he earned scholarships to study law in Frankfurt and Rome, and later worked as a researcher at the University of Cagliari, eventually becoming a Professor of Roman Law. A former member of the Italian Communist Party, he joined the Communist Refoundation Party following the breakup of his former party. First elected as a Member of Parliament in 1994 for the Communist Refoundation Party, he left the party in 1998 in opposition to the leadership's stance on a motion of no confidence that resulted in Romano Prodi's defeat. Alongside Armando Cossutta and others, he founded the Party of Italian Communists, of which he became secretary. He served as Minister of Justice in the first government of Massimo D'Alema, becoming one of only two party members in that government, holding the position until 2000 when he voluntarily stepped down to focus on party affairs. Upon taking office as Minister of Justice, he expressed pride in being "The second Communist appointed as Minister of Justice after Palmiro Togliatti" and had the same desk previously used by Togliatti restored and placed in his office. In November 2004, he faced widespread criticism for meeting with Hizbollah leader Sheik Hassan Nasrallah during a visit to Lebanon, prompting a protest note from the Israeli Ambassador in Rome. Before the April 2006 general election, which was won by the centre-left coalition, he declared he would not serve as minister if the centre-left won, instead remaining as party leader—a position he has maintained. In May 2006, he was elected to the City Council of Rome. He is currently a professor of Roman Law at the Faculty of Law of the "La Sapienza" University of Rome. Before the April 2008 snap general election, caused by the fall of the Prodi II Cabinet, he refused to run for the Camera dei Deputati in the Turin constituency for the left-wing alliance The Left – The Rainbow, on the grounds of giving a chance to a junior party fellow—a steel worker at the local Thyssen-Krupp steelworks, who died in a fire on 6 December 2007 that killed seven colleagues. After the poor results of both the 2008 general election and the 2009 European election, in which the Italian left-wing parties failed to reach the minimum threshold, Diliberto was confirmed as party secretary with a mandate to promote unity among left-wing parties. Diliberto has been married twice: he married Ms. Delia Cardia in 1985, after which they separated, and is currently married (since 1997) to Ms. Gabriella Serrenti, whom he met in 1978 at the university where he was an assistant lecturer.

Olton Willem van Genderen (17 October 1921 – 9 November 1990) was a Surinamese civil servant and politician who served as Deputy Prime Minister of Suriname from 24 December 1973 until the coup d'état of 25 February 1980. He was one of the main negotiators for Suriname's independence. Born on 17 October 1921 in Albina, he worked for the customs agency and, in the 1950s, went to Rotterdam for four years where he became a licensed customs officer. He became active in trade unions and politics and was given the honorary title Da Djendé (Ndyuka: Beautiful teacher). In 1958, he was first elected to the Estates of Suriname and was re-elected five times. On 16 May 1967, he was elected Chairman of the Estates of Suriname, serving until 1 September 1969. On 15 December 1973, he was re-elected as Chairman, but resigned on 28 December because he had been elected Deputy Prime Minister on 24 December in the Arron cabinet. He also served as Minister of District Administration and Decentralisation. The Arron government negotiated with the Dutch government regarding Suriname's independence, and van Genderen was a key negotiator. On 25 November 1975, Suriname gained independence. In 1977, he was appointed Minister of the Interior, the successor to the Ministry of District Administration and Decentralisation. On 25 February 1980, Desi Bouterse carried out a coup d'état; Arron went into hiding, while van Genderen was captured. On 26 February, van Genderen and Minister Badrising announced the government's surrender on television, urging the population not to resist the military regime. On 28 February, Arron surrendered to the regime. Van Genderen was placed under house arrest until February 1981. On 19 June 1981, he was sentenced to four months imprisonment minus time served under house arrest and fined a total of ƒ 55,000. Van Genderen died on 9 November 1990 at the age of 69. In 2021, the Emmastraat in Albina was renamed Olton Willem van Genderen Boulevard in his honor.

One on One is an American sitcom created by Eunetta T. Boone and aired on UPN from September 3, 2001, to May 15, 2006. The series stars Flex Alexander as a single sportscaster who becomes a full-time father when his ex-wife, Nicole Barnes (Tichina Arnold), takes a job in Nova Scotia and his teenage daughter Breanna Barnes (Kyla Pratt) moves in with him. Flex, who previously blew out his knee during an NBA game and used his communications degree—though he failed the class twice—to transition into sportscasting, works for the fictional WYNX-TV and lives in a luxury bachelor pad. He is a ladies' man who strives to be a responsible parent and best friend to Breanna, being very protective of her, especially from boys. His only serious relationship was with Nicole, whom he impregnated at 18. The show is set in Baltimore for the first four seasons before shifting to Los Angeles for the final season. It was a joint production of Greenblatt/Janollari Studio and Daddy's Girl Productions in association with Paramount Network Television, though it was not originally a Paramount production. The show was initially pitched to ABC in 1999 when the pilot was shot, but ABC declined due to declining sitcom audiences. It was then pitched to The WB, which passed on it because it wasn’t “teen enough,” and later to Fox Television Studios, which also declined due to it not fitting their financial model. After ABC, The WB, and Fox rejected the show, UPN executives took interest, especially due to the success of Moesha’s cancellation, and picked it up. Fox Television Studios dropped out last minute over financial concerns, prompting Paramount Television to step in. The series featured guest appearances from celebrities and athletes such as Lil' Zane, Chris Brown, Lil' Romeo, Eve, Lloyd, Floetry, Angie Stone, Mario, Omarion, Brandy, Solange Knowles, Nina Sky, Marques Houston, Smokey Robinson, Kim Fields, Avant, Jennifer Freeman, Nate Dogg, Bobby V, Claudia Jordan, Ruben Studdard, and Lisa Leslie. The show was cancelled months before UPN and The WB merged to form The CW. A spin-off series, Cuts, premiered as a mid-season replacement in the 2004–2005 season and followed Flex’s younger stepbrother Kevin Barnes running a barbershop/day spa with a spoiled brat named Tiffany Sherwood after her father Jack Sherwood purchased the shop. Cuts also lasted two seasons and was cancelled when UPN and The WB merged. The series centers on Flex Washington (Alexander) and his daughter Breanna Barnes (Pratt), beginning with Breanna wanting to stay with Flex, whom she previously saw only two weeks a year. Flex’s best friend and Breanna’s godfather, Duane Odell Knox (Kelly Perine), is a used-car salesman who lives across the hall and is a constant presence; he is often repelled by women, though his only serious girlfriend was Candy (Shondrella Avery), whom he dated for two years before breaking up. Breanna’s best friend is Spirit Jones (Sicily Sewell), with whom she creates mischief, and her other best friend, Arnaz Ballard (Robert Ri'chard), is the object of her on-again, off-again affection. Breanna becomes jealous of Arnaz’s old girlfriend, Ginger (Khanya Mkhize), and Arnaz becomes jealous when Breanna starts dating Josh (Josh Henderson). They eventually become a couple in the latter part of the series, break up in season 3, and later rekindle their relationship, ending with Arnaz chasing after Michelle (Brandy Norwood), D-Mack’s sister, while Breanna is shown in bed with D-Mack (Ray J). The show’s theme song, "Living One on One," was written and performed by Shanice (Flex Alexander’s wife) and Tonex, with music composed by Jonathan Wolff and Becky Kneubuhl, who also composed the scene-change music for the first season. For the fifth season, the theme was slightly shortened and remixed by Detail and Ray J, and a truncated version with only the words "One on One" was used as a closing theme in syndicated airings. The opening titles for the first three seasons featured the cast playing basketball on an outdoor court, with additional scenes showing Spirit checking out a boy and Arnaz playing guitar interrupted by a bouncing basketball. The fourth-season opening featured the cast in a dressing room preparing for a night out, ending with a pan shot of them in mirrors wearing different outfits. The first four seasons included a closeup of Flex, Breanna, and Arnaz before cutting to a shot of the entire cast. The final season’s opening showed the main cast (Breanna, Arnaz, D-Mack, Sara, Cash, and Lisa) at various locations on the Venice Beach Boardwalk before meeting at a beach house for a photo. The show began airing in syndication in September 2006, with CBS Paramount Domestic Television holding distribution rights for the first year, and CBS Media Ventures taking over since September 2007. In the U.S., it aired on local stations (mostly Fox, The CW, and MyNetworkTV) from September 2006 to September 2009, and was rerun on Noggin’s teen block, The N, starting in October 2006. It continued on The N after it became a 24-hour channel in December 2007, running until October 2008, then returned to The N on September 14, 2009, and moved to TeenNick on September 28, 2009, airing in two-hour morning and late-night blocks before being removed in 2013. The show aired on BET in 2009 in two one-hour blocks (one weekday morning and one afternoon) and on Saturdays. Formerly, Bounce TV and TV One also broadcast the series. It joined Netflix on October 15, 2020. As of 2024, reruns can be seen on Cleo TV and Dabl. Overseas, the series is broadcast in Canada on BET and local affiliates, in Australia on Nine Network, in South Africa on SABC1, and in the Middle East on the Paramount Comedy Channel (though the fifth season has not been aired in full). It is also broadcast across Africa via the Sony Entertainment Channel through DSTV.

Onsari Gharti Magar (Nepali: ओनसरी घर्तिमगर) is a Nepali communist politician and current parliamentarian. She made history by becoming the first female Speaker of the Parliament of Nepal, a position she was elected to unopposed on October 16, 2015.[2][3] Prior to this, she served as Deputy Speaker of Parliament[3] and held the office of Minister of Youth and Sports in the cabinet led by Jhala Nath Khanal.[2] Gharti Magar was elected to the Constituent Assembly (CA) from Rolpa constituency-2 in the second CA election. She later entered the House of Representatives in 2017 through a party list.[citation needed] In the 2013 Constituent Assembly election, she contested from Rolpa-2. She is married to Barsha Man Pun, who was formerly the secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist-Centre).[2] This article about a politician from Lumbini Province is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Oprah Gail Winfrey (/ˈoʊprə/; born Orpah Gail Winfrey; January 29, 1954) is an American talk show host, television producer, actress, author, and media proprietor. She is best known for her talk show, The Oprah Winfrey Show, which aired in national syndication from Chicago from 1986 to 2011, spanning 25 years. Globally, she is the richest Black woman and the wealthiest female celebrity. Dubbed the "Queen of All Media," she was the richest African-American of the 20th century and once the world's only Black billionaire. By 2007, she was frequently ranked as the most influential woman in the world. Winfrey was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi, to a teenaged mother, Vernita Lee, and father Vernon Winfrey; her parents never married. Her mother worked as a housemaid, and her father was a coal miner who later became a barber and city councilman. A 2006 genetic test revealed her matrilineal ancestry originated among the Kpelle ethnic group from Liberia, with 89% Sub-Saharan African, 8% Native American, and 3% East Asian heritage. After birth, her mother moved north, and Winfrey lived in rural poverty with her maternal grandmother, Hattie Mae Lee, who taught her to read before age three and nicknamed her "The Preacher" for reciting Bible verses. Her grandmother beat her daily and often dressed her in potato sack dresses, which other children mocked. At age six, Winfrey moved to an inner-city neighborhood in Milwaukee, where her mother worked long hours as a maid. Around this time, Lee gave birth to Winfrey’s younger half-sister, Patricia, who died in 2003 from cocaine-related causes, and a third daughter also named Patricia, who was adopted to ease financial strain. Winfrey did not learn of her second half-sister until 2010. By 1962, Lee gave birth to Winfrey’s half-brother Jeffrey, who died of AIDS-related causes in 1989. At age eight, she was baptized in a Baptist church. Winfrey reported being molested by her cousin, uncle, and a family friend starting at age nine, which she first disclosed on a 1986 episode of her show. A biographer claimed that when she shared this with family at age 24, they refused to believe her. She once said she chose not to be a mother because she had not been mothered well. At age 13, after years of abuse, she ran away from home. At 14, she became pregnant, but her son was born prematurely and died shortly after. She later expressed betrayal over a family member who sold the story of her son to the National Enquirer in 1990. Winfrey attended Lincoln Middle and High School in Milwaukee, then transferred to Nicolet High School after early success in the Upward Bound program. She was reminded of her poverty on the bus, leading her to steal money from her mother to keep up with peers. Her mother sent her to live with Vernon in Nashville, where he was strict but encouraging and made education a priority. Winfrey became an honors student, was voted Most Popular Girl, and placed second nationally in dramatic interpretation. In 1986, she said, "When my father took me, it changed the course of my life. He saved me. He simply knew what he wanted and expected. He would take nothing less." Her first job was at a local grocery store. At 17, she won the Miss Black Tennessee pageant and gained attention from WVOL, a local black radio station, which hired her for part-time news work during high school and her first two years of college. She won an oratory contest, securing a full scholarship to Tennessee State University, a historically black institution, where she studied communication. She did not deliver her final paper until 1987, by which time she was a successful television personality, and only then earned her degree. Her grandmother once said that ever since Winfrey could talk, she was on stage, and she played games interviewing her corncob doll and crows. Winfrey acknowledged her grandmother’s influence, saying she encouraged her to speak in public and gave her a positive sense of self. Winfrey worked at WLAC-TV in Nashville as the youngest news anchor and the first black female news anchor, covering stories alongside John Tesh. In 1976, she moved to Baltimore’s WJZ-TV to co-anchor the six o’clock news, but was removed from that role and later joined Richard Sher as co-host of People Are Talking, which premiered on August 14, 1978. She also hosted Dialing for Dollars. In 1984, she moved to Chicago to host WLS-TV’s low-rated morning talk show, AM Chicago, which aired on January 2, 1984. Within months, the show rose from last place to overtaking Donahue as the highest-rated in Chicago. Roger Ebert persuaded her to sign a syndication deal with King World, predicting she would generate 40 times as much revenue as his show, At the Movies. The show was renamed The Oprah Winfrey Show and expanded to a full hour, with its first national broadcast on September 8, 1986. The syndicated show brought in double Donahue’s national audience, displacing him as the number-one daytime talk show in America. Time magazine noted that despite lacking journalistic toughness, Winfrey excelled in empathy, often making guests reveal personal stories they would not share with a national audience, likening the show to a group therapy session. Howard Rosenberg described her as "roundhouse, a full course meal, big, brassy, loud, aggressive, hyper, laughable, lovable, soulful, tender, low-down, earthy, and hungry," and said she may know Donahue’s jugular. Les Payne observed she was sharper, wittier, more genuine, and better attuned to her audience than Donahue, while Martha Bayles called her a relief for having cultural and religious roots. In the early years, the show was classified as a tabloid talk show. In the mid-1990s, Winfrey shifted focus to broader topics such as heart disease, geopolitics, spirituality, and meditation, interviewing celebrities on social issues like cancer, charity, and substance abuse, and hosting giveaways. Later, the show faced criticism for promoting junk science, particularly regarding guests like Jenny McCarthy’s unfounded claims about vaccines and Suzanne Somers’s promotion of bioidenticals. In addition to her talk show, Winfrey moderated three ABC Afterschool Specials from 1992 to 1994 and produced and co-starred in The Women of Brewster Place (1989) and its spin-off, Brewster Place. She co-founded Oxygen, the initial network for her Oprah After the Show program from 2002 to 2006, before moving to Oprah.com when she sold her stake. She is also president of Harpo Productions (Oprah spelled backwards), a production company behind The Oprah Winfrey Show, Dr. Phil, Rachael Ray, and The Dr. Oz Show. Dr. Phil has been criticized as simplistic or harmful, with the National Alliance on Mental Illness calling his conduct "unethical" and "incredibly irresponsible." Dr. Oz has been criticized by medical publications for spreading pseudoscience, including promoting "miracle pills" for weight loss. Science-Based Medicine stated no other TV show offers as much bad health advice as The Dr. Oz Show, all while appearing credible. Multiple publications have urged Winfrey to denounce medical statements made by former guests long after their shows ended, including calls to denounce Dr. Oz in 2020 over his coronavirus comments and promotion of a poorly vetted drug as a cure. On January 15, 2008, Winfrey and Discovery Communications announced plans to rebrand Discovery Health into the Oprah Winfrey Network (OWN), which was scheduled to launch in 2009 but delayed and officially launched on January 1, 2011. The final episode of The Oprah Winfrey Show aired on May 25, 2011. In January 2017, CBS announced Winfrey would join 60 Minutes as a special contributor starting in September 2017, and she left by the end of 2018. In June 2018, Apple announced a multi-year content partnership with Winfrey to create original programs for Apple TV+. The first show, Oprah's Book Club, premiered on November 1, 2019, based on a segment from her talk show. The second, Oprah Talks COVID-19, debuted on March 21, 2020, during the pandemic. A third show, The Oprah Conversation, premiered on July 30, 2020, to explore impactful topics with global thought leaders. In 1993, Winfrey hosted a prime-time interview with Michael Jackson titled Michael Jackson Talks ... to Oprah, which became the fourth most-watched event in American television history with 36.5 million viewers and the most-watched interview ever. On December 1, 2005, she appeared on The Late Show with David Letterman for the first time in 16 years to promote The Color Purple, which she produced. The episode was hailed as a "television event of the decade" and drew 13.45 million viewers, the largest audience in Letterman’s 11-year span. Although rumors of a feud were reported, both Winfrey and Letterman denied it, with Winfrey stating, "It's really over, whatever you thought was happening." On September 10, 2007, Letterman made his first appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show, as the season premiere was filmed in New York City. In 2006, rappers Ludacris, 50 Cent, and Ice Cube criticized Winfrey for what they saw as anti-hip hop bias. Ludacris said she gave him a hard time about his lyrics, edited comments during an appearance with the Crash cast, and did not initially invite him. Winfrey responded that she opposes rap lyrics that marginalize women but enjoys artists like Kanye West, and said she spoke with Ludacris backstage to explain her position, understanding his music was for entertainment but that some listeners might take it literally.

Both Winfrey and Letterman rejected discussions about a potential collaboration, with Winfrey stating, "I want you to know, it's really over, whatever you thought was happening." On September 10, 2007, Letterman made his first appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show, which was filmed in New York City. In 2006, rappers Ludacris, 50 Cent, and Ice Cube criticized Winfrey for what they saw as anti-hip hop bias; Ludacris claimed she gave him a hard time about his lyrics and edited comments he made during an appearance with the cast of Crash, and that he wasn't initially invited on the show. Winfrey responded by saying she opposes rap lyrics that "marginalize women" but enjoys artists like Kanye West, and that she spoke with Ludacris backstage to explain her position, acknowledging his music was for entertainment but noting some listeners might take it literally. In September 2008, Matt Drudge reported that Winfrey refused to have Sarah Palin on her show due to her support for Barack Obama; Winfrey denied the report, stating she had no discussion about Palin and that after publicly supporting Obama, she decided not to use her show as a platform for any candidates, though Obama appeared twice prior to his candidacy. She later said Palin would be a fantastic guest and did invite her on November 18, 2009. In 2009, Winfrey faced criticism for allowing actress Suzanne Somers to discuss hormone treatments not accepted by mainstream medicine, and critics suggested she is not tough enough when questioning guests she likes; Lisa de Moraes of The Washington Post noted that Oprah only asks follow-up questions of authors who have embarrassed her with fabricated memoirs, referencing James Frey's A Million Little Pieces. In 2021, Winfrey conducted a global interview with Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Prince Harry, which received international media attention. In 2024, ABC aired "AI and the Future of Us: An Oprah Winfrey Special," a one-hour show exploring artificial intelligence's impact on daily life, featuring interviews with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Bill Gates. Winfrey co-starred in Steven Spielberg's The Color Purple (1985) as Sofia, earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress; the Alice Walker novel later became a Broadway musical opening in late 2005 with Winfrey credited as a producer. In October 1998, Winfrey produced and starred in Beloved, based on Toni Morrison's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel; to prepare for her role as Sethe, she underwent a 24-hour simulation of slavery involving being tied up, blindfolded, and left alone in the woods. Despite major advertising and moderate to good reviews, the film opened to poor box-office results, losing approximately $30 million. Co-star Thandiwe Newton described Winfrey as "a very strong technical actress and it's because she's so smart. She's acute. She's got a mind like a razor blade." Harpo Films released a made-for-television film adaptation of Zora Neale Hurston's 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God in 2005, based on a teleplay by Suzan-Lori Parks and starring Halle Berry. In late 2008, Harpo Films signed an exclusive output pact with HBO to develop and produce scripted series, documentaries, and movies. In 2013, Winfrey starred in The Butler directed by Lee Daniels, which garnered significant Oscar buzz but did not result in a nomination. Winfrey voiced Gussie the goose in Charlotte's Web (2006) and Judge Bumbleton in Bee Movie (2007), co-starring Jerry Seinfeld and Renée Zellweger; in 2009, she voiced Eudora, the mother of Princess Tiana, in Disney's The Princess and the Frog, and in 2010 narrated the US version of the BBC nature program Life for Discovery.
