In 2018, she starred as Mrs. Which in the film adaptation of Madeleine L'Engle's A Wrinkle in Time and lent her voice to an animated virtual-reality short film written and directed by Eric Darnell, starring John Legend, titled Crow: The Legend, telling a Native American origin tale. Winfrey has co-authored five books; when her 2005 weight-loss book with Bob Greene was announced, it was reported that her undisclosed advance broke the world record for the highest book advance, previously held by Bill Clinton's autobiography. In 2015, her memoir The Life You Want was announced following a tour of the same name, scheduled for publication in 2017, but was "indefinitely postponed" in 2016. Winfrey publishes Oprah Daily and from 2004 to 2008 also published O At Home; in 2002, Fortune called O, the Oprah Magazine the most successful start-up in the industry; although circulation declined by over 10 percent to 2.4 million from 2005 to 2008, the January 2009 issue was the best-selling since 2006; the magazine's audience is more upscale than her TV show, with average readers earning above the U.S. median for women. In July 2020, it was announced that O Magazine would end regular print publications after the December 2020 issue; in that issue, Winfrey thanked readers and acknowledged it was the magazine's "final monthly print edition." Winfrey's company created Oprah.com, which averages over 70 million page views and more than six million users per month, receiving about 20,000 emails weekly; she initiated "Oprah's Child Predator Watch List" through her show and website, leading to the capture of two men within 48 hours. On February 9, 2006, Winfrey signed a three-year, $55-million contract with XM Satellite Radio to launch Oprah Radio, featuring contributors like Nate Berkus, Dr. Mehmet Oz, Bob Greene, Dr. Robin Smith, and Marianne Williamson; Oprah & Friends began broadcasting at 11:00 a.m. ET on September 25, 2006, from a new studio in Chicago, airing 24 hours a day, seven days a week on XM Channel 156; the contract requires her to be on air 30 minutes a week, 39 weeks a year. Winfrey's extensive real-estate portfolio has drawn attention, with industry outlets calling her a "tycoon," and her investments estimated at approximately $127 million as of 2022. She first purchased a condominium in Chicago's Water Tower Place in 1985, then bought adjoining units in 1992, 1993, and 1994. In 1988, she bought a 164-acre property in Rolling Prairie, Indiana, including main and guest residences, orchard, and stables. In 1992, she purchased an 80-acre compound in Telluride, Colorado, which she sold around late 2000. In 1994, she bought an apartment at the Four Seasons Hotel Chicago. Between 1996 and 2000, she purchased five condos in Fisher Island, Florida. In 2000, through her Chicago-based LLC Overground Railroad, she purchased an estate in Greenwich, Connecticut for her friend Gayle King. In 2001, she sold all five Fisher Island condos and bought what became her "main home base," called "The Promised Land," a 42-acre estate with ocean and mountain views in Montecito, California, as of 2022. That year, she also purchased homes in Elmwood Park, Illinois, and Merrillville, Indiana for family and friends. In 2002, she bought her father's home in Franklin, Tennessee and a lakefront condo in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. In 2003, she listed her Rolling Prairie property and sold it in 2004. From 2003 to 2005, she acquired several properties totaling 163 acres in Kula and Hana, Hawaii, and a penthouse in Atlanta, Georgia. In 2005, she purchased a home in Douglasville, Georgia, which was gifted in 2011 to a family member. In 2006, she bought a co-op apartment along Lake Shore Drive in downtown Chicago, reportedly with plans to move permanently from her Water Tower Place unit; for unknown reasons, it remained unused until sold in 2012. In 2008, she sold her Atlanta penthouse and listed Gayle King's estate, then purchased a penthouse in midtown Manhattan through her second LLC, Sophie's Penthouse, which was later sold in 2012. In early 2014, she listed her Chicago duplex; later that year, she returned to Telluride to buy a 60-acre lot with plans to build, and a lawsuit by a retired nuclear physicist over trail access rights was dismissed due to lack of case law and other issues; the extent of the agreement remains undisclosed. In 2015, she purchased another property in Telluride, expanded her Montecito compound by 23 acres, and acquired another 44-acre dedicated crop and equestrian preserve; she also sold both of her downtown Chicago homes. In 2018, she obtained two adjoining parcels totaling 23 acres including the Madroneagle compound on Orcas Island, Washington, and sold her last Chicago-area home in Elmwood Park. In late 2019, she expanded her Montecito home-base to 70 contiguous acres by purchasing a four-acre complex from actor Jeff Bridges. In 2021, she sold her Orcas Island compound as she said she was too busy to use it and purchased another compound in Montecito further from her main base, flipping the latter in 2022 with split properties—one sold to her property manager and longtime personal trainer Bob Greene, the other to actress Jennifer Aniston. In 2023, Winfrey purchased 870 acres of land in Maui for $6.6 million. Winfrey's high school sweetheart Anthony Otey recalled an innocent courtship beginning in her senior year, during which he saved hundreds of love notes; she conducted herself with dignity and was a model student. The two spoke of marriage, but Otey claimed he always knew she was destined for a greater life than he could provide; she broke up with him on Valentine's Day of her senior year. In 1971, months after ending her relationship with Otey, Winfrey met William "Bubba" Taylor at Tennessee State University, whom CBS journalist George Mair described as her "first intense, to-die-for love affair"; Winfrey helped get Taylor a job at WVOL and "did everything to keep him, including literally begging him on her knees to stay with her." Taylor refused to leave Nashville when she moved to Baltimore to work at WJZ-TV in June 1976; Winfrey later recalled they shared a deep love and that she would never forget it. In the 1970s, Winfrey had a romantic relationship with John Tesh; biographer Kitty Kelley claims Tesh ended the relationship due to pressures of an interracial relationship. When WJZ-TV management criticized Winfrey for crying on air during tragedies and her hair falling out from a bad perm, she turned to reporter Lloyd Kramer for comfort; she later recalled Kramer was "the best," loved her even when bald, and was the most fun romance she ever had. According to Mair, when Kramer moved to NBC in New York, Winfrey had a love affair with a married man who had no intention of leaving his wife; she recalled being with him for four years, never living with him, and feeling powerless and depleted, eventually pleading on her knees; on September 8, 1981, she wrote a suicide note to best friend Gayle King instructing her to water her plants. Winfrey later said the suicide note was "much overplayed" and that she couldn't kill herself because she feared missing something good. She attributed her weight gain and history of abusive relationships to a deep need for approval and self-worth, saying she would accept cruel self-absorbed men's criticism because she didn't believe she deserved anything else, and that this was also how she cushioned against disapproval. Winfrey later confessed to smoking crack cocaine with a man she was romantically involved with during that era, explaining that she was addicted to the man, not the drug, and that she would have done anything for him. She was allegedly involved in a second drug-related relationship with Randolph Cook, who claimed they lived together for several months in 1985 and used drugs; in 1997, Cook sued Winfrey for $20 million over an alleged tell-all book about their relationship. In the mid-1980s, Winfrey briefly dated movie critic Roger Ebert, whom she credits with advising her to take her show into syndication. In 1985, before her Chicago talk show went national, Haitian filmmaker Reginald Chevalier claims he appeared in a look-alike segment and began a relationship with Winfrey involving romantic evenings, candlelit baths, and dinners with Michael Jordan and Danny Glover; Chevalier says Winfrey ended the relationship when she met Stedman Graham. Winfrey and her partner Stedman Graham have been together since 1986; they were engaged in November 1992, but the ceremony never took place. Winfrey's best friend since their early twenties is Gayle King, who was formerly the host of The Gayle King Show and is currently an editor of O, the Oprah Magazine; since 1997, when Winfrey played the therapist on an episode of the sitcom Ellen.

Oprah Winfrey has faced legal threats, with one individual suing her for $20 million, alleging she blocked the publication of a tell-all book about their alleged relationship. In the mid-1980s, Winfrey briefly dated movie critic Roger Ebert, whom she credits with advising her to take her talk show into syndication. In 1985, before her show went national, Haitian filmmaker Reginald Chevalier claims he appeared in a look-alike segment and began a romantic relationship with Winfrey, which included evenings at home, candlelit baths, and dinners with Michael Jordan and Danny Glover; he says Winfrey ended the relationship when she met Stedman Graham. Winfrey and Stedman Graham have been together since 1986 and were engaged in November 1992, though the ceremony never occurred. Winfrey's best friend since their early twenties is Gayle King, who previously hosted The Gayle King Show and is now an editor of O, the Oprah Magazine. Since 1997, when Winfrey played therapist in an episode of Ellen in which Ellen DeGeneres came out, the two have been the subject of persistent rumors they are gay; Winfrey acknowledges the cultural lack of definition for such a close female bond and states she is not ashamed of being gay. Winfrey has also maintained a long friendship with Maria Shriver, whom she met in Baltimore, and considers Maya Angelou, author of I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, her mentor and close friend, calling her "mother-sister-friend." In 1998, Winfrey hosted a week-long Caribbean cruise for Angelou and 150 guests to celebrate her 70th birthday and in 2008, threw her an extravagant 80th birthday celebration at Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. Raised in rural poverty by a mother dependent on government welfare in a poor urban neighborhood, Winfrey became a millionaire at age 32 when her show received national syndication. She negotiated ownership rights and founded her own production company. At age 41, her net worth was $340 million, making her the only African American on the Forbes 400; by 2000, her net worth reached $800 million, and she is believed to have been the richest African American of the 20th century. A course on her business acumen, "History 298: Oprah Winfrey, the Tycoon," is taught at the University of Illinois. In 2006, Winfrey was the highest-paid television entertainer in the U.S., earning an estimated $260 million—five times more than second-place music executive Simon Cowell—and by 2008, her yearly income had increased to $275 million. Forbes listed her as the world's only black billionaire from 2004 to 2006 and recognized her as the first black woman billionaire in 2003. As of 2014, her net worth exceeded $2.9 billion, and she overtook former eBay CEO Meg Whitman as the richest self-made woman in America. Winfrey was raised a Baptist and has spoken about her faith, stating she believes in a "God force" that lives within all people and that doubt is a signal to pause and reflect. She cites Acts 17:28 as her favorite Bible verse and attends The Potter's House, an Evangelical church in Dallas. After losing her infant child at age 14, Winfrey did not want more children, explaining in a 2017 Vanity Fair interview that she lacks the patience for babies, though she has patience for puppies. Winfrey has been called "arguably the world's most powerful woman" by CNN and TIME, "arguably the most influential woman in the world" by The American Spectator, and "one of the 100 people who most influenced the 20th Century" and "one of the most influential people" from 2004 to 2011 by TIME—being the only person to appear on the latter list ten times. At the end of the 20th century, Life named her the most influential woman and most influential black person of her generation, calling her "America's most powerful woman"; in 2007, USA Today ranked her the most influential woman and most influential black person of the previous quarter-century. Ladies' Home Journal ranked her number one among the most powerful women in America, and Senator Barack Obama said in 2007 she "may be the most influential woman in the country." In 1998, Winfrey became the first woman and first African American to top Entertainment Weekly's list of the 101 most powerful people in entertainment. Forbes named her the world's most powerful celebrity in 2005, 2007, 2008, 2010, and 2013. As chairman of Harpo Inc., she was named the most powerful woman in entertainment by The Hollywood Reporter in 2008. She has been listed as one of the world's 100 most powerful women by Forbes, ranking 14th in 2014 and 31st in 2023. In 2010, Life named her one of the 100 people who changed the world, alongside Jesus Christ, Elvis Presley, and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu—she was the only living woman on the list. Columnist Maureen Dowd called her the "top alpha female" in the country, stating she has more credibility than the president and that no other successful woman had to be publicly criticized to advance. Vanity Fair claimed Oprah has more cultural influence than any university president, politician, or religious leader except perhaps the Pope. Bill O'Reilly described her as a woman who rose from nothing to become the most powerful woman in the world, noting her loyal following, credibility, talent, and self-made success. In 2005, Winfrey was named the greatest woman in American history in a public poll as part of The Greatest American, ranking No. 9 overall. Polls on her popularity have been inconsistent: a November 2003 Gallup poll found 73% of Americans had a favorable view of her, which rose to 74% in January 2007 but dropped to 66% in October 2007 and to 55% in a December 2007 Fox News poll. Gallup consistently ranks her among the most admired women in the world, with her highest rating in 2007 when she was tied with Hillary Clinton for first place. In a 2010 New Statesman list, she was ranked 38th in "The World's 50 Most Influential Figures 2010." In 1989, she was inducted into the NAACP Image Award Hall of Fame. The Wall Street Journal coined the term "Oprahfication," referring to public confession as therapy. By sharing intimate details about her weight, love life, and sexual abuse and crying with guests, Winfrey is credited by Time with creating "rapport talk," distinct from Phil Donahue's "report talk," emphasizing the emotional connection between viewer and host. Observers have noted the "Oprahfication" of politics, including "Oprah-style debates," and Bill Clinton being described as "the man who brought Oprah-style psychobabble and misty confessions to politics." Newsweek stated that every time a politician shows emotion or a cable anchor "emotes," they are nodding to the cult of confession Oprah helped create. The November 1988 Ms. magazine noted that in a society where fat is taboo, Winfrey made it sexy, elegant, and nearly gorgeous through her wardrobe and sensuality. While Phil Donahue pioneered the tabloid talk show genre, Winfrey's warmth, intimacy, and personal confession popularized and transformed it. In the book Freaks Talk Back, Yale professor Joshua Gamson credits the genre with providing high-impact media visibility for LGBT people and making them more socially acceptable than any other 20th-century development. Michael Bronski wrote that before tabloid talk shows, LGBT people had almost no presence on television, and shows like Jerry Springer, Jenny Jones, Oprah, and Geraldo brought them into living rooms daily. Gamson believes these shows helped make alternative sexual identities more acceptable in mainstream society, contributing to increased gay visibility and declining suicide rates. In April 1997, Winfrey played therapist in "The Puppy Episode" on Ellen, where the character and real-life Ellen DeGeneres came out as a lesbian. The power of Winfrey's opinions and endorsements to influence public opinion—especially consumer behavior—has been dubbed "the Oprah Effect." This influence has been documented in book sales, beef markets, and election voting. In late 1996, Winfrey launched the Oprah's Book Club segment, which focused on new and classic books and brought obscure novels to prominence; when she selected East of Eden, it soared to the top of the charts. Being recognized by her often leads to a million additional book sales. In Reading with Oprah: The Book Club that Changed America (2005), Kathleen Rooney describes her as a serious American intellectual who used electronic media to promote reading and motivate millions of non-readers. When Jonathan Franzen's book was selected, he reportedly "cringed" and said such selections tend to be "schmaltzy." After James Frey's A Million Little Pieces was found to contain fabrications in 2006, Winfrey confronted him on her show over the breach of trust, and in 2009 apologized to Frey. During a 1996 show on mad cow disease with Howard Lyman, Winfrey said she was stopped from eating another burger; Texas cattlemen sued her and Lyman in early 1998 for "false defamation of perishable food" and "business disparagement," claiming their remarks caused cattle prices to fall and cost producers $11 million. Winfrey was represented by attorney Chip Babcock, and after a two-month trial in Amarillo, Texas, a jury found her and Lyman not liable. Her success in launching other talk shows such as Dr. Phil, The Dr. Oz Show, and Rachael Ray has also been cited as evidence of "The Oprah Effect." Matthew Baum and Angela Jamison conducted a study showing that politically unaware individuals who watch soft news shows like The Oprah Winfrey Show are 14% more likely to vote consistently than those who only watch hard news. Winfrey identifies as a political independent who says she "earned the right to think for myself and to vote for myself." She endorsed Barack Obama in the 2008 presidential election, making her first public endorsement on Larry King Live in September 2006. Two economists estimate her endorsement was worth over a million votes in the Democratic primary and that without it, Obama would have lost the nomination. She held a fundraiser for Obama at her Santa Barbara estate in September 2007 and joined him in rallies in Iowa, New Hampshire, and South Carolina in December 2007, with the Columbia event drawing nearly 30,000 attendees—the largest political event of 2007. An analysis by economists at the University of Maryland estimated her endorsement caused between 420,000 and 1.6 million votes for Obama in the Democratic primary, based on states excluding Texas, Michigan, North Dakota, Kansas, and Alaska, and that it contributed to the popular vote difference between Obama and Hillary Clinton. Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich said Winfrey's endorsement was so impactful he considered offering her his vacant Senate seat, calling her "the most instrumental person in electing Barack Obama president" with a voice "larger than all 100 senators combined." Winfrey responded by stating she was not interested in being a senator but did feel she could be one. The Topps trading card company honored her involvement in the campaign by featuring her on a card in a set commemorating Obama.

Oprah Winfrey drew a crowd of nearly 30,000 at a political event in 2007, the largest for any political event that year. An analysis by two economists at the University of Maryland, College Park estimated that Winfrey's endorsement was responsible for between 420,000 and 1,600,000 votes for Barack Obama in the Democratic primary, based on a sample of states excluding Texas, Michigan, North Dakota, Kansas, and Alaska. The results indicate that Winfrey's endorsement accounted for the difference in the popular vote between Obama and Hillary Clinton. Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich stated he considered offering Winfrey Obama's vacant Senate seat, calling her "the most instrumental person in electing Barack Obama president" and saying she had "a voice larger than all 100 senators combined." Winfrey responded that while she was not interested in running for Senate, she did feel she could be a senator. Topps trading card company featured Winfrey on a card in a set commemorating Obama's road to the White House. In April 2014, Winfrey spoke for over 20 minutes at a fundraiser in Arlington, Virginia, for Lavern Chatman, a Democratic primary candidate, despite reports that Chatman had been found liable in 2001 for defrauding hundreds of District of Columbia nursing-home employees of at least $1.4 million in owed wages. Winfrey endorsed Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election and referred to Donald Trump as a "demagogue." In 2018, she canvassed door-to-door for Georgia gubernatorial Democratic nominee Stacey Abrams and donated $500,000 to the March for Our Lives student demonstration advocating for gun control. Media speculation about Winfrey running for president, especially in the lead-up to the 2020 election, was noted, but she denied any plans, stating in 2018 that while it was "a humbling thing to have people think you can run the country," she "would not be able to do it. It's not a clean business. It would kill me." She suggested she would publicly endorse a candidate in the 2020 Democratic primaries but ultimately did not. She later campaigned for Joe Biden during the general election. In early 2018, Winfrey met with Mohammad bin Salman, the crown prince and de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia, during his visit to the United States. In the 2022 Pennsylvania Senate election, she endorsed Democrat John Fetterman over Republican Mehmet Oz, whose show she promoted. In the 2022 Maryland gubernatorial election, she endorsed Baltimore author Wes Moore in the Democratic primary and co-hosted a virtual fundraiser for him in June. She attended and spoke at Moore's gubernatorial inauguration on January 18, 2023. In 2022, Winfrey established OWN Your Vote, a nonpartisan group focused on voter registration and a get-out-the-vote campaign aimed at providing Black women with tools and resources to vote in the November election. The group's partners include Advancement Project, African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME), Color Of Change, Delta Sigma Theta sorority, The King Center, The Lawyers' Committee, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, National Action Network, National Bar Association, National Council of Negro Women, Sigma Gamma Rho, Southern Poverty Law Center, VoteRunLead, and Vote.org. On August 21, 2024, Winfrey endorsed Kamala Harris at the 2024 Democratic National Convention. In 2000, she received the Spingarn Medal from the NAACP. In 2002, Christianity Today published an article titled "The Church of O," concluding that Winfrey had become an influential spiritual leader, noting that since 1994, when she shifted to more edifying content, and 1998, when she launched "Change Your Life TV," her most significant role became that of a spiritual leader. The article described her as a "postmodern priestess—an icon of church-free spirituality" to her audience of over 22 million mostly female viewers. This sentiment was echoed by Marcia Z. Nelson in her book The Gospel According to Oprah. Since the mid-1990s, Winfrey's show has emphasized uplifting and inspirational topics, and some viewers say it has motivated them to perform acts of altruism, such as helping Congolese women and building an orphanage. A scientific study by psychological scientists at the University of Cambridge, University of Plymouth, and University of California found that watching an uplifting clip from The Oprah Winfrey Show caused subjects to become twice as helpful as those who watched a British comedy or nature documentary. In 1998, Winfrey began an ongoing conversation with Gary Zukav, a spiritual teacher, who appeared on her show 35 times. Winfrey keeps a copy of Zukav's The Seat of the Soul at her bedside, calling it one of her all-time favorites. On the premiere of her 13th season, Roseanne Barr told Winfrey "you're the African Mother Goddess of us all," which inspired enthusiasm from the studio audience. The animated series Futurama referenced her spiritual influence by suggesting "Oprahism" is a mainstream religion in 3000 AD. Twelve days after the September 11 attacks, New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani asked Winfrey to host a Prayer for America service at Yankee Stadium, attended by former President Bill Clinton and Senator Hillary Clinton. Leading up to the U.S.-led 2001 invasion of Afghanistan, less than a month after September 11, Winfrey aired a controversial show called "Islam 101," portraying Islam as a religion of peace and calling it "the most misunderstood of the three major religions." In 2002, George W. Bush invited Winfrey to join a U.S. delegation including adviser Karen Hughes and Condoleezza Rice to go to Afghanistan to celebrate the return of Afghan girls to school; the "Oprah strategy" aimed to portray the war on terror positively, but when Winfrey refused to participate, the trip was postponed. Leading up to the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, Winfrey's show faced criticism for allegedly having an anti-war bias. Ben Shapiro of Townhall.com wrote that Winfrey was a "dangerous political force" with "unpredictable and mercurial attitudes." In 2006, Winfrey recalled receiving intense hate mail, including "Go back to Africa" messages, after a show titled "Is War the Only Answer?" which she said led to accusations of being un-American. Filmmaker Michael Moore defended Winfrey for showing antiwar footage that other media avoided and begged her to run for president. A February 2003 series, in which Winfrey showed clips from people worldwide urging America not to go to war, was interrupted in several East Coast markets by network broadcasts of a press conference by President George W. Bush and Colin Powell summarizing the case for war. In 2007, Winfrey began endorsing the self-help program The Secret, which claims people can change their lives through positive thoughts or 'vibrations' that attract more positive outcomes. Peter Birkenhead of Salon argued this idea is pseudoscience and psychologically damaging, promoting a quick-fix material culture, and criticized Winfrey's promotion as irresponsible. In 2007, skeptic and magician James Randi accused Winfrey of being deliberately deceptive and uncritical in handling paranormal claims on her show. In 2008, Winfrey endorsed author and spiritual teacher Eckhart Tolle and his book A New Earth: Awakening to Your Life's Purpose, which sold several million extra copies after being selected for her book club. During a webinar promoting the book, Winfrey stated "God is a feeling experience and not a believing experience. If your religion is a believing experience [...] then that's not truly God." Christian radio host Frank Pastore criticized Winfrey's views, saying if she is a Christian, she is "an ignorant one because Christianity is incompatible with New Age thought." In 2008, Winfrey was named Person of the Year by PETA for using her fame to help the less fortunate, including animals, and for exposing cruelty in puppy mills and factory farms, and for promoting a cruelty-free vegan diet. In 2009, Winfrey filmed interviews in Denmark highlighting its citizens as the happiest people in the world. In 2010, Bill O'Reilly of Fox News criticized these shows for promoting a left-wing society. Following the launch of Super Soul Sunday and SuperSoul Sessions on Harpo Productions' SuperSoul TV in 2016, Winfrey selected 100 people for the SuperSoul 100 list of innovators and visionaries aligned on a mission to move humanity forward. On the use of the N-word, Winfrey said, "You cannot be my friend and use that word around me. ... I always think of the people who heard that as their last word as they were hanging from a tree." The viewership for The Oprah Winfrey Show peaked during the 1991–92 season at about 13.1 million daily viewers. By 2003, ratings declined to 7.4 million daily viewers. Ratings briefly rose to about 9 million in 2005 and then declined to around 7.3 million in 2008, though the show remained the highest-rated talk show. In 2008, the show was airing in 140 countries and reached an estimated 46 million people weekly in the U.S. According to Harris poll data, Winfrey was America's favorite television personality in 1998, 2000, 2002–06, and 2009, especially among women, Democrats, political moderates, Baby Boomers, Generation X, Southern Americans, and East Coast Americans. Outside the U.S., Winfrey became increasingly popular in the Arab world; in 2007, MBC 4, an Arab satellite channel, centered its programming around reruns of her show due to record female viewership in Saudi Arabia. In 2008, The New York Times reported that The Oprah Winfrey Show with Arabic subtitles aired twice each weekday on MBC 4. Winfrey's modest dress and attitude of triumph over adversity and abuse have caused some women in Saudi Arabia to idealize her. In 2004, Winfrey became the first Black person to rank among the 50 most generous Americans and remained in the top 50 until 2010. By 2012, she had given away about $400 million to educational causes. As of 2012, she had also given over 400 scholarships to Morehouse College in Atlanta, Georgia. Winfrey received the first Bob Hope Humanitarian Award at the 2002 Emmy Awards for services to television and film. To celebrate two decades on national TV and thank her employees, Winfrey took her staff and their families (1,065 people total) on vacation to Hawaii in summer 2006. In 2013, Winfrey donated $12 million to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom that same year. Winfrey purchased 2,130 acres of land in Maui and established a bed and breakfast for entertaining friends and a (unprofitable) organic farm dedicated to keeping the area unoccupied and growing native species to restore damaged watersheds. She distributed pillows, diapers, and other supplies to survivors of a devastating fire and, with Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson, set up the People’s Fund of Maui, personally donating $25 million. In 1998, Winfrey created Oprah's Angel Network, a charity that supported charitable projects and provided grants to nonprofit organizations worldwide. The network raised over $80 million ($1 million from Jon Bon Jovi), with Winfrey covering all administrative costs so 100% of funds went to charity programs. In May 2010, with the end of her show, the charity stopped accepting donations and was shut down. In 2004, Winfrey and her team filmed an episode titled "Oprah's Christmas Kindness" in South Africa, traveling to bring attention to children affected by poverty and AIDS. During a 21-day trip, Winfrey and her crew visited schools and orphanages, distributing Christmas presents to 50,000 children—dolls for girls and soccer balls for boys, along with school supplies. Throughout the show, Winfrey appealed to viewers to donate to Oprah's Angel Network for poor and AIDS-affected children in Africa. From that show alone, viewers donated over $7 million. Winfrey invested $40 million and some of her time to establish the Oprah Winfrey Leadership Academy for Girls in Henley on Klip, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. The school, spanning 22 acres, opened in January 2007 with 150 pupils (increasing to 450) and includes state-of-the-art classrooms, computer and science labs, a library, a theater, and a beauty salon. Nelson Mandela praised Winfrey for overcoming her own disadvantaged youth to become a benefactor. Critics viewed the school as elitist and unnecessarily luxurious. Winfrey rejected these claims, saying, "If you are surrounded by beautiful things and wonderful teachers who inspire you, that beauty brings out the beauty in you." Winfrey, who has no surviving biological children, described maternal feelings toward the girls at the academy. She teaches a class at the school via satellite.

doc_name: Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment
text: The Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment (OAE) is a British period instrument orchestra with its headquarters at Acland Burghley School. It is the resident orchestra at Southbank Centre and Glyndebourne Festival Opera, and serves as Artistic Associate at Kings Place. The leadership is rotated among four musicians: Matthew Truscott, Kati Debretzeni, Huw Daniel, and Margaret Faultless. Formed in 1986 as a self-governing ensemble by a group of period instrumentalists, the OAE takes its name from the late 18th century, the historical period that forms the core of its repertoire. The orchestra does not have a principal conductor and instead selects conductors individually. The current Principal Artists are Sir Simon Rattle, Vladimir Jurowski, Iván Fischer, John Butt, Sir Mark Elder, and András Schiff. William Christie is Emeritus Conductor, as are the late Frans Brüggen, Sir Roger Norrington, and Sir Charles Mackerras. Other conductors who have worked with the OAE include Marin Alsop, Anu Tali, Yannick Nézet-Séguin, Sian Edwards, Edward Gardner, Suzi Digby, Robin Ticciati, Joanna Tomlinson, Philippe Herreweghe, Gustav Leonhardt, René Jacobs, Harry Bicket, Christopher Hogwood, Sigiswald Kuijken, Ivor Bolton, Monica Huggett, and Bruno Weil. Sir Martin Smith played a key role in establishing the OAE, securing private funding for its founding and serving on the Board for many years, and is now Life President. The OAE's ethos is democratic, with players actively guiding the artistic direction and having the right to join regardless of whether they are asked to play. Responsibility for concert planning lies with the Players' Artistic Committee, elected annually by members and also sitting on the OAE Board of Directors. An early mission statement stated the orchestra aimed to "Avoid the dangers implicit in:" The OAE's first concerts, held in June 1986 at Oxford's Town Hall and London's Queen Elizabeth Hall, were conducted by Sigiswald Kuijken and featured Telemann's Overture Suite, Rameau's Suite from Dardanus, Gossec's symphony, and Haydn's Symphony No. 83. The founding leaders were Catherine Mackintosh, Elizabeth Wallfisch, Alison Bury, and Margaret Faultless. The OAE's recurring season at Southbank Centre includes concerts at the Queen Elizabeth Hall and Royal Festival Hall. In May 2006, the OAE launched "The Night Shift," a series of informal late-night concerts, which has twice been nominated for a Royal Philharmonic Society Award for audience development. The Night Shift, established in 2006, presents classical music in a relaxed setting with performances of concise length, the allowance of alcoholic drinks, and the ability to clap and talk freely. More than 80% of its audience is under 35, and about 20% are attending a classical concert for the first time. In 2007, the OAE celebrated its 21st anniversary with a concert at the Royal Festival Hall, conducted by Norrington, Elder, Mackerras, and Jurowski respectively. That year, it won the RPS Ensemble award for its broad repertoire, advocacy of original instruments, pioneering education initiatives, and the artistry of its members. In July 2008, the OAE moved its headquarters to Kings Place in London, sharing office space with the London Sinfonietta. On 29 January 2010, The Night Shift made its first appearance at The Roundhouse in Camden. In August 2010, the OAE performed at the Royal Albert Hall during the BBC Proms, conducting Wagner's Tristan und Isolde (Act 2) and the Love Scene from Romeo and Juliet by Berlioz, with soloists Sarah Connolly, Ben Heppner, and Violeta Urmana. In September 2020, the OAE, led by Jonathan Cohen and featuring Nicola Benedetti, Rodolfo Richter, and Matthew Truscott, performed at the Royal Albert Hall during the BBC Proms, playing Vivaldi's Concerto in D major for two violins, Concerto in D minor for two violins, Concerto in A minor for two oboes, Handel's Concerto grosso in B flat major and Passacaglia from Radamisto, Charles Avison's Concerto grosso no. 5 in D minor, and Bach's Concerto in D minor for two violins. In September 2020, the OAE moved its headquarters to Acland Burghley Secondary School in Tufnell Park, Camden, where the administrative office, library, and recording studio are located on campus, and musicians use the school's Grade II listed assembly hall for rehearsals, workshops, and small performances. The partnership, initially underwritten by £120,000 from the Sainsbury family's Linbury Trust for three years, allows Burghley pupils to attend rehearsals and collaborate on artistic projects, such as exploring Rameau's music with the school's dance students. The OAE believes this presence will be transformational, improving academic performance, language skills, engagement with music, and even enhancing the orchestra's own playing, a model inspired by the Deutsche Kammerphilharmonie's project in Bremen, Germany. The OAE has toured extensively, including South America and the US in 2002 and South East Asia in autumn 2003. Its discography includes over fifty recordings from Henry Purcell to Verdi, featuring guest artists such as Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, Renée Fleming, Susan Graham, Andreas Scholl, Ian Bostridge, Elizabeth Wallfisch, Emanuel Ax, Thomas Hampson, Cecilia Bartoli, Gerald Finley, Bob van Asperen, Anner Bylsma, Viktoria Mullova, and Michael Chance. The OAE is highly active in school engagement, especially in the area around Kings Place, offering concerts, leading youth projects, and teaching children to play instruments. In the spring/summer of 2010, it ran a series of three concerts inspired by Monteverdi's Vespers for schools. The Ann and Peter Law OAE Experience is an apprenticeship scheme for young period instrumentalists, established in 2002 and the only such scheme with a period orchestra. It is consistently over-subscribed and offers participants mentorship from OAE musicians, rehearsal opportunities with guest conductors, performances with the OAE, and sometimes concerts as an ensemble.

Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease caused by the breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone, and it is considered the most common form of arthritis, affecting approximately 237 million people or 3.3% of the global population as of 2015. It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide, with an estimated 240 million people experiencing activity-limiting symptoms. The primary symptoms are joint pain and stiffness, which typically progress slowly over years and are worsened by prolonged activity and relieved by rest; morning stiffness usually lasts less than thirty minutes but may return after periods of inactivity. Other symptoms include joint swelling, decreased range of motion, and, when involving the back, weakness or numbness in the arms and legs. The most commonly affected joints are the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers, the base of the thumbs, the knees, hips, neck, and lower back. In smaller joints, Heberden's nodes (on the distal interphalangeal joints) and Bouchard's nodes (on the proximal interphalangeal joints) may form, limiting finger movement, and osteoarthritis of the toes can contribute to bunion development. The condition affects the joints without involving internal organs. Possible causes include prior joint injury, abnormal joint or limb development, inherited factors, mechanical stress on joints, and low-grade inflammatory processes. Risk factors include being overweight, having legs of different lengths, jobs involving high joint stress (such as manual handling, kneeling, squatting, or standing), and a history of joint injury or family history of the disease. Obesity increases the risk of hip and knee osteoarthritis, with those who are obese having twice the risk of developing it. Women, especially post-menopausal women, are more likely to develop osteoarthritis and tend to have more severe symptoms and imaging findings than men, though differences between African Americans and Caucasians remain conflicting. Osteoarthritis is more common in people over 60, with about 10% of males and 18% of females affected. It accounts for about 2% of years lived with disability, and individuals with hip or knee osteoarthritis have a 20% increased risk of mortality, possibly due to reduced activity. Early changes involve a disorganized collagen matrix and reduced proteoglycan content, leading to increased water content in cartilage, while ligaments become thickened, menisci are damaged, and new bone outgrowths (osteophytes) form. Subchondral bone becomes more dense and less mineralized, and inflammation in the joint lining involves macrophages rather than T-cells. Diagnosis is based on clinical signs and symptoms, with X-rays showing joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes, and the combination of joint pain and osteophytes on imaging has good sensitivity and specificity. In 1990, the American College of Rheumatology established criteria for hand osteoarthritis with 92% sensitivity and 98% specificity. Treatment primarily includes lifestyle modifications such as weight loss and exercise, along with pain medications like paracetamol (acetaminophen) and NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen, ibuprofen), which are first-line options. Topical NSAIDs (e.g., diclofenac) may provide relief, though recessed joints respond less well. COX-2 inhibitors are equally effective as nonselective NSAIDs but carry higher cardiovascular risks and are more expensive; rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004 due to cardiovascular events. Acetaminophen has only a small short-term benefit and may affect liver function, while NSAIDs are more effective for severe pain but carry greater gastrointestinal risks. Opioids are not recommended due to limited benefit and significant risks of addiction and side effects, and their use is reserved for cases where first-line treatments fail. Oral steroids and doxycycline are not recommended. Intra-articular injections of steroids, hyaluronic acid, or platelet-rich plasma may offer short-term pain relief in knee osteoarthritis. Joint injections may be more effective and safer due to increased bioavailability and reduced systemic exposure. Therapeutic exercise, such as walking or swimming, is recommended at least three times per week, under supervision, to reduce pain and improve function, with supervised programs showing the best results for knee osteoarthritis. High-impact exercise increases joint injury risk, while low-impact activities are safer. Functional, gait, and balance training are recommended for lower extremity arthritis to reduce fall risk. For hand osteoarthritis, exercises may offer small benefits in hand function and stiffness. Weak knee extensor muscles may increase the risk of knee osteoarthritis, and strengthening them could prevent it. Lateral wedge insoles and neutral insoles are not helpful, and knee braces have disputed benefits. Heat can relieve stiffness, cold can reduce muscle spasms, and ice massage may improve range of motion, though evidence for pain relief is limited. Hot packs do not reduce swelling, and there is no strong evidence for benefit from hot packs. Education improves self-management and can lead to about 20% more pain relief than NSAIDs alone. If pain relief is not achieved after two weeks, treatment should be reassessed. Remote peer mentorship may help improve self-management in people with socioeconomic disadvantage. Weight loss and exercise are the most safe and effective long-term treatments, with benefits lasting up to six months after a program ends. There is insufficient evidence for massage therapy or manual therapy, and aquatic therapy is safe and effective as an adjunct for knee osteoarthritis, reducing pain and disability in the short term. Medications that alter the disease course have not been found as of 2025. More than 90% of hip and knee joint replacements are due to osteoarthritis, and artificial joints typically last over 20 years.

Several NSAIDs are available for topical use, including diclofenac, which may provide symptomatic relief for osteoarthritis; however, recessed joints, such as the hips, may respond less well to topical therapies. Transdermal opioid pain medications are not typically recommended for osteoarthritis treatment. Topical capsaicin use for osteoarthritis is controversial, as some reviews report benefit while others find no benefit. Intra-articular injections of steroids, hyaluronic acid, or platelet-rich plasma (PRP) may be used for pain relief in knee osteoarthritis. Local drug delivery via intra-articular injection may offer greater effectiveness and safety due to increased bioavailability, less systemic exposure, and reduced adverse events. Several such medications are available. Glucocorticoid injections, such as hydrocortisone, provide short-term pain relief lasting a few weeks to a few months. A 2015 Cochrane review found that knee corticosteroid injections did not improve quality of life or knee joint space, and clinical effects one to six weeks after injection could not be clearly determined due to poor study quality. Higher-dose injections were associated with negative effects in one 2015 study, and a 2017 trial showed reduced cartilage thickness with triamcinolone injections every 12 weeks for two years compared to placebo. A 2018 study linked intra-articular triamcinolone to increased intraocular pressure. High-quality studies on hyaluronic acid injections for hip and knee osteoarthritis only show minor benefit; in other studies, hyaluronic acid injections did not improve knee arthritis compared to placebo and were associated with an increased risk of further pain. Evidence for hyaluronic acid in ankle osteoarthritis is unclear. PRP injections have unclear effectiveness; some suggest they improve function but not pain and are associated with increased risk. A 2014 Cochrane review found the evidence for PRP to be insufficient. Low-dose radiotherapy improves pain and mobility in affected joints, particularly in extremities, with approximately 70–90% effectiveness and minimal side effects. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of sensory knee nerves—also known as genicular neurotomy or genicular RFA—is an outpatient procedure used to reduce knee osteoarthritis pain. During the procedure, a guide cannula is directed under local anesthesia and imaging (ultrasound or fluoroscopy) to each target genicular nerve, and a radiofrequency electrode is passed through it, heating the tip to about 80 °C (176 °F) for one minute to cauterize a segment of the nerve, thereby blocking pain signals. As of 2023, reviews indicate that ablating three or more genicular nerve branches reduces knee pain, with some sources suggesting 4–5 targets may be justified and a 2022 analysis indicating up to 10 targets could provide better long-term pain relief. Pain relief of 50% or more following genicular RFA may last from several months to two years and can be repeated through the same outpatient procedure when pain returns. Phenol injection may be used as a neurolytic treatment to relieve chronic knee osteoarthritis pain. Arthrodesis (joint fusion) may be considered in severe cases of ankle osteoarthritis unresponsive to other treatments. If osteoarthritis symptoms significantly impact quality of life and conservative management fails, joint replacement surgery is an option; evidence supports its use for both knees and hips as clinically effective and cost-effective. People who underwent total knee replacement reported improved quality of life and better pain and function compared to those who did not have surgery, with a less than 1% risk of death within 90 days and less than 5% risk of serious complications (such as prosthetic joint infections, blood clots, or dislocations) after hip or knee replacement. Ninety percent of hip replacement patients and 80% of knee replacement patients reported little or no arthritis-related pain after surgery. Less than 10% of artificial knees and less than 20% of artificial hips required revision over 20 years. Arthroscopic debridement of the knee, also known as joint resurfacing, is not recommended for knee osteoarthritis and has a limited role only in patients with a meniscal tear who have failed other treatments. For shoulder osteoarthritis unresponsive to medications, surgical options include shoulder hemiarthroplasty or total shoulder arthroplasty; demand for these procedures is expected to increase by 750% by 2030. However, there is a lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials to determine which surgical approach is most effective, the associated risks, or how it compares to other treatments. Low-quality evidence suggests no significant short-term clinical benefit when comparing total shoulder arthroplasty to hemiarthroplasty, and it is unclear whether the risk of harm differs between the two. Osteotomy may be useful in knee osteoarthritis but has not been well studied and its effectiveness relative to non-surgical treatments or other surgeries is unclear. Arthroscopic surgery is not recommended for knee osteoarthritis as it does not improve outcomes and may cause harm; its benefit in mild to moderate cases is unclear. Glucosamine’s effectiveness is controversial; reviews show it is equal to or slightly better than placebo, with possible differences between glucosamine sulfate (which shows benefit) and glucosamine hydrochloride (which does not). Evidence for glucosamine sulfate affecting disease progression is unclear and likely modest. The Osteoarthritis Research Society International recommends discontinuing glucosamine if no effect is seen after six months, and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence no longer recommends its use. Despite uncertainty, glucosamine remains a treatment option. The European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis recommends glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate for knee osteoarthritis. Its use is generally safe. A 2015 Cochrane review of chondroitin found most trials were of low quality, but some evidence of short-term pain improvement with few side effects; it does not appear to improve or maintain joint health. Avocado–soybean unsaponifiables (ASU), an extract from avocado and soybean oils sold as a dietary supplement or prescription drug in France, may provide short-term pain relief in some osteoarthritis patients, but does not improve or maintain joint health. A two-year high-quality trial comparing ASU to chondroitin found no difference between them, and there is insufficient evidence on ASU safety. Only a few moderate-quality studies of Boswellia serrata show small improvements in pain and function. Curcumin and s-adenosyl methionine (SAMe) show little effect on pain; a 2009 Cochrane review recommended against routine SAMe use due to insufficient high-quality research. A 2021 review found hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) had no benefit in reducing pain or improving physical function in hand or knee osteoarthritis, and its off-label use should be discouraged. There is no evidence for colchicine in treating hand or knee arthritis pain. Limited evidence supports the use of hyaluronan, methylsulfonylmethane, rose hip, capsaicin, or vitamin D. Acupuncture provides small pain relief, which may be of questionable importance, and waiting list–controlled trials show clinically relevant benefits possibly due to placebo effects; long-term benefits are not established. TENS and low-level laser therapy have no conclusive evidence of reducing pain or disability; one review found unclear benefit, while another found short-term pain relief for osteoarthritic knees. Research is needed to determine if balneotherapy improves quality of life or function. Low-quality evidence suggests therapeutic ultrasound may be beneficial for knee osteoarthritis, though further research is needed; it is safe, reduces pain, and improves physical function, while phonophoresis may offer greater pain relief than standard non-drug ultrasound. Weak evidence suggests electromagnetic field treatment may provide moderate pain relief, but further research is needed to determine if it improves quality of life or function. Globally, as of 2010, approximately 250 million people had knee osteoarthritis (3.6% of the population), and hip osteoarthritis affected about 0.85% of the population. In 2004, osteoarthritis caused moderate to severe disability in 43.4 million people, ranking as the 11th most disabling condition globally among 291 diseases. In the Middle East and North Africa, hip osteoarthritis prevalence increased three-fold (from 1.28 million to 1.28 million cases) from 1990 to 2019, and knee osteoarthritis increased 2.88-fold (from 6.16 million to 17.75 million cases). Hand osteoarthritis in MENA increased 2.7-fold (from 1.6 million to 4.3 million cases). As of 2012, osteoarthritis affected 52.5 million people in the United States, about 50% of whom were 65 years or older; 80% of the population have radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis by age 65, though only 60% experience symptoms. The U.S. rate is projected to reach 78 million (26%) adults by 2040. In 2011, there were approximately 964,000 hospitalizations for osteoarthritis, at a rate of 31 stays per 10,000 population, with an aggregate cost of $14.8 billion ($15,400 per stay), making it the second-most expensive condition in U.S. hospital stays and the second-most costly billed to Medicare and private insurance. In Europe, osteoarthritis prevalence increased from 27.9 million in 1990 to 50.8 million in 2019; hand osteoarthritis was the second most prevalent type, affecting 12.5 million people. In 2019, knee osteoarthritis was the 18th most common cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) in Europe, accounting for 1.28% of all YLDs (up from 1.12% in 1990). In India, osteoarthritis increased from 23.46 million in 1990 to 62.35 million in 2019; knee osteoarthritis was the most prevalent type, followed by hand osteoarthritis. In 2019, osteoarthritis was the 20th most common cause of YLDs in India (1.48% of all YLDs), up from 1.25% and previously the 23rd most common cause. Osteoarthritis comes from the Greek "ostéon" (bone) and "arthritis" (joint inflammation), though inflammation is not a prominent feature; some clinicians use "osteoarthrosis" to emphasize the non-inflammatory nature. The condition has been reported in various animals, including cats, rodents, cattle, deer, rabbits, sheep, camels, elephants, buffalo, hyenas, lions, mules, pigs, tigers, kangaroos, dolphins, dugongs, and horses, and in fossils of the dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis. Disease-modifying therapies aim to alter disease progression by arresting structural joint changes and ameliorating symptoms. Emerging evidence suggests a system-based approach is needed to identify osteoarthritis causes. A University of Twente study found that osmolarity-induced intracellular molecular crowding may drive disease pathology. Guidelines for including soluble biomarkers in osteoarthritis clinical trials were published in 2015, but as of 2021, no validated biomarkers are used clinically. A 2015 systematic review identified 37 biochemical markers of bone and cartilage turnover.

Osteoarthritis has been observed in the fossils of the large carnivorous dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis. Pharmaceutical agents that modify the natural course of the disease by halting joint structural deterioration and relieving symptoms are referred to as disease-modifying therapies. Current therapies under investigation include various agents aimed at altering disease progression. There is growing evidence that a system-based approach is required to identify the underlying causes of osteoarthritis; a study by scientists at the University of Twente suggested that osmolarity-induced intracellular molecular crowding may contribute to disease pathology. Guidelines for including soluble biomarkers in osteoarthritis clinical trials were published in 2015, but as of 2021, no validated biomarkers are used clinically to diagnose osteoarthritis. A 2015 systematic review of biomarkers for osteoarthritis, analyzing 25 publications, identified 37 different biochemical markers of bone and cartilage turnover. The strongest evidence supported urinary C-terminal telopeptide of type II collagen (uCTX-II) as a prognostic marker for knee osteoarthritis progression and serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) levels as a prognostic marker for both knee and hip osteoarthritis incidence. A review of biomarkers in hip osteoarthritis also noted associations with uCTX-II. Procollagen type II C-terminal propeptide (PIICP) levels indicate type II collagen synthesis in the body and within joint fluid, and PIICP levels can serve as a prognostic marker for early osteoarthritis.

Otto Georg Thierack (19 April 1889 – 26 October 1946) was a German Nazi jurist and politician. Born in Wurzen in Saxony, he served in the First World War from 1914 to 1918 as a volunteer, reaching the rank of lieutenant, and suffered a facial injury; he was awarded the Iron Cross, second class. After the war, he resumed his law studies and completed them in 1920 with his Assessor (junior lawyer) examination. That same year, he was hired as a court Assessor in Saxony. On 1 August 1932, Thierack joined the Nazi Party. Following the Nazis' seizure of power in 1933, he rapidly advanced from prosecutor to President of the People's Court (Volksgerichtshof), a rise facilitated not only by his Nazi Party membership but also by his leadership of the National Socialist jurists' organization, the Rechtswahrerbund. Appointed Saxony's justice minister on 12 May 1933, Thierack was tasked with "nazifying" the region's judicial administration. After holding several mid-level judicial positions, he became vice president of the Reich Court in 1935 and, in May 1936, president of the Volksgerichtshof, which had been established in 1934. He held this position until August 1942, when he was succeeded by Roland Freisler, despite two interruptions due to service in the armed forces. On 20 August 1942, he succeeded Hans Frank as President of the Academy for German Law. On the same date, he became Reich Minister of Justice. In October 1942, he introduced the monthly Richterbriefe, which provided model judicial decisions from the Nazi perspective, with names omitted, to guide German jurisprudence. He also introduced the Vorschauen and Nachschauen ("previews" and "inspections"), requiring higher state court presidents, in cases of public interest, to discuss with the public prosecutor's office and the State Court president—whom they had to forward to responsible criminal courts—how a case would be judged before a final decision. Upon becoming Reich Minister of Justice in August 1942, Thierack streamlined the lengthy clemency procedures for death sentences. In September 1942, he classified all prisoners who were "Jews, Gypsies, Russians, Poles sentenced to over three years, Czechs, or Germans serving a sentence of over eight years" as "asocial elements" and transferred them to Reichsführer-SS Heinrich Himmler for forced labor to death. At Thierack's initiative, the execution shed at Plötzensee Prison in Berlin was equipped with eight iron hooks in December 1942 to enable the simultaneous hanging of multiple individuals (a guillotine had already existed there). Mass executions began on 7 September 1943, though some prisoners were hanged by mistake; Thierack dismissed these as errors and insisted that the hangings continue. Thierack was named to continue as Minister of Justice in Hitler's political testament. He served in the brief Goebbels cabinet but was dismissed on 5 May 1945 by Hitler's successor, Reichspräsident Karl Dönitz. After the end of World War II, the Allies arrested Thierack. Before being tried at the Nuremberg Judges' Trial, he committed suicide in Sennelager, Paderborn, by poisoning himself.

Outlaw Run is a wooden roller coaster located at Silver Dollar City in Branson, Missouri, designed by Alan Schilke and manufactured by Rocky Mountain Construction (RMC), making it RMC's first wooden roller coaster. It became the first wooden roller coaster to feature multiple inversions and has a 162-foot (49 m) drop at an 81-degree angle, which is the fourth steepest and fourth tallest among wooden roller coasters. The ride reaches a maximum speed of 68 mph (109 km/h), placing it as the sixth-fastest wooden coaster in the world, and it includes three inversions, one of which is a double heartline roll. Outlaw Run is tied with Wildfire at Kolmården Wildlife Park, also built by RMC, for the most inversions on a wooden coaster. Development of the concept began in 2009, with planning for a new 2013 attraction initiated by Herschend Family Entertainment, who sought a "world first" ride with marketing appeal, including a double barrel roll. Joel Manby, CEO of Herschend, wanted a wooden coaster with a unique element, and after Rocky Mountain Construction demonstrated their steel coaster, New Texas Giant, in 2011, the contract was secured. Marketing began in 2011 at the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions trade show, with a teaser website launched during construction that revealed a Western stagecoach theme and an announcement date of August 9, 2012. On that date, Silver Dollar City officially announced Outlaw Run would open in the second quarter of 2013. The ride opened to a limited audience on March 13, 2013, with a public opening two days later, and official celebrations occurred in April. At a cost of $10 million, it was the most expensive attraction at Silver Dollar City in over a decade. The 2,937-foot-long (895 m) ride uses laminated wood with a steel plate called Topper Track in the upper layers, a technology developed by RMC to reduce maintenance and improve ride smoothness. The track features twisted wooden beams developed over four years, enabling dynamic elements. Each train holds twelve pairs of riders, with riders needing to be at least 48 inches (122 cm) tall and secured in fiberglass seats with a U-shaped lap bar; the ride uses steel wheels instead of polyurethane. The ride's theme centers on stagecoaches and the Wild West, with a storyline where outlaws attempt to rob stagecoaches, and the "good guys" always win. The ride begins with a chain lift hill, a small pre-drop, and a 162-foot (49 m) 81-degree drop, followed by an outside banked turn, a 100-foot (30 m) double down, a 70-foot (21 m) double up, a twist and turn, a wave turn, a high-speed float, and two heartline rolls before returning to the station. A single ride cycle takes about 1 minute and 27 seconds. Outlaw Run debuted with the steepest drop on any wooden roller coaster at the time, though it no longer claims to be the only wooden coaster with inversions due to the opening of Hades 360, which also features inversions. It is also the fifth-fastest wooden coaster in the world, with a top speed of 68 mph (109 km/h), though this record was later surpassed by Goliath at Six Flags Great America in 2014. Outlaw Run retains the record for the wooden roller coaster with the most inversions. The ride received favorable reviews, with Arthur Levine of About.com praising its layout, Brady MacDonald of the Los Angeles Times including it in his top 13 most anticipated 2013 attractions, and Marcus Leshock, Brandy McDonnell, and Tim Baldwin offering positive feedback. In its debut year, Outlaw Run won the Golden Ticket Award for Best New Ride with 45% of the vote and ranked as the seventh-best wooden roller coaster worldwide.

P-Model, an electronic rock band formed in 1979 by members of the defunct progressive rock band Mandrake, has undergone numerous lineup changes over the years but has always been led by frontman Susumu Hirasawa. The band officially disbanded in 2000, though many of its members continue to release solo albums and collaborate on various projects. Hirasawa has since released work under the name "Kaku P-Model" (核P-Model; lit. 'nucleus of P-Model'), effectively marking a solo revival of the band. All videos from the albums *Great Brain* to *Harm Harmonizer* were directed by Yuichi "You1" Hirasawa, Susumu's brother. The tracks "Fu-Ru-He-He-He," "2D or Not 2D," and "Grid" are included in *Bitmap 1979–1992*; "Monotone Grid" in *Photon-3*; "http" in *Rocket Shoot*; and "Logic Airforce" in *Live Video Music Industrial Wastes〜P-Model or Die*. P-Model and Susumu Hirasawa have been influential on both musicians and artists in other mediums, particularly within the manga and anime industries. Several of their collaborators, including six band members, began as major fans of their work: Berserk mangaka Kentaro Miura has stated that listening to Hirasawa's music has helped him refocus on the themes of his writing; anime director Satoshi Kon described Hirasawa's work as "a source of imagination and creativity for me" over the past 20 years; and film director Daihachi Yoshida considers Hirasawa the creator of "about half of my way of thinking." Musicians such as Fukusuke of Metronome, Hiroyuki Hayashi of Polysics, Daoko (whose song "Welcome to the Parade" from 2012's *HyperGirl: Mukōgawa no Onna no Ko* was directly influenced by Hirasawa's worldview), Toby Driver of Kayo Dot (who claims *Plastic House on Base of Sky* was an attempt to create his own version of Hirasawa's music), and Kenshi Yonezu (who said a Hirasawa song "changed [his] life") have cited P-Model or Hirasawa as influences. Other artists who have expressed admiration include Klaha of Malice Mizer, Ryoko Yamagishi of *Shiroi Heya no Futari*, Arika Takarano of Ali Project, Hiroyuki Kitakubo (director of *Roujin Z* and *JoJo's Bizarre Adventure*), Sumire Uesaka, Gen Hoshino, Kouta Hirano (mangaka of *Hellsing*), Koyoharu Gotouge (mangaka of *Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba*), Seiji Mizushima (director of *Fullmetal Alchemist* and *Concrete Revolutio*), Satoshi "hil" Ishikawa (composer of *Fate/stay night [Réalta Nua]* and *Taiko no Tatsujin*), and Ko Shibasaki. The five main characters of the *K-On!* franchise—Yui Hirasawa, Mio Akiyama, Ritsu Tainaka, Tsumugi Kotobuki, and Azusa Nakano—are in a band, share the surnames of late '80s P-Model members, and play their respective primary instruments (except Nakano). All active members referenced have acknowledged this connection. Additionally, P-Model references appear in the manga *The Sorrow of a Perfectly Healthy Girl* and *Opus*, as well as in the anime *Sailor Moon*, *Perfect Blue*, *BECK: Mongolian Chop Squad*, and *Space Dandy*. In theatre, musician/playwright Keralino Sandorovich (ja) named two of his stage plays—*Frozen Beach* and *Blue Cross*—after P-Model songs and one, *Haldyn Hotel*, after a Hirasawa solo song.

Pieter Willem Botha, DMS (locally /ˈbʊərtə/ BOOR-tə; Afrikaans pronunciation: [ˈpitər ˈvələm ˈbuəta]; 12 January 1916 – 31 October 2006), was a South African politician who served as the last Prime Minister of South Africa from 1978 to 1984 and as the first executive State President from 1984 until his resignation in 1989. Nicknamed 'Die Groot Krokodil' (Afrikaans for 'The Big Crocodile') due to his tough political stance, he was considered the final hardline leader of South Africa during the apartheid era. Born on 12 January 1916 on a small farm in the Paul Roux district of the Orange Free State Province (now Free State Province), Botha was the son of Afrikaner parents; his father, Pieter Willem Botha Sr., fought as a commando against the British in the Second Boer War, and his mother, Hendrina Christina Botha (née de Wet), was interned in a British concentration camp during that war. Raised in a conservative Afrikaner family with strong nationalist beliefs, Botha was influenced by Afrikaner culture and Calvinist religious teachings, emphasizing discipline, hard work, and loyalty to the Afrikaner cause. Growing up in the aftermath of the Second Boer War and amid rising Afrikaner nationalism, he internalized the belief that Afrikaners needed to assert political and economic control over South Africa. He initially attended the Paul Roux School and matriculated from Bethlehem Voortrekker High School. In 1934, he entered Grey University College (now the University of the Free State) in Bloemfontein to study law but left early at age twenty to pursue politics. He began working for the National Party as a political organizer in the neighbouring Cape Province, joined the Ossewabrandwag—an Afrikaner nationalist group sympathetic to the German Nazi Party—and helped found its Cape Town branch in 1939. After the German attack on the USSR, Botha condemned the Ossewabrandwag in August 1941, shifting to Christian nationalism and being expelled from the group. In 1943, he married Anna Elizabeth Rossouw (Elize), with whom he had five children: two sons (Piet and Rossouw) and three daughters (Elsa, Amelia, and Rozanne). In the 1980s, Rozanne emerged as a minor celebrity, releasing Afrikaans pop songs and appearing on magazine covers such as Sarie and Style, where she was dubbed "First Daughter of the Land." In 1998, he married Barbara Robertson, a legal secretary 25 years his junior, following Elize's death. In 2022, two of his daughters died: Amelia Paschke in a car crash driving back from Betty's Bay, and Rozanne from cancer. Botha was elected to parliament in 1948 as an MP for the National Party from George, coinciding with the party's rise to power under Prime Minister D.F. Malan, who formally instituted apartheid. As a staunch supporter of Afrikaner nationalism, he aligned with the baasskap faction, advocating for stricter racial policies and white minority rule. He gained a reputation for tough, uncompromising rhetoric, often warning of communist threats, black liberation movements, and international pressure, and displayed authoritarian tendencies by advocating for increased state power to suppress opposition. His main opponents in Parliament were Helen Suzman and Harry Schwarz, whom he frequently attacked. After retaining his seat in the 1953 and 1958 elections, he was appointed Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs by Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd, assisting in enforcing the Population Registration Act that classified all South Africans into four racial groups. In 1961, he became Minister of Community Development and Coloured Affairs, overseeing forced removals including the clearance of District Six. In 1966, he was appointed Minister of Defence by Prime Minister John Vorster, a role he held for over 15 years. As Defence Minister, he expanded the military, increased spending to 20% of the national budget from 1.3% in 1968, implemented conscription, launched covert operations against anti-apartheid movements, and initiated South Africa's nuclear weapons program under a doctrine of "strategic deterrence" to counter Soviet-backed forces in Southern Africa. He also established the policy of "total onslaught," framing racial policies as a Cold War struggle against communism and black liberation. The South African Defence Force (SADF) reached a peak under his leadership and was involved in the South African Border War. When Prime Minister John Vorster resigned in 1978 following allegations in the Muldergate Scandal, Botha was elected as his successor by the National Party caucus, defeating Foreign Minister Pik Botha and Connie Mulder in a 78–72 vote. On 5 December 1978, he was absolved of blame in the scandal. Upon becoming Prime Minister, he retained the defence portfolio until October 1980, when he appointed SADF Chief General Magnus Malan. He pursued an ambitious military policy to strengthen South Africa's military capabilities, sought improved relations with the West—especially the United States—but with mixed results, arguing that preserving the apartheid government was essential to countering African communism spreading into Angola and Mozambique after their independence. In one of his first moves, he appointed Piet Koornhof as minister responsible for black affairs, who later joined the ANC in the post-apartheid era and was regarded as one of the most reform-minded ministers. Botha led a campaign to demolish Crossroads, a high-density township in Cape Town in 1978, and later agreed with Koornhof to "indefinitely delay" the demolitions amid opposition. A challenge arose when Andries Treurnicht was elected leader of the Transvaal province, opposing apartheid reforms and holding a strong majority in the all-white parliament, highlighting differences between Afrikaners in Botha's Cape Province and Treurnicht's. In 1979, Botha became the first premier to visit Robben Island, declining to say if he met any prisoners, calling it a "routine" visit. In April 1979, he offered military and economic support to Abel Muzorewa's government in Zimbabwe Rhodesia and held high-level talks with Muzorewa in June 1979. In the weeks before the 1981 general election, he faced hard-line Afrikaner hecklers, some supporters of the Herstigte Nasionale Party, resisting changes to apartheid. On the final night of the campaign, he vowed that "As long as there is a National Party Government, we won't hand over South-West Africa to the authority of SWAPO." His party won 58% of the all-white vote and 131 seats, down from 65% and 134 seats in 1977, losing ground to the Herstigte Nasionale Party. In April 1981, Desmond Tutu's passport was seized after he visited Europe and the United States to call for economic pressure on South Africa; Botha was angered and had vowed to seize Tutu's passport. In the same year, he authorized Operation Beanbag, a series of raids by the SADF against safe houses of uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK), the armed wing of the ANC in Mozambique. In February 1982, he survived a leadership challenge from Andries Treurnicht, securing 172 votes to 36 on a motion of support. On 22 April 1983, Botha announced a special commission to consider repealing the Immorality Act and the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, 1949, stating: "I am personally opposed to immoral practices, but the Government does not see these two laws as guarantees for the survival of South Africa." On 19 May 1983, the International Press Institute issued resolutions condemning the "continued harassment and persecution" of the media in South Africa, appealing to Botha to accept press freedom as a prerequisite for being part of the democratic world and citing difficulties for foreign journalists obtaining visas, as well as the upcoming trials of journalists Allister Sparks, his wife Suzanne, and Bernard Simon, which were dropped in March 1984. In May 1983, he condemned the Church Street, Pretoria bombing by uMkhonto weSizwe, calling it evidence of a "Communist-inspired onslaught." In 1983, Botha proposed a new constitution, put to a vote of the white population on 2 November, which was endorsed by the white electorate. Though it did not implement a federal system, it introduced a power-sharing arrangement with Coloureds and Indians by creating two new houses of parliament—the House of Representatives for Coloureds and the House of Delegates for Indians—alongside the existing white-only House of Assembly. Each chamber had sole jurisdiction over matters relating to their communities, and legislation on "general affairs" such as foreign policy and race relations had to pass all three chambers after joint committee review. White South Africans outnumbered Coloureds and Indians together, preserving white dominance. The plan included no representation for the black majority, allocating each Black ethno-linguistic group a 'homeland' initially as a semi-autonomous area, with blacks legally considered citizens of the Bantustans, not of South Africa, and expected to exercise political rights there. Bantustans were to gradually move toward independence, with sovereign nation status as the final goal. During Botha's tenure, Ciskei, Bophutatswana, and Venda achieved nominal sovereignty and nationhood, recognized only by each other and South Africa, and remained economically dependent. Over half of the Bantustans, notably KwaZulu led by Mangosuthu Buthelezi, rejected independence due to their leaders' opposition to apartheid. The new constitution changed the executive branch from a parliamentary system to a presidential system, abolishing the prime minister's office and merging its functions with the state president, who became an executive with sweeping powers. The president was elected by an electoral college composed of members from the three chambers, not by universal suffrage. The state president and cabinet had sole jurisdiction over "general affairs," and disputes were resolved by the President's Council, composed of members from the three chambers and members directly appointed by the president. In practice, the composition of the electoral college and President's Council made it impossible for Coloured and Indian chambers to outvote the white chamber, even if they voted as a bloc, so real power remained in white hands and in Botha's National Party, which held a large majority in the white chamber due to the first-past-the-post system. Only the challenge from the Conservative Party, which opposed the reforms due to fears of apartheid breaking up, questioned Botha's position. The new constitution was criticized by the black majority for failing to grant them any formal role in government, with the African National Congress and Chief Buthelezi among its opponents, supported by many Coloured, white, and Indian groups including the Progressive Federal Party. International commentators such as the Reagan Administration praised it as a "first step" in a series of reforms. On 14 September 1984, Botha was elected as the first executive State President under the new constitution. Implementing the presidential system was a key step in consolidating his personal power, having previously passed strict laws limiting freedom of speech and frequently declaring states of emergency, including extrajudicial killings by special forces like the Koevoet. In many Western countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Commonwealth, there was debate over imposing economic sanctions to weaken Botha and undermine the white regime. By the late 1980s, as foreign investment declined, disinvestment significantly affected South Africa's economy. After suffering a stroke in 1989, Botha resigned as Leader of the National Party and later as State President, and was succeeded by F. W. de Klerk. After resigning as State President, Botha remained influential in South African politics, opposing de Klerk's reforms, particularly the negotiations to dismantle apartheid and the unbanning of the ANC, and advocating for a no vote in the 1992 referendum. He became a vocal critic of the move toward democracy, maintaining his belief in the necessity of apartheid. In the late 1990s, he faced legal challenges related to his role in apartheid-era policies, notably during Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearings, where he was called to account but refused to fully cooperate. His health declined, and he died on 31 October 2006, at the age of 90.
