Lezi were among South Africa's opponents, and their stance was supported by various coloured, white, and Indian groups, including the official opposition, the Progressive Federal Party. International commentators, such as the Reagan Administration, praised the reforms as a "first step" in a series of anticipated changes. On 14 September 1984, Botha was elected as the first state president under the newly approved constitution, a move seen as a key step in consolidating his personal power. In prior years, he had passed strict laws limiting freedom of speech and frequently declared states of emergency, which included extrajudicial killings during riots or by special forces like Koevoet. In Western countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Commonwealth, there was significant debate over imposing economic sanctions to weaken Botha and undermine the white regime; by the late 1980s, as foreign investment declined, disinvestment severely affected South Africa’s economy. Botha’s loss of influence was directly linked to decisions at the Reagan/Gorbachev summit in Moscow (29 May – 1 June 1988), which aimed to resolve the Namibia issue, as foreign minister Pik Botha stated it was destabilizing the region and "seriously complicating" South Africa’s own challenges. Soviet military aid would cease and Cuban troops would be withdrawn from Angola once South Africa complied with UN Security Council Resolution 435 by ending its control of Namibia and allowing UN-supervised elections. The Tripartite Agreement, implementing these decisions, was signed at UN headquarters in New York on 22 December 1988 by Angola, Cuba, and South Africa. On 18 January 1989, Botha (aged 73) suffered a mild stroke, preventing him from attending a meeting with Namibian leaders on 20 January; he was replaced by acting president J. Christiaan Heunis. On 2 February 1989, Botha resigned as leader of the National Party, anticipating that his nominee, finance minister Barend du Plessis, would succeed him; instead, the party’s parliamentary caucus elected education minister F. W. de Klerk, who quickly consolidated his position as a reformist, while hardliners supported Botha. In March 1989, the NP elected de Klerk as state president, but Botha refused to resign, claiming constitutional entitlement to remain until March 1990 and even considering a five-year re-election. After acrimonious meetings in Cape Town and following the implementation of UNSCR 435 in Namibia on 1 April 1989, Botha and de Klerk reached a compromise: Botha would retire after the parliamentary elections in September, allowing de Klerk to assume the presidency. However, Botha abruptly resigned from the state presidency on 14 August 1989, citing lack of consultation by de Klerk regarding his visit to Zambia’s President Kenneth Kaunda. De Klerk was sworn in as acting state president on 14 August 1989 and was subsequently nominated by the electoral college for a five-year term. De Klerk quickly removed legislation against anti-apartheid groups, including the African National Congress, and released Nelson Mandela. His term led to the dismantling of apartheid and negotiations culminating in South Africa’s first racially inclusive democratic elections on 27 April 1994. In a 2006 statement on Botha’s death, de Klerk acknowledged that Botha introduced some changes to apartheid, including legalizing interracial marriage and miscegenation, lifting the constitutional ban on multiracial political parties, and relaxing the Group Areas Act by creating "Open Group Areas" – racially mixed neighborhoods requiring government permits, local white support, and being located in upper-class areas of major cities. In 1983, constitutional reforms granted limited political rights to "Coloureds" and "Indians," and Botha became the first South African leader to authorize contact with Nelson Mandela. Despite these reforms, NP hardliners, led by Andries Treurnicht, rejected them, with the group splitting in 1982 to form the Conservative Party, which failed to meet opposition demands. Facing rising discontent and violence, Botha refused to transfer power to blacks and imposed stricter security measures against anti-apartheid activists, refusing to negotiate with the ANC. In 1985, Botha delivered the Rubicon speech, refusing to yield to black demands, including Mandela’s release. His defiance isolated South Africa, leading to economic sanctions and a sharp decline in the rand. The following year, when the United States passed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act, Botha declared a nationwide state of emergency and famously stated, "This uprising will bring out the beast in us." As sanctions and diplomatic pressure increased, civil unrest spread among the black population, supported by the ANC and neighboring black-majority governments. On 16 May 1986, Botha warned neighboring states against "unsolicited interference" in South Africa’s affairs; four days later, he ordered air strikes against targets in Lusaka, Harare, and Gaborone, including ANC exiled activists, claiming these were a "first installment" showing South Africa’s capacity and will to dismantle the ANC. Despite concessions, Botha’s rule remained repressive: thousands were detained without trial, tortured, or killed. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found Botha responsible for gross human rights violations and directly authorized unlawful activities, including killings. He declined to apologize for apartheid and, in a 2006 birthday interview, claimed he had no regrets about his leadership. He denied holding black South Africans in inferiority to whites but admitted that "some" whites did; he also stated that apartheid laws originated in Lord Milner’s time and that the National Party merely inherited them, though he conceded that the Afrikaner population had been "happy to perpetuate [apartheid]" as many were, and some still were, "racists at heart." Botha and his wife Elize retired to Die Anker, a home 16 kilometers (9.9 miles) from George on the Indian Ocean coast of the Western Cape. Elize died in 1997 from a heart attack. He was briefly engaged to Reinette Water Naude, 31 years his junior, but on 22 June 1998 married Barbara Robertson, 25 years his junior. Botha remained largely out of the public eye and was widely believed to oppose de Klerk’s reforms; he resigned from the Afrikaner Broederbond. President Nelson Mandela arranged a dinner with Botha’s daughters, Rozanne and Elsa, and their husbands, hoping to persuade them to have their father testify at the TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. There was no consensus within the family, with Rozanne strongly opposing, fearing prosecution or humiliation. The TRC found Botha responsible for the 1988 bombing of the South African Council of Churches headquarters in Johannesburg. In August 1998, he was fined and given a suspended jail sentence for refusing to testify on human rights violations and violence sanctioned by the State Security Council (SSC), which he directed as president until 1989. In June 1999, Botha successfully appealed to the High Court, with Judge Selikowitz (and Judge Foxcroft concurring) ruling that the notice to appear before the TRC was technically invalid. Botha died of natural causes on 31 October 2006, at age 90, at his home in Wilderness. His death was met with magnanimity by many former opponents, with Mandela stating that while Botha remained a symbol of apartheid, he also contributed to the peaceful settlement of the country. President Thabo Mbeki announced flags would be flown at half-mast and a state funeral offered, though the family declined the state funeral and a private one was held on 8 November in George, where Botha was buried. Mbeki attended. However, the government’s decision to honor Botha with official gestures drew public criticism, with organizations like the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) and COSATU opposing it, arguing that a man widely seen as a symbol of apartheid oppression should not receive national recognition.

The Padma Bhushan (IAST: Padma Bhūṣaṇa, lit. 'Lotus Decoration') is the third-highest civilian award in the Republic of India, coming after the Bharat Ratna and the Padma Vibhushan and before the Padma Shri. Instituted on 2 January 1954, it is awarded for "distinguished service of a high order...without distinction of race, occupation, position or sex," including service in any field such as that rendered by government servants, with exceptions for those working in public sector undertakings, except doctors and scientists. As of 2025, the award has been conferred upon 1341 individuals, including 38 posthumous and 101 non-citizen recipients. The recommendations for the award are submitted annually between 1 May and 15 September by state and union territory governments, Ministries of the Government of India, Bharat Ratna and Padma Vibhushan awardees, Institutes of Excellence, Ministers, Chief Ministers, Governors, Members of Parliament, and private individuals. These recommendations are processed by the Padma Awards Committee, convened annually by the Prime Minister of India, which then submits its findings to the Prime Minister and the President of India for approval. Recipients are announced on 26 January, the Republic Day of India, and their names are registered in The Gazette of India, a weekly publication by the Department of Publication, Ministry of Urban Development, which is required for the conferral to be considered official. Recipients whose awards are revoked or restored—both actions requiring presidential authority—must surrender their medals when their names are struck from the register. Initially, the award was not given posthumously, but this was changed in the January 1955 statute; D. C. Kizhakemuri became the first posthumous recipient in 1999. The original design featured a silver circle 1+3⁄8 inches (35 mm) in diameter with a lotus flower embossed on the obverse and "Padma Bhushan" in Devanagari script above it, a floral wreath on the lower edge, and the State Emblem of India on the reverse with "Desh Seva" in Devanagari script on the lower edge, suspended by a pink ribbon 1+1⁄4 inches (32 mm) wide with two white vertical lines. In 1955, the design was modified to a bronze-toned medallion 1+3⁄4 inches (44 mm) in diameter and 1⁄8 inch (3.2 mm) thick, with a central raised circular space and a lotus flower, "Padma" above and "Bhushan" below, and the State Emblem on the reverse with "Satyameva Jayate" in Devanagari script. The rim and all embossing are in standard gold with "Padma Bhushan" in gold gilt, and the ribbon has a broad white stripe in the middle. The award ranks fifth in the order of precedence for wearing medals and decorations and is produced at the Alipore Mint, Kolkata, alongside other civilian and military awards. The Padma Bhushan, along with other personal civil honours, was briefly suspended twice: from July 1977 to January 1980 and from August 1992 to December 1995. The first suspension occurred when Morarji Desai became Prime Minister, criticized as "worthless and politicized," and was rescinded on 25 January 1980 after Indira Gandhi took office. The second suspension followed two Public-Interest Litigations in 1992—one in the Kerala High Court by Balaji Raghavan and another in the Madhya Pradesh High Court (Indore Bench) by Satya Pal Anand—questioning the awards as "titles" under Article 18 of the Constitution. On 25 August 1992, the Madhya Pradesh High Court issued a temporary suspension. A Special Division Bench of the Supreme Court, comprising A. M. Ahmadi C. J., Kuldip Singh, B. P. Jeevan Reddy, N. P. Singh, and S. Saghir Ahmad, restored the awards on 15 December 1995, ruling that the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18. Several recipients have refused or returned the award: Sisir Bhaduri (1959) refused, stating that state awards create a sycophantic environment and do not reflect the government's seriousness about theatre; Vilayat Khan declined in 1968, citing incompetent selection committees, having previously refused the Padma Shri in 1964 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2000; Nikhil Chakravarty rejected it in 1990, saying journalists should not be identified with the establishment; Romila Thapar declined twice—first in 1992 and again in 2005—stating she would accept awards only from academic institutions or those linked to her professional work, and sent a clarification letter to President A. P. J. Abdul Kalam explaining her prior refusal; K. Subrahmanyam refused his 1999 award, arguing bureaucrats and journalists should not accept government awards due to potential favouritism; Dattopant Thengadi (RSS volunteer) rejected the 2003 award until K. B. Hedgewar and M. S. Golwalkar were offered the Bharat Ratna; S. R. Sankaran turned down the 2005 award without explanation; S. Janaki refused in 2013, stating the award came late in her five-and-a-half-decade career and requesting more recognition for southern artists; family members of J. S. Verma, the 27th Chief Justice of India, refused the posthumous award, saying Verma would not have accepted it as he never sought acclaim; K. Shivaram Karanth returned his 1968 award in protest against the 1975 Emergency; Khushwant Singh returned his 1974 award in 1984 in protest against Operation Blue Star, later receiving the Padma Vibhushan in 2007; Pushpa Mittra Bhargava returned his 1986 award in 2015 in protest against the Dadri mob lynching and due to concerns about the socio-political climate. In 2010, Indian-American businessman Sant Singh Chatwal was awarded the Padma Bhushan in the field of Public Affairs, which sparked controversy due to his guilty plea for violating the Federal Election Campaign Act and witness tampering in the 2008 U.S. presidential election, and allegations of lobbying for the award through contacts in the Prime Minister's Office and U.S. Congress. The government clarified that Chatwal is a "tireless advocate" of India's interests abroad and stated that a due diligence process was conducted, with three of five CBI-registered cases against him closed by the CBI and two others resulting in his discharge by courts, with no adverse records found. Media reports indicate several cases filed after April 2009, including three with Kerala Police and four in Delhi and Kerala High Courts, and Chatwal received a summons in January 2010; however, Union Home Secretary Gopal Krishna Pillai stated no probe had been ordered or report sought. In 2008, Chatwal was considered for the Padma Shri but the Indian Embassy in Washington, D.C. declined to nominate him, citing controversy over his financial dealings and that his contributions were less significant than others, and that the award would demoralize those who had done more and create the impression that lack of transparency disqualifies individuals from honours. In 2022, former West Bengal Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharya refused his award on the eve of the 73rd Republic Day, reportedly not being intimated about his nomination and publicly stating that if he had been awarded, he would refuse it; his name appeared on the official list, and he has since refused the award.

The Pakistan Cycling Federation (PCF) is the national governing body for cycle racing in Pakistan, established in 1947 and currently headquartered in Peshawar. SYED AZHAR ALI SHAH serves as the President, and MUHAMMAD HAROON GENERAL is the General Secretary. Recent elections have resolved the federation’s 13-year-long dispute, with the newly elected leadership committed to restoring Pakistan’s cycling prestige. The PCF was formed in 1947 following Pakistan’s independence and held its first National Cycling Championship in 1948 during the National Games in Karachi, which were officially opened by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, who also became the first honorary president of the PCF. The federation is affiliated with the Union Cycliste Internationale, which it joined in 1952, the Asian Cycling Confederation, and the Pakistan Sports Board. Major events organized by the PCF include the Tour de Pakistan, Tour De Khunjrab, Tour of Islamabad, and Tour De Galyat.

Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) is the flag carrier of Pakistan, with its primary hub at Jinnah International Airport in Karachi, and secondary hubs at Allama Iqbal International Airport in Lahore and Islamabad International Airport. PIA was under the administrative control of the Secretary to the Government of Pakistan for Aviation until its privatization in 2025. The airline traces its origins to Orient Airways, founded on 29 October 1946 by Mirza Ahmad Ispahani and Adamjee Haji Dawood in Calcutta, British India, and became the first and only Muslim-owned airline in the British Raj. After Pakistan's independence on 14 August 1947, Orient Airways began relief operations and served routes between East and West Pakistan. In 1952, the government subsidized Orient Airways by purchasing three Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellations through a newly established subsidiary, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), at a cost of 25 million rupees. On 1 October 1953, Orient Airways and PIA were formally merged under the Pakistan International Airlines Corporation Ordinance, 1955, with the government taking majority control. The merged airline operated a fleet of three Super Constellations, two Convair CV-240s, and eleven DC-3s. On 11 March 1955, Orient Airways ceased operations. PIA inaugurated its first international route on 11 March 1955, flying from Karachi to London Heathrow via Cairo and Rome using Super Constellations, carrying 113,165 passengers in 1955—50% more than in 1954. In May 1956, PIA ordered five Vickers Viscount 815s and partnered with Pan Am to train personnel. Passenger numbers rose to 208,000 between 1957 and 1958, prompting the purchase of two additional Super Constellations. In February 1960, PIA wet-leased a Boeing 707 from Pan American Airlines and introduced it on the Karachi-London route on 7 March 1960, becoming the second Asian airline to operate a jet aircraft commercially, with an all-Pakistani crew beginning operations on 20 June 1960. By the end of 1960, PIA achieved financial profitability. On 5 May 1961, it launched its first trans-Atlantic route, Karachi to New York JFK via London, which was suspended in February 1963. In 1961, PIA ordered three Boeing 720s, delivered in 1962. On 2 January 1962, a PIA Boeing 720B set a world record speed of 938.78 km/h (582.98 mph) from London to Karachi, a record still held today. In 1963, Fokker F27 Friendships and Sikorsky helicopters were ordered; the latter served 20 towns in East Pakistan until 1966. In 1964, PIA began flying the Dhaka-Guangzhou-Shanghai route, becoming the first non-Communist airline to fly to China, and on 10 May 1964, became the first non-Soviet airline to offer flights to Europe via Moscow. During the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965, PIA's aircraft were used for military logistics. The Viscounts were phased out in 1966 and replaced by four Hawker Siddeley Tridents. PIA expanded its network in the 1960s, adding Dhahran in 1962, Cairo services resumed, and by 1966, Paris, Istanbul, Baghdad, Kuwait, Jeddah, and Nairobi were added. Bangkok was added in 1967, and Manila, Tokyo, and Damascus in 1969. On 11 May 1967, Air Marshal Asghar Khan announced that PIA had become the fifth largest profit-making airline in the world, carrying one million passengers annually. In July 1967, he announced plans to build 64-room hotels in Sylhet, Sargodha, Sukkur, Mohenjo-daro, Chitral, Gilgit, and Kaptai, and 88-room hotels in Khulna, Lyallpur, Multan, and Murree, with 20 cottages attached to the 644-room Kaptai Hotel, and 125-room hotels in Peshawar and Chittagong. These European-style motels, equipped with air conditioning, heating, parking, and swimming pools, were completed in 1970 and funded through private investment, with no government financial participation. A new holding company was established to attract domestic investment, and Pakistan Services Ltd. contributed significantly. Bechtel Corp. prepared the design and cost estimates, recommending standardized designs using local materials. On 3 December 1971, a French national's attempt to hijack a PIA flight from Paris to Karachi was thwarted by French security forces. Transatlantic flights to New York resumed in May 1972 with a European stopover. In 1972, PIA added Tripoli to its network following improved ties with Libya and leased two Boeing 707s to Yugoslav airline JAT (now Air Serbia). In 1973, PIA acquired McDonnell Douglas DC-10s to replace its Boeing 707-300s. Nur Khan was appointed PIA executive for a second term in 1974, and in 1974, PIA launched Pakistan International Cargo. In 1976, PIA leased its first two Boeing 747s from TAP Air Portugal. By 1976–7, PIA carried 2.2 million passengers, up from 698,000 in 1972–3, and revenues reached $134 million in July–December 1976. On 20 January 1978, a PIA Fokker 27 was hijacked en route to Karachi from Sukkur. PIA began providing technical and administrative assistance or leasing aircraft to foreign airlines including Air China, Air Malta, Choson Minhang (now Air Koryo), Philippine Airlines, Somali Airlines, and Yemenia. A PIA subsidiary also began offering hotel management services in the UAE. Political upheaval in Pakistan during the late 1970s negatively impacted PIA's operations. In the 1980s, PIA expanded operations with the opening of a cargo handling center at Karachi airport, duty-free shops, the first C and D safety checks on its fleet, and the introduction of its first Airbus A300B4-200. In 1981, PIA had nearly 24,000 employees, which declined to 20,000 by 1983, still maintaining the world's highest employee-to-aircraft ratio. Operations became increasingly decentralized during the early 1980s. PIA reported its highest ever profits in 1981–82 and again in 1983–84. In 1984, PIA introduced the Night Coach service as a low-cost domestic alternative. The PIA Planetarium was inaugurated in Karachi, followed by ones in Lahore and Peshawar, featuring retired PIA aircraft for educational use. Two retired Boeing 720B aircraft were donated to the Karachi and Lahore planetaria. PIA profits rose again in 1984–85. In June 1985, PIA became the first Asian airline to operate the Boeing 737-300, after six aircraft were delivered. PIA played a key role in establishing Emirates in 1985 by providing technical and administrative support, leasing a Boeing 737–300 and an Airbus A300B4-200. In late 1987 and early 1988, services to Malé, Manchester, and Toronto were introduced. Throughout the 1990s, PIA sustained operating losses and liquidity problems due to frequent pilot strikes, vendor issues, over-staffing, and political interference. In 1990, First Officer Maliha Sami became the first female pilot of PIA on the Karachi-Panjgur-Turbat-Gwadar route. In June 1991, PIA took delivery of its first of six Airbus A310-300s, introducing flights to Tashkent in 1992 and Zurich in 1993. In March 1993, AVM Farooq Umar became managing director. An Open Skies agreement between Karachi and Dubai was agreed upon in 1993, allowing 12 private airlines to operate domestically, which placed significant financial pressure on PIA. PIA operates a fleet of 32 aircraft, primarily Boeing 777 types, Airbus A320s, and ATR aircraft. It runs nearly 50 daily flights, serving 20 domestic and 28 international destinations across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America. PIA operates a frequent flyer program called Awards +Plus and is not part of any airline alliance. The airline owns Sofitel Paris, The Scribe Hotel in Paris, and The Roosevelt Hotel in New York City, which is now used as a homeless shelter. The Government of Pakistan's 2020 report noted that after Air Marshals Nur Khan and Asghar Khan—whose leadership was regarded as the "Golden Age of PIA"—departed, the airline entered a downward trajectory, suffering billions in losses, with declining assets, escalating disciplinary issues, and unions indirectly taking control. Capable aircraft were grounded, and repairable equipment was neglected. From 30 June 2020 until 29 November 2024, PIA was banned from flying in European airspace after the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) determined it was not capable of certifying or overseeing its operations in accordance with international standards. This ban was also implemented in other non-EU territories after it was revealed that at least a fourth of all pilot licenses issued in Pakistan were not genuine. Following prolonged financial losses, governance issues, and international operational restrictions, PIA was privatized in 2025, ending direct government ownership and transferring majority control to the private sector.

In late 1987 and early 1988, PIA introduced services to Malé, Manchester, and Toronto. Throughout the 1990s, the airline faced sustained operating losses and liquidity problems due to frequent pilot strikes, vendor issues, over-staffing, and political interference in management. In 1990, First Officer Maliha Sami became the first female pilot of PIA when she flew the Karachi-Panjgur-Turbat-Gwadar route. In June 1991, PIA received its first of six Airbus A310-300s, which enabled the airline to launch flights to Tashkent in 1992 and Zürich in 1993. In March 1993, AVM Farooq Umar became managing director. That year, an Open Skies agreement between Karachi and Dubai was agreed upon, allowing 12 private airlines to operate domestically in Pakistan, both of which placed significant pressure on PIA’s financial performance. In 1994, PIA launched six new routes to the Persian Gulf and CIS countries and introduced a tourist 'Air Safari' scenic flight over the Karakoram Mountains. Non-stop flights from Lahore and Islamabad to JFK and Canada were introduced, and PIA added Jakarta, Fujairah, Baku, and Al-Ain to its network. The airline also became a client of SABRE, Galileo, and Amadeus. In 1996, a Tupolev Tu-154 was briefly leased to manage increased passenger traffic during summer, and flights to Beirut were resumed that year before being discontinued later. In 1999, PIA leased five Boeing 747–300s from Cathay Pacific to replace its Boeing 747-200M fleet; these aircraft were painted with a new livery featuring a handwork Pashmina tail on a white body and large Pakistan titles on the front fuselage, a design adopted in the early 1990s but dropped due to copyright issues. The 747–300s retained the new livery with a plain green tail and PIA titles, while other aircraft were repainted in the early 1990s livery. The 9/11 attacks in Afghanistan in 2001 closed Afghan airspace, negatively impacting PIA’s operations. However, after restructuring under new management in April 2001, the airline became profitable again. Between 2000 and 2003, cost per employee dropped by 24%, and lower engineering and maintenance costs improved airline revenue. In July 2002, PIA purchased six Boeing 747–300s, five of which were already on lease, with the sixth arriving shortly after and used primarily on North American and European routes. In October 2002, after ten years without new orders, PIA placed an order for eight Boeing 777 aircraft, including three 777-200ER, two 777-200LR, and three 777-300ER variants, becoming the launch customer for the 777-200LR project. Boeing delivered the first 777-200ER to PIA in January 2004, and a new livery was introduced for the 777-200ERs and applied to most of the fleet. PIA also leased six additional Airbus A310-300s directly from Airbus. On 3 November 2005, PIA ordered seven ATR 42-500s to replace its ageing Fokker F27 Friendship fleet. On 10 November 2005, PIA used its 777-200LR to fly the world’s longest commercial flight, covering 21,000 kilometers from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 22 minutes—a record still standing as of late 2019. On 6 December 2005, PIA acquired a new Boeing 777-200ER on a ten-year lease. In the same year, Ayesha Rabia Naveed became the first Pakistani woman to captain a scheduled commercial flight and later captained a flight with the first all-woman crew. On 23 December 2006, PIA took delivery of its first Boeing 777-300ER, with the remaining aircraft delivered in January 2007. On 25 February 2006, Boeing delivered its first 777-200LR to PIA. ATR delivered two of the seven ATR 42s in May and December 2006, after which PIA ceased using military Lockheed C-130 Hercules for passenger services in northern Pakistan, having previously used them following the PIA Flight 688 accident. Under the supervision of Mr. Syed Shah, PIA initiated the introduction of long-range 777 aircraft, enabling non-stop flights from Toronto to Karachi, Islamabad, and Lahore beginning 3 March 2006. This strategic move allowed more efficient and seamless travel for passengers and positioned PIA as a prominent player in aviation. However, PIA had planned non-stop flights to New York City, Chicago, Washington, and Houston, which were denied by US authorities due to security concerns after 9/11 unless a European stopover was included. In July 2006, a PIA flight from Multan crashed, killing 45; a government inquiry blamed aging aircraft. Houston services ended in 2006. On 5 March 2007, the European Commission banned 33 of PIA’s 42 aircraft from flying to Europe due to safety concerns over aging planes, though the Boeing 777 fleet was exempted; by that time, 15 aircraft were over 20 years old. PIA argued the ban was discriminatory and unjustifiable. The ban was lifted after four months on 5 July 2007 following an EU Air Safety Administration inspection, with five Boeing 747-300s and six Airbus A310-300s allowed to resume operations. On 29 November 2007, the EU fully lifted the ban, permitting PIA’s entire fleet to fly to Europe. In 2010, PIA changed its livery, replacing the tail with a larger Pakistan national flag and adding "Pakistan International" in gold beneath the PIA logo on the fuselage, with a modified green stripe extended to the rear. By 2011, PIA became unprofitable again and required government subsidies. In 2014, PIA leased four Boeing 737-800s and issued a request for tender for four Boeing 777-300ERs, though the bids were not accepted. The airline leased Airbus A320 aircraft, inducted two A320-214s in 2014, and added two wet-leased A320-211s on 11 August 2014. In October 2014, PIA wet-leased three Boeing 737-800s and accepted bids to dry lease five ATR 72–500s for eight years. In 2015, the last of PIA’s Boeing 747-300s were phased out. In early 2016, PIA was grounded for a week as employees walked out en masse following the deaths of two employees in a protest against privatisation. In August 2016, PIA launched a "Premier Service" to London using an Airbus A330-300 wet-leased from SriLankan Airlines, which was returned after six months and the service discontinued. By the end of 2016, the airline had $3 billion in debt. In January 2017, PIA retired all Airbus A310-300s and leased four Boeing 737-800s from Pegasus Airlines, which were returned after the lease ended. After over 50 years of service, PIA ended its service to New York in October 2017 due to TSA regulations preventing nonstop flights between Pakistan and the US, leaving Toronto as the only North American destination, served by nonstop flights from Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad. In 2017, PIA replaced its Sabre reservation system with a Turkish-origin system called Hitit, successfully switching to the new system in September 2018. By the end of 2018, the airline had $3.3 billion in debt, up from $2.97 billion the prior year, requiring government bailouts. With the closure of Shaheen Air, PIA launched routes previously served only by Shaheen. In 2019, new profitable routes were launched, and profitable routes like Karachi-Toronto saw increased frequencies, while six unprofitable routes were discontinued. In April 2019, PIA reported that its revenues nearly matched operating costs. Following a visit by TSA officials to Islamabad International Airport in July 2019, PIA expressed hope that non-stop flights to the US would be permitted. In August 2019, PIA laid off 1,000 employees. In September 2019, PIA announced plans to lease additional aircraft to increase its fleet to 37 by 2020 and 45 by 2023. By the end of 2019, PIA reported a 41% year-on-year revenue increase due to route adjustments, reintroduction of grounded aircraft, and higher cargo space utilization. For the first time in its history, PIA operated a relief flight from Lahore to Melbourne during the COVID-19 pandemic. On 22 May 2020, a PIA Airbus A320-214 (AP-BLD) crashed near Karachi airport while en route from Lahore; Flight PK8303, carrying 91 passengers and eight crew members, crashed during descent to Jinnah International Airport, killing 97 and leaving two survivors. The crash was caused by damage from a first belly landing, with both engines flaming out during a go-around. The final report cited human error, non-adherence to SOPs, disregard of ATC instructions, and lack of communication between ATC and the flight crew. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) expressed concerns over "serious lapses in licensing and safety oversight" by the aviation regulator. In November 2020, PIA shut down its courier arm, SpeedEx, which had infrastructure across 74 domestic destinations, and laid off 320 employees. In December 2020, PIA announced plans to lay off half its employees and transferred its engineering arm, Precision Engineering Complex (PEC), to the Pakistan Air Force. On 24 June 2020, following the Flight 8303 crash, Aviation Minister Ghulam Sarwar Khan stated that 262 of Pakistan’s 860 licensed pilots had suspicious or fake licenses, suspected of paying others to take their certification exams. PIA grounded 150 of its 434 pilots and later terminated employment of seven pilots. Almost a week later, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) suspended PIA’s authorization, banning flights in European airspace for six months. On 9 July 2020, the US banned PIA over pilot certification concerns, and the airline was also banned from flying in the UK; Pakistani pilots in Vietnam and Malaysia were temporarily grounded. On 15 July 2020, the US Federal Aviation Administration downgraded Pakistan’s International Aviation Safety Assessment to Category 2, preventing Pakistani airlines from establishing new US services or using US codes. On 18 July 2020, PIA dismissed seven pilots and one cabin crew member whose licenses were revoked by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). On 28 December 2020, the EU extended its ban for three months, requiring an official CAA inspection. On 16 March 2021, the ban was extended to July, and then to indefinitely on 24 March 2021 following a safety concern about the CAA reported by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which had not yet conducted a safety audit of the CAA. EASA stated that ICAO’s audit would indicate improvement. On 6 November 2021, the CAA received positive feedback from Europe’s Safety Audit for Foreign-Origin Aircraft (SAFA). In late 2023, PIA was forced to cancel numerous flights due to unpaid fuel bills, leading to customer anger and viral social media content. Pakistan State Oil suspended fueling of PIA aircraft after the airline’s request for additional government funding was denied. On 8 March 2023, PIA completed an online safety audit conducted by EASA. On 29 November 2024, EASA lifted its ban on PIA, citing improvements in the CAA’s oversight, and PIA announced the resumption of flights to Europe, beginning with a flight to Paris on 10 January 2025. However, after advertising the event, PIA apologised for using imagery reminiscent of the September 11 attacks, prompting Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to announce an inquiry. In late December 2023, the Interim government announced a plan to privatise PIA, with Air Marshal (Retd) Farhat Hussain Khan stating that privatisation would occur under the government’s policy to privatise loss-making entities, initially as a flight entity with decisions on other properties to be made later. On 6 January 2025, PIA announced plans to expand its destinations to the Middle East using its Boeing 777 and Airbus A320 fleets. Starting 20 January 2025, PIA began two weekly flights between Sialkot and Bahrain, two weekly flights between Lahore and Dammam, and a once-a-week flight between Lahore and Kuwait. Additionally, weekly flights from Faisalabad to Jeddah and Sialkot to Doha, Qatar began on 20 and 21 January 2025, respectively. On 16 July 2025, the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority lifted its ban on PIA, citing safety improvements. PIA announced plans to resume flights to the UK with three weekly flights between Islamabad and Manchester, later reduced to two weekly. The inaugural flight was delayed due to delays in obtaining necessary approvals.

On 6 January 2025, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) announced it would expand its operations to the Middle East by introducing weekly flights using its Boeing 777 and Airbus A320 fleets. Starting 20 January 2025, two weekly flights began between Sialkot and Bahrain, and two weekly flights were launched between Lahore and Dammam, with an additional once-a-week flight starting on 25 January 2025 between Lahore and Kuwait. Weekly services from Faisalabad to Jeddah began on 20 January 2025, and a weekly flight from Sialkot to Doha, Qatar, commenced on 21 January 2025. On 16 July 2025, the UK's Civil Aviation Authority lifted its ban on PIA, citing safety improvements, and PIA announced plans to resume flights to the UK with three weekly flights between Islamabad and Manchester, later reduced to two weekly flights. Despite delays in obtaining a Third Country Operator certificate, the certificate was finally secured on 24 September 2025, and flights to the UK commenced in October 2025. On 23 December 2025, a consortium led by the Arif Habib Corporation was awarded a 75% majority stake in PIA through an auction offering 135 billion rupees ($482 million), with Fauji Fertilizer joining the consortium. PIA remains majority-owned by the Government of Pakistan (86%), with 14% held by private shareholders, and is administered by the Aviation Division under a president and chief executive officer, along with a board of nine independent non-executive members. The board has four sub-committees: Audit, Brand and Advertising, Finance, and Human Resource, each with a charter and chairman. The airline’s main headquarters are in Karachi, with smaller offices in several Pakistani cities. Seven of PIA’s ten departments are located in Islamabad—Marketing, Procedure Bureau, Central Reservation Control, Revenue Management, HR and Security and Vigilance—while the remaining three are in Karachi: finance, engineering, and situation room. In the late 1990s, the government proposed privatization due to persistent losses, but plans were not implemented; in 1997, a team from International Finance Corporation (IFC) was brought in for restructuring, but no agreement was reached. On 18 February 2009, PIA was removed from the privatization list. In 2013, the government attempted privatization by selling 26% of shares and management control, but the plan was abandoned after protests following the killing of two employees at Jinnah International Airport. In 2018, the new government decided against privatization and instead focused on profitability through management changes. On 6 February 2024, the interim government decided to split PIA into two entities: TopCo, which handles engineering, ground handling, flight kitchen, and training, and HoldCo, which manages Precision Engineering Complex, PIA Investment Limited, and subordinate departments and properties. On 4 June 2024, six companies—Air Blue, Arif Habib Corporation, Blue World City, Fly Jinnah, Pak Ethanol (Pvt) Consortium, and YB Holdings Consortium—were pre-qualified to bid for PIA’s privatization. On 30 October 2024, only Blue World City submitted a bid, offering 10 billion Pakistani rupees ($36 million) for a 60% stake, significantly below the government’s minimum of 85 billion rupees. On 13 November 2024, the government officially rejected the bid, stating the process would follow laws and regulations with decisions made in the national interest by the cabinet committee. On 9 July 2025, the government approved four potential investors: Air Blue, Fauji Fertilizers, Lucky Cement Consortium (including Hub Power, Kohat Cement, and Metro Ventures), and Arif Habib Consortium (including Fatima Fertilizer, City Schools, and Lake City Holdings). In December 2025, the Government of Pakistan sold its 75% stake in PIA to the Arif Habib-led consortium for 135 billion Pakistani rupees ($480 million), part of a long-delayed privatization linked to broader economic reforms. PIA became unprofitable in 2011, requiring government subsidies, and by the end of 2016, it carried $3 billion in debt, rising to $3.3 billion by the end of 2018, necessitating government bailouts. In April 2019, PIA reported that revenues nearly matched operating costs; an audit revealed 46 empty flights between 2016 and 2017, resulting in a $1.1 million loss, and 36 Hajj flights without passengers. By the end of 2019, PIA reported a 41% year-on-year revenue increase due to route rationalization, reintroduction of idle aircraft, and increased cargo utilization. PIA faces profitability challenges due to "capacity dumping" by Middle East airlines, such as Emirates operating up to seven daily flights to Karachi on high-capacity Boeing 777s under Pakistan’s Open Skies Agreement with the UAE. PIA discontinued profitable US routes due to TSA restrictions requiring costly diversions to European airports, and new routes to Najaf and Bangkok did not improve finances due to seasonality. Staffing issues, including an employee count of 18,014 in 2010 for a 40-aircraft fleet, remain a challenge, though 1,000 employees were laid off in August 2019. As of November 2019, PIA served 19 domestic and 28 international destinations across 20 countries in Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and North America. Through interline agreements and codeshare partnerships, PIA offers travel options in 102 international destinations across 40 countries. PIA’s hubs are Jinnah International Airport, Allama Iqbal International Airport, and Islamabad International Airport, with Karachi as the main hub and Islamabad and Lahore as secondary hubs. PIA has codeshare and interline agreements with various airlines and cargo special pro-rate agreements with others. As of December 2025, PIA operates a fleet of aircraft, with the government requiring 38 new aircraft over four years; the new owner, Arif Habib Consortium, plans to add 38 aircraft in the first phase and 65 in the second phase over four to six years. In December 2003, PIA introduced a new livery on its first Boeing 777-200ER and two leased Airbus A310s, featuring a white front and beige rear with a dark green stripe, a white tail with a dark green PIA acronym, and a raised "Pakistan" title; due to criticism, the design was modified, replacing the tail logo with a flowing Pakistan flag on beige, removing "Pakistan" titles, and enlarging the PIA acronym. In early 2006, four provincial tail designs were launched—Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan—each featuring cultural motifs and a city name, but were discontinued in 2009 due to high costs. In mid-April 2010, a new livery was launched featuring a green and gold strip down the fuselage and tail, white forward and off-white/beige rear, a large wavy Pakistan flag on the tail, and "PIA" in dark green and "Pakistan" in golden letters at the front. In July 2014, a "crescent and star" was introduced on the engine cowlings in place of the Urdu logo; in 2015, the 1960s livery was applied to three A320s and one Boeing 777-200ER. In April 2018, PIA launched a new brand identity with a Markhor, Pakistan’s national animal, on aircraft, symbolizing resilience, grace, and fortitude, with a forward leaping Markhor on the tail and two on the engines; however, the Supreme Court of Pakistan issued a suo motu notice halting the rebranding due to concerns over staff salaries, later allowing retention of the flag on the tail and dismissing the case, but the rebranding was ultimately abandoned. Currently, PIA operates a hybrid livery with a euro-white fuselage, gold Urdu logo at front exits and engine cowls, and retains the flag tail, English and Pakistan titles in dark green on the belly, and the PIA corporate website ahead of the aft exits. Five Boeing 777s and three A320s currently feature this livery. PIA Catering supplies meals at Islamabad and Karachi, producing 15,000 meals daily; flight kitchens were managed by Singapore Air Terminal Services (SATS) from 2006 to 2011, after which PIA managed them independently. In April 2019, an MOU was signed with McDonald’s for catering, and PIA provides special meals for dietary and religious needs, with no alcoholic beverages or pork served due to Islamic dietary laws. PIA Premier, a luxury service launched on 14 August 2016 using an A330 wet-leased from SriLankan Airlines, operated six weekly flights to London and three each from Islamabad and Lahore, but was discontinued due to a loss of 2.1 billion rupees. PIA was the first international airline to introduce a regularly scheduled film on board in 1962. In January 2017, PIA began trials of an on-board internet system for domestic flights, allowing passengers to access content via their mobile devices; Boeing 777s offer personal screens with movies, music, TV, maps, and air shows, and selected A320s have drop-down screens with maps and air shows. The Precision Engineering Complex (PEC), originally a PIA subsidiary, produces high-precision components for aerospace and engineering, with capabilities in investment casting, CNC machining, optics, PCB manufacturing, electronics, and composites, and is a supplier to General Electric, Airbus, and Boeing. In late 2025, ownership of PEC was transferred from PIAHCL to Precision Engineering Complex (Private) Limited, a company under the Pakistan Air Force, as part of the government-led restructuring and privatization effort.

The Precision Engineering Complex (PEC) is a specialized manufacturing and engineering facility that was originally part of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) and later became a subsidiary of the Pakistan International Airlines Holding Company Limited (PIAHCL). It is now owned by Precision Engineering Complex (Private) Limited, a company designated by the Pakistan Air Force, following an ownership transfer approved by PIAHCL shareholders in late 2025 as part of the government-led restructuring and privatization of the national flag carrier. The PEC is an integrated complex that produces high-precision components for the aerospace and broader engineering industries, with capabilities in investment casting, conventional and CNC machining, optics, PCB manufacturing, electrical, electronics, and composites. It holds international certifications and serves as a supplier to major global aerospace companies such as General Electric, Airbus Industries, and Boeing. PIA provides ground handling services to various airlines, operates PIA Cargo—a cargo airline that transports goods across Pakistan and internationally, including meat packing, vegetables, textiles, paper products, laboratory equipment, and postal mail—and previously operated Air Express in the 1970s, launching a dedicated cargo division in 1974 using two Boeing 707-320C aircraft, which operated to the Middle East and Europe before ending in the late 1990s. From 2004 to 2007, it operated two Airbus A300 Freighter aircraft chartered through MNG Airlines to Haan, Luton, Amsterdam, Basel, and Cologne, before discontinuing the service. In 2003, PIA launched PIA Speedex, a courier service initially in four cities that expanded to twelve within a year and now serves over 70 locations in Pakistan, collecting and delivering shipments from customers' homes. In 2019, the new PIA management increased cargo space utilization from 20 percent to nearly 80 percent. PIA currently offers cargo services to international destinations including Abu Dhabi, Bangkok, Barcelona, Birmingham, Beijing, Copenhagen, Doha, Dubai, Jeddah, Kabul, Kuala Lumpur, London, Manchester, Medina, Milan, Muscat, Najaf, Oslo, Paris, Riyadh, Sharjah, Tokyo–Narita, and Toronto–Canada. The airline sponsors various events domestically and abroad, including the three green stripe livery introduced in the 1990s to support sports, backing the PIA first-class cricket team in the Quaid-i-Azam Trophy and Patron's Trophy, the PIA football club, the A1 Team Pakistan in the A1 Grand Prix, and the annual Shandur Polo Gala in northern Pakistan. PIA has had a sports division since 1958, promoting cricket, hockey, football, squash, polo, tennis, bridge, chess, table tennis, cycling, and bodybuilding. It also operates a Boy Scouts Association (PIA-BSA) in partnership with the Pakistan Boy Scouts Association, which provided relief after the 2005 earthquake. PIA was an official sponsor of "Destination Pakistan 2007" and in 2008 partnered with Ufone to offer air miles to mobile network users, and with Standard Chartered Bank to launch air miles credit cards. In 2009, it was the gold sponsor of Logistics Pakistan and formed a strategic alliance with the Pakistan Remittance Initiative (PRI) to promote international money transfers. PIA operates planetariums in Karachi and Lahore featuring static aircraft and astronomy shows, and PIA Horticulture, established in 1996, supplies flowers for offices and events, winning awards nationally. The airline supports non-profit organizations such as Al-Shifa Trust, Zindagi Trust, The Citizens Foundation, and Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation. In 2009, it partnered with McDonald's to offer meal discounts and upgrades. PIA owns three hotels—Roosevelt Hotel, Scribe Hotel, and Skyrooms (Private) Limited—and has an agreement with Pearl Continental Hotels for UAE-based passengers. PIA has continuously transported government officials, including the President and Prime Minister, on overseas visits; during the late 1990s, a Boeing 737–300 was used for official trips, later transferred permanently to PIA after a military coup in 1999, and subsequently replaced by two Airbus A310-300s. In February 2007, Qatar gifted an Airbus A310 to the Pakistani government, ending the need for PIA aircraft for official travel, though occasional use of PIA's Airbus A320 or Boeing 777 is still made. PIA operates private charter flights using ATR 42s to Bhit, Kadanwari, and Sehwan Sharif in Sindh and other domestic locations for oil and gas companies and customers, and provides ad hoc charters for United Nations peacekeeping troops to Africa, Eastern Europe, Asia (South Korea, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, East Timor), and other international destinations through its Charter Team. The airline runs a two-month Hajj operation annually to Saudi Arabia, transporting over 100,000 pilgrims until its fleet reduced to 25 aircraft in 2011–2012, after which the Hajj quota was reduced to 60,000 to 70,000 pilgrims. On 27 September 2024, PIA received Pakistan's first National Tourism Award for Promoting Travel and Tourism, awarded to Air Vice Marshal Amir Hayat, CEO of PIA, in recognition of its efforts in promoting domestic travel. The airline has experienced more than 30 aircraft losses, including 20 fatal crashes, and has been involved in at least eight hijacking incidents between 1971 and 2017.

Morris Steinberg (DEM) and Isaac Glanzer (REP) are political figures associated with Palm Tree. Palm Tree is a town coterminous with the village of Kiryas Joel, which is inhabited by the Satmar Hasidic community and was previously part of the municipality of Monroe. The population of Palm Tree was 32,954 according to the 2020 census. The town of Palm Tree, comprising the entirety of Kiryas Joel, was officially established on January 1, 2019. Prior to 2019, the area underwent several geographic and name changes: until 1764, it was part of an enlarged Goshen, which was then divided, with Palm Tree joining Cornwall; by 1799, Cornwall was split, and Palm Tree became part of the town of Cheesekook (later renamed Smithfield or Southfield), which in 1808 became Monroe, either in honor of James Monroe or a local family. In 1974, Satmar rebbe Joel Teitelbaum founded the Kiryas Joel community, and in 1976, it was incorporated as a village in his honor as a semi-rural retreat for his Brooklyn-based community. As the population grew, zoning conflicts with Monroe arose, leading to a referendum on November 7, 2017, which passed overwhelmingly and resulted in the split from Monroe and the creation of Palm Tree, coterminous with Kiryas Joel. On June 14, 2018, special legislation was passed to move the official founding date forward by one year, signed by Governor Andrew Cuomo on July 1. The town became official on January 1, 2019, with officials elected in November 2018 being sworn in on that date. No candidates ran for town justice in 2018 or 2019; however, two non-resident lawyers were elected in the November 2019 elections through a write-in campaign supported by the leadership of the majority faction, as New York law normally requires town justices to be residents, but the town amended its laws to allow non-resident justices. In the same election, residents voted for a single consolidated town-village government to be governed as a village rather than a town. The name "Palm Tree" is a calque of Teitelbaum, meaning "date palm" from "teitel" (date) and "baum" (tree). According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the town has a total area of 1.5 square miles (3.9 km²), with only a small portion—specifically a duck pond called "Forest Road Lake"—covered in water. Palm Tree began with a 2019 founding population of 26,905, but since it shares the same boundaries as Kiryas Joel, its pre-incorporation demographics are known. As of the 2000 census, there were 13,138 people, 2,229 households, and 2,137 families in the village, with a population density of 11,962.2 inhabitants per square mile (4,618.6/km²) and 2,233 housing units at an average density of 2,033.2 units per square mile (785.0 units/km²). The racial composition was 99.02% White, 0.21% African American, 0.02% Asian, 0.12% from other races, and 0.63% from two or more races; Hispanic or Latino of any race made up 0.93%. Kiryas Joel had the highest percentage of people reporting Hungarian ancestry in the U.S., at 18.9% in 2000; 3% were Israeli, 2% Romanian, 1% Polish, and 1% European. In 2000, 6.3% of residents spoke only English at home, one of the lowest in the U.S., while 91.5% spoke Yiddish and 2.3% spoke Hebrew; 46% of Yiddish speakers spoke English "not well" or "not at all," and overall, 46% of residents spoke English "not well" or "not at all" when including those who primarily spoke Hebrew or European languages. There were 2,229 households, 79.5% of which had children under 18, 93.2% were married couples living together, 1.6% had a female householder with no husband, and 4.1% were non-families; 2.8% were made up of individuals, and 2.1% had someone living alone aged 65 or older. The average household size was 5.74, and the average family size was 5.84. The population was very young: 57.5% under 18, 17.2% aged 18–24, 16.5% aged 25–44, 7.2% aged 45–64, and 1.6% aged 65 or older; the median age was 15. For every 100 females, there were 116.3 males, and for every 100 females aged 18 and over, there were 118.0 males. The village follows strict Jewish customs, and its welcome sign (installed in 2010) asks visitors to dress conservatively and maintain gender separation in public areas, though the sign states there are no consequences for violating these guidelines.

The Panavia Tornado is a family of twin-engine, variable-sweep wing multi-role combat aircraft jointly developed and manufactured by Italy, the United Kingdom, and Germany. It consists of three primary variants: the Tornado IDS (interdictor/strike) fighter-bomber, the Tornado ECR (electronic combat/reconnaissance) SEAD aircraft, and the Tornado ADV (air defence variant) interceptor. Developed by Panavia Aircraft GmbH, a tri-national consortium comprising British Aerospace (formerly British Aircraft Corporation), MBB of West Germany, and Aeritalia of Italy, the Tornado first flew on 14 August 1974 and entered service between 1979 and 1980. Due to its multirole capabilities, it replaced several different aircraft types in the air forces of its operators. The Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF) is the only export operator of the Tornado, in addition to the three original partner nations. A training and evaluation unit, the Tri-National Tornado Training Establishment (TTTE), operated from RAF Cottesmore and maintained international cooperation beyond production. The Tornado is the only non-American-developed aircraft currently approved to carry United States nuclear weapons under NATO's Nuclear Planning Group. The Tornado was operated by the Royal Air Force (RAF), Italian Air Force, and RSAF during the Gulf War of 1991, conducting numerous low-altitude penetrating strike missions. It was also used in the Bosnian War, Kosovo War, Iraq War, the 2011 Libyan civil war, and in smaller roles in Afghanistan, Yemen, and Syria. Including all variants, 990 aircraft were built. The concept of variable-geometry wings was explored in the 1960s to combine the maneuverability of straight wings with the speed of swept wings. The UK cancelled the BAC TSR-2 and the US F-111K in 1965 and 1967, respectively, and sought a replacement for the Avro Vulcan and Blackburn Buccaneer. Britain and France initiated the BAC/Dassault AFVG project in 1965, which ended with French withdrawal in 1967. West Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, and Canada formed a working group in 1968 to replace the Lockheed F-104G Starfighter, initially called the Multi Role Aircraft (MRA) and later renamed the Multi Role Combat Aircraft (MRCA). Due to diverse requirements, a single multirole aircraft was developed. Britain joined in 1968, and a memorandum of agreement was signed between the UK, West Germany, and Italy in May 1969. By the end of 1968, the six countries planned to purchase 1,500 aircraft. Canada and Belgium withdrew before long-term commitments; Canada found the project politically unpalatable, and France offered Belgium the Dassault Mirage 5. On 26 March 1969, the UK, Germany, Italy, and the Netherlands agreed to form Panavia Aircraft GmbH to develop and manufacture the MRCA. The project aimed to produce an aircraft capable of tactical strike, reconnaissance, air defence, and maritime missions. Various design concepts, including fixed-wing and single-engine options, were studied. The Netherlands withdrew in 1970, citing complexity, and Germany reduced its order from 600 to 324 in 1972. It is suggested Germany initially placed a high order to secure design influence in Germany. The UK and West Germany each held a 42.5% share of the workload, with Italy holding 15%, influenced by political negotiations. The front fuselage and tail were assigned to BAC (now BAE Systems), the centre fuselage to MBB (now part of Airbus), and the wings to Aeritalia (now Leonardo). A separate company, Turbo-Union, formed in June 1970, developed the RB199 engines with ownership split 40% Rolls-Royce, 40% MTU, and 20% FIAT. In May 1970, two designs were selected: the single-seat Panavia 100 and the twin-seat Panavia 200, with the latter preferred by the RAF. The aircraft was briefly called the Panavia Panther. In September 1971, the three governments signed an Intention to Proceed (ITP) document, designating the aircraft for low-level strike missions, with the UK's Chief of the Defence Staff stating that two-thirds of the front-line fighting force would consist of this aircraft. The first of fifteen development aircraft, including nine prototypes (P01 to P09) and six pre-series (PS11 to PS16), flew on 14 August 1974 at Manching, Germany. Pilot Paul Millett described the flight as smooth and almost simulated. Flight testing required modifications, including re-profiling engine intakes and fuselage to reduce surging and buffeting at supersonic speeds. Jim Quinn, a developer of the Tornado simulation software and engine controls, noted that the prototype could reach supercruise safely, but engines had safety issues at high altitude during deceleration due to combustion pressure backfiring; engine controls automatically increased idle settings with altitude, leading to one aircraft being stuck at Mach 1.2 and unable to decelerate. A nose-wheel steering augmentation system was needed to counteract destabilization during landing with the thrust reverser deployed. Two prototypes were lost due to pilot error in ground collisions, and a third was seriously damaged by pilot-induced pitch oscillation. Designers incorporated advanced stability augmentation systems and autopilots, similar to those in the F-16. Failure testing of the triplex analogue CSAS was conducted on flight control rigs, complicated by variable-sweep wings and heavy payloads. The contract for Batch 1 aircraft was signed on 29 July 1976. The first production aircraft flew on 10 July 1979 at BAe Warton, with the first deliveries to the RAF and German Air Force on 5 and 6 June 1979, respectively. The first Italian Tornado was delivered on 25 September 1981. The TTTE officially opened on 29 January 1981 and remained active until 31 March 1999. The 500th Tornado was delivered to West Germany on 19 December 1987. Saudi Arabia was the only export customer, as part of the Al-Yamamah arms deal between British Aerospace and the Saudi government. Oman committed to purchasing eight Tornado F2s and associated equipment for £250 million in August 1985 but cancelled the order in 1990 due to financial difficulties. Australia considered joining the MRCA programme to replace its Dassault Mirage IIIs and ultimately selected the F/A-18 Hornet. Canada also chose the F/A-18 after considering the Tornado. Japan considered the Tornado in the 1980s, along with the F-16 and F/A-18, before selecting the Mitsubishi F-2. In the 1990s, Taiwan and South Korea expressed interest in acquiring small numbers of Tornado ECR aircraft. In 2001, EADS proposed a Tornado ECR variant with enhanced electronic warfare capabilities for Australia. Production ended in 1998, with the final batch going to the RSAF, which ordered 96 IDS Tornados. In June 2011, the Tornado fleet collectively flew over one million flying hours. Aviation author Jon Lake noted that the Panavia consortium produced just under 1,000 Tornados, making it one of the most successful postwar bomber programs. In 2008, AirForces Monthly called the Tornado "for more than a quarter of a century... the most important military aircraft in Western Europe." The Tornado is designed as a low-level penetration aircraft with variable-sweep wings enabling efficient high-speed and low-speed flight. Its mission during the Cold War involved delivering conventional and nuclear weapons against Warsaw Pact forces in Eastern Europe. The variable wing geometry minimizes drag during low-level flight. Advanced navigation and flight computers, including a fly-by-wire system, reduce pilot workload. For long-range missions, it has a retractable refuelling probe. As a multirole aircraft, it replaced multiple specialized aircraft types with a single platform, either through standard Tornados or modified variants like the Tornado ECR. The most extensive modification was the Tornado ADV, which was stretched and armed with long-range anti-aircraft missiles for interception. Operators have conducted life extension and upgrade programs, projecting continued service until 2025. To perform as a low-level supersonic strike aircraft, the Tornado required good high- and low-speed flight characteristics. A swept or delta wing is efficient at high speed but inefficient at low speed; the variable-sweep wing enables performance at both speeds. The wing sweep angle ranges from 25 to 67 degrees, with each angle having a specific speed range. Some Tornado ADVs had an automatic wing-sweep system. When wings are swept back, drag is reduced, aiding high-speed low-level flight. Weapons pylons pivot with the wing sweep so stores point in the direction of flight. Significant attention was given to short-field take-off and landing (STOL) performance, particularly in Germany. The Tornado can sweep wings to 25 degrees, deploy full-span flaps and leading edge slats, and use thrust reversers for excellent low-speed handling. The aircraft has a tandem-seat cockpit with a pilot and navigator/weapons officer, using electromechanical and electro-optical controls. Dials and switches are mounted on either side of a centrally placed CRT monitor for navigation, communications, and weapons control. BAE Systems developed the Tornado Advanced Radar Display Information System (TARDIS), a 32.5-centimetre multi-function display, replacing the rear cockpit's Combined Radar and Projected Map Display; the RAF began installing it on the GR4 fleet in 2004. The primary flight controls are a fly-by-wire hybrid, consisting of an analogue quadruplex Command and Stability Augmentation System (CSAS) connected to a digital Autopilot & Flight Director System (AFDS), with mechanical reversion retained for safety. Artificial feel is built into the controls, adjusting automatically to wing profile and flight attitude changes. The flight stability system compensates for changes in flight dynamics due to a wide range of munitions. The Tornado has a combined navigation/attack Doppler radar that scans for targets and conducts fully automated terrain-following for all-weather, hands-off low-level flight. The Tornado ADV uses the AI.24 Foxhunter radar, capable of tracking up to 20 targets at ranges up to 160 kilometres (100 miles). The Tornado was one of the first aircraft to feature a digital data bus, with Link 16 JTIDS integration on the F3 variant enabling data exchange with friendly aircraft. The Tornado ECR, operated by Germany and Italy, is dedicated to Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) and is equipped with an emitter-locator system (ELS) to detect radar use. German ECRs have a Honeywell infrared imaging system for reconnaissance. RAF and RSAF Tornados have the Laser Range Finder and Marked Target Seekers (LRMTS) for targeting laser-guided munitions. In 1991, the RAF introduced the Thermal Imaging and Laser Designator (TIALD) system.

The Tornado ADV features a different radar system, the AI.24 Foxhunter, designed for air defence operations, capable of tracking up to 20 targets at ranges of up to 160 kilometres (100 mi). It was one of the earliest aircraft to incorporate a digital data bus for data transmission, and the F3 variant includes Link 16 JTIDS integration, enabling the exchange of radar and sensory data with nearby friendly aircraft. Variants are equipped with mission-specific avionics: the German and Italian Tornado ECRs perform Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) missions and are fitted with an emitter-locator system (ELS) to detect radar use; German ECRs also have a Honeywell infrared imaging system for reconnaissance. RAF and RSAF Tornados are equipped with Laser Range Finder and Marked Target Seekers (LRMTS) for targeting laser-guided munitions; in 1991, the RAF introduced the Thermal Imaging and Laser Designator (TIALD), allowing Tornado GR1s to laser-designate their own targets. The GR1A and GR4A reconnaissance variants use the Tornado Infrared Reconnaissance System (TIRRS), which includes one SLIR sensor on each side of the fuselage forward of the engine intakes for oblique images and a single IRLS sensor on the underside for vertical images, with images recorded on six S-VHS video tapes; the RAPTOR reconnaissance pod replaced the built-in TIRRS system. The Tornado can carry a wide range of NATO air-launched weapons, including unguided and laser-guided bombs, anti-ship and anti-radiation missiles, and specialized munitions like anti-personnel mines and anti-runway weapons. To enhance combat survivability, it is equipped with onboard countermeasures such as flare and chaff dispensers and electronic countermeasure pods mounted under the wings; underwing fuel tanks and a buddy store aerial refuelling system allow range extension. Since its introduction, operators have conducted various upgrades to deploy new weapons, including the Enhanced Paveway and Joint Direct Attack Munition bombs and modern cruise missiles such as the Taurus and Storm Shadow, improving combat accuracy and capabilities; precision cruise missiles have replaced older munitions like cluster bombs. Strike variants have limited air-to-air capability with AIM-9 Sidewinder or AIM-132 ASRAAM missiles; the Tornado ADV is equipped with beyond visual range AAMs such as Skyflash and AIM-120 AMRAAM. The Tornado has two internally mounted 27 mm (1.063 in) Mauser BK-27 revolver cannons under the fuselage; the ADV variant has only one. When RAF GR1s were converted to GR4s, the FLIR sensor replaced the left cannon, leaving only one; the GR1A reconnaissance variant gave up both guns to accommodate sideways-looking infra-red sensors. The Mauser BK-27 was developed specifically for the Tornado and has since been used on other European fighters, including the Alpha Jet, JAS 39 Gripen, and Eurofighter Typhoon. The Tornado is capable of delivering air-launched nuclear weapons; in 1979, Britain considered replacing its Polaris submarines with either Trident or the Tornado as the primary nuclear deterrent, though it proceeded with Trident; several Tornado squadrons in Germany were assigned to SACEUR to deter a major Soviet offensive using conventional and nuclear weapons, including the WE.177, which was retired in 1998; German and Italian Tornados can deliver US B61 nuclear bombs through NATO. Britain insisted on Rolls-Royce developing the advanced engine for the MRCA, opposing American engine adoption, and in September 1969, Rolls-Royce's RB199 engine was selected; a technology transfer agreement led to joint development and manufacturing by Turbo-Union. The programme was delayed by Rolls-Royce's entry into receivership in 1971, but multinational collaboration prevented major disruption; research from the Concorde contributed to the RB199 and engine control unit development. The Tornado uses variable intake ramps to maximize air pressure entering the engine up to Mach 2; each engine drives an airframe gearbox with an electrical generator, hydraulic pump, and fuel boost pump, with both generators and hydraulic pumps capable of being driven by a single engine; in case of double-engine or double-generator failure, an emergency battery operates one fuel and one hydraulic pump for up to 13 minutes. The RB199 includes a thrust reverser to reduce landing distance, with a yaw damper connected to the nosewheel steering for greater stability when used. The first RB199 flight occurred under a Vulcan in April 1973; the first Tornado prototype, P01, flew on 14 August 1974 from Ingolstadt Manching Airport, West Germany, and the engine completed qualification tests in late 1978; the final production engine met reliability and performance standards, though development costs exceeded predictions due to ambitious performance requirements; early turbine blades had a shorter life, corrected by design revisions; several uprated engines were developed and used on most Tornado ADVs and German ECRs; the DECU (Digital Engine Control Unit) is the current engine control unit, replacing the analogue MECU (Main Engine Control Unit) or CUE. Designed for low-level operations, the Tornado required modifications for medium-level operations adopted by the RAF in the 1990s; the RAF re-manufactured its GR1 fleet into GR4s with upgrades including forward-looking infrared, a wide-angle HUD, improved cockpit displays, NVG capabilities, new avionics, and a GPS receiver, easing integration of new weapons and sensors such as the Storm Shadow cruise missile, Brimstone anti-tank missile, Paveway III bombs, and RAPTOR pod; the first GR4 flight was on 4 April 1997, with the first delivery on 31 October 1997 and completion of deliveries in 2003; in 2005, the RSAF upgraded its IDS fleet to match the RAF's GR4 configuration; in December 2007, BAE signed a £210m contract for CUSP, the Capability Upgrade Strategy (Pilot), which included integrating the Paveway IV bomb and a communications upgrade in Phase A, followed by a new tactical datalink in Phase B. German IDS and ECR Tornados began receiving the ASSTA 1 upgrade in 2000, which included a new weapons computer, GPS, and Laser Inertial navigation systems, enabling integration of HARM missiles, Taurus KEPD 350 missiles, Rafael Litening II pod, and Paveway III bombs; ASSTA 2, beginning in 2005, included new digital avionics and an ECM suite, applied to 85 aircraft (20 ECRs and 65 IDSs), as the Tornado is being phased out by the Eurofighter Typhoon; ASSTA 3, started in 2008, adds support for the laser-targeted Joint Direct Attack Munition and further software changes. In January 2016, Bild reported that the ASSTA 3.1 upgrade, featuring colour multifunctional LCD screens replacing monochrome CRT displays, interfered with helmet-mounted night-vision displays, rendering German Tornado bombers in Syria ineffective for night missions; the defence ministry acknowledged bright cockpit lights could distract pilots and said a solution would be implemented soon, but denied the need for night missions in Syria. TV TAB displays are used for route planning, FLIR sensors, and targeting pods such as TIALD and CLDP; the original MRCA TV TAB DU display (part number V22.498.90) uses a green CRT with a price of €33,852.64 per unit; high brightness levels caused CRT wear; an Active Matrix Liquid Crystal Display (AMLCD) drop-fit replacement (NSN 5895-99-597-1323) was developed to reduce lifecycle costs, featuring a color display and a bezel that reduces the viewing angle; the AMLCD has a built-in menu for selecting GR1, GR4, or F3, self-test, and display tests; the original CRT has two white domes with light sensors and white buttons, while the AMLCD has black buttons with white dots; the AMLCD requires only 28 VDC, unlike the CRT which needed both 115 VAC 400 Hz and 28 VDC, with a separate HVPS for the CRT; the AMLCD has a built-in 115 VAC to 28 VDC converter and no HVPS; it has a diagnostic connector and is considered a 'dumb' device compared to the original CRT, which only required a video signal and external waveform generator; the AMLCD has a self-test and display test features. In December 2013, BAE Systems test-flown a Tornado with 3D-printed parts, including a radio cover, landing-gear guard, and air-intake door support struts, demonstrating the feasibility of producing replacement parts quickly and cheaply at air bases; parts cost less than £100 to make, saving over £300,000, with potential savings reaching over £1.2 million by 2017. The first Tornado prototype flew on 14 August 1974 from Ingolstadt Manching Airport, West Germany; production deliveries began on 27 July 1979; a total of 247 Tornados were delivered to the German Air Force, including 35 ECR variants; originally, Tornados equipped five fighter-bomber wings, one tactical conversion unit, and four front-line wings, replacing the F-104 Starfighter; when one of the two German Navy Tornado wings was disbanded in 1994, its aircraft were used to re-equip a Luftwaffe reconnaissance wing previously equipped with RF-4E Phantoms. Fourteen German Tornados conducted combat operations during the Bosnian War as part of NATO's campaign, flying reconnaissance missions from Piacenza, Italy, to survey damage and scout new targets, significantly improving target selection. In 1999, German Tornados participated in Operation Allied Force, NATO's airstrikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the Kosovo War, marking Germany's first offensive air mission since WWII; ECRs escorted allied aircraft and carried AGM-88 HARM missiles to counter enemy radar; during the Kosovo conflict, IDS Tornados conducted reconnaissance to identify enemy ground forces and civilian refugees, flying 2108 hours and 446 sorties and firing 236 HARM missiles. In June 2007, two Luftwaffe Tornados flew reconnaissance missions over an anti-globalisation demonstration during the 33rd G8 summit in Heiligendamm; the German Defence Ministry admitted one aircraft breached the minimum flying altitude and acknowledged handling errors in summit security. In 2007, a detachment of six Tornados from Aufklärungsgeschwader 51 "Immelmann" was deployed to Mazar-i-Sharif, Northern Afghanistan, to support NATO forces; the deployment was controversial, with one political party launching an unsuccessful legal challenge; improvements to reconnaissance equipment were accelerated to enhance detection of hidden improvised explosive devices (IEDs); the German Tornados were withdrawn from Afghanistan in November 2010. Defence cuts announced in March 2003 led to the retirement of 90 Tornados, reducing Luftwaffe strength to four wings by September 2005; on 13 January 2004, German Defence Minister Peter Struck announced a plan to reduce the fighter fleet from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015, reducing the Tornado force to 85, with the type expected to remain in service until 2025; the retained aircraft are undergoing a service life extension programme. Currently, the Luftwaffe operates Tornados with Tactical Wings Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 33 at Cochem/Büchel Air Base, Rhineland-Palatinate, and Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 "Immelmann" at Jagel, Schleswig-Holstein. German Tornado aircrew training took place at Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico, US, starting in January 1996, at the Taktische Ausbildungskommando der Luftwaffe USA (TaktAusbKdoLw USA), which trained both German F-4 Phantom and Tornado crews.

A major part of the German defence announcement involved reducing the fighter fleet from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015, with the German Tornado force to be cut to 85, and the aircraft expected to remain in service with the Luftwaffe until 2025. The retained Tornados are undergoing a service life extension programme. Currently, the Luftwaffe operates Tornados with Tactical Wings Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 33 at Cochem/Büchel Air Base in Rhineland-Palatinate and Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 "Immelmann" at Jagel in Schleswig-Holstein. German Tornado aircrew training previously took place at Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico, US, from January 1996 through the Taktische Ausbildungskommando der Luftwaffe USA, which trained both German F-4 Phantom and Tornado crews; in 1999, the command was renamed Fliegerisches Ausbildungszentrum der Luftwaffe. In March 2015, Defence Minister Ursula von der Leyen decided to continue this training in Germany. In September 2017, flight training at Holloman for the Tornado was discontinued and transferred to Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 in Jagel, with the US location command dissolved in 2019. In April 2020, the German defence ministry planned to replace its Tornado fleet with 30 Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, 15 EA-18G Growlers, and 55 Eurofighter Typhoons, selecting the Super Hornet due to its compatibility with nuclear weapons and availability of an electronic attack version. In March 2020, the Super Hornet was not certified for the B61 nuclear bombs, though Dan Gillian, head of Boeing's Super Hornet program, stated that the German requirements could be met with U.S. government collaboration on the required timeline.
