In 2021, Airbus offered to replace 90 ageing Tornado IDS and ECR aircraft with 85 new Eurofighter Tranche 5 standard from 2030. In 2022, the German defence ministry announced that 35 Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning IIs would replace the Tornado fleet for nuclear sharing instead of the previously discussed 30 Boeing Super Hornets. In addition to the Luftwaffe order, the German Navy's Marineflieger received 112 IDS variants for anti-ship and marine reconnaissance roles, replacing the Starfighter, with two wings each having a nominal strength of 48 aircraft. The principal anti-ship weapon was the AS.34 Kormoran missile, initially supplemented by unguided bombs and BL755 cluster munitions, later by AGM-88 HARM anti-radar missiles, and reconnaissance missions used pods with panoramic optical cameras and infrared line scan. Following the end of the Cold War and the CFE Treaty, Germany reduced its armed forces, including combat aircraft; one Marineflieger Tornado wing was disbanded on 1 January 1994, with its aircraft replacing a Luftwaffe reconnaissance wing's Phantoms, and the second wing was enlarged and continued in anti-shipping, reconnaissance, and anti-radar roles until disbanded in 2005, with its aircraft and duties transferred to the Luftwaffe. The first Italian prototype of the Tornado made its maiden flight on 5 December 1975 from Turin; the Aeronautica Militare received 100 Tornado IDSs (known as A-200 in Italian service), with 16 converted to ECR configuration; the first Italian Tornado ECR (EA-200) was delivered on 27 February 1998. As a stop-gap, the Aeronautica Militare operated 24 Tornado ADVs in the air defence role, leased from the RAF to cover the gap between the retirement of the F-104 Starfighter and the introduction of the Eurofighter Typhoon. Italian Tornados, along with RAF Tornados, participated in the first Gulf War in 1991, with eight IDS interdictors deployed from Gioia del Colle to Al Dhafra, Abu Dhabi, as part of Italy's coalition contribution; one aircraft was lost to Iraqi anti-aircraft fire, with pilots ejecting safely and being captured. A total of 22 Italian Tornados were deployed in Operation Allied Force over Kosovo in 1999; A-200s served in bombing and EA-200s in radar suppression, firing 115 AGM-88 HARM missiles. In 2000, due to Eurofighter delays, Italy began searching for an interim fighter; while the Tornado was considered, long-term lease extensions requiring RAF CSP upgrades were deemed cost ineffective. In February 2001, Italy announced a lease of 35 F-16s from the US under the PEACE CAESAR programme. The Aeronautica Militare returned its Tornado ADVs to the RAF, with the final aircraft arriving at RAF St Athan on 7 December 2004; one was retained for static display at the Italian Air Force Museum. In July 2002, Italy signed a contract with the Tornado Management Agency (NETMA) and Panavia to upgrade 18 A-200s, the first received in 2003; the upgrade included improved navigation systems (integrated GPS and laser INS) and new weapons such as the Storm Shadow cruise missile, Joint Direct Attack Munition, and Paveway III laser-guided bombs. In response to anticipated violence during the 2010 Afghanistan elections, Italy dispatched four A-200 Tornados; it opted to extend the Tornado's service life over alternatives like the AMX, initiating a major upgrade and life extension programme in 2010 to include digital displays, Link 16 communications, night-vision goggles compatibility, and other upgrades. In the long term, Italy plans to replace its Tornado IDS/ECR fleet with the F-35 Lightning II, with the final Italian Tornado scheduled to be phased out in 2025; the first of 15 upgraded Tornado EA-200s was received on 15 June 2013. Italian Tornado A-200 and EA-200 aircraft participated in the UN no-fly zone enforcement during the 2011 Libya intervention; various coalition aircraft operated from Italy, including RAF Tornados; Italian military aircraft delivered 710 guided bombs and missiles, with 550 from A-200s and AMXs and 160 from Navy AV-8Bs; Tornados launched 20 to 30 Storm Shadow cruise missiles, the rest being Paveway and JDAM guided bombs. On 19 August 2014, two Italian Tornados collided mid-air during a training mission near Ascoli. On 14 November 2014, Italy announced it was sending four Tornado aircraft with 135 support staff to Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and two other bases in Kuwait for coalition operations against the Islamic State, using them for reconnaissance only. In October 2018, the EA-200 Tornado successfully completed operational testing of the AGM-88E AARGM, providing capabilities including expanded target set, counter-shutdown, advanced signals processing, geographic specificity, and weapon impact-assessment broadcast. Nicknamed the "Tonka" by the British, the first Tornado prototype (XX946) made its maiden flight on 30 October 1974 from BAC Warton; the first full production Tornado GR1 (ZA319) flew on 10 July 1979 from Warton; the first RAF Tornados (ZA320 and ZA322) were delivered to the TTTE at RAF Cottesmore on 1 July 1980. Crews qualified from the TTTE went to the Tornado Weapons Conversion Unit (TWCU), formed on 1 August 1981 at RAF Honington, before being posted to front-line squadrons. No. IX (B) Squadron became the first front-line squadron in the world to operate the Tornado upon reformation on 1 June 1982, receiving its first Tornado GR1 ZA586 on 6 January 1982; it was declared strike combat ready to SACEUR in January 1983. Two more squadrons were formed at RAF Marham in 1983—No. 617 Squadron on 1 January and No. 27 Squadron on 12 August. The first RAF Tornado GR1 loss occurred on 27 September 1983 when ZA586 suffered complete electrical failure and crashed; navigator Flt. Lt. Nigel Nickles ejected but pilot Sqn. Ldr. Michael Stephens died after ordering ejection. In January 1984, the TWCU became No. 45 (Reserve) Squadron. RAF Germany (RAFG) began receiving Tornados with the formation of No. XV (Designate) Squadron on 1 September 1983 at RAF Laarbruch, followed by No. 16 (Designate) Squadron in January 1984 (both former Buccaneer squadrons), and No. 20 (Designate) Squadron in May 1984 (operating SEPECAT Jaguar GR1 from RAF Brüggen). Unlike UK-based Tornado squadrons under British control, RAFG squadrons were under SACEUR, with aircraft on Quick Reaction Alert (Nuclear), "QRA (N)", equipped with the WE.177 nuclear bomb; in the event of a 'hot' Cold War, the majority were tasked with destroying Warsaw Pact airfields and SAM sites in East Germany; No. 20 Squadron had a separate mission to destroy bridges over the Elbe and Weser rivers. By early 1985, Nos. XV, 16, and 20 Squadrons at RAF Laarbruch were declared strike combat ready to SACEUR. Tornados began arriving at RAF Brüggen in September 1984 with No. 31 (Designate) Squadron, No. 17 (Designate) Squadron formed in December 1984, and No. 14 (Designate) Squadron in mid-1985. No. IX (B) Squadron relocated from RAF Honington to RAF Brüggen on 1 October 1986, arriving in a diamond formation. The Reykjavík Summit in October 1986 ended QRA (Nuclear) for the Tornado force. By the end of 1986, the Tornado GR1 fleet had been equipped with a Laser Ranger and Marked Target Seeker (LRMTS) under the nose and began receiving BOZ-107 chaff and flare dispensers. The Tornado made its combat debut in Operation Granby, the British contribution to the Gulf War in 1991, with 49 RAF Tornado GR1s deployed to Muharraq Airfield in Bahrain and to Tabuk and Dhahran Air Bases in Saudi Arabia. Eighteen Tornado F3s were deployed to provide air cover, deterring Iraqi pilots with long-range missiles. Early in the conflict, GR1s targeted Iraqi airfields using 450 kg unguided bombs in loft-bombing and JP233 runway denial weapons. On 17 January 1991, the first Tornado was shot down by an Iraqi SA-16 missile after a failed low-level bombing run; on 19 January, another was shot down during an intensive raid on Tallil Air Base. Six RAF Tornados were lost in the conflict—four with unguided bombs, one after JP233, and one attempting to deliver laser-guided bombs. The UK sent a detachment of Buccaneer aircraft with Pave Spike laser designators to allow Tornado GR1s to drop precision-guided weapons; a programme to fit GR1s with the TIALD laser designation system was accelerated, enabling the GR1 to achieve "probably the most accurate bombing in the RAF's history," according to Claus-Christian Szejnmann. Although effective, only 23 TIALD pods were purchased by 2000, causing shortages during operations over Kosovo. After the war's opening phase, GR1s switched to medium-level strike missions targeting munition depots and oil refineries; only the reconnaissance GR1As continued low-altitude, high-speed missions without incident. After the conflict, Britain maintained a military presence in the Gulf, with around six GR1s based at Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait contributing to the southern no-fly zone under Operation Southern Watch and six additional GR1s participating in Operation Provide Comfort over Northern Iraq. The upgraded Tornado GR4 made its operational debut in Operation Southern Watch, patrolling Iraq's southern airspace from Kuwait. Both GR1s and GR4s based at Ali Al Salem participated in coalition strikes during Operation Desert Fox in 1998. In December 1998, an Iraqi anti-aircraft battery fired six to eight missiles at a patrolling Tornado; the battery was later attacked in retaliation, with no aircraft lost. It was reported that during Desert Fox, RAF Tornados successfully destroyed 75% of their targets, with 28 of 36 planned missions completed. The GR1 participated in the Kosovo War in 1999, initially operating from RAF Brüggen and later from Solenzara Air Base, Corsica. Experiences from Kosovo led to the RAF procuring AGM-65 Maverick missiles and Enhanced Paveway smart bombs. Following the Kosovo War, the GR1 was phased out as aircraft were upgraded to GR4 standard; the final upgrade was returned to the RAF on 10 June 2003. The GR4 was used in Operation Telic, Britain's contribution to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, flying alongside American aircraft in the opening phase, striking Iraqi targets. Aiming to minimize civilian casualties, Tornados deployed the Storm Shadow cruise missile for the first time; while 25% of UK air-launched weapons in Kosovo were precision-guided, this ratio increased to 85% in Iraq. On 23 March 2003, a Tornado GR4 was shot down over Iraq by friendly fire from a US Patriot missile battery, killing both crew members. In July 2003, a US board of inquiry exonerated the battery's operators, noting the Tornado's "lack of functioning IFF (Identification Friend or Foe)."

The RAF operated Tornado GR1 and GR4 variants, with the GR1 initially entering service in the early 1980s, the first aircraft delivered on 5 June 1979. The GR1B, a specialized anti-shipping variant, replaced the Buccaneer, with 26 aircraft converted and based at RAF Lossiemouth, each capable of carrying up to four Sea Eagle anti-ship missiles; early GR1Bs lacked radar for tracking shipping and relied on missile seekers, later upgraded to pass target data from aircraft to missile. A single GR1 (ZA326) was rebuilt into a GR1P after a fire during testing and served with the Royal Aircraft Establishment and Empire Test Pilot's School until retired in 2005, becoming the last GR1 in service globally. The UK Ministry of Defence began studies for a GR1 Mid-Life Update in 1984, and in 1994, a GR4 upgrade was approved to improve medium-altitude capabilities based on lessons from the 1991 Gulf War. British Aerospace (later BAE Systems) upgraded 142 GR1s to GR4 standard between 1996 and 2003. Fifty-nine RAF GR4s later received the CUSP avionics upgrade, achieving Initial Service Date in March 2013, which included integration of Paveway IV bombs and new secure communications from Cassidian in Phase A and Tactical Information Exchange (TIE) datalink from General Dynamics in Phase B. The GR1A reconnaissance variant, operated by the RAF and RSAF, used the TIRRS system and replaced the cannon; 30 GR1As were ordered, 14 as rebuilds and 16 new. When upgraded to GR4 standard, GR1As became GR4A, and with the shift from low-level to medium/high-level operations, the internal TIRRS was no longer used, leading the RAF's Tactical Reconnaissance Wing to operate both GR4A and GR4 aircraft. The Tornado ADV, operated by the RAF (designated F2 or F3), Saudi Arabia, and Italy, was developed as a long-endurance interceptor, not a dogfighter, with 80% parts commonality with the IDS, greater acceleration, improved RB199 Mk.104 engines, a stretched body, greater fuel capacity, AI.24 Foxhunter radar, and software changes, featuring only one cannon for an inflight refuelling probe. The ECR variant, operated by Germany and Italy, was designed for Suppression of Enemy Air Defences, equipped with radar detection and AGM-88 HARM anti-radiation missiles; the Luftwaffe received 35 new ECRs, Italy received 16 converted IDSs, Italian ECRs lacked built-in reconnaissance and used RecceLite pods, only Luftwaffe ECRs had the RB199 Mk.105 engine with higher thrust, and German ECRs did not carry a cannon. The RAF used the IDS version in the SEAD role and modified some Tornado F.3s for this mission. The GR4 was used in Operation Telic, Britain's contribution to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, with RAF Tornados flying alongside American aircraft in the opening phase, striking Iraqi targets, and deploying the Storm Shadow cruise missile for the first time to minimize civilian casualties. While 25% of UK air-launched weapons in Kosovo were precision-guided, this ratio increased to 85% in Iraq four years later. On 23 March 2003, a Tornado GR4 was shot down over Iraq by friendly fire from a US Patriot missile battery, killing both crew members; a US board of inquiry in July 2003 exonerated the operators, citing the Tornado's "lack of functioning IFF" as a factor, with problems in Patriot systems also suggested, including a fatal shootdown of a US Navy F/A-18 a few weeks later. Britain withdrew the last of its Tornados from Iraq in June 2009. In early 2009, several GR4s arrived at Kandahar Airfield, Afghanistan, to replace Harrier GR7/9 aircraft deployed since November 2004. In 2009, Paveway IV guided bombs were introduced on RAF Tornados, previously used by Harriers in Afghanistan. In summer 2010, extra Tornados were dispatched to Kandahar for the 2010 Afghan election. British Tornados ended operations in Afghanistan in November 2014, having flown over 5,000 pairs of sorties for 33,500 hours, including 600 "shows of force" to deter Taliban attacks, with over 70 engagements deploying 140 Brimstone missiles and Paveway IV bombs and over 3,000 27 mm cannon shells. Prior to the 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review (SDSR), the Tornado's retirement was under consideration with £7.5 billion in anticipated savings; the SDSR retained the Tornado at the expense of the Harrier, with numbers declining as the fleet transitioned to Eurofighter Typhoon and F-35 Lightning II. By July 2013, 59 GR4s were receiving the CUSP avionics upgrade. On 18 March 2011, British Prime Minister David Cameron announced Tornados and Typhoons would enforce a no-fly zone in Libya; in March 2011, several Tornados flew 3,000-mile strike missions against targets inside Libya, the longest-range bombing mission by the RAF since the Falklands conflict, using laser-guided bombs and Brimstone missiles. In August 2014, Tornado GR4s were deployed to RAF Akrotiri, Cyprus, to support refugees from Islamic State militants in northern Iraq, following US air attacks; on 27 September 2014, after Parliament approved airstrikes in Iraq, two Tornados conducted their first armed reconnaissance mission with coalition aircraft, and the next day made the first airstrike on a heavy weapons post and armored vehicle, supporting Kurdish forces in northwest Iraq. By 1 March 2015, eight Tornados had been deployed to Akrotiri and conducted 159 airstrikes against IS targets in Iraq. On 2 December 2015, Parliament approved air strikes in Syria and Iraq to combat ISIL; Tornados began bombing that evening. On 14 April 2018, four Tornado GR4s from RAF Akrotiri struck a Syrian military facility with Storm Shadow cruise missiles in response to a suspected chemical attack on Douma by the Syrian regime. On 10 July 2018, nine Tornado GR4s from RAF Marham flew over London to celebrate 100 years of the RAF. In late 2018, the RAF commemorated the Tornado's service with three special schemes: ZG752 with green/grey camouflage, and ZG775 and ZD716 honoring the final operating units, No. IX (B) Squadron and No. 31 Squadron. On 31 January 2019, the Tornado GR4 flew its last operational sorties in Operation Shader. The eight Tornados from RAF Akrotiri returned to RAF Marham in early February 2019, their duties taken over by six Typhoons. Between September 2014 and January 2019, RAF Tornados accounted for 31% of the estimated 4,315 casualties inflicted on ISIL. On 19, 20, and 21 February 2019, flypasts were held over BAE Warton, RAF Honington, and RAF Lossiemouth to mark 40 years of service and retirement. On 28 February, nine Tornados flew a diamond nine formation flypast over a graduation parade at RAF Cranwell before returning and conducting passes over RAF Marham. On 14 March 2019, the final flight of an RAF Tornado was carried out by Tornado GR4 ZA463, the oldest remaining Tornado, over RAF Marham during the disbandment parade of No. IX (B) Squadron and No. 31 Squadron. The Tornado GR4 was officially retired from RAF service on 1 April 2019, the 101st anniversary of the RAF. Post-retirement, five Tornados returned to RAF Honington by road for the Complex Air Ground Environment (CAGE) training simulation. On 2 July 2023, pylons from decommissioned RAF Tornado GR4s were fitted to Ukrainian Su-24s to launch Storm Shadow missiles, with the Su-24s capable of carrying at least two Storm Shadows, requiring target coordinates to be entered before takeoff. In 1984, Royal Saudi Air Force pilots visited RAF Honington to evaluate the Tornado GR1. On 25 September 1985, the UK and Saudi Arabia signed the Al Yamamah I contract, including the sale of 48 IDS and 24 ADV Tornados. In October 1985, four RSAF crews joined the Tri-National Tornado Training Establishment at RAF Cottesmore. The first Saudi Tornado IDS (701) flew on 17 February 1986, and the first four IDS were delivered to King Abdul Aziz Air Base, Dharan on 26 March 1986. The first Saudi Tornado squadron, No. 7 Squadron, received 20 aircraft by 8 October 1987. The first Saudi ADV (2905) flew on 1 December 1988, with first deliveries arriving in Saudi Arabia on 20 March 1989. The first two RSAF ADV squadrons, Nos. 29 and 34, reached full strength of 12 aircraft each by 1990. In the run-up to the Gulf War, the RSAF pooled its Tornado squadrons, with a joint 24-aircraft ADV unit flying missions in Operation Desert Shield. Saudi Tornados participated in the Gulf War, with No. 7 Squadron conducting its first mission on the night of 17 January 1991; in total, the RSAF flew 665 IDS sorties and 451 ADV sorties, losing one IDS (765) on the night of 19/20 January. In June 1993, the Al Yamamah II contract was signed, including 48 additional IDSs. Following experience with the Tornado and F-15E, the RSAF discontinued low-level training in the F-15E due to the Tornado's superior low-altitude performance. Ten Saudi Tornados were fitted for reconnaissance missions. The 22 Tornado ADVs were replaced by the Eurofighter Typhoon; retired aircraft were purchased back by the UK. By 2007, both the Sea Eagle anti-ship missile and ALARM anti-radiation missile had been withdrawn from RSAF Tornado service. As of 2010, Saudi Arabia signed contracts for new weapon systems, including IRIS-T air-to-air, Brimstone, and Storm Shadow missiles. In September 2006, Saudi Arabia signed a £2.5 billion (US$4.7 billion) contract with BAE Systems to upgrade up to 80 RSAF Tornado IDS aircraft to remain in service until 2020 under the "Tornado Sustainment Programme" (TSP), to equip them with new precision-guided weapons and enhanced targeting equipment common with UK Tornado GR4 systems. The first RSAF Tornado was returned to BAE Systems Warton in December 2006 for upgrade, and the first modernized aircraft returned to Saudi Arabia in December 2007. Starting in November 2009, RSAF Tornados, along with F-15s, conducted air raids during the Shia insurgency in north Yemen, the first such operation since Operation Desert Storm in 1991. RSAF Tornados continue to play a central role in Saudi-led bombing campaigns in Yemen. On 7 January 2018, Houthi fighters claimed to have shot down a Saudi warplane conducting raids over northern Yemen; Saudi reports stated it was an RSAF Tornado lost for 'technical reasons' with both crew rescued. On 12 July 2018, another RSAF Tornado crashed in Asir region after returning from Saada, Yemen due to a technical malfunction. On 14 February 2020, a Saudi Tornado was shot down during a close air support mission in Yemen's Al Jouf governorate by Houthis; the next day, the Saudi command confirmed the loss, and a video showed the downing using a two-stage surface-to-air missile, with both pilots ejecting and being captured by Houthis.

The aircraft featured improvements such as increased acceleration, upgraded RB199 Mk.104 engines, a longer fuselage, enhanced fuel capacity, the AI.24 Foxhunter radar, and software updates. It was equipped with a single cannon to allow space for a retractable in-flight refuelling probe. Information is sourced from International Warbirds: An Illustrated Guide to World Military Aircraft, 1914–2000 and Tornado, Modern Fighting Aircraft. The document includes sections on general characteristics, performance, armament, avionics, related development, aircraft of comparable role, configuration, and era, and related lists.

Paola Severino, born on 22 October 1948 in Naples, is an Italian lawyer, academic, and politician. She studied law at La Sapienza University of Rome and graduated in 1971. She began her career as a researcher at the Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche (National Council of Research) in 1972, working there until 1975, after which she served as an assistant professor at La Sapienza from 1975 to 1987. She later worked at Perugia University, teaching penal commercial law at the Faculty of Economics. In 1997, she was appointed vice president of the Superior Council of Military Magistracy, becoming the first Italian woman to hold this position; her tenure lasted until 2002. She also worked with Giovanni Maria Flick, former President of the Italian Constitutional Court. Severino is recognized as one of Italy’s top criminal lawyers and has represented prominent clients such as former Prime Minister Romano Prodi, Cesare Geronzi, and Francesco Caltagirone in the Cirio trial, as well as the Italian energy giant Eni. She served as head of the law department at LUISS Guido Carli University from 2003 to 2006 and previously held positions as professor of penal law at the School for Carabinieri Officers and Pro-Rector Vicar at LUISS Guido Carli University. On 16 November 2011, she was appointed Minister of Justice in the Monti cabinet, becoming the first woman to hold this office in Italian history; her income in 2011 exceeded seven million euros, making her the highest-paid minister in the cabinet. Her term ended in April 2013, when Anna Maria Cancellieri succeeded her. She is married to former CONSOB executive Paolo Di Benedetto, with whom she has a daughter, and is an amputee who lost her right arm due to illness. On 3 October 2016, she was nominated rector of Libera Università Internazionale degli Studi Sociali Guido Carli. From 2018 to 2020, she served as Special Representative of the President-in-Office of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) for the fight against corruption, a role established by the Italian Presidency of the organization in 2018.

The Paris Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award is presented annually by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) to recognize specific theoretical achievements that have produced a significant and measurable impact on the practice of computing. Established in 1996, the award commemorates Paris C. Kanellakis, a computer scientist who died in a plane crash in South America in 1995, along with his immediate family, aboard American Airlines Flight 965. The award includes a prize of $10,000 and is funded by contributions from Kanellakis's parents, supplemented by financial support from four ACM Special Interest Groups—SIGACT, SIGDA, SIGMOD, and SIGPLAN—the ACM SIG Projects Fund, and individual donations.

Park Geun-hye, born on 2 February 1952 in Samdeok-dong, Jung District, Daegu, South Korea, is a South Korean politician who served as the 11th president of South Korea from 25 February 2013 until her removal from office in 2017. She is the eldest daughter of Park Chung Hee, who became the third president of South Korea after the May 16 military coup in 1961 and served from 1963 to 1979, and his wife, First Lady Yuk Young-soo. Both of her parents were assassinated; her mother, Yuk Young-soo, was killed on 15 August 1974 in the National Theater of Korea during an assassination attempt by Mun Se-gwang, and her father, Park Chung Hee, was assassinated on 26 October 1979 by his intelligence chief, Kim Jae-gyu. Park Geun-hye served as the first lady of South Korea from 1974 until her father's assassination. She has a younger sister, Park Geun-ryeong, a younger brother, Park Ji-man, and an older half-sister, Park Jae-ok. She is unmarried and has no children. Park graduated from Sogang University in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in electronic engineering and briefly studied at Joseph Fourier University in France before leaving after her mother's murder. She received honorary doctoral degrees from the Chinese Culture University in Taiwan in 1987, Pukyong National University and KAIST in 2008, Sogang University in 2010, and TU Dresden in 2014. Park served as a member of the National Assembly for four consecutive terms between 1998 and 2012, first elected in a 1998 by-election for Dalseong County (Daegu), and was re-elected three times in the same district until April 2012. In 2012, she announced she would not run for a constituency seat but instead for a proportional representative position to lead the Saenuri Party, which she won in the April 2012 election. She was leader of the conservative Grand National Party (GNP) from 2004 to 2006 and later the Liberty Korea Party (Saenuri Party) from 2011 to 2012. In 2006, she was attacked by Ji Chung-ho, who slashed her face with a utility knife, causing an 11-centimeter wound requiring 60 stitches; after recovery, she reportedly said, "How is Daejeon?" which contributed to the victory of the GNP candidate in the Daejeon mayoral race. She earned the nickname "Queen of Elections" for leading the GNP to win all 40 reelections and by-elections during her tenure as chairwoman from 2004 to 2006. In 2007, she visited Harvard University, where she advocated for a stronger U.S.-South Korea relationship. She was the leading candidate for the 2012 presidential election in every national poll between 2008 and September 2011, with approval ratings ranging from 25% to 45%, and was the top candidate in a national survey with a 45.5% approval rating in August 2012 and a 50.6% rating in a two-way competition against Ahn Cheol-soo in September. She was elected president on 19 December 2012 with 51.6% of the vote. Her inauguration on 25 February 2013, the largest in South Korean history with 70,000 participants, included diplomatic representatives from 24 countries. In her inauguration speech, she outlined a vision of "a new era of hope and happiness" with five administrative goals: a jobs-centered creative economy, tailored employment and welfare, creativity-oriented education and cultural enrichment, a safe and united society, and strong security measures for peace on the Korean Peninsula. She emphasized economic prosperity, people's happiness, cultural enrichment, and peaceful unification. She restructured the Blue House and government, launching new offices including the Office of National Security, the Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and revived the Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs. On 5 June 2013, she announced a plan to build a "Creative Economy" to revitalize the economy and create jobs. In April 2013, she emphasized the importance of timely economic policy and encouraged the gig economy. On 8 April 2014, she signed the Australia–Korea Free Trade Agreement with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Park proposed eliminating the "Four Major Social Evils"—sexual violence, domestic violence, school violence, and unsafe food—and launched the National Unity Committee on 17 June 2013, chaired by Han Kwang-ok, to resolve societal conflicts and promote co-existence. After taking office, she met with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and President Barack Obama, and made her first foreign trip to the United States in May 2013. In 2017, the National Intelligence Service admitted it had conducted an illicit campaign to influence the 2012 presidential election to ensure Park defeated Moon Jae-in. In 2016, Park was impeached by the National Assembly on charges of influence peddling by her aide, Choi Soon-sil, and Prime Minister Hwang Kyo-ahn assumed her duties as acting president. The Constitutional Court upheld the impeachment on 10 March 2017 by a unanimous 8–0 decision, making her the first Korean president to be removed from office. On 6 April 2018, South Korean courts sentenced her to 24 years in prison (later increased to 25 years) for corruption and abuse of power. In 2018, two separate criminal cases increased her sentence by seven years: five years for illegally taking off-the-books funds from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) and two years for illegally interfering in the Saenuri Party primaries in the 2016 legislative election. On 24 December 2021, she was granted a pardon on compassionate grounds by President Moon Jae-in, was released from prison on 31 December, and returned home on 24 March 2022. Park chose not to vote in the 2017 South Korean presidential election.

Park advocated for ordinary people to organize a supplementary budget promptly for economic policy, jobs, and livelihoods, and encouraged the growth of the gig economy. On 8 April 2014, she signed the Australia–Korea Free Trade Agreement with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. She proposed eliminating the "Four Major Social Evils"—sexual violence, domestic violence, school violence, and unsafe food, noting that statistics indicated increases in sexual and domestic violence during that period, though without citing data, school violence and food safety remained significant public concerns. On 17 June, she launched the National Unity Committee, chaired by former Democratic United Party Advisor Han Kwang-ok, to advise on resolving societal conflicts and fostering co-existence and co-prosperity. After taking office, Park met with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and President Barack Obama; her first foreign trip, in May 2013, included visits to Washington, D.C., New York City, and Los Angeles. During summit talks at the White House, Park and Obama issued a joint declaration strengthening the American-South Korean alliance, discussed peace in Northeast Asia, and agreed on a joint statement for comprehensive energy cooperation and the establishment of a policy cooperation committee on information and communication technology. Park also urged the U.S. to expand the annual visa quota for South Korean professionals to boost economic cooperation. In June 2013, she visited China, meeting with President Xi Jinping, and on 13 November 2013, held an extended meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose visit was the first among leaders of the U.S., China, Japan, and Russia; the two leaders considered combining Korea's Eurasian Initiative with Russia's Asia-Pacific Policy and issued a joint communique and held a joint press conference. Earlier, at the September 2013 G-20 Summit in St. Petersburg, Park met Putin separately to discuss economic cooperation and North Korean issues, marking the first Korea–Russia summit since her inauguration. During her meeting with Russian Far East Minister Viktor Ishaev, she stated Russia was a key strategic partner. North Korea conducted provocations, including violating a UN Security Council resolution, firing a long-range missile on 12 December 2012, and carrying out a third nuclear test on 12 February 2013, nullifying non-aggression agreements on 8 March, and withdrawing workers from the Kaesong Industrial Region on 8 April. Park maintained that South Korea would not yield to North Korean provocations and would seek policy coordination with the U.S., China, and the UN, a stance that gained support from South Koreans and major powers and contributed to the unanimous adoption of UN Security Council Resolution 2094 on 7 March 2013. As a result, North Korea ceased provocations on 6 June and proposed discussions on reopening the Kaesong Industrial Complex. Park stated that peace and unification are the shared wish of all 70 million Koreans and that her administration would work to achieve this goal, emphasizing that reunification should improve quality of life, expand freedom and human rights, and build a prosperous peninsula. She also stated that North Korea must accept her trust-building policy initiative. Her policy on North Korea and unification is reflected in the Korean Peninsula Trust-building Process, with the Ministry of Unification announcing a vision of "realizing a new unified Korea that ensures everyone's happiness," including normalizing inter-Korean relations, launching small-scale unification projects, and strengthening unification capabilities. Park outlined a three-stage unification initiative: securing peace, achieving economic integration, and reaching political integration, with humanitarian assistance, inter-Korean exchanges, and the "Vision Korea project" to establish a single economic community, contingent on mutual trust and North Korean denuclearization. On 28 March 2014, during a state visit to Germany, she proposed three steps to North Korea, starting with jointly managing rivers and forests across the two Koreas, and urged North Korea to attend the UN Convention on Biological Diversity conference in Pyeongchang in October. In May 2014, Park warned that a new North Korean nuclear test could trigger a "nuclear domino effect," potentially prompting neighbors to acquire nuclear weapons. On 18 May 2014, she announced plans to dismantle the South Korean Coast Guard after its poor response during the MV Sewol ferry disaster, transferring investigation and information roles to the National Police and rescue and ocean security roles to the Department for National Safety, with the Korean Ministry of Security and Public Administration being newly established. On 19 November 2014, the Korea Coast Guard and National Emergency Management Agency ceased control as the Ministry of Public Safety and Security was founded. On 26 May 2015, Park urged the head of the Asian Development Bank to cooperate with South Korea and the China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, following South Korea's official application to join the latter in late March 2015. On 1 May 2016, Park became the first South Korean president to visit Iran, leading a 236-member delegation of businessmen and entrepreneurs for a three-day visit to Tehran, where she met President Hassan Rouhani and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and signed 19 basic agreements to expand cooperation. Iran's President Rouhani stated that bilateral trade would grow from $6 billion to $18 billion. In the 2016 general elections on 13 April, the Saenuri Party lost its majority and first-party status in the National Assembly, with Park criticized for her role in the election and nomination process, and pro-Park faction members blamed for the defeat. Park loyalists also performed poorly in constituency elections, hindering her proposed economic reforms and leading conservative The Chosun Ilbo to state that her "lame duck period" began earlier than any previous administration. In July 2013, public support for Park reached 63 percent, higher than her 52 percent election vote share, attributed to her principled North Korea policy, constructive outcomes from U.S. and Chinese visits, and distancing from internal disputes. By January 2015, her approval rating had dropped to 30 percent due to the MV Sewol sinking and North Korea disputes, rising to 54 percent by September 2015 due to successful diplomacy defusing a military standoff with North Korea, but falling to 31.5 percent after the 2016 election loss, a drop of 8.1 percentage points. On 4 November 2016, her ratings fell to 4–5% as details of her relationship with Choi Soon-sil were exposed in the 2016 South Korean political scandal. Park was arrested on 31 March 2017 and held at the Seoul Detention Center in Uiwang, Gyeonggi Province. On 17 April 2017, she was formally charged with abuse of power, bribery, coercion, and leaking government secrets, denying the charges during five rounds of interrogation. Prosecutors sought a 30-year prison term and a fine of ₩188.5 billion (US$110,579,397). On 6 April 2018, a three-judge panel of the Central District Court in Seoul sentenced her to 24 years in prison and a fine of ₩18 billion (US$16,798,683), finding her guilty of 16 out of 18 charges. In June 2018, three former NIS directors—Lee Byung-kee, Lee Byung-ho, and Nam Jae-joon—were found guilty of bribery for illegally transferring funds from the NIS budget to Park's office, which were then used for private purposes and bribes. On 24 August 2018, Park's sentence was increased to 25 years. In July 2020, an appellate court reduced her sentence to 20 years, citing that she received little personal benefit and was cleared of alleged extortion from conglomerates donating to Choi Soon-sil's foundations. In January 2021, South Korea's top court upheld the 20-year sentence. On 24 December 2021, Park was pardoned by President Moon Jae-in, citing her deteriorating health and the need to "overcome unfortunate past history and promote national unity." She was released from prison on 31 December and returned home on 24 March 2022. New President Yoon Suk-yeol invited her to his inauguration ceremony on 10 May 2022. Park faced criticism for being the "daughter of a dictator" (Park Chung Hee), with supporters of Lee Myung-bak criticizing her lack of support for his administration. A 2012 national-level poll found that 59% of respondents did not believe she was a "daughter of a dictator," while 36% did. Park Chung Hee's legacy became contested after the 1997 financial crisis, with GNP party elites promoting his economic achievements to reshape his image. In a 2012 interview with CJB, Park stated her father's 1961 May 16 coup was a "revolution to save the country," asserting that politicians should not debate whether it was a coup or revolution. A July 2012 survey found that 50% of respondents disagreed with her view that the coup was "unavoidable, the best possible choice, and advisable," while 37% agreed. Another survey showed 42% agreed it was unavoidable, while 46% disagreed. Because Park inherited strong regional and generational support from her father and his economic legacy, opponents used this to criticize her. Park faced scrutiny over the Jeongsoo Scholarship Foundation, formerly known as Buil (linked to the Busan Ilbo newspaper), which her father and she headed; original owners claimed they were forced to transfer it to her father. Liberty Korea Party member Nam Kyung-pil criticized the party's Park-centered nature, stating that repeated instances of Park giving press conferences before party meetings and having her statements adopted as official positions suggested democracy had disappeared. Critics also noted that Park's behavior in the 2012 election campaign was a mix of trend-following and corner-cutting, contrasting with her principled opposition to revising the Sejong City multifunctional administrative city plan. For example, Yim Tae-hee criticized Park for voting down a motion to arrest Chung Doo-un, a lawmaker implicated in bank bribery, and Ahn Sang-soo accused her of "saying one thing yesterday and another today." Park fired Yoon Chang-jung, a Blue House spokesman, after allegations from Washington Police that he committed sexual assault against an intern at the South Korean Embassy in Washington during her first U.S. visit. Just before the 2012 presidential election, the opposition alleged that NIS public servants organized an online campaign promoting Park and attacking opponents, a violation of the Korean Constitution. To prove the allegation, the opposition, along with police and the Central Election Assistance Commission, investigated. A 29-year-old female agent, Ha-Young Kim, who ran an illegal online campaign, locked herself in her home, leading to a three-day standoff that provoked political tension. The opposition accused the intelligence service of blocking the investigation, while Park and her party accused the opposition of harassing the agent. Later, during the presidential debate, Kim Yong-pan, then chief of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, announced there was no evidence of illegal online postings from the agent's laptop, an announcement believed to have significantly affected the election outcome. After months of investigation, prosecutors concluded in mid-June 2013 that NIS chief Won Sei-hoon, who served under former President Lee Myung-bak, ordered agents to conduct a systematic online smear campaign against opposition candidates using hundreds of user IDs. The special investigation found that agents systematically intervened in domestic politics through thousands of cyber postings. Kim Yong-pan was prosecuted without physical detention on charges of abusing his authority to obstruct police investigations.

Park faced significant political and legal challenges throughout her presidency. In the lead-up to the presidential election, Park was criticized for allegedly harassing a woman during a presidential candidate debate, where she claimed the self-lock-in standoff violated a female right. Three days before the election, Kim Yong-pan, then chief of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency (SMPA), publicly stated there was no evidence of illegal online postings from a female agent’s laptop, an announcement that the opposing party believed significantly influenced the election outcome. Despite this, internal police CCTV recordings revealed that analysts had already identified illegal online postings targeting opposition candidates, suggesting intentional misinformation. The prosecution concluded in mid-June 2013 that Won Sei-hoon, former NIS chief under President Lee Myung-bak, ordered agents to conduct a systematic online smear campaign, resulting in 55,689 messages posted on Twitter over three months. The special investigation team, led by Yoon Suk-ryul, was disbanded, with Yoon returning to his original position as head of the Yeoju branch of the Supreme Prosecutors Office. Park also faced criticism for holding press conferences with pre-submitted questions and prepared answers, with opponents labeling her as "No communication" (Bultong). In November 2015, around 80,000 anti-government protesters clashed with security forces in Seoul, demanding her resignation over her business-friendly labor policies and the mandate for state-issued history textbooks in schools starting in 2017. Following the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster, the Park administration created a commission to monitor and prosecute social media critics, and Japanese journalist Tatsuya Kato was indicted for defamation after reporting on a relationship between Park and Choi Soon-sil’s husband, Chung Yoon-hoi. On 25 June 2015, Park made a statement criticizing Yu Seungmin of the Saenuri Party, which was criticized as an attempt to influence his election, though the National Election Commission ruled it did not violate the Public Official Election Act. In 2015, Park reached an agreement with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe on the comfort women issue, including a $8.8 million assistance fund and a commitment to "irreversibly resolve" the matter, though President Moon Jae-in later terminated the deal in 2017. Investigations into Park’s relationship with Choi Soon-sil began in October 2016, revealing that Choi, without official government status, accessed confidential information and acted as a close confidant, extorting ₩77.4 billion (about $75 million) from chaebols and establishing two foundations, Mir and K-sports. Choi was also accused of influencing Ewha Womans University’s admission criteria for her daughter, Chung Yoo-ra, and of misusing a South Korean overseas development project in Myanmar for personal gain. Ahn Jong-bum and Jeong Ho-sung, top aides, were arrested for abuse of power and aiding Choi, denying wrongdoing and claiming they followed Park’s orders. On 25 October 2016, Park publicly acknowledged her close ties with Choi, and on 28 October, she dismissed key staff, causing her approval rating to plummet to 4%, with ratings as low as 1–3% among those under 60, the worst in Korean history. This triggered mass protests, including over 1 million participants at Gwanghwamun Square on 12 November and another 1 million on 19 November, demanding her resignation or impeachment. Park fired cabinet members and the prime minister, Hwang Kyo-ahn, with controversy arising over the claim that the dismissal was via text message. The Supreme Prosecutors' Office charged Park with collusion with Choi and two aides, marking the first time a serving South Korean president was questioned by prosecutors. Massive demonstrations began in early November 2016. On 29 November 2016, Park offered to resign and requested a transfer of power, but opposition parties rejected the offer, accusing her of evading impeachment. The National Assembly filed an impeachment motion on 9 December 2016, which passed with 234 votes, suspending Park’s presidential powers and transferring them to Hwang Kyo-ahn as acting president. On 10 March 2017, the Constitutional Court unanimously (8–0) upheld the impeachment, removing Park from office. On 26 March 2017, prosecutors sought an arrest warrant, which was granted by the Seoul Central District Court on 31 March 2017, leading to Park’s arrest and eventual sentencing to 25 years in prison. In December 2021, President Moon Jae-in granted Park a pardon to promote national reconciliation and address the national crisis from the COVID-19 pandemic, citing her declining health. The pardon was part of a broader amnesty that benefited 700 prisoners, reducing or eliminating their remaining sentences. Park returned home in March 2022 after being hospitalized at Samsung Medical Center.

Patrick Nagel (November 25, 1945 – February 4, 1984) was an American artist and illustrator known for his distinctive style that combined elements of Art Deco and pop art, emphasizing the female form. Born in Dayton, Ohio, on November 25, 1945, he was raised and spent most of his life in the Los Angeles area. After serving in the United States Army with the 101st Airborne Division in Vietnam, he attended the Chouinard Art Institute in Los Angeles in 1969 and earned his Bachelor of Fine Arts degree from California State University, Fullerton that same year. In 1971, he worked as a graphic designer for ABC Television, and in 1972 began freelancing for major corporations and magazines, including Architectural Digest, Harper's Magazine, IBM, ITT Corporation, MGM, Oui, Rolling Stone, United Artists, and Universal Studios. He produced album covers for artists such as Tommy James, Charlene, Thelma Houston, and Cissy Houston. His 1982 painting for Duran Duran's Rio album cover, designed by Malcolm Garrett, became one of his most acclaimed works; the model, Marcie Hunt, was identified from a 1981 Vogue Paris feature and did not know she was used until forty-two years later. A lithograph of the cover is part of MoMA’s collection. Nagel also worked with commercial clients including Intel, Lucky Strike cigarettes, Ballantine's Whiskey, and Budweiser. From August 1975 to July 1984, he contributed illustrations to Playboy magazine, with one painting published in every issue, notably in the Playboy Advisor, Playboy Forum, and Playboy After Hours columns; he created roughly 285 artworks for the magazine. Initially given specific instructions, he later chose his own themes and approaches. In 1993, his widow Jennifer Dumas sued Playboy over rights to the artwork. In 1977, Nagel created his first poster for Mirage Editions, launching the popular "Nagel woman" series, which depicted idealized women with black hair and bright white skin. He used models such as Cathy St. George, Tracy Vaccaro, and Shannon Tweed, and painted portraits of celebrities like Joan Collins and Joanna Cassidy, often tracing photographs and editing hair and clothing to fit his style. Much of his source material came from fashion magazine spreads and advertisements, with many original models unaware their images were used. Art historians have speculated Nagel was influenced by Japanese woodblock prints, with figures silhouetted against neutral backgrounds, strong black and white contrasts, bold lines, and unusual angles, though no specific evidence exists; his mapmaking experience in Vietnam may have influenced his high-contrast imagery. Nagel died on February 4, 1984, after participating in a 15-minute celebrity "aerobathon" for the American Heart Association in Santa Monica; an autopsy revealed a heart attack caused by a congenital heart defect undetected throughout his life. He was survived by his wife Jennifer Dumas and his daughter Carole Nagel LaVigne. Against his parents' wishes, he was cremated and his ashes scattered over the Pacific Ocean. His works are seen as capturing the emotional state of 1980s American culture—materialistic aspirations and a "Less than Zero" mindset—echoed by Alex Israel, who created the 2015 Duran Duran album art Paper Gods, which references the Rio cover. The short-lived cartoon Moonbeam City, starring Rob Lowe and Elizabeth Banks, based its characters on Nagel’s models and adopted his minimalist architectural aesthetic, drawing from the Memphis Group’s deco-influenced designs of the 1980s. Nagel prints became widespread in the 1980s; his manager, Karl Bornstein, continued publishing his works posthumously, including open editions and mass-market posters. In 1991, the FBI dismantled a counterfeiting ring that flooded the market with forged serigraphs, contributing to Nagel’s cultural presence—his artwork was in about two million homes worldwide—but also devaluing his brand. By 2019, the market saw a resurgence, with one original 1982 work selling for $112,500 at auction, nearly doubling its estimated value, and limited-run silkscreen posters selling for several thousand dollars. In 2020, fast fashion retailer Forever 21 launched an apparel collection featuring Nagel portraits.

Paul Benedict Cullen, Lord Pentland, PC[1] (born 11 March 1957), is the current Lord President of the Court of Session and Lord Justice General, the most senior judge in Scotland. He is a former Solicitor General for Scotland, Senator of the College of Justice, and Chairman of the Scottish Law Commission. Born in Gosforth, Northumberland, he was educated at St Augustine's High School, Edinburgh, and at the School of Law of the University of Edinburgh.[2] Cullen was admitted to the Faculty of Advocates in 1982, devilling for Alan Rodger QC.[3] He tutored part-time at the Faculty of Law at the University of Edinburgh from 1982 to 1986, when he was elected Clerk of the Faculty of Advocates, serving until 1991. He was Standing Junior Counsel to the Department of the Environment in Scotland from 1988 to 1991 and appointed an Advocate Depute in 1992, becoming a Queen's Counsel in 1995. A member of the Conservative Party, he became Solicitor General for Scotland, the junior Law Officer in Scotland, in 1995, when Donald Mackay succeeded Lord Rodger of Earlsferry as Lord Advocate, the senior Law Officer. He held this post until the Labour election victory in 1997, when he was succeeded by Colin Boyd, who later became Lord Advocate.[4] He chaired the public inquiry into the Gilmerton Limestone Emergency from 2001 to 2002 and has served as Chairman of the Appeal Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland and of the Police Appeals Tribunal.[4][5] In 2003, The Scotsman named him the seventieth highest earner in Scotland and third highest earner at the Bar, after Richard Keen QC (sixty-first with earnings of £600,000 and a former dean of the Faculty) and Michael Jones, Lord Jones (fifty-fifth with earnings of £750,000).[6] He was involved in several high-profile cases, including the Countryside Alliance challenge to the Scottish fox-hunting ban, a judicial review related to the Stockline Plastics factory explosion, and the first two appeals to the Inner House of the Court of Session under the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002, as well as the first such appeal to the House of Lords.[5] In November 2008, Cullen was appointed as a Senator of the College of Justice, a judge of the High Court of Justiciary and Court of Session, the Supreme Courts of Scotland, and took the judicial title Lord Pentland.[2][4][7] In 2010 he was appointed as a member of the Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber). He has also served as an Intellectual Property judge. Lord Pentland was appointed Chairman of the Scottish Law Commission on 1 January 2014 for a five-year term until 31 December 2018. He was appointed to the First Division of the Inner House of the Court of Session in July 2020 and to the Privy Council in September 2020. On 9 January 2025, it was announced that Lord Pentland had been appointed as the next Lord President of the Court of Session and Lord Justice General.[8] He succeeded Lord Carloway on 3 February 2025.[9] On 17 October 2025, Lord Pentland celebrated the tenth anniversary of the creation of the Sheriff Appeal Court alongside Lord Carloway, Lord Gill, and Sheriff Principal Anwar.[10] The Regulation of Legal Services (Scotland) Act 2025 granted ultimate control and supervision of the Scottish legal profession to the Lord President. On 16 December 2025, consideration of possible detailed approaches was placed in the hands of Lord Ericht, appointed as Regulatory Judge.[11] Cullen contested the Eastwood constituency at the 1997 general election for the Conservative Party but finished in second place to Jim Murphy of the Labour Party. All Conservative Party representation was wiped out from Scottish constituencies at that election. Cullen served as Vice-President of the Edinburgh South Conservative Association from 1997 until he took the bench in 2008. He represented the Scottish Conservative Party on the Consultative Steering Group from 1998 to 1999, which helped prepare procedures for the new Scottish Parliament. He was appointed Chairman of the Disciplinary Panel of the Scottish Conservatives in 2000. Cullen is married to Joyce Nicol, former Chair of Brodies LLP (1983), with whom he has two sons and a daughter. He plays tennis and bridge and is a member of the New Club.

Paya is a town and municipality located in the La Libertad Province within the Colombian department of Boyacá. It shares borders with Pisba, Labranzagrande (in Boyacá), Támara, Nunchía, and Yopal (in Casanare). The name Paya in the Chibcha language means "People of hope." Prior to the Spanish conquest in the 1530s, the area was inhabited by the Muisca, who were part of the loose Muisca Confederation. Modern Paya was officially established on September 14, 1600. The primary economic activity in Paya is horticulture, contributing 47% to the local economy, followed by livestock farming at 37% and agriculture at 16%. Its geographic coordinates are 5°38′N 72°26′W (5.633°N 72.433°W).

doc_name: Peace at home, peace in the world
text: The slogan "Peace at home, peace in the world" (Turkish: Yurtta sulh, cihanda sulh, now rendered as Yurtta barış, dünyada barış due to Atatürk's language reforms) was first introduced by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk on 20 April 1931 during his tours of Anatolia and later became the foundation of the Republic of Turkey's foreign policy. The original full sentence was "To describe the stable and general diplomatic policy of the Republican People's Party, I think this short sentence is enough: We work for peace at home, peace in the world." This slogan became the center of a dispute during the Turkish Super Cup final between Galatasaray and Fenerbahçe held in Saudi Arabia in December 2023, on the centennial of the Turkish Republic, a date of special national significance. Fenerbahçe sought to display banners with the slogan "Peace at home, peace in the world," but Saudi authorities refused, stating it had not been previously discussed. Additionally, players were prohibited from entering the pitch wearing T-shirts featuring Atatürk's image, and the Turkish National Anthem was initially barred from being played. Saudi authorities claimed that no political slogans were permitted and that entry to the stadium should be via official jerseys approved by the Turkish Football Federation. However, both clubs maintained that Atatürk's image and the National Anthem were not considered political, and they had not requested permission from the Turkish Football Federation for these elements, leading to a major misunderstanding. For hours after the issue became public, an unofficial diplomatic crisis ensued. As it became clear that a resolution honoring the match's significance could not be reached, the game was cancelled hours before kick-off.

Pedro Antonio de Aragón (7 November 1611 – 1 September 1690) was a Spanish nobleman, military leader, and politician who served under Kings Philip IV and Charles II of Spain. He was the brother of Cardinal Pascual de Aragón, who served as Viceroy of Naples from 1664 to 1666, and the son of Enrique Ramón Folch de Cardona y Córdoba and Catalina Fernández de Córdoba y Figueroa. Born in Lucena, now in the Province of Córdoba, he was a well-educated individual who held several high-ranking positions at the Court, including Viceroy of Catalonia from 1642 to 1644, ambassador in Rome from 1664 to 1666, Viceroy of Naples from 1666 to 1671, and Commander in Chief of Catalonia. In 1670, he claimed the joint titles of 8th Duke of Segorbe and 9th Duke of Cardona following the deaths of his brother Luis Raimundo Folch de Cardona (January 1670) and his infant son Joaquín (March 1670), leaving only seven daughters. He was brought before the Justice Courts by two of his nieces and their husbands, but died in Madrid before the case was resolved, leading to ongoing issues regarding the numbering of the Dukedoms due to his self-appointed succession. During his ten-year stay in Italy (1662–1672), he built a personal library of approximately 3,600 volumes. As a patron of Poblet Monastery, he donated his library in 1677 in exchange for burial among its revered figures and sent back to Naples in 1671 the body of King Alfonso V of Aragon. He served as President of the Council of Aragon from 1677 to 1690 and published a work on Geometria Militar in 1671. This article about an Andalusian politician is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Pedro Alonso López (born 5 October 1948 – disappeared 22 September 1999), also known as the Monster of the Andes, is a Colombian serial killer, child rapist, and fugitive who murdered a minimum of 110 people, mostly pre-teen girls, from 1978 to 1980. López claimed to have murdered over 300 people in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. He is considered by many as one of the most prolific serial killers and rapists in history. Born in the Tolima Department, Colombia, as the seventh of thirteen children, López was the son of Benilda López de Castañeda, a laundry worker, and Midardo Reyes, a rancher who was murdered six months before López's birth in an ambush during La Violencia. Benilda stated that Midardo was a local leader of a self-protection group aligned with the Colombian Liberal Party, while later accounts describe him as a member of the Conservative Party. After his father's death, Benilda fled to her mother's home in El Espinal, where she remained bedridden under midwives' care until López's birth. López claimed a difficult childhood due to household violence and the absence of a father, describing his mother as a prostitute who "was only good for putting children into this world, each from different men," and stating he often saw her and his stepfather have sex in front of him. Childhood neighbors reported that his mother was strict and forbade him from playing with them, and his mother claimed that López expressed hatred for her early on, telling her he couldn't stand her as a young child. According to López, he was banished from the house at age eight after his mother caught him groping his sister, spending a year homeless in Tolima, during which he was raped by a man who lured him with false promises of shelter and food. His mother claimed he ran away on 5 April 1958 in rebellion, asserting he did not want to live with her. At age ten, López moved to Bogotá, where he joined a gang of street children for protection and began using basuco and cannabis to combat malnutrition; he was occasionally sexually assaulted. At age twelve, he was adopted by an American immigrant family but ran away the same year, claiming a male teacher at the orphan's school had sexually harassed him, though biographers note no such incident occurred and that he left due to a lack of trust in his adoptive family. In 1969, López was sentenced to seven years in prison for auto theft; two days after arriving at La Modelo prison, he was raped by four inmates, and instead of reporting the assault, he killed three of them with a makeshift knife over two weeks. The killings were considered self-defense by prison staff, but his sentence was extended by two years. After his release in 1978, López wandered through the northwestern region of South America, staying in Bogotá and traveling through Tolima, Huila, Cauca, and Nariño to enter Ecuador, then Peru, claiming to do migrant work in the Llanos near Venezuela. He claimed between 1978 and 1980 to have killed over 100 girls, mainly street children and those from indigenous tribes. Though unverifiable, it is known that he was briefly captured by indigenous Peruvians in the Ayacucho region after attempting to abduct a 9-year-old girl; they beat him for several hours, stripped him of his clothes, and buried him up to the neck in sand, with reports stating their intention was to kill him through live burial, though López later claimed they poured syrup on him to allow ants to eat him alive. An American missionary convinced them to release him and turn him over to police, who did not detain him and instead expelled him from the country. After deportation, López resumed his killing spree in Ecuador, and although authorities noticed an increase in missing young girls, they concluded the disappearances were likely due to human trafficking. On 5 May 1979, López met Hortensia Garcés Lozada in Ambato, gave her 100 sucres to follow her, and raped and killed her under a nearby bridge. On 14 December 1979, in his hometown of El Espinal, he raped and murdered Flor Alba Sánchez. Two other girls were murdered in El Espinal on 21 December 1979 and 3 January 1980; Sánchez was found 20 days later buried on municipal property alongside Blanca Bautista, both bearing signs of torture. Sánchez is the only Colombian victim for whom López was tried; other cases were lost in a fire at the El Espinal courthouse. On 10 January 1980, he abducted Ivanova Jácome at a parking lot in Totoras [de], a suburb of Ambato, raped and murdered her in a nearby shack, with her body discovered at Ambato's Plaza Urbina on 15 February. López frequently visited Plaza Urbina, claiming to be a street merchant, but was usually seen at market stalls manned by young girls, offering them 100 sucres to accompany him, typically claiming to need directions to a bus stop. He was easily identified by his tall stature, prominent nose, lack of upper front teeth, and a large scar on his right cheek. In early 1980, two vendors, Luz Marina Lozada and Marina Cuenca, declined his offer and informed merchants of his behavior. On 9 March 1980, López tried to abduct 9-year-old Carmen Lozada, but her cries alerted bystanders, and he fled. Carmen identified him as the man who had previously offered her sister Luz Marina money. The plaza's merchant board president, Carolina Román Poveda, ran to rally others, was ignored due to heavy business, followed López out of the market, caught him talking to another 9-year-old girl, and intervened as he led her to a secluded path, shouting he was going to sell the child. Bystanders initially believed López, who claimed ignorance and called Román crazy, but due to her insistence and her assertion that he had previously tried to kidnap two girls, the crowd convinced them to bring López back, shoving and punching him. Román's fellow merchants criticized her, but she demanded he be handed over to authorities. López was taken to a police station but released shortly after. In April 1980, flash flooding in the Ambato area uncovered the remains of four missing girls, whose bodies showed signs of strangulation, prompting police to reopen investigations and contributing to López's eventual arrest. Three days after the flood, López approached 12-year-old Marina (or María) Román Poveda at Plaza Rosa market, flirted with her, offered 100 sucres to show him around, and she refused. She told her mother, Carolina, of his advances, recognized him, screamed at him, and grabbed his arm. She told bystanders he had tried to abduct her daughter and was responsible for the recently discovered girls. Local merchants overpowered López and held him until police arrived. While in police custody, López initially refused to cooperate, choosing to remain silent. Eventually, he began confessing to police captain Pastor Córdova Gudino, who shared a cell with him for 27 days. López boasted he had murdered a hundred in Colombia, at least 110 in Ecuador, and "many more" in Peru. He described his modus operandi as luring victims away from public spaces with a trinket, money, candy, or a job offer, then raping and strangling them with his bare hands for about 15 minutes, embracing their corpses as "muñequitas" ("dollies") until they became cold, leaving them at the scene and later covering them up. He claimed to occasionally exhume bodies and have "tea parties" with them. When asked about his motive, López said: "I lost my innocence at age eight. So I decided to do the same to as many girls as I could." In a 1992 interview, he admitted killing solely for sexual pleasure, stating: "It's like eating chicken. Why have old chicken when you can have young chicken?" He emphasized that he found it important that victims stay conscious until their eyes lost their light, calling it a "divine moment" and "terribly exciting." Because police doubted the authenticity of his confession, López offered to direct authorities to sites where he had left victims. He led Ambato police and families to a canyon of the Ambato River, where officers found the body of Hortensia Garcés Lozada beneath a bridge, held down by rocks. Police had to lock López in a patrol car to prevent lynchings. While driving to a second location, López described how he lured Garcés away with pedestrians nearby, and police found a decomposing body in an empty house. He later recounted meeting the victim in central Ambato, convincing her to accompany him out of town by bus, walking her around for hours, and raping her for twelve hours before killing her. Officers maintained an amicable tone with López to ensure cooperation. He led investigators to several more sites, mostly along the highway from Ambato to Quito, and recalled many murders before refusing to talk further, claiming his "friendship" with police had been betrayed. Ultimately, the bodies of 53 girls, aged eight to thirteen, were found, several in a forest near Ambato. While 28 sites named by López yielded no remains, police attributed this to scavenging animals unearthing and scattering body parts. Given the discovery of the mass grave, his estimate of 110 murders in Ecuador was accepted as legitimate. Authorities did not charge him with the total of 350 confessed murders because most occurred outside Ecuador and it was considered too costly to hold additional trials in Colombia and Peru. In 1980, López's trial began in Ambato under judge José Roberto Cobos Moscoso, charged with 57 counts of murder. On 27 January 1981, he was found guilty of three murders and received a 16-year sentence, the maximum available in Ecuador at the time. López served his sentence at the Garcia Moreno prison near Quito, where he was frequently attacked by fellow inmates, leading to increased security. Throughout the 1990s, he was often interviewed by journalists and made contradictory statements. He bragged about the rush he felt during strangulation but at other times claimed he was only an accomplice to Jorge Patiño, stating he only helped Patiño bury bodies after being raped by him and that he later murdered Patiño with a knife in Durán. His projected release date was controversial, with numerous lawyers petitioning for extensions or additional convictions. He was released two years early, on 31 August 1994. In an interview before his release, López called himself "the man of the century" and said he was released for "good behavior." He was transported from Quito to Ibarra, where a judge ordered his deportation. Press and public were present at the court, and López shook hands with several people. After the deportation order was read, police seized him and took him to a different vehicle for transport to the Colombian border, driving for five hours until nightfall to avoid pursuers, as families of victims had placed bounties on him, the highest being $25,000. In Colombia, he was received by DAS officers but, lacking a warrant, was temporarily held at a hotel in Pasto, with his room under surveillance but the door left unlocked, though he did not attempt escape due to fear of vigilantes. After a week, an arrest warrant was issued from El Espinal over suspicion of over a dozen murders, though no official case had been filed. He was transported to El Espinal, but after a van was ambushed by an angry mob of 2,000 people, he was taken to Bogotá for a medical examination until the situation calmed. López pleaded with doctors to release him, but was returned to El Espinal, where Alba Sánchez had filed a complaint over the murder of her daughter, as the state of her body resembled that of the girls murdered in Ecuador. López was convicted of the murder of Flor Alba Sánchez, though a physician believed he had signs of psychosis, requiring psychological treatment. The diagnosis was challenged, and he was designated as having "unhealthy personality traits" rather than a mental disorder, and was sent to the psychiatric ward of La Modelo prison. He did not receive medication and was noted as an unremarkable patient, engaging in heavy exercise, reading, and watching television. He maintained a well-groomed appearance but was never interviewed by the Colombian press due to lack of interest. In February 1998, López was declared sane and released on bail equivalent to US$70, on the condition of periodic reporting and therapy appointments; he almost immediately absconded. Ecuador's press and AFP reported on several alleged sightings in Tulcán and Ibarra, and a supposed capture in Cuenca that ended in his escape, but these claims were never verified. Within the year, López visited his mother to ask for money, but after she rejected him due to her poverty, he took her mattress and chair, sold them on the street, and left. The last reported sighting of López was on 22 September 1999, when he visited the National Civil Registry in Bogotá to renew his citizenship card, using the identity of a 60-year-old man from Aipe named Israel Césped to bypass checkpoints. In 2002, Colombian National Police and Interpol issued warrants for his arrest over a murder resembling his modus operandi. The Interpol warrant was deactivated in 2005 based on a claim by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine that an abandoned corpse had been identified as López, accepted by the National Registry, but he remains a fugitive. López has also been named as a possible suspect in the 2012 killing of Andrea Marcela García Buitrago in Tunja, Colombia, due to similarities with his 1979 murder of Flor Alba Sánchez. The most commonly reported victim count of 110 (not including the three prisoners killed by López in Colombia) is cited.

The last reported sighting of López was on 22 September 1999, when he visited the National Civil Registry in Bogotá to renew his citizenship card, using the identity card of a 60-year-old man from Aipe named Israel Césped to bypass checkpoints. In 2002, Colombian National Police and Interpol issued warrants for his arrest over a murder resembling his modus operandi; the Interpol warrant was deactivated in 2005 based on a claim by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine that an abandoned corpse had been identified as López, a claim accepted by the National Registry, though he remains a fugitive. López has also been named as a possible suspect in the 2012 killing of Andrea Marcela García Buitrago in Tunja, Colombia, due to similarities with his 1979 murder of Flor Alba Sánchez. The most commonly reported victim count of 110 (excluding the three prisoners killed by López in 1969) comes from his admission to Ecuadorian authorities, who only pursued those he stated he killed within Ecuador. Police searches in "almost every province" recovered several remains around Ambato and Santo Domingo, as well as individual gravesites near villages in cantons including La Troncal, Tulcán, Quito, Azogues, Manta, and Salcedo; of the Ecuadorian victims, only 17 were identified. Although López stated he killed a hundred victims in Colombia, he only confirmed the murder of two children in El Espinal. There are no known records about the victims murdered in Peru. Colombian journalist Jairo Enrique Gómez Remolina was one of the first to write about Pedro López (pseudonymised as Pablo Alonso Lopera); he travelled through Colombia's Andean Region to speak with parents whose daughters had gone missing and confronted López during a 1981 prison interview. Gómez Remolina is credited with linking López to child disappearances and killings in El Espinal, Pasto, Neiva, La Plata, Popayán, and El Bordo, though these were not definitively proven. He also speculated that López was responsible for the murders of young boys committed by the unidentified Monster of the Mangones (López denied travelling through Cali) and those of teenage girls by the Sadist of El Charquito (later attributed to Daniel Camargo Barbosa), later writing about López's prison interactions with Camargo Barbosa. Gómez Remolina was killed in 1986 during the Pozzetto massacre, having sat directly next to the perpetrator, Campo Elías Delgado. In 1992, López was filmed and interviewed by American journalist Ronald Laytner of the National Examiner. While media interest outside of Latin America was initially low, he received more coverage in the years leading up to his release and disappearance, often being referenced as a comparison to newly discovered serial killers such as Luis Garavito and Harold Shipman. Editions of Guinness World Records up to 2005 credited López as the "most prolific serial killer," but the listing was removed in newer editions after complaints that it made a competition out of murder.

Pehr Löfling (31 January 1729 – 22 February 1756) was a Swedish botanist and a devoted follower of Carl Linnaeus. Born in Tolvfors Bruk, Gävle, Sweden, he studied at the University of Uppsala, where he took courses taught by Linnaeus. When the Spanish ambassador requested Linnaeus to appoint a botanist for service in the American colonies, Linnaeus immediately selected Löfling. Löfling traveled to Spain in 1751 to learn Spanish and then joined a scientific expedition to South America in February 1754. The Treaty of Madrid, signed on 13 January 1750, had established the colonial borders between Spain and Portugal. In Cumaná, Venezuela (then a Spanish colony), Löfling participated in the Expedicion de Limites al Orinoco, a project to demarcate the border with Brazil, and was assigned to lead the natural history department responsible for evaluating the region’s resources. He worked on the expedition with two young Spanish doctors and remained involved throughout his life. Löfling died in a remote mission called San Antonio de Caroni, located on the banks of the Caroní River near the present-day city of Ciudad Guayana, Venezuela. His death was seen as a significant loss to natural history, particularly to botany, and Carl Linnaeus regarded it as irreparable. After his death, his manuscripts were preserved by his two assistants. In 1753, Linnaeus named the genus Loeflingia for plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, one species of which is found in Spain and another in Spanish America. In 1923, Sprague published Pehria, a monotypic genus of plants from South America in the family Lythraceae, also named in honor of Löfling. A park named Parque Löefling in Ciudad Guayana, Venezuela, is dedicated to him and includes a zoo. Linnaeus posthumously published his Iter Hispanicum, eller resa til Spanska Länderna uti Europa och America 1751 til 1756 in 1758.

doc_name: Penny Crane Award for Distinguished Service
text: The Penny Crane Award for Distinguished Service is presented by the Association for Computing Machinery's Special Interest Group on University and College Computing Services. The award was founded in 2000 to honor individuals who have made substantial contributions to the Special Interest Group and to the field of computing in higher education.

The Perkin Medal is an annual award presented by the Society of Chemical Industry (American Section) to a scientist living in the United States for an "innovation in applied chemistry resulting in outstanding commercial development." It is recognized as the highest honor in the U.S. chemical industry. The medal was first awarded in 1906 to mark the 50th anniversary of the discovery of mauveine, the world's first synthetic aniline dye, by Sir William Henry Perkin, an English chemist. The award was given to Sir William during his visit to the United States the year before his death. It was subsequently awarded in 1908 and has been presented every year since then.

The Perkin Prize for Organic Chemistry is a distinguished award founded in 2008 by the Royal Society of Chemistry to recognize sustained originality and significant achievement in research across all areas of organic chemistry. The prize is named in honor of Sir William Henry Perkin (1838–1907), who invented the first aniline dye, and is presented every two years. The recipient is awarded £5000, a medal, and a certificate, which are presented during an awards ceremony in November, and is also required to participate in a UK lecture tour.
