Persina Nature Park (Bulgarian: Природен парк Персина) is a wetland area on the Bulgarian side of the Danube, established on December 4, 2000. It spans 21,762 ha (53,780 acres) and lies within the territories of three municipalities: Nikopol, Belene, and Svishtov. The park's primary goal is the conservation and restoration of Danube wetlands, with special focus on the numerous islands and their natural condition. Named after Persin Island, which is part of the Belene Islands Complex, the island is 15 km (9.3 mi) long and 6 km (3.7 mi) wide, making it the fourth largest Danube island and the largest in Bulgaria. A separate island group near Nikopol is also significant and was designated a Ramsar site on September 24, 2002, covering 18,330 ha (45,300 acres), the largest such site in Bulgaria. Key ecosystems within the park include flooded forests along the Danube and inland marshes, and several protected areas have been created to safeguard these habitats. A visitor centre for the park is located in Belene. This Pleven Province, Bulgaria location article is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

Peter George Doyle (June 1843 – April 19, 1907) was an Irish-born American transit worker who served as an intimate companion to Walt Whitman from approximately 1865 to 1876, and to some extent until Whitman's death in 1892. Doyle was born in early June 1843 in Ireland to Peter George Doyle, a blacksmith, and Catherine Nash Doyle, the sixth of nine children; he was baptized on June 16, 1843, in Limerick. The family moved to Alexandria, Virginia, in 1853, arriving in Baltimore on May 10 before settling there. Doyle received little formal education and stood about 5 feet 8 inches tall. His niece described him as "a homosexual." Between 1856 and 1859, the Doyles relocated to Richmond, Virginia, where Peter Sr. worked at the Tredegar Iron Works. When the American Civil War began, Doyle enlisted in the Confederate States Army on April 25, 1861, fought in several battles including the Battle of Antietam (where he was wounded), and was discharged on November 7, 1862. He likely re-joined the army in 1863 before deserting and fleeing north, where he was briefly imprisoned near Old Capitol Prison in April 1863 and released on May 11. He then worked at the Washington Navy Yard in Washington, D.C., until 1865. After the war, he lived in Washington, D.C., and worked as a streetcar conductor for the Washington and Georgetown Railroad Company. Doyle was an eyewitness to the assassination of Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, and Whitman later referenced his account. Doyle first met Whitman in 1865 on a "cold, stormy night" when Whitman was the only passenger on Doyle’s streetcar; the two became close friends, corresponding regularly and meeting frequently. Whitman often rode Doyle’s streetcar, went on hikes together, and wrote many letters, addressing Doyle as "boy" or "son," while Doyle signed his name "Pete the Great." Historian Martin G. Murray suggested that Doyle may have influenced Whitman’s poem "O Captain! My Captain!" by prompting a shift to a more conventional form, and that the hero in "Come Up From the Fields, Father" is named "Pete," with Murray arguing Doyle may have inspired some poems in Drum-Taps. In May 1870, the two traveled briefly to New York City to see the opera Poliuto; Whitman abbreviated Doyle’s name in his diary as "16.4" (P being the 16th letter, D the fourth). Whitman may have begun to suspect he loved Doyle, though Doyle did not reciprocate fully, as he was supporting his mother; by the end of 1870, Whitman was more confident in their bond. In 1872 or 1873, Doyle began working as a braker on the Pennsylvania Railroad. After Whitman suffered a stroke in 1873, Doyle helped nurse him. Doyle grew increasingly dissatisfied with his job and continued visiting Whitman even after he moved to Camden, New Jersey, in 1874. After 1876, their correspondence and visits declined significantly. In 1880, Doyle met Richard Maurice Bucke, a promoter and early biographer of Whitman. After 1885, he moved permanently to Philadelphia, where he was a member of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks and joined the United Confederate Veterans. The last known contact between Doyle and Whitman may have been in 1889, though they likely met at least once afterward. Whitman left Doyle his watch, and Doyle visited Whitman’s body after his death in 1892, though he was nearly denied entry to the funeral. Doyle was also friends with Horace Traubel and his wife Anne Traubel, as well as Gustave Percival Wiksell. Whitman’s letters to Doyle were published in 1895 as *Calamus, A Series of Letters Written During the Years 1868–1880 by Walt Whitman To A Young Friend (Peter Doyle)*, which is generally recognized as a collection of love letters and received mixed reviews. After Whitman’s death, Doyle kept a coat that Whitman had worn, describing it as "like Aladdin's lamp." For the rest of his life, Doyle was regarded as a celebrity by Whitman’s friends and followers. A portrait of Doyle and Whitman, taken around 1865 by M. P. Rice, is the earliest known portrait of Whitman with someone else. John Burroughs paraphrased Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" to describe Doyle as "a mute inglorious Whitman." Doyle is considered the most likely candidate for Whitman’s lifelong love, and biographer Justin Kaplan wrote in 1980 that Whitman extended himself with Doyle more than with any other man, at greater risk to his psychological well-being. Their relationship is often described as a "romantic friendship," though its exact nature remains unknown. Doyle died on April 19, 1907, in Philadelphia from uremia and is buried in the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, D.C.

Philip Leder (November 19, 1934 – February 2, 2020) was an American geneticist born in Washington, D.C., who studied at Harvard University and graduated in 1956. He completed his medical education at Harvard Medical School in 1960 and finished his medical residency at the University of Minnesota. From the 1960s through the 1990s, Leder made significant contributions to molecular genetics, immunology, and the genetics of cancer. He is best known for his early work with Marshall Nirenberg in determining the genetic code through the Nirenberg and Leder experiment. His team defined the base sequence of the complete mammalian beta globin gene, revealing its detailed organization including associated control signals. His research on antibody gene structure was pivotal in explaining how a limited number of genes generate the vast diversity of antibody molecules. This work was later extended to the study of Burkitt's lymphoma, a tumor of antibody-producing cells involving the oncogene c-myc, which was crucial in understanding the tumor's origin. In 1988, Leder and Timothy Stewart received the first patent for a genetically engineered animal—a mouse with genes injected into its embryo to increase cancer susceptibility, known as the "oncomouse," used in cancer therapy research. In 1968, he led the Biochemistry Department of the Graduate Program at the National Institute of Health; in 1972, he became director of the Laboratory for Molecular Genetics at the same institution, a role he held until 1980. He then returned to Harvard Medical School in 1980 as the founder of the Department of Genetics, holding the John Emory Andrus Chair. He retired from this position in 2008 and died of complications from Parkinson's disease on February 2, 2020. Leder was a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Institute of Medicine. He received numerous honors, including the Golden Plate Award of the American Academy of Achievement in 1981, the Lasker Award in 1987, the National Medal of Science in 1991, the Harvey Prize, and the Heineken Prize from the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences. In November 2015, he was awarded an honorary doctoral degree from the Medical Faculty of the University of Basel for his lifetime achievements.

Dame Gillian Phyllida Barlow DBE RA (4 April 1944 – 12 March 2023) was a British visual artist who studied at Chelsea College of Art from 1960 to 1963 and the Slade School of Art from 1963 to 1966. She joined the Slade faculty in the late 1960s and taught there for over forty years, retiring in 2009 as an emerita professor of fine art. Her students included Rachel Whiteread and Ángela de la Cruz, and she significantly influenced younger artists. Born in Newcastle upon Tyne in 1944, the daughter of psychiatrist Erasmus Darwin Barlow, a great-grandson of Charles Darwin, she was raised in London after the Second World War, where her experiences of bomb damage deeply informed her artistic practice. At Chelsea, she studied under George Fullard, whose teachings emphasized the adventure of making, and she developed a fascination with the potential of materials like cardboard, polystyrene, scrim, and cement. She found a strong affinity for clay and focused on creating abstract works that invited viewers to engage with the materials and processes. Barlow believed art schools overemphasized a single model of artistic success. After graduating from the Slade in 1966, she began teaching at the West of England College of Art (now the University of the West of England, Bristol), where she learned traditional sculpture techniques and discovered the malleability of clay. In 2004, she was appointed professor of fine art and director of undergraduate studies at the Slade before retiring in 2009. Her artistic breakthrough came in 2004 when her work was shown at the BALTIC, Gateshead, followed by representation by Hauser & Wirth. In 2018 and 2019, she served as 'provocateur' for the Yorkshire Sculpture international. Barlow’s work combines playful, childlike colours with industrial materials and large scale, creating forms that appear both heavy and light, imposing and unstable. Her sculptures often evoke a sense of environment, blocking or interrupting space, and she openly exposed her processes and materials. Known for her use of inexpensive materials such as plywood, cardboard, plaster, cement, fabric, and paint, her practice is rooted in an anti-monumental tradition, drawing on everyday objects and physical material handling. Her works have been exhibited globally, including a solo show at the Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain in 2014, a solo exhibition titled HOARD at The Norton Museum of Art in 2013 as part of the RAW – Recognition of Art by Women – series, and a show called 'Set' at the Fruitmarket Gallery in Edinburgh in 2015. In 2016, she exhibited at the Kunsthalle Zurich and was one of four artists nominated for the inaugural Hepworth Prize, with her work displayed at Hepworth Wakefield. For the 2017 Venice Biennale, she presented her Folly series, which occupied both indoor and outdoor spaces; initially planned as hanging 'baubles' from the pavilion facade, the installation was altered due to cost and instead resembled lollipops. She was selected for her "challenging and imposing sculptures" and commanded a powerful presence at the 57th Biennale. In 2018, she had solo exhibitions at Hauser & Wirth in New York titled 'tilt', with High Line Art in New York titled 'prop', and at Jupiter Artland in Edinburgh titled 'Quarry'. In 2019, the Royal Academy of Art hosted a site-specific exhibition of her large-scale, brutalist sculptures titled cultural-de-sac in the Gabrielle Jungels-Winkler Galleries, responding to the RA’s architecture. Barlow was elected a Royal Academician in 2011, awarded a CBE in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to the arts, and promoted to DBE in the 2021 Birthday Honours for services to art. She was also a member of the juries that selected Doris Salcedo (2016), Pierre Huyghe (2017), Isa Genzken (2019), and Michael Rakowitz (2020) for the Nasher Prize. Barlow died on 12 March 2023, at the age of 78.

The Piasecki VZ-8 Airgeep (company designation PA-59) was a prototype vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) aircraft developed by Piasecki Aircraft to fulfill a U.S. Army Transportation Research Command contract for a flying jeep in 1957. The design aimed to be smaller and easier to fly than a helicopter. To meet the Army's requirement, Piasecki's aircraft featured two tandem, three-blade ducted rotors, with the crew of two seated between them. Power was provided by two 180 hp (134.2 kW) Lycoming O-360-A2A piston engines, driving the rotors via a central gearbox. The first of two aircraft ordered by the Army, initially called the Model 59K Skycar (later renamed Airgeep) by Piasecki and designated VZ-8P by the Army, made its first flight on 22 September 1958. It was later re-engined with a single 425 hp (317 kW) Turbomeca Artouste IIB turboshaft engine, flying in this configuration in June 1959. After being loaned to the U.S. Navy for evaluation as the Model 59N, where it was fitted with floats, it was returned to the Army and had its engine replaced with a lighter and more powerful 550 hp (410.1 kW) Garrett AiResearch TPE331-6 engine. The second prototype was completed with a modified design, designated Model 59H AirGeep II by Piasecki and VZ-8P (B) by the Army, powered by two Artouste engines, including ejection seats for the pilot and co-pilot/gunner and three additional seats for passengers. It also had a powered tricycle undercarriage to improve land mobility. The AirGeep II's first flight occurred on 15 February 1962, piloted by "Tommy" Atkins. While the Airgeep typically operated close to the ground and could fly to several thousand feet, demonstrating stability in flight and the ability to evade radar detection, the U.S. Army concluded that the "Flying Jeep concept was unsuitable for the modern battlefield" and instead focused on conventional helicopter development, despite its superiority over the other two vehicles evaluated—Chrysler VZ-6 and Curtiss-Wright VZ-7.

The PlayStation 5 (PS5) is a home video game console developed by Sony Interactive Entertainment as the fifth iteration of the PlayStation brand. It was announced as the successor to the PlayStation 4 in April 2019 and launched on November 12, 2020, in Australia, Japan, New Zealand, North America, and South Korea, with a worldwide release one week later. The PS5 is part of the ninth generation of video game consoles, alongside Microsoft's Xbox Series X/S, which were released in the same month. The base model includes an optical disc drive compatible with Ultra HD Blu-ray discs, while the Digital Edition lacks this drive and is a lower-cost model for purchasing games exclusively through download. Both variants were launched simultaneously. Slimmer hardware revisions of both models replaced the original versions on sale in November 2023, colloquially referred to as the "PlayStation 5 Slim." A PlayStation 5 Pro model was released on November 7, 2024, featuring a GPU approximately 45% faster than the original PS5, twice as fast ray tracing performance, and an AI-driven upscaling technology called PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), enabling 4K at 60 frames per second for optimized games. The Pro model ships with 2 TB of internal SSD storage, does not include an optical disc drive or vertical stand (which can be purchased separately), and supports Wi-Fi 7 and 8K resolution output. It was priced at US$699 / £699 / €799 and launched globally on that date. The PS5's main hardware includes a custom system-on-a-chip (SoC) developed by AMD in collaboration with Sony, integrating a CPU and GPU. The eight-core CPU is based on AMD's Zen 2 architecture, built on a 7 nm process, operating up to 3.5 GHz, and the GPU is based on AMD's RDNA 2 architecture with 36 compute units running at up to 2.23 GHz, delivering a theoretical peak performance of 10.28 teraFLOPS. It supports hardware-accelerated real-time ray tracing and uses Sony's AGC graphics API. The console features a custom "boost" system based on AMD's SmartShift technology that dynamically adjusts CPU and GPU speeds. It includes 16 GB of GDDR6 SDRAM via a 256-bit interface, capable of 448 GB/s peak bandwidth, shared between CPU and GPU. The console has 825 GB of built-in solid-state storage (667 GB available to users), with a 12-channel interface providing 5.5 GB/s raw bandwidth and a dedicated decompression unit supporting zlib and Oodle Kraken formats for throughput of 8–9 GB/s, peaking at 22 GB/s. An internal M.2 SSD slot supports user-installed NVMe drives up to 8 TB, with SSD support added via a system update in September 2021. Games must be installed on the built-in SSD or an M.2 SSD, though developers may allow selective installation of features like multiplayer modes. External USB drives (up to 8 TB) are supported, but only PlayStation 4 games can be played directly from them; PlayStation 5 games must be transferred to internal or SSD storage. The standard model supports Ultra HD Blu-ray, standard Blu-ray, and DVD formats, but not CDs or 3D Blu-rays, with game discs holding up to 100 GB of data. The launch model has a two-tone design with a black central unit flanked by white side panels, blue LED accents, and can be oriented vertically or horizontally. Long air intake vents run along the front, and heat is exhausted through rear vents. The side panels are removable, allowing access to the SSD expansion slot, optional Ultra HD Blu-ray drive, and dust collection channels. Front ports include one USB-C (USB 3.1 Gen 2) and one USB-A (USB 2.0), while the rear offers two USB-A (USB 3.1 Gen 2), an HDMI 2.1 port, Gigabit Ethernet, and power. In vertical position, the optical drive model measures 390 mm high, 260 mm deep, 104 mm wide, and weighs 4.5 kg; the digital edition is slightly slimmer at 92 mm wide and initially weighed 3.9 kg. A minor revision in August 2021 (1100 series) reduced weight and eliminated the need for a screwdriver to attach the stand. A 1200-series revision in August 2022 featured a die shrink, reducing power consumption and allowing a redesigned heatsink, resulting in a lighter model (3.9 kg for optical, 3.4 kg for digital). The 2023 Slim revisions reduced the size and included 1 TB of internal storage at launch, though the Digital Edition was later reduced to 825 GB. The Slim Digital Edition was priced higher than the original, with a $50 increase in the US, and an optional Ultra HD Blu-ray drive can be purchased separately for $80. The Slim model with an optical drive measures 358 mm high, 216 mm deep, 96 mm wide, and weighs 3.9 kg; the digital edition is 80 mm wide and weighs 2.6 kg. The DualSense controller was revealed on April 7, 2020, and includes adaptive triggers with force feedback, a new built-in microphone array, and a speaker. The controller maintains the same buttons as the DualShock 4, with the "Share" button renamed to "Create" and additional content creation features. The PS5 supports backward compatibility with the majority of PlayStation 4 and PlayStation VR games and includes the PlayStation VR2 headset. Mark Cerny, the lead architect of the PlayStation console line, implemented a two-year feedback cycle after the PlayStation 4 launch, visiting first-party developers to gather input on hardware improvements. During PS5 development, a central challenge was reducing loading times, as developers like Tim Sweeney from Epic Games identified the slow I/O speed of hard disk drives as a limiting factor in game development. The PS5's custom SSD enables high-speed data streaming, significantly improving storage performance. The console's cooling system uses a 120 mm double-sided intake fan and a large heat sink with a heat pipe design, including a layer of liquid metal for improved heat transfer. It uses a 350-watt internal power supply and consumes less energy in rest mode than the PlayStation 4. Jim Ryan, then CEO of Sony Interactive Entertainment, concluded that a low-priced, reduced-spec version of the PS5, similar to Microsoft's Xbox Series S, would not succeed due to rapid obsolescence. Cerny first publicly described the console in a Wired interview in April 2019, and Sony's financial report for the quarter ending March 31, 2019, confirmed next-generation hardware was in development but would not ship before April 2020. A second Wired interview in October 2019 stated the console would ship worldwide by the end of 2020. Full specifications were revealed in an online presentation by Cerny on March 18, 2020, and a detailed "deep dive" was published by Digital Foundry on April 2. A major game library showcase planned for June 4, 2020, was postponed to June 11 due to the George Floyd protests and also premiered the PS5's external design. Sony planned a launch during the 2020 end-of-year holiday period. The release date and pricing were confirmed on September 16, 2020, with the console launching in Australia, Japan, New Zealand, North America, and South Korea on November 12, 2020, and worldwide on November 19, 2020. The console launched in the Philippines on December 11, 2020. Its release in India was delayed, with speculation over a trademark dispute involving the name "PS5," which was eventually resolved, leading to a release on February 2, 2021. It launched in Indonesia on January 22, 2021, and in China on May 15, 2021. Pre-orders opened on September 17, 2020, but caused a rush and scalping, prompting Sony to apologize on September 19, 2020 and commit to increased deliveries. Worldwide supply remained low from 2020 to 2023 due to a global chip shortage, with Sony expecting short retail stock until 2023. In August 2022, Sony announced a price increase of up to 20% in most markets except the US, citing economic, inflationary, and supply chain pressures; a US price increase took effect in August 2025. Accessories were not affected. Starting in September 2025, the Digital Edition of the PS5 Slim was downgraded from 1 TB to 825 GB of internal storage without announcement in Europe (September 13, 2025) and the US (October 3, 2025), with an announcement in Japan (November 11, 2025). Limited quantities of the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro with gray cases and special branding were released on November 21, 2024, to celebrate the brand's 30th anniversary, along with branded DualSense, DualSense Edge, and PlayStation Portal devices.

Limited quantities of the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro, featuring gray cases and special branding, were released on November 21, 2024, to celebrate the brand's 30th anniversary. Similar branded versions of the PlayStation DualSense, DualSense Edge, and PlayStation Portal were also made available. The DualSense wireless controller for the PlayStation 5 was revealed on April 7, 2020, and is based on the DualShock controller with modifications informed by discussions with game designers and players. It includes adaptive triggers with force feedback via voice coil actuators that adjust resistance for experiences like drawing an arrow from a bow. The controller retains the same buttons as the DualShock 4, with the "Share" button renamed to "Create" and additional tools for creating and sharing content. A new built-in microphone array allows players to communicate using only the controller, and the included speaker has been improved. The controller features two-tone coloring, primarily white with a detachable black piece, and its light bar is positioned on the sides of the touchpad. It supports USB-C connectivity, has a higher-rated battery, and includes an audio jack. An Easter egg features miniature versions of the four PlayStation button symbols (cross, circle, square, and triangle) on the controller's texture. The DualSense Edge (CFI-ZCP1), a more modular controller with replaceable stick modules, multiple control profiles, and the ability to relocate map inputs, was revealed by Sony in August 2022 and initially released on January 26, 2023, via PlayStation Direct, becoming available through other retailers on February 23, 2023. Accessories include a DualSense charging station, a new HD camera, a media remote control, and the Pulse 3D wireless headset, which integrates with the PS5's Tempest Engine 3D audio technology. The PS5 is backward compatible with most existing PS4 controllers and accessories for PS4 games, though some have limited functionality; Rock Band peripherals are supported since Rock Band 2, and PS5 games can use existing PlayStation Move, PlayStation Camera, PlayStation VR Aim Controller, officially licensed headsets, and specialty controllers like flight sticks and racing wheels. The PlayStation Portal, developed by Sony Interactive Entertainment and first released on November 15, 2023, is a handheld accessory for the PS5 that streams video games and media via Remote Play using Wi-Fi. It uses its built-in screen and a DualSense-like controller to control the console but does not run games or media natively. Sony announced the PlayStation VR2 for the PS5 in January 2022; it features a headset with dual OLED panels supporting 4K resolution, HDR, and 90/120 Hz refresh rates, along with two Sense controllers that include 14 embedded IR LEDs for tracking, haptic feedback, and adaptive triggers similar to the DualSense. The headset includes eye-tracking for foveated rendering and in-game features in select titles and supports finger touch detection to show thumb, index, and middle finger positions. Unlike the previous PS VR, it does not require external cameras and uses four internal cameras to track position via its USB-C cable. The PS VR2 launched on February 22, 2023, priced at $549.99 in the U.S., €599.99 in the EU, and £529.99 in the U.K., with launch games including Horizon Call of the Mountain, Gran Turismo 7, and Resident Evil Village. It is not compatible with PS VR games by default, requiring developer updates. The headset received positive reviews but later faced criticism for lack of continued support. The PS5's user interface is described as "accessible and informative," providing updates on friends' activities, multiplayer options, and single-player missions and rewards. Cerny stated that players should not have to repeatedly boot games to check updates, so these features are visible in the UI. Matt MacLaurin, vice president of UX design at PlayStation, described the redesigned interface as a "very interesting evolution of the OS" and a "100 percent overhaul of the PS4 UI," noting its speed and robust visual language. Eurogamer praised the interface for responsiveness, accessibility, clarity, and simplicity, rendered in 4K with high dynamic range. Users are greeted with a stylistic boot-up animation and new login screen, and the central design concepts from the PS4 were redesigned into a new home screen. The top of the screen features a row of applications and two upper tabs to switch between games and media. Selecting a game reveals specific activities like levels or multiplayer modes. The PlayStation Store is no longer a standalone app and is fully integrated into the home screen. The most significant change is the Control Center, accessed by pressing the PS button at the bottom of the screen. The upper section includes cards suggesting actions based on current or recent game activities, such as progress reports or challenges, with PlayStation Plus subscribers receiving hints, tips, screenshots, or videos. System-level cards offer options like store sales or user screenshots. The lower section contains a customizable row of icons including notifications, status updates, friends list, and system settings. According to internal materials reviewed by Vice, the "activities"-focused UI was designed to help players commit time to games, especially single-player titles, recognizing that many players have limited time and that activity cards help them plan gameplay. The PS5 supports multiple streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube, with support for others expected in the future. Sony Pictures Core was released in 2023, and the system includes support for PlayStation Now, Sony's cloud gaming service, while available. Sony's Remote Play application, available on PlayStation 4, Windows, iOS, and Android, was updated before the PS5 launch to allow remote play of PS5 games over a local network. In April 2021, Sony released a software update enabling users to transfer downloaded PS5 games to an external USB hard drive. A PlayStation 5 system software beta program was announced in June 2021, similar to the Xbox Insider program, allowing signed-up users to test early software updates. One of the first major features in the beta was internal SSD expansion via the M.2 port, added in July 2021. In September 2021, a software update introduced a new trophy tracker, Control Center customization, 3D audio support for built-in TV speakers, internal SSD expansion, and various UX enhancements. Game Trials were introduced in October 2021, initially available in the UK for Death Stranding: Director's Cut and Sackboy: A Big Adventure, allowing users to play full versions for a fixed time before needing to purchase the game. In March 2022, software update 5.00 added accessibility improvements such as an improved screen reader with support for mono audio, reading notifications aloud, additional language support, and a check mark for enabled settings. Voice command support was introduced for users in the U.S. and U.K., allowing control via "Hey, PlayStation," and Ukrainian language support was added. Game Base was enhanced with a new "Friends" tab, easier friend request declines, and other updates. Various improvements were made to trophies, child accounts, the home screen, and other features. On March 8, 2023, software update 7.00 added VRR support for 1440p, data transfer between PS5 consoles, voice chat on Discord, and the ability to save gameplay clips via voice (available only in English for the U.S. and U.K. at release). On September 13, 2023, software update 8.00 added Dolby Atmos support, increased M.2 SSD capacity to 8 TB (up from 4 TB), and the ability to mute the start-up beep. On March 13, 2024, software update 9.00 allowed adjustment of the PS5 power indicator brightness, added new features in Parties and Share Screen, and improved the mic input quality of the DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers using a new AI machine-learning model. On September 12, 2024, software update 10.00 introduced the Welcome hub, Party Share, personalized 3D audio profiles, adaptive controller charging, and support for enabling remote play for individual users. On March 25, 2025, software update 11.00 added full details on activity cards, support for Unicode 16.0 emojis, parental control adjustments, system performance and stability improvements, and refinements to messages and usability on certain screens. On September 17, 2025, software update 12.00 introduced a power saver for supported PS5 games and a feature allowing wireless controllers to be paired across multiple devices simultaneously. Each PS5 console comes preinstalled with Astro's Playroom, a game designed to demonstrate the DualSense controller. Games are not region locked, so purchases in one region can be played on consoles in all regions. Sony stated its commitment to supporting the PlayStation 4 community while embracing the PS5 as a major technological advancement. In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Ryan emphasized that next-gen consoles should include features not available on previous generations and that developers should create games that take advantage of these features. General manager Eric Lempel affirmed that Sony wants to evolve every part of the experience, noting that new hardware and devices are necessary to deliver the intended experiences. Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart was highlighted as a next-gen game not possible on older hardware. Lempel assured that interest in PS4 will not end abruptly, with more titles to come. Sony's definition of distinct console generations was interpreted as a shift toward PS5-exclusive games leveraging the console's capabilities, rather than cross-generation releases. Ryan stated there should be no disappointment as PS5 versions take advantage of advanced features and initially planned free upgrades for PS4 versions. Few major games, such as Horizon Forbidden West, are developed as concurrent releases for both PS5 and PS4, and Sony supports publishers offering enhanced PS4 versions at no additional cost. However, in May 2021, Sony announced a shift, with Gran Turismo 7 and God of War Ragnarök now available on both PS5 and PS4, a move attributed to the global semiconductor shortage affecting PS5 availability. Sony initially planned to charge PS4 users to upgrade to the PS5 version of Horizon Forbidden West upon preorder, but after negative consumer feedback—since Sony had previously stated the upgrade would be free—reversed course and made the upgrade free, though all future PS4 to PS5 upgrades from first-party games will be at cost. Eurogamer reported that Sony's certification program, as of May 2020, required PS4 games submitted after July 13, 2020, to be natively compatible with the PS5. Hideaki Nishino, Sony's senior vice president of Platform Planning and Management, stated that the PS5 is backward compatible with over 99% of PS4's 4,000+ game library, playable from launch. The console is compatible with PlayStation VR. Due to its high-speed SSD and increased processing power, many PS4 games benefit from faster loading times, improved gameplay speeds, higher or more stable frame rates, and potentially higher resolutions. Players can synchronize saved game files via cloud storage or transfer them using a USB device to avoid losing progress. Backward compatibility is enabled by hardware similarities, such as "extra logic" in the RDNA 2 GPU that ensures compatibility with PS4's GCN-based GPU. Mark Cerny explained during a March 2020 presentation and in interviews with Digital Foundry that CPU clock timing required special attention; while the Zen 2 CPU supports the PS4's Jaguar CPU instruction set, timing differences required close collaboration with AMD to match Jaguar's performance. Some PS4 games may exhibit errors when played on the PS5, and backward compatibility does not include games from previous generations. However, older PlayStation games are available through the PlayStation Plus game streaming service. The PS4's Share menu cannot be displayed, but the PS5's Create menu can be used to capture screenshots or video. All compatible downloaded PS4 games are visible in the PS5 library and available for download, can be copied via USB or Wi-Fi, and save data can be copied similarly or via cloud storage. On October 9, 2020, Sony released a list of ten PS4 games identified as incompatible with the PS5; the list has since shortened as developers released compatibility updates. As of December 16, 2021, six PS4 games remain incompatible: Afro Samurai 2: Revenge of Kuma Volume One, Hitman Go: Definitive Edition, Just Deal With It!, Robinson: The Journey, Shadwen, and We Sing. The PlayStation 4 bundled game, The Playroom, is also not supported. The PS5 was generally well received at launch, with praise for the DualSense controller's improved haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Astro's Playroom, preinstalled on every PS5 and designed to demonstrate the controller, was praised by Laptop Mag as "deceptively cute." The exclusive launch lineup, including Spider-Man: Miles Morales and Demon's Souls, was highly praised, though some reviewers, such as TechRadar, felt there should have been more launch titles. The user interface was generally praised for being fast and easy to navigate. Many reviewers found the console's design polarizing; CNET described the black and white scheme as "clearly meant to be a sculptural conversation piece," while Tom's Guide criticized the large size as "inelegant," and others found it frustrating to integrate into a home entertainment center. However, many acknowledged the size improved cooling and reduced noise. The comparatively small 667 GB of usable SSD space was also criticized.

The PlayStation 5 was generally well received at launch, with widespread praise for its DualSense controller's improved haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. The preinstalled game Astro's Playroom, designed to showcase the controller's features, was lauded by Laptop Mag as "deceptively cute." The exclusive launch lineup, including Spider-Man: Miles Morales and Demon's Souls, was highly praised, though some reviewers, like TechRadar, noted there should have been more launch titles. The console's user interface was generally commended for being fast and easy to navigate. However, the console's design was seen as polarizing; CNET described its black and white scheme as "clearly meant to be a sculptural conversation piece," while Tom's Guide criticized the large size as "inelegant," and others found it frustrating for home entertainment integration. Despite this, many acknowledged the size helped improve cooling and reduce noise. The comparatively small 667 GB of usable SSD space was criticized. Technical reviews, such as those by Digital Foundry, noted that features like variable refresh rate and 8K video output were not available at launch, but praised the ray tracing, SSD speed, and 120 Hz output capabilities. The PS5 faced limited supply at launch and throughout 2021 due to a global semiconductor shortage and increased demand driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, with Sony expecting supply to remain limited until at least 2022. Scalpers exploited the shortage, attempting to sell consoles for thousands of dollars, prompting Sony to expand its PlayStation Direct program to sell consoles directly to consumers in Europe in November 2021 to bypass scalpers. Two weeks after launch, Sony declared the largest launch in PlayStation history, surpassing the PlayStation 4's 2.1 million units sold in its first two weeks in 2013. In Japan, during its first week of release, 103,901 standard consoles and 14,181 Digital Editions were sold, totaling 118,082 units, making it the best-selling console in the country that week; by September 2021, Sony reported over a million PS5 sales in Japan, compared to its predecessor, which did not reach a million units until a year after release. In the UK, the PS5 was the best-selling video game console in November. In Spain, it sold over 43,000 units in its first week. Sony reported 4.5 million PS5 shipments through its fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2020, similar to the PS4's launch shipments. By March 31, 2021, total shipments reached 7.8 million, surpassing the PS4's 7.6 million units in its first two quarters. As of July 18, 2021, 10 million PS5 units had been sold, marking the fastest-selling console in PlayStation history. Sony later confirmed that by June 30, 2021, it had shipped 10.1 million consoles, indicating nearly every shipped unit was sold immediately. Shipments surpassed 13.4 million by September 30, 2021. In August, Sony anticipated shipping over 22 million units by the end of its 2021 fiscal year in March 2022, but revised this to 15 million units in November. Despite the revision, sales during the 2022 fiscal year were forecast to reach 22.6 million units. Bloomberg News reported in January 2022 that Sony continued PS4 production to help alleviate the PS5 shortage during the ongoing chip shortage. By the end of September 2024, total PS5 shipments had reached 65 million units. Sony's Q2 2025 financial results stated that the PlayStation 5 had shipped 84.2 million units. Sales reached 20 million units by May 2022, 40 million by July 2023, 50 million by December 2023, and 75 million by February 2025.

The Pleasant Stay hotel case involved Jayalalithaa, the former Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu during 1991–1996, and her colleagues V. R. Nedunchezhiyan and T. M. Selvaganapathy, who were charged with misusing their office to allow Rakesh Mittal’s Pleasant Stay Hotel in Kodaikanal to build seven floors, violating development norms. In April 1991, Mittal was permitted to construct two floors; in January 1992, he sought approval for seven floors, which was rejected by the Kodaikanal township, prompting an appeal. He began constructing four floors without permission. On 13 May 1994, the Jayalalithaa government passed Government Order (G.O.) Ms. No.126, permitting five extra floors for a total of seven, against the norms. The order was passed by Jayalalithaa, Selvaganapathy, and water supply secretary H.M. Pandey, despite the Architectural and Aesthetics Aspects Committee (AAAC)’s recommendation against it. A subsequent G.O. Ms. No.317, effective from 13 May 1994, exempted the building from Development Control Rules. On 31 March 1994, the Madras High Court had ordered Mittal to use only the zero and first floors, an order later quashed along with the May 1994 G.O. The Palani Hills Conservation Council (PHCC) obtained a stay from the Madras High Court in December 1997 and won the legal battle. The trial, presided over by special judge Radhakrishnan in Chennai, was conducted by special public prosecutors N. Natarajan, S. Ramasamy, K.E. Venkataraman, R. Karunakaran, and advocate Sunder Mohan. The judge noted the First Investigation Report (FIR) was filed two years after the incident and that while there was a pecuniary advantage to the hotel management, no direct proof linked the government orders to personal gain for officials. Pandey, who knew the case details, did not pass the file directly to Jayalalithaa via Selvaganapathy. On 2 February 2000, the five accused—Jayalalithaa, Selvaganapathy, Pandey, Rakesh Mittal, and Palai N. Shanmugham—were convicted of criminal conspiracy and criminal misconduct by public servants; Jayalalithaa was sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment and fined ₹2,000, with the judge stating there was sufficient circumstantial evidence proving their involvement. On 9 February 2000, the Madras High Court suspended the sentence on appeal. The verdict triggered statewide protests and violence, including the burning of five buses, damage to fifty buses, and injuries to 40 people. In Dharmapuri, on 2 February 2000, three girls—Hemalatha, V. Gayathri, and Kokilavani—were burnt alive when a petrol bomb was thrown during a study tour return trip, with 16 others injured; the incident was broadcast on Sun TV and led to student protests and school closures. Two AIADMK cadres committed suicide by setting themselves on fire. The DMK accused AIADMK of inciting the violence, while AIADMK demanded a CBI probe, alleging DMK-supported Sun TV was present during the incident. The three AIADMK men convicted in the Dharmapuri incident were sentenced to death on 5 December 2007, later commuted to life imprisonment. Twenty-five other AIADMK cadres were convicted on lesser charges and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. The verdict occurred during a period when the Tamil Maanila Congress, allied with DMK in the 1996 elections, supported AIADMK in upcoming by-elections. Jayalalithaa was disqualified from contesting the 2001 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election due to the conviction, and the Supreme Court disqualified her on 21 September 2001, ruling that a convicted person cannot hold office of Chief Minister, despite claims of popular mandate. The governor of Tamil Nadu, Fathima Beevi, who administered the oath, was advised to step down by the Union Ministry, which submitted the report to the President of India; it was a rare instance of a constitutional functionary being removed for omission of duties. She resigned on 1 July 2001, and C. Rangarajan, then governor of Andhra Pradesh, was appointed as the acting governor. Following her disqualification, no clear successor emerged, and at an AIADMK meeting, O. Panneerselvam was chosen as Chief Minister. On 4 December 2001, the Madras High Court acquitted Jayalalithaa and four others of all charges in both the Pleasant Stay hotel and TANSI land acquisition cases. She contested and won the Andipatti assembly by-election in March 2002 and was sworn in as Chief Minister again. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal on 24 November 2003, citing lack of legal evidence despite strong suspicion, and ordered that she "must atone her conscience in the whole controversy." It was later reported that she returned the land to the agency at a throwaway price.

The Pleiades (/ˈpliː.ədiːz, ˈpleɪ-, ˈplaɪ-/ PLEE-ə-deez, PLAY-, PLY-), also known as Seven Sisters and Messier 45 (M45), is an asterism of an open star cluster containing young B-type stars in the northwest of the constellation Taurus. At a distance of about 444 light-years, it is among the nearest star clusters to Earth and the nearest Messier object to Earth, being the most obvious star cluster to the naked eye in the night sky. It contains the reflection nebulae NGC 1432, an HII region, and NGC 1435, known as the Merope Nebula. Around 2330 BC the Pleiades marked the vernal point. Due to the brightness of its stars, the Pleiades is viewable from most areas on Earth, even in locations with significant light pollution. The cluster is dominated by hot blue luminous stars that have formed within the last 100 million years. Reflection nebulae around the brightest stars were once thought to be leftover material from their formation, but are now considered likely to be an unrelated dust cloud in the interstellar medium through which the stars are currently passing, estimated to be moving at a speed of approximately 18 km/s relative to the stars in the cluster. Computer simulations have shown that the Pleiades were probably formed from a compact configuration that once resembled the Orion Nebula. Astronomers estimate that the cluster will survive for approximately another 250 million years, after which the clustering will be lost due to gravitational interactions with the galactic neighborhood. Together with the open star cluster of the Hyades, the Pleiades form the Golden Gate of the Ecliptic. The Pleiades have been said to "resemble a tiny dipper," and should not be confused with the "Little Dipper," or Ursa Minor. The name, Pleiades, comes from Ancient Greek: Πλειάδες. It probably derives from plein (πλεῖν 'to sail') because of the cluster's importance in delimiting the sailing season in the Mediterranean Sea: "the season of navigation began with their heliacal rising." In Classical Greek mythology the name was used for seven divine sisters called the Pleiades. In time, the name was said to be derived from that of a mythical mother, Pleione, effectively meaning "daughters of Pleione." In reality, the ancient name of the star cluster related to sailing almost certainly came first in the culture, naming of a relationship to the sister deities followed, and eventually appearing in later myths, to interpret the group name, a mother, Pleione. The M45 group played an important role in ancient times for the establishment of many calendars thanks to the combination of two remarkable elements. The first, which is still valid, is its unique and easily identifiable appearance on the celestial vault near the ecliptic. The second, essential for the ancients, is that in the middle of the third millennium BC, this asterism marked the vernal point (2330 BC with ecliptic latitude about +3.5° according to Stellarium). The importance of this asterism is also evident in northern Europe. The Pleiades cluster is displayed on the Nebra sky disc that was found in Germany and is dated to around 1600 BC. On the disk the cluster is represented in a high position between the Sun and the Moon. This asterism also marks the beginning of several ancient calendars: The Pleiades are a prominent sight in winter in the Northern Hemisphere, and are easily visible from mid-southern latitudes. They have been known since antiquity to cultures all around the world, including the Celts (Welsh: Tŵr Tewdws, Irish: Streoillín); pre-colonial Filipinos (who called it Mapúlon, Mulo‑pulo or Muró‑púro, among other names), for whom it indicated the beginning of the year; Hawaiians (who call them Makaliʻi); Māori (who call them Matariki); Indigenous Australians (from several traditions); the Achaemenid Empire, whence in Persians (who called them Parvīn پروین or Parvī پروی); the Arabs (who call them al-Thurayyā; الثريا); the Chinese (who called them mǎo; 昴); the Quechua (who call them Qullqa or the storehouse); the Japanese (who call them Subaru; 昴); the Maya; the Aztec; the Sioux; the Kiowa; and the Cherokee. In Hinduism, the Pleiades are known as Kṛttikā; कृत्तिका and are scripturally associated with the war deity Kartikeya (कार्त्तिकेय) and are also identified or associated with the Saptamatrika(s) (Seven Mothers). Hindus celebrate the first day (new moon) of the month of Kartik as Diwali, a festival of abundance and lamps. The Pleiades are also mentioned three times in the Bible, using the constellation's Hebrew name Kimah; כִּימָה. The earliest known depiction of the Pleiades is likely a Northern German Bronze Age artifact known as the Nebra sky disk, dated to approximately 1600 BC. The Babylonian star catalogues name the Pleiades MULMUL (𒀯𒀯), meaning 'stars' (literally 'star star'), and they head the list of stars along the ecliptic, reflecting the fact that they were close to the point of the vernal equinox around the twenty-third century BC. The Ancient Egyptians may have used the names "Followers" and "Ennead" in the prognosis texts of the Calendar of Lucky and Unlucky Days of papyrus Cairo 86637. Some Greek astronomers considered them to be a distinct constellation, and they are mentioned by Hesiod's Works and Days, Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and the Geoponica. The Pleiades was the most well-known "star" among pre-Islamic Arabs and so often referred to simply as "the Star" (an-Najm; النجم). Some scholars of Islam suggested that the Pleiades are the "star" mentioned in Surah An-Najm ('The Star') in the Quran. On numerous cylinder seals from the beginning of the first millennium BC, M45 is represented by seven points, while the Seven Gods appear, on low-reliefs of Neo-Assyrian royal palaces, wearing long open robes and large cylindrical headdresses surmounted by short feathers and adorned with three frontal rows of horns and a crown of feathers, while carrying both an ax and a knife, as well as a bow and a quiver. As noted by scholar Stith Thompson, the constellation was "nearly always imagined" as a group of seven sisters, and their myths explain why there are only six. Some scientists suggest that these may come from observations as far back as 100,000 BC when Pleione was farther from Atlas and hence, more visible as a separate star to the unaided eye. In Japan, the cluster is mentioned under the name Mutsuraboshi ("six stars") in the eighth-century Kojiki. The cluster is now known in Japan as Subaru, from the intransitive verb subaru, meaning "to cluster together." The Subaru Telescope, the 8.2-meter (320 in) flagship telescope of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, located at the Mauna Kea Observatory on the island of Hawaii, was named after the cluster. It had the largest monolithic primary mirror in the world from its commissioning in 1998 until 2005. It also was chosen as the brand name of Subaru automobiles to reflect the origins of the firm as the joining of five companies, and is depicted in the firm's six-star logo. In J. R. R. Tolkien's legendarium, where The Lord of the Rings is set, Pleiades is referred to as Remmirath, the netted stars, as are several other celestial bodies, such as the constellation Orion as Menelvagor, swordsman of the Sky. Galileo Galilei was the first astronomer to view the Pleiades through a telescope. He thereby discovered that the cluster contains many stars too dim to be seen with the naked eye. He published his observations, including a sketch of the Pleiades showing 36 stars, in his treatise Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610. The Pleiades have long been known to be a physically related group of stars rather than any chance alignment. John Michell calculated in 1767 that the probability of a chance alignment of so many bright stars was only 1 in 500,000, and so surmised that the Pleiades and many other clusters must consist of physically related stars. When studies were first made of the proper motions of the stars, it was found that they are all moving in the same direction across the sky, at the same rate, further demonstrating that they were related. Charles Messier measured the position of the cluster and included it as "M45" in his catalogue of comet-like objects, published in 1771. Along with the Orion Nebula and the Praesepe cluster, Messier's inclusion of the Pleiades has been noted as curious, as most of Messier's objects were much fainter and more easily confused with comets—something that seems scarcely possible for the Pleiades. One possibility is that Messier simply wanted to have a larger catalogue than his scientific rival Lacaille, whose 1755 catalogue contained 42 objects, and so he added some bright, well-known objects to boost the number on his list. Edme-Sébastien Jeaurat then drew in 1782 a map of 64 stars of the Pleiades from his observations in 1779, which he published in 1786. The distance to the Pleiades can be used as a key first step to calibrate the cosmic distance ladder. As the cluster is relatively close to the Earth, the distance should be relatively easy to measure and has been estimated by many methods. Accurate knowledge of the distance allows astronomers to plot a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram for the cluster, which, when compared with those plotted for clusters whose distance is not known, allows their distances to be estimated. Other methods may then extend the distance scale from open clusters to galaxies and clusters of galaxies, and a cosmic distance ladder may be constructed. Ultimately astronomers' understanding of the age and future evolution of the universe is influenced by their knowledge of the distance to the Pleiades. Yet some authors argue that the controversy over the distance to the Pleiades discussed below is a red herring, since the cosmic distance ladder can (presently) rely on a suite of other nearby clusters where consensus exists regarding the distances as established by the Hipparcos satellite and independent means (e.g., the Hyades, the Coma Berenices cluster, etc.). Measurements of the distance have elicited much controversy. Results prior to the launch of the Hipparcos satellite generally found that the Pleiades were approximately 135 parsecs (pc) away from Earth. Data from Hipparcos yielded a surprising result, namely a distance of only 118 pc, by measuring the parallax of stars in the cluster—a technique that should yield the most direct and accurate results. Later work consistently argued that the Hipparcos distance measurement for the Pleiades was erroneous: In particular, distances derived to the cluster via the Hubble Space Telescope and infrared color–magnitude diagram fitting (so-called "spectroscopic parallax") favor a distance between 135 and 140 pc; a dynamical distance from optical interferometric observations of the inner pair of stars within Atlas (a bright triple star in the Pleiades) favors a distance of 133 to 137 pc. However, the author of the 2007–2009 catalog of revised Hipparcos parallaxes reasserted that the distance to the Pleiades is ~120 pc and challenged the dissenting evidence. In 2012, Francis and Anderson proposed that a systematic effect on Hipparcos parallax errors for stars in clusters would bias calculation using the weighted mean; they gave a Hipparcos parallax distance of 126 pc and photometric distance of 132 pc based on stars in the AB Doradus, Tucana-Horologium and Beta Pictoris moving groups, which are all similar in age and composition to the Pleiades. Those authors note that the difference between these results may be attributed to random error. More recent results using very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) (August 2014), and preliminary solutions using Gaia Data Release 1 (September 2016) and Gaia Data Release 2 (August 2018), determine distances of 136.2 ± 1.2 pc, 134 ± 6 pc, and 136.2 ± 5.0 pc, respectively. The Gaia Data Release 1 team were cautious about their result, and the VLBI authors assert "that the Hipparcos-measured distance to the Pleiades cluster is in error." The most recent distance estimate of the distance to the Pleiades based on the Gaia Data Release 3 is 135.74±0.10 pc. The cluster core radius is approximately 8 light-years and tidal radius is approximately 43 light-years. The cluster contains more than 1,000 statistically confirmed members, not counting the number that would be added if all binary stars could be resolved. Its light is dominated by young, hot blue stars, up to 14 of which may be seen with the naked eye, depending on local observing conditions and visual acuity of the observer. The brightest stars form a shape somewhat similar to that of Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. The total mass contained in the cluster is estimated to be approximately 800 solar masses and is dominated by fainter and redder stars. An estimate of the frequency of binary stars in the Pleiades is approximately 57%. The cluster contains many brown dwarfs, such as Teide 1. These are objects with less than approximately 8% of the Sun's mass, insufficient for the nuclear fusion of hydrogen to start in their cores and become proper stars. They may constitute up to 25% of the total population of the cluster, although they contribute less than 2% of the total mass. Astronomers have made great efforts to find and analyze brown dwarfs in the Pleiades and other young clusters, because they are still relatively bright and observable, while brown dwarfs in older clusters have faded and are much more difficult to study. The brightest stars of the cluster are named the Seven Sisters in early Greek mythology: Sterope, Merope, Electra, Maia, Taygeta, Celaeno, and Alcyone. Later, they were assigned parents, Pleione and Atlas. As daughters of Atlas, the Hyades were sisters of the Pleiades. The following table gives details of the brightest stars in the cluster. Ages for star clusters may be estimated by comparing the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram for the cluster with theoretical models of stellar evolution. Using this technique, ages for the Pleiades of between 75 and 150 million years have been estimated. The wide spread in estimated ages is a result of uncertainties in stellar evolution models, which include factors such as convective overshoot, in which a convective zone within a star penetrates an otherwise non-convective zone, resulting in higher apparent ages. Another way of estimating the age of the cluster is by looking at the lowest-mass objects. In normal main-sequence stars, lithium is rapidly destroyed in nuclear fusion reactions. Brown dwarfs can retain their lithium, however. Due to lithium's very low ignition temperature of 2.5 million K, the highest-mass brown dwarfs will burn it eventually, and so determining the highest mass of brown dwarfs still containing lithium in the cluster may give an idea of its age. Applying this technique to the Pleiades gives an age of about 115 million years. The cluster is slowly moving in the direction of the feet of what is currently the constellation of Orion. Like most open clusters, the Pleiades will not stay gravitationally bound forever. Some component stars will be ejected after close encounters with other stars; others will be stripped by tidal gravitational fields. Calculations suggest that the cluster will take approximately 250 million years to disperse, because of gravitational interactions with giant molecular clouds and the spiral arms of our galaxy hastening its demise. With larger amateur telescopes, the nebulosity around some of the stars may be easily seen, especially when long-exposure photographs are taken. Under ideal observing conditions, some hint of nebulosity around the cluster may be seen even with small telescopes or average binoculars. It is a reflection nebula, caused by dust reflecting the blue light of the hot, young stars. It was formerly thought that the dust was left over from the formation of the cluster, but at the age of approximately 100 million years generally accepted for the cluster, almost all the dust originally present would have been dispersed by radiation pressure. Instead, it seems that the cluster is simply passing through a particularly dusty region of the interstellar medium. Studies show that the dust responsible for the nebulosity is not uniformly distributed, but is concentrated mainly in two layers along the line of sight to the cluster. These layers may have been formed by deceleration due to radiation pressure as the dust has moved toward the stars. Analyzing deep-infrared images obtained by the Spitzer Space Telescope and Gemini North telescope, astronomers discovered that one of the stars in the cluster, HD 23514, which has a mass and luminosity a bit greater than that of the Sun, is surrounded by.

Nebulosity around some of the stars in the cluster can be easily observed, particularly in long-exposure photographs, and under ideal observing conditions, a faint hint of this nebulosity may be visible even through small telescopes or average binoculars. The nebulosity is a reflection nebula, formed when dust reflects the blue light from the hot, young stars. Previously, it was believed that the dust originated from the cluster's formation, but given the cluster's age of about 100 million years, most of the original dust would have been dispersed by radiation pressure. Current evidence suggests instead that the cluster is passing through a particularly dusty region of the interstellar medium. Studies indicate that the dust causing the nebulosity is not evenly distributed but is concentrated in two layers along the line of sight to the cluster, possibly formed by deceleration due to radiation pressure as the dust moves toward the stars. Analysis of deep-infrared images from the Spitzer Space Telescope and Gemini North telescope revealed that one of the cluster's stars, HD 23514—having a mass and luminosity slightly greater than the Sun—is surrounded by a large number of hot dust particles, which may indicate ongoing planet formation around HD 23514.

Pluto, designated as minor-planet 134340, is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond Neptune's orbit. It is the ninth-largest and tenth-most-massive known object directly orbiting the Sun, the largest known trans-Neptunian object by volume, though less massive than Eris. Composed primarily of ice and rock, Pluto is much smaller than the inner planets and has roughly one-sixth the mass and one-third the volume of the Moon. Originally classified as a planet, its status changed when the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 2006 adopted a new definition of planet that excluded dwarf planets like Pluto. Pluto has a moderately eccentric and inclined orbit, ranging from 30 to 49 astronomical units (4.5 to 7.3 billion kilometers; 2.8 to 4.6 billion miles) from the Sun, with light from the Sun taking 5.5 hours to reach it at its average distance of 39.5 AU (5.91 billion km; 3.67 billion mi). Despite occasionally being closer to the Sun than Neptune, a stable orbital resonance prevents collision. Pluto has five known moons: Charon, the largest with a diameter just over half that of Pluto; Styx; Nix; Kerberos; and Hydra. Pluto and Charon are considered a binary system because their barycenter lies outside both bodies, and they are tidally locked. The New Horizons spacecraft made the first flyby of Pluto and its moons on July 14, 2015, taking detailed measurements and observations. Discovered in 1930 by Clyde W. Tombaugh at the Lowell Observatory, Pluto was initially hailed as the ninth planet. Doubts arose due to its small size, especially after the discovery of Eris in 2005, a more massive scattered disk object. In 2006, the IAU formally redefined a planet, requiring an object to orbit the Sun, be spherical, and have cleared its orbit of other debris—conditions Pluto fails to meet, as its mass is only 0.07 times that of the combined mass of other objects in its orbit. The IAU classified Pluto, Eris, and Eris's moon Dysnomia as dwarf planets, assigning them minor-planet designations (134340) Pluto, (136199) Eris, and (136199) Eris I Dysnomia. The name Pluto, derived from the Roman god of the underworld and an epithet for Hades, was proposed by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, and selected by a vote at the Lowell Observatory, which unanimously approved it. The name was published on May 1, 1930. The symbol for Pluto, a monogram of "PL," was created at the time but is rarely used in astronomy, though common in astrology. The name inspired Mickey Mouse's dog, Pluto, and the element plutonium, named by Glenn T. Seaborg in 1940. Most languages use "Pluto," with Japanese, Chinese, and Korean adopting Meiōsei (冥王星), while Hindi and other Indian languages use Yama, the Hindu god of death. Polynesian languages use indigenous underworld deities, such as Māori Whiro. Vietnamese uses Yama as Sao Diêm Vương due to phonological constraints. Early estimates of Pluto's mass were high—initially thought to be Earth-sized in 1931, then Mars-sized in 1948—before being revised to 0.2% of Earth's mass in 1978 after the discovery of Charon, which allowed accurate mass measurement. This mass was too small to explain orbital discrepancies in Uranus, which were later resolved by updated Neptune mass estimates from Voyager 2 data in 1992. By 2000, most scientists agreed that Lowell's Planet X did not exist, though his 1915 prediction was close to Pluto's actual orbit, a coincidence noted by Ernest W. Brown. The discovery of numerous Kuiper belt objects, including those as large as Pluto, intensified debate over its planetary status. In 1998, Brian G. Marsden suggested assigning Pluto minor-planet number 10000 while retaining its planetary status, prompting public outcry and the IAU clarifying it was not proposing removal. In 2005, the discovery of Eris, more massive than Pluto, intensified the debate, with many viewing it as a strong argument for reclassifying Pluto. At the 2006 IAU triennial meeting, astronomers Julio Ángel Fernández and Gonzalo Tancredi proposed the three criteria for planetary status, which Pluto fails due to not clearing its orbit. The IAU's decision faced resistance from planetary scientists, including Alan Stern and Marc W. Buie, who rejected it, while some, like Mike Brown, supported it. Public reaction was mixed, with a California Assembly resolution calling the decision a "scientific heresy" and New Mexico and Illinois passing resolutions honoring Clyde Tombaugh and affirming Pluto's planetary status. The American Dialect Society named "plutoed" word of the year in 2006, defining it as to demote or devalue. In April 2024, Arizona passed a law designating Pluto as the official state planet. In 2008, a conference at Johns Hopkins titled "The Great Planet Debate" concluded that scientists could not reach consensus on the definition of a planet. The IAU later introduced the term "plutoid" for Pluto-like objects beyond Neptune, though it has not gained widespread use. Pluto's orbital period is about 248 years, with a significant inclination of over 17° and moderate eccentricity, placing it in a region occasionally closer to the Sun than Neptune. The Pluto–Charon barycenter reached perihelion on September 5, 1989.

Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory hosted a conference titled "The Great Planet Debate" that featured back-to-back talks on the IAU definition of a planet, concluding with a post-conference press release stating that scientists could not reach a consensus on the definition. In June 2008, the IAU announced the term "plutoid" to describe Pluto and other planetary-mass objects with an orbital semi-major axis greater than Neptune’s, though this term has not seen significant use. Pluto’s orbital period is approximately 248 years, with a moderately inclined orbit (over 17°) relative to the ecliptic and moderately eccentric (elliptical), meaning a small portion of its orbit lies closer to the Sun than Neptune’s. The Pluto–Charon barycenter reached perihelion on September 5, 1989, and was last closer to the Sun than Neptune between February 7, 1979, and February 11, 1999. Despite the 2:3 resonance with Neptune, Pluto’s inclination and eccentricity behave chaotically, and computer simulations can only reliably predict its position for up to about 10–20 million years due to sensitivity to immeasurably small Solar System details. Pluto’s semi-major axis varies between 39.3 and 39.6 AU with a 19,951-year period, corresponding to an orbital period between 246 and 249 years, and this is currently increasing. Although Pluto’s orbit appears to cross Neptune’s when viewed from certain angles, the two bodies do not intersect; Pluto passes about 8 AU north of Neptune’s orbit, preventing a collision. This is further protected by the 2:3 orbital resonance: for every two orbits Pluto completes, Neptune completes three, in a rotating frame where Pluto’s perihelion precesses at about 0.97×10−4 degrees per year, with each cycle lasting about 495 years. When Pluto is at perihelion, Neptune is initially 57° ahead, and by the second perihelion, Neptune is 123° behind, resulting in a minimum separation of over 17 AU—greater than Pluto’s minimum distance from Uranus. This resonance is highly stable and has persisted over millions of years, preventing any close approach. When Pluto’s orbital period slightly deviates from 3/2 of Neptune’s, its distance from Neptune drifts; near perihelion, it moves interior to Neptune’s orbit and approaches from behind, remaining between 50° and 65° behind Neptune for about 100 years (e.g., 1937–2036). Gravitational interactions transfer angular momentum to Pluto, increasing its orbital radius and period, and after several cycles, the system returns to a stable state over about 20,000 years. Numerical studies show that the general alignment between Pluto and Neptune’s orbits remains unchanged over millions of years, with additional stability from two mechanisms: first, Pluto’s argument of perihelion librates around 90°, meaning it is farthest north when closest to the Sun, preventing encounters with Neptune; the amplitude of this libration is 38°, so the angular separation between Pluto’s perihelion and Neptune’s orbit is always greater than 52°, with the closest separation occurring every 10,000 years. Second, the longitudes of ascending nodes of Pluto and Neptune are in near-resonance, forming a 1:1 superresonance when aligned, placing Pluto’s perihelion at 90° and ensuring it is farthest north when closest to the Sun; this superresonance is influenced by all four Jovian planets. Pluto’s rotation period is 6.387 Earth days, with an axial tilt of 120°, causing extreme seasonal variation—where one-fourth of its surface experiences continuous daylight and another fourth continuous darkness at solstices. Research from the University of Arizona suggests this tilt results from polar wander due to the buildup of frozen nitrogen in shadowed areas, caused by temperatures as low as −240 °C (33.1 K) at the equator, which leads to nitrogen freezing. This polar wandering effect would be observable on Earth if the Antarctic ice sheet were much larger. Pluto’s surface is composed of over 98% nitrogen ice, with traces of methane and carbon monoxide; nitrogen and carbon monoxide are most abundant on the anti-Charon face (around 180° longitude, including Sputnik Planitia), while methane is most abundant near 300° east; mountains are made of water ice. The surface shows large variations in brightness and color, ranging from charcoal black to dark orange and white, with notable features including Tombaugh Regio ("Heart"), Belton Regio ("Whale"), and the "Brass Knuckles." Sputnik Planitia, a 1,000 km-wide basin of frozen nitrogen and carbon monoxide, features polygonal cells interpreted as convection cells, sublimation pits, and glacial flows, with no visible craters to New Horizons, indicating a surface younger than 10 million years—recent studies estimate its age at 180,000±90,000−40,000 years. The New Horizons team described Pluto as displaying a wide variety of geological landforms, including those from glacial and surface-atmosphere interactions, impacts, tectonics, possible cryovolcanism, and mass-wasting. In western Sputnik Planitia, transverse dunes formed by winds from the basin to surrounding mountains have wavelengths of 0.4–1 km and consist of methane particles 200–300 μm in size. Pluto’s density is 1.853±0.004 g/cm³, and scientists expect its internal structure to be differentiated, with a rocky core (pre-New Horizons estimate: 1700 km in diameter, 70% of Pluto’s diameter) surrounded by a water-ice mantle. Evidence suggests a subsurface ocean of liquid water 100 to 180 km thick at the core–mantle boundary, supported by Brown University simulations in September 2016 showing liquid water upwelling after a collision that formed Sputnik Planitia. In June 2020, astronomers reported evidence that Pluto may have had a subsurface ocean and could have been habitable when first formed; in March 2022, researchers proposed that Wright Mons and Piccard Mons are mergers of smaller cryovolcanic domes, indicating previously unanticipated internal heat. Pluto’s diameter is 2,376.6±3.2 km and its mass is (1.303±0.003)×10²² kg, which is 17.7% of the Moon’s mass (0.22% of Earth’s). Its surface area is 1.774443×10⁷ km², slightly larger than Russia or Antarctica (especially including winter sea ice), and its surface gravity is 0.063 g (compared to 1 g on Earth and 0.17 g on the Moon), giving it an escape velocity of 4,363.2 km/h (2,711.167 mph), more than twice the diameter and a dozen times the mass of Ceres. It is less massive than Eris, though it has a larger diameter (2,376.6 km vs. Eris’s ~2,326 km). With less than 0.2 lunar masses, Pluto is less massive than the terrestrial planets and seven moons (Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, Moon, Europa, and Triton). The discovery of Charon in 1978 enabled accurate determination of the Pluto–Charon system’s mass via Newton’s version of Kepler’s third law, allowing more precise measurements of Pluto’s diameter and shape through occultation and adaptive optics. Size determinations were complicated by Pluto’s atmosphere and hydrocarbon haze; in March 2014, Lellouch, de Bergh et al. found methane mixing ratios consistent with a diameter greater than 2,360 km, with a best estimate of 2,368 km. New Horizons data from July 13, 2015, initially measured Pluto’s diameter at 2,370 km, revised to 2,372 km on July 24, and later to 2,374±8 km; radio occultation data from the New Horizons Radio Science Experiment (REX) confirmed the diameter as 2,376.6±3.2 km. Pluto has a tenuous atmosphere of nitrogen, methane, and carbon monoxide in equilibrium with surface ices, with a surface pressure of about 1 Pa (10 μbar)—one million to 100,000 times less than Earth’s. New Horizons data show that atmospheric density increases as Pluto moves away from the Sun, and the atmosphere likely remains gaseous throughout its orbit. Nitrogen escape is 10,000 times less than expected; Alan Stern suggests even a small temperature increase could exponentially raise atmospheric density, potentially leading to liquid nitrogen flow. Sublimation of the atmosphere cools Pluto’s surface; it has no or almost no troposphere, with only a thin, discontinuous boundary layer about 4 km thick and at 37±3 K. In July 2019, an occultation revealed a 20% drop in atmospheric pressure since 2016, confirmed in 2021 by data from a 2018 occultation showing a thinner atmosphere. Methane, a greenhouse gas, creates a temperature inversion, with the atmosphere averaging tens of degrees warmer than the surface, though upper atmosphere observations show temperatures of 70 K (vs. expected ~100 K). The atmosphere has about 20 regularly spaced haze layers up to 150 km high, likely formed by pressure waves from airflow over mountains. Pluto has five known natural satellites; Charon, discovered in 1978 by James Christy, is the largest and the only moon of Pluto believed to be in hydrostatic equilibrium, with its mass causing the Pluto–Charon barycenter to lie outside Pluto; beyond Charon are four smaller circumbinary moons.

Astronomers at the Southwest Research Institute confirmed data from a 2018 occultation event, which revealed that light from behind Pluto's disc appeared to diminish less gradually, indicating a thinning atmosphere. Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, is present in Pluto's atmosphere and causes a temperature inversion, making the average atmospheric temperature tens of degrees warmer than the surface, although New Horizons observations found the upper atmosphere to be significantly colder than expected—around 70 K instead of about 100 K. Pluto's atmosphere consists of roughly 20 regularly spaced haze layers extending up to 150 km in height, believed to form due to pressure waves generated by airflow over Pluto's mountains. Pluto has five known natural satellites: Charon, the largest and closest, first identified in 1978 by James Christy, which is the only moon of Pluto thought to be in hydrostatic equilibrium; Charon's mass causes the barycenter of the Pluto–Charon system to lie outside Pluto. Beyond Charon are four smaller circumbinary moons—Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra—discovered in 2012 (Styx), 2005 (Nix and Hydra), and 2011 (Kerberos), respectively. Their orbits are circular (eccentricity less than 0.006) and coplanar with Pluto's equator (inclination less than 1°), tilted approximately 120° relative to Pluto's orbital plane, and they all orbit within the inner 3% of the region where prograde orbits would be stable. The moons exhibit orbital resonances and near-resonances: when precession is considered, Styx, Nix, and Hydra have an exact 18:22:33 period ratio, and there is a sequence of approximate 3:4:5:6 ratios between Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra and Charon, becoming more precise with greater distance. The Pluto–Charon system is unique in having its barycenter outside the primary body, with the Sun–Jupiter system being the only larger example and the Patroclus–Menoetius system being a smaller one; some astronomers refer to it as a double dwarf planet due to the similarity in size. Both bodies are tidally locked to each other, meaning they always show the same hemisphere to one another, a trait shared only with Eris and Dysnomia, and from any point on either body, the other remains in a fixed position in the sky or is always obscured. This tidal locking means each body's rotation period equals the system's orbital period around its barycenter. A collision between Pluto and a similar-sized body early in the Solar System is hypothesized to have formed the moons. In 2012, calculations suggested that 15810 Arawn could be a quasi-satellite of Pluto, remaining in such a configuration for about 350,000 years every two million years; New Horizons observations in 2015 refined Arawn's orbit and confirmed earlier data, though astronomers remain divided on whether Arawn should be classified as a quasi-satellite due to its primary orbital influence from Neptune. Early theories proposing Pluto as an escaped moon of Neptune were rejected because Pluto never approaches Neptune in its orbit. Pluto's true place in the Solar System became clear in 1992 when similar icy objects beyond Neptune were discovered, revealing a trans-Neptunian population; Pluto is the largest known member of the Kuiper belt, located between 30 and 50 AU from the Sun, and as of 2011, any remaining Pluto-sized objects are expected beyond 100 AU.
