Like other Kuiper belt objects, Pluto shares comet-like features, such as solar wind gradually eroding its surface; claims that Pluto would develop a tail if placed near Earth have been disputed due to its high escape velocity. Pluto may have formed from the aggregation of numerous comets and Kuiper belt objects. Though Pluto is the largest Kuiper belt object discovered, Neptune's moon Triton—larger than Pluto—is geologically and atmospherically similar and is believed to be a captured Kuiper belt object; Eris, similar in size to Pluto but more massive, is not considered a Kuiper belt object but rather part of the scattered disc. Pluto is thought to be a residual planetesimal from the original protoplanetary disc and its position results from Neptune's early migration outward, which disrupted the proto-Kuiper belt, captured some objects into orbit (like Triton), locked others into resonances, and scattered others into chaotic orbits; the scattered disc is thought to have formed from interactions with Neptune's migrating resonances. A 2004 model by Alessandro Morbidelli suggested Neptune's migration was triggered by a 1:2 resonance between Jupiter and Saturn, which pushed Uranus and Neptune into higher orbits and caused them to switch places, doubling Neptune's distance from the Sun, and this migration may have expelled objects from the proto-Kuiper belt, explaining the Late Heavy Bombardment and the origin of Jupiter trojans; Pluto may have had a near-circular orbit at about 33 AU before being perturbed into a resonant orbit. The Nice model requires about a thousand Pluto-sized bodies in the original planetesimal disk, including Triton and Eris. Pluto's great distance from Earth makes direct study difficult; its average visual magnitude is 15.1, brightening to 13.65 at perihelion, requiring a telescope with at least a 30 cm aperture to observe it, and it appears star-like without a visible disk due to its maximum angular diameter of 0.11". Early maps from the late 1980s were brightness maps derived from eclipses by Charon, measuring brightness changes during eclipses to infer surface features; Hubble Space Telescope images provided higher resolution, revealing details several hundred kilometers across, including polar regions and large bright spots, though these maps were later surpassed by New Horizons. The New Horizons spacecraft, launched in 2006, captured its first distant images of Pluto in late 2006 from about 4.2 billion kilometers away, confirming its ability to track distant targets, and used a Jupiter gravity assist in early 2007. It made its closest approach to Pluto on July 14, 2015, after a 3,462-day journey, with scientific observations beginning five months prior and continuing for at least a month afterward, using remote sensing instruments, spectroscopy, and radio science tools to study Pluto's geology, surface composition, and atmosphere. The final data from the encounter, totaling 50 billion bits or 6.25 gigabytes, was received on October 25, 2016. Since the flyby, scientists have called for an orbiter mission to fulfill new objectives, including mapping at 9.1 m per pixel, studying smaller moons, observing rotational changes, investigating a possible subsurface ocean, and creating topographic maps of permanently dark regions using laser pulses. Alan Stern has proposed a Cassini-style orbiter launched around 2030, the 100th anniversary of Pluto's discovery, using Charon's gravity for orbital adjustments and later leaving the system to study other Kuiper belt objects; a conceptual fusion-powered orbiter and lander based on the Princeton field-reversed configuration reactor has been funded by NASA's NIAC program. New Horizons imaged all of Pluto's northern hemisphere and equatorial regions down to about 30° South, while higher southern latitudes were only observed at low resolution from Earth; Hubble images from 1996 covered 85% of Pluto, showing large albedo features down to about 75° South, sufficient to reveal temperate-zone maculae, with slightly improved resolution later due to instrument upgrades. The equatorial region of the sub-Charon hemisphere was only imaged at low resolution due to the spacecraft's closest approach to the anti-Charon hemisphere. Some albedo variations in the southern latitudes were detectable via Charon-shine, and the south polar region appears darker than the north, though a high-albedo area in the southern hemisphere may represent a regional deposit of nitrogen or methane ice.

The Polanyi Medal is a biennial award given by the Royal Society of Chemistry to recognize outstanding contributions to the field of gas kinetics. It is presented at the International Symposium on Gas Kinetics following a plenary lecture delivered by the recipient. The medal is named in honor of Michael Polanyi, the Hungarian-British polymath who lived from 1891 to 1976 and whose research played a key role in establishing gas kinetics and reaction dynamics. John Polanyi, Michael's son, was awarded the Polanyi Medal in 1988.

Poliomyelitis, commonly known as polio, is an infectious disease caused by the poliovirus. Approximately 75% of cases are asymptomatic; mild symptoms such as sore throat and fever may occur in about 25% of cases and typically resolve within one or two weeks. In about 1% of infections, the virus spreads to the central nervous system (CNS), leading to nonparalytic aseptic meningitis with symptoms like headache, neck stiffness, fever, and vomiting, while in one to five in 1,000 cases, it progresses to paralytic disease, characterized by muscle weakness, floppiness, and paralysis—known as acute flaccid paralysis—most commonly affecting the legs, though it may also involve the head, neck, or diaphragm. Paralytic polio is classified as spinal, bulbar, or bulbospinal, depending on the CNS region affected; spinal polio results from damage to motor neurons in the spinal cord’s anterior horn, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy; bulbar polio affects the brain stem, causing difficulties with breathing, swallowing, and speech; and bulbospinal polio involves both bulbar and spinal regions, often resulting in diaphragm paralysis and respiratory failure. Between 2 and 10% of those with paralysis die due to respiratory complications. The disease is caused by infection with one of three serotypes of poliovirus—WPV1, WPV2, and WPV3—each with a distinct capsid protein, with WPV1 being the most commonly associated with paralysis. WPV2 was certified eradicated in 2015 and WPV3 in 2019. Polio occurs only in humans and spreads through fecal–oral or oral–oral routes, with transmission possible for up to six weeks after infection, even in asymptomatic individuals. The incubation period ranges from three to six days for nonparalytic cases and seven to 21 days if paralysis develops. The virus enters via the mouth, binds to CD155 receptors on cells, replicates in the gastrointestinal tract, and spreads to lymphoid tissues before entering the bloodstream, where it may circulate for up to 17 weeks. In rare cases, it invades the CNS, which is likely a chance event unrelated to age or socioeconomic status. Immunity develops through infection or vaccination, with IgA antibodies blocking replication in the gut and IgG and IgM preventing spread to motor neurons; however, immunity to one serotype does not protect against others. Two types of vaccines are used: the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), developed by Jonas Salk in 1952 and administered by injection, and the oral polio vaccine (OPV), introduced in 1961 and containing weakened live virus, which can be transmitted to others and, in low-vaccination settings, may revert to a virulent form, leading to circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV). An improved oral vaccine, nOPV2, with greater genetic stability, was granted full licensure and prequalification by the World Health Organization in December 2023. The global incidence of wild polio has dropped dramatically from an estimated 350,000 cases in 1988 to 30 confirmed cases in 2022, confined to Pakistan and Afghanistan as of October 2023. The term "poliomyelitis" comes from Ancient Greek, meaning inflammation of the spinal cord’s grey matter, first used in 1874 by Adolf Kussmaul, and the abbreviated term "polio" first appeared in 1911. Polio does not affect any species other than humans and is caused by a member of the Enterovirus genus. A rare condition, nonpoliovirus poliomyelitis, can result from other enteroviruses. Risk factors include pregnancy, being very young or old, immune deficiency, and malnutrition; maternal antibodies provide passive immunity to infants. Laboratory diagnosis involves detecting the virus in feces or pharyngeal swabs, or in blood or cerebrospinal fluid, with RT-PCR or genomic sequencing used to determine serotype and strain. In 1950, William Hammon developed a gamma globulin therapy from polio survivor plasma, which was about 80% effective in preventing paralytic polio and reducing disease severity, though its limited supply led to the focus on vaccine development. Both IPV and OPV are effective in providing lifelong protection and are used globally to prevent polio.

In 1950, William Hammon at the University of Pittsburgh purified the gamma globulin component from the blood plasma of polio survivors, proposing that it contained antibodies to poliovirus and could halt infection, prevent disease, and reduce its severity in other patients. A large clinical trial showed the gamma globulin was about 80 percent effective in preventing paralytic poliomyelitis and reduced disease severity in those who developed polio. However, due to limited blood plasma supply, it was deemed impractical for widespread use, leading the medical community to focus on developing a polio vaccine. Two types of polio vaccines are used globally: an inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) given by injection, developed in 1952 by Jonas Salk at the University of Pittsburgh and announced on 12 April 1955, which uses poliovirus grown in monkey kidney tissue culture (vero cell line) and chemically inactivated with formalin; after two doses, 90 percent or more of individuals develop protective antibodies to all three serotypes, and at least 99 percent are immune after three doses. Albert Sabin developed an oral polio vaccine (OPV) comprising a live, attenuated virus produced by repeated passage through nonhuman cells at subphysiological temperatures; the vaccine replicates efficiently in the gut but not in nervous system tissue. A single dose of Sabin’s trivalent OPV produces immunity in about 50 percent of recipients, and three doses provide protective antibodies in over 95 percent. Human trials began in 1957, and in 1958, the US National Institutes of Health selected it over other live attenuated vaccines; it was licensed in 1962 and became the only oral polio vaccine used worldwide. OPV efficiently blocks person-to-person transmission via oral–oral and fecal–oral routes, providing both individual and community immunity, while IPV confers good immunity but is less effective at preventing fecal–oral spread. OPV is preferred in many countries due to its low cost, ease of administration, and strong intestinal immunity, especially in endemic areas. However, on rare occasions, the attenuated virus in Sabin’s OPV can revert to a virulent form, leading to vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV); in 2017, cVDPV cases outnumbered wild poliovirus cases for the first time due to declining wild polio cases. Most industrialized countries have switched to IPV, which cannot revert, either alone or in combination with OPV. An improved oral vaccine, novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2), began development in 2011, received emergency licensing in 2021, and full licensure in December 2023; it has greater genetic stability and is less likely to revert. There is no cure for polio; treatment focuses on symptom relief, speeding recovery, and preventing complications, including antibiotics, analgesics, moderate exercise, and a nutritious diet. Long-term rehabilitation involving occupational therapy, physical therapy, braces, corrective shoes, and orthopedic surgery is often required. Portable ventilators may be needed; historically, iron lungs were used to support breathing during acute infection until patients could breathe independently (typically one to two weeks), but their use is now largely obsolete due to advances in therapy and polio’s eradication. Other historical treatments include hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, massage, passive motion, and surgical interventions such as tendon lengthening and nerve grafting. Patients with abortive polio recover completely; those with aseptic meningitis experience symptoms lasting two to ten days followed by full recovery. In spinal polio, if nerve cells are completely destroyed, paralysis is permanent; if not, temporary loss of function may recover within four to six weeks. Half of spinal polio patients recover fully, one-quarter with mild disability, and one-quarter with severe disability. The degree of acute and residual paralysis is proportional to viremia and inversely proportional to immunity. Spinal polio is rarely fatal; without respiratory support, suffocation or pneumonia from aspiration can occur, with 5 to 10 percent of paralytic polio patients dying, and case fatality rates ranging from 2–5 percent in children to 15–30 percent in adults. Bulbar polio is often fatal without respiratory support, with CFR ranging from 25 to 75 percent depending on age, reducible to 15 percent with intermittent positive pressure ventilation. Many cases result in temporary paralysis; nerve impulses return within a month, and recovery is complete in six to eight months. Recovery involves nerve terminal sprouting, where remaining motor neurons form new branches to reinnervate denervated muscle fibers, increasing the number of muscle cells controlled by a single neuron. Other mechanisms include myofiber hypertrophy and transformation of type II to type I muscle fibers. The body compensates for residual paralysis by using weaker muscles at higher intensity, developing little-used muscles, and using ligaments for stability. Residual complications include skeletal deformities, joint tightening, and movement disability; equinus foot occurs when downward-pulling muscles work but upward-pulling ones do not, leading to a foot that drops and retracts Achilles tendons, impairing walking. If one leg grows slower than the other, it causes limb length discrepancy and spinal deformities like scoliosis; interventions include epiphysiodesis or custom footwear. Prolonged immobility can lead to pulmonary edema, aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infections, kidney stones, paralytic ileus, myocarditis, and cor pulmonale. Between 25 and 50 percent of individuals who recovered from paralytic polio in childhood develop post-polio syndrome (PPS) decades later, characterized by new muscle weakness and extreme fatigue, thought to result from failure of oversized motor units created during recovery. Contributing factors include aging, permanent residual impairment, and overuse or disuse of neurons; PPS is progressive and has no specific treatment. Paralysis and limb length differences impair gait, and orthotics—such as stance phase control knee joints—can improve walking by providing mechanical support and enabling a natural gait pattern. Locked knee joints prevent flexion during swing phase, requiring compensatory mechanisms like Duchenne limping or circumduction. Polio epidemics were unknown before the 20th century; prior to that, it was an endemic disease worldwide. Mothers who survived polio passed temporary immunity to their babies in utero and through breast milk, so infants generally had mild symptoms and long-term immunity. Improvements in sanitation during the 19th century reduced herd immunity, leading to frequent epidemics, which killed or paralyzed over half a million people annually. After widespread vaccine use in the mid-1950s, polio cases declined dramatically in industrialized nations. Global eradication efforts began in 1988, led by the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and The Rotary Foundation, and are ongoing. Polio is one of only two diseases under a global eradication program, the other being Guinea worm disease. Smallpox and rinderpest are the only diseases completely eradicated by humans; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, rinderpest in 2011. In April 2012, the World Health Assembly declared failure to eradicate polio a programmatic emergency and stated it "must not happen." Efforts have greatly reduced cases, from 350,000 in 1988 to 483 in 2001, then stabilizing at about 1,000–2,000 annually. By 2015, wild polio remained in only Pakistan and Afghanistan, with outbreaks in neighboring countries due to hidden or re-established transmission. Global surveillance includes testing acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases and environmental/wastewater samples to detect circulating virus. The last region with wild polio is South Asia, specifically Afghanistan and Pakistan. In 2011, the CIA ran a fake hepatitis vaccination clinic in Abbottabad, Pakistan, damaging trust in vaccination programs; 66 vaccinators were killed in 2013 and 2014. In Afghanistan, the Taliban banned house-to-house polio vaccination from 2018 to 2021, hindering eradication efforts. In Afghanistan, polio cases dropped from 80 in 2011 to 4 in 2021. In Pakistan, cases fell by 97 percent from 2014 to 2018, due to a 440 million dirham donation from the UAE, changes in military conditions, and arrests of attackers. The Americas were declared polio-free in 1994, with the last known case in Peru in 1991. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends polio boosters for travelers and residents in endemic areas. In July 2022, New York reported its first polio case in nearly a decade, attributed to a vaccine-derived strain. In 2000, polio was declared eliminated in 37 Western Pacific countries, including China and Australia. Despite eradication, an outbreak involving a Pakistan strain was confirmed in China in September 2011. In September 2019, the Philippines declared a polio outbreak after a single case in a 3-year-old girl.

The Americas were declared polio-free in 1994, with the last known case occurring in a boy in Peru in 1991. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends polio vaccination boosters for travelers and individuals living in countries where the disease is endemic. In July 2022, New York reported its first polio case in nearly a decade, attributed to a vaccine-derived strain. In 2000, polio was officially eliminated in 37 Western Pacific countries, including China and Australia. Despite eradication ten years earlier, China experienced an outbreak in September 2011 involving a strain common in Pakistan. In September 2019, the Philippines declared a polio outbreak after a single case in a 3-year-old girl, and in December 2019, acute poliomyelitis was confirmed in an infant in Sabah, Malaysia, with three additional cases reported, the last in January 2020; both outbreaks were linked to vaccine-derived poliomyelitis. Europe was declared polio-free in 2002. On 27 March 2014, the WHO announced the eradication of poliomyelitis in the South-East Asia Region, which includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, North Korea, India, Indonesia, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Timor-Leste, bringing 80% of the world population into polio-free regions. As of January 2023, Syria is considered polio-free but remains at high risk for imported outbreaks; difficulties in immunization programs during the civil war led to a return of wild polio in 2012–2013, with 15 cases confirmed in Deir Ezzor between October and November 2013, and two more cases in rural Damascus and Aleppo; a vaccination campaign conducted under gunfire resulted in the deaths of several vaccinators but restored pre-war vaccination coverage; an outbreak in 2017 was caused by circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2, both of which were contained through intensive vaccination and surveillance. In 2022, before the Israel-Hamas conflict, routine immunization coverage in Israel exceeded 99%, but fell to less than 90% by the first quarter of 2024, according to the WHO; in 2024, the Gaza Health Ministry reported symptoms consistent with polio in several children, with laboratory confirmation of a 10-month-old child infected; United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres called for a weeklong cease-fire to enable vaccinations and prevent a potential outbreak. In 2003, a fatwa in northern Nigeria declared the polio vaccine designed to render children sterile, leading to polio's reappearance and spread to other countries; in 2013, nine health workers administering the vaccine were killed in Kano, though this was the only attack; local traditional and religious leaders and polio survivors helped revive the campaign, and Nigeria was removed from the polio-endemic list in September 2015 after over a year without cases, only to be restored in 2016 after two cases were detected. Africa was declared free of wild polio in August 2020, though circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 continues to appear in several countries; a single wild polio case in Malawi in February 2022 and another in Mozambique in May 2022, both imported from Pakistan, do not affect Africa’s wild poliovirus-free status. Polio’s effects have been known since prehistory, with Egyptian art depicting people with withered limbs and children using canes; the earliest known case is from a 4000-year-old burial site in the UAE involving a teenage girl. The first clinical description was by English physician Michael Underwood in 1789, who referred to it as "a debility of the lower extremities"; it was later known as Heine–Medin disease due to the work of Jakob Heine in 1840 and Karl Oskar Medin in 1890, and called infantile paralysis due to its effect on children. Before the 20th century, polio infections were rare in infants under six months, mostly affecting children aged six months to four years; poor sanitation led to constant exposure and natural immunity, but improvements in sanitation in developed countries during the late 19th and early 20th centuries reduced childhood exposure and immunity, increasing risk of paralytic polio. Small paralytic epidemics began in Europe and the US around 1900, reaching pandemic levels in Europe, North America, Australia, and New Zealand during the first half of the 20th century; by 1950, the peak age incidence in the US shifted to children aged five to nine, with about one-third of cases in persons over 15; the 1952 epidemic was the worst in US history, with nearly 58,000 cases, 3,145 deaths, and 21,269 left with mild to disabling paralysis; intensive care medicine originated in the fight against polio, with respiratory centers established in 1952 at Blegdam Hospital in Copenhagen by Bjørn Ibsen, who later founded the world’s first dedicated ICU. Polio epidemics altered lives and brought cultural changes, including grassroots fundraising and the development of rehabilitation therapy; polio survivors helped advance the disability rights movement, with the WHO estimating 10 to 20 million survivors worldwide; in 1977, 254,000 US residents were paralyzed by polio; in 2001, estimates showed 40,000 survivors in Germany, 30,000 in Japan, 24,000 in France, 16,000 in Australia, 12,000 in Canada, and 12,000 in the UK; many notable individuals credit polio with shaping their careers. The disease was widely publicized in the 1950s, and 15 scientists and two laymen who contributed to polio research are honored in the Polio Hall of Fame, established in 1957 at the Roosevelt Warm Springs Institute for Rehabilitation, with four organizations—Rotary International, WHO, CDC, and UNICEF—added in 2008. World Polio Day (24 October) was established by Rotary International to commemorate the birth of Jonas Salk, who led the first team to develop a polio vaccine. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), launched in 1988 by WHO, UNICEF, and The Rotary Foundation, has reduced polio worldwide by 99 percent and continues. In 2010, wild poliovirus was detected through importation in 13 countries: Chad, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Republic of Congo, Kazakhstan, Liberia, Mali, Nepal, Niger, the Russian Federation, Senegal, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uganda. In 2021, types 2 and 3 were fully eradicated globally, though type 1 cases still persist in Pakistan and Afghanistan; these two countries remain the only ones with endemic poliovirus. Countries considered polio-free but not confirmed as of April 2024 include Somalia, Djibouti, Sudan, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Yemen, the UAE, Iraq, Kuwait, and Iran. Since 2018, GPEI has coordinated efforts to eliminate polio and improve surveillance and prevention, employing 4,000 people across 75 countries and managing a budget of nearly US $1 billion. As of 2021, GPEI had raised 18 billion dollars in funding, with annual contributions between 800 million and 1 billion dollars; approximately 30% came from the Gates Foundation, 30% from developed governments, 27% from polio-risk countries, and the remainder from nonprofits, private funders, and other foundations. GPEI has identified six research directions, including continuing vaccination programs for at least ten years after eradication and gradually reducing the retention of live poliovirus samples in laboratories and manufacturing facilities due to escape risks; vaccines under development use virus-like particles or modified viruses that cannot reproduce in humans.

Ponyo is a 2008 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, animated by Studio Ghibli for the Nippon Television Network, Dentsu, Hakuhodo DY Media Partners, Buena Vista Home Entertainment, Mitsubishi, and distributed by Toho. The film stars Yuria Nara, Hiroki Doi, Tomoko Yamaguchi, Kazushige Nagashima, Yūki Amami, George Tokoro, Rumi Hiiragi, Akiko Yano, Kazuko Yoshiyuki, and Tomoko Naraoka. It is the eighth film Miyazaki directed for Studio Ghibli and his tenth overall. The story follows Ponyo, a goldfish-like creature who escapes from the ocean and is helped by a five-year-old human boy named Sōsuke after she is washed ashore while trapped in a glass jar. As they bond, Ponyo desires to become a human girl, using magic granted by Sōsuke's human blood that she licked. Fujimoto, a misanthropic wizard who was once a human, lives underwater with his daughter Brunhilde and her numerous smaller sisters, who are goldfish-like creatures with human faces. During an outing in his four-flippered submarine, Brunhilde sneaks off and floats away on a jellyfish, gets trapped in a glass jar, and is rescued by Sōsuke. When Sōsuke shatters the jar with a rock, he cuts his finger, and Brunhilde licks the blood, healing the wound instantly. Sōsuke names her Ponyo and promises to protect her. Fujimoto, distraught, searches for his daughter and calls his wave spirits to recover her, leaving Sōsuke heartbroken. Ponyo refuses to be called by her birth name, declaring her desire to be a human named Ponyo. With Sōsuke's blood, she begins transforming into a human, but Fujimoto forces her back into her true form and leaves to summon her mother, Gran Mamare. Meanwhile, Ponyo and her sisters break away and use Fujimoto's magic to become human, causing a massive release of magic that leads to a tsunami. After the tsunami, Sōsuke is overjoyed to see her, and his mother, Lisa, allows her to stay at their house. Lisa leaves to check on residents of a nursing home where she works, promising to return soon. Gran Mamare arrives at Fujimoto's submarine, where Sōsuke's father, Kōichi, recognizes her as the Goddess of Mercy. Fujimoto notices the moon falling out of orbit and satellites falling like shooting stars, signs of nature's imbalance. Gran Mamare declares that if Sōsuke passes a test, Ponyo can live as a human and nature will be restored; if he fails, Ponyo will turn into sea foam. The next day, Sōske and Ponyo find most of the land covered by the ocean. Since Lisa cannot return, they decide to find her. Using Ponyo's magic, they enlarge Sōsuke's pop-pop boat to see marine life from the Late Devonian period and more people on boats. When they reach the forest, Ponyo tires and falls asleep, and the boat reverts to its original size. Sōsuke drags Ponyo to shore, where he finds Lisa's abandoned car. As they walk, Ponyo mysteriously reverts to her fish form. Gran Mamare grants Lisa and the nursing home residents the ability to breathe underwater. Ponyo and Sōske encounter Fujimoto, who warns them about the imbalance and begs them to return Ponyo. Despite trying to escape, Fujimoto captures them and transports them to the nursing home. Sōske reunites with Lisa and meets Gran Mamare, who asks if he can love Ponyo whether she is a fish or human; Sōske confirms he does. Gran Mamare then tells Ponyo she must give up her magical powers to permanently become human. She agrees and is encased in a bubble given to Sōske, who is instructed to kiss it to complete her transformation, restoring nature's balance. The stranded ships return to port. Fujimoto respects his daughter's choice and decides to trust Sōske. Ponyo joyfully jumps and kisses Sōske, completing her transformation into a human. Miyazaki was prompted to create Ponyo after producer Toshio Suzuki suggested a film aimed at children, noting the success of Howl's Moving Castle (2004). The film combines real-world and fictional influences with new art and animation approaches developed by Studio Ghibli staff. In 2004 and 2005, Miyazaki spent time in Tomonoura, a seaside town in Setonaikai National Park, where he studied its community and environment. He read the complete works of Natsume Sōseki, particularly The Gate, which features a character named Sōsuke living at the bottom of a cliff, providing inspiration for characters and settings. Initially, Miyazaki considered a film about a stormy sea with waves higher than a house on a hillside, later creating the character Ponyo, a name he thought of as an onomatopoeia for the soft, squishy feeling of touch. He recalled borrowing Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid" as a child and struggling with the idea that the protagonist lacked a soul. Before visiting the Tate Britain art museum, Miyazaki faced a creative block; upon seeing the 1852 painting Ophelia by John Everett Millais, he was struck by its detail and realized his animation style needed to evolve. Katsuya Kondō, who had directed the short film House Hunting (2006), was hired as animation supervisor for Ponyo and helped develop a direction emphasizing traditional hand-drawn animation with simple, solid lines. The film features frame-by-frame animation of ships, unlike typical cel animation, and the computer graphics section was closed to prioritize hand-drawn work. Elements of Richard Wagner's opera Die Walküre are present, with Ponyo's birth name, Brunhilde, referencing the Valkyrie Brünnhilde. The character of Sōsuke is based on Miyazaki's son Gorō when he was five. Miyazaki intended a sequel to Ponyo, but Toshio Suzuki convinced him to make The Wind Rises instead. The eponymous theme song, "Gake no Ue no Ponyo," was released on December 5, 2007, performed by Fujioka Fujimaki and eight-year-old Nozomi Ōhashi. It entered the Oricon Weekly Charts, reaching 6th on July 28 and 3rd on August 4, and became the 14th highest-selling single on the Oricon Yearly Charts by the end of 2008. Ōhashi was the youngest participant in the 59th NHK Kōhaku Uta Gassen at age 11, breaking Mai Hagiwara's record, and later announced the disbanding of her unit with Fujioka Fujimaki. An English-translated pop version was recorded by Jonas and Cyrus and plays over the second half of the English closing credits, with the first half being a translated version. The film score was composed by Joe Hisaishi, Miyazaki's regular collaborator, and the score album was released in Japan by Tokuma Japan Communications, in South Korea by Pony Canyon Korea, and throughout Europe by Colosseum. The film premiered in Japan on July 19, 2008, on 481 screens, a record for a domestic film, grossing ¥10 billion ($91 million) in its first month and a total of ¥15.0 billion ($153.1 million) by November 9, 2008. It was named Animation of the Year at the Tokyo Anime Fair in 2008. The film was released on VHS and DVD by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment on July 3, 2009, and on Blu-ray on December 8, 2009, making it the last Studio Ghibli film and the last anime film to be released on VHS, and the first Studio Ghibli film released on Blu-ray in the U.S. It was released in the U.S. and Canada on August 14, 2009, by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures through their Walt Disney Pictures banner and The Kennedy/Marshall Company, opening in 927 theaters—the widest release for a Studio Ghibli film in the U.S., compared to Spirited Away (26), Howl's Moving Castle (36), and Princess Mononoke (38). The English dub was directed by John Lasseter, Brad Lewis, and Peter Sohn of Pixar and produced by Frank Marshall, Hayao Miyazaki, John Lasseter, Steve Alpert, and Kathleen Kennedy; the English script was written by Melissa Mathison. In July 2009, there were multiple pre-screenings in California, and Miyazaki traveled to the U.S. to promote the film at the University of California, Berkeley, and San Diego Comic-Con. The film was released in Southeast Asia on January 1, 2009. Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment released it on DVD and Blu-ray on March 2, 2010, as the first Ghibli film directed by Miyazaki or Takahata to be released on Blu-ray in America. GKIDS re-issued it on Blu-ray and DVD on October 17, 2017, under a new deal with Studio Ghibli, and it was re-released from March 25 to 28, 2018, for its 10th anniversary. On its opening weekend in the U.S. and Canada, it earned $3,585,852 on 927 screens, with a per-screen average of $3,868, opening at number nine on the box office. The film made $15,743,471 in the U.S. and Canada and $187,461,411 in other countries for a worldwide total of $203,204,882. It received critical acclaim, with Rotten Tomatoes compiling 174 reviews and giving it a 91% positive rating with an average score of 7.6/10, and a Metacritic score of 86 out of 100 based on 29 reviews, indicating universal acclaim. The Japan Times gave it four out of five stars, praising its simple themes and visual design and comparing it to My Neighbor Totoro. Critics at the Venice International Film Festival gave high praise; Wendy Ide of The Times called it "as chaotic and exuberant as a story told by a hyperactive toddler" and gave it 4 stars out of 5, while Roger Ebert gave it four out of four stars, calling it "magical" and "visually breathtaking." The film was ranked #2 on Dentsu's list of "2008 Hit Products in Japan" after the Wii console. It was an entrant in the 65th Venice International Film Festival and received a special mention at the Bologna Future Film Festival for its high artistic and expressive quality. In 2009, it won five awards at the 8th annual Tokyo Anime Awards, including "Anime of the Year" and "Best Domestic Feature," with Miyazaki winning best director and best original story, and Noboru Yoshida winning best art direction. The film also won Animation of the Year and Outstanding Achievement in Music at the 32nd Japan Academy Prize.

Onyo was an entrant in the 65th Venice International Film Festival and received a special mention at the Bologna Future Film Festival, recognized for "the high artistic and expressive quality of animation able to give form to wonderful imagination of the worldwide cinema master". In 2009, Ponyo won five awards at the 8th annual Tokyo Anime Awards, including "Anime of the Year" and "Best domestic feature". Miyazaki was awarded best director and best original story, while Noboru Yoshida received the award for best art direction. The film also won the awards for Animation of the Year and Outstanding Achievement in Music at the 32nd Japan Academy Prize.

Prabhunath Singh is a politician from Bihar, India, who served as a member of the 12th, 13th, and 14th Lok Sabha. He represented the Masrakh assembly constituency from 1985 to 1995 and the Maharajganj Lok Sabha constituency from 1998 to 2009. In 2013, he won a bypoll and remained as a Member of Parliament until 2014. Singh is a member of the Janata Dal (United) (JD(U)) and is currently serving a life imprisonment sentence in a murder case. Born in Mashrakh, Saran district, Bihar, he studied up to class-12 from Bihar University, Muzaffarpur, in 1972. His brothers, Dina Singh, Madan Singh, and Kedar Singh, are also politicians. He is married to Binda Devi, and his son, Randhir Kumar Singh, is a politician who currently serves as MLA from the Manjhi Assembly constituency but lost in the 2019 Indian general election to Janardan Singh Sigriwal of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Before entering politics, Singh owned a brick-making factory. He won his first election as an independent candidate due to his support among Rajputs in his area. He is a four-time member of parliament from the Saran district. In the 1995 elections, he ran as a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) but left the party after losing and joined the Janata Dal (United) (JD(U)). He won elections as a JD(U) member but later joined the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) due to Nitish Kumar's dictatorship in the JD(U). He represented the Maharajganj constituency from 2004 to 2009 on the JD(U) ticket. In 2009, he contested on the JD(U) ticket but narrowly lost to Uma Shankar Singh of the RJD. After Uma Shankar Singh's death, which left the seat vacant, Singh contested on the RJD ticket and defeated JD(U)'s nominee P.K. Shahi. On 23 May 2017, Singh was sentenced to life imprisonment by the Hazaribagh Court for his involvement in the murder of MLA Ashok Singh, which occurred 22 years earlier. Singh had been elected as MLA twice and as a Lok Sabha MP four times.

doc_name: Premier League Manager of the Month
text: The Premier League Manager of the Month is an award that recognises the best-performing manager each month during the Premier League season. The winner is determined by a combination of a 10% public online vote and a panel of experts. The award was previously known as the Carling Premiership Manager of the Month (1993–2001) and the Barclaycard Premiership Manager of the Month (2001–2004), and is currently called the Barclays Manager of the Month. The Premier League was established in 1992 when the First Division clubs withdrew from the Football League to form a commercially independent league that negotiated its own broadcast and sponsorship deals. The Manager of the Month award was introduced for the 1993–94 season, supplementing existing Player of the Year awards from the Football Writers' Association and Professional Footballers' Association; the first recipient was Manchester United's Alex Ferguson in August 1993. The Player of the Month award was introduced for the 1994–95 season and is presented alongside the Manager of the Month award. Ferguson holds the record with 27 Manager of the Month awards, while Harry Redknapp has won the award in five of his six spells managing Premier League clubs—West Ham United, Portsmouth, Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, and Queens Park Rangers. Sixteen other managers have won the award with two or more clubs: Gordon Strachan (Coventry City, Southampton), Stuart Pearce (Nottingham Forest, Manchester City), Martin O'Neill (Leicester City, Aston Villa, Sunderland), Roy Hodgson (Blackburn Rovers, Fulham), Rafael Benítez (Liverpool, Chelsea, Newcastle United), Brendan Rodgers (Swansea City, Liverpool), Alan Pardew (West Ham United, Newcastle United), Sam Allardyce (Bolton Wanderers, West Ham United), Tony Pulis (Crystal Palace, West Bromwich Albion), Mauricio Pochettino (Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur), Claudio Ranieri (Chelsea, Leicester City), Carlo Ancelotti (Chelsea, Everton), José Mourinho (Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur), Nuno Espírito Santo (Wolverhampton Wanderers, Tottenham Hotspur, Nottingham Forest), Eddie Howe (Bournemouth, Newcastle United), and Sean Dyche (Burnley, Everton). Seventeen managers have won the award in consecutive months: Joe Kinnear, Kevin Keegan, Roy Evans, Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, David O'Leary, Stuart Pearce, Paul Jewell, Rafael Benítez, Carlo Ancelotti, Manuel Pellegrini, Claudio Ranieri, Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp, Mikel Arteta, and Ange Postecoglou. Guardiola is the only manager to have won the award in four successive months, Klopp is the first to win it five times in a single season, and Postecoglou is the only manager to win it in each of his first three months in charge. The award was shared once, in March 2002, when Liverpool's Gérard Houllier and caretaker manager Phil Thompson were jointly awarded the prize due to Houllier's absence for medical reasons. As of December 2025, the most recent recipient is Aston Villa head coach Unai Emery. The award has been given monthly from the 1993–94 season through to the 2025–26 season. A table lists the number of awards won by managers with at least two wins, with managers in bold still active in the Premier League.

The presidency of Carlos Saúl Menem lasted from July 8, 1989, to December 10, 1999, when his successor, Fernando de la Rúa, took office. It was a liberal-conservative government, typically associated with the right in Argentina. Menem won the 1989 presidential election in the first round with 48.51% of the votes and was re-elected in 1995 with 49.95% of the votes. Upon taking office, Argentina faced severe hyperinflation and recession; his first measure was a mandatory conversion of time deposits into government bonds, which worsened recession but reduced hyperinflation. Despite being a Peronist, Menem privatized several state-owned enterprises, including telephones and airlines, with YPF, the company involved in oil and gas exploration and production, being one of the most significant privatizations. As fourth economy minister, Domingo Cavallo implemented deeper neoliberal reforms, introducing the Convertibility Plan that established a one-to-one fixed exchange rate between the Argentine peso and the US dollar, while also limiting public expenditures—though this was often ignored. This policy, combined with a surge in foreign direct investment, reduced inflation from 5,000% annually in 1989 to single digits by 1993 and boosted productivity, albeit at the cost of high unemployment. Argentina's GDP, below 1973 levels when Menem began his term, increased by 35% from 1990 to 1994, and fixed investment rose by 150%. In March 1991, negotiations with Brazil led to the formation of the Mercosur customs union; on November 14 of that year, Menem addressed a joint session of the U.S. Congress, one of only three Argentine presidents to do so (the others being Raúl Alfonsín and Arturo Frondizi). His re-election in 1995 was by a large majority, though the early success of the dollar peg, which worked when the dollar was falling, gave way to economic difficulties when the dollar rose from 1995 onward, compounded by high external debt. Financial crises in Mexico (Tequila Crisis), East Asia, and Russia (1998) led to higher interest rates for Argentina, and by the end of his term, Argentina's country risk premium was 6.10 percentage points above the yield on comparable U.S. Treasuries. Menem began his presidency with a nonconfrontational approach, appointing conservative opposition members and business leaders to his cabinet. His economic recovery, driven by Cavallo’s policies, was bolstered by Justicialist Party victories in the 1991 and 1993 mid-term elections and his 1995 re-election campaign. Domestically, his administration launched programs to improve AIDS awareness, flood prevention, vaccination, and child nutrition, and introduced a Social Plan to increase spending on antipoverty initiatives, with other social programs addressing the needs of poor Argentines. These policies likely contributed to a decline in poverty during his first term. The Argentine quota law, proposed by the UCR, increased the number of women in the Argentine Congress. In 1994, after the Olivos Pact with Radical Civic Union leader Raúl Alfonsín, Menem succeeded in modifying the Constitution to allow presidential re-election. The new Constitution also introduced checks and balances, making the Mayor of Buenos Aires an elective position (previously a political appointee with significant budget control), and resulting in an opposition candidate winning the mayoral election in 1996. The president of the Central Bank and the Director of the AFIP (Federal Tax & Customs Central Agency), though political appointees, could be removed only with congressional approval. The Constitution also established an ombudsman and a board to review and propose new judicial candidates. Despite these reforms, the majority of the population and some members of the Catholic Church criticized Menem’s neoliberal policies, with unemployed workers forming the Piquetero movement and some economists labeling his financial policies as anti-liberal. These issues, along with rising crime rates, led to a defeat for his party in the 1997 mid-term elections, marking the first time his administration faltered. On December 3, 1990, Menem ordered the forceful suppression of a politically motivated uprising led by Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín, ending military involvement in politics. He faced strong criticism for pardoning Jorge Videla, Emilio Massera, Leopoldo Galtieri, and other leaders of the 1976–83 military dictatorship, who were convicted in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas for terrorism and the disappearance of approximately 15,000 political prisoners; he also pardoned some guerrilla leaders on grounds of national reconciliation. Nearly 50,000 people protested in Buenos Aires, and former President Raúl Alfonsín called it "the saddest day in Argentine history." Menem drastically reduced the military budget and appointed Lt. Gen. Martín Balza as Army General Chief of Staff, a figure with strong democratic convictions and a critic of the Falklands War who had defended the legitimate government in all coups and delivered the first institutional self-criticism regarding the military’s role in the 1976 coup and the subsequent terror. After the death of a conscript, Menem abolished conscription in 1994, ending military control over society. Carlos Menem Jr., the president’s son, died in a helicopter accident on March 15, 1995, at age 26; his death remains a mystery, with his parents, Zulema Yoma de Menem, suspecting murder, and ballistics expert Roberto Locles believing "Carlitos" died in an attempted assassination. Menem re-established relations with the United Kingdom, which had been suspended since the Falklands War, within months of taking office, and earned praise for resolving territorial disputes with Chile, peacefully settling over 20 border issues, including the Laguna del Desierto dispute. His tenure was most negatively affected by the Mexican peso crisis of 1995 and was marred by repeated accusations of corruption. His administration’s handling of the 1992 Israeli Embassy bombing and the 1994 AMIA Jewish community center bombing in Buenos Aires was criticized as dishonest and superficial, with suspicions that he diverted investigations from Iranian involvement to avoid confronting that power and to cover up possible links to his family friend, Alberto Kanoore Edul, a Syrian-Argentine businessman suspected of involvement in the attacks.

Raúl Alfonsín served as president of Argentina from 1983 to 1989. He inherited an economic crisis rooted in the 1981–82 financial collapse, which left Argentina with a US$43 billion foreign debt and interest payments that consumed its entire US$3 billion trade surplus. Although the economy showed modest recovery in 1983 due to the lifting of wage freezes and the Central Bank's "Circular 1050," inflation soared to 400%, GDP per capita remained at its lowest level since 1968, and fixed investment was 40% below 1980 levels. Alfonsín appointed a center-left cabinet led by Foreign Minister Dante Caputo and Economy Minister Bernardo Grinspun, fulfilling campaign promises such as a nutritional assistance program for the 27% of Argentines living in poverty and reversing Bignone's blanket amnesty for human rights abuses and warrantless wiretapping. Defense Minister Raúl Borrás advised removing Fabricaciones Militares from military control, resulting in the retirement of 70 generals and admirals opposed to the transfer. He appointed playwright Carlos Gorostiza as Secretary of Culture and exiled scientist Dr. Manuel Sadosky as Secretary of Science and Technology, leading to hundreds of artists and scientists returning in 1984. Gorostiza abolished the National Film Rating Entity, contributing to a doubling of film and theatre production, and the film *La historia oficial* was released in April 1985 and won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Alfonsín established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), led by Ernesto Sábato, which documented 8,960 forced disappearances and presented its findings to the President on September 20; the report's victim count was lower than Amnesty International's estimate of 16,000 and the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo's estimate of 30,000. Alfonsín prosecuted members of leftist groups, including Mario Firmenich of the Montoneros, and pardoned former President Isabel Perón in May 1984 for her role in the Dirty War and alleged embezzlement, though his legislation for secret ballot labor union elections was rejected by the Senate by one vote. Relations with the United States deteriorated when Alfonsín ended support for the Contras, and two meetings with President Ronald Reagan failed to secure economic concessions. He initiated diplomatic contact with the United Kingdom, lifting British trade sanctions, and proposed a treaty with Chile to resolve the Beagle Channel border dispute, which was approved by voters with 82% support. Facing a foreign debt crisis worsened by high global interest rates, Alfonsín dealt with shattered business confidence and record budget deficits; GDP grew by 2% in 1984, but fixed investment declined and inflation rose to 700%. The federal budget had a US$10 billion shortfall in 1984 (13% of GDP), prompting the Central Bank to print money, which pushed inflation from 18% monthly to 30% in June 1985—the world's highest at the time. Economy Minister Juan Sourrouille introduced the Austral Plan, freezing prices and replacing the peso with the austral at 1,000 to one. Sharp budget cuts, especially in military spending, reduced it to about half of 1983 levels. A mechanism called desagio was introduced to compensate debtors affected by inflation drops, reducing inflation from 30% in June to 2% monthly by the end of 1985 and cutting the fiscal deficit by two-thirds. Military discontent grew, with bomb threats and sabotage blamed on hard-line officers, including former 1st Army Corps head Gen. Guillermo Suárez Mason, who fled to Miami after an October arrest order. Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, beginning on April 22, 1985, which prosecuted top military leaders for Dirty War crimes; in December, former President Jorge Videla and Navy Chief Emilio Massera received life sentences, and three others received 17-year sentences. Four defendants were acquitted, including former President Leopoldo Galtieri, who was later court-martialed in May 1986 for malfeasance during the Falklands War and sentenced to 12 years. For these actions, Alfonsín received the first Prize For Freedom of the Liberal International and the Human Rights Prize by the Council of Europe. In the November 1985 legislative elections, the UCR gained one seat in the Lower House and controlled 130 of 254 seats, while the Justicialists lost eight (leaving 103). In April 1986, Alfonsín announced a panel to plan the transfer of the capital to Viedma, 800 km south of Buenos Aires, proposing constitutional amendments for a parliamentary system with a prime minister, which was well received by the Lower House but opposed in the Senate. Economic concerns persisted, and a fall in global commodity prices in 1986 reduced the trade surplus from US$4.5 billion to half and inflation dropped to 50% by June 1986 (from 1,130% in June 1985), though it soon rose above 80%. GDP, which had declined 5% in 1985, grew 7% in 1986, driven by machinery purchases and consumer spending. Repeated wage freezes under Sourrouille caused real wages to fall by about 20%, triggering seven general strikes by the CGT. Alfonsín appointed conservative economist José Luis Machinea as Central Bank president, pleasing the financial sector but failing to stop capital flight, with affluent Argentines believed to hold over US$50 billion in overseas deposits. He made several state visits abroad to secure trade deals. His international reputation for human rights was damaged in December 1986 when Congress passed the Full Stop Law, limiting civil trials against roughly 600 officers to those indicted within 60 days of the law's passage. In 1987, during Easter weekend, a group known as the Carapintadas, loyal to Army Major Aldo Rico, staged a mutiny at Campo de Mayo and near Córdoba; Alfonsín negotiated their surrender and announced: "La casa está en orden y no hay sangre en Argentina. ¡Felices pascuas!" to signal the end of the crisis. His appointment of General Dante Caridi as Army Chief of Staff further strained military relations, and in June, Congress passed the Law of Due Obedience, granting immunity to officers implicated in crimes against humanity based on "due obedience," a law condemned by Amnesty International and effectively halting further prosecutions. Tensions were heightened by the suspicious death of Defense Minister Roque Carranza in 1986 and the September 1987 discovery of banker Osvaldo Sivak, kidnapped by police for a ransom of over one million US dollars. Despite this, Alfonsín passed the legalization of divorce, resolving the legal status of 3 million adults (1 in 6), and the Antidiscrimination Law of 1987, supported by Argentina's Jewish and Gypsy communities, earning him the Moisés Prize from the Argentine Jewish community. A severe drought in early 1987 reduced exports to their lowest level in a decade, canceling the trade surplus and creating a US$6 billion current account deficit. Alfonsín's debt negotiator, Daniel Marx, secured a record US$19 billion debt rescheduling (one-third of total debt), but speculators caused the austral to lose half its value between June and October, leading to higher inflation rising from 5% monthly to 20% in October. Unimpressed by the appointment of a Labor Minister from within the CGT, the union's leader Saúl Ubaldini called two more general strikes, and hundreds of sectoral strikes erupted. A positive relationship with Brazil's newly elected President José Sarney led to initial agreements for a common market with Uruguay in January 1988, including a special currency, the Gaucho, for subsidizing intra-regional exports. New Minister of Public Works Rodolfo Terragno advocated for privatizations to generate foreign exchange, resulting in the sale of Austral Airlines in September 1987. Subsequent instability and the Wall Street Crash of 1987 led to tax increases, and GDP rose 3% in 1987, driven by construction spending, though inflation reached 175% and real wages declined by about 10%, falling below 1983 levels. This economic downturn significantly weakened the UCR in local and legislative elections in September 1987, losing 13 seats in Congress (leaving 117) and losing its absolute majority in the Lower House and a majority in the Senate, suspending much of its legislative agenda, including the capital transfer plan. UCR governors fared poorly, with only two remaining, including Governor Armendáriz of Buenos Aires. Military discontent peaked when Major Aldo Rico escaped house arrest and organized a second mutiny in January 1988, which was quickly suppressed. The resulting tension and stagflation prompted Alfonsín to move the October 1989 elections five months earlier. During the May 1988 Justicialist Party convention, the CGT opposed frontrunner Buenos Aires Governor Antonio Cafiero, and Alfonsín supported pairing his struggling UCR (14 points behind in polls) against Cafiero's rival, Carlos Menem, a little-known governor from a small province. The primaries resulted in an upset, and Menem was nominated. The UCR selected Eduardo Angeloz, the centrist governor of Córdoba, as its candidate. The Austral Plan continued to fail, with inflation remaining at 15–20% monthly and reaching 27% in August. In April, foreign debt payments fell into arrears when Alfonsín ordered the Central Bank to halt payments. On August 3, Economy Minister Sourrouille announced the Plan Primavera, featuring a price truce with 53 wholesalers and a new wage freeze, triggering a violent September 9 general strike by the CGT at Plaza de Mayo. Despite the conviction of Banco Alas executives for fraud totaling US$110 million, their suspended sentences and the discovery of a "parallel customs" operation by National Customs Director Juan Carlos Delconte raised doubts about Alfonsín's anti-corruption efforts. Alfonsín obtained INTERPOL's cooperation to extradite fugitive Army Corps leader Gen. Guillermo Suárez Mason and Argentine Anticommunist Alliance mastermind José López Rega, who were returned to Argentina in 1987 to stand trial. The military relationship remained tense, with continued budget cuts and opposition to democracy leading to a third mutiny on December 1, supported by disaffected Coast Guard members; the leader, Col. Mohamed Alí Seineldín, was arrested after six days. In a compromise, Alfonsín announced a modest military budget increase and dismissed moderate General Dante Caridi as Army Chief of Staff. A January 23, 1989 attack on the Regiment of La Tablada by a leftist armed group killed 39 people, testing Alfonsín's improved military rapport, which allowed the military to prosecute the case, though allegations of torture emerged. Inflation fell from 27% in August to 5–10% monthly by the end of 1988, but GDP declined 2% and inflation rose to 380% while real wages continued to fall. Exports recovered, and the trade surplus rose to nearly US$4 billion. The Springtime Plan increasingly relied on reserves to stabilize the austral, which lost nearly all of its US$3 billion in reserves. On "Black Tuesday," February 7, 1989, the U.S. dollar gained 40% against the austral, triggering a sharp decline in the austral's value, which traded at 17 to the dollar in January and reached over 100 australes by May 14. Inflation, which had been below 10% monthly as late as February, surged to 78.5% in May, shattering records and leading to a landslide victory for Justicialist candidate Carlos Menem. Polling showed that economic anxieties were central to two-thirds of voters, and Menem won in 19 of 22 provinces.

Exports recovered, and the trade surplus increased to nearly US$4 billion. The Springtime Plan increasingly relied on its foreign reserves to support the austral, whose stability helped maintain lower inflation rates. In this process, the Central Bank depleted almost all of its US$3 billion in reserves. On "Black Tuesday," February 7, 1989, the Central Bank engaged in heavy trading, causing the U.S. dollar to rise by about 40% against the austral. The sharp depreciation of the austral undermined the country's fragile financial situation. Later that month, the World Bank recalled a major portion of a loan agreement from 1988, triggering a sharp decline in the austral's value: it traded at 17 to the dollar in January and reached over 100 australes per dollar by election day, May 14. Inflation, which had remained below 10% per month as late as February, surged to 78.5% in May, breaking records and contributing to a decisive victory for Justicialist candidate Carlos Menem. Polling showed that economic concerns were a top priority for two-thirds of voters, and Menem won in 19 of 22 provinces, while losing in the traditionally anti-Peronist Federal District (Buenos Aires). The nation's finances did not stabilize after the election as expected. The dollar doubled in value the following week, and on May 29, riots and looting erupted in the poorer areas of several cities, especially Rosario. Inflation continued to escalate: it reached 114% per month in June and 197% in July. Income poverty rose from about 30% to 47% during this period, and the economy contracted by 7% in 1989, bringing per capita GDP to its lowest level since 1964. Having committed to remain in office until December 10, Alfonsín transferred power to President-elect Menem on July 8 due to the ongoing financial crisis and escalating economic instability.

doc_name: President of the Supreme Federal Court
text: The President of the Supreme Federal Court is the highest-ranking official in the Brazilian judiciary and also serves as president of the National Council of Justice (CNJ). Their duties include representing both the Court and the CNJ before other branches of government and authorities, presiding over plenary sessions of both bodies, enforcing their bylaws, deciding points of order during sessions, ruling on injunctions when the institutions are in recess or vacation, and administering oaths to Supreme Court justices and CNJ councillors. The President is fourth in the Brazilian presidential line of succession and presides over all federal impeachment trials. The President and Vice President of the Supreme Court are elected by their peers via a secret ballot, requiring a quorum of at least eight justices, using a two-round system, and serve a single, non-renewable two-year term. Historically, a tradition of rotation has existed, where the most senior justice who has not yet served becomes President and the second-most senior becomes Vice President, though this practice is not codified by law. Self-governance in selecting the Court’s president was absent during two periods: under the monarchy, when the Emperor appointed the President for a renewable three-year term; and under the 1937 Constitution, when the President of Brazil appointed the Court’s President from among the current justices for an indefinite term. The longest presidency lasted 13 years and 312 days, held by Hermínio do Espírito Santo, while the shortest lasted 23 days, held by Leoni Ramos. The current President is Justice Edson Fachin, who has held the position since 29 September 2025.

Princess Bathildis of Anhalt-Dessau (German: Prinzessin Bathildis Amalgunde von Anhalt-Dessau; 29 December 1837 – 10 February 1902) was a member of the House of Anhalt by birth and held the title of Princess of Anhalt-Dessau. Through her marriage to Prince William of Schaumburg-Lippe, she became a Princess of Schaumburg-Lippe. She was born in Dessau, Anhalt-Dessau, as the second child of Prince Frederick Augustus of Anhalt-Dessau, son of Frederick, Hereditary Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, and Landgravine Amalie of Hesse-Homburg, and Princess Marie Luise Charlotte of Hesse-Kassel, daughter of Landgrave William of Hesse-Kassel and Princess Charlotte of Denmark. She was the younger sister of Grand Duchess Adelaide of Luxembourg. On 30 May 1862 in Dessau, she married Prince William of Schaumburg-Lippe, the seventh child and third son of George William, Prince of Schaumburg-Lippe, and Princess Ida of Waldeck and Pyrmont. The couple had eight children. Bathildis died on 10 February 1902 at Náchod Castle, Kingdom of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), at the age of 64. Her body was buried alongside her husband Friedrich in a Waldeck family Crypt in Rhoden, Harz, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.

Princess Shruti Rajya Lakshmi Devi Shah of Nepal (Nepali: श्रुती राज्य लक्ष्मी देवी शाह) (15 October 1976 – 1 June 2001) was the daughter of King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya, and sister of King Dipendra and Prince Nirajan. She was widely admired by the public as a compassionate and approachable figure, earning the affectionate nickname 'the people's princess' in Nepal. Known for her active involvement in social and humanitarian causes, Princess Shruti participated in charitable activities focused on education, children’s welfare, and women’s empowerment. She supported initiatives to improve access to schooling for underprivileged children in rural Nepal and was involved in programs promoting skill development and self-reliance among women. Passionate about Nepalese culture, she contributed to the preservation of traditional arts and music. Her philanthropic efforts, though cut short by her untimely death, remain a significant part of her legacy. She studied at Kanti Ishwari Sishu Vidhyalaya in Tripureswar, Nepal, St. Mary's School in Kathmandu, Nepal, and later at Mayo College Girls School in Ajmer, India, completing her bachelor's degree at Padma Kanya Campus in Nepal. She was a meritorious painter. Princess Shruti married Kumar Gorakh Shumsher Jang Bahadur Rana, a member of the aristocratic Rana family of Nepal, descendants of Maharaja Chandra Shumsher Jang Bahadur Rana through Field Marshal Sir Kaiser Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana; he is head of Global Banking and Commercial Banking for Standard Chartered Bank Nepal Limited. The couple married on 7 May 1997 in Kathmandu and had two daughters. On 5 December 2008 in Kathmandu, Kumar Gorakh Shumsher Jang Bahadur Rana married Deepti Chand, a humanities student at Kathmandu's Padma Kanya Multiple Campus, who is also the niece of former royalist prime minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand. The name Shruti means "that which is heard." Princess Shruti, along with her mother, father, brother Nirajan, and six other royal relatives, was killed in the Nepalese royal massacre on 1 June 2001. This biography of a member of a Nepalese royal house is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

The Progress Rail PR43C was a 4,300 hp (3,210 kW) C-C genset diesel-electric locomotive developed by Progress Rail Services Corporation through the conversion of existing EMD SD50 locomotives. This conversion involved replacing the original EMD 645 prime mover with a 3,600 hp (2,680 kW) 12-cylinder Caterpillar C175 engine and a 700 hp (522 kW) Caterpillar C18 engine. The design was jointly created by Progress Rail and Norfolk Southern Railway, with development beginning in 2008. A total of three PR43Cs were built at Progress Rail's Mayfield, Kentucky factory. Two were used in revenue freight service on Norfolk Southern, while the third served as a demonstrator unit. Norfolk Southern had four additional PR43Cs on order at one time. These locomotives operated on freight trains in central Illinois, leading to speculation about testing due to Caterpillar's headquarters being located in Peoria, Illinois. The conversion altered the locomotive's external appearance, replacing the original radiator section with a larger one resembling that of an EMD SD70ACe or SD70M-2. Due to repeated mechanical failures, all PR43Cs were retired in 2017 and subsequently cut up for scrap in 2018. Prior to retirement, they were renumbered to prevent number conflicts with the AC44C6Ms.

doc_name: Proposed political status for Puerto Rico
text: Proposed political status options for Puerto Rico include maintaining its current status, becoming a U.S. state, achieving full independence, or establishing a free association with the United States. Puerto Rico was a Spanish colony for about four centuries until it was ceded to the United States in 1898 through the Treaty of Paris, which ended the Spanish–American War. In 1917, the Jones Act granted Puerto Ricans U.S. citizenship, though with limited rights, such as the inability to vote in presidential elections. The 1950s and 1960s saw significant developments: in 1950, President Harry S. Truman signed Public Act 600, enabling Puerto Ricans to draft their own constitution, and on July 25, 1952, the Constitution of Puerto Rico was approved by referendum, establishing the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico (Estado Libre Asociado). This status, granted by U.S. Congress, enhanced Puerto Rico’s political autonomy from a protectorate to a commonwealth, allowing it to have its own elected governor and a Resident Commissioner in Congress, who serves on committees but cannot vote on final legislation. Puerto Ricans remain U.S. citizens but do not vote in presidential elections or elect U.S. Senators or Representatives. The U.S. has five inhabited territories, including Puerto Rico, and the power to change Puerto Rico’s status lies with Congress, which must pass a bill with a simple majority in both houses and secure presidential approval; once enacted, such a change cannot be repealed. Since 2012, referendums have consistently shown statehood as the most favored option, with results in 1967 (39.0% for statehood), 1993 (46.3%), 1998 (46.49%), 2012 (61.3%), 2017 (97.2%), 2020 (52.52%), and 2024 (56.82%), though the 2024 vote did not include the Commonwealth option and the 2017 vote was criticized for low turnout due to a political boycott. The federal government has funded subsequent referendums, and the Puerto Rico Status Act in Congress aims to support the island’s decision. Various U.S. presidents, including Reagan, Bush, Obama, and Trump, have expressed support for Puerto Rico’s right to self-determination, with Trump stating in 2016 that Puerto Ricans should determine their status through constitutional and congressional protocols. The U.S. Congress has the authority to grant independence, statehood, or free association, with free association modeled after Palau, Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands, where the U.S. provides defense and economic aid but citizens are not U.S. citizens. The UN Special Committee on Decolonization has at times classified Puerto Rico as a colony, particularly after 1972, though it was removed in 1952 after the establishment of commonwealth status. Despite the 1952 commonwealth status, debates over Puerto Rico’s political status continue to dominate society and have been discussed in UN hearings. The Foraker Act (1900) established a civil government with an appointed governor, a legislative body, and a Resident Commissioner, while the Jones Act (1917) formalized Puerto Rico as an unincorporated territory with restricted citizenship rights. Operation Bootstrap, initiated in 1950 by Governor Luis Muñoz Marín, transformed Puerto Rico’s economy from agricultural to industrial, stimulating growth through tax incentives and access to U.S. markets, though it required importing 80% of its food. The 2005, 2007, and 2011 President’s Task Forces on Puerto Rico’s Status affirmed that Congress has plenary authority over Puerto Rico until its status changes through statehood, independence, or free association, and that no other options are constitutionally permissible. The 2011 Obama Task Force specifically outlined free association as a viable path, similar to the Compact of Free Association with Palau, Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands. Washington, D.C. gained the right to vote in presidential elections through the 23rd Amendment, highlighting that constitutional changes are required for such shifts.

doc_name: Proposed political status for Puerto Rico
text: The political status of Puerto Rico has been the subject of multiple plebiscites, beginning with the first on July 23, 1967, where 60.4% of voters chose to maintain Commonwealth status, 39% supported statehood, and 0.6% favored independence. Subsequent referendums in 1993 and 1998 also upheld the status quo, though with smaller margins. In October 2011, Governor Luis Fortuño set August 12, 2012, as the date for a two-part plebiscite, with the first question asking whether voters preferred to maintain the current territorial status or opt for a non-territorial option, and the second presenting three non-territorial choices: statehood, independence, or free association. A bill to implement this process passed the Legislative Assembly on December 28, 2011. On November 6, 2012, both questions were combined on a single ballot; the New Progressive Party supported statehood, the Popular Democratic Party advocated for the current Commonwealth status and called for abstention on the second question, and the Puerto Rico Independence Party supported independence. The 2012 referendum resulted in a 54% majority voting against the territorial status and in favor of a new status, with 61.1% of those voting for a new status choosing statehood—marking the most successful statehood referendum to date. Despite nearly 500,000 blank ballots causing confusion, Congress chose to ignore the vote but provided funding for a future one. The 2017 plebiscite, held on June 11, 2017, offered statehood, independence/free association, and the current Commonwealth status, with 97% voting for statehood, though turnout was only 23%. Governor Ricardo Rosselló supported statehood to address economic challenges and end what he called a 500-year-old colonial dilemma, citing benefits such as $10 billion in annual federal funds, the right to vote in presidential elections, higher Social Security and Medicare benefits, and the ability for government agencies to file for bankruptcy—currently prohibited. Statehood would also bring increased disability benefits, Medicaid funding, the federal minimum wage, and full representation in Congress, with Puerto Rico gaining two Senate seats and a population-based number of House seats and electoral votes. A 2018 bill, the Puerto Rico Admission Act, introduced by Jenniffer González Colón with 34 co-sponsors, aimed to make Puerto Rico a state by the start of 2021. In 2020, a yes-no vote on statehood was held, though it was not approved by the U.S. Justice Department. Congresswomen Nydia Velázquez and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed a convention instead of a referendum, arguing that pushing statehood could be seen as the culmination of colonization, while Governor González-Colón maintained that the people’s decision through voting is definitive. A new referendum was scheduled for November 5, 2024, alongside the Puerto Rican general election and the U.S. elections. The 2024 non-binding vote offered three choices: statehood, independence, and independence with free association, with 57% voting for statehood from 528,000 ballots. To become a state, U.S. Congress must pass a bill signed by the President, and the bill cannot be repealed. Four referendums in 12 years have favored statehood, though the 2024 vote did not include the option to retain the Commonwealth, which was considered a choice not required for voters. As a Commonwealth, Puerto Rico receives less federal funding, lower Social Security and Medicare benefits, and neither Commonwealth nor municipal governments can file for bankruptcy. Puerto Ricans cannot vote in presidential elections but are represented in the U.S. House by a Resident Commissioner with committee duties and voting rights on legislation except final passage. In 2022, the U.S. House passed the Puerto Rico Status Act, aiming to resolve Puerto Rico’s status through a binding plebiscite, and in April 2023, the bill was reintroduced in the House by Democrats. In September 2023, Senator Roger Wicker proposed a two-round process with a vote on August 4, 2024, offering four options: annexation, independence, sovereignty in free association, or a free state associated with the U.S. In July 2024, Governor Pedro Pierluisi called for a plebiscite in November 2024, the first time the current territorial status would not be an option. Voters would choose between statehood, independence, or independence with free association, with terms to be negotiated on foreign affairs, U.S. citizenship, and use of the U.S. dollar. If granted, Puerto Rico would become the 51st state, with two senators and a population-based delegation in the House, and a corresponding number of electoral votes. The outcome would only be effective if Congress acts under the Territorial Clause of the U.S. Constitution. Admission requires a congressional majority vote in both chambers and presidential approval. Puerto Rico’s population in 2017 was about 3.4 million, comparable to Iowa or Connecticut, with a land area larger than only Rhode Island and Delaware, and a coastline of 700 miles, similar to Wisconsin or Connecticut. Its GDP in 2017 was over $100 million, placing it between Mississippi and New Mexico. It is a two-to-three hour flight from Miami and lies between Florida and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Free association would grant a status similar to Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau, with a Compact of Free Association covering military presence, currency use, trade, and U.S. citizenship, with the possibility of renegotiation every 15 years and a path to full independence if agreement is not reached. Full independence would result in a sovereign nation with full control over domestic and foreign policy, with no formal U.S. obligations. A return to Spain as an autonomous community, like the Canary Islands, is a historical option supported by some, with potential for EU citizenship under the European Union citizenship rules. A confederation with Cuba and the Dominican Republic is a historical proposal with a few current supporters. In 1953, the UN began considering Puerto Rico’s political status, and in 1978, the Special Committee concluded that a colonial relationship exists between the U.S. and Puerto Rico, referring to Puerto Rico as a nation in its reports due to international recognition of its people’s status.

doc_name: Proposed political status for Puerto Rico
text: Puerto Ricans have recently requested Spanish citizenship under the Historical Memory Law, and joining Spain again would enable them to move to the European Union under EU citizenship rules. This idea was widely supported by Puerto Rican political leaders in the late nineteenth century, who proposed a confederation involving Puerto Rico, Cuba, and the Dominican Republic, though a small number of supporters remain today. Ron Lauder suggested to Donald Trump that the United States purchase Greenland, a proposal discussed in the White House Situation Room and reported by Elizabeth Neumann. Since 1953, the United Nations has been examining Puerto Rico’s political status and supporting its path to "independence" or "decolonization." In 1978, the UN Special Committee concluded that a "colonial relationship" exists between the United States and Puerto Rico. The Committee has consistently referred to Puerto Rico as a nation in its reports, reflecting the international recognition of Puerto Ricans as a distinct Caribbean nation with a national identity. Most recently, in a June 2016 report, the Special Committee urged the United States to accelerate the process of self-determination, emphasizing full exercise of the right to independence and sovereignty, and calling for decisions that address urgent economic and social challenges such as unemployment, marginalization, insolvency, and poverty. In June 2025, the United Nations adopted a resolution in favor of self-determination and independence for the state of Puerto Rico.

The prosecutor general of the Republic (Portuguese: procurador-geral da República) serves as the head of the Brazilian Federal Prosecution Office, an autonomous body responsible for criminal prosecution and the protection of society at large.
