Robert C. Harvey (May 31, 1937 – July 7, 2022) was an American author, critic, and cartoonist known for his work on the history and theory of cartooning, with a particular focus on the comic strip. He worked as a freelance cartoonist and described drawing cartoons since age 7. He earned a B.A. from the University of Colorado, where he submitted cartoons to the campus humor magazine, The Flatiron. After graduating in 1959, he tried to make a living as a freelance cartoonist in New York but was interrupted by service in the U.S. Navy from 1960 to 1963, during which he served as paymaster aboard the USS Saratoga. Upon discharge, he taught high school English for five years (1964–1969) before working for 30 years as a convention manager for the National Council of Teachers of English. He obtained a Master's Degree in English from New York University in 1968 and a Ph.D. in English literature from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in 1978. While at NCTE, he freelanced cartoons to magazines from 1978 to 1982. In 1973, he began writing about comics and cartooning for The Menomonee Falls Gazette, and in 1976, his columns started appearing in The Comics Journal, where he had a regular column. During the 1990s, Fantagraphics Books published two volumes of Cartoons of the Roaring Twenties, collected and edited by Harvey. He also contributed biographies of several cartoonists to Oxford University Press' American National Biography. In 1994, his first work of comics scholarship, The Art of the Funnies, was published by the University Press of Mississippi, followed by The Art of the Comic Book in 1996. He served as an associate editor for the journal Inks: Cartoon and Comic Art Studies, handling submissions related to the comic strip. In 1998, Harvey was guest curator for the Children of the Yellow Kid exhibition at the Frye Museum in Seattle, for which he also provided the catalogue. Harvey authored or edited thirteen books on comics and cartooning, including Milton Caniff: Conversations (2002) from the University Press of Mississippi, followed by a full biography of Caniff, Meanwhile... A Biography of Milton Caniff, Creator of Terry and the Pirates and Steve Canyon (2007) published by Fantagraphics. His most recent book is Insider Histories of Cartooning: Rediscovering Forgotten Famous Comics and Their Creators (2014) from the University Press of Mississippi. A complete list of his books is available on his website. He interviewed cartoonists for the long-running quarterly magazine Cartoonist PROfiles and contributed a column briefly to the Comics Buyer's Guide. Harvey was a member of the National Cartoonists Society and an associate member of the Association of American Editorial Cartoonists. He received awards including the All-Navy Cartoonist in 1960, the AAEC Ink Bottle Award in 2013 "in recognition of dedicated service to the Association and distinguished efforts to promote the art of editorial cartooning," and the San Diego Comic-Con's Inkpot Award in 2018 "for achievement in comic arts." He married his wife Linda née Kubicek in 1971 and had twin daughters, Julia (Jill) and Katherine (Kit), born in May 1975. In late June 2022, Harvey fell and unknowingly broke six ribs; he was hospitalized and died from complications of the fall on July 7, 2022, at the age of 85.

Rached Ghannouchi (Arabic: راشد الغنوشي, romanized: Rāshid al-Ghannūshī; born 22 June 1941), also spelled Rachid al-Ghannouchi or Rached el-Ghannouchi, is a Tunisian politician and the co-founder of the Ennahdha Party, serving as its intellectual leader. He was born Rashad Khriji (راشد الخريجي) in El Hamma, in the governorate of Gabès in southern Tunisia, where his village had no electricity or paved roads. His father was a poor farmer, and the family worked in the fields daily, with meat only a few times a year; after the harvest, they wove baskets from palm leaves to supplement income. Rached attended a local branch of the traditional Arabic-language Zaytouna school with financial help from an older brother. He earned a certificate of attainment equivalent to the Baccalauréat in 1962 from the University of Ez-Zitouna (Zaytouna), then entered the school of agriculture at Cairo University in 1964 before leaving due to the expulsion of Tunisians from Egypt. He moved to Syria and studied philosophy at the University of Damascus, graduating in 1968. In his 20s, he traveled and worked in Europe as a grape picker and dish washer. In April 1981, Ghannouchi founded the Islamic Tendency Movement (Ḥarakat al-Ittijāh al-Islāmī), which described itself as rooted in non-violent Islamism and advocated for equitable economic life, the end of single-party politics, and political pluralism and democracy. By the end of July, he and his followers were arrested, sentenced to eleven years in prison in Bizerte, and tortured; both religious and secular communities, including secular political organizations, rallied in his support. While in prison, he translated works and wrote on democracy, women's rights, and Palestine, producing his most noted work, Al‐Hurriyat al‐'Ammah (Public Liberties). He was released in 1984, returned to prison in 1987 with a life sentence, and was released again in 1988. He moved to the United Kingdom as a political exile, living there for 22 years. In 1989, he attended the Islamic Committee for Palestine conference in Chicago. Following the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, he denounced King Fahd of Saudi Arabia for inviting U.S. forces and called for a Muslim boycott of American goods, planes, and ships. He has also been criticized for calling for jihad against Israel. He continued to criticize Tunisian politics and President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali. After Ben Ali was ousted in popular unrest, Ghannouchi returned to Tunisia on 30 January 2011, after twenty-two years in exile, welcomed by thousands. His party won 37.04% of the vote in the 2011 Tunisian Constituent Assembly election—more than the next four parties combined—and Ghannouchi did not take a government position; Hamadi Jebali became Prime Minister. Ennahda led Tunisia through the aftermath of the Jasmine Revolution, characterized by greater transparency, lack of corruption, and consensus-building. In March 2012, Ennahda declared it would not support making sharia the main source of legislation in the new constitution, maintaining the secular nature of the state, a stance criticized by hardline Islamists but welcomed by secular parties. The government faced criticism for mediocre economic performance, failure to stimulate tourism, poor relations with France, and tolerance of radical Islamists demanding Sharia law, gender equality, and restrictions on polygamy, some of whom were responsible for the September 2012 ransacking and burning of the American embassy and school following the assassinations of Chokri Belaid (February 2013) and Mohamed Brahmi (July 2013). During the 2013–14 Tunisian political crisis, secularists demanded the government step down or a Sisi-style coup, while Ennahda militants opposed early elections and booed Ghannouchi’s calls for national unity. Ghannouchi worked with secularist leader Beji Caid Essebsi to forge a compromise, signing a "road map" on October 5, 2013, whereby Ennahda would step down for a caretaker government after the new constitution was agreed upon and until new elections were held. Both leaders faced criticism from their party ranks, and Ghannouchi secured agreement from the Ennahda shura council only by threatening to resign. In January 2014, after the new Tunisian Constitution was approved, Ennahda peacefully quit government and handed power to a technocratic government led by Mehdi Jomaa. Ennahda placed second in the October 2014 parliamentary election with 27.79% of the vote and formed a coalition government with the larger secularist party Nidaa Tounes despite rank-and-file opposition. Ennahda did not put forth a presidential candidate in the November 2014 election; Ghannouchi "hinted broadly" that he personally supported Beji Caid Essebsi, who won with over 55% of the vote. Ghannouchi argued that the country was too fragile and the economy too in need of reform for Ennahda to remain in opposition. He supported a crackdown on jihadi indoctrination at radical mosques, as over 60 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed in 2015 by jihadis, severely damaging Tunisia’s tourism industry. Despite his Islamist background, he had always been "reviled" by jihadis and now appeared near the top of the jihadi "wanted list." On 22 October 2011, The Economist published an apology for previously attributing false statements to Ghannouchi, claiming he opposed the liberal Code of Personal Status and threatened to hang a Tunisian feminist, Raja bin Salama; the apology stated that Ghannouchi expressly accepted the Code of Personal Status and never threatened to hang bin Salama. On 9 October 2012, The Independent apologized for suggesting Ennahda had accepted foreign funds, clarifying that Ghannouchi and his party had not received any foreign donations in breach of Tunisian party funding laws. On 17 May 2013, the BBC apologized for previously accusing Ghannouchi of threatening to deploy troops if Ennahda did not achieve desired election results and suggesting he condoned the violent Salafist attack on the U.S. embassy and school in September 2012; the retraction acknowledged these claims were false and apologized for the distress caused. In 2020, the UK High Court ruled in Ghannouchi’s favor in a libel case against Middle East Online (MEO) and its editor Haitham El Zobaidi, who claimed Ennahda supported terrorism—a charge Ghannouchi "vigorously denied." According to Ahmed Yusuf, the article was part of a "systematic campaign" against Ghannouchi by media backed by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Egypt. On 1 February 2024, Ghannouchi and his son-in-law were sentenced to three years in prison by a Tunisian court for illicit foreign financing and ordered to pay a fine of $1.17 million on behalf of his party. On 19 February, he began a hunger strike in prison in solidarity with other opposition figures imprisoned by President Saied’s government. On 13 July 2024, his three-year sentence was confirmed by the Criminal Chamber of the Judicial and Financial Unit. On 8 July 2025, he was sentenced to 14 years’ imprisonment on terrorism charges. Ghannouchi’s willingness to compromise with secularists and Tunisia’s democratic success post-Arab Spring has been credited by at least one observer, Robert Worth, to his background—unlike many Islamists, he lived abroad for decades, reading widely in three languages, including Karl Marx, Sigmund Freud, and Jean-Paul Sartre—and admired leftist protesters who were arrested and tortured. Watching the collapse of the Algerian Islamists during civil war while in exile left a deep impact. According to Azzam S. Tamimi, he was influenced by Malik Bennabi and his treatise "Islam and Democracy," which laid the foundations for Ghannouchi’s "masterpiece" Al‐Hurriyat al‐'Ammah (Public Liberties). In 2002, a Western source (Martin Kramer) described him as differing from other Islamists in his insistence that Islam accepts multi-party democracy. In 2015, he told French journalist Olivier Ravanello that homosexuality should not be criminalized, though he opposed gay marriage; he has also been interviewed by Michael Moore in Where to Invade Next and stated that homosexuality is a "private affair." On 13 July 2021, the official TAP news agency reported that Ghannouchi, already vaccinated, tested positive for COVID-19. On 1 August, he was discharged a few hours after being readmitted to a hospital.

Rachel Karen Green is a fictional character from the American sitcom Friends, one of the six main characters who appeared in all 236 episodes from the show's premiere on September 22, 1994, to its finale on May 6, 2004. Created by David Crane and Marta Kauffman, she is portrayed by Jennifer Aniston, who originally auditioned for the role after turning down a position as a cast member on Saturday Night Live. The role was initially offered to Téa Leoni, who declined to star in The Naked Truth, and Courteney Cox, who chose to play Monica Geller; Aniston, at the time a relatively unknown actress with prior experience in five short-lived sitcoms, was cast after the producers had already begun auditioning other actresses, including Elizabeth Berkley, Denise Richards, Melissa Rivers, Nicollette Sheridan, Parker Posey, Tiffani Thiessen, and Jami Gertz. Although Aniston was simultaneously starring in the CBS sitcom Muddling Through, which was ultimately canceled after only three months and 10 episodes—two weeks before Friends premiered—this allowed her to remain on the show. The character was originally named Rachel Robbins in the pilot and was conceived as a young woman unprepared for adulthood, relying on her parents’ wealth and initially described as spoiled and unskilled, with a personality that is "spoiled yet courageous" and "equipped to do nothing." Introduced in the pilot as a runaway bride who leaves her fiancé Barry Farber at the altar and moves in with her childhood friend Monica Geller, Rachel begins working as a waitress at Central Perk. Her relationship with Monica’s brother Ross Geller, whom she meets during her move to New York, becomes central to the series, beginning with Ross expressing his love for her at the end of the first season, despite her initially not knowing. Their on-again, off-again relationship spans the entire series, including Ross choosing Rachel over his girlfriend, their breakup during a "break," Ross marrying Emily (Helen Baxendale) after accidentally saying Rachel’s name in vows, divorcing Emily when she demands he stop being friends with Rachel, drunkenly marrying in Las Vegas during season five, and later co-parenting their daughter Emma, born in season eight from a one-night stand. Rachel briefly dates Joey Tribbiani in season nine, ending the relationship in season ten after realizing they are better as friends. Despite receiving a job offer in France, she decides to stay in New York and rekindle her relationship with Ross in the series finale, de-boarding her flight at the last minute. By the end of the series, Rachel has evolved from a dependent, spoiled "daddy's girl" into a successful businesswoman and self-assured woman. The character's second season haircut, known as the "Rachel," became an international phenomenon and remains one of the most popular hairstyles in history, despite Aniston personally disliking it. Rachel is regarded as a style icon due to her influence on 1990s womenswear, and her relationship with Ross is widely considered one of television’s most beloved. Critical reception has consistently praised Rachel, with The A.V. Club citing her as a major factor in the show’s early success. Aniston won an Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series and a Golden Globe Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a Television Series – Comedy or Musical, and her performance is credited with launching her successful film career and making her the show’s most famous cast member. The writers initially intended for Joey and Monica to be the show’s defining couple, but after seeing Aniston and David Schwimmer’s on-screen chemistry, they decided to focus on Ross and Rachel, creating a long-running "will they or won't they" dynamic that became a hallmark of the series. The first-season finale "The One Where Rachel Finds Out" marked a turning point, as Rachel learns of Ross’s true feelings and reciprocates, ending the "he’s pining, she’s oblivious" pattern. Their first kiss in season two’s "The One Where Ross Finds Out" was met with enthusiastic audience applause. Despite challenges, including Schwimmer’s initial objection to Ross divorcing Rachel, the writers ultimately decided to end the series with Ross and Rachel together, fulfilling audience expectations after ten years of anticipation. Post-series material, such as the spin-off Joey, suggests they eventually remarry. Rachel is the youngest of the six main characters and was raised in Long Island, New York. The ensemble format of Friends, which emphasized equal importance for all characters, was a key creative decision by Crane and Kauffman, and the cast became the first in television history to negotiate as a group for equal salaries, eventually earning $1 million per episode by seasons nine and ten. Aniston, who became the highest-paid television actress of all time alongside Cox and Lisa Kudrow, was initially hesitant to return for the final season but agreed after considering her own career and the show’s popularity. The character’s popularity has led to her being named one of the greatest television characters of all time.

Rachel Green, one of the six main characters of Friends, was raised in Long Island, New York, and is frequently described as spoiled, especially in her early appearances. Encyclopædia Britannica characterizes her as spoiled and funny, while her original pilot description by Crane and Kauffman portrays her as a spoiled yet courageous young woman who "has worked for none of what she has," unlike best friend Monica, and is initially "equipped to do nothing." James Endrst of the Hartford Courant labeled her "a spoiled rich kid," and the Daily News called her an "endearingly spoiled Daddy's girl." Kim Etingoff noted she is "spunky and sometimes spoiled," and TV Land described her as "naive." The Guardian's Ryan Gilbey observed that Rachel is neither insulated by self-regard like Monica nor swaddled in gormlessness like Phoebe. Frequently seen as fitting the "girl next door" archetype, Anne Bilson described her as "funny but not too funny, pretty but not too pretty, sexy but not too sexy, scatterbrained but not too scatterbrained," while Dominic Wills of TalkTalk called her "smart but ditzy, determined but undisciplined." Liat Kornowski of The Huffington Post described her as "beautiful, coveted, slightly neurotic, borderline egocentric." Jonathan Bernstein of The Daily Telegraph identified Rachel as "the self-absorbed one who goes from riches to rags," and Reign Magazine described her as "a human being full of vulnerability, humor and strength while aesthetically donning an undeniable beauty and allure." Originally unprepared for adult life, Rachel's personality evolved over time to become more self-sufficient and sympathetic, with Murray Pomerance noting that the growing boundary between Jennifer Aniston and Rachel made Aniston more authentic, and that both share normalcy, relatability, and expressiveness through hand gestures. Madeline Dimaggio wrote that Rachel struggled with being the spoiled, image-conscious "Daddy's girl" who fled from her wedding in the pilot, while BuddyTV stated she remains the most image-centric among the six, and Vogue's Edward Barsamian noted she was the most stylish and unabashedly fashion-obsessed character. TV Land summarized her as a "born shopper" who is "not necessarily a born worker," having never worked before moving in with Monica, but who is smart, resourceful, and chic, with a bright future. Splitsider's Mike D'Avria found Rachel had the third most sexual partners (14) and the highest percentage of serious monogamous relationships (71%), noting she continually meets men she wants to impress, and that her flirtations typically fail but result in serious relationships. Rachel is also the only female character to admit to having had a homosexual experience, alongside Chandler's admission of kissing a man in season 7, episode 4. In an interview with the Jewish Telegraph, Kauffman confirmed Rachel is Jewish, explaining that the name "Rachel Green" inherently implies Jewish identity. Vulture's Lindsey Weber noted similarities to Jewish culture, including referring to her grandmother as "Bubbe," Long Island origin, and engagement to a Jewish doctor. Stacy Wolf identified Rachel as embodying Jewish stereotypes in the 1990s, often serving as "the butt of the shows' jokes," and JDate's Rebecca Frankel cited her as one of the earliest and most prominent examples of the Jewish American Princess stereotype. Alicia R. Korenman described Rachel as spoiled, dependent on her father's and fiancé's money, horrified at the thought of working, inept in her attempts, and eventually overcoming a nose job. Evan Cooper described Rachel as a "de-semitized" Jew due to the absence of Jewish cultural experiences, Yiddish, or family members with Jewish surnames, noting she is more aligned with the "little woman" stereotype, while Robert Rorke labeled her a "rehabilitated Jewish American Princess," contrasting her with Amy (Christina Applegate), who remains selfish and narcissistic. Critical response to Rachel remained mostly positive throughout the show's ten-season run. John Reid of The A.V. Club credited Rachel with the pilot's success, calling her "the perfect stranger for this plot" and stating her arrival was a catalyst for the other characters' growth, as she is interested in finding meaning in life. Sonia Saraiya praised Rachel's first awkward encounter with Ross for displaying empathy and hailed her as a model for women coming of age in the 1990s—popular, pretty, dissatisfied with illusions, yet unwilling to embrace aggressive feminism. Joseph Hanania of The New York Times found Rachel's phone conversation with her father humorous, and Bob Shayne of the Los Angeles Times joked that his feelings for Rachel mirrored those of Gunther. Cosmopolitan called her "the best fictional gal pal we've ever had," People called her "spoiled-but-lovable," and TV Guide described her as "neurotic and adorable." Ellen Kerry of Heat hailed Rachel's transformation from waitress to businesswoman as "the best thing on tv." USA Today's Robert Bianco credited Rachel's pregnancy storyline with saving the show, noting it increased ratings and reversed decline, concluding that without it, Friends likely would have ended sooner. BDCwire ranked five episodes as Rachel's strongest: "The One with the Ball," "The One with Rachel's Inadvertent Kiss," "The One With The Football," "The One with the Fake Party," and "The One In Vegas, Part One." TVLine criticized Rachel for sleeping with ex-fiancé Barry in season one's "The One With the Evil Orthodontist" and for her role in season four's "The One With The Fake Party." The second-season episode "The One Where Dr. Ramoray Dies" generated mild controversy when Rachel and Monica argued over the last condom, with Rachel winning via rock-paper-scissors. Fans often criticized Aniston for Rachel's decisions. Within the first two seasons, Rachel became extremely popular among women, and her success remained a fan favorite throughout all ten seasons. Dominic Wills of TalkTalk noted that while Rachel was the general favorite, no one had a bad word to say about Jennifer Aniston, whose performance audiences instantly fell in love. Ken Tucker of Entertainment Weekly praised Aniston's portrayal of Rachel as having "prickly intelligence," David Zurawik of The Baltimore Sun cited her among the show's "very strong cast," and Tony Scott of Variety noted the principals displayed sharp sitcom skills. Robert Bianco of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette praised the female cast equally, TV Guide wrote that Aniston "instantly charmed audiences with her perfect looks and endearingly flawed persona," and Kevin Fallon of The Daily Beast described her tenure as not a "leading lady performance" but "the work of a brilliant character actress." Ryan Gilbey of The Guardian highlighted Aniston as the cast member "least reliant on goofball caricature," noting she was the only character a sane viewer might reasonably identify with. Andrew Collins of Radio Times called her a "natural comic performer, as adept with a subtle nose wrinkle as a full-on pratfall, and fluent in quick-fire patter." In 2002, Aniston won the Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series, and in 2003, she won the Golden Globe Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a Television Series – Comedy or Musical. Dominic Wills believes these awards were due to her "brilliant comic performances." Rachel has had several romantic relationships, most notably her on-again, off-again relationship with Ross. Though popular, the couple received mixed reviews; Katherine Hassel of the Daily Express called their relationship "the heart of the show," China Daily cited their reunion in the finale as a highlight, and Gary Susman of Rolling Stone believed audiences would not have been happy without their reunion. Joe Reid of The Wire considered the second season the only time Ross/Rachel was truly great, while Virgin Media stated their dynamics became "mightily tedious" by season ten. E! ranked them ninth among the greatest Friends couples, noting their relationship provided "enough iconic quotes to fill a book," with Phoebe's line "See? [Ross is] her lobster!" being among the most iconic. The season three breakup sparked debate over fault—Rachel for suggesting a break or Ross for sleeping with another woman afterward—leading E!'s Jenna Mullins to rule in Rachel's favor, stating Ross "blew it." The Jewish community welcomed the presence of a Jewish-American couple on prime time television, described by Lilith magazine as a "televisual first." Rachel and Ross are considered among television's greatest and most beloved couples, with Ninemsn calling them "everyone's favourite on ... off ... on (a break!) duo," Us Weekly and BuzzFeed ranking them first and second best television couples, respectively, and TV Guide placing them third as "the most iconic TV couple in recent memory." Extra ranked them eighth, writing "Never did we want two people to get together more than Ross ... and Rachel," and Refinery29 included them in a list of couples fans want to be together forever. They are often ranked among television's greatest "will they or won't they" couples, with Network Ten and Suggest naming them the greatest such couple, and Sarah Doran of Radio Times noting they became synonymous with the phrase "we're on a break." Phoebe's line has become one of the show's most popular and quoted. Kaitlin Reilly of Bustle defined the term as "the person of whom another is meant to be with forever," and Tara Aquino of Complex stated that "Every other person can tell you what exactly a 'Ross and Rachel' relationship means." Rachel's season eight pregnancy arc is credited with reviving the show's ratings and reviews. During season ten, Rachel's brief romance with Joey drew strong criticism from critics and fans, with Joshua Kurp of Splitsider attributing the show's final two seasons' performance to the Rachel/Joey/Ross love triangle, and Eric Goldman of IGN calling the storyline "questionable." Entertainment Tonight Canada ranked "The One After Rachel and Joey Kiss" among the show's ten worst episodes at number five, with I. P. Johnson calling it "desperate" and concluding "Jeers for even conceiving this romantic plot; cheers for abandoning it." E! enjoyed the Rachel and Joey relationship for bringing out positive aspects and shared humor, though Jenna Mullins of E! argued it was too late in the series, felt forced, and didn't make sense. After their breakup, there were many hints they would reunite, especially in seasons 8–10. In the final season, Rachel wants to sleep with Ross when her father has a heart attack, seeking "sympathy sex," which he declines. However, they sleep together the night before she leaves for Paris, leading Ross to admit he still loves her and wants to get back together. Rachel turns down the Paris job to be with Ross, realizing she still loves him, and the two agree "this is it," getting back together for good. Jennifer Aniston, who played Rachel, confirmed that after the series finale, Ross and Rachel got remarried, happily, and had at least one more child. Rachel's popularity established her as the show's breakout character; she is often ranked among the greatest characters in television history. Us Weekly ranked her the most beloved television character of the past two decades, citing her as "one of TV's most endearing personalities," Entertainment Weekly ranked her sixth on a similar list, and AOL TV included her among television's hundred "Greatest Women" at number 23, with author Kim Potts observing that Rachel grew from a one-note character into a more independent, caring pal.

Rachel, portrayed by Jennifer Aniston, becomes the show's breakout character and is widely recognized as one of the greatest television characters of all time, frequently ranked among the most beloved and influential female characters in TV history. Us Weekly named her the most beloved television character of the past two decades, while Entertainment Weekly ranked her sixth on a similar list, and AOL TV placed her at number 23 among television's hundred greatest women, noting her growth from a one-note character into an independent and caring friend. BuddyTV ranked her 15th as the funniest female sitcom character, and ChaCha listed her, Monica, and Phoebe at 11th, 12th, and 13th on their "Top 16 Female TV Characters of All Time." The Hollywood Reporter named her the 29th best female character in 2016, and Harper's Bazaar ranked her third most influential female TV character who changed the landscape of television, citing her promotion of female independence, open discussions about sex and pleasure, and her role in educating men on respectful treatment of women. Georgina Littlejohn of Entertainmentwise noted that Rachel inspired the character Penny from The Big Bang Theory, both being blonde, cute, funny, and likeable "girls-next-door." The name "Rachel" is commonly associated with baby names due to the character's popularity. Both Rachel and Aniston became fashion icons in the 1990s, especially among British women, with Vogue's Edward Barsamian crediting Rachel with inspiring "the cool New York look," and Stylist noting her revival of denim shirts and dungarees. Mahogany Clayton of StyleBlazer praised her for dominating fashion trends in stylish ways, while Heat magazine called her the "Fash Queen" for her influence on plaid skirts, denim, and overalls. BuzzFeed identified the mullet dress as a trend popularized by Rachel in the first season, and TV Guide published a list of "The 17 Ways Rachel from Friends Changed '90s Fashion." Rachel is often considered one of television's best-dressed characters, appearing on Elle's "50 Best Dressed Women on TV" list and PopSugar's list of "50 TV Shows That Changed the Way We Dress," where Friends was ranked 15th. InStyle ranked Friends 36th as the most fashionable TV show, praising the costumes of Rachel, Monica, and Phoebe. StyleCaster placed Rachel at number 28 among "The 50 Most Stylish TV Characters Of All Time," and Cosmopolitan compiled a list of 16 work outfits Rachel wore that are still wearable today. Virgin Media ranked her among television's sexiest, and Brides included her wedding dress in "The Best TV Wedding Dresses," commending its role in setting the tone for their decade-long relationship. Aniston, as the show's breakout star, became one of the most popular television actresses of her era, with USA Today dubbing her "our favorite Friend" and Kim Etingoff noting her fame "outshone" that of her co-stars, making her the first cast member to rise to prominence and the one with the most post-Friends success. Her performance in Friends launched her successful film career, with The Inquisitr News stating that Rachel "launched [Aniston's] success" and Splitsider asserting that she likely wouldn't have become a major movie star without Friends. Complex magazine ranked her the most attractive sitcom star of the 1990s, attributing her rise to her haircut, TV fame, and comedic talent, replacing Courteney Cox as the show's "established hottie." Steve Charnock of Yahoo! Movies noted that Aniston is the only main cast member to become a bona fide movie star since the show ended. Critics argue that many of her film roles are variations of Rachel, with Ryan Gilbey of The Guardian and Andrew Collins of Radio Times noting that she is "trapped" playing Rachel-like roles, and TV Guide stating she is usually cast as a variation of her neurotic and adorable Friends character. Aniston cites Rachel as one of three roles she is most grateful for and admits that being typecast has challenged her, as audiences struggle to move past the "Rachel" tag. The hairstyle known as the "Rachel," named after the character, is a bouncy layered shag inspired by Aniston's hair during the first and second seasons of Friends (1994–1996), debuting in the 20th episode, "The One with the Evil Orthodontist." Aniston believes her stylist, Chris McMillan, created it while under the influence of marijuana. The hairstyle became an international trend, with Marie Claire estimating 11 million women adopting it during the decade, and the Daily Express noting its popularity among British women, who visited salons with magazine pictures of Aniston asking for the look. Vanity Fair credited the hairstyle's popularity in the show's first year as cementing Friends' influence on style. The "Rachel" remains one of the most popular and iconic hairstyles in history, becoming the most popular in the U.S. since Farrah Fawcett's, and is frequently ranked among the greatest hairstyles of all time, with Redbook placing it fourth and Time ninth. The Huffington Post named it one of "The Most Famous TV Hairstyles Of All Time," US Weekly ranked it 17th most iconic, Glamour ranked it fourth on their "100 Best Hairstyles of All Time" and called it the most memorable hairstyle in television history, while The Sydney Morning Herald ranked it second greatest television hairstyle and Metro ranked it as the character's second-best hairstyle. It was also ranked sixth on Entertainment Weekly's list of "25 Fashion Moments That Changed Entertainment" and declared the most "desired" hairstyle of the Clinton era. Self's Zahra Barnes joked that Rachel's hair was the "true star of the show," and Elle's Sarah Carrillo believed the hairstyle helped make Friends a cultural phenomenon. Tom Jicha of The Baltimore Sun noted that the hairstyle was the show's only major cultural trend, while Complex's Josh Robertson and Glamour's Hannah Lyons Powell credited it as making Aniston the definitive hair icon of the '90s and the owner of arguably the most infamous and influential hairstyle of all time. Jim Vorel of Paste called it "the definition of influence," and Rebecca Cox of Glamour expressed gratitude that it remained a 1990s trend. In the second-season episode "The One with the Lesbian Wedding," Rachel jokes about her mother trying to reinvent her life by copying her haircut. Despite her association with the style, Aniston disliked it, finding it difficult to maintain without McMillan, stating she would curse him every time she blow-dried it, that it required three brushes like "doing surgery," and that she would rather shave her head than wear it for life. Since Aniston, numerous celebrities have worn variations of the "Rachel," including Cameron Diaz, Rachel McAdams, Emma Watson, Reese Witherspoon, Julia Roberts, Tina Fey, Tyra Banks, and Lily Allen.

The Railpower GG20B Green Goat is a low-emissions diesel hybrid switcher locomotive manufactured by Railpower Technologies Corp. It is powered by a single Caterpillar C9 six-cylinder inline engine producing 300 horsepower (224 kW), which is paired with a large battery bank, resulting in a combined total power output of 2,000 horsepower (1,490 kW). Since their first introduction in 2004, more than 50 GG20B diesel-electric hybrid switchers have been produced. BNSF Railway and Vehicle Projects converted one GG20B into an experimental hydrogen fuel cell locomotive, designated HH20B. This locomotive was first publicly demonstrated on June 29, 2009, in Topeka, Kansas. The locomotive, originally built in 1957 as Canadian Pacific 8637 (renumbered 1544 in the 1980s), was a GMD GP9 locomotive. In 2006, it was rebuilt into a GG20B for Canadian Pacific but was not delivered due to the cancellation of the order. It was sold to BNSF in 2008 and shipped to BNSF's shops in Topeka, Kansas, where the diesel generator set was removed and a fuel cell power unit installed in its place. Hydrogen storage is provided by a set of tanks located in a heavily vented enclosure on top of the locomotive's long hood, above the batteries. To date, this locomotive is the largest land vehicle on Earth powered exclusively by hydrogen fuel cells. In 2023, the locomotive, without its hydrogen components, was donated to the Oklahoma Railroad Museum, where it is planned to be used as a control car and for electricity generation at the end of excursion trains.

Ramiriquí is a town and municipality located in the Colombian Department of Boyacá, within the Márquez Province subregion. It shares borders with Tunja to the north, Chinavita and Zetaquirá to the south, Rondón and Ciénaga to the east, and Chivatá, Tibaná, and Jenesano to the west. The town is named after the last cacique, Ramirique, and in the Chibcha language of the Muisca, "Ramirraquí" translates to "white earth"; an alternative etymology, "Ca-mi-quiquí," means "our strength over the grasslands." Before the arrival of Spanish conquistadors in the Altiplano Cundiboyacense during the 1530s, the area was inhabited by the Muisca people. The northern Muisca Confederation was later established in Hunza, present-day Tunja, following the mythological and violent cacique Goranchacha's relocation from Ramiriquí, with Hunzahúa becoming the first ruler of Hunza and the city being named after him. Quemuenchatocha, the second-last ruler of the Muisca, died in Ramiriquí after being defeated by Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada. The modern town was officially founded on December 21, 1541, by Spanish friar Pedro Durán. Petroglyphs have been discovered within the municipal boundaries. Key economic activities in Ramiriquí include agriculture—specifically uchuva, tree tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, blackberries, and maize—fishing, and crafts. Its geographic coordinates are 5°24′N 73°20′W (5.400°N 73.333°W).

Rana Ayyub, born on 1 May 1984 in Mumbai, India, is an Indian journalist and opinion columnist for The Washington Post. She is the author of the investigative book Gujarat Files: Anatomy of a Cover Up. Her father, Mohammad Ayyub Waqif, was a writer for Blitz, a Mumbai-based magazine, and a member of the progressive writers movement; her uncle, Abdul Haq Azmi, was a distinguished Hadith scholar and senior professor at Darul Uloom Deoband. Ayyub contracted polio at age five, which left her left hand and right leg immobile, but she eventually recovered. During the 1992–93 Mumbai riots, her father warned her that local men were targeting his daughters; at nine years old, Rana fled with her sister to stay with a Sikh friend’s relatives for three months before returning to Deonar, a Muslim-majority suburb, where she grew up. She is a practising Muslim and graduated in English literature from Sophia College, Mumbai, where she studied with Richa Chada and Shuchi Talati. At Tehelka, a Delhi-based investigative news magazine, Ayyub conducted an eight-month undercover sting operation posing as Maithili Tyagi, a student of the American Film Institute with ideological ties to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, to gather recordings from Gujarat bureaucrats and police officers regarding encounter killings and the aftermath of the 2002 Gujarat riots. The recordings, made using a concealed device, were documented in her book Gujarat Files. However, Tehelka’s management refused to publish any story based on the recordings, citing that the data was incomplete or of inadequate quality. Ayyub continued working with Tehelka for several months before resigning in November 2013 in protest against the handling of sexual harassment allegations against editor-in-chief Tarun Tejpal. She now works independently. In September 2019, The Washington Post nominated her as a Contributing Global Opinions Writer. In 2021, on HARDtalk, she explained her ability to critique the government due to Indian media censorship. In October 2020, she published an open letter in Inquilab: A Decade of Protest, protesting the appointment of Gajendra Chauhan as chairman of FTII. Historian Ramachandra Guha called Gujarat Files "a brave book," and several journalists have privately praised her courage. Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay noted the bravery required in conducting undercover interviews during the investigation. The investigation was listed by Outlook as one of the twenty greatest magazine stories of all time. In 2018, Ayyub was awarded "most Resilient Global journalist" by Free Press Unlimited for resisting attempts to silence her. In the Haren Pandya murder case, the Supreme Court dismissed her book, stating it was based on surmises and had no evidentiary value; Ayyub called the ruling "puzzling," noting the CBI had used her work as evidence and that no official had denied her claims. In 2019, she accompanied Dexter Filkins from The New Yorker on a trip to Kashmir to report on government violence following the revocation of Kashmir’s special status, highlighting torture of Kashmiri civilians, including minors, which contrasted with official claims. In February 2022, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) froze assets worth over ₹1.77 crore of hers in a money laundering case alleging she embezzled public funds raised for pandemic relief. The ITAT in Mumbai found that only 10 per cent of the relief funds were used for relief work, with the rest transferred to her father’s and sister’s accounts and then to her personal account. International observers have described the charges as sham, part of a broader campaign to intimidate her and silence her criticism of the Modi government. A FIR was filed against her in Dharwad for allegedly calling anti-hijab protestors Hindu terrorists. In 2022, UN experts urged India to stop judicial harassment against her, including repeated bank freezes, calling the fund allegations "bogus" and linked to a far-right social media group. Online abuse against Ayyub is primarily driven by Twitter users aligned with Hindu nationalism and the ruling BJP; an ICFJ report found that Twitter failed to address the abuse and withheld her tweets at the request of the Indian government, with abuse often arriving within 14 seconds of her posting. In 2018, she received multiple death and rape threats, her personal details were leaked, and a deepfake pornographic video was released; Delhi Police closed the case in August 2020 due to inability to identify the perpetrators. Several UN Special Rapporteurs have intervened three times, warning of a serious risk to her life and calling on Indian authorities to protect her. The U.S. State Department’s 2020 Human Rights Report specifically mentioned the online trolling and threats against her. Reporters Without Borders also documented the hate speech against her and called on the government and Delhi police to protect her. In 2022, Hindu nationalist alt-right groups created the app Bulli Bai, which falsely auctioned Muslim women, and the secret app Tek Fog, used by BJP supporters to spread right-wing propaganda, targeted Ayyub and other prominent women journalists. In November 2024, Ayyub was doxxed, with her phone number leaked by a right-wing account on X, resulting in hundreds of calls and messages, with no respite despite filing a police complaint. In November 2025, she received threats of violence against herself and her father from an unknown international number, which she claimed were intended to intimidate her into writing a column on the 1984 anti-Sikh riots following the assassination of Indira Gandhi.

Randolph College is a private liberal arts and sciences college located in Lynchburg, Virginia, United States. It was founded in 1891 as Randolph-Macon Woman's College by William Waugh Smith, then-president of Randolph-Macon College, under Randolph-Macon's charter after he failed to convince R-MC to become coeducational. The college has historic ties to the United Methodist Church and received 50 acres from the city of Lynchburg for its establishment. In 1916, it became the first women's college in the South to earn a Phi Beta Kappa charter. Beginning in 1953, the two colleges were governed by separate boards of trustees. Main Hall, built in 1891, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. In August 2006, Randolph-Macon Woman's College announced it would become coeducational and change its name, a decision supported by former Interim president Ginger H. Worden, who argued in a September 17, 2006 editorial for The Washington Post that only 3 percent of college-age women consider women's colleges, and that most applicants were not seeking single-sex education, with seven of the top 10 colleges applicants also being coed. The decision was not universally accepted, with alumnae and students organizing protests covered by local and national media, accusing the administration of recruiting students without informing them of the coeducation plan, and leading to lawsuits. The college was officially renamed Randolph College on July 1, 2007, when it became coeducational. The transition was difficult, with the first full-time male students facing vandalism to mailboxes and doors and experiencing polarization. The last class to receive diplomas from Randolph-Macon Woman's College graduated on May 16, 2010. The college is named after John Randolph of Roanoke, Virginia (1773–1833), an eccentric planter and politician who freed hundreds of slaves in his will and once fought a duel with Henry Clay. Randolph College is primarily an undergraduate institution offering Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Science, and Bachelor of Fine Arts degrees in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and also offers Master's programs including a Master of Arts in Teaching, a Master of Fine Arts in Creative Writing, a Master of Fine Arts in Theatre, and a Master of Coaching and Sport Leadership. In the fall of 2021, the college launched a new curriculum model called TAKE2, which divides each semester into seven-week sessions during which students take two courses at a time, differing from the traditional model of taking four or five courses over an entire semester. The Maier Museum of Art, which has been collecting American art since 1920, features works by 19th and 20th-century American artists and houses several thousand paintings, prints, drawings, and photographs in its permanent collection. The museum hosts special exhibitions and education programs annually. In 2007, the college faced controversy when it announced it would sell four paintings from its collection. The college has a tradition of rivalry between 'odd' and 'even' graduating classes, based on whether their graduation year is odd or even, resulting in two odd and two even 'sister-classes' that participate in shared events. Since 1968, the college has hosted a study abroad program at the University of Reading, England, selecting up to 35 students each year, commonly during the junior year, who may enroll for the full academic year or for a semester, living in one of three Randolph-owned houses near the campus and traveling together to various cities in England. In 2018, the Randolph College Board of Trustees decided to end the World in Britain program after the following academic year. A minor in American Culture allows students to study American society and culture through interdisciplinary approaches and also accepts visiting students from other U.S. colleges for a one-semester intensive study of themes or regions, including literature, art, history, and travel. Randolph College is affiliated with NCAA Division III and competes in the Old Dominion Athletic Conference (ODAC), offering intercollegiate sports in nine varsity disciplines: basketball, cross country, lacrosse, soccer, swimming, tennis, track and field, volleyball, and wrestling. The college fields six men's and eight women's varsity teams.

Ranuccio Bianchi Bandinelli (19 February 1900 – 17 January 1975) was an Italian archaeologist and art historian. He was born in Siena to Mario Bianchi Bandinelli (1859–1930) and Margherita Ottilie "Lily" von Korn (Bianchi Bandinelli, 1878–1905), both of whom were descended from ancient aristocracy in Siena. His early research focused on the Etruscan centers near his family lands, Clusium in 1925 and Suana in 1929. Despite having shown Hitler around Rome under Mussolini, he became disillusioned with Italian fascism and converted to communism after World War II, becoming a Marxist. In 1945, he co-founded the magazine Società with Cesare Luporini and Romano Bilenchi. As an anti-fascist, he was appointed to several key art-historical positions after the war, including director of the government's fine arts and antiquities ministry (Antichità e Belle Arti) from 1945 to 1948. His memoir on fascism in Italy, titled Hitler e Mussolini, 1938: il viaggio del Führer in Italia, was published in 1995. From his positions at the universities of Florence and Rome, he guided a new generation of Italian archaeologists grounded in dialectical materialism, and he also taught at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. In the 1950s and 1960s, he wrote comprehensive texts on classical art for a broad, literate audience. In 1958, he founded the Enciclopedia dell'arte antica and was elected a foreign member of the Soviet Academy of Sciences that same year. In the mid-1960s, he was commissioned to write two volumes on Roman art for the French Arts of Mankind series, which expanded his influence and introduced social criteria for art to a wider, English-speaking audience. In 1967, he founded the Dialoghi di archeologia with his students, a highly innovative and controversial journal in classical archaeology. He was frequently a maverick in his interpretations, with arguments that were not always convincing but were forcefully grounded. For example, regarding the Belvedere Apollo—a Roman copy of a Greek work now believed to date to the fourth century B.C.—he argued it was a frigid copy of a Hellenistic work unrelated to the Greek master Leochares, contrary to the mainstream view. His work emphasized the interrelation between Hellenistic, Etruscan, and Roman art. Among his students were influential 20th-century Italian archaeologists, including Giovanni Becatti, Antonio Giuliano, Mario Torelli, Andrea Carandini, and Filippo Coarelli. He was elected a foreign member of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1966.

Rare is the third studio album by American singer Selena Gomez, released by Interscope Records on January 10, 2020. As the executive producer, she collaborated with producers including Ian Kirkpatrick, Jason Evigan, Mattman & Robin, Sir Nolan, Simon Says, The Monsters & Strangerz, and David Pramik. Described by Gomez as her "diary from the past few years," the album is a midtempo pop and dance-pop record influenced by electronic, Latin pop, and R&B styles. Lyrically, it centers on themes of self-love, self-empowerment, self-acceptance, and self-worth. Guest features on the album include singer 6lack and rapper Kid Cudi. The album was promoted by two singles before its release: "Lose You to Love Me," released on October 23, 2019, topped the Billboard Hot 100 and became Gomez's first number-one single in the United States; "Look at Her Now," released the next day, peaked at number 27. The title track was released as the third single on the album's release day and reached number 30 on the Hot 100. Rare received positive critical reception, with many calling it Gomez's best album to date, and it earned a normalized Metacritic score of 76 based on 12 reviews, indicating generally favorable reviews. The album debuted at number one in Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Estonia, Lithuania, Mexico, Norway, Portugal, Scotland, and the United States, and was certified platinum by the RIAA for over 1 million equivalent units in the U.S. A Target-exclusive edition includes five standalone singles from 2017–2018: "Bad Liar," "Fetish" featuring Gucci Mane, "It Ain't Me" with Kygo, "Back to You," and "Wolves" with Marshmello. The vinyl edition adds "Feel Me" as a bonus track, and a deluxe edition with three new tracks, including the single "Boyfriend," was released on April 9, 2020. In a November 2019 interview for Apple Music, Gomez stated that the unreleased tracks were where she was at creatively and that the songs on the tracklist fit well together after being ordered. She also said on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon that the album would have a "sense of strong pop" and that she experimented with electric guitar, adding that it took her four years to feel ready for the album. According to Semrush, Rare was one of 2020's three most-searched albums on Google, with 1.2 million monthly searches, alongside Taylor Swift's Folklore and J Balvin's Colores. The album is primarily pop and dance-pop with a dark tone, drawing from R&B, electro, funk-pop, reggaeton, alternative pop, and electronic music, with main themes of "love, loss and dating." Gomez described the album as "honest, empowering and uplifting," with core messages of self-love, acceptance, and empowerment, and stated that the songs are "the most honest music I've ever made." The standard edition contains 13 tracks, beginning with a quiet but impactful self-love anthem titled "Rare," which discusses a lover's wavering interest and the realization that the partner isn't valuing her adequately; its sound is described as muffled, as if "dunked underwater." The following track, "Dance Again," blends funk, dance, electro, and electropop, featuring an "infectious" and "mellifluous" melody, a "Cure-like" bass, "fuzzy" synths, and a "walloping disco bassline," and has been called "lite-Daft Punk" and "low-key yet deeply infectious." Co-written with Julia Michaels and Justin Tranter, "Look at Her Now" is an upbeat dance-pop and electropop track about moving on from a toxic relationship. "Lose You to Love Me," the only ballad, features "bare-bones" production with plucked violins, booming bass, tearjerker piano, an orchestra, and multi-tracked Gomez vocals, and is about self-love and discovering one's true self after losing a lover; critics speculated it may reference her relationship with Justin Bieber. "Ring," a Latin-infused track about toying with noncommittal lovers, draws comparisons to Camila Cabello's "Havana," Gotye's "Somebody That I Used to Know," and Santana's "Smooth." Produced by The Monsters & Strangerz with Jon Bellion, "Vulnerable" is a warm disco and electropop track with a moody synth groove and elements of italo disco and tropical house. "Let Me Get Me" features Latin music influences and is described as "dancefloor-ready." "Crowded Room," the first collaboration with 6lack, is an R&B song. Tracks 10, 11, and 12 have a funk sound; "Kinda Crazy" is a tongue-in-cheek, sinuous kiss-off driven by a clean bluesy guitar lick and horns; "Cut You Off" is a slinky, funk-inflected downtempo pop song about ending a draining relationship and has been compared to Taylor Swift. The album concludes with "A Sweeter Place," a collaboration with Kid Cudi that documents life lessons and expresses hope for brighter days. The vinyl and digital bonus editions include "Feel Me," previously on Gomez's 2016 Revival Tour setlist, released on digital platforms on February 21, 2020, the same day as the vinyl release. The album and its title were first announced on Gomez's Instagram page, which revealed the cover art and included a snippet of the title track. The standard edition was promoted by the release of "Lose You to Love Me" on October 23, 2019, and "Look at Her Now" on October 24, 2019; on November 24, 2019, Gomez performed both songs at the 2019 American Music Awards. She also promoted the album on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, The Ellen Degeneres Show, and The Kelly Clarkson Show. "Dance Again" was scheduled to promote CBS Sports and Turner Sports' 2020 NCAA tournament coverage but was not used due to the event's cancellation over the COVID-19 pandemic; proceeds from the song supported the MusiCares COVID-19 Relief Fund, and a performance video was posted on YouTube on March 26, 2020. In the U.S., Rare debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, earning 112,000 album-equivalent units (including 53,000 pure sales) in its first week, becoming Gomez's third U.S. number-one debut and the first album released in the 2020s to top the chart; it also accumulated 79.3 million on-demand streams that week. In its second week, it dropped to number six, earning 38,000 units; as of December 2020, it had 703,000 album-equivalent units in the U.S., and by July 2021, it had sold 123,000 pure copies. In the U.K., it debuted at number two, earning 17,661 album-equivalent units, becoming her highest-charting and highest-selling album in the country, and was certified gold by the BPI in April 2021 for 100,000 units. In Australia, it debuted at number one, becoming her first number-one debut there, and also achieved number one in Argentina, Belgium (Flanders), Lithuania, Portugal, and Scotland. Rare was featured on several year-end lists, including number 30 on Uproxx's "Best Albums of 2020," where editors noted its idiosyncratic lyrics, vocal performances, and earworm hooks; Rolling Stone ranked it number 24, with Julia Childing stating it was cathartic to hear Gomez release her past struggles, and also named "Cut You Off" the 19th best song of 2020; Billboard listed the title track as one of the best pop songs of 2020. UMI Yearlies named Rare album of the year in 2020.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (Nepali: राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी, lit. 'National Independence Party', abbr. RSP) is a centrist political party in Nepal.[2][3][5] It was announced by Rabi Lamichhane in June 2022[10] and registered with the Election Commission of Nepal on 1 July 2022, ahead of the 2022 Nepalese general election.[11][12] The party was formally registered on that date with Rabi Lamichhane as the founding president and a bell inside a circle as its election symbol.[15] On 16 June 2022, Lamichhane resigned as managing director of Galaxy 4K television and announced his candidacy for the House of Representatives in the 2022 general elections.[13] On 21 June 2022, he announced the formation of the RSP along with a 21-member central committee.[10][14] The party fielded 131 candidates in First Past the Post constituencies and submitted a closed list of 107 prospective members for proportional representation seats in the House of Representatives, without fielding any candidates for provincial assemblies. Candidates were selected through primary elections.[16] The RSP emerged as the fourth-largest national party in Nepal after the 2022 election, securing victory in seven constituencies—four in Kathmandu, one in Lalitpur, and two in Chitwan—and receiving 10.70% of the party list vote, becoming one of the seven national parties in the Federal Parliament. It won 13 seats via proportional representation, bringing its total parliamentary strength to 20.[18][19] The party later won the Tanahun 1 constituency, where Swarnim Wagle was elected and advocated for reducing the number of army personnel. The party was a junior ally in the Prachanda-led government from 26 December 2022 to 5 February 2023 and served as a coalition partner with four cabinet ministries from 6 March 2024 to 12 July 2024.[6][7][8][9] Party president Rabi Lamichhane fled from Nakkhu jail during the 2025 Nepalese Gen Z protests, claiming it was per the decision of the Ministry of Home Affairs, a claim rejected by the prison administration and criticized as indirectly enabling imprisoned individuals to escape.[21][22][23] Party leaders were divided over dissolving parliament, with Sobita Gautam condemning such a move.[24] Joint general secretary and former MP Sumana Shrestha resigned from her post and from party membership on 14 September 2025 amid protests, citing a culture of leader worship.[25][26] Party chief whip Santosh Pariyar left the party to form the Pragatisheel Loktantrik Party, stating that personality-based leadership cannot lead to national development.[27][28] The party announced it would have no sister organizations, only members, not cadres, and emphasized primary elections for candidate selection.[14][10] The RSP supports constitutional socialism, market socialism, progressivism, political pragmatism, participatory democracy, economic liberalism,[2] and political freedom.[29] It endorses a "capitalistic" economy with individual rights, asserting that industrial and commercial activities are off-limits to government interference, as economic freedom drives prosperity and government planning disrupts the economy.[33][34][35][36] The party supports recall elections, the right to reject, and absentee ballots, and advocates for a directly elected prime minister and directly elected chief ministers for the seven provinces.[10][14][37] In its 2022 election manifesto, it proposed a non-partisan president elected by an expanded electoral college including ward chairs and federal lawmakers, and suggested the chairman of the National Assembly act as de facto vice-president. It also called for ending political appointments in constitutional bodies, scrapping the Constitutional Council, and having appointments recommended by the National Assembly and confirmed by the House of Representatives. The party advocated dissolving provincial assemblies and district coordination committees, favoring instead a provincial council elected by local government heads. Rabi Lamichhane did not cast a vote in the 2022 provincial elections.[39][40] The party views the private sector, cooperatives, and public sector as the three pillars of the economy, favors competition, and seeks to expand the private sector's role as an alternative to the public sector for service delivery and economic growth. It supports ending income tax for individuals in the lowest octile of earners, establishing food banks in every ward, and providing nutrition assistance to those below the poverty line through ration cards. It also seeks to expand the social welfare system and include private insurance companies. The party supports a single-payer healthcare system, with at least one laboratory and a 750-bed hospital in each province, a 50 to 100-bed hospital in each of the 77 districts, a 6 to 25-bed hospital in each local unit, and a clinic in every ward. It wants a centralized national ambulance service, a health and quality assurance accreditation board, a food and drug department, a central disease board, and a health innovation & development board, along with a health workers act for public healthcare workers.[41] To combat corruption, it supports a Whistleblower Protection Act and an Anti-Corruption Police under the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority.[41] The party also calls for shelters for abuse victims and a fund for victims of human trafficking, domestic violence, and acid attacks, and promotes entrepreneurship among women and sexual minorities by establishing funds where at least sixty percent of shareholders or employees are female or from a sexual minority group.[41] The party nominated 131 candidates for the First Past the Post seats in the 2022 general election.[42] This list of MPs is based on the order of power holdings within the party, ministry level, and length of presence in House of Representatives meetings.

The Ratcatcher, Otis Flannegan, is a character in American comic books and other media published by DC Comics, primarily known as an enemy of Batman and part of the Dark Knight's rogues gallery. Once a rat-catcher in the Gotham City Sanitation Department, Flannegan turned to a life of crime after stabbing a man to death in a street fight, leading to a ten-year sentence at Gotham State Penitentiary. After his release, he kidnapped the officials who arrested him and tortured them using his trained rats. Following five years in captivity, one of his prisoners escaped; though Flannegan ordered his rats to kill him, the prisoner reached the surface, where Batman discovered his body, tracked him down, and defeated him by dispersing his rats. After being re-incarcerated, Flannegan escaped his parole hearing by using a flute he carved to control rats through a high-pitched frequency, but was captured again by Dick Grayson disguised as Batman. In Infinite Crisis, Flannegan is revealed to be an OMAC before being killed by a civilian. In the The New 52 continuity reboot, he is resurrected and makes a minor appearance in Batman Eternal. The Ratcatcher has the ability to communicate with and control an army of rats, possesses in-depth knowledge of Gotham City's sewer system and Blackgate Penitentiary's layout, and wields a gas gun capable of manipulating objects with cyanide gas. A female version of the character, Cleo Cazo / Ratcatcher 2, appears in the DC Extended Universe film The Suicide Squad (2021), portrayed by Daniela Melchior. She is the daughter of an unnamed previous Ratcatcher (portrayed by Taika Waititi), who was originally from Portugal and died from a heroin overdose. Cazo moved to America and used her father's equipment to become a criminal, eventually being arrested for armed bank robbery and incarcerated in Belle Reve Penitentiary. Later, she joined the eponymous squad to infiltrate and destroy Jötenheim, a Corto Maltesean laboratory containing the alien Starro, forming bonds with teammates Bloodsport and King Shark, despite Bloodsport's fear of rats. Her pet rat, Sebastian, has vocal effects provided by Dee Bradley Baker. The Ratcatcher first appeared in Detective Comics #585 (April 1988) and was created by writers Alan Grant and John Wagner and artist Norm Breyfogle.

"Rattlestar Ricklactica" is the fifth episode of the fourth season and the 36th episode overall of the Adult Swim animated series Rick and Morty. Written by James Siciliano and directed by Jacob Hair, it originally aired on December 15, 2019. While setting up Christmas lights, Jerry falls off the roof and is zapped by Rick with a ray that renders him lighter than air for 10 hours, then makes his shoes heavier than air, resulting in neutral buoyancy and allowing him to jump higher than usual. Rick and Morty leave for an adventure, but their ship breaks down in space; while repairing it, Morty is bitten by a snake astronaut and kills it. To atone for the snake's death, Morty buys another snake from a pet store and sends her to a race-war-ridden snake planet, where the snakes quickly realize she is from a different world. This leads to an increasing number of snakes that alternately attack or protect the Smiths. Rick explains that Morty's actions caused the snakes to unite and invent time travel. Rick and Morty travel to the Snake Pentagon to end the war, but the snakes' time machine is incomplete. A future version of Rick and Morty, who has a black eye, appears with a snake-language book containing time travel instructions and insults their past selves. Current Rick and Morty travel to 1985 and leave the book at Snake MIT. Meanwhile, Jerry loses one of his shoes, causing him to float away helplessly. Believing he will either survive unassisted or be blamed by Rick and Beth if he dies, he refuses help. With minutes left on the ray and high above the ground, Jerry prepares to fall when a jet passes by, which he attaches himself to. The plane crashes after colliding with a flying snake, but Jerry survives. Back on present-day Earth, the large amount of time travel alerts the Time Cops from "A Rickle in Time," who travel back in time and kill the first primitive snake to use tools, preventing snake civilization and causing the snakes to vanish. Jerry reveals he has been on the roof the entire time, turns on the Christmas lights, then falls off and breaks his leg, which Rick heals to 50% capacity, leaving the rest of the healing to Jerry. Rick and Morty are reminded by their future selves to make the time travel notes. In the post-credits scene, while waiting for their past selves on the snake planet, Rick tells Morty to stay in the car next time and punches him in the eye. Rick and Morty's journey to Snake MIT is set to a chalkboard displaying mathematics related to quantum mechanics, known as the snake equation. The notation on the board was inspired by a research paper by Christopher Wood, Jacob Biamonte, and David G. Cory published in the journal Quantum Information & Computation and later included in a book by Jacob Biamonte. The episode aired on Adult Swim on December 15, 2019. According to Nielsen Media Research, it was viewed by 1.32 million household viewers in the United States and achieved a 0.75 rating among the 18–49 adult demographic, making it the lowest-rated episode of the series (excluding the unannounced season three premiere) since season one's "M. Night Shaym-Aliens!". Zack Handlen of The A.V. Club awarded the episode an A, calling it the best episode of the season so far and a pure joy from start to finish, noting it is funny despite not being revolutionary or emotionally impactful, and restoring faith in the show. Joe Matar of Den of Geek gave it a 5 out of 5, stating that the first half of Rick and Morty's fourth season ends strongly with this not-so-festive Christmas episode.

Raylene May Keightley (born 19 November 1961 in Kokstad, former Cape Province) is a South African judge of the Supreme Court of Appeal. She was admitted as an attorney in 1986 and as an advocate in 2006. She matriculated at Umtata High School in Mthatha and earned a BA and LLB from the University of Natal in 1984. Between 1987 and 1988, she completed an LLM at the University of Cambridge, winning the Gonville and Caius College Sir William McNair Prize for the best LLM student. From 1985 to 1986, she was a candidate attorney at Balsillie, Watermeyer and Cawood in Cape Town. Upon returning to South Africa in 1988, she joined the law faculty at the University of Cape Town, teaching as a lecturer until 1995 and then as a senior lecturer from 1991. In 1996, she moved to Johannesburg to become a senior lecturer at the University of the Witwatersrand's School of Law, where she was promoted to professor in 1999 and served as assistant dean that year. Between 1999 and 2001, she was senior state advocate in the Asset Forfeiture Unit of the National Prosecuting Authority. In 2001, she was admitted as an advocate of the High Court of South Africa and was promoted to deputy director of Public Prosecutions in the Asset Forfeiture Unit, before leaving in 2003 to become its regional head in Johannesburg. In July 2006, she left the National Prosecuting Authority to serve her pupillage at the Johannesburg Bar. From 2006 to 2015, she practised law at the Johannesburg Bar, first at the Island Group of Advocates and then at Thulamela Chambers, and served as director of the Centre for Applied Legal Studies at the University of the Witwatersrand from 2008 to 2011. She also served as an acting judge in the Gauteng Division of the High Court for four periods between October 2013 and August 2015. In October 2015, the Judicial Service Commission shortlisted and interviewed her for a permanent vacancy in the Gauteng High Court, recommending her for appointment after interviews, and President Jacob Zuma confirmed her appointment with effect from 1 January 2016. In October 2017, she delivered a landmark ruling declaring corporal punishment by parents unconstitutional, finding that neither religious defences nor the common-law defence of "reasonable chastisement" justified it, a decision upheld by the Constitutional Court in September 2019 in Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development. Other notable rulings include a July 2019 decision prohibiting the application of set-off to credit agreements under the National Credit Act and an October 2022 ruling reinstating Mpho Phalatse as Mayor of Johannesburg following an unconstitutional vote of no confidence. Keightley served as an acting judge in the Supreme Court of Appeal for two terms between July 2023 and March 2024, during which the court heard an appeal of an Equality Court decision on whether singing 'Dubul' ibhunu’ (“Kill the Boer”) constituted hate speech. AfriForum requested her recusal, citing alleged bias from a 2018 High Court case where Keightley reportedly said AfriForum was “barking up the wrong tree” and suggested counsel might wish to apply for her recusal, but the application was refused. In May 2024, the Judicial Service Commission recommended her for permanent elevation to the Supreme Court of Appeal, which was confirmed by President Cyril Ramaphosa, and she joined the bench on 1 July 2024. She is married to Alan Dodson SC, a prominent advocate and former acting justice of the Constitutional Court, with whom she has three sons.

Raúl Ricardo Alfonsín (Spanish pronunciation: [raˈul alfonˈsin]; 12 March 1927 – 31 March 2009) was an Argentine lawyer and statesman who served as president of Argentina from 10 December 1983 to 8 July 1989. He was the first democratically elected president after the National Reorganization Process. Ideologically, he identified as a radical and a social democrat, serving as the leader of the Radical Civic Union (UCR) from 1983 to 1991, 1993 to 1995, and 1999 to 2001 [not verified in body]. His political approach was known as "Alfonsinism." Born in Chascomús, Buenos Aires Province, Alfonsín began his law studies at the National University of La Plata and graduated from the University of Buenos Aires at the age of 23. He was affiliated with the UCR, joining the faction of Ricardo Balbín after the party split. He was elected a deputy in the legislature of the Buenos Aires province in 1958, during the presidency of Arturo Frondizi, and a national deputy during the presidency of Arturo Umberto Illia. He opposed both sides of the Dirty War and filed several writs of Habeas corpus, requesting the freedom of victims of forced disappearances, during the National Reorganization Process. He denounced the crimes of military dictatorships in other countries and opposed the actions of both sides in the Falklands War. He became the leader of the UCR after Balbín's death and won the presidency in the 1983 elections as the Radical candidate. After being elected president, Alfonsín revoked the self-amnesty law established by the military. He established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons to investigate the crimes committed by the military, which led to the Trial of the Juntas and resulted in the sentencing of the heads of the former regime. Discontent within the military led to the mutinies of the Carapintadas, which Alfonsín appeased with the full stop law and the law of Due Obedience. He also had conflicts with the unions, which were controlled by the opposing Justicialist Party. He resolved the Beagle conflict, increased trade with Brazil, and proposed the creation of the Contadora support group to mediate between the United States and Nicaragua. He passed the first divorce law of Argentina. He initiated the Austral plan to improve the national economy, but that plan, as well as the Spring plan, failed. The resulting hyperinflation and riots led to his party's defeat in the 1989 presidential elections, which was won by Peronist Carlos Menem. Alfonsín continued as the leader of the UCR and opposed the presidency of Carlos Menem. He initiated the Pact of Olivos with Menem to negotiate the terms for the 1994 amendment of the Argentine Constitution. Fernando de la Rúa led a faction of the UCR that opposed the pact, and eventually became president in 1999. Following de la Rúa's resignation during the December 2001 riots, Alfonsín's faction provided the support needed for the Peronist Eduardo Duhalde to be appointed president by the Congress. He died of lung cancer on 31 March 2009, at the age of 82, and was given a large state funeral. Raúl Alfonsín was born on 12 March 1927 in Chascomús, 123 km (76 mi) south of Buenos Aires. His parents, Serafín Raúl Alfonsín Ochoa and Ana María Foulkes, were shopkeepers. His father was of Galician and German descent, and his mother was the daughter of Welsh immigrant Ricardo Foulkes and Falkland Islander María Elena Ford. After elementary schooling, Alfonsín enrolled at the General San Martín Military Lyceum. Although his father disliked the military, he believed it would offer a quality education similar to a private school without the cost. Alfonsín disliked the military but this education helped him understand the military mindset. He graduated after five years as a second lieutenant and did not pursue a military career, instead beginning law studies at the National University of La Plata and completing them at the University of Buenos Aires. He was not a successful lawyer: he was frequently absent from work and in debt. He married María Lorenza Barreneche, whom he met in 1949 at a masquerade ball. They moved to Mendoza, La Plata, and returned to Chascomús. They had six sons, of whom only Ricardo Alfonsín would follow a political career. Alfonsín bought a local newspaper (El Imparcial). He joined the UCR in 1946 as a member of the Intransigent Renewal Movement, a faction that opposed the UCR's incorporation into the Democratic Union coalition. He was appointed president of the party committee in Chascomús in 1951 and elected to the city council in 1954. He was briefly detained during the government of Juan Perón's reaction to the bombing of Plaza de Mayo. The Revolución Libertadora ousted Perón from the national government; Alfonsín was again briefly detained and forced to leave his office in the city council. The UCR split into two parties: the Intransigent Radical Civic Union (UCRI), led by Arturo Frondizi, and the People's Radical Civic Union (UCRP), led by Ricardo Balbín and Crisólogo Larralde. Alfonsín did not like the split but opted to follow the UCRP. He was elected deputy for the legislature of the Buenos Aires province in 1958 on the UCRP ticket and reelected in 1962. He moved to La Plata, the capital of the province, during his tenure. President Frondizi was ousted by a military coup on 29 March 1962, which also closed the provincial legislature. Alfonsín returned to Chascomús. The UCRP prevailed over the UCRI the following year, leading to the presidency of Arturo Umberto Illia. Alfonsín was elected a national deputy and then vice president of the UCRP bloc in congress. In 1963 he was appointed president of the party committee for the province of Buenos Aires. Still in his formative years, Alfonsín held no noteworthy role in the administrations of Frondizi and Illia. Illia was deposed by a new military coup in June 1966, the Argentine Revolution. Alfonsín was detained while trying to hold a political rally in La Plata and a second time when he tried to re-open the UCRP committee. He was forced to resign as a deputy in November 1966. He was detained a third time in 1968 after a political rally in La Plata. He also wrote opinion articles in newspapers under the pseudonyms Alfonso Carrido Lura and Serafín Feijó. The Dirty War began during this time, as many guerrilla groups rejected both the right-wing military dictatorship and civil governments, preferring instead a left-wing dictatorship aligned with the Soviet Union, as in the Cuban Revolution. Alfonsín clarified in his articles that he rejected both the military dictatorship and the guerrillas, advocating for free elections.
