The UCRP became the UCR once more, and the UCRI was turned into the Intransigent Party. Alfonsín created the Movement for Renewal and Change within the UCR to challenge Balbín's leadership. The military dictatorship called for free elections, allowing Peronism (which had been banned since 1955) to take part. Balbín defeated Alfonsín in the primary elections but lost in the main ones. Alfonsín was elected deputy once more. Illia was invited in 1975 to a diplomatic mission to the Soviet Union; he declined and proposed Alfonsín instead. Upon his return, Alfonsín became one of the founding members of the Permanent Assembly for Human Rights. He served as the defense lawyer for Mario Roberto Santucho, leader of the ERP guerrillas, but only to carry out due process of law, not because of a genuine desire to support him. The 1976 Argentine coup d'état against President Isabel Perón started the National Reorganization Process. Alfonsín filed several Habeas corpus motions, requesting the freedom of victims of forced disappearances. The UCR stayed silent over the disappearances, but Alfonsín urged the party to protest the kidnapping of senators Hipólito Yrigoyen (nephew of the former president of the same name) and Mario Anaya. He also visited other countries, denouncing those disappearances and violations of human rights. He established the magazine Propuesta y control in 1976, one of the few magazines that criticized the military dictatorship during its early stages. The magazine was published up to 1978. His editorials were collected in 1980 in the book La cuestión argentina. Alfonsín expressed opposition to the 1982 Falklands War, criticizing the deployment of troops by both sides during the conflict. He rejected the invasion of the islands, which he considered an inevitable logistic and diplomatic failure, being one of the few politicians who opposed the war from the start. He proposed an emergency government headed by Illia, with ministers from all political parties, who would call for a ceasefire with the British and call for elections. He reasoned that the British would be magnanimous in victory if negotiating the transition with a civilian government, that all Argentine parties would be involved with such negotiations, and provide greater guarantees. The proposal did not get enough support, as Peronist Deolindo Bittel proposed another post-war scenario: electing a prime minister selected by a committee of generals and politicians, who would keep a veto power and guide the new government for at least two years. This proposal implicitly intended to remove Bignone and appoint a figure akin to the late Juan Perón, but it did not get support either because the current context did not provide any such figure that would have both support from the military and from the population. Antonio Trocolli, former leader of the Radical Congress, rejected both proposals as impracticable. The Falklands Wars were lost, and the military lifted the ban on political activities on the promise to hold elections. This was a calculated move to make the politicians focus on internal infighting, instead of blaming the military for the defeat. The plan did not work as intended, as the political parties united in a temporary coalition, the "Multipartidaria," that rejected the military attempt to control the new government and asked to speed up the elections, which were called for October 1983. The Movement for Renewal and Change organized the first political event in a stadium in the Buenos Aires suburbs. As Balbín had died in 1981, the UCR had no strong leadership at the time. Alfonsín disputed the leadership of the UCR with Carlos Contín, but was unable to pass through the complex internal regulations of the party. He made a new political rally at the Luna Park, with a success comparable to a United States presidential primary. This new rally convinced Contín, who also ambitioned to be president, that he had no chances fighting against Alfonsín in proper primary elections. Fernando de la Rúa, who would have run in the primary elections against him, declined his candidacy because of Alfonsín's huge popularity. Antonio Trocolli, another precandidate, declined to run as well. Alfonsín was then appointed candidate of the UCR for the 1983 general elections, with Víctor Martínez as the candidate for the vice-presidency. The UCR proposed Alfonsín to run with De la Rúa as the candidate for the vice-presidency, to secure the conservative votes, but Alfonsín was confident to win the elections without help. The publicity was managed by David Ratto, who created the slogan "Ahora Alfonsín" (Spanish: "Now Alfonsín"), and the gesture of shaking hands. His campaign used a non-confrontational approach, in stark contrast with the Peronist candidate for the governorship of the Buenos Aires province, Herminio Iglesias. Iglesias burned a coffin with the seals of the UCR on live television, which generated a political scandal. Both Iglesias and Ítalo Luder, the Peronist candidate for the presidency, saw a decrease in their public image as a result. A group of UCR supporters drew graffiti that praised Alfonsín manliness and mocked Luder as effeminate; Alfonsín ordered to remove the graffitis as soon as he knew about them. During the campaign, both parties made similar proposals to reduce authoritarianism and the political influence of the military, and to maintain the Argentine claim in the Falkland Islands sovereignty dispute. Alfonsín denounced a pact between the military and the Peronist unions that sought an amnesty for the military. He maintained that the armed forces should be subject to the civilian government and that unions should be regulated. He also proposed an investigation into the actions of the military during the Dirty War. He closed his campaign by reading the preamble of the constitution of Argentina. The last rally was at the Plaza de la República, and was attended by 400,000 people. Opinion polls placed the UCR behind the PJ, but also placed Alfonsín as the most popular politician at the time. The elections were held on 30 October. The Alfonsín–Martínez ticket won with 51.7% of the vote, followed by Luder–Bittel with 40.1%. It was the first time since the rise of Juan Domingo Perón that the Peronist party was defeated in elections without electoral fraud or proscription. The UCR won 128 seats in the Assembly, forming a majority; and 18 seats in the Senate, constituting a minority. 18 provinces elected radical governors and 17 elected governors from either the Justicialist or local parties. Alfonsín took office on 10 December and gave a speech from the Buenos Aires Cabildo. The presidential inauguration of Alfonsín was attended by Isabel Perón. Despite internal recriminations for the defeat, the Peronist party agreed to support Alfonsín as president, to prevent a return of the military. There were still factions in the military ambitious to keep an authoritarian government, and groups such as the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo seeking reparations for the actions of the military during the Dirty War. Three days after taking office, Alfonsín sent a bill to Congress to revoke the self-amnesty law established by the military. This made it possible for the judiciary to investigate the crimes committed during the Dirty War. During the campaign, Alfonsín had promised that he would do this while Luder had been non-committal. Alfonsín also ordered the initiation of judicial cases against guerrilla leaders Mario Firmenich, Fernando Vaca Narvaja, Ricardo Obregón Cano, Rodolfo Galimberti, Roberto Perdía, Héctor Pardo and Enrique Gorriarán Merlo; and military leaders Jorge Videla, Emilio Massera, Orlando Agosti, Roberto Viola, Armando Lambruschini, Omar Graffigna, Leopoldo Galtieri, Jorge Anaya and Basilio Lami Dozo. He also requested the extradition of guerrilla leaders who were living abroad. Most of the first cabinet, organized in Chascomús, was composed of trusted colleagues of Alfonsín. Alfonsín appointed as minister of labor Antonio Mucci, who belonged to a faction of the UCR that sought to reduce the influence of Peronism among labor unions, and promptly sent a bill to Congress designed to promote independent unions. Facing an economic crisis, he appointed Bernardo Grinspun as minister of the economy. He appointed Aldo Neri minister of health, Dante Caputo minister of foreign relations, Antonio Tróccoli minister of interior affairs, Roque Carranza minister of public works, Carlos Alconada Aramburu minister of education, and Raúl Borrás minister of defense. Juan Carlos Pugliese led the Chamber of Deputies, and Edison Otero was the provisional President of the Senate. Many presidential negotiations took place at the Quinta de Olivos, the official residence of the president, rather than at the Casa Rosada. The priority of Raúl Alfonsín was to consolidate democracy, incorporate the armed forces into their standard role in a civilian government, and prevent further military coups. Alfonsín first tried to reduce the political power of the military with budget cuts, reductions of military personnel and changing their political tasks. As for the crimes committed during the Dirty War, Alfonsín was willing to respect the command responsibility and accept the "superior orders" defense for the military of lower ranks, as long as the Junta leaders were sentenced under military justice. This project was resisted by human rights organizations such as Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo and public opinion, as it was expected that the defendants would be acquitted or receive low sentences. The military considered that the Dirty War was legally sanctioned, and considered the prosecutions to be unjustified. Alfonsín also established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), composed of several well-known personalities, to document cases of forced disappearances, human rights violations and abduction of children. Alfonsín sent a military code bill to Congress so that the military would use it. In its "Nunca más" report (Spanish: Never again), the CONADEP revealed the wide scope of the crimes committed during the Dirty War, and how the Supreme Council of the military had supported the military's actions against the guerrillas. As a result, Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, in which, for the first time, the leaders of a military coup in Argentina were on trial. The first hearings began at the Supreme Court in April 1985 and lasted for the remainder of the year. In December, the tribunal handed down life sentences for Jorge Videla and former Navy Chief Emilio Massera, as well as 17-year sentences for.

It was expected that the defendants in the Dirty War prosecutions would be acquitted or receive light sentences, as the military viewed the conflict as legally sanctioned and considered the trials unjustified. President Alfonsín established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), composed of prominent figures, to document forced disappearances, human rights violations, and the abduction of children. He introduced a military code bill to Congress to regulate military conduct. The "Nunca más" report by CONADEP revealed the extensive nature of the crimes and how the Supreme Council of the military supported its actions against guerrillas. Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, marking the first time military coup leaders were prosecuted; the first hearings began at the Supreme Court in April 1985 and continued through the year. In December, Jorge Videla and Emilio Massera received life sentences, and Roberto Eduardo Viola was sentenced to 17 years; President Leopoldo Galtieri was acquitted of repression charges but was court-martialed in May 1986 for malfeasance during the Falklands War; Ramón Camps received a 25-year sentence. The trials also included Mario Firmenich, captured in Brazil in 1984 and extradited in 1984, and José López Rega, extradited from Miami in 1986 due to his ties with the Argentine Anticommunist Alliance. The military was supported by the families of subversion victims, a group formed to counter the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, though it had few followers. The trials were followed by bomb attacks, rumors of military protests, and a possible coup. Alfonsín sought to calm the military by increasing their budget, but when that failed, he proposed the Full Stop Law, setting a deadline for Dirty War-related prosecutions. Congress approved the law despite strong public opposition. Prosecutors filed 487 charges against 300 officers, including 100 still in active service. Major Ernesto Barreiro refused to appear in court and initiated a mutiny in Córdoba; Lieutenant Colonel Aldo Rico launched another mutiny at Campo de Mayo, supporting Barreiro. The rebels were known as "Carapintadas" due to their use of military camouflage. The CGT called a general strike in support of Alfonsín, and large crowds gathered in the Plaza de Mayo. Alfonsín negotiated directly with the rebels and secured their surrender, announcing the end of the crisis from the Casa Rosada balcony. The mutineers eventually surrendered, but the government proceeded with the Law of Due Obedience to regulate the trials. The timing of both events was exploited by the military, and opposition parties described the outcome as a surrender by Alfonsín. Aldo Rico escaped from prison in January 1988 and launched a new mutiny in a distant northeast regiment; this time, military support and public outcry were minimal. The army attacked him, and Rico surrendered after brief combat. Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín launched another mutiny in late 1988; the mutineers were defeated and jailed, but the military avoided opening fire. Alfonsín’s goal of reconciling the military with the civilian population failed, as the public rejected military complaints and the military focused on internal issues. The Movimiento Todos por la Patria, a small guerrilla group led by Enrique Gorriarán Merlo, attacked the Regiment of La Tablada in 1989; the army killed many members and quickly defeated the uprising. During his presidency, Alfonsín clashed with labor unions over economic reforms and trade liberalization, as Peronism still controlled the unions, the most powerful in Latin America, with the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) being the largest. Alfonsín sought to reduce Peronist influence, rejecting single-candidate internal elections, which he deemed totalitarian, and proposing changes to election laws, removal of dictatorship-appointed union leaders, and new elections. The CGT rejected the proposal as interventionist, prompting Peronist politicians to oppose it. The law passed the Chamber of Deputies but failed in the Senate by one vote. A second bill calling only for elections without government supervision was approved, leaving unions Peronist. The CGT was internally divided: Lorenzo Miguel, aligned with the Justicialist party, led "the 62 organizations" faction; Saúl Ubaldini, more confrontational and distrustful of PJ politicians, became secretary general; his lack of political ties enabled him to mediate between factions. Carlos Alderete led a faction closer to Alfonsín, known as "the 15" unions. The government sought to deepen divisions by appointing Alderete as minister of labor and promoting legislation favoring his faction; he was removed after the 1987 midterm election defeat, but the government maintained good relations with his faction. Alfonsín maintained a dictatorship-era regulation allowing wage regulation, authorizing wage increases every three months to match inflation. The CGT rejected this, proposing instead free negotiations. Alfonsín allowed strikes, previously forbidden during the dictatorship, giving unions another avenue to expand influence. There were thirteen general strikes and thousands of minor labor conflicts. Unlike past situations, the CGT supported Alfonsín during military rebellions and did not back removing a non-Peronist president. The conflicts stemmed from high inflation, prompting unions to demand higher wages, with support from non-unionized retirees, the church, and left-wing factions. Popular support enabled the government to endure despite union opposition. After the end of the military dictatorship, Alfonsín promoted cultural and educational reforms to reduce authoritarianism and supported press freedom. Many intellectuals and scientists who had left the country returned, improving university quality, with the University of Buenos Aires regaining 1960s standards. Many intellectuals entered politics, enriching political discourse, benefiting both Alfonsín and Peronist Antonio Cafiero. Divorce was legalized in 1987; the church opposed it, but it had broad popular support, including Catholic factions who argued that marital separation already existed and divorce merely formalized it. The church opposed Alfonsín afterward and successfully pressured to prevent the abolition of religious education. In line with Pope John Paul II’s teachings, the church criticized rising drug use, terrorism, abortion, and pornography. Alfonsín intended to decriminalize abortion but abandoned the idea to avoid further conflict with the church. Argentina had a tense relationship with the United Kingdom due to the Falklands War; the UK temporarily banned foreign ships from entering the exclusion zone in 1986. Argentina responded with air and marine patrols and military exercises in Patagonia, but this did not satisfy military hard-liners. Alfonsín proposed postponing sovereignty discussions and instead negotiating a de jure cease of hostilities, reduced military forces, and normalized relations with the UK. The UK did not trust the proposal, suspecting it was a cover for sovereignty talks. The Beagle conflict with Chile remained unresolved despite 1978 Papal mediation. The military, disturbed by the juntas trial, rejected the proposed agreement and continued claiming the islands. Alfonsín called for a referendum to settle the dispute. Despite opposition from the military and the Justicialist party, which urged abstention, support reached 82%. The bill passed the Senate by a single vote, as the PJ resisted. The Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1984 between Chile and Argentina was signed the following year, ending the conflict. Human rights violations by Chilean President Augusto Pinochet and revelations of Chilean support for British forces during the Falklands War remained contentious. The Argentine church invited Pope John Paul II for a second visit in 1987 to celebrate his successful mediation; he celebrated World Youth Day near the Obelisk of Buenos Aires and gave a mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján. Argentina allied with Brazil, Uruguay, and Peru—countries that had recently ended military dictatorships—to mediate the U.S.-Nicaragua conflict. They formed the Contadora support group, which later shifted focus to foreign debt and diplomacy with the UK regarding the Falklands. Initially, Alfonsín refused to establish diplomatic relations with the Brazilian military government, doing so only after its end and José Sarney’s presidency. Their initial concern was increasing trade. The two presidents met in Foz do Iguaçu and issued a joint declaration on peaceful nuclear use. A second meeting in Buenos Aires strengthened trade agreements. Argentina and Brazil signed the Program of Integration and Economic Cooperation (PICE), and in 1988, with Uruguay, agreed to create a common market, leading to the 1991 Treaty of Asunción establishing Mercosur. Alfonsín was the first Argentine head of state to visit the USSR. He began his term facing severe economic problems: the economy had contracted by 15% in the previous decade, foreign debt was nearly $43 billion, and the country narrowly avoided sovereign default in 1982. In 1982, GDP fell by 5.6% and manufacturing profits by 55%; unemployment was nearly 10%, inflation nearly 209%, and foreign investment seemed unlikely. The country had a $6.7 billion deficit. Possible solutions like currency devaluation, privatization, or import restrictions would have been unpopular. Initially, the government took no strong action. Bernardo Grinspun, the first minister of economy, raised wages to 1975 levels, causing inflation to reach 32%. He failed to secure favorable foreign debt terms and, risking default, negotiated with the IMF, which demanded spending cuts. International credits prevented default by the end of 1984, but Grinspun resigned in March 1985 when debt reached $1 billion and the IMF denied further credits. He was succeeded by Juan Vital Sourrouille, who introduced the Austral plan in 1985. The plan froze prices and wages, stopped money printing, implemented spending cuts, and introduced the Austral, worth 1 USD. The plan succeeded short-term in curbing inflation. However, by this point, most of Alfonsín’s initial popularity had declined, and he could not convince many of the long-term benefits of austerity. Inflation rose again by year-end, the CGT opposed the wage freeze, and the business community opposed the price freeze. Alfonsín believed privatization and deregulation might work, but both the PJ and his own party opposed them. The Austral plan was undermined by populist economic policies. With World Bank support, the government tried new measures in 1987, including tax increases, privatizations, and spending cuts. These could not be enforced; the government lost the 1987 midterm elections, the "15" unions distanced themselves, and the business community offered no clear path. The PJ, aiming for a 1989 presidential victory, opposed measures it saw as socially harmful. The "Spring plan" aimed to stabilize the economy until the elections by freezing prices and wages and reducing the federal deficit. It had a worse reception than the Austral plan and received no party support. The World Bank and IMF refused to extend credits; big exporters refused to sell dollars to the Central Bank, depleting reserves. The austral was devalued in February 1989, and inflation turned into hyperinflation. The US dollar was worth 14 australes at the beginning of 1989 and 17,000 by May. The 1989 presidential elections occurred during the crisis, and Justicialist Carlos Menem won. By winter 1989, inflation was so severe that Alfonsín transferred power to Menem on 8 July, five months earlier than scheduled. Alfonsín remained president of the UCR after leaving office, staying until the party’s defeat in the 1991 legislative elections. Damaged by the 1989 hyperinflation, the UCR lost in several districts. Alfonsín returned as party president in 1993. He supported a special budget for Buenos Aires, led by governor Eduardo Duhalde. Radical legislator Leopoldo Moreau supported the budget more strongly than the Peronists. Both parties formed an informal alliance in the province. Alfonsín also supported a constitutional amendment allowing Duhalde to run for re-election. President Menem sought a constitutional amendment to allow his re-election, which Alfonsín opposed. The 1993 midterm victory strengthened the PJ, which approved the bill in the Senate. Menem proposed a referendum to force radical deputies to support it and introduced a bill allowing a constitutional amendment with a simple majority in Congress. As a result, Alfonsín signed the Pact of Olivos with Menem. Under the pact, the UCR would support Menem’s proposal with amendments reducing presidential power. The Council of Magistracy reduced executive influence over the judiciary, Buenos Aires became an autonomous territory with elected mayor, and the presidential term was reduced to four years. The election system adopted a two-round system, and the electoral college was abolished. Alfonsín was elected to the constituent assembly that drafted the 1994 constitutional amendment. A faction of the UCR, led by Fernando de la Rúa, opposed the pact, but the party as a whole supported Alfonsín. The UCR received only 19% of the vote in the 1995 elections, finishing third behind Frepaso when Menem was re-elected. Alfonsín resigned as party president in that year. Raúl Alfonsín made the Pact of Olivos with President Carlos Menem, leading the UCR to support Menem's constitutional amendment proposals with modifications that reduced presidential power. These changes included limiting executive influence over the judiciary, granting the city of Buenos Aires autonomy to elect its mayor, and shortening the presidential term to four years. The presidential election system was changed to include a two-round system, and the electoral college was abolished. Alfonsín was elected to the constituent assembly that drafted the 1994 constitutional amendment. A faction of the UCR, led by Fernando de la Rúa, opposed the pact, but the party as a whole backed Alfonsín. In the 1995 presidential elections, the UCR received only 19% of the vote, finishing third behind the Frepaso, and Alfonsín resigned as party president that year. The UCR and Frepaso formed the Alliance for Work, Justice, and Education, led by Alfonsín, de la Rúa, and Rodolfo Terragno from the UCR, and Carlos Álvarez and Graciela Fernández Meijide from the Frepaso, which won the 1997 legislative elections. Alfonsín disagreed with de la Rúa on the fixed exchange rate, believing it had become harmful to the economy despite its past benefits. In 1999, Alfonsín suffered a car crash on Route 6 in Río Negro province during a campaign for governor Pablo Verani, was ejected from the vehicle due to not wearing a seat belt, and was hospitalized for 39 days. De la Rúa won the 1999 presidential election, defeating Eduardo Duhalde, the governor of Buenos Aires. Alfonsín was elected Senator for Buenos Aires Province in October 2001. When de la Rúa resigned during the December 2001 riots, Congress appointed Adolfo Rodríguez Saá, who also resigned, and Alfonsín instructed Radical legislators to support Duhalde as president, appointing him with ministers Horacio Jaunarena for Defense and Jorge Vanossi for Justice, helping Duhalde surpass the ambitions of Carlos Ruckauf and José Manuel de la Sota. Later in the year, due to health issues, Alfonsín stepped down, being replaced by Diana Conti. In 2006, Alfonsín supported a UCR faction advocating for an independent candidate in the 2007 presidential election, and the party endorsed Roberto Lavagna, a center-left economist who led Argentina’s economic recovery from 2002 until his departure from President Néstor Kirchner in December 2005; Lavagna finished in third place. On 1 October 2008, President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner honored Alfonsín with a bust at the Casa Rosada, marking his last public appearance. Alfonsín died at home on 31 March 2009 at age 82 after being diagnosed with lung cancer a year earlier. Hundreds gathered around his house on Santa Fe avenue, starting a candlelight vigil. Radical Julio Cobos, Fernández de Kirchner’s vice president, served as acting president and declared three days of national mourning. A ceremony in Congress, where his body was displayed in the Blue Hall, was attended by nearly a thousand people; his widow María Lorenza Barreneche could not attend due to poor health. The event was attended by former presidents Carlos Menem, Fernando de la Rúa, Eduardo Duhalde, and Néstor Kirchner, all Supreme Court justices, mayor Mauricio Macri, governor Daniel Scioli, Uruguayan president Tabaré Vázquez, and other politicians. The coffin was moved to La Recoleta Cemetery, where he was buried next to Leandro N. Alem, Hipólito Yrigoyen, and Arturo Illia. Perú and Paraguay declared national mourning, with Brazil, Chile, Colombia, France, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Spain, Uruguay, and the United States sending messages of condolence. Julio María Sanguinetti of Uruguay and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil also attended the ceremony. Historians Félix Luna, Miguel Ángel de Marco, and Fernando Rocchi praise Alfonsín for his role in ending the Dirty War and restoring democracy, with Luna calling him an effective president who avoided using state power for personal gain. De Marco notes that the period was delicate, and any error could have led to a coup, though all three historians disagree on the Pact of Olivos: Luna sees it as a necessary compromise to prevent chaos, while De Marco and Rocchi view it as the greatest mistake of Alfonsín’s career. Alfonsín received the 1985 Princess of Asturias Award for international cooperation for resolving the Beagle dispute and restoring democracy. He was named "Illustrious Citizen of Buenos Aires Province" in 2008 and "Illustrious Citizen of Buenos Aires" in 2009, the latter posthumously received by his son Ricardo Alfonsín, ambassador to Spain.

Raúl Fajardo Moreno, born on December 3, 1929, and passing away in July 2012, was a prominent Colombian architect. He co-designed the Coltejer Building, which is Medellín's tallest building, alongside Hernando Vélez, Germán Samper, and Jorge Manjarrés. When asked about his favorite projects, he listed the City University U. of A., the Coltejer building, the Headquarters of Southamerican Insurance, and several other works, but stated that he would redesign each one if given the opportunity to create them anew. Fajardo married María Valderrama Tobón and had five children: Sergio Fajardo, who served as Mayor of Medellín and later Governor of Antioquia, María Isabel, Andrés, Rodrigo, and Silvia. He died at the end of July 2012.

Reinhold Rudenberg (or Rüdenberg) was a German-American electrical engineer and inventor recognized for numerous innovations in electric power and related fields, including improvements in large alternating current generators, the electrostatic-lens electron microscope, carrier-current communications on power lines, a form of phased array radar, an explanation of power blackouts, preferred number series, and the number prefix "Giga-". Born in Hannover to a Jewish family, he had a father, Georg, who ran a plant for preparing and cleaning feathers and down, and a mother who was the daughter of the Chief Rabbi of Braunschweig. He studied at Leibniz University Hannover (then Technische Hochschule), earning both his electrical engineering degree (Dipl. Ing.) and doctorate (Dr. Ing.) in 1906. He worked as a teaching assistant for Professor Ludwig Prandtl at Göttingen University, where he also took courses in physics and the Advanced Electrodynamics course taught by Emil Wiechert, a former discoverer of the electron. In 1919, he married Lily Minkowski, daughter of Hermann Minkowski and Auguste née Adler; their son, H. Gunther Rudenberg, was born from this marriage. Rudenberg taught at Göttingen, Berlin, London, and in the United States at MIT and Harvard University, serving as head of the Department of Electrical Engineering at Harvard’s Graduate School of Engineering from 1939 to 1952, when he retired. After leaving Göttingen in 1908, he joined Siemens-Schuckertwerke (SSW), a Siemens company in Berlin, starting as a machine design engineer and quickly advancing to head the machine design department. His work expanded to include transmission lines, distribution systems, and protective relays and switches. In 1923, he was appointed Director of the Scientific Department (Wissenschaftliche Abteilung) of SSW and named Chief Electrical Engineer (Chef-Elektriker) of the firm. In 1916, he designed the electric generator for the main power station in Cologne, which was then the largest known. He was a prolific inventor and author, with his books on electrical transients widely used as college texts. In 1930, shortly after returning from a summer vacation in the Netherlands, his 2 3⁄4-year-old son fell ill with poliomyelitis, a disease with a 10–25% death rate that affected the legs and could progress to the lungs; at the time, the virus was known to be too small to be seen under an optical microscope. Determined to visualize such small particles, Rudenberg, inspired by his studies of electrons under Wiechert’s guidance, believed electrons could resolve virus particles and began investigating methods to focus them to create enlarged images. In 1927, Hans Busch, a friend from Göttingen, had published an analysis of a magnetic coil acting as a lens. Rudenberg reasoned that an electron beam from a point on an object in an axially symmetric electrostatic system could be focused back to an image point if the radial electric field was proportional to the electron’s distance from the axis, enabling real magnified images. As a public lecture on electron optics approached, Siemens applied for a patent on Rudenberg’s electrostatic-lens instrument and general electron microscope principles on May 30, 1931, securing patents in six other countries. Germany later granted patents on this or related inventions between 1938 and 1954. Some competitors raised objections to the Rudenberg patents but failed to acknowledge that he began his work in 1930, the specific stimulus that prompted it, or the technical differences between his electrostatic lenses and the magnetic lenses used by others.

"Resistance Is Futile" is the ninth episode of the second season and twenty-first overall episode of the American television drama series Dexter, which first aired on November 25, 2007 on Showtime in the United States. The episode was written by Melissa Rosenberg, who earned her fifth writing credit, and directed by Marcos Siega, who received his second directing credit. Set in Miami, the series follows Dexter Morgan, a forensic technician specializing in bloodstain pattern analysis for the fictional Miami Metro Police Department, who leads a secret parallel life as a vigilante serial killer, hunting down murderers who have not been adequately punished by the justice system due to corruption or legal technicalities. In this episode, Dexter discovers that the FBI is following him and that Doakes has taken his blood slides. While staying guard outside her house, Dexter (Michael C. Hall) apologizes to Rita (Julie Benz) for his affair with Lila (Jaime Murray). He drives off to dispose of Jimenez's body at the cabin but finds a car following him; the car belongs to the FBI, and agents check his office to examine the blood work database. In Port-au-Prince, Doakes meets with a friend, Leones (Peter Macon), asking him to analyze Dexter's blood slides, but he does not have them. Dexter realizes the slides are missing and believes Lundy (Keith Carradine) has them. FBI agents arrive and ask him to accompany them to the department, where Lundy and Matthews (Geoff Pierson) await him with the blood slides. Dexter believes he has been caught until Lundy and Matthews state they suspect Doakes is the Bay Harbor Butcher, having raided his car and found the slides. To cover himself, Dexter agrees with their theory, allowing the FBI to protect him while appointing him to analyze the blood slides, during which he uses the opportunity to cover his fingerprints. Despite Dexter's warning, Lila flirts with Angel (David Zayas) and goes out with him and others from the station for drinks, forcing Dexter to go along with them as he fears she will expose his connection to Jimenez. Doakes contacts LaGuerta (Lauren Vélez) to claim his innocence, which she believes. Doakes refuses to surrender and sets out to find evidence, destroying his cell phone in the process. When Lundy plans to reveal Doakes as the prime suspect to the press, LaGuerta tries to get Debra (Jennifer Carpenter) to act, leading to an argument in which Debra yells that she is in a relationship with Lundy. That night, Dexter escapes from his apartment and uses his boat to return to the cabin, where he chops Jimenez's body. As he leaves with the bags, he is held at gunpoint by Doakes, who tracks him with a GPS in the boat. Having discovered the trash bags, Dexter realizes he is the Butcher. Doakes forces Dexter to handcuff himself and walk toward him, but Dexter attacks him. During the fight, Dexter is shot in the leg and they fall into the water, where Dexter uses the handcuffs to knock Doakes unconscious. Doakes later wakes up inside a cage in the cabin, and Dexter locks the door behind him. In its original American broadcast, the episode was seen by an estimated 1.03 million household viewers and gained a 0.5 ratings share among adults aged 18–49, meaning 0.5 percent of all households with televisions watched it. This represented a 17% decrease in viewership from the previous episode, which was watched by an estimated 1.23 million household viewers with a 0.6/1 in the 18–49 demographics. The episode received critical acclaim, with Eric Goldman of IGN giving it an "amazing" 9.5 out of 10, praising it as a nailbiting, suspenseful scenario that felt like the penultimate episode of the season. Scott Tobias of The A.V. Club gave it a "B+" grade, noting that each solution created new problems and that the showdown with Doakes was a surprising reversal of their cat-and-mouse dynamic. Alan Sepinwall wrote that while the episode wasn't bad, it was the first time viewers were genuinely concerned about the show's forward plan, and that the writers' strings were visible. Paula Paige of TV Guide called Michael C. Hall's expressions award-worthy and noted that his self-reflection was unhealthy, while the killing made him more attractive. Keith McDuffee of TV Squad stated it was not surprising that Doakes was brought in as the prime suspect due to prior clues, including taking the blood slides and Doakes' father being a butcher, but was surprised when Doakes appeared on the dock at the end. Television Without Pity gave the episode an "A" grade. Lauren Vélez submitted this episode for consideration for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Drama Series at the 60th Primetime Emmy Awards.

Reza Aslan (Persian: رضا اصلان, IPA: [ˈɾezɒː æsˈlɒːn]; born May 3, 1972) is an Iranian-American scholar of sociology, writer, and television host. Born into a Twelver Shia Muslim family, he converted to evangelical Christianity at age 15 and reverted to Islam the summer before attending Harvard, where he completed his degree in 1999. Aslan holds a B.A. in religious studies from Santa Clara University, a Master of Theological Studies (MTS) from Harvard Divinity School, a Master of Fine Arts (M.F.A.) in fiction writing from the University of Iowa's Writers' Workshop, and a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of California, Santa Barbara. His 2009 dissertation, "Global Jihadism as a Transnational Social Movement: A Theoretical Framework," discusses contemporary Muslim political activism. Aslan has written four books: No God but God: The Origins, Evolution, and Future of Islam (2005), How to Win a Cosmic War: God, Globalization, and the End of Terror (2009), re-released in 2010 as Beyond Fundamentalism: Confronting Religious Extremism in the Age of Globalization, Zealot: The Life and Times of Jesus of Nazareth (2013), and An American Martyr in Persia: The Epic Life and Tragic Death of Howard Baskerville (2022). He has also edited two anthologies: Tablet and Pen: Literary Landscapes from the Modern Middle East (2011) and Muslims and Jews in America: Commonalities, Contentions, and Complexities (2011). Aslan has written for numerous media outlets, including The Daily Beast, The Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, Slate, The Boston Globe, The Guardian, The Nation, and The Christian Science Monitor. He is a professor of creative writing at the University of California, Riverside, and a board member of the National Iranian American Council (NIAC). Aslan's family fled Iran in 1979 and settled in the San Francisco Bay Area; he attended Del Mar High School in San Jose and graduated in 1990. In the early 1990s, he taught at De La Salle High School in Concord, California. He served as a visiting faculty member in Islamic and Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Iowa in August 2000 while at the Iowa Writers' Workshop and was the 2012–13 Wallerstein Distinguished Visiting Professor at the Drew University Center on Religion, Culture & Conflict. He is an Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations from 2012 to 2013, a member of the Los Angeles Institute for the Humanities and the Pacific Council on International Policy, and serves on the boards of the Ploughshares Fund, PEN Center USA, The Markaz, the Chicago Theological Seminary, and the Yale Humanist Community. Aslan founded Aslan Media and partnered with Mahyad Tousi to create BoomGen Studios in 2006, which produced projects such as National Geographic's Amreeka, Disney's Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, the Broadway adaptation of Aladdin, Miral, Desert Dancer, The Trials of Spring, Rosewater, and The Square. In January 2015, ABC picked up Of Kings and Prophets, a biblical epic produced by Aslan, Tousi, and Jason Reed, which followed the story of King David and was set in the Kingdom of Israel but filmed in Cape Town, South Africa. Aslan joined HBO's The Leftovers as a consulting producer for its second and third seasons, playing a key role in shaping protagonist Kevin Garvey's character arc. In March 2016, Ovation premiered Rough Draft with Reza Aslan, a talk show featuring Aslan discussing topics with authors and writers. In 2015, Aslan began production on the documentary series Believer, which follows his immersive experiences with various religious traditions, focusing on fringe sects. The first episode featured the Aghori sect of Hinduism, where Aslan ate part of a human brain, leading to accusations of sensationalism and anti-Hinduism. Critics, including the United States India Political Action Committee, Vamsee Juluri, Aseem Shukla, and US Congresswoman Tulsi Gabbard, condemned the episode for misrepresenting Hinduism, calling it racist, anti-immigrant, and inaccurate. Aslan claimed he had planned to cover the Ashura festival in Pakistan but abandoned it due to insurance costs and pledged to cover Islam if a second season of Believer were produced. On June 9, 2017, CNN announced it would not proceed with a second season of Believer after Aslan's anti-Trump tweets were criticized for using vulgar language. Aslan defended the episode in a Facebook post and stated he is not a journalist but a social commentator and scholar, agreeing with CNN that it was best to part ways. Aslan also wrote a sitcom pilot titled "Allah in the Family" based on his experiences as an Iranian immigrant in Oklahoma, which ABC bought but has not yet produced. After the 2017 London Bridge attack, Aslan criticized President Donald Trump on Twitter, calling him "a piece of shit" and a "man-baby," leading to CNN's decision to end their collaboration. Aslan has made numerous media appearances on NPR, Fox News, PBS, The Rachel Maddow Show, Meet the Press, The Daily Show, The Colbert Report, Anderson Cooper 360°, Hardball, Nightline, Real Time with Bill Maher, Fareed Zakaria GPS, and ABC Australia's Big Ideas. In a 2013 Fox News interview, Aslan defended his right to write about Jesus as a scholar of religion, despite criticism from Fox host Lauren Green, who questioned his credentials. The interview went viral and boosted sales of Zealot, which reached number four on The New York Times best-seller list and topped Amazon's U.S. list by late July 2013. Academic scholars, including Elizabeth Castelli of Barnard College and Manuel Roig-Franzia of The Washington Post, criticized Aslan's claims of being a historian, noting that his university does not offer degrees in the history or sociology of religion, though his dissertation adviser, Mark Juergensmeyer, acknowledged that Aslan completed most of his coursework in religion and was placed in sociology to avoid language requirements. Aslan is a sitting member of the advisory board for the National Iranian American Council and, in 2015, co-signed with 73 other Middle East scholars a statement supporting the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. Aslan refers to Al Qaeda's jihad against the West as "a cosmic war," distinct from holy war, in which rival religious groups are engaged in an earthly battle for material goals, and he argues that American rhetoric of "war on terrorism" mirrors this cosmic dualism. He distinguishes between Islamism and Jihadism, asserting that Islamists have legitimate goals and can be negotiated with, while Jihadists seek a pan-Islamic, borderless religious communalism. Aslan's solution to the cosmic war is to engage moderate Islamic political forces in democratic processes, noting that such participation has reduced support for extremist groups. The New Yorker called Beyond Fundamentalism a "thoughtful analysis of America's War on Terror," and The Washington Post described it as offering a "very persuasive argument for the best way to counter jihadism." In Zealot, Aslan presents Jesus as a political, rebellious, and eschatological Jew who called for regime change to end Roman hegemony and oppressive religious leadership. In a 2013 interview with WNYC, Aslan stated that all religions are languages of symbols and metaphors to express faith, and in a 2014 interview with Cenk Uygur, he described Islam as a man-made institution composed of symbols and metaphors that provide a language for the inexpressible, not more right or wrong than other religions. Kirkus Reviews called An American Martyr in Persia "an intriguing read that breathes life into a pivotal moment of Persian/Iranian history."

Aslan is a professor of creative writing at the University of California, Riverside and a board member of the National Iranian American Council (NIAC), serving as a sitting member of its advisory board. In 2015, as part of the group, he signed a statement of support for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action alongside 73 other prominent International Relations and Middle East scholars. He describes Al Qaeda's jihad against the West as a "cosmic war," distinct from holy war, which he views as a ritual drama reflecting a battle occurring in the heavens, contrasting with American rhetoric of a "war on terrorism" that operates within the same structure of "cosmic dualism." Aslan distinguishes between Islamism and Jihadism, asserting that Islamists have legitimate goals and can be negotiated with, whereas Jihadists seek an idealized, pan-Islamic, borderless "religious communalism" and are not open to dialogue. His solution to the cosmic war is engagement with moderate Islamic political forces through democratic participation, noting that in the Middle East, when moderate Islamist parties have been allowed into the political process, support for extremist groups has declined. Aslan advocates for religious freedom and protection of religious minorities in the Middle East, calling on Iran to stop the "horrific human rights abuses" against its Baháʼí community and condemning the persecution and displacement of Middle Eastern Christian communities as a "regional religious cleansing" that will be a historic disaster for both Christians and Muslims. In a 2014 interview, he criticized "armchair atheism" among figures like Sam Harris and Bill Maher, who lack formal training in religion and thus cannot meaningfully discuss how religion influences human behavior, and he called Richard Dawkins a "buffoon, embarrassing himself every day," contrasting the New Atheists with earlier thinkers who were experts in religion and offered critiques grounded in education and research. On September 29, 2014, Antonia Blumberg of The Huffington Post reported that Aslan criticized Bill Maher for portraying female genital mutilation as an "Islamic problem" and for making sweeping generalizations about Islam, stating that equating Pakistan and Turkey as similar is "stupid," and he expressed broader concerns about how Muslims are portrayed in mainstream media. Prachi Gupta of Salon noted Aslan's claim that the U.S. was partnering with Saudi Arabia while condemning ISIS. In an October 8, 2014 article in The New York Times titled "Bill Maher Isn't the Only One Who Misunderstands Religion," Aslan argued that while Maher is right to condemn religious practices that violate human rights, failing to recognize religion's cultural embedding and making blanket judgments about Islam is bigotry. Eric Sasson of The New Republic challenged Aslan's claims that women are treated equally in Indonesia and Turkey due to elected female leaders, citing Human Rights Watch reports of a significant rollback of women's rights in both countries, and disputed his assertion that female genital mutilation is only a problem in central Africa, noting it also occurs in Malaysia. David Pakman also questioned some of Aslan's claims from the interview, and Sam Harris criticized Aslan for attributing violence in the Muslim world to individuals rather than Islam as a whole, calling his approach "post-modernist nonsense." Aslan and his former fiancée, journalist Amanda Fortini, ended their engagement in 2008. He married entrepreneur and author Jessica Jackley, a Christian, in 2011, forming an interfaith family with three sons. His aunt is the Iranian-American pop singer Leila Forouhar, and he is a fan of the professional football team the Las Vegas Raiders.

The Ribenboim Prize, named in honour of Paulo Ribenboim, is awarded by the Canadian Number Theory Association to recognize distinguished research in number theory by a mathematician who is Canadian or has significant ties to Canadian mathematics. Typically, the recipient has obtained their Ph.D. within the past 12 years, and is expected to deliver a plenary talk at the award ceremony. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the prizes for 2020, 2022, and 2024 were all conferred in 2024.

Ricco (October 13, 1915 – March 27, 1972), born Erich Wassmer, was a Swiss painter known for depicting idealizing dream worlds in the genre of magic realism. Erich Wassmer was born in Allschwil into an upper-class environment as the son of cement factory owner and art patron Max Wassmer (1887–1970). From the age of three, he lived at Bremgarten Castle near Bern, a home rich in art and culture, where his parents socialized with notable figures such as Hermann Hesse, Louis Moilliet, Cuno Amiet, Paul Basilius Barth, and Othmar Schoeck. Early on, Erich developed an interest in painting, which the family supported due to the continued success of the family’s cement factory, secured by his two brothers. In 1937, he adopted the name Ricco—described as a "magic word"—to sign his works, replacing his father’s well-known industrialist identity. Ricco studied in Munich and Paris under Cuno Amiet, though the influence of his teachers was minimal. He was deeply fascinated by the sea and the idea of exploring lost paradises and uncharted territories, and he had an anchor tattooed on his arm, which he later incorporated into his signature. During the 1940s, he traveled by freighter across the ocean and lived in Tahiti. In the 1950s, he settled at Bompré Castle near Vichy. In 1963, French police discovered in his studio photographs of nude boys that served as the basis for his paintings. A French court convicted him—without a formal indictment—of sexual "exploitation" of young boys and breach of morality, sentencing him to eight months in prison. Ricco never fully recovered from this imprisonment. After his release, he returned to Switzerland and settled in a mansion in Ropraz, where he died in 1972 at the age of 56. Until his death, Ricco Wassmer remained a family shareholder in Portland-Cement-Werke AG. His early works, such as paintings of castle life, are classified as primitivist, while his mature work includes still lifes, harbor scenes, exotic motifs, and allegorical figures. He frequently painted dream worlds in the style of magic realism, featuring lean boys in surreal arrangements, reflecting his longing for androgynous, youthful perfection. His work is described as being rooted in everyday reality but possessing overtones of fantasy or wonder, creating a surreal atmosphere.

Richard Evelyn Byrd Jr. (October 25, 1888 – March 11, 1957) was an American naval officer, pioneering aviator, polar explorer, and organizer of polar logistics. He served as a navigator and expedition leader in aircraft flights that crossed the Atlantic Ocean, a segment of the Arctic Ocean, and a segment of the Antarctic Plateau. He is credited with discovering Mount Sidley, the largest dormant volcano in Antarctica. Byrd claimed to be the first to reach both the North and South Poles by air, though there is controversy over whether he actually reached the North Pole, with some evidence suggesting the distance he claimed to have flown exceeded the possible fuel range of his aircraft. He received the Medal of Honor, the highest military decoration in the U.S. Armed Forces, and the Navy Cross, the second-highest honor for valor in the U.S. Navy. Born in Winchester, Virginia, to Esther Bolling (Flood) and Richard Evelyn Byrd Sr., he was a descendant of the First Families of Virginia, including John Rolfe, Pocahontas, William Byrd II, William Byrd I, Robert "King" Carter, George Yeardley, Francis Wyatt, and Samuel Argall. He was the brother of Virginia Governor and U.S. Senator Harry F. Byrd, whose father served as Speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates. On January 20, 1915, Byrd married Marie Ames Byrd (d. 1974); he named Marie Byrd Land and the Ames Range after her and her father, respectively. They had four children: Richard Evelyn Byrd III, Evelyn Bolling Byrd Clarke, Katharine Agnes Byrd Breyer, and Helen Byrd Stabler. The family moved to a brownstone at 9 Brimmer Street in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood in late 1924, purchased by Marie’s father, a wealthy industrialist. Byrd was friends with Edsel Ford and Henry Ford, whose admiration for his polar exploits helped secure Ford Motor Company sponsorship for his expeditions. He owned a pet dog named Igloo, who accompanied him to both poles and is buried at the Pine Ridge Pet Cemetery with a tombstone reading "He was more than a friend." Byrd attended the Virginia Military Institute for two years, transferred to the University of Virginia, and then entered the United States Naval Academy on May 28, 1908. He graduated on June 8, 1912, as an ensign and was assigned to the USS Wyoming; during service in the Caribbean, he received a letter of commendation and a Silver Lifesaving Medal for rescuing sailors twice by diving fully clothed. In April 1914, he transferred to the USS Washington and served in Mexican waters. He later served on the USS Dolphin, which also served as the yacht of the Secretary of the Navy, where he met future Fleet Admiral William D. Leahy and Assistant Secretary of the Navy Franklin Roosevelt. He was promoted to lieutenant (junior grade) on June 8, 1915. His last assignment before forced retirement was on the presidential yacht USS Mayflower. On March 15, 1916, he was medically retired on three-quarters pay due to an ankle injury sustained on the Mayflower. He was then assigned as inspector and instructor for the Rhode Island Naval Militia, where he was commended by Brigadier General Charles W. Abbot for improving its efficiency. After the U.S. entered World War I in April 1917, Byrd oversaw the mobilization of the Rhode Island Naval Militia and was recalled to active duty, serving in the Office of Naval Operations as secretary and organizer of the Navy Department Commission on Training Camps. In the autumn of 1917, he attended naval aviation school at Pensacola, Florida, and qualified as a naval aviator (number 608) in June 1918. He commanded naval air forces at Naval Air Station Halifax, Canada, from July 1918 until the armistice in November, during which he was promoted to the permanent rank of lieutenant and the temporary rank of lieutenant commander. For his wartime service, he received a letter of commendation from Secretary of the Navy Josephus Daniels, later converted to a Navy Commendation Medal. After the war, Byrd volunteered for the U.S. Navy’s 1919 aerial transatlantic crossing, the first time the Atlantic was flown across by aircraft. Though his service in Newfoundland was considered overseas, he contributed by planning the flight path. Only Lieutenant Commander Albert Read’s NC-4 completed the flight on May 18, 1919. In 1921, Byrd attempted a solo nonstop Atlantic crossing, six years before Charles Lindbergh, but was denied due to concerns over risk by acting Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt Jr. He was then assigned to the ill-fated dirigible ZR-2 (formerly the British R-38), which broke apart in midair on August 24, 1921, killing 44 of 49 crew members. Byrd lost friends in the accident and participated in recovery and investigation, an event that deeply affected him and led him to prioritize safety in future expeditions. Due to postwar Navy reductions, Byrd reverted to the rank of lieutenant in 1921. In summer 1923, he and other World War I Navy veterans founded the Naval Reserve Air Station (NRAS) at Squantum Point near Boston, using an unused seaplane hangar, which was commissioned on August 15, 1923, and is considered the first air base in the Naval Reserve program. From June to October 1925, Byrd commanded the aviation unit of an arctic expedition to North Greenland led by Donald B. MacMillan, though the expedition did not reach the pole. Byrd’s aviation contributions, however, earned him recognition as a pioneer of aircraft in exploration. During this expedition, he met Navy Chief Aviation Pilot Floyd Bennett and Norwegian pilot Bernt Balchen, both of whom later contributed to his expeditions. Bennett piloted Byrd’s 1926 North Pole flight, and Balchen became the primary pilot on the 1929 South Pole flight. On May 9, 1926, Byrd and Bennett flew a Fokker F.VIIa/3m tri-motor monoplane named Josephine Ford from Spitsbergen (Svalbard) to the North Pole and back, lasting 15 hours and 57 minutes, including 13 minutes circling at their farthest north, covering a distance of 1,535 miles (1,335 nautical miles). Upon returning to the U.S., Byrd became a national hero, was paraded in New York City, and on December 21, 1926, Congress promoted him to commander and awarded both him and Bennett the Medal of Honor. The Josephine Ford was flown across the country in celebration, and Bennett was promoted to warrant officer rank of machinist. Byrd and Bennett received Tiffany Cross versions of the Medal of Honor on March 5, 1927, at the White House from President Calvin Coolidge. Since 1926, doubts have arisen about whether Byrd actually reached the North Pole. In 1958, Bernt Balchen questioned Byrd’s claim, stating that Bennett had confessed months later that they had not reached the pole. Bennett, who had not fully recovered from a prior crash, died of pneumonia in April 1928 after participating in a rescue flight. However, Bennett had written memoirs, given interviews, and published an article confirming Byrd’s account before his death. The 1996 release of Byrd’s diary revealed erased sextant sights that differ from his later official report: at 7:07:10 GCT, his diary shows a solar altitude of 19°25'30", while his official report states 18°18'18". Dennis Rawlins concluded that Byrd flew about 80% of the distance to the pole before turning back due to an engine oil leak and later falsified his official report to claim reaching the pole. A defender of Byrd suggests a westerly-moving anticyclone provided tailwinds that boosted ground speed, allowing the claimed distance to be covered in the stated time, though this theory is challenged by Rawlins, who notes that the precision of the sextant data in the official typewritten report (to 1 second) is not feasible for 1926 Navy sextants, unlike the more accurate data in Byrd’s diary. If Byrd and Bennett did not reach the North Pole, the first flight over the pole occurred on May 12, 1926, when the airship Norge, piloted by Roald Amundsen, Umberto Nobile, Oscar Wisting, and Lincoln Ellsworth, flew from Spitsbergen to Alaska. In 1927, Byrd announced support from the American Trans-Oceanic Company, established in 1914 by Rodman Wanamaker, to attempt the first nonstop transatlantic flight. He named Floyd Bennett as chief pilot, with Bernt Balchen, Bert Acosta, and Lieutenant George Noville as crew. During a practice takeoff, the Fokker Trimotor America crashed, severely injuring Bennett and slightly injuring Byrd. Charles Lindbergh won the Orteig Prize on May 21, 1927, completing the first nonstop transatlantic flight. Byrd then named Balchen as chief pilot to replace Bennett. On June 29, 1927, Byrd, Balchen, Acosta, and Noville flew the America from Roosevelt Field, New York, to France, arriving the next day but being prevented from landing in Paris due to cloud cover. They crash-landed near Ver-sur-Mer (Gold Beach) on July 1, 1927, without fatalities. In France, Byrd and his crew were received as heroes and Byrd was invested as an Officer of the French Legion of Honor by Prime Minister Raymond Poincaré on July 6. After returning to the U.S., an elaborate dinner was held in New York City on July 19, where Byrd and Noville were awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross by Secretary of the Navy Curtis D. Wilbur; Acosta and Balchen were not awarded due to the Distinguished Flying Cross being limited to military personnel at the time. Byrd wrote an article for the August 1927 edition of Popular Science Monthly, accurately predicting that specially modified aircraft with one to three crewmen could fly the Atlantic nonstop, though commercial realization would take another 20 years. In 1928, Byrd began his first Antarctic expedition with two ships—the City of New York (formerly Samson, noted for being near the Titanic) and the Eleanor Bolling (named after his mother)—and three aircraft: a Ford Trimotor named Floyd Bennett (after Bennett), a Fairchild FC-2W2 named Stars And Stripes (now at the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center), and a Fokker Super Universal named Virginia (named after his birth state). A base camp named "Little America" was established on the Ross Ice Shelf, and scientific expeditions using snowshoes, dog sleds, snowmobiles, and airplanes began. A 19-year-old Boy Scout, Paul Allman Siple, was selected to join, later earning a doctorate and participating in all five of Byrd’s Antarctic expeditions. Photographic expeditions and geological surveys were conducted, and constant radio communication was maintained. After their first winter, expeditions resumed, and on November 28, 1929, the first flight to the South Pole and back was launched. Byrd, with pilot Bernt Balchen, co-pilot/radioman Harold June, and photographer Ashley McKinley, flew the Floyd Bennett to the South Pole and back in 18 hours and 41 minutes. They struggled to gain altitude and had to dump empty gas tanks and emergency supplies to reach the Antarctic Plateau, but ultimately succeeded. In November 1929, Byrd led a privately financed expedition where his aircraft crew successfully flew over the South Pole. He strongly advocated for ski-equipped aircraft, despite significant operational, logistical, and maintenance challenges, which required the establishment of substantial onshore bases. As a result of this achievement, Byrd was promoted to the next rank.

Other than Byrd himself, no one else participated in all five of Byrd's Antarctic expeditions. During the summer of 1929, photographic expeditions and geological surveys were conducted, with constant radio communications maintained with the outside world. After their first winter, the expedition resumed, and on November 28, 1929, the first flight to the South Pole and back was launched by Byrd, pilot Bernt Balchen, co-pilot/radioman Harold June, and photographer Ashley McKinley, who flew the Floyd Bennett to the South Pole and back in 18 hours, 41 minutes. They struggled to gain sufficient altitude and had to dump empty gas tanks and emergency supplies to reach the Antarctic Plateau, but ultimately succeeded. In November 1929, Byrd led a privately financed expedition that successfully flew over the South Pole, strongly advocating for ski-equipped aircraft despite significant operational, logistical, and maintenance challenges that required large onshore bases. As a result, Byrd was promoted to rear admiral by special act of Congress on December 21, 1929, becoming the youngest admiral in U.S. Navy history at age 41; none of his Annapolis classmates became admirals until 1942 after 30 years of service. He is one of only four persons, including Admiral David Dixon Porter, Rear Admiral Donald Baxter MacMillan, and Rear Admiral Frederic R. Harris, to have been promoted to rear admiral without first holding the rank of captain. The expedition returned to North America on June 18, 1930, and was honored with the gold medal of the American Geographical Society; it was also featured in the film With Byrd at the South Pole (1930). Byrd, now an internationally recognized polar explorer and aviator, served as Honorary National President of Pi Gamma Mu (1931–1935), carrying the society's flag during his first Antarctic expedition to highlight the spirit of adventure in both natural and social sciences. To secure political and public support, Byrd cultivated relationships with powerful individuals such as President Franklin Roosevelt, Henry Ford, Edsel Ford, John D. Rockefeller Jr., and Vincent Astor, naming geographic features in Antarctica after them. During his second expedition (1933–1934), winter in the Northern Hemisphere, Byrd spent five months alone at Advance Base, narrowly escaping death from carbon monoxide poisoning due to a poorly ventilated stove. Unusual radio transmissions alarmed base camp personnel, who attempted to reach him; the first two trips failed due to darkness, snow, and mechanical issues. Thomas Poulter, E. J. Demas, and Amory Waite eventually reached Advance Base, where they found Byrd in poor health; they remained until October 12, when an airplane picked up Dr. Poulter and Byrd, and the rest returned with a tractor. This experience is detailed in Byrd’s autobiography Alone. During the summer, days were long with twilight evenings, and Byrd maintained a large calendar in the headquarters to track each day. A CBS radio station, KFZ, was established on the base camp ship, the Bear of Oakland, and the program The Adventures of Admiral Byrd was broadcast via shortwave to Buenos Aires and then to New York. Sponsored by General Foods, it aired on Saturday nights at 10:00 pm and reached #16 on the Hooper rating for the 1933–34 season with an average audience of 19.1 million. President Roosevelt and the U.S. Postmaster General honored the expedition in 1933 with a U.S. commemorative stamp, which helped fund the mission. The stamp, numbered 753 in Scott’s Catalog, required a 3-cent Byrd II stamp and 53 cents in additional postage for mail to Antarctica, which was processed through a special U.S. Post Office established at Little America on October 6, 1933. Approximately 150,000 pieces of mail passed through the post office between 1933 and 1934. Only authorized post office personnel could handle mail, and Charles F. Anderson, a special representative of the Postmaster General, was assigned to Little America. In late 1938, Byrd visited Hamburg to present his Antarctic film to members of the German Antarctic Expedition 1938/39, answering questions and offering practical advice based on his polar experience in a private event with no press. Byrd's third expedition was the first U.S. government-financed one, including studies in geology, biology, meteorology, and exploration, and featured the innovative Antarctic Snow Cruiser, which broke down shortly after arrival. By March 1940, Byrd was recalled to active duty in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations; the expedition continued until its last participants left on March 22, 1941. In March 1942, Byrd was recalled again and served as confidential advisor to Admiral Ernest J. King, participating in the South Pacific Island Base Inspection Board from 1942 to 1945, which toured South Pacific bases in May and June 1942 and submitted a report analyzing base conditions and offering recommendations for future planning. On September 1, 1943, Byrd was ordered to lead a survey of East and South Pacific islands related to national defense and commercial air bases and routes. The Special Navy Mission sailed from Balboa on USS Concord, commanded by Captain Irving Reynold Chambers, in September 1943. On October 7, 1943, a large explosion at sea, caused by gasoline fumes at the stern, killed 24 crewmen, including executive officer Commander Rogers Elliott, and injured others; some were thrown overboard or killed by concussion, burns, or broken bones. The dead were buried at sea on October 8. On October 23, 1943, Byrd wrote to Chambers commending his crew for "courage and efficiency," expressing pride in their heroism. Byrd completed the mission in December and participated in the United States Strategic Bombing Survey (USSBS) from 1944 to 1945. On February 10, 1945, Byrd received the Order of Christopher Columbus from the Dominican Republic. He was present at the Japanese surrender in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, and was released from active duty on October 1, 1945. For his World War II service, he received two awards of the Legion of Merit. In 1946, Secretary of the Navy James Forrestal appointed Byrd as officer in charge of the Antarctic Developments Project. His fourth expedition, Operation Highjump, was the largest to date and was expected to last 6–8 months. It was supported by a large naval force (Task Force 68), including 13 U.S. Navy support ships (besides the flagship USS Mount Olympus and aircraft carrier USS Philippine Sea), six helicopters, six flying boats, two seaplane tenders, and 15 other aircraft, involving over 4,000 personnel. The armada arrived in the Ross Sea on December 31, 1946, and conducted aerial explorations of an area half the size of the United States, recording 10 new mountain ranges, primarily along the eastern coastline of Antarctica from 150°E to the Greenwich meridian. In an interview with Lee van Atta of International News Service aboard the USS Mount Olympus, Byrd warned that the U.S. should prepare for attacks by hostile planes from polar regions, stating that the shrinking world meant isolation was no longer a guarantee of safety. The interview appeared in the March 5, 1947, edition of Chilean newspaper El Mercurio. In 1948, the U.S. Navy produced The Secret Land, a documentary about Operation Highjump that won the Academy Award for Best Documentary. On December 8, 1954, Byrd appeared on Longines Chronoscope, where he discussed his Antarctic voyages and stated that Antarctica would become the most important scientific location in the world. As part of the International Geophysical Year (1957–58), Byrd was appointed officer in charge of U.S. Navy Operation Deep Freeze I in 1955–56, which established permanent bases at McMurdo Sound, the Bay of Whales, and the South Pole—marking the beginning of a permanent U.S. military presence in Antarctica. Byrd spent only one week in Antarctica and began his return to the U.S. on February 3, 1956. He died in his sleep of a heart ailment at age 68 on March 11, 1957, at his home in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Byrd was an active Freemason, raised in Federal Lodge No. 1, Washington, D.C., on March 19, 1921, and affiliated with Kane Lodge No. 454, New York City, on September 18, 1928, and was a member of National Sojourners Chapter No. 3 at Washington. In 1930, he received a gold medal from Kane Lodge. In 1931, Byrd became a compatriot of the Tennessee Society of the Sons of the American Revolution, receiving state membership number 605 and national number 50430, and was awarded the War Service Medal for First World War service. He was also a member of the Explorers Club, American Legion, and National Geographic Society. By the time of his death, Byrd had 22 citations and special commendations, nine for bravery and two for extraordinary heroism in saving lives; he also received the Medal of Honor, Silver Lifesaving Medal, Navy Distinguished Service Medal, Distinguished Flying Cross, and Navy Cross. He is the only person to have three ticker-tape parades in New York City (1926, 1927, 1930). He was one of only four American military officers entitled to wear a medal with his own image, including Admiral George Dewey, General John J. Pershing, and Admiral William T. Sampson; Byrd’s image appears on both the first and second Byrd Antarctic Expedition Medals, making him the only American to wear two such medals. He received the Langley Gold Medal from the Smithsonian Institution and was the seventh recipient of the Hubbard Medal from the National Geographic Society for his North Pole flight, alongside Robert Peary, Roald Amundsen, and Charles Lindbergh. He also received the David Livingstone Centenary Medal, Loczy Medal, Vega Medal, and Elisha Kent Kane Medal from various geographical societies. In 1927, the Boy Scouts of America made Byrd an Honorary Scout, a new category created that year for citizens whose achievements in exploration and adventure inspired boys. In 1927, the City of Richmond dedicated the Richard Evelyn Byrd Flying Field, now Richmond International Airport, in Henrico County, Virginia; Byrd's Fairchild FC-2W2, NX8006, Stars And Stripes, is on display at the Virginia Aviation Museum. In 1929, Byrd received the Silver Buffalo Award and the Langley Gold Medal. Lunar crater Byrd, the U.S. Navy dry cargo ship USNS Richard E. Byrd (T-AKE-4), and the decommissioned guided missile destroyer USS Richard E. Byrd (DDG-23) are named after him. In 1930, Byrd was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In Glen Rock, New Jersey, the Richard E. Byrd School was dedicated in 1931. On March 31, 1934, during a scheduled broadcast, Byrd was awarded the CBS Medal for Distinguished Contribution to Radio, recognizing his short-wave relay broadcasts from the second expedition as a milestone in communication history; he was the sixth recipient. The Institute of Polar Studies at Ohio State University changed its name to the Byrd Polar Research Center (BPRC) on January 21, 1987, after acquiring Byrd’s expedition records, personal papers, and memorabilia from Marie A. Byrd’s estate in 1985; his papers formed the nucleus of the BPRC Polar Archival Program in 1990. In 1958, the Richard Byrd Library opened in Springfield, Virginia, as part of the Fairfax County Public Library system. Richard E. Byrd Elementary School in Negishi, Yokohama, Japan, opened on September 20, 1948, and was renamed R.E. Byrd Elementary School on April 5, 1960. Memorials to Byrd exist in Wellington and Dunedin, New Zealand, which served as his departure point for several expeditions. In 1979, the Australian Antarctic Territory issued a set of two postage stamps commemorating the 50th anniversary of Byrd’s first flight over the South Pole, along with a commemorative flag. The long-range short-wave voice transmissions from Byrd’s 1934 expedition were named an IEEE Milestone in 2001.

Admiral Richard E. Byrd, born October 25, 1888, in Winchester, Virginia, and appointed from Virginia, was a Commander in the United States Navy and one of the most highly decorated officers in U.S. Navy history. He is probably the only individual to have received the Medal of Honor, Navy Cross, Distinguished Flying Cross, and the Silver Life Saving Medal, and one of only a few to have earned all three Antarctic expedition medals issued before World War II. Byrd was awarded the Medal of Honor by President Calvin Coolidge on March 5, 1927, for courage and intrepidity in demonstrating that aircraft could fly continuously from a populated area over the North Pole and return, alongside Machinist Floyd Bennett. The Navy Cross was awarded in 1929 for leading the flight to the South Pole on November 29, 1929, from Little America, Antarctica, under extreme cold and high-altitude conditions, with a forced landing being beyond probable rescue. In 1926, he received a Gold Star in lieu of a second Navy Distinguished Service Medal for organizing the U.S. Antarctic Service, establishing two bases 1,500 miles apart, and conducting significant explorations, including four flights that discovered new mountain ranges, islands, over 100,000 square miles of land, a peninsula, and 700 miles of previously unknown Antarctic coast. He also earned the Legion of Merit in 1943 for surveying thirty-three Pacific islands for air base sites and a second Gold Star in lieu of a second Legion of Merit from 1942 to 1945 for his role as a confidential advisor to the Commander in Chief, United States Fleet, providing strategic counsel that contributed to the war effort. He received the Distinguished Flying Cross in 1927 for flying the "America" from New York to France under adverse weather, landing safely at Ver sur Mer after 39 hours and 56 minutes. Byrd was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa as an honorary member at the University of Virginia and into the International Air and Space Hall of Fame in 1968. His papers, including 985 documents from the estate of Marie A. Byrd, the late wife of Admiral Byrd, formed the foundation of the BPRC Polar Archival Program in 1990. The Richard Byrd Library, part of the Fairfax County Public Library system, opened in Springfield, Virginia, in 1958. Richard E. Byrd Elementary School in Negishi, Yokohama, Japan, opened on September 20, 1948, and was renamed R.E. Byrd Elementary School on April 5, 1960. Admiral Byrd Middle School in Frederick County, Virginia, opened in 2005 and is decorated with images and letters from his life and career. A school in Sun Valley, California, named Richard E. Byrd Middle School, opened in its current location in 2008 after its original site became Sun Valley High School. Memorials to Byrd are located in Wellington and Dunedin, New Zealand, where he used the country as a departure point for several Antarctic expeditions. The 50th anniversary of his first flight over the South Pole was commemorated in 1979 by Australian Antarctic Territory with a set of two postage stamps and a commemorative flag. Long-range short-wave voice transmissions from his 1934 Antarctic expedition were named an IEEE Milestone in 2001. Byrd was posthumously eligible for the Antarctic Service Medal, established in 1960, for his participation in Operation Highjump (1946–1947) and Operation Deep Freeze (1955–1956). He also received numerous other awards from U.S. governmental and private entities. In Great Circle by Maggie Shipstead, Byrd and the Little America bases are the final stop in Marian Graves' journey to circle the globe by flight over the North and South Poles. Jacques Vallée, in his book Confrontations, references a "spurious story" about "holes in the pole" allegedly found by Byrd, citing Clint Chapin of the Copper Medic case as believing UFOs originated from within the Earth.

Richard Manning Karp, born on January 3, 1935, is an American computer scientist and computational theorist at the University of California, Berkeley. He is best known for his research in the theory of algorithms, for which he received the 1985 ACM Turing Award, the Benjamin Franklin Medal in Computer and Cognitive Science in 2004, and the Kyoto Prize in 2008. Karp was elected a member of the National Academy of Engineering in 1992 for major contributions to the theory and application of NP-completeness, constructing efficient combinatorial algorithms, and applying probabilistic methods in computer science. Born to Abraham and Rose Karp in Boston, Massachusetts, he has three younger siblings: Robert, David, and Carolyn. His family was Jewish, and he grew up in a small apartment in the then mostly Jewish neighborhood of Dorchester in Boston.
