Both parents were Harvard graduates; his mother earned her degree at age 57 through evening courses, and his father, who had intended to attend medical school after Harvard, became a mathematics teacher due to financial constraints. Karp attended Harvard University, where he earned his bachelor's degree in 1955, master's degree in 1956, and Ph.D. in applied mathematics in 1959. He began working at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center. In 1968, he became a professor of computer science, mathematics, and operations research at the University of California, Berkeley, and was the first associate chair of the Computer Science Division within the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. Aside from a four-year period as a professor at the University of Washington, he has remained at Berkeley. From 1988 to 1995 and from 1999 to the present, he has also served as a research scientist at the International Computer Science Institute in Berkeley, where he currently leads the Algorithms Group. Karp was awarded the National Medal of Science and received the Harvey Prize from the Technion and the 2004 Benjamin Franklin Medal in Computer and Cognitive Science for his insights into computational complexity. In 1994, he was inducted as a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery, and in 2002, he was elected a Fellow of the Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences. He has received several honorary degrees and is a member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Philosophical Society. In 2012, Karp became the founding director of the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing at the University of California, Berkeley. Karp has made significant discoveries in computer science, combinatorial algorithms, and operations research, with current research interests including bioinformatics. In 1962, he co-developed with Michael Held the Held–Karp algorithm, an exact exponential-time algorithm for the traveling salesman problem. In 1971, he co-developed with Jack Edmonds the Edmonds–Karp algorithm for solving the maximum flow problem on networks, and in 1972, he published a landmark paper in complexity theory, "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems," in which he proved 21 problems to be NP-complete. In 1973, he and John Hopcroft published the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm, the fastest known method for finding maximum cardinality matchings in bipartite graphs. In 1980, along with Richard J. Lipton, Karp proved the Karp–Lipton theorem, which shows that if SAT can be solved by Boolean circuits with a polynomial number of logic gates, then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. In 1987, he co-developed with Michael O. Rabin the Rabin–Karp string search algorithm. His citation for the 1985 Turing Award stated that he was recognized for his continuing contributions to the theory of algorithms, including the development of efficient algorithms for network flow and other combinatorial optimization problems, the identification of polynomial-time computability with the intuitive notion of algorithmic efficiency, and, most notably, contributions to the theory of NP-completeness, introducing the now-standard methodology for proving problems to be NP-complete, which has led to the identification of many theoretical and practical problems as being computationally difficult.

Richard Meier, born October 12, 1934, is an American abstract artist and architect known for his geometric designs that prominently feature the color white. A recipient of the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1984, Meier has designed several iconic buildings, including the Barcelona Museum of Contemporary Art, the Getty Center in Los Angeles (completed 1997), the High Museum of Art in Atlanta (completed 1983), and San Jose City Hall (completed 2005). He was born to a Jewish family in Newark, New Jersey, the oldest of three sons of Carolyn (Kaltenbacher) and Jerome Meier, a wholesale wine and liquor salesman, and grew up in nearby Maplewood, where he attended Columbia High School. Meier earned a Bachelor of Architecture degree from Cornell University in 1957. After graduation, he traveled to Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, and Italy to network with architects. He worked briefly in 1959 for Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and then for three years with Marcel Breuer before founding his own firm in 1963. In 1972, Meier was identified as one of The New York Five, a group of modernist architects alongside Peter Eisenman, Michael Graves, Charles Gwathmey, and John Hejduk. Early in his career, he worked with artist Frank Stella and favored white, geometric structures. Meier gained recognition for his designs of various houses, The Atheneum (completed 1979), and the High Museum of Art in Atlanta. His design for the Getty Center brought him widespread acclaim. Other notable commissions from this period include the Barcelona Museum of Contemporary Art (completed 1995), the Paley Center for Media (completed 1996), The Hague City Hall (completed 1995), San Jose City Hall (completed 2005), the reconstruction of City Tower in Prague (completed 2008), and residential projects such as 173 and 176 Perry Street in Manhattan (completed 2002) and Meier on Rothschild in Tel Aviv (completed 2015). MeierPartners has offices in New York and Los Angeles, with projects in China, Tel Aviv, Paris, and Hamburg. Much of Meier's work is influenced by early to mid-20th-century architects, especially Le Corbusier, particularly his early works like the Villa Savoye and the Swiss Pavilion; Meier is considered to have implemented more of Corbusier's ideas than anyone, including Corbusier himself. His work also reflects influences from Mies Van der Rohe, Frank Lloyd Wright, and Luis Barragán (without color). White has been used in historical architectural landmarks such as cathedrals and white-washed villages in Spain, southern Italy, and Greece. In 2013, the Mayor of Rome, Gianni Alemanno, promised to remove the large travertine wall of Meier's Museum of the Ara Pacis, agreeing to reduce its height between an open-air space and a road along the Tiber River, with plans to build a wide pedestrian area and run the road underneath. Meier supported the plan, stating that the wall was originally built for traffic and noise, and that opening the piazza to the river would be beneficial. The mayor's office stated the project was intended to be completed by the end of his term in 2013, but the underpass project has not progressed and remained unchanged by 2024. In 1984, Meier received the Pritzker Prize, with the jury citing his "personal, vigorous, original" structures. In 2008, he won the gold medal from the Academy of Arts and Letters, and his project Jesolo Lido Village received the Dedalo Minosse International Prize. Meier is a Senior Fellow of the Design Futures Council and received the AIA Gold Medal in 1997 and the A+ Lifetime Achievement Award in 2013. He also received the Golden Plate Award in 1996 and in 2010, Cornell University established a professorship named for him. In 2014, Meier opened a 15,000-square-foot exhibition space at Mana Contemporary in Jersey City, which gathers much of his life's work, including his sculptures, architectural drawings, and collages, for the first time, and includes a planned research library. This replaced a smaller venue in Long Island City, Queens, which was open only by appointment to students and tour groups until 2013. On March 13, 2018, The New York Times reported allegations from women that Meier had sexually harassed or assaulted them; Meier responded by taking a six-month leave from his firm. In response, Cornell University declined his intended endowment and reviewed his previous donations. On April 6, 2018, four additional women who had worked at his firm came forward with allegations, some dating to 2009. On October 9, 2018, the firm announced that Meier's resignation was permanent. Major works by Meier include the High Museum of Art in Atlanta, the Barcelona Museum of Contemporary Art, the Getty Center, Meier on Rothschild, and On Prospect Park.

Richard Serra (November 2, 1938 – March 26, 2024) was an American artist renowned for his large-scale abstract sculptures installed in site-specific landscape, urban, and architectural environments, and is primarily associated with postminimalism. Described as "one of his era's greatest sculptors," Serra emphasized the material qualities of his works and explored the relationship between the viewer, the artwork, and its site. Born in San Francisco on November 2, 1938, to Tony and Gladys Serra—second of three sons—the son of a Spanish father from Mallorca and a mother, Gladys (née Fineberg), daughter of Russian Jewish immigrants from Odessa, USSR—was encouraged to draw by his mother, who introduced him as "Richard the artist." His father worked as a pipe fitter at a shipyard near San Francisco, and Serra recalled a memory of watching a boat launch at age four, noting, "All the raw material that I needed is contained in the reserve of this memory." His father, related to the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí, later worked as a candy plant foreman. Serra studied English literature at the University of California, Berkeley in 1957 before transferring to the University of California, Santa Barbara, where he graduated in 1961 with a B.A. in English Literature, meeting muralists Rico Lebrun and Howard Warshaw. To support himself, he worked in steel mills from ages 16 to 25. He then attended Yale University, earning a B.A. in art history and an M.F.A. in 1964. During a one-year traveling fellowship in Paris in 1964, he met composer Philip Glass, who became a collaborator and long-time friend, and visited Constantin Brâncuși's studio, partially reconstructed at the Musée national d'Art moderne on the Avenue du Président Wilson, which influenced his sculptural approach. Serra spent 1965 in Florence, Italy on a Fulbright Grant and visited the Prado Museum in Madrid in 1966, where he saw Diego Velázquez's painting *Las Meninas* and decided to move away from painting. In Europe, he began experimenting with nontraditional materials, exhibiting "Animal Habitats" at Galleria Salita in Rome, which referenced early Arte Povera works. Returning to the United States in 1966, he continued using experimental materials such as rubber, neon, latex, fiberglass, and lead. His Belt Pieces used gravity to form rubber strips hung on walls, and he created *Belts (1966–67)* by combining neon with rubber, referencing Jackson Pollock's *Mural (1963)*. He wrote *Verb List (1967)*, a list of transitive verbs like "cast," "roll," "tear," and "prop," which guided his sculptures. Works such as *To Lift (1967)*, where a 10-foot sheet of rubber was lifted into a free-standing form, and *Thirty-Five Feet of Lead Rolled Up (1968)*, created with the help of Philip Glass, reflected his interest in industrial materials and physical properties. In 1968, he exhibited *Prop (1968)*, *Scatter Piece (1968)*, and *Splashing (1968)* at the Castelli Warehouse in New York, where molten lead was thrown against walls and floors. In 1969, *Casting* was included in the Whitney Museum's *Anti-Illusion: Procedures/Materials* exhibition, where molten lead was splashed and pulled away from walls to create free-standing forms. The verb "to prop" led to a series of lead plate and pole assemblages, with *One Ton Prop: House of Cards (1969)*—a self-supporting structure of four lead plates weighing one ton—marking a move away from wall dependency. In 1969, while working with Jasper Johns, Serra created *Strike: To Roberta and Rudy (1969–71)*, a steel plate wedged into a corner that divided a room into two equal spaces, altering the viewer's perception as they moved around it. In 1969, during the "Art and Technology" exhibition at LACMA, Serra developed the Skullcracker Series, building ephemeral steel stacks up to 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 meters) high and weighing 60 to 70 tons (54.4 to 63.5 tons), which were knocked down daily by steelworkers, marking a shift toward large-scale works beyond gallery settings. In 1970, Serra received a Guggenheim Fellowship and traveled to Japan, where he created his first outdoor sculptures, *To Encircle Base Plate (Hexagram) (1970)* and *Sugi Tree (1970)*, installed in Ueno Park, Tokyo as part of the Tokyo Biennale. While in Kyoto, he studied Zen gardens and temples at Myoshin-ji, which influenced his perception of space in relation to time. Upon returning, he created *To Encircle Base Plate Hexagram, Right Angles Inverted (1970)*, embedding two semi-circular steel flanges—1 inch and 8 inches wide—into 183rd Street in the Bronx, visible from two perspectives. Throughout the 1970s, Serra produced outdoor site-specific works exploring landscape topography and viewer movement. His first landscape work, *Pulitzer Piece: Stepped Elevation (1970–71)*, was commissioned by Joseph and Emily Rauh Pulitzer for their property outside St. Louis, Missouri, consisting of three plates 5 feet high by 40 to 50 feet long placed across approximately 3 acres, impaled into the ground so their rise was 5 feet, acting as surrogate horizons. *Shift (1970–1972)*, built in King City, Ontario, consisted of six rectilinear concrete sections along a sloping field, with the top edges forming a horizon at specific elevational intervals; it was designated a Heritage Site in 2013. Notable landscape works include *Porten i Slugten (1983–1986)* at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Humlebaek, Denmark, where two angled plates at the end of a path form a gate-like structure that appears to swing as viewers walk toward the sea; *Carnegie (1985)* outside the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh; *Afangar (Stations, Stops on the Road, To Stop and Look: Forward and Back, To Take It All In) (1990)* on Videy Island, Iceland, consisting of nine pairs of basalt columns placed at elevations of 9 and 10 meters, with stones measuring 3 meters at higher and 4 meters at lower levels, varying in spacing due to topography; *Schunnemunk Fork (1991)* in Storm King Art Center, New York; *Snake Eyes and Box Cars (1993)* in Sonoma County, California; *Te Tuhirangi Contour (2000–2002)* in Kaipara, New Zealand, a 20-foot-high, 844-foot-long contour following the rolling hills; and *East-West/West-East (2014)* in Qatar, consisting of four steel plates—543⁄4 or 481⁄2 feet high—placed at irregular intervals in a valley between two gypsum plateaus, all level with each other and the adjacent plateaus, visible from either end. In urban settings, Serra's site-specific works, such as *Sight Point (1972–1975)* at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, *Terminal (1977)* in Bochum, Germany, *T.W.U. (1980)* at Deichtorhallen in Hamburg, *Fulcrum (1986–87)* in Broadgate, London, *Exchange (1996)* outside Luxembourg, and *7 (2011)* on a pier in Doha, Qatar, reflect verticality and balance, often inviting viewers to walk through or around them. Curved works like *St. John's Rotary Arc (1980)*, temporarily installed at the Holland Tunnel entrance in New York City; *Tilted Arc (1981)*, installed and later removed from Federal Plaza in New York City; *Clara-Clara (1983)* at Tuileries, Place de la Concorde, Paris; and *Berlin Junction (1987)* outside the Berlin Philharmonic, open and close depending on the viewer's direction of movement. Serra was married to artist Nancy Graves from 1965 to 1970 and to Clara Weyergraf from 1981 until his death in 2024.

Deichtorhallen in Hamburg, Germany; Fulcrum (1986–87), installed in Broadgate, London; Exchange (1996) outside the City of Luxembourg; or 7 (2011) on a pier in Doha, Qatar, reflect the verticality of their surrounding architecture. Outdoor sculptures such as St. John's Rotary Arc (1980), temporarily installed outside the Holland Tunnel entrance in New York City; Tilted Arc (1981), installed and later removed from New York City's Federal Plaza; Clara-Clara (1983), temporarily installed at Tuileries, Place de la Concorde, Paris; and Berlin Junction (1987), installed outside the Berlin Philharmonic, are all curved forms or arcs that open and close depending on the direction the viewer takes while walking around them. Sight Point (1972–1975) was Serra's first vertical Urban work and a continuation of the balance and counterbalance principles of his earlier work Prop. It stands outside the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam, the Netherlands, consisting of three vertical steel plates 10 feet (3 m) wide and 40 feet (12 m) high that lean in at an angle, forming a triangular space on the ground with three openings that can be walked through; once inside, the viewer can look up and see the sky framed by the triangular shape made by the leaning plates. Another vertical sculpture, Terminal (1977), was conceived for "Documenta VI" in 1977 and permanently installed on a traffic island between street car tracks in front of a train station in Bochum, Germany. Serra chose the site due to its proximity to a high-traffic area. Exchange (1996), sited in a vehicular round-about on top of a highway tunnel, is made of seven trapezoidal plates and stands 60 feet (18 m) high, visible to drivers entering and leaving the City of Luxembourg. In 1980, Serra installed two sculptures with the support of the Public Art Fund in New York City: T.W.U. (1980), a vertical sculpture consisting of three vertical plates each 36 feet (11 m) high, installed at a subway entrance near West Broadway between Leonard and Franklin Streets, is now permanently installed outside the Deichtorhallen, Hamburg, Germany; and St. John's Rotary Arc (1980), one of Serra's earliest curved sculptures, 12 feet (3.6 m) high and spanning 180 feet (55 m), was installed from 1980 to 1988 on the rotary at the entrance and exit to the Holland Tunnel. In 1981, Tilted Arc (1981) was installed in New York City's Federal Plaza, commissioned by the U.S. General Services Administration's Art-in-Architecture Program after a rigorous selection process; the sculpture's arc spanned 120 feet (36 m) and was 12 feet (3.6 m) high, tilting and leaning away from its base, anchored at both ends with the center raised. Serra intended the sculpture to draw pedestrians' attention as they crossed the plaza. It faced resistance from Federal building workers, leading to an eight-year campaign to remove it, which concluded with its removal on March 15, 1989. In defense of the sculpture, Serra stated, "To remove Tilted Arc, therefore, is to destroy it," advocating an art-for-art's-sake approach to site-specific artworks. Following the hearing and GSA's decision, Serra responded that he would deny authorship of Tilted Arc if it were relocated and would consider it a "derivative work." The case of Tilted Arc continues to highlight tensions surrounding public art and its intended audience. Serra's work has been featured in numerous gallery and museum exhibitions, with his site-specific gallery installations sometimes used to test ideas. His first U.S. solo exhibition was at the Leo Castelli Warehouse, New York City in 1969, where he exhibited ten lead Prop Pieces, a Scatter Piece: Cutting Device: Base Plate Measure (1969), and a Splash Piece: Splashing with Four Molds (To Eva Hesse) (1969). After his process-based works of the late 1960s and early 1970s, Serra began to solely use rolled or forged steel in his sculptures. Berlin Block (for Charlie Chaplin) (1977) was his first forged sculpture, made for the plaza outside the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and weighing 70 tons. Other forged sculptures include Elevation for Mies (1985–88) at Museum Haus Esters, Krefeld, Germany; Philibert et Marguerite (1985) in the Musee de Brou, Bourg-en-Bresse, France; Weight and Measure (1992), a temporary site-specific installation at the Tate Gallery, London; Santa Fe Depot (2004) in the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego; and Equal (2015) in the Museum of Modern Art, New York. Serra's most known series of sculptures using rolled steel plates are the Torqued Ellipses. In 1991, after visiting Borromini's Church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane in Rome and mistaking the ovals of the dome and floor as offset, he conceived a torqued form. He created models in his studio by cutting two ellipse-shaped pieces of wood and nailing a dowel between them, then turning the ellipses at a right angle and wrapping a sheet of lead around the form. After making a template, he worked with an engineer to fabricate the sculptures. There are seven Torqued Ellipses and four Double Torqued Ellipses (an ellipse inside an ellipse) dated between 1996 and 2004. Each sculpture has a different degree of torque and measures up to 13 feet (3.9 m) high, with an opening for walking through and around. Three Torqued Ellipses are on permanent view at Dia Beacon, New York. In 2005, "The Matter of Time," a commissioned installation at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain, opened, consisting of eight sculptures spanning from 1994 to 2005 and highlighting the evolution of Serra's forms. It includes five sculptures derived from the initial torqued ellipse: one single, one double ellipse, and three torqued spirals. The Torqued Spirals followed the Double Torqued Ellipses when Serra connected a double ellipse into a single wound form that can be entered and walked through. The remaining sculptures are one closed (Blind Spot Reversed) and one open (Between the Torus and the Sphere) torus and spherical sculpture; and Snake, made of three parts, each comprising two identical conical sections inverted relative to each other and spanning 104 feet (31.7 m) overall. The sculptures are organized with intention, creating a sensation of varying scale and proportion and an awareness of the passage of time as the viewer moves through the space. In 2008, Serra participated in Monumenta at Paris's Grand Palais, installing Promenade (2008), consisting of five plates, each 55 feet (16.8 m) tall and 13 feet (4 m) wide, placed 100 feet (30 m) apart across the interior, not in a line but side by side off the center axis, tilting left or right and leaning toward or away from each other and the viewer as they stroll around them. Equal (2015), in the collection of The Museum of Modern Art, New York, consists of eight forged blocks, each measuring 5 by 5 1/2 by 6 feet (1.5 × 1.7 × 1.8 m) and weighing 40 tons, stacked in pairs and positioned on their longer or shorter sides so each stack measures 11 feet (3.4 m) tall; walking among the four stacks makes the viewer aware of their own sense of weight, balance, and gravity in relation to the sculptures. Four Rounds: Equal Weight, Unequal Measure (2017), consisting of four 82-ton (74 t) forged cylinders of varying dimensions, is permanently installed at Glenstone in Potomac, Maryland, within a building designed by Thomas Phifer of Thomas Phifer and Partners, in collaboration with Serra to highlight the sculpture's mass within the building's interior. Drawing was integral to Serra's practice; he made drawings on large sheets of canvas or handmade paper, including horizontal or vertical compositions, overlapping sheets, or line drawings, primarily in paintstick, lithographic crayon, or charcoal, always black, experimenting with techniques to create a tactile, phenomenological experience of movement, time, and space. He stated that his drawing practice involves "repetition, knowing there's no possibility of repeating, knowing that it's going to yield something different each time." After his break into space with sculptures like Strike: To Roberta and Rudy (1969–1971), Serra became interested in redefining architectural space through drawing. In 1974, he began making Installation Drawings—large-scale site-specific sheets of canvas completely covered in paintstick and stapled to the wall. Shafrazi and Zadikians were two of his first Installation Drawings, exhibited at Leo Castelli Gallery, New York City in 1974, measuring approximately 10 1/2 feet (3.2 m) high and 18 feet (5.5 m) wide. He continued making Installation Drawings throughout his career, with notable series including Diptychs (1989); Dead Weight (1991–92); Weight and Measure (1993–94); Videy Afangar (1989–1991); Rounds (1996–97); out-of-rounds (1999–2000); Line Drawings (2000–2002); Solids (2008); Greenpoint Rounds (2009); Elevational Weights (2010); Rifts (2011–2018); Transparencies (2011–2013); Horizontal Reversals (2014); Rambles (2015–16); Composites (2016); Horizontals and Verticals (2016–17); and Orchard Street (2018). National and international survey exhibitions of Serra's drawings include Richard Serra: Tekeningen/Drawings 1971–1977 at the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam in 1978; Richard Serra: Tekeningen/Drawings at the Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht in 1990; Richard Serra Drawing: A Retrospective at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Menil Collection, Houston from 2011 to 2012; and Richard Serra: Drawings 2015–2017: Rambles, Composites, Rotterdam Verticals, Rotterdam Horizontals, Rifts at the Museum Boijmans van Beuningen, Rotterdam, The Netherlands in 2017. Serra began making prints in 1972, working closely with Gemini G.E.L. in Los Angeles, developing unconventional techniques and producing over 200 printed works that reflect an interest in process, scale, and material experimentation. His early lithographs from 1972 include Circuit; Balance; Eight by Eight; or 183rd & Webster Avenue, each titled after a sculpture created around the same time. In 1981, he produced his first lithograph series, Sketch #1 through Sketch #7, and began making larger-scale prints such as Malcolm X; Goslar, or The Moral Majority Sucks. After pushing lithography to its limit, Serra began working with silkscreen, applying a layer of ink to paper and then a layer of paintstick through a second screen to create a saturated and textured surface. He continued using this technique, sometimes combining it with etching and aquatint, with print series including Videy Afanger (1991); Hreppholer (1991); WM (1996); Rounds (1999); Venice Notebook (2001); Between the Torus and the Sphere (2006); Paths and Edges (2007); Level (2008); Junction (2010); Reversal (2015); Elevational Weight (2016); Equal (2018); and (?) (2019). From 1968 to 1979, Serra made a collection of films and videos, recognizing the different material capacities of each medium and not extending sculptural problems into his films and videos. He collaborated with artists including Joan Jonas, Nancy Holt, and Robert Fiore. His first films, Hand Catching Lead (1968), Hands Scraping (1968), and Hand Tied (1968), involve actions such as a hand trying to catch falling lead, pairs of hands moving lead shavings, and bound hands untieing themselves. A later film, Railroad Turnbridge (1976), frames the Willamette River in Portland, Oregon as the bridge turns. Steelmill/Stahwerk (1979), made in collaboration with art historian Clara Weyergraf, is divided into two parts: interviews with German steel factory workers about their work and the forging of Serra's sculpture Berlin Block (for Charlie Chaplin). Survey exhibitions and screenings of his films have been held at the Kunstmuseum Basel, Switzerland in 2017; Anthology Film Archives, New York, October 17–23, 2019; and Harvard Film Archive, January 27 – February 9, 2020. In 2019, Serra donated his entire film and video works to the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan, New York. Serra's first solo exhibition was in 1966 at Galleria Salita in Rome, Italy. His first solo exhibition in the U.S. was at the Leo Castelli Warehouse, New York, in 1969. His first solo museum exhibition was at the Pasadena Art Museum in Pasadena, California in 1970. The first retrospective of his work was held at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986. A second retrospective was held at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 2007. The first survey exhibition of his drawings was at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam in 1977 and traveled to the Kunsthalle Tübingen in 1978. A second retrospective of drawings was presented at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; and The Menil Collection, Houston from 2011 to 2012. An overview of Serra's work in film and video was on view at the Kunstmuseum Basel in 2017. Serra enjoyed solo exhibitions at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden in 1978; Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 1980; Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou, Paris, 1983–1984; Museum Haus Lange, Krefeld, in 1985; The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986 and 2007; Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in 1986; Westphalian State Museum of Art and Cultural History, Münster, in 1987; Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus, Munich, in 1987; Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven, in 1988; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, in 1988.

Richard Serra moved to New York City in 1966 and bought a house in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia in 1970, where he spent summers working. He married art historian Clara Weyergraf in 1981. As of 2019, Serra maintained a home in Manhattan and studios in Nova Scotia and on the North Fork of Long Island. His brother is noted San Francisco attorney Tony Serra. Serra enjoyed solo exhibitions at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden in 1978; Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 1980; Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou, Paris, from 1983 to 1984; Museum Haus Lange, Krefeld, in 1985; The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986 and 2007; Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in 1986; Westphalian State Museum of Art and Cultural History, Münster, in 1987; Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus, Munich, in 1987; Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven, in 1988; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, in 1990; Kunsthaus Zürich, in 1990; CAPC Musée d'Art Contemporain, Bordeaux, in 1990; Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, in 1992; Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, Düsseldorf, in 1992; Dia Center for the Arts, New York, in 1997; Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, from 1998 to 1999; Centro de Arte Hélio Oiticica, Rio de Janeiro, from 1997 to 1998; Trajan's Market, Rome, from 1999 to 2000; Pulitzer Foundation for the Arts, St. Louis, in 2003; National Archaeological Museum, Naples, in 2004; and Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 2017. An overview of his work in film and video was on view at the Kunstmuseum Basel in 2017. Serra's work is included in numerous museums and public collections worldwide, such as The Museum of Modern Art, New York; The Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto; Art Institute of Chicago; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, The Netherlands; Centre Cultural Fundació La Caixa, Barcelona; Centre Georges Pompidou, Musée National d'Art Moderne, Paris; Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, Texas; Dia Art Foundation, New York; Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and New York; Pérez Art Museum Miami, Florida; Hamburger Kunsthalle, Hamburg, Germany; Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC; Moderna Museet, Stockholm; and Glenstone Museum, Potomac, Maryland. Selected public collections include the City of Bochum, Germany; City of Chicago, Public Art Collection; City of Goslar, Germany; City of Hamburg, Germany; City of St. Louis, Missouri; City of Tokyo, Japan; City of Berlin, Germany; City of Paris, France; and Collection City of Reykjavík, Iceland. Serra received numerous awards, including the Fulbright Grant (1965–66); Guggenheim Fellowship (1970); République Française, Ministère de la Culture et de la Communication Chevalier de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (1985 and 1991); Japan Arts Association, Tokyo Praemium Imperiale (1994); a Leone d'Oro for lifetime achievement at the Venice Biennale, Italy (2001); American Academy of Arts and Letters (2001); Orden pour le Mérite für Wissenschaften und Künste, Federal Republic of Germany (2002); Orden de las Artes y las Letras de España, Spain (2008); The National Arts Award: Lifetime Achievement Award (bestowed by Americans for the Arts in 2014); Hermitage Museum Foundation's Award for Lifetime Contributions to the World of Art (2014); Chevalier de l'Ordre national de la Légion d'honneur, Republic of France (2015); Landesmuseum Wiesbaden Alexej-von-Jawlensky-Preis (2017); and a J. Paul Getty Medal (2018). Serra is also featured as an architect who is a third level Mason in Matthew Barney's film Cremaster 3, part of the five-part Cremaster Cycle. All writings and interviews in the following anthologies are solely by Richard Serra unless otherwise indicated. Richard Serra died from pneumonia at his home in Orient, New York, on March 26, 2024, at the age of 85.

Richard George Whittle, born on 31 December 1979 in Oldham, England, to Harry and Maggie (Goodwin) Whittle, is a British actor and the oldest of three children. His mother is English and his father is Jamaican; his father served in the Royal Air Force, causing the family to move to different countries every few years. Whittle was primarily raised in Northern Ireland and recalled being bullied as a child for being the only black child in school, at one point telling his mother he wanted to be white to fit in. He studied law at Southampton Solent University, where he was football team captain, and began modelling to pay for textbooks, eventually leaving university just before graduation. He took up modelling in college and became the face of Reebok in 2000. Whittle made his acting debut in 2002 on the Sky 1 series Dream Team, which he described as a "dream job," after being sent for an audition by his co-star Terence Maynard. He left the show in 2006 and joined Channel 4's soap opera Hollyoaks in May 2006 as Calvin Valentine. In December 2009, it was announced he would leave Hollyoaks, with the character killed off in 2010; he cited plans to pursue American television and film and intended to stay for only four years. In summer 2009, he competed in Series 7 of the BBC reality show Strictly Come Dancing, pairing with professional dancer Natalie Lowe, and finished second to Chris Hollins. He permanently relocated to Los Angeles in summer 2011. Upon arriving in the US, he met with someone to create an audition reel, leading to a signing with manager Ken Jacobsen, who has also represented James Franco, Michelle Williams, and Hilary Swank. He was cast in the film Austinland opposite Keri Russell, Jane Seymour, and Jennifer Coolidge, joking that his audition tape cut off his head and that the film was shot in the UK despite his move to Los Angeles. His immigration status caused him to withdraw from several projects, including an episode of the NBC sitcom Up All Night, after management informed him the network would not accept his visa, prompting him to apply for a green card. In March 2012, he was cast in a recurring role as Charles on VH1's Single Ladies, initially for two episodes but later expanded to six after making a strong impression on producer Stacy A. Littlejohn, who wrote him into the rest of the season. The series was filmed in Atlanta from January to June 2012. In 2013, he appeared in an episode of the CBS drama NCIS titled "Detour." In 2014, he joined The CW's post-apocalyptic drama The 100 as Lincoln, and on 25 July 2014 at San Diego Comic-Con, it was announced he was promoted to series regular for season 2. Around the same time, he booked a recurring role as Daniel on ABC's Mistresses, the love interest of April (Rochelle Aytes), appearing in 10 episodes. In January 2016, it was reported he was in talks for a lead role on another series; during an April 2016 interview with AfterBuzz TV, he announced his departure from The 100, accusing creator Jason Rothenberg of bullying him by marginalizing his character, and stated that after Warner Bros. Television President Peter Roth and The CW President Mark Pedowitz learned of the situation, he was allowed to audition for other projects. In January 2016, he was cast as Shadow Moon, the lead in Starz's television adaptation of Neil Gaiman's 2001 novel American Gods, opposite Ian McShane. Though he had no prior knowledge of the novel, he was a fan-favorite choice for the role, and out of 2,000 audition tapes submitted, he was selected from approximately 600 actors who met with producers after submitting 16 audition tapes over a five-month period. In September 2017, he was cast opposite Sanaa Lathan in the Netflix original film Nappily Ever After, based on a novel by Trisha R. Thomas. On 16 April 2018, he signed with talent agency William Morris Endeavor. Whittle dated his Hollyoaks co-star Carley Stenson from 2007 to 2009 and remained close friends with her; he dated Kirstina Colonna from 2016 to 2018.

River Monsters is a British wildlife documentary series produced by Icon Films of Bristol, UK, for Animal Planet. Hosted by angler and biologist Jeremy Wade, the show follows his global journeys to investigate large and dangerous fish linked to local folklore and reported attacks. The series premiered on ITV in the UK and became one of the most-watched programs in Animal Planet's history, as well as one of the most-viewed series on Discovery Channel in the United States. Wade, born in Suffolk, travels to numerous countries including England, Scotland, Cambodia, Canada, Germany, Spain, Colombia, Bolivia, Iceland, Norway, Austria, Greenland, Argentina, Australia, Fiji, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, India, Japan, France, Russia, Suriname, Brazil, Guyana, the Solomon Islands, Indonesia, Zambia, Malaysia, Nepal, The Bahamas, The Cayman Islands, Mexico, Peru, Uganda, South Africa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nicaragua, Mongolia, Ukraine, Botswana, and U.S. states such as Alaska, Florida, Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, Washington, Illinois, Oregon, and Vermont. In its first season, Wade searched for piranha, goonch catfish (during investigations of Kali River attacks), alligator gar, wels catfish, arapaima, piraíba, and bull shark—all known to be potentially deadly and poorly understood. The show details the feeding habits, behavior, and conservation status of these creatures, and rebroadcasts with behind-the-scenes commentary from Wade are available under the title River Monsters: Unhooked. The second season began airing on 24 April 2010, with the first episode, "Demon Fish," premiering on Discovery Channel on 28 March 2010; it consisted of seven episodes and included visits to the River Congo and other remote locations. In the episode "Death Ray," Wade caught a pregnant giant freshwater stingray, the largest fish he ever landed, which later gave birth to two pups during examination by Wade and biologists. This season also featured the white sturgeon, Wade’s second-largest catch. The ninth season was announced as the final season. Featured animals include sharks such as the bull shark, which can swim miles up rivers and has been found breeding in freshwater, including in Australia and South Africa, where a record-breaking bull shark was caught in a river. In Argentina’s Paraná River, Wade investigated the short-tailed river stingray, which grows to 6 feet and delivers a venomous sting, leading to a battle that became his longest. In Zambia, Wade explored the Zambezi River after reports of fishermen disappearing, identifying the vundu as the deadly fish, a southern African species believed to be responsible for attacks and drownings, and found it beneath the Kariba Dam. In India, Wade investigated the sareng catfish, a sacred fish in Hinduism, which is believed to bring bad luck if harmed; he faced resistance due to religious restrictions and eventually returned to perform a blessing to appease the gods. Episodes include "Electric Executioner," where Wade caught a stingray; "Silent Assassin," where he landed a massive river stingray in the longest battle on the show; "River Monsters Goes Tribal," where he reeled in a full-grown shark barehanded; "Freshwater Shark," which revealed bull sharks breed in rivers; and "Hidden Predator," where he caught a large bull shark in a populated river. Other featured animals include the Japanese giant salamander, white sturgeon, taimen, New Zealand longfin eel, candiru, and the giant snakehead. Wade also encountered the sea lamprey in Lake Champlain, where he used himself as bait and later caught them with a native tribe in the Pacific Northwest. The series also covers encounters with the electric eel, red-bellied piranha, tiger sorubim, golden dorado, arapaima, piraiba, black caiman, green anaconda, and various catfish species. Episodes such as "Jungle Killer" involved a lightning strike in Suriname, "Amazon Assassins" included catching a 150 lb arapaima, and "American Killers" featured catches of blue and channel catfish in Oklahoma. Wade also faced challenges with the giant snakehead in Thailand using a hand-made spear gun and encountered crocodiles and hippos in Rift Valley. The show includes a wide range of species such as the Greenland shark, European eel, Atlantic cod, Arctic char, and various fish from the Pacific and Atlantic regions. The ninth season was confirmed as the final season of the series.

Promoted as a special season under the title River Monsters: Mysteries of the Ocean, this season sees Jeremy Wade shift his focus from freshwater to oceanic fish. Featured animals include Fang's puffer, Asian redtail catfish, Mekong giant catfish, giant barb, giant snakehead, Cantor's giant softshell turtle, Xenacanthus, alligator gar, Xiphactinus, Indo-Pacific sailfish, Leedsichthys, whale shark, Megapiranha, red bellied piranha, Helicoprion, Dunkleosteus, white sturgeon, Rhizodus, saltwater crocodile, Pacific halibut, Chinook salmon, salmon shark, China rockfish, lingcod, giant mottled eel, giant trevally, narrow-barred Spanish mackerel, spot-fin porcupinefish, bull shark, saltwater crocodile, African tigerfish, blackspotted squeaker, humpback largemouth, vundu catfish, Nile crocodile, African fish eagle, Salp, Common ling, European conger, Moray eel, Atlantic horseshoe crab, Stomatopoda, Giant oarfish, Great barracuda, Pacific cubera snapper, Lemon shark, Southern stingray, skipjack tuna, Mahi-mahi, barracuda, snoek, bluntnose sixgill shark, oceanic whitetip shark, tiger shark, cookiecutter shark, brown fur seal, dolphin, isopod, pig, Greenland shark, Atlantic cod, Atlantic halibut, Rose fish, Cusk, dog, seagull, black marlin, needlefish, Bluespotted stingray, Goonch catfish, golden mahseer, gharial, giant snakehead, golden snapper, Leopard coral grouper, barracuda, giant trevally, Papuan black bass, bull shark, Wallago leerii, arapaima, giant snakehead, pig, Asian water monitor, arapaima, river stingray, black piranha, redtail catfish, goonch, golden mahseer, dwarf snakehead, carp, Indian flapshell turtle, mully catfish, flathead catfish. Wade revisits some of his previous adventures and investigates the spiritual and mythological events behind them. Jeremy also revisits some of the many scientific projects he has worked with over his career and presents new information discovered since his time with the researchers. This season was dubbed "the final season", as it is the last season of River Monsters. The season only had one episode, "Jeremy's Monster Story". River Monsters had the best series premiere in Animal Planet's network history by delivering 1.3 million viewers. It was also its most watched regularly airing primetime telecast in over six years. The second episode of Animal Planet's River Monsters delivered a 39% boost in total viewers (1.866 million) compared to the series premiere. Those numbers made it the best performing regularly scheduled primetime telecast in Animal Planet's history. The first season of River Monsters made it the best performing show in Animal Planet's history with every episode averaging over 1 million households. The season finale delivered about 1.47 million households. The second season premiere episode became the network's best season premiere ever. It drew in 1.7 million total viewers.

Jaime Royal "Robbie" Robertson OC (July 5, 1943 – August 9, 2023) was a Canadian musician, composer, and producer. He was the lead guitarist for Bob Dylan's backing band and the guitarist and primary songwriter of The Band from its formation until his departure in 1976. In his later solo career, he released six albums. Robertson's work with The Band was instrumental in creating the Americana music genre. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Canadian Music Hall of Fame as a member of The Band, and also into Canada's Walk of Fame, both with The Band and individually. He is ranked 59th in Rolling Stone magazine's 2011 list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time. He co-wrote "The Weight" and "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down" with The Band and had a solo hit with "Somewhere Down the Crazy River." He was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the National Academy of Songwriters. Robertson collaborated on film and television soundtracks, primarily with director Martin Scorsese. His soundtrack work began with The Band's farewell rockumentary film The Last Waltz (1978) and included dramatic films such as Raging Bull (1980), The King of Comedy (1983), The Color of Money (1986), The Irishman (2019), and Killers of the Flower Moon (2023), the latter dedicated to his memory and earning him a posthumous Academy Award nomination for Best Original Score. Born on July 5, 1943, Robertson's mother, Rosemarie Dolly Chrysler, was born on February 6, 1922. Chrysler was Cayuga and Mohawk, raised on the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve southwest of Toronto near Hamilton, and later lived with an aunt in Toronto's Cabbagetown neighbourhood, working at the Coro jewellery plating factory, where she met James Patrick Robertson and married him in 1942. James and Rosemarie Robertson continued working at the Coro factory and lived in several Toronto neighbourhoods while Robbie was a child. An only child, Robertson often visited the Six Nations reserve with his mother, where he was taught guitar by his older cousin Herb Myke. He became a fan of rock and roll and rhythm and blues through radio, listening to disc jockey George "Hound Dog" Lorenz on WKBW from Buffalo, New York, and John R.'s all-night blues show on WLAC, a clear-channel station in Nashville, Tennessee. At age 12, his mother told him his biological father was Alexander David Klegerman, a Jewish-American gambler with whom she had been involved before marrying James Robertson; Klegerman died in a hit-and-run accident on the Queen Elizabeth Way before Robbie was born. Robertson's mother arranged for him to meet his paternal uncles, Morris (Morrie) and Nathan (Natie) Klegerman, who "quickly pulled me into their world and went out of their way to make me feel like family." At 14, he worked two brief summer jobs in the travelling carnival circuit, first in a Toronto suburb and later as an assistant at a freak show during the Canadian National Exhibition. He later drew from this experience for the song "Life is a Carnival" (with The Band) and the movie Carny (1980), which he both produced and starred in. His first band was Little Caesar and the Consuls, formed in 1956 by Bruce Morshead and Gene MacLellan, which he joined for almost a year. In 1957, he formed Robbie and the Rhythm Chords with Pete "Thumper" Traynor, later changing the name to Robbie and the Robots after watching Forbidden Planet and liking its character Robby the Robot. Traynor customized Robertson's guitar with antennae and wires. The group later became The Suedes with pianist Scott Cushnie. At a show on October 5, 1959, at CHUM Radio's Hif Fi Club on Toronto's Merton Street, Ronnie Hawkins first became aware of them and was impressed enough to join them for a few numbers. Robertson began shadowing Hawkins after the Suedes opened for him at Dixie Arena. One afternoon, he overheard Hawkins say he needed new songs for a studio session, so he stayed up all night and wrote "Someone Like You" and "Hey Boba Lu," which he played for Hawkins the next day. Hawkins recorded both for his album Mr Dynamo (1959) and brought Robertson to the Brill Building in New York to help choose songs. Hawkins hired pianist Scott Cushnie away from The Suedes and took him on tour in Arkansas. When the Hawks' bass player left, Cushnie recommended hiring Robertson to replace him on bass. Hawkins invited Robertson to Arkansas and then flew to the UK to perform there. Left in Arkansas, Robertson spent his living allowance on records and practiced daily. Upon returning, Hawkins hired him to play bass. Cushnie left the band a few months later. Robertson soon switched from bass to lead guitar for the Hawks, developing into a guitar virtuoso. Roy Buchanan, a few years older than Robertson, briefly joined the Hawks and influenced Robertson's guitar style through his volume speed dial use, string bending, rapid sweep picking, and passion for bending past root and fifth notes. Drummer/singer Levon Helm was already a member of the Hawks and soon became close friends with Robertson. The Hawks continued touring the U.S. and Canada, adding Rick Danko, Richard Manuel, and Garth Hudson in 1961, forming the lineup that later became The Band. They toured with Hawkins throughout 1962 and into 1963 and also hired saxophonists Jerry Penfound and Bruce Bruno. The Hawks recorded sessions for Roulette Records from 1961 to 1963, producing three singles: "Come Love" b/w "I Feel Good" (Roulette 4400, 1961); "Who Do You Love" b/w "Bo Diddley" (Roulette 4483, 1963); and "There's A Screw Loose" b/w "High Blood Pressure" (Roulette 4502, 1963). In early 1964, the group left Ronnie Hawkins and began seeking new direction, losing interest in rockabilly and favoring blues and soul. They approached agent Harold Kudlets, who agreed to represent them and booked them in the same circuits as before. Initially dubbed The Levon Helm Sextet, the group included all future members of The Band, plus Jerry Penfound and Bob Bruno. After Bruno left in May 1964, the group changed their name to Levon and the Hawks. Penfound stayed until 1965. Kudlets kept them busy performing throughout 1964 and 1965, booking two lengthy summer engagements at Tony Mart's in Somers Point, New Jersey, playing six nights a week alongside Conway Twitty. In 1964, the group befriended blues artist John P. Hammond in Toronto. Later that year, they worked on Hammond's album So Many Roads (released in 1965), with Robertson playing guitar and being billed as "Jaime R. Robertson" in the credits. In March 1965, under the name the Canadian Squires, they released the single "Uh Uh Uh" b/w "Leave Me Alone," both songs written by Robertson, recorded in New York, and released on Apex Records in the U.S. and Ware Records in Canada. In 1965, as Levon and the Hawks, they recorded an afternoon session for Atco Records, yielding two singles: "The Stones I Throw" b/w "He Don't Love You" (Atco 6383) and "Go, Go, Liza Jane" b/w "He Don't Love You" (Atco 6625), all written by Robertson. In August 1965, Robertson received a call from Albert Grossman Management requesting a meeting with Bob Dylan. The group had been recommended to both Grossman and Dylan by Mary Martin, a Toronto-born employee of Grossman and a friend of the band, and Dylan was also aware of them through John Hammond, whose album So Many Roads the group had performed on. Robertson agreed to meet with Dylan, initially refusing to join as guitarist but agreeing to play two shows: one at the Forest Hills Tennis Stadium on August 28 and one at the Hollywood Bowl on September 3, suggesting Levon Helm play drums. The first show received a hostile response, while the second was slightly more favorable. Dylan flew to Toronto and rehearsed with Levon and the Hawks from September 15 to 17, after which he hired the full band for his upcoming tour, making Robertson his guitarist during his "legendary electric period." Dylan and the Hawks toured the U.S. from October to December 1965, with each show featuring two sets: an acoustic set with Dylan alone and an electric set with the Hawks. The tours were met with hostility from fans who viewed Dylan's shift to rock as a betrayal. Helm left after the November 28 performance in Washington, D.C. On November 30, 1965, Dylan recorded a studio session with the Hawks, producing the non-LP single "Can You Please Crawl Out Your Window?" Dylan completed the Blonde on Blonde album in Nashville in mid-February 1966, with Robertson participating in a session on February 14. Dylan and the Hawks played more dates in the continental U.S. from February to March 1966, followed by tours in Hawaii, Australia, Europe, and the UK and Ireland from April 9 to May 27. The Australian and European legs received particularly harsh reactions from disgruntled folk fans. The May 17 Manchester Free Trade Hall show is best known for an audience member yelling "Judas!" at Dylan, becoming a frequently-bootlegged live recording later officially released as The Bootleg Series Vol. 4: Bob Dylan Live 1966, The "Royal Albert Hall" Concert. On July 29, 1966, Dylan suffered a neck injury in a motorcycle accident and retreated to a quiet life in upstate New York. Some Hawks members lived at the Chelsea Hotel in New York and were kept on a weekly retainer by Dylan's management. In February 1967, Dylan invited the Hawks to Woodstock, New York to work on music. Robertson had met a French-Canadian woman during a stop on Dylan's 1966 world tour and moved into a house in the Woodstock area. The remaining three members of the Hawks rented a house near West Saugerties, New York, later known as "Big Pink" due to its pink exterior. Dylan and the Hawks worked daily at Big Pink to rehearse and generate song ideas, many of which were recorded in the basement studio between late spring and autumn of 1967. Previous Hawks member Levon Helm returned to the group in August 1967. By this time, Robertson's guitar style had evolved to be more supportive of the songs and less focused on speed and virtuosity. In 1968, Rolling Stone co-founder Jann Wenner highlighted these sessions in an article titled "Dylan's Basement Tape Should Be Released." In 1969, a bootleg album with a plain white cover, compiled by two incognito music industry insiders, featured seven tracks from these sessions and became known as The Great White Wonder. It gained popularity in independent record stores and on radio, becoming a runaway success and helping to launch the bootleg recording industry. In 1975, Robertson produced an official compilation, The Basement Tapes, which included selected tracks from the sessions. An exhaustive collection of all 138 extant recordings was released in 2014 as The Bootleg Series Vol. 11: The Basement Tapes Complete. In late 1967, Dylan left to record John Wesley Harding (1967). After recording the basic tracks, Dylan asked Robertson and Garth Hudson to play on the album to fill out the sound, but Robertson liked the starkness and recommended leaving the tracks as they were. Dylan worked with the Hawks again for two Woody Guthrie memorial concerts at Carnegie Hall in January 1968, with three performances later released on the LP A Tribute to Woody Guthrie, Vol. 1 (1972). During the "Basement Tapes" period, the group developed their own sound. Grossman went to Los Angeles to shop the group to a major label, securing a contract with Capitol Records. The group went to New York to begin recording with music producer John Simon, and Capitol brought them to Los Angeles.

In late 1967, Dylan left to record John Wesley Harding (1967), after which he asked Robertson and Garth Hudson if they would play on the album to complete the sound; Robertson appreciated the raw quality and advised leaving the tracks as is. Dylan later worked with the Hawks again during two Woody Guthrie memorial concerts at Carnegie Hall in January 1968, with three of these performances released as A Tribute to Woody Guthrie, Vol. 1 (1972). Over the "Basement Tapes" period, the group developed their own sound; Grossman moved to Los Angeles to secure a contract with Capitol Records, and the group began recording with producer John Simon in New York before finishing in Los Angeles. The resulting album, Music from Big Pink, was released in August 1968 and marked the debut studio album of the group, which called itself The Band. Robertson was the principal songwriter and lead guitarist, writing four songs for Music from Big Pink—“The Weight,” “Chest Fever,” “Caledonia Mission,” and “To Kingdom Come”—credited as “J.R. Robertson,” and sang lead on “To Kingdom Come”; he did not sing on another public Band song until “Knockin’ Lost John” on 1977’s Islands. “The Weight” was influenced by Luis Buñuel’s films, particularly Nazarín (1959) and Viridiana (1961), reflecting the theme of sainthood being unattainable, and the mention of “Nazareth” referenced the C. F. Martin & Company guitar manufacturer in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, where Robertson saw the word in his guitar. Although “The Weight” reached No. 21 on the British radio charts and initially stalled at No. 63 on the American charts, it became the Band’s best-known song, covered by many artists and appearing in numerous films and documentaries. The Band began performing regularly in spring 1969, with their first live dates at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco, and notable performances at the 1969 Woodstock Festival and the UK Isle of Wight Festival with Bob Dylan in August. Their self-titled second album, released in September 1969, was a critical and commercial success, peaking at No. 9 on the U.S. pop charts and staying in the Top 40 for 24 weeks; Robertson wrote or co-wrote every song, and the album is recognized as a foundational work in the Americana music genre and was included in the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry in 2009. “The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down,” written by Robertson over eight months, tells of the suffering of Virgil Caine, a poor white Southerner during the final days of the American Civil War; Robertson developed the concept with help from Helm, a native of Arkansas, and the song was first released as the B side of “Up on Cripple Creek,” which reached No. 3 in 1971, helping popularize it. The song was ranked number 245 on Rolling Stone’s 2004 list of the 500 greatest songs of all time, named the forty-second best song of the 1960s by Pitchfork, and included in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame’s “500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll” and Time magazine’s All-Time 100. On November 2, 1969, the Band appeared on the Ed Sullivan Show, one of only two television appearances they made; on January 12, 1970, they were featured on the cover of Time magazine. Planning to record a live album at The Woodstock Playhouse, the city council denied the request, so they recorded without an audience; Robertson handled most songwriting duties and brought in Todd Rundgren to engineer the sessions, which took two weeks and resulted in Stage Fright, the Band’s highest-charting album, peaking at No. 5 and staying in the Top 40 for 14 weeks. Their next album, Cahoots, recorded at Albert Grossman’s Bearsville Studios and released in October 1971, received mixed reviews, peaked at No. 24, and remained in the Top 40 for five weeks; it included a cover of Bob Dylan’s “When I Paint My Masterpiece,” which came about when Dylan played an unfinished version to Robertson, leading to the Band recording it; the album also featured “Life Is a Carnival.” The Band toured throughout 1970–1971, and a live album from shows at the Academy of Music in New York City from December 28–31, 1971, was released in 1972 as Rock of Ages, which peaked at No. 6 and stayed in the Top 40 for 14 weeks. After the Academy of Music shows, the Band stopped touring and returned to the stage on July 28, 1973, performing at the Summer Jam at Watkins Glen alongside the Allman Brothers Band and the Grateful Dead; the performance was released as Live at Watkins Glen in 1995 and drew over 600,000 attendees, setting a record for “Pop Festival Attendance” in the Guinness Book of World Records (first published in 1976). In October 1973, the Band released Moondog Matinee, which peaked at No. 28; during its recording, Robertson began working on an unfinished project called Works. One lyric from Works, “Lay a flower in the snow,” was used in Robertson’s song “Fallen Angel” on his 1987 solo album. Bill Graham ran a full-page advertisement in The New York Times to promote the 1974 tour with Bob Dylan and received between five and six million ticket requests for 650,000 seats; tickets were sold via lottery, and Dylan and the Band earned $2 million. While preparing for the tour, the Band recorded Planet Waves (1974) with Dylan at Village Recorder in West Los Angeles from November 2–14, 1973; the album was released on February 9, 1974, reached No. 1 on the Billboard charts for four weeks, and spent 12 weeks in the Top 40; it was Bob Dylan’s first No. 1 album and the only studio album recorded together with the Band. The 1974 tour began on January 3 in Chicago and ended on February 14 at The Forum in Inglewood, California; the final three shows were compiled into Before the Flood, released on July 20, 1974, credited to “Bob Dylan/The Band,” debuted at No. 3, and spent ten weeks in the Top 40. After the tour, manager Elliot Roberts booked the Band with Crosby, Stills, Nash, and Young, who performed together at Wembley Stadium in London on September 4 with Jesse Colin Young and Joni Mitchell. After moving to Malibu in 1973, Robertson and the Band leased a ranch near Zuma Beach called “Shangri-La”; the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes, credited to Bob Dylan and the Band, was the first album produced at the new studio, featuring selected tapes from the 1967 sessions and demos for Music from Big Pink, with Robertson cleaning up the tracks and releasing it in July 1975. One of the most notable tracks on Northern Lights – Southern Cross (1975), released on November 1, is “Acadian Driftwood,” the Band’s first song with Canadian subject matter, inspired by the 1971 documentary Acadia, Acadia (L'Acadie, L'Acadie?!?) seen by Robertson in Montreal; the album received positive reviews and reached No. 26 on the Billboard charts, staying in the Top 40 for five weeks. The Band began touring again in June 1976, performing through the summer, but Richard Manuel suffered a neck injury in a boating accident, canceling ten dates. Robertson suggested the group cease touring, agreeing to a “grand finale” show, parting ways to pursue individual projects, and then regrouping; Helm later claimed Robertson forced the breakup, citing concerns about heroin use by Danko, Helm, and Manuel as reasons for Robertson’s departure. On November 25, 1976, the Band performed at the Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving, with ticket prices of $25 and a Thanksgiving dinner served; the event, called The Last Waltz, included musical guests and was filmed by director Martin Scorsese, with a 200-page script developed by Robertson and Scorsese. Warner Bros. Records offered to fund the film in exchange for the right to release the music, and the Band recorded Islands for Capitol between rehearsals, with Robertson writing or co-writing eight of the ten tracks; “Knockin’ Lost John” featured Robertson on vocals, the first since “To Kingdom Come,” and “Christmas Must Be Tonight” was inspired by the birth of Robertson’s son, Sebastian, in July 1974. Approximately 5,000 people attended The Last Waltz; after the concert, Scorsese had 400 reels of raw footage. The Last Waltz album, released on April 7, 1978, as a 3-LP set, featured live performances on the first five sides and studio recordings on the last, including Out of the Blue, which became the third and final Band song with Robertson on lead vocals; it peaked at No. 16 and stayed in the Top 40 for 8 weeks. The film premiered in theaters on April 26, 1978, and received positive reviews from both rock and film critics; Robertson and Scorsese promoted it across America and Europe. Over time, The Last Waltz has been recognized as a pioneering rockumentary, influencing films like Talking Heads’ Stop Making Sense (1984) and U2’s Rattle and Hum (1988); Roger Ebert offered a mixed review, noting the musicians seemed to have bad memories, Scorsese focused on close-ups and ignored the audience, and the film was made during a difficult period in Scorsese’s life. Robertson left the Band in 1976 but performed with them one final time on March 1, 1978, at the Roxy in Los Angeles. Robertson is credited as writer or co-writer of most of The Band’s songs and has received the majority of the songwriting royalties, leading to disputes, especially with Helm, who in his 1993 autobiography, This Wheel’s on Fire, argued that the songs were developed collaboratively and that the credits were invalid; Danko agreed, stating, “I think Levon.”

The Last Waltz was made during a difficult period in Martin Scorsese's life, coinciding with his work on New York, New York, and features mostly closeups and medium shots of performances, ignoring the audience; it does not portray serene or nostalgic scenes of friends enjoying each other's company. Robertson left The Band in 1976 but performed with them one final time on March 1, 1978 at the Roxy in Los Angeles. He is credited as writer or co-writer of most of The Band's songs and thus received the majority of the songwriting royalties, leading to disputes, especially with Helm, who argued in his 1993 autobiography This Wheel's on Fire that the songs were collaboratively developed by all members; Danko agreed, stating that the Band stopped being a true group when Robbie and Albert Grossman took themselves too seriously. Robertson denied Helm wrote any songs attributed to him. He produced and played guitar on Jesse Winchester's 1970 self-titled debut album on Ampex Records, co-crediting "Snow" to himself. He played guitar on Ringo Starr's 1973 album Ringo on the track "Sunshine Life For Me (Sail Away Raymond)" with four-fifths of The Band and contributed a guitar solo to "Snookeroo" on Starr's 1974 album Goodnight Vienna. In 1974, he played guitar on Joni Mitchell's "Raised on Robbery" from Court and Spark and on Carly Simon's version of "Mockingbird" with James Taylor. In 1975, he produced and played guitar on Hirth Martinez's debut album Hirth From Earth, which Bob Dylan had recommended to him; he also played guitar on Martinez's follow-up album Big Bright Street (1977). That same year, Eric Clapton recorded No Reason to Cry at The Band's Shangri-La Studios with members of The Band, with Robertson playing lead guitar on "Sign Language." In the mid-1970s, Robertson collaborated with Neil Diamond on a concept album about a Tin Pan Alley songwriter, Beautiful Noise, recorded at Shangri-La Studios in early 1976; it reached No. 6 on the Billboard charts and stayed in the Top 40 for sixteen weeks. Robertson produced the album, co-wrote "Dry Your Eyes" with Diamond (which he later performed at The Last Waltz), and played guitar on "Dry Your Eyes," "Lady-Oh," and "Jungletime." He also produced Diamond's live double album Love at the Greek (1977), recorded in 1976 at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, which reached No. 8 on the Billboard charts and stayed in the Top 40 for nine weeks. In 1977, he played guitar on "Java Blues" for Rick Danko's self-titled debut and on "Sing, Sing, Sing" for Levon Helm & the RCO All-Stars. He also contributed to Libby Titus's second self-titled album, producing "The Night You Took Me To Barbados In My Dreams" (co-written by Titus and Hirth Martinez) and producing and playing guitar on "Miss Otis Regrets." He co-produced "The Best of Everything," originally intended for the film The King of Comedy, which instead appeared on Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers' Southern Accents album; he also worked on the horn arrangements and brought in Band alumni Richard Manuel and Garth Hudson as guests. In 1986, he played guitar on the track "The Morning" for the album Reconciled by the Call. That same year, he was brought on as creative consultant for Hail! Hail! Rock 'n' Roll (1987), a film honoring Chuck Berry, appearing on camera interviewing Berry and playing guitar while Berry recited poetry. In 1988, he collaborated with Maria McKee on the song "Nobody's Child," released on her 1989 debut album. In 1992, he produced "Love in Time" for Roy Orbison's posthumous album King of Hearts, a basic demo Orbison had recorded and rediscovered, which Robertson enhanced with new arrangements to make it sound as if the arrangements were original. Robertson began work on his first solo album, Robbie Robertson, in July 1986 after signing with Geffen Records, choosing Daniel Lanois as producer. The album was recorded at The Village Recorder in West Los Angeles, Bearsville Studios near Woodstock, in Dublin with U2, and in Bath, England with Peter Gabriel; it featured guest appearances by U2, Gabriel, Bodeans, and Maria McKee, with Garth Hudson and Rick Danko also contributing. He wrote "Fallen Angel" in honor of Richard Manuel after his death in March 1986. Released on October 26, 1987, the album peaked at No. 35 on the Billboard 200, remaining in the top 40 for three weeks and reached No. 23 on the UK Albums Chart, staying on the chart for 14 weeks. It received critical acclaim and was listed among the top 10 albums of 1987 by Billboard and ranked No. 77 on Rolling Stone's 1989 list of the 100 Best Albums of the Eighties. His biggest UK hit was "Somewhere Down the Crazy River," which reached No. 15 and stayed in the chart for 11 weeks; its video was directed by Martin Scorsese and featured Maria McKee in an acting role. In the U.S., the album had several hits on the Billboard Mainstream Rock charts, with "Showdown At Big Sky" reaching #2 and "Sweet Fire Of Love" reaching #7. The album was nominated for a Grammy for "Best Rock / Vocal Album" and certified gold in the U.S. in 1991. In Canada, Robertson won Album of the Year, Best Male Vocalist of the Year, and Producer of the Year at the 1989 Juno Awards. In 1991, Rod Stewart recorded a version of "Broken Arrow" for his album Vagabond Heart, which reached No. 20 on the Billboard 100 and No. 2 on the Top Canadian Hit Singles chart; the song was also performed live by the Grateful Dead with Phil Lesh on vocals. Storyville was released on September 30, 1991; Robertson collaborated with New Orleans natives like Aaron and Ivan Neville and the Rebirth Brass Band, bringing in Garth Hudson and Rick Danko as contributors. The album reached No. 69 on the Billboard 200 and received positive reviews, with Rolling Stone giving it 4 1/2 stars and the Los Angeles Times 3 stars. Two tracks, "What About Now" and "Go Back To Your Woods," charted on the Mainstream Rock charts at No. 15 and No. 32 respectively. The album was nominated for Grammy Awards in "Best Rock Vocal Performance (solo)" and "Best Engineer." In 1994, Robertson formed the Red Road Ensemble and recorded Music for the Native Americans, which accompanied a TBS documentary series; the song "Ghost Dance" outlines the Battle of Wounded Knee and the near-extinction of the bison. On Contact from the Underworld of Redboy, he explored rock, native, and electronic music with Howie B, DJ Premier, and Marius de Vries (Björk, Massive Attack), examining native traditions like Peyote healing; Rolling Stone gave it 4 out of 5 stars, and he won a Juno Award for Best Music of Aboriginal Canada Recording. Released on April 5, 2011, How to Become Clairvoyant was his fifth solo release, stemming from impromptu demo sessions in Los Angeles with Eric Clapton; he performed "Straight Down The Line" with Robert Randolph and the Roots on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. The deluxe edition included five bonus tracks (four demos and "Houdini," named after Harry Houdini) and was released with a limited collector's edition featuring an art book, five lithographs (including by Richard Prince and Anton Corbijn), original tarot cards, original tracks, and ten bonuses. Released on September 20, 2019, Sinematic was his sixth solo album, featuring Van Morrison on "I Hear You Paint Houses" and allusions to Scorsese's films, with guest appearances by Citizen Cope, Derek Trucks, and Frédéric Yonnet. Robertson assisted Scorsese on the music for Raging Bull (1980), which sparked his interest in film music; he produced three newly recorded instrumental jazz tracks featuring guitar and performances by Garth Hudson and Richard Manuel, one co-written with Hudson, and selected the film's opening theme from Cavalleria Rusticana by Pietro Mascagni; the soundtrack was released in 2005 as a 37-track, 2-CD set. He worked with Scorsese on The King of Comedy (1983), credited for "Music Production," and contributed the original song "Between Trains" in tribute to assistant "Cowboy" Dan Johnson. In June 1986, he began work on The Color of Money, composing the score for the first time and bringing in Canadian jazz composer Gil Evans for orchestration; the best-known song, "It's in the Way That You Use It," co-written by Robertson and Eric Clapton, reached No. 1 on the Billboard Mainstream Rock Songs chart in January 1987; he also produced "Don't Tell Me Nothin'" with blues player Willie Dixon, co-written with Robertson. In 1999, he contributed songs to Oliver Stone's film Any Given Sunday. He scored Scorsese's 2019 film The Irishman and consulted with music supervisor Randall Poster on the soundtrack; the film is dedicated to him and he received a posthumous Academy Award nomination for Best Original Score, becoming the first Indigenous person nominated in that category. After The Last Waltz, MGM/UA viewed Robertson as a potential film actor and provided him with an office on the MGM lot; Martin Scorsese's agent contacted him about producing a film about traveling carnivals, which he found appealing due to his childhood carnival experiences. The screenplay was directed by Robert Kaylor. Although initially only intended as producer, Robertson became the third lead actor, playing Patch, with Gary Busey as Frankie and Jodie Foster as Donna; real-life carnies were cast alongside professional actors, creating a difficult on-set atmosphere. Carny opened on June 13, 1980, and Warner Bros. released a soundtrack co-credited to Robertson and Alex North, re-released on CD in 2015. In November 2024, Robertson posthumously appeared in the documentary Return of the King: The Fall and Rise of Elvis Presley. In October 2025, he posthumously appeared in the documentary series Mr. Scorsese. He co-authored Legends, Icons and Rebels: Music That Changed the World with his son Sebastian Robertson and colleagues Jim Guerinot and Jared Levine, and wrote Hiawatha and the Peacemaker, illustrated by David Shannon. His autobiography, Testimony, was published by Crown Archetype in November 2016. In April 2025, Penguin Random House Canada announced a second volume of his memoirs, focusing on his relationship with Martin Scorsese, to be published in November 2025. On March 24, 1968, Robertson married Dominique Bourgeois.

Robertson was ranked 59th in Rolling Stone magazine's 2011 list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time. The soundtrack for the film was re-released on compact disc by Real Gone Music in 2015. In November 2024, Robertson posthumously appeared in the documentary Return of the King: The Fall and Rise of Elvis Presley. In October 2025, he posthumously appeared in the documentary series Mr. Scorsese. Robertson co-authored Legends, Icons and Rebels: Music That Changed the World with his son, Sebastian Robertson, and colleagues Jim Guerinot and Jared Levine. He also wrote Hiawatha and the Peacemaker, illustrated by David Shannon. His autobiography, Testimony, written over the course of five years, was published by Crown Archetype in November 2016. In April 2025, Penguin Random House Canada announced that a second volume of Robertson's memoirs, focusing on his working relationship with Martin Scorsese, would be published in November 2025. On March 24, 1968, Robertson married Dominique Bourgeois, a Canadian journalist; they had two daughters and a son named Sebastian, and the marriage ended in divorce. On March 12, 2023, Robertson married his girlfriend of four years, Canadian entrepreneur, restaurateur, and Top Chef Canada judge Janet Zuccarini; their marriage occurred only five months before his death. Robertson was involved in social causes and was a member of the Canadian charity Artists Against Racism, using his platform to support anti-racism initiatives and public awareness campaigns. Robertson died at a Los Angeles hospital on August 9, 2023, at the age of 80, after a year-long battle with prostate cancer. His longtime manager, Jared Levine, stated that Robertson was surrounded by his family at the time of his death. In lieu of flowers, Levine requested that donations be made to the Six Nations of the Grand River, honoring Robertson’s heritage and lifelong connection to the community. In November 2023, director Martin Scorsese held a tribute concert for Robertson in Los Angeles, with notable guests including Joni Mitchell, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Lily Gladstone. In October 2024, another tribute concert with Scorsese's involvement was held at the Kia Forum. In May 2024, Robertson's three adult children filed a lawsuit against his wife, Janet Zuccarini, alleging elder abuse and undue influence, claiming that during a period of significant health decline, Zuccarini took advantage of Robertson's weakened condition to have him sign legal documents that would financially benefit her in the event of his death, without the full awareness or involvement of his children. The Band (including Robertson) was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 1989 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1994. In 1997, Robertson received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the National Academy of Songwriters. In 2003, Robertson received the Indspire Aboriginal Lifetime Achievement Award and was inducted into Canada's Walk of Fame. In 2005, Robertson received an honorary doctorate from York University. In 2006, he received the Governor General's Performing Arts Award for Lifetime Artistic Achievement, Canada's highest honour in the performing arts. In 2008, Robertson and the Band received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. In 2011, Robertson was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame. On May 27, 2011, Robertson was made an Officer of the Order of Canada by Governor General David Johnston. In 2014, the Band was inducted into Canada's Walk of Fame. On October 14, 2017, Robertson received the first Lifetime Achievement Award from the community of Six Nations. In 2019, Robertson was given a key to the city of Toronto by Mayor John Tory during a TIFF press conference for Once Were Brothers: Robbie Robertson and The Band. In 2019, Robertson received the Lifetime Achievement Award in the Canadian Music Industry Hall of Fame from Canadian Music Week (CMW).

Robert Adams (5 October 1917 – 5 April 1984) was an English sculptor and designer who, though not widely known outside artistic circles, was regarded as one of the foremost sculptors of his generation. In a 1993 retrospective review by Brian Glasser of Time Out magazine, Adams was described as "the neglected genius of post-war British sculpture," a view also expressed by Tim Hilton in the Sunday Independent, who ranked his work above that of contemporaries Ken Armitage, Reg Butler, Lynn Chadwick, and Bernard Meadows. Adams attended the village school in Hardingstone, Northamptonshire, now a suburb of Northampton, and lived there until 1951.
