He left school at age 14 and worked in various manual jobs, first as a van-boy for a printer and later with the agricultural engineering company Cooch & Sons, where experience in metal crafting proved valuable in his later art. From 1937 to 1946, he attended evening classes in life drawing and painting at the Northampton School of Art. During the Second World War, Adams was a conscientious objector but joined the Civil Defence as a fire warden. Some of his early sculptures were exhibited in London between 1942 and 1944 in group shows by Civil Defence artists. In April 1946, he exhibited fourteen early oil portraits at the Northampton Public Library. Between 23 November 1947 and 3 January 1948, he held his first one-man exhibition at Gimpel Fils Gallery, 84 Duke Street, London. From 1949 to 1959, he taught at the Central School of Art and Design in London, where he interacted with Victor Pasmore, Kenneth Martin, and Mary Martin, who were advancing Constructivist ideas in Britain. From 1950 to 1980, he was recognized as one of Britain's leading abstract sculptors, with his work exhibited at the Venice Biennale in 1952 and again in 1962 when he represented Britain with a retrospective in two galleries. Some of his works are held in the Tate Britain collection and in modern art museums in New York, Rome, Turin, São Paulo, and several other global locations, though he remains virtually unknown in his hometown. The Apocalyptic Figure was commissioned by the Arts Council England for the Festival of Britain in 1951. Large-scale sculptures by Adams can be seen at The Custom House, London, Heathrow Airport, Shell Mex House, London, and the Musiktheater im Revier, Gelsenkirchen, Germany, and one of his works is in the Contemporary Art Museum of Macedonia. He also had a retrospective at the Northampton Art Gallery in 1971.

doc_name: Robert Boyle Prize for Analytical Science
text: The Robert Boyle Prize for Analytical Science, previously known as the Boyle Medal, is a biennial award given by the Royal Society of Chemistry for outstanding contributions in the field of analytical chemistry. It carries a monetary value of £5,000 and is named in honor of Robert Boyle. The prize was awarded from 1982 until 2020, after which it was discontinued. It was replaced by the RSC's Analytical Science Horizon Prize, which is awarded every two years to groups or teams for recent and innovative advances in analytical chemistry.

Robin Roberts, born November 23, 1960, is an American television broadcaster who co-anchors ABC's Good Morning America. She was born in Tuskegee, Alabama, and grew up in Pass Christian, Mississippi, where she played basketball and tennis and graduated as the salutatorian of Pass Christian High School in 1979. She is the daughter of Lucimarian (née Tolliver) and Colonel Lawrence E. Roberts, a Tuskegee Airman, and is the youngest of four siblings, following Sally-Ann, Lawrence Jr. (nicknamed Butch), and Dorothy. Roberts attended Southeastern Louisiana University in Hammond, Louisiana, graduating cum laude in 1983 with a degree in communication, where she was a standout on the women's basketball team, ending her career as the school's third all-time leading scorer with 1,446 points and 1,034 rebounds—making her one of only three Lady Lions to reach 1,000 points and 1,000 rebounds. During her senior season, she averaged 27.6 points per game, and her jersey number 21 was retired by Southeastern on February 5, 2011. She began her career in 1983 as a sports anchor and reporter for WDAM-TV in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, then moved to WLOX-TV in Biloxi in 1984, WSMV-TV in Nashville in 1986, and WAGA-TV in Atlanta from 1988 to 1990, where she also hosted on radio station V-103. In February 1990, she joined ESPN as a sportscaster, working there until 2005, during which time she co-hosted NFL Primetime and used the catchphrase "Go on with your bad self!" She began working for ABC News as a featured reporter on Good Morning America in June 1995 and hosted ABC's Wide World of Sports from 1996 to 1998. In 2005, she was promoted to co-anchor of Good Morning America. After Diane Sawyer left in December 2009, George Stephanopoulos joined her as co-anchor, and their partnership led the program back to number one in the ratings by April 2012, surpassing NBC's Today, which had held the top spot for 16 years. In the fall of 2005, Roberts anchored emotional reports from the Mississippi Gulf Coast following Hurricane Katrina, which severely impacted her hometown of Pass Christian, where her high school was reduced to rubble. She hosted the Academy Awards preshow for ABC on February 22, 2009, and again in 2011. In 2010, she guest-starred on Disney Channel's Hannah Montana in season 4, episode 10, "Can You See the Real Me?", and drove the Pace Car for the 2010 Indianapolis 500 on May 30, 2010. In 2012, she was inducted into the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame for her contributions to women's basketball through broadcasting and play. In 2014, she was named one of ESPNW's Impact 25 and founded Rock'n Robin Productions. She executive-produced and narrated the documentary Tuskegee Airmen: Legacy of Courage, which premiered on History on February 10, 2021. Roberts is Presbyterian and practices Transcendental Meditation. In 2005, she began a romantic relationship with massage therapist Amber Laign, which she publicly acknowledged in late December 2013, and they married in September 2023. In 2007, she was diagnosed with early breast cancer, underwent surgery on August 3, and completed eight chemotherapy treatments by January 2008. In 2012, she was diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), a bone marrow disease, which led to a 1,800 percent spike in bone marrow donors for Be the Match Registry on the day she went public with her illness. She took a leave from GMA to undergo a bone marrow transplant, returning to the show on February 20, 2013, after going home in October 2012. Her coverage of her MDS diagnosis earned her a 2012 Peabody Award for allowing her network to document her battle and inspire hundreds of potential donors to register, raising awareness of the need for more bone marrow donors. ESPN awarded her the Arthur Ashe Courage Award at the 2013 ESPYs, and the NBA honored her with the Sager Strong Award at its June 20, 2019, ceremony. On May 19, 2018, she co-anchored the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle at St. George's Chapel in Windsor. In 2021, she served as a guest host on Jeopardy! for five episodes from July 19 to 23, following Alex Trebek's death in November 2020, and launched the Disney+ interview series Turning the Tables with Robin Roberts. She also performed as a backup singer in the film Pitch Perfect 2. On October 10, 2018, she was selected as a mentor for Disney's #DreamBigPrincess campaign.

Rolling Papers 2 (sometimes stylized as Rolling Papers II) is the sixth studio album by American rapper Wiz Khalifa, released on July 13, 2018, by Taylor Gang Entertainment and Atlantic Records. It serves as the sequel to his major-label debut Rolling Papers (2011). The album features guest appearances by Gucci Mane, Swae Lee, Ty Dolla Sign, PartyNextDoor, Bone Thugs-n-Harmony, and Snoop Dogg, as well as R&B duo THEMXXNLIGHT and Jimmy Wopo, who is credited posthumously after his death on June 18, 2018, less than a month before the album's release. Production is handled by Cardo, Mike Will Made It, Tay Keith, and Young Chop, among others. The album was supported by the singles "Something New", "Real Rich", "Hopeless Romantic", and "Gin & Drugs"; "Something New" and "Hopeless Romantic" were both modest hits and eventually certified platinum by the RIAA. It debuted at number 2 on the Billboard 200, driven by 84.2 million streams and 14,000 pure album sales, which Billboard equated to 80,000 album-equivalent units, marking Khalifa's fifth top-ten album in the United States. The album earned 33,000 album-equivalent units in its second week. In Canada, it debuted at number four on the Canadian Albums Chart, serving as Khalifa's third non-consecutive top-ten album in the country. In 2018, Rolling Papers 2 was ranked as the 128th most popular album of the year on the Billboard 200 and was certified Gold by the RIAA eleven months after its release. In an episode of Genius' For the Record, Wiz Khalifa spoke with hip hop journalist Rob Markman, stating that the album represented a new phase in his career and felt as important as his debut. The album received generally mixed reviews from critics, with Metacritic assigning it an average score of 56 based on 6 reviews. Sales and streaming figures are based on certification alone.

Roman Gregory Chatov (1900–1987) was a Russian-born American artist, painter, designer, and illustrator. Born in Rostov-on-Don, Russia, to a theater impresario and his wife, Chatov began drawing in his teenage years, creating magazine illustrations at age 16 and serving as a military-correspondent painter near the end of World War I. He received his initial art training in Russia and Paris, France. In 1922, he moved to New York with his family due to the Bolshevik Revolution and the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War. He later joined the Art Students League and the National Academy of Art to further develop his skills. Chatov initially designed costumes and painted murals, including works for the Ford and Palestinian Pavilions at the 1939 New York World's Fair under a commission from the New Deal Works Progress Administration. Among his most notable works was a set of murals for New York City's Russian Tea Room restaurant, which are now held in a New York City museum. These achievements led to numerous painting commissions across the United States. He also designed costumes for Florenz Ziegfeld, and dancer Isadora Duncan admired his designs; he painted a silk scarf for her, which later caused her death when it became entangled in the wheel of a moving car. In New York, Chatov met prominent artists such as Willem de Kooning, with whom he shared studio space. Under commission from MGM, Chatov and his brother Constantin painted portraits of famous Hollywood celebrities, including Vivien Leigh and Clark Gable. Chatov married Geneva McCormack in 1942. In his later years, he focused primarily on portraiture and opened an art studio in Atlanta with his brother Constantin. He received the Governor's Award from the Georgia Council for the Arts and Humanities in 1983 and died in 1987 at the age of 86 or 87. His son Marc Chatov (born in 1953) continues his father's legacy as an artist and art instructor.

Ronnie Lee Milsap, born Ronald Lee Millsaps on January 16, 1943, in Robbinsville, North Carolina, is an American country music singer and pianist who was one of the most popular and influential performers of the 1970s and 1980s. Nearly completely blind from birth due to a congenital disorder, he became one of the most successful and versatile country "crossover" singers, appealing to both country and pop audiences with hit songs that blended pop, R&B, and rock and roll elements. His biggest crossover hits include "It Was Almost Like a Song", "Smoky Mountain Rain", "(There's) No Gettin' Over Me", "I Wouldn't Have Missed It for the World", "Any Day Now", "Is It Over", and "Stranger in My House". He is credited with six Grammy Awards and 35 number-one country hits, fourth only to George Strait, Conway Twitty, and Merle Haggard. Milsap was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2014. He was abandoned by his mother as an infant and raised in poverty by his grandparents in the Smoky Mountains until age five, when he was sent to the North Carolina State School for the Blind and Deaf in Raleigh. During childhood, he developed a passion for music, especially late-night radio broadcasts of country, gospel, and rhythm and blues; at age seven, his instructors recognized his musical talent, and he began formal study of classical music at Governor Morehead School, eventually mastering the piano. At age 14, he lost the remaining vision in his left eye after a slap from a houseparent. Inspired by Elvis Presley's 1956 breakthrough, he formed a rock band called the Apparitions with high school classmates and has often paid tribute to Ray Charles, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Presley. He received a full college scholarship to Young Harris College in Georgia with plans to become a lawyer, where he joined the local R&B band the Dimensions and became a regular at the Royal Peacock Club. In 1963, he met Atlanta disc jockey Pat Hughes, who supported his career; his first single, "Total Disaster/It Went to Your Head", sold 15,000 copies with Hughes' radio promotion. He auditioned for a keyboardist role with J. J. Cale and signed with Scepter Records in 1965, recording several obscure singles and working briefly with Ray Charles and Stevie Wonder. That year, he scored his first hit with "Never Had It So Good", which reached No. 19 on the R&B chart, and recorded "Let's Go Get Stoned" as a B-side. In the late 1960s, after moving to Memphis, Tennessee, he worked with producer Chips Moman, became a popular weekly performer at T.J.'s nightclub, and contributed to recordings with Elvis Presley, including "Don't Cry Daddy" (1969) and "Kentucky Rain" (1970), and had a pop chart appearance with "Loving You Is a Natural Thing". He released his debut album, Ronnie Milsap, on Warner Brothers in 1971. In December 1972, after a chance meeting with country music star Charley Pride at Whiskey A-Go-Go in Los Angeles, Milsap relocated to Nashville, where Pride encouraged him to focus on country music. He began working with Pride's manager, Jack D. Johnson, and was signed to RCA Records in 1973. His first RCA single, "I Hate You", peaked at No. 10 on the country chart. In 1974, he toured with Pride and had two No. 1 singles: "Pure Love" (written by Eddie Rabbitt) and "Please Don't Tell Me How the Story Ends" (a Kris Kristofferson composition), which won him his first Grammy. In 1975, he revived the Don Gibson song "(I'd Be) A Legend in My Time" and scored another No. 1 hit with "Daydreams About Night Things". From 1976 to 1978, he achieved seven consecutive No. 1 country singles, including the Grammy-winning "(I'm a) Stand by My Woman Man" and "What a Difference You've Made in My Life". His most significant 1970s success was "It Was Almost Like a Song" in 1977, a piano-based ballad that topped the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, reached No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100, and entered the Adult Contemporary Chart at No. 7—his first entry on that chart since "Please Don't Tell Me How the Story Ends" reached No. 95. It was his only crossover success of the 1970s, though he continued to have country chart hits. In the late 1970s, his sound shifted toward string-laden pop ballads, leading to crossover success on the pop charts beginning in the early 1980s. From 1980 to 1983, he scored eleven No. 1 singles. His Greatest Hits album, released in 1980, included "Smoky Mountain Rain", which became a No. 1 country hit and reached the Top 20 on the pop chart and the first of two Milsap songs to reach No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. Other crossover successes included the Top 5 pop single "(There's) No Gettin' Over Me", and Top 20 songs "I Wouldn't Have Missed It For the World" and "Any Day Now", the latter spending five weeks at No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. All four songs reached No. 1 on the country chart. Although the No. 1 streak ended in 1983, "Stranger in My House" remained successful, peaking at No. 5 on the country chart, No. 23 on the pop chart, and No. 8 on the Adult Contemporary chart. "Don't You Know How Much I Love You", released shortly after, became his last significant pop chart entry, peaking at No. 58, though it and others achieved major success on the Adult Contemporary chart, including "Show Her", "Still Losing You", and the Grammy-winning "Lost in the Fifties Tonight" in 1985. Between 1985 and 1987, he had a series of uninterrupted No. 1 country singles, including "She Keeps the Home Fires Burning", "In Love", "Snap Your Fingers", "Where Do the Nights Go", and the Grammy-winning duet with Kenny Rogers, "Make No Mistake, She's Mine". In 1987, he contributed the theme song to the NBC television series J.J. Starbuck. In 1989, he had his last No. 1 song with "A Woman in Love", remaining successful on the charts. Other Top 10 singles between 1989 and 1991 include "Houston Solution", "Stranger Things Have Happened", "Turn That Radio On", a remake of the 1950s hit "Since I Don't Have You" (his last adult contemporary hit), and "Are You Loving Me Like I'm Loving You". With writer Tom Carter, he released his autobiography, Almost like a Song, in 1990. In 1992, he had major success with "All Is Fair in Love and War", which featured rock guitarist Mark Knopfler and peaked at No. 11; his last top-40 country hit, "True Believer", peaked at No. 30 in 1993. By that time, his chart success had declined. Despite this, he remained one of country music's most beloved performers. In 1993, he released True Believer on Liberty Records and achieved a Top 30 country hit with the title track, even as contemporaries were no longer played on country radio. In 2000, his two-disc retrospective 40 No. 1 Hits reached the Country Top 20 and earned gold certification, and his life and career were profiled in a Biography episode. In 2004, he released Just for a Thrill, a collection of pop and jazz standards, which marked a stylistic departure and earned a Grammy nomination. He returned to RCA Records in 2006 with a mainstream country sound on My Life. His two-disc gospel set Then Sings My Soul (2009) reached the Southern gospel charts, and Country Again (2011) reflected a more traditional country style. In 2014, Rolling Stone included "Smoky Mountain Rain" among its 100 greatest country songs. That year, he released Summer #17, an album of nostalgic pop and R&B covers. In 2016, he was among 30 artists featured on "Forever Country", a mash-up honoring the 50th CMA Awards. In 2019, he returned to the charts with Ronnie Milsap: The Duets, featuring collaborations with Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, George Strait, and others; a duet version of "Smoky Mountain Rain" with Parton reached the Adult Contemporary top 30. By 2020, he had installed a new home studio and continued to record, releasing A Better Word for Love in 2021. In 2022, he contributed "Oh, Lady Be Good!" to Michael Feinstein’s Gershwin Country and launched a podcast, Music and Milsap; that year, he inducted Ray Charles into the Country Music Hall of Fame and was later inducted into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame. His final concert, held on October 3, 2023, at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, marked the end of his touring career, several months after celebrating his 80th birthday on stage at the Grand Ole Opry. Though retired from touring, he continues to record. Milsap is an Advanced-class amateur radio operator with call sign WB4KCG. In 1965, he married Joyce Reeves; they had one son, Ronald "Todd" Milsap, who was found dead on his houseboat at age 49 on February 23, 2019, from an apparent medical condition; Todd's son discovered the body after not hearing from his father for two days. Joyce, who had been battling leukemia since 2014, died on September 6, 2021, at age 81. On December 2, 2020, six miles of U.S. 129 in Graham County, North Carolina, from Yellow Creek near Robbinsville to the Swain County line, was designated Ronnie Milsap Highway.

Rosa Whitaker Duncan-Williams is an American lobbyist and former trade negotiator who served as the first Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Africa during the administrations of Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. She currently operates a consulting firm called The Whitaker Group. Whitaker was born in Washington, D.C., and earned both a master's and bachelor's degree from American University in Washington, D.C., and also studied at the Foreign Service Institute in the United Kingdom and Italy. While serving as a Senior Trade Advisor to Congressman Charlie Rangel, she played a key role in drafting the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which was enacted in 2000. AGOA, America’s first comprehensive trade law targeting Africa, continues to serve as the foundation of U.S. economic policy toward the continent, facilitating billions of dollars in duty-free African products entering the U.S. market each year and supporting job creation and investment across Africa. She co-founded and co-chaired the bipartisan advocacy group AGOA Action Coalition with Jack Kemp. After leaving the U.S. Trade Representative’s office in 2003, Whitaker launched The Whitaker Group, which is headquartered in Northern Virginia and Accra, Ghana, and provides advice on trade, investment, and project development across Africa. The firm, established in 2003, has attracted clients from Fortune 500 companies seeking opportunities in both commercial and human development in Africa. In 2017, Whitaker led The Whitaker Group’s first direct investment in Africa by acquiring shares and management control of Dominion TV, a Pan-African television, entertainment, and multimedia company that broadcasts in 48 African countries via DStv, Africa’s largest satellite platform. The firm has also worked with the authoritarian Faure Gnassingbé regime in Togo. In 2005, Whitaker became involved in a controversy over her firm’s lobbying relationship with the Ugandan government, as The Whitaker Group was contracted by Uganda to enhance its international image at an annual cost of $350,000, making it one of the first well-known firms to manage Uganda’s public relations abroad.

Rosario Crocetta, born on 8 February 1951 in Gela, Sicily, is an Italian politician and openly gay man. He became the first openly gay mayor in Italy when he was elected Mayor of Gela in 2003, a position he held until 2009. His election followed a court ruling in 2003 that declared electoral fraud in the mayoral election, overturning the initial victory of right-wing candidate Giovanni Scaglione, who had won by a narrow margin of 197 votes. Telephone intercepts revealed that a local Mafia boss ordered a returning officer to prevent Crocetta, a center-left candidate, from winning, describing the effort as needing to "move heaven and earth in order to avoid the communist faggot to win." Crocetta, the son of a water-worker and a seamstress, began his political career in the 1980s with the Italian Communist Party, later joining the Communist Refoundation Party and the Party of Italian Communists. In 1998, he served as Councillor for Culture in Gela with the Federation of the Greens, focusing on cultural projects among Mediterranean countries, and from 2001 to 2002, he was Councillor for Public Education. In May 2002, he contested the mayoral election as a center-left candidate, and after the fraud was exposed, he was officially declared mayor. In 2007, he was re-elected with 64.4 percent of the vote. In 2008, he joined the Democratic Party and in the 2009 European elections, he was elected as a Member of the European Parliament for the Italian Islands constituency with 150,091 votes. In 2012, he ran for President of Sicily against Sebastiano "Nello" Musumeci of the PDL and eight other minor candidates on the platform of La Rivoluzione è Già Iniziata (The Revolution Has Already Started), winning 30.5 percent of the vote and becoming the first left-wing governor of Sicily since 1947. He served as President of Sicily from 2012 to 2017, making him the second openly gay head of a regional government in Italy after Nichi Vendola. From 2013 to 2017, he was also a member of the Committee of the Regions. On 19 July 2017, he announced his candidacy for the regional presidency with the list The Megaphone – Crocetta List, without Democratic Party support. After the party nominated Fabrizio Micari, Crocetta withdrew on 3 September 2017 and supported Micari with his list. Throughout his career, Crocetta has been a strong advocate against organized crime in Sicily and has faced multiple assassination plots. In 2003, a plot involving a Lithuanian killer targeting him during the patronal feast of the Immaculate Conception was thwarted by the Carabinieri. In 2008, a failed assassination attempt was revealed by the district attorney of Caltanissetta, leading to tighter security for Crocetta. In 2010, another assassination plot was stopped, resulting in the arrest of five individuals linked to the local Mafia. Crocetta speaks four languages—Italian, Arabic, English, and French—and has spoken and posted on social media in the Sicilian language. He worked for ENI in Gela after receiving his diploma and has an older brother, former PCI senator Salvatore Crocetta.

Rose Matafeo (/ˌmætəˈfeɪoʊ/; born 25 February 1992) is a New Zealand comedian, actress, and TV presenter. She was a writer and performer on the New Zealand late-night comedy sketch show Funny Girls. In 2018, she won the Edinburgh Comedy Award for Best Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe for her show Horndog, collecting a £10,000 prize. She was the first person of colour to win the prestigious award for a solo show and the first New Zealander to do so, joining only four other female solo stand-up comedians who had previously won the award. Matafeo was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1992 to parents John Matafeo and Diane Vuletich. Her parents are Rastafarians who first met through the Twelve Tribes of Israel denomination; as a child, she attended monthly services at their local headquarters in New Lynn, Auckland. John, a Samoan man and first-generation immigrant to New Zealand, joined the Polynesian Panthers movement as a teenager and worked in an administrative role at the Rastafarian Church. Diane, a Pākehā New Zealander of Scottish and Croatian heritage, works as a teacher and moved to Kampala, Uganda to teach English in the 2010s. Matafeo grew up in Ponsonby, Auckland, and attended Auckland Girls' Grammar School, where she was head girl; she has two older brothers and describes her upbringing as "quite relaxed." At 15, she began stand-up comedy through the New Zealand Comedy Trust's "Class Comedians" programme and won the "Nailed It on the Night" award at the New Zealand International Comedy Festival in 2007. She has been a regular at the festival since and won best newcomer at the 2010 festival. She became a host of the comedy festival show "Fanfiction Comedy" in 2012 and had success with her solo stand-up shows: Life Lessons I've Learnt from the 60s Based on Things I've Seen on Television (2011), Scout's Honour (2012), and The Rose Matafeo Variety Hour (2013). She won the Billy T Award for The Rose Matafeo Variety Hour in 2013, having been previously nominated for Scout's Honour in 2012. Her 2014 festival show was titled Pizza Party. In 2015, she performed a duo show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe with Guy Montgomery titled Rose Matafeo and Guy Montgomery Are Friends. She was a TV presenter and host of U Live on the TVNZ U channel from 13 March 2011 until 31 August 2013, when the channel ended. After that, she became a writer for Jono and Ben at Ten. She co-created and starred in the New Zealand sketch comedy show Funny Girls for three seasons from 2015 to 2018. Since 2018, she has played the role of Talia in the ABC comedy Squinters. She appeared on Jon Richardson: Ultimate Worrier as an investigator and on 8 Out of 10 Cats Does Countdown (S19, Ep1) for Channel 4 TV in January 2020. She was a contestant on series three of Richard Osman's House of Games and the ninth series of Taskmaster. After ten years touring as a stand-up comedian, Matafeo said in 2018 she wanted to "take a break from hour long comedy" and instead act more, write more, and direct. She directed five episodes of the 2019 New Zealand TV comedy Golden Boy. In 2019, she made her US television debut as a comedian on Conan O'Brien's talk show Conan on TBS. She appeared on James Acaster and Josh Widdicombe's show Hypothetical on Dave. She currently hosts the podcast Boners of the Heart with comedian and writer Alice Snedden on the Little Empire Podcast Network and has been a guest on Deborah Frances-White's The Guilty Feminist podcast and the RHLSTP podcast with Richard Herring. In 2019, she directed five episodes in the first season of Golden Boy and returned to the show in 2020 as a supporting cast member in the second season. In July 2020, she joined Guy Montgomery on the comedy show Tiny Tour of Aotearoa, travelling across New Zealand. On 20 August 2020, her comedy special Horndog was released on HBO Max. She was cast as the lead in the 2020 comedy film Baby Done. In April 2021, Starstruck, a six-part rom-com created by and starring Matafeo, aired on the BBC (UK), HBO (US), TVNZ (New Zealand), and ABC (Australia). Co-written by Matafeo and Alice Snedden, the show featured actor Nikesh Patel as leading man and love interest Tom. Filming for the first series was delayed due to the COVID pandemic, but a second series was commissioned before filming began. A third series was released in September 2023. In 2023, she guest presented the British quiz show Pointless. In 2024, she appeared in Moana 2 as Loto, an engineer who works on boats, and took on the role of Taskmaster in Junior Taskmaster, a Taskmaster spin-off for children aged 9–11, with Mike Wozniak as the assistant. Matafeo previously dated New Zealand comedian Guy Williams. In 2015, she moved to London, where her then-boyfriend James Acaster lived; she shared a flat with comedian Nish Kumar. The two broke up in 2017. One of her interests is mukbang videos; in July 2018, she made a mukbang video using takeaways from Double Happy Takeaways in Auckland, which was featured on The Spinoff. Matafeo is a supporter of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand and was scheduled to host their campaign launch for the 2020 general election, but was later asked to step down due to a miscommunication within the party.

Rosemarie Trockel, born on 13 November 1952 in Schwerte, Nordrhein-Westfalen, West Germany, is a German conceptual artist known for her work in drawings, paintings, sculptures, videos, installations, and mixed media. From 1985, she began creating large-scale paintings using industrial knitting machines, which often featured geometric motifs, logos such as the Playboy Bunny or a hammer and sickle, and the phrase "Made in West Germany." Between 1974 and 1978, she studied anthropology, mathematics, sociology, and theology while attending the Werkkunstschule in Cologne, a period marked by the strong influence of Joseph Beuys. In the early 1980s, she met members of the Mülheimer Freiheit artist group, founded by Jiří Georg Dokoupil and Walter Dahn, and exhibited at the women-only gallery of Monika Sprüth in Cologne. Her work frequently critiques other artists or artistic styles, such as minimal art. During the 1980s, she also contributed to the magazine Eau de Cologne, which focused on women artists. In 1994, she created the Frankfurter Engel monument for Frankfurt. For Documenta in 1997, she collaborated with Carsten Höller on an installation in one of the exhibition's outbuildings. Since the late 1990s, she has worked extensively with clay and continued producing both hand and machine knitted "paintings," several of which were shown in the 2005 retrospective Post-Menopause at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne. In 2013, her work was included in the Italian Pavilion, and she represented Germany at the Venice Biennale in 1999; she also participated in Documenta in 1997 and 2012. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she collaborated with Bottega Veneta designer Daniel Lee on the brand’s 2021 ad campaign. Trockel is a professor at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in Düsseldorf, Nordrhein-Westfalen, and her students have included Tea Jorjadze, Michail Pirgelis, and Bettina Pousttchi. She has been represented by Sprüth Magers and Gladstone.

Royal Eason Ingersoll (20 June 1883 – 20 May 1976) was a United States Navy four-star admiral who served as Commander in Chief, U.S. Atlantic Fleet (CINCLANT) from January 1, 1942 to late 1944; Commander, Western Sea Frontier from late 1944 to 1946; and Deputy Commander in Chief, U.S. Fleet/Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (DCOMINCH/DCNO) from late 1944 to late 1945. Born in Washington, D.C., on 20 June 1883, he was second in a line of three generations of U.S. Naval officers: his father, Rear Admiral Royal R. Ingersoll—United States Naval Academy class of 1868—and his son, Lieutenant Royal Rodney Ingersoll II—USNA class of 1934—was killed in a friendly fire accident on board the aircraft carrier Hornet (CV-8) on 4 June 1942 during the naval Battle of Midway. Ingersoll graduated from the Naval Academy in 1905, along with Chester W. Nimitz, and reported as a passed midshipman to the battleship Missouri (BB-11). In August 1905, he was assigned special temporary duty to attend the Russian-Japanese Peace Conference at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine. After being detached from the Missouri in May 1906, he served briefly on the Marietta (PG-15) and later the Hancock (AP-3), then assisted in fitting out the Connecticut (BB-18) at the New York Navy Yard, serving on that battleship from her commissioning on 29 September 1906 until October 1907. He served as an instructor of Seamanship and International Law, and later of English, at the Naval Academy between 1911 and 1913, preceding his assignment to the Asiatic Squadron, where he joined the armored cruiser Saratoga (ACR-2), the flagship of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet, serving briefly as her First Lieutenant and later as Aide and Flag Lieutenant to the Chief-of-Staff of the Asiatic Fleet's Commander. He returned to the United States and on 1 June 1916 reported as Assistant for Communications and Communication Officer in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department. He wrote that the work in this office intensified as diplomatic tensions with Germany rose, and on 2 February 1917, when diplomatic relations with Germany were broken, the workload overwhelmed the office. For organizing the greatly expanded Naval Communications Office during World War I, he was awarded the Navy Cross and cited "for distinguished service in the line of his profession in organizing, developing, and administering the Communication Office of the Navy Department." After the Armistice in November 1918, he was ordered to join Admiral William S. Benson, USN, then Chief of Naval Operations, to establish a communication office for that commission. In February 1919, he returned home aboard the George Washington with the Presidential party, handling messages for President Woodrow Wilson across the Atlantic. In March 1919, he rejoined the Connecticut as her executive officer until September 1920, then transferred to the Arizona (BB-39). In June 1921, he reported to the Navy Department for a tour of duty in the Office of Naval Intelligence, and on 26 March 1924, assumed command of the Nokomis (SP-609). Under his command, the gunboat was fitted out as a survey ship and cruised in the Cuban–Haitian area, producing new charts of the north coast of Cuba. Completing the Senior Course at the Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island in June 1927, he served as a member of that staff the following year. In June 1928, he reported as Assistant Chief of Staff to Commander Battle Fleet in the California (BB-44) and continued in similar duty on the Staff when Admiral William V. Pratt became Commander in Chief, United States Fleet, with his flag in the Texas (BB-35). In August 1930, he was assigned to the Division of Fleet Training, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department, where he served until May 1933. He then became Commanding Officer of the heavy cruiser Augusta (CA-31), and in November 1933, was transferred to the Mare Island Naval Shipyard to fit out the San Francisco (CA-38), which he commanded from her commissioning on 10 February 1934 until June 1935. His three-year assignment in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations as Director of the War Plans Division included his role in June 1936 as Technical Assistant to the American Delegation at the London Naval Conference (1935–36). He again traveled to London in December 1937, addressing requirements arising from the London Naval Treaty limiting naval armament. On 16 July 1938, Ingersoll took command of Cruiser Division Six of the Scouting Force, with his flag in the cruiser Minneapolis (CA-36). Two years later, he returned to the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations as assistant to the Chief, and on 1 January 1942, with the rank of Vice Admiral, was designated Commander in Chief, U.S. Atlantic Fleet, with the Augusta as his flagship. Ingersoll was promoted to the rank of admiral on 1 July 1942 and broke his flag on the converted yacht USS Vixen (PG-53) on 17 July. Having organized the movements of thousands of ships across the Atlantic to deliver men and supplies at the precise hour for the North African landings in November 1942, he also planned the composition of naval escort forces to ensure the safe arrival of troop convoys. Following the North African invasion, the Atlantic Fleet was tasked with running troop convoys and transporting stores, munitions, and fuel to the United Kingdom and the Mediterranean, as well as operating convoys along the coast of Brazil and continuously conducting the anti-submarine war, a primary concern since the outbreak of hostilities. Ingersoll is generally credited with solving the U-boat and Atlantic logistics problems. Additionally, he was responsible for the defense of the Western Hemisphere by U.S. naval forces and made changes in the disposition of air and surface forces stationed in North and South America. For his service in this command, he was awarded the Distinguished Service Medal and cited as a "forceful and resolute leader under the critical conditions existing throughout a period of approximately three years... against a determined and ruthless enemy intent on world domination..." In November 1944, he was detached from the Atlantic Fleet and became Commander Western Sea Frontier, with headquarters in San Francisco. In addition to commanding naval forces protecting shipping in coastal waters, he managed the flow of supplies to the Pacific Fleet through West Coast ports. In this role, he held the status of Deputy Commander in Chief, U.S. Fleet, and Deputy Chief of Naval Operations. After the navy's reorganization in October 1945, he continued as Commander Western Sea Frontier until 10 April 1946, when he was relieved of all active duty pending his retirement, which became official on 1 August 1946. Ingersoll was married in 1910 to Louise Van Harlingen of Atlanta, Georgia, and had two children. He died on 20 May 1976. In 1979, Mrs. Louise Ingersoll was the sponsor for USS Ingersoll (DD-990); their daughter, Alice Jean Ingersoll Nagle, acted as proxy sponsor. Their son, Royal Rodney II, had been (with Admiral Ingersoll's father) the namesake of the USS Ingersoll (DD-652). In addition to the Navy Cross and the Distinguished Service Medal, Ingersoll was awarded the World War I Victory Medal; the American Defense Service Medal; European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal; and the World War II Victory Medal. He also received the Chevalier of the Legion of Honor from the French Government, the Order of Naval Merit (Grand Cross) from the Government of Brazil, and the Grand Officer of the Order of Orange Nassau with Swords from the Government of The Netherlands.

The fourth season of RuPaul's Drag Race began airing on January 30, 2012, and concluded on April 30, 2012. The cast was announced on November 13, 2011. The winner of the season was Sharon Needles, with Chad Michaels and Phi Phi O'Hara as runners-up, marking the first time in the show's history that two runners-up were named. The final featured a three-way lip-sync battle instead of the usual two, and the winner was not crowned in the studio but during the "Reunited" episode, which was filmed in front of a live audience. This was also the first season in which three versions of the finale were filmed, with each Top 3 contestant being crowned to prevent spoilers, following the leak of Raja's Season 3 win by Perez Hilton in 2011. Santino Rice and Billy B (Billy Brasfield), a celebrity makeup artist and star of the HGTV mini-series Hometown Renovation, shared the judges' seat alternately, with Brasfield filling in for Rice when needed, and both appeared side-by-side in the audience during the "Reunited" episode. The theme song played during the runway every episode was "Glamazon," and the song played during the credits was "The Beginning," both from RuPaul's album Glamazon. This season marked the first time a contestant, Willam Belli, was disqualified for breaking the rules, and the second consecutive season in which a contestant, Kenya Michaels, was brought back after being eliminated earlier. Jiggly Caliente, who placed 8th, later served as a judge on Drag Race Philippines and died on April 27, 2025. The premiere episode averaged a 0.6 rating in the 18-49 demographic, totaling 481,000 viewers, making it the highest-rated premiere in Logo's network history, while the finale scored a 0.7 rating and drew 601,000 viewers, with the "Reunited" episode becoming the highest-rated episode of the season and the highest-rated reunion in the franchise's history, seeing a 33% increase in the 18-49 demographic compared to Season 3. The season finale also registered five trending topics on Twitter, including Sharon Needles, Phi Phi, Willam, and the portmanteau "RuPaulogize," and ranked 4th among non-sports cable programs on Trendrr. During the season, the show's Twitter following increased by 77% and the Facebook page saw a 36% increase in likes. Logo released the second running of Fantasy Drag Race, an online fan contest inspired by fantasy football, where viewers assembled a team of three season four contestants, earning points based on performance and completing tasks, with the highest scorers receiving Drag Race and NYX Cosmetics products and one player winning a trip for two to the first stop on Logo's Drag Race Tour. The season also saw increased engagement on social media platforms, with Logo expanding its presence on Facebook, Twitter, Tumblr, GetGlue, and Foursquare, hosting live tweets from RuPaul and contestants, and LogoTalk! chat parties. Season four specifically increased its focus on Tumblr, publishing animated GIFs, contestant trading cards, and internet meme-based images. TV.com named it the best reality show on television. In January 2012, the premiere episode generated eight US trending topics on Twitter and reached a 7th place ranking on Trendrr, and the show's Facebook page saw an 89% increase in followers, earning over half a million fans. At the end of the season, RuPaul revealed that Kenya Michaels had been voted back into the competition, and Latrice Royale was named Miss Congeniality. The final challenge involved the queens starring in RuPaul's music video "Glamazon" and acting in a dramatic scene with RuPaul. All three finalists lip-synced to "Glamazon" during the runway, and RuPaul announced that the winner would be revealed in the live "Reunited" episode. The live grand finale included a reunion with all eliminated queens, with RuPaul revealing she had invited her husband to her hotel, a breach of contract, and officially crowned Sharon Needles as the winner. Ages, names, and cities stated are at the time of filming.

RuPaul Andre Charles (born November 17, 1960) is an American drag queen, television host, singer, producer, writer, and actor. He produces, hosts, and judges the reality competition series RuPaul's Drag Race and has received several accolades, including 14 Primetime Emmy Awards, three GLAAD Media Awards, a Critics' Choice Television Award, two Billboard Music Awards, a Tony Award, and a Guinness World Records title. He has been dubbed the "Queen of Drag" and is considered the most commercially successful drag queen in the United States, with Fortune saying that he is "easily the world's most famous drag queen." In 2017, RuPaul was included in the annual Time 100 list of the most influential people in the world. Born and raised in San Diego, California, RuPaul studied performing arts in Atlanta, Georgia, before relocating to New York City, where he became a popular fixture on the LGBTQ nightclub scene. He achieved international fame as a drag queen with the release of his debut single, "Supermodel (You Better Work)" (1993). RuPaul was a spokesperson for MAC Cosmetics in 1994, raising money for the Mac AIDS Fund and becoming the first drag queen to land a major cosmetics campaign. RuPaul's Drag Race was created in 2009 and has gone on to produce eighteen seasons in the United States. The show has also seen success internationally and there are several international variants of the show, including RuPaul's Drag Race UK (2019–present) and Canada's Drag Race (2020–present). There are also several spin-offs of the main show, such as RuPaul's Drag U (2010–2012), RuPaul's Drag Race All Stars (2012–present), and RuPaul's Secret Celebrity Drag Race (2020–2022). His other television work includes The RuPaul Show (1996–1998), Skin Wars (2014–2016), Good Work (2015), Gay for Play Game Show Starring RuPaul (2016–2017), and RuPaul (2019). In 2018, RuPaul received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for his contributions to the television industry. RuPaul has made appearances in films, including Crooklyn (1994), The Brady Bunch Movie (1995), and But I'm a Cheerleader (1999), as well as television series, including Girlboss and Broad City (both 2017). He created and starred in the Netflix original series AJ and the Queen (2020). As a recording artist, RuPaul has released fifteen studio albums. He has also published four books: Lettin' It All Hang Out (1995), Workin' It! RuPaul's Guide to Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Style (2010), GuRu (2018), and The House of Hidden Meanings (2024). RuPaul was born in San Diego on November 17, 1960, the son of Ernestine "Toni" (née Fontenette) and Irving Andrew Charles. His parents were both from Louisiana. He was named by his mother; "Ru" came from roux, the French term for the base of gumbo and other creole stews and soups. According to DNA analysis by Finding Your Roots staff, his ancestry is 70% African and 30% European. RuPaul was raised in a Catholic household and grew up poor in a "broken home" with an absent father and volatile mother. After his mother discovered his father was having an affair, she poured gasoline on his car and attempted to set the house on fire. He described this traumatic event as a "pivotal moment" which caused him to dissociate from his body and deeply impacted him. After his parents divorced in 1967, he and his three sisters lived with their mother. He attended Patrick Henry High School but dropped out in 10th grade. At 15, RuPaul and his sister Renetta moved to Atlanta, where they studied performing arts. RuPaul struggled as a musician and filmmaker during the 1980s, working at Atlanta's Plaza Theatre. In 1982, he debuted on an Atlanta public access variety show called The American Music Show, and went on to appear on the show frequently. He also took part in underground cinema, helping create the low-budget film Star Booty and an album of the same name. In Atlanta he often performed at the Celebrity Club, managed by Larry Tee, as a bar dancer or with his band, Wee Wee Pole. RuPaul also performed as a backup singer to Glen Meadmore along with drag queen Vaginal Davis. His first prominent national exposure came in 1989, when he danced as an extra in the video for The B-52s' "Love Shack", and also appeared in Tom Rubnitz's video "Pickle Surprise". In the early 1990s, RuPaul worked the Georgia club scene and was known by his full birth name. Initially participating in gender bender-style performances, he performed solo and in collaboration with other bands at several New York City nightclubs, most notably the Pyramid Club. He played opposite New York City drag performer Mona Foot (Nashom Benjamin) in the one-act science-fiction parody "My Pet Homo", written and directed by Jon Michael Johnson for Cooper Square Productions. He performed for many years at the annual Wigstock drag festival and appeared in the documentary Wigstock: The Movie. In the 1990s, RuPaul appeared on the UK Channel 4 series Manhattan Cable, a weekly series produced by World of Wonder and presented by American Laurie Pike about New York's public-access television system. In 1993, RuPaul recorded the dance/house album Supermodel of the World. It was released through the rap label Tommy Boy, spawning the dance track hit "Supermodel (You Better Work)". The song peaked at 45 on the Billboard Hot 100. It charted on the UK Singles Chart, peaking on the top 40 at 39. The song found the most success on the Billboard Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart, where it peaked at 2. Radio airplay, heavy rotation of the music video on MTV, and television appearances on popular programs like The Arsenio Hall Show popularized the song. His next two singles/videos, "Back to My Roots" and "A Shade Shady (Now Prance)", both went to the top spot on the Billboard Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart. His following release "House of Love" failed to place on any U.S. charts but peaked at 68 on the UK Singles Chart. In 1994, he released "Don't Go Breaking My Heart", a duet with Elton John. RuPaul was signed to a modeling contract for MAC Cosmetics. Various billboards featured him in full drag, often with the text "I am the MAC girl". He also released his autobiography, Lettin' It All Hang Out. He promoted the book in part with a 1995 guest appearance on ABC's All My Children, in a storyline that put it on the set of Erica Kane's talk show "The Cutting Edge". The same year, he was featured in his first of two appearances in the Brady Bunch movies, in which he played Jan's female guidance counselor. In 1994 he had a duet with Elton John who was of the superguests of the Sanremo Festival in Italy as superguests, one of the main festivals worldwide; the performance generated both positive and concerned reactions from the public. In 1996, he landed a talk show of his own on VH1, called The RuPaul Show interviewing celebrity guests and musical acts. Cher, Diana Ross, Nirvana, Duran Duran, Pat Benatar, Mary J. Blige, Bea Arthur, Dionne Warwick, Cyndi Lauper, Olivia Newton-John, Beenie Man, Pete Burns, Bow Wow Wow, and the Backstreet Boys were notable guests. His co-host was Michelle Visage with whom he also co-hosted on WKTU radio. On one episode, RuPaul featured guests Chi Chi LaRue and Tom Chase speaking about the gay porn industry. Later in the year he released his second album, Foxy Lady, this time on the L.A.-based Rhino Records label. The album failed to chart on the Billboard 200. However, its first single "Snapshot" went to number four on the Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart. It also enjoyed limited mainstream success, charting at 95 on the Billboard Hot 100, which was his second and final solo Hot 100 entry to date. The album's second single "A Little Bit of Love" was not as successful, peaking at 28 on the Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart. During this time, RuPaul hosted a morning radio show at WKTU radio in New York City and would serve as host until 1998. In 1997, he released his third album, the Christmas-themed Ho Ho Ho. That year, RuPaul teamed with Martha Wash to remake the classic disco anthem, "It's Raining Men". The song was included on the 1998 compilation CD RuPaul's Go Go Box Classics. During this time, he appeared in Webex TV commercials and magazine ads. In 2002, he was featured on the Eurodance track "You're No Lady" alongside Brigitte Nielsen. In 2004, RuPaul released his fourth album, Red Hot, on his own RuCo Inc. music label. It received dance radio and club play, but very little press coverage. RuPaul later noted, "I don't know what happened. It seemed I couldn't get press on my album unless I was willing to play into the role that the mainstream press has assigned to gay people, which is as servants of straight ideals." Red Hot's lead single "Looking Good, Feeling Gorgeous" peaked at number two on the dance chart. The second, "WorkOut", peaked at number five. The third and final single from the album "People Are People" a duet with Tom Trujillo, peaked at number 10. The album itself only charted on the Top Electronic Albums chart, where it hit number nine. In September, he was hired at WNEW. On June 13, 2006, RuPaul released ReWorked, his first remix album. The only single released from the album was a re-recording of "Supermodel (You Better Work)", which reached number 21 on the U.S. dance chart. June 20, 2007, saw the release of Starrbooty: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack in the United States. The single "Call Me Starrbooty" was digitally released in 2007. The album contains new tracks as well as interludes with dialogue from the movie. The film was released on DVD in October 2007. In mid-2008, RuPaul began producing RuPaul's Drag Race, a reality television game show which aired on Logo in February 2009. On the program drag queens compete to be selected by RuPaul and a panel of judges as "America's next drag superstar". The first season's winner was BeBe Zahara Benet, and first runner-up Nina Flowers was chosen by fans as "Miss Congeniality" through voting via the show's official website. To publicize the new show, RuPaul appeared on several other shows in 2008, including Project Runway, as guest judge, and on Paula's Party as a guest "chef". In March 2009, RuPaul released the album Champion. The album spawned four singles "Cover Girl", "Jealous of My Boogie", "Devil Made Me Do It", and "Tranny Chaser". The album peaked at number 12 on the Billboard Dance/Electronic Albums as well as 26 on the Billboard Top Heatseekers chart. Logo's second annual NewNowNext Awards in 2009 were hosted by RuPaul. There he performed "Jealous of My Boogie (Gomi & RasJek Edit)". In March 2010, RuPaul released his second remix album, Drag Race, the album features remixes of songs from the 2009 album Champion. In April 2011, coinciding with the finale of season 3 of RuPaul's Drag Race, RuPaul released his sixth studio album Glamazon, produced by Revolucian. The album charted on Billboard's Dance/Electronic Albums and the Billboard Top Heatseekers chart at 11 and 8 respectively. In July 2011, he released another remix EP entitled SuperGlam DQ which features remixes of tracks from Glamazon, remixes of the "Drag U Theme Song", and a new song, "Sexy Drag Queen". The second season of RuPaul's Drag U began in June 2011. In late 2011, RuPaul made appearances on The Rosie Show and The Chew, and also attended a Drag Race NY Premiere party at Patricia Field's store in New York. Season 4 of RuPaul's Drag Race premiered on Logo on January 30, 2012, with RuPaul returning as the main host and judge. In the fall of 2012, the spin-off RuPaul's Drag Race All Stars premiered and featured past contestants of the previous four seasons. Season 5 of RuPaul's Drag Race premiered on January 28, 2013. On April 30, 2013, he released "Lick It Lollipop" featuring Lady Bunny. In fall of 2013, RuPaul joined forces with cosmetic manufacturers Colorevolution to launch his debut make-up line featuring ultra-rich pigment cosmetics and a beauty collection. Released alongside the line was a unisex perfume entitled "Glamazon". Talking to World of Wonder he said: "Glamazon is for women and men of all ages and preferences who share one thing in common: They are not afraid to be fierce. For me, glamour should be accessible to all, and I am committed to helping the world look and smell more beautiful." The line was exclusively sold on the Colorevolution website in various gift sets. On January 28, 2014, RuPaul released RuPaul Presents The CoverGurlz, a collaborative album featuring new versions of RuPaul songs from 2009 to 2013. His seventh studio album, Born Naked, was released on February 24, 2014, to coincide with the premiere of the sixth season of RuPaul's Drag Race. Born Naked placed at number 4 on the US Billboard dance chart and 85 on the Billboard 200 chart. On April 9, 2014, RuPaul and Michelle Visage released the first episode of their podcast, RuPaul: What's the Tee? with Michelle Visage. In August, he joined the reality competition show Skin Wars acting as a judge. On March 2, 2015, RuPaul released his eighth studio album, Realness. The release coincided with the premiere of the seventh season of RuPaul's Drag Race. In April, he launched and began hosting a new show, Good Work, a plastic surgery-themed talk show for E!. In October he released his second Christmas album, and ninth studio album, Slay Belles. The album contains ten original Christmas-themed songs and features collaborations with Michelle Visage, Siedah Garrett, Todrick Hall, and Big Freedia. The album charted at 21 on the US Billboard Dance chart. In January 2016, it was announced RuPaul would present a new game show for Logo TV called Gay for Play Game Show Starring RuPaul which premiered on April 11, 2016, after RuPaul's Drag Race. In March 2016, he released his tenth album, Butch Queen, just prior to the premiere of the eighth season of RuPaul's Drag Race. A song from the album, "U Wear It Well" was featured in the teaser campaigns for the season and was released as its first single. The album charted at number 3 on the US Billboard Dance chart. "'Be Someone" featuring American singer Taylor Dayne was released as the album's second and final single. Additionally, Butch Queen: The Ru-Mixes was released. In July 2016, it was announced that RuPaul was nominated for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Host for a Reality or Reality-Competition Program. He was presented the award at the September Creative Arts Emmy Awards Ceremony. 2016 also saw the release of the single "Read U Wrote U" that features rap parts by the RuPaul's Drag Race All Stars 2 finalists Roxxxy Andrews, Katya Zamolodchikova, Alaska Thunderfuck, and Detox Icunt with production by Ellis Miah. On February 3, 2017, RuPaul released the album Remember Me: Essential, Vol. 1. It is a collection of new songs and remakes of RuPaul hits that feature new artists. Two singles were released from the album: "Rock It (To The Moon)", and an updated version of RuPaul's 1996 single "Snapshot" from Foxy Lady. The album debuted at number four on the Billboard Dance Albums Sales Chart in the United States and at number eleven on the UK Dance Albums Chart. On March 24, 2017, RuPaul released his eleventh studio album, American. On the same day, the ninth regular season of RuPaul's Drag Race debuted on basic cable channel VH1. It moved from the expanded cable channel Logo TV which aired all previous seasons of the show. The season 9 premiere featured singer Lady Gaga as its guest judge and was a success, with ratings of nearly 1,000,000 viewers, making it the series' most viewed episode. On June 9, 2017, Essential, Vol. 2 was released. It was preceded by the single "Crying on the Dance Floor", a re-recording of the 2010 single "Main Event" from Champion.

A collection of new songs and remakes of RuPaul's hits featuring new artists was released, with two singles, "Rock It (To The Moon)" and an updated version of RuPaul's 1996 single "Snapshot" from Foxy Lady, released from the album. The album debuted at number four on the Billboard Dance Albums Sales Chart in the United States and at number eleven on the UK Dance Albums Chart. On March 24, 2017, RuPaul released his eleventh studio album, American, and on the same day, the ninth regular season of RuPaul's Drag Race premiered on VH1, moving from Logo TV. The season 9 premiere, which featured Lady Gaga as guest judge, attracted nearly 1,000,000 viewers, becoming the series' most viewed episode. On June 9, 2017, Essential, Vol. 2 was released, preceded by the single "Crying on the Dance Floor," a re-recording of the 2010 single "Main Event" from Champion. On March 16, 2018, RuPaul received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, becoming the first drag queen to be honored with the award. He released his third Christmas album in October 2018. In June 2019, the daytime talk show RuPaul premiered but was cancelled after a three-week test run; he also appeared in Taylor Swift's "You Need to Calm Down" music video. In late 2019, the first season of RuPaul's Drag Race UK was released on BBC3 and was renewed for a second season in 2021. RuPaul created and starred in the Netflix drama-comedy show AJ and the Queen, released on January 10, 2020, which was cancelled on March 6, 2020. He hosted Saturday Night Live on February 8, 2020, and made an appearance on The Price Is Right at Night on May 11. He also appeared in the premiere episode of Canada's Drag Race. In August 2021, RuPaul guest hosted two episodes of Jimmy Kimmel Live. He provided voice work in Amphibia as FBI agent Mr. X and won the Tony Award for Best Musical in 2022 as a producer of A Strange Loop. He voices himself as the announcer on The Tiny Chef Show and began hosting a revival of the game show Lingo for CBS in 2023, as well as Celebrity Lingo on ITV. HarperCollins published the RuPaul memoir The House of Hidden Meanings in March 2024. The podcast RuPaul: What's the Tee? With Michelle Visage debuted on April 6, 2014, co-hosted by RuPaul and Michelle Visage, featuring discussions on RuPaul's Drag Race, life advice, beauty tips, and entertainment guests. In 2018, RuPaul voiced the audiobook A Day in the Life of Marlon Bundo. RuPaul's DragCon LA, launched through World of Wonder in 2015, and RuPaul's DragCon NYC, which began in 2017, are annual drag-themed conventions in Los Angeles and New York City, featuring performances, meet-and-greets, merchandise, and panel discussions. RuPaul has supported voter registration, producing a public service announcement for National Voter Registration Day and urging registration, noting that voter ID laws vary by state and that one in five LGBTQ adults are not registered. Several RuPaul's Drag Race stars serve as Ambassadors for Drag Out the Vote. In March 2023, in response to the Tennessee Adult Entertainment Act, RuPaul, World of Wonder producers Randy Barbarto and Fenton Bailey, and MTV launched a fund to oppose anti-drag initiatives, supported by the ACLU and funded by DragCon LA 2023, the "Drag Isn't Dangerous" livestream, "Can't Hold us Down," "Born This Way," "God Save the Queens," and a small donation from the Manhattan Association of Cabarets. RuPaul's Instagram post prior to the fund called on followers to vote, stating, "Register to vote so we can get those stunt queens out of office," ending with, "By the way, a social media post has never been as powerful as a registered vote." Lauren Herold of Mic.com called RuPaul "arguably the most commercially successful drag queen in America," and Sami Main of Adweek credited him with expanding drag queens' visibility in mainstream society through chart success and RuPaul's Drag Race's rising viewership. His talk show The RuPaul Show was the first national talk show hosted by a drag queen, featuring high-profile guests like Cher, Lil Kim, and Diana Ross over 100 episodes and discussing topics such as black and female empowerment, misogyny, and liberal politics, which were rare in 1990s television. In 1999, RuPaul received the Vito Russo Award at the GLAAD Media Awards for promoting LGBTQ equality. RuPaul has significantly contributed to RuPaul's Drag Race's television success by pioneering queer representation, earning his first Emmy in 2016 and a second consecutive win for Outstanding Host for a Reality or Reality-Competition Program in 2017, when the show received eight Primetime Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Reality Competition Program. In 2017, he was included in Time 100 as one of the world's most influential people, and in 2019, Fortune named him "easily the world's most famous" drag queen. RuPaul has faced controversy over his comments regarding the transgender community, with critics citing his use of terms like "tranny" and "shemale" and the "You've got she-mail" phrase, which former contestants and activists criticized as transphobic. In 2014, Logo TV removed the phrase and replaced it with "She done already done had herses," and RuPaul defended the use of such terms, stating they refer to transvestites and drag queens, not just trans women. In 2018, RuPaul stated that a post-transition trans woman would "probably not" be accepted onto the show, noting Peppermint had not yet had breast implants, which drew criticism; he later expressed regret and clarified that the only screening criteria are charisma, uniqueness, nerve, and talent. Since then, multiple transgender contestants have competed and won on the show. RuPaul met painter Georges LeBar in 1994 at the Limelight nightclub in New York City and married him in January 2017; they have an open marriage and split their time between a home in Los Angeles and a 60,000-acre ranch in Wyoming. Environmentalists criticized them in 2020 for leasing mineral rights and selling water to oil companies and allowing fracking on the ranch, which has at least 35 active wells. RuPaul previously held a climate-themed ball to raise environmental awareness, leading to accusations of hypocrisy. In 2016, RuPaul publicly endorsed Hillary Clinton and expressed dismay at her defeat by Donald Trump, saying the narrative of love, peace, liberty, and equality felt dead. He described drag as a "very, very political" act that challenges fixed identities by asserting, "Drag says 'I'm a shapeshifter, I do whatever the hell I want at any given time.'" Since 1999, RuPaul has been sober, abstaining from alcohol, drugs, and tobacco. In 2020, he learned from Finding Your Roots that he and New Jersey Senator Cory Booker are "DNA cousins." In a 2013 interview, RuPaul said he is not religious but practices spiritual routines like yoga and meditation and prays. RuPaul has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, was inducted into the California Hall of Fame in 2019, and has won 14 Primetime Emmy Awards, including eight for Outstanding Host for a Reality or Competition Program, making him the most awarded in that category and the most-awarded person of color in Emmy history. His other accolades include a Tony Award, two Billboard Music Awards, four Canadian Screen Awards, ten Critics' Choice Real TV Awards, a Critics' Choice Award, four GLAAD Media Awards including the 1999 Vito Russo Award, five Producers Guild of America Awards, and a Guinness World Records title. In 2020, a species of Australian soldier fly was named Opaluma rupaul, referencing its "costume of shiny metallic rainbow colours," with other species named O. ednae and O. fabulosa.

Karl Wilhelm Rudolf von Bennigsen (10 July 1824, Lüneburg – 7 August 1902, Bennigsen near Springe) was a German politician from an old Hanoverian family. He was born in Lüneburg on 10 July 1824; his father, Karl von Bennigsen, was a general in the Hanoverian Army and held diplomatic positions. His nephew was the anthropologist Moritz von Leonhardi. After studying at the University of Göttingen, where he joined the Corps Hannovera, Bennigsen entered the Hanoverian civil service. In 1855, he was elected to the second chamber, but resigned due to the government’s refusal to grant him leave from his duties. He then became the recognized leader of the Liberal opposition to the reactionary government, distinct from Alexander Levin, Count of Bennigsen, a member of the same family and son of the Russian General Bennigsen, who served as Hanover’s minister-president between 1848 and 1850 and later as president of both chambers of the Estates Assembly. Bennigsen’s significance extended across Germany through his role as founder and president of the German National Association, established in response to the Austro-Sardinian War, which aimed to promote national unity and constitutional liberty. The association united moderate Liberals and became a major political force despite government suppression, especially by King George V of Hanover. He was also a founder of the Protestantenverein in 1863. In 1866, as leader of the liberal opposition in the second chamber, he attempted to keep Hanover neutral in the Austro-Prussian War, though unsuccessfully; his brother, a Prussian Army officer, was killed in Bohemia. In May 1866, he had a significant meeting with Bismarck, who sought his support for reforming the German Confederation. After the war, Bennigsen became a Prussian subject and took a seat in the diet and the Prussian House of Representatives. He advocated for maximum autonomy for Hanover and opposed the Guelph Party. Alongside Ludwig Windthorst and Johann von Miquel, he was one of three Hanoverians who led the province’s representatives in both the Prussian and North German parliaments. The Nationalverein was dissolved after its work was completed, but Bennigsen was central in founding the National Liberals, who supported Bismarck’s national policy while seeking constitutional development. For the next thirty years, he served as president of the party and was the most influential parliamentary leader, helping avoid open conflict between Bismarck and parliament. He introduced numerous constitutional amendments and, in 1870, undertook a mission to Southern Germany to strengthen the national party, and was consulted by Bismarck at Versailles. He secured the compromise on the military bill in 1874. In 1877, he was offered the position of vice-chancellor with a seat in the Prussian ministry, but declined due to disagreements with Bismarck or the king over his conditions. From then on, his relations with the government became less friendly, and in 1878 he led the rejection of the first Socialist Bill. In 1883, he resigned from parliament due to reactionary government measures that ended his cooperation with Bismarck, but returned in 1887 to support a coalition of national parties. One of Emperor Wilhelm II’s first actions was to appoint him upper president of the Province of Hanover. In 1897, he resigned this post and retired from public life, dying on 7 August 1902.

Rugged Lark (May 1, 1981 – October 26, 2004) was a Quarter Horse stallion who achieved two American Quarter Horse Association (AQHA) World Show Superhorse titles in 1985 and 1987, and was also recognized as a three-time AQHA World Champion. He won the Silver Spur Award. Rugged Lark was the son of the Thoroughbred stallion Really Rugged and the Quarter Horse mare Alisa Lark, who was a great-granddaughter of Leo and a great-great-granddaughter of both King P-234 and Joe Hancock P-455. He earned AQHA points in Hunter Under Saddle, Western Pleasure, Trail, Hunter Hack, Reining, Working Hunter, Western Riding, Pleasure Driving, and Barrel Racing. In 1985, he was crowned World Champion Pleasure Driving Horse and in 1987, he became World Champion Senior Hunter Under Saddle Horse. Among his offspring are The Lark Ascending, Rugged Painted Lark, Look Whos Larkin (1999 AQHA World Show Superhorse), Jolena Lark, Rugged Lark II, and Forever a Lark. He is one of only two stallions to sire offspring that also won Superhorse titles. Rugged Lark was euthanized in October 2004 due to colic and was inducted into the AQHA Hall of Fame.

doc_name: Russian annexation of Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts
text: On 30 September 2022, Russia unilaterally declared the annexation of areas in and around four Ukrainian oblasts—Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia, despite none of the oblasts being fully under Russian control at the time or since. The annexation followed internationally unrecognized referendums held from 23 to 27 September, organized by Russian occupation authorities in territories where hostilities were ongoing and much of the population had fled. The boundaries of the annexed areas were not defined, with Russian officials stating they would be determined later. The areas under Russian control at the time amounted to about 90,000 km² (15% of Ukraine’s territory, roughly the size of Portugal or Hungary), including about 60% of Donetsk Oblast, most of Luhansk Oblast, almost all of Kherson Oblast, and about 70% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Russia had previously occupied Crimea in 2014 and recognized the Donetsk and Luhansk People's Republics in February 2022, launching a full-scale invasion on 23 February 2022, which included military occupations in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. On 29 September, Russian authorities declared the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions independent as an intermediate step before annexation, and on 30 September, President Vladimir Putin signed accession treaties with the leaders of the four regions—Leonid Pasechnik, Denis Pushilin, Yevgeny Balitsky, and Volodymyr Saldo—while stating that the Donbas regions would maintain their 2014 borders and that other areas’ borders would be defined through consultations with residents. The annexation was condemned by the international community, including Ukraine, the European Union, the United States, and the United Nations, which rejected the referendums and the annexation as having no legal basis. The UN Security Council failed to pass a resolution condemning the annexation due to a Russian veto, and the UN General Assembly passed a resolution in October 2022 condemning the annexation and demanding Russia withdraw its forces. Only North Korea and formerly Ba'athist Syria recognized the annexation. On 19 October, Russia introduced martial law in the annexed areas, restricting public gatherings and personal liberties. The Ukrainian Kharkiv and Kherson counteroffensives enabled Ukraine to recapture parts of its territory, including Kherson on 11 November 2022. Russia’s State Duma and Federation Council unanimously approved the annexations, which were carried out in violation of Russian law. On 3 October, Putin stated that Donetsk and Luhansk would be annexed in their 2014 borders, while Kherson and Zaporizhzhia would have borders defined through consultations. A YouGov poll in February 2023 found that 63% of Swedes supported Ukraine in a war with Russia until Russian troops withdrew, and a Gallup poll in June 2023 showed that 62% of Americans supported Ukraine regaining lost territory, even if it prolonged the war. In response, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared that Ukraine would not negotiate with Russia as long as Putin was president and requested expedited NATO membership. A Kyiv International Institute of Sociology poll in May 2022 found that 82% of Ukrainians opposed any territorial concessions to Russia, and a September 2022 poll showed 87% opposed such concessions. Mykhailo Podolyak, an advisor to Zelenskyy, called the annexation a "Kremlin freak show" with no legal sense. In July 2024, a British Army official estimated that Russia would need five years and over 1.5 million casualties to fully control the annexed regions, with no winners in the conflict. In a 37-minute speech delivered on 30 September in the Grand Kremlin Palace, Putin justified the annexation as reflecting the "will of millions" of people, citing Article 1 of the UN Charter, while denouncing the West as totalitarian, despot, and Satanist, and accusing it of attempting to create a neo-colonial world order. Reuters noted that formal annexation would escalate the war and risk direct military confrontation with the United States and its allies. The Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the referendums as "sham elections" on 9 September 2023.

Ruth Wilson Gilmore, born on April 2, 1950, in New Haven, Connecticut, is a prison abolitionist and prison scholar. She serves as the Director of the Center for Place, Culture, and Politics and is a professor of geography in Earth and Environmental Sciences at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York. Gilmore has made significant contributions to carceral geography, defined as the study of the interrelationships across space, institutions, and political economy that shape and define modern incarceration. She received the 2020 Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Association of Geographers. Born in New Haven, Wilson’s grandfather organized the first blue collar workers' union at Yale University; her father, Courtland Seymour Wilson, was a tool-and-die maker for Winchester Repeating Arms Company and was active in the machinists' union, later serving as assistant dean of student affairs at Yale Medical School and working in the Office of Government and Community Relations at Yale-New Haven Hospital. In 1960, she attended a private school in New Haven as one of its few working-class students and the first, and mostly only, African American student. In 1968, she enrolled at Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania, where she became involved in campus activism; in 1969, she, Fania Davis (the younger sister of radical activist Angela Davis), and other students occupied the school's admissions office to advocate for admitting more Black students. After the sudden death of the university president, white students spread false rumors blaming the occupying students, and the next morning, Gilmore learned that her cousin, John Huggins, and Black Panther Bunchy Carter had been murdered at the University of California, Los Angeles. Following these events, she left Swarthmore and returned home to New Haven, where she enrolled at Yale and earned a bachelor's degree in drama. Gilmore earned her Ph.D. from Rutgers University in 1998 in economic geography and social theory, inspired by Neil Smith. After completing her Ph.D., she was hired as an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley, where she began developing her concept of carceral geography, which examines the relationships between landscape, natural resources, political economy, infrastructure, and the policing, jailing, caging, and controlling of populations. The academic community in this field is associated with the Carceral Geography Working Group (CGWG) of the Royal Geographical Society with the Institute of British Geographers, and Gilmore delivered a keynote address at the 2nd International Conference for Carceral Geography at the University of Birmingham, UK, on December 12, 2017. She is a cofounder of numerous social justice organizations, including the California Prison Moratorium Project and, in 1998, Critical Resistance alongside Angela Davis. In 2003, she co-founded Californians United for a Responsible Budget (CURB) to oppose jail and prison construction and currently serves on its board. Gilmore is a leading scholar and speaker on prisons, decarceration, racial capitalism, oppositional movements, and state-making. She authored the book Golden Gulag, which won the Lora Romero First Book Publication Prize for the best book in American Studies from the American Studies Association in 2008. Her work has been published in journals such as Race & Class, The Professional Geographer, Social Justice, Global Lockdown: Race, Gender, and the Prison Industrial Complex, and the critical anthology The Revolution Will Not Be Funded: Beyond the Non-Profit Industrial Complex, edited by the Incite! collective. In 2011, she was the keynote speaker at the National Women's Studies Association annual conference in Atlanta, Georgia. In 2012, the American Studies Association awarded her its first Angela Y. Davis Prize for Public Scholarship, recognizing scholars who apply their scholarship to the public good through education, policy influence, or addressing inequalities.
