In 2014, she received the Harold M. Rose Award for Anti-Racism Research and Practice from the Association of American Geographers. In 2017, she earned the American Studies Association Richard A. Yarborough Award for excellence in teaching and mentoring. In 2020, Prospect listed her as the seventh-greatest thinker for the COVID-19 era, noting that she has spent nearly 30 years developing carceral geography and has helped shift the conversation about crime from punishment to rehabilitation, making her radical ideas especially relevant as the U.S. justice system's failures come to light. An Antipode journal documentary film highlighted her work on geography, racial capitalism, the prison industrial complex, and abolition geographies. In 2021, she was elected a Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2023, she was honored with a mural painted by artist and filmmaker Jess X. Snow and local community members on the outside of the Possible Futures bookstore in New Haven, Connecticut.

Somanahalli Mallaiah Krishna (1 May 1932 – 10 December 2024) was an Indian politician who served as Minister of External Affairs of India from 2009 to October 2012. He was the 10th Chief Minister of Karnataka from 1999 to 2004 and the 19th Governor of Maharashtra from 2004 to 2008. He served as Speaker of the Karnataka Vidhana Soudha from December 1989 to January 1993. He was a member of both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha from 1971 to 2014. He is widely credited with putting Bengaluru on the world map by building the foundation for it to become the IT Hub that it is today during his tenure as Chief Minister. In 2023, Krishna was awarded the Padma Vibhushan, the second highest civilian award of India. Born on 1 May 1932 to a Vokkaliga family in Somanahalli, Maddur Taluk of Mandya district, Karnataka, he completed his High School at Sri Ramakrishna Vidyashala, Mysore, and earned a Bachelor of Arts from Maharaja's College, Mysore. He obtained a law degree from University Law College, then known as Government Law College in Bangalore. He studied in the United States, graduating with a Master of Laws from Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas, and The George Washington University Law School in Washington D.C., where he was a Fulbright Scholar. As a student in the US, he campaigned for John F. Kennedy during the 1960 United States presidential election in areas dominated by Indian Americans; after Kennedy became President, he wrote to Krishna in 1961 expressing his "warm appreciation of your efforts during the campaign." Upon returning to India, he worked as a professor of international law at Renukacharya Law College, Bangalore. He began his electoral political career in 1962 when elected to the Mysore Legislative Assembly from Maddur as an independent, defeating K. V. Shankar Gowda, a prominent Indian National Congress (INC) leader for whom Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru had campaigned. He joined the Praja Socialist Party (PSP) but lost to M. Manchegowda of the INC in the 1967 election. He was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1968 at by-polls from Mandya following the death of the sitting parliamentarian. In 1968, he played a key role in reconciling members of the Indian National Congress and the PSP. He served three terms as a member of parliament from Mandya, starting with the 1968 by-poll as a PSP candidate, followed by wins in 1971 and 1980. He resigned from the Lok Sabha in 1972, joined the Karnataka Legislative Council, and was appointed a minister by Devaraj Urs. After returning to the Lok Sabha in 1980, he served as a minister under Indira Gandhi between 1983 and 1984. He lost his bid for the Mandya Lok Sabha seat in the 1984 elections but was reelected to the Karnataka Legislative Assembly in 1985. He served as Speaker of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly from 18 December 1989 to 20 January 1993 and as Deputy Chief Minister of Karnataka from 1993 to 1994. He was a member of the Rajya Sabha from April 1996 to 1999. In 1999, as president of the Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee, he led his party to victory in the assembly polls and became Chief Minister of Karnataka, a position he held until being defeated in the 2004 Karnataka Legislative Assembly elections. He was instrumental in creating power reforms with ESCOMS and digitizing land records through the BHOOMI initiative, and promoted private-public participation, sponsoring the Bangalore Advance Task Force. He was appointed Governor of Maharashtra on 6 December 2004 and resigned on 5 March 2008, reportedly to return to active politics in Karnataka; President Pratibha Patil accepted his resignation on 6 March. He entered the Rajya Sabha and took oath as Union Cabinet Minister of External Affairs under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on 22 May 2009. During his tenure, he visited countries including Tajikistan in 2012 to strengthen economic and energy ties. He resigned as External Affairs Minister on 26 October 2012, signaling a return to Karnataka state politics. On 29 January 2017, he resigned from the Indian National Congress, citing the party's "state of confusion" regarding its need for mass leaders and claiming he had been sidelined, stating the party was "dependent on managers and not time-tested people like himself." After speculation about joining the Bharatiya Janata Party, he formally joined the party in March 2017. He announced his retirement from politics in January 2023, citing age-related issues. He was married to Prema and had two daughters; his daughter Malavika Krishna was married to the Late V. G. Siddhartha, a businessman and founder of Cafe Coffee Day. He had a younger brother, Shankar (who died in 2019), who was a member of the Karnataka Legislative Council. At the end of his political life, he released his biography, Smritivahini, in the presence of many dignitaries, including anecdotes such as the Veerappan kidnapping of Rajkumar during his tenure as Chief Minister, and noted that former Prime Minister H. D. Devegowda had strong plans to join the Indian National Congress twice during the period of National Emergency. He died from a long illness at his residence in Bengaluru on 10 December 2024, at the age of 92. He was cremated with state honours, including a gun salute, at his ancestral village of Somanahalli in Maddur taluk of Mandya district on 11 December. The Karnataka Government declared a three-day mourning period.

Sarv Mittra Sikri (26 April 1908 – 24 September 1992) was an Indian lawyer and judge who served as the 13th Chief Justice of India.[1] He previously held the position of the first Advocate-General for Punjab and was the first judge of the Supreme Court of India to be directly appointed from the Bar; he is one of only two judges to have become CJI directly from the Bar.[2] Born in Lahore on 26 April 1908,[3] Sikri moved to London to study medicine but switched to law, studying at Trinity College, Cambridge.[1] Before returning to Lahore in 1930, he served as a barrister-at-law at Lincoln's Inn in London. He began his legal practice in the chambers of Jagannath Agarwal, a leading advocate in the Lahore High Court who specialized in criminal and civil law. After independence, he was appointed Assistant Advocate General of Punjab in 1949 and became the Advocate General in 1951, holding that position almost continuously until his elevation to the Supreme Court of India in 1964.[4] As an advocate, he appeared and practised in various courts, including the Lahore High Court, other courts in Punjab, the Federal Court of India, and eventually the Supreme Court of India.[5] In the case of I.C. Golaknath and Ors. v. State of Punjab and Anrs., Sikri was part of a 6:5 minority that reversed the court's earlier decision upholding Parliament's power to amend all parts of the Constitution, including Part III on Fundamental Rights, thereby effectively removing Parliament's power to curtail Fundamental Rights.[4] This Indian law–related biographical article is a stub. doc_name: SIGMOD Edgar F. Codd Innovations Award
text: The ACM SIGMOD Edgar F. Codd Innovations Award is a lifetime research achievement honor bestowed by the ACM Special Interest Group on Management of Data at its annual flagship conference, commonly referred to as SIGMOD. As stated on its official website, the award recognizes "innovative and highly significant contributions of enduring value to the development, understanding, or use of database systems and databases." The award has been presented since 1992. Prior to 2003, it was known as the "SIGMOD Innovations Award." In 2004, SIGMOD, with the unanimous approval of the ACM Council, renamed the award to honor Dr. E.F. (Ted) Codd (1923 – 2003), who invented the relational data model and played a pivotal role in establishing the database field as a scientific discipline.

SIGPLAN is the Association for Computing Machinery's Special Interest Group (SIG) on programming languages, focusing on programming language concepts and tools across design, implementation, practice, and theory. Its members include programming language developers, educators, implementers, researchers, theoreticians, and users. SIGPLAN recognizes an individual or individuals who have made a significant and lasting contribution to the field of programming languages. It also honors outstanding contributions by young researchers in programming languages, with the award named after computer scientist Robin Milner. Additionally, it awards an institution or individual(s) for the development of a software system that has had a significant impact on programming language research, implementations, and tools. The John C. Reynolds Doctoral Dissertation Award, named after computer scientist John C. Reynolds, is presented annually to the author of the outstanding doctoral dissertation in programming languages. This award is given to the authors of a paper presented at PLDI 10 years prior to the award year, in recognition of its influence over the past decade, and similarly, to the authors of a paper presented at POPL 10 years prior to the award year, in recognition of its influence over the past decade.

The SS Columbia (1880–1907) was a cargo and passenger steamship owned initially by the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company and later by the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company. Constructed in 1880 by the John Roach & Sons shipyard in Chester, Pennsylvania, as Hull No. 193 for the Oregon Steamship Company, which was acquired by the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company in 1879, construction began in September 1879 and the ship was launched on February 24, 1880 at 11:40 a.m. Both the Bureau Veritas and American Shipmasters' Association oversaw its building. Despite Roach’s initial refusal to install incandescent light bulbs due to fire concerns, the ship became the first to carry a dynamo powering electric lights instead of oil lamps and the first commercial use of electric light bulbs outside of Thomas Edison's Menlo Park, New Jersey laboratory. After attending Edison’s New Year's Eve demonstration, Henry Villard, president of the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company, ordered the installation of an Edison Lighting System, making Columbia the first commercial vessel to use the incandescent bulb and Edison’s first commercial order for the light bulb. The lighting system was installed in May 1880, with the first lighting occurring on May 2, 1880, and the bulbs carried aboard by Francis R. Upton. The system was successful, with chief engineers reporting no failures after 415 hours and 45 minutes of continuous use. The ship completed sea trials, sailed around Cape Horn to San Francisco with 13 locomotives, 200 railroad cars, and supplies, made a stop in Rio de Janeiro where Emperor Pedro II of Brazil viewed the electric lights, and used light bulbs attached to a tallow-covered cable to inspect the propeller shaft and rudder while passing through the Straits of Magellan. Upon arrival in San Francisco, the original carbon filament bulbs were replaced with newer bamboo filament bulbs sent by Edison. The ship safely arrived in Portland on August 24, 1880, though insurance companies were initially reluctant to underwrite it. Columbia operated a regular service between Portland and San Francisco and, after the Alaskan was sunk in 1889, carried its captain and crew to Astoria. The success of the Edison lighting system led to adoption by other shipping companies, including the British Cunard Line, with the SS Servia becoming the first major ocean liner lit by incandescent bulbs in 1881. The Columbia was highly reliable, with a record of being on the route for less than one night in fifteen years. In July 1895, the original Edison generators were removed and replaced with modern ones, and the dynamos were later donated to the Smithsonian Institution and The Henry Ford in Dearborn, Michigan. The Oregon Railway and Navigation Company was taken over by the Union Pacific Railroad in 1904, and the Columbia and the George W. Elder were transferred to the new subsidiary, the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company. In 1905, the George W. Elder struck a rock and sank, later being refloated and purchased by the North Pacific Steamship Company, and the Columbia collided with a wood barge in the Columbia River, resulting in damage requiring repair in San Francisco. On February 1, 1906, the Columbia collided with a log raft in dense fog, with no damage to the ship, though the captain anchored until the fog lifted. On January 30, 1898, the Columbia broke the speed record between San Francisco and Portland, traveling in just under two days with a delay of one hour due to stops, shaving one hour off the previous record. On October 3, 1900, the Columbia collided with the ferryboat Berkeley in San Francisco due to misinterpreted signals, damaging the bow of the Columbia and destroying one of the Berkeley’s lifeboats, leading both ships to be taken out of service. The George W. Elder temporarily replaced the Columbia on its route. On September 14, 1902, the Columbia ran aground near Astoria due to low tide and was refloated at high tide and returned to Portland the following night. During a refit at the Union Iron Works in 1906, the ship was damaged by the San Francisco earthquake, knocking off its supports, rolling to starboard, and hitting the dock, with its iron hull damaging the hydraulic drydock. The ship was sent to Hunter’s Point for permanent repairs, during which the crew abandoned ship after a steam pipe explosion. The Columbia was temporarily replaced by the steamer Costa Rica and the Barracouta. It returned to service on January 17, 1907, and was trapped in an ice pack near St. Helens, Oregon for four days, with the Aragonia successfully breaking through the ice to free it. After returning to San Francisco, the ship appeared unscathed. Designed by Edward Faron, the Columbia was 300 feet (91 m) long with 310 feet (94 m) above water, had a beam of 38 feet 6 inches (11.73 m), a depth of 23 feet (7.0 m), and was powered by two compound condensing steam engines with 42.5-inch and 82-inch by 54-inch strokes driving a single Hirsch four-bladed propeller of 16 feet (4.9 m) diameter and 27 feet (8.2 m) mean pitch, operating at 65 revolutions per minute. The propeller could be removed individually or all at once. The ship had six boilers, each 12 feet (3.7 m) in diameter and 12 feet 6 inches (3.81 m) long, operating at 80 pounds per square inch (550 kPa) pressure. It carried a maximum of 300 tons of coal, had an estimated top speed of 16 knots (30 km/h; 18 mph), and included a single donkey boiler and an auxiliary steam engine for bilge and water supply, plus a second auxiliary engine for electricity. It had a Brigantine rig with over 15,000 yards (14,000 m) of canvas on two iron masts. The ship had four decks—Spar, Main, Hurricane, and a fourth—each with iron framing and four watertight compartments. It featured electric fire alarms, annunciators, hydrants, electric head and side lights powered by an auxiliary dynamo, and telegraph communication between the bridge and engine room. The cargo holds had double steam-powered elevators. Passenger amenities were highly innovative and luxurious, including a large refrigeration room in the stern capable of maintaining a constant cold temperature, ventilation and heating systems, a Bohemian glass shade illuminated by an electric bulb in the main saloon, frosted glass fixtures for other bulbs, French walnut, Hungarian ash, mahogany, and maple paneling in the dining room, wooden furniture and carpeting, telephones in key rooms, and electrical indicators and monitoring equipment on the bridge. First-class staterooms accommodated 250 individuals and steerage 600 passengers, with paneling and furniture similar to first-class Pullman rail cars, including folding berths. Fresh-water plumbing was included. All 120 light bulbs were connected via separate circuits to four 6-kilowatt Edison A Type "long legged Mary-Ann" dynamos, with the fourth boosting the magnetic fields of the others at a lower voltage, each capable of powering 60 bulbs. Voltage adjustments were made by observing bulb brightness in the engine room. Wiring used molten paraffin and cotton in rubber tube casings, with wires painted to distinguish positive and negative charges. The electrical system mirrored Menlo Park designs, with oil lamps available as backup. On July 20, 1907, Columbia departed San Francisco with 251 passengers and crew for Portland under Captain Peter Doran. As evening approached, the ship became shrouded in fog about 12 miles (19 km) off Shelter Cove, and Doran refused to slow down despite the whistle of the lumber schooner San Pedro being heard nearby. Neither vessel reduced speed, and the rolling waves caused many passengers to go to their cabins due to seasickness. Fifteen minutes later, San Pedro approached directly. Doran ordered full reverse, but it was too late. At 12:22 a.m. on July 21, 1907, San Pedro struck the starboard side of Columbia, damaging the bow of the wooden-hulled San Pedro and holed the Columbia, causing it to list to starboard and sink by the bow. Passenger William L. Smith described the impact as "soft," while Otilla Liedelt reported it as severe. Doran ordered lifeboats to be launched, with Smith going from cabin to cabin to ensure passenger safety. Many passengers were seasick and did not respond, while others prepared to abandon ship. Smith observed a family holding hands in their cabin. As the ship sank, Liedelt noted that Doran tied the whistle cord down on the bridge and remained there, waving his hands in a final salute. After the bridge submerged, the whistle stopped. The ship developed a noticeable list to starboard, allowing Lifeboat Number Four to be launched without lowering. Eight and a half minutes after the collision, the ship began its final plunge, with the stern rising and the bow entering the water in seconds. A large explosion occurred, dragging many people back to the surface. While survivors believed the explosion was from a boiler, Chief Engineer Jackson stated it did not explode, as he stood directly above them when the ship pitched. Another theory is that a massive release of trapped air caused the explosion. Among those in the water was 16-year-old Maybelle Watson from Berkeley, who, after being thrown from a capsizing lifeboat, found a young schoolteacher flailing due to a lifebelt fastened backwards. Maybelle helped her stand upright and keep her head above water until rescued by Officer Hawse’s lifeboat. A total of 88 passengers and crew, including all children on board, perished in the sinking. Due to the rapid sinking, many lifeboats could not be launched. After the sinking, the lifeboats of Columbia and San Pedro launched a rescue effort assisted by the steamers Roanoke and George W. Elder. The San Pedro, carrying 390,000 ft (118,872 m) of redwood, remained afloat and rescued nearly 80 survivors, many of whom were forced to hold on to each other to avoid being carried away by lapping waves.

During the sinking of the Columbia, 88 passengers and crew, including all children on board, lost their lives due to the rapid descent of the ship. Many lifeboats could not be launched because of the speed of the sinking. After the disaster, the lifeboats from the Columbia and San Pedro launched a rescue operation, assisted by the steamers Roanoke and George W. Elder, the latter being one of Columbia’s previous running mates. Although severely damaged and partially sunk with a noticeable list, the San Pedro’s hull, carrying 390,000 ft (118,872 m) of redwood, remained afloat. Nearly 80 survivors were brought aboard the San Pedro, many of whom had to hold onto each other to avoid being swept away by lapping waves on the semi-submerged deck. The George W. Elder also towed the damaged San Pedro to shore. Hull inspector John K. Bulger, who had inspected the Columbia eight months earlier with O.F. Bolles—coincidentally the ship’s first captain—testified that the vessel had four watertight bulkheads, meeting modern safety standards requiring only three. However, Bulger admitted that if one compartment was punctured, water would cascade over the bulkheads, causing the ship to sink, a scenario similar to the RMS Titanic’s sinking in 1912. He later retestified that two flooded compartments would lead to disaster, not one. Despite this, the bulkheads likely provided little delay in water ingress. The San Francisco Examiner reported that the Columbia, an iron-hulled vessel, suffered a major impact, with its brittle, aged iron plates cracking and a seven-foot gash at the forward hatch allowing unimpeded water entry. Captain Doran of the Columbia and First Officer Hendrickson of the San Pedro were found most responsible for the collision; Hendrickson’s license was revoked for five years, and Captain Magnus Hanson of the San Pedro was found to have given insufficient orders and failed to reach the bridge when warned of fog, resulting in a one-year license revocation. Despite these errors, survivors and the press commended most crew members for their bravery and lifesaving actions. Third Officer Hawse of the Columbia, however, received little praise; he was reported to have shown aggressive and indifferent behavior, threatening to throw survivors overboard and claiming he would have shot them if he had a .45. He blamed Captain Hanson for denying survivors boarding his vessel, which he claimed caused many deaths. Survivors denied Hawse’s account of Hanson’s actions, and rumors spread about Hawse having a morphine addiction; Doctor S.B. Foster at the U.S. Marine Hospital noted Hawse had requested the drug three times. Hawse was arrested on July 29, 1907, while living in Second Officer Richard Agerup’s home in San Francisco, showing signs of paranoia during arrest and was admitted to the Central Emergency Hospital’s detention ward. After the sinking, the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company leased the City of Panama to replace the Columbia. On August 8, 1907, the City of Panama collided with the grounded steam schooner Alliance near the Willamette and Columbia Rivers; due to the Alliance’s wooden hull, the City of Panama sustained only minor damage. Richard Agerup, the City of Panama’s second officer, had been on the Columbia’s bridge the night it sank. The Columbia’s sinking, along with earlier losses of the Valencia, Clallam, and City of Rio de Janeiro, eroded public confidence in shipping lines and inspectors. Despite the tragedy, key lessons were not learned. On August 29, 1929, over 22 years later, the passenger steamer San Juan collided with the oil tanker S.C.T. Dodd in dense fog, sinking in just three minutes and killing 77 people. The San Juan’s sinking closely mirrored that of the Columbia, sharing similar design, shipyard, route, and being outdated iron-hulled steamers. The San Pedro was repaired and continued serving along the California coast until being sold to foreign owners in 1920, after which it sank that same year. The Punta Gorda Light was established in response to the disaster, and rusting debris from the Columbia—including a boiler and bulkhead—remains visible near the northern section of the Lost Coast Hiking Trail. Between 1899 and 1907, at least eight other ships sank in the area, including the St. Paul, whose rusted boilers are still visible in the surf at Punta Gorda. The coordinates of the incident are 39°57′29.43″N 124°11′2.26″W (39.9581750°N 124.1839611°W).

SS Olympia was a steamship that operated in the northwest United States and Alaska during the Klondike Gold Rush and was wrecked in 1910. Originally laid down as SS Doune Castle, she was launched in 1883 as SS Dunbar Castle by Barclay, Curle and Co. of Glasgow, Scotland, for the Castle Mail Packet Company. In 1895, Dunbar Castle was sold to Fairfield Ship Building and Engineering Co. and renamed SS Olympia. In 1897, the Scottish American Steamship Company purchased her, and later that year, the Northern Pacific Steamship Line acquired her. In 1898, she operated under the North America Mail Steamship Company of Tacoma, Washington. In 1903, she served with the North Western Steam Ship Company of Seattle, Washington, which sold her to the Alaska Steam Ship Company in 1904; that year, lifeboats were installed. On 10 December 1910, Olympia ran aground on Bligh Reef off Alaska's Prince William Sound and sank, with no loss of life. After the incident, steamboat inspectors accused Captain Daniels, who was in command at the time of the grounding, of "unskillful navigation." The coordinates of the wreck site are 60°50′26″N 146°52′48″W (60.840529°N 146.880015°W).

Saba Valadkhan (Persian: صبا ولدخان) is an Iranian American biomedical scientist who serves as an Assistant Professor and RNA researcher at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio.[1] In 2005, she received the GE / Science Young Scientist Award for her groundbreaking work on the mechanism of spliceosomes—described as "akin to finding the Holy Grail of the splicing catalysis field"[2]—a field critical because "20 percent or 30 percent of all human genetic diseases are caused by mistakes that the spliceosome makes."[3] She earned her medical degree from Tehran University of Medical Sciences in Iran in 1996 and moved to the United States to pursue her Ph.D. at Columbia University, New York.[4] In 2004, she joined Case Western Reserve University as an Assistant Professor.[5] Her research focuses on the role of small nuclear RNAs in the human spliceosome under the supervision of Prof. James Manley.[2] She has developed a novel minimal spliceosome consisting of only two spliceosomal snRNAs that catalyzes a reaction identical to the natural splicing reaction. This system provides direct evidence for RNA catalysis in the spliceosome, thereby resolving the long-standing question of the catalytic domain's identity, and also serves as a powerful tool for studying the structure and function of the spliceosome. Valadkhan was awarded the Harold Weintraub award from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle for her doctoral thesis.[4] She was named a Searle Scholar in 2004 and also received the American Association for Advancement of Science (AAAS) Young Scientist Grand Prize that same year.[4][6] In 2006, she became a founding member of the Rosalind Franklin Society and was honored with the Nsoroma Award from the Cleveland Chapter of the National Technical Association.[7]

Saboyá is a town and municipality located in the Western Boyacá Province, within the Colombian department of Boyacá. The name Saboyá is of Italian origin and was introduced by European colonizers. Prior to the Spanish conquest of the Muisca in the central highlands of the Colombian Andes, the area was governed by a cacique named Saboyá. Pedro de Galeano, who was the brother of Martín Galeano and a soldier in the army of Hernán Pérez de Quesada—brother of the Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada—served as the first encomendero of Saboyá. Modern Saboyá was officially founded on October 4, 1556. Simón Bolívar visited the town on three separate occasions: January 2, 1821; September 6, 1827; and June 9, 1828. The primary economic activities in Saboyá are agriculture and livestock farming, with cultivated products including potatoes, maize, and fruits such as curuba, blackberries, tree tomatoes, and strawberries. The geographical coordinates of Saboyá are 5°42′N 73°46′W (5.700°N 73.767°W).

Sajood Sailani, born Ghulam Mohammed Wani in 1936 in Dalgate Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, was a Kashmiri playwright, painter, theater artist, cartoonist, and poet. He is primarily known for his radio plays written in regional languages, producing about 150 radio plays, 27 stage dramas, and 40 comedies throughout his career. His work was primarily in Urdu and Kashmiri, and he gained recognition for the play Kaej Raath (Dumb Night), which earned him the Sahitya Akademi Award under the Kashmiri category in 1994. He served on the Sahitya Akademi advisory board from 1973 to 1977 and again in 1990. He began his career while studying in the 10th class and never attended college for further studies. Inspired by All India Radio's night show Hawa Mahal, he started writing short sketch comedies and later worked for Radio Kashmir Srinagar (modern-day AIR Srinagar), where he produced many of his literary works, including prominent dramas such as Kaej Raath, Gaashe Taaruk (Guiding Star), Ropye Rood (Money Shower), Zalur (Spider), Vutri binyul (Catastrophe), Fundbaz (Swindler), and Tentykor (Catgut). He also recorded nohakhwaani (the tragedy of Husayn ibn Ali) and wrote scripts of noha depicting the battle of Karbala. As a painter, he established the Wani Art Gallery and received an uncertain cultural award from the government of Jammu and Kashmir's Department of Cultural Academy in 1970. He is sometimes regarded as the only Kashmiri writer in the 20th century to have written a radio play in Bhojpuri. He was suffering from a chronic condition for several years and passed away on 17 November 2020 in Zafran Colony, Srinagar, and is buried in Pandrethan cemetery, Srinagar. He is survived by three children, including two sons—Showkat Shehri (playwright and writer) and Manzoor Ahmad (psychiatrist)—and a daughter.

Salvador Domingo Felipe Jacinto Dalí i Domènech, Marquess of Dalí de Púbol (11 May 1904 – 23 January 1989), known as Salvador Dalí, was a Spanish surrealist artist celebrated for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre imagery. Born on 11 May 1904 at 8:45 am on the first floor of Carrer Monturiol, 20 in Figueres, Catalonia, Spain, near the French border, Dalí's older brother, also named Salvador (born 12 October 1901), had died of gastroenteritis on 1 August 1903. His father, Salvador Luca Rafael Aniceto Dalí Cusí (1872–1950), was a middle-class lawyer and notary, an anti-clerical atheist and Catalan federalist, whose strict discipline was softened by his wife, Felipa Domènech Ferrés (1874–1921), who encouraged Dalí’s artistic development. In 1912, the family moved to the top floor of Carrer Monturiol 24 (now 10). Dalí later attributed his love for luxury, gilded things, and oriental clothing to an "Arab lineage," claiming his ancestors were descendants of the Moors. He was haunted by his dead brother throughout his life, describing them as "like two drops of water, but with different reflections," and later referred to his brother as "probably the first version of myself but conceived too much in the absolute." Images of his brother reappeared in works such as Portrait of My Dead Brother (1963). Dalí also had a sister, Anna Maria, who was three years younger, and he painted her 12 times between 1923 and 1926. Childhood friends included future FC Barcelona footballers Emili Sagi-Barba and Josep Samitier, with whom they played football during holidays in Cadaqués. Dalí attended the Municipal Drawing School in Figueres in 1916 and discovered modern painting during a summer trip to Cadaqués with the family of Ramon Pichot, a local artist who traveled to Paris. In 1918, he held his first public exhibition at the Municipal Theatre in Figueres, a venue he returned to decades later. In 1921, the Pichot family introduced him to Futurism, and his uncle Anselm Domènech, who owned a bookshop in Barcelona, supplied him with books on Cubism and contemporary art. On 6 February 1921, Dalí’s mother died of uterine cancer; at 16, he later described the loss as the greatest blow in his life, saying he worshipped her and could not accept her death. After her death, his father married her sister, which Dalí did not resent due to his deep respect for his aunt. In 1922, Dalí moved to the Residencia de Estudiantes in Madrid and studied at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando. Standing 1.72 metres tall, he was known as an eccentric and dandy with long hair, sideburns, a coat, stockings, and knee-breeches in the style of late 19th-century English aesthetes. At the Residencia, he became close to Pepín Bello, Luis Buñuel, Federico García Lorca, and others in the Madrid avant-garde group Ultra; his friendship with Lorca was emotionally intense, though Dalí rejected the poet’s sexual advances, and the relationship remained significant until Lorca’s death in 1936 during the Spanish Civil War. In 1922, he began a lifelong relationship with the Prado Museum, visiting every Sunday to study the masters, which he described as the start of a "monk-like period" devoted to solitary work. His Cubist paintings, such as Cabaret Scene (1922) and Night-Walking Dreams (1922), drew attention from peers, as there were no Cubist artists in Madrid at the time. In May 1925, he exhibited eleven works at the Sociedad Ibérica de Artistas in Madrid, seven in Cubist style and four in realism, earning praise from critics. His first solo exhibition at Galeries Dalmau in Barcelona, from 14 to 27 November 1925, included twenty-two works and was a critical and commercial success. In April 1926, Dalí traveled to Paris, where he met Pablo Picasso, whom he revered, and was influenced by Yves Tanguy, later claiming to have "pinched everything from your uncle Yves." He left the Royal Academy in 1926, shortly before his final exams, and demonstrated mastery through his realistic painting The Basket of Bread (1926). In December 1926 to January 1927, he exhibited again at Galeries Dalmau with the support of critic Sebastià Gasch, featuring twenty-three paintings and seven drawings, with the Cubist works separated from the objective ones; the critical response was generally positive, with Composition with Three Figures (Neo-Cubist Academy) receiving special attention. From 1927, Dalí’s work became increasingly influenced by Surrealism. Works such as Honey is Sweeter than Blood (1927) and Gadget and Hand (1927), shown at the Barcelona Autumn Salon in October 1927, were described by Dalí as "equidistant between Cubism and Surrealism" and featured dreamlike images, precise draftsmanship, idiosyncratic iconography (like rotting donkeys and dismembered bodies), and landscapes evocative of Catalonia. These works caused bemusement among the public and debate among critics about whether he had become a Surrealist. Influenced by Freud and Lautréamont, Dalí introduced suggestive sexual imagery into his work; Dialogue on the Beach (Unsatisfied Desires) (1928) was rejected by the Barcelona Autumn Salon for being too provocative, sparking a scandal widely covered in the press and prompting a Madrid illustrated weekly to publish an interview with Dalí. Throughout the 1920s, Dalí was influenced by a range of styles, from classical masters like Raphael, Bronzino, Francisco de Zurbarán, Vermeer, and Velázquez to avant-garde movements, resulting in a mixture of praise and puzzled debate from critics due to the blend of traditional and modern techniques. In the mid-1920s, he grew a neatly trimmed mustache, later cultivating a more flamboyant one in the style of Diego Velázquez, which became a well-known Dalí icon. In 1929, Dalí collaborated with Luis Buñuel on the short film Un Chien Andalou (An Andalusian Dog), contributing to the script, though contemporary accounts do not substantiate a significant role in filming. That same year, he met his lifelong muse and future wife Gala, born Elena Ivanovna Diakonova, a Russian immigrant ten years his senior who was then married to poet Paul Éluard. In works such as The First Days of Spring, The Great Masturbator, and The Lugubrious Game, Dalí explored themes of sexual anxiety and unconscious desires. His first Paris exhibition at the Goemans Gallery in November 1929 featured eleven works, with André Breton describing the work as "the most hallucinatory that has been produced up to now"; the exhibition was commercially successful but critically divided. In 1929, Dalí officially joined the Surrealist group in Montparnasse, Paris, and the Surrealists recognized his paranoiac-critical method of accessing the subconscious. His relationship with his father deteriorated due to his romance with Gala and his association with Surrealism; the final incident occurred when his father read in a Barcelona newspaper that Dalí had exhibited a drawing of the Sacred Heart of Jesus with the inscription "Sometimes, I spit for fun on my mother's portrait," leading to a public demand for recantation. Dalí refused, possibly fearing expulsion from the Surrealist group, and was violently thrown out of his home on 28 December 1929, with his father declaring he would be disinherited and barred from Cadaqués. The following summer, Dalí and Gala rented a small fisherman’s cabin in Port Lligat, which he later bought and expanded into a beloved seaside villa. His father eventually accepted his son’s companion. In 1931, Dalí painted The Persistence of Memory, featuring soft, melting pocket watches, interpreted as a rejection of rigid time, supported by expansive landscapes and watches being devoured by ants. In June 1931 and May–June 1932, he held two exhibitions at the Pierre Colle Gallery in Paris, with the first including sixteen paintings, of which The Persistence of Memory drew the most attention. The exhibitions featured images of Gala and Surrealist objects such as Hypnagogic Clock and Clock Based on the Decomposition of Bodies. His largest exhibition at Pierre Colle in June 1933 included twenty-two paintings, ten drawings, and two objects, with one critic noting his precise draftsmanship and calling him a "paranoiac of geometrical temperament." His first New York exhibition at Julien Levy’s gallery in November–December 1933 featured twenty-six works and was a commercial and critical success, with The New Yorker praising the precision and lack of sentimentality, calling them "frozen nightmares." Dalí and Gala were civilly married on 30 January 1934 in Paris and later remarried in a church ceremony on 8 August 1958 at Sant Martí Vell. Gala managed Dalí’s business affairs, supporting their extravagant lifestyle while avoiding insolvency, and despite her own extra-marital affairs, she tolerated Dalí’s relationships with younger muses, remaining his primary partner. Dalí continued to paint Gala as they aged, producing sympathetic and adoring images. Their long, tense, complex, and ambiguous relationship, lasting over 50 years, became the subject of the opera Jo, Dalí (I, Dalí) by Catalan composer Xavier Benguerel. Dalí’s first U.S. visit in November 1934 attracted widespread press coverage; his second New York exhibition at Julien Levy in November–December 1934 was again a commercial and critical success. He delivered three lectures on Surrealism at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and other venues, stating for the first time that "[t]he only difference between me and a madman is that I am not mad." The heiress Caresse Crosby organized a farewell fancy dress ball on 18 January 1935, where Dalí wore a glass case on his chest containing a brassiere and Gala dressed as a woman giving birth through her head; a Paris newspaper claimed the Dalís dressed as the Lindbergh baby and his kidnapper, a claim Dalí denied. While most Surrealists aligned with leftist politics, Dalí maintained an ambiguous stance on politics and art. André Breton accused Dalí of defending the "new" and "irrational" in "the Hitler phenomenon," but Dalí rejected the claim, stating, "I am Hitlerian neither in fact nor intention," and insisted that Surrealism could exist in an apolitical context, refusing to explicitly denounce fascism.

Salvador Dalí delivered three lectures on Surrealism at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and other venues, during which he first stated that "[t]he only difference between me and a madman is that I am not mad." In January 1935, the heiress Caresse Crosby, inventor of the brassiere, organized a farewell fancy dress ball for Dalí, where Dalí wore a glass case on his chest containing a brassiere and Gala dressed as a woman giving birth through her head; a Paris newspaper later claimed the Dalís had dressed as the Lindbergh baby and his kidnapper, a claim Dalí denied. While most Surrealists aligned with leftist politics, Dalí maintained an ambiguous stance on politics and art; André Breton accused Dalí of supporting the "Hitler phenomenon," but Dalí rejected this, stating, "I am Hitlerian neither in fact nor intention," and insisted Surrealism could exist apolitically, refusing to denounce fascism. In 1934, Dalí narrowly avoided expulsion from the Surrealist group during a "trial," to which he responded, "The difference between the Surrealists and me is that I am a Surrealist." In 1936, Dalí participated in the London International Surrealist Exhibition, delivering a lecture titled *Fantômes paranoiacs authentiques* while wearing a deep-sea diving suit and helmet; he had arrived with a billiard cue and Russian wolfhounds and required the helmet to be unscrewed as he gasped for breath, commenting that he wanted to show he was "plunging deeply into the human mind." His first solo London exhibition at the Alex, Reid, and Lefevre Gallery that year included twenty-nine paintings and eighteen drawings, receiving generally favorable critical response, though the Daily Telegraph critic noted the artist's return to full consciousness was "awaited with interest." In December 1936, Dalí participated in the Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism exhibition at MoMA and a solo exhibition at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York, both drawing large crowds and widespread press coverage; the painting *Soft Construction with Boiled Beans (Premonition of Civil War)* (1936) attracted particular attention, with Dalí describing it as "a vast human body breaking out into monstrous excrescences of arms and legs tearing at one another in a delirium of auto-strangulation." On 14 December, aged 32, Dalí was featured on the cover of Time magazine. From 1933, Dalí was supported by Zodiac, a group of affluent admirers who contributed monthly to his stipend in exchange for a painting of their choice; from 1936, Edward James became his primary patron in London, supporting him financially for two years, and they collaborated on *The Metamorphosis of Narcissus* (1937) and the iconic works *Lobster Telephone* and *Mae West Lips Sofa*. Dalí was in London when the Spanish Civil War broke out in July 1936; upon learning that his friend Lorca had been executed by Nationalist forces, he reportedly shouted "Olé," a reference he included in his art and writings for the rest of his life, though he avoided taking a public stance for or against the Republic during the conflict. In January 1938, Dalí unveiled *Rainy Taxi*, a three-dimensional artwork featuring an automobile and two mannequin occupants being soaked with rain from within, first displayed at the Galerie Beaux-Arts in Paris at the Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme, organized by André Breton and Paul Éluard, designed by Marcel Duchamp, who also hosted the event. In March 1938, Dalí met Sigmund Freud through Stefan Zweig; as Dalí sketched Freud's portrait, Freud whispered, "That boy looks like a fanatic," which Dalí later found delightful; the next day Freud wrote to Zweig, "until now I have been inclined to regard the Surrealists... as complete fools... that young Spaniard, with his candid fanatical eyes and his undeniable technical mastery, has changed my estimate. It would indeed be very interesting to investigate analytically how he came to create that picture [i.e. Metamorphosis of Narcissus]." In September 1938, Dalí was invited by Gabrielle Coco Chanel to her house "La Pausa" in Roquebrune on the French Riviera, where he painted numerous works later exhibited at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in March–April 1939, including twenty-one paintings and eleven drawings; Life reported the exhibition was the most popular in New York since Whistler's Mother in 1934. At the 1939 New York World's Fair, Dalí debuted his *Dream of Venus* Surrealist pavilion in the Amusements Area, featuring bizarre sculptures, statues, mermaids, and live nude models in "costumes" made of fresh seafood, photographed by Horst P. Horst, George Platt Lynes, and Murray Korman; Dalí was angered by design changes, railing against mediocrities who thought "a woman with the tail of a fish is possible; a woman with the head of a fish impossible." After Franco's victory in the Spanish Civil War in April 1939, Dalí wrote to Luis Buñuel denouncing socialism and Marxism and praising Catholicism and the Falange, leading Buñuel to break off relations with Dalí. In the May issue of *Minotaure*, André Breton announced Dalí's expulsion from the Surrealist group, claiming Dalí had espoused race war and that the over-refinement of his paranoiac-critical method repudiated Surrealist automatism, causing many Surrealists to sever ties with him; in 1949, Breton coined the derogatory nickname "Avida Dollars" (avid for dollars), an anagram for "Salvador Dalí," a derisive reference to the commercialization of Dalí's work and his perceived pursuit of fame and fortune. The outbreak of World War II in September 1939 found the Dalís in France; following the German invasion, they escaped after being issued visas by Aristides de Sousa Mendes, Portuguese consul in Bordeaux, on 20 June 1940, crossing into Portugal and sailing on the Excambion from Lisbon to New York in August 1940. Dalí and Gala lived in the United States for eight years, splitting their time between New York and the Monterey Peninsula, California. Dalí spent the winter of 1940–41 at Hampton Manor, the residence of Caresse Crosby in Caroline County, Virginia, where he worked on his autobiography and paintings for an upcoming exhibition. In April–May 1941, Dalí announced the death of the Surrealist movement and the return of classicism in an exhibition at the Julien Levy Gallery, which included nineteen paintings (among them *Slave Market with the Disappearing Bust of Voltaire* and *The Face of War*) and other works; in his catalog essay and media comments, he proclaimed a return to form, control, structure, and the Golden Section, though sales were disappointing and most critics did not see a major shift in his work. On 2 September 1941, he hosted *A Surrealistic Night in an Enchanted Forest* in Monterey, a charity event that attracted national attention but raised little money. MoMA held two major, simultaneous retrospectives of Dalí and Joan Miró from November 1941 to February 1942, with Dalí represented by forty-two paintings and sixteen drawings; the exhibition attracted significant critical attention and later toured eight American cities, enhancing his reputation in America. In October 1942, Dalí's autobiography, *The Secret Life of Salvador Dalí*, was published simultaneously in New York and London and widely reviewed; Time magazine's reviewer called it "one of the most irresistible books of the year," while George Orwell wrote a scathing review in the *Saturday Book*; a passage in which Dalí claimed Buñuel was solely responsible for the anti-clericalism in *L'Age d'Or* may have indirectly led to Buñuel resigning from MoMA in 1943 under pressure from the State Department. Dalí also published a novel, *Hidden Faces*, in 1944 with less critical and commercial success. In the catalog essay for his 1943 exhibition at the Knoedler Gallery, Dalí continued his attack on Surrealism, writing: "Surrealism will at least have served to give experimental proof that total sterility and attempts at automatizations have gone too far and have led to a totalitarian system. ... Today's laziness and the total lack of technique have reached their paroxysm in the psychological signification of the current use of the college [collage]." The critical response to the society portraits in the exhibition was generally negative. From November to December 1945, Dalí exhibited new work at the Bignou Gallery in New York, including eleven oil paintings, watercolors, drawings, and illustrations such as *Basket of Bread*, *Atomic and Uranian Melancholic Ideal*, and *My Wife Nude Contemplating her own Body Transformed into Steps, the Three Vertebrae of a Column, Sky and Architecture*; the exhibition was notable for works in Dalí's new classicism style and those heralding his "atomic period." During the war years, Dalí worked on ballet designs including *Labyrinth* (1942), *Sentimental Colloquy*, *Mad Tristan*, and *The Cafe of Chinitas* (all 1944), and in 1945 created the dream sequence for Alfred Hitchcock's film *Spellbound*; he also produced artwork and designs for perfumes, cosmetics, hosiery, and ties. In 1946, Dalí collaborated with Walt Disney and animator John Hench on an unfinished animated film, *Destino*. In November 1947 to January 1948, Dalí exhibited new work at the Bignou Gallery, including 14 oil paintings and other works reflecting his growing interest in atomic physics; notable works included *Dematerialization Near the Nose of Nero (The Separation of the Atom)*, *Intra-Atomic Equilibrium of a Swan's Feather*, and a study for *Leda Atomica*, whose proportions were worked out with a mathematician. In early 1948, Dalí's *50 Secrets of Magic Craftsmanship* was published, a mixture of anecdotes, practical advice on painting, and Dalínian polemics. In 1948, Dalí and Gala moved back into their house in Port Lligat, near Cadaqués, where they would spend most of their time for the next three decades, spending winters in Paris and New York; Dalí's decision to live in Spain under Franco and his public support for the regime provoked outrage from many anti-Francoist artists and intellectuals, with Pablo Picasso refusing to mention Dalí's name or acknowledge him for the rest of his life. In 1960, André Breton unsuccessfully opposed the inclusion of Dalí's *Sistine Madonna* in the Surrealist Intrusion in the Enchanter's Domain exhibition organized by Marcel Duchamp in New York; Breton and other Surrealists issued a tract denouncing Dalí as "the ex-apologist of Hitler ... and friend of Franco." In December 1949, Dalí's sister Anna Maria published *Salvador Dalí Seen by his Sister*, which Dalí found derogatory toward Gala, leading to a break with his family; when Dalí's father died in September 1950, he learned he had been virtually disinherited in his will, triggering a two-year legal dispute over paintings and drawings left in the family home, during which Dalí was accused of assaulting a public notary. As Dalí embraced Catholicism, he introduced more religious iconography in his work; in 1949 he painted a study for *The Madonna of Port Lligat* (first version, 1949) and showed it to Pope Pius XII during an audience about his marriage to Gala; this work preceded his "Nuclear Mysticism" phase, a fusion of Einsteinian physics, classicism, and Catholic mysticism, evident in paintings such as *The Madonna of Port Lligat*, *The Christ of Saint John of the Cross*, and *The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory*, with later works including *La Gare de Perpignan* (1965) and *The Hallucinogenic Toreador* (1968–70). Dalí's interest in natural science and mathematics grew, with images of DNA and rhinoceros horn shapes appearing in mid-1950s works; according to Dalí, the rhinoceros horn grows in a logarithmic spiral, signifying divine geometry; he was also fascinated by the Tesseract (a four-dimensional cube), using it in *Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)*. Dalí had long used optical illusions such as double images, anamorphosis, negative space, visual puns, and trompe-l'œil, continuing these in his later work; at some point, he installed a glass floor in a room near his studio in Port Lligat to study foreshortening from above and below, incorporating dramatic perspectives into his paintings. He also experimented with the bulletist technique, pointillism, enlarged half-tone dot grids, and stereoscopic images; he was among the first artists to employ holography artistically. In his later years, young artists such as Andy Warhol proclaimed him an important influence on pop art. In 1960, Dalí began work on his Theatre-Museum in his hometown of Figueres, which became his largest single project and a main focus until its opening in 1974, with continued additions through the mid-1980s. In 1955, Dalí met Nanita Kalaschnikoff, who became a close friend, muse, and model; at a French nightclub in 1965, he met Amanda Lear, then known as Peki Oslo, who became his protégée and muse; according to Lear, she and Dalí were united in a "spiritual marriage" on a deserted mountaintop. In 1968, Dalí bought the Castle of Púbol for Gala, and from 1971 she retreated there for weeks at a time, with Dalí agreeing not to visit without her written permission; his fears of abandonment and estrangement from his muse contributed to depression and failing health. In 1980, at age 76, Dalí's health deteriorated sharply, with treatment for depression, drug addiction, and Parkinson-like symptoms, including a severe tremor in his right arm; there were allegations that Gala had been supplying Dalí with pharmaceuticals from her own prescriptions. Gala died on 10 June 1982, at age 87; after her death, Dalí moved from Figueres to the castle in Púbol, where she was entombed. In 1982, King Juan Carlos bestowed on Dalí the title of Marqués de Dalí de Púbol (Marquess of Dalí de Púbol) in the nobility of Spain, with Púbol being where Dalí lived; the title was initially hereditary but changed to life-only at Dalí's request in 1983. In May 1983, what was said to be Dalí's last painting, *The Swallow's Tail*, was revealed, heavily influenced by the mathematical catastrophe theory of René Thom; however, some critics questioned how Dalí could have executed such a precise painting given the severe tremor in his painting arm. From early 1984, Dalí's depression worsened and he refused food.

Gala died on 10 June 1982 at the age of 87. After her death, Dalí moved from Figueres to the castle in Púbol, where she was entombed. In 1982, King Juan Carlos bestowed on Dalí the title of Marqués de Dalí de Púbol in the nobility of Spain, Púbol being where Dalí then lived. The title was initially hereditary but at Dalí's request was changed to life-only in 1983. In May 1983, what was said to be Dalí's last painting, The Swallow's Tail, was revealed. The work was heavily influenced by the mathematical catastrophe theory of René Thom. However, some critics have questioned how Dalí could have executed a painting with such precision given the severe tremor in his painting arm. From early 1984, Dalí's depression worsened and he refused food, leading to severe undernourishment. Dalí had previously stated his intention to put himself into a state of suspended animation as he had read that some microorganisms could do. In August 1984 a fire broke out in Dalí's bedroom and he was hospitalized with severe burns. Two judicial inquiries found that the fire was caused by an electrical fault and no findings of negligence were made. After his release from hospital Dalí moved to the Torre Galatea, an annex to the Dalí Theatre-Museum. There have been allegations that Dalí was forced by his guardians to sign blank canvases that could later be used in forgeries. It is also alleged that he knowingly sold otherwise-blank lithograph paper which he had signed, possibly producing over 50,000 such sheets from 1965 until his death. As a result, art dealers tend to be wary of late graphic works attributed to Dalí. In July 1986, Dalí had a pacemaker implanted. On his return to his Theatre-Museum he made a brief public appearance, saying: "When you are a genius, you do not have the right to die, because we are necessary for the progress of humanity." In November 1988, Dalí entered hospital with heart failure. On 5 December 1988, he was visited by King Juan Carlos, who confessed that he had always been a serious devotee of Dalí. Dalí gave the king a drawing, Head of Europa, which would turn out to be Dalí's final drawing. On the morning of 23 January 1989, Dalí died of cardiac arrest at the age of 84. He is buried in the crypt below the stage of his Theatre-Museum in Figueres. The location is across the street from the church of Sant Pere, where he had his baptism, first communion, and funeral, and is only 450 metres (1,480 ft) from the house where he was born. On 26 June 2017, it was announced that a judge in Madrid had ordered the exhumation of Dalí's body in order to obtain samples for a paternity suit. Joan Manuel Sevillano, manager of the Fundación Gala Salvador Dalí (The Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation), denounced the exhumation as inappropriate. The exhumation took place on the evening of 20 July, and his DNA was extracted. On 6 September 2017, the Foundation stated that the tests carried out proved conclusively that Dalí and the claimant were not related. On 18 May 2020, a Spanish court dismissed an appeal from the claimant and ordered her to pay the costs of the exhumation. From the late 1920s, Dalí progressively introduced many bizarre or incongruous images into his work which invite symbolic interpretation. While some of these images suggest a straightforward sexual or Freudian interpretation (Dalí read Freud in the 1920s), others (such as locusts, rotting donkeys, and sea urchins) are idiosyncratic and have been variously interpreted. Some commentators have cautioned that Dalí's own comments on these images are not always reliable. Food and eating have a central place in Dalí's thoughts and work. He associated food with beauty and sex and was obsessed with the image of the female praying mantis eating her mate after copulation. Bread was a recurring image in Dalí's art, from his early work The Basket of Bread to later public performances such as in 1958 when he gave a lecture in Paris using a 12-meter-long baguette an illustrative prop. He saw bread as "the elementary basis of continuity" and "sacred subsistence". The egg is another common Dalínian image. He connects the egg to the prenatal and intrauterine, thus using it to symbolize hope and love. It appears in The Great Masturbator, The Metamorphosis of Narcissus and many other works. There are also giant sculptures of eggs in various locations at Dalí's house in Portlligat as well as at the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres. The radial symmetry of the sea urchin intrigued Dalí. He had enjoyed eating them with his father at Cadaqués and, along with other foods, they became a recurring theme in his work. The famous "melting watches" that appear in The Persistence of Memory suggest Einstein's theory that time is relative and not fixed. Dalí later claimed that the idea for clocks functioning symbolically in this way came to him when he was contemplating Camembert cheese. The rhinoceros and rhinoceros horn shapes began to proliferate in Dalí's work from the mid-1950s. According to Dalí, the rhinoceros horn signifies divine geometry because it grows in a logarithmic spiral. He linked the rhinoceros to themes of chastity and to the Virgin Mary. However, he also used it as an obvious phallic symbol as in Young Virgin Auto-Sodomized by the Horns of Her Own Chastity. Various other animals appear throughout Dalí's work: rotting donkeys and ants have been interpreted as pointing to death, decay, and sexual desire; the snail as connected to the human head (he saw a snail on a bicycle outside Freud's house when he first met him); and locusts as a symbol of waste and fear. The elephant is also a recurring image in his work; for example, Dream Caused by the Flight of a Bee Around a Pomegranate a Second Before Awakening. The elephants are inspired by Gian Lorenzo Bernini's sculpture base in Rome of an elephant carrying an ancient obelisk. Dalí's life-long interest in science and mathematics was often reflected in his work. His soft watches have been interpreted as references to Einstein's theory of the relativity of time and space. Images of atomic particles appeared in his work soon after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and strands of DNA appeared from the mid-1950s. In 1958 he wrote in his Anti-Matter Manifesto: "In the Surrealist period, I wanted to create the iconography of the interior world and the world of the marvelous, of my father Freud. Today, the exterior world and that of physics have transcended the one of psychology. My father today is Dr. Heisenberg." The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory (1954) harks back to The Persistence of Memory (1931) and in portraying that painting in fragmentation and disintegration has been interpreted as a reference to Heisenberg's quantum mechanics. Dalí was a versatile artist. Some of his more popular works are sculptures and other objects, and he is also noted for his contributions to theater, fashion, and photography, among other areas. From the early 1930s, Dalí was an enthusiastic proponent of the proliferation of three-dimensional Surrealist Objects to subvert perceptions of conventional reality, writing: "museums will fast fill with objects whose uselessness, size and crowding will necessitate the construction, in deserts, of special towers to contain them." His more notable early objects include Board of Demented Associations (1930–31), Retrospective Bust of a Woman (1933), Venus de Milo with Chest of Drawers (1936) and Aphrodisiac Dinner Jacket (1936). Two of the most popular objects of the Surrealist movement were Lobster Telephone (1936) and Mae West Lips Sofa (1937) which were commissioned by art patron Edward James. Lobsters and telephones had strong sexual connotations for Dalí who drew a close analogy between food and sex. The telephone was functional, and James purchased four of them from Dalí to replace the phones in his home. The Mae West Lips Sofa was shaped after the lips of actress Mae West, who was previously the subject of Dalí's watercolor, The Face of Mae West which may be used as a Surrealist Apartment (1934–35). In December 1936 Dalí sent Harpo Marx a Christmas present of a harp with barbed-wire strings. After World War II Dalí authorized many sculptures derived from his most famous works and images. In his later years other sculptures also appeared, often in large editions, whose authenticity has sometimes been questioned. Between 1941 and 1970, Dalí created an ensemble of 39 pieces of jewelry, many of which are intricate, some containing moving parts. The most famous assemblage, The Royal Heart, is made of gold and is encrusted with 46 rubies, 42 diamonds, and four emeralds, created in such a way that the center "beats" like a heart. Dalí ventured into industrial design in the 1970s with a 500-piece run of Suomi tableware by Timo Sarpaneva that Dalí decorated for the German Rosenthal porcelain maker's "Studio Linie". In 1969 he designed the Chupa Chups logo. He facilitated the design of the advertising campaign for the 1969 Eurovision Song Contest and created a large on-stage metal sculpture that stood at the Teatro Real in Madrid. In theater, Dalí designed the scenery for Federico García Lorca's 1927 romantic play Mariana Pineda. For Bacchanale (1939), a ballet based on and set to the music of Richard Wagner's 1845 opera Tannhäuser, Dalí provided both the set design and the libretto. He executed designs for a number of other ballets including Labyrinth (1942), Sentimental Colloquy, Mad Tristan, The Cafe of Chinitas (all 1944) and The Three-Cornered Hat (1949). Dalí became interested in film when he was young, going to the theater most Sundays. By the late 1920s he was fascinated by the potential of film to reveal "the unlimited fantasy born of things themselves" and went on to collaborate with the director Luis Buñuel on two Surrealist films: the 17-minute short Un Chien Andalou (1929) and the feature film L'Age d'Or (1930). Dalí and Buñuel agree that they jointly developed the script and imagery of Un Chien Andalou, but there is controversy over the extent of Dalí's contribution to L'Age d'Or. Un Chien Andalou features a graphic opening scene of a human eyeball being slashed with a razor and develops surreal imagery and irrational discontinuities in time and space to produce a dreamlike quality. L'Age d'Or is more overtly anti-clerical and anti-establishment, and was banned after right-wing groups staged a riot in the Parisian theater where it was being shown. Summarizing the impact of these two films on the Surrealist film movement, one commentator has stated: "If Un Chien Andalou stands as the supreme record of Surrealism's adventures into the realm of the unconscious, then L'Âge d'Or is perhaps the most trenchant and implacable expression of its revolutionary intent." After he collaborated with Buñuel, Dalí worked on several unrealized film projects including a published script for a film, Babaouo (1932); a scenario for Harpo Marx called Giraffes on Horseback Salad (1937); and an abandoned dream sequence for the film Moontide (1942). In 1945 Dalí created the dream sequence in Hitchcock's Spellbound, but neither Dalí nor the director was satisfied with the result. Dalí also worked with Walt Disney and animator John Hench on the short film Destino in 1946. After initially being abandoned, the animated film was completed in 2003 by Baker Bloodworth and Walt Disney's nephew Roy E. Disney. Between 1954 and 1961 Dalí worked with photographer Robert Descharnes on The Prodigious History of the Lacemaker and the Rhinoceros, but the film was never completed. In the 1960s Dalí worked with some directors on documentary and performance films including with Philippe Halsman on Chaos and Creation (1960), Jack Bond on Dalí in New York (1966) and Jean-Christophe Averty on Soft Self-Portrait of Salvador Dalí (1966). Dalí collaborated with director José-Montes Baquer on the pseudo-documentary film Impressions of Upper Mongolia (1975), in which Dalí narrates a story about an expedition in search of giant hallucinogenic mushrooms. In the mid-1970s film director Alejandro Jodorowsky initially cast Dalí in the role of the Padishah Emperor in a production of Dune, based on the novel by Frank Herbert. However, Jodorowsky changed his mind after Dalí publicly supported the execution of alleged ETA terrorists in December 1975. The film was ultimately never made. In 1972 Dalí began to write the scenario for an opera-poem called Être Dieu (To Be God). The Spanish writer Manuel Vázquez Montalbán wrote the libretto and Igor Wakhévitch the music. The opera poem was recorded in Paris in 1974 with Dalí in the role of the protagonist. Fashion designer Elsa Schiaparelli worked with Dalí from the 1930s and commissioned him to produce a white dress with a lobster print. Other designs Dalí made for her include a shoe-shaped hat and a pink belt with lips for a buckle. He was also involved in creating textile designs and perfume bottles. In 1950, Dalí created a special "costume for the year 2045" with Christian Dior. Photographers with whom he collaborated include Man Ray, Brassaï, Cecil Beaton, and Philippe Halsman. Halsman produced the Dalí Atomica series (1948) – inspired by Dalí's painting Leda Atomica – which in one photograph depicts "a painter's easel, three cats, a bucket of water, and Dalí himself floating in the air". Dalí's architectural achievements include his Port Lligat house near Cadaqués, as well as his Theatre Museum in Figueres. A major work outside of Spain was the temporary Dream of Venus Surrealist pavilion at the 1939 New York World's Fair, which contained several unusual sculptures and statues, including live performers posing as statues. In 1958, Dalí completed Crisalida, a temporary installation promoting a drug, which was exhibited at a medical convention in San Francisco. In his only novel, Hidden Faces (1944), Dalí describes the intrigues of a group of eccentric aristocrats whose extravagant lifestyle symbolizes the decadence of the 1930s. The Comte de Grandsailles and Solange de Cléda pursue a love affair, but interwar political turmoil and other vicissitudes drive them apart. It is variously set in Paris, rural France, Casablanca in North Africa, and Palm Springs in the United States. Secondary characters include aging widow Barbara Rogers, her bisexual daughter Veronica, Veronica's sometime female lover Betka, and Baba, a disfigured U.S. fighter pilot. The novel was written in New York, and translated by Haakon Chevalier. His other literary works include The Secret Life of Salvador Dalí (1942), Diary of a Genius (1966), and Oui: The Paranoid-Critical Revolution (1971). Dalí also published poetry, essays, art criticism, and a technical manual on art. Dalí worked extensively in the graphic arts, producing many drawings, etchings, and lithographs. Among the most notable of these works are forty etchings for an edition of Lautréamont's The Songs of Maldoror (1933) and eighty drypoint reworkings of Goya's Caprichos (1973–77). From the 1960s, however, Dalí would often sell the rights to images but not be involved in the print production itself. In addition, a large number of fakes were produced in the 1980s and 1990s, thus further confusing the Dalí print market.

Salvador Dalí, a disfigured U.S. fighter pilot, is known for his extensive body of work, which includes The Secret Life of Salvador Dalí (1942), Diary of a Genius (1966), and Oui: The Paranoid-Critical Revolution (1971), as well as poetry, essays, art criticism, and a technical manual on art. He worked extensively in the graphic arts, producing many drawings, etchings, and lithographs, including forty etchings for an edition of Lautréamont's The Songs of Maldoror (1933) and eighty drypoint reworkings of Goya's Caprichos (1973–77). From the 1960s, Dalí often sold the rights to images without participating in print production, and a large number of fakes were produced in the 1980s and 1990s, further complicating the Dalí print market. Book illustrations were central to his career; his first was for the 1924 Catalan poem Les bruixes de Llers by Carles Fages de Climent, and other notable illustrations include 101 watercolors and engravings for The Divine Comedy (1960) and 100 drawings and watercolors for The Arabian Nights (1964). As a youth, Dalí identified as communist, anti-monarchist, and anti-clerical, and was briefly imprisoned in 1924 by the Primo de Rivera dictatorship for being "intensely liable to cause public disorder." In 1929, he joined the Surrealist group, where his political activism initially increased; he contributed to the Workers' and Peasants' Front in 1931 and delivered lectures, but as divisions grew, he adopted a more apolitical stance, refusing to denounce fascism. In 1934, André Breton accused him of sympathizing with Hitler, and Dalí narrowly avoided expulsion; in 1935, he wrote a letter to Breton suggesting non-white races should be enslaved. During the Spanish Civil War in 1936, Dalí avoided taking a public stand, but after Franco's victory in 1939, he praised Catholicism and the Falange and was expelled from the Surrealists. After returning to Catalonia in 1948, he publicly supported Franco’s regime and returned to the Catholic faith; he was granted audiences with Pope Pius XII in 1949 and Pope John XXIII in 1959, and had official meetings with General Franco in June 1956, October 1968, and May 1974. In 1968, Dalí stated that upon Franco’s death, Spain should become an absolute monarchy and there should be no return to democracy. In September 1975, he publicly supported Franco’s execution of three alleged Basque terrorists and reiterated his support for an absolute monarchy, saying, "Personally, I'm against freedom; I'm for the Holy Inquisition." Following this, he fled to New York after his home in Port Lligat was stoned and he received numerous death threats. When King Juan Carlos visited the ailing Dalí in August 1981, he told him: "I have always been an anarchist and a monarchist." Dalí espoused a mystical view of Catholicism and claimed to be both a Catholic and an agnostic, showing interest in the writings of Jesuit priest and philosopher Teilhard de Chardin and his Omega Point theory; his painting Tuna Fishing (Homage to Meissonier) (1967) was inspired by Chardin. Dalí's sexuality profoundly influenced his work; he stated that as a child seeing graphic illustrations of venereal diseases led to a lifelong disgust of female genitalia and fear of impotence and sexual intimacy. He described his main sexual activity as voyeurism and masturbation, with a preferred orifice being the anus, and claimed that his wife Gala was the only person with whom he achieved complete coitus. From 1927, his work featured graphic and symbolic sexual images associated with shame and disgust, including anal and fecal imagery, evident in works such as The First Days of Spring (1929), The Great Masturbator (1929), and The Lugubrious Game (1929). Several intimates from the 1960s and 1970s reported that he arranged choreographed sexual activities for selected guests to aid his voyeurism and masturbation. Dalí was known for his eccentric and ostentatious behavior; in 1941, MoMA’s Director of Exhibitions wrote that while his conduct was undignified, his art was sincere. When elected to the French Academy of Fine Arts in 1979, a fellow academic hoped he would abandon his "clowneries." In 1936, at the premiere of Joseph Cornell’s film Rose Hobart at Julien Levy’s gallery, Dalí knocked over the projector and said, "My idea for a film is exactly that," adding he had never written it down. In 1939, after creating a window display for Bonwit Teller, he pushed a bathtub through a plate glass window due to unauthorized changes. In 1955, he delivered a lecture at the Sorbonne arriving in a Rolls-Royce full of cauliflowers. To promote Robert Descharnes' 1962 book The World of Salvador Dalí, he appeared in a Manhattan bookstore on a bed, wired to a machine measuring his brain waves and blood pressure, autographing books while monitored and giving buyers the paper charts. After World War II, Dalí became one of the world’s most recognized artists, with his long cape, walking stick, haughty expression, and upturned waxed mustache becoming iconic; he famously declared, "every morning upon awakening, I experience a supreme pleasure: that of being Salvador Dalí." He was a frequent television guest in Spain, France, and the United States, including appearances on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson (7 January 1963), The Mike Wallace Interview, and What's My Line?, and participated in advertising campaigns for Jack Winters sportswear and Lanvin chocolates. He often appeared in public with his pet anteater and ocelot Babou. By 1966, critics like Carlton Lake complained that his self-promotion overshadowed his art. Two major museums are dedicated to Dalí: the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres, Catalonia, Spain, and the Salvador Dalí Museum in St. Petersburg, Florida, U.S. His life and work have influenced pop art, other Surrealists, and contemporary artists such as Jeff Koons and Damien Hirst, and continue to impact contemporary culture, with portrayals in films like Little Ashes (2008), Midnight in Paris (2011), and Dalíland, and the Spanish television series Money Heist (2017–2021) featuring characters in red jumpsuits and Dalí masks, with the creator noting the mask was chosen as an iconic Spanish image. The Salvador Dalí Desert in Bolivia and the Dalí crater on Mercury are named after him, and the container ship MV Dali was named after him in 2015. The Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation serves as his official estate, with the Artists Rights Society acting as the U.S. copyright representative. Dalí produced over 1,600 paintings and numerous graphic works, sculptures, three-dimensional objects, and designs. Some of his major works are listed, and important books by or about Dalí are readily available in English.

Satyanarayan Gangaram Pitroda, popularly known as Sam Pitroda (born 16 November 1942), is an Indian official, telecommunications engineer, innovator, and entrepreneur. He was born in Titlagarh, in the eastern Indian state of Odisha, into a Gujarati family. He served as an advisor to Rajiv Gandhi and Manmohan Singh during their respective tenures as the Prime Minister of India, as well as to the United Nations.[3][4] He is the chairman of the Indian Overseas Congress.[5] He is often credited as the “Father of India’s Telecom Revolution” for his role in modernizing the country’s communications infrastructure and shaping India’s technology landscape during the 1980s.[6][7][8] In 1966, he began working for GTE in Chicago.[9] He is considered a pioneer of portable computing, as he invented the electronic diary in 1975.[10] He holds a master's degree in Physics and Electronics from Maharaja Sayajirao University (India) and a Master's in Electrical Engineering from the Illinois Institute of Technology (USA). Between 2005 and 2009, he chaired the National Knowledge Commission in India and served as an advisor to Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in the area of Public Information Infrastructure and Innovations. Since 2010, he has been the chairman of the National Innovation Council.[11] On a trip back to India in 1981, Pitroda was frustrated by how hard it was to call his family back in Chicago, and decided he could help modernize India's telecommunications system.[12] In 1984, Pitroda was invited to return to India by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. On his return, he started the Center for Development of Telematics (C-DOT), an autonomous telecom R&D organization. He had previously become a naturalized US citizen but renounced his US citizenship to take Indian citizenship again to work in the Indian Government.[13] In the 1990s Pitroda returned to Chicago to resume his business interests. In May 1995, he became the first chairman of the WorldTel initiative of the International Telecommunication Union.[14] In 1993, Pitroda helped establish (with Darshan Shankar) the Foundation for Revitalisation of Local Health Tradition and The University of Trans-Disciplinary Health Sciences and Technology near Bangalore in India. The foundation promotes Ayurveda, India's traditional medicinal knowledge.[15] In October 2009, Pitroda was appointed as advisor to Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Public Information Infrastructure and Innovations with the rank of Cabinet Minister.[16] In 1992, his biography Sam Pitroda: A Biography was published.[17] The Enforcement Directorate, on 15 April 2025, filed a chargesheet against him over his alleged involvement in the National Herald case.[18][19]

Samacá is a town and municipality located in the Central Boyacá Province within the Colombian Department of Boyacá. It shares borders with Cucaita and Tunja to the east, Ráquira to the west, Sáchica, Sora, and Cucaita to the north, and Ventaquemada, Ráquira, and Guachetá (in Cundinamarca) to the south.
