Shawnee Slopes is a residential neighbourhood located in the southwest quadrant of Calgary, Alberta, Canada, bordered to the south by James McKevitt Road, to the east by Macleod Trail, to the north by Fish Creek Provincial Park, and to the west by Evergreen Street SW. The neighbourhood is named after the Shawnee native people and is represented in the Calgary City Council by Ward 13 councillors. At its center lies the Shawnee Slopes Golf Course, which served as a primary amenity for residents and the public. On 13 June 2011, it was announced that the golf course would permanently close to the public on 2 October 2011. In February 2013, the city council approved the redevelopment of the golf course lands to construct 1,400 new homes. Shawnee Slopes is closely linked to the northern section of the adjacent Evergreen community, sharing the same community association, while the remainder of Evergreen operates independently. According to the City of Calgary's 2012 municipal census, Shawnee Slopes had a population of 1,565 living in 866 dwellings, representing a 2.4% increase from its 2011 population of 1,529. With a land area of 1.2 km² (0.46 sq mi), the population density was 1,300/km² (3,380/sq mi) in 2012. In 2005, residents had a median household income of $106,379, with 3.4% living in low-income households; in 2006, 26.9% of residents were immigrants. Additionally, 12.9% of the buildings were condominiums or apartments, and 1.6% of the housing was used for renting.

doc_name: She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye (album)
text: She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye is the thirteenth studio album by American musician and pianist Jerry Lee Lewis, released on Mercury Records in January 1970. It was Lewis's sixth album for Mercury following his 1968 comeback album Another Place, Another Time. During this period, Shelby Singleton, who purchased the entire Sun Records catalog from Sam Phillips on July 1, 1969, began releasing albums featuring unheard recordings by Lewis, many of them country songs, to capitalize on Jerry Lee's revitalized commercial appeal. As country music historian Colin Escott recounts in his essay for the 1986 Bear Family retrospective The Killer: The Smash/Mercury Years, "Singleton continued to release titles from the old Sun catalog (sometimes with new overdubs) as though they were current product, usually timing the releases so that they appeared just as Jerry's new smash single had peaked...Singleton began programming albums with vague themes, using contemporary photos wherever possible to create the illusion that these might be new recordings." Consequently, the market was flooded with product, turning Lewis into one of the most in-demand country artists in the business. By the dawn of the new decade, Lewis had scored five straight Top 5 country hits for Smash in less than two years (including the chart topper "To Make Love Sweeter For You"), and his streak continued with "She Even Woke Me Up To Say Goodbye," which made it all the way to number 2. The song was co-written by Mickey Newbury, who would become best known for his arrangement of "An American Trilogy," later made famous by Elvis Presley, but it was Lewis who had been the first major artist to cover one of Newbury's compositions, having recorded "Just Dropped In (To See What Condition My Condition Was In)" for his 1967 album Soul My Way. Lewis's vocal on "She Even Woke Me Up To Say Goodbye" has been widely praised, with biographer Rick Bragg opining in Jerry Lee Lewis: His Own Story, "Some songs make people think they were written for them. This is the opposite: in this song, it's as if Jerry were living inside the lyrics." In the book Jerry Lee Lewis: Lost and Found, producer Jerry Kennedy marvelled to Joe Bonomo, "He learned 'She Even Woke Me Up To Say Goodbye' and did that cut of it after hearing the song one time. He really is a genius." The album also features the top 5 hit "Once More with Feeling," which was written by Kris Kristofferson and Shel Silverstein. Bonomo quotes Kristofferson: "I consider Jerry Lee Lewis one of the great singers of all time. Put him up there with opera singers. He had a way of transforming my songs into something I couldn't believe I was hearing." The album continues with the winning formula established on Lewis's recent country albums like Another Place, Another Time and She Still Comes Around (To Love What's Left Of Me), pairing Jerry Lee's unmistakable piano playing and soulful vocals with top shelf Nashville musicians on a mixed bag of honky-tonk drinking songs and sad ballads. As on those two previous albums, Lewis covers a Merle Haggard song, this time the blue collar anthem "Workin' Man Blues" ("Down in Lou'siana," he adlibs during the instrumental break, "we call that boogie woogie!") and pays tribute to one of his musical heroes, Jimmie Rodgers, on the song "Waiting for a Train." However, Lewis's rock and roll roots also began showing through on several cuts, with AllMusic noting: "He had been riding high on his new hits - so successful that new collections of his Sun singles made it to the country Top Ten - and took that as encouragement to do whatever he damn well pleased on this new record. So, he cut pure rock & roll (a thundering cover of "Brown Eyed Handsome Man"), inserted his name in every other song (in every verse on "Since I Met You Baby," where he manages to find a place to say his full name), laughed and leered, growled and crooned, pounding and gliding down the keyboard in equal measure." According to the liner notes for the 2006 collection A Half Century of Hits, Kennedy didn’t dare release an uptempo single because he couldn't risk radio programmers declaring that Lewis was returning to his rockabilly past, so up-tempo songs like "Workin’ Man Blues" were consigned to LPs. Although Kennedy liked to record in closed sessions, he eventually came to appreciate that Lewis needed an audience: “Bad as I hated it, he did better with a crowd. I can remember 70 or 80 people in the control room and standing around the studio. One time we almost had a song nailed and there was a thunk right at the end. Some guy had left the studio and slammed the door. The engineer went down and was chewing him out. 'Why’d you do that?' The guy said, 'The ice in Jerry’s drink was melting.'" The ease with which Lewis conveyed these often bitterly sad country songs came as no surprise to him, as he explained in the 1990 documentary The Jerry Lee Lewis Story: "I am a rock and roll artist and I can cover the other country-type territory if I have to sneak in the back door...If you wanna be an ass-dragging hillbilly singer, you can be one if you really want to." She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye was released in January 1970 and rose to number 9 on the Billboard country album charts. Stephen Erlewine of AllMusic calls the album "the fieriest, loosest performances he's given since leaving Sun (not counting, of course, the then-unreleased Star Club live recording), which jolts the hardcore country of Another Place and She Still Comes Around to a different stratosphere. Those were spectacular pure country records by any measure, but this is a spectacular pure Jerry Lee country record, where he's the center of every cut, every performance, and the record is tremendously addictive for it." In 2009, Lewis biographer Joe Bonomo echoed these sentiments, writing that "Jerry Lee's last pure country record is the apex of his resurgence...Even Another Place, Another Time and She Still Comes Around (To Love What's Left Of Me) fall short of the kind of devotions to the rich traditions and history of honky-tonk music that this album reveals."

Sheila Levrant de Bretteville, born in 1940 in Brooklyn, New York, is an American graphic designer, artist, and educator whose work emphasizes feminist principles and user participation in design. Her parents were Polish immigrants who fled anti-semitism in the 1920s and worked in the textile and millinery industries; her mother introduced her to painting lessons at the Brooklyn Museum as a child. She graduated from Abraham Lincoln High School in 1959, where she studied under Leon Friend, who introduced her to modern graphic design and its social responsibilities and encouraged her to enter design and painting competitions. De Bretteville earned a BA in art history from Barnard College in 1962 and an MFA in graphic design from Yale University in 1964. She has received honorary doctorates from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts), the Moore College of Art, and the California College of the Arts. In 1969, she moved to Los Angeles, working as an in-house graphic designer at CalArts before becoming the first woman faculty member in its design department in 1970. In 1971, she founded the first design program for women at CalArts, and two years later co-founded the Woman's Building, a public center in Los Angeles focused on women's education and culture. In 1973, she founded the Women's Graphic Center and co-founded the Feminist Studio Workshop with Judy Chicago and Arlene Raven, both based at the Woman's Building. She designed a necklace featuring an eye bolt on a chain, symbolizing "strength without a fist" and the biological identity of women; she gave the first to Arlene Raven and Judy Chicago when they started the Feminist Studio Workshop in 1972 and has since given similar necklaces to other women aligned with her vision for women's culture. Members of the Feminist Studio Workshop from 1978–79 produced 500 such necklaces to celebrate the fifth anniversary of the Woman's Building. The feminist art group Sisters of Jam (Mikaela & Moa Krestesen) transformed the necklace into a mobile monument, interpreting the eye bolt as a symbol of completed and ongoing work, and installed "Hello Sheila" at the Survival Kit Festival in Umeå in 2014. In 1980, she initiated the communication design program at the Otis College of Art and Design, a division of the New School. De Bretteville has long advocated for communal forms of art as central to the U.S. feminist art movement; in 1973, she created "Pink," a broadside exploring gender and the color pink for an American Institute of Graphic Arts exhibition, which was the only entry on that color. She arranged paper squares into a "quilt" from which posters were printed and distributed in Los Angeles, earning her the nickname "Pinky." She has created numerous public artworks embedded in city neighborhoods, including "Biddy Mason's Place: A Passage of Time," an 82-foot concrete wall with embedded objects in downtown Los Angeles that chronicles the life of Biddy Mason, a former slave who became a midwife in Los Angeles and lived near the site, which she created in collaboration with Betye Saar. In 1994, she completed "Path of Stars" in a New Haven neighborhood, featuring 21 granite stars embedded in the sidewalk documenting the lives of local residents—past and present. In 1996, she collaborated with artist Sonya Ishii on "Remembering Little Tokyo" in Los Angeles, where they interviewed residents and created brass tiles etched with symbols representing local history and Japanese American identities. She also designed the mural "At the Start... At Long Last" for the Inwood-207th Street station in New York City, inspired by the song "Take the A Train" by Billy Strayhorn. De Bretteville was interviewed for the film !Women Art Revolution and is a member of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences. She has received numerous awards, including a 2009 "Grandmaster" award from the New York Art Directors Club, a "Design Legend Gold Medal" from the American Institute of Graphic Arts in 2004, a "Best Public Artwork" recognition from Americans for the Arts in 2005, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Women's Caucus for Art in 2016. In 1990, she became the director of the Yale University Graduate Program in Graphic Design and the first woman to receive tenure at the Yale University School of Art. In 2010, she was named the Caroline M. Street Professor of Graphic Design.

Shepard Alonzo Mount (1804–1868) was an American artist trained at the National Academy of Design during the mid-nineteenth century, known for his realistic portrayals in still-life and landscape genres, with portraiture being his most celebrated work. Born on July 17, 1804, in Setauket, New York, he was one of five children of Julia Ann Hawkins (1782–1841) and Thomas Shepard Mount (1778–1814), with siblings Henry Smith Mount (1802–1841), Robert Nelson (1806–1883), William Sidney Mount (1807–1868), and Ruth Hawkins (1808–1888). The family operated an inn and farm until Thomas Shepard’s death in 1814, after which they moved to Stony Brook, New York, to live with Julia Ann’s parents, Ruth and Jonas Hawkins. Shepard’s introduction to the fine arts came through practical craftsmanship. Julia Ann apprenticed him to carriage builder James Brewster in New Haven, Connecticut, where he worked from 1821 to about 1828, refining his understanding of color theory, style, and design. In 1827, he ended the apprenticeship and reunited with his brothers Henry and William in New York City, enrolling in drawing classes at the National Academy of Design. Henry had opened a business in ornamental painting, and William worked alongside him; the brothers practiced drawing in the evenings. In 1828, Shepard and William opened a portrait studio at 15 Cherry Street in New York City, which closed due to lack of success, prompting their move to Athens, Pennsylvania. Shepard returned to New York and studied portrait painting with Henry Inman. Early in his career, he focused on still-life paintings, with his first exhibition in 1829 at the Academy titled *Still Life; Composition*. He was particularly skilled in fish still lifes, noting in a letter to William that he believed fish were the only subjects he painted well. He admired nature and created landscape paintings, though he rarely exhibited them. His 1861 painting *Hudson River Scene* depicts two ornately dressed Native Americans gazing across the Hudson River, with a man in a rowboat symbolizing the journey through life and the passage of time; most of his landscapes were based on the Susquehanna River near the New York-Pennsylvania state line near Athens. After the brothers closed the portrait shop in 1829, Shepard worked in Athens, painting portraits for relatives and friends for over a half year until returning to Stony Brook in 1830, where he painted the now-lost portrait of Dr. Henry S. Dering and created his earliest surviving portrait, *Tamer*, of an African American woman who worked at the St. James estate of William and Eliza Mills. His portraits later became more traditional, with tighter brushwork and compositional formats, often including background elements that reflected the subject’s occupation or social status. Influenced by Henry Inman, Shepard learned portraiture techniques through shared outdoor activities like hunting and fishing, abandoning background details in favor of using color and brushstroke to convey individuality. In 1833, he painted John Bedell using strong contrast, linear brushstrokes, and crisp colors to highlight Bedell’s nature, and in 1834, he painted his sister Ruth with looser, more romantic brushwork and playful color to reflect her delicate personality. The portrait of John Bedell was exhibited in 1833 as his first public piece, and later that year he was elected an associate member of the National Academy of Design. His reputation grew, and he began receiving commissions from New York City socialites, including business owners and Wall Street executives from the rising upper-middle class. His first major professional portrait was of his wife, Elizabeth Elliott Mount, completed in 1838, the year after their marriage, and exhibited at the National Academy of Design. In 1838, the couple began a family, with their children William Shepard Mount (born 1839), Ruth (known as Tutie, born 1842), Joshua (born 1845), and Robert (born 1853); Shepard often used his children as models. His peak career achievement was *Rose of Sharon* (1850), a portrait of his daughter Ruth (1842–1861), or Tutie, painted gently holding flowers to highlight her delicate beauty and youthful fertility. The painting features advanced color use and a glowing skin, with landscape elements in the background—a technique he frequently employed. Goupil et Cie, a Paris-based publishing firm, commissioned a lithograph reproduction of *Rose of Sharon*, which was distributed commercially in the U.S. and Europe, significantly increasing his fame. Elizabeth died in August 1858 at age 42, and Shepard left his children in his sister Ruth’s care in Stony Brook for six weeks. In 1861, Tutie died of consumption at age 19, four months after marriage. In 1863, his eldest son William Shepard was drafted into the Confederate Army in Mississippi and later captured by Union soldiers, who mistook him for a spy. Shepard secured his release through a letter from artist Francis Bicknell Carpenter, who was painting a portrait of Abraham Lincoln and endorsed William’s plea; Lincoln ordered his release. Shepard continued painting into his later years, completing his final work, *Camille Mount*, a portrait of his deceased granddaughter, on September 12, 1868. He died in Stony Brook six days later at age 64 from cholera and is buried in the Saint James Episcopal Church Graveyard in Saint James, New York.

Dr. Sher Afgan Khan Niazi (Urdu: شیر افگن خان نیازی; died 11 October 2012) was a Pakistani politician who served as Minister of Parliamentary Affairs of Pakistan. His real uncle was AK Niazi, also known as General Niazi. He was elected for a fourth time to the National Assembly in 2002 as a member of the Pakistan Peoples Party (Parliamentarians), but later switched his allegiance to the PPPP (Patriot) and then joined the Pakistan Muslim League (Q). Sher Afgan Niazi supported President Pervez Musharraf's actions in 2007, including the ousting, detention, and replacement of Supreme Court judges, and backed Musharraf's military operation at Lal Masjid in Islamabad. On 18 February 2008, he lost the general election to independent candidate Humair Hayat Khan Rokhri. On April 8, 2008, he was attacked in Lahore, Punjab, by lawyers protesting against his support for the dismissal of Supreme Court judges and the Lal Masjid operation, an incident that sparked strong protests in his home town. Niazi joined President Pervez Musharraf's newly formed political party, the All Pakistan Muslim League (APML), but later resigned due to differences with the party leadership. He was highly knowledgeable in constitutional affairs and had a strong command over the Constitution of Pakistan. He completed his M.B.B.S degree from Nishtar Medical College in Multan, Punjab. Niazi was known for memorizing all the articles of the Constitution of Pakistan. His health declined gradually after one of his sons died in a car accident in Rawalpindi, and he was diagnosed with liver cancer in 2012. Pankaj Singh Pundir, popularly known as Sher Singh Rana or S. Rana, is an Indian politician born on 17 May 1976 in a Hindu Rajput family in Roorkee, Uttarakhand, India.[8][9] He was sentenced in August 2014 to life imprisonment and a fine of ₹100,000 (approximately US$1,600) for the 2001 assassination of Phoolan Devi, a dacoit-turned-parliamentarian who was a sitting Member of Parliament in the 13th Lok Sabha, along with charges of conspiracy after a 10-year trial.[5][6] Rana, along with two other men, murdered Phoolan Devi outside her home in New Delhi in July 2001, claiming revenge for her actions as a leader of a bandit gang that targeted higher castes in the late 1970s and early 1980s. He was arrested and confessed to the murder.[11][12] On 17 February 2004, Rana escaped from Tihar jail, a high-security prison in Delhi, went to Moradabad, checked into a hotel, and received ₹1 lakh from relatives. From Ranchi, he applied for a passport in the name of Sanjay Gupta.[14] During a two-month wait for the passport, he visited Gaya and Benaras, then went to Kolkata where he obtained a three-month Bangladesh visa. Rana claimed he rented a house in Khulna and lived there posing as Sanjay Gupta. After fleeing to Bangladesh, he bought a satellite phone for ₹16,500 to contact relatives and friends without being tracked. He traveled from Moradabad to Ranchi, Kolkata, Bangladesh, Dubai, and later to Afghanistan, where he is said to have brought back the ashes of the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan.[17] He received approximately ₹15,000 to ₹20,000 per month and visited Kolkata regularly to extend his visa, sometimes in Dhaka.[18] On 25 April 2006, he was re-arrested in Kolkata by the SIT, who tracked him down through his subscription to a Hindi newspaper, one of the few people in the Dharmatala area who did so.[19][20] In January 2012, a trial court allowed Rana to file nomination papers from Tihar to contest the Uttar Pradesh assembly election.[21] The Delhi High Court granted him bail, and he was released on 24 October 2016.[22] On 28 February 2018, he married Pratima Singh, daughter of Pratap Singh; however, some newspapers incorrectly stated that Pratap Singh was a former Member of Legislative Assembly from Madhya Pradesh; in fact, Rekha Yadav was the MLA from Malhara in 2008.[23] The marriage was conducted with a shagun of only a silver coin and without accepting a dowry of 10 crore rupees worth property and 31 lakh rupees in cash.[24][25][26] In 2019, Rana formed his own political party, the Rashtravadi Janlok Party (RJP).[27]

Sherri Louise Graeff-Papini, who was 34 years old at the time, disappeared on November 2, 2016, while jogging a mile from her home in Redding, California. She reappeared on Thanksgiving Day, November 24, 2016, at 4:30 a.m. on County Road 17 near Interstate 5 in Yolo County, about 150 miles (240 km) south of where she disappeared, still wearing restraints. The case attracted widespread media attention, with law enforcement experts questioning the credibility of her reported abduction due to inconsistent and unlikely details. In August 2020, Papini maintained her story during questioning by a federal agent and a detective from the Shasta County Sheriff's Office. Between 2017 and 2021, she received over $30,000 from the California Victim Compensation Board. On March 3, 2022, Papini was arrested on federal charges for fabricating the kidnapping; she had been staying with her former boyfriend, James Reyes, during the time she was allegedly missing, and according to Reyes, she had asked him to harm her to support her false claims. Six weeks later, on April 3, 2022, she pleaded guilty to one count of mail fraud and one count of making false statements, admitting she had orchestrated the hoax. In September 2022, she was sentenced to 18 months in prison and three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay $309,902, including restitution for the multi-state police investigation. Her husband, Keith Papini, filed for divorce and sought sole custody of their two children shortly after her guilty plea, and the couple separated on March 3, 2022, the day of her arrest. On November 2, 2016, Keith returned home to find Sherri missing and eventually discovered her cell phone and earbuds at an intersection about a mile away. In interviews, Papini claimed she was held by two Hispanic women who masked their faces or kept her head covered and was branded on her right shoulder with the word "EXODUS," which she said resembled a verse from the Book of Exodus. Keith stated that Sherri was physically abused during captivity, with her nose broken, hair cut off, and her weight reduced to 87 pounds (39 kg) when released. Authorities were actively investigating, seeking a dark-colored SUV with two Hispanic females armed with a handgun, and issued nearly 20 search warrants, including in Michigan, examining cellphone records, bank accounts, emails, and social media. The FBI assisted in the investigation. DNA found on Papini did not match her or her husband, and CODIS showed no matches; however, DNA on her clothing matched James Reyes, who confirmed she stayed with him in Southern California during the disappearance. On March 3, 2022, the FBI arrested her, accusing her of lying to federal agents and faking her kidnapping to spend time with Reyes. In April 2022, she pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in Sacramento to one count of making false statements and one count of mail fraud, with 33 other mail fraud counts dropped. At sentencing, she apologized and accepted responsibility; her attorney cited past mental health issues. She was released from prison in August 2023 and placed in a halfway house. The case was widely covered in national news and true crime programming, including a People front cover profile and multiple documentaries and podcasts. In a 2025 interview with Inside Edition, Papini admitted difficulty finding employment due to the case's global attention. A 2023 Lifetime film, Hoax: The Kidnapping of Sherri Papini, was the first scripted film based on the hoax, with Jaime King playing Papini and Lossen Chambers portraying the lead detective (though in reality, the lead detective was Shasta County Sheriff Sergeant Kyle Wallace). Hulu released the limited documentary series Perfect Wife: The Mysterious Disappearance of Sherri Papini on June 19, 2024. Eminem references the hoax in his song "Houdini" with the line "...Caught sleepin' and see the kidnappin' never did happen (no), Like Sherri Papini, Harry Houdini, I vanish into the thin air as I'm leaving like...". The Investigation Discovery series Sherri Papini: Caught in the Lie premiered on May 26, 2025, featuring Papini’s first public interview since conviction and exploring her marriage to Keith, their custody dispute, her relationship with James Reyes, the post-nuptial agreement, and the FBI’s investigative rationale. In the series, Papini claimed her injuries—including bruises, a waist chain, and a brand—were non-consensually inflicted by Reyes, but Reyes denied the allegations and passed a polygraph, stating she voluntarily stayed with him and that she both inflicted and asked for some injuries, including the branding. Medical examiners and an FBI criminal analyst concluded the wounds were consistent with deliberate, self-inflicted or controlled injuries, not prolonged abuse. Papini also claimed to have bite marks, which forensic experts later identified as rashes. Papini has a documented history of self-harm and false abuse reports, including a 2003 incident when her mother filed a report with the Shasta County Sheriff's Office alleging self-harm and blaming others for the injuries.

Shubhneet Singh, born on 10 August 1997, is an Indian rapper-singer and songwriter based in Canada, known professionally as Shubh, and associated with Punjabi music. He rose to mainstream popularity in 2021 with the single "We Rollin" and released his debut album, Still Rollin, in 2023. His singles, including "Elevated," "Offshore," "No Love," "Baller," and "Her," have charted on the Canadian Hot 100, New Zealand Chart, UK Singles Chart, and Billboard India. "Baller," produced by Ikky, became his most streamed track and reached number 68 on the Canadian Hot 100. The album Still Rollin debuted at number 16 on the Billboard Canadian Albums Chart and charted on the New Zealand Albums Chart; "Cheques" from the album peaked at number 3 on Billboard India Songs. Shubh was born in Punjab, India, to a Punjabi Sikh family and has an elder brother, Ravneet Singh, who is an actor, singer, vocalist, and host. He began his musical career in Brampton, Canada. In August 2023, he announced the Still Rolling world tour across seven countries—India, UK, Australia, New Zealand, UAE, USA, and Canada—divided into seven phases. The India phase included 10 cities and a cruise event at Cruise Control 4.0 in Mumbai aboard the Cordelia Cruise, but on 20 September 2023, BookMyShow announced the cancellation of the India tour, following the withdrawal of sponsorship by electronics brand boAt due to controversy. The UK phase featured concerts in London and Birmingham. On 5 January 2024, Shubh released his first EP, Leo, under his own label. On 29 March 2024, he released the single "Bandana" without prior announcement. On 10 April 2024, he announced the Aus/Nz phase, including concerts in Melbourne, Brisbane, Auckland, and Sydney, with tickets available on Shubhtour.com starting 3 May 2024; the Brisbane show on 4 May was cancelled due to promoter mismanagement and lack of communication, resulting in the revocation of the show permit due to venue load issues. On 3 May in Melbourne, Shubh performed his unreleased song "MVP," which was later released on his YouTube channel on 10 May 2024. In March 2023, during a curfew in Punjab due to a police search for pro-Khalistan separatist Amritpal Singh and internet shutdowns, Shubh shared an Instagram story titled "Pray for Punjab," featuring a distorted map created by Amandeep Singh (pseudonym Inkquisitive), showing Punjab, Haryana, and Himachal Pradesh darkened and omitting northeastern states and Jammu and Kashmir, which drew criticism for misrepresenting India. Actress Kangana Ranaut accused the post of indirect support for the Khalistan movement. Shubh removed the story and replaced it with "Pray for Punjab" on a black background. Inkquisitive later apologised, stating it was not intended to provoke a separate state agenda but to depict a "blackout in Punjab." On 19 September 2023, Inkquisitive reiterated the intent and blamed Ranaut for giving it a "pro-khalistan angle." On 21 September, Shubh clarified his concern over the internet shutdown in Punjab and expressed disappointment over the tour cancellation, stating, "India is my country too." Artists such as AP Dhillon, Karan Aujla, and Sidhu Moose Wala's team, along with politicians including Harsimrat Kaur Badal, Amrinder Singh Raja Warring, and Bikram Singh Majithia, publicly supported him. During a London concert on 29 October 2023, Shubh held up a black hoodie thrown by the audience, allegedly bearing the date and image of the assassination of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by her bodyguards Satwant Singh and Beant Singh on a map of Punjab; he later posted that many items, including clothing, jewellery, and phones, were thrown at him, which he did not inspect, along with a video.

Sidney Abbott (July 11, 1937 – April 15, 2015) was an American feminist and lesbian activist and writer. Born on July 11, 1937, into a military family, she described herself as a military brat. She attended Smith College for three years and graduated from the University of New Mexico in 1961. She then pursued graduate studies in urban planning at Columbia University. In 1969, she joined the National Organization for Women (NOW) and became one of the first individuals to advocate for lesbian rights on panels at the New York chapter of NOW and at Columbia University. A member of the Lavender Menace, she co-authored Sappho Was a Right-on Woman: A Liberated View of Lesbianism with Barbara Love in 1971. In the mid-1970s, with Barbara Love, she lobbied for the establishment of a NOW task force focused on lesbian issues, which was eventually created and initially named the "sexuality and lesbian task force"; Abbott co-chaired the task force with a heterosexual woman. At the NOW national conference in Philadelphia in 1976, she successfully demanded that 1% of the organization’s budget be allocated to the task force, a resolution that passed as one of only two to do so. She served on the founding board of the National Gay and Lesbian Task Force and worked to ensure the organization’s board had equal representation of gay men and lesbian women. She was named by the Manhattan Borough President to the community planning board, becoming the first openly gay person to hold that position. She also served as program developer for two departments in the New York City government, co-chaired the New York Performing Arts Center, and was politically active in the North Fork area of Long Island, New York. Abbott and Kate Millett, Phyllis Birkby, Alma Routsong, and Artemis March were among the members of CR One, the first lesbian-feminist consciousness-raising group. She lived in Southold, New York, where in 2007 she founded the Women's Rights are Human Rights nonprofit and in 2008 launched a newsletter, In Our Shoes, covering politics, class, and poverty. Her personal archives are housed in the Sophia Smith Collection at Smith College and in the Radcliff College feminist collection of NOW biographies. Abbott died in a house fire in Southold, New York on April 15, 2015, at the age of 77.

Sigurd Arthur Aalefjær (14 September 1917 – 10 March 1991) was a Norwegian engineer, civil servant, and director of Norwegian hydropower plants. He was born in Bend, Oregon, as the son of Wilhelm Torjussen Aalefjær (1881–1969) and Inger Larsen Kostøl (1890–1975), and the family relocated to Vennesla in Vest-Agder, Norway. He married Magda Synnøve Berg (1920–2002) in 1943 and lived and died in Bærum. He completed his secondary education at Kristiansand Cathedral School in 1937 and earned a construction engineering degree from the Norwegian Institute of Technology in Trondheim in 1941. He worked for the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Agency from 1942 to 1946, then at Drammens Elektrisitetsverk from 1946 to 1949, and returned to the Water Resources and Energy Agency in 1949. From 1960 until his retirement in 1984, he served as the director of Statskraftverkene (now Statkraft). He was awarded the Knight, First Class of the Order of St. Olav in 1983. This article about a Norwegian engineer is a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

Silas Alexander Holcomb (August 25, 1858 – April 25, 1920) was a Nebraska lawyer and politician who served as the ninth Governor of Nebraska from 1895 to 1899, running under a fusion ticket between the Populist and Democratic Parties. Born in Gibson County, Indiana, he helped on the family farm and attended local schools during the winter. At seventeen, he began teaching school. After his father's death in 1878, he moved with his mother and siblings to Hamilton County, Nebraska in 1879. He worked at the Thummel & Platt law office in Grand Island and was admitted to the Nebraska bar in 1882. On April 13, 1882, he married Martha Alice Brinson in Mills County, Iowa. They moved to Broken Bow, where he farmed and practiced law. From 1891 to 1894, Holcomb served as a 12th District judge. In 1894, with the support of William Jennings Bryan, he was elected Governor of Nebraska and was re-elected in 1896. During his tenure, sounder financial policies were initiated, corruption and mismanagement in the state treasurer's office were addressed, and reforms in state government programs were begun. Following his time as governor, Holcomb was appointed a judge of the Nebraska Supreme Court in 1899 and served as chief judge from 1904 to 1906. He left the Court in 1906 but later served on the Nebraska Board of Commissioners of State Institutions from 1913 until his failing health required him to resign. In 1896, Holcomb was accused of tampering with ballots concerning constitutional amendments. In 1899, The Norfolk Weekly News accused him of ballot fraud in an attempt to "steal two seats on the supreme bench" during a party meeting, alleging that votes were changed and that when a recount was requested, "Holcomb paid no attention to their suggestions." He was ultimately appointed to serve on the court in 1899. Holcomb moved to Bellingham, Washington, where he lived with his daughter until his death on April 25, 1920. His body was returned to Nebraska, and he is interred at Broken Bow Cemetery, Broken Bow, Custer County, Nebraska.

Harsimrat Kahlon (1982 – October 4, 2009) was an Indian-Canadian serial killer who murdered three of her newborn infants between 2005 and 2009 in Calgary. After her death from complications of childbirth on October 4, 2009, her common-law husband Harnek Mahal discovered the infants' bodies stuffed in a suitcase and a box, reporting the findings to police, who later determined the children had been murdered by their mother. Kahlon was born in Chandigarh, India in 1982, to Sikh parents. In 1999, she emigrated to Canada, settling with her aunt and uncle in Martindale. She worked as an assistant and receptionist at a law firm, where colleagues described her as a hard worker who appeared happy. Her live-in boyfriend, Harnek Mahal, was a long-haul trucker who worked away from home, and the couple were described as quiet and reserved. They initially lived in a basement suite in Falconridge before moving to Taradale in 2006. On October 4, 2009, after returning home from work, Mahal found Kahlon lying face-down in her bedroom, motionless; he called the police, who ruled her death as non-suspicious due to childbirth complications. The next day, Mahal reported finding a suspicious suitcase in a garbage bag with blood and other fluids dripping from it. A medical examiner opened the bag and found a newborn infant inside. A more thorough search, conducted by Mahal's sister just hours later, uncovered another box containing two additional corpses and a placenta. Mahal stated he knew Kahlon had been pregnant in the early 2000s and that they had agreed she would have an abortion, but he was unaware of the other two pregnancies. Forensic psychologist Dr. J. Thomas Dalby concluded Kahlon likely suffered from a personality disorder or depression, resulting in an unstable personality and self-loathing. In her secret diary, Kahlon expressed no guilt about the children's deaths but showed some attachment to them, as she kept the bodies on her property after their deaths. The first child, Reet Kahlon, was a girl born in 2005 at the Peter Lougheed Centre to an unknown father and was found wearing a hospital ID bracelet. The other two infants, unnamed, were born alive at home in the summer of 2009 while Mahal was away. Bloodied towels, sheets, clothing, cloths, and a garden hose were used as crude instruments during the killings, and Kahlon hid the bodies in her bedroom, spraying air freshener to mask the odor of decaying flesh. Questions about why Kahlon killed the children and why she kept the bodies remain unanswered, and the case has been officially closed by authorities.

Sing Sing Correctional Facility is a maximum-security prison for men operated by the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, located in the village of Ossining, New York, United States, approximately 30 miles (48 km) north of Midtown Manhattan on the east bank of the Hudson River. It holds about 1,500 inmates as of 2019 and employed around 900 people, hosting over 5,000 visitors per month. The prison originally opened in 1826 as the fifth prison built by New York state authorities, with construction beginning in 1825 after the legislature appropriated $20,100 (roughly $559,000 in 2024) to purchase a 130-acre (53 ha) site in Mount Pleasant, near the village of Sing Sing. The name "Sing Sing" comes from the Wappinger Native American words sinck sinck, meaning 'stone upon stone,' and was formerly the name of the village. In 1970, the prison was renamed Ossining Correctional Facility, but reverted to Sing Sing in 1985. The prison property is bisected by the Metro-North Railroad's four-track Hudson Line. Sing Sing was initially considered a model prison because it turned a profit, and its early operations included a hard labor system centered on quarrying, with stones used to build notable structures like Lyndhurst mansion and Grace Church. Warden Elam Lynds implemented the Auburn system, enforcing absolute silence through whippings and other punishments. In 1844, the New York Prison Association was formed to promote humane treatment and prisoner rehabilitation, leading to Eliza Farnham being appointed to lead the women's ward at Sing Sing, where she introduced social engagement and secular literature, including novels by Charles Dickens, to the prison library. Thomas Mott Osborne, a radical reformer, served briefly as warden in 1914, criticizing traditional prison administration and writing the influential book Society and Prisons: Some Suggestions for a New Penology. After facing political opposition and being indicted, he was vindicated in court and returned to Sing Sing, where he was celebrated by inmates. Lewis Lawes served as warden from 1920 to 1941, transforming the prison into a modern facility with sports, education, and new disciplinary methods, and retired in 1941, dying six years later. In 1943, the original cellblock was closed, and its metal bars and doors were donated to the war effort. Sing Sing housed the state's execution chamber until 1963, when the last execution occurred on August 15, 1963, involving Eddie Lee Mays for murder; the final execution in New York state. A total of 614 men and women—including four under federal death sentences—were executed at Sing Sing until the abolition of the death penalty in 1972. A new Death House was built in 1920 and began executions in 1922, with high-profile cases including the Rosenbergs on June 19, 1953, and Gerhard Puff on August 12, 1954. In 1972, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Furman v. Georgia that the death penalty was unconstitutional due to inconsistency and arbitrariness, leading to a temporary nationwide moratorium, though executions resumed in other states in 1977. The electric chair at Sing Sing was moved to Green Haven Correctional Facility in the early 1970s and never used again. In 1996, Katherine Vockins founded Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA) at Sing Sing, offering year-round theater workshops that improved cognitive behavior and reduced recidivism, with a formal evaluation by John Jay College for Criminal Justice showing that longer participation led to fewer inmate violations. RTA now operates at five other New York state prisons. The program was dramatized in the 2023 film Sing Sing, starring Colman Domingo and featuring real-life former inmates. Hudson Link for Higher Education in Prison, founded in 1998 by Anne Reissner through private funding after state and federal support was halted during a get-tough-on-crime campaign, provides college courses to reduce recidivism and strengthen families. In 1931, prisoners were allowed recreation opportunities, including baseball and football teams, vaudeville, and concerts, funded by ticket sales; Tim Mara sponsored the Sing Sing Black Sheep football team, providing equipment and coaching, though the program ended in 1936 when the state banned ticket sales and revenue from events, cutting off funding for prisoner families and staff. The expression "up the river" to describe someone going to prison originated in 1891 from the practice of sentencing individuals to Sing Sing, located up the Hudson River from New York City. The wardens of Sing Sing are appointed by the Commissioner of the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision. Plans to convert the original 1825 cell block into a period museum began in 2002, with local officials proposing a $5 million project linked to a retired cell block, later seeking $12.5 million in federal funding in 2007, with the museum intended to display the prison's history. The prison's coordinates are 41°9′6″N 73°52′8″W.

The Sir George Stokes Award, commonly referred to as the Stokes Medal, is named in honor of George Gabriel Stokes and is presented every two years by the Analytical Division of the Royal Society of Chemistry. Established in 1999, the award was created to acknowledge the multidisciplinary aspects of analytical chemistry[1] and is bestowed upon individuals from complementary fields who have made outstanding and sustained contributions to analytical science, resulting in developments of seminal significance to chemical analysis. There are no restrictions on the nationality of candidates eligible for the award. Source: Royal Society of Chemistry

Siri (/ˈsɪri/ ⓘ SEER-ee) is a virtual assistant and chatbot developed and popularized by Apple Inc., included in iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, macOS, Apple TV, audioOS, and visionOS. It uses voice queries, gesture-based control, focus-tracking, and a natural-language interface to answer questions, make recommendations, and perform actions by delegating requests to Internet services. Over time, Siri adapts to users' individual language use, searches, and preferences, delivering personalized results. Originating from a project at the SRI International Artificial Intelligence Center, Siri is a spin-off of the DARPA-funded CALO project and was co-founded by Dag Kittlaus, Tom Gruber, and Adam Cheyer. The name Siri, a short form of the Old Norse name Sigrid (composed of "sigr" meaning victory and "fríðr" meaning beautiful), was named by Kittlaus after a co-worker in Norway. Siri's speech recognition engine was provided by Nuance Communications, which was acquired by Scansoft, later bought by Nuance; Apple licensed the recordings. The original American voice was recorded in July 2005 by Susan Bennett, unaware of its future use; a report in 2013 suggested Allison Dufty was the voice, but she denied it, and Bennett confirmed her role with audio forensics support. The original British male voice was provided by Jon Briggs, who narrated The Weakest Link and discovered his role in 2011; the original Australian voice was provided by Karen Jacobsen, known as the GPS girl. The initial prototype used the Active platform, a joint project between SRI International and École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, led by Didier Guzzoni, who became Siri’s chief scientist. Apple acquired Siri in April 2010 under Steve Jobs’ direction, and it was first released as a standalone app for iOS in February 2010, with plans for Android and BlackBerry devices. On October 4, 2011, Apple introduced Siri as a built-in feature of the iPhone 4S, removing the standalone app from the App Store. Third-party developers like Steven Troughton-Smith and "Chpwn" later ported and hacked Siri to run on older devices. Siri supports a wide range of commands, including phone actions, information checks, scheduling, device settings, Internet searches, navigation, entertainment queries, and interactions with iOS-integrated apps. With iOS 10 (2016), Apple opened limited third-party access via an API for messaging, payments, ride-sharing, and calling apps. iOS 11 added support for follow-up questions, language translation, and expanded third-party actions, including task management. In iOS 11, Apple also introduced typing to Siri and implemented on-device learning to improve suggestions. iOS 17 and iPadOS 17 enabled users to activate Siri by saying "Siri," while "Hey Siri" remains supported. In 2024, Apple introduced initial large language model (LLM) functionality to Siri in iOS 18, iPadOS 18, and macOS Sequoia, including ChatGPT integration, under the "Apple Intelligence" umbrella. In 2025, Apple announced a broader overhaul of Siri based on Apple Intelligence would be delayed due to technical challenges. In 2026, Apple selected Google Gemini to power AI features like Siri. Siri received mixed reviews upon its 2011 release, praised for voice recognition and contextual knowledge but criticized for stiff commands, lack of flexibility, poor understanding of accents, and limited information on nearby places. Critics noted Siri's lack of innovation compared to competitors like Amazon's Alexa, Microsoft's Cortana, and Google's Assistant, with concerns over voice recognition, service integrations, and Apple's prioritization of user privacy and internal power struggles. In 2017, a report highlighted Apple's slow progress in voice assistant innovation, citing privacy policies and internal conflicts. In 2019, a former Apple contractor revealed that Siri occasionally records user conversations when activated and sends them to contractors evaluating responses. Siri has also faced criticism from pro-abortion rights groups, including the ACLU and NARAL Pro-Choice America, for failing to provide information on birth control or abortion providers and instead directing users to crisis pregnancy centers. Apple stated these were not intentional omissions, and while Siri began offering more comprehensive lists of Planned Parenthood facilities, adoption clinics still appear near the bottom of results. Siri has also struggled with users having distinctive English accents, such as Scottish or Southern U.S. accents. In March 2012, Frank M. Fazio filed a class-action lawsuit claiming Apple misrepresented Siri’s capabilities, alleging the iPhone 4S was merely a more expensive iPhone 4. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2013 due to insufficient documentation of misrepresentation. In June 2016, The Verge reported that Siri's core flaws—poor voice recognition and clunky results—remained unresolved, especially as competitors advanced. In October 2016, Bloomberg reported Apple planned to unify its cloud services teams to improve Siri’s query processing, though The Verge later reiterated in 2017 that Siri's voice recognition remained "bad." Apple has expanded Siri to newer iPhone models, iPad, iPod Touch, Mac, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod, and Apple Vision Pro. In 2021, Apple announced Siri integration for third-party devices on the same network as a HomePod or HomePod Mini, with the Ecobee SmartThermostat becoming the first such device in October 2021. In 2024, Denon added Siri control to select soundbars and smart speakers. Siri also offers humorous pre-programmed responses, such as "All evidence to date suggests it's chocolate" to "What is the meaning of life?" or "My End User Licensing Agreement does not cover marriage" to "Will you marry me?" Initially limited to female voices in most countries, Apple added a male voice option in June 2013, with notable exceptions in the UK, France, and the Netherlands. In September 2014, users could say "Hey Siri" to activate the assistant without holding the device, and in September 2015, individualized voice recognition was introduced to prevent unauthorized activation. In iOS 17 and iPadOS 17, Siri supports back-to-back requests and bilingual queries. In iOS 18, iPadOS 18, and macOS Sequoia, Siri features an updated interface, improved natural language processing, and text interaction via double-tapping the home bar (without enabling in Accessibility). Apple states Siri now uses device context to make conversations more natural, provides device support, and offers larger app support via the Siri App Intents API. For example, a user can ask, "When is Mom's flight landing?" and Siri will cross-reference flight details with real-time tracking. Siri also summarizes messages across apps like Discord and Slack, though users note this can be inappropriate in certain situations. Apple Intelligence enables Siri to deliver personalized, context-aware intelligence using on-device information. Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt acknowledged that Siri could threaten Google's core search business.

Siri's voice recognition has been described as "bad."[88] In June 2017, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was falling behind in voice assistant innovation due to competitors like Amazon and Google advancing in the field, noting that Apple workers' anxiety levels "went up a notch" upon learning of Amazon's Alexa. The report attributed this lag to Apple's emphasis on user privacy—such as storing randomly-tagged six-month Siri searches—compared to Google and Amazon, which retain data until users actively delete it,[clarification needed] and internal executive power struggles at Apple. Apple did not respond to the report, though Eddy Cue stated: "Apple often uses generic data rather than user data to train its systems and has the ability to improve Siri's performance for individual users with information kept on their iPhones."[15][89] In July 2019, an anonymous former Apple contractor, Thomas le Bonniec, revealed that Siri regularly records user conversations when activated, often unintentionally, and sends these recordings to Apple contractors who grade Siri's performance on various factors. These recordings include private doctor-patient conversations, business deals, and intimate moments between couples. Apple did not disclose this in its privacy documentation and provided no opt-in or opt-out option.[90] In August 2019, Apple apologized, suspended the Siri grading program, and stated it would resume "later this fall when software updates are released to [its] users."[91] The company also announced it would no longer listen to Siri recordings without user permission.[92] iOS 13.2, released in October 2019, introduced the ability for users to opt out of the grading program and delete all stored voice recordings on Apple's servers.[93] Users could choose whether their audio data was sent to Apple, with the ability to change their decision at any time, making the program opt-in. In May 2020, Thomas le Bonniec revealed himself as the whistleblower and sent a letter to European data protection regulators, urging them to investigate Apple's "past and present" use of Siri recordings, arguing that despite the apology, Apple has not faced consequences for its years-long grading program.[94][95] In December 2024, Apple agreed to a $95 million class-action settlement to compensate users of Siri-enabled devices from the past ten years and committed to confirming the deletion of Siri recordings before 2019 (when the feature became opt-in) and issuing new guidance on data collection and user participation in improving Siri.[96] Apple has developed various accessibility features to make its devices more inclusive for individuals with disabilities, allowing users to share feedback via email.[97] Features include live speech, personal voice, Siri's atypical speech pattern recognition, and more.[98] Siri, like many AI systems, can perpetuate gender and racial biases; The Conversation argued that Siri reinforces the role of women as secondary and submissive to men due to its default soft, female voice.[103] According to The Scientific American, Claudia Lloreda noted that non-native English speakers must "adapt our way of speaking to interact with speech-recognition technologies."[104] Due to repeated learning from a large user base, Siri may unintentionally reflect a Western perspective, limiting representation and reinforcing biases in interactions. Despite these issues, Siri offers significant benefits, especially for people with disabilities who face barriers in using technology and accessing the internet. Apple has since expanded Siri's voice options to include various accents and languages.[105] The iOS version of Siri includes a vulgar content filter, but it is disabled by default and must be enabled manually by the user.[106] In 2018, Ars Technica reported a glitch where requesting the definition of "mother" caused Siri to respond by saying "mother" is short for "motherfucker" when the user replies "yes"—a response derived from third-party sources like the Oxford English Dictionary, not from Apple.[107] This led to numerous YouTube videos showing the responses or how to trigger them. Apple silently fixed the issue. Siri also provided the voice of 'Puter in The Lego Batman Movie.[109]

The Soko 522 was a two-seater military training and light attack aircraft developed in the 1950s by SOKO in Yugoslavia. It was designed by Yugoslav engineers Šostarić, Marjanović, and Čurčić at the Ikarus Aircraft Factory in Zemun, with the first prototype flying in February 1955. Following its initial success, production was moved to the Soko aircraft factory in Mostar and continued until 1961, resulting in a total of 110 units built. The aircraft served as the primary trainer for the Yugoslav air force until its retirement in 1978. It became well known for its appearances in war films produced in Yugoslavia during the 1960s and 1970s, where it was used to depict the Fw 190 German fighter. Notable film roles included the Yugoslav Oscar candidate *Battle of Neretva* and *Kelly's Heroes*, starring Clint Eastwood. According to Jane's All The World's Aircraft 1961–62[7], the Soko 522 had avionics including a radio system (AN-ARC-3) operating in the VKT 100-156 MHz range, with a communication range of 45 km at 1000 ft and 200 km at 10,000 ft, and a radiocompass (AN-ARN-6) operating between 100–1750 kHz or using the AD-722 system. The aircraft is listed among other aircraft of similar role, configuration, and era.

Solanum incanum Ruiz & Pav.[2]  
Solanum albidum is a species of nightshade native to western South America, ranging from southern Ecuador to northern Argentina, and thrives at mid elevations in the Andes. It is known by common names such as lumo (in Ecuador), huaritar (in Peru), and lavaplato plateado (in Bolivia). The plant can grow as either a shrub or a small tree. Its berries are dull yellow and measure 0.8–1.5 cm (0.31–0.59 in) in diameter.[2]

Solid State Logic Ltd. (SSL) is a British company headquartered in Begbroke, Oxfordshire, England, that designs and markets audio mixing consoles, signal processors, and other audio technologies for the post-production, video production, broadcast, sound reinforcement, and music recording industries. The company employs over 160 people worldwide and maintains regional offices in Los Angeles, Milan, New York City, Paris, and Tokyo, supported by an international network of distributors. SSL is part of the Audiotonix Group. Founded by Colin Sanders in 1969, SSL began as the first manufacturer of solid-state control systems for pipe organs, with Sanders naming the company to reflect the use of transistor and FET switching. Sanders also owned Acorn Studios in Stonesfield, Oxfordshire, where he designed and built two prototype mixing consoles with computer control, featuring one-button switching between recording, tracking, and mixdown modes, designated as the SL 4000 A. In 1976, SSL combined the SL 4000's in-line mixing console design with a computer that enabled fader automation and programmable tape transport auto-location; six B Series consoles were built and sold to studios, including Abbey Road Studios in London, Le Studio in Morin-Heights, Canada, Virgin Records' Townhouse Studios in London, and Tocano Studio in Copenhagen. The SL 4000 E Series, introduced in 1979, included a new 4-band EQ developed in collaboration with George Martin, introduced the ability to save and recall mixer settings, and was the first mixer to feature a compressor/gate on every channel as well as a master bus compressor. SSL launched the SL 4000 G Series at the AES New York Convention in 1987 with a redesigned EQ and other improvements. The ability to save and recall settings, along with dedicated compressors and noise gates on every channel in the E Series and its successors, led to widespread adoption in professional studios such as The Power Station, Sarm Studios, Larrabee Sound Studios, Battery Studios, Record One, Eden Studios, and RG Jones Recording Studios, and was used by engineers including Bob Clearmountain, Steve Lillywhite, Tom Lord-Alge, Alan Moulder, and Trevor Horn. The E Series and G Series were later offered in 5000, 6000, and 8000 Series formats to meet the needs of recording, film, video, and broadcast markets. SSL introduced SuperAnalogue design in the SL 9000 J Series, which used a capacitor-free signal path to achieve high bandwidth and extremely low distortion. In 1996, Billboard reported that 83% of number one singles that year were produced using an SSL mixing console, and the company claims more platinum albums have been recorded on its consoles than on any other company's equipment combined. By 2004, over 3,000 SSL-equipped facilities existed worldwide. In the 1990s, SSL developed products for post-production and motion pictures, introducing the A Series digital mixing consoles; in the 2000s, it launched the C Series consoles for broadcast production. In 2003, SSL introduced outboard signal processors offering processing previously available only in its large-format consoles, including the XLogic family, with the Logic Channel as its first standalone channel strip. In 2005, additional processors such as the E Series channel strip and G Series Compressor were released, using SSL's classic G Series center compressor design within a SuperAnalogue topology, and the X-Rack provided a modular outboard solution. In late 2004, SSL launched the AWS 900, an integrated analogue console and DAW controller, followed by its successor, the AWS 900+, two years later, with over 300 studios using the AWS 900. SSL later introduced the AWS 916, 924, and 948 with support for SSL's delta control plug-in. In late 2006, SSL launched Duality, a large-format console combining the mixing functionality of the XL 9000K with the control surface of the AWS 900, featuring updated signal routing accessible from the center section, channel strips with E and G Series EQ selected via a single button per channel, and 'Variable Harmonic Drive' (VHD) preamps that offer standard or distorted output. In the same year, SSL introduced the Duende DSP platform to emulate SSL channel strip features for home recording, including filters, SSL E and G Series EQ, and dynamics processing, with the SSL Stereo Bus Compressor; based on the digital technology of its C-Series consoles, Duende integrates into DAWs via FireWire or PCI-e as VST or Audio Units plug-ins. On 25 April 2007, SSL released Drumstrip, a Duende plug-in with a noise gate, transient shaper, high and low frequency enhancers, and a Listening Mic Compressor. In 2006, SSL also announced expansion into broadcast video content management and delivery with the MediaWAN system. In 2002, SSL sold its organ division, now known as Solid State Organ Systems; the proprietary aptX-codec was sold in a management buyout, with APT Licensing Ltd. incorporated on 1 March 2005 in Belfast. In 2005, musician Peter Gabriel and broadcast entrepreneur David Engelke became majority shareholders. In 2017, SSL was acquired by the Audiotonix Group, with Gabriel becoming a major investor in the group. The company received The Queen's Award for Enterprise: International Trade (Export) in 1981 and The Queen's Award for Enterprise: Innovation (Technology) in 1993 and 2020. In February 2004, SSL received a Special Merit/Technical Grammy Award at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards for its contributions to the recording field. Two SSL products were inducted into the TEC Awards TECnology Hall of Fame: the SL 4000 series in 2004 and the AWS studio console in 2018.

Sonam Wangchuk, born on 1 September 1966 in near Alchi, Leh district of Jammu and Kashmir (now in the Union Territory of Ladakh), is an Indian activist, innovator, education reformer, and environmentalist. He was not enrolled in school until the age of 9, as there were no schools in his village, and his mother taught him the basics in his mother tongue. In 1975, his father, Sonam Wangyal, became a minister in the Jammu and Kashmir Government. At age 9, Wangchuk was enrolled in a school in Srinagar, where he faced mistreatment due to his appearance, being addressed in a language he did not understand, which led to him being wrongly perceived as stupid. Unable to bear this, he escaped to Delhi in 1977 and pleaded with the school principal at a Kendriya Vidyalaya. He completed his B.Tech. in Mechanical Engineering from National Institute of Technology Srinagar (then REC Srinagar) in 1987, financing his education independently after a disagreement with his father over his engineering stream. He later pursued two years of higher studies in Earthen Architecture at Craterre School of Architecture in Grenoble, France, in 2011. In 1988, Wangchuk, along with his brother and five peers, founded the Students' Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh (SECMOL), which began experimenting with school reforms at the government high school in Saspol, leading to the launch of Operation New Hope in 1994 in collaboration with the government education department and village communities. From June 1993 to August 2005, he served as the editor of Ladakh's only print magazine, Ladags Melong. In 2001, he was appointed an education advisor to the Hill Council Government; in 2002, he co-founded the Ladakh Voluntary Network (LVN) and served as its secretary until 2005. He was part of the Drafting Committee for the Ladakh Hill Council Government’s Vision Document Ladakh 2025, which was formally launched by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in 2005, and in 2005, he was appointed a member of the National Governing Council for Elementary Education in the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India. From 2007 to 2010, he worked as an education advisor for MS, a Danish NGO. In late 2013, Wangchuk invented and built a prototype of the Ice Stupa, an artificial glacier that stores winter stream water in cone-shaped ice heaps, releasing it during late spring when farmers need it most. By the end of February 2014, his team had constructed a two-storey prototype capable of storing about 150,000 litres of water. In 2015, during a landslide that blocked the Phugtal river and created a 15 km long lake in Zanskar, Wangchuk proposed using a siphon technique and water jet erosion to safely drain the lake, but his advice was ignored, and blasting proceeded, leading to a flash flood on 7 May 2015 that destroyed 12 bridges and many fields. In 2016, he applied the Ice Stupa technique for disaster mitigation at high-altitude glacier lakes, leading a three-week expedition to South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, installing a siphoning system to reduce the lake’s level. In late 2016, he was invited by the municipality of Pontresina, Switzerland, to build Ice Stupas as winter tourism attractions, and in October 2016, his team began constructing the first Ice Stupa in Europe with Swiss partners. In February 2018, local Ladakhi artists built a 10-foot-high ice stupa, completed in 25 days at around -12°C, housed within a larger ice tower. In February 2021, Wangchuk developed solar-powered tents for the Indian army, each accommodating about 10 soldiers, designed to trap daytime heat and retain warmth during the night, responding to the needs of around 50,000 soldiers working in harsh high-altitude conditions. In 2013, on student requests, he launched the New Ladakh Movement (NLM), a social campaign aimed at promoting sustainable education, environment, and economy, eventually becoming a non-political movement. In June 2020, in response to India-China border skirmishes at Galwan, he urged Indians to boycott Chinese products, a call that received widespread media coverage and celebrity support. On 26 January 2023, Wangchuk attempted a fast at Khardungla pass to highlight climate change impacts and demand protection for Ladakh under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, but authorities allegedly prevented him from reaching the pass by placing him under house arrest, citing unsuitable temperatures below -40°C; the Ladakh police denied the charges. In March 2024, he initiated a fast-unto-death to demand constitutional safeguards for Ladakh and protection from industrial and mining activities, and began a 21-day Climate Fast for Ladakh’s statehood under the Sixth Schedule. On 30 September 2024, during a foot march from Ladakh to Delhi, he and supporters were detained by Delhi Police at the Singhu border and released on 2 October 2024. On 24 September 2025, a protest in Leh resulted in the burning of the BJP office and vandalism of the Ladakh Hill Council premises, leading to a police crackdown that killed four civilians and injured dozens, with a curfew imposed and mass arrests conducted. The Ministry of Home Affairs blamed Wangchuk for inciting the protests, which he denied, stating the protests reflected public frustration with the government. Two days later, on 2 October 2025, Wangchuk was detained by hundreds of police officers, led by the Ladakh Director General of Police, under the National Security Act (NSA). Internet services were suspended in Leh, and a curfew continued. Despite no formal detention order being issued to his family, Wangchuk was moved to Jodhpur Central Jail. The Home Ministry accused SECMOL of accepting dubious foreign funds and revoked its FCRA licence, while the CBI opened an inquiry into HIAL, and CRPF personnel were deployed against it. His wife, Gitanjali J Angmo, claimed the Ladakh DGP falsely accused Wangchuk of having "Pakistani links" because he attended a Himalayan Climate Convention in Pakistan in February with her, organized by the United Nations and Dawn Media, and was denied information about his health or condition, with authorities refusing her access to him. On 2 October, Angmo filed a Habeas corpus petition before the Supreme Court to challenge Wangchuk’s arrest. Wangchuk gained national attention in 2009 when his story inspired Aamir Khan’s character Phunsukh Wangdu in the film 3 Idiots, leading to him being referred to as "The real life Phunsukh Wangdu," though he has disavowed the comparison. Wangchuk is also known for designing the SECMOL campus, which runs on solar energy and uses no fossil fuels for cooking, lighting, or heating. His innovative contributions to Ladakh’s education and climate challenges have earned him numerous accolades, including the Ramon Magsaysay Award (2018), the title of Eminent Technologist of the Himalayan Region by IIT Mandi (2018), and the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2017), with around 15 awards as of 2025. He founded the Himalayan Institute of Alternatives Ladakh (HIAL) in 2015 with Gitanjali J Angmo, motivated by the need to address Ladakh’s unique geographical and cultural educational and developmental challenges, continuing his commitment to educational reform through HIAL, aiming to provide higher education and equip youth with skills for sustainable living in their environment. He has also designed and overseen the construction of several passive solar mud buildings in Ladakh, Sikkim, and Nepal, which remain warm even in winter temperatures as low as -30°C. In July 2016, SECMOL won the International Terra Award for the best building at the 12th World Congress on Earthen Architecture in Lyon, France, for its rammed earth 'Big Building' constructed using traditional, low-cost techniques and passive solar principles.

Sonqorabad (Persian: سنقرآباد) is a village and the capital of Chahardangeh Rural District in the Central District. The previous capital of the rural district was the village of Chahar Dangeh, which is now the city of Chaharbagh. During the 2006 National Census, the village had a population of 1,376 people living in 337 households, at that time located in the Ramjin Rural District of the Chaharbagh District in Savojbolagh County, Tehran province. The 2016 census recorded the population as 1,777 people in 564 households, occurring when the county had been transferred from Tehran province to the newly established Alborz province. In 2020, the district was separated from the county to form Chaharbagh County, and the Central District was created. As part of this reorganization, the rural district was transferred to the new Ramjin District, and Sonqorabad was moved to Chahardangeh Rural District within the Central District.

Sopore is a city in the Baramulla district of Jammu and Kashmir, India, located 45 km (28 mi) north-west of Srinagar and 16 km (10 mi) north-east of Baramulla. It is one of the largest subdivisions in Jammu and Kashmir, comprising seven tehsils and is the state's oldest existing subdivision, recognized as an urban area since the 1911 census. Sopore serves as a central business hub in North Kashmir, with its historical and economic significance reinforcing its prominence. The city hosts Asia's second-largest fruit mandi at Nowpora Kalan Sopore, about 2 km from the main town, which generates an annual turnover of over ₹3000 crore and handles around 40 percent of the apple production and sales in the Kashmir Valley, earning it the title of the 'Apple Town of Kashmir'. Wular Lake, one of Asia's largest freshwater lakes, lies between Sopore and the Bandipore district and is a major source of fish and known for its water chestnut production, contributing to the region's economic and ecological value. The Municipal Council Sopore administers the city, consisting of 21 wards and two outgrowths: Amargarh and Nowpora Kalan. Old Sopore is situated on both banks of the Jhelum River and features a densely packed network of 30–35 mohallas, including Hatishah, Jamia Qadeem, Khanqah, Chankhan, Untoo Hamam, Sofi Hamam, Now Hamam, Batpora, Ashpeer, Khushal Matoo, Muslim Peer, Kralteng, Sangrampora, Maharajpora, Arampora, Teliyan, and Takyabal, each with unique character and history. New Sopore began developing in the mid-20th century with the establishment of New Colony and later expanded to include Noor Bagh, Iqbal Nagar, Badam Bagh, Baba Raza, Siddiq Colony, Model Town, Shah Kirman Colony, Krankshivan Colony, and New Light Colony, all designed with modern infrastructure. The Sopore division includes the city, nearby villages such as Tarzoo, Wagub, Adipora, Seer Jagir, and the Zaingair belt, which comprises Dangerpora, Dooru, Mundji, Hardshiva, Warpora, Botingoo, Hathlangoo, Wadoora, Tujar Sharif, Brath Kalan, Bomai, Seelo, Logripora, Zaloora, and others, all contributing to the region's economy. Old Sopore is home to Bada Bazar, a historic marketplace that has functioned as a central trade hub for over a century, alongside Chota Bazar, a narrower market that includes a prominent fish market known as Gaade Bazar. Main Chowk Sopore, formerly known as Samad Talkies Chowk due to the historic cinema that once stood there, is the town's central intersection, linking Bada Bazar and Chota Bazar, Iqbal Market, Super Bazar, and Tehsil Road. Since 1947, the town's market has expanded at least fivefold, with Iqbal Market emerging as a key commercial center, especially known for its bustling Sunday market and its connection to Shah Faisal Market and the General Bus Stand Market. Other notable markets include Chankhan Market, Downtown, and Tehsil Road (commonly called Bugu), while New Colony, near the General Bus Stand, has grown into a major commercial hub, and Amargarh and the Sopore Bypass are rapidly developing into prominent commercial zones. Sopore was historically known as Suyyapura, founded by the Kashmiri engineer Suyya during the reign of Raja Awantivarma (855–883 A.D.), in commemoration of his name. J.P. Ferguson, in his book 'Kashmir', describes Suyya as being hundreds of years ahead of his time for his technical skills in draining floodwaters that had previously made land cultivation impossible, leading to famine; Kalhana, in 'Rajatarangini', regarded Suyya as an incarnation of the Lord of Food. M.A. Stein, in his 1899 book 'Memoir on maps illustrating the Ancient Geography of Kashmir', notes that Sopore lies near where the Vitasta leaves Wular and remains a town of over 8,000 inhabitants, having served as the official headquarters for Kamraj during recent times and earlier periods. According to Srivara, a great conflagration destroyed Suyyapura during Zain-ul-Abidin's reign, destroying the official archives of Kamarajya, though the royal residence survived and the town was rebuilt in great splendour; however, no older remains of interest remain today. In 1459, Sopur was attacked by Adam Khan, son of Zain-ul-Abidin, during a rebellion, resulting in the defeat and death of the town's governor and the destruction of the town. Zain-ul-Abidin responded by sending an army, routing Adam's forces in a pitched battle, and during the retreat, the bridge collapsed, causing 300 of Adam's followers to drown in the Jhelum. At some point during Zain-ul-Abidin's reign, Sopur was destroyed by fire (possibly a duplicate reference to Adam Khan's attack), after which Zain-ul-Abidin built a new palace at Sopore, using materials from the demolished palace in Baramulla, and also constructed a swinging bridge at Sopore. This bridge remained the sole river crossing until 1955, when it was replaced by an R.C.C. bridge about half a mile downstream; the old bridge has since been reconstructed and reopened to traffic. As per the 2011 India census, the Sopore urban area had a population of 71,292 and an area of 18.9 km² (7.3 sq mi), consisting of the city and outgrowths; the city alone had a population of 61,098 and an area of 9.90 km² (3.82 sq mi). The urban area had 37,570 males (53%) and 33,722 females (47%). Of the population, 9,329 (13.1%) were aged 0–6: 5,042 males (54%) and 4,287 females (46%). The literacy rate for those over six was 70.8% (males 78.6%, females 62.3%). Sh. Shabir Ahmad Raina is the Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) of Sopore, and Iftkhar Talib (JKPS) is the Superintendent of Police (SP) of Sopore.
