Sora is a town and municipality located in the Central Boyacá Province, within the Colombian Department of Boyacá. It is bordered by Motavita and Chíquiza to the north, Cucaita and Samacá to the south, Motavita and the department capital Tunja to the east, and Sáchica and Chíquiza to the west.[1] The name Sora originates from the Chibcha language and translates to "Devil worshipper."[2] Prior to the Spanish conquest, the region was inhabited by the Muisca, who were part of the loose Muisca Confederation, and Sora was governed by the zaque based in nearby Hunza. Modern Sora was officially established on August 12, 1556, by Tomás Gualba Castellanos.[1] Its geographical coordinates are 5°34′N 73°26′W, or 5.567°N 73.433°W.

The Southern Baptist Convention (SBC), also known as the Great Commission Baptists (GCB), is a Christian denomination based in the United States and is the world's largest Baptist organization, the largest Protestant denomination, and the second-largest Christian body in the U.S. It consists of fully autonomous, independent churches that share common essential beliefs and pool resources for missions. Churches are evangelical, emphasizing individual conversion, which is affirmed through complete immersion baptism—a public, symbolic act representing burial of the old life and resurrection to new life, not a requirement for salvation. The denomination maintains a male pastorate, citing 1 Timothy 2:12, and denies the legitimacy of same-sex marriage, asserting that marriage is exclusively between a man and a woman and that all sexual relations must occur within marriage. Beliefs vary by congregation due to local autonomy. In 1845, Southern Baptists split from the Triennial Convention to support slavery, as American society divided over the issue preceding the Civil War. In 1995, the SBC apologized for its historical racial positions, and today it is racially diverse, with one in four congregations having a nonwhite majority. Since the 1940s, it has expanded across the U.S., with tens of thousands of affiliated churches and 41 state conventions. A conservative movement gained control of the SBC leadership by the 1990s. Self-reported membership peaked in 2006 at about 16 million, declined by an estimated 13.6% since then, with 2020 marking the 14th year of continuous decline, and weekly attendance dropped about 27% between 2006 and 2020. In 2024, the convention reported increased participation and a slowing of membership decline, with 12,722,266 members. The name "Southern" originates from the 1845 founding in Augusta, Georgia, by white Baptists who supported slavery and separated from northern Baptists, who opposed funding evangelists involved in slavery. In 2012, the SBC adopted the descriptor "Great Commission Baptists" after electing its first African American president, and in 2020, some leaders proposed changing the name to distance it from its white supremacist origins and reflect its no longer being a specifically Southern church; some affiliated churches have also adopted the descriptor. Early Baptists in British colonies came from England in the 17th century due to dissent from the Church of England. Roger Williams founded the first Baptist church in British America in 1638 in Providence Plantations, Rhode Island. The oldest Baptist church in the South, First Baptist Church of Charleston, South Carolina, was organized in 1682 by William Screven. Baptist churches were formed in Virginia in 1715 through Robert Norden and in North Carolina in 1727 through Paul Palmer. Baptists followed a congregational polity, operating independently of the state-established Anglican churches in the South, where non-Anglicans were barred from political office. By 1740, there were about eight Baptist churches in Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina with 300 to 400 members. New members, both black and white, were converted by Baptist preachers during the 18th and 19th centuries, especially during the First and Second Great Awakenings. Black churches were founded in Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia before the American Revolution, and some maintained independence after Nat Turner's Rebellion of 1831. Before the Revolution, Baptist and Methodist evangelicals promoted the equality of all people before God, including enslaved people and free blacks, challenging class and racial hierarchies and urging planters to abolish slavery. There was a divide between the plain-living, common-people-oriented Baptists and the opulent, slave-owning Anglican gentry, who viewed Baptist discipline as radical but saw it as a way to maintain order. Baptists strictly monitored moral conduct, expelling members for sexual transgressions, cursing, or excessive drinking. In Virginia and other southern colonies, the Church of England was the established church and opposed Baptist growth, prosecuting preachers for "disturbing the peace" and having them defended by Patrick Henry and James Madison. In 1779, Thomas Jefferson wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, enacted in 1786, and James Madison later incorporated religious freedom into the U.S. Constitution. The struggle for religious tolerance intensified during the American Revolution, with Baptists opposing the Anglican establishment, and the conflict between evangelical and gentry styles becoming bitter. In 1814, leaders like Luther Rice helped unify Baptists nationally under the Triennial Convention, which met every three years and supported missions abroad. The Home Mission Society, established in 1832, supported missions in U.S. frontier territories. By the mid-19th century, social, cultural, economic, and political differences emerged between northern, western, and southern groups, with slavery being the most divisive issue, followed by missions. Northern Baptists, along with Quakers and Methodists, increasingly argued that enslavers must free enslaved people during the Second Great Awakening. While most southern Baptists were yeomen and common planters, many attracted major planters who interpreted the Bible as supporting slavery and encouraged paternalistic practices. They preached to enslaved people to accept their status and obey enslavers and welcomed enslaved people and free blacks as members, though whites controlled leadership and often segregated seating. In 1821, Gillfield Baptist in Petersburg, Virginia, had the largest congregation in the Portsmouth Association with 441 members, more than twice the size of the next-largest church. Before 1831, Gillfield had a black preacher; after Nat Turner's Rebellion, the state required white men to oversee black congregations, and Gillfield could not appoint a black preacher until after the Civil War and emancipation. After the rebellion, whites passed laws requiring white ministers to lead or be present at meetings, and many enslaved people evaded these restrictions. The Triennial Convention and the Home Mission Society maintained neutrality on slavery, refusing to endorse or condemn it. In 1844, during the "Georgia Test Case," the Georgia State Convention proposed appointing enslaver Elder James E. Reeve as a missionary, but the Foreign Mission Board refused, citing neutrality. In 1844, University of Alabama president Basil Manly Sr., who enslaved 40 people, drafted the "Alabama Resolutions" demanding that enslavers be eligible for denominational offices, which were not adopted. Many southern Baptists tested neutrality by recommending an enslaver to the Home Mission Society, which refused, noting missionaries could not take servants and would not appear to endorse slavery. Many southerners viewed the northern stance that "slaveholding brethren were less than followers of Jesus" as a justification for seceding. This conflict culminated in 1845 when northern representatives refused to appoint missionaries whose families enslaved people, leading many southern Baptists to split and form the Southern Baptist Convention. A secondary concern was that the American Baptist Home Mission Society did not appoint a sufficient number of missionaries to the South, likely due to not appointing enslavers. Northern Baptists favored a loose structure with individual annual dues and single-ministry societies, while southern Baptists preferred a centralized, association-based structure with multiple ministries under one organization. Increasing tensions and southern discontent over criticism of slavery and mission policies led to their withdrawal from national Baptist organizations. The Southern Baptists met in May 1845 at the First Baptist Church of Augusta and formed the Southern Baptist Convention, electing William Bullein Johnson as its first president, who had previously served as president of the Triennial Convention in 1841. African Americans founded churches early on, such as in Petersburg, Virginia (1774) and Savannah, Georgia (1788), and later in frontier areas like First African Baptist Church of Lexington, Kentucky, which joined the Elkhorn Association in 1824 and had 1,820 members by 1850 and 2,223 by 1861. Southern whites generally required black churches to have white ministers and trustees, with segregated seating, and white preaching often emphasized that enslaved people should accept their place and behave well toward enslavers. After the Civil War, freedmen formed independent black congregations, regional associations, and state and national conventions, seeking independence from white supervision. They saw their liberation as analogous to the Exodus and viewed John Brown as their Moses. In 1866, black Baptists formed the Consolidated American Baptist Convention, and in 1895, they merged three national conventions to create the National Baptist Convention, USA, which now has over eight million members and is the largest African American religious organization, second only to the Southern Baptists. Free black people in the North founded independent churches in the early 19th century. During Reconstruction, missionaries from northern denominations, especially the African Methodist Episcopal Church, attracted tens and hundreds of thousands of freedmen, leading many white Southern Baptist churches to lose black members to new denominations and independent congregations. During the civil rights movement, many Southern Baptist pastors and members rejected racial integration and upheld white supremacy, further alienating African Americans. Historian Wayne Flynt described the church as "the last bastion of segregation," and the SBC did not integrate seminary classrooms until 1951. In 1995, the SBC voted to adopt a resolution renouncing its racist roots and apologizing for its past defense of slavery, segregation, and white supremacy, marking its first formal acknowledgment of racism's role in its history. By the early 21st century, ethnically diverse congregations were increasing, with nearly 20% of congregations being majority African American, Asian, Hispanic, or Latino in 2008, and an estimated one million African American members in cooperating churches. The SBC has passed resolutions recommending greater inclusion of black members and appointing more African American leaders. In 2012, it elected Pastor Fred Luter of the Franklin Avenue Baptist Church as its first African American president. In 2005, proposals to rename the SBC to "North American Baptist Convention" or "Scriptural Baptist Convention" were defeated. In 2012, messengers voted to adopt the descriptor "Great Commission Baptists," with the legal name remaining "Southern Baptist Convention," though affiliated churches and entities could voluntarily use it. Almost a year after the Charleston church shooting, the denomination approved a resolution urging member churches and families to stop flying the Confederate flag. It also approved a resolution, "On Refugee Ministry," encouraging churches and families to welcome refugees. Russell Moore of the Southern Baptist Ethics and Religious Liberty Commission responded to a pastor's question about supporting Muslim mosque construction by stating that religious freedom must be for all religions and that such questions are not simple. From February to June 2016, the SBC collaborated with the National Baptist Convention, USA, on racial reconciliation, with presidents Ronnie Floyd and Jerry Young assembling ten pastors from each convention to discuss race relations; in 2016, Baptist Press and The New York Times reported tension within the National Baptist Convention, with President Jerry Young stating that while he understood the history and pain of slavery, he saw it as reverse racism to oppose collaboration, emphasizing that the Gospel demands reconciliation. After an initial resolution against the alt-right failed to pass, the denomination officially denounced the alt-right at its 2017 convention. On November 5, 2017, a mass shooting occurred at the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, the deadliest shooting at any affiliated church in its history and the deadliest at an American place of worship in modern times. In 2020, the denomination canceled its convention due to COVID-19 concerns.

Fellowship members in the same denomination contacted Dr. Jerry Young, asking, "What are you doing? I mean, are you not aware of the history?" He responded that he is fully aware of the history and the pain associated with it, but emphasized that from his perspective, using the history of slavery as a reason to avoid involvement with the Southern Baptists is reverse racism. He affirmed that if the Gospel is to have any effect, it must demand that we not only preach but also practice reconciliation. In 2017, after an initial resolution denouncing the alt-right movement failed to reach the convention floor, the Southern Baptist Convention officially condemned the alt-right at its convention. On November 5, 2017, a mass shooting occurred at the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, which was the deadliest shooting at any affiliated church in its history and the deadliest at an American place of worship in modern times. In 2020, the denomination canceled its convention due to COVID-19 concerns and rescheduled it for June 2021. In a September 15, 2020, Washington Post story, J. D. Greear stated that some SBC leaders wanted to rename the church "Great Commission Baptists" to distance it from its historical ties to slavery and to reflect that it is no longer solely a Southern church; since then, several churches have adopted this alternative name. In 2018, investigations revealed that the SBC suppressed reports of sexual abuse and protected over 700 accused ministers and church workers. In 2022, a report found that church leaders had stonewalled and disparaged survivors of clergy sexual abuse for nearly two decades; reform efforts were criticized or dismissed by other leaders; and known abusers were allowed to retain their positions without informing their local churches. On August 12, 2022, the denomination announced it was facing a federal investigation into the abuse scandal. A joint investigation by the Houston Chronicle and the San Antonio Express in 2019 found over 700 victims of sexual abuse by nearly 400 church leaders, pastors, and volunteers over 20 years. The Chronicle examined federal and state court databases, prison records, and official documents from over 20 states and sex offender registries nationwide, compiling a list of pastors, leaders, employees, and volunteers convicted or who pleaded guilty to sex crimes as of June 2019. On June 12, 2019, during its annual meeting in Birmingham, Alabama, convention messengers approved a resolution condemning sex abuse and establishing a special committee to investigate it and to make it easier for the convention to excommunicate churches. Reverend J. D. Greear called it a "defining moment," and Ronnie Floyd, president of the executive committee, called it a "very, very significant moment in the history of the Southern Baptist Convention." In June 2021, leaked letters from former policy director Russell D. Moore to convention leadership revealed that the convention had mishandled claims of sexual abuse. On May 22, 2022, Guidepost Solutions, an independent firm hired by the executive committee, released a report detailing that church leaders had stonewalled and disparaged survivors for nearly two decades, spending $4 million on the inquiry; it also found that known abusers were allowed to keep their positions without informing their churches. The report noted that although Greear, elected president in 2018, made addressing sexual abuse a central agenda, nearly all reform efforts were met with criticism and dismissal by other leaders. On June 14, 2022, the denomination voted to create a system to track pastors and other church workers credibly accused of sex abuse and to launch a new task force to oversee further reforms after a consultant revealed that leaders had mishandled abuse cases and stonewalled victims for years. The task force will operate for one year, with the option to continue. On August 12, 2022, the organization announced it was facing a federal investigation into the sex abuse scandal. As abuse revelations and lawsuits continued into 2023, the SBC's Abuse Reform Implementation Task Force announced ongoing development of a database of sexual offenders. The Baptist Faith and Message (BF&M) represents the general theological perspective of the denomination's churches. The convention first drafted the BF&M in 1925 as a revision of the 1833 New Hampshire Confession of Faith, revised it significantly in 1963, amended it in 1998 to add a section on the family, and revised it again in 2000. The 1998 and 2000 changes sparked controversy, especially regarding women's roles in the church. The BF&M is not a creed like the Nicene Creed; members are not required to adhere to it, and churches or state conventions are not required to use it as their statement of faith, though many do. However, key leaders, faculty in denomination-owned seminaries, and missionaries applying through missionary agencies must affirm that their practices, doctrine, and preaching are consistent with the BF&M. In 2012, a LifeWay Research survey found that 30% of churches identified as Calvinist or Reformed, and 30% as Arminian or Wesleyan; Ed Stetzer noted that historically many Baptists have considered themselves neither, holding a unique theological approach. The survey also found that 60% of pastors were concerned about Calvinism's influence within the convention. Nathan Finn noted that the debate over Calvinism has intensified, with non-Calvinists especially concerned about Founders Ministries and Calvinists especially concerned about revivalism and Keswick theology. Historically, the denomination has not considered glossolalia or other Charismatic beliefs to be in accordance with Scriptural teaching, though the BF&M does not mention it. In 2015, the International Mission Board lifted a ban on glossolalia for its missionaries while reaffirming it should not be taught as normative. The convention brings together fundamentalist and moderate churches. In addition to the BF&M, the denomination has issued position statements affirming the autonomy of the local church, the importance of the Cooperative Program of missions, that statements of belief are revisable in light of Scripture though the Bible is the final word, honoring the indigenous principle in missions without compromising doctrine, that laypersons have the same right as ordained ministers to communicate with God, interpret Scripture, and minister in Christ's name, that at the moment of conception a new being enters the universe, created in God's image, and should be protected regardless of circumstances, that God's plan for marriage and sexual intimacy is a lifelong relationship of one man and one woman, rejecting homosexuality, and that the Bible forbids any form of extramarital sexual relations, affirming individual accountability before God, and that women are not eligible to serve as pastors. In 2022, the convention passed a resolution against prosperity theology, which it considers a heretical distortion of the Bible. The denomination's position on abortion has changed significantly over time, evolving from acceptance under certain circumstances to firm opposition. In 1971, the SBC passed a resolution urging a loosening of U.S. abortion laws, calling for legislation allowing abortion in cases of rape, incest, severe fetal deformity, or when a mother's emotional, mental, or physical health is at risk. In 1973, a Baptist Standard poll found that 90% of Texas Baptists believed their state's abortion laws were too restrictive. During this era, a majority of Southern Baptists, including some conservatives, supported a moderate expansion of abortion rights, viewing it as a matter of religious liberty, lacking biblical condemnation, and believing in non-intrusive government. Their initial reaction to Roe v. Wade was support or indifference, seeing anti-abortion movements as sectarian and Catholic. By the mid-1970s, this began to shift, and the movement to change Southern Baptist opinions on abortion substantially influenced their views. Over time, the SBC changed, and today it strongly opposes abortion. The denomination officially subscribes to a complementarian view of gender roles. Beginning in the early 1970s, as a reaction to women's liberation movements, the church and other historically conservative Baptist groups began asserting traditional gender roles. In 1973, at the annual meeting, delegates passed a resolution stating, "Man was not made for woman, but the woman for the man. Woman is the glory of man. Woman would not have existed without man." In 1998, the convention added a male leadership understanding of marriage to the 1963 BF&M with an official amendment: Article XVIII, "The Family." In 2000, it revised the document to support a male-only pastorate with no mention of the office of deacon. In 1984, when there were about 250 women pastors, the convention adopted a resolution affirming the exclusion of women from pastoral leadership. Since 1987, local associations and regional conventions have considered churches that authorize women as pastors to be not in friendly cooperation (or "disfellowshipped") without national convention intervention. By explicitly defining the pastoral office as the exclusive domain of males, the 2000 BF&M became the denomination's first official position against women pastors. Because individual churches are autonomous, they cannot be forced to adopt a male-only pastorate. Some churches that have appointed women as pastors have been disfellowshipped from local associations; a smaller number from state conventions. In February 2023, the Executive Committee first deemed five churches that had appointed women pastors to not be in friendly cooperation. In June 2023, when two churches requested a review, 88% of convention representatives voted to uphold the decision. American Reformer magazine estimated the convention would have 1,844 female pastors in 2023. The crystallization of the church's positions on gender roles and restrictions on women's pastoral roles contributed to the split of members joining the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, which broke from the convention in 1991. The Alliance of Baptists also accepts women's ordination. The 2000 BF&M prescribes a husband-headship authority structure, closely following a complementarian reading of Paul's exhortations in Ephesians 5:21–33. Article XVIII. The Family. The husband and wife are of equal worth before God, both created in God's image. The marriage relationship models how God relates to His people. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church, has the God-given responsibility to provide for, protect, and lead his family. A wife is to submit graciously to her husband's servant leadership, even as the church submits to Christ's headship; she, being in God's image as is her husband, has the God-given responsibility to respect her husband and serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation. Southern/Great Commission Baptists observe two ordinances: the Lord's Supper and believer's baptism (also known as credo-baptism, from the Latin for "I believe"). They hold the historic Baptist belief that immersion is the only valid mode of baptism. The BF&M describes baptism as a symbolic act of obedience and a testimony of the believer's faith in Jesus Christ to others and notes that it is a precondition to congregational church membership. The BF&M holds to memorialism, the belief that the Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience in which believers commemorate Christ's death and look forward to His Second Coming. Individual churches are free to practice open or closed communion due to the convention's belief in congregational polity and local church autonomy, though most practice open communion. The frequency of the Lord's Supper varies; churches commonly observe it quarterly, some monthly, and a small minority weekly. Because the organization traditionally opposes alcoholic beverage consumption, grape juice is used instead of wine. Most members observe a low church form of worship, less formal and without a stated liturgy. The form of worship depends on whether the congregation uses traditional or contemporary services or a mix of both—main differences are in music and the response to the sermon. In both types, there is a prayer at the beginning, before the sermon, and at the end. Offerings are taken, either mid-service or at the end; with the rise of electronic systems, some churches offer online or app-based giving. Responsive Scripture readings are uncommon but may occur on special occasions. In a traditional service, music typically features hymns with piano or organ (churches have generally phased out organ due to changing preferences), sometimes with a soloist or choir. Smaller churches allow anyone to participate in the choir regardless of singing ability; larger churches limit participation to those who have successfully tried out. After the sermon, an invitation to respond (sometimes called an altar call) may be given; people may respond by receiving Christ as Lord and Savior, beginning discipleship, seeking baptism, joining the congregation, or entering vocational ministry. Churches may schedule baptisms on specific weekends or offer them when a baptistry is available. In a contemporary service, music generally features modern songs led by a praise team or similar group with featured singers; choirs are less common. An altar call may or may not be given; if not, interested persons are directed to the lobby to speak with someone. Baptismal services are usually scheduled as special events. Church membership is typically done through periodic classes on church history, beliefs, goals, and expectations. Controversially, churches may require a member to sign a "membership covenant," a document with promises such as regular attendance, regular giving (sometimes including tithing), and service within the church. Such covenants are controversial because they may not allow a member to withdraw voluntarily from membership or, in some cases, to leave at all without leadership approval. A Dallas/Fort Worth church was forced to apologize to a member who attempted to annul her marriage after her husband admitted to viewing child pornography. According to a 2024 census published by the convention, it had 46,876 churches, 4.3 million weekly worshippers, and 12,722,266 members. The global convention has more than 1,161 local associations, 41 state conventions, and fellowships covering all 50 states and territories of the United States.

A prospective member of the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC) may be asked to sign a "membership covenant," a document outlining commitments such as regular attendance at main services and small groups, consistent giving—sometimes including tithing—and service within the church. These covenants are controversial because they may restrict a member’s ability to voluntarily withdraw from membership to avoid church discipline, or in some cases, prevent leaving the church entirely without leadership approval. For example, a Dallas/Fort Worth church was forced to apologize when a member attempted to annul her marriage after her husband admitted to viewing child pornography, as the church had not requested permission for the annulment. According to a 2024 census, the SBC comprises 46,876 churches, 4.3 million weekly worshippers, and 12,722,266 members. The global convention includes more than 1,161 local associations, 41 state conventions, and fellowships covering all 50 U.S. states and territories. The states with the highest membership rates are Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, Florida, and Tennessee, with Texas having the largest number of members—estimated at 2.75 million—divided between the more traditionalist Southern Baptists of Texas Convention and the more moderate, diversified Baptist General Convention of Texas, which is more financially and organizationally autonomous than most state conventions. Southern/Great Commission Baptists support thousands of missionaries through the Cooperative Program. Data from church sources and independent surveys show that since 1990, SBC membership as a proportion of the American population has declined. The convention grew historically until 2007, when membership decreased by nearly 40,000, with total membership at about 16.2 million remaining flat over the period, falling by 38,482 or 0.2%. New baptisms have declined annually for seven of the last eight years, reaching their lowest levels since 1987 by 2008, and continued to decline through 2012. The 2014 statistical summary recorded a loss of 236,467 members, the largest one-year decline since 1881, and by 2018, membership fell below 15 million for the first time since 1989, reaching its lowest level in over 30 years. This decline has led some researchers to describe the SBC as a "denomination in decline," with former president Frank Page suggesting in 2008 that half of the convention’s churches could close permanently by 2030. A 2004 survey found that 70% of SBC churches had declining or plateaued membership. The decline is attributed to four factors: increased immigration by non-European groups, stagnant growth among predominantly European American churches, the aging of current members, and reduced participation by younger generations. Some believe Baptists have not sufficiently attracted minorities, though state conventions in Mississippi and Texas report rising minority membership. In 1990, 5% of congregations were non-white; by 2012, that proportion had risen to 20%, with 60% of minority congregations located in Texas, especially in Houston and Dallas suburbs. By 2020, an estimated 22.3% of affiliated churches were non-white. The decline may be more significant than statistics suggest because churches are not required to remove inactive members, leading to inflated numbers, and hundreds of moderate congregations have shifted allegiance to other Baptist groups like the American Baptist Churches USA, the Alliance of Baptists, or the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship while remaining on the SBC’s rolls. Groups have withdrawn due to conservative trends; for instance, in 2000, the Baptist General Convention of Texas cut contributions to Southern Baptist seminaries and redirected over $5 million to more moderate seminaries, including the Hispanic Baptist Theological School in San Antonio, Baylor’s George W. Truett Theological Seminary in Waco, and Hardin–Simmons’ Logsdon School of Theology in Abilene. Since the 1980s controversies, the convention has established over 20 theological programs for moderate and progressive Baptists in the Southeast, including in Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina, and Alabama. Texas and Virginia have the largest state conventions with moderate theological approaches. On June 4, 2020, the SBC reported a 13th consecutive year of membership decline, dropping nearly 2% to 14,525,579 from 2018 to 2019, and in 2022 lost 457,371 members—its largest drop in over a century—to 13,223,122, a level similar to the late 1970s. The denomination has four organizational levels: local congregation, local association, state convention, and national convention, with 41 affiliated state conventions or fellowships. Churches voluntarily pool resources through cooperative associations to support missionary and other work, but the national convention, state conventions, and local associations have no administrative or ecclesiastical control over local churches; they may disfellowship a congregation on an issue but cannot terminate leadership, members, or force closure. The national convention does not claim authority over any other Baptist body, as stated in Article IV. Authority. The national convention maintains a central administrative office in Nashville, Tennessee, where its executive committee controls seminaries and other institutions. As of 2008, the denomination had around 10,000 ethnic churches. The executive committee rejected a proposal to create a convention-wide database of clergy accused of sexual crimes due to the principle of local church autonomy. A 2009 Lifeway Christian Resources study found that one in eight background checks for church workers revealed a history of crime that could have prevented them from working. The Baptist Faith and Message is not binding on churches or members, though national employees and missionaries must agree to it. Southern/Great Commission Baptists are generally conservative, opposing homosexual activity and abortion. Baptists recognize only two scriptural offices: pastor-teacher and deacon, with a 1980s resolution officially restricting ordained offices to men, based on New Testament scriptures. The annual meeting, held in June over two days, includes delegates ("messengers") from cooperating churches who determine programs, policies, and budgets, elect officers, and committees. Each church may send up to two messengers, with a maximum of 12. The Cooperative Program (CP) collects and distributes funds from congregations to support regional, national, and international ministries. In the fiscal year ending September 30, 2008, local congregations reported $11.1 billion in gift receipts, sending $548 million—about 5%—to state conventions via the CP, of which $344 million was retained by state conventions and $204 million went to the national CP. The denomination was founded in 1845 to establish a mission board. The North American Mission Board (NAMB) in Alpharetta, Georgia, supports missionaries in the U.S. and Canada, while the International Mission Board (IMB) in Richmond, Virginia, supports missionaries worldwide. Baptist Men is the mission organization for men under NAMB. The Woman's Missionary Union, founded in 1888, supports two major annual missions: the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering. Southern Baptist Disaster Relief, initiated in 1967, responded to 166 named disasters in 2005, preparing 17,124,738 meals, repairing 7,246 homes, and removing debris from 13,986 yards. The organization provides free, essential services such as food, water, child care, and rebuilding. The SBC has affiliated primary and secondary schools and universities. The national convention directly supports six theological seminaries. Other notable organizations include Baptist Press (founded 1946), Baptist Collegiate Network, GuideStone Financial Resources (founded 1918), LifeWay Christian Resources (founded 1891), the Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, and the Southern Baptist Historical Library and Archives in Nashville. The SBC has experienced major internal controversies, including Landmarkism in the 1850s–1860s, which led to the formation of the American Baptist Association and many independent churches. The Whitsitt controversy (1896–99) challenged the timeline of Baptist immersion. From the 19th to 20th century, the SBC supported white supremacy, racial segregation, the Confederacy, and opposed interracial marriage. A conservative movement gained control from the late 1970s onward, culminating in 1995 when the SBC officially denounced racism. In the 21st century, after electing its first Black president, the SBC adopted the "Great Commission Baptists" descriptor to distance itself from its white supremacist past. By 2008, nearly 20% of SBC congregations were majority African American, Asian, Hispanic, or Latino, with an estimated one million African American members. By 2018, the denomination passed resolutions to increase black membership and appoint more African American leaders. The Southern Baptist Convention conservative resurgence (c. 1970–2000) was a struggle for control of resources and ideology. In 1961, Professor Ralph Elliott published a book rejecting biblical inerrancy. In the 1970s, other seminary professors were criticized for liberal views. In response, a group led by Judge Paul Pressler and Pastor Paige Patterson campaigned for a conservative direction, resulting in Adrian Rogers being elected president in 1979. New leaders replaced all agency heads with more conservative individuals, a move called the "conservative resurgence" by supporters and "fundamentalist takeover" by opponents. Russell H. Dilday described the resurgence as a "self-destructive, contentious, one-sided feud." In 1984, a resolution was passed excluding women from pastoral leadership. In 1987, churches opposed to fundamentalist control founded the Alliance of Baptists; in 1991, moderate churches formed the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship over similar concerns.

From 1978 to 1994, the resurgence fragmented Southern Baptist fellowship and was described as "far more serious than [a controversy]" and a "self-destructive, contentious, one-sided feud that at times took on combative characteristics." Since 1979, Southern Baptists had become polarized into two major groups: moderates and conservatives. Reflecting the conservative majority votes of messengers at the 1979 annual meeting of the SBC, the new national organization officers replaced all leaders of Southern Baptist agencies with presumably more conservative individuals, often labeled "fundamentalist" by dissenters. In 1984, this group passed a resolution excluding women from pastoral leadership. In 1987, a group of churches criticized the fundamentalists for controlling leadership and founded the Alliance of Baptists. A group of moderate churches also criticized the denomination for leadership control and opposition to women's ministry, and founded the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship in 1991. In 2019, after sexual abuse scandals involving deacon Paul Pressler and cover-ups involving former president Paige Patterson, Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary removed the stained-glass windows from the MacGorman Chapel opened in 2011 that depicted them as actors of a "conservative resurgence." Since 1976, the Convention has adopted 22 resolutions supporting only marriage between a man and a woman and opposing same-sex marriage. Since 1992, the national convention has "disfellowshipped" various churches that support LGBTQ inclusion; in 2018, the District of Columbia Baptist Convention was disfellowshipped for this reason. On June 10, 2025, at the annual meeting in Dallas, the convention voted overwhelmingly in favor of working to overturn the legal right to same-sex marriage, marking the first time the SBC had asked its member churches to do so. The resolution also opposed "transgender ideology." The resolution, "On Restoring Moral Clarity through God's Design for Gender, Marriage, and the Family," was written by Andrew T. Walker, an ethicist at a Kentucky seminary. By November 2020, the six convention seminary presidents called critical race theory "unbiblical," emphasizing the importance of not turning to secular ideas to confront racism; four African American churches left the SBC over the leadership's charged statement on the issue.

Soy tu fan (English: I'm your fan) is a Mexican romantic comedy television series produced by Canana Films, Fox Television Studios, and Once TV México, and is an adaptation of the Argentine series of the same name created by Dolores Fonzi and Constanza Novick. The series is directed by Álvaro Hernández, Mariana Chenillo, and Gerardo Naranjo, produced by Pablo Cruz, Constanza Novick, Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna, Geminiano Pineda, Jorge Mondragón, Diego Martínez Ulanosky, and Ana Claudia Talancón, and written by Constanza Novick. It premiered on Wednesday, April 28, 2010, in Mexico on Once TV México and in the United States on mun2 on October 17, 2010. Season 2 began airing on October 19, 2011, on Once TV in Mexico. Charly (played by Ana Claudia Talancón) and Nicolas meet in a coffee shop in Mexico City after Charly's breakup with Julián, the frontman of an upcoming band. Nicolas shows interest in Charly and tells her to inform her therapist, with whom she has an appointment later, that she has just met the love of her life. Charly appreciates the attention but feels harassed by him, until after Nicolas makes endless attempts to get her to go out with him, he gives up and starts dating a struggling actress. The lack of attention causes Charly to reconsider and re-engage in a relationship with Nicolas. Rocío and Fernanda, Charly's best friends, witness her struggle to make the relationship work while still trying to move on from Julián and endure his obnoxious new girlfriend, Vanesa.

Speak Your Mind is the debut studio album by English singer Anne-Marie, released on 27 April 2018, through Major Tom's, Asylum Records, and Atlantic Records. Anne-Marie announced the album, described as a pop and EDM record, on 21 February 2018, and it became available for pre-order two days later. The album was recorded from 2015 to 2018 at various studios, with production handled by Jennifer Decilveo, Nick Monson, Amir Amor, Chris Loco, Marshmello, The Invisible Men, MNEK, TMS, Teddy Geiger, Fred Ball, Fraser T. Smith, Jack Patterson of Clean Bandit, Mark Ralph, David Guetta, and Steve Mac, among others. Marshmello makes a guest appearance and is the sole guest on the standard track listing, while Clean Bandit and David Guetta, along with Sean Paul, appear on various reissues. The album was supported by seven singles: "Alarm," "Ciao Adios," "Heavy," "Then," "Friends" (featuring Marshmello), "2002," and "Perfect to Me," a remix of "Perfect." "Alarm," released on 20 May 2016, charted at number 16 on the UK Singles Chart and number 7 on the ARIA Charts in Australia, where it was certified 2× Platinum, and reached number 3 on the Billboard Bubbling Under Hot 100. "Ciao Adios," released on 10 February 2017, peaked at number 9 in the UK and was certified 2× Platinum in the UK and Netherlands, with Platinum in Australia, Germany, and Poland, and Gold in Canada. "Heavy" and "Then" had modest success in the UK, with "Then" reaching number 87 in the UK and certifying Silver by the BPI. "Friends," released on 9 February 2018, became Anne-Marie's first entry on the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at number 11, and was certified 6× Platinum in Canada, 4× Platinum in the US and Australia, and 3× Platinum in the UK. "2002," released on 20 April 2018, debuted at number 8 in the UK and climbed to number 3, becoming Anne-Marie's highest-charting solo single there, and was certified 8× Platinum in the US, 5× Platinum in Canada, and 4× Platinum in the UK. "Perfect to Me," released on 2 November 2018, reached number 57 in the UK and was certified Gold. A stripped version of "Peak," released on 21 October 2016, became the main version of the song and was included as a bonus track on the Japan and digital deluxe editions. "Can I Get Your Number" and "Trigger" also charted, with "Trigger" peaking at number 59 on the Irish Singles Chart. The album received generally favorable reviews, with a Metacritic score of 62 based on eight reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews." It peaked at number 3 on the UK Albums (OCC) and Scottish Albums (OCC) charts, number 4 on the Irish Albums (IRMA) chart, and number 31 on the Billboard Hot 100. It was certified Platinum by the BPI (300,000 units), Platinum by the RIAA (1,000,000 units), and 2× Platinum by Music Canada (160,000 units). The album was reissued with bonus tracks, including the chart-topping "Rockabye" (Clean Bandit featuring Sean Paul and Anne-Marie) and the modestly successful "Don't Leave Me Alone" (David Guetta featuring Anne-Marie). Anne-Marie promoted the album with the Speak Your Mind Tour from 2018 to 2019, featuring supporting acts such as Lennon Stella and Goody Grace. Speaking to Luvpop, Anne-Marie explained that the title reflects her honesty and openness, stating she "doesn't hold anything in" and "speak[s] my mind a lot." The album charted in numerous countries, including number 18 in Australia, number 16 in Canada, number 10 in Switzerland, number 66 in France (certified Gold), number 24 in Germany, number 4 in Ireland, number 9 in the Czech Republic, number 11 in Finland, number 78 in Italy, number 17 in the Netherlands, number 33 in Sweden, number 27 in Spain, number 31 in New Zealand, number 16 in Austria, number 3 in Scotland, number 50 in Portugal, number 9 in Slovakia, and number 185 in Japan. In South Korea, it charted at number 3 on the Circle Music Chart. The album was certified Gold in Norway (60,000 units) and Singapore (5,000 units), and reached number 3 in Scotland. The digital deluxe edition later included "Don't Leave Me Alone." "Rockabye," originally released on 21 October 2016, topped charts in the UK, Australia, Austria, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, and Switzerland, and reached number 4 in Canada and number 9 on the Billboard Hot 100, with certifications including 7× Platinum in Canada and Italy, 5× Platinum in Australia, 4× Platinum in the UK, 3× Platinum in the US, and 2× Platinum in Germany and Switzerland. "Don't Leave Me Alone," released on 27 July 2018, charted at number 18 in the UK and reached number 2 on the Ultratop Belgium Dance chart, and was certified Platinum in Australia, Canada, and Poland. The tour began on 20 August 2018 in Los Angeles and concluded on 19 June 2019 in London, with supporting acts including Goody Grace, Mahalia, Kojey Radical, Ella Watson, Cellarr (then known as "OpenSide"), Glades, and Lennon Stella. The setlist from the O2 Academy in Leeds may not represent all tour performances. Sales figures are based on certification alone, and streaming is included in certification.

doc_name: Speaker of the House of Representatives (Nepal)
text: The Speaker of the House of Representatives in Nepal serves as the presiding officer of the lower house of parliament, the House of Representatives. This position plays a crucial role in the legislative process by overseeing proceedings, maintaining order, and ensuring fair debate and discussion. The Speaker's office is vacated under the following conditions: (a) if the Speaker ceases to be a member of the House of Representatives, with the exception that during the dissolution of the House, both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker continue in office until the day before nominations for a new election are filed; (b) if the Speaker submits a written resignation; or (c) if a resolution is passed by a majority of two-thirds of the then total members of the House of Representatives declaring that the Speaker's conduct is incompatible with the office.

doc_name: Spring Rock Township, Clinton County, Iowa
text: Spring Rock Township is located in Clinton County, Iowa, United States. As of the 2000 census, the population of the township was 1,142. It was organized in 1844 and derives its name from a large rock found at a spring in Scott County. The township spans an area of 36.25 square miles (93.9 km²) and includes one incorporated settlement, Wheatland, as well as unincorporated settlements such as Big Rock. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, it contains four cemeteries: Homigrahusen, Pine Hill, Rose Hill, and Saint Pauls. The streams that flow through the township are Calamus Creek, Lizard Creek, Rock Creek, and Yankee Run. This article about the geography of Clinton County, Iowa is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

The Springfield Doughnut is a pink doughnut sculpture with sprinkles situated in Springfield, New Zealand. It is inspired by the doughnut commonly seen in the American animated sitcom The Simpsons, which is set in a city also named Springfield. The sculpture was donated to the town by 20th Century Fox to promote the 2007 film The Simpsons Movie. The original version, made from polystyrene encased in fibreglass, was first unveiled in July 2007 and had a diameter of 3.5 metres (11 ft) and weighed 6 tonnes (5.9 long tons; 6.6 short tons). It received a resource consent allowing it to remain for only six weeks. In September 2009, an arsonist set the sculpture on fire, destroying it. This incident occurred on the same day as consent hearings about whether the sculpture should stay permanently, leading to suspicion that the attacker was opposed to the doughnut, viewing it as a degradation of the landscape or believing Springfield should not associate with American cartoons depicting dysfunctional families. In response, local residents painted a tractor tyre pink and tan, removed a "bite" from it, and added sprinkles to replace the destroyed sculpture. On 1 July 2012, a new replacement was unveiled, constructed from concrete, with the same dimensions and weight—3.5 metres (11 ft) in diameter and 6 tonnes (5.9 long tons; 6.6 short tons). This version is fireproof and includes steps that allow people to take photos with their heads poking through the center. Between 2020 and 2023, due to flaking and falling paint, the sculpture was repainted four times at a cost of $17,864.

The Stampacchia Gold Medal is an international award given every three years by the Italian Mathematical Union (Unione Matematica Italiana – UMI {it}) in collaboration with the Ettore Majorana Foundation (Erice), honoring exceptional achievements in the field of Calculus of Variations and its related applications.[1] The medal is named after the Italian mathematician Guido Stampacchia and is awarded to a mathematician who is not older than 35 years of age.

Starr Andrews, born on June 23, 2001, in Los Angeles, California, is an American figure skater who was home-schooled and has a brother and two sisters, including Skylar, a gymnast, and Ashton, a baseball player. Her mother, Toshawa Andrews, suffers from cardiac microvascular disease, which has resulted in a dozen heart attacks. Andrews became interested in figure skating when her mother took her to an ice rink at age three, and she began learning to skate in 2005. A video of nine-year-old Andrews skating to "Whip My Hair" went viral on YouTube in December 2010 and reached 53 million views by March 2018. Derrick Delmore became her coach around 2013, and she placed sixth on the novice level at the 2016 U.S. Championships. She moved up to the junior level under Delmore and Peter Kongkasem in Lakewood and Riverside, California, and won the junior ladies title at the Golden Bear of Zagreb in October 2016. She earned a junior silver medal at the 2017 U.S. Championships and was added to the U.S. team for the 2017 World Junior Championships in Taipei, where she finished twelfth after placing ninth in the short program. Beginning her junior season, she placed fifth at the ISU Junior Grand Prix in Austria and made her senior international debut at the 2017 CS Golden Spin of Zagreb, where she placed sixth and achieved the minimum technical scores for senior-level ISU Championships. In 2018, she finished sixth at the U.S. Championships, placing eighth in the short program and fifth in the free skate, and competed at the Four Continents and World Junior Championships (withdrawing from the latter and being replaced by Emmy Ma). At the 2018 CS Asian Open, she placed second in the short program but dropped to fifth after the free skate; at the 2018 CS Autumn Classic International, she ranked fifth in the short and seventh overall, attempting a triple Axel that was downgraded due to insufficient rotation. She made her Grand Prix debut at the 2018 Skate America, placing ninth in the short program, tenth in the free skate, and tenth overall, and later competed at the 2018 Skate Canada International, where she placed fourth in the short program, ninth in the free skate, and seventh overall. She finished eighth at the 2019 U.S. Championships, won silver at the 2019 International Challenge Cup and the 2019 Egna Spring Trophy, and placed fifth at both the 2019 CS Lombardia Trophy and CS Finlandia Trophy. At the 2019 Internationaux de France, she placed fourth in the short program and fifth overall in the free skate. She finished sixth at the 2020 U.S. Championships and eighth at the 2020 World Junior Championships. In 2020, she competed in a virtual U.S. domestic event, placing fourth, and at the 2020 Skate America in Las Vegas, she placed eighth. At the 2021 U.S. Championships in Las Vegas, she placed twelfth. She placed fifth at the 2021 CS Autumn Classic International and was named to replace Bradie Tennell at the 2021 Skate America, where she placed tenth; she also finished fifth at the 2021 CS Cup of Austria and withdrew from the 2021 Internationaux de France due to injury. At the 2022 U.S. Championships, she placed ninth, earning a spot at the 2022 Four Continents Championships, where she finished ninth. She underwent surgery for supraventricular tachycardia, a condition she had experienced for nearly a decade. She placed sixth at the 2022 CS Nebelhorn Trophy and finished fifth in the short program at the 2022 Skate Canada International before "surprising" many by winning silver in the free skate, becoming the first Black American woman to win a Grand Prix medal in singles since the 1995 era and the second Black woman after Surya Bonaly. She noted the significance, saying it was a huge deal for her as one of the few people of color in the sport. At the 2022 NHK Trophy, she planned to add a second flip to her free skate after recovering from an ankle "tweak," but dropped to ninth after the free skate when she did not execute the planned flip. At the 2023 U.S. Championships, she placed third in the short program, made two jump errors in the free skate, and was overtaken for bronze by Amber Glenn, but still won a pewter medal and stood on the senior podium for the first time, becoming the first African-American woman to do so since Debi Thomas in 1988. She had her preparation delayed due to a planned Coachella appearance that did not happen and later underwent heart surgery for atrial tachycardia, a condition she had managed for a decade. She began working on her programs by July and debuted at the Kings Cup International in early October, winning silver. At the 2023 Skate Canada International, she finished sixth in the short program and eighth overall due to jump problems in the free skate; she placed tenth at the 2023 Grand Prix of Espoo. At the 2023 CS Golden Spin of Zagreb, she won the bronze medal. At the 2024 U.S. Championships, she placed ninth in the short program but delivered a strong fifth-place free skate, moving up to sixth overall. She began the 2024–25 ISU Challenger Series with fifth at the Cranberry Cup International and tenth at the Denis Ten Memorial Challenge, won silver at the 2025 Pacific Coast Sectional Championships, qualifying for the U.S. Championships, and won gold at the 2024 Santa Claus Cup. At the 2025 U.S. Championships, she placed twelfth in the short program but fifth in the free skate, finishing sixth overall, and closed the season with a fourth-place finish at the 2025 International Challenge Cup. She recorded the vocals for the track "Turning Page" used in her free skate. Beginning the 2025–26 Challenger Series, she placed seventh at the 2025 CS Nepela Memorial and twelfth at the 2025 CS Trialeti Trophy. In November, she announced that the 2025–26 season would be her last as a singles skater and that she would switch to pair skating beginning with the 2026–27 season. Selected as a host pick for 2025 Skate America, she delivered two clean programs, earning a new personal best free skate and combined total score, placing fifth overall, and also finished fifth at the 2025 CS Tallinn Trophy. At the 2026 U.S. Championships in January, she finished seventh and was named to the 2026 Four Continents team.

Stars Dance is the debut solo album by American singer Selena Gomez, released on July 19, 2013, by Hollywood Records. Gomez began planning the project in 2012, announcing that her band Selena Gomez & the Scene would take an indefinite hiatus. The album is an EDM and electropop record that incorporates elements of dubstep, techno, disco, electro house, and worldbeat. She worked on the album through March 2013 with producers including Rock Mafia and the Cataracs. Upon release, Stars Dance received generally mixed reviews, with critics praising Gomez's maturing image and vocal and lyrical content, while criticizing its electronic-heavy production. The album debuted at number 1 on the Billboard 200, selling 97,000 copies domestically in its first week, a figure later surpassed by her 2015 album Revival, which sold 117,000 units in its first week. Stars Dance became her fourth Top 20 entry in the United Kingdom, peaking at number 14, and topped the charts in Canada, Norway, Mexico, Taiwan, and China. By 2017, it had sold an estimated 410,000 copies in the United States. The lead single, "Come & Get It," featured heavy electronic and worldbeat themes and became Gomez's first Top 10 entry in the United States, entering the Top 10 in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada, and reached number 2 on the Mainstream Top 40 chart. "Slow Down" reached the Top 30 in the United States and also reached the Top 10 of the Mainstream Top 40. Gomez promoted the album through high-profile performances, including the 2013 Billboard Music Awards, and embarked on the Stars Dance Tour (2013). Selena Gomez & the Scene's third studio album, When the Sun Goes Down (2011), was musically rooted in electropop and dance-pop, similar to their second album, A Year Without Rain (2010). Although reviews for that album were mixed, it was a commercial success. In January 2012, Gomez announced a musical hiatus to focus on acting, stating the band would go their separate ways. Despite this, she confirmed in October 2012 that work had begun on an upcoming solo album, which she later described as her debut. She announced the lead single would be released the following month and the album would follow in the summer. On April 15, she revealed plans for her first world tour, the Stars Dance Tour. On June 3, she officially confirmed the album's title, Stars Dance, and revealed the track listing and cover art. On her return to music, Gomez stated she wanted to write about personal experiences and tell a story, as she had not had time before. For the album, she worked with The Cataracs, Stargate, and Rock Mafia, with Rock Mafia having previously worked on singles with The Scene. She emphasized greater creative control, stating it was the hardest record she had ever worked on. Jason Evigan noted that Gomez had grown into a respected electronic pop dance artist. Prior to the album's release, Gomez announced she would take a musical hiatus after Stars Dance, citing her love for acting and film. Following the album's announcement, rumors spread that most of the album was about her relationship with Justin Bieber. After the release of "Come & Get It," these rumors intensified, and Gomez confirmed the song was not about Bieber, though she later stated that "Love Will Remember" is about her relationship with Bieber, citing an early leaked version with a voicemail from Bieber that was removed. She called "Love Will Remember" the most personal track on the record and said it was a sweet way to release it. "Birthday" was the first song recorded for the album. Gomez listed "Forget Forever" as one of her favorite tracks, describing it as a beautiful song with emotional meaning and a special studio experience, and noted it was about forgetting past troubles. She later said it was about enjoying the present. Recording artist Jennifer Lopez wanted to record "Save the Day" for her 2013 album but failed to secure it from Gomez. "Come & Get It" was initially recorded by Rihanna for her 2011 album Talk That Talk, but she decided not to use it. Musically, Stars Dance is rooted in EDM and pop, specifically electropop, with strong elements of dubstep, techno, disco, and worldbeat. Jocelyn Vena of MTV News described it as "dance-song-heavy" dubstep with wobbly synths, loopy vocals, fist-pumping beats, and crunchy breakdowns. Caroline Sullivan of The Guardian noted its efficient movement from EDM to Bollywood. Most tracks feature dubstep breakdowns, synth stabs, and according to Jim Farber of the New York Daily News, a frisson of sex previously absent from her work. Jason Evigan noted ethnic influences, such as tribal dance drums, similar to Jennifer Lopez's music. August Brown of the Los Angeles Times called it a "sassy" pop-EDM album with "oxygen-sucking" sub-bass and trap snares, noting Spring Breakers' influence. He described it as a blend of pop sugar from the Disney era with broken glass and club bathroom nosebleeds. The title track "Stars Dance" is described as "kind of sensual" and features an orchestral-dubstep beat. "Like a Champion" includes Jamaican and reggae influences and features Gomez singing in a Bajan accent, drawing comparisons to Rihanna. "Save the Day" is about moments when one doesn't want a moment to end, and is described as a "thumping" Latin pop and house song. "Write Your Name" is about falling in love and features a rap verse by Gomez and dubstep elements. "B.E.A.T." is a "sexy" urban hip-hop song with minimal spoken word electro, described as "infectious and definitely racier than usual." Gomez cited Britney Spears, Janet Jackson, Skrillex, Taylor Swift, and Christina Aguilera as major influences. She noted Skrillex inspired her with baby dubstep, having previously worked on the Spring Breakers soundtrack. In an interview with Teen Vogue, she mentioned Ellie Goulding, describing the record as "a little Ellie Goulding-ish, a little island-y feel." The album opens with "Birthday," an electropunk song with sparse drums, trap snares, and vocal chants, described as a "candy-coated, clap-happy club anthem" with girl power and sex appeal. "Slow Down" is a high-octane, uptempo dance-pop and EDM song with a dubstep chorus, funk guitars, a four-on-the-floor beat, and a spoken word outro, lyrically speaking of slowing down a relationship. "Stars Dance" is a "breathy and sultry" dubstep song with an orchestral-dubstep beat, with Gomez's soft voice taking center stage over sexy synth-beats and wallowing melodies. "Like a Champion" is a dancehall song with funk, reggae, and soca influences. "Come & Get It" is a tribal electropop and popstep song with a Bhangra beat, sonic drops, and Indian music influences, lyrically about a female lover rekindling a past romance. "Forget Forever" is a dance-pop and synthpop song with an EDM beat and house music breakdowns, lyrically about a breakup. Sam Lansky of Idolator called it an "electrifying dance-pop banger" with a strong chorus and anthemic beat, while Nate Jones of Popdust called it "bright and expansive" with vocals flying over an EDM beat. "Save the Day" is a "thumping" Latin pop and house song. "B.E.A.T." is described as "minimal spoken word electro" and "infectious and definitely racier than usual." "Write Your Name" is an "exotic" electronic dance and house music song with a rap verse and dubstep elements. "Forget Forever" and "Write Your Name" both avoid the bombast of typical Guetta-style tracks. Gomez promoted the album through interviews and televised performances, including On Air with Ryan Seacrest on April 8, 2013, her first televised performance of "Come & Get It" at the 2013 MTV Movie Awards on April 14, a performance on Dancing with the Stars on April 16, a performance on The Ellen Degeneres Show on April 18, a performance on The Late Show with David Letterman on April 25, and at the 2013 Radio Disney Music Awards on April 27. She performed "Come & Get It" again at the 2013 Billboard Music Awards on May 19 and on The Graham Norton Show days later. She performed "Slow Down" for the first time at MuchMusic Headquarters on May 30 and performed both "Come & Get It" and "Slow Down" at the Macy's 4th of July Fireworks Spectacular on July 4. She performed "Come & Get It" on This Morning in the United Kingdom and on Good Morning America to coincide with the album's release, and on Live! With Kelly and Michael in September. Following the release of "Slow Down," she performed it on The View and The Late Show with David Letterman, and on The X Factor in the United States. She was selected as the halftime performer for the Dallas Cowboys vs. Oakland Raiders Thanksgiving game, performing a medley of "Like a Champion," "Slow Down," and "Come & Get It." The Stars Dance Tour (2013) promoted the album and visited the United States and Asia, earning over $36 million at the box office, though dates in Australia and Japan were canceled due to personal issues. "Come & Get It" was released as the lead single on April 7, 2013, and by July 2013 had become one of Gomez's most successful singles, peaking at number 6 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and the Canadian Hot 100, and was certified 3× Platinum by the RIAA. The music video premiered on MTV on May 7, 2013.

Selena Gomez was selected to perform as the halftime act during the Dallas Cowboys vs. Oakland Raiders game on Thanksgiving, where she performed a medley of "Like a Champion," "Slow Down," and "Come & Get It." The Stars Dance Tour (2013), which was originally scheduled to include dates in Australia and Japan, was cancelled due to personal issues and instead promoted the tour through performances in the United States and Asia, earning over $36 million at the box office. "Come & Get It" was released as the lead single on April 7, 2013, and by July 2013 had reached number 6 on both the US Billboard Hot 100 and the Canadian Hot 100, earning 3× Platinum certification from the RIAA; its music video premiered on MTV on May 7, 2013, directed by Anthony Mandler. "Slow Down" was released as a promotional single on June 3, 2013, via instant digital download with the pre-order of the album on iTunes, co-produced by The Cataracs and David Kuncio, and later released as the official second single on August 13, 2013, peaking at number 27 on the Billboard Hot 100; its official video was uploaded to YouTube on July 19, 2013. Stars Dance received mixed reviews; critics praised the album's production, lyrics, and Gomez's vocals, but criticized her lack of a distinct musical identity, often comparing her to Rihanna. At Metacritic, the album received an average score of 59, indicating "mixed or average reviews." Tim Sendra from AllMusic awarded it three-and-a-half stars, highlighting "Slow Down," "Save the Day," and "Undercover" as highlights and calling it another strong entry in her catalog. Stephen Unwin from Express.co.uk compared it to Vanessa Hudgens, noting the album's shift to more adult themes. Two Guardian reviews were issued: Kitty Empire awarded three stars, while Hermione Hoby gave two stars, criticizing Gomez for lacking a strong hit-making ability and comparing the work to Rihanna. August Brown from the Los Angeles Times described the album as blending pop sugar from her Disney era with "broken glass and a club bathroom nosebleed," rooted in today's pop-EDM trends. Natalie Palmer from Entertainmentwise praised the album for attempting something new, noting it diverged from bubblegum pop or angry rock, opting for an edgier sound. Matthew Horton from Virgin Media gave two stars, criticizing the lack of personality and vocal strength, calling the album "identikit" and unoriginal. Simon Price from The Independent awarded one star, stating there was no standout track to redeem the record. Ron Harris from The Huffington Post felt the album failed to meet expectations, saying Gomez "punched the clock" and worked through a pre-written musical plot, and noted it had less personality than her earlier work with The Scene. Stars Dance debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, selling 97,000 copies in its first week—Gomez's first number one and highest first-week sales until surpassed by Revival, which sold 117,000 copies in its first week. The album fell to number eight in its second week (selling 31,000 copies, a 68% drop), then to number thirteen, number eighteen, and number twenty-five in its fifth week, rising to number twenty-four after a 23% sales increase (selling 17,213 copies) and reaching number twenty-one, before dropping to number thirty-three the following week (selling just over 7,000 copies). The album spent a total of twenty-five weeks on the Billboard 200, with its last appearance on the week ending January 25, 2014. It debuted at number one on the Canadian Albums Chart with 16,500 copies sold in its first week—her first number one in Canada and surpassing her previous album's first-week sales by over 5,000. On August 27, 2013, it received a Gold certification from the CRIA for sales exceeding 40,000. It entered the top five at number five on the New Zealand Albums Chart. In the UK, it debuted and peaked at number fourteen, spending four weeks on the chart; in Ireland, it peaked at number nine and spent six weeks; in Australia, it peaked at number eight. The album was more successful internationally: it debuted at number one in Mexico, was certified Gold for 30,000 sales, reached number two in Portugal (certified Platinum), peaked at number eight in Brazil (certified Platinum), and reached number eight in Australia. Credits are adapted from the album's liner notes. Sampling credits and shipment/sales figures are based on certification alone.

The statue of Søren Kierkegaard is situated in the Royal Library Garden on Slotsholmen in central Copenhagen, Denmark. It was unveiled in 1918 and is based on an earlier statuette by Louis Hasselriis, which was created in 1878 and 1879. Kierkegaard is portrayed sitting on a chair, writing with a quill on a sheet of paper, with books placed next to him. The monument was enlarged by sculptors Carl Aarsleff and H.P. Petersen-Dan and cast in bronze at Lauritz Tasmussen's Bronze Foundry in 1918. Hasselriis' original plaster statuette is housed in the Danish National Gallery. The enlarged plaster copy was part of Aarsleff's private collection and later donated to Østfyns Museum, where it was previously displayed in the assembly hall of Nyborg Gymnasium and is now located outside the Søren Kierkegaard Auditorium in the University of Copenhagen's Department of Theology in Copenhagen. A second statue of Søren Kierkegaard in Copenhagen is found on the exterior of Frederik's Church and was created in 1972 by Knud Nellemose. Stefan Parkman, born on 22 June 1952 in Uppsala, is a Swedish conductor. He serves as a professor at Uppsala University, holding the Eric Ericson chair of choral conducting. From 2002 to 2005, he was the head conductor of the Swedish Radio Choir, and he has also conducted the Danish Radio Choir and the Boys' Choir of Uppsala Cathedral. Since 1983, he has led Uppsala Akademiska Kammarkör. Parkman received the Danish Order of the Dannebrog in 1997 and was elected a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Music in 1998. Stephen Rodger Waugh AO (born 2 June 1965) is an Australian former international cricketer and twin brother of cricketer Mark Waugh. A right-handed batsman and medium-pace bowler, Waugh is considered one of the greatest cricketers of all time. He was part of the Australian team that won their first World Cup title in 1987. As captain from 1997 to 2004, he led Australia to fifteen of their record sixteen consecutive Test wins and to victory in the 1999 Cricket World Cup. Waugh is regarded as the most successful Test captain in history with 41 victories and a winning ratio of 72%. Born in New South Wales, he began his first-class cricket career in 1984 and captained the Australian Test team from 1999 to 2004, becoming the most capped Test player in history with 168 appearances until Sachin Tendulkar of India surpassed this record in 2010. He was the world number 1 all-rounder in both Test and One Day International (ODI) cricket until back issues forced him to stop bowling, after which he focused solely on batting and became one of the leading batsmen of his era. He is one of only fourteen players to have scored more than 10,000 Test runs. Waugh was named Australian of the Year in 2004 for his philanthropy and was inducted into the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in January 2010 in front of his home fans at the Sydney Cricket Ground. He has been included in the National Trust of Australia's list of one hundred Australian Living Treasures and has received the Order of Australia and the Australian Sports Medal. Known as an attacking and sometimes ruthlessly efficient captain, cricket columnist Simon Barnes described him in 2003 as a "cold-blooded, scientific" leader, noting that "Waugh wants to defeat you personally." At the end of his final Test match, he was carried by teammates in a lap of honour at the Sydney Cricket Ground. In a 2017 fan poll by the CA, he was named in the country's best Ashes XI in the last 40 years. Born at Canterbury Hospital in Campsie, South-Western Sydney, Waugh was one of twin boys born to Rodger and Beverley Waugh, arriving four minutes before Mark, who also played for Australia. Their father was a bank official and their mother a teacher in the New South Wales Department of Education. The family settled in Panania. The twins were later joined by brothers Dean (who played first-class cricket) and Danny (who played first grade for Sydney University Cricket Club). From an early age, the children were introduced to sport; by six, they were playing organised soccer, tennis, and cricket, and both were dismissed for ducks in their first match. Their paternal grandfather Edward was a greyhound trainer who played for the New South Wales Country rugby league team and was about to join Eastern Suburbs before retiring due to family reasons. Rodger was Edward's only son and was a promising junior tennis player, ranked eighth in Australia and state champion at under-14 level. On the maternal side, Bev was a tennis player who won the under-14 singles at the South Australian Championships; her eldest brother Dion Bourne was an opening batsman who played for Bankstown and remains the club's leading runscorer. The twins joined the Bankstown District under-10s at age eight and were the youngest ever selected for the New South Wales Primary Schools' soccer team in 1976. They won the Umbro International Shield, scoring all three goals in the final, and were key in their school's consecutive state cricket championships and second place in the state tennis final. In his final year, Steve was vice-captain of the cricket team and captained the state soccer team. They were instrumental in New South Wales winning the cricket carnival without a defeat, combining for a 150-run partnership in one match. As their sports demands increased, conflicts arose, and one of them was delisted from a team due to commitment issues. They attended East Hills Boys Technology High School, known for producing Australian international athletes. At 13, they were invited by their uncle Bourne, then captain of Bankstown's first grade team, to trial for the under-16 Green Shield team, and both were selected. At 14, they made their senior grade cricket debut in 1979–1980 in the Fourth XI and broke into the East Hills Boys First XI that season, achieving the same in soccer. In 1980–81, they were promoted to the Third XI mid-season. They often formed a two-man team, taking 16/85 between them. In 1980, they were selected for the state under-16 team at the national carnival. They changed soccer teams to play in the reserve grade for Sydney Croatia, earning small professional payments, but left quickly as cricket took precedence. They were promoted to Bankstown's Second XI before being selected for the First XI in the 1982–83 season at age 17, both making their debut against Western Suburbs, though Waugh was later dropped back to the Second XI. He was regarded as an aggressive player, a trait that defined his early international career. The twins finished high school in 1983. In 1983–84, both were part of New South Wales Combined High Schools and the state under-19 team; Waugh scored 170 against Great Public Schools. They were first selected for Australia in the national under-19 team to play a Test and ODI series against Sri Lanka. In the Third Test at Melbourne, Waugh scored 187 as Australia won 1–0. After high school, Waugh enrolled in a teaching course but withdrew after a few lectures. He made his maiden First XI century during the season, scoring a ton against Sydney University and Waverley. At the start of the 1984–85 season, both were included in the New South Wales state squad. At the end of the season, they signed a contract to play for Egerton Cricket Club in the Bolton League in Lancashire, with Steve officially designated as a professional but splitting earnings with Mark. They were billeted with a local family. During the year, the Australian rebel tour to South Africa occurred, breaking the apartheid boycott, leading to some players defecting; Dave Gilbert was promoted to the national squad, forfeiting his Esso scholarship, and Steve was selected to replace him with Essex, leaving Mark as the only professional. In December 2017, his son Austin Waugh was named in Australia's squad for the 2018 Under-19 Cricket World Cup. Waugh made his first-class debut for New South Wales in 1984–85, batting at number nine and bowling medium pace. In the Sheffield Shield final that season, he scored 71 while batting with the tail to help NSW win. After ten first-class matches for NSW, he made his Test debut against India in the 1985–86 season in the Second Test at Melbourne, scoring 13 and 5 and taking 2/36 in the first innings. He scored only 26 runs in four innings during the series and was retained for the tour of New Zealand, where he had a good all-round performance in the Second Test at Christchurch, scoring 74 and claiming 4/56, though his batting average remained 17.40. In the one-day format, he made his debut against New Zealand at the MCG, taking 1/13 and a catch, and did not bat as the match was washed out. He played in all 12 matches of the triangular tournament, scoring 266 runs at 38.00 with two half-centuries, including a top score of 81 in the Australia Day victory over India, and took seven wickets at 33.00. He played in all four ODIs on the tour of New Zealand, scoring 111 runs at 27.75 and taking four wickets at 39.75. The Australian selectors retained him for a tour of India in 1986, despite scoring only 113 runs at 12.56 in his Test career. In the three Tests, he scored 59 runs once and took two wickets. As a bowler, he bore a heavy workload, though selected primarily for his batting. He played in all six ODIs, scoring 111 runs at 55.50 and taking seven wickets at 35.86. In the First Test against England at Brisbane in 1986–87, he bowled a long spell, taking 3/76, then scored 0 and 28 as Australia lost.
