In the Second Test at Perth, he made 71 and had match figures of 5/159, including 5/69 in the second innings, and scored 79 not out in the drawn Third Test at Adelaide. His scores of 49 and 73 in the last two Tests gave him series figures of 310 runs (at 44.29) and ten wickets (at 33.60), a fighting effort in a team defeated 1–2. The win in the Fifth Test was the first time Waugh was in a victorious Test team in his 13th match. He played in all 13 ODIs for the home season, scoring 372 runs at 37.20 with two half-centuries and taking 21 wickets at 21.80. He regularly performed with both bat and ball; against Pakistan, he scored 82 and took 4/48 but could not stop a one-wicket victory, then scored 83* and took 2/30 in an Australia Day win over England. He failed to maintain form in the finals, scoring one and one and taking 1/78 as England won 2–0. Early in his career, Waugh was a natural, uninhibited strokeplayer who liked to drive off the back foot, scoring quickly but inconsistently at Test level and was better suited to ODI cricket. As a bowler, he was known for his astute change of pace and was the pioneer in inventing a carefully disguised slower ball bowled from the back of the hand, regularly used in the final overs, where his change of pace was difficult to score from. Allan Border often used Waugh as a final overs specialist in crucial situations, and at his peak, he was the top slog overs specialist bowler for any conditions. The 1987 World Cup, played on the Indian subcontinent, marked a turning point in Waugh's career. He scored 19* in the death overs against India in the first match, and his tight bowling in the closing overs ended with the dismissal of Maninder Singh in the final over, securing a one-run victory. In the match against Zimbabwe, he scored 45 and conceded only seven runs in six overs, leading to a 96-run win. Against New Zealand, he bowled the last over when the Kiwis needed seven runs, restricting them to three runs by taking two wickets, ending with 2/36. In the second round robin, he took 1/59 and scored 42 in a 56-run loss to India, then took 2/37 in a 17-run win over New Zealand. In Australia's final group match, he scored 10* and took 1/9 from four overs in a 70-run win over Zimbabwe. Australia qualified for the semi-finals and faced co-hosts Pakistan in Lahore. Batting first, Waugh hit 16 from the final over of the innings in a cameo of 32*, helping Australia win by 18 runs. In the final, he scored an unbeaten five in a brief innings at the end of the innings. He was a key player as Australia defended a target of 254 against England at Kolkata, claiming the wickets of Allan Lamb and Phillip DeFreitas in the 47th and 49th overs as England faltered. Australia won by seven runs to claim the World Cup for the first time. Waugh compiled 167 runs at 55.66 and took 11 wickets at 26.18. These performances in tight situations earned him the nickname "Iceman." However, he remained inconsistent in Test matches, scoring only 194 runs at 32.33 in five Tests in 1987–88 against New Zealand, England, and Sri Lanka, with nine wickets at 29.67. His ODI form remained strong, playing in all 11 ODIs, scoring 226 runs at 32.29 and taking 18 wickets at 23.50, including a 4/33 in a match against Sri Lanka. In a Test tour of Pakistan in late 1988, he scored 92 runs at 18.40 with one half-century and two wickets at 108.00. In 1988–89 against the West Indies, he mixed batting failures with two entertaining innings of 90 and 91 on the faster pitches of Brisbane and Perth. He bowled bouncers at Viv Richards at Brisbane, claiming 3/77 and 5/92 in the Third Test at Melbourne. Bill O'Reilly wrote that the most significant incident of the Brisbane Test was the three consecutive bouncers Waugh served up to Viv Richards, which he described as an uncompromising message to the West Indies captain about the end of the bouncer policy. Waugh continued to perform well in ODIs, scoring 270 runs at 38.57 and taking seven wickets at 49.42, with his highest score and best bowling analysis occurring in the same match—taking 3/57 before scoring 54 against the West Indies in Melbourne. Despite this, Australia lost the match. Heading into the 1989 Ashes series, Waugh's batting average was 30.52 from 26 Tests. In the three-match ODI series before the Tests, he scored 113 runs at 37.66 and took three wickets at 54.00. Waugh finally scored his maiden Test century, 177 not out in the First Test at Leeds, a free-flowing innings marked by square driving that lasted just over five hours and helped Australia set a strong platform for a win. He followed this with an unbeaten 152 in the Second Test at Lord's, effectively guiding his tail-end partners to set up a 242-run first-innings lead. He was not dismissed until...

Waugh scored 270 runs at 38.57 and took seven wickets at 49.42, with his highest score and best bowling analysis occurring in the same match—taking 3/57 before scoring 54 against West Indies in Melbourne—despite Australia losing the game. Heading into the 1989 Ashes series, his batting average was 30.52 from 26 Tests; in the preceding three-match ODI series, he scored 113 runs at 37.66 and took three wickets at 54.00. He scored his maiden Test century, 177 not out, in the First Test at Leeds, a free-flowing innings marked by square driving that lasted over five hours and helped Australia set a large first-innings total. He followed with an unbeaten 152 in the Second Test at Lord's, guiding his tail partners to build a 242-run first-innings lead, and was not dismissed until the first innings of the Third Test for 43, by which time he had 393 runs. He scored 92 in the Fourth Test at Old Trafford in a win and did not pass 20 in the last two Tests, finishing the series with 506 runs at 126.5; he bowled only twice, taking two wickets, and first experienced back problems that would hinder his bowling. On the brief India Nehru Cup ODI tour after the Ashes, he played as a specialist batsman, scoring 88 runs at 22.00 and not bowling. During the 1989/90 international season, he scored 378 runs at 37.8 in six Tests in Australia and one in New Zealand; the highlight was an unbeaten 134 against Sri Lanka in the Second Test in Hobart, following twin half-centuries in the First Test. His focus on batting resulted in only 1/19 with the ball in seven Tests. His Test form tapered off thereafter. In ODIs, Australia played ten at home and five in New Zealand; after taking two wickets at 38.50 in the first three ODIs, Waugh did not bowl again. After scoring only 99 runs at 19.80 in the first nine ODIs in Australia, he was dropped for the Second Final against Pakistan, which Australia won. He played in all five ODIs in New Zealand, scoring only 72 runs at 18.00. He returned to bowling in the Sharjah tournament, taking four wickets at 28.00 and scoring 98 runs at 49.00. In 1990, Waugh and his twin brother Mark scored an unbeaten 464 in 407 minutes for NSW against Western Australia at the WACA Ground, setting a world first-class record; both teams were at full strength and WA's attack included Test bowlers Terry Alderman, Bruce Reid, and Chris Matthews, with the twins ending on 216 and 229 respectively. During the 1990–91 Ashes series in Australia, Waugh suffered a form slump, making only 82 runs at 20.50, and was dropped for the Fourth Test at Adelaide; he was replaced by his twin Mark, who scored a century on debut. However, he remained a regular in the ODI team, playing in all ten ODIs, scoring 141 runs at 35.25 and taking seven wickets at 49.42. Recalled for the Third Test in Trinidad during the 1991 Caribbean tour, he and Mark became the first twins to play in a Test match together; however, he failed to post a significant score and was dropped for the Fifth Test, Australia's only win in the series. He played in all five ODIs, scoring 86 runs at 28.66 and taking five wickets at 30.60. Waugh remained out of the Test team for eighteen months and did not play in the five-day format during the 1991–92 season. Nevertheless, he played in all 18 ODIs, scoring only 146 runs at 18.25 but consistently taking 16 wickets at 19.00. As a result, he retained his position in the team for all eight of Australia's group matches in the 1992 Cricket World Cup in Australia and New Zealand, scoring 187 runs at 26.71 and taking eight wickets at 34.63; he scored 55 and took 2/28 in a 128-run win over Zimbabwe as Australia failed to progress beyond the group stage. He returned as number three batsman for the 1992–93 home Test series against the West Indies, with a 228-run average at 25.33 bolstered by a 100 in the Third Test in Sydney; Waugh called this "probably the most important hundred of my Test career ... word had reached me that if I didn't get runs, then I was going to be dropped." He continued to be a fixture in the ODI team, playing in all ten matches and scoring 213 runs at 23.66 with one half-century and taking nine wickets at 39.22. Solid performances in New Zealand, where he scored 178 Test runs at 44.50, enabled him to hold his position on the 1993 Ashes tour of England. He completed the tour with 120 runs at 30.00 and three wickets at 57.66 in five ODIs; the three-match ODI series in England preceded the Tests and Waugh scored 41 runs at 20.50 and took five wickets at 30.20. During the Test series, Michael Slater became the regular opener and Boon returned to the middle order; Waugh gained the number six position ahead of two promising Western Australians, Justin Langer and Damien Martyn. In the Fourth Test at Headingley, Waugh's 157 not out earned comparisons to his 1989 efforts and he shared an unbroken stand of 332 with Allan Border. He also scored half-centuries in the First and Fifth Tests and ended with 416 at 83.2 from limited opportunities—playing nine innings, only five of which were completed. Australia's top order dominated the English attack, and the tourists retained the Ashes 4–1. Returning to Australia, he solidified his position by scoring an unbeaten 147 against New Zealand in an innings victory in the Third Test at Brisbane, ending the series with 216 runs once dismissed. He missed part of the 1993–94 triangular ODI tournament with New Zealand and South Africa due to a hamstring injury in late December, as well as the first two Tests against the South Africans. He returned for the end of the ODIs and ended with 141 runs at 23.50 and taking four wickets at 54.50. Waugh played in the Third Test at Adelaide Oval in late January with Australia trailing 1–0; he scored a 160 and took 4/26 as Australia won the Test and levelled the series. He was named international player of the [Australian] season. He took 5/28 and scored 86 in the Second Test of the return series in South Africa at Newlands, Cape Town, helping Australia level the series 1–1 after losing the first at Wanderers in Johannesburg. Another half-century saw him end with 195 runs at 65.00 and his bowling was at its most productive in five years, with 10 wickets at 13.00. In the ODI series, he received the player of the series for his all-round efforts, which hauled Australia back from a deficit of 2–4 to draw the series at 4–4; he took 2/48 in the final match as Australia levelled the series by one run, ending with 291 runs at 48.50 and five wickets at 56.40. At the conclusion of the tour, the Australian Cricket Board interviewed Waugh, along with David Boon, Mark Taylor, and Ian Healy to determine their opinions on the team's direction after Allan Border's impending retirement; despite Waugh's greater experience, Taylor was granted the captaincy and Healy was made vice-captain. The new leadership took the team to Sri Lanka for the Singer World Series ODI tournament and then on a Test-playing tour of Pakistan; Waugh scored 53 runs at 17.66 and took five wickets in 16.20. On the latter tour, he made 73 in the First Test, which Australia lost by one wicket; his 98 in the Second Test at Rawalpindi was notable for his survival against a hostile barrage of short-pitched bowling from Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, falling when a bouncer struck his body and rolled onto the stumps. A shoulder injury forced him out of the final Test, which Australia drew and therefore lost the series. Waugh scored 153 runs at 38.25 with two half-centuries and took two wickets at 72.00 as Australia won the ODI tournament. During the 1994–95 Ashes series against England, he narrowly missed centuries in the Second and Fifth Test in Melbourne and Perth, scoring 94 and 99 not out respectively when the last wicket fell; in the second instance, his brother Mark was run out after a mix-up while running for the injured Craig McDermott. It was an uneven series performance, scoring 94* and 26* in the Second Test and 99* and 80 in the Fifth, but not passing 20 in the six innings of the other three Tests; he ended the series with 345 at 49.28 and did not bowl for the entire series. Waugh played only one ODI for the season, scoring a duck and not bowling a ball. The season ended with a short ODI tournament in New Zealand, which Australia won; Waugh scored 81 runs at 27.00 in four matches and did not bowl. The West Indies had been Australia's bête noire since winning the Frank Worrell Trophy in 1978; at the beginning of Australia's 1995 tour of the Caribbean, the West Indies had not lost a Test series since 1980 and had not lost a Test series to Australia at home since 1973. The Tests were preceded by an ODI series lost 1–4; Waugh scored 164 runs at 32.80 and took three wickets at 41.00. In a low-scoring, four-Test series, Waugh compiled 429 runs at an average of 107.25 and claimed five wickets (for 62 runs), winning the player of the series award; his twin Mark was the next best batsman with 240 runs at 40.00. During the First Test at Barbados, Waugh claimed a low catch from Brian Lara in the first innings; television replays were inconclusive but suggested the ball may have hit the ground; Lara, known for accepting the word of the fielder without question, left the field. Following his dismissal, the West Indies' batting collapsed, and Australia won by ten wickets. Waugh later faced accusations of dishonesty and cheating over the incident. After scoring 65 not out in the drawn Second Test at Antigua, Waugh defied the Caribbean pacemen on a green pitch at Trinidad suited to their hostile bowling during the Third Test. In the first innings, he scored an unbeaten 63 of Australia's 128 and had a mid-pitch confrontation with Curtly Ambrose; after evading a bouncer from Ambrose, the pair exchanged glares, Waugh swore and told Ambrose to return to his bowling mark; an angry Ambrose had to be physically dragged away by his captain—a photograph of this moment became one of the iconic images of cricket in the 1990s, symbolising when Australia was no longer intimidated by the West Indies. Waugh "showed he was prepared to put it all on the line," said Justin Langer, "in the toughest conditions [...] against probably the best fast bowler of our time. To stand up to him [Ambrose] and go toe to toe [...] gave us a huge boost." Nevertheless, the West Indies won the match and levelled the series. In the decider in Jamaica, Waugh took 2/14 in the West Indies' first innings of 265 and then arrived at the crease with Australia at 73 for three in reply; he compiled a long partnership of 231 runs with his brother Mark, who was eventually out for 126; Waugh was the last man to go, out for 200 after nine hours of batting. "Steve had made up his mind to bat and bat," wrote Paul Reiffel, "to stay out there and anchor the proceedings. [... H]e copped a lot of blows on his arms, chest and ribs. When he came back to the dressing room at the end of day two, we could see the spots and bruises on his body [...]. I remember when I walked in [...] he didn't say anything to me, but then he didn't need to. We all pretty much knew that we just had to support him." He was in a trance-like state; in the wee hours of the second morning, a security guard was found rifling through Steve's kit bag. That incident did not affect his concentration. It all just went to show how strong a character he was. Waugh played patiently and reached his double century with an all-run four to fine-leg off a quicker ball from Carl Hooper; he was the last man out. With a large lead on first innings, Australia dismissed the opposition for a low score to win a crushing victory. After some post-win wassailing, Waugh retired to bed in his cricket whites, socks, and baggy green. "[Y]ou could say that Steve's legacy gained a lot of momentum from his efforts at Jamaica," wrote Reiffel. Waugh started the 1995–96 Australian season ranked as the world's leading Test batsman. He made an unbeaten 112 as Australia defeated Pakistan in the First Test at Brisbane and scored 200 runs at 50.00 for the series. Suffering an injury in December, he missed the First Test against Sri Lanka and part of the triangular ODI tournament, then returned for the Boxing Day Test at Melbourne to score 131 not out. Waugh returned during the latter stages of the triangular tournament, playing in the last four matches after missing the first six. He scored his maiden ODI century, ten years after his ODI debut, with an unbeaten 102 against Sri Lanka in Melbourne. Despite this, Australia lost by three wickets. Waugh ended with 128 runs at 42.66 and did not take a wicket, bowling only four overs on his comeback from injury. He helped Australia to a 3–0 result in the Test series by scoring 170 and 61 not out at Adelaide to end the series with 362 runs for once out. He also took 4/34 in the Third Test. During the 1996 Cricket World Cup on the subcontinent, Waugh scored 82 and featured in a 207-run partnership with his brother during Australia's first match against Kenya—an Australian record partnership at the World Cup. He made an unbeaten half-century in the quarter-final against New Zealand at Madras, sealing a successful run chase. However, he was less effective in the semi-final and final, failing to pass 20 on either occasion. Australia lost the final to Sri Lanka at Lahore. After the World Cup, Geoff Marsh replaced Bob Simpson as coach. The Australians started the new era with two ODI tournaments in Sri Lanka and India. Waugh scored 366 runs at 40.66 with three half-centuries and took five wickets at 37.40 across nine matches. The tour ended with a solitary Test against India in Delhi, where Waugh was the only Australian to make a half-century in a defeat. Waugh failed to make a century in the five Tests of the 1996–97 Australian season against the West Indies, scoring 255 runs at 36.42 with three half-centuries.

In Australia's first match against Kenya at the World Cup, Waugh scored 82 and shared a 207-run partnership with his brother, setting an Australian record for the tournament. He made an unbeaten half-century in the quarter-final against New Zealand at Madras, securing a successful run chase. However, he failed to pass 20 in the semi-final and final, and Australia lost the final to Sri Lanka in Lahore. After the World Cup, Geoff Marsh replaced Bob Simpson as coach. The Australians began the new era with two ODI tournaments in Sri Lanka and India, where Waugh scored 366 runs at 40.66 with three half-centuries and took five wickets at 37.40 across nine matches. The tour concluded with a solitary Test against India in Delhi, where Waugh was the only Australian to score a half-century in a defeat. Waugh failed to make a century in the five Tests against the West Indies during the 1996–97 season, scoring 255 runs at 36.42 with three half-centuries, and missed the Second Test after injuring his groin while bowling in the First. The injury limited his availability to six of Australia's eight ODI matches in the annual triangular tournament, where he managed only 159 runs at 26.50 and bowled three overs without taking a wicket, as Australia missed the finals. Waugh returned to form on the 1997 tour of South Africa, averaging 78.25, scoring 160 in the First Test at Johannesburg in a 385-run partnership with Greg Blewett, and top-scoring with half-centuries in both innings of the Third Test, which Australia lost. After Ian Healy was suspended for throwing his bat, Waugh replaced him as Mark Taylor's deputy. In seven ODIs, he scored 301 runs at 50.16 with four half-centuries, including 50 and 50* in the first two matches, 89 in a run chase in the sixth match to seal a 4–2 series win with one over in hand, and 91 in the final match in a vain run chase. In the 1997 Ashes tour, Australia started poorly with a 0–3 loss in the ODI series, with Waugh scoring only 60 runs at 20.00. Australia lost the First Test by nine wickets, drew the Second Test, won the toss in the Third Test at Manchester, and after gambling on batting first on a green pitch, slumped to 3/42 in the first hour when Waugh came out to bat, scoring 108; he then began his second innings with Australia on 3/39 and scored 116, both centuries in a low-scoring match that won the game. Australia levelled the series and retained the Ashes 3–2, with Waugh finishing the series with 390 runs at 39 average. Waugh took over the captaincy of the one-day side in 1997–98 after Mark Taylor and Ian Healy were dropped following Australia's failure to qualify for the tri-nations tournament in 1996–97. Planning began for a more modern team for the 1999 Cricket World Cup, with Adam Gilchrist's batting prowess critical. The new team started poorly, losing all four preliminary matches against South Africa, with Michael di Venuto, Tom Moody, and Stuart Law all tried as Waugh's opening partner. Waugh struggled, scoring only 12 runs, including three ducks in his first six innings, before scoring 45* in the last round-robin match to ensure qualification for the finals ahead of New Zealand. With Gilchrist elevated to opener in the finals, Australia defeated South Africa 2–1. Waugh scored 53 and 71 in his two innings, ending the series with 181 runs at 22.63 and taking a solitary wicket, his first ODI wicket in over a year. In the 1997–98 Test season against New Zealand and South Africa, Waugh scored 80 three times in six Tests without a century, averaging 40.89, and Australia won both series. He bowled more frequently than before, taking six wickets at 17.33. After the southern hemisphere season, Waugh led a four-match ODI tour of New Zealand, scoring 112 runs at 37.33 and taking three wickets at 42.00, drawing the series 2–2. On the 1998 tour of India, he scored 80 in the Second Test at Calcutta but missed the following Test due to injury, ending with 152 runs at 38. He recovered to lead in the triangular tournament in India, winning both games against Zimbabwe but losing both to India. In the final, Waugh contributed with bat and ball, taking 2/42 and scoring 57, and Australia beat India by four wickets. In the Sharjah triangular tournament, Australia won all four group matches against India and New Zealand, but India won the final by six wickets despite Waugh's 70. Waugh totalled 254 runs at 28.22 and eight wickets at 33.50 across the two tournaments. Later in the year, he top-scored with 157 in the First Test against Pakistan at Karachi, enabling Australia to force an innings victory and gain their first win in Pakistan in 39 years, forming the basis of a 1–0 series win, in which Waugh scored 235 runs at 58.75. Waugh led the ODI team in a 3–0 sweep of Pakistan after the Tests, but managed only 40 runs at 13.33. The following season, Waugh suffered hamstring injuries and missed most of the ODI tournament; in the two matches he played, he made only a duck and 20, and Australia lost both. Shane Warne led Australia to victory in his absence, winning eight of the remaining 10 matches. Waugh began the Ashes series with centuries in the First Test at Brisbane (112) and the Third Test at Melbourne, but was criticised for taking singles off the first ball of an over, exposing tail-end batsmen. Stuart MacGill and Glenn McGrath fell to Darren Gough after one such instance, leading to Australia's collapse in the second innings while chasing a small target. In the Fifth Test, Waugh shared a century partnership with brother Mark for the second consecutive year, scoring 96 while his brother reached a century; Australia won the Test and the series 3–1. Mark Taylor retired at the end of the 1998–99 season, and Waugh replaced him as Test captain, beginning with a tour of the Caribbean. Australia was expected to win as the West Indies had been whitewashed 5–0 by South Africa. After easily winning the First Test, Australia was stymied by West Indies skipper Brian Lara, who batted with Jimmy Adams for the entire second day of the Second Test, leading to a home side victory. In the Third Test, Lara batted for the entire final day to secure an unlikely one-wicket win. This result placed Waugh under pressure, and he controversially dropped Shane Warne from the team for the final Fourth Test. Australia won the final Test despite a third consecutive century from Lara and retained the Frank Worrell Trophy 2–2. The subsequent ODI series between the two teams was drawn 3–3. The series was notable for two incidents: in the fifth match at Georgetown, Guyana, Waugh faced Keith Arthurton with his team needing four runs from the final over to win; he struck the last ball into the outfield and attempted three runs to tie the match. A crowd invasion removed all stumps, with Waugh out of his ground when the ball was returned by the fielder, and the match was declared a tie. During the West Indies run-chase in the final match in Barbados, local batsman Sherwin Campbell was run out after falling over due to a collision with bowler Brendon Julian, resulting in a crowd riot and Waugh nearly being struck in the head with a glass bottle. The match continued after Campbell was reinstated, but Waugh criticised the security and questioned the integrity of the match. Waugh struggled in the lead-up to the World Cup, scoring 135 runs at 22.50 and taking two wickets at 33.00. Australia had a slow start to the 1999 World Cup in England, winning a scratchy match against Scotland but suffering defeats to New Zealand and Pakistan, so they had to win two remaining group matches (against Bangladesh and the West Indies) and all three "Super Six" matches to progress to the semi-finals—this meant seven consecutive matches without defeat to win the World Cup. After defeating Bangladesh, Waugh and Michael Bevan were criticised for deliberately batting slowly to minimise damage to the net run rate of the West Indies, enhancing Australia's chances: if the West Indies' run rate remained high, they would qualify ahead of New Zealand. Since Australia had lost to New Zealand, it would be the Kiwis that carried two points if the West Indies were eliminated. If the West Indies proceeded, Australia would carry over two points from the win. When questioned about the ethics of this manipulation, Waugh retorted, "We're not here to win friends mate." After beating India and Zimbabwe in their first two Super Six matches, Waugh saved his best for two must-win games against South Africa: he scored an unbeaten 120 against South Africa in the "Super Six" phase and 56 in the semi-final. The latter match was tied, and Australia progressed to the final, where they crushed Pakistan by eight wickets to win the trophy. The World Cup victory did not immediately improve Waugh's Test form. The tour to Sri Lanka continued difficulties, with Australia losing the First Test in Kandy, exacerbated by a fielding collision between Waugh and Jason Gillespie, where Waugh's nose made contact with Gillespie's shin, resulting in Gillespie suffering a broken leg that sidelined him for 15 months and Waugh having his nose broken. Although Waugh returned for the next match, the last two Tests were drawn due to monsoonal weather interruptions. Waugh had a lean series with 52 runs at 17.33. The team then played an inaugural Test against Zimbabwe at Harare, winning by ten wickets, with Waugh's 151 not out being the first century in Tests between the nations. After the team's return home, John Buchanan replaced Geoff Marsh as team coach. In the 1999–2000 Test season, his first as captain in a home series, Gilchrist ousted Healy from the wicket-keeper's position. With Gilchrist averaging over 50, the team claimed a clean-sweep of both Test series, 3–0 against Pakistan and India. Waugh had a lean stretch during the Pakistan series, scoring 58 runs at 14.50, but the team won by margins of ten wickets, four wickets, and an innings. Waugh returned to form in the First Test against India at the Adelaide Oval, scoring 150 in the first innings. He only passed fifty once more in the series, ending with 276 runs at 55.20. Australia won all three Tests by comfortable margins of 285 runs, 180 runs, and an innings. After losing their first match, the team won the season's triangular ODI tournament without further defeat. They then toured New Zealand and won the ODI series 5–1, losing their final match, ending a world record of 14 consecutive ODI victories. They then swept the Tests against New Zealand 3–0 in early 2000, taking the Tests by 62 runs, six wickets, and six wickets respectively. Waugh led the way in the Second Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington with an unbeaten 151 but otherwise did not pass 20, totalling 214 runs at 53.50. His men won all nine of their Tests during the southern hemisphere summer. The team continued their winning streak with an undefeated home season in 2000–01, whitewashing the West Indies 5–0. The first two Tests were won by an innings, and the Second Test at the WACA brought a twelfth consecutive Test victory, surpassing the record held by the 1980s West Indies team led by Clive Lloyd. Waugh missed the Third Test with injury, and Gilchrist led the team in his absence, keeping the winning streak alive. Waugh returned for the last two Tests and scored centuries in the first innings of both Tests with 121* and 103 respectively, which Australia won by 352 runs and six wickets respectively. Waugh compiled 349 runs at 69.80. Waugh then led the Australians undefeated in the triangular ODI tournament against the West Indies and Zimbabwe, despite using a rotation system that often left the team understrength with players rested. The only significant result Australia had failed to achieve during Waugh's international career was a Test series victory in India. Waugh began calling this the "Final Frontier" as Australia had not won there since 1969–70. Australia easily won the First Test at Mumbai by ten wickets to extend the winning sequence to 16. India looked set for defeat in the Second Test at Eden Gardens in Kolkata after conceding a first innings lead of 274. Waugh top-scored in the first innings with 110. He chose to enforce the follow-on, the only time Australia had done so in over five years. However, VVS Laxman (281) and Rahul Dravid (180) batted for the entire fourth day's play and set Australia a target of 384 on a dusty, spinning wicket. The Australians were unable to cope with the spin of Harbhajan Singh on the final day, becoming only the third team to lose a Test after enforcing the follow-on. Starting the final Test well, Australia's batting collapsed on the second morning, losing 6/26 after Waugh became the sixth batsman to be given out for handling the ball—he pushed a ball from Harbhajan away from the stumps after being hit on the pads. Waugh's pair of 47s was not enough as Harbhajan finished with 15 wickets in the match to lead India to a two-wicket win. Waugh's team regrouped and won a 4–1 series victory over England during the 2001 Ashes tour. He scored 105 in the First Test at Edgbaston as the Australians started with an innings victory. Waugh did not pass 50 in the next two Tests, but Australia won both by eight and seven wickets respectively to retain the Ashes. However, Waugh pulled a calf muscle and missed the Fourth Test at Headingley, which Australia lost. In his final Test innings on English soil at The Oval, he combined with brother Mark (120) in a partnership of 197 and scored 157 not out. Australia won by an innings to seal the series 4–1, with Waugh scoring 321 runs at 107.00. He was unable to maintain this form during the 2001–02 Australian season, failing to score a century in the six Tests against New Zealand and South Africa. The first two Tests against New Zealand were drawn due to rain, and the Third also ended in a draw. Waugh failed to pass double figures until scoring.

Steve Waugh played a key role in Australia's success during the 2001–02 season, scoring 105 in the First Test at Edgbaston as the Australians began the Ashes series with an innings victory. Although he failed to pass 50 in the next two Tests, Australia won both by eight and seven wickets respectively, retaining the Ashes. Waugh pulled a calf muscle and missed the Fourth Test at Headingley, which Australia lost. In his final Test innings on English soil at The Oval, he shared a 197-run partnership with brother Mark (who scored 120) and finished with 157 not out, helping Australia win by an innings to seal the series 4–1, with Waugh scoring 321 runs at 107.00. During the 2001–02 Australian season, he failed to score a century in six Tests against New Zealand and South Africa; the first two Tests against New Zealand were drawn due to rain, and the Third also ended in a draw. Waugh scored only 8 and 13 in the First Test against South Africa, but Australia won by 246 runs. His best score of the series was 90 in the Second Test at the MCG, which was ended by a run-out decision not referred to the video umpire; he faced criticism for not leaving the ground until he watched a replay on the stadium's video screen. Australia won the Third Test at the SCG by ten wickets, with Waugh scoring 30. Australia started the 2001–02 VB Series poorly, losing the first three preliminary matches due to a rotation policy that unsettled the team and was later scrapped. The team won four of the last five matches but failed to qualify for the finals for only the third time in 23 years. In their final match, Australia needed a win and a bonus point against South Africa, as New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming had previously conceded a bonus point in retaliation to Waugh's tactics in the World Cup. The team's performance sparked a reaction similar to 1997, and with an eye toward the next World Cup, selectors dropped the Waugh brothers and appointed Ricky Ponting as captain. Waugh publicly expressed his displeasure and stated a desire to return to the side. As Test captain, Waugh led Australia to a 2–1 victory in South Africa, retaining Australia's number one ranking. Australia won the First Test by an innings and 360 runs, won the Second Test by four wickets, and lost the Third. Waugh's form was poor, with 95 runs at 19.00, and he left the tour when the ODI series began. Arriving in Australia alone, he faced media questions about his playing future, responding: "We've just beaten the next best team in the world 5–1, and all you want to talk about is getting me out of the team." Speculation about the Waugh brothers' futures continued ahead of the mid-2002 Test series against Pakistan, hosted in the UAE and Sri Lanka due to security concerns after a bomb blast in Pakistan. Australia won 3–0, winning the last two matches by an innings, but the Waughs had little influence. Steve scored 103 not out in his final innings after consecutive ducks, which may have saved his career; his brother was dropped for the 2002–03 Ashes series and announced his retirement. Despite Australia being well ahead, Waugh struggled in the early part of the Ashes series, scoring only 106 runs in four innings in the first three Tests. Australia crushed England in the First Test by 384 runs and recorded consecutive innings victories. In the Fourth Test at the MCG, he scored 77 in the first innings and took his first Test wicket in four years; he did not bowl often as captain. His 14 in the second innings was marked by many inside edges and false strokes, leading to speculation he would be dropped. Australia reached their target with five wickets down despite a stumble on the final morning. The Fifth Test in Sydney began with speculation it would be Waugh's last unless he reversed his form slump. Asked to name a defining moment of a career likely to end, he said: "It might be yet to come." On the second day, he fulfilled this prophecy by scoring a chanceless century, bringing up three figures with a cover drive off the last ball of the day (bowled by off-spinner Richard Dawson), equaling Sir Donald Bradman's then Australian record of 29 Test centuries and saving his career. In the second innings, Australia faced a large target and lost by 225 on a deteriorating pitch, their only loss of the series. When dismissed cheaply, Waugh ran off the field as the crowd gave him a standing ovation, with speculation he might retire after the fairytale century. Waugh was denied a fifth World Cup in 2003. A last-minute reprieve came when all-rounder Shane Watson was injured. Waugh had promoted his bowling abilities through his newspaper column and increasingly used himself as a bowler to strengthen his case for return, but Ricky Ponting advocated for Andrew Symonds, who was included despite controversy and went on to establish himself. During the April 2003 tour to the West Indies, Waugh scored 25 in the First Test and did not bat in the Second, then scored 115 in the Third Test victory. Australia won all three Tests by nine wickets, 118 runs, and nine wickets respectively. He finished the series with 226 runs at 75.33, including 41 and 45* in the Fourth Test. In that match, Australia lost as the hosts broke the record for the highest successful Test run chase. Waugh faced criticism for refusing to control his players after a heated confrontation between Glenn McGrath and West Indian batsman Ramnaresh Sarwan. In the 2003 winter, Waugh scored consecutive unbeaten centuries of 100 and 156 as Australia took a 2–0 sweep over Bangladesh with innings victories. In late-2003, after scoring 78 and 61 in two Tests against Zimbabwe, which Australia won by an innings and nine wickets respectively, Waugh announced the 2003–04 series against India would be his last. In the First Test, Waugh was involved in a controversial run-out when he had a mix-up with Damien Martyn, who walked out to allow Waugh to stay at the crease, generating criticism that his farewell series was prioritized over team victory. With Shane Warne and McGrath unavailable due to drug suspension and injury, Australia struggled to bowl out Indian batsmen. After a rain-affected draw in the First Test, the next two Tests were shared, and Australia needed a win to reclaim the Border–Gavaskar Trophy in the final Fourth Test at the Sydney Cricket Ground. Promoters handed out giant red handkerchiefs to spectators in tribute to Waugh, who had always used a red handkerchief to wipe sweat while batting. Australia's hopes of a win vanished when India batted into the third morning and amassed 7/705 (with Sachin Tendulkar scoring 241*), forcing Australia to chase 449 with just over one day's play. Waugh's highest Test score of the season was his final: 80 in the Fourth Test at Sydney, securing a draw. After a slow start, he adopted an aggressive style once Australia was safe, striking several fours, achieving the highest fourth-innings score of his Test career. When he passed 50, ferries on Sydney Harbour sounded their horns. A record fifth-day SCG crowd gathered to watch his final day as an Australian player. Waugh's leadership led to 16 consecutive Test match victories, surpassing the previous record of 11 by the West Indies. His 168 Test matches were the record until 2010; he captained Australia on 57 occasions, the fourth-highest of all time, and Australia's 41 victories under his leadership were the most until Ricky Ponting surpassed him in December 2009. He holds the record for scoring over 150 runs in one innings against each Test-playing nation at the time. Waugh developed a "slog sweep" shot during the 1998 Commonwealth Games, which is technically unsound but effective against spin and sometimes faster bowlers. Notably, he avoided the 'risky' hook shot, instead playing defensively with back-foot sways or ducks, which made his batting safer and more reliable, raising his Test average to around 50. His ability to continue playing despite a back injury that limited his bowling enhanced his reputation. He contributed to many one-day victories but did not score his first one-day hundred until his 187th match, against Sri Lanka at Melbourne in 1995–96. Early in his career, he was a bowler and all-rounder with a strong leg cutter—full-length, aimed at off stump to tempt middle-order batsmen to hit over mid-wicket or down the ground, or aimed outside off to tempt lower-order batsmen to drive into the infield. Waugh supports a leper children's colony, Udayan, in Kolkata, and encouraged his players to learn about and enjoy the countries they visited. He is a keen photographer and has produced several "tour diaries" featuring his images. In his later years, he wrote for newspapers, insisting on writing them himself, and is a prolific author with books including Never Say Die, The Meaning of Luck, and an autobiography, Out of my Comfort Zone. He was named Australian of the Year in 2004 for his sporting achievements and charity work, married Lynette with three children, and was named Australian Father of the Year in 2005. After retirement, he established the Steve Waugh Foundation, aimed at children with diseases, illnesses, or afflictions not covered by other charities. Waugh has declined multiple approaches by the Australian Labor Party to run for political office, stating he is not suited to politics.

SunPass is an electronic toll collection system in Florida, United States, created in 1999 by the Florida Department of Transportation's (FDOT's) Office of Toll Operations, operating as a division of Florida's Turnpike Enterprise (FTE). The system uses windshield-mounted RFID transponders manufactured by TransCore and lane equipment designed by TransCore, SAIC, and Raytheon. It was introduced on April 24, 1999, and by October 1 of that year, over 100,000 SunPass transponders had been sold. In early 2009, all Easy Pay customers automatically became SunPass Plus customers if they opted in to use their transponders for airport parking at Tampa, Orlando, Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, and Miami airports, with the option to opt out. The SunPass Mini was introduced on July 1, 2008, and became available at retail locations; it is a passive RFID transponder about the size of a credit card, requiring no batteries, and must be mounted on a glass windshield to function properly, with removal damaging the pass; it does not work on motorcycle windshields. SunPass Portable (or SunPass Pro) transponders can be transferred between vehicles. SunPass-only toll lanes on most Florida toll roads allow vehicles to pass at speeds up to 25 mph (40 km/h) for safety, while the Turnpike uses all-electronic tolling (AET) and toll by plate for highway speeds, with mainline toll barriers having dedicated lanes for full-speed automatic toll collection up to 65 mph (105 km/h). In September 2010, February 2011, April 2014, and June 2014, Florida's Turnpike Enterprise converted the Homestead Extension of Florida's Turnpike, the Sawgrass Expressway, the Veterans Expressway, and the Veterans Expressway to open road tolling using SunPass, ending cash collection; motorists without a SunPass are billed via toll by plate, which uses cameras and sends a bill to the registered vehicle owner including a toll and administrative fee; failure to pay results in a $100 fine plus tolls owed, with possible court costs, license points, license suspension, or registration suspension. SunPass is fully interoperable with E-Pass (Central Florida Expressway Authority), O-Pass (Osceola County, now folded into E-Pass), LeeWay (Lee County toll bridges), and Miami-Dade Expressway Authority (MDX) toll roads. Initially, SunPass was not compatible with out-of-state systems; the federal Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act (MAP-21), adopted in July 2012, required all toll facilities to be interoperable by October 1, 2016. SunPass announced in 2012 plans to become interoperable with E-ZPass; by the end of 2015, older battery-powered transponders were phased out, and new batteryless models support out-of-state tolling. On July 29, 2013, Florida's Turnpike Enterprise entered into an interoperability agreement with North Carolina Turnpike Authority and NC Quick Pass, allowing SunPass holders to use North Carolina toll roads and lanes. On November 12, 2014, an interoperability agreement was made with Georgia's Peach Pass, enabling SunPass use on I-85 Express lanes and future toll roads or lanes in Georgia. The C-Pass system on the Rickenbacker and Venetian Causeways was replaced by SunPass and pay-by-plate on September 23, 2014. In July 2020, E-ZPass announced SunPass would be compatible with E-ZPass by the end of 2020 and Peach Pass in 2021; on May 28, 2021, Florida Turnpike Enterprise began accepting E-ZPass, and E-ZPass facilities began accepting SunPass Pro transponders, but not earlier models like SunPass Portable or SunPass Mini. On February 27, 2023, SunPass was announced as compatible with toll roads in Kansas and Oklahoma and certain toll roads in Texas, supporting both SunPass Mini and SunPass Pro transponders; however, transponders from Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas cannot be used on any tolled roads maintained by the Central Florida Expressway Authority. In March 2025, the Harris County Toll Road Authority reached an interoperability agreement with Florida Turnpike Enterprise, making SunPass accepted statewide in Texas, with EZ Tag and TxTag accepted on all Florida Turnpike Enterprise roads. In November 2025, the E-470 Public Highway Authority reached an interoperability agreement with Florida Turnpike Enterprise, allowing SunPass use on E-470 and the express lanes network in Colorado, and ExpressToll acceptance on all Florida Turnpike Enterprise roads.

The RSC Supramolecular Chemistry Award was a distinguished award established by the Royal Society of Chemistry to recognize research contributing to the design of functionally useful supramolecular species. The award was first presented in 2001 and concluded in 2020 after a review of the RSC Awards structure, being given biennially. In 2022, the award was revived by the RSC Macrocyclic and Supramolecular Chemistry interest group as the MASC Supramolecular Chemistry Award, sponsored by Chem from Cell Press, and is now awarded annually.

doc_name: Supreme Court of Justice of Bolivia
text: The Supreme Court of Bolivia (Spanish: Corte Suprema de Justicia de Bolivia) served as the country's highest court from 1825 to 2012 and was located in Sucre, 410 kilometres to the south-east of La Paz, Bolivia's capital. It was established by the Supreme Decree (Decreto Supremo) of April 27, 1825, which converted the Royal Audience of Charcas (Audiencia y Cancillería Real de La Plata de los Charcas) of imperial Spain into the Supreme Court of the newly independent Bolivia. The court was officially inaugurated on July 16, 1827. It consisted of 12 ministers (judges) who were elected by the National Congress and served 10-year terms. Manuel María Urcullo was the first President of the Supreme Court of Bolivia, appointed in 1827, and was joined by Ministers Mariano Guzmán, Juan de la Cruz Monje y Ortega, and Casimiro Olañeta. Among the 56 individuals who served as presidents of the court were these and others. The Supreme Court of Bolivia was replaced in January 2012 by the Supreme Court of Justice, as established by the 2009 constitution.

Susan Victoria Lucci, born December 23, 1946, in Scarsdale, New York, is an American actress best known for portraying Erica Kane on the ABC daytime drama All My Children from January 16, 1970, to September 23, 2011, during the show's entire network run. The character is considered an icon in American soap opera history and is regarded as the most popular character in the genre; TV Guide has called her "unequivocally the most famous soap opera character in the history of daytime TV" and included her in their 2013 list of The 60 Nastiest Villains of All Time. Lucci was nominated 21 times for the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series, winning once in 1999 after the 19th nomination, with her status as a perpetual nominee drawing significant media attention since the late 1980s. Her image became widely recognized as synonymous with never winning an Emmy, a phenomenon highlighted by NBC's Saturday Night Live, which featured her hosting an episode with cast and crew using Emmys as props, and a 1989 Sweet One commercial in which she shouted, "Eleven years without an Emmy! What does a person have to do around here to get an Emmy?" After 18 nominations, she won the award in 1999, receiving a standing ovation presented by Shemar Moore. She was named one of VH1's 200 Top Icons of All Time and one of Barbara Walters's Ten Most Fascinating People. Lucci graduated from Garden City High School in 1964 and Marymount College, Tarrytown, in 1968 with a BA in drama. She began her television career with bit parts on Love Is a Many Splendored Thing and The Doctors, and had uncredited roles in the 1969 films Goodbye, Columbus and Me, Natalie. She also appeared in a 1982 cameo in Young Doctors in Love, guest-starred in prime time series such as The Love Boat, Fantasy Island, and The Fall Guy, and played leading roles in films including Invitation to Hell (1984), Anastasia: The Mystery of Anna (1986), Mafia Princess (1986), Haunted by Her Past (1985), Lady Mobster (1988), and The Bride in Black (1990). In 1995, she starred as Elizabeth 'Ebbie' Scrooge in the Lifetime film Ebbie, a Christmas Carol update, which received positive reviews. In 1999, she played Annie Oakley in the revival of Annie Get Your Gun. She guest-starred in episodes of Hope & Faith (2004), That's So Raven (2005), and appeared in the 2015 film Joy. From 2010 to 2014, she made multiple appearances on Hot in Cleveland as herself, including the episode "Life with Lucci," and appeared in Gloria Estefan's music video "Hotel Nacional" in February 2012. She guest-starred in multi-episodes of Army Wives in 2012 and hosted and narrated the 2012–2014 Investigation Discovery series Deadly Affairs. In 2013, she began starring as Geneviève Delatour in the Lifetime series Devious Maids, which ran until 2016, and her comedic performance was well received. In 2017, she appeared in Sia's music video "Santa's Coming for Us" and guest-starred in an episode of Difficult People, as well as in Progressive Insurance television ads styled as soap operas. In 2023, she received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the 50th Daytime Emmy Awards. In 2024, after a seven-year acting hiatus, she returned to film in the black comedy Outcome, starring alongside Keanu Reeves, Jonah Hill, and Cameron Diaz. Lucci married Helmut Huber on September 13, 1969; they have two children, actress Liza Huber and son Andreas Huber, and were married for 52 years until his death on March 28, 2022, at age 84. She is a registered Republican and has hosted fundraising events for Rudy Giuliani, and is a supporter of LGBT rights, inspired by a 2000 All My Children storyline in which her character Erica's daughter, Bianca Montgomery, came out as a lesbian. In late 2018, she underwent an emergency procedure to place two arterial stents in her heart due to blocked arteries, and postponed publicizing the event until shortly before the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women event in February 2019. Lucci also owns The Susan Lucci Collection, a line of hair care, perfumes, lingerie, and skin care products.

The Swami Vivekananda Planetarium, also known as Pilikula Planetarium, is located at Pilikula Nisargadhama in Mangaluru and is the first 3D planetarium in India. It is the only such planetarium in the country equipped with hybrid modern technology, combining 8K digital and opto-mechanical (hybrid) projection systems. Part of the Pilikula Nisargadhama, which spans 370 acres (150 ha) and is named Dr. Shivaram Karanth Biological Park, the planetarium was initiated in 2013 to commemorate the 150th birth anniversary of Swami Vivekananda by then Karnataka Chief Minister Jagadish Shettar. The foundation stone was laid by Shettar, and the project was undertaken at a cost of ₹35.69 crore (US$4.2 million), with the construction completed two years later than planned, opening on 1 March 2018. The planetarium was established with grants from KSTePS (Karnataka Science and Technology Promotion Society). It is operated by the Pilikula Regional Science Centre and aims to provide viewers—especially students and the public—with immersive experiences of stars and planetary systems. The planetarium features an 18 m (59 ft) diameter dome with a seating capacity of 170, where seats can be tilted by 15 degrees to improve viewing. It uses a Megastar IIA optical projector integrated with a Digistar and active stereo 3D 8K digital system manufactured by Evans & Sutherland Computer Corporation in the US, along with 32 lenses from Ohira Tech Japan, capable of projecting "20 million stars uniformly and seamlessly" across the dome’s nano-seam panels without visual overlap. Five technical personnel were initially trained in Utah, US, to operate the facility, and the planetarium includes a ₹1.5 crore (US$180,000) annual maintenance fund. It inaugurated on 1 March 2018 and began its first public show on 2 March 2018, offering eight shows daily, each lasting 25 minutes. The shows, such as We are stars, Dawn of the space age, and Mysteries of the unseen world, cover space technology, planets, nature, environment science, history, and geography in English, Hindi, and Kannada. The inaugural show, We are stars, narrates the story of space from the Big Bang to the present day. The planetarium is situated at Moodushedde, 9 kilometres (5.6 mi) from Mangalore, well connected by road, rail, and air. Mangalore Railway Station links to major cities like Chennai, Mumbai, and New Delhi, while Mangalore International Airport is about 7 kilometres (4.3 mi) from the city centre. By road, it is 350 kilometres (220 mi) west of Bengaluru, the capital of Karnataka.

Syed Bashir Ahmad (Kashmiri: سید بشیر احمد) (born 2 January 1952 in Sheikhar, Pulwama district in Jammu and Kashmir)[1][2] is a Kashmiri politician who has worked for the social upliftment of people in rural areas and has advocated for the rights of weaker sections. He served as the Member of Legislative Assembly from Rajpora Constituency[3] and was the Chairman of the Petitions Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly.[4] He entered politics at a young age and was associated with the Janata Dal, Indian National Congress, and Jan Morcha. In the 1996 state assembly elections, he contested from the Pulwama constituency on a Janata Dal ticket against the National Conference candidate but lost by a narrow margin.[5] In 1999, he co-founded the Jammu & Kashmir Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), which was led by Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, the former Home Minister of India and Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister. In 2002, he won the Assembly Elections from Rajpora Constituency and was appointed Minister for Education in Mufti Mohammad Sayeed's government.[2][6] He later held the portfolios of 'PHE, Irrigation and Flood Control' and 'Roads & Buildings'.[7] He won again from Rajpora in the 2008 Assembly Elections.[6] In July 2005, militants attempted to assassinate him at crowded Budshah Chowk in Srinagar while he was en route from the Civil Secretariat; he escaped unharmed, but two of his personnel security officers (PSO) and a civilian were injured.[8][9] In July 2014, the PDP removed Syed Bashir Ahmad from its candidate list for the 2014 Assembly elections. Shortly thereafter, hundreds of his party workers from Rajpora Constituency staged a large protest outside Housing Colony in Pulwama, where top politicians and legislative members reside, criticizing Mufti Mohammad Sayeed for ignoring Syed Bashir. The protesters later drove to Srinagar and held a demonstration outside the PDP president’s official Gupkar residence, demanding a mandate in favor of Syed Bashir. Syed Bashir later stated that he was not consulted before being dropped from the list and was only informed over the phone that he was no longer the candidate.[11] In October 2014, Syed Bashir was expelled from the PDP, according to a party statement citing anti-party activities.[12] In a press interview, he denied the allegations, saying he was not given any notice of the expulsion, had not engaged in any anti-party activities, and had respected the party symbol even when denied the mandate.[13] On 30 October 2014, Syed Bashir announced his intention to contest the J&K Legislative Assembly elections 2014 as an independent candidate. At a press conference held at his Sheikhar residence, he stated that although several political parties offered him a ticket, he declined them as his workers and supporters wanted him to run independently, and he had no choice but to honor their wishes.[14][15] On 22 August 2024, Syed Bashir Ahmad rejoined the People's Democratic Party.[16]

Szentes (Hungarian pronunciation: [ˈsɛntɛʃ]) is a town in south-eastern Hungary, located in Csongrád county near the Tisza river. It serves as a cultural and educational center in the region and is the third most populous town in Csongrád county, after Szeged and Hódmezővásárhely. The town is 82,6 km away from Kerekegyháza. The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic period, with the discovery of the Szegvár-tűzkövesi idol, one of the few Neolithic depictions of a male deity, found there. During the barbarian invasions, archaeological evidence shows hundreds of graves belonging to the Iazyges, Sarmatians, Gepids, Huns, and Avars, and certain accounts claim the legendary camp of Atilla the Hun was located at the confluence of the Tisza and Körös rivers. The town was first documented in a land-division in 1332 under the name "Scenthus" and was said to be inhabited by descendants of the Ond tribe, one of the seven tribes of Hungary, and also contained a stone church dedicated to Andrew the Apostle. Local tradition holds that Csongrad castle stood on the town's boundaries until the first Mongol invasion. After Hungary's defeat at the Battle of Mohács by Ottoman forces, taxes were imposed on Szentes by three different powers, prompting those who could leave to flee. The region endured severe hardship under Ottoman rule, with entire towns erased, and further losses occurred during the Long Turkish War, when many towns disappeared and Szentes' inhabitants sought refuge in nearby wetlands. In 1647, Ferdinand III was defeated by Ottoman forces outside Szentes, but the Ottoman forces withdrew from the region. In 1693, the area was scorched and pillaged by Crimean Tatars seeking food after their failed attempt to capture Gyula. In 1709, the town experienced a plague outbreak that killed over 1,000 inhabitants. The townspeople actively participated in the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and Kossuth Lajos visited to recruit troops. Following the Habsburg suppression of the revolution, many young men were forcibly conscripted into the Imperial Army as punishment, and the mayor was sentenced to hard labour. Szentes is twinned with: [5]. This Csongrád-Csanád County location article is a stub. You can help Wikipedia by adding missing information.

The Taddei Tondo, also known as The Virgin and Child with the Infant St. John, is an unfinished marble relief tondo created by the Italian Renaissance artist Michelangelo Buonarroti. It is the only marble sculpture by Michelangelo in Great Britain and is part of the permanent collection of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. Dating to Michelangelo's time in Florence before his move to Rome in 1505, the tondo was commissioned by Taddeo Taddei, a patron and friend of Raphael. According to art historian Vasari, while working on his David, Michelangelo blocked out but did not finish two marble tondi—one for Taddeo Taddei, now in his house, and another for Bartolomeo Pitti, which was begun but left unfinished. The tondo features a seated Virgin Mary with the baby Jesus dynamically sprawled across her lap, turning and looking back over his right shoulder toward the infant Saint John the Baptist, who stands before him, looking down and holding a fluttering bird. The bird is most likely a goldfinch, symbolizing the Passion, and the unfinished portion below it may have been intended as a crown of thorns. John, patron saint of Florence, with his attribute of a baptismal bowl, crosses his arms, possibly alluding to the cross. The work is executed using only a point and claw chisel, driven hard and with great energy, creating a sense of surface unity without drill marks. The Christ child is the only figure highly finished (except for the feet), St. John is less finished, Mary is the least finished, and the background is only roughly executed. These variations in texture are believed to establish the relative status of the figures and enhance compositional depth. On the reverse of the relief, a ligature combining the letters L and A is present, likely the mark of Lapo d'Antonio di Lapo, a carver and assistant active at the Opera del Duomo from 1506–1507; a chisel blow from this phase caused a hairline crack in the Virgin’s face, possibly due to Michelangelo’s decision to continue working despite the damage, possibly due to material constraints or confidence in his ability to work around flaws. The missing segment at the bottom right may result from an excess of Michelangelo’s "direct attack." Work on the tondo ceased at some point; five holes in the outer rim were intended for fixings and are variously dated. The tondo was originally in the Palazzo Taddei and documented there in 1568, but by 1678, the family had moved to a new residence near San Remigio. It was later taken to Rome, where it was acquired by Sir George Beaumont in 1822 from Jean-Baptiste Wicar. Initially displayed at Beaumont’s house in Grosvenor Square, it was bequeathed to the Royal Academy in 1830 and installed at Somerset House, then moved with the Academy to the east wing of the new National Gallery building in 1836, remaining there until the Academy relocated to Burlington House in 1868. Except for an exhibition at the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1960, it has been housed in various Academy locations since. In 1989, the discovery of a hairline crack led to the decision to provide a permanent home for the tondo. It was cleaned with dichloromethane swabs and clay poultices to remove residues of nineteenth-century plaster casts, oil-based release agents, packing materials, beeswax, pine resin adhesives, and other surface accretions. The tondo was left unwaxed and without any coating, as it is not finished and was originally unpolished, like Michelangelo’s David when completed. Since the opening of the Sackler Wing of Galleries in 1991, it has been on free public display on the top floor, behind protective glass for preventive conservation against air pollution and vandalism. The tondo format was a hallmark of the Florentine Renaissance, with leading artists such as Filippo Lippi, Botticelli, Luca Signorelli, Piero di Cosimo, Fra Bartolomeo, Andrea del Sarto, Leonardo da Vinci (in a lost work), and Raphael creating tondi. Michelangelo experimented with the form, producing the Doni tondo (his only panel painting documented in contemporary sources) and beginning two unfinished tondo sculptures—the Pitti and Taddei tondi—after which he never returned to the tondo form in either medium. Raphael studied and reworked the tondo in two drawings: the versi of The Storming of Perugia at the Louvre and compositional studies for the Madonna del Prato at Chatsworth House, and also applied Michelangelo’s twisting Christ child pose in the Bridgewater Madonna. Shortly after arriving in England, the tondo was sketched by Wilkie, who wrote to Beaumont that it was "the chief talk of all our artists" and a "great addition to our stock of art," justifying Michelangelo’s great reputation. Cockerell noted in his diary that the subject "seems growing from the marble & emerging into life," as if being formed from an unformed mass. Constable, upon its arrival at the Royal Academy, published a letter in the Athenaeum of 3 July 1830 praising its lighting, which highlighted the more finished parts and made the less perfect areas appear as masses of shadow, creating the effect of a rich picture in chiaroscuro. The tondo is an outstanding technical study piece, with plaster casts found at the Victoria and Albert Museum and Fitzwilliam Museum. Many of Michelangelo’s works are unfinished, and while some are viewed as completed, the nineteenth-century critic Eugène Guillaume described his "non finito" as an expressive device for infinite suggestiveness.

The Taj Mahal, meaning "Crown of the Palace" in Urdu and derived from Arabic and Persian words for "crown" and "palace," is an ivory-white marble mausoleum located on the right bank of the Yamuna river in Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India. It was commissioned in 1631 by Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), the fifth Mughal emperor, to house the tomb of his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died on 17 June 1631 while giving birth to their 14th child, Gauhara Begum. Construction began in 1632, with the mausoleum completed in 1648 and the surrounding buildings and garden finished in 1653. The first ceremony held at the site was on 6 February 1643, marking the 12th anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal's death. The entire complex, spanning 17 hectares (42 acres), includes a mosque, a guest house, and formal gardens bounded on three sides by a crenellated wall. The building complex incorporates Indo-Islamic and Mughal architectural traditions, featuring symmetrical designs with various shapes and symbols. The mausoleum is constructed of white marble inlaid with semi-precious stones, while red sandstone is used for other structures, similar to Mughal-era buildings. The complex sits on a 300-metre (980 ft) long by 8.7-metre (28.5 ft) high platform built with varying patterns of dark and light sandstone. The mausoleum itself stands on a 6-metre (20 ft) high square plinth measuring 95.5 metres (313 ft) per side, with a large multi-chambered cube and chamfered corners forming an eight-sided structure approximately 57.3 metres (188 ft) long. It has four identical sides with iwans (arch-shaped doorways), each topped by a 33-metre (108 ft) high pishtaq (vaulted archway) and two arched balconies, replicated on chamfered corners for symmetry. Access to the mausoleum is provided by two flights of stairs on the southern side. The central feature is a 23-metre (75 ft) high marble dome on a 12-metre (39 ft) high cylindrical drum with an inner diameter of 18.4 metres (60 ft), slightly asymmetrical and topped by a 9.6-metre (31 ft) high gilded finial. Four smaller chattris, shaped like the main dome, are placed at the corners, supported by columns and decorated with lotus motifs. Tall guldastas extend from the walls as decorative spires. The main dome and chattris are adorned with Persian and Indian design elements, with the main finial originally made of gold and later replaced by a gilded bronze copy in the early 19th century, topped by a moon motif pointing heavenward. Four minarets, each over 40 metres (130 ft) tall, flank the tomb at the corners of the plinth, each composed of three equal parts with balconies and smaller chattris, designed to fall away from the tomb in case of collapse. The external surfaces are decorated with delicate reliefs, inlays, and carvings using precious and semi-precious stones, including pietra dura inlays of geometric patterns of vines, flowers, and fruits. The calligraphy on the gateway arches, composed of thuluth script in jasper or black marble inlaid in white marble, includes Qur'anic passages, with one on the southern gate translating to "O Soul, thou art at rest. Return to the Lord at peace with Him, and He at peace with you." This calligraphy is attributed to Abdul Haq, who was granted the title "Amanat Khan" by Shah Jahan. The main chamber is an octagon with 7.3-metre (24 ft) sides, with two tiers of eight pishtaq arches along the walls, and balconies on the central upper arches, each with intricate jali windows. The inner walls are open along the axes with jali screens transmitting light from outside. The chamber has an open elongated room on three sides, flanked by square cells with decorated ceilings, likely used for visitors and Qur'an reciters. Staircases lead to the roof level, with ventilation shafts. The interior walls are 25 metres (82 ft) high and topped by a "false" interior dome with a sun motif, decorated with inlay work of gemstones. The walls are highly decorated with dado bas-reliefs, intricate lapidary inlays, and calligraphy. The main chamber contains the false cenotaphs of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan, with the real tombs located in the basement. The cenotaphs are aligned north–south, with heads facing north and bodies laid on their sides with faces turned toward the west, facing Mecca. Mumtaz's cenotaph is centered on a 1.5 by 2.5-metre (4 ft 11 in by 8 ft 2 in) marble base, and Shah Jahan's is on a larger base to the west, marked by a small pen box sculpture. The cenotaphs are adorned with detailed inlays: Mumtaz's features natural plum fruits, buds, and blossoms with the epitaph "The illumined grave of Arjumand Bano Begam, entided Mumtaz Mahal, who died in the year 1631," and Shah Jahan's has a similar decoration with the epitaph "This is the sacred grave of His Most Exalted Majesty... Shah Jahan, Padshah; may it ever be fragrant! The year 1076 [AD 1666]." The original burial chamber is undecorated, with the Ninety Nine Names of God inscribed on its side. The complex is set within a charbagh garden, inspired by Persian gardens and symbolizing Paradise (Jannah), divided into four quadrants by walkways and further subdivided into 16 sunken parterres. A raised marble water tank, called al Hawd al-Kawthar, is positioned halfway between the tomb and the gateway on a north–south axis, reflecting the mausoleum. The garden includes avenues of trees and fountains, and in the north-western quadrant, there is a site marking where Mumtaz Mahal was first buried before being moved to the main chamber. The tomb is located at the end of the garden, unlike most Mughal gardens, and the Archaeological Survey of India has hypothesized that the Yamuna river was incorporated into the design as one of the rivers of Paradise, based on the discovery of Mahtab Bagh on the opposite bank. The Taj Mahal was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 for being "the jewel of Islamic art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage." It is regarded as one of the best examples of Mughal architecture and a symbol of Indian history. It is a major tourist attraction, drawing over five million visitors annually, and was declared a winner of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007. The Taj Mahal and its surroundings are a Monument of National Importance, administered by the Archaeological Survey of India. The construction project employed more than 20,000 workers and artisans under the guidance of a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the emperor's court architect. The complex was completed at a cost estimated at the time to be around ₹32 million, equivalent to approximately ₹52.8 billion (US$827 million) in 2015. Abdul Hamid Lahori, in his 1636 book Padshahnama, refers to the Taj Mahal as rauza-i munawwara, meaning the illumined or illustrious tomb. The imperial court records illustrate Shah Jahan's deep grief, including avoiding royal affairs for a week and giving up music and lavish dressing for two years, highlighting his devotion to Mumtaz Mahal. Shah Jahan chose the site south of Agra, where a mansion of Raja Jai Singh I stood, and in exchange, Jai Singh agreed to give the land to the emperor for a large palace in the center of Agra. The design of the Taj Mahal draws inspiration from Timurid and Mughal buildings, including the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand and Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, which influenced the Charbagh gardens and hasht-behesht plan. The entire complex is symmetrical, with the use of various shapes and symbols, and the use of contrasting colors and tessellation patterns in floors and walkways. The plinth is differentiated by an interlocking pattern of octagonal white marble pieces set into four-pointed stars made of red sandstone, surrounded by a border. The building features many lattice windows or jalis with interlocking hexagonal patterns. The calligraphy on the buildings was created in 1609 by Abdul Haq, and the inscription at the base of the interior dome reads "Written by the insignificant being, Amanat Khan Shirazi."

The Taj Mahal complex, built between 1631 and 1653, was commissioned by Shah Jahan in exchange for a palace in Agra from Raja Jai Singh I, and construction began in 1632. The site, located south of the walled city of Agra, was prepared by excavating an area of about 1.2 hectares (3 acres), filling it with dirt to reduce seepage, and leveling it at 50 metres (160 ft) above the riverbank. The tomb complex was constructed primarily of brick and lime mortar, with the external surface and interior of the main cenotaph veneered in white marble from Makrana, Rajasthan, and other interior surfaces and accessory buildings lined with red sandstone from Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh, coated with a red octet. Over 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones, including jade, crystal from China, turquoise from Tibet, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, sapphire from Sri Lanka, and carnelian from Arabia, were inlaid into the white marble. More than 20,000 artisans, labourers, painters, and specialists—such as sculptors from Bukhara, calligraphers from Syria and Persia, designers from southern India, stone cutters from Baluchistan, and Italian artisans—were involved in the construction. A 15 km (9.3 mi) long earthen ramp was built to transport materials, hauled by oxen and elephants on specially constructed wagons, and a colossal brick scaffold mirrored the tomb’s structure. An elaborate post-and-beam pulley system, powered by animals, was used to raise marble blocks. Water for the gardens was drawn from the Yamuna River via animal-powered devices, transported through a channel into an underground reservoir along the eastern wall, lifted by pulleys and wheels to a tank, and then carried via an aqueduct southward to the western wall before turning east. The water was distributed through earthenware pipes underground, with fountains in the central tank powered by the drop from 9.47 m (31.1 ft) high walls, using large copper vessels interconnected by copper pipes. The charbagh garden, inspired by Persian gardens, symbolizes the Paradise garden (Jannah) with four rivers flowing from a central spring or mountain, dividing the garden into four quadrants. The main tomb is located at the end of the garden, unlike most Mughal gardens which place a tomb in the center. The north-western quadrant marks the site where Mumtaz Mahal was first buried before being moved to the main chamber. The discovery of Mahtab Bagh on the other side of the Yamuna river led the Archaeological Survey of India to hypothesize that the river itself was incorporated into the garden design as one of the rivers of Paradise. Similarities in layout and architectural features with the Shalimar Gardens suggest both may have been designed by the same architect, Ali Mardan. Early accounts describe abundant vegetation, including roses, daffodils, and fruit trees. As the Mughal Empire declined, the gardens were neglected, and when the British Raj took over, they were redesigned to resemble 19th-century London lawns. The Taj Mahal complex is enclosed by crenellated red sandstone walls on three sides, with the Yamuna-facing side open. Outside the walls are mausoleums for Shah Jahan’s other wives, royals, and favorite servants. The inner walls feature columned arcades with domed chattris and smaller structures like the Music House. The main gateway, built of marble, mirrors the tomb’s architecture and includes intricate bas-relief and pietra dura inlays. At the far end stand two similar red sandstone buildings: one a mosque and the other a jawab, lacking a mihrab. The complex was partially completed in 1643 with a ceremony held by Shah Jahan on 6 February to mark the 12th anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal’s death. Construction of the mausoleum ended in 1648, with additional work continuing for five years, and the entire complex completed in 1653 at a cost of approximately ₹32 million (equivalent to ₹52.8 billion or US$827 million in 2015). In December 1652, Aurangzeb wrote to Shah Jahan about leaks in the tomb, mosque, and assembly hall. In 1658, Shah Jahan was deposed and placed under house arrest at Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal. Upon his death in 1666, Aurangzeb buried him next to Mumtaz Mahal. In the 18th century, the Jat rulers of Bharatpur attacked the Taj Mahal, removing two chandeliers—one agate, one silver—and the gold and silver screen; the gold shield covering the 4.6-metre-high (15 ft) finial of the main dome was also taken. By the late 19th century, the buildings fell into disrepair, and in 1908, Lord Curzon ordered and completed a restoration project, also commissioning a large interior lamp and replacing the gardens with European-style lawns. In 1942, scaffolding was erected to hide the monument from Japanese air attacks; during the 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan wars, scaffolding was again used to mislead bomber pilots. Since Indian independence in 1947, the Archaeological Survey of India has maintained the monument. In 1983, the Taj Mahal was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site for being "the jewel of Islamic art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage." Since the late 20th century, environmental pollution, including acid rain and emissions from the Mathura Oil Refinery affecting the Yamuna River, has caused the monument to turn yellow-brown. After the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India & Ors., the Indian government established the Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ), a 10,400-square-kilometre (4,000 sq mi) area with strict emissions standards. Concerns about structural integrity have arisen due to declining groundwater levels, with cracks appearing in 2010 and minarets showing tilting; minor damage occurred in April 2018 and May 2020. In the 2020s, the government has undertaken restoration efforts, including placing mud packs to restore the white color and replacing broken marble. The Taj Mahal is a major tourist attraction, drawing about five million visitors in the 2022–23 financial year, with a three-tier pricing system: ₹50 for Indian citizens, ₹540 for SAARC and BIMSTEC nationals, and ₹1,100 for foreign tourists. Visitors enter through three gates, and polluting vehicles are banned; tourists must walk or take electric buses from designated parking areas. The complex is open daily except Fridays, from one hour before sunrise to 45 minutes before sunset, and limited night viewing is offered on full moon days, excluding Ramadan. In 2019, fines were introduced for visitors staying over three hours.
