A 2025 government report stated the Taj Mahal earned ₹297 crore (US$35 million) over five years, making it the highest-earning ASI monument. The small town of Taj Ganji or Mumtazabad, located south of the Taj, was built with caravanserais, bazaars, and markets to serve visitors and workers. The Taj Mahal is frequently listed in travel guides and the New Seven Wonders of the World (a 2007 poll), and is a common destination for foreign dignitaries. The monument has long been admired across cultures, with personal and emotional responses surpassing scholarly analysis. A myth claims Shah Jahan planned a black marble mausoleum across the Yamuna, known as the Black Taj Mahal, originating from Jean-Baptiste Tavernier’s 1665 writings; however, excavations in the 1990s disproved the presence of blackened marble, revealing discolored white stones. In 2006, archaeologists reconstructed the Mehtab Bagh pool and confirmed a dark reflection of the white mausoleum, supporting the theory that the idea stemmed from Shah Jahan’s obsession with symmetry. There is no concrete evidence for claims that Shah Jahan mutilated or killed architects and craftsmen, nor for stories that Lord William Bentinck planned to demolish the Taj and auction its marble—such claims are linked to Bentinck’s sale of discarded Agra Fort marble. Another myth suggests that beating the finial’s silhouette will cause water to flow, with broken bangles found nearby. Several unfounded theories claim other people built the Taj Mahal, including Hindu kings like Paramardi in 1196; these were dismissed by the Supreme Court in 2000 and the Allahabad High Court in 2005. Right-wing politicians have promoted such claims, but in November 2015 and August 2017, the Union Minister of Culture and the Archaeological Survey of India respectively stated there is no evidence the monument ever housed a temple. Theories that the Taj was designed by an Italian, Geronimo Vereneo, or a Frenchman, Austin of Bordeaux, were promoted by Henry George Keene and William Henry Sleeman, based on misinterpreted texts, and later revived by Father Hosten and E. B. Havell.

The concept was first introduced by Henry George Keene in 1879, who derived it from a translation of a Spanish work, *Itinerario* (The Travels of Fray Sebastian Manrique, 1629–1643). An alternative theory, suggesting that a Frenchman named Austin of Bordeaux designed the Taj Mahal, was advanced by William Henry Sleeman, drawing upon the writings of Jean-Baptiste Tavernier. These theories were later revived by Father Hosten and further discussed by E. B. Havell, forming the foundation for subsequent debates and controversies.

Takashi Masuzaki (増崎孝司, Masuzaki Takashi; born 8 December 1962, in Nagasaki, Japan) is a Japanese guitarist, composer, and arranger under Being Inc. and a member of the fusion band DIMENSION [ja]. His career began in 1983 when he signed with a music agency and became primarily active as a musician and back band member. In 1987, he joined the band Bluew (1987–1989) as a guitarist and simultaneously became a consistent member of the live tours for singer Mari Hamada. In 1990, he released his first solo work, "Speaks," under BMG Victor, and joined the group B.B. Queens, which won the 32nd Japan Record Award and appeared in the national new-year program Kōhaku Uta Gassen. After the group's dissolution in 1992, he joined the fusion band Dimension with saxophonist Kazuki Katsuta and keyboardist Akira Onozuka, remaining an active member as of 2023. In 2003, he released his first collaborative album, Tsuki, with Japanese guitarist Koichi Yabori from the band Fragile. In 2005, he participated in a guitarist session with Michiya Haruhata from Tube and Yoshinobu Ohga from OOM, contributing to the compilation album "Theatre Of Strings," produced and composed by Japanese guitarist Tak Matsumoto from the rock band B'z. In 2011, he took part in the B.B. Queens reunion, contributing to the recording of a compilation and new original album. However, unlike other members, he did not participate in the Live Tour "Being Legend" in 2012. Since 2012, his agency has launched an annual event, Being Legend: Guitar summit, in which he performs live with younger musicians such as Akihide from Breakerz, Hiroshi Shibazaki from Wands, Shinji Tagawa from Deen, Takashi Gomi from T-BOLAN, and Michiya Haruhata from Tube. In 2014, he became a member of the Mario Kart band, performing in the games Super Mario Kart 8, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, and Super Mario Odyssey. As of 2023, he has released 3 studio albums and 3 collaborative albums. Note: this list contains only credits for lyrics, composition, and arrangement. Note: this list contains only credits for performer as guitarist.

Talat Ahmad, born on 23 December 1955, is an Indian Earth Scientist and former Professor at the Department of Geology, University of Delhi, who also served as Indian National Science Academy (INSA) Senior Scientist. He served as Chairman of the Governing Body overseeing the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Dehradun from 1 December 2021 (full charge from 1 June 2022) until 30 November 2024, and thereafter continued as a member of the Governing Body (WIHG) from 1 December 2024 to 30 November 2027. He previously served as Vice-Chancellor of the University of Kashmir from 6 August 2018 to 20 May 2022, marking his second tenure, and had earlier held the position from 1 June 2011 to 2014, taking over from Professor Riyaz Punjabi. Before that, he served as Vice-Chancellor of Jamia Millia Islamia, though he resigned a few months short of his full term, following a search committee headed by Prof. Abid Hussain, former Indian ambassador to the US, and including Prof. G. K. Chadha, Prof. Seyed E. Hasnain, and other eminent figures. He is the first Vice-Chancellor to serve a second term and the second to be appointed from outside Jammu and Kashmir in the past two decades, with Jalees Ahmad Khan Tareen being the first such appointee from outside the state (2001–2004). Ahmad was born and raised in Giridih, Jharkhand, and his father was Moinuddin Ahmad. He completed his schooling at Giridih Higher Secondary School, joined Aligarh Muslim University in 1972 for a BSc in geology (completed 1975), pursued an MSc in geology (1977), M.Phil in Ore Petrology from Jawaharlal Nehru University (1980), and a PhD in Igneous Petrology from JNU (1985). He held postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Leicester (1988–89) under a Government of India Fellowship, the University of Cambridge (1997–98) under the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC), and Nagoya University, Japan (1999–2000) under the Japanese Society for Promotion of Science (JSPS). In 1979, he was selected by the UPSC and joined the Geological Survey of India (GSI) in February 1980, working there for a year before leaving due to its survey-oriented nature. He then worked as a Scientist at the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Dehradun from 16 July 1984 to 3 September 1989, and served as a scientist under DST for nineteen years (1984–2003). He joined the Department of Geology, University of Delhi as a professor on 31 October 2003, where he initiated research projects in central India and Rajasthan, and later secured a project from the Russian Foundation for Basic Research (RFBR) in the Kashmir valley. He was appointed Vice-Chancellor of Jamia Millia Islamia on 29 April 2014, taking over from Prof. S M Sajid and succeeding Najeeb Jung, who became the 20th Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in April 2013, and was relieved by A M Shah, dean of academic affairs. Ahmad has over 65 research publications and has supervised numerous M.Phil. and PhD research studies at the University of Delhi and the Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra. He has led several sponsored projects, including Geochemical, Isotopic and Geochronological characterisation of Granotoids from the Central Indian Tectonic Zones (CITZ) and Central Indian Shear Zones (CISZ)—Constraints on Pre-Cambrian Crystal Evolution, funded by Indo-Russian collaboration and the ILTP Project, and Proterozoic mafic magmatism in the Central Indian Tectonic Zone (CITZ): elemental and isotopic constraints on crystal evolution and geodynamics. He is a member of several prestigious societies and has received numerous fellowships and awards.

Tantalum is a chemical element with the symbol Ta and atomic number 73, named after the Greek mythological figure Tantalus. It is a hard, ductile, lustrous, blue-gray transition metal known for its high corrosion resistance and extremely high melting point of 3017 °C (boiling point 5458 °C), which is exceeded only by tungsten, rhenium, osmium, and carbon among metals. Tantalum is part of group 5, along with vanadium and niobium, and is always found in nature together with niobium in mineral groups such as tantalite, columbite, and coltan. It is chemically inert and highly resistant to acids, especially aqua regia at temperatures below 150 °C, though it can be dissolved by hydrofluoric acid or acidic solutions containing fluoride ions and sulfur trioxide, as well as molten potassium hydroxide. Tantalum exists in two crystalline phases: the alpha phase, which is stable up to the melting point and has a body-centered cubic structure with lattice constant a = 0.33029 nm at 20 °C, and the beta phase, which is hard, brittle, tetragonal, and metastable, converting to the alpha phase upon heating to 750–775 °C. Bulk tantalum is mostly alpha phase, while the beta phase is typically produced as thin films via magnetron sputtering, chemical vapor deposition, or electrochemical deposition. Natural tantalum consists of two stable isotopes: 180mTa (0.012%) and 181Ta (99.988%), with 180mTa being a metastable isomer predicted to decay via isomeric transition, beta decay, or electron capture, though its radioactivity has never been observed and only a lower limit of 2.9×10¹⁷ years on its half-life has been established; the ground state of 180Ta has a half-life of 8 hours. Tantalum forms compounds in oxidation states from −3 to +5, with Ta(V) oxides being the most common, and it is barely soluble in dilute hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric, or phosphoric acids due to precipitation of hydrous Ta(V) oxide, but can be solubilized in basic media via polyoxotantalate species. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta₂O₅) is the most important compound for applications. Tantalates, such as lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) and lanthanum tantalate (LaTaO₄), are well-known compounds. The hardest known compounds of tantalum are its nitrides and carbides; tantalum carbide (TaC) is used in cutting tools, and tantalum(III) nitride is used as a thin film insulator in microelectronics. Tantalum sulfide (TaS₂) is a layered semiconductor, and a tantalum-tellurium alloy forms quasicrystals. Tantalum halides include TaF₅ (melting point 97.0 °C), [TaF₇]²⁻ (used for separation from niobium), and TaCl₅ (a dimer that hydrolyzes readily), with lower halides TaX₄ and TaX₃ featuring Ta-Ta bonds. Organotantalum compounds include pentamethyltantalum, mixed alkyltantalum chlorides, alkyltantalum hydrides, alkylidene complexes, and cyclopentadienyl derivatives, as well as salts and substituted derivatives of hexacarbonyl [Ta(CO)₆]⁻ and related isocyanides. Tantalum is estimated to make up about 1–2 ppm of the Earth's crust. Key tantalum minerals include tantalite (Fe, Mn)Ta₂O₆, which is the most important for extraction, microlite, wodginite, euxenite (euxenite-(Y)), polycrase (polycrase-(Y)), samarskite, and fergusonite; tantalite and columbite have the same structure, with tantalite containing more tantalum and columbite more niobium. Gravitational separation is used due to the high density of these minerals. Australia was the main producer of tantalum before the 2010s, with Global Advanced Metals (formerly Talison Minerals) operating mines at Greenbushes and Wodgina in Western Australia; the Wodgina mine reopened in January 2011 after being suspended in 2008 due to the financial crisis, but operations ceased in February 2012 due to softening demand. Wodgina produces a primary tantalum concentrate upgraded at Greenbushes. While Brazil and Canada are major niobium producers, their ores also contain small amounts of tantalum. China, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Thailand, and Malaysia mine ores with higher tantalum content, with Thailand and Malaysia producing tantalum as a by-product of tin mining, where tantalite is found in placer deposits and recovered from tin smelter slag. Since the start of the 21st century, tantalum production has shifted significantly from Australia and Brazil to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, and other African countries, with Congo producing nearly 40% and Rwanda and Burundi contributing about 18% of global production by 2021. Tantalum is considered a conflict resource because coltan, the mineral from which it is extracted, is found in Central Africa and has been linked to conflict in the DRC, where smuggling of coltan has contributed to war resulting in approximately 5.4 million deaths since 1998, making it one of the world's deadliest conflicts since WWII. Ethical concerns arise over corporate responsibility, human rights, and environmental damage in conflict zones. The United States Geological Survey reported that the DRC produced less than 1% of global tantalum output from 2002–2006, peaking at 10% in 2000 and 2008. Extraction begins with crushing and gravity separation of the ore, followed by leaching with hydrofluoric acid and sulfuric or hydrochloric acid to separate tantalum and niobium from impurities. The resulting fluoride complexes are separated via liquid-liquid extraction into organic solvents like cyclohexanone, octanol, or methyl isobutyl ketone, removing impurities. Niobium is then separated by lowering ionic strength, forming oxyfluoride H₂[NbOF₅], while purified H₂[TaF₇] is neutralized with ammonia to precipitate hydrated tantalum oxide, which is calcined to Ta₂O₅. Alternatively, H₂[TaF₇] can be treated with potassium fluoride to form K₂[TaF₇], which is easily crystallized and reduced to metallic tantalum using sodium at approximately 800 °C in molten salt. The older Marignac process involves converting the mixture to K₂[TaF₇] and K₂[NbOF₅] and separating them by fractional crystallization based on water solubility. Tantalum can also be refined by electrolysis using a modified Hall–Héroult process, where powdered metal oxides are reduced in a molten salt bath with a carbon anode and a powdered oxide cathode, first demonstrated in 1997 by Cambridge University researchers.

H2[TaF7] can be treated with potassium fluoride to produce potassium heptafluorotantalate (K2[TaF7]), which is readily crystallized and handled as a solid. K2[TaF7] can be converted to metallic tantalum through reduction with sodium at approximately 800 °C in molten salt. In the older Marignac process, a mixture of H2[TaF7] and H2[NbOF5] is converted to a mixture of K2[TaF7] and K2[NbOF5], which is separated by fractional crystallization based on their differing water solubilities. Tantalum can also be refined by electrolysis using a modified Hall–Héroult process that operates on non-liquid powdered oxides; this method was first discovered in 1997 by Cambridge University researchers who immersed oxide samples in molten salt baths and reduced them with electric current. In this process, the cathode uses powdered metal oxide, the anode is carbon, and the molten salt at 1,000 °C (1,830 °F) serves as the electrolyte. The first refinery using this method has enough capacity to supply 3–4% of annual global demand. All welding of tantalum must be performed in an inert atmosphere of argon or helium to prevent contamination, and tantalum is not solderable; grinding is difficult, especially for annealed tantalum, which is extremely ductile and can be readily formed into metal sheets. The primary use of tantalum metal powder is in electronic components, especially capacitors and some high-power resistors. Tantalum electrolytic capacitors use tantalum powder pressed into a pellet as one plate, the oxide layer as the dielectric, and an electrolytic solution or conductive solid as the other plate. Because the dielectric layer can be thinner than in aluminum capacitors, high capacitance is achieved in a small volume, making tantalum capacitors ideal for portable telephones, personal computers, automotive electronics, and cameras. Tantalum is also used in alloys with high melting points, strength, and ductility, including carbide tools for metalworking and superalloys for jet engine components, chemical process equipment, nuclear reactors, missile parts, heat exchangers, tanks, and vessels. Due to its ductility, tantalum can be drawn into fine wires or filaments for evaporating metals like aluminium. Tantalum is inert to most acids except hydrofluoric acid and hot sulfuric acid, and hot alkaline solutions cause corrosion, making it suitable for chemical reaction vessels and pipes for corrosive liquids, including heat-exchanging coils for steam heating of hydrochloric acid. Historically, tantalum was used in ultra high frequency electron tubes for radio transmitters, where its ability to form oxides and nitrides helped maintain high vacuum in internal parts such as grids and plates. In surgery, tantalum is valued for its hardness, ductility, and use in sharp instruments and monofilament sutures; additionally, its unique ability to form a durable bond with human hard tissue makes it ideal for bone and dental implants. Tantalum coatings are increasingly used in complex titanium surgical implants due to their strong, biologically stable bond with hard tissue. Because tantalum is non-ferrous and non-magnetic, implants are acceptable for MRI procedures. NASA used tantalum to shield spacecraft components such as Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 from radiation. Its high melting point and oxidation resistance make it suitable for vacuum furnace parts and corrosion-resistant components like thermowells, valve bodies, and fasteners. Due to its high density, tantalum is used in shaped charge and explosively formed penetrator liners, enhancing armor penetration capabilities. It is also occasionally used in precious watches, such as those by Audemars Piguet, F. P. Journe, Hublot, Montblanc, Omega, and Panerai. Tantalum oxide is used to produce special high refractive index glass for camera lenses. Spherical tantalum powder, produced by atomizing molten tantalum with gas or liquid, is commonly used in additive manufacturing due to its uniform shape, excellent flowability, and high melting point. Tantalum receives little attention in environmental studies; upper crust concentration (UCC) is 0.92 ppm and the Nb/Ta(w/w) ratio is 12.7. Reliable data on tantalum concentrations in natural waters are lacking, with dissolved concentrations in seawater and freshwaters not reliably measured and likely below 1 ng L−1 due to analytical limitations. Tantalum appears mostly as particulate matter in natural waters. Soil concentrations are near 1 ppm, indicating a detrital origin; atmospheric aerosol values are scattered and limited, with enrichment likely due to loss of more water-soluble elements in clouds. No pollution linked to human use has been detected, and tantalum is considered a very conservative element in biogeochemical terms, though its cycling and reactivity are not fully understood. Tantalum compounds are rarely encountered in the laboratory; the metal is highly biocompatible and used in body implants and coatings, so focus may be on other elements or the physical properties of the compounds. Workplace exposure to tantalum can occur through inhalation, skin contact, or eye contact. OSHA sets the permissible exposure limit at 5 mg/m³ over an 8-hour workday, and NIOSH recommends a 5 mg/m³ limit over 8 hours and a short-term limit of 10 mg/m³. A paradox exists because tantalum's strong bonding to bone tissue means that at 2500 mg/m³, tantalum dust becomes immediately dangerous to life and health if it bonds with incorrect tissues.

Tara Chand is a politician and leader from Jammu and Kashmir. He served as Deputy Chief Minister of the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir from 2009 to 2014 and had previously held the position of Speaker of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly. On 30 August 2022, he resigned from the Indian National Congress in support of Ghulam Nabi Azad and was subsequently appointed as Vice Chairperson of the Democratic Azad Party. However, on 22 December 2022, he was removed from the Democratic Azad Party due to allegations of 'anti-party' activities. In the 2014 elections, Chand lost to BJP candidate Dr. Krishan Lal in the Chhamb Assembly constituency of Jammu district. In the 2024 election, he finished in third place.

Tatsuo Miyajima (宮島 達男, Miyajima Tatsuo; January 16, 1957 –) is a Japanese sculptor and installation artist who resides in Moriya, Ibaraki prefecture, Japan. His artistic practice frequently involves digital LED counters and centers on the themes of time and space, particularly within Buddhist philosophy. Born in Edogawa City, Tokyo on January 16, 1957, Miyajima graduated from the Oil Painting course in the Fine Arts department of Tokyo National University of Fine Arts and Music in 1984 and completed his MA at the same institution in 1986. Although he initially trained as a painter and briefly identified as a performance artist, his current work primarily consists of installations and sculptures, which he describes as "performing" on his behalf. His core artistic principles are "Keep Changing, Connect with Everything, Continue Forever." In the 1970s, he practiced performance art, influenced by Joseph Beuys, Allan Krapow, and Christo, viewing these works as "actions for society"; however, his desire to create lasting art—contrasting with the ephemeral nature of performance—led him to shift toward sculpture and installation. Miyajima created his first LED counter in 1988, which has become foundational to his later works. These counters typically display two digits in red or green, counting from 1 to 9, and never reach zero, as Miyajima views zero as a purely Western concept. He has connected various displays into interactive systems he calls 'regions.' On August 9, 1945, an atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands and destroying much of the city, but a kaki tree survived with over half its trunk blackened and nearly dead. In 1994, arborist Masayuki Ebinuma began treating the tree and restored it, enabling it to produce seedlings. Ebinuma then distributed these saplings to children visiting Nagasaki as a symbol of peace. After learning about this, Miyajima decided to support Ebinuma artistically. In 1995, at an art exhibition, he displayed the saplings and recruited foster parents, receiving ten applications and selecting the former Ryuhoku Elementary School in Taito-ku, Tokyo as the planting site. This led to the conception of the art project "Revive Time: Kaki Tree Project," which established an executive committee. In 1996, the first planting occurred at the former Ryuhoku Elementary School, with Miyajima conducting a workshop at the ceremony. In his works, the LED counters symbolize the lives of anonymous individuals. Miyajima's first solo exhibitions were "Human Stone" at Gallery Parergon, Tokyo in 1983, and "Time" at Maki Gallery, Tokyo in 1986. More recently, he has exhibited at the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth (1996), Fondation Cartier pour l'Art Contemporain (1996), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1997), Miyanomori Art Museum, Hokkaido (2010), and Ullens Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing (2011). He has also participated in numerous group exhibitions, including the Venice Biennale in 1988 and 1999, the Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art (2008), the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney (2012), and the Third Asia-Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art, Queensland Art Gallery, Brisbane (1999). In 2020, Miyajima's works will be featured in the STARS: Six Contemporary Artists from Japan to the World exhibition in Tokyo, which includes a new work titled "Sea of Time – TOHOKU" and documentary footage of the public helping to set counter speeds. The following museums and institutions hold works by Miyajima in their collections.

Taylor Harry Fritz, born on 28 October 1997, is an American professional tennis player with a career-high singles ranking of world No. 4, achieved on 18 November 2024, and a best doubles ranking of No. 104, reached on 26 July 2021. He has won ten ATP Tour singles titles, including a Masters 1000 title at the 2022 Indian Wells Open, and was a finalist at the 2024 US Open and the 2024 ATP Finals. Fritz won a junior major singles title at the 2015 US Open and was the runner-up in junior singles at the 2015 French Open. He reached his first ATP Tour final in his third career event, the 2016 Memphis Open. He is the youngest of three boys, born to Kathy May, a former top-10 WTA player, and Guy Henry Fritz, who played professional tennis and was named US Olympic Development Coach of the Year in 2016; they divorced when he was 18. Through his mother, he is the great-great-grandson of David May, founder of The May Department Stores Company, which merged with Macy's. Fritz has two older maternal half-brothers, Chris and Kyle, and his uncle, Harry Fritz, also played professional tennis and won the longest Davis Cup match in history by number of games. His aunt, Laura Fritz, was a competitive swimmer who reached a top-5 world ranking in the 100 freestyle and was part of the world record 400 X4 freestyle relay team. Fritz grew up in Rancho Santa Fe in the San Diego metropolitan area with his brothers and attended Torrey Pines High School, where he won the CIF singles title in the San Diego section as a freshman. He switched to an online high school during his sophomore year to play full-time ITF junior events. He did not play any ITF events until he was 15, when he competed in a Grade-4 tournament in March 2013 in Clairemont. He began competing regularly on the ITF Circuit at the 2013 Junior US Open, shortly before turning 16, and reached the semifinals at the 2014 Junior Wimbledon tournament. He won his first Grade A tournament at the 2014 Osaka Mayor's Cup. In 2015, he reached at least the quarterfinal of all four junior Grand Slam tournaments, including the final at the French Open where he lost to Tommy Paul and the final at the US Open where he defeated Paul, finishing the year as the number-one-ranked boy's junior tennis player and being named the 2015 ITF Junior World Champion—making him the first American to hold the title since Donald Young in 2005 and Andy Roddick in 2000. He played his first ATP Tour tournament at Nottingham, where he received a wild card and won his first ATP match against Pablo Carreño Busta. In September 2015, after winning the Junior US Open, he turned pro and quickly rose from the 600s into the top 250 of the ATP rankings by becoming the 9th player at age 17 to win multiple Challenger Tour titles in back-to-back weeks, joining Top 20 players Bernard Tomic, Tomáš Berdych, Richard Gasquet, and Juan Martín del Potro, as well as Number 1 players Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic. After losing in the final of his last tournament in 2015, he reached a final again in his first tournament of 2016, winning against top-100 player Dudi Sela at Happy Valley to reach the 150s in the rankings. He advanced through Australian Open Qualifying to reach his first main draw of a Grand Slam tournament at the Australian Open, where he lost in the first round to Jack Sock in five sets. He was awarded a wildcard into his first ATP 250 tournament of 2016 at Memphis, where he defeated second-seeded Steve Johnson, the highest-ranked player he had ever defeated, and then beat Ričardas Berankis in the semifinal to become the youngest American to reach an ATP final since Michael Chang in 1988 and the second-fastest American to reach an ATP final, doing so in just his third career ATP tournament, behind only John Isner. He lost in the final to Kei Nishikori. In February 2016, he cracked the top 100 for the first time by reaching the quarterfinals in Acapulco at his first ATP 500 event. His grass-court season was highlighted by a close three-set loss to Roger Federer at Stuttgart, and he peaked in the rankings at No. 53 toward the end of the summer. At the US Open, he drew Jack Sock in the first round for the second time that year and lost in five sets. He won the ATP Star of Tomorrow award in 2016 for being the youngest player in the top 100 at age 19. In 2017, he achieved his first victory over a top-10 ATP player at Indian Wells, defeating sixth seed Marin Čilić in the second round. He struggled with injuries in the first half of the year and skipped the clay court season to recover. He returned in the summer with quarterfinals at Los Cabos and Winston-Salem. In his seventh Grand Slam appearance, he won his first match at a major by defeating Marcos Baghdatis at the US Open before losing in the second round to Dominic Thiem. After finishing 2017 just outside the top 100, he had a strong start to 2018, reaching two Challenger finals in January. He returned to the Top 100 by reaching the final in New Caledonia, where he lost to Noah Rubin. After a loss in qualifying at the Australian Open, he won his first Challenger title in two years at the inaugural event in Newport Beach, near his current residence in Palos Verdes. He continued his strong start by reaching the fourth round at Indian Wells, his first round of 16 appearance at a Masters event. He began the clay-court season with a semifinals appearance at the US Men's Clay Court Championships in Houston, the best result on clay of his career, where he upset Ryan Harrison and Jack Sock before losing to Steve Johnson, helping him return to No. 66 in the world. At the US Open, he reached his first Grand Slam third round, defeating Mischa Zverev and Jason Kubler, before losing to 9th-seeded Dominic Thiem in four sets. Earlier in the season, he began working with Paul Annacone, who helped him reach a career-high ranking of world No. 47 on November 5, 2018. He made the third round at the Australian Open, losing to Roger Federer in three sets. He won the Challenger at Newport Beach, defeating Brayden Schnur of Canada in straight sets. In June, he won his first ATP Tour title at the Eastbourne International by defeating Sam Querrey in straight sets. In the first round of Wimbledon, he defeated Tomáš Berdych in straight sets before losing to Jan-Lennard Struff in four sets. At the US Open, he was seeded 26th, his first-ever Grand Slam seeding, but lost in the first round to Feliciano López. He represented Team World in the third annual Laver Cup in Geneva. In his first singles match, he lost to Stefanos Tsitsipas, but bounced back on the final day by defeating Dominic Thiem. At the Swiss Indoors, he defeated 2nd-seeded Alexander Zverev in the first round in straight sets. After achieving a career-high ranking of world No. 25 on August 5, 2019, he ended the year ranked No. 32 in the world. He began his 2020 season at the inaugural ATP Cup, representing Team USA, going 1–2 in singles and being eliminated in the round-robin stage. At the Australian Open, he reached the third round with a five-set victory over Kevin Anderson before losing to Dominic Thiem. He reached his first ATP 500 final in Acapulco, where he lost to Rafael Nadal, and this runner-up finish propelled him to a new career-high ranking of world No. 24 on March 2, 2020. At the US Open, he was seeded 19th, defeated Dominik Koepfer in four sets, beat Gilles Simon in the second round, and lost to Denis Shapovalov in the third round in five sets. At the French Open, he was seeded 27th, defeated Tomáš Macháč in five sets and Radu Albot in straight sets before losing to Lorenzo Sonego in the third round in straight sets. The match against Sonego had the longest tie-break in French Open history, with Fritz losing 17–19. He started his 2021 season at the first edition of the Murray River Open, seeded sixth, reaching the third round before losing to Jérémy Chardy. Seeded 27th at the Australian Open, he reached the third round, where he was defeated by top seed, eight-time champion, and eventual champion Novak Djokovic in five sets, despite coming back from two sets to love down. In Doha, he reached the semifinals, defeating Lorenzo Sonego, sixth seed David Goffin, and fourth seed Denis Shapovalov before losing to Nikoloz Basilashvili. Seeded 15th at the Dubai Championships, he defeated Basilashvili in the second round in three sets, and was beaten in the third round by second seed Andrey Rublev. Seeded 22nd at the Miami Open, he reached the fourth round, losing to 32nd seed Alexander Bublik, which was his best showing at the event and only his second fourth-round appearance at a Masters 1000. He dropped out of the top 30 on May 10, 2021, after first-round losses at Monte-Carlo and Madrid, marking the first time no American men were in the Top 30 in nearly half a century. At the 2021 French Open, he was seeded 30th, defeated João Sousa in the first round in straight sets, and suffered a torn meniscus during a 4-set loss to Dominik Koepfer. After surgery, he returned in time for Wimbledon and reached the third round, where he lost to Alexander Zverev. At the 2021 BNP Paribas Open, he earned his first top 10 win in two years by beating world No. 7 and 5th seed Matteo Berrettini to reach the second fourth round at a Masters 1000, only the third in his career. It was his first win against a Top-10 opponent in 2021 and the seventh of his career. He then beat 10th seed Jannik Sinner to advance to his first Masters 1000 quarterfinal. There, he saved two match points to earn his biggest win of the year, defeating world No. 4 and 3rd seed Alexander Zverev to reach his first Masters 1000 semifinal, where he lost to Nikoloz Basilashvili. At the 2021 St. Petersburg Open, he turned 24 and won against countryman Tommy Paul, reaching the final where he lost to Marin Čilić. At the 2021 Rolex Paris Masters, he reached his second Masters 1000 quarterfinal, defeating Lorenzo Sonego, 5th seed and world No. 6 Andrey Rublev, and 10th seed and Indian Wells champion Cameron Norrie, for his third Top-10 win of the year and 10th Top-10 win of his career. He lost to Novak Djokovic in the quarterfinals. With this successful run, he reached a new career-high ranking in the top 25 at world No. 23 and became the No. 1 American player in singles on November 8, 2021. He ended the year ranked 23. Fritz started his 2022 season by representing the U.S. at the ATP Cup, where the U.S. was in Group C with Canada, Great Britain, and Germany. He defeated Félix Auger-Aliassime of Canada and Cameron Norrie of Great Britain but lost to Alexander Zverev of Germany, resulting in the U.S. finishing fourth in Group C. Seeded 20th at the Australian Open, he reached the second week of a Grand Slam for the first time after defeating 15th seed Roberto Bautista Agut in the third round in five sets. He fell in the fourth round to fourth seed Stefanos Tsitsipas in five sets, making his debut in the top 20 of the singles rankings on January 31. As the top seed at the Dallas Open, he reached the quarterfinals, where he was eliminated by seventh seed and compatriot Marcos Giron. Seeded seventh in Acapulco, he lost in the second round to qualifier Yoshihito Nishioka. Representing the U.S. in the Davis Cup tie against Colombia, he played one match and beat Alejandro González, helping the U.S. win 4–0 to make up for a previous loss to Colombia. Seeded 20th in Indian Wells, he became the first American to reach the final at the event since John Isner in 2012 by defeating 29th seed Alex de Minaur in the fourth round, Miomir Kecmanović in the quarterfinals, and seventh seed Andrey Rublev in the semifinals. He then defeated fourth seed, three-time champion, and then-21 Grand Slam champion Rafael Nadal in the final in straight sets, claiming his maiden Masters 1000 title, his second career ATP title, and ending Nadal's 20-match winning streak. It was his first win over a member of the Big Three in nine career matches and marked the first time an American man had won the Indian Wells title since Andre Agassi in 2001. This victory marked his top 15 debut and reached a career-high ranking of No. 13. Seeded 11th at the Miami Open, he entered the tournament aiming to complete the Sunshine Double but lost in the fourth round to Miomir Kecmanović in three sets. He started his clay-court season at the U.S. Clay Court Championships in Houston, Texas, seeded second, reaching the quarterfinals before losing to fifth seed and 2019 champion Cristian Garín. Seeded 10th at the Monte-Carlo Masters, he lost in the quarterfinals to eventual finalist Alejandro Davidovich Fokina. He missed the Madrid Open and Italian Open due to a left foot injury. Seeded 13th at the French Open, he was defeated in the second round by qualifier Bernabé Zapata Miralles. He began his grass-court season at the Libéma Open, seeded third, suffering a second-round upset to Dutch wildcard and eventual champion Tim van Rijthoven. Seeded fourth at the Queen's Club Championships, he was eliminated in the first round by British wildcard Jack Draper. Seeded third at the Eastbourne International, he beat sixth seed and defending champion Alex de Minaur in the semifinals to reach the final for the first time since 2019 when he won the title. He defeated compatriot Maxime Cressy in the final to win his third ATP Tour title and second in Eastbourne. Seeded 11th at Wimbledon, he defeated Alex Molčan and qualifier Jason Kubler in the third and fourth rounds respectively to reach his first Major quarterfinal. In the quarterfinals, he pushed world No. 4, second seed, and two-time champion Rafael Nadal to five sets but lost in a fifth-set tiebreak. His American swing began in Washington, where he was the third seed. After defeating Alexei Popyrin in straight sets, he retired against Dan Evans in the third round due to the heat, despite having a match point in the second set. At the Canada Masters, he beat Andy Murray and Frances.

At the Eastbourne International, seeded third, Fritz reached the final by defeating sixth seed and defending champion Alex de Minaur in the semifinals, marking his first final appearance since 2019 when he won the title; he then defeated compatriot Maxime Cressy to win his third ATP Tour title and second in Eastbourne. Seeded 11th at Wimbledon, he advanced to his first Major quarterfinal by defeating Alex Molčan and qualifier Jason Kubler in the third and fourth rounds, but lost in a five-set match to world No. 4 and second seed Rafael Nadal in the quarterfinals. In Washington, as the third seed, he beat Alexei Popyrin in straight sets before retiring against Dan Evans in the third round due to heat, despite having a match point in the second set; at the Canada Masters, he defeated Andy Murray and Frances Tiafoe before losing to Evans in three sets. In Cincinnati, he reached the quarterfinals by defeating Sebastián Báez, Nick Kyrgios, and sixth seed Andrey Rublev, but lost to world No. 1 Daniil Medvedev; at the US Open, he suffered a first-round defeat to first-time qualifier Brandon Holt, who earned his first ATP Tour win. Fritz withdrew from the Korea Open due to COVID-19 but reached his second ATP 500 final in Tokyo, where, as the third seed, he beat James Duckworth, Hiroki Moriya, received a walkover from Nick Kyrgios, and defeated Denis Shapovalov; he defeated Tiafoe in straight sets to become the first American champion since Pete Sampras in 1996, reaching a career-high ranking of World No. 8 on October 10, 2022, the first American to crack the Top 10 since Jack Sock in 2017. At the Paris Masters, he won against Alejandro Davidovich Fokina in the first round before losing to French wildcard Gilles Simon in a three-set match lasting 3 hours and 5 minutes, missing qualification for the 2022 ATP Finals but becoming an alternate; after Carlos Alcaraz’s withdrawal due to injury, Fritz qualified for the 2022 ATP Finals, the first American since John Isner in 2018; in the round robin, he defeated Rafael Nadal on his debut, his first win over a top-3 player, lost to Casper Ruud, and defeated Félix Auger-Aliassime to reach the semifinals, the first American since Jack Sock in 2017 to reach that stage, marking his 45th tour-level win of the season; he lost to Novak Djokovic in straight sets. Fritz finished the year ranked inside the top-10 for the first time, at world No. 9. At the inaugural 2023 United Cup, as the No. 1 American male player, the United States team won the championship by defeating Italy in the final; at the Australian Open, he lost in the second round to wildcard Alexei Popyrin, saving a match point in the fourth set to make it two sets all, but lost a match lasting over four hours. At the 2023 Dallas Open, he reached the semifinals, losing to Wu Yibing, and reached a new career-high ranking of world No. 7, the highest ranked American since Mardy Fish in 2011; as the top seed, he reached back-to-back semifinals at the 2023 Delray Beach Open, defeated Mackenzie McDonald to reach his first ATP final of the season and tenth overall, and defeated Miomir Kecmanović to win his fifth ATP Tour title, moving to world No. 5 on February 27, 2023. At the Mexican Open, he defeated Frances Tiafoe to reach his third straight semifinal, losing to Tommy Paul in an epic match lasting three and a half hours, setting a record for the longest match in the 30-year history of the Abierto Mexicano Telcel. In Indian Wells and Miami, he reached back-to-back quarterfinals by defeating Sebastián Báez, Márton Fucsovics, and Denis Shapovalov, Holger Rune respectively. In Monte Carlo, he reached his third consecutive Masters quarterfinal by defeating Stan Wawrinka and Jiří Lehečka, then defeated two-time defending champion Stefanos Tsitsipas to reach the semifinals, recording his 200th win and becoming the first American in 20 years to reach the semifinals at this Masters since Vince Spadea; he lost in three sets to Andrey Rublev after winning the first set. Seeded second at the 2023 BMW Open, he reached the semifinals with wins over Márton Fucsovics and Dominic Thiem; in Madrid, he lost to Zhizhen Zhang after Zhang saved three match points to reach the quarterfinals; in Rome, he lost in the second round to qualifier Yannick Hanfmann. He won his sixth title at the 2023 Atlanta Open by defeating Aleksandar Vukic; at the US Open, he reached the quarterfinals for the first time at a Major but lost to Novak Djokovic. At the 2023 Japan Open, as the defending champion, he lost to wildcard Shintaro Mochizuki after being a set up and serving at 5–2 in the third set. Seeded fifth in Basel, he lost to Alexander Shevchenko after missing 15 break point opportunities in a match lasting nearly three hours with three tiebreaks; in Paris, he withdrew before the second round due to injury, ending the season early, though potentially remaining as an alternate at the 2023 ATP Finals. He reached his first quarterfinal at the Australian Open by defeating Stefanos Tsitsipas in four sets; he successfully defended his Delray Beach title by defeating Tommy Paul; at the 2024 Miami Open, he lost in the second round to qualifier Thiago Seyboth Wild, having received a bye. He had a successful start to the clay season at the Bavarian International Tennis Championships in Munich, reaching his first clay court final by defeating Cristian Garín and regaining the American No. 1 ranking; at the 2024 Mutua Madrid Open, he reached his second clay Masters quarterfinal and tenth overall, defeating Luciano Darderi, Sebastián Báez, and Hubert Hurkacz, his second top-10 career win on clay; he defeated Francisco Cerúndolo for his 250th career win, becoming the sixth man born in 1995 or later to reach that milestone and the first American man to reach the semifinals of Madrid since it switched to clay in 2009 and the third after Andre Agassi and Robby Ginepri; at the 2024 Italian Open, he reached back-to-back quarterfinals by defeating Fabio Fognini, Sebastian Korda, and Grigor Dimitrov, becoming the first American man to reach the quarterfinals or better at all three clay court Masters tournaments; it was also the first time multiple American players (with Tommy Paul) reached the quarterfinals in Rome since 2008; at the 2024 French Open, he reached the fourth round of a clay Major for the first time with a five-set win over Thanasi Kokkinakis. Seeded third, he reached the Paris Olympics semifinals with Tommy Paul and won the bronze medal by defeating the Czech duo Tomáš Macháč and Adam Pavlásek. Seeded 12th at the US Open, Fritz reached his first Grand Slam semifinal by defeating Camilo Ugo Carabelli, Matteo Berrettini, Francisco Comesaña, Casper Ruud, and Alexander Zverev, his first two consecutive top-10 wins in a Major; he became the first American since Andre Agassi in 2001 to reach the fourth round at each Grand Slam in the same season; by reaching the semifinals, he set up an all-American matchup with Frances Tiafoe, the first at a Grand Slam since 2005 at the US Open; he won the match in five sets to reach his first Grand Slam final, but lost to Jannik Sinner in straight sets; in an interview on the Nothing Major podcast, he admitted the emotional toll of the loss. At the ATP Finals in November, Fritz reached the semifinals after two wins and one loss in the group stages, beating Daniil Medvedev and Alex De Minaur; he defeated Alexander Zverev in the semifinals to reach his first final at the end-of-season event, becoming the first American to reach the championship match at the ATP Finals since James Blake in 2006; he lost the final to Jannik Sinner in straight sets; despite the loss, he ended the season with a new career-high singles ranking of world No. 4 on November 18. Opening the year as a career-high No. 4 in the world rankings, Fritz helped the United States win the United Cup title, their second in three years, winning four of five matches over Borna Coric, Zhizhen Zhang, Tomas Machac, and Hubert Hurkacz. Entering the 2025 Australian Open as the fourth seed, he cruised through his first two matches, dropping only 8 games against Jenson Brooksby and Christian Garin, but lost in four sets to Gael Monfils, marking his earliest exit at a Grand Slam since the 2023 Wimbledon Championships. After disappointing early exits in Delray Beach and Dallas, Fritz entered Indian Wells aiming to recapture his 2022 win; he reached the fourth round for the fifth straight time but lost to Jack Draper in straight sets. Entering the Miami Open as the third seed, aiming for his second ATP 1000 title, he reached the quarterfinals for the second time after defeating Lorenzo Sonego, Denis Shapovalov, and Adam Walton; in the quarterfinal, he defeated Matteo Berrettini in three sets to reach his first semifinal at the tournament; in the semifinal, he lost a close three-set match to eventual champion Jakub Menšík. During the 2025 grass season, Fritz won two titles: the BOSS Open after a fifth straight victory over Alexander Zverev, and the Eastbourne International, defeating Jenson Brooksby in the final. At Wimbledon, he defeated Karen Khachanov to reach the semifinals for the first time in that tournament, becoming the first American man to do so since John Isner in 2018; he lost to Carlos Alcaraz in four sets. At the US Open, he reached the quarterfinals and lost to Novak Djokovic in four sets. At the 2025 Japan Open in Tokyo, he reached the final and lost to world No. 1 Carlos Alcaraz, who avenged his loss at the 2025 Laver Cup, where team World defeated team Europe. At the 2025 Rolex Shanghai Masters, he reached the third round, recording his 50th win of the season, becoming the first American in 20 years to reach that milestone and to do so in three consecutive seasons (54 in 2023, 53 in 2024) since Andy Roddick. Since early 2024, Fritz wears Hugo Boss clothing on court, previously sponsored by Nike; he uses ASICS Gel-Resolution tennis shoes and a Head Radical MP racquet. He has partnerships with Motorola, Eight Sleep, La Roche Posay, and Chipotle Mexican Grill. Fritz is an offensive baseliner with powerful, penetrating groundstrokes that force errors or end points as winners; his most consistent stroke is his forehand, and he has a strong, flatter backhand; though not comfortable at the net, he has significantly improved his net game and movement. Standing 6 feet 5 inches (1.96 meters) tall, he has a dominant serve reaching 149 miles per hour (240 km/h) and solid groundstrokes off both wings; he uses an almost full-western grip on his forehand, bordering on Hawaiian, a defining aspect of his style; he excels at sharp angle cross-court shots on both sides and has a good topspin lob. He has a son, Jordan (born in 2017), with former pro tennis player Raquel Pedraza, whom he married from 2016 to 2019. Fritz is an avid player of World of Warcraft and Rust, and occasionally live streams his gaming on Twitch under the name TaylorFritz97. Since June 2020, he has been in a relationship with fashion influencer Morgan Riddle. He appeared in the tennis docuseries Break Point, which premiered on Netflix on January 13, 2023 and concluded in 2024. Fritz has played three seasons with World TeamTennis, making his debut in 2015 with the San Diego Aviators, playing two additional seasons with them in 2018 and 2019; he joined the Philadelphia Freedoms in 2020 at The Greenbrier, advancing to the WTT Playoffs as the No. 1 seed but losing to the New York Empire in the semifinal; he was named the WTT 2020 Male MVP. Current through the 2025 US Open.

Telegram, also known as Telegram Messenger, is a cloud-based, cross-platform social media and instant messaging service that launched for iOS on 14 August 2013 and for Android on 20 October 2013. It enables users to exchange messages, share media and files, and conduct private and group voice or video calls, as well as public livestreams. Available on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux, and web browsers, Telegram offers end-to-end encryption in voice and video calls and optionally in private chats if both participants use a mobile device. The service includes social networking features such as posting stories, creating public groups with up to 200,000 members, and sharing one-way updates to unlimited audiences via channels. Founded in 2013 by Pavel and Nikolai Durov, Telegram previously had its roots in the Russian social network VK, which the brothers left in 2014, citing government control. Nikolai developed the MTProto protocol, the foundation of the messenger, while Pavel provided financial support through his Digital Fortress fund. Telegram is registered as a company in the British Virgin Islands and as an LLC in Dubai, with its headquarters in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Its servers are distributed worldwide through a complex network of shell companies to avoid compliance with government subpoenas, and the company claims it does not process requests related to illegal content in chats or group chats, stating it has disclosed zero bytes of user messages to third parties, including governments. However, Pavel reported that Telegram disclosed data for 203 legal requests from Brazil and 6,992 from India between January and September 2024. Users can check their country's legal requests via Telegram’s transparency bot. As of March 2025, Telegram has more than 1 billion monthly active users, with India being the country with the most users. The app reached 100,000 daily active users in October 2013, 35 million monthly users and 15 million daily active users by March 2014, 50 million active users and 1 billion daily messages by December 2014, 60 million active users and 12 billion daily messages in September 2015, 100 million monthly active users and 15 billion daily messages in February 2016, 180 million in December 2017, 200 million by March 2018, 300 million monthly active users by October 2019, 400 million in April 2020, 500 million in January 2021, 700 million in June 2022, 800 million in July 2023, 900 million in March 2024, 950 million in July 2024, and surpassed 1 billion monthly active users in March 2025. Registration requires either a phone number and a smartphone or one of a limited number of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) issued in 2022. Users must sign up on an Android or iOS device, and changing a phone number automatically reassigns the account without notifying contacts or exporting data. Messages are tied to the user’s number and custom username, not the device, and are synced across logged-in devices via cloud storage, except for device-specific secret chats. Inactive accounts are deleted after six months, with a range of up to 18 months. Groups and channels can be verified if they have a verified social media or Wikipedia page, but individual user accounts cannot. Messages support formatted text, media, files up to 2 GB (4 GB with Premium), locations, and audio or video messages; private chat messages can be edited for up to 48 hours with an "edited" icon, and messages or entire chats can be deleted without a trace. Chat history can be imported from WhatsApp, Line, and KakaoTalk. Users can start a message on one device and finish it on another via cloud drafts. Messages can be translated, with Premium users able to translate entire chats with one click and hide the translate button for specific languages. Reactions with emoji are available in private chats and can be enabled by admins in groups and channels, with Premium users having more options and the ability to leave multiple reactions. Stickers, including static, animated, or video types, are supported and use WebP or WebM formats, with full-screen effects possible. Messages can be scheduled to send at a specific time or when a conversation partner comes online, or sent without sound. Private chat messages can be forwarded with the original sender hidden or captions hidden, and forwarded messages retain reply formatting. A "Saved Messages" chat allows users to bookmark messages, visible only to themselves. Chats can be sorted into folders with preset or custom categories, and Premium users can set any folder as the default screen. Secret Chats are end-to-end encrypted, accessible only on the device where they started, and self-destruct upon logout; they restrict screenshots on Android and warn on iOS, hide content from screenshots, and support perfect forward secrecy with key rotation after 100 uses or weekly. Secret Chats are available on Android, iOS, and macOS. Messages in both secret and regular chats can self-destruct after being read, with a user-set duration from one day to one year. Groups support up to 200,000 members and can be public or private, with flexible admin rights and bots for moderation. Groups can be split into topics, and admins can hide member lists or post anonymously. Content protection prevents screenshots, forwarding, and downloading of media. Ownership of groups and channels can be transferred to an admin. Groups support threaded replies and tagging users with @username. Polls can be open or anonymous with multiple choices, and votes retain when forwarded. Channels are one-way feeds where owners or admins post content, and followers can only read, react, and comment if enabled. Channels can reach unlimited subscribers and show detailed statistics only to admins. Channel owners can run giveaways to award prizes like Telegram Premium subscriptions. Premium users can give "boosts" to channels, unlocking features such as custom messages or posting stories. In December 2019, Bloomberg News moved its newsletter from WhatsApp to Telegram after WhatsApp banned bulk messaging. Other news organizations with official channels include the Financial Times, Business Insider, and The New York Times. Channels have been used by governments and heads of state, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Emmanuel Macron, and by journalists in oppressive regimes to create independent news networks. Telegram offers an open API for third-party bots, many built on the 8XR game engine, with Mini Apps reaching 500 million monthly active users in July 2024. Since 2017, users have been able to initiate one-on-one calls; video calls were introduced in August 2020, and a neural network is used to improve call quality. Group voice chats were launched in December 2020 and group video chats in June 2021, supporting picture-in-picture, screen sharing, recording, noise suppression, and selective muting. Channels support livestreams that integrate with third-party apps like OBS Studio and XSplit. Group voice chats remain open until an admin closes them. In April 2025, Telegram launched secure group calls with end-to-end encryption using blockchain-like technology, supporting up to 200 participants with voice, video, and screen sharing. Login requires either an SMS or a code from another active session, with two-step verification and recovery email options added in late 2022, and support for Sign in with Apple, Google, or email. A login alert is sent when a new device logs in. Users can hide their "Last Seen" status, phone number, and profile photo, with Premium users able to restrict who can send them text or voice messages. The Devices submenu shows active devices and allows remote logout. Media autoplay and automatic downloads can be disabled for WiFi and mobile data, with settings adjustable by chat type. Cache can be cleared when it reaches a certain size or time, with visual storage usage and media sorting by size available. In June 2015, Telegram launched a bot platform allowing third-party developers to create bots that respond to messages, integrate services, or host mini apps. Bots can accept payments via Paymentwall and Yandex.Money. Inline bots can be accessed from any chat screen by typing a username and query, and certain approved bots integrate into the attachment menu. A Dutch report noted that an invited bot can potentially read all group messages if access is changed silently, and Telegram indicated it would announce such changes in the group.

In June 2015, Telegram launched a platform enabling third-party developers to create bots, which are Telegram accounts operated by programs capable of responding to messages or mentions, being invited into groups, performing tasks, integrating with other programs, and hosting mini apps. These bots can accept online payments via Paymentwall, Yandex.Money, Stripe, Ravepay, Razorpay, QiWi, and Google Pay, depending on the country. Bots power Telegram’s gaming platform using HTML5, with games loading on-demand and compatible with iPhone 4 and newer, and Android 4.4 and newer devices. Through IFTTT, users can interact with Internet of Things (IoT) services. In April 2021, the Payments 2.0 upgrade allowed bot payments in any chat using third-party services such as Sberbank, Tranzoo, Payme, CLICK, LiqPay, and ECOMMPAY to process credit card information. Bots are widely used by businesses to communicate with customers via APIs integrated with communication platforms, enabling omnichannel inbox functionality, website chat widgets, and automated or human-assisted conversations; platforms like respond.io, Manychat, and Trengo offer such integrations. In February 2018, Telegram introduced Telegram Login, a website widget allowing users to sign into third-party sites with their Telegram account, sharing only their name, username, and profile picture while keeping their phone number hidden, with the gateway linked to a bot tied to the developer’s domain. In June 2021, a new bot menu was introduced, allowing users to browse and send commands during chats. In April 2022, bots gained support for customized interfaces and inline page loading, with interfaces adjustable to match the app’s theme even during interactions. In October 2024, Telegram increased messaging limits for bots to 1000 messages per second, with messages beyond the free 30-per-second limit charged using Telegram Stars. In December 2024, Telegram introduced affiliate programs enabling developers to create programs where users earn commissions for referring others to bots or mini apps. Telegram has over 40,000 stickers, which are cloud-based, high-resolution images used to provide expressive emoji, organized into collections called "packs," with one default pack included; stickers are automatically available across all clients and use the WebP format, with animated emoji introduced in August 2019, interactive emoji added in September 2021, and video stickers in January 2022 using the WebM format. In August 2022, users could upload custom emoji via Telegram’s emoji platform, though only Premium users can use them in chats. Reactions were introduced in 2021 and expanded in September 2022 to include dozens of options for free users, with the reaction panel redesigned. Features People Nearby and Groups Near Me, which used GPS to connect users nearby, were removed in 2024 due to issues with bots and scammers. Telegram users can post stories with dual-camera mode, privacy settings, post-editing, and rewind/fast-forward capabilities. Telegram Premium, launched on 19 June 2022 with regional pricing, offers increased limits such as larger file uploads, faster downloads, unlimited voice message transcription, more pinned chats and folders, extra stickers, emoji, reactions, customization features like a special badge, and message appearance changes, as well as instant chat translation and restrictions on who can send text or voice messages. Premium can be purchased via Apple and Google in-app purchases, through Telegram’s @PremiumBot, or with cryptocurrency on the Fragment platform, and can be bought for oneself or as a gift, or won through official Channel Giveaways. In October 2024, Telegram launched Gifts, virtual cosmetic items purchasable and sendable using Telegram Stars, and in January 2025, Collectible Gifts were introduced—unique collections with special artwork and attributes, some of which can be upgraded to unlock random appearances and other features, registered on the TON blockchain as NFTs and tradeable on Telegram’s in-app Gift Marketplace or external platforms. In July 2025, Telegram partnered with Snoop Dogg to release limited-edition collectible gifts with his music video "Gifts," and in November 2025, partnered with Khabib Nurmagomedov and UFC for two limited-edition releases using an auction-based system. Users can publish articles on Telegraph, a minimalistic text editor and publisher, with anonymous publishing and the ability to check view counts and edit content later; articles support Instant View, allowing full reading in chats without opening a browser. The URL is auto-generated from the title, with non-Latin characters transliterated, spaces replaced by hyphens, and the publication date appended, e.g., /Telegraph-blog-platform-11-17 for an article titled "Telegraph (blog platform)" published on 17 November. Text formatting includes two levels of headings, single-level lists, bold, italics, quotes, hyperlinks, image and video uploads (limited to 5 MB, disabled since September 2024), and direct embedding of YouTube, Vimeo, or Twitter links. In July 2018, Telegram introduced Telegram Passport, a real-life identification system allowing users to upload official documents like passports or driver’s licenses, with data shared only with authorized recipients and no access by Telegram; however, the service was criticized for vulnerability to brute-force attacks. In December 2020, Telegram launched a Bugs and Suggestions platform where users submit bug reports and feature ideas, which others can vote on and comment. In October 2024, Telegram introduced a verification platform, Telegram Gateway, enabling third-party services to authenticate users via verification codes sent through Telegram. For encrypted chats (Secret Chats), Telegram uses MTProto, a custom symmetric encryption scheme developed by Nikolai Durov and other developers, based on 256-bit AES, 2048-bit RSA, and Diffie–Hellman key exchange; MTProto 1.0 was deprecated in December 2017 in favor of MTProto 2.0, deployed starting with version 4.6, which was formally proven correct in December 2020 by a team from the University of Udine, Italy, using ProVerif, confirming its security properties including authentication, integrity, confidentiality, and perfect forward secrecy, though the team noted that the server is not trusted and man-in-the-middle attacks are possible if users fail to verify shared key fingerprints, and that full computational model proofs are needed for definitive security. Telegram uses centralized servers in multiple countries, with closed-source, proprietary server-side software; Pavel Durov stated that connecting independent servers would require a major architectural redesign. For users in the European Economic Area (EEA) or UK, GDPR is supported by storing data only in the Netherlands and designating a London-based company as responsible data controller. Telegram offers various client apps, many free and open-source under the GNU GPL version 2 or 3, with official clients supporting all file formats and media types including JPEG, PNG, WebP, H.264, HEVC, MP4, and MP3, FLAC, Vorbis, Opus, AAC; clients are available for non-traditional platforms like KaiOS (Telekram) and S30+/Mocor feature phones. In 2021, Telegram announced a direct build of its Android app, available directly from the Telegram website, automatically updated and faster than versions in app stores, with a unique feature allowing access to channels/groups on specific topics without censorship due to app store policies. The iOS version was written in Swift, the Android version uses TDLib, and the iOS version was discontinued with its code merged into the main app. Telegram provides public APIs for developers to build instant messaging apps, and in February 2015, the creators of WhatsApp+ released Telegram Plus, later renamed Plus Messenger, after receiving a cease-and-desist from WhatsApp; Samsung released a messaging app based on these APIs in September 2015. Telegram also offers a bot API for developers to create bots, used for emulating old games and informing users about vaccine availability during the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, Telegram enables direct payments within the platform using external services like Stripe. In 2025, Telegram’s founder claimed that xAI signed a $300 million program with Telegram for Grok to provide full functions within Telegram starting in Summer 2025, funded by a mix of cash and xAI equity, though the initiative has since been abandoned with no new announcements or feature releases. Initially supported by Pavel Durov’s personal funds after selling his VK stake, Telegram conducted a private placement in January 2018, raising $1.7 billion from investors including Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia Capital, and Benchmark; after the TON project shutdown, the company had to repay investors for funds not spent on development. On 15 March 2021, Telegram issued a $1 billion five-year public bonds placement to cover $625.7 million in debts, including $433 million from investors who bought Gram token futures, such as David Yakobashvili; on 23 March, it sold an additional $150 million to Mubadala Investment Company and Abu Dhabi Catalyst Partners. The next day, Mubadala stated that Russia’s sovereign wealth fund participated in the deal through a joint UAE-Russia investment platform, though Telegram denied RDIF was among investors, confirming that the funds involved did not include RDIF. Bondholders have the option to convert bonds to shares at a 10% discount if Telegram conducts an open IPO. Durov stated the bond move aimed to enable global growth while maintaining independence and values, having previously rejected offers for a 5–10% stake, valuing the company at $30–40 billion. In March 2024, Telegram sold an additional $330 million in bonds, with Durov stating it would further solidify Telegram’s position as an independent platform challenging industry 'Goliaths'. Telegram has stated it will never serve advertisements in private chats; in late 2020, Durov announced work on an internal ad platform to integrate non-targeted advertising.

Durov stated that Telegram’s bond issuance aimed to "enable Telegram to continue growing globally while sticking to its values and remaining independent." Prior to the bond placement, Durov had rejected investment offers for a 5–10% stake in the company, valuing it between $30–40 billion, and in March 2024, Telegram sold an additional $330 million in bonds. Durov said the bond sale "will further solidify our position as an independent platform that is able to challenge the 'Goliaths' of our industry." According to the bond contract, holders will be given the option to convert their bonds into shares at a 10% discount if the company conducts an open IPO. Telegram has stated it will never serve advertisements in private chats, but began offering non-targeted ads in public one-to-many channels through its "Sponsored Messages" platform in October 2021, starting with channels having more than 1,000 followers. In late 2020, Durov announced Telegram would consider adding paid enterprise features requiring more bandwidth, with costs covered by feature prices and partially offsetting regular user costs. In June 2024, Telegram launched Telegram Stars to facilitate in-app purchases of digital goods and services, in compliance with App Store and Play Store policies, and later expanded functionality to allow Stars to unlock media in channels or buy gifts for other users. In December 2024, Telegram CEO Pavel Durov announced the company had reached profitability due to significant growth in Premium subscriptions and ad sales, supported by other monetization features launched in 2024. In 2017, Telegram began developing a blockchain platform called "The Open Network" (TON) and its native cryptocurrency "Gram," announced in mid-December 2017 and with a 132-page technical paper released in January 2018. The codebase was developed by Pavel Durov’s brother Nikolai Durov, the core developer of Telegram’s MTProto protocol. In January and February 2018, Telegram conducted a private sale of Gram futures, raising around $1.7 billion, with no public offering. The TON development was isolated and delayed, with a test network launched in January 2019 and the main network scheduled for 31 October 2019. On 30 October, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission obtained a temporary restraining order to block Gram distribution to initial purchasers, considering the offering an unregistered securities transaction. Judge P. Kevin Castel agreed with the SEC, maintaining the ban, which applied to non-U.S.-based purchasers due to Telegram’s inability to prevent resale to U.S. citizens on secondary markets, given user anonymity. Durov announced the end of Telegram’s active involvement with TON, and on 26 June, the judge approved a settlement where Telegram paid an $18.5 million penalty and returned $1.22 billion to Gram purchasers. In March 2021, Telegram launched a bonds offering to cover the debt and fund further growth. The TON ecosystem was later developed by others and began offering decentralized domain names and cloud storage via TON DNS. Telegram’s mixed nature—combining private communication with social media features and minimal content restrictions—has led to its use by organizations for recruitment and spreading agendas, including in Belarus, Russia, Hong Kong, and Iran, as well as for state propaganda and extremist views. Research institutions and monitoring bodies have criticized Telegram for being used by violent groups like ISIS, the Proud Boys, and the Myanmar junta for private and public communication. Telegram has made efforts to ban illegal content, including child abuse and pro-terrorist channels, including a partnership with Europol to eliminate IS presence, though far-right extremist communities remain active. Durov argued that removing conspiracy theories strengthens them, as their content is removed. In September 2024, Telegram announced it would hand over users’ IP addresses and phone numbers to authorities with valid legal requests. Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s BND, warned Russia was recruiting saboteurs across Europe via Telegram by monitoring pro-Russian channels. A study by OpenMinds, published before the 2025 Moldovan parliamentary election, found a third of Telegram channels in Moldova systematically spread Russian propaganda and one in eight comments came from bots; Moldovan President Maia Sandu criticized Telegram for refusing to collaborate with state authorities on illegal activities like vote buying. In September 2015, Durov stated privacy was more important than fear of terrorism and sarcastically suggested banning words used by terrorists. ISIS used Telegram for recruitment, and in France, initial investigations of a terrorist act revealed Telegram use, though the extent was unclear. Telegram began publishing daily moderation statistics on terror-related content in an official channel named @ISISwatch, and after removing such content, ISIS reportedly moved its recruitment groups to the dark web, with U.S. officials citing the deplatforming as effective. In 2023, Saudi Arabia’s Etidal reported over 59 million pieces of extremist content were removed from Telegram since 2022. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps used Telegram to dox citizens and share propaganda in 2020, and after the 2021 Myanmar coup, the junta used the platform to spread propaganda and organize misinformation campaigns, prompting Telegram to ban 13 accounts linked to the military. On 26 April 2023, Telegram was temporarily suspended in Brazil and fined R$1 million per day for failing to comply with a Federal Police investigation into neo-Nazi activities; the company only partially fulfilled a data request, which authorities deemed intentional lack of cooperation, and the suspension was lifted three days later but the fine remained. Telegram’s CEO claimed the requested data was technologically impossible to obtain. Twelve days later, Telegram warned users that Brazil’s upcoming Congressional Bill No. 2630 would end freedom of speech. Far-right and white supremacist groups on Telegram have shared videos of the Christchurch and Halle shootings after they were removed from Twitch. British far-right publication TR.news launched a Telegram channel after multiple deplatformings, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue reported Irish far-right groups grew substantially between 2019 and 2020. Oxford University research suggests Telegram’s lack of sorting algorithms keeps many extremist groups obscure while some gain attention. Telegram has been used to distribute illegal pornography, including child pornography, and has a reporting system for child abuse content, including specific messages, with a verified channel "Stop Child Abuse" posting daily statistics on banned groups and channels and an email for abuse reports. In January 2021, a banned Telegram group called "Public Room" ("Јавна соба") with over 7,000 members shared nude photos of women and teenage girls, including their private information like phone numbers and social media profiles, encouraging contact for sexual favors without consent, causing public backlash and demands from North Macedonian leaders for action; the group was banned without a public statement. In August 2024, a BBC investigation found Telegram had not joined the U.S. National Center for Missing & Exploited Children or the UK Internet Watch Foundation, and Telegram responded that it proactively moderates harmful content within industry standards. In August 2024, journalist Ko Narin exposed Telegram chats where teenagers used generative AI to deepfake images of classmates and teachers for porn. In May 2020, Volodymyr Flents of "Electronic Democracy" reported a Telegram bot selling personal data of Ukrainian citizens, estimated to contain data from 26 million Ukrainians in the Diia app; deputy prime minister Mykhailo Fedorov denied data leaks, and 25 people were confirmed as involved with 30 databases seized. In 2020, Apple blocked a Telegram bot for posting deepfake pornography, and Telegram reportedly banned over 350,000 bots and channels containing child abuse and terrorism-related content. In 2021, a bot was found selling leaked Facebook phone numbers. Telegram has faced criticism for fraud, primarily involving scammers offering online jobs with "prepaid tasks" that entice users to deposit money with false promises of returns. In July 2023, Hyderabad Police uncovered a fraud where 15,000 Indian citizens lost ₹712 crore (US$84 million) in less than a year through such tasks, originating in China and laundered via cryptocurrency wallets. In September 2023, Singapore Police reported over 6,600 Singaporeans lost S$96.8 million (US$72.24 million) to prepaid job scams on Telegram and WhatsApp. In March 2024, a Spanish judge ordered the temporary blocking of Telegram in Spain following complaints from media organizations about unauthorized sharing of copyrighted content; the order was suspended pending a police report and later annulled as "disproportionate." In recent years, Telegram has become popular for illicit drug trading, with a 2024 paper by Sociology Compass exploring this trend. In August 2024, an EU probe was launched to determine if Telegram breached EU digital rules by failing to provide accurate user numbers. Telegram stated in February 2024 it had 41 million users in the EU, but under the EU Digital Services Act, it was required to provide an updated number by August 2024 and only declared it had "significantly fewer than 45 million average monthly active recipients in the EU." As part of its monetization model, Telegram displays advertisement banners in public channels with over 1,000 subscribers, with revenue shared with channel owners in Toncoin cryptocurrency; as of August 2025, there was no opt-out option, which is seen as problematic for non-profit organizations. In August 2025, Germany’s public broadcaster NDR closed its tagesschau Telegram channel after editorial staff discovered unsolicited advertisements, which they argued violated the Rundfunkstaatsvertrag, especially "shady" or "fraudulent" sports betting ads; NDR stated the accumulation of Toncoin from unsolicited ads was unacceptable. In 2025, Telegram blocked Huione Guarantee, an escrow-style marketplace operating across thousands of Telegram channels and widely used by online scammers based in Cambodia, with Hun To, cousin of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, listed as a director. Channels have been used by celebrities such as Arnold Schwarzenegger and Snoop Dogg, and politicians including President Emmanuel Macron of France, former President Jair Bolsonaro of Brazil, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, President Maia Sandu of Moldova, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine, former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador of Mexico, and former Singaporean Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.

Not noticed these ads before, but closed the channel, stating that an advertisement-based accumulation of Toncoin, albeit unsolicited and not withdrawn, was unacceptable for a German public media broadcaster. In 2025, Telegram said it blocked Huione Guarantee, which Elliptic described as an escrow-style marketplace operating across thousands of Telegram channels and widely used by online scammers based in scam centers in Cambodia; Huione lists businessman Hun To, cousin of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a director.
