Channels have been used by celebrities such as Arnold Schwarzenegger and Snoop Dogg and politicians: President of France Emmanuel Macron, former President of Brazil Jair Bolsonaro, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, President of Moldova Maia Sandu, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, former Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, former Singaporean Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev, former Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and others. Telegram's security model has received notable criticism by cryptography experts, who criticized how, unless modified first, the default general security model stores all contacts, messages and media together with their decryption keys on its servers continuously, and that it does not enable end-to-end encryption for messages by default; Pavel Durov has argued that this is because it helps to avoid third-party unsecured backups and to allow users to access messages and files from any device. Criticisms were also aimed at Telegram's use of a custom-designed encryption protocol. In December 2020, a study titled "Automated Symbolic Verification of Telegram's MTProto 2.0" was published, confirming the security of the updated MTProto 2.0 and reviewing it while pointing out several theoretical vulnerabilities; the paper provides "fully automated proof of the soundness of MTProto 2.0's authentication, normal chat, end-to-end encrypted chat, and re-keying mechanisms with respect to several security properties, including authentication, integrity, confidentiality and perfect forward secrecy" and "proves the formal correctness of MTProto 2.0", partially addressing concerns about lack of scrutiny while confirming the formal security of the protocol's latest version. The desktop clients, excluding the macOS client, do not feature options for end-to-end encrypted messages; when the user assigns a local password in the desktop application, data is also locally encrypted. Telegram has defended the lack of ubiquitous end-to-end encryption by saying that online-backups that do not use client-side encryption are "the most secure solution currently possible". Telegram has organized two cryptography contests to challenge its own security; third parties were asked to break the service's cryptography and disclose the information contained within a secret chat between two computer-controlled users, with rewards of US$200,000 and US$300,000 offered; both contests expired with no winners. Security researcher Moxie Marlinspike, founder of the competing Signal messenger, and commenters on Hacker News criticized the first contest for being rigged or framed in Telegram's favor and said that Telegram's statements on the value of these contests as proof of the cryptography's quality are misleading, because the cryptography contest could not be won even with completely broken algorithms such as MD2 (hash function) used as key stream extractor, and primitives such as the Dual EC DRBG that is known to be backdoored. Telegram has been blocked temporarily or permanently by some governments including Iran, China, Brazil, and Pakistan; the Russian government blocked Telegram for several years before lifting the ban in 2020. The company's founder has said he wants the app to have an anti-censorship tool for Iran and China similar to the app's role in fighting censorship in Russia. On 19 April 2024, Apple removed Telegram from the App Store in China. In September 2024, Ukraine banned the usage of Telegram by government officials, military personnel, and key workers on official devices, citing fears of Russian espionage; the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine enforced the restrictions following evidence reported to them by Kyrylo Budanov, showing Russia's ability to access messages and user data on the platform; Andriy Kovalenko, head of the security council's centre on countering disinformation, clarified that the ban was limited to official devices and did not extend to personal phones. Telegram was the main subject surrounding the 2019 Puerto Rico riots that ended up in the resignation of then-Governor Ricardo Rosselló; hundreds of pages of a group chat between Rosselló and members of his staff were leaked, with the messages considered vulgar, racist, and homophobic, and members of the chat discussing how they would use the media to target potential political opponents. In September 2021, prior to the regional elections in Russia, Telegram suspended several bots spreading information about the election, including a bot run by the opposition party and critics of incumbent president Vladimir Putin's government, citing election silence as the reason, though a blog post by the company's CEO implied the company was following Apple and Google, which "dictate the rules of the game to developers"; the blocking of the main Smart Voting bot was criticized by allies of Alexei Navalny, a Kremlin critic and former opposition leader; Navalny's spokeswoman Kira Yarmysh called the block and the deletion of the tactical voting app from app stores "censorship [...] imposed by private companies". In a later blog post, Durov directly stated that the block was a result of pressure from Google and Apple as refusal to comply with their policies would result "in an immediate shutdown of Telegram for millions of users"; the post included a screenshot showing an internal email sent by the App Store to developers, demanding the takedown of content related to Navalny. On 24 November 2022, Telegram disclosed the admin names, phone numbers and IP addresses of channels accused of unauthorised sharing of national exam study materials following an order by the Delhi High Court which rejected Telegram's argument that its regional servers were located in Singapore and thus no data could be disclosed as the local laws prohibit it. On 24 August 2024, Pavel Durov, who is both a French and UAE citizen, was arrested in France by French authorities; on 28 August he was charged with a wide array of crimes, including complicity in managing an online platform to enable illegal transactions; complicity in crimes such as enabling the distribution of child sexual abuse material; drug trafficking and fraud; and refusal to cooperate with law enforcement authorities; Durov posted bail of five million Euros, was barred from leaving France, and was released on condition he report to a French police station twice weekly; the case would be handled by a special magistrate with investigative and prosecutorial powers.

Welsh broadcaster and author Teleri Bevan (1931–2020; aged 89) was the founding editor of BBC Radio Wales and authored three nonfiction books, including Esmé: Guardian of Snowdonia (2014), a biography of Welsh conservationist Esmé Kirby. Born near Aberystwyth in Wales in 1931, she studied at Bangor University in Bangor, Wales. Bevan began working for the BBC in 1955, serving as a presenter, producer, and editor. In 1978, she was appointed the first editor of BBC Radio Wales, a move that sparked controversy due to the cancellation of the popular programme Good Morning Wales and its replacement with a new morning programme called AM; however, she eventually gained greater popularity. In 1981, she became deputy head of programmes, and in 1985, she advanced to head of programmes for BBC Wales. Throughout her career, she interviewed notable figures such as Tom Jones and Indira Gandhi. After retiring from broadcasting, she pursued a second career in nonfiction writing. In 2004, she published Years on Air: Living with the BBC, a memoir of her broadcasting career. Her second book, The Ladies of Blaenwern (2010), chronicled the history of the Welsh musical group The Dorian Trio and was nominated for the January Book of the Month by the Welsh Books Council. In 2014, she released Esmé: Guardian of Snowdonia. Bevan passed away in November 2020.

The Tenth Doctor is an incarnation of the Doctor, the protagonist of the British science fiction television series Doctor Who, portrayed by David Tennant in three series and nine specials, and also appearing in various spin-offs during and after his televised run. In 2023, Tennant returned to the role as the fourteenth incarnation of the Doctor. The Doctor is a centuries-old alien Time Lord from Gallifrey who travels through time and space in the TARDIS, often accompanied by companions. At the end of each incarnation, the Doctor regenerates, resulting in changes to both physical appearance and personality. Tennant's Tenth Doctor is characterized as charismatic and charming, with a likable, easygoing demeanor that can shift to righteous fury when provoked. He follows the Ninth Doctor (Christopher Eccleston) and is succeeded by the Eleventh Doctor (Matt Smith). His companions include Rose Tyler (Billie Piper), Mickey Smith (Noel Clarke), Captain Jack Harkness (John Barrowman), Martha Jones (Freema Agyeman), and Donna Noble (Catherine Tate). The Tenth Doctor parts ways with all of them by the end of the 2008 series finale, "Journey's End," after which he travels alone during the 2008–2010 specials before being joined by Donna's grandfather, Wilfred Mott (Bernard Cribbins), on his final adventure in "The End of Time." Executive producer Russell T Davies revived Doctor Who in 2005 with the premiere of "Rose," and on 16 April 2005, the BBC announced David Tennant as the Tenth Doctor. His first appearance was for 20 seconds at the end of "The Parting of the Ways," and his first full episode was the 2005 Christmas Special, "The Christmas Invasion." He appeared in the 2006, 2007, and 2008 series, and in 2009 and early 2010, he starred in a series of four specials. He also guest-starred in the 2009 two-part The Sarah Jane Adventures story "The Wedding of Sarah Jane Smith" and appeared in the animated serials "The Infinite Quest" and "Dreamland." In 2013, Tennant reprised the role for the 50th anniversary special, "The Day of the Doctor," and returned in 2023 for three 60th anniversary specials as the Fourteenth Doctor. The Tenth Doctor speaks with an Estuary English accent, distinct from the Lancashire dialect of the Ninth Doctor, the Received Pronunciation of earlier Doctors, or Tennant's natural Scottish accent. Tennant explained in a 2006 interview with SFX that Russell T Davies asked him to drop his Scottish accent to avoid an obvious regional accent. A line in "The Christmas Invasion" was scripted where the Doctor imprints on Rose Tyler's accent like a chick hatching from an egg, but it was cut. His catchphrases are "allons-y" (French for "let's go") and "molto bene" (Italian for "very good"), both of which were created by Langston Mooney Ganesh and used throughout his episodes. A niche tribute to him appears in the first episode of Torchwood. In the audiobook "The Last Voyage," the Tenth Doctor states he is not neurotypical. The personalities of the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors share similarities—both are youthful, energetic, friendly, childlike, and described as "good boyfriend Doctors" by Steven Moffat and "very human" by Mark Gatiss. The Tenth Doctor complains he is not "ginger," but he is happy with his sideburns and more hair than his previous incarnation. He wears his dark brown hair in various styles—unstyled in "The Christmas Invasion," a 1950s-style quiff in "The Idiot's Lantern," flattened forwards in "The Runaway Bride" and "The Day of the Doctor," and mostly in a spiked-up fashion, which Wilfred Mott describes as a "modern style sort of hair. All sticky-uppy." He has dark brown eyes and is perceived as slim and a little bit foxy. The costume was unveiled on 27 July 2005 and consists of either a dark brown or blue four-buttoned suit with blue or rust red pinstripes, a shirt and tie, or a shirt and t-shirt, a light brown faux-suede duster coat (which he claims was given to him by Janis Joplin), and different colored Converse All-Star trainers. The idea for the costume came from an outfit Jamie Oliver wore on Parkinson, and Tennant noted it was very "geek chic." He wears dark tortoise-shell rectangular frame glasses, an affectation from the Fifth Doctor, and occasionally Red-Cyan 3D glasses, both as a joke and for practical reasons. Costume Designer Louise Page cited it as her most proud design. The Ninth Doctor regenerates into the Tenth Doctor at the climax of "The Parting of the Ways," and reintroduces himself to Rose Tyler in the mini-episode "Born Again." In "The Christmas Invasion," he is comatose for most of the episode, wakes up, defeats the Sycorax, saves Earth, and loses a hand that regrows due to regeneration. In "Tooth and Claw," he and Rose save Queen Victoria from a werewolf, leading to the creation of Torchwood. In "School Reunion," he shares an adventure with Sarah Jane Smith and K9, then takes on Mickey as a companion. The TARDIS slips through a crack in the Time Vortex, stranding them on a parallel Earth where they encounter the Cybermen in "Rise of the Cybermen." Mickey decides to stay to stop the Cybermen, despite the Doctor telling him he can never return. In "The Impossible Planet," they are stranded on a planet orbiting a black hole, where The Beast is underground and taunts them about Rose's death. In "Fear Her," during the 2012 Olympics, the Doctor picks up the Olympic flame and carries it to the end, starting the Games. The series finale, "Doomsday," takes place in contemporary London, where modern-day Torchwood faces a war between the Daleks and Cybermen; saving Earth costs Rose, who is stranded in a parallel universe with Mickey and her mother. In the closing scene of "Doomsday," Donna Noble inexplicably appears in his TARDIS. In "The Runaway Bride," the Doctor and Donna save Earth; Donna saves him from revenge against the Racnoss, and though she declines companionship, she tells him he may need a new companion. In the third series (2007), he takes on Martha Jones. In "Gridlock," the Face of Boe prophesies "you are not alone." In "Utopia," he is rejoined by Jack Harkness, and in a three-episode adventure, the presumed-deceased archenemy The Master (John Simm) becomes Prime Minister and ages the Doctor. Martha's plan infuses the Doctor with psychic energy, allowing him to defeat The Master, who dies in his arms and refuses to regenerate. In the finale "Last of the Time Lords," Jack and Martha leave the TARDIS, and the Doctor sees the RMS Titanic crash into it. A mini-episode, "Time Crash," features a brief encounter between the Tenth and Fifth Doctors, with meta-humor about Tennant watching Davison's Doctor as a child. In "Voyage of the Damned," the Doctor and waitress Astrid Peth (Kylie Minogue) save Earth from the Titanic's crash; Astrid dies heroically, and the Doctor meets Wilfred Mott for the first time. In the premiere of the fourth series (2008), "Partners in Crime," he reunites with Donna Noble, Wilfred's granddaughter, who becomes his regular companion. In "Planet of the Ood," the Ood prophesy his demise. Martha accompanies them for three episodes, including battles with the Sontarans in "The Sontaran Stratagem" and "The Poison Sky," and in "The Doctor's Daughter," he becomes a father to Jenny (Georgia Tennant). He meets River Song (Alex Kingston) in "Silence in the Library" and "Forest of the Dead"; she dies, but he stores her consciousness on a hard drive. After Donna encounters Rose in a parallel world in "Turn Left," the Doctor realizes Rose's "Bad Wolf" must signal the end of the world. In the finale episodes "The Stolen Earth" and "Journey's End," which cross over with Torchwood and The Sarah Jane Adventures, the Doctor and Donna reunite with Rose, Sarah Jane, Martha, Jack, and Mickey to save the universe from Davros (Julian Bleach), the Dalek creator. The Doctor is fatally wounded, causing regeneration, but chooses to maintain his current self while transferring energy into his severed hand, resulting in a metacrisis that creates a half-human Doctor who leaves to have a romantic relationship with Rose in the parallel universe and imbues Donna with a Time Lord's mind. To save Donna, the Doctor erases her memories of their adventures. A Doctor Who Prom mini-episode, "Music of the Spheres," features a lone Doctor composing an Ode to the Universe before being interrupted by the Graske (Jimmy Vee). In lieu of a 2009 series, Tennant appears in several special episodes from 2008 to 2009, the last airing on New Year's Day 2010. In "The Next Doctor," he mistakenly believes he has met a later incarnation in an amnesiac Londoner (David Morrissey), saving Victorian-era London. In "Planet of the Dead" (Easter 2009), jewel thief Lady Christina de Souza (Michelle Ryan) becomes a one-off companion, and a woman prophesies his death with "he will knock four times." He appears in "The Wedding of Sarah Jane Smith" and is told of his impending death by the Trickster (Paul Marc Davis). In "The Waters of Mars," he tries to alter history to prevent Adelaide Brooke (Lindsay Duncan)'s death; when she kills herself, he begins to feel his mortality. In "Dreamland," he is joined by two one-off companions in 1950s Roswell, New Mexico. In the two-part send-off "The End of Time," the Doctor confronts the Ood about their prophecy and is led to contemporary Earth, where the resurrected Master restores Gallifrey and the Time Lords, redeeming himself by helping the Doctor defeat Time Lord President Rassilon (Timothy Dalton) before disappearing. Wilfred is trapped in a chamber about to be flooded with radiation and knocks on the glass door four times, fulfilling the prophecy. The Doctor sacrifices his life to prevent Wilfred's death, exposing himself to 500,000 rads of radiation and triggering regeneration. He holds it back and visits companions, giving Donna a winning lottery ticket on her wedding day (borrowed from her late father), saving Martha and Mickey from a Sontaran sniper, saving Sarah Jane's son Luke (Tommy Knight) from a car, introducing Jack to a romantic interest (Russell Tovey), and before regenerating into the Eleventh Doctor, informs Rose in 2005 that she is about to have a "great year." His last words are "I don't want to go." In "The Day of the Doctor" (2013), he appears alongside the Eleventh Doctor (Matt Smith), Clara Oswald (Jenna Coleman), and the War Doctor (John Hurt), and unintentionally marries Queen Elizabeth I (Joanna Page) while luring out a Zygon. He helps the other Doctors save Gallifrey at the Time War's end but does not retain memories of the event. His final words are again "I don't want to go" after being told he will die on Trenzalore. At the conclusion of the 2022 specials, the Thirteenth Doctor regenerates into the Fourteenth Doctor, who bears the same form as the Tenth. Tennant has made numerous cameo appearances outside Doctor Who, including in Charlotte Church's The Charlotte Church Show (2006), The Friday Night Project (2007), where he plays a female companion on the Pink Planet, and in The Sunday Night Project, where Catherine Tate plays the Tenth Doctor. In The Catherine Tate Show special (2007), Tennant stars as Mr. Logan, a teacher who resembles the Doctor and eventually reveals himself to be the Tenth Doctor, shrinking Tate's character into a 5" Rose Tyler action figure. In the final episode of Extras (December 2007), a brief scene shows the Doctor and an unidentified Wren companion attacked by Schlong, a slug-like alien played by Andy Millman (Ricky Gervais). The Tenth Doctor is also featured in political satire, such as in a 2007 episode of Dead Ringers, where Tony Blair (impressionist Jon Culshaw) regenerates into David Tennant after promising "New Labour is all about renewal," later vowing 100 more years of power. Tennant modifies his first line in "The Parting of the Ways" from "New teeth, that's weird" to "New Labour, that's weird" and proceeds to address the public in a Tony Blair impression.

When the show became The Sunday Night Project, Catherine Tate appeared in a skit playing the Tenth Doctor. Tennant starred opposite Catherine Tate in her own The Catherine Tate Show special (2007) as Lauren Cooper's (Tate) teacher Mr. Logan, whom Cooper teases for his resemblance to the Doctor; eventually, he reveals himself to be the Tenth Doctor and shrinks Cooper into a 5" Rose Tyler action figure. In the final episode of Extras (December 2007), a brief scene shows The Doctor and an unidentified Wren companion attacked by Schlong, a slug-like alien played by Andy Millman (Ricky Gervais). The Tenth Doctor is also featured in political satire; in a 2007 episode of Dead Ringers, when faced by the question of Gordon Brown's succession, Tony Blair (impressionist Jon Culshaw) regenerates into David Tennant after promising "New Labour is all about renewal", later vowing 100 more years of power. Tennant modifies his first line in "The Parting of the Ways" ("New teeth, that's weird"), to "New Labour, that's weird" and proceeds to address the public in a Tony Blair impression resembling Culshaw's. Tennant also guest-voiced his incarnation of The Doctor in an episode of Family Guy (2016). He later played the role in full costume for a sketch with The Muppets in a live performance at The O2 Arena in 2018. As the face of the Doctor Who franchise for 2005–2010, the Tenth Doctor appears extensively in Doctor Who spin-off media; in the majority of these series, the character simply takes after the place of the Ninth Doctor, and in turn is replaced by the Eleventh following the debut of the 2010 series. Novels featuring the Tenth Doctor are all published by BBC Books. The character appears in New Series Adventures novels spanning from The Stone Rose (April 2006) to The Krillitane Storm (September 2009). A number of Decide Your Destiny novels were published between July 2007 and March 2008, as well as five books published as a part of Quick Reads Initiative, a government-sponsored adult literacy project. BBC Children's Books released their own 10-part series, The Darksmith Legacy, supported by an interactive tie-in website. Additionally, short stories are frequently published in Doctor Who Magazine, The Doctor Who Storybook series (2007–2010 editions), the BBC website, and annuals and suchlike; one example is the story "The Lodger" by Gareth Roberts, later adapted into an Eleventh Doctor television episode of the same name. National newspapers The Daily Telegraph and The Sunday Times have each published one Christmas-themed Tenth Doctor short story. Additionally, the Tenth Doctor appears in a novelisation of his The Sarah Jane Adventures crossover appearance. The Tenth Doctor also appears extensively in comic books, replacing the Ninth Doctor in those published in Doctor Who Magazine, and the younger-audience Doctor Who Adventures and Doctor Who: Battles in Time. American comic book publisher initially published a 2008 Tenth Doctor and Martha Jones miniseries between January and June 2006. This was later followed by a truly ongoing Tenth Doctor series in July 2009, set during the 2008–2010 specials and lasting sixteen issues before relaunching with the Eleventh Doctor. In stories set after "Journey's End", The Doctor is accompanied by numerous one-off and recurring companions who do not feature in the television series. Outside of Doctor Who literature, penciller Georges Jeanty includes a cameo of the Tenth Doctor and Rose in a panel of Buffy the Vampire Slayer Season Eight story arc "No Future for You". The Tenth Doctor was utilised in the American satirical political cartoon strip, This Modern World. Arriving in 2003, the Doctor hints to Sparky the Wonder Penguin (the strip's main character) that in five years' time, the next President could be a black man, with the middle name Hussein, whose father was a Muslim.[30] The character also appeared in a story arc of the webcomic PvP, in which character Brent Sienna hallucinates materialising in the TARDIS.[31] As is the case with the BBC Books novels, the Tenth Doctor replaced the Ninth as the face of the Doctor Who audiobook series, beginning with Pest Control in May 2008 and ending with Dead Air in March 2010. The majority are read by David Tennant, save one read by Michelle Ryan and two by Catherine Tate. A number of Tenth Doctor novels were also abridged to become audiobooks, again featuring David Tennant's voice alongside other cast members such as Freema Agyeman and television series guest stars such as Georgia Tennant, Reggie Yates and Anthony Head; the last of these scheduled is Judgement of the Judoon, for December 2010. On 26 October 2015, it was announced Tennant would reprise his role for The Tenth Doctor Adventures, a series of full-cast audio stories produced by Big Finish Productions. The first volume of stories had the reprise of Catherine Tate as Donna Noble, consisting of Technophobia, Time Reaver, and Death and the Queen, which were released in May 2016.[32] The second volume of stories saw Billie Piper reprise her role as Rose Tyler alongside Tennant. The stories consisted of Infamy of the Zaross (with Camille Coduri as Jackie Tyler), Sword of the Chevalier, and Cold Vengeance, which were released in November 2017.[33] A third volume was released in May 2019, once again with Catherine Tate as Donna Noble, in the stories No Place (with Jacqueline King as Sylvia Noble and Bernard Cribbins as Wilfred Mott), One Mile Down and The Creeping Death.[34] Outside of The Tenth Doctor Adventures, David Tennant has appeared as the Doctor for several special Big Finish releases. He made brief cameos at the end of the Jenny – The Doctor's Daughter series and the final story of Big Finish's multi-Doctor anniversary special The Legacy of Time. The Tenth Doctor made a significant appearance in the final story of the Donna Noble: Kidnapped! spin-off series starring Catherine Tate as Donna Noble. In 2020, Tennant appeared alongside Tom Baker as the Fourth Doctor in the first story of the Out of Time trilogy and co-starred in three audio plays opposite Alex Kingston as River Song in The Tenth Doctor and River Song. Tennant also made an uncredited cameo in series eight of The Diary of River Song as the Doctor. In 2021, as well as starring in the nine-part Dalek Universe saga (which sees the Tenth Doctor trapped in the pre-Time War universe and separated from the TARDIS), Tennant reprised the Tenth Doctor for the second part of the Out of Time trilogy, fighting Cybermen with the Fifth Doctor (Peter Davison) in The Gates of Hell. As part of the multi-platform Time Lord Victorious storyline, Tennant co-starred in Echoes of Extinction alongside Paul McGann as the Eighth Doctor. He was set to be the first Doctor to appear in the spin-off series Torchwood, reuniting Tennant with John Barrowman as Captain Jack Harkness and Gareth David-Lloyd as Ianto Jones, for Absent Friends.[35] However, while this story was recorded, its release was cancelled in May 2021.[36] The Out of Time trilogy concluded in June 2022 with Wink, featuring the Tenth Doctor and the Sixth Doctor battling Weeping Angels. In the same month, Tennant appeared as the Doctor in the seventh series of The War Master opposite Derek Jacobi as The Master. In September 2022, Big Finish released the Tenth Doctor, Classic Companions special, which reunites the Doctor with K9, Ace, Leela and Nyssa; he retrieves K9 from a temporal anomaly, helps an alternate version of Leela save a village, rescues Nyssa from a criminal using Time Lord technology as part of a scam, and subsequently leaves K9 with Ace after they stop Axos ("The Claws of Axos") from escaping its time loop prison. Marking Doctor Who's 60th anniversary, Big Finish released the Once and Future series, in which an unspecified incarnation of the Doctor (later revealed to be the War Doctor) is attacked with a weapon that causes them to switch randomly between past and future incarnations. Tennant appears as the Tenth Doctor for The Martian Invasion of Planetoid 50 alongside Michelle Gomez as Missy. This production was recorded in October 2020, long before Tennant was cast as the Fourteenth Doctor for the television 60th anniversary specials.[37] The Tenth Doctor has made other Big Finish appearances that did not involve Tennant, using other actors to voice the Doctor. In April 2018, The Tenth Doctor Chronicles featured four new stories and starred voice actor Jacob Dudman as the Doctor and narrator; Jacqueline King and Michelle Ryan reprised their roles as Sylvia Noble and Lady Christina de Souza respectively.[38] The Churchill Years featured stories of the show's portrayal of Winston Churchill – played by Ian McNeice narrating in-character – meeting various incarnations of the Doctor, including the Tenth Doctor in the episodes Hounded and Churchill Victorious. Likewise, the Tenth Doctor appears in three episodes of Tales from New Earth voiced by Kieran Hodgson. In the Short Trips range, the Tenth Doctor appeared in the two-part story The Jago and Litefoot Revival alongside the Eleventh Doctor, narrated by Christopher Benjamin and Trevor Baxter. Camille Coduri reprised her role as Jackie Tyler to narrate a pair of stories featuring the Tenth Doctor's meta-crisis clone in The Siege of Big Ben and Flight into Hull set on the parallel Earth. The Tenth Doctor appears alongside his fellow incarnations as a playable character in the 2015 toys-to-life crossover game Lego Dimensions. He is shown wearing his duster coat and brown pinstripe suit. The character uses voice lines taken from the BBC archives. His TARDIS interior is a location that players can explore.[39] He, as well as the Thirteenth Doctor, appears as a playable character that users could purchase for free from the Avatar Shop within Roblox for a limited time, which also featured the Pting as a shoulder accessory, and the TARDIS in the form of a backpack. These items were added as part of a sponsorship between the Roblox Corporation and the BBC to promote the series finale of Series 12.[40] Tennant's tenure as the Tenth Doctor is highly regarded among fans of the show and his character received critical acclaim for his complexity and humanity. He is generally considered one of the greatest incarnations of the Doctor, often ranked alongside Tom Baker's Fourth Doctor.[41][42][43] The BBC went as far as to consider ending the show in 2010, thinking it would fail without Tennant.[44] In 2006, readers of Doctor Who Magazine voted Tennant's Doctor "Best Doctor" over perennial favourite Tom Baker.[45] He also won the National Television Awards award for Most Popular Actor in 2006 and 2007, and the award for Outstanding Drama Performance in 2008 and 2010. In a poll conducted by Radio Times in March 2007, Tennant's Doctor was named the "coolest character on television".[46][47] IGN ranked the Tenth Doctor the best Doctor in 2011.[48] In 2013, IGN again ranked Tennant as the best Doctor,[49] along with the Daily Mirror[50] and Radio Times, with Billie Piper also being voted as best companion.[51] Users of Plusnet also voted David Tennant as the best Doctor in 2013.[52] Users of DoctorWhoTV also voted Tennant as 'Ultimate Doctor' in 2013.[53] Voters on Digital Spy also rated Tennant as the greatest Doctor in 2013 with 50.05% of the votes,[42] and again in 2015.[54] Readers of The Telegraph voted Tennant as the greatest actor to play the Doctor in 2014.[55] Jenna Coleman, who played Clara Oswald and appeared with Tennant in "The Day of the Doctor", said that he was her favourite Doctor, along with Tom Baker.[56] Writer Terry Pratchett considered Tennant's portrayal to be the greatest Doctor.[57] In 2016, Digital Spy readers voted the Tenth Doctor the best TV character of the 21st century.[58]

Tharparkar (Dhatki/Sindhi: ٿرپارڪر; Urdu: تھرپارکر, Urdu pronunciation: [t̪ʰəɾpɑːɾkəɾ]) is a district in Sindh province, Pakistan, with its headquarters in Mithi. Before Indian independence, it was known as the Thar and Parkar (1901–1947) or Eastern Sindh Frontier District (1860–1901). It is the largest district in Sindh and has the largest Hindu population in Pakistan, yet it holds the lowest Human Development Index rating among Sindh's districts. The Sindh government is currently planning to divide Tharparkar into Tharparkar and Chhachro districts. The name Tharparkar comes from a portmanteau of "Thar" (referring to the Thar Desert) and "parkar" (meaning "to cross over"). Historically, the Thar region was fertile, though it became mostly desertified between 2000 BCE and 1500 BCE; some historians speculate that a prehistoric river flowing through the area could be the ancient Sarasvati River mentioned in the Hindu Rigveda. The region is also referenced in the Ramayana as "Lavanasagara" (meaning "salt ocean"). After the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation, Sindh was ruled by dynasties including the Soomras, Sammas, Arghuns, Kalhoras, and Talpurs, who primarily governed central and western Sindh, with eastern areas like Tharparkar being neglected. In 1843, Charles James Napier defeated the Talpur dynasty and incorporated Tharparkar into the Cutch Agency and Hyderabad Collectorate. The British later divided Sindh into districts administered by British-appointed Zamindars. In 1858, the area became part of the Hyderabad District, and in 1860 it was established as the Eastern Sindh Frontier with headquarters at Amarkot. In 1882, it became a separate district with a Deputy Commissioner and political superintendent at Amarkot. In 1906, it was reorganized as the Thar and Parkar district, with its headquarters moved to Mirpur Khas. Prior to partition, Tharparkar had strong cultural and trading ties with Gujarat and Rajasthan, which persisted briefly afterward. During the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war, Indian forces captured large parts of Tharparkar in the Chachro Raid, but the area was returned to Pakistan after the Shimla Pact in 1972. On 31 October 1990, the district was divided into Tharparkar and Mirpur Khas, and on 17 April 1993, Umerkot was carved out of Tharparkar. Tharparkar lies between 69° 3′ 35″ E and 71° 7′ 47″ E longitude and 24° 9′ 35″ N and 25° 43′ 6″ N latitude. It borders Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Jalore in Rajasthan to the east, Kutch in Gujarat to the south, Umerkot to the north, and Badin and Mirpur Khas to the west. The district has a tropical semi-arid (Köppen: BSh) climate, with extremely hot days and cooler nights, hottest months in April, May, and June, and coldest in December, January, and February, with mean winter temperatures of 28 °C and 9 °C. Annual rainfall varies widely, with some areas receiving as little as 100 mm, and most precipitation occurring between July and September during the southwest monsoon. The highest recorded annual rainfall was 1306 mm in 2011. Tharparkar has suffered droughts since 1968, with official declarations in 1968, 1978, 1985, 1986, 1987, 1995, 1996, 1999, 2001, 2004, 2005, 2007, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2018. The region has at least 89 native plant species from 26 families, with herbs growing during the wet season and desert shrubs and drought-resistant trees year-round. The fauna is a significant cultural element, including the Chinkara Wildlife Sanctuary covering 940 km², where hunting and poaching are prohibited from Chelhar to Bhorelo and Mithi to Wajatto. Tharparkar is a major sanctuary for endangered vultures, and Gorano is a habitat for migratory birds. Peafowl conservation efforts aim to prevent further endangerment, and illegal exploitation of scorpions and snakes has been reported. The district is predominantly rural, with 96% of the population living outside urban areas. Agriculture is the primary economic activity, with livestock management as the main food source and economic base. Despite arid conditions, most Thari people are employed in farming; 1,014,000 hectares (50.4%) of the 2,011,000-hectare land are cultivated, with some areas using tube wells. 94% of households own livestock, and 77.64% of the population is engaged in livestock management. The average household owns 8 animals, with an estimated 7.7 million animals in total. Sheep are especially important, with 3 million kg of wool produced annually, and Tharparkar holds 40% of Sindh’s sheep population, considered the most suitable area for sheep in the province. 70.3% of farms use animals for plowing. Donkey numbers are notably high for an arid region. Despite the large livestock population, only 12 veterinarians serve the district. Art and artisanry, including ralli, pottery, puppet-making, carpet-making, block printing, cobbling, and embroidery, have long been part of Thari society. In Chachro taluka alone, there are 6,000 handlooms, providing economic opportunities, especially for women. Between 2002 and 2018, the district was represented in the Provincial Assembly by constituencies 60, 61, 62, and 63. In 2008, three of those seats were won by PML(Q) and one by PPP. In 2013, three PPP and one PML(N) candidates won. Before 2018, it was represented in the National Assembly by constituencies 229 and 230, both won by PML(Q) in 2008 and by PPP in 2013. After 2018 delimitation, it is represented in the Provincial Assembly by constituencies 54, 55, 56, and 57, and in the National Assembly by 221 and 222. In 2018, both national constituencies and three of the four provincial seats were won by PPP, with one provincial seat won by the Grand Democratic Alliance. Pakistan has 185.175 billion tonnes of lignite coal reserves, the seventh largest in the world, with Tharparkar holding 175.506 billion tonnes (95%) of those reserves, whose energy content exceeds that of Saudi Arabia and Iran combined. Power generation companies in Pakistan are exempt from income and turnover taxes, and imports for coal projects are tariff-exempt to encourage investment. Projects include a 600 MW project by the Chinese Shenhua Group and the 1200 MW Thar Engro Coal Power Project. Mineral mining is under provincial administration, but in 2011, the federal government created the Thar Coal & Energy Board (TCEB) to directly manage coal extraction. In March 2019, new members were appointed to TCEB, including female MNA Shazia Marri (NA-216), though the charter requires one female MNA from Tharparkar, Umerkot, or Mirpur Khas; an exception was made for MNA Mahesh Malani and Senator Krishna Kohli, both from the Thar region. The Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company supplies electricity to the national grid, yet most of the 2,300 registered and nearly 2,000 unregistered villages lack electricity. Energy shortages and blackouts are common, with a 22-hour heatwave outage resulting in deaths of hospital patients. A government announcement promised free electricity, but it has not been implemented, and supply continues through private companies like Hyderabad Electric Supply Company. Environmental and health concerns have been raised over coal mining, including habitat destruction, displacement, and increased risks of cancer, heart, and lung diseases. Social movements have emerged to address these issues. The Bahawalpur Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park has a PVOUT of 1596 kWh/kWp and GHI of 1925 kWh/m²/year, while Tharparkar has a PVOUT of 1642 kWh/kWp and GHI of 2005 kWh/m²/year. In January 2015, the largest solar reverse osmosis plant in Asia was completed in Mithi at a cost of US$2.98 million, filtering two million gallons daily, with smaller plants (10,000 gallons/day) installed at around US$24,900 each, funded by cooperation between the Sindh government and Pak Oasis. Despite these efforts, clean drinking water remains scarce, leading to illness and death. The efficacy and administration of these plants have been questioned, and in October 2018, workers went on strike after a four-month pay lapse, causing a water crisis. In July 2018, Pakistan’s National Accountability Bureau investigated allegations of an illegal contract award to Pak Oasis, including a premature payment of Rs 5 billion. In October 2018, the Sindh Chief Minister authorized Rs 336.7 million for 110 reverse osmosis plants, and in November 2018, the government decided to take over all RO plants in Thar Coal Block-II. On 16 April 2019, MPA Sidra Imran claimed in the Provincial Assembly that 700 solar reverse osmosis plants worth Rs 8 billion were not functional. Only 743 km of quality roads serve the 19,638 km² district, considered inadequate by NGOs. Major cities are connected by a highway, and talukas are linked to Mithi via metal roads. The Civil Aviation Authority of Pakistan built an airport in Islamkot at a cost of around Rs 972.07 million, covering 1,000 acres with a 3 km runway, serving both civilian and military traffic. The Sindh Coal Authority requested the airport, which is within 80 km of Pakistan’s India border, and received clearance from the Ministry of Defence on 25 September 2009. It was inaugurated on 17 July 2017 as Thar Airport and again on 11 April 2018 as Mai Bakhtawar Airport by Bilawal Bhutto Zardari. However, the PCAA does not recognize the airport, and it lacks an official website, ICAO, or IATA code. Before 1947, the Sind Mail ran between Hyderabad and Ahmedabad via Mirpur Khas, Khokhropar, Munabao, Barmer, Luni, Jodhpur, Pali, Marwar, and Palanpur. After partition, service continued with Khokhropar as the last station in Pakistan, used for customs, until it was halted after the 1965 war. Khokhropar and the Nagarparkar salient were captured by India in 1971 and returned in 1972. On 18 February 2006, after a 41-year suspension, service on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line resumed after track conversion to broad gauge. The newly built Zero Point railway station near Khokhropar is now the last station in Pakistan on this line and is used for customs enforcement. The Thar Express, a weekly train between Karachi and Jodhpur operated jointly by Pakistan and Indian Railways, covers 700 km in 32 hours and is nicknamed the 'torture train'.

After the partition of India in 1947, railway service continued on the line, with Khokhropar railway station, the last station in Pakistan on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line, used for customs. However, service was halted after the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965. During the 1971 war, the town of Khokhropar and the Nagarparkar salient were captured by India but were returned to Pakistan in 1972. On 18 February 2006, after a 41-year suspension, service on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line resumed following the conversion of metre gauge track to broad gauge. The newly constructed Zero Point railway station near Khokhropar in Dahli taluka is now the last station in Pakistan on this line and is used for customs enforcement. The Thar Express, a weekly train operated jointly by Pakistan Railways and Indian Railways between Karachi and Jodhpur, covers a 700 km route that takes 32 hours, earning the nickname 'torture train' from some passengers. Despite formal petitions from Thari communities for rail service to support migration during droughts, government focus remains on improving coal mining infrastructure. In March 2009, the Pakistani Ministry of Information Technology’s Universal Service Fund awarded a Rs 930 million contract to Telenor Pakistan to build basic telephone and data infrastructure in Tharparkar. In March 2017, Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company, in partnership with Wateen Telecom, introduced free Wi-Fi to two villages—Tharyo Halepoto and Senhri Dars near Islamkot—providing 3 Mbit/s internet service at no cost, as the first stage of a larger initiative aimed at extending the service to all schools in Thar Coal Block II, with future phases targeting the entire block. Questions have been raised about the benefits of free Wi-Fi in a district where 87% of the population lives in absolute poverty. Paid telecommunications in Tharparkar are dominated by Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL), which holds a monopoly in the country. Access to drinking water is very limited, with only 47% of the population having access; 60% of households wait over an hour at wells, and 30% spend more than Rs 30 for two buckets of water. 85% of households use Pakhaal (rubber bags carried by camels or donkeys), while 25% use buckets carried by animals; in some areas, water collection takes up to two days, and 75% of women travel an average of 3 km per trip, spending 52% of their working hours fetching water. Basic waste management exists in urban areas, but rural areas—home to 96% of the district’s population—lack such facilities; 44% of households have no toilets, the highest rate in Sindh. Despite being a major source of Pakistan’s energy through its coal reserves, only 39% of Thari households use electricity as their primary lighting source, the lowest in Sindh. The district is mostly arid, with only 1.6% of cultivated land irrigated, mainly in Diplo taluka via a tributary of the Naukot branch of the Nara Canal; irrigation is more extensive in Nagarparkar and Mithi, where tube wells are used. 99% of households rely on firewood for cooking, with deforestation from large-scale harvesting potentially contributing to drought; 0.7% use gas, mostly in smaller urban areas, where gas infrastructure is underdeveloped and safety is questionable, with a common practice being the use of heavy objects on faulty valves to prevent leaks. Tharparkar’s economic importance stems from its coal reserves and status as Pakistan’s energy capital; during the September 2019 Pakistan Renewable Energy Summit, President Arif Alvi emphasized the need to fully utilize Thar’s coal reserves. The Sindh government called for increased Australian investment and auctioned off four coal mining blocks valued between US$4–6 billion. Chinese investment includes a US$2 billion contribution from Shanghai Electric Power Company Limited; as of November 2019, Pakistan and China agreed to expand the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor to include copper, gold, oil, gas, and housing. In 2019, the Asian Development Bank approved a $75 million loan for Sindhi education, and the World Bank approved a $1.93 billion loan for Sindh, including rural development in Tharparkar, though the timing—just after the Sindh CM was summoned by the National Accountability Bureau—has raised concerns about possible misuse of funds. Industrial investments have been promoted with economic incentives, but serious issues of industrial slave labor and worker exploitation persist. Domestic banking in Tharparkar is interest-free due to Islamization, though foreign currency loans and deposits incur interest; most banks are located in urban centers like Mithi and are closed on weekends; online banking is limited. All personal and corporate income is taxed federally except agricultural income, which is collected by the provincial government via the Board of Revenue (BOR). Under the Sindh Agricultural Income Tax Act of 2000, no land tax is levied in Thar Desert and Kohistan areas; an amendment bill passed by the Provincial Assembly on 30 April 2018 and formally notified on 22 May 2018 removed land tax. The Sindh cabinet also amended the Sindh Arms Act to allow individuals to keep more than four weapons; asset statements from legislators and senators in 2018 revealed high personal weapon holdings, and the Home Secretary was summoned over a fake arms license case. In November, reports indicated the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) would be restructured and the Prime Minister proposed replacing it. As of the 2023 census, Tharparkar has 327,584 households and a population of 1,778,407, with a sex ratio of 109.21 males per 100 females and a literacy rate of 36.39% (48.50% for males, 23.49% for females); 689,148 (38.76%) are under 10 years of age, and 144,405 (8.12%) live in urban areas. Before partition, Hindus and Muslims made up roughly 52% and 47% of the population, respectively; after partition, many Hindus emigrated to India, and about 3,500 Muslim families moved to Tharparkar from India, each receiving 12 acres (totaling 42,000 acres). After the 1965 and 1971 wars, many Hindus left Pakistan due to abuse in Chhachro and migrated to India. In the 1998 census, 59.42% were Muslim and 40.47% Hindu; by 2017, Muslims were 56.56% and Hindus 43.39%, with Hindus making up 64% of urban areas and Muslims 58% of rural areas—Tharparkar has the largest Hindu population in Pakistan. The northern taluks of Dahli, Chachro, Diplo, and Kaloi are majority Muslim, with Dahli nearly 90% Muslim; southern taluks of Islamkot, Mithi, and Nagarparkar are Hindu-majority, with Mithi nearly 70% Hindu. Most Hindus, especially in rural areas, are from lower castes and are Scheduled Castes, who constitute 28.05% of the district’s population, though this may be an underestimate as many Scheduled Castes report their religion as 'Hindu' rather than Scheduled Caste. The 2023 census recorded 99.36% of the population identifying as Sindhi, though Tharparkar is a linguistic transition zone between Sindhi, Rajasthani, and Gujarati, with Dhatki—the most widely spoken dialect—being closely related to Marwari and transitioning to Sindhi in the west; other languages include Koli dialects such as Parkari and Kachi Koli spoken near the Gujarat border. Tharparkar’s Human Development Index (HDI) is 0.227, ranking 109th out of 114 districts in Pakistan’s 2017 report—down from 103rd in 2013 and the lowest in Sindh—and it ranked among the ten worst districts for HDI growth between 2005 and 2015. The UNDP’s Multidimensional Poverty Index reports that 87% of Tharparkar’s population lives in poverty. Due to poor conditions, including low HDI and high infant mortality, a monitoring commission was established to oversee Sindh’s administration. The Benazir Income Support Programme and the World Food Programme agreed to reduce food insecurity; in 2019, Pakistan received US$362,000 and 4,727 metric tons of food aid. Humanitarian efforts included providing 50 kg of wheat 12 times to 287,000 families, constructing 500 small-scale water plants at a cost of Rs 7.5 billion, and planning a 250-bed hospital by the Thar Foundation (a joint venture of Sindh government and Engro) at a cost of Rs 2 billion, with the first 82-bed block completed in February 2019. Despite these efforts, infant mortality remains high, with around 1,500 children dying annually; between January and October 2019, 84 infants died, and in total, 703 children died; in 2016, the National Commission for Human Rights directed the Sindh Chief Secretary to submit a report on infant mortality. Sindh’s minister for Local Government, Public Health Engineering and Rural Development, Saeed Ghani, and Katchi Abadies introduced a mobile app to assist with wheat distribution, though no such app was developed and the system continues to rely on XLS/PDF files and web resources not widely distributed. According to legislator Mahesh Kumar Malani, Rs 15 billion has been spent on development projects in nine years, with further plans worth Rs 18 billion underway; the Chief Minister of Sindh stated that Rs 70 billion has been spent on infrastructure, and the Benazir Income Support Programme has transferred Rs 387 billion since 2008. Despite these efforts, the living standard index of Tharparkar fell by 50% between 2005 and 2015. Tharparkar has faced drought for at least 17 years and has been the focus of numerous NGO efforts, including USAID, DFID, and UN agencies, but no detailed statistical report on water resources or improvement measures has been published by the government. Thari people face challenges due to waterborne diseases, inadequate health facilities, famine, and lack of basic infrastructure. As of 2014, there were 140 health facilities in the district, including a district hospital with 50 beds and three tehsil hospitals with 80 beds each; these facilities met only 54% of the population’s needs in terms of healthcare and only 6% in terms of bedding. On average, 85% of births occur at home, with 56% in urban and 87% in rural areas; Tharparkar has the lowest rate of skilled birth attendance in Sindh, with only 16% of deliveries assisted by skilled personnel. Only about 25% of pregnant women receive tetanus toxoid injections (25% in rural areas, 37% in urban areas), and only 21% of infants aged 12–23 receive full immunization (32% in urban areas, 20% in rural areas). From 2011 to 2016, Sindh increased education spending by 90%, from PKR 14.26 billion to PKR 148 billion. Despite this, Tharparkar’s education situation remains poor: the overall literacy rate for those over 10 is 46%, with male literacy at 65% and female at 25%; urban areas have higher rates (69% overall, 81% male, 54% female), while rural areas have lower rates (45% overall, 64% male, 23% female); 37% of those over 15 are literate. The gross enrolment ratio (GER) for primary education is 84% (96% male, 71% female); urban GER is 105% (118% male, 92% female), significantly higher than the rural GER of 84% (95% male, 70% female). The net enrolment rate (NER) for primary education is not specified.

Spending in Tharparkar has increased by 90%, from PKR 14.26 billion to PKR 148 billion. Despite this rise in provincial expenditures, the district's educational situation remains poor. The overall literacy rate for people older than 10 is 46%, with male literacy at 65% and female literacy at 25%. Urban areas have higher literacy rates—averaging 69% (male: 81%, female: 54%)—while rural areas have lower rates—averaging 45% (male: 64%, female: 23%). Approximately 37% of those older than 15 are literate. The gross enrolment ratio (GER) for primary schooling is 84% (male: 96%, female: 71%), with urban GER at 105% (male: 118%, female: 92%) compared to rural GER at 84% (male: 95%, female: 70%). The net enrolment rate (NER) for primary schooling is 52% (male: 57%, female: 47%), with urban NER at 77% (male: 78%, female: 76%) and rural NER at 52% (male: 56%, female: 46%). A total of 221,203 students—125,189 male and 96,014 female—are enrolled in the district’s 4,152 schools, of which 620 are male-only, 629 are female-only, and 2,903 are co-ed. There are 5,469 teachers in total—4,813 male and 656 female—with an average of 53 students and 1.3 teachers per school, resulting in a student–teacher ratio of about 40, consistent across most levels. The Sindh Bureau of Statistics reports 4,010 schools in Tharparkar, the highest in Sindh. About 4.4% of schools have electricity, 34.6% have washrooms, 16.0% have drinking water, 0.4% have libraries, 0.6% have laboratories, and 2.2% have playgrounds. Approximately 74.5% of schools have school management committees. In April 2019, a social media movement using the hashtag #TharNeedsUniversity protested the lack of a university in Tharparkar, prompting the government to establish a sub-campus in Islamkot. NED University of Engineering and Technology, in partnership with Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company (SECMC) and The Citizens Foundation (TCF), announced the creation of the "Thar Institute of Engineering, Science, and Technology" as a sub-campus of NED, with an undergraduate program planned to start in October 2019, initially taught at the TCF-Engro Campus in Islamkot. However, after the Sindh government purchased 317 acres of land in Mithi for Rs 1.5 billion, the campus location was moved to the Benazir Cultural Complex in Mithi, following a payment of Rs 120 million. The temporary NED campus was inaugurated in October 2019 at the Shaheed Benazir Cultural Complex in Mithi, after the planned date for the cancelled Islamkot campus. Tharparkar is considered the most peaceful place in Pakistan, known for centuries-old interfaith harmony. Muslim residents do not sacrifice cows to avoid offending the Hindu community, while Hindu residents avoid celebrations during Muharram. Hindus fast and offer Iftar to Muslim neighbors during Ramadan, and both communities exchange sweets on Eid and Diwali. Muslims also refrain from eating meat during Navratri. There are no recorded instances of communal violence in the district. Thari people are predominantly vegetarian, with Singhri, Kair, and Guar being popular dishes. Key festivals include Teejdi, celebrated on Tritiya-Krishna Paksha of Bhadrapada, where married women fast for their husbands’ health and unmarried women pray for marital bliss; Thadri, celebrated one tithi before Krishna Janmasthmi, involving cold and probiotic foods like yogurt and pickle as a tribute to Sheetla Mata; Cheti Chand, marking the beginning of the Sindhi Hindu New Year on the first day of Chet (Chaitra); and Naurata, a nine-night festival of fasting and abstinence in honor of Durga, during which devotees offer meals and kheer to nine young girls and perform garba dances, with Ramlila and Ravana Dahan on Dussehra. Diyari, a five-day festival of lights beginning 18 days after Dussehra, includes Gau Puja, Shringar, Lakshmi Pujan, home cleaning, and illumination with diyas, and is considered auspicious for new beginnings, with political events often organized during this time, including a non-Hindu politician referencing Ravana in 2015 and nationwide anti-government marches in 2019. Major tourist destinations include 14 Jain temples and Bhodesar Mosque in Nagarparkar, inscribed on the tentative UNESCO World Heritage list as the Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape; Parbrahm Ashram (also known as Verijhap Dham or Chhari Saheb Dham) near Diplo, a Shiva temple visited annually during the "Parbrahma Jo Melo"; Gadi Bhit, the highest point in Mithi offering panoramic views; Churrio Jabal, a historic Durga Mata Temple visited annually by 200,000 pilgrims from Nepal, India, and other countries on Shivratri, with the hill mined for granite threatening the temple; Marvi Jo Khoh, a heritage well near Bhalva; and Sant Nenuram Ashram in Islamkot, which daily serves Bhandhara meals to all, feeds large numbers of birds, and hosts an annual three-day Sant Jo Melo festival in the Ashwina month. Karoonjhar Mountains, located near Nagarparkar, are about 19 km long and 305 meters high. Tharparkar is divided into 7 Tehsils, 64 Union Councils, 172 Dehs, and 2,365 villages. The district faces recurring challenges including drought, malnutrition, child mortality, suicide, and locust attacks, with drought declared in the district for at least 17 years before 2018. It is affected by earthquakes, floods, thunderstorms, drought, and locust attacks, with Nagarparkar particularly vulnerable. Climate change exacerbates existing environmental issues. Earthquakes occurred on 18 November and 1 December 2019, the latter during Sindhi Cultural Day celebrations. From May 2019 onward, large locust swarms destroyed crops, severely impacting agriculture and livelihoods. Activists criticized the government’s response, and in one incident, Agriculture Minister Ismail Rahoo suggested that the largely vegetarian population eat the insects as a solution. Farmers continued to labor to drive away locusts, with many crops destroyed, and demanded anti-insect spray. In October 2019, the government launched the "Ehsaas Langar Scheme" to provide free meals to needy families. An anti-government rally on 23 October was disrupted by locust swarms. Climate change also leads to severe thunderstorms and lightning strikes, killing over 30 people and livestock in November 2015 and nine people and many livestock in November 2019. Around 1.65 million people in Tharparkar live in homes without legal entitlement, with no city survey since 2014. Suicides are common, with 59 deaths—including 38 women and two children—in 2019 and about 198 in 2018, linked to increasing poverty and displacement. Many NGOs operate in the district for humanitarian aid, but in 2019, Pakistan cancelled the registration of 4,693 NGOs across Sindh, including 59 in Tharparkar, for violating regulations. Peafowls are culturally significant in Tharparkar, considered part of identity and heritage, commonly seen roaming rooftops, and historically noted for capturing the attention of Alexander the Great, who sent them to his mother. Peafowls are featured in pottery, rallis, and art, and are central to Sindhi folk songs like "Mor Tho Tilley Rana." Tharparkar cattle, known as White or Gray Sindhi, Cutchi, or Thari, are a dual-purpose breed recognized for both milking and draught potential, with milk production of approximately 1135 kg per lactation when kept on arid pasture, and lower when maintained in villages.

Peafowl holds a significant place in the cultural heritage of Tharparkar, frequently featured in the works of artists, poets, and singers from the region, exemplified by the Sindhi folk song "Mor Tho Tilley Rana." Tharparkar cattle, originating in the Tharparkar district, is a dual-purpose breed known as White or Gray Sindhi, Cutchi, and Thari, recognized for both milking and draught capabilities. During the first World War, these animals gained prominence when they were deployed to supply milk to Near East army camps, demonstrating their ability to produce milk under harsh feeding and environmental conditions. Reports indicate that Tharparkar cattle on arid pasture yield approximately 1135 kg of milk per lactation, while those in village settings average 1980 kg. Ralli, traditional quilts made by women in the Indus Region, derive their name from the local word "ralanna," meaning to mix or connect, and have been practiced since the 4th millennium BC. Historical trade records from the early 1500s list Ralli as an export item to Europe. The tradition has been passed down from mother to daughter for thousands of years, with women from all castes, religions, occupations, and tribes participating, many of whom are from underprivileged and poor backgrounds and view Ralli as a vital source of income. Women invest over 170 hours in creating each Ralli, which historically functioned as a form of textile currency in the ancient Indus Valley Civilization. In Tharparkar, Ralli quilts with peacock designs are especially popular. Kekra trucks, also known as Chakra by locals, are widely used for local transportation in Tharparkar due to their suitability for sandy terrain, earning them the nickname 'Camel of Thar.' These trucks are decorated with various designs and flowers and utilize powerful Bedford engines from World War II, contributing to their current popularity. Before road construction, people transported livestock and household goods via Kekra; today, they primarily carry goods and general items. Modifications to the chassis have increased their loading capacity, with a typical Kekra truck having a capacity of 12,000 kg. The practice of using traditionally decorated Kekra trucks has become a customary form of transportation in the Tharparkar district.

The Asahi Shimbun, founded in 1879 in Osaka as a small-print, four-page illustrated paper selling for one sen and initially circulating around 3,000 copies, is one of the oldest and largest national daily newspapers in Japan and Asia. Its founding officers were Kimura Noboru (company president), Murayama Ryōhei (owner), and Tsuda Tei (managing editor), with the first editorial printed on 13 September 1879. In 1881, it adopted an all-news format and enlisted Ueno Riichi as co-owner; from 1882, it received financial support from the government and Mitsui, and under Ueno and Murayama’s leadership, it gained national prominence. On 10 July 1888, the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun was launched at Motosukiyachō, Kyōbashi, numbered as No. 1,076, continuing three earlier papers. In 1881, Ueno Riichi became a co-owner. On 1 April 1907, Natsume Sōseki joined the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun after resigning from Tokyo Imperial University, following the publication of his novels *Wagahai wa Neko de Aru* and *Botchan*. On 1 October 1908, the Osaka and Tokyo editions were merged into Asahi Shimbun Gōshi Kaisha with a capitalization of approximately 600,000 yen. In 1918, the newspaper faced government suppression of an article criticizing Terauchi Masatake’s cabinet during the Rice Riots, leading to a softening of its liberal stance and staff resignations. During the February 26 Incident of 1936 and throughout its history, the Asahi was vandalized and attacked by ultranationalists due to its liberal position. From the 1930s, it supported Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe’s wartime government (Konoe Shin Taisei) and criticized capitalism under Editor-in-Chief Taketora Ogata. Influential editorial writers such as Shintarō Ryū, Hiroo Sassa, and Hotsumi Ozaki (a spy informant for Richard Sorge) were members of the Shōwa Kenkyūkai, a political think tank for Konoe. Ogata was a leading member of the Genyōsha, an ultranationalist group including Kōki Hirota, who was later executed as a Class A war criminal and a close friend of Ogata. Ryū, formerly a Marxist economist, advocated centrally planned economies in *Nihon Keizai no Saihensei* (1939), while Sassa, son of ultranationalist politician Sassa Tomofusa, allied with far-right generals and terrorists who assassinated Junnosuke Inoue, Dan Takuma, and Inukai Tsuyoshi, and attempted to assassinate Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō in 1944. On 9 April 1937, the Kamikaze, a Mitsubishi aircraft sponsored by Asahi and flown by Masaaki Iinuma, arrived in London, becoming the first Japanese-built aircraft to fly to Europe. On 1 September 1940, the Osaka and Tokyo editions unified under the name Asahi Shimbun. On 1 January 1943, the government halted publication after Seigō Nakano, a Genyōsha member and Ogata’s friend, published a critical essay. On 27 December 1943, Nagataka Murayama, son-in-law of Murayama Ryōhei and Asahi president, removed Ogata from Editor-in-Chief and demoted him to Vice President. On 22 July 1944, Ogata became Minister without Portfolio and President of Cabinet Intelligence Agency in Kuniaki Koiso’s cabinet. On 7 April 1945, Hiroshi Shimomura, former Vice President, held the same position in Kantarō Suzuki’s cabinet. On 17 August 1945, Ogata became Minister without Portfolio, Chief Cabinet Secretary, and President of Cabinet Intelligence Agency in Prince Higashikuni’s cabinet. On 5 November 1945, the Asahi’s president and senior executives resigned en masse to take responsibility for compromising the paper’s principles during the war. On 21 November 1946, the newspaper adopted the modern kana usage system (shin kanazukai). On 30 November 1949, it began publishing the serialized cartoon strip *Sazae-san* by Machiko Hasegawa, a landmark in Japan’s postwar era. Between 1954 and 1971, it published a glossy, large-format annual in English titled *This is Japan*. In April–May 1989, the paper reported that a coral reef near Okinawa was defaced by a man with a dissolute Japanese mind, later revealed to be a fabricated report by the reporter himself, known as the Asahi Shimbun coral article hoax incident; the president resigned. On 26 June 2007, Yoichi Funabashi became the third editor-in-chief. Shōichi Ueno, co-owner since 1997, died on 29 February 2016. Under Shin-ichi Hakojima, the Asahi partnered with the International Herald Tribune to launch the *International Herald Tribune/Asahi Shimbun*, which ran from April 2001 to February 2011, replacing the *Asahi Evening News*; the partnership ended in 2010 due to unprofitability, and the Asahi now operates the Asia & Japan Watch online portal for English readers. The Tribune (now The International New York Times) collaborates with Asahi on Aera English, a glossy magazine for English learners. The Asahi is considered left-leaning, described as “the intellectual flagship of Japan’s political left,” with a tradition of reporting on political scandals more than conservative papers, and is regarded as a newspaper of record in Japan. It criticizes right-wing nationalism and shows progressive views on cultural and diplomatic issues, though it has a neoliberal economic stance, contrasting with Mainichi Shimbun’s Keynesian view. It supports Japan’s postwar Constitution, especially Article 9, opposing changes in interpretation, including the 2014 right of collective self-defense. While retracting discredited testimonies of Seiji Yoshida in August 2014, it affirmed that women were coerced into prostitution for the Japanese military, though no official documents proved direct military recruitment on the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan, citing poverty and patriarchal systems as enabling factors. In March 2011, following criticism for aligning too closely with the government during the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, the Asahi strengthened its investigative unit, the Tokubetsu Hodobu (Special Reports Section), which won awards in 2012 and 2013. In May 2014, it published a testimony from Masao Yoshida, the plant manager during the meltdown, stating that 90% of employees had left despite his orders, and that his instructions had not reached them. The headline “Workers Evacuated, Violating Plant Manager Orders” sparked controversy, with criticism that it implied cowardice, when many viewed the workers as heroes. Japanese journalist Ryusho Kadota criticized the mischaracterization, and the Asahi initially defended the story, demanding an apology. However, by August, the Yomiuri Shimbun, Sankei Shimbun, Kyodo News, and NHK obtained the same testimony and used it to attack the Asahi. In September, facing criticism from media and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, the Asahi retracted the story, and president Tadakazu Kimura resigned. Reporters and editors were punished, the Special Reports Section was reduced in size, and two top reporters left to found the Tokyo Investigative Newsroom Tansa, a non-profit investigative journalism organization. The section was told to avoid Fukushima coverage and has since faded. In the evening edition of 20 April 1989, an article described damage to the world’s largest Azami coral in Okinawa, with the initial “KY” scratched, later proven to be fabricated by the Asahi photographer; president Toichiro Hitotsuyanagi resigned. On 27 September 1950, a solo interview with Japanese Communist Party executive Ritsu Ito was published, later revealed to be forged by the Asahi reporter. The Asahi Shimbun Asia Network (AAN), established in 1999, promotes information exchange in Asia and hosts annual symposia and publishes research reports; Gong Ro Myung became its president in 2003. The Asahi Prize, established in 1929 and since 1992 awarded by the Asahi Shimbun Foundation, recognizes achievements in scholarship or the arts that contribute to Japanese culture or society. Past issues are available in three forms: CD-ROMs (with headlines from 1945–1999), microfilm (from 1888), and shukusatsuban (reduced-sized print editions from 1931), widely used in research universities. The CD-ROM database includes advertisements and is accessible at Harvard-Yenching Library; researchers typically use the CD-ROM index before accessing microfilm or shukusatsuban. Issues from August 1984 onward are available through Lexis-Nexis Academic. The Asahi Shimbun was an official supporter of several Asian initiatives.

Shukusatsuban is a technology developed and popularized by the Asahi Shimbun in the 1930s to compress and archive newspapers by reducing print size so that multiple pages of a daily newspaper can fit onto a single page. These are primarily used by libraries and archives and are typically organized and released by month. Shukusatsuban resources are accessible at many leading research universities worldwide, especially those with strong Japanese studies programs. The Asahi Shimbun maintains a CD-ROM database indexing headlines and sub-headlines from 1945 to 1999. A more expensive, full-text searchable database, which includes advertisements, is available exclusively at the Harvard-Yenching Library at Harvard University. Researchers at other university libraries generally begin with the CD-ROM index and then consult microfilm or shukusatsuban versions. Microfilm versions of the Asahi Shimbun are available starting from 1888, while shukusatsuban versions begin from 1931. Issues of the Asahi Shimbun published since August 1984 are accessible through Lexis-Nexis Academic. The Asahi Shimbun has been an official supporter of several Asian Football Confederation (AFC) competitions, most recently the 2019 AFC Asian Cup. It previously sponsored both the AFC Champions League and AFC Cup until the 2018 season. The newspaper was also an official sponsor of the 2002 FIFA World Cup.

The Bear is an American comedy-drama series created by Christopher Storer for FX on Hulu. Jeremy Allen White stars as Carmy Berzatto, a talented chef who returns to his hometown of Chicago to manage the chaotic kitchen at his deceased brother's Italian beef sandwich shop, leaving behind his career in Michelin-starred restaurants. The regular cast includes Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Ayo Edebiri, Lionel Boyce, Liza Colón-Zayas, Abby Elliott, Matty Matheson, and Edwin Lee Gibson. The series premiered on FX on Hulu on June 23, 2022, with all episodes of the first season released on that date; the second season followed on June 22, 2023. In November 2023, the series was renewed for a third season, released on June 26, 2024, and in March 2024, it was renewed for a fourth season, which premiered on June 25, 2025. In July 2025, the series was renewed for a fifth season. The show's storyline is divided into parts marked by onscreen title cards, with Part II appearing in the first episode of season 2 and Part III in the first episode of season 3, which concluded with a "to be continued" card. Most episodes are about 30 minutes long, ranging from 20 minutes to 70 minutes. FX ordered a pilot in March 2021, written and directed by Christopher Storer, and then ordered the series in October 2021 for a 2022 premiere. The sandwich shop interior is modeled after Mr. Beef on Orleans Street in River North, a shop frequently visited by Storer, who is a friend of Christopher Zucchero, the current owner. The show's culinary production is overseen by co-executive producer Courtney Storer (sister of Christopher Storer) and culinary co-producer C. J. Capace, with additional team members including chefs Justin Selk, Nicole Biyani, Danielle Stefanick, Gabriel Wallace, Jeffrey Thomas, and Brian Lockwood. The lead costume designer is Courtney Wheeler, with Lariana Santiago as assistant; Ally Vickers leads the hair department; Laura Roeper (sister of Chicago Sun-Times critic Richard Roeper) is the Chicago-based prop master; Merje Veski is the production designer; Lisa Korpan is the art director; and Eric Frankel heads the set decoration department. The primary cinematographer is Andrew Wehde, with A-camera operator Gary Malouf and B-camera operator Chris Dame having worked with Storer and Wehde previously; Scott D. Smith has led the sound mixing team since the pilot, Steve "Major" Giammaria is the supervising sound editor, and Evan Benjamin is the dialogue sound editor; the episode cuts are handled by Joanna Naugle, Adam Epstein, and Megan Mancini. The show's soundtrack features 1980s to 2000s alternative and mainstream rock songs, including tracks by Wilco, Radiohead, Van Morrison, Pearl Jam, Sufjan Stevens, John Mayer, Refused, The Breeders, Erasure, The Replacements, Counting Crows, Genesis, Nine Inch Nails, John Mellencamp, R.E.M., Weezer, The Smashing Pumpkins, Led Zeppelin, Oasis, and Taylor Swift (with "Love Story (Taylor's Version)", "Long Live (Taylor's Version)", and "Style (Taylor's Version)"), selected by Storer and executive producer Josh Senior. The primary composers are Chicago-based Jeffrey "JQ" Qaiyum and Johnny Iguana, whose instrumentals are used primarily in back-of-house scenes; Iguana described JQ as a "wizard producer" who creates the beats and handles the chords and notes. The Bear premiered in the U.S. on June 23, 2022, and became available internationally on Disney+'s Star hub; it was also accessible on Hulu via Disney+ in the U.S. starting December 6, 2023. The series has received critical acclaim, with a 93% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and an 83 out of 100 score on Metacritic. The first season earned a 100% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes with a Metacritic score of 88; the second season received 99% positive reviews and a Metacritic score of 92; the third season had an 89% approval rating and a Metacritic score of 80; the fourth season received an 84% approval rating and a Metacritic score of 72. The American Film Institute named it one of the ten best television programs of the year in both 2022 and 2023, and The Guardian ranked it number one of the best 100 TV shows of 2022, calling it "the best workplace drama since Mad Men." It appeared on numerous "Best of 2022" and "Best of 2023" lists. The show was the most-nominated series in comedy categories at the 2024 Emmys with 23 nominations, surpassing 30 Rock's 22 from 2009, but lost the Outstanding Comedy Series award to Hacks, with industry observers suggesting voter resentment over its lack of comedic content. Reelgood and JustWatch reported that The Bear was among the most-streamed programs in the U.S., with peak viewership during July 2024 and 2025, and it was the most-watched comedy series in FX history for its first season and the most-watched season premiere in the network's history for its second season. The season 3 premiere garnered 5.4 million views in its first four days, making it the most-watched season premiere for any scripted series on Hulu and the best FX premiere on Hulu, with 1,233 million minutes of viewing recorded from June 24–30, surpassing the previous peak of 1.01 billion minutes. The Bear was the third most-streamed show in the U.S. in 2024 and the second most-streamed in Canada that year.

The second season of The Circle premiered on April 14, 2021, and concluded on May 5, 2021, following its announcement in March 2020 when Netflix renewed the series for a second and third season. Michelle Buteau returned as host. Players compete to become the most popular without meeting face-to-face; instead, they communicate through a custom social media app where they can portray themselves in any way they choose, a practice known as catfishing. The first eight players were revealed on April 5, 2021, with additional contestants added during the season. On May 5, 2021, DeLeesa St. Agathe won the season by playing as her husband, Trevor, and received the US$100,000 prize, while Chloe Veitch finished as runner-up and won the Fan Favorite award along with US$10,000. All players live in separate apartments within the same building and communicate exclusively through the app. Players rate each other from first to last, and at the end of each round, their average ratings are shared from lowest to highest. Typically, the two highest-rated players become Influencers, while others are at risk of being Blocked by the Influencers. However, twists may occur, such as instant blocking of the lowest-rated players, secret Influencers, or multiple blocks. Blocked players are eliminated but get to meet one remaining player in person, with a video message revealing whether they were real or fake the day after. In the finale, the highest-rated player wins US$100,000, and fans vote for their favorite player, who earns US$10,000 as Fan Favorite. The initial players introduced were Bryant, Savannah, Chloe, Courtney, "Trevor"/DeLeesa, "Emily"/Jack, "River"/Lee, and Terilisha. Suspicion arises when "Trevor," a single dad, is revealed to be played by DeLeesa, who is 32 years old. Bryant begins a private chat with Courtney, offering support, while Jack, playing a 21-year-old sorority girl named Emily, starts a group chat with the girls. Savannah and Terilisha are named Influencers and are given 24 hours to decide who to save from elimination. They choose to save "Emily"/Jack and "Trevor"/DeLeesa. The other players begin conversations with the Influencers. Bryant convinces Terilisha not to eliminate him, which succeeds.
