Courtney forms an alliance with Savannah, and Chloe and "Trevor"/DeLeesa flirt. Savannah wants to block "River"/Lee, but Terilisha opposes it. Ultimately, Bryant is voted off and chooses to meet "River"/Lee in person before leaving. After the season, the Circle announces a new player joining. A video reveals Bryant is not a catfish. New player Lisa joins as "Lance," a former NSYNC member. Skepticism grows after "Lance"’s identity is revealed. Savannah accidentally reveals Terilisha attempted to block Courtney, leading to an alliance. Terilisha starts a group chat with Chloe and "Emily"/Jack, expressing suspicions about Savannah. Terilisha accuses Savannah of being a game player, and Savannah accuses Terilisha of being untrustworthy. "Trevor"/DeLeesa reaches out to Savannah after the conflict, offering support. Terilisha warns Courtney that Savannah is causing drama, which Courtney believes is due to Terilisha. Savannah reaches out to Chloe and "Emily"/Jack for support. Savannah’s video reveals she is not a catfish and states there are still multiple catfish in the game. Courtney is in the Inner Circle and unlocks a secret identity, "The Joker," who speaks to new players, Mitchell and Khat, before they join. Courtney warns them not to trust Chloe or Terilisha. Courtney returns to the Inner Circle and selects one player to become an influencer at the next blocking. Chloe flirts with both Mitchell and "Trevor"/DeLeesa. "River"/Lee is chosen as the influencer. The players are told one of them was a catfish but not who. Terilisha talks to Khat to learn what "The Joker" said and assumes it was "Emily"/Jack. The ratings reveal Courtney as the second influencer. Terilisha is blocked and meets Chloe. Her video reveals she knows who "The Joker" is and what was said to Khat and Mitchell. Khat, "Lance"/Lisa, and Mitchell discuss and believe "Lance"/Lisa is a catfish. Mitchell friend zones Chloe after "Trevor"/DeLeesa tells him they are close. "Emily"/Jack is upset, believing the game cost him and that everyone thinks he is catfishing. The players receive an alert that two players will be blocked the next day. "Emily"/Jack and "Lance"/Lisa form a friendship. Khat and "Trevor"/DeLeesa discuss their suspicions with "Emily"/Jack and "Lance"/Lisa. Chloe, Courtney, and "River"/Lee discuss their suspicions with "Emily"/Jack. "Trevor"/DeLeesa suspects "River"/Lee of sending a catfish message about her. The ratings show no influencers, and "Emily"/Jack and "Lance"/Lisa are instantly blocked. "Lance"/Lisa chooses to meet "River"/Lee, and "Emily"/Jack chooses "Trevor"/DeLeesa. They meet and receive a second chance with a shared profile set up by The Circle. Jack and Lisa now play as "John," a 64-year-old psychic. Their videos are posted, revealing both were catfishing. The Circle chat opens, and players are unaware that "John"/Jack and Lisa are lurking. No one confirms if "Emily"/Jack or "Lance"/Lisa visited them after being blocked, leading to suspicion. The "John"/Jack and Lisa profile is revealed. Khat tells Courtney and "River"/Lee that she believes Chloe is a liar and unaware they are both close to her. Chloe starts a chat with "Trevor"/DeLeesa and admits her feelings. "Trevor"/DeLeesa continues to flirt despite knowing she is catfishing. Courtney and "River"/Lee inform Chloe about Khat’s claims. Chloe says she thinks Khat is a game player. Courtney informs "Trevor"/DeLeesa about Khat’s feelings toward Chloe. The players rate each other, and the ratings reveal Chloe and "Trevor"/DeLeesa as the influencers. Khat is blocked and meets "Trevor"/DeLeesa. Her video shows she was not a catfish and advises players not to believe everything. Courtney and "River"/Lee decide to monitor Mitchell, who hasn’t spoken to either of them. Mitchell and "Trevor"/DeLeesa plan to break up Courtney and "River"/Lee’s alliance. "Trevor"/DeLeesa begins by talking to "River"/Lee. Mitchell talks to Chloe to join his alliance. The players receive an alert that the final blocking occurs the next day. Mitchell’s video is posted. Final ratings are submitted. Players get to meet face-to-face. Chloe meets "Trevor"/DeLeesa and sees she was catfishing. "River"/Lee is revealed as a catfish to Chloe, Courtney, and "Trevor"/DeLeesa. "John"/Jack and Lisa are revealed as catfish to the remaining finalists.

The third season of the American reality competition streaming series The Circle began on Netflix on September 8, 2021, and concluded on September 29, 2021. The season was announced in March 2020 when Netflix renewed The Circle for a second and third season, with Michelle Buteau returning as host. Like previous seasons, players compete to become the most popular without meeting face-to-face; instead, they communicate through a specially designed app where they can portray themselves in any way they choose, including catfishing. The contestants live in separate apartments within the same building and rate one another from first to last place. At the end of each rating period, their average ratings are revealed from lowest to highest, with the two highest-rated players typically becoming "Influencers" and the rest at risk of being "blocked" by them. Occasionally, the blocking process includes twists such as instantly blocking the lowest-rated players, keeping the Influencers' identities secret, or blocking multiple players at once. Blocked players are eliminated but are given the chance to meet one remaining player in person, with a video message shown the next day to reveal if they were real or fake. The season finale features a final rating, with the highest-rated player winning the US$100,000 prize, and fans voting for their favorite player, who wins the Fan Favorite award and US$10,000. James Andre Jefferson Jr. won the season by playing as himself and receiving the US$100,000 prize, while Matthew Pappadia as "Ashley" was the runner-up. Keisha "Kai" Ghost won the Fan Favorite award and US$10,000. The first eight players—Matt, Calvin, Nick, Kai, Ruksana, Michelle, Daniel, Ava, and Chanel—enter the apartment building and create their profiles. Initially, Calvin and Kai place in the top two, but The Circle reveals Kai is the sole influencer, who decides to block Ava and Chanel. Ava and Chanel choose to clone Michelle, re-entering as "Blue Michelle" and leaving the original Michelle as "Orange Michelle." The players have one day to decide which Michelle to keep. Orange Michelle is blocked unanimously and visits Blue Michelle before leaving. Later, two new players, "Isabella" and "Jackson," enter and are able to talk to each other before meeting the rest. Isabella and Jackson settle in, with Jackson starting a private chat with Kai and flirting with her. The players rate each other from first to sixth, with new players unable to be rated. After the ratings, Kai places second and Ruksana places first; both influencers chat and decide who to block. Kai visits Michelle after deciding to block her, learning she is not the real Michelle but instead Ava and Chanel. Later, the players learn that Orange Michelle was the real Michelle and Blue Michelle was the clone, confirmed by their goodbye messages. The players rate each other from first to seventh, with Nick placing first and Daniel second; both become Influencers and choose one player to block. Daniel blocks Jackson, and Nick blocks Ruksana. "Jackson" visits Nick and reveals she is actually Rachel. Nick confides with Rachel that "Vince" is his burner profile, received as a parting gift from Calvin. Ruksana visits Daniel. The next morning, "Vince" is removed from the game before the Circle reveals it was a burner profile handled by an existing player. New player Jacki joins the game. James brings Jacki up to speed on events in The Circle. The two main alliances—James, Kai, and Daniel on one side; Nick, Ashley, and Isabella on the other—each try to bring Jacki to their side, resulting in her receiving simultaneous group chat invites and choosing James’s group. Jacki later explains the situation to Nick to clear the air. James and Nick decide to block Daniel. When Daniel is allowed to visit a player, he chooses Isabella (Sophia), who shares her story with him. After the circle votes for the yearbook, there is a circle prom where players share their plans for the prize money if they win. In 2023, Calvin Crooks and Nick Uhlenhuth competed on the first season of Perfect Match; Crooks was eliminated in Episode Two, and Uhlenhuth finished as a finalist alongside LC Chamblin. Nick Uhlenhuth also competed on the first season of Battle Camp, where he was eliminated tenth. Rachel Ward appeared on the comedy game show Game Changer, appearing as a suitor in a Bachelor-themed episode.

The Haunted Mansion is a horror-themed dark-ride attraction located at Disneyland, Magic Kingdom, and Tokyo Disneyland. The ride features a ride-through tour in Omnimover vehicles known as "Doom Buggies" and a walk-through show for the queue line. Each location has slight design differences, using a range of technology from century-old theatrical effects to modern special effects, including Audio-Animatronics. The attraction was in development for over a decade after the parks opened and was one of the last projects created under Walt Disney's direction. It inspired two distinct but loosely similar attractions: Phantom Manor at Disneyland Park Paris and Mystic Manor at Hong Kong Disneyland. Franchise media includes television specials, merchandise, comic strips, and two feature films: The Haunted Mansion released in 2003 and Haunted Mansion released in 2023. Guests enter through the front gate of a typical antebellum mansion, passing through gardens with a pet cemetery and a carriage led by an invisible horse. The deep voice of the Ghost Host introduces himself in the foyer. Guests enter an art gallery with four paintings showing people from the chest up; as the room stretches vertically, the portrait frames elongate, revealing the subjects' grim yet humorous fates. This room is actually an elevator transporting guests beneath the railroad berm to the main attraction. The room goes dark, the ceiling vanishes, and lightning flashes to reveal the cupola, where the Ghost Host's skeletal corpse hangs from the rafters by a noose, implying suicide; a shriek follows, then bones shatter. The Ghost Host apologizes, a wall opens, exposing a portrait corridor leading to the loading area—this corridor is a tunnel under the Disneyland Railroad to the ride building. The portraits on the right briefly flicker into macabre versions when lighting flashes from the left. At the corridor's end are two busts that appear to "follow" guests due to the Hollow-Face illusion. In the loading area, Doom Buggies descend one staircase and ascend another to the second floor, with fog pumped into the back. Guests pass a candelabra floating down an endless hallway, near which is a moving suit of armor and a chair with an abstract face. The Doom Buggies then view a glass conservatory with dead flora surrounding a casket; the occupant is heard calling for help, with bony hands trying to pry the lid open. The vehicles travel down a hallway of doors where sounds of pounding, calls for help, screams, knocking, and maniacal laughter are heard; knockers and handles move independently, and some doors appear to "breathe." A demonic grandfather clock chimes 13 as the minute hand spins backward, with a shadow of a claw passing over it. Guests enter a dark séance room with occult objects; Madame Leota, a blue-haired medium with a disembodied head in a levitating crystal ball, summons spirits, and floating musical instruments respond to her spell. After the séance, guests move to a mezzanine overlooking a massive ballroom where ghosts are enjoying a birthday party. Ghosts fly in from a crashed hearse and windows; one ghost girl blows out the candles, and the others disappear and reappear when she inhales. Drunken ghosts play with glasses of red wine on the chandelier; six ghost couples waltz to music from a gentleman's spirit on a pipe organ, with wraiths emerging from its pipes. Two duelists' portraits on the wall come to life and fire their revolvers. In the attic, guests see portraits of a bride with different grooms, each disappearing and reappearing; a shadow of a pianist plays a sinister version of the "Bridal March." The ghost of bride Constance Hatchaway floats nearby, holding the same candelabra as earlier, with her heart glowing pink and beating in time with the music. The Doom Buggies drift out of an attic window onto a balcony under a starry night sky, then fall backward beneath dead trees with humanoid faces. On reaching the ground, they turn toward a private graveyard where a frightened caretaker holds a lantern and shovel, with a scrawny dog cowering at his feet, whimpering. Around the corner, ghosts rise and party; comical scenes include a skeleton's hand popping from a tomb, a duo singing opera, a king and queen balancing on a gravestone, and a duchess sipping tea. Five busts sing the theme song "Grim Grinning Ghosts" near the end. The Doom Buggies enter a large crypt where the Ghost Host warns about hitchhiking ghosts as vehicles pass a group of three ghosts thumbing for a ride; in large mirrors, guests see one of the trio inside their buggy. Guests then disembark and begin leaving the mansion; a small ghost named Little Leota encourages them to return and to bring their "death certificate." The Haunted Mansion opened on day one at Magic Kingdom in Walt Disney World, located in Liberty Square. During production, duplicates of props and audio-animatronics were made for the Florida version, which was decided to be longer and more elaborate than the California version, with extra scenes like the library and music room. Paul Frees recorded additional voice-overs, including the Ghost Host, for these scenes. Due to more space in the park, the show building is larger and not restricted by a railroad berm. In the Foyer, there is a portrait of the Aging Man from the Disneyland version. Unlike the California version, the stretching rooms do not use elevators; instead, ceilings rise. After this, the door opens to the Doom Buggy loading area. Upon boarding, guests pass under a staircase with a floating candelabra, then pass changing portraits as seen in the Disneyland queue. An on-ride photo is taken here. Guests then enter the library, where ghost writers' busts stare and follow them. In the music room, an invisible pianist plays a sinister version of "Grim Grinning Ghosts," and guests proceed to the Endless Staircase, where footprints are visible and candelabras are occasionally blown out by unseen ghosts. Passing bat-eyed wallpaper that glows in the dark, guests see the Endless Hallway, with the Hatbox Ghost appearing next to it from a blue door, his footprints visible. After passing through the conservatory where a corpse cries for help, guests travel through a corridor of doors, where a demonic grandfather clock chimes 13. Guests enter the seance room, where Madame Leota floats and recites her spell, with instruments playing and a green specter floating alongside. The Doom Buggies enter the mezzanine of the ballroom, where ghosts gather for a party, then proceed to the attic. A piano player can be heard but not seen; the bride is now blue and white with a stained hatchet. The Doom Buggies pass through the cemetery, where ghosts sing "Grim Grinning Ghosts," and enter the crypt, where hitchhiking ghosts play in mirrors. Little Leota appears above the vehicles as guests disembark and pass a mausoleum and a pet cemetery. The Tokyo Disneyland version opened on day one and is located in Fantasyland; it is largely a duplicate of the Magic Kingdom version, with minor differences such as a haunted painting of a man resembling Peter Lorre whose face pops out and stretches, a tall, legless ghost in the Séance Room, and more advanced lighting. It did not receive the 2007 refurbishment changes made to the Magic Kingdom version. The idea for the Mansion predates Disneyland and WED Enterprises, originating when Walt Disney hired his first Imagineers. In 1951, a park illustration showed a main street, green fields, western village, and a carnival. Disney Legend Harper Goff developed a sketch of a crooked street leading to a peaceful church and graveyard, with a run-down manor perched high on a hill. Disney assigned Imagineer Ken Anderson to develop a story using Goff's idea. Plans were made for a New Orleans-themed land between Frontierland and Adventureland, promising a thieves' market, pirate wax museum, and a haunted house walk-through. Anderson studied New Orleans and old plantations, landing on the Shipley-Lydecker House in Baltimore, Maryland, and created a drawing of an antebellum manor with overgrown weeds, dead trees, swarms of bats, and a screeching cat as a weathervane. Disney rejected the idea of a run-down building. He visited the Winchester Mystery House in San Jose, California, and was captivated by its massive structure with stairs to nowhere, doors opening to walls and holes, and elevators. Anderson envisioned stories including a ghostly sea captain who killed his nosy bride and hanged himself, a family's misfortune, and a ghostly wedding party with Disney villains and spooks. In 1961, handbills announced a 1963 opening at Disneyland. Construction began a year later, with the exterior completed in 1963. The attraction was previewed in a 1965 episode of Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color, but did not open until 1969, due to Disney's involvement in the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair and the attraction redesign after his death in 1966. After the fair, Imagineers Marc Davis, X Atencio, and Claude Coats contributed ideas; Anderson had left the project. Rolly Crump presented designs including coffin clocks, candle men, talking chairs, man-eating plants, tiki-like busts, living gypsy wagons, and a mirror with a face. Disney accepted these ideas and wanted to create a "Museum of the Weird," a restaurant side to the Haunted Mansion, similar to Blue Bayou at Pirates of the Caribbean. When Disney assigned Crump and Yale Gracey to create illusions, they intended to make the "Museum of the Weird" a separate walk-through section using the Pepper's ghost technique. Crump and Gracey were given a large workshop to develop their ideas. One night, they played a prank on the night cleaning crew by leaving lights on with motion sensors that triggered ghost effects; the next morning, the janitors found the effects still running and a broom in the center. Davis and Coats disagreed on whether the ride should be frightening or funny: Coats wanted a scary adventure with moody, bleak environments; Davis proposed a silly, gag-filled experience. Atencio combined both approaches, creating a transition from dark foreboding to spirited entertainment. The ride narration was performed by Paul Frees as the Ghost Host; the theme song "Grim Grinning Ghosts" was composed by Buddy Baker with lyrics by Atencio and is heard in nearly every area. After Disney's death in December 1966, the project evolved significantly. The "Museum of the Weird" idea was abandoned. Imagineers objected to a walk-through attraction's low capacity, suggesting two identical attractions to serve twice as many guests. A solution emerged with the development of the Omnimover system for Adventure Thru Inner Space, renamed the Doom Buggy. The system's continuous chain of semi-enclosed vehicles offered high capacity and allowed control over what guests saw and heard. Each car holds one to three people, making it ideal for the story of individuals wandering alone through a haunted house. Employee previews occurred on August 6, 7, and 8, followed by soft openings on August 9 and 10, and a "Midnight" Press Event on August 11. The attraction officially opened to all guests on August 12, 1969. Around 1977, WDI considered using Rolly Crump's unused designs and effects for Professor Marvel's Gallery, a tent show in Discovery Bay, but the expansion plans were dropped. In 1994, Disneyland's Haunted Mansion was updated with a phantom piano player in the attic and a full-fleshed bride replacing the original faceless one. In 2001, a new, more detailed safety spiel was added to the Doom Buggies' onboard audio, recorded by Joe Leahy in English and Fabio Rodriguez in Spanish, in a recreation of Paul Frees' Ghost Host voice, as part of a park-wide safety campaign. The seasonal overlay Haunted Mansion Holiday premiered in October, featuring characters from the 1993 film The Nightmare Before Christmas. In 2004, the Seance Room was updated so the crystal ball with Madame Leota's talking head floated above the table instead of sitting on it, with the original projection-mapped effect replaced by a rear-projection effect. In 2006, the original attic bride was replaced by Constance Hatchaway with a new storyline. In 2007, the attraction was renovated with the addition of changing portraits and lightning-filled windows from the Disneyland version, and new vocals for most of the graveyard ghosts. In the Walt Disney World version, an endless staircase was added after a dark space with spider webs. The Sinister 11 portraits, originally with eyes that stared at guests, were moved to the loading area during the refurbishment and no longer follow guests. In March 2011, a new "interactive queue" debuted at Walt Disney World, featuring crypts and tombstones honoring Imagineers; a murder mystery involving the sinister Dread Family; the Composer Crypt with musical instruments that play variations of "Grim Grinning Ghosts" when touched, including a pipe organ named after Thurl Ravenscroft; the Mariner's brine-filled sepulcher, whose ghost sings and sneezes; and a crypt for poetess Prudence Pock, featuring haunted moving books and Prudence's ghost writing invisibly in her poem book. Guests can solve unfinished poems by speaking into microphones. The FastPass+ line skips the queue and leads directly to the Foyer doors. There is also an extended queue using the former Mike Fink Keel Boats dock. On April 10, 2015, it was officially confirmed that The Hatbox Ghost would return to Disneyland's Haunted Mansion. The character returned on May 9, 2015. The Hatbox Ghost was originally part of the attraction when it opened in 1969 but was removed because the illusion was not convincing. The character was added to Disney World's Haunted Mansion on November 30.

The Haunted Mansion at Disneyland features the "Ravenscroft" company, named for Thurl Ravenscroft, one of the vocalists for "Grim Grinning Ghosts"; a brine-filled sepulcher where a ghost sings and sneezes; and a crypt dedicated to Prudence Pock, the poetess, which includes haunted moving books and Prudence's ghost writing invisibly in her poem book. Guests can solve unfinished poems by speaking into microphones located in the crypt. The FastPass+ line skips the queue entirely and leads guests directly to the Foyer doors. An extended queue line uses the former Mike Fink Keel Boats dock. On April 10, 2015, it was confirmed that The Hatbox Ghost would return to Disneyland's Haunted Mansion, debuting on May 9, 2015; the character was originally part of the attraction when it opened in 1969 but was removed due to an unconvincing illusion; it was added to Disney World's Haunted Mansion on November 30, 2023, as part of The Walt Disney Company's 100th Anniversary celebration. On April 2, 2019, PhotoPass ride photography was introduced at Magic Kingdom, with a hidden camera capturing riders as they pass the final portrait, the flash disguised as flickering lightning, and a black-and-white photo framed by surrounding ghosts automatically added to the guest's PhotoPass account via RFID from their second-generation MagicBand. On January 21, 2020, Disneyland's Haunted Mansion closed for an extensive refurbishment to install lighted steel panels, improved lighting, mechanical touch-ups, and new paint and trims, originally scheduled for completion in spring 2020 but delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic; it reopened on April 30, 2021, with a refreshed pet cemetery featuring new greenery, new drapes in the portrait gallery, more decorative wallpaper in the loading area, and the return of the original portrait "April to December," along with a statue of the one-eyed cat; the rest of the attraction received repairs and new lighting. A new secret entrance was added using an exit: once the crypt door opens, visitors go down a flight of stairs and through a utility passageway used by cast members. In January 2024, the Disneyland Haunted Mansion began another major refurbishment to expand the outdoor queue, modify nearby Magnolia Park in New Orleans Square, and add a gift shop at the ride's exit; the expansion opened on November 26, 2024, including an accessible elevator, and the gift shop, themed as the mansion's carriage house, opened on December 23, 2024. In January 2025, the attraction received a new bride inspired by the original character and storyline, and the hitchhiking ghosts scene was updated. The Haunted Mansion at Disneyland and Tokyo Disneyland transforms into Haunted Mansion Holiday during the Halloween and Christmas seasons since 2001, inspired by Tim Burton's 1993 film The Nightmare Before Christmas; it closes in mid to late August for a few weeks to revamp the attraction with new props and Audio-Animatronics from the movie, then reopens in September, closing again in early January to restore the original version and reopening late January. The Magic Kingdom does not have a holiday edition and operates continuously during the holidays. Disneyland Park Paris features Phantom Manor in Frontierland, a "re-imagined" version in Western Victorian, Second Empire style based on the Fourth Ward School House in Virginia City, Nevada, with a Western plot aligned with Thunder Mesa and Frontierland; unlike Disneyland and Magic Kingdom, which use English narration by Paul Frees, Phantom Manor features Vincent Price throughout. Mystic Manor opened at Hong Kong Disneyland in spring 2013 in Mystic Point, differing from the Haunted Mansion or Phantom Manor by not referencing departed spirits or the afterlife due to cultural differences in traditional Chinese culture; it continues the Society of Explorers and Adventurers theme of Tokyo DisneySea, telling the story of Lord Henry Mystic and his monkey Albert, who opens an enchanted music box that brings the house's artifacts to life; the exterior is a large Victorian mansion in Queen Anne style, with a trackless system and a musical score by Danny Elfman. On October 5, 2025, a woman in her 60s was found unresponsive after riding The Haunted Mansion; Disneyland security administered CPR until Anaheim Fire and Rescue arrived; she was transported to a local hospital and pronounced dead; no autopsy was performed, and no ride issues were found. Walt Disney Pictures produced two standalone live-action film adaptations: The first, The Haunted Mansion, directed by Rob Minkoff and starring Eddie Murphy, was released on November 26, 2003; the second, Haunted Mansion, directed by Justin Simien, was released on July 28, 2023. In July 2010, Guillermo del Toro announced he would write and produce a darker film adaptation, which was officially confirmed in July 2021, with Tiffany Haddish playing a hired psychic attempting to commune with the dead and LaKeith Stanfield playing a lackluster tour guide in New Orleans's French Quarter.

The Jeffersons is an American sitcom created by Norman Lear that aired on CBS from January 18, 1975, to July 2, 1985, spanning eleven seasons and 253 episodes. Starring Isabel Sanford as Louise Jefferson and Sherman Hemsley as George Jefferson, the show follows a prosperous African-American couple who move from Queens to a high-rise apartment in Manhattan, New York City, due to the success of George's dry-cleaning chain, Jefferson Cleaners. It is a spin-off of All in the Family, where the Jeffersons were neighbors of the Bunkers; George's character was specifically created for Hemsley, who was initially unavailable due to starring in the Broadway musical Purlie, leading Lear to introduce Henry Jefferson, played by Mel Stewart, as George's younger brother until Purlie ended. The Jeffersons premiered the week after the All in the Family episode "The Jeffersons Move Up," which aired on January 11, 1975, and featured Louise, her son Lionel (played by Mike Evans), and George moving into the Colby East high-rise. The show's concept was inspired by feedback from Black Panthers who criticized the portrayal of Black people on television, prompting Lear to develop a series highlighting upward mobility. The series evolved into a traditional sitcom but occasionally addressed serious issues such as alcoholism, racism, suicide, gun control, transgender identity, the KKK, and adult illiteracy, with the epithets "nigger" and "honky" used occasionally, especially in early seasons. The show had one spin-off, Checking In, centered on Florence Johnston (Marla Gibbs), who becomes a hotel cleaning manager, lasting only four episodes before returning to The Jeffersons with the story that the hotel burned down. The Jeffersons shared continuity with E/R, featuring Lynne Moody in a guest role, and Sherman Hemsley guest-starred as George in two episodes of a one-season series. The show ended controversially when CBS canceled it without a proper finale, announcing the cancellation at the upfront presentation the day before the final episode aired on July 2, 1985, nearly two months prior; cast members learned through newspapers, tabloids, or Entertainment Tonight. Isabel Sanford criticized the cancellation as disrespectful. The cast later reunited in a stage play, "The Jeffersons Live: The Movin' On Up Tour," and made guest appearances in later series, including The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air (1995 and 1996) and Tyler Perry's House of Payne (2011). In 1985, Hemsley and Sanford made a joint guest appearance in the Italian comedy Grand Hotel, with their voices dubbed by Enzo Garinei and Isa di Marzio. As of 2023, surviving main cast members include Marla Gibbs, Berlinda Tolbert, Damon Evans, and Jay Hammer. The Jeffersons' theme song, "Movin' On Up," was co-written by Ja'Net DuBois and Jeff Barry, inspired by DuBois's dream of providing her mother with a comfortable retirement. The show changed time slots at least 15 times during its run, most commonly airing on Sunday nights. It initially ranked fourth in its first season, later entering the Top 30, peaking at No. 3 in 1982, and remaining in the Top 20 for several seasons. The series was rebroadcast on CBS from February 4, 1980, to September 25, 1981, and released on DVD by Sony Pictures Home Entertainment from 2002 to 2007, later acquired by Mill Creek and Shout! Factory, with the complete series released in a 33-disc collection in 2014. The Jeffersons earned 14 Emmy nominations, winning two: Marla Gibbs won Best Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series from 1981 to 1985, Sherman Hemsley received a nomination in 1984, and Larry M. Harris won Outstanding Video Tape Editing in 1983; Isabel Sanford was nominated for seven consecutive Best Actress Emmys from 1979 to 1985, winning in 1981, making her the first African-American actress to win that award. The show received five Golden Globe nominations. Critics have criticized it as stereotypical, with Gregory Kane calling it demeaning in 1999. The series had many two-part episodes and was known for its recurring characters, including Tom and Helen Willis (played by Franklin Cover and Roxie Roker), who were an interracial couple; Allan (Jay Hammer) and Jenny (Berlinda Tolbert), who married in 1976 and had a daughter, Jessica; and Paul Benedict as Harry Bentley, a British neighbor with a bad back and a habit of being slammed in the door. Ned Wertimer played Ralph Hart, the tip-hungry doorman, and Danny Wells portrayed Charlie, the bar owner and alcoholic, whose drinking issue was addressed in a season 11 episode. Mike Evans (Lionel) left after the first season, with Damon Evans (no relation) taking over until halfway through season 4, and Evans made his final appearance in "Lionel Gets the Business." Mike Evans and Tolbert returned in 1979–1980, with Tolbert's character pregnant, and Evans appeared in only one more season. The series' eighth season reached No. 3, becoming the first African-American sitcom in years to peak in the top 5. Paul Benedict left for a season and a half in 1981, returning in the final two seasons. The show's ratings declined after 1980, and it ended with the episode "Red Robins" on July 2, 1985. On May 22, 2019, ABC aired a live stage production of Norman Lear's All in the Family and The Jeffersons, featuring Marla Gibbs as Florence Johnston.

The stage show featured recreations of the episodes "A Whole Lot of Trouble," "Social Insecurity," and "My Wife... I Think I'll Keep Her." The tour started in Detroit, Michigan, with a six-city run, and although Roker dropped out, Berlinda Tolbert (who played Jenny) and Ned Wertimer (who played Ralph) returned to reprise their roles for the Los Angeles performance in 1994. On May 22, 2019, ABC aired Live in Front of a Studio Audience: Norman Lear's All in the Family and The Jeffersons, produced by Norman Lear and Jimmy Kimmel, starring Woody Harrelson, Marisa Tomei, Jamie Foxx, Wanda Sykes, Ike Barinholtz, Kerry Washington, and Ellie Kemper, with Marla Gibbs reprising her role as Florence Johnston.

doc_name: The Story of God with Morgan Freeman
text: The Story of God with Morgan Freeman is an American television documentary series that first aired on the National Geographic Channel on April 3, 2016. The series stars actor Morgan Freeman as he investigates different cultures and religions, focusing on their perspectives regarding a God or a higher power. The second season premiered on January 16, 2017, and the third season began on March 5, 2019. This article, concerning a non-fiction television series in the United States, is currently a stub and can be expanded with additional information.

Theodore von Kármán (Hungarian: (szőlőskislaki) Kármán Tódor [(sølløːʃkiʃlɒki) ˈkaːrmaːn ˈtoːdor]; 11 May 1881 – 6 May 1963) was a Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer, and physicist known for his key advances in aerodynamics, particularly in supersonic and hypersonic airflow characterization, and is regarded as the outstanding aerodynamic theoretician of the twentieth century. Born into a Jewish family in Budapest, Austria-Hungary, he was the son of Helen (Kohn or Konn, Hungarian: Kohn Ilka) and Mór Kármán, with one ancestor being Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel. He studied engineering at the Royal Joseph Technical University, now known as Budapest University of Technology and Economics, and after graduating in 1902, moved to the German Empire to join Ludwig Prandtl at the University of Göttingen, where he earned his doctorate in 1908 and taught for four years. In 1912, he became director of the Aeronautical Institute at RWTH Aachen University, one of Germany’s leading institutions, though his tenure was interrupted by service in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1915 to 1918, during which he designed the Petróczy-Kármán-Žurovec, an early helicopter. After the war, he returned to Aachen with his mother and sister Josephine de Karman, who encouraged him to expand his scientific influence beyond national borders; they organized the first international conference in mechanics in September 1922 in Innsbruck, leading to the formation of the International Union of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics. Kármán left RWTH Aachen in 1930. Concerned about European developments, he accepted the directorship of the Guggenheim Aeronautical Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology (GALCIT) in 1930, appointing Frank Wattendorf as his research assistant. His student Ernest Edwin Sechler, with Kármán’s support, developed an understanding of aeroelasticity for reliable airframes. In 1936, Kármán formed the Aerojet Corporation with graduate student Frank Malina and collaborator Jack Parsons to manufacture JATO rocket motors, later becoming a naturalized U.S. citizen. During World War II, U.S. military interest in rocket research grew due to German advances; in early 1943, the U.S. Army Air Forces received reports from British intelligence about German rockets capable of traveling over 100 miles (160 km), and Kármán provided an analysis in a letter dated 2 August 1943. In 1944, he and others affiliated with GALCIT founded the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), now a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech under NASA. In 1946, he became the first chairman of the Scientific Advisory Group for the U.S. Army Air Forces and helped establish AGARD (1951), the International Council of the Aeronautical Sciences (1956), the International Academy of Astronautics (1960), and the Von Karman Institute for Fluid Dynamics in Brussels (1956). He was instrumental in recognizing the importance of swept-back wings in modern jet aircraft and made significant contributions to theories of non-elastic buckling, unsteady wakes in circum-cylinder flow, stability of laminar flow, turbulence, airfoils in steady and unsteady flow, boundary layers, and supersonic aerodynamics, as well as to elasticity, vibration, heat transfer, and crystallography. In June 1944, Kármán underwent surgery for intestinal cancer in New York City, which caused two hernias and resulted in a slow recovery; in September, while still in New York, he met U.S. Army Air Forces Commanding General Henry H. Arnold on a runway at LaGuardia Airport, who proposed that Kármán move to Washington, D.C. to lead the Scientific Advisory Group and serve as a long-range planning consultant. Kármán returned to Pasadena in mid-September, was appointed to the SAG position on October 23, 1944, and left Caltech in December 1944. At age 81, he received the first National Medal of Science in a White House ceremony by President John F. Kennedy, recognized for his leadership in aeronautical science and engineering, effective teaching, distinguished counsel to the Armed Services, and promotion of international cooperation in science and engineering. Kármán never married; he died on a trip to Aachen, Germany, in 1963, and his body was returned to the United States to be entombed in the Beth Olam Mausoleum at Hollywood Forever Cemetery. He has sometimes been described as one of The Martians. His fame stemmed from using mathematical tools to study fluid flow and interpreting results to guide practical designs. His autobiography, *The Wind and Beyond*, published in 1965 by Lee Edson with Little, Brown and Company, received enthusiastic reviews from J. Kestin, who advised readers to study it as a reference, while Charles Süsskind criticized it for lacking engagement with Wernher von Braun’s arrival in America and the Hsue-shen Tsien affair, and labeled Kármán a militarist due to his lifelong association with military authorities. Sydney Goldstein, who wrote the Royal Society memoir, remembered Kármán as a warm-hearted, witty, internationally recognized engineer and scientist who found the military to be the most comfortable group to work with. On creativity, Kármán wrote that the finest creative thought arises from the quiet of one’s own world, and I. B. Holley noted his penetrating insights into the creative process, while also noting his fondness for convivial drinking and the company of beautiful women.

Therapy is the second studio album by English singer-songwriter Anne-Marie, released on 23 July 2021 through Major Tom's, Asylum Records, and Atlantic Records. It is a pop record produced by TMS, who also produced her debut album Speak Your Mind (2018), alongside Digital Farm Animals, Mojam, Nathan Dawe, Grades, Sire Noah, Lostboye, Cameron Gower Poole, Oak, Jean-Marie, Rudimental, Elvira Anderfjärd, Blake Slatkin, and Fred Ball. The album features guest appearances from Digital Farm Animals, Nathan Dawe, Rudimental, KSI, Little Mix, Niall Horan (formerly of One Direction), and MoStack, with Raye providing backing vocals on the opening track, "x2". Before its release, four non-album singles were released, including "To Be Young" featuring Doja Cat. The album was supported by four singles: "Don't Play" (featuring KSI and Digital Farm Animals), released on 15 January 2021, peaked at number 2 on the UK Singles Chart (Anne-Marie's highest-charting single as of 2025), number 9 in Ireland, and was certified Platinum in the UK; "Way Too Long" (featuring Nathan Dawe and MoStack), released on 9 April 2021, peaked at number 37 in both the UK and Ireland and was certified Silver; "Our Song" (featuring Niall Horan), released on 21 May 2021, peaked at number 13 in the UK and number 7 in Ireland, and was certified Platinum in the UK; and "Kiss My (Uh-Oh)", released on 23 July 2021, peaked at number 10 on the UK Singles Chart and was certified Platinum. The album received generally favorable reviews from critics, who praised the guest appearances and Anne-Marie's vocals but criticized its lack of a unique sound and confusing direction. Commercially, it charted higher in the UK than her debut, peaking at number 2 on the UK Albums Chart, and reached number 4 and 2 in Ireland and Scotland, and number 3 on Ultratop's Belgian Albums Chart in Flanders. It was certified Gold by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) for 100,000 equivalent units sold. To promote the album, Anne-Marie embarked on the Dysfunctional Tour, which featured Gracey, Billen Ted, and Mimi Webb, and a deluxe edition was later released, including the non-album singles "To Be Young" with Doja Cat and "Birthday," along with a guest appearance from JJ Lin. Planning for the album began in 2019; in a March 2019 interview with Music Week, Anne-Marie stated she had spent a week in the studio "having therapy with her own brain" and emphasized writing fresh, unreleased material, contrasting with the more curated approach of her debut. During 2020, she released standalone singles "Birthday," "Her," "To Be Young" (featuring Doja Cat), and "Problems," with "Birthday" and "To Be Young" later included in the Japanese edition of Therapy. On 15 January 2021, "Don't Play" was released as the lead single; on 9 April 2021, "Way Too Long" followed; on 21 May 2021, "Our Song" was released, and Anne-Marie announced the title, cover art, and release date of Therapy. She later announced the Dysfunctional Tour for 3 to 11 May 2022 and Therapy: The Live Experience on 7 August 2021. On 6 July 2021, Anne-Marie launched a fan-driven website to determine the track listing, with new tracks revealed daily; on 7 July, followers received DMs with snippets and partial titles of songs, with "Kiss My (Uh-Oh)" revealed on 8 July, featuring Little Mix and sampling Lumidee's "Never Leave You (Uh Oooh, Uh Oooh)," announced as the fourth single on 9 July with a release date of 23 July. A snippet was shared on TikTok, the cover was revealed on 21 July, and the music video, directed by Hannah Lux Davis, parodied the 2011 film Bridesmaids. The album is described as genre-hopping pop, drawing from trance, indie, electronic, trap, UK garage, and pop rock. "x2" begins soulfully before turning into a revenge track; "Don't Play" is a 2-step-influenced UK garage track about heartache; "Kiss My (Uh-Oh)" is a calypso-pop song compared to Beyoncé; "Who I Am" is a defiant, self-accepting pop song; "Unlovable" with Rudimental is a "fist-pumping" dance track; "Beautiful" features lyrics about insecurities with swaying percussion; "Tell Your Girlfriend" and "Better Not Together" explore turning heartbreak into self-confidence; and the title track is a trop-pop closer. On 28 May 2021, Anne-Marie announced the Dysfunctional Tour for 3 to 11 May 2022 across the UK and Ireland, with tickets released to the public on 4 June at 10 am BST and pre-sale tickets available from 2 to 4 June (for London and Leeds only); North American dates were announced on 30 November 2021, European shows on 7 June 2022, and the Asian leg on 15 July 2022. In September 2022, both European and North American legs were cancelled due to scheduling conflicts, though no official statement was issued; the tour ultimately ran for two legs and 11 shows, with Gracey, Billen Ted, and Mimi Webb as supporting acts during the UK & Ireland leg. The setlist from Dublin on 3 May 2022 does not represent the full tour. At Metacritic, Therapy has an average score of 65 based on six reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews." Ali Shutler of NME praised it as more confident than her debut, giving it four out of five stars; Robin Murray of Clash rated it seven out of ten, noting it pushes her story forward but lacks a singular sound; Ben Devlin of musicOMH gave it four out of five stars, highlighting Anne-Marie's ability to unify diverse sounds with her relatable delivery. Lauren Murphy of The Irish Times was slightly more mixed, criticizing "Beautiful" and "Better Not Together," but noted most tracks "land with a thud." Dani Blum of Pitchfork called it "crisply rendered and competently hooky," though it "promises a more personal self-portrait" that ends in vague songwriting and anodyne dance-pop. Michael Cragg of The Guardian called it a "missed opportunity," criticizing the heavy use of collaborators and giving it two out of five stars. In its first week, Therapy opened at number two on the UK Albums Chart with 18,260 sales (12,463 physical copies), and by the end of 2021, it was at number 98. It was certified Gold by the BPI for 100,000 units. In Australia, it charted at number 60 on the ARIA Charts; in New Zealand at number 36; in Austria at number 15; in Belgium at number 50 in Wallonia and number 3 in Flanders; in the Netherlands at number 19; in France at number 135; in Germany at number 22; in Hungary at number 5; in Ireland at number 4; in Lithuania at number 54; in Slovakia at number 78; in Spain at number 76; in Switzerland at number 36; in Japan at number 178 on the Japanese Albums Chart and number 66 on the Billboard Japan Hot Albums chart; and in Scotland at number 2.

Theresa Aba Kufuor (née Mensah; 25 October 1935 – 1 October 2023) was the wife of John Kufuor, the second President of the Fourth Republic of Ghana, and served as First Lady of Ghana from 2001 to 2009. She was a nurse and midwife. Born Theresa Mensah on 25 October 1935, she was the youngest child in her family, with her older brother being Joseph Henry Mensah, an economist and New Patriotic Party politician. She began her education at the Catholic Convent, OLA, in Keta, Volta Region, Ghana, and later studied in London, where she became a Registered General Nurse at the Southern Hospital Group of Nursing in Edinburgh, Scotland. She further trained at the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford and Paddington General Hospital in London, qualifying as a State Certified Midwife with a Certificate in Premature Nursing. Theresa married John Kufuor when he was 23 after meeting him at a Republic Day Anniversary Dance in London in 1961; they married in 1962. Together, they had five children: J. Addo Kufuor, Nana Ama Gyamfi, Saah Kufuor, Agyekum Kufuor, and Owusu Afriyie Kufuor. She was a mother of five and a grandmother of eight, and a devout Roman Catholic. Despite serving as First Lady for eight years between 2001 and 2009, she maintained a low political profile. In 2007, she advocated for policy changes in the Government's white paper on Educational Reforms to implement UNESCO's Free Compulsory Universal Basic Education (FCUBE) program for kindergarten children. John Kufuor founded the Mother and Child Community Development Foundation (MCCDF), a non-governmental organization operating in Ghana and Canada that supports work in preventing mother-to-child transmission. Theresa Kufuor died at her home in Peduase on 1 October 2023, at the age of 87. Her funeral took place on November 16 at Accra's State House, featuring hymns and tributes, followed by the transportation of her remains to Kumasi for a three-day funeral at Heroes Park, culminating in her burial in the Ashanti Regional capital. On 25 October 2010, Pope Benedict XVI awarded her husband, President John Kufuor, the Papal Award of Knight Commander of St. Gregory the Great for his service to mankind and the Catholic Church, and conferred on Theresa Kufuor the Papal Award Dame of St. Gregory the Great for her commitment to the plight of poor children and their mothers.

These Two Windows is the debut studio album by American singer Alec Benjamin. The album was released by Warner Music on May 29, 2020, and reached number 75 on the Billboard 200. On the UK Albums Chart, it debuted at No. 52 with 1,677 sales units, representing Benjamin's first appearance on that chart.

Third Day is a Christian rock band formed in Marietta, Georgia in 1991 by lead singer Mac Powell, guitarist Mark Lee, and pianist Billy Wilkins. The band's name references the biblical resurrection of Jesus on the third day after his crucifixion. In 1992, they performed at a church event with the Bullard Family Singers, featuring David Carr and Tai Anderson, who were later invited to join the band. In 1993, they began playing regularly in the Atlanta area to fund album recording; Wilkins left to pursue teaching. Their debut album, Long Time Forgotten, was recorded at Furies Studios with production help from Carr and sold 2,000 copies. In 1994, they added August McCoy as a second guitarist and released the self-financed album Contagious for $3,000, which included 1,000 CDs and cassettes; McCoy left that year to attend college. At a show in Marietta, they signed with Gray Dot Records, releasing the album Third Day that sold 20,000 copies; Reunion Records later bought the contract and signed them for a multi-album deal. In 1995, Brad Avery joined after auditioning and playing "Consuming Fire," and the official version of Third Day was released, selling over 300,000 copies and earning a mainstream rock hit, "Nothing at All," which reached No. 34 on the Billboard rock charts. The band opened for Newsboys on five West Coast shows and launched a 65-city tour with All Star United and Seven Day Jesus. In 1996, they were nominated for a Dove Award for New Artist of the Year and won a Billboard Music Award for the "Consuming Fire" video, shot in Bombay Beach and around the Salton Sea, which later inspired the artwork for Revelation. In 1997, they began work on Conspiracy No. 5 with producer Sam Taylor, which was Grammy-nominated and won Dove Awards for Rock Album of the Year and Rock Song of the Year ("Alien"). In 1998, they worked with Monroe Jones, whose produced album Time was Grammy-nominated and won a Dove Award; songs left out were released on the EP Southern Tracks. They released Offerings: A Worship Album, recorded in a week, and toured with Jennifer Knapp in 2000. That year, they also collaborated on City on a Hill: Songs of Worship and Praise with FFH, Caedmon's Call, SonicFlood, Jars of Clay, and others. In 2001, they toured Australia and New Zealand following the success of Offerings and recorded a concert with 15,000 fans at the HiFi Buys Amphitheatre, released as The Offerings Experience. The year also saw them win five Dove Awards and their first Grammy, with the album Come Together winning two Dove Awards and a Grammy, and being certified gold the following year. The band appeared in the 2002 film Joshua, with "My Hope is You" included in the soundtrack. In 2003, they released Offerings II: All I Have to Give. In 2004, they released Wire, toured with tobyMac and Warren Barfield, and went to Europe for a two-week tour; they recorded a live concert in Louisville and released it as Live Wire. They also contributed to the soundtrack of Mel Gibson's The Passion of the Christ, played at the Republican National Convention, and were featured on 60 Minutes. In January 2007, they performed in Melbourne, Brisbane, and Sydney, Australia. Their album Wherever You Are debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200 and won their third Grammy. In 2006, they released their first Christmas-themed album, Christmas Offerings, and in 2007, their first hits compilation, Chronology. On February 28, 2008, Brad Avery announced his departure after 13 years and over 1,000 concerts to pursue solo projects, and the band continued as a quartet. They performed at the 2008 Papal Youth Rally in Yonkers, N.Y. In support of the July 29, 2008, release of Revelation, they performed on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno and The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson. "Call My Name" reached No. 1 and was the fifth most-played song on R&R's Christian CHR chart in 2008. In April 2009, they released Live Revelations, a live version of Revelation, and were inducted into the Georgia Music Hall of Fame on September 19, 2009. Live Revelations won the Grammy for Best Rock or Rap Gospel Album, their fourth Grammy, and was certified Gold, becoming their eighth Gold album. In 2010, they appeared at Winter Jam with the Newsboys, Fireflight, and Tenth Avenue North, released the single "Lift Up Your Face," and released their tenth studio album, Move, on October 19. They concluded the Make a Difference Tour 2010 with TobyMac, Michael W. Smith, Jason Gray, and Max Lucado in Fayetteville, NC. The song "Follow Me There" from Move became the theme song for the TLC show Sarah Palin's Alaska, which debuted in 2010. In 2012, they released Miracle, touring with Colton Dixon and Josh Wilson from February 21, 2013, to May 19, 2014. In 2015, they released the worship album Lead Us Back: Songs of Worship, produced by The Sound Kids, which peaked at No. 20 on the Billboard 200, No. 1 on the Christian Albums chart, No. 5 on the Top Rock Albums chart, and No. 13 on the Digital Albums chart; the single "Soul on Fire" spent 19 weeks on the Billboard charts, peaking at No. 2 on Hot Christian Songs and No. 3 on Christian Digital Songs. In 2015, bassist Tai Anderson announced a break from touring after 23 years with the band. To celebrate their 25th anniversary, they released their thirteenth and final album, Revival, on August 4, 2017, recorded at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, and reunited with producer Monroe Jones. On March 2, 2018, the band announced a farewell tour with 12 shows, later expanded to 20 concerts, with the final show in Denver on June 27, 2018. In June 2025, they announced a reunion with the lineup of Mac Powell, Mark Lee, David Carr, and Tai Anderson to celebrate their 30th anniversary, with a limited tour beginning in spring 2026. As of 2020, the band has earned 4 Grammy Awards and 25 Dove Awards. They have sold over 7 million albums in the United States and had 28 number one Christian album chart hits. Their fans are known as "Gomers" after a song on their second album about Gomer. The band was inducted into the Georgia Music Hall of Fame on September 19, 2009.

Thomas Chrowder Chamberlin (/ˈkraʊdər/; September 25, 1843 – November 15, 1928) was an American geologist and educator who founded the Journal of Geology in 1893 and served as its editor for many years. Born in Mattoon, Illinois, he moved to near Beloit, Wisconsin, when he was three years old. His father was a Methodist circuit minister and farmer. Chamberlin attended a preparatory academy before studying at Beloit College, where he received a classical education in Greek and Latin and developed an interest in natural science. While at Beloit, he directed a church choir and participated in athletics and debate. After graduating in 1866, he worked as a teacher and later principal in a high school near Beloit and married Alma Wilson in 1867. From 1868 to 1869, he took graduate courses in geology at the University of Michigan. He then served as professor of natural science at Whitewater Normal School from 1869 to 1873, joined the Beloit faculty in 1873 as professor of geology, zoology, and botany, and became one of several part-time participants in a comprehensive geological survey of Wisconsin. His geological mapping in southeastern Wisconsin, which had thick glacial deposits, led him to identify multiple episodes of glaciation during the Pleistocene, a terminology still in use with minor modifications. In 1875, he started a business with his brother selling spring water. In 1876, he became chief geologist for the Wisconsin geological survey, supervising the completion of a four-volume report in which he authored sections on glacial deposits, Paleozoic and Precambrian bedrock geology, lead-zinc ore deposits, artesian wells, and soils, bringing him national attention and leading to his appointment as head of the glacial division of the US Geological Survey in 1881. He later served as president of the University of Wisconsin from 1887 to 1892. In 1890 and again in 1897, Chamberlin published "The method of multiple working hypotheses," advocating the evaluation of several hypotheses simultaneously, rejecting those inconsistent with data, and concluding with the one supported by evidence—contrasting with the "single ruling theory" that encouraged uncritical acceptance of a dominant hypothesis. The paper is considered a landmark in the scientific method, inspired the strong inference approach, and was reprinted in 1965. In 1892, he accepted a position to organize a geology department at the University of Chicago, where he remained a professor until 1918. From 1898 to 1914, he served as president of the Chicago Academy of Sciences. In 1899, he wrote "An Attempt to Frame a Working Hypothesis of the Cause of Glacial Periods on an Atmospheric Basis," proposing that climate changes could result from variations in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration, noting that during warming after glacial episodes, oceans release carbon dioxide, accelerating climate improvement. He observed notable fluctuations in the total mass of living matter over geological periods, suggesting that life activity was greatest during times of sea extension and mild climates and least during climatic disruptions, which counteracted the carbon dioxide effects. He concluded that agencies capable of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at rates above normal during certain times could cause glaciation, and agencies capable of restoring it during other times could produce mild climates. Chamberlin was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1901 and the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1903. In 1905, he and Forest Ray Moulton proposed the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis, challenging the Laplacian nebular hypothesis; it received favorable support for nearly a third of a century but fell out of favor by the late 1930s and was ultimately discarded in the 1940s due to incompatibility with Jupiter’s angular momentum, though the idea that planetesimals gradually collided to form planets through accretion remains well-regarded. Chamberlin also concluded that Earth was much older than Lord Kelvin’s estimate of about 100 million years, and his speculations about the Sun’s energy source—derived from internal atomic processes—were prescient. In 1905, he was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In 1909, he and his son Rollin Thomas Chamberlin traveled to the East as members of the Oriental Educational Investigation Commission led by Ernest DeWitt Burton and supported by John D. Rockefeller to assess Eastern regions for potential humanitarian projects of the Rockefeller Foundation. Chamberlin received the inaugural Penrose Gold Medal of the Society of Economic Geologists in 1924 and the inaugural Penrose Medal of the Geological Society of America in 1927. He served as president of the Geological Society of America in 1894. He remained professionally active until his death in Chicago on November 15, 1928. His papers are held at the University of Chicago and Beloit College archives, with the latter also containing the papers of his son, Rollin T. Chamberlin (1881–1948), who was a geologist and later chaired the geology department at the University of Chicago. Buildings are named for him at Beloit College and the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and a house in Burton-Judson Courts at the University of Chicago bears his name. The lunar crater Chamberlin and a Martian crater are named in his honor, and Mount Chamberlin in California is named after him. A 42-ton Precambrian glacial erratic known as the Chamberlin Rock stood on Observatory Hill at the University of Wisconsin–Madison for over 100 years before being moved to a university property on Lake Kegonsa in 2021.

Thomas Eisner (June 25, 1929 – March 25, 2011) was a German-American entomologist and ecologist known as the "father of chemical ecology." He held the Jacob Gould Schurman Professorship in Chemical Ecology at Cornell University and served as director of the Cornell Institute for Research in Chemical Ecology (CIRCE). A world authority on animal behavior, ecology, and evolution, Eisner, along with his Cornell colleague Jerrold Meinwald, was a pioneer in chemical ecology, the study of chemical interactions among organisms. He authored or co-authored 400 scientific articles and seven books. Born in Berlin, Germany, on June 25, 1929, Eisner's father, Hans Eisner, was a Jewish chemist who worked with Fritz Haber at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Electrochemistry and later held a chemistry chair at Cornell; his mother, Margarete Heil-Eisner, was an artist. After escaping the Nazi regime, the family moved to Barcelona and then to Uruguay, before relocating to the United States in 1947. Eisner became a naturalized American citizen and, though rejected as an undergraduate at Cornell, earned his B.S. and PhD from Harvard University. He joined Cornell's entomology faculty in 1957 and married Maria Eisner, a member of his lab. In 1964, he helped establish the Department of Neurobiology and Behavior, where he worked until his death. A passionate nature photographer and videographer, Eisner's film *Secret Weapons* won the Grand Award at the New York Film Festival and was named Best Science Film by the British Association for the Advancement of Science. He was also an avid pianist and occasional conductor. Eisner died on March 25, 2011, from Parkinson's disease. He was an atheist. His primary research focused on chemical defenses in insects against predation, including his discovery that the bombardier beetle produces a chemical reaction to expel a boiling, noxious liquid from a nozzle in its abdomen. With field experience across four continents, Eisner was an active conservationist, serving on the boards of the National Audubon Society, the National Scientific Council of the Nature Conservancy, and the World Resources Institute Council. He was past president of the American Society of Naturalists and chairman of the Biology Section of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and played a key role in launching the Congressional Fellow Program in Washington, D.C., as well as in preserving wilderness areas in Florida and Texas. He was a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Philosophical Society. Eisner received numerous honors, including the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement, the Harvard Centennial Medal, the 1994 National Medal of Science, and the Lewis Thomas Prize for Writing about Science. He held honorary degrees from universities in Sweden, Germany, Switzerland, and the United States and was a foreign fellow of the Royal Society. He was also a member of the Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher Leopoldina and Academia Europaea. In 2008, he was awarded the John J. Carty Award by the National Academy of Sciences.

Thomas Randolph (1523–1590) was an English ambassador to Elizabeth I of England and spent much of his professional life in Scotland, serving at the courts of Mary, Queen of Scots, and her son James VI. He was involved in marriage negotiations and various political upheavals. Between 1568 and 1569, he was sent on a special mission to Russia, where he visited the court of Ivan the Terrible and secured privileges for English merchants, leading to the formation of the Muscovy Company. Randolph served as a Member of Parliament for New Romney in 1558, Maidstone in 1584, 1586, and 1589, Grantham in 1559, St Ives in 1558 and 1572. Born in 1523 to Avery Randolph of Badlesmere, Kent, and Anne Gainsford (not the lady-in-waiting to Anne Boleyn), he entered Christ Church, Oxford at its foundation, graduated with a B.A. in October 1545 and a B.C.L. in 1548, became a public notary, and was principal of Broadgates Hall (now Pembroke College), Oxford until 1553. Due to Protestant persecutions under Queen Mary, he resigned and retired to France, where he resided in Paris and was influenced by George Buchanan, whom he praised in a letter to Peter Young, tutor of James VI. Among his fellow students in Paris was Sir William Kirkcaldy of Grange. After Elizabeth's accession in 1558, Randolph acted as an agent in Germany before returning to England and purchasing a farm in Kent—the house where he was born. His knowledge of Scottish Protestants in Paris led Elizabeth to employ him in bringing the Earl of Arran from Geneva to England. He sometimes signed his letters with the Latin phrase "Virtus pro divitiis," which he wrote in a copy of John Jewel's Apologia ecclesiae Anglicanae (1562), now held by the University of Edinburgh. Under the name Barnabie and using the codename Pamphilus, he was sent in autumn 1559 to secretly transport James Hamilton, 3rd Earl of Arran, into Scotland. He returned to London on 25 November but was again sent to Scotland in March 1560, where his efforts influenced Protestant opposition to the queen-regent and helped establish an understanding with Elizabeth. His continued role as a confidential agent for Elizabeth, and also for William Cecil, the secretary of state, gave him significant influence in Scottish politics despite lacking diplomatic skill compared to Maitland of Lethington. His numerous letters remain vital sources on the Queen of Scots' court, political plots, and social intrigues. At the marriage of Lord James Stewart and Agnes Keith in February 1562, Mary toasted Elizabeth from a gold cup and presented it to Randolph, discussing the "amity" between England and Scotland; Mary was also sent a portrait of Elizabeth, which Randolph verified. In autumn 1562, Randolph accompanied Mary on a northern expedition that resulted in the defeat and death of George Gordon, 4th Earl of Huntly, and he participated in the campaign, stating he was "ashamed to sit still where so many were occupied." In January 1563, he attended the wedding of James Stewart, Commendator of Inchcolm, and Margaret Campbell at Castle Campbell, describing feasts, banqueting, masking, and running at the ring. In June 1563, he met a servant of Catholic priest John Black at St Andrews, bribed him to reveal correspondence, and copied it. On 5 June 1563, Elizabeth granted him a license to return to England for private business. In April 1563, he was sent to Scotland to entangle Mary in marriage negotiations with Lord Robert Dudley, Elizabeth's favourite; initially unenthusiastic, Mary eventually accepted the proposal after Elizabeth declared her official heir on the condition of marriage. In September 1564, Elizabeth granted Dudley the earldom of Leicester to improve his appeal, and in early 1565, Mary accepted the match. However, Dudley refused to marry Mary and showed passive resistance, which Randolph repeatedly tried to overcome through letters. Elizabeth later withdrew her support for the succession declaration. When Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, became a serious candidate, Elizabeth sought to prevent the marriage, and Randolph received instructions to push for a union with Dudley or another noble; if the proposal was irreversible, he was to report how it would distress her. Randolph reported on a Roman antiquity discovered near Edinburgh at Musselburgh, including an inscribed altar and hypocaust, and courted Mary Beaton, one of Mary's companions. In April 1565, Beaton and Randolph played bowls at Stirling Castle with the queen and Darnley, winning and receiving a ring and brooch worth fifty crowns from Darnley. A letter from Alexander Clark mocked their relationship with nonsense words: "And as to your mistress Marie Beton, she is both darimpus and sclenbrunit, and you in like manner without contrebaxion or kylteperante, so you are both worth little money." Randolph failed to prevent Mary's marriage to Darnley and declined to recognize Darnley's authority. His representations may have contributed to the rebellion of James Stewart, 1st Earl of Moray, known as the Chaseabout Raid. On 16 January 1566, he reported that Mary had withheld the "Matrimonial crown" from Darnley and was now pregnant, noting she felt the movement on New Year's Day and had milk in her breasts. On 14 February 1566, he wrote to the Earl of Leicester that he could not commit to writing about Mary's actions due to fear of appearing "malicieus foolyshe and unadvised." In February 1566, Mary accused him of aiding Moray and her rebels with a gift of three thousand crowns, requiring him to leave the country within six days. He retired to Berwick upon Tweed, where after Riccio's murder, he was accused of writing a book against Mary called Mr. Randolph's Phantasy. He was recalled to England around June 1566 and appointed "Master of the King's Post," later becoming postmaster general. On 2 November 1567, he obtained from Robert Constable an assignment as constable of Queenborough Castle and steward of the manor of Middleton and Merden in Kent. In June 1568, he was sent to Russia to support English merchants, securing privileges from Ivan IV that led to the Muscovy Company's formation; he returned in autumn 1569. Following representations by Regent Moray's agent Nicolas Elphinstone in January 1570, he was sent to Scotland despite uncertain news of Moray's assassination. He remained in Scotland for a year. In October 1573 and April 1576, he conducted special embassies to France. In February 1578, he was sent to Scotland but too late to prevent the fall of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton. After Morton's imprisonment in 1580, he returned to Scotland to negotiate on his behalf. At a convention of the estates on 20 February 1581, he presented a paper on the Queen's intentions and offers to the King of Scotland and delivered a two-hour speech denouncing Esme Stewart, created Duke of Lennox, as a Roman agent. His bold action only sealed Morton's fate. He then attempted, with Elizabeth's approval, to plot the seizure of Lennox and the young king, but the plot was betrayed, and he fled to Berwick after narrowly escaping death from a shot fired in the provost's house in Edinburgh. His advice directly influenced English policy, advising Elizabeth against military intervention in Scotland against the Lennox government. In January 1586, he was sent on his final mission to Scotland with Thomas Mills to negotiate a treaty between England and Scotland, which he successfully secured through the signature of James VI despite opposition from French diplomat Charles de Prunelé, Baron d'Esneval. In August 1586, Randolph and the Scottish ambassador Archibald Douglas sent male deer and huntsmen to James VI at Falkland Palace; the huntsmen likely included Cuthbert Rayne. He wrote: "I have sent the Kynge two hunting men, verie good and skillful, with one footman, that can hoop, hollow and crye, that all the trees in Fawkland will quake for fear. Pray the Kynge's Majestie to be mercifull to the poor bucks; but let him spare and look well to himself." He presented £4,000 to James VI from Elizabeth, the first regular subsidy, noting that James VI, like previous regents, did not issue receipts for such payments, explaining that princes avoid "bills of their hands" to prevent "danger or reproach." Randolph held the joint offices of Chamberlain of the Exchequer and Master of the Post until his death on 8 June 1590, at age sixty-seven, in his house on St. Peter's Hill, near Thames Street, London, and was buried in the church of St. Peter's, Paul's Wharf. Throughout his embassies, he was frequently short of money and struggled to pay expenses. Despite his significant services, he received no substantial reward beyond these modest offices. The claim that he was knighted in 1571 is not supported by evidence. He is believed to have authored the original short Latin Life of George Buchanan, though this is at least doubtful; he showed strong interest in Buchanan's History and offered financial support for its completion. In July 1593, the Scottish ambassador, with Roger Aston, claimed that Randolph had promised in 1586 to pay James VI an annual subsidy of £5,000, a claim William Cecil deemed unlikely and which prompted a search of Randolph's papers. In late 1571, he married Anne Walsingham, daughter of Thomas Walsingham of Chislehurst and cousin once removed of Francis Walsingham. Before the marriage, on 1 October 1571, he received letters patent from Thomas Walsingham and William Crowner granting custody of the manor and hundred of Middleton and Merden at a rent of 100 pounds per annum to be paid to his wife. In 1572, he was appointed Chamberlain of the Exchequer for life. His friend George Buchanan teased him about the marriage, saying: "If you had been in your right wit, you being once escaped the tempestous storms and naufrage (shipwreck) of marriage, had never entered again the same dangers, for I cannot take you for a Stoic philosopher, having one head inexpugnable (not to be captured) with the frenetic tortures of jealousy, or a careless heart sceptic that takes cuckoldry as thing indifferent." Their children included: Thomas Randolph married secondly Ursula Copinger, daughter of Henry Copinger of Allhallows Hoo, Kent, and Buxhall, Suffolk, and his wife Agnes, daughter of Thomas Jermyn (died 1552); their children are listed. Randolph died in 1590.

Thomas Ryder (1746–1810), an engraver, studied under James Basire and, during his apprenticeship, submitted drawings to the Society of Artists in 1766 and 1767. He was among the first students at the Royal Academy's schools. Ryder produced a few engravings in the line manner, including "The Politician" (a portrait of Benjamin Franklin) after S. Elmer in 1782, and "Vortigern and Rowena" after A. Kauffman in 1802. However, he is most renowned for his stipple engravings, which are considered some of the finest in their category. These include "The Last Supper" after Benjamin West, "The Murder of James I of Scotland" after Opie, "Prudence and Beauty" after A. Kauffman, nine plates from the large edition of Boydell's "Shakspeare," and others based on designs by Bigg, Bunbury, Cipriani, Cosway, Ryley, and Shelley. He also engraved portraits of Mrs. Damer after Kauffman, Henry Bunbury after Lawrence, Sir William Watson, M.D., after Abbot, and Maria Linley after Westall. His engravings were typically printed in brown ink and sometimes in colour. Ryder had a son with the same name who was also an engraver, and together they created the whole-length portrait of Queen Charlotte after Beechey, which appeared as a front piece in the second volume of Boydell's ‘Shakspeare.’ This article draws from a now-public domain publication: "Ryder, Thomas (1746-1810)" in the Dictionary of National Biography, London: Smith, Elder & Co., 1885–1900. This article is a stub about a British engraver, etcher, or printmaker and can be expanded with additional information.

To Serve and Protect, also known as Under Arrest on streaming platforms, is a Canadian reality crime television series that follows city police in Edmonton, Alberta; Winnipeg, Manitoba; Vancouver, Penticton, New Westminster, Summerland, and Surrey, British Columbia. A few episodes include visits to Las Vegas and Memphis. The program premiered on KVOS-TV in 1993 using footage recorded in 1991 and 1992 and is based on the American series Cops. Created by Dwayne Mitchell and Dan Forrer for KF Media Inc., it debuted in 1993 on KVOS-TV in Bellingham, Washington. Most viewers were in the Vancouver, British Columbia region. Mitchell filmed five hundred "ride alongs" during the program’s first two years. KVOS aired it on Sunday nights in the 1990s and weeknights at midnight in the early 2000s. Future Edmonton Police whistleblower Derek Huff appeared on the show. With a new audience on Netflix, the program is now regarded as a camp classic due to its dramatic characters and 1990s aesthetic. As of 2023, 26 episodes are available for streaming on Peacock. After the first season, the Vancouver Police Department refused ride-along access because the production company refused to blur suspects' faces; police constable Anne Drenan stated that Forrer’s negative attitude after the request to black out faces led to the police board ending participation. The provincial government ruled that broadcasting a suspect’s face without consent was illegal. The original version of To Serve and Protect was cancelled in 1995; executive producer Dan Forrer attributed the cancellation to "senior officers in the Vancouver police department and RCMP." He claimed the final episode included footage that Vancouver Police Chief Ray Canuel had wanted the public to see, and that the chief sought to end access to ride-alongs because the prior chief, Bill Marshall, had approved the show. The program captured several instances of excessive force and illegal maneuvers, which were aired as routine, causing concern for the new police chief who was distressed by the negative portrayal of his force. Forrer and Mitchell secured access to other departments and began new episodes in 1997, with the RCMP of Surrey, British Columbia, featured prominently. Located thirty minutes east of Vancouver, Surrey was known for mullets, mustaches, and alcohol-related incidents, often compared to Heavy Metal Parking Lot and Trailer Park Boys. Some of the most memorable moments occurred in Surrey episodes, leading the Surrey City Council to revoke filming permission and request removal of all Surrey-based episodes from KVOS reruns. Councillor Judy Villeneuve stated that repeatedly airing the same incidents gave the impression that such events still occur and that the show unfairly portrayed Surrey as "crime-ridden." Forrer responded that he would not accept the suggestion to stop showing the content, calling it "ludicrous," and argued that if the city is pressuring the show, it is also pressuring the police. However, the Surrey RCMP had been troubled for months and suspended participation in November 1997, citing that the show did not present a balanced view of police work but instead focused on sensational incidents. Forrer acknowledged the show was unrehearsed but admitted it was formatted for maximum television impact. He stated that they simply entered police cars and followed dispatches, noting that what they showed was not 100 per cent of reality, nor was it entirely different from what viewers see on BCTV News. He added that some individuals appear multiple times because they repeatedly cause trouble and that he has no sympathy for them, attributing this to "bleeding hearts and political correctness" and the fact that the show embarrasses or exposes some offenders. In 1997, Dwayne Mitchell sold a syndicated, half-hour version of the program to American markets under the title Mounties: True Stories of the Royal Canadian Police, which aired in eighty regional markets including Elko, Nevada; St. Joseph, Missouri; Salina, Kansas; Tucson, Arizona; West Palm Beach, Florida; and Agana, Guam.
