It generally aired around 2 a.m., and Forrer referred to it as "filler" for the American market. The show is currently available on video-on-demand platforms such as Netflix, Peacock, The Roku Channel, Pluto TV, Crackle, Tubi, and Amazon Freevee (with the latter six versions provided by FilmRise) under the title Under Arrest, with episodes condensed from their original hour length into eight "Best of" seasons, each episode running 20 minutes.

Tonya Maxene Price, born November 12, 1970, in Portland, Oregon, is an American former figure skater, boxer, and reality television personality. She was raised in East Portland by her mother, LaVona Golden (born 1940), and father, Albert Harding (1933–2009), who held various odd jobs and was often underemployed due to poor health. Harding began ice skating at age three with coach Diane Rawlinson and also learned hunting, drag racing, and auto mechanics from her father. LaVona struggled to support the family, hand-sewing her daughter’s skating costumes to save money, and the couple divorced after 19 years in 1987 when Harding was 16. She dropped out of Milwaukie High School during her sophomore year to focus on skating and earned a GED in 1988. Harding claimed she suffered frequent physical and psychological abuse from her mother, with LaVona admitting to one instance of hitting her at an ice rink. In her 2008 biography, The Tonya Tapes, she stated she was the victim of acquaintance rape in 1991 and that her half-brother, Chris Davison, molested her as a child; she reported the abuse in 1986, and Davison was briefly imprisoned before being killed in an unsolved hit-and-run in 1988. She later said Davison was the only person in her life she hated and unworthy of forgiveness. Harding trained with Rawlinson through the mid-1980s, placing sixth in 1986, fifth in 1987 and 1988, and third in 1989. After the 1989 Nationals, she trained with Dody Teachman and won Skate America in October 1989. In 1991, she completed her first triple Axel in competition on February 16, becoming the first American woman to do so and the second woman in history (after Midori Ito) to land it internationally. She won the 1991 U.S. Ladies' Singles title with the event’s first 6.0 technical merit score since Janet Lynn’s 1973 performance and finished second at the March 1991 World Championships behind Kristi Yamaguchi and ahead of Nancy Kerrigan, marking the first time one country swept the ladies’ medal podium. At the September 1991 Skate America, she recorded three more firsts. Despite these achievements, she never successfully completed the triple Axel again after 1991, and her results declined. She placed third at the January 1992 U.S. Championships despite a twisted ankle and finished fourth at the February 1992 Winter Olympics. On March 1, 1992, she dismissed Teachman and returned to Rawlinson. She placed sixth at the 1992 World Championships and fourth at the November 1992 Skate Canada International. In the 1993 season, she skated poorly at the U.S. Championships and failed to qualify for the World team. In January 1994, she won the U.S. Championships but was later stripped of the title when the USFSA voted to vacate it in June 1994 following an investigation into the attack on Nancy Kerrigan. Despite the controversy, she remained on the U.S. Olympic team for the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer. After a broken skate lace in her long program, she was given a re-skate and finished eighth, behind Oksana Baiul (gold) and Nancy Kerrigan (silver). On January 6, 1994, one day before the U.S. Championships, Kerrigan was attacked in a corridor at the Detroit Cobo Arena by Shane Stant, who used a 21-inch ASP telescopic baton to strike her right leg above the knee. Stant, hired by Harding’s ex-husband Jeff Gillooly and bodyguard Shawn Eckardt, turned himself in on January 14. The attack was intended to prevent Kerrigan from competing in the Nationals or Olympics. On January 11, Harding was interviewed by KOIN-TV, where she said, “I have definitely thought about it,” with Gillooly standing behind her. She confirmed speaking with FBI agents in Detroit and Portland. On January 13, Eckardt and Smith were arrested. On January 16, Harding’s lawyer held a press conference denying her involvement. On January 18, she submitted to over ten hours of questioning by the DA and FBI, during which she admitted knowing of the plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith on January 10 and 11, and lying to FBI agents on January 18. In the transcript, she stated, “I hope everyone understands. I'm telling on someone I really care about. I know now [Jeff] is involved. I'm sorry.” On January 19, Gillooly surrendered to the FBI. On January 20, Diane Sawyer asked Harding on Primetime whether she had done anything wrong; she said she had not. On January 27, Gillooly testified, possibly implicating Harding, and her friend Stephanie Quintero said Harding was shocked and hurt, believing in Jeff. On February 1, 1994, Gillooly’s attorney negotiated a plea bargain, resulting in Gillooly and Eckardt pleading guilty to racketeering, Stant and Smith to conspiracy to commit second-degree assault, and Gillooly sentenced to two years in prison and publicly apologizing to Kerrigan, calling the apology “hollow.” Judge Donald Londer noted the attack could have injured Kerrigan more seriously. Eckardt died in 2007. On February 1, the USFSA disciplinary panel found reasonable grounds to believe Harding violated the sport’s code of ethics due to her failure to report the assault, leading to a formal charge of making false statements about her knowledge. Claire Ferguson, USFSA president, decided not to suspend Harding before a hearing. The panel reviewed testimonies from Stant and Smith, telephone records, and notes found in a Portland saloon trash bin. Harding was given 30 days to respond. News media attended her practices and filmed her barefoot running to stop a tow truck on February 7. On February 10, Connie Chung interviewed her, saying, “I never did anything to hurt [Jeff]. If I ever did anything, it was to stick up for him and protect him.” Chung also flew with Harding to Oslo on February 15. On February 17, Harding and Kerrigan practiced together at the Hamar Olympic Amphitheatre, with approximately 400 press members present; Kerrigan wore the same costume as during the attack, which she later said was deliberate and empowering. The February 23 technical program broadcast was one of the most-watched telecasts in the U.S. On February 25, Harding finished eighth after a bootlace broke early in her free skate, and she was allowed a re-skate. Kerrigan won silver behind Oksana Baiul. On March 9, 1994, Judge Owen Panner granted Harding a stay until June on her disciplinary hearing. Portland authorities stated the criminal investigation would conclude by March 21. On March 16, 1994, Harding pled guilty to conspiracy to hinder prosecution as a Class C felony, negotiating a plea bargain with her lawyer Robert Weaver to avoid further prosecution. Judge Donald Londer confirmed she entered the plea knowingly and voluntarily. Her plea admissions included knowing of the assault plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith on January 10 and 11, and lying to FBI agents on January 18. The attack received widespread media coverage, appearing on the covers of Sports Illustrated, Newsweek, and Time. Abby Haight and J.E. Vader wrote a biography of Harding called Fire on Ice, including excerpts from her January 18 FBI interview. Harding later competed professionally from 2003 to 2004, placing second at the ESPN Pro Skating Championship in 1999. Her life has been the subject of numerous books, films, documentaries, and academic studies. In 2014, two documentaries, Nancy & Tonya and The Price of Gold, were released, inspiring Steven Rogers to write the film I, Tonya in 2017, in which Margot Robbie portrayed Harding. In 2018, she was a contestant on season 26 of Dancing with the Stars, finishing third, and in 2019, she won season 16 of Worst Cooks in America. The United States Figure Skating Association banned her for life on June 30, 1994, after her involvement in covering up the assault.

Nancy Kerrigan, after recovering from her injury, won a silver medal behind Oksana Baiul from Ukraine. On March 9, 1994, Judge Owen Panner granted Harding a stay until June on her disciplinary hearing. Portland authorities stated the criminal investigation would conclude by March 21, with any indictments and a grand jury report to be issued at that time. On March 16, 1994, Harding pled guilty to conspiracy to hinder prosecution as a Class C felony offense at a Multnomah County court hearing, with her lawyer Robert Weaver negotiating a plea bargain that ensured no further prosecution. Judge Donald Londer confirmed Harding entered her plea knowingly and voluntarily. Her admissions included knowing of the assault plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith affirming the story on January 10 and 11, and lying to the FBI with the story on January 18. Law enforcement had been following and videotaping the co-conspirators since January 10. Her penalties were three years of probation, a $100,000 fine, 500 hours of community service, reimbursement of $10,000 in legal expenses to Multnomah County, a psychiatric examination, and a $50,000 donation to Special Olympics Oregon (SOOR). Oregon sentencing guidelines carried a maximum penalty of five years in prison. The plea agreement required Harding to resign from the U.S. Figure Skating Association, forcing her withdrawal from the 1994 Worlds (scheduled for March 17). District Attorney Norman Frink stated that if Harding had not agreed to the plea, she would have faced an indictment on all possible charges and punishment including loss of skating privileges. Phil Knight, CEO of Nike, donated $25,000 toward Harding's legal fees, and she had earned approximately $600,000 from an Inside Edition deal. Weaver said the plea agreement was satisfactory because it avoided prison, stating "We would have prevailed at trial." A USFSA executive commented that they did not know if Harding was innocent or guilty, if she was involved before the national championship. On March 18, Claire Ferguson decided the disciplinary hearing would proceed in June. The USFSA executive committee discussed Harding's reinstatement and whether to strip her of the 1994 National Championship title, but no decision was made. On March 21, 1994, a Portland grand jury issued an indictment stating there was evidence Harding participated in the attack plot, based on more than two months of investigation and testimonies from Diane Rawlinson, choreographer Erika Bakacs, writer Vera Marano, and Eckardt's college instructor and classmates. The indictment stated there was evidence Harding fraudulently used USFSA-provided skating monies to finance the assault and that Harding, Gillooly, Eckardt, Smith, and Stant agreed to "knowingly cause physical injury ... by means of a dangerous weapon," implying she was involved from the beginning or very closely. She was not charged due to the terms of her March 16 plea agreement. On June 29, 1994, the USFSA disciplinary panel met for nine hours over two days to consider Harding's alleged role in the attack. On June 30, chairman William Hybl stated that the panel found the FBI reports, court documents, and Harding's March 16 plea agreement presented sufficient evidence. Harding did not attend or participate in the hearing. Weaver said the decision disappointed her but was not surprising, and that she had not decided on an appeal. Harding was stripped of her 1994 U.S. Championship title and banned for life from USFSA events as a skater or coach. The USFSA has no authority over professional skating, but after the scandal, Harding became persona non grata on the pro circuit, with few skaters or promoters working with her and she did not benefit from the subsequent rise in professional skating. Shortly before the 1998 Winter Olympics, CBS and Fox aired two televised special reports on the scandal. Harry Smith hosted the CBS special, where Harding reiterated her January 27, 1994 statement: "I had no prior knowledge of the planned assault on Nancy Kerrigan." Smith then interviewed Kerrigan, who, after reviewing transcripts from Harding's January 18, 1994 FBI interview, concluded that "[Tonya] knew more than she admits." The Fox special, titled Breaking the Ice: The Women of '94 Revisited, hosted by James Brown, featured interviews with Harding, Gillooly, and Kerrigan. Gillooly (later renamed Jeff Stone in 1995) said Harding avoiding prison did not anger him and that he felt his own punishment was just. Stone reflected on Harding's "limited involvement" and speculated a "guilty conscience" still troubled her. Brown mediated a joint interview between Kerrigan and Harding, where both expressed sincere desires for happy families and well-wishes. Kerrigan said she hoped Harding could learn from her mistakes and "find happiness," and Harding said she was grateful to personally express remorse to Kerrigan. In her 2008 biography, The Tonya Tapes (transcribed by Lynda D. Prouse), Harding stated she wanted to call the FBI in 1994 to reveal what she knew but decided not to when Gillooly allegedly threatened her with death after a gunpoint gang rape by him and two other men she did not know. Gillooly responded with surprise that "groundless claims" against him could be published and claimed her gang rape accusation was "utterly ridiculous." In 2013, Deadspin sought Gillooly for an interview, and he again defended himself, expressing regret that Harding is often remembered for what he said she did, meaning allegedly plotting to injure Kerrigan. He admitted his past "stupidity" contributed to her 1994 downfall and maintained she was a great figure skater, saying, "I've had it easy, compared to poor Tonya... she tends to be the butt of the joke. It's kind of sad to me." In 2014, Nancy Kerrigan addressed the scandal in a brief interview with Bob Costas, stating, "Whatever apology Tonya has given, I accept it. It's time for all us—I've always wished [Tonya] well. She has her own family, I have my family. It's time to make that our focus, and move on with our lives." On February 15, 1994, an explicit 1991 videotape clip of Harding topless was shown on A Current Affair; three still frames were published in The Sun (a British tabloid). The New York Post reported that Gillooly supplied the videotape for an undisclosed sum. On June 22, 1994, in Portland, Oregon, Harding appeared on an AAA professional wrestling show as the manager for Los Gringos Locos, which included Art Barr and Eddie Guerrero. A promotional musical event in 1995 in Portland was unsuccessful when Harding and her band, the Golden Blades, were booed off stage. On July 26, 1994, Penthouse announced its September issue would feature stills of Harding and Gillooly having sex from the same extended videotape, which was copied and marketed exclusively by Penthouse. Both used the same agent to negotiate equal payment. In 1994, Harding was cast in Breakaway, an action film with Teri Fruichantie and Joseph "Joe" Estévez, centered on her being unwittingly involved in an organized crime syndicate's attempt to recover $300,000 of stolen money, released in 1996. Harding appeared on television on The Weakest Link: "15 Minutes of Fame Edition" in 2002 with Kato Kaelin, and in March 2008 became a commentator for TruTV's truTV Presents: World's Dumbest. Since leaving skating and boxing, Harding has worked as a welder, a painter at a metal fabrication company, and a hardware sales clerk at Sears. In 2017, she stated she worked as a painter and deck builder. She lives in Vancouver, Washington. In August 2019, Harding appeared in a U.S. television commercial promoting Direct Auto Insurance. In 2002, Harding boxed against Paula Jones on the Fox Network Celebrity Boxing event, winning the fight. On February 22, 2003, she made her official women's professional boxing debut, losing a four-round split decision against Samantha Browning on the undercard of Mike Tyson vs. Clifford Etienne. Her boxing career began amid rumors of financial difficulties and needed fighting to earn money. She fought on The Man Show and won against co-host Doug Stanhope, who later claimed on his podcast the fight was fixed because Harding refused to "fight a man." On March 23, 2004, she canceled a planned boxing match against Tracy Carlton in Oakland, California, due to an alleged death threat. On June 24, 2004, she was defeated by Amy Johnson in a match in Edmonton, Alberta, with fans booing her as she entered the ring and cheering for Johnson when she won in the third round. Her boxing career was cut short by asthma, with an overall record of three wins and three losses. On August 12, 2009, Harding set a new land speed record for a vintage gas coupe at 97.177 mph (156.391 km/h; 43.442 m/s) driving a 1931 Ford Model A named Lickity-Split on the Bonneville Salt Flats. On April 13, 2018, Harding was announced as one of the celebrities competing on season 26 of Dancing with the Stars, with professional partner Sasha Farber, finishing in third place. In August 2018, she was announced as one of the celebrities competing in the fifth celebrity edition of Food Network's Worst Cooks in America, set to broadcast in April 2019. Learning under Chef Anne Burrell, Harding ultimately won the competition, with the $25,000 prize going to St. Jude Children's Research Hospital. Harding is the only child of Albert Gordon Harding and LaVona Golden, who had been married three times and had four other children. The two divorced in 1987. Harding had a tumultuous relationship with her mother, alleging both physical and emotional abuse, including one incident where her mother threw a knife at her. LaVona denied the incident and claimed her daughter has a history of dishonesty. Harding began a relationship with 17-year-old Jeff Gillooly in September 1986 when she was 15. They moved into a home together in 1988 when he worked at the Oregon Liquor Control Commission. They married on March 18, 1990, when she was 19 and he was 22. In January 1992, Harding told Terry Richard of The Oregonian, "Jeff always put food on the table and a roof over my head. He paid for my skating for a couple of years. If it hadn't been for him during that time, I wouldn't have been skating." They divorced on August 28, 1993. During autumn 1993, Gillooly worked part-time managing Harding's career and took real estate classes. Harding and Gillooly continued seeing each other from early October 1993 until January 18, 1994, sharing a rented chalet in Beavercreek, Oregon. Harding married Michael Smith in 1995; they divorced in 1996. On October 29, 1996, Harding received media attention after using mouth-to-mouth resuscitation to revive an 81-year-old woman who collapsed at a bar in Portland while playing video poker. On February 22, 2000, Harding attacked her then-boyfriend Darren Silver, punching him repeatedly and throwing a hubcap at his head, leaving him with a bloodied face. She was arrested and initially pleaded not guilty to misdemeanor charges; in a May trial in Clark County District Court, she admitted to the attack and was sentenced to three days in jail, 10 days of community service, and a suspended jail sentence of 167 days. She married 42-year-old Joseph Price on June 23, 2010, when she was 39, and gave birth to a son named Gordon on February 19, 2011. On February 26, 2018, Harding stated on The Ellen DeGeneres Show that she is still active in skating and practices three times a week, performing several jumps and spins with her former coach Dody Teachman. Her life, career, and role in the 1994 attack have been widely referenced in popular culture, including a 2007 primary campaign speech by Barack Obama, in which he said, "Folks said there's no way Obama has a chance unless he goes and kneecaps the person ahead of us, does a Tonya Harding." In 2014, Matt Harkins and Viviana Olen created the Nancy Kerrigan and Tonya Harding Museum in their Brooklyn apartment, collecting and archiving memorabilia related to both. A contemporaneous Vogue article noted that Harding had developed a "cult following" over the years. In 1995, the book Women on Ice: Feminist Essays on the Tonya Harding/Nancy Kerrigan Spectacle was published, containing essays analyzing Harding's public image. Abigail Feder wrote that there existed "overdetermined femininity in Ladies' Figure Skating...femininity and athleticism are mutually exclusive concepts in American culture." Sam Stoloff wrote that during the scandal, the media emphasized Harding's class over her gender, subjecting her to a "litany of vaguely pejorative or mocking expressions" associated with "low class" cultural attributes, sometimes due to her personal interests. Stoloff theorized that Harding represented an American social class requiring interpretation ("the class Other") as referenced in Susan Orlean's 1994 essay "Figures in a Mall" in The New Yorker. In Sarah Marshall's 2014 essay "Remote Control: Tonya Harding, Nancy Kerrigan, and the Spectacles of Female Power and Pain," she noted the media's pervasive role in the 1994 scandal: "Somehow, in the scandal's aftermath, the form of the Tonya-bash was able to alchemize even the most chilling details of Tonya's life into tabloid gold." Marshall also examined Harding's "tomboy" persona in the context of figure skating, theorizing that she was rejected by the figure skating ethos because she did not conform to appearing as "beautiful without being sexual, strong without being intimidating, and vulnerable without being weak."

Top Dance Albums, previously known as Top Electronic Albums and later as Top Dance/Electronic Albums, is a weekly music chart published by Billboard magazine that ranks the top-selling dance music albums in the United States based on sales data collected by Nielsen SoundScan. The chart first appeared on the June 30, 2001, issue under the title Top Electronic Albums, with the original soundtrack to the film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider holding the first number-one position. It initially consisted of fifteen positions and has since expanded to include twenty-five albums. The chart includes full-length albums by artists associated with electronic dance music genres such as house, techno, IDM, and trance, as well as pop-oriented dance music and electronic-leaning hip hop. Remix albums by non-electronic artists and DJ-mixed compilation albums or film soundtracks featuring a majority of electronic or dance music are also eligible. In 2019, Billboard introduced a companion chart, Dance/Electronic Album Sales, which ranks the top 15 albums based exclusively on physical sales, focusing on core dance/electronic artists. Starting with the first full chart week of 2025, the chart was renamed to Top Dance Albums to better reflect the cross-reference of dance titles on the ranking. As of the issue dated January 17, the current number-one album is ABBA Gold by ABBA. Additionally, there is a list of albums that achieved number-one status on the Billboard Top Dance/Electronic Albums Year-End chart.

Caroline "Tottie" Goldsmith OAM (born 27 August 1962) is an Australian actress and singer known for her roles as Trixie Sheldon in Starting Out, Toni Sheffield in The Young Doctors, Marilyn "Tex" Perez in Fire, and Cassandra Freedman in Neighbours. She hosted the Network Ten program Sex/Life in 1996 and was a contestant on the 8th season of the Australian version of I'm a Celebrity...Get Me Out of Here! in 2022. A founding member of the Chantoozies, a pop group formed in 1986, she was one of four female lead vocalists from 1986 until she left to pursue a solo singing career before the band released their second album, Gild the Lily in 1991. She rejoined the group temporarily in 2006 for the Countdown Spectacular concert series and permanently in 2012, before leaving again in 2020. With Chantoozies member Eve von Bibra, she performed as the duo the Toozies, who opened for the 2010 Antenna Awards. On 8 January 2023, she returned to music after a three-year break by performing with the 3XY Allstars in St. Kilda, and on 30 July 2023, invited former bandmate Ally Fowler to cover Olivia Newton-John's "You're the One That I Want," her first performance with a Chantoozies member since leaving the band. She also returned to the Chantoozies at a concert at the Sandstone Point Hotel on the Sunshine Coast on 26 July, filling in for Fowler. In the late 1990s, she co-hosted a breakfast program on Melbourne radio station TTFM, replacing Nicky Buckley. She played Janet in a season of the New Rocky Horror Show and participated in an arena version of Grease. Goldsmith works as a marriage celebrant and has released two meditation and relaxation albums: Unwind Your Mind (2004) and Falling Asleep (2005). After experiencing chronic fatigue syndrome and long-term sleep issues, she partnered with sleep specialist Chris Bunney to record Falling Asleep, which has since been prescribed by doctors. In 2007, she collaborated with a child psychologist on A Sleep Story, aimed at children. She was known as a sex symbol early in her career and posed nude for art magazine Black+White in August 1996. She is the daughter of Melbourne restaurateur and nightclub owner Brian Goldsmith and British-born actress Rona Newton-John (1941–2013), with her great-grandfather, the father of her grandmother Irene, being German-British physicist, mathematician, and Nobel Prize winner Max Born. Olivia Newton-John is her maternal aunt, Brett Goldsmith is her elder brother, and racecar driver Emerson Newton-John is her half brother; she has six other siblings. Goldsmith was married to skier Steven Lee, with whom she has one daughter, and became engaged to businessman James Mayo in January 2008. In the 2020 Queen's Birthday Honours, she was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) for "service to the community, and to the performing arts." She made guest appearances in Australian television series such as The Young Doctors, Starting Out, Prisoner, Saturdee, The Henderson Kids, Mission: Impossible (1989 episode), G.P., and Embassy. In 1996, she starred as Marilyn "Tex" Perez in the second season of Fire and also hosted Sex/Life, appeared in Twisted Tales and Shark Bay, and was a panellist on Beauty and the Beast and All-Star Squares. In the 2000s, she made guest appearances on The Secret Life of Us, Bert's Family Feud, Big Questions, Surprise Surprise Gotcha, Pizza, and Celebrity Singing Bee, and had a three-episode run on Blue Heelers. She appeared in a 2001 episode of Stingers and another in 2004. In 2009, she appeared in Neighbours for three months as Cassandra Freedman. She acted in two episodes of Swift and Shift Couriers, appeared in the 2010 film Ricky! The Movie as the ex-girlfriend of Ricky T, and as a gangster's girlfriend in the 2011 television film Underbelly Files: Infiltration. She had a supporting role in the 2012 Jack Irish telefilm Bad Debts. The Chantoozies released four singles: "Witch Queen", "He's Gonna Step On You Again", "Wanna Be Up", "Kiss and Tell", and an album, Chantoozies.

Western European militaries generally show a greater tendency toward including LGBT individuals compared to other armed forces. On 18 July 1980, Sweden became the first country to allow legally recognized transgender individuals—those who had completed transition and obtained legal gender status under the 1972 gender-recognition law—to be medically classified as fit for duty and serve openly in their affirmed gender within the armed forces. As of 2025, eight North Atlantic Treaty Organization members—Italy, Albania, Poland, Turkey, Hungary (ban effective 29 May 2020), Bulgaria (ban effective 20 February 2023), the United States (ban effective 8 May 2025), and Slovakia (ban effective 1 November 2025)—have prohibited transgender people from serving in their armed forces. Arguments against transgender inclusion include the view that being transgender is a mental illness, leading to concerns about depression, suicide, and the effects of hormone therapy, which may affect mood and well-being. Complications from estrogen and testosterone therapies—such as increased risk of thromboembolic disease, myocardial infarction, breast cancer, fertility problems, stroke, abnormal liver function, renal disease, endometrial cancer, and osteoporosis—may also impact military service, especially in remote or field settings. The cost of treating transgender members is cited as a concern; estimates show that 30 to 140 transgender soldiers annually pursue hormone treatment and 25 to 100 undergo surgical reassignment, with male-to-female transitions costing $7,000 to $24,000 and female-to-male transitions exceeding $50,000. The Defense Department’s annual healthcare budget is $6 billion, and treating service members with gender dysphoria would cost between $2.4 million and $8.4 million—0.04 to 0.14 percent of the budget. Critics argue that transgender individuals would negatively affect unit cohesion and morale, though this overlooks the need for structural accommodations that could maintain trust and performance. Excluding transgender personnel reinforces civic inferiority and contradicts the principle that all citizens are obligated to serve. Current medical understanding, including the DSM’s classification of gender dysphoria as a distinct condition rather than a paraphilic disorder, suggests that excluding transgender individuals on grounds of mental illness is inconsistent with modern medical standards. There is no empirical evidence that transgender individuals are unfit for service; issues like depression and anxiety are common in the broader LGBT community and do not justify exclusion. Research from 18 countries allowing transgender service, including the Israeli Defense Forces, British Armed Forces, and Canadian Armed Forces, found no negative impacts on performance, unit cohesion, or morale. A 2016 survey of U.S. military academy, ROTC, and civilian undergraduates found that 50.8% disagreed with the ban, 72.6% believed transgender inclusion would not affect productivity, and 21.8% said they would want to know transgender individuals’ gender preferences, while 56.1% had no preference. In October 2017, U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly ruled that the evidence against transgender service was contradicted by military studies. Albania has never established a legal pathway for gender recognition in civil status; its 2010 anti-discrimination law protects gender identity in employment but does not allow changes to civil registry data, meaning transgender individuals cannot serve in their affirmed gender due to lack of legal gender recognition. Similarly, Bulgaria has no general legal procedure for gender recognition, with the Supreme Court in February 2023 ruling that courts cannot authorize gender changes in civil status, resulting in a de facto nationwide ban. As of 2025, Bulgaria’s ban is under review by the Court of Justice of the European Union. The Australian Defence Force lifted its ban on transgender service in 2013, with inclusion reportedly still in effect in 2017; it was the last agency to allow firing employees for transitioning gender. The ADF supports diversity and includes gender diversity as a priority, with approximately 15 openly transgender service members supported by DEFGLIS. In 2013, Australia formally codified gender identity protections in the Sex Discrimination Act 1984. In 1997, Sergeant Sylvia Durand became the first military member worldwide to transition openly while serving; she was officially recognized in 1998, underwent surgery in 1999, and retired in 2012 after 31 years of service. As of 2014, Austria, Belgium, Bolivia, Canada, Chile, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, and France allowed transgender people to serve openly, with the policy reportedly still in effect in 2017. In France, while the military may be initially more accepting, civilian court rulings impose strict requirements for changing identity documents, as seen in the case of Delphine Ravisé-Giard, who was reintegrated smoothly in 2009 but faced difficulties in civilian life.

As of 2014, France allowed transgender people to serve openly in its military forces, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. The military is sometimes more accepting of transgender service members than civilian authorities, though this varies by locality and jurisdiction, and is influenced by civilian court rulings that impose strict requirements for changing identity documents. In 2009, a transgender Adjutant in the French Air Force, Delphine Ravisé-Giard, who had served 18 years as a man, returned to her unit in Nancy as a woman after a sick leave. Her superiors provided her with new uniforms and military papers under her new name, and she was reintegrated smoothly. However, she faced difficulties in civilian life, such as presenting her driver's license, passport, or other documents. The military requested the Nancy District Court to alter her gender and name on her birth certificate, but the court denied the request because she had not undergone sex reassignment surgery, citing that her situation was reversible. A 1992 decision by the Cour de cassation requires individuals seeking to change legal documents to show a diagnosis of "transsexual syndrome," listed as a long-term psychiatric disorder in France, and to have undergone surgical intervention; the Adjutant stated she had no such disorder and considered any discussion of surgery a private matter. Her lawyer suggested the denial was due to concerns about her ability to have children, implying the court’s goal was sterilization, which the Commissioner for Human Rights of the European Council stated should not be required for gender identity recognition. Following the court’s decision in December, Minister Hervé Morin ordered her to surrender her military papers, which she did. She later discovered her name on her pay stub reverted to her old name, the military supplement for feminine undergarments was removed, and she was to be docked pay for the supplement she received during two years as a woman. As of 2014, Germany also allowed transgender people to serve openly, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. Since at least 1947, transgender individuals have been de facto banned from serving in the Indian Armed Forces through inherited military regulations and medical fitness standards, despite no formal law targeting them. Since 1980, transgender individuals in Iran have been de facto banned from military service due to medical and psychiatric classifications that label gender nonconformity as a mental disorder. Following the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Iran implemented mandatory conscription for male citizens over 18, and transgender individuals are medically exempted under "psychosexual disorders," which bars them from service and exposes them to discrimination and stigma. A 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini recognized sex reassignment surgery as permissible under Islamic law, but this did not change military policy, and transgender people remain classified as disqualified. Iran requires all male citizens over 18 to serve, except transgender women, who are classified as having mental disorders, and new military identity cards list this exemption. In July 2017, Taoiseach Leo Varadkar of Ireland stated he did not agree with the Trump administration’s decision to ban openly transgender personnel, noting Ireland had never formally banned such service and would not consider introducing such a ban. From 4 May 1861 to the present, the Italian Armed Forces have never formally permitted transgender people to serve openly. Military medical regulations have historically classified gender identity variance as a mental or sexual disorder, resulting in disqualification. The earliest explicit exclusion was on 28 May 1964 with Decreto del Presidente della Repubblica (D.P.R.) n. 496, which listed "invertiti sessuali" as a psychiatric abnormality disqualifying individuals from conscription. On 2 September 1985 (published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale on 21 April 1986), D.P.R. n. 1008 updated the list, removing that phrase but continuing to exclude individuals for "devianze sessuali." A Ministerial Decree of 29 November 1995 introduced "disturbi dell’identità di genere (disturbi della sessualità)" as disqualifying conditions. The 14 April 1999 revision reaffirmed this exclusion, listing "parafilie e disturbi dell’identità di genere" among psychiatric disorders incompatible with military fitness. Under D.P.R. n. 90 of 15 March 2010 (Testo Unico dell'Ordinamento Militare), Article 582 confirmed that medical standards set by the Ministry of Defence govern eligibility, maintaining prior exclusions. On 4 June 2014, the Ministry issued an updated technical directive (published 9 June 2014) reaffirming "parafilie e disturbi dell’identità di genere" as causes of non-fitness, a classification still applied. Although Italy enacted Law 164/1982 allowing legal gender change through judicial authorization, this did not alter military fitness standards, and as of 2025, the Italian Armed Forces continue to exclude transgender individuals. As of 2014, Israel allowed transgender people to serve openly, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. There is no explicit legal prohibition on transgender individuals serving in the Lithuanian Armed Forces. The official medical fitness criteria (Order No. V-449 of 3 June 2020, consolidated version of 27 September 2025) do not list gender identity or gender transition as disqualifying conditions. Suitability is assessed individually by the Military Medical Expertise Commission. As of 2014, the Netherlands allowed transgender people to serve openly, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. The New Zealand Defence Force is recognized as a world leader in diversity and LGBTQI integration, ranked number one for inclusion of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender personnel. With the addition of the Human Rights Act to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act in 1994, discrimination based on sexual orientation was criminalized. Although there is no specific reference to transgender people in the statute, the Solicitor General has held that protections for transgender people fall under the sex discrimination provision. While the Human Rights Commission and activists continue to call for an express provision, the NZDF does not discriminate on gender identity. The Chief of Defence Force approved a support group for LGBTI personnel, and in 2012, the NZDF Overwatch was launched to provide peer support, networking, education, and guidance to command and commanders. The NZDF and Overwatch won the Supreme award for equal employment opportunity at the ANZ and Equal Employment Opportunities Trust, Diversity Awards NZ 2013. On 16 December 2024, the Harmonised Armed Forces Terms and Conditions of Service, signed by President Bola Tinubu, explicitly banned transgender individuals and cross-dressing in the Nigerian Armed Forces, effective immediately, aiming to enforce strict military ethics and discipline. As of 2014, Norway allowed transgender people to serve openly, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. In 2017, the Philippines allowed members of the LGBT community, including transgender people, to serve in its military, though gender expression is restricted, particularly through uniform regulations, and service is based on the gender reflected on the certificate of live birth. From 12 October 1918 to the present, the Polish Armed Forces have never officially permitted open service by transgender people. Military medical regulations have treated “transsexualism” or gender-identity variance as disqualifying, assigning an “E” (permanently unfit) category or excluding candidates under psychiatric criteria. Eligibility is set by ministerial regulations (rozporządzenia) with annexed lists of diseases and defects used by Military Medical Commissions. A 2005 regulation updated procedures and lists, and subsequent regulations in 2010 carried forward the framework. On 25 March 2024, the Ministry of National Defence issued a consolidated regulation (Dz.U. 2024 poz. 466), specifying the disease/defect list, including psychiatric conditions that disqualify service, which entered into force upon publication. In April–June 2024, the Commissioner for Human Rights (Rzecznik Praw Obywatelskich) noted that “transseksualizm” had been “again recognized as a disqualifying premise” and requested legal and factual justification. On 1 July 2025, an amending regulation (Dz.U. 2025 poz. 887) retained the same legal framework, continuing reliance on the annexed list without creating a route for open transgender service. As of 2025, mainstream legal summaries continue to describe Poland as not allowing open service by transgender people, with LGB personnel able to serve but transgender status treated as disqualifying under medical-fitness rules. From 2 November 1721 to the present, the Russian Armed Forces (including predecessors in the Russian Empire and Soviet Armed Forces) have never officially permitted open service by transgender people. Historical and contemporary medical-fitness rules have treated “transsexualism” as a disqualifying condition. On 1 January 1968, the Ministry of Health adopted the Soviet adaptation of the eighth revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-8), classifying transseksualizm as a mental disorder. A 1969 revision of the Schedule of Diseases listed “psychosexual deviations” and “sexual perversions” as disqualifying conditions, interpreted to include homosexuality and transsexualism. After 1991, the Russian Federation retained an exclusionary framework. The Government’s 4 July 2013 decree No. 565 “On approval of the Regulations on military-medical examination,” in force since 1 January 2014 and amended multiple times (including 27 February 2020 and 29 August 2025), sets the legal basis and annexed Schedule of Diseases used by military medical commissions to assign fitness categories (A, B, V, G, D). Mental and behavioral disorders (ICD-10 “F” block), applied via the Schedule (notably Article 18), are grounds for limited-fit or unfit classification, which practice has applied to gender-identity diagnoses (e.g., F64). Civil-society and legal-aid guides explain that a confirmed F64 diagnosis is assessed under Article 18 and typically leads to a “D” (completely unfit) or “V” (limited fit/reserve) category, precluding open service in one’s affirmed gender. As of 2025, the same regulatory architecture remains in force: military medical commissions apply the Government’s Schedule of Diseases, and gender-identity diagnoses fall within disqualifying psychiatric grounds. No policy authorizing open transgender service has been promulgated by the Ministry of Defence. As of 2014, Spain allowed transgender people to serve openly, and the policy of inclusion was reportedly still in effect in 2017. Since 1998, South Africa has allowed transgender individuals to serve in the South African National Defence Force (SANDF), becoming the first and only African country to do so. Since at least 1978, South Korea has excluded transgender individuals from military service through medical classifications such as "sexual perversion" and later "gender identity disorder," used by the Military Manpower Administration to disqualify or exempt them. The Swedish Army traces its origins to 14 January 1521, when Gustav Eriksson was appointed commander in Dalarna. Modern policy on transgender personnel begins in the twentieth century; earlier eras lacked a legal or medical category for "transgender," and there is no evidence of an explicit ban in military statutes. On 1 January 1972, Sweden enacted the Law on the Determination of Gender in Certain Cases (SFS 1972:119), creating the world’s first statutory procedure to change legal sex in the civil register. Despite this, the Armed Forces relied on their medical regulation code (Medicinska undersökningsreglementet, Med U), under which "transsexualism" was a ground for exemption. In 1976, Med U was revised to allow "homosexuals as well as transsexuals" to be considered for service in various divisions, though transgender conscripts were still commonly exempted and open service was not established. A decisive reform occurred on 18 July 1980, when the Defence Medical Administration issued an amendment (reg. no. 440–1279) removing "homosexuality" as a medical exclusion and specifying that for "transsexual" conscripts, "exemption is no longer the sole recommendation," permitting medical officers to find transgender individuals fit for service. Because legal gender recognition already existed by statute, this change enabled transgender people to serve openly in their affirmed gender—identified as the first documented instance in any national military. Sweden subsequently embedded non-discrimination into general law. The Discrimination Act (SFS 2008:567), enacted on 5 June 2008 and in force from 1 January 2009, prohibits discrimination on grounds of "transgender identity or expression" and applies to recruitment, training, and service in the total-defence system, binding the Armed Forces. On 3 July 2008, the Swedish Armed Forces appointed Petra Jäppinen as its first LGBT (HBT) officer, formalizing internal support and inclusion work for transgender personnel. The sterilization prerequisite for legal gender recognition was removed following litigation and legislative change in 2012–2013; from 1 July 2013, transgender people could obtain legal recognition without sterilization, eliminating a barrier to full administrative recognition, including in defence records. In the 2010s and 2020s, the Swedish Armed Forces presented inclusion as institutional policy and practice, participating in Pride events and running diversity-focused messaging that includes gender identity. In Thailand, males 21 years of age and above can serve voluntarily for six months in the military. If they opt not to serve, they are not required to.

On 5 June 2008 and in force from 1 January 2009, Sweden prohibited discrimination on the grounds of "transgender identity or expression" and applied this to recruitment, training, and service in the total-defence system, binding the Armed Forces. On 3 July 2008, the Swedish Armed Forces appointed Petra Jäppinen as its first LGBT (HBT) officer, formalizing internal support and inclusion work that explicitly covered transgender personnel. In 2012–2013, following litigation and legislative change, the sterilization prerequisite for legal gender recognition was removed, allowing transgender people to obtain legal recognition without sterilization from 1 July 2013, eliminating a barrier to full administrative recognition, including in defence personnel records. In the 2010s and 2020s, the Swedish Armed Forces presented inclusion as institutional policy and practice, participating publicly in Pride events and running diversity-focused messaging that includes gender identity alongside other protected characteristics. In Thailand, males aged 21 and above can serve voluntarily for six months; if selected in the annual draft lottery and they choose not to serve, they must serve for two years. Transgender women/kathoeys are not exempted and are legally required to appear for the military conscription event on draft day regardless of their transition status or presentation. Identity documents cannot be legally changed in Thailand. Those who have undergone sex reassignment surgery (SRS) or are deemed to have adopted a female appearance are automatically exempted from being drafted; those with a male appearance must undergo a medical test to obtain an exemption. Those who underwent SRS are exempted for the next two years, while those diagnosed with gender identity disorder are exempted for life. On draft day, lines may include transgender women in makeup and feminine attire waiting alongside male draftees. Despite the perception of acceptance, many transgender women report being treated as second-class citizens and face stress from being undressed or publicly humiliated; some were still drafted. From the establishment of the Turkish Armed Forces in May 1920 until 1 January 1968, there were no explicit legal provisions addressing transgender or homosexual individuals in military regulations, though broad medical and moral fitness standards effectively excluded those considered to have "sexual disorders" or who deviated from norms of masculinity and morality. On 1 January 1968, the Turkish Armed Forces introduced a revised version of the Türk Silahlı Kuvvetleri Sağlık Yeteneği Yönetmeliği (Health Capability Regulation) that for the first time included provisions on cinsel terslik ("sexual inversion"), classifying homosexuality, transvestism, and transsexualism as disqualifying medical conditions, marking individuals as having a "psychosexual disorder" and issuing them exemption/discharge certificates ("pink certificate"). On 24 November 1986, Turkey formally reissued the Health Capability Regulation, maintaining psychosexual classifications as disqualifying grounds. Independent summaries confirm that the regulation bars those with "high-level psychosexual disorders," a category applied in practice to transsexuality and transvestism. On 12 May 1988, the Turkish Civil Code was amended to permit some post-operative transgender people to change their legal sex on identity documents; this framework was later recodified in Law No. 4721, Article 40, in force from 1 January 2002. Legal gender recognition did not alter armed forces’ medical-fitness exclusions, and transgender people continued to be classified as unfit and issued "pink certificates." The exclusion extends beyond conscription to career officers and voluntary personnel through disciplinary provisions allowing dismissal on broad morality grounds, leaving no room for open transgender service; a 2015 Military Supreme Court referral did not lead to repeal. In a 2015 incident widely reported, a woman known as Bihter was recorded in army files as a deserter because she had not completed conscription, despite being a transgender woman legally identified as male. As of 2024–2025, Turkey is still listed as not permitting open transgender military service, with exclusion enforced through the medical-fitness regime rather than a distinct service-eligibility statute. A Williams Institute analysis of the 2017 Global Attitudes Toward Transgender People survey found that 36.5% agreed (19.2% strongly and 17.3% somewhat), while 55.9% disagreed (30.6% strongly and 25.3% somewhat), and 7.6% responded "don't know" when asked if transgender people should be allowed to serve in the military. Since the Royal Navy's establishment on 24 April 1546, the British Armed Forces did not permit open service by individuals of a gender different from their sex assigned at birth; women and gender-nonconforming people could enlist only by concealing their identities. During the 18th and 19th centuries, a small number of people assigned female at birth disguised themselves as men to enlist, such as Hannah Snell (served in the Royal Marines 1747–1750) and James Barry (Army medical officer, whose assigned sex was discovered after his death on 25 July 1865). In the 20th century, armed forces regulations classified gender transition or "transsexualism" as a psychiatric disorder rendering individuals medically unfit. Royal Navy medic Lynda Cash was dismissed in 1986 after beginning gender transition, officially on grounds of "emotional instability," and later won a pension and apology on 3 June 1999 after the service admitted wrongful dismissal. In 1993, a Royal Air Force technician known as "Officer M" was discharged after disclosing a diagnosis of gender identity disorder; the RAF classified her as "unfit for duty" on 12 February 1993. On 30 April 1996, the European Court of Justice ruled that dismissal for gender reassignment constituted sex discrimination under European law. On 27 September 1999, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Smith and Grady v United Kingdom that the ban on homosexual service members violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, leading the UK to reform its wider LGBT service policies. On 2 August 1999, the Ministry of Defence issued new internal guidance allowing transgender personnel to remain in service if medically and operationally fit, ending automatic dismissal on grounds of gender reassignment. In late 1999, Caroline Paige became the first openly serving transgender officer in the Royal Air Force, continuing her career after transitioning. On 12 January 2000, the UK government formally lifted the ban on gay, lesbian, and bisexual personnel and introduced a new Armed Forces Code of Social Conduct neutral on sexual orientation and gender identity. The Gender Recognition Act 2004, passed on 4 April 2004, established a legal mechanism for transgender people to obtain recognition of their affirmed gender, affecting service documentation and pensions. The Equality Act 2010, which received Royal Assent on 8 April 2010, prohibited discrimination on grounds of “gender reassignment” in employment, including military service. On 19 July 2023, the UK Government formally apologized to LGBT veterans who had been discharged under earlier discriminatory military policies. As of 2025, transgender people serve openly in all branches of the British Armed Forces, protected under law and by Joint Service Publication 889, which sets out Defence policy on gender identity and transition. In the United States, military policy previously excluded transgender people on medical grounds; while cisgender gay, lesbian, and bisexual service members were allowed to serve openly since 2011, transgender service members risked discharge if they did not pass as their assigned sex, requiring them to conceal their gender identities. It was estimated that in 2008–2009 there were approximately 15,500 transgender individuals serving on active duty or in the National Guard or Army Reserve. A 2016 study estimated that between 1,320 and 6,630 transgender individuals served on active duty and between 830 and 4,160 in reserve duty, with midrange figures of 2,450 in active duty and 1,510 in reserves. Regardless of the number, transgender individuals are between 2-5 times more likely to serve than their cisgender counterparts, primarily due to financial security and a sense of belonging to a community, leading to the belief that the U.S. Armed Forces is one of the largest, if not the largest, employers of transgender Americans. A key concern is the use of military medical services to transition. On 22 August 2013, U.S. soldier Chelsea Manning issued a public statement declaring herself a transgender woman. In 2014, while incarcerated, Manning filed a lawsuit against Secretary of Defense Hagel for failing to provide appropriate medical treatment for her gender transition. In early 2015, hormone therapy to assist with gender conformity was approved as a military first, along with cosmetics and female undergarments. Air Force Secretary Deborah Lee James openly supported a policy change in 2014, stating it was likely to be reviewed in the next year or so. In February 2015, Secretary of Defense Ashton Carter stated he was open-minded about including transgender people in the military, saying nothing but individual lack of merit should preclude service, a statement later endorsed by President Obama. On 19 August 2015, Carter stated in a memo that the Defense Department had begun dismantling the ban and that transgender people would be able to openly serve by 27 May 2016. Department of Defense regulations banning transgender persons from military service were repealed on 30 June 2016. Beginning on that date, otherwise qualified service members could no longer be discharged, denied reenlistment, involuntarily separated, or denied continuation of service due to being transgender. On 26 July 2017, President Donald Trump announced that transgender people would no longer be allowed to serve in the U.S. military. The following day, General Joseph Dunford stated openly transgender people would continue to serve until Trump provided direction to Secretary of Defense James Mattis. On 1 August 2017, the Palm Center released a letter signed by 56 retired generals and admirals opposing the proposed ban, stating it would cause significant disruptions, deprive the military of mission-critical talent, and force transgender troops to live a lie, as well as non-transgender peers to choose between reporting comrades or disobeying policy. On 9 August 2017, five transgender U.S. military personnel sued Trump and top Pentagon officials over the proposed ban, asking the court to prevent its implementation. Two major LGBT-rights organizations filed a petition in U.S. District Court in Washington on behalf of the five service members. Trump signed a presidential memorandum on 25 August 2017 directing the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Homeland Security to submit an implementation plan by 21 February 2018 to reinstate the ban and halt the use of military funds for sex reassignment surgery. On 30 October 2017, U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly barred the administration from excluding transgender people from military service in Jane Doe v. Trump, stating that all reasons proffered by the president were contradicted by military studies and judgments. In November 2017, the Defense Health Agency approved payment for sex reassignment surgery for an active-duty service member, an infantry soldier who is a trans woman, who had already begun treatment and underwent the procedure on 14 November at a private hospital due to lack of surgical expertise in military hospitals. On 11 December, Kollar-Kotelly ruled that the government must accept transgender recruits into the military by 1 January 2018. After the ruling, the Department of Justice appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to issue a stay. The Pentagon confirmed on 26 February 2018 that the first transgender recruit had signed a contract to join the military. On 23 March 2018, President Trump banned transgender and transsexual people with current or previous gender dysphoria from serving. The Pentagon stated they would comply with the court decision until reversed. The policy was stayed in Karnoski v. Trump on 13 April 2018, when the court ruled the 2018 memorandum repeated the same issues as the 2017 order, classifying transgender individuals as a protected class entitled to strict scrutiny, and ordered the matter to proceed to a full trial. On 22 January 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Trump's transgender military ban to go into effect while litigation continued in lower courts. On 12 March 2019, acting Deputy Defense Secretary David Norquist signed a directive to allow the policy to take effect in 30 days. On Biden's first day in office, his press secretary, Jen Psaki, announced he would soon reverse the ban, though no specific date was given. Although Biden had originally said the reversal would occur "on day one," it could not happen due to the unconfirmed nomination of Lloyd Austin for Secretary of Defense. On 25 January 2021, President Biden signed an executive order to reverse the ban, allowing most transgender individuals to serve in the U.S. military. The order required the Department of Homeland Security to lift its transgender service ban and immediately revoked both the Presidential Memorandum of 23 March 2018 and the 25 August 2017 memorandum. It also required the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Homeland Security, with respect to the Coast Guard, to consult with the Joint Chiefs of Staff on implementation. The order prohibited any service member from being forced out of the military on the basis of gender identity. On 30 April 2021, the Pentagon enacted a new policy providing better medical service access and gender marker assistance to transgender people in the military. Executive Order 14183, titled "Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness," was issued by President Donald Trump on 27 January 2025, banning transgender people from military service. In March 2025, a federal judge blocked the order; in May 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to reinstate the ban while legal challenges continue in the Ninth Circuit.

The Chiefs of Staff were tasked with determining the best approach to implement a full reversal. President Biden issued an order that prohibited any service member from being forced out of the military due to their gender identity. On 30 April 2021, the Pentagon implemented a new policy aimed at improving medical service access and providing gender marker assistance to transgender individuals in the U.S. military. Executive Order 14183, titled "Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness," was signed by President Donald Trump on January 27, 2025, and banned transgender people from serving in the military. In March 2025, a federal judge blocked this executive order; however, in May of that year, the Supreme Court permitted the Trump administration to reinstate the ban, while legal challenges to the policy continued in the Ninth Circuit.

Tuai is a rural settlement and village situated around Lake Whakamarino in the Wairoa District of the Hawke's Bay Region on New Zealand's North Island. The local Tuai Power Station, opened in 1929 as part of the Waikaremoana power scheme, is located on the lake's shores and has been remotely controlled by Genesis Energy from Tokaanu power station since the early 2000s. Artist Doris Lusk painted the power station in 1948, describing it as a “gothic building in the middle of the wild hills.” Lake Whakamarino, also known as Tuai Lake, is popular with anglers and can be accessed by fly-fishers using small unanchored boats. Statistics New Zealand classifies Tuai as a rural settlement covering 21.99 km² (8.49 sq mi), with an estimated population of 230 as of June 2025, a population density of 10 people per km², and is part of the Maungataniwha-Raupunga statistical area. The 2023 census recorded a population of 222, an increase of 6 people (2.8%) from 2018 and 9 people (4.2%) from 2013; there were 108 males and 114 females in 87 dwellings. 1.4% of residents identified as LGBTIQ+. The median age was 32.4 years (compared to 38.1 years nationally), with 63 people (28.4%) under 15, 42 (18.9%) aged 15 to 29, 90 (40.5%) aged 30 to 64, and 30 (13.5%) aged 65 or older. Ethnicity data shows 25.7% European (Pākehā), 87.8% Māori, and 1.4% Pasifika; English was spoken by 94.6%, Māori by 54.1%, and other languages by 2.7%; 2.7% of people could not speak a language (e.g., too young to talk). The percentage of people born overseas was 6.8%, compared to 28.8% nationally. Religious affiliations included 20.3% Christian, 32.4% Māori religious beliefs, 1.4% New Age, and 1.4% other religions; 40.5% had no religion, and 6.8% did not answer the census question. Among those aged 15 and over, 24 (15.1%) held a bachelor's or higher degree, 99 (62.3%) had a post-high school certificate or diploma, and 45 (28.3%) held only high school qualifications. The median income was $31,200 (compared to $41,500 nationally), with 3 people (1.9%) earning over $100,000 (compared to 12.1% nationally); employment status showed 63 (39.6%) full-time, 21 (13.2%) part-time, and 12 (7.5%) unemployed. Te Kūhā Tārewa Marae and Te Poho o Hinekura or Ruapani meeting house serves the Tūhoe hapū of Ngāti Hinekura and the Ngāti Ruapani hapū of Ngāti Hinekura and Tuwai. In October 2020, the Government committed $1,949,075 from the Provincial Growth Fund to upgrade the marae and 23 other Ngāti Kahungunu marae, expected to create 164 jobs. Te Kura o Waikaremoana is a Year 1–8 co-educational state primary school, a decile 2 school with a roll of 27 as of October 2025. It was formed in 2005 by the merger of Tuai School, established by 1929, and Kokako School, established between 1896 and 1898.

The ACM A. M. Turing Award is an annual honor bestowed by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) for significant and enduring technical contributions to computer science. It is widely regarded as the highest achievement in the field and is commonly known as the "Nobel Prize of Computing." As of 2025, 79 individuals have received the award, with Andrew Barto and Richard S. Sutton being the most recent recipients, awarded in 2024. The award is named after Alan Turing, often called the "Father of Computer Science," a British mathematician and former reader in mathematics at the University of Manchester. Turing is credited as the founder of theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence and played a crucial role in the Allied decryption of the Enigma cipher during World War II. From 2007 to 2013, the award included a US$250,000 prize, funded by Intel and Google. Since 2014, the prize has been US$1 million, also supported by Google. The first recipient was Alan Perlis in 1966. Donald Knuth was the youngest recipient, winning in 1974 at age 36, while Alfred Aho was the oldest, receiving it in 2020 at age 79. Only three women have been awarded the prize: Frances Allen in 2006, Barbara Liskov in 2008, and Shafi Goldwasser in 2012.

Twisted Timbers is a hybrid roller coaster built by American manufacturer Rocky Mountain Construction (RMC) and located at Kings Dominion in Doswell, Virginia. It originally opened in 1994 as a wooden coaster named Hurler, designed and manufactured by International Coasters, Inc., as an exact clone of Hurler at Carowinds. The ride closed for "extensive maintenance" in 2015, and in 2016, Kings Dominion teased that Hurler would reopen in 2018, hinting at a renovation by RMC with the message, "There's really more coming." The park contracted RMC to revamp the aging coaster, during which the wooden track was replaced with steel using RMC's I-Box track technology, enabling more aggressive elements and inversions. The ride reemerged as Twisted Timbers on March 24, 2018, featuring three overbanked turns, three inversions, and twenty airtime moments, and reaches a maximum speed of 54 mph (87 km/h), which is faster than its predecessor. It ranked third among new rides in 2018 in the annual Golden Ticket Awards from Amusement Today. On August 16, 2017, Kings Dominion officially confirmed that Hurler would reopen as Twisted Timbers and open in 2018, with promotional artwork and ride specifications released in a press release. The ride includes a barrel roll drop, similar to Wind Chaser at Kentucky Kingdom. A soft opening was scheduled for March 22, 2018, for media and American Coaster Enthusiasts members, with a second for season ticket holders, but due to inclement weather on March 21, both were held on March 23. The grand opening to the public occurred on March 24, 2018. When Hurler closed in fall 2015, no renovation signs were visible, but on March 25, 2017, RMC I-Box track was spotted in a storage yard, and amateur drone footage four days later revealed track removal had begun. On May 20, new wood and steel supports appeared on the old structure for the first time. On May 21, the park tweeted the first in a series of teasers setting the announcement date for August 16. On August 8, just over a week before the formal announcement and three days before ride details leaked online, the ride's lift hill was topped off. After a winter hiatus, the final track pieces and two custom trains were installed on February 17, 2018, with the signatures of the park's full-time employees placed on the final piece as an "Easter egg." Kings Dominion tested the completed attraction on February 21, and on March 20, four days before the grand opening, the two trains—one blue and one green—tested together. The ride is set in the fictional Hanover Hill Orchard, a rustic apple orchard named after Hanover County, Virginia, where the park is located. Signage throughout the queue tells the story that in 1950, a mysterious force destroyed the orchard and froze it in time, and in the present day, a local businessman has reopened it as it appeared in 1950. Guests are encouraged to tour the abandoned orchard, with the queue line passing mangled trees, flipped farm vehicles, and other signs of destruction. The station is themed as a partially destroyed apple shipping warehouse, and the trains resemble weathered 1937 Ford pickup trucks. Along with the ride's opening in 2018, the surrounding Candy Apple Grove section was rethemed to continue the 1950s orchard theme. Twisted Timbers, previously known as Hurler, is located in the Candy Apple Grove section and takes riders to a height of 111 feet (34 m) before entering a barrel roll inversion and dropping them 109 feet (33 m) down the first hill. It features twenty airtime moments, three overbanked turns, and two additional inversions, including a cutback and zero-g roll. In its debut year, Twisted Timbers placed third in the category of "Best New Ride for 2018" in the Golden Ticket Awards from Amusement Today, and ranked 38th on the publication's list of top 50 steel roller coasters. Amusement Today praised the ride for its dramatic maneuvers, abundance of airtime, inversions, and remarkable smoothness compared to its former life. In June 2018, a woman was hit in the forehead by a mobile phone while riding Twisted Timbers and was taken to the hospital, receiving three stitches.

Tyndale Biscoe School is located in the Sheikh Bagh neighbourhood of Lal Chowk, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir. Founded in 1880 CE, it is one of the oldest schools in the region, with S.P. School, established in 1874 CE, being the oldest. The school was initiated by Christian missionaries and named after Canon Cecil Tyndale-Biscoe (1863–1949). It maintains current affiliations with the Church Mission Society, and its first principal was Reverend J. H. Knowles. The institution has five departments. It is well known for its extra-curricular activities, particularly swimming, skiing, mountain climbing, camping, and regatta. The school emphasizes physical activities such as mountaineering, trekking, boating, football, cricket, and swimming to foster courage, masculinity, and physical fitness. When football was introduced, students initially resisted due to the belief that cow leather, used in the balls, was holy, and touching it was blasphemous; instead, they played using wooden clogs (known as Khraav in Kashmiri) in their feet. Similarly, when boating was introduced, students disliked it because boatmen were not considered respectable in Kashmiri society; however, over time, the activity was adopted, and the school boys became proficient paddlers and rowers. In 1880, Reverend J. H. Knowles laid the foundation of the C.M.S. School on the premises of the Modern Chest Disease Hospital (Drugjan) in Srinagar, starting with five pupils. By 1883, the number of boys increased to 30. In 1890, the Government allowed the C.M.S. to relocate the school to downtown, moving it to a large house and compound on the riverbank at Fateh Kadal, where the student population grew to about 200. In 1891, Canon C.E. Tyndale-Biscoe joined the school, when the roll stood at 250 pupils. The primary school evolved into a middle school and later into a high school, which was later named the Hadow Memorial School in honour of its honorary treasurer for 40 years. Eventually, five additional mission schools were established—one in each part of the capital city and one in Anantnag.

Un'alma innamorata (HWV 173) is a dramatic secular cantata for soprano and instruments composed by George Frideric Handel in 1707. It is also listed in other catalogues as HG liiB,92 and HHA v/5,97. The title translates to "A soul in love." The piece was composed for the Ruspoli family to be performed at their country estate in Vignanello, near Rome, with the copyist's bill dated 30 June 1707. It is possible that the soprano part was written for Vittoria Tarquini, a singer with whom Handel is rumored to have had a relationship, and she was present at the Vignanello estate around the time of composition. The text may have been authored by Abbé Francesco Mazziotti, who served as tutor to Ruspoli's eldest son. Despite being performed by a female voice, the text does not specify whether the "voice" is male or female. It describes a heart that is faithful in love becoming angry when wounded, yet the singer is content because it loves more than one heart and rejects the harsh rules and rigors of love as defined by Cupid. The work is scored for violin and keyboard, with occasional figured bass markings in the second movement, and includes three recitative-aria pairings. A typical performance lasts approximately fifteen and a half minutes. The cantata comprises six movements, beginning with: "Sia il solo dolore geloso timore, le pene e catene martire crudel." (Let its only pain be jealous fear, and let cruel torments be its chains.) Movements do not contain repeat markings unless specified; the bar count given is the raw number from the manuscript, not including repeat markings. This information is drawn from volume 52B, starting at page 92, of the Händel-Gesellschaft edition. This article about a classical composition is a stub.
