Upon release, Song Cycle elicited positive reviews from critics associated with the New Journalism movement, but yielded confusion from retailers, radio programmers, and the label's marketing staff.[80] To address poor sales, the company, without consulting Parks, launched an unconventional ad campaign declaring the album a commercial flop.[81] According to Parks, "there was every expectation that the recording costs would be recovered, and they were, within three years."[82][nb 10]

We didn't know whom we were selling Ry [Cooder] or Randy [Newman] to, it was strictly on a wing and a prayer, but we did our darnedest to sell them anyway.

After completing Song Cycle Parks relocated to Laurel Canyon and co-produced Newman's 1968 self-titled debut album with Waronker, which faced a similar reception.[86][65][nb 11] The Parks-Waronker production team reunited for folk singer Arlo Guthrie's 1969 album Running Down the Road, featuring contributions from Los Angeles session musicians such as Ry Cooder.[88] They then produced Cooder's 1970 self-titled debut album, containing an ornate orchestral rendition of "One Meat Ball" arranged by Parks.[87][nb 12]

Following the Beach Boys' departure from Capitol Records, the band signed to Reprise in 1969 through a deal brokered by Parks. Amid concerns about the group's contractual complexities and declining record sales, Parks later stated that he "put [his] job on the line" to facilitate the deal.[90] The band's second album for the label, Surf's Up (1971), included the title track, co-written by Parks originally for Smile, and "A Day in the Life of a Tree", featuring Parks singing part of the coda.[91]

In the 1970s, Parks collaborated extensively with Little Feat founder Lowell George, contributing to the band's recordings and co-writing material throughout the decade.[93] Parks and George first met during sessions for the Fraternity of Man's second album Get It On! (1969), which featured future Little Feat members Richie Hayward and George's songwriting collaborator Martin Kibbee. Their friendship grew after Little Feat's self-titled 1971 debut album, with Parks periodically co-writing, producing, and advising George on music business matters.[94]

After Warner Bros. had considered dropping the band, Parks invited George to contribute guitar to his forthcoming follow-up to Song Cycle and record their collaborative song "Sailin' Shoes", with the results later reaffirming Little Feat's value to Warner Bros.[94][nb 13] Hayward later stated, "Van Dyke Parks got us our record deal and produced us. He's an amazing human being—the Oscar Levant of rock music. [...] He's old school. You can tell by his violin scores."[96][nb 14]

From the late 1960s to early 1970s, Parks transitioned to an executive role at Warner Bros., having proposed alternative revenue streams to reduce artists' reliance on touring. He spearheaded the creation of Audio-Visual Services, a division producing promotional films for acts such as Zappa, Joni Mitchell, Earth, Wind & Fire, and Captain Beefheart.[88][nb 15] Directors and crews were recruited from the advertising industry to realize these projects,[97] intended for screening before Warner Bros. theatrical features[98] and potential educational or cable television distribution.[97] The films combined performance footage with surrealist visuals, exemplified by Beefheart's Lick My Decals Off short.[98] Parks was appointed as the division's head in August 1970.[97] According to Henderson, Song-length, musical film shorts called Panoram Soundies had been tried in a jukebox-style format by the Mills Novelty Co. during the 1940s, and the Beatles filmed promotional TV/movie theater clips in 1967–68 [...] but no record company had ever established an in-house department for the production of what would prove the forerunner of music videos.[97] The division dissolved by mid-1971.[97] According to some writers, Ostin deemed the initiative financially unsustainable due to limited distribution avenues and costs exceeding $500,000 (equivalent to $3.88 million in 2024).[97][99] Parks stated in a 2013 interview that only one of the films produced had exceeded costs of $18,500: "I provided that each artist would get 25% of the net profits of the rentals or sales. [...] Warners soon tired of what I thought was a fair equation of participation in creative profits, and basically isolated me to the extent that I left."[100]

Parks had achieved the kind of oracular stature at the company that transcends any one title or job. His opinion was sought out on matters large and small. He was heavily involved in A&R decisions [...].

Unrealized plans included a dedicated cable channel;[97] internal memos from Parks referenced early concepts for what became Music Television, including the phrase "I want my music television" and the acronym "MTV".[102] Parks remained under Ostin, later saying, "I was directly under Mo Ostin at WB Records [...] I answered to only one man. That was Mo."[102] His initiatives had also extended to facilitating logistical support for filming at the 1969 Woodstock Festival, though he later distanced himself from the festival: "I had other priorities than queuing at a rock concert's mud flat latrine."[102]

In 1970, Parks and Newman recommended electronic music duo Beaver & Krause to Smith, leading to their signing.[103] In 1972, Parks became involved in the career of musician Peter Ivers through mutual associate Buell Neidlinger. Parks admired Ivers' songwriting and technical skill on harmonica, leading to Ivers signing with Warner Bros. and recording his third album, Terminal Love (1974). Ivers also contributed as a session musician on Parks' projects.[104]

The 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill profoundly influenced Parks' artistic direction, prompting him to pursue environmental and racial justice causes through his work and deepen his engagement with Caribbean music. He sought to elevate the recognition of Caribbean traditions, particularly calypso and steel pan, as vehicles for political consciousness, and to subvert the oil industry's cultural influence. From 1970 to 1975, he promoted West Indian music in the U.S., however, logistical challenges in touring with a large steel band and resistance from corporate interests hindered broader acceptance.[105]

Parks produced the Esso Trinidad Steel Band's 1971 album of covers by artists like the Kinks and the Jackson 5, as well as the 1974 calypso collection Hot & Sweet by Trinidadian artist Mighty Sparrow.[106] He dedicated the Esso Trinidad Steel Band's album to Prince Bernhard of the World Wildlife Fund as part of his environmental advocacy: "Everything was directed to making it a proper, political, green album."[105] Parks' second album, Discover America (1972), reinterpreted Trinidadian calypso standards alongside compositions by songwriters such as Allen Toussaint and the sole original "Sailin' Shoes".[106] He delayed the album's release to allow Little Feat's version of the song to debut first on their second album Sailin' Shoes (1972).[95] Parks' focus on calypso during this period also led to friction with Bob Marley, whose requests for production assistance he declined.[105]

Parks' third album, Clang of the Yankee Reaper (1976), co-produced with Andrew Wickham and Trevor Lawrence, revisited calypso music while exploring themes of British colonial influence in the Caribbean. It featured one original composition alongside reimagined Trinidadian songs.[107] Limited production resources led to scaled-back arrangements, including the use of an ARP String Synthesizer instead of live orchestration.[108] The sessions were further affected by the death of a close friend of Parks prior to recording; he later dismissed the album as "brain-dead", disowning it in subsequent years.[109]

While recording the Discover America version of "Sailin' Shoes", Parks and George encountered the Japanese band Happy End, who visited their studio unannounced. Parks later recounted that the group had sought guidance on creating "the California Sound". Though initially hesitant due to his workload, George noticed a briefcase filled with cash brought by Happy End's representatives, prompting an impromptu collaboration. The two wrote "Goodbye America, Goodbye Japan" ("さよならアメリカ　さよならニッポン", "Sayonara America Sayonara Nippon"), which became a chart-topping hit in Japan,[110] while Parks produced Happy End's final album, Happy End (1973).[111] This marked the first meeting between Parks' and band member Haruomi Hosono, who later performed alongside Parks at numerous concerts in Japan.[112]

Parks was the primary composer of the Beach Boys' 1973 single "Sail On, Sailor", which reached number 79 on the Billboard charts.[113][nb 16] He joined initial recording sessions for Little Feat's fourth album Feats Don't Fail Me Now at Hollywood's Sound Factory between January and March 1974.[115] The track "Spanish Moon", produced by Parks and co-written with George, featured a prominent Parks-assisted horn arrangement by Tower of Power and other production elements distinguishing the track from the remainder of the album.[116] A truncated version of the song was released as a single in March 1975.[117]

Parks' involvement did not extend beyond these early sessions, having sparked tensions with Warner Bros. due to budgetary disputes, as recalled by George, who added that Parks "was going to do more" before the band "got stuck [and] broke up for about two weeks".[115][nb 17] The album's title origin remains contested between Parks and guitarist Paul Barrère.[118] Alongside members of Little Feat, Parks also contributed to Kathy Dalton's 1973 solo debut Amazing and Howdy Moon's 1974 self-titled album.[119]

During the 1970s, Parks collaborated extensively with singer-songwriter Harry Nilsson,[120] contributing to albums such as Nilsson Schmilsson (1971), where he played accordion on "The Moonbeam Song",[121] and Duit on Mon Dei (1975), where he provided Caribbean-inspired arrangements after completing Clang of the Yankee Reaper.[120][nb 18] Parks introduced Nilsson to steel pan player and Desperadoes Steel Orchestra member Robert Greenidge for Duit on Mon Dei and performed piano on several tracks.[123][nb 19] He characterized his role as Nilsson's "musical secretary", translating his fragmentary concepts into fully realized compositions,[125] and Parks' organizational skills proved vital during the chaotic, drug-fueled sessions.[126]

My life basically gravitated toward [Harry Nilsson], who was truly a genius-- the smartest guy I ever met in the music business. He turned my head around because he could be retro without shame.

Nilsson drew inspiration from Parks' Trinidadian musical explorations and both musicians had a longtime familiarity with the session players, including Jesse Ed Davis, Jim Keltner, Bobby Keys, and Klaus Voormann, whom Parks had previously worked with throughout 1974.[127][nb 20] Plans for live performances involving Parks and the studio ensemble, plus Jesse Ed Davis and Ringo Starr, were abandoned due to challenges securing Nilsson's ideal venue.[129] Parks involvement extended to the 1975 follow-up Sandman, where he expanded Nilsson's "Jesus Christ, You're Tall", and whose Voorman-designed sleeve featured caricatures of Parks and other members of the studio ensemble.[130]

Having brought Toussaint to Warners' attention via Discover America, Parks traveled to Louisiana to work on Toussaint's 1975 album Southern Nights, though he was ultimately denied a production credit due to intervention by Toussaint's management.[93] That year, Parks and Brian Wilson recorded "Come to the Sunshine", intended for the Beach Boys album that became 15 Big Ones (1976), but the recording was lost.[131] In 1976, he appeared as one of the interviewees in the band's NBC television special It's OK!.[132]

By the late 1970s, Parks had entered a period of personal and professional transition.[107] Having ensconced himself in the American southeast, he returned to Los Angeles after being commissioned by Jack Nicholson to compose the score for Goin' South (1978), which Nicholson directed.[109] The film's music, characterized by unconventional instrumentation and silent-film-era piano motifs, echoed the style of Parks' earlier solo work, particularly Song Cycle. This project marked his shift toward film composition, though his later screen scores seldom retained the sonic signatures of his standalone recordings.[133]

George's 1979 solo debut, Thanks, I'll Eat It Here, included "Cheek to Cheek", a song co-written with Parks.[134] Little Feat biographer Mark Brend surmised that the track "Himmler's Ring", written by Jimmy Webb, was arranged by Parks, citing a resemblance to Discover America.[135] Parks' partnership with Nilsson continued with Flash Harry (1980), an album that reunited the extant RCA house band and included Nilsson's version of "Cheek to Cheek".[136][nb 21]

Parks and Nilsson also collaborated on the soundtrack for Robert Altman's film Popeye (1980), where Parks appeared onscreen as a pianist.[137] The film's soundtrack elicited a mostly unfavorable critical response; Parks later suggested that Tom Pierson's incidental score had overshadowed the sparse, character-driven songs, disrupting his aim at a subdued musical atmosphere inspired by the original Popeye cartoons.[138] Elements of Parks' Popeye arrangements were later sampled in Jon Brion's score for Punch-Drunk Love (2002).[137] Later in 1980, Parks joined Nilsson as part of a studio band for Starr's unreleased album Can't Fight Lightning, but the sessions halted abruptly following John Lennon's murder that December.[139]

In the 1980s, Parks shifted focus to composing for television and low-budget films. In a 2011 interview, he reflected: "I withdrew from the popular music field as a producer and even as an arranger and started scoring countless television shows that mean nothing and B movies with A scores, in my view. I worked hard to get my children their college and stayed insulated, basically."[27] This included Shelley Duvall's Faerie Tale Theatre (1982–1987).[140]

Parks revived his solo career with his fourth album, Jump! (1984), conceived as the soundtrack to a musical adaptation of Joel Chandler Harris' Uncle Remus stories. The album showcases acoustic orchestrations inspired by early 20th-century brass bands and American folk traditions.[141] It received critical praise[37] and Parks, collaborating with artist Barry Moser, expanded the project into a trilogy of illustrated children's books: Jump!, Jump Again!, and Jump On Over!.[141] The first volume received a Caldecott Medal in 1986.[142]

In 1988, Parks played accordion on the Beach Boys' single "Kokomo"[143] and contributed four songs – "City of Light", "It's a B-Movie", "Cutting Edge", and "Worthless"—to the 1987 film The Brave Little Toaster, directed by Jerry Rees.[citation needed] He also co-produced Hal Wilner's multi-artist albums Lost in the Stars: The Music of Kurt Weill (1985) and Stay Awake: Various Interpretations of Music from Vintage Disney Films (1988).[144]

Parks' fifth album Tokyo Rose (1989) continued his exploration of cross-cultural themes, revisiting Japanese-American relations initially addressed in the Song Cycle song "Pot Pourri".[145] To promote the album, he performed concerts in Japan with Haruomi Hosono, songwriter Syd Straw, harmonicist Tommy Morgan, and steelpan player Yann Tomita as his supporting band.[146]

In 1990, Parks appeared on Twin Peaks, playing a defense attorney in the episode "The Orchid's Curse",[147] and in 1991 he composed the music for an album pairing Jodie Foster's narration of The Fisherman & His Wife with his original score.[37] During this period, he also provided arrangements for U2's Rattle and Hum (1988), Sesame Street's Follow That Bird (1985), T-Bone Burnett's The Talking Animals (1988), Stan Ridgway's Mosquitos (1989), Divinyls' Divinyls (1991), and Fiona Apple's Tidal (1996).[110]

In October 1995, Warner Bros. issued the album Orange Crate Art, credited jointly to Parks and Brian Wilson.[148] A concept album centered on California's cultural heritage, Wilson provided lead vocals for nearly all tracks.[149] The album received critical praise[150] and, on October 8, 1996, Parks and Wilson performed a concert together at the Will Geer Theater in Topanga, California.[148] In 2000, Parks was commissioned to write an overture.

The episode "The Orchid's Curse," and in 1991 he composed the music for an album pairing Jodie Foster's narration of The Fisherman & His Wife with his original score. During this period, he also provided arrangements for U2's Rattle and Hum (1988), Sesame Street's Follow That Bird (1985), T-Bone Burnett's The Talking Animals (1988), Stan Ridgway's Mosquitos (1989), Divinyls' Divinyls (1991), and Fiona Apple's Tidal (1996). In October 1995, Warner Bros. issued the album Orange Crate Art, credited jointly to Parks and Brian Wilson, a concept album centered on California's cultural heritage, with Wilson providing lead vocals for nearly all tracks. The album received critical praise and, on October 8, 1996, Parks and Wilson performed a concert together at the Will Geer Theater in Topanga, California. In 2000, Parks was commissioned to write an overture arrangement of Wilson's songs for Wilson's Pet Sounds concert performances. Parks attended the 2001 tribute show held in Wilson's honor at the Radio City Music Hall in New York and appeared as a featured guest on his Gettin' In over My Head (2004). Through the 2000s, Parks remained active as an arranger and collaborator, contributing to albums by Victoria Williams, Sam Phillips, Joanna Newsom, and Rufus Wainwright, and providing songs for the children's television series Harold and the Purple Crayon (2001–2002). Parks' association with Australian rock band Silverchair began with his work on their fourth studio album Diorama in 2002, when he was attracted to the music of lead singer and guitarist Daniel Johns. He composed orchestral arrangements for Silverchair's fifth album Young Modern in 2007, with Johns traveling to Prague with Parks to have the arrangements recorded by the Czech Philharmonic; the album's title is a nickname Parks uses for Johns. In 2003, Parks was contacted by Wilson to assist with live performances of Smile, billed as Brian Wilson Presents Smile, which began with a premiere performance at the Royal Festival Hall in London in 2004, which Parks attended. He subsequently provided lyrics and narration to select tracks on Wilson's That Lucky Old Sun (2008). During this period, Parks provided arrangements for Wainwright's Want and Want Two (2004), Newsom's Ys (2006), and Scissor Sisters' Ta-Dah (2006). He contributed the Smile parody song "Black Sheep" to the 2007 comedy film Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story. In the late 2000s, Parks worked with Inara George, daughter of Lowell, on An Invitation (2008), an album combining Inara's vocal narratives with Parks' orchestral backdrops, and they performed two songs together on January 8, 2008, at the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles, as part of the program Concrete Frequency: Songs of the City. In 2009, Parks performed in The People Speak, a documentary feature film based on historian Howard Zinn's A People's History of the United States, using dramatic and musical performances of the letters, diaries, and speeches of everyday Americans; Parks performed with Bob Dylan and Ry Cooder on the December 13, 2009, broadcast on the History Channel, playing "Do Re Mi" and reportedly a couple of other Guthrie songs that were excluded from the final edit. In 2011, Parks released Arrangements, Vol. 1 through his label Bananastan, a curation of previously released songs he had arranged for other artists in the 1960s. That year, he began releasing a series of vinyl singles featuring original songs, archival recordings, cover songs, and re-recordings, which were compiled into the album Songs Cycled, released on May 6, 2013, through Bella Union. It was followed later in the year with Super Chief: Music for the Silver Screen, an orchestral concept album that compiled music originating from his various television and film scores over the previous decades. In January 2013, Parks performed with Haruomi Hosono in Tokyo for the first time in many years. That March, he performed at the Adelaide Festival with Daniel Johns and Kimbra. In September, he curated a "Best-of" CD for New Orleans pianist Tom McDermott, titled Bamboula. On November 22, Parks released a 7-inch single, "I'm History", to mark the 50th anniversary of John F. Kennedy's assassination. In 2014, Parks underwent unsuccessful hand surgery, which resulted in his hands freezing after about forty minutes of playing the piano. On May 9, 2015, he performed what he described as his "final piano performance" at the Largo nightclub in Los Angeles, with guest performers including Gaby Moreno, Joe Henry, Edward Droste of Grizzly Bear, Kimbra, and Grant Geissman. In 2019, Parks partnered with Moreno on ¡Spangled!, creating orchestral arrangements for traditional songs from South and Central America. He arranged four compositions by Mexican poet and harpist Verónica Valerio for their 2021 EP Van Dyke Parks Orchestrates Verónica Valerio: Only in America. Additional collaborative work includes contributions as an arranger and instrumentalist for Brian Woodbury's Antipathy & Ideology (2022), Oliver Sim's Hideous Bastard (2022), Tommy McLain's I Ran Down Every Dream (2022), and Wainwright's Folkocracy (2023). Parks' overall sound and music style has been categorized as orchestral pop, Americana, art pop, baroque pop, and experimental pop. His musical influences include Percy Grainger, Louis Moreau Gottschalk, Spike Jones, Juan García Esquivel, and Les Paul, as well as Bach, Beethoven, Charles Ives, Chopin, Antonín Dvořák, Bedřich Smetana, Vaughn Williams, George Gershwin, Woody Guthrie, and Howlin' Wolf. According to Parks, hearing Jones' "Cocktails for Two" (1944) and Les Paul and Mary Ford's "How High the Moon" (1951) as a child convinced him of the creative possibilities of recorded and multitracked sound and set him on a lifelong path in studio music. His affinity for "tuneful percussion" originated from attending Grainger's chamber-folk symphony performances in his youth. Lyrically, Parks is characterized by a free-associative approach, with influences on his lyric style including James Joyce, Lawrence Ferlinghetti, e.e. cummings, William Saroyan, and John Steinbeck; the Discover America album title derived from Ferlinghetti's poem "I Am Waiting". In his AllMusic summary, contributor Mark Dehming wrote that Parks remains "widely regarded as one of the most talented behind-the-scenes figures in rock and pop music and a respected, cult-favorite singer/songwriter in his own right". Pitchfork contributor Jayson Greene recognized Parks as placing "an inimitable stamp on American pop, though the vast majority of music fans have no idea when they are listening to his work". I honestly knew that I wasn't an artist, even when I signed at Warner Bros. I knew I was simply a musician who wanted to record in the studio, and I signed an artist contract basically kicking and screaming. Writing in 2002, Brend summarized Parks' career as eclectic and resistant to categorization, marked by his multidisciplinary approach across prolific collaborative work, involvement in 1960s and 1970s West Coast music scenes, "unique" solo projects, and ambiguously defined role at Warner Bros. Parks himself reflected on his role as a behind-the-scenes collaborator rather than a conventional solo artist, citing his work with figures such as Randy Newman, Ry Cooder, and Little Feat as examples of his preference for supporting others' creative visions. Song Cycle influenced the 1970s singer-songwriter movement and inspired many other recording artists to experiment with studio artifice. Author and musician Bob Stanley credits Parks, among others, with originating soft rock styles leading to the offshoot genre later termed "sunshine pop", and with presaging the more complex pop styles associated with early forms of progressive rock. In his 2010-published 33⅓ book covering Song Cycle, Richard Henderson credits Parks as influential on music production in his consideration for the studio as a compositional tool alongside "the potential of a record's production to suggest scenery and location". Parks is the great-nephew of 19th-century poet Will Carleton, whose book Farm Ballads originated the title of Parks' Clang of the Yankee Reaper. His brother Carson wrote the song "Somethin' Stupid", which became a hit for Frank and Nancy Sinatra in 1967.

Vault 7 is a series of documents published by WikiLeaks starting on 7 March 2017, revealing the activities and capabilities of the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) in conducting electronic surveillance and cyber warfare. The files, spanning from 2013 to 2016, detail the agency’s software tools capable of compromising cars, smart TVs, and web browsers including Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and Opera, as well as smartphone operating systems such as Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android, and computer operating systems including Microsoft Windows, macOS, and Linux. A CIA internal audit found that 91 out of more than 500 malware tools in use in 2016 were compromised by the release, all developed by the Operations Support Branch of the CIA. The Vault 7 release prompted the CIA to reclassify WikiLeaks as a "non-state hostile intelligence service." In July 2022, former CIA software engineer Joshua Schulte was convicted of leaking the documents to WikiLeaks and in February 2024 sentenced to 40 years' imprisonment on espionage charges and 80 months for child pornography charges. WikiLeaks first teased the Vault 7 release in February 2017 via cryptic messages on Twitter (now X), followed by the release of classified documents on the 2012 French presidential election as context for the upcoming Vault 7 series. US intelligence and law enforcement officials told Reuters in March 2017 that they had been aware of the CIA security breach since late 2016 and were focusing on "contractors" as a possible source. Federal law enforcement identified Joshua Adam Schulte as a suspected source in 2017, and he later pled not guilty before being convicted in July 2022. On 13 April 2017, CIA Director Mike Pompeo declared WikiLeaks a "hostile intelligence service," and in September 2021, Yahoo! News reported that the CIA considered kidnapping or assassinating Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, as well as spying on his associates, sowing discord among them, and stealing their electronic devices—though all such plans were scrapped due to legal and moral objections, with a former Trump national security official stating, "We should never act out of a desire for revenge." The first batch, named "Year Zero," was released on 7 March 2017 and consisted of 7,818 web pages with 943 attachments, more than Edward Snowden’s 2013 NSA leak. The documents were placed in a locked archive earlier in the week, with the passphrase revealed on the 7th, referencing President John F. Kennedy’s quote about splintering the CIA. WikiLeaks did not name its source but stated the files had circulated among former U.S. government hackers and contractors, one of whom provided the archive. The source reportedly wished to initiate a public debate about the security, creation, use, proliferation, and democratic control of cyberweapons, raising urgent questions about whether the CIA’s hacking capabilities exceed its mandate and the need for public oversight. WikiLeaks attempted to redact identifying information from the documents but faced criticism for leaving key details unredacted and also tried to allow connections between individuals through unique identifiers. It also postponed releasing the source code for the cyberweapons, which is reportedly several hundred million lines long, until a consensus on the technical and political nature of the CIA’s program and how such tools should be analyzed, disarmed, and published emerged. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange claimed this was only part of a larger series. The CIA issued a statement expressing deep concern over disclosures that could damage the Intelligence Community’s ability to protect the U.S. from terrorists or adversaries, stating such leaks jeopardize personnel and operations and provide adversaries with tools to cause harm. On 19 March 2017, Assange stated that technology companies contacted had not agreed to, disagreed with, or questioned WikiLeaks’ standard industry disclosure plan, which sets a 90-day window for vulnerability disclosure after the company is given full details. Only Mozilla received information on the vulnerabilities, while Google and other companies only confirmed receiving initial notifications. WikiLeaks argued that most companies have conflicts of interest due to their classified work with U.S. government agencies, limiting staff with security clearances from fixing flaws based on leaked information, and suggested users may prefer organizations like Mozilla or European firms that prioritize user privacy over government contracts. On 23 March 2017, WikiLeaks released "Dark Matter," detailing CIA efforts to hack Apple’s iPhones and Mac devices, including the Sonic Screwdriver malware that could bypass Apple’s password firmware via the Thunderbolt interface. On 31 March 2017, "Marble" was published, containing 676 source code files for the CIA’s Marble Framework, used to obfuscate malware to evade detection by antivirus software and include a de-obfuscator to reverse the process. On 7 April 2017, "Grasshopper" was released, consisting of 27 documents on a framework used to build customized, persistent malware for Microsoft Windows, focusing on avoiding Personal Security Products like MS Security Essentials, Symantec Endpoint, or Kaspersky IS. On 14 April 2017, "HIVE" was published, covering a top-secret CIA virus program developed by its Embedded Development Branch (EDB), including six documents on the HIVE multi-platform malware suite, which used a public-facing HTTPS interface to transfer data from target devices to the CIA and allowed remote command execution while hiding behind unsuspicious domains via a "Switchblade" masking interface. On 21 April 2017, "Weeping Angel" was released, a tool co-developed by the CIA and MI5 to exploit early smart TVs for covert intelligence gathering, enabling microphones and cameras to record surroundings while the TV appears off, with data stored locally or sent to the CIA. Allegedly, both agencies collaborated on the tool during Joint Development Workshops. On 28 April 2017, "Scribbles" was published, including documentation and source code for a tool to track documents leaked to whistleblowers and journalists by embedding web beacon tags into classified documents to trace the leakers. The tool affects Microsoft Office documents from versions 97 to 2016 (excluding 95) and non-locked, unencrypted files; when opened, an invisible image hosted on a CIA server generates an HTTP request logged on the server, revealing who opened it and where. If opened in an alternative word processor, the image may be visible; if opened offline or in protected view, the beacon won’t connect, unless editing is enabled. On 5 May 2017, "Archimedes" was released, previously known as "Fulcrum," which allows CIA operators to redirect local area network web browser sessions through a controlled computer, performing a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attack. WikiLeaks included hashes to help identify and guard against the virus, with experts like Pierluigi Paganini suggesting that targeted computers could search for these hashes to detect an attack. On 12 May 2017, "AfterMidnight" and "Assassin" were published. AfterMidnight is malware installed on a target computer as a DLL file, executed during a reboot, then connects to a CIA Command and Control (C2) server to download modules and run tasks. Assassin is similar but runs inside a Windows service process, acting as a C2 to collect and send user data to CIA Listening Posts (LPs), with both being persistent, beacons, and self-uninstalling on a set date. On 19 May 2017, "Athena" was released, a malware allegedly developed by the CIA in August 2015, shortly after Microsoft released Windows 10, with a secondary malware named "Hera." Both were developed with Siege Technologies, a New Hampshire private corporation, and exploit persistent DLL files to create backdoors, steal data, and send it to CIA servers or delete data. Athena hijacks Windows’ Remote Access services, while Hera hijacks the Dnscache service, affecting all versions of Windows including Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10. The encryption differs between infected computers and CIA Listening Posts. While the documents describe the malware, WikiLeaks did not provide evidence that the CIA used Athena. On 1 June 2017, "Pandemic" was released, a persistent implant on Windows machines with shared folders that functions as a file system filter driver, listening to Server Message Block traffic and replacing legitimate files with malware during downloads, only modifying files in transit while leaving originals unchanged. It can modify up to 20 files at a time, with a maximum individual file size of 800 MB, and possibly allows infected computers to become file servers, spreading to new targets. On 15 June 2017, "Cherry Blossom" was published, using a command and control server called Cherry Tree and custom router firmware called FlyTrap to monitor internet activity, scan for email addresses, chat usernames, MAC addresses, and VoIP numbers, and redirect traffic. On 22 June 2017, "Brutal Kangaroo" was released, a project focused on compromising air-gapped networks via infected USB drives, including tools such as Drifting Deadline, Shattered Assurance, Shadow, and Broken Promise for data exfiltration. On 28 June 2017, "Elsa" was published, a tool for tracking Windows devices on nearby WiFi networks. On 29 June 2017, "OutlawCountry" was released, a Linux 2.6 kernel module that allowed CIA agents to spy on Linux servers and redirect outgoing traffic to a chosen site. On 6 July 2017, "BothanSpy" was published, a tool designed to steal SSH credentials from Windows computers. On 13 July 2017, "Highrise" was released, a tool used to intercept and redirect SMS messages on Android phones running versions 4.0 through 4.3 and also serve as an encrypted communication channel between CIA agents and supervisors. On 19 July 2017, documents from Raytheon Blackbird Technologies on the "UMBRAGE Component Library" (UCL) were published, analyzing real-world malware attacks and providing recommendations to CIA development teams for further investigation and proof-of-concept development. On 27 July 2017, "Imperial" was released, including three tools: Achilles, which turns MacOS DMG install files into trojan malware; Aeris, a malware implant for POSIX systems; and SeaPea, an OS X rootkit. On 3 August 2017, "Dumbo" was published, a tool used to disable webcams, microphones, and other surveillance tools over WiFi and Bluetooth to allow field agents to operate undetected. On 10 August 2017, "CouchPotato" was released, a tool for intercepting and saving remote video streams to enable the CIA to tap into other people’s surveillance systems. On 24 August 2017, "ExpressLane" was published, highlighting a covert information collection tool used by the CIA to exfiltrate biometric data collection systems of services it liaises with, such as the NSA, DHS, and FBI. ExpressLane was installed under the cover of upgrading biometric software by CIA’s Office of Technical Services (OTS) agents without their knowledge. On 31 August 2017, "Angelfire" was released, a malware framework for Windows XP and Windows 7 made of five parts: Solartime modified the boot sector to load Wolfcreek, a self-loading driver that loaded other drivers; Keystone loaded other malware; BadMFS was a covert file system hiding malware; and Windows Transitory File System was a newer alternative to BadMFS. The manual included a long list of problems with the tools.

On 7 March 2017, WikiLeaks released Vault 7 "Year Zero," revealing that a top-secret CIA unit used the German Consulate General in Frankfurt as a base for cyber operations targeting Europe, China, and the Middle East. The hackers, part of the Center for Cyber Intelligence Europe (CCIE), operated under cover identities and diplomatic passports to avoid detection by customs officials. The documents showed the CIA had amassed a large collection of cyberattack techniques and malware from other sources, maintained by the UMBRAGE group within the CIA's Remote Devices Branch, with these techniques stored in a "Umbrage Component Library" git repository. WikiLeaks described UMBRAGE as a library of attack methods "stolen" from malware produced by other nations, including the Russian Federation, to enable false flag attacks, allowing the CIA to mislead forensic investigators by disguising its actions as those of other groups. Among the techniques borrowed was the file wiping method used by Shamoon. The Marble framework, a string obfuscator used to hide text fragments in malware, reached version 1.0 in 2015 and was used by the CIA throughout 2016. It included foreign language text—such as Chinese, Russian, Korean, Arabic, and Persian—to mask the origin of attacks, though technical analysis disputed this claim, suggesting its primary purpose was to evade antivirus detection. Marble also included a deobfuscator tool to reverse the obfuscation. The "ExpressLane" project involved the CIA using a covert tool to exfiltrate biometric data from liaison services like the NSA, DHS, and FBI, installed under the guise of software upgrades by the CIA's Office of Technical Services (OTS). On 31 August 2017, WikiLeaks published the Angelfire manual, a malware framework for Windows XP and Windows 7 composed of five parts: Solartime modified the boot sector to load Wolfcreek, a self-loading driver that loaded other drivers; Keystone loaded additional malware; BadMFS and Windows Transitory File System were covert file systems that hid malware. The manual listed numerous flaws in the tools. On 7 September 2017, Protego, described as a PIC-based missile control system developed by Raytheon, was released. On 9 November 2017, WikiLeaks began publishing Vault 8, which included source code and development logs for Hive, a covert communications platform for CIA malware, previously released as part of Vault 7 on 14 April 2017. In October 2021, a backdoor based on Hive's source code, named xdr33, was discovered targeting an unspecified F5 appliance, allowing file uploads/downloads, network traffic spying, and command execution. Researchers released a report on it in January 2022. The documents originated from a high-security network inside the CIA's Center for Cyber Intelligence (CCI) in Langley, Virginia, and revealed the CCI had a unit focused on compromising Apple products. Symantec found that some of the described software matched cyberattacks by "Longhorn," a group it had monitored since 2014, suspected to be government-sponsored and active against 40 targets in 16 countries. The Vault 7 documents also detailed the CIA's use of tools like HammerDrill, a CD/DVD collection tool that logs insertion/removal events and collects files, and a "Windows FAX DLL injection" exploit in Windows XP, Vista, and 7 that allows malware to be hidden under another application's DLL, requiring prior compromise. The CIA's tools were capable of compromising both Apple's iOS and Google's Android operating systems, enabling access to audio and message traffic before encryption, including through keylogging and touch input recording, though end-to-end encrypted apps like Telegram, WhatsApp, and Signal were not cracked. Edward Snowden stated the leaks revealed the U.S. government was developing vulnerabilities in its own products and intentionally keeping them unpatched, calling this reckless. Nathan White of Access Now criticized the practice of stockpiling vulnerabilities, arguing they should be responsibly disclosed. Lee Mathews noted that many of the techniques were already known to cybersecurity experts and were likely used for targeted surveillance. Ashley Gorski emphasized that such vulnerabilities could be exploited by foreign governments and cybercriminals. Cindy Cohn of the Electronic Frontier Foundation argued that if the CIA knew of a security flaw in a device, it should disclose it and fix it, as the freedom to have private conversations is essential to a free society. Microsoft President Brad Smith stated that both the NSA and CIA had stockpiled vulnerabilities, which were later leaked, and called for a "digital Geneva Convention" requiring governments to report such vulnerabilities to vendors.

Velma Springstead (22 August 1906 – 27 March 1927) was a Canadian track and field athlete born in Hamilton, Ontario. She won the gold medal in the high jump at the 1925 Canadian Track and Field Championships and became a member of the first women's track and field team of Canada to compete internationally. In July 1925, she participated in a track and field qualification at Varsity Stadium for the Amateur Athletic Union of Canada, which earned her a spot on that historic team. The following month, she finished third in the high jump and fourth in the hurdles at a track and field meet in London, England, where she was presented a trophy by Lord Decies for her courage. Outside of athletics, Springstead worked as a teacher at Calvin Presbyterian Church and as a secretary for Tuckett Tobacco Company. She died of pneumonia on 27 March 1927 in Hamilton, Ontario. After her death, the Velma Springstead Trophy was established to award the best Canadian sportswoman of the year, and in 2011, she was posthumously inducted into the Hamilton Sports Hall of Fame.

Vibha Saraf is an Indian singer-songwriter and Bollywood playback singer who performs and writes music primarily inspired by Kashmiri folk traditions. She has contributed to the soundtracks of the films Raazi, which won Best Film at the 64th Filmfare Awards, and Gully Boy, the fourth highest-grossing Bollywood film of 2019. In 2019, she was jointly nominated with Harshdeep Kaur for Best Female Playback Singer at both the 65th Filmfare Awards and the 20th International Indian Film Academy (IIFA) Awards for the song "Dilbaro" from the 2018 film Raazi. Born in the Fateh Kadal neighbourhood of Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, Saraf's family relocated to New Delhi when she was three years old during the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits. She studied Hindustani classical music for four years at Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra before pursuing pop music for five years, and worked as a management consultant for five years before leaving to focus on music. In 2013, she moved to Mumbai to pursue her music career, recording her first soundtrack song, "O Soniye," a duet with Arijit Singh for Titoo MBA in 2014, and later singing "Feeling Avnavi" with Advait Nemlekar for Gujjubhai the Great in 2015. Her debut single, "Harmokh Bartal," was released in 2016, a Kashmiri bhajan reinterpreted with Tapas Relia composing and Ashwin Srinivasan on flute and Ankur Mukherjee on guitar. In 2018, she performed "Dilbaro" for Raazi, a song written by Shankar–Ehsaan–Loy and inspired by the Kashmiri folk wedding song "Khanmoj koor," which earned her a nomination for an IIFA Award in 2019. In February 2019, she released "Kab Se Kab Tak" as a duet with Ranveer Singh, and co-sang "Dil Mein Mars Hai" with Benny Dayal for the Mission Mangal soundtrack, released in summer 2019. That same year, she performed on the Gully Boy soundtrack in the duet "Kab Se Kab Tak" with Ranveer Singh. She has written music for Nucleya, whom she met briefly at an airport, and has composed two songs for him, performing one, "Behka," in the film High Jack. Saraf appears in music videos, including as a co-singer with Rajasthani folk singer Dapu Khan in the "Mumal" video and with Absar Zahoor in her own "Jalwe" video. She has sung in Hindi, Kashmiri, Telugu, Bengali, and Tamil, and writes and composes for both film and independent music. Her music is influenced by traditional music from Kashmir, Jammu, and Ladakh, which she heard from her grandparents and mother, shaping her subconscious connection to Kashmiri music. She expresses a desire to promote the sufism present in her songs and draws inspiration from Kashmiri literature, including the poetry of Habba Khatoon and Lalleshwari. In a 2019 interview with The Hindu, she described her responsibility to share Kashmir-inspired folk music with a broader audience as a duty "falling on our generation" to "stick to our roots," and also expressed appreciation for the preservation and popularity of Punjabi music. Vibha Saraf won the Best Female Playback Singer award for "Dilbaro" from Raazi at the 20th IIFA Awards on 18 September 2019 in Mumbai, India, and also jointly won the Best Female Playback Singer award at the REEL Movie Awards 2019 and the Zee Cine Award for Best Playback Singer – Female for the same song.

Victoria Manalo Draves (née Manalo; December 31, 1924 – April 11, 2010) was a Filipino American competitive diver who won gold medals in both platform and springboard diving at the 1948 Summer Olympics in London. She became the first woman to earn gold medals in both the ten-meter platform and three-meter springboard events and was the first American woman to win two gold medals in diving, as well as the first Asian American to win Olympic gold medals. Born in San Francisco’s South-of-Market district, she was the daughter of Philippine chef and musician Teofilo Manalo and English maid Gertrude Taylor, who met and married in San Francisco. She grew up with her parents, twin sister Connie, older sister Frankie, and younger brother Sonny, who died as a child. Unable to afford swimming lessons until age 10, she took summer lessons from the Red Cross, paying five cents for pool admission in the Mission District. She played badminton, basketball, and softball in high school and graduated from Commerce High School on Van Ness Avenue in 1942, working temporarily in the Army Port Surgeon's office to support her family. Introduced to diving at age 16 by Jack Lavery, she trained under Phil Patterson at the Fairmont Hotel Swimming and Diving Club, where racial discrimination led her to change her name to Vicki Taylor. Patterson’s military service during World War II caused her to pause diving, during which she worked at the Presidio military base. She later joined the Crystal Plunge in North Beach under coach Charlie Sava and trained with Jimmy Hughes, continuing her 50–100 dive after-school practices even while attending San Francisco Junior College (now City College of San Francisco). At 19, she finished third in her first national AAU diving competition at the Indiana meet in 1943. In 1944, she was befriended by Sammy Lee, who introduced her to Lyle Draves, who coached at the Athens Athletic Club in Oakland. Draves began training with Lyle Draves, adding platform diving to her springboard repertoire. After Lyle Draves left the San Francisco Bay Area due to racism at the Fairmont Hotel, she commuted to Los Angeles, placing second and third at the Outdoor Nationals. In 1945, following her father’s death, she returned to her job at the Army Port Surgeon's office in San Francisco. After the war, she moved permanently to Southern California, married Lyle Draves on July 12, 1946, and won the National Tower Diving Championship (10-meter platform) in 1946, 1947, and 1948. She won a total of five United States diving championships prior to the 1948 Olympics, despite not finishing first in either springboard or platform events at the Olympic trials in Detroit. On August 3, 1948, she won the springboard gold medal in London, followed by the 10-meter platform gold on August 6, becoming the first woman to win both titles. After her Olympic victory, she and her husband visited the Philippines, staying in a Malacañang Palace suite and visiting her father’s relatives in Orani, Bataan, where he was born. She gave platform diving exhibitions at Rizal Stadium and other venues, including for Philippine President Elpidio Quirino, and was named one of Life magazine’s top two U.S. athletes at the 1948 Olympics. After the Olympics, she turned professional, joining Larry Crosby’s “Rhapsody in Swimtime” aquatic show for her debut at Soldier Field in Chicago in 1948, and also performed at the L.A. Coliseum with Esther Williams and at the General Motors convention in Detroit. From 1949 to 1950, she toured the U.S., Canada, and Europe with Buster Crabbe’s “Aqua Parade.” After performing regularly at the El Mirador Hotel in Palm Springs and the Shadow Mountain Resort & Club in Palm Desert, she retired from diving. In the early 1950s, she started a family in Glendale and, with her husband, operated a swimming and diving training program at Indian Springs in Montrose, later moving it to Encino. They lived in Tarzana for 35 years, raising their four sons—David, Jeffery, Dale, and Kim—into skilled divers. Draves worked as a secretary while her husband remained a coach and swimming director. In the mid-1960s, she advocated for the Filipino Education Center as the second wave of Filipino immigrants settled in the South of Market district. In 1968, she joined Jesse Owens, Tommy Harmon, and Sam Hanks at the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas to raise $700,000 for the City of Hope National Medical Center. She was inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1969. In 2005, she was named the year’s Most Outstanding Alumnus of City College of San Francisco, receiving her award and speaking at the commencement ceremonies at the SF Masonic Auditorium, where she received a resounding ovation from the graduating students. That same year, she was recognized as one of Los Angeles Athletics Club’s outstanding athletes. In October 2006, a two-acre park in San Francisco—named Victoria Manalo Draves Park—was dedicated in her honor, located on Folsom and Sherman streets, the site of her former Franklin Elementary School, four blocks from where she was born and raised. Draves and her husband moved to Palm Springs, California in 1995. She died on April 11, 2010, aged 85, from pancreatic cancer aggravated by pneumonia. On August 3, 2020, she was honored with a Google Doodle in recognition of her achievements.

The Victor A. Prather Award, established by the American Astronautical Society, aims to promote understanding of the human body's response to high altitude environments. It is given to researchers, engineers, and flight crew members who contribute to the field of extravehicular protection or activity in space. The award is named in honor of Victor A. Prather, a Naval flight surgeon. The award was terminated in 2013.

Victor Newman is a fictional character from the American CBS soap opera The Young and the Restless, portrayed by Eric Braeden since 1980. Initially created by William J. Bell as a "despicable, contemptible, unfaithful wife abuser" intended to last only eight to twelve weeks and be killed off by his wife, the character was saved after Bell saw Braeden's performance and recognized his "voice, the power, the inner strength," deciding to sign him to a contract. Braeden was initially hesitant to work in a daytime soap opera, believing it was "too confining," but eventually signed a six-month contract and has remained a regular cast member for over 45 years. Victor is widely described as a ruthless villain with a powerful presence and a low-toned voice, yet he is loving and protective toward family and loved ones, as noted by the show's official website and critics. He arrived in Genoa City, Wisconsin for business and eventually built Newman Enterprises into a worldwide conglomerate. Victor's first marriage was to Julia Newman (Meg Bennett), after which he formed a long-term romance with stripper Nikki Reed (Melody Thomas Scott), who became his wife and mother of their children Victoria (Amelia Heinle) and Nicholas Newman (Joshua Morrow). During his marriage to Nikki, he had an affair with Ashley Abbott (Eileen Davidson), leading to Ashley's pregnancy and the birth of their daughter Abby Newman (Melissa Ordway), who was believed to be Brad Carlton's daughter until age five. Victor was briefly married to Hope Wilson (Signy Coleman), with whom he had a son, Adam Newman (Mark Grossman), who grew up unaware of Victor as his father. Victor has a long-standing business rivalry with Jack Abbott (Peter Bergman) and has had other romantic relationships, including one with his former daughter-in-law Sharon Newman (Sharon Case), which was criticized by both actors and the public. Victor and Nikki are recognized as one of daytime television's most prominent couples, with fans dubbing them "Niktor," and their relationship has been described as a "dominant force" in the show, featuring a continuous cycle of marriage, divorce, and reconciliation. The couple's weddings have been covered by mainstream media, and their dynamic has been praised for its enduring appeal and conflict. Victor has been nominated eight times for the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series, winning in 1998 and being pre-nominated three times; he also won the "Favorite Male Performer in a Daytime Serial" award at the 18th Annual People's Choice Awards in 1992. In 2007, Braeden received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. In January 1999, Braeden's character appeared on The Bold and the Beautiful in a crossover event from January 25 to 28. In 2008, Victor married Sabrina Costelana (Raya Meddine), a marriage that was short-lived after her accidental death. He later reconnected with Ashley, remarried her, and she became pregnant, though the pregnancy ended in miscarriage. Victor and Sharon Newman's relationship began as a father-daughter bond, evolved into a kiss in 2003, and later included a proposed platonic marriage in December 2011, which was annulled shortly after, followed by a genuine romance. Despite the controversy, Sharon described Victor as her "security blanket" and noted the relationship had "daddy issues" elements, which she said most people do not want to watch. The relationship was criticized as incestuous by Sharon, with fans and actors expressing strong negative reactions. In 2009, Victor and Nikki were temporarily removed from the show due to sudden salary cuts during contract negotiations, with Braeden criticizing the process as "cold and hard-nosed" and "insulting," though a new contract was quickly reached, allowing Victor's return on January 15, 2010. Onscreen, Victor left on November 2, 2009, and returned in 2010. In 2012, further contract negotiations sparked speculation about Victor's departure, with reports indicating a two-week absence and an expiring contract in November, but no final departure occurred. The character has been described as complex, with Braeden noting Victor's deep-seated loneliness, his need for love, and his inability to trust relationships, stemming from his childhood. Braeden stated that Victor "doesn't take any shit" and that he is "defensive and always self-protective," and that he enjoys portraying the character more than anything, despite not being like Victor in personality, as he does not use money to manipulate people. Victor met his mother, Cora Miller (Dorothy McGuire), for the first time at age 7, a scene Braeden called a "deeply-felt" turning point in his career. In 2011, Michael Logan of TV Guide criticized Victor for throwing his ex-wife Diane from an ambulance, calling it "pushing it with the fans," and Braeden defended the character by stating he "doesn't give a shit" and "doesn't take any shit." Victor is considered an icon of the soap opera genre, with his performance widely praised as "legendary" and "enthralling," and he was made a spokesperson for Zellers.

The character of Victor Newman, born Christian Miller on March 7, 1947, in Buffalo, New York, was placed in an orphanage at age seven by his mother Cora Miller (Dorothy McGuire); his father was Albert Miller. By adolescence, he left the orphanage and rose to become one of the world's wealthiest tycoons, changing his name to "Victor Christian Newman," with "Victor" meaning "victorious" and "Newman" meaning "new man." In 1970, he married Julia Newman (Meg Bennet) as he built a strong business reputation. In 1980, the couple moved to Genoa City to assist Katherine Chancellor (Jeanne Cooper) with Chancellor Industries; Julia felt neglected and slept with photographer Michael Scott (Nick Benedict), while Victor cheated on her with Eve Howard (Margaret Mason) and later Lorie Brooks (Jaime Lyn Bauer). Julia became pregnant, believed to be Michael's child, and Victor attacked Michael, resulting in Julia losing the child, which was later revealed to be Victor's. Eve later had child Cole Howard (J. Eddie Peck), believed to be Victor's son. Julia and Victor divorced, and Julia left town with Michael, as Victor began a romance with stripper Nikki Reed (Melody Thomas Scott). Victor taught Nikki about society, took over Prentiss Industries, and schemed to regain it by using Lorie to seduce him into marriage, which failed when Lorie stood him up. Victor later tried to return to Nikki, who had married Kevin Bancroft; Nikki became pregnant with Victor's child but was manipulated into marrying Tony DiSalvo to preserve her relationship with Kevin. Nikki gave birth to daughter Victoria Newman (Ashley Nicole Millan). Nikki later became involved with Rick Daros, who nearly killed her, and was saved by Victor. Eve returned with her boyfriend, demanding money for Cole in Victor's will and later working as his assistant, prompting Julia to return to protect Victor. Victor planned to marry Eve but faked his death on their wedding day and instead married Nikki in April 1984. While vacationing, Eve reappeared with Rick, stole money from them, and escaped. Nikki facilitated Victor's reunion with his mother Cora Miller, who died. Despite loving Nikki, Victor began an affair with Ashley Abbott (Brenda Epperson), enraging Nikki, who then slept with Jack Abbott (Peter Bergman), Ashley's brother and Victor's business rival. Ashley became pregnant, and Victor left Nikki, but when Nikki was diagnosed with cancer, Victor returned to her, and Ashley aborted the child. After Nikki recovered, Victor wanted to be with Ashley, who had moved on with her psychiatrist Steven Lassiter (Rod Arrants); Steven later died, and although Ashley wanted Victor back, he returned to Nikki, resulting in the birth of their son Nicholas Newman (Joshua Morrow). Victor and Jack hired Leanna Love (Barbara Crampton) to write a biography on Victor, when in reality Jack wanted it to be a tell-all exposé. Leanna wrote a chapter about Victor's affair with Ashley and Nikki's illness, leading Victor to believe Nikki was behind it. He divorced her and married Leanna to prove to the press he didn't want to be with Ashley; their marriage was invalid because the divorce wasn't finalized. Victor later took over Jack's family company, Jabot Cosmetics, replacing him with Brad Carlton (Don Diamont), causing Jack to spitefully marry Nikki, making their relationship bitter. Victor married Ashley, and years later told Jack he would give him back Jabot Cosmetics if he divorced Nikki. Jack agreed, but due to a legal loophole, he wasn't given full control. Victor had a heart attack during a confrontation with Jack, left him for dead, and recovered. As Jack and Nikki's marriage strained due to Nikki's alcoholism and painkiller addiction, she reconnected with Victor, who had decided to divorce Ashley. Eve returned with her grown son Cole, who romanced Victor's daughter Victoria, unaware he was believed to be Victor's son. Victor left Genoa City and went to Kansas, letting Nikki and the Newman family believe he had died. He met Hope Adams (Signy Coleman) and returned to Genoa City to marry her. While in Kansas, Cole and Victoria eloped, and when Victor revealed their sibling relationship, the marriage was annulled. After Eve's death, it was revealed Cole was never Victor's son; Victoria and Cole remarried. Victor and Hope had a son, Victor Adam Newman Jr. Hope wanted to return to Kansas, and Victor was not interested; he divorced her, and Victor Jr. was raised without knowing Victor was his father. Nikki was engaged to Brad, which upset Victor. On their wedding night, Victor was shot and Nikki returned to him; the mentally unstable Mari Jo Mason (Diana Barton) was revealed as the gunwoman. Victor and Nikki briefly reunited before he returned to Kansas after Hope's new husband, Cliff Wilson, died. In 1997, Victor married Diane Jenkins (Alex Donnelley), Jack's ex-girlfriend. Nikki had Victor have a vasectomy but froze sperm for future use. Nikki later married Joshua Landers (Heath Kizzier), and in 1998, she was shot by Joshua's ex-wife, Veronica Landers (Candice Daly); Victor divorced Diane to marry Nikki on her deathbed, promising to remarry Diane after Nikki's death. When Nikki survived, their second marriage was invalidated because Victor and Diane's divorce was never processed. Victor and Diane had a bitter divorce over months, during which Nikki reunited with Brad, and Jack and Tucker took control of Newman Enterprises. Diane remained in love with Victor and stole his frozen sperm to artificially inseminate herself; unknowingly, Ashley also stole Victor's sperm. Diane gave birth to Christian Victor Newman, but discovered the sperm was Jack's. Ashley received Victor's actual sperm and gave birth to Abby Carlton, whom she passed off as Brad's child. Victor and Nikki later reunited, and in 2002, Maxwell Hollister (Sam Behrens) attempted to destroy Victor using Lorie Brooks, who had been Victor's estranged wife; Max tried to lead a hostile takeover of Julia Newman Martin's design firm, which Victor prevented. Max then used Lorie to keep Victor and Nikki apart, but Lorie failed, and Max left town. Months later, Victor and Nikki remarried in front of their loved ones. Ashley revealed Abby was Victor's daughter due to her cancer diagnosis, and Victor welcomed her. After rescuing Nikki from a carjacker, Victor was diagnosed with temporal lobe epilepsy. Victor and Nikki's marriage strained as he fought to take Jabot Cosmetics from Jack, managed NVP Retreats, and dealt with Nikki's campaign for State Senator, which led to an affair with her campaign manager David Chow. They eventually divorced after six years in 2008. Soon after, Hope died, and Victor's estranged son, now known as Adam Newman (Michael Muhney), came to Genoa City and worked at Newman Enterprises. Victor fell in love with Sabrina Costelana (Raya Meddine), but she died in a car accident with Nikki's devious husband David Chow. Victor traveled to Mexico and nearly died; Ashley found him and they rekindled their romance. They remarried when Ashley became pregnant, but she miscarried when Adam gaslighted her into believing she was still pregnant. Despite Adam stealing Nicholas' daughter Faith and passing her off as Ashley's, she and Victor divorced as he reunited with Nikki. Victor was later shot by Patty Williams (Stacy Haiduk) and needed a heart transplant, receiving Colleen Carlton's (Tammin Sursok) heart. Victor and Nikki went to treatment in Europe, and upon return, Adam's scheme was revealed—he had faked his death. Victor searched for him in Canada, met Meggie McClaine (Sean Young), brought her to Genoa City, and she worked as Nikki's assistant but caused her to relapse into alcoholism. In reality, Meggie tried to stop Victor and Nikki's union to marry Victor for his money. Victor married her but had her arrested soon after; Nikki moved on with Deacon Sharpe (Sean Kanan). Afterward, Victor's children filed a lawsuit against him over a cosmetics line, which they won. Diane (Maura West), who returned to Genoa City, reconnected with Victor and they remarried, but the marriage was annulled shortly after she found Victor sleeping with Nikki and learned of her affair with Tucker McCall (Stephen Nichols) and Jack. Victor then sent Nikki to a rehabilitation center for her alcoholism. Diane was murdered in August 2011, with Victor as a suspect. Nikki actually murdered Diane in self-defense, causing Victor to falsely confess to the murder to protect Nikki. While in jail, Victor married his former daughter-in-law Sharon Newman (Sharon Case) to push Nikki away; when the entire murder plot was revealed, Nikki was not charged and Victor was freed. Victor and Sharon's marriage was annulled, and he reunited with Nikki, but she left him when some of his past schemes involving Victoria's marriage were exposed. To gain control of the cosmetics line Beauty of Nature, Victor slept with Genevieve Atkinson (Genie Francis). When Nikki reunited with Jack, Victor developed a genuine romance with Sharon to spite her. They married a second time, but he disappeared shortly after, and Sharon believed he was abandoning her. She burned their prenuptial agreement and took over Newman Enterprises, while Jack and Tucker bought up its stocks. While away, Victor lost his memory and worked as a dock worker in Los Angeles, demanding better conditions; workers planned to kill him in an explosion, leading Genoa City to believe he had died, but he returned shortly after. Upon return, he annulled his marriage to Sharon and reunited with Nikki, just before Jack announced he was taking over Newman Enterprises, firing all Newman family members and appointing Adam. However, due to his painkiller addiction, Jack gave up control of the company, leaving it to Adam. Victor and Nikki finally remarried in March 2013, just before Nikki was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. At their wedding, an assassin attempted to shoot Victor, but Adam took the bullet and nearly died for his father. As a result, Adam offered Victor the position of co-CEO at Newman, and they began working together. However, their partnership ended several months later when Victor discovered Adam's silent partner had previously taken Newman private again was Jack. Victor feared Adam and Jack had been scheming to take back the company without him. In retaliation, Victor, who now owned Chancellor Industries according to Katherine Chancellor's will, had all major Newman clients sign with Chancellor, making Newman worthless so he could build up Chancellor. Adam signed over his shares in Newman to Victor, who planned to merge Chancellor Industries with Newman. Nikki revealed she had given birth to another son decades earlier before being with Victor, revealed to be Dylan McAvoy (Steve Burton). A subsidiary of the merged conglomerate, Bonaventure Industries, produced an illegal speed drug that Summer Newman (Hunter King) overdosed on. Jack reported Victor to the FDA, and he and his company were put under investigation. Dylan's supposed father and Nikki's former lover Ian Ward (Ray Wise) arrived in town, causing chaos, and Victor tried to get him out of town. It was later revealed Victor had hired a lookalike to his granddaughter Cassie, named Mariah Copeland (Camryn Grimes), to haunt Sharon and learn a supposed secret she had. When the scheme was revealed, Nick and Sharon shunned him, and Nikki decided to move out temporarily, but she and Victor later reunited. Victor and Nikki learned Ian was incapable of fathering children, causing confusion. It was later revealed Paul Williams (Doug Davidson), Nikki's ex-lover and longtime friend, was actually Dylan's father, causing tension in Victor and Nikki's marriage, which continued when Victor went to great lengths to awaken Phyllis (Gina Tognoni) from a coma to find out more about Sharon's supposed secret. Nikki fell off the wagon and began drinking again; she left Victor and refused to take him back. Victor also sold Chancellor Industries back to Jill (Jess Walton), leaving the rest of the Newman family confused about why he gave it up so easily. In 2015, Victor had Jack kidnapped and replaced by a lookalike, revealed to be a Peruvian drug lord named Marco Annicelli, to take over Jabot Cosmetics and merge it with Newman, forming Newman Abbott Enterprises. Meanwhile, Victor and his children discovered Nikki had fallen off the wagon; they convinced her to quit drinking again, and she and Victor reunited. Jack returned to Genoa City just as Victor learned Marco was dangerous; he planned to shoot Marco in the park, but it was actually Jack who he shot, who had finally returned to confront him. Jack fell into a coma while Victor frantically tried to get rid of Marco, who continued to masquerade around town. When Jack awakened, he reluctantly agreed to help Victor get Marco out of town and back into prison, which they succeeded in doing. With the real Jack back in Genoa City, the Newman Abbott merger ended, and both companies returned to separate states. Meanwhile, Adam, who returned to town under the false identity of Gabriel Bingham, teamed up with Ian (who had escaped prison) to create a computer virus, known as the Paragon project, to destroy Newman Enterprises for revenge; Ian made no promise to stop it. On Halloween, during a party at the Newman Enterprises ballroom, Ian caused the building to catch fire, creating a major panic. As a result, Ashley and Billy (Burgess Jenkins) offered to share office space at Jabot with Newman while the building was repaired, but Victor refused to trust them. It was later revealed Billy revived Paragon as an act of revenge against Victor, leading to Jack firing him and Victor filing a lawsuit against Jabot. "Newman has become a daytime television icon during his unparalleled tenure as soap opera's biggest star ... Victor Newman quickly developed into a main character and firmly planted himself into the hearts of millions of fans across the globe."[57] Chris Jancelewicz of The Huffington Post described Victor as "the very definition of daytime TV icon" and noted that, "Even people who have never seen an episode in their lives know his name, his face, and his powerful low voice."[16] In the early 1990s, he was described as a heartthrob.[58] He is credited as one of the soap opera world's leading stars.[59] Jamey Giddens of Zap2it considers Braeden the soap opera's leading male.[60] Tommy Garrett of Highlight Hollywood stated that Braeden "is known in the industry as the biggest daytime leading man of all time".[61] In 1993, Nancy Reichardt of The Los Angeles Times stated: "Victor Newman is one of those characters. When Eric Braeden first came on the show in the role, Victor was a villain, and what a villain! His portrayal proved so dynamic that this 'minor' plot point has been ignored over the years. Today, Braeden is one of the show's leading men. The character has never lost his edge, but his knife-wielding days are long forgotten."[62] In 1997, The Museum of Television and Radio wrote that with the arrival of the character, who was an "enigmatic stranger popular with women", "the show's revived tableau was complete", saying it was an "amazingly seamless transition" and praised William J. Eric Braeden first joined *The Young and the Restless* in 1980 as a baddy in a mini-stint, but stayed on to transform the show, becoming one of daytime television's most recognizable figures. The character of Victor Newman, a ruthless businessman, was introduced in 1997 as an "enigmatic stranger popular with women," and The Museum of Television and Radio praised the introduction as an "amazingly seamless transition," crediting William J. Bell for the character's impact. Over the years, Victor has remained a symbol of power in Genoa City, with critics noting his dynamic and complex nature. Deanna Barnert of MSN Entertainment stated that Braeden's tenure changed the game in Genoa City forever, and his portrayal has been described as compelling, with critics highlighting his ability to balance villainy and vulnerability. In 1997, the character's arrival completed the show's revived tableau. BuddyTV identified the storyline where Victor locked his wife Julia's lover in a bomb shelter as the turning point that made him a villain. Victor has been used as a spokesperson for Zellers, appearing in commercials that aired in November 1998, where he breaks the fourth wall, praises shoppers, and squashes his nose against the camera lens. According to StrategyOnline, the Zellers campaign was the most popular to date and received considerable praise for balancing affordability with strong branding. Victor's long-standing relationship with Nikki Reed has been called "epic" and has received positive reviews, though it has always been troubled by poor timing and miscommunication. Critics have noted Victor's multiple marriages, including to Ashley Abbott in 1990, Hope in 1995, and their third wedding in 2002 and fourth in 2013, with Entertainment Weekly stating that Victor knows who is best for him—Nikki. His rivalry with Jack Abbott has been a soap opera legend, with Allison Waldman of AOL TV noting their shared wives, corporations, and deep-seated hatred. Waldman praised Braeden for making Victor a compelling, dynamic villain with a heart and vulnerability, likening him to a "big jungle cat" who can turn on those he once loved. Victor has earned nicknames such as "The Mustache" and "The Dark Night." When asked about Victor's commercial appeal, Braeden attributed it to his emotional authenticity and life experiences, suggesting viewers sense his empathy. Tommy Garrett of Highlight Hollywood compared Braeden's performance as Victor to his role as John Jacob Astor IV in *Titanic*, calling both equally enthralling. Victor's voice is described as "gravel," and Toby Goldstein of The Orlando Sentinel credited him as a key factor in the show's enduring popularity. Shelley Fralic of the Winnipeg Free Press named Braeden and Susan Lucci as the soap opera genre's biggest icons, calling Victor the "eye of the Genoa City hurricane" and stating that the show would be unthinkable without him, much like *Dallas* without J.R. Ewing or *The Sopranos* without Tony. In 2022, Charlie Mason from Soaps She Knows ranked Victor second on his list of the best 25 characters from *The Young and the Restless*, noting that his mustache has a space at the Smithsonian and that he has a former-wives wing at the American Museum of Natural History rivaling Henry VIII's.

Victor and Nikki Newman are fictional characters and a supercouple from the American CBS soap opera The Young and the Restless. Victor is portrayed by Eric Braeden and Nikki by Melody Thomas Scott. The couple has shared three marriages and two children: Victoria and Nicholas Newman (Amelia Heinle and Joshua Morrow). They are often referred to by fans as "Niktor" on internet message boards and in magazines. Nikki was originally from the lower walks of life, having been a stripper and prostitute. After multiple failed relationships, she began a romance with Victor, who taught her about society. They fell in love and had a daughter, Victoria Newman (Heather Tom), and later a son, Nicholas Newman (Joshua Morrow). Their pairing was originally written to follow a continuous cycle of marriage and divorce, a take on the original supercouple formula, which has persisted throughout their time on the show and is regarded as an "inspired decision," leading to them becoming the most successful supercouple on The Young and the Restless. The couple's first wedding took place on the episode that aired on April 13, 1984. Nikki gave birth to Victoria in 1982, and the pair married in 1984. Ashley Abbott (Eileen Davidson, Brenda Epperson) came between them, causing their divorce, after which both remarried—Victor to Ashley and Nikki to Jack Abbott (Peter Bergman). However, they remained linked, with an affair resulting in the birth of Nicholas. Despite Victor marrying architect Diane Jenkins (Alex Donnelley) in 1997, Nikki suffered a gunshot wound the following year and came close to death, leading Victor to supposedly divorce Diane and remarry Nikki on her deathbed. However, Victor and Diane's divorce was never legal, invalidating their remarriage. An actual divorce between Victor and Diane occurred, resulting in their reunion. In September 2002, they remarried again at the site of their first wedding, a union that lasted six years. In 2008, Nikki began an affair with David Chow (Vincent Irizarry), leading to their second divorce. Melody Thomas Scott has stated that the couple always has to get back together, but "not without a challenge," and that the writers must create believable storylines because people care about them. In March 2013, after four years of an on-and-off relationship, Victor and Nikki remarried for the third time, coinciding with the 40th anniversary of The Young and the Restless. Victor and Nikki are recognized as one of daytime television's most prominent pairings and have received positive reviews from critics. The News & Advance cited their romance as part of the "epic" romances of the early supercouple era. The couple has a large fan following and their weddings have been reported by mainstream media. Scott has said that Victor and Nikki will always be a huge dynamic, having been in a circular cycle for over 30 years. Braeden has stated that the storyline is an "honestly felt love story with great material for conflict with Nikki." Former As the World Turns actress Martha Byrne has said that Victor and Nikki exemplify a couple who are repeatedly torn apart and reunited, and that the writers do it well because the characters are stable. Daytime expert Michael Fairman stated that Victor and Nikki just can't get together long enough to find happiness, and that they "deserve" each other and the baggage that comes with their co-dependent relationship.

Vincent Joseph Schaefer (July 4, 1906 – July 25, 1993) was an American chemist and meteorologist who developed cloud seeding. On November 13, 1946, while working at the General Electric Research Laboratory, he seeded clouds in the Berkshire Mountains using dry ice. Self-taught and never having completed high school, Schaefer held 14 patents. He was the oldest son of Peter Aloysius Schaefer and Rose Agnes (Holtslag) Schaefer, and had two younger brothers, Paul and Carl, and two younger sisters, Gertrude and Margaret. The family resided in Schenectady, New York, and due to his mother's health, began summer trips to the Adirondack Mountains in 1921. Schaefer maintained a lifelong connection with the Adirondacks and had interests in hiking, natural history, and archaeology. In his youth, he founded a local group of the Lone Scouts and co-wrote and printed a publication called "Archaeological Research," which introduced him to key figures in Schenectady, including Dr. Willis Rodney Whitney of the General Electric Research Laboratory. During the late 1920s and early 1930s, he built a personal library on natural history and science and organized several groups, including the Mohawk Valley Hiking Club (1929), the Van Epps-Hartley Chapter of the New York Archaeological Association (1931), and the Schenectady Wintersport Club (1933–34), which established snow trains to ski slopes in the Adirondacks. In 1931, he began work on creating the Long Path of New York, a hiking trail from near New York City to Whiteface Mountain. He also developed adult education programs on natural history, expanding his community connections, including with John S.
