The tournament resulted in a tie between Chigorin and Max Weiss, with a four-draw play-off, and Weiss conceding the title to Chigorin, while Isidor Gunsberg, the third-place finisher, was prepared to play for the title. A Steinitz–Gunsberg match in 1890 ended with a 10½–8½ victory for Steinitz. The experiment was not repeated, and Steinitz's last three matches were private arrangements. In 1891, the Saint Petersburg Chess Society and Havana Chess Club offered another Steinitz–Chigorin match for the world championship, which was played in Havana in 1892 and won by Steinitz (ten wins, five draws, eight losses). Dr. Siegbert Tarrasch declined a 1892 challenge due to medical commitments. Around this time, Steinitz publicly announced his retirement but changed his mind when Emanuel Lasker, 32 years younger and relatively untested, challenged him. Lasker had previously been refused a non-title challenge by Tarrasch, who was the world's dominant tournament player at the time. Initially, Lasker wanted $5,000 per side, and the match was agreed at $3,000 per side, but Steinitz reduced the stakes due to financial difficulties, settling on $2,000 each (equivalent to about $114,000 in 2016 values), which was publicly praised as sportsmanship but may have been necessary for Steinitz. The match took place in 1894 in New York, Philadelphia, and Montreal, Canada, with a 32-year age difference between the players—the largest in world championship history and still the largest today. Steinitz had previously declared he would win without doubt, but Lasker won the first game. Steinitz won the second and maintained balance until the sixth, but Lasker won games seven through eleven, and Steinitz requested a one-week rest. When the match resumed, Steinitz looked in better form.

Initz agreed to a series of reductions in stakes when Lasker found it difficult to raise funds, resulting in a final payment of $2,000 each, which was less than in some of Steinitz's earlier matches; the combined final stake of $4,000 would be worth about $114,000 at 2016 values. Although this was publicly praised as an act of sportsmanship, Steinitz may have desperately needed the money. The match took place in 1894 at venues in New York, Philadelphia, and Montreal, Canada, and featured the largest age difference between combatants in world championship history—32 years—which remains unbroken today. Steinitz had previously declared he would win without doubt, but it came as a shock when Lasker won the first game; Steinitz responded by winning the second and maintained balance until the sixth. Lasker then won all games from the seventh to the eleventh, and Steinitz requested a one-week rest. Upon resuming, Steinitz won the 13th and 14th games, but Lasker regained the lead in the 15th and 16th, and Steinitz could not recover, resulting in Lasker winning with ten wins, five losses, and four draws. Some commentators believed Steinitz's habit of playing "experimental" moves in serious competition contributed significantly to his downfall. After losing the title, Steinitz played more frequently in tournaments; he won at New York City 1894 and placed fifth at Hastings 1895, winning the first brilliancy prize for his game against Curt von Bardeleben. At Saint Petersburg 1895, a strong four-player, multi-round-robin event with Lasker, Chigorin, and Pillsbury, he finished second behind Lasker. His results declined afterward: sixth in Nuremberg 1896, fifth in Cologne 1898, and tenth in London 1899. In early 1896, Steinitz defeated Emanuel Schiffers in a match, winning 6 games, drawing 1, and losing 4. From November 1896 to January 1897, he played a return match with Lasker in Moscow, winning only 2 games, drawing 5, and losing 10—this was the last world chess championship match for eleven years. Shortly after, Steinitz suffered a mental breakdown and was confined for 40 days in a Moscow sanatorium, where he played chess with inmates. There is ongoing debate among chess writers about whether Steinitz's reign as World Chess Champion began in 1866, when he beat Anderssen, or in 1886, when he defeated Zukertort. In April 1894, the British Chess Magazine described Steinitz as holding the chess championship of the world for 28 years, though there is no evidence he claimed the title in 1866, and he had claimed to be champion since his 1880s victory over Anderssen. It is suggested he could not claim the title while Paul Morphy was alive, as Morphy had defeated Anderssen 8–3 in 1858 and retired in 1859, dying in 1884. The 1886 match between Steinitz and Zukertort was the first explicitly described as being for the World Championship, though Howard Staunton and Paul Morphy had been unofficially called "World Chess Champion" in the mid-19th century. One organizer of the 1851 London International tournament referred to the event as being for "the baton of the World's Chess Champion," and Ludwig Bledow suggested in 1845 organizing a world championship in Germany. Some commentators described Steinitz as "the champion" after his 1872 victory over Zukertort, but in the late 1870s and early 1880s, both Steinitz and Zukertort were regarded as champions, and the 1886 match was seen as resolving conflicting claims rather than creating the title. George Alcock MacDonnell hailed Joseph Blackburne as "World Champion" in 1881, George Henry Mackenzie as having "won the Chess Championship of the World" in 1887, and Isidore Gunsberg as "among the champions of the world" after his 1888 win at "Bradford Place." Steinitz regarded MacDonnell as "one of my bitterest and most untruthful persecutors." Steinitz lived with Caroline Golder (born 1846) in the 1860s, and their only daughter, Flora, was born in 1866; Flora died in 1888 at age 21, and Caroline died in 1892. He married his second wife a few years later and had two children with her. In 1897, he dedicated a pamphlet to the memory of his first wife and daughter. In February 1897, The New York Times prematurely reported his death in a New York mental asylum. Some authors claim he contracted syphilis, which may have contributed to his mental breakdowns. In the months before his death, he spent time in institutions due to failing mental health. Before confinement, Steinitz was attempting to publish an essay on the emancipation of Austrian Jews and attributed his symptoms entirely to mental fatigue. His chess activities did not yield significant financial rewards, and he died a pauper in the Manhattan State Hospital (Wards Island) on August 12, 1900, from a heart attack. Steinitz is buried in the Cemetery of the Evergreens in Brooklyn, New York. His second wife and their two young children were still alive at the time of his death. The book of the Hastings 1895 tournament described Steinitz as a strong theoretician and writer with a powerful pen, who strives to be fair to friends and foes but sometimes fails to see that he is like many others. He is described as having a fine intellect and being extremely fond of chess, often losing sight of other considerations. His play up to and including 1872 mirrored that of his contemporaries: sharp, aggressive, and full of sacrificial play, which led to his rise as "world number one" after beating Adolf Anderssen in 1866 and confirming his position by defeating Zukertort in 1872 and winning the 1872 London International tournament (Zukertort had claimed second place by beating Anderssen in 1871). In 1873, Steinitz's style changed, prioritizing positional elements such as pawn structure, space, knight outposts, and the advantage of two bishops. Although he often accepted difficult defensive positions to demonstrate his theories, he also showed that his methods could support powerful attacks. Lasker summarized the new style as: "In the beginning of the game ignore the search for combinations, abstain from violent moves, aim for small advantages, accumulate them, and only after having attained these ends search for the combination—and then with all the power of will and intellect, because then the combination must exist, however deeply hidden." Steinitz stated he had been thinking along these lines for years, citing Paulsen's games at the 1862 London Congress as a key influence. During his nine-year layoff from tournaments (1873–1882) and later in his career, he used chess writings to present his theories—writing for The Field in the UK from 1873 to 1882, founding the International Chess Magazine in New York in 1885 and editing it until 1891, and editing the book of the 1889 New York tournament (won by Chigorin and Weiss), which was designed to produce his successor as World Champion. Many writers found his new approach incomprehensible, boring, or even cowardly; Adolf Anderssen criticized him as a "pick-pocket" who wins by stealing a pawn. However, in his 1886 match against Zukertort, Steinitz clearly played at a higher level, outmaneuvering Zukertort through positional principles despite Zukertort's superior attacking ability. By the 1890–91 match against Gunsberg, some commentators began to understand and appreciate his theories. Before the 1894 match with Lasker, even The New York Times, which had previously attacked his play and character, paid tribute to his record, theories, and sportsmanship in agreeing to the most difficult match of his career despite his intention to retire. By the end of his career, Steinitz was more highly esteemed as a theoretician than as a player; the Hastings 1895 tournament comments focus on his theories and writings, and Lasker explicitly stated, "He was a thinker worthy of a seat in the halls of a University. A player, as the world believed he was, he was not; his studious temperament made that impossible; and thus he was conquered by a player." As a result of his play and writings, Steinitz, along with Paul Morphy, is considered by many commentators the founder of modern chess. Lasker, who succeeded him, wrote, "I who vanquished him must see to it that his great achievement, his theories should find justice, and I must avenge the wrongs he suffered." Vladimir Kramnik emphasized Steinitz's role as a pioneer in chess theory, stating he was the first to realize that chess, despite being complex, obeys common principles, though he was an experimenter rather than a founder of a complete theory. Steinitz was the main chess correspondent of The Field from 1873 to 1882, using it to present his strategic ideas. In 1885, he founded the International Chess Magazine in New York and edited it until 1891. He wrote articles on Paul Morphy, who died in 1884, and authored the book of the 1889 New York tournament, annotating all 432 games, and published the textbook The Modern Chess Instructor in 1889. He also allegedly wrote a pamphlet entitled Capital, Labor, and Charity while confined at River Crest Sanitarium in New York during his final months. Statistical rating systems are unkind to Steinitz; "Warriors of the Mind" ranks him 47th, below several obscure Soviet grandmasters, and Chessmetrics places him only 15th on its all-time list. Chessmetrics penalizes players who play infrequently; opportunities for competitive chess were rare in Steinitz's best years, and he had several long absences from play (1873–1876, 1876–1882, 1883–1886, 1886–1889). However, in 2005, Chessmetrics author Jeff Sonas found that Steinitz was ahead of his contemporaries in the 1870s compared to Bobby Fischer's peak (1970–1972), had the third-highest total number of years as world's top player (behind Lasker and Kasparov), and placed 7th in a comparison of how long players were ranked in the world's top three. Between his victory over Anderssen in 1866 and his loss to Lasker in 1894, Steinitz won all his "normal" matches, often by wide margins, and his worst tournament result in that 28-year period was third place in Paris (1867). He also lost two handicap matches and a match by telegraph in 1890 against Mikhail Chigorin, where Chigorin chose the openings and won both. The Edo rating system (1821–1937) places Steinitz third in peak rating, behind Jose Capablanca and Paul Morphy but ahead of Emanuel Lasker and Alexander Alekhine. Initially, Steinitz played in the all-out attacking style of contemporaries like Anderssen, then shifted to the positional style that dominated competitive chess in the 1870s and 1880s. Max Euwe noted that Steinitz aimed at positions with clear-cut features to which his theory was best applicable. He retained his capacity for brilliant attacks until the end; for example, at Hastings 1895 (when he was 59), he defeated von Bardeleben in a spectacular game where he deliberately exposed all his pieces to attack simultaneously (except his king). His significant weaknesses included playing "experimental" moves and entering unnecessarily difficult defensive positions in top-level games. Traditional accounts describe him as having a sharp tongue and violent temper, possibly due to his short stature (barely five feet) and congenital lameness. He admitted, "Like the Duke of Parma, I always hold the sword in one hand and the olive branch in the other," and could become abusive in published articles under provocation. He acknowledged early in his career that his frankness would offend and make enemies, and his brutally honest review of Wormald's The Chess Openings in 1875 confirmed this. His personal correspondence, articles, and third-party writings show he had long and friendly relationships with many in the chess world, including Ignác Kolisch, Mikhail Chigorin, Harry Nelson Pillsbury, Bernhard Horwitz, Amos Burn, and the Cuban and Russian chess communities. He also cooperated with the American Chess Congress in its project to regulate future world title contests that he had earned. Steinitz strove to be objective in his writings; for example, he attributed a poor tournament score by Henry Edward Bird to bad luck, despite not being a friend of Bird's, and was generous in praising great play by even his enemies. He also poked fun at his own rhetoric, such as saying he would rather die in America than live in England, and that he would rather lose a match in America than win one in England, but later concluded that he neither.

Steinitz was proven correct on two points. His personal letters, his own articles, and some third-party articles reveal that he maintained long and friendly relationships with numerous individuals and groups in the chess world, including Ignác Kolisch (one of his earliest sponsors), Mikhail Chigorin, Harry Nelson Pillsbury, Bernhard Horwitz, Amos Burn, and the Cuban and Russian chess communities. He also collaborated with the American Chess Congress on its initiative to regulate future world title contests, which he had won. Steinitz aimed for objectivity in his commentary on chess events; for instance, he credited Henry Edward Bird’s poor tournament performance to bad luck, despite considering Bird no friend, and he praised exceptional play even from his bitter rivals. He also self-ironized his own statements, such as saying he would rather die in America than live in England or lose a match in America than win one in England, later clarifying that he no longer meant to die or lose the match. During a joint simultaneous display in Russia around the time of the 1895–96 Saint Petersburg tournament, Emanuel Lasker and Steinitz formed an impromptu comedy double act. Although Steinitz valued honor in repaying debts, he struggled with financial management: he allowed a competitor to take many of his clients between 1862 and 1863, offered to play the 1886 world title match against Johannes Zukertort for free, and died in poverty in 1900, leaving his widow to survive by running a small shop.

Will Hicok Low (May 31, 1853 – November 27, 1932) was an American artist, muralist, and writer on art. Born in Albany, New York, he entered the atelier of Jean-Léon Gérôme at the École des Beaux Arts in Paris in 1873 and later joined the classes of Carolus-Duran, remaining with him until 1877. He spent lengthy and painterly periods in Barbizon and Montigny-sur-Loing. Returning to New York, he became a member of the Society of American Artists in 1878 and the National Academy of Design in 1890. His depictions of New England types and illustrations of John Keats brought him recognition. Low created panels and medallions for the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York City, a panel for the Essex County Court House in Newark, New Jersey, and numerous panels for private residences, as well as stained glass windows for various churches, including St. Paul's Methodist Episcopal Church in Newark. He taught at Cooper Union in New York from 1882 to 1885 and at the National Academy of Design from 1889 to 1892. Known as a close friend of R. L. Stevenson, Low published reminiscences titled A Chronicle of Friendships, 1873–1900 (1908). The obverse of the United States silver certificate History Instructing Youth was his design, which was used for the obverse of the bill. The engraving for the obverse of the one-dollar History Instructing Youth note was done by Charles Schlecht. In 1896, he began working for American artist John La Farge, spending two years in New York decorating buildings. After Berthe's death in 1909, he married Mary Fairchild, the former wife of sculptor Frederick William MacMonnies. He painted a series of murals in the New York State Education Department rotunda in Albany, New York, using figures and symbols from Roman and Greek mythology paired with New York buildings and landscapes to chart major milestones in human progress—such as art, science, technology, modernization, liberty, democracy, and quality of life. The earliest panels, including Architecture, Astronomy & Geography, and Medicine & Chemistry, combine theory and practical skills. Another eight panels, such as Theseus, the Pathfinder, feature modern inventions to illustrate human progress by the early 20th century. The final paintings reflect a patriotic theme, with subjects like The Standard, The United States Military Academy, and the Shaft of Union. These murals, originally displayed at the entrances of the State Library Main Reading Room, the Law Library, and the Periodicals Library, complement the Rotunda's architectural nobility and its atmosphere of intellectual enlightenment.

Willer Bordon (16 January 1949 – 14 July 2015) was an Italian academic, businessman, and politician who held various cabinet positions during the late 1990s and 2000s. He was born in Muggia, Province of Trieste, on 16 January 1949. Bordon served as mayor of Muggia for eleven years and was elected to the Italian parliament in 1987 as a deputy representing Trieste. In 1992, he founded the Democratic Alliance, a small centre-left party, but resigned from it in June 1994 after poor performance in the general election. He later joined the Margherita party. From 1998 to 1999, he served as minister for public works. In April 2000, he was appointed minister of environment in the cabinet led by Prime Minister Giuliano Amato, taking over the role from Edo Ronchi. Bordon also served as a member of the Italian Senate, retiring from the Senate in 2008. After leaving politics, he became president of Enalg SpA and began working as a professor of political science at La Sapienza University. Bordon died at the age of 66 on 14 July 2015.

William Butts Ittner (September 4, 1864 – 1936) was an American architect based in St. Louis, Missouri, who designed over 430 school buildings across Missouri and other regions. He served as president of the St. Louis Chapter of the American Institute of Architects from 1893 to 1895, was awarded an honorary degree by the University of Missouri in 1930, and held the presidency of the Architectural League of America from 1903 to 1904. At the time of his death, he was president of the St. Louis Plaza Commission and was a fellow and life member of the American Institute of Architects, as well as a thirty-third degree Mason. Ittner is recognized as the most influential man in school architecture in the United States and has a star on the St. Louis Walk of Fame. He was appointed St. Louis School Board commissioner in 1897 and held the position until his resignation in 1910, continuing as a consulting architect until October 1914. His first school design was the Eliot School (1898–99), and his last was Bryan Mullanphy (1914–15). He is credited with designing over 430 schools nationwide and has more than 35 school buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places. E-shaped school designs are considered his trademark. Many of the architectural planning and design principles used in schools today originated with Ittner. His parents were Anthony F. and Mary Butts Ittner; his father, a U.S. Congressman, worked at a lead plant and as a bricklayer before founding Ittner Bros. with his brother Conrad in 1859. Ittner's father helped establish the trade school from which his son graduated in 1884 as part of the first class to receive diplomas from Washington University's Manual Training School. William Ittner graduated with a degree in architecture from Cornell University College of Architecture, Art, and Planning, traveled in Europe, married Lottie Crane Allen in St. Louis, and worked in the office of Eames & Young from 1889 to 1891 before practicing independently, first in partnership with William Foster and then with T. C. Link and Alfred Rosenheim.

Sir William Beechey RA (12 December 1753 – 28 January 1839) was a British portraitist active during the golden age of British painting. Born in Burford, Oxfordshire, on 12 December 1753, he was the son of William Beechey, a solicitor, and Hannah Read. Both parents died in the early 1760s, and he and his siblings were raised by his uncle Samuel, a solicitor in Chipping Norton. Samuel intended for William to follow a legal career, and at an appropriate age, he was apprenticed as a clerk to a conveyancer near Stow-on-the-Wold. However, as recorded in The Monthly Mirror in July 1798, he was "Early foredoomed his [uncle's] soul to cross/ And paint a picture where he should engross." Beechey entered the Royal Academy Schools in 1772, where he is believed to have studied under Johan Zoffany. He first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1776, with his earliest surviving works being small-scale full-length and conversation pieces reminiscent of Zoffany. In 1782, he moved to Norwich, where he received commissions such as a portrait of John Wodehouse and a series of civic portraits for St. Andrew's Hall. By 1787, he had returned to London, and in 1789, he exhibited a celebrated portrait of John Douglas, Bishop of Carlisle (now in Lambeth Palace). His early career featured portraits in the restrained style of Joshua Reynolds. Beechey's style aligned well with the royal family's tastes, and in 1793, he was commissioned to paint a full-length portrait of Queen Charlotte and appointed her official portrait painter. That same year, he was elected an associate member of the Royal Academy. Following this appointment, royal commissions increased significantly, and in 1797 he exhibited six royal portraits. In 1798, he was elected a full member of the Royal Academy and painted George III and the Prince of Wales Reviewing Troops for the Academy's exhibition—an enormous composition depicting the King, the Prince of Wales, and staff officers on horseback at an imagined cavalry review in Hyde Park. The King was pleased with the painting and awarded Beechey a knighthood. Joseph Farington's Diaries document Beechey's relationships with the royal family, including a temporary fall from favour in 1804, which Farington attributed to George III's mental condition. Beechey's portraits at the turn of the century are regarded as his most colourful and lively, reflecting the flamboyant and free techniques of his younger rivals, John Hoppner and Sir Thomas Lawrence. Royal patronage resumed around 1813 when Beechey was appointed portrait painter to Prince William Frederick, Duke of Gloucester and Edinburgh, culminating in his appointment in 1830 as principal portrait painter to William IV. In 1830, he stood for election as President of the Royal Academy following Thomas Lawrence's death, finishing second to Martin Archer Shee. In 1836, Beechey retired to Hampstead, and on 9–11 June of that year, the contents of his studio and collection were sold at Christie's. Despite being capable of impetuousness and irascibility, Beechey was known for his generosity to students, particularly supporting the young John Constable. Over a half-century-long career, he painted many leading figures of his time, including Capt. Jack Aubrey, whose portrait—showing him in Royal Navy uniform with the insignia of the Order of the Bath—was described by Patrick O'Brian in his 1978 novel Desolation Island as having hung in Aubrey's home, Ashgrove Cottage. His first marriage was to Mary Ann Jones (c. 1760–1793) in 1772 (some sources state 1778); they had a son, British painter and Egyptologist Henry William Beechey (1788–1862). After Mary Ann's death, he married the successful miniature painter Anne Phyllis Jessop (1764–1833) in 1793; they had several children, including Royal Navy captain, geographer, and politician Frederick William Beechey (1796–1856); painter George Duncan Beechey (1798–1852); clergyman St. Vincent Beechey (1806–1899); and painter and admiral Richard Brydges Beechey (1808–1895). Beechey's Portrait of James Watt sold for £153,440 at Sotheby's on 20 March 2003; his Portrait of Mirza Abu'l Hassan Khan, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of King George III, sold for £181,600 at Christie's on 8 June 2006; his Portrait of George Douglas, 16th Earl of Morton in the dress of the Royal Company of Archers, sold for £481,250 at Christie's on 5 July 2011; and his portrait of The Dashwood Children sold for $821,000 including premium at Christie's on 29 January 2014. His works are held in many of the world's leading collections, including the Louvre, the Smithsonian Institution, the Royal Collection, the Royal Academy of Arts, the National Portrait Gallery, London, the Tate, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Beechey was granted arms on 16 February 1829.

William Blake (28 November 1757 – 12 August 1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker who remained largely unrecognized during his lifetime but has since become a seminal figure in the history of Romantic-era poetry and visual art. His "prophetic works" were described by 20th-century critic Northrop Frye as forming "what is in proportion to its merits the least read body of poetry in the English language." Born on 28 November 1757 at 28 Broad Street (now Broadwick Street) in Soho, London, he was the third of seven children, two of whom died in infancy; his father, James, was a hosier who lived in London. William attended school only until age 10, after which he was educated at home by his mother, Catherine Blake (née Wright). Though the Blakes were English Dissenters, William was baptized on 11 December at St James's Church, Piccadilly, London. The Bible profoundly influenced him from an early age, and he recalled mystical experiences such as seeing God's face against his window, angels among haystacks, and being visited by the prophet Ezekiel. At age 10, he enrolled in drawing classes at Henry Pars's school in the Strand and began studying classical art through drawings of Greek antiquities purchased by his father, influenced by Raphael, Michelangelo, Maarten van Heemskerck, and Albrecht Dürer. On 4 August 1772, he was apprenticed to engraver James Basire for seven years at £52.10, becoming a professional engraver at age 21. Basire's line-engraving style was considered outdated, and Blake later crossed out Basire's name from a list of artistic adversaries. After two years, Blake copied images from Gothic churches in London, including Westminster Abbey, where he experienced visions of Christ with the Apostles and a procession of monks and priests, and heard their chants. He was briefly interrupted by schoolboys from Westminster School, one of whom he knocked off a scaffold, leading to the withdrawal of their access. In 1780, Blake became a student at the Royal Academy in Old Somerset House, where he rebelled against President Joshua Reynolds' emphasis on "general truth" and "general beauty," responding in marginalia with "To Generalize is to be an Idiot; To Particularize is the Alone Distinction of Merit." He also disliked Reynolds' apparent humility, which he viewed as hypocrisy. Blake became friends with John Flaxman, Thomas Stothard, and George Cumberland, who shared radical views, with Stothard and Cumberland joining the Society for Constitutional Information. In June 1780, Blake was reportedly in the front rank of a mob that attacked Newgate Prison during the Gordon Riots, a protest against a parliamentary bill revoking sanctions against Roman Catholicism. In 1781, Blake met Catherine Boucher, whom he loved after expressing his heartbreak and asking if she pitied him; he married her on 18 August 1782 in St Mary's Church, Battersea, with Catherine signing the contract with an X. The marriage was successful, and Catherine became his "partner in both life and work," assisting as an engraver and colourist, mixing and applying paint, including colouring the cover of Europe: A Prophecy. According to Alexander Gilchrist, the poet and wife did everything in making books except manufacturing paper, and they made the ink or colour. In 2019, Tate Britain's Blake exhibition highlighted Catherine's role. Around 1783, Blake published his first collection of poems, Poetical Sketches. In 1784, after his father's death, he and former apprentice James Parker opened a print shop and began working with radical publisher Joseph Johnson, whose house hosted intellectuals such as Joseph Priestley, Richard Price, John Henry Fuseli, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Thomas Paine. Blake supported the French and American revolutions, wore a Phrygian cap in solidarity, and composed the unfinished manuscript An Island in the Moon in 1784. He illustrated Original Stories from Real Life (1791) by Wollstonecraft, and in Visions of the Daughters of Albion (1793), condemned enforced chastity and marriage without love, defending women's right to self-fulfilment. From 1790 to 1800, Blake lived at 13 Hercules Buildings, Hercules Road, North Lambeth, London, a site now marked by a plaque and commemorated by 70 mosaics at Waterloo Station. In 1788, at age 31, Blake developed relief etching, which he used for most of his illuminated books, paintings, and poems. This method, also known as illuminated printing, involved writing text on copper plates with pens and brushes using an acid-resistant medium, then etching the plates to leave designs in relief. The resulting books were hand-coloured and stitched into volumes. Though relief etching is his most innovative technique, his commercial work primarily used intaglio engraving, a laborious process where images were incised into copper plates, taking months or years to complete. Europe Supported by Africa and America, an engraving for John Gabriel Stedman's The Narrative of a Five Years Expedition against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam (1796), depicts three women embracing, with Black Africa and White Europe holding hands in a gesture of equality, while the barren earth blooms beneath them; Europe wears pearls, and Africa and America wear slave bracelets. Some scholars interpret the bracelets as representing the historical reality of slavery, while the handclasp reflects Stedman's belief that people of different colors are created by the same hand. Blake used intaglio engraving for works such as the Illustrations of the Book of Job, completed just before his death. A 2009 study noted his use of "repoussage," a technique of hammering out mistakes by hitting the back of the plate, indicating the laborious nature of intaglio work. Blake and Catherine's marriage was close and devoted; he taught Catherine to write and she helped him colour his poems. Some biographers suggest he attempted to bring a concubine into the marriage according to Swedenborgian beliefs, though this is disputed. Samuel Foster Damon speculates that Catherine may have had a stillborn daughter for which The Book of Thel is an elegy. In 1800, Blake moved to a cottage in Felpham, West Sussex, to illustrate works by William Hayley, where he began Milton (title page dated 1804, completed in 1808). The preface to Milton includes a poem beginning "And did those feet in ancient time," which became the anthem "Jerusalem." Blake grew resentful of Hayley, believing he was preoccupied with "the meer drudgery of business," and wrote in Milton: A Poem, "Corporeal Friends are Spiritual Enemies." In August 1803, Blake was involved in a physical altercation with soldier John Schofield, who claimed Blake said "Damn the king. The soldiers are all slaves." Blake was cleared at the Chichester assizes, with the report noting the evidence was "invented" and thus led to acquittal. Schofield was later depicted wearing "mind forged manacles" in an illustration to Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion. In 1804, Blake returned to London and began working on Jerusalem (1804–20), his most ambitious work. After approaching dealer Robert Cromek to market an engraving based on Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, he was cheated when Cromek commissioned Thomas Stothard instead. Blake broke off contact with Stothard and held an independent exhibition in his brother's haberdashery shop at 27 Broad Street in Soho, showcasing his own version of the Canterbury illustration, titled The Canterbury Pilgrims. He wrote a Descriptive Catalogue (1809), which includes a "brilliant analysis" of Chaucer and is regularly anthologised as a classic of Chaucer criticism, along with detailed explanations of his other works. The exhibition was very successful.

Blake was later depicted wearing "mind forged manacles" in an illustration to Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion.[59] He returned to London in 1804 and began writing and illustrating Jerusalem (1804–20), his most ambitious work. Having conceived the idea of portraying characters from Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, Blake approached dealer Robert Cromek, intending to market an engraving; however, knowing Blake was too eccentric to produce a popular work, Cromek commissioned his friend Thomas Stothard to execute the concept. Upon learning he had been cheated, Blake severed contact with Stothard and held an independent exhibition in his brother's haberdashery shop at 27 Broad Street in Soho, designed to promote his own version of the Canterbury illustration (titled The Canterbury Pilgrims) along with other works. As a result, he wrote his Descriptive Catalogue (1809), which Anthony Blunt called a "brilliant analysis" of Chaucer and is regularly anthologised as a classic of Chaucer criticism; it also included detailed explanations of his other paintings. The exhibition was poorly attended, selling none of the temperas or watercolours, and its only review in The Examiner was hostile.[61] Around this time (circa 1808), Blake expressed strong views on art in a series of polemical annotations to Sir Joshua Reynolds' Discourses, denouncing the Royal Academy as a fraud and proclaiming, "To Generalize is to be an Idiot."[62] In 1818, he was introduced by George Cumberland's son to young artist John Linnell.[63] A blue plaque commemorates Blake and Linnell at Old Wyldes' in North End, Hampstead.[64] Through Linnell, Blake met Samuel Palmer, a member of the Shoreham Ancients, a group of artists who shared his rejection of modern trends and belief in a spiritual and artistic New Age. At age 65, Blake began work on illustrations for the Book of Job, later admired by John Ruskin, who compared Blake favourably to Rembrandt, and by Vaughan Williams, who based his ballet Job: A Masque for Dancing on a selection of the illustrations.[citation needed] In later life, Blake began selling a large number of his works, particularly his Bible illustrations, to Thomas Butts, a patron who viewed him more as a friend than as an artist of merit—this reflects the general opinion of Blake throughout his life.[citation needed] In 1826, a commission for Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy came to Blake through Linnell, with the aim of producing a series of engravings. Blake's death in 1827 cut short the project, and only a handful of watercolours were completed, with only seven engravings reaching proof form. Nevertheless, the Dante watercolours are among Blake's richest achievements, engaging fully with the complexity of the poem, and the mastery of watercolour reached a higher level, used to extraordinary effect in differentiating the atmosphere of the three states of being in the text. The illustrations are not merely accompanying works but appear to critically revise or comment on certain spiritual or moral aspects of the poem. Because the project was incomplete, Blake's original intent may be obscured; however, in the margin of Homer Bearing the Sword and His Companions, Blake notes, "Every thing in Dantes Comedia shews That for Tyrannical Purposes he has made This World the Foundation of All & the Goddess Nature & not the Holy Ghost," indicating his dissent from Dante's admiration of ancient Greece and his apparent glee in Hell's punishments. At the same time, Blake shared Dante's distrust of materialism and the corrupting nature of power and relished the opportunity to represent the atmosphere and imagery of Dante's work. Even near death, Blake's central preoccupation was his work on the illustrations for Dante's Inferno; he is said to have spent one of his last shillings on a pencil to continue sketching.[66] Blake's final years were spent at Fountain Court off the Strand (the property was demolished in the 1880s when the Savoy Hotel was built).[1] On the day of his death (12 August 1827), he worked relentlessly on the Dante series. Eventually, he ceased working and turned to his wife, who was in tears by his bedside. Beholding her, Blake is said to have cried, "Stay Kate! Keep just as you are – I will draw your portrait – for you have ever been an angel to me." Having completed this portrait (now lost), Blake laid down his tools and began to sing hymns and verses. At six that evening, after promising his wife he would be with her always, Blake died. Gilchrist reports that a female lodger present at his death said, "I have been at the death, not of a man, but of a blessed angel."[68] George Richmond described Blake's death in a letter to Samuel Palmer: "He died ... in a most glorious manner. He said He was going to that Country he had all His life wished to see & expressed Himself Happy, hoping for Salvation through Jesus Christ – Just before he died His Countenance became fair. His eyes Brighten'd and he burst out Singing of the things he saw in Heaven."[69] Catherine paid for Blake's funeral with money lent to her by Linnell. Blake's body was buried in a shared plot, five days after his death—on the eve of his 45th wedding anniversary—at the Dissenters' burial ground in Bunhill Fields, in the City of London area. His parents' bodies were also buried there. Present at the ceremonies were Catherine, Edward Calvert, George Richmond, Frederick Tatham, and John Linnell. After Blake's death, Catherine moved into Tatham's house as a housekeeper and believed she was regularly visited by Blake's spirit. She continued selling his illuminated works and paintings but entertained no business transaction without first "consulting Mr. Blake."[71] On her death in October 1831, she was calm and cheerful, calling out to him "as if he were only in the next room, to say she was coming to him, and it would not be long now."[72] Following her death, Frederick Tatham took possession of Blake's works and continued selling them. Tatham later joined the fundamentalist Irvingite church and, under conservative influence, burned manuscripts he deemed heretical; the exact number of destroyed works is unknown, but shortly before his death Blake told a friend he had written "twenty tragedies as long as Macbeth", none of which survive.[74] William Michael Rossetti also burned works by Blake he considered lacking in quality,[75] and John Linnell erased sexual imagery from a number of Blake's drawings.[76] At the same time, some unpublished works were preserved by friends, such as his notebook and An Island in the Moon. Blake's grave is commemorated by two stones. The first reads "Near by lie the remains of the poet-painter William Blake 1757–1827 and his wife Catherine Sophia 1762–1831" and is located approximately 20 metres (66 ft) from the actual grave, which was not marked until 12 August 2018.[44] Since 1965, the exact location of Blake's grave had been lost and forgotten due to damage from the Second World War; gravestones were removed and a garden created. The memorial stone, indicating the burial sites are "nearby," was listed as a Grade II listed structure in 2011.[77][78] A Portuguese couple, Carol and Luís Garrido, rediscovered the exact burial location after 14 years of investigation, and the Blake Society organised a permanent memorial slab, unveiled at a public ceremony on 12 August 2018.[44][78][79][80] The new stone is inscribed "Here lies William Blake 1757–1827 Poet Artist Prophet" above a verse from his poem Jerusalem. The Blake Prize for Religious Art was established in Australia in 1949. In 1957, a memorial to Blake and his wife was erected in Westminster Abbey.[81] Another memorial lies in St James's Church, Piccadilly, where he was baptised. At the time of his death, Blake had sold fewer than 30 copies of Songs of Innocence and of Experience.[82] Blake was not active in any well-established political party. His poetry consistently reflects a rebellion against the abuse of class power, as documented in David Erdman's Blake: Prophet Against Empire: A Poet's Interpretation of the History of His Own Times (1954). Blake was concerned about senseless wars and the blighting effects of the Industrial Revolution, and much of his poetry uses symbolic allegory to recount the effects of the French and American revolutions. Erdman claims Blake was disillusioned with the political outcomes, believing they had replaced monarchy with irresponsible mercantilism. Erdman also notes Blake was deeply opposed to slavery and that some of his poems, read primarily as championing "free love," had their anti-slavery implications underemphasised.[83] A more recent study, William Blake: Visionary Anarchist by Peter Marshall (1988), classifies Blake and his contemporary William Godwin as forerunners of modern anarchism.[84] The British Marxist historian E. P. Thompson's final work, Witness Against the Beast: William Blake and the Moral Law (1993), argues that Blake was inspired by dissident religious ideas rooted in the thinking of the most radical opponents of the monarchy during the English Civil War. Because Blake's later poetry contains a private mythology with complex symbolism, his late work has been less published than his earlier, more accessible work. The Vintage anthology of Blake edited by Patti Smith focuses heavily on the earlier work, as do many critical studies such as William Blake by D. G. Gillham. The earlier work is primarily rebellious and can be seen as a protest against dogmatic religion, especially in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, where the figure represented by the "Devil" is a hero rebelling against an imposter authoritarian deity. In later works, such as Milton and Jerusalem, Blake presents a distinctive vision of humanity redeemed by self-sacrifice and forgiveness, while retaining his earlier negative attitude toward the rigid and morbid authoritarianism of traditional religion. Not all readers agree on the continuity between Blake's earlier and later works. Psychoanalyst June Singer writes that Blake's late work shows a development of ideas first introduced in his earlier works, namely, the humanitarian goal of achieving personal wholeness of body and spirit. In the final section of her expanded edition of The Unholy Bible, she suggests the later works are the "Bible of Hell" promised in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. Regarding Blake's final poem, Jerusalem, she writes: "The promise of the divine in man, made in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is at last fulfilled."[86] John Middleton Murry notes a discontinuity between Marriage and the late works, in that while the early Blake focused on a "sheer negative opposition between Energy and Reason," the later Blake emphasized self-sacrifice and forgiveness as the path to interior wholeness. This renunciation of the sharper dualism of Marriage of Heaven and Hell is evident in the humanisation of the character of Urizen in the later works. Murry characterises the later Blake as having found "mutual understanding" and "mutual forgiveness."[87] Regarding conventional religion, Blake was a satirist and ironist, as illustrated and summarised in his poem Vala, or The Four Zoas, one of his uncompleted prophetic books begun in 1797. The demi-mythological and demi-religious main characters of the book are the Four Zoas (Urthona, Urizen, Luvah and Tharmas), created by the fall of Albion in Blake's mythology. The work consists of nine books, referred to as "nights," outlining the interactions of the Zoas, their fallen forms, and their Emanations. Blake intended the book to be a summation of his mythic universe. The Four Zoas represent four aspects of the Almighty God, and Vala is the first work to mention them. In particular, Blake's God/Man union is broken down into the bodily components of Urizen (head), Urthona (loins), Luvah (heart), and Tharmas (unity of the body), with paired Emanations being Ahania (wisdom, from the head), Enitharmon (what can't be attained in nature, from the loins), Vala (nature, from the heart), and Enion (earth mother, from the separation of unity).[88] As connected to Blake's understanding of the divine, the Zoas are the God the Father (Tharmas, sense), the Son of God (Luvah, love), the Holy Ghost (Urthona, imagination), and Satan who was originally of divine substance (Urizen, reason), with their Emanations representing Sexual Urges (Enion), Nature (Vala), Inspiration (Enitharmon), and Pleasure (Ahania).[90] Blake believed each person had a twofold identity, one half good and the other evil. In Vala, both the character Orc and The Eternal Man discuss their selves as divided. By the time he was working on his later works, including Vala, Blake felt he had overcome his inner battle but was concerned about losing his artistic abilities. These thoughts carried over into Vala as the character Los (imagination) is connected to the image of Christ, and he added a Christian element to his mythic world. In the revised version of Vala, Blake added Christian and Hebrew images and describes how Los experiences a vision of the Lamb of God that regenerates his spirit. In opposition to Christ is Urizen and the Synagogue of Satan, who later crucify Christ, from whom Deism is born.[91] Blake did not subscribe to the notion of a body distinct from the soul that must submit to the rule of the soul, but saw the body as an extension of the soul, derived from the "discernment" of the senses. Thus, the emphasis in orthodoxy on denying bodily urges is a dualistic error born of misapprehension of the relationship between body and soul. Elsewhere, he describes Satan as the "state of error," and as beyond salvation.[92] Blake opposed the sophistry of theological thought that excuses pain, admits evil, and apologises for injustice. He abhorred self-denial,[93] which he associated with religious repression and particularly sexual repression:[94] "Prudence is a rich ugly old maid courted by Incapacity. He who desires but acts not breeds pestilence." (7.4–5, E35) He saw the concept of "sin" as a trap to bind men's desires (the briars of Garden of Love) and believed that restraint in obedience to a moral code imposed from the outside was against the spirit of life: "Abstinence sows sand all over / The ruddy limbs & flaming hair / But Desire Gratified / Plants fruits & beauty there." (E474) He did not hold with the doctrine of God as Lord, an entity separate from and superior to mankind;[95] this is shown clearly in his words about Jesus Christ: "He is the only God ... and so am I, and so are you." A telling phrase in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell is "men forgot that All deities reside in the human breast." Blake had a complex relationship with Enlightenment philosophy. His championing of the imagination as the most important element of human existence ran contrary to Enlightenment ideals of rationalism and empiricism.[96] Due to his visionary religious beliefs, he opposed the Newtonian view of the universe. This mindset is reflected in an excerpt from Blake's Jerusalem: "I turn my eyes to the Schools & Universities of Europe / And there behold the Loom of Locke whose Woof rages dire / Washd by the Water-wheels of Newton. black the cloth / In heavy wreathes folds over every Nation; cruel Works / Of many Wheels I view, wheel without wheel, with cogs tyrannic / Moving by compulsion each other: not as those in Eden: which / Wheel within Wheel in freedom revolve in harmony & peace." (15.14–20, E159) Blake believed the paintings of Sir Joshua Reynolds, which depict the naturalistic fall of light upon objects, were products entirely of the "vegetative eye," and he saw Locke and Newton as "the true progenitors of Sir Joshua Reynolds' aesthetic."[100] The popular taste in England at the time for such paintings was satisfied with mezzotints, prints produced by a process that created an image from thousands of tiny dots upon the page. Blake saw an analogy between this and Newton's particle theory of light.[101] Accordingly, Blake never used the technique, opting instead to develop a method of engraving purely in fluid line, insisting that: "a Line or Lineament is not formed by Chance a Line is a Line in its Minutest Subdivision[s] Strait or Crooked It is Itself & Not Intermeasurable with or by any Thing Else Such is Job." (E784) It has been supposed that, despite his opposition to Enlightenment principles, Blake arrived at a linear aesthetic that was in many ways more similar to the Neoclassical engravings of John Flaxman than to the works of the Romantics, with whom he is often classified.[102] However, Blake's relationship with Flaxman seems to have grown more distant after Blake's return from Felpham, and there are surviving letters between Flaxman and Hayley wherein Flaxman speaks ill of Blake's theories of art.[103] Blake further criticised Flaxman's styles and theories of art in his responses to criticism made against his print of Chaucer's.

Blake's work involves prints made through a process that creates an image from thousands of tiny dots, a method he compared to Newton's particle theory of light, though he never used it, instead developing a technique of engraving in fluid line, asserting that a line is not formed by chance but is itself, in its minutest subdivision, straight or crooked, and not measurable by or against anything else, as stated in "Such is Job" (E784). Though often classified with the Romantics, Blake's aesthetic is more aligned with John Flaxman's Neoclassical engravings, but his relationship with Flaxman deteriorated after Blake's return from Felpham, with Flaxman criticizing Blake's artistic theories in letters to Hayley, and Blake responding to criticism of his print *Chaucer's Caunterbury Pilgrims* in 1810 by rejecting Flaxman's styles and theories. After his death, Blake has been claimed by various movements for his use of symbolism and allegory, particularly as a forerunner of the 19th-century "free love" movement, which began in the 1820s and viewed state-sanctioned marriage as "legal prostitution" and monopolistic, aligning more with early feminist thought, especially Mary Wollstonecraft's writings, which Blake admired. Blake criticized contemporary marriage laws and traditional Christian notions of chastity, advocating for a second wife during a strained marriage due to Catherine's inability to bear children, and his poetry, such as "Why should I be bound to thee, O my lovely Myrtle-tree?" and "Earth's Answer," suggests support for multiple sexual partners; in "London," he references "the Marriage-Hearse" under the "youthful Harlot's curse," and *Visions of the Daughters of Albion* is widely read as a tribute to free love, with Bromion and Oothoon bound only by law, not love. Blake opposed law and love, condemning the "frozen marriage-bed," and in *Visions*, wrote: "Till she who burns with youth, and knows no fixed lot, is bound / In spells of law to one she loathes? and must she drag the chain / Of life in weary lust?" (5.21–3, E49). Algernon Charles Swinburne highlighted Blake's praise of "sacred natural love" unbound by possessive jealousy, which Blake described as a "creeping skeleton," and Swinburne noted Blake's *Marriage of Heaven and Hell* condemned "pale religious letchery." Edward Carpenter (1844–1929) was influenced by Blake's mystical emphasis on energy free from external restrictions. Pierre Berger noted that Blake's early views celebrated authentic love over duty, and Irene Langridge observed that free love in Blake's creed was intended for the edification of the soul. Michael Davis (1977) argued that jealousy separates man from divine unity, condemning him to a frozen death. S. Foster Damon noted that for Blake, the main obstacles to free love were corrupt human nature and hypocritical communication, not just societal intolerance or male jealousy. Thomas Wright (1928) observed that marriage should afford joy but often fails to do so, as couples' awareness of being chained diminishes their joy, and Pierre Berger analyzed Blake's early mythological poems like *Ahania* as showing marriage laws as a result of human fallenness from pride and jealousy. Some scholars note Blake's views on free love were qualified and evolved, with late poems like *The Sick Rose* warning of predatory sexuality; Magnus Ankarsjö observed that in *Visions of the Daughters of Albion*, the heroine becomes more cautious as she gains awareness of sexuality's dark side, asking "Can this be love which drinks another as a sponge drinks water?" and that Blake, like Mary Wollstonecraft, developed more circumspect views late in life. Given Blake's sense of human fallenness, Ankarsjö argues Blake does not fully endorse sensual indulgence in defiance of law, as all love in the fallen world is enchained; he records Blake supporting a commune with shared partners, though David Worrall read *The Book of Thel* as rejecting the proposal to take concubines from the Swedenborgian church. Blake's later writings show renewed interest in Christianity, reinterpreting Christian morality to embrace sensual pleasure, though with less emphasis on sexual libertarianism and more on "self-denial" inspired by love rather than authoritarian compulsion. Berger, more than Swinburne, emphasizes a shift in sensibility from early to later Blake, believing the young Blake overemphasized following impulses, while the older Blake developed a better-formed ideal of true love involving self-sacrifice. Mystical sensuality remains in late poems, notably in Blake's denial of the virginity of Jesus's mother, while later works emphasize forgiveness, redemption, and emotional authenticity. Northrop Frye noted Blake's consistency, stating that his notes on Reynolds at fifty were "exactly similar" to those on Locke and Bacon when young, and that phrases and lines reappeared up to forty years later; consistency was a central principle, and self-contradiction was one of his most contemptuous critiques. Blake abhorred slavery and believed in racial and sexual equality, with poems expressing universal humanity: "As all men are alike (tho' infinitely various)," and in one poem, a black child narrates that white and black bodies are like shaded groves or clouds, existing until one learns "to bear the beams of love," stating: "When I from black and he from white cloud free, / And round the tent of God like lambs we joy: / I'll shade him from the heat till he can bear, / To lean in joy upon our fathers knee. / And then I'll stand and stroke his silver hair, / And be like him and he will then love me" (23–8, E9). Blake remained engaged with social and political issues, opposing institutional restrictions, including the Church, and in *Songs of Experience* (1794), distinguished between the Old Testament God, whom he rejected for his restrictions, and the New Testament God, whom he viewed positively. From a young age, Blake claimed to have seen visions: at age four, he saw God "put his head to the window," causing him to scream; at age eight or ten, he saw "a tree filled with angels, bright angelic wings bespangling every bough like stars," which he reported to his parents, escaping punishment due to his mother's intervention. His mother was especially supportive, and early drawings and poems adorned her chamber. He also saw angelic figures among haymakers. Blake claimed to experience visions throughout his life, often involving beautiful religious themes, and believed he was personally instructed by Archangels, who actively read and enjoyed his works. In a letter to William Hayley (6 May 1800), he wrote: "I know that our deceased friends are more really with us than when they were apparent to our mortal part. Thirteen years ago I lost a brother, and with his spirit I converse daily and hourly in the spirit, and see him in my remembrance, in the region of my imagination. I hear his advice, and even now write from his dictate." In a letter to John Flaxman (21 September 1800), he wrote: "[Felpham] is a sweet place for Study, because it is more spiritual than London. Heaven opens here on all sides her golden Gates; her windows are not obstructed by vapours; voices of Celestial inhabitants are more distinctly heard, & their forms more distinctly seen; & my Cottage is also a Shadow of their houses. My Wife & Sister are both well, courting Neptune for an embrace... I am more famed in Heaven for my works than I could well conceive. In my Brain are studies & Chambers filled with books & pictures of old, which I wrote & painted in ages of Eternity before my mortal life; & those works are the delight & Study of Archangels." In a letter to Thomas Butts (25 April 1803), he wrote: "Now I may say to you, what perhaps I should not dare to say to anyone else: That I can alone carry on my visionary studies in London unannoy'd, & that I may converse with my friends in Eternity, See Visions, Dream Dreams & prophecy & speak Parables unobserv'd & at liberty from the Doubts of other Mortals; perhaps Doubts proceeding from Kindness, but Doubts are always pernicious, Especially when we Doubt our Friends." In *A Vision of the Last Judgement*, he wrote: "Error is Created Truth is Eternal Error or Creation will be Burned Up & then & not till then Truth or Eternity will appear It is Burnt up the Moment Men cease to behold it I assert for My self that I do not behold the Outward Creation & that to me it is hindrance & not Action it is as the Dirt upon my feet No part of Me. What it will be Questiond When the Sun rises do you not see a round Disk of fire somewhat like a Guinea O no no I see an Innumerable company of the Heavenly host crying Holy Holy Holy is the Lord God Almighty I question not my Corporeal or Vegetative Eye any more than I would Question a Window concerning a Sight I look thro it & not with it." (E565–6) Despite seeing angels and God, Blake also claimed to have seen Satan on the staircase of his South Molton Street home in London. William Wordsworth commented, "There was no doubt that this poor man was mad, but there is something in the madness of this man which interests me more than the sanity of Lord Byron and Walter Scott." John William Cousins wrote that Blake was "a truly pious and loving soul, neglected and misunderstood by the world, but appreciated by an elect few," who "led a cheerful and contented life of poverty illumined by visions and celestial inspirations." The 1911 *Encyclopædia Britannica* entry questioned whether Blake was mad, noting he was under the influence of illusions with no outward facts to account for them, and that much of his writing lacks logical coherence. Blake's work was neglected for a generation after his death and nearly forgotten until Alexander Gilchrist began his biography in the 1860s, which transformed his reputation, especially through adoption by Pre-Raphaelites like Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Algernon Charles Swinburne. In the 20th century, scholars such as S. Foster Damon, Geoffrey Keynes, Northrop Frye, and David V. Erdman helped establish Blake's standing. Blake influenced figures like William Butler Yeats, who edited his works in 1893, and British surrealists such as Paul Nash and Graham Sutherland, drawing on Blake's non-mimetic, visionary approach. British classical composers set Blake's poems, beginning with Doyne Bell's 1876 setting of "Can I see another's woe," followed by notable settings by Benjamin Britten, Ralph Vaughan Williams, and John Tavener, who set "The Lamb" (1982) and "The Tyger." June Singer argued Blake's views on human nature anticipate Carl Jung's ideas, with Jung noting Blake compiled half-digested knowledge in fantasies, which are artistic rather than authentic unconscious representations. Diana Hume George claimed Blake is a precursor to Freud's ideas. Blake influenced the beat poets of the 1950s and the 1960s counterculture, cited by Allen Ginsberg, Bob Dylan, Richard Ashcroft, Jim Morrison, Van Morrison, Bruce Dickinson, and Aldous Huxley. William Bolcom composed a Pulitzer Prize-winning setting of *Songs of Innocence and of Experience*, using diverse musical styles, from modern to Broadway to Country/Western and reggae. Much of Philip Pullman's *His Dark Materials* trilogy is rooted in Blake's *The Marriage of Heaven and Hell*, and Blake features as a significant character in Brian Catling's *The Erstwhile*, where his visions of angelic beings are incorporated. Kathleen Yearwood is one of many contemporary musicians who have set Blake's poems to music. After WWII, Blake's influence expanded into popular music, film, and graphic novels, with Edward Larrissy asserting that "Blake is the Romantic writer who has exerted the most powerful influence on the twentieth century." Major recent exhibitions have focused on William Blake, with the works with * constituting the prophetic books. Digital editions and research are available in the specified categories.

William Blake's poems have been set to music by various artists, including com set Songs of Innocence and of Experience to music, with different poems assigned to distinct musical styles, ranging from modern techniques to Broadway, Country/Western, and reggae. The central theme of Philip Pullman's fantasy trilogy, His Dark Materials, is inspired by the world depicted in Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and Blake also appears as a significant character in Brian Catling's fantasy novel The Erstwhile, where his visions of angelic beings are incorporated into the narrative.
