William Kentridge, born on 28 April 1955 in Johannesburg to Sydney Kentridge and Felicia Geffen, a Jewish family of lawyers who defended victims of apartheid, is a South African artist renowned for his prints, drawings, and animated films. He began showing artistic promise at age eight, taking charcoal classes, and earned a Bachelor of Arts in Politics and African Studies from the University of the Witwatersrand, followed by a diploma in Fine Arts from the Johannesburg Art Foundation. In the early 1980s, he studied mime and theatre at the L'École Internationale de Théâtre Jacques Lecoq in Paris, where he realized he was not suited for acting and transitioned to becoming an artist. Between 1975 and 1991, he acted and directed with Johannesburg's Junction Avenue Theatre Company and worked on television films as an art director. Kentridge's work is deeply rooted in South Africa's socio-political history, and he views his ethnic Jewish identity as offering a third-party perspective. He practices expressionist art where form and content are interwoven, and his sparse, rough handwriting evokes a sombre, vulnerable atmosphere. His art frequently addresses social injustice, such as in *Casspirs Full of Love*, a print that appears as heads in boxes to outsiders but symbolizes apartheid-era crowd-control vehicles used against lower-class populations. By the mid-1970s, he produced prints and drawings, including the "Pit" series (1979) and "Domestic Scenes" (1980), which established his artistic identity. In 1986, he created charcoal and pastel drawings inspired by Watteau's *The Embarkation for Cythera*, depicting a dystopic urban landscape. In 1996–1997, he produced *Ubu Tells the Truth*, a portfolio based on Alfred Jarry's *Ubu Roi*, relating to South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. In 2012, he delivered the Norton Lectures at Harvard University, discussing studio practice and a series of large tree drawings made on torn encyclopedia pages. Kentridge's animated films, beginning with *Johannesburg, 2nd Greatest City After Paris* in 1989 and continuing through *Tide Table* (2003) and *Other Faces* (2011), use a unique technique of successive charcoal drawings on the same sheet, with erasures and re-drawings giving each change a quarter to two seconds of screen time, preserving traces of previous images to convey fading memory and time's passage. These films feature characters Soho Eckstein and Felix Teitlebaum, reflecting the emotional and political struggles of pre-democracy South Africa. His work explores themes of time, change, and suppressed history, often through ambiguity, contradiction, and unfinished narratives. In 1988, he co-founded the Free Film-makers Co-Operative in Johannesburg; in 1999, he was appointed a filmmaker by Stereoscope. His political perspective is evident in his opera productions, including *Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria*, *Die Zauberflöte*, and *The Nose*, and in the collaborative show *Telegrams from the Nose*. In 2015, his staging of Berg's *Lulu* premiered at the Metropolitan Opera, and in 2017, his *Wozzeck* premiered at the Salzburg Festival. In 2023, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for Outstanding Achievement in Opera for *Sybil* at the Barbican Theatre. Kentridge began a series of tapestries in 2001, using shadowy figures from ripped construction paper and nineteenth-century atlas maps, collaborating with the Johannesburg-based Stephens Tapestry Studio to create locally spun mohair tapestries. In 2009, he created the 10m-tall sculpture *Fire Walker* in Johannesburg and *Il cavaliere di Toledo* in Naples; in 2013, he produced *Rebus*, a series of bronze sculptures that form a nude when paired at a certain angle. In 2016, he unveiled *Triumphs and Laments*, a 550m-long mural along the Tiber River in Rome, celebrating the city's founding in 753BC with over 80 figures from mythology to the present, accompanied by live shadow play and music. Kentridge is married to Anne Stanwix and has three children; he is of third-generation South African Lithuanian-Jewish heritage. His films were shown at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival. His works are held in permanent collections at the Honolulu Museum of Art, Kalamazoo Institute of Arts, Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, Museum of Modern Art (New York), and Tate Modern (London). An edition of *The Refusal of Time* (2012) was acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. In 2015, he donated his complete archive of films, videos, and digital works to the George Eastman Museum. His *Five Themes* exhibit was included in the 2009 Time 100 and won First Place in the 2009 AICA Best Monographic Museum Show Nationally category. In 2012, he was invited to deliver the Charles Eliot Norton Lectures at Harvard University and was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In 2017, he founded The Centre For The Less Good Idea in Maboneng, Johannesburg, with Bronwyn Lace, currently led by Neo Muyanga. Kentridge's artworks are among the most valuable in South Africa, with a major charcoal drawing selling for £250,000; a bronze piece reached $1.5 million at Sotheby's New York in 2013, and a record of R6.6 million ($320,000) was set in 2018 at Aspire Art Auctions in Johannesburg. He is represented by Goodman Gallery, Lia Rumma Gallery, and Hauser & Wirth (since 2024), having worked with Goodman Gallery from 1999 to 2024.

Sir William Ramsay KCB FRS FRSE (/ˈræmzi/; 2 October 1852 – 23 July 1916) was a Scottish chemist who discovered the noble gases and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904 "in recognition of his services in the discovery of the inert gaseous elements in air" alongside John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh, who received the Nobel Prize in Physics that same year for their discovery of argon. After identifying argon, Ramsay investigated other atmospheric gases, isolating argon, helium, neon, krypton, and xenon, which led to the creation of a new section of the periodic table. Born on 2 October 1852 at 2 Clifton Street in Glasgow, the son of civil engineer William C. Ramsay and Catherine Robertson, he lived in a three-storey and basement Georgian townhouse at 2 Clifton Street before moving to 1 Oakvale Place in Hillhead as a youth. He was a nephew of geologist Sir Andrew Ramsay. Educated at Glasgow Academy, he apprenticed with Robert Napier in Govan before studying chemistry at the University of Glasgow, matriculating in 1866 and graduating in 1869. He then trained with chemist Thomas Anderson and studied in Germany at the University of Tübingen under Wilhelm Rudolph Fittig, completing a doctoral thesis on Investigations in the Toluic and Nitrotoluic Acids. He returned to Glasgow as Anderson's assistant and was appointed Professor of Chemistry at University College of Bristol in 1879, marrying Margaret Buchanan in 1881 and becoming Principal of the college that same year while conducting active research in organic chemistry and gases. In 1876, he synthesized pyridine from acetylene and hydrogen cyanide in an iron-tube furnace, marking the first synthesis of a heteroaromatic compound. In 1887, he succeeded Alexander Williamson as chair of Chemistry at University College London (UCL), where he made his most significant discoveries. As early as 1885–1890, he published notable papers on nitrogen oxides. On 19 April 1894, after attending a lecture by Lord Rayleigh, who had observed a discrepancy in nitrogen density, Ramsay and Rayleigh began investigating the issue. In August 1894, Ramsay informed Rayleigh of a new, heavy, chemically inert component of air, which he named argon from the Greek word meaning "lazy." In subsequent years, working with Morris Travers, he discovered neon, krypton, and xenon. He also isolated helium, previously only observed in the sun's spectrum, and in 1910 isolated and characterized radon. Between 1893 and 1902, he collaborated with British chemist Emily Aston on mineral analysis and atomic weight determination, including studies on the molecular surface energies of mixtures of non-associating liquids. He was elected an International Member of the American Philosophical Society in 1899 and an International Member of the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1904. In 1902, he was appointed a Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath (KCB) in the Coronation Honours list, invested by King Edward VII at Buckingham Palace on 24 October 1902. Ramsay served as president of the British Association from 1911 to 1912. He married Margaret Johnstone Marshall (née Buchanan) in 1881; they had a daughter, Catherine Elizabeth (Elska), and a son, William George, who died at age 40. He lived in Hazlemere, Buckinghamshire, and died in High Wycombe on 23 July 1916 at the age of 63 from nasal cancer and was buried in Hazlemere parish church. A blue plaque at 12 Arundel Gardens, Notting Hill, commemorates his life and work. The Sir William Ramsay School in Hazlemere and Ramsay grease are named after him. A memorial to him is located in the north aisle of the choir at Westminster Abbey by Charles Hartwell. In 1923, University College London named its Chemical Engineering department and seat after Ramsay, funded by the Ramsay Memorial Fund, with H. E. Watson, one of his former graduates, serving as the third Ramsay professor of chemical engineering. On 2 October 2019, Google celebrated his 167th birthday with a Google Doodle.

Windows 2000 is a major release of the Windows NT operating system developed by Microsoft, targeting the server and business markets as the direct successor to Windows NT 4.0. It was released to manufacturing on December 15, 1999, and to retail on February 17, 2000 for all versions, with Windows 2000 Datacenter Server released to retail on September 26, 2000. The operating system introduced NTFS 3.0, the Encrypting File System, and support for basic and dynamic disk storage. It improved support for people with disabilities through new assistive technologies and expanded language and locale support. The Windows 2000 Server family included Active Directory, which became widely used in business environments. Although support for the Alpha architecture was present in early development builds, including 64-bit versions, it was discontinued during the final stages of development after Compaq dropped support, and no 64-bit version of Windows 2000 was officially released. The decision to drop the "NT" name from the product line was the result of a debate between Jim Allchin and Bill Gates, with Allchin advocating for modernization and Gates favoring integration with the existing series; Allchin ultimately won. Four editions were released: Professional, Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server, with the latter launched months after the others. All editions share core features such as the Microsoft Management Console and standard system administration tools. Microsoft marketed Windows 2000 as the most secure Windows version at the time, though it faced high-profile virus attacks like Code Red and Nimda. It was succeeded by Windows XP, released on October 2001, and Windows Server 2003, released on April 2003, more than three years after the initial release of Windows 2000 Server. Support for Windows 2000 ended on July 13, 2010, the same day support ended for Windows XP SP2. Both the original Xbox and Xbox 360 used a modified version of the Windows 2000 kernel, with the former's source code leaked in 2020. Originally named Windows NT 5.0, the operating system began development in early 1997 with beta builds identical to Windows NT 4.0, and the first official beta was released in September 1997, followed by Beta 2 in August 1998. On October 27, 1998, Microsoft announced the final name would be Windows 2000, referencing its projected release date. Windows 2000 Beta 3 was released in May 1999, and the new login prompt, icons, and boot screen first appeared in that build. The operating system did not have a codename, as Jim Allchin did not like them; Service Pack 1 was codenamed "Asteroid." Microsoft released three release candidates between July and November 1999, followed by a partner release on December 12, 1999, and manufacturing on December 15, 1999. A leaked memo revealed over 63,000 known defects in the system, though Microsoft claimed it was the most reliable and stable operating system shipped to that point due to mature source code, stress testing, and error detection. InformationWeek and Wired News described the launch as meeting expectations but lacking excitement, and Novell criticized Active Directory as less scalable than its own NDS. Windows 2000 was initially planned to replace both Windows 98 and Windows NT 4.0, but this changed when Windows 98 Second Edition was released in 1999. On or shortly before February 12, 2004, portions of Windows 2000 and Windows NT 4.0 source code were illegally made available online, traced to Mainsoft, and Microsoft issued a statement warning against distribution. An exploit allegedly discovered by someone studying the leaked code was reported on February 16, 2004, and GitHub removed a repository containing Windows NT 4.0 source code on April 15, 2015. Microsoft had planned a 64-bit version for Itanium, codenamed "Janus," but the first officially released 64-bit version was Windows XP 64-Bit Edition, released on October 25, 2001, followed by limited server editions based on pre-release Windows Server 2003 code, released in 2002 and superseded by final Server 2003 versions on April 24, 2003. Windows 2000 incorporated features from Windows 98 and 98 SE, such as the Windows Desktop Update, Internet Explorer 5, Outlook Express, FAT32 support, 3DNow!, SSE, SSE2, Windows Driver Model, Internet Connection Sharing, Windows Media Player 6.4, WebDAV, Bluetooth 1.0, USB device class drivers, and improved FireWire support. It introduced USB 2.0 support in SP4, Wireless Zero Configuration, and SSE3. It was the first Windows version to support hibernation at the OS level (ACPI S4 sleep state). Windows File Protection was introduced to prevent unauthorized modification of critical system files, with the System File Checker allowing manual scans and repairs. A system setting enabled automatic reboot on stop errors, with options to create minidumps or full memory dumps and log events. Administrators could optimize memory and processor usage for background services or applications. Core system administration features like Windows Installer, Windows Management Instrumentation, and Event Tracing for Windows were introduced. A major improvement over Windows NT 4.0 was full Plug and Play with ACPI and Windows Driver Model support, enabling automatic hardware recognition, resource allocation, driver loading, and device notifications. Version 3 print drivers based on Unidrv were introduced, and generic 5-button mouse support was added. Driver Verifier was introduced to detect driver bugs. Windows 2000 introduced layered windows with transparency, translucency, and effects like shadows and alpha-blended GUI elements, and menus supported a Fade transition. The Start menu included personalized menus, expandable special folders, and the ability to launch multiple programs by holding SHIFT, with a Re-sort button to sort by name. The Taskbar supported balloon notifications. Windows Explorer introduced customizable toolbars, auto-complete in the address bar and Run box, advanced file type associations, comments in shortcuts as tooltips, extensible columns, icon overlays, an integrated search pane, sort by name, and a Places bar. Active Desktop, introduced in Internet Explorer 4.0, was included and allowed HTML-based folder customization, though it was exploited by viruses like VBS/Roor-C and VBS.Redlof.a. The "Web-style" folders view with left-pane details and media previews was default, and until Windows Vista, Windows 2000 was the only Windows release with an interactive media player as a default previewer. Default tooltips displayed file title, author, subject, and comments, readable from NTFS streams or OLE structured storage, and all Microsoft Office documents since Office 4.0 displayed this metadata. File shortcuts could store comments displayed as tooltips. The shell introduced extensibility via metadata, icon overlay, and column handlers. The right pane of Explorer could be customized, with system folders showing warnings by default and additional panes defined via DIV elements in folder templates. A DHTML-based search pane was integrated into Explorer, and the Indexing Service was built into the OS, enabling file searches through its database. Windows 2000 also introduced disk quotas, file-system-level encryption, sparse files, and reparse points, with sparse files enabling efficient storage of large data sets with zero-filled areas and reparse points allowing transparent file system functionality changes.

A warning is provided to users that modifying system folder contents could harm their computer. In Windows 2000, additional Explorer panes can be defined using DIV elements in folder template files, a level of customizability not available in Windows 98 or the Desktop Update. The new DHTML-based search pane is integrated into Windows 2000 Explorer, unlike the separate search dialog in earlier versions, and works with the integrated Indexing Service to search files indexed by its database. Microsoft released version 3.0 of NTFS as part of Windows 2000 (sometimes incorrectly called "NTFS 5"), introducing disk quotas (via QuotaAdvisor), file-system-level encryption, sparse files, and reparse points. Sparse files enable efficient storage of large data sets with many zero-filled areas, while reparse points allow the object manager to reset file namespace lookups and enable transparent functionality changes, used for volume mount points, junctions, Hierarchical Storage Management, Native Structured Storage, and Single Instance Storage. Volume mount points and directory junctions allow transparent file references between locations. Windows 2000 introduced Distributed Link Tracking to ensure file shortcuts remain functional if the target is moved or renamed; the target's unique identifier is stored in the shortcut on NTFS 3.0, and the service silently updates the shortcut if the target changes. The Encrypting File System (EFS) provides strong file system-level encryption, allowing transparent encryption of any folder or drive on an NTFS volume. EFS uses a bulk symmetric key (File Encryption Key or FEK) for fast encryption and decryption of large data, which is then encrypted with the user's public key and stored in the file header. Decryption uses the user's private key to retrieve the FEK, which is then used to decrypt the file. EFS includes recovery agents—users authorized by a public key recovery certificate—to decrypt files; by default, local administrators are recovery agents, configurable via Group Policy. Windows 2000 introduced the Logical Disk Manager and diskpart command-line tool for dynamic storage, supporting simple, spanned, and striped volumes in all editions. Windows 2000 Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server also support mirrored volumes and striped volumes with parity. Windows 2000 brought accessibility features from the Windows 9x line to the NT line, including support for visual and auditory impairments, and added new accessibility features. It introduced the Multilingual User Interface (MUI), supporting Arabic, Armenian, Baltic, Central European, Cyrillic, Georgian, Greek, Hebrew, Indic, Japanese, Korean, simplified Chinese, Thai, traditional Chinese, Turkic, and Vietnamese, along with many locales. English versions support right-to-left and CJKV languages, but require installation of related files in Control Panel. Windows 2000 includes DirectX 7.0 and supports up to DirectX 9.0c (Shader Model 3.0), which shipped with Windows XP Service Pack 2; Microsoft released quarterly updates to DirectX 9.0c through February 2010, after which support ended in June 2010, with bug fixes and libraries like D3DX, XAudio 2, XInput, and Managed DirectX. Most DirectX 9.0c games run on Windows 2000. It includes the same games as Windows NT 4.0: FreeCell, Minesweeper, Pinball, and Solitaire. Windows 2000 introduced the Microsoft Management Console (MMC), used to create, save, and open administrative tools; each is a console containing one or more snap-ins, which can be standalone or extensions. Consoles can be created in author mode (allowing snap-in addition, window creation, and saving) or user mode (with restricted access, allowing viewing but not adding snap-ins or multiple windows). The main tools are in the Computer Management console (in Administrative Tools), including Event Viewer, system information, backup utility, Task Scheduler, shared folder management, COM+ configuration, Group Policy, user and group management, device manager, Disk Management, Removable Storage, disk defragmenter, performance diagnostic console, service configuration, and CHKDSK with performance improvements. Two registry editors are included: REGEDIT.EXE, ported from Windows 98 and lacking registry permission editing, and REGEDT32.EXE, which supports permission editing via an older MDI interface and displays keys and values in separate windows. Windows XP later merged both into a single utility. The System File Checker (SFC) is a command-line tool that verifies system file integrity and signs, and can repair files in the Dllcache folder. The Recovery Console runs outside the installed Windows to perform maintenance tasks when booting fails, including commands like fixmbr; it can check, repair drives, restore boot information, replace corrupted files from the CD, or enable/disable services/drivers. It can be accessed via bootable media or other methods. Windows 2000 introduced Windows Script Host 2.0 with an expanded object model and support for logon and logoff scripts. The Windows 2000 Server family includes Windows 2000 Server, Advanced Server, Small Business Server, and Datacenter Server. All server editions include core services and features. Server editions add Microsoft Distributed File System (DFS), Active Directory support, and fault-tolerant storage. DFS groups network shares under a single DFS root, which can only exist on a server version and only one per server. DFS can be implemented as a standalone root (local only, no Active Directory) or domain-based root (within Active Directory, with fault tolerance via replication through the Microsoft File Replication Service). Active Directory replaces Windows NT's domain model with a hierarchical structure, enabling centralized user and computer policy management, automatic program deployment, and scalable user account management; it supports domains from a few hundred to millions of objects, linking domains into trees and forests. Active Directory services can be installed on Server Standard, Advanced, or Datacenter editions but not on Windows 2000 Professional, though Professional is the first client OS to use its features. Active Directory requires a DNS server supporting SRV resource records or upgraded DNS infrastructure, and at least one domain controller to hold the database and provide directory services. Server editions support mirrored volumes and RAID-5 volumes in addition to simple, spanned, and striped volumes. Windows 2000 can be deployed via traditional media (CD) or shared folders, with attended or unattended installations. Unattended installations use an answer file or INI script with pre-filled options, passed to Winnt.exe or Winnt32.exe. Deployment methods include bootable CD, Microsoft Systems Management Server (SMS), System Preparation Tool (Sysprep), Winnt32.exe with /syspart, or Remote Installation Services (RIS). Sysprep allows duplication of a disk image from a reference computer to multiple target servers, with the same HALs, ACPI support, and mass storage devices (though Windows 2000 auto-detects plug and play devices); the Winnt.exe command must include /unattend and /s switches. Sysprep enables rapid deployment to sites with standard hardware. SMS upgrades multiple computers running Windows NT 3.51, NT 4.0, 98, or 95 OSR2.x with the SMS client agent, enabling wide-area, centralized upgrades. RIS automatically installs Windows 2000 Professional over a network from a central server, without requiring hardware-specific images; security settings are configured post-installation via a unique SID generated for each machine. RIS requires client computers to boot over the network via a PXE-enabled NIC or supported network card, and the server must be Windows 2000 Server with access to DNS, DHCP, and Active Directory services. Microsoft released editions of Windows 2000 for different markets: Professional, Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server. Windows 2000 Professional is the client version for businesses and power users, offering greater security and stability than prior desktop versions, supporting up to two processors and 4 GB of RAM, with minimum system requirements of a Pentium processor (133 MHz or higher), 32 MB RAM, 650 MB hard drive space, and a CD-ROM drive (recommended: Pentium II, 128 MB RAM, 2 GB hard drive, CD-ROM). It can be installed on 4th-generation x86 CPUs like the 80486. Windows 2000 Embedded and Windows 2000 Professional Embedded/Windows 2000 Professional for Embedded Systems are embedded versions designed for ATMs, vending machines, and similar devices; Windows 2000 Embedded was canceled in favor of Windows XP Embedded, but binary-identical FES versions were released for embedded licensing. Windows 2000 Server shares the same user interface as Professional but includes server components for infrastructure and application roles. A major new component is Active Directory, an enterprise directory service based on LDAP. Microsoft also integrated Kerberos authentication, replacing NTLM, enabling transitive trust between domains in a forest. Windows 2000 Server includes a Domain Name Server for dynamic IP address registration. It supports up to four processors and 4 GB of RAM, with a minimum requirement of 12 MHz.

Windows 2000 Embedded was cancelled during development in favor of Windows XP Embedded, although binary-identical FES versions were released and function exactly like their retail counterparts, but are licensed for embedded use. Windows 2000 Server shares the same user interface as Windows 2000 Professional and includes additional components for server roles and infrastructure and application software, with Active Directory—an enterprise-wide directory service based on LDAP—being a major new feature. Microsoft also integrated Kerberos network authentication, replacing the previously criticized NTLM system, enabling a purely transitive-trust relationship between domains in a forest, which consists of one or more domains sharing a common schema, configuration, and global catalog with two-way transitive trusts. Windows 2000 Server includes a Domain Name Server for dynamic IP address registration, supports up to 4 processors and 4 GB of RAM, with a minimum requirement of 128 MB of RAM and 1 GB of hard disk space, though requirements may increase based on installed components. Windows 2000 Server Embedded and Windows 2000 Server for Embedded Systems are binary-identical versions targeted at the embedded market, functioning identically to the retail version but licensed for embedded use. Windows 2000 Advanced Server is designed for medium-to-large businesses, supporting up to 8 CPUs, up to 8 GB of RAM on PAE systems, 8-way SMP, TCP/IP load balancing, and enhanced two-node clustering built on Microsoft Cluster Server. System requirements are similar to Windows 2000 Server, though higher for larger infrastructures. Windows 2000 Datacenter Server is designed for large businesses handling large volumes of sensitive data, supporting clustering, failover, and load balancing; it has minimum requirements similar to Advanced Server but is built for advanced, fault-tolerant, and scalable hardware, such as up to 32 CPUs and 32 GB of RAM, with rigorous testing, hardware partitioning, and change control. It was released to manufacturing on August 11, 2000, and launched on September 26, 2000, based on Windows 2000 with Service Pack 1 and was not available at retail. Windows 2000 received four full service packs and one rollup update package after SP4, the last service pack; Microsoft cancelled a planned fifth service pack and instead released Update Rollup 1 for SP4, which includes security-related hotfixes and some significant issues but excludes non-security hotfixes and undergoes less regression testing than a full service pack. Microsoft stated this update better meets customer needs, helps secure systems, reduces support costs, and supports existing hardware. Several components of Windows 2000 can be upgraded to later versions, and major Microsoft applications are available. During the Windows 2000 era, attacks increasingly came from remote Internet sources, with many malicious programs exploiting IIS services, particularly buffer overflow vulnerabilities—configuration-specific rather than OS-specific—and a common criticism is that default installations include numerous security issues, such as unnecessary enabled services and no active local security policy. According to the SANS Institute, remotely exploitable buffer overflow vulnerabilities are the most common flaws, and vulnerable encryption techniques are also criticized. Code Red and Code Red II worms exploited vulnerabilities in the Windows Indexing Service of IIS, and in August 2003, Sobig and Blaster infected over half a million Windows computers. The 2005 Zotob worm compromised Windows 2000 systems at ABC, CNN, the New York Times Company, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. On September 8, 2009, Microsoft skipped patching two of five flaws in a monthly update, citing that fixing one critical vulnerability was "infeasible" due to the lack of TCP/IP protection architecture in Windows 2000 SP4, which would require re-architecting the OS and risking application compatibility; no patches were released for newer Windows XP versions either, and Microsoft recommended enabling Windows Firewall. Windows 2000 and its Server edition were superseded by Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP Professional, respectively. The Windows 2000 family moved from mainstream support to extended support on June 30, 2005, during which Microsoft provided only critical security updates monthly and paid per-incident support, with no new service packs or non-security updates. Extended support ended on July 13, 2010, after which no new security updates or hotfixes were provided. Updated versions of components like Windows Media Player 11 and Internet Explorer 7 were not released for Windows 2000, as Microsoft noted that security work in IE7 relies on XP SP2 functionality not feasible to port back. Users of Windows 2000 could purchase upgrade licenses for Windows Vista Business or Windows Server 2008, but neither supports direct upgrade from Windows 2000; a clean install or a two-step upgrade via XP/2003 is required, and no upgrade path exists to Windows 7. Despite being the last NT-based Windows version without product activation, Microsoft introduced Windows Genuine Advantage for certain downloads and non-critical updates. Windows 2000 reached end-of-life on July 13, 2010, alongside Windows XP SP2, and will not receive new security updates or hotfixes after that date. In Japan, over 130,000 servers and 500,000 PCs in local governments were affected, with many citing lack of funds to replace systems. As of 2011, Windows Update still supported Windows 2000 updates available on July 2010 Patch Tuesday, if older optional features are enabled later; Internet Explorer 6 under Windows 2000 did not receive security patches after its end of support, unlike IE6 on Windows XP. The Windows Malicious Software Removal Tool, available monthly for XP and later, can still be manually downloaded for Windows 2000. In 2020, Microsoft disabled Windows Update for SHA-1 endpoints for older versions, and since Windows 2000 lacked a SHA-2 update, Windows Update services were discontinued as of late July 2020. As of March 2024, many old Windows 2000 updates remain available on the Microsoft Update Catalog, and a third-party tool named Legacy Update allows installation from the catalog. An independent project named Windows Update Restored, available since 2022, aims to restore Windows Update websites for older versions, including Windows 2000. In October 2002, Microsoft commissioned IDC to compare the total cost of ownership (TCO) of enterprise applications on Windows 2000 versus Linux over five years for an average organization of 100 employees. IDC found Windows 2000 had a better TCO in file, print, network infrastructure, and security infrastructure, but Linux had a better TCO for web serving. The greatest cost was staffing and downtime, with Linux servers showing less unplanned downtime than Windows 2000 servers, running less workload per server, and no businesses using 4-way SMP Linux systems. The report emphasized that TCO is only one factor in choosing an IT platform and noted that improved management and server software could alter the findings.

The Winnipeg Falcons were a senior men's amateur ice hockey team based in Winnipeg, Manitoba. The team won the 1920 Allan Cup as part of the Manitoba Hockey League, where they defeated the Selkirk Fishermen 5–3 to claim the championship, and this victory earned them the right to represent Canada at the 1920 Summer Olympics in Antwerp, Belgium. There, the Falcons won Canada's first Olympic gold medal in ice hockey by outscoring their opponents 29–1 over three games. The team was founded in 1911, primarily composed of Icelandic Canadian players who faced ethnic prejudice and were excluded from other Winnipeg teams; their roots trace back to the Icelandic Athletic Club formed in 1898, which merged in 1908 into a single team. In their first season, 1911–1912, they finished last in their league, but after Konnie Johannesson and Frank Fredrickson joined in 1912, they became league champions. During the First World War, seven of the eight players enlisted and went overseas; two, Frank Thorsteinson and George Cumbers, died in the war, and the remaining five returned in 1919 to reassemble the team. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association (CAHA) selected the Falcons as the Allan Cup champions to represent Canada at the Olympics instead of forming a national all-star team. W. A. Hewitt, who oversaw finances and reported on the Games for Canadian newspapers, served as a father and mother figure to the team and sailed with them aboard the SS Melita from Saint John to Liverpool and then to Antwerp. Upon returning home via the SS Grampian from Le Havre to Quebec City, the Falcons were celebrated as conquering heroes, with each player receiving a gold watch from the City of Winnipeg and a private dinner held in honor of Hewitt and his wife, who were presented with a silver cup inscribed with the number 13—representing the number of people who traveled to the Olympics and the team's lucky number. The Falcons were inducted into the Manitoba Hockey Hall of Fame in the team category, and their legacy is honored in the Hockey Hall of Fame, Manitoba Sports Hall of Fame and Museum, and in a 2014 Heritage Minute segment narrated by George Stroumboulopoulos and featuring Jared Keeso. In 2004, Hockey Canada used a replica yellow and black jersey of the Falcons as alternate uniforms during the World Cup of Hockey against Team USA, and later that year, the national junior team wore replicas of the Falcons' gold and black uniforms in a pre-tournament game in Winnipeg. On July 31, 2019, Parks Canada designated the Falcons' 1920 Olympic victory as a "National Historical Event." The Icelandic national hockey team features the Icelandic Falcon and the Canadian maple leaf on their jerseys in honor of the Falcons. Five other players—Harvey Benson, Ed Stephenson, Connie Neil, Babs Dunlop, and Sam Laxdal—contributed to the 1919–20 season but were not part of the Olympic roster. The first member to pass away was Chris Fridfinnson, who died in 1938 at age 40; the last surviving member was Mike Goodman, who died in 1991 at age 93.

The Wolf Prize in Mathematics is awarded nearly every year by the Wolf Foundation in Israel and is one of six Wolf Prizes established by the Foundation, which have been awarded since 1978; the other prizes are in Agriculture, Chemistry, Medicine, Physics, and Arts. The prize includes a monetary award of $100,000. A reputation survey conducted in 2013 and 2014 ranked the Wolf Prize in Mathematics as the third most prestigious international academic award in mathematics, following the Abel Prize and the Fields Medal. Woodlands House School is located in Srinagar, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, India, and serves students from the pre-nursery stage up to 12th grade. The school has a separate boys' wing and a girls' wing. It was founded in 1966 by Mrs. Rup SP Singh, who served as both founder and principal, and is situated under the foothills of the Takht-e-Sulaiman/Shankaracharya Temple. Initially starting with a small number of students, the school gained popularity due to Mrs. Singh's leadership, attracting families from Jammu and Kashmir and especially from Srinagar. Her efforts were acknowledged by then Chief Minister Bakshi Gulam Mohammad and later by Sheikh Mohammed Abdullah, who supported her in establishing a junior wing at Shivpora, Srinagar, which eventually became the girls' wing. The school addressed a critical gap in the region by offering English-medium education, and it has since developed in academic, co-curricular, and infrastructural areas. Mrs. Singh emphasized the importance of social and moral values in education. She retired in 1995, after which her son, Mr. Riki Singh, took over as chairman and principal. The boys' wing is located at Gupkar Road, Sonwar Bagh, Srinagar, while the girls' wing is located at Shivpora, Srinagar.
