Worcester Reed Warner (May 16, 1846 – June 25, 1929) was an American mechanical engineer, entrepreneur, manager, astronomer, and philanthropist. He co-founded the Warner & Swasey Company with Ambrose Swasey. The Moon's crater Warner is named after him. Born and raised on a farm near Cummington, Massachusetts, Warner met Swasey while both were apprentices at the Exeter Machine Works. In 1870, they both joined Pratt & Whitney in Hartford, Connecticut. In 1880, Warner and Swasey co-founded a business to manufacture sewing machines and lathes, but soon shifted to telescope manufacturing due to Warner’s interest in astronomy. The firm, initially located in Chicago, moved to Cleveland. In 1880, Beloit College purchased one of its telescopes, helping establish the company’s reputation in the telescope industry. Warner & Swasey designed and built the framework and mounting for the 36-inch refracting telescope installed at Lick Observatory in 1888, which was the world’s largest refractor at the time. The company later built telescopes used in Canada and Argentina. Warner was a charter member of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers and served as its 16th president from 1897 to 1898; Ambrose Swasey later became the 23rd president. In 1900, the firm was incorporated as the Warner & Swasey Company. Warner served as president and chairman of the board until his retirement in 1911. Both Warner and Swasey became trustees of the Case School of Applied Science and donated an entire observatory, which became the Warner and Swasey Observatory, dedicated in 1920. The Worcester Reed Warner Laboratory, located in the Warner Building at Case Western Reserve University, is named after Warner and was partly funded by him. In 1911, Warner and his family moved to Wilholm in the Wilson Park neighborhood of Tarrytown, New York, where he built a celestial observatory for stargazing sessions, inviting guests such as John D. Rockefeller and President Herbert Hoover. The Warner Library in Tarrytown, built and gifted by Warner and his wife Cornelia in 1929, is constructed of Vermont limestone and designed by Walter Dabney Blair. It cost $250,000 (approximately $4,700,000 in 2025 dollars) to build and was further endowed with $50,000 (about $950,000 in 2025 dollars) for books. Warner married Cornelia Blakemore of Philadelphia in 1890; they had three children, two of whom—Worcester Reed Warner Jr. and Marion Holbrook Warner—died at a young age. He was survived by daughter Helen Blakemore Warner (1894–1971), who used her inheritance to continue his philanthropy. She collaborated with John D. Rockefeller Jr. in saving and restoring the Philipsburg Manor House in Sleepy Hollow and established the Helen B. Warner Prize for Astronomy, awarded annually by the American Astronomical Society. In memory of her father’s birthplace, Cummington, Massachusetts, she founded the Cummington Museum, now known as the Kingman Tavern Historical Museum. She also supported the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Phelps Hospital. Warner died on a trip in Eisenach, Saxe-Weimar, Germany, four months after the dedication of the Warner Library, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery. The Worcester Reed Warner Medal, established by his bequest in 1930, is awarded by the ASME for "outstanding contribution to the permanent literature of engineering."

The "Word of the Year" (sometimes capitalized as "Word(s) of the Year" and abbreviated as "WOTY" or "WotY") refers to various annual assessments identifying the most significant word(s) or expression(s) in the public sphere during a specific year. The German tradition of "Wort des Jahres" began in 1971 and has been selected annually by the Society of the German Language, with an additional "Unwort des Jahres" (Most Unpleasant Word of the Year) introduced in 1991 to highlight socially inappropriate terms, such as "Überfremdung." Since 1999, Austria has included its own "Word of the Year," organized by the Society for Austrian German (GSÖD), reflecting the pluricentric nature of German; notable selections include the 52-letter word "Bundespräsidentenstichwahlwiederholungsverschiebung" in 2016 and "Elk Emil" in 2025. Similar word-of-the-year selections have occurred in Liechtenstein since 2002, Switzerland since 2003, and Slovenia since 2016, with the Slovenian Sign Language gesture of the year also announced annually in January. In addition, various German dialects have their own Wort des Jahres selections, including Plattdeutsches Wort des Jahres, Wort des Jahres (Sachsen), and Wort des Jahres (Südtirol). The American Dialect Society's Word of the Year, the oldest English-language version, is announced after the end of the calendar year by a vote of independent linguists and is not tied to commercial interests; since 1990, it has designated one or more words or terms, and also selects words in categories such as "Most Outrageous," "Most Creative," and "Most Likely to Succeed." The Australian National Dictionary Centre has announced a Word of the Year since 2006, chosen by editorial staff based on prominence in the Australian social and cultural landscape, though it is not always an Australian word. The Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, published annually since 2015 by Cambridge University Press & Assessment, is selected based on user data, zeitgeist, and language trends; in 2024, "manifest" was chosen, traditionally meaning "obvious" or "to show clearly," but used in 2024 as a verb meaning "to imagine achieving something you want, in the belief doing so will make it more likely to happen," especially by celebrities on social media. Collins English Dictionary has announced a Word of the Year since 2013, with a shortlist of ten words typically released at the end of the year, though only four were announced in 2014; the selection is made by lexicographers, editorial, marketing, and publicity staff in Glasgow and London, with public input previously allowed; words are not required to be new, and usage statistics and a large corpus are used to support selections, with international relevance often considered, such as "fake news" in 2017. Dictionary.com began selecting a Word of the Year in 2010 with "change" and has done so annually in December, based on search trends and news events. Since 2021, The Economist has published a Word of the Year. The Macquarie Dictionary, which covers Australian English, selects a Word of the Year each year by reviewing new words and definitions added to its online dictionary; a public vote in November determines the People's Choice winner, while the Word of the Year Committee—comprising the Editorial Team, David Astle, and language specialist Tiger Webb—selects the most influential word. Merriam-Webster has published a ten-word list annually since 2003, initially based on website page hits and searches, and since 2006 by an online poll and visitor suggestions. Oxford University Press announces both an Oxford Dictionaries UK Word of the Year and a US Word of the Year (which may be the same), selected by editorial staff and lexicographers, with no guarantee of inclusion in any Oxford dictionary. Since 2004, lexicographer Grant Barrett has published an unranked list of words of the year, usually in The New York Times, and Susie Dent, an English lexicographer working for Oxford University Press, has published a column "A Word a Year" since 2004, selecting one word from each of the past 101 years to reflect contemporary preoccupations; her list is subjective and often mistakenly referred to as the "Oxford Dictionary's Word of the Year." Japan has held an annual "New Word/Trendy Phrase Award" since 1984, sponsored by Jiyu Kokuminsha (and U-CAN since 2004), and has selected a "Kanji of the Year" since 1995, with both reflecting current events and attitudes; for example, in 2011, following the Fukushima disaster, the phrase "the possibility of recriticality is not zero" became the top phrase, and the kanji for "bond" (representing family or friendship) was chosen as the kanji of the year. Word of the Year polls have also been conducted in Denmark (2006–2012 and since 2009 with Sproglaboratoriet and Dansk Sprognævn), Norway (since 2012), Portugal (since 2009), Russia (since 2007), and the Netherlands (since 2007), with Spain selecting a word since 2013 and Ukraine since 2013.

World of Warcraft Classic is a 2019 massively multiplayer online role-playing game developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment, released globally on August 26, 2019. It runs alongside the main game and recreates World of Warcraft in its vanilla state, as it existed before the launch of the first expansion, The Burning Crusade, specifically at patch 1.12.1, around September 2006. The maximum character level is set to 60, all expansion content is absent, and nearly all original gameplay mechanics are preserved. Modern interface and functional enhancements from later expansions have been integrated, along with bug and exploit fixes from the original release. The game emphasizes social interaction, a feature many players felt was missing in more recent versions. Players can choose from the original eight races—humans, dwarves, gnomes, night elves (Alliance) and orcs, trolls, tauren, Forsaken (Horde)—and the original nine classes: druid, hunter, mage, paladin, priest, rogue, shaman, warlock, and warrior. Only Alliance players can become paladins, and only Horde players can become shamans; no expansion-added races or classes are available. The game world is restored to its pre-Cataclysm state, and expansion areas like Outland are inaccessible. Content was released in six phases to emulate the original patch cycle, with no changes to core game mechanics, which remain set to the 1.12.1 version. The demand for Classic and legacy realms grew significantly after Cataclysm made original content permanently inaccessible. Blizzard previously refused to create such servers, citing high development and support costs, and stated in 2008 that maintaining classic realms was not justified. Private servers, such as Nostalrius, emerged to replicate older versions, with Nostalrius reaching 800,000 registered accounts and 150,000 active players before shutting down in April 2016 due to a cease and desist letter. A Change.org petition with over 200,000 signatures was created and delivered to Blizzard leadership, prompting internal discussions. Blizzard acknowledged the community's interest and stated they had been considering legacy servers for years, though technical challenges delayed implementation. The Nostalrius team shared their source code with Valkyrie-WoW, and the servers returned as the Elysium Project on December 17, 2016. At BlizzCon 2017, J. Allen Brack announced Classic on stage, describing it as a faithful recreation of the original game on modern infrastructure. The game was developed by porting original 1.12.1 data and assets to modern servers and clients, allowing shared source code and access to performance and security improvements. In March 2020, Blizzard surveyed Classic players about a Burning Crusade version, which was confirmed in February 2021 and launched on June 1, 2021. In April 2022, Blizzard announced Wrath of the Lich King Classic, released on September 26, 2022. The developers aimed for minimal changes to preserve the original game feel, contrasting with Classic’s approach of preserving all original interactions. Both official and private servers traditionally used the end-patch state for each expansion. In Wrath of the Lich King Classic, the Dungeon Finder was excluded in favor of an improved bulletin board to promote social interaction. A limited-time 50% experience buff, Joyous Journeys, was introduced during the pre-patch and returned before each new content phase. Previously, players had to reach level 55 to unlock Death Knight, but this was changed to allow immediate creation, later reverted to prevent bot abuse. In the first phase, Naxxramas mob health and damage were increased due to original undertuning. In the second phase, Phase 1 bosses dropped 25-man difficulty items, and 10-man items were scattered in Heroic Dungeons via a new "Titan Rune Dungeon" difficulty, known as "Heroic+". All Ulduar bosses were released in their pre-nerf state, and gear on all difficulties had higher stats and item levels. Class balancing changes were introduced to improve performance and eliminate detrimental play styles. Cosmetic changes included full character recustomization, which was made available to all players in Classic, including gender (now called Body Type). Race and Faction Change features, introduced in the original Wrath of the Lich King, were added in Phase 2. The WoW Token, introduced during Warlords of Draenor, became available in Wrath of the Lich King Classic on May 23, 2023. Phase 3 launched on June 20, 2023, adding Argent Tournament, daily quests, Trial of the Champion, Trial of the Crusader and Grand Crusader raids, Onyxia's Lair, and Defense Protocol: Beta, a new dungeon difficulty. "Heroic" difficulty for raids was introduced immediately and could be toggled per boss, unlike the original 2008 release. Phase 4, released on October 10, 2023, added Icecrown Citadel, three Frozen Halls dungeons, Defense Protocol: Gamma, and introduced Random Dungeon Finder and Pets and Collections systems. Phase 5, released on January 11, 2024, added the Ruby Sanctum raid. At BlizzCon 2023, Blizzard announced that Wrath of the Lich King Classic would continue into Cataclysm content in the first half of 2024, with gameplay changes including continued use of the Titan Rune Dungeon system, faster leveling, and a faster content release. The 4.0 Cataclysm pre-patch launched on April 30, 2024, adding Worgen and Goblin races, new race/class combinations, and revamped 0-60 zones and quests. The expansion officially launched on May 20, 2024, unlocking level 80-85 zones and dungeons. The Rise of the Zandalari patch, released on July 30, 2024, introduced reimagined Zul'Gurub and Zul'Aman as 5-player dungeons for max-level characters. Content in the Rage of the Firelands patch became available on October 29, 2024, including the Firelands raid and "Elemental Rune Protocol: Inferno" dungeons, which allowed players to earn tokens for tier 11 raid items; the raid itself opened on November 6, 2024. The Hour of Twilight patch, released on February 18, 2025, added Dragon Soul, Hour of Twilight Dungeons, and "Elemental Rune Protocol: Twilight" difficulty, excluding Looking For Raid (LFR), which was instead accessible through Protocol: Twilight dungeons. In November 2024, during a 30th Anniversary livestream, Blizzard announced that Mists of Pandaria would launch in summer 2025. In April 2025, users began beta testing Mists of Pandaria Classic. The expansion launched on July 21, 2025, including original 85-90 quests, zones, dungeons, and raids, plus "Celestial Dungeons," modeled after the Elemental and Titan Rune dungeon systems from earlier expansions. Celestial Dungeons replaced the Raid Finder mode, which was not implemented. The first raid tier featured a staggered rollout of the three raid instances, with each raid's loot table integrated into the Celestial Dungeon system. In September 2025, Blizzard opened free character transfers to consolidate players onto "Mega Realms" in each region, citing benefits observed from prior transfers in Season of Discovery and Classic Era realms.

Mists of Pandaria Classic launched on July 21, 2025, offering the original 85-90 quests, zones, dungeons, and raids, along with new "Celestial Dungeons" modeled after the "Elemental Rune" and "Titan Rune" dungeon modes from Cataclysm Classic and Wrath of the Lich King Classic. These Celestial Dungeons were introduced as a replacement for the Raid Finder difficult mode, since Blizzard chose not to include Raid Finder in Mists of Pandaria Classic. The first raid tier featured a staggered rollout of the three raid instances, with each raid's loot table later integrated into the Celestial Dungeon system. In September 2025, Blizzard opened free character transfers to consolidate players onto "Mega Realms" in each region, based on observed benefits from prior transfers during Season of Discovery and Classic Era realms. On December 9, 2025, Phase 3 "The Thunder King" launched, adding the Isle of Thunder and Isle of Giants zones, the Throne of Thunder raid, and new story content centered on the Shado-Pan Assault faction and the continuation of the legendary questline; the Throne of Thunder raid opened two days later on December 11, 2025, marking the second-to-last raid in the Mists of Pandaria Expansion. During Warcraft Direct 2024, Blizzard announced a re-release of the 2004 version of World of Warcraft, launched on November 21, 2024, as the "20th Anniversary Edition," which retains most features from the 2019 Classic release and includes quality-of-life updates such as the Chronoboon Displacer, updated Honor System, removal of Buff and Debuff Limits, a native LFG tool, and a modern guild panel UI. Blizzard stated this edition would continue into The Burning Crusade starting in late 2025 or early 2026. On February 5, 2026, the 20th Anniversary Edition servers will transition into The Burning Crusade Classic. Hardcore-only servers were released with the 20th Anniversary Edition, featuring permadeath and an optional "Self-Found Mode," and Blizzard confirmed these servers will not progress to The Burning Crusade; characters can transfer to Normal realms to continue playing in The Burning Crusade Classic. Before Burning Crusade Classic launched, Blizzard created separate copies of each server known as Classic Era servers, while original realms automatically progressed with Burning Crusade content. Players could pay to create copies of their existing characters on Classic Era servers, which remained in a 1.12.1 state with all content phases unlocked, or freely create new characters to replay content in that state. Reinvented versions of World of Warcraft Classic have launched as separate servers to provide players with a fresh experience. Blizzard began seasonal Classic servers in November 2021 with Season of Mastery, which introduced more challenging mechanics and an "ironman" mode allowing players to progress without letting their characters die; Season of Mastery concluded on February 14, 2023. On August 24, 2023, official Hardcore Classic servers launched, featuring permadeath and the "Mak'gora" duel-to-death mode, inspired by community-created permadeath experiences using addons with restrictions like auction house access or trading; characters that die on Hardcore servers cannot log back in or resurrect but can transfer to Classic Era realms. On February 29, 2024, Self-Found Mode was added to Hardcore servers, preventing auction house use and mail sending/receiving, available only for new characters during creation and not reversible once disabled. On November 30, 2023, Season of Discovery launched as a seasonal server with new content in the base "Vanilla" world, including runes for class abilities and updated professions, featuring gated leveling (level 25 in Phase 1, incrementally increasing) and forced faction balance that locked players from creating a new character of the dominant faction. Each phase included reworked PvE and PvP content, such as a 10-player Blackfathom Deeps raid and a world PvP event in Ashenvale, and Blizzard tested anti-RMT measures like restricting new accounts from trading, sending mail, or using the auction house for 30 days. Phase 2 raised the level cap to 40, converted Gnomeregan into a 10-player raid, added a PvP event in Stranglethorn Vale called The Blood Moon, and introduced restrictions on GDKP runs. Phase 3 raised the level cap to 50, converted the Temple of Atal'Hakkar ("Sunken Temple") into a 20-player raid, and introduced persistent world events called Nightmare Incursions for reputation and rewards. Phase 4 increased the level cap to 60, added a new 5-player dungeon, Demon Fall Canyon, and unlocked a reworked Molten Core (20-player) and a reworked 40-man Onyxia's Lair. Phase 5 introduced updated versions of Zul'Gurub and Blackwing Lair raids, the new raid Crystal Vale, and a new boss in Demon Fall Canyon. Phase 6 added the "48-Hour War" event leading to the opening of the Ruins of Ahn'Qiraj and Temple of Ahn'Qiraj raids, with Ruins retuned for 10+ players and Temple changed to 20+ players, and the emerald dragons of Emeriss, Ysondre, Lethon, and Taerar moved into a special "Nightmare Grove" raid. Phase 7 introduced Naxxramas and the Scourge Invasion event, along with the Karazhan Crypts, a new 5-player dungeon in Deadwind Pass with new quests and items, originally planned as the final full patch but expanded due to community feedback. Phase 8 introduced the first all-new raid, Scarlet Enclave, added New Avalon—the first new zone in the Classic world—with new quests and supporting content, and marked the final content addition to Season of Discovery. PC Gamer scored Classic 80 out of 100, calling it a window into a time when online interactions felt novel and exciting, while Polygon praised its difficulty and design for fostering social connections, calling it a "faithful snapshot of a moment in time." Since launch, Blizzard has faced criticism for using layering technology to split communities and exploit the in-game economy, though as of October 10, 2019, most realms operate on a single layer, with only high-population servers still using multiple layers. The game won "PC Game of the Year" at the 2019 Golden Joystick Awards and was nominated for "Game, Classic Revival" at the NAVGTR Awards.

Wynne Neilly, born in 1990, is a Canadian artist and photographer based in Toronto who specializes in photographing queer and transgender individuals. He completed the Image Arts program at Ryerson University, graduating in 2012. Neilly began creating portraiture in the early 2010s and is currently based in Toronto. He identifies as queer and transmasculine, and in 2018, he stated that his maleness is "really only based on my physical appearance," emphasizing that "there is a lot more to me and my gender identity." His artistic focus is on exploring gender and sexuality, particularly "the queer and trans body." In 2014, at the age of 24, a photograph he took was featured on the cover of Original Plumbing, part of a series titled Female to "Male" that centers on gender transitioning and Neilly's own transition. In 2015, he won the "Flash Forward" photography competition hosted by the Magenta Foundation. In 2021, Elliot Page requested that Neilly photograph him for the cover of Time following Page's transition, seeking a transgender photographer. Neilly initially doubted the email, believing the pandemic had ended his career, but he photographed Page on March 5, 2021, for the March 29 – April 5 issue, making him the first transgender man to appear on the magazine's cover. He later expressed that the experience "really meant the world to me to be able to help [Page] tell his story." Neilly draws inspiration from Catherine Opie, as well as Cassils, Michelle Groskopf, and Robert Mapplethorpe. His work has been exhibited at the International Center of Photography, The Annenberg Space for Photography, Southern Norway Art Museum, and the Ryerson Image Centre.

Zhang Xiang JP (Chinese: 张翔; pinyin: Zhāng Xiáng; born December 1963) is a Chinese-American mechanical engineer who has served as the 16th president and vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong since July 2018. He was the inaugural Ernest S. Kuh Endowed Chaired Professor at the University of California, Berkeley, served as director of the National Science Foundation Nano-scale Science and Engineering Center, directed the materials science division, and held the position of senior faculty scientist at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Zhang earned a Bachelor of Science and a Master of Science from Nanjing University, a Master of Science from the University of Minnesota, and a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of California, Berkeley in 1996. From 1996 to 1999, he was an assistant professor at Pennsylvania State University, and from 1999 to 2004, he held positions as associate professor and then full professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, before joining UC Berkeley. He is an elected member of the United States National Academy of Engineering and Academia Sinica, a foreign member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a Fellow of the American Physical Society, the Optical Society of America (OSA), the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the International Society for Optical Engineering. Zhang has published more than 390 journal papers, with research focusing on materials physics, metamaterials, and nano-photonics. On 15 December 2017, The University of Hong Kong appointed Zhang to the roles of president and vice-chancellor, marking the first time a candidate born and educated to undergraduate degree level in mainland China had been appointed to such a position; he assumed office in July 2018. On 3 July 2019, in response to the Storming of the Legislative Council Complex two days earlier, Zhang stated he was "disheartened by the violence" and that he "would like to condemn such acts"; in response to backlash from approximately 2,000 HKU students, alumni, and staff, he affirmed on 11 July that he opposed violence "by any party, and at any juncture" and agreed to participate in a forum open to students, staff, alumni, and the media. In April 2021, the Hong Kong University Students' Union criticized Zhang, claiming he was promoting national security education as a "political task" and was "destroying the autonomy of institutions." In October 2023, Zhang was accused by whistleblowers of potential misconduct, including the purchase of a HK$2 million (US$255,370) BMW vehicle without going through an open tender.

The Young British Artists, or YBAs—also known as Brit artists or Britart—are a loose collective of visual artists who first exhibited together in London in 1988. Many of the group graduated from the BA Fine Art course at Goldsmiths between 1987 and 1990, with some having trained at the Royal College of Art. The scene originated through artist-led exhibitions held in warehouses and factories, starting with Damien Hirst’s Freeze in 1988, followed by the East Country Yard Show and Modern Medicine in 1990. These exhibitions were notable for their "shock tactics," use of everyday or throwaway materials, wild lifestyles, and an attitude that was both oppositional and entrepreneurial. The group gained significant media attention and dominated British art during the 1990s, with international exhibitions such as Brilliant! and Sensation showcasing their work. Charles Saatchi was a key supporter and collector of many YBAs, though Angus Fairhurst was a notable exception. Leading figures include Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin, with key works such as Hirst’s The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living—a shark preserved in formaldehyde—and Emin’s My Bed, a dishevelled bed surrounded by personal detritus. There is debate over the first use of the term "young British artists": Tate claims it was Michael Corris in a 1992 Artforum footnote, while others argue Saatchi used it in his 1992 exhibition Young British Artists I; the acronym "YBA" was coined in 1994. Most YBAs were born in the mid-1960s. Core group members graduated from Goldsmiths in specific classes: Liam Gillick, Fiona Rae, Steve Park, and Sarah Lucas in 1987; Ian Davenport, Michael Landy, Gary Hume, Anya Gallaccio, Lala Meredith-Vula, Henry Bond, and Angela Bulloch in 1988; Damien Hirst, Angus Fairhurst, Mat Collishaw, Simon Patterson, and Abigail Lane in 1989; Gillian Wearing and Sam Taylor-Wood in 1990; and Jason Martin in 1993. Teaching staff during this period included Jon Thompson, Richard Wentworth, Michael Craig-Martin, Ian Jeffrey, Helen Chadwick, Mark Wallinger, Judith Cowan, and Glen Baxter. Gavin Turk and Mark Francis, who studied at Chelsea School of Art (1986–1989) and the Royal College of Art (1989–1991), were also part of the group and exhibited in the Saatchi Sensation show. Freeze, organized by Hirst during his second year of study, was held in a London Docklands warehouse and lacked major press coverage but inspired the model of artist-as-curator, influencing later independent spaces. A smaller precursor, Progress by Degree, organized by Angus Fairhurst, took place shortly before Freeze. In 1990, Henry Bond and Sarah Lucas staged the East Country Yard Show in a 16,000m² warehouse in London Docklands. Art critic Andrew Graham-Dixon noted the shows' ambition and impact, comparing them favorably to exhibitions by the Liverpool Tate. Established alternative spaces like City Racing and Milch, as well as activity in Hoxton/Shoreditch, provided early exposure. The Serpentine Gallery held a survey of the group in 1991 titled Broken English, and in 1992, Charles Saatchi launched a series of exhibitions featuring Sarah Lucas, Rachel Whiteread, and Damien Hirst. A second wave of YBAs emerged in 1992–1993 through exhibitions such as New Contemporaries, New British Summertime, and Minky Manky, including Douglas Gordon, Christine Borland, Fiona Banner, Tracey Emin, Tacita Dean, Georgina Starr, and Jane and Louise Wilson. The 1995 British Art Show included several YBA artists. The YBAs helped revitalize the contemporary art market, spawning commercial galleries such as Karsten Schubert, Sadie Coles, Victoria Miro, Maureen Paley’s Interim Art, and Jay Jopling’s White Cube. Frieze launched in 1991 and embraced the YBAs, while publications like Art Monthly, Art Review, Modern Painters, and Contemporary Art shifted focus to emerging British artists. Charles Saatchi, a major art collector and co-founder of Saatchi and Saatchi, visited Freeze and was astonished by Hirst’s installation A Thousand Years, which he later bought. Saatchi became the primary collector and sponsor of the YBAs, shifting his focus from American and German art to emerging British artists. His collection was exhibited in a converted paint factory in St John’s Wood, inspiring large-scale concept artworks. His 1992 exhibition featured Hirst’s shark, which became a defining work of British art and a global symbol of Britart. The artists gained intense media coverage due to their prominence in the Turner Prize, which had several nominees and winners from the group, amplified by Channel 4’s sponsorship. The group’s status solidified in 1995 with the exhibition Brilliant! at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. The term "yBa" was used as early as 1994 and later featured in Simon Ford’s 1996 article in Art Monthly. Jay Jopling represented several YBAs, including Jake & Dinos Chapman, Tracey Emin, Marcus Harvey, Damien Hirst, Gary Hume, Marc Quinn, Gavin Turk, and Sam Taylor-Wood, whom he married in 1998. Karsten Schubert was the first major dealer of YBA artists, exhibiting Ian Davenport, Gary Hume, and Michael Landy in November 1988. In 1997, the Royal Academy held Sensation, a show of Saatchi’s private collection that included major YBA works, sparking controversy—especially over Marcus Harvey’s Myra and Chris Ofili’s The Holy Virgin Mary—and leading to three Academicians resigning. In 1997, Gillian Wearing won the Turner Prize; in 1998, Chris Ofili did the same. In 1999, Tracey Emin was nominated, with her exhibit My Bed generating significant media attention and contributing to the rise of the anti-YBA group The Stuckists, co-founded by her ex-boyfriend Billy Childish. In 2003, Jake and Dinos Chapman and Anya Gallaccio were nominated. On 24 May 2004, a fire in a storage warehouse destroyed works from the Saatchi collection, including the Chapman Brothers’ Hell and Tracey Emin’s tent, Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963–1995. In 2008, Angus Fairhurst died by suicide. In the 2011 Birthday Honours List, Sam Taylor-Wood and Gillian Wearing were appointed to the Order of the British Empire by Queen Elizabeth II. Several YBAs have been elected as lifetime members of the Royal Academy of Arts, earning the title "Royal Academician" and the designation "RA." Critics such as Richard Cork, Louisa Buck, Sarah Kent, and Sir Nicholas Serota have supported the artists, with Serota advancing their inclusion in the Tate collection. Maureen Paley stated that the YBA generation was defined by boldness and a belief that "you can get away with anything." Iwona Blazwick, director of the Whitechapel Art Gallery, said in 2009 that the YBA moment was over, but that their influence continued to grow. In 1998, John Windsor noted that YBA work seemed tame compared to the "shock art" of the 1970s, such as Mandy Havers’ Pink Crucifixion. In 1999, The Stuckists were founded with an anti-YBA stance. In 2002, Sir Simon Rattle criticized Britart, leading to accusations of poor understanding of conceptual art. Playwright Tom Stoppard and critics like Brian Sewell, David Lee, and Rolf Harris—whom criticized Tracey Emin’s My Bed as a "con"—were hostile to the movement. James Heartfield argued that the 1990s art boom encouraged sloppiness, with YBAs favoring gestures over patient work and using public outrage, which faded quickly. The group is parodied in a Private Eye cartoon strip and in Jilly Cooper’s Pandora. Female artists were a minority in the male-dominated YBA scene; Sarah Lucas, Jenny Saville, and Rachel Whiteread faced underrepresentation and less media attention compared to male peers like Hirst. Feminist influences in the 1980s shaped female YBA work, with artists subverting feminine stereotypes. Rachel Whiteread’s work, such as Nine Tables, exists in a gender-neutral space while still being viewed as feminine, and Daniel Ogilivie linked this to Judith Butler’s theory that the act of casting creates gender. Jenny Saville, influenced by feminist ideology, discovered the absence of women in art history and began painting female nudes that rejected idealization, showing natural flaws like pubic hair and discolored skin. She stated she aimed not to teach but to prompt discussion about how women have been constructed by patriarchal structures, asserting that beauty is often defined by the male image of the female body.

The document examines how women have been shaped by male perspectives. It questions the concept of beauty, stating that beauty is typically defined by the male ideal of the female body. However, it also asserts that the speaker's view of women is that they are beautiful in their individuality.

Yusef Salaam, born in 1974 in New York City to Sharonne Salaam, is an American politician, motivational speaker, and activist who has served as a member of the New York City Council representing the 9th council district since 2024. A member of the Democratic Party, Salaam was one of the Central Park Five, a group of five Black and Latino teenagers—along with Korey Wise, Kevin Richardson, Antron McCray, and Raymond Santana—who were wrongly convicted in 1990 of assaulting and raping Trisha Meili, a woman jogging in Central Park on April 19, 1989, an incident committed by Matias Reyes. At the time, Salaam was 15 years old. The teenagers initially confessed but later claimed their confessions were obtained through beatings and threats by police, with Salaam stating that officers deprived them of food, drink, or sleep for over a day. His conviction was upheld by the Appellate Division in 1990 and again by the Court of Appeals of the State of New York in 1993. He was released from prison in 1997, and his conviction was vacated in 2002. In 2014, New York City settled a civil rights lawsuit brought by the Central Park Five for $41 million. While incarcerated, Salaam deepened his connection to Islam, stating that his faith helped him endure his sentence and that he found parallels between his experience and the story of Prophet Yusuf (as) in the Quran. He served as imam of a youth facility for five years, as Qadi (religious judge) for about one and a half years, and as Naib (assistant leader) before his release. After being released, Salaam worked as a construction worker in the Mitchell–Lama Housing Program, was later fired after his identity was discovered, and then worked at Weill Cornell Medicine. He has served on the board of the Innocence Project. In 2021, he considered running for the New York State Legislature but declined due to residency requirements. He moved back to New York City from Georgia in 2022. On February 4, 2023, Salaam announced his candidacy for the 9th City Council District, representing Harlem, and was endorsed by Cornel West. He won the Democratic primary on July 5, defeating assemblymembers Inez Dickens and Al Taylor, and was unopposed in the general election, succeeding councilwoman Kristin Richardson Jordan for a term ending January 1, 2026. He was re-elected in November 2025. In January 2024, his car, which had Georgia license plates and dark-tinted windows illegal in New York, was stopped in Harlem by a police officer. When the officer approached, Salaam identified himself as a city council member on city business; he was on a business call with colleagues including City Council member Sandy Nurse, who heard the interaction. The officer, upon learning Salaam’s position, cut off the interaction and walked away, saying, "Take care, sir." Salaam said the police should have given a reason for the stop, though officers are not required to do so; critics claimed he used his position to avoid a ticket. After the second 2024 presidential debate, Salaam confronted former president Donald Trump, who had previously called for Salaam to be executed, but refused to retract those statements. Salaam is a practicing Muslim with ten children, three of whom are stepchildren. In 2016, he received a Lifetime Achievement Award from President Barack Obama, and in 2021, he was awarded the Muhammad Ali Confident Muslim of the Year by the Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research. He is featured in Ken Burns’s documentary The Central Park Five (2012), portrayed as an adult by Chris Chalk and as a child by Ethan Herisse in Ava DuVernay’s television miniseries When They See Us. In 2022, "Gate of the Exonerated" was dedicated at the northern end of Central Park in honor of Salaam and the other members of the Exonerated Five.

Zanele Muholi FRPS (born 1972) is a South African artist and visual activist working in photography, video, and installation. Their work centers on race, gender, and sexuality, documenting and celebrating the lives of South Africa's Black lesbian, gay, transgender, and intersex communities since the early 2000s. Muholi is non-binary and uses they/them pronouns, stating "I'm just human." They identify as a visual activist rather than an artist, dedicated to increasing the visibility of Black LGBTQI people. Muholi researched and documented hate crimes, including "corrective rape," assault, and HIV/AIDS, to bring these realities to public attention. Born and raised in Umlazi, Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, Muholi’s father, Ashwell Tanji Banda Muholi, died shortly after their birth, and their mother, Bester Muholi, was a domestic worker who left her children to work for a white family during apartheid; Muholi was raised by an extended family. They completed an Advanced Photography course at the Market Photo Workshop in Newtown, Johannesburg in 2003 and held their first solo exhibition at the Johannesburg Art Gallery in 2004. In 2009, Muholi earned a Master of Fine Arts degree in Documentary Media from Ryerson University in Toronto, with a thesis mapping the visual history of Black lesbian identity and politics in post-Apartheid South Africa. On 28 October 2013, they were appointed Honorary Professor – video and photography at the University of the Arts Bremen in Germany. Muholi’s photography is compared to W.E.B. DuBois’s subversion of African American representations, as both created archives to dismantle dominant perceptions. Muholi views their work as collaborative, referring to participants as "participants" rather than subjects, allowing them to co-create poses and speak at events, thus empowering the subjects. Their work documents the African queer community as a record for future generations, portraying the LGBTQI community without negativity or focus on violence, aiming to promote unity. Before 1994, Black lesbian voices were largely excluded from the formal queer movement, and Muholi’s efforts combat homophobic violence, especially against Black lesbians, who are often viewed negatively in patriarchal and heteronormative contexts, leading to rejection and violence. In Zukiswa (2010), a Black lesbian woman makes eye contact with the viewer, displaying confidence, self-awareness, and determination, encouraging awareness and acceptance. Muholi began recognizing "gender within gender" in 2003 and included trans people in their community. They worked as a photographer and reporter for Behind the Mask, an online magazine on LGBTI issues in Africa. Muholi gained global attention in 2012 at Documenta in Germany for the Faces and Phases series of portraits of lesbians and transgender participants, which was also exhibited at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. Their first solo exhibition, Visual Sexuality: Only Half the Picture, held at the Johannesburg Art Gallery in 2004, featured photographs of survivors of rape and hate crimes, including an image with a rape and assault case number, with the individuals' gender concealed—only showing above-the-knee and hip shots with hands over the genital region—while maintaining anonymity due to fears of violence and lack of trust in reporting hate crimes. In 2006, Muholi launched the Faces and Phases project, comprising around three hundred portraits of lesbians, beginning with activist and survivor Busi Sigasa, who endured corrective rape and contracted HIV from the attack. Muholi ensured all participants were of age and fully out for safety. The project challenges colonial "art-in-service-to-science" practices, such as 18th-century botanical imagery, which erase cultural context; Muholi instead provides names, dates, locations, and places participants in a public sphere, highlighting both suffering and joy. In June 2014, Muholi showed Faces and Phases at the Ryerson Image Centre during WorldPride and at the Singapore International Arts Festival’s O.P.E.N., speaking on legacies of violence. In 2009, their work was featured in the Innovative Women exhibition in Durban and Cape Town, curated by Bongi Bhengu, which was canceled by Minister of Arts and Culture Lulu Xingwana, who called the photography immoral, offensive, and against nation-building; Muholi responded that it was paralysing and intended to create dialogue. Their Trans(figures) (2010–2011) project includes portraits of lesbian and trans individuals in urban and rural South African and international settings. In 2014, Muholi exhibited Of Love & Loss at the Brooklyn Museum, focusing on violence and hate crimes in the LGBTQIA community, juxtaposing wedding and funeral images, including video works and installations, and featuring images of Muholi and their partner, illustrating their role as a visual activist and their personal battle scars. In 2014, Muholi began the 365 self-portrait series Somnyama Ngonyama, which includes portraits with exaggerated dark skin tones to reclaim Blackness from its appropriation in minstrel performance; the series features Zulu names and directly confronts the face as a site of violence and identity. The series debuted at Yancey Richardson Gallery in New York in 2015, was shown in London in 2017, and appeared as digital billboards in Times Square during the 2017 Performa Biennial; previews were sold out, and the series was published in a 2018 book by Aperture. In 2019, Muholi won the Photography Book Award from the Kraszna-Krausz Foundation for Somnyama Ngonyama: Hail, the Dark Lioness. In 2002, Muholi co-founded the Forum for the Empowerment of Women (FEW), a Black lesbian organization providing a safe space for women. In 2006, they conceptualized a platform for Queer Activism = Queer media. In 2009, Muholi founded Inkanyiso ("illuminate" in Zulu), a non-profit organization focused on queer visual activism, registered with the Department of Social Services (NPO 073–402), with a vision statement of "Produce. Educate. Disseminate." In 2018, Muholi collaborated with Lindeka Qampi and the Philadelphia Photo Arts Center (PPAC) to create the Women's Mobile Museum, mentoring a cohort of women artists in Philadelphia, culminating in a special exhibition at PPAC, with participants undergoing technical workshops and exhibition development. In 2021, Muholi produced a coloring book of Somnyama Ngonyama to engage South African youth (categorized as youth until age 35 due to apartheid), organizing workshops in underprivileged regions to provide art education, as a personal concern stemming from their own upbringing. In 2010, Muholi co-directed the documentary Difficult Love, commissioned by SABC, which explores their life and the lives of Black lesbians in South Africa, shown in South Africa, the USA, Spain, Sweden, the UK, Amsterdam, Paris (Festival Cinefable), and Italy. In 2013, Muholi co-directed We Live in Fear, released by Human Rights Watch. On 20 April 2012, Muholi’s flat in Vredehoek was robbed, with over twenty external hard drives and their laptop containing five years of photos and videos—records of funerals of Black South African lesbians murdered in hate crimes—stolen; Muholi was overseas at the time, and the incident raised suspicions that their documentation of Black lesbian life was targeted, effectively erasing five years of work. A few weeks later, Muholi stated they were still traumatized and found it difficult to sleep in the space, now a crime scene. In July 2017, Muholi’s collaborator Sibahle Nkumbi was pushed down a staircase in Amsterdam by their Airbnb host while covering the opening of Muholi’s exhibition at the Stedelijk Museum; Nkumbi was hospitalized with a concussion and bruising, and video footage went viral, leading to the host being charged with attempted manslaughter. Muholi’s work is held in public collections.

Zippo Pine Bar (1969–1998) is recognized as the leading Western Pleasure sire of Quarter Horses. He was a 1969 sorrel foal sired by Zippo Pat Bars and born from Dollie Pine, a daughter of Poco Pine, who in turn was a son of Poco Bueno. Dollie Pine’s mother was a descendant of Joe Moore, who was a half brother to Joe Reed P-3 and also a descendant of Traveler. Norman Reynolds purchased Zippo Pine Bar as a weanling at Lloyd Geweke's dispersal sale in 1969, with the intention of acquiring a halter horse. During his show career, he earned an AQHA Championship, a Performance Register of Merit, and a Superior Western Pleasure Horse Award. He was named the 1972 AQHA High Point Junior Western Pleasure Stallion and the 1972 AQHA High Point Junior Western Riding Horse. In 1992, he was inducted into the National Snaffle Bit Association Hall of Fame. He sired 1648 Quarter Horses, 68 Appaloosas, and 72 Paints, which together have accumulated over 50,000 show points. Five of his offspring—Mr Zippo Pine, Zippo By Moonlight, Zips Chocolate Chip, Zippos Mr Good Bar, and Zippos Amblin Easy—have been inducted into the NSBA Hall of Fame. His son Zippos Mr Good Bar was inducted into the AQHA Hall of Fame in 2019 and also into the National Snaffle Bit Association Hall of Fame in 2000. Other notable offspring include Melody Zipper, Flashy Zipper, Zippo Cash Bar, Zippo Jack Bar, Zippos Honeybee, and Don't Skip Zip. In 1991, his offspring won World Championships in Western Pleasure in the AQHA, the American Paint Horse Association (APHA), and the Appaloosa Horse Club (ApHC). Zippo Pine Bar was euthanized on January 12, 1998, at the age of 29 after suffering a major stroke. He was inducted into the AQHA Hall of Fame in 2000.

Zofia Emilia Kielan-Jaworowska (25 April 1925 – 13 March 2015) was a Polish paleobiologist born in Sokołów Podlaski, Poland. In 1928, her family moved to Warsaw when her father, Franciszek Kielan, was offered a job with the Association of Agriculture and Trade Cooperatives, a stay lasting five years; they returned to Warsaw in 1934 and lived in Żoliborz. After the war, when Warsaw was destroyed by the Nazis, the Department of Geology was among the ruins, and she attended lectures by Polish paleontologist Roman Kozłowski in his home, sparking her passion for paleontology. She earned a master's degree in zoology and a doctorate in paleontology from Warsaw University, later becoming a professor there. In 1948, she began working as an assistant in the University of Warsaw's Department of Paleontology, teaching paleontology to students in biology and geology, and completed her master's research on trilobites in the Świętokrzyskie Mountains, collecting over one hundred specimens over several summers. She received her master's degree in 1949 and worked at the university until 1952. From 1963 to 1971, she led Polish-Mongolian paleontological expeditions to the Gobi Desert, returning seven times, and unearthed numerous dinosaurs and mammals from the Cretaceous and early Tertiary periods. In 1965, her team shipped over 20 tons of fossils back to Poland; one notable find in 1971 was a Protoceratops and a young Velociraptor tangled in a struggle, with the fossilization process of their position still debated. Her research shifted from Paleozoic invertebrates, especially trilobites (studied from 1949 to 1963), to Mesozoic mammals in 1963. She authored the book *Hunting for Dinosaurs* (written in Polish and translated to English, published in 1969), which details her work in the Gobi Desert, her interactions with Mongolian people, and the hardships she faced, and co-authored *Mammals from the Age of Dinosaurs*, which won the Prize of the Foundation for Polish Science in 2005 for a creative synthesis of Mesozoic mammalian evolution. Her work was widely published in peer-reviewed journals, books, and monographs. She served as director of the Institute of Paleobiology from 1960 to 1982, then held a visiting professorship at the Musée national d’Histoire naturelle in Paris (1982–1984), followed by a professorship at the University of Oslo (1986–1995), becoming Professor Emerita in 1995. She was awarded the Walter Granger Memorial Award in 1988, the Romer-Simpson Medal in 1996 (the 8th recipient), the Commander's Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta in 2002, and the Righteous Among the Nations Medal in 1999. She was a member of the Polish Geological Society, Academia Europaea, Palaeontological Association, Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters, Norwegian Paleontological Society, Polish Academy of Sciences, and an honorary member of the Linnean Society of London, Polish Copernicus Society of Naturalists, and the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. She also worked at Harvard University (1973–1974), Paris Diderot University (1982–1984), and the Polish Academy of Sciences. Several extinct animals were named in her honor, including Deinocheirus, Gallimimus, Kielanodon, Zofiabaatar, Kielantherium, Zofiagale, and Indobaatar zofiae. She married Zbigniew Jaworowski, a professor of radiobiology, in 1958. She was the first woman to serve on the executive committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences. In her obituary in *Nature*, Richard L. Cifelli noted that "Much of what we know about the origin and early evolution of mammals stems, directly or indirectly, from [her work]". Her co-author, Zhe-Xi Lou, stated that her contributions to paleontology are unmatched by any living expert and that only George Gaylord Simpson would be her equal in the field of Mesozoic mammalian studies over the past century, describing her as a rare leader and charismatic figure who improved both the science and the community of paleontology. During World War II, she helped hide two Jewish women with her family.

The iPad Air, retrospectively known as the original iPad Air or iPad Air 1, was announced on October 22, 2013, and released on November 1, 2013, marking a major design change for the iPad since the iPad 2. It features a thinner profile, measuring 7.5 millimeters in thickness, with a smaller screen bezel similar to the iPad Mini 2, and retains the 9.7-inch screen size from earlier models. Apple reduced the device's overall volume using thinner components, resulting in a 22% weight reduction compared to the iPad 2. The iPad Air is available in space gray and silver, and its enclosure is milled from a solid block of aluminum, making it 100% recyclable and free of harmful materials like BFRs and PVC. It launched with iOS 7, which introduced a flat, colorful design replacing skeuomorphic elements from iOS 6, with Jonathan Ive describing the update as "bringing order to complexity" through refined typography, new icons, translucency, layering, physics, and gyroscope-driven parallaxing. The device includes an A7 system-on-chip with a Secure Enclave and an M7 motion processor, though it does not support Touch ID due to retaining the same home button design as earlier 9.7-inch iPads. The A7 chip in the iPad Air uses a different design than in the iPhone 5S, lacking a PoP configuration and featuring a metal heat spreader for better thermal management. It includes a 5-megapixel rear-facing iSight camera with a 5 MP CMOS, hybrid IR filter, and fixed ƒ/2.4 aperture, and a FaceTime HD front-facing camera capable of 720p HD video with face detection and backside illumination. The iPad Air supports Wi-Fi (802.11n), dual-band Wi-Fi, and cellular connectivity in various variants, including nano-SIM, quad-band GSM, penta-band UMTS, dual-band CDMA EV-DO Rev. A and B, and LTE bands depending on the model, with one variant supporting LTE bands 1–5, 7, 8, 13, 17–20, 25 and 26, and another supporting bands 1–3, 5, 7, 8, 18–20 and TD-LTE bands 38, 39, and 40. It can act as a hotspot via Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or USB and access the Apple App Store. The device comes with applications such as Safari, Mail, Photos, Video, Music, iTunes Store, App Store, Maps, Notes, Calendar, Game Center, Photo Booth, and Contacts, and supports syncing with Mac or Windows computers via iTunes. It includes iLife (iPhoto, iMovie, GarageBand) and iWork (Pages, Keynote, Numbers) apps. The iPad Air supports iOS 8 (2014), iOS 9 (2015), which introduced Slide Over and Picture in Picture multitasking features (but not Split View), iOS 10 (2016), which added support for AirPods, and iOS 11 (2017), which redesigned the Control Center. Apple confirmed in June 2018 that the first-generation iPad Air would receive iOS 12, making it part of a group of devices receiving six major iOS updates from iOS 7 to iOS 12. Support for the iPad Air was dropped with the release of iPadOS 13 in September 2019, and the latest update available is iOS 12.5.7, released on January 23, 2023. The device has stereo audio with two speakers on either side of the Lightning connector and includes ambient light and 3-axis accelerometer sensors for screen brightness adjustment and orientation detection. It supports all four screen orientations, including upside-down, with the home button's position changing relative to orientation. The iPad Air is available in 16, 32, 64, or 128 GB of internal storage with no expansion option, and a camera connection kit with an SD card reader is available for transferring photos and videos. The cellular model weighs 478 grams, while the Wi-Fi model weighs 469 grams—over 25% lighter than their predecessors. The iPad Air's successor, the iPad Air 2, was announced on October 16, 2014, and released on October 22, 2014, with 64 GB and 128 GB variants discontinued after the iPad Pro 9.7-inch announcement in March 2016, and 16 GB and 32 GB variants discontinued on March 21, 2016. The iPad Air sold out in Hong Kong just two hours after going online, and received generally positive reviews, with praise for its design, performance, and display, though some critics noted the muddled speakers and lack of a fingerprint reader. Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak criticized the focus on reducing size and weight over increasing storage, and Dave Smith of the International Business Times noted the device brought only slight improvements and lacked a fingerprint scanner. The launch saw less turnout than usual, expected due to the delayed release of the iPad Mini 2. The device is manufactured with various model numbers including A1475, A1476, A2902, A2903, A2904, A2898, A2899, A2900, A3266, A3267, A3270, A3268, A3269, A3271, iPad14,9, iPad14,11, iPad15,4, and iPad15,6, with weights ranging from 1.014 to 1.362 pounds.

Seán William "Jack" McLoughlin (/məˈɡlɒklɪn/ mə-GLOK-lin; born 7 February 1990), known online as jacksepticeye, is an Irish YouTuber whose content centers on gaming, comedy, and vlogging. Born the youngest of five children to John (c. 1936 – 27 January 2021) and Florrie McLoughlin, he was raised in Cloghan, County Offaly, Ireland, and also lived in Banagher. His father worked for the Electricity Supply Board and his mother worked various jobs before becoming a caregiver for his grandmother. McLoughlin began playing video games at age seven, often spending time in a treehouse with a Nintendo Game Boy, where he found a sense of belonging. He was commonly called Jack in childhood and received the nickname "Jack Septic Eye" after injuring his eye during a football match. At 18, he and his family moved to a cabin in Ballycumber, where he studied music technology and production at Limerick Institute of Technology before dropping out to return home. He later moved to Athlone, County Westmeath, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts (Honours) degree in hotel management from the Athlone Institute of Technology. In 2017, he moved to Brighton, England, partly due to privacy concerns after fans discovered his home in Athlone and to access the city’s strong LGBTQ and vegan communities. He began uploading videos to YouTube under the name "jacksepticeye" in December 2012, initially focusing on voice impressions before shifting to gameplay content. His channel gained rapid traction, reaching 15,000 subscribers in four days after being mentioned in a PewDiePie video, hitting one million subscribers in August 2014, 1.5 million by year-end, one billion views and 3.2 million subscribers by February 2015, and adding six million subscribers the following year. In January 2016, he was one of the first YouTubers signed under PewDiePie’s Revelmode network, co-hosted the SXSW Gaming Awards, and appeared in the 2016 YouTube Rewind. The Revelmode network was shut down by Disney in 2017 due to controversy over anti-semitic imagery in a planned Scare PewDiePie season, after which McLoughlin was signed to Disney’s Digital Network. In June 2017, he was featured in Polaris: Player Select on Disney XD as part of the D | XP programming block and was included in RTÉ 2’s Ireland's Rich List as one of the "top 30 earners under 30." He toured the US and UK in 2017 and 2018 with his How Did We Get Here tour and the Game Grumps' Ready Player 3 tour, with the show featuring a biographical retelling of his life and fan gameplay segments. In February 2018, he announced US and Canada dates for the tour, performing at the Just for Laughs comedy festival in Montreal in July 2018. In 2018, he began streaming exclusive content on Twitch under a multi-year deal with Disney Digital Network. In January 2019, he signed with WME and later joined Studio71. In 2020, he participated in Summer Game Fest following the cancellation of E3. He appeared in the film Free Guy starring Ryan Reynolds, which was released in August 2021, and previously played Deadpool with Reynolds in a video. He also advised director Shawn Levy on making the film authentic to video game culture. In July 2021, he released a short film titled "15 MONTHS" about his pandemic experience, and later signed with CAA. In February 2022, a biographical documentary entitled How Did We Get Here? premiered on Moment House, featuring footage from his tour. In July 2022, he stated he would likely stop streaming on Twitch to focus on edited YouTube content. In 2023, he co-hosted The Gamer and the Mouth with Chris Redd. In 2025, he voiced the character 'Punch Up' in the video game Dispatch, starring Aaron Paul. He has also worked on production and behind-the-scenes roles for a cancelled animated show based on Soma and an independent horror film called Godmother. McLoughlin has been recognized in numerous media lists, including Forbes' Top Gaming Influencers 2017, as the eighth highest-paid YouTuber in 2018 (estimated $16 million), eighth highest-paid gamer in 2019 ($11 million), and third most talked-about gaming personality on Twitter. He was featured in the 2020 Forbes 30 Under 30 list under "Sports & Games" as Ireland's most popular YouTuber. In 2021, he was the sixth most popular gaming streamer according to Currys, and ranked 15th in Forbes' Top Creators 2022 and 2023, with estimated incomes of €7.3 million (2022) and $27 million (2023), and $18 million in 2024. His channel has consistently been noted as the most subscribed in Ireland by publications such as Tubefilter, The Irish Examiner, The Irish Times, The Times, and The Guardian. His content primarily consists of Let's Plays, comedy gaming videos, and vlogs, featuring a mix of conventional and unusual games, collaborations with Markiplier and PewDiePie, interviews with celebrities like Tom Holland, Dwayne Johnson, Brad Pitt, Chris Hemsworth, and Margot Robbie, and regular appearances of comedy sketches, charity livestreams, and Q&A sessions. Videos typically begin with a high five and the catchphrase "Top of the morning to ya, laddies," though he used it less by 2023, and end with "punch the 'like' button in the face, like a boss!" The color green, representing his Irish heritage, appears in his YouTube logo "Septic Eye Sam." His commentary is improvised, humorous, and includes swearing, described as "genuine" and "authentic," and he calls himself the "most energetic video-game commentator on YouTube," noting his content is an "assault on the senses" that people either love or hate. He attributes his success to energy, positivity, honesty, and consistency and emphasizes building an inclusive community, promoting the slogan "positive mental attitude." Elements of gothic storytelling appear in his horror game Let's Plays and in the character Antisepticeye, which originated in response to Markiplier’s Darkiplier and involves direct audience interaction on social media. His audience creates fan fiction, and he produces short-form videos for TikTok focusing on personal content. For the first five years, he uploaded two videos per day, later reducing to one per day. In July 2018, he announced a break due to mental health and burnout, a trend he repeated in July 2020 and January 2021 (after his father’s death) and again in July 2021, stating he needed to step back to avoid burnout. In October 2018, he co-founded the clothing brand Cloak with Markiplier, which later added Pokimane as a partner and created special editions with franchises like Minecraft Dungeons and Five Nights at Freddy's, donating a percentage of sales to charities such as the World Health Organization and The Trevor Project; he left the brand in 2023. On 15 June 2020, he launched Top of The Mornin' Coffee, partnering with the Feya Foundation to combat world hunger. In April 2023, he launched a podcast with Ethan Nestor titled Brain Leak and announced a comic book with Bad Egg.

Twitch streamer Pokimane serves as a third partner and creative director for the brand, which has launched special edition collections in collaboration with franchises and internet personalities such as Minecraft Dungeons, Five Nights at Freddy's, Rhett & Link, and Pokimane. The brand donates a percentage of its sales revenue to charities, having contributed to the World Health Organization's COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund and The Trevor Project. A person named He left the business in 2023. On 15 June 2020, McLoughlin announced the launch of his coffee company, Top of The Mornin' Coffee, which began pre-orders on that day, and partnered with the Feya Foundation to combat world hunger. In April 2023, he launched a podcast with YouTuber Ethan Nestor titled Brain Leak. He also announced a comic book with publisher Bad Egg, inspired by their collaboration with MoistCr1TiKaL on Godslap; the series, Altrverse, features characters from his YouTube content and had its first issue released in December 2023. Business Insider has labeled McLoughlin "one of YouTube's most prolific philanthropists." In 2019, he received a Humanitarian Stream Team award from Save the Children for fundraising efforts. In 2021, he was named one of Junior Chamber International Ireland's "Ten Outstanding Young Persons" for raising over $6 million in charity between 2017 and 2021. In 2022, he won Best Philanthropic Streamer at The Streamer Awards. In December 2016, McLoughlin participated in the Revelmode charity livestream #Cringemas with PewDiePie, Markiplier, Emma Blackery, and PJ Liguori, raising over $1.3 million under the #EndAIDS hashtag with matching donations from the Gates Foundation and YouTube. In December 2017, he hosted two charity streams with Blackery and Liguori for Save The Children, raising over $260,000. Throughout 2018, he hosted multiple fundraiser livestreams for charities including the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, the Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance, GameChanger, AbleGamers, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, and Crisis Text Line, raising over $1 million that year; his Crisis Text Line stream in December was titled "Thankmas," a name he later used annually. In January 2019, he raised over $100,000 for the Make-A-Wish Foundation. In March 2019, he headlined a Charity: Water livestream, raising over $100,000. In May 2019, he raised over $110,000 in nine hours for Red Nose Day 2019. In September 2019, he hosted a stream with actor Emilia Clarke, raising $260,000 for SameYou, a charity focused on brain injury recovery. In December 2019, he raised over $300,000 for Child's Play during his annual Thankmas stream. In January 2020, he raised over $200,000 in four hours for Australian bushfires. In April 2020, he raised over $650,000 in 12 hours for COVID-19 relief, with the #HopeFromHome campaign raising over $1.7 million in total through subsequent streams. In June 2020, he raised over $600,000 for Black Lives Matter organizations including The Bail Project, NAACP Empowerment Programs, Color of Change, and the Advancement Project. In October 2020, he participated in MrBeast's Team Trees campaign, raising over $150,000 for the Arbor Day Foundation. In December 2020, his Thankmas stream raised over $1.4 million in 10 hours for Red Nose Day, with the campaign raising over $4.6 million in total. In December 2021, he partnered with Tiltify for a Thankmas stream supporting New Story, which combats homelessness through 3D-printed houses; Tiltify enabled influencers to host additional streams, and the campaign raised $7.6 million. In November 2022, he announced a new partnership with Tiltify to raise $10 million for World Central Kitchen during his annual Thankmas stream, a goal that was successfully met in the final hour. His 2023 Thankmas stream, presented live from the Orpheum Theater in Los Angeles, raised $6 million for World Central Kitchen, bringing the total from his Thankmas streams to over $25 million. His 2024 Thankmas stream was also broadcast live from the Orpheum Theater in support of Crisis Text Line. McLoughlin has criticized YouTube's changing algorithms and policies, stating in November 2016 that removing ads from "unsuitable content" was a "shitty thing to do" and accusing the platform of using "shady tactics" and "manipulating viewers" after algorithm changes reduced views and subscribers. In May 2018, he objected to a surprise algorithm test that altered video order in subscription feeds, urging YouTube to keep such changes on the home page and recommendations. In March 2022, he released a video criticizing increased scams and spam comments on his videos, a concern echoed by Linus Sebastian and Marques Brownlee, leading YouTube to implement new policies that removed the ability for channels to hide subscriber counts or use special characters in channel names to prevent impersonation and expanded enhanced comment moderation access. McLoughlin has criticized the YouTube algorithm for pressuring creators to constantly produce content and has discussed creator mental health, suggesting the platform could hide view counts or remove the dislike button, while also noting that YouTube provided him with "purpose" and reduced his loneliness and depression. He believes YouTube's strength lies in its sense of community, stating that people seek community wherever they can. He has positively reviewed YouTube Gaming following policy changes at Twitch that reduced revenue shares, saying "What a mess. Owned by Amazon and acting like some amateur platform. It's no wonder so many of your partners are jumping ship to YT." In 2023, McLoughlin claimed MrBeast had damaged YouTube by making it more focused on views, money, and popularity than fun; MrBeast initially called the comments "insanely disrespectful" but later stated they had a private conversation and there was no animosity. McLoughlin believes video game culture should be more inclusive, criticizing controversies involving companies like Activision Blizzard and the use of slurs or "gamer words" on Twitch as evidence of toxic "chad energy," and stating that a more accepting, open culture is needed, similar to progress in real life and LGBTQ representation. He dated Danish influencer Signe "Wiishu" Hansen from 2015 to 2018 and has been in a relationship with Dutch YouTuber Evelien "Gab" Smolders since 2019. McLoughlin has played the drums since childhood and became a fan of heavy metal music through his older brother. He was formerly in a melodic death metal-influenced metalcore band called Raised to the Ground. He has autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Şahika Ercümen (born 16 January 1985) is a Turkish dietitian and world record holder in free diving. Born in Çanakkale, she attended Gazi Primary School and completed her secondary education at Milli Piyango Anatolian High School in her hometown. She moved to Ankara for higher education and graduated from the Department of Nutrition and Dietetics at Başkent University's Faculty of Health Sciences. Her involvement in underwater sports began with scuba diving and underwater rugby, and she has been actively engaged in various underwater disciplines for twelve years, serving as a member of four national teams since 2001, including those for underwater hockey, underwater rugby, underwater orienteering, and free diving, participating in World and European Championships. On February 11, 2011, in Lake Weissensee, Austria, she achieved a 110 m (360 ft) dynamic apnea under ice (DYN), which was recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records for both men and women, surpassing the previous women's record of 70 m (230 ft) and the men's record of 108 m (354 ft). Prior to this, on November 10, 2011, in Dahab, Egypt, she set a world record in constant weight with fins at sea (CWT) at 70 m (230 ft), recognized by CMAS, previously held by Tanya Streeter at 67 m (220 ft). On the same day, she also set a CMAS-recognized record in variable weight apnea without fins at sea (VNF) at 60 m (200 ft). On June 1, 2013, she broke her own VNF record to 61 m (200 ft) in saline soda waters of Lake Van, eastern Turkey, citing her desire to highlight the migration of Pearl Mullet (Chalcalburnus tarichi), also known as Lake Van fish. On July 23, 2014, in Kaş, Antalya, southern Turkey, she reached 91 m (299 ft) in VNF in 2:49 minutes, surpassing Derya Can’s previous record. On October 22, 2016, off Kaş, Turkey, she set a new VWT record at 110 m (360 ft) in 2:44 minutes, recognized by CMAS. In a separate record, on an unspecified date, she reached 65 m (213 ft) in sweet water at Lake Salda in Yeşilova, Burdur Province, Turkey, in 1:58 minutes, surpassing the previous record of 55 m (180 ft). On October 26, 2021, in Kaş, Antalya, Turkey, she set a new VNF world record at 100 m (330 ft), valid for both women and men. In October 2025, she set a new world record in the variable weight apnea without fins at sea category, reaching 106 meters, with a dive to 107 meters under the slogan “Let Gaza breathe, let darkness turn to light” to draw attention to Gaza.
